# John

## 1:1 Introduction
[Philipp Melanchthon, Opera (Vol. 15 · Annotations on the Gospels; Romans; Corinthians; Colossians). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
XII. ANNOTATIONS ON THE GOSPELS. (CONTINUATION) "EXPOSITION ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN" It was indeed published by Caspar Cruciger under his own name, but written by Philipp Melanchthon, who in the year 1536, when he was making a journey into the Palatinate, gave the papers written by himself to Cruciger to be read publicly in the school at Wittenberg.

How these lectures gave Conrad Cordatus the occasion to accuse both Cruciger and Melanchthon before Luther, as if they had deviated from the genuine doctrine of Luther concerning justification by faith alone, appears sufficiently from the Epistles pertaining to the years 1536 and 1537, which we provided above in Vol. III, p. 159 ff. and p. 347 ff.

From the same, however, it is understood that Melanchthon certainly wrote this exposition, which is also confirmed by the testimony of Ratzemberger, which you have in the Epistles above in Vol. IV, p. 1037.

That Peucer, Melanchthon's son-in-law, also held Melanchthon to be the author of this exposition, he sufficiently professed by the fact that he inserted it into the works of Melanchthon, published by him at Wittenberg, Vol. IV, p. 592.

Nor did Mylius contradict this, who in his "Chronology of the writings of Ph. Mel." for the year 1546 has these words: "Exposition on the Gospel of John the Apostle, published by Cruciger. It exists in Vol. 4 of the works of Philipp, p. 592." For while Luther was living, Cruciger did not dare to publish this exposition, fearing without doubt that Luther might be offended by it.

But after his death, Cruciger published it under his own name, and dedicated it to Maurice, Duke of Saxony, inscribed thus: Caspar Cruciger's exposition on the Gospel of John the Apostle. Strasbourg 1546. 8vo. (2 Alph. 18 sheets) Since there is no doubt that Cruciger used Melanchthon's papers, we also have not hesitated to insert this exposition together with the letter of Cruciger into the Works of Melanchthon.

TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE AND LORD, Lord MAURICE, Duke of Saxony, Landgrave of Thuringia, Margrave of Meissen, his most clement Lord, Caspar Cruciger, Doctor of Theology, sends greetings.

Although the human race was created by God principally for this reason, that it might rightly acknowledge, invoke, and celebrate God, and for that reason the light showing God was also implanted in the nature of men, and God himself immediately revealed himself to our first parents by an express voice: yet after the nature of men was oppressed by death and other evils following the most sorrowful fall of our first parents, these shadows are most of all to be deplored, because although God afterwards revealed himself again by an express voice and by many illustrious testimonies, as in the family of Noah saved in the flood, in the leading of the Israelites out of Egypt, and finally in the sending of his Son: yet the madness of a great multitude of men is so great that they either, in a completely Cyclopean manner, consider that there is no God, no providence, and no distinction between virtues and vices, or, having rejected the divine voice and revelation, most audaciously invent new deities and wander away from the true God.

Since, however, God does not wish the whole human race to perish, He has often manifested Himself by clear testimonies, and has delivered to us the secret decree concerning the Son as Mediator, and by that doctrine He gathers an inheritance for the Son, and the Church, which by the joyful communion of God will enjoy eternal life. Although many raging people despise this benefit of God, there is nevertheless always some God-taught (θεοδίδακτος) assembly, and always will be, which will testify that the doctrine concerning God handed down through the Prophets, Christ, and the Apostles is not an empty tragedy, but the true voice of God.

And this unique assembly embraces that doctrine handed down through the Prophets, Christ, and the Apostles, recognizes and celebrates the magnitude of this benefit, that God, coming forth from His secret hiding places, has familiarly revealed Himself to us, and calls upon God, just as He Himself taught that He should be called upon, retains His Gospel, and experiences by the voice of the Gospel light and eternal life being kindled in their minds: since we are in this assembly, let us know that the rages of the Cyclopes and others are to be execrated, who mock us because we read, embrace, and interpret the prophetic and apostolic writings.

For godless (ἄθεοι) men judge that we follow this whole study through some error of the mind.

But let us despise their judgments, and let us confirm ourselves by the thought of the divine testimonies of the resurrection of the dead and similar miracles, and let us determine that a judgment will follow, in which God will openly show to the whole human race that the Church has been called to eternal salvation.

Confirmed by this conviction, let us read the writings handed down divinely, because there never was, nor will there be, a Church of God, except where these writings are read.

Just as the Son of God says: He who loves me will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him, and make our dwelling with him.

Let us hold this sweetest promise fixed in our minds, which openly affirms that the Church of God will certainly be there where the voice of the Gospel will sound, where these very books, which contain the Gospel, will be read, heard, and loved.

Since these things are most true, our labor, which we sustain in reading and expounding, is to be approved, which is undertaken so that these heavenly writings may be transmitted to posterity whole and uncorrupted.

God wills that these books be in the hands of men, and by their reading and contemplation He kindles true and eternal light in their minds.

And so that these books may be in the hands of men, He preserves, and from time to time restores, the ministry of the Gospel, that is, He wills there to be teachers and interpreters.

Nor should interpretation be a game of wits, but it should be a true exposition, which the compared parts of the divine discourse produce, in which matter, however, the interpreter is aided by certain testimonies of the ancient and purer Church.

For although the divine discourse is not ambiguous, and like the leaves of the Sibyl, yet the more unlearned, without the voice of an interpreter, do not everywhere understand the type of discourse, the phrasing, and the figures of words.

And because it is spoken about things placed outside human sight, heavenly sayings are easily transferred, or distorted, to human opinions.

Lest that happen, pious interpreters ought to warn.

Samosatenus was corrupting this saying: ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος (in the beginning was the Word), nor did he want λόγον (the Word) to be understood as subsisting (ὑφιστάμενον).

Therefore, lest the corruption of Samosatenus destroy the true meaning, it is necessary for interpreters to defend the native meaning, which is perceived by comparing the parts, as I said before.

And it is not entirely unheard of, because it has been propagated from the very beginning by the Apostles.

Therefore, let antiquity be known to the interpreter, let the struggles of all times be known, so that he may have approved witnesses of the true meaning.

For this reason, creeds were established in the beginning, so that the pure meaning of the first antiquity might be known to all.

Thus, when the Pelagians corrupt the term "Grace," and say that the law is called grace, the interpreter shows that this corruption fights against the sources, and that grace signifies the remission of sins and gratuitous reconciliation, with which the gift of the Holy Spirit is joined.

Thus, when the Monks corrupt the saying: We are justified by faith, and command minds struggling with great terrors and fleeing from God to doubt concerning the remission of sins, let the interpreter refute this corruption, and show that it must be overcome by faith. doubt, and therefore that faith is trust in mercy, establishing that we are received by God, and that this trust is commanded in these words: Being justified by faith, we have peace with God.

In these and similar disputes, the matter shows that the voice of a pious interpreter in the Church is not useless.

But, as I have said, let interpretation not be a game of wits, but let it be taken from the sources, and let it agree with the creeds; and the mind of a pious interpreter, diligently and skillfully comparing divine sayings and antiquity, is aided by God.

Furthermore, let there also be in the Church judges and censors of interpretation, as Paul says: Let those who sit judge.

I have prefaced these things so that I might show the reason for my study and purpose to everyone.

Even if we are mocked by atheists, nevertheless let all in the Church of God know that the Prophetic and Apostolic Books must necessarily be understood.

Then, since I am now indeed performing some part of the Gospel ministry, the matter sometimes compels me to add an interpretation, or certainly some admonition, to brief sayings in some narrative.

Moreover, I profess with my whole heart that I embrace the doctrine of the Apostolic and Nicene Creeds, and the consensus of the Catholic Church of God, which indeed the Churches of these Universities, Wittenberg and Leipzig, also follow, which I also wish to be the judges of my writings.

As for the fact that I have published this my exposition on the Gospel of John under the auspices of your name, this is the principal cause: that since you show that you prefer the true invocation of God before all human things, and that you love the Church of God, I might first in this public writing give thanks to God, because He turns the hearts of some Princes to the love of the Gospel and the Church, and then that I might also show my gratitude and devotion to you.

I therefore give thanks to God the eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, because He has kindled the light of His Gospel in you and in certain other Princes, and brings it about that some polities are shelters for the Church.

For there is need of schools as a seat for doctrine, and Psalm 46 says: That God is greatly exalted when the Princes of the peoples are gathered together with the God of Abraham, because many are moved by example, and doctrine can be propagated more easily, and discipline governed with greater severity.

Then, I congratulate you on this spirit, that you strive to adorn the glory of God and to consult the salvation of many nations, and I pray to God the eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, that He may rule and preserve you.

And since Paul truly says: That God brings it about that we both will and perform a salutary course, so that some things may become pleasing to Him, you also, since God has kindled the light in your breast, will seek and expect help thereafter, so that your governance may be auspicious and happy for you and the Church, and that you may direct your labors to this end, which many pious people also seek for you with ardent prayers.

Moreover, God will advance pious endeavors, so that some things may become pleasing to Him.

Too many things are done throughout the whole human race that are insulting to God.

Epicureans, Mohammedans, and many others, as if waging war on heaven, not only do things displeasing to God, but also most audaciously defend false and foul opinions about God, and exercise cruelty against those who truly celebrate God.

Then, how many prefer their ambition, lusts, and avarice to God?

Since all these do things displeasing to God, God nevertheless wills that some part of the human race, namely, the Church, should do things pleasing to Him—which, to be sure, invokes Him rightly, takes care that true doctrine is propagated, and honestly governs discipline.

That you may always be in this number, and always do things salutary and pleasing to God, may the eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ grant.

Given at Wittenberg, in the year 1546, on the 18th day of February, on which day 1708 years ago, Nicanor having been slain, the temple was recovered and the school of heavenly doctrine restored in the city of Jerusalem; by which example being admonished, let us seek and expect now also from God the defense of the Church and of pious doctrine.

The End.

ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN PROLEGOMENA.

On the distinction between Law and Gospel. At the beginning of the narration of the Gospels, it is necessary to speak of the distinction between the Law and the Gospel. But John himself delivers this very thing immediately in the first chapter. For he himself judged that this distinction must necessarily be taught, propagated, and preserved in the Church. Unless this exists and is seen, it is inevitable that horrendous darkness will follow regarding the sum of doctrine, the benefits of Christ, true invocation, and faith. Therefore, let us give thanks to God that He has restored this light to His Church, so that the true distinction between Law and Gospel may be understood, and let us pray to Him that He may kindle our minds, so that we may use such a great gift in the invocation of God and in the exercises of faith.

I shall, however, defer the doctrine concerning this distinction to the narration of that passage in chapter 1: The Law was given through Moses, grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.

Now, from the beginning of the world, promises were delivered to the Church concerning the Messiah, whom the eternal Father willed to become a victim for us, and whom He willed to be the redeemer and savior of the human race. And the Fathers and Prophets propagated those promises at all times, until the Messiah himself came. Thus, later, the Apostles testify that this Messiah has been exhibited, and they recount his doctrine, death, and resurrection. With this purpose, John also wrote this history, so that he might be a witness in the Church concerning the exhibited Messiah, and might set forth his death and resurrection, and show the benefits on account of which men are liberated from sin, from the wrath of God, and are granted eternal life.

This is the sum of this history, just as John himself wisely warns concerning the sum and scope of his purpose, chapter 20: These are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, and that believing you may have life in his name. And since John is a witness to such a great matter, and points out the author of eternal life, certain things must be recounted concerning John himself.

On John.

From the other writers of the evangelical history, it appears that John was the son of Zebedee, and the brother of James, who was killed by Herod in the fourth year after the resurrection of Christ, as Eusebius noted.

Whether he was born of the sister of Mary is not certain, but it is nevertheless consistent that they were kinswomen. But as for the fact that Christ commended his mother to him, although the example pertains to all, I nevertheless judge it to be signified that he would govern the Church among the Apostles for the longest time.

Christ especially willed this mother to be his care, and Sophronius writes that in the 68th year after the resurrection of Christ, John died at Ephesus, namely, in the third year of Trajan, when the other Apostles and Paul had long since been extinguished. He taught, therefore, for no small time, namely about 67 years.

Meanwhile, he also went into exile for some time under Domitian, whose acts being rescinded under Trajan, he returned to Ephesus. He left behind him as auditors Ignatius, Bishop of Antioch, Polycarp, Bishop of Smyrna, and Papias, Bishop of Hierapolis. What a harvest of the Gospel, what happiness of the Church it was, to hear an Apostle and his disciples for such a long time!

But yet, at this very time, many fanatical teachers wandered about everywhere: already Ebion and Cerinthus were troubling the Churches, who contended that there was only a human nature in Christ; to repress and refute these, John wrote his Gospel, so that he might testify clearly and expressly that there are two natures in Christ, divine and human, united in such a way that Christ, the Son of God and our mediator, is one person.

There are recounted histories concerning the death of Cerinthus, likewise concerning a certain youth recalled by John, which are worthy of memory. For the example concerning repentance confirms the pious, and the death of Cerinthus threatens the blasphemous. But let these histories be read in their entirety in Eusebius. Now we approach the exposition. And because John is a witness concerning the Messiah having been exhibited, he first describes who he is, and the other Evangelists testify that he was born from the seed of David according to the promises, John therefore preaches concerning the divine nature.

Latin:

XII. ANNOTATIONES IN EVANGELIA. (CONTINUATIO) „ENARRATIO IN EVANGELIUM IOANNIS” edita quidem est a Casp. Crucigero suo nomine, sed scripta a Philippo Melanthone, qui anno 1536, cum iter in Palatinatum faceret, chartas a se perscriptas Crucigero dedit publice praelegendas in schola Witebergensi.

Quo modo hae praelectiones Conradum Cordatum occasionem dederint accusandi et Crucigerum et Melanthonem apud Lutherum, quasi deflexerint a genuina Lutheri doctrina de iustificatione ex sola fide, satis apparet ex Epistolis, ad annum 1536 et 1537 pertinentibus, quae supra Vol. III., p. 159 sqq. et p. 347 sqq. dedimus.

Ex iisdem vero intelligitur, Melanthonem utique scripsisse hanc enarrationem, quod etiam confirmat testimonium Ratzembergeri, quod habes in Epistolis supra Vol. IV., p. 1037.

Peucerum, generum Melanthonis, quoque habuisse Melanthonem auctorem huius enarrationis, satis professus est eo, quod eam operibus Melanthonis, ab ipso Witebergae editis, Tom. IV. p. 592. inseruit.

Neque contradixit Mylius, qui in „Chronologia scriptorum Ph. Mel.” ad annum 1546. haec habet: „Edita a Crucigero enarratio in Evangelium Iohannis Apostoli. Extat 4 Tom. operum Philippi p. 592.” Vivente enim Luthero Cruciger non ausus est hanc enarrationem edere, haud dubie timens, ne Lutherus ea offenderetur. Post huius vero obitum Cruciger illam edidit suo nomine, eamque dicavit Mauritio Duci Saxoniae sic inscriptam: Caspari Crucigeri enarratio in Evangelium Iohannis Apostoli.

Argentorati 1546. 8. (2 Alph. 18 pl.) Quum dubium non sit, quin Cruciger usus sit chartis Melanthonis, etiam nos hunc enarrationem simul cum epistola Crucigeri Operibus Melanthonis inserere non haesitavimus.

ILLUSTRISSIMO PRINCIPI ET DOMINO, Domino MAURICIO Duci Saxoniae, Landgravio Turingiae, Marchioni Mysiae, Domino suo clementissimo, Caspar Cruciger Theologiae Doctor, S.

D. Etsi genus humanum praecipue hanc ob causam a Deo conditum est, ut Deum recte agnoscat, invocet, et celebret, eamque ob causam et insita fuit naturae hominum lux monstrans Deum, et Deus ipse statim expressa voce primis parentibus se patefecit: tamen postquam post tristissimum lapsum primorum parentum natura hominum morte, et aliis malis oppressa est, hae tenebrae omnium maxime deplorandae sunt, quod quanquam se Deus postea rursus expressa voce, et multis illustribus testimoniis patefecit, ut in diluvio servata familia Nohae, in eductione Israëlitarum ex Aegypto, denique misso filio: tamen furor tantus est magnae multitudinis hominum, ut aut prorsus Cyclopico more, nihil esse Deum, nullam providentiam, nullum discrimen virtutum et vitiorum ducat, aut reiecta voce et patefactione divina, audacissime fingat nova numina, et a vero Deo aberret.

Cum autem Deus non velit universum genus humanum perire, saepe manifestis testimoniis se patefecit, et arcanum decretum de filio Mediatore nobis tradidit, eaque doctrina filio haereditatem, ac Ecclesiam colligit, quae laeta consuetudine Dei- aeterna fruetur. Etsi autem multi furentes hoc Dei beneficium contemnunt: tamen semper est coetus aliquis θεοδίδακτος, et semper erit, qui testabitur doctrinam de Deo traditam per Prophetas, Christum et Apostolos, non esse inanem tragoediam, sed veram Dei vocem.

Et hic coetus unicus amplectitur doctrinam illam per Prophetas, Christum et Apostolos traditam, agnoscit et celebrat magnitudinem huius beneficii, quod Deus ex arcanis latebris suis prodiens, se nobis familiariter patefecit, et Deum invocat, sicut ipse invocandum se esse docuit, retinet eius Evangelium, et experitur voce Evangelii lucem, et vitam aeternam in mentibus accendi: quo in coetu nos cum simus, sciamus Cyclopum, et aliorum furores execrandos esse, qui nos derident, propterea quod scripta prophetica et apostolica legimus, amplectimur, interpretamur.

Nam homines ἄθεοι iudicant nos hoc totum studium quodam errore mentis sequi.

Sed illorum iudicia aspernemur, nosque cogitatione divinorum testimoniorum resuscitationis mortuorum, et similium miraculorum confirmemus, ac statuamus sequuturum esse iudicium, in quo palam ostendet Deus universo generi humano Ecclesiam ad aeternam salutem vocatam esse.

Hac confirmati sententia, legamus scripta divinitus tradita, quia nusquam aut fuit, aut erit Dei Ecclesia, nisi ubi haec scripta leguntur.

Sicut filius Dei inquit: Qui diligit me, sermonem meum servabit, et pater meus diliget eum, et ad eum veniemus, et mansionem apud eum faciemus.

Hanc dulcissimam promissionem infixam animis teneamus, quae palam affirmat ibi certo futuram esse Dei Ecclesiam, ubi sonabit vox Evangelii, ubi hi ipsi libri, qui Evangelium continent, legentur, audientur, amabuntur.

Haec cum sint verissima, labor noster, quem in legendo et enarrando sustinemus, probandus est, qui eo suscipitur, ut ad posteritatem haec coelestia scripta integra et incorrupta transmittantur.

Vult Deus hos libros in manibus hominum esse, et eorum lectione et cogitatione in mentibus accendit veram et aeternam lucem.

Et ut hi libri sint in hominum manibus, servat, et subinde instaurat Evangelii ministerium, hoc est, vult esse doctores et interpretes.

Nec interpretatio sit ludus ingeniorum, sed sit vera enarratio, quam gignunt collata membra sermonis divini, qua in re tamen interpres adiuvatur certis vetustae et purioris Ecclesiae testimoniis.

Etsi enim sermo divinus non est ambiguus, et similis foliorum Sibyllae: tamen rudiores sine voce interpretis non ubique genus sermonis, phrasin, figuras verborum intelligunt.

Et quia de rebus positis extra conspectum humanum dicitur, facile transferuntur, seu detorquentur coelestia dicta ad humanas opiniones.

Id ne fiat, pii interpretes monere debent.

Depravabat hoc dictum Samosatenus: ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, nec volebat λόγον intelligi ὑφιστάμενον.

Ne igitur corruptela Samosateni deleat veram sententiam, necesse est interpretes nativam sententiam propugnare, quae collatis membris, ut ante dixi, cernitur.

Et ea non est prorsus inaudita, quia inde usque ab initio ab Apostolis propagata est.

Sit igitur nota interpreti vetustas, sint nota omnium temporum certamina, ut verae sententiae probatos testes habeat.

Hanc ob causam initio symbola condita sunt, ut primae antiquitatis pura sententia omnibus nota esset.

Sic cum Pelagiani vocabulum Gratiae corrumpunt, ac dicunt legem dici gratiam, ostendit interpres hanc corruptelam cum fontibus pugnare, et gratiam significare remissionem peccatorum, et reconciliationem gratuitam, cum qua donatio Spiritus sancti coniuncta est.

Sic cum Monachi corrumpunt dictum: Fide iustificamur, ac iubent de remissione peccatorum mentes luctantes cum magnis pavoribus, ac fugientes Deum, dubitare, refutet interpres hanc corruptelam, et ostendat fide vincendam esse dubitationem, ideoque fidem esse fiduciam misericordiae, statuentem nos a Deo recipi, ac praecipi hanc fiduciam in his dictis: Fide iustificati, pacem habemus apud Deum.

In his et similibus disputationibus res ostendit vocem pii interpretis in Ecclesia non inutilem esse.

Sed, ut dixi, non sit interpretatio ludus ingeniorum, verum sit ex fontibus sumta, et congruat ad symbola, et mens interpretis pii, diligenter et dextre conferentis dicta divina, et antiquitatem, a Deo adiuvatur.

Praeterea sint in Ecclesia etiam iudices et censores interpretationis, ut Paulus inquit: Sedentes iudicent.

Haec praefatus sum, ut mei studii et consilii rationem omnibus ostendam.

Etiamsi ridemur ab atheis, tamen omnes in Ecclesia Dei sciant necessario cognoscendos esse Libros Propheticos et Apostolicos.

Deinde cum nunc quidem parte aliqua ministerii Evangelici fungar, res cogit interdum interpretationem, aut certe commonefactionem aliquam addere brevibus dictis in narratione aliqua.

Profiteor autem toto pectore me amplecti doctrinam Symbolorum Apostolici et Niceni, et consensum Catholicae Ecclesiae Dei, quem quidem et Ecclesiae harum Academiarum, Witembergensis et Lipsicae sequuntur, quas etiam iudices esse meorum scriptorum volo.

Quod autem hanc meam enarrationem in Iohannis Evangelium tui nominis auspicio edidi, haec praecipua causa est, ut cum ostendas te veram Dei invocationem omnibus rebus humanis anteferre, et amare Ecclesiam Dei, primum in hoc publico scripto Deo gratias agam, quod aliquorum Principum pectora ad Evangelii et Ecclesiae amorem flectit, deinde ut tibi quoque meam gratitudinem et studium ostendam.

Ago itaque gratias Deo aeterno Patri Domini nostri Iesu Christi, quod lucem Evangelii sui in te et aliis quibusdam Principibus accendit, et efficit, ut aliquae politiae hospitia sint Ecclesiae.

Nam opus est scholis sede aliqua doctrinae, et Psalmus 46. inquit: Deum valde exaltari, cum Principes populorum congregantur cum Deo Abraham, quia multi exemplo moventur, et doctrina propagari facilius potest, et maiore severitate regi disciplina.

Deinde hunc animum tibi gratulor, quod gloriam Dei ornare, et multarum gentium saluti consulere studes, ac precor Deum aeternum Patrem Domini nostri Iesu Christi, ut te regat ac servet.

Et cum Paulus vere dicat: Deum efficere, ut et velimus et perficiamus salutare curriculum, ut aliqua ipsi grata fiant, tu quoque, cum accenderit Deus lucem in pectore tuo, petes et expectabis auxilium deinceps, ut tua gubernatio fausta sit, et felix tibi et Ecclesiae, et ad hunc finem tuos labores dirigas, quod et multi pii ardentibus votis pro te petunt.

Provehet autem Deus pios conatus, ut aliqua ipsi grata fiant.

Nimis multa in tota genere humano fiunt contumeliosa in Deum.

Epicurei, Mahometistae, et multi alii tanquam coelo bellum inferentes, non solum ingrata Deo faciunt, sed etiam audacissime falsas et tetras opiniones de Deo defendunt, et saevitiam in eos exercent, qui Deum vere celebrant.

Deinde, quam multi ambitionem, libidines, avaritiam suam Deo anteferunt?

Hi cum omnes Deo ingrata faciant, vult tamen Deus aliquam partem generis humani, scilicet, Ecclesiam grata ipsi facere, quae videlicet eum recte invocat, curat veram doctrinam propagari, et honeste disciplinam regit, quo in numero, ut semper sis, et salutaria et grata Deo semper agas, faciat aeternus Pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi.

Datae Witebergae, anno 1546. die 18.

Februarii, quo ante annos 1708 Nicanore interfecto, recuperatum templum, et restituta schola doctrinae coelestis in urbe Ierosolyma, quo exemplo commonefacti petamus et expectemus nunc quoque a Deo Ecclesiae, et piae doctrinae defensionem.

Finis.

IN EVANGELIUM IOANNIS ΠΡΟΛΕΓΟΜΕΝΑ.

De discrimine Legis et Evangelii. Initio enarrationis Evangeliorum necesse est dici de discrimine Legis et Evangelii. Sed hoc ipsum tradit Ioannes statim in primo capite. Nam et ipse iudicavit necessario in Ecclesia hoc discrimen tradendum, propagandum, et conservandum esse. Quod nisi extet et conspiciatur, horrendas tenebras de summa doctrinae, de beneficiis Christi, de vera invocatione, de fide, necesse est sequi. Quare Deo gratias agamus, quod hanc lucem Ecclesiae suae restituit, ut verum discrimen Legis et Evangelii intelligatur, et precemur eum, ut mentes nostras accendat, ut tanto munere in invocatione Dei, et exercitiis fidei, grati utamur.

Differam autem doctrinam de hoc discrimine ad enarrationem eius loci in 1. cap.: Lex per Mosen data est, gratia et veritas per Iesum Christum facta est.

Ut autem ab initio mundi Ecclesiae traditae sunt promissiones de Messia, quem aeternus pater pro nobis voluit fieri victimam, et quem voluit esse redemptorem et salvatorem generis humani. Et promissiones illas Patres et Prophetae omnibus temporibus, donec ipse Messias venit, propagaverunt. Ita postea Apostoli testantur hunc Messiam exhibitum esse, et ipsius recitant doctrinam, mortem, et resurrectionem. Hoc consilio Ioannes et hanc historiam conscripsit, ut in Ecclesia testis esset de exhibito Messia, et mortem et resurrectionem eius exponeret, et beneficia monstraret, propter quae liberantur a peccato, ab ira Dei, et donantur vita aeterna.

Haec est huius historiae summa, sicut ipse Ioannes sapienter monet de summa et scopo consilii, cap. 20.: Haec scripta sunt, ut credatis quod Iesus est Christus, et ut credentes vitam habeatis in nomine eius. Et quoniam testis est Ioannes tantae rei, et monstrat autorem vitae aeternae, quaedam de ipso Ioanne recitanda sunt.

De Ioanne.

Ex caeteris scriptoribus historiae evangelicae apparet Ioannem fuisse filium Zebedaei, et fratrem eius Iacobum, qui ab Herode interfectus est, anno quarto post resurrectionem Christi, ut annotavit Eusebius.

An fuerit natus ex sorore Mariae, non constat, sed tamen cognatas fuisse consentaneum est. Quod vero Christus commenda-vit ei matrem, etsi exemplum ad omnes pertinet, tamen significatum arbitror, hunc inter Apostolos diutissime gubernaturum Ecclesiam.

Hanc ei matrem praecipue Christus voluit esse curae, ac scribit Sophronius 68. anno post resurrectionem Christi Ioannem esse mortuum Ephesi, videlicet, tertio Traiani anno, cum caeteri Apostoli et Paulus multo ante extincti essent.

Docuit igitur non exiguo tempore, videlicet annos circiter 67. Interim et exulavit aliquandiu sub Domitiano, cuius actis rescissis sub Traiano, Ephesum rediit. Auditores post se reliquit Ignatium Episcopum Antiochenum, Polycarpum Episcopum Smyrnaeum, et Papiam Episcopum Hierapoleos.

Quanta messis Evangelii, quanta Ecclesiae felicitas fuit, tam longo tempore audire Apostolum et eius discipulos? Sed tamen hoc ipso tempore multi fanatici doctores passim vagati sunt: iam Ebion et Cerinthus turbârant Ecclesias, qui contendebant in Christo esset tantum humanam naturam, ad hos reprimendos et refutandos Ioannes scripsit Evangelium suum, ut testaretur clare et expresse, in Christo duas esse naturas, divinam et humanam, unitas ita, ut sit una persona Christus filius Dei, et mediator noster.

Recitantur historiae de morte Cerinthi, item de quodam ado- lescente revocato a Ioanne, quae sunt dignae me- moria. Nam exemplum de poenitentia confirmat pios, et mors Cerinthi minatur blasphemis. Sed hae historiae integrae legantur apud Eusebium. Nunc accedimus ad enarrationem. Et quia Ioan- nes testis est de exhibito Messia, primum descri- bit quis sit, ac caeteri Evangelistae testantur na- tum esse ex semine David iuxta promissiones, Ioannes igitur de natura divina concionatur.

## 1:1 Argument
Chapter I.

Latin:

Caput I.

## 1:1
In the beginning was the Word.

True knowledge and invocation of God shines only in the Church of God. Therefore, the Prophets and Apostles especially hand down the doctrine concerning the nature and the will of God. And Moses indeed begins from the creation of things, and inserts a description by which he declares what God is. For he says: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. Likewise: God said. Likewise: God saw what he had made, and all things were very good. God is therefore an eternal essence, creating, omnipotent, speaking, good, just, etc. For he testifies that God was before the creatures, and to create things from nothing is the work of the omnipotent. But when he says: Speaking, Likewise: He saw all things which he had made, and they were very good, he testifies that God is a mind that is intelligent, wise, good, just, etc. Since therefore John was about to describe the son of God, he leads us himself also to that narrative in Genesis, where it is read: And God said. From this he takes the name which he attributes to the son, namely, the Word. Nor was this nomenclature, or the description of the son, discovered by the sharpness of human wit, but without doubt handed down divinely.

Let us weave together, however, all the members. In the beginning was the word, and the word was with God, and the word was God. These propositions all mean this, that the Word is a person coeternal with the eternal father, who nevertheless is not the father, and yet is of the essence of the father. He preaches therefore concerning two divine persons, the eternal Father, and the Son. He calls the son therefore the Word. So that this may be declared, let other sayings concerning the son of God be sought, in which he is called the image of the father, as to the Colossians. Likewise to Heb. 1: In these last days he has spoken to us in his son, whom he made heir of all things, through whom also he made the ages, who is the brightness of his glory, and the image of his substance, bearing all things by the word of his power. As therefore the son is called the brightness of the paternal glory, and the image of the paternal substance, so they say the word is also called. For words are images of things thought, and rays are a certain image of light, or, as is said here, ἀπαύγασμα. But these comparisons do not altogether fit. For the son of God is a person, and a substantial image. I call a person, however, an intelligent, individual, incommunicable substance.

But the ancients declared these things somehow for the sake of teaching, namely that the eternal father, looking upon himself and understanding himself, begets an image of himself, to which he communicates his essence. This begotten substantial image is the son, and is called the word, because he is begotten by thinking. This description is of Basil and Augustine. For these are the words of Basil. Why is he called λόγος? so that it may be shown that he proceeded from the mind, and is the image of the begetter, showing the begetter entirely in himself, and existing properly, just as our speech is an effigy of the whole thought. And although I approve of this declaration, and it is without doubt most true that the eternal father first looks upon, understands, and thinks of himself, and the son is begotten by thought, so that he is the image of the father, nevertheless we shall learn the sublime and secret declaration later. Now let us be content with the old saying of Irenaeus, who signifies that the son is called the word, because he is a person sounding and speaking with the fathers, and issuing promises. Which John also seems to signify, when he says: No one has ever seen God, the only-begotten son who is in the bosom of the father, he has explained him to you. And soon more will be said concerning this sentiment.

After I have explained what the Church understands in this place, and what John intended by writing: In the beginning was the word. Now we will run through the individual members in order.

The first proposition is: In the beginning was the word, that is, the son of the eternal father was before the condition of the world. For the word signifies in this place the son of the eternal father, who is his image, and a person begotten by the eternal father. And we understand a person, not, as they speak on the stages, Roscius sustains the person of Agamemnon. But as the Church speaks, an individual, intelligent, and incommunicable substance. And that it is necessary for a person to be understood in this way here, we will show more copiously later in the refutation of Samosatenus. But that he says: He was in the beginning, he testifies that this existed when the world was being founded, therefore the Son existed before the foundation of the world, and before creatures, coeternal with the Father, but yet begotten by the Father speaking.

Latin:

In principio erat Verbum.

Vera notitia et invocatio Dei in sola Ecclesia Dei lucet. Ideo praecipue tradunt Prophetae et Apostoli doctrinam de natura, et de voluntate Dei. Ac Moses quidem incipit a creatione rerum, et inserit descriptionem, qua declarat quid sit Deus. Ait enim: In principio creavit Deus coe- lum et terram. Item: Dixit Deus. Item: Vidit Deus quae fecerat, et omnia erant valde bona. Est igitur Deus essentia aeterna, creans, omni- potens, dicens, bona, iusta etc. Testatur enim Deum fuisse ante creaturas, et creare ex nihilo res est omnipotentis. Cum vero ait: Dicens, Item: Vidit omnia quae fecerat, et erant valde bona, testatur Deum esse mentem intelligentem, sapientem, bonam, iustam etc. Cum igitur Ioannes descripturus esset filium Dei, deducit nos et ipse ad illam narrationem in Genesi, ubi legitur: Et dixit Deus. Hinc sumit nomen quod filio tribuit, scilicet Verbum. Nec acie ingenii humani deprehensa est haec nomenclatura, aut filii descriptio, sed haud dubie divinitus tradita.

Contexamus autem omnia membra. In prin- cipio erat verbum, et verbum erat apud Deum, et Deus erat verbum. Hae propositiones omnes hoc volunt, Verbum esse personam coaeternam patri aeterno, quae tamen non sit pater, et tamen sit de essentia patris. Concionatur ergo de dua- bus personis divinis, Patre aeterno, et Filio. Vo- cat igitur filium Verbum. Id ut declarari possit, quaerantur et alia dicta de filio Dei, in quibus dicitur imago patris, ut ad Colossen. Item ad Heb. 1.: Novissime locutus est nobis in filio, quem fecit haeredem omnium, per quem et se- cula fecit, qui est fulgor gloriae, et imago sub- stantiae eius, ferens omnia verbo potentiae suae. Ut igitur filius vocatur fulgor paternae gloriae, et imago substantiae paternae, sic dicunt et verbum vocari. Verba enim sunt imagines rerum cogita- tarum, et radii sunt quaedam imago lucis, seu, ut hic dicitur, ἀπαύγασμα. Sed hae collationes non omnino quadrant. Nam filius Dei est per- sona, et substantialis imago. Voco autem per- sonam substantiam intelligentem, individuam, non communicabilem.

Sed veteres haec utcunque docendi causa de- clarabant, quod videlicet aeternus pater se in- tuens, atque intelligens, gignat imaginem sui ipsius, cui communicat essentiam suam. Haec genita substantialis imago est filius, et vocatur verbum, quia est cogitando genitus. Haec de- scriptio est Basilii et Augustini. Haec enim sunt verba Basilii. Quare dicitur λόγος? ut osten- datur quod ex mente prodierit, et sit imago geni- toris, totum in se ostendens genitorem, et exi- stens proprie, sicut et noster sermo effigies est totius cogitationis. Etsi autem probo hanc de- clarationem, et haud dubie verissimum est, aeter- num patrem sese primum intueri, intelligere, et cogitare, et gigni filium cogitatione, ut sit imago patris, tamen sublimem et arcanam declaratio- nem coram discemus. Nunc simus contenti ve- teri dicto Irenaei, qui significat filium dici ver- bum, quia sit persona sonans et loquens cum pa- tribus, et edens promissiones. Quod videtur et Ioannes significare, cum ait: Deum nemo vidit unquam, unigenitus filius qui est in sinu patris, ipse enarravit vobis. Et mox de hac sententia plura dicentur.

Postquam exposui quid hoc loco Ecclesia in- telligat, et quid Ioannes voluerit scribens: In principio erat verbum. Iam ordine singula mem- bra percurremus.

Prima propositio est: In principio erat ver- bum, id est, filius aeterni patris erat ante mundi conditionem. Nam verbum significat hoc loco filium aeterni patris, qui est eius imago, et per- sona genita ab aeterno patre. Et personam intel- ligimus, non, ut in scenis loquuntur, Roscius sustinet personam Agamemnonis. Sed ut Eccle- sia loquitur, substantiam individuam, intelli- gentem et incommunicabilem. Et quod opor- teat hic personam hoc modo intelligi, postea in refutatione Samosateni copiosius ostendemus. Quod autem ait: Erat in principio, testatur hunc fuisse, cum mundus conderetur, ergo filius ante conditionem mundi fuit, et ante creaturas, coae- ternus patri, sed tamem a patre dicente genitus.

## 1:1
And the Word was with God.

This particle, 'with', distinguishes the persons. The Word, that is, the Son, was with the eternal Father. There are therefore two persons, the eternal Father, and the Son of God coeternal, begotten by the Father.

Latin:

Et Verbum erat apud Deum.

Haec particula, apud, discernit personas. Verbum, id est, filius erat apud patrem aeter- num. Sunt igitur duae personae, aeternus pater, et filius Dei coaeternus genitus a patre.

## 1:1
And the Word was God.

After he distinguished the persons, lest anyone should think the Son is a creature, or created out of nothing, it is expressly added: The Word was God, that is, of the essence of the Father and ὁμοούσιος. Here, however, the Greek reading must be diligently observed, which is clearer. For the article aids the interpretation, which testifies in this statement, as the Dialecticians speak, that 'Word' is the subject, and the other term, namely 'God', is the predicate. Thus the speech becomes more perspicuous, when God is said of the Word, as a more common term describing the substance of the Word: And the nature of discourse demands that narrower terms be placed in the subject, and more common ones in the place of the predicate. This arrangement, therefore, brings much light to this statement: The Word is God, as if he were to say: That very image was not created by the Father out of nothing, but is of the eternal substance of the Father, and is truly God. For here 'God' is not understood allegorically, but properly, namely of the eternal and omnipotent God. Because here true divinity is described. Nor are the significations here discrepant regarding the substance of God. Afterwards he repeats the first statement: This was in the beginning with God. For again he admonishes that there are two persons, and that they are coeternal, but in such a way that it is understood, the eternal Father who begat, and the begotten Son, who is the image of the eternal Father, etc.

Latin:

Et Deus erat Verbum.

Postquam personas discrevit, ne quis existi- met filium esse creaturam, aut ex nihilo condi- tum, diserte additur: Verbum erat Deus, id est, de essentia patris et ὁμοούσιος. Hic autem dili- genter observanda est Graeca lectio, quae est illustrior. Nam articulus adiuvat interpretatio- nem, qui testatur in hoc dicto, ut Dialectici lo- quuntur, verbum, esse subiectum, et alteram vocem, scilicet Deus, esse praedicatum. Ita fit magis perspicua oratio, cum Deus dicitur de ver- bo, tanquam vocabulum communius describens substantiam verbi: Et natura sermonis postulat vocabula angustiora in subiecto collocari, et com- muniora in loco praedicati. Haec igitur collo- catio multum lucis affert huic dicto: Verbum est Deus, quasi dicat: Illa ipsa imago a patre non est creata ex nihilo, sed est de substantia aeterna patris, et vere Deus. Nam hic Deus non intelli- gitur allegorice, sed proprie, videlicet de aeterno et omnipotente Deo. Quia hic describitur vera divinitas. Nec sunt significationes hic de sub- stantia Dei discrepantes. Postea repetit primum dictum: Hoc erat in principio apud Deum. Rur- sus enim admonet duas esse personas, easque coaeternas, sed ita ut intelligatur, pater aeternus qui genuit, et filius genitus, qui est imago aeterni patris, etc.

## 1:3
All things were made through him, and without him was made nothing that was made.

There is no doubt that these words were taken from Genesis, where 'God said' is always placed before creation. Therefore it is said here that all things were founded through him, and Paul speaks in the same way several times, at 1 Corinthians 8: There is one God the Father, from whom are all things, and we in him, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him. Likewise Colossians 1: All things were founded through him and in him. At Hebrews 1: Through whom he also made the ages. It is a secret wisdom, and placed far outside the sight of all creatures, the understanding of creation, which nevertheless God has revealed to us, so that he might confirm us concerning providence, that he truly cares for creatures, that he wills to look upon, help, nourish, and save those who call upon him, and punish those who despise him, so that this faith may be kindled in us, the doctrine concerning creation has also been divinely revealed. And a pious and useful rule must be held: that all creatures were created by the whole divinity, by the eternal Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit equally. This rule is confirmed by the statement, John 5: My Father works until now, and I work. But why it is said to be from the Father and through the Son, and with the Holy Spirit fostering, as in Genesis, this is not perceived by the sharpness of the human mind, and yet let us hold these forms of speaking divinely handed down. In Genesis, concerning the creation of man, it is written, God said: Let us make man. Here it is signified that things are created by a certain deliberation of the eternal Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Creatures are therefore created, because the decree shines in the Son and the image of the paternal mind. Thus it is said that things are created through the Son. But because he says that all things were created through the Son, he understands both all creatures, and all the works of God in the Church, as we shall say later. For it must first be explained why he adds as an exception: And without him was made nothing that was made. This is said for this reason, because many huge evils are in sight, which, since they greatly move the minds of all, all wonder from where they have arisen. Since therefore he had said before that all things were created through the Son of God, it was necessary to add this exception, lest anyone should reason from this that sin and death were also created through the Son of God; therefore he adds the exception, those things, I say, which were made, were created through the Son of God. But certain things have broken into nature not created. These were not made through the Son of God. Here let us contemplate with our mind the whole nature of things, and the nature of angels and men, in which we shall see a huge and horrible deformity and confusion, in the devil hatred of God, and tyranny impelling men to all flagitious acts, and raging against men with every kind of calamity and death. Then in men the most sad servitude, by which they obey the devil, rushing by contempt of God into horrible crimes, and destruction. These evils are all more conspicuous than the creatures of God themselves; wherefore John excepts from that condition of creatures, and restricts his statement, saying; that only the works of God were created through the Son. He warns, therefore, that certain things are perceived in created things which are neither works of God nor created through the Son, namely sin and death. These two designations signify the destruction of the entire nature, the fury of the devil, the total depravity of the human race, and all the sins of all men, all calamities, death, and eternal torments. No creature can perceive the magnitude of these evils. Wherefore let us not think that light inconveniences are signified when we hear sin and death named.

John teaches, however, in other places also, that these evils are not things created by God, as in chapter 8: When the devil speaks a lie, he speaks from his own: for he is a liar, and the father of it; and in 1 Epist. chapter 2: The lust of the flesh is not of the Father, but of the world; and chapter 3: He who commits sin is of the devil, because the devil sins from the beginning. Since, therefore, the devil and the will of man assenting to the devil is the cause of sin and death, the exception must be diligently observed, which provides the distinction between created things and the uncreated destruction of things. And from this a definition of evil can be taken. That evil is not a thing created by God, but the destruction of a created thing, originated by the devil, and then by the will of man. Sin, that is, the aversion of the will from God, extinguished the knowledge of God in minds, and the fear of God, faith, and the love of God in the will, and impels the will to rush against the law of God and horribly offend God. Death is the destruction of human nature, following sin, and the sense of the wrath of God against sin, as is said in Psalm 90: For we have failed in thy wrath, and are troubled in thy fury; and Psalm 38: Because of iniquity thou chastenest man. Likewise Paul says briefly and clearly: Through sin death. Likewise: The wages of sin is death. Likewise: The sting of death is sin.

I have explained the reason why John added the exception, as it were, that only created things were made through the Son, so that we may know that evils, sin and death, which are the destruction of the work of God, did not originate from the Son of God. Although these evils are privations or destructions, yet we should not think that they are therefore to be extenuated: but they are like the ruin of a huge building. We have judged that the reader should be briefly warned of this in this place. For although certain things are subtly disputed by the learned concerning the definition of sin, yet let us remember this, that no creature sufficiently perceives the magnitude of sin, but let us learn in the exercises of repentance what sin is, and what the wrath of God against sin is; let us also contemplate the saddest examples of all ages, in which God declared his wrath in this life, in the flood, in the conflagration of Sodom, in all the wars and calamities of the human race, in the changes of kingdoms, in the destruction of Jerusalem, in the devastations which are now being done by the Turkish tyranny. In these such great evils God allows the fury of the devil to rage against the human race, so that punishments may warn us that God is truly angry at sin, and casts men into eternal destruction. But such is the hardness of the human heart that it is not sufficiently moved even by these examples, yet it behooves the Church to consider these things, and in some way to tremble.

After I have spoken about the cause of evil, and about the exception placed in the text, I now return to the other particle. All things were made through him. I said before that here not only the first creation of things should be understood, but also the governance and defense of the Church of all times. The creation of the world from nothing is a work to be admired, but the first restoration of Adam and Eve after the fall is no less a work, where through the Son of God, and because of him, human nature was snatched back again from the devil, and liberation was promised through the coming seed; to this work and the following ones, the statement must also be applied: All things were made through him. For in such works the Son of God fought wonderfully against the devil. Nor should it be thought that it was a light business to utter the first word about the remission of sins, to promise a liberator, and to receive the fallen.

What kind of dread was in our first parents before that first liberation? How difficult was it even afterwards to retain this consolation, when our first parents saw so many contrary examples, the slaughter of their sons, and other sins? Nor is there any doubt that the devil laid snares in various ways for our first parents, and for other pious people, so that he might destroy both their bodies and their souls. Against these snares the saints were defended through the Son of God.

Afterwards through him Noah was saved in the flood, the Israelites were led out of Egypt with him defending them, just as Paul says: They drank of the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ. Which passage, Theophylact rightly explains, saying: 'While he was accompanying them,' to show that Christ was present here with them and everywhere, and had performed all the miracles. And Jacob in the blessing of the sons of Joseph makes mention of this deliverer, when he says: 'The angel who delivered me from all evils, bless these boys.' The angel blessing, and delivering from all evils, is properly the Son of God. For angelic creatures, who are ministers, cannot deliver men from sin, from the wrath of God, and from death. Let there be added also the other glorious struggles, such as those of Joshua, Samuel, David, Jehoshaphat, Elijah, Elisha, and the like. The Son of God governed and helped all these. Thus, let this saying be applied to all deliverances in the Church: 'All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that has been made.' Why this clause was added, I have mentioned above the reason. Students, however, must be admonished to follow the Greek reading here, and not to tear the last clause away from the preceding one. For mutilation casts shadows and confuses the sentences.

Latin:

Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, et sine ipso factum est nihil, quod factum est.

Non dubium est, haec verba sumta esse ex Genesi, ubi creationi semper praeponitur dixit Deus. Ideo hic dicitur, omnia per ipsum condita esse, et Paulus aliquoties eodem modo loquitur, ad Corinth. 8.: Unus est Deus pater, ex quo sunt omnia, et nos in eum, Et unus dominus Iesus Christus, per quem sunt omnia, et nos per eum. Item Coloss. 1.: Omnia per ipsum et in ipso con- dita sunt. Ad Heb. 1.: Per quem et secula fecit. Arcana sapientia est, et longe posita extra conspectum omnium creaturarum, intellectus creationis, quam tamen Deus revelavit nobis, ut nos confirmet de providentia, quod vere curet creaturas, quod velit respicere, iuvare, alere et salvare invocantes ipsum, et punire contemnentes eum, ut haec in nobis fides accendatur, etiam doctrina de creatione divinitus revelata est. Et tenenda est regula pia et utilis: Creaturas omnes a tota divinitate, ab aeterno patre, filio, et Spiritu sancto pariter conditas esse. Hanc regulam confirmat dictum, Ioh. 5.: Pater meus usque modo operatur, et ego operor. Cur autem dicatur ex patre et per filium, et fovente Spiritu sancto, ut in Genesi, hoc non perspicitur acie humanae mentis, et tamen nos teneamus has formas loquendi divinitus traditas. In Genesi de conditione hominis scribitur, dixit Deus: Faciamus hominem. Hic significatur, condi res quadam deliberatione aeterni patris, filii, et Spiritus sancti. Conduntur ergo creaturae, quia lucet decretum in filio et imagine mentis paternae. Ita dicitur, per filium condi res. Quod autem omnia condita esse dicit per filium, intelligit et creaturas omnes, et omnia opera Dei in Ecclesia, sicut postea dicemus. Prius enim exponendum est, quare addat velut exceptionem: Et sine ipso factum est nihil, quod factum est. Hoc ideo dicitur, quia multa ingentia mala sunt in conspectu, quae cum valde moveant omnium animos, mirantur omnes, unde sint orta. Cum igitur antea dixisset, omnia per filium Dei condita esse, necesse fuit addi hanc exceptionem, ne quis hinc ratiocinetur etiam peccatum et mortem condita esse per filium Dei; ideo addit exceptionem, illa inquam, quae facta sunt, condita sunt per filium Dei. Sed quaedam irruperunt in naturam non condita. Haec non sunt facta per filium Dei. Hic totam naturam rerum, et naturam angelorum et hominum mente intueamur, in qua videbimus ingentem et horribilem deformitatem et confusionem, in diabolo odium Dei, et tyrannidem impellentem homines ad omnia flagitia, et saevientem in homines omni genere calamitatum et morte. Deinde in hominibus tristissimam servitutem, qua diabolo obtemperant, ruunt contemtu Dei in horribilia scelera, et exitium. Haec mala omnia sunt conspectiora, quam ipsae creaturae Dei; quare Ioannes excipit ea a conditione creaturarum, et contrahit suum dictum, inquiens; tantum opera Dei per filium condita esse. Admonet igitur quaedam in rebus conditis cerni, quae nec sunt opera Dei, nec condita per Filium, videlicet peccatum et mortem. Hae duae appellationes significant universam naturae destructionem, furorem diaboli, totam humani generis depravationem, et omnia peccata omnium hominum, omnes calamitates, mortem, et perpetuos cruciatus. Horum malorum magnitudinem nulla creatura perspicere potest. Quare non existimemus levia incommoda significari, cum audimus nominari peccatum et mortem.

Docet autem et in aliis locis Ioannes, haec mala non esse res a Deo conditas, ut cap. 8.: Quando mendacium loquitur diabolus, ex propriis loquitur: quia mendax est, et pater mendacii; et in 1. Epist. cap. 2.: Concupiscentia carnis non est ex patre, sed ex mundo; et cap. 3.: Qui facit peccatum, ex diabolo est, quia initio diabolus peccat. Cum igitur diabolus et hominis voluntas assentiens diabolo, sit causa peccati et mortis, diligenter observanda exceptio, quae discrimen tradit inter res conditas, et rerum destructionem non conditam. Et hinc definitio mali sumi potest. Malum esse non rem conditam a Deo, sed destructionem rei conditae, ortam a diabolo, et deinde a voluntate hominis. Peccatum, id est, aversio voluntatis a Deo extinxit noticiam Dei in mentibus, et timorem Dei, fidem, et dilectionem Dei in voluntate, et impellit voluntatem, ut ruat contra legem Dei, et Deum horribiliter offendat. Mors est naturae hominis destructio, secuta peccatum, et sensus irae Dei adversus peccatum, sicut in Psal. 90. dicitur: Quia defecimus in ira tua, et in furore tuo turbati sumus; et Psal. 38.: Propter iniquitatem corripis hominem. Item Paulus breviter et clare dicit: Per peccatum mors. Item: Stipendium peccati mors. Item: Aculeus mortis peccatum est.

Exposui causam, cur Ioannes velut addiderit exceptionem, tantum res conditas factas esse per filium, ut sciamus mala, peccatum et mortem, quae sunt destructio operis Dei, non esse orta a filio Dei. Quanquam autem haec mala sunt privationes seu destructiones, tamen non propterea extenuari putemus: sed sunt velut ruina ingentis aedificii. Haec lectorem hoc loco breviter monendum esse censuimus. Etsi enim a doctis quaedam subtiliter disputantur de defini- tione peccati, tamen hoc meminerimus, nullam creaturam satis perspicere magnitudinem peccati, sed discamus in exercitiis poenitentiae, quid sit peccatum, et quid sit ira Dei adversus peccatum, intueamur etiam tristissima omnium aetatum exem- pla, in quibus Deus iram suam in hac vita de- claravit, in diluvio, in conflagratione Sodomae, in omnibus bellis et calamitatibus humani gene- ris, in mutationibus regnorum, in excidio Iero- solymae, in vastationibus, quae nunc fiunt per tyrannidem Turcicam. In his tantis malis sinit Deus diaboli furorem grassari in genus humanum, ut poenae nos admoneant, Deum vere irasci pec- cato, et abiicere homines in aeternum exitium. Sed tanta est humani cordis durities, ut nec his exemplis satis moveatur, sed tamen Ecclesiam oportet haec considerare, et aliquo modo expa- vescere.

Postquam dixi de causa mali, et de exce- ptione in textu posita, nunc redeo ad alteram particulam. Omnia per ipsum facta sunt. Dixi antea hic non tantum primam conditionem rerum intelligi debere, sed etiam gubernationem et de- fensionem Ecclesiae omnium temporum. Admi- randum opus est creatio mundi ex nihilo, sed non est minus opus prima restitutio Adae et Evae, post lapsum, ubi per filium Dei, et propter eum diabolo rursus erepta est humana natura, et pro- missa liberatio, per venturum semen, ad hoc opus et sequentia, etiam oportet accommodari dictum: Omnia per ipsum facta sunt. Nam in talibus operibus mirabiliter praeliatus est filius Dei adversus diabolum. Nec enim existimandum est leve quoddam negotium fuisse, edere primam vocem de remissione peccatorum, promittere li- beratorem, et lapsos recipere.

Qualis pavor fuit in primis parentibus ante pri- mam illam liberationem? quam difficile fuit etiam postea retinere hanc consolationem, cum primi parentes tot contraria exempla, caedes filiorum, et alia peccata cernerent? Nec dubium est, dia- bolum variis modis insidiatum esse primis paren- tibus, et aliis piis, ut cum corpora, tum animas eorum perderet. Adversus has insidias sancti de- fensi sunt per filium Dei.

Postea per eum Noë servatus est in diluvio, educti ex Aepypto Israëlitae ipso defendente, si- cut Paulus inquit: Bibebant ex spirituali comi- tante eos petra, petra autem erat Christus. Quem locum enarrans Theophylactus recte ait: Comi- tante autem eos dixit, ut ostenderet Christum hic illis et ubique adfuisse, et miracula omnia fecisse. Et Iacob in benedictione filiorum Ioseph mentionem facit huius liberatoris, cum ait: An- gelus qui liberavit me ex omnibus malis, bene- dicat pueris istis. Angelus benedicens, et libe- rans ex omnibus malis, proprie est filius Dei. Nam creaturae angelicae, quae sunt ministrae, non possunt homines a peccato, ab ira Dei, et a morte liberare. Addantur et caetera gloriosa certamina, ut Iosue, Samuelis, Davidis, Iosaphat, Eliae, Eli- saei, et similia. Haec omnia gubernavit et ad- iuvit filius Dei. Ita ad omnes liberationes in Ec- clesia accommodetur hoc dictum: Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, et sine ipso factum est nihil, quod factum est. Quare haec particula sit addi- ta, supra rationem memoravi. Admonendi au- tem sunt studiosi, ut sequantur hic graecam le- ctionem, nec avellant a superiori postremam par- ticulam. Nam mutilatio tenebras offundit, et sententias turbat.

## 1:4
In him was life, and the life was the light of men.

Most interpreters apply these words to creation. They say that through the Son, life and light were implanted in creatures. For there is no doubt that these wonderful works were founded through the Son of God: Life, that is, the duration or preservation, and the motion of things and the degrees of living beings, then also the light of bodies, and the notions of the mind, the distinctions of just and unjust implanted in minds, and the remaining notions. We indeed perceive these things, but we cannot thoroughly discern what kind of works these are: the perpetual agitation which is life, likewise the light of the Sun, the light of the eyes, the notion of the mind. We are struck with wonder at these most beautiful things when we look at them in any way, but we cannot look into them thoroughly. Therefore, the usual interpretation is: 'In him was life,' that is, through him life was founded; with the decree shining in the Son, things were fashioned by God such as they are, and through the Son they are sustained and preserved. But John does not speak of creation alone, but of the perpetual life of man, into whom life was implanted at the beginning, which was the image of God and perpetual; then, this having been lost, perpetual life is rendered through the Son, the image is renewed; therefore, one must speak here of this perpetual life, and light, which is the image of God. For just as the Son of God is the image of the eternal Father, so in him the life of the Father shines forth, and wisdom shines, understanding and glorifying the Father. Genesis teaches at the beginning that men were also created according to this image, so that they might live a perpetual life, and have a notion acknowledging and celebrating God. Furthermore, this image having been lost after the fall, when death and darkness had oppressed human nature, the Son of God was again given to us by an ineffable counsel, because by his efficacy he would again kindle in us perpetual life and light.

The meaning, therefore, is that in the Son there is perpetual life, and the light understanding God, which is the image of the eternal Father. And the Son was given to us for this reason, that he might be effective and restore a similar life and light in us. Nor is there any doubt that the most serious doctrine is contained here, wrapped up concerning the Son, how he is the image of the eternal Father, likewise concerning the condition of man according to this image, likewise concerning the counsel of restoring the human race, because he who is the image of the Father was sent so that he might restore the image of God in us. Let the pious think of these things in prayer, when this ineffable counsel concerning the Son appointed as mediator must be thought upon: we cannot attain the magnitude of these things with words.

However, it is necessary to warn of that which John undoubtedly also wished to be distinguished here in these words: the Messiah from all other Prophets, and this very distinction is often repeated afterwards. Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, the Apostles, carrying around the doctrine commended by God, are ministers of an external voice, and they are not victims, or prices for the human race, nor do they themselves effect perpetual life and new light in the minds of men. But the Messiah, the Son of God, not only proposes an external voice, but he himself is at the same time the propitiator and effects in the minds that assent to the Gospel a new life and light.

This distinction is opposed to the imagination of the Jews, who only dreamed of a worldly empire, and thought that the Messiah would bring good laws, just government, and external peace, nor did they understand the fall of human nature, the causes of sin and death, nor did they think that these evils were to be abolished from the foundation, and that the Messiah would in a wonderful way render life and perpetual justice. These sayings must also be opposed to our adversaries, who dream that Christ is only a legislator, and do not acknowledge that he is the author of life and new righteousness in the minds. But these things will have to be taught more fully below.

Latin:

In ipso vita erat, et vita erat lux hominum.

Haec plerique interpretes accommodant ad creationem. Dicunt, per filium vitam et lucem creaturis inditam esse. Non enim dubium est, per filium Dei condita esse haec miranda opera: Vitam, id est, durationem seu conservationem, et motum rerum et gradus viventium, deinde et lucem corporum, et mentis noticias, discrimina iusti et iniusti mentibus indita, et reliquas noti- cias. Haec sentimus quidem, sed non possumus penitus perspicere, qualia sint haec opera, Agi- tatio perpetua quae est vita, item lux Solis, lux oculorum, noticia mentis. Obstupescimus ad- miratione harum pulcerrimarum rerum, cum eas quoquo modo aspicimus, sed penitus introspicere non possumus. Est ergo usitata interpretatio: In ipso vita erat, id est, per ipsum vita est condita, lucente decreto in filio, res a Deo tales fabricatae sunt, et per filium sustentantur et conservantur. Sed Ioannes non de sola creatione loquitur, sed de vita perpetua hominis, cui initio vita in- dita est, quae erat imago Dei et perpetua, deinde hac amissa, redditur vita perpetua per filium, re- novatur imago, ideo de hac vita perpetua, et luce, quae est imago Dei, hic dicendum est. Ut enim filius Dei est imago aeterni patris, ita in eo vita patris resplendet, et lucet sapientia intelligens et glorificans patrem. Ad hanc imaginem docet Genesis initio et homines conditos esse, ut viverent vita perpetua, et haberent noticiam agnoscentem et celebrantem Deum. Porro amissa hac imagine post lapsum, cum mors et tenebrae naturam humanam oppressissent, rursus inenarrabili consilio donatus est nobis filius Dei, quia sua efficacia in nobis iterum accenderet vitam perpetuam, et lucem.

Est ergo sententia, in filio esse vitam perpetuam, et lucem intelligentem Deum, quae est aeterni patris imago. Ideo autem nobis donatus est filius, ut sit efficax et similem vitam et lucem in nobis restituat. Nec dubium est, gravissimam doctrinam hic involutam contineri de filio, quomodo sit imago aeterni patris, item de conditione hominis ad hanc imaginem, item de consilio restituendi generis humani, quod is, qui est imago patris missus est, ut imaginem Dei in nobis restituat. Haec pii in invocatione cogitent, cum hoc inenarrabile consilium de filio mediatore constituto cogitandum est: verbis assequi magnitudinem harum rerum non possumus.

Illud autem monere necesse est, quod haud dubie et Ioannes hic voluit in his verbis discerni Messiam a caeteris Prophetis omnibus, et hoc ipsum discrimen postea saepe repetitur. Adam, Noë, Abraham, Moises, Apostoli, circumferentes doctrinam a Deo commendatam, externae vocis ministri sunt, nec sunt victimae, aut pretia pro genere humano, nec efficiunt ipsi in mentibus hominum perpetuam vitam et novam lucem. At Messias filius Dei non solum vocem externam proponit, sed ipse simul est propiciator et efficit in mentibus, quae Evangelio assentiuntur, novam vitam et lucem.

Hoc discrimen oppositum est imaginationi Iudaeorum, qui tantum somniabant imperium mundanum, et Messiam arbitrabantur allaturum esse bonas leges, iustam gubernationem, externam pacem, nec intelligebant naturae humanae lapsum, causas peccati et mortis, nec cogitabant haec mala funditus abolenda esse, et Messiam mirabili modo redditurum esse vitam et iusticiam perpetuam. Opponenda sunt et haec dicta adversariis nostris, qui somniant Christum tantum esse legislatorem, nec agnoscunt esse autorem vitae et novae iusticiae in mentibus. Sed haec copiosius infra docenda erunt.

## 1:5
And the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.

Let the antithesis be observed. He calls the Son of God the light; he calls the human race, oppressed by sin, the darkness. However, the Son of God himself was always present to the human race, and always after the first promise given to the first parents, a voice sounded concerning him, in which he wished to be recognized and seen, and through which he was effective in some, and in them he initiated new light and life. He was present, therefore, and wished to be recognized in the promise, and he declared his presence and efficacy by many wondrous liberations, as the examples of the Fathers and Prophets show, and yet the darkness did not recognize him. Always the greatest part of the human race, raging with horrible contempt for God, judged the Gospel to be an empty fable. Many even hated it as a pernicious doctrine, and attempted to destroy it.

This narrative, therefore, warns what the nature of the Church is like. Just as a small spark shines in the night, so the Gospel is a little flame shining in some, while meanwhile all the rest are darkness. We experience, however, that human judgments abhor this nature of the Church; we marvel that the greatest part of the human race perishes and is cast into eternal punishments. But because of this offense to reason, let us not fall away from God, but rather let us fear his judgment and wrath all the more, and let us obey the Gospel.

Latin:

Et lux in tenebris lucet, et tenebrae eam non comprehenderunt.

Antithesis observetur. Filium Dei vocat lucem, genus humanum oppressum peccato vocat tenebras. Semper autem adfuit filius Dei ipse ge- neri humano, et semper post primam promissio- nem datam primis parentibus, sonuit vox de eo, in qua agnosci et conspici voluit, et per quam fuit efficax in aliquibus, et in eis novam lucem et vitam incoavit. Adfuit igitur et agnosci in pro- missione voluit, et suam praesentiam atque effi- caciam multis mirandis liberationibus declaravit, ut exempla Patrum et Prophetarum ostendunt, et tamen tenebrae eum non agnoverunt. Semper maxima pars generis humani, furens horribili contemtu Dei, iudicavit Evangelium inanem fa- bulam esse. Multi etiam tanquam perniciosam doctrinam oderunt, et delere conati sunt.

Haec igitur narratio monet, qualis sit Ec- clesiae species. Velut parva scintilla fulget in nocte, sic Evangelium est flammula fulgens in aliquibus, cum interim caeteri omnes sint tene- brae. Experimur autem humana iudicia abhor- rere ab hac specie Ecclesiae, miramur maximam humani generis partem interire, et in aeternas poenas abiici. Sed propter hanc offensionem ra- tionis non deficiamus a Deo, ac eo magis eius iudicium et iram metuamus, et Evangelio obe- diamus.

## 1:6
There was a man sent from God whose name was John.

The previous part teaches the reader about the nature of the Son of God, which existed even before the assumption of human nature. The following narrative will discourse on the assumption of human nature, and before it speaks of the advent of the Son of God, it makes mention of John the Baptist for two reasons, the former of which is to adduce the testimony of the Baptist concerning the Messiah, the second to distinguish the Messiah from the Baptist and from all the Prophets and other ministers of heavenly doctrine.

Concerning the former I shall speak briefly: The affairs of empires, such as the victories of Alexander, Scipio, or Julius, strike the eyes of men and have evident testimonies of the whole multitude in many great nations. But those things which are carried out in the Church are not so perceived by the whole multitude, and yet there is some assembly in which certain and firm testimonies exist concerning divine deeds or the voice of God. For God wishes the faith of the Church to be certain. There are many examples of this matter; the eternal Father from heaven issued this voice: This is my beloved Son, hear him, and Moses and Elijah were present. Although this command pertains to the whole world, yet only three disciples were present then, Peter, James, and John. These were later witnesses of that voice, and God confirmed their testimony with new miracles. Thus, many testimonies concerning the advent of the Son of God were proposed, which benefited the pious and sufficiently confirmed them, even though they were mocked by the impious. As it was established that an angel had spoken with Zechariah, that later John was born from a barren and worn-out mother, and was specifically destined for this, to show that the Messiah was now about to come. Later, by the divine calling of John, a new kind of doctrine and baptism began; there he saw the Holy Spirit descending, and he saw and heard the clear voice of the eternal Father: This is my beloved Son. Many miracles, therefore, concur—those of Zechariah, Elizabeth, and John—all of which must be gathered together to confirm the testimony of John, which he spoke concerning the son of Mary, and many pious people knew these things. The rest of the impious multitude mocked.

I have prefaced these things for this reason, that we might hold the authority of testimonies in the Church in high regard, even if the spectacles of empires strike the eyes more than the wondrous events which God bestows upon the Church. God had predicted through Malachi that he would send an excellent messenger to testify concerning the advent of the Messiah, and lest authority be lacking, he attached many miracles to this testimony in Zechariah, Elizabeth, and John. Mention of John is made, therefore, so that the faith of the Church might be confirmed, with all those testimonies and miracles collected, and so that, warned of the promise in Malachi, we might recognize that the event corresponds to the prophecy, and we might seek the doctrine concerning the Messiah from the Prophets to confirm our faith. It is enough to have warned of these things concerning the former cause.

I have also added a second reason why mention of the Baptist is made, so that the ministers might be distinguished from the person of Christ. Therefore he adds:

He was not that light, but that he might bear testimony concerning the light.

The difference between the Messiah and the rest of the whole assembly of Prophets, Apostles, and Doctors is infinite, as I said above. Only the Son of God was the victim and the price for the human race. He abolishes sin and death, and in the minds of believers awakens a new light, that is, the knowledge of God, righteousness, and eternal life, and effects it, and gives the life-giving Holy Spirit. These things are done in us by faith, that is, trust in Him, not trust in Moses, Elijah, the Baptist, Peter, or anyone else. The Baptist himself preaches about this distinction several times in the text: I baptize you with water, He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire. Let the reader observe these sayings, and refer them to this distinction, which I wished to touch upon briefly here. Furthermore, we shall speak of the baptism of John a little later.

He was the true light which illuminates every man.

Again he inculcates that the Son of God is the light, and I do not interpret light or the word illuminate ambiguously. I call it light because the Son of God, through the Gospel which He brought from the bosom of the Father, gives the Holy Spirit, and in us effects light, that is, the knowledge of God, righteousness, and eternal life; that is what he calls illuminating.

But why is the universal particle added, He illuminates every man? Because the Word proposes this new light to all, even though not all receive it. Thus it should be understood, He illuminates every man, namely, the one receiving the Gospel, through which light, righteousness, and life shine into the minds. This very interpretation is added: As many as received Him, to them He gave the power to become children of God; and a little later: Of His fullness we have all received; and we shall speak more about these universals in their proper place.

He was in the world, and the world was made through Him, and the world did not know Him.

Above he affirmed that all things were created through the Son of God, and that He was always present with the Church. Now he speaks of His visible presence, because he expressly adds: He was in the world, signifying His visible conversation with men. But the following particle must be diligently observed, which clearly testifies that there are two natures in Christ, and that the Word, of whom he spoke above, must be understood as a person. For there is no doubt that it is said here of Christ: He was in the world, and the world was made through Him. However, it is certain that the world was not created through the human nature of Christ, therefore it is necessary that there be in Him another nature prior to the creation of the world, which with the eternal Father created all things. It is useful to remember this testimony to refute Samosatenus, as I shall say later.

Then he repeats the complaint about the darkness of the world, that the world does not believe in God, indeed that that very people, who are called the people of God, are so fascinated by their own persuasions about the righteousness of the law and the empire of the world, which they think the Messiah is going to occupy, that they most fiercely oppose this Son of God, because He does not give the empire which they were expecting, and likewise He abrogates the law, and preaches about a certain other righteousness. We are admonished also by this brief saying that the Church is both small and is attacked by those very people who are called the people of God, that is, who bear the title of the Church, who hold the ordinary power, as they call it. When, therefore, similar struggles occur, let us be confirmed by this saying of the Evangelist, so that we do not fall away from the Gospel on account of adversaries who excel in authority.

But as many as received Him, He gave to them, etc.

Before he spoke of the person, now he adds about the benefit which is given through this person, and indeed he shows the manner by which we obtain this benefit. And thus he proposes the sum or the chief sentiment and voice of the Gospel, and briefly embraces many things: what Christ brings, to whom He exhibits it, how we obtain it, and what happens in those who receive it.

Let the first thing therefore be what He brings, namely, the power to become children of God.
