Since this is said more briefly than the magnitude of the matter requires, explanations from other passages must be added, for the Apostle signifies that the human race is oppressed by sin, death, the wrath of God, and eternal punishments, and cannot be freed from these great evils by the law or any wisdom or human righteousness, indeed that the wrath of God could not be appeased by anything except this one victim, namely, the Son of God given for the human race. Therefore, by an ineffable counsel, this Son was divinely promised and exhibited, who in turn gives the power to become children of God, that is, He gives this gift, that we may be children of God, and when he names children, he embraces all the benefits of the Gospel. Children signify those to whom the wrath of God is appeased, who have been justified, and made heirs of eternal life.

And he expressly says, children, in order to distinguish the elect Church from the people of the law. For this is called a people, because it serves God in the eternal polity, and receives bodily promises, even though many did not receive righteousness and eternal life, but children pro- prie are called sons, to whom God is gracious, and who are reborn and heirs of eternal life. This distinction between the appellation of people and sons often occurs, as in Hosea 1: And it shall be in the place where it is said to them, you are not my people, it shall be said to them, sons of the living God. I have reviewed what benefit it brings, which will be declared shortly in more words in the text itself, therefore I have been briefer. I come to the second part. To which text itself, therefore I have been briefer. I come to the second particle. To whom he may show.

The universal proposition must be diligently observed, both placed above and often repeated, which testifies that God offers salvation to all, according to that: Come to me all you who labor. And it is said here, so that all might believe. Likewise, he illuminates every man, that is, he was indeed sent to illuminate all. And it is of great benefit to fix this doctrine in the mind, that both sentences are a universal evangelical promise, and a command that we believe in the Son of God. Concerning the promise there are many examples, Rom. 3: The justice of God unto all, and upon all. Likewise John 3: That everyone who believes in him may not perish. To this also pertains the saying of Paul: God wants all men to be saved. Because the promise offers salvation to all. But it is clear that the command pertains to all, namely that voice which sounded from heaven: Hear him. Likewise: He who does not believe God, makes him a liar. [3] These universals must be held, but a will is required that assents, not one that resists the Gospel. Therefore he says: But as many as received him. For the Son of God illuminates these through the Gospel and the Holy Spirit, who do not resist, but hear the Gospel, and sustain themselves in invocation by the voice of the Gospel, as it is said elsewhere: He will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask, not to those who despise or who attempt to oppress the Gospel with stubborn fury.

Concerning the third particle, how we obtain, he says: He gave the power to become sons of God, to those believing in his name. Expressly, he says, by faith in Christ we become sons of God. This voice is unknown to human judgments, for men to become sons of God in this way, namely, by faith, that is, by trust in this savior given to us freely, not because of our justice. And indeed it is difficult for the believers themselves to retain that they please God freely, although they are weak and unworthy, yet they please him certainly, because of the Son Jesus Christ given to us. Men cannot retain this voice of the Gospel without a struggle, but it is profitable to have before one's eyes the testimonies, which are very many, which hand down to us this doctrine of faith, which we will explain more copiously a little later, when this very proposition about faith will have to be repeated.

Concerning the fourth particle, what happens in us: He says, that the sons of God are born of God.

Not of blood, nor of the will etc.

He learnedly describes justification and regeneration. It is necessary to acknowledge the Son of God, who was given to us so that he might become a victim for us, and rose again, so that he might reign and sanctify the Church of God. By trust in this savior we are received, we are reckoned just, and we are made sons. And when this happens, that we are sons of God, we are also regenerated by God through the Holy Spirit, as the Gospel teaches everywhere, at Gal. 3: That we might receive the promise of the spirit through faith. At Rom. 8: Those who are led by the spirit of God, these are the sons of God. And John 7: He who believes in me, from his belly shall flow rivers of living water. And Zech. 12: I will pour out upon the house of David the spirit of grace and of prayers. He calls it the spirit of grace, because through the Gospel he moves hearts, so that they may acknowledge the ineffable mercy of God toward us, and may conclude that our sins are forgiven, and that we are in grace. Then, having acknowledged such great goodness, let us invoke and submit ourselves to God. [8] To these words of Zechariah, the saying of Paul in Rom. 8 fits most aptly: You have received the spirit of adoption of sons, by which we cry Abba Father. The same spirit testifies to our spirit that we are the sons of God. This embraces the acknowledgment of grace, and invocation, with which are joined other spiritual movements, and the beginning of new justice and life in the hearts. This is the perpetual doctrine concerning the benefits of the Gospel, which John briefly embraced at the beginning, for he will repeat it later.

Moreover, he adds negatives, so that he may distinguish the people of the law from the true seed of Abraham. The Israelites boasted that they were the people of God, and that the promise given concerning blessing, justice, and eternal kingdom pertained to them, and they attributed this whole prerogative to carnal generation, or legal succession, just as now Bishops contend that they are the Church because of ordinary succession. This error must necessarily be refuted. Because God, having rejected those who were insolent because of the prerogatives of the flesh, often called others to the society of his kingdom with illustrious examples, as with Cain and Esau, the firstborn, being rejected, Abel and Jacob were called. And the Church is not in the hands of those who arrogate the title to themselves because of carnal prerogatives or ordinary succession, but in the hands of others who are ignoble, in whom the Gospel shines, and who are born of God, as John says here: This is the summary of this passage, consistent with many similar disputations in the Prophets and Paul to the Romans 9. And John, distinguishing three members: Not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man etc., considers all the modes by which kingdoms or political assemblies are propagated, because the world thinks the Church is propagated like the kingdoms of the world, or assemblies, or human colleges. He therefore delivers useful doctrine, distinguishes the Church from polities, and shows the mode of propagation. The first mode is to be propagated by carnal generation, just as Cambyses is the heir of Cyrus, because he was born from him. Just as the Mosaic polity was by carnal propagation, but in such a way that circumcision was added. Thus, the opinion first clung to Adam, that the son Cain would be the heir, because he had been born from him. Thus Isaac imagined concerning Esau, thus David concerning Absalom, and we individuals each think there is some prerogative of generation and family. The Israelites therefore contended that they were the people of God or sons, because they had been born from the seed of Abraham, and they retained the circumcision received from the fathers. And there was a persuasion of the Levitical high priests that the Church was bound to a series of ordinary successors. The Baptist also taxes this error when he says: Do not say within yourselves, we have Abraham as father, etc. The second mode of propagation is by adoption, or election, as Tiberius succeeds Augustus. Thus, after it is established that the Church, after the destroyed Mosaic polity, is not bound to a certain family, another persuasion crept in, that the Church is bound to the succession of those who hold ordinary government by human election. This is the nerve of pontifical power; by this persuasion they hold the whole world fascinated, that the Church is propagated by canonical election or the ordinary succession of Bishops. They bind the Church to this in such a way that they contend that all are damned who are not under such Bishops, or do not obey their laws. But John openly protests: Not of the will of the flesh. The Church is another assembly, not propagated by human elections, like empires or the dignities of pontiffs. The third degree is propagation by imitation. This is much more excellent than the second degree, therefore he says: Not of the will of man, by the counsel, study, or industry of excellent men. Germanicus was more of a successor to Augustus than Tiberius. For the empire was governed by the virtue and labors of Germanicus. Antigonus excelled Arideus, the brother of Alexander, who was elected. Thus learned and wise men, who succeed the fathers by imitation, excel elected Bishops, and here are included all who without the Holy Spirit imitate external rites, exercises, and the discipline of the saints. Just as honest priests imitate the ceremonies of Bishops, Monks imitate the harsh exercises of some fathers, Baptists, or Anthony, etc. Erudite men imitate doctrine without the spirit, and mix in human wisdom.

These three degrees are the modes by which kingdoms and political assemblies are propagated, and there are no other nor more modes.

But the fourth degree of the Church, that is, of the people reborn to eternal life, is proper: to be born of God through the Gospel, as he says: He gave them power to become sons of God, to those believing, etc.

Let us learn therefore not only to refute the persuasions of the Israelites, but also similar ones. Anabaptists also err at this time, who contend that those born of Christians do not bring original sin. They err who contend that the Church is where there is an ordinary succession of governing Bishops, which succession truly and properly, as John speaks here: Is made by the will of the flesh, that is, by human counsel, as Caiaphas is not a son of God, even if by ordinary succession he is high priest, because he is not born of God. But Zacharias is a son of God, because he is reborn through the Word and the Holy Spirit. They also err who think they become sons because of the imitation of ceremonies or moral works without the Holy Spirit, and without faith, that is, without trust in mercy, just as hypocrites feigned merit of congruity. For this imagination also thinks that sons of God are made, and sin is erased, by the effort and study of reason without trust in Christ the mediator, and without the Holy Spirit. I do not doubt that John includes these opinions in those exclusive particles. Having therefore finished this preface concerning the benefits of Christ, and the mode by which we obtain them, the Evangelist returns to the description of the person.

Latin:

Fuit homo missus a Deo cui nomen Ioannes.

Superior pars docet lectorem de natura filii Dei, quae etiam ante assumtionem naturae huma- nae fuit. Sequens narratio concionabitur de as- sumtione naturae humanae, et priusquam de ad- ventu filii Dei loquatur, mentionem facit Ioannis Baptistae propter duas causas, quarum prior est, ut alleget testimonium Baptistae de Messia, se- cunda, ut discernat Messiam a Baptista, et omni- bus Prophetis et aliis ministris doctrinae coelestis.

De priori breviter dicam: Negotia imperio- rum, ut victoriae Alexandri, Scipionis aut Iulii, incurrunt in oculos hominum, et habent eviden- tia testimonia universae multitudinis in multis magnis gentibus. Sed ea quae geruntur in Ec- clesia non ita cernuntur ab universa multitudine, et tamen aliquis est coetus, in quo certa et firma testimonia extant de factis divinis aut de voce Dei. Vult enim Deus fidem Ecclesiae certam esse. Exempla huius rei multa sunt, pater aeternus ex coelo hanc edidit vocem: Hic est filius meus di- lectus, hunc audite, et adfuerunt Moses et Elias. Hoc mandatum cum pertineat ad totum mundum, tamen tantum tunc adfuerunt tres discipuli, Pe- trus, Iacobus et Ioannes. Hi postea testes fue- runt eius vocis, et Deus testimonium eorum no- vis miraculis confirmavit. Ita de adventu filii Dei multa testimonia proposita sunt, quae piis proderant, et satis confirmabant eos, etsi ab im- piis deridebantur. Ut constabat angelum cum Zacharia locutum esse, postea ex sterili et effoeta matre Ioannem natum esse, et nominatim ad hoc destinatum, ut ostenderet iam venturum Messiam. Postea Ioannis vocatione divina novum genus do- ctrinae et baptismum incoavit, ibi vidit descen- dentem Spiritum sanctum, et vidit et audivit cla- ram vocem aeterni patris: Hic est filius meus di- lectus. Multa igitur miracula concurrunt, Zacha- riae, Elizabeth, Ioannis, quae omnia colligenda sunt, ut confirment testimonium Ioannis, quod de filio Mariae dixit, et haec multi pii norant. Reliqua multitudo impia deridebat.

Haec ideo praefatus sum, ut autoritatem te- stimoniorum in Ecclesia magnifaciamus, etiamsi spectacula imperiorum magis incurrunt in oculos, quam mirandi eventus, quos Deus impertit Ec- clesiae. Praedixerat Deus per Malachiam se mis- surum esse nuncium eximium, testificaturum de Messiae adventu, et ne deesset autoritas, huic testimonio multa miracula in Zacharia, Eliza- beth, Ioanne affixit. Fit igitur mentio Ioannis, ut fides Ecclesiae confirmetur, collectis omnibus illis testimoniis et miraculis, et ut admoniti de promissione in Malachia, agnoscamus eventum congruere prophetiae, et doctrinam de Messia ex Prophetis ad confirmandam fidem requiramus. Haec de priore causa monuisse satis est.

Adieci et alteram causam, fieri mentionem Baptistae, ut discernantur ministri a persona Christi. Ideo addit:

Non erat ille lux, sed ut testimonium per- hiberet de lumine.

Infinitum est discrimen inter Messiam et re- liquum totum coetum Prophetarum, Apostolo- rum et Doctorum, ut supra dixi. Solus filius Dei fuit victima, et pretium pro genere humano. Hic abolet peccatum et mortem, et in mentibus credentium novam lucem, id est, noticiam Dei, iusticiam, et vitam aeternam exuscitat, et efficit, dat Spiritum sanctum vivificantem. Haec fiunt in nobis fide, hoc est, fiducia ipsius, non fiducia Mosi, Eliae, Baptistae, Petri, aut cuiusquam alterius. De hoc discrimine aliquoties conciona- tur ipse Baptista in textu: Ego vos baptizo aqua, ille vos baptizabit Spiritu sancto et igni. Haec dicta observet lector, et ad hoc discrimen referat, quod breviter hic volui attingere. Caeterum de baptismo Ioannis dicemus aliquanto post.

Erat lux vera quae illuminat omnem ho- minem.

Iterum inculcat filium Dei esse lucem, nec ambigue interpretor lucem, aut verbum illumi- nare. Lucem voco, quia filius Dei per Evange- lium, quod ex sinu patris attulit, dat Spiritum sanctum, et in nobis lucem, hoc est, noticiam Dei, iusticiam, et vitam aeternam efficit, id vo- cat illuminare.

Sed cur addita est particula universalis, il- luminat omnem hominem? Quia verbum omni- bus proponit hanc novam lucem, tametsi non omnes accipiunt. Sic intelligatur, illuminat omnem hominem, scilicet, accipientem Evange- lium, per quod lux, iusticia et vita illucescit in mentibus. Haec ipsa interpretatio additur: Quot- quot receperunt eum, dedit eis potestatem filios Dei fieri; et aliquanto post: Ex plenitudine eius omnes accepimus; ac de his universalibus suo loco plura dicemus.

In mundo erat, et mundus per ipsum factus est, et mundus eum non cognovit.

Supra affirmavit per filium Dei omnia con- dita esse, et semper affuisse eum Ecclesiae. Nunc loquitur de visibili praesentia, quia diserte addit: In mundo erat, significans visibilem conversatio- nem cum hominibus. Sed sequens particula dili- genter observanda est, quae perspicue testatur, in Christo duas esse naturas, et verbum, de quo supra dixit, intelligi oportere personam. Non enim dubium est hic de Christo dici: In mundo erat, et mundus per eum factus est. Constat au- tem mundum non esse conditum per humanam naturam Christi, ergo necesse est in eo et alteram naturam esse priorem conditione mundi, quae cum patre aeterno res condidit. Hoc testimonium meminisse utile est, ad refutandum Samosatenum, ut postea dicam.

Deinde repetit querelam de tenebris mundi, quod mundus non credit Deo, imo quod ille ipse populus, qui dicitur populus Dei, ita fascinatus sit propriis persuasionibus de iusticia legis et im- perio mundi, quod putat Messiam occupaturum esse, ut huic filio Dei accerrime adversetur, quia non dat imperium quod ipsi expectabant, item abrogat legem, et de alia quadam iusticia concio- natur. Admonemur et hoc brevi dicto Ecclesiam et exiguam esse et oppugnari ab illis ipsis, qui vocantur populus Dei, hoc est, qui gerunt titu- lum Ecclesiae, qui tenent ordinariam potestatem, ut vocant. Cum igitur similia certamina incidunt, hoc dicto Evangelistae confirmemur, ne propter adversarios, qui autoritate antecellunt, deficia- mus ab Evangelio.

Quotquot autem receperunt eum, dedit eis, etc.

Antea de persona dixit, nunc addit de bene- ficio, quod per hanc personam datur, et quidem modum, quo hoc beneficium consequimur, osten- dit. Atque ita summam seu praecipuam Evangelii sententiam et vocem proponit, et multa breviter complectitur, quid afferat Christus, quibus exhi- beat, quomodo consequamur, quid in accipienti- bus fiat.

Sit igitur primum quid afferat, videlicet po- testatem filios Dei fieri. Hoc cum brevius dicatur, quam magnitudo rei postulat, addendae sunt ex- plicationes ex aliis locis, significat enim Apostolus genus humanum oppressum esse peccato, morte, ira Dei, et poenis aeternis, nec posse ab his tan- tis malis per legem aut ullam sapientiam, aut iu- sticiam humanam liberari, imo nulla re potuisse placari iram Dei, nisi hac una victima, scilicet, dato filio Dei pro genere humano. Itaque ineffa- bili consilio divinitus hic filius promissus et exhi- bitus est, qui rursus dat potestatem filios Dei fieri, id est, dat hoc munus, ut simus filii Dei, et cum filios nominat, complectitur omnia beneficia Evangelii. Filii significant eos, quibus placata est ira Dei, qui iustificati sunt, et facti haeredes vitae aeternae.

Et diserte dicit, filii, ut discernat Ecclesiam electam a populo legis. Hic enim dicitur popu- lus, quia in aeterna politia servit Deo, et accipit promissiones corporales, etiamsi iusticiam et vi- tam aeternam multi non accipiebant, sed filii pro- prie dicuntur hi, quibus Deus propicius est, et qui sunt renati et haeredes vitae aeternae. Hoc discrimen appellationis populi et filiorum saepe occurrit, ut Oseae 1.: Et erit in loco, ubi dice- tur eis, non populus meus vos, dicetur eis, filii Dei viventis. Recensui quod beneficium afferat, quod subinde pluribus verbis in ipso textu decla- rabitur, ideo fui brevior. Venio ad secundam particulam. Quibus exhibeat.

Diligenter observanda est propositio univer- salis, et supra posita, et saepe repetita, quae te- statur Deum omnibus offerre salutem, iuxta illud: Venite ad me omnes qui laboratis. Et hic dictum est, ut omnes crederent. Item, illuminat omnem hominem, id est, missus est quidem ut omnes illuminet. Ac magnopere prodest animis infigere hanc doctrinam, quod utraque sententia sit uni- versalis promissio evangelica, et mandatum ut credamus filio Dei. De promissione multa sunt exempla, Rom. 3.: Iusticia Dei in omnes, et su- per omnes. Item Ioan. 3.: Ut omnis qui credit in eum, non pereat. Huc et dictum Pauli perti- net: Deus vult omnes homines salvos fieri. Quia promissio omnibus offert salutem. Mandatum vero ad omnes pertinere constat, videlicet vocem illam quae de coelo sonuit: Hunc audite. Item: Qui non credit Deo, mendacem facit eum. Hae universales tenendae sunt, sed requiritur volun- tas assentiens, non repugnans Evangelio. Ideo dicit: Quotquot autem receperunt eum. Nam hos per Evangelium et Spiritum sanctum illuminat filius Dei, qui non repugnant, sed audiunt Evan- gelium, et in invocatione se sustentant voce Evan- gelii, sicut alibi dicitur: Dabit Spiritum sanctum petentibus, non vel contemnentibus, vel perti- naci furore opprimere Evangelium conantibus.

De tertia particula, quomodo consequamur, ait: Dedit potestatem filios Dei fieri, credentibus in nomine eius. Expresse, inquit, fide in Chri- stum fieri nos filios Dei. Haec vox ignota est hu- manis iudiciis, fieri homines filios Dei hoc mo- do, scilicet, fide, id est, fiducia huius salvatoris nobis donati gratis, non propter nostram iusti- ciam. Et quidem ipsis credentibus difficile est retinere, quod placeant Deo gratis, quanquam infirmi et indigni, sed placeant tamen certo, pro- pter filium Iesum Christum nobis donatum. Non sine certamine retinere hanc Evangelii vocem ho- mines possunt, sed prodest in conspectu habere testimonia, quae sunt plurima, quae hanc de fide doctrinam nobis tradunt, quam aliquanto post copiosius exponemus, cum haec ipsa de fide pro- positio repetenda erit.

De quarta particula, quid fiat in nobis: Ait, filios Dei ex Deo nasci.

Non ex sanguinibus, nec ex voluntate etc.

Erudite describit iustificationem et regenera- tionem. Necesse est agnosci filium Dei, qui no- bis donatus est ut fieret victima pro nobis, et re- surrexit, ut regnet et sanctificet Ecclesiam Dei. Huius salvatoris fiducia recipimur, reputamur iusti, et efficimur filii. Et hoc cum fit, ut simus filii Dei, etiam a Deo per Spiritum sanctum rege- neramur, ut ubique docet Evangelium, ad Gal. 3.: Ut promissionem spiritus accipiamus per fidem. Ad Rom. 8.: Qui spiritu Dei aguntur, hi sunt filii Dei. Et Ioan. 7.: Qui credit in me, flumina de ventre eius fluent aquae vivae. Et Zach. 12.: Effundam super domum David spiritum gratiae et precum. Vocat spiritum gratiae, quia per Evan- gelium movet corda, ut agnoscant inenarrabilem misericordiam Dei erga nos, et statuant nobis re- mitti peccata, nos esse in gratia. Deinde agnita tanta bonitate invocemus, et nos subiiciamus Deo. Ad haec Zachariae verba convenit aptissime di- ctum Pauli Rom. 8.: Accepistis spiritum adoptio- nis filiorum, quo clamamus Abba pater. Idem spiritus testificatur spiritui nostro, quod simus filii Dei. Hic complectitur agnitionem gratiae, et invocationem, cum qua coniuncti sunt alii mo- tus spirituales, et incoatio novae iusticiae et vitae in cordibus. Haec est perpetua doctrina de be- neficiis Evangelii, quam Ioannes initio breviter complexus, postea enim repetet.

Addit autem negativas, ut discernat popu- lum legis a vero semine Abrahae, gloriabantur Israëlitae se esse populum Dei, et ad se pertinere promissionem datam de benedictione, iusticia, et regno aeterno, et hanc totam praerogativam tri- buebant carnali generationi, seu legali succes- sioni, sicut nunc Episcopi contendunt se esse Ec- clesiam propter ordinariam successionem. Hic error necessario refellendus est. Quia Deus re- pudiatis his, qui insolescebant propter carnis praerogativas, saepe illustribus exemplis vocavit alios ad societatem regni sui, ut reiecto Cain, Esau, primogenitis, vocati sunt Abel, Iacob. Estque Ecclesia non penes eos qui sibi arrogant titulum, propter carnales praerogativas seu ordi- nariam successionem, sed penes alios ignobiles, in quibus lucet Evangelium, et qui sunt nati ex Deo, ut Ioannes hic inquit: Haec est summa huius loci, congruens cum multis similibus dispu- tationibus in Prophetis et Paulo ad Rom. 9. Et Ioannes discernens tria membra: Non ex sangui- nibus, nec ex voluntate carnis, neque ex voluntate viri etc., considerat modos omnes, quibus pro- pagantur regna aut politici coetus, quia mundus putat propagari Ecclesiam, sicut regna mundi, vel coetus, aut collegia humana. Tradit igitur utilem doctrinam discernit Ecclesiam a politiis, et modum propagationis ostendit. Primus modus est, propagari carnali generatione, sicut haeres est Cambyses Cyri, quia ex eo natus est. Sicut politia Mosaica fuit propagatione carnali, sed ita, ut accederet circumcisio. Sic haerebat primum in Adam opinio, filium Cain fore haeredem, quia ex ipso natus esset. Sic imaginabatur Isaac de Esau, sic David de Absalon, et nos singuli cogi- tamus aliquam praerogativam esse generationis et familiae. Contendebant igitur Israëlitae se esse populum Dei seu filios, propterea quod nati es- sent ex semine Abraham, et circumcisionem a pa- tribus acceptam retinebant. Et erat persuasio pontificum Leviticorum, alligatam esse Ecclesiam ad seriem ordinariorum successorum. Hunc er- rorem et Baptista taxat, cum inquit: Ne dicatis intra vosmetipsos, patrem habemus Abraham, etc. Secundus modus propagationis est per ad- optionem, vel electionem, ut Augusto succedit Tiberius. Sic postquam constat Ecclesiam post destructam politiam Mosaicam non esse alligatam ad familiam certam, obrepsit alia persuasio, Ec- clesiam alligatam esse ad successionem eorum, qui humana electione ordinariam gubernationem tenent. Hic nervus est potentiae pontificiae, hac persuasione tenent fascinatum totum orbem ter- rarum, quod Ecclesia sit propagata electione ca- nonica seu successione ordinaria Episcoporum. Ad hanc ita alligant Ecclesiam, ut contendant damnatos esse omnes, qui non sunt sub talibus Episcopis, aut non obtemperant eorum legibus. Sed Ioannes palam reclamat: Non ex voluntate carnis. Alius coetus est Ecclesia, non propaga- tus humanis electionibus, ut imperia, aut digni- tates pontificum. Tertius gradus est, propagatio per imitatio- nem. Haec est multo excellentior secundo gradu, ideo dicit: Non ex voluntate viri, consilio, stu- dio, industria excellentium virorum. Magis erat successor Augusti Germanicus, quam Tiberius. Nam virtute et laboribus Germanici regebatur imperium. Antigonus antecellebat Arideo fratri Alexandri electo. Sic antecellunt Episcopis electis viri docti et sapientes, qui imitatione patribus succedunt, et comprehenduntur hic omnes qui sine Spiritu sancto imitantur externos ritus, exer- citia, disciplinam sanctorum. Sicut honesti sa- cerdotes imitantur ceremonias Episcoporum, Mo- nachi imitantur dura exercitia aliquorum patrum, Baptistae, aut Antonii, etc. Homines eruditi imitantur doctrinam sine spiritu, et miscent hu- manam sapientiam.

Hi tres gradus sunt modi, quibus propagan- tur regna et politici coetus, nec sunt alii nec plu- res modi.

Sed quartus gradus Ecclesiae, hoc est, po- puli renascentis ad perpetuam vitam proprius est, ex Deo nasci per Evangelium, sicut ait: Dedit illis potestatem filios Dei fieri, credentibus, etc.

Discamus ergo non solum Israëlitarum per- suasiones refutare, sed etiam similes. Errant et hoc tempore Anabaptistae, qui contendunt natos ex Christianis non afferre peccatum originis. Er- rant qui contendnnt ibi esse Ecclesiam, ubi est ordinaria successio Episcoporum gubernantium, quae successio vere et proprie, ut Ioannes hic lo- quitur: Fit voluntate carnis, id est, humano con- silio, ut Caiphas non est filius Dei, etiamsi ordi- naria successione est pontifex, quia non est natus ex Deo. At Zacharias est filius Dei, quia per verbum et Spiritum sanctum est renatus. Errant etiam qui putant fieri filios propter imitationem ceremoniarum aut operum moralium sine Spiritu sancto, et sine fide, hoc est, sine fiducia miseri- cordiae, sicut hypocritae finxerunt meritum con- grui. Nam haec imaginatio etiam putat filios Dei fieri, deleri peccatum, conatu et studio rationis sine fiducia Christi mediatoris, et sine Spiritu sancto. Has sententias in illis exclusivis particu- lis complecti Ioannem non dubito. Absoluta igi- tur hac praefatione de beneficiis Christi, de modo quo ea consequimur, redit Evangelista ad perso- nae descriptionem.

## 1:14
And the Word was made flesh.

By this saying, Samosatenus, Servetus, and their likes are refuted, who contend that the λόγον ought not to be understood as a person, but these deceits and calumnies we shall refute later. For first I will recite the simple and perpetual opinion of the Church, and I exhort the pious to retain the phrasing of the ancients, who spoke thus: The Word assumed human nature, so that Jesus Christ is one person. Nor must it be imagined that the human nature was merely a lodging for the divine nature them. But the two natures, divine and human, are united by a hypostatic union, as the ancients spoke, that is, so that there is one person. Therefore the Evangelist says here: The Word was made flesh, as if to say: The Word was not merely joined, as a separable companion, but was made man, shining in the whole human nature which is united to him, so that he is one person. I think that Paul also wished to say the same when he says: In Christ the fullness of the divinity dwells bodily, that is, personally. For as we now commonly say person, so the Greeks most commonly said σώματα.

Secondly, when it is said: The Word was made flesh. Let there be no thought of a transmutation or conversion of the Word into human nature, as when you say: Water was made wine. Wax was made fire. For it was said above that the Word is a divine person. Therefore it is not extinguished nor converted into another thing, but having assumed human nature, it remains, and shines in it.

Thirdly, let flesh be understood not only as the body, but the whole man. For the Word assumed a body and a human soul. But why did the Evangelist prefer to use the appellation of flesh? Why did he not say, the Word was made man? Although he meant this: For Christ is truly also man, having a body and a soul, as many other testimonies witness, yet by the phrasing of scripture he said flesh for man, to signify weakness and mortality. For such a nature was assumed, which is mortal, and indeed subject to the horrible wrath and judgment of God against the sin of the human race. Which wrath this weak and mortal flesh sustained in Christ. This ineffable humiliation the Evangelist signified by the appellation of flesh, as Isaiah says: Because he will set his soul as sin, that is, an expiation, or a sacrifice for sin, he will see a long-lived seed. And to the Galatians 3: Made a curse for us, that he might redeem us from the curse. Nor must it be thought that this is an appellation of a light thing. Human reason does not understand the magnitude of the wrath of God against sin. Therefore it does not understand what it is to be cast off and cursed by God. But Christ understood, and feeling this great wrath, he sustained it for us. Paul teaches the same to the Philippians 2: Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus, who when he was in the form of God, did not think it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and found in habit as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Although others add other interpretations, yet the simplest is the meaning in that passage of Paul. Form signifies likeness in both places. Who when he was in the form of God, that is, was like God, wise, just, strong, superior to death, the giver of life, in short having divine power, yet he did not arrogate to himself the equality of God, that is, he did not conduct himself as equal to God, so that he could not suffer and die, but he emptied himself, that is, he put off that likeness of God, not to be able to suffer, not to be able to die, and was made like men, that is, truly a mortal man, and found in habit as a man, that is, endowed with all natural affections, he hungered, thirsted, was wearied, feared, hoped, grieved, rejoiced, wept, was angry, felt such great sadness that he sweated blood. For when he was a victim for the human race, he experienced the sense of the wrath of God against sin in the human race. These things are declared next. Made obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Therefore as the Evangelist used the name of flesh, signifying both human nature and weakness. So Paul both embraces human nature and describes the weakness, when he names the form of a servant, and says: Found in habit, that is, in affections as a man. Furthermore, this also must be said: Although in Christ the human nature was mortal, it was truly human nature, yet it was without sin, there were in him all ordered appetites, such as God created, there was the appetite for food, drink, weariness, bodily pain, fear, hope, sadness, joy, anger, zeal, but these were ordered and without sin, as it is said in 2 Corinthians 5: Him who knew no sin, he made sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in him. And to the Hebrews 4: We do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our infirmities, but one tempted in all things according to our likeness without sin. Let us therefore approach with confidence, etc.

Latin:

Et Verbum caro factum est.

Hoc dicto refutatur Samosatenus, Servetus, et similes, qui contendunt λόγον non debere in- telligi personam, sed has praestigias et calumnias postea refellemus. Prius enim simplicem et perpetuam Ecclesiae sententiam recitabo, et adhortor pios, ut retineant phrasin veterum, qui sic locuti sunt: Verbum assumsit naturam humanam, ita ut sit una persona Iesus Christus. Nec imaginandum est humanam naturam tantum fuisse hospitium divinae naturae. Sicut habitat Spiritus sanctus in renatis, et est in eis efficax. Sed duae naturae divina et humana sunt unitae unione hypostatica, ut veteres locuti sunt, hoc est, ita ut una sit persona. Ideo Evangelista hic dicit: Verbum caro factum est, quasi dicat: Verbum non tantum adiunctum est, ut comes separabilis, sed factum est homo, lucens in tota natura humana, quae est ei unita, ita ut sit una persona. Arbitror et Paulum voluisse idem dicere, cum ait: In Christo plenitudinem divinitatis habitare corporaliter, id est, personaliter. Nam ut nunc usitate dicimus personam, ita Graeci usitatissime dixerunt σώματα.

Secundo cum dicitur: Verbum caro factum est. Non cogitetur transmutatio seu conversio verbi in naturam humanam, ut cum dicis: Aqua est facta vinum. Cera est facta ignis. Nam supra dictum est λόγον esse personam divinam. Non igitur extinguitur neque convertitur in aliam rem, sed assumta humana natura manet, et in ea lucet.

Tertio caro intelligatur non tantum corpus, sed totus homo. Nam λόγος assumsit corpus et animam humanam. Sed cur maluit Evangelista uti appellatione carnis? Cur non dixit, λόγος factus est homo? Etsi hoc voluit: Nam Christus vere etiam est homo, habens corpus et animam, ut alia multa testimonia testantur, tamen phrasi scripturae pro homine dixit carnem, ut significaret imbecillitatem et mortalitatem. Talis enim natura assumta est, quae est mortalis, et quidem subiecta horrendae irae et iudicio Dei adversus peccatum humani generis. Quam iram haec imbecillis et mortalis caro in Christo sustinuit. Hanc inenarrabilem humiliationem significavit Evangelista appellatione carnis, ut Esaias inquit: Quia ponet animam suam peccatum, id est, piaculum, seu hostiam pro peccato, videbit semen longaevum. Et ad Gal. 3.: Factus pro nobis maledictum, ut nos a maledictione redimeret. Nec cogitandum est hanc esse appellationem rei levis. Humana ratio non intelligit magnitudinem irae Dei adversus peccatum. Ideo nec quid sit esse abiectum et maledictum a Deo, intelligit. Chri- stus autem intellexit et sentiens hanc tantam iram, pro nobis eam sustinuit. Idem docet Paulus ad Philip. 2.: Hoc sentite inter vos, quod et in Christo Iesu, qui cum esset in forma Dei, non rapinam duxit se aequare Deo, sed seipsum exinanivit, formam servi accipiens, in similitudine hominum factus, et habitu inven- tus ut homo, humiliavit seipsum, factus obediens usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis. Etsi alii alias interpretationes addunt, tamen simpli- cissima est in eo Pauli loco sententia. Forma significat utroque loco similitudinem. Qui cum esset in forma Dei, id est, esset similis Deo, sa- piens, iustus, fortis, superior morte, dator vi- tae, denique divinam habens potentiam, tamen non arrogavit sibi aequalitatem Dei, id est, non gessit se tanquam aequalem Deo, ut non posset pati et mori, sed seipsum exinanivit, id est, exuit illam Dei similitudinem, non posse pati, non posse mori, et factus est similis hominum, id est, vere homo mortalis, et habitu inventus ut homo, id est, affectibus naturalibus omnibus praeditus, esuriit, sitiit, defatigatus est, metuit, speravit, doluit, laetatus est, lacrymavit, iratus est, sensit tantam moesticiam, ut sudaret sanguinem. Cum enim esset victima pro genere humano, expertus est sensum irae Dei adversus peccatum in genere humano. Haec deinde declarantur. Factus obe- diens usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis. Itaque ut Evangelista usus est nomine carnis, et naturam humanam, et imbecillitatem significans. Ita Paulus et humanam naturam complectitur, et describit imbecillitatem, cum nominat formam servi, et inquit: Habitu, id est, affectibus inven- tus ut homo. Caeterum et hoc dicendum est: Etsi in Chri- sto humana natura mortalis, vere fuit humana natura, tamen fuit sine peccato, fuerunt in eo omnes appetitiones ordinatae, quales Deus condi- dit, fuit appetitio cibi, potus, defatigatio, dolor corporis, metus, spes, tristitia, laetitia, ira, ze- lus, sed haec fuerunt ordinata et sine peccato, ut 2. Corinth. 5. dicitur: Eum qui non novit pecca- tum, pro nobis peccatum fecit, ut nos fieremus iusticia Dei in eo. Et ad Ebraeos 4.: Non habe- mus pontificem qui non possit compati infirmita- tibus nostris, tentatum autem per omnia secun- dum similitudinem nostram sine peccato. Acce- damus igitur cum fiducia, etc.

## 1:14
And he dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only-begotten.

He had spoken of the assumption of human nature, now he adds testimonies, and a little later he says why the Son of God was sent, why he lived among men. He says, therefore, that he dwelt among men, that is, that he lived openly with men, that he lived in the human manner.

Let this be understood, as I explained above the particle of the Pauline saying: Being found in fashion as a man. Then follow the testimonies, that this Messiah lived with men, although he had put on mortality, and is truly man, yet he is also the powerful Son of God. Therefore he says: We saw his glory, that is, miracles, we saw him raising the dead, we saw him also after death living again, and living familiarly with us, so that we might know that through him sin and death are taken away, and that he reigns, and gives to believers the Holy Spirit, righteousness, and eternal life. These things cannot be done, unless by divine power. Therefore he says it is the glory of the only-begotten from the Father.

He names Christ the only-begotten, however, to distinguish him from the other saints, who are sons by adoption. But this Christ is Son by nature, that is, of the substance of the Father, as we said above.

Latin:

Et habitavit in nobis, et conspeximus glo- riam eius, gloriam tanquam unigeniti.

Dixerat de assumtione humanae naturae, nunc addit testimonia, et paulo post dicit, cur missus sit filius Dei, cur versatus inter homines. Dicit igitur eum habitasse inter homines, id est, palam conversatum esse cum hominibus, humano more vixisse.

Quod intelligatur, ut supra enarravi parti- culam Paulini dicti: Habitu inventus ut homo. Deinde sequuntur testimonia, quod hic Messias conversatus cum hominibus, quanquam induerat mortalitatem, et sit vere homo, tamen etiam sit filius Dei potens. Ideo ait: Vidimus eius glo- riam, id est, miracula, vidimus eum resuscitan- tem mortuos, vidimus et ipsum post mortem rur- sus viventem, et nobiscum familiariter versan- tem, ut sciremus per eum tolli peccatum et mor- tem, et regnare eum, ac dare credentibus Spiri- tum sanctum, iusticiam et vitam aeternam. Haec non possunt fieri, nisi divina potentia. Ideo di- cit esse gloriam unigeniti a patre.

Nominat autem Christum unigenitum, ut discernat eum a caeteris sanctis, qui sunt filii adoptione. At hic Christus est natura filius, id est, de substantia patris, ut supra diximus.

## 1:14
Full of grace and truth.

There is no doubt that he is speaking of the Son: For the fact that some labor over the syntax in this place is a superfluous quibble. For it refers to the preceding: The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, full of grace and truth. Grace undoubtedly signifies the favor of God, and the meaning is: This Son is primarily and naturally loved by God, and is the cause for which others are chosen and loved. Eph. 1: He loved us in the beloved, that is, on account of the beloved Son, through whom we have redemption through his blood. The heavenly voice teaches the same: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased, hear him. He testifies, therefore, that this Son is loved first, and that on account of him the Church is chosen and loved, which hears this Son, Eph. 1: As he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before God, in love predestinating us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself; and Rom. 3: Through redemption in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as a propitiator. All these sentences declare the saying of the Evangelist, that the Son of God is said to be: Full of grace, that is, truly and naturally loved by the Father, and obtaining that the human race does not utterly perish, but that some on his account are chosen and loved, and imparting to believers the remission of sins, so that they too may be loved.

Let grace be understood, therefore, not only of private love, but also of that which is to be communicated to other elect, namely that on account of this Son the human race has been snatched from the tyranny of the devil, and believers have been chosen, and are loved. Below he will again repeat both appellations with the same meaning, where he declares himself more clearly, saying: We have received grace for grace, that is, favor toward us, for favor toward him, just as it was said before: He chose us in him, that is, on account of him.

He adds, however: Full of truth, that is, the true knowledge of God, and true righteousness, proper and to be communicated. For in the Son truly shines the knowledge of God, as he says in Matthew 11: No one knows the Son, but the Father, nor does anyone know the Father, but the Son, and he to whom the Son will reveal him. Likewise to the Hebrews 1: Through the Son, who is the brightness of his glory and the express image of his substance. Therefore in the Son is the true and entire knowledge of the eternal God, such as is in no creature, nor is it revealed to others except through the Son. As he himself says: No one knows the Father but the Son, and he to whom the Son will reveal him. Through him, therefore, the promise concerning the will of the Father was published, in the beginning after the fall of Adam, and through him this knowledge shines into the minds of believers, when through his word he gives the Holy Spirit. Furthermore, true righteousness, ardent love of God, and true obedience accompany the true knowledge of God, of which it is often said elsewhere, as in Isaiah 6: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; and Colossians 2: In him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily. Wherefore in him is true righteousness, and the entire fulfillment of the law. But just as the Evangelist speaks of the knowledge of God being communicated, so also he speaks of righteousness being communicated. When Christ communicates the knowledge of God to believers through the word and the Holy Spirit, true righteousness is also effected in the hearts of believers. For when, having acknowledged our sin and condemnation, we have also acknowledged through the Gospel the mercy of God forgiving sins, liberating us from condemnation, receiving, helping, and saving us, we begin to call upon him, and to submit ourselves to him, and to love him, as in Rom. 8. It is said: You have received the spirit of adoption of sons, by which we cry Abba Father. Likewise, Jer. 31: I will put my law in their hearts. Likewise Zach. 12: I will pour out upon the house of David the spirit of grace and of supplications. He calls the Holy Spirit the spirit of grace, that is, by which hearts are confirmed, so that we may acknowledge that we are in grace, and that God is propitious to us. He also calls it the spirit of supplications, by which hearts are impelled to true invocation, which is the chief worship and the beginning of obedience.

And an antithesis is to be considered in this saying. The whole remaining human race without Christ is under sin, and guilty of the wrath of God; it is not accepted by God, but believers are received on account of the Son. It is also full of darkness and falsehood, that is, it is without light and firm knowledge of God, it remains in doubt, and flees from God or is angry at Him, much less does it love God who judges and punishes and burdens this weak race with such great miseries. Furthermore, even if there is some external discipline in some, this is not yet true justice, but hypocrisy without knowledge and conversion to God. As although Atticus is an honest man, yet he doubts about providence, and has a will averse to God, and neither truly fears nor loves God: but he trusts in human resources, in human wisdom, he does not trust in God's help. This antithesis, when diligently considered, illustrates somewhat the word of truth, and it will have to be repeated a little later.

John testifies concerning Him and cries out, saying: This was He of whom I spoke.

He sometimes cites the sermons of John the Baptist, so that both his testimonies may confirm us and his doctrine may instruct us. For the testimony of that man ought to be of the greatest value, who heard the voice of the eternal Father from heaven, saying of Christ: This is my beloved Son. He also saw the Holy Spirit descending upon Christ. This miracle surpasses the wonderful deeds of all the Prophets, because here the three persons of the divinity revealed themselves with a clear distinction. There was, therefore, a most weighty reason why he thought the testimony of John should be recounted, and would that he had recited more and longer sermons of his. The saying of the Baptist, however, embraces the chief articles concerning the person of the Messiah, concerning his benefits, and concerning the distinction between Moses and the Messiah.

The first part speaks of the person. He who is to come after me, that is, who is to perform his office.

He is before me, that is, more excellent in calling, and in glory or power, and the reason is added: Because he is prior to me, that is, the first, on account of whom God both chose the Church and wishes to save it, and who was the first helper and liberator of all the elect, Adam, Noah, Abraham, and others. I judge this to be the simplest meaning. Others have understood the particle ἔμπροσθεν as, he is before me, which interpretation I do not criticize, but I am moved by the sequence of the discourse to follow the other opinion. The Baptist therefore testifies that the Messiah excels in calling and power. Because he was called not only to be a teacher, as other ministers, but to become a propitiator for the human race, and he excels in power, because he gives the Holy Spirit and eternal life.

Moreover, it is added: Because he is prior to me. That is rightly referred to eternity, or the beginning of the Church: therefore the Messiah excels, because he is the first on account of whom God chose the Church, as was said above, and he was effective from then on from the beginning in the Church. By an admirable counsel, on account of him the eternal Father received the fallen first parents, and issued the first voice of the Gospel, when the first parents had been oppressed by death, and could think of nothing else but that they would now remain in eternal wrath. Here let us consider what kind of grief, what thoughts the first parents had. In such great sadness, on account of the Son, the eternal Father raised them up again; the Baptist signifies this liberation and the remaining wonderful liberations when he says: That this Lord is the first, namely, on account of whom the Church is chosen and is saved. He declares that in the following words.

Latin:

Plenum gratiae et veritatis.

Non dubium est, quin de filio loquatur: Quod enim laborant quidam hoc loco de syntaxi, supervacanea cavillatio est. Refertur enim ad superiora: Verbum caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis, plenum gratiae et veritatis. Gratia significat haud dubie favorem Dei, estque sen- tentia: Hic filius primum et naturaliter a Deo diligitur, estque causa, propter quam caeteri sunt electi et diliguntur. Ephes. 1.: Dilexit nos in dilecto, id est, propter filium dilectum, per quem habemus redemtionem per sanguinem eius. Idem docet vox coelestis: Hic est filius meus dilectus, quo delector, hunc audite. Testatur ergo hunc filium primum amari, et propter hunc electam esse et diligi Ecclesiam, quae audit hunc filium, Ephes. 1.: Sicut elegit nos in ipso ante conditionem mundi, ut essemus sancti et immaculati coram Deo, per dilectionem praede- stinans nos ad adoptionem filiorum per Iesum Christum in ipsum; et Rom. 3.: Per redemtio- nem in Christo Iesu, quem proposuit Deus pro- piciatorem. Hae sententiae omnes declarant di- ctum Evangelistae, quod videlicet filius Dei di- catur: Plenus gratia, id est, vere et naturaliter dilectus patri, et impetrans ne genus humanum prorsus pereat, sed ut aliqui propter ipsum sint electi et diligantur, et impertiens credentibus re- missionem peccatorum, ut diligantur et ipsi.

Intelligatur igitur gratia non tantum de pri- vata dilectione, sed etiam de communicanda cae- teris electis, videlicet quod propter hunc filium genus humanum sit ereptum tyrannidi diaboli, et credentes sint electi, et diligantur. Infra rur- sus utranque appellationem repetet eadem signi- ficatione, ubi se clarius declarat, dicens: Acce- pimus gratiam pro gratia, id est, favorem erga nos, pro favore erga ipsum, sicut ante dictum est: Elegit nos in ipso, id est, propter ipsum.

Addit autem: Plenus veritate, id est, vera Dei noticia, et vera iusticia, propria et commu- nicanda. Nam in filio vere lucet noticia Dei, si- cut ait Matthaei 11.: Nemo novit filium, nisi pa- ter, neque patrem quisquam novit, nisi filius, et cui voluerit filius revelare. Item ad Ebraeos 1.: Per filium, qui est fulgor gloriae et effigies sub- stantiae eius. Ergo in filio est vera et integra noticia aeterni Dei, qualis in nulla creatura est, nec patefit aliis nisi per filium. Sicut ipse ait: Nemo novit patrem nisi filius, et cui volet filius revelare. Per hunc igitur edita est promissio de voluntate patris, initio post lapsum Adae, et per ipsum illucescit haec noticia mentibus credentium, cum per verbum suum dat Spiritum sanctum. Porro, veram Dei noticiam comitatur vera iusti- cia, ardens dilectio Dei, et vera obedientia, de qua saepe alias dicitur, ut Esaiae 6.: Spiritus domini super me, eo quod unxerit me; et Colos- senses 2.: In ipso habitat omnis plenitudo divi- nitatis corporaliter. Quare in eo vera iusticia est, et integra legis impletio. Ut autem de noticia Dei communicanda, sic et de communicanda iu- sticia loquitur Evangelista. Cum Christus noti- ciam Dei credentibus communicat per verbum et Spiritum sanctum, etiam iusticia nova efficitur in cordibus credentium. Cum enim agnito peccato et damnatione nostri, agnovimus etiam per Evan- gelium misericordiam Dei remittentis peccata, liberantis nos a damnatione, recipientis, adiu- vantis et servantis nos, incipimus eum invocare, et nos ei subiicere, et eum diligere, sicut Rom. 8. dicitur: Accepistis spiritum adoptionis filiorum, quo clamamus Abba pater. Item, Ierem. 31.: Dabo legem meam in corda eorum. Item Zach. 12.: Effundam super domum David spiritum gra- tiae et precum. Vocat Spiritum sanctum spiri- tum gratiae, id est, quo confirmantur corda, ut agnoscamus, nos esse in gratia, Deum esse nobis propicium. Vocat et spiritum precum, quo corda impelluntur ad veram invocationem, quae est praecipuus cultus, et initium obedientiae.

Estque antithesis consideranda in hoc dicto. Totum reliquum genus humanum sine Christo est sub peccato, et reum irae Dei, non est acceptum Deo, sed recipiuntur credentes propter filium. Est et plenum tenebris et mendacio, id est, est sine luce et noticia firma Dei, manet in dubita- tione, ac fugit Deum aut ei irascitur, multo mi- nus diligit Deum iudicantem et punientem, et onerantem hoc imbecille genus tantis aerumnis. Deinde etiamsi quae est externa disciplina in ali- quibus, haec nondum est vera iusticia, sed hypo- crisis sine noticia et conversione ad Deum. Ut quamvis Atticus est honestus vir, tamen de pro- videntia dubitat, et voluntatem habet aversam a Deo, nec vere timet, nec diligit Deum: sed con- fidit humanis praesidiis, humana sapientia, non confidit Dei auxilio. Haec antithesis diligenter considerata, nonnihil illustrat vocabulum veri- tatis, ac paulo post repetenda erit.

Ioannes testatur de ipso et clamitat, dicens: Hic erat de quo dixi.

Aliquoties citat Ioannis Baptistae conciones, ut et testimonia eius nos confirment, et doctrina erudiat. Plurimum enim valere debet testimo- nium eius viri, qui de coelo vocem aeterni patris audivit, dicentis de Christo: Hic est filius meus dilectus. Vidit et Spiritum sanctum descenden- tem ad Christum. Hoc miraculum omnium Pro- phetarum miranda facta superat, quia hic tres personae divinitatis illustri discrimine se patefe- cerunt. Fuit igitur gravissima causa, cur testi- monium Ioannis recensendum duxerit, atque uti- nam plures et longiores eius conciones recitasset. Complectitur autem dictum Baptistae praecipuos articulos, de persona Messiae, de beneficiis, de discrimine Mosi et Messiae.

Prima pars loquitur de persona. Is qui post me venturus est, id est, functurus officio suo.

Ante me est, id est, praestantior vocatione, et gloria seu potentia, et additur ratio: Quia prior me est, id est, primus, propter quem Deus Ecclesiam et elegit, et salvare vult, et qui primus fuit adiutor et liberator omnium electorum, Adae, Noë, Abrahae, et aliorum. Hanc iudico simplicissimam esse sententiam. Alii particulam ἔμπροσθεν intellexerunt, coram me est, quam interpretationem non reprehendo, sed serie orationis moveor, ut alteram sententiam sequar. Testatur ergo Baptista Messiam antecellere vocatione et potentia. Quia vocatus est non solum ut sit doctor, ut caeteri ministri, sed ut fiat propiciator pro genere humano, et antecellit potentia, quia dat Spiritum sanctum et vitam aeternam.

Additur autem: Quia prior me est. Id recte ad aeternitatem refertur, seu initium Ecclesiae: ideo Messias antecellit, quia primus est propter quem Deus elegit Ecclesiam, ut supra dictum est, et fuit efficax inde usque ab initio in Ecclesia. Admirando consilio propter eum aeternus pater recepit lapsos primos parentes, et vocem Evangelii primam edidit, cum primi parentes oppressi essent morte, nec possent aliud cogitare, nisi iam se in aeterna ira mansuros esse. Hic cogitemus qualis dolor, quae cogitationes fuerint primorum parentum. Hos in tanta moesticia, propter filium, aeternus pater rursus erexit, hanc liberationem et reliquas mirandas liberationes significat Baptista, cum ait: Primum esse hunc dominum, scilicet, propter quem Ecclesia electa est, et salvatur. Id declarat sequentibus verbis.

## 1:16
Out of his fullness we have all received grace for grace.

The Messiah does not only precede others, as Moses excelled Samuel or others, nor does the Messiah only teach others, but he is the propitiator and life-giver; he was sent to be a victim, and to merit reconciliation for us. Likewise, that he might be effective, that he might give the Holy Spirit beginning a new light in believers, and eternal life, and that he might raise the dead, and grant eternal life. He calls this fullness, that is, the merit of reconciliation, and power or efficacy. From this merit and efficacy we have all received. The force of the universal particle in excluding [others] in this sentiment is noted. All who receive justice and eternal life receive it from this one, not from another. It embraces therefore the whole Church, just as Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses and all the rest of the elect were saved, drawing from this fountain, that is, from this merit, and from his power, that is, on account of this victim they obtained reconciliation, and he himself was effective in them, he gave them the Holy Spirit beginning a new light, and eternal life in them.

That this is the very meaning is testified by the following words: Grace for grace, that is, our reconciliation for the love towards the Son. As it is written in Ephesians 1: He chose us in him. Likewise: He loved us in the beloved, that is, on account of the beloved Son. But let us not read and hear these with idle minds, but let faith or trust approach, which may sustain us in true terrors, looking into the Son of God, and drawing from his fullness, merit, and power. And when we shall determine that we are truly loved by the eternal Father, let us also determine that we are truly loved, received, heard, and saved on account of him, even if we are unworthy. In such an exercise of faith, and consolation, and invocation, these sayings will grow sweet to us, and will be understood more clearly. I am, however, briefer in explaining these most rich sayings, because the same sentiments will often be repeated, as soon in the comparison of Moses and the Messiah.

The law was given through Moses, grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.

This is a notable passage, delivering the distinction between the Law and the Gospel, which ought especially to exist in the Church. For just as the Pharisees imagined themselves to be righteous by the law, and knew not the benefits of the Messiah, so many in the Church contend that men are righteous by the works of the Decalogue and the ceremonies of the Bishops, and do not understand the benefits of Christ, and the doctrine of faith. These shadows embrace many errors, which it is necessary to refute and explode.

The first error is to imagine that men can satisfy the law of God.

The second, that interior doubt concerning providence, concerning the wrath of God against sins, concerning remission, likewise security neglecting the wrath of God, diffidence not assenting to the promises, not to burn with love, to admire oneself, to trust in one's own powers and to despise others, likewise vicious concupiscence, are not sins, nor are they repugnant to the law of God.

The third error, that external discipline is righteousness before God.

The fourth, that the true and proper honor of justifier and mediator is detracted from Christ.

The fifth, the whole doctrine concerning faith is extinguished, and God is accused of lying, if the delusion is confirmed that one must doubt concerning the remission of sins.

The sixth, timid minds are driven to despair, and certain consolation and the harbor of consciences is taken away.

The seventh, true invocation is taken away, which cannot happen when the mind flees from God. Finally, this whole Pharisaical imagination concerning the law is only an ethnic and rational doctrine, and does not progress further. It is manifest, therefore, that these great errors must be censured, and Christ often contends about these with the Jews, as in chapter 3 with Nicodemus, chapter 8: If the Son has set you free, you will be truly free. And often elsewhere. Paul does the same to the Romans and elsewhere, and the Baptist undoubtedly explained these in more words.

This sentiment is therefore in antithesis; the persons are unlike, Moses and the Messiah. Moses was only a teacher and a political governor, he was not a propitiator, he did not take away sin and death. The Messiah, however, is not only a teacher, but also a propitiator, he takes away sin and death, he gives the Holy Spirit and eternal life, nor is he a political governor, as you Jews dream, but he has a far different office, he is a victim for sin, he is a perpetual priest and mediator between God and men, he gives the remission of sins, new righteousness, and eternal life. I have spoken concerning the distinction of the persons.

Now let the distinction between the Law and the Gospel be observed, which the text shows when it says: Grace and truth came by Jesus Christ. The words will be clear if you consider that the Baptist is speaking of the complete and consummated benefit of Christ. Grace signifies reconciliation, by which in this life the remission of sins is given to us freely on account of the Son of God, not on account of the law or our merits. Truth signifies the true knowledge of God, not captive to sin, true life, not captive to death, and finally true and eternal goods, which although they are begun in this mortal life, yet after the resurrection will be exhibited in their entirety. He therefore gives such knowledge, righteousness, and life, which then is without error, without sin, without death. He therefore names the truth, true and eternal goods, and the saying of the Baptist can be understood more easily when we look at that consummation than if we think only of the saints in this mortal life, although, as con- it stands, it is necessary that these things be begun in this life; here we apprehend grace, by which we are reconciled, and are reckoned righteous, and are sons of God, and heirs of eternal life, even if a huge mass of sins still clings to this corrupted nature; yet it is necessary that there be begun both a true knowledge of God, a true invocation, a true righteousness victorious over sin, and a true life victorious over death. By faith we establish that God is merciful, that we are received, heard, helped, and saved on account of the mediator. This is a new light unknown to the flesh, and it overcomes doubt, and when faith establishes [itself] concerning reconciliation, it already overcomes sin and death, and begins to invoke God with a true motion, to flee to him, and to await eternal life.

But the comparison is more illustrious if the consummated benefits are opposed to the law. Christ gives a new light, by which we shall behold God without any error; he gives righteousness, which will be without any sin; he gives eternal life, entirely free from death, and enjoying eternal joy in the knowledge of God. What similar thing does the law bring? The righteousness of the law is only an external discipline, that is, a certain miserable and unclean hypocrisy, captive to errors and doubt, to sin and death. For if the mind hears nothing but the law, it remains oppressed by manifold doubt, it flees God, it does not establish that it is heard or saved, just as Saul fled God. And therefore there is no true invocation in such a mind. It is therefore overcome in horrible sin, that is, because it does not acknowledge nor invoke God; it is also overcome by death, because, doubting, it rushes into despair and eternal wrath. Indeed, the law is the ministry of this wrath, because it is a voice showing the wrath of God against sin, only crying out that God is angry at sin, and accusing us. Therefore, the voice of the Gospel is far different, namely, announcing grace and truth through Christ, that is, announcing that reconciliation and eternal life are given on account of Christ the mediator. Christ revealed this voice from the bosom of the eternal Father, as he will say shortly, nor did he bring the law, which God willed to be promulgated through Moses. Thus also Paul says: Now the righteousness of God has appeared without the law, that is, some other righteousness is revealed, namely, gratuitous reconciliation, which the law does not teach, nor is it given on account of the law, but on account of the Son the mediator. These things concerning the distinction between Moses and Christ, between the law and the Gospel, must be diligently observed, lest the highest benefits given to the Church through the Son of God—liberation from sin and eternal death, and the gift of reconciliation, righteousness, and eternal life—be overwhelmed and obscured.

Latin:

Ex plenitudine eius omnes accepimus gratiam pro gratia.

Non tantum antecedit caeteris Messias, ut Moses antecelluit Samueli, aut aliis, neque tantum docet Messias caeteros, sed est propiciator et vivificator, missus est ut sit victima, et mereatur nobis reconciliationem. Item ut sit efficax, det Spiritum sanctum incoantem in credentibus novam lucem, et vitam aeternam, et resuscitet mortuos, ac donet vitam aeternam. Hanc vocat plenitudinem, id est, meritum reconciliationis, et potentiam seu efficaciam. Ex hoc merito et efficacia omnes accepimus. Nota est vis particulae universalis in excludendo in hanc sententiam. Omnes qui iusticiam et vitam aeternam accipimus ab hoc uno accipimus, non ab alio. Complecti- tur igitur universam Ecclesiam, sic Adam, Noë, Abraham, Moses et reliqui electi omnes salvati sunt, haurientes ex hoc fonte, id est, ex hoc merito, et ex potentia eius, id est, propter hanc victimam consecuti sunt reconciliationem, et ipse fuit in eis efficax, dedit eis Spiritum sanctum incoantem novam lucem, et vitam aeternam in ipsis.

Hanc ipsam esse sententiam testantur verba sequentia: Gratiam pro gratia, id est, reconciliationem nostri pro amore erga filium. Sicut ad Ephes. 1. scriptum est: Elegit nos in ipso. Item: Dilexit nos in dilecto, id est, propter filium dilectum. Sed haec non legamus et audiamus otiosis animis, sed accedat fides seu fiducia, quae sustentet nos in veris pavoribus, intuens in filium Dei, et ex eius plenitudine, merito et potentia hauriens. Et cum statuemus ab aeterno patre vere diligi, statuamus et nos propter eum vere diligi, recipi, exaudiri, et salvari, etiamsi sumus indigni. In tali exercitio fidei, et consolatione, et invocatione, dulcescent nobis haec dicta, et clarius intelligentur. Sum autem brevior in his, uberrimis dictis enarrandis, quia eaedem sententiae saepe repetentur, ut mox in collatione Mosi et Messiae.

Lex per Mosen data est, gratia et veritas per Iesum Christum facta est.

Hic est insignis locus, tradens discrimen Legis et Evangelii, quod in Ecclesia maxime oportet existere. Ut enim Pharisaei imaginabantur se lege iustos esse, nec norant beneficia Messiae, sic multi in Ecclesia contendunt homines iustos esse operibus Decalogi et ceremoniis et Episcoporum, nec intelligunt beneficia Christi, et doctrinam fidei. Hae tenebrae multos errores complectuntur, quos necesse est refutari et explodi.

Primus error est imaginari quod homines possint legi Dei satisfacere.

Secundus, quod interior dubitatio de providentia, de ira Dei adversus peccata, de remissione, item securitas negligens iram Dei, diffidentia non assentiens promissionibus, non ardere dilectione, admirari sese, confidere propriis viribus et despicere alios, item vitiosa concupiscentia, non sint peccata, nec repugnent legi Dei.

Tertius error, quod externa disciplina sit iusticia coram Deo.

Quartus, quod Christo detrahitur verus et proprius honos, iustificatoris et mediatoris.

Quintus, extinguitur tota doctrina de fide, et Deus accusatur mendacii, si confirmatur deli- rium, quod sit dubitandum de remissione pecca- torum.

Sextus, pavidae mentes adiguntur ad despe- rationem, et tollitur certa consolatio, et portus conscientiarum.

Septimus, tollitur vera invocatio, quae non potest fieri, cum mens fugit Deum. Denique tota haec pharisaica imaginatio de lege, tantum est ethnica et rationalis doctrina, nec progreditur ulterius. Hos igitur tantos errores taxari opor- tere manifestum est, et de his Christus saepe di- micat cum Iudaeis, ut cap. 3. cum Nicodemo, cap. 8.: Si filius vos liberavit, vere liberi eritis. Et alias saepe. Idem agit Paulus ad Rom. et ali- bi, et Baptista haud dubie pluribus verbis haec exposuit.

Est igitur haec sententia in antithesi, dissi- miles sunt personae, Moses et Messias. Moses tantum fuit doctor et politicus gubernator, non fuit propiciator, non sustulit peccatum et mortem. Messias vero non tantum est doctor, sed etiam propiciator, tollit peccatum et mortem, dat Spi- ritum sanctum et vitam aeternam, nec est poli- ticus gubernator, ut vos Iudaei somniatis, sed habet longe aliud officium, est victima pro pecca- to, est perpetuus sacerdos et mediator inter Deum et homines, dat remissionem peccatorum, novam iusticiam et vitam aeternam. Dixi de discri- mine personarum.

Nunc discrimen Legis et Evangelii conspi- ciatur, quod ostendit textus, cum ait: Gratia et veritas per Iesum Christum facta est. Verba erunt perspicua, si cogitabis Baptistam loqui de integro et consummato beneficio Christi. Gratia significat reconciliationem, qua in hac vita dona- tur nobis remissio peccatorum gratis propter filium Dei, non propter legem aut nostra merita. Ve- ritas significat veram Dei noticiam, non captivam peccati, veram vitam, non captivam mortis, de- nique vera et aeterna bona, quae etsi incoantur in hac mortali vita, tamen post resurrectionem exhibebuntur integre. Donat igitur talem noti- ciam, iusticiam et vitam, quae tunc est sine erro- re, sine peccato, sine morte. Nominat igitur veritatem, vera et aeterna bona, ac facilius in- telligi dictum Baptistae potest, cum illam con- summationem aspicimus, quam si tantum de san- ctis in hac mortali vita cogitemus, etsi, ut con- stat, haec incoari necesse est in hac vita, hic gratiam apprehendimus, qua reconciliamur, et reputamur iusti, et sumus filii Dei, et haeredes vitae aeternae, etiamsi haeret adhuc in hac cor- rupta natura ingens moles peccatorum, incoari tamen et veram noticiam Dei, veram invocatio- nem, veram iusticiam victricem peccati, et veram vitam victricem mortis, oportet. Fide statuimus Deum esse misericordem, nos propter mediato- rem recipi, exaudiri, iuvari, salvari. Haec est nova lux ignota carni, et vincens dubitationem, et cum fides statuit de reconciliatione, iam vin- cit peccatum et mortem, et incipit Deum invo- care vero motu, ad eum confugere, et expectare vitam aeternam.

Sed collatio est illustrior, si consummata beneficia opponantur legi. Christus donat novam lucem, qua sine ullo errore Deum intuebimur, donat iusticiam, quae sine ullo peccato erit, do- nat vitam aeternam prorsus liberam a morte, et fruentem aeterna laetitia in agnitione Dei. Quid simile adfert lex? Iusticia legis tantum est exter- na disciplina, id est, quaedam misera et immunda hypocrisis, captiva errorum ac dubitationis, pec- cati ac mortis. Nam si nihil audiat mens nisi le- gem, manet oppressa dubitatione multiplici, fugit Deum, non statuit se exaudiri, aut salvari, ut Saul fugit Deum. Ideoque nulla vera est invo- catio in tali mente. Vincitur ergo in horrendo peccato, id est, quod Deum non agnoscit, nec invocat, vincitur et morte, quia dubitans ruit in desperationem et aeternam iram. Imo lex est ministerium huius irae, quia est vox ostendens iram Dei adversus peccatum, tantum clamitans, Deum irasci peccato, et nos accusans. Proinde longe alia est Evangelii vox, videlicet, annun- cians gratiam et veritatem per Christum, id est, annuncians donari reconciliationem et vitam aeter- nam propter Christum mediatorem. Hanc vocem patefecit Christus ex sinu aeterni patris, ut mox dicet, nec attulit legem, quam voluit Deus pro- mulgari per Mosen. Sic et Paulus inquit: Nunc iusticia Dei apparuit sine lege, id est, alia quae- dam iusticia patefit, scilicet, reconciliatio gratui- ta, quam non docet lex, nec datur propter legem, sed propter filium mediatorem. Haec de discri- mine Mosi et Christi, legis et Evangelii, dili- genter observanda sunt, ne obruantur et ob- scurentur summa beneficia per filium Dei Eccle- siae donata, liberatio a peccato, et morte aeter- na, ac donatio reconciliationis iusticiae ac vitae aeternae.

## 1:18
No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him.

This passage coheres with the next narrative, and declares more clearly the distinction between the law and the Gospel. For the law is a doctrine implanted in human minds at the creation of man, which even after the fall of Adam was not entirely extinguished. For God willed that some knowledge of himself remain in our minds, so that judgment against sin might remain. This knowledge, which argues against sin, Paul calls a chirograph, by which human nature is condemned, guilty of the wrath of God, and oppressed by sin. Therefore, there is born with us a certain light, which is the knowledge of the law; this is knowledge commanding what sort of people we ought to be, and what things are to be done, what are to be omitted, and denouncing the wrath of God to those who do not obey. This knowledge was later renewed in the Decalogue, so that a voice from heaven might be a witness that that knowledge had been divinely handed down and implanted in our minds, and at the same time it might kindle it in this darkness of ours.

But human reason, without divine promise, is entirely ignorant of the will of God concerning the gratuitous remission of sins and the restoration of eternal life on account of the Son. This sentiment is far distant from the voice of the law, nor is it born with us, but as it is said here: The Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has revealed it to us. Many, because they see that in ethnic laws or writings many things are honestly commanded, argue that there is no difference between the doctrine of the Church and the ethnic. But these err in the whole way; precepts concerning morals, or laws, agree because they are naturally known, just like the knowledge of numbers. But the voice of the Gospel concerning the gratuitous remission of sins and the restoration of eternal life was unknown to the ethnic, and is very far distant from laws. These things must be observed so that the kinds of doctrines may be distinguished, because the confusion of the law and the Gospel produces many pernicious errors.

But the distinction will be more illustrious if we look at our first parents after the fall. When they were called into judgment, they knew the law, that there is a God, that he is a judge, and being accused, they felt terrors which no human voice can express. And because no promise existed concerning the remission of sins, they could think nothing else but that they had been cast off by God, and would remain in eternal punishments. Idle and secure men cannot imagine how great this consternation was in our first parents, who had heard nothing about the remission of sins, nay, had heard that a great multitude of spirits, after the fall, had been cast into eternal punishments. Let us think, therefore, that there were terrors far greater than those which can be described in words. Here, when the knowledge of the law was present, the voice of the Gospel was lacking. Wherefore, by an admirable counsel, it was decreed that the Son of God, sent to men, should put on human nature, should become a victim for the human race, and should restore eternal life to us. This admirable counsel of the eternal Father the Son himself then also declared to our first parents, and published the promise concerning the future seed, and the future liberation from sin and death. This is the first revelation of the Gospel, placed entirely outside of natural judgment, which indeed was made then by the Son of God, and afterwards often repeated in conversations with the fathers. And at length it sounded through him, when, having put on flesh, he openly promulgated the Gospel.

From this comparison let us learn the distinction between the Law and the Gospel. Then also let us give thanks to God, because by this wonderful counsel through the Son he delivered the human race from eternal wrath. And this is the sentiment of the discourse in the text. He wished to declare the distinction of the Law and the Gospel, and to testify that the Gospel was revealed to us through the Son of God, and that it is not a doctrine born with us, as are doctrines known to the heathens, the wisdom of laws, or the knowledge of numbers and figures. Let us know, therefore, that this word was delivered by a singular and ineffable goodness, and the Son sent, lest the human race should perish, as the devils perished.

This is the sum of the words in the text. Now let us briefly consider the words: No one has ever seen God. Since the text in this place asks how this will of God was known, that God willed to restore the human race, and how he willed to appease his wrath, there is no need for a disputation about the vision of the essence, but it is enough to establish this. No one has ever seen God, that is, no one has seen this secret will concerning the saving of the human race, and concerning the mode of salvation. Angels see God, but they did not know this secret decree before the Son brought it forth. Human minds in some way know God, they know the law of God, but the will concerning salvation is entirely outside the sight of human reason.

This is a simple, and as far as I can judge, a proper interpretation of this text. For as to what others ask here, why the text says, No one has seen God? when yet Moses saw him? There is no need for this disputation. For Moses learned the will concerning the saving of the human race from the promises which he had received from the fathers, nor did he first bring them forth from the aspect in which he saw God, nor do I dispute now how or how much Moses saw; certainly neither angels, nor fathers, nor Moses could see that inscrutable will before it was revealed through the Son by the voice of the promises, and in Exodus 33 it is clearly said: You will not be able to see my face, but also the Son says, Matthew 11: No one knows the Son, except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father, except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal him.

This is the proper glory of the Son, to have perfectly known the Father, because he is the image of the Father. Therefore, the decree of the divine will concerning the wonderful salvation of the human race shines in the Son. Our hearts, harder than the rocks of the Caucasus and colder than ice, cannot think what the wrath of the Father was against sin, what the deliberation was concerning the victim and concerning the remission. We think in the Stoic manner that these things happened as if by fatal necessity; we do not think that there was a true and ardent wrath, and true deliberations. But the text in this place wishes to admonish us that we should think that the wrath was true, and that it is an admirable work of mercy that it was decreed that the Son should become a victim and a savior.

The Son who is in the bosom of the Father, that is, penetrating the intimate parts of the Father, perfectly looking into the Father, as was said before, that the Father is perfectly known to the Son alone. He declared it, namely, not first then when he taught in Judea having put on human nature, but he declared it from then on from the beginning by the voice of the Son; the promises sounded to Adam, Eve, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, and other Prophets. This is the embassy of the one Son, to preach first concerning this huge mercy, and to reveal this secret decree concerning salvation, concerning the abolishing of sin, concerning eternal life. Therefore, he both delivered the promises in the beginning, and afterwards, born of a virgin, he illustrated them.

But it must be diligently observed, the very word he declared.
