He binds us to this very word which the Son exhibited to the fathers, the Prophets, the Apostles; through this word he wishes God to be known, through this word he testifies that sin is abolished, and that eternal life is begun, just as it is said later in chapter 16: Sanctify them in the truth, your word is truth. I do not pray for them only, but also for those who are going to believe in me through their word. This is the proper wisdom of the Church, not to inquire about God or the will of God through human opinions, but to acknowledge Him through the word, and to establish that He is certainly effective through His word, and certainly performs those things which He promised in His word. As Paul says: The Gospel is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes. This sentiment brings the richest consolation to the pious. For human minds easily wander outside the word of God, they seek other testimonies about God, other illuminations, they easily doubt whether such great things, which are shown in the promises, are performed. Therefore, it is necessary to instruct them about the use and efficacy of the word of God. Furthermore, the sum of this passage is that the law must be distinguished from the Gospel, as I said above. And that the law is a natural notion, but the Gospel is another wonderful counsel unknown to human reason, concerning the salvation of the human race, revealed from the beginning in the Church through the Son of God, and confirmed by wonderful testimonies.

Latin:

Deum nemo vidit unquam, unigenitus filius qui est in sinu patris, ipse enarravit.

Cohaeret haec particula cum proxima narra- tione, et magis declarat discrimen legis et Evan- gelii. Nam lex est doctrina insita mentibus hu- manis in creatione hominis, quae etiam post la- psum Adae non prorsus extincta est. Voluit enim Deus aliquam manere in nostris mentibus noticiam sui, ut maneret iudicium adversus pec- catum. Hanc noticiam arguentem peccatum Pau- lus vocat Chirographum, quo condemnatur hu- mana natura, rea irae Dei, et oppressa peccato. Nascitur ergo nobiscum qualecunque lumen, quod est noticia legis, hoc est, noticia praecipiens, quales nos esse oportebat, et quae sint facienda, quae omittenda, et iram Dei denuncians iis, qui non obtemperant. Haec noticia postea in Deca- logo renovata est, ut vox de coelo testis esset, no- ticiam illam divinitus traditam, et mentibus no- stris insitam fuisse, et simul eam in hac caligine nostra accenderet.

Sed ratio humana sine promissione divina prorsus ignorat voluntatem Dei de remissione pec- catorum gratuita, et restitutione vitae aeternae propter filium. Haec sententia longe distat a voce legis, nec nascitur nobiscum, sed ut hic dicitur: Filius qui est in sinu patris, patefecit eam nobis. Multi, quia vident in ethnicis legibus aut scri- ptis multa honeste praecipi, disputant nihil in- teresse inter doctrinam Ecclesiae et ethnicam. Sed hi tota via errant, praecepta de moribus, seu leges congruunt, quia sunt naturaliter notae, si- cut numerorum noticiae. At vox Evangelii de re- missione peccatorum gratuita et restitutione vitae aeternae, fuit ignota ethnicis, et longissime di- stat a legibus. Haec observanda sunt, ut discer- nantur doctrinarum genera, quia confusio legis et Evangelii multos perniciosos errores parit.

Erit autem illustrius discrimen, si primos parentes post lapsum intueamur. Cum vocati essent in iudicium, norant legem, esse Deum, esse iudicem, et accusati senserunt pavores, quos nulla vox humana eloqui potest. Et quia de re- missione peccatorum nulla promissio extabat, nihil aliud cogitare poterant, nisi se a Deo ab- iectos esse, ac mansuros in aeterna morte ac aeternis poenis. Homines otiosi et securi non possunt existimare, quanta fuerit in primis pa- rentibus haec consternatio, qui nihil audierant de remissione peccatorum, imo audierant magnam multitudinem spirituum, post lapsum, in aeter- nas poenas abiectam esse. Cogitemus igitur fuisse terrores longe maiores, quam qui verbis describi possint. Hic cum adesset legis noticia, deerat vox Evangelii. Quare admirando consilio decre- tum est, ut filius Dei missus ad homines, indue- ret humanam naturam, fieret victima pro genere humano, et restitueret nobis vitam aeternam. Hoc admirandum consilium aeterni patris tunc quoque filius ipse enarravit primis parentibus, ac edidit promissionem de futuro semine, ac futura liberatione a peccato et morte. Haec est prima Evangelii revelatio prorsus extra naturale iudi- cium posita, quae quidem et tunc a filio Dei facta est, et postea saepe repetita in colloquiis cum pa- tribus. Et tandem sonuit per eum, cum induta carne palam promulgavit Evangelium.

Ex hac collatione discamus discrimen inter Legem et Evangelium. Deinde et gratias aga- mus Deo, quod hoc mirabili consilio per filium liberavit genus humanum ab aeterna ira. Et haec est sententia concionis in textu. Discrimen legis et Evangelii declarare voluit, et testari Evange- lium per filium Dei nobis revelatum, nec esse doctrinam nobiscum nascentem, ut sunt doctri- nae ethnicis notae, legum sapientia, aut nume- rorum et figurarum noticia. Sciamus igitur sin- gulari et inenarrabili bonitate traditum hoc ver- bum, et missum filium, ne genus humanum periret, sicut diaboli perierunt.

Haec est summa verborum in textu. Nunc breviter verba consideremus: Deum nemo vidit unquam. Cum hoc loco textus quaerat, quo- modo haec voluntas Dei agnita sit, quod voluerit Deus restituere genus humanum, et quomodo placari iram suam voluerit, non est opus dispu- tatione de visione essentiae, sed satis est hoc con- stituere. Deum nemo vidit unquam, id est, hanc arcanam voluntatem de salvando humano genere, et de modo salvationis nemo vidit. Vident Deum angeli, sed hoc arcanum decretum non norant, priusquam filius protulit. Mentes humanae ali- quo modo norunt Deum, norunt legem Dei, sed voluntas de salvatione prorsus est extra conspe- ctum humanae rationis.

Haec est simplex, et quantum iudicare pos- sum, propria interpretatio huius textus. Quod enim alii hic quaerunt, cur dicat textus, Deum nemo vidit? cum tamen Moses viderit? Non est opus hac disputatione. Nam voluntatem de sal- vando genere humano Moses dedicit ex promis- sionibus, quas acceperat a patribus, nec primus protulit eas ex aspectu, quo vidit Deum, nec disputo nunc quomodo aut quantum Moses vide- rit, certe illam inscrutabilem voluntatem nec an- geli, nec patres, nec Moses videre potuerunt, antequam per filium voce promissionum patefacta est, et Exo. 37. clare dicitur: Faciem meam vi- dere non poteris, sed et filius inquit, Matth. 11.: Nemo novit filium, nisi pater, nec patrem quis novit, nisi filius, et cui voluerit filius revelare.

Propria haec filii gloria est perfecte novisse patrem, quia est imago patris. Lucet ergo in filio decretum voluntatis divinae, de miranda sal- vatione generis humani. Nostra pectora duriora Caucasi rupibus et frigidiora glacie non possunt cogitare, qualis fuerit ira patris adversus pecca- tum, qualis deliberatio de victima et de remis- sione. Cogitamus Stoico more haec ita quasi fa- tali necessitate accidisse, non cogitamus veram et ardentem iram, et veras deliberationes fuisse. Sed textus hoc loco vult nos admonere, ut cogite- mus veram fuisse iram, et admirandum opus mi- sericordiae esse, quod decretum est, ut filius fieret victima et salvator.

Filius qui est in sinu patris, id est, intima patris penetrans, perfecte introspiciens patrem, sicut antea dictum est, uni filio perfecte notum esse patrem. Ipse enarravit, videlicet non pri- mum tunc cum indutus humana natura in Iu- daea docuit, sed enarravit inde usque ab initio voce filii, Adae, Evae, Abrahae, Isaac, Iacob, Mosi et aliis Prophetis sonuerunt promissiones. Unius filii legatio haec est de hac ingenti miseri- cordia primum concionari, et hoc decretum arca- num de salvatione, de abolendo peccato, de vita aeterna, patefacere. Ergo et initio promissiones tradidit, et postea natus ex virgine, eas illu- stravit.

Diligenter autem observandum est ipsum vo- cabulum enarravit. Alligat nos ad hoc ipsum verbum, quod exhibuit filius patribus, Prophetis, Apostolis, per hoc verbum vult agnosci Deum, per hoc verbum testatur aboleri peccatum, et in- coari vitam aeternam, sicut et postea dicitur cap. 16.: Sanctifica eos in veritate, sermo tuus veritas est, Non pro eis rogo tantum, sed et pro iis qui credituri sunt per verbum eorum in me. Haec est propria Ecclesiae sapientia, non humanis opi- nionibus quaerere de Deo, aut de Dei voluntate, sed agnoscere eum per verbum, et statuere quod certo sit efficax per verbum suum, certo praestet ea, quae in verbo suo promisit. Sicut Paulus inquit: Evangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti. Haec sententia uberrimam con- solationem affert piis. Nam humanae mentes fa- cile vagantur extra verbum Dei, requirunt testi- monia alia de Deo, alias illuminationes, facile dubitant, an praestentur res tantae, quae in pro- missionibus monstrantur. Ideo necesse est eru- diri eas, de usu et efficacia verbi Dei. Porro summa huius loci est, discernendam esse legem ab Evangelio, ut supra dixi. Ac legem esse na- turalem noticiam, sed Evangelium esse aliud mi- randum consilium ignotum humanae rationi, de salvatione generis humani, patefactum ab initio in Ecclesia per filium Dei, et mirandis testimoniis confirmatum.

## 1:19
And this is the testimony of John, when the Jews sent priests, etc.

He adds another narrative about John, to show that he often testified about the Messiah. And the testimonies of John, Joseph, the Shepherds, the Magi, Simeon, and others are written down, so that they may confirm us. For although those things which are done in the Church do not strike the eyes in the same way as the battles of Alexander and Caesar, nevertheless God wants the Church to be some assembly, and for there to be certain witnesses of the great things that are done. Thus, from the very beginning, the word has been propagated by certain testimonies. Adam and Eve testified about the creation, likewise about the fall, and about the promises given. Thus also, one after another, some were always spectators and witnesses of the propagated divine word. And let this be enough to have warned about the testimonies.

Nor is there any need here to declaim about the constancy of John. Another question must be agitated, which also provided the occasion for the embassy. Since John was handing down a new article of the greatest moment, namely about the time of the coming of the Messiah, and likewise was changing the kind of doctrine, receiving the Gentiles, withdrawing from the temple, omitting the sacrifices commanded in the law, although he was born of the priestly lineage, and was instituting a new ceremony of baptism, by which a schism and distraction of the people was being made. Finally, since he was departing from the ordinary authority, and was saying and doing many things against it, there was a great and grave cause for the high priest and the priests to inquire by what authority John was making such a change in the Church, just as it is now often debated why we depart from the ordinary authority, why we make a change in the Church, not a mediocre one. That novelty and appearance of schism was therefore the cause of the embassy.

This dispute is the principal one: whether it is ever permitted to depart from the ordinary authority, and to change doctrine and rites in the Church. One thing politicians hate most bitterly and detest most of all, namely the changing of laws, which is accustomed to beget the desertion of ordinary authority, seditions, and discords, which are the ruin of all empires and states. Hence those sayings of Plato, that just as the delusions of parents, so certain vices of governors must be tolerated: and many things are discussed most gravely by the wisest men to this effect. These political discourses are transferred to the Church, and indeed they are exaggerated; they say that the Church must be spared more, because dissensions in the Church bring more dangers to consciences, and can be healed with more difficulty.

But although these political discourses have their place, nevertheless it must be known that this government is far different from human empires. We have a rule as to how far the ordinary authority in the Church must be obeyed, and when it is necessary to oppose it. The general rule is immutable: Whenever the governors of the Church hand down impious doctrine, it is necessary to oppose them, to refute the impious doctrine, and to profess and propose the true one. This rule is taken from the first and second commandment: You shall have no other gods. Likewise: You shall not take the name of God in vain. Likewise to the Galatians 1: If anyone teaches another Gospel, let him be anathema. Therefore, although political men take it ill that concord is disturbed, nevertheless if the ordinary authority dissents from the truth, it is necessary that the truth be preferred. This rule in general commands all those teaching this faith, as Paul says: This is required, that we be faithful. Wherefore, even if John had served only in a common vocation, nevertheless it would have behooved him to tax the errors of the synagogue, just as Zacharias, Simeon, and others were undoubtedly taxing them then.

But there is another certain peculiar prophetic vocation, by which God effects notable changes, as when He raises up Moses, and establishes a new polity for Israel. Likewise when He later raises up Samuel, Elijah, Elisha, Jeremiah, who all stirred up great matters against the ordinary power. For they both renewed the doctrine previously handed down, and did certain other things by singular mandate, they called kings, and deposed some. For they had a singular calling, singular mandates and divine testimonies. Thus God from time to time renews the Church, and shows that it is not ruled only by human counsels or ordinances. Therefore it is written: He ascended, He gave gifts to men, some indeed Prophets, others Apostles, etc. And let the ordinary governors rage as much as they want, yet God in His immense mercy values the Church more than the ordinary power. For He sends better governors and teachers, Moses, Elijah, Elisha, Jeremiah, so that they may restore the Church collapsed by the wickedness of the ordinary power.

Such also was John; he had a singular calling, a singular mandate, and singular testimonies. It was necessary to obey this calling and mandate, and because he had singular testimonies, it was necessary to assent to his doctrine. Now the testimonies were that this son was promised to his father Zacharias by the voice of an angel, that he was born from a barren and aged mother, and that speech was taken from and restored to his father, and that the father prophesied about the coming of the Messiah.

Then John himself was confirmed by an illustrious testimony, nor is any revelation of such a great matter described, nor in the visions of the Fathers or Prophets, as in the vision of John, concerning which he himself indeed says: I saw, and I am a witness. The whole Godhead showed itself to John, so that the distinction of the persons might be seen. The eternal Father, opening the heavens, revealing Himself, sounds a voice by which He testifies concerning the Son. The Son is bathed in water before him in the Jordan, the Holy Spirit descends in a visible form. Minds, when they hear such great things, imagine that it was an idle spectacle, and they marvel with a certain curiosity. But let us know that this revelation was exhibited by the singular counsel of God, and that there were great causes. John learned very many things in this great revelation, about which he later instructed others as well. Although therefore John is not said to have performed miracles, that is, like the others on the bodies of men, or in political government, yet he had testimonies of his doctrine so wondrous and illustrious that they were not inferior to the testimonies of Moses and Elijah.

Although these testimonies confirmed the pious and John, which indeed when they were publicly preached ought to have bent even the adversaries, yet when questioned by the adversaries, he alleges the saying of the Prophet Isaiah, so that he may show that he also has testimonies of his calling from the word of God, and that he preaches by divine authority. The chief priests and Levites had already heard from his father Zacharias that this John would be the herald of the Messiah, and they had read in Malachi about the angel who would precede the Savior. Thus also Isaiah preaches about a voice crying in the desert. These prophetic sayings agreed with the other testimonies of John. Wherefore it was necessary for John to serve his calling, and all ought to have heard him. Nor could it be objected that he was the author of a schism, and that he was stirring up sedition among the people, and that he was instituting new cults without divine authority and had diminished the authority of the law. Concerning these great matters the adversaries were expostulating with him. This was the cause and sum of the embassy, as now hypocrites complain, that we depart from the ordinary power, and are authors of schisms and new dogmas.

But for us the answer is easier than for John. Because John was the author of a new rite of baptism, and he was receiving the Gentiles, and neglecting the sacrifices, which nevertheless had been handed down by divine right. We, however, know that after the promulgation of the Gospel no other word is to be pressed, but simply the voice of the Gospel is to be retained, until the Son of God shows Himself openly to the world again. This mandate concerning the Son: Hear Him, is absolutely immutable. Wherefore if any have taught, or are teaching, things conflicting with the Gospel, at any time, they are to be refuted, and the pure voice of the Gospel is to be retained. This is a general mandate pertaining to all without any distinction. Therefore we can easily wash away the crime of schism, but I come to the text.

Why, they say, do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor a Prophet? As if they were saying: Why do you institute a new rite, which is permitted to no one except the Messiah, or perhaps Elijah who is to precede the Messiah, as it is written in Malachi, or some similar Prophet who is to precede the Messiah. John answers without ambiguity, and at the same time explains what he is not, and commemorates in what calling he is engaged, and what is the sum of his doctrine. First, he denies that he is the Messiah, and often distinguishes his own person and office from the person of the Messiah, and the benefits, as was said above, and a little later the same passage will be repeated. Next, he denies that he is Elijah: for although the name of Elijah is attributed to John in Malachi, yet the chief priests were expecting Elijah himself, and indeed one warring against tyrants and driving out the Romans; such an Elijah he denies that he is.

Regarding the third question, more is disputed, why he denied that he was the Prophet, and some say that he was not being asked in a general sense whether he is a prophet, but about a certain prophet who was to precede the Messiah. For in the text the article is added: Are you that Prophet? But whether they are asking about a prophet in a general sense, or about a certain prophet, there is no great difference. And although most say that for the sake of modesty he did not wish to accept the title of Prophet, yet since he is answering regarding his calling, he did not wish here to mix in ironies or concealments. It is an ingenuous confession. The chief priests understood the Prophet to be not only a teacher of the Gospel, but a political governor, such as were Samuel, Elijah, Elisha, Jeremiah, and others. They wanted to hear whether he promised that he would recover the liberty of the kingdom by driving out the Romans; here he answers that he is not the Prophet, that is, a political governor. Christ says in Matthew 11 that he excels the prophets, because it is a greater office to deliver the voice of the Gospel, through which Jews and Gentiles are saved, and indeed openly to receive the Gentiles and show Christ, than to defend the polity of the Israelites, as Samuel, Jeremiah, and the like had done. This is the simplest explanation regarding the Prophet in this place: Nor are these things recounted in the text without cause. For we are warned that the ministry of the Gospel should be distinguished from the prophetic calling. John does not establish a new polity, he does not bear the sword, he does not anoint new kings, as Samuel and Elisha did, but only brings the voice of the Gospel, by which God founds the Church and receives believers. It matters much to retain this distinction, but the legates imagine that he has no authority if he does not have political authority. Therefore they ask insultingly: Why do you baptize? If you are neither Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet? John refutes them and signifies that their enumeration is not complete: Nay, he says, I have authority, even if I am not the Prophet, for I am a minister of the voice of the Gospel. I have, therefore, a ministry, not political, but one which serves the new and eternal justice and life. He adds, therefore, the saying of Isaiah, by which he teaches at the same time what his ministry is, and warns them to listen to him, because he is the one whom the Prophet there signified should be heard, as a witness of the coming of the Messiah.

Latin:

Et hoc est testimonium Ioannis, cum Iudaei miserunt sacerdotes, etc.

Addit aliam narrationem de Ioanne, ut ostendat eum saepe testatum esse de Messia. Suntque testimonia Ioannis, Ioseph, Pastorum, Magorum, Simeonis, et aliorum perscripta, ut nos confirment. Etsi enim ea, quae geruntur in Ecclesia, non perinde incurrunt in oculos, ut Alexandri et Caesaris pugnae, tamen Deus vult Ecclesiam esse aliquem coetum, ac testes esse cer- tos magnarum rerum quae geruntur. Sic inde usque ab initio certis testimoniis verbum propa- gatum est. Adam et Eva testati sunt de condi- tione, item de lapsu, et de datis promissionibus. Sic et deinceps aliqui semper spectatores, et te- stes fuerunt propagati verbi divini. Atque haec de testimoniis monuisse satis sit.

Nec opus est hic declamare de constantia Ioannis. Alia quaestio agitanda est, quae et oc- casionem legationi praebuit. Cum Ioannes arti- culum novum maximi momenti traderet, videli- cet de tempore adventus Messiae, item mutaret genus doctrinae, reciperet gentes, secederet a tem- plo, omitteret mactationes in lege mandatas, cum quidem esset natus genere sacerdotum, institueret et novam ceremoniam baptismi, qua fiebat schi- sma et distractio populi. Denique cum discederet ab ordinaria potestate, et multa contra eam di- ceret et faceret, magna ac gravis causa fuit pon- tifici et sacerdotibus interrogandi, qua autoritate Ioannes tantam mutationem in Ecclesia faceret, ut nunc disputari solet, cur ab ordinaria potestate discedamus, cur mutationem in Ecclesia, non mediocrem, faciamus. Fuit igitur novitas illa et species schismatis causa legationis.

Haec disputatio praecipua est, liceatne ali- quando discedere ab ordinaria potestate, et mu- tare doctrinam, et ritus in Ecclesia. Unam rem omnium acerrime oderunt maximeque detestan- tur viri politici, videlicet mutationem legum, quae desertionem ordinariae potestatis, seditio- nes et discordias gignere solet, quae sunt exitio omnibus imperiis et civitatibus. Hinc sunt illae voces Platonis, ut parentum deliria, ita quaedam gubernatorum vitia toleranda esse: et in hanc sententiam a sapientissimis viris plurima gravissi- me disseruntur. Transferuntur hi politici ser- mones ad Ecclesiam, et quidem exaggerantur, magis parcendum esse dicunt Ecclesiae, quod dis- sidia in Ecclesia plus periculorum conscientiis afferant, et difficilius sanari possint.

Etsi autem hi politici sermones suum habent locum, tamen sciendum est, hanc gubernatio- nem longe dissimilem esse humanis imperiis. Ha- bemus regulam quatenus ordinariae potestati in Ecclesia parendum sit, et quando adversari ne- cesse sit. Generalis regula est et immutabilis: Quandocunque gubernatores Ecclesiae tradunt impiam doctrinam, necesse est eis adversari, re- futare impiam doctrinam, profiteri ac proponere veram. Haec regula sumitur ex primo et secundo praecepto: Non habebis deos alienos. Item: Non usurpabis nomen Dei vane. Item ad Galat. 1.: Si quis aliud Evangelium docet, anathema sit. Etsi igitur politici viri aegre ferunt turbari concordiam, tamen si ordinaria potestas dissentit a veritate, necesse est anteferri veritatem. Haec regula in genere praecipit omnibus docentibus hanc fidem, ut Paulus inquit: Hoc requiri, ut fideles simus. Quare etiamsi Ioannes tantum in communi vocatione serviisset, tamen errores sy- nagogae taxare eum oportuisset, ut taxabant haud dubie tunc Zacharias, Simeon et alii.

Sed alia quaedam est peculiaris vocatio pro- phetica, qua Deus insignes mutationes efficit, ut cum Mosen excitat, ac novam politiam Israël con- stituit. Item cum postea excitat Samuelem, Eliam, Elisaeum, Ieremiam, qui omnes contra ordina- riam potestatem maximas res moverunt. Nam et doctrinam prius traditam renovaverunt, et certas res alias singulari mandato egerunt, vocaverunt reges, et quosdam excusserunt. Habuerunt enim singularem vocationem, singularia mandata et testimonia divina. Sic Deus subinde renovat Ec- clesiam, et ostendit eam non regi tantum huma- nis consiliis aut ordinationibus. Ideo scriptum est: Ascendit, dedit dona hominibus, alios qui- dem Prophetas, alios Apostolos, etc. Ac fre- mant quantum volunt ordinarii gubernatores, ta- men Deus sua ingenti misericordia pluris facit Ecclesiam, quam ordinariam potestatem. Mittit enim meliores gubernatores et doctores, Mosen, Eliam, Elisaeum, Ieremiam, ut Ecclesiam col- lapsam scelere ordinariae potestatis rursus in- staurent.

Talis fuit et Ioannes, hic singularem voca- tionem, singulare mandatum, et singularia testi- monia habuit. Huic vocationi et mandato parere necesse fuit, et quia singularia testimonia habuit, necesse fuit assentiri eius doctrinae. Erant autem testimonia, quod patri Zachariae voce angeli hic filius promissus fuit, quod natus ex sterili et effoeta matre, et quod patri ademtus est et reddi- tus sermo, quod pater vaticinatur de adventu Messiae.

Deinde ipse Ioannes confirmatus est illustri testimonio, nec ulla describitur tantae rei reve- latio, nec in Patrum aut Prophetarum visionibus, ut in visione Ioannis, de qua quidem ipse inquit: Ego vidi, et testis sum. Ostendit se Ioanni tota divinitas, ita ut personarum discrimen conspice- retur. Aeternus pater coelo aperto sese patefa- ciens vocem sonat, qua de filio testatur. Filius coram in Iordane aqua perfunditur, descendit Spiritus sanctus visibili speciei. Mentes, cum res tantas audiunt, imaginantur fuisse otiosum spectaculum, et curiositate quadam mirantur. Sed sciamus singulari Dei consilio hanc revela- tionem exhibitam esse, et magnas fuisse causas. Plurima Ioannes didicit in hac tanta revelatione, de quibus postea et caeteros erudiit. Quanquam igitur Ioannes non dicitur fecisse miracula, scili- cet, ut caeteri in corporibus hominum, aut in politica gubernatione, tamen doctrinae testimonia tam miranda et illustria habuit, ut non fuerint inferiora testimoniis Mosi et Eliae.

Quanquam autem pios et Ioannem haec te- stimonia confirmabant, quae quidem cum publice praedicarentur, etiam adversarios flectere debe- bant, tamen interrogatus ab adversariis, allegat dictum Prophetae Esaiae, ut ostendat se etiam ex verbo Dei testimonia suae vocationis habere, ac divina autoritate concionari. Audiverant iam Pontifices et Levitae ex patre Zacharia, hunc Ioan- nem praenuncium fore Messiae, et legerant apud Malachiam de angelo praecessuro salvatorem. Ita et Esaias concionatur de voce clamante in deserto. Haec dicta prophetica congruebant cum caeteris te- stimoniis Ioannis. Quare oportuit Ioannem servire suae vocationi, et audire eum omnes debebant. Nec poterat obiici, quod schismatis autor esset, et quod in populo seditionem moveret, et sine auto- ritate divina novos cultus institueret ac legis auto- ritatem minuerit. De his tantis rebus cum eo ex- postulabant adversarii. Haec fuit legationis causa et summa, ut nunc hypocritae quaeruntur, nos discedere ab ordinaria potestate, esse schismatum et novorum dogmatum autores.

Sed nobis facilior est responsio, quam Ioan- ni. Quia Ioannes erat autor novi ritus baptismi, et recipiebat gentes, et sacrificia negligebat, quae tamen iure divino tradita erant. Nos vero sci- mus post promulgationem Evangelii non instare aliud verbum, sed simpliciter vocem Evangelii retinendam esse, donec se palam mundo rursus ostendat filius Dei. Hoc mandatum de filio: Hunc audite, prorsus immutabile est. Quare si qui pugnantia cum Evangelio docuerunt, aut do- cent, quocunque tempore, refutandi sunt, et pura vox Evangelii retinenda. Hoc est generale mandatum ad omnes sine ullo discrimine, perti- nens. Ideo facile possumus diluere crimen schi- smatis, sed venio ad textum.

Cur, inquiunt, baptizas, si non es Chri- stus, nec Elias, nec Propheta? Quasi dicant: Cur novum ritum iustituis, quod nulli licet nisi Messiae, aut fortassis Eliae praecessuro Messiam, ut in Malachia scriptum est, aut alicui simili Pro- phetae praecessuro Messiam. Ioannes sine am- biguitate respondet, ac simul quid non sit, ex- ponit, et commemorat in qua vocatione versetur, et quae sit suae doctrinae summa. Primum negat se esse Messiam, et saepe discernit suam perso- nam officium, a persona Messiae, et beneficiis, ut supra dictum est, et paulo post idem locus re- petetur. Deinde negat se esse Eliam: etsi enim nomen Eliae tribuitur Ioanni in Malachia, ta- men pontifices expectabant ipsum Eliam, et qui- dem belligerantem cum tyrannis, et depellentem Romanos, talem se Eliam esse negat.

De tertia quaestione plura disputantur, cur se negarit Prophetam esse, et dicunt quidam in- terrogari non in genere, an sit Propheta, sed de certo Propheta praecessuro Messiam. Nam in textu articulus additur: Es tu Propheta ille? Sed sive in genere de Propheta interrogant, sive de certo Propheta, non magnum discrimen est. Et quanquam plerique dicunt modestiae causa non velle recipere titulum Prophetae, tamen cum de vocatione respondeat, non voluit hic miscere iro- nias aut occultationes. Ingenua confessio est. Pontifices Prophetam intelligebant, non solum doctorem Evangelii, sed gubernatorem politicum, quales fuerunt Samuel, Elias, Elisaeus, Iere- mias, et alii. Volebant audire, an promitteret se recuperaturum libertatem regni depulsis Ro- manis, hic respondet se non esse Prophetam, id est, politicum gubernatorem. Christus Matth. 11. dicit, eum antecellere Prophetis, quia maius est officium vocem Evangelii tradere, per quam Iudaei et gentes servantur, et quidem aperte gen- tes recipere et monstrare Christum, quam tueri politiam Israëlitarum, ut fecerant Samuel, Iere- mias, et similes. Haec est simplicissima enarra- tio de Propheta in hoc loco: Nec sine causa haec recensentur in textu. Monemur enim ut discer- natur ministerium Evangelii a vocatione prophe- tica. Ioannes non constituit novam politiam, non gerit gladium, non ungit reges novos, ut Sa- muel et Elisaeus, sed tantum vocem Evangelii affert, qua Deus Ecclesiam condit, et recipit cre- dentes. Hoc discrimen retinere multum refert, sed legati imaginantur, nullam eum autoritatem habere, si politicam non habeat. Ideo contu- meliose inquiunt: Cur baptizas? si nec es Chri- stus, nec Elias, nec Propheta? Refutat eos Ioannes, et significat enumerationem eorum non esse integrum: Imo, inquit, habeo autoritatem, etiamsi non Propheta, sum enim minister vocis Evangelii. Habeo igitur ministerium, non poli- ticum, sed quod servit novae et aeternae iusticiae et vitae. Addit igitur dictum Esaiae, quo simul docet, quale sit suum ministerium, et monet, ut ipsum audiant, quod sit is, quem ibi Propheta audiendum esse significaverit, tanquam testem adventus Messiae.

## 1:23
I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness.

He expressly says that he is a voice, to signify that he only has the ministry of teaching, and is not a leader or a political governor, such as Samuel and Elisha were. The sum of the doctrine, although it is contained in the saying of Isaiah, is nevertheless expressed more clearly in the sermons of John.

Latin:

Ego sum vox clamantis in deserto.

Diserte ait se vocem esse, ut significet se tantum habere ministerium docendi, non esse ducem, aut politicum gubernatorem, qualis fuit Samuel et Elisaeus. Summa vero doctrinae, etsi in dicto Esaiae continetur, tamen concionibus Ioannis clarius expressa est.

## 1:23
Prepare the way of the Lord.

That is, repent. For to prepare the way is to present oneself as a way to the coming Lord, in which he may be received. Those who defend their idols or other vices do not prepare the way for the Lord, but keep away the coming Messiah, they despise him, they do not seek his benefits, but mock the remission of sins and the new justice and eternal life. Therefore, to prepare the way for the Lord is properly to repent, to acknowledge sins, to seek the coming deliverer who takes away our evils. These things are declared thus in Isaiah: All flesh is grass, and all its glory as the flower of the field, that is, acknowledge that human nature is subject to sin and death, and cannot be freed by wisdom or one's own justice. Wherefore let us tremble at the recognition of our miseries, and let us receive the coming deliverer. As it is said there in Isaiah: Behold the Lord God will come in strength, he will feed his flock like a shepherd, he will gather the lambs in his arm, and will lift them in his bosom, and he himself will carry those that are nursing. The Baptist interprets this sermon; first he cries out that we should repent. Then he points out the Messiah, as he says here: In the midst of you stands, etc. Likewise: Behold the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. He therefore recited the testimony concerning his calling and the sum of his doctrine.

Latin:

Parate viam Domino.

Id est, agite poenitentiam. Nam parare viam est venienti domino sese tanquam viam exhibere, in qua excipi possit. Hi qui defendunt sua idola aut alia vitia, non parant viam domino, sed arcent venientem Messiam, contemnunt eum, non expetunt beneficia eius, sed derident remissionem peccatorum et novam iusticiam, ac vitam aeternam. Est ergo parare viam domino proprie, agere poenitentiam, agnoscere peccata, expetere venientem liberatorem, qui tollit mala nostra. Haec ita declarantur in Esaia: Omnis caro foenum, et omnis gloria eius, quasi flos agri, id est, agnoscite humanam naturam subiectam esse peccato et morti, nec posse liberari sapientia aut iusticia propria. Quare expavescamus agnitione nostrarum miseriarum, et excipiamus venientem liberatorem. Sicut ibi dicitur apud Esaiam: Ecce dominus Deus in fortitudine veniet, sicut pastor gregem suum pascet, in brachio suo congregabit agnos, et in sinu levabit, et lactentes ipse portabit. Hanc concionem interpretatur Baptista, primum clamat, ut agamus poenitentiam. Deinde monstrat Messiam, sicut hic inquit: Medius vestrum stat, etc. Item: Ecce agnus Dei qui tollit peccatum mundi. Recitavit igitur testimonium de vocatione sua, et doctrinae summam.

## 1:26
I baptize with water.

Before, he showed that he was called to this duty by God, and signified that there is a difference between his calling and that of the former prophets. Now he declares more clearly the difference between his person and the Messiah's, and to this must be added the parts of the sermon which exist in the other evangelists. The Messiah alone baptizes with the Holy Spirit, that is, the Son of God gives the Holy Spirit, and effects a new and perpetual light, justice, and life in believers, and fire, that is, the judgment and sense of the wrath of God against sin, in which some are converted, and being raised up by faith are saved, others are oppressed by eternal death. And these things are done through the external voice of the ministers, but yet they are done by the power of the Messiah, who gives the Holy Spirit; they are not done by the power of the other ministers. We, however, the other ministers, baptize with water unto repentance, that is, we are ministers of the voice of the Gospel, and of the Sacrament or sign, which is a testimony, by which God signifies that this human nature is, through the Gospel, immersed into death and the acknowledgment of sin, and washed, and gifted with new righteousness and life. One is the Messiah, the giver of the Holy Spirit, who kindles a fire in our hearts, that is, who shows the wrath of God against sin, and again, in consolation, begins a new and perpetual righteousness and life. But these things are done through the external voice, which sounds through the ministry of John, the Apostles, and all who teach rightly in the Church. For just as John distinguishes his person from the Messiah, so he distinguishes from the one Messiah all the ministers of the evangelical voice, the Apostles and the others who teach rightly.

Here it is usually asked what the difference is between the baptism of John and that of the Apostles and the subsequent ministers of the Gospel. The answer is not difficult for us who understand the office of John. It is true that the person of the Messiah must be distinguished from the ministers, as has already been said, yet the ministry of John and of the subsequent teachers of the New Testament has the same meaning and effect. For John is the beginner of the preaching of the Gospel. At the beginning of the New Testament, when the voice of John was heard, the elect felt the wrath of God against sin and were terrified, and again, believing the voice that pointed [to Him], they received the remission of sins, and a new and perpetual righteousness was begun in them. The same things happen in the preaching of the Apostles and their successors, until the end of the world. Therefore it is said in Luke: Preaching the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins, as if he were saying: The preaching of John was not an empty sound, but God willed it to be effective through the voice of John, whom He willed to be a witness concerning the Messiah born and the beginner of the preaching of the Gospel.

Lombard and his interpreters wrote somewhat differently about the distinction between the ministry of John and the Apostles, but the opinion which we have recited is true. Nor must it be imagined that the voice of John was merely a testimony in the human manner, such as are spoken in the forum. This imagination is too profane. But it must be known that great things, and those pertaining to eternal life, are transacted in the Church. God willed through the preaching of John to show the Messiah, and to deliver testimonies concerning Him; He willed also to gather again some Church, and by the voice of John to impart eternal life to it. These things differ greatly from forensic testimonies, and one must think far otherwise about these miraculous works of God in the Church than about profane business. I have spoken briefly about the common question, concerning which some things are said absurdly in the 4th book of Lombard, about which it is not difficult to judge for one who understands the power of the ministry of the Gospel, but I proceed to what is said in the text: He who is before me. I interpret as above concerning the excellence of the calling and the power: he is before me, that is, he excels me in calling and power. The Messiah was called first, and He excels all in power, because He Himself is the redeemer, the savior, and the giver of the Holy Spirit, and of new and perpetual righteousness and life. What is added: Whose shoe's latchet I am not worthy to unloose, is a figure by which John signifies that he is not worthy to be His minister; and customarily feet and shoes signify messengers, that is, heralds of the Gospel. He signifies, therefore, that he is not worthy of this so great ministry of the Gospel, which, even if it is despised in the world, yet in reality there is no greater function. Nor let us doubt that God is present to this function, and governs it miraculously, and defends it against the hatreds of the devil and the world. John signifies many things briefly in this place concerning the greatness of the ministry, which are to be pondered by the pious reader. For to recite everything in the exposition would be too long.

At the end of the passage, mention is made of where this most serious disputation with the legates was held. These things were done, he says, in Bethabara; the conjecture of those who think it should be read Betharaba, that is, house of the desert, does not displease, which seems to have been the name of some village in the desert, and the same name of a place is in the history of Joshua, chapter 15. It signifies, however, what kind of dwelling John's was, and it admonishes the Church and pious teachers to have such lodgings as they may in the desert, and to endure exiles, not to hold royal seats or riches. Those who retain the other reading, Bethabara, say that a crossing or ferry is signified, for this is what the word Abara sounds like, because John baptized in such a place at the Jordan, where, since it was a crossing, many who wished to be carried across the river were accustomed to gather daily, etc.

Latin:

Ego baptizo aqua.

Antea ostendit se divinitus ad hoc munus vocatum esse, et significavit discrimen esse suae vocationis, et priorum Prophetarum. Nunc magis declarat discrimen suae personae et Messiae, et huc addenda sunt membra concionis, quae extant apud caeteros Evangelistas. Messias solus baptizat Spiritu sancto, id est, filius Dei dat Spiritum sanctum, ac novam ac perpetuam lucem, iusticiam et vitam efficit in credentibus, et ignem, id est, iudicium ac sensum irae Dei adversus pec- catum, in quo alii convertuntur, et fide erecti salvantur, alii opprimuntur aeterna morte. Et haec fiunt per vocem externam ministrorum, sed tamen fiunt potentia Messiae, qui dat Spiritum sanctum, non fiunt potentia caeterorum mini- strorum. Nos vero caeteri ministri baptizamus aqua ad poenitentiam, id est, sumus ministri vocis Evangelii, et Sacramenti seu signi, quod est testimonium, quo Deus significat hanc huma- nam naturam per Evangelium mergi in mortem, ac agnitionem peccati, et ablui, ac donari nova iusticia et vita. Unus est Messias dator Spiritus sancti, accendentis ignem in cordibus nostris, id est, ostendentis iram Dei adversus peccatum, ac rursus in consolatione incoantis novam et per- petuam iusticiam ac vitam. Sed haec fiunt per vocem externam, quae sonat per ministerium Ioannis, Apostolorum, et omnium recte docen- tium in Ecclesia. Ut enim Ioannes suam perso- nam discernit a Messia, sic ab uno Messia discer- nit omnes ministros vocis evangelicae, Aposto- los ac caeteros recte docentes.

Hic quaeri solet, quid intersit inter bapti- smum Ioannis et Apostolorum, et sequentium ministrorum Evangelii. Non est difficilis respon- sio nobis intelligentibus officium Ioannis. Ve- rum est, discernendam esse personam Messiae a ministris, ut iam dictum est, tamen ministerium Ioannis et sequentium doctorum novi testamenti, significationem et effectum eundem habet. Ioan- nes enim est incoator praedicationis Evangelii. Sub initium novi testamenti audita voce Ioannis, senserunt electi iram Dei adversus peccatum, ac expaverunt, et rursus credentes voci monstranti, acceperunt remissionem peccatorum, et incoata est in eis nova et perpetua iusticia. Eadem fiunt in concione Apostolorum, et sequentium, usque ad finem mundi. Ideo in Luca dicitur: Praedi- cans baptismum poenitentia ad remissionem pec- catorum, quasi dicat: Ioannis concio non erat inanis sonitus, sed Deus voluit esse efficax per vocem Ioannis, quem voluit esse testem de Messia nato et incoatoremn praedicationis Evangelii.

Paulo aliter scripserunt de discrimine mini- sterii Ioannis et Apostolorum Longobardus et eius interpretes, sed sententia quam recitavimus vera est. Nec imaginandum est, Ioannis vocem tan- tum fuisse testimonium humano more, qualia in foro dicuntur. Haec imaginatio nimis profana est. Sed sciendum est res magnas, et ad vitam aeternam pertinentes in Ecclesia geri. Deus vo- luit per Ioannis concionem monstrare Messiam, et de eo testimonia tradere, voluit et rursus col- ligere aliquam Ecclesiam, et voce Ioannis ei vi- tam aeternam impertiri. Haec plurimum diffe- runt a forensibus testimoniis, et de his mirandis operibus Dei in Ecclesia longe aliter sentiendum est, quam de negociis profanis. Dixi breviter de quaestione communi, de qua in 4. libro Lon- gobardi quaedam absurde dicuntur, de quibus non difficile est iudicare, intelligenti vim mini- sterii Evangelii, sed pergo, quod in textu dici- tur: Qui prior me est. Interpretor ut supra de praestantia vocationis et potentia, prior me est, id est, antecellit me vocatione et potentia. Mes- sias primum vocatus est, et antecellit omnibus potentia, quia ipse est redemtor, salvator, et dator Spiritus sancti, et novae ac perpetuae iusti- ciae ac vitae. Quod additur: Cuius non sum dignus solvere lorum calceamenti, figura est, qua Ioannes significat se non esse dignum, qui sit illius minister; et usitate pedes, calcei, signi- ficant nuncios, hoc est, Evangelii praecones. Significat igitur se non esse dignum hoc tanto mi- nisterio Evangelii, quod etsi spretum est in mun- do, tamen reipsa nulla functio maior est. Nec dubitemus Deum adesse huic functioni, eamque mirabiliter gubernare, et adversus diaboli et mundi odia tueri. Multa hoc loco breviter Ioan- nes de magnitudine ministerii significat, quae pio lectori cogitanda sunt. Nam recitate omnia in enarratione, nimis longum esset.

In fine loci mentio fit, ubi haec gravissima disputatio cum legatis habita est. Haec facta sunt, inquit, in Bethabara, non displicet con- iectura eorum, qui putant legendum esse Betha- raba, id est, domus deserti, quod videtur fuisse nomen alicuius vici in deserto, et idem nomen loci est in historia Iosuae cap. 15. Significat au- tem quale Ioannis domicilium fuerit, et admonet Ecclesiam et pios doctores habere hospitia qualia- cunque in deserto, et perpeti exilia, non tenere regias sedes aut opes. Qui retinent alteram le- ctionem, Bethabara, dicunt significari transitum seu traiectum, hoc enim sonat vocabulum Abara, quod Ioannes tali loco ad Iordanem baptizarit, ubi cum esse traiectus, quotidie convenire soliti sint multi, qui per flumen transvehi vellent, etc.

## 1:29
Behold the Lamb of God.

Let us diligently compare all the sermons of John. For he also sets forth the doctrine of repentance, most severely arguing against sins, the contempt of God, hypocrisy, and other vices, and clearly setting forth eternal punishments for all who despise the wrath of God and do not believe in the Messiah. Then he adds the Gospel concerning the office of the Messiah, whom he says is a victim for sin, as these words teach: Behold the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world. He also preaches the remission of sins and the righteousness of faith in clear words in chapter 3: He who believes in the Son has eternal life, but he who does not believe in the Son, the wrath of God remains upon him. These sermons were very new to the Pharisees, who were expecting a Messiah not to be crucified, but to occupy the empires of the world; to divide the provinces. Nor did they know the righteousness of faith, but dreamed that they were righteous by the law. Since, therefore, there was such great darkness in the Church, God again kindled the light of true doctrine through John. It was, therefore, an excellent calling, and truly a greater prophecy, because John was sent to correct the huge errors that were spreading in the Church.

I said that he had delivered the doctrine concerning repentance, concerning the eternal punishments of the impious, concerning the office of the Messiah, concerning the remission of sins, concerning the righteousness of faith, and eternal life. He also shows the Messiah himself born, and already dwelling among men, so that the Church might know that the promises had been fulfilled; he called the nations to the fellowship of the Gospel and the benefits of the Messiah. Finally, he also delivered the doctrine of good works, and instructed individual orders of men, soldiers, judges, spouses, and showed true good works, omitting hypocritical ceremonies, and at length testified by his death that he truly professed these things for the sake of God, and expected a testimony from God in eternal life. I have reviewed these things so that we may consider that the calling of John was a huge benefit of God, and see that it contained the whole doctrine of the Church. This also must be added, that no revelation so clear has been delivered concerning the three persons of the divinity as this one is, which is described in the baptism of Christ, where John sees heaven opened, hears the voice of the eternal Father concerning the Son who was standing before him, and sees the Holy Spirit descending. Let us therefore listen to such a teacher and witness, and meditate with the sharpest zeal upon his sermons, which, although they have been delivered to us briefly, nevertheless embrace the universal doctrine of the Church. I have prefaced these things so that students, being admonished, may join and compare all the sermons of John, and seek the entire doctrine.

But now we shall speak of one particle, which itself also embraces a great part of the Gospel, and censured many errors of the Pharisees: Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world. The particle: Behold, points out the person, and distinguishes this one pointed out from all other men, as if he were saying: Look upon this one, this alone is the Messiah and Savior. Lamb is a metaphor for a victim. This is the lamb, that is, the victim. For he takes the appellation of lamb from the ceremonies of the fathers, and the Levitical ones, in which the slaughter of a lamb had been used to signify this victim, namely the Messiah: for because God had instituted certain slaughters, and wished them to be called offerings for sins, the fathers understood that another victim remained, whose true obedience was to undergo our punishments, and to appease the wrath of God. Nor should it be thought that the name of victim signifies a light thing; nothing sadder can be said. For it signifies a thing upon which God exerts, or pours out, his wrath, with which he burns against sin. It is, therefore, a thing guilty of the wrath of God, and destined for death, or destruction, because of the wrath of God against sin. Thus, in Paul, Christ is called sin, or a curse. In the same way, Isaiah also speaks in chapter 53: Because he will set his soul as sin, that is, a sacrifice for sin, he will see long-lived seed.

There is, therefore, in the appellation of lamb not only a metaphor of innocence and patience, as the unlearned think, but another, signifying a most great and secret thing, namely the metaphor of a victim, sustaining the true, huge, and ineffable wrath of God, with which he is averse to sin in human nature, and destined for destruction. The human mind's stupor cannot attain to the magnitude of this wrath by thinking. But let us conclude that God is seriously angry, since he is a mind acting most freely, and truly averse to sin. Wherefore he horribly declares his judgment, and indignation against sin, in the infinite punishments of the devil and the human race. Thus far I have spoken briefly concerning the appellation of lamb, or victim.

He names, however, the Lamb of God. This description is also added with a singular purpose. The other lambs slaughtered by the fathers or priests, although they were types, nevertheless were not consecrated and anointed by God so that they might become victims, nor were they peculiarly given to us for this purpose, so that they might become sacrifices. Finally, they neither felt, nor did they appease the wrath of God, nor could they take away sin and death. They were therefore the lambs of those sacrificing, that is, chosen by them for the sake of type and image, so that others might be admonished, not so that God might be appeased by this slaughter: But the Messiah alone is the lamb of God, that is, appointed by the ineffable counsel of God, so that he might become a victim, and for this purpose consecrated and anointed, sent, and given to us, for this very thing, he felt the wrath of God, and he alone is the appeaser, and obtains that sin and death be taken away, and that righteousness and eternal life be restored to us. This comparison indicates that there were grave and great reasons why John spoke thus, and thought that this lamb, appointed by God, consecrated, anointed, feeling the wrath of God, and the appeaser, should be distinguished from the other victims, which, although they were types, yet were not properly appointed, consecrated, or anointed by God for this office, nor had they felt the wrath of God, nor had they appeased it.

Similar is the saying of Isaiah, which John seems to have expressed. For Isaiah says expressly: The Lord willed to crush him. Likewise: We saw him struck by God. Likewise: The Lord laid upon him the iniquities of us all, that is, God appointed this victim, and declared the magnitude of his wrath against sin, because no other victim could appease it except the death of the son, and upon him he poured out his wrath against sin. He alone truly knows how great a thing sin is, and has perceived the magnitude of the divine wrath. He is therefore the victim of God, that is, feeling the wrath of God and appeasing God. These things must be diligently pondered by the pious; the magnitude of these things cannot be explained in words. There is in the very words of Isaiah in his own language a singular emphasis, but I proceed to the rest.

Latin:

Ecce agnus Dei.

Diligenter conferamus omnes conciones Ioan- nis. Nam et doctrinam poenitentiae proponit, severissime arguens peccata, comtemtum Dei, hy- pocrisin, et alia vitia, et clare proponens aeter- nas poenas omnibus qui contemnunt iram Dei, et non credunt in Messiam. Deinde addit Evan- gelium de officio Messiae, quem ait victimam esse pro peccato, ut haec verba docent: Ecce agnus Dei qui tollit peccata mundi. Praedicat et remis- sionem peccatorum, et iusticiam fidei claris ver- bis cap. 3.: Qui credit in filium, habet vitam aeter- nam, qui autem non credit filio, ira Dei manet super eum. Hae conciones valde novae erant Pharisaeis, qui Messiam expectabant, non cru- cifigendum, sed occupaturum imperia mundi; partiturum provincias. Nec iusticiam fidei no- rant, sed somniabant se lege iustos. Cum igitur tantae essent in Ecclesia tenebrae, Deus lucem verae doctrinae rursus accendit per Ioannem. Fuit igitur excellens vocatio, et vere maior pro- phetia, quia missus est Ioannes ad ingentes erro- res, qui in Ecclesia grassabantur, corrigendos.

Dixi eum tradidisse doctrinam de poeniten- tia, de aeternis poenis impiorum, de officio Mes- siae, de remissione peccatorum, de iusticia fidei, et vita aeterna. Monstrat etiam ipsum Messiam natum, et iam versantem inter homines, ut Ec- clesia sciret exhibitas esse promissiones, vocavit gentes ad societatem Evangelii et beneficiorum Messiae. Postremo etiam tradidit bonorum ope- rum doctrinam, et erudiit singulos ordines homi- num, milites, iudices, coniuges, et monstravit vera bona opera omissis ceremoniis hypocriticis, et tandem morte testatus est, se haec vere profiteri propter Deum, et expectare a Deo testimonium in vita aeterna. Haec recensui, ut cogitemus vo- cationem Ioannis ingens Dei beneficium fuisse, et videamus complexum esse totam doctrinam Eccle- siae. Addendum est et hoc, nullam tam claram revelationem traditam esse de tribus personis di- vinitatis, quanta haec est, quae describitur in baptismo Christi, ubi videt Ioannes aperiri coe- lum, audit vocem aeterni patris de filio, qui co- ram astabat, videt Spiritum sanctum descendere. Tantum igitur doctorem et testem audiamus, et eius conciones acerrimo studio meditemur, quae etsi breviter nobis sunt traditae, tamen univer- sam Ecclesiae doctrinam complectuntur. Haec praefatus sum, ut studiosi admoniti coniungant, et conferant omnes Ioannis conciones, et inte- gram doctrinam quaerant.

Nunc vero de una particula dicemus, quae et ipsa magnam partem Evangelii complectitur, et taxavit multos Pharisaeorum errores: Ecce agnus Dei, qui tollit peccata mundi. Particula: Ecce, monstrat personam, et discernit hunc monstratum ab omnibus aliis hominibus, quasi dicat: Hunc in- tuemini, hic solus est Messias et Salvator. Agnus metaphora est victimae. Hic est agnus, id est, victima. Sumit enim appellationem agni ex cere- moniis patrum, et Leviticis, in quibus fuerat usur- pata mactatio agni, ad significandam hanc victi- mam, scilicet Messiam: quia enim Deus insti- tuerat certas mactationes, et volebat vocari obla- tiones pro peccatis, intelligebant patres restare aliam victimam, cuius vera obedientia esset subi- tura nostras poenas, et placatura iram Dei. Nec existimetur nomen victimae rem levem significare, nihil tristius dici potest. Significat enim rem, in quam Deus exerit, seu effundit iram suam, qua ardet adversus peccatum. Est ergo res rea irae Dei, et destinata morti, seu exitio, propter iram Dei adversus peccatum. Sic apud Paulum Chri- stus dicitur peccatum, seu maledictum. Eodem modo et Esaias loquitur cap. 53.: Quia ponet ani- mam suam peccatum, id est, hostiam pro peccato, videbit semen longaevum.

Est ergo in appellatione agni non tantum in- nocentiae et patientiae metaphora, ut indocti pu- tant, sed alia, rem maximam et arcanam signifi- cans, videlicet metaphora victimae, sustinentis veram, ingentem et ineffabilem iram Dei, qua aversatur peccatum in natura humana, et desti- nata ad exitium. Huius irae magnitudinem hu- mani animi stupor non potest assequi cogitando. Sed serio irasci Deum statuamus, cum sit mens liberrime agens, et vere aversans peccatum. Qua- re horribiliter declarat suum iudicium, et indigna- tionem adversus peccatum, in poenis diaboli, et humani generis infinitis. Hactenus de appella- tione agni, seu victimae, breviter dixi.

Nominat autem agnum Dei. Haec descriptio etiam singulari consilio addita est. Caeteri agni mactati a patribus aut sacerdotibus etsi erant typi, tamen non erant a Deo consecrati et uncti, ut fie- rent victimae, nec peculiariter ad hoc donati no- bis erant, ut fierent hostiae. Postremo nec sen- tiebant, nec placabant iram Dei, nec poterant tol- lere peccatum et mortem. Erant igitur agni sacri- ficantium, id est, ab ipsis electi, typi et imaginis causa, ut alii admonerentur, non ut hac macta- tione placaretur Deus: Sed solus Messias est Dei agnus, hoc est, inenarrabili Dei consilio consti- tutus, ut fieret victima, et ad hoc consecratus at- que unctus, missus, ac donatus nobis, ad hanc ipsam rem, sensit iram Dei, et solus est placator, ac impetrat deleri peccatum et mortem, ac restitui nobis iusticiam, et vitam aeternam. Haec collatio indicat graves et magnas causas fuisse, cur Ioan- nes sic locutus sit, et hunc agnum a Deo constitu- tum, consecratum, unctum, sentientem iram Dei, et placatorem discernendum putarit a caeteris vi- ctimis, quae etsi erant typi, tamen a Deo non erant proprie ad hoc munus constitutae, consecra- tae, aut unctae, nec senserant iram Dei, nec pla- caverant.

Simile est dictum Esaiae, quod videtur ex- pressisse Ioannes. Ait enim Esaias diserte: Do- minus voluit conterere eum. Item: Vidimus eum percussum a Deo. Item: Dominus posuit in eo iniquitates omnium nostrum, id est, Deus hanc victimam constituit, et declarauit irae suae magni- tudinem adversus peccatum, quod alia nulla victi- ma placari potuit nisi morte filii, et in hunc effu- dit iram adversus peccatum. Hic solus revera scit, quanta res sit peccatum, et irae divinae magnitu- dinem perspexit. Est ergo victima Dei, id est, sentiens iram Dei et placans Deum. Haec a piis diligenter cogitanda sunt, magnitudo harum re- rum verbis explicari non potest. Est in ipsis ver- bis Esaiae in sua lingua singularis emphasis, sed pergo ad caetera.

## 1:29
Who takes away the sin of the world.

In Isaiah there are two verbs: to take away and to bear, which John has undoubtedly expressed: Truly he himself bore our infirmities, and he himself carried our sins. Likewise: He himself carried their iniquities, and again: He bore the sins of many. And there is no doubt that by the other verb is signified the carrying, as we bear a burden imposed upon us. Thus says Isaiah, that the Messiah sustains and endures the punishments which the human race ought to have borne for sin. By the other verb both are signified, to lift up and to take away, and there is no doubt that in Greek the verb which he uses here signifies both, to take up to be carried and to take away. Let us also embrace both. For although by the title of victim, the carrying is already previously included, yet the exposition is more ready: He takes away sin, that is, he sustains the punishment of sin for the whole world. For although not all receive the benefit of Christ, yet for all he was made a sufficient victim, as is said elsewhere: He is the propitiation for our sins, and not indeed for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world. Then because the end of the immolation is appeasement and liberation, it embraces also the other meaning. He takes away the sins of the world, that is, he removes them. Thus he also speaks below in the epistle: He appeared, that he might take away our sins, that is, remove them. He says, however, expressly, sin in the singular number. By a Hebrew phrase, for universal damnation. He takes away sin, that is, universal damnation, namely the disobedience of the human race, the guilt of the wrath of God, death, and eternal punishments. This whole damnation he says is blotted out by the Messiah.

I have explained as best I could the words of this sermon. Now it is necessary to compare this victim to the types. If this lamb alone abolishes sins, what then were the victims worth, concerning which the law had commanded? By these slaughters the Pharisees thought they were earning the remission of sins, and becoming heirs of eternal life. This error John also taxes here, when he testifies that sin is not taken away, except through this lamb. It could not therefore be taken away through the other victims, and Isaiah had previously rebuked the same error saying: Because he will lay down his soul as a sacrifice for sin, he will see long-lived seed, that is, the death of this one alone will truly appease the wrath of God, and he, having been resurrected, will restore to us eternal life. Wherefore both the sermons of Isaiah and the Baptist testify that in the New Testament those Levitical slaughters were to cease, the true victim having been exhibited.

But here also the doctrine concerning faith must be held, how the application of the sacrifice of Christ is made, namely by faith. Concerning this application the Baptist preaches below in chapter 3: He who believes in the son has eternal life; he who does not believe the son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him. Faith, however, is the trust by which we determine that God is appeased toward us on account of Christ, as is said in Romans 5: Through whom we have access by faith into this grace. This trust does not rely on our dignity, or our virtues, but on the mediator himself, the son of God. This doctrine concerning application through faith, it is necessary to include here, because the adversaries, although they admit this saying: this is the lamb etc., yet afterwards they bury the son of God, and say that it must be doubted whether we are in grace, or they say, that a man is righteous on account of his own virtues: but more will be said below concerning the same matter.

Latin:

Qui tollit peccatum mundi.

Apud Esaiam duo verba sunt: tollere et ge- stare, quae haud dubie expressit Ioannes: Vere languores nostros ipse tulit, et peccata nostra ipse portavit. Item: Iniquitates eorum ipse portavit, et rursus: Peccata multorum tulit. Nec dubium est altero verbo significari gestationem, ut onus nobis impositum gerimus. Ita inquit Esaias, Mes- siam sustinere et perferre poenas, quas pro pec- cato genus humanum ferre debebat. Altero verbo utrunque significatur, levare et auferre, nec du- bium est Graecis id verbum, quo hic utitur utrun- que significare, suscipere gestandum et auferre. Complectamur et nos utrunque. Nam etsi appel- latione victimae, iam antea comprehensa est gesta- tio, tamen expeditior est expositio: Tollit pecca- tum, id est, sustinet poenam peccati pro toto mundo. Etsi enim non omnes accipiunt benefi- cium Christi, tamen pro omnibus facta est victima sufficiens, ut alias dicitur: Ipse est propiciatio pro peccatis nostris, nec vero pro nostris tantum, sed etiam pro peccatis totius mundi. Deinde quia finis immolationis est placatio et liberatio, complectitur et alteram significationem. Tollit peccata mundi, id est, aufert. Sic et infra loquitur in epistola: Ille apparuit, ut peccata nostra tollat, id est, au- ferat. Dicit autem diserte, peccatum singulari numero. Ebraica phrasi, pro universa damna- tione. Tollit peccatum, id est, universam damna- tionem, videlicet inobedientiam generis humani, reatum irae Dei, mortem, et aeternas poenas. Hanc totam damnationem ait deleri a Messia.

Enarravi utcunque verba huius concionis. Iam necesse est conferri victimam hanc ad typos. Si hic solus agnus abolet peccata, quid igitur va- lebant victimae, de quibus lex praeceperat? His mactationibus Pharisaei putabant se mereri remis- sionem peccatorum, et fieri haeredes vitae aeter- nae. Hunc errorem et hic Ioannes taxat, cum te- statur peccatum non auferri, nisi per hunc agnum. Non igitur poterat auferri, per victimas caeteras, et reprehenderat eundem errorem antea Esaias in- quiens: Quia ponet animam suam hostiam pro peccato, videbit semen longaevum, id est, huius unius mors vere placabit iram Dei, et hic resusci- tatus, restituet nobis vitam aeternam. Quare et Esaiae et Baptistae conciones testantur, in novo testamento illas mactationes Leviticas cessuras esse, exhibita vera victima.

Sed hic etiam doctrina de fide tenenda est, quomodo fiat applicatio sacrificii Christi, scilicet fide. De hac applicatione infra Baptista conciona- tur cap. 3.: Qui credit in filium, habet vitam aeternam; qui non credit filio, non videbit vitam, sed manet ira Dei super eum. Est autem fides, fiducia, qua statuimus Deum nobis placatum esse propter Christum, ut dicitur Rom. 5.: Per quem accessum habemus fide in hanc gratiam. Haec fiducia non nititur nostra dignitate, seu nostris virtutibus, sed ipso mediatore filio Dei. Hanc doctrinam de applicatione per fidem, necesse est hic complecti, quia adversarii, etsi hoc dictum ad- mittunt: hic est agnus etc., tamen postea sepeliunt filium Dei, et dicunt, dubitandum esse, an simus in gratia, aut dicunt, hominem iustum esse pro- pter proprias virtutes: sed infra de eadem materia rursus dicetur.

## 1:30
This is he, of whom I said: After me comes a man, who is before me.

He repeats the testimony by which he points out the Messiah, because, as was said above, this is his calling, that he should initiate the preaching of the New Testament and baptism, point out the Messiah himself, and tax the errors of the Church of his time, as it was called. But we have declared these words above: This is the man who was to come after me, he speaks of the office; because the Messiah finished his course after the Baptist, for which he was sent, he preached, and was made a victim, and was resurrected. He is before me, that is, more excellent in glory and calling; because the calling of the Messiah is far superior to the calling of John: the Messiah is the price for the human race, and the savior, the Baptist is a minister of the voice of the Gospel, like the Apostles and other faithful ministers.

Latin:

Hic est, de quo ego dixi: Post me venit vir, qui ante me est.

Repetit testimonium, quo monstrat Messiam, quia ut supra dictum est, haec est eius vocatio, ut incoët novi testamenti praedicationem, et baptis- mum, monstret ipsum Messiam, et taxet errores Ecclesiae eius temporis, ut vocabatur. Supra au- tem declaravimus haec verba: Hic est vir post me venturus, de officio loquitur; quia Messias post Baptistam absolvit suum cursum, ad quem missus erat, concionatus est, et factus victima, et resusci- tatus. Ante me est, id est, praestantior gloria et vocatione; quia vocatio Messiae longe superior est vocatione Ioannis: Messias est pretium pro genere humano, et salvator, Baptista est minister vocis Evangelii, ut Apostoli et caeteri fideles mi- nistri.

## 1:30
Because he was before me.

The reason is added why he excels in calling, because he is the first, for whose sake God chose the Church, he also preceded in time and was present to the fathers, Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, and the other saints.

And I did not know him.

There is a dispute about this particle, how these things agree. Before baptism John knew the Messiah, when he said: I need to be baptized by you. But here he says that he only then recognized him when he saw the Holy Spirit descending from heaven upon him. That revelation was made soon after baptism. This criticism of the history is odious, and has no utility. But it can be answered very briefly, which is undoubtedly true, that the Baptist recognized the Messiah by some notable revelation of the Holy Spirit whenever he recognized him, even long before baptism, although he had not known him before, and he speaks of recognition not only of the body, but of the recognition by which he learned that he is the Son of God, having a divine and human nature, and that he was not to be a worldly king, but would redeem the Church by his death, and would reign in eternal life. These things were shown to John divinely, and confirmed by many testimonies, so that the Church might be confirmed by his voice and testimony, as is added soon in the text.

That he might be manifested to Israel, for this reason I came baptizing with water.

As if he were to say: My ministry was divinely instituted so that I might be a witness as to who the Messiah is, and what his kingdom is to be. God wills these things to be made known to the Church, he wills certain testimonies to exist, he wills the voice of his Gospel to be spread far and wide, he wills the Son to be recognized, so that many may be saved. These are the greatest things of all that can be thought of, the mission of the Son of God, his death and resurrection, the redemption of the human race: God does not will these such great things to happen secretly in the world without certain and illustrious testimonies, even though these admirable deeds and benefits of God are seen differently than the victories of Alexander or Julius. Let us therefore diligently consider the testimonies and sermons of the Baptist, to confirm our faith, and let us add the other testimonies which are recounted in the evangelical history, such as those of Mary, Joseph, Zechariah, Simeon, Elizabeth, Anna, and the Apostles; mention is made of all these for this very reason which is recounted here, namely, that the Messiah might be manifested in Israel, and be recognized in the whole Church.

And John testified, saying: I saw the Holy Spirit as a dove, etc.

The narrative is brief, but no other more illustrious revelation is described concerning the three persons of the divinity; John sees the eternal Father, and testifying concerning the Son, when he says: This is my beloved Son; he sees also the Son standing before him, having come out of the waters; he sees also the Holy Spirit, who embraces the Son in the form of a dove. Here, therefore, the persons are distinguished. If the Holy Spirit were only a created motion in souls, he would not appear in a singular form, outside the minds of men. This great revelation was not exhibited and described without the most serious reasons. We are more moved by the promulgation of the law, when on Mount Sinai the voice of God sounded amidst thunders and lightnings, issuing the Decalogue, and the whole multitude was a spectator of the flames on the mountain, and heard the sounding voice on the great mountain with dread. These things strike the eyes, these signs we perceive to have been exhibited, so that we might have certain testimonies concerning God and concerning the law, and we judge that wrath is denounced to all who despise the law of God. Let us conclude the same also concerning the revelation made to John. Although the pomp of the spectacle is not similar, because the glory of the Gospel is different from that of the law, nevertheless let us know that these revelations pertain to the whole Church. First, it teaches us not obscurely about the three persons. Second, it indicates benefits, and shows true worship; the Father sends the Son, and commands him to be heard, and testifies that he is loved by him, and is the giver of the Holy Spirit, through whom a new and eternal righteousness will come to pass in those who hear the Son. Third, true worship is to acknowledge him to be truly the eternal God, the creator and preserver of all things, and one who wills to take away sin and death, and to grant us eternal life, who is the father of this Messiah standing here before the Baptist, and to call upon God with this faith, that on account of this Messiah, who has been made the lamb of God or victim, he may remit our sins, and is about to give eternal life, and that this Messiah truly sanctifies us with his Holy Spirit, who has embraced him here, so that we may know that we all receive from his fullness, as was said above.

These things, as often as we call upon him, must be thought about regarding the three persons, for two reasons: that we may distinguish our invocation from the invocation of the Jews and Turks, who even if they say they call upon God, nevertheless reject the Son, and do not call upon this God who is the father of Jesus Christ crucified for us and raised again. Then, that faith may exist in the invocation, that God truly wills to hear and receive us on account of the Son, and that he truly wills to rule and sanctify those who call upon him with the Holy Spirit. Let us therefore contemplate in our minds, when we say prayers, this very history of the baptism of Christ, and let us think about this God, who revealed himself with this voice crying out about the Son: This is my beloved Son, hear him; and let us call upon this father of this Jesus Christ, the creator of all things, and let us believe that he is propitious to us on account of the Son, and let us ask that he may sanctify us with his Holy Spirit.

Those who in this way confirm their faith from the testimony of the Baptist, and look to this in their invocation, they will understand that it has been exhibited for a great cause of the Church. As the voice of the law is a testimony about God, and about the wrath of God against sin: so this revelation is a testimony about God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and about mercy and salvation.

Latin:

Quia prior me erat.

Additur ratio, cur antecellat vocatione, quia primus est, propter quem elegit Deus Ecclesiam, tempore etiam antecessit et adfuit patribus, Adae, Noae, Abrahae, Mosi, et caeteris sanctis.

Et ego non noram eum.

De hac particula disputatur, quomodo haec conveniant. Ante baptismum norat Ioannes Mes- siam, cum diceret: Mihi opus est, ut abs te bapti- zer. Hic vero ait, se tunc demum agnovisse eum, cum vidit de coelo Spiritum sanctum descenden- tem super eum. Ea revelatio facta est mox post baptismum. Haec reprehensio historiae odiosa est, et nihil habet utilitatis. Sed potest brevissi- me responderi, quod haud dubie verum est, Bapti- stam aliqua insigni revelatione Spiritus sancti agnovisse Messiam quandocunque agnovit, etiam multo ante baptismum, cum antea non novisset, et loquitur de agnitione non tantum corporis, sed de agnitione, qua didicit esse filium Dei, haben- tem divinam naturam et humanam, et non mun- danum regem futurum esse, sed sua morte redem- turum esse Ecclesiam, et regnaturum in vita aeterna. Haec Ioanni divinitus monstrata sunt, et pluribus testimoniis confirmata, ut eius voce ac testimonio Ecclesia confirmaretur, sicut mox in textu additur.

Ut manifestetur Israëli, ideo veni ego bapti- zans aqua.

Quasi dicat: Meum ministerium divinitus in- stitutum est, ut sim testis, quis sit Messias, et quale sit futurum eius regnum. Haec Deus vult patefieri Ecclesiae, vult extare certa testimonia, vult late spargi vocem Evangelii sui, vult agnosci filium, ut multi salventur. Maximae res sunt omnium, quae cogitari possunt, missio filii Dei, mors et resurrectio eius, redemtio generis huma- ni: has tantas res Deus non vult clam in mundo sine certis et illustribus testimoniis fieri, tametsi aliter haec admiranda Dei facta et beneficia con- spiciuntur, quam Alexandri aut Iulii victoriae. Nos igitur Baptistae testimonia et conciones dili- genter consideremus, ad fidem nostram confir- mandam, et adiungamus caetera testimonia, quae in evangelica historia recitantur, ut Mariae, Io- seph, Zachariae, Simeonis, Elizabeth, Annae et Apostolorum, horum omnium mentio fit, pro- pter hanc ipsam causam, quae hic recensetur, vi- delicet, ut manifestetur Messias in Israël, et agnoscatur in tota Ecclesia.

Et testatus est Ioannes, dicens: Vidi Spiri- tum sanctum tanquam columbam, etc.

Brevis est narratio, sed non alia revelatio illustrior describitur de tribus personis divinita- tis, Ioannes videt aeternum patrem, et testifican- tem de filio, cum ait: Hic est filius meus dilectus, videt et filium coram astantem, egressum ex aquis, videt et Spiritum sanctum, qui amplectitur filium specie columbae. Hic ergo discernuntur perso- nae. Si Spiritus sanctus esset tantum motio crea- ta in animis, non appareret singulari specie, extra mentes hominum. Haec tanta revelatio non siue gravissimis causis exhibita, et descripta est. Ma- gis movemur promulgatione legis, cum in monte Sina inter tonitrua et fulgura sonuit vox Dei, edens Decalogum, et universa multitudo fuit spe- ctatrix flammarum in monte, et sonantem vocem in monte magno cum pavore audivit. Haec in- currunt in oculos, haec signa sentimus exhibita esse, ut de Deo, et de lege certa testimonia ha- beremus, et iudicamus omnibus denunciari iram contemnentibus legem Dei. Sic statuamus etiam de revelatione facta Ioanni. Etsi spectaculi pom- pa non est similis, quia Evangelii gloria alia est, quam legis, tamen ad totam Ecclesiam has revela- tiones pertinere sciamus. Primum docet nos non obscure de tribus personis. Secundo indicat beneficia, et veros cultus monstrat, Pater mittit Filium, et iubet hunc audiri, testaturque hunc a se diligi, et datorem esse Spiritus sancti, per quem nova et aeterna iusticia in his, qui filium audiunt, fiet. Tertio, cultus verus est agnoscere hunc vere esse Deum aeternum, rerum omnium conditorem et conservatorem, ac volentem tollere peccatum et mortem, ac donare nobis vitam aeternam, qui est pater huius Messiae hic astantis coram Baptista, et invocare Deum hac fide, quod propter hunc Messiam, qui factus est agnus Dei seu victima, nobis remittat peccata, et sit daturus vitam aeternam, et quod hic Messias vere sanctificet nos Spiritu sancto suo, qui hic ipsum amplexus est, ut sciamus ex plenitudine eius omnes accipere, ut supra dictum est.
