Haec, quoties invocamus, de tribus personis cogitanda sunt, propter duas causas, ut discernamus nostram invocationem a Iudaeorum et Turcarum invocatione, qui etiamsi dicunt se invocare Deum, tamen reiiciunt filium, non invocant hunc Deum, qui est pater Iesu Christi crucifixi pro nobis, et resuscitati. Deinde ut in invocatione existat fides, quod Deus vere velit nos exaudire et recipere propter filium, et quod invocantes vere velit regere et sanctificare Spiritu sancto. Intueamur ergo animis, cum dicimus precationes, in hanc ipsam historiam baptismi Christi, et de hoc Deo cogitemus, qui se patefecit hac voce de filio clamitans: Hic est filius meus dilectus, hunc audite; et hunc patrem huius Iesu Christi conditorem omnium rerum invocemus, et credamus eum propicium nobis esse propter filium, et petamus, ut nos sanctificet Spiritu sancto suo.

Qui hoc modo confirmant suam fidem ex testimonio Baptistae, idque in invocatione intuentur, hi intelligent magna de causa Ecclesiae exhibitum esse. Ut legis vox est testimonium de Deo, et de ira Dei adversus peccatum: ita haec revelatio est testimonium de Deo patre, filio et Spiritu sancto, et de misericordia et de salvatione.

## 1:35
On the next day John was standing again.

This is a repetition of the previous sermon about the lamb, and witnesses are cited who heard this very sermon. This repetition and citation of witnesses confirm the Church, so that we may more certainly conclude that this Jesus born of Mary is the Messiah.

what the Holy Spirit wills to be believed and thought about concerning the lamb, that is, the victim, in these narratives, I have already reviewed in some way.

Latin:

Die crastino iterum stabat Ioannes.

Repetitio est superioris concionis de agno, et allegantur testes, qui hanc ipsam concionem audiverunt. Haec repetitio et allegatio testium confirmant Ecclesiam, ut certius statuamus, hunc Iesum natum ex Maria esse Messiam.

quae de agno, id est, victima credi et cogitari vult Spiritus sanctus in his narrationibus, supra utcunque recensui.

## 1:40
Andrew was of Simon.

The disciples also confirm the testimony, who afterwards accompanied Christ: Andrew, John, Simon, Philip, and Nathanael. These seek out the lodging to hear him teaching, then they openly say he is the Messiah. Andrew says: We have found the Messiah. Neither in the narratives nor in the deeds themselves is there that pomp which seems to befit the magnitude of the events. Such is the appearance of the true Church; the word sounds, the lamb of God is shown, the benefits of God are recounted, so that God may be called upon and celebrated. The true glory of these things is not seen in this life, but will be seen in eternal life. Let this narrative therefore admonish us that the Church does not consist in ranks of dignities, but is a gathering of those teaching and hearing the word of God, and testifying about Christ; the testimonies are confirmed by miracles; Christ recognized Simon and Nathanael, previously unknown, even though no one had indicated who they were.

To Simon he attributes the name Cephas, which the text itself interprets as a rock or stone: for that is what it signifies in Greek, πέτρος. And that was the vernacular of the Jews, Cephas. We read this reason for the appellation in Matthew 16, that the whole ministry of the Gospel is called a rock, which will be firm, immovable, and perpetual, and wherever the voice of the Gospel sounds, there will be the Church, which will be freed from sin and death, and will not remain in the bonds of sin and the tyranny of the devil. Therefore it is said: The gates of hell shall not prevail against it. Nor will the Turks utterly destroy the Gospel and the Church, and wherever the Gospel is, there it will be effective against the devil, and believers will be freed from sin and death, and will be heirs of eternal life. Wherefore, even if some members of the Church are slaughtered by Diocletian and other tyrants, and by the Turks, nevertheless they will revive and be glorified. Nor can the whole body of the Church be destroyed in this life. Let us take this doctrine from the word Peter or Cephas, which signifies a rock. This exposition is more useful to the pious than the dispute about the dignity and primacy of the Roman Pontiff, which they append here, since that primacy is manifestly prohibited in Matthew 20, and now is only a barbaric tyranny, full of idolatry and cruelty: but the dispute about the primacy must be treated elsewhere. Now I return to the text, in which the reader must also be warned of this, that some have most foolishly interpreted the word κηφᾶς as κεφαλῆ, that is, head, when it is an entirely different word, κηφᾶ, foreign to the Greek language, meaning a rock.

Latin:

Erat Andreas Simonis.

Confirmant testimonium et discipuli, qui postea comitati sunt Christum, Andreas, Ioannes, Simon, Philippus, et Nathanaël. Hi de diversorio quaerunt ut audiant docentem, deinde palam dicunt esse Messiam. Andreas inquit: Invenimus Messiam. Nec in narrationibus, nec in ipsis factis illa pompa est, quae magnitudini rerum convenire videtur. Talis est verae Ecclesiae species, sonat verbum, ostenditur agnus Dei, narrantur beneficia Dei, ut invocetur et celebretur Deus. Harum rerum vera gloria in hac vita non conspicitur, sed in vita aeterna conspicietur. Admoneat ergo nos haec narratio, Ecclesiam non in gradibus dignitatum consistere, sed esse coetum docentium et audientium verbum Dei, et testificantium de Christo, confirmantur testimonia et miraculis, Christus agnovit Simonem et Nathanaëlem antea ignotos, cum tamen nemo indicasset, qui essent.

Simoni attribuit nomen Cephae, quod ipse textus interpretatur rupem seu lapidem: id enim significat Graece πέτρος. Idque Iudaeorum vernacula erat Cepha. Hanc rationem appellationis legimus Matth. 16. vocari rupem, ipsum totum ministerium Evangelii, quod firmum, immotum ac perpetuum erit, et ubicunque vox Evangelii sonat, ibi erit Ecclesia, quae liberabitur a peccato et morte, nec manebit in vinculis peccati, et tyrannide diaboli. Ideo dicitur: Portae inferi non praevalebunt adversus eam. Nec Turcae delebunt funditus Evangelium et Ecclesiam, et ubicunque est Evangelium, ibi erit efficax adversus diabolum, et credentes liberabuntur a peccato et morte, et erunt haeredes vitae aeternae. Quare etiamsi aliqua membra Ecclesiae trucidantur a Diocletiano et aliis tyrannis, et a Turcis, tamen reviviscent, et glorificabuntur. Nec totum corpus Ecclesiae in hac vita deleri potest. Hanc doctrinam sumamus ex vocabulo Petri seu Cephae, quod rupem significat. Haec enarratio utilior est piis, quam disputatio de dignitate et primatu Romani Pontificis, quam hic assuunt, cum primatus ille manifeste prohibitus sit, Matth. 20., et nunc tantum sit barbarica tyrannis, idolatriae et saevitiae plena: sed disputatio de primatu alias tractanda est. Nunc ad textum redeo, in quo et hoc monendus est lector, quod insulsissime quidam interpretati sunt vocabulum κηφᾶς pro κεφαλῆ, id est, capite, cum prorsus alia vox sit, κηφᾶ, aliena a Graeca lingua, rupem significans.

## 1:43
On the next day Jesus wished to go out into Galilee.

This history which is narrated in the first chapter contains those things which happened immediately after the baptism of Christ, when he had already completed his 30th year toward the beginning of spring, at which time he began to teach, and a series of three years can be detected from this Evangelist. Christ therefore now begins his school, and calls his disciples, Andrew, John, Peter, Philip, and Nathanael. But Nathanael is also offended by the humble appearance of Christ. First, a question is raised about his homeland; it seemed absurd that the Messiah should come from the village of Nazareth, from Galilee, whom they knew was to come from a royal lineage. And they imagined that his parents would be grand and powerful, and that he himself, especially now as an adult, would have crowds of nobles attached to him, and that he would be in the government of the republic, just as they knew the advancements of the greatest men in Israel had been illustrious before, such as Samuel and David. Therefore Nathanael, doubting and offended by the absurdity regarding his homeland, says: Can anything good come from Nazareth? as if to say: Our prophecies do not bring the Messiah from Galilee. This example warns us again not to be offended by the humble appearance of the Church, but to inquire into the word of God and divine testimonies. Thus here Nathanael is confirmed by a miracle, when he understands that he was seen while absent, under the fig tree.

Latin:

Die crastino voluit Iesus egredi in Galilaeam.

Haec historia quae in primo capite narratur, continet ea quae acciderunt statim post baptismum Christi, cum iam complesse annum 30. sub initium veris, quo tempore docere coepit, ac trium annorum series ex hoc Evangelista deprehendi potest. Incoat igitur iam Christus suam scholam, et vocat discipulos, Andream, Ioannem, Petrum, Philippum et Nathanaëlem. Offenditur autem et Nathanaël humili specie Christi. Primum movetur quaestio de patria, videbatur absurdum ex pago Nazareth, ex Galilaea venire Messiam, quem sciebant ex regio genere venturum esse. Et imaginabantur parentes fore amplos et potentes, et ipsum praesertim iam adultum, habiturum esse catervas procerum adiunctas, futurum in gubernatione reipub. ut norant antea summorum virorum incrementa in Israël illustria fuisse, ut Samuelis, Davidis. Ergo Nathanaël dubitans et offensus absurditate de patria, inquit: Num ex Nazareth aliquid boni orietur? quasi dicat: Nostra vaticinia non adducunt Messiam ex Galilaea. Hoc exemplum rursus admonet, ne offendamur humili specie Ecclesiae, sed inquiramus verbum Dei, et testimonia divina. Ita hic confirmatur Nathanaël miraculo, cum intelligit se absentem conspectum esse a Christo, sub fico.

## 1:51
Hereafter you shall see heaven opened.

This is a sweet description of the Messiah and the Church taken from Genesis chapter 28, concerning the ladder of Jacob. The ladder is Christ himself, touching heaven with its top, as is said in Genesis: because the divine nature is in him. Therefore it is clearly said in Genesis that God was leaning upon the ladder. But it stands on the earth, because the λόγος assumed human nature, subject to sorrows and death. But this ladder nevertheless joins heaven and earth, that is, God and the Church. And that heaven is said to be opened signifies that God is now propitious and looks upon those who call upon him, and saves.

But that angels ascend and descend on this ladder signifies that Christ himself bears

the Church, and leads it to the eternal Father. First he himself bears the punishments of our sins, and appeases the Father. Then, when he has appeased him, he also brings us. Just as it is said in Romans 5: Through him we have access into this grace. But he himself also says: I am the way, the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me. Thus, therefore, we approach God standing on this ladder, namely in Christ, that is, by faith, which is truly establishing that on account of him the eternal Father wishes to be propitious to us, to hear us, to give us eternal life: by this faith we receive the remission of sins on account of this mediator and high priest, by this faith the invocation that is made is heard, by this faith we obtain eternal life.

But that he names the Angels signifies the whole Church, and especially the teachers, and these first ascend, afterwards descend; that also seems wonderful. But by this let it be understood that they first ascend, because we must each first seek reconciliation with God, and receive gifts from him on account of the Son. Afterwards, however, they descend, and impart these gifts to others, doctrine, government, and ministries according to their calling. And this is the sweetest image of the Church, which God himself proposed, the ladder of Jacob having been shown, and concerning which Christ here warns us that it must always be kept in sight. For he warns the pious about many great things, namely, that through this Messiah alone is there access to the eternal Father, not through human opinions, not through our merits. Likewise that this person is God and man. Likewise that we must first ascend, and receive reconciliation and gifts from God, and then they must be brought forth and exercised, so that God may be celebrated, and the benefits of the Son of God may become known. Just as Peter says, that we have been called to declare his mighty works, who called us into his marvelous light.

I have briefly explained the principal sayings of the first chapter, concerning which huge struggles have often arisen, but I follow and retain with the best faith the old, true, and perpetual opinion of the Catholic Church of Christ. It is useful, however, for the pious to be warned what controversies have existed concerning this passage, and how they are to be refuted, so that, ignorant of those contentions, we do not assent to light minds, by whose petulance old errors are renewed.

And the principal struggle is with Samosatenus, whose quibble seems most plausible in appearance to profane men. For it seems foreign to the common custom of speakers to call the λόγον a person. Therefore Samosatenus astutely contends that there is no need for this foreign interpretation, and that the common custom of speaking must be retained, and he wished the λόγον to be understood only as a thought, or deliberation, or purpose in the divine mind, which is not a person, or an existing ὑπόστασις, distinct from the Father. The Father, he says, deliberating from eternity, decreed that he would reveal himself, and for that reason was about to create the world, and men, and for the sins of men was about to send a victim. This decree, not a person, but only a purpose in the mind of the Father, he interpreted here as the λόγον. This imagination is plausible among the profane, and has been recently renewed by Servetus. Therefore, the pious are to be warned what the Church of Christ has always felt, and firm testimonies are to be collected.

Let us take, however, the first testimony from the text of John itself. That the λόγος does not signify a thought, which is the Father, nor a passing voice, is confirmed first by this saying: And the word was made flesh. It is certain, however, that the Father was not made flesh; the λόγος, therefore, is not a thought, which is the Father, nor can it be said thus of a passing voice, because if the voice passed, it is not joined with flesh: but the λόγος, of whom it is spoken here, remains joined with flesh, that is, with the assumed human nature, which is also confirmed by the text, because John, speaking of Christ, who has already appeared, says: He was in the world, and the world was made by him. It is established, however, that the world was not made by the human nature of Christ. There remains, therefore, in Christ another nature, namely the divine. Hence it is clear that the λόγον is not a passing voice, nor the Father, but a person to be distinguished from the Father.

To this argument let other sayings be added, which speak of Christ after he appeared, and yet describe two natures, as in Heb. 1: He has spoken to us by his son, whom he appointed heir of all things, by whom also he made the ages, who is the brightness of his glory, and the image of his substance, upholding all things by the word of his power. He clearly says that all things were made by the son, which, since it cannot be said of the human nature, it is necessary that another nature also remains in Christ.

In the same way it is written in Coloss. 1: And he is before all things, and all things consist by him. There remains, therefore, in Christ the divine nature, which is the λόγος.

John 17: Glorify me, Father, with the glory which I had with you before the world was. The λόγος was, therefore, a person with the Father before the creation of the world. For if it were a passing voice, what glory would he have had? Or if this person were not to be distinguished from the Father, how would he say that he had glory from the Father?

The opinion of the Church is confirmed also by other testimonies, which speak of omnipotence, which certainly belong to the divine nature. John 5: My Father works until now, and I work. Likewise: Whatever he does, the son does likewise. Here he openly testifies that he acts and creates equally with the Father. And John 10: I give eternal life, which is of an omnipotent nature.

I have recited testimonies from the very discourses of the Gospel, which refute Samosatenus quite clearly, and show that the λόγον must be understood as a person, and confirmed by these testimonies we believe this article, and we invoke the son of God: just as Psalm 71 says: Prayer shall be made for him always, daily they shall bless him. And since this article is necessary for the Church, it was not unknown to the first fathers. They too invoked God with confidence in the coming liberator, and recognized even then that they were helped by that Lord, and defended against the devil.

Therefore Jacob says: The God of my father, and the angel who delivered me from all evils, bless these boys. He undoubtedly understood this angel to be the son of God. For he delivers from sin and death. And in Daniel this Lord speaks: These testimonies must be considered, so that we may learn that the son of God has always been present with the Church, and will be present, and that we may invoke him with this confidence, just as in 1 Corinth. 10 it is said of the rock accompanying them. These histories also contain an illustrious argument that the λόγος is a person.

Although this article must be believed because of the word of God, yet it is also useful to know the sayings of the pious and approved writers, who were closest to the Apostles. It is established that the pious in the Church, who heard the Apostles themselves as interpreters of their doctrine, felt and taught thus. I will therefore add some ancient testimonies. When Samosatenus had moved this controversy, Gregory, Bishop of Neocaesarea, who was distinguished by his doctrine and miracles, was summoned to refute him. Basil also cites this Gregory as a weighty witness, and says that he received from his nurse the doctrine which she had heard from Gregory of Neocaesarea. Moreover, there exists a clear testimony of this Gregory concerning the three persons of the divinity in book 7 of the Ecclesiastical History: One God, the Father of the living Word, of the subsistent Wisdom. One Son, the image of the Father, the creating Word. One Holy Spirit, having substance from God, who appeared through the Son, through whom God is known above all things, the cause of sanctification. Servetus, with an impudent lie, attempted to deceive the unlearned when he said that Tertullian and Irenaeus say that the λόγος is not a person. But it is most manifest that an injury is being done to these praised writers.

Tertullian, in Against Praxeas, expressly raises this question: whether the λόγος is a subsistent nature, or, as we now say, a person. And he answers, affirming that it is a person, or ὑπόστασις, and he dwells for a long time on this matter, and finally says: Whatever, therefore, the substance of the Word was, that I call a person, and to it I claim the name of Son.

Irenaeus also openly affirms that the λόγος was a person before he assumed human nature. For thus he says in chapter 20 of book 3: Having shown manifestly that the λόγος, existing in the beginning with God, through whom all things were made, who also was always present to the human race. Him, in the last times, according to the preordained time, the Father sent, united to his own creation, having been made a passible man. These words of Irenaeus contain both a useful testimony and a doctrine pleasing to the pious, namely that the Son of God was present to the Church from the very beginning, and is its guardian and defender against the devil. Just as he was also an intercessor in the council of the eternal Father after the fall of Adam, so that the human race might not perish entirely through the severity of divine wrath against sin.

Thus far we have refuted Samosatenus; now we shall speak of Arius. He concedes that the λόγος is a person, but says that he is a creature, albeit by far the most excellent of all, created from nothing. And because it appears that some are less angry with Arius, the pious must be diligently warned what the principal state of the controversy was, so that we may with our whole heart execrate the error of Arius, and not seek specious excuses, as others say: Why is there a need to dispute about words, whether he was begotten or created? Indeed, it was a disagreement about the greatest matters, not a λογομαχία (war of words). For Arius contended that the Son is not of the essence of the Father. The Church adores the only-begotten Son of the eternal Father, and understands the Son to be a Son by nature, born of the essence or substance of the eternal Father, as we speak. This is what the symbol also intends when it calls him ὁμοούσιον.

Let us therefore recite the testimonies against Arius. John 1: And the Word was God; this was in the beginning with God; all things were made through him, and without him was made nothing that was made. Arius confesses that the λόγος is a person, and this passage affirms that he is God, and the name of God is properly taken from an intelligent, eternal, and omnipotent essence. And truly it is a wonderful thing, and a narrative to be revered, that the Word is God. For as was said above, λόγος is placed in the position of the subject, because of the nature of the article, and then God is placed in the position of the predicate. Now if anyone attentively considers the majesty of this statement: And the Word was God, he cannot but be astonished, thinking that the name of God is understood here, not metaphorically, but properly, of an intelligent, eternal, and omnipotent essence. This description, therefore, was very new and admirable to the Jews, but the following narrative confirms this interpretation: All things were made through him, and without him was made nothing that was made. This description fits no one except the creating divine essence. Now if the Son is properly God and Creator, it is necessary that he be of the essence of the Father. The other sentences which testify that all things were created and are preserved through the Son effect the same, for they attribute to him omnipotence, which belongs to the divine essence.

The statement in Hebrews 1 pertains to the same: Where the Son is called the radiance of his glory and the image of his substance, upholding all things by the word of his power. The Son would not be the image of the divine substance if he were of another substance; but, so that I may not be too long-winded, since Arius confesses that the λόγος is a person, he can be sufficiently convinced from the 1st chapter of John that he is God by nature. Wherefore it is necessary to believe that the Son is of the essence of the Father, and was not brought forth from nothing. That he is indeed omnipotent, many most clear testimonies bear witness, nor can omnipotence be attributed to any nature outside the divine. I have added these things briefly to the first chapter, so that we may testify that we disapprove of the ravings of Samosatenus, Arius, and the like, and that the reader may diligently consider what the perpetual sentiment of the true Church has been, which we also strive to retain faithfully. Many other ravings have been scattered against the doctrine concerning God handed down through the Prophets and Apostles, as the Manichaeans imagined two Gods, a good one and an evil one, or light and darkness, disagreeing, equally eternal, creating different things. These monstrous opinions can easily be refuted. Therefore I pass over them.

Latin:

Posthac videbitis coelum apertum.

Haec est dulcis descriptio Messiae et Ecclesiae sumta ex Genes. cap. 28. de scala Iacob. Scala est ipse Christus, cacumine tangens coelum, ut in Genesi dicitur: quia est in eo natura divina. Ideo in Genesi clare dicitur, Deus innixus fuisse scalae. Consistit autem in terra, quia λόγος assumsit humanam naturam, obnoxiam doloribus et morti. Sed haec scala tamen coniungit coelum et terram, id est, Deum et Ecclesiam. Quodque coelum dicitur esse apertum, significat iam Deum propicium esse et respicere invocantes ipsum, et salvare.

Quod vero in hac scala ascendunt et descendunt angeli, significat Christum ipsum gestare

Ecclesiam, et perducere ad aeternum patrem. Primum ipse gestat poenas peccatorum nostrorum, et placat patrem. Deinde cum placavit, etiam nos adducit. Sicut Rom. 5. dicitur: Per hunc habemus accessum in gratiam hanc. Sed et ipse inquit: Ego sum via, veritas et vita, nemo ve- nit ad patrem nisi per me. Sic igitur accedimus ad Deum stantes in hac scala, videlicet in Christo, scilicet fide, hoc est, vere statuentes, quod propter hunc aeternus pater nobis velit esse pro- picius, nos exaudire, nobis dare vitam aeter- nam: hac fide accipimus remissionem peccatorum propter hunc mediatorem et pontificem, hac fide facta invocatio exauditur, hac fide consequimur vitam aeternam.

Quod vero nominat Angelos, significat totam Ecclesiam, ac praecipue doctores, et hi primum ascendunt, postea descendunt, id quoque vide- tur mirandum. Sed eo intelligantur primum ascendere, quia singuli prius debemus quaerere reconciliationem cum Deo, et ab eo accipere dona propter filium. Postea vero descendere, et im- pertiri haec dona aliis, doctrinam, gubernatio- nem, et ministeria iuxta vocationem. Estque haec dulcissima imago Ecclesiae, quam Deus ipse proposuit, ostensa scala Iacob, et de qua Christus hic nos admonet semper in conspectu habenda. Nam de multis magnis rebus pios admonet, vide- licet, quod per solum hunc Messiam sit aditus ad aeternum patrem, non per opiniones humanas, non per merita nostra. Item quod haec persona sit Deus, et homo. Item quod ascendere nos pri- mum, et a Deo reconciliationem, et dona acci- pere oporteat, et deinde ea proferri et exerceri, ut Deus celebretur, et beneficia filii Dei inno- tescant. Sicut Petrus inquit, nos vocatos esse, ut enarremus virtutes eius, qui nos in admiran- dum lumen vocavit.

Exposui breviter praecipua dicta primi capi- tis, de quo saepe extiterunt ingentia certamina, sed sequor et retineo optima fide veterem, veram et perpetuam catholicae Ecclesiae Christi senten- tiam. Utile est autem moneri pios, quae de hoc loco extiterint controversiae, et quomodo sint re- futandae, ne ignari earum contentionum assen- tiamur levibus ingeniis, quorum petulantia vete- res errores renovantur.

Ac praecipua dimicatio est cum Samosateno, cuius cavillatio in speciem profanis hominibus maxime videtur concinna. Alienum enim vide- tur a communi loquentium consuetudine, dicere λόγον personam. Ideo astute contendit Samosa- tenus, nihil opus esse hac peregrina interpreta- tione, ac retinendam esse communem loquendi consuetudinem, et λόγον intelligi voluit tantum de cogitatione, seu deliberatione, seu proposito in mente divina, quod non sit persona, seu exi- stens ὑπόστασις, distincta a patre. Pater, inquit, ab aeterno deliberans decrevit, quod se patefactu- rus esset, eamque ob causam conditurus mundum, et homines, et pro hominum peccatis missurus victimam. Hoc decretum non personam, sed tan- tum propositum in mente patris, hic interpretatus est λόγον. Haec imaginatio plausibilis est apud profanos, et recens renovata est a Serveto. Sunt igitur monendi pii, quid semper Ecclesia Christi senserit, et firma testimonia colligenda.

Sumamus autem primum testimonium ex ipso textu Ioannis. Quod λόγος non significet co- gitationem, quae est pater, nec transeuntem vo- cem, primum ex hoc dicto confirmatur: Et ver- bum caro factum est. Certum est autem patrem non factum esse carnem, λόγος igitur non est co- gitatio, quae pater est, nec de voce transeunte sic dici potest, quia si transiit vox, non est coniuncta cum carne: at λόγος, de quo hic dicitur, manet coniunctus cum carne, id est, cum natura hu- mana assumta, quod etiam confirmatur ex textu, quia Ioannes de Christo, qui iam apparuit, lo- quens, ait: In mundo erat, et mundus per ipsum factus est. Constat autem mundum non per hu- manam naturam Christi factam esse. Manet igi- tur in Christo altera natura, scilicet divina. Hinc perspicuum est λόγον non esse vocem trans- euntem, nec patrem, sed personam discernen- dam a patre.

Ad hoc argumentum adiungantur caetera dicta, quae de Christo, postquam apparuit, lo- quuntur, et tamen duas naturas describunt, ut ad Ebr. 1.: Locutus est nobis per filium, quem posuit haeredem omnium, per quem et secula fe- cit, qui est fulgor gloriae, et imago substantiae eius, ferens omnia verbo potentiae suae. Clare dicit, per filium omnia facta esse, quod cum de natura humana dici non possit, necesse est, in Christo manere etiam alteram naturam.

Eodem modo scribitur ad Coloss. 1.: Et ipse est ante omnia, et omnia per ipsum consistunt. Manet igitur in Christo divina natura, quae est λόγος.

Ioann. 17.: Glorifica me pater ea gloria quam habui ante mundum apud te. Erat igitur λόγος persona apud patrem ante conditionem mundi. Nam si vox transiens esset, quam ha- buisset gloriam? aut si non discernenda esset haec persona a patre, quomodo diceret se habuisse gloriam a patre?

Confirmatur sententia Ecclesiae et caeteris testimoniis, quae loquuntur de omnipotentia, quae certe competunt naturae divinae. Ioann. 5.: Pa- ter meus adhuc operatur, et ego operor. Item: Quaecunque ille facit, filius similiter facit. Hic aperte testatur se pariter cum patre agere et creare. Et Ioann. 10.: Ego do vitam aeternam, quod est naturae omnipotentis.

Recitavi testimonia ex ipsis concionibus Evangelii, quae satis perspicue refutant Samosa- tenum, et ostendunt λόγον oportere intelligi per- sonam, et confirmati his testimoniis credimus hunc articulum, et filium Dei invocamus: sicut Psalm. 71. dicit: Orabitur coram eo semper, quo- tidie benedicent ei. Et cum hic articulus sit ne- cessarius Ecclesiae, non fuit ignotus primis patri- bus. Hi quoque invocabant Deum fiducia venturi liberatoris, et agnoscebant iam tum se iuvari ab illo domino, et propugnari contra diabolum.

Ideo Iacob ait: Deus patris mei, et angelus qui eruit me cunctis malis, benedicat pueris istis. Hunc angelum haud dubie intellexit filium Dei. Nam hic liberat a peccato et morte. Et apud Daniëlem loquitur hic dominus: Haec testimonia consideranda sunt, ut discamus filium Dei; Ec- clesiae semper affuisse, et adfuturum esse, et hac fiducia eum invocemus, sicut 1. Corinth. 10. dici- tur de comitante eos petra. Continent etiam hae historiae illustre argumentum, quod λόγος sit persona.

Etsi autem hic articulus credendus est pro- pter verbum Dei, tamen prodest etiam nosse dicta piorum, et probatorum scriptorum, qui proximi fuerunt Apostolis. Constat sic sensisse et docuisse pios in Ecclesia, qui audiverunt ipsos Apostolos interpretes suae doctrinae. Addam igitur vetera quaedam testimonia. Cum Samosatenus movisset hanc controversiam, accersitus est ad eum refu- tandum Gregorius Neocaesariensis Episcopus, qui doctrina et miraculis claruit. Hunc Gregorium et Basilius allegat, tanquam gravem testem, seque ait a sua nutrice accepisse doctrinam, quam illa a Gregoria Neocaesariensi audierat. Extat autem huius Gregorii testimonium perspicuum de tribus personis divinitatis lib. 7. Ecclesiasticae histo- riae: Unus Deus, Pater verbi viventis, sapientiae subsistentis. Unus Filius imago patris, verbum creans. Unus Spiritus sanctus ex Deo substan- tiam habens, qui per Filium apparuit, per quem Deus super omnia cognoscitur, sanctificationis causa. Servetus impudenti mendacio, fucum fa- cere indoctis conatus est, cum ait, Tertullianum et Irenaeum dicere λόγον non esse personam. Sed est manifestissimum iniuriam fieri his laudatis scriptoribus.

Tertullianus adversus Praxeam diserte movet hanc quaestionem, an λόγος sit natura subsistens, seu, ut nunc dicimus, persona. Et respondet, affirmans esse personam, seu ὑπόστασιν, et diu huic materiae immoratur, ac tandem ait: Quae- cunque ergo substantia sermonis fuit, illam dico personam, et illi nomen filii vendico.

Irenaeus etiam aperte affirmat λόγον fuisse personam, antequam assumsit naturam huma- nam. Sic enim ait cap. 20. lib. 3.: Ostenso ma- nifeste, quod in principio λόγος existens apud Deum, per quem omnia facta sunt, qui et semper aderat humano generi. Hunc novissimis tempo- ribus secundum praefinitum tempus a patre uni- tum suo plasmati, passibilem hominem factum, misit. Haec Irenaei verba et testimonium utile continent, et doctrinam piis gratam, quod vide- licet filius Dei inde usque ab initio adfuerit Ec- clesiae, sit eius custos et propugnator contra dia- bolum. Sicut etiam in concilio aeterni patris in- tercessor fuit post lapsum Adae, ne severitate irae divinae contra peccatum prorsus periret genus humanum.

Hactenus refutavimus Samosatenum, nunc de Ario dicemus. Is concedit λόγον esse perso- nam, sed ait creaturam esse, etsi longe omnium praestantissimam, ex nihilo conditam. Et quia apparet aliquos minus succensere Ario, diligenter monendi sunt pii, qui fuerit praecipuus status controversiae, ut toto pectore execremur errorem Arii, et non quaeramus fucosas excusationes, si- cut alii dicunt: Quorsum opus est disputare de vocabulis, genitus sit, an conditus. Imo rerum maximarum dissensio fuit, non λογομαχία. Nam Arius contendebat filium non esse de essentia pa- tris. Ecclesia adorat filium unigenitum aeterni patris, ac filium intelligit natura filium, natum de patris aeterni essentia, seu substantia, ut lo- quimur. Hoc vult et symbolum, cum vocat eum ὁμοούσιον.

Recitemus igitur testimonia contra Arium. Ioann. 1.: Et Deus erat verbum, hoc erat in principio apud Deum, omnia per ipsum facta sunt, et sine ipso factum est nihil, quod factum est. Fatetur Arius λόγον esse personam, et hic locus affirmat esse Deum, et nomen Dei proprie sumitur de essentia intelligente, aeterna, omni- potente. Ac profecto mira res est, et suspicienda narratio, verbum est Deus. Nam ut supra dictum est, λόγος subiecti loco ponitur, propter articuli naturam, deinde in loco praedicati ponitur Deus. Iam si quis attente consideret huius dicti maiesta- tem: Et verbum erat Deus, non poterit non ob- stupescere, cogitans hic intelligi nomen Dei, non metaphorice, sed proprie, de essentia intelligente, aeterna et omnipotente. Erat igitur haec de- scriptio valde nova, et admiranda Iudaeis, sed sequens narratio confirmat hanc interpretatio- nem: Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, et sine ipso factum est nihil, quod factum est. Haec descri- ptio nulli convenit, nisi essentiae divinae creanti. Iam si filius est proprie Deus, et creator, necesse est eum de essentia patris esse. Idem efficiunt cae- terae sententiae quae testantur per filium omnia condita esse et conservari, tribuunt enim ei omni- potentiam, quae est essentiae divinae.

Eodem pertinet dictum Ebr. 1.: Ubi filius dicitur fulgor gloriae, et imago substantiae eius, ferens omnia verbo potentiae suae. Non esset filius imago substantiae divinae, si alia esset sub- stantia, sed ne sim prolixior, cum fateatur Arius λόγον esse personam, satis convinci potest ex 1. capite Ioannis, quod sit natura Deus. Quare ne- cesse est sentire, quod filius sit de essentia patris, et non sit ex nihilo editus. Quod vero sit omni- potens, multa clarissima testimonia testantur, nec potest tribui omnipotentia naturae ulli extra divinam. Haec breviter adieci ad primum caput, ut testemur nos improbare deliria Samosateni, Arii, et similia, et lector diligenter consideret, quae fuerit perpetua verae Ecclesiae sententia, quam et nos fideliter retinere studemus. Multa alia deliria sparsa sunt contra doctrinam de Deo traditam, per Prophetas et Apostolos, ut Mani- chaei finxerunt duos Deos, bonum et malum, seu lumen et tenebras, dissentientes, pariter aeter- 'nos, diversa condentes. Hae portentosae opi- niones facile refutari possunt. Ideo eas prae- tereo.

## 2:1 Argument
Chapter II.

Luke says that Christ was baptized when he was 30 years old, and they relate that the day of January, which is called ἡ ἐπιφάνεια, is the day of the baptism. And that name is most justly attributed to that day, because the divinity showed itself in such a way that the distinct persons were seen by the Baptist, as has been said above. After the baptism, Christ withdrew into the desert, where he stayed for 40 days, afterwards he returned to the Baptist, from there on the third day he came into Galilee to the wedding, around the end of the month of February, shortly after the text recounts the Passover, which is the first after the baptism of Christ. I mention these things because the distinction of times is pleasant to the reader, and brings some light. And the beginnings of the ministry are to be admired; in the baptism an illustrious testimony was brought forth, by which Christ himself was both confirmed, and his authority commended to us by this voice: Hear him. This calling, this promotion, as they call it, this ordination is the public one of this teacher. He did not therefore creep in, he did not invade the ministry without a manifest calling, but he awaited the calling, so that we may remember that no government is to be invaded without a true calling, according to that in Hebrews 5: No one should take the honor to himself, but he should be called by God, as Aaron was. For government is not happy unless God helps, as the Baptist says: No one can take anything to himself, unless it has been given to him from above.

This doctrine must be diligently thought upon in great matters, lest by human confidence, without a calling, without legitimate causes, we move great things, as in Leviticus 10. The two eldest sons of Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, relying on the prerogative that they preceded the others in age, sacrificed without a calling, and in Numbers chapter 16, Korah, Dathan, and Abiram perish when they invade the priesthood without a calling. Thus, innumerable leaders have perished because they invaded empires without a calling, such as Antony and others. The order of history demanded that I say these things as briefly as possible about the calling, and since the topic is very broad, many things must be thought upon here by the reader.

After the calling, Christ is prepared by wondrous temptations, nor can that struggle be described in words, in which the Son of God is tempted to fail in his calling, to strive for glorious things outside of his calling, to invade the empires of the world, to establish idolatry. The struggle between Christ and the devil was not about small matters: and although we in this our infirmity do not understand what that contest was like, nevertheless, because of the sequence of the history, I will add something briefly about the temptations.

First, as often as it is spoken of these and other temptations of Christ, let us think at the beginning of the contest that was in Paradise. With what hostile spirit the devil is toward the human race, he declared there, and infinite examples of horrible impiety and the destruction of the greatest part of men declare it afterwards. How the devil also fights, he showed there; first he turned Eve away from the word of God to her own splendid thoughts: You shall not die. Likewise: You shall be as gods, etc. But when the devil had won in Paradise, and God, by a wonderful plan on account of the Son, had again taken pity on the human race and had received the first parents: here the war between the Church and the devil began, and the devil felt afterwards that he did not always win, so that, although he had driven Cain to crime, he could not drive Adam, Eve, Seth, Enoch, Noah, and the like to impiety and despair in the same way. And he saw many of their notable victories and divine liberations. Concerning this war, it was said immediately in Paradise: The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent, and the serpent shall bite his heel. A liberator was therefore promised, who would crush the head, that is, the power and kingdom of the devil; thus John says: For this the Son of God appeared, that he might destroy the works of the devil.

Wherefore, let us learn at the beginning that the name of the devil is not an empty scarecrow, but that the devil is truly the enemy of God and the human race, and that he rages horribly and destroys many. But that the Son of God has been given to the Church so that he may defend, help, and liberate us, with the devil repressed, and that we ought to repel the attacks of the devil by the confidence and invocation of the Son of God, and thus the raging enemy is to be overcome, just as Joseph overcame the devil when he avoided adultery. David overcame the devil when, driven into exile, he was not broken by despair. These struggles ought to be known to us in some way in the Church, and at the same time it ought to be understood by us that the presence of Christ is helping us, who is Emmanuel, and who has always been present to the Church in such struggles. Let these things be considered first in this history, that we are attacked atrociously, and that the enemy must be repressed by confidence in the Son of God, and that the Son of God himself was tempted may be, and he has conquered, so that he may show that he is affected by our dangers, and that he will be the victor.

And temptations themselves contain the chief dangers of the Church. The first is concerning bodily persecution, poverty, hunger, exiles, death. This first thing distresses the minds of all. If you wish to obey God, to embrace the Gospel, poverty must be endured, the hatreds of the powerful must be suffered, the cruelty of princes must be undergone; you will wander without a home, or you will be killed. Human nature fears these things by itself, and the devil presents opportunities, so that he may shake minds more vehemently with these thoughts. This is the sum of the words: If you are the Son of God, say that these stones may become bread, that is, if you are a care to God, from where will you live? From stones? And it is a sarcasm of the devil mocking Christ, as if to say: It is going excellently with you, if you think that you are serving God, that you are the sons of God, who, if he cared for you, would not allow tyrants to exercise cruelty upon you, would not allow you and your children to be killed by hunger, to be most cruelly put to death. Thus the devil attacks and shakes minds, presenting thoughts about providence, and bringing into doubt whether God is present with us, helps us, cares for us.

Christ receives these darts of the devil with an opposing shield, and teaches what kind of battle this is, and how this enemy is to be conquered, how one must judge concerning the will of God. Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God. From this response it can be noticed that this was especially the struggle, which I mentioned, concerning defense. Christ therefore answers, fortifying and confirming himself with the word of God. Hence he testifies that he learns the will of God, who has promised that he will be present to the Church. The Church will therefore live and will have sustenance and defense, even if we are destitute of human aid. For me, he says, it is enough to follow the word of God, the calling, the command, and the promise; I entrust the care of sustenance, of defense, and the outcome to God, and if I do these things, I shall live. For we live miraculously, with God sustaining us. As he says in Psalm 4: Know that God makes his holy one wonderful, that is, he rules and delivers him in wonderful ways.

The other temptations are more arcane, and we, occupied with gross desires, do not understand those arcane struggles of wisdom and glory. The second temptation is concerning wisdom and glory. The devil casts into Christ the thought of how God cares for him, whether it is so even that he will be present to one doing something without a calling, or serving a rash desire, not the utility of the Church or of one's neighbor. Cast yourself down, he says, because it is written: You will not strike your foot against a stone. By this temptation of wisdom the Church has been harshly shaken; teachers sit on the pinnacle of the temple, and because they have a magnificent persuasion of wisdom concerning themselves, they cast themselves down, that is, they show off their beautiful imaginations to the people, concocted without the word and without a calling, just as because the cavil about the Word, or λόγῳ, which he invented, pleases the Samosatene, he scatters it among the people, departing from the perpetual meaning of the text, John 1. Thus it seemed convenient to the pontiffs to establish laws concerning worship and celibacy. For that order of ceremonies and rank of persons is a specious thing. Therefore these were instituted without a calling and without the word. It pleases wise men in Israel to create a king, that they may have a certain leader and defender, after the manner of other nations. Thus, since men are naturally delighted by their own wisdom and seek plausible refinements in the word of God. Likewise, since we are all naturally φιλαρχικοὶ, and desire to order and constitute many things, we boldly undertake many things outside of a calling and without the word; this is to cast oneself down from the pinnacle of the temple.

Here again Christ opposes a most weighty saying: You shall not tempt the Lord your God. For to tempt God is properly to contend with God, in reliance on one's own wisdom, justice, or strength, and in this reliance to depart from the word of God and the calling or ordinance of God. Thus all heretics sin, thus the authors of new forms of worship sin, who, departing from the word of God, imagined that Monasticism was a distinguished thing, which would be of more value before God than the works of common life. Thus the people of Israel sinned by their own wisdom, demanding a king, when they ought to have known that in the people of God a form of polity was not to be constituted without a clear command of God, and that God wished that they should expect defense from him alone.

The third temptation is more horrible than the others; the devil impudently demands to be worshipped, and for this service promises the empires of the world. Nor is it to be thought that this was a light struggle. He cast before that excellent man how great an honor empire is, how much Christ himself excels all kings in genius and virtue. That such a man is worthy of a monarchy, that such a prince would be salutary to the world. What of the fact that the inheritance of the world was promised to the Messiah? These and many other things the devil cast before him. And although Christ conquered and repelled the devil, nevertheless this temptation devastated the Church in the end. Mahomet, the Pope, because of empires, devised idolatrous cults, and we see the power of the world conspiring to defend idolatry: just as once emperors protected ethnic idol-manias, so now Pontiffs and kings establish impious Masses, the cult of saints, and celibacy. Not that they feel these things should be approved, but only so that they may retain wealth, dignities, and pleasures. The devil, knowing this conspiracy of the powerful, promises Christ the empire of the world, not because he thought that, with God unwilling, he could transfer empires. For he knows that polities are of God, but because he notices that those who hold empires are for the most part impious, and he finds that they protect idols with huge fury, so that they may retain authority and wealth.

the Church as bride. Therefore, in many places the description of weddings in sacred histories rightly signifies the Church, as here the allegory is very fitting, but we will first run through the history. The principal points are the approval of weddings, the example of the hardships of marriage: the testimony of the presence of God helping in these domestic miseries. Concerning invocation, as here the mother intercedes with Christ, and he answers harshly, yet afterwards he helps. All these things contain useful doctrine.

Concerning the first point, the reader is to be briefly admonished, because since Christ is present and adorns the wedding with a miracle, he certainly approves of them. And to this must be added sentences from many other places, which testify that legitimate weddings please God, and refute the impious opinions of all fanatics who have condemned or prohibited legitimate marriage. Such were Marcion, the Manichaeans, the Encratites, and the Pontiffs, who still defend the law concerning celibacy, and the Monks, who pretend that celibacy is an excellent cult of God, and merits the remission of sins, and many other rewards. How these delusions are to be refuted is often said elsewhere: And here they are refuted by the sufficiently illustrious testimony of the presence of Christ, who shows that he favors weddings, since he is both present and adorns them with a miracle. And this one saying, when Christ says: 'What God has joined,' testifies clearly enough that weddings were instituted by God and please God. And indeed this passage embraces copious doctrine, when it warns that marriage is a divine conjunction, that is, a society instituted by God, which God not only approves, but also helps, rules, protects, and preserves in this life, and wishes for its own sake to be loved, magnified, and kept by a certain law.

Christ conquered these temptations, and he wished these things to be written, so that the Church, being admonished, might know that it is going to undergo similar temptations and similar struggles. There will therefore be some who will resist the devil, mindful of the victory of Christ, who will undergo the struggle by his example, and will seek help from him. For the Son of God came for this reason, that he might destroy the works of the devil. Thus all saints conquer the devil, but others, preferring power, wealth, dignity, and pleasures, obey the devil in worshiping and retaining idols. But Christ warns all men beforehand, repeating this voice: 'You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve.' Warned by this example of Christ and by this victory, let us know that in all temptations these two things are especially to be done. Let us look at the word of God, and seek counsel from there, and let us not suffer ourselves to be torn away from the word of God. Let us likewise seek help from the victorious Christ, and let us know that the Church is exercised by such struggles, and that the Son of God wishes to be present for those struggling. I have said these things briefly concerning temptations because of the sequence of the history.

The second point is the example of the hardships of marriage; a common burden is poverty, and yet it is not light, but many other harder things happen: diseases, unhappy births, the funerals of children, the faults or sad accidents of children. As the first parents looked with great grief upon the murder of their son Abel, but the crime of their other son, the parricide, brought them much greater and sharper grief. Human miseries are the punishments of sin, as is evident, and these press most heavily upon this part of the human race which lives in marriage. For this is the principal one. The others who flee matrimony do not flee the society itself, which is sweet in itself, but that mass of hardships which is added, and they seek leisure and

After the temptations, with the 40 days completed, Christ returned to the Baptist, and it is consistent that in the meantime they were together several times: and when in the middle of February he was returning to Galilee, after those wonderful exercises he began to teach, and to confirm his doctrine with public miracles, and first it is narrated here concerning the wine made at the wedding.

Latin:

Caput II.

Lucas ait Christum baptizatum esse, cum natus esset annos 30, ac narrant eam diem Ianua- rii, quae vocatur ἡ ἐπιφάνεια, diem esse bapti- smi. Idque nomen iustissime illi diei tribuitur, quod divinitas ita se ostendit, ut distinctae perso- nae conspicerentur a Baptista, ut supra dictum est. Post baptismum Christus secessit in deser- tum, ubi dies 40 commoratus, postea ad Bapti- stam rediit, inde tertio die venit in Galilaeam ad nuptias, circa finem mensis Februarii, brevi post recenset textus Pascha, quod primum est post baptismum Christi. Haec eo commemoro, quia temporum distinctio iucunda est lectori, et non- nihil lucis affert. Suntque initia ministerii ad- miranda, in baptismo editum est illustre testimo- nium, quo et confirmatus est ipse Christus, et commendata nobis eius autoritas hac voce: Hunc audite. Haec vocatio, haec promotio, ut vocant, haec ordinatio publica est huius doctoris. Non igitur obrepsit, non sine manifesta vocatione in- vasit in ministerium, sed vocationem expectavit, ut meminerimus gubernationem nullam invaden- dam esse sine vera vocatione, iuxta illud ad Ebr. 5.: Nemo sibi sumat honorem, sed vocetur a Deo, sicut Aaron. Nec enim felix est gubernatio, nisi Deo adiuvante, ut Baptista inquit: Nemo potest quicquam sibi sumere, nisi sit ei datum desuper.

Haec doctrina diligenter cogitanda est in magnis rebus, ne fiducia humana, sine voca- tione, sine legitimis causis, res magnas movea- mus, ut Levit. 10. Duo filii Aaron maximi natu, Nadab et Abihu, freti praerogativa, quod ante- cederent caeteros aetate, sacrificabant sine voca- tione, et in Num. cap. 16. Chore, Dathan et Abiram pereunt, cum invadunt sacerdotium sine vocatione. Sic innumerabiles duces perierunt, propterea quod imperia sine vocatione invaserunt, ut Antonius, et alii. Haec ut brevissime de vo- catione dicerem, ordo historiae postulabat, cum- que locus sit amplissimus, multa lectori hic co- gitanda sunt.

Post vocationem praeparatur Christus miran- dis tentationibus, nec verbis describi illa pugna potest, in qua filius Dei tentatur, ut deficiat a vo- catione, ut moliatur res gloriosas extra vocatio- nem, ut invadat mundi imperia, ut stabiliat ido- latriam. Non de parvis rebus dimicatio fuit inter Christum et diabolum: et quanquam nos in hac nostra infirmitate quale fuerit illud certamen non intelligimus, tamen propter seriem historiae ali- quid breviter de tentationibus adiiciam.

Primum quoties de his et aliis tentationibus Christi dicitur, initio cogitemus certamen quod fuit in Paradiso. Quam hostili animo sit diabo- lus erga genus humanum, ibi declaravit, et de- clarant postea infinita exempla horrendae impieta- tis, et exitii maximae partis hominum. Quomodo etiam praelietur diabolus, ibi ostendit, primum avertit Evam a verbo Dei, ad proprias et splen- didas cogitationes: Non moriemini. Item: Eritis sicut dii, etc. Cum autem vicisset diabolus in Paradiso, et rursus mirabili consilio propter filium misertus Deus generis humani, recepisset primos parentes: hic bellum inter Ecclesiam et diabolum esse coepit, ac sensit postea diabolus, se non semper vincere, ut, quanquam impulerat Cain ad scelus, tamen non sic impellere Adam, Evam, Seth, Enoch, Noë, et similes ad impietatem et desperationem potuit. Et vidit horum multas in- signes victorias, et liberationes divinas. De hoc bello statim in Paradiso dictum est: Semen mu- lieris conteret caput serpentis, et serpens morde- bit calcaneum eius. Promissus est ergo liberator, qui caput, id est, potentiam et regnum diaboli conterat, sic Ioannes inquit: Ad hoc apparuit filius Dei, ut destruat opera diaboli.

Quare principio discamus non esse inane terriculamentum nomen diaboli, sed vere esse hostem Dei, et generis humani diabolum, et hor- ribiliter grassari, et multos perdere. Ecclesiae vero datum esse filium Dei, ut nos defendat, ad- iuvet, liberet represso diabolo, nosque fiducia et invocatione filii Dei debere impetus diaboli depel- lere, et sic vinci grassantem hostem, ut Ioseph superavit diabolum, cum vitavit adulterium. Da- vid superavit diabolum, cum pulsus in exilium non fractus est desperatione. Haec certamina aliquo modo in Ecclesia nobis nota esse debent, et simul intelligi a nobis debet praesentia Christi adiuvantis nos, qui est Emanuel, et adfuit sem- per Ecclesiae in talibus certaminibus. Haec pri- mum in hac historia considerentur, quod oppu- gnemur atrociter, et quod fiducia filii Dei hostis reprimendus sit, et quod filius Dei ipse tentatus sit, et vicerit, ut ostendat se affici nostris periculis, et fore victorem.

Ac tentationes ipsae pericula Ecclesiae praecipua continent. Primum est de corporali persecutione, inopia, fame, exiliis, nece. Hoc primum angit omnium animos. Si voles Deo obedire, amplecti Evangelium, erit ferenda paupertas, patienda odia potentum, subeunda saevitia principum, miserere errabis sine domo, aut interficieris. Haec humana natura per sese formidat, et diabolus obiicit occasiones, ut his cogitationibus vehementius animos concutiat. Haec est summa verborum: Si filius Dei es, dic, ut hi lapides fiant panes, id est, si es Deo curae, unde victitabis? num ex lapidibus? Estque sarcasmus diaboli irridentis Christum, scilicet egregie vobiscum agitur, si putatis vos servire Deo, vos esse filios Dei, qui, si vos curaret, non concederet tyrannis in vos exercere saevitiam, non sineret vos, vestros liberos fame necari, crudelissime interfici. Ita diabolus oppugnat et concutit mentes, obiiciens cogitationes de providentia, et adducens in dubitationem, an Deus adsit nobis, iuvet, curet nos.

Haec diaboli tela Christus excipit opposito clypeo, ac docet, quale sit hoc genus pugnae, et quomodo vincendus sit hic hostis, quomodo de voluntate Dei iudicandum sit. Non solo pane vivit homo, sed omni verbo quod procedit ex ore Dei. Ex hac responsione animadverti potest, praecipue hanc fuisse dimicationem, quam dixi, de defensione. Respondet igitur Christus, se muniens et confirmans verbo Dei. Hinc testatur se discere voluntatem Dei, qui pollicitus est se adfuturum esse Ecclesiae. Vivet igitur Ecclesia et habebit victum, defensionem, etiamsi humana ope destituimur. Mihi, inquit, satis est sequi verbum Dei, vocationem, mandatum, et promissionem, curam victus, defensionis, eventum Deo commendo, et haec si fecero, vivam. Vivimus enim mirabiliter, Deo nos sustentante. Sicut inquit Psalm. 4.: Scitote quod Deus mirificat sanctum suum, id est, mirabilibus modis regit, ac liberat.

Caeterae tentationes sunt magis arcanae, et nos crassis cupiditatibus occupati non intelligimus illa arcana certamina sapientiae et gloriae. Secunda tentatio est de sapientia et de gloria. Offundit diabolus Christo cogitationem, quomodo Deo curae sit, num sic etiam, ut adfuturus sit facienti aliquid sine vocatione, aut servienti te- merariae cupiditati, non utilitati Ecclesiae, seu proximi. Deiicias te, inquit, quia scriptum est: Non offendes ad lapidem pedem tuum. Hac sa- pientiae tentatione duriter quassata est Ecclesia, sedent doctores in culmine templi, et quia persua- sionem sapientiae, de se magnificam habent, de- iiciunt se, id est, ostentant populo suas bellas imaginationes, sine verbo et sine vocatione con- fictas, ut quia Samosateno placet cavillatio de verbo, seu λόγῳ, quam finxit, spargit eam in populum, discedens a perpetua sententia textus, Ioan. 1. Sic commodum visum est pontificibus condere leges de cultibus et coelibatu. Nam spe- ciosa res est ille ceremoniarum ordo, et persona- rum gradus. Ideo haec sine vocatione, et sine verbo instituta sunt. Placet sapientibus viris in Israël creare regem, habeant certum ducem, et defensorem, more aliarum gentium. Ita cum homines naturaliter delectentur sua sapientia, et quaerant concinnitates in verbo Dei plausibiles. Item cum omnes simus naturaliter φιλαρχικοὶ, et multa ordinare, et constituere cupiamus, multa extra vocationem, et sine verbo audacter suscipi- mus, hoc est, se deiicere de culmine templi.

Hic rursus opponit Christus dictum gravissi- mum: Non tentabis dominum Deum tuum. Est enim tentare Deum proprie certare cum Deo, fi- ducia propriae sapientiae, iusticiae, aut virium, et hac fiducia discedere a verbo Dei, et vocatione seu ordinatione Dei. Sic peccant omnes haere- tici, sic peccant autores novorum cultuum, qui discedentes a verbo Dei, imaginati sunt Monasti- cen esse rem insignem, quae plus apud Deum va- litura esset, quam opera communis vitae. Sic peccavit populus Israël sua sapientia, regem fla- gitans, cum scire deberet in populo Dei non esse constituendam formam politiae, sine claro man- dato Dei, et Deum velle, ut ab eo ipso defensio- nem expectaret.

Tertia tentatio est magis horrenda caeteris, diabolus impudenter postulat se adorari, et pro hoc officio promittit imperia mundi. Nec cogi- tandum est fuisse hoc leve certamen. Offudit illi praestanti viro, quantum decus sit imperium, quantum ipse Christus ingenio et virtute antecel- lat omnibus regibus. Talem virum dignum esse monarchia, talem principem fore salutarem mundo. Quid, quod Messiae promissa sit mun- di haereditas? Haec et alia multa obiecit dia- bolus. Etsi autem vicit Christus, ac repulit diabolum, tamen ad extremum Ecclesiam vastavit haec tentatio. Mahometh, Papa, propter imperia excogitarunt idolatricos cultus, et videmus conspirare potentiam mundi ad defendendam idolatriam: ut olim imperatores tuebantur ethnicas idolomanias, ita nunc Pontifices et reges stabiliunt impias Missas, cultum sanctorum, coelibatum. Non quod sentiant probanda esse, sed tantum ut opes, dignitates, et voluptates retineant. Hanc conspirationem potentum, sciens diabolus, promittit Christo imperium mundi, non quod arbitraretur, se invito Deo posse imperia transferre. Scit enim politias esse Dei, sed quod eos, qui tenent imperia, plerunque impios esse animadvertit, et ingenti furore tueri idola comperit, ut autoritatem et opes retineant.

clesiam sponsam. Ideo multis locis descriptio nuptiarum in historiis sacris recte significat Ecclesiam, ut hic valde concinna est allegoria, sed nos prius historiam percurremus. Praecipui loci sunt approbatio nuptiarum, exemplum aerumnarum coniugii: testimonium praesentiae Dei opitulantis in his oeconomicis miseriis. De invocatione, ut hic mater interpellat Christum, et is duriter respondet, tamen postea opitulatur. Haec omnia continent utilem doctrinam.

De primo loco breviter admonendus est lector, quia enim adest Christus, et ornat miraculo nuptias, certe eas approbat. Et huc addendae sunt sententiae ex aliis locis multis, quae testantur legitimas nuptias Deo placere, et refutant impias opiniones omnium fanaticorum, qui damnaverunt, aut prohibuerunt legitimum coniugium. Quales fuerunt Marcion, Manichaei, Encratitae et Pontifices, qui adhuc defendunt legem de coelibatu, et Monachi, qui fingunt coelibatum esse eximium Dei cultum, et mereri remissionem peccatorum, et alia multa praemia. Haec deliria quomodo refutanda sint, alias saepe dicitur: Et hic satis illustri testimonio refutantur praesentia Christi, qui ostendit se favere nuptiis, cum et adest, et eas miraculo ornat. Et unum hoc dictum, cum ait Christus: Quos Deus coniunxit, satis clare testatur nuptias institutas esse a Deo, et placere Deo. Et quidem copiosam doctrinam complectitur haec particula, cum monet coniugium esse coniunctionem divinam, id est, societatem institutam a Deo, quam Deus non solum approbat, sed etiam adiuvat, regit, tuetur, servat in hac vita, et vult propter ipsam amari, magnifieri, et certa lege servari.

Vicit autem Christus has tentationes, et haec scribi voluit, ut Ecclesia admonita, sciat se similes tentationes, et similia certamina subituram esse. Erunt igitur aliqui, qui diabolo repugnabunt, memores victoriae Christi, qui eius exemplo dimicationem subibunt, et ab eo auxilium petent. Ideo enim filius Dei venit, ut destruat opera diaboli. Ita omnes sancti vincunt diabolum, sed alii anteferentes potentiam, opes, dignitatem, voluptates, obtemperant diabolo in colendis et retinendis idolis. Praemonet autem Christus omnes homines, hanc vocem repetens: Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, et huic soli servies. Hoc exemplo Christi, et hac victoria moniti, sciamus in omnibus tentationibus haec duo praecipue facienda esse. Intueamur verbum Dei, et inde consilium petamus, nec avelli nos a verbo Dei patiamur. Petamus item auxilium a victore Christo, et sciamus Ecclesiam talibus certaminibus exerceri, et velle certantibus adesse filium Dei. Haec breviter de tentationibus propter seriem historiae dixi.

Secundus locus est exemplum aerumnarum coniugii, vulgare onus est inopia, et tamen non leve, sed alia multa incidunt duriora, morbi, infelices partus, funera natorum, delicta, aut tristes casus liberorum. Ut magno cum dolore spectarunt primi parentes necem filii Abel, sed multo maiorem et acriorem dolorem attulit eis alterius filii parricidae scelus. Humanae miseriae sunt poenae peccati, ut constat, et hae maxime premunt hanc partem generis humani, quae vivit in coniugio. Haec enim est praecipua. Caeteri qui fugiunt matrimonium, non ipsam societatem, quae per se dulcis est, fugiunt, sed illam aerumnarum molem, quae accedit, ac quaerunt otium ac

Post tentationes exactis 40 diebus, rediit Christus ad Baptistam, et consentaneum est interim aliquoties eos una fuisse: cumque mense Februario pene medio rediret in Galilaeam, post illa mira exercitia coepit docere, et doctrinam confirmare publicis miraculis, ac primum hic narratur de vino in nuptiis facto.

## 2:1
And on the third day the wedding was taking place.

There is no doubt that legitimate weddings are an image of the love between the Son of God, the bridegroom, and the Church pleasures. Since, therefore, mention is made here of one burden, namely poverty, let us also consider the others, and at the same time consider the cause, namely that the human race is subject to immense miseries on account of sin, and that God wishes us to be obedient in enduring these; the complaint of the anxious mother of the family is therefore described here, when the mother says: They have no wine.

The third passage, when Christ relieves poverty, testifies that God is present to the miseries of spouses and alleviates them. Let us therefore apply the example to all difficulties. For we are subject to these so that we may acknowledge sin, be called to repentance, raise ourselves up by faith, call upon God, and from Him seek, hope for, and expect help, and celebrate Him as Creator, Helper, and Savior, so that others also may acknowledge Him, fear Him, and learn to call upon Him. Thus, the first Church is the society of spouses; in this, God wishes to be seen, called upon, and celebrated. Let us therefore contemplate the promises here. Psalm 34: There is no poverty for those who fear Him. But Psalm 128 pertains properly to spouses: Behold, thus shall the man be blessed who fears the Lord. This voice testifies that God is present to pious husbands and matrons, and indeed that He blesses them, that is, favors them, gives them offspring, protects their families, and helps them in the duties of their calling, both in the household and in the state; fruitfulness is promised to the wife: Your wife shall be like a fruitful vine. Offspring flourishing in the strength of body and spirit are also promised, like olive shoots. Happiness is promised in the duties of one's calling: Because you shall eat the labors of your hands, you are blessed, that is, God will bring it about that you enjoy your labors, have sustenance, and have success in private and public life. Finally, a far greater gift is promised: public tranquility, peace, and the longevity of the government. This is a great matter: Pious spouses see that the changes of kingdoms are wondrous and daily, that wars easily arise everywhere, by which citizens are driven from their possessions, spouses are separated, children are torn from the embrace of their parents, churches are dissipated, the knowledge of God is extinguished, and wise men see that there is such inconstancy in human affairs that nowhere is there lasting and certain tranquility. The Psalm therefore consoles pious spouses, and as if building walls and a fortress, it promises divine defense; pious spouses will be safe, their posterity will have some seats, states, and churches, just as Jeconiah, obeying Jeremiah, remained safe, although in exile, and he also had a son as a successor, to whom the ancestral seat was restored. Therefore it says here: May you see your children's children, and peace upon Israel. With these promises, let pious spouses console themselves and believe that they are a care to God, and that they are defended and helped by Him. Certainly the times themselves should help us to seek these consolations. For we see all kingdoms everywhere shaken by great commotions; yet, among these commotions, God will preserve some seat for the Churches. He will therefore preserve pious spouses and some states.

The fourth passage is about Invocation. To the mother interceding, the Son answers harshly; indeed, He seems to turn away from her as if she were a stranger. First, this is the reason: Because those things which pertained to the calling of the Messiah, He does not wish to be governed by the human affections of a mother and others, just as He says elsewhere: Did you not know that I must be about my Father's business? Then, this is also signified concerning the very miseries of spouses: often spouses pray to be relieved of a certain kind of misery, and yet they do not immediately obtain relief; indeed, sometimes difficulties increase. When Abraham was forced to cast out his son Ishmael and his mother, in what pain was he? Likewise, in what mourning was Jacob when Rachel was dead, and likewise when his son Joseph was lost? God hears the vows and groans of pious spouses and preserves them wondrously, even though not everything happens that we ask for or as we ask for it. To the old man Jacob, Joseph is restored in the 23rd year after he had been lost. To David, Absalom is not preserved at all. Let the pious consider this variety, because God does not rule us by human counsels, but by His own, and He wishes that we depend on Him by faith. He preserves, but in a way far different from what we dreamed. Moses, leading the people out of Egypt, by no means thought that such a great multitude would wander in the desert for 40 years without certain seats, and yet here he is wondrously preserved.

This is a useful doctrine for the pious in bodily miseries, so that they may know that they are not cast off for that reason, even if that which they would prefer does not come. For even if God wishes us to be exercised by some certain kind of trial, yet in the meantime He does not desert us, and He preserves us in another way. He permitted Jerusalem to be overturned, the pious to be led to Babylon, and there He adorned them with greater glory than what they had had at home. This doctrine preaches equally about obedience and about faith; it commands us to be convinced that we are a care to God, and that we are protected by Him, and yet to endure in the meantime, if there are any things to be borne. As Christ says: They shall receive a hundredfold in this life, but with tribulation. Thus here there was some anxiety for the mother, especially having suffered a rejection, but afterwards it is amply compensated by the delay. For Christ honorably bestowed a gift, which could suffice for the whole year, namely six amphorae, as we call them. For one hydria contained two metretae, that is sixty of our canthari, as we call them. The hydria therefore corresponded to our amphora.

Thus far I have run through the history most simply, which undoubtedly proposes doctrine and consolation concerning marriage. But as I said at the beginning, paintings of marriage usually signify the Church, and here the image fits the Church most aptly. The Church is conflicted by many and various miseries, is shaken by wars, is dissipated by the cruelty of tyrants, is pressed by domestic hatreds, labors under poverty, is torn apart by the dissensions of governors and by perverse opinions: with no light grief, Mary is tormented in these such great evils, that is, the sincere part of the Church, so that there was great despair of many, under the reign of Antiochus, the heavenly doctrine seemed about to perish utterly. Thus in the time of Diocletian the pious were in great grief, on account of the cruelty of the tyrants: Mary therefore cried out, that is, the better part of the Church to Christ, and he did not immediately deliver her, because we, often exhausted by the magnitude of afflictions, seek deliverance with carnal affection, as Paul says, Rom. 8: We do not know what we should pray for as we ought. But yet Christ does not forget his Church, and he delivers it at an opportune time. As it is said in Isaiah 49: Can a mother forget her infant, so as not to have mercy on the son of her womb? and even if she should forget, yet I will not forget you. It is enough to have known this concerning the allegory. For there is a close comparison of private and public miseries, and in both, invocation ought to shine. To the allegory this is also more fitting, that the ruler of the feast admires that the good wine is given last. For finally, after many and long struggles, the Church is glorified.

Latin:

Et die tertia nuptiae fiebant.

Non dubium est, legitimas nuptias esse imaginem amoris inter filium Dei sponsum, et Eccle- voluptates. Cum igitur hic fit mentio unius one- ris, scilicet inopiae, caetera etiam cogitemus, et simul causam consideremus, quod videlicet ge- nus humanum subiectum sit ingentibus aerumnis propter peccatum, quod Deus velit nos obedire in his perferendis; querela igitur hic anxiae ma- trisfamilias describitur, cum inquit mater: Vi- num non habent.

Tertius locus, cum Christus sarcit inopiam, testatur Deum adesse coniugum aerumnis, easque lenire. Exemplum igitur transferamus ad omnes difficultates. Ideo enim his subiecti sumus, ut agnoscamus peccatum, vocemur ad poenitentiam, erigamus nos fide, invocemus Deum, et ab eo petamus, speremus, ac expectemus auxilium, eumque celebremus conditorem, opitulatorem, salvatorem, ut et alii eum agnoscant, timeant, et invocare discant. Ita prima Ecclesia est con- iugum societas, in hac vult Deus conspici, in- vocari et celebrari. Hic igitur promissiones contemplemur. Psalm. 34.: Non est inopia ti- mentibus eum. Sed proprie ad coniuges perti- net Psalm. 138. Ecce sic benedicetur homo, qui timet dominum. Haec vox testatur Deum ad- esse piis maritis et matronis, et quidem benedi- cere illis, id est, favere, dare sobolem, tueri familias, adiuvare officia vocationis, tum in oeco- nomia, tum in politia, uxori foecunditas pro- mittitur: Uxor tua sicut vitis abundans. Promit- titur et soboles florens viribus corporis, et spiri- tu, sicut novellae olivarum. Promittitur felici- tas in officiis vocationis: Labores manuum tua- rum quia manducabis, beatus es, id est, efficiet Deus, ut fruaris laboribus tuis, habeas victum, successus in vita privata et publica. Postremo longe amplius munus promittitur, tranquillitas publica, pax et diuturnitas imperii. Haec ma- gna res est: Vident pii coniuges, miras esse et quotidianas mutationes regnorum, facile ubique oriri bella, quibus cives excutiuntur ex possessio- nibus, distrahuntur coniuges, avelluntur liberi a complexu parentum, dissipantur Ecclesiae, ex- tinguitur noticia Dei, ac vident sapientes tantam esse inconstantiam rerum humanarum, ut nus- quam sit diuturna et certa tranquillitas. Conso- latur ergo Psalmus pios coniuges, et tanquam muros et arcem extruens, pollicetur divinam de- fensionem, pii coniuges erunt tuti, posteritas eorum habebit aliquas sedes, politias, Ecclesias, ut Iechonias obtemperans Ieremiae, mansit in- columis, quanquam in exilio, habuit et filium successorem, cui reddita est patria sedes. Ideo hic inquit: Videas filios filiorum tuorum, et pa- cem super Israël. His promissionibus pii con- iuges se consolentur, et credant se curae esse Deo, defendi et iuvari ab eo. Certe tempora nos ipsa adiuvent, ut has consolationes quaeramus. Vi- demus enim omnia regna ubique magnis motibus concuti, inter hos motus tamen Deus Ecclesiis aliquam sedem servabit. Servabit igitur pios coniuges et aliquas politias.

Quartus locus est de Invocatione. Matri interpellanti duriter respondet filius, imo eam quasi alienam aversari videtur. Primum haec causa est: Quia illa, quae ad vocationem Messiae pertinebant, non vult gubernari humanis affecti- bus matris et aliorum, sicut alibi dicit: Nescic- batis me oportere in negotiis esse mei patris. De- inde et hoc de ipsis coniugum aerumnis significa- tur, saepe coniuges orant levari certum genus miseriae, nec tamen subito impetrant levationem, imo interdum crescunt difficultates. Cum Abra- ham extrudere filium Ismaël et matrem eius coge- retur, in quanto dolore fuit? Item, quanto in luctu fuit Iacob extincta Rachel, item amisso filio Ioseph? Exaudit Deus vota et gemitus piorum coniugum, eosque mirabiliter servat, tametsi non omnia eveniunt, quae petimus aut ut petimus. Seni Iacob redditur Ioseph, anno 23. postquam fuerat amissus. Davidi omnino non servatur Ab- solon. Hanc varietatem pii considerent, quia Deus nos non humanis consiliis regit, sed suo, et vult, ut fide ex ipso pendeamus. Servat, sed longe aliter, quam nos somniabamus. Moses educens populum ex Aegypto, nequaquam fore cogitavit, ut tanta multitudo sine certis sedibus in deserto 40 annis vagaretur, et tamen hic mi- rabiliter servatur.

Haec est utilis doctrina piis in corporatibus aerumnis, ut sciant se non propterea abiectos esse, etiamsi non venit hoc, quod mallent ipsi. Deus enim etiamsi vult nos aliquo certo genere exerceri, tamen interim non deserit, et alio modo nos ser- vat. Permittebat everti Ierosolymam, perduci pios Babylonem, et ibi eos maiore gloria ornabat, quam qualem domi habuerant. Haec doctrina pariter de obedientia, et de fide concionatur, iu- bet statuere quod Deo curae simus, et ab eo pro- tegamur, et tamen perferre interim, si quae sunt ferenda. Sicut Christus ait: Recipient centuplum in hac vita, sed cum tribulatione. Ita hic fuit aliqua matris solicitudo, praesertim passae repul- sam, sed postea cumulate sarcitur mora. Nam Christus honorifice munus tribuit, quod poterat toto anno sufficere, videlicet sex amphoras, ut nos vocamus. Nam una hydria continebat duas metretas, hoc est sexaginta nostros cantharos, ut vocamus. Respondebat igitur hydria nostrae amphorae.

Hactenus historiam simplicissime percurri, quae haud dubie doctrinam et consolationem de coniugio proponit. Ut autem initio dixi, plae- runque picturae coniugii significant Ecclesiam, et hic aptissime quadrat imago ad Ecclesiam. Conflictatur Ecclesia multis et variis aerumnis, concutitur bellis, dissipatur saevitia tyrannorum, premitur odiis domesticis, laborat inopia, dila- ceratur dissidiis gubernatorum et pravis opinio- nibus: non levi dolore, in his tantis malis ex- cruciatur Maria, id est, pars Ecclesiae, sincera, ut magna desperatio fuit multorum, regnante Antiocho, visa est penitus interitura coelestis do- ctrina. Sic Diocletiani tempore magno in dolore fuerunt pii, propter tyrannorum saevitiam: Cla- mabat igitur Maria, id est, pars Ecclesiae melior ad Christum, et is non statim eam liberavit, quia plaerunque defessi magnitudine afflictionum, car- nali affectu expetimus liberationem, ut Paulus inquit, Rom. 8.: Quid oremus, sicut oportet non scimus. Sed tamen non obliviscitur Chri- stus suae Ecclesiae, et eam oportuno tempore liberat. Sicut dicitur Esaiae 49.: Num oblivisci potest mater infantem suum, ut non misereatur filii uteri sui? etsi illa oblita fuerit, ego tamen non obliviscar tui. Haec de allegoria satis est novisse. Est enim vicina collatio privatarum et publicarum aerumnarum, et in utrisque lucere debet invocatio.
