Ad allegoriam etiam hoc accom- modatius est, quod architriclinus admiratur bo- num vinum postremo dari. Postremo enim post multa et longa certamina glorificatur Ecclesia.

## 2:11
Jesus did this as the beginning of signs.

The utility of miracles is described. For he warns that these deeds above nature are testimonies to the doctrine, because they show that God is present with this teacher. For many things have been done which the power of no creature, neither of angels nor of devils, can imitate, such as the resuscitation of the dead, the fertilization of an effete and barren woman. These proper miracles of the Church must be diligently considered.

Latin:

Hoc fecit initium signorum Iesus.

Utilitas miraculorum describitur. Monet enim haec facta supra naturam, testimonia esse doctrinae, quia ostendunt Deum adesse huic do- ctori. Multa enim facta sunt, quae imitari nul- lius creaturae, nec angelorum, nec diabolorum potentia potest, ut resuscitatio mortuorum, foecundatio effoetae mulieris et sterilis. Haec propria miracula Ecclesiae diligenter consideranda sunt.

## 2:13
And the Passover of the Jews was near, and he went up, etc.

From the very series of the preceding narrative, it sufficiently appears that the Evangelist speaks here of the first Passover, which was after the baptism and the beginning of Christ's preaching, and this narrative shows that not only at the last Passover were the money-changers and merchants driven from the temple by Christ, but also before, and perhaps he flared up thus more often. For it is not consistent that such a man could have watched the manifest baseness of these marketings without great indignation. It is consistent, therefore, that this crowd of merchants was often dissipated by him. John here recounts the expulsion made at the first Passover. Matthew and Luke recount the expulsion made on Palm Sunday. Mark recounts another made the day after the Palm festival; therefore, three are counted.

But here it is disputed, if he did not wish to have political government, why did he drive the merchants from the temple? It is asked likewise concerning the example: Whether it is permitted to other ministers of the Church to use bodily force against the impious for the sake of propagating doctrine. The answer is very easy for those piously instructed. First, this deed of Christ was not a work of political government, nor was it done by bodily force, but by the impulse of the Holy Spirit with which such a great man burned against the impious: like the work of Elijah, who had ordered fire to descend from heaven and consume the soldiers. These deeds are truly divine and singular, and are not to be referred to common deliberations or rules. Such also is the deed of Peter, when by his voice alone he killed the lying Ananias. Such was the deed of the Corinthian Church, when the incestuous man, having been excommunicated, began to be tormented by the devil. Such was the deed of Ambrose, when the excommunicated scribe of Stilicho began to rave. All these examples pertain to the ministry of the Gospel, or the spirit, because punishments are not inflicted by hand or bodily force, but by the voice of the teacher, through whom the Holy Spirit is effective. And often similar things happen in the Church, often such is the voice of true excommunication, as it is written: I will bless those who bless you, I will curse those who curse you, and as the prayer of the saints has a promise, according to that: if two shall agree upon the earth, whatever they ask, will be done for them by my heavenly Father: thus also a curse against the impious is effective, like the voice of David: Confound, O God, the counsels of Ahithophel. These sentences exhort us to prayer, likewise to fearing true excommunication, they warn also what the weapons of the Church are; by these weapons devils are driven away, tyrants are repressed, nay, they are shaken out of their very kingdoms, the Amalekite army is routed. Because God wishes the Church to exercise faith in invocation, and he hears these prayers, lest the Church perish utterly. Likewise, that he may testify that the Church is his concern, and that he hears prayers.

For as Christ with burning spirit drove out the hucksters, so pious teachers ought always to drive out from the Church with the word and with excommunication the impious, who turn the sacraments into gain or accumulate ceremonies so that they may capture profits, just as the Lord's supper has been depraved and turned to gain, and infinite examples could be cited. Nor indeed is that voice of the Holy Spirit in pious teachers, arguing against those profanations and wicked huckstering, empty, but by the wonderful work of God the power of the impious mass-priests, who have deformed the gift of God with those snares of gain, will collapse and be weakened.

But what the duty of the magistrate is toward the worshippers of idols, and those turning the sacraments into gain, will be said in another place. Here it is enough to have admonished that the magistrate, after error has been rejected by the Gospel, ought to abolish by force the external cults of idols, and those snares of gain in the temples, and punish the authors. This the divine law commands concerning the punishing of blasphemers, which also pertains to the political magistrate.

Latin:

Et prope erat Pascha Iudaeorum, et ascendit, etc.

Ex ipsa serie superioris narrationis, satis apparet Evangelistam hic de primo Paschate loqui, quod fuit post baptismum et initium praedicationis Christi, et haec narratio ostendit non tantum in postremo Paschate nummularios et caupones ex templo pulsos esse a Christo, sed etiam ante, ac fortassis saepius ita incanduit. Nec enim consentaneum est talem virum sine magna indignatione potuisse spectare manifestam turpitudinem harum nundinationum. Consentaneum est igitur saepe ab eo hanc turbam cauponum dissipatam esse. Ioannes hic recenset expulsionem factam primo Paschate. Matthaeus et Lucas recensent expulsionem factam in die Palmarum. Marcus recenset aliam factam postridie festi Palmarum, tres ergo numerantur.

Hic autem disputatur, si noluit habere politicam gubernationem, quare expulit caupones e templo? Quaeritur item de exemplo: An liceat caeteris ministris Ecclesiae, corporali vi adversus impios, doctrinae propagandae causa, uti. Facillima est responsio pie institutis. Primum, hoc factum Christi non fuit opus politicae gubernationis, nec factum est vi corporali, sed impetu Spiritus S. quo exarsit tantus vir contra impios: sicut Eliae opus, qui iusserat ignem de coelo descendere, et absumere milites. Haec facta sunt vere divina et singularia, nec referenda sunt ad communes deliberationes, aut regulas. Tale est et Petri factum, cum sola voce occidit Ananiam mentientem. Tale erat factum Ecclesiae Corinthiae, cum excommunicatus incestus excruciari coepit a diabolo. Tale erat factum Ambrosii, cum Stilliconis scriba excommunicatus furere coepit. Haec exempla omnia ad ministerium Evangelii, seu spiritus pertinent, quia poenae non manu aut vi corporali irrogantur, sed voce docentis, per quam Spiritus sanctus est efficax. Ac saepe similia in Ecclesia accidunt, saepe talis est vox verae excommunicationis, sicut scriptum est: Benedicam benedicentibus tibi, maledicam maledicentibus tibi, et ut oratio sanctorum habet promissionem, iuxta illud si duo consenserint super terram, quicquid petent, fiet eis a patre meo coe- lesti: ita et imprecatio adversus impios est efficax, ut Davidis vox: Infatua Deus consilia Ahitophel. Hae sententiae hortantur nos ad precationem, item ad timendam veram excommunicationem, monent etiam quae sint arma Ecclesiae, his armis depelluntur diaboli, reprimuntur tyranni, imo ex ipsis regnis excutiuntur, profligantur exercitus Amalechiticus. Quia Deus vult Ecclesiam exer- cere fidem in invocatione, et exaudit has preces, ne funditus pereat Ecclesia. Item, ut testetur sibi curae esse Ecclesiam, et exaudire preces.

Nam ut Christus ardenti spiritu expulit cau- pones, ita semper pii doctores verbo, et excom- municatione expellere ex Ecclesia debent impios, qui sacramenta in quaestum conferunt aut cumu- lant ceremonias, ut lucra captent, sicut coena Domini depravata et ad quaestum collata est, et possent infinita exempla recitari. Nec vero ina- nis est vox illa Spiritus sancti in piis doctoribus, arguentibus illas prophanationes et nefarias nun- dinationes, sed mirabili opere Dei ruet, et labe- fiet potentia impiorum sacrificulorum, qui illis aucupiis quaestus deformavereunt donum Dei.

Caeterum quod sit officium magistratus ad- versus cultores idolorum, et conferentes sacra- menta in quaestum, alio loco dicetur. Hic satis est admonuisse, quod magistratus, postquam error per Evangelium reiectus est, debet manu abolere externos cultus idolorum, et illa aucupia quaestuum in templis, et punire autores. Haec praecipit lex divina de puniendis blasphemis, quae etiam ad politicum magistratum pertinet.

## 2:16
My house shall be called a house of prayer.

The other saying stands in Isaiah chapter 56: My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations. It is a brief description of the true Church, and of true and chief worship. First, therefore, let the sentence of Isaiah be understood of the people of God themselves, for the Prophet speaks of this: Christ, however, adapts it to the place of ministry. Furthermore, what the Church is, has been said elsewhere; now it is enough to know this, that it is a people truly invoking God, that it is in the acknowledgment of that word which he himself delivered. And let individuals transfer the saying to themselves; let every pious person know that he is a house of God. Why? Not because he gives great gifts to God, but because he invokes God, and because he truly asks from him, and expects good things. This work, namely true invocation, distinguishes the Church from the nations, as is often said elsewhere. And this same Prophet Isaiah in chapter 43, defining the Church, says: Everyone who calls upon my name, I have created him for my glory, that is, the pious alone truly glorify me, they alone are the living members of the Church, who perform this worship, namely invocation. It is certain, however, that invocation cannot happen except in the acknowledgment of the word which God delivered, and the acknowledgment of the Son, as Christ says: Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give to you. Invocation therefore embraces the acknowledgment of the word of God, and faith in Christ. These, as is evident, distinguish the Church from the nations. Nor indeed can the Church exist in this life without an external place of ministry. Therefore, Christ also says concerning the place: My house is a house of prayer. Here again, prayer embraces the whole ministry, the preaching of the Gospel, and the sacraments. All these are destined for this end, namely for invocation, which is the highest worship. But when Christ casts the merchants out of the place of the temple, let us understand that they are being thrust from the ministry. Just as God subsequently, purging the Church, punishes impious teachers, as he destroyed the Levitical High Priests and later the heretics. Thus, in his own time, he will also destroy the High Priests who now, because of wealth or dignities, retain idolomanias.

Latin:

Domus mea, domus orationis vocabitur.

Alterum dictum extat apud Esaiam cap. 56.: Domus mea, domus orationis vocabitur cunctis gentibus. Brevis descriptio est verae Ecclesiae, ac veri et praecipui cultus. Primum ergo senten- tia Esaiae intelligatur de ipso populo Dei, nam de hoc loquitur Propheta: Christus autem ad lo- cum ministerii accommodat. Porro quid sit Ec- clesia, alias dictum est, nunc satis est hoc scire, quod sit populus vere invocans Deum, quod sit in agnitione eius verbi, quod ipse tradidit. Et transferant dictum singuli ad sese, sciat quisque pius, se esse domum Dei. Quare? Non quod magna munera det Deo, sed quod invocet Deum, et quod ab ipso vere petat, et expectet bona. Hoc opus, videlicet vera invocatio, discernit Eccle- siam a gentibus, ut alias saepe dicitur. Et hic ipse Propheta Esaias cap. 43. definiens Ecclesiam, inquit: Omnem, qui invocat nomen meum, in gloriam meam creavi eum, id est, pii soli vere me glorificant, soli sunt Ecclesiae viva membra, qui hunc cultum, videlicet invocationem prae- stant. Constat autem invocationem non posse fieri, nisi in agnitione verbi, quod Deus tradidit, et agnitione filii, ut Christus inquit: Quicquid petieritis patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis. Complectitur ergo invocatio agnitionem verbi Dei, et fidem in Christum. Haec, ut constat, discer- nunt Ecclesiam a gentibus. Nec vero potest Ec- clesia in hac vita existere, sine externo loco mi- nisterii. Ergo et de loco dicit Christus: Domus mea, domus orationis est. Hic rursus oratio complectitur totum ministerium, praedicationem Evangelii, et sacramenta. Haec omnia destinata sunt ad hunc finem, scilicet ad invocationem, quae est summus cultus. Cum autem Christus ex loco templi caupones eiicit, intelligamus eos a ministerio detrudi. Sicut subinde Deus repur- gans Ecclesiam, punit impios doctores, ut Levi- ticos Pontifices et postea haereticos delevit. Sic delebit suo tempore etiam Pontifices, qui nunc propter opes, aut dignitates retinent idolomanias.

## 2:17
The zeal of your house consumes me.

Two sentences are cited in this history: the one declares whence this anger of Christ arose, and teaches that this work was a singular movement in the saints, and exhorts that a similar anger or emulation should burn in the saints. Now zeal is indignation driving away injury from a beloved one, or fighting so that the beloved person may not be snatched away from oneself. As when Samson's wife is snatched away, the magnanimous man conceives huge grief, from desire for his wife, he conceives also anger, so that he may either punish the Philistines or recover his wife, and many affections are mixed. As Virgil says: Madness is mixed with grief. Thus Scipio had participated in three great battles, in which he had seen his fatherland defeated; these disasters brought him huge grief, and kindled anger to restore the former glory of the fatherland, and to repress Hannibal. Thus generally it behooves good governors to burn with zeal, as the Psalms often say: I have hated the wicked, and I have loved your law. The emperor Aurelian, when he had learned that a soldier had raped his hostess, tore him apart tied to two bent trees. Thus in government [there should be] love of justice, modesty, truth, and burning hatred of vices, so that with true indignation he may undertake the labor to punish the wicked and sanction discipline. This most sharp affection was in Elijah, in Elisha, and it was in Christ. But Christ did not often exercise this huge movement in punishing; he exercised it more in tolerating adversities, which had to be borne to restore the glory of the eternal Father, and to liberate the Church, which he also ardently loved, and knew could not be liberated otherwise, unless he himself became the victim. Therefore it is said in Psalm 68: The zeal of your house consumes me, that is, it exhausts me, I bring my life into danger to liberate the Church, which I love, and to drive away the insults with which God is afflicted, which bring me huge grief, and kindle me to anger against blasphemers.

Latin:

Zelus domus tuae comedit me.

Duae sententiae citantur in hac historia: altera declarat, unde haec ira Christi orta sit, et docet hoc opus, motum esse singularem in sanctis, et hortatur, ut similis ira seu aemulatio flagret in sanctis. Est autem zelus indignatio de- pellens iniuriam ab amato, aut pugnans ne sibi persona amata eripiatur. Ut cum Samsoni eripi- tur uxor, concipit vir magnanimus ingentem do- lorem, desiderio uxoris, concipit et iram, ut vel puniat Philistaeos, vel recipiat uxorem, et mi- scentur multi affectus. Sicut Virgilius inquit: Mixta est insania luctu. Sic Scipio tribus magnis praeliis interfuerat, quibus viderat vinci patriam, hae clades, et ingentem dolorem ei attulerunt, et accenderunt iram ad restituendam pristinam gloriam patriae, et ad reprimendum Annibalem. Sic generaliter ardere zelo bonos gubernatores oportet, ut saepe Psalmi dicunt: Iniquos odio habui, et legem tuam dilexi. Aurelianus impe- rator, cum rescisset militem vi stuprasse hospitam, discerpsit eum alligatum duabus arboribus incur- vatis. Sic in gubernatione amor iusticiae, pudi- citiae, veritatis, et ardens odium vitiorum, ut vera indignatione suscipiat laborem ad puniendos sceleratos, et sanciendam disciplinam. Hic affe- ctus acerrimus fuit in Elia, Eliseo, fuit et in Christo. Sed non saepe in puniendo Christus hunc ingentem motum exercuit, magis exercuit eum in tolerandis adversis, quae ferenda erant ad restituendam gloriam aeterni patris, et ad libe- randam Ecclesiam, quam et ardenter diligebat, et sciebat aliter non posse liberari, nisi ipse fieret victima. Ideo dicitur in Psal. 68.: Zelus domus tuae comedit me, id est, absumit me, adduco vitam in discrimen ad liberandam Ecclesiam, quam diligo, et ad depellendas contumelias, qui- bus Deus afficitur, quae mihi ingentem dolorem afferunt, et ad iram accendunt adversus blas- phemos.

## 2:20
Forty and six years was this temple in building.

When they had demanded a miracle, Christ speaks covertly about the chief miracle, and one proper to his own person, namely about his resurrection, as he often did elsewhere; but the adversaries, raging with hatred and impiety, do not understand what was said figuratively, and they introduce a memory of the building of the temple foreign to the purpose, alleging a thing, as it seemed to them, impossible, since a resurrection from the dead is more impossible. But why do they say this temple was built in 46 years? This history admonishes much about the wonderful return from Babylon, which contains an example of punishments, calamities, liberation, and many things in the Church. Daniel had obtained edicts from Cyrus, so that the Jews might be granted a return to their homeland, and the temple might be rebuilt. The building of the temple was therefore begun in the second year of Cyrus, and there was good hope, now that the pious prince Cyrus was reigning, that it would come to pass that the temple and city would soon be restored, and the people would enjoy tranquility. But behold, as it happens, a great calamity intervenes. Cyrus departs far from the kingdom, waging war with the Scythians, and a little later is killed; at home, his impious son Cambyses governs the kingdom, who again prohibits the building and the return; neighboring nations try to hinder the building by force of arms. Here, what a wound did Daniel and other pious men receive when the pious king was lost and the edict of Cyrus was abolished? Thus, the restoration of the Church is hindered in various ways, and divine liberations do not proceed according to human plans. When Cambyses died, new wars arose in the Babylonian kingdom itself. Darius killed the Magi and recovered Babylon. The king, therefore, being occupied with domestic wars, could not hear the causes of the provinces. Thus the building is deferred for nearly 42 years. For during the whole time of Cambyses and Darius it was hindered; these are 40 years. Afterwards, Longimanus succeeded, milder than the previous kings, and understanding the true worship of God. For he used to listen to Ezra and Nehemiah, and is thought to have been the son of Esther. Therefore, in the second year of this Longimanus, it was again granted that the benefit of Cyrus should be renewed, and the building completed. Therefore, in the following 4 years, the building of the temple was completed in the 5th year of Longimanus, as history testifies in the book of Ezra. What is therefore said in the text of John, that the building lasted forty-six years, should not be understood as continuous building, but the works were interrupted and hindered for nearly forty-two years. Therefore, Daniel predicted in chapter 9 that it would come to pass that Jerusalem would be built in anguish, that is, that the building would be hindered by various difficulties and hardships.

I have recounted these historical matters, not only for the sake of explaining the text, but also for admonishing the reader concerning the calamities of the Church: for here we see it, by the wonderful counsel of God, harshly shaken in empires, and yet preserved divinely, but not in the way that human minds think. And this admonition contains a most serious and useful doctrine, namely, that we should faithfully obey our calling in the Church, and not be deterred by the fear of impending dangers, nor depend on human protections, but ask for and expect the governing of actions and favorable outcomes from God by faith. Just as Psalm 36 says: Commit your way to the Lord, and he will act. The governing of the Church, especially, is properly God's, and the Son of God wars with the devil, nor can human wisdom foresee the changes of affairs, of polities, of princes, and fortify the Church with human protections. Therefore, let faith look to God, and let us do our duty rightly, that is, let us teach purely and faithfully, and commend the outcomes to God, as Christ says: Seek first the kingdom of God, etc.

Latin:

Quadraginta et sex annis aedificatum est hoc templum.

Cum flagitassent miraculum, Christus tecte de miraculo praecipuo, et proprio personae ipsius concionatur, scilicet de sua resurrectione, sicut alias saepe, sed adversarii furentes odio et impie- tate, figurate dictum non intelligunt, et de aedi- ficio templi memoriam iniiciunt alienam a propo- sito, allegantes rem, ut ipsis videbatur, impos- sibilem, cum resurrectio ex mortuis magis sit im- possibilis. Sed cur dicunt hoc templum aedifica- tum esse annis 46? Multa admonet haec historia de mirabili reditu ex Babylone, qui continet exemplum poenarum, calamitatum, liberationis, et multarum rerum in Ecclesia. Daniel impetra- verat a Cyro edicta, ut Iudaeis concederetur redi- tus in patriam, et templum reaedificaretur. In- coata est igitur aedificatio templi anno secundo Cyri, et bona spes erat, iam regnante pio prin- cipe Cyro, futurum, ut cito restituerentur tem- plum et civitas, et populus frueretur tranquilli- tate. Sed ecce, ut fit, intervenit magna calami- tas. Cyrus procul ex regno discedit, bellum ge- rens cum Scythis, et paulo post interficitur; do- mi filius Cambyses impius regnum gubernat, qui iterum prohibet aedificationem et reditum, co- nantur ex armis vicinae gentes impedire aedi- ficationem. Hic quantum vulnus acceperunt Daniel et alii pii amisso pio rege, et abo- lito edicto Cyri? Ita Ecclesiae instauratio va- riis modis impeditur, et divinae liberationes non procedunt humanis consiliis. Cambyse mor- tuo nova bella in ipso regno Babylonico orta sunt. Darius Magos interfecit, recuperavit Ba- bylonem. Occupatis igitur rex domesticis bellis, audire provinciarum causas non potuit. Ita dif- fertur aedificatio, annos fere 42. Nam toto tem- pore Cambysis et Darii impedita est, hi sunt anni 40. Successit postea Longimanus mitior regibus prioribus, et intelligens verum cultum Dei. Nam hic audiebat Esdram et Neaemiam, et putatur fuisse filius Esther. Huius igitur Longimani anno secundo rursus concessum est, ut beneficium Cyri renovaretur, et aedificatio absolveretur. Ergo sequentibus annis 4 templi aedificatio abso- luta est 5. anno Longimani, ut testatur historia in libro Esdrae. Quod ergo in textu Ioannis di- citur, aedificatio durasse annos sex et quadraginta, non de continua aedificatione intelligatur, sed in- terruptae sunt et impeditae operae, fere duos et quadraginta annos. Ideo praedixit Daniel cap. 9. futurum, ut aedificaretur Ierusalem in angustia, id est, ut variis difficultatibus et aerumnis impe- diretur aedificatio.

Haec historica recensui, non solum decla- randi textus causa, sed etiam admonendi lectoris, de calamitatibus Ecclesiae: Hic enim videmus eam mirabili consilio Dei in imperiis duriter quas- sari, et tamen servari divinitus, sed non eo modo, quem cogitant mentes humanae. Et haec admo- nitio gravissimam et utilissimam doctrinam conti- net, videlicet, ut nos in Ecclesia nostrae voca- tioni fideliter pareamus, nec deterreamur metu impendentium periculorum, nec pendeamus ex humanis praesidiis, sed a Deo fide petamus, et expectemus gubernationem actionum et secun- dos eventus. Sicut Psal. 36. ait: Revela do- mino viam tuam, et ipse faciet. Gubernatio praesertim Ecclesiae proprie Dei est, et filius Dei belligeratur cum diabolo, nec potest humana sapientia prospicere mutationes rerum, politia- rum, principum, et munire Ecclesiam humanis praesidiis. Ideo fides Deum intueatur, et nos nostrum officium recte faciamus, id est, pure et fideliter doceamus, exitus Deo commendemus, sicut Christus inquit: Primum quaerite regnum Dei, etc.

## 2:25
For he himself knew what was in man.

…At the end of this chapter, an admonition is proposed concerning the inconstancy of human wills, or human perfidy. Jesus did not trust himself to them. He For he knew what was in man, that is, that the wills of all are weak, and of many even treacherous, as it is said elsewhere: Do not trust in princes, nor in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation. And it is a common complaint in friendships, both within the Church and outside the Church, that the wills of friends are easily changed. Hence that saying of Virgil: Nowhere is faith safe; and there exist infinite such maxims. Cicero says: That saying of Epicharmus is the sinews and joints of wisdom: Remember to distrust. But here we are taught first not to undertake unjust or unnecessary matters, trusting in friends or associates. Secondly, let us conduct even good, just, and necessary matters in such a way that we seek and hope for guidance and success from God, and with a sincere mind look to the end, namely, of duty, or the glory of God. Nor should trust rely chiefly on the alliance of friends or the leagues of associates, nor should we entangle ourselves too closely in the friendships of men, who sometimes drag others with them, against their will and desire, into unjust and ruinous affairs. It is a common saying about fellowships: Make yourself no one's companion too much; you will rejoice less, and you will grieve less.

But someone might say that these are paradoxes, because nothing in life can be done without friends. David cannot protect his own safety without his friend Jonathan. I answer: Let there be friendships, and let us candidly love all, but especially friends, that is, those joined by duties, whose services we may also use, and return our services in turn. Let a leader have a benevolent, obedient army. These things do not conflict with those sayings that command us to distrust, because love and candor should be shown toward men. But at the same time, let us know that the wills of men are mutable, just as we know that man is mortal. Likewise, let us know that success is to be expected from God; He will confirm the wills of men as long as He wills. Again, let us know that just causes are not to be abandoned, even if we are forsaken by human aid. Thus Daniel is constant in his confession, even if he is deserted by his friend King Darius.

Here it is objected again: Therefore is it a virtue to be suspicious? By no means, for this conflicts with love, that is, with candor, which is a part of truth, that is, to attribute to another truly and from the heart what he deserves in reality. David thinks well of Joab, until he detects no fraud of his, but yet he knows him to be mutable, as he is mortal, and he trusts in God, even if he has been deserted by Joab. He is therefore suspicious who interprets the right actions of friends calumniously, and without probable arguments thinks ill of another's mind. Paul censures this vice when he says: Love believes all things, namely, those things which are to be believed of a man, and so far as contrary arguments do not appear. We ought not to believe friends regarding false doctrine, but to seek the word of God. Cicero ought not to have believed that Octavius would be more friendly to the senate than to Antony. For in youth there is neither firm judgment nor constancy of will. And Octavius did not have in his power the armies, which were more inclined toward Antony, and the whole matter depended more on the will of the soldiers. But Phocylides most correctly says: Λαῷ μὴ πίστευε, πολύτροπος ἐστὶν ὅμιλος. Do not trust the people, because the wills of the people are inconstant. But these things can be easily distinguished by the prudent: what is to be attributed to a friend, what to God; especially in the Church, much is sinned in this kind. Wise men, because they distrust God, applaud the errors of the powerful. Others sin by perverse trust, because they seek defenses against the will of God, and stir up tumults, both in good and in bad causes, as often happens. Monetarius and his associates stirred up tumults without a calling, relying on the desires of the mob, which are more changeable than the winds. To such cases pertains this admonition in this text: That we do not entangle ourselves too closely in the friendships of men, nor, elated by trust in human defenses, undertake anything without a calling.

Latin:

Ipse enim sciebat quid esset in homine.

In fine huius capitis proponitur admonitio de inconstantia humanarum voluntatum, seu per- fidia humana. Iesus non credebat se eis. Scie- bat enim quid esset in homine, id est, omnium voluntates esse infirmas, multorum etiam perfi- diosas, ut alibi dicitur: Nolite confidere in prin- cipibus, neque in filiis hominum, in quibus non est salus. Et vulgaris querela est in amicitiis, cum in Ecclesia, tum extra Ecclesiam, facile mu- tari voluntates amicorum. Hinc illud Virgilii: Nusquam tuta fides; et extant infinitae tales sen- tentiae. Cicero ait: Nervos atque artus esse sa- pientiae illud Epicharmi: Memento diffidere. Primum autem hic docemur ne res iniustas, aut non necessarias moveamus confisi amicis, aut so- ciis. Secundo, etiam res bonas, iustas, neces- sarias sic agamus, ut a Deo gubernationem et suc- cessus petamus, et speremus, et sincero animo num finem spectemus, videlicet officii, seu gloriam Dei. Nec fiducia nitatur praecipue con- iunctione amicorum, aut foederibus sociorum, nec implicemus nos arctius amicitiis hominum, qui interdum invitos ac nolentes rapiunt secum in negotia iniusta et exitiosa. Vulgare est de so- dalitiis: Nulli te facias nimis sodalem; Gaudebis minus, et minus dolebis.

Sed dicat aliquis, haec esse paradoxa, quia nihil in vita sine amicis geri potest. David non potest tueri suam salutem, sine amico Ionathan. Respondeo: Sint amicitiae, et nos candide dili- gamus omnes, maxime vero amicos, id est, offi- ciis coniunctos, quorum etiam opera utamur, et reddamus vicissim nostras operas. Dux habeat exercitum benevolum, obedientem. Haec non pugnant cum illis dictis, quae iubent diffidere, quia dilectio et candor praestentur erga homines. Sed simul sciamus, voluntates hominum esse mu- tabiles, ut scimus hominem esse mortalem. Item, sciamus a Deo expectandos esse successus, hic confirmabit voluntates hominum, quoad volet: Rursus sciamus iustas causas non abiiciendas esse, etiamsi destituamur humanis praesidiis. Sic con- stans est Daniel in confessione, etiamsi ab amico rege Dario deseritur.

Hic rursus obiicitur: Ergo virtus est esse suspicacem? Nequaquam, hoc enim cum di- lectione pugnat, hoc est, cum candore, qui est pars veritatis, id est, vere et ex animo tribuere alteri, quod re ipsa meretur, David bene sentit de Ioab, donec nullam eius fraudem deprehendit, sed tamen scit esse mutabilem, ut mortalem, et Deo confidit, etiamsi a Ioab fuerit desertus. Est ergo suspicax, qui recte facta amicorum calum- niose interpretatur, et sine probabilibus argu- mentis de alterius animo male sentit. Hoc vi- tium taxat Paulus, cum ait: Dilectio omnia cre- dit, scilicet, quae sunt homini credenda, et qua- tenus non apparent contraria argumenta. Non debemus amicis credere de falsa doctrina, sed quaerere verbum Dei. Non debebat Cicero cre- dere, Octavium futurum amiciorem senatui, quam Antonio. Nam in adolescentia nec iudi- cium firmum, nec constantia voluntatum est. Et Octavius non habebat in potestate exercitus, qui erant aequiores Antonio, et tota res magis pen- debat a voluntate militum. Rectissime autem in- quit Phocylides: Λαῷ μὴ πίστευε, πολύτροπος ἐστὶν ὅμιλος. Nec confide populo, quia inconstantes sunt voluntates populi. Sed haec a prudentibus facile discerni possunt quid sit tribuendum amico, quid Deo, inprimis autem in Ecclesia multum pecca- tur in hoc genere. Sapientes quia diffidunt Deo, applaudunt potentum erroribus. Alii peccant fiducia prava, quia quaerunt praesidia contra vo- luntatem Dei, ac movent tumultus, cum in bo- nis, tum in malis causis, ut saepe accidit. Mo- netarius et eius socii movebant tumultus sine vocatione, freti studiis vulgi, quae sunt mutabi- liora ventis. Ad tales casus pertinet haec admo- nitio in hoc textu: Ne nos implicemus arctius amicitiis hominum, neve elati fiducia humano- rum praesidiorum aliquid moveamus sine voca- tione.

## 3:1 Argument
Chapter III.

This chapter at the beginning contains a most learned disputation concerning justification, concerning the distinction between the justice of the law and the justice of faith, and concerning the proper office of the Messiah. Then the illustrious testimony of the Baptist is repeated, along with his sermon, which is most sweet to pious minds. But before I come to the disputation, a few things must be said about the sects of the Jewish people, so that the history may be considered. For this comparison of the times of the Church warns us that the Church is not bound to titles, ranks of dignities, and human ceremonies, but only to the word of God, just as it is said in John 10: My sheep hear my voice; and Christ expressly denies that others, who do not believe, are his sheep. After the Maccabees by divine aid defeated the army of Antiochus and expelled them from Judea, and Now there was a moderate peace, and because of the kinship of the Greek language the Jews began in their leisure to devote effort even to Greek philosophy; here, having neglected the ancient doctrine of the Prophets, they began to devise various opinions, from which diverse sects arose. Three principal ones are named.

Pharisees; these, the learned consider to be named from explaining, as if you were to say interpreters, or narrators, or expositors. For although these embraced Moses and all the Prophets, yet they attached their own expositions, smelling of philosophy, or born from human superstition. Although they rightly thought that the souls of men were immortal, yet they erred concerning sin, concerning the law, and concerning justice; they dreamed that sins were only external offenses, and that the law of God was to be preached only concerning external deeds or attempts, not condemning inner doubt and contumacy. They did not know the disease of origin; they feigned that men could satisfy the law of God, and merit the remission of sins by sacrifices and by the rest of good works and the law. Concerning the Messiah they erred in various ways; they did not know he was the Son of God, they did not understand that he was to come in order to become a victim, they did not know the justice of faith, but imagined that he would be a most powerful king, who according to the law of Moses was to restore peace in the whole world and civil peace, with tyrants destroyed and all unjust government abolished.

They imagined that the kingdom of the Messiah would be a certain golden age of this kind. To these false imaginations concerning sin, concerning the Son of God, and concerning the kingdom of the Messiah, they added a great mass of human traditions. And Epiphanius writes that their exercises were quite harsh, fasts, vigils, and other labors, and there was added the error that by these human ceremonies they were righteous before God and merited the remission of sins. And if anyone will attentively consider the whole doctrine of the Pharisees, he will understand that it does not differ much from the monastic [doctrine] which crept into the Church.

The second sect was that of the Sadducees, who with a most arrogant title called themselves after justice, as if you were to say the just, when in reality they were Epicureans. They seem, however, to have taken this title for themselves out of a certain emulation, since others had a glorious appellation from the learning of interpreters, these attributed to themselves a more glorious one from justice. For there is more of true praise in justice than in doctrine. The Sadducees, however, received only Moses, and repudiated all the other Prophets. For they feigned that neither were the souls of men immortal, nor was there to be a resurrection of the dead. And therefore they exploded the Prophets, so that they could not be refuted by their testimonies. They asserted, however, that one must live justly, and that on account of justice useful things are given to men by God in this life, good health, faculties, power, happiness in conducting affairs; concerning the kingdom of the Messiah, the ravings of the three sects were almost the same.

The third sect was that of the Essenes, who wished to appear to excel both, the Pharisees and the Sadducees. Therefore they took for themselves a name from acting, as if signifying that others profess religion with words and disputes, but they themselves with actions. These differed from the Pharisees in that they contributed their possessions into common, [but] in other things they almost agreed with the Pharisees.

Such was the appearance of the Church or the people of God at that time; most and the principal ones had embraced sects, some one, some another, and these disagreed among themselves. And the Pontiffs, Priests, and those who seemed to be the heads of the Church and had ordinary authority, were sometimes Pharisees, sometimes Sadducees, but both defended many ravings. Therefore these erring assemblies were not the Church of God, but meanwhile there were among the people a few who thought rightly and called upon God in the true acknowledgment of the Messiah and in faith, such as Simeon the elder, Anna, Zacharias, Elizabeth, and the hearers of these; these were the Church of God. It must be confessed, therefore, that pontiffs and others who hold the ordinary government, as it is called, can err. And indeed it is a wonder that in the Jewish nation, which had the most serious discipline, such profane audacity should have arisen, that it was openly permitted to deny the resurrection of the dead and the immortality of human souls. This example shows that, once the light of the word of God is lost, the densest darkness follows, just as in the pontifical kingdom the most absurd opinions concerning the worship of saints, concerning transubstantiation, concerning the funeral rites of the dead, and concerning the ceremonies of Monks have been handed down with great applause.

Let us therefore consider the example of the Jewish people of that time, and let us learn that the true Church is not bound to those titles and ranks of dignities, or human traditions, but to the word of God: and let us confirm ourselves, lest on account of the titles of pontiffs, or on account of the fewness of those who think rightly, we fall away from the word of God. For even in that people there were few who thought rightly, and these dissented from the pontiffs and those sects; which the greater part of the people embraced, or at least followed. Now I come to the narrative in John.

Latin:

Caput III.

Hoc caput initio continet eruditissimam dis- putationem de iustificatione, de discrimine iusti- ciae legis et iusticiae fidei, de officio proprio Mes- siae. Deinde repetitur illustre testimonium Ba- ptistae, cum concione eius dulcissima piis menti- bus. Sed priusquam venio ad disputationem, pauca de sectis populi Iudaici dicenda sunt, ut historiae considerentur. Nam haec collatio tem- porum Ecclesiae admonet nos, Ecclesiam non esse alligatam titulis, gradibus dignitatum, et hu- manis ceremoniis, sed tantum verbo Dei, sicut Ioann. 10. dicitur: Oves meae vocem meam au- diunt; et expresse negat Christus suas esse oves caeteros, qui non credunt. Postquam Maccabaei divina ope Antiochi exercitum vicerunt, et ex Iudaea expulerunt, et iam mediocris pax esset, et propter cognationem Graecae linguae inciperent Iudaei in otio etiam philosophiae Graecae operam dare, hic neglecta veteri Prophetarum doctrina, ceperunt varias opi- niones comminisci, unde diversae sectae ortae sunt. Nominantur autem tres praecipuae.

Pharisaei, hos eruditi nominatos esse cen- sent, ab exponendo, quasi dicas interpretes, aut enarratores, seu expositores. Nam hi etsi Mosen et omnes Prophetas amplectebantur, tamen affin- gebant suas expositiones, philosophiam redolen- tes, aut natas ex humana superstitione. Etsi recte sentiebant animas hominum immortales esse, ta- men de peccato, de lege et de iusticia errabant, somniabant peccata esse tantum externa delicta, legem Dei tantum de externis factis, seu conati- bus concionari, non damnare dubitationem et contumaciam interiorem. Non norant morbum originis, fingebant homines legi Dei satis facere posse, mereri remissionem peccatorum sacrificiis, et reliquis bonis operibus et lege. De Messia va- rie errabant, non norant esse filium Dei, non in- telligebant venturum esse, ut fieret victima, non norant iusticiam fidei, sed existimabant fore po- tentissimum regem, qui iuxta legem Mosi in toto orbe, et pacem civilem instauraturus esset, dele- tis tyrannis et abolita omni iniusta gubernatione.

Talem quandam auream aetatem imagina- bantur regnum Messiae fore. Ad has falsas ima- ginationes de peccato, de filio Dei, de regno Messiae, addebant magnam molem traditionum humanarum. Et scribit Epiphanius, fuisse eo- rum exercitia admodum aspera, ieiunia, vigilias et alios labores, et accessit error, quod his hu- manis ceremoniis iusti essent coram Deo, et re- missionem peccatorum mererentur. Ac si quis totam doctrinam Pharisaeorum attente considera- bit, intelliget eam non multum differre a mona- stica, quae in Ecclesiam irrepsit.

Secunda secta fuit Sadducaeorum, qui arro- gantissimo titulo se cognominarunt a iusticia, quasi dicas iustos, cum re ipsa essent Epicurei. Videntur autem hunc titulum aemulatione qua- dam sibi sumsisse, cum alii ab eruditione glorio- sam appellationem haberent interpretum, hi ma- gis gloriosam a iusticia sibi attribuerunt. Plus est enim verae laudis in iusticia, quam in do- ctrina. Tantum autem recipiebant Sadducaei Mosen, et repudiabant omnes Prophetas caeteros. Fingebant enim nec animas hominum esse immor- tales, nec futuram esse resuscitationem mortuo- rum. Ideoque Prophetas explodebant, ne eorum testimoniis refutari possent. Asseverabant autem iuste vivendum esse, et propter iusticiam a Deo hominibus in hac vita dari res utiles, bonam va- letudinem, facultates, potentiam, felicitatem in rebus gerendis, de regno Messiae fere eadem de- liramenta erant trium sectarum.

Tertia secta fuit Essaeorum, qui volebant videri utrisque antecellere, Pharisaeis et Zaddu- caeis. Ideo sibi nomen sumserunt ab agendo, quasi significantes caeteros verbis et disputationi- bus profiteri religionem, se vero actionibus. Hi differebant a Pharisaeis, quod res suas in com- mune conferebant, caetera fere conveniebant cum Pharisaeis.

Talis fuit species Ecclesiae seu populi Dei eo tempore, plurimi et praecipui sectas amplexi erant, alii alias, et hi inter se dissidebant. Et Pontifices, Sacerdotes, et qui videbantur esse ca- pita Ecclesiae, et ordinariam potestatem habe- bant, alias erant Pharisaei, alias Sadducaei, utri- que autem multa deliria defendebant. Itaque hi coetus errantes non erant Ecclesia Dei, sed inte- rim erant in populo pauci recte sentientes et in- vocantes Deum in agnitione vera Messiae, et fide, ut Simeon senex, Anna, Zacharias, Elizabeth, et horum auditores, hi erant Ecclesia Dei. Fa- tendum est igitur pontifices et alios qui tenent gu- bernationem ordinariam, ut vocatur, posse er- rare. Ac profecto mirum est, in gente Iudaica, quae disciplinam gravissimam habuit, tam pro- phanam audaciam extitisse, ut palam licuerit ne- gare resuscitationem mortuorum, et animarum humanarum immortalitatem. Ostendit hoc exem- plum, amissa luce verbi Dei densissimas tenebras sequi, sicut in regno pontificio absurdissimae opi- niones, de cultu sanctorum, de transsubstantia- tione, de inferiis mortuorum, de Monachorum ceremoniis, magno plausu traditae sunt.

Consideremus igitur exemplum populi Iu- daici eius temporis, et discamus Ecclesiam veram non alligatam esse ad illos titulos, et gradus di- gnitatum, aut traditiones humanas, sed ad ver- bum Dei: ac nos confirmemus, ne propter pon- tificum titulos, aut propter paucitatem recte sen- tientium, deficiamus a verbo Dei. Nam et in illo populo pauci erant recte sentientes, et hi dissen- tiebant a pontificibus et sectis illis; quas ample- ctebatur aut certe sequebatur maior pars populi. Nunc venio ad narrationem in Ioanne.

## 3:1
There was a man from the Pharisees.

He added this for the reason that he might signify that a certain one of the chief teachers and rulers, who excelled others in erudition and doctrine, had posed a question to Christ concerning righteousness. But just as among the Monks some inquired more studiously after the truth, and did not stubbornly defend their errors, but were teachable, and listened to others, many of whom emerged from the darkness: so also Nicodemus desired to hear Christ concerning this new kind of doctrine. Because he had heard that the Baptist and Christ were criticizing the opinions of the Pharisees so harshly, and there was not such hard and iron-like stubbornness that he was not moved by the miracles, which signified that these men had been sent by God. The occasion of the question is therefore this: We know that the law of Moses was given by God, and that God demands these acts of worship and these works. Why therefore do you and the Baptist shout that we, performing these works, are not righteous, are not pleasing to God, but are under sin? Why do you condemn our exercises, by which we strive to tame the flesh, so that it may more easily obey the law of God? To these very interrogations the first proposition corresponds properly and aptly.

Unless one is born again, he will not be able to see the kingdom of God.

This general and not yet explained proposition is only a preparation for the following explanation, and is a refutation of the error of Nicodemus. You are mistaken, Nicodemus, he says: although it is true that the law was given by God, and these works are demanded, yet the law does not abolish the sin which is born with us. This external discipline of yours does not satisfy the law; hearts doubt concerning God, they are void of the fear of God, of trust, of love. In short, the nature of men is at war with that most beautiful order instituted in the law. Therefore you are not righteous by the law, and heirs of eternal life, on account of this discipline of yours, which many excellent men among the Gentiles also performed. There is need of another newness, so that with sin recognized, the recognition of God may begin to shine, and sin may be taken away, and true trust, love, and obedience may be kindled. In short, that discipline of yours is one thing, and this righteousness, which is the heir of eternal life, is quite another.

He declares this proposition with these words: That which is born of the flesh is flesh, that which is born of the spirit is spirit. Syllogisms are instituted, which it is necessary for me to weave together. Those born of a corrupt nature are corrupt flesh, captive to sin and death: the law does not abolish this captivity, it does not take away sin and death, therefore by the law you cannot attain righteousness and eternal life. The other syllogism is: That which is born of the spirit is spirit. Eternal life is a spiritual thing, true light, and the recognition of God, true love of God. Therefore it is necessary for the heirs of eternal life to be born again of the spirit. When the syllogisms are woven together in this way, it sufficiently appears that it is a declaration of the refutation, namely that by the law the captivity of sin and death in the flesh cannot be abolished: likewise, that it is necessary for the heirs of eternal life to be born again of the spirit. Furthermore, this whole refutation is a sermon of repentance: It teaches that this discipline of the law is not righteousness before God, and does not take away sin.

But observe here in passing the antithesis of the words; it is certain that the spirit is called, not a part of man, but God moving and sanctifying minds, and the very modes arising from the Holy Spirit; therefore, on the contrary, flesh signifies not only the appetite of the senses, as Origen thought, but the whole nature of the unregenerate man, the appetite of the senses, the intellect, and the will; thus also Paul speaks in Romans 7 and 8.

But having heard this refutation, the Pharisee is stunned, because human reason sees no other righteousness except that of the law; what riddles, he says, are you speaking? Unless one is born again, can this nature be refashioned? I understand righteousness to be what this nature can perform. It is absurd that impossible things are required of us; it is enough to sweat and struggle, he thinks, for him who in this stadium of ours now urges the course of virtue so that he may not knowingly fall into vices. This very righteousness which we perform is a great and difficult thing. It is absurd that something else is required. This is certainly what the interrogation of the Pharisee means. How can these things be? Nor is it obscure that all political men most vehemently abhor this belittling of the righteousness of the law, or of the study of virtue, as they call it, nor do they think any speech is more pernicious to life than when the reverence of the law is diminished. Hence such great bitterness of hatred against the Gospel arises, especially in such men, just as Paul says: Ignorant of the righteousness of God, they seek to establish their own righteousness.

Latin:

Erat homo ex Pharisaeis.

Ideo asscripsit, ut significaret quendam ex praecipuis doctoribus et gubernatoribus, qui antecelluit eruditione et doctrina caeteris, movisse Christo quaestionem de iusticia. Ut autem inter Monachos aliqui studiosius inquisiverunt veritatem, nec pertinaciter defenderunt errores suos, sed fuerunt dociles, et alios audiverunt, quorum multi ex tenebris emerserunt: ita et Nicodemus audire Christum de hoc novo genere doctrinae cupiebat. Quia audierat, Baptistam et Christum tam duriter taxare Pharisaeorum opiniones, nec erat adeo dura et ferrea pertinacia, ut non moveretur miraculis, quae significabant hos viros a Deo missos esse. Est ergo occasio quaestionis haec: Scimus, legem Mosi a Deo datam esse, hos cultus, et haec opera Deum postulare. Cur ergo Baptista et tu clamitatis, Nos praestantes haec opera non esse iustos, non placere Deo, sed sub peccato esse? Cur damnatis exercitia nostra, quibus domare carnem studemus, ut facilius legi Dei obtemperet? Ad has ipsas interrogationes proprie et apte quadrat prima propositio.

Nisi quis renatus fuerit denuo, non poterit videre regnum Dei.

Haec generalis et nondum explicata propositio tantum est praeparatio ad sequentem explicationem, estque refutatio erroris Nicodemi. Erras Nicodeme, inquit: etsi verum est legem a Deo datam esse, et postulari haec opera, tamen lex non abolet peccatum, quod nobiscum nascitur. Haec vestra externa disciplina non satisfacit legi, corda dubitant de Deo, vacant timore Dei, fiducia, dilectione. Denique natura hominum belligeratur cum illo pulcerrimo ordine instituto in lege. Non igitur estis iusti lege, ac haeredes vitae aeternae, propter hanc vestram disciplinam, quam et ethnici multi excellentes viri praestiterunt. Alia novitate opus est, ut cognito peccato, incipiat lucere agnitio Dei, et tolli peccatum, et accendi vera fiducia, dilectio et obedientia. Denique prorsus aliud est ista vestra disciplina, aliud ista iusticia, quae est haeres vitae aeternae.

Hanc propositionem declarat his verbis: Quod natum est ex carne, caro est, quod natum est ex spiritu, spiritus est. Syllogismi instituun- tur, quos pertexi ambos oportet. Nati ex cor- rupta natura, sunt caro corrupta, captiva peccati et mortis: lex non abolet hanc captivitatem, non tollit peccatum et mortem, ergo lege non potestis consequi iusticiam, et vitam aeternam. Alter syllogismus est: Quod natum est ex spiritu, spi- ritus est. Vita aeterna est res spiritualis, vera lux, et Dei agnitio, vera dilectio Dei. Ergo ne- cesse est haeredes vitae aeternae renasci ex spiritu. Cum hoc modo pertexuntur syllogismi, satis ap- paret esse declarationem refutationis, scilicet quod lege non possit aboleri captivitas peccati et mortis in carne: item, quod oporteat haeredes vitae aeternae renasci ex spiritu. Porro haec tota refutatio est concio poenitentiae: Docet hanc di- sciplinam legis non esse iusticiam coram Deo, non tollere peccatum.

Obiter autem hic observa antithesin vocabu- lorum, certum est vocari spiritum, non partem hominis, sed Deum moventem et sanctificantem mentes, et ipsos modus a Spiritu sancto ortos, ergo econtra caro significat non tantum appetitum sensuum, ut Origenes putavit: sed totam natu- ram hominis non renati appetitum sensuum, in- tellectum et voluntatem, sic et Paulus loquitur Rom. 7. et 8.

Audita autem hac refutatione, Pharisaeus obstupescit, quia humana ratio non aliam iusti- ciam videt, nisi legis, quae aenigmata, inquit, dicis? Nisi quis renatus fuerit, num potest haec natura refingi? Ego iusticiam intelligo, quam haec natura praestare potest. Absurdum est re- quiri a nobis impossibilia, satis sudandum, et de- certandum ei esse puta, qui in hoc nostro stadio nunc cursum virtutis ita urget, ne ruat sciens in vitia. Magna et difficilis res est haec ipsa iusticia, quam nos praestamus. Absurdum est aliud re- quiri. Hoc certe vult interrogatio Pharisaei. Quomodo possunt haec fieri? Nec obscurum est omnes politicos viros vehementissime abhorrere ab hac extenuatione iusticiae legis, seu studii vir- tutis, ut ipsi loquuntur, nec ullam orationem existimant magis perniciosam esse vitae, quam cum reverentia legis minuitur. Hinc tanta acer- bitas odii adversus Evangelium oritur, praecipue in talibus viris, sicut Paulus dicit: Ignoran- tes Dei iusticiam, suam iusticiam stabilire co- nantur.

## 3:5
Unless one is born again of water, etc.

The refutation of the Pharisee is first proposed generally: Unless one is born again. Afterwards the same sentiment is repeated, with the addition of a brief, but not yet complete, declaration which makes mention of the ministry. For Christ leads us at the beginning to the ministry of the Gospel, as if he were saying: I understand, Nicodemus, that you are offended by the new sermons of the Baptist and my own, because we say that sin is not taken away by your exercises and discipline, but I affirm this absolutely, and I lead you to this new ministry. You must be born again through this new ministry of baptism, which is performed by water and spirit. Therefore, he first points out the ministry, but the matter is not yet fully explained. It must also be added how it is effective through this ministry.

Furthermore, Nicodemus is more astonished, having heard the mention of baptism; what is this thing? Is this new ceremony worth more than circumcision? More than the law of Moses, delivered with such great miracles? How little is this, to be dipped in water? To a wise man, and one comparing external works among themselves, all these things seem quite absurd; wherefore he confesses his ignorance, and as if indignant, and about to leave this teacher, he again asks that absurd, inept, and impossible things be spoken: How, he says, can these things be? And so, before Christ finishes the entire sermon, he interposes a very harsh rebuke: Are you a teacher in Israel, and do you not know these things? As if he were saying: You and your like are the governors of the Church of God, and you are ignorant of the doctrine which is proper to the Church alone. Since, therefore, you neither understand nor perform your duty, you will pay the most serious penalties to God, and you will be shaken out of your governance: Do you think there is no difference between the Gentiles and the Church of God? The things which you teach concerning honest exercises and discipline, the nations also know, but to you not only was the law delivered, but also the promises concerning the Messiah; these you pervert and twist toward worldly empires; you have not known sin, nor justice, nor the office of the Messiah, and yet in the Church you boast yourselves to be teachers of true justice and co-heirs of the kingdom of the Messiah.

Latin:

Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua, etc.

Refutatio Pharisaei primum generaliter pro- ponitur: Nisi quis renatus fuerit. Postea repe- titur eadem sententia, adiecta brevi, sed non- dum integra declaratione, quae facit mentionem ministerii. Deducit enim Christus nos initio ad ministerium Evangelii, quasi dicat: Intelligo te Nicodeme offendi novis concionibus Baptistae et meis, quod dicimus vestris exercitiis et disciplina non tolli peccatum, sed hoc prorsus affirmo, te- que ad hoc novum ministerium deduco. Renasci te oportet per hoc novum ministerium baptismi, qui fit aqua et spiritu. Primum igitur monstrat ministerium, sed nondum integre explicata res est. Addendum est etiam quomodo sit efficax per hoc ministerium.

Porro Nicodemus magis obstupescit, audita mentione baptismi, quid hoc rei est? Num plus valet haec nova ceremonia, quam circumcisio? plusne, quam lex Mosi, tradita tantis miraculis? quantulum est hoc mergi in aquam? Haec omnia viro sapienti, et externa opera inter sese confe- renti, admodum videntur absurda, quare suam ignorantiam confitetur, et quasi stomachans, et relicturus hunc magistrum, rursus quaeritur ab- surda, inepta et impossibilia dici: Quomodo, inquit, possunt haec fieri? Itaque Christus prius- quam integram concionem absolvit, interponit obiurgationem durissimam: Tune es magister in Israël, et haec ignoras? quasi dicat: Tu et tui si- miles estis gubernatores Ecclesiae Dei, et do- ctrinam, quae solius Ecclesiae propria est, igno- ratis. Cum igitur officium vestrum nec intellige- tis, nec faciatis, Deo poenas gravissimas dabitis, et ex gubernatione vestra excutiemini: Nihilne interesse inter Ethnicos et Ecclesiam Dei censes? ea quae de honestis exercitiis, et disciplina doce- tis, norunt et gentes, sed vobis non tantum lex tradita est, sed etiam promissiones de Messia, has depravatis et detorquetis ad mundi imperia, non peccatum, non iusticiam, non Messiae offi- cium novistis, et tamen in Ecclesia iactatis vos doctores verae iusticiae, et cohaeredes regni Messiae.

## 3:11
But we speak what we know, etc.

Here the antithesis must be considered. For the Pharisees are censured, who, having omitted the true doctrine delivered from heaven, the law of God, and the promises, proposed uncertain opinions and traditions fabricated by human authority, or rather by audacity. But in the Church the voice of God ought to sound, not uncertain and fictitious opinions, such as were, to the nations, the religions of Numa Pompilius and the like. Therefore Peter says in 1 Peter 4:11: He who speaks (namely, in the Church) let him speak the oracles of God. For Peter there gives instructions concerning the ministry of the Church.

Then Christ begins to preach about the Messiah, on account of whom baptism is effective, and he fully declares that former proposition. He led us to the ministry, to baptism. Why was this instituted here, and how is it effective? On account of the Messiah. Concerning this matter he now preaches, and he now proposes to the Pharisee sentiments more new and wonderful than the former ones were. For the Pharisee, thinking about the Messiah, expects only an empire of the world, flourishing with justice, peace, and other virtues, like a poetic golden age. Christ censures these errors and shows that the Messiah will not only not have worldly empires, but will also be a victim to be slaughtered for the human race, and this is the first proposition.

Latin:

Nos vero quod scimus loquimur, etc.

Hic antithesis consideranda est. Taxantur enim Pharisaei, qui omissa vera doctrina de coelo tradita, lege Dei, et promissionibus, propone- bant incertas opiniones et traditiones confictas humana autoritate, seu audacia potius. At in Ecclesia vox Dei sonare debet, non incertae et commentitiae opiniones, ut fuerunt ad gentes, Numae Pompilii religiones, et similes. Ideo Pe- trus inquit 1. Petri 8.: Qui loquitur (videlicet in Ecclesia) loquatur sermones Dei. Nam Petrus ibi de ministerio Ecclesiae praecipit.

Deinde Christus incipit de Messia concio- nari, propter quem baptismus est efficax, et illam superiorem propositionem integre declarat. De- duxit nos ad ministerium, ad baptismum. Cur hic est institutus, et quomodo est efficax? Propter Messiam. Hac de re iam concionatur, et senten- tias Pharisaeo iam proponit magis novas et mi- randas, quam fuerunt superiores. Nam Phari- saeus de Messia cogitans, tantum expectat impe- rium mundi, florens iusticia, pace, et aliis vir- tutibus, tanquam auream aetatem poëticam. Hos errores Christus taxat, et ostendit, Messiam non solum non habiturum imperia mundana, sed etiam fore victimam mactandam pro humano ge- nere, estque prima propositio.

## 3:13
No one has ascended into heaven, except he who descended from heaven.

The error of the Pharisees is refuted, who thought that sin was taken away, and the wrath of God appeased, by those exercises of theirs. Christ takes away this praise from all men, Noah, Abraham, Moses, and all the saints. No one has ascended into heaven, namely, appeasing the wrath of God. No one has ascended without a mediator appeasing the wrath of God, except me; and the reason is added: Because I descended from heaven, I am he whom God promised that he would send, so that he might take away sin and death; this liberator was to come from heaven, as he says in another place: Glorify me, Father, with yourself with that glory which I had with you before the world was. This sentiment was new to the Pharisee, who was ignorant that the Son of God had been from the beginning. And the following sentiment has more obscurity, when he says: Who is in heaven. How does he both descend, and is in heaven? The Son of God descended, because he both put on human nature, and is humbled below every human grasp, while he becomes a victim for the sins of the human race, and yet he is in heaven, that is, he sees the Father, and retains divine power, just as it is said in chapter 5: My Father works until now, and I work. Let thoughts about place be omitted here; in the descent mention is made of humiliation and mortality. While he says that he is in heaven, he makes mention of the eternal society with God, by which he sees the Father, and is efficacious with him, although, as Irenaeus says, he restrained his power when the flesh was suffering; these are the words of Irenaeus: that Christ suffered while the Word was at rest, so that he could be crucified and die.

Latin:

Nemo ascendit in coelum, nisi qui descendit de coelo.

Refutatur error Pharisaeorum, qui putabant tolli peccatum, et placari iram Dei, illis suis exer- citiis. Christus detrahit hanc laudem omnibus hominibus, Noae, Abrahae, Mosi, et omnibus sanctis. Nemo ascendit in coelum, videlicet, placans iram Dei. Nemo ascendit sine mediatore placante iram Dei, nisi ego; et adiicitur ratio: Quia ego descendi de coelo, ego sum ille, quem Deus pollicitus est, se missurum esse, ut tollat peccatum et mortem, de coelo venturus erat hic liberator, ut alio loco dicit: Glorifica me pater apud te ea gloria, quam habui ante mundum apud te. Haec sententia Pharisaeo nova erat, qui ignorabat filium Dei fuisse ab initio. Ac sequens sententia plus habet obscuritatis, cum ait: Qui est in coelo. Quomodo et descendit, et est in coelo? Descendit filius Dei, quia et induit natu- ram humanam, et humiliatur infra omnem ca- ptum humanum, dum fit victima pro peccatis ge- neris humani, et tamen est in coelo, id est, cer- nit patrem, et retinet potentiam divinam, sicut cap. 5. dicitur: Pater meus usque modo operatur, et ego operor. Omittantur hic cogitationes de loco, in descensu fit mentio humiliationis et mortalitatis. Dum ait, se esse in coelo, facit mentionem aeternae societatis cum Deo, qua patrem videt, et cum eo est efficax, tametsi, ut inquit Irenaeus, potentiam cohibuit, cum caro pateretur, verba Irenaei haec sunt: Christum passum esse requiescente verbo, ut crucifigi ac mori posset.

## 3:14
As Moses lifted up the serpent.

The previous proposition said: That the wrath of God is appeased only through the Messiah, that only the Messiah ascends into heaven, that is, that he is the mediator and appeaser of the wrath of God. There follows a second proposition, which preaches about the death of the Messiah, and about the manner in which we apprehend his benefit. As Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the son of man be lifted up, that is, just as the dead serpent was set before you in the desert to be looked upon, and those who looked upon it were healed: so your Messiah will hang dead, but this death will be salutary for you if you look upon him, that is, if you recognize the Messiah, and by trust in him believe that you are received by God and healed. The Pharisee was more amazed at this sermon. For he dreams of a golden age, he does not think of the most foul punishment of the Messiah, nor does he know that he is sent to become a victim to appease the wrath of God. No creature can comprehend the magnitude of the divine wrath against sin. Therefore human minds think securely about God, as if about an oblivious king, but the magnitude of human calamities signifies that there is a true and horrible wrath, but the offering of the son declares this much more, which testifies that the force of the wrath of God is so great that God would not have been willing to be swayed except by the intercession, obedience, and death of the son. The Pharisee did not understand this, not discerning the deformity of sin, and thinking coldly about wrath, and admiring his own righteousness immoderately. Let us therefore listen to Christ, who rebukes these shadows of human hypocrisy, and testifies that the wrath of God is not appeased except through the son interceding for us, and diverting the wrath onto himself.

This is also signified by the type which Christ adapts here, from the 21st chapter of Numbers. Struck by fiery serpents, when they looked upon the bronze serpent, ordained for this purpose by the command of God, they were healed. The explanation is easy; human nature was horribly struck by the serpent in the fall of our parents. Fiery and most sharp was the force of the poison which that serpent breathed, that is, of the persuasion or deception which impelled minds to disobedience, which was followed by the despoiling of heavenly goods and death. But because these things are common to all, we consider them lighter. This serpent does not rest, but with new bites inflames the old poison in individuals, nor is there anyone who is not wounded by some significant wound, so that he might snatch a friend's spouse or kill a husband. When the serpent had made this wound in the heart of David, what slaughters of sons, what sedition, what raped spouses followed afterwards? By these such great evils, the wound of David was most cruelly lacerated. Here he felt that he was not righteous by his own purity, here he felt the magnitude of human misery, and the force of the curse, and he opposed the promise and learned to understand the blessing promised on account of the Messiah, that he was about to liberate us from the cruelty of the devil and the kingdom of sin. As it is written later in John: The Son of God appeared that he might destroy the works of the devil. By this faith in the mercy of God promised on account of the Messiah as intercessor and liberator, David sustained himself.

But as the bronze serpent is erected in the desert by divine command, so also the Messiah is sent by the command of the eternal Father, and becomes a victim. As therefore the dead serpent, so Christ hangs dead on the cross, who himself also bears the figure of a serpent, because he put on a similar nature of sinful flesh, and one sustaining the punishments of sin, the sense of the wrath of God and death: but as those looking upon that figure were healed, so God wishes the Messiah to be looked upon, that is, to be acknowledged and believed, that by his interceding and liberating we are healed. Let these things be declared thus in the text itself, for it follows.

So must the son of man be lifted up, that everyone who believes in him may not perish.

Now this part of the sermon is added to the previous one, when it was being spoken about the ministry: Unless one has been reborn of water and the spirit. How does this regeneration happen? How is the Holy Spirit efficacious? How does new and eternal righteousness and life shine forth in a man? He answers by looking into the crucified Christ, that is, by faith or trust apprehending mercy. When in repentance and true terrors we are sustained and raised up by faith, it is certain that reconciliation happens, that sins are forgiven, and the Holy Spirit is given. For at the same time, when we are sustained by this very faith, the Holy Spirit is received, as it is said in Galatians 3: That we might receive the promise of the spirit through faith. Therefore also Habakkuk 2 says: The righteous shall live by his faith, that is, by faith we obtain, [we are] righteous, that is, we are accounted accepted by God, and we are made alive, that is, we are clothed with new life and light, which is the beginning of eternal life. And Zech. 12: I will pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitant of Israel the spirit of grace and of prayers. This is also a clear description of reconciliation and regeneration. The spirit of grace, that is, which testifies in us that we are pleasing and accepted by God, this happens when we are raised up by faith, and we determine that our sins are forgiven us on account of Christ. Then, having acknowledged the mercy of God, we begin to call upon him, and to submit ourselves to him, just as Paul says, Rom. 8: You have received the spirit of adoption of sons, by which we cry Abba Father. Wherefore Zechariah most aptly names the spirit of prayers, because invocation is the proper worship of the Church alone, and then it embraces the rest of obedience.

Latin:

Sicut Moses exaltavit serpentem.

Prior propositio dixit: Per solum Messiam placari iram Dei, solum Messiam ascendere in coelum, hoc est, esse mediatorem et placatorem irae Dei. Sequitur secunda propositio, quae concionatur de morte Messiae, et de modo, quo beneficium eius apprehendimus. Sicut Moses exaltavit serpentem in deserto, sic exaltari oportet filium hominis, id est, ut mortuus serpens in deserto proponebatur vobis conspiciendus, et sanabantur illi, qui eum aspiciebant: ita vester Messias pendebit mortuus, sed haec mors erit vobis salutaris, si aspicietis, id est, si cognoscetis Messiam, et fiducia ipsius credetis vos recipi a Deo, ac sanari. Hanc concionem Pharisaeus magis miratus est. Is enim somniat aureum seculum, non cogitat Messiae foedissimum supplicium, nec scit mitti eum, ut fiat victima ad placandam iram Dei. Nulla creatura magnitudinem irae divinae adversus peccatum comprehendere potest. Ideo humanae mentes secure de Deo, tanquam de oblivioso rege cogitant, sed veram et horribilem iram esse magnitudo calamitatum humanarum significat, verum multo magis id declarat filii oblatio, quae testatur tantam vim irae Dei esse, ut nisi deprecatione, obedientia et morte filii, flecti Deus non voluerit. Haec non intellexit Pharisaeus, non cernens peccati deformitatem, et de ira frigide cogitans, et suam iusticiam immodice admirans. Nos igitur audiamus Christum, qui reprehendit has tenebras humanae hypocrisis, ac testatur non placari iram Dei, nisi per filium deprecantem pro nobis, et derivantem iram in sese.

Haec significat et typus, quem Christus huc accommodat, ex 21. cap. Num. Icti a serpentibus igneis, cum aspiciebant aeneum serpentem, ad hoc ordinatum mandato Dei, sanabantur. Facilis est enarratio, natura humana horribiliter icta est a serpente in lapsu parentum. Ignea et acerrima fuit vis veneni, quod afflavit ille serpens, id est, persuasionis seu deceptionis, quae impulit mentes ad inobedientiam, quam secuta est bono- rum coelestium spoliatio et mors. Sed haec quia communia sunt omnium, leviora ducimus. Non quiescit hic serpens, sed novis morsibus ac- cendit vetus venenum in singulis, nec quisquam est, qui non saucietur aliquo in signi vulnere, ut raperet amici coniugem, interficeret maritum. Hoc vulnus cum fecisset serpens in corde Davidis, quae postea secutae sunt caedes filiorum, seditio, stupratae coniuges? His tantis malis vulnus Da- vidis crudelissime laceratum est. Hic sensit se non esse iustum sua munditie, hic sensit magni- tudinem miseriae humanae, et vim maledictionis, et opposuit promissionem ac didicit intelligere be- nedictionem promissam propter Messiam, quod a saevitia diaboli et regno peccati nos liberatu- rus sit. Sicut postea in Ioanne scriptum est: Fi- lius Dei apparuit, ut destruat opera diaboli. Hac fide misericordiae Dei promissae propter Messiam deprecatorem et liberatorem, David se susten- tabat.

Ut autem in deserto aeneus serpens erigitur mandato divino, ita et Messias mandato aeterni patris mittitur, et fit victima. Ut igitur mortuus serpens, pendet in cruce Christus mortuus, qui et ipse figuram gerit serpentis, quia induit simi- lem naturam carnis peccati, ac sustinentem poe- nas peccati, sensum irae Dei et mortem: sed ut sanabantur aspicientes figuram illam, ita vult Deus aspici Messiam, id est, agnosci et credi, quod ipso deprecante et liberante sanemur. Haec ita declarentur in ipso textu, sequitur enim.

Sic oportet filium hominis exaltari, ut omnis qui credit in eum, non pereat.

Iam haec pars concionis superiori additur, cum de ministerio diceretur: Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua et spiritu. Quomodo fit haec re- generatio? quomodo est efficax Spiritus sanctus? quomodo illucescit in homine nova et aeterna iu- sticia et vita? Respondet intuendo in Christum crucifixum, hoc est, fide seu fiducia apprehen- dente misericordiam. Cum in poenitentia et ve- ris terroribus fide sustentamur et erigimur, cer- tum est fieri reconciliationem, remitti peccata, et donari Spiritum sanctum. Simul enim, cum hac ipsa fide sustentamur, accipitur Spiritus san- ctus, ut ad Gal. 3. dicitur: Ut promissionem spiritus accipiamus per fidem. Ideo et Hab. 2 ait: Iustus fide sua vivet, id est, fide utrunq consequimur, iusti, hoc est, accepti Deo reputa- mur, et vivificamur, hoc est, nova vita et luce induimur, quae est incoatio vitae aeternae. Et Zach. 12.: Effundam super domum David et su- per habitatorem Israël spiritum gratiae et pre- cum. Est et haec luculenta descriptio reconcilia- tionis et regenerationis. Spiritus gratiae, id est, qui testificatur in nobis, nos Deo gratos et ac- ceptos esse, id fit, cum fide erigimur, ac statui- mus nobis remitti peccata propter Christum. Deinde agnita misericordia Dei, incipimus eum invocare, et nos ei subiicere, sicut Paulus inquit, Rom. 8.: Accepistis spiritum adoptionis filiorum, quo clamamus Abba pater. Quare Zacharias ap- tissime nominat spiritum precum, quia invocatio proprius cultus est solius Ecclesiae, ac deinde re- liquam obedientiam complectitur.

## 3:15
He who believes in him is not judged.

Sin clings to all men, on account of which all are guilty, and another sin is added in many, the contempt of the Son of God, as will be said below: The Holy Spirit will convict the world of sin, because they do not believe in me. Where, therefore, there is no acknowledgment of mercy and of reconciliation promised on account of the Son, it is necessary that eternal wrath follow: because sin is not remitted, but accumulated. On the contrary, where the remission of sins is received by the acknowledgment of the Son of God and by faith, minds are freed from the wrath of God. The saying of Christ has nothing of obscurity, but the antithesis must be considered. The Pharisee thought that sin and the wrath of God were taken away and eternal life given on account of the law; he thought nothing of the sort about the Messiah, but dreamed that he would govern the empire of the world. But on the contrary, Christ says: sin and the wrath of God are taken away, and eternal life is given, if we believe in this Son, the Messiah and Savior.

Latin:

Qui credit in ipsum, non iudicatur.

Haeret peccatum in omnibus hominibus, propter quod omnes sunt rei, et accedit alterum peccatum in multis, contemtu filii Dei, sicut in- fra dicetur: Spiritus sanctus arguet mundum de peccato, quia non credunt in me. Ubi igitur non est agnitio misericordiae, et reconciliationis propter filium promissae, necesse est sequi aeter- nam iram: quia peccatum non est remissum, sed cumulatum. Econtra, ubi agnitione filii Dei, et fide accipitur remissio peccatorum, liberantur mentes ab ira Dei. Dictum Christi nihil habet obscuritatis, sed antithesis consideranda est. Pharisaeus putabat tolli peccatum, et iram Dei, et dari vitam aeternam propter legem, de Messia nihil tale cogitabat, sed somniabat gubernaturum esse mundi imperium. At econtra Christus ait: ita tolli peccatum et iram Dei, ac dari vitam ae- ternam, si credamus in hunc Filium, Messiam et Salvatorem.

## 3:16
For God so loved the world, etc.

Christ has already preached quite clearly concerning faith and justification, yet he now inculcates the same sentiment again, with the addition of a brief commemoration of the cause. For God so loved the world. This part of the sermon even more surpasses human comprehension than the former. Reason does not perceive that men are loved by God, since human nature is oppressed by such great miseries and calamities; then the voice of the law is added, which even more denounces wrath, and the judgment of conscience is added, which is, as Paul says: A handwriting written against us, that testifies that we are stubborn against the law of God. Whence therefore is it certain that we are loved by God? Here Christ brings forth this Gospel with his own voice, from the bosom of the eternal Father. Indeed, he says, God loves men, and adds an evident testimony, because he gave his only-begotten son, he made him a victim for the human race.

It is a wonderful counsel, and one far surpassing the comprehension of all angels and men, and at the thought of which all men ought to have trembled, just as the whole of nature trembled when the son of God hung on the cross. Nor is there any more illustrious testimony on both sides, of the wrath of God and of mercy, than the death of the son. There are many other signs of the wrath of God against sin, such as the death of the whole human race, and singular punishments above nature, such as the flood common to the whole world, the conflagration of Sodom, the destruction of Pharaoh in the water, when Israel had not perished on the same path, finally the infinite calamities of all men, but these punishments are all inferior to the death of the son of God.
