It is necessary therefore that there be a true and huge wrath, which could not be appeased in any other way, not by the murder of Abel, not by the death and other miseries of all the saints. Now let us consider how great an impiety it is, with such great examples of wrath proposed, nevertheless securely either to neglect or to despise the judgment of God. But as sin is accumulated in those who despise the death of the son of God, so again for those who are terrified, it is the highest testimony of the mercy of God; this distinction Christ delivers below: He who does evil, hates the light. The secure, the iron-hearted, not doing penance, despise the death of the son of God, but others, who do the truth, who are not secure Epicureans or hypocrites, but acknowledge the judgment of God, and yield to the truth, confess themselves to be guilty, are terrified and flee to God according to the promises, to these the death of the son of God will be a pledge of mercy, and of these it is said: That everyone who believes in him, may not perish, but have eternal life. Moreover, this passage warns: What faith is, namely to believe that we are loved by God on account of the son, or, which is the same thing, stated in other words, trust in mercy on account of the son. And to explain these, it is necessary to add from Paul the particle freely, that is, that we are received on account of the son, although we are unworthy. For monks everywhere in the histories of the Gospel overwhelm and deprave all these sermons about faith, inventing a false interpretation: You are loved thus, it is profitable to believe in the son thus, if you have enough merits. This interpretation transforms the Gospel into law, and extinguishes faith. For the Gospel shows Christ for this reason, because we do not have merits, and we do not satisfy the law. Wherefore the particle Freely must be diligently observed, so that it may be truly understood what Christ calls faith here, namely the trust that we are loved and received by God on account of the son the mediator freely, when indeed we are unworthy and guilty; moreover, the particle must be observed, that the son is named only-begotten, for here he is distinguished from adopted sons. For since Christ is called properly begotten by the father, it is necessary that he be of the substance of the father, as was said above.

Latin:

Sic enim Deus dilexit mundum, etc.

De fide et iustificatione iam satis perspicue concionatus est Christus, tamen eandem senten- tiam iam rursus inculcat, addita brevi comme- moratione causae. Sic Deus dilexit mundum. Haec pars concionis etiam magis superat captum humanum, quam superiora. Non cernit ratio diligi homines a Deo, cum tantis aerumnis et ca- lamitatibus humana natura oppressa sit, deinde accedit vox legis, quae magis etiam denunciat iram, accedit et iudicium conscientiae, quod est ut Paulus inquit: Chirographum scriptum contra nos, id testatur nos contumaces esse legi Dei. Unde igitur constat nos diligi a Deo? Hic Chri- stus sua voce profert hoc Evangelium, ex sinu aeterni patris. Imo, inquit, Deus diligit homi- nes, et testimonium evidens addit, quia filium suum unigenitum dedit, fecit victimam pro ge- nere humano.

Mirum est consilium, et longe superans omnium angelorum atque hominum captum, et cuius cogitatione omnes homines contremiscere oportebat, sicut tota natura contremuit, cum filius Dei in cruce penderet. Nec ullum est illustrius testimonium in utranque partem, irae Dei et mi- sericordiae, quam mors filii. Multa sunt alia signa irae Dei adversus peccatum, ut mors totius generis humani, et singulares poenae supra natu- ram, ut diluvium commune toti orbi, Sodomo- rum conflagratio, Pharaonis interitus in aqua, cum Israël in eadem via non interiisset, denique infinitae omnium hominum calamitates, sed hae poenae omnes inferiores sunt morte filii Dei. Ne- cesse est igitur veram et ingentem iram esse, quae placari alio modo non potuit, non nece Abel, non morte, et aliis miseriis omnium sanctorum. Iam cogitemus quanta sit impietas, propositis tantis exemplis irae, tamen secure, vel negligere, vel contemnere iudicium Dei. Sed ut peccatum cumulatur in his, qui mor- tem filii Dei contemnunt, ita rursus his qui expa- vescunt, est testimonium summum misericordiae Dei, hoc discrimen Christus infra tradit: Qui mala agit, odit lucem. Securi, ferrei, non agen- tes poenitentiam, contemnunt mortem filii Dei, sed alii, qui veritatem faciunt, qui non sunt se- curi Epicurei, vel hypocritae, sed agnoscunt iu- dicium Dei, et veritati cedunt, fatentur se esse reos, expavescunt et confugiunt ad Deum iuxta promissiones, his mors filii Dei erit pignus mise- ricordiae, et de his dicitur: Ut omnis qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam. Monet autem hic locus: Quid sit fides, scili- cet credere quod diligamur a Deo propter filium, seu, quod idem est, dictum aliis verbis, fiducia misericordiae propter filium. Et ad has explican- das, oportet addi ex Paulo particulam gratis, hoc est, quod propter filium recipiamur, quanquam indigni. Nam omnes has conciones de fide pas- sim in historiis Evangelii obruunt et depravant Monachi affingentes falsam interpretationem: Sic dligeris, sic prodest credere in filium, si satis habeas meritorum. Haec interpretatio transfor- mat Evangelium in legem, et extinguit fidem. Nam Evangelium ideo monstrat Christum, quia non habemus merita, et legi non satisfacimus. Quare diligenter observanda est particula Gratis, ut vere intelligatur, quid hic fidem nominet Chri- stus, videlicet fiduciam, quod a Deo diligamur et recipiamur propter filium mediatorem gratis, cum quidem simus indigni et rei, observanda est autem particula, quod filius nominatur unige- nitus, nam hic discernitur a filiis adoptatis. Nam cum Christus vocetur proprie genitus a patre, ne- cesse est eum esse de substantia patris, ut supra dictum est.

## 3:17
For God did not send his son, that he might judge, etc.

He repeats the same sermon much more sweetly, even if the son judges the world, as is said elsewhere, John 9: I have come into this world for judgment etc., yet he speaks here of the principal cause of his mission, and soon meets the objection: He who does not believe is already judged. A sentence has already been passed upon all who despise this savior, but yet there will be some who do not despise him; the whole human race will not perish; there will be some group that will hear this son, and will believe in him, and will be saved.

Latin:

Non enim misit Deus filium suum, ut iu- dicet, etc.

Repetit eandem concionem multo dulcius, etsi filius iudicat mundum, ut alias dicitur, Ioann. 9.: In iudicium veni in hunc mundum etc., ta- men hic loquitur de principali causa suae missio- nis, et mox occurrit obiectioni: Qui non credit, iam iudicatus est. Iam est lata sententia de omni- bus contemnentibus hunc salvatorem, sed tamen erunt aliqui non contemnentes, non peribit totum genus humanum, erit aliquis coetus, qui audiet hunc filium, et credet ei, ac salvabitur.

## 3:18
But he who does not believe is already judged, etc.

The sentence of condemnation does not need a new promulgation, because immediately after the fall of our first parents, the entire posterity was oppressed by sin and death, on account of the sentence passed before in Paradise: You shall die the death. Therefore, all men are already judged, that is, condemned. As Paul says, Rom. 5: All have sinned, that is, they are guilty and lack the glory of God. And to the Ephesians 2: We were by nature children of wrath. But liberation happens in this way, when by faith we acknowledge the Son, and receive reconciliation, and are transferred from the kingdom of darkness into the kingdom of the Son of God, and are gifted with new light and eternal life through the voice of the Gospel. Since, therefore, a condemnation has preceded that encompasses the whole human race, and those who are not liberated remain in that condemnation, it is rightly said here: He who does not believe is already judged. Furthermore, this very condemnation, or wrath of God, although it ought to have been understood from death and other calamities, yet it has also been declared by the word of God through the Fathers, Prophets, Christ, and the Apostles, and this voice showing the wrath of God ought always to sound in the Church. Therefore, Paul begins his sermon thus: The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and injustice of men. Likewise Psalm 13: God looked down from heaven upon the sons of men, etc. All have turned aside, etc. These sermons are sentences already passed upon all, but those who receive reconciliation by the acknowledgment of the word of God, or faith, are snatched from this condemnation. But it must be diligently considered that he says the cause of condemnation is not believing in the Son of God. For although sin clinging to nature is also a cause in the unbeliever, yet because this sin is ruled by faith in those who believe, even if it remains in reality, it does not condemn, but grace abounds over sin.

All these things seemed new and absurd to the Pharisee, and in general they are alien to human judgments, which only understand the justice of the law. It is a wonder to you yourself, also acknowledging your own weakness, that God affirms that he wants to give you eternal life on account of the Son, when you are so vicious; it would seem more consistent to you to become an heir of eternal life if you discovered in yourself wonderful virtues, flames of the love of God, excellent divine light. Because you do not discover these in yourself, you doubt, but the voice of the Gospel rebukes this very doubt, which commands you to believe that God, on account of the Son the mediator, truly wants to receive and hear you. These exercises ought to be known to the pious.

Latin:

Qui autem non credit, iam iudicatus est, etc.

Sententia damnationis non habet opus nova promulgatione, quia statim post lapsum primo- rum parentum, oppressa est peccato et morte uni- versa posteritas, propter sententiam ante latam in Paradiso: Morte morieris. Iam igitur iudicati, hoc est, damnati sunt omnes homines. Sicut Paulus inquit, Rom. 5.: Omnes peccaverunt, id est, rei sunt, et carent gloria Dei. Et ad Ephes. 2.: Eramus natura filii irae. Sic autem fit libe- ratio, cum fide agnoscimus filium, et accipimus reconciliationem, et ex regno tenebrarum tradu- cimur in regnum filii Dei, et per vocem Evangelii nova luce, et vita aeterna donamur. Cum igitur praecesserit damnatio complexa totum genus hu- manum, et hi qui non liberantur, maneant in ea damnatione, recte hic dicitur: Qui non credit, iam iudicatus est. Porro haec ipsa damnatio, seu ira Dei, etsi ex morte et caeteris calamitatibus in- telligi debebat, tamen etiam verbo Dei per Patres, Prophetas, Christum et Apostolos declarata est, et semper haec vox ostendens iram Dei, in Ecclesia sonare debet. Ideo Paulus sic orditur suam con- cionem: Revelatur ira Dei de coelo super omnem iniquitatem et iniusticiam hominum. Item Psal. 13.: Deus de coelo respexit super filios homi- num, etc. Omnes declinaverunt etc. Hae con- ciones sunt sententiae iam latae de omnibus, sed ab hac condemnatione eripiuntur hi, qui agni- tione verbi Dei, seu fide accipiunt reconciliatio- nem. Diligenter autem considerandum est, quod causam damnationis ait esse, non credere in filium Dei. Etsi enim peccatum haerens in natura etiam causa est in non credente, tamen quia hoc pecca- tum regitur fide in his qui credunt, etiamsi ma- neat reipsa, tamen non damnat, sed gratia exu- berat supra peccatum.

Haec omnia videbantur Pharisaeo nova et absurda, et in universum aliena sunt a iudiciis humanis, quae tantum intelligunt iusticiam legis. Mirum est tibi ipsi quoque agnoscenti tuam im- becillitatem, quod Deus affirmet se tibi velle vi- tam aeternam dare, propter filium, cum adeo sis vitiosus, magis consentaneum tibi videretur, fieri haeredem vitae aeternae, si in te deprehenderes mirificas virtutes, flammas amoris Dei, excellen- tem lucem divinam. Haec quia non deprehendis in te, dubitas, at hanc ipsam dubitationem re- prehendit vox Evangelii, quae iubet credere, quod Deus propter filium mediatorem vere velit te recipere, et exaudire. Haec exercitia piis nota esse debent.

## 3:19
But this is the judgment, that light has come into the world.

He distinguishes, as I said above, between men; some receive the Son, others do not. But only those who receive the Son become saved; the rest perish. But those who hear the Gospel receive him, acknowledge that they are guilty, and that life is brought through the Son; he calls this judgment, that is, the preaching of the Gospel concerning repentance and the remission of sins. The light has come into the world, that is, Christ himself preaching this Gospel of repentance and remission of sins, which also always sounds in the Church on account of Christ. But the greatest part of the world despises this Christ and this Gospel; men love darkness, they do not acknowledge sin, nor the wrath of God, nor do they call upon God, nor do they seek a mediator, and the word in which God has revealed his will concerning the future judgment, concerning the remission of sins, concerning eternal life, where it is established that the greatest part of men are either Epicurean or hypocritical, and both love darkness. Concerning the Epicureans there is no doubt, because those who think the word of God to be fabulous remain in darkness and in ignorance of God, and are oppressed by eternal wrath. Thus also perish the hypocrites, like Saul, Judas, and others, although they do not wish to appear ἄθεοι, but boast that they acknowledge and fear God, yet they prefer certain opinions or desires of their own before the word of God, and in others there are other errors, other desires. In the Pharisees, the persuasion concerning a worldly kingdom and the admiration of the law were so deeply fixed that they most vehemently abhorred Christ, whom they saw was not a worldly king, and heard to diminish human justice. Fascinated by these opinions, they hated the word of God, nor did they call upon God in true faith, but rather variously provoked Him with blasphemies and tyranny. Therefore they remained in darkness, and were oppressed by punishments and the eternal wrath of God.

This is the history of the world in all times; the greatest part of men now also is Epicurean, others are hypocrites, as are wise men among the adversaries of the Gospel; in these, the most bitter hatreds of the Gospel exist for two reasons: when they see the present form of the polity, or Church, as they call it, being undermined and shaken, they cannot but be indignant, and they have many human reasons for this their grief. Then, when they hear certain things in the doctrine that are not very plausible, their fury is confirmed, as now, when the adversaries hear these sentences: That we are reputed righteous by faith on account of Christ, not on account of our virtues; that the invocation of the dead and the papistical Masses are idolatrous; their rage is wonderfully kindled. They remain, therefore, in darkness, as has been said above concerning others.

Latin:

Hoc est autem iudicium, quod lux venit in mundum.

Discernit, ut supra dixi, homines, alii acci- piunt filium, alii non accipiunt. Soli autem accipientes filium, fiunt salvi, caeteri pereunt. Accipiunt autem hi qui Evangelium audiunt, agnoscunt se reos esse, et afferri vitam per filium, hoc vocat iudicium, id est, praedi- cationem Evangelii de poenitentia et remissio- ne peccatorum. Lumen venit in mundum, id est, Christus ipse praedicans hoc Evangelium de poenitentia et remissione peccatorum, quod etiam propter Christum semper in Ecclesia sonat. Sed maxima pars mundi hunc Christum et hoc Evangelium contemnunt, diligunt homines te- nebras, non agnoscunt peccatum, nec iram Dei, nec invocant Deum, nec quaerunt mediatorem, et verbum, in quo Deus patefecit suam volunta- tem de futuro iudicio, de remissione peccatorum, de vita aeterna, u constat maximam partem ho- minum, aut esse Epicuream, aut hypocriticam, et utrique diligunt tenebras. De Epicureis non est dubium, quia, qui verbum Dei fabulosum esse existimant, manent in tenebris et in ignora- tione Dei, et aeterna ira opprimuntur. Sic per- eunt et hypocritae, ut Saul, Iudas, et alii, etsi non volunt videri ἄθεοι, sed iactitant se agno- scere et timere Deum, tamen suas quasdam vel opiniones, vel cupiditates anteferunt verbo Dei, et in aliis alii sunt errores, aliae cupiditates. Pharisaeis adeo infixa erat persuasio de regno mundano, et admiratio legis, ut vehementissime abhorrerent a Christo, quem videbant non esse mundanum regem, et audiebant extenuare iusti- ciam humanam. His opinionibus fascinati, ode- rant verbum Dei, nec invocabant Deum in vera fide, imo varie irritabant blasphemiis et tyran- nide. Ideo manserunt in tenebris, et oppressi sunt poenis et aeterna ira Dei.

Haec est mundi historia omnibus tempori- bus, maxima pars hominum nunc quoque est Epi- curea, alii sunt hypocritae, ut sapientes viri inter adversarios Evangelii, in his acerrima odia Evan- gelii existunt, propter duas causas, cum praesen- tem formam politiae, seu Ecclesiae, ut vocant, labefieri et concuti videant, non possunt non in- dignari, et multas habent humanas causas huius sui doloris. Deinde cum audiunt in doctrina quaedam parum plausibilia, confirmatur eorum furor, ut nunc, cum audiunt adversarii has sen- tentias: Quod fide iusti reputemur propter Chri- stump, non propter nostras virtutes, quod sit ido- latrica invocatio mortuorum, et Missae papisti- cae, mirabiliter accenditur rabies. Manent igi- tur in tenebris, ut de aliis supra dictum est.

## 3:21
On the contrary, he who does the truth comes to the light.

That is, acknowledging sin and the wrath of God, and preferring the word of God to his own opinions and desires. He hears the Gospel, and believing, becomes a son of God. Thus his works are done in God, that is, with God now governing.

Latin:

Econtra faciens veritatem venit ad lucem.

Id est, agnoscens peccatum et iram Dei, et anteferens verbum Dei propriis opinionibus et cu- piditatibus. Is audit Evangelium, et credens fit filius Dei. Ita fiunt eius opera in Deo, id est, Deo iam gubernante.

## 3:22
After these things came Jesus and his disciples, etc.

The first year after the baptism of Christ is still passing, and Christ had returned after the Passover into Galilee; now perhaps he returns to Judea for Pentecost; the Baptist had not yet been cast into prison, because he had now approached closer to Galilee, and was staying in a place near Tiberias by the Sea of Gennesaret. For not far from that lake were Aenon and Salem, of which mention is made here. For Jerome says that even in his own age there was a village whose name was Salimias, not far from Scythopolis, distant from Jerusalem about 10 of our miles.

But the question is repeated here concerning baptism, by whom it was instituted. Whether it is permitted for this Jesus and his disciples to baptize, or what difference there is between the two baptisms, what also the difference is between the persons, John and Jesus. Here a most serious discourse is recited, in which John distinguishes the persons, and most fully delivers the sum of the Gospel, and at the same time teaches that he performs a ministry which serves Him, that he does not seek or join the people to himself, but to lead them to Him, and that the ministry is effective on account of Him. He begins, however, from a general sentence most memorable; although he speaks properly of the Church, yet it is also a political precept, and because political examples are more easily understood, I shall begin the interpretation from these.

A man can receive nothing to himself, etc.

He discourses concerning events and progress. A man cannot manage great and salutary things for himself and the Republic, possess empires, establish a durable and lasting state, or retain authority, unless he is helped divinely. Antony, Cassius, Dolabella, and many others were seeking that place in the Roman empire which Julius had held; they had seen his example, and thought that they could attain by their own counsels and preparations the same things that he had attained. This κακοζηλία always deceives innumerable men in the world. But because God does not help Antony and the others, they are not only frustrated in their hope, but also bring destruction upon themselves, and entangle the Republic in pernicious wars. Meanwhile, God raises up the weak youth Augustus, lifts him up, fortifies, guards, and helps him, and hands over the Republic to him, with the others being driven away. So many illustrious examples warned this man to acknowledge that it is in vain for men to seek empires and governments unless they are divinely helped.

All ages and all histories are full of similar examples. Lentulus envies the glory of Scipio, and desires the praise of the finished Punic war to be transferred to himself, but the foolish man does not see that he is by no means like Scipio. He ought therefore to acknowledge his own mediocrity, and by no means compare himself to a superior. What is more common than that many attempt to pass laws, to reform their states, as they call it, but nothing salutary or durable is established unless God helps, as the laws of Solon, Augustus, and certain similar men were useful to the citizens and endured: meanwhile, how many futile amendments have disturbed the Attic and Roman state.

In such affairs of life let us consider this maxim: A man can take nothing to himself, unless it be given him from heaven. Let this maxim teach us that government is the work of God, let it warn us not to undertake great things without a calling; this modesty is useful to public peace and concord.

Although therefore it is also a political precept, yet because the Baptist speaks of the Church, let us speak of the ministries of the Church. Ministries, governments, worship, neither please God, nor are they effective, nor durable, unless God is the author and helper. John was a minister of baptism, to which he was divinely called by certain testimonies. This ministry therefore pleased God, was effective and durable. The same John acknowledged the manner of his calling, and so often professes that he is not the Messiah. If he were to take to himself another's honor, he would be cast off by God, and his government would quickly be dissipated. Therefore he prefaced it thus: A man cannot take anything to himself, unless it be given him from heaven. The government of King Ahaz was unhappy, although he labored much, attempted much, and diligently fortified himself with the defenses of neighboring kings. On the contrary, the government of Hezekiah was happy and salutary, because he was divinely helped. Jeremiah saved the people with a new and unusual plan, which kings, priests, and all the wise men opposed. Let us know that examples of this kind pertain to this maxim, and let us ourselves learn that nothing is to be attempted without a calling, nor should we trust in human plans or strengths, but let us know that governments are truly the works of God, and are not happy unless God helps. Wherefore let us do only the necessary things which the calling demands, and let us implore the help of God, just as Psalm 36 commands: Commit your way to the Lord, and he will act. Likewise: Be subject to God and hope in him, that is, undertake the necessary works of your calling, and endure those troubles and those dangers which the calling brings, and trust that God will be with you, just as it is said in 2 Chronicles 19: Be strong, and act, because the Lord will be with the good.

Latin:

Post haec venit Iesus et discipuli eius, etc.

Adhuc agitur primus annus post baptismum Christi, et redierat Christus post Pascha in Ga- lilaeam, nunc fortassis ad Pentecosten redit in Iu- daeam, nondum coniectus erat Baptista in car- cerem, quia iam propius Galilaeam accesserat, versabaturque in loco vicino Tyberiadis ad lacum Genezareth. Nam non procul ab eo lacu erant Aenon et Salem, cuius hic fit mentio. Nam Hieronymus ait etiam sua aetate vicum fuisse, cui nomen fuit Salimias, non procul a Scythopoli, distans a Ierosolymis circiter 10 miliaria no- stratia.

Quaestio autem hic repetitur de baptismo, a quo sit institutus. An liceat huic Iesu et eius discipulis baptizare, aut quid intersit inter utrun- que baptismum, quid etiam intersit inter perso- nas, Ioannem et Iesum. Hic recitatur gravis- sima concio, in qua Ioannes personas discernit, et plenissime tradit summam Evangelii, et simul docet se fungi ministerio, quod illi serviat, se non sibi quaerere aut adiungere populum, sed ad illum deducere, et efficax esse ministerium pro- pter ipsum. Orditer autem a generali sententia maxime memorabili, etsi de Ecclesia proprie lo- quitur, tamen etiam politicum praeceptum est, et quia politica exempla facilius intelliguntur, ab his ordiar interpretationem.

Non potest sibi homo sumere quicquam, etc.

De eventibus et profectu concionatur. Homo non potest gerere res magnas, et salutares sibi et Reipublicae, potiri imperiis, constituere durabi- lem et mansurum statum, retinere autoritatem, nisi adiuvetur divinitus. Antonius, Cassius, Dolabella, et multi alii appetebant eum locum in imperio Romano, quem Iulius tenuerat, viderant illius exemplum, et existimabant se suis consiliis ac apparatibus posse consequi eadem, quae ille adeptus fuisset. Haec κακοζηλία semper in mun- do innumerabiles homines fallit. Quia vero Deus non adiuvat Antonium et caeteros, non solum fru- strantur sua spe, sed etiam sibi ipsis exitium ac- cersunt, et implicant Rempublicam perniciosis bellis. Interim Deus excitat adolescentem imbe- cillem Augustum, hunc evehit, munit, custodit, adiuvat, huic Rempublicam tradit, caeteris de- pulsis. Hunc tot illustria exempla admonuerunt, ut agnosceret frustra homines appetere imperia et gubernationes, nisi divinitus adiuventur.

Similium exemplorum plenae sunt omnes aetates, et omnes historiae. Lentulus invidet gloriae Scipionis, et cupit ad se transferri laudem finiti belli Punici, sed non videt ineptus, se ne- quaquam similem esse Scipioni. Debebat igitur agnoscere suam mediocritatem, et nequaquam se conferre superiori. Quid est usitatius, quam quod multi conantur leges ferre, reformare suas civitates, ut vocant, sed nihil salutare, aut dura- bile constituitur, nisi Deo adiuvante, ut Solonis, Augusti, et similium quorundam leges fuerunt utiles civibus, et duraverunt: interim quam mul- torum futiles emendationes turbaverunt Atticam civitatem et Romanam.

In talibus vitae negotiis cogitemus hanc sen- tentiam: Non potest homo sibi quicquam sumere, nisi sit ei datum de coelo. Haec sententia doceat nos, gubernationem esse opus Dei, moneat, ne sine vocatione res magnas suscipiamus, haec mo- destia utilis est paci et concordiae publicae.

Quanquam igitur et politicum praeceptum est, tamen quia Baptista de Ecclesia loquitur, di- camus de ministeriis Ecclesiae. Ministeria, gu- bernationes, cultus, nec placent Deo, nec sunt efficaces, nec durabiles, nisi Deus sit autor et adiutor. Ioannes minister fuit baptismi, ad quem divinitus certis testimoniis vocatus fuit. Hoc igi- tur ministerium placuit Deo, fuit efficax et du- rabile. Idem Ioannes agnovit modum suae voca- tionis, ac toties profitetur se non esse Messiam. Si sibi sumeret alienum honorem, abiiceretur a Deo, et cito dissiparetur eius gubernatio. Ideo sic praefatus est: Non potest sibi homo sumere quicquam, nisi sit ei datum de coelo. Fuit in- felix gubernatio regis Achas, etsi multa molitus, multa conatus est, et praesidiis vicinorum regum diligenter se communiit. Econtra Ezechiae gu- bernatio fuit felix et salutaris, quia divinitus ad- iuvabatur. Ieremias servavit populum, novo et inusitato consilio, cui reges, sacerdotes, et omnes sapientes adversabantur. Huiusmodi exempla innamers sciamus pertinere ad hanc sententiam, et nos ipsi discamus nihil tentandum esse sine vocatione, nec confidamus humanis consiliis, aut viribus, sed sciamus gubernationes vere esse opera Dei, et non esse felices, nisi Deo iuvante. Quare necessaria tantum, quae postulat vocatio, facia- mus, et auxilium Dei imploremus, sicut Psal. 36. praecipit: Commenda domino viam tuam, et ipse faciet. Item: Subditus esto Deo et spera in eum, id est, suscipe opera vocationis necessaria, et sustine eas aerumnas, et ea pericula, quae affert vocatio, et confide Deum tibi affuturum esse, sicut 2. Pa- ral. 19. dicitur: Sitis fortes, et facite, quia erit dominus cum bono.

## 3:28
You yourselves are witnesses that I have said.

The discourse coheres aptly; before, as in a syllogism, he proposed the major premise, now he attaches the minor. I am mindful of my calling, I clearly profess that I am not the Messiah, but his minister, and a witness sent before him, that is, that I may announce that he is soon to be present. It matters a great deal in the Church that the distinction be understood between the person of Christ and the Prophets, Apostles, and all teachers. Only the Son of God is the victim for us and the mediator, on account of him alone are we received by the Father through trust in him, he alone gives the Holy Spirit and eternal life: but the Prophets, Apostles, and other teachers propose the Gospel, they testify about that Savior, nor do they have the authority to devise new doctrine and new forms of worship, nor are they to be invoked, nor is trust to be placed in them. Although many think they understand this distinction, who follow and recite the words however they may, yet in truth they do not understand it, those who are ignorant of the righteousness of faith, or who dream that they are righteous, that is, that they please God and are accepted for eternal life, on account of their own virtues or the fulfillment of the law. These only imagine that Christ is a teacher or a demonstrator, such as Moses was, or other Prophets. Often, therefore, the Baptist preaches about this distinction, and he repeats this sermon here with the most serious words.

Latin:

Ipsi vos testes estis quod dixerim.

Apte cohaeret oratio, ante, ut in syllogi- smo, maiorem proposuit, nunc minorem attexit. Memini meae vocationis, clare profiteor me non esse Messiam, sed ministerium eius, et testem missum ante eum, id est, ut annunciem ipsum mox affuturum esse. Plurimum refert in Ecclesia discrimen intelligi, inter personam Christi et Prophetas, Apostolos ac omnes doctores. Solus filius Dei est victima pro nobis et mediator, pro- pter hunc solum recipimur a patre fiducia ipsius, solus hic dat Spiritum sanctum et vitam aeter- nam: sed Prophetae, Apostoli et caeteri docto- res proponunt Evangelium, testantur de salva- tore illo, nec habent autoritatem excogitandi no- vam doctrinam et novos cultus, nec invocandi sunt, nec fiducia in ipsos collocanda est. Hoc discrimen etsi se multi intelligere putant, qui verba utcunque sequuntur, et recitant, tamen re vera non intelligunt isti, qui iusticiam fidei igno- rant, seu qui somniant se iustos esse, id est, pla- cere Deo, et acceptos esse ad vitam aeternam, propter suas virtutes, aut impletionem legis. Hi tantum imaginantur Christum doctorem esse, aut monstratorem, qualis fuit Moses, aut alii Pro- phetae. Saepe igitur Baptista de hoc discrimine concionatur, et hanc concionem hic gravissimis verbis repetit.

## 3:29
He who has the bride is the bridegroom.

By a simile he declares the distinction, as the bridegroom joins the bride to himself by a perpetual covenant and love, and dedicates his body and all his fortunes to her. But the friends who are invited are witnesses, and they congratulate the bridegroom on the honor. Thus Christ is the bridegroom of the Church, he joins her to himself by an eternal covenant and love, and gives all his goods to her, wisdom, that is, the Gospel or the true knowledge of God and mercy, righteousness, admirable defense, resurrection from death, and eternal life. And it is wonderful that Scripture sometimes warns of the love of the bridegroom and the bride. Likewise, that the perpetual union of the bridegroom and the bride is an image of the love and covenant of Christ and the Church. If we could truly see these things as they are ordained by God, the comparison would teach and console us most abundantly, therefore it follows:

Latin:

Qui habet sponsam, sponsus est.

Similitudine declarat discrimen, ut sponsus perpetuo foedere et amore sibi sponsam iungit, ac corpus ei, ac omnes fortunas addicit. Amici vero invitati sunt testes, et sponso gratulantur honorem. Ita Christus est sponsus Ecclesiae, iungit hanc sibi aeterno foedere et amore, et omnia sua bona ei donat, sapientiam, id est, Evangelium seu agnitionem veram, Dei et mise- ricordiae, iusticiam, defensionem admirabilem, resuscitationem ex morte, et vitam aeternam. Ac mirum est, quod scriptura aliquoties monet, amo- rem sponsi et sponsae. Item, perpetuam con- iunctionem sponsi et sponsae, esse imaginem amoris et foederis Christi et Ecclesiae. Haec si pos- semus re vera aspicere, ut sunt ordinata a Deo, collatio doceret et consolaretur nos uberrime, ideo sequitur:

## 3:29
My joy is fulfilled, etc.

The Baptist recognizes this bridegroom, sees with what love he embraces the Church, knows that there is an eternal and indissoluble covenant between the son of God and the Church, of which he also determines himself to be a member, knows that this bridegroom imparts to us righteousness, defense, and liberation from death, and eternal life.

Latin:

Gaudium meum impletum est, etc.

Baptista agnoscit hunc sponsum, videt quo amore Ecclesiam complectatur, scit aeternum et indissolubile foedus esse inter filium Dei, et Ec- clesiam, cuius se quoque membrum esse statuit, scit hunc sponsum impertire nobis iusticiam, de- fensionem, et liberationem a morte, et vitam aeternam.

## 3:30
He must increase, but I must decrease.

He repeats the sermon concerning the person of Christ, whom, as has often been said, he diligently and with many words distinguishes from the Prophets, Apostles, and all teachers. Although I hold a great office, I teach, I reform the Church, I have disciples, yet I am a minister of the Messiah, to whom I lead my hearers. Let us ministers know that we are only messengers of this lord, and let us prefer the lord himself to ourselves, let us not change his commands, let us not think that the Church is ruled or preserved by human counsels, but let us know that the lord himself is effective in this ministry, and in a wonderful way rules and preserves the Church. I must decrease. I do not want to be called anything other than a minister of this lord, but let the Church approach him, let it seek from him liberation from sins and from death, not from me or other ministers.

Latin:

Illum oportet crescere, me autem minui.

Repetit concionem de persona Christi, quem, ut saepe dictum est, diligenter et multis verbis discernit a Prophetis, Apostolis et omnibus do- ctoribus. Etsi gero magnum munus, doceo, re- purgo Ecclesiam, habeo discipulos, tamen mini- ster sum Messiae, ad hunc deduco auditores. Nos ministri sciamus nos tantum nuncios esse hu- ius domini, et dominum ipsum nobis antefera- mus, non mutemus mandata, non existimemus humanis consiliis regi aut conservari Ecclesiam, sed sciamus ipsum dominum efficacem esse in hoc ministerio, et mirabili modo regere et servare Ecclesiam. Me oportet minui. Nolo me aliud dici, nisi huius domini ministrum, ad ipsum vero accedat Ecclesia, ab ipso petat liberationem a pec- catis et a morte, non a me, aut caeteris mi- nistris.

## 3:31
He who comes from above is above all.

Here he indicates more clearly the distinction, why the Messiah excels all, because he comes from heaven.

Here he signifies that there are two natures in Christ, as he also signified above, and testifies that the son of God was with the eternal father before the assumption of human nature, and that he subjected himself to the will of the father for the Church, immediately after the fall. And therefore that he was sent from heaven, that he might put on human nature. He is therefore above all, because he is by nature the son of God, born of the substance of the eternal father. To the same point pertains what follows.

Latin:

Qui de supernis venit, super omnia est.

Hic discrimen clarius indicat, quare omni- bus antecellat Messias, quia de coelo venit.

Hic significat in Christo esse duas naturas, ut et supra significavit, et testatur filium Dei ante assumtionem humanae naturae apud aeternum pa- trem fuisse, et se pro Ecclesia voluntati patris subiecisse, statim post lapsum. Ideoque missum esse de coelo, ut indueret naturam humanam. Est igitur supra omnes, quia est natura filius Dei, natus de substantia aeterni patris. Eodem perti- net quod sequitur.

## 3:31
He who is from the earth speaks of earthly things.

To these words he opposes others. He who is from the earth, is from the earth, and speaks of earthly things. It is a general statement pertaining to human nature, he who is from the earth, that is, is mortal, not having spiritual light, wisdom discerning and glorifying God, and righteousness, which satisfies the law of God. He speaks from the earth, that is, he understands and speaks of things subject to reason, he does not discern the will of God, as Plato, Cicero, and the like, understand goods, which ones? Civil honesty, the comforts of life, good health, bodily strength, power, faculties, wealth, and these they desire, and when they have attained them, they see nothing greater. When they lose these, they are ignorant of the will of God, they do not determine that they are regarded and heard by God, nay, oppressed by calamity, they especially begin to doubt about providence. All human wisdom, therefore, and all philosophy is comprised here. He speaks of the earth, that is, of perishable goods, not of God, not of the will of God, not of light, wisdom, and eternal righteousness. Such is the wisdom of all without the word and light, which the Messiah brings by the given Holy Spirit, but insofar as a new light is kindled by the Gospel of God, to that extent the reborn begin to understand and speak not only of earthly, but also of divine things. Thus the antithesis in the text is to be taken, so that this statement may be understood of human nature not reborn by the word and the Holy Spirit. He who is from the earth, is earthly, that is, mortal, and speaks of earthly things, is the other part of the antithesis.

Latin:

Qui ex terra est, terrena loquitur.

His dictis opponit alia. Qui est ex terra, ex terra est, et terrena loquitur. Generale dictum est ad naturam humanam pertinens, qui est ex terra, id est, mortalis est, non habens lucem spiritualem, sapientiam cernentem et glorifican- tem Deum, et iusticiam, quae legi Dei satisfacit. Ex terra loquitur, id est, intelligit ac loquitur de rebus rationi subiectis, non cernit voluntatem Dei, ut Plato, Cicero, et similes, intelligunt bona, quaenam? Honestum civile, commoda vitae, bonam valetudinem, vires corporis, poten- tiam, facultates, opes, et haec appetunt, eaque cum sunt adepti, nihil vident maius. Haec cum amittunt voluntatem Dei ignorant, non statuunt se respici, et exaudiri a Deo, imo oppressi cala- mitate, maxime incipiunt dubitare de providen- tia. Tota ergo sapientia humana, et tota philo- sophia hic comprehensa est. De terra loquitur, id est, de perituris bonis, non de Deo, non de voluntate Dei, non de luce, sapientia et iusticia aeterna. Talis est sapientia omnium sine verbo et luce, quam affert Messias dato Spiritu sancto, sed quatenus accenditur Evangelio Dei nova lux, eatenus incipiunt renati, non tantum terrena, sed etiam divina intelligere, et loqui. Sic acci- pienda est in textu antithesis, ut hoc dictum de natura humana non renata verbo et Spiritu san- cto, intelligatur. Qui ex terra est, terrenus est, id est, mortalis, et terrena loquitur, altera pars antithesis est.

## 3:32
What he has seen and heard he testifies.

That is, the son has revealed the secret will of God, unknown to all creatures, concerning the remission of sins, concerning the restoration of eternal life, just as he said above: The Son who is in the bosom of the father, he has declared him to us. And Matt. 21: No one knows the son except the father, nor does anyone know the father, except the son, and he to whom the son wills to reveal him.

Latin:

Quod vidit et audivit testatur.

Id est, filius patefecit arcanam voluntatem Dei, ignotam omnibus creaturis de remissione peccatorum, de restituenda vita aeterna, sicut supra dixit: Filius qui est in sinu patris, ipse enarravit nobis. Et Matth. 21.: Nemo novit filium nisi pater, neque patrem quis novit, nisi filius, et cui voluerit filius revelare.

## 3:32
And no one accepts his testimony.

To wit, except him whom the Father has drawn. The rest, being rebels, resist God even when He is drawing them. Likewise, He admonishes them concerning the appearance of the Church. The Jews were expecting a Messiah who, having subdued the nations, would reign gloriously, and whose power would be visible to the eyes of all nations. In short, they were thinking of a king similar to Alexander, but more powerful and more just. But the Baptist describes a far different appearance of the leader and the people. This Messiah will preach, will be slaughtered as a victim, will be without arms, without human power; few will follow this leader. Because no one accepts the testimony, that is, his doctrine testifying concerning the will of God, to wit, except he who is drawn by God. Therefore, let this part of the antithesis also be understood again concerning human nature, not aided by the Holy Spirit. The following statement proves this mitigation.

Latin:

Et testimonium eius nemo accipit.

Videlicet, nisi quem pater traxerit. Caeteri rebelles etiam trahenti Deo repugnant. Item eos admonet de specie Ecclesiae. Iudaei expectabant Messiam, qui domitis gentibus gloriose regnatu- rus esset, et cuius potentia omnium gentium ocu- lis conspicienda esset. Denique regem cogitabant Alexandri similem, sed potentiorem et iustio- rem. Sed longe aliam speciem ducis et populi describit Baptista. Hic Messias concionabitur, trucidabitur, ut victima, erit sine armis, sine humana potentia, hunc ducem pauci sequentur. Quia testimonium, id est, doctrinam eius testi- ficantem de voluntate Dei, nemo accipit, videli- cet, nisi qui trahitur a Deo. Rursus ergo et haec pars antithesis intelligatur de natura humana, non adiuta a Spiritu sancto. Hanc mitigationem probat sequens dictum.

## 3:32
But he who receives.

Here he testifies that some follow this leader, but few. The Church will therefore be small, without power and human protections, unlike the empires of the world, scattered, etc. He who receives his testimony, he seals (that is, testifies with certainty) that God is truthful. Brevity increases obscurity, wherefore if the antithesis is compared, perhaps some light will be added. Those who do not believe the Gospel, they neither understand nor judge the doctrine to be true, but despise it as a monstrous fable, as all the impious have always judged the Gospel. But on the contrary, believers recognize the doctrine to be truly heavenly, concerning the will of God. But whence arises this certainty, or πληροφορία? Formerly the Enthusiasts and many Fanatics afterwards, neglecting the word of God, sought through certain preparations and fasts singular motions of the Holy Spirit, and singular light, and revelations, but these delusions are to be rejected, and the infallible rule is to be held: Faith comes from hearing, hearing through the word of God. Likewise: Your word is a lamp to my feet. Likewise 2 Pet. 1: We have a more sure prophetic word, to which you do well to pay attention, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts. These sentences testify that revelations are not to be sought outside the word of God, or without the word of God. Therefore, for the certainty of conscience, or πληροφορία, the first necessity is to hold to the certain and plain word of God.

But why does David assent, while Saul does not assent? Why does David judge the doctrine of the people of Israel to be from God, and that he obtains the promises which the doctrine offers? Saul thinks that he is no more a concern to God than neighboring kings, nor that the opinions of this nation are any more from God than those of others. Here the distinction is made in this way, because David assents to the word of God, the Holy Spirit is simultaneously effective, and arouses appropriate motions in the heart. The doctrine of repentance concerning the wrath of God against sin strikes true terrors into them; in these he truly recognizes that God is angry at sin, and in his own example he understands that others also do not fall into punishments by chance, but by the judgment and will of God. Saul thought that the Philistines now, the Israelites then, succumbed by chance, and without the governance and providence of God. Again, when David, having heard the consolation concerning the remission of sins, assents to that voice, the Holy Spirit is simultaneously effective, and truly produces peace and tranquility in his heart. There David feels himself resting in the recognition and faith of the mercy of God. This consolation shows the word of God to be effective, and kindles a new light, by which David now feels that he is truly received and cared for by God, and truly asks from Him and expects rewards, defense, governance, victories, and eternal life.

Therefore it is said in Rom. 8: You have received the spirit of adoption of sons, by which we cry Abba Father. This same spirit testifies with our spirit that we are sons. And 2 Cor. 3: When they shall have returned to the Lord, the veil will be taken away. Here he says that darkness and doubt are taken away when conversion to Christ occurs. A little later he adds: But we all, with unveiled face beholding the glory of God, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as from the Spirit of the Lord.

This is a notable sentence, and truly pertaining to this passage of the Baptist, where it is said: He who receives his testimony, seals or testifies that God is truthful. Paul signifies, however, that when in true terrors and the recognition of the wrath of God against sin we flee to Christ, and determine that we are truly received by God on account of the Son the mediator, and sustain ourselves with this confidence, there arises in us a firmer knowledge of the mercy of God toward us, which also produces other virtues.

Hence, therefore, is certainty, when, assenting to the Gospel, we are confirmed by the Holy Spirit, and conceive a firmer knowledge of providence, of the wrath of God against sins, and of the mercy of God toward us. Therefore the Baptist also says: He who receives his testimony, that is, he who assents to the voice of Christ, testifies, is confirmed by the Holy Spirit, and conceives a firm knowledge, by which he determines that God is truthful, and that the Gospel is not a fabricated fable, as Epicureans and the like imagine. What could have seemed more ridiculous to the Roman Senate than what Paul was narrating: that the Roman Senate was not a gathering pleasing to God, but that he and his listeners, miserable wanderers, were pleasing to God, and would have an eternal kingdom in heaven. For Paul, assenting to the Gospel, had conceived a firm knowledge, had felt the wrath of God against sin, had felt the consolations born from faith, or confidence in the Son of God. According to that: The Holy Spirit testifies with our spirit, that we are children of God. The Roman senate knew not these terrors and these consolations. Why? Because it did not assent to the Gospel. Finally, the Holy Spirit is not effective in those who do not assent to the Gospel. In those, however, who in true repentance assent to the voice of the Gospel, He is undoubtedly effective. This is the testimony and σφραγίς, or seal, of which he speaks here, and the anointing, which is otherwise called thus in the Epistle of John.

handed down by the fathers, and they declared it. Therefore, that Holy Spirit was given to a certain measure, to a certain calling; Samuel performed great deeds, but yet by a certain measure; at another time David performed them, at another Elijah, at another Jeremiah; there was a great dissimilarity among them. And it is prudence for each one to understand his own measure, and not to attempt or strive for things above his calling, just as Saul attempted. Wherefore it is also commanded in Rom. 12: That each one should recognize the mode, or measure given to him, and not attempt greater things above that measure. This moderation is difficult for great men. Here Gideon stumbled, having established a cult; Saul sinned with a much sadder fall. David also offended somewhat when he numbered the people, thinking perhaps about the constitution of the kingdom which was not commanded.

Latin:

Qui autem accipiet.

Hic testatur aliquos sequi hunc ducem, sed paucos. Erit igitur Ecclesia exigua, sine potentia et praesidiis humanis, dissimilis imperiis mundi, dissipata, etc. Qui accipit testimonium eius, is signat (id est, testificatur certo), quod Deus sit verax. Brevitas auget obscuritatem, quare si conferatur antithesis, fortassis aliquid accedet lucis. Qui non credunt Evangelio, hi nec intelligunt, nec iudicant veram esse doctrinam, sed aspernantur, tanquam portentosaın fabulam, ut omnes impii de Evangelio semper iudicarunt. Sed econtra, credentes agnoscunt vere coelestem doctrinam esse, de voluntate Dei. Unde autem oritur haec certitudo, seu πληροφορία? Olim Enthusiastae et multi postea Fanatici, neglecto verbo Dei, certis praeparationibus et ieiuniis, quaesierunt singulares motus Spiritus sancti, et singulare lumen, et revelationes, sed haec deliria repudianda sunt, et tenenda regula infallibilis: Fides ex auditu est, auditus per verbum Dei. Item: Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum. Item 2. Petr. 1.: Habemus firmiorem propheticum sermonem, cui, recte facitis, attendentes, tanquam lychno lucenti in loco caliginoso, donec dies illucescat, et oriatur lucifer in cordibus vestris. Hae sententiae testantur, non esse revelationes extra verbum Dei, aut sine verbo Dei quaerendas. Ergo ad certitudinem conscientiae, seu πληροφορίαν primum opus est tenere certum et planum verbum Dei.

Sed cur assentitur David, Saul non assentitur? Cur David iudicat doctrinam populi Israël a Deo esse, et se consequi promissiones, quas offert doctrina? Saul cogitat se nihilo magis Deo curae esse, quam vicinos reges, nec magis a Deo esse huius gentis opiniones, quam aliarum. Hic discrimen fit hoc modo, quia David assentitur verbo Dei, Spiritus sanctus simul efficax est, et convenientes motus in corde exuscitat. Doctrina poenitentiae de ira Dei adversus peccatum incutit eis veros terrores, in his agnoscit vere Deum irasci peccato, et in suo exemplo intelligit etiam alios, non casu in poenas incidere, sed Dei iudicio et voluntate, Saul existimabat casu, et sine gubernatione et providentia Dei, nunc Philistaeos, nunc Israëlitas succumbere. Rursus, cum David audita consolatione de remissione peccatorum as- sentitur illi voci, simul est efficax Spiritus san- ctus, et vere pacem in corde eius, et tranquilli- tatem efficit. Ibi sentit se acquiescere David in agnitione et fide misericordiae Dei. Haec conso- latio ostendit verbum Dei esse efficax, et accendit novam lucem, qua iam sentit David vere se a Deo recipi et curari, vere ab eo petit et expectat prae- mia, defensionem, gubernationem, victorias, et vitam aeternam.

Ideo dicitur ad Rom. 8.: Accepistis spiritum adoptionis filiorum, quo clamamus Abba pater. Idem hic spiritus testificatur cum spiritu nostro, quod sumus filii. Et 2. Corinth. 3.: Cum redierint ad dominum, auferetur velum.. Hic dicit, auferri caliginem et dubitationem, cum fit conversio ad Christum. Aliquanto post addit: Nos autem omnes retecta facie gloriam Dei speculantes, in eandem imaginem transformamur a claritate in claritatem, tanquam a domini spiritu.

Haec est insignis sententia, et vere pertinens ad hunc locum Baptistae, quo dicitur: Qui testi- monium eius accipit, signat seu testificatur, quod Deus sit verax. Significat autem Paulus, cum in veris terroribus et agnitione irae Dei adversus peccatum confugimus ad Christum, et statuimus vere nos recipi a Deo propter filium mediatorem, et hac fiducia nos sustentamus, exoriri in nobis firmiorem noticiam misericordiae Dei erga nos, quae etiam alias virtutes parit.

Hinc igitur est certitudo, cum assentientes Evangelio, confirmamur per Spiritum sanctum, ac firmiorem noticiam providentiae, irae Dei ad- versus peccata, et misericordiae Dei erga nos con- cipimus. Ideo et Baptista dicit: Qui testimonium eius accipit, id est, qui assentitur voci Christi, testificatur, confirmatur a Spiritu sancto, et con- cipit firmam noticiam, qua statuit Deum veracem esse, Evangelium non esse commentitiam fabu- lam, ut Epicurei et similes imaginantur. Quid magis ridiculum senatui Romano videri potuit, quam quod Paulus narrabat: Senatum Romanum non esse coetum Deo placentem, sed se et suos auditores, miseros errones, Deo placere, et ha- bituros regnum aeternum in coelo. Paulus enim assentiens Evangelio, conceperat firmam noticiam, senserat iram Dei adversus peccatum, senserat consolationes ex fide, seu fiducia filii Dei ortas. Iuxta illud: Spiritus sanctus testificatur cum spi- ritu nostro, quod simus filii Dei. Hos terrores et has consolationes nesciebat senatus Romanus. Quare? Quia non assentiebatur Evangelio. De- nique Spiritus sanctus non est efficax in his, qui Evangelio non assentiuntur. In his vero, qui in vera poenitentia assentiuntur voci Evangelii, haud dubie est efficax. Haec est testificatio et σφραγίς, seu sigillum, de quo hic loquitur, et unctio, quae alias sic dicitur in Epistola Ioannis.

patribus traditam, et declarabant. Erat igitur is datus Spiritus sanctus ad certam mensuram, ad certam vocationem, Samuel gessit res magnas, sed tamen certa mensura, alias gessit David, alias Elias, alias Ieremias, magna horum dissimili- tudo fuit. Et prudentia est, unumquemque in- telligere suam mensuram, nec conari aut moliri res supra vocationem, sicut Saul conabatur. Quare et ad Rom. 12. praecipitur: Ut unusquis- que agnoscat modum, seu mensuram sibi datam, nec supra eam mensuram, res maiores conetur. Haec moderatio difficilis est magnis viris. Hic Gedeon impegit, constituto cultu, Saul multo tristiore lapsu peccavit. David etiam nonnihil offendit, cum numeraret populum, cogitans for- tasse de regni constitutione non mandata.

## 3:34
For He whom God has sent speaks the words of God.

He speaks of Christ, as he has also testified several times above: that this Jesus is the Messiah sent by God, and that He must be heard; indeed, he even added a mysterious sentiment: He who is in the bosom of the Father, He has declared Him to us. By which saying he testifies that this One is far above all the Prophets, indeed that the Prophets received from Him the doctrine concerning the secret counsel of God, namely, concerning the redemption of the human race, concerning the abolishing of sin, concerning the restoring of eternal life, concerning the remission of sins; the Son alone, who knows the Father, first revealed this will of the Father. Thus the Baptist preached about Him above, and now he repeats almost the same sentiment: He whom God has sent speaks the words of God; he commands that He be heard, and testifies that He was sent by God, and he speaks of the mission of the Messiah. For the question was concerning Him: Whether this Jesus were the Messiah, and whether He should be heard as the Messiah, and the preceding words speak of the Messiah, of the Son of God, as the words show quite clearly.

But Christ is far above all the Prophets, in the fullness of the Spirit and in calling. The divinity dwells in Him bodily, as Paul says to the Colossians. Therefore, the knowledge of God and justice abound in Him; He also has a greater calling; He frees from death, from sin; He restores perpetual justice and life, and in order to effect this, He so abounds in the Holy Spirit that He imparts the Spirit to others, kindling this light in them, the knowledge of God, justice, and perpetual life.

The Baptist declares this more in the following saying.

Latin:

Quem enim misit Deus, verba Dei loquitur.

De Christo loquitur, ut et supra aliquoties testificatus est: Hunc Iesum esse Messiam a Deo missum, et audiendum esse, imo etiam arcanam sententiam addidit: Qui est in sinu patris, ipse enarravit nobis. Quo dicto testificatur, hunc longe supra omnes Prophetas esse, imo Prophe- tas ab ipso accepisse doctrinam de arcano consilio Dei, videlicet, de redemtione generis humani, de abolendo peccato de restituenda vita aeterna, de remissione peccatorum, hanc voluntatem pa- tris solus filius, qui novit patrem, primum reve- lavit. Ita supra de eo Baptista concionatus est, et nunc eandem sententiam fere repetit: Quem misit Deus, verba Dei loquitur, iubet hunc audi- ri, et testatur a Deo missum esse, et loquitur de missione Messiae. Nam de eo erat quaestio: An hic Iesus esset Messias, et an ut Messias audien- dus esset, et proxima dicta loquuntur de Messia, de filio Dei, ut verba satis perspicue ostendunt.

Sed Christus longe supra omnes Prophetas est, plenitudine spiritus et vocatione. Habitat in eo divinitas corporaliter, sicut inquit Paulus ad Coloss. Abundat igitur noticia Dei, et iusti- cia, habet et vocationem maiorem, liberat a mor- te, a peccato, reddit perpetuam iusticiam et vi- tam, et ut hoc efficiat, ita abundat Spiritu san- cto, ut impertiat aliis spiritum, accendentem hanc lucem in eis, noticiam Dei, iusticiam et vitam perpetuam.

Haec magis declarat Baptista sequenti dicto.

## 3:34
God does not give the Spirit by measure.

The love with which God loves His only-begotten Son differs from the love with which He loves us. He loves us on account of the Son, and being appeased by His death. But He loves the Son not on account of any mediator, but by His own ineffable στοργῇ, because He was born of Him, which indeed is so great that on His account He receives us also. If we could here cast aside the Stoic opinions about God, and think that there is a true and ardent love in the eternal Father, with which He loves the Son, and on account of the Son others, this recognition of divine love toward the Son would bring us most abundant consolation: but these things cannot be explained in words; let us meditate upon them somehow with piety of mind. The Baptist declares the power of love, and adds: Because the Father truly loves the Son, therefore He has handed over all things into His hands, that is, He has constituted Him the giver of wisdom, justice, and eternal life. To Him He handed over the power of destroying the works of the devil, sin, and death; He also handed over the power of ruling and preserving the Church,

Namely to the Son, whom He sent; for as he said above: From His fullness we all receive, so now he says: that the Messiah has been endowed with the fullness of the Holy Spirit, with perfect wisdom and justice, and indeed with the power of sanctifying and vivifying other saints. Moses had a glorious calling; he led the people out of Egypt, and ruled them in the desert, but yet this calling did not free the people from eternal death. Furthermore, even in this present justice he had many confusions. Moses himself also had only an incipient light and knowledge of God, and an incipient justice, and there still clung to him a huge doubt, which showed itself when he struck the rock with these. Thus it can be said of the calling, light, and justice of each of the Prophets: and in sum, the Prophets had ruled that polity, and had been ministers of the word; they sounded the promise even in this life, and for the sake of restraining the rampant devil, he therefore glorifies the Church with illustrious works even in this life, just as he has always preserved it with miraculous works, as in the flood, in Egypt, in the desert, and afterwards in the time of the Judges and the Kings of Judah and Israel, all things are full of miraculous works. And although these preservations do not strike the eyes in the same way, nevertheless, right up to the end of the world, certain miraculous deliverances will always take place, as he says in Hosea: I will save them, but not by bow, nor by sword. It is necessary for us to maintain this doctrine in the Church, when the terrible power of the world strikes the eyes, and it seems that it is about to overwhelm the Church, as now the Turkish power, likewise the cruelty of other kings.

Latin:

Non ad mensuram dat Deus Spiritum.

Differunt dilectio, qua Deus diligit unigeni- tum filium, et dilectio, qua nos diligit. Nos di- ligit propter filium, et placatus eius morte. Sed filium diligit non propter aliquem mediatorem, sed sua inenarrabili στοργῇ, quia ex ipso natus est, quae quidem tanta est, ut propter ipsum et nos recipiat. Si possemus hic stoicas opiniones de Deo abiicere, et cogitare verum, et ardentem amorem esse in patre aeterno, quo filium diligit, et propter filium alios, uberrimam consolationem haec agnitio divini amoris erga filium nobis affer- ret: sed haec verbis explicari non possunt, pie- tate mentis utcunque ea meditemur. Baptista de- clarat vim amoris, et addit: Quia vere diligit pa- ter filium, ideo omnia tradidit in manus eius, id est, hunc constituit datorem sapientiae, iusti- ciae, vitae aeternae. Huic tradidit potentiam de- struendi opera diaboli, peccatum et mortem, tra- didit et potentiam regendae et servandae Ecclesiae,

Scilicet filio, quem misit, ut enim supra dixit: Ex plenitudine eius omnes accipimus, ita nunc ait: donatum esse Messiam plenitudine Spi- ritus sancti, perfecta sapientia et iusticia, et qui- dem potentia sanctificante et vivificante caeteros sanctos. Moses habuit gloriosam vocationem, edu- xit populum ex Aegypto, et rexit in deserto, sed tamen haec vocatio non liberabat populum a morte aeterna. Deinde etiam in hac praesente iusticia multum habebat confusionum. Ipse etiam Moses tantum habebat incoatam lucem et agnitionem Dei, et incoatam iusticiam, et adhuc haerebat in eo ingens dubitatio, quae se ostendit, cum his percuteret petram. Sic de singulorum Propheta- rum vocatione, luce, iusticia, dici potest: et in summa, Prophetae rexerant illam politiam, et fuerant ministri verbi, sonabant promissionem etiam in hac vita, et reprimendi grassantem dia- bolum, ideo illustribus operibus glorificat Eccle- siam etiam in hac vita, sic ut mirabilibus operi- bus semper servavit, ut in diluvio, in Aegypto, in deserto, et postea tempore Iudicum et Regum Iuda et Israël, omnia plena sunt mirabilium ope- rum. Et quanquam non eodem modo hae serva- tiones incurrunt in oculos, tamen semper usque ad finem mundi fient mirabiles quaedam libera- tiones, sicut in Osea dicit: Salvabo eos, sed non in arcu, neque in gladio. Hanc doctrinam nos in Ecclesia tueri necesse est, cum terribilis mundi potentia in oculos incurrit, et videtur Ecclesiam obruitura esse, ut nunc Turcica potentia, item aliorum regum saevitia.

## 3:35
The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into His hands.

Latin:

Pater diligit filium, et omnia dedit in ma- nus eius.

## 3:36
He who believes in the Son, will have eternal life, etc.

He spoke concerning the person of the Messiah: That this Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, that he has the fullness of the Spirit, and the power of giving a new and perpetual light, wisdom, righteousness, and life. Now he preaches about the application, how we may obtain these benefits, how the Messiah is to be received or worshipped. But the Pharisees vehemently abhorred this sermon, who understood that by these words divine honor was attributed to the Messiah, they understood likewise that the Messiah was called by the Baptist, not an establisher of a political kingdom, but a giver of eternal life. The world does not seek this in such a way that it does not prefer the present empire to flourish with the glory of victories, with tranquility, good order, wealth, etc. All these magnificent hopes about the empire of the world the Baptist commands to be cast away, and he preaches about eternal things, righteousness and eternal life, and about the eternal wrath of God.

The consensus of the doctrine concerning righteousness and faith must be diligently observed. He speaks about faith in exactly the same way as Christ, the Apostles in Acts, and Paul speak; thus Christ said above: God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that everyone believing in him might not perish, but have eternal life. Thus also the Apostles in Acts say: To him all the Prophets bear witness, that everyone believing in him receives remission of sins through his name; and Paul: Being justified by faith we have peace. So here the Baptist clearly says: He who believes in the Son, has eternal life, but he who does not believe the Son, will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him. It is manifest that the words agree. But what does such a great consensus mean? Let us retain the propriety of the words, nor let us invent foreign opinions, let us be disciples of such great teachers, let us not beget another kind of doctrine in the Church: the words clearly command that you believe that your sins are remitted to you, and that you are received by God, and become an heir of eternal life, on account of the Son of God, not on account of the law, not on account of your own virtues.

But the Monks oppose this most simple exposition, who invent that the remission of sins is given on account of our merits, then they contend that by faith only the knowledge of history is signified, such as is even in the devils, they deny that it is trust in the mercy promised on account of Christ, nay, in order to extinguish that trust, they command one to doubt whether you have the remission of sins, or whether God is propitious to you. There is therefore in all these sermons, of the Baptist, of Christ, of Paul, of the Apostles, a principal question. What faith signifies: Whether it truly signifies to trust in Christ. If it does not signify to trust in Christ, but only to know and profess the history, these sayings signify nothing, and are very improper, we are justified by faith. Likewise: He who believes in the Son, has eternal life. But let us retain, as I said, the propriety of the words, let us know that the statement is true, we are justified by faith, that is, we are reconciled by trust in the Son of God, not on account of the law, or our own virtues. That this is the meaning sufficiently appears from Paul, who compares faith and the promise among themselves, and commands that the promise be received by faith. Likewise for this reason he contends about the particle freely, that he may teach that trust is to be transferred to the Son of God, who is the victim for us, and that one is not to trust in our own dignity, nor is our dignity the price, or merit, or cause of the remission of sins,

Latin:

Qui credit in filium, habebit vitam aeter- nam, etc.

Dixit de persona Messiae: Hunc Iesum esse Messiam, filium Dei, habere plenitudinem spiri- tus, ac potentiam dandae novae ac perpetuae lu- cis, sapientiae, iusticiae et vitae. Nunc de ap- plicatione concionatur, quomodo haec beneficia consequamur, quomodo excipiendus, aut colen- dus sit Messias. Vehementer autem abhorrebant ab hac concione Pharisaei, qui intelligebant his verbis tribui Messiae honorem divinum, intellige- bant item Messiam dici a Baptista, non instaura- torem regni politici, sed datorem vitae aeternae. Hanc non sic expetit mundus, ut non malit prae- sens imperium florere gloria victoriarum, tran- quillitate, bono ordine, opibus etc. Has magni- ficas spes omnes de imperio mundi iubet Baptista abiicere, et concionatur de rebus aeternis, iusti- cia et vita aeterna, et de ira Dei aeterna.

Diligenter observandus est consensus doctri- nae de iusticia et fide. Prorsus eodem modo lo- quitur de fide, sicut Christus, Apostoli in Actis, et Paulus loquuntur, sic Christus supra inquit: Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut filium suum unige- nitum daret, ut omnis credens in eum non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam. Sic et Apostoli in Actis dicunt: Huic omnes Prophetae testimo- nium perhibent, remissionem peccatorum acci- pere per nomen eius omnes credentes in eum; et Paulus: Iustificati fide pacem habemus. Ita hic plane inquit Baptista: Qui credit in filium, ha- bet vitam aeternam, qui autem non credit filio, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super ipsum. Verba congruere manifestum est. Quid autem vult hic tantus consensus? Retineamus proprieta- tem verborum, nec fingamus peregrinas opinio- nes, simus discipuli tantorum doctorum, non gignamus in Ecclesia aliud doctrinae genus: verba clare iubent, ut credas tibi remitti peccata, et te recipi a Deo, et fieri haeredem vitae aeternae, propter filium Dei, non propter legem, non pro- pter virtutes proprias.

Sed hanc simplicissimam enarrationem op- pugnant Monachi, qui fingunt dari remissionem peccatorum propter nostra merita, deinde conten- dunt fide tantum significari noticiam historiae, qualis et in diabolis est, negant esse fiduciam mi- sericordiae propter Christum promissae, imo ut illam fiduciam extinguant, iubent dubitare an ha- beas remissionem peccatorum, seu an Deus sit tibi propicius. Est ergo in omnibus his concio- nibus, Baptistae, Christi, Pauli, Apostolorum, praecipua quaestio. Quid significet fides: An vere significet confidere Christo. Si non significat confidere Christo, sed tantum nosse, et profiteri historiam, haec dicta nihil significant, et valde sunt impropria, fide iustificamur. Item: Qui credit in filium, habet vitam aeternam. Sed nos retineamus, ut dixi, proprietatem verborum, sciamus veram esse orationem, fide iustificamur, id est, fiducia filii Dei reconciliamur, non propter legem, aut nostras virtutes. Hanc esse senten- tiam ex Paulo satis apparet, qui fidem et pro- missionem inter se confert, et iubet fide promis- sionem accipi. Item hanc ob causam contendit de particula gratis, ut doceat fiduciam transferendam esse in filium Dei, qui est victima pro nobis, nec esse confidendum nostra dignitate, nec nostram dignitatem esse pretium, seu meritum seu causam remissionis peccatorum,

## 4:1 Argument
Chapter IV.

Latin:

Caput IV.

## 4:1
When therefore Jesus knew that they had heard.

This chapter also contains a useful disputation concerning the kingdom of the Messiah, concerning the distinction of the New and Old Testament, concerning true worship, about which the Samaritan woman discourses with Christ. But first the series of the history should be considered. The first year after the baptism of Christ is still being dealt with, and now for the first time after the Passover he returns into Galilee, when in the meantime he had stayed for some time in Judea, and there had commanded his disciples to perform the ministry of baptizing, about which was discussed above. I said that baptism is a ceremony of the New Testament instituted by God through John, who first begins the rite, and afterwards Christ commands the Apostles to administer the same rite. And the baptism of John and of the Apostles is the same, and it profits in the same way; it shows the reconciliation promised through the Son of God: and it requires that the baptized believe this promise, and those who believe truly obtain the remission of sins, and are sanctified by the Holy Spirit, and become heirs of eternal life, on account of Christ. Let this brief repetition suffice concerning the baptism of John and the Apostles.

sometimes he also declares with tears. And in the Epistle to the Hebrews it is said: We have a high priest who can sympathize with our infirmities, that is, who truly loves us and truly endured immense sorrows for our sake.

Latin:

Ut igitur cognovit Iesus quod audissent.

Continet et hoc caput utilem disputationem de regno Messiae, de discrimine novi et veteris Testamenti, de vero cultu, de quo mulier Samar- ritana disserit cum Christo. Sed prius series hi- storiae consideretur. Adhuc agitur primus annus post baptismum Christi, et iam primum post Pa- scha redit in Galilaeam, cum interim aliquandiu moratus esset in Iudaea, et ibi iussisset discipulos fungi ministerio baptizandi, de quo supra dispu- tetum est. Dixi baptismum ceremoniam esse novi Testamenti a Deo institutam per Ioannem, qui pri- mus incoat ritum, postea praecipit Christus Apo- stolis eundem ritum administrare. Estque idem baptismus Ioannis et Apostolorum, ac prodest eodem modo, monstrat reconciliationem per filium Dei promissam: et postulat, ut baptizati credant huic promissioni, et credentes vere consequuntur remissionem peccatorum, et sanctificantur Spiritu sancto, et fiunt haeredes vitae aeternae, propter Christum. Haec brevis repetitio sufficiat de ba- ptismo Ioannis et Apostolorum.

interdum et lacrymis declarat. Et in Epistola ad Hebr. dicitur: Habemus pontificem, qui potest compati nostris infirmitatibus, id est, qui vere nos diligit et vere sustinuit ingentes dolores no- stra causa.

## 4:4
And he had to pass through Samaria.

Samaria is the name of both the city and the neighboring region in the borders of the tribe of Ephraim, namely, almost in the middle of the road between Jerusalem and Galilee; there was also Sichem or Salem in the border of Manasseh and Ephraim. And there is no doubt from Gen. 48 that the place was given there to Joseph; they also say that the tomb of Joseph was in that place. In Gen. 33 it is written that Jacob bought a field near Salem or Sichem, in which he built an altar. Most people think that this Sichem is called Sychar here with a somewhat corrupted word, and it is consistent that it is either the same or a neighboring place, since it was near the estate which Jacob gave to Joseph.

Latin:

Oportebat autem ipsum transire per Samariam.

Samaria et urbis et regionis vicinae nomen est in finibus tribus Ephraim, videlicet fere in media via inter Ierusalem et Galilaeam, fuit et Sichem seu Salem in confinio Manasse et Ephraim. Nec dubium est ex cap. 48. Genes. ibi locum fuisse donatum Ioseph, aiunt et sepulcrum Ioseph eo loco fuisse. Gen. 33. scribitur, Iacob emisse agrum prope Salem seu Sichem, in quo altare condidit. Hanc Sichem plerique arbitrantur hic nonnihil corrupta voce dici Sychar, et vel eandem, vel vi- cinam esse consentaneum, siquidem vicina fuit praedio, quod Iacob donavit Ioseph.

## 4:6
Now he was tired from the journey.

It is noted here concerning weariness, what affections and what infirmities were in the human nature of Christ; concerning this question it was said above in the passage: And the Word was made flesh. Just as in Christ there was a truly human nature, but not contaminated by sin, so there were members appropriate to human nature, organs, appetites, affections, motions, but these were ordered, just, and congruent to the law of God. And just as naturally, when nourishment is consumed, the veins excite hunger and thirst, so naturally, by more vehement motion, the nerves and other instruments of motion are exhausted. Thus the same things happened in Christ; he hungered, he thirsted, he was wearied, because his nature was truly human, and indeed also subject to death and injury, but not contaminated by sin. He had also other affections, which are properly in the heart; he rejoiced, he grieved, he had compassion, he loved the pious, he was inflamed with anger, he hated the devil, but these motions and στοργαὶ were ordered. In other men, too, the created nature must be distinguished from concupiscence, that is, from the depravity and ἀταξίᾳ that has been added. This is a ready answer to this question, what affections were in Christ, concerning which there are many perplexed disputes among the Sententiaries.

Now Christ departs, because he understands that the Pharisees are lying in wait for him. Although Christ and the Prophets have their own peculiar impulses, yet in this place Christ obeys the common rule: If they cast you out of one place, go into another. For then obedience and constancy in affliction are pleasing to God, when it is necessary to suffer, as Peter says: Not when we ourselves bring destruction upon ourselves without necessity or without a calling. For this rashness is not obedience, but ἐθελοθρησκεία, as when the priests of Baal gashed themselves.

Latin:

Erat autem defatigatus ex itinere.

Annotatur hic de fatigatione, qui affectus et quae infirmitates fuerint in natura humana Chri- sti, de hac quaestione supra dictum est in loco: Et Verbum caro factum est. Ut in Christo natura vere humana fuit, sed non contaminata peccato, ita fuerunt membra convenientia naturae huma- nae, organa, appetitiones, affectus, motus, sed haec fuerunt ordinata, iusta et congruentia legi Dei. Et sicut naturaliter consumto nutrimento, venae famem et sitim excitant, ita naturaliter motu vehementiore nervi et caetera motus instru- menta delassantur. Ita fiebant eadem in Christo, esuriebat, sitiebat, defatigabatur, quia natura erat vere humana, et quidem etiam obnoxia morti et laesioni, sed non contaminata peccato. Habe- bat et alios affectus, qui proprie sunt in corde, laetatus est, doluit, misertus est, dilexit pios, excanduit ira, odit diabolum, sed hi motus et στοργαὶ fuerunt ordinatae. Est et in caeteris hominibus discernenda natura condita a concu- piscentia, id est, a depravatione et ἀταξίᾳ, quae accessit. Haec est expedita responsio ad hanc quaestionem, qui affectus in Christo fuerint, de qua multae perplexae sunt disputationes apud sententiarios.

Discedit autem Christus, quia intelligit sibi Pharisaeos insidiari. Etsi Christus et Prophetae habent suos peculiares impetus, tamen hoc loco Christus obtemperat communi regulae: Si eiece- rint vos ex uno loco, ite in alium. Tunc enim placet Deo obedientia et constantia in afflictione, cum necesse est pati, ut Petrus inquit: Non cum ipsi nobis sine necessitate, aut sine vocatione ac- cersimus exitium. Haec enim temeritas non est obedientia, sed ἐθελοθρησκεία, ut cum se fode- rent sacerdotes Baal.

## 4:7
Jesus says to her: Give me to drink.

Here a conversation is instituted between Christ and the woman, in which Christ delivers the doctrine of the Gospel, and preaches about the calling of the Gentiles, and distinguishes the Old and New Testament, as well as true and false worship. It is also a peculiar testimony of mercy that he offers his Gospel to a miserable adulteress, and expressly says to her that he is the Messiah, and afterwards goes with her into the town, and stays there for two days, in order to confirm a disciple and to call others to the light of the Gospel. By this testimony let us also be confirmed, let us know that sinners are truly received, and that the Church is a humble and despised gathering, but one that is doing penance and believing the Gospel, and that the Church is not to be bound to Pontiffs, Kings, Princes, etc.

Now the Evangelist seems not without cause to have inserted the description of the place. Because since the domicile of Melchizedek was there, and Jacob had built an altar there, the sight of the place excited immense motions in Christ, as he thought about the old Church, and about the calling of the fathers, about the promises, about the rejection of the people, and many other things: for it appears that his mind was not idle, because he could not enjoy the food brought afterwards. It is useful to consider these affections in Christ, so that we may conclude that we are truly loved by him, and that he is truly afflicted by our evils, just as it is often said in the histories of the Gospel that he is moved with mercy, which
