The first question, however, arises from human tradition: there is no social intercourse between Jews and Samaritans. For although God had forbidden the Israelites from marriages and idols of neighboring impious nations, he had not, however, forbidden contracts, purchases, sales, or the duties of sharing food and drink. The Pharisees, however, had added superstitious traditions so that they might accumulate works by an opinion of righteousness, and they pretended that they were righteous on account of the law and their own traditions. Furthermore, the Samaritans, although they had received the doctrine concerning the one God the Creator, whom they professed to be the one who had revealed himself to the fathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, nevertheless did not know the promises and the doctrine concerning faith, and they retained many ethnic superstitions, as the book of 4 Kings 17 shows. Christ, having omitted the tradition, proceeds to perform his duty; he begins to say who he is and what he teaches, but he has at the beginning a crude disciple, not yet capable of the Gospel. Therefore, after he has prefaced a few things, he preaches to the woman about repentance. He spoke obscurely: If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, etc. Afterwards, he declares more clearly that he is the Messiah, the giver of eternal life. Whoever drinks from the water that I will give him, there will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life. The woman does not yet understand what this wonderful sermon means for her, and she mixes in human ineptitudes about drawing water. Here Christ proposes to her a sermon of repentance, so that with sin acknowledged and the wrath of God acknowledged, she might be instructed about the Messiah and about the remission of sins. He rebukes her on account of her adulteries. Here she, becoming terrified, begins now to inquire about doctrine and about the worship of God. The Jews rightly felt that there should be no other temple for the people of Israel where sacrifices should be made except in Jerusalem, but the Samaritans opposed the examples of the fathers. To imitate the examples of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the worship of God is most pious. Here Jacob sacrificed, therefore we also do piously because we sacrifice here. The impious priests, who desired to lead the people away from the doctrine of Moses, undoubtedly exaggerated these things. Christ judges the question: Wherever the word of God is, there worship is rightly performed. The fathers who worshipped here, that is, sacrificed, were guardians and teachers of the word, commended and handed down to them by God. They proposed this to others and taught true invocation, and they themselves invoked, kindled by faith through this word. Afterwards, this same word of God was commended to the tribe of Levi, so that they might teach at the tabernacle or temple; God wanted his word to be sought there, so that true invocation could be performed. But you Samaritans now perform worship and sacrifices here without the word of God. Therefore your worship is rejected. We Jews retain the word. For there were some, such as Simeon and Zacharias, who had retained it. Therefore at the temple, and in this Church in which the word of God sounds, the worship of those who hear the word of God and, kindled by faith, invoke him, is pleasing. This is the part of the response in which he says what thing distinguishes places, namely, the word of God, and this part still censures only the Samaritans, who bound worship to a place in which the word of God did not sound. It was necessary for this error to be censured.

Afterwards he adds more. That the word of God is not bound to a certain place, and he distinguishes external worship bound to places from true worship, and he censures the error of both peoples, the Samaritans and the Jews. The Samaritans pretended there was a Church without the word of God; the Jews had the word of God, but they pretended that worship was their sacrifices, and they did not understand the invocation which must be done by faith. Let us therefore speak in order about the individual parts of the sermon.

Latin:

Dicit ei Iesus: Da mihi bibere.

Hic colloquium instituitur Christi et mulie- ris, in quo Christus tradit doctrinam Evangelii, et concionatur de vocatione gentium, et discernit vetus et novum Testamentum, item cultus veros et falsos. Est autem peculiare testimonium mise- ricordiae, quod miserae adulterae suum Evange- lium offert, et huic expresse dicit, sese esse Mes- siam, et postea cum ea pergit in oppidum, et ibi biduum commoratur, ut discipulam confirmet, et alios vocet ad Evangelii lucem. Hoc testimonio et nos confirmemus, sciamus vere recipi peccato- res, et Ecclesiam esse coetum humilem et despe- ctum, sed agentem poenitentiam et credentem Evangelio, nec alligandam esse Ecclesiam ad Pon- tifices, Reges, Principes etc.

Videtur autem Evangelista non sine causa in- seruisse loci descriptionem. Quia cum ibi domi- cilium fuerit Melchisedec, et Iacob ibi altare con- diderit, loci conspectus excitavit ingentes motus in Christo, cogitante de veteri Ecclesia, et de pa- trum vocatione, de promissionibus, de reiectione populi, et alia multa: apparet enim eius animum non fuisse otiosum, quia cibo allato postea frui non potuit. Hos affectus utile est in Christo con- siderare, ut vere nos ab eo diligi, et vere eum afficti nostris malis statuamus, sicut saepe in hi- storiis Evangelii dicitur affici misericordia, quam

Prima autem quaestio oritur ex traditione humana, non sunt commercia Iudaeis et Samaritanis. Etsi enim Deus interdixerat Israëlitis vicinarum gentium impiarum connubiis et idolis, tamen non interdixerat contractibus, emtionibus, venditionibus, aut officiis communicandi cibi et potus. Addiderant autem Pharisaei superstitiosas traditiones, ut cumularent opera opinione iusticiae, et fingebant se propter legem, et suas traditiones iustos esse. Porro Samaritani, etsi receperant doctrinam de uno Deo creatore, quem profitebantur hunc esse, qui se patribus, Abrahae, Isaac, et Iacob revelaverat, tamen promissiones et doctrinam de fide non norant, et retinebant multas superstitiones ethnicas, ut ostendit liber 4. Reg. 17. Christus omissa traditione, pergit suum officium facere, incipit dicere quis sit, et quid doceat, sed habet initio rudem discipulam, nondum capacem Evangelii. Ideo postquam pauca praefatus est, concionatur mulieri de poenitentia. Dixit obscure: Si agnosceres donum Dei, et quis sit, qui dicit tibi etc. Postea clarius narrat, se esse Messiam, vitae aeternae datorem. Qui biberit ex aqua, quam ego dabo ei, fiet in eo fons aquae salientis in vitam aeternam. Nondum intelligit mulier, quid sibi velit haec miranda concio, et miscet humanas ineptias de aquatione. Hic Christus proponit ei concionem poenitentiae, ut agnito peccato, agnita ira Dei, possit erudiri de Messia, de remissione peccatorum. Obiurgat eam propter adulteria. Hic illa expavescens, incipit iam de doctrina, et de cultu Dei quaerere. Iudaei recte sentiebant non aliud templum esse debere populi Israël, ubi fierent sacrificia, nisi Ierosolymis, sed Samaritani opponebant exempla patrum. Imitari Abrahae, Isaac, Iacob exempla in cultu Dei, maxime pium est. Hic sacrificavit Iacob, ergo et nos pie facimus, quod hic sacrificamus. Haec haud dubie sacerdotes impii exaggerabant, qui cupiebant abducere populum a doctrina Mosi, Christus diiudicat quaestionem: Ubicunque verbum Dei est, ibi recte fit adoratio. Patres qui hic adoraverunt, id est, sacrificaverunt, erant custodes et doctores verbi, a Deo ipsis commendati et traditi. Hoc proponebant aliis, et docebant veram invocationem, et invocabant ipsi, fide accensi per hoc verbum. Postea hoc idem verbum Dei commendatum est tribui Levi, ut ad tabernaculum, seu templum docerent, ibi Deus quaeri verbum suum voluit, ut vera invocatio fieri posset. Sed vos Samaritani iam hic facitis adorationem et sacrificia, sine verbo Dei. Ideo vestra adoratio reiecta est. Nos Iudaei retinemus verbum. Erant enim aliqui, ut Simeon, Zacharias, retinuerant. Ideo ad tem- plum, et in hac Ecclesia, in qua sonat verbum Dei, placet adoratio eorum, qui verbum Dei au- diunt, et fide accensi invocant. Haec est pars responsionis, in qua dicit, quae res discernat loca, scilicet, verbum Dei, et haec pars taxat adhuc tantum Samaritanos, qui alligabant adora- tionem loco, in quo non sonabat verbum Dei. Hunc errorem taxari necesse fuit.

Postea addit amplius. Verbum Dei non esse alligatum ad certum locum, et discernit externam adorationem alligatam locis a vera, et taxat utriusque populi errorem, Samaritanorum et Iu- daeorum. Samaritani fingebant Ecclesiam sine verbo Dei, Iudaei habebant verbum Dei, sed fin- gebant adorationem esse sua sacrificia, nec intel- ligebant invocationem, quae facienda est fide. Dicamus igitur ordine de singulis partibus con- cionis.

## 4:21
The hour comes when neither on the mountain, etc.

He speaks about the propagation of the Gospel in the whole world, and let it not be understood only as the Church in this life, but also the Church resurrected and already enjoying eternal blessedness, and without any weakness now celebrating God and giving thanks to him, as if he were saying: The Messiah establishes an eternal kingdom gathered from all nations, in which God will be perpetually celebrated, and there will be no external worship bound to the Jewish temple or to this mountain. Not on this mountain, nor in Jerusalem, that is, you will not worship God in ceremonies bound to a place. It is therefore a prediction about the eternal kingdom, which is begun in the preaching of the Gospel, scattered through the whole world, as it is said in Hosea 1: And it will be in the place where it will be said to them: You are not my people, there it will be said to them, sons of the living God. The first sentence here therefore admonishes the woman about another worship, namely, spiritual and eternal, and rejects the ceremony bound to a place. This sentence will be explained more clearly in the statements that follow.

Latin:

Venit hora, quando neque in monte, etc.

Loquitur de propagatione Evangelii in toto orbe terrarum, nec tantum intelligatur Ecclesia in hac vita, sed etiam Ecclesia resuscitata et fruens iam aeterna beatitudine, et sine ulla imbe- cillitate iam celebrans Deum, et ei gratias agens, quasi dicat: Messias regnum aeternum constituit collectum ex omnibus gentibus, in quo Deus per- petuo celebrabitur, nec erit cultus externus, alli- gatus ad templum Iudaicum, aut ad hunc mon- tem. Non in hoc monte, nec Ierosolymis, id est, non in ceremoniis alligatis loco, coletis Deum. Est igitur praedictio de aeterno regno, quod in- coatur in praedicatione Evangelii, sparsa per to- tum orbem, ut Oseae 1. dicitur: Et erit in loco ubi dicetur eis: Non populus meus vos, ibi dice- tur eis, filii Dei viventis. Prima igitur sententia hic admonet mulierem de alio cultu, scilicet, spi- rituali et aeterno, et reiicit ceremoniam alligatam loco. Haec sententia clarius exponetur in dictis, quae sequuntur.

## 4:22
You worship what you do not know.

Here he only distinguishes the Gentiles and the Church, in which the word of God handed down through the Prophets sounds. and the Apostles, he does not yet censure Jewish worship. All nations and groups, such as Mahometans and others calling upon God, without the word delivered through the Prophets and Apostles, call upon what they do not know. And although it is briefly stated, yet it contains a most copious doctrine, and convicts the blindness of the whole world. The greatest part of men worship religions in appearance, on account of custom; thus Alexander, Julius, Augustus, and the like, felt that common customs should be obeyed. All such confess that they do not know what they adore, they confess they do not know whether God cares for, judges, and hears men. There are others, like Plato, Cicero, who are moved by reason to feel that God is some eternal mind, as Plato says, the cause of good. But yet what He is, how He wishes to be called upon, and to hear, they are ignorant. Therefore when they cry out to God, soon doubts press in upon them: what thing God is, whether He regards individuals, whether He hears you who are calling upon Him. Similar is the blindness in Mahometans, indeed even in all who are ignorant of the Gospel. As in the island of Crete it is said there was a statue of Jupiter without ears: so all nations ignorant of the Gospel in their invocation doubt what thing they are addressing, whether a deaf one, or one that is intelligent, caring, hearing, truly effective and saving men. And although this doubt in human minds is not obscure, nor does the disease lie hidden, yet the stupor is so great that we do not think about what and how great the evil is. Let us learn therefore to recognize, deplore, and flee this plague, and let us take refuge in the light in which the eternal God has revealed Himself, to the word delivered through the Prophets, Christ, and the Apostles, so that we may truly call upon God, therefore it follows.

Latin:

Vos adoratis quod nescitis.

Hic tantum discernit Ethnicos et Ecclesiam, in qua sonat verbum Dei traditum per Prophetas et Apostolos, nondum vituperat cultus Iudaicos. Omnes gentes et coetus, ut Mahometistae et aliae invocantes Deum, sine verbo tradito per Prophe- tas et Apostolos, invocant quod nesciunt. Etsi autem breve dictum est, tamen copiosissimam do- ctrinam continet, et coecitatem totius mundi ar- guit. Maxima pars hominum religiones in spe- ciem colit, propter consuetudinem, sic Alexan- der, Iulius, Augustus, et similes, sentiebant moribus communibus obtemperandum esse. Ta- les omnes fatentur se nescire quid adorent, faten- tur se nescire, an Deus curet, iudicet, et exau- diat homines. Alii sunt, ut Plato, Cicero, qui moventur ratione, ut sentiant Deum esse aliquam mentem aeternam, sicut Plato dicit, causam boni. Sed tamen quae sit, quomodo velit invocari, et exaudire, ignorant. Ergo cum clamant ad Deum, mox obstrepunt eis dubitationes, quae res sit Deus, an singulos respiciat, an te invocantem exaudiat. Similis est coecitas in Mahometistis, imo et omni- bus ignaris Evangelii. Ut in Creta insula dicitur fuisse Iovis statua sine auribus: ita omnes gentes ignarae Evangelii in invocatione dubitant, quam rem alloquantur, surdamne, an intelligentem, curantem, audientem, vere efficacem et salvan- tem homines. Etsi autem haec in humanis men- tibus dubitatio non obscura est, nec latet morbus, tamen stupor tantus est, ut non cogitemus, quid et quantum sit mali. Discamus ergo agnoscere, deplorare et fugere hanc pestem, et confugiamus ad lucem, in qua se Deus aeternus patefecit, ad verbum traditum per Prophetas, Christum et Apostolos, ut vere invocemus Deum, sequitur ergo.

## 4:22
We worship what we know.

That is, we know that the will of God is not seen without His own revelation, as was said above: No one has ever seen God, but the Son who is in the bosom of the Father, He has declared Him to us. We know likewise that He does not wish that we ourselves should fashion opinions about Him by our own judgment, or devise forms of worship. Therefore we receive that word in which He has revealed Himself, and we call upon this eternal, wise, good, just God, the judge and father of Jesus Christ, who also has promised us salvation on account of the Son, whom by a wonderful and ineffable counsel He made a victim for us. On account of Him we know certainly that we are regarded, heard, and saved; we know this voice

of the Gospel to be the first, one, and perpetual in the Church, delivered by certain testimonies through the Prophets, Christ, and the Apostles.

These things which I now recite, and which Christ certainly says here, are daily to be contemplated in the mind during invocation. Your invocation must be distinguished from the clamor of the Gentiles, Jews, and Mahometans, who, if asked, would all confess that they call upon a deaf God, and doubt what thing God is, and what His will is, and whether He hears the prayers of men, or is affected by our miseries; they would confess likewise that they have no certain testimonies of their doctrine, nor whence or how it was propagated, nor do they know whether God has promised that He will hear, or how He wishes to be appeased. Therefore separate yourself from the invocation of these, and join yourself to the whole Church of the Fathers, Prophets, and Apostles; through these consider that the word was delivered by certain testimony, and recognize and confess that this is the God who has revealed Himself through His word. This God is neither mute nor deaf; He spoke in the beginning with the Fathers and Prophets, He exhibited also other certain and evident testimonies, such as by raising the dead, and with a clear voice He commanded us all concerning the Son: Hear Him. Furthermore, He is not deaf, but truly wishes on account of the Son to hear and to save, and believers know that they are not deceived. All these things are to be thought upon daily in invocation, the testimonies of the Church delivered thence from the beginning are to be contemplated.

The prayer of the fathers teaches this very thing, God of Abraham, that is, I call upon Thee, O God, who deliveredst Thy word to Abraham by certain testimony, by which Thou also didst testify that Thou wouldst hear; by faith in this word I call upon Thee, and I believe that I am heard, regarded, and I do not call upon Thee like the others, who are ignorant of the word of Abraham, like the Egyptians, or others, not knowing what God is, how He wishes to be recognized and worshipped, whether He has promised anything concerning His will. God therefore added also in the first commandment a testimony by which He wishes to be recognized, when He says: I am the God who brought thee out of the land of Egypt; thus He always proposed some certain testimony. But let all things be referred to the sum, that is, to the Son; let us contemplate Him, as He said: He who sees Me, sees the Father also. Therefore call upon this God, who has revealed Himself both through the Son, and has published the promise of mercy and salvation through Him, and on account of Him He grants it, therefore it follows.

Latin:

Nos adoramus quod scimus.

Id est, nos scimus voluntatem Dei non con- spici sine ipsius revelatione, sicut supra dictum est: Deum nemo vidit unquam, sed filius qui est in sinu patris, ipse enarravit nobis. Scimus item, nolle eum, ut nos ipsi fingamus de eo opiniones nostro iudicio, aut excogitemus cultus. Ideo ac- cipimus id verbum in quo se patefecit, et hunc Deum aeternum, sapientem, bonum, iustum, iudicem, et patrem Iesu Christi invocamus, qui et pollicitus est nobis salutem propter filium, quem mirabili et inenarrabili consilio pro nobis victimam fecit. Propter hunc scimus certo nos respici, exaudiri, et salvari, scimus hanc vocem

Evangelii primam unam et perpetuam esse in Ecclesia, traditam certis testimoniis per Prophe- tas, Christum et Apostolos.

Haec quae nunc recito, et quae certe hic Christus dicit, quotidie in invocatione animo in- tuenda sunt. Discernenda est tua invocatio ab Ethnicorum, Iudaeorum, Mahometistarum cla- more, qui interrogati, omnes faterentur se invo- care surdum Deum, ac dubitare quae res sit Deus, et quae sit eius voluntas, et an audiat hominum vota, an afficiatur nostris miseriis, faterentur item se nulla habere certa testimonia suae doctrinae, nec unde aut quomodo propagata sit, nec scire an promiserit Deus se exauditurum esse, aut quo- modo velit esse placatus. Ergo ab horum invo- catione te seiungas, et te ad totam Ecclesiam Pa- trum Prophetarum, et Apostolorum adiungito, per hos cogita verbum certo testimonio traditum esse, et hunc esse Deum, qui se patefecit per suum verbum, agnoscas et fatearis. Hic Deus nec mu- tus est, nec surdus, locutus est initio cum Patri- bus et Prophetis, exhibuit et alia certa et eviden- tia testimonia, ut resuscitatis mortuis, et clara voce nobis omnibus de filio praecepit: Hunc au- dite. Deinde nec surdus est, sed vere vult pro- pter filium exaudire, et salvare, et credentes sciunt se non falli. Haec omnia quotidie in in- vocatione cogitanda sunt, intuenda testimonia Ecclesiae tradita inde usque ab initio.

Hoc ipsum docet patrum precatio, Deus Abraham, id est, te Deum invoco, qui Abrahae tradidisti certo testimonio verbum tuum, quo et testatus es te exauditurum esse, huius verbi fide te invoco, et credo me audiri, respici, nec in- voco ut caeteri, ignorantes verbum Abrahae, ut Aegyptii, aut alii, nescientes quid sit Deus, quo- modo velit agnosci et coli, an promiserit aliquid de sua voluntate. Addidit igitur Deus et in primo praecepto testimonium, quo vult agnosci, cum ait: Ego sum Deus, qui eduxit te de terra Ae- gypti, sic semper aliquod certum testimonium proposuit. Sed omnia referantur ad summam, id est, ad filium, hunc nos intueamur, sicut dixit: Qui videt me, videt et patrem. Hunc igi- tur Deum invoca, qui se, et per filium patefecit, et promissionem misericordiae, et salutis per ipsum edidit, et propter eum praestat, ideo se- quitur.

## 4:22
Because salvation is from the Jews.

Salvation signifies the promises, or the word handed down by certain testimonies, and the Mediator himself. These are known only to the Jews, that is, to the people holding the word of God, namely the true Church of God, and at that time in that Jewish Church there was not only knowledge of the promises and the mediator, but the mediator himself was born in that people, according to the promises.

Latin:

Quia salus ex Iudaeis est.

Salus significat promissiones, seu verbum certis testimoniis traditum, et ipsum Mediatorem. Haec sunt tantum nota Iudaeis, id est, populo tenenti verbum Dei, videlicet verae Ecclesiae Dei, et tunc in illa Ecclesia Iudaica non solum erat no- ticia promissionum et mediatoris, sed etiam ipse mediator in eo populo natus erat, iuxta promis- siones.

## 4:23
But the hour is coming, and now is, when the true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth.

Above, he distinguished the Church from the other nations, and rejected the invocation which is done outside the Church. Now he adds a doctrine concerning true invocation, taxing also the worship of the Jews, as if he were saying: Neither in the Church are external sacrifices true worship. The Pharisees thought their sacrifices excelled because they were done in a place established by God, but the place does nothing to the matter; God wanted those rites to be observed in a certain place so that it might be known for certain to which people the word of God had been handed down, but he wanted greater worship taught than those external sacrifices. Which ones? That the Father be worshipped in spirit and in truth. Spirit is opposed to external work or ceremony, and signifies a spiritual motion kindled by the Holy Spirit, by which the heart is turned to God and beholds God, namely the fear of God and faith. Truth is opposed to two things: doubt, and a righteousness that is about to die. For the worship of the New Testament is not only a motion of the heart, but also such a motion with which there is true confidence, certainly establishing that God is propitious to you, that he hears you, that he wishes to save you. This confidence is the beginning of eternal and perpetual life, not of a light concerning God and righteousness that is about to die. On the contrary, however, hypocrisy either busies itself in ceremonies or in philosophical works. Meanwhile, however, it retains doubt, just as Ahab perpetually remains in this doubt, whether he has God as propitious, whether he is heard. Hezekiah, however, does not doubt that he has God as propitious; by this faith he raises himself in the highest danger, asks for, and expects help from God, and this very faith kindles a light concerning God, and righteousness, which is the beginning of eternal life, just as it is said in John 17: This is eternal life, that they may know you to be the only God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.

By this saying are also described the worship of the New Testament, which bring eternal life, and are perpetual things in the soul; they are not external ceremonies, nor philosophical works, with which is joined doubt concerning the will of God, concerning wrath and mercy, but they are a light in the heart by which we recognize that God is truly angry at sin, we truly tremble, and we feel that God is not idle, as reason thinks. Then by which we again establish that, for those fleeing to the mediator, sins are remitted, and we are truly received, not neglected in adversities and in death, and we submit ourselves to God, we confess that we owe him obedience in all works, struggles, and afflictions to which he calls us, and we do not grow proud in the admiration of our own wisdom or righteousness, we do not rage against God in punishments, but we obey that eternal majesty, and we feel that on account of the Son we are pleasing, even if we are unworthy.

These sayings of John 4 and 17 embrace this interior worship, which ought to be held as common rules, so that they may admonish us concerning the proper worship of the Church, and so that we may have in readiness clear testimonies to refute the Pharisaic and ethnic opinions concerning ceremonies ex opere operato scattered in the Church. For Christ also opposes these sentences to that very delusion; thus the woman thought, that the sacrifices which were done either in Jerusalem or on that mountain Gerizim, where the Samaritans had built a temple, merited the remission of sins for men ex opere operato, that is, that they were righteousness and merits, even if in the heart of the doer there remained doubt concerning the wrath and mercy of God. The Papists have taught, and still defend, the same delusions when they speak of the sacrifice of the Mass and of many other ceremonies, which they pretend are righteousness and merits, even if in the heart of the doer there remains doubt concerning the wrath of God and the remission of sins.

Furthermore, the reader must again be warned: When there is talk of the knowledge of God in this saying, likewise of spirit and truth, that is, of true motions of the heart and true faith, it must always be understood that the Gospel is required here, in which God has revealed himself. There is no knowledge without the word shining before it, no faith without a promise. Indeed, let us know that this light is kindled in hearts by the Holy Spirit through the Gospel, and not otherwise. Wherefore, where there is no word of God, there cannot be worship of God, just as he said above: You worship what you do not know; without the word of God you invent the will of God and worship, when you know neither what the will of God is toward you, nor what kind of worship he approves. Such is ethnic worship, and all who rely only on human traditions. Therefore it is said: In vain do they worship me with the commandments of men.

God is a spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and in truth.

There have been those who attributed the shape of a human body to God, but that delirium is refuted by this saying of Christ: God is a spirit, that is, a spiritual essence, without bodily mass. But this must be declared: when he names spirit, he understands a certain essence that is intelligent, willing, free, wise, good, just, strong, life-giving, judging, etc. These effects in some way indicate and describe a spiritual nature, just as our reasoning, will, free choice, discernment of honorable and base things, or of virtues and vices, vices and motions, in some way indicate the human mind, which is the image of God. Therefore, the nature of spirit is to be estimated by thought in some way, not by imagining a mass of body.

However, the argument of Christ must be considered. God is a spirit, therefore he must be worshipped in spirit and in truth. Why does this follow? Because all worship or invocation is truly an acknowledgment of the will of God. A spirit cannot be acknowledged unless a spiritual light is kindled, and truth in the heart. It is necessary, therefore, that God be invoked in spirit and in truth. There is no invocation without acknowledgment, as a great part of men practice heathen invocation, thinking nothing in their mind about the will of God, doubting whether they are heard. To these, God is either nothing, or a deaf thing, just as in Crete there was a statue of Jupiter without ears. Such, however, are all the cults of ceremonies among all the impious, by whatever name they may be called. Such is the invocation of the Jews, Mahometans, and Papists, who imagine that their cults are valid by the work performed, without a good motion of the doer, that is, even if you do not think of the will of God, either as angry at sin or as receiving those who flee to him.

Therefore, let this be held first: that in invocation there must be an acknowledgment of the will of God, namely of his wrath and mercy. Paul commands the same when he says: Offer a rational cult, that is, a cult of the mind, in which the mind truly deals with something with God, acknowledging wrath and mercy. And in the first commandment, where the true and highest cults are handed down, it is said: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart; and in Isaiah 29, external cult without the invocation of the heart is condemned: This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. But it is not enough for there to be motions of the heart, such as a man meditates upon without the word of God and without the Holy Spirit. For doubt remains in such a heart, but through the word of God, a light must be kindled by the Holy Spirit, in which the wrath and mercy of God are truly perceived. Thus, when David was rebuked, a new light was kindled in his heart, by which he acknowledged that God is not idle, negligent of human crimes, but is truly angry at sins. But again, having heard the absolution, he acknowledged that he is truly merciful, life-giving, and freeing from eternal wrath. Such motions are spirit and truth, that is, spiritual motions and true knowledge of God, attributing to God wisdom, justice, and goodness, wherefore God is affected by true honor by such motions. The sum of this discourse is the rejection of the Pharisaic opinion, which imagines that ceremonies and external works please God by the work performed, as they call it. This heathen persuasion had oppressed the Church of that time, and always wanders in the world. Therefore, remember this discourse, so that you may have a refutation at hand.

Latin:

Sed venit hora, et nunc est, quando veri ado- ratores adorabunt patrem spiritu et veri- tate.

Supra distinxit Ecclesiam a caeteris gentibus, et reiecit invocationem, quae fit extra Ecclesiam. Nunc addit doctrinam de vera invocatione, taxans etiam Iudaeorum cultus, quasi dicat: Nec in Ec- clesia externa sacrificia sunt veri cultus. Phari- saei putabant antecellere sua sacrificia, quia fie- bant loco constituto a Deo, sed locus nihil ad rem facit, Deus voluit certo loco servari eos ritus, ut certo sciretur, cui populo traditum esset ver- bum Dei, sed alios maiores cultus, quam illa ex- terna sacrificia doceri voluit. Quosnam? Ut pa- ter adoretur in spiritu et veritate. Spiritus oppo- nitur externo operi seu ceremoniae, et significat spiritualem motum incensum a Spiritu sancto, quo cor ad Deum convertitur, et Deum intuetur, videlicet timorem Dei et fidem. Veritas opponi- tur duabus rebus, dubitationi, et moriturae iu- sticiae. Nam cultus novi Testamenti non solum est motus cordis, sed etiam talis motus, cum quo est vera fiducia, certo statuens, quod Deus sit tibi propicius, quod exaudiat te, quod velit te salvare. Haec fiducia est incoatio vitae aeternae et perpetuae, non moriturae lucis de Deo et iu- sticiae. Econtra vero hypocrisis aut versatur in ceremoniis, aut in philosophicis operibus. Inte- rim vero retinet dubitationem, ut Achas perpetuo manet in hac dubitatione, an habeat Deum pro- picium, an exaudiatur. Ezechias vero non du- bitat se habere Deum propicium, hac fide in sum- mo periculo se erigit, petit, et expectat auxilium a Deo, et accendit haec ipsa fides lucem de Deo, et iusticiam, quae est incoatio vitae aeternae, sicut Ioann. 17. dicitur: Haec est vita aeterna, ut co- gnoscant te solum esse Deum, et quem misisti Ie- sum esse Christum.

Describuntur et hoc dicto cultus novi Testa- menti, qui afferunt vitam aeternam, et sunt res perpetuae in anima, non sunt externae ceremo- niae, nec opera philosophica, cum quibus est coniuncta dubitatio de voluntate Dei, de ira et de misericordia, sed sunt lux in corde, qua agno- scimus Deum vere irasci peccato, vere expavesci- mus, et sentimus Deum non esse otiosum, ut ra- tio cogitat. Deinde qua rursus statuimus, con- fugientibus ad mediatorem remitti peccata, et nos vere recipi, non negligi in adversis et in morte, et subiicimus nos Deo, fatemur nos ei debere obedientiam in omnibus operibus, certaminibus et afflictionibus, ad quas vocat nos, et non su- perbimus admiratione nostrae sapientiae, aut iu- sticiae, non fremimus adversus Deum in poenis, sed illi aeternae maiestati obtemperamus, et sen- timus propter filium nos placere, etiamsi sumus indigni.

Hos cultus interiores complectuntur haec dicta Ioannis 4. et 17. quae tanquam communes regulae teneri debent, ut nos de propriis Eccle- siae cultibus admoneant, et ut habeamus in promtu perspicua testimonia, ad refutandas pha- risaicas et ethnicas opiniones de ceremoniis ex opere operato sparsas in Ecclesia. Nam et Chri- stus prorsus illi ipsi delirio opponit has sententias, sic sentiebat mulier, sacrificia, quae fiebant vel Ierosolymis, vel in illo monte Garizim, ubi tem- plum Samaritani condiderant, mereri hominibus remissionem peccatorum ex opere operato, id est, esse iusticiam et merita, etiamsi in corde facien- tis maneat dubitatio de ira et de misericordia Dei. Eadem deliria docuerunt, et adhuc defendunt Pa- pistae, cum de sacrificio Missae et de ceremoniis aliis multis loquuntur, quas fingunt esse iusticiam et merita, etiamsi in corde facientis maneat dubi- tatio de ira Dei, et de remissione peccatorum.

Caeterum rursus monendus est lector: Cum dicitur de noticia Dei in hoc dicto, item de spiritu et veritate, id est, veris motibus cordis, et vera fide, semper intelligendum est, hic requiri Evan- gelium, in quo se patefecit Deus. Nulla est no- ticia sine verbo praelucente, nulla fides sine pro- missione. Imo sciamus hanc lucem accendi in cordibus a Spiritu sancto per Evangelium, et non aliter. Quare ubi nullum est verbum Dei, ibi non possunt esse cultus Dei, sicut supra dixit: Vos adoratis quod nescitis, sine verbo Dei fingitis voluntatem Dei et cultus, cum non sciatis, neque quae sit voluntas Dei erga vos, neque quales cul- tus approbet. Tales sunt ethnici cultus, et omnes qui tantum nituntur traditionibus humanis. Ideo dictum est: Frustra colunt me mandatis ho- minum.

Deus spiritus est, et adorantes ipsum, in spi- ritu et veritate oportet adorare.

Fuerunt qui Deo figuram corporis humani tribuerunt, sed id delirium refutatur hoc dicto Christi: Deus est spiritus, id est, essentia spiri- tualis, sine mole corporea. Sed id declarandum est, cum nominat spiritum, intelligit essentiam quandam intelligentem, ac volentem, liberam, sapientem, bonam, iustam, fortem, vivificatri- cem, iudicantem, etc. Hi effectus utcunque in- dicant et describunt naturam spiritualem, sicut humanam mentem, quae est effigies Dei, utcun- que indicant nostra ratiocinatio, voluntas, electio libera, discrimen honestorum et turpium, seu virtutum et vitiorum, vitia et motus. Cogita- tione ergo utcunque aestimanda est natura spiri- tus, non fingenda est moles corporis.

Considerandum est autem argumentum Chri- sti. Deus est spiritus, ergo spiritu et veritate adorandus est. Cur hoc sequitur? Quia omnis adoratio seu invocatio vere est agnitio voluntatis Dei. Spiritus non potest agnosci, nisi accensa spirituali luce, et veritate in corde. Necesse est igitur Deum invocari in spiritu et veritate. Non est invocatio sine agnitione, ut magna hominum pars ethnicam invocationem exercet, nihil cogitat in mente de voluntate Dei, dubitat an exaudiatur. His Deus aut nihil est, aut res surda est, sicut in Creta erat statua Iovis sine auribus. Tales autem sunt omnes cultus ceremoniarum apud omnes impios, quocunque nomine vocentur. Talis est Iudaeorum, Mahometistarum et Papistarum in- vocatio, qui fingunt suos cultus valere ex opere operato, sine bono motu facientis, id est, etiamsi non cogites Dei voluntatem, vel irascentem pec- cato, vel recipientem confugientes ad eum.

Primum igitur hoc teneatur, in invocatione oportere esse agnitionem voluntatis Dei, videlicet irae et misericordiae. Idem praecipit Paulus, cum ait: Offerte cultum rationalem, id est, cul- tum mentis, in quo mens vere aliquid cum Deo agit, agnoscens iram et misericordiam. Et in praecepto primo, ubi veri et summi cultus tra- duntur, dicitur: Diliges dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde; et Esaias 29. damnatur cultus exter- nus, sine invocatione cordis: Populus hic labiis me honorat, cor autem procul est a me. Sed non satis est esse motus cordis, quales homo sine verbo Dei, et sine Spiritu sancto meditatur. Ma- net enim in tali corde dubitatio, sed per verbum Dei oportet accendi lucem a Spiritu sancto, in qua vere cernatur ira et misericordia Dei. Sic cum David obiurgaretur, accensa est in corde eius nova lux, qua agnovit Deum non esse otiosum, negligentem humana scelera, sed vere irasci pec- catis. Rursus autem audita absolutione, agnovit vere esse misericordem, vivificantem et liberan- tem ab aeterna ira. Tales motus sunt spiritus et veritas, id est, spirituales motus et vera Dei no- ticia, tribuens Deo sapientiam, iusticiam, boni- tatem, quare talibus motibus Deus vero honore afficitur. Summa vero huius concionis est reie- ctio pharisaicae opinionis, quae fingit ceremonias et externa opera placere Deo ex opere operato, ut vocant. Haec ethnica persuasio et illius tempo- ris Ecclesiam oppresserat, et semper vagatur in mundo. Ideo hanc concionem memineris, ut in promtu refutationem habeas.

## 4:25
I know that the Messiah is coming.

The woman heard the discourse about repentance when she was rebuked on account of her adulteries; afterwards she heard the reproof of false cults, but she does not yet understand this, wherefore, as if doubting, she now begins to desire a more illustrious doctrine. When the Messiah comes, she says, he will teach us these things, just as many now await synods and new judgments of controversies, and do not acquiesce in the word of God. Thus this woman still fluctuates in her mind, nor is she moved by that magnificent voice which she had heard: The water that I will give him will become in him a fountain of life leaping up into eternal life. But yet, because she is teachable, she is not rejected, but is freed from error, and is truly led to the acknowledgment of God and the Messiah, so that henceforth she may serve God. She hears, therefore, an express voice testifying about the Messiah: I, he says, who speak with you, am the Messiah: see a notable example. The Gospel is revealed to the despised, and to those not swelling with confidence in their own wisdom, just as Christ says: You have revealed it to little ones, and hidden it from the wise. This miserable woman hears this so clear voice about the Messiah, and although Christ signified the same by many testimonies publicly, yet he does not approach any high priest or Pharisee privately, nor does he teach those wise men so calmly, so clearly. But what is the reason why wise men less often arrive at the light of the Gospel? Paul says this is the reason: Because human wisdom is pleased with itself and plays with infinite opinions about God; therefore, it generally despises the word of God, as it is said in 1 Corinthians 1: We preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to the Jews, but to the Greeks foolishness. Likewise: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise. And in 2 Corinthians 10, he exhorts us to take captive every thought to the obedience of Christ. Let us not think these are trivial precepts, but the matter shows that the most serious lapses have always been those of human wisdom, whether judging doctrine or other great affairs without the word of God. The counsel of the people of Israel, asking for a king, was wise, but this wisdom displeased God, because He wanted this people to be ruled by His word and to expect defense from God. The counsel of Jeroboam, instituting a peculiar cult so that the ten tribes would not again join themselves to the city of Jerusalem, was wise, but from this, infinite εἰδωλομανία (idolatry) arose, and punishments and the destruction of the whole kingdom followed. Thus, after the Apostles, how many heresies has human wisdom produced? Why are manifest idols defended now, if not because of the arguments of human wisdom? They argue that the concord of the Church is salutary, that defection from the ordinary authority produces infinite dissipations, tumults, and wars. Therefore, they order us to take a favorable view of, excuse, and mitigate customary errors, etc. But to speak of the lapses that arise properly from human wisdom is an infinite task; I only wished to warn the reader to consider that the mind must be curbed and ruled by the word of God, and not played with by inventing opinions. Let us know that this audacity displeases God and is destructive, as it has been said: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise. Ethnic examples also show that the wisest men have often brought destructive calamities upon both themselves and their empires, such as Themistocles, Theramenes, Pericles, Cicero, and many others. Because God hates the confidence of human wisdom and wants us to be ruled by His word, which keeps us in our calling and forbids us to tempt God, that is, to undertake things not commanded.

Meanwhile his disciples came, etc. Likewise: She left her water jar, etc.

The individual parts of this narrative have their own meanings. This woman, having heard the sermon of Christ, becomes herself a herald of the Gospel. Thus, in a wonderful way, the light of the Gospel is spread. But she leaves her water jar at the well, having omitted the cares of bodily things, or having left the old fountain, that is, her former doctrine, she undertook a new ministry. She begins, however, from the miracle, that this unknown guest had recounted her secrets and had called her to repentance and had taught her about the true worship of God, concerning which the sentences that are in the text were undoubtedly explained more copiously.

My food is to do the will of Him who sent me.

This conversation between Christ and the Apostles is somewhat obscure, but in summary, Christ signifies three sentiments in veiled words. The first is about his own sorrow. The second about the Prophets and the old Church. The third about the Apostles. The first sentiment, about his own sorrow, is signified: because although he was exhausted by the labor of the journey and had sought food, yet now he does not enjoy the food brought to him, not out of any superstition, but because his mind is occupied by some new sadness or care, which brings a distaste for food, or rather so weakens the stomach that it does not even admit food; this languor is very well known to those who feel sharp pains of the mind. But from where did this sudden sadness arise in Christ? Undoubtedly from many concurrent causes; thinking of the blindness of the neighboring Samaritan people, he is affected with sorrow for them, and he desires to liberate some, and prays for them. These things were happening in this man, not without great movements. His mind burns with sorrow because of the miseries of the whole human race, because of the destruction of the greatest part of men; he prays with vehement emotion, he thinks also of his own death and of redemption: He recalls in his mind the hardships of the Fathers and the Prophets. This is the first part of this conversation: My food is to do the will of the Father, and to complete his work, that is: I am now occupied with the care and thought of my calling, I am tormented by a certain very sharp pain, and I pray for this people. These affairs of the calling are to be preferred to food. Indeed, a pious and diligent minister, when he is exercised by these cares, cannot even admit food. Now he compares to this image those who seek ministries because of their belly, and because of leisure and wealth assent to false opinions.

All these are condemned by this voice of Christ: My food is to do the will of Him who sent me.

The second part of the conversation is about the Fathers and the Prophets, and he makes a comparison of the Fathers and Prophets with the Apostles. For because he recalls to mind the Church of all times, he signifies that the government of the Prophets was more difficult than that of the Apostles will be. For the Prophets sustained two things: political government and the propagation of doctrine concerning the promises, concerning the Messiah, and concerning eternal life. The administration of Samuel, Elijah, Elisha, Jeremiah, and Daniel was much more difficult than that of the Apostles. And not to speak of the others, how difficult was the government of Jeremiah? Who for 40 continuous years quarreled with kings, high priests, and princes. And he persuaded them to surrender, contrary to the examples of all the Prophets who had been before him, and by this unusual counsel he saved the people. What insults did he endure, how often was he shut up in prison, how often was he cast into deep pits, where he was about to perish in the mire, had he not been divinely delivered? And although it is no light burden to bear insults and bodily tortures, yet mental sorrows exercise a governor much more harshly. Jeremiah acknowledged the wrath of God against the sins of the people, and he was shaken by horrible terrors; he mourned the destruction of the people, he fought with prayer for the people, he quarreled with impious teachers, he was disturbed by scandals arising one after another. In short, no human mind can foresee or enumerate all the difficulties which government brings, especially in a restless, seditious, and now collapsing republic, as are most of the empires of these times. The course of Jeremiah was therefore much more difficult than that of the Apostles, who, free from political government, only carried about the Gospel. Therefore Christ says: the harvest is at hand, but there were others who did the sowing first, that is, the Fathers, the Prophets, and himself. This is, as it seems to me, the second part of the discourse, nor is the comparison difficult. He says the harvest is at hand, taking the occasion from the sight of the crops. And because this journey was made some time after the Passover, the first which is described in John, namely at the end of March or the beginning of April, he says: In 4 months the harvest will be here, and the crops are already turning yellow. The harvest is therefore at hand; go, he says, and for you Apostles a harvest is at hand much easier than for the Fathers, the Prophets, and me. Great was the glory of the Apostles, that in a short time they converted many nations to the true knowledge and invocation of God, and that they were not burdened with political government, but they themselves meanwhile had their own hardships, of which this is the greatest: that they, alone and private men without the appearance of authority, were compelled to contradict all the powers in the whole world. How difficult this matter is for good and moderate men cannot be explained by any reason. They also had infinite dangers to their bodies, and secret struggles with the specters and snares of the devil, and endless contentions with fanatical teachers. But in these hardships shines the glory and presence of God, who by wondrous deliverances testifies that he cares for this despised and weak flock, as Christ says: Take heart, for I have overcome the world. Likewise: He who is in you is greater than he who is in the world. Likewise: I will not leave you orphans, etc.

For we ourselves have heard, and we know that this is the savior of the world.

Immediately at the beginning in Paradise after the fall of Adam, the ministry of the Gospel was instituted, namely, both of preaching repentance and of the promise. This one and the same ministry is perpetual, and will be until the resurrection of the dead. God therefore wishes to call the Church by the voice of the Gospel, but he also wishes this, that those who hear should believe, and believe not in human authority, but in the word and testimonies of God. We are warned of this in this history: First, the woman performs an apostolic duty, she calls the people to the Messiah; the dispute about ordinary authority has nothing to do with the Gospel. Whoever brings the voice of God must be heard, whether he be an ordinary Bishop or a private man. For the Gospel of God must necessarily be obeyed, whoever it is through whom it sounds. Thus, when Christ was born, the Apostles were shepherds; when Christ hung on the cross, the Apostles were the thief and the centurion. To this effect Paul says: God does not accept the person of man.

The argument therefore does not hold: These things the Bishops have decreed, therefore they must be received as certain, true, and necessary. In the Synod of Antioch, the Deacon Malchion especially opposed Paul of Samosata, and the opinion of Malchion was rightly preferred, because he retained the writing of the Apostle John, which Samosata was corrupting. It is enough to warn briefly about this regarding ordinary authority, namely, that the word of God must be preferred.

Secondly, the example warns that individuals must be judges of doctrine for themselves, even if this seems to be said arrogantly and absurdly, that it is not enough to follow the judgments of synods and doctors, but that there ought to be added the proper judgment of each person, as is said in this place: We have heard and we know. Thus, faith in individuals should rest not on human authority, but on the word of God and testimonies. You believe the Nicene synod not because of the judgment of this multitude which gathered there, but because you understand the decree to agree with certain testimonies of the word of God. Human and political judgments invert this order; they do not want those things which have been judged once to be called into dispute, just as it is not permitted to call into dispute again those things which have been deliberated and decreed by a king and princes in any kingdom. But let us know that faith does not depend on any human authority; the conscience could not invoke the Son of God and attribute omnipotence to him if it had no testimony except that of a synod, but because the very words of Christ and the Apostles teach this, faith is kindled and truly invokes.

But you might ask, is it not enough to hear the ministers of the Gospel? I answer: It is enough, just as it is clearly said below in chapter 17: I pray not for them only, but also for all who will believe through their word; but when we hear ministers, we ought to know whence they received the doctrine, that is, whether they bring the doctrine of the Son of God, just as the Samaritans inquired here whence the woman had received the doctrine. Let faith look to the sources, the word and the testimonies, etc.

Latin:

Scio quod Messias venit.

Audivit mulier concionem de poenitentia, cum obiurgata est propter adulteria, postea audi- vit reprehensionem falsorum cultuum, sed hanc nondum intelligit, quare velut dubitans iam inci- pit desiderare illustriorem doctrinam. Cum ve- niet, inquit Messias, haec nos docebit, ut nunc multi expectant synodos et novas diiudicationes controversiarum, nec acquiescunt in verbo Dei. Ita haec mulier adhuc fluctuat animo, nec illa magnifica voce movetur, quam audierat: Aqua, quam ego dabo ei, fiet in eo fons vitae salientis in vitam aeternam. Sed tamen, quia docilis est, non reiicitur, sed liberatur ab errore, et vere ad agnitionem Dei, et Messiae traducitur, ut dein- ceps Deo serviat. Audit igitur expressam vocem testificantem de Messia: Ego, inquit, qui loquor tecum, sum Messias: vide insigne exemplum. Revelatur Evangelium spretis, et non tumentibus fiducia suae sapientiae, sicut inquit Christus: Re- velasti parvulis, et abscondisti a sapientibus. Haec misera mulier audit hanc tam claram vocem de Messia, et quanquam idem significavit Christus multis testimoniis publice, tamen non accedit pri- vatim ullum pontificem, aut Pharisaeum, nec tam placide, tam perspicue sapientes illos docet. Sed quae causa est, cur sapientes minus per- veniant ad lucem Evangelii? Hanc esse dicit Pau- lus: Quia humana sapientia sibi placet, et ludit opinionibus de Deo infinitis: ideo plerunque con- temnit verbum Dei, ut 1. Corinth. 1. dicitur: Praedicamus Christum crucifixum, Iudaeis scan- dalum, Graecis vero stultitiam. Item: Perdam sapientiam sapientum. Et 2. Corinth. 10. horta- tur, ut captivemus intellectum ad obedientiam Christo. Non existimemus haec esse frivola prae- cepta, sed res ostendit, gravissimos lapsus sem- per fuisse humanae sapientiae, vel doctrinam, vel alia magna negotia iudicantis sine verbo Dei. Erat sapiens consilium populi Israël, postulantis regem, sed Deo displicuit haec sapientia, quia voluit hunc populum regi verbo, et expectare a Deo defensionem. Erat sapiens consilium Iero- boam, instituentis peculiarem cultum, ne decem tribus rursus se adiungerent civitati Ierosolymae, sed hinc infinita εἰδωλομανία orta est, et secutae poenae et excidium totius regni. Sic post Apo- stolos, quantum haeresium peperit humana sa- pientia? Cur nunc manifesta idola defenduntur, nisi propter humanae sapientiae rationes? dispu- tant salutarem esse concordiam Ecclesiae, defe- ctionem ab ordinaria potestate gignere infinitas dissipationes, tumultus, bella. Ideo iubent usi- tatos errores boni consulere, excusare, mitigare, etc. Sed dicere de lapsibus, qui proprie ab hu- mana sapientia oriuntur, infinitum est, tantum monere lectorem volui, ut cogitet frenandam esse mentem, et regendam verbo Dei, et non luden- dum fingendis opinionibus. Sciamus hanc auda- ciam Deo displicere, et exitiosam esse, sicut di- ctum est: Perdam sapientiam sapientum. Osten- dunt etiam ethnica exempla, sapientissimos ho- mines, et sibi et imperiis saepe accersivisse exitio- sas calamitates, ut Themistoclem, Theramenem, Periclem, Ciceronem, et alios multos. Quia Deus odit fiduciam humanae sapientiae, et vult nos regi suo verbo, quod retinet nos in vocatione, et vetat tentare Deum, id est, suscipere res non man- datas.

Inter haec venerunt discipuli eius, etc. Item: Reliquit hydriam suam, etc.

Singulae partes huius narrationis habent suas significationes. Haec mulier audita concione Chri- sti, fit et ipsa Evangelii annunciatrix. Ita mira- bili modo spargitur lux Evangelii. Sed relinquit ad fontem hydriam, omissis rerum corporalium curis, seu relicto veteri fonte, hoc est, doctrina priore, suscepit novum ministerium. Orditur autem a miraculo, quod arcana ipsius recitaverit hic hospes ignotus, et eam ad poenitentiam voca- verit, et de vero cultu Dei docuerit, de quo sen- tentiae, quae sunt in textu, haud dubie copiosius enarratae sunt.

Meus cibus est, ut faciam voluntatem eius, qui me misit.

Hoc colloquium Christi et Apostolorum sub- obscurum est, sed in summa significat Christus tectis verbis tres sententias. Prima est de suo do- lore. Secunda de Prophetis, et veteri Ecclesia. Tertia de Apostolis. Prima sententia de suo do- lore, significatur: quia etsi labore itineris defa- tigatus erat, et cibum expetiverat, tamen nunc non fruitur allato cibo, non superstitione aliqua, sed quia animus nova aliqua moestitia seu cura occupatus est, quae affert fastidia cibi, vel potius ita languefacit ventriculum, ut ne quidem admit- tat cibum, hic languor notissimus est his, qui acres animi dolores sentiunt. Unde autem exti- tit haec subita moestitia in Christo? Haud dubie ex multis causis concurrentibus, cogitans caecita- tem vicinae gentis Samaritanae, afficitur dolore propter ipsam, et cupit aliquos liberare, ac pro ea orat. Haec in isto viro fiebant, non sine ma- gnis motibus. Ardet animus dolore propter to- tius generis humani miserias, propter exitium maximae partis hominum, precatur vehementi motu, cogitat etiam de sua morte et de redem- tione: Repetit animo Patrum et Prophetarum aerumnas. Haec est prima pars huius colloquii: Meus cibus est, ut faciam voluntatem patris, et perficiam opus eius, id est: Iam sum occupatus cura, et cogitatione meae vocationis, excrucior acerrimo quodam dolore, et precor pro hoc po- pulo. Haec negotia vocationis sunt anteferenda cibo. Imo pius et sedulus minister, cum exerce- tur his curis, ne potest quidem admittere cibum. Iam confert ad hanc imaginem eos, qui propter ventrem appetunt ministeria, et propter otium ac opes assentiuntur falsis opinionibus.

Omnes hi damnantur hac voce Christi: Meus cibus est, ut faciam voluntatem eius, qui misit me.

Secunda pars colloquii est de Patribus et Pro- phetis, et collationem facit Patrum ac Propheta- rum, cum Apostolis. Quia enim repetit animo Ecclesiam omnium temporum, significat diffici- liorem fuisse gubernationem Prophetarum, quam futura sit Apostolorum. Nam Prophetae duas res sustinuerunt, politicam gubernationem, et pro- pagationem doctrinae, de promissionibus, de Messia, et de vita aeterna. Samuelis, Eliae, Eli- saei, Ieremiae, Danielis, multo difficilior fuit administratio, quam Apostolorum. Et ut de caeteris non dicam, quam difficilis fuit guberna- tio Ieremiae? qui annos 40 continuos rixatus est cum regibus, pontificibus et principibus. Et suasit deditionem contra omnium Prophetarum exempla, qui ante eum fuerant, et hoc inusitato consilio servavit populum. Hic quas tulit con- tumelias, quoties inclusus est carceri, quoties ab- iectus in fossas profundas, ubi in coeno periturus erat, nisi divinitus liberatus fuisset? Et quan- quam non est leve onus ferre contumelias et cru- ciatus corporis, tamen gubernatorem multo du- rius exercent animi dolores, agnoscebat Ieremias iram Dei adversus populi peccata, et horribilibus terroribus concutiebatur, lugebat populi interi- tum, pugnabat oratione pro populo, rixabatur cum impiis doctoribus, perturbabatur exorienti- bus subinde scandalis. Denique nulla mens hu- mana prospicere aut enumerare omnes difficulia- tes potest, quas affert gubernatio, praesertim in republica inquieta, seditiosa, et iam ruente, ut sunt imperia horum temporum pleraque. Fuit igitur Ieremiae cursus multo difficilior, quam Apostolorum, qui liberi a gubernatione politica, tantum circumtulerunt Evangelium. Ideo inquit Christus: instare messem, sed fuisse alios, qui prius sementem fecerunt, id est, Patres, Prophe- tas, et sese. Haec est, ut mihi videtur, secunda pars colloquii, nec difficilis est similitudo. Ait instare messem, sumta occasione a conspectu se- getum. Et quia hoc iter factum est aliquanto post Pascha, primum quod in Ioanne describitur, vi- delicet in fine Martii, aut initio Aprilis, ait: Post 4 menses fore messem, et iam flavescere se- getes. Instat igitur messis, ite inquit, et vobis instat Apostolis messis multo facilior, quam Pa- tribus, Prophetis et mihi. Magna fuit gloria Apostolorum, quod brevi tempore multas gentes converterunt ad veram agnitionem et invocatio- nem Dei, et quod non fuerunt onerati politica gubernatione, sed ipsi interim habuerunt suas aerumnas, quarum haec est maxima, . quod soli et privati homines sine specie imperii, coacti sunt contradicere omnibus potestatibus in toto orbe terrarum. Haec res quam sit difficilis bonis et moderatis, non potest ulla ratione explicari. Ha- buerunt et infinita pericula corporum, et arcana certamina cum diaboli spectris et insidiis, et con- tentiones sine fine cum fanaticis doctoribus. Sed in his aerumnis lucet gloria et praesentia Dei, qui mirandis liberationibus testatur, se curare hunc despectum et infirmum gregem, sicut inquit Chri- stus: Confide, quia ego vici mundum. Item: Maior est, qui in vobis est, quam qui est in mundo. Item: Non relinquam vos orphanos, etc.

Ipsi enim audivimus, et scimus quod hic est salvator mundi.

Statim initio in Paradiso post lapsum Adae institutum est ministerium Evangelii, videlicet, et poenitentiae praedicandae, et promissionis. Hoc unum et idem ministerium perpetuum est, et erit usque ad resuscitationem mortuorum. Vult igitur Deus voce Evangelii vocare Ecclesiam, sed vult hoc quoque, ut audientes credant, et cre- dant non autoritati humanae, sed verbo et testi- moniis Dei. Haec monemur in hac historia: Pri- mum mulier fungitur munere apostolico, vocat populum ad Messiam, nihil ad Evangelium per- tinet disputatio de ordinaria potestate. Quisquis affert vocem Dei, audiendus est, sive sit ordina- rius Episcopus, sive privatus homo. Nam Evan- gelii Dei necessario parendum est, quisquis est, per quem sonat. Ita nato Christo erant Apostoli, pastores: cum Christus in cruce penderet, erant Apostoli, latro, et centurio. In hanc senten- tiam inquit Paulus: Deus personam hominis non accipit.

Non igitur valet argumentum: Haec Episcopi decreverunt, quare pro certis, veris, necessariis recipienda sunt. In Synodo Antiochena adver- sabatur Paulo Samosateno praecipue Diaconus Malchion, et recte praeferebatur sententia Mal- chionis, quia retinebat Ioannis Apostoli scriptum, quod Samosatenus corrumpebat. Haec de auto- ritate ordinaria breviter monere satis est, videli- cet, quod oporteat anteferri verbum Dei.

Secundo monet exemplum, oportere singulos per sese iudices esse doctrinae, etsi hoc videtur arroganter et absurde dici, non satis esse sequi synodorum ac doctorum iudicia, sed debere acce- dere proprium cuiusque iudicium, ut hoc loco di- citur: Ipsi audivimus et scimus. Ita fides in sin- gulis nitatur non autoritate humana, sed Dei verbo et testimoniis. Credis synodo Nicenae non pro- pter huius multitudinis iudicium, quae ibi conve- nit, sed quia intelligis congruere decretum cum certis testimoniis verbi Dei. Hunc ordinem in- vertunt humana et politica iudicia, non volunt in disputationem vocari ea, quae semel iudicata sunt, ut non licet rursus vocare in disputationem ea, quae in aliquo regno re deliberata a rege et prin- cipibus decreta sunt. Sed nos sciamus fidem non pendere ex ulla humana autoritate, non posset conscientia invocare filium Dei, et tribuere ei omnipotentiam, si nullum haberet testimonium, nisi synodi, sed quia verba ipsa Christi et Apo- stolorum hoc docent, accenditur fides et vere in- vocat.

Sed quaeras, an non satis est audire mini- stros Evangelii? Respondeo: Satis est, sicut infra cap. 17. clare dicitur: Rogo non pro eis tantum, sed etiam pro omnibus credituris per verbum eorum, sed cum audimus ministros, scire debe- mus unde acceperint doctrinam, id est, an affe- rant doctrinam filii Dei, sicut hic inquisiverunt Samaritani, unde mulier acceperit doctrinam. Fides intueatur fontes, verbum et testimonia etc.

## 4:46
And there was a royal official, whose son, etc.

Now after the first Passover he returns to Galilee, where he immediately calls to the Gospel with a new miracle the household of a powerful man, serving King Herod. It is, however, an illustrious example of weak faith; Christ censures the weakness. But nevertheless, he receives one who has the beginning and spark of faith, just as elsewhere in Mark 9: I believe, Lord, help my unbelief. Thus also Paul says in Romans 14 about the weak: God receives him. So the Apostles are sometimes rebuked: you of little faith, why did you doubt? Let us diligently consider these examples, both that we may acknowledge the feebleness of our faith and ask for an increase, and yet sustain ourselves with this consolation, that those who have some spark of faith are not cast away. Just as it is said in Isaiah: A smoldering wick he will not extinguish.

The feebleness of faith is, however, rebuked in these words: Unless you see signs, you do not believe. Christ looks into the hesitation of that petitioner, and at the same time judges the others who were present. They did not yet believe his word, and they were struggling with manifold doubt. But the whole human race ought to believe the divine voice, especially since it is never without certain testimonies. Long ago, Simeon, Joseph, Anna, Zacharias, John the Baptist had already testified about Christ, and a voice had been heard from heaven: This is my beloved Son. These had as yet moved few to acknowledge the Messiah. Therefore, in these words, both the hesitation of this petitioner and the hardness of the others are censured.

But this petitioner, although he is weak, is nevertheless received and heard; his hesitation or trepidation appears because he fears that unless he is helped while his son is still living, there is no hope after death: nor does he understand that this Messiah can restore life not only to the sick, but also to the dead. Indeed, that blind courtier does not understand that this very life, after sin, is a journey of death, and that the Messiah, the author of life, will give a life which is outside the tyranny of this death. He can therefore restore both the sick and the dead alike. Although there are errors and hesitations in this listener, yet because it is a beginning of faith, he is received and helped. Let these examples confirm us, so that, not deterred by our own feebleness, we may not flee from Christ, but rather approach, invited by his most sweet voice, by which he says: Come to me all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Likewise: Ask, and you shall receive.

But the human mind does not understand these acts of worship, petition and invocation of God, but, hindered and oppressed by the opinions of the law, it thinks that acts of worship are only when we offer excellent deeds to God; it is hindered by natural doubt, so that it cannot establish that God truly wishes to be present with us and to help in so many affairs; reason thinks it would be most miserable occupations for God if he were to be present for this one in fevers, for that one in shipwreck, for others in battle, for others in the guarding of a house, family, or children. But let us cast these Epicurean thoughts out of our mind, and let us think that all human dangers are great, and that in all of them the snares of the devil are to be feared, and let us kindle ourselves to invocation by precepts and promises. We cannot overcome death, the dangers of body and soul, and the snares of the devil without the help of God. Therefore Christ says: Without me you can do nothing. But let us learn that this is the chief act of worship of God, to seek help from him by trust in the Mediator, just as Psalm 49 says: Call upon me in the day of trouble, etc.

Latin:

Et erat Regulus, cuius filius, etc.

Nunc post primum Pascha redit in Galilaeam, ubi statim novo miraculo vocat ad Evangelium familiam hominis potentis, servientis regi Herodi. Est autem illustre exemplum infirmae fidei, taxat Christus infirmitatem. Sed tamen recipit haben- tem fidei initium et scintillam, sicut alibi Marci 9.: Credo domine, opitulare diffidentiae meae. Ita et Paulus Rom. 14. dicit de infirmo: Deus eum reci- pit. Sic aliquoties obiurgantur Apostoli, vos pa- rum fidentes, quid dubitastis? Haec exempla di- ligenter consideremus, et ut fidei nostrae imbe- cillitatem agnoscamus, et petamus incrementum, et tamen hac nos consolatione sustentemus, quod non abiiciantur, qui aliquam scintillam fidei ha- bent. Sicut apud Esaiam dicitur: Linum fumi- gans non extinguet.

Reprehenditur autem fidei imbecillitas in his verbis: Nisi signa videtis, non creditis. Intro- spicit Christus illius petentis haesitationem, et simul de caeteris iudicat, qui aderant. Hi non- dum credebant eius verbo, et laborabant multi- plici dubitatione. Debet autem totum genus hu- manum voci divinae credere, praesertim cum nun- quam sit sine testimoniis certis. De Christo iam olim testificati erant Simeon, Ioseph, Anna, Za- charias, Ioannes Baptista, et vox de coelo audita erat: Hic est filius meus dilectus. Haec paucos adhuc moverant, ut Messiam agnoscerent. Est igitur his verbis taxata, et huius petentis haesita- tio, et caeterorum durities.

Sed hic petens, etsi est infirmus, tamen re- cipitur et exauditur, haesitatio seu trepidatio ap- paret, quia veretur, nisi viventi adhuc filio co- ram opituletur, post mortem nihil esse spei: nec intelligit hunc Messiam non solum aegrotis, sed etiam mortuis posse vitam reddere. Imo non in- telligit ille coecus aulicus, hanc ipsam vitam post peccatum, mortis iter esse, et Messiam autorem vitae, daturum esse vitam, quae sit extra huius mortis tyrannidem. Potest igitur pariter et aegro- tum et mortuum restituere. Quanquam autem sunt errores et haesitationes in hoc auditore, ta- men quia initium est fidei, recipitur et adiuvatur. Haec exempla nos confirment, ne deterriti imbe- cillitate nostra, fugiamus Christum, sed potius accedamus invitati dulcissima voce ipsius, qua in- quit: Venite ad me omnes qui laboratis, et one- rati estis, ego reficiam vos. Item: Petite, et acci- pietis.

Sed humana mens non intelligit hos cultus, Dei petitionem et invocationem, sed impedita et oppressa opinionibus legis, cogitat tantum cultus esse, cum nos egregia facta Deo offerimus, impe- dita est et naturali dubitatione, ut non potest sta- tuere, Deum vere velle nobis adesse, et opitulari in tam multis negotiis, cogitat ratio miserrimas esse occupationes Dei, si huic in febribus, illi in naufragio, aliis in acie, aliis in custodia domus, familiae, liberorum adsit. Sed has epicureas co- gitationes eiiciamus ex animo, et cogitemus omnia humana pericula magna esse, et in omnibus me- tuendas esse insidias diaboli, et nos praeceptis et promissionibus ad invocationem accendamus. Non possumus mortem, pericula corporis et ani- mae, insidias diaboli, sine auxilio Dei vincere. Ideo Christus inquit: Sine me nihil potestis facere. Discamus autem hunc esse praecipuum cultum Dei, auxilium ab eo fiducia mediatoris petere, sicut Psal. 49. ait: Invoca me in die tribulatio- nis, etc.

## 4:53
And he himself believed, and his house.

The former passage is an example of weak faith, which nevertheless obtains what it asks for. The latter passage is a confirmation following the event, and the conversion of many. After victory, faith becomes more ardent, as Paul says: Testing produces hope, when we struggle and conquer, faith and hope are confirmed, so that we may henceforth more eagerly await the help of God, and 2 Corinthians 1: We had the sentence of death in ourselves, that we should not be confident in ourselves, but in God, who raises the dead, who delivered us from so great a death, and does deliver, in whom we hope, that he will also deliver us again, with your prayers helping. Both teach that God allows us to be overwhelmed by the storms of afflictions, so that we may learn the fear of God, amend our security, and lay aside confidence in ourselves, just as God punished King Nebuchadnezzar, so that he would lay aside confidence in himself: again it also teaches that He delivers us, so that we may have testimonies of His presence and mercy, that He truly helps. Just as Hagar, helped in exile by the showing of a spring, afterwards becomes firmer in faith, and with greater constancy awaits the help of God, just as it is said in the Pauline statement: Who will also deliver us again, etc. Thus faith grows and is confirmed in this courtier, when he discovers that his petition was not in vain, and his family is moved by the testimony of the miracle, so that they now believe the author of the benefit is the Messiah. Such are the deliverances, such are the victories, such are the triumphs of Christ, which we will understand then, when the Church is glorified, how in such actions He fought with the devil, so that He might deliver many from his snares.

Latin:

Et credidit ipse, et domus eius.

Prior locus est exemplum infirmae fidei, quae tamen impetrat, quod petit. Alter locus est con- firmatio secuta eventum, et multorum conversio. Post victoriam fides fit ardentior, sicut Paulus in- quit: Probatio spem efficit, cum dimicamus et vincimus, confirmatur fides et spes, ut deinceps alacrius expectemus auxilium Dei, et 2. Corinth. 1.: Responsum mortis in nobis habuimus, ut non simus confidentes in nobis, sed in Deo, qui exusci- tat mortuos, qui ex tanta morte liberavit nos, et liberat, in quem speramus, quod et iterum nos liberaturus sit, adiuvantibus vestris precibus. Utrunque docet quod Deus sinat nos obrui pro- cellis afflictionum, ut discamus timorem Dei, emendemus securitatem, deponamus fiduciam no- stri, sicut Deus regem Nabuchodonosor punivit, ut deponeret fiduciam sui: rursus etiam docet, quod liberet nos, ut testimonia habeamus prae- sentiae et misericordiae eius, quod vere opitule- tur. Sicut Agar adiuta in exilio monstrato fonte, postea fit firmior in fide, et maiore constantia expectat auxilium Dei, sicut et in dicto Paulino dicitur: Qui et iterum liberabit nos, etc. Ita crescit et confirmatur fides in hoc aulico, cum comperit non fuisse irritam petitionem, et move- tur familia testimonio miraculi, ut iam credat au- torem beneficii esse Messiam. Tales sunt libera- tiones, tales sunt victoriae, tales triumphi Chri- sti, quos intelligemus tunc, cum glorificabitur Ecclesia, quomodo in talibus actionibus praelia- tus sit cum diabolo, ut plures a laqueis eius libe- raret.

## 5:1 Argument
Chapter V.

Latin:

Caput V.

## 5:1
Afterwards there was a feast of the Jews.

From the series of the history it appears that the first year since the baptism of Christ is still being conducted, and the feast, of which mention is made here, is written by Cyril to be Pentecost, who adds that on that day an angel was accustomed to descend from heaven, and to stir this pool, so that the first one who was brought in might be healed. We say, however, concerning the miracles of Christ, the same things everywhere in general, which I also briefly repeat here. First: Miracles are so many and consistent testimonies that this word, which the teacher scatters here, is truly divine, and that the teacher was sent by God, because the matter shows that he is helped by God. Second, these miracles are testimonies of divine power in this teacher. As he clearly affirms here: My Father is working until now, and I am working, what He does, the Son also does likewise. Here Christ affirms these things are done both by the eternal Father and by Himself. And it is a notable testimony, as will be said later, concerning the divine nature of the Son. Third, miracles are examples of promises, which ought to move us to ask for and seek help, just as the promises themselves and all things are referred to this statement: The Son of God appeared, that He might destroy the works of the devil. So that it may be certain that sin and death are destroyed by the Son of God, He often removes diseases, and raises the dead, therefore let us also, whether overwhelmed by sin or by the punishments of sin, flee to Christ, and ask for and await deliverance. These are the acts of worship that affect this Messiah with special honor, and they are not understood by human reason without the light of the Gospel. For human minds are occupied with the opinions of the law, and they always bring this philosophy to God: you will truly worship God if you bring excellent virtues to Him; because you do not bring these, you are not worthy of His gifts. Furthermore, it is absurd to ask God to run to your fever, to your poverty, and to the subduing of some foolish desire; why do you not repress it yourself? These imaginations harshly exercise human minds, but let us learn that the Son of God was sent for this reason, that the voice of the Gospel was published for this reason, so that we might amend that philosophy of human reason, and know that it is truly the worship of God to ask for help, as Christ says: Without me you can do nothing. Let it be enough to have said these things about miracles in general.

Latin:

Postea erat festum Iudaeorum.

Ex serie historiae apparet adhuc agi primum annum a baptismo Christi, et festum, cuius hic fit mentio, scribitur a Cyrillo esse Pentecoste, qui addit, eo die solitum angelum de coelo descen- dere, et hanc piscinam agitare, ut sanaretur pri- mus, qui inferebatur. Dicimus autem de mira- culis Christi ubique eadem in genere, quae et hic breviter repeto. Primum: Miracula tot et con- gruentia sunt testimonia, hoc verbum, quod hic doctor spargit, vere divinum esse, et doctorem a Deo missum esse, quia res ostendit, eum iuvari a Deo. Secundo, haec miracula testimonia sunt potentiae divinae in hoc doctore. Sicut hic clare affirmat: Pater meus etiamnum operatur, et ego operor, quae ille facit, et filius similiter facit. Hic affirmat Christus haec facta, et ab aeterno patre, et a sese fieri. Estque insigne testimonium, ut postea dicetur, de divina natura filii. Tertio, mi- racula sunt exempla promissionum, quae nos ad petendum et expetendum auxilium movere debent, perinde ut ipsae promissiones et omnia referantur ad hanc sententiam: Apparuit filius Dei, ut de- struat opera diaboli. Ut certum sit destrui a filio Dei peccatum et mortem, saepe tollit morbos, et resuscitat mortuos, ergo et nos vel peccato, vel peccati poenis obruti, confugiamus ad Christum, et petamus et expectemus liberationem. Hi sunt cultus, qui praecipuo honore hunc Messiam affi- ciunt, et non intelliguntur ab humana ratione, sine luce Evangelii. Nam humanae mentes sunt occupatae opinionibus legis, et semper afferunt ad Deum hanc philosophiam, sic vere coles Deum, si eximias virtutes ad ipsum afferes, has quia non affers, non es dignus eius muneribus. Praeterea absurdum est a Deo petere, ut accurrat ad tuam febrim, ad tuam inopiam, et ad domandam ali- quam stultam cupiditatem, cur ipse eam non re- primis? Hae imaginationes duriter exercent men- tes humanas, sed discamus ideo missum esse filium Dei, ideo editam vocem Evangelii, ut illam philosophiam rationis humanae emendemus, et sciamus vere cultus Dei esse, petere auxilium, sicut Christus inquit: Sine me nihil potestis fa- cere. Haec de miraculis in genere dixisse satis sit.

## 5:4
An angel at a set time used to descend into the pool.

There were many miracles among this people, by which God gave testimony to His word, among which this also is to be numbered, that on Pentecost itself, they discovered every year that the water was moved by an angel, and the first one who was brought in after the water was moved was healed, nor is there any doubt that God wished to adorn this day of the given law with this testimony in a peculiar way. The angel troubling the water signifies the voice of the law, troubling consciences that recognize the horrible wrath of God against sins. But this happens, not so that the troubled minds may perish, but so that the firstfruits may be saved; therefore only the first one was healed. For the voice of the law troubles the whole human race, but the firstfruits are saved, that is, the elect, who recognize the Son of God; let this be the brief explanation of the meaning. For it is certain that by this troubling of the waters the ministry of the law was signified, so that the people might be admonished for what purpose the law was given, and why that Pentecost had been instituted, namely, that all might acknowledge the wrath of God against sins.

I think this also pertains to the signification, that these things were done in the pool of Bethesda, that is, the sheep-pool, in which the sacrificial victims were washed.
