For by the voice of the law, victims are plunged into death, that is, the law testifies that we are destined for death on account of sin and are guilty of the wrath of God. For it is not a light or trivial matter that is signified when mention is made of victims. For a victim signifies something guilty and destined for death on account of the wrath of God. Furthermore, this must also be considered: just as men abuse other benefits of God, so they abused this one; the poor were kept away, nor could they be cured, but the rich were brought in first, and without doubt this matter was profitable to the priests. Cruelty against the poor is therefore covertly rebuked. The word Βηθεσδὰ seems to signify house of benefit or of alms, and the whole matter is a wonderful image of the Church, which is properly a house of alms, in which the sick are cured by heavenly ministry.

That he had done these things on the Sabbath.

It is a notable example of calumnies; the Jews cloak this cause with hatred of Christ, that he violates the Sabbath. It must therefore be asked whether he violated the law by healing, and likewise whether the one healed violated the law by carrying his bed. I answer that neither violated it. First, concerning Christ, there is a plain and clear defense, and one which most declares the law concerning the Sabbath. The law does not command idleness simply, but commands holy works which conduce to the ministry of the word of God, and it prohibits other external works of the body which hinder the ministry: this is the simplest meaning of this principal law. Now this work of Christ was a testimony of the ministry and word of Christ, just as other healings done on the Sabbath, and it confirmed faith in many and excited them to true invocation; all these were most properly works of the Sabbath. Wherefore this healing also was truly a work of the Sabbath. Secondly, the law was given to man, and not to God, and is a discipline prohibiting certain works of this carnal and weak nature which serve the belly. But this healing done by Christ was properly a work of God, sanctifying this one who was cured and beginning a new life in him.

Concerning the one healed carrying his bed, I also answer that he did not act against the law. Because the law does not prohibit works testifying to the ministry. This public carrying on Pentecost itself was a work testifying to Christ, therefore it was not prohibited by law. Secondly: The Lord is the son of man even of the Sabbath, says Christ, and testifies that he is above the priesthood and the polity of the law; he commands therefore, as the priest of the new Sabbath and the new Pentecost, something other than the Levitical priest; therefore the one healed had to obey the superior Lord, and indeed the end of the law and the polity was signified by this very spectacle. The one healed on the Sabbath, or Pentecost, that is, in the beginning of the new and eternal Testament; he no longer lies on his bed, that is, in the polity of Israel, but he takes this very polity and law with him by the liberty of the spirit; he does not seek righteousness by ceremonies or by works of the law, but he now has health, that is, true and heavenly light and righteousness in his soul. Outwardly, however, as long as he is in the body, he uses whatever polities there are, like a guest soon to go into eternal life,

Sin no more.

Christ testifies that diseases are punishments for sins, and he exhorts the one healed to take care, lest by falling again he bring new punishments upon himself. Thus Paul says to the Corinthians: If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged by the Lord. Likewise Psalm 38: For iniquity you correct man. And indeed let us learn that the punishments of this life, which is short and momentary, do not yet satisfy the wrath of God, but are signs of the eternal wrath of God. Caligula, Nero, even if they were killed, yet by this brief punishment they did not yet satisfy the wrath of God, but there are two ends of these present punishments. The one is that those who are curable, being admonished by both their own and others' punishments, may be called to repentance. For these understand that these torments are signs of eternal wrath against those who are not amended. Therefore it is written: When we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord, that we may not be condemned with this world. Likewise Apocalypse 3: Those whom I love, I rebuke and chasten. The other end is that the incurable may be restrained, repressed, and removed. Therefore in Psalm 32 it is said: Bind their jaws with bit and bridle, who do not approach you, that is, human nature is burdened with huge miseries, so that stubbornness may be restrained.

Solomon says in Ecclesiastes chapter eight: He who keeps the commandment will not be affected by punishments, but for the wicked there will be no help on the day of death, nor will there be deliverance in war, nor escape. Blasphemers, like Rabshakeh, Judas, Arius; perjurers, like Metius; murderers, like Cain, and tyrants, like Alexander, Caligula, Nero; adulterers, like Paris, Tereus, and countless others are punished, so that they may cease to rage, and the example of punishments deters others. It is enough to have warned of this passage: That you may not sin henceforth, lest something worse happen to you. Let us know that this sermon is proposed to us all, and that the examples of this sermon are the greatest part of human calamities, which may warn us of the wrath of God, deter us from contumacy, and exhort us to repentance.

Latin:

Angelus stato tempore descendebat in pisci- nam.

Multa fuerunt miracula in hoc populo, quibus Deus testimonium dedit verbo suo, inter quae et hoc numerandum est, quod in ipsa Pentecoste, quotannis compererunt aquam ab angelo moveri, et primum, qui post motam aquam inferebatur, sanari, nec dubium est, quin hunc diem datae legis ornare hoc testimonio peculiariter Deus vo- luerit. Angelus conturbans aquam, significat vo- cem legis, conturbantem conscientias, agnoscen- tes horribilem iram Dei adversus peccata. Sed id fit, non ut pereant conturbatae mentes, sed ut primitiae salventur, ideo tantum primus sanaba- tur. Nam vox legis conturbat universum genus humanum, sed salvantur primitiae, id est, electi, qui agnoscunt filium Dei, haec sit brevis signi- ficationis enarratio. Certum est enim hac contur- batione aquarum significatum esse ministerium legis, ut admoneretur populus, ad quem usum data lex esset, et quare illa Pentecoste instituta esset, videlicet, ut omnes agnoscerent iram Dei adversus peccata.

Arbitror et hoc ad significationem pertinere, quod haec fiebant in piscina probatica, id est, ovilla, in qua lavabantur hostiae. Nam voce legis hostiae in mortem merguntur, id est, lex testatur nos destinatos esse morti, propter pecca- tum, et reos irae Dei. Non enim levis aut exigua res significatur, cum fit mentio hostiarum. Nam hostia significat quiddam reum, et destinatum morti, propter iram Dei. Caeterum et hoc con- siderandum est, ut caeteris beneficiis Dei abutun- tur homines, ita et hoc abusos esse, pauperes ar- cebantur, nec curari possent, sed divites prius inferebantur, et haud dubie haec res quaestuosa fuit sacerdotibus. Tecte igitur reprehenditur cru- delitas adversus pauperes. Vocabulum Βηθεσδὰ videtur significare domum beneficii, seu eleemo- synae, et tota res mirifica imago est Ecclesiae, quae proprie est domus eleemosynae, in qua ae- groti curantur ministerio coelesti.

Quod haec fecisset in Sabbato.

Insigne exemplum est calumniarum, prae- texunt Iudaei odio Christi hanc causam, quod sabbatum violet. Quaerendum est igitur, an le- gem violarit sanando, item an sanatus violarit legem, gestando grabhatum. Respondeo, neu- trum violasse. Primum de Christo plana et per- spicua defensio est, et quae maxime declarat le- gem de sabbato. Lex non praecipit otium sim- pliciter, sed praecipit sancta opera, quae mini- sterio verbi Dei conducunt, et prohibet alia ex- terna opera corporis, quae impediunt ministe- rium: haec simplicissima est huius legis princi- palis sententia. Iam hoc opus Christi erat testi- monium ministerii et verbi Christi, sicut aliae curationes in sabbato factae, et confirmabat fidem in multis, et excitabat eos ad veram invocationem, haec omnia erat propriissime opera sabbati. Quare et haec sanatio vere fuit sabbati opus. Secundo, lex homini lata est, et non Deo, et est disciplina prohibens certa opera huius carnalis et infirmae naturae, quae serviunt ventri. Sed haec sanatio facta a Christo proprie erat opus Dei, sancti- ficans istum curatum, et novam in eo vitam in- coans.

De sanato gestante grabhatum, etiam respon- deo, eum non fecisse contra legem. Quia lex non prohibet opera testificantia de ministerio. Haec publica gestatio in ipsa Pentecoste erat opus te- stificans de Christo, non igitur erat lege prohibi- tum. Secundo: Dominus est filius hominis etiam sabbati, inquit Christus, et testatur se supra sa- cerdotium, et politiam legis esse, mandat igitur tanquam sacerdos novi sabbati et novae Penteco- stes aliud, quam sacerdos Leviticus, igitur sana- tus, superiori domino obtemperare debuit, et quidem finis legis et politiae, hoc ipso spectaculo significatus est. Sanatus in sabbato, seu Pente- coste, id est, in incoatione novi et aeterni Testa- menti; non iam iacet in lecto suo, id est, in po- litia Israël, sed hanc ipsam politiam et legem, libertate spiritus secum aufert, non quaerit iusti- ciam ceremoniis, vel operibus legis, sed habet iam sanitatem, hoc est, veram et coelestem lucem et iusticiam in anima. Foris autem, donec est in corpore, utitur politiis quibuscunque, tanquam hospes mox iturus in vitam aeternam,

Ne amplius pecces.

Christus testatur morbos esse poenas pecca- torum, et hortatur sanatum, ut caveat, ne lapsus denuo accersat sibi novas poenas. Ita Paulus in- quit ad Corinthios: Si nos ipsi iudicaremus, non iudicaremur a domino. Item Psal. 38.: Propter iniquitatem corripis hominem. Et quidem disca- mus poenas huius vitae, quae est brevis et mo- mentanea, nondum satisfacere irae Dei, sed signa esse irae Dei aeternae. Caligula, Nero, etiamsi interfecti sunt, tamen hoc brevi supplicio non- dum satisfecerunt irae Dei, sed harum praesen- tium poenarum duo sunt fines. Alter est, ut sa- nabiles admoniti et suis et alienis poenis, vocen- tur ad poenitentiam. Hi enim intelligunt haec supplicia esse signa aeternae irae adversus eos, qui non emendantur. Ideo scriptum est: Cum iudicamur, a domino corripimur, ne cum hoc mundo damnemur. Item Apocal. 3.: Ego quos diligo, arguo et castigo. Alter finis est, ut in- sanabiles coërceantur, reprimantur et tollantur. Ideo in Psal. 32. dicitur: In chamo et freno ma- xillas eorum constringe, qui non accedunt ad te, id est, humana natura est onerata ingentibus aerumnis, ut contumacia coërceatur.

mon inquit in Ecclésiaste capite octavo: Qui cu- stodit praeceptum, non afficietur poenis, sed im- pio non erit auxilium in die mortis, nec erit libe- ratio in bello, nec evasio. Blasphemi, ut Rabsa- ces, Iudas, Arius; periuri, ut Metius; homici- dae, ut Cain, et tyranni, ut Alexander, Caligu- la, Nero; adulteri, ut Paris, Tereus, et alii innumerabiles puniuntur, ut desinant furere, et exemplum poenarum deterret alios. Haec satis est monuisse de hoc loco: Ne deinceps pecces, ne quid deterius tibi accidat. Hanc concionem nobis omnibus proponi sciamus, et exempla huius con- cionis esse maximam partem calamitatum huma- narum, quae nos de ira Dei admoneant, deter- reant a contumacia, et hortentur nos ad poeni- tentiam.

## 5:17
My Father is working until now.

This is the defense which Christ opposes to the charge of violating the law of the Sabbath. And it is the second reason from those which I reviewed above, but much richer. For Christ embraces three statements, one of which is that this healing, about which it was then being discussed, is the work of God. The second, that he with the eternal Father has done the same works from that time from the beginning, and is doing them now. The third, that the Father is not idle, or has ceased to act after he fashioned the creature, as the Jews, according to the dream of human reason, imagined that God, having founded things, afterwards left them, just as a smith leaves a ship once it is built. We must speak in order about these three very rich statements, which also contain an illustrious testimony about the Son, that he is of the divine substance.

Let us therefore speak first about the third statement: My Father is working until today. This is a refutation of the Jewish argument about the Sabbath, as if he were saying: You err, and you do not correctly understand the law, when it says in Exodus 20: In six days God made heaven and earth, and rested on the seventh day: from this you reason that God is now idle, and certainly does nothing on the Sabbath. Therefore you deny that the healing performed by me is the work of God. To this imagination of yours I oppose this saying. That the Father, after the nature of things was founded, did not cease to act, but has since always been present to his work, and has sustained it, and preserved it, making the earth fruitful every year, imparting the power of procreation, and life to living creatures. Likewise, in the Church, he performs wonderful deliverances from time to time. God was not idle when he opened a way for the people through the Red Sea, when he stopped the course of the Sun while Joshua was fighting; Christ's saying embraces these and similar things, which indeed we ought to remember diligently, and add to the other testimonies which teach us about the general action of God preserving nature, so that we do not imagine that things are now carried by their own momentum, without God, nor that life, the fruitfulness of the earth, and other works of nature are not to be sought from God; let us oppose this delirium of human reason with these sayings: In God we live, and move, and have our being. To the Hebrews 1: Upholding all things by the word of his power. Colossians 1: All things consist in him. Matthew 10: Two sparrows are sold for a penny, and one of them will not fall upon the ground without your Father. Likewise Psalm 103: All things wait for you, that you may give them food in due season.

Besides this general action of God, there also occur daily peculiar deliverances in the Church, of which many other testimonies speak, such as ask and you shall receive. Psalm 33: Many are the tribulations of the righteous, but the Lord will deliver them from them all. And both kinds of actions must be understood by faith, so that we may truly establish that God is present to the nature of things, and we may ask of him that he protect our life, that he make the earth fruitful, that he defend us. This faith is to believe the article about creation. For he who only imagines that things were founded by God in such a way, and afterwards left, just as a smith leaves a ship once made, and hands it over to the sailors, he does not think correctly about creation. But since the human mind without faith judges otherwise, the true statement about the conservation of things and the constant works of God must be learned from the testimonies, so that faith, once kindled, may recognize the presence of God, and rightly call upon him.

But why was it said in the law that God ceased, or rested? I answer: There is no doubt that secret doctrine is contained in this description and condition of the Sabbath. However, to unfold such great things is difficult. First, God is said to have rested because he founds no new species in nature, and God makes mention of cessation so that he may clearly testify that he will not found another species after man has been cast aside, but that man is the final and highest work, in which he may delight, and in which he may wish to rest, and the immense dignity of man is signified, and the love of God toward man, in this very testimony, that God pronounces this to be the final work, toward which the deliberation and desire of the whole Creator had been directed. This work God indeed wished to be for himself, in which he himself might properly delight, and in which he might be celebrated perpetually and without end.

There is also a number of days written down for a certainty, so that the distinction might be signified between life in this ψυχικῇ nature, as it is called, and the other life, in which we shall truly celebrate the Sabbath, when this nature will live in a new way without food and drink and generation, enjoying the sight of God face to face. For that new and illustrious knowledge and glorification of God will be the true celebration of the Sabbath, and it is consistent that the saying of Elijah was taken from this number of days: Six thousand years the world, and afterwards there will be destruction. Hence they think that when the six thousand years are finished, there will be the beginning of that new and eternal life in the seventh, in which the Church of God will truly sanctify the Sabbath in perpetual life, without darkness and sin, will perform holy works, will see God face to face, and will enjoy His immense wisdom. All feel that this is the principal meaning of the Sabbath, and the Epistle to the Hebrews testifies to it.

But just as that Sabbath was prepared for us in creation, so after the nature of man fell, God first consecrated the Sabbath in another way, so that He might restore to us the lost feast. For the Son of God performed the Sabbath by His death, when He rested the whole seventh day in the sepulcher; here God rested in an ineffable way, both because the Son was in the sepulcher, and because the Father permitted Him to rest that whole day, as if forsaken. This Sabbath can be declared much less than that future one, but just as the Son, before the honor of the future Sabbath, first rested in death, so the whole Church begins the honor of the Sabbath from a similar rest, or cessation, that is, from death, in which, although we seem forsaken, yet we shall certainly be resurrected to the honor of the eternal Sabbath. The magnitude of these things cannot be sufficiently declared in words, but must be pondered with pious meditation, so that in the cross we may learn that this is the beginning of the Sabbath.

Let the Sabbaths therefore be distinguished. The first is pedagogical, namely a ceremony instituted for the sake of teaching, and so that it may admonish men of the future Sabbath, in which we shall perfectly acknowledge God, and shall celebrate without any sin; the law silently signifies that these things are to be, and this pedagogy was not handed down to rule Christ, who has no need of discipline, but the remaining are the Sabbaths which properly pertain to Christ. Another in which He Himself rests in death or the sepulcher, as if forsaken by God. Another in which He celebrates the Father with eternal honor. These Sabbaths are in the same way also the Church's, from the beginning. As Abel sustains the cross, and lies in death as if forsaken by God, but afterwards resurrected will have a glorious Sabbath. Thus far I have spoken about one particle: My Father works until now; and I have recited the doctrine of the Church concerning the general action or perpetual preservation of the whole of nature, and concerning the wondrous works of God in the Church. I come to the second part.

Latin:

Pater meus huc usque operatur.

Haec est defensio, quam Christus opponit crimini de violata lege sabbati. Estque secunda ratio ex his, quas supra recensui, sed multo ube- rior. Nam Christus tres sententias complectitur, quarum una est, hanc sanationem, de qua tunc disserebatur, opus Dei esse. Secunda, se cum aeterno patre eadem opera inde usque ab initio fecisse, et nunc facere. Tertia, patrem non esse otiosum, aut desiisse agere, postquam fabricavit creaturam, sicut Iudaei iuxta somnium humanae rationis fingebant, Deum conditis rebus postea eas reliquisse, sicut faber navim fabricatam relinquit. De his tribus sententiis uberrimis ordine dicen- dum est, quae etiam continent illustre testimo- nium de filio, quod sit substantiae divinae.

Primum ergo de tertia sententia dicatur: Pater meus usque hodie operatur. Haec est refu- tatio argumenti Iudaici de sabbato, quasi dicat: Erratis, nec recte intelligitis legem, cum ait Exod. 20.: Sex diebus fecit Deus coelum et ter- ram, et requievit die septimo: hinc ratiocinami- ni, Deum nunc otiosum esse, et certe in sabbato nihil agere. Quare sanationem a me factam ne- gatis esse Dei opus. Huic vestrae imaginationi oppono hoc dictum. Patrem post conditam natu- ram rerum non desiisse agere, sed deinceps sem- per affuisse suo operi, et id sustentasse, et con- servasse, foecundare terram quotannis, impertire vim procreationis, et vitam animantibus. Item in Ecclesia subinde mirandas liberationes facere. Non erat otiosus Deus, cum viam populo patefa- ceret per mare rubrum, cum sisteret cursum Solis praeliante Iosua, haec et similia complectitur dictum Christi, quod quidem diligenter memi- nisse debemus, et adiungere caeteris testimoniis, quae docent nos de generali actione Dei conser- vantis naturam, ne fingamus res nunc suo im- petu ferri, sine Deo, nec a Deo petendam esse vitam, terrae foecunditatem, et alia naturae ope- ra, huic delirio humanae rationis opponamus haec dicta: In Deo sumus, vivimus, et move- mur. Ad Heb. 1.: Ferens omnia verbo potentiae suae. Coloss. 1.: Omnia in eo consistunt. Matth. 10.: Duo passeres asse veneunt, et unus ex illis non cadet super terram sine patre vestro. Item Psalm. 103.: Omnia a te expectant, ut des eis escam in tempore oportuno.

Praeter hanc generalem actionem Dei, etiam fiunt quotidianae peculiares liberationes in Eccle- sia, de quibus loquuntur alia multa testimonia, ut petite et accipietis. Psal. 33.: Multae tribu- lationes iustorum, sed de his omnibus liberabit eos dominus. Et utrunque genus actionum fide intelligendum est, ut vere statuamus Deum adesse naturae rerum, et petamus ab ipso, ut vitam nostram tueatur, ut foecundet terram, ut defen- dat nos. Haec fides est credere articulum de crea- tione. Nam qui sic tantum fingit a Deo conditas esse res, et postea relictas, ut cum faber navim factam, postea relinquit, et tradit nautis, hic non recte cogitat de creatione. Cum autem hu- mana mens sine fide non aliter iudicet, discenda est vera sententia de conservatione rerum, et assi- duis Dei operibus ex testimoniis, ut fides accensa agnoscat Dei praesentiam, et recte invocet eum.

Sed cur dictum est in lege cessasse, seu quie- visse Deum? Respondeo: Non dubium est arca- nam doctrinam contineri in hac sabbati descri- ptione et conditione. Evolvere autem res tantas difficile est. Primum ideo dicitur quievisse Deus, quia nullam novam speciem in natura condit, et facit mentionem cessationis Deus, ut clare teste- tur, se non aliam speciem abiecto homine con- diturum esse, sed hominem esse extremum et summum opus, quo delectetur, et in quo quie- scere velit, ac significatur ingens dignitas homi- nis, et amor Dei erga hominem, in hoc ipso te- stimonio, quod Deus pronunciat hunc esse extre- mum opus, ad quod fuerit directa totius opificis deliberatio et appetitio. Hoc opus voluit sibi Deus quidem esse, quo ipse proprie delectaretur, et in quo perpetuo et sine fine celebraretur.

Est et numerus dierum certo conscriptus, ut significaretur discrimen vitae in hac natura ψυχι- κῇ, ut vocatur, et alterius vitae, in qua vere sabbatum celebrabimus, cum haec natura sine cibo et potu et generatione vivet novo modo, co- ram fruens aspectu Dei. Nam illa nova, et illu- stris noticia et glorificatio Dei, erit vera sabbati celebratio, et consentaneum est ex hoc numero dierum dictum Eliae sumtum esse: Sex millia mundus, et postea erit destructio. Hinc existi- mant confectis sex millibus annorum, deinceps in septenario initium fore illius novae et aeternae vitae, in qua Ecclesia Dei in vita perpetua vere, sine caligine et peccato, sanctificabit sabbatum, faciet sancta opera, coram cernet Deum, et eius immensa sapientia fruetur. Hanc esse principa- lem significationem sabbati omnes sentiunt, et testatur Epistola ad Ebraeos.

Sed ut nobis in creatione paratum est illud sabbatum, ita postquam natura hominis lapsa est, Deus prius sabbatum alio modo consecravit, ut nobis restitueret amissum festum. Nam filius Dei morte sua egit sabbatum, cum quievit toto septi- mo die in sepulcro, hic Deus inenarrabili modo quievit, et quia filius fuit in sepulcro, et quia pater quiescere eum toto illo die, tanquam deser- tum, permisit. Hoc sabbatum multo minus de- clarari potest, quam futurum illud, sed ut filius ante sabbati futuri honorem, prius in morte quie- vit, ita sabbati honorem tota Ecclesia incoat a simili quiete, seu cessatione, id est, a morte, in qua etsi deserti videmur, tamen certo resuscita- bimur ad honorem aeterni sabbati. Harum re- rum magnitudo non satis declarari verbis potest, sed pia meditatione cogitanda est, ut in cruce discamus hoc esse initium sabbati.

Discernantur igitur sabbata. Primum est paedagogicum, videlicet ceremonia instituta et docendi causa, et ut admoneat homines de futuro sabbato, in quo Deum perfecte agnoscemus, et sine ullo peccato celebrabimus, haec tacite signi- ficat lex futura esse et haec paedagogia non est tradita, ut Christum regat, qui non habet opus disciplina, sed reliqua sunt sabbata, quae pro- prie ad Christum pertinent. Alterum in quo ipse quiescit in morte seu sepulcro, tanquam desertus a Deo. Alterum in quo celebrat patrem aeterno honore. Haec sabbata eodem modo etiam sunt Ecclesiae, inde usque ab initio. Ut Abel sustinet crucem, et iacet in morte velut desertus a Deo, sed postea resuscitatus habebit gloriosum sabba- tum. Hactenus dixi de una particula: Pater meus usque modo operatur; et recitavi doctrinam Ecclesiae, de generali actione seu perpetua con- servatione totius naturae, et de mirandis operibus Dei in Ecclesia. Venio ad secundam partem.

## 5:17
And I work.

This saying is afterwards declared in more words: What the Father does, the Son does likewise. Item: He shows the Son all things which the Father does, etc. These sayings are recounted among the clearest testimonies concerning the Son, that He is of the substance of the Father, and that He created and sustains things together with the Father, just as was said above: All things were made through Him; and to Heb. 1: Upholding all things by the word of His power. Let us propose these sentences to ourselves in invocation, so that invoking God the eternal Father of Jesus Christ, the creator and preserver of things, we may think that the Son and the Holy Spirit together with the Father created and preserve all things, and let us invoke them together, and directing the invocation to Christ the mediator, that He may intercede for us, let us truly establish that He is omnipotent, and hears us, and that the Father wills absolutely the same thing that the Son wills, and what He has testified that He wills. This sentence must therefore be pondered while praying: My Father works until now, and I work. Let it be enough to have briefly pointed this out, so that the reader may observe this testimony concerning the divinity of the Son, and piously weigh it with himself. Nor do I wish to recount the cavils of Samosatenus and Arius, by which they attempted to elude this passage. For the clarity of the saying is so great that it cannot be speciously shaken: For the Jews recognized that Christ was making Himself equal to God.

The saying pertains to the same thing: The Father shows all things to the Son, therefore the wisdom of the Father and the Son is equal, thus He also equates the power, nay, He makes Himself a partner of the action of God, which He does, the Son does likewise. Afterwards He also equates the honor, so that all may honor the Son, just as they honor the Father. This sentence repeats the previous ones, for this is the true honor, of which He spoke above: To attribute immense wisdom and power equally to the Father and the Son.

I come to the third sentence, namely to the conclusion refuting the Jews: The Father is not idle, nor is He bound by carnal pedagogy. I act with the Father, and I do nothing, except what I see the Father acting; therefore this healing done by me is divine, and not subject to your law concerning the Sabbath, which is a pedagogy of this weak and miserable human nature, signifying a far different Sabbath, namely the future and eternal rest, in which, with the functions of the body—generation, nutrition, and the like—ceasing, we shall perform only the works of the Sabbath. We shall behold and celebrate God, and He himself will impart to us the fellowship of His light and of eternal life. For the type in the law of the Sabbath foreshadows this future rest, as was said above.

Amen, amen, I say to you, he who hears my word and believes in Him who sent me has eternal life.

I said above that the testimonies concerning the divine nature in Christ are to be observed in this place, which I commend to the meditation of the pious. For they are sufficiently clear, even without a long explanation. We see wisdom, power, and honor being equated; therefore, omnipotence is also attributed to the Son. Furthermore, let us also observe this thunderbolt, by which the righteousness of all who do not attribute honor to the Son of God is condemned, such as Jews, Gentiles, Heretics, and all enemies of the Gospel. Even if the virtue of Fabius, Ebion, Arius, Pelagius, of some Jews who are enemies of the Gospel, likewise of Monks and other wise men who now oppose the Gospel, is excellent, yet because they do not attribute honor to the Son of God, they are clearly condemned here: He who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father; and again, for us who acknowledge the Son as mediator, and who, with Him leading, approach the Father, a huge consolation is proposed in this sentence. We know certainly that we are received by the Father, because we attribute honor to the Son, of whom the Gospel teaches, which narrates who the Son is and why He was sent. For to attribute honor to the Son is to believe the Gospel concerning all the articles about Christ, and with confidence in Him to approach God and to invoke Him. Therefore, the sentence immediately follows which interprets this honor with these words: Amen, amen, I say to you, he who hears my word and believes in Him who sent me has eternal life. Here He teaches how honor is to be attributed to the Son, namely by hearing His word and by believing both in the Son Himself and in the Father who sent Him, and for this work He promises eternal life. The Jews execrated these sermons as foul blasphemies, because He demanded that honor equal to the Son and the Father be attributed, and likewise because He promises eternal life for this work.

therefore was the law given? Or is this vile work, to believe in this crucified Messiah, of such value that eternal life is given for it? These things seem absurd to human wisdom, and especially to those who are fascinated by the admiration of their own righteousness. But the true Church of God understands these sayings, and rightly understands the promises concerning the Messiah and the law. It knows why the law was given, namely, that it might be a voice showing the judgment and wrath of God against sin, not that men are righteous by the law. It knows why the Messiah was promised, namely, that He might become a victim for our sins and begin eternal life in those who believe. Here, therefore, let those things be repeated which were said above concerning the righteousness of faith in chapter 3 and elsewhere. But why does He say?

He will not come into judgment, but has passed from death into life.

Will believers not be judged? I answer: He speaks of the proper and principal effect of faith; as all men besides Christ have sins, so God judges and accuses all, just as Paul says: All are under sin; but after faith, or confidence in Christ, has shone in the heart, by which we acknowledge that we are truly received, heard, ruled, and defended by God, there follows peace and joy, which is the beginning of eternal life, and it covers the sins which still cling to us in our weakness. Therefore it is said: Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. Thus, the believer does not even come into judgment, that is, even if he has sins, yet these are covered after faith has shone; but without faith, and before faith, terrors and death dominate, just as Paul says: The sting of death is sin: the power of sin is the law, but thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.

Because the hour is coming when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God.

See the series of the whole sermon. In the beginning, He said who He is, namely the Son of God; afterwards, what benefit He brings, namely eternal life. Now He adds how He is going to give eternal life, namely, by raising the dead, and He affirms that He Himself will be the raiser of the dead. And here are two testimonies expressed and proposed, one concerning the resurrection of the dead, the other concerning the omnipotence of the Son, but yet in such a way that it has been communicated by the Father. Therefore He says:

Latin:

Et ego operor.

Hoc dictum postea pluribus verbis declara- tur: Quod pater facit, facit filius similiter. Item: Omnia ostendit filio, quae facit pater, etc. Haec dicta recensentur inter clarissima testimonia de filio, quod sit de substantia patris, et simul cum pater condiderit, et sustentet res, sicut supra di- ctum est: Omnia per ipsum facta sunt; et ad Heb. 1.: Ferens omnia verbo virtutis suae. Has sententias in invocatione nobis proponamus, ut invocantes Deum aeternum patrem Iesu Christi conditorem et conservatorem rerum, cogitemus simul cum patre filium et Spiritum sanctum omnia condidisse et conservare, et simul invo- cemus, et dirigentes invocationem ad Christum mediatorem, ut pro nobis intercedat, vere sta- tuamus eum esse omnipotentem, et nos exaudire, et patrem prorsus idem velle, quod vult filius, et quod testatus est se velle. Cogitanda est igitur haec sententia inter precandum: Pater meus usque modo operatur, et ego operor. Haec breviter monuisse satis sit, ut lector hoc testimonium de divinitate filii observet, et secum pie expendat. Nec volo recensere Samosateni et Arii cavallatio- nes, quibus eludere hunc locum conati sunt. Nam perspicuitas dicti tanta est, ut labefactari speciose non possit: Nam Iudaei agnoscebant Christum se aequare Deo.

Eodem pertinet dictum: Pater omnia mon- strat filio, ergo aequalis est sapientia patris et filii, sic et potentiam aequat, imo facit se socium actio- nis Dei, quae ille facit, filius similiter facit. Postea et honorem aequat, ut omnes honorent filium, sicut honorant patrem. Haec sententia repetit superiores, nam hic est honos verus, de quo supra dixit: Tribuere immensam sapientiam, et potentiam pariter patri et filio.

Venio ad tertiam sententiam, videlicet ad conclusionem refutantem Iudaeos: Pater non est otiosus, nec tenetur carnali paedagogia. Ego ago cum patre, et nihil facio, nisi quod video patrem facientem, ergo haec sanatio a me facta, divina est, et non subiecta vestrae legi de sabba- to, quae est paedagogia huius infirmae et miserae naturae humanae, significans longe aliud sabba- tum, scilicet futuram et aeternam quietem, in qua cessantibus officiis corporis, generatione, nu- tritione et similibus, tantum opera sabbati facie- mus. Intuebimur et celebrabimus Deum, et ipse nobis impertiet societatem suae lucis, et vitae aeternae. Nam hanc futuram quietem adumbrat typus in lege sabbati, ut supra dictum est.

Amen dico vobis, qui audit sermonem meum, et credit ei, qui misit me, habet vitam aeternam.

Dixi supra observanda esse hoc loco testimo- nia de divina natura in Christo, quae meditationi piorum commendo. Sunt enim satis perspicua, etiam sine longa enarratione. Videmus aequari sapientiam, potentiam et honorem, tribuitur ergo et filio omnipotentia. Caeterum et hoc ful- men observemus, quo damnatur omnium iusti- cia, qui filio Dei non tribuunt honorem, quales sunt Iudaei, Ethnici, Haeretici, et omnes hostes Evangelii. Sit licet excellens virtus Fabii, Ebio- nis, Arii, Pelagii, Iudaeorum aliquorum, qui sunt inimici Evangelii, item Monachorum et alio- rum sapientum, qui nunc Evangelio adversantur, tamen quia filio Dei non tribuunt honorem, hic clare damnantur: Qui non honorat filium, non honorat patrem; ac rursus nobis, qui agnosci- mus mediatorem filium, et ipso ducente accedi- mus ad patrem, ingens consolatio in hac senten- tia proponitur. Scimus certo nos recipi a patre, quia filio tribuimus honorem, de quo docet Evan- gelium, quod narrat quis sit filius, et quare sit missus. Nam tribuere honorem filio est credere Evangelio de omnibus articulis de Christo, et fiducia eius accedere ad Deum, et eum invocare. Ideo statim sequitur sententia, quae interpreta- tur hunc honorem his verbis: Amen, amen dico vobis, qui sermonem meum audit, et credit ei, qui misit me, habet vitam aeternam. Hic docet quomodo tribuatur honos filio, scilicet audiendo verbum eius, et credendo tum ipsi filio, tum patri qui misit eum, et pro hoc opere promittit vitam aeternam. Has conciones Iudaei tanquam tetras blasphemias execrabantur, quod tribui po- stulabat honorem parem filio et patri, item quod pro hoc opere promittit vitam aeternam.

igitur data est lex? An hoc vile opus, credere in hunc crucifixum Messiam, tanti est, ut pro eo detur vita aeterna? Videntur haec absurda hu- manae sapientiae, et praesertim, his qui fascinati sunt admiratione suae iusticiae. Sed vera Eccle- sia Dei intelligit haec dicta, et recte intelligit pro- missiones de Messia, et legem. Scit cur data sit lex, scilicet, ut sit vox ostendens iudicium et iram Dei adversus peccatum, non quod homines sint lege iusti. Scit cur promissus sit Messias, scilicet, ut fieret victima pro peccatis nostris, et incoët in credentibus vitam aeternam. Hic igitur repetantur ea, quae supra de iusticia fidei in cap. 3. et alias dicta sunt. Sed cur ait?

Non veniet in iudicium, sed transivit ex morte in vitam.

An non iudicabuntur credentes? Respondeo: de proprio et principali effectu fidei loquitur, ut omnes homines praeter Christum habent peccata, sic omnes iudicat et accusat Deus, sicut Paulus inquit: Omnes sunt sub peccato; sed postquam illuxit fides, seu fiducia Christi in corde, qua agnoscimus nos vere a Deo recipi, exaudiri, regi, defendi, sequitnr pax et laetitia, quae est incoa- tio vitae aeternae, et tegit peccata, quae adhuc in imbecillitate nostra haerent. Ideo dicitur: Beati quorum remissae sunt iniquitates, et quo- rum tecta sunt peccata. Sic credens ne quidem venit in iudicium, id est, etsi habet peccata, ta- men haec tecta sunt, postquam illuxit fides, sed sine fide, et ante fidem dominantur terrores et mors, sicut inquit Paulus: Aculeus mortis pecca- tum est: Potentia peccati lex, sed Deo sit gratia, qui dat nobis victoriam per dominum nostrum Ie- sum Christum.

Quia venit hora quando mortui audient vo- cem filii Dei.

Vide seriem universae concionis. Initio dixit quis sit, videlicet filius Dei, postea quod bene- ficium afferat, scilicet vitam aeternam. Nunc addit quomodo daturus sit vitam aeternam, scili- cet, resuscitatis mortuis, et affirmat seipsum fore resuscitatorem mortuorum. Suntque hic expressa testimonia duo proposita, alterum de resuscita- tione mortuorum, alterum de filii omnipotentia, sed tamen ita, ut a patre sit communicata. Ideo ait:

## 5:26
He has given the Son to have life in himself.

And there is an emphasis in this saying, to have life in himself, that is, in another way than creatures, angels, and men. For God has life in himself, namely eternal, and which can in no way be extinguished, nay, in such a way that he even imparts it to others; an angel and a man cannot impart life to a dead thing. These are only of the omnipotent nature: since therefore the Son is a resuscitator, it is necessary that he be omnipotent. Let this be enough to have noted concerning such sublime sayings, concerning which you should especially remember this, that they are testimonies of the divinity of the Son.

Afterwards, at the end, he adds a rebuke, that they did not believe the Baptist testifying concerning him. And that he may abundantly confirm the Church, he alleges not only the testimonies of the Baptist, but also the sayings and miracles of the eternal Father, which make us certain that this Jesus is the Son of God and the Messiah, but a very harsh rebuke follows in these words:

Neither have you heard his voice, nor have you seen his form.

It is true that God revealed himself to the fathers of this people alone by a clear voice and a certain form, just as it is written of Moses, that he saw God face to face. It is also certain that the voice sounding at Sinai to the whole people was a testimony by which God testified that this word, which he had delivered to Moses, was his word; but yet there is an infinite difference between the knowledge by which the Son knows the essence of the eternal Father, and those revealed voices, just as Christ says sometimes in Matthew 11: No one knows the Father, except the Son; and in this chapter of John 5: Whatever the Son sees the Father doing, those things the Son also does likewise. Wherefore, concerning the knowledge of the essence, there is no doubt that creatures do not know the voice and the form as the Son knows them. Nor indeed do I think it should be said concerning this secret knowledge in this place: For the Jews did not boast of this knowledge, but of the revelation by which God had certainly testified that he had received this people. This prerogative without any doubt surpassed the glory of all nations, and Christ disputes concerning this prerogative, as if he were saying: It is most true and most certain that you were called by the voice of God, but you did not hear it, namely, you did not receive it with your heart; you heard the words, but not the life-giving ones, not received with the heart. Therefore you cried out in Exodus 20: Let not the Lord speak to us, lest we die. Abraham hears the voice of God, but he receives it by faith, and feels that he conceives light and life by this voice. The people also hear the voice, but they flee, and cannot sustain it. Rightly, therefore, the boasting of the Jews is taxed, who contended that they were the Church of God because of this prerogative, that they had heard the voice. Christ refutes them: even if you were called, yet you did not listen, you could not hear, nor did you want to: To hear that sound does not make you the people of God, just as he will say below in chapter 8: He who is of God hears the words of God. Therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God: If you were the people of God, then at Mount Sinai you would have heard God speaking, but as you fled then, so you flee now; therefore you are not the people of God, nor do you care for the voice of God. Thus, therefore, let this whole passage be understood, that the opinion of the Pontiffs and Princes is condemned, who boasted that they were the Church of God because of this prerogative of calling, when yet they did not believe the voice of God, and that to hear the voice of God is to believe with the heart, and by faith to conceive new light and life, as was said above.

He who hears my words, and believes him who sent me, shall have eternal life, and does not come into judgment, but shall pass from death into life.

The dispute concerning the Church is similar in all ages. So now also the Bishops and governors argue that they are the chief members of the Church of God, because of ordinary succession, because those to whom they succeeded in the human manner heard the voice of Christ, therefore they twist the promises to themselves, but they are to be refuted in the same way. Only those are living members of the Church who receive the voice of God by faith, and conceive new light and life in their heart. Certainly those are not members of the people of God who oppose the Gospel, as Paul says: If anyone teaches another Gospel, let him be anathema; but concerning the Church it will be said often afterwards, I return to the text.

Search the scriptures.

Before, he cited the testimonies of miracles, but if miracles dissent from the word of God, the law in Deuteronomy 13 commands the word of God to be preferred, and detracts authority from miracles. Therefore Christ cites miracles in such a way that he simultaneously testifies that they agree with the sayings of the Prophets: It is impious obstinacy not to assent to the agreeing testimonies of the Prophets and miracles. But both the Prophets and miracles testify that I was sent by God, and that I teach the truth. It was therefore fitting for all to believe my voice, but Which scriptures does he cite? After the resurrection there were more illustrious testimonies, because it is written of Christ both that he was to suffer, and yet not to remain in death, but to reign. Wherefore it was necessary for him to come to life again. And it was manifest that this man, without the voice of any other human, was recalled from death to life. He was therefore the Messiah, just as they predicted concerning his death and resurrection, chapter 53 of Isaiah, and Psalm 16: Thou wilt not leave my soul in hell, nor wilt thou suffer thy holy one to see corruption.

Then after Jerusalem was overturned, the ruins of the temple and the overthrow of this entire polity testified that the Messiah had come. Because it is an irrefutable argument, since the Messiah must come while the second temple is standing and the Mosaic polity is still enduring, it is necessary that he has come, since the second temple was utterly destroyed and the whole polity overturned. And it is useful to remember this argument against the madness of the Jews, who still expect the Messiah. And this argument is clearly handed down in Daniel and Haggai.

But the Jews also had testimonies in the Prophets concerning Christ preaching, namely concerning the time, concerning his miracles, and that he was not going to rule in a royal manner, but was going to spread the Gospel, and afterwards was going to suffer and rise again from death. The time was fitting, because the weeks of Daniel were already running to an end, and foreign kings were in charge. The Prophets had also spoken concerning the miracles. That the Messiah would declare his power by such testimonies, as is said in Isaiah.

But because a persuasion concerning the royal dominion of the Messiah was fixed in the Jews, this appearance especially deterred them from believing in this Nazarene man, because they saw him not ruling in a royal manner. They could have corrected this error most of all from the sayings of the Prophets and all the examples of the saints, which show that the Church is subject to the cross, and the Prophets prophesy most clearly concerning the death and eternal kingdom of the Messiah. Wherefore Christ recalls the Jews from the ravings of the Pharisees to the Prophets. For the Pharisees were confirming that false persuasion among the people concerning royal dominion.

He repeats this sentiment, however, at the end: there is one who accuses you, Moses: because he wrote of me. This is a notable interpretation of the whole of Moses. That all those first revelations and promises were made so that the Church might know from the very beginning that it was being received by God on account of the coming deliverer. The first promise contains this: The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent. This promise was afterwards repeated to Abraham: In thy seed shall all nations be blessed. Then again Jacob says: Until the savior comes, to whom the nations shall adhere. Afterwards it is clearly said in Deut. 18: I will raise up a prophet for them from the midst of their brethren, like unto thee, etc. God commands that this one be heard after Moses. Furthermore, the whole law and the whole polity is a type of eternal things. The lamb signified the lamb that was to come, and that polity is by no means the eternal kingdom promised to the people, nor is that blessing, of which the promises speak, which signifies that sin and death are taken away through the Messiah, and he restored eternal life; these have not yet been exhibited through the law. Wherefore Moses is a certain witness concerning the Messiah, who was to bring the blessing, that is, righteousness and eternal life.

Do not think that I am going to accuse you.

After he alleged the testimony of Moses and the other Prophets against the Jews, he adds the conclusion, that Moses would be the accuser, not himself. But since they thought they were defending Moses most of all, they by no means thought that he would be the accuser. It would be a long narration, if one wished to pursue everything, why Moses is the accuser; first, because God refutes and convicts the people through the handed-down word, and there is no need for another accuser. Now in that word both parts accuse the people. The law was given, and it is manifest that the people do not satisfy the law. Moses will therefore be the accuser. Secondly, promises concerning the Messiah were handed down; these they distort toward an earthly kingdom, and they corrupt them, they do not embrace them as they ought, nor do they receive the interpretation of the other Prophets. They therefore contradict God, and pollute themselves with horrible blasphemies, they violate the law, and not only reject, but even corrupt the promises. God will show them these sins, and will convict them by the testimonies of Moses and the Prophets. God gave his word to the Prophets and Apostles, and added manifest testimonies, such as all the miracles done from the beginning in the Church, the preservation of Noah in the flood, the leading of the people out of Egypt, the defense of the kingdom through Samuel, David, Elijah, Elisha, Isaiah, the resurrection of Christ, the resuscitation of the dead done through the Apostles. All these things together will be terrible testimonies against all the impious, Jews and Gentiles. Therefore Christ says in John 12: The word which I have spoken will judge him on the last day. For Christ embraces both the word and all the testimonies published concerning the word, which convict all the impious, Jews and Gentiles.

How can you believe, who receive glory from one another?

He adds two things at the end: the reason why they do not believe, and a warning. The reason is that they seek human glory. A great impediment to faith and confession is anxiety about sustenance and life, but the anxiety about glory and reputation is much greater. Prominent men do not wish to appear seditious and disturbers of the public peace and of the established state in empires; they judge it honorable to think with the leaders who excel in authority, and to be defenders of the common concord, and the mention of the pursuit of peace and concord is plausible. For in truth it is honorable to maintain peace and concord in their proper order, but when the idols and errors of the powerful are taxed, wise men know how to follow great changes and disturbances of affairs. Therefore they flee the profession of the truth, or even hate it, nor is it possible for wise men to overcome this affection without divine light; indeed, it is harder than death to come into the hatred of the wise, and to be called seditious and an overthrower of the Church and of the good state. Against this temptation Isaiah consoles us in chapter 51: Do not fear the reproaches of men, and do not be afraid of their blasphemies. And Paul opposes many sentences to this affection, and among these also: I am not ashamed of the Gospel of Christ. The warning is: Another will come in his own name, him you will receive. The punishment for having despised the Gospel is greater blindness and madness, at Romans 11: That with eyes they may not see, etc. 2 Thessalonians 2: Because they did not receive the love of the truth; therefore God sends them an effective deception, as the outcome shows; in the Jews, obstinacy and fury grew so much that at length they utterly destroyed the whole nation. The Gentiles were also punished on account of the neglect of the Gospel; first came the heretics, afterwards Mahomet, and the errors of the Popes and Monks, who horribly devastated the Church.

Latin:

Dedit filio vitam habere in sese.

Et est emphasis in hoc dicto, vitam habere in sese, id est, alio modo, quam creaturae, an- geli et homines. Habet enim Deus vitam in sese, videlicet aeternam, et quae nullo modo extingui potest, imo sic, ut aliis etiam impertiat, Angelus et homo non potest rei mortuae vitam impertire. Haec tantum sunt naturae omnipotentis: cum igi- tur filius sit resuscitator, necesse est omnipoten- tem esse. Haec satis sit annotasse de tam subli- mibus dictis, de quibus praecipue hoc memine- ris, quod sint testimonia divinitatis filii.

Postea in fine addit obiurgationem, quod Baptistae testificanti de ipso non crediderint. Et ut Ecclesiam abunde confirmet, allegat non solum Baptistae testimonia, sed etiam aeterni patris dicta et miracula, quae nos certos reddunt hunc Iesum filium Dei et Messiam esse, sed durissima obiur- gatio sequitur his verbis:

Neque vocem eius audistis, neque speciem eius vidistis.

Verum est, Deum se solis patribus huius po- puli patefecisse clara voce, et certa specie, sicut de Mose scriptum est, quod viderit Deum facie ad faciem. Certum est etiam vocem sonantem in Sina ad universum populum fuisse testimonium, quo Deus testatus est, hoc verbum quod Mosi tradiderat, suum esse verbum, sed tamen infinita differentia est inter noticiam, qua filius novit es- sentiam aeterni patris, et inter illas revelatas vo- ces, sicut Christus aliquoties Matth. 11.: Nemo novit patrem, nisi filius; et in hoc cap. Ioan. 5.: Quicquid videt filius patrem facientem, quae ille facit, similiter et filius facit. Quare de noticia essentiae non est dubium, quin vocem et speciem non norint creaturae, sicut filius novit. Nec vero dicendum puto de hac arcana noticia hoc loco: Nam Iudaei non gloriabantur de hac noticia, sed de revelatione, qua Deus certo testatus erat, se recepisse hunc populum. Haec praerogativa sine ulla dubitatione superabat omnium gentium glo- riam, et de hac praerogativa disputat Christus, quasi dicat: Verissimum est, et certissimum vos Dei voce vocatos esse, sed vos eam non audistis, videlicet, corde non accepistis, verba audistis, sed non vivificantia, non accepta corde. Ideo clamastis Exod. 22. Non loquatur nobis domi- nus, ne moriamur, audit vocem Dei Abraham, sed fide eam accipit, et sentit se hac voce lucem et vitam concipere. Audit vocem et populus, sed fugit, et sustinere eam non potest. Iure igitur gloriatio Iudaeorum taxatur, qui se propter hanc praerogativam contendebant esse Ecclesiam Dei, quod vocem audissent. Refutat eos Christus etiamsi vocati estis, tamen non auscultastis, au- dire nec potuistis, nec voluistis: Audire sonum illum, non facit vos populum Dei, sicut infra di- cet cap. 8.: Qui est ex Deo, verba Dei audit. Ideo vos non auditis, quia ex Deo non estis: Si essetis populus Dei, tunc ad montem Sina audivissetis Deum loquentem, sed ut tunc fugiebatis, ita nunc fugitis, non igitur estis populus Dei, nec vocem Dei curatis. Sic igitur intelligatur hic totus lo- cus, quod damnetur opinio Pontificum et Princi- pum, qui gloriabantur se esse Ecclesiam Dei, pro- pter hanc praerogativam vocationis, cum tamen non crederent voci Dei, et quod audire vocem Dei sit corde credere, et fide novam lucem et vi- tam concipere, sicut supra dictum est.

Qui verba Dei, et credit ei qui misit me, ha- bebit vitam aeternam, et in iudicium non venit, sed transibit ex morte in vitam.

Similis est disputatio de Ecclesia omnibus ae- tatibus. Ita nunc quoque disputant Episcopi et gubernatores, se esse praecipua membra Ecclesiae Dei, propter successionem ordinariam, quia illi, quibus humano more successerunt, audierunt vo- cem Christi, ideo promissiones ad se detorquent, sed eodem modo refutandi sunt. Soli hi sunt viva membra Ecclesiae, qui vocem Dei fide accipiunt, et in corde novam lucem et vitam concipiunt. Certe hi non sunt membra populi Dei, qui Evan- gelio adversantur, ut Paulus inquit: Si quis aliud Evangelium docet, anathema sit; sed de Eccle- sia postea saepe dicetur, redeo ad textum.

Scrutamini scripturas.

Antea citavit testimonia miraculorum, sed si miracula dissentiant a verbo Dei, iubet lex Deut. 13. anteferri verbum Dei, et detrahit auto- ritatem miraculis. Ideo Christus ita citat mira- cula, ut simul testetur congruere ea cum Prophe- tarum dictis: Impia pertinacia est non assentiri congruentibus testimoniis Prophetarum et mira- culorum. Testantur autem et Prophetae et mira- cula, me a Deo missum esse, et vera docere. Oportuit igitur omnes meae voci credere, sed quas scripturas citat? Post resurrectionem erant illustriora testimonia, quia de Christo utrunque scribitur et passurum esse, et tamen non mansu- rum in morte, sed regnaturum. Quare oportuit eum reviviscere. Et manifestum fuit, hunc sine voce ullius hominis alterius ex morte in vitam re- vocatum esse. Fuit igitur Messias, sicut de morte et resurrectione praedixerunt, cap. 53. Esaiae, et Psal. 16.: Non relinques animam meam in in- ferno, nec sines sanctum tuum videre corru- ptionem.

Deinde post eversam Ierosolymam, ruinae templi, et eversio totius huius politiae testabantur venisse Messiam. Quia irrefragabile argumentum est, cum oporteat Messiam venire, stante secundo templo, et adhuc durante politia Mosaica, necesse est venisse eum, cum secundum templum funditus deletum erat, et eversa tota politia. Ac prodest hoc argumentum meminisse adversus amentiam Iudaeorum, qui adhuc expectant Messiam. Est- que perspicue traditum hoc argumentum in Da- niele et Haggaeo.

Sed etiam de praedicante Christo habebant testimonia Iudaei in Prophetis, videlicet de tem- pore, de miraculis eius, et quod non esset regio more dominaturus, sed sparsurus Evangelium, et postea passurus et resurrecturus ex morte. Tempus conveniebat, quia iam Danielis hebdo- mades decurrebant ad finem, et peregrini reges praeerant. De miraculis etiam dixerant Prophe- tae. Messiam talibus testimoniis declaraturum esse suam potentiam, ut in Esaia dicitur.

Sed quia Iudaeis infixa erat persuasio de re- gia dominatione Messiae, haec species maxime deterrebat eos, ne huic viro Nazareno crederent, quia videbant eum non dominari regio more. Hunc errorem maxime poterant ex Prophetarum dictis et omnibus exemplis sanctorum corrigere, quae ostendunt Ecclesiam subiectam esse cruci, et Prophetae clarissime vaticinantur de morte, et regno aeterno Messiae. Quare Christus revocat Iudaeos a Pharisaeorum deliramentis ad Prophe- tas. Nam Pharisaei falsam illam persuasionem in populo de regia dominatione confirmabant.

Repetit autem hanc sententiam in fine, est qui accusat vos Moses: Quia ille de me scripsit. Haec est insignis interpretatio totius Moysi. Quod omnes illae primae revelationes et promissiones factae sunt, ut sciret Ecclesia inde usque ab initio se recipi a Deo, propter venturum liberatorem. Hoc continet promissio prima: Semen mulieris conculcabit caput serpentis. Haec promissio postea repetita est Abrahae: In semine tuo benedi- centur omnes gentes. Deinde rursus Iacob inquit: Donec veniet salvator, cui adhaerebunt gentes. Postea clare dicitur Deut. 18.: Prophetam susci- tabo eis de medio fratrum suorum, sicut te, etc. Hunc praecipit Deus audiri post Mosen. Prae- terea tota lex et tota politia typus est rerum aeter- narum. Agnus significavit venturum agnum, et politia illa nequaquam est aeternum regnum, pro- missum populo, nec benedictio illa, de qua di- cunt promissiones, quae significat per Messiam tolli peccatum et mortem, et reddidit vitam aeter- nam, haec nondum sunt exhibita per legem. Quare Moses certus testis est de Messia, allaturo benedictionem, id est, iusticiam et vitam ae- ternam.

Ne existimetis quod ego accusaturus sim vos.

Postquam allegavit Mosi, et aliorum Prophe- tarum testimonium contra Iudaeos, addit conclu- sionem, Mosen fore accusatorem, non se. Cum autem putarent se maxime tueri Mosen, nequa- quam existimabant hunc fore accusatorem. Esset autem longa enarratio, si quis omnia persequi vellet, cur Moses sit accusator, primum quia Deus per traditum verbum redarguit et convincit populum, nec opus est alio accusatore. Iam in eo verbo utraque pars accusat populum. Data est lex, et manifestum est, populum non satisfa- cere legi. Erit igitur accusator Moses. Secundo, traditae sunt promissiones de Messia, has detor- quent ad regnum mundanum, et depravant, non amplectuntur ut debebant, nec recipiunt caetero- rum Prophetarum interpretationem. Contradi- cunt igitur Deo, et horrendis blasphemiis se pol- luunt, violant legem, et non solum abiiciunt, sed etiam corrumpunt promissiones. Haec pec- cata ostendet eis Deus, et convincet eos testimo- niis Mosi et Prophetarum. Deus dedit verbum suum Prophetis et Apostolis, et addidit manifesta testimonia, ut omnia miracula facta ab initio in Ecclesia, servationem Noae in diluvio, eductio- nem populi ex Aegypto, defensionem regni per Samuëlem, Davidem, Eliam, Elisaeum, Esaiam, resurrectionem Christi, resuscitationem mortuo- rum factam per Apostolos. Haec omnia simul erunt terribilia testimonia contra omnes impios, Iudaeos et gentes. Ideo dicit Christus Ioan. 12.: Sermo, quem locutus sum, iudicabit eum novis- simo die. Complectitur enim Christus et verbum, et omnia testimonia edita de verbo, quae convin- cunt omnes impios, Iudaeos et gentes.

Quomodo potestis vos credere, qui gloriam alius ab alio accipitis?

Duo in fine addit, causam, quare non credant, et comminationem. Causa est, quia gloriam hu- manam quaerunt. Magnum impedimentum est fidei et confessionis, solicitudo de victu et de vita, sed multo maius est de gloria et opinione. Praestantes viri nolunt videri seditiosi et pertur- batores publicae pacis, et constituti status in im- periis, iudicant honestum esse sentire cum prae- cipuis, qui autoritate antecellunt, et defensores esse concordiae communis, et est plausibilis men- tio studii pacis et concordiae. Nam revera hone- stum est, pacem et concordiam suo ordine tueri, sed cum taxantur potentum idola et errores, sciunt sapientes sequi magnas rerum mutationes et perturbationes. Ideo fugiunt professionem ve- ritatis, aut etiam oderunt, nec possibile est sa- pientibus sine luce divina hunc affectum vincere, imo durius est morte, venire in odium sapientum, et dici seditiosum, et eversorem Ecclesiae, et boni status. Adversus hanc tentationem consolatur nos Esaias cap. 51.: Nolite timere probra homi- num, et blasphemias eorum ne metuatis. Et Paulus huic affectui opponit multas sententias, et in his quoque: Non pudet me Evangelii Christi. Comminatio est. Alius veniet in nomine suo, il- lum accipietis. Poena est comtemti Evangelii ma- ior caecitas et amentia, ad Rom. 11.: Oculis ne videant, etc. 2. Thes. 2.: Quia dilectionem veri- tatis non receperunt; ideo mittit eis Deus effica- cem deceptionem, ut eventus ostendit, in Iudaeis ita creverunt pertinacia et furor, ut tandem pror- sus perderent totam gentem. Punitae sunt et gen- tes propter neglectionem Evangelii, venerunt primum haeretici, postea Mahometus, et errores Pontificum et Monachorum, qui Ecclesiam horri- biliter vastarunt.

## 6:1 Argument
Chapter VI.

At the beginning of this chapter, something must be said about the series of history and the order of the years of Christ's preaching. For because mention is made here of the Passover, and the history of the miracle done at this time is narrated in exactly the same way also by the remaining three writers of evangelical history, it is certain that the time corresponds, that it was done at the beginning of spring, and under the feast of that Passover, when John had been killed not long before, as the others clearly write, but of what year was that Passover? For concerning the first Passover it has been said above quite clearly that Christ, from the first miracle done at the wedding in Cana, had ascended to Jerusalem for the feast, and I judge that the continuous history of the same is described in the first year, in the previous five chapters, concerning the return of Christ into Galilee and the passage through Samaria and the return to the feast of Pentecost: but in this chapter a new series is instituted, and it appears that an entire year has been omitted, in which Christ also began to preach everywhere, especially in Galilee, after John was captured and afterwards killed, when hitherto in his first year he had preached almost only in Judea and Jerusalem, and had yielded Galilee to John.

But that the third Passover of the time in which Christ preached is to be numbered from this chapter, the narrations of the remaining Evangelists indicate, from which it can be gathered that John preached for about two years. For when he had begun his baptism in the beginning in a place very near to Judea at the Jordan, from which Mark writes that a great multitude had gone out from the city of Jerusalem, afterwards he withdrew into Galilee, going around the banks of the Jordan, and he approached the remaining shores, until Christ also from Nazareth, when he was in the vicinity, approached to Bethabara (or Bethabara) to be baptized by him, then having stayed for a while in Galilee, at the city of Salim, as John narrated above in chapter 3, and having baptized, before he was captured by Herod, and he preached for some time afterwards to Herod, and was often heard by him, but at length was thrown into prison, and was held in it for some time before he was killed, because he sends disciples to Christ from the prison. This course of John could not be completed suddenly, but a time of more than a year intervened, when Christ in the meantime had begun his ministry in Judea, and now for the first time, with John having been handed over into prison, he was preaching in Galilee, and was going around it, until it became known even to Herod, just as Mark in chapter 1 says that Christ, after John was handed over, came into Galilee. From here now follows the Passover, which was the beginning of the third year from the preaching of John, of which mention is made here, when Christ also had now preached for almost a year and a half, and was already going about Galilee here and there, and indeed he neither went up to Jerusalem under this Passover, nor even afterwards until the feast of tabernacles, as is said in the history of the following chapter. From the remaining narratives of the evangelical history it appears that a little before this Passover, John the Baptist was killed, and Herod, when he heard of the miracles of Christ, being dismayed, had even laid snares for Christ, as the words of Luke 11 signify. It was said, however, above, that the Baptist in the last time before he was snatched into prison had stayed near Salim, which, since it is in Galilee, John obeyed Herod, and it seems he withdrew there for fear of the chief priests and the Pharisees. Therefore he was captured by Herod, and killed. Christ, however, withdrew from Galilee, crossing the lake of Gennesaret into the desert, towards the region of Trachonitis. For in the towns of Galilee the soldiers of Herod were wandering more, who were about to attack anyone they met more quickly: wherefore he departs from their sight, but I come to the recitation of the miracle, which contains useful doctrine, which I shall distribute into topics. The first topic, consolation is proposed against the temptation concerning food and defense, and the deed agrees with the rule: Seek first the kingdom of God, and the rest shall be added unto you. For we are admonished that the Church wanders in the desert, is shaken here and there by tyrants, is harshly afflicted, but in these miseries God nevertheless preserves some assembly, in a wonderful way, even if some members, as in battle, are killed. The second topic, that the Apostles distribute, these are admonished especially, who preside, that they should perform their ministry, feed the people with the Gospel, nay even with the remaining duties help the poor, as much as they can, and in this very matter shine before them with faith, when dangers of food or body occur, let them confirm the hearers, that they may expect defense. Just as Moses confirmed the people on the shore of the Red Sea: and Isaiah when the city was surrounded by the siege of Sennacherib. The third, that fragments remain, is a notable testimony, that goods are increased, not diminished, by bestowing alms, as the voice of Christ testifies: Give and it shall be given unto you. The fourth, that he orders the fragments to be gathered, and the remains to be preserved: It is a precept worthy of observation concerning Frugality. For God wishes us to use his gifts reverently, that is, he wishes that we acknowledge that food is given divinely, he wishes faith to be exercised, and invocation by seeking, and expecting from God the things necessary for protecting life, and he wishes them to be arranged for uses ordained by himself, he wishes also our gratitude to be seen, by proclaiming the benefits of God, as the Psalm teaches: Call upon me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me. And let the prodigal learn here that they violate this command of Christ, who clearly says: Gather the remains that nothing may perish. For immoderate expenses, and profusions, what are they, but a vain wasting of faculties, and divine gifts? And because no one can tolerate profusions for long, there follow afterwards evil pursuits of money and rapacities. Thus vices arise from vices, or sins from sins.

The fifth topic. Thus far I have adapted the history without allegory to certain topics of the doctrine of the Gospel. For such deeds are examples proposed, so that we may be admonished concerning faith and the precepts. The principal topic is therefore, that we may learn that food and defense are to be sought and expected from God by faith. Furthermore, the bread and the bodily distribution are also images of the evangelical ministry, and it is a sweet allegory. Distribution is commanded to the Apostles, especially of the Gospel, and when they are faithful in their office and zeal, spiritual gifts grow in them, the light of doctrine, faith, prudence, fortitude, chastity, success in government. And here the fragments ought to be preserved with great care, that is, the doctrine revealed to them, as we preserve the remains of Augustine, that is, the books by which he refuted Pelagius, the Manichaeans, the Donatists, Arius: and now the remains are to be preserved, that is, the pious writings of those who again kindled the light of the Gospel, concerning repentance, concerning the free remission of sins, which is granted on account of Christ by faith, concerning the distinction of works commanded by God, and human traditions, concerning the fleeing of the idols of the Masses, and the invocation of the dead.

Finally, the baskets also signify the studies of letters, and discipline, or external government. For by these things the fragments are contained, that is, memory is retained, and propagated, and it is necessary to join letters, discipline, or external government, because without discipline even those things which are committed to letters cannot be read, so that although many are learned in other arts, yet because Bishops have not accustomed the youth to the studies of the doctrine of the Gospel by some useful discipline, pure doctrine comes into oblivion. And now it is to be feared, because superiors do not care for studies and discipline, that darkness will follow again, wherefore it was necessary for these baskets, that is, for the Apostles, that is, the governors, to care for studies and discipline.

Latin:

Caput VI.

Initio huius capitis aliquid de serie historiae, et ordine annorum praedicationis Christi dicen- dum est. Quia enim hic fit mentio Paschae, et historia miraculi hoc tempore facti, etiam a reli- quis tribus evangelicae historiae scriptoribus, prorsus eodem modo narratur: certum est tem- pus congruere, quod factum fuerit initio veris, et sub festum illius Paschae, cum non multo ante interfectus esset Ioannes, sicut clare scribunt cae- teri, sed quoti anni id Pascha fuit? Nam de primo Paschate supra satis perspicue dictum est, Chri- stum a primo miraculo facto in nuptiis in Cana, ascendisse Ierosolymam ad festum, ac iudico de- scribi continuam historiam eiusdem, primo anno, in prioribus quinque capitibus, de reditu Christi in Galilaeam et transitu per Samariam et reditu ad festum Pentecostes: sed in hoc capite nova se- ries instituitur, et apparet omissum esse annum integrum, in quo et Christus coepit passim prae- dicare, praesertim in Galilaea, postquam Ioan- nes captus, et postea interfectus est, cum hacte- nus primo suo anno fere in Iudaea et Ierosolymis esset concionatus, et Ioanni Galilaeam cesserit.

Quod vero ab hoc capite tertium Pascha numerandum sit eius temporis, quo Christus prae- dicavit, reliquorum Evangelistarum narrationes indicant, ex quibus colligi potest, Ioannem cir- citer biennium concionatum esse. Nam cum is principio in loco maxime vicino Iudaeae ad Iorda- nem incoasset suum baptismum, quo magnam multitudinem ex urbe Ierosolyma egressam esse, scribit Marcus, postea secessit in Galilaeam, cir- cumiens ripas Iordanis, et reliquas oras accessit, donec Christus etiam ex Nazareth, cum in vicinia esset ad Betharabam (seu Bethabaram) accederet, ut ab eo baptizaretur, deinde aliquantisper com- moratus in Galilaea, ad Salim urbem, ut supra cap. 3. narravit Ioannes, et baptizasset, ante- quam ab Herode caperetur, et aliquandiu postea concionatus est Herodi, et saepe ab eo auditus, sed tandem in carcerem coniectus, et in eo ali- quandiu detentus priusquam interficeretur, quia Christo ex carcere mittit discipulos. Hic cursus Ioannis non subito perfici potuit, sed intercessit tempus amplius anno, cum Christus interim in Iudaea incoasset ministerium, et nunc primum tradito Ioanne in carcerem, in Galilaea conciona- retur, et eam circumiret, quoad etiam Herodi innotuit, sicut Marcus cap. 1. ait, Christum post- quam Ioannes traditus est, venisse in Galilaeam. Hinc iam sequitur Pascha, quod fuit initium tertii anni a praedicatione Ioannis, cuius hic fit mentio, cum et Christus iam fere sesquiannum praedicas- set, et iam Galilaeam passim obiret, et quidem nec sub hoc Pascha ascenderet Ierosolymam, nec etiam postea usque ad festum tabernaculorum, ut in sequentis capitis historia dicitur. Ex reliquis narrationibus historiae evange- licae apparet paulo ante hoc Pascha, Ioannem Baptistam interfectum esse, et Herodem cum au- diret miracula Christi, consternatum etiam Chri- sto insidias instruxisse, sicut significant verba Lu- cae 11. Dictum est autem supra, Baptistam po- stremo tempore antequam in carcerem raperetur versatum esse prope Salim, quae cum sit in Gali- laea, paruit Ioannes Herodi, videturque eo se- cessisse metu Pontificum et Pharisaeorum. Ideo ab Herode captus, et interfectus est. Secessit au- tem Christus ex Galilaea traiiciens lacum Gene- zareth in desertum, versus Trachonitidem regio- nem. Nam in oppidis Galilaeae magis vagaban- tur milites Herodis, qui obvium citius invasuri erant: quare ex conspectu illorum discedit, sed venio ad miraculi recitationem, quae continet uti- lem doctrinam, quam distribuam in locos. Primus locus, consolatio proponitur contra tentationem de victu et defensione, et congruit factum cum regula: Primum quaerite regnum Dei, et caetera adiicientur vobis. Admonemur enim Ecclesiam vagari in de- serto, passim a tyrannis excuti, duriter affligi, sed in his aerumnis Deum tamen servare aliquem coetum, mirabili modo, etiamsi membra aliqua, ut in acie interficiuntur. Secundus locus, quod Apostoli distribuunt, admonentur hi praecipue, qui praesunt, ut fun- gantur ministerio suo, pascant populum Evange- lio, imo etiam reliquis officiis iuvent pauperes, quantum possunt, et in hac ipsa re praeluceant eis fide, cum incidunt pericula victus, aut corpo- ris, confirment auditores, ut expectent defensio- nem. Sicut Moses confirmabat populum in lit- tore maris rubri: et Esaias cum urbs cincta esset obsidione a Senacherib. Tertius, quod supersunt fragmenta, insigne testimonium est, augeri bona, non minui, lar- giendis eleemosynis, ut testatur vox Christi: Date et dabitur vobis. Quartus, quod iubet colligi fragmenta, et asservari reliquias: Praeceptum est dignum ob- servatione de Parsimonia. Vult enim Deus nos reverenter uti donis suis, hoc est, vult, ut agno- scamus dari victum divinitus, vult exerceri fidem, et invocationem petendis, et expectandis a Deo rebus necessariis ad tuendam vitam, et vult collo- cari eas ad usus ab ipso ordinatos, vult et gratitu- dinem nostram conspici, praedicandis Dei bene- ficiis, sicut Psalmus docet: Invoca me in die tri- bulationis, et eripiam te, et glorificabis me. Et discant hic prodigi se violare hoc mandatum Chri- sti, qui diserte ait: Colligite reliquias ne quid pereat. Nam immodici sumtus, et profusiones, quid sunt, nisi inanis perditio facultatum, ac mu- nerum divinorum? Et quia profusiones nemo to- lerare diu potest, sequuntur postea mala aucupia pecuniae et rapacitates. Ita vitia ex vitiis, seu peccata ex peccatis oriuntur.

Quintus locus. Hactenus historiam sine al- legoria accommodavi ad locos quosdam doctrinae Evangelii. Nam talia facta sunt exempla propo- sita, ut nos de fide et de praeceptis admoneamur. Praecipuus est igitur locus, ut discamus fide pe- tendum et expectandum esse victum, et defensio- nem a Deo. Caeterum panis et corporalis distri- butio sunt imagines etiam ministerii evangelici, estque dulcis allegoria. Apostolis mandatur dis- tributio, praecipue Evangelii, et cum sunt fide- les in munere suo ac studio, crescunt in ipsis dona spiritualia, lux doctrinae, fides, prudentia, fortitudo, castitas, successus in gubernatione. Et hic fragmenta asservari magna cura debent, id est, doctrina ipsis patefacta, ut Augustini reli- quias asservamus, hoc est, libros quibus refuta- vit Pelagium, Manichaeos, Donatistas, Arium: et nunc asservandae sunt reliquiae, id est, pia scripta eorum, qui rursus accenderunt lucem Evangelii, de poenitentia, de remissione pecca- torum gratuita, quae donatur propter Christum fide, de discrimine operum a Deo mandatorum, et traditionum humanarum, de fugiendis idolis Missarum, et invocationis mortuorum.

Postremo et cophini significant studia litera- rum, et disciplinam, seu gubernationem exter- nam. Nam his rebus continentur fragmenta, id est, retinetur memoria, et propagatur, et con- iungi literas, disciplinam, seu externam guber- nationem oportet, quia sine disciplina etiam ea, quae sunt mandata literis, legi non possunt, ut quamvis multi sunt docti in aliis artibus, tamen quia Episcopi non assuefecerunt iuventutem ad studia doctrinae Evangelii quadam utili disciplina, venit in oblivionem pura doctrina. Et nunc me- tuendum est, quia superiores non curant studia et disciplinam, rursus secuturas esse tenebras, quare hos cophinos, id est, studia et disciplinam curare Apostolos, id est, gubernatores oportebat.

## 6:15
He withdrew into the mountain by himself.

The miracle is pleasing to the multitude, to be fed without any expense of their own, and this man seemed by this art to be able to gather and lead the greatest armies.
