Therefore they hoped that the beginnings of that kingdom of the Messiah, which they dreamed of, were now at hand: therefore they run together, and are about to proclaim this Nazarene king, and to compel him to accept the kingdom, and to lead an army into Judea under a royal name, nor is there any doubt that in this deliberation, many sentences of the Prophets concerning the kingdom of the Messiah were alleged, of which they thought such beginnings would one day be, but Christ flees a new danger by a new method. Before, he had withdrawn from the cities, fleeing Herod, now he flees from the desert into the cities, where he knew such gatherings, or any talk about a new king, were not permitted to the people.

But why does he refuse to receive the kingdom? Let those insipid thoughts be laid aside, that it is a virtue to live in miseries, to flee wealth and power, just as Monks pretend that their hiding places and filth are a great virtue, and a worship of God, but let the calling be looked to. Christ was sent, only to teach the Gospel, and to become a victim for the human race, not to occupy a worldly empire. He obeys this calling of his, and because of this he does not permit himself to be proclaimed king. Meanwhile, he professes that he holds a much greater office than a royal one, namely that he is the giver of righteousness and eternal life, as I have said so often before. This was a much greater boasting than if he had professed himself king, or even had administered a kingdom. Let us learn therefore what virtue is, which is called humility, and again what glory is, and how it is to be fled, or sought.

Humility is truly to fear God, and to acknowledge one's own weakness, and yet in faith to obey the calling of God, and to expect help and governance from him, and not to desire those things to which God does not call, nor to become more bold, as if by our own wisdom, by our own strengths, we perform great and salutary things, but truly to conclude that with God helping we perform useful things, to acknowledge also the measure of our gift, and not to despise other members, through whom God is effective, but rather to pray that God may also help the others, and to treat them with honor, as

God's instruments, and to think that God can perform even more useful things through them. Such are Moses, David, and the like, who acknowledged their own weakness, understood that they were by no means equal to the burden of governance, and yet because of the calling they do not refuse to undergo such a mass, and they sustain this by faith, they expect help from God, they do not judge that they can rule such dangerous things by their own counsels and strengths. But if they perform anything happily, they know they perform it by the help of God, nor do they despise other instruments of God. Moses does not despise Joshua, David does not despise Jonathan, nay they venerate those whom they see to be partners of such great labor. Jonathan is humble, he does not desire the kingdom, when he sees that he is not called, but he serves faithfully in his own calling, nor does he envy David, whom he sees to excel, and to be called to the kingdom, himself although the son of the king being excluded. This was a great and excellent virtue in Jonathan, to comply with the will of God, and being willing to yield to another the inheritance of the kingdom, which seemed due to himself. The world is ignorant of this true humility, which neither desires other things outside of one's calling, and obeys the calling by faith. It is therefore a virtue intermediate between these extremes, between sloth, and arrogance or pride.

Sloth is the desertion of one's calling, or out of simulation and superstition to desire filth, as Monks do. On the contrary, Arrogance is to take upon oneself things greater than one's calling, likewise to trust in one's own strengths, and to despise other instruments of God, or to envy them, as Cain, Goliath, Saul, Antonius, and the greatest part of men.

Glory is the true approval of our conscience, and the testimony of others judging rightly, concerning honest deeds. But true approval of our conscience embraces many things. For then the conscience truly indicates, when it acknowledges its own weakness, fears God, and yet obeys the calling by faith, and performs those things which the calling demands, does not desire other things, and acknowledges itself to be helped by God, thus Samuel, David, Paul boast, that is, they have true testimonies of conscience, they know they did not seize dominions, but obeyed the calling, and did not mix in private desires, and that what they performed happily, was governed by God. This glory, that is, this testimony of conscience is to be sought. Because God wants us to live with a good conscience. Nay, a polluted conscience cannot call upon him. But yet let us not trust that we have reconciliation with God, because of this testimony of conscience, this is declared elsewhere. Again, glory, that is, glorious functions, without a calling, are not to be sought. Nor let us imagine that we perform saving works by our own strength, but let us know that it is true what Christ says: Without me you can do nothing. It is therefore pride to seek functions without a calling, likewise to trust in one's own strength.

From this it can be judged that humility and the seeking of glory are related virtues, just as thrift and liberality are related, and that each of these moves between these extremes, between sloth and pride. Humility, however, is spoken of insofar as it does not seek functions without a calling, and acknowledges its own infirmity, and does not trust in its own strength. Glory, truly, is spoken of insofar as it obeys a calling. Therefore Christ rightly and without arrogance proclaims of himself: I am the light and the life, because it was necessary for him to declare his calling, which far surpassed all worldly kingdoms. It was far greater glory to be called the author of justice and of eternal life than to be called Augustus, Emperor of the Roman people. Again, he rightly and without simulation proclaims of himself when he says: I am humble of heart, and in truth Christ excelled all angels and all men in this virtue, which is called humility, because he himself perfectly knows the eternal Father, wherefore he perfectly submits himself to him, and casts himself further beneath him, understands that obedience is owed to him more than all angels and all men understand, nor does he despise other organs of God, but embraces, helps, and protects them with immense love.

Let this be enough to have touched upon briefly, so that we may consider the true causes why Christ fled, namely, because his calling did not allow him to rule in the royal manner: therefore let each one learn what his own calling requires. This rule the Bishops have long since neglected, and forgetful of their primary calling, and having neglected the ministry of the Gospel, they now only rule worldly empires, and after doctrine was neglected on account of the occupation of empires, great errors crept into the Church, and many evils were added. The magnitude and punishments of which the last day will show, and these sins are often and justly censured elsewhere.

Latin:

Secessit in montem ipse solus.

Gratum est miraculum multitudini, pasci sine suo sumtu aliquo, et hic vir hac arte videbatur maximos exercitus posse contrahere et ducere. Ideo sperabant iam initia fore eius imperii Messiae, quod somniabant: ideo concurrunt, et hunc Nazarenum regem renunciaturi sunt, et coacturi, ut imperium accipiat, et regio nomine exercitum in Iudaeam ducat, nec dubium est in hac deliberatione, multas Prophetarum sententias de regno Messiae allegatas esse, cuius existimabant aliquando talia initia fore, sed Christus novum periculum fugit nova ratione. Antea secesserat ex urbibus, fugiens Herodem, nunc fugit ex deserto in urbes, ubi sciebat populo non concedi tales concursus, aut ullos sermones de novo rege.

Cur autem recusat recipere regnum? Deponantur illae insulsae cogitationes, quod sit virtus vivere in miseriis, fugere opes et potentiam, sicut Monachi fingunt suas latebras et sordes esse magnam virtutem, et cultum Dei, sed vocatio spectetur. Missus est Christus, tantum ut doceat Evangelium, et fiat victima pro humano genere, non ut occupet imperium mundanum. Huic suae vocationi obtemperat, et propter hanc non permittit se renunciari regem. Interim profitetur se multo maius officium gerere, quam regium, videlicet se esse datorem iusticiae et vitae aeternae, ut toties ante dixi. Haec erat multo maior gloriatio, quam si regem se professus esset, aut etiam regnum administrasset. Discamus igitur quid sit virtus, quae vocatur humilitas, et rursus quid sit gloria, et quomodo sit fugienda, aut appetenda.

Humilitas est vere timere Deum, et agnoscere propriam infirmitatem, et tamen in fide obedire vocationi Dei, et expectare ab ipso auxilium et gubernationem, nec appetere ea, ad quae Deus non vocat, nec fieri audaciorem, quasi nostra sapientia, nostris viribus, res magnas et salutares geramus, sed vere statuere, quod Deo adiuvante res utiles geramus, agnoscere et modum nostri doni, nec despicere alia membra, per quae Deus est efficax, sed potius petere, ut Deus etiam caeteros adiuvet, et illos honore afficere, tanquam

Dei organa, et existimare, quod Deus etiam utiliora per eos gerere possit. Tales sunt Moses, David, et similes, qui agnoscebant suam infirmitatem, intelligebant se nequaquam pares esse oneri gubernationis, et tamen propter vocationem non recusant subire tantam molem, et hanc fide sustinent, expectant auxilium a Deo, non iudicant se suis consiliis et viribus res tam periculosas regere posse. Sed si quid feliciter gerunt, sciunt se Dei auxilio gerere, nec despiciunt alia organa Dei. Moses non despicit Iosue, David non despicit Ionathan, imo venerantur eos, quos vident socios esse tanti laboris. Humilis est Ionathas, non appetit regnum, cum videt se non esse vocatum, sed servit fideliter in sua vocatione, nec invidet Davidi, quem videt antecellere, et ad regnum vocatum esse, se quanquam filio regis excluso. Haec fuit magna et excellens virtus in Ionatha, obsequi voluntati Dei, et volentem de haereditate regni, quae ipsi debita videbatur, alteri cedere. Hanc veram humilitatem ignorat mundus, quae nec appetit alia extra vocationem, et vocationi obtemperat fide. Est igitur virtus media inter haec extrema, inter ignaviam, et arrogantiam seu superbiam.

Ignavia est desertio vocationis, aut ex simulatioe et superstitione appetere sordes, ut Monachi faciunt. Econtra Arrogantia est maiora vocatione sibi sumere, item confidere propriis viribus, et alia organa Dei despicere, vel eis invidere, ut Cain, Goliath, Saul, Antonius, et maxima pars hominum.

Gloria est vera approbatio conscientiae nostrae, et testimonium aliorum recte iudicantium, de honestis factis. Multa autem complectitur vera approbatio nostrae conscientiae. Tunc enim conscientia vere indicat, cum agnoscit suam infirmitatem, timet Deum, et tamen vocationi obtemperat fide, et gerit ea, quae postulat vocatio, non appetit alia, et agnoscit se iuvari a Deo, sic gloriantur Samuël, David, Paulus, id est, vera testimonia habent conscientiae, sciunt se non rapuisse dominationes, sed vocationi obedivisse, et non miscuisse privatas cupiditates, et quae feliciter gesserunt, a Deo gubernata esse. Haec gloria, id est, hoc testimonium conscientiae est appetendum. Quia Deus vult nos vivere bona conscientia. Imo polluta conscientia non potest eum invocare. Sed tamen non confidamus nos habere reconciliationem apud Deum, propter hoc testi- monium conscientiae, hoc alias declaratur. Rur- sus glorio, id est, gloriosae functiones, sine vo- catione, non sunt appetendae. Nec imaginemur nos nostris viribus res salutares gerere, sed scia- mus verum esse, quod ait Christus: Sine me ni- hil potestis facere. Est igitur superbia appetere functiones sine vocatione, item confidere propriis viribus.

Hinc iudicari potest, cognatas virtutes esse, humilitatem, et gloriae appetitionem, sicut co- gnatae sunt parsimonia et liberalitas, et utranque inter haec extrema versari, inter ignaviam et su- perbiam. Dicitur autem humilitas, quatenus non appetit functiones sine vocatione, et agnoscit suam infirmitatem, et non confidit suis viribus. Gloria vero dicitur quatenus obtemperat voca- tioni. Ergo Christus recte et sine arrogantia de se praedicat: Ego sum lux et vita, quia oportuit eum declarare suam vocationem, quae longe su- perabat omnia regna mundana. Longe maior gloria erat dici autorem iusticiae, et vitae aeter- nae, quam dici Augustum Imperatorem populi Romani. Rursus recte, et sine simulatione de se praedicat, cum ait: Ego sum humilis corde, et revera excelluit Christus hac virtute, quae voca- tur humilitas, omnes angelos et omnes homines, quia ipse perfecte novit aeternum patrem, quare perfecte se ei subiicit, et longius se infra eum abiicit, intelligit magis deberi ei obedientiam, quam intelligunt omnes angeli et omnes homi- nes, nec despicit alia organa Dei, sed ingenti amore complectitur, adiuvat et tuetur.

Haec satis sit breviter attigisse, ut veras causas cogitemus, cur fugerit Christus, scilicet, quia vocatio eius non sinebat eum regio more do- minari: ideo singuli discant, quid propria voca- tio postulet. Hanc regulam iam olim neglexerunt Episcopi, et primae vocationis obliti, et neglecto ministerio Evangelii, iam tantum regunt imperia mundana, et postquam doctrina propter occupa- tionis imperiorum neglecta est, magni errores in Ecclesiam irrepserunt, et multa mala accesserunt. Quorum magnitudinem et poenas ostendet dies novissimus, et haec peccata alias saepe et iuste taxantur.

## 6:16
But after it became evening, the disciples went down, etc.

Let the historical matters be considered: Christ had left the whole multitude, and had withdrawn somewhere, lest in the gathering of the crowd he be called King, and from that fact pernicious tumults might arise. The disciples, however, betake themselves to the ships, so that they might sleep there and wait for the Lord; finally, because he is not present, when now darkness was deepening, the Apostles begin to cross the river, intending to return to the town of Capernaum, situated on the southern bank. But they see Christ coming, walking upon the river, when now the ship had been carried forward thirty stadia, that is, almost a German mile. Consider therefore how many great virtues concur: he taught, he healed the sick, he fed the people without any abundance of things, he withdrew lest he be called King, now he walks upon the river.

The next morning the people came to their northern bank, and since they knew that Christ had not been carried away with the Apostles, nor had there been another ship there except the one which the Apostles had used, they wonder where Christ had departed, and while they doubt, it seems most convenient to follow the Apostles, and by chance other ships arrive at that bank, which had come from Tiberias.

And when they come to Christ, they are first rebuked because they do not seek the glory of God and eternal goods, but present comforts, as is customary for this miserable and weak nature of men, to be more anxious about food, about the tranquility of the body, than about the glory of God and eternal goods, just as Esau preferred a morsel to the right of primogeniture, that is, of the priesthood, which was a divine ministry.

He therefore proposes a proposition which contains a rebuke and a doctrine. Work for food not that which perishes, but that which remains unto eternal life, which the son of man will give to you, for him the Father, God, has sealed. First, he speaks about his person, who he is. Then he explains what kind of food he is about to give, and testifies that he is the Messiah, the giver of eternal life, and clearly refutes the persuasion of the Jews, who were expecting an empire of the world, and neither understood nor sought the remission of sins, justice, eternal life. I said, however, in the beginning that the description of the person must be observed. He says he is sealed by the Father; it is an altogether singular description, signifying two things, namely, that this person is destined for a certain duty above all men, and adorned with singular gifts, by which he excels all men.

For what is said here: Sealed, that is said in the Psalm and in Isaiah and Daniel Anointed. Isaiah 61: The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because he has anointed me. The word is taken from the rite of anointing priests and kings. Therefore, to be anointed, or to be sealed, is to be destined for the office of priest and king. And indeed, when it is said of this person, one must understand the priest who truly appeases the wrath of God, and the king who utterly destroys the kingdom of the devil, of sin, and of death, and gives an eternal kingdom. Nor does the word anoint signify only such an ordination to perform this office, but it also signifies the imparting of gifts, as Isaiah says: The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me. But as the Baptist said above: The Father does not give the Spirit to him by measure: so it is signified here that this person excels all others in a peculiar way, which is explained more copiously in other places, because Christ is heaped with the gifts of the Holy Spirit above all men, indeed because the divinity dwells in him bodily, that is, because he is by nature the Son of God, he is of equal power with the Father, as he said above: My Father works until now, and I work; he therefore sanctifies, and gives life, and gives new light, righteousness, and eternal life. Thus is Christ sealed and anointed, that he may anoint believers, as it was said above: Of his fullness we all receive.

The Greeks emphasize the word 'sealed,' and adapt it to the image of God; Christ is σφραγὶς, that is, the image of the eternal Father, as it is said in Hebrews 1: The Son is the χαρακτὴρ of the Father's substance. Nor does this interpretation displease me, but the word σφραγίζω is thus attributed to Christ alone and uniquely, by which, however, John and Paul also use it regarding other saints, as in 2 Corinthians 1: God who has sealed us, that is, ordained, gifted, and fortified us with the Holy Spirit. Likewise: In whom you were sealed for the day of redemption. In sum, however, Christ in this discourse of the sixth chapter says that he is sealed, that is, that he alone is the Messiah certainly ordained and given for all men for this office, that he may give eternal life. This was a new discourse, and unknown to the people, who were fascinated by persuasions about an empire of the world.

Latin:

Postquam autem sero factum est, descende- runt discipuli, etc.

Historica considerentur, reliquerat totam multitudinem Christus, et secesserat aliquo, ne in vulgi concursu Rex appellaretur, eaque ex re perniciosi tumultus orirentur. Discipuli vero se ad naves recipiunt, ut ibi cubarent, et dominum expectarent, tandem quia is non adest, cum iam tenebrae intenderentur, Apostoli flumen traiicere incipiunt, redituri in oppidum Capernaum, si- tum in ripa meridiana. Vident autem advenire Christum supra flumen ingredientem, cum iam navis provecta esset stadia triginta, id est, fere miliare germanicum. Cogita ergo quam multae magnae virtutes concurrunt, docuit, sanavit ae- grotos, pavit populum sine aliqua rerum copia, secessit, ne Rex appellaretur, nunc incedit supra flumen.

Postridie mane venit populus ad suam ripam Arctoam, cumque scirent Christum non avectum esse cum Apostolis, nec aliam ibi navem fuisse praeter unam, qua erant usi Apostoli, mirantur quo Christus discesserit, cumque dubitant, vide- tur commodissimum sequi Apostolos, et casu aliae naves ad eam ripam applicant, quae ex Tyberiade venerant.

Cumque veniunt ad Christum, primum ob- iurgantur, quod non quaerant gloriam Dei et bona aeterna, sed praesentia commoda, sicut usi- tatum est huic miserae et infirmae naturae homi- num, magis angi de victu, de tranquillitate cor- poris, quam de gloria Dei et de bonis aeternis, sicut Esau praetulit offam iuri primogeniturae, hoc est, sacerdotii, quod erat ministerium di- vinum.

Proponit igitur propositionem, quae conti- net obiurgationem et doctrinam. Parate cibum non periturum, sed manentem in vitam aeter- nam, quem filius hominis dabit vobis, hunc enim pater signavit Deus. Primum de persona dicit, quis sit. Deinde exponit qualem cibum daturus sit, et testatur se esse Messiam datorem vitae ae- ternae, ac clare refutat persuasionem Iudaeorum, qui expectabant imperium mundi, nec intellige- bant, nec expetebant remissionem peccatorum, iusticiam, vitam aeternam. Dixi autem principio descriptionem personae observandam esse. Ait se obsignatum a patre, omnino singularis descri- ptio est, significans duo, videlicet, hanc perso- nam destinatam esse ad certum munus prae omni- bus hominibus, et ornatam singularibus donis, quibus antecellat omnes homines.

Quod enim hic dicitur: Obsignatus, id in Psalmo et apud Esaiam et Daniëlem, dicitur unctus. Esaiae 61.: Spiritus Domini Dei super me, eo quod unxerit me. Est autem sumtum verbum a ritu ungendi sacerdotes et reges. Est ergo ungi, seu obsignari, destinari ad munus sa- cerdotis et regis. Et quidem cum de hac persona dicitur, intelligendus est sacerdos vere placans iram Dei, et rex qui prorsus deleat regnum dia- boli, peccati et mortis, et det regnum aeternum. Nec vero tantum significat vocabulum ungere ta- lem ordinationem ad fungendum hoc munere, sed significat etiam impartire dona, sicut ait Esaias: Spiritus Domini Dei super me. Ut autem Baptista supra dixit: Non ad mensuram ei dat pa- ter spiritum: ita hic significatur hanc personam antecellere omnibus peculiari modo, qui in aliis locis copiosius exponitur, quia Christus cumula- tus est donis Spiritus sancti supra omnes homines, imo quia in eo divinitas habitat corporaliter, id est, quia natura est filius Dei, est pari potentia cum patre, ut supra dixit: Pater meus usque mo- do operatur, et ego operor, sanctificat igitur, et vivificat, dat novam lucem, iusticiam, et vitam aeternam. Sic est obsignatus et unctus Christus, ut ungat credentes, sicut supra dictum est: Ex plenitudine eius omnes accipimus.

Graeci urgent vocabulum obsignatus est, et accommodant ad imaginem Dei, Christus est σφραγὶς, id est, imago patris aeterni, sicut ad Heb. 1. dicitur: Filius est χαρακτὴρ substantiae patris. Nec mihi displicet haec interpretatio, sed ita verbum σφραγίζω tribuitur soli et uni Chri- sto, quo tamen et alias utuntur Ioannes et Paulus, de caeteris sanctis, ut 2. Corinth. 1.: Deus qui obsignavit nos, id est, ordinavit, donavit, et munivit Spiritu sancto. Item: In quo obsignati estis in diem redemtionis. In summa vero Chri- stus in hac concione sexti capitis dicit, se esse ob- signatum, id est, se unum esse Messiam certo modo ordinatum, et donatum pro omnibus homi- nibus ad hoc munus, ut det vitam aeternam. Haec erat nova concio, et ignota populo, fasci- nato persuasionibus de imperio mundi.

## 6:28
What shall we do, that we may work the works of God?

At the beginning of the chapter he recounted some miracles, which are testimonies of his doctrine: afterwards follows the narrative of the constancy of Christ fleeing the royal name. Thirdly, the rebuke of the people is described, seeking Christ, not because of the Gospel and the glory of God, but because of their own advantages, food, liberty, the shaking off of tributes, and a kingdom. Fourthly, doctrine is added: If we sin, what then must be done, that we may please God? Fifthly, the struggle is renewed: because the Jews are offended by the voice of the Gospel, and there is a comparison of Moses and the Messiah. Sixthly, doctrine is again interposed concerning the difference between human wisdom and the Gospel, that human reason does not embrace the Gospel unless it is helped by the Holy Spirit, and this passage refutes the Pelagians, and also distinguishes the Church from the people of the law. Seventhly, discourses are added about eating the Messiah, which are opposed to the food given to them in the desert. Eighthly, new and greater offenses arise when they hear about the eating of the Messiah, and there is no doubt that all who excel in human wisdom, when they read this discourse about eating, are astonished and wonder to what end this so obscure and seemingly absurd reasoning pertains. Ninthly, he breaks off the whole altercation, and repeats the cause of these offenses, which he mentioned above, namely, that the human mind is oppressed by darkness, and does not embrace the Gospel unless God helps. Tenthly, the confession of the Apostles is tested, who expressly affirm that this their master is the Messiah, the Son of God. I have recited the series of passages which are the principal ones in this long and obscure discourse, so that the reader may see more clearly how the members fit together.

I return therefore to the fourth point concerning doctrine, which is the principal one in this chapter. When the Jews had been rebuked while indignant, they ask, what work does he want to be done? He himself proposes this work, concerning which the Gospel properly discourses, namely, that they believe in Christ, and a little later he affirms that he is the giver of eternal life, and that men obtain this if they believe in the Messiah. This is the principal doctrine in this whole dispute, which is indeed the sum of the Gospel, as has often been said above, and is a sentiment opposed to the law and to the empty confidence of this people, who because of the law thought they had the remission of sins and the inheritance of eternal life. Therefore they ask ironically: What shall we do, that we may work the works of God? as if they were saying: Why do you rebuke us? why do you command eternal food to be sought, when we are righteous by the law, what more do you require? Christ answers, nay, I require something else: This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent. He calls this faith the work of God, not only because it is commanded by God, for in this way the law is also a work of God, but also because it pleases God, and it is that work, which receives men, and gives them eternal life. This is the simple meaning of the saying. The exercises of the law are not this work, by which God saves, but are discipline and political justice, which although it is necessary in this bodily life, yet it does not merit the remission of sins, as is evident, and at Gal. 3 it is said: As many as are of the works of the law are under the curse, that is, those who think they satisfy the law, and by this discipline are righteous before God, and do not know that reconciliation is given on account of the Messiah, these err utterly, and perish. Now this doctrine stirs up new offenses and new conflict.

Latin:

Quid faciemus, ut operemur opera Dei?

Initio capitis miracula recitavit aliquot, quae sunt testimonia doctrinae: postea sequitur narra- tio constantiae Christi fugientis regium nomen. Tertio, describitur obiurgatio populi, quaerentis Christum, non propter Evangelium et gloriam Dei, sed propter proprias utilitates, victum, li- bertatem, excussionem tributorum, regnum. Quarto additur doctrina: Si peccamus, quid igi- tur faciendum est, ut Deo placeamus? Quinto renovatur certamen: quia voce Evangelii offen- duntur Iudaei, et sit collatio Mosi et Messiae. Sexto, rursus interponitur doctrina de discrimine humanae sapientiae, et Evangelii, quod humana ratio non amplectatur Evangelium, nisi adiuve- tur a Spiritu sancto, et hic locus refutat Pelagia- nos, discernit etiam Ecclesiam a populo legis. Septimo, adduntur conciones de manducando Messia, quae opponuntur esui sibi dati in deserto. Octavo, novae et maiores offensiones oriuntur, cum audiunt de manducatione Messiae, nec du- bium est omnes sapientia humana antecellentes, cum legunt hanc concionem de manducatione, obstupefieri et mirari, quorsum haec tam ob- scura ratio, et in speciem absurda pertineat. No- no, abrumpit totam altercationem, et causam re- petit harum offensionum, quam supra dixit, vi- delicet, quod mens humana sit oppressa tenebris, nec amplectatur Evangelium, nisi Deo iuvante. Decimo, tentatur confessio Apostolorum, qui expresse affirmant, hunc suum dominum esse Messiam filium Dei. Recitavi seriem locorum, qui in hac longa et obscura concione praecipui sunt, ut lector magis videat, quomodo membra congruant.

Redeo igitur ad quartum locum de doctrina, quae in hoc capite praecipua est. Cum Iudaei stomachantes obiurgati essent, interrogant, quod opus fieri velit? Ipse proponit hoc opus, de quo proprie concionatur Evangelium, videlicet, ut credant in Christum, et aliquanto post affirmat, se esse datorem vitae aeternae, et hanc ita conse- qui homines, si credant in Messiam. Haec est principalis doctrina in hac tota disputatione, quae quidem est summa Evangelii, ut saepe dictum est supra, et est sententia opposita legi, et inani fiducia populi huius, qui propter legem existima- bat se habere remissionem peccatorum et haere- ditatem vitae aeternae. Ideo ironice interrogant: Quid faciemus, ut operemur opera Dei? quasi dicant: Cur nos obiurgas? cur iubes aeternum cibum quaeri, cum simus iusti lege, quidnam re- quiris amplius? Respondet Christus, imo aliud requiro: Hoc est opus Dei, ut credatis in eum, quem ille misit. Vocat hanc fidem opus Dei, non solum quia a Deo mandatum est, nam hoc modo et lex est opus Dei, sed etiam quia placet Deo, et est illud opus, quod recipit homines, et dat eis vitam aeternam. Haec est simplex sententia dicti. Exercitia legis non sunt hoc opus, quo salvat Deus, sed sunt disciplina et politica iusticia, quae etiamsi in hac corporali vita necessaria est, tamen non meretur remissionem peccatorum, ut constat, et ad Gal. 3. dicitur: Qui ex operibus legis sunt, sub maledictione sunt, id est, qui arbitrantur se legi satisfacere, et hac disciplina coram Deo iustos esse, nec norunt propter Messiam donari recon- ciliationem, hi prorsus errant, et pereunt. Iam haec doctrina novas offensiones et novum certa- men excitat.

## 6:30
What sign do you perform then?

I come therefore to the fifth place, in which there is a harsh altercation. The Jews, offended because Christ says he is the Messiah, and demands to be believed, begin to dispute about the comparison of Moses and the Messiah, and return to their inveterate disease and error concerning an earthly kingdom. And thus they argue, Christ will be greater than Moses, Moses led the people out of Egypt, destroyed enemies, fed the people in the desert, finally performed such great deeds, therefore since the Messiah ought to perform greater and more glorious deeds, and you perform nothing, but leave us in servitude and miseries, it is not to be thought that you are the Messiah. It was a specious argument, and one which, fascinated by the persuasion of an earthly kingdom, they can by no means explain. But Christ refutes their argument. The Messiah will perform greater deeds, because he will give eternal goods: The bread of God is he who descends from heaven, and gives life to the world. He refutes the other part also. Moses gave Manna, nay, he says, Moses did not give it, but my father, as if to say: Moses is only a minister, he could no more give life by his own power than any other most miserable man. I want Moses the minister to be distinguished from the Messiah the Lord and author of life, this author of life descended from heaven, he is the son of the eternal father, working with him, as he said above: What he does, the son also does likewise. This son takes away death, and restores eternal life.

But let this passage be diligently observed against those who only pretend that Christ is a teacher, as were Moses, or Phocylides, or others, who handed down precepts of morals, and who transform the Gospel into law. This pernicious error has often been taxed above, and the distinction ought always to be in sight for the pious. There is also a testimony to be observed concerning the divine nature in Christ, which although it is more obscure, yet joined to the others it becomes clearer. He who descends from heaven is bread, giving life, he affirms that he descended from heaven, and does not only carry around a human nature. Furthermore, this is clear, here bread is said metaphorically to be a life-giving thing. For the occasion was taken from the words of the Jews, who cited the history of Manna, and afterwards Christ will repeat the same sentiment in more words, and will say that men are thus made alive through him, when they believe in him. But Christ is interrupted by the ironies of his hearers: Give us, they say, that food, which once tasted, we shall henceforth live without hunger, without food, and without expense.

Latin:

Quod igitur facis signum?

Venio igitur ad quintum locum, in quo est dura altercatio. Offensi Iudaei, quod Christus ait se esse Messiam, et postulat sibi credi, inci- piunt de collatione Mosi et Messiae disputare, et redeunt ad suum inveteratum morbum atque er- rorem de regno mundano. Et sic argumentan- tur, Christus erit maior Mose, Moses eduxit po- pulum ex Aegypto, delevit hostes, pavit popu- lum in deserto, denique res tantas gessit, ergo cum Messiam maiora et gloriosiora gerere opor- teat, et tu nihil geras, sed relinquas nos in ser- vitute et miseriis, non est existimandum te esse Messiam. Speciosum argumentum erat, et quod fascinati parsuasione de regno mundano, nequa- quam possunt explicare. Refutat autem Christus argumentum eorum. Messias maiora geret, quia dabit aeterna bona: Panis Dei est, qui de coelo descendit, et vitam dat mundo. Refutat et alte- ram partem. Moses dedit Manna, imo inquit, Moses non dedit, sed pater meus, quasi dicat: Moses tantum minister est, nihilo magis poterat dare sua potentia vitam, quam alius quilibet ho- mo miserrimus. Discerni volo Mosen ministrum a Messia domino et autore vitae, hic autor vitae de coelo descendit, filius est aeterni patris, cum eo operans, ut supra dixit: Quae ille facit, et filius similiter facit. Hic filius tollit mortem, et reddit vitam aeternam.

Diligenter autem observetur hic locus adver- sus eos, qui de Christo tantum fingunt eum esse doctorem, ut fuerunt Moses, vel Phocylides, vel alii, qui praecepta morum tradiderunt, et qui Evangelium in legem transformant. Hic perni- ciosus error saepe taxatus est supra, et discrimen semper in conspectu esse piis debet. Est et testi- monium observandum de divina natura in Chri- sto, quod etsi obscurius est, tamen adiunctum caeteris fit clarius. Hic qui de coelo descendit est panis, dans vitam, affirmat se de coelo de- scendisse, nec tantum circumferre humanam na- turam. Caeterum hoc perspicuum est, hic pa- nem metaphorice dici rem vivificam. Sumta est enim occasio a verbis Iudaeorum, qui citaverunt historiam de Manna, et postea Christus pluribus verbis repetet eandem sententiam, et dicet sic vivificari homines per ipsum, cum credunt in eum. Interpellatur autem Christus ironiis audi- torum: Da nobis, inquiunt, cibum illum, quo gustato, postea victuri sumus sine fame, sine ci- bo, et sine sumtu.

## 6:37
All that the father gives me will come to me.

Here follows the sixth place, concerning the distinction between the Gospel and human wisdom and the Church, and the people of the law. And first a sad rebuke is interposed concerning the rejection of the people. I said to you, he says: That you would see me, and yet would not believe. This voice alludes to the predictions of the Prophets concerning the rejection of the people. For these are well-known sentences: If the people were as the sand of the sea, yet only a remnant will be saved. But let us know that this sermon not only threatens the Jews, but also the remaining nations, out of the whole human race, a small part will be saved, wherefore profane imaginations are to be corrected, which pretend that the Church is a larger and more powerful multitude. The people of the law were the whole circumcised multitude, and joined in the Mosaic polity, but the true Church is another assembly, namely the one elected from Jews and Gentiles, which is drawn by the father, so that it may come to the son, and believe in him.

These things are afterwards declared more broadly, with the passage of Isaiah 54 cited: I will give all your children taught by the Lord. This is a brief and compendious description of the Church, but yet one encompassing the sum of the matter, namely, that the Church is an assembly, not bound to the polity of Moses, but to the Gospel, and truly believing in Christ, with God teaching hearts through the Gospel.

Furthermore, from these sentences long and intricate disputes are built up concerning predestination, which there is no need to mix in, and Christ himself cuts this off here, when he says: Him who comes to me I will not cast out. Let us hold to the promise of the Gospel to be undoubtedly universal and free, and let us include ourselves in that universal, and let us approach Christ. We know likewise that the commandment of God is immutable, which commands that we believe. With this true and firm doctrine we have confirmed ourselves, let us know that these sayings in John and elsewhere, which are cited concerning predestination, are not said so that they may weaken faith and overturn the promise, but they contain a doctrine reminding us what the Church is, lest, offended by its meager and humble appearance, we wander away from it. And they speak of the effect of predestination more than of the cause. It is impossible for human reason not to be stunned if it compares the Church to the empires of the world. When Augustus, a wise prince and beneficial to the world, was reigning at Rome, and was sustaining great labors in ruling the empire and maintaining peace, and the senate was a great assembly of honest and prudent men who were managing great affairs and sustaining the mass of government in the whole world, who would say that this assembly was not the Church of God, but that a few certain and miserable men in Judea, Zechariah, Elizabeth, Simeon, Anna, Mary, Joseph, and some similar ones were the Church, and were the care of God, and that only this small and miserable assembly would be a partner of the eternal kingdom of God? Since, therefore, reason is moved by this appearance, it is necessary that a reminder or consolation be handed down to us, which confirms us so that we may know that the Church is bound to the Gospel, not to lineage, not to multitude, not to power, empires, wisdom, and the justice of the law.

This is without doubt the meaning of the sayings in John and Paul. Meanwhile, however, it is true that God wishes all to be saved, and that the promise is universal, which no one can deny. Therefore, the cause of damnation arises from our sin. But concerning salvation, it must be thought thus: that we are called through the Gospel, and that we ought to assent, and when we assent, without doubt we are drawn and obtain the promised reconciliation.

Human reason is shaken by many offenses as often as it sees those who are not the Church excelling in multitude, power, empires, wisdom, fortitude, and many virtues. Here the mind first disputes whether there is providence, whether God cares for men? For it reasons from the law that it ought to be better for the just, that the just ought to flourish in empires and dignity. But in the world the impious hold the empires, and those fighting against that doctrine which the Church affirms was handed down by God. Therefore, many, offended by this appearance, fall away from God, and it is difficult to struggle out of this temptation, but it is necessary to oppose to it the wonderful testimonies by which the word of God was handed down and propagated from the beginning, and the examples of the first fathers. God shows by manifest testimonies of miracles that He is present with the small assembly embracing His word.

After the mind has conquered those Epicurean thoughts with a great struggle, a second struggle arises, also born from the law: if there are any who are the care of God, it is consistent that those who are worthy, well-deserving, excelling in talents, wisdom, justice, and other virtues are chosen by God. I feel myself to be far inferior to Saul, Aristides, Plato, Scipio, Augustus; how is it consistent that I am more chosen than these greatest men? This, however, is much more difficult than the former, and here now the voice of the Gospel concerning Christ and the particle 'Freely' must be opposed to the thought of dignity. I am nothing compared to Saul, Aristides, Scipio, Plato, Augustus, but the dignity of the Son of God is greater than all the virtues of all the greatest men. Profane men despise these things, but we in the Church will not despise the Son of God. Let us know that this one has been appointed as propitiator, and that no human wisdom and justice is to be preferred to this mediator. This is the reason for the particle 'Freely,' why it has been repeated so often by Paul, because he wants to tear us away and abstract us from the comparison of the merits and dignity of men, to the sight of the one mediator Christ. The third temptation is concerning particularity. When we have heard the argument of the law concerning dignity and merits rejected, here indeed new tumults arise in the mind. Because one departs from the law and the comparison of merits, the mind disputes that God is a respecter of persons, that He picks out certain ones from the whole human race whom He joins to Himself, and rejects the rest who are equal. Such an election without causes seems tyrannical. Let the universal promise be opposed to this temptation, which testifies that God offers salvation to all, and there is no doubt that it is the commandment of God that all should believe this promise, likewise that all should hear the Son of God. Whom, therefore, does He choose? I answer: He chooses those who sustain themselves with the promise which has been proposed on account of the Son. Although, therefore, He does not choose on account of the merits of men, yet there is a distinction between those who are received and the rest. For those who are received retain the voice of the Gospel, they assent to this, and sustain themselves by the acknowledgment of Christ.

Fourthly, a new struggle arises here: whether this is worth so much, that I believe in the Gospel. Why is this work made so important? Why is it preferred to all the noble deeds of Saul or Scipio? I acknowledge the reasoning of offense, which indicates that this work is light and inferior to others, but it is great not because of its own dignity, but because of the mediator Christ, whom it apprehends. Therefore it is said here:

This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he sent.

That is, the work which God approves, and by which he saves you. This is the singular wisdom of the Church, which Christ confesses in this discourse is not understood by the world. Therefore he says that minds are drawn by the Father, and likewise taught by the Holy Spirit. Nor is the human will idle on that account; indeed, he who thinks there is idleness for the will in such a great struggle has not tasted these most difficult conflicts. The human will can cast away faith in these temptations, and many do cast it away, who had pious and joyful beginnings, like Saul, and indeed they cast it away willingly; others retain it, like David and Peter, and they feel the great weakness of the will, but yet they are not so broken that they cast it away willingly; they do not approach despair and insults against God of their own accord, but they are helped in the meantime by the Holy Spirit, as Paul says: The Spirit helps our weakness. These things are delivered in that very place in Romans 8 and in this 6th chapter to this effect, as I said: That the pious may be instructed about the Church, and may oppose these consolations to the offenses of reason and to many cruel temptations. In these, experience teaches that there is no idleness for the will, but that in a great struggle these causes are joined: the word of God, the Holy Spirit, and the human will.

This is the will of him who sent me, that everyone who sees the son, etc.

As in the preceding verses he spoke of the distinction between Moses and the Messiah, so now he repeats the same sentiment. Before he said figuratively: He who believes in me shall never thirst; now he says simply without a figure: This is the will of the Father who sent me, that everyone who sees the son and believes in him may have eternal life; and a declaration about eternal life is added: And I will raise him up on the last day. At the same time he meets many questions; he teaches that he gives greater benefits than Moses gave, namely righteousness, resurrection from death, and eternal life: he also proposes the manner by which men are to obtain that ineffable benefit, namely not by the law, but by faith in Christ. Thirdly, he adds a universal particle, which refutes the Jews, who thought the benefits of the Messiah pertained only to themselves; he also refutes in general human thoughts about election, which undermine faith and pour forth imaginations, lest we establish that the promise of grace pertains to ourselves.

Although the Monks retain these words: Everyone who believes in the son will have eternal life, yet as I have warned several times above, they attach corruptions; they understand believing only as knowing the history. Afterwards they add: He who believes, that is, knows the history and satisfies the law, merits reconciliation, but yet because you do not know when you have enough works, they command you to doubt. We have often refuted these errors above, but to retain the light of the Gospel, from time to time, when similar passages recur, the reader must be warned to retain the propriety of the words. When he commands us to believe, he wants not only for the history to be known, but he wants us to assent to the promise which is added to the history, that God receives us freely for the sake of the son, not for the sake of the law or our own dignity; this is what he wants you to believe, this is the confidence he wants you to conceive, as it is often said: He who believes in him will not be put to shame. Likewise: Being justified by faith we have peace. Furthermore, in this sentiment of Christ: He who believes in the son, etc. And in similar ones, the mind should always look to the exclusive particle, Freely, which Paul inculcates so often, which testifies that we are received for the sake of the son, not for the sake of the fulfillment of the law. With this light, simplicity, and propriety of words retained, then indeed such sentiments of the Gospel will become sweet to us, and will show true and grateful consolations, and there is no doubt that this one, which we have already repeated so often, is the native interpretation of these sentiments.

However, with this sentiment established, consider also the preface. This is the will of the Father who sent me. Let the antithesis be considered: the law announces to you the will of God, punishing the sins of the human race with eternal death. But I, from the bosom of the Father, bring another voice, which testifies that this is truly the eternal, unmoved, and immutable will of the Father: That he truly receives those who trust that they are accepted on account of the Son, and in these He truly takes away sin and death. Christ repeats this same sentiment so often and with such clarity that the Jews could not have complained that the benefits of the Messiah were not stated with sufficient explicitness, and the perversity of those who later cast a shadow over these very clear sayings in ecclesiastical doctrine is rightly rebuked.

Latin:

Omne quod dat mihi pater ad me veniet.

Hic sequitur sextus locus, de discrimine Evangelii et humanae sapientiae et Ecclesiae, ac populi legis. Et primum tristis obiurgatio inter- ponitur de reiectione populi. Dixi vobis, inquit: Vos me visuros esse, et tamen non credituros. Haec vox alludit ad Prophetarum praedictiones de reiectione populi. Sunt enim notae senten- tiae: Si fuerit populus, ut arena maris, tamen reliquiae tantum salvae erunt. Nos vero sciamus concionem hanc non solum minari Iudaeis, sed etiam reliquis gentibus, ex toto genere humano, exigua pars servabitur, quare prophanae imagi- nationes corrigendae sunt, quae fingunt Eccle- siam esse maiorem multitudinem et potentiorem. Populus legis erat universa multitudo circumcisa, et coniuncta in politia Mosaica, sed vera Ecclesia est alius coetus, scilicet electus ex Iudaeis et gentibus, qui trahitur a patre, ut veniat ad filium, et in eum credat.

Haec postea latius declarantur, citato loco Esaiae 54.: Dabo universos filios tuos doctos a domino. Haec est brevis et compendiaria descri- ptio Ecclesiae, sed tamen summam rei comple- ctens, videlicet, quod Ecclesia sit coetus, non alligatus ad politiam Mosi, sed ad Evangelium, et vere credens Christo, Deo docente corda per Evangelium.

Porro ex his sententiis extruuntur longae et intricatae disputationes de praedestinatione, quas admiscere nihil opus est, et Christus hic praecidit ipse, cum ait: Venientem ad me non eiiciam fo- ras. Nos teneamus promissionem Evangelii haud dubie universalem et gratuitam esse, et nos in illam universalem includamus, et ad Christum accedamus. Scimus item mandatum Dei immu- tabile esse, quod praecipit, ut credamus. Cum hac doctrina vera et firma nos confirmavimus, sciamus haec dicta in Ioanne et alibi, quae de praedestinatione citantur, non eo dici, ut labe- faciant fidem, et evertant promissionem, sed do- ctrinam continent commonefacientem nos, qua- lis sit Ecclesia, ne offensi exigua et humili specie ab ea aberremus. Ac de effectu praedestinationis magis quam de causa loquuntur. Impossibile est non obstupescere rationem humanam, si con- ferat Ecclesiam ad imperia mundi. Cum Romae regnabat Augustus sapiens princeps, et salutaris orbi terrarum, et magnos labores sustineret in re- gendo imperio, et tuenda pace, et senatus esset magnus coetus virorum honestorum et pruden- tum, qui magnas res gerebant, et molem guber- nationis in toto orbe sustinebant, quis diceret hunc coetum non esse Ecclesiam Dei, sed paucos quosdam, et miseros homines in Iudaea, Zacha- riam, Elizabeth, Simeonem, Annam, Mariam, Ioseph et aliquot similes esse Ecclesiam, et Deo curae esse, et tantum hunc exiguum et miserum coetum socium fore aeterni regni Dei? Cum igi- tur hac specie ratio moveatur, necesse est nobis tradi commonefactionem, seu consolationem, quae confirmet nos, ut Ecclesiam sciamus alligatam esse ad Evangelium, non ad genus, non multitu- dinem, non potentiam, imperia, sapientiam, et iusticiam legis.

Haec est haud dubie sententia dictorum in Ioanne et Paulo. Interim tamen verum est Deum velle omnes salvos fieri, et promissionem univer- salem esse, quod nemo negare potest. Causam igitur damnationis oriri a nostro peccato. De sa- lute vero sic sentiendum, vocari nos per Evange- lium, et assentiri nos debere, et cum assentimur, haud dubie nos trahi et consequi reconciliationem promissam.

Concutitur humana ratio multis offensioni- bus, quoties videt eos, qui non sunt Ecclesia, antecellere multitudine, potentia, imperiis, sa- pientia, fortitudine, et multis virtutibus. Hic primum disputat mens, an sit providentia, an Deus curet homines? Ratiocinatur enim ex lege, de- bere melius esse iustis, iustos debere imperiis et dignitate florere. At in mundo tenent imperia impii, et pugnantes cum ea doctrina, quam Ec- clesia affirmat a Deo traditam esse. Hac igitur specie multi offensi a Deo deficiunt, et difficile est eluctari ex hac tentatione, sed opponi ei opor- tet miranda testimonia, quibus verbum Dei tra- ditum et propagatum est inde usque ab initio, et exempla primorum patrum. Deus manifestis te- stimonlis miraculorum ostendit se adesse exiguo coetui amplectenti eius verbum.

Postquam magno certamine vicit mens epi- cureas illas cogitationes, exoritur secundum cer- tamen etiam a lege ortum, si qui sunt curae Deo, consentaneum est a Deo eligi dignos, bene me- rentes, praestantes ingenils, sapientia, iusticia, et aliis virtutibus. Ego me sentio longe inferio- rem esse Saule, Aristide, Platone, Scipione, Augusto, quomodo consentaneum est me magis electum esse, quam hos summos viros? Hoc cer- tamen multo difficilius est superiore, et hic iam opponenda est cogitationi dignitatis, vox Evan- gelii de Christo, et particula Gratis. Ego nihil sum collatus ad Saulem, Aristidem, Scipionem, Platonem, Augustum, sed filii Dei dignitas maior est, quam omnes omnium summorum hominum virtutes. Aspernantur haec homines prophani, sed nos in Ecclesia non aspernemur filium Dei. Hunc unum sciamus constitutum esse propiciato- rem, nec ullam esse sapientiam, et iusticiam hu- manam anteferendam huic mediatori. Haec est causa particulae Gratis, cur toties repetita sit a Paulo, quia vult nos avellere et abstrahere a col- latione meritorum et dignitatis hominum, ad con- spectum unius Christi mediatoris. Tertia tenta- tio est de particularitate. Cum audivimus reiici argumentum legis de dignitate et meritis, hic vero novi tumultus in mente existunt. Quia a lege et collatione meritorum disceditur, disputat mens Deum esse personarum acceptorem, ex toto genere humano quosdam excerpere, quos sibi adiungat, caeteros pares reiicere. Talis electio sine causis videtur tyrannica. Huic tentationi opponatur universalis promissio, quae testatur Deum offerre omnibus salutem, nec dubium est mandatum esse Dei, ut huic promissioni omnes credant, item ut omnes audiant filium Dei. Quos igitur elegit? Respondeo: Eligit eos, qui se sustentant promis- sione, quae propter filium proposita est. Quan- quam igitur non propter hominum merita eligit, tamen discrimen est inter eos qui recipiuntur, et caeteros. Nam hi qui recipiuntur, retinent vo- cem Evangelii, huic assentiuntur, et se susten- tant agnitione Christi.

Quarto novum hic certamen oritur, an hoc sit tanti, quod credo Evangelio. Cur hoc opus tanti fit? cur antefertur omnibus egregiis factis Saulis, vel Scipionis? Agnosco offendi rationem, quae indicat hoc opus esse leve et inferius cae- teris, sed est magnum non propter suam dignita- tem, sed propter mediatorem Christum, quem apprehendit. Ideo hic dicitur:

Hoc opus Dei, ut credatis in eum, quem misit.

Id est, opus quod approbat Deus, et quo salvat vos. Haec est sapientia singularis Eccle- siae, quam in hac concione fatetur Christus non intelligi a mundo. Ideo inquit, mentes a patre trahi, item, doceri a Spiritu sancto. Nec pro- pterea voluntas humana est otiosa, imo qui in tanto certamine putat otium esse voluntati, non degustavit has difficilimas luctas. Potest humana voluntas effundere fidem in his tentationibus, et effundunt multi, qui habuerunt initia pia et lae- ta, sicut Saul, et quidem volentes effundunt, alii retinent, ut David, Petrus, et sentiunt magnam infirmitatem voluntatis, sed tamen non ita fran- guntur, ut volentes abiiciant, non sua sponte ac- cessunt desperationem, et contumelias adversus Deum, sed adiuvantur interim a Spiritu sancto, sicut inquit Paulus: Spiritus opitulatur infirmi- tati nostrae. Haec illo ipso loco ad Rom. 8. et in hoc 6. capite traduntur in hanc sententiam ut dixi: Ut pii erudiantur de Ecclesia, et has con- solationes opponant offensionibus rationis, et multis saevis tentationibus. In his experientia docet, non esse otium voluntati, sed in magno certamine iungi has causas, verbum Dei, Spiri- tum sanctum, et humanam voluntatem.

Haec est voluntas eius, qui misit me, ut omnis qui videt filium, etc.

Ut in proximis versibus dixit de discrimine Mosi et Messiae, ita nunc repetit eandem senten- tiam. Prius dixit figurate: Qui credit in me, non sitiet unquam; nunc simpliciter sine figura dicit: Haec est voluntas patris, qui misit me, ut omnis qui videt filium, et credit in eum, habeat vitam aeternam; et additur declaratio de vita aeterna: Et ego resuscitabo eum in extremo die. Simul occurrit multis quaestionibus, docet se maiora beneficia dare, quam dedit Moses, sci- licet iusticiam, resuscitationem ex morte, et vitam aeternam: proponit et modum, quo illud inenarrabile beneficium consecuturi sunt homines, scilicet non lege, sed fide in Christum. Tertio, addit particulam universalem, quae refutat Iu- daeos, qui ad se tantum pertinere beneficia Mes- siae putabant, refutat et in genere humanas cogi- tationes de electione, quae labefactant fidem et offundunt imaginationes, ne promissionem gratiae ad nos ipsos pertinere statuamus.

Etsi autem haec verba retinent Monachi: Omnis qui credit in filium, habebit vitam aeter- nam, tamen ut supra aliquoties admonui, affin- gunt corruptelas, credere intelligunt tantum nosse historiam. Postea addunt: Qui credit, id est, novit historiam et legi satisfacit, meretur recon- ciliationem, sed tamen quia nescis quando satis operum habeas, iubent dubitare. Hos errores saepe refutavimus supra, sed ad retinendam lucem Evangelii subinde, cum similes loci recurrunt, lector admonendus est, ut proprietatem verbo- rum retineat. Cum iubet nos credere, vult non tantum historiam sciri, sed vult nos promissioni assentiri, quae est addita historiae, recipit nos Deus propter filium gratis, non propter legem, vel propter nostram dignitatem, hoc vult te cre- dere, hanc fiduciam vult te concipere, sicut saepe dicitur: Qui credit in eum, non confundetur. Item: Iustificati fide pacem habemus. Praeterea in hac sententia Christi: Qui credit in filium, etc. Et in similibus semper respiciat mens ad particu- lam exclusivam, Gratis, quam toties inculcat Paulus, quae testatur nos recipi propter filium, non propter impletionem legis. Hac luce, sim- plicitate et proprietate verborum retenta, tum vero dulcescent nobis tales sententiae Evangelii, et veras ac gratas consolationes ostendent, et hanc unam, quam toties iam repetivimus, nativam esse harum sententiarum interpretationem, nihil dubium est.

Constituta autem hac sententia etiam prae- fationem considera. Haec est voluntas patris, qui misit me. Antithesis consideretur, lex de- nunciat vobis voluntatem Dei, punientem peccata generis humani, aeterna morte. At ego ex sinu patris affero aliam vocem, quae testatur vere hanc esse voluntatem patris aeternam, immotam et immutabilem: Quod vere recipiat eos, qui con- fidunt se propter filium recipi, et in his vere tol- lat peccatum et mortem. Toties hanc eandem sententiam tanta perspicuitate repetit Christus, ut Iudaei quaeri non potuerint, non satis explicate dici de beneficiis Messiae, et iure reprehenditur perversitas eorum, qui his tam perspicuis dictis offuderunt caliginem postea in doctrina eccle- siastica.

## 6:41
But the Jews murmured about Him, etc.

We are still engaged with the sixth passage, according to the order we have established. For having previously repeated the summary of the Gospel, when He said that this is the will of the Father, that he who believes in the Son should have eternal life: Now, as the offense grows, He again compares human wisdom and the Gospel, and the people of the Law and the Church, just as Pharaoh was not swayed, but the longer he heard Moses, the more his hatred against his doctrine was inflamed. So here, as the discourse proceeds, the hypocrites raged all the more. Why, they ask, does He say He has descended from heaven? Because the Jews thought their Messiah would have no other nature but human, and would reign in this mortal life after the manner of other monarchs. They therefore execrated these words as blasphemous and insulting toward God, in which Christ said He was the Son of God and had descended from heaven. Christ therefore interrupts the sermon and warns them of the cause of their error. Namely, because the human mind, without divine light and without divine motion, does not assent to the Word of God; this is what He means when He says: No one comes to me unless the Father draws him. And the testimony from Isaiah 54 is cited: I will make all your children taught by the Lord. This passage contains the peculiar doctrine of the Church, namely, concerning the darkness and contumacy of human nature, which is original sin. This darkness is not only to be ignorant of God and His Gospel, but also, without the light and motion of the Holy Spirit, not to assent to the Gospel. This passage therefore refutes the Pelagian shadows, which correspond entirely with Pharisaic opinions and are a kind of diluted philosophy. For because man, by natural judgment, understands the Law to some extent and can perform external discipline without the Holy Spirit. Therefore the Pharisees and Pelagians invented—and many today feel the same—that man is righteous by that discipline, and that the doctrine of righteousness is nothing other than that philosophy. But Christ here testifies that those who are converted to God are drawn by divine motion. The mind is drawn by the Holy Spirit through the Word of God, and the Holy Spirit is efficacious in those who do not resist the Word of God, as the ancients said: No one comes to me unless the Father has drawn him. He draws, however, the willing, just as I said above: that the will is not idle in this difficult struggle.

And how this drawing happens, the following words indicate, namely: I will make all your children taught by the Lord. Likewise: He who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me. That teaching and learning happens through the word or voice of the Gospel, which is, so to speak, the instrument by which the Holy Spirit kindles new light in the mind and new motions in the heart, as it is said in Romans 8: Those who are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God. The same sentiment distinguishes the people of the Law from those who are living members of the Church within that people. The people of the Law are those who are restrained by external discipline, but the living members of the Church are those of whom Christ says here: All shall be taught by God, and Zechariah 12: I will pour out upon the house of David a spirit of grace and of prayers, that is, the Holy Spirit, by whom the reborn may be assured that they are in grace and please God, and by whom they may be impelled to true invocation and obedience. For by the designation of prayers, or invocation, He embraces all true worship of the New Testament,

Latin:

Murmurabant autem Iudaei de eo etc.

Adhuc versamur in sexto loco, iuxta seriem, quam instituimus. Repetita enim Evangelii summa prius, cum dixit hanc esse voluntatem patris, ut qui credit in filium habeat vitam aeter- nam: Nunc crescente offensione rursus confert humanam sapientiam et Evangelium, et populum legis et Ecclesiam, ut Pharao non flectebatur, sed quo diutius audiebat Mosen, eo magis in- flammabatur odium adversus eius doctrinam. Ita hic procedcute disputatione hypocritae magis fre- mebant. Cur, inquiunt, dicit se de coelo descen- disse? Quia Iudaei cogitabant suum Messiam non aliam naturam habiturum esse, nisi huma- nam, et regnaturum in hac mortali vita, more aliorum monarcharum. Istas igitur voces exe- crabantur tanquam blasphemas et contumeliosas adversus Deum, in quibus Christus dicebat se esse filium Dei, et de coelo descendisse. Interrumpit igitur Christus concionem, et monet de causa er- roris. Quia videlicet mens humana sine luce di- vina, et sine motu divino non assentitur verbo Dei, hoc vult, cum ait: Nemo venit ad me, nisi pater traxerit eum. Et citatur testimonium ex Esaiae 54.: Dabo universos filios tuos doctos a domino. Hic locus peculiarem Ecclesiae doctri- nam continet, videlicet de caligine et contumacia naturae humanae, quae est peccatum originis. Haec caligo est non solum ignorare Deum et eius Evangelium, sed etiam sine luce et motu Spiritus sancti non assentiri Evangelio. Refutat ergo hic locus Pelagianas tenebras, quae prorsus congruunt cum pharisaicis opinionibus, et sunt quaedam diluta philosophia. Quia enim homo naturali iudicio utcunque legem intelligit, et sine Spiritu sancto externam disciplinam praestare potest. Ideo finxerunt Pharisaei et Pelagiani, et hodie sic sen- tiunt plurimi, hominem illa disciplina iustum esse, nec aliud esse doctrinam de iusticia, nisi illam philosophiam. Sed Christus hic testatur eos, qui ad Deum convertuntur, trahi motu di- vino. Trahitur mens Spiritu sancto per verbum Dei, et est efficax Spiritus sanctus in his, qui non repugnant verbo Dei, sicut veteres dixerunt: Nemo venit ad me, nisi pater traxerit eum. Tra- hit autem volentem, sicut et supra dixi: Volun- tatem in hac difficili lucta non esse otiosam.

Et quomodo fiat hic tractus, sequentia indi- cant, scilicet: Dabo universos filios tuos doctos a domino. Item: Qui audivit et didicit a patre, venit ad me. Fit autem illud docere et discere per verbum seu vocem Evangelii, quae est, ut ita di- cam, instrumentum, quo Spiritus sanctus in mente novam lucem et in corde novos motus ac- cendit, ut ad Romanos 8. dicitur: Qui ducuntur spiritu Dei, hi sunt filii Dei. Eadem sententia discernit populum legis, et eos qui in populo sunt viva membra Ecclesiae. Populus legis est, qui coërcetur externa disciplina, sed viva membra Ecclesiae sunt hi, de quibus hic dicit Christus: Omnes erunt docti a Deo, et Zachar. 12.: Effun- dam super domum David spiritum gratiae et pre- cum, id est, Spiritum sanctum, quo renati sta- tuant se esse in gratia, et placere Deo, et quo im- pellantur ad veram invocationem et obedientiam. Nam appellatione precum, seu invocationis, com- plectitur veros cultus omnes novi testamenti,

## 6:46
Not that anyone has seen the Father, except He who is from God.

This is a notable saying, and it is opposed to the revelation to Moses, of whom it is said in Exodus 33: The Lord used to speak to Moses face to face, just as a man is accustomed to speak to his friend. And the Jews, because of this prerogative, greatly exalted themselves above other nations, and this carnal confidence bred security in them and confirmed their obstinacy in retaining the Law, and their persuasion of righteousness on account of whatever discipline they performed in imitation of the Law. Opposed to this false boasting are these words: Not that anyone has seen God, except He who is from God, He has seen the Father. Likewise: No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, He has declared Him. And Luke 10: No one knows who the Son is except the Father, and who the Father is except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal Him.

But you might ask, how do these things agree with the passage in Exodus? I answer, in the same chapter 33 it is expressly said: You will not be able to see my face, because no man shall see me and live. Wherefore He Himself Moses testifies that he did not see the face, but heard the speaker in person. For the text says: He spoke face to face, that is, in person and with a clear voice, not in an obscure appearance or dream, just as the same sentiment is repeated in Num. ch. 12, where he uses these words: I will speak to him mouth to mouth. Furthermore, there is an infinite difference between a revealed voice and the knowledge that beholds the substance of God. Therefore, the words of Christ do not dissent from Moses, but testify that Christ is far above Moses. Moses heard a revealed voice, but the Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, divinely looks into the substance of the Father. This passage, therefore, also testifies that in Christ there is not only a human or carnal nature. Because he says that he is from God, and that he has seen the Father, which in Greek is said more significantly, ὁ ὢν παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ. And although it is a brief statement, yet when joined to the others, it confirms the sentiment concerning the divine nature in the Son. But what does that admirable history in Exod. 33 signify? For there is no more abstruse history in all of Moses. The first sentence can be understood in some way. Moses asks that God himself be present at his governance, because governance without God is certainly unhappy. He says, therefore, if you yourself do not go before us, do not lead us out of this place. These things can be understood in some way, but Moses adds: Show me your face. Likewise: Show me your glory. Some explain it thus: that Moses is asking that God might show beforehand the course of this whole governance of the people, but that God replies that He does not wish His face to be seen, that is, His counsels before the end of the completed Church. But that we see the back parts, that is, that we shall see the glory at the consummation. Meanwhile, the people lie hidden in the cleft of the rock, that is, in the present Church subject to the cross, and yet it is covered by the hand of God. This sentiment proposes a most welcome consolation to us, because it testifies that the Church is now covered by the hand of God, and is to be glorified afterwards. To lie hidden in the cleft of the rock, however, is to be in the present state, leaning upon the rock, Christ. But if we understand the inspection of God to be requested, eternal life and the highest glorification are being sought, and the interpretation will agree with that which I have just recited. The Church cannot yet see God, or have the glory which has been promised, but still standing upon the rock, that is, Christ by faith, and in this cleft subject to the cross, it awaits glory until God has passed by, that is, has brought the whole Church to completion. Meanwhile, however, He covers us with His hand, and we see the back parts, that is, we recognize Him in the Word, about to see His face then, when we shall be glorified at the end.

Amen, amen, I say to you, he who believes in me has eternal life.

He repeats the principal proposition of this long discourse and disputation, and again inculcates, as often, that he gives eternal life, which Moses could not give, and indeed gives it not because of the law, but to those who will believe in him that it is given because of this Son. This proposition, placed in his own words, he afterwards exaggerates by comparison and allegories, explaining, namely, the Mosaic types: The fathers ate Manna, and are dead; now another heavenly bread is given to you, by eating which one will have eternal life. I said above that this is the seventh passage of this chapter concerning eating: He affirms that he himself is the bread, likewise, that it is his flesh, and adds that it is to be given for the life of the world, that is, that it is to suffer. Here I think another type is being looked back to, namely the Passover, so that as the bodily foods were Manna and the Passover, and yet signifying something else: so know now that not a bodily food, not a shadow is being proposed, but the life-giver himself—I say—and indeed my flesh about to suffer for the life of the world; thus he calls himself food.

But what is this eating, or how will this food be to be eaten? Many have accommodated the text to the Lord's Supper, because it is said here: My flesh is food indeed, and my blood is drink indeed, and in the Lord's Supper it is said concerning the distribution of flesh and blood. And Gerson disputes about those who contended that the Lord's Supper should be given to infants, and said they were moved by these words, signifying necessity: Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man, and drink his blood, you do not have life in you. But if any feel that the Lord's Supper is a work which, without a true movement of faith, makes a man righteous, that is, accepted before God, and merits eternal life, these err, ignorant of the doctrine of the righteousness of faith. For the use of the Lord's Supper without the exercise of faith, by which we both recognize the benefits of Christ and true invocation is excited, is an idle ceremony. Furthermore, it is certain that the Lord's Supper was instituted so that it might be a ceremony of public assembly, joined with the preaching of the Gospel, and Paul says: Let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread. These things are appropriate not for infants, but for those whose age already however he understands the doctrine, and he is able to examine his own conscience, and the text says: As often as you eat this bread etc., proclaim the death of the Lord. Here no other necessity is imposed, except that a commemoration of the death of Christ be made at the same time when the sacrament is received. Although, therefore, that age which already understands the doctrine ought sometimes to use the sacrament, in order to profess its faith publicly before the Church, yet necessity is not imposed upon those who do not yet understand the profession, and it is enough that infants be incorporated into the Church through baptism. I have said these things in passing about those who have adapted the passage of John to the ceremony of the Lord's Supper, and have contended more harshly about the necessity than is needed.

I do not understand this sermon of this sixth chapter as being about the ceremony of the Lord's Supper, nor about ceremonial eating, but just as Christ previously spoke about the faith by which we believe that the wrath of God is appeased by the death of the Son, who offers his body for us and sheds his blood, and that we are received by God into grace on account of this victim, and are gifted with eternal life. Thus I understand the rest as being about the same faith, by which believers are made alive, because they rely on Christ, who offered his body for us and shed his blood. This doctrine about his passion, and about our faith signified, he inculcates beforehand to the Jews in the eating of the lamb, who had entirely other opinions about Christ; they did not think he was going to suffer, they did not know that reconciliation was granted on account of him, finally they knew nothing about the trust in this victim, but only had their dreams about a worldly empire.

Moreover, Christ shows the distinction between the other Prophets and himself. The flesh and blood of the other Prophets is not eaten, but their doctrine is only heard: it is another thing to eat the flesh of this Messiah and to drink his blood. For here he becomes a victim for us, and it must be felt that by trust in this sacrifice God is appeased toward us. Other saints were also killed, such as Abel, and many Prophets, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and others, but the flesh of these is not food, nor is their blood drink, that is, it is not to be felt that these were victims appeasing the wrath of God, but Christ alone is that victim upon whom it is necessary for us to rely, and concerning whom it must be determined that on account of him God remits our sins. This faith is necessary; therefore, when he speaks about necessary eating, let us understand not ceremonial, but this faith: Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man, and drink his blood, you will not have life in you, that is, unless your faith relies upon the oblation of my body and the shedding of my blood. Much light is added to the text when you consider that in these words a distinction is shown between the other Prophets and the Messiah, who alone is the lamb to be eaten, that is, faith relies upon the oblation of this person alone. The other Prophets are not to be eaten, nor does faith rely upon their persons. And the others, although they sound the voice of the Gospel, yet they are not persons giving eternal life. This one person, who is the Messiah, the Son of God, gives light, righteousness, and eternal life. I indicate this to be the simple and native meaning of this saying.

He said these things in the synagogue, etc. Likewise: This is a hard saying.

Eighth passage. Having heard the sermon about the eating of the true lamb, the Jews are offended all the more, although the ceremony of the lamb ought to have reminded them of this doctrine. Certainly, this eating was not instituted in vain. The lamb signified Christ, the slaughter signified his passion or death, the eating signified faith relying upon this very person, and the association by which we are made brothers and co-heirs of Christ, and participants of his Spirit, and as Peter speaks, of the divine nature. Moses, Joshua, and the like understood these things when they ate the paschal lamb, and Christ is preaching here about this association of brothers and co-heirs, but the Jews, fascinated by the persuasion of a worldly empire, understood neither their type of the lamb, nor the sermon of Christ. Therefore Christ refutes their error, with the form of his kingdom opposed: The sermon about eating seems absurd to you; a more wondrous thing will be the resurrection from death and the form of the kingdom, when I shall reign with divine power. He means this when he says: You will see the Son of Man ascending where he was before, that is, he will ascend to the Father, about to reign with divine power, about to give the Holy Spirit and eternal life, about to defend the Church. You expect a Messiah who gives you an empire of the world; I am about to give myself, which is more, and the fellowship of eternal glory: for I shall reign with divine power, etc.

The flesh profits you nothing; it is the spirit that gives life.

This is the ninth passage, in which he breaks off the disputation, and returns to the passage treated above, see namely to the comparison of the Gospel and human wisdom. The flesh profits nothing, that is, the carnal imagination concerning eating, the carnal opinions concerning the Messiah, profit nothing. This is the simplest meaning, just as it is said elsewhere: The natural man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God. On the contrary, the spirit gives life, that is, the light and motion of the Holy Spirit, which is effective through the Gospel, are the beginning of life, just as it is also said elsewhere: Those who are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God. Likewise: The mind of the spirit is life and peace. The following sentence, which connects the Gospel and the Holy Spirit, must be observed most diligently.

The words that I speak to you are spirit and life, but there are some among you who do not believe. Here he connects these three: the Gospel, the Holy Spirit, and faith. He teaches, therefore, that without the Gospel the Holy Spirit is not effective; he teaches also how it is effective, namely, when we assent to the Gospel and do not resist. For example: When David had heard this voice: The Lord has taken away your sin, many contrary reasons were resisting this voice; David felt the punishments, the fratricides of his sons, exile, sedition, the defilement of his wives: here he saw that from one adultery and one slaughter of Uriah, innumerable sins had arisen. When he saw these new sins, how could he conclude that his sin had been blotted out, or that he was not guilty? But against this huge mass he sustained himself with this voice: The Lord has taken away your sin. When he did this, he felt these words to be spirit and life, that is, spiritual light, by which he both truly acknowledged the mercy of God and conceived the consolation by which eternal life is begun. Thus the saying of Christ can be rightly and simply understood when it is transferred to practice.

This, therefore, is the sum: human wisdom dissents from the Gospel and resists the Holy Spirit, but when we hear the Gospel and assent, the Holy Spirit is effective and illuminates the darkness of the human mind. To the same point belongs what follows: No one can come to me unless it has been given to him by my Father. Let us join these, as was said before: the Gospel, the Holy Spirit, and the assenting will. No one comes to Christ unless he is drawn by the Father.
