Therefore Christ says here: There are some among you who do not believe, that is, by your own will you resist the Gospel and stubbornly retain a false persuasion; you do not want to believe my voice; these are the reasons why you are not drawn by my Father. These being removed, the Father draws those who assent, because he certainly wants all to be saved, and commands that we all be sustained by his promise, and that we include ourselves in the universal promise. These things are simple and plain, and there is no need here for longer disputations about election or predestination; let this sum be held: that the human will, persisting in sins, is the cause of rejection; on the contrary, however, the mercy of God receiving us for Christ's sake is the cause of election; but because we are received for Christ's sake, it is necessary that Christ be acknowledged and apprehended by faith. Those, therefore, are the elect who believe that they are received for Christ's sake, and do not cast away this faith.

Latin:

Non quod patrem quis viderit, nisi qui est ex Deo.

Insigne dictum est, et oppositum revelationi Mosi, de quo dicitur Exo. 33.: Loquebatur autem dominus ad Mosen facie ad faciem, sicut loqui solet homo ad amicum suum. Et Iudaei propter hanc praerogativam valde efferebant se supra cae- teras gentes, et haec carnalis fiducia securitatem in eis pariebat, et confirmabat pertinaciam reti- nendae legis, persuasionem iusticiae propter qua- lemcunque disciplinam, quam imitatione legis praestabant. Huic falsae gloriationi opponuntur haec verba, non quod Deum viderit quisquam, nisi qui est a Deo, hic vidit patrem. Item: Nemo Deum vidit unquam, filius unigenitus, qui est in sinu patris, ipse enarravit. Et Lucae 10.: Nemo novit quis sit filius, nisi pater, et quis sit pater, nisi filius, et cui voluerit filius revelare.

Sed dicas quomodo haec ad locum Exodi con- veniant? Respondeo, in eodem cap. 33. diserte dicitur: Non poteris videre faciem meam, quia non videbit me homo, et vivet. Quare ipse Moses testatur se non vidisse faciem, sed loquen- tem coram audivisse. Textus enim ait: Loque- batur facie ad faciem, id est, coram et clara voce, non obscura specie, vel somnio, sicut eadem sen- tentia repetita est in Num. cap. 12. ubi his verbis utitur: Ore ad os ei loquar. Porro infinitum discrimen est inter vocem patefactam, et inter noticiam, quae intuetur substantiam Dei. Non igitur dissentiunt verba Christi a Mose, sed te- stantur Christum longe supra Mosen esse. Moses audivit vocem patefactam, sed filius, qui est in sinu patris, divinitus introspicit substantiam pa- tris. Testatur ergo et hic locus, in Christo non tantum esse humanam naturam seu carnalem. Quia inquit, se esse a Deo, et se vidisse patrem, quod Graece signifiantius dicitur, ὁ ὢν παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ. Etsi autem breve dictum est, tamen adiunctum caeteris, confirmat sententiam de di- vina natura in filio. Quid autem significat illa admiranda historia, Exod. 33. Non est enim alia abstrusior historia in toto Mose. Prima sententia utcunque intelligi potest. Petit Moses, ut Deus ipse adsit suae gu- bernationi, quia certe gubernatio sine Deo infelix est. Ait igitur, si non tu ipse praecedas nos, ne educas nos de loco isto. Haec utcunque intelligi possunt, sed addit Moses: Ostende mihi faciem tuam. Item: Ostende mihi gloriam tuam. Qui- dam sic exponunt, petere Mosen, ut Deus prae- monstret cursum totius huius gubernationis po- puli, Deum vero respondere, nolle se cerni fa- ciem, id est, consilia sua ante finem consumma- tae Ecclesiae. Sed videre nos posteriora, id est, in consummatione visuros esse gloriam. Interim latet populus in foramine petrae, id est, in prae- senti Ecclesia subiecta cruci, et tamen tegi eam manu Dei. Haec sententia gratissimam consola- tionem nobis proponit, quia testatur Ecclesiam nunc tegi manu Dei, et postea glorificandam esse. Latere autem in foramine petrae, id est, in prae- senti statu innixam petrae Christo. Sed si intel- ligimns peti inspectionem Dei, petitur vita aeterna et summa glorificatio, et congruet interpretatio cum ea, quam nunc recitavi. Nondum potest Ecclesia videre Deum, seu habere gloriam, quae promissa est, sed adhuc stans super petram, id est, Christum fide, et in hoc foramine subiecta cruci, expectat gloriam, donec Deus transierit, id est, totam Ecclesiam consummaverit. Interim autem tegit nos manu sua, et nos videmus poste- riora, id est, in verbo agnoscimus eum visuri faciem tunc, cum glorificabimur in fine.

Amen Amen dico vobis, qui credit in me, habet vitam aeternam.

Repetit principalem propositionem huius lon- gae concionis et disputationis, ac rursus inculcat, ut saepe, se dare vitam aeternam, quam Moses non potuerit dare, et quidem dare eam non pro- pter legem, sed his qui credent sibi eam propter hunc filium donari. Hanc propositionem propriis verbis positam, postea exaggerat collatione et allegoriis, enarrans, videlicet typos Mosaicos: Patres comederunt Manna, et mortui sunt, nunc datur vobis alius panis coelestis, quo vescens ha- bebit vitam aeternam. Hunc supra dixi septi- mum esse locum huius cap. de manducatione: Panem ipse affirmat sese esse, item, suam carnem esse, et addit dandam pro mundi vita, id est, passuram esse. Hic existimo respici alium typum, scilicet Pascha, ut corporales cibi fuerunt Manna et Pascha, et tamen significantes aliud: ita sci- tote nunc non corporalem cibum, non umbram proponi, sed ipsum vivificatorem me, inquam, et quidem carnem meam passuram pro mundi vita, ita sese cibum vocat.

Sed quid est haec manducatio, aut quomodo manducandus erit hic cibus? Multi accomoda- runt textum ad coenam Domini, quia hic dicitur: Caro mea vere est cibus, et sanguis meus vere po- tus, et in coena Domini dicitur de distributione carnis et sanguinis. Et Gerson disputat de his, qui contenderunt infantibus dandam esse coenam Domini, et dixerunt se moveri his verbis, signi- ficantibus necessitatem: Nisi manducaveritis car- nem filii hominis, et biberitis sanguinem eius, non habetis vitam in vobis. Sed si qui sentiunt coenam Domini opus esse, quod sine vero motu fidei efficit hominem iustum, id est, acceptum coram Deo, et meretur vitam aeternam, hi errant, ignari doctrinae de iusticia fidei. Nam usus coe- nae Domini sine exercitio fidei, qua et beneficia Christi agnoscimus, et vera invocatio excitatur, otiosa ceremonia est. Praeterea certum est coe- nam Domini institutam esse, ut sit ceremonia pu- blici congressus, coniuncta cum praedicatione Evangelii, et Paulus inquit: Probet seipsum ho- mo, et sic de illo pane manducet. Haec conve- niunt non infantibus, sed iis quorum aetas iam utcunque intelligit doctrinam, et explorare con- scientiam suam potest, et textus dicit: Quoties panem hunc manducabitis etc., mortem domini praedicate. Hic non alia necessitas imponitur, nisi ut simul fiat commemoratio de morte Christi, cum sumitur sacramentum. Quanquam igitur aetas illa, quae iam intelligit doctrinam, aliquan- do debet uti sacramento, ut publice profiteatur suam fidem coram Ecclesia, tamen necessitas non imponitur his, qui professionem nondum intelli- gunt, et satis est infantes insertos esse Ecclesiae per baptismum. Haec obiter dixi de his, qui lo- cum Ioannis ad ceremoniam coenae Domini ac- commodarunt, et durius contenderunt de necessi- tate, quam opus est.

Ego hanc concionem huius sexti capitis, nec de ceremonia coenae Domini, nec de manduca- tione ceremoniali intelligo, sed sicut supra Chri- stus praefatus est de fide, qua credimus placatam esse iram Dei morte filii, corpus suum offerentis pro nobis, et sanguinem suum fundentis, et nos propter hanc victimam recipi a Deo in gratiam, et donari vita aeterna. Ita caetera de eadem fide intelligo, qua vivificantur credentes, quia nitun- tur Christo, qui pro nobis corpus suum obtulit, et sanguinem suum fudit. Hanc doctrinam de passione sua, et de fide nostra significatam, ante in manducatione agni inculcat Iudaeis, qui pror- sus alias habebant opiniones de Christo, non co- gitabant eum passurum esse, non sciebant donari reconciliationem propter ipsum, denique nihil no- rant de fiducia huius victimae, sed tantum habe- bant sua somnia de imperio mundano.

Ostendit autem Christus discrimen inter Pro- phetas caeteros et sese. Caeterorum Propheta- rum caro et sanguis non manducatur, sed doctri- na tantum auditur: aliud est carnem huius Mes- siae manducare et bibere sanguinem. Hic enim fit victima pro nobis, et sentiendum est fiducia huius sacrificii nobis Deum placatum esse. Inter- fecti sunt et alii sancti, ut Abel, et multi Prophe- tae, Esaias, Ieremias, et alii, sed horum caro non est cibus, nec sanguis est potus, id est, non est sentiendum hos fuisse victimas placantes iram Dei, sed solus Christus est illa victima, qua niti nos oportet, et de qua statuendum est, quod propter eam Deus nobis remittat peccata. Haec fides est necessaria, ideo cum de manducatione necessaria loquatur, non ceremonialem, sed hanc fidem intelligamus: Nisi manducaveritis carnem filii hominis, et biberitis sanguinem, non habe- bitis vitam in vobis, id est, nisi fides vestra ni- tatur mei corporis oblatione, et sanguinis effu- sione. Multum lucis accedit textui, cum cogi- tabis his verbis discrimen ostendi inter caeteros Prophetas, et inter Messiam, qui solus est agnus manducandus, id est, solius huius personae obla- tione nititur fides. Caeteri Prophetae non sunt manducandi, nec nititur fides ipsorum personis. Et caeteri, quanquam sonant vocem Evangelii, tamen non sunt personae dantes vitam aeternam. Haec una persona, quae est Messias, filius Dei, dat lucem, iusticiam, et vitam aeternam. Hanc indico simplicem et nativam sententiam esse huius dicti.

Haec dixit in synagoga, etc. Item: Durus est hic sermo.

Octavus locus. Audita concione de esu veri agni, magis offenduntur Iudaei, cum tamen eos admonere ceremonia agni, de hac doctrina de- buerit. Certe non frustra fuit instituta haec man- ducatio. Agnus significabat Christum, mactatio passionem, seu mortem, manducatio fidem ni- tentem hac ipsa persona, et consociationem, qua efficimur fratres et cohaeredes Christi, ac partici- pes spiritus ipsius, et sicut Petrus loquitur, di- vinae naturae. Haec intelligebant Moses, Iosue, et similes, cum vescerentur agno paschatis, et de hac consociatione fratrum et cohaeredum Chri- stus hic concionatur, sed Iudaei fascinati persua- sione de imperio mundano, nec suum typum de agno, nec Christi concionem intelligebant. Ideo errorem eorum refutat Christus, opposita forma sui regni: Absurda vobis concio de manducatione videtur, magis mira res erit resurrectio a morte et forma regni, cum potentia divina regnabo. Hoc sentit cum ait: Videbitis filium hominis ascendentem, ubi erat prius, id est, ascendet ad patrem, regnaturus divina potentia, daturus Spiritum sanctum et vitam aeternam, defensu- rus Ecclesiam. Vos expectatis Messiam, qui det vobis imperium mundi, ego me ipsum daturus sum, quod plus est, et societatem aeternae glo- riae: regnabo enim divina potentia, etc.

Caro non prodest vobis quicquam, spiritus est, qui vivificat.

Hic nonus locus est, in quo abrumpit dispu- tationem, ac redit ad locum supra tractatum, vi- delicet ad collationem Evangelii, et humanae sa- pientiae. Caro non prodest quicquam, id est, carnalis imaginatio de manducatione, carnales opiniones de Messia non prosunt quicquam. Haec est simplicissima sententia, sicut alias dicitur: Animalis homo non percipit ea, quae sunt spiri- tus Dei. Econtra spiritus vivificat, id est, lu- men et motus Spiritus sancti, qui per Evangelium est efficax, sunt incoatio vitae, sicut et alias dici- tur: Qui spiritu Dei ducuntur, hi sunt filii Dei. Item: Sensus spiritus vita est et pax. Diligentis- sime observanda est sequens sententia, quae con- nectit Evangelium et Spiritum sanctum.

Verba quae ego loquor vobis, sunt spiritus et vita, sed sunt quidam ex vobis qui non cre- dunt. Hic connectit haec tria, Evangelium, Spi- ritum sanctum, et fidem. Docet igitur sine Evan- gelio non esse efficacem Spiritum sanctum, docet item, quomodo sit efficax, scilicet, cum nos as- sentimur Evangelio, nec repugnamus. Exempli causa: Cum audisset hanc vocem David: Domi- nus abstulit peccatum tuum, multae contrariae rationes huic voci refragabantur, sensit poenas David, parricidia filiorum, exilium, seditionem, stupra coniugum: hic videbat ex uno adulterio et una caede Uriae orta esse innumerabilia pec- cata. Cum haec nova peccata videret, quomodo potuit statuere suum peccatum deletum esse, aut se non esse reum? Sed adversus hanc ingentem molem se sustentabat hac voce: Dominus abstulit peccatum tuum. Quod cum faceret, sensit haec verba esse spiritum et vitam, id est, spirituale lumen, quo et agnoscebat vere misericordiam Dei, et consolationem concipiebat, qua incoatur vita aeterna. Ita poterit recte et simpliciter in- telligi dictum Christi, cum ad usum transfe- retur.

Est ergo haec summa, dissentit ab Evange- lio humana sapientia, et repugnat Spiritu sancto, sed cum audimus Evangelium, et assentimur, Spiritus sanctus est efficax, et tenebras humanae mentis illustrat. Eodem pertinet, quod sequitur: Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi datum ei sit a pa- tre meo. Iungamus haec, ut ante dictum est, Evangelium, Spiritum sanctum, et voluntatem assentientem. Nemo venit ad Christum, nisi tra- hatur a patre. Trahit autem pater volentes. Ideo hic inquit Christus: Sunt quidam inter vos, qui non credunt, id est, vestra voluntate repugnatis Evangelio, et pertinaciter retinetis falsam per- suasionem, non vultis credere voci meae, hae sunt causae, cur non trahimini a patre meo, his remotis, trahit pater eos, qui assentiuntur, quia certe vult omnes salvos fieri, et mandat, ut omnes sua promissione sustentemur, et in promissionem universalem nos includamus. Haec simplicia et plana sunt, et non est opus hic longioribus dispu- tationibus de electione, seu de praedestinatione, teneatur haec summa: quod humana voluntas perseverans in peccatis, sit causa reiectionis, econtra vero misericordia Dei propter Christum recipientis nos, causa est electionis, sed quia pro- pter Christum recipimur, necesse est fide agnosci et apprehendi Christum. Illi ergo sunt electi, qui credunt se propter Christum receptos esse, et hanc fidem non abiiciunt.

## 6:70
And we have believed and have known that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God.

The tenth passage is the notable and clear confession of the Apostles, just as another similar to this one, made at Caesarea, of which mention is made in Matthew 16. Up to this point, the beginnings of Christ's preaching had been more joyful and pleasant. The magnitude of the miracles and the correction of the doctrine of the Pharisees had attracted many who had the sweetest hopes of a new liberty and of that kingdom which they dreamed of for themselves. But because Christ now more often exposes the Pharisees, and gradually preaches less pleasant things about the cross, about faith, and condemns those sweet dreams about the kingdom, he is therefore completely deserted, just as our age has seen a similar example; at the beginning, how great was the ardor of minds? how great a light did men judge to have been shown? When many errors were censured and a purer doctrine was proposed, but because the minds of bishops and powerful men were gradually to be offended more by the reproof of the Messiah and of certain other opinions, which are the nerves of impiety, many powerful and learned men fell away. By the example of these defections, other weak ones are not lightly disturbed, as we see now. Christ therefore questions the Apostles, that he may hear their confession and confirm them.

This example therefore warns us not to be moved or disturbed by the defection of others. There are sad complaints about this offense, even in the Psalms, as in Psalm 40: The man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has increased his cruelty against me. Whenever there are factions and dissensions in a Republic, many defections occur. Because a great part follows fortune, and inclines to the more prosperous side of the ship. But especially in the Church there are defections, because not only must the hatreds, bitterness, and cruelty of enemies be endured, but also the scandals of allies make the spirits of some grow faint: just as David's adultery alienated many from him. Let the pious therefore learn to confirm themselves by the knowledge of doctrine, and let them hold to this, even if there are blemishes in persons. Again, let us each be the more diligent in avoiding scandals, so that we do not deter the weak. Christ says to Peter: And you, when you have turned, confirm your brothers. Let this precept always be in our sight, and let it exhort us to be more cautious, so that all our words and deeds may benefit others.

Now let us speak of the confession of the Apostles; they clearly affirm that they approve of the doctrine of Christ, and that they will not depart from him. For others were departing, offended by the novelty of the doctrine, but these on the contrary reply: You have the words of eternal life. They affirm that Christ teaches the truth, and because they believe his doctrine, they therefore acknowledge it to be salutary, and they clearly profess: You are the Christ, the son of the living God. This is the chief article of the Church, just as it is said in another place: Upon this rock I will build my Church. At that time, the struggle of the Church with the people of the Jews was about this article. The people of the Jews denied that this Jesus born of Mary was the promised Messiah, they likewise denied that he was the son of God, but the Apostles profess both, and by this profession they constitute the Church, and separate themselves from the impious.

Now it must be considered how much this article embraces: You are the promised Messiah, to take away sin and death, and to restore righteousness and everlasting life. The Son of God, the image of the eternal Father, begotten by the Father, coeternal, knowing the Father, creating with him, giving the Holy Spirit and eternal life. It is certain that these things are truly comprehended in this confession from the declarations scattered everywhere in the doctrine of the Apostles, and when we hear this brief saying, let us gather in our minds those declarations handed down in other places, and let us learn to be confirmed by the acknowledgment and invocation of this Lord.

But after Christ heard their confession, he warns them again that the end of defections is not yet; this is signified for this reason, that each may be vigilant, and not invite the devil through negligence or curiosity, just as curious minds, while they indulge themselves too much and take delight in their own subtleties and inventions, entangle themselves in the snares of the devil; afterwards, the warning also is useful, so that when some fall away, the others may not despair, but may know that the Church will nevertheless not perish.

Latin:

Et nos credidimus et cognovimus, quod tu es Christus filius Dei viventis.

Decimus locus est confessio Apostolorum in- signis et perspicua, sicut et altera similis huius, facta ad Caesaream, cuius fit mentio Matth. 16. Hactenus initia praedicationis Christi laetiora et gratiora fuerant. Magnitudo miraculorum et emendatio doctrinae Pharisaeorum multos at- traxerant, qui dulcissimas spes habebant novae libertatis et regni illius, quod sibi somniabant. Sed quia saepius iam ostendit Christus Pharisaeos, et paulatim concionatur minus grata de cruce, de fide, et damnat illa dulcia somnia de regno, ideo deseritur prorsus, ut nostra aetas vidit exemplum simile, initio quantus ardor erat animorum? quantum lumen iudicabant homines ostensum esse? cum multi errores taxarentur, et doctrina purior proponeretur, sed quia paulatim magis erant offendendi Episcoporum et potentum animi, reprehensione Messiae et quarundam aliarum opi- nionum, quae sunt nervi impietatis, deficiebant multi potentes et docti. Harum defectionum exemplo non leviter perturbantur alii imbecilles, sicut nunc videmus. Interrogat igitur Christus Apostolos, ut audiat eorum confessionem, et eos confirmet.

Monet igitur hoc exemplum, ne moveamur, nec perturbemur defectione aliorum. De hac of- fensione tristes querelae sunt, et in Psalmis, ut Psalm. 40.: Homo pacis meae, in quo speravi, qui edebat panes meos, auxit saevitiam inimico- rum adversus me. Quandocunque sunt in Re- publ. partes et dissidia, accidunt multae defe- ctiones. Quia magna pars sequitur fortunam, et inclinat ad navis latus felicius. Maxime vero in Ecclesia sunt defectiones, quia non solum ho- stium odia, acerbitates, saevitia subeunda est, sed etiam sociorum scandala, aliquorum animos languefaciunt: ut Davidis adulterium multos ab eo alienavit. Discant igitur pii se confirmare co- gnitione doctrinae, et hanc teneant, etiamsi in personis sunt naevi. Rursus etiam singuli eo si- mus diligentiores in cavendis scandalis, ne deter- reamus infirmos. Christus inquit Petro: Et tu conversus confirma fratres tuos. Hoc praeceptum semper nobis sit in conspectu, ac hortetur nos ut simus cautiores, ut omnia nostra dicta et facta prosint aliis.

Iam de confessione Apostolorum dicamus, clare affirmant se approbare doctrinam Christi, nec ab eo discessuros esse. Alii enim discede- bant novitate doctrinae offensi, hi contra respon- dent: Verba vitae aeternae habes. Affirmant Christum vera docere, et quia credunt eius do- ctrinae, ideo agnoscunt eam salutarem esse, et clare profitentur: Tu es Christus filius Dei viven- tis. Hic est articulus praecipuus Ecclesiae, sicut alio loco dicitur: Super hanc petram aedificabo Ecclesiam meam. De eo articulo tunc certamen erat Ecclesiae cum populo Iudaeorum. Populus Iudaeorum negabat hunc Iesum natum ex Maria esse Messiam promissum, negabat item esse filium Dei, sed Apostoli utrunque profitentur, et hac professione constituunt Ecclesiam, et sese ab im- piis seiungunt.

Iam considerandum est, quam multa com- plectatur hic articulus: Tu es Messias promissus, ut auferas peccatum et mortem, et reddas iusti- ciam, ac vitam perpetuam. Filius Dei imago ae- terni patris, genita a patre, coaeterna, intelligens patrem, cum eo creans, dans Spiritum sanctum et vitam aeternam. Haec revera comprehendi in hac confessione constat ex declarationibus pas- sim sparsis in doctrina Apostolorum, et cum hoc breve dictum audimus, colligamus animo decla- rationes illas in aliis locis traditas, et discamus nos agnitione et invocatione huius domini con- firmari.

Postquam autem Christus confessionem eo- rum audivit, rursus praemonet nondum finem esse defectionum, hoc ideo significatur, ut singuli sint vigilantes, nec negligentia aut curiositate in- vitent diabolum, sicut ingenia curiosa, dum nimium sibi indulgent, et delectantur suis argutiis et inventis, implicant se laqueis diaboli, postea prodest etiam praemonitio, ut cum deficiunt aliqui, caeteri non desperent, sed sciant tamen Ecclesiam non interituram esse.

## 7:1 Argument
Chapter VII. Now the feast of the Jews was near.

John, after the mention of the Passover, having omitted a great part of the history, now attaches the winter of the last year of Christ's preaching, and begins from the feast of tabernacles, which was started on the 15th of September, and is celebrated for the whole octave, as is written in Leviticus 23, and the meaning of the feast is added: That I made the children of Israel dwell in tabernacles, when I brought them out of the land of Egypt. It is therefore a memorial of the bringing out of Egypt, and of the defense in the desert, which embraces huge miracles; indeed, it is by far the greatest of all histories, of all ages from the beginning of the world until the end, except for the passion and resurrection of Christ itself. And it is not only an image of the Church of all times, but a chief part, which shows notable examples in other times, which testify that the Church is preserved and ruled by God without human safeguards, and is exercised by various calamities, that a great part of the people, which bears the name of the Church of God, is corrupted and punished, but that some remnants of the people remain uncorrupted, and retain the purity of doctrine, faith, and true invocation, and experience wondrous liberations, just as the history indicates in order: Manna was given, meat was given, the rock struck by the rod of Moses poured forth abundant springs, the multitude was covered by a cloud by day, and by shining flames at night; the multitude fell and was polluted by a great crime, when in the absence of Moses they worshiped the calf. A great multitude is therefore killed, the seditions of Korah and others occur, and again fourteen thousand and seven hundred men perished by heavenly fire; the people bring new punishments upon themselves by whoredom and idols; meanwhile various battles also occur, and illustrious testimonies of the presence of God are exhibited. Finally, in the desert, the glory of this people was greater than it ever was when the kingdom was flourishing in the land of Canaan.

We are therefore taught by the mention of this solemnity, concerning the wondrous governance and preservation of the Church, that God indeed began from the beginning of the world after the fall of Adam, to lead the Church out of the kingdom of sin and death, and in the desert to rule and preserve it miraculously in this world, even though meanwhile a great multitude fails and rushes into eternal wrath and eternal punishments. Since, therefore, we see the most powerful kings of the world and the greatest multitude of men despising the doctrine handed down through the Prophets and Apostles, and that there is a small assembly of those professing that doctrine, stripped of protections and struggling with various miseries, let us contemplate that image of the Church in the desert, and let us not fail from God, but let us know that the Church is being led now also through the desert, and is being covered by a cloud and heavenly flames, and that Christ the leader is present, just as he was present to them. Exactly the same thing is happening, and will happen until the end of the world, when the Church will be introduced into the eternal tabernacles and the fellowship of God.

Latin:

Caput VII. Erat autem prope festum Iudaeorum.

Ioannes post Paschatis mentionem, omissa magna parte historiae, iam attexit hiemem postremi anni praedicationis Christi, et orditur a festo tabernaculorum, quod incoabatur die 15. Septembris, et celebratur toto octiduo, ut scribitur Levit. 23. et significatio festi adscripta est: Quod in tabernaculis fecerim habitare filios Israël, cum educerem eos de terra Aegypti. Est ergo memoria eductionis ex Aegypto, et defensionis in deserto, quae ingentia miracula complectitur, imo est omnium historiarum, omnium aetatum a principio mundi usque ad finem, excepta ipsa Christi passione et resurrectione, longe maxima. Nec solum est imago Ecclesiae omnium temporum, sed pars praecipua, quae caeteris temporibus exempla insignia monstrat, quae testantur Ecclesiam servari et regi a Deo sine praesidiis humanis, et variis calamitatibus exerceri, magnam partem populi, quae gerit nomen Ecclesiae Dei, corrumpi et puniri, sed aliquas populi reliquias manere incorruptas, et retinere doctrinae puritatem, fidem, et veram invocationem, et experiri mirandas liberationes, sicut ordine historia indicat, datum est Manna, datae carnes, percussa rupes virga Mosi effudit largos fontes, tecta est multitudo nube interdiu, et noctu praelucentibus flammis, lapsa et polluta est multitudo magno scelere, cum absente Mose colunt vitulum. Magna igitur multitudo interficitur, fiunt seditiones Chorae et aliorum, et rursus quatuordecim millia hominum et septingenti perierunt coelesti flamma, populus scortatione, et idolis novas poenas accersit, fiunt et interim varia praelia, et exhibentur illustria testimonia praesentiae Dei. Denique in deserto maior fuit gloria huius populi, quam unquam florente regno in terra Canaan.

Docemur igitur mentione huius solennitatis, de miranda gubernatione et conservatione Ecclesiae, quod videlicet coeperit Deus a principio mundi post Adae lapsum, Ecclesiam ex regno peccati et mortis educere, et in deserto eam in hoc mundo mirabiliter regat et servet, etsi inte- rim magna multitudo deficit, et ruit in aeternam iram et aeternas poenas. Cum igitur videmus potentissimos reges orbis terrarum, et maximam hominum multitudinem contemnere doctrinam per Prophetas et Apostolos traditam, et exiguum coetum esse profitentium eam doctrinam, orba- tum praesidiis, et conflictantem variis aerumnis, illam imaginem Ecclesiae in deserto, intueamur, et non deficiamus a Deo, sed sciamus duci Eccle- siam nunc quoque per desertum, et tegi nube et flammis coelestibus, et adesse ducem Christum, sicut illis adfuit. Prorsus eadem res geritur, et geretur usque ad finem mundi, cum in aeterna tabernacula et consuetudinem Dei introducetur Ecclesia.

## 7:5
For neither did his brothers believe.

The beginning of the chapter recounts the dangers of Christ, and narrates that he was despised and mocked by his own relatives. Therefore, the image of the Church is proposed, and we are warned that the profession of the Gospel is not to be abandoned, even if the hatreds of the highest and of friends must be endured. This common place often offers itself in the whole history of the Gospel, and has nothing of obscurity. For we see daily examples. Therefore it does not need a long declaration, but let us remember this, let us confirm ourselves with these and similar discourses of Christ, lest, broken by hatreds and persecution, we fail from God and from the doctrine divinely handed down.

Latin:

Neque enim fratres eius credebant.

Initium capitis recitat pericula Christi, et narrat eum contemtum et derisum esse a suis co- gnatis. Proponitur ergo imago Ecclesiae, et mo- nemur Evangelii professionem non esse relin- quendam, etiamsi odia summorum et amicorum subeunda sint. Hic locus communis saepe se in tota historia Evangelii offert, et nihil habet ob- scuritatis. Videmus enim quotidiana exempla. Ideo non indiget longa declaratione, sed illud meminerimus, his et similibus Christi concioni- bus confirmemus nos, ne fracti odiis et persecu- tione, deficiamus a Deo et a doctrina divinitus tradita.

## 7:17
If anyone wishes to do his will, let him know about the doctrine.

Here he begins a useful discourse, and first he affirms concerning the doctrine that it is divine. My doctrine is not mine, but his who sent me. Afterwards he teaches how this doctrine can be perceived. Concerning human doctrines we first discern experience, afterwards we assent, as we first experience that the hand is burned by fire, afterwards we determine that fire is hot. With the voice of the Gospel the order is contrary. First God requires assent, afterwards follows efficacy and experience. As Moses first believes God commanding him to lead out the people, afterwards he discerns the help of God and the wonderful defense. It is therefore very profitable to remember this rule. The impious spurn the Gospel of God, who wish to experience the power and efficacy first, and afterwards to assent. Therefore they remain in darkness, nor do they understand the Gospel, nor do they receive its benefits, but those who believe, because they receive by faith and sustain themselves with the voice of God, experience the efficacy, and are gifted with the Holy Spirit and new light.

Therefore, let this sentence of Christ always be in our sight in our invocation. For in all men human reason naturally seeks experience first. We all willingly think thus, that we would invoke God if we saw that the invocation would profit us. But God wants us to believe first that the invocation will be profitable, afterwards we shall discern the efficacy. If anyone wishes to do his will, that is, to receive by faith this word which I propose, this person will afterwards experience the efficacy, he will feel that it is truly from God. Just as Paul also says elsewhere: You have received the spirit of adoption of sons, by which we cry Abba Father. The spirit itself testifies to our spirit that we are the sons of God. Therefore, those who believe understand the Gospel, and are gifted with new light, as it is said in 2 Corinthians 3: When you have turned to the Lord, the veil will be taken away. Likewise: We are transformed as if by the spirit of the Lord, from glory to glory, that is, from divine light into light shining in us. But those who do not believe, their hearts are blinded all the more. Therefore, the more they are refuted, the greater flames of hatred they conceive against the Gospel, as it is said in Romans 2: Let their eyes be darkened. And 2 Corinthians 4: If our Gospel is veiled, it is veiled in those who are perishing, in whom the unbelieving mind has been blinded, that is, because the mind does not wish to believe, it becomes more blind, nor does it see what kind of doctrine the Gospel is.

He who seeks the glory of him who sent him, he is truthful. Did not Moses give you the law?

It is an assertion by which he again, as often at other times, testifies that he is a truthful teacher, sent by God, and that he is just. And it is a preface to the following altercation. For the Jews, since they could blame nothing in the morals and deeds of Christ, were accustomed to slander the violation of the Sabbath: For many healings were done on the Sabbaths. Here Christ makes an antithesis at the beginning, he affirms that he is a truthful teacher and just, but that they are unjust. And although some Philosopher, like Socrates, might think these things are said more boastfully than is fitting for a man, when he says, no that there is injustice in itself, and it is true that this cannot be said of other men: yet this doctrine is necessary concerning Christ, who distinguishes himself from all men by such descriptions.

But the antithesis must be diligently considered, I am righteous: None of you keeps the law of Moses. Nor will I dispute more subtly about this universal proposition, even though it is true that all except Christ have sins, but yet here a comparison is made between Christ and his enemies: None of you, he says, keeps the law. And this voice condemns all worship, discipline, and exercises of virtue in the enemies of Christ, just as it is said in Psalm 15: I will not take their names upon my lips. Likewise: Let their prayer become sin, Psalm 109. All sects are condemned, Jewish, Mahometan, Heretics, defenders of idols, in short, all who fight against the Gospel, and this crime is attributed to all: You seek to kill me, that is, all burn with hatred for Christ and his members, and desire to satisfy their hatred with the slaughter of the saints. Perhaps someone might marvel at this statement, and think that there is not such great cruelty in men.

But Christ wants us to be reminded, he wants us to know what a savage enemy we have in the devil, so that we may be more vigilant in all the business that we will have with the enemies of the Gospel, and know that they do not consult the utility of the Church, even when they pretend to. But after Christ convicts them of homicide, they add a greater sin, namely blasphemy, when they say: You have a demon; this blasphemy is an indication of what spirit they are driven by.

Latin:

Si quis vult voluntatem ipsius facere, cogno- scat de doctrina.

Hic orditur utilem concionem, ac primum af- firmat de doctrina, quod sit divina. Mea do- ctrina non est mea, sed eius qui misit me. Po- stea docet quomodo percipi haec doctrina possit. De humanis doctrinis prius cernimus experien- tiam, postea assentimur, ut prius experimur igne uri manum, postea statuimus ignem esse calidum. De voce Evangelii contrarius est ordo. Prius re- quirit Deus assensum, postea sequitur efficacia et experientia. Ut prius credit Moses Deo iubenti ipsum educere populum, postea cernit auxilium Dei, et mirandam defensionem. Valde igitur prodest hanc regulam meminisse. Impii asper- nantur Evangelium Dei, qui vim et efficaciam experiri prius volunt, et postea assentiri. Ideo manent in tenebris, nec intelligunt Evangelium, nec beneficia eius accipiunt, sed credentes, ideo quia fide accipiunt, et se sustentant voce Dei, experiuntur efficaciam, et donantur Spiritu san- cto et nova luce.

Semper igitur nobis in invocatione nostra sit in conspectu haec sententia Christi. Nam in omnibus hominibus ratio humana naturaliter quaerit primum experientiam. Omnes sic cogi- tamus libenter, nos Deum invocaturos esse, si vi- deremus nobis prodesse invocationem. Sed Deus vult nos prius credere profuturam esse invocatio- nem, postea cernemus efficaciam. Si quis vult voluntatem eius facere, id est, fide accipere hoc verbum quod propono, hic postea experietur ef- ficaciam, sentiet revera ex Deo esse. Sicut et alibi Paulus inquit: Accepistis spiritum adoptio- nis filiorum, quo clamamus Abba pater. Ipse spiritus testificatur spiritui nostro, quod simus filii Dei. Itaque credentes intelligunt Evange- lium, et nova luce donantur, ut 2. Corinth. 3. dicitur: Cum conversus fueris ad dominum, au- feretur velamen. Item: Transformamur tan- quam a domini spiritu, a gloria in gloriam, id est, a luce divina in lucem splendentem in nobis. Qui vero non credunt, horum corda magis excae- cantur. Ideo quo magis refutantur, eo maiores odii flammas contra Evangelium concipiunt, sicut Roman. 2. dicitur: Obscurentur oculi eorum. Et 2. Corinth. 4.: Si est velatum Evangelium nostrum, in pereuntibus est velatum, in quibus excaecata est mens incredula, id est, quia mens non vult credere, fit magis caeca, nec videt qualis sit do- ctrina Evangelii.

Qui quaerit gloriam eius qui misit se, hic verax est. Nonne Moses dedit vobis le- gem?

Asseveratio est, qua iterum, ut saepe alias, testatur se doctorem veracem esse, a Deo missum et iustum esse. Estque praefatio sequentis alter- cationis. Iudaei enim, cum nihil possent in mo- ribus et factis Christi culpare, calumniari viola- tionem sabbati solebant: Multae enim fiebant in sabbatis curationes. Hic Christus facit initio an- tithesin, affirmat se veracem doctorem, et iustum esse, illos vero iniustos. Et quanquam Philoso- phus aliquis, ut Socrates putaret haec gloriosius dici, quam homini conveniat, cum ait, nullam in se iniusticiam esse, et verum est de caeteris hominibus non posse dici: tamen de Christo ne- cessaria haec doctrina est, qui se talibus descri- ptionibus discernit ab omnibus hominibus.

Diligenter autem consideranda est antithesis, Ego sum iustus: Nemo vestrum facit legem Mosi. Nec disputabo subtilius de hac universali propo- sitione, etsi verum est, omnes praeter Christum habere peccata, sed tamen hic fit collatio Christi et hostium: Nemo ex vobis, inquit, facit legem. Et damnat haec vox omnes cultus, disciplinam, exercitia virtutis in hostibus Christi, sicut et Psalm. 15. dicitur: Non sumam nomina eorum in labia mea. Item: Fiat oratio eorum peccatum, Psalm. 109. Damnatae sunt omnes sectae, Iudai- ca, Mahometica, Haeretici, defensores idolorum, denique omnes pugnantes cum Evangelio, et tri- buitur hoc crimen omnibus: Quaeritis me inter- ficere, id est, omnes ardent odio Christi et mem- brorum eius, et cupiunt explere odia caede san- ctorum. Miretur fortassis aliquis hoc dictum, et existimet non tantam esse crudelitatem in homi- nibus.

Sed Christus vult nos commonefactos esse, vult nos scire, quam saevum hostem habeamus diabolum, ut simus vigilantiores in omnibus ne- gotiis, quae nobis futura sunt cum Evangelii ho- stibus, et sciamus eos non consulere utilitati Ec- clesiae, etiam cum hoc simulant. Postquam vero Christus eos arguit homicidii, ipsi addunt pecca- tum maius, scilicet blasphemiam, cum aiunt: Daemonium habes, haec blasphemia indicio est, quo spiritu agantur.

## 7:22
On the Sabbath you circumcise a man.

John includes many very grave arguments, which it is consistent that Christ explained more fully. And although the same calumny is refuted above in chapter 5, yet the solution is taken from a more abstruse doctrine concerning creation and the continuous works of God, namely from the distinction between the works of God and human works. The Sabbath forbids the works of men that hinder the ministry, it does not forbid the works of God: My Father is working until now, and I am working. Therefore, the law concerning the Sabbath does not hinder these divine works of mine, the healing and the donation of eternal life, thus he answered above. Now the refutation is taken from another source, namely from the example of the fathers and of circumcision. There are, however, many subtle consequences, which I will explain as much as I can. This is the first: Circumcision is a work of the fathers, and yet it is kept, notwithstanding the law concerning the Sabbath, therefore the law concerning the Sabbath does not entirely forbid all works. The second consequence, the work of the fathers is preferred to the law concerning the Sabbath, therefore my work is much more to be preferred, because the Messiah is more excellent than the fathers, and the work of the Messiah, which is not only healing, but at the same time the donation of eternal life, is more excellent than circumcision. This is the third: The law itself compels certain works to be done on the Sabbath, as circumcision must be done on the Sabbath, lest the law be broken, namely, that which commands concerning circumcision; thus the law concerning healing and saving one's neighbor must be done on the Sabbath, lest the law be broken, namely, that which teaches the necessary duties of love. When two laws concur, one concerning a ceremony, the other concerning a necessary duty of love, the ceremony yields to love, outside the case of confession. The Prophets hand down this rule, and say: I desire mercy, not sacrifice. When the army of Antiochus was invading the Jews on the Sabbath, the duty of defense was necessary. Therefore Maccabaeus acted rightly when he repelled the enemies on that day. But in a case of confession, the ceremony is preferred to love: as Eleazar ought rather to seek death than to eat swine's flesh, then, when the Gentiles demand it for that reason, so that he may show by his testimony that he casts off the law of God and despises the God who is the author of this law. But this dispute concerning the Sabbath has been treated more fully above, and it is clear what should be thought about the Sabbath after the Mosaic polity has been rejected, and the Levitical rites have been rejected. We ought to retain the genus of the third commandment, namely, that the public ministry be preserved, that gatherings be held at some time, as Paul says: As often as you gather. For although the Church is unlike empires, yet God does not want it to be unknown and hidden in secret places, but so that the doctrine may become known, and the name of Christ be widely celebrated, he wants there to be honest and public gatherings, in which the Church can be seen and heard, as the Psalm says: Their sound has gone out into all the earth. This sentence is the genus of the works of the third commandment, which pertain to all times. Furthermore, the species concerning a certain day, and concerning the manner of rest, ceases after the Jewish polity. Although therefore Christ alleges other reasons why it was permitted to violate that manner of rest, yet this is the reason. By these examples he shows himself, as he himself says: To be Lord of the Sabbath, that is, that he is above the law, that he gives remission of sins, and another eternal righteousness, which will be the true celebration of the eternal Sabbath. Let this suffice to have touched briefly upon the Sabbath.

Cyril transposes the clause, so that the law may not be broken, because since circumcision seems to break the law of the Sabbath, he thinks these do not cohere well. If a man receives circumcision on the Sabbath, so that the law may not be broken. But it is simpler not to change the order, and let these words be understood thus: If a man receives circumcision on the Sabbath, so that the law (namely, that delivered to the fathers concerning circumcision) may not be broken, and so forth.

Latin:

In sabbato circumciditis hominem.

Multa gravissima argumenta complectitur Ioannes, quae consentaneum est a Christo copio- sius explicata esse. Etsi autem supra cap. 5. re- futatur eadem calumnia, tamen solutio ex abstru- siore doctrina de creatione, et de continuis Dei operibus sumta est, videlicet a distinctione ope- rum Dei et humanorum. Sabbatum prohibet opera hominum impedientia ministerium, non prohibet Dei opera: Pater usque modo operatur, et ego operor. Ergo lex de sabbato non impedit haec mea opera divina, sanationem, et donatio- nem vitae aeternae, sic supra respondit. Nunc ex alio fonte sumitur refutatio, videlicet ab exem- plo patrum et circumcisionis. Sunt autem mul- tae argutae consequentiae, quas quantum potero explicabo. Prima haec est: Circumcisio est opus pa- trum, et tamen servatur, non obstante lege de sabbato, ergo lex de sabbato non prorsus omnia opera prohibet. Secunda consequentia, patrum opus antefertur legi de sabbato, ergo multo magis meum opus anteferendum est, quia Messias prae- stantior est patribus, et opus Messiae, quod est non solum sanatio, sed simul donatio vitae aeter- nae est praestantius, quam circumcisio. Tertia haec est: Lex ipsa cogit quaedam opera in sabbato facere, ut circumcisio facienda est in sabbato, ne lex solvatur, videlicet, quae praecipit de circum- cisione, sic lex de sanando et salvando proximo facienda est in sabbato, ne lex solvatur, scilicet, quae docet officia necessaria dilectionis. Cum concurrunt duae leges, altera de cere- monia, altera de necessario officio dilectionis, ce- dit ceremonia dilectioni, extra casum confessio- nis. Hanc regulam tradunt Prophetae, et dicunt: Misericordiam volo, non sacrificium. Cum exer- citus Antiochi in sabbato invaderet Iudaeos, erat officium defensionis necessarium. Ideo recte fe- cit Maccabaeus, cum eo die repressit hostes. Sed in casu confessionis praefertur dilectioni cere- monia: ut potius debet Eleazarus mortem oppe- tere, quam vesci carne suilla, tunc, cum Ethnici ideo postulant, ut vescatur, ut testimonium ostendat, se legem Dei abiicere, et contemnere Deum huius legis autorem. Sed haec disputatio de sabbato supra copio- sius tractata est, et quid post reiectam politiam Mosaicam, et reiectos cultus Leviticos sentien- dum sit de sabbato, constat. Genus tertii prae- cepti retinere debemus, videlicet, ut ministerium publicum conservetur, fiant congressus aliquo tempore, sicut Paulus inquit: Quotiescunque conveneritis. Etsi enim Ecclesia dissimilis est imperiis, tamen Deus non vult eam ignotam et abditam esse in latebris, sed ut innotescat doctri- na, et late celebretur nomen Christi, vult esse honestos et publicos congressus, in quibus con- spici et audiri Ecclesia possit, ut ait Psalmus: In omnem terram exivit sonus eorum. Haec sen- tentia est genus operum tertii praecepti, quae ad omnia tempora pertinent. Caeterum species de certo die, et de modo otii cessat post politiam Iu- daicam. Etsi igitur allegat Christus et alias cau- sas, cur licuerit illum modum otii violare, tamen haec est causa. His exemplis ostendit se, ut ipse inquit: Dominum esse sabbati, id est, se supra legem esse, dare remissionem peccatorum, et aliam iusticiam aeternam, quae erit vera sabbati aeterni celebratio. Haec breviter de sabbato at- tigisse satis sit.

Cyrillus transponit particulam, ne lex sol- vatur, quia cum circumcisio videatur solvere le- gem sabbati, putat haec male cohaerere. Si cir- cumcisionem accipit homo in sabbato, ne lex sol- vatur. Sed simplicius est non mutare ordinem, et intelligantur haec verba sic: Si circumcisionem accipit homo in sabbato, ne lex (scilicet tradita patribus de circumcisione) solvatur, et caetera.

## 7:24
Do not judge according to appearance, but judge righteous judgment.

He accuses the Jews because they judge wrongly: because it is a calumny to disparage a good and holy work, and to praise an impious work. He says therefore: Do not judge according to the face, that is, do not look only at the external appearance of the work, but at the true causes, as the work of David eating the showbread could be reprehended in appearance. Thus above, the carrying of a bed on the Sabbath could be reprehended in appearance, but the causes of the work must be looked at, commands Christ, who is above the Sabbath, and that carrying celebrates a miracle, which offers testimony to the Gospel, and Christ healing, heals by a divine work, which is not subject to the law of the Sabbath, nay, it is truly the very observance of the Sabbath. Because it is a testimony concerning his word, and the eternal Sabbath will be the eternal celebration of God vivifying and working in those who are resurrected. Therefore when he says: Judge righteous judgment, he commands one to truly consider what kind of work is prohibited by the law, namely, works hindering the ministry of the Gospel, not a divine action, or one testifying to the Gospel, or a necessary duty of love.

Latin:

Non iudicate secundum speciem, sed iustum iudicium iudicate.

Accusat Iudaeos, quod male iudicent: quia calumniae sunt, bonum et sanctum opus vitupe- rare, et impium opus laudare. Ait ergo: Ne iu- dicate secundum faciem, id est, non tantum ex- ternam operis speciem spectate, sed veras causas, ut Davidis opus comedentis panes propositionis, reprehendi in speciem poterat. Sic supra in spe- ciem reprehendi poterat gestatio lecti in sabbato, sed causae operis spectandae sunt, iubet Christus, qui est supra sabbatum, et gestatio illa celebrat miraculum, quod praebet testimonium Evangelio, et Christus curans, curat divino opere, quod non est subiectum legi sabbati, imo vere est ipsa ob- servatio sabbati. Quia est testimonium de eius verbo, et aeternum sabbatum erit aeterna cele- bratio Dei vivificantis et operantis in resuscitatis. Ergo cum ait: Verum iudicium iudicate, iubet vere considerare, quale opus sit prohibitum lege, videlicet operae impedientes ministerium Evan- gelii, non actio divina, aut testificans de Evan- gelio, aut necessarium officium dilectionis.

## 7:25
Therefore some were saying: Is this not he, whom they seek to kill?

He recounts the diverse judgments concerning Christ, and the snares laid and frustrated. This narrative has nothing obscure, but it is to be considered because it is an image of the Church of all times; the judgments of men are various, the snares many, and the deliverances to be wondered at. Let us therefore confirm ourselves with the examples of all times, so that we may know that these dangers are not to be fled, and yet let us hope for divine defense amidst these very struggles, just as Daniel is saved among the lions; David is snatched so often from Saul; the entire people is saved in the midst of the Red Sea: and it is certain that the Church is always and in all ages miraculously protected, even if such works of God do not fall into the eyes of men, like the journey through the Red Sea.

Latin:

Dicebat ergo quidam: Nunquid hic est, quem quaerunt occidere?

Recitat diversa iudicia de Christo, et structas insidias et frustratas. Haec narratio nihil habet obscuri, sed ideo consideranda est, quia est ima- go Ecclesiae omnium temporum, varia sunt iu- dicia hominum, multae insidiae, et mirandae li- berationes. Confirmemus igitur nos exemplis omnium temporum, ut sciamus non fugienda esse haec pericula, et tamen speremus inter haec ipsa certamina defensionem divinam, ut Daniel serva- tur inter leones; David eripitur toties Sauli; universus populus servatur in medio mari rubro: et certum est, semper et omnibus aetatibus Ecclesiam mirabiliter protegi, etiamsi talia Dei opera non incurrunt in hominum oculos, sicut iter per mare rubrum.

## 7:37
On the last day of the feast Jesus stood, and cried out.

Above he said that these sermons were held at the Feast of Tabernacles, which preceded the last winter of Christ's preaching. Moreover, the eighth day of the feast was the most celebrated, on which a maximum frequency of people gathered for sacrifice, heard sermons, and contributed money to the temple, or for the uses of the poor, because, as I said above, God wills that assemblies be public, and the voice of his Gospel to sound in public assemblies. Here Christ preaches in the maximum frequency of the people, which was accustomed to gather from all neighboring places at these feasts, just as Josephus writes, that more than two million people gathered at Jerusalem for the feast of the Passover: therefore the text says he cried out. But see how many offenses occur; it was a seditious appearance, that he shouts in such a multitude, and shows himself as if he were to be the leader of the multitude. Likewise, that he teaches, when he is not from the Levitical tribe. Then also the very sentence has how much absurdity to human judgment: If anyone thirsts, let him come to me, and drink. He who believes in me, etc. Since therefore such various offenses arose, the Pharisees are greatly in an uproar, but let us learn the true and necessary causes of this whole deed and saying. He preaches in such a frequency. Because God wills the ministry to be public, and willed it to be testified, that the Messiah had been exhibited to all. But that he teaches, although he is not from the Levitical tribe, it was customary for Prophets to be sent from other tribes. And Christ is the chief priest, on account of whom alone the ministry of others is effective from the beginning of the world until the end. The sentence itself is the sum of the Gospel, which although it is new and unknown to human judgments, which nevertheless know the law, yet to the Church discerning the law and the Gospel, it is known and most acceptable. For what can be said more sweetly to a pious mind in repentance, than what Christ says here? If anyone thirsts, let him come to me; and elsewhere: Come to me all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. For the sentence is the same in both places, and here in few words is set forth the summary of the sermon, which was undoubtedly explained at length by Christ.

And observe the occasion: Christ looks upon the multitude among the people of God wandering, without teachers, following Mosaic rites without knowledge of the Gospel. Just as the whole human race without Christ was in dense darkness, lacking true knowledge of God, and because it has some knowledge of the law, it seeks rites and works by which to please God, and yet remains in doubt, it does not find the consolation by which it might struggle out of terrors and overcome sin and death. Thus, when He sees the people without heavenly doctrine, and as is said elsewhere: wandering like a flock without a shepherd, He is moved with compassion, and burning with a great impulse, He begins to preach about His benefits; He calls the people back from those rites of the law to Himself, He teaches that consolation must be sought in Him, not in the law; wherefore here we are also admonished concerning the distinction between the law and the Gospel, as often elsewhere, that the doctrine of the law does not free one from terrors.

But because it shows and condemns sin, which clings to nature, which never satisfies the law, it drives minds to despair, by which, being oppressed, they rush into eternal death. On the contrary, this is the proper voice of the Gospel, which Christ sounds: If anyone thirsts, let him come to me, and drink. He calls these very ones who, terrified by the law, struggle with fears; to these He promises and shows the consolation by which they may overcome the terrors of sin and eternal death.

But as we are admonished elsewhere, in such sayings one must always look to the exclusive particle, Gratis (freely), which Paul urges especially in the doctrine of justification, because by this he properly makes the distinction between the law and the Gospel: so also this sermon will then finally grow sweet if we consider that Christ wills that we should certainly hold this consolation, that our sins are remitted to us, and eternal life is given, freely, on account of the Son of God Himself, by faith, not on account of the law or our own dignity, and that this is the will of God, that we should certainly conclude that we are received, heard, and saved on account of the mediator Christ, even though we are unworthy. For the mind would never find rest, nor could it overcome doubt, if it had to be felt that we only then obtain these benefits if we had enough merits.

Moreover, Christ Himself adds the other part of the doctrine, how we may obtain His benefit, when He says: He who believes in me, rivers shall flow from his belly. And from the very context of the sermon it can easily be understood what He calls faith. He clearly signifies that faith is required, which, hearing the voice of the Gospel concerning free remission, assents, and receives the pardon, and overcomes doubt and terrors, and a little later it is added that by this faith Christ is effective in those who believe, and gives the Holy Spirit, when the text says that Christ spoke of the Holy Spirit, whom the believers were to receive. Therefore, faith does not signify only knowledge of history, or a profession of doctrine, but such an impulse, which the Holy Spirit effects in those who assent to the Gospel, by which hearts are quickened, and fears are overcome, just as Paul says of this faith: Being justified by faith we have peace with God. The universal must also be considered, because Christ calls all, nor does He make a distinction. For this reason the condition of the law is removed, so that all may conclude that they are received, provided they themselves do not resist, and know that it is the universal command of God that all should believe this voice of the Gospel, which the Son of God sounds. What He says: Rivers shall flow from his belly, living waters, is a customary metaphor of Scripture, which here not only signifies quickening and consolation, but embraces all the benefits of Christ, who is effective in believers, sanctifies them by the given Holy Spirit, and imparts to the Church new light, and other immense gifts, by which the knowledge of God is propagated, and He defends and preserves the Church, until the end of the world, against the power and snares of the devil, by wondrous liberations. Concerning these benefits the Prophets prophesied long before, to whose sayings Christ alludes, and says that the Prophets spoke of these very benefits while preaching about the kingdom of Christ. Just as promises are everywhere extant delivered in this very figure of speech, which Christ uses here, as in Isaiah 44: I will pour waters upon the thirsty, and streams upon the dry ground, I will pour my spirit upon your seed, etc. And 41: The needy and poor seek waters, and there are none: I the Lord will hear them, I will open rivers on the hills. And indeed John himself adds the interpretation of Christ's saying, he says that He spoke of the Holy Spirit, whom those who believed in Him were to receive. Wondrous was this sermon of Christ, nor were such prophetic sayings understood even by those who heard them. For the Jewish people were utterly fascinated by the imagination of a bodily kingdom of the Messiah, who was to liberate the people from the servitude of foreign domination, to shake off tyrants from their kingdoms, and to occupy the empires of the world. Therefore, reading or hearing such prophecies, they imagined that it was spoken of a huge abundance of bodily goods, they dreamed of a golden age, in which the Messiah was to bring them liberty and empires, so that they might enjoy riches, pleasures, etc.

This imagination is refuted in this place, and an interpretation is added, that these prophetic sayings are not to be understood concerning a polity or worldly kingdom, but concerning other spiritual and eternal benefits, which are attained by those who believe the voice of the Gospel, through which the Holy Spirit is effective in the minds of those who, oppressed by the terrors of the wrath of God and eternal death on account of sin, assenting by faith to the promises, are raised up again, and receive consolation, and are gifted with new light, righteousness, and eternal life. Christ says that he effects these things in the Church in those who believe, and these benefits also bring forth huge fruits; not only do new motions exist in the believers themselves, the fear of God, true faith, true invocation, and similar spiritual motions, but also by their ministry the doctrine of the Gospel is propagated, the unlearned are instructed by their confession, and others are invited by their examples. Concerning all these benefits the Psalm says: You have ascended on high, you have led captivity captive, you have received gifts for men, and concerning the same things the saying of Joel prophesies: I will pour out of my spirit upon all flesh.

These sentences therefore teach us what the kingdom of Christ is, namely, that it is not the righteousness of the law, or any bodily or political discipline whatsoever: but eternal things, which are effected in the hearts of believers, the Holy Spirit having been given, as is signified in these words: Rivers shall flow from his belly or from his bowels, just as it is said elsewhere: The kingdom of God is within you. We are taught likewise that Christ is not idle, or reigning for himself alone, but is effective by divine power in the Church, and indeed imparts eternal benefits, justifies believers, sanctifies them by the Holy Spirit having been given, defends and preserves the Church against the power of the devil, and begins a new and eternal life in believers. Let us learn therefore to acknowledge these benefits, and in repentance to exercise faith; let us determine that Christ will be effective in us also, when with this faith we shall invoke him according to the promise: He will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him.

As to what he adds: The Holy Spirit was not yet, because Christ was not yet glorified. It is plain that this is not said because the person of the Holy Spirit did not exist, or because the Holy Spirit was not effective in the Church before Christ was glorified. For above in the history of the Gospel the admirable revelation made to the Baptist was clearly recited, by which the persons of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit are manifestly distinguished, and it is evident from that, that from the beginning the Church was always ruled and sanctified by the Holy Spirit, just as Peter says concerning the Prophets, that they inquired about the salvation to be revealed, searching what time the spirit of Christ which was in them signified, and 2 Pet. 1 it is said: that the Prophets spoke being inspired by the Holy Spirit, etc. Wherefore it is necessary that this saying be understood concerning the manifest showing of the Holy Spirit, or concerning the ministry openly and publicly promulgated through the Holy Spirit, just as the preceding words. But he was saying these things about the spirit, which the believers were about to receive; he clearly signifies that he spoke about this public ministry, through which the Holy Spirit is effective in believers.

Let it be understood therefore that ministries are here being contrasted. There was indeed then among the people of Israel a public ministry of the doctrine of the law and of the Levitical ceremonies, published long before by manifest revelation and miracles; the people knew and admired only this: therefore they imagined nothing else about the Messiah than that he would be such a governor who would propagate this Mosaic polity, divinely constituted, into the whole world; they did not think that he would bring another kind of doctrine, nor did they understand that his kingdom would not be an external polity, but that he would gather and govern the Church, without arms and bodily power, by the ministry of the Gospel alone, the Holy Spirit having been given. Wherefore after Christ appeared, it was necessary that a public testimony of this new doctrine, or of the ministry to be spread among all nations, be divinely published. This was done by the Holy Spirit being sent in a manifest form, and by miracles after Christ's resuscitation, when he was taken up into heaven, so that it might be evident that his kingdom is not bodily, nor the doctrine of the law, or the polity of the Jewish people, but a ministry concerning the benefits of the son of God, who gives the Holy Spirit, and begins a new and eternal righteousness and life in believers.

Thus this saying will be understood more clearly, if the distinction between the ministry of the old and new testament is considered, concerning which it is spoken more copiously elsewhere.

The Old Testament is only a ministry of the doctrine of the law, and in that people of the Mosaic polity, which had bodily promises, it neither preaches about the free remission of sins, nor promises or brings the Holy Spirit; on the contrary, the ministry of the New Testament brings and exhibits the promise concerning the remission of sins and the donation of eternal righteousness and life, which is offered to all who believe, not because of the law, but because of the Son of God, and through this ministry the Holy Spirit is given and is efficacious in those who believe the Gospel, kindling a new light in their minds, sanctifying their hearts, and beginning a new and eternal righteousness. This ministry or this efficacy of the Holy Spirit could not be known openly before Christ was resurrected. For although promises had been published before in the Prophets, and Christ himself had begun the doctrine of the Gospel, yet it was necessary for a manifest revelation to arrive, with the Holy Spirit sent, so that there might exist a testimony by which God would testify that this Messiah is the Son of God, and that He wills that all should believe in this ministry, and know that through it the Holy Spirit is given, and that believers are saved, not through the law.

The meaning of this saying is therefore: The Holy Spirit was not yet, that is, by heavenly and manifest revelation, or by the showing forth of the Holy Spirit, this ministry had not yet been promulgated, through which the Holy Spirit is given, just as after the resurrection of Christ the Holy Spirit showed Himself in a manifest form, and it appears that the appellation of the Holy Spirit was commonly used at the beginning in the Church simply for the manifest showing forth, or testimony of the exhibited Holy Spirit, just as happened at the beginning of the Church, where the Gospel was first spread by the Apostles; thus in the Acts certain disciples speak: We have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.

Many therefore of the people who had heard the sermon, etc.

The renewed struggle and dissensions of opinions concerning Christ indicate that it was a vehement and wonderful sermon, which moved the minds of the hearers so that they felt far differently about this teacher than about others; they heard him preaching in a new and marvelous way about the greatest things, about the eternal benefits of the Messiah, about the donation of the Holy Spirit. For there is no doubt that he interpreted at length these sentiments, which are noted here very briefly. By this magnificent promise the people are moved, so that they cannot despise this teacher, even though they saw him to be in hatred among the chief priests and Pharisees; but the judgments are diverse: some feel that he is indeed an excellent teacher, not inferior to the Prophets, but they do not assent so as to believe he is the Messiah, offended by his humble appearance, because he was born not from some famous family of the powerful or noble, but from unknown parents, from the common people, and that in the extreme borders of the Jewish nation; likewise, because he wanders here and there, erring without a fixed seat, and is not in any part of the government, nor does he have the support or recommendations of the powerful, but being spurned by those who are in government, he is neglected also by the rest of the people. Offended by this form, even those who did not disapprove of the doctrine fall away.

This is always the face of the Church in the world. Struggles and dissensions remain, and although the world does not seek the truth, yet it takes upon itself a judgment concerning the doctrine, and is not moved to believe, even though it is convinced by manifest testimonies. Many also at the beginning approve of the reformation of doctrine and applaud, but afterwards, because the outcome does not correspond to human judgments and expectations, they easily fail when they see the doctrine condemned by the opinions of others who excel in wisdom and authority. Thus the Church is always a small group of certain people who retain constancy in confession, and because of it they themselves also incur the contempt and hatred of others. Truly, against these judgments, God nevertheless wills that testimonies of the doctrine exist; wherefore it is necessary that there be some who retain the confession, it is necessary that this voice sound publicly, that this is Christ the Son of God. Likewise, it is necessary that testimony be given to the doctrine, even by some of those who are addicted to the enemies. Just as here the ministers of the chief priests sent to seize Christ now dare to oppose their own opinion to their judgments and authority; they not only pronounce that he is unjustly sought for death, but they add an excellent testimony, that this teacher excels all others, and that his doctrine cannot be refuted, etc. But not even refuted and convinced by the testimony of these do the Pharisees and chief priests assent.

And since in this chapter there are various struggles and disputes concerning Christ, two arguments in particular are agitated, which most of all hold back obstinate minds from assenting to his doctrine. The one is taken from the authority of the ordinary power, which in that people was of the greatest value, and at all times it is customary to oppose the doctrine of the Gospel, just as now the Bishops deny that one should depart from that which has once been received by public consent, and they allege ordinary succession. This assembly they call the Church, which by the authority of perpetual succession has for many centuries held possession of doctrine without doubt those who depart from this assembly are to be detested; thus they reason here from the authority of those who are chief among the people of God and hold the government instituted divinely. Wherefore, against the authority and judgment of these, one should not assent to the doctrine of one private and unknown man.

This is what they say: Have any of the rulers believed in him, or of the Pharisees? Because among this people the Pharisees had the chief authority, as those excelling in wisdom, doctrine, and zeal for religion, and among them many presided in government; from the judgment of such they affirm that it is better to decide concerning doctrine than that of the foolish and unskilled multitude, which, since it opposes itself to the authority of ordinary power, they securely pronounce to be damned and cursed by God.

The other argument from the testimony of scripture, taken from the lineage and birthplace of the Messiah, is more specious. It is urged most strongly in these altercations that scripture testifies that the promised Messiah was to arise from the royal lineage and family of David in Bethlehem, which was in the tribe of Judah, as Micah says clearly in chapter 5: Out of thee shall come forth the leader of my people, etc. Hence they argue against Christ, that this teacher's family is not known, and his parents are obscure, and he was born in an ignoble place, far removed in the furthest border adjacent to the Gentiles, from whence not only is the Messiah not to be expected, but not even any Prophet has arisen; but this argument, although it pretends the testimony of scripture, yet in reality reasons from human judgment, or human imagination, which the Jews had concerning Christ, namely, that he was to have a worldly empire. Therefore they think he will come forth from a most noble family, and will reign, surrounded and fortified by hosts of powerful and noble men, and in such a place where he would be conspicuous to all, adorned with royal honor and glory. Because these things do not fit the person of this teacher, they therefore confidently deny that this is the Christ.

But scripture often refutes these imaginations, which clearly affirms that the kingdom of the Messiah was not to be such a worldly domination, nor was his person to be conspicuous in the world, according to the expectation of men. These things had been predicted without obscurity in the Prophets, as Isaiah chapter 53 testifies, in which it is clearly said concerning the Messiah: He has no form nor comeliness, and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him, etc. Wherefore the Jews ought to have considered these testimonies, and not to have reasoned from their own imaginations and external appearance concerning his person, especially when testimonies concerning the time were added, that the Messiah had already been born, and miracles testified to his person. Meanwhile, also concerning his family and place, it could easily have been established, if they had wished to inquire. For there were also public records extant which contained the series and nomenclatures of persons in individual families, and there were still living witnesses who remembered this Jesus born in Bethlehem, even though his parents and kin did not have a domicile there. Because when the people had already for a long time been oppressed by foreign domination, the posterity of the family of David, which because of the royal name was most exposed to injury, since there was no place for it in Judea, was forced to withdraw to the furthest border of Galilee; but yet this also had been predicted, that Christ would be born at that very time, when the people and the royal family had been oppressed by the sad servitude of foreign domination, as it is said in Genesis: The scepter shall not depart from Judah, until the Messiah comes, etc.

I have said these things so that they may be considered, and these calumnies may be refuted, by which the adversaries of the Gospel with great appearance detract from the doctrine of Christ. For the same struggles exist in all ages; as the Jews here dispute so as not to assent to Christ, so the wise always object these two things: first, concerning ordinary power, that this is to be heard, and one must not dissent from its judgment and authority. Then they say that a new doctrine is brought by unknown, obscure men, without testimony or the approval of the governors. For human wisdom, just as it judges in the same way concerning the kingdom of Christ or the Church, so it does concerning doctrine; it seeks a Church which has the testimonies and approval of princes, the powerful, the wise, etc. Conversely, when it sees a small assembly without authority and power, despised and rejected in the world, it is offended, and does not judge this to be the people of God, wherefore neither to the doctrine does it assent: thus now very many reject the doctrine of the Gospel, moved by similar arguments, that one must not dissent from public consensus and the judgment of so many ages. Likewise that this doctrine did not proceed from those who hold the government in the Church and are in ordinary power, therefore it is not to be received. But let us know that heavenly doctrine is not to be judged by human imaginations or political wisdom, by ordinary power, or by the consensus of the greater part received for many centuries, but that the true testimonies of the word divinely handed down must be sought. Let us hold this doctrine, which it is certain was handed down by the Prophets, Christ, and the Apostles, and confirmed by the testimonies of miracles, nor let us be moved by diverse judgments or the conspiracy of the powerful and the wise, however long-lasting. We see that there has always been in the world a small group of the true Church, in which the purity of doctrine remained. Nor is it new that the greater part errs, and that εἰδωλομανίας and impious doctrine are defended by those who are in ordinary power, just as in the people of Israel the Prophets, Elijah, Elisha, and others were forced to oppose themselves openly to kings and priests defending idolatry. And Jeremiah alone withstood the assembly of the Pontiffs and Prophets in the tribe of Judah etc.

Latin:

In extremo die festi stabat Iesus, et clamabat.

Supra dixit has conciones habitas esse in festo tabernaculorum, quod praecessit postremam hiemem praedicationis Christi. Erat autem octavus dies festi celeberrimus, quo maxima frequentia populi ad sacrificium conveniebat, audiebat conciones, et conferebat pecunias ad templum, seu usus pauperum, quia, ut supra dixi, Deus vult publicos esse congressus, et vocem Evangelii sui in publicis congressibus sonare. Hic Christus in maxima frequentia populi concionatur, quae ex omnibus vicinis locis in his festis solebat convenire, sicut Iosephus scribit, sub festum Paschae convenisse Ierosolymis amplius vicies centena millia hominum: ideo textus inquit eum clamasse. Vide autem quam multae offensiones occurrant, seditiosa species erat, quod in tanta multitudine vociferatur, et quasi ducem fore se multitudinis ostendit. Item, quod docet, cum non sit ex Levitica tribu. Deinde et ipsa sententia quantum habet absurditatis iudicio humano: Si quis sitit, veniat ad me, et bibat. Qui credit in me, etc. Cum igitur tam variae offensiones extiterint, Pharisaei valde tumultuantur, sed nos discamus veras et necessarias causas huius totius facti et dicti. Concionatur in tanta frequentia. Quia Deus vult ministerium esse publicum, et voluit esse testatum, universis exhibitum esse Messiam. Quod vero docet, quanquam non sit ex Levitica tribu, usitatum erat mitti Prophetas ex aliis tribubus. Et Christus est praecipuus sacerdos, propter quem solum caeterorum ministerium est efficax ab initio mundi usque ad finem. Ipsa vero sententia est summa Evangelii, quae etsi est nova et ignota iudiciis humanis, quae tamen legem norunt, tamen Ecclesiae discernenti legem et Evangelium, est nota et acceptissima. Quid enim dulcius piae menti in poenitentia dici potest, quam quod ait Christus hic? Si quis sitit, veniat ad me; et alibi: Venite ad me omnes qui laboratis et onerati estis, et ego reficiam vos. Est enim eadem utrobique sententia, et hic paucis verbis pro- ponitur summa concionis, quae haud dubie a Christo copiose explicata est.

Ac vide occasionem, intuetur Christus mul- titudinem in populo Dei errantem, sine doctori- bus, sectantem cultus Mosaicos sine noticia Evan- gelii. Sicut totum genus humanum sine Christo erat in densa caligine, carens vera noticia Dei, et quia habet aliquam legis noticiam, quaerit cultus et opera, quibus placet Deum, et tamen manet in dubitatione, non invenit consolationem, qua eluctetur ex terroribus, et vincat peccatum et mortem. Ita cum videt populum sine doctrina coelesti, et sicut alibi dicitur: tanquam gregem sine pastore errare, afficitur misericordia, et ar- dens ingenti motu incipit concionari de suis be- neficiis, revocat populum ab illis cultibus legis ad sese, docet apud sese quaerendam esse conso- lationem, non in lege, quare hic etiam admone- mur de discrimine legis et Evangelii, ut saepe alias doctrina legis non liberat a terroribus.
