Sed quia ostendit, et damnat peccatum, quod haeret in natura, quae nunquam satisfacit legi, adigit mentes ad desperationem, qua op- pressae, ruunt in aeternam mortem. Econtra haec est propria Evangelii vox, quam sonat Chri- stus: Si quis sitit, veniat ad me, et bibat. Vocat hos ipsos, qui perterrefacti lege luctantur cum pavoribus, his promittit et ostendit consolatio- nem, qua vincant terrores peccati, et mortis ae- ternae.

Ut autem alibi admonemur, in talibus dictis semper respiciendum esse ad particulam exclusi- vam, Gratis, quam praecipue in doctrina iustifi- cationis urget Paulus, quia hac proprie facit dis- crimen legis et Evangelii: ita et haec concio tum demum dulcescet, si consideremus Christum velle, ut certo hanc consolationem teneamus, no- bis remitti peccata, ac donari vitam aeternam, Gratis, propter ipsum filium Dei, fide, non pro- pter legem, seu propriam dignitatem, et hanc esse Dei voluntatem, ut statuamus certo nos re- cipi, exaudiri et salvari propter mediatorem Christum, etiamsi sumus indigni. Nunquam enim acquiesceret mens, nec posset vincere du- bitationem, si sentiendum esset, tum demum nos consequi haec beneficia, si haberemus satis meritorum.

Addit autem Christus ipse et alteram partem doctrinae, quomodo consequamur ipsius benefi- cium, cum inquit: Qui credit in me, flumina de ventre eius fluent. Ac ex ipso contextu concio- nis facile intelligi potest, quid vocet fidem. Clare significat requiri fidem, quae audiens vocem Evangelii de gratuita remissione, assentitur, et accipit condonationem, et vincit dubitationem et terrores, et paulo post additur, hac fide Christum efficacem esse in his, qui credunt, et dare Spiri- tum sanctum, cum ait textus, Christum locutum esse de Spiritu sancto, quem accepturi essent credentes. Non igitur fides significat tantum no- ticiam historiae, aut professionem doctrinae, sed talem motum, quem efficit Spiritus sanctus in his, qui assentiuntur Evangelio, quo vivificantur cor- da, et vincuntur pavores, sicut de hac fide Pau- lus ait: Iustificati fide pacem habemus apud Deum. Consideranda est etiam universalis, quia Christus omnes vocat, nec facit discrimen. Ideo enim tollitur conditio legis, ut omnes statuant sese recipi, modo ipsi non repugnent, et sciant universale mandatum Dei esse, ut omnes credant huic voci Evangelii, quam sonat filius Dei. Quod ait: Flumina de ventre eius fluent oquae vivae, usitata metaphora scripturae est, quae hic non tantum significat vivificationem et consolationem, sed complectitur omnia beneficia Christi, qui est efficax in credentibus, sanctificat eos dato Spiritu sancto, et impertit Ecclesiae no- vam lucem, et alia ingentia dona, quibus propa- gatur noticia Dei, defendit et servat Ecclesiam, usque ad finem mundi, adversus potentiam et in- sidias diaboli, mirandis liberationibus. De his beneficiis multo ante vaticinati sunt Prophetae, ad quorum dicta alludit Christus, et ait de his ipsis beneficiis locutos esse Prophetas concionan- tes de regno Christi. Sicut passim extant promis- siones traditae hac ipsa figura sermonis, qua hic utitur Christus, ut Esaiae 44.: Effundam aquas super sitientem, et fluenta super aridam, effun- dam spiritum meum super semen tuum, etc. Et 41.: Egeni et pauperes quaerunt aquas, et non sunt: Ego dominus exaudiam eos, aperiam in collibus flumina. Et quidem Ioannes ipse addit interpretationem dicti Christi, ait eum locutum esse de Spiritu sancto, quem accepturi erant cre- dentes in ipsum. Miranda fuit haec concio Christi, nec ab ipsis, qui audierunt, intellecta sunt talia dicta prophetica. Prorsus enim fascinatus erat populus Iudaicus imaginatione de regno Messiae corporali, qui esset liberaturus populum a servitute alienae dominationis, excussurus tyrannos e regnis, et occupaturus imperia mundi. Itaque legentes aut audientes talia vaticinia, imaginabantur dici de ingenti ubertate honorum corporalium, somnia- bant auream aetatem, in qua Messias allaturus esset eis libertatem et imperia, ut fruerentur opi- bus, voluptatibus, etc.

Haec imaginatio hoc loco refutatur, et addi- tur interpretatio, haec dicta prophetica non esse intelligenda de politia aut regno mundano, sed de aliis spiritualibus, et aeternis beneficiis, quae consequuntur hi, qui credunt voci Evangelii, per quam efficax est Spiritus sanctus in mentibus eo- rum, qui oppressi terroribus irae Dei, ac mortis aeternae, propter peccatum, fide assentientes pro- missionibus, rursus eriguntur, et accipiunt con- solationem, et donantur nova luce, iusticia et vita aeterna. Haec ait Christus se efficere in Ec- clesia in his, qui credunt, et haec beneficia affe- runt etiam ingentes fructus, non tantum in ipsis credentibus existunt novi motus, timor Dei, vera fides, vera invocatio, et similes motus spirituales, sed etiam ipsorum ministerio propagatur doctrina Evangelii, instituuntur rudes ipsorum confes- sione, et exemplis invitantur alii. De his omni- bus beneficiis ait Psalmus: Ascendisti in altum, captivam duxisti captivitatem, accepisti dona ho- minibus, et de iisdem vaticinatur dictum Ioëlis: Effundam de spiritu meo super omnem carnem.

Docent igitur nos hae sententiae, quale sit regnum Christi, videlicet, non esse iusticiam le- gis, aut qualemcunque corporalem seu politicam disciplinam: sed res aeternas, quae efficiuntur in cordibus credentium, dato Spiritu sancto, ut significatur in his verbis: Flumina de ventre seu de visceribus eius fluent, sicut alibi dicitur: Re- gnum Dei intra vos est. Docemur item, Chri- stum non esse otiosum, aut sibi tantum regnare, sed esse efficacem divina potentia in Ecclesia, et quidem impertire aeterna beneficia, iustificare credentes, sanctificare dato Spiritu sancto, de- fendere et servare Ecclesiam adversus potestatem diaboli, incoare novam et aeternam vitam in cre- dentibus. Discamus ergo agnoscere haec benefi- cia, ac in poenitentia exercere fidem, statuamus Christum in nobis quoque efficacem fore, cum hac fide invocabimus eum iuxta promissionem: Dabit Spiritum sanctum petentibus se.

Quod addit: Spiritus sanctus nondum erat, quia Christus nondum erat glorificatus. Palam est non hoc dici, quod non extiterit persona Spiritus sancti, aut quod Spiritus sanctus non fuerit efficax in Ecclesia ante Christum glorificatum. Nam supra in historia Evangelii clare recitata est admiranda revelatio, facta Baptistae, qua manifeste discernuntur personae Patris, et Filii, et Spiritus sancti, et constat inde usque ab initio semper Ecclesiam regi et sanctificari Spiritu sancto, sicut Petrus de Prophetis ait, eos exquisivisse de revelanda salute, scrutantes, quod tempus significaret spiritus Christi, qui in eis erat, et 2. Pet. 1. dicitur: Spiritu sancto inspiratos locutos esse Prophetas, etc. Quare necesse est intelligi hoc dictum de manifesta ostensione Spiritus sancti, seu de ministerio palam et publice promulgato per Spiritum sanctum, sicut praecedentia verba. Haec autem dicebat de spiritu, quem accepturi erant credentes, clare significant eum locutum esse de hoc publico ministerio, per quod Spiritus sanctus efficax est in credentibus.

Intelligatur ergo hic opponi ministeria. Erat tunc quidem in populo Israël publicum ministerium doctrinae legis, et ceremoniarum Leviticarum multo ante editum, manifesta revelatione et miraculis, hoc tantum norat et mirabatur populus: ideo de Messia nihil aliud imaginabatur, quam eum fore talem gubernatorem, qui propagaturus esset hanc politiam Mosaicam, divinitus constitutam, in totum orbem terrarum, non existimabant eum allaturum esse aliud genus doctrinae, nec intelligebant eius regnum fore non externam politiam, sed collecturum ac gubernaturum Ecclesiam, sine armis et potentia corporali, solo ministerio Evangelii, dato Spiritu sancto. Quare postquam apparuit Christus, necesse fuit divinitus edi publicum testimonium huius novae doctrinae, seu ministerii spargendi in omnes gentes. Id factum est misso Spiritu sancto manifesta specie, et miraculis post Christi resuscitationem, cum assumtus est in coelum, ut constaret ipsius regnum non esse corporale, nec doctrinam legis, aut politiam Iudaici populi, sed ministerium de beneficiis filii Dei, dantis Spiritum sanctum, et incoantis novam et aeternam iusticiam et vitam in credentibus.

Sic clarius intelligetur hoc dictum, si consideretur discrimen inter ministerium veteris ac novi testamenti, de quo alibi copiosius dicitur.

Vetus testamentum tantum est ministerium do- ctrinae legis, et in illo populo politiae Mosaicae, quae habebat promissiones corporales, nec con- cionatur de remissione peccatorum gratuita, nec promittit aut adfert Spiritum sanctum, econtra novi testamenti ministerium affert et exhibet pro- missionem de remissione peccatorum, et dona- tione aeternae iusticiae et vitae, quae offertur omnibus qui credunt, non propter legem, sed propter filium Dei, et per hoc ministerium datur, et efficax est Spiritus sanctus in his, qui credunt Evangelio, accendens in mentibus novam lucem, sanctificans corda, et incoans novam et aeternam iusticiam. Hoc ministerium seu haec efficacia Spiritus sancti non potuit cognosci palam, prius- quam resuscitatus est Christus. Etsi enim ante editae erant promissiones in Prophetis, et Chri- stus ipse incoarat doctrinam Evangelii, tamen oportuit accedere manifestam revelationem, misso Spiritu sancto, ut extaret testimonium, quo Deus testaretur hunc Messiam esse filium Dei, et se velle, ut omnes huic ministerio credant, ac sciant per hoc dari Spiritum sanctum, et salvari cre- dentes, non per legem.

Est ergo sententia huius dicti: Nondum erat Spiritus sanctus, id est, nondum coelesti ac ma- nifesta revelatione, seu ostensione Spiritus sancti, promulgatum erat hoc ministerium, per quod da- tur Spiritus sanctus, sicut post resurrectionem Christi, manifesta specie sese ostendit Spiritus sanctus, ac apparet usitate Spiritus sancti appel- lationem initio in Ecclesia simpliciter usurpatam esse pro manifesta ostensione, seu testimonio ex- hibiti Spiritus sancti, sicut fiebat initio Ecclesiae, ubi primum spargebatur Evangelium ab Aposto- lis, sic in Actis loquuntur quidam discipuli: Ne quidem quod sit Spiritus sanctus audivimus.

Multi igitur de plebe qui audierant concio- nem, etc.

Renovatum certamen et dissensiones iudicio- rum de Christo, indicant vehementem et mirifi- cam concionem fuisse, quae moverit animos au- dientium, ut longe aliter sentirent de hoc docto- re, quam de aliis, audiebant eum novo et mi- rando modo concionari de rebus maximis, de ae- ternis beneficiis Messiae, de donatione Spiritus sancti. Non enim dubium est, quin has senten- tias, quae hic brevissime notantur, copiose inter- pretatus sit. Hac magnifica promissione movetur populus, ut non possit contemnere hunc docto- rem, etiamsi videbat eum in odio esse apud Pon- tifices et Pharisaeos, sed diversa sunt iudicia, alii sentiunt esse quidem excellentem doctorem, non inferiorem Prophetis, sed non assentiuntur, ut credant esse Messiam, offensi humili specie, quod erat ortus non ex celebri aliqua familia potentum aut nobilium, sed ex ignotis parentibus, de me- dia plebe, idque in extremis finibus gentis Iudai- cae, item, quod vagatur passim errans sine certa sede, nec est in aliqua parte gubernationis, nec habet studia aut suffragationes potentum, sed spretus ab his, qui sunt in gubernatione, negli- gitur etiam a reliquo populo. Hac forma offensi, resiliunt etiam hi, qui doctrinam non impro- babant.

Haec semper est in mundo facies Ecclesiae. Manent certamina et dissensiones, et mundus etsi non quaerit veritatem, tamen sibi iudicium sumit de doctrina, nec movetur, ut credat, etiamsi convincitur manifestis testimoniis. Multi etiam initio approbant doctrinae emendationem, et ap- plaudunt, sed postea, quia non respondet even- tus humanis iudiciis, et expectationi, facile defi- ciunt, cum vident sententiis aliorum, qui prae- stant sapientia et autoritate, damnari doctrinam. Ita Ecclesia semper est exiguus coetus quorun- dam, qui retinent constantiam in confessione, et propter eam etiam ipsi incurrunt in comtemtum et odia aliorum. Verum adversus haec iudicia tamen Deus vult extare testimonia doctrinae, quare oportet esse aliquos, qui retineant confes- sionem, oportet publice sonare hanc vocem, quod hic sit Christus filius Dei. Item oportet testimo- nium dari doctrinae, etiam ab aliquibus eorum, qui sunt addicti hostibus. Sicut hic ministri pon- tificum missi ad prehendendum Christum, iam audent illorum iudiciis et autoritati suam senten- tiam opponere, non solum pronunciant ipsum iniuste appeti ad necem, sed addunt egregium testimonium, hunc doctorem antecellere omni- bus, nec posse eius doctrinam reprehendi etc. Sed nec horum testimonio refutati ac convicti as- sentiuntur Pharisaei et Pontifices.

Ac cum in hoc capite sint varia certamina, et disputationes de Christo, praecipue duo argu- menta agitantur, quae maxime retinent animos obstinatos, ne assentiantur doctrinae eius. Al- terum est sumtum ab autoritate ordinariae pote- statis, quod in illo populo plurimum valebat, et omnibus temporibus solet opponi doctrinae Evan- gelii, sicut nunc Episcopi negant discedendum esse ab eo, quod semel publico consensu receptum est, et allegant successionem ordinariam. Hunc coetum vocant Ecclesiam, qui autoritate perpe- tuae successionis iam multis seculis tenet posses- sionem doctrinae et gubernationis, hunc con- tendunt non posse errare, et sine dubitatione de- testandos esse eos, qui ab hoc coetu discedunt, ita hic ratiocinantur ab autoritate eorum, qui sunt praecipui in populo Dei, et tenent guberna- tionem institutam divinitus. Quare contra ho- rum autoritatem et iudicium, non esse assentien- dum doctrinae unius hominis privati et ignoti.

Hoc est, quod aiunt: Nunquis ex principi- bus credit in ipsum, aut ex Pharisaeis? Quia in hoc populo Pharisaeorum erat praecipua autori- tas, tanquam praestantium sapientia, doctrina, et studio religionis, ac inter eos multi praeerant in gubernatione, ex talium iudicio affirmant po- tius statuendum esse de doctrina, quam stultae et imperitae multitudinis, quae cum sese opponat autoritati ordinariae potestatis, secure pronun- ciant eam a Deo damnatam et maledictam esse.

Alterum argumentum ex testimonio scriptu- rae, de genere et loco natali Messiae sumtum, magis est speciosum. Maxime urgetur in his al- tercationibus, quod scriptura testatur Messiam promissum, oriturum esse ex regio genere, et fa- milia Davidis in Bethlehem, quae erat in tribu Iuda, sicut clare ait Michaeas cap. 5.: Ex te egre- dietur dux populi mei, etc. Hinc argumentan- tur contra Christum, huius doctoris nec familiam esse notam, et parentes esse obscuros, et ortum esse loco ignobili, procul dissito in extrema ora finitima gentibus, unde non solum Messias non sit sperandus, sed ne quidem Propheta aliquis ex- titerit, sed hoc argumentum, etsi praetexit testi- monium scripturae, tamen revera ratiocinatur ex humano iudicio, seu imaginatione humana, quam habebant Iudaei de Christo, videlicet, quod esset habiturus imperium mundanum. Ideo cogi- tant eum proditurum ex nobilissima familia, et regnaturum, septum et munitum agminibus po- tentum et nobilium, et tali loco, ubi esset omni- bus conspicuus, ornatus honore et gloria regia. Haec quia non conveniunt in personam huius doctoris, ideo confidenter negant hunc esse Christum.

Sed has imaginationes saepe refutat scriptura, quae clare affirmat regnum Messiae non futurum esse talem mundanam dominationem, nec personam ipsius futuram esse conspicuam in mundo, iuxta hominum expectationem. Haec sine obscuritate praedicta erant in Prophetis, ut cap. Esaiae 53. testatur, in quo clare dicitur de Messia: Non est species ei neque decor, cum aspiceremus eum, non erat species, quae placeret, etc. Quare haec testimonia debebant Iudaei considerare, nec ex suis imaginationibus et externa specie de persona ratiocinari, praesertim cum accederent testimonia de tempore, quod iam natus esset Messias, et de persona miracula testarentur. Interim etiam de familia et loco facile poterat constare, si voluissent inquirere. Nam et publice extabant indices, qui continebant seriem et nomenclaturas personarum in singulis familiis, et erant adhuc vivi testes, qui meminerant hunc Iesum natum in Bethlehem, etsi eius parentes et cognatio non habebant ibi domicilium. Quia cum populus iam longo tempore oppressus esset aliena dominatione, posteritas familiae Davidis, quae propter regium nomen, maxime erat obnoxia iniuriae, cum nusquam esset ei locus in Iudaea, coacta est secedere in ultimam oram Galileae, sed tamen praedictum et hoc erat, eo ipso tempore Christum nasciturum esse, cum populus et regia familia oppressa esset tristi servitute alienae dominationis, sicut in Genesi dicitur: Non auferetur sceptrum a Iuda, donec veniat Messias, etc.

Haec dixi, ut considerentur, et refutari possint hae calumniae, quibus adversarii Evangelii magna specie detrahunt doctrinae Christi. Nam eadem sunt certamina omnibus aetatibus, ut hic disputant Iudaei, ne assentiantur Christo, ita semper haec duo obiiciunt sapientes, primum de potestate ordinaria, hanc esse audiendam, nec dissentiendum ab eius iudicio et autoritate. Deinde aiunt afferri novam doctrinam ab hominibus ignotis, obscuris, sine testimonio, aut approbatione gubernatorum. Nam humana sapientia, sicut de regno Christi seu Ecclesia, ita de doctrina semper eodem modo iudicat, quaerit Ecclesiam, quae habeat testimonia et comprobationem principum, potentum, sapientum, etc. Contra, cum videt exiguum coetum sine autoritate et potentia, contemtum et spretum in mundo, offenditur, nec iudicat hunc esse populum Dei, quare nec doctri- nae assentitur: ita nunc plurimi repudiant doctri- nam Evangelii, moti similibus argumentis, quod non sit dissentiendum a publico consensu, et iu- dicio tot aetatum. Item quod haec doctrina non prodierit ab his, qui tenent gubernationem in Ec- clesia, et sunt in potestate ordinaria, ideo non esse recipiendam. Sed nos sciamus de doctrina coelesti non esse iudicandum ex humanis imaginationibus aut sa- pientia politica, de ordinaria potestate, aut con- sensu maioris partis multis seculis recepto, sed quaerenda esse vera testimonia verbi divinitus traditi. Teneamus hanc doctrinam, quam con- stat certo traditam esse a Prophetis, Christo et Apostolis, et confirmatam testimoniis miraculo- rum, nec moveamur diversis iudiciis aut conspi- ratione potentum et sapientum, quantumvis diu- turna. Videmus semper in mundo fuisse exi- guum coetum verae Ecclesiae, in quo mansit pu- ritas doctrinae. Nec novum est maiorem partem errare, et defendi εἰδωλομανίας et impiam doctri- nam ab his, qui sunt in ordinaria potestate, sicut in populo Israël Prophetae, Elias, Elisaeus, et alii coacti sunt sese palam opponere regibus et sa- cerdotibus defendentibus idololatriam. Et Iere- mias solus obstitit coetui Pontificum et Propheta- rum in tribu Iuda etc.

## 8:1 Argument
Chapter VIII.

Latin:

Caput VIII.

## 8:1
But Jesus went to the Mount of Olives.

Christ continues to teach in the temple: for although the feast had already passed, and he understands that he is being sought by the snares of the Pharisees, yet he remains for some time, so that he may both teach more people and confirm those who had heard him; he sees the people, like a flock wandering without a shepherd, having need of doctrine, wherefore the next morning he returns to the temple, not deterred by danger and snares. But before the remaining sermons and new altercations of the Jews with Christ are described, at the beginning the history of the adulterous woman brought to Christ is recited, which although the ancients, especially the Greeks, did not interpret, yet it appears it was always held among the received and approved. For Eusebius also mentions it, but citing from the Gospel according to the Hebrews. Certainly it does not seem to have been inserted rashly into this place, nor does any disturbance of the context appear, and in the style of the discourse it differs in nothing. And so it has been received by later writers without doubt.

He explains, however, the new frauds of the Pharisees, who when they see that their snares have not succeeded, nor do they find a cause so that they may openly attack Christ, now they seek something else, and eagerly seize an opportunity offered by chance; they produce the adulteress caught and convicted in the act, they set her before Christ, intending to make him the judge, they ask what he may answer, whether he wishes to condemn and order that she be stoned, which not even they themselves in this place and in this multitude would have dared to do, or to absolve, against the law, which ordered that adulterers and adulteresses be put to death. But they do not do this so that the adultery might be punished by a legitimate judgment, as it ought to have been. For they do not produce her to the judges to whom capital judgments were entrusted, but by conspiracy they lay snares for Christ, so that whatever he may answer, they may have something to accuse him of on either side. They had heard his sermon, which did not in the manner of the law condemn and repel sinners and the unworthy, but comforted the terrified and the miserable, and promised forgiveness; wherefore if he absolves this adulteress, and pronounces that she is not to be punished, they judge that they have a most just cause for atrocious slander, namely that he is much more worthy to be stoned than the miserable little woman, because he openly abolishes the Mosaic law, and grants license to sin with impunity. But if he condemns the woman, it would happen that he would completely alienate the multitude from himself. Because by this very act he would go against his own doctrine, and they do not think he will escape from these straits.

These are the customary Pharisaical snares, just as similar ones are described elsewhere. But Christ artfully repels the snares, and the history is altogether wonderful, which both hands down and depicts useful doctrine: and in the gesture and in the response of Christ there is something to be wondered at, and a singular counsel, just as everywhere in the evangelical history, in the deeds and speech of Christ, especially when he is attacked by the snares of hypocrites, certain singular and sharp movements and wonderfully conceived responses are discerned.

But the series of the history itself reveals the doctrine of this place. At the beginning when the woman is accused, Christ answers nothing, as if intent on another matter, namely, completely rejecting from himself this question, which pertains to the cognizance of the political magistrate. Afterwards when he is urged, he answers, not about the woman, but about the sins of those who were accusing her; but it is more wonderful that, sitting in the temple and bending down, he writes on the ground with his finger, and persists in this gesture for so long until they all go out of the temple; finally, turning to the woman, he denies that he is a judge who would condemn, but dismisses her, adding a word of pardon or remission of sin. which teaches about the distinction of ministries, namely, the ministry of the law, which sanctions discipline and corporal punishments, and the ministry which is proper to the Gospel; but I will speak of this distinction a little later, for first let this be considered, that Christ teaches by this example that it is not his office to pass sentences on the punishments of crimes, in the manner of a political magistrate, nor does he want those who are in the ministry of teaching the Gospel to take upon themselves the power or right of taking cognizance of capital actions, or other forensic or judicial business which pertains to political jurisdiction; for he wants ministries to be distinct, lest a carnal imagination creep in, as if the kingdom of Christ were an external or corporal dominion, or a polity which either passes new laws about empires, about the division of property, about contracts, about punishments, and civil discipline, or permits Christians the liberty of freeing themselves from the bonds of public laws. It is profitable to hold this rule for many reasons, that the kingdom of Christ does not establish or change political ordinances or laws. Because Christ did not appear to be a legislator, but brings other eternal benefits, heavenly doctrine about the will of God, about the remission of sins, the gift of the Holy Spirit, and the beginning of a new and eternal righteousness in the hearts of believers. Meanwhile, however, he grants the pious in this corporal life to use legitimate political ordinances, just as this light, air, food and drink, and similar things necessary for corporal life. Provided that the pious know that the kingdom of Christ is not situated in these things, but that the administration of political affairs must be distinguished from the ministry of the Gospel, and these ministries must not be confounded, as the Anabaptists and their like, under the pretext of ministry, criticize or change legitimate ordinances concerning tithes, contracts, or sanction new laws concerning the communion of property, concerning judgments, etc. Or as the Roman Pontiffs, under the pretext of ecclesiastical power, took royal dominion to themselves, arrogated to themselves the right of taking away kingdoms from whom they wished, and transferring them to others, etc. To these errors must be opposed this example of Christ, and similar sayings and deeds, by which Christ clearly refutes such imaginations and shows the distinctions and ends of the ministries, namely, of the spiritual ministry, or the doctrine of the Gospel, and of political government, as a similar example is written in Luke 12, when Christ, to someone asking that he order his brother to hand over to him a part of the inheritance, replies: Who has appointed me a judge or divider between you?

Secondly, that Christ writes on the ground, and to the pressing Pharisees replies: He who is without sin among you, let him be the first to throw a stone at the woman. Without doubt, by this whole gesture he notes the hypocrisy of the Pharisees, that they falsely put on a singular zeal, as if they greatly detested and hated sin, and wished it to be punished according to the law, when nevertheless they themselves are no less guilty before God and condemned by the judgment of the law than those who are openly and manifestly sinners, namely, because they are without repentance and fear of divine judgment, likewise full of interior uncleanness, vicious affections, and contumacy against the law: therefore Christ, omitting the woman, preaches to them. And when they pronounce from the law that the adulteress must be punished, he signifies in turn that they themselves are condemned by the law. Wherefore he says: If any of you is without sin, as if to say: Since you allege the law and require my sentence, I determine nothing about corporal punishment, because this does not pertain to my office; let the woman indeed be stoned according to the law, but because my ministry is spiritual, I order you to hear the law, which judges equally all who do not repent, and pronounces them guilty of wrath and eternal death. Let you acknowledge this first, and hear the law judging you, before you condemn this miserable woman.

He indicates this also by the gesture itself, when he writes on the ground, as if by a sign, namely, admonishing them of the interior hypocrisy of the judging law, and the uncleanness of the heart, which he silently signifies is seen and judged by God, even if men do not judge, just as elsewhere he preaches to such people: You are they who justify yourselves before men. But God knows your hearts. But that he writes on the ground, I think it is most simply signified that by a similar phrase in Jeremiah seventeen it is said: Those who depart from you shall be written in the earth, etc. Which phrase is opposite to that by which it is said elsewhere: Your names are written in heaven, namely, that to be written in the earth signifies that such people before God are not considered the people of God, even if they have the title and the name, and display a singular zeal or devotion to justice, but are guilty and condemned by the very sentence and judgment of the law. Thus, therefore, Christ by word and gesture interprets the law, as it were, and teaches that all men are condemned who are without repentance, and do not seek or receive the remission of sins from Christ by faith, etc.

If anyone should ask, since Christ replies to the Pharisees: He who is without sin among you, let him be the first to cast a stone at her. Is it not permitted for the guilty to be condemned or punished, except by those who are just and without sin? Who, therefore, shall be the ministers of the law? The answer is simple and easy: The magistrate or judge does not pronounce judgment or inflict penalties in a private capacity or in his own name, but is a minister of God, as Paul says, Rom. 13: That is, he exercises his office by divine command and authority, just as it is said in 2 Chron. 19: You do not exercise the judgment of man, but of God; therefore the magistrate acts rightly when he punishes adulterers or the guilty by legitimate judgment, even if he who is in office is neither pious nor otherwise free from reproach. For the vice of the person detracts nothing from the ministry.

Why, therefore, does Christ demand that they be without sin? I answer: Christ does not do this to lay down laws for the magistrate concerning the punishments of evildoers, but he uses a spiritual ministry against hypocrites; from the law he shows that they are no less guilty and to be condemned before God than this adulteress. He wants them to acknowledge this, lest they think themselves just or not condemned by the law of God, even if they cannot be accused of manifest crimes, but that they may know that they are condemned by the judgment of God for this very reason, that they seem to themselves to be without sin. Therefore, Christ pronounces this sentence of the law, by which all are judged who think themselves just by any observance of the discipline of the law, just as Paul shows in Rom. 2: that not even those who boast in the law or discipline keep the law.

Latin:

Iesus autem perrexit in montem Olivaram.

Pergit Christus docere in templo: etsi enim festum iam praeterierat, et intelligit se peti insi- diis Pharisaeorum, tamen manet aliquandiu, ut et plures doceat, et confirmet eos, qui ipsum au- dierant, videt populum, velut gregem errantem sine pastore, opus habere doctrina, quare postri- die mane redit in templum, non deterritus peri- culo ac insidiis. Sed priusquam reliquae concio- nes et novae altercationes Iudaeorum cum Christo describuntur, initio recitatur historia de muliere adultera adducta ad Christum, quam etsi veteres, praesertim Graeci, non sunt interpretati, tamen apparet semper habitam esse inter receptas et ap- probatas. Nam et Eusebius eius meminit, sed citans ex Evangelio secundum Ebraeos. Certe huic loco nec temere inserta videtur, nec aliqua contextus perturbatio apparet, et in genere ser- monis nihil discrepat. Itaque a posterioribus sine dubitatione recepta est.

Exponit autem novas fraudes Pharisaeorum, qui cum vident non successisse insidias, nec in- veniunt causam, ut Christum palam adoriantur, nunc aliud captant, et cupide arripiunt occasio- nem forte oblatam, adulteram manifesto depre- hensam, et convictam producunt, hanc sistunt Christo, ipsum facturi iudicem, quaerunt quid respondeat, damnare ne velit, et iubere ut lapi- detur, quod ne ipsi quidem hoc loco, et in hac multitudine ausi essent facere, an absolvere, con- tra legem, quae iubebat interfici moechos et adul- teras. Sed isti non hoc agunt, ut legitimo iudi- cio, sicut debebat, puniretur adulterium. Non enim producunt ad iudices, quibus erant mandata iudicia capitalia, sed ex composito insidiantur Christo, ut quicquid respondeat, in utramque partem habeant quod accusent. Audierant eius concionem, quae non more legis damnabat et re- pellebat peccatores et indignos, sed consolaba- tur perterrefactos et miseros, et promittebat con- donationem, quare si hanc adulteram absolvat, et pronunciet non esse puniendam, iudicant se habere iustissimam causam atrocis calumniae, vi- delicet hunc multo digniorem esse qui lapidetur, quam misera muliercula, quia palam aboleat le- gem Mosaicam, concedat licentiam impune pec- candi. Si vero mulierem condemnet, futurum esse ut multitudinem a sese prorsus abalienet. Quia hoc ipso facto contra eat suae doctrinae, nec existimant ex his angustiis evasurum esse.

Hae sunt usitatae insidiae pharisaicae, sicut et alibi similes describuntur. Sed Christus arte repellit insidias, et prorsus mirifica est historia, quae et doctrinam utilem tradit et pingit: et in gestu, et in responso Christi mirandum, et sin- gulare consilium, sicut passim in historia evan- gelica, in factis et oratione Christi, praesertim cum hypocritarum insidiis petitur, singulares quidam et acres motus et mirifice cogitata responsa cernuntur.

Sed doctrinam huius loci ipsa historiae se- ries aperit. Initio cum accusatur mulier, nihil respondet Christus, tanquam in aliam rem inten- tus, videlicet prorsus a sese reiiciens hanc quae- stionem, pertinentem ad cognitionem magistratus politici. Postea cum urgetur, respondet, non de muliere, sed de illorum peccatis, qui ipsam accusabant, sed mirabilius est, quod sedens in templo, et inclinans sese digito scribit in terram, et in hoc gestu perseverat tantisper, dum illi omnes egrediuntur e templo, tandem ad mulie- rem conversus, negat se esse iudicem qui con- demnet, sed dimittit eam, addita voce condona- tionis, seu remissionis peccati. In hac tota historia praecipuus locus est, qui docet de discrimine ministeriorum, videlicet mini- sterii legis, quod sancit disciplinam et poenas cor- porales, et ministerii, quod est proprium Evan- gelii, sed de hoc discrimine paulo post dicam, prius enim hoc consideretur, quod Christus hoc exemplo docet, non esse suum munus ferre sen- tentias de poenis delictorum, more politici magi- stratus, nec vult eos, qui sunt in ministerio do- cendi Evangelii sumere sibi potestatem seu ius cognoscendi actiones capitales, aut alia forensia seu iudicialia negotia, quae pertinent ad iuris- dictionem politicam, vult enim esse distincta mi- nisteria, ne obrepat carnalis imaginatio, quasi regnum Christi sit externa seu corporalis domina- tio, seu politia, quae aut ferat novas leges de im- periis, de divisione rerum, de contractibus, de poenis, et disciplina civili, aut permittat liberta- tem Christianis exsolvendi se vinculis publicarum legum. Hanc regulam multis de causis prodest te- nere, quod regnum Christi non condat aut mutet ordinationes seu leges politicas. Quia Christus non apparuit, ut esset legislator, sed affert alia aeterna beneficia, doctrinam coelestem de volun- tate Dei, de remissione peccatorum, donationem Spiritus sancti, et incoationem novae et aeternae iusticiae in cordibus credentium. Interim tamen concedit piis in hac vita corporali uti legitimis ordinationibus politicis, sicut hac luce, aëre, cibo et potu, et similibus rebus necessariis ad vitam corporalem. Modo sciant pii, in his non esse situm regnum Christi, sed discernendam esse ad- ministrationem politicarum rerum, a ministerio Evangelii, nec confundenda esse haec ministeria, sicut Anabaptistae et similes, praetextu ministe- rii, reprehendunt, aut mutant legitimas ordina- tiones de decimis, contractibus, aut novas leges sanciunt de communione rerum, de iudiciis, etc. Aut ut Pontifices Romani, praetextu potestatis ec- clesiasticae, sibi sumserunt regiam dominatio- nem, arrogarunt sibi ius adimendi regna, quibus vellent, et ad alios transferendi, etc. His erro- ribus opponendum est hoc exemplum Christi, et similia dicta et facta, quibus Christus clare refu- tat tales imaginationes, ac ostendit discrimina et fines ministeriorum, videlicet ministerii spiritua- lis, seu doctrinae Evangelii, et gubernationis po- liticae, ut simile exemplum Lucae 12. scribitur, cum Christus cuidam petenti, ut fratrem iubeat sibi tradere partem haereditatis, respondet: Quis me constituit iudicem aut divisorem inter vos?

Secundo, quod Christus scribit in terram, et instantibus Pharisaeis respondet: Qui ex vobis sine peccato est, primus iaciat lapidem in mulie- rem. Haud dubie hoc toto gestu notat Pharisaeo- rum hypocrisin, quod falso prae se ferant singu- larem zelum, quasi valde detestentur et oderint peccatum, ac iuxta legem velint esse punitum, cum tamen ipsi non minus sint rei coram Deo et damnati iudicio legis, quam qui palam et mani- festo sint peccatores, videlicet, quia sunt sine poenitentia et metu iudicii divini, item pleni in- teriori immunditia, vitiosis affectibus et contu- macia contra legem: igitur Christus omissa mu- liere ipsis concionatur. Cumque illi ex lege pro- nuncient, adulteram plectendam esse, vicissim significat ipsos lege damnari. Quare inquit: Si quis vestrum sine peccato est, quasi dicat: Quia legem allegatis, et meam sententiam requiritis, ego de poena corporali nihil statuo, quia hoc non pertinet ad meum munus, sit sane mulier secun- dum legem lapidanda, sed quia meum ministe- rium spirituale est, iubeo vos legem audire, quae ex aequo iudicat omnes, qui non agunt poeniten- tiam, et pronunciat reos irae et mortis aeternae. Hoc prius agnoscatis, et legem de vobis iudican- tem audiatis, quam miseram hanc mulierem con- demnetis.

Hoc et ipso gestu, cum scribit in terram, velut signo indicat, videlicet admonens eos legis iudicantis interiorem hypocrisin, et immunditiem cordis, quam tacite significat a Deo cerni et iudi- cari, etiamsi homines non iudicant, sicut alibi concionatur talibus: Vos estis qui iustificatis vos- metipsos coram hominibus. Deus autem novit corda vestra. Quod autem in terram scribit, simplicissime significari existimo, quod simili phrasi Ieremiae decimo septimo dicitur: Rece- dentes abs te, in terra scribentur, etc. Quae phrasis opposita est illi, qua alibi dicitur: No- mina vestra scripta sunt in coelis, videlicet ut in terram scribi, significet tales coram Deo non ha- beri pro populo Dei, etiamsi habeant titulum et nomen, ac prae se ferant singularem zelum, aut studium iusticiae, sed esse reos et damnatos ipsa sententia et iudicio legis. Sic ergo Christus dicto et gestu velut interpretatur legem, et docet dam- nari omnes homines, qui sunt sine poenitentia, nec quaerunt aut accipiunt remissionem peccato- rum a Christo fide, etc.

Si quis quaerat, cum Christus respondeat Pharisaeis: Qui ex vobis sine peccato est, primus iaciat lapidem in illam. An non licet condem- nari aut puniri sontes, nisi ab his qui sunt iusti et sine peccato? Qui ergo erunt legis ministri? Simplex et facilis responsio est: Magistratus, aut iudex non privato, seu suo ipsius nomine dicit ius, aut irrogat poenas, sed Dei minister est, sicut Paulus inquit, Rom. 13.: Hoc est, man- dato et autoritate divina exercet officium, sicut et 2. Paral. 19. dicitur: Non hominis iudicium exer- cetis, sed Dei, ideo recte facit magistratus, cum legitimo iudicio punit adulteros, aut nocentes, etiamsi is, qui est in officio, nec pius est, nec alioqui caret reprehensione. Nam personae vi- tium nihil derogat ministerio.

Quare igitur Christus postulat, ut sint sine peccato? Respondeo: Christus non hoc agit, ut magistratui leges ferat de poenis malefactorum, sed utitur ministerio spirituali adversus hypocri- tas, ex lege ostendit eos coram Deo non minus esse reos et damnandos, quam hanc adulteram, hoc vult illos agnoscere, ne putent sese iustos esse, aut non damnari lege Dei, etiamsi non pos- sint accusari manifestorum criminum, sed sciant se propter hoc ipsum iudicio Dei damnari, quod sibi videntur sine peccato esse. Ideo hanc sen- tentiam legis pronunciat Christus, qua iudican- tur omnes, qui sese existimant iustos esse quali- cunque observatione disciplinae legis, sicut ad Rom. 2. Paulus ostendit: ne eos quidem, qui gloriantur lege, seu disciplina, servare legem.

## 8:10
Where are your accusers? Has no one condemned you? etc.

Especially in this place, the sentence is to be observed, when Christ says to the woman: Neither do I condemn you, and indeed he adds the word of absolution: Go in peace. For these words clearly teach concerning the proper office of Christ, and distinguish the ministry of the law and the Gospel; Christ clearly denies that it pertains to his office to accuse, or to demand, or to inflict punishments, in the manner of the law or of the political magistrate, and not even to condemn those who have been condemned by the sentence of the law. Therefore, Christ is not a minister of the law, which pronounces a sentence of condemnation against all who have sinned, and denounces eternal and bodily punishments. And indeed, the magistrate performs a part of this ministry, punishing manifest crimes with bodily punishments, as it is said in Rom. 13: He is a minister of God, an avenger for wrath to him who does evil. But the proper ministry of condemnation is the very voice of the law, when it accuses and terrifies hearts, showing the eternal wrath of God and the punishment of eternal death: therefore it is called by Paul the ministry of death.

On the contrary, Christ clearly pronounces that he is not a minister of condemnation against those who, according to the law, have deserved the wrath of God or eternal and bodily punishments. But on the contrary, he testifies with a manifest voice that he brings a sentence of pardon, or remission of sins, to those who have been condemned by the law, when they feel the terrors of divine wrath and punishments. Therefore, in this example, a peculiar testimony of mercy, or of gratuitous pardon, is proposed. For he testifies that he freely remits the sins of the miserable woman, and indeed he signifies that the remission of sins is given by the external ministry of the voice of the Gospel, and that this is received by those who apply this voice to themselves by faith. This is the sweetest consolation for terrified consciences, which struggle with the sense of the wrath of God and eternal death. Meanwhile, however, those who have obtained the remission of sins are admonished that obedience is subsequently required, namely, that they take care not to continue to rush against the will of God, because to those who are justified by faith, the Holy Spirit is given at the same time, who is effective in those who do not resist, and begins a new obedience. Therefore, it is necessary for those who are converted to obey the Spirit, so that they may retain faith, and not lose the pardon, and cast out the Holy Spirit, as is often said elsewhere.

I am the light of the world.

The summary of the new discourse is recited very briefly, which undoubtedly was explained at length by Christ, as Evangelists are accustomed to often encompass lengthy discourses in a few words. Again, however, he discourses concerning his benefit, he shows what his office is, to which he was called and sent, and what he brings, so that he may invite the people to receive the doc- the doctrine of the Gospel, just as it was necessary for this sermon to be often repeated and inculcated, because this people, while they had the doctrine of the law and the Mosaic rites, did not think they had need of another doctrine; they thought they would be acceptable and righteous to God if they strove to perform the law and observe those rites handed down divinely, they did not think the Messiah… would bring another kind of doctrine. Therefore, when they heard these voices: I am the light of the world, if anyone thirsts, let him come to me, and similar ones, it was necessary that those who were the chief teachers of the people be greatly offended, and the wise governors from on high mocked both this teacher and the stupidity of the people who would listen to him preaching such absurd things, as they judged them, about himself, just as the Evangelist later narrates that it was objected to Christ by the Pharisees that his testimony is not true because he bears testimony about himself.

But Christ does not delay over these judgments; he knows that this doctrine, which he himself brings, does not agree with the opinions of human wisdom, which only understands the law in some way, yet does not see that it does not perform it, but that all men are accused and condemned by it. Christ has compassion on those immersed in this dense darkness and overwhelmed under the wrath of God and eternal death. Therefore, he inculcates these voices: I am the light of the world, he who follows me will not walk in darkness, etc. I said above, however, in these sermons, when Christ is called light, that he is distinguished far from the remaining teachers and ministers, just as in the 1st chapter the office of the Baptist is clearly distinguished from the person and office of Christ. Moses, the Fathers, the Prophets, the Apostles, although they are the chief members and lights of the Church, nevertheless are only ministers of the heavenly doctrine; they themselves do not create new light and life in the minds of man. But this Messiah is the illuminator, who not only brings doctrine from the heavenly Father, but is at the same time effective in the minds of those who assent to the Gospel, by the given Holy Spirit, kindling a new light, so that we may certainly conclude that for his sake the Father is appeased toward us, and we are received, and giving new and eternal righteousness and peace. These things can be said of no one else but the Son of God, wherefore he alone is rightly called the light of the world, that is, not just a minister, like others, and not even a teacher of the law, like Moses and the Levites, but he who himself effects new light and perpetual life in those who believe.

He speaks of this effect when he adds: He who follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life, that is, he will be gifted with true light and the knowledge of God, which will bring true consolation, by which he will overcome terrors and be liberated from eternal death. In order that these sayings may be understood more clearly, the antithesis must again be considered; let both these be compared, both the doctrine of the law and of the Gospel, and the effect of each; although men naturally have some knowledge of the law, and the law had been handed down to the people of Israel by singular revelation and heavenly testimony, nevertheless this knowledge does not bring light, it does not liberate from the darkness and gloom in which the human race is immersed. Human minds, when they have heard the law and perform external and bodily discipline, and add some rites of works, think that this study and imitation of the law, whatever it may be, is righteousness before God; they do not see nor acknowledge that they themselves and this whole nature are immersed in sin, polluted with interior and exterior impurity, guilty of the wrath of God and eternal death; for these the face of Moses is completely veiled, and they are involved in the thickest darkness and errors; they do not at all understand or feel the power of the law, without the knowledge of the will of God, without repentance; blind and secure, they rush into manifest contempt of God and impiety. In certain others, although the law exercises its power when it shows and convicts of sin, nevertheless even here it effects nothing except the terrors of the wrath of God and eternal death: it does not show how doubt and dreads are to be overcome. Finally, if no other light approaches which shows liberation, minds are driven to despair and rush into eternal death, etc.

Christ, the Son of God, sees and understands this misery of the human race. Therefore, from the beginning he published the promise of the Gospel, unknown to reason, and later he himself handed it down by his own voice and commanded it in the Church, which teaches that those terrified by the law and doing penance are received by God and obtain the remission of sins by faith, freely, on account of this very Son of God the propitiator, and by this faith or trust in the Son of God are pronounced righteous, that is, accepted and pleasing to God, and become heirs of eternal life; and indeed by the ministry of this voice, which he ordered to be spread in the Church, he himself is effective, by the given Holy Spirit, who moves hearts so that they assent to the Gospel, and when they receive the promise with faith, hearts are raised up and vivified, so that they overcome terrors and conclude that they are now truly received by God. Wherefore the Holy Spirit now effects in them new motions, which are the beginning of a new and eternal life. A new light is kindled, and the recognition of the mercy and benefits of God is increased; faith grows and is exercised in invocation, in confession, and in obedience in the cross and afflictions, and together with faith, love also exists, and the other virtues come into being. Thus, the law is already begun in these, but meanwhile, by faith, they determine that they are pronounced righteous, and are certainly heirs of eternal life, not because of these begun virtues, but because of Christ, because these virtues are still far removed from this perfection which the law requires: these things are done only by the ministry of the Gospel, and the efficacy or power of this Messiah, the Son of God. Wherefore he alone is the light of the world, truly effecting in believers a new light, which frees minds from doubt and terrors, and consoles and vivifies hearts, so that perpetual righteousness and life may truly be begun in them. Christ therefore refutes by this statement the Pharisaical opinion concerning the law and the righteousness of the law; he teaches that, apart from the recognition of the Gospel, the whole human race lies oppressed by eternal darkness, without true recognition of God, without consolation, and is not liberated except by the recognition of this Messiah, concerning whom promises had been published, that he would bring a new word, and through it would be efficacious, and would give the Holy Spirit, a new light and life, just as the Prophets often use this very word of light concerning the kingdom of the Messiah, and signify that Christ, by the new ministry of the heavenly voice, would be efficacious, so that minds might be liberated from gloom and darkness, that is, from doubt and despair, from which they cannot be liberated by the law.

Christ signifies that he applies these benefits to us, and that they are received by faith, when he says: He who follows me. For just as he is called light, not because he is merely a teacher, but because he is the giver and effector of new light and life. Thus, when he commands us to follow him, he does not speak only of imitation, such as that of the doctrine of the law or of virtues, the examples of which shine in a teacher, but he speaks of faith, which apprehends this benefit which Christ brings, that is, it determines for itself that by the power of Christ, and on account of him, light, righteousness, and eternal life are given.

The Jews therefore said: You bear witness of yourself, etc.

Again, the struggles of the Pharisees with Christ are described, which indeed are intensified more and more until the end of this chapter, and they depict the form of the Church, which must always be conflicted by the hatreds and calumnies of the impious, and they confirm and console the pious, so that they may not be broken in spirit on account of such judgments and calumnies, but may know that the heavenly doctrine delivered by Christ shines forth all the more among these struggles, and remains invincible.

But the Pharisees, first of all offended by so magnificent and, as it seemed, arrogant a discourse, attempt to refute Christ by opposing a grave argument in appearance, concerning the authority of testimony, which certainly holds weight in human judgments: No one is believed when testifying about himself, without the testimonies of others, and every appearance of arrogance diminishes the authority of the teacher; wherefore the objection of the Pharisees is grave, when they say: You bear witness of yourself, therefore your testimony is not true: and certainly the matter is so; the doctrine of the Gospel does not agree with the judgment of reason, it does not have the testimonies or endorsements of the wise, the powerful, or the multitude. Wherefore, with great appearance, its authority and credibility are detracted from; the wise cry out that a doctrine recently brought forth by one or another, without proven authors, dissenting from the received consensus approved by many centuries, is not to be heard. Thus the Pharisees oppose the doctrine and rites delivered by Moses with huge divine miracles, and the testimony of the whole people, who were spectators when the law was promulgated, which, since it has such illustrious testimonies, means that another teacher who arrogates to himself authority equal to Moses is not to be heard, when no similar testimonies appear.

It was necessary to answer this objection, and Christ refutes it in two ways. First, he speaks of his vocation, that this is truly divine; then he adds concerning the testimonies, namely, of the word of God and of miracles. For he first answers the consequence of the proposed argument. He denies that his testimony or doctrine is false for that reason, even if it does not rely on human testimonies or judgments; then he answered the antecedent, that he has divine testimonies. In the former member of the refutation, he alleges his vocation, that he was sent by God, and has the command of the eternal Father, which he inculcates everywhere in these discourses, as above in chapter 7: My doctrine is not mine, but his who sent me; and below he will say: I do nothing of myself, but as the Father taught me, so I speak.

Thus also here he says: Even if I bear witness of myself, my testimony is true, because I know whence I came, and whither I go, as if to say: I do not do my own business, but I bring a heavenly command, and I carry out the office committed to me by God, namely, that I may deliver this word, which truly reveals the will of God, how he wishes to be acknowledged, how one may arrive at him. I know for certain that this word is his own mandate, wherefore I teach truly and rightly, nor do I care for the judgments of the world or of you, who cannot testify concerning me, because my calling is unknown to you, nor do you acknowledge the mandate of the eternal Father. Therefore your argumentation concerning human testimonies is of no value, nor are you to be heard, when you take upon yourselves the judgment concerning doctrine. Thus he both defends the authority of the doctrine or of the office entrusted to him, and refutes the objection of those seeking human testimonies, and takes away from them the right of judging concerning an unknown doctrine.

This refutation can therefore be included in two syllogisms, of which the one dissolves the objection concerning testimony, in this way. The testimony of him who has a calling and a mandate for his office or doctrine is true. Therefore I know whence I was sent, and I bring a heavenly mandate, therefore you falsely condemn my testimony. The other syllogism is an exception against these judges. Let no one take upon himself the judgment concerning an unknown matter. You do not know him by whom I was sent, and whose mandate I bring, therefore it is not for you to judge concerning the doctrine.

This refutation is to be considered for this reason, because it delivers useful rules. The first is that the judgment concerning the doctrine of the Church does not depend upon human authority or approval. The second is concerning the calling. It is necessary for the Church to have the testimony of a heavenly calling and mandate concerning doctrine, namely, that we may be certain that this doctrine is truly the word of God. The doctrine of the Gospel is unknown, as has often been said already, to the wisdom of the world, and it disagrees with the judgment of reason. Wherefore it cannot be decided by human judgments, nor is that adjudication of any value which is made (as in other controversies concerning matters subject to the judgment of reason) from the suffrage or consent of the greater part of those who are thought to excel in wisdom, authority, judgment, etc.

It is necessary therefore that the certainty of the doctrine be sought from elsewhere, namely, that it be established concerning the calling, that the doctrine has been delivered by the mandate of God, and has true testimonies, thence even from the beginning of the Church, by which God testifies that this is a heavenly doctrine, even if the testimonies or authority of men do not approach.

Therefore, although boasting seems inept and unworthy of a wise man, and elsewhere that which is commanded, let another man praise you, etc., has its place, nevertheless for the ministry of the Gospel the boasting of a divine calling is necessary, so that it may be established that the doctrine which is delivered certainly has the mandate of God, just as Peter says: If any man speak, let him speak as the oracles of God, for this cause, and Christ everywhere in the Gospel sounds these voices: He that believeth in me, believeth not in me, but in him that sent me. Likewise: I have not spoken of myself, but the Father who sent me, he gave me a commandment etc. And Paul alleges a heavenly calling, so that it may be established that he brings a doctrine delivered by God, and that it is the mandate of God that we should assent to it.

The other part of the refutation is taken from the sentence of the law, and answers the antecedent of the objection of the Pharisees. The law says that the testimony of two is valid. For thus the text says, Deut. 19: In the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word be established: I bear testimony concerning the doctrine, and the testimony of the Father approaches, therefore these testimonies are to be believed. It is a clever piece of reasoning, and the minor premise, although it could have been eluded before, nevertheless now is valid, after he has shown in the former member of the refutation that his doctrine is true, brought from heaven, etc. But what he says: that the Father testifies concerning himself, let it be understood to embrace both, namely the testimony of the word of God and of miracles.

Concerning the former, the sayings of the Prophets are often alleged, and in John 5 it was said: Search the scriptures, for they are they which testify of me. Likewise: If you believed Moses, you would believe me also, for he wrote of me. The testimony of John is also alleged, to whom that admirable revelation was shown, in which the whole divinity exhibited itself in a visible form, and the voice of the eternal Father sounded openly from heaven, testifying concerning the Son: This is my beloved Son, etc. To these testimonies of scripture, and of the divine voice, he looks both here and elsewhere, when he says that he was sent by the Father. For there are promises concerning Christ published before in the scriptures and by the voice of the Prophets and of the Baptist. Then, with these testimonies, miracles also agree, which were both performed and are alleged by Christ, for the purpose of confirming the faith of the pious that this is the Messiah the Son of God, sent by the Father according to the promises. Because it is established that these miracles are performed only by divine power, just as he himself says: What things soever the Father doeth, these also doeth the Son likewise. But concerning these testimonies, it has been said elsewhere, as above in chapter 5.

I judge no one.

What Christ says, rejecting the judgment of the Pharisees, I judge no one, and if I do judge, my judgment is true, he speaks in the way in which he often does elsewhere regarding the proper and principal cause of his mission; he denies that he was sent to judge, because he does not bring the word of the law, which judges hearts, accuses and condemns all men, but he has another ministry, which shows how men may be freed from wrath and from condemnation, and be saved, namely, if they receive by faith the reconciliation promised on account of the Son of God himself, and yet he adds, if he does judge, that his judgment is true. Because just as now that the Gospel is revealed, those who believe are saved, nor does the law have the right to condemn them, so conversely a sentence has been passed, and remains irrevocable: that no one who does not believe is saved, and that all who despise the Son of God are now rightly condemned. Therefore he says elsewhere: I came into this world for judgment, etc.

Latin:

Ubi sunt accusatores tui? Nemo te condem- navit? etc.

Praecipue in hoc loco observanda est senten- tia, cum Christus ait mulieri: Nec ego te con- demno, et quidem addit vocem absolutionis: Vade in pace. Nam haec dicta perspicue docent de pro- prio officio Christi, et discernunt ministerium le- gis et Evangelii, clare negat Christus pertinere ad suum officium accusare, aut deposcere, seu infli- gere poenas, more legis, aut magistratus politici, ac ne eos quidem damnare, qui sententia legis damnati sunt. Quare Christus non est minister legis, quae pronunciat sententiam damnationis adversus omnes, qui peccarunt, et denunciat poenas aeternas et corporales. Et quidem par- tem huius ministerii gerit magistratus, puniens manifesta delicta corporalibus poenis, sicut dici- tur Rom. 13.: Dei minister est vindex in iram ei, qui male agit. Sed proprium ministerium condemnationis est ipsa vox legis, cum accusat, et perterrefacit corda, ostendens aeternam iram Dei, et poenam mortis aeternae: ideo vocatur a Paulo ministerium mortis.

Econtra Christus clare pronunciat, se non esse ministrum condemnationis adversus hos, qui iuxta legem meriti sunt iram Dei, aut aeternas et corporales poenas. Sed contra, manifesta voce testatur se afferre sententiam condonationis, seu remissionis peccatorum his, qui lege damnati sunt, cum sentiunt terrores irae divinae et poe- narum. Proponitur ergo in hoc exemplo pecu- liare testimonium misericordiae, seu condonatio- nis gratuitae. Testatur enim se gratis remittere peccata miserae mulieri, et quidem significat ex- terno ministerio vocis Evangelii dari remissionem peccatorum, et hanc accipi ab his, qui fide sibi hanc vocem applicant. Haec est dulcissima con- solatio perterrefactis conscientiis, quae luctantur cum sensu irae Dei, et mortis aeternae. Interim tamen admonentur hi, qui consecuti sunt remis- sionem peccatorum, deinceps requiri obedien- tiam, videlicet, ut caveant ne pergant ruere contra voluntatem Dei, quia his, qui iustifican- tur fide, simul datur Spiritus sanctus, qui est ef- ficax in non repugnantibus, et incoat novam obe- dientiam. Quare necesse est, eos qui sunt con- versi, obsequi spiritui, ut retineant fidem, nec amittant condonationem, et excutiant Spiritum sanctum, ut saepe alias dicitur.

Ego sum lux mundi.

Brevissime recitatur summa novae concionis, quae haud dubie copiose explicata est a Christo, ut solent Evangelistae prolixas conciones saepe paucis verbis complecti. Rursus autem concio- natur de suo beneficio, ostendit quod sit suum munus, ad quod vocatus et missus erat, et quid afferat, ut invitet populum ad accipiendam do- ctrinam Evangelii, sicut necesse fuit hanc con- cionem saepe repeti et inculcari, quia hic popu- lus, cum haberet doctrinam legis et cultus Mo- saicos, non existimabat se opus habere alia do- ctrina, putabant se ita Deo acceptos et iustos fore, si conarentur legem praestare et illos cul- tus divinitus traditos servare, non cogitabant Messiam allaturum aliud doctrinae genus. Ideo cum audierunt has voces: Ego sum lux mundi, si quis sitit, veniat ad me, et similes, necesse fuit valde offendi eos, qui erant praecipui docto- res populi, et sapientes gubernatores ex sublimi deriserunt et hunc doctorem, et stultitiam po- puli, qui eum audiret tam absurda, ut ipsi iudi- cabant, de sese praedicantem, sicut postea Evan- gelista narrat obiici Christo a Pharisaeis, quod eius testimonium non sit verum, quia testimo- nium perhibeat de se ipso.

Sed haec iudicia Christus non moratur, scit hanc doctrinam, quam ipse affert, non congruere cum opinionibus humanae sapientiae, quae tan- tum legem aliquo modo intelligit, nec tamen vi- det se eam non praestare, sed ab ea accusari et damnari omnes homines. Hac densa caligine de- mersos et obrutos sub ira Dei, et morte aeterna, miseratur Christus. Ideo has voces inculcat: Ego sum lux mundi, qui sequitur me, non am- bulabit in tenebris, etc. Dixi autem supra in his concionibus cum Christus vocatur lux, longe discerni hunc a reliquis doctoribus et ministris, ut clare in 1. cap. discernitur Baptistae munus a persona et officio Christi. Moses, Patres, Pro- phetae, Apostoli, etsi sunt praecipua membra et lumina Ecclesiae, tamen tantum sunt ministri doctrinae coelestis, non efficiunt ipsi novam lu- cem et vitam in mentibus hominis. Sed hic Messias est illuminator, qui non solum doctri- nam affert a patre coelesti, sed simul est efficax in mentibus eorum, qui assentiuntur Evangelio, dato Spiritu sancto, accendens novam lucem, ut certo statuamus propter ipsum nobis placari pa- trem, et nos recipi, et dans novam et aeternam iusticiam et pacem. Haec de nemine alio, quam de filio Dei dici possunt, quare solus recte voca- tur lux mundi, hoc est, non tantum minister, ut alii, et ne quidem doctor legis, ut Moses et Le- vitae, sed qui ipse efficit novam lucem et per- petuam vitam in his, qui credunt.

De hoc effectu loquitur, cum addit: Qui se- quitur me, non ambulabit in tenebris, sed habe- bit lumen vitae, id est, donabitur vera luce et agnitione Dei, quae afferet veram consolationem, qua vincet terrores, liberabitur a morte aeterna. Haec dicta ut clarius intelligantur, rursus consi- deranda est antithesis, conferantur haec ambo, et doctrina legis ac Evangelii, et utriusque effe- ctus, etsi homines naturaliter habent aliquam no- ticiam legis, et populo Israël singulari revela- tione et testimonio coelesti tradita erat lex, tamen haec noticia non affert lucem, non liberat a cali- gine et tenebris, quibus immersum est genus hu- manum. Mentes humanae, cum audierunt le- gem, et praestant disciplinam externam et corpo- ralem, et addunt aliquos cultus operum, putant hoc qualecunque studium et imitationem legis, esse iusticiam coram Deo, non vident nec agno- scunt, sese et hanc totam naturam esse immer- sam peccato, pollutam interiore et exteriore im- munditia, ream irae Dei et mortis aeternae, his prorsus velata est facies Mosi, et versantur in crassissimis tenebris et erroribus, prorsus non in- telligunt nec sentiunt vim legis, sine agnitione voluntatis Dei, sine poenitentia, caeci et securi ruunt manifesto contemtu Dei, et impietate. In aliis quibusdam, etsi lex exercet suam vim, cum ostendit et arguit peccatum, tamen hic etiam ni- hil efficit, nisi terrores irae Dei, et mortis aeter- nae: non ostendit, quomodo vincatur dubitatio et pavores. Denique si non accedit alia lux, quae monstrat liberationem, adiguntur mentes ad de- sperationem, et ruunt in aeternam mortem, etc.

Hanc miseriam generis humani videt et in- telligit Christus filius Dei. Ideo ab initio edidit promissionem Evangelii, ignotam rationi, et eam postea ipse sua voce tradidit, et mandavit in Ec- clesia, quae docet perterrefactos lege et agentes poenitentiam, recipi a Deo, et consequi remis- sionem peccatorum fide, Gratis, propter hunc ipsum filium Dei propiciatorem, et hac fide seu fiducia filii Dei pronunciari iustos, hoc est, acce- ptos et placentes Deo, et fieri haeredes vitae ae- ternae, et quidem ministerio huius vocis, quam iussit spargi in Ecclesia, ipse est efficax, dato Spi- ritu sancto, qui movet corda, ut assentiantur Evangelio, et cum fide accipiunt promissionem, eriguntur corda et vivificantur, ut vineant ter- rores, ac statuant se iam vere receptos esse a Deo. Quare Spiritus sanctus iam efficit in eis novos mo- tus, qui sunt incoatio novae et aeternae vitae, Accenditur nova lux, et augetur agnitio miseri- ordiae et beneficiorum Dei, crescit et exercetur fides in invocatione, in confessione, et obedientia in cruce et afflictionibus, et cum fide simul etiam dilectio, et caeterae virtutes existunt. Ita iam in his incoatur lex, sed interim fide statuunt se iu- stus pronunciari, et certo esse haeredes vitae ae- ternae, non propter has incoatas virtutes, sed propter Christum, quia hae virtutes adhuc pro- cul absunt ab hac perfectione, quam lex requirit: haec tantum fiunt ministerio Evangelii, et effi- cacia seu potentia huius Messiae filii Dei. Quare hic solus est lux mundi, vere efficiens in creden- tibus novam lucem, quae liberat mentes a dubi- tatione et terroribus, et consolatur ac vivificat corda, ut vere incoëtur in ipsis perpetua iusticia et vita. Refutat ergo Christus hoc dicto opinio- nem pharisaicam de lege et iusticia legis, docet citra agnitionem Evangelii totum genus humanum iacere oppressum aeternis tenebris, sine vera agnitione Dei, sine consolatione, nec liberari nisi agnitione huius Messiae, de quo editae erant promissiones, quod esset allaturus novum ver- bum, et per illud futurus efficax, daturus Spiri- tum sanctum, novam lucem ac vitam, sicut saepe Prophetae hac ipsa voce lucis de regno Messiae utuntur, et significant Christum novo ministerio vocis coelestis fore efficacem, ut liberentur men- tes a caligine et tenebris, hoc est, a dubitatione et desperatione, a qua non possunt liberari lege.

Haec beneficia Christus significat sese nobis applicare, et accipi fide, cum ait: Qui sequitur me. Nam sicut lux dicitur, non quia tantum sit doctor, sed quia dator et effector est novae lucis et vitae. Ita cum se sequi iubet, non tantum loquitur de imitatione, qualis est doctrinae legis seu virtutum, quarum exempla lucent in doctore, sed loquitur de fide, quae apprehendit hoc bene- ficium, quod affert Christus, hoc est, statuit sibi potentia Christi, et propter ipsum donari lucem, iusticiam et vitam aeternam.

Dicebant igitur Iudaei: Tu de teipso, etc.

Rursus describuntur certamina Pharisaeorum cum Christo, quae quidem magis, ac magis in- tenduntur usque ad finem huius capitis, et pin- gunt formam Ecclesiae, quam necesse est semper conflictari odiis et calumniis impiorum, et con- firmant, ac consolantur pios, ne propter talia iudicia, et calumnias frangantur animis, sed sciant doctrinam coelestem traditam a Christo in- ter haec certamina magis elucescere, et manere invictam.

Primum autem Pharisaei offensi tam magni- fica, et ut videbatur, arroganti concione, conan- tur refutare Christum, opposito gravi argumento in speciem, de autoritate testimonii, quod certe valet in iudiciis humanis: Nemini creditur de seipso praedicanti, sine aliorum testimoniis, et elevat autoritatem docentis, omnis arrogantiae species, quare gravis est obiectio Pharisaeorum, cum aiunt: Tu de teipso testimonium dicis, igi- tur testimonium dicis, igitur testimonium tuum non est verum: ac certe ita se res habet, doctri- na Evangelii non congruit cum iudicio rationis, non habet testimonia aut suffragationes sapientum, potentum, multitudinis. Quare magna specie detrahitur ei autoritas et fides, clamant sapientes, non esse audiendam doctrinam recens ab uno et altero prolatam, sine probatis autoribus, dissen- tientem a recepto, et multis seculis approbato consensu. Sic Pharisaei opponunt doctrinam et ritus traditos a Mose ingentibus miraculis divinis, et testimonio totius populi, qui fuit spectator, cum lex promulgaretur, quae cum habeat tam illustria testimonia, non esse audiendum alium doctorem, qui sibi arroget autoritatem parem Mosi, cum nulla appareant similia testimonia.

Huic obiectioni necesse erat respondere, et Christus eam dupliciter refutat. Primum de sua vocatione dicit, quod haec sit vere divina, de- inde addit de testimoniis, videlicet verbi Dei et miraculorum. Prius enim respondet ad con- sequentiam propositi argumenti. Negat ideo suum testimonium seu doctrinam falsam esse, etiamsi non nitatur testimoniis aut iudiciis huma- nis, deinde ad antecedens respondebat, se habere testimonia divina. In priori membro refutatio- nis allegat vocationem, quod sit missus a Deo, et habeat mandatum aeterni patris, quod passim in his concionibus inculcat, ut supra capite 7.: Mea doctrina non est mea, sed eius qui misit me; et infra dicet: A meipso facto nihil, sed sicut docuit me pater, sic loquor.

Ita et hic ait: Etsi testimonium perhibeo de meipso, testimonium meum verum est, quia scio unde veni, et quo vado, quasi dicat: Non ago meum negotium, sed affero mandatum coeleste, et gero munus mihi commissum a Deo, videlicet, ut tradam hoc verbum, quod vere patefacit vo- luntatem Dei, quomodo velit agnosci, quomodo perveniatur ad ipsum. Hoc verbum certo scio esse ipsius mandatum, quare vere et recte doceo, nec moror mundi aut vestra iudicia, qui de me non potestis testari, quia ignota est vobis mea vocatio, nec agnoscitis mandatum aeterni patris. Itaque non valet vestra argumentatio de testimo- niis humanis, nec estis audiendi, cum sumitis vobis iudicium de doctrina. Ita simul et tuetur autoritatem doctrinae seu muneris sibi mandati, et refutat obiectionem quaerentium humana testi- monia, et detrahit eis ius iudicandi de doctrina ignota.

Potest igitur haec refutatio includi duobus syllogismis, quorum alter diluit obiectionem de testimonio, hoc modo. Verum est testimonium eius, qui habet vocationem et mandatum sui mu- neris seu doctrinae. Ergo scio unde missus sim, et affero coeleste mandatum, ergo falso meum testimonium damnatis. Alter syllogismus est ex- ceptio contra hos iudices. Nemo sumat sibi iudi- cium de re ignota. Vos non nostis eum a quo missus sum, et cuius affero mandatum, ergo non est vestrum iudicare de doctrina.

Haec refutatio ideo consideranda est, quia tradit utiles regulas. Prima est quod iudicium de doctrina Ecclesiae non pendeat ab autoritate vel approbatione humana. Altera de vocatione. Necesse est Ecclesiam habere testimonium voca- tionis et mandati coelestis de doctrina, videlicet, ut certi simus, hanc doctrinam vere esse verbum Dei. Ignota est, ut saepe iam dictum est, do- ctrina Evangelii sapientiae mundi, et discrepat a iudicio rationis. Quare de ea non potest de- cerni humanis iudiciis, nec valet diiudicatio, quae fit (ut in aliis controversiis de rebus subiectis iudicio rationis) ex suffragatione aut consensu ma- ioris partis eorum, qui existimantur praestare sa- pientia, autoritate, iudicio, etc.

Necesse est igitur aliunde peti certitudinem doctrinae, videlicet, ut constet de vocatione, quod doctrina sit tradita mandato Deo, et habeat vera testimonia, inde usque ab initio Ecclesiae, quibus Deus testetur hanc esse doctrinam coele- stem, etiamsi non accedant testimonia aut auto- ritas hominum.

Ideo etsi videtur inepta et indigna sapiente gloriatio, et alibi suum locum habet illud, quod praecipitur, praedicet te os alienum etc., tamen ministerio Evangelii necessaria est gloriatio voca- tionis divinae, ut constet doctrinam, quae tradi- tur, certo habere mandatum Dei, sicut Petrus in- quit: Qui loquitnr, loquatur tanquam sermones Dei, propter hanc causam, et Christus passim in Evangelio sonat has voces: Qui credit in me, non credit in me, sed in eum, qui me misit. Item: Ego non ex me ipso sum locutus, sed qui misit me, pater, is mihi mandatum dedit etc. Et Pau- lus allegat vocationem coelestem, ut constet eum afferre doctrinam traditam a Deo, et esse man- datum Dei, ut illi assentiamur.

Altera pars refutationis sumta est ex senten- tia legis, et respondet ad antecedens obiectionis Pharisaeorum. Lex ait, duorum testimonium valere. Sic enim inquit textus, Deut. 19.: In ore duorum aut trium testium stabiliatur omne verbum: ego testimonium perhibeo de doctrina, et accedit testimonium patris, ergo his testimo- niis credendum est. Arguta ratiocinatio est, et minor, etsi ante eludi poterat, tamen nunc valet, postquam in priore membro refutationis ostendit suam doctrinam esse veram, allatam e coelo, etc. Quod autem ait: Patrem testari de sese, intelli- gatur utrunque complecti, videlicet testimonium verbi Dei et miraculorum.

De priore saepe allegantur Prophetarum di- cta, et Ioan. 5. dictum est: Scrutamini scriptu- ras, ipsae enim sunt, quae testimonium perhi- bent de me. Item: Si crederetis Mosi, credere- tis etiam mihi, de me enim ille scripsit. Allega- tur etiam testimonium Ioannis, cui ostensa est illa admiranda revelatio, in qua se visibili specie exhibuit tota divinitas, et palam sonuit de coelo vox aeterni patris, testantis de filio: Hic est filius meus dilectus, etc. Ad haec testimonia scriptu- rae, et vocis divinae, respicit et hic et alibi, cum ait, se missum esse a patre. Sunt enim ante in scripturis et voce Prophetarum et Baptistae, edi- tae promissiones de Christo. Deinde cum his testimoniis congruunt etiam miracula, quae et edita sunt, et allegantur a Christo, ideo ut con- firment fidem piorum, hunc esse Messiam filium Dei, missum a patre iuxta promissiones. Quia haec miracula constat fieri tantum divina poten- tia, sicut ipse ait: Quae pater facit, similiter et filius facit. Sed de his testimoniis et alibi, ut supra cap. 5. dictum est.

Ego non iudico quenquam.

Quod ait Christus, reiiciens iudicium Pha- risaeorum, Ego non iudico quenquam, et si iu- dico, iudicium meum verum est, loquitur eo modo, quo saepe alias de propria et principali causa suae missionis, negat se missum esse, ut iudicet, quia affert non verbum legis, quod iudi- cat corda, accusat et damnat omnes homines, sed habet aliud ministerium, quod ostendit quomodo liberentur homines ab ira et a damnatione, et salvi fiant, videlicet, si fide accipiant reconcilia- tionem promissam propter ipsum filium Dei, et tamen addit, si iudicet, suum iudicium verum esse. Quia sicut iam revelato Evangelio, hi qui credunt salvantur, nec lex habet ius eos con- demnandi, ita contra lata est, et manet irrevoca- bilis sententia: neminem salvari non credentem, et iam iure condemnari omnes qui contemnunt filium Dei. Ideo alibi ait: In iudicium in hunc mundum veni, etc.

## 8:19
The Jews said to him: Where is your father?

The Jews, in order to evade the response concerning the testimony, ask about the father, where he is, as if they were saying: You cite the testimony of the father very splendidly indeed, who is both absent and unknown; come now, if you demand to be believed, present the father to us in person, so that we may hear him testifying about you. This is a calumnious and virulent mockery, such as are the voices of the impious, who, driven by the devil by hatred of the truth, boldly exert blasphemous tongues against the open testimonies of miracles, but Christ answers gravely concerning the father: If you had known me, you would have known my father also. This is the simplest meaning: that they would then finally understand concerning the father, that he truly testifies about this Messiah, if they believe his voice and the miracles by which he shows and proves that he was sent by the eternal father; wherefore by this saying he recalls them to the testimony of the word of God and of miracles: he teaches that for this purpose, that God may be acknowledged, faith is required, or assent to the doctrine handed down divinely by the voice of the Fathers and Prophets concerning this Messiah, and that one cannot rightly judge concerning the will of God unless one first assents to this word, much as he said above: If anyone wishes to do the will of my father, he will know about the doctrine.

But this saying also embraces a broader doctrine concerning the acknowledgment of the secret will of God, about which it is said elsewhere, and will be repeated often below.
