Concerning the first point he has spoken thus far: The Jews are offended by the doctrine of Christ for this reason, because they judge that from it follows the dissolution of that polity divinely established, which they thought ought to be perpetual, and that the Messiah would come in order to restore it, and render it far more flourishing, increased by the empire of the world, and by huge corporal glory. But

Christ denies that he has come to establish a polity or a corporal kingdom: he says that he is not of this world, but that he was sent so that he might become a victim, and only then would they be safe, if they believe his voice, because truly they do not want to agree, it will come to pass that all that polity is overturned. This was the first offense. The second is not lighter in the question which is agitated here concerning religion, or worships; here they fight, lest religion and worship be undermined, concerning which they were especially boasting that the law and Mosaic rites had been divinely handed down to them, and that this religion had been preserved in this people by a singular benefit of God from then all the way from Moses and the fathers. Therefore they are more gravely offended because Christ says: Not on account of the law and those worships are men freed from sin, and pleasing to God, but he affirms them to be under sin and the wrath of God. Here therefore arises a long and atrocious struggle. But before this is settled, a third conflict approaches, which is the hardest of all, concerning the person of the Messiah, when he says that he is the Son of God, who has existed from eternity; they judge this to be blasphemy, to be refuted not by arguments, but by stones.

I have briefly recited the sum of the topics which are agitated in this whole sermon up to the end of the chapter; now I return to the text, when Christ commands them to persevere in faith, and thus promises liberty, if they believe his word. The Jews oppose a response concerning the law, and the doctrine of religion, received from the fathers, and up to this point preserved in the people of God. They argue that they are the seed of Abraham and the fathers, to whom had been given the promises concerning the posterity and the people in whom the Messiah would be born.

That these promises had always been valid, and that it was necessary that this polity be preserved, and the doctrine of religion, and the worships handed down by Moses, on account of the coming Messiah, who is to be the lord of this people, and is to bring a perpetual kingdom. That this liberty had remained intact for them up to this point, because they had never been forced by violence or foreign empire to cast away their religion, and their laws, not even in the Babylonian exile; nay, even then, when they were forced to bear the Roman empire, they nevertheless retained their autonomy, they defended their religion, and lived by their own laws, and this very confidence of liberty, conceived from the promises concerning the Messiah, animated them so that they hoped they would shake off this bridle of the Roman empire.

Wherefore they confidently explode the voice of Christ, when he says: The truth will set you free, they do not suffer themselves to be called servants because they hold the religion, worship, and polity handed down divinely, and they reason that God by this very benefit of defended and preserved liberty testifies that this is the people of God, pleasing to God. This is the sentiment of this response, which boasts of the posterity of Abraham, and liberty, shown as now the pontifical assembly boasts of the prescription of the title of Church, that the profession of religion and the ordinary power or government of the Church had always been in their possession, and therefore one must not dissent from their opinions and dogmas.

Latin:

Semen Abrahae sumus.

Prorsus alienum responsum subiiciunt gra- vissimae sententiae Christi, quod testatur illos, quorum quidam coeperant credere, ut assentiren- tur hunc esse Messiam, tamen adhuc tenere in- fixam animis imaginationem de regno corporali, adhuc somniant, siquidem hic sit Messias, futu- rum esse potentem regem, florentem opibus, sti- patum agminibus procerum et multitudinis, et in his se quoque beatos fore. Hac spe adducti, fa- cilius assentiebantur. Nunc cum incipit concio- nari de agnitione veritatis et fide, et ait: Ita de- mum felices fore, et habituros libertatem, si fide teneant eius verbum, et in ea perseverent, offensi resiliunt, et contra disputant, negant se esse ser- vos, subditos alienae potestati, quod ad profes- sionem, seu doctrinam religionis attinet, sed esse semen Abrahae, semper usque ab initio fuisse po- pulum Dei, nunquam fuisse idolatras, gentium more, sed tenuisse doctrinam religionis, legem, circumcisionem et alios ritus traditos quidem a Mose, sed acceptos per manus a patribus inde usque ad Abraham. Ita hic novum certamen oritur Christo, et quidem multo durius supe- riore.

Ac ut rectius intelligi possint totius huius capitis altercationes, capita controversiarum in- tueamur. De tribus rebus praecipue certamen est in his quaestionibus, quae agitantur de Messia. Primum de politia disputatur, secundo de culti- bus, tertio de persona Messiae.

De primo loco hactenus dixit: Ideo offendun- tur Iudaei doctrina Christi, quia iudicant ex ea sequi dissolutionem istius politiae divinitus con- stitutae, quam ipsi existimabant debere esse per- petuam, et Messiam venturum, ut eam instaura- ret, et longe florentiorem redderet, auctam im- perio mundi, et ingenti gloria corporali. Sed

Christus negat se venisse, ut constituat politiam aut regnum corporale: ait se non esse ex hoc mundo, sed missum esse, ut fiat victima, et ita demum salvos fore, si credant ipsius voci, quia vero nolint assentiri, futurum ut evertatur tota illa politia. Haec fuit prima offensio. Altera est non levior in quaestione, quae hic agitatur de re- ligione, seu cultibus, hic pugnant, ne religio et cultus labefactentur, de quibus praecipue gloria- bantur sibi divinitus traditam esse legem et ritus Mosaicos, hanc religionem inde usque a Mose et patribus in hoc populo singulari Dei beneficio conservatam esse. Gravius ergo offenduntur, quod Christus ait: Non propter legem et illos cul- tus liberari homines a peccato, et placere Deo, sed affirmat eos esse sub peccato et ira Dei. Hic ergo oritur longum et atrox certamen. Sed prius- quam hoc dirimitur, accedit tertia conflictatio, quae est omnium durissima de persona Messiae, cum se dicit esse Filium Dei, qui extiterit ab ae- terno, hanc iudicant esse blasphemiam, non ar- gumentis, sed saxis revincendam.

Recitavi breviter summam locorum, quae in hac tota concione usque ad finem capitis agitan- tur, nunc redeo ad textum, cum Christus iubet eos perseverare in fide, et ita promittit liberta- tem, si credant ipsius verbo. Iudaei opponunt responsionem de lege, et doctrina religionis, ac- cepta a patribus, et huc usque conservata in po- pulo Dei. Argumentantur se esse semen Abra- hae et patrum, quibus datae erant promissiones de posteritate et populo, in quo nasceretur Messias.

Has promissiones semper ratas fuisse, et opoltere et hanc politiam conservari, et doctri- nam religionis, ac cultus traditos a Mose, pro- pter venturum Messiam, qui futurus sit dominus huius populi, et allaturus regnum perpetuum. Hanc libertatem hactenus ipsis mansisse integram, quia nunquam vi aut imperio alieno coacti sint abiicere religionem, et suas leges, ne quidem in exilio Babylonico, imo etiam tum, cum cogeban- tur ferre Romanum imperium, tamen retinebant αὐτονομίαν, tuebantur religionem, et vivebant suis legibus, et haec ipsa fiducia libertatis con- cepta ex promissionibus de Messia, animabat eos, ut sperarent se excussuros hoc frenum Romani imperii.

Quare confidenter explodunt Christi vocem, cum inquit: Veritas liberabit vos, non patiuntur se dici servos, quia teneant religionem, cultus, politiam traditam divinitus, et ratiocinantur Deum hoc ipso beneficio defensae et conservatae libertatis testari, quod hic sit populus Dei, Deo placens. Haec est sententia huius responsionis, quae gloriatur de posteritate Abrahae, et liber- tate, ostensa in promissionibus, quae erant factae patribus, prorsus ut nunc coetus pontificius glo- riatur de praescriptione tituli Ecclesiae, semper penes ipsos fuisse professionem religionis, et or- dinariam potestatem seu gubernationem Ecclesiae, ideo non esse dissentiendum ab ipsorum sententiis et dogmatis.

## 8:34
Everyone who commits sin is a servant of sin.

It is a most serious refutation of carnal boasting about liberty, which contains an excellent doctrine as to what is the true liberty of the people of God, or of the pious, and it preaches about the manner in which it comes about, and shows the distinction between the true and the false Church. Let the sentences therefore be distinguished. The first is a definition of liberty, which, so that it may be more illustrious, is proposed by antithesis. And it is a negative syllogism. No one doing sin has liberty before God; you serve sin; therefore you are not free. This syllogism clearly refutes the boasting of the Jews about the defended and preserved liberty of the doctrine of the law and of the polity. He simply denies that they, on account of the law or the profession of the doctrine and Mosaic rites, have liberty before God, or the glory that they are the people of God, that they are pleasing to God, and it is a sentiment consistent with the saying of John 1: Who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God. For just as there he denies that they are children of God on account of the propagation of carnal generation, as the Jews imagined: so here he denies that they are the people of God on account of that prerogative, that they retain the title and profession of the law and of the rites received from the fathers. This is the sum of the conclusion, which denies that they are free, namely before God, that is, the people of God, accepted by God, an heir of eternal life.

But the major premise of the syllogism must be observed, from which the definition of liberty is taken, namely, that liberty before God is not to have the title of the people of God, or the profession of the doctrine of the law and the Mosaic polity, but to be free from sins, that is, to have the remission of sins, and to be reckoned righteous by God, or to be accepted by God. But in order for this definition to be declared, it is necessary to apply an explanation of the manner. Therefore another sentence is added, how men attain this liberty, because the saying of Christ: He who commits sin is a servant of sin, takes away from all the glory of liberty or righteousness before God; he also says that these, who boast of the law, are servants of sin, that is, guilty and subject to the wrath of God and to damnation, and that they are not made accepted to God on account of the law.

He therefore adds the necessary doctrine concerning the cause and manner of liberation. If the son shall have set you free, you will be truly free, as if he were to say: Since you are servants of sin, and the law does not take away sin and the wrath of God, it is necessary for you to be liberated by another's benefit, and indeed by the son of God, who is without sin, the lord and giver of righteousness and eternal life, sent by God, so that he might bring and impart reconciliation to those believing his voice, just as he said a little before: If you have remained in my word, the truth will set you free. Thus therefore liberty will come to you, if, having heard the voice of the Gospel, you believe that your sins are remitted to you, that you are received by God on account of this propitiator. It is a brief saying: If the son shall have set you free, you will be truly free, but the weight of the words must be diligently considered. For it is a most serious sentence, simply removing from the cause or merit of reconciliation all confidence in that own dignity or merits, as if he were to say: I know that you have many prerogatives, the propagation of the race from Abraham and the fathers, the law and the polity handed down divinely, the priesthood, the worship, etc. I know that there are some men in this people who are excellent, endowed with virtue, but you are not free from sin on that account; all men remain guilty of wrath and eternal death. Nor is there any thing on account of which liberation or reconciliation comes about, except the son of God himself, sent by God, so that he might become a victim. In this, God wishes both things to be seen: both the magnitude of the wrath against sin, because it could be appeased by no other sacrifice except the death of the son, and again the immense mercy, because he willed the son to become a victim, so that the human race might not perish, which he wishes to receive on account of him who believe. The son of God himself brought forth this secret counsel of the eternal father. God therefore wishes that we believe the voice of this one, and thus determine that liberation from sin and from death truly comes to us on account of the son. It is necessary that this faith be added. Because this benefit, or liberation, cannot be apprehended or received in any other way. Therefore Christ preached about it above.

Latin:

Omnis qui facit peccatum, servus est peccati.

Gravissima refutatio est carnalis gloríationis de libertate, quae continet egregiam doctrinam, quae sit vera libertas populi Dei, seu piorum, et concionatur de modo, quomodo contingat, et ostendit discrimen verae et falsae Ecclesiae. Di- stinguantur igitur sententiae. Prima est definitio libertatis, quae, ut sit illustrior, per antithesin proponitur. Estque syllogismus negativus. Ne- mo faciens peccatum, habet libertatem coram Deo, vos servitis peccato, ergo non estis liberi. Hic syllogismus clare refutat gloriationem Iudaeo- rum de defensa et conservata libertate doctrinae legis ac politiae. Simpliciter negat ipsos propter legem seu professionem doctrinae et rituum Mo- saicorum habere libertatem coram Deo, seu glo- riam, quod sint populus Dei, quod placeant Deo, estque sententia congruens cum dicto Ioannis 1.: Qui non ex sanguinibus, neque ex voluntate car- nis, neque ex voluntate viri, sed ex Deo nati sunt. Sicut enim illic negat filios Dei esse pro- pter propagationem generationis carnalis, ut Iu- daei imaginabantur: ita hic negat esse populum Dei propter illam praerogativam, quod retineant titulum, ac professionem legis, ac rituum acce- ptorum a patribus. Haec est summa conclusio- nis, quae negat eos esse liberos, videlicet coram Deo, hoc est, populum Dei, acceptum Deo, hae- redem vitae aeternae.

Sed observanda est maior syllogismi, ex qua sumitur definitio libertatis, videlicet, quod liber- tas coram Deo sit, non habere titulum populi Dei, aut professionem doctrinae legis et politiae Mo- saicae, sed liberum esse a peccatis, hoc est, ha- bere remissionem peccatorum, et iustum reputari a Deo, seu esse acceptum Deo. Sed ut haec de- finitio declaretur, necesse est adhibere explicatio- nem de modo. Ideo additur altera sententia, quomodo homines consequantur hanc libertatem, quia dictum Christi: Qui facit peccatum, servus est peccati, omnibus detrahit gloriam libertatis seu iusticiae coram Deo, dicit etiam hos, qui glo- riantur lege, esse servos peccati, hoc est, reos et subiectos irae Dei, et damnationi, nec propter legem fieri acceptos Deo.

Addit ergo necessariam doctrinam de causa et modo liberationis. Si filius vos liberaverit, vere liberi eritis, quasi dicat: Cum servi sitis peccati, nec lex tollat peccatum et iram Dei, ne- cesse est vos alieno beneficio liberari, et quidem filii Dei, qui est sine peccato, dominus et dator iusticiae et vitae aeternae, missus a Deo, ut affe- rat et impertiat reconciliationem credentibus voci ipsius, sicut paulo ante dixit: Si manseritis in sermone meo, veritas liberabit vos. Ita ergo con- tinget vobis libertas, si audita voce Evangelii credetis vobis remitti peccata, vos recipi a Deo propter hunc propiciatorem. Breve dictum est: Si filius vos liberaverit, vere liberi eritis, sed di- ligenter considerandum est pondus verborum. Est enim gravissima sententia, simpliciter remo- vens a causa seu merito reconciliationis omnem fiduciam illius propriae dignitatis aut meritorum, quasi dicat: Scio vos habere multas praerogativas, propagationem generis ab Abraham et patribus, legem et politiam divinitus traditam, sacerdo- tium, cultus, etc. Scio esse aliquos in hoc po- pulo viros excellentes, praeditos virtute, sed non ideo liberi estis a peccato, manent rei irae et mortis aeternae omnes homines. Nec ulla res est, propter quam contingit liberatio seu reconci- liatio, nisi ipse filius Dei, missus a Deo, ut fiat victima. In hoc utrunque Deus vult conspici, et magnitudinem irae adversus peccatum, quod nulla alia hostia potuerit placari, nisi morte filii, et rursus ingentem misericordiam, quod voluit filium fieri victimam, ne periret genus humanum, quod propter ipsum vult recipere credentes. Hoc arcanum consilium aeterni patris protulit ipse filius Dei. Vult igitur Deus, ut credamus voci huius, et ita statuamus vere nobis contingere li- berationem a peccato, et a morte propter filium. Hanc fidem necesse est accedere. Quia hoc be- neficium, seu liberatio non potest aliter appre- hendi seu accipi. Ideo de ea Christus supra con- cionatus est.

## 8:35
A slave does not remain in the house forever.

It is a general statement that a slave does not remain in the family, that is, is not an heir, and yet it is much more to be a slave of sin, as he said before: The slave of sin is guilty of the eternal wrath of God and eternal death, and nothing more atrocious or sad can be said about human nature than that it is a slave of sin. All these things are contained in this saying: that human nature is averse to God, stubborn against God, cast off by God, destined for eternal and horrible punishments, subject to the tyranny of the devil, and unable to be freed from the wrath of God and eternal punishments by its own righteousness. The magnitude of these evils is not comprehended by any creature, but the Church, which performs penance and knows itself to be subject to that huge mass of miseries on account of sin, recognizes these great calamities to some extent, amidst so many horrendous signs of the wrath of God and amidst daily punishments. It is therefore more to say 'slave of sin' than to be called a slave in a general sense. For a slave in a general or civil manner is a captive of his master, kept for certain tasks and receiving a ration. Such was also the people of the law, in a better condition than the Gentiles. All alike, the descendants of Abraham and the Gentiles, are slaves of sin by nature, but yet God chose the seed of Abraham so that it might serve Him in this polity, in which He wished to reveal Himself, and to promulgate the word, and to send the son of this household, as a steward or manager, to this people born from Abraham, in whom, however, He wished there to be at the same time some participants of the promised inheritance, but not on account of the polity, just as He also called some from the Gentiles to the promised inheritance. But the Jews contended that they, on account of the polity and the works of the law, were heirs of righteousness and eternal glory; Christ refutes this in two ways: First, by an atrocious condemnation: 'Whoever commits sin is a slave of sin.' Then, by a general example, from which arises the argument that they call 'a maiore': No slave is an heir of the master's property, therefore much less you, who are slaves of sin. And although you were chosen for a certain polity, yet on account of this you are not heirs. Afterwards, he adds an antithesis.

Latin:

Servus non manet in domo perpetuo.

Generale dictum est, servum non manere in familia, id est, non esse haeredem, et tamen multo plus est, esse servum peccati, ut antea dixit: Servus peccati est reus aeternae irae Dei et mortis aeternae, nec quicquam dici atrocius aut tristius de natura humana potest, quam esse ser- vum peccati. Omnia haec insunt in hoc dicto, naturam humanam esse aversam a Deo, contu- macem adversus Deum, abiectam a Deo, desti- natam ad aeternas et horribiles poenas, subiectam tyrannidi diaboli, non posse liberari ab ira Dei, et poenis aeternis, propria iusticia. Horum malo- rum magnitudo non comprehenditur ab ulla crea- tura, sed aliqua ex parte agnoscit has tantas ae- rumnas, inter tot horrenda signa irae Dei, et in- ter poenas quotidianas, Ecclesia, quae agit poe- nitentiam, et scit se subiectam illi ingenti moli aerumnarum propter peccatum. Plus est igitur dicere servum peccati, quam generaliter dici ser- vum. Nam servus generaliter seu civili more est captivus heri sui, servatus ad aliquas operas, et demensum accipiens. Talis erat et populus le- gis, meliore conditione, quam Ethnici. Omnes pariter, posteri Abrahae et Ethnici, sunt servi peccati secundum naturam, sed tamen Deus de- legit semen Abrahae, ut serviret ipsi in hac poli- tia, in qua se patefacere voluit, et promulgare verbum, et mittere filium huius hospitii, quasi atriensem seu villicum, hunc populum natum ex Abraham, in quo tamen voluit simul esse aliquos participes promissae haereditatis, sed non propter politiam, sicut etiam ex Ethnicis vocavit aliquos ad promissam haereditatem. Sed Iudaei conten- debant se propter politiam et legis opera esse hae- redes iusticiae et gloriae aeternae, id refutat Chri- stus duobus modis: Primum atroci condemnatio- ne: Qui facit peccatum, servus est peccati. Deinde generali exemplo, unde nascitur argumentum, quod vocant a maiore: Nullus servus est haeres facultatum heri, ergo multo minus vos, qui estis servi peccati. Et quanquam delecti estis ad cer- tam politiam, tamen propter hanc non estis hae- redes. Postea addit antithesin.

## 8:36
But if the son sets you free, you will be truly free.

As above, nothing sadder could be said than this utterance: 'Whoever commits sin is a slave of sin.' For it embraces universally all the evils of the human race, sin and the wrath of God, and all present and eternal punishments. So, in turn, this utterance proposes the sweetest consolation: 'If the son sets you free, you are truly free.' For it embraces liberation from sins, from the wrath of God, and from punishments, that is, the restoration of righteousness and the gift of eternal glory and joy. Because they did not understand these gifts, they therefore, like drunkards and delirious men, wander away from the meaning of Christ and dream of political liberty and empires, and show that they understand neither human miseries nor the promise of Abraham at all.

Latin:

Sed si filius vos liberaverit, vere liberi eritis.

Ut supra nihil tristius dici potuit hac voce: Qui peccatum facit, servus est peccati. Comple- ctitur enim universaliter omnia mala generis hu- mani, peccatum et iram Dei, et omnes poenas praesentes et aeternas. Ita rursus haec vox proponit dulcissimam consolationem: Si filius vos liberaverit, vere liberi estis. Complectitur enim liberationem a peccatis, ab ira Dei et a poenis, hoc est, restitutionem iusticiae, et donationem gloriae aeternae et laetitiae. Quae munera quia non intelligebant, ideo tanquam ebrii et deliri aberrant a sententia Christi, et somniant libertatem politicam et imperia, et ostendunt se prorsus nec miserias humanas, nec promissionem Abrahae intelligere.

## 8:37
I know that you are the seed of Abraham.

When the Jews said that they were free, they were using this argument: Because we are the seed of Abraham, to whom the promise of the kingdom and liberty was made, and whom God has hitherto preserved so that he would not be oppressed by perpetual slavery, even if He chastised him for a time. Christ previously refuted that argument by the description of slavery: 'Whoever commits sin is a slave of sin,' and showed that he was not speaking of political slavery. Now he adds a more odious refutation, taken from their own persons: Although you are the seed of Abraham according to the flesh, yet because you are children of the devil, you are not that posterity which is a participant in the promise of Abraham. This saying, 'I know that you are the seed of Abraham,' is the voice of one lamenting that those very people who ought to be the Church are enemies of God and the Church. I know that you are born from the seed of Abraham, I know that you have been called by great miracles to the knowledge of God, and for many centuries defended and placed in the highest honor among the whole human race, so that you might be the guardians and heralds of my word and promise, by which salvation has been rendered to the human race. All these things are greater than can be sufficiently explained in words. I agree, therefore, that you are the seed of Abraham according to the flesh, and called to the kingdom of God, and I grieve that you do not recognize your calling, and that you fight rabidly against it. You are not, therefore, the true posterity of Abraham, a participant in the promised blessing, but miserable dregs, cast off by God, because, having neglected the word of God, you have fashioned for yourselves new opinions, and now you oppose the Gospel. For he alleges this cause.

Latin:

Scio quod semen Abrahae estis.

Cum Iudaei dicerent se liberos esse, utebantur hoc argumento: Quia sumus semen Abrahae, cui facta est promissio regni et libertatis, et quod Deus hactenus servavit, ne servitute perpetua opprimeretur, etiamsi ad tempus castigavit. Id argumentum prius refutavit Christus descriptione servitutis: Qui facit peccatum, servus est peccati, et ostendit se non loqui de politica servitute. Nunc addit magis odiosam refutationem, ab ipsorum personis sumtam: Vos etsi estis semen Abrahae secundum carnem, tamen quia estis filii diaboli, non estis illa posteritas particeps promissionis Abrahae. Hoc dictum: Scio quod estis semen Abrahae, vox est deplorantis, quod illi ipsi, qui debebant esse Ecclesia, sunt hostes Dei et Ecclesiae. Scio vos esse natos ex Abrahae semine, scio vos magnis miraculis vocatos esse ad agnitionem Dei, et multis seculis defensos et collocatos in summo honore in toto genere humano, ut sitis custodes et praecones mei verbi et promissionis, qua reddita est salus humano generi. Haec omnia maiora sunt, quam ut verbis explicari satis possint. Assentior ergo vos esse semen Abrahae secundum carnem, et vocatos ad regnum Dei, et doleo vos non agnoscere vestram vocationem, et cum ea rabiose pugnare. Non estis igitur vera posteritas Abrahae, particeps promissae benedictionis, sed miserae feces, abiectae a Deo, quia neglecto verbo Dei finxistis vobis novas opiniones, et nunc adversamini Evangelio. Hanc enim causam allegat.

## 8:37
My word does not take hold in you, etc.

Nor is there any need to bring in here longer disputes about predestination. The cause of the present rejection Christ himself cites, therefore you are not the Church, because there is no place for my word in you. For this is the meaning of this idiom. There is no place for my discourse in you, that is, it does not enter your minds. Because, clearly, by your own fault you resist, and you do not wish to assent, although I convince you with manifest testimonies of God, so many miracles, and the sayings of the Prophets. He therefore attributes the cause of the rejection not to God, but to the will of those who oppose the Gospel, just as he says elsewhere: How often I wanted to gather you and you would not.

first commandment: You shall have no other gods. Likewise: Flee from idols. Likewise, the commandment concerning confession: Whoever shall deny me before men, I will deny him before my heavenly Father. Likewise: If anyone shall teach another Gospel, let him be anathema. To these passages let us add a clear testimony in this place, who concerning these very ones who held the title of governors of the people, and were born from the seed of Abraham, were circumcised, and performed the ordinary ministry in the temple, he expressly says: You are from your father the devil, and in chapter 10: You are not of my sheep. To these sayings let us add the examples of the Prophets, of Christ, and of the Apostles, who all dissented from the ordinary authority. Instructed and fortified by these testimonies, let us not be deterred from the right opinion when the title of the Church is opposed for the defense of errors, but let us not ourselves invent new opinions, nor rashly disturb the Church on account of our own delusions, but let us oppose the ordinary authority only there where certain truth, handed down in the word of God and apostolic testimonies, compels us to oppose false opinions.

I speak what I have seen with my Father.

Since he had previously conceded that the opposing Jews were the seed of Abraham, here he adds a correction. You are the seed according to the flesh, but in truth and in spirit you are not the children of Abraham, but the children of the devil, because you are enemies of the Gospel, and you kill the members of the true Church of God. Here he hands down a doctrine necessary to be known in such a variety of judgments: often those who dominate in the Church, and on account of their title boast that they are the chief members of the people of God, are entirely outside the Church, and yet they demand obedience, they want their errors to be heard and approved on account of their position or ordinary succession, and they condemn the reproof of errors as seditious and as dissipating the Church of God. Furthermore, moderate governments by nature love political order and ordinary authority, and they depart from it with difficulty; therefore, many weak people are always, on account of these pretexts, even if they recognize the errors, nevertheless, out of a certain zeal for concord, they dissimulate their own judgment. Thus, for those who are prudent and truly fear God, there is need of certain and clear confirmation that it is necessary to oppose errors, and that on account of the title of ecclesiastical authority, they are not members of the Church, but on account of their pertinacity in errors and their cruelty, they are enemies of God, cast out by God from the Church and to be abandoned. We have great need of this consolation now. The chief argument of wise and political men is that the Church has felt this way for many centuries. That when the authority of the highest rank in the Church is shaken, infinite dissipations follow, which bring about the oblivion and destruction of all religion, and on this pretext errors are established.

A long struggle is described here in the text, where the adversaries of Christ contend that they are the people of God; on the contrary, Christ denies it. This whole passage contains this doctrine especially, namely, that we should not be moved by the title of the Church in the refutation of errors, but that we should know that the pertinacious defenders of impious opinions are outside the Church. This is a necessary and sweet consolation for the pious; on the contrary, let it be considered what a sad condemnation it is that he says his enemies are from their father the devil, that is, enemies of God, cast into eternal destruction, captives of the devil, blinded, rushing with blind fury against God, against the Gospel, against the true invocation of God, against true worship, against the true people of God, just as they are snatched by the devil, as Saul is driven from one crime into another; Marcion, Mahomet, Arius have fallen from other delusions into others, and have polluted themselves with lusts and every turpitude. The text describes this misery of such blinded ones in the saddest words, reciting what kind of being the devil is.

He was a murderer from the beginning, and he did not stand in the truth.

Although sane men cannot but be moved by this plausible argument, yet we should know that this human wisdom must be preferred to the first. Not without great sorrow were these things said by Christ, that the devil was a murderer from the beginning; he remembers the first human fall, and he considers that the devil, out of hatred for God, tore the human race away from God, and on account of that all men are oppressed by this fall, and by the immense and ineffable wrath of God, in which a great multitude is to remain forever. The thought of these evils brings to Christ a sorrow such as no other mind can conceive. But let all the particulars be gathered together: He attributes two things properly to the devil, homicide and lying, and then adds that the devil is the father, that is, the cause and author of these evils. Homicide is to wish to harm a man against the will of God; lying is any error, false opinion, and false doctrine about God, and then universally any deception contrived for the purpose of harming, such as all the sophistry and sycophancy in religions, in government, and in common life. These are the sources of all evils in life, the ignorance of God, or lies about God. For it is of these especially that he speaks here, and he says that the devil is the cause of homicide, that is, the desire to harm, and of these evils. But often in the Church great tumults have arisen concerning the cause of evil. Wherefore pious minds are most especially to be confirmed by this saying of Christ, which testifies that God is not the cause of sin, that is, that He neither wills, nor approves, nor effects sin, but that sin has arisen simply from the will of the devil and of man, which freely turns itself away from God. This opinion must be held most firmly, and one must never depart from it, even if sayings seem to occur somewhere that introduce some clouding of the true opinion, and it must be seen to that the contrary things are explained dexterously and without sophistry.

But first let the mind be fortified and confirmed by certain testimonies which show that sin has arisen, and arises, not from the will of God, but entirely and simply from the will of the devil and of man, Gen. 1: God saw all things which He had made, and they were very good, that is, pleasing to God, rightly ordered, obedient to God. For the word 'good' properly signifies these things, and the particle 'very' is not placed idly in Moses, which, although it pertains to all creatures, yet most especially describes the excellence of human nature, which was very good, that is, very pleasing to God, very beloved by God, endowed with gifts far exceeding present strengths, very ordered, perfectly obedient to God. This particle therefore warns us from what dignity we have been cast out.

Psalm 5: You are not a God who wills impiety. Zech. 8: Do not think evil against your neighbor, and do not love a false oath. For the Lord says that He hates all these things. But although some attempt to elude these two testimonies with futile quibbling, yet it is certain that they are firm. They imagine that another will is expressed in the law, and yet that a contrary one exists in the mind of God. This imagination must be repudiated, for the will of God is so good and just, and wills this order which it expresses in the law, that it is impossible for it to will, effect, aid, or approve the contrary: it is impossible for God to will the lusts of Nero, but it is the eternal and immutable will of God to will chastity. But that He permits evils, hiding His wrath for a little while, it is sufficiently evident that permission is not to will positively, or to effect, or to aid, or to approve.

1 John 3: He who commits sin is of the devil, because the devil sins from the beginning, that is, the devil is the originator of sin, as if he were to say: The nature of spirits and of man was created by God in such a way that it was pleasing to God, rightly ordered, and obedient to God. But the will of the devil freely turned itself away from God. This turning away is sin, because it is disobedience fighting against the will of God, and is neglect, contempt, or hatred of God. Afterwards the devil also impelled human wills, having cast a false imagination upon them, so that they would turn themselves away from God.

1 John 2: The concupiscence of the flesh is not of the Father, but of the world. This saying states quite clearly and explicitly that sin does not arise from God.

To this also may be added that from Rom. 5: Through one man sin entered into the world.

But the most illustrious testimony is the saying of this place. John 8: When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own, because he is a liar and the father of lies. When he says 'from his own,' he distinguishes created things from non-created things. The nature of a spirit is a thing created by God, but besides this there is something 'own' in the devil, that is, not created by God, namely the turning away from God, which is disobedience fighting against God. And Christ clearly says that the devil is the father of lies. He affirms, therefore, that lying and sin did not arise from God. And sin is properly the turning away of an intelligent nature from God, fighting against the law of God. Nor do these things fight against each other, that the nature of man arose from God, and that sin is not from God. Because sin is a horrible destruction of the work and of the divine order, truly displeasing to God, because it is His he had not wished the work to be violated. These things must be carefully considered, and the simple truth, which I have reviewed, must be retained; let us learn to accuse ourselves, not God, let us seek from God the remedies for our evils, as it is said in Hosea 13: Your destruction is from yourself, O Israel, only in me is your help.

however, the dispute speaks of doctrine, I think therefore that this is what is being asked. Convict me concerning the doctrine. Who among you can accuse me, that I teach false things, that I am a false prophet? This is the principal question concerning doctrine and calling. This must first be judged from the word of God, afterwards from the miracles and private morals of the teachers; Christ has the testimonies of the word of God, then of miracles, finally his private morals are not signs of an evil spirit.

But as for what some object with these sayings: I will harden the heart of Pharaoh, and similar ones, the certain and true explanation is that these sayings speak of permission; I will harden, that is, I will allow to be hardened. For the Hebrew phrase does not require such words to be interpreted harshly, as when we say: Lead us not into temptation, that is, do not allow us to be led, or to perish once led. God foresees the furies of Pharaoh, Saul, and others, and permits them to happen, as if hiding his wrath, and yet he determines them, that is, he sets boundaries for those furies, which he does not allow them to cross. This determination is described by an illustrious figure in Sennacherib, 4 Kings 19: I will put a bridle on your lips, and I will lead you back, etc.

This order must be observed in judgments concerning doctrine, which the law also sanctions, Deut. 18: The first and highest judge of doctrine is the word of God delivered first through the Prophets and Apostles; the law does not even want miracles to be preferred to the word of God. Afterwards, when the word of God agrees, miracles and private morals should be considered, and in private morals there is a twofold consideration: either they are vices which the teachers themselves disapprove of and amend, as when Peter fell; or they are vices which the teachers defend. These are evil fruits, and signs of the devil, as when the Anabaptists defend seditions, and contend that they have a mandate from the Gospel to wage wars against others, and to establish a new kingdom. Such delirium is not only a lapse in morals, but is an error in doctrine and an abuse of the divine name, against the second commandment. Let us therefore observe these rules in judging spirits, as Christ says: By their fruits you shall know them, that is, first by the testimonies of doctrine, afterwards by miracles, finally by the vices that are defended.

Latin:

Sermo meus non capit in vobis, etc.

Nec opus est huc accersere disputationes de praedestinatione longiores. Causam reiectionis praesentis allegat ipse Christus, ideo non estis Ecclesia, quia verbo meo non est locus in vobis. Haec enim est huius idiotismi significatio. Non est locus meo sermoni in vobis, id est, non subit animos vestros. Quia scilicet vestra culpa re- pugnatis, et non vultis assentiri, cum manifestis testimoniis Dei, tot miraculis et Prophetarum di- ctis vos convincam. Causam igitur reiectionis non Deo, sed voluntati istorum tribuit, qui ad- versantur Evangelio, sicut alias dicit: Quoties volui vos congregare et noluistis.

mum praeceptum: Non habebis Deos alienos. Item: Fugite idola. Item, praeceptum de con- fessione: Qui negaverit me coram hominibus, ne- gabo eum coram patre meo coelesti. Item: Si quis aliud Evangelium docuerit, anathema sit. Ad haec loca addamus clarum testimonium hoc loco, qui de his ipsis qui titulum tenebant guber- natorum populi, et ex semine Abrahae nati erant, erant circumcisi, et fungebantur ministerio ordi- nario in templo, expresse inquit: Vos ex patre diabolo estis, et capite 10.: Vos non estis ex ovi- bus meis. Ad haec dicta adiungamus exempla Pro- phetarum, Christi et Apostolorum, qui omnes ab ordinaria potestate dissenserunt. His eruditi ac muniti testimoniis, non deterreamur a recta sententia, cum opponitur titulus Ecclesiae ad de- fensionem errorum, sed non fingamus ipsi novas opiniones, nec temere propter nostra deliria con- turbemus Ecclesiam, sed tantum ibi adversemur ordinariae potestati, ubi certa veritas tradita in verbo Dei et apostolicis testimoniis, cogit nos adversari falsis opinionibus.

Ego quod vidi apud patrem meum loquor.

Cum antea concessisset Iudaeos adversantes esse semen Abrahae, hic addit correctionem. Estis semen secundum carnem, sed revera et spi- ritu non estis filii Abrahae, sed filii diaboli, quia estis hostes Evangelii, et interficitis membra verae Ecclesiae Dei. Hic doctrinam tradit necessariam cognitu in tanta iudiciorum varietate, saepe hi, qui dominantur in Ecclesia, et propter titulum iactitant se esse praecipua membra populi Dei, sunt prorsus extra Ecclesiam, et tamen flagitant obedientiam, volunt audiri et approbari suos erro- res propter locum, seu successionem ordinariam, damnant errorum reprehensionem, tanquam se- ditiosam et dissipantem Ecclesiam Dei. Porro moderata imperia natura amant politicum ordi- nem et potestatem ordinariam, et aegre disce- dant ab ea, ideo semper multi imbecilles propter hos praetextus, etiamsi agnoscunt errores, tamen quodam studio concordiae suum iudicium dissi- mulant. Itaque prudentibus et vere Deum timen- tibus, certa et perspicua confirmatione opus est, quod necesse sit adversari erroribus, et quod pro- pter titulum potestatis ecclesiasticae, non sint membra Ecclesiae, sed propter pertinaciam in erroribus, et crudelitatem, sint hostes Dei, extra Ecclesiam a Deo eiecti et relinquendi. Hac con- solatione nobis nunc valde opus est. Praecipuum argumentum est sapientum et politicorum viro- rum, quod sic sentiat Ecclesia multis seculis. Quod labefactata autoritate summi gradus in Ec- clesia sequantur infinitae dissipationes, quae obli- vionem et interitum universae religionis afferant, et hoc praetextu stabiliuntur errores.

Longum hic certamen describitur in textu, ubi contendunt adversarii Christi, se esse popu- lum Dei, econtra Christus negat. Totus hic lo- cus praecipue hanc doctrinam continet, videlicet, ne moveamur titulo Ecclesiae in refutatione erro- rum, sed sciamus pertinaces defensores impiarum opinionum extra Ecclesiam esse. Haec est piis necessaria et dulcis consolatio, econtra cogitetur quam tristis condemnatio sit, quod dicit hostes suos ex patre diabolo esse, hoc est, hostes Dei, abiectos in aeternum exitium, captivos diaboli, excaecatos, caeco furore ruentes contra Deum, contra Evangelium, contra veram Dei invocatio- nem, contra veros cultus, contra verum Dei po- pulum, sicut rapiuntur a diabolo, ut Saul ex alio scelere in aliud impellitur, Marcion, Mahome- tus, Arius, ex aliis deliriis in alia lapsi sunt, et polluerunt se libidinibus et omni turpitudine. Hanc miseriam talium excaecatorum describit tri- stissimis verbis textus, recitans qualis sit diabolus.

Ille homicida erat ab initio, et in veritate non stetit.

Etsi autem homines sani non possunt non moveri hoc plausibili argumento, tamen huic hu- manae sapientiae sciamus anteferendum esse pri- Non sine magno dolore haec a Christo dicta sunt, diabolum initio fuisse homicidam, meminit primi lapsus humani, et cogitat diabolum odio Dei avulsisse a Deo genus humanum, et propter hunc lapsum omnes homines oppressos esse in- genti, et inerrabili ira Dei, in qua magna multi- tudo perpetuo mansura est. Horum malorum cogitatio parit Christo dolorem, quantum nulla alia mens concipere potest. Colligantur autem omnes particulae: Duo tribuit proprie diabolo, homicidium et mendacium, et deinde addit dia- bolum patrem, id est, causam et autorem horum malorum esse. Homicidium est, velle nocere homini contra voluntatem Dei, mendacium est quilibet error, falsa opinio et falsa doctrina de Deo, deinde universaliter quaelibet deceptio ad nocendum comparata, ut tota sophistica et syco- phantica in religionibus, in gubernatione et com- muni vita. Hi sunt fontes malorum omnium in vita, ignoratio Dei, seu mendacia de Deo. Nam de his praecipue hic loquitur, et homicidium, id est, cupiditas nocendi, et horum malorum cau- sam esse inquit diabolum. Saepe autem in Ec- clesia magni tumultus exorti sunt de causa mali. Quare maxime confirmandae sunt piae mentes hoc dicto Christi, quod testatur Deum non esse cau- sam peccati, hoc est, neque velle, neque appro- bare, neque efficere peccatum, sed simpliciter ortum esse peccatum a voluntate diaboli et homi- nis, quae libere se avertit a Deo. Haec senten- tia firmissime tenenda est, neque unquam ab ea est discedendum, etiamsi alicubi videntur occur- rere dicta, quae aliquid caliginis verae sententiae inducunt, ac videndum est, ut dextre, ac sine sophistica explicentur contraria.

Primum autem sit munita et confirmata mens certis testimoniis, quae ostendunt peccatum ortum esse, et oriri non a voluntate Dei, sed prorsus et simpliciter a voluntate diaboli et hominis, Ge- nes. 1.: Vidit Deus cuncta, quae fecerat, et erant valde bona, id est, Deo placentia, recte ordi- nata, Deo obedientia. Haec enim proprie signi- ficat vocabulum bonum, nec otiose posita est in Mose particula valde, quod etsi ad omnes crea- turas pertinet, tamen maxime describit humanae naturae praestantiam, quae erat valde bona, id est, valde placens Deo, valde dilecta a Deo, praedita donis longe superantibus praesentes vi- res, valde ordinata; perfecte obediens Deo. Ad- monet igitur haec particula ex quanta dignitate excutti simus.

Psalm. 5.: Non Deus volens impietatem tu es. Zach. 8.: Malum contra proximum ne cogi- tetis, et iuramentum falsum ne diligatis. Omnia enim haec odi, dicit dominus. Etsi autem haec duo testimonia quidam futili cavillatione eludere conantur, tamen firma esse, certum est. Fin- gunt aliam voluntatem in lege expressam esse, et tamen contrariam in mente Dei esse. Haec ima- ginatio repudianda est, nam voluntas Dei ita est bona et iusta, et volens hunc ordinem, quem lege exprimit, ut impossibile sit eam velle, efficere, adiuvare, aut approbare contrarium: impossibile est Deum velle libidines Neronis, sed est aeterna et immutabilis Dei voluntas, velle castitatem. Quod autem mala permittit, abscondens suam iram ali- quantisper, satis constat permissionem non esse velle positive, aut efficere, vel adiuvare, vel approbare.

1. Ioan. 3.: Qui facit peccatum, ex diabolo est, quia ab initio diabolus peccat, id est, dia- bolus est incoator peccati, quasi dicat: Natura spirituum et hominis condita fuit a Deo sic, ut Deo placeret, recte ordinata esset, et Deo obe- diens. Sed diaboli voluntas sese libere avertit a Deo. Haec aversio est peccatum, quia est inobe- dientia pugnans cum voluntate Dei, et est negle- ctio, contemtus, aut odium Dei. Postea diabo- lus etiam humanas voluntates impulit, offusa falsa imaginatione, ut se averterent a Deo.

1. Ioan. 2.: Concupiscentia carnis non est ex patre, sed ex mundo. Hoc dictum satis per- spicue et diserte inquit, non oriri a Deo pec- catum.

Huc etiam illud addi potest ad Rom. 5.: Per unum hominem peccatum introiit in mundum.

Sed maxime illustre testimonium est dictum huius loci. Ioan. 8.: Quando loquitur menda- cium, ex propriis loquitur, quia mendax est et pater mendacii. Cum ait ex propriis, discernit res conditas a non conditis. Natura spiritus est res a Deo condita, sed praeter hanc quiddam est proprium in diabolo, id est, non conditum a Deo, videlicet aversio a Deo, quae est inobe- dientia pugnans cum Deo. Et clare dicit Chri- stus, diabolum esse patrem mendacii. Affirmat igitur mendacium et peccatum non esse a Deo ortum. Estque peccatum proprie aversio intelli- gentis naturae a Deo, pugnans cum lege Dei. Nec pugnant haec inter sese, naturam hominis a Deo ortam esse, et peccatum non esse a Deo. Quia peccatum est horribilis destructio operis, et ordinis divini, vere displicens Deo, quia suum opus violari noluerat. Haec diligenter conside- randa sunt, et simplex veritas, quam recensui, retinenda est, discamus nos ipsos accusare, non Deum, petamus a Deo remedia nostrorum malo- rum, sicut Oseae 13. dicitur: Perditio tua ex te Israël, tantum in me auxilium tuum.

tamen disputatio loquitur de doctrina, existimo igitur hoc quaeri. De doctrina me convincite. Quis vestrum accusare me potest, quod falsa do- ceam, quod sim pseudopropheta? Haec est prin- cipalis quaestio de doctrina et vocatione. Haec primum iudicanda est ex verbo Dei, postea ex miraculis et privatis moribus docentium, Chri- stus testimonia habet verbi Dei, deinde miracu- lorum, postremo privati mores eius non sunt in- dicia mali spiritus.

Quod vero obiiciunt aliqui haec dicta: Ego indurabo cor Pharaonis, et similia, certa et vera explicatio est, haec dicta loqui de permissione, indurabo, id est, sinam indurari. Nam phrasis Ebraica non postulat huiusmodi verba durius ex- poni, ut cum dicimus: Ne nos inducas intenta- tionem, id est, ne sinas nos induci, aut inductos perire. Praevidet Deus Pharaonis, Saulis, et aliorum furores, ac fieri permittit, tanquam suam iram abscondens, ac determinat tamen, id est, metas illis furoribus constituit, quas transire illos non sinit. Haec determinatio illustri figura de- scribitur in Sennaherib, 4. Regum 19.: Impo- nam frenum labiis tuis, et reducam te, etc.

Hic ordo observandus est in iudiciis de do- ctrina, quam sancit et lex, Deut. 18.: Primus et summus iudex doctrinae est verbum Dei traditum prius per Prophetas et Apostolos, ne miracula quidem vult lex anteferri verbo Dei. Postea cum congruit verbum Dei, considerentur miracula et privati mores, et in privatis moribus duplex est consideratio, aut sunt vitia, quae ipsi doctores improbant et emendant, ut cum Petrus lapsus est: aut sunt vitia, quae doctores defendunt. Haec sunt mali fructus, et signa diaboli, ut cum Anabaptistae defendunt seditiones, ac contendunt se mandato Evangelii aliis bella inferre, et novum regnum constituere. Tale delirium non est tan- tum lapsus in moribus, sed est error in doctrina et abusus nominis divini, contra secundum prae- ceptum. Has igitur regulas observemus in iudi- candis spiritibus, sicut Christus inquit: Ex fru- ctibus eorum cognoscetis eos, id est, primum ex doctrinae testimoniis, postea ex miraculis, po- stremo ex vitiis quae defenduntur.

## 8:46
Who of you will convict me of sin?

The dispute is about the calling, whether this Jesus is sent by God, or rather whether he is the Messiah, as they ask above, who he is. The Jews, however, criticize his sayings, because he had brought such a sad judgment, namely, that these children of Abraham, and governors of the people of God, were from the devil. This voice seems so absurd and impious, as if someone were to say that the synod and the Bishops at this time opposing true doctrine are not the Church of God. Therefore, as the dispute proceeds as if after the contestation of the suit, Christ seeks the cause: If you condemn me, set forth the cause; I allege my cause against you as plain and ready. All members of the Church have heard the word of God. You do not hear, therefore you are not members of the people of God. By this reason I manifestly convict you; you in turn convict me. A similar dispute recurs whenever struggles arise concerning doctrine. For it is always disputed about the source, whence the doctrine is; thus they asked about John, about Jeremiah, and others, whether they taught truly, whether they were sent by God. Thus now it is disputed whence this kind of doctrine is, which has now arisen.

Latin:

Quis ex vobis arguet me de peccato?

Disputatio est de vocatione, an sit missus a Deo hic Iesus, imo an sit Messias, sicut supra interrogant, quis sit. Iudaei autem reprehen- dunt eius dicta, quod tam tristem sententiam tu- lerat, videlicet, hos filios Abrahae, et guberna- tores populi Dei esse a diabolo. Haec vox tam absurda et impia videtur, ut si quis dicat syno- dum et Episcopos hoc tempore adversantes verae doctrinae, non esse Ecclesiam Dei. Procedente igitur disputatione tanquam post litis contestatio- nem, quaerit Christus causam: Si me condemna- tis, causam exponite, ego meam causam contra vos planam et expeditam allego. Omnia membra Ecclesiae audiverunt verbum Dei. Vos non audi- tis, ergo non estis membra populi Dei. Hac ra- tione manifeste vos convinco, vos contra et me convincite. Similis disputatio recurrit, quoties oriuntur certamina de doctrina. Semper enim de fonte disputatur, unde sit doctrina, sic de Ioanne, de Ieremia, et aliis quaerebant, an vera docerent, an essent divinitus missi. Sic nunc disputatur unde sit hoc genus doctrinae, quod nunc exortum est.

## 8:48
You are a Samaritan, and have a demon.

The Jews cannot bring forward a cause why they condemn this teacher, but they repeat and increase the insults. Here it is customary to dispute about refutation and vengeance, but the explanation is very easy. Although the world mixes these two, defense and vengeance, yet the law and the judgment of God want them to be distinguished; universally the defense of the truth is granted, but it is one thing to testify with words which opinion is true, it is another thing afterwards to take up arms. Christ refutes his adversaries with words, he does not move arms. Then he observes these degrees: He does not refute all insults, but only those which expressly harmed the glory of God; he answers nothing concerning the insult of being a Samaritan, and because it was a manifest and notorious falsehood, there is no need to refute it, as is commonly said: And because he himself was gathering the Church even from the Samaritans, he was teaching the people

Christ therefore answered, and sets forth the thesis, which must remain firm in the Church. Who of you accuses me of sin? Although many interpret these things only concerning the private morals of Christ,

that they belong to God, not only those born of Abraham and observing the ceremonies of Moses, but all in all nations who were about to embrace the Gospel; but he refutes the other reproach, 'You have a demon': here he answers plainly and clearly: 'I do not have a demon.' For here one must fight, one must not be silent for any creature, when the truth of God is said to be a lie of the devil, or vice versa. These are the blasphemies which he also refutes elsewhere, as in Matthew 12: 'He who is not with me is against me,' etc. Let us therefore remember these refutations, and let us know that it is commanded to us likewise that we defend the glory of God by our confession, let us attribute to God what is God's, and let us not allow them to be depraved. This duty is commanded universally to all, when it is said: 'Whoever shall have confessed me before men, I will confess him before my heavenly Father,' etc.

If anyone shall keep my word, he shall not see death, etc.

He emphasizes his confession and repeats the sum of his doctrine; he not only denies that he has a demon, but also testifies further that he honors his Father. Then he repeats the sum of his doctrine and proposes a statement more wonderful to these listeners; he affirms that he gives eternal life, and shows the way. 'If anyone shall keep my word, he shall not see death.' Since this voice is the sum of the Gospel, it must be diligently fixed in our minds, and nothing greater can be said after it, and this saying must be opposed to the law. The Jews thought they were made safe on account of the law. Christ proposes another voice, namely his word, which he has already repeated so often, as above in chapter 3: 'God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son, that everyone who believes in him may not perish, but have eternal life.' Those who retain this word shall not see and shall not taste death.

Neither the profane nor the secure hypocrites understand this saving consolation, who dream that men are righteous on account of some discipline or other; and discipline is a great and necessary ornament, but yet no one in this corruption of nature is without sin, and the pious understand that sin is a great and horrible mass, which always accuses and condemns our hearts, commands us to flee from God, and forbids us to hope for grace and help, just as all the pious learn in daily experience. Therefore, the law does not save, but the mediator must be acknowledged.

There is also in this particle a sweet consolation, in that he says: 'If anyone shall have kept my word.' For timid minds are harshly vexed; they think, 'I would hope for grace if I saw Christ present with me, if the situation showed that I was being freed from the present calamity, if I had burning motions of the Holy Spirit and new revelations.' These temptations are known to the pious, who ought to hold onto these sayings. Behold, we are led to the word; thus we apprehend God, thus we are freed from eternal wrath, thus by this word, by this promise, we sustain ourselves, which Christ delivered, just as Paul also says: 'The word is near in your mouth and in your heart, this is the word of faith which we preach.' Therefore, having heard and known the voice of the Gospel, let us determine that this very thing is truly the will of God, which he declares to us there; let us determine that we are truly received on account of the Son according to these promises, and although present punishments attack this faith, yet let us not be broken by the delay. Therefore he says: 'If anyone shall have kept.' For it is difficult to retain faith amidst present miseries, which signify the wrath of God against sin, etc.

But why does he say: 'He shall not see death,' and afterwards repeats the saying: 'He shall not taste death'? There is emphasis in the word 'seeing.' Likewise in the word 'tasting.' Not to see, not to taste death, is not to rush into eternal wrath and not to feel condemnation. The damned see and taste death perpetually, that is, they feel eternal punishments and the horrible wrath of God. But the heirs of eternal life shall not see, shall not taste death; rather, they shall be in joy and perpetual life; indeed, even when the dissolution of bodies occurs, they do not see nor taste death, that is, they have life already begun in themselves, nor are they oppressed by the terrors of the wrath of God, as Saul and Judas are oppressed by ineffable terror. He said, therefore: 'He shall not see death,' so that he might clearly signify that he was not denying the dissolution of mortal bodies, but that he was preaching about liberation from the horrible wrath of God; to feel, to see, to taste this is eternal death. Although these things ought to be explained more at length, yet because these sentences have been repeated often, I am briefer here,

Latin:

Samaritanus es, et daemonium habes.

Non possunt afferre causam Iudaei, cur damnent hunc doctorem, sed repetunt et augent convicia. Hic disputari solet de refutatione, et vindicta, sed facillima est explicatio. Etsi mun- dus miscet haec duo, defensionem et vindictam, tamen lex et iudicium Dei vult ea distingui, uni- versaliter defensio veritatis concessa est, sed aliud est verbis testificari, quae sententia sit vera, aliud est postea arma capere. Christus verbis refutat adversarios, non movet arma. Deinde servat hos gradus: Non refutat omnia convicia, sed illa tantum, quae expresse laedebant gloriam Dei, de convicio Samaritani nihil respondet, et quia ma- nifesta falsitas erat, et notoria, refutare nihil opus est, ut vulgo dicitur: Et quia ipse colligebat Ecclesiam etiam ex Samaritanis, docebat populum

Respondit igitur Christus, et ponit thesin, quam oportet firmam manere in Ecclesia. Quis vestrum accusat me de peccato? Etsi multi haec interpretantur tantum de privatis moribus Christi,

Dei esse non solum natos ex Abraham et obser- vantes ceremonias Mosi, sed omnes in omnibus gentibus, qui Evangelium amplexuri erant, sed alterum convicium refutat, daemonium habes: hic plane et diserte respondet: Daemonium non habeo. Nam hic pugnandum est, nulli creaturae tacendum est, cum veritas Dei dicitur esse men- dacium diaboli, aut econtra. Hae sunt blasphe- miae, quas etiam alibi refutat, ut Matth. 12.: Qui non est mecum, contra me est, etc. Has igitur refutationes meminerimus, et sciamus no- bis similiter praecipi, ut gloriam Dei nostra con- fessione defendamus, tribuamus Deo, quae sunt Dei, et non sinamus ea depravari. Hoc officium mandatum est universaliter omnibus, cum dici- tur: Qui confessus fuerit me coram hominibus, confitebor eum coram patre coelesti, etc.

Si quis sermonem meum servabit, mortem non, etc.

Exaggerat suam confessionem, et repetit summam doctrinae, non solum negat se daemo- nium habere, sed etiam amplius testatur, se pa- trem honore afficere. Deinde summam doctrinae repetit, et proponit sententiam magis mirandam istis auditoribus, affirmat se vitam aeternam dare, et modum ostendit. Si quis sermonem meum servabit, mortem non videbit. Haec vox cum sit Evangelii summa, diligenter animis infigenda est, nec dici quicquam maius post, estque hoc dictum legi opponendum. Iudaei putabant se propter legem salvos fieri. Christus aliam vocem proponit, scilicet suum sermonem, quem toties iam repetivit, ut supra cap. 3.: Sic dilexit Deus mundum, ut filium suum unigenitum dederit, ut omnis qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam. Hunc sermonem qui retinent, mortem non videbunt et non gustabunt.

Hanc salutarem consolationem nec profani nec securi hypocritae intelligunt, qui somniant homines propter qualemcunque disciplinam iustos esse, et est magnum et necessarium decus disci- plina, sed tamen nemo in hac corruptione natu- rae sine peccato est, et pii intelligunt peccatum esse magnam et horrendam molem, quae semper accusat ac damnat nostra corda, iubet fugere Deum, vetat sperare gratiam et auxilium, sicut in quotidiana experientia omnes pii discunt. Non igitur lex salvat, sed agnoscendus est mediator.

Est et in hac particula dulcis consolatio, quod ait: Si quis sermonem meum servaverit. Duriter enim vexantur pavidae mentes, tunc spe- rarem gratiam, si viderem mihi adesse Christum, si res ostenderet me liberari ex praesenti calami- tate, si haberem flagrantes motus Spiritus sancti, ac novas revelationes. Hae tentationes notae sunt piis, qui tenere haec dicta debent. Ecce ad ser- monem deducimur, sic apprehendimus Deum, sic liberamur ab aeterna ira, sic hoc sermone, hac promissione nos sustentamus, quam Christus tradidit, sicut et Paulus inquit: Probe est ver- bum in ore tuo, et in corde tuo, hoc est, ver- bum fidei, quod praedicamus. Quare audita et cognita voce Evangelii, statuamus hanc ipsam vere esse voluntatem Dei, quam ibi nobis decla- rat, statuamus nos iuxta has promissiones propter filium vere recipi, et quanquam poenae praesen- tes hanc fidem oppugnant, tamen non frangamur mora. Ideo dicit: Si quis servaverit. Difficile enim est retinere fidem inter praesentes miserias, quae significant iram Dei adversus peccatum, etc.

Sed cur inquit: Non videbit mortem, et postea dictum repetit: Non gustabit mortem. Em- phasis est in verbo videndi. Item in verbo gu- standi. Non videre, non gustare mortem, est non ruere in aeternam iram, et non sentire damnationem. Damnati vident, et gustant mor- tem perpetuo, id est, sentiunt aeternas poenas, et horribilem iram Dei. Sed haeredes vitae aeter- nae non videbunt, non gustabunt mortem, imo erunt in laetitia, et vita perpetua, imo etiam cum fit dissolutio corporum, non vident nec gustant mortem, id est, habent in seipsis iam incoatam vitam, nec sunt oppressi terroribus irae Dei, si- cut Saul et Iudas sunt oppressi ineffabili terrore. Dixit ergo: Non videbit mortem, ut diserte signi- ficaret, se non negare corporum mortalium disso- lutionem, sed concionari se de liberatione ab hor- ribili ira Dei, hanc sentire, videre, gustare, est mors aeterna. Haec etsi prolixius explicanda essent, tamen quia saepe repetitae sunt hae sen- tentiae, hic sum brevior,

## 8:53
Are you greater than our father Abraham?

Here the Jews remarkably declare their ignorance, who think that the Messiah will not be greater than father Abraham, nor do they understand that Abraham was freed from death through the Messiah; in short, entirely they are ignorant of the benefits of the Messiah, and they only dream of that worldly kingdom of theirs; therefore Christ repeats his assertions concerning his mission and doctrine, and explains the objection concerning Abraham. Abraham your father rejoiced to see my day. This new absurdity irritates the adversaries even more; it mixes ages, his own and Abraham's. What is the meaning of this? But he says specifically: Abraham desired to see my day. Although he speaks of the preaching of victory and of the liberation of the human race, yet he also says concerning his own person: Abraham ardently desired to see both, this propitiator, and the very preaching of the Gospel, and the glory of the victory in the resurrection, and the triumph of Christ ascending into the heavens, where the Apostles saw the form of his kingdom, which will be after the resurrection. How, therefore, did Abraham see these things? I answer: He knew the person, that is, he knew the Son of God was to come in the flesh, and that this one is our propitiator and guardian; thus Jacob also knew the Son of God, who says: May God bless these boys, and the angel who delivered me from all evils. This angel, who delivers from all evils, is certainly the Son of God, our guardian and savior; the fathers knew this, and therefore the meeting is understood to be with the Son of God, when God appeared to Abraham in the valley of Mamre, where he received three men into hospitality, and worships one, namely, the Son of God walking among the angels. And we think too coldly about the promise given to Abraham, if we do not think that he considered how great a thing was promised. Abraham understood that not only was a worldly kingdom promised to him, since the promise says: In your seed shall all nations be blessed. The worldly government of the Israelite kingdom profited the other nations nothing, but Abraham knew that liberation from sin and from eternal death, and the restoration of eternal justice and life, had been promised. Thus, therefore, he saw the day of the coming Messiah; he understood the promise; he knew that the coming seed would be a sacrifice for sin, and that for his sake the remission of sins and eternal life were given; indeed, he even knew the Son of God himself, whom he had seen would come in the flesh. Hence, therefore, he rejoiced, because the acknowledgment of mercy promised for the sake of the Son delivers from sins and from eternal death, and brings eternal life, just as Paul says: Justified by faith we have peace toward God.

And Christ teaches in this place how all the heirs of eternal life were saved before Christ was born of the virgin. The Pharisees thought that all were saved by the discipline of the law, just as the monks also wrote, who invented three laws, and added that everyone was saved because of their own law. These ravings are to be execrated, and it must be known that there is one eternal law, which is the eternal judgment of God concerning sin. Adultery can never please God, nor does the sin of any man please him, but wrath falls upon the Son; for the sake of this one, the person fleeing to the Son is received. Therefore the law always argues and accused sins, nor was anyone saved because of that discipline. But in the same way all the heirs of eternal life were saved, by faith, that is, by trust in the mercy promised for the sake of the Messiah. These things were entirely unknown to the Pharisees, who only dreamed of a worldly empire, nor did they understand the promise concerning the blessing, nor did they think about what the acknowledgment of the Messiah had profited Abraham and all the fathers after the fall, from that time on from the beginning. Finally, they were entirely ignorant of the true doctrine concerning the Messiah.

Therefore let us remember this saying of Christ concerning the salvation of the fathers, to which corresponds the saying of Peter in Acts chapter 15: Why do you tempt God, by putting a yoke upon the neck of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear, but we believe that we are saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, just as they also? And so that we may understand gratuitous mercy more clearly, and stir up faith, let us look at the fathers before the law, sustaining themselves by the promise, not the law, just as Paul also proposes this saying to us with singular counsel: Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness. In this example he bids us look, and teaches us that we are received into grace, not because of the law, but by faith, that is, by trust in the mercy promised for the sake of the Messiah, just as Abraham was received. Nor is there any doubt that Christ in this narrative of the Evangelist looks back to that passage in Genesis, when he says of Abraham: He saw and rejoiced. This is clearly the same thing that is said in Genesis: He believed, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness. Even though this sentiment differed entirely from the dreams of the Pharisees.

Moreover, there are ardent affections in the words: Abraham desired to see my day, that is, he desired both to know me, and to see the glory of my coming, that is, the beginning of the eternal kingdom. He saw, that is, he knew me to be the Son of God, and that I would assume human nature from his own seed, he knew that I would be a victim, he saw that sin would be taken away, and the wrath of God appeased through me, and eternal life restored. Sustaining himself with this faith, he felt a new light kindled within him, the knowledge of God and eternal life. Thus he saw my day, that is, in himself, and he rejoiced.

Latin:

Nunquid tu maior es patre nostro Abraham?

Hic insigniter declarant Iudaei inscitiam suam, qui Messiam arbitrantur, non maiorem fore patre Abraham, nec intelligunt Abraham per Messiam liberatum esse a morte, denique prorsus ignorant beneficia Messiae, et tantum somniant suum illud mundanum regnum, repetit igitur Christus suas asseverationes de missione et de doctrina, et explicat obiectionem de Abraham. Abraham pater vester exultavit, ut videret diem meum. Haec nova absurditas magis etiam irritat ad- versarios, miscet aetates, suam et Abrahae. Quid hoc rei est? Sed nominatim dicit: Abraham optavit videre diem meum. Etsi de prae- dicatione victoriae et de liberatione generis hu- mani loquitur, tamen de sua persona etiam dicit: Abraham videre utrunque ardenter cupivit, hunc propiciatorem, et ipsam praedicationem Evange- lii, et gloriam victoriae in resurrectione, ac trium- phum Christi ascendentis in coelos, ubi Apostoli viderunt formam eius regni, quod erit post resur- rectionem. Quomodo igitur vidit haec Abraham? Re- spondeo: Personam novit, hoc est, novit filium Dei venturum in carnem, et hunc esse propicia- torem nostrum et custodem, sic norat filium Dei et Iacob, qui inquit: Benedicat pueris istis Deus, et angelus, qui eripuit me ex omnibus malis. Hic angelus, qui liberat ab omnibus malis, certe est filius Dei, custos et salvator noster, id norant patres, ideo et de filio Deo intelligitur congressus, cum apparuit Deus Abrahae in valle Mamre, ubi tres viros hospitio excipit, et unum adorat, vide- licet, inter angelos euntem filium Dei. Ac de promissione data Abrahae nimis fri- gide cogitamus, si non existimamus eum conside- rasse, quanta res promissa fuerit. Intelligebat Abraham non tantum sibi promitti regnum mun- danum, cum promissio dicat: In semine tuo be- nedicentur omnes gentes. Gubernatio mundana regni Israëlitici nihil proderat caeteris gentibus, sed sciebat Abraham promissam esse liberationem a peccato et a morte aeterna, et restitutionem aeternae iusticiae et vitae. Sic igitur vidit diem venturi Messiae, intellexit promissionem, sciebat venturum semen fore hostiam pro peccato, et pro- pter ipsum dari remissionem peccatorum et vi- tam aeternam, imo norat etiam ipsum filium Dei, quem viderat venturum in carnem. Hinc igitur laetatus est, quia agnitio misericordiae propter filium promissae, liberat a peccatis et a morte aeterna, et affert vitam aeternam, sicut Paulus inquit: Fide iustificati pacem habemus erga Deum.

Ac docet hoc loco Christus, quomodo salvati sint omnes haeredes vitae aeternae, antequam Christus ex virgine natus est. Pharisaei putabant omnes disciplina legis salvatos esse, sicut scripse- runt et Monachi, qui finxerunt tres leges, et ad- diderunt unumquemque salvatum esse propter suam legem. Haec deliramenta execranda sunt, ac sciendum unam esse legem aeternam, quae est iudicium aeternum Dei de peccato. Nunquam potest Deo placere adulterium Davidis, nec placet ullius hominis peccatum, sed ira incurrit in filium, propter hunc recipitur persona confugiens ad filium. Semper igitur lex arguit, et accusavit peccata, nec quisquam propter disciplinam illam salvatus est. Sed eodem modo salvati sunt omnes haeredes vitae aeternae, fide, id est, fiducia mi- sericordiae propter Messiam promissae. Haec prorsus ignota fuerunt Pharisaeis, qui tantum somniabant mundanum imperium, nec intellige- bant promissionem de benedictione, nec cogita- bant quid Abrahae et omnibus patribus post lapsum inde usque ab initio profuisset agnitio Messiae. Denique prorsus ignorabant veram de Messia doctrinam.

Hoc igitur dictum Christi meminerimus, de salvatione patrum, ad quod congruit dictum Petri in Actis capite 15.: Quid tentatis Deum, impo- nentes iugum super collum discipulorum, quod neque patres nostri, neque nos portare potuimus, sed gratia domini Iesu Christi credimus salvari, sicut et ipsi, et ut nos gratuitam misericordiam clarius intelligamus, et fidem excitemus, intuea- mur patres ante legem, sustentantes se promis- sione, non lege, sicut et Paulus nobis singulari consilio hoc dictum proponit: Credidit Abraham Deo, et imputatum est ei ad iusticiam. In hoc exemplum intueri nos iubet, et docet nos recipi in gratiam, non propter legem, sed fide, id est, fiducia misericordiae propter Messiam promissae, sicut Abraham receptus est. Nec dubium est quin Christus in hac narratione Evangelistae ad illum locum in Genesi respiciat, cum ait de Abraham: Vidit et laetatus est. Hoc plane idem est, quod in Genesi dicitur: Credidit, et imputatum est ei ad iusticiam. Etsi haec sententia a somniis Phari- saeorum prorsus discrepabat.

Sunt autem in verbis ardentes affectus: Abraham optavit videre diem meum, id est, opta- vit et me nosse, et mei adventus gloriam, id est, incoationem regni aeterni videre. Vidit, id est, novit me filium Dei, et assumturum humanam na- turam ex ipsius semine, scivit me futurum victi- mam, vidit tolli peccatum, et placari iram Dei per me, et restitui vitam aeternam. Hac fide se sustentans, sensit accendi in se novam lucem, agnitionem Dei et vitam aeternam. Sic vidit diem meum, id est, me, et regni mei beneficia in seipso, et laetatus est.

## 8:57
You are not yet fifty years old, etc.

But this new discourse irritates the raging Jews all the more, ignorant of who the Messiah is, and what kind of kingdom it is, and what the benefits are. They demand an explanation, therefore, regarding the absurdity, whether he had seen Abraham, who had died almost two thousand years before. By this very objection, they show that they do not understand what the Messiah profited the fathers, and all those born before that kingdom, which they were dreaming of. Christ therefore adds a new assertion: Before Abraham was born, I am, and indeed he swears twice: Amen, amen. The words are plain, and have always been understood in the Church in this way, that there are two natures in Christ, of which one, namely the λόγος, is coeternal with God the Father, as was said above in chapter 1. Therefore Christ says that he existed before Abraham was born. And this testimony is to be diligently observed among those which are preached concerning the two natures in Christ, so that it may be in sight among the rest, for confirming the faith for us and others, in the defense of dogmas and in invocation.

Although it seems rather clever to dispute subtly about the manner of speaking, that he says, I am: yet I think it is not without cause that it is said thus, and that there is an allusion to the statement in Exodus chapter 3, where to Moses asking about the name of God, it is answered: I am who I am, he who is, has sent me to you, and it is added: The God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob has sent me to you, this is my name forever, and my memorial from generation to generation. Why does Moses ask about the name? So that he might bring some testimony of his revelation. Therefore, a most salutary doctrine is delivered in that place; that God who speaks with Moses testifies that he is truly God. He who is, that is, he who alone is truly God, the others are not gods, and this God is truly eternal essence, omnipotent, not subject to any corruption, and the creator of things, which are all by their nature weak and languid, and could not endure unless they were preserved by God. Then he teaches how this true God wishes to be acknowledged, this one, I say, who alone is, is to be distinguished from fictitious gods, and is to be distinguished by this title, that he is the God of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob etc., that is, that God who delivered his word to them, by which he wishes to be acknowledged and distinguished from fictitious gods.

Therefore the Church must often be warned to learn to distinguish its invocation from the Heathen, Jewish, and Mahometan. For all the wise men of all sects say that they invoke some one eternal mind, the creator of things, but yet they do not truly invoke it. For they err in two ways: First concerning the essence, afterwards concerning being heard. They err concerning the essence, because they do not want to acknowledge, believe, and confess that this is truly God, who revealed himself through his son Jesus Christ, but they invent for themselves an unknown God, having rejected this true God, who truly is. Then they doubt concerning being heard; they cannot invoke, since they remain entirely in doubt, nor do they believe that they are forgiven, or that they are heard.
