Let us therefore distinguish our invocation, and direct it to this God, who, as is said here: Truly is, that is, let us know that the gods of other sects are nothing, but that this one is truly God, the creator of all things, who revealed himself through this word, which he delivered in the beginning to the fathers and Prophets, and through his son Jesus Christ. Just as it is said here in a clear and remarkable description, that this title, God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, would be an everlasting memorial. A remarkable revelation and promise is contained in these words: God testifies that he will perpetually preserve this one and the same word, which he delivered to the fathers; therefore the Church of the fathers is always to remain.

Then also in this part let us distinguish, as often as we invoke, let us think why we are heard, namely on account of the son, wherefore some such form of invocation should be thought of. I invoke you omnipotent, eternal and living God, eternal father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who revealed yourself with immense goodness, and proclaimed concerning your son our Lord Jesus Christ: creator of all things and preserver, with your coeternal son our Lord Jesus Christ and your Holy Spirit, poured out upon the Apostles, wise, good, merciful, judge, strong, have mercy on me on account of Jesus Christ your son, whom you willed to be for us a victim, mediator, intercessor and our advocate, and sanctify and rule me by your Holy Spirit, rule your Church and governments etc. I often think that this too is signified by this description. He who is, that is, the Son of God himself, who has already been promised to you before: This same one has now sent me, this same one will also be the liberator. Nor is it far from this interpretation what others explain, urging the verb of future tense. I will be who I will be, that is, I, that liberator promised to you, will be present, who some time later will be your brother, having assumed human nature, and I will truly free you from sin and from death, and rising from death among you in the flesh, I will initiate an eternal kingdom. This interpretation, concerning the Son of God speaking and signifying his future advent, simultaneously admonishes the listener about the divine nature in Christ, and aptly corresponds to the promises, as if he were saying: Why do you doubt about the liberation? I will be who I will be, that is, I, since I have promised that I will be your brother, and bone of your bones, and that I will gather for myself an eternal Church, will now also be present, I will save you, so that this tyrant does not oppress you: I, that very God, who later will be your brother, am now about to be present. Thus that also will square: He who will be, has sent me, that is, that liberator of ours who will be our brother having assumed flesh, who has been promised to you, has sent me. I have reviewed the pious interpretations of the passage in Moses, from which the reader may choose whichever he wishes, even though they are all close, but the last one is more suitable to the person of Christ.

Latin:

Quinquaginta annos nondum habes, etc.

Sed haec nova concio magis irritat furentes Iudaeos, ignorantes quis sit Messias, et quale sit regnum, et quae sint beneficia. Expostulant igi- tur de absurditate, num viderit Abraham, qui fere ante duo millia annorum mortuus fuerat. Hac ipsa obiectione ostendunt se non intelligere quid Messias profuerit patribus, et omnibus ante regnum illud natis, quod somniabant. Addit igi- tur Christus novam asseverationem: Antequam nasceretur Abraham, ego sum, et quidem bis iu- rat: Amen, amen. Verba plana sunt, et semper in Ecclesia sic intellecta, in Christo duas esse na- turas, quarum altera, scilicet λόγος, est coaeterna Deo patri, ut supra in 1. cap. dictum est. Ideo Christus inquit, se fuisse ante natum Abraham. Estque hoc testimonium inter ea, quae de duabus naturis in Christo concionantur, diligenter obser- vandum, ut sit in conspectu inter caetera, ad con- firmandam fidem nobis et aliis, in dogmatum de- fensione et invocatione.

Etsi autem videtur argutius, subtiliter dispu- tare de modo loquendi, quod ait, sum: tamen opinor non sine causa sic dici, et alludi ad dictum in Exod. cap. 3., ubi Mosi de nomine Dei inter- roganti, respondetur: Sum qui sum, qui est, mi- sit me ad vos, et additur: Deus pater vestrorum, Deus Abraham, Deus Isaac, et Deus Iacob misit me ad vos, hoc est, nomen meum in aeternum, et memoriale meum in generationem et generatio- nem. Cur quaerit Moses de nomine? ut afferat testimonium aliquod suae revelationis. Traditur ergo doctrina maxime salutaris eo loco, testatur ille Deus, qui cum Mose loquitur, se vere Deum esse. Qui est, id est, is qui unus est vere Deus, caeteri non sunt dii, et hic Deus vere est essentia aeterna, omnipotens, non obnoxia ulli corruptio- ni, ac conditrix rerum, quae omnes natura sua sunt imbecilles et languidae, nec possent durare, nisi a Deo conservarentur. Deinde docet, quo- modo hic verus Deus velit agnosci, hic inquam, qui solus est, discernendus est a ficticiis diis, et hoc titulo discernendus, quod sit Deus Abrahae, Isaac, Iacob etc., id est, ille Deus, qui ipsis ver- bum suum tradidit, quo agnosci vult et discerni a ficticiis diis.

Ideo saepe monenda est Ecclesia, ut discat discernere suam invocationem ab Ethnica, Iudai- ca, et Mahometica. Nam omnes sapientes omnium sectarum dicunt, se invocare unam aliquam aeter- nam mentem, conditricem rerum, sed tamen non vere invocant. Errant enim dupliciter: Primum de essentia, postea de exauditione. De essentia errant, quia nolunt agnoscere, credere et fateri hunc esse vere Deum, qui se patefecit per filium Iesum Christum, sed fingunt sibi Deum ignotum, reiecto hoc vero Deo, qui vere est. Deinde de exauditione dubitant, non possunt invocare, cum prorsus maneant in dubitatione, nec credant sibi ignosci, aut se exaudiri. Nos igitur discernamus nostram invocationem, et dirigamus eam ad hunc Deum, qui, ut hic dicitur: Vere est, id est, scia- mus aliarum sectarum Deos nihil esse, sed hunc vere esse Deum, conditorem omnium rerum, qui se patefecit per hoc verbum, quod initio tradidit patribus et Prophetis, et per filium suum Iesum Christum. Sicut hic luculenta et insigni descri- ptione dictum est, hunc titulum, Deus Abraham, Deus Iacob, Deus Isaac, fore sempiternum memo- riale. Insignis revelatio et promissio continetur in his verbis: Deus testatur se perpetuo servatu- rum esse hoc unum et idem verbum, quod patri- bus tradidit, semper ergo patrum Ecclesia man- sura est.

Deinde et hac parte discernamus, quoties in- vocamus, cogitemus cur exaudiamur, scilicet propter filium, quare talis aliqua forma invocatio- nis cogitetur. Invoco te omnipotens, aeterne et vive Deus, aeterne pater domini nostri Iesu Chri- sti, qui te immensa bonitate patefecisti, et clama- sti de filio tuo domino nostro Iesu Christo: con- ditor omnium rerum et conservator, cum filio tuo coaeterno domino nostro Iesu Christo et Spiritu S. tuo, effuso in Apostolos, sapiens, bone, mi- sericors, iudex, fortis, miserere mei propter Ie- sum Christum filium tuum, quem voluisti pro no- bis esse victimam, mediatorem, interpellatorem et deprecatorem nostrum, et sanctifica ac rege me Spiritu Sancto tuo, rege Ecclesiam tuam et po- litias etc. Saepe et hoc cogito hac descriptione signifi- cari. Qui est, id est, illius ipse filius Dei, qui iam ante vobis est promissus: Idem hic iam misit me, hic idem iam quoque liberator erit. Nec ab hac interpretatione procul abest, quod alii enar- rant, futuri temporis vocem urgentes. Ego ero qui ero, id est, ego ille promissus vobis liberator adero, qui aliquanto post ero frater vester, as- sumta humana natura, et vos vere liberabo a pec- cato et a morte, et inter vos in carne resurgens a morte, regnum aeternum incoabo. Haec inter- pretatio de filio Dei loquente et significante futu- rum adventum, simul admonet auditorem de na- tura divina in Christo, et apte congruit ad pro- missiones, quasi dicat: Quid dubitas de libera- tione? Ego ero qui ero, id est, ego cum promi- serim me futurum fratrem vestrum, et os ex ossi- bus vestris, et collecturum mihi Ecclesiam aeter- nam, nunc etiam adero, vos servabo, ne hic ty- rannus vos opprimat: Ego ille ipse Deus, qui po- stea ero frater vester, nunc affuturus sum. Sic quadrabit et illud: Qui erit, misit me, id est, ille noster liberator qui erit frater noster assumta carne, qui vobis promissus est, misit me. Re- censui interpretationes loci in Mose pias, ex qui- bus deligat lector, quam volet, etsi vicinae sunt omnes, sed postrema accommodatior est ad Chri- sti personam.

## 8:59
They took up stones therefore.

This is the outcome of disputes in the Church: For the defeated impious ones rage all the more, just as Isaiah 6 says: Hear and hear, and do not understand, blind the heart of this people, and Psalm 68: Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see. It is truly a terrible spectacle that the greatest and seemingly most excellent part of the human race is driven by such furies; that it opposes the manifest voice of God against its conscience, they see in Christ, the Prophets, and the Apostles, manifest testimonies of God, and yet they resist, and not only do they resist, but they even attempt to remove the teachers from the midst, just as here they take up stones to overwhelm Christ. But let us learn these two things: first, although many oppose, yet it is necessary that some embrace the Gospel, just as it is written in Isaiah 55: My word shall not return to me void, etc. And many sayings testify that some Church will always remain, as in Isaiah 59: This is my covenant with them, says the Lord: My spirit which is in you, and my words, which I have put in your mouth, shall not depart from your mouth, nor from the mouth of your seed, forever. This promise testifies that there will always be some Church. And indeed it expressly defines this assembly to be that in whose mouth is the word handed down through the Prophets, and in whom is the spirit speaking through the Prophets. Therefore the preaching of the Gospel is not in vain; there will always be some who will embrace the word, just as it is said in Romans 9: A remnant shall be saved, that is, a part of the people, neither the greatest, nor excelling in power, honors, or wealth. This sentiment is adorned with an illustrious figure. Amos 3: Thus says the Lord, As a shepherd rescues from the mouth of the lion two legs, or the tip of an ear, so shall the children of Israel be delivered.

The other thing which this passage warns is that Christ often escaped from the hands of the Jews, nor could he be dragged to execution before it was divinely ordained. We are admonished that the Church is guarded divinely. Although therefore God wills that some be taken away like soldiers from the battle line, yet he preserves them so that they may first complete their course: Paul was often preserved when he was closer to death than when Nero ordered him to be killed; the beasts in the circus spared him, but he allowed him to be killed at last by Nero, a beast much worse than any wild animals, so that he might show a notable testimony of the future judgment. God had shown before by many miracles that Paul was pleasing to him, and it was established that Nero was polluted with the most shameful crimes of all. Since therefore he was killed while pleasing to God, by such a monster, it is an evident argument that another judgment remains, in which God will show that he has not forgotten Paul, whom he had previously approved, and that Paul is loved by him, but Nero is cast into horrendous punishments.

But as Paul had often been preserved before, so let us know that the whole Church is preserved, not by the human counsels of princes, but miraculously by God, as very many sayings testify. Psalm 71: He has delivered the poor from the powerful, the poor who had no helper, and Hosea 1: I will save them in the Lord their God, and I will not save them by bow and sword. And now let us especially set before ourselves such sayings and corresponding examples, because we clearly see that human protections are lacking to the Churches everywhere, and elsewhere the Turks, elsewhere other kings, exercise cruelty against the Churches. In these miseries and consolation let us sustain ourselves, that God will nevertheless preserve a remnant, just as it is promised in Daniel concerning this very time:

At that time Michael the great prince shall stand, for the children of his people.

Latin:

Tulerunt ergo lapides.

Hic disputationum in Ecclesia exitus est: Victi enim impii magis insaniunt, sicut inquit Esa. 6.: Audite audientes, et nolite intelligere, excaeca cor populi huius, et Psal. 68.: Obscuren- tur oculi eorum, ne videant. Terribile profecto spectaculum est, quod maxima et in speciem prae- stantissima pars generis humani talibus furiis agi- tatur; ut manifestae voci Dei contra conscientiam adversetur, vident in Christo, Prophetis et Apo- stolis, manifesta Dei testimonia, et tamen repu- gnant, nec tantum repugnant, sed etiam e medio tollere doctores conantur, sicut hic lapides tollunt ad obruendum Christum. Sed duo haec discamus, primum etsi multi adversantur, tamen aliquos amplecti Evangelium necesse est, sicut scriptum est Esaiae 55.: Verbum meum non revertetur ad vacuum, etc. Et semper mansuram esse aliquam Ecclesiam, multa dicta testantur, ut Esaiae 59.: Hoc foedus meum cum eis, dicit dominus: Spiri- tus meus qui est in te, et verba mea, quae posui in ore tuo, non recedent ab ore tuo, nec ab ore seminis tui, in sempiternum. Haec promissio testatur semper aliquam futuram esse Ecclesiam. Et quidem eam expresse definit hunc coetum esse, in cuius ore sit verbum traditum per Prophetas, et in quibus sit spiritus loquens per Prophetas. Non igitur inanis est Evangelii praedicatio, sem- per erunt aliqui, qui amplectentur verbum, sicut Rom. 9. dicitur: Reliquiae salvae fient, id est, pars populi, nec maxima, nec antecellens poten- tia, honoribus, opibus. Haec sententia illustri figura ornata est. Amos 3.: Haec dicit Dominus, Sicut eruit pastor ex faucibus leonis duo crura, et extremam auriculae, sic liberabuntur filii Israël.

Alterum est, quod hic locus monet, quod Christus saepe evasit ex manibus Iudaeorum, nec prius ad supplicium rapi potuit, quam divinitus constitutum erat. Admonemur Ecclesiam custo- diri divinitus. Quanquam igitur vult Deus ali- quos, tanquam milites ex acie absumi, tamen hos servat, ut prius curriculum suum absolvant: Saepe erat servatus Paulus, cum propior morti fuit, quam cum Nero eum iussit interfici, peper- cerunt ei bestiae in circo, at a Nerone bellua multo deteriore, quam ullae ferae erant, permi- sit eum tandem interfici, ut testimonium insigne ostenderet futuri iudicii. Ostenderat Deus antea multis miraculis, sibi placere Paulum, et consta- bat Neronem pollutum esse sceleribus omnium turpissimis. Cum igitur interficeretur Deo pla- cens, a tali portento, evidens argumentum est, restare aliud iudicium, in quo Deus ostendet, se non oblitum esse Pauli, quem antea approbave- rat, et a se Paulum diligi, Neronem vero in hor- rendas poenas abiici.

Ut autem Paulus antea saepe servatus erat, sic sciamus totam Ecclesiam servari, non humanis consiliis principum, sed a Deo mirabiliter, sicut plurima dicta testantur. Psalm. 71.: Liberavit pauperem a potente, pauperem, cui non erat ad- iutor, et Oseae 1.: Salvabo eos in domino Deo suo, et non salvabo eos in arcu et gladio. Ac nunc maxime proponamus nobis huiusmodi dicta et exempla congruentia, quia manifeste videmus Ecclesiis passim deesse praesidia humana, et alibi Turcos, alibi alios reges exercere saevitiam in Ec- clesias. In his aerumnis ac consolatione nos sus- tentemus, Deum tamen servaturum esse reliquias, sicut in Daniele de hoc ipso tempore promittitur:

In tempore illo stabit Michaël dux magnus, pro filiis populi sui.

## 9:1 Argument
Chapter IX. Neither this man has sinned.

This history is placed between the feast of tabernacles and the ἐγκαίνια of the last year of Christ's preaching. Now the ἐγκαίνια were on the 25th of November, as I shall say below, and it is useful to consider those times, so that we may observe that as the conflict gradually increased, hatreds and furies grew among the impious. But the first discussion in this place arises concerning this saying: Neither this man has sinned, nor his parents. Here many things are asked. Whether children are punished for the sins of their parents. Next, whether all calamities are punishments for sin, and particular punishments for particular offenses. Finally, whether Christ pronounces that these were without sin. I shall speak in order concerning the individual questions.

The Decalogue clearly testifies that because of the offenses of parents, descendants are also punished, and it speaks of punishments in this life; thus it is said also in Deut. 28: If you will not hear the voice of the Lord your God etc., cursed shall be the fruit of your womb, likewise your sons and your daughters shall be given to a foreign people. The tender and delicate woman shall begrudge her husband, her sons and her daughters the flesh and the filth of the afterbirth, and Psalm 108: Let his children be beggars, and let them be cast out from their dwellings. Examples are gathered here. Because of the crimes of Saul, the whole family and posterity was destroyed, except for the son of Jonathan; indeed, even the holy man Jonathan, a stranger to his father's crime, God nevertheless willed to be killed together with them: because of David's adultery, slaughters raged for a long time among his sons: because of Solomon's idols, his son loses the greatest part of the kingdom. Finally, there are many examples in the scriptures, and they can be seen daily in life: how many splendid families perish because of the lusts of their ancestors, or other crimes. Rightly, therefore, the Apostles ask: Who sinned, he himself, or his parents? For it is true that the crimes of parents are punished by the calamities of their children. Conversely, children born of them are also adorned with rewards for the good deeds of their parents, as the posterity of Jonathan remained until the time of the Babylonian exile.

But why is this sentiment retracted in Ezekiel chapter 18? The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the children's teeth are set on edge. I answer: The discourse of Ezekiel is the voice of the Gospel, announcing the remission of sin. The Law always threatens punishments for our sins and those of our parents, and when we do not repent, the judgment of the Law remains, the wrath of God remains, and we are oppressed by punishments both eternal and present. But Ezekiel proposes the voice of the Gospel: if you repent, neither will eternal punishments oppress you, and present punishments will be mitigated or removed. This is a simple and true reconciliation. It is useful, however, to think diligently on this doctrine and the examples concerning punishments, so that, having considered the magnitude of the wrath of God and of the punishments, we may with greater care avoid sins, lest we heap miseries upon our children, as happens very often, even if the profane and secure world neither sees nor fears this cause of calamities. The second question [requires] a more lengthy discussion: whether human calamities are universally punishments for sin, and whether there are particular punishments for particular offenses. I answer: Although this sentiment is universally true: that death and all calamities are punishments for original sin, nevertheless, the degrees of calamities afterwards have many other causes: that Isaiah, Jeremiah, and John the Baptist were killed, the general cause is that they had original sin. But that they were subjected to huge hardships above other men, this degree has many other causes, which must be diligently gathered. For human reason and philosophy, when it contemplates the magnitude of human miseries, indeed wonders that this excellent nature has been oppressed by such a sad burden, and seeks the causes, but cannot detect the principal ones, and it is the proper doctrine of the Church to show the causes of human evils and the true remedies. Philosophers argue that the flux of matter, as in plants and cattle, so in the human race, is the cause of generations and corruptions, and of diseases. But the divine voice testifies that the human race was created otherwise, namely, so that it would live without sin and death in an admirable way, but that the first parents voluntarily admitted sin, to which this huge punishment was proposed, that afterwards the nature of men, having lost its former light and integrity, would be subject to sin and death. Concerning other calamities, Philosophers say that they arise either from matter, or are brought on by the errors and will of men. As Alexander, by drinking, brings destruction upon himself; they rightly see some proximate causes in some things, but they are ignorant of the sources: why Alexander is mortal, why such excellence of intellect is so prone to vices. Likewise, many fall into calamities, not through any error of their own, or petulance, like Jeremiah, John the Baptist, etc. Here philosophy also accuses the judgment of God, wondering why He allows the good to be torn apart by the wicked. Let us therefore listen to the Church discoursing on the causes of human miseries, so that we may consider both the wrath of God and true consolations, and that the catalog may always be in sight.

The first cause is the common sin of the human race, on account of which all men are universally subject to death, diseases, and many common evils.

The second cause, since the world does not acknowledge that disease, and the contempt of God, and the wrath against this evil, God presses the Church more, so that it may acknowledge these evils, and that we may be called to repentance.

The third cause, because the devil rages more furiously against the Church.

The fourth, God wishes the recognition of our infirmity to grow in us, and our confidence in ourselves to be laid aside, and the invocation of God to be kindled; therefore He exercises the saints more, as in 2 Corinthians 1: We had the sentence of death in ourselves, that we should not be confident in our own strength, but should invoke God. God also wishes His power against the devil to be seen in our infirmity.

The fifth, that afflictions may be a testimony of immortality and future glory. For because God allows Jeremiah, the Baptist, Paul, and the like, whom He had previously testified were of concern to Him, to be killed here by tyrants, it is necessary that another judgment remain, in which it may again appear that these are also of concern to God after death, and that the tyrants are punished.

The sixth, that afflictions may be testimonies of doctrine. For because the saints prefer confession to their own life, it appears that they seriously feel this way.

The seventh, that we may be made similar to the image of the Son of God; thus Abel, Isaac, Isaiah, Jeremiah, the Baptist, were types of Christ.

The eighth, often afflictions are punishments for certain offenses, such as the exiles of David and Manasseh, and the disease of the Babylonian king.

The ninth, that it may appear that the saints perform obedience, not for the sake of their own pleasure, but on account of God.

The tenth, that the Church may know that it does not rely on human defenses, but has God as its guardian, as Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Jonah, and Paul, when they carry about the word of God, experience in their wanderings that they are divinely protected. It is profitable to always have these causes in sight, so that we may learn according to this saying of Peter: Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, etc., and that our obedience in afflictions pleases God, and that we are not rejected on account of calamities, but rather are then drawn to God, and that the chief end of all miseries is that we may be stirred to invocation, and faith may be confirmed, and God may be celebrated in deliverances.

Now therefore the answer to the question in this text is easy: Christ does not say this: That the parents and the blind man were without sin, but that the blindness was not the punishment of a specific crime in them. For although calamities are often punishments for specific crimes, as has been said concerning David and Manasseh, yet they are not always such punishments, as God Himself excuses Job. And even if they are punishments, yet we should not think only of wrath and punishment, but much more of the further end, that is, of invocation, of faith, of the glorification of God. David understands that he has been deformed by such great miseries on account of his lapses, and he submits himself to God who punishes, but he does not resist in this thought of wrath, but knows he is being admonished concerning repentance, concerning invocation, concerning faith, concerning the glorification of God, because he is not overwhelmed by such great miseries, nor is he utterly deserted, just as Saul had been deserted.

So also Christ in this place shows the Apostles these reasons, that care must be taken that our affliction may serve the glory of God, both in enduring and in proclaiming deliverance. David does not commit suicide, as Saul did, although he was in greater calamity, but he sets forth his miseries without notable deformity, meanwhile he both calls upon God and shows constancy of mind, because he governs a huge war with his counsels. The sight of these virtues adorned the glory of God, and David himself gave thanks to God, because he felt himself to be sustained.

But afterwards the presence of God was more visible in the deliverance, and many testified that God is present to those who call upon Him, many gave thanks to God, thus Paul in 2 Corinthians 1 exhorts that he be helped by the prayers of many, so that thanksgiving by many may again be offered to God. These forms of worship are unknown to human reason, but the Church ought to learn them from the word of God, namely obedience in miseries, invocation, faith, hope of help or deliverance, and thanksgiving, and celebration of the mercy of God, as the Psalm says: Call upon me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me etc.

Latin:

Caput IX. Neque hic peccavit.

Haec historia inter festum tabernaculorum et ἐγκαίνια postremi anni praedicationis Christi collocatur. Fuerunt autem ἐγκαίνια die 25. No- vemb. ut infra dicam, ac prodest ea considerare tempora, ut observemus paulatim crescente cer- tamine, in impiis odia et furores crevisse. Prima autem in hoc loco disputatio oritur de hoc dicto: Neque hic peccavit, neque parentes eius. Hic multa quaeruntur. Num filii propter parentum peccata plectantur. Deinde, sintne calamitates omnes poenae peccati, et peculiarium delictorum peculiares poenae. Postremo, an Christus pro- nunciet hos sine peccato fuisse. Dicam ordine de singulis quaestionibus.

Decalogus manifeste testatur propter delicta parentum etiam posteros plecti, et loquitur de poenis in hac vita, sic dicitur et Deut. 28.: Si non audieris vocem domini Dei tui etc., maledictus fructus ventris tui, item filii tui et filiae tuae tradentur alieno populo. Tenera mulier et deli- cata invidebit viro suo, filii et filiae carnes, et il- luviem secundinae, et Psalm. 108.: Filii eius mendicent, et eiiciantur de habitationibus suis. Huc colligantur exempla. Propter Saulis scelera tota familia et posteritas deleta est, praeter filium Ionathae, imo et virum sanctum Ionathan alie- num a paterno scelere, tamen una interfici Deus voluit: propter Davidis adulterium diu grassatae sunt caedes inter filios: propter Salomonis idola filius amittit maximam regni partem. Denique exempla in scripturis multa sunt, et cerni quoti- die in vita possunt: quam multae splendidae fa- miliae pereunt propter maiorum libidines, aut alia scelera. Recte igitur Apostoli quaerunt: Quis peccavit, ipse, an parentes? Verum est enim puniri scelera parentum calamitatibus filio- rum. Rursus etiam pro benefactis parentum or- nari praemiis natos ex eis, ut manet Ionathae po- steritas usque ad tempus exilii Babylonici.

Sed cur apud Ezechielem cap. 18. retracta- tur haec sententia? Patres comederunt uvam acerbam, et dentes filiorum obstupuerunt. Re- spondeo: Ezechielis concio est vox Evangelii, an- nuncians remissionem peccati. Lex semper mi- natur poenas pro nostris et parentum peccatis, et cum non agimus poenitentiam, manet iudicium legis, manet ira Dei, et opprimimur poenis tum aeternis, tum praesentibus. Sed Ezechiel pro- ponit vocem Evangelii, si egeris poenitentiam, nec poenae aeternae oppriment te, et mitigabun- tur vel tollentur poena praesentes. Haec est sim- plex et vera conciliatio. Prodest autem hanc do- ctrinam et exempla de poenis diligenter cogitare, ut considerata magnitudine irae Dei et poenarum, maiore cura vitemus peccata, ne nostris liberis miserias cumulemus, ut fit saepissime, etsi mun- dus profanus et securus hanc causam calamitatum nec videt nec metuit. Secunda quaestio prolixiorem disputationem, sintne calamitates humanae universaliter poenae peccati, et an peculiares poenae sint peculiarium delictorum. Respondeo: Etsi universaliter vera est haec sententia: Mortem et omnes calamitates poenas esse peccati originalis, tamen postea gra- dus calamitatum habent alias plures causas: quod Esaias, Ieremias, Ioannes Baptista sunt inter- fecti, generalis causa est quia habuerunt peccatum originis. Sed quod supra caeteros homines sub- iecti fuerunt ingentibus aerumnis, hic gradus ha- bet alias causas multas, quae diligenter colligen- dae sunt. Nam humana ratio et philosophia, cum intueatur magnitudinem humanarum mise- riarum, miratur quidem hanc praestantem natu- ram tam tristi onere oppressam esse, et causas quaerit, sed praecipuas non potest deprehendere, estque propria Ecclesiae doctrina, causas huma- norum malorum et vera remedia ostendere. Phi- losophi disserunt fluxum materiae, ut in plantis et pecudibus, sic in genere humano, causam esse generationum et corruptionum, et morborum. Sed vox divina testatur, humanum genus aliter fuisse conditum, videlicet ita, ut sine peccato et morte viveret admirando modo, sed primos pa- rentes ultro peccatum admisisse, cui proposita fuit haec ingens poena, ut postea hominum na- tura amissa priori luce et integritate, obnoxia es- set peccato et morti. De caeteris calamitatibus Philosophi dicunt, eas aut ex materia oriri, aut accersi erroribus ac voluntate hominum. Ut Alexander volens, sibi potando accersit exitium, rect aliquas proximas causas in aliquibus cernunt, sed fontes ignorant, cur Alexander sit mortalis, cur tanta ingenii praestantia tam prona sit ad vi- tia. Item, multi incidunt in calamitates, non errore aliquo suo, aut petulantia, ut Ieremias, Ioannes Baptista, etc. Hic philosophia etiam accusat iudicium Dei, miratur cur bonos lacerari a malis sinat. Nos igitur audiamus Ecclesiam de causis aerumnarum humanarum concionantem, ut et iram Dei et veras consolationes considere- mus, et catalogus semper sit in conspectu.

Prima causa est peccatum commune generis humani, propter quod omnes homines universa- liter subiecti sunt morti, morbis et multis ma- lis communibus.

Secunda causa, cum mundus non agnoscat illum morbum, et contemtum Dei, et iram ad- versus hoc malum, Deus magis premit Ecclesiam, ut agnoscat haec mala, et ut vocemur ad poeni- tentiam.

Tertia causa, quia diabolus rabiosius saevit in Ecclesiam.

Quarta, vult Deus crescere in nobis agnitio- nem infirmitatis nostrae, et deponi fiduciam no- stri, et accendi invocationem Dei, ideo magis exercet sanctos, ut 2. Corinth. 1.: Responsum mortis in nobis habuimus, ne essemus confiden- tes nostra virtute, sed invocaremus Deum. Vult etiam conspici Deus in nostra infirmitate suam potentiam adversus diabolum.

Quinta, ut afflictiones sint testimonium im- mortalitatis et futurae gloriae. Quia enim hic sinit a tyrannis Deus interfici, Ieremiam, Bapti- stam, Paulum, et similes, quos antea testatus est sibi curae esse, necesse est restare aliud iudicium, in quo rursus appareat hos etiam post mortem Deo curae esse, et puniri tyrannos.

Sexta, ut afflictiones sint testimonia doctri- nae. Quia enim sancti anteferunt confessionem suae vitae, apparet eos serio sic sentire.

Septima, ut efficiamur similes imaginis filii Dei, sic Abel, Isaac, Esaias, Ieremias, Bapti- sta, fuerunt typi Christi.

Octava, saepe afflictiones sunt poenae certo- rum delictorum, ut Davidis, Manassae exilia, regis Babylonici morbus.

Nona, ut appareat sanctos obedientiam prae- stare, non suae voluptatis causa, sed propter Deum.

Decima, ut Ecclesia sciat se non humanis praesidiis niti, sed habere custodem Deum, ut Abraham, Isaac, Iacob, Ionas, Paulus, cum circumferunt verbum Dei, in suis peregrinationi- bus experiuntur se divinitus protegi. Has causas prodest semper in conspectu habere, ut discamus iuxta hoc dictum Petri: Humiliamini sub potenti manu Dei etc., et Deo placere obedientiam no- stram in afflictionibus, et nos non reiectos esse propter calamitates, sed potius tunc trahi ad Deum, et praecipuum finem omnium aerumna- rum esse, ut excitemur ad invocationem, et con- firmetur fides, et in liberationibus celebretur Deus.

Nunc igitur facilis est responsio ad quaestio- nem in hoc textu: Christus non hoc dicit: Pa- rentes et caecum sine peccato fuisse, sed caecita- tem non esse poenam certi sceleris in istis. Etsi enim saepe calamitates sunt poenae certorum sce- lerum, ut de Davide et Manasse dictum est, ta- men non semper tales poenae sunt, ut Deus ipse excusat Iob. Et ut maxime sint poenae, tamen nos non tantum de ira et poena cogitemus, sed multo magis de fine ulteriore, id est, de invoca- tione, de fide, de glorificatione Dei. David in- telligit se tantis miseriis propter lapsus suos de- formatum esse, ac subiicit se Deo punienti, sed non resistit in hac cogitatione irae, sed scit ad- moneri de poenitentia, de invocatione, de fide, de glorificatione Dei, quod tantis aerumnis non opprimitur, nec prorsus deseritur, sicut Saul de- sertus erat.

Ita et Christus hoc loco Apostolis ostendit has causas, curandum esse, ut nostra afflictio serviat gloriae Dei, cum in tolerando, tum in praedicanda liberatione. David non consciscit sibi mortem, ut Saul, etsi erat in maiore calami- tate, sed praefert sine insigni deformitate suas ae- rumnas, interim et Deum invocat, et animi con- stantiam ostendit, quod bellum ingens suis con- siliis gubernat. Harum virtutum conspectus or- nabat gloriam Dei, et agebat Deo gratias ipse Da- vid, quod sustentari se sentiebat.

Postea vero in liberatione magis conspecta est praesentia Dei, et multi testificati sunt, Deum adesse invocantibus ipsum, multi egerunt gratias Deo, sic Paulus 2. Corinth. 1. hortatur, ut mul- torum precibus iuvetur, ut rursus Deo offeratur multorum gratiarum actio. Hi cultus rationi hu- manae ignoti sunt, sed Ecclesia eos ex verbo Dei discere debet, scilicet obedientiam in aerumnis, invocationem, fidem, spem auxilii, seu libera- tionis, et gratiarum actionem, et celebrationem misericordiae Dei, sicut Psal. inquit: Invoca me in die tribulationis, et eripiam te, et glorificabis me etc.

## 9:3
But that the works of God may be made manifest.

The liberation of this blind man illustrates the glory of God in three ways; first, the healing itself is a testimony concerning Christ, that this teacher was sent by God. For miracles are universally testimonies of doctrine, and although some may seem greater than others, let us join them all together. It is certain that the raising of the dead is the work of God alone; therefore, Christ raising the dead is not a false prophet, but sent by God, and is divinely guided and helped, as is said in the text a little later: How can a sinful man do such signs? Next, the glory of God is illustrated through the healed man, who first privately gave thanks to God for so great a benefit, afterwards he celebrates the author, and with a clear confession, testifies that this man, by whom he was healed, is a Prophet sent by God; indeed, afterwards Christ even specifically teaches him about the highest article, commands him to believe in the Son of God, and this healed man answers: I believe, Lord. These things said here concerning the causes of afflictions and liberations bring some light to this narrative and similar ones, and usefully instruct us in our own troubles.

Latin:

Sed ut manifestentur opera Dei.

Liberatio huius caeci illustrat gloriam Dei tripliciter, primum ipsa sanatio est testimonium de Christo, hunc doctorem a Deo missum esse. Nam miracula universaliter sunt testimonia do- ctrinae, et cum alia aliis videantur maiora, omnia coniungamus. Certum est resuscitationem mor- tuorum solius Dei opus esse, ergo Christus re- suscitans mortuos, non est pseudopropheta, sed a Deo missus, et divinitus regitur ac adiuvatur, sicut in textu aliquanto post dicitur: Quomodo potest homo peccator talia signa facere. Deinde illustratur gloria Dei per sanatum, qui primum privatim Deo gratias egit pro tanto beneficio, po- stea autorem celebrat, et clara confessione, testa- tur, hunc, a quo sanatus est, Prophetam esse a Deo missum, imo postea Christus etiam nomina- tim eum docet de summo articulo, iubet eum cre- dere in filium Dei, et hic sanatus respondet: Cre- do domine. Haec de causis afflictionum et libe- rationum in hoc loco dicta, aliquid lucis huic narrationi et similibus afferunt, et nos in nostris aerumnis utiliter erudiunt.

## 9:4
I must work the works of him who sent me.

This sentence and similar ones, which give instructions concerning labor or the duties of one's calling, are to be diligently observed. For they teach us about the greatest matter and console us against the common temptation of wise men. We experience in every government, great and small, that there are many difficulties which cannot be eased by human diligence, that many huge dangers arise from everywhere which cannot be foreseen or avoided, and finally, often, just as the fury of storms overcomes the art of steering ships, so too are the plans of wise men completely defeated by unexpected events. Hence Demosthenes and Cicero are sought out, and from there the verse was born: Fortune rules life, not wisdom. Wherefore many wise men, having deserted the government of affairs, hid themselves in leisure, and handed down the precept λάθε βιώσας. Demosthenes also said as an old man that if it were now permitted for him to decide freely about his life, and two lives were proposed, one leading to the highest honors in the Republic, the other straight to death, he would prefer to enter that path leading straight to death rather than the other one proposing the greatest honors in the Republic. Because he had already learned by experience how many dangers there are in government, and how events do not correspond to plans. Aeschines, while in exile, writes that he congratulates himself on his leisure, that he has been freed from the government of the Republic as if from a rabid dog; and Plato narrates that Socrates fled the administration of the Republic. Finally, the sayings and examples of wise men are very many, which warn that it is safest to avoid all public business, and the affairs of others, great and small; finally, it is said concerning private associations: Do not make yourself too much of a companion, you will rejoice less, and you will grieve less.

Against this human wisdom Christ cries out: I must do the works of him who sent me, while it is day, that is, while this my calling of the sounding Gospel lasts; thus he commands the Apostles to teach, and not to fear terrors and dangers, nor to be broken in spirit, even if events do not correspond to human opinions. Thus Moses obeys God in leading out the people, and although enemies press in, he nevertheless commands the people to be of great heart: Stand, he says, because you will see the glorious works of God. Thus Paul says to the Ephesians 5: Walk diligently, not as unwise, but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil. At the same time, Paul includes the very mention of impediments, and yet commands them to resist with skill. The days are evil, that is, in the time of this life many difficulties hinder good plans, and great dangers deter many from advising the Republic well. Although, he says, these things happen in this way, nevertheless the government of affairs is not to be cast aside, one is not to cease.

What then is to be done, will Plato or similar men say, when we can accomplish nothing or little? Christ answers here: I must do the works of him who sent me, that is, the works of my calling, or mission, and 1 Corinthians 9: Woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel, and it is often commanded concerning one's calling, at Romans 12 and elsewhere, that each one should diligently perform his own calling, and not cast it aside because of terrors, hatreds, injuries, dangers, or sad events. And to this doctrine these two consolations are to be added: that help is to be expected from God by faith, and that salutary events are to be hoped for, even if we do not immediately perceive them with our own eyes. Just as Jeremiah, advising on a new matter, and one which seemed destined to be the destruction of that polity, namely surrender and help, nevertheless knew that this plan, sad in appearance, would afterward be salutary for the people. Concerning help, Christ says here: I must do the works of him who sent me, by which words he signifies both that he does the works commanded by God the Father, and that they are done with him himself helping; thus he also often consoles us: I will not leave you orphans. Likewise: I will ask the Father, and he will give you another paraclete, that he may remain with you forever, the spirit of truth. Likewise Matth. 10.: It will be given to you in that hour what you should speak: For it is not you who speak, but the spirit of the Father who speaks in you. Finally, testimonies about the help of God occur everywhere, which we ought to remember, and to ask that in such great dangers we may be ruled and helped, just as the Prophets cry out from time to time, and 2 Paralip. 20 it is said: When we do not know what should be done, we direct our eyes to you. Demosthenes, Cicero, and similar governors did not know this help. Therefore they are broken in spirit, and finally judge that the governing of affairs is to be avoided, but let us in the Church know that these great promises were not handed down to us in vain. Then let us gather sentences concerning the outcome or event, so that we may know our labors will not be empty. Psal. 1.: And he will be like a tree planted by the streams of waters, which will give its fruit in its time, and Matth. 13.: But he who sows into good soil brings forth fruit, and makes one a hundredfold etc., and 2 Corinth. 3. concerning the ministry: We have such confidence through Christ, not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything, as if from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God, and then how much more will this ministry be in glory, that is, effective, having such hope we use great confidence, and to Phil. 2.: It is God who works in you, both to will and to perform, so that some things may be done that are pleasing to him, that is, God helps us so that we may do pious and salutary things. Then he also helps us in acting, in the ministry, in government, in all necessary actions, finally he also governs the event and the cause, so that certain things may be done that are pleasing to him, as if he were saying: The Devil, out of hatred for God, instigates his organs so that they may do very many things horribly displeasing to God, he sows blasphemies, he impels them to fashion idols, to move useless wars, to loosen the rein for wicked lusts. By these furies God is most vehemently offended and irritated, so that the whole human race may not be born only for destruction, and do only things worthy of hatred, he himself helps some in his Church, so that many things may be done that are pleasing to him, and salutary to us, namely, when there is right teaching, when true invocation of God is performed, when polities rightly govern discipline, when morals are pious and chaste, etc. He confirms us concerning events also by that voice: The Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes. And in general concerning both, namely concerning help and outcome, it is said, 1 Corinth. 15.: Your labor is not in vain in the Lord.

The night comes, when no one can work, while I am in the world, I am the light of the world.

The latter sentence declares the former, while I am in the world, I am the light of the world, as long as Christ himself preaches, and as long as his voice sounds in the ministry, there is light, that is, men are gifted with light, with the true knowledge of God, with true worship, with eternal life. These do not happen otherwise than by the voice of the Gospel sounding through Christ, or his ministers. But where Christ is absent, that is, when the Gospel is extinguished, with Christ silent, and the ministers silent, he calls these shadows night here, then no one can work, namely, works pleasing to God, and initiating eternal life. As there was great wisdom in the Attic state in the time of Solon, or Pericles, there was great wisdom in the Roman state, in the time of Fabius, Scipio, Laelius, and similar supreme men. But what is all wisdom, without the true knowledge of God, they are deliberations about perishable things. And minds err in many ways, when they do not look toward the true and eternal end, they do not know God, they do not seek counsel and help from him, they do not see the causes why empires should be established, they do not know that justice which brings eternal life, and because they are subject to the tyranny of the Devil, they are horribly impelled to disturb Republics with evil counsels, and in private life to contaminate themselves with many great crimes, as Themistocles, Alexander, and countless others, although they excelled in wisdom and virtue, yet after victories they greatly degenerated from themselves, and by great crimes deformed the honor previously gained. As therefore there was night among the nations ignorant of God in the whole world: so Christ, prophesying about future miseries, signifies that night will come again, that is, a time when the light of the Gospel will be widely extinguished, as immediately in the Jewish people night followed, and subsequently with heresies having arisen, and later the law of Mahomet having been born, and then the Turkish kingdom having been established, which although it flourishes in wisdom in the administration of the empire and in riches, yet that empire is only night, that is, a blind multitude, ignorant of God, guilty of the wrath of God, and destined for eternal punishments.

Latin:

Me oportet operari opera eius, qui misit me.

Diligenter haec sententia et similes observan- dae sunt, quae de labore, seu de vocationis offi- ciis praecipiunt. Nam et docent nos de re maxi- ma et adversus communem tentationem sapien- tum consolantur. Experimur in omni guberna- tione magna et parva, multas esse difficultates, quae humana diligentia leniri non possunt, multa ingentia pericula undecunque oriri, quae prospici et caveri nequeunt, denique saepe, ut tempesta- tum saevitia ars navium gubernandarum supera- tur, ita prorsus vinci consilia sapientum inopina- tis eventibus. Id quaeruntur Demosthenes et Ci- cero, inde et versus natus est: Vitam regit for- tuna, non sapientia. Quare multi sapientes de- serta gubernatione rerum, abdiderunt se in otium, et praeceptum tradiderunt λάθε βιώσας. Demosthenes etiam dixit senex, se, si iam liceret sibi libere de sua vita statuere, essentque duae vitae propositae, altera ad summos honores in Repub. ducens, altera recta ad mortem, malle mox ingredi viam illam recta ducentem ad mor- tem, quam alteram proponentem maximos hono- res in Republica. Quod iam usu comperisset, quantum in gubernatione periculorum sit, quam non respondeant eventus consiliis. Aeschines exulans scribit se gratulari sibi otium suum, quod tanquam a rabiosa cane, a Reipub. gubernatione liberatus sit: et Plato Socratem narrat fugisse ad- ministrationem Reipub. Denique dicta sapientum et exempla sunt plurima, quae monent tutissi- mum esse vitare omnia negotia publica, et aliena, magna et parva, denique de privatis sodalitiis di- citur: Nulh te facias nimis sodalem, gaudebis minus, et minus dolebis.

Contra hanc humanam sapientiam clamat Christus: Me oportet facere opera eius, qui me misit, donec dies est, id est, donec haec mea vocatio sonantis Evangelii durat, sic Apostolis praecipit, ut doceant, nec metuant terrores ac pericula, nec frangantur animis, etiamsi eventus non respondent humanis opinionibus. Sic Mo- ses Deo obtemperat educens populum, et quan- quam instant hostes, tamen iubet populum magno animo esse: State, inquit, quia videbitis gloriosa opera Dei. Sic Paulus inquit ad Ephes. 5.: Am- bulate diligenter, non ut insipientes, sed ut sa- pientes, redimentes tempus, quia dies mali sunt. Simul complectitur Paulus ipsam impedimento- rum mentionem, et tamen iubet illis repugnare arte. Dies mali sunt, id est, in huius vitae tem- pore multae difficultates impediunt bona consilia, magna pericula deterrent multos bene consulere Reipub. Quanquam, inquit, haec ita fiunt, ta- men non abiicienda est gubernatio rerum, non cessandum.

Quid igitur faciendum est, dicet Plato, aut similes, cum nihil aut parum proficere possimus? Respondet hic Christus: Oportet me facere opera eius, qui misit me, id est, opera meae vocatio- nis, seu missionis, et 1. Corinth. 9.: Vae mihi, si non evangelizavero, et saepe de vocatione praecipitur, ad Rom. 12. et alibi, ut suam quis- que vocationem diligenter obeat, nec abiiciat eam, propter terrores, odia, iniurias, pericula, aut eventus tristes. Et ad hanc doctrinam addendae sunt hae duae consolationes, fide auxilium a Deo expectandum esse, et sperandos eventus salutares, etiamsi nos non statim cernimus eos nostris ocu- lis. Sicut Ieremias consulens rem novam, et quae videbatur exitio futura illi politiae, videlicet deditionem et auxilium, tamen sciebat hoc consi- lium in speciem triste, deinde salutare fore po- pulo. De auxilio hic dicit Christus: Oportet me facere opera eius, qui misit me, quibus verbis utrunque significat, se mandata opera a Deo pa- tre, facere, et fieri ea ipso iuvante, sic et nos saepe consolatur: Non relinquam vos orphanos. Item: Ego rogabo patrem, et alium paracletum dabit vobis, ut maneat vobiscum in aeternum, spiritum veritatis. Item Matth. 10.: Dabitur vo- bis in hora illa, quid loquamini: Non enim vos estis, qui loquimini, sed spiritus patris est, qui loquitur in vobis. Denique passim occurrunt te- stimonia de auxilio Dei, quae meminisse debe- mus, et petere ut in tantis periculis regamur et adiuvemur, sicut subinde clamant Prophetae, et 2. Paralip. 20. dicitur: Cum ignoramus quid agen- dum sit, oculos nostros ad te dirigimus. Hoc auxilium non norant Demosthenes, Cicero, et similes gubernatores. Ideo franguntur animis, et tandem iudicant fugiendam esse rerum guberna- tionem, sed nos in Ecclesia sciamus, non frustra nobis has tantas promissiones traditas esse. Dein- de de exitu seu eventu colligamus sententias, ut sciamus labores nostros non inanes fore. Psal. 1.: Et erit tanquam arbor plantata ad rivos aquarum, quae fructum suum dabit in tempore suo, et Matth. 13.: Qui vero in terram bonam seminat, fructum affert, et facit aliud centuplum etc., et 2. Corinth. 3. de ministerio: Fiduciam habemus talem per Christum, non quod sufficientes simus ex nobis aliquid cogitare, tanquam ex nobis ipsis, sed sufficientia nostra ex Deo est, et deinde quanto magis hoc ministerium erit in gloria, id est, effi- cax, habentes talem spem magna fiducia utimur, et ad Phil. 2.: Deus est qui operatur in vobis, ut velitis et perficiatis, ut aliqua fiant ipsi grata, id est, Deus adiuvat nos, ut pia et salutaria facia- mus. Deinde etiam adiuvat nos in agendo, in ministerio, in gubernatione, in omnibus neces- sariis actionibus, denique et eventus gubernet et causam, ut fiant quaedam ipsi grata, quasi dicat: Diabolus odio Dei instigat sua organa, ut plurima faciant horribiliter displicentia Deo, serit blas- phemias, impellit ad fingenda idola, ad movenda bella inutilia, ad laxandum frenum flagitiosis li- bidinibus. His furoribus vehementissime offen- ditur et irritatur Deus, ne igitur totum genus humanum tantum ad perniciem nascatur, ac tan- tum odio digna faciat, ipse in Ecclesia sua aliquos adiuvat, ut fiant multa ipsi grata, et nobis salu- taria, videlicet, cum recte docetur, cum fit vera invocatio Dei, cum politiae recte regunt discipli- nam, cum mores sunt pii et casti, etc. Con- firmat nos de eventibus et illa vox: Evangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti. Et in genere de utroque, scilicet de auxilio et exitu dicitur, 1. Corinth. 15.: Labor vester non est inanis in domino.

Venit nox, cum nemo operari potest, donec in mundo sum, lux sum mundi.

Posterior sententia declarat priorem, donec in mundo sum, lux sum mundi, donec Christus praedicat ipse, et donec vox eius sonat in mini- sterio, lux est, id est, homines donantur luce, agnitione vera Dei, veris cultibus, vita aeterna. Haec non aliter nisi voce Evangelii sonantis per Christum, aut ministros contingunt. Sed ubi Christus abest, id est, cum Evangelium extin- guitur, tacente Christo, et tacentibus ministris, eas tenebras hic vocat noctem, tunc nemo operari potest, videlicet, opera Deo placentia, et aeter- nam vitam incoantia. Ut magna fuit sapientia Atticae civitatis tempore Solonis, aut Periclis, magna fuit Romanae civitatis, tempore Fabii, Scipionis, Laelii, et similium summorum viro- rum. Sed quid est universa sapientia, sine agni- tione vera Dei, deliberationes sunt de rebus ca- ducis. Et errant animi multipliciter, cum verum et aeternum finem non prospiciunt, non norunt Deum, non petunt ab eo consilium et auxilium, non vident causas, cur imperia constituenda sint, non norunt illam iusticiam, quae affert vitam ae- ternam, et quia sunt subiecti tyrannidi diaboli, impelluntur horribiliter, ut turbent Respub. ma- lis consiliis, et in privata vita contaminent se multis magnis sceleribus, ut Themistocles, Ale- xander, et alii innumerabiles, quanquam sapien- tia et virtute excelluerunt, tamen post victorias valde a seipsis degenerarunt, et magnis sceleri- bus decus antea partum deformavereunt. Ut ergo nox erat apud gentes ignaras Dei toto orbe terra- rum: sic Christus vaticinans de futuris miseriis, significat rursus venturam noctem, id est, tem- pus quo late extinguetur lux Evangelii, ut statim in populo Iudaico nox secuta est, et deinceps or- tis haeresibus, et postea nata lege Mahometi, ac deinde constituto regno Turcico, quod etsi floret sapientia in administratione imperii et opibus, tamen illud tantum imperium nox est, id est, caeca multitudo, ignara Dei, rea irae Dei, et destinata aeternis poenis.

## 9:6
He spat on the ground, and made clay, etc.

God always establishes certain signs of his promises and actions, which we call Sacraments, which are efficacious, even if there are no physical causes; just as an infant who was circumcised was pleasing to God, and one who despised circumcision was not pleasing to God, so afterwards other signs were instituted, Baptism and the Supper of the Lord. These works of God are attacked in two ways. The devil devises similar things and feigns ceremonies, such as the deeds of the Magi and many deceptions in the worship of idols. A girl standing on the Delphic tripod began to rave and prophesy. Those celebrating the orgies of Bacchus were also moved by a certain inspiration of their own, and it is still customary for people gathering for a feast and the dances of Vitus, as they call them, to be seized by frenzy. But the devil incites other impious people to likewise mock all ceremonies, as if they were empty superstitions, whether they come from God or elsewhere. Therefore, ceremonies instituted by God must be prudently distinguished from human ones. Baptism is valid because it was ordained by the command of God. Thus this ceremony, which Christ here applies to the eyes of the healed man, is valid. Because the Lord and creator of nature himself administers it, it is not a superstitious or empty work, but good and efficacious on account of the creator.

And this misplaced zeal (κακοζηλία) is not valid: 'Christ used such a ceremony, therefore it is permitted for us also to institute similar things, and holy water, and the touching of bones, and I know not what else.' Indeed, this false persuasion has filled the whole world with idols, because men, when they had seen that some ceremonies were commanded by God, through error feigned similar ones and attributed great efficacy to them; this misplaced zeal is to be condemned, and the rule is to be held that only those ceremonies are pleasing to God and truly efficacious which God has instituted by his word and handed down to us, and this very example of this history is a testimony that ceremonies instituted by God are certainly efficacious; just as the eyes are healed by the mass smeared on them, made from spittle and earth by Christ, so it is certain that a man baptized is received by God and gifted with the Holy Spirit. Christ could have healed this man even without this mass, by his word alone, as he helped many, but he added a ceremony so that he might testify that the ceremonies instituted by him are efficacious.

There is also this reason, that the faith of the blind man is exercised by this delay, for he is sent to the pool so that he may wash off the smeared mass there, and it is consistent that there was a great crowd of spectators who followed to see the outcome, and perhaps he heard the laughter and abusive voices of many. 'Why do you believe this impostor? Are you so delirious that you think perpetual blindness can be cured?' But whatever kind of spectacle it was, in the delay itself his faith was tested, but the outcome showed it to have been firm and constant. Thus delay exercises the Canaanite woman, thus delay exercised the Israelites after Moses promised liberation, and he did not immediately lead the people out of Egypt; indeed, he provoked the tyrant so that he would exacerbate their servitude. Let these examples confirm us, so that we may not be broken in spirit, nor cast away hope of help, even if it is deferred. The saying of Christ and the parable in Luke 18 advise the same: 'It is necessary always to pray, and not to grow weary.'

Latin:

Expuit in terram, et fecit lutum, etc.

Semper Deus signa quaedam suarum promissionum et actionum instituit, quae vocamus Sacramenta, quae sunt efficacia, etiamsi causae physicae nullae sunt, ut infans circumcisus placebat Deo, spreta circumcisione non placebat Deo, sic postea alia signa instituta sunt, Baptismus et Coena Domini. Haec Dei opera dupliciter oppugnantur. Diabolus similia excogitat, et fingit ceremonias, ut sunt Magorum facta et multae praestigiae in cultu idolorum. Puella stans in tripode delphica coepit furere et vaticinari. Celebrantes orgia Bacchi, etiam suo quodam afflatu movebantur, et adhuc usitatum est corripi furore homines convenientes ad festum et choreas Viti, ut vocant. Alios vero impios instigat diabolus, ut pariter derideant omnes ceremonias, tanquam inanes superstitiones, sive a Deo, sive aliunde sint. Quare prudenter discernendae sunt ceremoniae a Deo institutae ab humanis. Valet baptismus, quia mandato Dei ordinatus est. Sic valet haec ceremonia, quam hic Christus adhibet oculis sanati. Quia ipse dominus et conditor naturae eam administrat, nec opus est superstitiosum, aut inane, sed bonum et efficax propter creatorem.

Nec valet κακοζηλία, Christus usus est tali ceremonia, ergo nobis quoque licet similia instituere, et aquam consecratam, et ossium contactum, et nescio quae alia. Imo haec falsa persuasio implevit totum mundum idolis, quod homines, cum vidissent divinitus aliquas ceremonias mandatas esse, errore finxerunt similes, et eis attribuerunt magnam efficaciam, haec κακοζηλία damnanda est, et tenenda regula, solas illas ceremonias Deo placere, et vere efficaces esse, quas Deus suo verbo instituit et nobis tradidit, et hoc ipsum exemplum huius historiae testimonium est, ceremonias a Deo institutas, certo efficaces esse, sicut sanantur oculi illita massa, facta ex sputo et terra a Christo, sic certum est hominem baptizatum a Deo recipi, et donari Spiritu sancto. Poterat sanare hunc Christus etiam sine hac massa, solo verbo, ut multis opitulatus est, sed addidit ceremoniam, ut testaretur ceremonias a se institutas efficaces esse.

Accedit et haec causa, quod fides caeci exer- cetur hac mora, mittitur enim ad stagnum, ut ibi abluat massam illitam, et consentaneum est magnam fuisse spectatorum turbam, quae secuta est, ut eventum videret, fortassis et cachinnos, et voces maledicas multorum audivit. Quid cre- dis huic impostori? adeo ne deliras, ut curari perpetuam caecitatem putes? sed qualecunque spectaculum fuit, in ipsa more fides tentata est, sed eventus ostendit firmam et constantem fuisse. Sic mora exercet Cananaeam, sic mora exercebat Israëlitas, postquam Moses promisit liberationem, nec statim eduxit populum ex Aegypto, imo irri- tavit tyrannum, ut servitutem exasperaret. Haec exempla confirment nos, ne frangamur animis, nec abiiciamus spem auxilii, etiamsi differtur. Idem monet dictum Christi, et similitudo, Lucae 18.: Oportet semper orare, et non languefieri.

## 9:7
He went away, therefore, and washed, and returned seeing.

This healing is an image of baptism. Therefore the type fits; the blind man washes himself in the pool, but commanded by the voice of Christ. Thus baptism is valid on account of the command and promise of Christ, and it is called the pool of Siloam, that is, 'sent,' so that it may be signified that that pool must be approached in the Church, to which we are sent by the word of God.

Then in the narrative various discourses about this healing are recited, and the contentions that followed, so that the miracle might become better known and more celebrated, and so that the confession of the healed man might become more illustrious, and faith might grow. And these struggles are an image of the dangers of the Church. Thus it has been and will be customary for the Church in all ages, as often as impious doctrine is censured and true doctrine is restored, for dissensions and schisms to arise, as Christ says in Matthew 10: 'Brother will deliver brother to death, etc.' And courage is necessary for us, not to cast away the profession of true and salutary doctrine for fear of discord or human hatreds, as it is said in Isaiah 51: 'Do not fear the reproaches of men, and do not be afraid of their blasphemies.' Let it suffice to have said this in summary about this example. Again they seek a jejune calumny about the violation of the Sabbath; Christ refuted this most copiously above.

Latin:

Abiit ergo, et lavit, et rediit videns.

Haec sanatio imago est baptismi. Ideo ty- pus congruit, lavat se in piscina caecus, sed ius- sus voce Christi. Sic baptismus valet propter mandatum et promissionem Christi, et dicitur stagnum Siloam, id est, missi, ut significetur stagnum illud adeundum esse in Ecclesia, ad quod verbo Dei mittimur.

Deinde in enarratione recitantur sermones varii de hac sanatione, et contentiones, quae se- cutae sunt, ut miraculum fieret notius, et magis celebraretur, et ut sanati confessio fieret illustrior, et fides cresceret. Et haec certamina sunt imago periculorum Ecclesiae. Sic omnibus aetatibus usitatum fuit et erit Ecclesiae, quoties doctrina impia taxatur, et vera instauratur, exoriri dis- sensiones et schismata, sicut inquit Christus Matth. 10.: Tradet frater fratrem, etc. Et vir- tus necessaria est nobis, non abiicere professio- nem verae et salutaris doctrinae, metu discordiae, aut odiorum humanorum, ut Esa. 51. dicitur: Ne timeatis opprobria hominum, et blasphemias eorum ne formidetis. Haec in summa de hoc exemplo dixisse satis sit. Iterum quaerunt ieiu- nam calumniam de violatione sabbati, hanc supra copiosissime refutavit Christus.

## 9:28
We are disciples of Moses.

And this arrogance is also refuted above, chapter 5: 'If you believed Moses, you would believe me also,' for he wrote about me. And in this narrative, the fury of the hypocrites must be considered and dreaded. Men fascinated by carnal opinions about the law, and swelling with the persuasion of their own righteousness, as now Wicelius or certain others most proudly and from on high deride the doctrine of grace and faith, and and well-composed morals, think this to be the one and highest honor, feign this to be perfect righteousness, the satisfaction of the law of God, finally preach it as a certain divinity, and value Aristides or Cato far more than Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the like, whose life seems in appearance more rustic. Although civil righteousness and the moderation of morals is a great honor, and is a necessary thing, yet we in the Church know that this righteousness of the flesh is far from the perfection of the law, nay, it does not even begin the first table. For hearts are full of doubts about God, they are secure, without the fear of God, without repentance, without the acknowledgment of their own weakness, and much more without any acknowledgment of mercy and trust in God. Then they admire and exalt themselves, and trust in their own wisdom, and most pertinaciously defend their false persuasions by self-admiration. These hypocrites are often described in the Prophets, as in Isaiah 6: Blind the heart of this people, and make its ears heavy, and Rom. 11: God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that they should not see, etc. I recite these things, so that the pious may consider what a great evil hypocrisy is, and what kind of blindness it is, so that they may dread it and hear the voice of the Gospel, and seek from God the true light, and the Holy Spirit, who removes the veil with which hearts are covered, as Paul says: in the doctrine of the law.

Latin:

Nos Mosi discipuli sumus.

Est et haec arrogantia supra refutata, cap. 5.: Si Mosi crederetis, mihi quoque crederetis, nam de me scripsit ille. Estque in hac narra- tione furor hypocritarum considerandus et ex- pavescendus. Homines fascinati opinionibus car- nalibus de lege, et tumentes persuasione propriae iusticiae, ut nunc Wicelius aut alii quidam su- perbissime et ex alto derident doctrinam de gratia et fide, ac mere fanatica somnia esse iudicant, et econtra admirantur disciplinam et mores bene compositos, hoc decus unum et summum esse pu- tant, hoc fingunt esse perfectam iusticiam, satis- factionem legis Dei, denique praedicant tanquam divinitatem quandam, ac longe pluris faciunt Ari- stidem, aut Catonem, quam Abraham, Isaac, Iacob, et similes, quorum vita in speciem vide- tur agrestior. Quanquam autem magnum decus est civilis iusticia et moderatio morum, et res ne- cessaria est, tamen nos in Ecclesia scimus hanc iusticiam carnis longe abesse a perfectione legis, imo nec quidem incoare primam tabulam. Nam corda sunt plena dubitationum de Deo, sunt se- cura, sine timore Dei, sine poenitentia, sine agnitione propriae infirmitatis, et multo magis sine ulla agnitione misericordiae et fiduciae Dei. Deinde admirantur ac efferunt sese, et confidunt sua sapientia, et suas falsas persuasiones admira- tione sui, pertinacissime propugnant. Hi hypo- critae saepe in Prophetis describuntur, ut Esaiae 6.: Excaeca cor populi huius, et aures eius ag- grava, et Rom. 11.: Dedit eis Deus spiritum ex- acerbatum, oculos ne videant, etc. Haec recito, ut considerent pii, quantum malum sit hypocri- sis, et qualis caecitas sit, ut expavescant et au- diant vocem Evangelii, et petant a Deo verum lumen, et Spiritum sanctum, qui tollit velum, quo corda velata sunt, ut Paulus inquit: in do- ctrina legis.

## 9:31
But we know that God does not hear sinners.

This saying contains a twofold doctrine; it teaches that miracles are testimonies of doctrine, and it hands down a common sentiment, which it is necessary to know in every invocation. First, it argues thus concerning miracles: Whoever performs miracles in the name of God, and proper to the Church, it is certain that this one is from God. But Christ performed miracles in the name of God, just as He says: The Son can do nothing of Himself, unless He sees the Father doing it, and He performed miracles proper to the Church, that is, which the devil or any creature cannot imitate.

For He restored life to the dead, etc. Furthermore, He taught what had already been handed down before by the Prophets, He did not beget a kind of doctrine conflicting with the Prophets. It was certain, therefore, that this teacher was sent by God.

But someone will object that even the Gentiles performed miracles, as they tell of the whetstone being cut with a razor in the time of Servius Tullius. To all ethnic things there is an easy answer, that they are the illusions of the devil, which can be confirmed by three causes: the first is because they are not done with the invocation of the true God. The second cause, because they are done to establish manifest turpitudes, as Calchas prophesies about the years of the Trojan War, and orders a human victim to be sacrificed. The third, because they are miracles which the devil can imitate. They are not testimonies of omnipotent nature, such as the resurrection of the dead, stopping the course of the sun, making a barren old woman fruitful. These causes must be diligently thought upon, so that true testimonies may be discerned from ethnic and fallacious ones. Nor are most things that are told to confirm the invocation of the dead unlike the ethnic ones.

Then if anyone objects: But false prophets will perform prodigies, as it is said in Matt. 24: And they will perform them in the name of God. To these I answer: Even if they perform them under the pretext of the name of God, yet they perform them to establish certain errors against the doctrine previously handed down by God. Furthermore, in the Church, miracles and the doctrine previously handed down by God ought to be compared; if miracles conflict with the doctrine previously handed down by God, they are fallacious, and they will always be such as the devil can imitate, they will not be proper to the Church, such as the resurrection of the dead, or something similar. It is profitable to consider these things concerning the diversity of miracles and their different ends, and let not fallacious miracles, and those conflicting with the certain word of God, lead minds away from the true invocation of God to idols and false opinions.

Let another common doctrine be observed in this place. God does not hear sinners, namely those persevering in sins against conscience. For both errors must be censured: some, secure while retaining the purpose of sinning, think that invocation is valid. This imagination is false and must be fled from with the whole heart, because it is clearly said in Psalm 5: You are not a God who wills impiety, and 1 John 3: If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence toward God, and if we ask anything, we shall receive it from Him. It is therefore vain babbling to come into the sight of God without repentance, but on the contrary others who are fearful must be instructed, lest they be deterred by despair from invocation. This voice of the law is always clamoring against us: God does not hear sinners, therefore you cry out to God in vain, since you are manifoldly guilty of the wrath of God. Here it is necessary to hold to the doctrine of repentance and faith. Let us bring to God a contrite heart, as the Psalm says: A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise, and let us determine by faith that we are heard on account of the mediator, just as it is said in Rom. 5: By faith we have access to God. And thus, by repentance and faith, let an evil conscience be put away, that is, the purpose of sinning. It is necessary that this be taught in the Church concerning both, concerning the secure and the fearful, so that invocation, which is the highest worship of God and the proper work of the Church, may be rightly performed.

Latin:

Scimus autem, quod Deus peccatores non exaudit.

Duplicem doctrinam continet hoc dictum, do- cet miracula testimonia esse doctrinae, et tradit communem sententiam, quam in omni invoca- tione nosse oportet. Primum de miraculis sic ar- gumentatur: Quicunque facit miracula nomine Dei, et Ecclesiae propria, hunc certum est a Deo esse. Faciebat autem Christus miracula nomine Dei, sicut inquit: Non potest filius facere ex sese quicquam, nisi viderit patrem facientem, et fa- ciebat miracula Ecclesiae propria, id est, quae non imitari diabolus, aut ulla creatura potest.

Nam mortuis reddebat vitam, etc. Praeterea et tradita iam ante per Prophetas docebat, non gi- gnebat genus doctrinae, pugnans cum Prophetis. Certum igitur erat hunc doctorem a Deo mis- sum esse.

Sed obiiciet aliquis, etiam Ethnicos fecisse miracula, ut narrant cotem dissectam esse nova- cula apud Servium Tullum. Ad ethnica omnia facilis responsio est, praestigias esse diaboli, quod tribus causis confirmari potest, prima est, quia non fiunt cum invocatione veri Dei. Secun- da causa, quia ad manifestas turpitudines stabi- liendas, ut Calchas vaticinatur de annis belli Tro- iani, et iubet mactari humanam hostiam. Ter- tia, quia sunt miracula, quae diabolus imitari potest. Non sunt testimonia naturae omnipoten- tis, ut resuscitatio mortuorum, sistere cursum solis, anum effoetam foecundam facere. Hae causae diligenter cogitandae sunt, ut discernan- tur vera testimonia ab ethnicis et fallacibus. Nec dissimilia sunt ethnicis pleraque, quae narrantur ad confirmandam invocationem mortuorum.

Deinde si quis obiiciet: At pseudoprophetae facient prodigia, ut Matth. 24. dicitur: Eaque facient nomine Dei. Ad haec respondeo: Etiamsi faciunt praetextu nominis Dei, tamen faciunt ad stabiliendos aliquos errores contra doctrinam cer- tam a Deo traditam. Porro in Ecclesia conferri oportet miracula, et doctrinam prius a Deo tra- ditam, si miracula pugnant cum doctrina prius a Deo tradita, sunt fallacia, et semper erunt talia, quae diabolus imitari potest, non erunt propria Ecclesiae, ut resuscitatio mortuorum, aut simile quiddam. Haec de diversitate miraculorum, et diversis eorum finibus prodest considerare, nec miracula fallacia, et pugnantia cum certo verbo Dei, abducant animos a vera invocatione Dei, ad idola et falsas opiniones.

Altera doctrina communis hoc loco observe- tur. Peccatores Deus non exaudit, scilicet per- severantes in peccatis contra conscientiam. Nam uterque error taxandus est: aliqui securi retinen- tes propositum peccandi, putant valere invocatio- nem. Haec imaginatio falsa et toto pectore fu- gienda est, quia Psal. 5. clare dicitur: Non Deus volens impietatem tu es, et 1. Ioann. 3.: Si cor nostrum non condemnat nos, fiduciam habemus erga Deum, et si quid petemus, accipiemus ab eo. Est ergo inanis βαττολογία, venire in con- spectum Dei sine poenitentia, econtra vero alii pavidi erudiendi sunt, ne desperatione deterrean- tur ab invocatione. Semper obstrepit nobis haec vox legis: Deus non exaudit peccatores, frustra igitur clamas ad Deum, cum sis multipliciter reus irae Dei. Hic doctrinam poenitentiae et fidei te- nere necesse est. Afferamus ad Deum cor con- tritum, ut inquit Psalmus: Cor contritum et hu- miliatum Deus non despicies, et fide statuamus nos propter mediatorem exaudiri, sicut ad Rom. 5. dicitur: Fide habemus accessum ad Deum. Et sic poenitentia ac fide deponatur mala conscien- tia, id est, propositum peccandi. Haec doceri in Ecclesia de utrisque, de securis et pavidis necesse est, ut invocatio, quae est summus cultus Dei et proprium Ecclesiae opus, recte fieri possit.

## 9:35
Do you believe in the Son of God.

As Christ said elsewhere: To him who has it will be given, so here gifts grow, after plain confession and the cross. For excommunication had followed confession. There follows, therefore, a new and remarkable confirmation, nor does Christ propose a common question, saying: Do you believe in the Son of God? The Jews more easily endured this teacher being called the Messiah, or a Prophet sent by God, than the Son of God. When they hear this surname, then indeed they burn with rage, and think they are defending the glory of God; he makes himself equal to God, they say above, and afterwards: because he made himself the Son of God, these they judge to be horrible and execrable blasphemies, but the Apostles issue the confession, Matt. 16: You are the Christ the Son of the living God. These embrace a description of both office and nature: We confess you to be the Messiah promised to the fathers, on account of whom God will be appeased toward us. Then we also profess this, that you, the Messiah, have a divine nature from the eternal Father, of whom you are the only-begotten Son. The Apostles understood these things somewhat more clearly than this man who was healed, and yet the profession is the same, and to this very person confessing it was later explained more fully.

It is an altogether wonderful voice of the Church, that it proclaims the Messiah to be by nature the Son of God, and it horribly offends the Jews and the wise Gentiles. The heathens always felt that the world is ruled by providence. For they saw heroic men suddenly raised up for the restoration and establishment of empires, such as Hercules, Cyrus, Alexander, Augustus, and others at other times. These also they called sons of God, not because they thought they were born from the nature of God, but because they saw them being helped by God, and wonderfully ruled and protected. Thus the Jews thought Solomon was called the Son of God, and they thought of the Messiah in the same way; thus also Mahomet contends that Moses, Christ, himself, and many other Prophets and Kings were sons of God. The same did Ebion, Samosatenus, Nestorius, and many others think, and perhaps many are always even Christians by title, who silently carry this opinion around with them in their minds.

But the Church of God, although it does not yet see in this life what that wonderful union of human and divine nature is, nevertheless is compelled by the command of God to sound this doctrine, that the Son of God, the λόγος, begotten by the Father from eternity, afterwards assumed human nature. For he wills this covenant, and this society of the divine nature and the human, to be an evident testimony of divine love toward human nature. If human minds could in any way conceive the magnitude of this work, that the divine nature so humbles itself, that it joins human nature to itself, and makes an immutable covenant with it, then indeed we would be inflamed with love of God, reverence, faith, thanksgiving, joy, and zeal for obedience, just as the angels sing: And on earth peace, good will toward men. And although we are very weak, nevertheless let us rouse ourselves to the pious contemplation of so great a work, and let us oppose the voice of God to the fury of the devil, and of the impious, who deny this conjunction of divine and human nature in Christ. Let us gather for ourselves testimonies, such as exist above in the first chapter, which affirm that the divine nature is in Christ.
