These pertain to the exposition of this passage, since Christ here commands the one who was healed to believe in the Son of God, he commands that he believe this healer to be the Son of God and the Messiah: he commands likewise that the one who was healed trust that he has God propitious on account of this Son of God, and is an heir of eternal life. This brief colloquy embraces all these things, in which the one who was healed is confirmed, and by another testimony confesses his faith, namely by voice, when he says: I believe, Lord, and by adoration.

Finally, let the example concerning the most necessary doctrine be observed, that unjust excommunication does not harm before God; after this beggar was cast out of the synagogue, Christ embraces him with a singular sign of benevolence, addresses him, and confirms him. By this example, let us at this time be comforted against the unjust judgments of those who because of the profession of true doctrine, attempt to cast us out of the Church.

Latin:

Tu credis in filium Dei.

Ut alias dixit Christus: Habenti dabitur, ita hic crescunt dona, post planam confessionem et crucem. Nam confessionem secuta erat excommu- nicatio. Sequitur ergo nova et insignis confirma- tio, nec vulgarem quaestionem proponit Christus, inquiens: Credis in filium Dei? facilius patieban- tur Iudaei hunc doctorem dici Messiam, aut Pro- phetam a Deo missum, quam filium Dei. Hoc cognomen cum audiunt, tum vero furenter incan- descunt, et se propugnare gloriam Dei putant, aequalem se facit Deo, inquiunt supra, et postea: quia filium Dei se fecit, has iudicant horrendas et execrandas blasphemias, sed Apostoli edunt confessionem, Matth. 16.: Tu es Christus filius Dei viventis. Hi complectuntur et officii, et na- turae descriptionem: Fatemur te esse Messiam promissum patribus, propter quem Deus erit pla- catus nobis. Deinde et hoc profitemur, te Mes- siam habere divinam naturam ab aeterno patre, cuius es unigenitus filius. Haec Apostoli aliquan- to clarius intelligebant, quam hic sanatus, et tamen professio eadem est, et huic ipsi confitenti postea magis explicata est.

Mira omnino vox est Ecclesiae, quod Mes- siam praedicat esse natura filium Dei, et horribi- liter offendit Iudaeos, et gentes sapientes. Ethnici semper senserunt, mundum providentia regi. Viderunt enim viros heroicos subito excitari ad instaurationem et constitutionem imperiorum, ut Herculem, Cyrum, Alexandrum, Augustum, et alios alias. Hos quoque vocabant filios Dei, non quod arbitrarentur ex natura Dei ortos esse, sed quia videbant eos a Deo iuvari, ac mirabiliter regi et protegi. Sic Iudaei cogitabant Salomonem dictum esse filium Dei, et de Messia eodem modo cogitabant, sic et Mahometus contendit Mosen, Christum, se, et alios multos Prophetas et Reges fuisse filios Dei. Idem Ebion, Samosatenus, Nestorius, et alii multi cogitarunt, et fortasse multi semper sunt etiam titulo Christiani, qui hanc opinionem secum tacite in animis circumferunt.

Sed Ecclesia Dei, etsi nondum in hac vita videt, qualis sit illa miranda unio humanae et divinae naturae, tamen mandato Dei cogitur sonare hanc doctrinam, quod filius Dei λόγος, genitus a patre ab aeterno, postea assumserit humanam naturam. Vult enim hoc foedus, et hanc societatem divinae naturae et humanae, esse evidens testimonium amoris divinae erga humanam naturam. Si possent animi humani cogitare aliquo modo magnitudinem huius operis, quod divina natura se adeo demittit, quod humanam sibi adiungit, et immutabile foedus cum ea facit, tum vero incenderemur amore Dei, reverentia, fide, gratiarum actione, laetitia, et studio obediendi, sicut angeli canunt: Et hominibus laetitia. Etsi autem sumus valde infirmi, tamen excitemus nos ad piam cogitationem tanti operis, et opponamus vocem Dei furori diaboli, et impiorum, qui negant hanc coniunctionem divinae et humanae naturae in Christo. Colligamus nobis testimonia, qualia supra extant in primo capite, quae affirmant in Christo divinam naturam esse. Haec pertinent ad huius loci enarrationem, cum Christus hic iubet sanatum credere in filium Dei, iubet ut credat hunc sanatorem esse filium Dei et Messiam: iubet item ut confidat sanatus, se propter hunc filium Dei habere Deum propicium, et haeredem esse vitae aeternae. Haec omnia complectitur hoc breve colloquium, in quo sanatus confirmatur, et alio testimonio profitetur suam fidem, videlicet voce, cum ait: Credo domine, et adoratione.

Postremo observetur exemplum de doctrina maxime necessaria, quod iniusta excommunicatio non noceat coram Deo, postquam hic mendicus ex synagoga eiectus est, Christus eum singulari significatione benevolentiae complectitur, alloquitur et confirmat. Hoc exemplo nos hoc tempore adversus iniusta iudicia eorum, qui nos propter professionem verae doctrinae ex Ecclesia eiicere conantur, consolemur.

## 9:39
For judgment into this world.

There are two very grave opinions, strongly conflicting with human law and wisdom. The one, that the Gospel offers salvation to the unworthy. The other, that it rejects those who seem most worthy, and excel in wisdom, virtue, and discipline, but because of this glory despise the voice of the Gospel. Human reason naturally holds opinions born from the law, makes much of discipline, and judges that the righteous please God, or if it receives any who have fallen, it certainly does not receive them except because of some merits. And because it never knows what merits are sufficient, it therefore always doubts about grace. This opinion is innate in the minds of all; therefore the Pharisees do not want the Church to be gathered from that number which lives without discipline, as from the Gentiles.

But here the immense mercy of God is most observed, that He spreads His Gospel, His voice, not only among those who are restrained by discipline, but absolutely among all men, even those contaminated by horrible vices. He calls all to repentance, and offers salvation because of the Son of God to all who are converted, even if they previously lived without discipline. And the magnitude of the mercy of God is better understood in comparison and in the histories themselves. Compare Nazareth and Rome in the time of Nero; it is less wonderful for the voice of God to sound and the Church to be gathered in Nazareth, where discipline flourished, and the true doctrine about one God, the creator of all things, caring for men, hearing the righteous, and punishing atrocious crimes, was still retained there. There were also honest morals, and the magistrates punished all manifest crimes. But at Rome, especially in the time of Nero, what kind of filth was there? The greatest multitude was entirely Epicurean, and most securely laughed at all religions; a few others worshipped idols. Furthermore, very many were horribly polluted by wandering and flagitious lusts, which were so far from being punished that they were even thought to be permitted pleasures, and the most excellent were the most contaminated. Likewise, usury and various ways of hunting for money were considered praiseworthy. And there was a nearly similar madness of the Gentiles throughout the whole world. Since Rome was such in the time of Nero, nevertheless the voice of God sounds there, and gathers a Church, when Paul preaches the Gospel there. This magnitude of mercy must be attentively considered. For it seems alien to human reason for the voice of God to sound among those polluted by such great filth, and to gather the Church of God from such people. Therefore the Jews were vehemently indignant at the beginning when they saw the Gospel being spread among the Gentiles.

To this judgment of human reason must be opposed these voices of Christ, and similar ones: I came that those who do not see may see, so that what is preached here and there about the calling of the Gentiles, and Paul struggles about the particle 'freely', cries out that discipline does not take away sin before God, but that Gentiles and Jews without the knowledge of the Son are under sin and are guilty, and all who flee to Him are received freely because of the Son. This was an unknown discourse to the hypocrites, but it behooves us to know and hold it in the Church, for many reasons: that due honor may be attributed to the Son of God, and also that consciences may hold firm consolation. Likewise, that we may not be deterred from the Gospel because it is preached among men, the greatest part of whom is full of madness and crimes. Concerning this great scandal there was a great and difficult struggle for Christ and the Apostles with the hypocrites, and Christ preaches on this argument about the lost sheep, and about the prodigal son, and adds the sweetest voice: There is more joy in heaven over one sinner repenting than over ninety-nine righteous who do not need repentance.

On the other hand, however, Christ says in this place: I came that those who see may become blind. Likewise, if you were blind, you would not have sin: Now you say you see, therefore your sin remains. Of all human things, the best thing is, and the most beautiful, discipline, that is, the order of external life, agreeing with the law of God; this human nature has nothing better or more beautiful, and the command of God is added, by which it is most severely enjoined, and yet, endowed with such a great good and most excellently behaved, He says they are blind, for this very reason, that by confidence in discipline they despise the Gospel. But the world does not understand this blindness and this sin, and there is darkness in the mind, namely, doubts about God, carnal security, distrust, contempt of the mediator, false invocation of a mind doubting and fleeing from God. There are also other motions innumerable that deviate from the law of God. Although, therefore, external morals are well composed, yet because the mind rages against the Son of God, it does not receive the remission of sins, and remains guilty of eternal wrath, because of the contempt of the Son of God, and many other sins. This judgment against hypocrites who please themselves because of external morals better composed must be observed, lest the pious be moved by the appearance and authority of such hypocrites to fall away from the Gospel.

Latin:

In iudicium in hunc mundum.

Duae sunt sententiae gravissimae, valde pu- gnantes cum lege et sapientia humana. Altera, quod Evangelium offerat salutem indignis. Alte- ra, quod eos qui videntur maxime digni, et ex- cellunt sapientia, virtute et disciplina, sed pro- pter hoc decus contemnunt vocem Evangelii, reii- ciat. Ratio humana naturaliter opiniones ex lege ortas tenet, disciplinam magni facit, et iudicat Deo placere iustos, aut si quos lapsos recipit, certe non recipere, nisi propter aliqua merita. Et quia nunquam scit, quae merita sufficiant, ideo semper dubitat de gratia. Haec opinio omnium animis innata est, ideo Pharisaei nolunt Ecclesiam colligi ex eo numero, qui vivit sine disciplina, ut ex gentibus.

Sed hic maxime conspicitur ingens miseri- cordia Dei, quod suum Evangelium, suam vo- cem non solum spargit inter eos, qui disciplina frenati sunt, sed prorsus inter omnes homines, etiam horribilibus vitiis contaminatos. Omnes vocat ad poenitentiam, et offert salutem propter filium Dei omnibus, qui convertuntur, etiamsi antea sine disciplina vixerunt. Ac magnitudo misericordiae Dei magis intelligitur in collatione et ipsis historiis. Confer Nazareth et Romam Ne- ronis tempore, minus mirum est, sonare vocem Dei et colligi Ecclesiam in Nazareth, ubi disci- plina florebat, adhuc retinebatur ibi vera doctrina de uno Deo, conditore omnium rerum, curante homines, exaudiente iustos, et puniente atrocia scelera. Erant et mores honesti, ac magistratus puniebant omnia manifesta scelera. At Romae praesertim Neronis tempore, qualis erat turpi- tudo? Maxima multitudo prorsus erat epicurea, et securissime ridebat omnes religiones, pauci alii colebant idola. Deinde horribiliter polluti fuerunt plurimi vagis et flagitiosis libidinibus, quae adeo non puniebantur, ut etiam concessae voluptates esse putarentur, ac praestantissimi maxime erant contaminati. Item usurae, et varia aucupia pe- cuniae laudi ducebantur. Et fere similis furor erat gentium toto orbe terrarum. Talis cum esset Roma Neronis tempore, tamen ibi sonat vox Dei, et Ecclesiam colligit, cum Paulus ibi Evangelium praedicat. Haec magnitudo misericordiae attente consideranda est. Alienum enim videtur huma- nae rationi, sonare vocem Dei inter pollutos tanta turpitudine, et colligere ex talibus Ecclesiam Dei. Ideo Iudaei vehementer stomachabantur initio, cum viderent Evangelium spargi inter gentes.

Huic iudicio humanae rationis opponendae sunt hae voces Christi, et similes: Veni et non videntes videant, ut quae de vocatione gentium passim concionantur, et Paulus dimicat de parti- cula Gratis, clamatat disciplina non tolli pecca- tum coram Deo, sed gentes et Iudaeos sine agni- tione filii, sub peccato et reos esse, et recipi gra- tis propter filium omnes, qui ad eum confugiunt. Haec erat ignota concio hypocritis, sed nos eam in Ecclesia nosse et tenere oportet, propter mul- tas causas, ut filio Dei tribuatur debitus honos, item, ut conscientiae firmam consolationem te- neant. Item, ne deterreamur ab Evangelio, pro- pterea quod inter homines, quorum maxima pars plena est furoris et scelerum, praedicatur. De hoc tanto scandalo magnum et difficile certamen fuit Christo et Apostolis cum hypocritis, et Chri- stus hoc argumento concionatur de ove perdita, et de filio prodigo, et addit dulcissimam vocem: Gaudium est in coelis maius de uno peccatore agente poenitentiam, quam de nonaginta novem iustis, qui poenitentia non indigent.

Econtra vero inquit Christus hoc loco: Veni, ut videntes caeci fiant. Item, si caeci essetis, non haberetis peccatum: Nunc dicitis vos videre, ideo peccatum vestrum manet. Omnium rerum hu- manarum optima res est, et pulcerrima disciplina, id est, ordo vitae externae, congruens legi Dei, nihil melius aut pulcrius habet haec humana na- tura, et accedit mandatum Dei, quo severissime praecipitur, et tamen hoc tanto bono praeditos, et optime moratos, ait caecos esse, hanc ipsam ob causam, quod fiducia disciplinae contemnunt Evangelium. Sed hanc caecitatem et hoc pecca- tum mundus non intelligit, suntque tenebrae in mente, videlicet dubitationes de Deo, securitas carnalis, diffidentia, contemtus mediatoris, falsa invocatio animi dubitantis et fugientis Deum. Sunt et alii motus aberrantes a lege Dei innume- rabiles. Etsi igitur mores externi bene compo- siti sunt, tamen quia mens furit adversus filium Dei, non accipit remissionem peccatorum, et ma- net rea aeternae irae, propter contemtum filii Dei, et alia multa peccata. Hoc iudicium adversus hy- pocritas sibi placentes propter externos mores me- lius compositos, observandum est, ne pii movean- tur specie et autoritate talium hypocritarum, ut ab Evangelio deficiant.

## 10:1 Argument
Chapter X.

Truly, truly I say to you, he who enters through the door, etc.

There is a long discourse concerning good and bad shepherds, in which at the beginning the reader must be warned to distinguish Christ from all other governors, from the Prophets, teachers, and governors of peoples, and we shall speak of that distinction later. At the beginning, however, we shall recount the degrees by which human governors differ. For Christ makes degrees here, so that by making a comparison He may declare His own governance to us more clearly.

There are three degrees of princes or governors. The first are shepherds who rightly perform their duty and manage necessary and salutary things, and are not broken by fear so as to desert their office, but constantly serve the public utility rather than their own. Such were Camillus, Fabius, Scipio, and others outstanding in virtue when the Roman Republic was flourishing. Such were Miltiades, Aristides, Cimon, Conon, and a few others in Athens.

In the second degree are listed the hirelings, who perform their duty moderately, but in such a way that they consult their own utility more than the public one. Therefore, in dangers they languish, are silent, and flee; such were Scaevola, Lucullus, Hortensius, and Servius Sulpitius in Rome. In Athens, Lysias, Demades, Aeschines, and in all courts and towns there is a great number of such men who serve moderately, but in dangers prefer their own safety to the common necessity, hide themselves, are silent, or bend their opinions to the wills of the powerful, just as Cicero courts the benevolence now of the flourishing Pompey, now of the reigning Caesar.

In the third degree are thieves and robbers, that is, sycophants and tyrants, who do not even strive to do right, but for the sake of their own utility devise frauds or go about with violence, as in Rome Saturninus, Glaucia, Rullus, and similar tribunes of the people, who carried agrarian laws and, having stirred up seditions, shook the Republic. Others seized dominion by arms, as Marius, Antony, and others. The frauds and perfidies of Alcibiades almost utterly overturned the Attic Republic; before that, it was oppressed by force by Pisistratus, and in all ages there are in power both cunning men who practice Simonian frauds and violent ones who go about more openly.

Let us compare teachers to this image of political men. Good shepherds were the Prophets and Apostles, and many other salutary teachers, Athanasius, Basil, Ambrose, Augustine. For they both performed their duty rightly and did not desert their service, broken by fear. Then there have always been innumerable other hirelings who served moderately in tranquil times. But they consulted their own utility more than the public one, and did not have enough strength to oppose impious teachers, like Osius of Spain, who, out of a certain weakness of spirit, assented to the impious decree of the Synod of Sirmium, which he did not approve. And Nazianzenus tells a similar thing about his own father, the Bishop. There is a huge multitude of such men at this time who teach moderately, but nevertheless, out of fear of tyrants, dissemble certain things and do not confess purely. In the third degree are thieves and robbers, that is, heretics who sow false dogmas and corruptions of true doctrine, and tyrannical Pontiffs and Princes who defend and establish them by force, such as Arius, Mahomet, and many others, and at this time teachers, Pontiffs, and Princes who defend various cults of idols in the Church. Likewise Anabaptists, etc.

These degrees having been considered, the discourse in the text becomes clearer. Now this must be said about good shepherds. Good shepherds are the Prophets and Apostles sent by God, and all who are duly called, and who perform their duty rightly and constantly: and although Christ is such a one, nevertheless He must be placed above the Prophets and Apostles. For He is not only a shepherd in that He teaches, as the others do, and performs an external ministry, but He is also a shepherd because He gives life by His own power, and gives the Holy Spirit; through Him the promise of grace was brought forth from the bosom of the Father and delivered to the Prophets and Apostles. He Himself is the victim for us, appeasing the wrath of God; He Himself is the giver of justice and eternal life.

Latin:

Caput X.

Amen, amen dico vobis, qui intrat per ostium, etc.

Longa concio est de Pastoribus bonis et ma- lis, in qua initio monendus est lector, ut discer- nat Christum ab omnibus gubernatoribus caeteris, a Prophetis, doctoribus, et gubernatoribus popu- lorum, ac de eo discrimine postea dicemus. Ini- tio vero gradus, quibus differunt humani guber- natores, recensebimus. Nam Christus hic gra- dus facit, ut facta collatione suam gubernationem nobis magis declaret.

Tres sunt gradus principum seu gubernato- rum. Primi sunt pastores, qui recte faciunt offi- cium suum, et res gerunt necessarias et salutares, nec franguntur metu, ut deserant suum munus, sed constanter serviunt utilitati publicae, potius quam suae. Tales fuerunt Romae florente Re- pub. Camillus, Fabius, Scipio, et alii virtute praestantes. Tales Athenis fuerunt Miltiades, Aristides, Cimon, Conon et pauci alii.

Secundo gradu recensentur mercenarii, qui mediocriter faciunt officium suum, sed ita, ut suae utilitati magis consulant, quam publicae. Quare in periculis languent, tacent, fugiunt, ta- les fuerunt Romae Scaevola, Lucullus, Horten- sius, Servius Sulpitius. Athenis Lysias, Dema- des, Aeschines, et in omnibus aulis ac oppidis talium magnus numerus est, qui mediocriter ser- viunt, sed in periculis anteferunt suam salutem communi necessitati, abdunt se, tacent, aut in- flectunt sententias ad potentum voluntates, ut Ci- cero nunc florentis Pompeii, nunc regnantis Cae- saris benevolentiam aucupatur.

Tertio gradu sunt fures et latrones, id est, sycophantae et tyranni, qui ne student quidem recte facere, sed suae utilitatis causa fraudes struunt, aut vi grassantur, ut Romae Saturninus, Glaucia, Rullus, et similes tribuni plebis, qui agrarias leges tulerunt, et motis seditionibus con- cusserunt Rempub. Alii armis rapuerunt domi- nationem, ut Marius, Antonius et alii. Atti- cam Rempub. fraudes et perfidiae Alcibiadis pene funditus everterunt, antea vi a Pisistrato oppressa fuit, et omnibus aetatibus sunt in imperiis, tum astuti homines, qui Simonias fraudes exercent, tum violenti, qui manifestius grassantur.

Ad hanc imaginem politicorum virorum conferamus doctores. Boni pastores fuerunt Prophetae et Apostoli, et multi alii salutares doctores, Athanasius, Basilius, Ambrosius, Augustinus. Nam et recte fecerunt officium suum, nec deseruerunt suam militiam, fracti metu. Deinde alii mercenarii semper innumerabiles fuerunt, qui mediocriter servierunt tranquillis temporibus. Sed suae utilitati magis quam publicae consuluerunt, nec tantum roboris habuerunt, ut impiis doctoribus se opponerent, ut Osius Hispanus, qui impio decreto Syrmiensis Synodi, quod non probabat, quadam tamen animi imbecillitate assensit. Et simile quiddam de suo patre Episcopo narrat Nazianzenus. Talium hoc tempore ingens est multitudo, qui mediocriter docent: sed tamen metu tyrannorum quaedam dissimulant, nec pure confitentur. Tertio gradu sunt fures et latrones, id est, haeretici, qui serunt falsa dogmata et corruptelas verae doctrinae, et tyrannici Pontifices et Principes, qui vi defendunt et stabiliunt, ut Arius, Mahomet et alii multi, et hoc tempore doctores, Pontifices et Principes, qui defendunt varios idolorum cultus in Ecclesia. Item Anabaptistae, etc.

His gradibus consideratis, concio in textu fit dilucidior. Iam de bonis pastoribus hoc dicendum. Boni pastores sunt Prophetae et Apostoli a Deo missi, et omnes rite vocati, et recte et constanter facientes officium suum: etsi autem talis est et Christus, tamen supra Prophetas et Apostolos collocandus est. Nam non solum est pastor, eo quod doceat, ut caeteri, et externo ministerio fungatur, sed etiam est pastor, quia vivificat sua potentia, et dat Spiritum sanctum, per ipsum ex sinu patris prolata est promissio gratiae, et tradita Prophetis et Apostolis. Ipse est victima pro nobis placans iram Dei, ipse est dator iusticiae et vitae aeternae.

## 10:1
He who does not enter through the door, etc.

At the beginning of the chapter an image is recited, to which He later compares Himself in the interpretation, and compares the teachers sent by Him, and opposes the hirelings and thieves. Furthermore, the text itself adds an interpretation to the image, with which we should be content, and I have recited the summary above in that by the distinction of three degrees, He who does not enter by the door is a thief and a robber: I, he says, am the door, as it is said in the Psalm: The stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner. And Paul says: Other foundation can no man lay than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ. God chose the Church for the sake of the Son, and willed it to be redeemed through him, and delivered the Gospel concerning him, and the Fathers, Prophets, and Apostles received the Gospel through the Son. No Church of God, therefore, is to be thought of without the acknowledgment of this mediator and the Gospel which he delivered, but all good shepherds, by whose voice God imparted salvation and righteousness to men, knew this Son, and embraced his Gospel, and propagated it, and were sent and aided by him. This is the sum of the first sentence: I am the door, the leader, sending the Fathers, Prophets, Apostles, Pastors, delivering the Gospel to them and aiding them. There follows, therefore, the antithesis.

All who came before me are thieves and robbers, that is, all who came without my sending or leading, without my Gospel, and with me neglected. The particle 'before me' is a signification not of time, but of distraction. The text itself indicates this, for it says: If anyone has climbed up some other way, he is a thief, that is, not through the door. The first fathers, Adam, Noah, Abraham, Samuel, David, did not come before the Son of God, but with him leading and sending them and giving the Gospel. As Paul says: He ascended, he gave gifts to men, Prophets, Apostles, Evangelists, Pastors, Teachers. Thus the Son of God was always present to the Church, he raised up teachers and governors, nor should we think that the purity of doctrine was retained by human counsels, but rather human wisdom from time to time cast a fog over the doctrine, not only through blasphemous men and heretics, but even through mediocre governors and teachers, as formerly through the Levitical Pontiffs. Afterwards through Gregory, Chrysostom, and others, who established many superstitions. Nor did empires retain the true state of the Church, but rather disturbed it, as all monarchies exercised cruelty, and finally Kings and Princes, who gave wealth to the Church, oppressed the ministry by that very opulence, for Bishops, occupied with the cares of maintaining wealth, utterly neglected the study of letters and the duty of teaching. Among these evils, however, the Son of God preserved the remnants of the Church, from time to time raising up some pious teachers who censured errors and proposed the voice of the Gospel more purely, some more, some less.

Latin:

Qui non intrat per ostium, etc.

Initio capitis recitatur imago, ad quam postea in interpretatione confert se, et a se missos doctores, et opponit mercenarios et fures. Porro ipse textus addit imagini interpretationem, qua contenti simus, et summam recitavi supra in illa distinctione trium graduum, Qui non intrat per ianuam, est fur et latro: Ego inquit sum ianua, ut in Psal. dicitur: Lapis quem reprobaverunt aedificantes, hic factus est in caput anguli. Et Paulus inquit: Fundamentum aliud poni non po- test, praeter id, quod positum est, quod est Iesus Christus. Deus elegit Ecclesiam propter filium, eamque voluit redimi per eum, et tradidit Evan- gelium de ipso, et Patres, Prophetae, Apostoli per filium acceperunt Evangelium. Nulla igitur cogitanda est Ecclesia Dei, sine agnitione huius mediatoris et Evangelii, quod tradidit, sed omne boni pastores, quorum voce Deus impertiit salutem et iusticiam hominibus, noverunt hunc filium, et Evangelium eius amplexi sunt, ac pro- pagarunt, et sunt missi, ac adiuti per eum. Haec est summa primae sententiae: Ego sum ianua, dux, mittens Patres, Prophetas, Apostolos, Pa- stores, Evangelium eis tradens et adiuvans. Se- quitur ergo antithesis.

Omnes qui ante me venerunt, fures sunt ac latrones, id est, omnes qui venerunt, non mit- tente, seu non ducente me, sine meo Evangelio, et me neglecto. Non temporis, sed distractionis significatio est in particula ante me. Id ipse tex- tus indicat, ait enim: Si quis aliunde ascenderit, fur est, hoc est, non per ianuam. Primi patres, Adam, Noha, Abraham, Samuel, David, non venerunt ante filium Dei, sed ipso ducente, ac mittente eos et dante Evangelium. Sicut inquit Paulus: Ascendit, dedit dona hominibus, Pro- phetas, Apostolos, Evangelistas, Pastores, Do- ctores. Ita semper filius Dei adfuit Ecclesiae, ex- citavit doctores et gubernatores, nec putemus hu- manis consiliis, doctrinae puritatem retentam esse, sed potius humana sapientia subinde cali- ginem doctrinae offudit, non solum per homines blasphemos et haereticos, sed etiam per guber- natores et doctores mediocres, ut olim per Pon- tifices leviticos. Postea per Gregorium, Chry- sostomum, et alios, qui stabilierunt multas su- perstitiones. Nec imperia retinuerunt verum Ec- clesiae statum, sed potius turbaverunt, ut omnes monarchiae saevitiam exercuerunt, et postremo Reges et Principes, qui dederunt opes Ecclesiae, ministerium oppresserunt ipsa opulentia, Episco- pi enim occupati curis opum tuendarum, prorsus neglexerunt studia literarum, et munus docendi. Inter haec mala filius Dei tamen Ecclesiae reli- quias servavit, subinde excitatis aliquibus piis doctoribus, qui errores taxarunt, et Evangelii vocem purius proposuerunt, alii magis, alii minus.

## 10:3
But the sheep did not hear them.

Concerning the remnants he says: The sheep did not hear them. For the greatest multitude in all ages heard the impious. He testifies, therefore, that there is always some true Church which hears the voice of the Gospel, even if at one time this assembly is larger, at another smaller, at one time it has more, at another less light, as it is said to Elijah: I have left for myself seven thousand, and Isaiah 1: Unless God had left us a seed, we would have been destroyed like Sodom.

Latin:

Sed non audiverunt ipsos oves.

De reliquiis dicit: Oves non audierunt eos. Nam maxima multitudo omnibus aetatibus audi- vit impios. Testatur ergo semper aliquam esse veram Ecclesiam, quae Evangelii vocem audit, etsi alias hic coetus maior, alias minor est, alias plus, alias minus lucis habet, sicut dicitur ad Eliam: Reliqui mihi septem millia, et Esaiae 1.: Nisi Deus reliquisset nobis semen, sicut Sodoma funditus deleti essemus.

## 10:9
If anyone enters through me, he shall be saved.

It is a most sweet description of pious Pastors and the Church. He recounts four benefits: 1. He shall be saved. 2. He shall enter. 3. He shall go out. 4. He shall find pasture. If he enters through me, that is, with me leading, sending, and giving the Gospel, if he acknowledges and confesses me, and sounds my Gospel, he shall be saved. First, he himself shall obtain my benefits, the remission of sins and righteousness, and shall be an heir of eternal life. Then he shall enter, that is, he shall approach God, he shall have the right of invoking him, he shall receive the gifts of the Holy Spirit. And he shall go out instructed with gifts, he shall serve the Church, he shall call many to the fellowship of eternal life. And he shall find pasture, that is, because he shall serve the calling, he shall propagate the Gospel, and shall exercise the gifts of the Holy Spirit in invocation, in confession, in various struggles, and finally in governing private morals, he shall find pasture, that is, consolation and help, etc.

Let us know, therefore, that a most ample and sweet promise is delivered to us here, which testifies to us that the Son of God, the shepherd, will be present, will give salvation, and will help with counsel and aid in all dangers and struggles, as he says elsewhere: I will not leave you orphans.

Latin:

Per me si quis ingredietur, servabitur.

Dulcissima descriptio est piorum Pastorum et Ecclesiae. Quatuor beneficia recenset, 1. Sal- vabitur. 2. Intrabit. 3. Exibit. 4. Pabulum inve- niet. Si per me, id est, me ducente, mittente, dante Evangelium intrabit, si me agnoscet ac pro- fitebitur, et meum Evangelium sonabit, salvabi- tur. Primum ipse consequetur beneficia mea, re- missionem peccatorum ac iusticiam, et erit haeres vitae aeternae. Deinde ingredietur, id est, acce- det ad Deum, habebit ius invocandi, accipiet dona Spiritus sancti. Et egredietur instructus donis, serviet Ecclesiae, multos vocabit ad socie- tatem vitae aeternae. Et pabulum inveniet, id est, quia serviet vocationi, propagabit Evange- lium, et exercebit dona Spiritus sancti in invo- catione, in confessione, in variis certaminibus, denique et in privatis moribus regendis, inveniet pabulum, hoc est, consolationem et auxilium, etc.

Sciamus igitur promissionem amplissimam et dulcissimam hic nobis tradi, quae testatur nobis pastorem filium Dei affuturum esse, daturum sa- lutem, consilio et auxilio opitulaturum in omni- bus periculis et certaminibus, sicut alias dicit: Non relinquam vos orphanos.

## 10:10
I came that they might have life.

He confirms and increases this very promise, and here Christ clearly distinguishes not only bad shepherds and good ones, but also prefers himself to the Prophets and other ministers. This is to be observed universally in these comparisons, that Christ is not only a teacher, or a minister of the external voice, but also the giver of the Holy Spirit and of new light, of righteousness and eternal life, as was said at the beginning of the first chapter: Grace and truth came by Jesus Christ, and below in John 10: I give them eternal life. And this honor is to be attributed to Christ in such a way that, when we have acknowledged him to be such, we truly believe that we are received into grace on his account, that we call upon God with confidence in him, and that we rest on his account in the expectation of help and eternal life.

Latin:

Ego veni, ut vitam habeant.

Hanc ipsam promissionem confirmat et auget, et hic clare non solum malos pastores et bonos discernit Christus, sed etiam sese Prophetis et aliis ministris antefert. Id universaliter in his collationibus observandum est, Christum non tan- tum doctorem esse, seu ministrum externae vocis, sed etiam datorem Spiritus sancti, et novae lucis, iusticiae et vitae aeternae, sicut initio primi capitis dictum est: Gratia et veritas per Iesum Christum facta est, et infra Ioan. 10.: Ego vitam aeternam do eis. Et hic honos ita tribuendus est Christo, ut cum agnovimus eum esse talem, vere credamus nos propter ipsum recipi in gratiam, fiducia ipsius invocemus Deum, ac quiescamus propter ipsum expectatione auxilii, et vitae aeternae.

## 10:11
The good shepherd lays down his life.

Christ returns to the distribution of shepherds, handed down above. Good shepherds prefer the salvation of the Church to their own life and all bodily comforts, according to the commandment of God: He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me: but hirelings, whom he called cowards above, are silent for the sake of their own tranquility, or they twist the Gospel to the affections of men, as there are very many now who are not ignorant of the true doctrine, but yet out of fear dissemble their opinion, and by their dissimulation confirm the rage of tyrants. Christ speaks atrociously here concerning these: when, the wolf coming, the hireling flees, the wolf scatters the sheep, and tears some, as there are examples now in sight. In many courts the learned know the true doctrine, and yet, lest they offend the wills of princes, they either are silent, or they soften and excuse errors, thus confirming the rage of wolves, that is, the furies of impious teachers and tyrants. Against these it is said in Matthew 12: He who is not with me is against me, and he who does not gather with me, scatters. And Mark 8: Whoever will be ashamed of me and my words in this adulterous generation, the Son will in turn be ashamed of him, and to the Romans 10: Confession is made unto salvation. And Isaiah 5: Woe to you who call evil good, woe to you who approve the impious and condemn the just.

Some think themselves excused if they are silent and are not instigators of cruelty, but by this very silence they confirm impiety and cruelty. Therefore let them know that confession is necessary, both for the glory of God and to liberate others who are dragged to punishments on account of confession. Here the reader must again be warned about the distinction between good political governors, Prophets, and Apostles, and Christ. Christ lays down his life for the sheep in a different way than Scipio, David, or Jeremiah: for Christ's passion is a unique sacrifice, ordained to this huge and ineffable good, that it appeases the wrath of God and is a satisfaction for our sins. But the punishments of David, Jeremiah, and Paul do not merit the remission of sins for others, nor are they sacrifices appeasing the wrath of God, but they are due obedience in those things, which nevertheless, because of confession and the propagation of doctrine, benefits others. So says Paul in Philippians 2: But even if I am poured out as a drink offering for the sacrifice and service of your faith, that is, I am poured out so that my confession may shine in punishment and be a testimony of the Gospel, confirming your faith, which is the true sacrifice and true offering.

Latin:

Bonus pastor animam suam ponit.

Redit Christus ad distributionem pastorum, supra traditam. Boni pastores anteferunt suae vitae et omnibus corporalibus commodis salutem Ecclesiae, iuxta praeceptum Dei: Qui diligit patrem aut matrem plus quam me, non est dignus me: sed mercenarii, quos supra vocavit ignavos, suae tranquillitatis causa tacent, aut inflectunt Evangelium ad hominum affectus, ut nunc plurimi sunt, qui non ignorant veram doctrinam, sed tamen metu sententiam suam dissimulant, et sua dissimulatione rabiem tyrannorum confirmant. De his atrociter hic loquitur Christus: cum, veniente lupo, mercenarius fugit, lupus dissipat oves, et aliquas lacerat, ut nunc exempla sunt in conspectu. In multis aulis docti norunt veram doctrinam, et tamen ne offendant principum voluntates, vel tacent, vel errores leniunt, et excusant, ita luporum rabiem, id est, furores impiorum doctorum et tyrannorum confirmant. Adversus hos dicitur Mat. 12.: Qui non est mecum, contra me est, et qui non congregat mecum, dissipat. Et Marci 8.: Quem pudebit mei et sermonum meorum in hac adultera generatione, hunc vicissim confundet filius, et ad Rom. 10.: Confessio fit ad salutem. Et Esaiae 5.: Vae, qui dicitis malum, bonum, vae qui approbatis impium, et damnatis iustum.

Quidam se excusatos putant, si taceant, nec sint hortatores ad saevitiam, sed hoc ipso silentio confirmant impietatem et crudelitatem. Ideo sciant necessariam esse confessionem, et propter gloriam Dei, et ad liberandos alios, qui propter confessionem rapiuntur ad supplicia. Hic rursus monendus est lector de discrimine bonorum gubernatorum politicorum, Prophetarum, et Apostolorum, et Christi. Aliter Christus animam suam pro ovibus ponit, quam Scipio, David, Ieremias: nam Christi passio singulare sacrificium est, ordinatum ad hoc ingens et inenarrabile bonum, ut iram Dei placet, et sit satisfactio pro pec- catis nostris. At Davidis, Ieremiae, Pauli sup- plicia non merentur aliis remissionem peccato- rum, nec sunt sacrificia placantia iram Dei, sed sunt debita obedientia in istis, quae tamen pro- pter confessionem et propagationem doctrinae aliis prodest. Ita inquit Paulus Philip. 2.: Sed et immolor propter sacrificium et oblationem fidei vestrae, id est, immolor, ut confessio mea luceat in supplicio, et sit testimonium Evangelii, con- firmans fidem vestram, quae est verum sacrificium et vera oblatio.

## 10:16
I have other sheep, which are not of this fold.

There is no doubt that these things are said concerning the calling of the Gentiles, nor is any other meaning to be sought for this saying: There will be one fold and one shepherd, he says there will be one Church, gathered from the Gentiles and the Jews, for which there will be one shepherd, one head the Son of God, who will rule that Church both by his Gospel and by the Holy Spirit, and will kindle in it the knowledge of God and invocation, a new and eternal righteousness and life, as is said to the Ephesians 1: And he gave him as head over all things to the Church, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all, just as he himself says above: I came that they may have life, and have it abundantly.

Let us learn, therefore, that the Church is bound to this shepherd Christ, and to his voice, that it is not a gathering approving dogmas fighting against the Gospel, nor let us banish this shepherd far away, nor think that he is now idle because he is not seen by the eyes. But he wishes to be acknowledged and worshipped in such a way that we now seek good things from him, and feel that God is propitious to us on his account, let us seek from him governance, the Holy Spirit, and defense. Therefore it is written: He ascended, he gives gifts to men, and in Acts 2 it is said: Exalted to the right hand of God, receiving the promise of the Holy Spirit from the Father, he poured it out, as you now see and hear. Likewise John 20: He breathed on them, and says to them: Receive the Holy Spirit. John 14: I will not leave you orphans, I will come to you. Thus in daily invocation let us remember that we are the sheep of this shepherd, and let us flee to him, let us seek help, defense, and governance from him, and unless we acknowledge his presence in such invocation, and experience these promises of his to be true, these sermons about the shepherd will not be understood. Finally, that delusion must be entirely rejected which fanatical men have fashioned from this passage, that there will be an empire in the world before the resurrection of the dead, in which the saints, with the wicked oppressed, will rule in the highest harmony of true doctrine and justice. Christ refutes this when he says: It will be as in the days of Noah, etc. Likewise: Unless those days were shortened, no flesh would be saved. Huge dangers are denounced to us; therefore, let us be vigilant, and let us pray that the calamities may be mitigated and the errors, which the devil scatters and confirms in the whole world, may be suppressed.

Latin:

Habeo et alias oves, quae non sunt de hoc ovili.

Non dubium est haec de vocatione gentium dici, nec alia sententia quaerenda est huius dicti: Erit unum ovile et unus pastor, unam inquit Ec- clesiam fore, collectam ex gentibus et Iudaeis, cui unus erit pastor, unum caput Filius Dei, qui illam Ecclesiam et Evangelio suo et Spiritu sancto re- get, et in ea agnitionem Dei et invocationem, no- vam et aeternam iusticiam ac vitam accendet, si- cut ad Ephes. 1. dicitur: Et dedit eum caput Ec- clesiae super omnia, quae est corpus eius, et in- teger coetus omnia in omnibus perficientis, sicut et ipse supra inquit: Ego veni, ut vitam habeant, et abunde habeant.

Discamus ergo Ecclesiam ad hunc pastorem Christum, et ad eius vocem alligatam esse, non esse coetum approbantem dogmata pugnantia cum Evangelio, nec pastorem hunc procul ablegemus, nec putemus eum iam otiosum esse, quia non cer- nitur oculis. Sed sic vult agnosci et coli, ut ab ipso iam petamus bona, et sentiamus propter eum nobis Deum propicium esse, petamus ab ipso gu- bernationem, Spiritum sanctum, et defensionem. Ideo scriptum est: Ascendit, dat dona homini- bus, et Act. 2. dicitur: Ad dexteram Dei exalta- tus, promissionem Spiritus sancti a patre acci- piens, effudit ipsum, ut nunc videtis et auditis. Item Ioan. 20.: Insufflavit, et dicit eis: Accipite Spiritum sanctum. Ioan. 14.: Non relinquam vos orphanos, veniam ad vos. Ita in quotidiana in- vocatione meminerimus nos esse oves huius pasto- ris, et ad eum confugiamus, auxilium, defensio- nem et gubernationem ab ipso petamus, ac nisi in tali invocatione eius praesentiam cognoscemus, et has promissiones eius veras esse experiemur, non intelligentur hae conciones de pastore. Postremo illud deliramentum prorsus reii- ciendum est, quod ex hoc loco finxerunt homines fanatici, futurum in mundo ante resurrectionem mortuorum imperium, in quo sancti oppressis impiis dominaturi sint, summa concordia verae doctrinae, et iusticia. Christus haec refutat cum ait: Erit sicut in diebus Noae, etc. Item: Nisi abbreviati essent isti dies, non fieret salva omnis caro. Ingentia pericula nobis denunciantur, quare simus vigilantes, et mitigari calamitates et reprimi errores, quos spargit et confirmat diabolus in toto orbe, oremus.

## 10:17
Therefore the Father loves me, etc.

This is the meaning of the secret counsel of God, which cannot be fully told, concerning the manner of the redemption of the human race, but look nevertheless at this saying: He affirms that his sacrifice is pleasing to the Father, nay, that he is loved because of this obedience, because he lays down his life for the sheep. Therefore, the love of the Father toward us is immense, not willing that we should perish, as he says elsewhere: God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, etc. By the thought of this immense love, let us kindle our hearts, that we may believe in God, call upon him, expect salvation from him, and submit ourselves to him.

Latin:

Propterea pater diligit me, etc.

Haec est sententia arcani consilii Dei, quod enarrari non potest, de modo redemtionis generis humani, sed aspice tamen hoc dictum: Affirmat suum sacrificium placere patri, imo se diligi pro- pter hanc obedientiam, quia ponat animam suam pro ovibus. Igitur immensus amor est patris erga nos, nolentis nos perire, sicut alias inquit: Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut filium suum unigenitum dederit, etc. Huius immensi amoris cogitatione accendamus pectora nostra, ut Deo credamus, in- vocemus eum, expectemus ab eo salutem, et nos ei subiiciamus.

## 10:18
No one takes it from me, etc.

Two notable sentences are contained in this place: the former concerning voluntary death, the latter concerning the divine nature in Christ. No one, he says, takes my soul from me, that is, even though I die for men, yet I will do it willingly; the power of no creature could forcibly snatch my soul from me, as Isaiah 53 says: He was offered, because he willed it. And at Philippians 2 it is said: He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, he humbled himself, becoming obedient even unto death. O incomprehensible humility. The Son of God, equal to the eternal Father, submits himself to the Father, derives upon himself the wrath of God against our sins, lies prostrate before God as if he were contaminated by those very crimes which we committed: this burden was much greater than the death of the body. Let us therefore consider how far the Son of God cast himself down, that we may acknowledge that the wrath of God against sin is great, and that we may give thanks to the Redeemer, and that we also may submit ourselves to God, who have deserved punishments in many ways.

The other part of the saying is a testimony concerning the divinity of Christ: I have the power of laying down my soul, and of taking it up again. There are therefore two natures in Christ, the divine not dying, and the human dying, which is recalled to life by the divine nature. It is an illustrious testimony, and to be added to the others which affirm that there are two natures in Christ, as in chapter 1: In the beginning was the Word, and then: The Word was made flesh. Let immortality therefore be attributed to the divine, which is called the Word, but mortality to the human nature, as it was then. And thus Irenaeus said most learnedly that Christ suffered while the Word was at rest, so that he could be crucified and die. After this wonderful discourse, various judgments follow. Some pious people approve of it, others, having become more rabid, utter horrible and insulting voices against God: He has a demon. There is no greater insult. Warned, however, by these examples, let us know that because of the judgments of the wicked, the Gospel is not to be cast aside, just as Isaiah comforts us in chapter 51: Do not fear the reproaches of men, etc.

Latin:

Nemo tollit eam a me, etc.

Duae insignes sententiae hoc loco continen- tur: prior de morte spontanea, altera de natura divina in Christo. Nemo, inquit, aufert a me animam, id est, etsi morior pro hominibus, ta- men volens id faciam, nullius creaturae potentia vi mihi animam eripere posset, sicut Esaias 53. inquit: Oblatus est, quia voluit. Et ad Philip. 2. dicitur: Seipsum exinanivit, formam servi acci- piens, humiliavit se, factus obediens usque ad mortem. O incomprehensibilem humilitatem. Filius Dei aequalis aeterno patri subiicit se patri, derivat in se iram Dei adversus nostra peccata, ia- cet prostratus coram Deo, quasi contaminatus es- set illis ipsis sceleribus, quae nos fecimus: hoc onus multo maius fuit morte corporis. Cogite- mus ergo quam procul se deiecerit filius Dei, ut agnoscamus magnam esse iram Dei adversus pec- catum, ac gratias redemtori agamus, et nos quo- que Deo subiiciamus, qui poenas multipliciter meruimus.

Altera pars dicti est testimonium de Christi divinitate: Habeo facultatem ponendae animae, et rursus sumendae. Sunt igitur duae naturae in Christo, divina non moriens, et humana moriens, quae a divina natura in vitam revocatur. Illustre testimonium est, et addendum ad caetera, quae duas naturas in Christo esse affirmant, ut in 1. cap.: In principio erat verbum, et deinde: Verbum caro factum est. Tribuatur ergo immortalitas divinae, quae vocatur Verbum, mortalitas vero naturae humanae, ut tunc erat. Et sic dixit eruditissime Irenaeus, Christum passum esse requiescente ver- bo, ut crucifigi et mori posset. Post hanc miran- dam concionem, sequuntur diversa iudicia. Ali- qui pii approbant eam, alii facti rabiosiores, hor- rendas voces et contumeliosas in Deum edunt: Daemonium habet. Nullum est maius convicium. Moniti autem his exemplis, sciamus propter im- piorum iudicia, non abiiciendum esse Evange- lium, sicut consolatur nos Esaias cap. 51.: Ne timete probra hominum, etc.

## 10:22
And the feast of the dedication took place.

On the twenty-fifth day of the month of November, which in the common calendars is the day of Catherine, Judas Maccabaeus recovered the temple, as is read in 1 Maccabees 4, and the history adds that it was instituted that the dedication should then be celebrated every year for eight days. And indeed he did not add it rashly, because the recovery of the temple agrees with the time when, after the return from Babylon, the foundations of the temple were laid, namely on the twenty-fourth day of November, as is read in Zechariah 2. Therefore some think the dedication was celebrated even before the Maccabees, but from whichever history the beginning of the dedication is, the time agrees, as I said, and the text makes mention of winter.

Wherefore it is useful to remember in what month the dedication was, namely November. And this was the winter nearest before the passion of Christ.

The feast itself, however, was instituted so that the memory of the restored or recovered temple might be celebrated, in which men were to be taught that the Church has always been wonderfully defended and restored by God, and to be exhorted to give thanks to God and to seek the governance and defense of the Church.

These dedication festivals Christ also celebrated at that time, undoubtedly giving thanks to God that He had chosen an eternal Church from the human race, that He had not utterly cast away the human race after the fall, as the devil was cast away, that He had heard the prayers of the mediator, and that He had always preserved the Church in a wonderful manner. Christ was also contemplating the future true ἐγκαίνια, that is, the restoration of human nature, with sin and death abolished, which he himself was about to begin a little later. Thus let us also celebrate the dedication with Christ, let us think about the governance and defense of the Church, and with ardent vows let us ask that it now be defended against the furies of the devil, raging with Turkish arms, and the tumults of other kings. Let us also ask for those future dedications of eternal life, and let us prepare ourselves for them with repentance and faith.

Latin:

Facta sunt autem encaenia.

Mense Novembri die vicesimo quinto, qui in Calendariis usitatis Catharinae dies est, Iudas Maccabaeus templum recuperavit, ut legitur 1. Maccab. 4. et addit historia, institutum esse, ut tunc encaenia quotannis celebrarentur octiduo. Nec vero temere addidit, quod recuperatio templi convenit ad tempus, quo post reditum ex Baby- lone iacta sunt fundamenta templi, videlicet die vicesimo quarto Novembris, ut Zachariae 2. legi- tur. Ideo encaenia arbitrantur nonnulli celebrata fuisse, etiam ante Maccabaeos, sed ab utra histo- ria initium est encaeniorum, tempus congruit, ut dixi, et textus mentionem facit hiemis.

Quare utile est meminisse quo mense fuerint ἐγκαίνια, videlicet Novembri. Fuitque haec pro- xima hiems ante passionem Christi.

Ipsum vero festum institutum est, ut memo- ria celebraretur seu instaurati, seu recuperati templi, in qua docendi erant homines, semper mirabiliter Ecclesiam a Deo defensam et restitu- tam esse, et hortandi, ut agerent gratias Deo, et peterent gubernationem et defensionem Ecclesiae.

Haec encaenia et tunc Christus celebravit, haud dubie gratias agens Deo, quod Ecclesiam aeternam ex genere humano elegerit, quod non prorsus abiecerit genus humanum post lapsum, ut diabolus est abiectus, quod mediatoris preces au- dierit, quod semper Ecclesiam mirabiliter serva- verit. Cogitabat etiam Christus futura vera ἐγκαί- ria, id est, naturae humanae revocationem, abo- lito peccato et morte, quam ipse paulo post incoa- turus erat. Sic et nos cum Christo celebremus encaenia, cogitemus de gubernatione et defensione Ecclesiae, et ardentibus votis petamus, eam nunc adversus diaboli furores, grassantis Turcicis armis, et aliorum regum tumultibus, defendi. Petamus et illa futura encaenia vitae aeternae, et ad ea nos poenitentia et fide praeparemus.

## 10:24
If you are the Christ, tell us freely.

Here again a huge struggle concerning the greatest matter of all is narrated. The Jews demand that Jesus say plainly and clearly who he is, whether he is the Messiah, through whom they knew great goods were promised to the nation, and they themselves were expecting liberty, wealth, and empires. This Jesus seemed to bring none of these things; therefore they despise him, hate him, and execrate him, just as all men in this weakness of ours, we desire a pleasant state for the Church, in which we have leisure, have wealth, have firm protections against injuries, have our polities tranquil and without dissensions, let them flourish in glory, let them hold empires, and let us be safe, let us not be dragged to punishments, in short, we dream of a poetic golden age. Wherefore very many, after they see that with the light of the Gospel having arisen, horrible distractions of princes, governors, and private men occur, abhor the Gospel as the most pernicious plague of all to human society; such savage hatred of the Gospel and of the name of Christ burns in the souls of very many.

To such things Christ here responds, taxing their impiety and stubbornness: I told you, he says, that I am the Messiah; the Baptist had clearly affirmed that this is the Messiah, and he himself affirmed it often, John 4, 5, 6, 8: Before Abraham was born, I am, and chapter 11 to the blind man: Do you believe in the Son of God? And Matthew 11: All things have been given to me by the Father. Come to me all you who labor, and Matthew 16: You are the Christ the Son of the living God, and Matthew 17: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased, listen to him. So many times already it had been said with a clear voice that this is the Messiah, and yet the more powerful and greater part of the Jews did not believe him. Let us know, therefore, that the more powerful and greater part in that assembly which holds the title of the Church can err, and let us be instructed about this scandal, so that we too may not be deterred from the Gospel on account of the dissensions and judgments of the impious.

Latin:

Si tu es Christus dic nobis libere.

Hic rursus ingens certamen, de re omnium maxima narratur. Postulant Iudaei, ut plane et clare dicat Iesus, quis sit, an sit Messias, per quem sciebant genti magna bona promissa esse, et ipsi expectabant libertatem, opes, imperia. Ho- rum nihil videbatur hic Iesus afferre, ideo eum contemnunt, oderunt, et execrantur, sicut omnes homines in hac imbecillitate, optamus Ecclesiae statum suavem, in quo nobis sit otium, sint opes, sint praesidia firma contra iniurias, sint politiae nostrae tranquillae, et sine dissidiis, floreant glo- ria, teneant imperia, et nos simus tuti, non ra- piamur ad supplicia, denique somniamus auream aetatem poëticam. Quare plurimi postquam vi- dent exorta luce Evangelii, fieri horrendas distra- ctiones principum, gubernatorum, et privatorum hominum, abhorrent ab Evangelio, ut a peste omnium perniciosissima humanae societati, tam saevum odium Evangelii, et nominis Christi ardet in plurimorum animis.

Talibus hic respondet Christus, taxans im- pietatem et pertinaciam: Dixi vobis, inquit, me esse Messiam, Baptista clare affirmaverat hunc esse Messiam, affirmavit et ipse saepe, Ioan. 4. 5. 6. 8.: Priusquam Abraham nasceretur, ego sum, et cap. 11. ad caecum: Credis in filium Dei? Et Matth. 11.: Omnia mihi data sunt a patre. Ve- nite ad me omnes qui laboratis, et Matth. 16.: Tu es Christus filius Dei viventis, et Matth. 17.: Hic est filius meus dilectus, quo delector, hunc au- dite. Toties iam clara voce dictum erat, hunc esse Messiam, et tamen potentior et maior pars Iudaeorum non credebant ei. Sciamus ergo po- tentiorem et maiorem partem in illo coetu, qui tenet Ecclesiae titulum, errare posse, et nos eru- diamus de hoc scandalo, ne propter dissidia et iu- dicia impiorum nos quoque ab Evangelio deter- reamur.

## 10:25
The works that I do.

For in order to clearly convince them and to exaggerate their sin and stubbornness, he alleges the wonderful deeds, which, since no creature can imitate them, it was manifest that he was sent by God, etc. The devil cannot recall the dead to life, but that is the work of divine power alone. Therefore they ought to have believed this teacher who was raising the dead.

Latin:

Opera quae ego facio.

Ut enim clare convincat eos, et peccatum eorum ac pertinaciam exaggeret, allegat miranda facta, quae cum nulla creatura possit imitari, ma- nifestum erat a Deo missum esse, etc. Diabolus non potest mortuos in vitam revocare, sed id so- lius divinae potentiae opus est. Credere ergo huic doctori resuscitanti mortuus debebant.

## 10:27
My sheep hear my voice.

Here follows a sweet description of the Church of God, properly so called, that is, beloved by God, just, rightly invoking God, and obeying him. This is first described by an external and principal sign, namely, by the voice of Christ. This alone is the Church which hears and embraces the doctrine of Christ. Therefore, all who abolish the Gospel, either in whole or in part, are excluded from the Church. Such is a great part of the human race, atheists, idolaters, Mahometans, Jews, heretics, defenders of impious cults, etc.

And I acknowledge them.

Then he adds what he himself in turn provides for those who hear. And I know them, it is a Hebrew phrase: I know, I acknowledge, I cherish, I care for, as in the Psalm: The Lord knows the way of the just, that is, he approves and cares for it. But let us remember this assertion and promise of Christ. It is difficult, when we feel not only the inconveniences of the body or of things, but are also moved by the sight of our own weakness and our vices, to establish that we are truly the care of God, that we are truly loved by God; it was difficult for the thief on the cross to establish that, and we individuals, as often as we begin our prayers, ask ourselves whether God cares for, regards, and hears us. Here these promises are to be gathered, which teach that we are truly and certainly received, regarded, heard, and helped, on account of this Son, just as Paul says so often in Romans 5 and Ephesians 3: Through him we have access by faith.

Latin:

Oves meae vocem meam audiunt.

Hic sequitur dulcis descriptio Ecclesiae Dei, proprie dictae, id est, dilectae Deo, iustae, recte invocantis Deum, et ei obtemperantis. Haec pri- mum ab externo et praecipuo signo describitur, scilicet, a voce Christi. Haec sola est Ecclesia, quae audit et amplectitur Christi doctrinam. Ex- clusi sunt igitur ab Ecclesia omnes, qui Evange- lium, vel totum, vel aliqua ex parte abolent. Talis est magna pars generis humani, ἄθεοι, Ido- latrae, Mahometistae, Iudaei, Haeretici, defen- sores impiorum cultuum, etc.

Et ego eos agnosco.

Deinde addit, quid vicissim ipse praestet audientibus. Et ego novi eas, Hebraica phrasis est: Novi, agnosco, foveo, curo, ut in Psal.: Novit Dominus viam iustorum, id est, approbat et curat. Meminerimus autem hanc asseveratio- nem et promissionem Christi. Difficile est, cum sentiamus non solum corporis aut rerum incom- moda, sed etiam moveamur conspectu nostrae infirmitatis, et vitiorum nostrorum; statuere, quod vere simus curae Deo, quod vere diligamur a Deo, difficile erat id latroni in cruce statuere, et nos singuli quoties incoamus nostras preces, quaerimus ipsi nobiscum, an curet, respiciat, exaudiat nos Deus. Hic colligendae sunt hae pro- missiones, quae docent vere et certo nos recipi, respici, exaudiri, iuvari, propter hunc filium, sicut toties inquit Paulus Rom. 5. Ephes. 3.: Per hunc habemus accessum fide.

## 10:28
And they follow me, and I give them eternal life, and they shall not perish forever, etc.

He inculcates the same sentiments, repeated so often, to show that he clearly and absolutely means and intends what the words signify, and that no other interpretation is to be attached to his statements. He says clearly and plainly that the Church is those who hear this voice of the Gospel, and the following, that is, embracing, and in turn he says: To this Church he gives eternal life, and he adds a consolation concerning the stability of the Church, as if he were saying: The wise in such great confusion of empires think that religions never remain long in the same state, but that one is extinguished and another arises in its place. When the Chaldeans held the Babylonian empire, Baal was worshipped there; afterwards, Alexander's victory introduced Olympian Jupiter, and the thing itself shows that the ruins of kingdoms drag with them changes of religion, as in Asia and Africa, where the doctrine of Christ having been wiped out, Mahometan frenzies rage. Many are moved by these examples to think that the doctrine of Christ is similar, and that it perishes like the delusions of the nations. And Christ sees the devil fighting most fiercely, and disturbing empires, Churches, and dogmas, especially with this design, that he may destroy the whole Church of God. Against this great danger he opposes this consolation: No one shall snatch them from my hand, just as he says elsewhere: And the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. Likewise: I am with you even to the end of the age. These sentences both affirm that the Church will remain in this life, and teach concerning the departure from this life, that we are received by the Son of God, and defended against the devils.

Let us therefore fix this consolation in our minds, and let us now set it before ourselves in present dangers; we see the Turks raging more widely every day, we see the tumults of the princes of the Christian name arising among themselves, pernicious to the Churches, and the defenders of popish idols burn with most bitter hatred against the pious, they forbid the Gospel to be propagated, and they cruelly kill many honest men. What else can human reason think in these spectacles? Unless that in a little while the true doctrine and the studies of this doctrine are going to perish utterly. But against this human reasoning let us think of this voice: No one shall snatch them from my hand. Let us think also that the Church has always been wonderfully defended against similar frenzies of the world, as when in Egypt an edict was proposed by the king, that newly born infants should be killed, and all ways of pressing and destroying the people of Israel were attempted for eighty whole years, yet God wonderfully preserved that nation, and increased it, defended it, and afterwards in the desert, likewise in the Babylonian exile. Finally, the whole history of the Church from the beginning of the world contains very many examples of this kind, which show that the Church is assiduously involved in dangers, which cannot be resolved by human counsels, and yet that it is preserved, restored, and raised up divinely; thus let us learn to adapt the sentences of this place to use. I have added this admonition; there is no need to add an interpretation to words that are most clear.

Finally, let that saying be observed: I and the Father are one. In this place he certainly speaks of power, he attributes to the Father, and to himself, the same power; therefore this saying is rightly adapted to confirm the doctrine that in Christ there is a divine, omnipotent nature. But the Arians used to elude this with a quibble; they said that a unity of wills was signified: I and the Father are one, that is, we are in agreement, willing the same thing, just as it is said below in chapter 17 concerning the members of the Church, that they may be one, just as we are one, that is, that they may be in agreement. Be it so, let the interpretation concerning the agreement of wills be acceptable in that place, and since we have other more illustrious and firmer testimonies, which clearly teach that the eternal God begat a co-eternal image, the Son, and that he afterwards assumed human nature, let us be content with those testimonies, and hold them with a firm heart. It is sufficiently subtle what Augustine says: Because, he says, I and the Father are one, it expresses two persons, and what he adds, one, not one person, signifies the unity of essence.

That also must be added, that much is disputed here concerning election because of Christ's saying: No one shall snatch them from my hand, nor does it displease me that it is said here concerning the firmness of election, but let these things be treated in such a way, not that Stoic fate is mixed in, but that faith is kindled in us. At the same time, this sentence is a doctrine concerning election, and a promise confirming us. Concerning election, it teaches that there is a certain Church of the elect, which God will not allow to be torn from him, but this belongs to all who truly believe the Gospel, or having fallen are again converted to God, and return to the Gospel; for thus it behooves us to judge from the word of God, it is commanded to all universally, that they should hear the Son of God. There is also a promise of universal grace, and it is commanded to all, that they should receive it. These things are true and firm: It is certain that Pharaoh, Saul, Judas, by their own will resist the calling God, who so often admonishes them to be converted. Since therefore they willingly repel the calling God, they finally rush into eternal punishments. Therefore they do not belong to the number of the elect, and the cause of their destruction is entirely in themselves. But David, Peter, Paul, do not resist the calling God, but assent, and obey the moving Holy Spirit, they struggle with doubts, distrust, and other vicious affections, and they experience the voice to be true: Come to me all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Because such people persevere at length in this obedience, they are chosen.

Let us therefore contemplate with our whole mind the will of God, expressed in the very word of God, so that when we seek the will of God concerning the remission of sins, we do not disturb ourselves with other disputations about the causes of election. Thus David understands the mercy of God calling and moving to be the cause of election, but that nevertheless the offered mercy must be accepted, and that one must assent to the calling God. Here now the saying of Christ becomes sweet to us, when we think of our weakness and dangers, we see that we can by no means sustain such great struggles. Adam and Eve could not by their own strength sustain the grief arising from the spectacle of the first murder. David could by no means sustain his grief arising from the consciousness of his crime and the evils of exile, but these, because they knew there was an eternal Church, knew it to be helped by God, therefore they raise themselves up, and are helped.

May this voice thus confirm us: No one shall snatch them from my hand. There is a certain eternal Church, wherefore it will be helped in such great struggles; indeed, let us use it as a promise, let us know that help is promised to us here in so many huge dangers, we do not foresee all the snares of the devil. God therefore guards us while we sleep, we are sometimes entangled in affairs which are utterly inextricable by human counsel, as David expelled from the kingdom, as the people of Israel having lost the ark, and afterwards led away into captivity, indeed, as Adam by his fall, here again we are recalled from the midst of hell. Let us therefore love this saying of Christ, and impress it upon ourselves, so that it may excite us to invocation, and console us in such a variety of private and public dangers: No one shall snatch them from my hand. Defend us therefore, Christ, who are attacked on all sides by our infirmity, by the devil, by various scandals and dangers. Let us think also about public movements. Where is the Church to remain, where will there be pious studies, if the Turks shall range more widely, if kings and princes of the Christian name shall continue to exercise cruelty, or shall cause devastations in their regions with civil wars? If the studies of letters shall be extinguished, if the teachers themselves shall tear the Churches apart with private and ambitious disputes, and shall cause confusions of dogmas? In these most sad spectacles let us turn our eyes to these promises: The gates of hell shall not prevail against it. Likewise: No one shall snatch them from my hand, etc. Let it be enough to have warned these things about the disputations of predestination, let us remove philosophical imaginations. The minds of all men without heavenly light either feel that all things rush by chance, without divine governance, as Epicurus felt, this madness is to be execrated, or they feel that God is bound to secondary causes, and does not act otherwise than as they drive him, or certainly that he drives wills and events by his eternal determination, whether we want it or not, so that they fall according to an immutable determination. These are Stoic things, which are not to be brought into the Church, and they beget in us either contempt of God, or hatred, or negligence. But let us hear the voice of the eternal Father, who says of the Son: Hear him. Wherefore it is necessary that the word of God be heard, that his threats be feared, and that one assent to the promises, and know, according to this word: that God deals with us freely and certainly, as a wise, just, and merciful head of a household deals with his children. Help from God must therefore be sought and certainly hoped for, just as Christ says: Ask and you shall receive. Likewise: How much more will your Father who is in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask.

They were therefore taking up stones again.

That the sermons of Christ were not ambiguous, his adversaries confess, who understand Christ to preach that he is God, equal to the Father, as in John 5 they say: He makes himself equal to God, and here, when you are a man, you make yourself God. Nor is it a wonder that the minds of this people, who were accustomed with the greatest care to the doctrine concerning the unity of God, vehemently abhorred these sermons. They therefore take up stones, so that they may crush him as a blasphemer. He therefore renews the struggle, first mitigating the contention about the name; indeed, Scripture calls even those gods to whom the custody of the word of God has been especially entrusted. Why therefore do you consider it blasphemy that the name of God be attributed to another? The saying in Psalm 82 is alleged: I said, You are gods, which signifies the guardians of the word of God, and the instruments of the works of God, through which God rules men. Moses, Samuel, Nathan, David are guardians of the word of God, and through them God does wonderful works. Such also were Saul and other kings and priests, even if they mixed their tyrannies with their office, as the Psalm there accuses them and threatens punishments.

After Christ proposes this mitigation, he then adds: That the title of God more truly belongs to himself, who was sanctified by the Father, sent into the world, doing the works of the Father. Here he shows the dissimilarity between the others, who are called Gods, Prophets, Priests, Kings, and himself. They are called Gods because they are guardians of the word and instruments of the works of God. But this Christ was with the Father before the foundation of the world, and was afterwards sent and revealed, and yet he is still in the Father, that is, reigning and working with the Father, and beholding the Father.

The Arians with great contention twisted this passage to their own cause, as if Christ, by bringing forward an example, wished to show that he is not God by nature, but is called God on account of his office, like the Prophets, priests, and kings, just as these are named Gods in the Psalm: I said, you are Gods. Although Christ himself delivers a sufficiently clear distinction here, when he says: The Father is in me, and I in the Father, yet it is profitable to join all other testimonies from the first chapter of John, from the fifth, and from other places, so that by comparing the testimonies, without sophistry, the native and uncorrupted meaning may be chosen, namely, that there are two natures in Christ, divine and human, and that the divine is the image of God, eternally begotten by the Father, through whom all things were created, ὁμοούσιος to the Father. That is, the joined testimonies show this, and the rest will be a declaration of this saying in this place: The Father is in me, and I in the Father, that is, one reigning, and one creating, and working.

Wherefore also let the sanctification be understood otherwise than the sanctification of Elijah or Jeremiah. He is not only sanctified, that is, set apart, so as to be a teacher and a victim, nor only gifted with the Holy Spirit by measure, as Elijah or Elisha, but the divinity dwells in this man Christ bodily, as Paul says, that is, personally. Thus, therefore, he is sanctified, so that he himself may sanctify others, and impart to us light and eternal life, as the Baptist says: Of his fullness we have all received, and Psalm 45: Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows. Here he names this king: God, he says, your God has anointed you with the oil of gladness, that is, the fullness of the Holy Spirit, so that you may sanctify others, and he adds, above your fellows, or because of your fellows, that is, you far excel all the Prophets, and you were sent so that they might draw from your fountain.

Let us therefore pray with our whole heart to this king Christ, the God who sanctifies his fellows, that he may also rule and sanctify us, and pour into us the rivulets of his fullness, light, knowledge, and love of God, and kindle us, so that we may truly acknowledge, invoke, and celebrate God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the Son sent into the world, and given to us by immense mercy, and joined to us by a wondrous covenant, namely, the fellowship of our nature.

O anointed one of the eternal Father with joyful breath, Son of God, anoint your fellows, O Christ.

These things have been said briefly, so that the warned students may be able to refute the furies of Arius more sharply.

They sought therefore to seize him.

He departs, so that he may confirm in reality that which he said before, that he has the power of laying down his soul, and of taking it up again. He also proposes an example to us, so that we may know that the members of the Church are guarded by God, and cannot be snatched to death whenever tyrants burning with fury desire to rage against us, but that a course is given to each, which being finished, God calls them out of this life. Jeremiah, although he is endangered so often, yet is not killed before the destruction of the city. Paul, so often captured, so often exposed to beasts, yet finishes his course. Afterwards, Jeremiah is killed by the king of Egypt, Apries, and Paul by Nero. Although human reason argues that it is by chance that one remains unharmed longer than another in such great dangers, yet let us know from the Gospel that we are certainly guarded by God, and are then finally led away from this course when it has seemed so to God, just as Christ clearly says, Luke 12: All the hairs of your head are numbered, etc.

Latin:

Et sequuntur me, et ego vitam aeternam do eis, et non peribunt in aeternum, etc.

Inculcat easdem sententias toties repetitas, ut ostendat se plane ac prorsus hoc, quod verba so- nant, sentire et velle, nec aliam dictis interpre- tationem affingendam esse. Clare et plane dicit, Ecclesiam esse audientes hanc vocem Evangelii, ac sequentes, id est, amplectentes, et vicissim ait: Huic Ecclesiae se dare vitam aeternam, et addit consolationem de stabilitate Ecclesiae, quasi dicat: Sapientes in tanta confusione imperiorum existimant nunquam religiones in eodem statu diu permanere, sed subinde alias extingui, et oriri alias. Cum tenerent Chaldaei imperium Babylo- nicum, colebatur ibi Baal, postea Alexandri victoria Iovem Olympium invexit, et res ipsa ostendit, ruinas regnorum secum trahere muta- tiones religionum, ut in Asia et Africa deleta Christi doctrina, grassantur furores Mahometici. His exemplis moventur multi, ut existiment simi- lem esse Christi doctrinam, et interire ut gentium deliria. Et videt Christus acerrime pugnare dia- bolum, et turbare imperia, Ecclesias, dogmata, praecipue hoc consilio, ut deleat totam Ecclesiam Dei. Huic tanto periculo opponit hanc consola- tionem: Nemo rapiet eas de manu mea, sicut alias dicit: Et portae inferorum non praevalebunt adversus eam. Item: Ego vobiscum sum usque ad consummationem seculi. Hae sententiae et in hac vita mansuram esse Ecclesiam affirmant, et de exitu ex hac vita docent, nos a filio Dei re- cipi, et adversus diabolos defendi.

Hanc igitur consolationem infigamus animis, et iam eam in praesentibus periculis nobis propo- namus, videmus Turcos quotidie latius grassari, videmus oriri tumultus principum Christiani no- minis inter sese, perniciosos Ecclesiis, et defen- sores idolorum pontificiorum ardent acerbissimis odiis adversus pios, vetant propagari Evangelium, et multos honestos homines crudeliter interficiunt. Quid in his spectaculis aliud cogitare potest hu- mana ratio? nisi paulo post veram doctrinam et studia huius doctrinae funditus interitura esse. Sed contra hanc humanam ratiocinationem cogi- temus hanc vocem: Nemo rapiet eas de manu mea. Cogitemus item Ecclesiam semper adversus similes mundi furores mirabiliter defensam esse, ut cum in Aegypto edictum a rege propositum es- set, ut recens editi foetus necarentur, et tenta- rentur omnes viae premendi et delendi populi Is- raël annis totis octoginta, tamen Deus mirabili- ter eam gentem servavit, et auxit, defendit et po- stea in deserto, item in exilio Babylonico. De- nique tota historia Ecclesiae inde usque ab initio mundi continet huius generis exempla plurima, quae ostendunt Ecclesiam assidue versari in peri- culis, quae humanis consiliis discuti non possunt, et tamen servari eam, restitui, et erigi divinitus, ita discamus sententias huius loci ad usum accom- modare.
