Hanc commonefactionem adieci, inter- pretationem addere verbis maxime perspicuis, non opus est.

Postremo illud dictum observetur: Ego et pater unum sumus. Hoc loco certe de potentia loquitur, tribuit patri, et sibi eandem potentiam, ideo hoc dictum recte accommodatur ad confir- mandam doctrinam, quod in Christo sit natura divina, omnipotens. Sed Ariani eludebant hanc cavillatione, dicebant voluntatum unitatem signi- ficari: Ego et pater unum sumus, id est, concor- des, idem volentes, sicut infra dicitur cap. 17. de membris Ecclesiae, ut unum sint, sicut nos unum sumus, id est, ut sint concordes. Esto sane, conveniat eo loco interpretatio de volunta- tum concordia, et cum alia habeamus illustriora et firmiora testimonia, quae clare docent Deum aeternum genuisse coaeternam imaginem, filium, et hunc postea assumsisss humanam naturam, contenti simus illis testimoniis, et firmo pectore ea teneamus. Satis argutum est, quod Augusti- nus dicit: Quia, inquit, ego et pater unum su- mus, duas exprimit personas, et quod addit, unum, non unus, unitatem significat essentiae.

Illud etiam adiiciendum est, disputari hic multa de electione propter Christi dictum: Nemo rapiet eas de manu mea, nec displicet mihi hic de electionis firmitate dici, sed ita haec tractentur, non ut misceatur stoicum fatum, sed ut accenda- tur in nobis fides. Simul haec sententia est do- ctrina de electione, et promissio nos confirmans. De electione docet, esse quandam electorum Ec- clesiam, quam Deus non sinet a se avelli, sed haec omnium est, qui vere credunt Evangelio, aut lapsi rursus convertuntur ad Deum, et re- deunt ad Evangelium, sic enim nos ex verbo Dei iudicare oportet, omnibus universaliter praecipi- tur, ut audiant filium Dei. Est et promissio gra- tiae universalis, et praecipitur omnibus, ut eam accipiant. Haec sunt vera et firma: Certum est Pharaonem, Saulem, Iudam, sua voluntate re- pugnare vocanti Deo, qui toties eos admonet ut convertantur. Cum igitur volentes repellant vo- cantem Deum, tandem ruunt in aeternas poenas. Non igitur pertinent ad electorum numerum, et causa exitii tota in ipsis est. At David, Petrus, Paulus, vocanti Deo non repugnant, sed assen- tiuntur, ac moventi Spiritui sancto obtemperant, luctantur cum dubitationibus, diffidentia, et aliis vitiosis affectibus, et experiuntur veram esse vo- cem: Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis et one- rati estis, et ego reficiam vos. Tales quia perse- verant tandem in hac obedientia, sunt electi.

Intueamur ergo tota mente voluntatem Dei, in ipso verbo Dei expressam, ut cum de remis- sione peccatorum, quaerimus voluntatem Dei, nec nos ipsos conturbemus aliis disputationibus de causis electionis. Ita intelligit David miseri- cordiam Dei vocantis, et moventis, esse causam electionis, sed tamen accipi oportere oblatam mi- sericordiam, et vocanti Deo assentiendum esse. Hic iam dulcescit nobis dictum Christi, cum im- becillitatem nostram et pericula cogitamus, vi- demus nequaquam nos tanta certamina sustinere posse. Adam et Eva non poterant suis viribus sustinere dolorem, ex spectaculo primae caedis ortum. David nequaquam poterat sustinere suum dolorem, ex conscientia sui sceleris et exilii ma- lis ortum, sed hi, quia sciebant aliquam esse aeternam Ecclesiam, norant eam a Deo adiuvari, erigunt igitur se, et adiuvantur.

Ita nos confirmet haec vox: Nemo rapiet eas de manu mea. Est quaedam aeterna Ecclesia, quare iuvabitur in tantis certaminibus, imo uta- mur ea tanquam promissione, sciamus nobis hic in tot ingentibus periculis promitti auxilium, non praevidemus omnes diaboli insidias. Custodit igitur nos dormientes Deus, implicamur inter- dum negotiis, quae prorsus inextricabilia sunt humano consilio, ut David expulsus regno, ut populus Israël amissa arca, et postea abductus in captivitatem, imo, ut Adam suo lapsu, hic rur- sus ex mediis inferis revocamur. Amemus ergo hoc dictum Christi, et nobis inculcemus, ut nos ad invocationem excitet, et in tanta varietate pe- riculorum privatorum et publicorum consoletur: Nemo rapiet eas de manu mea. Defende igitur nos Christe, qui undique oppugnamur ab infir- mitate nostra, a diabolo, variis scandalis et pe- riculis. Cogitemus et de publicis motibus. Ubi mansura est Ecclesia, ubi erunt pia studia, si Turci latius grassabuntur, si reges et principes Christiani nominis, vel saevitiam exercere per- gent, vel intestinis bellis vastitates in suis regio- nibus facient? Si studia literarum extinguentur, si doctores ipsi privatis et ambitiosis certamini- bus dilacerabunt Ecclesias, et confusiones dogma- tum facient? In his spectaculis tristissimis refe- ramus oculos nostros ad has promissiones: Non praevalebunt portae inferni adversus eam. Item: Nemo rapiet eas de manu mea, etc. Haec de disputationibus praedestinationis monuisse satis sit, removeamus philosophicas imaginationes. Omnium hominum animi sine luce coelesti, aut sentiunt casu omnia ruere, sine gubernatione divina, ut sentiebat Epicurus, hic furor execrandus est, aut sentiunt Deum alliga- tum esse causis secundis, nec aliter agere, quam ut illae eum rapiunt, aut certe sua aeterna deter- minatione rapere voluntates, et eventus, sive ve- limus, sive nolimus, ita cadere iuxta immutabi- lem determinationem. Haec sunt Stoica, quae non sunt invehenda in Ecclesiam, et vel contem- tum Dei, vel odium, vel negligentiam in nobis gignunt. Sed nos audiamus vocem aeterni patris, qui inquit de filio: Hunc audite. Quare necesse est audiri verbum Dei, metuere minas, et assen- tiri promissionibus, et scire, iuxta hoc verbum: libere Deum ac certo nobiscum agere, ut erga suos liberos agit sapiens, iustus et clemens pa- terfamilias. Petendum igitur et certo sperandum est auxilium Dei, sicut Christus ait: Petite et ac- cipietis. Item: Quanto magis pater vester qui in coelis est, dabit Spiritum sanctum petentibus.

Tollebant igitur iterum lapides.

Non fuisse ambiguas conciones Christi, fa- tentur eius adversarii, qui intelligunt Christum praedicare, se esse Deum, patri aequalem, ut Ioann. 5. dicunt: Aequalem se Deo facit, et hic, cum homo sis, facies te Deum. Nec mirum est, vehementer animos huius populi abhorruisse ab his concionibus, qui erat summa cura ad doctri- nam de unitate Dei assuefactus. Tollunt ergo lapides, ut velut blasphemum obruant. Renovat igitur certamen, primum mitigans contentionem de nomine, imo scriptura Deos etiam illos vocat, quibus verbi Dei custodia praecipue commendata est. Cur igitur blasphemiam esse ducitis, nomen Dei alteri tribui? Allegatur autem dictum in Psal. 82.: Ego dixi, Dii estis, quod significat custodes verbi Dei, et organa operum Dei, per quae Deus regit homines. Moses, Samuel, Na- than, David, sunt custodes verbi Dei, et per eos miranda opera Deus facit. Tales erant et Saul, et alii reges ac sacerdotes, etiamsi miscuerunt of- ficio suas tyrannides, ut ibi Psal. eos accusat, et poenas minatur.

Postquam autem hanc mitigationem propo- nit Christus, deinde addit: Verius sibi competere appellationem Dei, qui sit a patre sanctificatus, missus in mundum, faciens opera patris. Hic dissimilitudinem ostendit inter caeteros, qui di- cuntur Dii, Prophetas, Sacerdotes, Reges, et se. Illi dicuntur Dii, quia sunt custodes verbi, et or- gana operum Dei. Sed hic Christus apud patrem fuit ante mundi conditionem, et postea missus et patefactus est, et tamen adhuc est in patre, id est, regnans et operans cum patre, et intuens patrem.

Ariani magna contentione hunc locum de- torserunt ad suam causam, quasi Christus col- lato exemplo voluerit, se non esse natura Deum, sed propter officium dici Deum, ut Prophetas, sacerdotes ac reges, sicut hi in Psalmo nominan- tur Dii: Ego dixi, Dii estis. Etsi autem Christus ipse satis luculentum discrimen hic tradit, cum ait: Pater in me est, et ego in patre, tamen pro- dest omnia alia testimonia ex primo cap. Ioann., ex quinto et ex aliis locis coniungere, ut collatis testimoniis, sine sophistica, nativa et incorrupta sententia eligatur, videlicet, quod in Christo sint duae naturae, divina et humana, et quod divina sit imago Dei, ab aeterno genita a patre, per quem omnia condita sunt, ὁμοούσιος patri. Id est, ostendunt testimonia coniuncta, et caetera erunt declaratio huius dicti hoc loco: Pater in me est, et ego in patre, id est, una regnans, et una creans, et operans.

Quare et sanctificatio intelligatur aliter, quam Eliae aut Ieremiae sanctificatio. Non so- lum sanctificatus est, id est, segregatus, ut sit doctor, et victima, nec solum donatus Spiritu sancto ad mensuram, ut Elias, aut Elisaeus, sed divinitas in hoc homine Christo habitat corpora- liter, ut Paulus inquit, id est, personaliter. Sic igitur sanctificatus est, ut ipse caeteros sanctificet, et lucem ac vitam aeternam nobis impertiat, sicut Baptista inquit: Ex plenitudine eius omnes acce- pimus, et Psal. 45.: Propterea unxit te Deus, Deus tuus, oleo laetitiae prae consortibus tuis. Hic nominat hunc regem: Te Deum, inquit, unxit Deus tuus oleo laetitiae, id est, plenitudine Spi- ritus sancti, ut alios sanctifices, et addit, prae consortibus, seu propter consortes, id est, longe antecellis omnibus Prophetis, et ut illi ex tuo fonte sumant, tu missus es.

Hunc igitur regem Christum Deum sanctifi- cantem consortes, toto pectore oremus, ut nos quoque regat et sanctificet, et in nos rivulos suae plenitudinis, lucis, notitiae, et dilectionis Dei effundat, et accendat nos, ut vere agnosca- mus, invocemus et celebremus Deum patrem Do- mini nostri Iesu Christi, et filium in terras mis- sum, et nobis immensa misericordia donatum, et mirando foedere, videlicet societate naturae no- strae copulatum.

O uncte aeterni laeto spiramine patris Nate Dei, socios ungito Christe tuos.

Haec breviter dicta sunt, ut moniti studiosi acrius refutare Arii furores possint.

Quaerebant igitur ipsum prehendere.

Discedit, ut reipsa confirmet id quod antea dixit, se habere potestatem ponendae animae suae, et rursus sumendae. Nobis etiam exem- plum proponit, ut sciamus Ecclesiae membra cu- stodiri a Deo, nec ad necem rapi posse, quando- cunque tyranni ardentes furore in nos saevire cu- piunt, sed dari singulis curriculum, quo con- fecto, Deus evocat eos ex hac vita. Ieremias etsi toties periclitatur, tamen ante excidium urbis non interficitur. Paulus toties captus, toties obiectus bestiis, tamen perficit suum curriculum. Postea interficitur Ieremias a rege Aegypti Aprye, Pau- lus a Nerone. Etsi autem humana ratio disputat, casu alium alio diutius incolumem manere in tan- tis periculis, tamen nos ex Evangelio sciamus, certo custodiri nos a Deo, et tunc demum ex hoc curriculo abduci, cum Deo ita visum est, sicut clare inquit Christus, Lucae 12.: Omnes capilli capitis vestri numerati sunt, etc.

## 10:41
John indeed performed no sign.

Below, Christ says, John 14: He who believes in me, the works that I do, he will do, and greater than these he will do. How, therefore, do these things agree, that John did not perform miraculous deeds, when indeed there are many unusual works of God in his history, so that they are testimonies of his calling? He was born of a sterile and barren mother, his father saw an angel speaking to him, and when he had been made mute, he began to speak again when the son was born. Afterwards, the son John saw heaven opened, he heard the voice of the eternal God concerning the Son Jesus Christ: This is my beloved Son. He was divinely warned concerning the Holy Spirit descending upon

Christ. To whom of all the elect, in any age, have the three persons of the divinity been thus exhibited, distinguished by clear differences? Indeed, this very revelation is the clearest testimony to the whole Church of all times concerning the three persons; why then do they say here that John did not perform miracles?

I answer: Miracles are of two kinds, others striking the eyes and the senses of the people, done divinely above the common order of nature, such as raising the dead, restoring sight to the blind, continually replenishing consumed bread or oil, as Christ fed some thousands, and Elijah and Elisha helped widows. These and similar particular things striking the eyes of all are miracles, which are exhibited for the sake of the unbelievers, as it is said in 1 Corinthians 14: namely, that moved by these testimonies they might assent to the doctrine; it is not necessary for such miracles to be performed by all the saints, nor could many sustain this external glory without pride. But there are other, much greater miracles, not striking the eyes of the people, which are done universally in the Church, such as a new light in the hearts of the pious, at times more, at times less illustrious. But yet this is common, which Paul says: You have received the spirit of adoption of sons, by which we cry Abba Father. Likewise, The anointing teaches you. These far greater miracles are also done; by the voice and ministry of men many are converted to God, as it is said in Romans 1: The Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth. Likewise, For the sake of the Church many houses, cities, regions, etc., are wonderfully preserved and defended.

When the Israelites were making their journey through the Red Sea, they saw the wonderful work of God, but in truth the Church is always protected in this way, indeed individual pious people, even if the modes of defense do not strike the eyes; when Hagar was departing from the house of Abraham, together with her son Ishmael, she was wandering miserably in desert places, and when she was almost consumed by thirst, finally a spring is shown to her as she wept. She heard an angel speaking; but Elizabeth, Mary, and many similar virgins and matrons were defended wonderfully, even if they did not see or hear angels, when in that turbulent time the Roman, Parthian, and Herodian armies were constantly wandering in the Jewish land.

And for this reason, sometimes the mode of defense, as in the Red Sea and other unusual examples, is proposed to be looked upon, so that we may know that the Church is always protected and preserved by God, and that daily defenses, although the mode is not seen in them, are nevertheless the works of God, as it is said in Isaiah 46: You who are carried in my womb, and borne in my belly, even to old age I will carry you, I have made, I will bear, I will save. Likewise Isaiah chapter 51: I have put my words in your mouth, and I have protected you with the shadow of my hand, that you may plant the heavens. Here it is clearly said: The ministers of the Gospel are covered by the shadow of the hand of God, and the final cause is added, that as a flourishing garden, the heavens may be planted with new plants, that is, that many may become heirs of the heavenly kingdom. God wills, however, that these benefits be acknowledged, sought, and preached. Thus there is no doubt that for the sake of the propagation of the Gospel these regions of ours have been defended in many dangers. For this benefit let us give thanks to God, and let us pray that for the sake of his son he may protect us longer. Such miracles of perpetual defense are therefore done daily in the Church, and many things are granted by the prayers of the Church. Therefore Christ says that the Apostles would do greater things, namely than those striking the eyes of the people. Finally, the Fathers, Prophets, and Apostles also had singular testimonies. Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, and many others were called by the proper voice of God. God showed John a clear distinction of the persons. Paul was caught up into heaven. These testimonies were exhibited to such men so that as teachers they might be endowed with greater light, and their testimonies are profitable to us. The universal Church at every time after the preaching of John is confirmed by his testimony concerning the three persons.

Latin:

Ioannes quidem signum fecit nullum.

Infra inquit Christus, Ioann. 14.: Qui credit in me, opera quae ego facio, faciet, et maiora horum faciet. Quomodo igitur haec conveniunt, Ioannem non fecisse miranda facta, cum quidem multa sint in eius historia opera Dei inusitata, ut sint testimonia vocationis eius. Natus est ex ma- tre sterili et effoeta, pater vidit angelum collo- quentem, et cum mutus factus esset, rursus nato filio loqui coepit. Postea filius Ioannes vidit coe- lum apertum, audivit vocem aeterni Dei de filio Iesu Christo: Hic est filius meus dilectus. Divi- nitus monitus est de Spiritu sancto descendente in

Christum. Cui omnium electorum, ulla aetate sic exhibitae sunt tres personae divinitatis, di- stinctae perspicuis discriminibus? Imo haec ipsa revelatio clarissimum testimonium est, toti Ec- clesiae omnium temporum, de tribus personis, cur igitur hic dicunt, Ioannem non fecisse signa?

Respondeo: Signa duplicia sunt, alia incur- rentia in oculos, et sensus populi, facta divinitus supra communem naturae ordinem, ut excitare mortuos, reddere visum caeco, assidue sarcire absumtum panem aut oleum, ut Christus pavit aliquot millia, et Elias et Elisaeus viduis opitu- lati sunt. Haec et similia particularia incurrentia in oculos omnium sunt signa, quae exhibentur propter infideles, ut 1. Corinth. 14. dicitur: ut videlicet moti his testimoniis assentiantur doctri- nae, talia signa non necesse est ab omnibus san- ctis fieri, nec possent hanc externam gloriam multi sustinere, sine superbia. Sed alia sunt signa multo maiora, non incurrentia in oculos populi, quae universaliter fiunt in Ecclesia, ut nova lux in cordibus piorum, alias magis, alias minus il- lustris. Sed tamen commune hoc est, quod Pau- lus dicit: Accepistis spiritum adoptionis filiorum, quo clamamus Abba pater. Item, Unctio vos docet. Fiunt et haec signa longe maxima, voce et ministerio hominum multi ad Deum conver- tuntur, sicut Rom. 1. dicitur: Evangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti. Item, Propter Ecclesiam mirabiliter servantur ac defen- duntur multae domus, urbes, regiones, etc.

Cum Israëlitae iter facerent per mare rubrum, videbant opus Dei mirandum, sed revera semper sic protegitur Ecclesia, imo singuli pii, etiamsi non incurrit in oculos modos defensionis, cum Agar discederet ex domo Abrahae, una cum filio Ismaël, misera errabat in locis desertis, et cum siti pene consumta esset, tandem lacrymanti mon- stratur fons. Haec audivit loquentem angelum: sed Elizabeth, Maria, et multae similes virgines et matronae defensae sunt mirabiliter, etiamsi non viderunt, vel audierunt angelos, cum illo turbulento tempore assidui exercitus Romani, Parthici, Herodiani vagarentur in terra Iudaica.

Ideo autem, interdum modus defensionis, ut in mari rubro, et aliis inusitatis exemplis pro- ponitur conspiciendus, ut sciamus Ecclesiam sem- per a Deo protegi et servari, et quotidianas de- fensiones, quanquam in eis modus non conspici- tur, tamen esse opera Dei, sicut Esaiae 46. dici- tur: Qui portamini in utero meo, et gestamini in alvo mea, senescentes ego vos portabo, ego feci, ego gestabo, ego salvabo. Item Esaiae cap. 51.: Posui verba mea in ore tuo, et umbra ma- nus meae protexi te, ut plantes coelos. Hic clare dicitur: Tegi ministros Evangelii umbra manus Dei, et additur causa finalis, ut tanquam vernans hortus, coeli conserantur novis plantis, id est, multi fiant haeredes regni coelestis. Vult autem Deus haec beneficia agnosci, peti, et praedicari. Sic non dubium est propter propagationem Evan- gelii has nostras regiones in multis periculis de- fensas esse. Pro hoc beneficio gratias Deo aga- mus, et oremus, ut propter filium suum nos diu- tius protegat. Talia igitur miracula perpetuae defensionis quotidie fiunt in Ecclesia, et multa precibus Ec- clesiae donantur. Ideo inquit Christus, maiora facturos Apostolos, scilicet quam illa incurrentia in oculos populi. Postremo, Patres, Prophetae, Apostoli, etiam singularia testimonia habuerunt. Adam, Noë, Abraham, Moses, et alii multi vo- cati sunt propria voce Dei. Ioanni Deus discri- men clarum personarum ostendit. Paulus in coe- lum raptus est. Haec testimonia talibus exhibita sunt, ut tanquam doctores maiori luce donaren- tur, et prosunt eorum testimonia nobis. Uni- versa Ecclesia omni tempore post Ioannis praedi- cationem confirmatur testimonio eius, de tribus personis.

## 11:1 Argument
Chapter XI.

The text begins the admirable history of Lazarus, recalled to life after death. And because messengers were sent by the sisters of Lazarus to Christ, and Christ first came to Bethany after the fourth day from the death of Lazarus, it is useful to consider the intervals of the places. Christ was in the desert, not far from Jericho and Bethabara. Jericho, however, was distant from the Jordan by sixty stadia, that is, almost two of our miles. From Jerusalem, however, by one hundred and fifty stadia, that is, almost five of our miles. Bethabara, however, was on the other bank, in the desert, and was further distant from Jerusalem, wherefore in the desert to Bethany, which was only half of our mile distant from Jerusalem, the interval was almost eight of our miles, for which it is necessary for one going with a company to have a journey of two days. Christ remained, however, for two days after the arrival of the messenger, and it is consistent that, before the messenger had come to Christ, Lazarus had already been dead. Christ therefore came on the fourth or fifth day to the village of Bethany, since Lazarus had been buried before the fourth day. This delay exercised Christ in the meantime with various thoughts, and increased the wonder of the deed, just as the text itself signifies.

Latin:

Caput XI.

Textus orditur admirandam historiam de La- zaro, post mortem in vitam revocato. Et quia missi sunt nuncii a Lazari sororibus ad Christum, et Christus primum venit Bethaniam, post quar- tum diem a morte Lazari, utile est locorum inter- valla considerare. Fuit Christus in deserto, non procul a Iericho et Bethabara. Iericho autem distabat a Iordane sexaginta stadiis, id est, fere duobus nostris miliaribus. A Ierusalem vero centum quinquaginta stadiis, hoc est, fere quin- que nostris miliaribus. Bethabara vero in altera ripa erat, in deserto, ac longius distabat a Ieru- salem, quare in deserto ad Bethaniam, quae tan- tum dimidio nostro miliari distabat a Ierusalem, intervallum fuit, fere octo nostrorum miliarium, ad quae opus est eunti cum comitatu itinere bidui. Mansit autem Christus post nuncii adventum bi- duo, et consentaneum est, priusquam nuncius venisset ad Christum, Lazarum iam fuisse mor- tuum. Venit ergo Christus quarto aut quinto die in vicum Bethaniam, cum Lazarus ante quar- tum diem sepultus esset. Haec mora exercuit Christum interim variis cogitationibus, et auxit admirationem facti, sicut ipse textus significat.

## 11:9
Are there not twelve hours in the day?

Before the journey of Christ, and before the resuscitation of Lazarus, there is a long narrative in the text concerning the sickness of Lazarus, concerning the messenger sent to Christ, and concerning Christ's conversation with the Apostles, to whom, before the departure, when no one had announced it, he explains that Lazarus is dead. This whole preparation was then performed by Christ in such a way that the Apostles might consider this resuscitation more diligently: and it was subsequently described in the text for this reason, that we might be stirred to the consideration of so great a matter. There was an interval of many days after the death and after the burial of Lazarus. It was certain, therefore, that he was truly dead. And although in reality other resuscitations of the dead were no less great, yet this one moved the minds of men more, as this very history indicates, that the chief priests were more dismayed by the wonder of this deed than of others. Because soon there is held a deliberation concerning the death of Christ. For they fear, on account of the magnitude of the deed, the defection of the people to him, which if it were to happen, they feared that they themselves would be oppressed by the people and cast out from their dignities and wealth. Let this suffice to have pointed out concerning the preparation.

Regarding the fact that he says there are twelve hours of the day, let students know that there are other equal hours, as ours are, when, namely, the natural day is divided into twenty-four equal hours; according to this reasoning, there are more hours of the artificial day in the summer solstice than in the winter. And this custom, now in use, is sufficiently known to all. Others were once in use, unequal hours, which the Greeks call καιρικὰς, to which they attributed twelve for any artificial day throughout the whole year, whether long or short. The diurnal hours were therefore longer around the summer solstice than around the winter.

And although to those ignorant of antiquity this dissimilarity seems absurd, yet it is certain that this custom existed. And although the time of the resuscitated Lazarus falls into the vernal equinox, when the artificial day is everywhere of twelve equal hours, Christ speaks of the universal custom, which throughout the whole year divided individual artificial days into twelve hours, καιρικὰς, as they called them. Christ, however, allegorically cites the saying: There are twelve hours of the day, signifying that a certain course, or space of his calling, is given to each, within which it is necessary for him to obey his calling, just as he says elsewhere: The day's own affliction is sufficient, that is, let us do and endure what is present according to our calling, let us not omit commanded works through sloth, nor summon others to ourselves, which is customary for restless and curious minds through πολυπραγμοσύνῃ, thus he himself interprets his own saying in the following words.

If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble. Each has his own day, his own calling; in this he commands one to walk, and he who obeys this does rightly, whether the outcomes are pleasant or sad. The Apostles urge Christ not to return to Jerusalem because of the danger. Thus men very often omit the duties of their calling because of terrors and dangers. But Christ commands us to regard the mandate concerning our calling, and to commend the outcomes to God, just as it is often commanded elsewhere in Psalm 36: Wait for the Lord, and keep his ways. Likewise: Be subject to the Lord, pray and [wait for] him. And Moses says in Exodus 14: Stand, and you will see the magnificent works of the Lord; therefore it is said here: If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, that is, if anyone is devoted to his calling, in faith and the invocation of God, he pleases God, and will be helped by him in dangers, and although he will be exercised by some troubles, yet he will conquer in the end, and his doctrine, counsels, and actions will be salutary to the Church and to polities. Conversely, with God not shining forth, that is, without a calling and without faith, it is entirely to wander in blind night, and not only not to progress, but even to slip everywhere, and to destroy oneself and others, as the counsels of Cassius and Brutus, concerning the killing of Julius, were darkness, destructive to them and to the whole Republic. Because they neither conformed to a calling, nor were they undertaken in the acknowledgment and invocation of God. Such were afterwards the counsels of Antony, desiring the monarchy. Concerning these it is said in Isaiah 59: Desolation and destruction are in their paths, that is, their counsels are pernicious to themselves and to the Republic. Wherefore let us avoid human counsels and ambition, and let us contain ourselves in the fear of God within the bounds of our calling, and let us do our duty, and seek help and success from God. Because no one can take anything for himself, unless it has been given to him from heaven.

Latin:

Nunquid duodecim sunt horae diei?

Ante iter Christi, et ante resuscitationem Lazari, narratio longa est in textu, de morbo Lazari, de nuncio ad Christum misso, de Christi colloquio cum Apostolis, qui eis ante profectio- nem, cum nemo nunciasset, exponit Lazarum esse mortuum. Haec tota praeparatio et tunc a Christo ita facta est, ut Apostoli diligentius con- siderarent hanc resuscitationem: et deinde in textu ideo descripta est, ut excitemur ad tantae rei considerationem. Tot dierum intervallum fuit post mortem et post sepulturam Lazari. Constabat igitur vere mortuum esse. Etsi autem reipsa non minora facta sunt aliae resuscitationes mortuorum, tamen haec magis movit animos ho- minum, sicut haec ipsa historia indicat, magis consternatos fuisse pontifices admiratione huius facti, quam aliorum. Quia mox habetur delibe- ratio de nece Christi. Metuunt enim propter magnitudinem facti defectionem populi ad ipsum, quae si fieret, opprimi sese a populo, et ex digni- tatibus et opibus excuti metuebant. Haec de prae- paratione satis sit monuisse.

Quod ait duodecim horas diei esse, sciant studiosi alias esse horas aequales, ut nostrae sunt, cum videlicet dies naturalis in viginti quatuor ae- quales horas dividitur, secundum hanc rationem plures sunt horae diei artificialis in solstitio ae- stivo, quam in bruma. Estque haec consuetudo nunc usitata satis nota omnibus. Aliae quondam in usu fuerunt inaequales horae, quas Graeci vo- cant καιρικὰς, quarum toto anno cuilibet diei artificiali, seu longo, seu brevi, duodecim attri- buerunt. Fuerunt igitur diurnae horae circa sol- stitium aestivum longiores, quam circa brumam.

Etsi autem ignaris antiquitatis haec dissimi- titudo videtur absurda, tamen fuisse hanc consue- tudinem certum est. Et quanquam tempus Lazari resuscitati incurrit in aequinoctium vernum, quo dies artificialis ubique est horarum aequalium duodecim, Christus de universali consuetudine loquitur, quae toto anno dividebat singulos dies artificiales in duodecim horas καιρικὰς, ut ipsi vocabant. Christus autem allegorice citat dictum: Duodecim sunt horae diei, significans certum cuique datum esse curriculum, seu spatium suae vocationis, intra quod necesse sit eum obsequi vocationi suae, sicut alias inquit: Sufficit diei afflictio sua, id est, praesentia iuxta vocationem faciamus, et perferamus, non omittamus mandatas operas per ignaviam, nec accersamus nobis alias, usitata ingeniis inquietis et curiosis πολυπραγμοσύνῃ, sic ipse interpretatur suum dictum sequentibus verbis.

Si quis ambulat in die, non impingit. Sua cuique dies est, sua vocatio, in hac iubet ambulare, et huic obtemperans recte facit, sive eventus sint placidi, sive tristes. Hortantur Christum Apostoli, ne redeat Ierosolymam propter periculum. Sic homines saepissime omittunt vocationis officia propter terrores et pericula. At Christus iubet nos mandatum de vocatione respicere, et exitus Deo commendare, sicut saepe praecipitur alias Psal. 36.: Expecta dominum, et custodi vias eius. Item: Subditus esto Domino, ora et eum. Et Moses inquit Exod. 14.: State, et videbitis magnifica opera Domini, ideo hic dicitur: Si quis ambulat in die, non impingit, id est, si quis suae vocationi inseruit, in fide et invocatione Dei, placet Deo, et ab eo adiuvabitur in periculis, et quanquam exercebitur aliquibus aerumnis, tamen vincet tandem, et eius doctrina, consilia, et actiones erunt salutares Ecclesiae et politiis. Econtra non praelucente Deo, id est, sine vocatione et sive fide, prorsus est in caeca nocte errare, et non modo non proficere, sed etiam passim labi, et sese et alios perdere, ut consilia Cassii, et Bruti, de Iulio interficiendo, tenebrae erant, exitiales ipsis et toti Reipublicae. Quia nec vocationi congruebant, nec suscipiebantur in agnitione et invocatione Dei. Talia erant postea et Antonii consilia, appetentis monarchiam. De his dicitur Esa. 59.: Vastitas et contritio in viis eorum, id est, eorum consilia sunt perniciosa ipsis et Reipublicae. Quare humana consilia et ambitionem vitemus, et nos in timore Dei intra vocationis metas contineamus, et nostrum officium faciamus, ac petamus auxilium et successus a Deo. Quia nemo potest sibi quicquam sumere, nisi sit ei datum e coelo.

## 11:14
Lazarus is dead, etc.

Not only was the resuscitation an act surpassing the powers of a creature, but this knowledge of an event which had happened far away also surpasses human nature. There are, therefore, many things joined to this one miracle, and all these things were primarily brought forth so that they might testify that God has revealed Himself to the human race and has confirmed the doctrine handed down in His Church. And therefore the Church has certain miracles of its own, which no creature can imitate, so that we may be certain that this doctrine written by the Prophets and Apostles is the voice and judgment of God. The Gentiles had miracles, as when the Augur cut the whetstone with a razor, and prophecies sometimes predicted true outcomes, but these are far inferior to the miracles of the Church, such as the frequent resuscitation of the dead, the recalled course of the Sun, as in the history of Joshua and Hezekiah, and the conception by an aged woman. Creatures cannot imitate such things, nor were these testimonies proposed in vain; God wishes them to be looked upon and pondered by us, so that they may confirm faith in us, just as Christ says in this very place: I rejoice for your sakes, that you may believe. Likewise: Because of the crowd standing around I said these things, that they may believe that you sent me, that is, I call upon you, so that it may be established that these miracles are done by the invocation of the name of God, and that they are testimonies that this one who calls upon God is pleasing to God, is sent by God, is a truthful teacher, etc.

Latin:

Lazarus mortuus est, etc.

Non solum resuscitatio factum est superans vires creaturae, sed etiam haec notitia eventus, qui procul acciderat, superat hominum naturam. Sunt igitur uni miraculo multa coniuncta, et haec omnia principaliter edita sunt, ut testentur Deum sese patefecisse generi humano, et confirmasse doctrinam traditam in Ecclesia sua. Ideoque Ecclesia habet propria quaedam miracula, quae nulla creatura potest imitari, ut certi simus hanc doctrinam scriptam per Prophetas et Apostolos, Dei vocem et sententiam esse. Habuerunt Ethnici miracula, ut Aruspex dissecuit cotem novacula, vaticinia interdum veros exitus praedixerunt, sed haec longe inferiora sunt Ecclesiae miraculis, resuscitatione mortuorum crebra, et revocato cursu Solis, ut in historia Iosuae et Ezechiae, et conceptu anili. Talia non possunt imitari creaturae, nec frustra proposita sunt haec testimonia, vult ea Deus conspici et cogitari a nobis, ut confirment fidem in nobis, quemadmodum hoc ipso loco inquit Christus: Gaudeo propter vos, ut credatis. Item: Propter turbam circumstantem haec dixi, ut credant, quod tu me miseris, id est, te invoco, ut constet invocatione nominis Dei haec miracula fieri, eaque testimonia esse, quod hic invocans Deo placeat, sit a Deo missus, sit verax doctor, etc.

## 11:24
I know that he will rise again in the resurrection, at the last day.

The conversation between Martha and Christ is long, in which Martha signifies a petition concerning the resurrection, and at the beginning affirms that Christ could have warded off the disease while Lazarus was alive, and now can recall the dead man to life; this is the first confession concerning the power of Christ. There follows, therefore, a promise concerning His will, which the woman does not immediately understand: Your brother will rise again. The woman understands this statement as referring to the future resurrection at the last day. Although some here ask whence the woman holds the opinion concerning the universal resurrection, whether she had recently learned it from the sermons of Christ, or whether this opinion had indeed always remained publicly among the people of Israel, that there would be a universal resurrection of the dead, and that God would judge all men and would give eternal joys to His Church and punishments to the wicked: yet it is manifest that pious men among the people of Israel had always thought thus, that there would be a resurrection of the dead and a future judgment. For the Prophets preach manifestly concerning the resurrection, as in Isaiah 26: The dead shall live, my slain shall rise again. And Isaiah 25: And death shall be swallowed up altogether. Ezekiel 37: Behold, I will open your graves. Daniel 12: And many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to eternal life, others to reproach, that they may see always, and Psalm 16: My flesh rests in hope, you will not abandon my soul in hell, nor will you give your holy one to see corruption. Job 19: I know that my redeemer lives, and in the last day I shall rise from the earth, and I shall be clothed again with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God, whom I myself shall see, and my eyes shall behold, and not another. Pious men did not spurn these such illustrious testimonies, and many are scattered here and there throughout the whole prophetic scripture which agree with these; therefore also the Pharisees, who although they professed many other delusions, yet defended this article most fiercely against the Sadducees, namely that there would be a resurrection of the dead, as is evident from Acts chapter 23. Martha therefore held this opinion from the customary doctrine of the pious among that people, and yet it is credible that she had often and diligently heard Christ concerning this article and the whole doctrine of the Gospel.

Latin:

Scio quod resurget in resurrectione, in novissimo die.

Longum colloquium est Marthae et Christi, in quo Martha significat petitionem de resurrectione, et initio affirmat, potuisse Christum depellere morbum, vivente Lazaro, et nunc posse revocare mortuum in vitam, haec prima est confessio de potentia Christi. Accedit igitur promissio de voluntate, quam mulier non statim intelligit: Resurget frater tuus. Hanc vocem mulier intelligit de resurrectione futura in novissimo die. Etsi autem hic quaerunt aliqui, unde mulier teneat sententiam de resurrectione universali, an ex Christi concionibus recens didicerit, an vero semper in populo Israël publice haec sententia manserit, futuram resurrectionem mortuorum universalem, et Deum iudicaturum esse de omnibus hominibus, et daturum Ecclesiae suae gaudia aeterna, et impiis poenas: tamen manifestum est semper homines pios in populo Israël sic sen- sisse, futuram esse resurrectionem mortuorum, et futurum iudicium. Nam Prophetae manifeste de resurrectione concionantur, ut Esaiae 36.: Vivent mortui, interfecti mei resurgent. Et Esa. 25.: Et mors devorabitur omnino. Ezech. 37.: Ecce ego aperiam tumulos vestros. Danielis 12.: Et multi de his qui dormiunt in terrae pul- vere, evigilabunt, alii in vitam aeternam, alii in opprobrium, ut videant semper, et Psal. 16.: Caro mea requiescit in spe, non derelinquas ani- mam meam in inferno, nec dabis sanctum tuum videre corruptionem. Hiob 19.: Scio quod re- demtor meus vivit, et in novissima die de terra resurrecturus sum, et rursus circumdabor pelle mea, et in carne mea videbo Deum, quem visu- rus sum ego ipse, et oculi mei conspecturi sunt, et non alius. Haec tam illustria testimonia pii non aspernabantur, et multa sunt passim sparsa in tota scriptura prophetica, quae cum his con- gruunt, ideo et Pharisaei, qui etsi alia multa de- liria profitebantur, tamen hunc articulum contra Sadducaeos acerrime defendebant, videlicet futu- ram esse resurrectionem mortuorum, ut constat ex Actis cap. 23. Tenebat igitur Martha hanc sententiam ex usitata doctrina piorum in isto po- pulo, et tamen credibile est, eam et de hoc arti- culo et universa doctrina Evangelii saepe et dili- genter audivisse Christum.

## 11:25
I am the resurrection and the life, etc.

There are two notable statements, comprising the sum of the whole Gospel. We have often warned, however, that those testimonies are especially to be observed and excerpted in which the sum of the Gospel is contained. For Christ wished to hand down things that were certain and explained; He did not wish to sow ambiguous and equivocal disputes, which would produce doubts and confusions of mind: I am the resurrection and the life, that is, the resuscitator and giver of life, as it is said in Isaiah: Father of eternal life, and He says several times above: I give them eternal life, etc. But so that the distinction may be known between those who obtain the benefit of Christ and others who do not obtain it, He adds: He who believes in me, even if he shall have died, shall live.

It is a plain and clear statement that by faith on account of Christ we are freed from eternal death and obtain eternal life. Nor is there any need to add longer explanations to statements that are manifest and perspicuous in themselves.

Let the reader only remember those things which ought to be most well-known in the Church, what faith signifies, namely, to assent to the promise concerning Christ, and to trust that on account of Christ we are truly received by God, heard, and gifted with the inheritance of eternal life. He who believes in me, that is, who assents to my promise, and trusts that through me the Father is appeased, that he himself is received on my account, and gifted with eternal life. And the same sentiment is repeated concerning the living: Every one living, and believing in me, shall not die. For although those who truly believe and are reborn by the light of the Gospel lay aside this flesh contaminated by sin, yet they do not die, that is, by the trust of Christ they retain peace and joy toward God, nor are they overwhelmed by the sense of the wrath of God, and dread, and despair, as Saul, Judas, and the like, but raised up by faith they pass from this life into the other, as it is said in chapter 8: He who will keep my word, shall not taste death.

But after Christ explained his discourse, and clearly testified that he was sent so that, with sin abolished and death abolished, he might restore righteousness and eternal life to those who believe, he finally demands faith from his listener, and a confession of faith, saying: Do you believe this? This final voice must also be diligently considered, so that we may learn how severely faith is required, and what a great thing it is to acquiesce by faith, which, how difficult it is, and what it is, must be learned in true invocation and true struggle, it cannot be sufficiently declared in words. Minds wander without faith, and do not admit certain consolation, but when they acquiesce by faith in the promise delivered by God, they cease to wander, and tranquilly await consolation and help from God; as therefore Christ asks the woman: Do you believe this? So let everyone know that he is being asked: Do you hear this voice? Come to me all you who labor, and are burdened, I will refresh you. Here you should know that the interrogation is soon added, Do you believe this? Those who do not believe, loathe this consolation, nay, they silently hate it and seek others, but those who believe acquiesce to the voice of Christ, and expect consolation and help from him.

Latin:

Ego sum resurrectio et vita etc.

Duae sunt insignes sententiae, complectentes summam totius Evangelii. Saepe autem monui- mus praecipue illa testimonia observanda et ex- cerpenda esse, in quibus summa Evangelii com- prehensa est. Voluit enim Christus certa et ex- plicata tradere, non voluit ambiguas et flexilo- quas disputationes serere, quae animorum dubi- tationes et confusiones parerent: Ego sum re- surrectio et vita, id est, resuscitator et dator vi- tae, ut apud Esaiam dicitur: Pater vitae aeternae, et aliquoties supra dicit: Vitam aeternam do eis, etc. Ut autem discrimen sciatur, inter eos qui beneficium Christi consequuntur, et inter alios qui non consequuntur, addit: Qui credit in me, etiamsi mortuus fuerit, vivet.

Plana et clara sententia est, fide propter Christum nos liberari a morte aeterna, et conse- qui vitam aeternam. Nec opus est sententiis per sese manifestis et perspicuis addere longiores enar- rationes.

Tantum illa meminerit lector, quae in Ec- clesia debent esse notissima, quid significet fides, videlicet assentiri promissioni de Christo, et con- fidere, quod propter Christum vere recipiamur a Deo, exaudiamur, et donemur haereditate vitae aeternae. Qui credit in me, id est, qui assentitur meae promissioni, et confidit per me placatum esse patrem, recipi se propter me, et donari vita aeterna. Et repetitur eadem sententia de vi- vente: Omnis vivens, et credens in me, non mo- rietur. Etsi enim vere credentes et renati luce Evangelii, hanc carnem contaminatam peccato deponunt, tamen non moriuntur, id est, fiducia Christi retinent pacem, et laetitiam erga Deum, nec opprimuntur sensu irae Dei, et pavore, ac desperatione, sicut Saul, Iudas, et similes, sed erecti fide transeunt ex hac vita in alteram, sicut cap. 8. dicitur: Qui sermonem meum servabit, non gustabit mortem.

Postquam autem Christus suam concionem exposuit, et plane testatus est, se missum esse, ut abolito peccato, et abolita morte, restituat cre- dentibus iusticiam et vitam aeternam, tandem po- stulat ab auditrice fidem, et fidei confessionem, inquiens: Credis hoc? Haec postrema vox etiam diligenter consideranda est, ut discamus quam severe requiratur fides, et quanta res sit acquie- scere fide, quod quam difficile sit, et quid sit, in vera invocatione et vero agone discendum est, verbis non satis declarari potest. Vagantur animi sine fide, et non admittunt certam consolationem, sed cum fide acquiescunt in promissione tradita a Deo, vagari desinunt, et tranquilli expectant con- solationem, et auxilium a Deo, ut igitur mulie- rem interrogat Christus: Credis hoc? Ita unus- quisque sese interrogari sciat: Audis hanc vocem? Venite ad me omnes qui laboratis, et onerati estis, ego reficiam vos. Hic scias mox addi in- terrogationem, Credis hoc? Qui non credunt, fastidiunt hanc consolationem, imo tacite oderunt et quaerunt alias, sed credentes voci Christi ac- quiescunt, et ab ipso consolationem et auxilium expectant.

## 11:27
I believe that you are the Christ.

The confession is clear concerning the Messiah, and as in other places these clear confessions are to be observed, as in Matthew 16, John 1, 3, and 9, so it is profitable to remember this passage, which teaches the reader about two greatest things, both that that Jesus born of Mary, then preaching, and raising the dead, is the promised Savior, and that the Messiah is the Son of God. Let us think about both sentences, why they have been delivered to us, and how they are to be exercised in invocation, and I will speak first and more briefly about the latter. We know from many certain testimonies of the Gospel that the divine nature is in Christ, and that Christ is by nature the Son of God. The Apostles confess this article, Matthew 16. And the Father says from heaven: This is my beloved Son, and the Baptist says, John 3: He who believes in the Son has eternal life, and in John 9 Christ himself asks: Do you believe in the Son of God? and in the 1st chapter the sentence is clearly delivered that in Christ is the divine nature, through which all things were created. Let us therefore acknowledge in invocation that the Mediator is not only man, but also by nature the Son of God, through whom all things were created and are sustained, as is said at Hebrews 1, who has always been present to his Church, and is about to be present, and therefore he is called Emmanuel.

But since invocation ought to be made by trust in the Son, it must always be thought of while praying, who that Mediator is, who derives the wrath of God into himself, and on account of whom we have been received, and who has always been present and will be present to the Church. All those who are ignorant of the Gospel, Gentiles, Jews, Mahometans, and other impious people, omit all these things in their invocation. They therefore wander away from God, since they deny that this is God, who sent the Son, and revealed himself by this word delivered through the Prophets, Christ, and the Apostles. But thus says Christ: He who does not honor the Son, does not honor the Father. Furthermore, those who are ignorant of the Gospel do not know whether God wishes to receive and hear us, and why he wishes to receive us, since the thing itself shows that we are unworthy. For everyone experiences that they are contaminated by some vices. Therefore, so that we may separate our invocation from the invocation of other nations, it must be thought of who the Son of God is. For although such great majesty cannot be comprehended, yet God wants us to hold his word, and to direct our invocation to that God who delivered this word, and thus revealed himself.

The other part pertains to the same thing, that namely it is necessary to believe that this Jesus born of Mary, crucified in Jerusalem at that time, is the Messiah. God defined the time and place, lest wandering minds seek various mediators, just as the Gentiles invented various deities, Ceres the giver of crops, Bacchus the giver of wine, Mars the helper in battles, Pallas showing counsels in the governing of the Republic, Juno heaping up riches. But let the mind be thinking of the word of God, bound to that God who has revealed himself by this word, and who sent his son born of a virgin, Jesus Christ crucified for us, and raised again, exhibited to the people of Israel, just as he had been promised, and preached at Jerusalem, and in all Judea, and testified to by miracles concerning the Gospel, and especially by the resurrection of the dead, at that very time of which the Apostles write, namely that the destruction of Jerusalem precedes by forty years. As therefore every invocation is to be excited by the consideration of the commandment and the divine promise, so it must always be thought of at the same time who that God is whom we invoke, where and how he has been revealed, how great his goodness is, that he has so revealed himself, that he has given a mediator, reconciliation, help, and salvation. Then who the mediator is, where and when he was revealed, why he suffered. Every invocation, however brief, ought to embrace all these things. Let us often remind both ourselves and the Church of this exercise. The diligence of the Philosophers is also to be praised, who wrote as accurately as could be done in philosophy about individual virtues. However, it is to be lamented that in the Church, concerning the highest of all virtues, the invocation of God, the doctrine handed down by God has not been collected with similar diligence in the precepts and promises which exist in the writings of the Prophets and Apostles; temperance is praised, and it is a virtue worthy of praise; clemency is praised in governors, and it is often salutary for great empires. Concerning these and other common virtues, the doctrine of the Philosophers exists written brilliantly, but concerning the queen of all virtues, the acknowledgment and invocation of God, how few, thin, and cold are the writings that are found? Few understand that it is a virtue; others think the doctrine is easy, known to all. Because naturally all of us, destitute of human help and having lost this visible aid, seek whether there is a God who is willing to help men, and in this discussion most people invoke God in some way or other, not thinking about who God is, how he has revealed himself, what he has commanded concerning invocation, what he has promised, how he is appeased, who the mediator is, whether and why he is willing to hear, what things he has promised by name, in what matters he requires our obedience, and yet has promised mitigation.

In Euripides, Hecuba, doubting what God is, invokes him thus: O Jupiter, whoever you are, difficult to know, who rule the earth, whether by the necessity of nature or by counsel. This doubt is common to all who are ignorant of the Gospel, or are held by the Stoic imagination that God acts necessarily without free counsel, just as secondary causes move, or if he acts freely, that he cares for certain great things but does not care for particular ones, as the same Euripides says. Finally, that even if he does care for particular things, he still does not hear the unworthy. These opinions clamor in the minds of all during invocation, and neither Gentiles, Mahometans, Jews, nor others ignorant of the Gospel struggle out of these errors. But faith, once the Gospel is acknowledged, struggles out and determines with certainty who God is, namely he who revealed himself by his word and by sending his son, and by adding wondrous testimonies, and that he is a most free agent, that he gave commandments and promises, and proposed his son as mediator, on account of whom he is certainly willing to hear, and that he has expressed by name what things he will certainly give, and in what matters he requires obedience, which he will nevertheless mitigate.

Therefore, so that we may excite ourselves to invocation, and invoke rightly, and distinguish our prayer from the Gentile, Turkish, and Jewish, I will briefly collect in this place what things are to be thought of, and concerning individual parts the word of God must be considered, because one approaches him only by thinking of the word of God, according to that in Rom. 10: Do not say in your heart, who shall ascend into heaven? but the word is near in your mouth and in your heart. Therefore, the first thing for one invoking is to seek the word, showing what God is. You do not invoke as Hecuba in Euripides, ignorant of who God is, whether he is an order of nature bound to secondary causes, or truly a free agent: You do not invoke as the Turks and Jews, heaping insults upon the son and not knowing the mediator, but you set before yourself the word of God, which certainly testifies that this is truly the almighty God, the creator of all creatures, and the preserver, who revealed himself by giving this word, adding testimonies from the beginning of the world, and sending his son crucified for us and raised again, and when we think of how he revealed himself, let there be mention of the persons in the address, as they have been revealed, as I shall say later.

Secondly, after it has been thought who God is, and you have joined yourself away from the Gentiles, Turks, and Jews, consider his commandment concerning invocation, It is a great thing to approach God and to ask of him not only those things which nature gives in the common course, but also other things, when he delivers us from our errors and troubles beyond the common course. However, our unworthiness deters us, especially since we know that God is just and is angry at sins, and that we are polluted with many sins. Here, therefore, there is need for the word of God, testifying of his will, that he commands himself to be invoked, and is willing to hear, receive, and help those who invoke him, although they are unworthy and polluted with sins. Wherefore let us diligently gather both the commands and the promises, as in Matt. 7: Ask, and it shall be given to you, etc. Luke 18: It is necessary always to pray, and not to grow weary. 1 Thess. 5: Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, in everything give thanks. For this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you. To Phil. 4: Be not anxious, but in everything by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.

Let the promises also be added, the chief of which, and the foundation of invocation for any matter whatsoever, is the promise of the remission of sins. For even when we think of the commands, yet this voice deters us: God does not hear sinners. Here, therefore, before other promises, let us set forth the doctrine concerning the remission of sins; let us know that to all who repent, sins are certainly remitted on account of Christ the mediator, not on account of our own worthiness. Indeed, that the remission of sins is received by faith, as is most clearly handed down in many places of the Gospel. And Rom. 3: The sum of his sentence is set forth, we are justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as a propitiator through faith in his blood.

This faith ought to shine forth in every invocation, that on account of the Son the mediator we are received, heard, and helped.

When we determine that we receive the remission of sins with this faith, here first the commands grow sweet, and the other promises concerning particular benefits. John 14: Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you. He commands to ask in his name, that is, with him named, with him invoked as mediator, on account of whom we are certainly received and heard, as it is said at Heb. 4: Having Jesus as High Priest, let us approach with confidence to the throne of grace.

Now, therefore, let us oppose the commands and promises to our unworthiness. Even though we are unworthy, yet God commanding must be obeyed, and although we are guilty, yet a propitiator has been given to us, and God promising must be believed, nor is God to be accused of lying. Let us therefore approach him, and ask for the remission of sins, the Holy Spirit, and other goods necessary for the Church, for political government, and for us privately. Concerning the Holy Spirit it is said by name, Luke 11: How much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask? Concerning other deliverances also, clear and many promises have been handed down, Ps. 3: The Lord is near to those who are of a troubled heart, and he will save the humble in spirit, and in the same Psalm: There is no lack for those who fear him. And Christ says: Seek first the kingdom of God, and the rest shall be added to you. And 1. Timoth. 4: Godliness has promises of the present and future life, etc.

Let many such sayings be in sight, and often thought upon in the mind, so that they may rouse us to invocation, and kindle in us some attention and faith while praying daily. Certainly always, as often as we begin a prayer, it must be thought upon, what God you invoke, whether he hears the unworthy, and why he hears, and to unworthiness must be opposed the commands and promises, and especially the promise of the remission of sins must be meditated upon and embraced. Then also the thing to be asked should be thought upon. For let not prayer be empty babbling, but let bodily and spiritual things necessary for common and private salvation be asked for. For this reason prayer is mostly cold, because we do not expect those benefits from God, nor does this light and faith burn in the heart, that God truly deals with us in something, gives the Holy Spirit, rules, helps, defends us, gives us sustenance, but minds are oppressed by doubt, nor can they raise themselves up to truly determine that those things are given by God, since with this our doubt we must especially struggle; we rely on our own counsels and visible advantages and human protections. When these are in sight, nothing is asked of God in any serious way. When these are snatched away, we begin to be anxious and to doubt whether we are a care to God, whether we are looked upon and helped. Wherefore let us acknowledge our weakness, that we have need of the government of the Holy Spirit, and that God truly wills to bestow him upon those who invoke him. Let us learn, and the advantages of the body, sustenance, defense, successes in our calling, with are present, are gifts of God, and it must be requested that God does not allow them to be snatched from us, and when they are snatched away, let us ask of God that in His wonderful goodness He may provide for us otherwise.

Latin:

Ego credo, quod tu es Christus.

Confessio perspicua est de Messia, et ut in caeteris locis hae clarae confessiones observandae sunt, ut Matth. 16. Ioann. 1. 3. et 9. ita hunc locum meminisse prodest, qui de duabus maxi- mis rebus lectorem docet, et quod ille Iesus natus ex Maria, tunc praedicans, et mortuos resusci- tans sit promissus Salvator, et quod Messias sit filius Dei. De utraque sententia cogitemus, cur nobis traditae sint, et quomodo in invocatione exercendae sint, ac prius et brevius de posteriore dicam. Nos scimus ex certis testimoniis Evange- lii multis, in Christo naturam divinam esse, et Christum natura filium Dei esse. Hunc articulum confitentur Apostoli, Matth. 16. Et pater de coelo dicit: Hic est filius meus dilectus, et Bapti- sta dicit, Ioann. 3.: Qui credit in filium, habet vitam aeternam, et Ioann. 9. ipse Christus inter- rogat: Tu credis in filium Dei? et in 1. capite clare tradita est sententia, quod in Christo sit na- tura divina, per quam omnia condita sunt. Agnoscamus igitur in invocatione Mediatorem, non tantum esse hominem, sed etiam natura filium Dei, per quem omnia condita sunt et sus- tentantur, sicut ad Heb. 1. dicitur, qui semper adfuit Ecclesiae suae, et affuturus est, ideoque dicitur Emanuel.

Cum autem invocatio fieri debeat fiducia filii, semper cogitandum est inter precandum, quis sit ille Mediator, qui in se derivat iram Dei, et pro- pter quem sumus recepti, et qui semper adfuit et aderit Ecclesiae. Haec omnia omittunt in sua invocatione omnes ignorantes Evangelium, Eth- nici, Iudaei, Mahometistae, et alii impii. Aber- rant igitur a Deo, cum negent hunc esse Deum, qui misit filium, et patefecit se hoc verbo tradito per Prophetas, Christum, et Apostolos. Sic au- tem inquit Christus: Qui non afficit honore filium, non afficit honore patrem. Deinde etiam ignorantes Evangelium, nesciunt an velit nos Deus recipere et exaudire, et cur velit recipere, cum res ipsa ostendat nos indignos esse. Omnes enim experiuntur, se aliquibus vitiis contamina- tos esse. Ut igitur nostram invocationem ab alia- rum gentium invocatione seiungamus, cogitan- dum est quis sit filius Dei. Etsi enim compre- hendi maiestas tanta non potest, tamen Deus vult nos verbum suum tenere, et dirigere invocatio- nem ad illum Deum, qui hoc verbum tradidit, et sic se patefecit.

Eodem pertinet altera pars, quod videlicet necesse sit credi hunc Iesum natum ex Maria, crucifixum in Ierosolyma in illo tempore, esse Messiam. Tempus et locum definivit Deus, ne vagabundae mentes quaerant varios mediatores, sicut finxerunt Ethnici varia numina, frugum da- tricem Cererem, vini datorem Bacchum, opitulatorem in praeliis Martem, Palladem monstrantem consilia in gubernatione Reipub. Iunonem divitias cumulantem. Sed sit mens cogitans verbum Dei, alligata ad illum Deum, qui se hoc verbo patefecit, et qui misit filium natum ex virgine, Iesum Christum crucifixum pro nobis, et resuscitatum, exhibitum populo Israël, sicut promissus erat, et concionatum Ierosolymae, et in tota Iudaea, et miraculis testificatum de Evangelio, ac praesertim resuscitatione mortuorum, illo ipso tempore de quo scribunt Apostoli, videlicet quod excidium Ierosolymae praecedit annis quadraginta. Ut igitur omnis invocatio excitanda est consideratione mandati, et promissionis divinae, ita semper simul cogitandum est, quis sit ille Deus, quem invocamus, ubi et quomodo patefactus, quanta bonitas sit, quod se sic patefecerit, quod donarit mediatorem, reconciliationem, auxilium et salutem. Deinde quis sit mediator, ubi, quando patefactus sit, cur passus sit. Haec omnia quaelibet, quamvis brevis, invocatio complecti debet. De hoc exercitio saepe et nos ipsos, et Ecclesiam commonefaciamus. Laudanda et Philosophorum diligentia, qui de singulis virtutibus tam accurate, quantum in philosophia fieri potuit, scripserunt. Dolendum est autem in Ecclesia de virtute omnium summa, de invocatione Dei, non collectam esse simili diligentia doctrinam a Deo traditam, in praeceptis et promissionibus, quae extant in scriptis Prophetarum et Apostolorum, laudatur temperantia, et est virtus digna laude, laudatur clementia in gubernatoribus, et saepe salutaris est magnis imperiis. De his et aliis vulgaribus virtutibus extat doctrina Philosophorum luculenter scripta, at de virtute omnium regina, de agnitione et invocatione Dei, quam pauca, tenuia et frigida scripta inveniuntur? pauci intelligunt esse virtutem, alii putant doctrinam facilem esse, notam omnibus. Quia naturaliter omnes destituti humana ope, et amisso hoc visibili auxilio, quaerimus an sit Deus, qui velit opitulari hominibus, et in hac disputatione plurimi quoquo modo Deum invocant, non cogitantes, quis sit Deus, quo modo se patefecerit, quid mandaverit de invocatione, quid promiserit, quomodo sit placatus, quis sit mediator, an et cur velit exaudire, quas res nominatim promiserit, in quibus rebus requirat obedientiam nostram, et tamen mitigationem promiserit.

Apud Euripidem Hecuba dubitans, quid sit Deus, sic invocat, o Iupiter, quisquis es, diffi- cilis cognitu, qui terram regis, sive necessitate naturae, sive consilio regens. Haec dubitatio communis est omnium, qui ignorant Evangelium, aut stoica imaginatione tenentur, Deum sine li- bero consilio sic agere necessario, ut movent cau- sae secundae, aut si libere agit, curare quaedam magna, non curare particularia, ut idem Euri- pides inquit. Postremo, ut maxime curet parti- cularia, tamen non exaudiri indignos. Hae opi- niones obstrepunt animis omnium in invocatione, nec eluctantur ex his erroribus Ethnici, Maho- metistae, Iudaei, et alii ignorantes Evangelium. Sed fides agnito Evangelio eluctatur, et statuit certo, quis sit Deus, nempe is, qui se patefecit verbo suo et misso filio, et additis mirandis te- stimoniis, et quod sit agens liberrimum, quod dederit mandata et promissiones, et proposuerit mediatorem filium, propter quem certo velit ex- audire, et quod expresserit nominatim, quas res certo daturus sit, et in quibus requirat obedien- tiam, quas tamen mitigaturus sit.

Ut igitur nos ad invocationem excitemus, et recte invocemus, et discernamus nostram preca- tionem ab Ethnica, Turcica, Iudaica, breviter colligam hoc loco, quae cogitanda sint, ac de singulis partibus considerandum est verbum Dei, quia tantum cogitatione verbi Dei ad eum acce- ditur iuxta illud Rom. 10.: Ne dixeris in corde tuo, quis ascendet in coelum? sed prope est ver- bum in ore tuo et in corde tuo. Primum igitur invocanti verbum quaerendum est, ostendens quid sit Deus. Non invocas, ut Hecuba apud Euri- pidem ignara quis sit Deus, an sit ordo naturae alligatus ad causas secundas, an vero agens libe- rum: Non invocas ut Turci et Iudaei contumelia afficientes filium, et nescientes mediatorem, sed verbum Dei tibi proponis, quod certo testatur, hunc vere esse Deum omnipotentem, conditorem omnium creaturarum, et conservatorem, qui se patefecit, dato hoc verbo, additis testimoniis a principio mundi, et misso filio crucifixo pro no- bis, et resuscitato, et cum cogitamus quomodo se patefecerit, in compellatione fiat mentio perso- narum, ut patefactae sunt, ut postea dicam.

Secundo, postquam, quis sit Deus, cogita- tum est, et se iunxisti te ab Ethnicis, Turcis et Iudaeis, mandatum eius de invocatione considera, magna res est, accedere ad Deum, ac petere ab eo, non solum ea, quae dat communi cursu na- turae, sed etiam alia, cum praeter communem cursum in nostris erratis et aerumnis nos liberat. Deterret autem nos indignitas nostra, praesertim cum sciamus Deum iustum esse, et irasci peccatis, nos autem multis peccatis pollutos esse. Hic igi- tur opus est verbo Dei, testificante de voluntate eius, quod iubeat se invocari, et velit exaudire, recipere, iuvare invocantes, quanquam indignos et pollutos peccatis. Quare diligenter colligamus et mandata, et promissiones, ut Matth. 7.: Peti- te, et dabitur vobis, etc. Lucae 18.: Oportet semper orare, et non languefieri. 1. Thess. 5.: Semper gaudete, incessanter orate, in omnibus gratias agite. Haec est enim voluntas Dei in Christo Iesu erga vos. Ad Phil. 4.: Non sitis so- liciti, sed in omnibus precatione et petitione, cum gratiarum actione postulationes vestrae ad Deum notae fiant.

Adiungantur et promissiones, quarum prae- cipua est et fundamentum invocationis de quacun- que re, promissio remissionis peccatorum. Nam etiam cum mandata cogitamus, tamen haec vox nos absterret: peccatores Deus non exaudit. Hic igitur ante caeteras promissiones proponamus do- ctrinam de remissione peccatorum, sciamus omni- bus agentibus poenitentiam, certo remitti peccata propter Christum mediatorem, non propter no- stram dignitatem. Accipi vero remissionem pec- catorum fide, ut clarissime traditur in multis Evangelii locis. Et Rom. 3.: Summa eius sen- tentiae proponitur, iustificamur gratis gratia ipsius, per redemtionem, quae est in Christo Iesu, quem proposuit Deus propiciatorem per fidem in sanguine ipsius.

Hanc fidem in omni invocatione praelucere oportet, quod propter filium mediatorem recipia- mur, exaudiamur et iuvemur.

Cum hac fide remissionem peccatorum acci- pere nos statuimus, hic primum dulcescunt man- data, et caeterae promissiones de particularibus beneficiis. Ioan. 14.: Quicquid petieritis patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis. Iubet petere no- mine suo, id est, se nominato, se invocato, tan- quam mediatore, propter quem certo recipimur et exaudimur, ut ad Heb. 4. dicitur: Habentes Pontificem Iesum, accedamus cum fiducia ad thro- num gratiae.

Iam igitur opponamus indignitati nostrae mandata et promissiones. Etiamsi sumus indigni, tamen mandanti Deo obtemperandum est, et quan- quam sumus rei, tamen donatus est nobis propi- ciator, et promittenti Deo credendum est, nec accusandus est Deus mendacii. Accedamus igi- tur ad eum, et petamus remissionem peccatorum, Spiritum sanctum, et alia bona necessaria Eccle- siae, politicae gubernationi, et nobis privatim. De Spiritu sancto nominatim dictum est, Lucae 11.: Quanto magis pater vester coelestis dabit Spi- ritum sanctum petentibus? De aliis liberationi- bus etiam perspicuae et multae promissiones tra- ditae sunt, Psal. 3.: Iuxta est dominus his, qui tribulato sunt corde, et humiles spiritu salvabit, et eodem Psalmo: Non est inopia timentibus eum. Et Christus inquit: Primum quaerite re- gnum Dei, et caetera adiicientur vobis. Et 1. Ti- moth. 4.: Pietas promissiones habet praesentis et futurae vitae, etc.

Talia dicta multa in conspectu sint, et saepe cogitentur animo, ut nos ad invocationem exusci- tent, et aliqua inter precandum quotidie atten- tionem, et fidem in nobis accendant. Certe sem- per, quoties precationem incoamus, cogitandum est, quem Deum invoces, an ille indignum ex- audiat, et cur exaudiat, et indignitati opponenda sunt mandata et promissiones, ac praecipue me- ditanda et amplectenda est promissio remissionis peccatorum. Deinde etiam res petenda cogitetur. Non enim sit oratio inanis βαττολογία, sed res corporales et spirituales necessariae communi et privatae saluti petantur. Ideo enim plerunque friget oratio, quia non expectamus illa beneficia a Deo, nec ardet in corde haec lux et fides, quod Deus vere aliquid nobiscum agat, det Spiritum sanctum, regat, iuvet, defendat nos, det victum nobis, sed mentes sunt oppressae dubitatione, nec possunt se erigere, ut res illas vere statuant a Deo dari, cum hac nostra dubitatione praecipue lu- ctandum est, nitimur nostris consiliis et commo- dis visibilibus et praesidiis humanis. Haec cum sint in conspectu, nihil admodum serio petitur a Deo. Cum haec eripiuntur, incipimus angi et dubitare, an Deo curae simus, an respiciamur et iuvemur. Quare agnoscamus imbecillitatem no- stram, quod sit nobis opus gubernatione Spiritus sancti, et quod Deus vere velit eum largiri invo- cantibus. Discamus, et commoda corporis, vi- ctum, defensionem, successus in vocatione, cum adsunt, esse Dei dona, et petendum, ut Deus ea nobis non eripi sinat, et cum eripiuntur, pe- tamus a Deo, ut sua mirabili bonitate nobis aliter prospiciat.

## 11:33
He groaned in spirit.

No miracle was performed by Christ without some great movement of the soul, just as He Himself says in Luke 8: I felt power go out from me. It appears, however, especially that there were great agitations of soul and great agonies in this resuscitation; He groans, He grieves, He is indignant, He weeps. These movements are unknown to us, but they signify a most bitter struggle; when He had decided to resuscitate Lazarus, He prayed to the eternal Father that this work might be done. Here the devil undoubtedly tries to hinder Him, by injecting various thoughts; He in turn resisted the devil, at times being angry at the devil, at times grieving and weeping on account of the huge misery of the human race, which He considered with great sorrow to be oppressed by sin, the wrath of God, the tyranny of the devil, infinite calamities, and bodily and eternal death; He grieved on account of the wrath of God, and was an intercessor for us, but He was angry at the devil and drove him away from Himself. Such were the agonies, which, even if we cannot understand them, let us nevertheless think that the soul of Christ was not idle, or iron-hearted, or without true sorrows and true indignation. For no one is affected by such sharp pain when he sees the extreme calamity of a most beloved daughter, as sharp as was the pain of Christ seeing our evils, because it is said in Hebrews 4: We do not have a High Priest who cannot sympathize with our infirmities, but one who was tempted in all things according to the likeness, without sin. Let us therefore approach with confidence. Let us be invited and let us more willingly flee to Christ, since we determine that He is truly affected by our pain, which many testimonies expressed in various histories certainly teach, as in Matthew 9: Seeing the crowds, He had compassion on them, and often otherwise.

And finally emerging from this struggle, Christ begins to give thanks to the Father because He heard Him. These words testify that those earlier sorrows and groanings were of a soul praying to God, and while praying, resisting the devil who was throwing up obstacles. And at the end He adds the principal reason for the whole deed, that His invocation was made so that it might appear that He was doing what He was doing by the power of this God, whose doctrine had been handed down among this people, and that this resuscitation was being done to confirm the doctrine. Thus let us also propose this history to ourselves; since miracles are testimonies of doctrine, let us diligently collect those which are proper to the Church, that is, which no creature can imitate, such as the resuscitation of the dead, stopping the course of the sun, and certain others. These manifestly show that this doctrine, concerning which they testify, was handed down by God.

Latin:

Infremuit spiritu.

Nullum miraculum sine magno aliquo motu animi a Christo factum est, sicut ipse dicit, Lu- cae 8.: Sensi virtutem a me exivisse. Apparet autem inprimis magnos aestus animi, magnos agones fuisse in hac resuscitatione, fremit, dolet, indignatur, lacrymat. Hi motus nobis ignoti sunt, sed significant luctam acerrimam, cum de- crevisset resuscitare Lazarum, precatus est aeter- num patrem, ut hoc opus fieret. Hic impedire eum haud dubie diabolus conatur, iniectis variis cogitationibus, ipse vicissim repugnavit diabolo, alias irascens diabolo, alias dolens, et illacry- mans propter humani generis ingentem miseriam, quod peccato, ira Dei, tyrannide diaboli, infini- tis calamitatibus, et morte corporali et aeterna oppressum esse magno cum moerore cogitabat, doluit propter iram Dei, et pro nobis fuit depre- cator, sed diabolo iratus est, et eum a se depulit. Tales agones fuerunt, quos etiamsi nos intelligere non possumus, tamen cogitemus animum Christi non fuisse otiosum, aut ferreum, aut sine veris doloribus et vera indignatione. Nullus enim tam acri dolore afficitur, cum videt carissimae filiae summam calamitatem, quam acris dolor fuit Christi mala nostra videntis, quia dicitur Ebr. 4.: Non habemus Pontificem, qui non possit compati nostris infirmitatibus, sed tentatum per omnia se- cundum similitudinem, sine peccato. Acceda- mus ergo cum fiducia. Invitemur et libentius ad Christum confugiamus, cum vere eum affici no- stro dolore statuimus, quod certe docent multa testimonia expressa in diversis historiis, ut Matth. 9.: Videns turbas, misertus est earum, et saepe alias.

Ac tandem emergens Christus ex hac lucta, incipit gratias agere patri, quod exaudierit ipsum. Haec verba testantur priores illos dolores ac fre- mitus fuisse animi precantis Deum, et inter pre- candum repugnantis diabolo obiicienti impedi- menta. Et addit in fine causam principalem to- tius facti, suam invocationem factam esse, ut ap- pareat se, quae faciebat potentia huius Dei, cuius in hoc populo doctrina tradita erat, facere, et hanc resuscitationem fieri ad confirmandam do- ctrinam. Sic et nobis hanc historiam proponamus, cum miracula sint testimonia doctrinae, diligenter illa colligamus, quae propria sunt Ecclesiae, hoc est, quae nulla creatura imitari potest, qualis est resuscitatio mortuorum, sistere cursum solis, et alia quaedam. Haec manifeste ostendunt hanc doctrinam, de qua testificantur, a Deo traditam esse.

## 11:44
And the dead man came out, bound hand and foot with strips of cloth.

That Lazarus is recalled from death by the voice of Christ, and is gifted with life again, is a testimony of the Gospel, that it is an efficacious voice, and, as Paul says, the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes; if He restores the life of the body to Lazarus by His voice, He will also, according to His promise, kindle eternal life and righteousness in hearts by the voice of the Gospel, as Christ Himself prays: Father, sanctify them in your truth, your word is truth; He wants them to be sanctified, that is, to be gifted with divine light, the knowledge of God, and righteousness; how? through the word of God.

Nor is mention made without cause of the shroud which covered his hands, feet, and face. For in Isaiah 25 it is clearly said concerning the abolishing of death, and on this mountain the face of those wrapped up will be devoured, with which all peoples are wrapped, and the covering with which all nations are covered, and death will be devoured entirely, and the Lord God will wipe away every tear from every face, and He will take away the reproach of His people from the whole earth. It is an illustrious and sweet testimony concerning the universal resurrection and the restoration of perpetual life, just as the resuscitation of Lazarus itself is a testimony that this Christ is the restorer of life; moreover, the form of the words agrees with the history of Lazarus; Isaiah says it will come to pass that the wrappings of faces will be taken away. Thus here Christ commands the shrouds and coverings to be taken away, with which the limbs of Lazarus were wrapped. Therefore the images in Isaiah and in the history of Lazarus correspond, and the same thing is signified in both readings. The shroud with which we are entangled is cast off, that is, the weakness and mortality of our body is put off, and we are adorned with a new garment, that is, the vivacity of the body, which will see God with its eyes and will burn with spiritual movements. These things, as they were signified in the words of Isaiah, so they were in the history of Lazarus, but in reality they will happen when the saints in the universal resurrection will be clothed in new and perpetual glory.

Latin:

Et egressus est mortuus, vinctus pedes et manus fasciolis.

Quod voce Christi Lazarus revocatur ex morte, et rursus vita donatur, testimonium est Evangelii, quod sit vox efficax, et, ut Paulus inquit, potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti, si voce restituit vitam corporis Lazaro, etiam iuxta promissionem suam voce Evangelii accendet vitam aeternam et iusticiam in cordibus, ut Christus ipse precatur: Pater sanctifica eos in veritate tua, sermo tuus est veritas, vult eos sanctificari, id est, luce divina, agnitione Dei, et iusticia donari, quomodo? per sermonem Dei.

Nec sine causa mentio fit stolae, quae texit manus, pedes et faciem.
