Nam Esaiae 25. clare dicitur de abolenda morte, et devorabitur in monte hoc facies involutorum, qua omnes populi involuti sunt, et tegumentum, quo omnes gentes coopertae sunt, et mors devorabitur omnino, et absterget dominus Deus omnem lacrymam ab omni facie, et opprobrium populi sui auferet de universa terra. Illustre et dulce testimonium est de universali resurrectione et de reddenda vita perpetua, sicut et ipsa Lazari resuscitatio testimonium est, hunc Christum instauratorem esse vitae, convenit autem forma verborum cum historia Lazari, Esaias inquit futurum, ut involucra facierum tollantur. Ita hic iubet Christus auferri stolas et tegmina, quibus involuta erant membra Lazari. Congruunt igitur imagines in Esaia et in historia Lazari, et res eadem in utraque lectione significatur. Stola, qua sumus impliciti, abiicitur, id est, corporis nostri imbecillitas et mortalitas exuitur, et nova veste, id est, corporis vivacitate ornamur, quae cernet oculis Deum, et ardebit motibus spiritualibus. Haec ut in verbis Esaiae, ita in historia Lazari significata sunt, sed revera fient, cum sancti in universali resurrectione nova et perpetua gloria vestientur.

## 11:45
Many therefore of the Jews, who had come to Martha.

After all miracles at all times these two events follow: the pious are confirmed, and somewhat more are converted to God, moved by the new testimony. On the contrary, however, in the impious, hatreds and furies grow, as it is said in Isaiah 6, and Romans 11, and John 12: He gave them eyes that they might not see, and ears that they might not hear. Let us compare these sayings to the histories, and let us console ourselves with these warnings against the judgments of great men who oppose the Gospel; let us know that there is always some assembly of God, but yet a small one, and that many endowed with great authority, power, and wisdom oppose it, as it is said in 1 Corinthians 1: God chose the weak things of the world, that he might confound the strong, etc.

But he did not say this of his own accord.

Great and difficult questions offer themselves here: whether Caiaphas is a member of the visible Church, since he is openly an enemy of the Gospel? Then, whether he is High Priest, since he is not a member of the Church? Thirdly, whether God wills the errors of governors? Fourthly, whether the impious are moved by the Holy Spirit in giving counsel?

To the first I answer that Caiaphas is not a member of the Church, even though he is the High Priest of that polity in which the Church of God was, that assembly which embraced the Gospel. For the rule must be held: My sheep hear my voice. And: If anyone preaches another Gospel, let him be anathema. And 1 Corinthians last: If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema, Maranatha, that is, the Lord comes. For by this form of words they invoked upon the cursed the judgment of God coming and punishing. Nor do these things conflict with each other, not to be a member of the Church, and yet to be a member of that polity which was then the domicile of the Church. Certainly it would be absurd to say that the Sadducees were members of the Church, whom, however, it can perhaps rightly be said were members of that polity.

Regarding the second question I answer: Because we distinguish the Church and the polity in that people, let us concede that Caiaphas was the High Priest of that polity, even though he was an enemy of the Church, just as when some Sadducee was High Priest. Thus Jason, Menelaus, and Alcimus were High Priests, when in reality they were enemies of the Church.

Regarding the third question I answer that God neither wills nor approves the sins or unjust counsels and unjust actions of governors, but rather is horribly angry at them, as He clearly says in Psalm 5: You are not a God willing impiety, and Christ clearly says: He who delivered me to you has the greater sin, and John 8: You are from your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father, and again Psalm 5: The Lord abominates the man of blood and deceit. Finally, there are very many most evident testimonies which affirm that God neither wills nor approves the unjust counsels and unjust actions of governors, but rather is horribly angry at these crimes and punishes them, as the outcomes themselves testify. Because of the murdered Prophets, Christ, and the Apostles, the Jewish nation paid the saddest penalties with the destruction of their entire Republic. Therefore, let us execrate as manifest madness the opinion which imagines that the unjust counsels of governors arise from God or please God. They are the impulses of the devil raging in the impious, who have shaken off God as their ruler, and for that reason have in turn been cast off, and become organs of wrath, plagues of the human race, and rush into eternal punishments, like Pharaoh, Judas, Caiaphas, Caligula, and Nero, at the thought of whom let us tremble, and let us pray to God that He may guard and rule us, lest we be implicated in unjust counsels and affairs.

To the fourth question the answer is clear. The impious are not moved by the Holy Spirit in giving unjust counsel, but are impelled by the devil, as it is clearly said: You are from your father the devil. Likewise: He who commits sin is from the devil. But that the text says Caiaphas prophesied because he was High Priest is similar to the history of Joseph, who says: You thought evil against me, but God turned it into good, that He might exalt me and save many peoples. God neither wills, nor approves, nor moves the minds of tyrants who rage against the Church, but He establishes the limits and the outcomes. The devil tries to destroy Joseph, but God preserves him, and this very calamity becomes, with God governing the manner, a salutary outcome. Thus the counsels and sayings of Caiaphas were condemned, but this very saying, which he himself utters with an impious will, becomes a means to a salutary outcome for the human race, with God governing, and thus God especially turns the furies of magistrates to the good of the Church. That turning to the good is the work of God, as Joseph says: God turned it into good. Thus the ungodly prophesy, that is, they contrive evil, which is a means to a glorious end, as when Ahithophel had given useful counsel to Absalom, Absalom nevertheless preferred the specious counsel of Hushai, by which he granted space to his father David to seek a retreat, to gather forces, and to prepare a defense. Thus Absalom, erring by that very counsel which he thinks is most safe for destroying his father, saves him. This example testifies that God sets limits both to the cruelty and to the counsels of the enemies of the Church, so that they cannot do as much harm as they wish.

Latin:

Multi igitur ex Iudaeis, qui venerant ad Martham.

Post miracula omnia omnibus temporibus sequuntur hi duo eventus, pii confirmantur, et aliquanto plures ad Deum convertuntur, moti novo testimonio. Econtra vero in impiis crescunt odia et furores, ut Esaiae 6. dicitur, et Roman. 11. et Ioan. 12.: Dedit eis oculos ne videant, et aures ne audiant. Haec dicta ad historias conferamus, et nos consolemur his praemonitionibus adversus iudicia magnorum hominum, qui Evangelio adversantur, sciamus semper aliquem esse Dei coetum, sed tamen exiguum, et huic adversari multos magna autoritate, potentia, sapientia praeditos, ut 1. ad Corinth. 1. dicitur: Infirma mundi elegit Deus, ut confundat fortia, etc.

Hoc autem a se ipso non dixit.

Magnae et difficiles quaestiones hic se offerunt, an Caiphas sit membrum Ecclesiae visibilis, cum aperte sit hostis Evangelii? Deinde, an sit Pontifex, cum non sit membrum Ecclesiae? Tertio, an Deus velit errata gubernatorum? Quarto, an Spiritu sancto moveantur impii in dandis consiliis?

Ad primam respondeo, Caipham non esse membrum Ecclesiae, etsi est Pontifex illius politiae, in qua erat Ecclesia Dei, coetus ille, qui amplectebatur Evangelium. Nam tenenda est regula: Oves meae vocem meam audiunt. Et: Si quis aliud Evangelium docet, anathema sit. Et 1. Corinth. ultimo: Si quis non diligit dominum Iesum Christum, sit anathema, Maranatha, id est, dominus venit. Hac enim forma verborum imprecabantur maledicto iudicium Dei venientis et punientis. Nec pugnant haec inter se, non esse membrum Ecclesiae, et tamen esse membrum politiae illius, quae tunc domicilium erat Ecclesiae. Certe absurdum esset dicere, Sadducaeos fuisse membra Ecclesiae, quos tamen fuisse membra illius politiae fortassis recte dici potest.

De secunda quaestione respondeo: Quia discernimus Ecclesiam et politiam in illo populo, concedamus Caipham fuisse Pontificem politiae istius, etiamsi erat hostis Ecclesiae, ut cum Sadducaeus aliquis erat Pontifex. Sic Iason, Menelaus, Alcimus erant Pontifices, cum revera essent hostes Ecclesiae.

De tertia quaestione respondeo, Deum nec velle, nec approbare peccata seu infusta consilia et iniustas actiones gubernatorum, sed potius horribiliter irascitur eis, sicut clare dicit, Psalm. 5.: Non Deus volens impietatem tu es, et Christus clare dicit: Qui tradidit me tibi, maius peccatum habet, et Ioan. 8.: Vos ex patre diabolo estis, et cupiditates patris vestri vultis facere, et rursus Psalm. 5.: Virum sanguinum et dolosum abominatur dominus. Denique plurima sunt evidentissima testimonia, quae affirmant Deum nec velle, nec approbare iniusta consilia, et iniustas actiones gubernatorum, sed potius horribiliter his sceleribus irasci, et ea punire, ut ipsi exitus testantur. Propter occisos Prophetas, Christum, Apostolos, gens Iudaica excidio totius suae Reipublicae tristissimas poenas dedit. Ideo tanquam manifestum furorem execrremur opinionem, quae a Deo fingit oriri, aut Deo placere iniusta consilia gubernatorum. Diaboli impetus sunt grassantis in impiis, qui Deum rectorem excusserunt, et propterea vicissim abiecti sunt, et fiunt organa irae, pestes generis humani, et ruunt in aeternas poenas, ut Pharao, Iudas, Caiphas, Caligula, Nero, quorum cogitatione expavescamus, et Deum oremus, ut custodiat et regat nos, ne iniustis consiliis et negociis implicemur.

Ad quartam quaestionem perspicua est responsio. Non moventur Spiritu S. impii in dandis consiliis iniustis, sed impelluntur a diabolo, ut clare dicitur: Vos ex patre diabolo estis. Item: Qui facit peccatum, ex diabolo est. Quod autem textus dicit Caipham prophetasse, eo quod Pontifex esset, simile est historiae Ioseph. Qui inquit: Vos cogitastis de me malum, sed Deus vertit illud in bonum, ut exaltaret me, et salvos faceret multos populos. Nec vult, nec approbat, nec movet Deus mentes tyrannorum, qui saeviunt in Ecclesiam, sed metas et exitus constituit. Diabolus conatur perdere Ioseph, sed Deus servat eum, et haec ipsa calamitas fit, Deo gubernante modum ad salutarem exitum. Ita consilia et dicta Caiphae damnata sunt, sed hoc ipsum dictum, quod ipse impia voluntate profert, fit modus ad exitum salutarem humano generi, Deo gubernante, et sic praecipue magistratuum furores Deus vertit ad Ecclesiae bonum. Versio illa ad bonum est Dei opus, sicut inquit Ioseph: Deus vertit illud in bonum. Sic impii prophetant, id est, malum struunt, quod sit modus ad gloriosum exitum, ut cum Achitophel dedisset consilium utile Absoloni, Absolon tamen consilium speciosum Chusai antefert, quo spatium concessit patri Davidi ad receptum quaerendum, colligendas copias et parandam defensionem. Ita Absolon errans eo ipso consilio, quod putat esse tutissimum ad perdendum patrem, servat eum. Hoc exemplum testatur, Deum metas constituere et saevitiae, et consiliis hostium Ecclesiae, ne possint nocere quantum volunt.

## 12:1 Argument
Chapter XII.

Latin:

Caput XII.

## 12:1
Six days before the Passover.

The series of narratives clearly shows that life was restored to Lazarus before Palm Sunday. For now, on the Saturday before Palm Sunday in Bethany, Lazarus, recently recalled to life, sits at the table and the banquet of Christ, which is narrated for this reason, that there might exist a testimony concerning the true restoration of the life of Lazarus, lest anyone think that he, like a phantom exhibited once, afterwards vanished. Indeed, this life was true and long-lasting after the resuscitation, and histories narrate that after the division of the Apostles, when other disciples were bringing the Gospel to other places, Lazarus came to Marseilles on the Gallic coast, and there taught the Gospel.

Moreover, this is also debated, whether the Evangelists recount different banquets in Bethany; although these questions are more curious than useful, yet that I may briefly break them off, I will state my opinion: I think different banquets are recounted; John narrates the banquet of the sixth day before the Passover, Matthew the banquet of the third day before the Passover. These have nothing of absurdity.

But let us see the service of Mary, the sister of Lazarus, and its significance. Mary anoints the feet of Christ; that was customary for that nation, in which both the most fragrant aromatics were produced, and there was a great use for them. For God wished to instruct His people with present remedies against wounds, when He wished them to be soldiers, and against the languors of the heart, which those burdened with cares sustain. But before I speak of the significance, I must first speak of the very kind of works. This work of Mary, and similar works of others, has been criticized by two arguments, the first of which is: only works commanded by God are to be done; this anointing was not commanded. Therefore it should not have been done. The other is: profusions are not to be made, especially with the defrauding of the poor. Mary pours out ointment, which could have been sold for three hundred denarii, that is, thirty crowns, from which it would have been better to help the poor; therefore, it is rightly criticized.

To the first I reply, and first to the minor premise I say: that this work was a work of confession, by which Mary testified that she revered this teacher and believed in him, when indeed he had already so often asserted that he was the Messiah, and for that reason the Chief Priests desired to remove him. Moreover, all works of confession that are not feigned please God, on account of the confession, and in general they are commanded. Thus this work pleases, not from the work performed, but because it is a testimony of confession, for it shows to others that she believes in this teacher and professes him to be the Messiah. Thus David performed a work of confession when, walking before the ark, he played the lyre. Nor do David or this woman add the opinion that this external work merits the remission of sins, or that it is of itself a worship of God; but they understand the soul of the work to be confession, and that this pleases God, according to that saying: Whoever shall have confessed me before men, him will I confess before my heavenly Father.

But confession is never exhibited in forbidden works; indeed, one doing forbidden works shows that he does not revere God, but rather despises His judgment, just as the adorations of statues, the carrying about of bread, and the sacrifices of the Mass are not signs of confession, as some now excuse those works. For they are in reality forbidden things, and they are not even done with this opinion, that they might be signs of the confession of the true doctrine of Christ, but they are done by superstition, that is, because the works themselves are thought to be merits and worship by their very nature. When this superstition is added, even good examples become vicious, just as many things become vicious. If Ahaz had danced before the ark like David, and had thought that by this work he was rendering distinguished honor to God, or that the work itself was a great merit, it would have been a vain and superstitious spectacle displeasing to God.

On the contrary, let confession shine in commanded works, as the Prophets, Apostles, Martyrs, and pious teachers in taxing the worship of idols and in the endurance of punishments, each in his own vocation, showed their confession. And that was a necessary work, which they could not omit without sin, wherefore in that matter their obedience was discerned, and it was seen to which God they were rendering obedience, and what kind of duties that true God demanded, as the Psalm says: For your sake we are killed all the day long. This rule being posited and remaining, that forbidden works should not be done, and that commandments should be done, there often approaches for the liberty of the spirit a third kind, that is, that which in kind agrees with the commandments, but in species is a middle thing, or not necessary, as is the dancing before the ark, which in kind agrees with the commandments, which order the God of Israel to be celebrated by invoking him by name. David therefore invokes in this rite, even if this form in species is not commanded, but let superstition be absent, lest this work be thought to be a merit for the remission of sins, or singular worship, beyond true invocation outside this rite.

Thus the observance of our Sabbath is a work pleasing to God. For the kind is a commandment, that the people should gather to hear the voice of the Gospel, and for the use of the sacrament, but the species is ordained for the liberty of the spirit, on which day and in what order one should gather. Such are the innumerable works of the liberty of the spirit. Rachel stole the idols of her father Laban, it was not necessary to take them away, but to warn him was enough, so that he might avoid the worship of idols. Irene, the daughter of the emperor Licinius, overturned the idols of her father with her own hands; it was not necessary to overturn them by hand, but to admonish her father was enough. Lawrence, when Decius was taking away the money of the ecclesiastical treasury, could have left it without sin, but by the liberty of the spirit he did not wish to yield to the tyrant. Such are many works of the free spirit in the saints, which are testimonies of confession and of an ardent spirit, which Christ approves here, especially when hypocrites criticize them. But Christ says that this duty is to be preached with the propagation of the Gospel in the whole world, because it was done so that she might declare that she would be mindful of Christ, that is, so that she might declare a confession. He therefore praises universally the works of confession done without superstition.

And because he makes mention of the burial, he alludes to the custom of those nations which preserved the bodies of the dead drenched in a great expense of ointment. He says therefore that the duty is pleasing to him, because it signifies that his burial is imminent, and that he himself awaits the preservation and resurrection of the buried body. The commendation of the duty is much broader than what the unlearned woman had thought. Thus are pious deeds of the spirit adorned, and often small duties produce huge benefits, and conversely small lapses often draw great ruins, as the history of Adam, Eve, and many other examples testify. Now I respond to the second argument: Profusions are not to be made, especially with the defrauding of the poor, but this ointment could have been sold for thirty crowns, therefore it should not have been poured out in such a way. To the major premise I respond, both kinds of works are necessary, to help the poor, and to give testimonies of faith, and the spirit in the saints does both, and sees the times convenient for both, as Samuel says in 1 Kings 10: Do whatever your hand finds, because the Lord is with you, that is: I cannot prescribe rules for individual moments, but the Holy Spirit will impel and rule you, so that you may rightly do present things, provided you serve your calling.

There is a great difference here between the works of the Holy Spirit and human counsels. Many wise men corrupt things, while, having omitted the works of their calling, they do other things which they think are more splendid. Likewise, while they omit present things, and out of fear and false suspicions they mix up affairs, so that they might guard against something in the future, which perhaps will never happen. Saul is broken by fear and diffidence, so that he does not wait for Samuel, and afterwards, so that he might do more splendid things, having neglected the command of God, he does not kill the captured king. Achas, because of diffidence, seeks the aid of the Assyrians, against the voice of Isaiah, just as often the Turks have been invited by kings of the Christian name. But when hearts are governed by the word of God and the Holy Spirit, they understand their calling, and do their own things; teachers teach, they do not seek the protection and alliances of princes. Princes administer their own affairs, they do not summon foreign business, nor do they disturb the public state out of fear. And it is great wisdom and fortitude to do present things rightly, as Christ says: Tomorrow will be anxious for itself, sufficient for the day is its own affliction, that is: Let us see what is to be done rightly in the present, and let us not do anything against the rule because of fear or uncertain hopes. These things cannot be judged unless hearts are confirmed by faith and the Holy Spirit.

Now I will add a few things about the significance of Mary's duty, because this work is praised especially for its significance. Feet usually signify messengers, that is, the Ministry of the Gospel, as in Isaiah: How beautiful are the feet of those who preach peace. But there is nothing more common in the world, than extremely to despise the ministers of the Gospel, and the ministry itself, as Paul says: that the Apostles are held as the offscouring of all things, than which nothing more detestable can be said. Against these impious judgments of the world, Christ confirms us with many sayings, and commands that we love and protect the ministers of the Gospel, as in Luke 10: He who hears you, hears me, and he who rejects you, rejects me. And Matt. 10: Whoever gives a cup of water to one of these little ones, because of the doctrine, amen I say to you, he shall not lose his reward, and in 1 Thess. the last chapter it is said: Those who preside over you in the Lord, love them exceedingly, because of the office which they bear. Paul knew the feelings of the people, who easily grow weary of teachers, and when slight occasions are offered, casts them off; against these wearinesses Paul strives to excite and confirm them with benevolence, which not only does not admit unjust hatreds, but also calmly tolerates some slight inconveniences in teachers who teach rightly and live without disgrace, and forgives them for the sake of their function and the common tranquility. These pious duties toward ministers are signified by the ointment poured upon the feet. Mary, that is, the Church as hearer, anoints the feet, that is, cherishes and protects the ministers of the Gospel, and the ministry for the studies of heavenly doctrine, just as Constantine, Theodosius, and a few other pious rulers cherished and covered the teachers and the studies of doctrine; this duty Christ commends to us by the example of this history with this praise. And from this ointment a sweet odor and fragrance is diffused into the whole house, that is, the Gospel is propagated more widely, the Church is gathered, the true invocation of God grows, and other virtues.

Latin:

Ante sex dies Paschae.

Series narrationum manifeste ostendit, Lazaro mortuo restitutam esse vitam ante diem Palmarum. Nunc enim Sabbato ante diem Palmarum in Bethania, Lazarus recens revocatus in vitam, accumbit mensae et convivio Christi, quod eo narratur, ut testimonium extet de vera restitutione vitae Lazari, ne quis existimet eum ut spectrum semel exhibitum, postea evanuisse. Imo haec vita, vera et diuturna post resuscitationem fuit, ac narrant historiae post divisionem Apostolorum, cum alii discipuli in alia loca Evangelium afferrent, Lazarum venisse Massiliam ad litus Gallicum, et ibi Evangelium docuisse.

Caeterum et hoc disputatur, an diversa convivia in Bethania recitent Evangelistae, etsi hae quaestiones magis curiosae sunt, quam utiles, tamen ut eas breviter abrumpam, meam opinionem dicam, existimo diversa convivia recitari, Ioannes narrat convivium sexti diei ante Pascha, Matthaeus convivium tertii diei ante Pascha. Haec nihil habent absurdi.

Sed officium Mariae sororis Lazari, et significationem videamus. Maria ungit pedes Christi, id fuit usitatum illi genti, in qua et nascebantur aromata fragrantissima, et magnus eorum usus erat. Voluit enim Deus suum populum instruere praesentibus remediis adversus vulnera, cum vellet esse milites, et adversus languores cordis, quos sustinent onerati curis. Priusquam autem de significatione dicam, prius de ipso genere operum dicendum est. Reprehensum est hoc opus Mariae, et similia opera aliarum duobus argumentis, quorum primum est, tantum opera mandata a Deo facienda sunt, haec unctio non fuit mandata. Non igitur facienda fuit. Alterum est: Non sunt faciendae profusiones, praesertim cum defraudatione pauperum. Maria profundit unguentum, quod potuit vendi trecentis denariis, id est, triginta coronatis, unde melius erat iuvare pauperes, iure igitur reprehenditur.

Ad primum respondeo, ac primum ad mi- norem dico: Hoc opus fuisse opus confessionis, quo Maria testificata est se hunc doctorem vene- rari, et ei credere, cum quidem toties iam asse- verasset, se esse Messiam, et propterea Pontifices eum tollere cuperent. Omnia autem opera con- fessionis non simulatae placent Deo, propter con- fessionem, et in genere mandata sunt. Ita pla- cet hoc opus, non ex opere operato, sed quia est testimonium confessionis, ostendit enim aliis, se credere huic doctori, et profiteri eum esse Mes- siam. Sic David faciebat opus confessionis, cum ante arcam incedens luderet cithara. Nec David aut haec mulier addunt opinionem, quod hoc opus externum mereatur remissionem peccatorum, aut per sese sit cultus Dei; sed animam operis in- telligunt esse confessionem, et hanc Deo placere, iuxta illud: Qui confessus fuerit me coram homi- nibus, illum confitebor coram patre meo coelesti.

Nunquam autem exhibetur confessio in ope- ribus prohibitis, imo faciens prohibita opera, ostendit se non venerari Deum, sed potius iudi- cium eius contemnere, sicut non sunt signa con- fessionis adorationes statuarum, circumgestatio panis, sacrificia Missarum, ut nunc illa opera quidam excusant. Sunt enim reipsa prohibitae res, ac ne fiunt quidem hac opinione, ut sint signa confessionis verae doctrinae Christi, sed fiunt superstitione, hoc est, quia ipsa opera per sese putantur esse merita et cultus. Haec super- stitio cum accedit etiam bona exempla, tamen fiunt vitiosa, ut multa fiunt vitiosa. Si Achas ante arcam saltasset sicut David, ac putasset se hoc opere insignem honorem Deo praestare, aut opus ipsum magnum meritum esse, fuisset inane et superstitiosum spectaculum Deo displicens.

Econtra vero luceat confessio in operibus praeceptis, ut Prophetae, Apostoli, Martyres, pii doctores in taxando cultu idolorum, et tole- rantia suppliciorum, singuli in sua vocatione, confessionem suam ostenderunt. Idque erat opus necessarium, quod sine peccato omittere non po- terant, quare in ea re cernebatur eorum obedien- tia, et conspiciebantur, cui Deo praestarent obe- dientiam, et qualia officia ille verus Deus postu- laret, sicut Psal. inquit: Propter te mactamur tota die. Posita et manente hac regula, ne fiant opera prohibita, et fiant praecepta, accedit saepe pro libertate spiritus tertium genus, id est, quod in genere cum praeceptis congruit, sed in specie medium est, seu non necessarium, ut est salta- tio ante arcam, quod in genere congruit cum praeceptis, quae iubent celebrari Deum Israël nominatim ipsum invocando. Invocat igitur Da- vid in hoc ritu, etiamsi haec forma in specie non sit praecepta, sed absit superstitio, ne hoc opus existimetur esse meritum remissionis peccatorum, aut singulares cultus, prae invocatione vera extra hunc ritum.

Ita observatio nostri sabbati est opus placens Deo. Nam genus est praeceptum, ut conveniat populus ad audiendam vocem Evangelii, et ad usum sacramenti, sed species pro libertate spiri- tus ordinata est, qno die et quo ordine conve- niendum sit. Talia sunt innumerabilia opera libertatis spiritus. Rahel rapuit idola patri La- ban, non fuit necesse auferre, sed monere satis erat, ut vitaret idolorum cultum. Irene filia im- peratoris Licinii evertit idola patris suis manibus, non necesse erat manu evertere, sed patrem ad- monere satis erat. Laurentius Decio auferenti pecuniam aerarii ecclesiastici, potuisset eam sine peccato relinquere, sed libertate spiritus noluit tyranno cedere. Talia multa sunt opera liberi spiritus in sanctis, quae sunt testimonia confes- sionis et ardentis spiritus, quae hic probat Chri- stus, praesertim cum hypocritae reprehendunt. Ait autem Christus praedicandum esse id officium cum propagatione Evangelii in toto mundo, quia factum sit, ut declararet se memorcm fore Chri- sti, id est, ut declararet confessionem. Laudat igitur universaliter opera confessionis sine super- stitione facta.

Et quod facit mentionem sepulturae, alludit ad morem earum gentium, quae corpora mortuo- rum magno sumtu unguenti perfusa asservabant. Ait ergo gratum sibi esse officium, quia significet instare eius sepulturam, et ipsam expectare se- pulti corporis conservationem et resurrectionem. Commendatio officii multo est amplior, quam quantum cogitarat inerudita mulier. Ita ornan- tur pia facta spiritus, et saepe parva officia ingen- tes utilitates pariunt, et econtra parvi lapsus tra- hunt saepe magnas ruinas, ut historia Adae, Evae, et alia multa exempla testantur. Nunc re- spondeo ad secundum argumentum: Non sunt fa- ciendae profusiones, praesertim cum defrauda- tione pauperum, sed hoc unguentum triginta co- ronatis vendi poterat, non igitur ita effundendum erat. Ad maiorem respondeo, utrunque genus operum necessarium est, iuvare pauperes, et ede- re testimonia fidei, et spiritus in sanctis utrun- que facit, et tempora convenientia utrique videt, sicut dicit Samuel Reg. 10.: Fac quaecunque in- venerit manus tua, quia dominus tecum est, id est: Non possum regulas singulorum momento- rum praescribere, sed Spiritus sanctus impellet et reget te, ut recte facias praesentia, modo ser- vias vocationi tuae.

Magna hic differentia est inter opera Spiri- tus sancti et inter humana consilia. Multa sa- pientes corrumpunt, dum omissis operibus voca- tionis alia agunt, quae putant esse splendidiora. Item dum omittunt praesentia, et metu et falsis suspicionibus miscent negocia, ut in posterum aliquid caveant, quod fortassis nunquam even- turum est. Saul frangitur metu et diffidentia, ne expectet Samuelem, et postea ut splendidiora faciat, neglecto mandato Dei, captum regem non interficit. Achas propter diffidentiam quaerit Assyriorum auxilia, contra vocem Esaiae, ut saepe Turci a regibus nominis Christiani invitati sunt. At cum corda verbo Dei et Spiritu sancto gubernantur, intelligunt vocationem suam, et suas res agunt, doctores docent, non quaerunt principum praesidia et foedera. Principes res suas administrant, non accersunt aliena negocia, nec turbant statum publicum metu. Et magna sapientia et fortitudo est praesentia recte facere, sicut Christus inquit: Crastinus dies pro sese so- licitus erit, sufficit diei afflictio sua, id est: Vi- deamus quid in praesentia recte fiat, nec propter metum aut incertas spes contra regulam aliquid agamus. Haec non possunt iudicari, nisi corda fide et Spiritu sancto confirmata sint.

Nunc pauca adiiciam de significatione officii Mariae, propter significationem maxime laudatur hoc opus. Pedes usitate significant nuncios, hoc est, Ministerium Evangelii, ut apud Esaiam: Quam speciosi pedes Evangelizantium pacem. Nihil est autem usitatius in mundo, quam extre- me contemnere ministros Evangelii, et ipsum mi- nisterium, sicut Paulus inquit: Apostolos haberi pro catharmatis, quo nihil detestabilius dici potest. Adversus haec impia iudicia mundi Christus confirmat nos multis dictis, ac praecipit ut ame- mus, ac tueamur Evangelii ministros, ut Lucae 10.: Qui vos audit, me audit, qui vos spernit, me spernit. Et Matth. 10.: Qui dederit potum aquae uni ex minimis istis, propter doctrinam, amen dico vobis, non perdet mercedem suam, et 1. ad Thessa. ult. dicitur: Eos qui praesunt vobis in domino, diligite excellenter, propter officium quod gerunt. Norat Paulus sensus populi, qui facile fastidit doctores, et levibus occasionibus oblatis, eos excutit, adversus haec fastidia Pau- lus studet excitare et confirmare benevolentia, quae non solum non admittit iniusta odia, sed etiam aliqua levia incommoda in doctoribus recte docentibus, et sine turpitudine viventibus placide tolerat, et condonat functioni et communi tran- quillitati. Haec officia pia erga ministros signifi- cantur unguento in pedes effuso. Maria, id est, Ecclesia auditrix ungit pedes, id est, fovet et tuetur ministros Evangelii, et ministerium ad studia doctrinae coelestis, ut Constantinus, Theo- dosius, et pauci alii pii gubernatores foverunt, et texerunt doctores, et studia doctrinae, id officium exemplo huius historiae Christus hac laudatione nobis commendat. Et ex hoc unguento suavis odor et fragrantia in totam domum diffunditur, id est, Evangelium latius propagatur, colligitur Ecclesia, crescit vera invocatio Dei, et aliae vir- tutes.

## 12:9
On the next day a great crowd, etc.

There are some pageants in the Gospel, such as the gathering of Angels, Shepherds, and Magi at the newborn Christ, likewise the wondrous revelation of divinity at the baptism of Christ and the testimonies of John, likewise the gathering for the resuscitation of Lazarus. Likewise the retinue of the people following Christ, and meeting him with branches of palms and olives, likewise the ascension of Christ into heaven. These pageants and all similar ones have one cause, that God willed there to exist certain and manifest testimonies, which would show that Christ had been exhibited as the Son. For although the deeds of Christ do not so strike the eyes of all, as the expeditions of Alexander or C. Caesar are seen by the eyes of all nations, and are celebrated by the voice and writings of all, yet God does not wish himself to be ignored, nor does he propose his revelations without great and certain testimonies; he wishes faith not to be a doubtful opinion, but to be kindled and confirmed by certain testimonies, therefore miracles were published, which would show the presence of an omnipotent nature, and many spectators and witnesses were added, as in the birth, baptism, and ascension of Christ. In these revelations let us always look with invocation, lest just as the minds of the Heathens wandered, doubting what or why they were invoking, or whether they would be heard, so also ours might wander and lose God; therefore, you should establish that he is truly God, the eternal Father, the creator of things, with his Son Jesus Christ, and the Spirit, who revealed himself by sending this Son, born of a virgin, crucified and resurrected, and whom a great multitude saw recall Lazarus from death, etc. Do not think that God is an empty name, nor that he revealed himself in vain, but that he revealed himself for this reason, to testify that he truly wishes to hear. With this confidence you should approach this revealed God, and you will experience that your prayer will not be in vain. First, therefore, in this narrative, or in the pageant of the entry into the city of Jerusalem, we shall remember this primary counsel of God, that he wishes there to exist testimonies that he has revealed himself.

Then the pageant itself is a most sweet image of the Church. There are four kinds of persons: Christ, the Apostles, the believing people, and the adversaries. These degrees are always to be considered in the Church; Christ the Son of God was sent so that he might become a victim for men, he gives the Gospel to his Church, and grants to believers the remission of sins, leads them back to the eternal Father, and gives the Holy Spirit and eternal life. Such a king he is; he does not come to divide the empires of the world, as the Jews dream of the kingdom of the Messiah for themselves, but he brings eternal things, justice, and eternal life; thus the Messiah is described in that very chapter of Zechariah, which is cited here: You also, by the blood of your testament, have sent forth the prisoners from the pit, in which there is no water, etc. That is, God gave a promise, which he calls a testament, and he wishes it to be sanctioned by the blood of the Messiah; by this blood of the Messiah poured out, he will lead the prisoners out of the pit, that is, having abolished death, he will restore eternal life. Finally, it is necessary that this primary person, Christ, be most recognized in this spectacle, and his benefits understood, which are often commemorated elsewhere.

After Christ, the Apostles should be considered, that is, the ministers of the Gospel; these lead to Christ the donkey and the colt, that is, the people of the law and the Gentiles, and they set Christ upon them, not themselves, that is, they want Christ to reign, they do not seek power and authority for themselves, nor do they invent a new doctrine, but they faithfully set forth the doctrine of Christ.

In the third place is the believing people; these perform a threefold duty: they sing praises to the coming Messiah, they carry branches of olive and palm, and they spread their garments. These duties the Church always ought to perform, and in some way does perform. The singing signifies the doctrine of the Gospel, invocation, confession, and thanksgiving. For this very assembly, sounding the voice of the Psalm, was professing in this song that this very teacher, who was being carried triumphantly into the city, was the Messiah. For it was customary to recite this Psalm in the synagogues, in the prayer by which the coming of the Messiah was sought. Moreover, the Psalm describes both the passion and the glory of the Messiah in these words: Hosanna, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel. The first part is a prayer to God that He may be present with the new kingdom, and having repressed the furies of the devil and the world, may help Christ, and may draw many from the world to the true knowledge of the Son, and to obedience to the Gospel and eternal life, may gather a great Church, and may impart the benefits of Christ to many. Therefore they say: Hosanna, that is, help this Messiah of yours and grant victory to him, and salvation to your Church.

In the remaining words is a profession of who this conqueror is, the King of Israel, namely the promised Messiah, blessed, that is, according to the promise given to Abraham. They know this one to be the blessed seed, pleasing to God, on account of which the Church will be blessed, that is, the curse will be taken away, the wrath of God appeased, sin and the punishments of sin, calamities and death will be removed, and this promised King comes in the name of the Lord, that is, by the command and power of God, who sent him, anointed him, and will help him, so that he may take away sin and death.

I have said these things briefly about the singing, so that we may remind ourselves what kind of worship this image requires of us. For first, as I said, it requires knowledge of doctrine, and preaching, invocation, confession, and thanksgiving.

Then the branches of olive and palm are signs of confession; formerly, those seeking peace from some leader would approach him carrying an olive branch, as in Livy, Book 10, Decade 3: The ship of the Carthaginians seeking peace came to Scipio, veiled with fillets and olive branches. This ceremony, therefore, also in this place signifies that this Messiah is the author of true peace with God, that through him and on account of him peace is given to us by God, our sins are forgiven, we are received by God, and wrath and eternal death are removed. The palm fronds, however, signified victories, and were carried in triumphs. Thus, praise is here attributed to Christ, that he is a victor. The devil bites the heel of Christ and the Church, and we are exercised by horrible miseries, but Christ conquers and represses the devil, and at length will utterly take away from him the power of ravaging, and will torment him with eternal punishments. And although he horribly attacks empires, the Church publicly and privately, stirs up dissensions, dissipations, scandals, and drives many into sins and huge miseries, yet in these Christ conquers, heals public and private wounds, and again raises up those who flee to him, just as he says: No one shall snatch them from my hands.

The third duty is to spread garments, that is, to contribute body and resources to the establishment and defense of the ministry; likewise, if there is need, to lose life and wealth rather than cast away the Gospel in confession, as it is written in Matthew 16: If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. Christ does not want his followers to have no resources; rather, just as it is necessary for many to live, and for there to be some polities and lodgings for the Church, so it is necessary for some to have patrimonies, houses, fields, and wealth; but just as he wants life, so he wants resources to be contributed to the preservation of the evangelical ministry, and he wants the confession of the Gospel to be preferred to these goods. Let the ravings of the Anabaptists, therefore, be exploded, who disturb the order of political life. and deny that Christians can retain property, even if no one snatches it away; but let us maintain a distinction, when it is permitted to retain it, when one must yield, and as long as God allows us to possess it, let us acknowledge his benefit, and for the polity, and for the lodging, let us give thanks.

Finally, there are in this triumphal procession adversaries condemning Christ, and forbidding him to be received and celebrated, as there always are the impious, who on account of their own gains and power defend errors and idols, and attempt to destroy the Gospel, but Christ chastises them, and confirms his own, and cites the sweetest consolation from Psalm 8: Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babes you have perfected praise,

God, he says, raises up the humble and the weak, so that they may sound the Gospel, even against the resistance of tyrants and the great governors of the world. A twofold consolation is proposed in this saying. We are warned not to despise the Gospel because we are moved by the weakness of the teachers, and indeed not to let our own weakness move us to abandon the ministry of the Gospel. Then help is promised, that God, he says, perfects praise; God helps those who teach, as it is said in Isaiah chapter 51: I have put my words in your mouth, and I have protected you in the shadow of my hand, that you may plant the heavens. We have noted these things briefly concerning the triumphal procession of Christ entering Jerusalem, so that students may recognize in that procession the image of the Church and its illustrious meanings.

Latin:

Postridie turba multa, etc.

Aliquae sunt in Evangelio pompae, ut con- ventus Angelorum, Pastorum, Magorum, recens nato Christo, item miranda revelatio divinitatis in baptismo Christi et testimonia Ioannis, item concursus ad resuscitationem Lazari. Item comi- tatus populi sequentis Christum, et ei occurren- tis cum frondibus palmarum et oleae, item ascen- sio Christi in coelum. Hae pompae et similes omnes habent unam causam, quod Deus voluit extare certa et manifesta testimonia, quae osten- derent Christum filium exhibitum esse. Etsi enim Christi facta non sic incurrunt in omnium oculos, ut Alexandri, aut C. Caesaris expeditiones omnium gentium oculis cernuntur, omnium voce et literis celebrantur, tamen Deus non vult ignorari sese, nec suas revelationes sine testimoniis magnis et certis proponit, vult fidem non esse dubiam opi- nionem, sed certis testimoniis accensam et confir- matam esse, ideo sunt edita miracula, quae osten- derent praesentiam naturae omnipotentis, sunt additi spectatores et testes multi, ut in nativitate, baptismo, ascensione Christi. In has patefactio- nes semper in invocatione intueamur, ne sicut Ethnicorum animi vagabantur dubitantes, quid, cur invocarent, an exaudirentur, ita et nostri vagentur, et amittant Deum, ergo illum statuas vere esse Deum, aeternum patrem, conditorem rerum, cum filio Iesu Christo, et Spiritu, qui se patefecit misso hoc filio, nato ex virgine, cruci- fixo et rsuscitato, et quem magna multitudo vidit revocare Lazarum ex morte etc. Non cogites Deum inane nomen esse, nec se frustra patefe- cisse, sed ideo se patefecisse, ut testaretur se vere velle exaudire. Hac fiducia accedas ad hunc pa- tefactum Deum, et experieris precationem tuam non fore irritam. Primum igitur in hac narra- tione, seu in pompa ingressus in urbem Ierosoly- mam, hoc praecipuum consilium Dei memineri- mus, quod vult extare testimonia, quod se pate- fecerit.

Deinde ipsa pompa imago est dulcissima Ec- clesiae. Personarum genera quatuor sunt, Chri- stus, Apostoli, populus credens, et adversarii. Hi gradus semper in Ecclesia considerandi sunt, Christus filius Dei missus est, ut fieret victima pro hominibus, dat Evangelium suae Ecclesiae, et credentibus donat remissionem peccatorum, re- ducit eos ad aeternum patrem, et dat Spiritum sanctum et vitam aeternam. Talis rex est, non venit ut imperia mundi partiatur, ut Iudaei sibi Messiae regnum somniant, sed res aeternas, iu- sticiam et vitam aeternam affert, sic describitur Messias in illo ipso cap. Zachariae, quod hic ci- tatur: Tu quoque in sanguine testamenti tui emi- sisti vinctos de lacu, in quo non est aqua, etc. Id est, Deus promissionem dedit, quam vocat testamentum, et id vult sanguine Messiae sanciri, hoc sanguine Messiae fuso educet vinctos e lacu, id est, abolita morte restituet vitam aeternam. Denique hanc praecipuam personam Christum in hoc spectaculo necesse est maxime agnosci, et eius beneficia intelligi, quae saepe alibi commemo- rantur.

Post Christum Apostoli considerentur, id est, ministri Evangelii, hi ad Christum adducunt asinam et pullum, id est, populum legis et gen- tes, et imponunt Christum, non sese, id est, vo- lunt Christum regnare, non quaerunt sibi impe- rium et potentiam, nec fingunt novam doctrinam, sed Christi doctrinam fideliter proponunt.

Tertio loco est populus credens, hi triplex officium praestant, canunt laudes venienti Mes- siae, gestant frondes oleae et palmarum, et sub- sternunt vestes. Haec officia semper et debet praestare, et utcunque praestat Ecclesia. Cantus significat doctrinam Evangelii, invocationem, confessionem et gratiarum actionem. Nam et hic ipse coetus sonans vocem Psalmi, profitebatur hoc carmine, hunc ipsum doctorem, qui invehe- batur triumphans in urbem, esse Messiam. Nam usitatum erat hunc Psalmum recitare in synago- gis, in precatione, qua petebatur adventus Mes- siae. Describit autem Psalmus et passionem, et gloriam Messiae, in his verbis: Ozianna, bene- dictus qui venit in nomine domini rex Israël. Pri- ma pars est precatio ad Deum, ut regno novo ad- sit, et repressis diaboli et mundi furoribus, Chri- stum adiuvet, et multos ex mundo ad veram agni- tionem filii, et obedientiam Evangelii et vitam aeternam pertrahat, colligat magnam Ecclesiam, et multis impertiat beneficia Christi. Ideo dicunt: Hozianna, id est, adiuva hunc tuum Messiam et victoriam ipsi, et Ecclesiae tuae salutem im- pertias.

In reliquis verbis est professio, quis sit hic triumphator, rex Israël, videlicet Messias pro- missus, benedictus, scilicet iuxta promissionem datam Abrahae. Hunc sciunt esse semen bene- dictum, Deo placens, propter quod benedicetur Ecclesiae, id est, auferetur maledictio placata ira Dei, tollentur peccatum, et poenae peccati, ca- lamitates et mors, et hic promissus rex venit in nomine domini, id est, mandato et potentia Dei, qui eum misit, unxit, iuvabit, ut tollat peccatum et mortem.

Haec breviter de cantu dixi, ut nos admo- neamus quales cultus a nobis haec imago postulet. Primum enim, ut dixi, postulat doctrinae cogni- tionem, et praedicationem, invocationem, con- fessionem, et gratiarum actionem.

Deinde rami oleae et palmarum signa sunt confessionis, olim petentes a duce aliquo pacem, ad eum accedebant gestantes oleae ramum, ut apud Livium lib. 10. Dec. 3.: Navis Carthaginem- sium petentium pacem venit ad Scipionem, velata infulis et ramis oleae. Haec igitur ceremonia et hoc loco significat hunc Messiam esse autorem verae pacis cum Deo, per eum et propter eum dari nobis pacem a Deo, remitti nobis peccata, et nos recipi a Deo, et tolli iram et mortem aeternam. Frondes vero palmarum significabant victorias, et in triumphis gestabantur. Ita hic tribuitur Christo laus, quod sit victor. Mordet calcaneum Christi et Ecclesiae diabolus, et exercemur horribilibus aerumnis, sed vincit Christus et reprimit diabolum, et tandem ei prorsus adimit potestatem grassandi, et excruciabit eum aeternis poenis. Et quanquam imperia horribiliter oppugnat, Ecclesiam publice et privatim, excitat dissidia, dissipationes, scandala, et multos impellit in peccata et aerumnas ingentes, tamen in his vincit Christus, sanat publica et privata vulnera, rursus erigit confugientes ad ipsum, sicut dicit: Nemo rapiet eas ex manibus meis.

Tertium officium est substernere vestes, id est, corpus et facultates conferre ad ministerii constitutionem et defensionem, item si sit opus, potius amittere vitam et opes, quam abiicere Evangelium in confessione, sicut scriptum est Matth. 16.: Si quis vult post me venire, abneget semetipsum, et tollat crucem suam, et sequatur me. Non vult Christus nullas esse facultates suorum, imo ut necesse est multos vivere, et esse politias aliquas et hospitia Ecclesiae: ita necesse est aliquos habere patrimonia, domos, agros, opes, sed ut vitam, ita et facultates vult conferri ad evangelici ministerii conservationem, et vult confessionem Evangelii anteferri his bonis. Explodantur ergo Anabaptistarum deliramenta, qui vitae politicae ordinem conturbant. et negant Christianos posse retinere proprium, etiamsi nemo eripiat, sed discrimen teneamus, quando liceat retinere, quando cedendum sit, et donec Deus possidere nos sinit, agnoscamus eius beneficium, et pro politia, ac pro hospitio gratias agamus.

Postremo sunt in hac triumphali pompa adversarii damnantes Christum, et prohibentes excipi, et celebrari eum, ut semper sunt impii, qui propter suos quaestus et potentiam defendunt errores et idola, et conantur delere Evangelium, sed Christus hos castigat, et confirmat suos, et citat consolationem dulcissimam ex Psal. 8.: Ex ore infantium et lactentium perfecisti laudem,

Excitat, inquit, Deus humiles et imbecilles, ut sonent Evangelium, etiam repugnantibus tyran- nis et magnis gubernatoribus mundi. Duplex consolatio proponitur in hoc dicto. Monemur, ne moti imbecillitate docentium contemnamus Evangelium, imo ne nos nostra imbecillitas mo- veat, ut deseramus ministerium Evangelii. Deinde auxilium promittitur, Deum, ait, perficere lau- dem, adiuvat Deus docentes, ut Esaiae cap. 51. dicitur: Posui verba mea in ore tuo, et umbra manus meae protexi te, ut plantes coelos. Haec breviter de pompa triumphali Christi ingredientis Ierosolymam annotavimus, ut studiosi agnoscant in illa pompa Ecclesiae imaginem et illustres significationes.

## 12:20
Now there were certain Greeks.

Brief and abrupt narratives are recounted; Christ begins a sermon which censures the desire for glory and testifies that the Church in this life is subject to the cross. In this very sermon, a sudden consternation of spirit befalls him, in which, crying out, he calls upon the Father, and a manifest voice from heaven is heard, which promises consolation; then new sentences follow. But let us speak in order and briefly about each one.

The occasion for the first sermon in this place is that the Apostles considered it honorable for Christ that Gentiles were coming to see him, and they dreamed of that golden kingdom now to be established by the Messiah, in which they thought Christ and his friends would be in great honor among the nations. However, nothing is sweeter to man than glory, especially when joined with tranquility, or the hope of a tranquil and glorious state; we all desire and seek this. But Christ condemns this error of the Apostles and others dreaming of such a kingdom in the Church, and this vicious desire, saying: Unless a grain of wheat falling into the ground dies, it remains alone. He who loves his soul will lose it.

There will indeed be a time when the Son of Man will be adorned with glory, and in his own time the whole Church is to have glory, but it is also necessary that I be crucified first, and that the whole Church first be subject to the cross and to immense miseries in this life. This is briefly the sum of the sermon and the principal proposition. And concerning Christ, the cause is known why it was necessary for him to suffer. For since God did not wish the whole human race to perish, and yet the justice of God demanded compensation and punishment for our sins, the Son became the intercessor and drew the punishment and the horrible wrath of God upon himself, so that the Father might be appeased for us; he suffered, therefore, not for his own sake, but for our sake, as John says: This is the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, and in Isaiah 53 the same sentiment is handed down at length. But why does the Church suffer? Not that it merits reconciliation by its own afflictions, but there are many other causes; the truth is the chief one: since sin clings to us, God wishes this mass of sin to be destroyed, so that we may be clothed with a new nature. Therefore death remains, and so that we may recognize the wrath of God against sin, if a new light is kindled in us once wicked inclinations are repressed, and it grows; therefore the Church is exercised more than other men, and other causes concur, recited in other places. Let us therefore put aside those sweet imaginations that our life will be more peaceful and tranquil because we are members of the Church of God. Rather, let us know that we carry sin around with us, and for that reason are plunged into immense miseries, so that we may learn to recognize the wrath of God against sin, nor does the light of the Holy Spirit grow in us without the cross, just as it is said in Psalm 38: Because of iniquity you correct man, and 1 Corinthians 4: Our outer man is being corrupted, so that the inner may be renewed day by day. Likewise Isaiah 28: Whom shall he teach knowledge? those weaned from the milk, and then: Vexation alone gives understanding. Likewise: His God will chastise him in judgment, that he may teach him, and Jeremiah 31: You have chastised me, O Lord, and I have been instructed. Isaiah 66: To whom shall I look, except to the afflicted and contrite in spirit, and him who trembles at my words. Finally, everywhere testimonies offer themselves in the Prophets and Apostles, and the histories of all the saints from the beginning are themselves illustrious sermons: Adam, Eve, Abel, Abraham, Jacob, Jeremiah, the Baptist, Christ, the Apostles, the Martyrs. Here someone might say, why then were those promises handed down: Blessed is the man who fears the Lord, wealth and riches are in his house, and the like? I answer: Both statements are true, that the Church is subject to the cross, and yet that it is helped by God, and in this the miseries of the pious differ from the miseries of the impious. David, Jeremiah, Daniel, Paul, and the like, know that even when they are plunged into miseries, they are nevertheless a care to God, and will have help and mitigation, and for as long as God wills that it serves in its course, miraculously raises up and frees the afflicted, as it is said in 2 Corinthians 4: We carry this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellence of the power may be of God, and not of us; we are troubled, but we do not lose heart; we are struck down, but we do not perish. But when great storms rush upon which human reason seeks aid, they are utterly overwhelmed by despair, and perish.

The promises of bodily deliverances are therefore profitable, because since the Church of God must remain in this life, the body is preserved in wondrous ways, just as the people were preserved in the desert, and many wondrous deliverances of individuals occur for the sake of the ministries, whether of the Church, or of the state, or of the household: as how often are David and Jeremiah miraculously snatched from death? Indeed, these present deliverances are an image of the complete future deliverance, and they admonish us of it, and nourish and confirm the faith by which we believe that God is present with us and helps us, and by which we await the future deliverance, as the example of Psalm 34 is cited: Approach him, and be enlightened; this poor man cried out, and the Lord heard him, etc. I have briefly reviewed these things here concerning the cross and the promises, for the sake of admonishing the reader, so that he might consider the sum of this sermon. Otherwise, this whole topic is usually treated more prolixly elsewhere.

That must be added in passing concerning the Greeks, who had come for the sake of worshiping: what kind of men does he understand? It is very profitable to know what kinds of men were then the Church of God. For not only the Israelites, that is, those born from the seed of Abraham, were then the Church of God, but also many Gentiles; there were therefore three kinds: Israelites, that is, those born from the seed of Abraham; these had to be circumcised and observe the Mosaic ceremonies. The second kind were Proselytes, who, converted from the nations, also wished to be circumcised and observe the Mosaic ceremonies. The third kind was undoubtedly great, of which he speaks here, and in the Acts of the Apostles they are called religious men, namely Gentiles, who without circumcision and the observation of ceremonies had learned of the promise of salvation given on account of the coming seed, by whom all nations were to be blessed, and by this faith they called upon the true God, who had revealed himself to the people of Israel and had handed down his word to them. Such were Naaman the Syrian, Nebuchadnezzar and his son, likewise Darius, Cyrus, Cornelius in the Acts of the Apostles, the Ethiopian eunuch, and many such Gentiles were members of the true Church, and therefore the Israelites were dispersed among the nations, so that many Gentiles might be called to the knowledge of the true God.

Latin:

Erant autem quidam Graeci.

Breves narrationes et abruptae recensentur, Christus concionem incoat, quae taxat cupidita- tem gloriae, et testatur Ecclesiam in hac vita sub- iectam esse cruci. In hac ipsa concione accidit ei subita consternatio animi, in qua exclamans in- vocat patrem, et exauditur manifesta vox de coelo, quae consolationem promittit, deinde sequuntur novae sententiae. Sed dicamus ordine ac brevi- ter de singulis.

Occasio primae concionis hoc loco est, quod Apostoli Christo honorificum esse duxerunt, ve- nire Ethnicos ad eum videndum, et somniarunt iam illud aureum regnum a Messia constituen- dum, in quo cogitabant Christum et eius amicos apud gentes in magno honore futuros esse. Ni- hil autem homini dulcius est gloria, praesertim cum tranquillitate coniuncta, seu spe tranquilli et gloriosi status, hunc omnes appetimus et quae- rimus. Sed Christus hunc errorem Apostolorum et aliorum somniantium tale regnum in Ecclesia, et hanc vitiosam cupiditatem damnat, inquiens: Nisi granum frumenti cadens in terram mortuum fuerit, ipsum solum manet. Qui amat animam suam, perdet eam.

Erit quidem cum filius hominis ornabitur gloria, et suo tempore universa Ecclesia gloriam habitura est, sed et me prius crucifigi oportet, et universam Ecclesiam prius in hac vita oportet subiectam esse cruci, et ingentibus aerumnis. Haec breviter summa est concionis et principalis propositio. Ac de Christo nota est causa, quare ipsum oportuit pati. Nam cum nollet Deus to- tum genus humanum perire, et tamen iusticia Dei compensationem, et poenam pro peccatis nostris postularet, Filius factus est deprecator, et poenam ac horrendam iram Dei in sese derivavit, ut no- bis pater placaretur, passus est igitur non propter sese, sed propter nos, ut Ioannes inquit: Hic est agnus Dei, qui tollit peccata mundi, et Esa. 53. eadem sententia prolixe tradita est. Sed cur Ecclesia patitur? Non ut propriis afflictionibus mereatur reconciliationem, sed aliae multae sunt causae, verum praecipua est, cum peccatum haereat in nobis, vult Deus hanc mas- sam peccati destrui, ut nova natura vestiamur. Ideo manet mors, et ut agnoscamus iram Dei ad- versus peccatum, si repressis pravis inclinationi- bus accendatur in nobis nova lux, et crescat, ideo magis exercetur Ecclesia, quam caeteri homines, et concurrunt aliae causae, recitatae aliis locis. Deponamus igitur illas suaves imaginationes, ma- gis placidam et tranquillam vitam nostram fore, quia sumus membra Ecclesiae Dei. Imo sciamus nos circumferre peccatum, et propterea mergi in aerumnas ingentes, ut discamus agnoscere iram Dei adversus peccatum, nec crescere lucem Spiri- tus sancti in nobis sine cruce, sicut Psalm. 38. di- citur: Propter iniquitatem corripis hominem, et 1. Corinth. 4.: Exterior noster homo corrumpi- tur, ut interior renovetur de die in diem. Item Esaiae 28.: Quem docebit scientiam? ablactatos a lacte, et deinde: Sola vexatio dat intellectum. Item: Castigabit eum Deus suus in iudicio, ut eum doceat, et Ieremiae 31.: Castigasti me do- mine, et eruditus sum. Esaiae 66.: Ad quem respiciam, nisi ad afflictum et contritum spiritu, et trementem sermones meos. Denique ubique se offerunt testimonia in Prophetis et Apostolis, et sunt illustres conciones ipsae historiae omnium sanctorum ab initio, Adae, Evae, Abel, Abra- hae, Iacob, Ieremiae, Baptistae, Christi, Apo- stolorum, Martyrum. Hic dicat aliquis, cur igitur traditae sunt promissiones illae: Beatus vir, qui timet domi- num, opes et divitiae domi eius, et similes? Re- spondeo: Utraque sententia vera est, et subiectam esse Ecclesiam cruci, et tamen eam iuvari a Deo, et hoc differunt piorum aerumnae ab impiorum aerumnis. David, Ieremias, Daniel, Paulus, et similes, sciunt se etiam cum merguntur in ae- rumnas, tamen Deo curae esse, et habituros auxi- lium et mitigationem, et tantisper dum vult Deus que in suo curriculo servire, mirabiliter erigit et liberat afflictos, ut 2. Corinth. 4. dicitur: Cir- cumferimus hunc thesaurum in vasis testaceis, ut excellentia virtutis sit Dei, et non ex nobis, an- gimur, sed non deficimus animo, quassamur, sed non perimus. At cum irruunt magnae pro- cellae in Saulem, Pompeium, Catonem, Anto- nium, et similes, destituti iis rebus, a quibus ratio humana opem petit, prorsus opprimuntur desperatione, et pereunt.

Prosunt igitur promissiones liberationum corporalium, quia cum in hac vita Ecclesiam Dei manere oporteat, servatur corpus mirandis mo- dis, ut populus in deserto servabatur, et multae singulorum mirandae liberationes fiunt propter ministeria, vel Ecclesiae, vel politiae, vel oeco- nomiae: ut quoties mirabiliter eripiuntur morti, David et Ieremias? Imo hae praesentes liberatio- nes sunt imago integrae liberationis futurae, et de ea nos admonent, et alunt ac confirmant fidem, qua credimus Deum nobis adesse, et opi- tulari, et qua expectamus futuram liberationem, ut allegatur exemplum Psal. 23.: Accedite ad eum, et illuminamini, iste pauper clamavit, et dominus exaudivit eum, etc. Haec de cruce, et promissionibus hic breviter recensui, admonendi lectoris causa, ut summam huius concionis con- sideret. Caeterum alibi prolixius totus hic locus tractari solet.

Illud obiter addendum est de Graecis, qui venerant adorandi causa, quale genus hominum intelligit? Valde prodest scire quae genera homi- num tunc fuerint Ecclesia Dei. Non enim soli Israëlitae, id est, nati ex semine Abrahae, fue- runt tunc Ecclesia Dei, sed etiam multi Ethnici, erant igitur genera tria: Israëlitae, id est, nati ex semine Abrahae, hos oportuit esse circumci- sos, et observare ceremonias Mosaicas. Secun- dum genus erant Proselyti, qui ex gentibus con- versi, etiam voluerunt circumcidi, et observare ceremonias Mosaicas. Tertium genus fuit haud dubie magnum, de quo hic loquitur, et in Actis Apostolorum vocantur viri religiosi, videlicet Ethnici, qui sine circumcisione et observatione ceremoniarum didicerant promissionem salutis datam propter venturum semen, quo benedicen- dae erant omnes gentes, et hac fide invocabant Deum verum, qui se populo Israël patefecerat, et verbum suum eis tradiderat. Tales fuerunt Naaman, Syrus, Nabuchodonosor, et eius filius, item Darius, Cyrus, Cornelius in Actis Aposto- lorum, Aethiops, Eunuchus, et multi tales Eth- nici fuerunt Ecclesiae verae membra, ideoque dispersi sunt inter gentes Israëlitae, ut multi Eth- nici ad ignitionem veri Dei vocarentur.

## 12:25
He who hates his soul.

Let us consider both, the precept and the promise. The precept is, as a command of God, that we prefer the confession of true doctrine to our life, and in this precept we are warned that there will be many and great enemies of the Gospel. Wherefore it will be a great danger to carry about the preaching of the Gospel, for what he says: He who loves his soul will lose it, is to be understood as he says elsewhere: He who loves father or mother more than me, etc. Thus here he condemns one loving his own soul, that is, his life, more than God, or the command of God. For order must be kept; life must be governed by the command of God, which first commands to obey God, and afterwards to love creatures on account of God, so that although he commands to love.

Then let us remember this sweetest promise, which preaches about the outcome. If anyone serves me, he will be honored by the Father. It is a brief saying, and one to be thought upon often. The teachers and disciples of the Gospel are despised and scorned by the powerful, but let them console themselves with this voice, that Christ here promises that it will come to pass that they will be adorned with glory by the Father; let us sustain ourselves with the same consolation in every kind of danger. Great discords have followed the exposing of errors, and the outcomes for those who teach rightly seem sad, often even deformed by the scandals of princes and the people, but let them know that the outcomes will be salutary. For the Father will adorn his ministers with glory, and although some may be killed, yet God will defend their cause, and at length in eternal life will reveal the glory of the whole Church, with the enemies condemned and cast into eternal torments. I have said these things briefly concerning these precepts and promises only for the sake of admonishing the reader, so that he might consider more attentively these brief sayings, which indeed are sufficiently clear.

Latin:

Qui odit animam suam.

Utrunque consideremus, praeceptum et pro- missionem. Praeceptum est, ut mandatum Dei, hoc est, confessionem verae doctrinae antefera- mus vitae nostrae, et in hoc praecepto monemur, multos et magnos fore hostes Evangelii. Quare magnum erit periculum, circumferre Evangelii praedicationem, nam quod ait: Qui amat ani- mam suam, perdet eam, intelligatur, ut alibi dicit: Qui diligit patrem aut matrem plus quam me, etc. Ita hic damnat amantem animam pro- priam, id est, vitam, plus quam Deum, seu mandatum Dei. Ordo enim servandus est, man- dato Dei regenda est vita, quod primum iubet Deo obedire, et postea propter Deum creaturas diligere, ita ut quamquam diligere praecipit.

Deinde hanc dulcissimam promissionem me- minerimus, quae concionatur de exitu. Si quis mihi ministrabit, honore ornabitur a patre. Bre- ve dictum est, et saepe cogitandum. Doctores et discipuli Evangelii sunt despecti, ac spreti a po- tentibus, sed se hac voce consolentur, quod Chri- stus hic promittit futurum esse, ut ornentur glo- ria a patre, eadem consolatione nos sustentemus in omni genere periculorum. Magnae discordiae secutae sunt taxatis erroribus, et videntur futuri exitus tristes recte docentium, saepe etiam scan- dalis principum, et populi deformantur, sed sciant exitus fore salutares. Pater enim ornabit gloria ministros suos, et quamvis aliqui interfi- ciantur, tamen Deus illorum causam defendet, et tandem in aeterna vita universae Ecclesiae glo- riam patefaciet, damnatis et abiectis hostibus in aeternos cruciatus. Haec breviter de his prae- ceptis et promissionibus tantum admonendi lecto- ris causa dixi, ut haec brevia dicta, quae quidem satis perspicua sunt, attentius consideret.

## 12:27
And now my soul is troubled.

His sermon is interrupted by such great consternation of soul that he had to be confirmed by the clear voice of the Father from heaven. But it is usually asked, since Christ always saw the Father, and was always blessed, How can consternation exist with that joy of soul, or sadness, such as is described elsewhere, when he says: My soul is sorrowful even unto death. Although no one can sufficiently explain the immense movements in Christ, both of joy and of sadness, yet it is necessary for the Church to think something about them, because it tastes both in some way, and both are often described in the Psalms, as the dismayed mind says: My God, why have you forsaken me? Likewise: There is no salvation for him in his God, and similar sayings are met with everywhere; but in order to embrace this whole discussion, we shall distribute it into several articles.

First: The Son of God assumed human nature, true, whole, uncorrupted, having all the powers and appetites proper to nature, likewise not vicious, but passible without sin, and mortal, which infirmities he willingly assumed for our sake, so that he could become a victim; thus it is said in Heb. 4: We do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our infirmities, but one who has been tempted in all things according to the likeness without sin. Although therefore Christ saw the Father, and was blessed, yet his human nature had its appetites, but ordered ones. And these are often recounted: he hungers, he thirsts, he rejoices, he is angry, he is affected by mercy, he grieves, he weeps, he is conflicted with immense sadness. These affections in Christ were not feigned, but were true and immense movements, and are illustrious testimonies, showing that human nature truly exists in Christ.

The second article, that the degrees of sorrows and consternations in Christ may be considered in some way, the powers may be distinguished, and what is proper to each may be established, so also the causes of the sorrows and consternations, and what kind of movements these were, may be stated in some part. The lowest degree is that of natural appetites, such as hunger and thirst, and of pain, which accompanies touch, such as the pain which follows the laceration of the body or of the nerves. That these were in Christ, and were not vicious, is certain, because they are things thus created by God. It is the nature of nerves, when they are lacerated, to cause torture, nor is this torture a rebellion against the mind, because it is a thing thus created; wherefore it can easily be understood not to be vicious. The second degree is that of the affections, which arise in the heart from the fear of that laceration and death, and, if I may so say, it is the trepidation of the heart fleeing death and laceration, and the heart in some part carries the will with it, but the heart and the will struggle, so that they may submit themselves to the will of God, as in other brave men, in Daniel or Jeremiah, there is a fear of death in the heart, and this carries the will with it, although the will and the heart are confirmed by the Holy Spirit, so that they overcome the fear, and calmly approach death, because the love of God inflames them, so that they wish to obey him.

Here it is asked, since the heart and the will in some part dissent from the judgment of the mind, whether this dissension in Christ, as in other men, is vicious. I answer: Just as pain arising from laceration is truly natural, and is not vicious: so a certain fear of that laceration is natural. Christ fears and recoils, but in an ordered way, not as we do, in an unordered way. For nature, when burdened above its strength, groans in an ordered way, nor is it broken without some sense of pain, and yet in this very groaning the mind retains its judgment, that God must be obeyed: and the will, loving God, overcomes its own trepidation and that of the heart, and wills to obey God, and with this will it calmly sustains death. This trepidation is therefore not vicious, because it is natural and ordered, not as in us, unordered, fleeing with softness and love of pleasures, and with doubts about God, or with raging against God.

But the third degree is that of the sorrows, or consternations, which are far above those natural sorrows, and natural causes, namely the sense of the wrath of God against sin. Christ acknowledges that God is horribly angry at the human race because of sin, and that this wrath is now being poured out upon himself, as a victim; he grieves that God has been offended by the human race, and he struggles with the temptation concerning rejection. This highest degree is a horrendous and ineffable consternation of the will, which consumes the powers of the whole nature like a fire, as Moses says: God is a consuming fire. And Hezekiah: Like a lion he crushed all my bones. Concerning this, the question is more difficult. But the same must be answered concerning it, as above, although this consternation is far greater in Christ than in David, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Hezekiah, and the like. For Christ bore the wrath and judgment of God for us. Nevertheless, it is dissimilar in Christ and in the others. For in all others, along with the flight, there exists a raging against the judgment of God, and in those who do not struggle by fleeing to the victory of Christ, namely in the damned, horrendous blasphemies follow. But Christ bears the terrors without indignation against the Father; therefore this trepidation is without sin, and is not vicious.

From this third degree I believe this sudden consternation also arose, which is mentioned in this chapter 12 of John, in which, since Christ was confirmed by a divine voice, there is no doubt that there was a huge terror. Nor have I recited these things for the sake of curiosity, but so that, thinking about the passion of Christ, we may not only consider the lacerations of the body, but may know that there were also huge and ineffable sorrows in his soul, and at the same time learn that the wrath of God against the sins of the human race is a great thing, and that the humility in the son of God is to be admired, who so cast himself down that he derived upon himself the wrath of God, as if he himself had been polluted by our filth. What prayer of angels or men can explain how great this humility and self-abasement was? I wish that we might also think to some extent about the love of Christ towards us, since he so abased himself for our sake, it must be an immense love. Looking upon him, let us flee to him, let us seek and expect help and salvation, and let us also declare our gratitude by our obedience. All these things must be thought about as often as the sufferings of Christ are spoken of.

I said above that two things are asked about the passion of Christ. First, since there was some trepidation, whether it was sinful. The second, how the joy proper to the blessed and such great consternation could exist in him at the same time. Regarding the former, it has already been said: although there were trepidations in Christ, yet they were not sinful. Because they were not like our disordered ones, in which the will rages against God, but they were the groans of a nature burdened beyond its strength, while the will nevertheless retained obedience without indignation against God.

Regarding the other question, the answers are long and various. But we answer briefly: times must be distinguished regarding Christ. One thing is the type of the passion and of this admirable obedience and abasement, or humility of Christ, another is the time outside the passion. For because it was decreed by the admirable counsel of God that the son should become a victim, it was necessary that there be some time for the slaughter of the victim. Although therefore Christ was always blessed, yet at that time which was destined for the passion, his blessedness did not shine as it did outside the passion, just as is said about the time, Psalm 8: You have diminished him a little from God. What that diminishing or desertion is, Isaiah expressed, saying: The Lord willed to crush him in infirmity. He says that it was the will and decree of God that he should be overwhelmed by such great wrath from God himself, so that he might be a λύτρον for our sins, because the justice of God demanded some compensation. For every law obliges either to obedience or to punishment. And it is not a small thing to be crushed by God. It is one thing to have the body lacerated by iron or by beasts. It is another, and a far greater thing, to be struck by God and to feel the wrath of God, that is, to struggle with the temptation of abasement. At such a time, the sight which produced blessedness, life, and joy was not clearly perceived. Irenaeus also said this learnedly: that Christ suffered while the Word was at rest, so that he could be crucified and die, that is, the Word was not then exercising its power. Thus, for a little while, Christ was deserted by God in his showing of power and blessedness, just as he himself cries out: My God, why have you forsaken me? He speaks of time, and Psalm 110, He shall drink of the torrent in the way, limits the time with this word, in the way. Then follows the revelation of glory, therefore he shall lift up his head. Thus Christ speaks of time, praying that he be adorned again with that glory which he had before the foundation of the world, John 17.

This answer is plainer than others which are recited by the Sententiaries, which whoever seeks, let him read in them. Let us think piously and reverently about these great and arcane matters, and having considered in some way the magnitude of the sufferings of Christ, let us acknowledge that God is truly and horribly angry at sins, that there is a huge force of love towards us in the son, who underwent punishment for us, and let us excite fear and faith with ardent thoughts.

Let this suffice to have said about the consternation in this place: there follows a manifest consolation, which was not only a confirmation of the terrified Christ, but also a testimony before the people that this Jesus was sent by God. For the divine voice says clearly: And I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again, as if to say: I am a witness that you were sent by me, the eternal Father, and I declared that because I raised the dead with you, and did other wonderful things, and afterwards I will again propose testimonies in your resurrection.

Latin:

Et nunc anima mea turbata est.

Interrumpitur eius concio tanta consterna- tione animi, ut fuerit clara voce patris de coelo confirmandus. Quaeri autem solet, cum Christus semper viderit patrem, et semper fuerit beatus, quomodo potest cum illa animi laetitia existere consternatio, aut moestitia, qualis alibi descri- bitur, cum ait: Tristis est anima mea usque ad mortem.
