Etsi autem ingentes motus in Christo tum laetitiae, tum tristitiae nemo potest satis ex- plicare, tamen Ecclesiam aliquid de eis cogitare necesse est, quia aliquo modo utrosque degustat, et in Psalmis saepe describuntur utrique, ut con- sternata mens dicit: Deus meus, quare dereliqui- sti me? Item: Non est salus ei in Deo suo, et similia dicta passim obvia sunt, ut autem hanc totam disputationem complectamur, distribuemus eam in aliquot articulos.

Primus: Assumpsit filius Dei naturam huma- nam, veram, integram, incorruptam, habentem omnes vires et appetitiones naturae proprias, item non vitiosam, sed passibilem sine peccato, et mortalem, quas infirmitates volens assumpsit pro- pter nos, ut posset fieri victima, sic ad Heb. 4. dicitur: Non habemus pontificem, qui non pos- sit compati infirmitatibus nostris, sed tentatum per omnia secundum similitudinem sine peccato. Etsi igitur Christus videbat patrem, et erat bea- tus, tamen humana natura habuit suas appetitio- nes, sed ordinatas. Et hae saepe recitantur, esu- rit, sitit, laetatur, irascitur, misericordia affici- tur, dolet, lacrymat, conflictatur ingenti moe- sticia. Hi affectus in Christo non fuerunt simu- lati, sed veri et ingentes motus, et sunt illustria testimonia, ostendentia in Christo vere esse hu- manam naturam.

Secundus articulus, ut gradus dolorum et consternationum in Christo aliquo modo conside- rentur, potentiae discernantur, et quid cuique proprium sit, constituatur, ita et causas dolorum et consternationum, et quales fuerint hi motus, aliqua ex parte dicatur. Infimus gradus est ap- petitionum naturalium, ut famis et sitis, et dolo- ris, qui tactum comitatur, ut dolor, qui lacera- tionem corporis seu nervorum sequitur. Haec fuisse in Christo, et non esse vitiosa constat, quia sunt res sic conditae a Deo. Natura nervorum est, cum lacerantur, cruciatum efficere, neque hic cruciatus est rebellio contra mentem, quia est res sic creata, quare facile intelligi potest non esse vitiosam. Secundus gradus est affectuum, qui in corde ex metu illius lacerationis et mortis oriuntur, et ut ita dicam, trepidatio est cordis fugientis mortem, et lacerationem, et cor rapit aliqua ex parte secum voluntatem, sed eluctantur cor et voluntas, ut se subiiciant voluntati Dei, ut in caeteris viris fortibus, in Daniele aut Ieremia est metus mortis in corde, et hic rapit secum voluntatem, etsi Spiritu sancto confirmantur voluntas et cor, ut superent metum, et placide adeant mortem, quia dilectio Dei accendit eos, ut obedire ei velint.

Hic quaeritur, cum cor et voluntas aliqua ex parte dissideant a iudicio mentis, an hoc dissidium in Christo, ut in caeteris hominibus sit vitiosum. Respondeo: Sicut dolor ex laceratione ortus, vere naturalis est, et non est vitiosus: ita metus quidam illius lacerationis est naturalis. Metuit et refugit Christus, sed ordinate, non ut nos, inordinate. Nam ordinate natura supra vires onerata gemit, nec frangitur sine aliquo sensu doloris, et tamen in hoc ipso gemitu mens retinet suum iudicium, quod Deo sit obediendum: et voluntas Deum diligens vincit trepidationem suam et cordis, et vult Deo obedire, et hac voluntate placide sustinet mortem. Non est igitur vitiosa haec trepidatio, quia est naturalis et ordinata, non ut in nobis, inordinata, fugiens mollitie et amore voluptatum, et cum dubitationibus de Deo, aut fremitu adversus Deum.

Sed tertius gradus est dolorum, seu consternationum, quae sunt longe supra naturales illos dolores, et causas naturales, videlicet sensus irae Dei adversus peccatum. Agnoscit Christus Deum horribiliter irasci generi humano propter peccatum, et hanc iram effundi nunc in se, tanquam victimam, dolet Deum offensum esse a genere humano, et luctatur cum tentatione de abiectione. Hic summus gradus est horrenda et inenarrabilis consternatio voluntatis, quae totius naturae vires velut incendium absumit, ut dicit Moses: Deus ignis consumens est. Et Ezechias: Sicut leo contrivit omnia ossa mea. De hac difficilior est quaestio. Sed idem de ea respondendum est, ut supra, etsi longe maior est haec consternatio in Christo, quam in Davide, Esaia, Ieremia, Ezechia, et similibus. Nam Christus pro nobis tulit iram et iudicium Dei. Tamen dissimilis est in Christo, et in caeteris. Nam in omnibus aliis cum fuga existit fremitus adversus iudicium Dei, et in his, qui non eluctantur confugientes ad victoriam Christi, videlicet in damnatis, sequuntur horrendae blasphemiae. At Christus fert terrores sine indignatione adversus patrem, ideo haec trepidatio est sine peccato, et non est vitiosa.

Ex hoc tertio gradu existimo fuisse et hanc subitam consternationem, cuius fit mentio in hoc cap. 12. Ioannis, in qua cum divina voce confir- matus sit Christus, non dubium est ingentem ter- rorem fuisse. Nec curiositatis causa haec recitavi, sed ut cogitantes de Christi passione, non tantum corporis lacerationes consideremus, sed sciamus in anima etiam ingentes et inenarrabiles moesti- cias fuisse, et simul discamus magnum quiddam esse iram Dei adversus peccata humani generis, et mirandam esse in filio Dei humilitatem, qui se sic abiecit, ut in sese derivarit iram Dei, quasi ipse pollutus fuisset nostris sordibus. Quae ora- tio angelorum aut hominum explicare potest, quanta fuerit haec humilitas et abiectio sui? Uti- nam etiam ex aliqua parte cogitemus de amore Christi erga nos, cum se adeo abiecerit propter nos, necesse est immensum amorem esse. Hunc intuentes confugiamus ad ipsum, petamus et ex- pectemus auxilium et salutem, gratitudinem etiam obedientia nostra declaremus. Haec omnia cogi- tanda sunt, quoties de Christi doloribus dicitur.

Dixi supra de passione Christi duo haec quaeri. Primum cum fuerit aliqua trepidatio, an fuerit vitiosa. Alterum quomodo potuerint in eo simul existere laetitia propria beatorum, et tanta consternatio. De priore iam dictum est: In Chri- sto etiamsi fuerunt trepidationes, tamen non fuisse eas vitiosas. Quia non fuerunt similes no- stris inordinatae, in quibus fremunt voluntates ad- versus Deum, sed fuerunt gemitus naturae onera- tae supra vires, cum tamen voluntas retineret obedientiam siue indignatione adversus Deum.

De altera quaestione longae et variae sunt responsiones. Sed nos breviter respondemus: Tempora discernenda esse de Christo. Aliud est typus passionis et huius admirandae obedientiae et abiectionis, seu humilitatis Christi, aliud tem- pus extra passionem. Quia enim admirando con- silio Dei decretum fuit, ut filius fieret victima, necesse fuit aliquod tempus esse mactationis victi- mae. Etsi igitur Christus semper fuit beatus, ta- men illo tempore, quod destinatum fuit passioni, non ita fulsit beatitudo, ut extra passionem, sicut dicitur de tempore, Psalm. 8.: Minuisti eum paulisper a Deo. Quid sit illud diminuere vel deserere, expressit Esaias, inquiens: Dominus voluit eum conterere in infirmitate. Voluntatem et decretum Dei fuisse inquit, ut a Deo ipso obrue- retur tanta ira, ut esset λύτρον pro nostris pec- catis, quia iusticia Dei flagitabat aliquam com- pensationem. Omnis enim lex vel ad obedien- tiam, vel ad poenam obligat. Nec est quiddam, conteri a Deo. Aliud est lacerari corpus ferro, aut a bestiis. Aliud, et longe maius est, percuti a Deo, et sentire iram Dei, hoc est, luctari cum tentatione de abiectione. Tali tempore conspe- ctus, qui beatitudinem, vitam, laetitiam efficie- bat, non clare cernebatur. Idem et Irenaeus erudite dixit: Verbo quiescente passum esse Chri- stum, ut crucifigi et mori posset, id est, verbum tunc non exercebat potentiam suam. Sic paulis- per Christus a Deo ostendente potentiam et bea- titudinem desertus est, sicut et ipse clamat: Deus meus, quare reliquisti me? Loquitur de tem- pore, et Psalm. 110. De torrente in via bibet, tempus circumscribit hoc verbum, in via. De- inde sequitur gloriae revelatio, propterea exalta- bit caput. Sic de tempore loquitur Christus, orans se rursus ea gloria ornari, quam habuerit ante mundi conditionem, Ioannis 17.

Haec responsio est planior, quam aliae quae a sententiariis recitantur, quas qui requiret, legat apud ipsos. Nos de his tantis et tam arcanis re- bus pie et reverenter cogitemus, et magnitudine dolorum Christi utcunque considerata, agnosca- mus Deum vere et horribiliter irasci peccatis, in- gentem vim esse amoris erga nos in filio, qui pro nobis poenam subiit, et timorem et fidem arden- tibus cogitationibus excitemus.

Haec de consternatione hoc loco satis sit di- xisse: Sequitur consolatio manifesta, quae non solum confirmatio fuit consternati Christi, sed etiam testimonium coram populo, hunc Iesum a Deo missum esse. Clare enim inquit vox divi- na: Et glorificavi, et rursus glorificabo, quasi dicat: Testis sum, te a me aeterno patre missum esse, idque declaravit, quia tecum resuscitavi mortuos, et alia feci miranda, et postea rursus proponam testimonia in tua resurrectione.

## 12:31
Now is the judgment of the world.

Here you see an example of that opinion which I just recited about distinguishing times. Christ had been weakened by sudden consternation, but he raises himself up again in this terror, especially confirmed by the divine voice; and just as he had been terrified before, so now he rejoices again, and joyfully recites the words of a most glorious triumph. Now is the judgment of this world, now the prince of this world will be cast out. These are obscure sayings to human judgments. For to Pilate and those like him, nothing new seemed to be happening or taking place in the world; he saw Christ going about, like Socrates, and censuring evil morals, and afterwards, being circumvented by unjust judgments, he thought he had been oppressed by chance, like Socrates: and that this matter brought no change to the human race or to empires. But then Pilate judged that the judgment of the world was taking place, when he saw restless princes being punished by Gaius Caesar, and afterwards by Augustus, avarice being punished, and the world being freed from their tyranny, and new laws, just and tolerable to the nations, being brought in, courts being restored, and peace being fortified. Pilate would have spoken of these deeds as the time when the judgment of the world was accomplished, and he would have spoken rightly concerning the judgment of empires or the polities of the world. With this image considered, the words of Christ will be understood more clearly, which speak of the overthrow of the tyranny of the devil and his members, and the destruction of the kingdom of sin, and of the constitution of a new and eternal kingdom, and the liberation of the elect; he says, that battle will now take place, in which I will overcome the devil and break his power.

Although, therefore, from the beginning of the world the fathers were saved by the voice of the Gospel and by faith in the mediator who was to come, and the mediator was always effective, yet the Prophets, Christ, and the Apostles speak in such a way that this very work, namely the passion and resurrection of Christ, is the consummation of the promises, because it is the cause, merit, and commencement of eternal life, and on account of this work the mediator was effective beforehand. Thus speaks Daniel in chapter 9: Then sin will be finished, and everlasting righteousness will be brought in, and prophecy will be fulfilled; the eternal life of the elect is commenced in the resurrection of Christ, and is consummated in the many who are raised. But some members await the consummation, yet the cause has been exhibited and the price paid, which was previously awaited. Thus it is said in this place: Now is the judgment of the world, that is, now that new state will be commenced in which the elect will be liberated from the tyranny of the devil, from sin, and from death, and on the other hand, the tyrant with his members will be condemned, repressed, and finally cast into eternal punishments. Therefore it is said in the text: Now the prince of this world will be cast out. For although the devil has been repressed from that time on from the beginning in the liberation of the fathers and the elect, yet now that work will take place on account of which the earlier liberations were made; the cause, the merit, and the manifest commencement of eternal life will be exhibited.

Furthermore, let us diligently inculcate this consolation in ourselves, that the devil is cast out by Christ; the words agree with that saying of John: The Son of God appeared that he might destroy the works of the devil. Which saying is an interpretation of the first promise, delivered in Genesis: The seed of the woman will crush the head of the serpent. This crushing is made manifest in the resurrection of Christ, and it happens universally as often as the devil is repressed by the help of Christ, so that he does not overthrow us. Therefore, so that we may learn that these promises are not empty sounds of words, but that these benefits are truly given at all times to those who call upon him, let faith shine in daily business, dangers, and struggles, seeking and expecting these benefits, just as Christ says: Ask, and you shall receive. This faith experiences that the promises are true, and that wondrous liberations are given to us.

Latin:

Nunc iudicium est mundi.

Exemplum hic cernis eius sententiae, quam nunc recitavi de discernendis temporibus. Lan- guefactus erat Christus subita consternatione, sed rursus in hoc terrore sese erigit, praesertim con- firmatus voce divina; et ut antea expaverat, ita nunc rursus laetatur, et verba gloriosissimi trium- phi laetus recitat. Nunc iudicium est mundi hu- ius, nunc princeps huius mundi foras eiicietur. Obscura dicta sunt humanis iudiciis. Nam Pilato et similibus nihil novi videbatur geri, aut fieri in mundo, videbat circumire Christum, ut Socratem, et taxare malos mores, et postea circumventum iniquis iudiciis, existimavit casu oppressum esse, ut Socratem: Nec eam rem afferre mutationem humano generi, vel imperiis. Sed tunc iudicavit Pilatus iudicium mundi fieri, cum vidit a Caio Caesare, et postea ab Augusto puniri inquietos principes, puniri avaritiam, et liberari orbem terrarum eorum tyrannide, et novas leges iustas et tolerabiles gentibus ferri, restitui iudicia, et muniri pacem. De his rebus gestis dixisset Pilatus, tunc iudicium mundi factum esse, et recte dixisset de iudicio imperiorum, seu politiarum mundi. Hac imagine considerata, verba Christi clarius intelligentur, quae loquuntur de eversione tyrannidis diaboli, et membrorum eius, et destructione regni peccati, et de novi regni et aeterni constitutione, et liberatione electorum, iam inquit illud praelium fiet, in quo ego superabo diabolum, et potentiam eius frangam.

Etsi igitur ab initio mundi patres salvati sunt voce Evangelii, et fide venturi mediatoris, et semper fuit efficax mediator, tamen sic Prophetae, Christus et Apostoli loquuntur, hoc ipsum opus, scilicet passionem et resurrectionem Christi esse consummationem promissionum, quia est causa, meritum et incoatio vitae aeternae, et propter hoc opus antea efficax fuit mediator. Sic loquitur Daniel cap. 9.: Tunc finietur peccatum, et adducetur iusticia sempiterna, et implebitur prophetia, incoatur vita aeterna electorum in resurrectione Christi, et consummatur in multis resuscitatis. Sed aliqua membra expectant consummationem, exhibita tamen est causa et persolutum pretium, quod antea expectabatur. Ita hoc loco dicitur: Nunc iudicium est mundi, id est, nunc novus ille status incoabitur, in quo electi liberabuntur a tyrannide diaboli, a peccato et a morte, et econtra tyrannus cum suis membris damnabitur, reprimetur, et tandem in aeternas poenas abiicietur. Ideo in textu dicitur: Nunc princeps mundi foras eiicietur. Etsi enim inde usque ab initio in patrum et electorum liberatione diabolus repressus est, tamen nunc illud opus fiet, propter quod priores liberationes factae sunt, causa, meritum, incoatio manifesta vitae aeternae exhibebuntur.

Caeterum diligenter nobis hanc consolatio- nem inculcemus, diabolum foras eiici a Christo, conveniunt verba ad illud dictum Ioannis: Filius Dei apparuit, ut destruat opera diaboli. Quod dictum interpretatio est primae promissionis, tra- ditae in Genesi: Semen mulieris conculcabit ca- put serpentis. Haec conculcatio palam fit in re- surrectione Christi, et fit universaliter, quoties Christi auxilio reprimitur diabolus, ne nos ever- tat. Ut igitur has promissiones discamus, non esse inanes sonitus verborum, sed revera haec beneficia omni tempore invocantibus dari, in quo- tidianis negotiis, periculis et certaminibus fides luceat, petens et expectans haec beneficia, sicut inquit Christus: Petite, et accipietis. Haec fides experitur promissiones veras esse, et donari nobis mirandas liberationes.

## 12:34
We have heard from the law.

Christ had said that he was to be exalted, that is, to be crucified, and that he would draw all to himself, Gentiles and Jews, and the people had understood without error that Christ was speaking of death. They add, therefore, questions about the contradiction which is common throughout the Prophets: Elsewhere they say that Christ is to die, as Isaiah and Daniel expressly say. Elsewhere they say that Christ is to reign perpetually without end. Neither the Pharisees then nor the Jews now could explain this contradiction. They invent, therefore, a polity of many centuries, and forget the heavenly kingdom in eternal life. For they argue that if he is born from the seed of David, he does not reign if he dies. But an eternal kingdom is promised not to some incorporeal nature, but to the son born from the seed of David. This contradiction is reconciled through the resurrection. Christ dies, but since it is necessary for the one born from the seed of David to reign, it is necessary for him to be raised; therefore, the one raised reigns in eternal life. This is enough to have admonished, so that the pious may understand that the New Testament is the light of the Prophets and may refute the Jews more easily by comparing the prophetic sayings. For some speak of death, others of the eternal kingdom of the seed of David, others clearly say that Christ will indeed die, but yet that he is to be snatched from death, as Isaiah says in chapter 53. And the Psalm says: You will not give your holy one to see corruption.

Latin:

Nos audivimus ex lege.

Dixerat Christus se exaltandum esse, id est, crucifigendum, et omnes ad se tracturum esse, Gentes et Iudaeos, et sine errore intellexerat po- pulus, Christum de morte loqui. Addunt igitur quaestiones de pugnantia, quae passim in Pro- phetis est obvia: Alibi dicunt, Christum moritu- rum, ut Esaias et Daniel expresse dicunt. Alibi dicunt, Christum regnaturum esse perpetuo sine fine. Hanc pugnantiam explicare nec Pharisaei tunc poterant, nec nunc possunt Iudaei. Fin- gunt igitur politiam multorum seculorum, et obli- viscuntur regni coelestis in vita aeterna. Dispu- tant enim natum ex semine David, si moriatur, non regnare. Promittitur autem regnum aeter- num non naturae alicui incorporeae, sed filio nato ex semine David. Haec pugnantia concilia- tur per resurrectionem. Moritur Christus, cum autem oporteat regnare natum ex semine David, necesse est eum resuscitari, regnat igitur resusci- tatus in vita aeterna. Haec satis est admonuisse, ut pii intelligant novum testamentum lucem esse Prophetarum et Iudaeos facilius refutent, colla- tis dictis propheticis. Nam alia de morte loquun- tur, alia de regno aeterno seminis David, alia clare dicunt, Christum moriturum quidem, sed tamen eripiendum esse ex morte, ut Esaias in- quit cap. 53. Et Psalm. ait: Non dabis sanctum tuum videre corruptionem.

## 12:39
Therefore they could not believe,

There are two opinions; the former says: That many, even after seeing miracles, did not believe. This example is recited so that the pious may not be moved by the small number of believers, so that they themselves might also fail. As there are many Turks, and men of other sects, who reason that so many nations would not seem to have been created in vain, and therefore they embrace errors because the multitude that approves of them is great. But often the Prophets, Christ, and the Apostles console us against this scandal, and the entire parable of the seed scattered on different soils preaches about this very point. For there is great need for all the pious to have this forewarning, because all are moved by the scarcity and miseries of the Church.

The second question in this place is about the cause of election and rejection. Is the will of God the cause of stubbornness in the impious, since it is said in this place that many could not believe because the Prophet said: He has blinded their eyes? I answer: This opinion must be held most firmly: that God neither wills sin, nor is the cause of sin, just as it is clearly said in Psalm 5: You are not a God who wills impiety, and above, Christ himself says that the devil is the cause of lying and murder, when he calls him the father of lies, and adds: When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own, that is, he himself turns away from God of his own accord, nor does he receive depravity or lying from God the creator, and in 1 John 3 it is said: He who commits sin is of the devil, because the devil sinned from the beginning. The true opinion, therefore, is that stubbornness in those who are damned is not from the will of God, but from the own will of those who are damned, and that this stubbornness is the cause, that is, the merit of damnation; thus also in Romans 10 it is said, with the sentence of Isaiah cited: All day long I have stretched out my hands to a people disobedient to me, and contradicting, it is said that salvation is offered by God to all, but not all embrace the offered benefit, but many oppose God. Therefore, the will of God is not the cause of stubbornness in them, but their own proper will.

Wherefore, what John says, that many do not believe because it was predicted: He has blinded their eyes, should be understood by way of consequence, the Prophet predicted: Because it was going to happen. Furthermore, the phrase should be understood correctly, which is most common among the Hebrews regarding permission: He has blinded their eyes, that is, he permitted them to be blind, he did not free them from blindness, he did not help them so that they might be healed. There is, however, a complaint in the Prophet, signifying the fury of the impious, who, having heard the voice of the Gospel, become more rabid, as if he were saying: What did teaching the Gospel profit? It rendered them harder, as we are accustomed to say in common parlance, by accident, that is, the rabies grew upon hearing the Gospel, because the will in them is turned away, it hates and flees the Gospel, not because God does anything in their will; indeed, Paul clearly says: That blindness is confirmed by the devil, who moves minds so that they think things contrary to the Gospel. As he moved the mind of Manichaeus, and of similar people, to devise monstrous lies. Nor is there any doubt that the Hebrew phrase in these words: I will harden the heart of Pharaoh, and similar ones, must be understood as permission, as in Isaiah 63: Why have you made us err, O Lord, from your ways? Here it is sufficiently clear that it is said by way of permission. This simple explanation regarding the merit of rejection, and regarding the cause of hardening, or pertinacity, is plain, and has nothing of perplexity, and is undoubtedly true, nor is it profitable to seek other disputations, which have many inexplicable labyrinths.

There is, however, a more expeditious answer regarding rejection, as I have said; the other disputation is more difficult regarding election; there is no doubt that the mercy, or the will of God showing mercy, is truly the cause of election. For after the fall of Adam, the whole human race had already perished, nor could Adam, or his posterity, recover the lost dignity by their own powers, but by the secret and wondrous counsel of God, with the Son interceding, reconciliation and the inheritance of eternal life were promised again, so that the whole nature of men might not have been created only for destruction. The cause, therefore, of election is without any doubt mercy, and the merit of the Son of God, just as it is said in John 3: God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life. And Paul in the second chapter to the Ephesians says: By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not of yourselves, it is the gift of God, not of works, lest anyone should boast, and in Romans nine and ten this opinion is handed down at greater length.

There is, therefore, in the will of God the cause of election, mercy, and the merit of Christ, but our apprehension must concur. For since the promise of grace is universal, as is most manifest, and it is necessary that we obey the promise, Some distinction must be made between the elect and the rejected based on our will, namely, that those who resist the promise are rejected. Conversely, we must feel that those who embrace the promise are received, as we must in a true struggle, because one cannot, nor is it permitted to, judge otherwise concerning the will of God than from the revealed promise. Indeed, what will the mind of David do when driven into exile, where will he take refuge, arguing especially in such great calamity, whether he is rejected? He will nowhere discern the will of God except in the universal promise; with this voice he will console himself: In your seed shall all nations be blessed.

Into this universal promise he will include himself also, and he will determine that God certainly wills and commands that we assent to the promise, and that those who assent are received. These things are learned better in the very exercises of faith than in idle speculations; let us not imagine, like the Manichaeans, that the human will is a stone, and that one must indulge in doubt until we feel ourselves compelled against our will to believe, but let us ourselves, with the thought-out voice of the Gospel, most sharply resist doubt; when we do this, faith is kindled in us, and the Holy Spirit is effective.

These things are true, certain, plain, and clear, and from these foundations they are built up, namely, that it is necessary to assent to the promise, that one must judge concerning the will of God from the very word proposed, just as Adam judged, who, as often as he was tormented about his fall, looked upon the promise of the coming reconciler, and sought no other opinions, but sustaining himself with the promise, he determined that he was received and elected. Let us also feel this, we who are drawn by the word, which must be received by faith, and let no other illuminations be sought. For when it is said: No one comes to me unless the Father has drawn him, let us know that we are drawn when we embrace the word of the Gospel by faith, just as it is said in the same place: Everyone who hears from the Father and learns, comes to me. Minds are drawn, he says, when they hear the Gospel and learn, that is, when they embrace it by faith, and do not resist, but believe. For afterwards Christ himself interprets that hearing and learning as believing the voice of the Gospel.

And as the promise of grace is universal, so let us understand these sayings to speak of the promise: God wills all to be saved. Likewise: With God there is no προσωποληψία, as is said in Acts 10 concerning this very question, what kind of people please God, and Deut. 10: Your God is a great, and powerful, and terrible God, who does not accept a person. Now, the acceptance of a person is not to be equal to equals in every respect. It is therefore the praise of the justice of God that He is equal to equals according to the rule which He has delivered; He condemns sin in all, and gave His Son as a propitiator for all. He therefore receives all who take refuge in the Son, He rejects all who despise the Son; this will of His He has clearly proposed in the promises. For thus He says in John 3: Everyone who believes in the Son has eternal life, and he who does not believe, the wrath of God remains upon him. These sayings define that equality, and show that there is no προσωποληψία with God.

Nor do these things contradict the words of Paul to the Romans 9: It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy. For it is true that the mercy and merit of Christ are the cause of election, and that the elect are drawn by God, but they are drawn by the word and the Holy Spirit. Here one must will, and one must not resist God who draws, nor must diffidence be retained and confirmed in the soul, or one must not wait until the will is compelled, as a stone is driven by force; and when the mind sustains itself in terrors with the promise of grace, at the same time the Holy Spirit is effective, according to that saying to the Galatians 3: That we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith. These things mentioned in this place concerning the causes of rejection and election should be transferred also to similar passages in John, in which it is spoken of rejection or election.

Latin:

Propterea non poterant credere, etc.

Duae sunt sententiae; prior ait: Multos etiam conspectis miraculis non credidisse. Id exemplum eo recitatur, ne paucitate credentium pii moveantur, ut ipsi quoque deficiant. Ut multi sunt Turci, et aliarum sectarum homines, qui ratiocinantur, non videri tot gentes frustra condi- tas esse, et propterea amplectuntur errores, quia magna est multitudo, quae illos approbat. At saepe nos Prophetae, Christus et Apostoli adver- sus hoc scandalum consolantur, et de hoc ipso loco tota parabola de semine in dissimiles terras sparso concionatur. Valde enim opus est omni- bus piis hac praemonitione, quia omnes moven- tur exiguitate et miseriis Ecclesiae.

Altera quaestio est hoc loco de causa ele- ctionis et reiectionis. Estne voluntas Dei causa contumaciae in impiis, cum hoc loco dicatur, ideo multos non potuisse credere, quia Propheta dixerit: Excaecavit oculos eorum. Respondeo: Firmissime tenenda est haec sententia: Deum nec velle peccatum, nec esse causam peccati, sicut Psal. 5. clare dicitur: Non volens Deus impieta- tem tu es, et supra Christus ipse inquit: diabo- lum causam esse mendacii et homicidii, cum vo- cat eum patrem mendacii, et addit: Cum menda- cium loquitur, ex propriis loquitur, id est, ipse se avertit a Deo sponte, nec accipit a Deo condi- tore depravationem seu mendacium, et 1. Ioan- nis 3. dicitur: Qui peccatum facit, ex diabolo est, quia diabolus primum peccavit. Vera est igitur sententia, contumaciam in damnandis non esse a voluntate Dei, sed a voluntate propria damnan- dorum, et hanc contumaciam causam esse, id est, meritum damnationis, sic et ad Roman. 10. dici- tur, citata sententia Esaiae: Tota die expandi manus meas ad populum repugnantem mihi, et contradicentem, ait offerri salutem a Deo omni- bus, sed non omnes amplecti oblatum beneficium, sed multos Deo repugnare. Non igitur voluntas Dei causa est contumaciae in ipsis, sed voluntas ipsorum propria.

Quare quod Ioannes dicit, ideo multos non credere, quia praedictum sit: Excaecavit eorum oculos, intelligatur ratione consequentiae, Pro- pheta praedixit: Quia erat eventurum. Deinde phrasis dextre intelligatur, quae usitatissima est Ebraeis de permissione: Excaecavit oculos eorum, id est, permisit esse caecos, non liberavit eos a caecitate, non adiuvit eos, ut sanarentur. Est autem querela apud Prophetam, significans furo- rem impiorum, qui audita voce Evangelii fiunt rabiosiores, quasi dicat: Quid profecit docens Evangelium? reddidit duriores, ut vulgo loqui solemus, per accidens, id est, rabies audito Evan- gelio crevit, quia voluntas in ipsis aversa, odit et fugit Evangelium, non quia Deus agat aliquid in voluntate eorum, imo Paulus clare dicit: Con- firmari caecitatem illam a diabolo, qui mentes movet, ut cogitent Evangelio contraria. Ut mo- vit mentem Manichaei, et similium, ad porten- tosa mendacia excogitanda. Nec vero dubium est phrasin Hebraicam in his verbis: Ego indurabo cor Pharaonis, et similibus de permissione in- telligendam esse, ut Esaiae 63.: Quare errare nos fecisti domine a viis tuis? Hic satis perspicuum est permissione dici. Haec simplex explicatio de merito reiectionis, et de causa indurationis, seu pertinaciae plana est, et nihil habet perplexita- tis, et haud dubie vera est, nec prodest quaerere alias disputationes, quae multos habent labyrin- thos inexplicabiles.

Est autem expeditior responsio de reiectione, ut dixi, altera disputatio difficilior est de electione, non dubium est misericordiam, seu voluntatem Dei miserentis vere esse causam electionis. Nam post lapsum Adae iam totum genus humanum pe- rierat, nec poterat Adam, aut posteritas eius, propriis viribus recuperare amissam dignitatem, sed arcano et mirando consilio Dei, deprecante filio, immensa misericordia rursus promissa est reconciliatio, et haereditas vitae aeternae, ne tota hominum natura tantum ad exitium condita esset. Causa igitur electionis est sine ulla dubi- tatione misericordia, et meritum filii Dei, sicut Ioann. 3. dicitur: Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut filium suum unigenitum dederit, ut omnis qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam. Et Paulus ad Ephesios secundo capite inquit: Gratia salvati estis per fidem, et hoc non ex vobis, Dei donum est, non ex operibus, ne quis glorietur, et ad Romanos nono et decimo prolixius haec sententia traditur.

Est igitur in voluntate Dei causa electionis, misericordia, et meritum Christi, sed concurrere oportet apprehensionem nostram. Cum enim promissio gratiae sit universalis, ut manifestissi- mum est, et necesse sit nos obedire promissioni, aliquod discrimen inter electos et reiectos a vo- luntate nostra sumendum est, videlicet, repu- gnantes promissioni, reiici. Econtra vero am- plectentes promissionem recipi, sic nos sentire necesse est in vero agone, quia de voluntate Dei nec potest, nec licet aliter iudicare, nisi ex reve- lata promissione. Imo quid aget mens Davidis pulsi in exilium, quo confugiet, disputans prae- sertim in tanta calamitate, an sit reiectus. Nus- quam voluntatem Dei cernet, nisi in promissione universali, hac se voce consolabitur: In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes.

In hanc universalem se quoque includet, et statuet, certo velle Deum, ac praecipere, ut pro- missioni assentiamur, et assentientes recipi. Haec in ipsis fidei exercitiis melius discuntur, quam in otiosis speculationibus, non fingamus, ut Mani- chaei, voluntatem humanam saxum esse, et in- dulgendum esse dubitationi, donec senserimus nos cogi invitos, ut credamus, sed ipsi cogitata voce Evangelii acerrime repugnemus dubitationi, quod cum facimus, accenditur in nobis fides, et Spiritus sanctus est efficax.

Haec vera, certa, plana et perspicua sunt, et ex his fundamentis extruuntur, videlicet, quod necesse sit assentiri promissioni, quod de volun- tate Dei iudicandum sit ex ipso verbo proposito, prorsus ut Adam iudicabat, qui quoties angeba- tur de suo lapsu, intuebatur promissionem ven- turi reconciliatoris, nec alias opiniones quaerebat, sed sustentans se promissione, statuebat se rece- ptum et electum esse. Ita et nos sentiamus, qui a verbo trahimur, quod fide accipi necesse est, nec aliae quaerantur illuminationes. Cum enim dicitur: Nemo venit ad me, nisi pater traxerit eum, trahi nos sciamus, cum verbum Evange- lii amplectimur fide, sicut eodem loco dicitur: Omnis qui audit a patre et discit, venit ad me. Trahi ergo mentes, inquit, cum audiunt Evan- gelium et discunt, id est, cum amplectuntur fide, nec repugnant, sed credunt. Nam postea ipse Christus illud audire et discere interpretatur cre- dere voci Evangelii.

Ac ut promissio gratiae est universalis, ita intelligamus haec dicta loqui de promissione: Deus vult omnes salvos fieri. Item: Apud Deum non est προσωποληψία, ut Act. 10. dicitur de hac ipsa quaestione, quales placeant Deo, et Deut. 10.: Deus vester est Deus magnus, et po- tens, et terribilis, qui personam non accipit. Est autem acceptio personae, non esse aequalem ae- qualibus omnino. Laus est igitur iusticiae Dei, quod est aequalis aequalibus iuxta regulam, quam tradidit, damnat peccatum in omnibus, et dedit filium propiciatorem pro omnibus. Recipit igi- tur omnes confugientes ad filium, reiicit omnes contemnentes filium, hanc voluntatem suam in promissionibus clare proposuit. Sic enim inquit Ioan. 3.: Omnis qui credit in filium, habet vitam aeternam, et qui non credit, manet ira Dei super eum. Haec dicta illam aequalitatem definiunt, et ostendunt non esse προσωποληψίαν apud Deum.

Nec adversantur haec dictis Pauli ad Roma- nos 9.: Non est volentis, neque currentis, sed Dei miserentis. Verum est enim misericordiam et meritum Christi esse causam electionis, et trahi electos a Deo, sed verbo et Spiritu san- cto trahuntur. Hic velle oportet, nec repu- gnandum est trahenti Deo, nec retinenda in animis et confirmanda diffidentia, seu expectan- dum donec cogatur voluntas, ut saxum vi impel- litur, cumque in pavoribus sustentat se mens pro- missione gratiae, simul est efficax Spiritus san- ctus, iuxta dictum illud, ad Galatas 3.: Ut pro- missionem Spiritus accipiamus per fidem. Haec de causis reiectionis et electionis hoc loco comme- morata, transferantur etiam ad similes locos in Ioanne, in quibus de reiectione aut electione dicitur.

## 12:41
These things Isaiah said when he saw His glory.

The simple opinion is that the Prophet said these things when he recognized in the spirit the kingdom, preaching, passion, and resurrection of the coming Christ. For chapter 53 of Isaiah is cited, in which the passion and resurrection of Christ are described, but there is another opinion, as I think, more proper, that the Prophet said these things when he saw the glory of Christ, that is, the visible appearance which is described in Isaiah 6: I saw the Lord sitting upon a high throne. For John signifies that the Son of God showed Himself to the Fathers and Prophets, and spoke with them, as not obscure sayings are read concerning Jacob, Moses, Joshua, and Daniel.

Latin:

Haec dixit Esaias quando vidit gloriam eius.

Simplex sententia est, dixisse haec Prophe- tam, quando spiritu agnovit venturi Christi re- gnum, praedicationem, passionem et resurrectio- nem. Citatur enim cap. 53. Esaiae, quo Christi passio et resurrectio describuntur, sed alia sen- tentia est, ut existimo, magis propria, dixisse haec Prophetam, cum vidit gloriam Christi, id est, visibilem speciem, quae describitur Esaiae 6.: Vidi Dominum sedentem supra solium excelsum. Significat enim Ioannes filium Dei se ostendisse Patribus et Prophetis, et cum eis collocutum esse, ut de Iacob, Mose, Iosue, Daniele, dicta non obscura leguntur.

## 12:44
Jesus, however, cried out: I do not judge.

At the end of this chapter he repeats the sum of the Gospel, and with great emotion of soul, and most grave asseveration, he alleges God as the author, and professes himself to have been sent by God. These assertions are repeated so often, so that the pious may be confirmed, and may more certainly conclude, that this is truly the will of God, which Christ proclaims, that it is truly received, and heard by God, and that all who take refuge in Christ are saved.

With what force of spirit are these voices poured forth? What shall I say? What shall I speak? I know that his commandment is eternal life. These repetitions signify love toward us, and a desire for our salvation, and burning wrath against the unbelieving. I did not come to judge the world, but to save it. This saying, rightly understood, does not dissent from other sayings which state that Christ is the judge. For here, and in similar places, he speaks of the principal cause of his own advent, and of the first advent, in which Christ becomes a victim. The principal cause for which Christ was sent is this: that, the wrath of God being appeased, the Church might be gathered to God in the human race through him, to whom justice and eternal life might be given. And indeed, in his first advent he only performs the office of a priest, he teaches and offers his sacrifice, but in his second advent he will show before the whole world that he also performs the duty of a judge. Furthermore, the whole human race has already been condemned beforehand, on account of the fall of Adam, and the sin which spreads through the whole nature of men, and on account of the contempt of the Son of God, as is said above: He who does not believe is already judged. Only those are excepted who believe the Gospel and take refuge in Christ.

Latin:

Iesus autem clamavit: Ego non iudico.

In fine huius capitis repetit summam Evan- gelii, et magno animi motu, et gravissima asse- veratione allegat Deum autorem, et profitetur se a Deo missum esse. Hae asseverationes toties repetuntur, ut pii confirmentur, et certius statuant, vere esse hanc voluntatem Dei, quam praedicat Christus, vere recipi, et exaudiri a Deo, ac salvos fieri omnes confugientes ad Christum.

Quanto animi impetu hae voces effunduntur? Quid dicam? quid loquar? Scio mandatum eius esse vitam aeternam. Hae repetitiones amorem erga nos, et desiderium nostrae salutis, et ardentem iram adversus incredulos significant. Non veni, ut iudicem mundum, sed ut salvum faciam, Hoc dictum dextre intellectum non dissentit a caeteris dictis, quae dicunt Christum iudicem esse. Hic enim et in similibus locis loquitur de causa principali adventus ipsius, et de primo adventu, quo Christus fit victima. Principalis causa, propter quam missus est Christus, haec est, ut placata ira Dei, per ipsum Ecclesia Deo in genere humano colligatur, cui detur iusticia et vita aeterna. Et quidem in primo adventu tantum fungitur officio sacerdotis, docet et offert suum sacrificium, sed in secundo adventu ostendet coram toto mundo, se fungi etiam munere iudicis. Praeterea totum genus humanum iam antea condemnatum est, propter lapsum Adae, et peccatum, quod grassatur in tota natura hominum, et propter contemtum filii Dei, ut supra dicitur: Qui non credit, iam iudicatus est. Tantum illi excipiuntur, qui credunt Evangelio, et confugiunt ad Christum.

## 13:1 Argument
Chapter XIII.

Latin:

Caput XIII.

## 13:1
Before the feast of the Passover.

Moses begins the day from the evening; therefore, that was the beginning of the fourteenth day, on which, according to the law, the paschal lamb ought to be eaten, wherefore he says concerning the beginning of that day: Before the feast of the Passover, but yet he speaks of that very day. For a consideration of the narrative in Luke shows that Christ, on the very fourteenth day, as the Jews described the day, both ate the lamb and was crucified. But just as John in his whole history deliberately passes over the narratives which exist in the writings of the other Evangelists, so here he omits the eating of the lamb and the institution of the supper to be observed in the Church, and only recites the washing of the feet and the most sweet sermons delivered afterwards.

There is, however, a twofold significance in this washing of the feet. First, the type signifies that sins and death are washed away, and that justice and eternal life are restored to us through Christ. He falls into this meaning when he says: Unless I wash you, you will have no part with me. Likewise: He who has been bathed does not need to have anything washed except his feet, but is clean all over. These sayings secretly signify the proper benefit of Christ: unless he himself washes us, that is, unless he himself redeems us with his blood, and unless we believe that we are redeemed by the blood of Christ, we shall not be heirs of eternal life. This sentiment does not need a longer declaration here. Then, without any doubt, he speaks of justification when he says: He who has been bathed does not need to have anything washed except his feet, that is, he who is just by faith and is sanctified is clean, that is, he is entirely pleasing to God, but yet in this life the feet must be washed assiduously, that is, the affections: weak nature in this life produces many wandering affections; these impurities must be assiduously washed away. And the interpretations are known: he who believes is clean all over, namely by imputation, but in this life newness is begun, not yet entirely completed. These things are said copiously elsewhere. Christ therefore warns the Church by this type concerning the principal washing, that is, concerning the redemption by which he purified the Church with his blood.

But the other significance is that of an example, as he, departing, afterwards preaches most diligently concerning the ministry of the Gospel and concerning the concord of ministers among themselves, and indeed he prays to the eternal Father that he may grant this to the Church; so here he proposes an example to teachers, that they should individually cast themselves below others and strive to heal the errors of others, not ulcerate them, not attempt to increase their power by the disparagement of others, not seize the occasion of exposing errors to deform and oppress others. But with true love let them all admonish one another, teach, rule with counsel, and cover errors. Finally, let private desires, ambition, malevolence, envy, desire for revenge, etc., be entirely absent, and with a true heart let us do only this: that we may adorn the glory of Christ and be of service to the Church.

Judge from that how great was the abjection of self in Christ. We are horribly terrified when we seriously think of our own impurities, and we consider ourselves unworthy of life and light. But thus Christ, prostrate before the eternal Father, endured the sense of the wrath of God against our sins, as if he himself had committed them, and had polluted himself with such great baseness. This is ineffable humility, to derive and transfer the baseness of others onto himself in this way. Let us therefore be ashamed of our pride, arrogance, vanity, and impatience, when we grumble if at any time we are pushed down a little from a higher rank, or when we desert, or even oppress, friends who are disfigured by some calamity or some fall. But someone may say, if infirmity is to be tolerated, if errors are to be covered, why is it commanded by authorities that they punish offenses? Why is it severely enjoined upon the Church that it should cast out the contumacious from the Church by its own jurisdiction? Finally, why is it commanded to individuals that they should avoid sinners, as if they were Gentiles, as Christ says: Let him be to you as a Gentile? I answer: Political government and ecclesiastical government differ. And yet both must observe a certain order, and distinguish the degrees of offenses. The political is not a ministry of eternal salvation, but a part of the law; therefore it punishes manifest offenses, even if no admonition precedes. But ecclesiastical jurisdiction, because it is a part of the Gospel, first calls those who have offended to repentance, and offers reconciliation to those who repent; thus it is a ministry of eternal salvation. But if the offense is manifest, and after admonition contumacy follows, then at last the Gospel commands the penalty to be inflicted, namely, excommunication. This order must be observed in manifest offenses which the law of God commands to be punished; the same must be thought concerning fraternal correction. Nor do the words of Christ concerning love in this place conflict with the right of magistrates, or ecclesiastical jurisdiction, or fraternal admonition. Justice has its own place, as has already been said, and this is exercised by the pious, without violating love.

But a neighboring virtue is equity or ἐπιείκεια, concerning which it is said: Forgive, and it will be forgiven you; concerning this it is properly said in this discourse of Christ, and it has a place in three degrees: in tolerating infirmity, which laws do not punish; in secret offenses; and in healing and covering manifest offenses before contumacy. These three degrees extend widely in life, and occasions for declaring leniency and equity in these are never lacking to love.

The first degree is that it is a great virtue to tolerate the morose, the suspicious, the irascible, the sluggish, the greedy for glory, those who take it too softly if they think they are being neglected, the meddlesome, and those more attentive to business than is necessary. These are of nature, and are not punished by laws, and yet they often produce great tumults if equity is lacking in colleagues, just as David bore the emulation in his brothers.

The second degree is not to twist ambiguous deeds calumniously into a worse sense, not to amplify light errors odiously, nor to divulge secret ones, but to cover and heal them. On these occasions, malevolent men often excite atrocious and tragic tumults. Thus the Pharisees accuse the Apostles for plucking ears of grain on the Sabbath; thus in the Church huge commotions have arisen because of ceremonies. Many have corrupted indifferent deeds with bitter interpretations. The Roman Bishop excommunicated some in the East because they did not want to observe Easter on the same day that the West observed it, and now there are great disputes about ceremonies; some condemn those singing in Latin in temples. Some reason is pretended, but minds contend with ambition, emulation, desire for revenge, and other depraved affections, and from a light error the envious person seizes the opportunity of oppressing him whom he envies, just as now hypocrites most virulently traduce our Churches because of some light faults, blaming the speck in another's eye while they neglect the beam in their own.

The third degree is, before contumacy, to admonish the erring and sinning person candidly and lovingly, and by this duty to recall him to the way, just as Paul recalls Peter to the way, and Christ most placidly receives those acting in repentance, such as the sinful woman, Zacchaeus, and others. In these three degrees, equity, or ἐπιείκεια, ought especially to reign. But severity, or the rigor of justice, as they call it, should be exercised against the contumacious in manifest offenses. And that judgment is not of man, but of God. Wherefore magistrates and the ecclesiastical judge, because they obey not their own desire but the command of God, nevertheless retain love when they rightly perform their duty.

Let this general distinction be held concerning severity and equity, as often as those precepts occur which seem in some way to disagree, of which some command to forgive, as 'forgive and it will be forgiven you,' others preach about punishment, as 1 Corinthians 5: 'Remove the evil from among yourselves.' And in the history of the washing of the feet, which contains the doctrine concerning love, the place required this distinction concerning severity and equity to be explained. Christ himself, however, applies the example, saying: 'I have given you an example, that just as I have done to you, so you also should do.'

The sermon is about love between brothers maintaining concord, for which duty many virtues are needed: gentleness, patience, equity. He commends the pursuit of concord to his own more ardently, as he is now about to depart from this world, so that these final commands might move their minds more. For these two things must be especially accomplished by a good governor: that he rightly teach the Gospel, and foster concord, and not disturb it with ambition, anger, or harshness, as happens very often in all governance. And as he gives precepts here, so afterwards he asks both from God, that He may rule the teachers, that they may teach the truth, and be in concord. This political doctrine is not obscure, but it is difficult to restrain the movements of the mind that are burning with ambition, anger, desire for revenge, and similar diseases.

Latin:

Ante festum Paschae.

Moses incoat diem a vespera, tunc igitur initium fuit diei quartidecimi, quo iuxta legem agnum paschalem manducari oportuit, quare de initio eius diei inquit: Ante festum Paschatis, sed tamen de eo ipso die loquitur. Nam consideratio narrationis in Luca ostendit Christum ipso die quartodecimo, sicut Iudaei diem describebant, et manducasse agnum, et crucifixum esse. Ut autem Ioannes in tota sua historia consulto praeterit narrationes, quae extant in aliorum Evangelistarum scriptis, ita hic omittit manducationem agni, et institutionem coenae in Ecclesia servandae, ac tantum recitat ablutionem pedum, et dulcissimas conciones postea habitas.

Duplex est autem significatio in hac ablu- tione pedum. Primum, typus significat ablui peccata et mortem, et reddi nobis iusticiam et vitam aeternam per Christum. In hanc significa- tionem incurrit, cum ait: Nisi lavero te, non habebis partem mecum. Item: Qui lotus est non indiget, nisi ut pedes laventur, sed est mundus totus. Haec dicta tecte significant beneficium Christi proprium, nisi ipso abluente nos, id est, nisi ipse suo sanguine nos redimat, et nisi creda- mus nos redemtos sanguine Christi, non erimus haeredes vitae aeternae. Haec sententia hic non indiget longiore declaratione. Deinde sine ulla dubitatione de iustificatione loquitur, cum ait: Qui lotus est, non indiget, nisi ut pedes laven- tur, id est, qui iustus est fide et sanctificatus est, est mundus, id est, placet Deo totus, sed tamen in hac vita pedes assidue lavandi sunt, id est, affectus: natura infirma in hac vita gignit multos errantes affectus, has sordes assidue ablui opor- tet. Et notae sunt interpretationes, credens, mundus est totus, scilicet imputatione, sed in hac vita incoata est novitas, nondum prorsus com- pleta. Haec alias copiose dicuntur. Monet igi- tur Christus hoc typo Ecclesiam de praecipua ab- lutione, id est, de redemtione, qua sanguine suo purificavit Ecclesiam.

Sed altera significatio est exempli, ut disce- dens postea diligentissime concionatur de mini- sterio Evangelii et de ministrorum inter sese concordia, et quidem orat aeternum patrem, ut hanc concedat Ecclesiae, ita hic doctoribus exem- plum proponit, ut singuli sese infra alios abii- ciant, et aliorum errata sanare studeant, non exulcerent, non obtrectatione aliorum augere po- tentiam conentur, non traducendis erratis captent occasionein alios deformandi et opprimendi. Sed vera dilectione se mutuo omnes admoneant, doceant, regant consilio, tegant errata. Deni- que absint prorsus privatae cupiditates, ambitio, malevolentia, livor, cupiditas vindictae, etc. et vero pectore hoc tantum agamus, ut ornemus gloriam Christi et prosimus Ecclesiae.

Quanta fuerit in Christo abiectio sui, inde aestima. Nos horribiliter expavescimus, cum ipsi nostras sordes serio cogitamus, nosque indignos vita et luce ducimus. Sic autem Christus coram aeterno patre prostratus sustinuit sensum irae Dei adversus nostra peccata, quasi ipse ea perpetras- set, et sese tanta turpitudine polluisset. Haec est inenarrabilis humilitas, aliorum turpitudinem sic in sese derivare et transferre. Pudeat igitur nos nostrae superbiae, arrogantiae, vanitatis, impattentiae, cum fremimus, si quando aliquan- tulum ex gradu superiori detrudimur, aut cum amicos aliqua calamitate vel aliquo lapsu defor- matos deserimus, aut etiam premimus. Sed di- cat aliquis, si toleranda est infirmitas, si tegenda sunt errata, cur imperiis mandatum est, ut pu- niant delicta? Cur severe praecipitur Ecclesiae, ut sua iurisdictione contumaces ex Ecclesia eiiciat? Denique cur singulis mandatum est, ut vitent peccantes, tanquam Ethnicos, ut Christus ait: Sit tibi velut Ethnicus? Respondeo: Differunt politica gubernatio et ecclesiastica. Et tamen utraque ordinem certum observare debet, et gra- dus delictorum discernere, Politica non est salu- tis aeternae ministerium, sed pars legis, ideo pu- nit delicta manifesta, etiamsi nulla praecedat ad- monitio. Sed ecclesiastica iurisdictio, quia pars est Evangelii, primum eos, qui deliquerunt, vo- cat ad poenitentiam, et offert reconciliationem resipiscentibus, ita est ministerium salutis aeter- nae. Sed si delictum est manifestum, et post ad- monitionem sequitur contumacia, tum demum praecipit Evangelium de poena irroganda, vide- licet de excommunicatione. Hic ordo in mani- festis delictis, quae lex Dei iubet puniri, servan- dus est, idem sentiendum est de castigatione fra- terna. Nec verba Christi de dilectione in hoc loco pugnant cum iure magistratuum, aut ecclesiastica iurisdictione, aut fraterna admonitione. Habet suum locum iusticiae, ut iam dictum est, et haec exercetur a piis, non violata dilectione.

Sed vicina virtus est aequitas seu ἐπιείκεια, de qua dicitur: Remittite, et remittetur vobis, de hac proprie dicitur in hac Christi concione, et habet locum in tribus gradibus, in toleranda infir- mitate, quam leges non puniunt, in arcanis de- lictis et in sanandis manifestis delictis tegendis ante contumaciam. Hi tres gradus in vita late patent, et nunquam dilectioni dseunt occasiones in his declarandae lenitatis et aequitatis.

Primus gradus est, ut magna virtus est tole- rare morosos, suspicaces, iracundos, segnes, avi- dos gloriae, mollius ferentes, si negligi se putent, πολυπράγμονας, attentiores ad rem, quam opus est. Haec naturae sunt, nec puniuntur legibus, et tamen saepe pariunt magnos tumultus, si desit ἐπιείκεια collegis, ut David tulit aemulationem in fratribus suis.

Secundus gradus est, ambigua facta non ca- lumniose in deteriorem partem flectere, levia er- rata non odiose amplificare, nec arcana traduce- re, sed tegere et sanare. His occasionibus homi- nes malevoli saepe atroces et tragicos tumultus excitant. Sic Pharisaei accusant Apostolos in sabbato vellentes spicas, sic in Ecclesia ingentes motus orti sunt propter ceremonias. Media facta, multi depravarunt acerbis interpretationibus. Epi- scopus Romanus excommunicavit aliquos in orien- te, quod nollent pascha servare eodem die, quo servabat occidens, et nunc magnae sunt lites de ceremoniis, aliqui damnant Latine canentes in templis. Praetexitur aliqua ratio, sed animi cer- tant ambitione, aemulatione, cupiditate vindi- ctae, et aliis pravis affectibus, et ex levi errato invidus arripit occasionem premendi eum, cui in- videt, ut nunc nostras Ecclesias, propter aliqua levia vitia, virulentissime traducunt hypocritae, festucam in alieno oculo culpantes, cum trabem in suo negligant.

Tertius gradus est, ante contumaciam can- dide et amanter monere errantem et peccantem, et hoc officio revocare eum in viam, ut Petrum revocat Paulus in viam, et Christus placidissime re- cipit agentes poenitentiam, ut mulierem peccatri- cem, Zachaeum, et alios. In his tribus gradibus regnare aequitas, seu ἐπιείκεια praecipue debet. Sed severitas seu iusticiae rigor, ut vocant, ad- versus contumaces in delictis manifestis exercea- tur. Idque iudicium non est hominis, sed Dei. Quare magistratus et iudex ecclesiasticus, quia non suae cupiditati, sed mandato Dei obtempe- rant, tamen retinent dilectionem, cum recte offi- cium faciunt.

Haec generalis distinctio teneatur de severi- tate et aequitate, quoties illa praecepta occurrunt, quae aliquo modo dissidere videntur, quorum alia iubent ignoscere, ut remittite et remittetur vobis, alia de poena concionantur, ut 1. Corinth. 5.: Auferte malum ex vobis ipsis. Ac in historia de ablutione pedum, quae doctrinam continet de di- lectione, locus poscebat hoc discrimen de severi- tate et de aequitate exponi. Applicat autem Chri- stus ipse exemplum, inquiens: Exemplum dedi vobis, ut sicut ego feci vobis, ita et vos faciatis.

Concio est de dilectione inter fratres tuente concordiam, ad quod officium multis virtutibus opus est, mansuetudine, patientia, aequitate. Ardentius autem commendat suis studium con- cordiae, iam ex hoc mundo discessurus, ut haec ultima mandata magis moveant animos. Nam haec duo praecipue efficienda sunt bono guberna- tori, ut recte doceat Evangelium, et foveat con- cordiam, nec turbet eam ambitione, iracundia, asperitate, ut saepissime fit in omni gubernatione. Et ut hic dat praecepta, ita postea petit utrunque a Deo, ut regat doctores, ut vera doceant, et sint concordes. Haec politica doctrina non est ob- scura, sed animi motus ardentes ambitione, ira- cundia, cupiditate vindictae, et similibus mor- bis, frenare difficile est.

## 13:18
He who eats bread with me.

The words are taken from Psalm 41: Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor, where an antithesis is recounted. A few are affected by mercy for the miserable Church; for this duty God promises rewards in that Psalm with the sweetest words. And Christ preaches about the rewards in Matthew 25: Come, you blessed, etc. And there are many examples which show that the friends of the Church are gloriously adorned in this life, such as the example of the widow of Zarephath. On the other hand, others, and indeed many and chief friends, desert the Church in calamities, or even attack it, just as Cain kills his brother. Esau lies in wait for the life of Jacob: Joseph is sold by his brothers. Against David, his son stirred up sedition. These domestic wounds cause far greater pain than the cruelty of strangers. Therefore this verse is cited by name, so that we may prepare our minds to tolerate the perfidy of friends: He who was eating bread with me, that is, he who was most closely joined to me by familiarity, benevolence, duties, and the society of a profession, now tries to oppress and destroy me. Moreover, there are other perfidies and distractions of friends customary among men even in the civil conduct of life, as the poet exclaimed: Nowhere is faith safe. But the Church has sadder and more pernicious examples, because in the dissensions of the Church, factions beget new errors and drag a great part of the people into extreme destruction; therefore, there are also many sermons here and there about their punishments, as in Matthew 25: Go, you cursed, into eternal fire, etc. And Psalm 55: But you, a man of one mind, my guide, and my acquaintance. Let death come upon them, and let them descend alive into hell. I have said these things briefly about the notable verse which Christ cites, so that we may consider these wounds of the Church, and confirm our minds with the example of Christ when we experience the perfidy of friends.

Latin:

Qui manducat mecum panem.

Verba sumta sunt ex Psalm. 41.: Beatus qui intelligit super egenum et pauperem, ubi recen- setur antithesis. Aliqui pauci afficiuntur miseri- cordia aerumnosae Ecclesiae, pro hoc officio Deus in eo Psalmo praemia dulcissimis verbis pollice- tur. Et de praemiis concionatur Christus Matth. 25.: Venite benedicti, etc. Et exempla multa sunt, quae ostendunt in hac vita gloriose ornatos esse amicos Ecclesiae, ut exemplum viduae Sare- ptanae. Rursus alii, et quidem multi et praeci- pui amici Ecclesiam in calamitatibus deserunt, aut etiam oppugnant, ut Cain fratrem interficit. Esau insidiatur vitae Iacob: Ioseph venditur a fratribus. Adversus Davidem filius seditionem movit. Haec domestica vulnera longe maiorem dolorem faciunt, quam alienorum hominum cru- delitas. Ideo nominatim citatur hic versiculus, ut praeparemus animos ad tolerandas perfidias amicorum: Qui mecum manducabat panem, id est, qui mihi familiaritate, benevolentia, officiis, societate professionis coniunctissimus fuit, nunc opprimere et delere conatur. Sunt autem aliae usitatae inter homines etiam in civili consuetudine vitae amicorum perfidiae et distractiones, ut poëta exclamarit: Nusquam tuta fides. Sed Ec- clesia habet exempla tristiora et perniciosiora, quia in dissidiis Ecclesiae factiones gignunt novos errores, et magnam partem populi trahunt in ex- tremum exitium, ideo et de poenis eorum passim multae sunt conciones, ut Matth. 25.: Ite maledicti in ignem aeternum, etc. Et Psalm. 45.: Tu vero homo unanimis, dux meus, et notus meus. Ve- niat mors super illos, et descendant in infernum viventes. Haec breviter de insigni versiculo, quem citat Christus, dixi, ut haec vulnera Ecclesiae consideremus, et animos confirmemus exemplo Christi, cum perfidias amicorum experimur.

## 13:19
I tell you before it happens, etc.

Christ adds the reason why he now indicates the traitor before it is done, namely so that the prediction may be a testimony of the presence of God in Christ. For to show future things beforehand, and to see the counsels of hearts, is proper to God. Furthermore, this prediction also signifies that Christ undergoes his passion of his own accord for the salvation of the human race, not being snatched to punishments unaware or unwilling. Then he attaches the often-delivered sentiment by which he commends the ministers of the Gospel to us: He who receives whom I send, receives me. He signifies, however, that similar dangers are to be for the ministers. Therefore, he promises rewards to those who are beneficent toward the Apostles and pious teachers, and threatens punishments to their enemies.

They looked, therefore.

It is an image of the pious, who, having heard mention of some crime in their own ranks, are terrified and grieve. First, they fear their own weakness, and fear some lapses, and anxiously pray that they may be confirmed and ruled. Then they are also moved by the scandal. Adversaries are confirmed when those very people fail who had previously defended the Gospel sharply. The whole group is also considered to be lighter on account of the inconstancy of others: It is manifest that good minds are burned by these scandals, just as Paul also says in 2 Corinthians 11: Who is weak, so that I am not also weak? Who is moved by some scandal, so that I am not also burned? It cannot be that the calamity of our body and our members does not bring us pain, as manifest experience testifies. Therefore, the solicitude and consternation of the Apostles is recited in this place.

But here consider the hardness of Judas. Although warned and chastised by several words of Christ, he nevertheless does not repent, he is not bent toward thinking of the magnitude of his sin and the wrath of God; such fury and iron hardness follows, after the beginnings of temptations are not resisted, so that, because Pharaoh, Saul, and Ahithophel did not extinguish the first flames of hatred, but fed them, a greater conflagration was made afterwards than they could extinguish. Warned, therefore, by those saddest examples, let us be vigilant and attentive, and let us resist the very first beginnings of temptations, let us not cherish, let us not nourish impious opinions in our minds. Resist the beginnings; the medicine is prepared too late, when evils have grown strong through long delays.

Satan entered into him.

It is a sad and horrible description, and a manifest testimony. That the devil is a spirit wandering in the air, and penetrating into men, and impelling them to crimes, just as Paul also calls the devils the powers of the air, and says they are effective in the impious. But although Judas had also been impelled by the devil before, yet now after the admonition, when he is not turned to repentance, the fury in him is increased; that is what is signified when it is now said that Satan entered into him. Now his obstinacy, madness, and fury are so confirmed that the end of admonitions is reached; what kind of person, therefore, is Judas now? An enemy of God, a dwelling-place of the devil, ignorant of himself, and raging, cast off by God, not yet indeed seeing the wrath of God, but about to feel it a little later, when he will wish to flee outside the entire nature of things, nay, will wish to be reduced to nothing, and yet will not be able to, he will be tormented with eternal pain, because he knows that he has offered the highest insult to God, who commanded that this Son be heard and honored, and showed evident testimonies of His will, because, spurning these testimonies of God, and furiously contemning His command, he has aided the slaughter of Christ, and has conspired with the enemies of God, and the whole kingdom of the devil who blasphemes God. The punishments for these greatest crimes are ineffable, but this horrible image must be pondered, so that we may be more vigilant, lest we be dragged by the devil's snares into similar falls.

This also must be said, that Judas freely and willingly assented to the temptation of the devil, and willingly fell, and that he did not sin by fatal or Stoic necessity, nor does God will the sin of Judas. For the rule handed down by John must be held: He who commits sin is of the devil, nor is the cause to be transferred to fatal necessity, or to the will of God.

Latin:

Dico vobis antequam fiat, etc.

Addit Christus rationem, cur proditorem nunc ante factum indicet, videlicet ut praedictio sit testimonium praesentiae Dei in Christo. Nam praemonstrare futura, et videre cordium consilia, proprium Deo est. Deinde haec praedictio etiam significat Christum sua sponte subire passionem pro salute generis humani, non rapi inscium aut invitum ad supplicia. Deinde attexit saepe traditam sententiam, qua commendat nobis ministros Evangelii. Qui recipit, si quem misero, me recipit. Significat autem similia pericula ministrorum futura esse. Promittit igitur beneficis erga Apostolos et pios doctores praemia, et minatur hostibus poenas.

Respexerunt igitur.

Imago est piorum, qui audita mentione sceleris alicuius in suo agmine, expavescunt et dolent. Primum, metuunt propriam infirmitatem, ac timent lapsus aliquos, et anxii orant, ut confirmentur et regantur. Deinde et scandalo moventur. Adversarii confirmantur, cum illi ipsi deficiunt, qui antea Evangelium acriter defenderant. Totus etiam coetus ducitur esse levior propter aliorum inconstantiam: His scandalis uri bonas mentes manifestum est, sicut et Paulus inquit 2. Corinth. 11.: Quis languet ita, ne simul et ipse langueam, quis movetur scandalo aliquo, ita ne ipse simul urar? Non potest fieri, quin calamitas nostri corporis et membrorum nostrorum dolorem nobis afferat, ut manifesta experientia testatur. Recitatur ergo hoc loco Apostolorum solicitudo et consternatio.

Sed hic considera Iudae duritiem. Ilic monitus et castigatus aliquot dictis Christi, tamen non agit poenitentiam, non flectitur ad cogitandam magnitudinem peccati sui et irae Dei, talis furor, et ferrea durities sequitur, postquam initiis tentationum non repugnatum est, ut, quia Pharao, Saul, Achitophel primas flammas odiorum non extinxerunt, sed aluerunt, postea incendium maius factum est, quam ut extinguere possent. Moniti igitur illis tristissimis exemplis, simus vigilantes et intenti, ac primis initiis ten- tationum repugnemus, non foveamus, non ala- mus impias opiniones in animis. Principiis obsta, sero medicina paratur, Cum mala per longas convaluere moras.

Ingressus est in illum satanas.

Tristis et horrenda descriptio est, et mani- festum testimonium. Diabolum esse spiritum vagantem in aëre, et penetrantem in homines, et impellentem ad scelera, sicut et Paulus nominat diabolos potestates aëris, et ait efficaces esse in impiis. Etsi autem antea quoque Iudas fuit im- pulsus a diabolo, tamen nunc post admonitio- nem, cum non flectitur ad poenitentiam, auge- tur in eo furor, id significatum est, cum nunc dicitur intrasse in eum satanas. Iam pertinacia, amentia, et furor ita confirmantur, ut admoni- tionum finis fiat, qualis est igitur iam Iudas? Hostis Dei, domicilium diaboli, ignorans sese, ac furens, abiectus a Deo, nondum quidem vi- dens iram Dei, sed aliquanto post sensurus, cuin volet fugere extra universam rerum naturam, imo volet in nihilum redigi, nec poterit tamen, ex- cruciabitur aeterno dolore, quod sciens Deum summa contumelia affecerit, qui iussit hunc filium audiri et honore affici, et testimonia suae volun- tatis evidentia ostendit, quod haec Dei testimo- nia spernens, et mandatum eius furiose conte- mnens, Christi necem adiuverit, et cum hosti- bus Dei, et toto regno diaboli blasphemantis Deum conspiraverit. Horum maximorum scele- rum poenae sunt inenarrabiles, sed cogitanda est haec horrenda imago, ut simus vigilantiores, ne diaboli insidiis pertrahamur ad similes lapsus.

Est et hoc dicendum, Iudam libere et vo- lentem assensisse tentationi diaboli, et volentem lapsum esse, nec necessitate fatali aut stoica pec- care, nec Deum velle peccatum Iudae. Tenenda est enim regula tradita a Ioanne: Qui facit pec- catum ex diabolo est, nec transferenda est causa ad fatalem necessitatem, aut ad voluntatem Dei.

## 13:31
Now is the Son of man glorified.

After the departure of Judas, Christ begins a discourse, which now signifies a less troubled mind, and He mixes consolation and doctrine, promises and precepts concerning the greatest matters. The discourse is consumed, however, in these topics: What the Gospel is, what kind of ministry the Gospel is, that the cross must be borne on account of confession, that He is about to send the Holy Spirit, who is effective in the ministry and in the hearts of individuals, that believers are to have eternal life. Finally, He adds most sweet prayers for the Church, which it was necessary to have fixed in our minds. And in this last part all the offices of a priest are clearly seen. Christ teaches the Gospel, prays for us, and afterwards offers His sacrifice. And it is necessary to remember the prayers, because in a sacrifice an application is necessary, that is, the one sacrificing ought to commemorate for whom he asks and offers. When, therefore, your mind asks about the application of these last prayers, you should ponder and know that Christ not only offered a sacrifice, but also applied it to all believers, and prayed for them, so that He may be understood to be a propitiator and intercessor. And let us be consoled here, since Christ has interceded for us, whom it is certain is heard, because the Father said: This is my Son, in whom I am well pleased; let us not doubt that we are received on account of this propitiator and intercessor. This is a sweet and salutary consolation for the pious, and it must be assiduously pondered.

He begins, however, in this place the consolation from the commemoration of His own joy; as long as Judas was present, there was some struggle in the mind of Christ, as consternations often recurred in this supper; He grieves according to nature, looking upon death, but He grieves far more, feeling the wrath of God being poured out upon Himself against the sins of the human race; He sees how much God is angered by sin, and He struggles almost as if fearing rejection; He grieves that a great part of the human race, ungrateful for this redemption, is rushing into eternal punishments. How great these sorrows are, no creature sufficiently understands. But yet there is some taste of it in the Church; at other times, however, the pain is felt more, at other times, the pain having been overcome, the mind rests and is raised up in the promise, presence, and hope of liberation from God. Thus here He says:

Now is the Son of man glorified, that is: Now I feel consolation again; this struggle and this pain, with which I was conflicted as long as Judas was present, having been overcome, I feel new strength, and joyfully and willingly I will obey the Father, and I hope for the salutary liberation of the entire Church; the mind is raised up, looking upon these two things: that He is performing a duty pleasing to God, and that He is being aided by God, and that this obedience will certainly be salutary to the Church of God. Therefore it follows: And God is glorified in Him, that is: After I have been confirmed by the Father, in turn the Father is and will be celebrated by my victory, by my preaching, by my obedience, and because of this obedience a little later the Father will again adorn me with new glory in the resurrection, and soon the discourse slips back again to the passion: Little children, I will not be with you for long and often repeated in this discourse.

Latin:

Nunc glorificatus est filius hominis.

Post exitum Iudae incoat Christus concio- nem, quae iam minus consternatum animum signi- ficat, et consolationem et doctrinam, promissio- nes et praecepta de maximis rebus miscet. Con- sumitur autem concio in his locis: Quid sit Evan- gelium, quale ministerium sit Evangelium, quod ferenda sit crux propter confessionem, quod sit missurus Spiritum sanctum, qui sit efficax in mi- nisterio, et singulorum cordibus, quod creden- tes habituri sint vitam aeternam. Postremo ad- dit dulcissimas precationes pro Ecclesia, quas in- fixas esse animis nostris oportebat. Et in hac postrema parte clare conspiciuntur omnia sacer- dotis officia. Docet Christus Evangelium preca- tur pro nobis, et postea offert suum sacrificium. Ideo autem necesse est meminisse precationes, quia in sacrificio necessaria est applicatio, id est, sacrificans, pro quo petat et offerat, commemo- rare debet. Cum igitur tua mens de applicatione quaerit has ultimas precationes, cogites ac scias Christum non solum obtulisse sacrificium, sed id etiam applicasse omnibus credentibus, et pro eis orasse, ut intelligatur esse propiciator, et inter- cessor. Et hic nos consolemur, cum Christus pro nobis intercesserit, quem exaudiri certum est, quia pater dixit: Hic est filius meus, quo delector, non dubitemus nos propter hunc pro- piciatorem et intercessorem recipi. Haec est piis dulcis et salutaris consolatio, et assidue cogi- tanda est.

Incoat autem hoc loco consolationem a com- memoratione sui gaudii, donec adfuit Iudas, fuit aliqua lucta in mente Christi, ut saepe recurre- runt consternationes in hac coena, dolet secun- dum naturam intuens mortem, sed longe magis dolet sentiens in se effundi iram Dei adversus pec- cata generis humani, videt quantum irascatur Deus peccato, et luctatur pene ut metuens ab- iectionem, dolet magnam partem generis humani ingratam pro hac redemtione, ruere in aeternas poenas. Hi dolores quanti sint, nulla creatura satis intelligit. Sed tamen gustus aliquis est in Ecclesia, alias autem dolor magis sentitur, alias superato dolore mens in Dei promissione, prae- sentia, et spe liberationis acquiescit, et erigitur. Ita hic dicit:

Nunc glorificatus est filius hominis, id est: Nunc rursus sentio consolationem, superata hac lucta et hoc dolore, quo conflictatus sum, donec aderat Iudas, sentio novum robur, ac laetus et volens patri obediam, et spero liberationem sa- lutarem universae Ecclesiae, erigitur mens in- tuens in haec duo, quod Deo gratum officium faciat, et quod a Deo adiuvetur, et certo haec obedientia futura sit salutaris Ecclesiae Dei. Ideo sequitur: Et Deus glorificatus est per eum, id est: Postquam ego a patre confirmatus sum, vi- cissim pater mea victoria, mea praedicatione, mea obedientia celebratur et celebrabitur, et propter hanc obedientiam paulo post rursus me pater nova gloria in resurrectione ornabit, ac mox delabitur sermo rursus ad passionem: Filioli non diu vobiscum ero. Et mox addit praece- ptum maxime necessarium, et saepe repetitum in hac concione.

## 13:34
A new commandment I give to you.

It is certain that the commandment concerning loving God and one's neighbor is eternal and immutable, because the divine mind has always ordained it so, and revealed this sentiment immediately from the beginning, impressed it upon human nature, and handed it down by the vocal word: Love your neighbor as yourself. Since these things are so, and the law concerning love has been repeated so often in the Prophets, why does Christ call it a new commandment? The usual answer is that it is called new, not because of the time when it began to be commanded, but because it is not fulfilled except by the gift of the new testament, namely by the Holy Spirit being given, and I do not criticize this opinion.
