However, it is sufficiently apparent that Christ calls this commandment new, as if to say, not customary to the world, that is, not because all men do not know the law itself, but because no one who is ignorant of the Gospel, and who does not have the fear of God and faith in Christ, performs this law concerning love and the pursuit of public concord, and Christ preaches this especially to rulers. For, being about to depart, he is very solicitous about the concord of the Church and of those who teach, therefore he often inculcates this precept, and with ardent affections signifies his solicitude for posterity.

The whole history of the world shows that the concord of rulers has been rare, and that destructive dissensions have most easily arisen among them; therefore, so that the Apostles may maintain concord, he commands them concerning love, because without love, conflicts are easily ignited. Saul envies the rising David, and grieves that he is being eclipsed. Pompey cannot bear the rising power of Caesar; Aristides and Themistocles are constantly quarreling among themselves. These things happen among those whose minds are without mutual love, but each one wants himself to be valued most highly, and catches at opportunities to suppress others; he does not admonish lovingly, he does not heal the troubles of another. But on the contrary, love first serves the glory of God; it wants this to be seen and celebrated. Then it casts itself down, and willingly yields the lead to others; it does not strive to harm or suppress; it desires to heal the errors of a colleague, therefore it admonishes calmly and lovingly. Since this diligence is full of difficulties, the precept is inculcated so often, so that, mindful of the voice of Christ, we may rather curb our affections, and take care lest we disturb the concord of the Church through ambition, anger, desire for revenge, malevolence, envy, or other diseases of the mind. Let this be enough to have briefly admonished concerning this precept, which experience will declare how necessary, how salutary, and how difficult it is. And let us ourselves, often thinking about this final discourse of Christ, be more diligent in maintaining concord.

Latin:

Mandatum novum do vobis.

Certum est mandatum de diligendo Deo et proximo aeternum et immutabile esse, quia sem- per ita statuit mens divina, et hanc sententiam statim ab initio revelavit, impressit humanae na- turae, et vocali verbo tradidit: Dilige proximum sicut teipsum. Haec cum ita sint, et lex de di- lectione toties sit repetita in Prophetis, cur Chri- stus vocat novum mandatum? usitata responsio est vocari novum, non propter tempus, quo prae- cipi coepit, sed propterea quod non impleatur, nisi novi testamenti dono, scilicet dato Spiritu sancto, nec reprehendo hanc sententiam. Cae- terum satis apparet Christum hoc mandatum vo- care novum, quasi dicat, non usitatum mundo, id est, non quia legem ipsam sciant omnes homi- nes, sed quia nemo ignarus Evangelii, et non habens timorem Dei, et fidem in Christum, prae- stat hanc legem de dilectione et studio publicae concordiae, et praecipue concionatur Christus gu- bernatoribus. Discessurus enim, valde solicitus est de concordia Ecclesiae et docentium, ideo saepe inculcat hoc praeceptum, et ardentibus af- fectibus significat suam solicitudinem de poste- ritate.

Tota mundi historia ostendit raram fuisse gubernatorum concordiam, et facilime exitialia dissidia inter eos exorta esse, ut igitur concor- diam tueantur Apostoli, praecipit de dilectione, quia sine dilectione facile accenduntur certamina. Invidet Saul crescenti Davidi, et se obscurari do- let. Non potest ferre Pompeius crescentem Cae- saris potentiam, assidue rixantur inter se Aristi- des et Themistocles. Haec fiunt inter illos, quo- rum animi sunt sine mutua dilectione, sed unus- quisque sese plurimi fieri vult, et occasiones pre- mendi alios captat, non amanter admonet, non sanat alterius incommoda. At econtra dilectio primum gloriae Dei servit, hanc vult conspici et celebrari. Deinde sese abiicit, et libenter aliis cedit de principatu, non studet laedere, aut pre- mere, errata collegae sanare cupit, ideo placide et amanter admonet. Haec diligentia cum sit difficultatum plena, toties inculcatur praeceptum, ut memores vocis Christi magis frenemus affectus nostros, et caveamus ne ambitione, iracundia, cupiditate vindictae, malevolentia, livore, aut aliis animi morbis turbemus Ecclesiae concordiam. Haec satis sit breviter de hoc praecepto monuisse, quod quam sit necessarium, quam salutare, quam difficile, experientia declarabit. Ac nos quidem ipsi de hac postrema Christi concione saepe cogi- tantes, diligentiores simus in concordia tuenda.

## 13:38
The cock will not crow.

An admonition concerning human weakness is inserted, and foolish confidence is rebuked; Peter dreams of battles and fighting, and confidently offers himself to death, but Christ taxes his confidence and predicts his fall. Let us learn, therefore, not to trust in our own righteousness, or vigilance, or wisdom: for human nature is of itself weak, and falls easily. Furthermore, the snares of the devil are most fierce, who in various ways drives weak nature, just as in Luke 22 Christ says: Simon, Simon, behold Satan has demanded you, that he might sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail, and you, when you have turned, confirm your brothers. This discourse contains many most grave and most ample sentiments. He says that the devil lies in wait for the Church, so that he may scatter and dissipate it. To this most sad voice he adds consolation, that he prays for us, so that our faith may not be extinguished. Finally, he also admonishes that we, having been confirmed, should also confirm others by our testimony. This discourse did not then enter the mind of Peter, occupied with the thought of battles and the worldly kingdom of Christ. But afterwards, when he gathered the words of Christ during his fall, he thought how necessary is the rebuke of human confidence, how sweet the consolation that Christ said he had prayed for him.

But below, one must speak more copiously concerning the fall of Peter, and to this example the falls of other excellent men should be added, so that we may learn to fear security and confidence, just as many sentiments admonish, 1 Corinthians 10: Let him who seems to stand, take heed lest he fall. Matthew 12, Christ says: The unclean spirit returns with seven others joined to him, into the idle house, that is, the secure one, not trembling at the recognition of the wrath of God, not seeking the help of God, but trusting in his own diligence, his own counsels and strengths, and 1 Peter last says: Be vigilant, because your adversary the devil as a roaring lion walks about, seeking whom he may devour, whom resist steadfast in the faith. Man in this depravity of nature is delighted with his own gifts, and when there is tranquility and quiet, he is pleased with himself on account of his gifts, and is puffed up and forgets God, and is often carried beyond the bounds, that is, beyond his calling, so that Josiah, although a holy king, yet in his successes becomes bolder, and moves war without necessity, so to all men many sad events happen, when in tranquility, trusting in human counsels or fortune, they undertake something more easily than they would in a sad time, as it is written: The people sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play. Let us therefore be vigilant, and let us especially fear tranquility, which is accustomed to bring some sad events to all, both high and low. But below, more will be said about Peter's fall and conversion.

Latin:

Non cantabit gallus.

Inseritur admonitio de imbecillitate humana, et reprehenditur stulta confidentia, Petrus so- mniat pugnas et dimicationem, et se morti confi- denter offert, sed Christus taxat confidentiam, ac praedicit eius lapsum. Discamus ergo non confi- dere propria iusticia, vel vigilantia, vel sapien- tia: nam humana natura per sese est imbecillis, et facile labitur. Deinde accerrimae sunt insidiae diaboli, qui variis modis imbecillem naturam im- pellit, sicut Lucae 22. inquit Christus: Simon, Simon, ecce Satanas expetivit vos, ut cribraret vos tanquam triticum. Ego autem rogavi pro te, ne deficiat fides tua, et tu conversus confirma fra- tres tuos. Haec concio multas gravissimas et am- plissimas sententias continet. Ait diabolum in- sidiari Ecclesiae, ut eam dispergat et dissipet. Huic tristissimae voci addit consolationem, quod pro nobis oret, ne fides nostra extinguatur. Po- stremo etiam monet, ut nos confirmati nostro te- stimonio etiam alios confirmemus. Haec concio tunc non subiit animum Petri, occupatum cogi- tatione de praeliis et regno mundano Christi. Sed postea cum in lapsu dicta Christi colligeret, cogitavit quam necessaria sit reprehensio huma- nae confidentiae, quam dulcis consolatio, quod pro se deprecatum esse dixit Christus.

Infra autem de lapsu Petri copiosius dicen- dum est, et huic exemplo aliorum excellentium virorum lapsus addantur, ut securitatem et confi- dentiam metuere discamus, sicut multae senten- tiae monent, 1. Corinth. 10. : Qui videtur stare, videat ne cadat. Matth. 12. ait Christus: Spiri- tum immundum redire adiunctis aliis septem, in domum otiosam, id est, securam, non expave- scentem agnitione irae Dei, non petentem auxi- lium Dei, sed confidentem propria diligentia, pro- priis consiliis et viribus, et 1. Petri ult. dicit: Vigilate, quia adversarius vester diabolus tan- quam leo rugiens circumit, quaerens quem de- voret, cui resistite fortes in fide. Homo in hac depravatione naturae delectatur suis donis, et cum est tranquillitas et quies, placet sibi propter dona, et effertur ac obliviscitur Dei, et saepe extra metas, id est, extra vocationem provehitur, ut Iosias quanquam sanctus rex, tamen in successi- bus fit audacior, et bellum movet sine necessi- tate, ita omnibus hominibus multi tristes casus accidunt, cum in tranquillitate confisi humanis consiliis aut fortuna, facilius aliquid suscipiunt, quam facerent tristi tempore, sicut scriptum est: Sedit populus manducare et bibere, et surrexit ludere. Simus igitur vigilantes, et maxime me- tuamus tranquillitatem, quae solet omnibus sum- mis et infimis afferre aliquos tristes casus. Infra autem de Petri lapsu et conversione plura dicentur.

## 14:1 Argument
Chapter XIV.

Latin:

Caput XIV.

## 14:1
Let not your heart be troubled.

Christ began a long discourse, in which he variously mixes consolations and doctrine, and an interruption provides an occasion for new statements, when he had said: Let not your heart be troubled, in my Father's house are many mansions, that is, Even if exiles, great hardships and deaths must be endured here, yet know that you will have life, joy, and eternal glory in heaven with the whole Church, and indeed there are many mansions. Although the Church is a small group, if it is compared to the multitude of the impious, yet it will be great, nor was the labor of the Fathers and Prophets in vain, nor will the labor of the Apostles and succeeding pastors be empty, as it is said in Isaiah ch. 55: My word, which goes forth from my mouth, shall not return to me empty, but shall do whatever I have willed, and shall prosper in those things for which I sent it. There always has been, is, and will be some Church of God and kingdom of Christ. Nor would the world stand, unless there were some elect, for whose sake God preserves the human race: although therefore in such a smallness of the Church pastors often doubt whether there are any members of the people of God among their hearers, yet let them remember these words: My word shall not return to me empty. Likewise: The Gospel is the power of God. And John 20: As the Father has sent me, so I send you. Matthew last: Behold I am with you all days even to the consummation of the age. Let us sustain ourselves with these sweetest and firmest consolations, when in such confusion of men minds seek about the efficacy of the ministry. The beginning therefore of this discourse consoles the Church and the ministers, and testifies that in this life labors will not be in vain, and after this life they will have eternal goods.

Then, interrupted by Thomas, as to where he is going, he again meets a new doubt. Minds are tormented, even if we know that great rewards, great glory are proposed to the Church, yet what must be done, by what counsels such a mass of affairs must be governed, what must be taught, how doctrine must be carried around against opposing empires, how men must be governed without armies and without weapons, this indeed is obscure. What seems more absurd than that a few weak men, equipped with no power, like wanderers, running through the whole world, should attempt a change of the world, and promise men eternal goods, when they themselves are involved in the greatest miseries? Christ cuts off these objections about the absurdity of such a plan and about the difficulty, commanding all that the Apostles should follow him as their leader, and trust in his help alone, that he will be the accomplisher of such a thing, that he will incline the minds of the people to embrace the Gospel, and will lead the believers to God, that he will cast a bridle upon tyrants. These are great promises, which far exceed all human counsels and human strengths. Therefore they are laughed at profusely by impious wise men. But let us in the Church know that this consolation is true, and must necessarily be inculcated to individuals, so that minds may be strengthened against the difficulties of the profession of the Gospel in private and public life. On this occasion he says:

I am the way, the truth, and the life,

And the emphasis is in the demonstration: I, I say, the Son of God, sent that I may be leader and liberator, will help you, I will be with you even to the consummation of the age. I will be the way, that is, the shower of the way, the giver of counsel, removing those things which, either privately or publicly, impede the journey of salvation. I am the truth, that is, the author of true doctrine concerning the will of God and concerning eternal salvation, flee and execrate all opinions fighting with my doctrine. Finally, I am the life, that is, my death appeases the wrath of God, and it deserves to be abolished, sin and death. And furthermore, I give righteousness and eternal life.

And he repeats the same sentence: No one comes to the Father, except through me. This sentence must be opposed to all the religions of all nations, which are outside the Gospel; neither the Eleusinian, nor the Mahometan, nor the Jewish religion leads to God. Indeed, not even in the Church, as it is called, does any monastic worship lead to God, nor any human works, once the true recognition and trust in Christ have been extinguished. Let us therefore remember this saying as a principal testimony to be opposed to all religions outside the Gospel, and likewise to the errors in the Church, which taught that one approaches God through monastic worship, through the invocation of the dead, through Masses and other works; but let the affirmative sentence also be held, that those who approach God with trust in Christ are certainly received by God and certainly heard, just as it is said in Romans 5: Through him we have access into this grace. Likewise John 16: Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you. Finally, always in every life, in every action, and in every invocation, let this sentence be in sight, containing wholesome doctrine and consolation: No one comes to the Father, except through me. Nor is it obscure to one who moderately understands the doctrine of faith, by which we are reconciled and righteous on account of Christ.

Latin:

Non turbetur cor vestrum.

Exorsus est Christus longam concionem, in qua varie miscet consolationes et doctrinam, et interpellatio praebet occasionem novis sententiis, cum dixisset: Non turbetur cor vestrum, in domo patris mei mansiones multae sunt, id est, Etiamsi hic toleranda erunt exilia, magnae aerumnae et neces, tamen scitote, vos in coelo vitam, laeti- tiam et gloriam sempiternam cum universa Ec- clesia habituros esse, et quidem multae sunt man- siones. Ecclesia etsi est exiguus coetus, si con- feratur ad impiorum multitudinem, tamen ma- gnus erit, nec fuit irritus labor Patrum et Pro- phetarum, nec Apostolorum et sequentium pa- storum labor inanis erit, sicut Esaiae cap. 55. di- citur: Verbum meum, quod egreditur de ore meo, non revertetur ad me vacuum, sed faciet quae- cunque volui, et prosperabitur in his, ad quae misi illud. Semper fuit, est, et erit aliqua Dei Ecclesia et regnum Christi. Nec staret mun- dus, nisi aliqui essent electi, propter quos Deus servat genus humanum: etsi igitur in tanta pau- citate Ecclesiae pastores saepe dubitant, an inter auditores suos sint aliqua membra populi Dei, ta- men haec dicta meminerint: Non revertetur ad me verbum vacuum. Item: Evangelium est po- tentia Dei. Et Ioan. 20.: Sicut misit me pater, sic et ego mitto vos. Matthaei ultimo: Ecce ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus usque ad con- summationem seculi. His dulcissimis et firmissi- mis consolationibus nos sustentemus, cum in tanta confusione hominum quaerunt animi de efficacia ministerii, Initium ergo huius concionis conso- latur Ecclesiam et ministros, ac testatur in hac vita labores non fore irritos, et post hanc vitam habituros esse aeterna bona.

Deinde interpellatus a Thoma, quo vadat, rursus occurrit novae dubitationi. Anguntur animi, etiamsi scimus magna praemia, magnam gloriam Ecclesiae propositam esse, tamen quid agendum sit, quibus consiliis tanta moles rerum regenda sit, quid docendum sit, quomodo adver- santibus imperiis circumferenda sit doctrina, quo- modo regendi sint homines sine exercitibus et sine armis, hoc vero obscurum est. Quid vide- tur absurdius, quam paucos imbecilles homines, nulla instructos potentia, velut errones, discur- rentes per totum orbem terrarum, moliri muta- tionem orbis terrarum, et polliceri hominibus aeterna bona, cum in maximis miseriis versentur ipsi? Has obiectiones de absurditate tanti consilii et de difficultate praecidit Christus, omnes iu- bens, ut sequantur Apostoli se ducem, et suo unius auxilio confidant, se fore perfectorem tan- tae rei, se populi animos inclinaturum esse ad Evangelium amplectendum, et ducturum creden- tes ad Deum, se frenum iniecturum esse tyran- nis. Magna haec promissa sunt, quae longe su- perant omnia humana consilia et humanas vires. Ideo ab impiis sapientibus effuse ridentur. Sed nos in Ecclesia sciamus hanc consolationem ve- ram, et necessario inculcandam esse singulis, ut animi adversus difficultates professionis Evange- lii in vita privata et publica confirmentur. Hac occasione dicit:

Ego sum via, veritas, et vita,

Et emphasis est in demonstratione: Ego ego inquam, filius Dei, missus ut sim dux, et li- berator adiuvabo vos, ero vobiscum usque ad con- summationem seculi. Ero via, id est, monstrator viae, dator consilii, tollens ea, quae vel priva- tim, vel publice iter salutis impediunt. Ego sum veritas, id est, verae doctrinae de voluntate Dei, et de salute aeterna autor, fugite et execramini omnes opiniones cum mea doctrina pugnantes. Denique, Ego sum vita, id est, mea mors placat iram Dei, et meretur aboleri peccatum et mor- tem. Ac insuper ego do iusticiam et vitam ae- ternam.

Et repetit eandem sententiam: Nemo venit ad patrem, nisi per me. Haec sententia oppo- nenda est omnibus omnium gentium religionibus, quae sunt extra Evangelium, non Eleusini, non Mahometica, non Iudaica religio perducit ad Deum. Imo nec in Ecclesia, quae sic vocatur, perducit ad Deum ullus cultus monasticus, non ulla humana opera, extincta vera agnitione et fiducia Christi. Meminerimus ergo hoc dictum, tanquam principale testimonium opponendum omnibus religionibus extra Evangelium, item er- roribus in Ecclesia, qui docuerunt accedere ad Deum per cultus monasticos, per invocationem mortuorum, per Missas et alia opera, sed te- neatur etiam affirmativa sententia certo recipi a Deo, et certo exaudiri accedentes ad Deum fidu- cia Christi, sicut ad Romanos 5. dicitur: Per hunc habemus accessum in gratiam hanc. Item Ioan. 16.: Quicquid petieritis patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis. Denique semper in omni vita, in omni actione, et in omni invocatione, sit in conspectu haec sententia, continens salutarem doctrinam et consolationem: Nemo venit ad pa- trem, nisi per me. Nec obscura est mediocriter intelligenti doctrinam de fide, qua propter Chri- stum reconciliati et iusti sumus.

## 14:8
Show us the Father, and it is enough for us.

Although this question seems to be proposed thoughtlessly, and to ask for too great and unusual a thing, yet in truth the minds of wise men from the beginning of the world until the end have sought and do seek this sight of God. We all wonder what God is, what his nature is like, what his counsels are in governance, why he allows such a multitude of people to perish, why he allows such various and monstrous opinions about the essence of God and about the variety of worships to spread, which is the one and true worship, why the Church of God in this life is subject to such great miseries. Finally, what kind of good is eternal life and communion with God. We think that all these mysteries could be comprehended in one glance if we saw God face to face. Certainly, if the Apostles had stood by this questioner, all the wise men of the world, Solon, Socrates, Plato, Xenophon, and others like them, would all have praised this petition and said that they were seeking the same thing.

But this thought about the manner of knowing God, and this desire, arise from the darkness of the human heart, which does not want to acknowledge God in the word, as he has revealed himself, but seeks God through its own imaginations, whence infinite opinions and infinite worships have always arisen in the world, and human minds do not understand how great this evil is.

But let us in the Church, being admonished, learn how God wishes to be sought and acknowledged, which is taught elsewhere often, but especially in this very saying: He who sees me, sees the Father; and 1 Corinthians 1: After the world did not know God in the wisdom of God through wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe; and at Romans 10: Do not say in your heart: Who will ascend into heaven? but the word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart. At Romans 1: The Gospel is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes. Let us diligently think upon these sayings and similar ones, for it is the singular wisdom of the Church not to seek God otherwise than through the word and testimonies handed down by him, nor to address any other God than this very one, who, by sending his Son and giving his Gospel, has so often revealed himself with certain testimonies. Christ teaches this doctrine especially in this saying: He who sees me, sees the Father.

Latin:

Ostende nobis patrem, et sufficit nobis.

Etsi haec quaestio videtur incogitanter pro- poni, et nimis magnam et inusitatam rem pe- tere, tamen revera ita hominum sapientum animi ab initio mundi usque ad finem expetiverunt, et expetunt hunc Dei conspectum. Omnes mira- mur quid sit Deus, qualis sit eius natura, qualia consilia in gubernatione, cur tantam multitudi- nem hominum perire sinat, cur tam varias et monstrosas opiniones de Dei essentia et de va- rietate cultuum grassari sinat, qui sit unicus et verus cultus, cur Ecclesia Dei in hac vita tantis aerumnis subiecta sit. Denique quale bonum sit vita aeterna et consuetudo cum Deo. Haec ar- cana omnia uno contuitu comprehendi posse co- gitamus, si Deum coram cerneremus. Certe si astitissent hoc interroganti Apostolo, omnes sa- pientes mundi, Solon, Socrates, Plato, Xeno- phon, et alii similes, omnes hanc petitionem laudassent, et se idem petere dixissent.

Sed haec cogitatio de modo cognoscendi Deum, et haec cupiditas ex tenebris humani cor- dis oriuntur, quod non vult Deum in verbo agno- scere, sicut se ipse patefecit, sed quaerit Deum propriis imaginationibus, unde infinitae opinio- nes et infiniti cultus in mundo semper exorti sunt, nec intelligunt humanae mentes quantum hoc malum sit.

Sed nos in Ecclesia admoniti discamus, quo- modo velit quaeri et agnosci Deus, quod alias saepe, sed praecipue traditur in hoc ipso dicto: Qui videt me, videt patrem, et 1. Corinth. 1.: Postquam mundus non novit Deum in sapientia Dei per sapientiam, placuit Deo per stultitiam praedicationis salvos facere credentes, et ad Rom. 10.: Ne dixeris in corde tuo: Quis ascen- det in coelum: sed prope est verbum in ore tuo et in corde tuo. Ad Rom. 1.: Evangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti. Haec dicta et similia assidue cogitemus, est enim sin- gularis sapientia Ecclesiae, non aliter quaerere Deum, nisi per verbum et testimonia ab ipso tra- dita, nec alium Deum alloqui, nisi hunc ipsum, qui se misso filio, et dato Evangelio suo, toties certis testimoniis patefecit. Hanc doctrinam prae- cipue tradit Christus in hoc dicto: Qui videt me, videt patrem.

## 14:9
I have been with you for so long a time.

Christ mixes a rebuke, by which he censures this huge evil and sin, that we all seek God otherwise, and seek other illuminations and revelations, omitting the voice of the Gospel, just as the Gentiles, Mahometans, Enthusiasts, and Anabaptists depart from the word of God and invent for themselves peculiar opinions outside the word of God, and either boast of or expect singular illuminations. But Christ draws us back to his person and his Gospel: Me, he says, the Father sent, that he might be testified of through me; invoke this Father who sent me and is in me, and think of me when you are about to approach the Father, as I said before: No one comes to the Father, except through me; and you will thus apprehend me if you hear, embrace, and believe this word of mine which I have handed down to you, just as it is said below: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him. Let hearts truly tremble when they have heard the voice of God rebuking sin, and let them truly believe that they are being rebuked and judged by this very God, who his with a voice he rebuked Adam for his fall in Paradise, and sent Christ, that he might preach repentance and the remission of sins. Again, let hearts also sustain themselves with the voice of the Gospel, and let them look upon the mediator crucified and raised from the dead, and truly know that they are received by the eternal Father on his account. Let them know that this mediator sits at the right hand of the Father, that he may give his gifts to the Church; let them call upon him, from him let them seek gifts, just as he promised.

Latin:

Tanto tempore vobiscum sum.

Miscet obiurgationem Christus, qua hoc in- gens malum et peccatum taxat, quod omnes quae- rimus Deum aliter, et expetimus alias illumina- tiones et revelationes, omissa voce Evangelii, sicut Ethnici, Mahometistae, Enthusiastae, Ana- baptistae, discedunt a verbo Dei, et fingunt sibi opiniones peculiares extra verbum Dei, et aut iactant, aut expectant singulares illuminationes. At Christus retrahit nos ad suam personam et suum Evangelium: Me, inquit, misit pater, ut de se testificetur, hunc patrem, qui me misit, et in me est, invoca, et de me cogita accessurus ad patrem, sicut antea dixi: Nemo venit ad patrem, nisi per me, ac me ita apprehendetis, si hoc meum verbum, quod tradidi vobis, audietis, amplecte- mini, credetis, sicut infra dicitur: Si quis dili- git me, sermonem meum servabit, et pater meus diliget eum, et ad eum veniemus, et mansionem apud eum faciemus. Corda vere expavescant au- dita voce Dei arguente peccatum, et vere credant se ab hoc ipso Deo obiurgari et iudicari, qui sua voce Adam lapsum in Paradiso obiurgabat, et misit Christum, ut praedicet poenitentiam et re- missionem peccatorum. Rursus etiam se susten- tent corda voce Evangelii, et intueantur media- torem crucifixum et resuscitatum, et revera sciant se propter eum recipi ab aeterno patre. Hunc mediatorem sciant sedere ad dextram patris, ut det dona sua Ecclesiae, hunc invocent, ab hoc petant dona, sicut promisit.

## 14:9
He who sees me, sees the Father.

This is the affirmation of this doctrine, that God must be sought through the knowledge of the Son crucified and raised from the dead, and of the Gospel, in which this Son of God is preached. He who is ignorant of the Son thinks rightly neither of the essence nor of the will of God. The wise, the Gentiles, the Mahometans, and recent Jews err openly concerning the essence, because they deny that this is the God the Creator who sent this Son crucified and raised from the dead. Nay, they abhor this Son as a most foul idol. And meanwhile they fashion for themselves some creator, and devise certain cults of their own by which they may celebrate him. Christ condemns this whole blindness, John 5, saying: He who does not honor the Son, does not honor the Father. Then they also err concerning the will, and although the knowledge of the law remains in some way, yet no one can certainly establish that he is received and heard by God, unless he acknowledges Christ the mediator through the Gospel: the Gentiles called upon [their gods], and recited long hymns; the Mahometans, Jews, Papists, and all who are ignorant of the Gospel call upon [God] now, but they by no means establish that they and their prayers are received. They judge in their minds that the unworthy are not received, and they acknowledge that they are each unworthy; therefore they doubt whether they are received, and at last are oppressed by despair.

Against both these darknesses, this sentence must be held: He who sees me, sees the Father. Seeking concerning the essence and will of God, look upon Christ crucified and raised from the dead. This is truly God, who has revealed himself through this Son, and this is truly his will, which this Son announces, who said: This is the will of the Father who sent me, that everyone who believes in the Son may have eternal life. This doctrine can neither be understood nor learned, except in the true struggle and true exercises of invocation. Looking upon the Son, know that he is always in the bosom of the eternal Father, just as he says here: I am in the Father, and the Father is in me. And John 1: The Son who is in the bosom of the Father. Likewise, chapter 8: No one has ascended into heaven, but he who descended from heaven, the Son of man, who is in heaven. Although these sayings far surpass the grasp of all creatures, yet they must be held by us by faith, and they teach that the divine nature is in Christ, and that the eternal Father and the Son are always together, and together perform all works which are done divinely, just as it is said in John 5: My Father works until now, and I work. They teach likewise that the will of the Father and the Son agree, and that no other will of God is to be thought of than that which has been announced through the Son in the Gospel. Just as he also says here: The words which I speak, I do not speak from myself, but the Father remaining in me, he himself does the works, etc. Let us therefore oppose these sayings to all speculations about God, which human reason devises having abandoned the Gospel, and let us bind our minds to this Christ crucified and raised from the dead, and to his Gospel, and let us not allow ourselves to be torn away from it, as many have always been torn away from it by human imaginations, and are being torn away.

He who believes in me, the works which I do, etc.

There is great consolation for the pious in such great miseries of the Church, which, when we look upon them, we seem to be neglected by God, and to carry the Gospel in vain, and that this voice of the Gospel is an empty sound, not changing men, not bringing the reconciliation of God and eternal life. Finally, we seem to move the world in vain, and only bring miseries and torments upon ourselves. Against this false imagination, Christ consoles and confirms us with this most ample promise: He who believes in me, the works which I do, he also will do, and he will do greater things than these. Christ does not speak only of miracles which strike the eyes, such as the healings of lepers, or of the blind, or of the lame. These are not the principal works for which Christ came, and for which the voice of the Gospel was given, but there are other greater ones, of which Paul says: The Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes. Those healings of bodies are indeed testimonies of the doctrine, and the Church always has some bodily miracles too, but sometimes more, sometimes less conspicuous and glorious, but let eternal benefits be placed far above these healings of bodies. The Gospel is not an empty sound, but it is truly a ministry by which God gives the remission of sins, the Holy Spirit, eternal life, and to those called to eternal life many wonderful deliverances occur, even if we ourselves do not know or understand them all, just as the infant Moses, the captive Joseph, David, and countless others were miraculously preserved and governed by God, and all things which they do are full of miracles.

Because I go to the Father, and whatever you shall ask, etc.

He adds the reason why the course of the Apostles will be effective and salutary, why they will perform great miracles, and accomplish salutary things.

Because, he says, I go to the Father, that is, because after I have redeemed the human race, I shall reign together with the Father, having been raised from the dead by my death; I shall be present with you, I shall be a helper and an effector. And soon the promise is added which contains the testimonies of two very great things. First, he teaches that Christ is God by nature. Christ says twice that he will do whatever the Church asks: he affirms, therefore, that he hears those who pray, and looks into the hearts of men, and is the effector of all the deliverances which are divinely given to us. These are things of an omnipotent, divine, and creative nature. Nor is there need of a long declaration in this testimony, for it is clear; the reader only needs to be admonished to weigh it, carry it about with him, and often think upon it, just as he said above in chapter 5: My Father works until now, and I work. Likewise, what the Father does, these things the Son also does in like manner. Let these and similar things be said in our sight, so that we may fortify ourselves against the impious furies of Samosatenus and Arius, and acknowledge the Son of God to be God by nature, and omnipotent and ὁμοούσιον to the Father, and truly call upon him. For unless this sentiment is retained, invocation cannot take place.

Secondly: This promise in the text teaches us about invocation, how it should be done, and affirms that our prayers are received, and that we certainly obtain those things which we ask. As often as we say our prayers, let us repeat this saying, and let us rouse our languishing, doubting, and fleeing minds. By this ample promise we are drawn to God, and we are commanded to invoke him; let us therefore obey, and let us approach God, just as this voice of Christ teaches us to approach. It was said above that five things must concur in prayer: thought about the commandment, the promise concerning God to whom the invocation is directed, which must be distinguished from the invocations of all impious nations, likewise about faith, and about the thing to be asked. This doctrine, even though it is often handed down, yet it is necessary to repeat it in this saying, because here the mode of invocation is proposed. The commandments are known: Ask and you shall receive. Likewise: Call upon me in the day of tribulation. Many promises also exist here and there, but in this very place the principal one is recited: Whatever you shall ask in my name, this I will do.

But how our invocation is to be distinguished from the Ethnic, Mahometan, and Jewish, these words teach: In my name. And there is a double distinction, one concerning the essence, the other concerning the will of God. For although Ethnics, Mahometans, or Jews confess that there is some one God, the creator of heaven and earth and of other created things, yet they do not believe in God as he has revealed himself, nor do they assent that this is truly the God the creator who sent his Son our Lord Jesus Christ, crucified for us and raised from the dead. But they wander in their minds, nor do they determine whom they invoke, who that God is, or by what testimony he has revealed himself, whom they seek. Therefore, Ethnics devise such varied divinities; one feigns that God is found by the worship of Pallas, another by the worship of Apollo, another by the worship of Jupiter, another by the worship of Mars. But God forbids minds to wander in this way, and binds us to the revelation and to this Son, as was said above: He who sees me, sees the Father. And here it is said: In my name, that is: Approach God by naming me, or having acknowledged me; invoke this God who has revealed himself through me, and who willed me to bring his word to you, by which he might be truly known. Furthermore, all nations ignorant of the Gospel err concerning his will, because they do not know whether and why they are heard: the Church knows that the promises were given on account of the Son, and knows that this mediator was appointed, and that we are heard on account of him, not on account of our own dignity. This sentiment also teaches this: Whatever you shall ask the Father in my name, that is, naming me, and acknowledging me as the mediator interceding for you before the Father. It is necessary that all these things be thought upon daily in invocation.

Fourthly: Let faith approach, or rather shine forth, which may determine concerning the remission of sins, given on account of Christ. For as long as the mind flees from God and does not believe in the remission of sins, it by no means determines that its prayers are received. Therefore, it is necessary that this faith shine forth, of which Paul says in Romans 5: By faith we have access to God through Christ. This very doctrine concerning faith is also comprehended in the saying of this place: Whatever you shall ask in my name, that is, acknowledging me as mediator, establishing that you are received on my account. And let this same faith establish that our prayers are received and heard, and that they will not be in vain.

Fifth: Let the things to be requested be considered in prayer, the goods of spirit and body, just as the daily petition itself embraces goods of both kinds.

I have briefly reviewed these things concerning prayer, because this saying of the text cannot be illustrated without this commemoration. Now in daily invocation let us propose this saying to ourselves, and let us impress it, that we may learn to approach God and to ask for good things. In this experience these words will become clearer: In my name, that is, acknowledging me as mediator, trusting in me as intercessor and advocate for you, to whom the eternal Father has especially delivered the promise of the priesthood, on my account he certainly wishes to hear, and wishes to be worshipped in this way, and to be affected with this honor, namely, invocation made by faith, or trust in our Lord Jesus Christ, and thus invoking we shall experience without any doubt that prayers are effective, and that we obtain the salutary things which we ask for, etc.

Latin:

Qui videt me, videt patrem.

Asseveratio est huius doctrinae, quaeren- dum esse Deum agnitione filii crucifixi et resus- citati, et Evangelii, in quo hic filius Dei praedi- catur. Nec de essentia, nec de voluntate Dei recte sentit, ignorans filium. Sapientes, Eth- nici, Mahometistae, Iudaei recentes, de essen- tia palam errant, quia negant hunc esse Deum creatorem, qui misit hunc filium crucifixum et resuscitatum. Imo hunc filium abominantur, ut teterrimum idolum. Ac interim fingunt sibi ali- quem creatorem, et suos quosdam cultus excogi- tant, quibus eum celebrent. Hanc totam caeci- tatem damnat Christus, Ioannis 5. dicens: Qui non honorat filium, non honorat patrem. Deinde et de voluntate errant, etiamsi legis noticia ut- cunque manet, tamen nemo potest certo statuere recipi et exaudiri se a Deo, nisi per Evangelium agnoscat Christum mediatorem: invocarunt Eth- nici, et longos hymnos recitarunt, invocant et nunc Mahometistae, Iudaei, Papistae, et omnes ignorantes Evangelium, sed nequaquam statuunt, se et preces suas recipi. Iudicant mentes, non recipi indignos, et agnoscunt se singuli esse in- dignos, dubitant igitur an recipiantur, et tan- dem desperatione opprimuntur.

Adversus has tenebras utrasque tenenda est sententia: Qui videt me, videt patrem. De Dei essentia et voluntate quaerens, intuearis Chri- stum crucifixum et resuscitatum. Hic est vere Deus, qui se per hunc filium patefecit, et haec vere eius voluntas est, quam hic filius annunciat, qui dixit: Haec est voluntas patris, qui misit me, ut omnis qui credit in filium, habeat vitam aeter- nam. Haec doctrina nec intelligi, nec disci po- test, nisi in vero agone et veris exercitiis invoca- tionis. Aspiciens filium, scito hunc semper in sinu esse aeterni patris, sicut hic inquit: Ego sum in patre, et pater in me est. Et Ioann. 1.: Filius qui est in sinu patris. Item, cap. 8.: Ne- mo ascendit in coelum, nisi qui ex coelo descendit, filius hominis, qui est in coelo. Haec dicta etsi longe omnium creaturarum captum superant, tamen a nobis fide tenenda sunt, ac docent in Christo naturam divinam esse, et aeternum patrem et filium semper simul esse, et simul efficere opera omnia, quae divinitus fiunt, sicut Ioann. 5. dicitur: Pater meus usque modo operatur, et ego operor. Docent item congruere voluntatem patris et filii, nec aliam cogitandam esse voluntatem Dei, quam illam quae in Evangelio per filium annunciata est. Sicut et hic ait: Verba quae ego loquor, a me ipso non loquor, sed pater in me manens, ipse facit opera, etc. Opponamus ergo haec dicta omnibus speculationibus de Deo, quas ratio humana relicto Evangelio comminiscitur, et ad hunc Christum crucifixum et resuscitatum, et ad Evangelium eius mentes nostras alligemus, nec inde nos avelli sinamus, ut multi inde imaginationibus humanis semper avulsi sunt, et avelluntur.

Qui credit in me, opera, quae ego facio, etc.

Magna consolatio est piis in tantis miseriis Ecclesiae, quas cum aspicimus, videmur a Deo negligi, et frustra circumferre Evangelium, et hanc vocem Evangelii inanem sonitum esse, non mutare homines, non afferre reconciliationem Dei et vitam aeternam. Denique videmur frustra movere orbem terrarum, et tantum nobis miserias et cruciatus accersere. Adversus hanc falsam imaginationem Christus consolatur, et confirmat nos hac amplissima promissione: Qui credit in me, opera, quae ego facio, et ipse faciet, et maiora his faciet. Non loquitur Christus tantum de miraculis, quae incurrunt in oculos, ut de sanationibus leprosorum, aut caecorum, aut claudorum. Haec non sunt praecipua opera propter quae venit Christus, et propter quae data est vox Evangelii, sed alia maiora sunt, de quibus dicit Paulus: Evangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti. Sanationes illae corporum sunt quidem testimonia doctrinae, et semper habet Ecclesia aliqua etiam corporalia miracula, sed alias magis, alias minus conspicua et gloriosa, sed longe supra has corporum sanationes collocentur beneficia aeterna. Evangelium non est inanis sonitus, sed vere est ministerium, quo Deus dat remissionem peccatorum, Spiritum sanctum, vitam aeternam, et vocatis ad vitam aeter- nam multae liberationes mirandae contingunt, etiamsi non omnes ipsi novimus aut intelligimus, sicut Moses infans, Ioseph captivus, David et alii innumeri, mirabiliter a Deo servati et guber- nati sunt, et plena sunt miraculorum omnia quae gerunt.

Quia ego vado ad patrem, et quicquid petie- ritis, etc.

Causam addit, cur futurus sit efficax et sa- lutaris cursus Apostolorum, cur magna miracula facturi sint, et res salutares effecturi.

Quia, inquit, ego vado ad patrem, id est, quia ego postquam redemero humanum genus, mea morte resuscitatus regnabo una cum patre, adero vobis, ero opitulator et effector. Et mox additur promissio quae duarum maximarum re- rum testimonia continet. Primum docet Chri- stum natura Deum esse. Bis inquit Christus, sese facturum esse, quicquid petit Ecclesia: affirmat ergo se exaudire precantes, et corda hominum introspicere, et effectorem esse omnium liberatio- num, quae nobis divinitus donantur. Haec sunt naturae omnipotentis, divinae et creatricis. Nec longa declaratione opus est in hoc testimonio, est enim perspicuum, tantum monendus est lector, ut expendat et secum circumferat, ac saepe cogi- tet, sic supra dixit cap. 5.: Pater meus usque modo operatur, et ego operor. Item, quae pater facit, haec et filius similiter facit. Haec et simi- lia dicta sint in conspectu, ut nos adversus impios furores Samosateni et Arii muniamus, et agno- scamus filium Dei natura Deum, et omnipoten- tem et ὁμοούσιον esse patri, et eum vere invo- cemus. Nisi enim haec sententia retinetur, non potest fieri invocatio.

Secundo: Haec promissio in textu docet nos de invocatione, quomodo facienda sit, et affirmat recipi nostras preces, et certo impetrare ea quae petimus. Quoties dicimus nostras preces, repe- tamus hoc dictum, et languentes, dubitantes, fu- gitantes animos excitemus. Hac ampla promis- sione trahimur ad Deum, et invocare iubemur, obtemperemus igitur, et accedamus ad Deum, sicut haec vox Christi accedere docet. Dictum est supra in precatione quinque res concurrere opor- tere, cogitationem de praecepto, promissione de Deo, ad quem dirigitur invocatio, discernenda ab invocationibus omnium gentium impiarum, item de fide, et de re petenda. Hanc doctrinam, etsi saepe traditur, tamen in hoc dicto repeti ne- cesse est, quia hic modus invocationis proponi- tur. Praecepta nota sunt: Petite et accipietis. Item: Invoca me in die tribulationis. Promis- siones etiam multae passim extant, sed in hoc ipso loco praecipua recitatur: Quicquid petetis in nomine meo, hoc faciam.

Sed quomodo discernenda sit nostra invoca- tio ab Ethnica, Mahometica et Iudaica, id do- cent haec verba: In nomine meo. Ac duplex discrimen est, alterum de essentia, alterum de voluntate Dei. Etsi enim Ethnici, Mahometistae, aut Iudaei fatentur unum aliquem esse Deum, conditorem coeli et terrae, et aliarum rerum crea- tarum, tamen non credunt Deum, ut se patefe- cit, nec assentiuntur hunc esse vere Deum condi- torem, qui misit filium dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, crucifixum pro nobis et resuscitatum. Sed vagantur animis, nec constituunt quid invo- cent, quid sit ille Deus, aut quo testimonio se patefecerit, quem quaerunt. Ideo Ethnici tam varia numina excogitant, alius fingit inveniri Deum cultu Palladis, alius cultu Apollinis, alius cultu Iovis, alius cultu Martis. Prohibet autem Deus sic vagari animos, et alligat nos ad patefa- ctionem et ad hunc filium, ut supra dictum est: Qui videt me, videt patrem. Et hic dicitur: In nomine meo, id est: Accedite ad Deum me nomi- nato, seu agnito, hunc Deum invocate qui se pa- tefecit per me, et me voluit ad vos perferre suum verbum, quo vere innotesceret. Deinde de vo- luntate errant omnes gentes ignarae Evangelii, quia non norunt, an et cur exaudiantur: Eccle- sia scit promissiones datas esse propter filium, et scit hunc mediatorem constitutum esse, et nos pro- pter eum exaudiri, non propter nostram dignita- tem. Id etiam docet haec sententia: Quicquid petieritis patrem in nomine meo, id est, me no- minantes, et me agnoscentes mediatorem interce- dentem pro vobis apud patrem. Haec omnia quotidie cogitari in invocatione necesse est.

Quarto: Accedat, imo praeluceat fides, quae statuat de remissione peccatorum, donata propter Christum. Nam mens donec fugit Deum nec cre- dit remissionem peccatorum, nequaquam statuit recipi preces suas. Ideo necesse est hanc fidem praelucere, de qua Paulus dicit ad Rom. 5.: Fide habemus accessum ad Deum per Christum. Haec ipsa doctrina de fide etiam comprehenditur in di- cto huius loci: Quicquid petieritis in nomine meo, id est, me agnoscentes mediatorem, statuentes vos propter me recipi. Et haec eadem fides statuat recipi, et exaudiri preces nostras, et non fore eas irritas.

Quinto: Cogitentur in petitione res petendae, bona spiritus et corporis, sicut et ipsa quotidiana petitio utriusque generis bona complectitur.

Haec de precatione breviter recensui, quia illustrari hoc dictum textus sine hac commemoratione non potest. Nunc in quotidiana invocatione hoc dictum nobis proponamus, et inculcemus, ut accedere ad Deum, et petere bona discamus. In hac experientia fient haec verba illustriora: In nomine meo, id est, me agnoscentes mediatorem, confisi me intercessore et deprecatore pro vobis, cui pater aeternus praecipue tradidit promissionem sacerdotii, propter me certo vult exaudire, et se vult sic coli, et hoc honore affici, videlicet invocatione facta fide, seu fiducia domini nostri Iesu Christi, et sic invocantes experiemur sine ulla dubitatione preces efficaces esse, et salutaria, quae petunt, impetrare, etc.

## 14:15
If you love me.

There are many notable sayings in this chapter, and very worthy of memory, as above: No one comes to the Father except through the Son. Likewise: He who sees me, sees the Father. Likewise: Whatever you ask the Father in my name, I will do. To these notable sayings, certain following clauses must also be added, among these is also this sentence: If you love me, keep my commandments, and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another paraclete. For this passage first teaches to whom the Holy Spirit is given. Then what it is: thirdly what are the proper benefits, or what are the proper effects. And here a description and consolation of the Church is proposed, most sweet.

But the first and chief question is, what and where is the Church, or to whom is the Holy Spirit given? The words of the text answer this question: If you love me, keep my commandments, and I will ask the Father etc., that is, that assembly which teaches, hears, and embraces my Gospel, is an assembly loving me, and it will be gifted, ruled, and sanctified by the Holy Spirit. This assembly is the Church of God. This is the true, simple, proper, and native meaning of this passage, nor should these words be understood concerning the doctrine of the law without the Gospel, as the Monks invent a meaning here that is entirely foreign, that you will love me when you have satisfied the law. This is not a Mosaic discourse, but Christ's, who commands the doctrine of his Gospel to be received and retained, and the Gospel to be believed, and to those who embrace the Gospel he promises the Holy Spirit, and affirms that this assembly is the Church, that is, it is an assembly beloved by God, which retains the commandments, that is, the doctrine which Christ delivered, and as he delivered it, namely the Gospel, which teaches us about repentance and the remission of sins, and about eternal life on account of Christ, and teaches who Christ the mediator is. And in this place Christ joins the Gospel and the Holy Spirit, nor does he promise the Holy Spirit to any except those who teach, hear, and embrace the Gospel. The same sentence will soon be repeated: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him, and make our dwelling with him. It is exactly the same as what I have already said about the Church. For this is the dwelling, that is, the temple of God, just as the Church is often and truly called the temple of God: Keeping my word, that is, embracing the Gospel, they will love me, they will truly worship me, and they will be loved by my Father, and we will dwell in them, who will be our eternal temple and Church, to them we will give life and eternal glory. It is therefore not uncertain which is, and where is the Church, it is not a Platonic polity, as impious men cavil, but it is some visible Church, for God wishes his doctrine to be scattered, to sound, to be heard among men, as it is written: Their sound has gone out into all the earth. He does not wish the Church to be hidden in secret places, or unknown, rather he always drew it into struggles with empires and hypocrites. It is therefore a visible assembly, namely, as it is described here, embracing and carrying about the Gospel, and reborn by the Holy Spirit, although in this life those not reborn are mixed into this visible assembly, who nevertheless, because they agree with the reborn concerning doctrine, are not excluded from the Church in this life. This mark can be known by sense, namely the voice of the Gospel, there the true Church of God certainly is, where the pure voice of the Gospel sounds, nor are the elect to be sought elsewhere, except in this assembly, according to that: Whom he chose, these he also called. It is profitable to consider these things about the Church first in this place, and let us add this saying of Christ to the other sayings which are cited concerning the description of the Church, such as: My sheep hear my voice. And to the Ephesians 2: You have been built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the cornerstone, that is, you have been built upon Christ through the prophetic and apostolic doctrine, which shows Christ to be the effective foundation, giving life, and truly bearing and saving the Church, and Isaiah 59: The redeemer shall come to Zion, and to those who return from iniquity in Jacob, this is my covenant with them, says the Lord, my spirit which is in you, and my words which I have put in your mouth, shall not depart from your mouth, nor from the mouth of your seed forever. This description affirms that the Messiah will bring the remission of sins to those who repent, and adds further that he will give to his people the word which is in the mouth of the Prophet, that is, preached by the Prophets, and the Holy Spirit. Thus he joins the Gospel, the Holy Spirit, the deletion of sin and death, that is, the donation of righteousness and eternal life. To these and similar descriptions, add the saying of Christ in this text.

Now follows the description of the Holy Spirit, in which he first testifies that the Holy Spirit is given at his request. For on account of Christ, the Church is received, loved, sanctified, and saved. Next, he names another spirit, the paraclete, the spirit of truth. All the learned in the Church have ordered the particle, another, to be considered. For this distinguishes the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, and refutes the impiety of many who contended that the Holy Spirit is not a person, but that by this word is signified either the Father acting, or a created agitation. But this particle, another, expressly distinguishes here the Holy Spirit from the Father. For Christ says: The Father will give you another paraclete. There is, therefore, a distinction, both from the Father and from the Son: nor does the Spirit signify the acting Father. Moreover, let other testimonies be added; in the baptism of Christ, the Holy Spirit appears in a peculiar form, and is distinguished from the Father and the Son. Now if it were only a created agitation in the mind, it would not appear in a peculiar form. It is therefore a person other than the Father and the Son, who is described in another place with these words: Proceeding from the Father and the Son, namely, a breath proceeding from the will of the Father and the will of the Son, and connecting the Father and the Son in mutual love, connecting also angels and men to God, into whom he is poured, and kindling minds with divine light, and stirring them with motions congruent to the will of God. O the immense and ineffable goodness of God, who thus imparts himself to us, and pours himself into us, just as he says again below: We will come to him, and make our dwelling with him.

Latin:

Si diligitis me.

Multa sunt huius capitis insignia dicta, et valde digna memoria, ut supra: Nemo venit ad patrem, nisi per filium. Item: Qui videt me, videt patrem. Item: Quicquid petieritis patrem in nomine meo, hoc faciam. His insignibus etiam quaedam sequentes particulae adnumerandae erunt, in his et haec sententia est: Si diligitis me, mandata mea servate, et ego rogabo patrem, et dabit vobis alium paracletum. Nam hic locus primum docet quibus detur Spiritus sanctus. Deinde quid sit: tertio quae sint beneficia propria, seu qui effectus proprii. Ac proponitur hic descriptio ac consolatio Ecclesiae dulcissima.

Est autem prima et praecipua quaestio, quidnam et ubi sit Ecclesia, seu quibus detur Spiritus sanctus? Ad hanc quaestionem respondent verba textus: Si diligitis me, mandata mea servate, et rogabo patrem etc., id est, ille coetus, qui meum Evangelium docet, audit, et amplectitur, est coetus diligens me, et donabitur, regetur, et sanctificabitur Spiritu sancto. Hic coetus est Ecclesia Dei. Haec est vera, simplex, propria et nativa sententia huius loci, nec intelligantur haec verba de legis doctrina sine Evangelio, ut Monachi prorsus alienam sententiam hic comminiscuntur, tunc diligetis me, cum legi sa- tisfeceritis. Non est haec Mosaica concio, sed Christi, qui mandat accipi et retineri doctrinam Evangelii sui, et credi Evangelio, et amplecten- tibus Evangelium promittit Spiritum sanctum, et affirmat hunc coetum esse Ecclesiam, id est, esse coetum dilectum Deo, qui retinet mandata, id est, doctrinam, quam Christus tradidit, et sicut tradidit, videlicet Evangelium, quod docet nos de poenitentia et remissione peccatorum, et de vita aeterna propter Christum, et docet quis sit Christus mediator. Et copulat hoc loco Christus Evangelium et Spiritum sanctum, nec ullis promittit Spiritum S. nisi iis, qui docent, audiunt et amplectun- tur Evangelium. Eadem sententia mox repete- tur: Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum serva- bit, et pater meus diliget eum, et ad eum venie- mus, et mansionem apud eum faciemus. Pror- sus idem est, quod jam dixi, de Ecclesia. Haec est enim mansio, id est, templum Dei, sicut saepe et vere Ecclesia vocatur templum Dei: Ser- vantes sermonem meum, id est, amplectentes Evangelium, diligent me, vere me colent, et di- ligentur a patre meo, et in his habitabimus, qui erunt templum et Ecclesia nostra aeterna, his vi- tam et gloriam aeternam dabimus. Non igitur incertum est quae sit, et ubi sit Ecclesia, non est politia Platonica, ut homines impii cavillantur, sed est aliqua visibilis Ecclesia, vult enim Deus suam doctrinam inter homines spargi, sonare, exaudiri, sicut scriptum est: In omnem terram exivit sonus eorum. Non vult Ecclesiam abdi- tam esse in latebris, aut ignotam, imo semper eam in certamina cum imperiis et hypocritis pro- traxit. Est igitur coetus visibilis, scilicet, ut hic describitur, amplectens et circumferens Evange- lium, et renatus Spiritu sancto, quanquam in hac vita huic visibili coetui non renati admixti sunt, qui tamen, quia de doctrina cum renatis consentiunt, in hac vita non excluduntur ex Ec- clesia. Sensu cognosci potest haec nota, scilicet vox Evangelii, ibi certo est Ecclesia vera Dei, ubi sonat pura vox Evangelii, nec alibi, nisi in hoc coetu quaerendi sunt electi, iuxta illud: Quos elegit, hos et vocavit. Haec de Ecclesia primum hoc loco considerare prodest, et hoc dictum Christi addamus caeteris dictis, quae citantur de descri- ptione Ecclesiae, ut oves meae vocem meam au- diunt. Et ad Ephes. 2.: Extructi estis super fundamentum Apostolorum et Prophetarum, exi- stente lapide angulari Iesu Christo, id est, ex- tructi estis super Christum per doctrinam prophe- ticam et apostolicam, quae monstrat Christum fundamentum efficax, dans vitam, et vere ge- stans, ac salvans Ecclesiam, et Esaiae 59.: Ve- niet Sion redemtor, et his qui redeunt ab iniqui- tate in Iacob, hoc est foedus meum cum eis, di- cit dominus, spiritus meus qui est in te, et verba mea quae posui in ore tuo, non recedent de ore tuo, nec de ore seminis tui in sempiternum. Haec descriptio affirmat Messiam allaturum esse remis- sionem peccatorum iis, qui agunt poenitentiam, et addit amplius daturum populo suo verbum, quod est in ore Prophetae, id est, praedicatum a Prophetis, et Spiritum sanctum. Ita coniungit Evangelium, Spiritum sanctum, deletionem pec- cati et mortis, hoc est, donationem iusticiae et vitae aeternae. Ad has et similes descriptiones dictum Christi in hoc textu adiungite.

Nunc sequitur descriptio Spiritus sancti, in qua primum testatur dari Spiritum sanctum se petente. Nam propter Christum recipitur, dili- gitur, sanctificatur et salvatur Ecclesia. Deinde nominat spiritum alium paracletum spiritum ve- ritatis. Omnes docti in Ecclesia iusserunt parti- culam, alium, considerari. Haec enim discer- nit Spiritum sanctum a patre et a filio, et re- futat impietatem multorum, qui contenderunt Spiritum sanctum non esse personam, sed hoc vocabulo significari aut patrem agitantem, aut creatam agitationem. Sed haec particula, alius, expresse discernit hic Spiritum sanctum a patre. Dicit enim Christus: Dabit pater vobis alium pa- racletum. Discrimen est igitur, et a patre et a filio: nec significat Spiritus agitantem patrem. Addantur autem et alia testimonia, in baptismo Christi peculiari specie apparet Spiritus sanctus, et discernitur a patre et filio. Iam si tantum agitatio creata esset in mente, non appareret pe- culiari specie. Est igitur persona alia a patre et filio, quae alio loco describitur his verbis: Pro- cedens a patre et filio, videlicet flatus a volun- tate patris, et voluntate filii procedens, ac con- nectens mutuo amore patrem et filium, connectens etiam angelos et homines Deo, in quos effusus est, et luce divina accendens mentes, et agitans moti- bus congruentibus voluntati Dei. O immensam et inenarrabilem bonitatem Dei, qui seipsum sic impertit nobis, et sese in nos effundit, sicut in- fra rursus inquit: Veniemus ad eum, et mansio- nem apud eum faciemus.

## 14:16
He will give you a Comforter.

After it has been established that by the appellation of the Holy Spirit a person is signified, when it is said what God is, now let the proper gifts also, which are effected through him in the Church, in the ministry, and in individuals, be considered. First, concerning the ministry, let us know that the Holy Spirit is certainly effective through the Gospel and the sacraments, as it is said in Romans 1: The Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes. And 2 Corinthians 3, the Gospel is said to be the Ministry of the spirit, that is, through which the Holy Spirit is effective, kindles new light and righteousness in hearts, for thus Paul himself interprets it. Therefore, the Holy Spirit preserves the light and purity of the Gospel in some in the public ministry, nor does he allow it to be utterly destroyed, and he is effective in those who hear the Gospel and use the sacraments. Secondly, in the hearts of individuals who are converted to God, the Holy Spirit kindles new light, so that they may assent to the Gospel, he excites motions of invocation, love, and other virtues congruent to the law of God, he comforts us, and begins in us eternal life, as it is said in Romans 8: You have received the spirit of adoption of sons, in which we cry Abba Father. And 2 Corinthians 3: We are transformed into the same image, namely of Christ, as if by the spirit of the Lord.

These gifts are also recited in this place; the Holy Spirit is called the Paraclete, which properly signifies an advocate, as in a trial. Christ has therefore encompassed many things; he has signified that the Church has constant struggles with the devil and his organs, and with our own infirmity. The Holy Spirit is therefore given, that he may be an advocate helping us with counsel and consolation, warning and confirming us, just as in the ministry he warns and confirms Jeremiah, the Baptist, Peter, against the authority of the synagogue, and against the cruelty of tyrants. Thus, to each of us he is a παράκλητος in all our dangers; he guides us with counsel, and confirms us, and stirs us up to invocation. David is guided by counsel, so that he does not kill Saul, and is confirmed, so that he does not fall into despair, and is stirred up to invoke. Paul has encompassed these things in Romans 8, saying: The Holy Spirit helps our infirmity. Experience makes doctrine more illustrious in great sorrows. And the gifts are described more clearly when he calls him the Spirit of truth, that is, the truthful one, and true wisdom, and true justice, and the one effecting life in us. For when we hear the Gospel, he himself moves minds so that they assent, and he governs thought, and helps, so that it does not wander, but sees the true meaning of the Gospel, and in the will he excites the flames of all virtues; kindled by this light and these flames, faith does not wander from God, but truly calls upon him, and brings the beginnings of eternal life, just as Christ says: This is eternal life, that they may know you the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent to be true. The Holy Spirit also retains the truth in the ministry, so that the doctrine is not entirely extinguished, as is said at Ephesians 4: And he kindles it in the hearts of those who truly believe. Pious people can judge in some way what kind and how great this benefit is, but a comparison declares it in some measure. How great are the frenzies of the impious, whom the devil agitates, so that they either embrace Epicurean blasphemies and a Cyclopean contempt of God, or fashion for themselves gods and idols at their own whim. Then, in what darkness are the more modest philosophers, who perpetually doubt whether there is providence. Thirdly, the Pharisees, oppressed by the opinions of the law, and conceding that there is providence and that delinquents are punished, nevertheless live without God, do not dare to call upon him, nor do they know how one must approach God, but they flee from God. All these carry around with them foul lies and pernicious errors about God, but once the Gospel is acknowledged, the truthful spirit is given, correcting those lies and kindling true light, just as John also says in his Epistle: The anointing teaches you about all things, and it is true, and it is not a lie, and just as it has taught you, remain in it.

Latin:

Consolatorem dabit vobis.

Postquam constitutum est appellatione Spi- ritus sancti personam significari, quando dicitur quid sit Deus, nunc etiam propria dona, quae per ipsum efficiuntur in Ecclesia, in ministerio, et in singulis considerentur. Primum de mini- sterio sciamus, certo Spiritum sanctum efficacem esse per Evangelium et sacramenta, ut ad Rom. 1. dicitur: Evangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti. Et 2. ad Corinth. 3. Evange- lium dicitur esse Ministerium spiritus, id est, per quod Spiritus sanctus est efficax, accendit novam lucem et iusticiam in cordibus, sic enim Paulus ipse interpretatur. Conservat ergo Spiritus san- ctus lucem et puritatem Evangelii in aliquibus in publico ministerio, nec penitus deleri sinit, et est efficax in his qui audiunt Evangelium et sa- cramentis utuntur. Secundo in cordibus singu- lorum qui convertuntur ad Deum, accendit Spi- ritus sanctus novam lucem, ut Evangelio assen- tiantur, excitat motus invocationis, dilectionis, et aliarum virtutum congruentis legi Dei, conso- latur nos, et incoat in nobis vitam aeternam, ut ad Ro. 8. dicitur: Accepistis spiritum adoptionis filiorum, in quo clamamus Abba pater. Et 2. Co- rinth. 3.: Transformamur in eandem imaginem, scilicet Christi, tanquam a domini spiritu.

Haec dona et hoc loco recitantur, Spiritus sanctus appellatur Paracletus, quod proprie signi- ficat advocatum, ut in iudicio. Multa igitur com- plexus est Christus, significavit Ecclesiam habere assidua certamina cum diabolo et eius organis, et cum nostra infirmitate. Datur ergo Spiritus sanctus, ut sit advocatus iuvans nos consilio et consolatione, monens et confirmans nos, ut in ministerio monet et confirmat Ieremiam, Bapti- stam. Petrum, contra autoritatem synagogae, et contra saevitiam tyrannorum. Sic nobis singulis est παράκλητος in omnibus nostris periculis, re- git nos consilio, et confirmat nos, et exuscitat nos ad invocationem. David regitur consilio, ne Saulem interficiat, et confirmatur, ne ruat in de- sperationem, et exuscitatur ad invocandum. Haec complexus est Paulus ad Rom. 8. inquiens: Spiri- tus sanctus opitulatur infirmitati nostrae. doctrinam in magnis doloribus experientia facit illustriorem. Et clarius describuntur dona, cum vocat eum Spiritum veritatis, id est, veracem, et veram sa- pientiam, ac veram iusticiam, et vitam in nobis efficientem. Nam cum audimus Evangelium, ipse movet mentes, ut assentiantur, et cogitationem regit, et adiuvat, ne aberret, sed veram senten- tiam Evangelii videat, et in voluntate flammas omnium virtutum exuscitat, hac luce et his flam- mis accensa, fides non aberrat a Deo, sed vere invocat, et affert initia vitae aeternae, sicut in- quit Christus: Haec est vita aeterna, ut agnoscant te verum Deum, et quem misisti verum esse Iesum Christum. Retinet et Spiritus sanctus veritatem in ministerio, ne penitus doctrina extinguatur, ut ad Ephes. 4. dicitur: Et accendit eam in singulo- rum vere credentium cordibus. Hoc beneficium quale et quantum sit, aliquo modo iudicare pos- sunt pii, sed collatio utcunque declarat. Quanti furores sunt impiorum, quos diabolus agitat, ut aut amplectantur epicureas blasphemias, et cy- clopicum contemtum Dei, aut fingant sibi ipsis deos et idola suo arbitrio. Deinde modestiores Philosophi in quantis tenebris sunt, qui perpetuo dubitant, an sit providentia. Tertio Pharisaei oppressi legis opinionibus, et concedentes esse providentiam, et puniri delinquentes, tamen vi- vunt sine Deo, non audent invocare, nec norunt quomodo accedendum sit ad Deum, sed fugiunt Deum. Omnes hi tetra mendacia et perniciosos errores de Deo secum circumferunt, sed agnito Evangelio spiritus verax datur, corrigens illa mendacia, et accendens veram lucem, sicut et Ioan- nes in Epistola ait: Unctio vos docet de omnibus, et vera est, et non est mendacium, et sicut do- cuit vos, manete in ea.

## 14:17
Whom the world cannot receive.

He calls the world all men not reborn by the Holy Spirit, but thinking about God as this corrupt nature thinks, and in life following the motions of this corrupt nature. Such people, he says, cannot take the Holy Spirit, nor do they know him, that is, as long as they persevere in the opinions and affections of corrupt nature, they do not admit the Holy Spirit, but resist him, like Caiaphas, even though he hears Christ, yet because he retains his imaginations, that men receive God on account of the law, and because no one knows when he has enough good works, that one must doubt about God, and he does not understand the gratuitous promise, nor the benefits of Christ, and remains in this doubt, he does not admit the Holy Spirit, nay, little by little darkness and frenzies grow in him. However, this opinion must be held against the Pelagians, who imagined that men without the Holy Spirit merit the remission of sins by good works, and can perform the law of God, and are just before God by these works. This opinion is akin to philosophy and the doctrine of the Pharisees, and many monks have embraced it, excessively amplifying free will and overwhelming the doctrine of the Gospel concerning the benefits of Christ.

But these frenzies are to be execrated, and on the contrary, the doctrine of grace must be held, that on account of Christ the remission of sins and the imputation of justice are given to us. And although we can in some measure perform the external discipline of honest and civil works, yet it must be known that we are far from the perfection of the law, and cannot have internal motions agreeable to the law of God, fear, faith, love, without the Holy Spirit, as is said in 1 Corinthians 2: The natural man, that is, living by natural life, does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God, and above in chapter 5 it was said: No one comes to me, unless the Father has drawn him. Let us not be so Cyclopean as to think that this miserable life in such darkness and such weakness of our powers can be governed without the Holy Spirit. Noah, Abraham, Joseph, Moses, Joshua, Samuel, David, Isaiah, and others did not perform such great and such salutary things in their functions by the powers of human nature without the Holy Spirit. But let us acknowledge our weakness, and let us hear that help is promised, and let us seek it, and let us sustain ourselves in all dangers with this consolation, that the Holy Spirit is present with us as governor and helper, just as Christ also promises elsewhere: How much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask. Observe, however, that it is expressly said, to those who ask; it is not said, to Epicureans who despise or hypocrites who resist the Gospel, but to those who flee to Christ through repentance, and seriously seek the remission of sins and the Holy Spirit.

Jeremiah says in chapter 10: I know, Lord, that the way of man is not his own, that is, in such weakness of the nature of men, and in such dangers of ours, in such difficulty of things to be done, in such snares of the devil, human powers cannot without the Holy Spirit govern vocations and conduct. Therefore David cries out so often in Psalm 118: Give me understanding. Likewise: Deal with thy servant according to thy mercy, and teach me thy statutes, and in 2 Chronicles 20 it is said: When we know not what we ought to do, our eyes look to thee. Let us exercise this doctrine in our daily dangers, which when we do, experience will teach us that these promises are true, and that we are truly ruled by counsel and helped by the consolation of the Holy Spirit, as Christ says: How much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him. Likewise: I will not leave you orphans, etc.

Latin:

Quem mundus non potest accipere.

Mundum vocat omnes homines non renatos Spiritu sancto, sed de Deo sentientes, ut sentit haec corrupta natura, et in vita sequentes motus huius corruptae naturae. Tales, inquit, non pos- sunt sumere Spiritum sanctum, nec norunt eum, id est, donec perseverant in opinionibus et af- fectibus corruptae naturae, non admittunt Spiri- tum sanctum, sed repugnant ei, ut Caiphas, etiam- si audit Christum, tamen quia retinet suas imagi- nationes, Deum recipere homines propter legem, et quia nemo scit, quando satis bonorum operum habeat, dubitandum esse de Deo, nec intelligit gratuitam promissionem, nec beneficia Christi, ac manet in hac dubitatione, non admittit Spiritum sanctum, imo paulatim in eo tenebrae et furores crescunt. Tenenda est autem haec sententia ad- versus Pelagianos, qui finxerunt homines sine Spiritu sancto, bonis operibus mereri remissio- nem peccatorum, et legem Dei facere posse, et his operibus coram Deo iustos esse. Haec opinio affinis est philosophiae, ac Pharisaeorum doctri- nae, et multi Monachi eam amplexi fuerunt, ni- mium amplificantes liberum arbitrium, et obruen- tes Evangelii doctrinam de beneficiis Christi.

Execrandi sunt autem hi furores, ac econtra tenenda doctrina de gratia, quod propter Chri- stum donentur nobis remissio peccatorum et im- putatio iusticiae. Et quanquam disciplinam ex- ternam honestorum et civilium operum utcunque praestare possimus, tamen sciendum est nos pro- cul abesse a perfectione legis, et nec posse motus interiores legi Dei convenientes, timorem, fidem, dilectionem habere sine Spiritu sancto, sicut 1. Co- rinth. 2. dicitur: Homo ψυχικὸς, id est, natu- rali vita vivens, non percipit ea quae sunt Spiri- tus Dei, et supra cap. 5. dictum est: Nemo venit ad me, nisi quem pater traxerit. Non simus adeo cyclopici, ut arbitremur hanc miseram vitam in tantis tenebris et tanta imbecillitate virium nostra- rum regi posse sine Spiritu sancto. Non gesse- runt res tantas, et tam salutares in suis functioni- bus Noe, Abraham, Ioseph, Moses, Iosue, Sa- muel, David, Esaias et alii, naturae humanae viribus sine Spiritu sancto. Sed agnoscamus no- stram imbecillitatem, et audiamus promitti auxi- lium, et id petamus, et hac consolatione nos in omnibus periculis sustentemus, quod adsit nobis Spiritus sanctus gubernator et adiutor, sicut Chri- stus et alibi promittit: Quanto magis pater vester coelestis dabit Spiritum sanctum petentibus. Ob- serva autem diserte dici, petentibus, non dicitur, Epicureis contemnentibus aut hypocritis repugnan- tibus Evangelio, sed confugientibus ad Christum per poenitentiam, et serio petentibus remissionem peccatorum et Spiritum sanctum.

Ieremias inquit cap. 10.: Scio domine, quod non est hominis via eius, id est, in tanta imbe- cillitate naturae hominum, et tantis periculis no- stris, in tanta difficultate rerum gerendarum, in tantis insidiis diaboli, humanae vires non pos- sunt sine Spiritu sancto regere vocationes et mo- res. Ideo toties clamat David Psalm. 118.: Da mihi intellectum. Item: Fac cum servo tuo se- cundum misericordiam tuam, et iustificationes doce me, et 2. Paral. 20. dicitur: Cum ignoramus quid agere debeamus, oculi nostri ad te respi- ciunt. Hanc doctrinam exerceamus in nostris periculis quotidianis, quod cum faciemus, expe- rientia docebit nos, has promissiones veras esse, ac vere nos regi consilio, et iuvari consolatione Spiritus sancti, sicut inquit Christus: Quanto ma- gis pater vester coelestis dabit Spiritum sanctum petentibus. Item: Non relinquam vos orpha- nos, etc.

## 14:17
He will be with you.

There is also a promise concerning perpetuity to be observed; he affirms that the Holy Spirit will remain in the Church forever, as is said in the last chapter of Matthew: Behold I am with you even unto the end of the world, and in 1 Timothy 3 the Church is called the seat of truth. Here, however, both things must be known: that the Holy Spirit will remain in the Church, so that men may not despair at any time, or any age think itself cast off, and yet that he is not bound to the ordinary succession, as they call it, or to the titles of dignities, but the Holy Spirit is present and effective without any doubt where the voice of the Gospel sounds rightly, or at least where the foundation of faith is retained. For that sentence remains unmoved, 2 Corinthians 3, that the Gospel is the ministry of the Holy Spirit. Likewise, that the Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth. Wherever, therefore, the voice of the Gospel sounds, there the Holy Spirit is effective.

Here let this huge benefit of God also be observed, that although the light of the Gospel is obscured, with the devil stirring up errors and men neglecting pious studies, yet the Son of God, sitting at the right hand of the Father and giving gifts to men, from time to time restores the ministry of the Gospel, as Paul says in Ephesians 4: And he recites the cause of this most ample gift, lest the Church, tossed by storms, should embrace various kinds of doctrine like children, and be carried about like the winds of doctrines to other and yet other frenzies, just as the heathens used to devise now the Bacchanalia, now the Salii of Mars, now the Corybantes, now other monstrosities. In all ages new restorations of the Church have been made. After Moses, Samuel was raised up; after Samuel, David; after David, Elijah; then Elisha; after these, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, Zechariah, Ezra,

Simon, Mattathias, Zechariah, the Baptist, Christ, the Apostles.

Latin:

Vobiscum erit.
