Est et promissio de perpetuitate observanda, affirmat perpetuo Spiritum sanctum in Ecclesia mansurum esse, sicut Matth. ult. dicitur: Ecce ego vobiscum sum usque ad consummationem se- culi, et 1. Tim. 3. Ecclesia dicitur sedes verita- tis. Hic autem utrunque sciendum est: et man surum esse in Ecclesia Spiritum sanctum, ne ullo tempore desperent homines, aut aliqua aetas se abiectam esse putet, et tamen non alligatum esse ad successionem ordinariam, ut vocant, aut titu- los dignitatum, sed ibi sine ulla dubitatione Spi- ritus sanctus adest, et est efficax, ubi recte sonat vox Evangelii, aut certe ubi fundamentum fidei retinetur. Manet enim illa sententia immota, 2. Corinth. 3. Evangelium esse ministerium Spi- ritus sancti. Item, Evangelium esse potentiam Dei ad salutem omni credenti. Ubicunque igitur sonat vox Evangelii, ibi Spiritus sanctus est efficax.

Hic observetur et hoc ingens beneficium Dei, quod quanquam lux Evangelii obscuratur, dia- bolo excitante errores, et hominibus negligentibus pia studia, tamen filius Dei sedens ad dextram pa- tris, ac dona dans hominibus, subinde instaurat ministerium Evangelii, ut Paulus ad Ephes. 4. inquit: Et causam huius amplissimi muneris re- citat, ne Ecclesiae procellis agitatae, velut pueri varia doctrinae genera amplectantur, et tanquam ventis doctrinarum circumferantur ad alios atque alios furores, ut Ethnici nunc Bacchanalia, nunc Martis Salios, nunc Corybantes, nunc alia por- tenta excogitabant. Omnibus seculis novae in- staurationes Ecclesiae factae sunt. Post Mosen excitatus est Samuel; post Samuelem David, post Davidem Elias, deinde Elisaeus, post hos Esaias, Ieremias, Daniel, Zacharias, Esdras,

Simon, Mathatias, Zacharias, Baptista, Christus, Apostoli.

## 14:18
I will not leave you orphans.

Before, the promise of the Holy Spirit was recited; now Christ speaks of his own person, and meets the silent question of the Apostles, who were undoubtedly debating among themselves: although another governor is promised to us, yet we desire to know what is to become of him. He answers: Nay, even though I depart for a little while, and die, and shall seem to be torn away from you, yet I shall soon revive from death, I will return to you, and I will always be with you. There is, however, a remarkable passage in the text, describing what the Church is like in this world, as far as human protection is concerned; thus all men reason: That no assembly is durable unless it has some certain seat and ordered governments by which it may be defended; the Church has neither a certain seat, nor is it defended by the consent of kings, but rather is oppressed and torn apart, and the teachers themselves cohere badly among themselves; they have no governors by whose authority concord may be maintained among them; they have no patrons and defenders against tyranny, or the hatreds of the people and of their own. In short, it is a miserable assembly, as the hardships of the Apostles and our own daily miseries show. For who looks upon us, embraces us, cherishes us, or defends us? Most kings and princes profess themselves to be enemies of our doctrine, and they drag us like victims to punishments where they can. The people who hear us, and the princes themselves who wish to appear not to abhor the Gospel, either care for us lightly or press us with craft. In short, we have absolutely no human protection, as it is written in the Psalms: My father and my mother have forsaken me. We are, therefore, as far as human protection is concerned, orphans.

But against this appearance Christ consoles us, saying: Nay, I will not leave you orphans; even if kings, princes, empires, the people, and teachers do not cover you, I will nevertheless protect and save you. The Church of God has need of this consolation, so that we may know that it will remain, even if it has no certain seat or the defense of empires. Therefore this consolation has been repeated often, as in Isaiah chapter 51: I have put my words in thy mouth, and I cover thee with the shadow of my hand, that thou mayest plant the heavens, that is: I am instituting the ministry of the Gospel; it will not be defended by empires, but rather will be cruelly attacked; therefore I myself promise the defense, for I will protect the ministers of the Gospel, the Churches, the schools, and pious studies, even if the raging world strives to destroy the Gospel. It is a sad sight to see a deserted Church; even individual private persons in death and other great dangers feel how miserable it is to lose all human aid in such straits. Let us set before ourselves these sayings, by which, if we stir up our faith, we shall… truly feel that Christ is present with us, that we are helped, ruled, and defended.

And here Christ specifically promises life to his hearers: I live, and you shall live; even if tyrants kill you with cruel tortures, yet I will restore life to you, in which you shall see the Father and me face to face.

Latin:

Non relinquam vos orphanos.

Antea recitata est promissio Spiritus sancti, nunc de sua persona Christus loquitur, ac occurrit tacitae quaestioni Apostolorum, qui haud dubie apud sese disputabant, etsi promittitur nobis alius gubernator, tamen scire cupimus, quid de ipso futurum sit. Respondet: Imo etsi paulisper discedam, moriar, videbor a vobis avulsus, tamen mox reviviscam ex morte, ad vos redibo, et semper vobiscum ero. Est autem insignis particula in textu, describens qualis sit Ecclesia in hoc mundo, quod ad praesidia humana attinet, sic omnes homines ratiocinantur: Nullum coetum durabilem esse, nisi habeat certam aliquam sedem et ordinata imperia, a quibus defendatur, Ecclesia nec sedem certam habet, nec defenditur consensu regum, sed potius opprimitur et laceratur, et ipsi inter sese doctores male cohaerent, non habent gubernatores, quorum autoritate concordia inter eos retineatur, non habent patronos ac defensores adversus tyrannidem, aut odia populi ac suorum. Denique miserabilis coetus est, ut Apostolorum aerumnae, et nostrae quotidianae miseriae ostendunt. Quis enim nos respicit, complectitur, fovet, aut defendit? Plurimi regum et principum profitentur se esse hostes nostrae doctrinae, et nos tanquam victimas ad supplicia rapiunt, ubi possunt. Populus, qui nos audit, et principes ipsi, qui videri volunt non abhorrere ab Evangelio, aut leviter curant nos, aut arte premunt. Denique humana praesidia prorsus nulla habemus, sicut in Psalmis scriptum est: Pater et mater dereliquerunt me. Sumus igitur, quod ad humana praesidia attinet, orphani.

Sed adversus hanc speciem Christus nos consolatur, inquiens: Imo non relinquam vos orphanos, etiamsi, reges, principes, imperia, populus, doctores vos non tegunt, ego tamen vos protegam ac servabo. Hac consolatione opus est Ecclesiae Dei, ut sciamus mansuram esse, etiamsi non habet certam sedem, aut imperiorum defensionem. Ideo saepe repetita est haec consolatio, ut Esaiae capite 51.: Posui verba mea in ore tuo, et umbra manus meae protego te, ut plantes coelos, id est: Instituo ministerium Evangelii, id ab imperiis non defendetur, sed potius atrociter oppugnabitur, ideo polliceor ipse defensionem, pro- tegam ministros Evangelii, Ecclesias, scholas, pia studia, etiamsi mundus furens delere Evangelium conatur. Tristis species est Ecclesiae desertae, sin- guli etiam privati in morte, et aliis magnis pericu- lis sentiunt, quam sit miserum amittere omnia hu- mana auxilia, in talibus angustiis. Proponamus nobis haec dicta, quibus si fidem excitabimus, sen- tiemus vere nobis adesse Christum, nos iuvari, regi, defendi.

Et nominatim hic promittit Christus suis au- ditoribus vitam: Ego vivo, et vos vivetis, etiamsi crudelibus suppliciis vos interficient tyranni, tamen ego vobis vitam reddam, in qua patrem et me co- ram videbitis.

## 14:21
He who has my commandments, and keeps them, etc.

It was said above that consolations and doctrine or commandments are mingled, as in a conversation of one approaching death. Here he inserts what the Church is and where it is, and this passage is to be carefully observed for this very reason, because it judges this controversy: what the Church is. Political men perpetually paint the Church as a worldly kingdom; they say it is a gathering of the reborn and the not-reborn, embracing the Gospel, bound to the Roman Bishop, reigning according to ordinary succession, and that this Bishop has the power of establishing laws and interpreting the Gospel, and that all men are bound to these laws established by him and to his interpretation; and they add that the Roman Bishop or his council cannot err in faith or in necessary matters, nay, some even add, in the empires of the world. They say that this supreme Bishop has the power of transferring kingdoms, and that he ought to be fortified with wealth and armies, and that kings owe him defense and must take up and lay down wars at his discretion; for this they allege the saying which, although it speaks of Christ alone, they twist toward the Roman Bishop: All power is given to me in heaven and on earth. Such a picture of the Church exists in the books of many. But it utterly transforms the Church into a worldly kingdom against many commandments of Christ, who says: The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them, but you shall not be so. Likewise: As the Father has sent me, even so I send you.

But since the Church has the promise that it is the pillar of truth, and those Bishops transfer the name of the Church to themselves, and under that pretext establish idols and errors, and an infinite multitude of men is moved by the mere name of the Church, it is necessary that good minds be taught what the Church is and where it is, and this doctrine must often be inculcated. An invisible Church is not to be imagined, like a Platonic idea, nor yet should we imagine the Church as similar to a worldly kingdom, but to an honest school. But as often as it is spoken of the Church, always before all things think of the saying of Paul: Whom he called, them he also chose; but the calling is visible. For the gathering of the called is a gathering of those embracing the Gospel by external profession. Therefore, let no election be thought of outside this visible gathering. And it is a great consolation for the pious to know that it is necessary that there always be some elect in this visible gathering, in these temples and these schools, and that there are no elect anywhere else. Therefore, this visible gathering and this ministry are to be loved, and it must be certainly established that he who perseveres in the doctrine of this visible gathering that teaches rightly is elected to eternal life. To think these things is useful for piety, for the tranquility of conscience, and for the Church, and many sayings in this text agree with this sentiment of Paul: He who loves me will keep my word.

Let this, therefore, be the definition of the visible Church: The Church is a gathering of those embracing the Gospel, and joined by the fellowship of the sacraments and the evangelical ministry, and reborn through the Holy Spirit, to which gathering many not reborn are admixed, who nevertheless agree with them in the profession of true doctrine, and have not been excommunicated on account of manifest crimes.

This definition is clear, and is taken from many testimonies, such as from the saying of Christ, John ch. 10: My sheep hear my voice; and to the Ephesians 2: You are therefore fellow citizens with the saints, and members of the household of God, built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief cornerstone, in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord, in whom you also are being built together for a dwelling place of the Holy Spirit. The parables also pertain to this, Matthew 13, concerning the net cast into the sea, and others. Nor can the parts which are enumerated in this definition be criticized by anyone. But hypocrites, fascinated by political opinions concerning the pontifical kingdom, do not want anything added, nor are they content when they hear that the Church is a gathering of those embracing the Gospel, joined by the fellowship of the sacraments and the evangelical ministry, but they want it added: bound to the Roman Pontiff and the ordinary succession of Bishops, and their interpretation and laws. There is a struggle at this time concerning this matter, and they accuse and execrate us most atrociously, as if we were enemies of the Church of God, and they cast against us crimes most detestable of all, of sedition stirred up in the Church, and of heresy, and they call us both schismatics and heretics. Nor can it be explained in words how much an honest man, who does not wish to be held as a ruin to the human race, is tormented by these insults; indeed, it would be easier for many to endure the most bitter bodily tortures, and to be killed, than to hear these insults. Many also, for fear of these insults, flee from the profession of the truth. Therefore, it is necessary for the pious to be well confirmed and fortified against this objection. For truly, those poisonous curses do not lightly wound sane and moderate men, especially when they come from such as have a reputation for doctrine and virtue, and many scandals are added, which make the accusation more plausible. There are many grave men, old, learned, excelling in virtue, who have long governed the counsels of the Republic, such as Cardinals, Campeggio, Sadoleto, and the like, who accuse us, first because we falsely tax the Church, and they say that this is bound to the Roman Pontiff and the ordinary succession of Bishops, and they deny that these can err in things necessary for salvation. Then they add that, even if there is some error, amendment should be awaited from the ordinary authority, and that seditions should not be stirred up. Because error is a lesser evil than sedition, and they cite the saying of Dionysius of Alexandria in Eusebius, book 6: that it is a greater crime to rend the Church than to sacrifice to idols. This speech is very plausible; therefore, true and not painted confirmations must be sought by the pious to refute these objections. And our first confirmation is this, which is true and cannot be taxed. Those who from the heart, and not feignedly, appeal to the judgments of the Church are by no means enemies of the Church, or seditious, or schismatics, or heretics. Because it is written: If he will not hear the Church, let him be to you as a heathen or a publican. Therefore, as long as one does not flee the judgment of the Church, he cannot be called an enemy or a schismatic. The second is a gross confirmation: however other disputes may stand, this is certain, that we ought not to be partners in manifest murders, as it is written: Do not communicate in other men's sins. Moreover, there are manifest murders, in that many pious men are killed on account of human traditions, and likewise many pious priests on account of marriage; Campeggio, Sadoleto, and the like, who boast that they are Catholics because they defend the pontifical polity, pollute themselves with the society of this cruelty.

The third confirmation is that the manifest command of God, 'Flee from idols,' is to be preferred to concord and to all human things, and that saying of Dionysius is to be understood rightly concerning the opinion of which he speaks; he compares idols and heresies. Here it is rightly said: it is no less a crime to sow false dogmas than to worship idols. For he is arguing against Novatus. However, it is certain that the Monks and their like defend manifest idol worship, namely the invocation of the dead at certain statues, and the horrendous profanations of the Lord's Supper in venal and funeral Masses. These evils are so manifest that they cannot be excused, which nevertheless they defend in such a way that they attempt to establish them, and they kill those who dissent.

The fourth confirmation: although the judgment of dogmas is difficult for the unlearned, yet the learned can see the difference and understand why one should not assent to the errors of the Monks. And although they do not now dare to profess many manifest errors, and mitigate them with painted interpretations, yet they retain the sinews of the errors. All universally defend this proposition, that a man ought always to doubt concerning the remission of sins, and that this doubt is a pious reverence toward God. Thus they abandon Christ, and abolish the doctrine of faith and invocation, which cannot happen when the mind flees God and is angry at Him, when in true dread doubt grows. Therefore, their imagination fights against these sayings: 'Being justified by faith, we have peace.' Likewise: 'Let us approach with confidence to the throne of grace,' and many errors concerning the distinction between Law and Gospel are implicated in this imagination of theirs. It is also manifest that their books concerning canonical satisfactions are full of errors and darkness, obscuring the Gospel. Finally, it is certain that their books do not speak rightly concerning the remission of sins, and that there is silence concerning the faith that receives the remission of sins. Indeed, the contrary dogma is defended, that one must always doubt concerning the remission. This must be rebuked, even if the world should fall broken: because the Gospel affirms this sentiment, that on account of the Son of God the mediator, there is freely offered to us the remission of sins and that it ought to be received by faith. It is necessary that this sentiment exist and be defended in the Church of God. For with this light extinguished, the benefit of Christ is not acknowledged, nor is the distinction between the Law and the Gospel perceived, nor is the difference between the doctrine of the Church and ethnic opinions discerned.

I have recounted these things because adversaries often declaim atrociously in general about how great the evils of discord and sedition are, and sometimes they disturb the Holy Spirit in moderate and weak men. But lest those clamors break the spirits of the pious, true, not sophistic, not specious causes must be held, as to why it is necessary for us to dissent from the defenders of unjust cruelty and errors. Now, therefore, I return to the definition of the Church; I say that the Church is bound to the Gospel and to the ministry of the Gospel, but not to the Roman Episcopate and ordinary succession. For when the Roman Bishop or others are enemies of the Gospel, it is necessary to dissent from them, just as this voice clearly teaches: If anyone teaches another Gospel, let him be anathema; and it is no light reproach to be called anathema, it is the extreme and highest of all curses. Let us know that the defenders of idols and impious dogmas have been rejected by God, and that errors are not to be embraced on account of the opinion of their authority. Let us therefore inculcate this sentiment in ourselves, let us fortify ourselves with this voice of Paul against those vituperations of dissensions, and let us respond: If anyone teaches another Gospel, let him be anathema, etc.

Christ says exactly the same thing in this discourse: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him, and we will make our abode with him. This is a plain and clear description of the Church: There, he says, the Father and I will dwell, and my Father will love those who will embrace my word, that is, the Gospel, which I have delivered to the Church, and will not corrupt it by mixing in depraved opinions. I have recounted the native sentiment of the text, which interpreters ignorant of the doctrine of the Gospel corrupt entirely, who think it is a discourse of the Law, and thus explain it: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, that is, if anyone loves God with his whole heart, with his whole soul, and with all his strength, he keeps the Law, he pleases God. This explanation is foreign, and does not pertain to this passage. Christ calls his word not only the Law, but the whole Gospel, that is, the promise of grace and eternal life, which God has revealed in a peculiar way, and wishes to be the interpreter of the Law. He delivers this whole doctrine here to his Church, and affirms that his people will be there, and that he will dwell there, where this doctrine will sound. Even the Gentiles know the Law in some way, but they are not the people of God because of this. But that assembly is the Church of God in which the voice of the Gospel sounds, and in that assembly it is necessary that some be elected to eternal life. And all are living members who embrace the Gospel by faith, and believe that they please God on account of the Son of God, and have begun obedience, just as the Gospel teaches concerning the Law. This admonition is necessary in this place, so that we may know that Christ is not speaking of the doctrine of the Law alone, as many have explained, but of the Gospel. And here the universal doctrine concerning the distinction between the Law and the Gospel must be repeated and considered in this explanation.

Latin:

Qui habet mandata mea, et servat, etc.

Dictum est supra, misceri consolationes, et doctrinam seu mandata, ut in colloquio adeuntis mortem. Hic inserit de Ecclesia quid sit, et ubi sit, estque hic locus diligenter observandus hanc ipsam ob causam, quia hanc controversiam, quid sit Ecclesia, diiudicat. Perpetuo viri politici pingunt Ecclesiam, ut regnum mundanum, di- cunt esse coetum renatorum, et non renatorum, amplectentium Evangelium, alligatum ad Roma- num Episcopum, regnantem iuxta ordinariam successionem, et hunc Episcopum habere pote- statem condendi leges, et interpretandi Evange- lii, et omnes homines ad has leges ab eo condi- tas, et eius interpretationem alligatos esse, et ad- dunt Romanum Episcopum seu concilium eius non posse errare in fide seu in necessariis, imo aliqui addunt, etiam mundi imperia. Dicunt hunc summum Episcopum habere potestatem re- gna transferendi, et oportere munitum esse opi- bus et exercitibus, ac reges debere ei defensio- nem et eius arbitrio bella sumere et deponere, ad hoc allegant dictum, quod cum de solo Christo loquatur, ipsi detorquent ad Romanum Episco- pum: Data est mihi omnis potestas in coelo et in terra, talis pictura Ecclesiae extat in libris mul- torum. Sed prorsus transformat Ecclesiam in regnum mundanum contra multa mandata Christi, qui inquit: Reges gentium dominantur, vos autem non sic. Item: Sicut me misit pater, sic ego mitto vos.

Cum autem Ecclesia habeat promissionem, quod sit columna veritatis, et illi Episcopi nomen Ecclesiae ad se transferant, et eo praetextu sta- biliant idola et errores, ac infinita multitudo ho- minum moveatur solo nomine Ecclesiae, necesse est doceri bonas mentes, quid sit et ubi sit Eccle- sia, et hanc doctrinam saepe inculcari necesse est. Non fingenda est invisibilis Ecclesia, sicut idea Platonica, nec tamen imaginemur Ecclesiam si- milem mundano regno, sed honestae scholae. Quoties autem de Ecclesia dicitur, semper ante omnia cogita dictum Pauli: Quos vocavit, hos elegit, vocatio autem visibilis est. Nam vocato- rum coetus est coetus externa professione ample- ctentium Evangelium. Nulla igitur electio cogi- tetur extra hunc visibilem coetum. Ac magna consolatio est piis scire, quod necesse sit semper in hoc visibili coetu, in his templis et his scho- lis aliquos esse electos, et quod nusquam alibi sint ulli electi. Amandus est igitur hic visibilis coetus et hoc ministerium, et certo statuendum, quod perseverans in doctrina huius visibilis coe- tus recte docentis, electus sit ad vitam aeternam. Haec cogitare ad pietatem, et tranquillitatem con- scientiae, et Ecclesiae utile est, et cum hac sen- tentia Pauli congruunt multa dicta in hoc textu: Qui diligit me, sermonem meum servabit.

Sit ergo haec definitio Ecclesiae visibilis: Ecclesia est coetus amplectentium Evangelium, et societate sacramentorum et ministerii evangelici coniunctorum, ac renatorum per Spiritum san- ctum, cui coetui multi non renati admixti sunt, qui tamen in professione verae doctrinae illis con- sentiunt, nec propter manifesta scelera excom- municati sunt.

Haec definitio perspicua est, et sumta est ex multis testimoniis, ut ex dicto Christi, cap. 10. Ioan.: Oves meae vocem meam audiunt, et ad Ephes. 2.: Estis igitur domestici Dei, extructi super fundamentum Apostolorum et Prophetarum, existente lapide angulari Iesu Christo, in quo omnis structura coagmentata crescit in templum sanctum domino, per quem et vos aedificati estis, ut sitis habitaculum Spiritus sancti. Huc et pa- rabolae pertinent, Matth. 13. de sagena missa in mare, et aliae. Nec partes quae in hac defini- tione recensentur, ab ullis reprehendi possunt. Sed aliquid addi nolunt hypocritae, fascinati opi- nionibus politicis, de regno pontificio, nec sunt contenti, cum audiunt Ecclesiam coetum esse am- plectentium Evangelium, coniunctum societate sacramentorum et ministerii evangelici, sed vo- lunt addi, alligatum ad Romanum Pontificem et ordinariam successionem Episcoporum, et eorum interpretationem et leges. De hac re hoc tem- pore dimicatio est, et nos atrocissime accusant et execrantur, tanquam hostes Ecclesiae Dei, et no- bis crimina omnium maxime detestanda obiiciunt, motae seditionis in Ecclesia, et haerescos, et vo- cant nos tum schismaticos, tum haereticos. Nec verbis explicari potest, quantum homo honestus, qui non vult se perhiberi perniciem esse generis humani, crucietur his conviciis, imo facilius esset multis perferre cruciatus corporis acerbissimos, ac interfici, quam haec convicia audire. Multi etiam metu horum conviciorum fugiunt professionem veritatis. Ideo necesse est pios bene confirmatos et munitos esse adversus hanc obiectionem. Nam profecto sanos et mode- ratos homines non leviter vulnerant illa venenata maledicta, praesertim a talibus, qui doctrinae et virtutis opinionem habent obiecta, et accedunt multa scandala, quae faciunt plausibiliorem cri- minationem. Multi sunt viri graves, senes, eru- diti, praestantes virtute, qui Reipub. consilia diu gubernaverunt, ut Cardinales, Campegius, Contarenus, Sadoletus, et similes, qui nos ac- cusant, primum quod falso Ecclesiam taxemus, et hanc dicunt alligatam esse ad Rom. Pontificem et Episcoporum ordinariam successionem, hos negant errare posse in necessariis ad salutem. Deinde addunt, etiamsi quid sit erroris, expe- ctandam esse emendationem ab ordinaria pote- state, nec movendas seditiones. Quia error mi- nus malum sit, quam seditio, et citant dictum Dionysii Alexandrini apud Euseb. lib. 6.: maius scelus esse scindere Ecclesiam, quam idolis sa- crificare. Haec oratio valde plausibilis est, ideo piis quaerendae sunt confirmationes verae, et non fucosae, ad has obiectiones refutandas. Ac prima confirmatio nobis est haec vera, et quae taxari non potest. Illi qui ex animo, et non simulate provocant ad iudicia Ecclesiae, nequa- quam sunt hostes Ecclesiae, aut seditiosi, aut schismatici, aut haeretici. Quia scriptum est: Si Ecclesiam non audierit, sit tibi velut Ethnicus aut Publicanus. Tantisper igitur donec non de- fugit iudicium Ecclesiae, non potest dici hostis, aut schismaticus. Secunda est crassa confirmatio, quoquo modo sese habent caeterae disputationes, hoc constat, nos non debere socios esse manifestorum parrici- diorum, sicut scriptum est: Non communices alie- nis peccatis. Sunt autem manifesta parricidia, quod multi pii homines propter traditiones hu- manas, item multi pii sacerdotes propter coniu- gium interficiuntur, huius crudelitatis societate se polluunt, Campegius, Sadoletus, et similes, qui gloriantur se esse catholicos, quia defendant po- litiam pontificiam.

Tertia confirmatio, quod manifestum est mandatum Dei: Fugite idola, anteponendum esse concordiae, et omnibus rebus humanis, ac di- ctum illud Dionysii dextre intelligendum est de ea sententia, de qua loquitur, confert idola et hae- reses. Hic recte dicitur: non minus scelus esse, falsa dogmata serere, quam idola colere. Dispu- tat enim contra Novatum. Constat autem Mo- nachos et similes tueri manifestos idolorum cultus, scilicet invocationem mortuorum ad certas sta- tuas, et horrendas profanationes coenae Domini in Missis venalibus et funebribus. Haec mala adeo manifesta sunt, ut excusari non possint, quae tamen ita defendunt, ut stabilire conentur, et in- terficiant eos qui dissentiunt.

Quarta confirmatio, etsi diiudicatio dogma- tum indoctis difficilis est, tamen eruditi possunt videre discrimen, et intelligere cur non sit assen- tiendum erroribus Monachorum. Et quanquam nunc multos manifestos errores profiteri non au- dent, et fucosis interpretationibus mitigant, ta- men nervos errorum retinent. Omnes universa- liter defendunt hanc propositionem, quod homo semper debeat dubitare de remissione peccatorum, et hanc dubitationem esse piam reverentiam erga Deum. Ita relinquunt Christum, et abolent do- ctrinam de fide et invocatione, quae fieri non potest, cum mens fugit Deum, et ei irascitur, cum in vero pavore dubitatio crescit. Pugnat ergo illorum imaginatio cum his dictis: Iustificati fide pacem habemus. Item: Accedamus cum fiducia ad thronum gratiae, ac multi errores de discrimine legis et Evangelii impliciti sunt huic eorum imaginationi. Manifestum est etiam li- bros eorum de satisfactionibus canonicis, plenos esse errorum et tenebrarum, obscurantium Evan- gelium. Denique certum est, de remissione pec- catorum non recte loqui eorum libros, et silen- tium esse de fide accipiente remissionem pecca- torum. Imo contrarium dogma defendi, quod semper sit dubitandum de remissione. Haec re- prehendi necesse est, vel si fractus illabitur or- bis: quia Evangelium affirmat hanc sententiam, quod propter filium Dei mediatorem gratis offera- tur nobis remissio peccatorum et quod fide eam accipi oporteat. Hanc sententiam necesse est in Ecclesia Dei extare, et propugnari. Nam hac luce extincta, non agnoscitur Christi beneficium, nec conspicitur discrimen legis et Evangelii, nec cernitur differentia inter Ecclesiae doctrinam et inter ethnicas opiniones.

Haec recensui, quia adversarii saepe atroci- ter declamitant in genere, quanta mala sint discor- diae et seditiones, et interdum in hominibus mo- deratis, et infirmis conturbant Spiritum sanctum. Ne autem clamores illi frangant animos piorum, verae, non sophisticae, non fucosae causae tenen- dae sunt, quod necesse sit nos dissentire a defen- soribus iniustae crudelitatis et errorum. Nunc igitur ad definitionem Ecclesiae redeo, dico alli- gatam esse Ecclesiam ad Evangelium et ad mini- sterium Evangelii, sed non ad Episcopatum Ro- manum et successionem ordinariam. Quia cum Episcopus Romanus vel alii sunt hostes Evangelii, dissentire ab eis necesse est, sicut clare haec vox docet: Si quis aliud Evangelium docet, anathema sit, nec leve convicium est vocari anathema, omnium maledictorum extremum et summum est, sciamus reiectos esse a Deo defensores idolorum et impiorum dogmatum, nec propter opinionem autoritatis eorum amplectendos esse errores. Hanc igitur sententiam nobis ipsi inculcemus, hac voce Pauli nos muniamus contra illas vituperationes dissidiorum, et respondeamus: Si quis aliud Evan- gelium docet, anathema sit, etc.

Idem prorsus in hac concione Christus dicit: Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum servabit, et pater meus diliget eum, et ad eum veniemus, et mansionem apud eum faciemus. Haec est plana et perspicua Ecclesiae descriptio: Ibi, inquit, ha- bitabimus pater et ego, et hos diliget pater meus, qui sermonem meum, id est, Evangelium, qui tradidi Ecclesiae, amplectentur, et non corrum- pent admixtis pravis opinionibus. Recensui nati- vam sententiam textus, quem prorsus corrumpunt interpretes ignari doctrinae Evangelii, qui putant esse concionem legis, et sic enarrant: Si quis di- ligit me, sermonem meum servabit, id est, si quis ex toto corde, ex tota anima, et omnib. viribus diligit Deum, is servat legem, is placet Deo. Haec enarratio aliena est, nec pertinet ad hunc locum. Christus vocat sermonem suum, non so- lam legem, sed totum Evangelium, id est, pro- missionem gratiae et vitae aeternae, quam Deus peculiariter revelavit, et vult esse legis interpre- tem. Totam hanc doctrinam hic tradit Ecclesiae suae, et affirmat ibi fore populum suum, et ibi se habitaturum esse, ubi haec doctrina sonabit. Norunt etiam Ethnici legem utcunque, sed pro- pter hanc non sunt populus Dei. At ille coetus est Ecclesia Dei, in quo sonat vox Evangelii, et in eo coetu necesse est aliquos esse electos ad vi- tam aeternam. Et sunt viva membra omnes, qui fide amplectuntur Evangelium, et propter filium Dei credunt se placere Deo, et habent incoatam obedientiam, sicut de lege docet Evangelium. Haec admonitio necessaria est hoc loco, ut scia- mus Christum non de sola legis doctrina loqui, ut multi enarrarunt, sed de Evangelio. Et hic universa doctrina de discrimine legis et Evangelii in hac enarratione repetenda et consideranda est.

## 14:26
But the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth.

He repeats the sweetest consolation, in which, as above, he promises the Holy Spirit to the Apostles and to his Church, and adds what his benefit and office is. But first let us learn here that the weak also pertain to the Church, just as Paul admonishes in Romans 14: Receive the weak in faith, for God has received them. Thus Christ signifies here that the Apostles do not yet understand these discourses, just as the event later showed they were not understood. But because they are not enemies of the Gospel, but hear and seek to be taught, therefore they are members of the Church.

But he says expressly: The Father will send the Holy Spirit in my name, that is, on account of me, and to those who acknowledge me. This is a huge prerogative of the Church, that is, of those professing the Gospel, that the Holy Spirit is certainly given in this assembly. Let us allow the Gentiles, Heretics, and Mahometans to preach their empires, riches, and pleasures; indeed, let us allow the Israelites to please themselves magnificently on account of the promise of the land of Canaan. This promise concerning the Holy Spirit far excels, which turns minds to the Gospel, and does not allow them to be entangled in errors, but begins a new light, righteousness, and eternal life, and sustains and consoles believers in all tribulations.

But that is to be lamented and deplored, that we, hard and blind, are not moved by so ample a promise: Human minds, on account of natural diffidence, and deterred by the Law, by no means assent that the goodness of God is so great that he would hear us, variously polluted though we are, and indeed bestow such great goods—reconciliation, the Holy Spirit, and eternal life. There are many sad impediments which either extinguish or weaken faith, just as Paul also says in Rom. 7: That sins through the law are effective in our members, that is, that faith and invocation are hindered by the terrors of the law, and that many other sins arise from diffidence. Let the pious understand these things, and let them resist diffidence, and let them be excited by the accumulation of these promises, so that they may believe them not to be empty sounds of words, but that we are truly heard when we call upon Him for Christ's sake, and that we truly obtain these very goods which are promised, nor does experience precede faith, but follows it: God wishes to be believed first, and He hears and helps those who believe. Therefore it is said in 2 Chron. 20: Believe in God, and you shall be secure, and in Mark 9: I believe, Lord; help my unbelief.

And this is also to be diligently observed, that the Holy Spirit is promised to that assembly in which there is the recognition of Christ, that is, in which the voice of the Gospel sounds, just as he also said above: If anyone keeps my words, we will come to him, etc., and below in chapter 15: If you remain in me, and my words remain in you, whatever you wish you shall ask, and it shall be done for you. This is a great consolation to the pious, to know for certain that the promise of the Holy Spirit is bound to the Gospel, that the Holy Spirit is given to those who believe the Gospel and ask with this faith. Likewise, that the Holy Spirit is certainly effective through the Gospel, as is said in Rom. 1: The Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes. Likewise 2 Cor. 3: The Gospel is the ministry of the spirit, that is, through which the Holy Spirit is given. These promises, on account of the narrowness of the human heart and manifold diffidence, are not sufficiently looked upon, but when we contemplate them in invocation, we experience them to be true and not void.

Latin:

Paracletus autem spiritus veritatis.

Repetit dulcissimam consolationem, in qua ut supra promittit Apostolis et Ecclesiae suae Spi- ritum sanctum, et addit quod sit eius beneficium et munus. Primum autem discamus hic ad Ec- clesiam etiam pertinere infirmos, sicut Paulus monet ad Romanos 14.: Infirmos in fide assu- mite, Deus enim recepit eos. Ita hic significat Christus Apostolos nondum intelligere has con- ciones, sicut postea Eventus ostendit non intel- lectas esse. Sed quia non sunt hostes Evangelii, sed audiunt et doceri expetunt, ideo sunt mem- bra Ecclesiae.

Diserte autem inquit: Pater mittet Spiritum sanctum in nomine meo, id est, propter me, et agnoscentibus me. Ingens haec praerogativa est Ecclesiae, hoc est profitentium Evangelium, quod certo in hoc coetu datur Spiritus sanctus. Sina- mus Ethnicos, Haereticos, et Mahometistas prae- dicare sua imperia, opes, voluptates, imo sina- mus Israëlitas magnifice sibi placere propter pro- missionem terrae Canaan. Haec promissio de Spiritu sancto longe antecellit, qui flectit mentes ad Evangelium, nec sinit eas intricari erroribus, sed incoat novam lucem, iusticiam et vitam ae- ternam, et sustentat ac consolatur credentes in omnibus aerumnis.

Sed illud est dolendum et deplorandum, quod nos duri et caeci non movemur tam ampla promissione: Humanae mentes propter naturalem diffidentiam, et absterriti lege, nequaquam as- sentiuntur tantam esse bonitatem Dei, ut nos va- rie pollutos exaudiat, et quidem tanta bona, re- conciliationem, Spiritum sanctum et vitam aeter- nam largiatur. Multa tristia impedimenta sunt, quae fidem aut extinguunt, aut languefaciunt, sicut et Paulus ad Rom. 7. ait: Peccata per legem efficacia esse in membris uostris, id est, terrori- bus legis impediri fidem et invocationem, et ex diffidentia oriri multa peccata alia. Haec intelli- gant pii, et repugnent diffidentiae, et harum pro- missionum cumulo excitentur, ut credant eas non esse inanes verborum sonos, sed revera nos ex- audiri invocantes propter Christum, et revera im- petrare haec ipsa bona, quae promittuntur, nec experientia praecurrit fidem, sed sequitur: Prius sibi vult credi Deus, et credentes exaudit, et ad- iuvat. Ideo dicitur 2. Paral. 20.: Credite Deo, et securi eritis, et Marci 9.: Credo Domine, opi- tulare meae incredulitati.

Est et hoc diligenter observandum, quod certo illi coetui promittitur Spiritus sanctus, in quo est agnitio Christi, hoc est, in quo sonat vox Evangelii, sicut et supra inquit: Si quis servabit sermones meos, ad eum veniemus etc., et infra cap. 15.: Si manseritis in me, et verba mea in vobis manserint, quod volueritis, petetis, et fiet vobis. Haec est magna consolatio piis, scire certo promissionem Spiritus sancti alligatam esse ad Evangelium, donari Spiritum sanctum iis, qui credunt Evangelio, et hac fide petunt. Item, certo efficacem esse Spiritum sanctum per Evan- gelium, sicut dicitur ad Rom. 1.: Evangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti. Item 2. ad Corinth. 3.: Evangelium est ministerium spiritus, id est, per quod datur Spiritus sanctus. Hae promissiones propter angustiam humani cor- dis et multiplicem diffidentiam non satis aspiciun- tur, sed cum eas in invocatione intuemur, expe- rimur eas veras, et non irritas esse.

## 14:26
He will teach you all things.

O great benefit of God, that He speaks with us so properly and clearly about the greatest matters, and that He has handed down promises in such lucid words that there can be no doubt about the meaning. But this is to be lamented, that there is such weakness and diffidence in our minds that we do not dare to ask for and expect such great goods, even though we are so often invited and commanded. But since He has previously openly affirmed that the Holy Spirit is given to the Church, that is, to those embracing the Gospel, as He says by name: Whom the Father will send in my name, that is, for my sake, and to those acknowledging me, now He speaks most clearly about the benefit, or gift, of the Holy Spirit. He will teach you, and will bring to your remembrance those things which I have said to you. The Jews expect from the Messiah victories, empires, wealth, money, pleasures: the world understands and admires these goods. But Christ here promises far different things, which the world does not value, true doctrine, light in the minds acknowledging and calling upon God, ardent motions of the heart which conform to the law of God, and consolations. The ungodly do not value these any more than if some new guest arriving were to promise that he would teach geometry. Therefore Christ said above that He would give the Holy Spirit, whom the world does not know. But let us in the Church give thanks to God for this so great a gift, and let us acknowledge what are properly the benefits of the Holy Spirit, how great these goods are, and how they are given and retained. This is the peculiar wisdom of the Church.

However, these two words must be joined: He will teach, and will bring to your remembrance those things which I have said to you. For He binds us to the Gospel handed down by Christ, He affirms that a kind of doctrine alien to the Gospel, or fighting against the Gospel, is not brought by the Holy Spirit. Often adversaries cite this saying: He will teach you all things, to establish opinions and rites which were not handed down by the Gospel, such as the abuses of Masses, invocations of dead men, monastic vows, and other feigned ceremonies. These, they say, are of that number of which it is said: The Holy Spirit will teach you all things. Thus also the ancient heretics abused this saying. But let the following clause be opposed: He will bring to your remembrance those things which I have said to you. The Holy Spirit teaches and illustrates those things which have already been handed down in the Gospel through Christ, concerning matters necessary for eternal life; concerning these, illuminations are not to be sought or expected outside the doctrine of the Gospel, as has often been said, and it is useful to remember the testimony of Paul pertaining to this: If anyone teaches another Gospel, let him be anathema.

Let us therefore hold here first this sentiment, that the Holy Spirit, in teaching, uses the voice of the Gospel, and teaches nothing besides the Gospel; then, that this teaching is to be understood in two ways, publicly in the ministry, and privately in the hearts. Thus we have embraced both benefits above, as often as it was said of the Holy Spirit. He is publicly present in the ministry, and retains the true meaning, and through the ministry itself he is effective, as these sayings most clearly testify: 1 Cor. 1 and 2 Cor. 3: The Gospel is the ministry of the Spirit, and to the Romans 1: The Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth. The Holy Spirit retains in the Church the light of true doctrine, sometimes in more, sometimes in fewer, and from time to time kindles it again, as is said in Ephesians 4: He gave gifts to men, Prophets, Apostles, Pastors, Teachers, and the cause of such a great benefit is added there, that men may not fluctuate, as if tossed by the winds of errors, that is, the Holy Spirit retains the Gospel handed down by Christ in the Church, and adds the gift of interpretation, whether in many or in few, so that one, true, perpetual, incorrupt meaning may always remain, lest, with the true knowledge and invocation of God extinguished, the whole human race be oppressed by ethnic furies and the like. These things concerning the public benefit must be diligently thought upon, and it must be prayed that the voice of the public ministry may always and everywhere be ruled by the Holy Spirit as teacher.

Then there is the private benefit, when minds hear the word of God, the Holy Spirit kindles light in hearts by this very voice, so that they may rightly understand the Gospel, and the mind, will, and heart may be bent toward believing, and motions consenting to the law of God may be excited, and consolations, which are the beginning of eternal life, as Christ says in John 17: This is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent, and concerning both benefits, public and private, it has often been said already, and it will have to be said again. And since the words of the text are so clear, there is no need for a long narration, but it is profitable for the reader to be reminded, then by pious thought in daily dangers and in invocation, these sweetest promises become more illustrious.

Latin:

Ille docebit vos omnia.

O magnum Dei beneficium, quod nobiscum tam proprie et perspicue de maximis rebus loqui- tur, et quod promissiones tradidit adeo dilucidis verbis, ut de sententia dubitari non possit. Sed hoc dolendum est, tantam esse imbecillitatem et diffidentiam in nostris mentibus, ut petere et ex- pectare tanta bona non ausimus, ne toties qui- dem invitati et iussi. Cum autem antea aperte affirmarit dari Spiritum sanctum Ecclesiae, hoc est, amplectentibus Evangelium, ut nominatim inquit: Quem mittet pater in nomine meo, id est, propter me, et agnoscentibus me, nunc cla- rissime dicit de beneficio, seu munere Spiritus sancti. Docebit vos, et rediget vobis in memo- riam ea, quae dixi vobis. Iudaei expectant a Messia victorias, imperia, opes, pecuniam, vo- luptates: haec bona mundus intelligit, et mira- tur. At Christus hic promittit longe alias res, quas mundus non magnifacit, veram doctrinam, lucem in mentibus agnoscentem et invocantem Deum, ardentes motus cordis, qui legi Dei con- gruunt, et consolationes. Haec impii non pluris faciunt, quam si quis novus hospes veniens pro- mittat se traditurum doctrinam geometricam. Ideo supra inquit Christus, se daturum Spiritum san- ctum, quem mundus non norit. Sed nos in Ec- clesia agamus Deo gratias pro hoc tanto munere, et agnoscamus, quae sint proprie beneficia Spiri- tus sancti, quanta bona sint, et quomodo dentur, ac retineantur. Haec est peculiaris Ecclesiae sa- pientia.

Coniungenda sunt autem haec duo verba: Docebit, et rediget in memoriam ea, quae dixi vobis. Alligat enim nos ad Evangelium tradi- tum a Christo, affirmat non afferri a Spiritu san- cto genus doctrinae alienum ab Evangelio, aut cum Evangelio pugnans. Saepe adversarii citant hoc dictum: Docebit vos omnia, ad stabiliendas opiniones et ritus, qui non sunt traditi ab Evan- gelio, ut Missarum abusus, invocationes homi- num mortuorum, vota monastica, et alias cere- monias commentitias. Haec inquiunt, sunt ex eo numero de quibus dicitur: Spiritus sanctus do- cebit vos omnia. Sic et haeretici veteres abute- bantur hoc dicto. Sed opponatur particula se- quens: Rediget vobis in memoriam ea, quae dixi vobis. Haec docet et illustrat Spiritus sanctus, quae iam in Evangelio tradita sunt per Christum, de rebus necessariis ad vitam aeternam, de his non sunt illuminationes quaerandae, aut expe- ctandae, extra doctrinam Evangelii, ut saepe di- ctum est, et meminisse Pauli testimonium huc pertinens utile est: Si quis aliud Evangelium do- cebit, anathema sit.

Teneamus ergo hic primum hanc sententiam, quod Spiritus sanctus docens utatur voce Evan- gelii, nec alia praeter Evangelium doceat, deinde hoc docere intelligatur dupliciter, publice in mi- nisterio, et privatim in cordibus. Ita supra utrun- que beneficium complexi sumus, quoties dictum est de S. S. Publice adest ministerio, ac retinet veram sententiam, et per ipsum ministerium est efficax, ut clarissime testantur haec dicta 1. ad Cor. 1. et 2. ad Corinth. 3.: Evangelium est mi- nisterium spiritus, et ad Romanos 1.: Evange- lium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti. Retinet Spiritus sanctus in Ecclesia lucem verae doctrinae, alias in pluribus, alias in paucioribus, et subinde rursus accendit, ut ad Ephesios quarto dicitur: Dedit dona hominibus, Prophetas, Apo- stolos, Pastores, Doctores, et additur ibi causa tanti beneficii, ne fluctuent homines, tanquam ventis errorum agitati, id est, Spiritus sanctus retinet Evangelium a Christo traditum in Eccle- sia, et addit donum interpretationis, seu in mul- tis, seu in paucis, ut una, vera, perpetua, in- corrupta sententia semper maneat, ne extincta vera agnitione et invocatione Dei, totum genus humanum opprimatur furoribus ethnicis et simi- libus. Haec de publico beneficio diligenter cogi- tanda sunt, et petendum est, ut doctore Spiritu sancto semper et ubique regatur vox ministerii publici.

Deinde privatum beneficium est, cum men- tes audiunt verbum Dei, Spiritus sanctus hac ipsa voce lucem in cordibus accendit, ut recte intelligant Evangelium, et flectantur mens, vo- luntas et cor ad credendum, et excitentur motus consentientes legi Dei, et consolationes, quae sunt incoatio vitae aeternae, ut Christus inquit Ioan. 17.: Haec est vita aeterna, ut agnoscant te solum verum esse Deum, et quem misisti Iesum esse Christum, ac de utroque beneficio, publico et privato, saepe iam dictum est, et rursus dicen- dum erit. Cumque verba textus adeo perspicua sint, non est opus longa enarratione, sed com- monefieri lectorem prodest, deinde pia cogita- tione in quotidianis periculis et in invocatione, hae dulcissimae promissiones fiunt illustriores.

## 14:27
My peace I give unto you.

Thus in this sentence the reader is to be reminded of what is being said. Afterwards, in afflictions and dangers, thought will render this promise more illustrious. Many have understood: I leave my peace with you, for this sentence: I want you to be in harmony among yourselves, and to tolerate injuries, and not to incite the populace against the enemies of the Gospel. But although he often preaches elsewhere about harmony and tolerance, yet the saying that is read here is not a precept, but is a promise and consolation, pertaining to individuals and to the whole Church. Therefore, peace in this place signifies, as often elsewhere, tranquility and joy of mind, arising from two causes, namely, because the mind understands that God must be obeyed in those miseries, and it foresees the outcome, that is, it knows that God is present with us, is even now bringing help, mitigating calamities, and will at length give peaceful outcomes.

These things will be understood more clearly from comparison. Demosthenes, Cicero, and the like sustain great dangers in their governance, and when they see their counsels to be unhappy, they accuse the treachery of their allies, they grieve that their labors are fruitless and vain, and they judge themselves to be neglected by God; therefore they become angry at God, and are oppressed by desperation and grief. In these there is no peace, of which Christ speaks, that is, tranquility or joy of heart, and the expectation of a good outcome. But on the contrary, in Jeremiah and in the Baptist there is peace, even though both sustain huge miseries, huge dangers, and at length are killed by tyrants. But whence does this peace arise in the heart? That is, what causes console and sustain them? These causes are: They know from heavenly doctrine why the Church is subjected to the cross, and that God demands this obedience; indeed, they know that the Son of God, who is the head of the Church, will be a victim, and will tolerate the most bitter tortures. Meanwhile, however, they know that they and the Church are helped and sustained by God, and that at length the outcomes will be joyful and glorious, and that their labors are not vain and fruitless.

Jeremiah's governance is unlike the counsels of all the previous Prophets; all the previous ones prohibited surrender and ordered them to fight, which the promises, which signified that the kingdom would remain in Judah, were persuading and promising. But Jeremiah persuades surrender, which was destructive to this whole polity and was going to dissipate the nation. These things seemed to fight with the promise, for it did not seem likely that a dissipated nation could after seventy years be gathered again into one place, or one form of Republic. Therefore the Princes, High Priests, and Priests hated and in many ways tortured Jeremiah. He tolerates these things with great strength of mind, and knows that his labors are salutary to the Church of God, even though he sees the destruction of the city, the dissipation, and the slaughter of the citizens; he knows also this, that he is protected and helped by God, although he is often cruelly vexed by enemies, and at length is killed in Egypt. In these most sad spectacles, however, this Prophet retains peace, that is, divine consolation and joy; he knows himself to be a minister of God, and sustains himself with the promise of God, and feels joy and the beginnings of eternal life in his heart.

This comparison renders the saying of Christ more illustrious. Now let us apply it to ourselves privately and publicly. Privately we are tormented on account of our sins, often also we are exercised by many private miseries; to all these sorrows let us oppose this saying of Christ: My peace I give to you. First, let us know that we, although we have fallen and are unworthy, are nevertheless truly received on account of the Son of God. Next, let us instruct ourselves concerning the causes of afflictions, and let us know that obedience is to be rendered to God, and help and mitigation are to be sought and expected. For the most part, however, public dangers terrify minds vehemently; kings, inflamed with hatreds, attempt to destroy the Church, and everywhere they kill many; no seat of studies seems likely to remain; we, without protection, without any defense, are exposed to enemies to be slaughtered. Here it is difficult to understand this voice of Christ: My peace I give to you. But yet the pious have these consolations; they know why the Church is subjected to the cross, and that obedience is to be rendered to God; they know also this, that the Church will remain, and that the labors which they undertake are not in vain, and that God is also present and helping them. These consolations are promised to us by these sayings: I will not leave you orphans. Likewise: My peace I give to you, and in Isaiah 46 it is said: I will carry the aging Church, I have founded it, I will carry it, I will save it.

With these consolations let us sustain ourselves in the dangers of these times, and with faith let us seek and expect help and good outcomes, and let us not abandon the studies of doctrine on account of the furies of enemies, nor let us think our labors will be in vain. And when we raise ourselves with faith, we shall feel the consolation and joy of which Paul [speaks] to the Philippians: The peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, shall guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus. The peace of God, that is, the consolation taken from the sweetest promises, which when faith embraces it, it knows God is present with us, as He says, that He dwells with a contrite heart, and it expects counsel, mitigation of dangers, and salutary outcomes. And therefore it confirms minds, so that they do not abandon the profession, studies, and labors of teaching and governing the Church, even if great impediments are thrown in the way; to all these Christ opposes this saying: My peace I give to you.

Latin:

Pacem meam do vobis.

Sic in hac sententia commonefaciendus est lector, qua de re dicatur. Postea in afflictioni- bus et periculis, hanc promissionem cogitatio reddet illustriorem. Multi intellexerunt: Pacem relinquo vobis, pro hac sententia: Volo vos esse concordes inter vos, et tolerare iniurias, nec con- citare plebem contra Evangelii hostes. Etsi au- tem alias saepe de concordia, et de tolerantia con- cionatur, tamen dictum quod hic legitur, non est praeceptum, sed est promissio et consolatio, ad singulos et ad universam Ecclesiam pertinens. Significat igitur pax hoc loco, ut saepe alias, tran- quillitatem et gaudium mentis, ortum a duabus causis, quia videlicet mens intelligit Deo in illis aerumnis obediendum esse, et prospicit exitum, id est, scit Deum nobis adesse, iam nunc opem ferre, mitigare calamitates, et tandem daturum placidos exitus.

Haec clarius intelligentur ex collatione. De- mosthenes, Cicero et similes magna pericula sus- tinent in sua gubernatione, et cum vident sua consilia esse infelicia, accusant sociorum perfi- diam, dolent suos labores esse irritos et inanes, et iudicant se a Deo negligi, irascuntur ergo Deo, et opprimuntur desperatione et dolore. In his non est pax, de qua Christus loquitur, id est, tran- quillitas seu gaudium cordis, et expectatio boni exitus. At econtra in Ieremia et in Baptista est pax, tametsi ambo sustinent ingentes aerumnas, ingentia pericula, et tandem a tyrannis interficiun- tur. Unde autem haec pax in corde oritur? id est, quae causae consolantur, et sustentant eos? Hae causae sunt. Norunt ex doctrina coelesti cur Ecclesia sit subiecta cruci, et quod Deus hanc obedientiam postulet, imo sciunt filium Dei, qui est caput Ecclesiae, futurum esse victimam, et toleraturum acerbissimos cruciatus. Interim ta- men sciunt, se et Ecclesiam iuvari, et sustentari a Deo, et tandem exitus fore laetos et gloriosos, nec labores suos inanes et irritos esse.

Ieremiae gubernatio dissimilis est omnium superiorum Prophetarum consiliis, omnes supe- riores prohibuerunt deditionem, et iusserunt di- micare, quod suadebant et promissiones, quae significabant regnum in Iuda mansurum esse. At Ieremias suadet deditionem, quae erat exitiosa huic toti politiae, et dissipatura erat gentem. Haec pugnare videbantur cum promissione, nec enim verisimile videbatur, dissipatam gentem post se- ptuaginta annos rursus congregari posse in unum locum, aut unam formam Reipub. Ideo Prin- cipes, Pontifices et Sacerdotes oderant, et multis modis excruciabant Ieremiam. Haec tolerat in- genti robore animi, et scit suos labores salutares esse Ecclesiae Dei, etiamsi videt excidium urbis, dissipationem, et neces civium, scit et hoc, se a Deo protegi et iuvari, quanquam saepe crudeliter vexetur ab inimicis, ac tandem in Aegypto interfi- citur. In his tristissimis spectaculis tamen reti- net hic Propheta pacem, id est, consolationem et laetitiam divinam, scit se Dei ministrum esse, et sustentat se promissione Dei, ac sentit laeti- tiam et initia vitae aeternae in corde.

Haec collatio dictum Christi reddit illustrius. Nunc accommodemus ad nos privatim et publice. Privatim angimur propter peccata nostra, saepe etiam exercemur multis privatis miseriis, his do- loribus omnibus opponamus hoc dictum Christi: Pacem meam do vobis. Primum sciamus nos, quanquam lapsi sumus, et sumus indigni, tamen vere recipi propter filium Dei. Deinde de causis afflictionum nos erudiamus, et sciamus Deo prae- standam esse obedientiam, et petendum et ex- pectandum auxilium et mitigationem. Plerum- que autem publica pericula vehementer terrent animos, reges incensi odiis, delere Ecclesiam co- nantur, et passim multos interficiunt, nulla se- des studiorum mansura videtur, nos sine praesi- diis, sine defensione ulla obiicimur hostibus tru- cidandi. Hic difficile est intelligere hanc vocem Christi: Pacem meam do vobis. Sed tamen pii habent has consolationes, sciunt cur Ecclesia cruci subiecta sit, et Deo obedientiam praestan- dam esse, norunt et hoc, Ecclesiam mansuram esse, nec irritos esse labores, quos suscipiunt, Deum etiam adesse, et opitulari ipsis. Hae con- solationes nobis his dictis promittuntur: Non re- linquam vos orphanus. Item: Pacem meam do vobis, et Esaiae 46. dicitur: Ego senescentem Ecclesiam gestabo, ego eam condidi, ego por- tabo, ego salvabo.

His consolationibus nos sustentemus in peri- culis horum temporum, et fide petamus et ex- pectemus auxilium, et bonos exitus, et non abii- ciamus studia doctrinae propter hostium furores, nec arbitremur nostros labores irritos fore. Cum- que fide nos erigemus, sentiemus consolationem et gaudium, de quo Paulus ad Philippenses: Pax Dei quae superat omnem sensum, custodiat corda vestra et sensus vestros in Christo Iesu. Pax Dei, id est, consolatio sumta ex dulcissimis pro- missionibus, quas fides cum amplectitur, scit Deum nobis adesse, sicut inquit, se habitare cum contrito corde, et expectat consilium, mitigatio- nem periculorum et salutares exitus. Ac pro- pterea confirmat animos, ne abiiciant professio- nem, studia, labores docendi, et gubernandi Ecclesiam, etiamsi magna impedimenta obiiciun- tur, his omnibus opponit Christus hoc dictum: Pacem meam do vobis.

## 14:28
I go to the Father, because the Father is greater than I.

He dwells on the forewarning and consolation: I, he says, will depart to the Father, that is, a little later I shall be killed, but that death will be a transition to eternal life and to the kingdom which, sitting at the right hand of the Father, that is, with equal power with the Father, I will administer, sanctifying, ruling, and vivifying the eternal Church. But the reason is added: Because the Father is greater than I, that is, you see me in this my vocation weak, about to die, as if deserted by God and all men, but as I said before: Know that I am not deserted. The Father, who sent me, is present with me, will raise me up, and will deliver to me the eternal kingdom, in which I will endow you and all who believe the Gospel with new righteousness, light, life, and eternal glory.

But especially the Arians cited this saying for the defense of their error, when they denied that the Son of God is God by nature. For if the Father is greater, the Son is not omnipotent, nor is He God by nature. To this interpretation of the Arians, let the sayings in the 1st chapter of John be opposed, where it is clearly said: And the Word was God. Likewise: All things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made that has been made. And to the Colossians 1: All things were created through Him and for Him, and all things consist through Him. These and many other testimonies clearly affirm that the Son of God is God by nature, omnipotent and the Creator. Confirmed therefore by these testimonies concerning the essence of the Son, let us afterwards consider the sayings concerning the present vocation to the ministry of the Gospel and to the passion. In this vocation He says: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? And John 8: If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing, but it is the Father who glorifies me. And John 17: Glorify me, Father, with yourself with the glory which I had with you before the world was.

These and similar sayings warn that times must be distinguished. One is the time of Christ reigning gloriously, another is the time of Christ humbled in ministry, passion, and death, when He becomes a victim for the human race; as far as this time and this ministry pertain, the Father is greater than Christ, because the one sending and glorifying, insofar as He sends and glorifies, is greater than the minister sent and subjected to horrendous punishments and temptations. And yet Christ alleges the sender, and by this mission He [confirms] Himself and us he consoles, so that we may know that the Father is present with him, and will restore life and glory. Nor must we dispute here about the essence, but about the time of the office. We do not invent this interpretation, but Christ himself delivers it in the saying in John 17: Glorify me with yourself with the glory which I had with you before the foundation of the world. He affirms that he existed before the foundation of the world, and that he was powerful and glorious. But now, for a time, he will be in this weakness, and will not declare his power, but after some time he will again be powerful in the resurrection.

Latin:

Vado ad patrem, quia pater maior me est.

Commoratur in praemonitione, et consola- tione: Ego, inquit, discedam ad patrem, id est, aliquanto post interficiar, sed illa mors erit transi- tus ad vitam aeternam, et ad regnum, quod se- dens ad dextram patris, id est, pari potentia cum patre administrabo, sanctificans, regens et vi- vificans Ecclesiam aeternam. Additur autem ra- tio: Quia pater maior me est, id est, me videtis in hac mea vocatione imbecillem, moriturum, velut desertum a Deo et omnibus hominibus, sed ut antea dixi: Scitote, me non desertum esse. Pater, qui me misit, adest mihi, resuscitabit me, et regnum aeternum tradet mihi, in quo vos et omnes qui credent Evangelio, donabo nova iu- sticia, luce, vita, et gloria aeterna.

Praecipue vero hoc dictum citaverunt Ariani ad defensionem erroris sui, cum negaverunt filium Dei esse natura Deum. Si enim pater maior est, filius non est omnipotens, nec est natura Deus. Huic Arianorum interpretationi opponantur dicta in 1. cap. Ioan. ubi clare dicitur: Et Deus erat verbum. Item: Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, et sine ipso factum est nihil quod factum est. Et ad Coloss. 1.: Omnia per ipsum, et in eum con- dita sunt, et omnia per eum consistunt. Haec et alia multa testimonia perspicue affirmant, filium Dei esse natura Deum, omnipotentem et crea- torem. Confirmati igitur his testimoniis de es- sentia filii, postea consideremus dicta de voca- tione praesenti ad ministerium Evangelii, et ad passionem. In hac vocatione dicit: Deus Deus meus, quare dereliquisti me. Et Ioan. 8.: Si ego glorifico meipsum, gloria mea nihil est, sed est pater, qui glorificat me. Et Iohan. 17.: Glo- rifica me pater apud te ea gloria, quam habui apud te, antequam mundus esset.

Haec et similia dicta monent, discernenda esse tempora. Aliud est tempus Christi gloriose regnantis, aliud est tempus humiliati Christi in ministerio, passione et morte, cum fit victima pro genere humano, quod ad hoc tempus et hoc ministerium attinet, Pater est maior Christo, quia mittens et glorificans, quatenus mittit et glorifi- cat, maior est ministro misso, et subiecto hor- rendis poenis et tentationibus. Et tamen allegat Christus mittentem, et hac missione se et nos con- solatur, ut sciamus patrem ipsi adesse, et redditurum esse vitam et gloriam. Nec disputandum est hic de essentia, sed de officii tempore. Hanc interpretationem non fingimus, sed Christus eam ipse tradit in dicto Ioan. 17.: Glorifica me apud te ea gloria, quam ante conditionem mundi apud te habui. Affirmat se fuisse ante conditionem mundi, et fuisse potentem et gloriosum. Nunc vero ad tempus se futurum in hac imbecillitate, et non declaraturum potentiam suam, sed aliquanto post rursus fore potentem in resurrectione.

## 14:30
For the Prince of this world comes.

The doctrine and consolation is notable, consistent with the saying in Genesis 3: The seed of the woman will crush the head of the serpent, and the serpent will bite his heel. The matter shows that the devil rages horribly with hatred of God against the Church, and by his own wondrous artifices overthrows many, just as in the beginning he overthrew Adam and Eve, and afterwards stirred up idols and heresies. Thus there is no doubt that Christ was tempted by the devil with most insidious and most cunningly devised frauds. Although we cannot say what kind of temptations they were in such great excellence, it is certain, however, that they were many and various, but Christ consoles the Church. He affirms that he was indeed tempted, but not overcome: The devil, he says, has nothing in me. Here let us learn that the victory of Christ pertains not only to his own person, but to all the members of the Church. He conquered the devil in his temptation, and overcomes death, so that he may testify that he blots out sin in us, and will repress the power and snares of the devil, just as it is written: The Son of God appeared, that he might destroy the works of the devil.

We would understand this power of Christ more if we were struggling with the snares of the devil, who at one time drives to other evils, sometimes weakens faith, and casts other specters that cause doubts, as is said of the Apostles: Satan has demanded you, that he might sift you; at other times he incites to other sins, as he drives David to adultery; Paul speaks of these various weapons of the devil in the last chapter to the Ephesians, and teaches that they are repelled by meditation on the Gospel and the invocation of Christ, who is present to those who call upon him, and delivers us, and when things happen that are inextricable by human counsel, as often occurs, he himself again provides salutary outcomes.

Latin:

Venit enim Princeps mundi huius.

Doctrina et consolatio insignis est, congruens cum dicto Gen. 3.: Semen mulieris conculcabit caput serpentis, et serpens mordebit calcaneum eius. Res ostendit, diabolum odio Dei horribiliter grassari adversus Ecclesiam, et suis mirandis artificiis multos evertere, ut initio evertit Adam et Evam, et postea idola et haereses excitavit. Ita non dubium est insidiosissime et astutissime cogitatis fraudibus tentatum esse a diabolo Christum. Etsi quales in tanta praestantia tentationes fuerint, nos dicere non possumus, certum est tamen, multas et varias fuisse, sed Christus Ecclesiam consolatur. Affirmat se quidem tentatum esse, sed non superatum: Non habet, inquit, diabolus in me quicquam. Hic discamus victoriam Christi, non tantum ad ipsius personam pertinere, sed ad omnia Ecclesiae membra. Vicit diabolum in sua tentatione, et superat mortem, ut testetur se delere peccatum in nobis, et repressurum diaboli potentiam et insidias, sicut scriptum est: Filius Dei apparuit, ut destruat opera diaboli.

Hanc Christi potentiam magis intelligeremus, si certaremus cum insidiis diaboli, qui alias impellit ad alia mala, interdum languefacit fidem, et offundit alia spectra moventia dubitationes, ut de Apostolis dicitur: Satanas vos expetivit, ut cribraret, alias incitat ad alia peccata, ut Davidem ad adulterium impellit, de his telis diaboli variis loquitur Paulus ultimo capite ad Ephesios, et docet ea repelli, meditatione Evangelii et invocatione Christi, qui adest invocantibus, et liberat nos, et cum inextricabilia humano consilio accidunt, ut saepe fit, ipse rursus praebet salutares exitus.

## 15:1 Argument
Chapter XV. I am the true vine.

The doctrine and consolation is most sweet concerning the presence and help of Christ, who rules and aids the Church and individuals who call upon him, and concerning the concord of the Church. And let the image itself be considered first. The Church is depicted as a vine, from which many branches are widely spread, and a vinedresser is added, who may care for the vine and the branches, and gathers the fruits. But mention is very often made of two trees in these comparisons, the olive and the vine, of which two trees they write that there is such great concord that the olive, when grafted onto the vine, produces both olives and grapes. This image most beautifully paints the Law and the Gospel, or the people of the Law and the Church. The vine is dry and rough, like the people of the Law, but yet teaching and learning the doctrine delivered through the Prophets: And when the knowledge of the Gospel approaches, it produces fruits; it teaches the Gospel and the Law. Indeed, then the Law is understood, and the discipline which the Law delivers begins to please God, and often wine signifies the doctrine of the Law or of repentance, but oil the Gospel, as in Luke 10: The Samaritan pours wine and oil into the wounds. For wine is sharp, and cleanses, but oil binds up, heals, and nourishes the flesh. Moreover, the age of both trees is long; they say the olive can live for two hundred years: but the vine, if it has been correctly pruned, much longer.

But in this place the vine signifies Christ, who, as the vine is a rough wood, yet producing a most salutary liquid, so he himself was of sad appearance when he endured death and other miseries in this life. But the branches signify all the other members of the Church. Christ therefore teaches that the other members of the Church live and are fruitful in this way, if they are grafted into him by faith, that is, when they retain the Gospel by faith, and new light and life is kindled in them by Christ himself through the Holy Spirit, and he says clearly and plainly: Those not remaining in him do not produce fruits. Heathens, Mahometans, and Heretics do not produce any salutary fruits, because they are cut off from this vine, Christ, but are rejected, and like vine-cuttings will be thrown into the fire; indeed, those who are not enemies of the Gospel, but yet live in contempt of God, and are not nourished by the native sap of the vine, that is, through the Holy Spirit, whom Christ gives, also do not produce salutary fruits, are not heirs of eternal life, do not resist the devil, but are dragged into destruction.

On the other hand, those who remain in Him, that is, who retain the Gospel with true faith, He says bear fruit, salutary for themselves and others, are freed from sin, are heirs of eternal life, are ruled by the Holy Spirit, are happy in their ministries and in governance, resist the devil, are defended in great dangers and against the furies of the devil; thus also the Baptist says: From His fullness we have all received. Noah, Samuel, David, Paul are saved because they are branches of this vine, and they perform wonderful things by the help of this governor; Saul, Ahab, and many others perish because they do not remain in this vine.

Let us learn, therefore, that both are condemned in this passage: the human opinion which thinks that by human strength and human diligence men are freed from sin, become heirs of eternal life, perform salutary deeds, and flee the snares of the devil, and avoid all sad occurrences, just as the philosophers wish life to be ruled by human diligence and think this is sufficient. But Christ expressly says here: Without me you can do nothing, and Jer. 10 says: I know, O Lord, that the way of man is not in himself, that is, a calling cannot be ruled by human counsels alone, nor is it effective and salutary unless God helps; in vain does Saul fight when deserted by God. I acknowledge, therefore, human weakness, and I pray to be ruled, helped, and defended by You. These sayings must be held among the chief dogmas of the Church against the philosophers and Pelagians and the like, who immoderately amplify the freedom of the human will and lead minds away from the thought, petition, and expectation of divine help, and from the sight of this vine of which it is spoken here; and in daily invocation these sayings should come to mind, so that we may acknowledge our weakness. We are weak, without any human protections, needy, despised, burdened with various calamities, we wander in uncertain dwellings, we have no defenders. What hope is there, therefore, that we can perform great things, gather or amend the Church, and establish a better and durable state?

When we think about these things concerning our infirmity, let us on the other hand propose to ourselves this sweetest consolation handed down here, which affirms that Christ is the vine and that we, grafted into this vine, are not sterile. It is difficult for individuals privately to retain faith and the true knowledge of God, and to rule their morals, when our infirmity is so great, the devil's snares so various, the furies of tyrants so great, and the judgments of the wise and powerful so unjust, and there are so many other impediments in human conversation. But there is a much greater difficulty in governance, many more impediments from our infirmity, from the devil, from the adversaries of doctrine, from tyrants and hypocrites, from feigned friends, from courts. Finally, no human mind can comprehend the magnitude of the dangers and miseries by which we are exercised. In these miseries let us think that Christ the Son of God is our vine, and that we are inserted into this vine, wherefore let us determine with certainty that we will not perish, nor will our labors be in vain. This is the meaning of the saying in the text: He who remains in me, and I in him, he will bear much fruit. These sayings will become more illustrious when they are applied to comforting us.

Two questions, however, are agitated here. The other, when He says: He who remains in me, and I in him. He seems to add an impossible condition, because there is no one without sin and without some lapses. The other is about the saying: Without me you can do nothing. Why are commandments given to us if human diligence is entirely useless? I answer regarding the former saying: The distinction between Law and Gospel must be held, and the sayings of the laws are useless without the Gospel. These sayings of Christ, therefore, should be understood according to the light of the Gospel: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word. Likewise: He who remains in me, and I in him, he will bear much fruit, that is, he who embraces the uncorrupted Gospel and is pleasing by faith on account of Christ, God will hear him when he calls, will rule and help him, so that he may do things salutary for himself and others: and although there are many errors in life, and some sad lapses, yet these evils are pardoned and healed in those who in true repentance flee back to Christ. David, Hezekiah, Peter are weak men, they have sins, they often err, and some sad lapses happen to them, but yet they do salutary things for themselves and others, and God corrects their lapses. Thus let this rule of Christ be understood according to the doctrine of the Gospel: He who remains in me, and I in him, he will bear much fruit. Let us also know that this is mutual or correlative: As long as we remain in Christ, that is, as long as we embrace the uncorrupted Gospel and have faith and a good conscience, in turn, without any doubt, Christ remains in us.

Regarding the other question, for the pious there is also an easy answer. If without Christ's help we do nothing, what does human diligence profit? Let the answer be taken from the text: First, let us be grafted into the vine, from which the branches draw sap, that is, let us hear the Gospel and embrace it, through which God draws and moves our hearts: But being moved, let us not resist but obey, nor is the will a stone or a trunk, but it can resist by its own malice, just as David, when he willed, shook off the guiding Holy Spirit. On the contrary, however, when the will is already helped by the Holy Spirit, it can retain the gift of God. And here a huge struggle and difficulty clearly testifies that the will is not idle, nor is diligence empty, just as Joseph does not retain the gift of God without a struggle. But if the will were like a stone, and only suffered the impression of a new power, there would be no struggle in retaining faith, or other virtues, etc. Therefore Paul says in 2 Corinthians 6: We exhort you not to receive the grace in vain, and in Philippians 2: Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, and in Luke 10 it is said: How much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask, where, when the particle 'to those who ask' is added, it is sufficiently understood that sloth and contempt are not confirmed. But let us acknowledge our weakness, let us set before ourselves those sins which hinder invocation and pollute the conscience, let us resist our weakness, and truly and seriously ask for divine help and guidance.
