The greatest part of men, even those who live without crime, in a philosophical manner, think they can govern their own morals, their own affairs and dangers, by their own rational diligence, and as long as there is tranquility, they carry around this secure confidence in their own wisdom and diligence, nor do they experience what true invocation or the petition for divine help is. But inextricable dangers are never lacking to those who are involved in government, and we ought each to consider our miseries more diligently, which if it were done, a true zeal for seeking help would be kindled. It is certainly necessary for Christians to progress in these exercises, namely, in the recognition of their own weakness, of the wrath of God, of the promises, and of the presence of God.

Therefore it is also said in the text: Everything that bears fruit, He prunes, so that it may bear more abundant fruit. Not without grave cause is mention made of this pruning, nor is this pruning a light exercise. It embraces, however, both the cross and consolation; Joseph is pruned when he is led away into prison. David when he is driven into exile: Hezekiah when the city of Jerusalem is besieged by Sennacherib: Daniel when he is thrown to the lions: Paul when he is exercised everywhere by new dangers. But these afflictions without consolations would be fatal to them, therefore the pruning also embraces consolation. And although other afflictions have other causes, nevertheless they all warn us of the cause of death, of the wrath of God against the sin born with us, of correcting our confidence in ourselves, of seeking God's help, of the tyranny and snares of the devil, and many are punished on account of certain lapses. Then, therefore, we are pruned, when we acknowledge these things, and do not murmur against God, but retain the light of faith, and are sustained by the Holy Spirit, lest we be oppressed by sorrow and despair, and we experience the mitigation, or lightening, of the terrible evils by which we are tormented. The Psalms describe this propagation everywhere, such as: O Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury. Likewise: It is good for me that you have humbled me, that I might learn your justifications. And Jeremiah says in chapter 31: You have chastised me, O Lord, and I have been instructed, like an untamed calf.

Latin:

Caput XV. Ego sum vitis vera.

Doctrina et consolatio est dulcissima de prae- sentia et auxilio Christi regentis et iuvantis Eccle- siam et singulos invocantes eum, et de concordia Ecclesiae. Ac imago ipsa primum consideretur. Ecclesia gingitur ut vitis, ex qua multi palmites late sparguntur, et additur vinitor, qui vitem et palmites curet, et decerpit fructus. Duarum au- tem arborum saepissime fit mentio in his collatio- nibus, oleae et vitis, quarum duarum arborum tantam esse concordiam scribunt, ut olea insita viti, et olivas et uvas gignat. Haec imago venu- stissime pingit legem et Evangelium, seu popu- lum legis et Ecclesiam. Vitis est arida et horrida, ut populus legis, sed tamen docens et discens doctrinam traditam per Prophetas: Cumque acce- dit Evangelii cognitio, gignit fructus, docet Evan- gelium et legem. Imo tunc lex intelligitur, et disciplina, quam lex tradit, incipit placere Deo, et saepe vinum significat legis seu poenitentiae do- ctrinam, oleum vero Evangelium, ut Lucae 10.: Samaritanus infundit vulneribus vinum et oleum. Nam vinum est acre, et purgat, oleum vero glu- tinat, sanat, et alit carnem. Longa est autem aetas utriusque arboris, oleam aiunt vivere posse annos ducentos: vitem vero, si recte fuerit putata, multo diutius.

Sed hoc loco vitis Christum significat, qui ut vitis est horridum lignum, gignens tamen sa- luberrimum liquorem, ita ipse fuit tristi specie, cum sustinuit mortem, et alias miserias in hac vita. Palmites autem significant omnia caetera membra Ecclesiae. Docet igitur Christus ita cae- tera membra Ecclesiae vivere, et foecunda esse, si ipsi sint inserti fide, hoc est, cum Evangelium fide retinent, et ab ipso Christo per Spiritum sanctum nova in eis lux et vita accenditur, et di- serte ac plane dicit: Non manentes in ipso, non gignere fructus. Ethnici, Mahometistae, Hae- retici non gignunt ullos salutares fructus, quia sunt praecisi ab hac vite Christo, sed sunt reiecti, et sicut sarmenta in ignem coniicientur, imo hi qui non sunt hostes Evangelii, sed tamen vivunt in contemtu Dei, nec aluntur nativo succo vitis, id est, per Spiritum sanctum, quem dat Chri- stus, etiam non gignunt fructus salutares, non sunt haeredes vitae aeternae, non resistunt dia- bolo, sed trahuntur in exitium.

Econtra vero manentes in ipso, id est, reti- nentes Evangelium vera fide, ait fructus gignere, sibi et aliis salutares, liberantur a peccato, sunt haeredes vitae aeternae, reguntur a Spiritu san- cto, sunt felices in ministeriis et in gubernatione, resistunt diabolo, defenduntur in magnis pericu- lis et adversus diaboli furores, sic et Baptista inquit: Ex plenitudine eius omnes accepimus. Noë, Samuel, David, Paulus, servantur, quia sunt huius vitis palmites, et res mirandas gerunt auxilio huius gubernatoris, Saul, Achas, et multi alii pereunt, quia non manent in hac vite.

Discamus igitur utrumque hoc loco damnari, opinionem humanam, quae putat humanis viri- bus et humana diligentia homines liberari a pec- cato, haeredes fieri vitae aeternae, gerere res sa- lutares, et fugere diaboli insidias, cavere omnes tristes casus, sicut Philosophi humana diligentia vitam regi volunt, et hanc sufficere arbitrantur. At Christus expresse hic inquit: Sine me nihil potestis facere, et Ierem. 10. ait: Scio Domine, non est hominis via eius, id est, vocatio non potest regi humanis tantum consiliis, nec est effi- cax et salutaris, nisi Deo iuvante, frustra prae- liatur Saul desertus a Deo. Agnosco igitur hu- manam imbecillitatem, et me oro a te regi, iu- vari, defendi. Haec dicta inter praecipua dog- mata Ecclesiae tenenda sunt adversus Philoso- phos et Pelagianos, et similes, qui libertatem humanae voluntatis immodice amplificant, et mentes abducunt a cogitatione, petitione, et ex- pectatione auxilii divini, et a conspectu huius vi- tis, de qua hic dicitur, et in quotidiana invoca- tione veniant in mentem haec dicta, ut agnosca- mus nostram imbecillitatem. Sumus imbecilles, sine nullis humanis praesidiis, inopes, despecti, calamitatibus variis onerati, vagamur incertis se- dibus, nullos defensores habemus. Quae est igi- tur spes, nos magnas res gerere posse, colligere aut emendare Ecclesiam et meliorem statum ac durabilem constituere?

Cum haec de infirmitate nostra cogitabimus, econtra hanc dulcissimam consolationem hic tra- ditam nobis proponamus, quae affirmat Christum vitem esse, et nos huic viti insitos, non esse ste- riles. Difficile est singulis privatim retinere fidem et agnitionem veram Dei, et regere mores, cum tanta sit infirmitas nostra, tam variae diaboli in- sidiae, tanti furores tyrannorum, et tam iniqua iudicia sapientum et potentum, et alia tam multa impedimenta in hominum conversatione. Sed multo maior difficultas est in gubernatione, multo plura impedimenta a nostra infirmitate, a diabolo, ab adversariis doctrinae, tyrannis et hypocritis, a fucatis amicis, ab aulis. Denique nulla mens humana complecti magnitudinem periculorum et aerumnarum potest, quibus exercemur. In his miseriis cogitemus Christum filium Dei vitem nostram esse, et nos huic viti insertos esse, quare statuamus certo nec perituros nos esse, nec labores nostros irritos fore. Haec sententia est dicti in textu: Qui manet in me, et ego in eo, hic copiosum fructum feret. Haec dicta fient magis illustria, cum ad nos consolandos accommodabuntur.

Duae autem quaestiones hic agitantur. Altera cum dicit: Qui manet in me, et ego in eo. Videtur conditionem impossibilem addere, quia nemo est sine peccato et sine aliquibus lapsibus. Altera de dicto: Sine me nihil potestis facere. Cur nobis praecepta dantur, si humana diligentia prorsus inutilis est? Respondeo de priore dicto: Tenendum est discrimen Legis et Evangelii, ac dicta legum sunt inutilia sine Evangelio. Haec igitur dicta Christi intelligantur iuxta Evangelii lucem: Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum servabit. Item: Qui manet in me, et ego in eo, hic copiosum fructum feret, id est, qui amplectitur Evangelium incorruptum, et fide placet propter Christum, hunc invocantem exaudiet Deus, hunc reget et iuvabit, ut salutaria sibi et aliis faciat: et quanquam sunt multa errata in vita, et aliqui tristes lapsus, tamen haec mala condonantur, et sanantur in illis, qui in vera poenitentia ad Christum rursus confugiunt. David, Ezechias, Petrus sunt infirmi homines, habent peccata, saepe errant, et accidunt eis aliqui tristes lapsus, sed tamen salutaria agunt sibi et aliis, et Deus eorum lapsus corrigit. Sic intelligatur haec regula Christi iuxta doctrinam Evangelii: Qui manet in me, et ego in eo, hic copiosum fructum feret. Hoc quoque sciamus mutuum seu correlativum esse: Donec nos in Christo manemus, id est, donec Evangelium incorruptum amplectimur, et fidem ac bonam conscientiam habemus, vicissim sine ulla dubitatione Christus manet in nobis.

De altera quaestione piis etiam est facilis responsio. Si sine Christi auxilio nihil agimus, quid prodest humana diligentia? Sumatur ex textu responsio: Primum simus insiti in vitem, a qua palmites succum trahunt, id est, audiamus Evangelium et amplectamur, per quod Deus tra- hit et movet corda nostra: Moti vero non repu- gnemus sed obtemperemus, nec voluntas est sa- xum, aut truncus, sed potest repugnare sua ma- litia, sicut David volens excussit gubernatorem Spiritum sanctum. Econtra vero, cum iam vo- luntas iuvetur Spiritu sancto, retinere donum Dei potest. Et hic ingens lucta et difficultas ma- nifeste testatur, voluntatem non esse otiosam, nec inanem esse diligentiam, ut Ioseph non sine lucta retinet Dei donum. Quod si voluntas se haberet ut saxum, ac tantum pateretur impressio- nem novae virtutis, nulla lucta esset retinendae fidei, seu aliarum virtutum, etc. Ideo inquit Paulus 2. Corinth. 6.: Hortamur, ne frustra gra- tiam acceperitis, et ad Philip. 2.: Cum timore et tremore vestram salutem operemini, et Lucae 10. dicitur: Quanto magis pater coelestis dabit Spi- ritum sanctum petentibus, ubi cum additur par- ticula petentibus, satis intelligitur non con- firmari ignaviam et contemtum. Sed agno- scamus imbecillitatem nostram, obiiciamus ea delicta, quae impediunt invocationem, et pol- luunt conscientiam, repugnemus imbecillitati nostrae, et vere ac serio petamus auxilium et gubernationem divinam. Maxima pars hominum, etiam eorum, qui vivunt sine crimine, more phi- losophico, arbitrantur se regere posse suos mores, sua negotia et pericula, sua rationali diligentia, et donec tranquillitas est, securi hanc fiduciam suae sapientiae et diligentiae circumferunt, nec experiuntur quid sit vera invocatio, seu petitio auxilii divini. Sed nunquam pericula inextrica- bilia desunt iis, qui sunt impliciti gubernationi, et singuli miserias nostras diligentius considerare deberemus, quod si fieret, accenderetur verum studium petendi auxilii. Proficere certe Chri- stianos his exercitiis necesse est, scilicet, agni- tione propriae imbecillitatis, irae Dei, promis- sionum et praesentiae Dei.

Ideo et in textu dicitur: Omne quod fru- ctum gignit, purgat, ut fructum uberiorem gi- gnat. Non sine gravi causa fit mentio huius pur- gationis, nec leve exercitium est haec purgatio. Complectitur autem et crucem et consolationem, Ioseph cum in carcerem abducitur, purgatur. David cum pellitur in exilium: Ezechias cum ob- sidetur civitas Hierosolyma a Sennacherib: Daniel cum obiicitur leonibus: Paulus cum passim no- vis periculis exercetur. Sed hae afflictiones sine consolationibus essent exitiales ipsis, ideo pur- gatio complectitur etiam consolationem. Etsi au- tem aliae afflictiones alias causas habent, tamen omnes admonent nos de causa mortis, de ira Dei adversus peccatum nobiscum nascens, de fiducia nostri corrigenda, de quaerendo Dei auxilio, de tyrannide et insidiis diaboli, et multi propter cer- tos lapsus plectuntur. Tunc igitur purgamur, cum haec agnoscimus, nec fremimus adversus Deum, sed retinemus lucem fidei, et sustentamur Spiritu sancto, ne opprimamur dolore et desperatione, et experimur mitigationem, seu levationem terri- bilium malorum, quibus excruciamur. Hanc propagationem describunt Psalmi passim, ut: Do- mine ne in furore tuo arguas me. Item: Bonum mihi quod humiliasti me, ut discerem iustificatio- nes tuas. Et Ieremias inquit capite 31.: Casti- gasti me Domine, et eruditus sum, quasi iuven- culus indomitus.

## 15:7
If you abide in me, and my words in you.

The previous description was an illustrious picture of the efficacy and presence of Christ in the Church. Now follow two very memorable sentences, which teach again where and what the Church is, and what the chief worship is. Let many sentences recited above, which are entirely similar and teach the same thing, be joined with this saying, that the Church is a gathering of those who embrace the Gospel, and we are not painting a Platonic idea, but we are speaking of the visible Church. There are no elect to eternal life except in this very visible gathering, which professes the Gospel of God, just as Paul says: Whom He chose, these He also called, and in the Psalm it is said: Their sound has gone out into all the earth. God wants to be rightly acknowledged and invoked, He wants His Gospel to be heard in the whole world and propagated everywhere. Wherefore He does not hide His Church in secret places, but wants it to be known, and its voice to be heard. When, therefore, we read these sweetest consolations of this discourse of Christ, and similar ones, let us not cast them away to another Church unknown to us, but let us accommodate them to this visible Church, and its members, that is, to ourselves. To us, therefore, this promise pertains: Whatever you will, you shall ask, and it shall be done for you.

There are many differences between ethnic religions and the one true doctrine about God, which sounds in the Church of God. For ethnic opinions err concerning the essence of God and His will, as has often been said above. And concerning the will, the heathens cannot determine why and whether God wills to hear, why in this nature of men it is oppressed by miseries, and whether after this life God will give life and tranquility. But in the Church this consolation exists, that God is not invoked in vain, that He truly wills to hear those who invoke Him, and to help them. And although by His secret counsel He governs others differently, yet He wills in this life to preserve the body of the Church, like an army, and for individuals either to mitigate miseries or to remove them entirely. Furthermore, after this life, to adorn all members of the Church with eternal glory. We ought always to bring the knowledge and faith of this doctrine, or promise, to God in prayer, namely that for Christ's sake we are received, heard, and helped, as has often been said elsewhere. This faith especially makes the distinction between heathen and Christian invocation.

The remaining doctrine concerning prayer has been recited often elsewhere, and must be assiduously inculcated into minds. First, one must consider who God is, and where, and how He has revealed Himself, whom you invoke, and what the difference is between true invocation and the heathen or impious ones of any nations whatsoever. Concerning this distinction, it has already been spoken. Next, why God is to be invoked, whether He hears those who invoke Him, and why He hears. Here, first, let us propose to ourselves the commands: it is necessary that God be invoked, because He commands this duty. He hears those who invoke Him, however, not because of our dignity, but because of the Son, the Mediator: and therefore He has delivered promises, and affirms that He will hear.

Thirdly, let the distinction be held between the proper promise of the Gospel concerning reconciliation and the promises of bodily benefits. Concerning the promise of reconciliation, it demands by name that we believe that our sins are remitted and that we are received into grace; therefore, this promise must be believed in prayer without exception, just as this sentence clearly demands this faith: This is the will of the Father, that everyone who believes in the Son may have eternal life. Likewise, to the Romans 3: We are justified, however, by faith freely. Always, however, even when bodily things are sought, the petition for the remission of sins should shine forth, as pious minds know.

But concerning the promises of bodily things, let faith always hold this in general: that they are not vain, but obtain either complete liberation or help and the mitigation of evil. But because the Church in this life is subject to the cross, we do not always immediately obtain complete liberation, and the will ought to be prepared for obedience. Therefore, it asks with this exception: If You will, and as You will. Just as David, while in exile, prays that he be brought back, and at the same time is prepared for obedience, he wishes to comply with the will of God, even if he is not brought back, nor does he cast away faith concerning the remission of sin, nor does he prescribe a manner to God; indeed, he would prefer not to be brought back, if he could free his son from eternal damnation, than to be brought back in such a way with his son and a great multitude of citizens cast into eternal destruction. This manner of liberation tormented David more than the loss of the kingdom, but he knew that God, who brings back, must be obeyed, and he acknowledged the wrath of God against his own sins and those of his son, in this magnitude of the son's punishment.

These examples, although their magnitude cannot be recounted, nevertheless remind the pious what the exercises of faith in invocation are like. They teach that one must certainly determine concerning the remission of sins, without any exception. They teach likewise concerning bodily miseries, that help must be sought certainly, without exception, but that the will ought to be prepared for the cross, even if liberation does not happen, and that a manner must not be prescribed to God. Experience, however, will show that all these things are very difficult; indeed, the first article, to determine concerning the remission of sins, is the most difficult of all, especially while the punishment lasts, and when the manner of liberation brings with it the destruction of others and brings us new miseries, as often happens. The people are led out of Egypt, but in the desert new sins, new seditions, and punishments follow.

Finally, since the promise in this text speaks universally: Whatever you will, you shall ask, let us know the kinds of things to be asked, namely eternal and bodily goods. For God has promised both, and let us remember the degrees. First, eternal things are to be asked, afterwards also bodily things, because God wills that in this life there always remain some Church and ministry of the Gospel. Therefore, we have need of life, good health, food, drink, lodging, governments, marriage, and households, so that offspring may be cherished and educated. To retain and protect these things, many more goods are necessary than those which we understand; so far is it from the case that all things can be provided for by human diligence, but it consoles us Christ, saying: That the heavenly Father knows and sees what things we have need of, etc. Since, therefore, we commend ourselves to God, our minds become tranquil through confidence in the presence and help of God, even if we ourselves never sufficiently understand how many and diverse things are needed. Hence are taken the fables by which human wisdom is mocked, when, having cast aside faith, it wishes to foresee everything, whereas it is the duty of man to serve his calling faithfully, and to commend to God the dangers and the means which we cannot sufficiently govern by our own counsel, and to await in faith the governance of things unknown to us, just as Psalm 26 says: Commend thy way to God, and he will do it. Known is the fable about the rustic to whom God had granted the right to ask for suitable weather, yet he had forgotten to ask for useful winds. Let us therefore ask also for bodily goods, because God commands this, and indeed for these reasons: he wishes us to acknowledge that life, sustenance, bodily strength, the happiness of children, and the good success of counsels in the Republic and in the household do not happen to us by chance or by natural order without the help of God, just as it is said in Deut. 30: God is thy life and the length of thy days. Furthermore, he testifies to this also by the promise of bodily goods, that he will always preserve some Church in this life; he wishes this to be believed, and that by this confidence we propagate the doctrine, and not abandon studies and governance out of despair. Thirdly, he also wishes the faith of reconciliation to be exercised by the petition for bodily things. For bodily things cannot be asked for unless this faith shines forth, that God receives, hears, and cares for us. Finally, we cannot approach God, whatever is to be asked, except by the faith of the mediator Christ. God wishes these three things to be always thought of in the petition for bodily goods, and faith to be kindled, believing these things, asking from God, and celebrating God for these benefits. Thus the petition for bodily goods becomes a worship pleasing to God. Thus all the saints asked for necessary defense and sustenance, from Adam onwards, and they will ask in this mortal life until the end. Here I briefly add the saying of 1 John at the end: If we ask anything according to his will, he hears us. In this saying John warns that we should not ask for things prohibited by God, just as David should not ask God to take away Uriah, and yet in the world these prayers arising from evil affections are most common. But let the pious, being warned, know that petition ought not to fight against the commandments of God, and that those things which are necessary for life are to be asked for, and must be asked for, piously and rightly.

These things about prayer I have briefly repeated in this place. Because a notable promise has been handed down in this text. I said, however, that the Church is described here, and that it is spoken of regarding invocation, which is the chief worship. Now another worship is also added, namely the propagation of doctrine, and confession.

In this is my Father glorified.

Let the reader diligently observe in this description of the Church that mention is made of two chief forms of worship, which are proper to the Church, namely true invocation and doctrine, or confession. Only the Church understands and performs these two forms of worship; other nations can have many other virtues, just as there was great honor of justice, chastity, and modesty in Aristides and Scipio, but the true invocation of God and the propagation of doctrine were lacking. This distinction between the Church and the Gentiles, or the impious, must often be repeated, so that we may rouse ourselves to these chief forms of worship, and so that we may now speak of the propagation of doctrine, let the studious consider the wills of men toward the ministry of the Gospel. The greatest part of the human race spurns the doctrine of the Gospel as if it were fabulous; many tyrants even attempt to destroy it; the remaining multitude not only outside the Church, but even within the Church, neglects the ministers and the studies of the Gospel, when this ought to have been the first care of all governors and of all men, namely, that each one in his own place should contribute counsel and effort to retaining the ministry of the Gospel, in the public administration of the Churches, to fostering the studies necessary for the Church, and to protecting and nourishing ministers, teachers, and disciples. It is evident that these duties are neglected everywhere in empires and cities by governors and by private individuals; suitable pastors are not sought for the Churches, moderate rewards or stipends are not given, youth are not driven to the studies necessary for the Church of God; nay, royal courts attribute the rewards due to the teachers of the Gospel, that is, priesthoods in colleges, to those whose work they use in the forum and in profane business.

I recite these things only for this reason, that the saying of this text may be properly understood and accommodated to use, that is, with this voice let us accuse the tyrants who attempt to destroy the ministry of the Gospel, and others who neglect it. But let us rouse ourselves to hear, to learn, to cultivate the Gospel, to the studies of doctrine necessary for the Church, to venerating the ministers of the Gospel, teachers and disciples. Let us exhort princes and cities to take care that the Gospel be purely and rightly proposed to the Churches, and let us console all who sustain dangers and hardships for the sake of the propagation of the Gospel. Finally, let us also inculcate this consolation upon ourselves, who for the sake of the study of the Gospel endure contempt, poverty, exiles, punishments, and manifold miseries. In this is my Father glorified, that you bear much fruit, and become my disciples. To bear fruit, and to become disciples of Christ, signifies to propagate the Gospel, or to serve in the ministry and studies of the Gospel; by this duty Christ affirms that God is glorified. Therefore, the propagation and study of the Gospel are good works, pleasing to God, necessary acts of worship of God, by which God affirms that He is honored. This is the simple meaning of this saying, which will be both more illustrious and sweeter to us when, as I have said, we accommodate it to use in this way.

Latin:

Si manseritis in me, et verba mea in vobis.

Prior descriptio illustris pictura fuit de effi- cacia et praesentia Christi in Ecclesia. Nunc se- quuntur duae sententiae valde memorabiles, quae docent rursus, ubi et quae sit Ecclesia, et qui sit praecipuus cultus. Coniungantur autem cum hoc dicto multae sententiae supra recitatae prorsus si- miles, quae idem docent, Ecclesiam esse coetum amplectentium Evangelium, nec pingimus ideam Platonicam, sed loquimur de visibili Ecclesia. Nulli sunt electi ad vitam aeternam, nisi in hoc ipso visibili coetu, qui profitetur Evangelium Dei, sicut Paulus inquit: Quos elegit, hos et vocavit, et in Psalmo dicitur: In omnem terram exivit so- nus eorum. Vult Deus recte agnosci et invocari, vult suum Evangelium exaudiri in toto orbe ter- rarum et ubique propagari. Quare non abdit Ecclesiam suam in latebras, sed vult eam notam esse, et vocem eius audiri. Cum igitur legimus has dulcissimas consolationes huius concionis Christi, et similium, non reiiciamus eas ad aliam Ecclesiam nobis ignotam, sed accommodemus ad hanc visibilem Ecclesiam, et eius membra, hoc est, ad nos ipsos. Ad nos igitur haec promissio pertinet: Quicquid volueritis, petetis, et fiet vobis.

Discrimina multa sunt inter ethnicas reli- giones, et unam veram doctrinam de Deo, quae sonat in Ecclesia Dei. Errant enim ethnicae opi- niones de essentia Dei et de voluntate, ut supra saepe dictum est. Ac de voluntate non possunt statuere Ethnici, cur et an velit exaudire Deus, cur in hac natura hominum sit oppressa aeru- mnis, et an post hanc vitam Deus sit daturus vi- tam et tranquillitatem. Sed in Ecclesia extat haec consolatio, quod Deus non frustra invocetur, quod vere velit exaudire invocantes, et eis opitu- lari. Et quanquam suo arcano consilio alios ali- ter gubernat, tamen velit in hac vita corpus Ec- clesiae, sicut exercitum servare, et singulis aut mitigare aerumnas, aut prorsus tollere. Deinde vero post hanc vitam ornare omnia membra Ec- clesiae aeterna gloria. Huius doctrinae, seu pro- missionis cognitionem et fidem nos semper in pre- catione afferre ad Deum oportet, quod videlicet propter Christum recipiamur, exaudiamur, et iuvemur, ut alias saepe dictum est. Haec fides praecipue discrimen facit inter ethnicam et Chri- stianam invocationem.

Reliqua doctrina de precatione alias saepe recitata est, et assidue mentibus est inculcanda. Primum cogitandum quis sit Deus, et ubi, ac quomodo se patefecerit, quem invoces, quid in- ter veram invocationem, et ethnicas, seu impias quarumcunque gentium intersit. De hoc discri- mine iam dictum est. Deinde cur sit invocandus Deus, an exaudiat invocantes, et cur exaudiat. Hic primum mandata nobis proponamus, necesse est invocari Deum, quia praecipit hoc officium. Exaudit autem invocantes non propter nostram dignitatem, sed propter filium mediatorem: ideo- que promissiones tradidit, et affirmat se exaudi- turum esse.

Tertio discrimen teneatur inter promissio- nem propriam Evangelii de reconciliatione, et promissiones corporalium beneficiorum. De pro- missione reconciliationis nominatim postulat, ut remitti nobis peccata, et recipi nos in gratiam credamus, ideo huic promissioni in precando sine exceptione credendum est, sicut clare postulat hanc fidem haec sententia: Haec est voluntas pa- tris, ut omnis, qui credit in filium, habeat vi- tam aeternam. Item ad Romanos 3.: Iustifica- mur autem fide gratis. Semper autem etiam cum petuntur corporalia, petitio remissionis peccato- rum praeluceat, sicut piae mentes norunt.

Sed de promissionibus rerum' corporalium semper hoc teneat fides in genere, non esse irri- tas, sed impetrare, vel integram liberationem, vel auxilium, et mitigationem mali. Quia vero Ecclesia in hac vita subiecta est cruci, non sem- per mox impetramus integram liberationem, de- betque voluntas parata esse ad obedientiam. Pe- tit igitur cum hac exceptione: Si vis, et sicut vis. Sicut David exulans, orat se reduci, et simul pa- ratus ad obedientiam, vult obsequi voluntati Dei, etiamsi non reducatur, nec tamen abiicit fidem de remissione peccati, nec modum praescribit Deo, imo mallet non reduci, si posset filium ab aeterna damnatione liberare, quam sic reduci abiectis in aeternum exitium filio, et magna multitudine ci- vium. Hic modus liberationis magis excruciavit Davidem, quam regni amissio, sed sciebat Deo reducenti obtemperandum esse, et agnoscebat iram Dei adversus peccata sua et filii, in hac ma- gnitudine poenae filii.

Haec exempla, etsi magnitudo eorum enar- rari non potest, tamen pios commonefaciunt, qua- lia sint fidei exercitia in invocatione. Docent certo statuendum esse de remissione peccatorum, sine ulla exceptione. Docent item de corporalibus aerumnis, certo petendum auxilium, sine exce- ptione, sed voluntatem debere paratam esse ad crucem, etiamsi non contingit liberatio, nec mo- dum praescribendum esse Deo. Experientia au- tem ostendet, haec omnia valde difficilia esse, imo primus articulus, statuere de remissione peccato- rum, omnium difficilimus est, praesertim du- rante poena, et cum modus liberationis exitium aliorum secum trahit, et nobis affert novas mise- rias, sicut saepe accidit. Educitur populus ex Aegypto, sed in deserto nova peccata, novae se- ditiones, et poenae sequuntur.

Postremo cum promissio in hoc textu loqua- tur universaliter: Quicquid volueritis, petetis, scia- mus genera rerum petendarum, videlicet bona aeterna et corporalia. Nam utraque promisit Deus, et gradus meminerimus. Primum aeterna petenda sunt, postea etiam corporalia, quia Deus vult in hac vita semper aliquam Ecclesiam et mi- nisterium Evangeli manere. Opus est igitur no- bis vita, bona valetudine, cibo, potu, hospitiis, politiis, coniugio, oeconomiis, ut soboles foveri et educari possit. Ad has res retinendas et tuen- das multo plura bona necessaria sunt, quam quae nos intelligimus, tantum abest, ut omnia pro- spici humana diligentia possint, sed consolatur nos Christus, inquiens: Patrem coelestem scire, ac videre quibus rebus nobis opus sit, etc. Cum igitur nos commendamus Deo, mentes fiducia praesentiae et auxilii Dei, fiunt tranquil- lae, etiamsi nunquam satis intelligimus ipsi, quam multis et diversis rebus opus sit. Hinc sunt sum- tae fabellae, quibus deridetur humana sapientia, cum abiecta fide, omnia perspicere vult, cum sit hominis fideliter servire vocationi, et pericula, ac media, quae consilio nostro non satis regere possumus, Deo commendare, et fide expectare rerum nobis ignotarum gubernationem, sicut Psalm. 26. inquit: Commenda Deo viam tuam, et ipse faciet. Nota est fabella de rustico, cui Deus concesserat petere tempestates idoneas, is tamen utiles ventos petere oblitus erat. Petamus igitur, et corporalia bona, quia id praecipit Deus, et quidem propter has causas, vult nos agnoscere, non casu aut naturali ordine, sine Dei ope nobis contingere vitam, victum, vi- res corporis, felicitatem liberorum, bonos suc- cessus consiliorum in Repub. et oeconomia, sicut Deut. 30. dicitur: Deus est vita tua, et longitudo dierum tuorum. Deinde testatur et hoc, promis- sione corporalium bonorum, se in hac vita sem- per aliquam Ecclesiam servaturum esse, id vult credi, et hac fiducia nos propagare doctrinam, nec desperatione studia ac gubernationem abii- cere. Tertio vult etiam fidem reconciliationis exerceri petitione corporalium. Non enim pos- sunt corporalia peti, nisi praelucente hac fide, quod Deus nos recipiat, exaudiat, curet. De- nique accedere ad Deum non possumus, quicquid petendum est, nisi fide mediatoris Christi. Haec tria vult Deus semper in petitione corporalium cogitari, et accendi fidem haec credentem, a Deo petentem, et Deum celebrantem propter haec be- neficia. Ita petitio corporalium fit cultus Deo placens. Sic petiverunt omnes sancti necessariam defensionem et sustentationem, inde usque ab Adam, et petent in hac mortali vita usque ad finem. Hic breviter adiicio dictum 1. Ioannis ul- timo: Si quid petiverimus secundum voluntatem eius, exaudit nos. In hoc dicto monet Ioannes, ne petamus res a Deo prohibitas, ut David non petat a Deo, ut tollat Uriam, et tamen in mundo haec vota a malis affectibus orta usitatissima sunt. Sed pii admoniti sciant, petitionem non debere pugnare cum praeceptis Dei, et quae vitae neces- saria sunt, pie et recte peti et petenda esse.

Haec de precatione breviter hoc loco repe- tivi. Quia insignis promissio in hoc textu tra- dita est. Dixi autem hic describi Ecclesiam, et dici de invocatione, quae est praecipuus cultus. Nunc additur et alius cultus, scilicet propaga- tio doctrinae, et confessio.

In hoc glorificatur pater meus.

Diligenter observet lector in hac descriptione Ecclesiae, mentionem fieri duorum praecipuorum cultuum, qui sunt proprii Ecclesiae, scilicet ve- rae invocationis, et doctrinae, seu confessionis. Hos duos cultus sola Ecclesia intelligit, et prae- stat, caeterae gentes possunt habere alias multas virtutes, ut magnum decus iusticiae, castitatis et modestiae fuit in Aristide, Scipione, sed defue- runt invocatio vera Dei, et propagatio doctrinae. Hoc discrimen Ecclesiae, et Ethnicorum, seu im- piorum, saepe repetendum est, ut nos ipsos ad hos praecipuos cultus excitemus, ac ut iam de pro- pagatione doctrinae dicamus, considerent stu- diosi hominum voluntates erga ministerium Evan- gelii. Maxima pars generis humani doctrinam Evangelii aspernatur, tanquam fabulosam, ty- ranni multi etiam delere eam conantur, reliqua multitudo non solum extra Ecclesiam, sed etiam in Ecclesia negligit ministros et studia Evangelii, cum hanc primam curam omnium gubernatorum et omnium hominum esse oportuerit, videlicet, ut consilium et operam suo quisque loco conferat ad retinendum ministerium Evangelii, in publica administratione Ecclesiarum, ad fovenda studia necessaria Ecclesiae, ad ministros, doctores, et discipulos tuendos et alendos. Haec officia con- stat in imperiis et civitatibus a gubernatoribus et a privatis passim negligi, non quaeri idoneos pa- stores Ecclesiis, non dari mercedes, seu stipen- dia mediocria, non adigi iuventutem ad studia necessaria Ecclesiae Dei, imo regiae aulae mer- cedes debitas doctoribus Evangelii, id est, sacer- dotia in collegiis attribuunt iis, quorum opera in foro et profanis negotiis utuntur.

Haec tantum eo recito, ut dictum huius tex- tus proprie intelligatur, et ad usum accommode- tur, id est, hac voce accusemus tyrannos, qui delere ministerium Evangelii conantur, et alios qui negligunt. Nos vero excitemus ad audien- dum, discendum, colendum Evangelium, ad stu- dia doctrinae necessaria Ecclesiae, ad venerandos Evangelii ministros, doctores et discipulos. Hor- temur principes et civitates, ut Evangelium pure et recte proponi Ecclesiis curent, et consolemur omnes, qui pericula et aerumnas sustinent pro- pter propagationem Evangelii. Denique et nobis ipsis, qui propter studium Evangelii toleramus contemtum, inopiam, exilia, supplicia et multi- plices miserias, hanc consolationem inculcemus. In hoc glorificatur pater meus, ut fructum mul- tum feratis, et fiatis mei discipuli. Fructum ferre, et fieri discipulos Christi, significat propagare Evangelium, seu servire in ministerio et studiis Evangelii, hoc officio affirmat Christus glorificari Deum. Itaque Evangelii propagatio et studium, sunt bona opera, Deo placentia, cultus Dei ne- cessarii, quibus Deus affirmat se honore affici. Haec est simplex huius dicti sententia, quae no- bis et illustrior et dulcior erit, cum hoc modo, ut dixi, eam ad usum accommodabimus.

## 15:9
As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you.

And to these very ones who are exercised by dangers and hardships for the sake of the studies and propagation of the Gospel, the highest consolation of all and an immense reward is proposed. As the Father has loved me, so I love you. Although the impious with burning hatreds persecute you who propagate and learn the Gospel, yet know that you are loved and defended by God the Father and by the Son our Lord Jesus Christ, as is often said elsewhere, and as it is said in Isaiah chapter 51: I have put my word in your mouth, and I have protected you with the shadow of my hand, that you may plant the heavens. These divine promises are to be opposed to tyrannical hatreds, and we must obey God who commands that we propagate the Gospel, and we must rejoice that we are loved by Him, and we must hope for not only defense, but also happiness in gathering the Church, because our labors will be perpetually salutary to ourselves and to a great multitude of the true Church.

This, moreover, is a true and firm consolation: to rejoice because we know that we are obeying God, and that our labors are pleasing to God, nay, that they are sacrifices pleasing to God, and that we are defended and helped by God, and that our contentions are not in vain, but are salutary to us and to the Church of God; eternity must be looked to, and those goods should be considered truly good which are to last forever, and are perpetual communion, joy, and glory with God. Pericles, Demosthenes, and others sustain great labors, but they are destructive to themselves and to their country. This is a great and ineffable misery, to be broken and consumed by merely pernicious labors: Scipio is less miserable, who performs deeds useful to his country and posterity, but yet he neither knows nor has invoked God, nor has he referred his labors to this end, that God might be rightly acknowledged and celebrated. Therefore, neither are his labors salutary to Scipio himself, nor do they serve divine things. But Samuel, David, Jeremiah, the Baptist, and the like, although they sustain huge hardships for a short time, yet they are blessed, because they both please God and perform deeds bringing perpetual salvation to themselves and to the Church. This consolation has been very often repeated, as it is said to Abraham, Gen. 15: I am your protector, and your reward exceeding great. He promises defense, rewards, and success, and 2 Corinthians 4, Paul says: Therefore we do not grow weary, but although our outward man is corrupted, yet the inward is renewed day by day. For tribulation, which, since it is momentary, is light, brings an excellent weight of eternal glory.

Latin:

Sicut dilexit me pater, ita dilexi vos.

Et his ipsis, qui exercentur periculis et ae- rumnis propter studia et propagationem Evange- lii, consolatio omnium summa et merces im- mensa proponitur. Sicut dilexit me pater, ita ego diligo vos. Etsi impii ardentibus odiis vos, qui Evangelium propagatis et discitis, persequen- tur, tamen scitote vos diligi et defendi a Deo patre et a filio Domino nostro Iesu Christo, sicut saepe alias dicitur, et Esaiae cap. 51. dictum est: Posui verbum meum in ore tuo, et umbra manus meae protexi te, ut plantes coelos. Hae promissiones divinae opponendae sunt odiis ty- rannicis, et obtemperandum est Deo praecipienti, ut Evangelium propagemus, et laetandum, quod ab ipso diligamur, ac speranda est, non solum defensio, sed etiam felicitas in colligenda Eccle- sia, quod videlicet nostri labores futuri sint per- petuo salutares nobis ipsis et magnae multitudini verae Ecclesiae.

Haec est autem vera et firma consolatio, lae- tari, quia scimus nos Deo obtemperare, et Deo placere nostros labores, imo sacrificia Deo grata esse, et nos defendi ac iuvari a Deo, nec esse ir- ritas contentiones, sed salutares nobis et Eccle- siae Dei, aeternitas intuenda est, ac vere bona ducantur illa bona, quae perpetuo duratura sunt, et sunt perpetua cum Deo consuetudo, laetitia et gloria. Magnos labores sustinent Pericles, De- mosthenes et alii, sed exitiales sibi ipsis et pa- triae. Haec magna et ineffabilis miseria est, frangi et consumi tantum perniciosis laboribus: minus miser est Scipio, qui res gerit utiles patriae et posteritati, sed tamen nec novit, nec invocavit Deum, nec retulit suos labores ad hunc finem, ut Deus recte agnoscatur et celebretur. Ideo nec ipsi Scipioni salutares sunt sui labores, nec serviunt rebus divinis. At Samuel, David, Ieremias, Baptista, et similes, etsi sustinent ingentes aeru- mnas exiguo tempore, tamen beati sunt, quia et Deo placent, et res gerunt perpetuam salutem af- ferentes ipsis et Ecclesiae. Haec consolatio sae- pissime repetita est, ut ad Abraham dicitur, Gen 15.: Ego protector tuus, et merces tua magna valde. Pollicetur defensionem, praemia et successus, et 2. Corinth. 4. dicit Paulus: Ideo non defatigamur, sed quamvis externus noster homo corrumpitur, tamen interior renovatur de die in diem. Nam tribulatio, quae, cum subita sit, levis est, affert excellens pondus aeternae gloriae.

## 15:13
Greater love than this no one has.

Regarding love, he proposes his own example: since I have loved you when you were unworthy, I want this debt to be repaid to me in turn, that you love your colleagues of your office as well-deserving and for my sake. Emulation is a sharp and vehement affection, and it is not easy for a rival to spare or yield, as the histories of many teach. Themistocles and Aristides, Pericles and Cimon, Sulla and Marius, Caesar and Pompey; but just as the emulations of these stirred up huge tumults and civil wars, so it happens in the Church. But Christ commands that hatreds be repressed and extinguished; he teaches that this duty is owed to him, that we love our colleagues and spare them, and approach them for his sake. Eusebius, Bishop of Caesarea, was pressing Basil the presbyter, incensed by emulation, because he saw him being magnified for his erudition; here Christ preaches to both: he commands Eusebius to embrace Basil with true benevolence and not to disparage him, but to give him the honor appropriate to him. In the same way, he commands Basil to overlook injuries and to show himself compliant to the Bishop, not to slander him, but to honor him with true reverence of mind because of the rank of his ministry, and thus to spare him for Christ's sake. He exaggerates this precept about mutual love and the pursuit of concord, recounting his own benefits, so that he may show that this duty is owed to him, that we love our colleagues. Therefore he says: I lay down my life for you, you are my friends: I no longer call you servants, I chose you, you did not choose me, therefore you are debtors to me.

Latin:

Maiorem hac dilectione nemo habet.

De dilectione suum exemplum proponit: cum ego vos dilexerim indignos, vicissim mihi rependi hoc debitum volo, ut bene meritum, et propter me collegas vestri muneris diligatis. Acer et ve- hemens affectus est aemulatio, nec facile est ae- mulo parcere, aut cedere, ut historiae plurimo- rum docent. Themistoclis et Aristidae, Periclis et Cimonis, Syllae et Marii, Caesaris et Pompeii, ut autem horum aemulationes ingentes tumultus et bella civilia excitarunt, sic in Ecclesia accidit. Sed Christus reprimi et extingui odia praecipit, hoc officium sibi deberi docet, ut collegas ame- mus, et eis parcamus, accedamus propter ipsum. Eusebius Episcopus Caesariensis Basilium pres- byterum, incensus aemulatione premebat, quia videbat eum propter eruditionem magnificri, hic utrique concionatur Christus, praecipit Eusebio, ut vera benevolentia complectatur Basilium, nec obtrectet ei, sed honorem ei convenientem tri- buat. Ad eundem modum et Basilio praecipit, ut dissimulet iniurias, ac morigerum se Episcopo praebeat, non suggillet eum, sed vera animi re- verentia eum colat propter ministerii gradum, at- que ita parcat ei propter Christum. Exaggerat autem hoc praeceptum de mutua dilectione, et studio concordiae, recensens sua beneficia, ut ostendat sibi hoc officium deberi, ut collegas dili- gamus. Ideo ait: Ego animam meam pro vobis pono, vos amici mei estis: Non iam nomino vos servos, ego elegi vos, non vos me elegistis, mihi igitur debitores estis.

## 15:15
All things which I have heard from my Father, I have made known to you.

In this saying, let the sentiment regarding the ministry of the Gospel be observed at the same time, namely, that God does not can be known and invoked in any other way, except as He has been revealed by the revelation of Christ. Likewise, that Christ has delivered all things necessary for salvation, and that new illuminations are not to be sought, nor other doctrine to be sought. Let these sentiments always be in sight, so that they may be opposed to philosophical opinions or carnal wisdom. Many imagine that God can be known and worshipped, even without the knowledge and ministry of the Gospel, because human reason also knows that there is one God, and knows the law. But here let us know that the will of God concerning the remission of sins to be granted on account of the mediator, the Son, was unknown to human reason and to all creatures, before it was brought forth from the secret bosom of the eternal Father through the Son. It is necessary, therefore, to hear the Gospel, as has often been said elsewhere concerning the distinction between the law and the Gospel.

Furthermore, even those who have heard the Gospel acquiesce with difficulty; they seek other illuminations or clearer visions, by which they desire to be made more certain, whence Enthusiasts, Anabaptists, and many fanatics have arisen, and all the pious experience that wandering minds must be repressed and constrained with great struggle, so that they may be bound to this word delivered by Christ and through the Apostles, and may acquiesce in it, and may determine that this is truly the will of God toward us, which He has revealed here. If now an angel were sent to you from heaven, announcing to you that God is appeased, and testimonies were added, namely the return of the sun, as in the time of Hezekiah, then indeed you would think that you would rejoice at such an illustrious signification of the will of God. But it is a greater benefit that the Son has been sent, and that He has been the messenger of such a great gift. By the word of this Son He wishes us to believe, and not to seek other doctrines or illuminations. To confirm this sentiment in us, let us remember this saying: All things which I have heard from my Father, I have made known to you. He affirms that He has brought doctrine, namely concerning reconciliation, unknown to all creatures, brought forth from the secret bosom of the Father. This He wishes us to embrace, in this He wishes us to acquiesce, and not to seek other opinions, other forms of worship, other revelations.

I have appointed you, that you should go, and bear fruit.

He adds consolation: If you will retain this doctrine of mine, you will bear fruit. It is miserable to sustain great labors which profit neither you nor others, as Sisyphus is said to roll a stone up a mountain in the underworld. But it is much sadder to bring upon oneself eternal punishments by labors and contentions, just as many who wage unjust wars, and others who defend impious dogmas. How mournful a spectacle was the destruction of Jerusalem for King Zedekiah and other princes, when, seeing the burning of the city, they thought that they had brought these huge evils upon themselves and the Church of God by their own counsels? And when Christ speaks of Judas, it would be better for that man not to have been born, He signifies that it is a huge misery to undertake counsels and labors by which the wrath of God is provoked, and the end of Judas shows that men who do unjust things are oppressed by horrendous darkness and furies. Just as Judas brings death upon himself, so that he may break off his pain, and yet afterwards feels eternal torments. Now consider that the greatest part of the human race is broken by either useless or pernicious contentions. There have been, are, and will be many like Judas, such as the impious teachers of all times. How many have there been endowed with excellent talents, who nevertheless performed deeds that were either useless or only pernicious to the human race. The deeds of Alcibiades from beginning to end harmed both himself and his country. The wars of the Bruti, the Cassii, the Antonii, and countless others, what are they but pernicious tumults? Now also, how few are the salutary princes.

Let us contemplate these things in histories and daily life, so that each one may think about his own vocation and its outcome. First, let your vocation be pleasing to God, then lay aside confidence in yourself, and know that great affairs are not governed by human wisdom, but by God showing counsels and opportunities, and helping. Therefore, set before yourself the divine promises, and on account of them invoke God, and seek help in the vocation which He Himself approves, and with confidence in the presence of God undertake the labors appropriate to your office. Thus, your ministry will be profitable to others, and you yourself will not lose eternal life, but will also be adorned with rewards in this life and after this life. This is the true and firm consolation, which Christ also inculcates here several times, and divine sermons often repeat, as I said above. And Paul cries out: Your labor is not in vain in the Lord.

And we in the Church especially have need of this consolation, where we carry around a doctrine hated by the world, and we seem to be able to accomplish nothing, because the highest kings oppose us, and there are many impediments, poverty, hunger, the fear of most cruel punishments. Among these evils, let us think of the promise of Christ so often repeated: He who remains in me, and I in him, he will bear much fruit. You are a preacher, a teacher, a scholar; know that your function pleases God if you obey your calling and teach or learn things that are salutary, and although many difficulties impede your course, and you seem to make little progress, yet by faith and the knowledge of the Son of God, ask that you may be helped, and do not doubt that your labors will be salutary for you and for others. And events in the present often show this. David, Isaiah, Daniel, and many others saw in the present that their labors were of benefit to many; Jeremiah did not see the return of the people, but yet he knew his counsel was happy and salutary for the whole Church of God.

And fix in the innermost senses of your mind what Christ explicitly adds in this place: And that your fruit should remain. The labors of pious ministers in the Church do not profit only for a short time, as the labors of Scipio or Augustus profit for a short time, who defended their polities and ruled them happily, which remained for a time: but the fruits of those who teach are eternal, who gather an eternal Church for God, and are themselves adorned with eternal rewards. No one in the senate at Rome thought that this doctrine which Paul was carrying around would remain for long, and yet Paul himself, his disciples, and the doctrine remain for all eternity.

Therefore, let us also console ourselves with this sweetest consolation. This state of the churches and schools, which has now been established by the benefit of God, with the light of the Gospel restored, does not seem as if it will remain. But it is going to remain, nevertheless, even if the empires of the world and the devil oppose it, just as Christ says elsewhere: The gates of hell shall not prevail against the Church. And because there are many impediments, Christ shows in this consolation also a helper, and affirms that God will be present to those who ask: Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you. God is present to us as a helper; he wishes to hear, rule, help, defend, and deliver us. Therefore, let us not be broken in spirit so as to cast away our profession, even if many impediments occur, but, reminded by this promise, let us flee to our helper.

Repeat, I pray, reader, this whole consolation, and weigh the arguments and the affections. It meets the chief cares and anxieties of our minds, and opposes them with the most fitting consolations. Are you troubled as to whether the course of those who teach in the Church pleases God? He affirms that it pleases. Are you troubled as to whether we are going to accomplish anything? He affirms that we are going to accomplish it.

For he says, that you may bear fruit, and that your fruit may remain. Are you troubled as to how we can sustain such a great mass of affairs? He promises help: Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you. Are you troubled about defense? He himself affirms that he will not desert the Church: I will not leave you orphans. Likewise: Behold, I am with you even to the end of the age. Since, therefore, he opposes all terrors with the sweetest and firmest consolations, let us often consider them, so that they may confirm us in these constant dangers which are joined with the profession of the Gospel, and by the thought of them, let us stir up in ourselves faith and trust in Christ.

Latin:

Omnia quae audivi a patre meo, patefeci vobis.

In hoc dicto simul observetur sententia de ministerio Evangelii, videlicet, quod Deus non aliter agnosci et invocari possit, nisi sicut Christi revelatione patefactus est. Item, quod omnia ad salutem necessaria tradiderit Christus, nec sint quaerenda novae illuminationes, nec quaerenda alia doctrina. Hae sententiae semper sint in con- spectu, ut philosophicis opinionibus, seu sapien- tiae carnali opponantur. Multi fingunt Deum posse agnosci et coli, etiam sine noticia et mini- sterio Evangelii, quia humana ratio etiam scit unum esse Deum, et novit legem. Sed hic scia- mus, voluntatem Dei de remissione peccatorum donanda propter mediatorem filium, ignotam fuisse humanae rationi et omnibus creaturis, priusquam prolata est ex sinu arcano aeterni pa- tris per filium. Necesse est igitur audire Evan- gelium, ut alias saepe dictum est de discrimine legis et Evangelii.

Deinde etiam hi, qui audierunt Evange- lium, difficulter acquiescunt, expetunt alias il- luminationes aut contuitus clariores, quibus optant se reddi certiores, unde Enthusiastae, anabapti- stae, et multi fanatici orti sunt, et experiuntur omnes pii, magno certamine reprimendos et coër- cendos esse vagantes animos, ut ad hoc verbum traditum a Christo, et per Apostolos, alligentur, et in eo acquiescant, ac statuant vere hanc Dei voluntatem erga nos esse, quam hic patefecit. Si nunc de coelo tibi mitteretur angelus, nuncians tibi Deum placatum esse, et adderentur testimo- nia, videlicet solis regressus, ut Ezechiae tem- pore, tum vero gavisurum te, tam illustri signifi- catione voluntatis Dei arbitraris. At maius be- neficium est, filium esse missum, ac fuisse nun- cium tanti muneris. Hnius filii verbo vult nos credere, nec alias doctrinas aut illuminationes quaerere. Ad hanc sententiam confirmandam in nobis, dictum hoc meminerimus: Omnia quae audivi a patre meo, patefeci vobis. Affirmat se attulisse doctrinam, videlicet de reconciliatione ignotam omnibus creaturis, prolatam ex arcano sinu patris. Hanc vult nos amplecti, in hac vult nos acquiescere, nec alias opiniones, alios cul- tus, alias revelationes expetere.

Posui vos, ut eatis, et fructum feratis.

Addit consolationem: Si hanc meam doctri- nam retinebitis, fructum feretis. Miserum est magnos labores sustinere, qui nec tibi, nec aliis prosint, ut apud inferos Sisyphus saxum adver- sus montem agere dicitur. Multo vero tristius est, laboribus et contentionibus tantum aeternas poenas accersere, sicut multi gerentes iniusta bella, et alii propugnantes impia dogmata. Quam lu- gubre spectaculum fuit excidium Ierosolymae regi Zedechiae, et aliis principibus, cum videntes ur- bis incendium, cogitarunt se suis consiliis haec ingentia mala sibi et Ecclesiae Dei accersivisse? Ac Christus cum de Iuda loquitur, melius esset isti homini non esse natum, significat ingentem miseriam esse, consilia et labores suscipere, qui- bus ira Dei irritatur et exitus Iudae ostendit hor- rendis tenebris et furiis opprimi homines iniusta gerentes. Sicut Iudas sibi mortem consciscit, ut abrumpat dolorem, et tamen postea aeternos cru- ciatus sentit. Iam cogita maximam partem gene- ris humani frangi, aut inutilibus, aut perniciosis contentionibus. Multi fuerunt, sunt, et erunt Iudae similes, ut impii doctores omnium tempo- rum. Quam multi fuerunt excellentibus ingeniis praediti, qui tamen res aut inutiles, aut tantum perniciosas generi humano gesserunt. Res gestae Alcibiadis omnes ab initio usque ad finem nocue- runt ipsi, et patriae. Bruti, Cassii, Antonii, et aliorum innumerabilium bella, quid sunt nisi per- niciosi tumultus? Nunc quoque quam pauci sunt salutares principes.

Haec in historiis et vita quotidiana contem- plemur, ut de sua quisque vocatione, et de exitu cogitet. Primum vocatio placeat Deo, deinde depone fiduciam tui, et scias non regi magnas res humana sapientia, sed Deo monstrante consilia et occasiones, et adiuvante. Proponas igitur tibi divinas promissiones, et propter eas invoca Deum, et pete auxilium in vocatione, quam ipse appro- bat, et fiducia praesentiae Dei suscipe labores, convenientes tuo muneri. Ita et aliis profuturum est tuum ministerium, et tu ipse non amittes vi- tam aeternam, sed etiam praemiis ornaberis in hac vita et post hanc vitam. Haec est vera et firma consolatio, quam et hic Christus aliquoties inculcat, et saepe repetunt conciones divinae, ut supra dixi. Et Paulus clamat: Labor vester non est irritus per Dominum.

Ac nobis in Ecclesia praecipue opus est hac consolatione, ubi circumferimus doctrinam invi- sam mundo, et videmur nihil proficere posse, quia adversantur nobis summi reges, et multa sunt impedimenta, inopia, fames, metus crudelissi- morum suppliciorum. Inter haec mala cogitemus promissionem Christi toties repetitam: Qui manet in me, et ego in eo, copiosum fructum feret. Es concionator, doctor, scholasticus, scito functio- nem Deo placere, si vocationi tuae obtemparas, et salutaria doces, aut discis, et quanquam mul- tae difficultates impediunt cursum tuum, et vide- ris parum proficere, tamen fide et agnitione filii Dei petas ut adiuveris, et non dubites labores tuos tibi, et aliis salutares fore. Idque saepe ostendunt eventus in praesentia. Viderunt Da- vid, Esaias, Daniel, et alii multi in praesentia suos labores multis prodesse, Ieremias non vidit reditum populi, sed tamen sciebat consilium suum felix et salutare esse et fore toti Ecclesiae Dei.

Ac infigas intimis sensibus animi, quod di- serte addit Christus hoc loco: Et fructus vester maneat. Non solum exiguo tempore prosunt la- bores piorum ministrorum in Ecclesia, ut exiguo tempore prosunt labores Scipionis aut Augusti, qui politias suas defenderunt, et feliciter rexerunt, quae ad tempus manserunt: sed aeterni fructus sunt docentium, qui colligunt Deo aeternam Ec- clesiam, et ornantur ipsi aeternis praemiis. Nemo Romae in senatu existimabat diu mansuram esse hanc doctrinam, quam Paulus circumferebat, ac manent Paulus ipse, discipuli, et doctrina ad omnem aeternitatem.

Hac igitur dulcissima consolatione nos quo- que consolemur. Non videtur mansurus esse hic status Ecclesiarum et scholarum, qui Dei benefi- cio iam constitutus est, luce Evangeli reddita. Sed mansurus est tamen, etiamsi imperia mundi, et diabolus adversantur, sicut alibi Christus in- quit: Portas inferorum non praevalituras adver- sus Ecclesiam. Et quia multa sunt impedimenta, monstrat Christus in hac consolatione etiam auxi- liatorem, affirmat petentibus Deum affuturum esse: Quicquid petieritis patrem in nomine meo, da- bit vobis. Adest nobis Deus adiutor, vult nos exaudire, regere, adiuvare, defendere, liberare. Ideo non frangamur animis, ut abiiciamus pro- fessionem, etiamsi multa impedimenta incidunt, sed hac promissione commonefacti, confugiamus ad nostrum adiutorem.

Repete quaeso lector hanc totam consolatio- nem, et expende argumenta et affectus. Occur- rit praecipuis animorum nostrorum curis et soli- citudinibus, et opponit consolationes maxime con- gruentes. Angeris, an Deo placeat cursus docen- tium in Ecclesia, affirmat placere. Angeris, an simus aliquid profecturi, affirmat profecturos esse.

Ait enim, ut fructum feratis, et fructus vester maneat. Angeris, quo modo tantam molem rerum susti- nere possimus, pollicetur auxilium: Quicquid petieritis patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis. Angeris de defensione, ipse affirmat se non deser- turum esse Ecclesiam: Non relinquam vos orpha- nos. Item: Ecce, ego vobiscum sum usque ad consummationem seculi. Cum igitur omnibus terroribus opponat consolationes dulcissimas et firmissimas, saepe eas consideremus, ut nos in his assiduis periculis, quae coniuncta sunt cum Evangelii professione confirment, et earum cogi- tatione fidem et fiduciam Christi in nobis exusci- temus.

## 15:17
This is my commandment, that you love one another.

Somewhat earlier he described the Church, he attributed to it worship, invocation, and the propagation of the Gospel. Now he preaches about the third worship or good work, which itself is not only necessary for individuals in private life, but also publicly in the propagation of doctrine and in the government of the Church, namely, about concord or mutual benevolence. The commandment is clear, and the sentiment is known to all: By concord small things grow, by discord great things fall apart, and no one is ignorant of the Psalm: Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity. Which Psalm preaches specifically about the concord of doctrine. Because when mention is made of the oil with which Aaron was anointed, doctrine is signified. As the oil distills from the head of Aaron onto his beard and the edges of his garment, so one doctrine from one high priest, and head Christ, being scattered, should be taught by the whole assembly of priests; let not men invent for themselves new opinions about God, but let them acknowledge Him as He has revealed Himself, and let them worship Him according to the word which He Himself has delivered. There is, however, a singular pathos signified by these particles, This is my commandment. Why does He call it properly His own, when it had been delivered so often before? Others answer in the usual way, that it is called Christ's commandment on account of the help, because Christ gives the Holy Spirit, by whom hearts are kindled, so that to this obey the commandment. It can also be rightly answered that this is Christ's commandment, because no one obeys this precept unless he has both rightly learned the Gospel and in some way imitates these two virtues of Christ, humility and patience. For dissensions arise from these three sources, either from ignorance, or from ambition, or from impatience.

Regarding ignorance, Paul says: They have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. Men not rightly instructed in the Gospel follow human imaginations, as many have depicted and still depict the Church as a worldly polity, some of whom defend this error not out of ambition or impatience, but only out of ignorance, because they are not rightly instructed. Therefore, first for the consensus of doctrine and wills, it is necessary to hold the Gospel rightly.

Then ambition inflames many to spread new or popular dogmas, so that they may attain fame or power. Against this madness, no one can be fortified by any excellence of virtue, however great, without the recognition and imitation of Christ. But by looking with a true heart in some way at Christ's humility, they can also restrain themselves, lest they swell with pride. David, acknowledging that he was polluted by adultery, slaughter, and the huge scandals of a stirred-up sedition, of violated wives, of countless slaughters committed, casts himself down and is forced to confess that he is wretched and horribly deformed; thus let each one think of his own filth. But now compare Christ to this image: what humility it is that Christ lies prostrate before the Father, enduring wrath as if he himself had been polluted by my, your, and David's crimes; he transferred this great deformity onto himself. This is not a rhetorical and empty amplification, but such was truly Christ's grief, deriving into himself the wrath of God, as if he himself had committed these our offenses. But who can recount the magnitude of this humility, that the Son of God submits himself as if he were guilty of such great turpitudes? When the Son of God performs this humility, when he derives our disgraces into himself, let us be ashamed that we are unwilling to suffer small losses to our opinion, but we exalt ourselves as if touching the sky with our heads, and we flatter ourselves as if we surpass everyone in wisdom and virtue.

The third disease is akin to ambition, namely impatience. Many, irritated by injuries, fall into a desire for revenge, so that they stir up discords. As Coriolanus, irritated by an unjust condemnation, brought war upon his fatherland. Thus it often happens in the Church that good men, unjustly harmed, have later moved unjust contests out of the pain of the injury. It is difficult for one who is angry and burning with a desire for revenge to restrain himself from breaking out beyond the limits. But these are the exercises of the pious, to endure not only just troubles but also injuries. For these reasons, I think this is properly called Christ's commandment, because no one can do these things unless he both understands the Gospel and in some way imitates these singular virtues in Christ, namely, humility and patience, of which he himself says: Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart.

Latin:

Hoc est mandatum meum, ut diligatis invicem.

Aliquanto superius descripsit Ecclesiam, at- tribuit cultus, invocationem, et propagationem Evangelii. Nunc de tertio cultu seu bono opere concionatur, quod et ipsum non solum singulis in privata vita necessarium est, sed etiam publice in propagatione doctrinae et in gubernatione Ec- clesiae, videlicet de concordia seu mutua bene- volentia. Perspicuum est mandatum, et nota omnibus sententia est: Concordia parvae res cre- scunt, discordia magnae dilabuntur, et nemo ignorat Psalmum: Ecce quam bonum et quam iu- cundum, habitare fratres in unum. Qui Psal- mus peculiariter de doctrinae concordia concio- natur. Quia cum fit mentio balsami, quo Aaron unctus est, doctrina significatur. Ut distillat balsamum a vertice Aaronis in barbam et oras vestimenti, ita una doctrina ab uno summo sa- cerdote, et vertice Christo sparsa, doceatur a toto coetu sacerdotum, non fingant sibi homines no- vas opiniones de Deo, sed agnoscant eum, sicut ipse se patefecit, et colant eum iuxta verbum quod ipse tradidit. Est autem singulare πάθος his par- ticulis significatum, Hoc praeceptum meum est. Cur vocat proprie suum, cum toties antea tradi- tum sit? Alii usitate respondent, dici Christi man- datum, propter auxilium, quia Christus dat Spi- ritum sanctum, quo corda accenduntur, ut huic mandato obtemperent. Potest et hoc recte re- sponderi, esse Christi mandatum, quia nemo ob- temperat huic praecepto, nisi et Evangelium recte didicerit, et aliquo modo imitetur has duas vir- tutes Christi, humilitatem et patientiam. Oriun- tur enim dissidia ex his tribus fontibus, vel ex ignorantia, vel ex ambitione, vel ex impatientia.

De ignorantia inquit Paulus: Habent zelum Dei, sed non secundum scientiam. Homines non recte instituti in Evangelio, sequuntur humanas imaginationes, ut multi Ecclesiam pinxerunt, et pingunt tanquam mundanam politiam, quorum aliqui non ambitione, aut impatientia defendunt hunc errorem, sed tantum inscitia, quia non sunt recte instituti. Primum igitur ad consensum doctrinae et voluntatum necesse est recte tenere Evangelium.

Deinde ambitio multos incendit, ut nova aut popularia dogmata spargant, ut claritatem aut potentiam consequantur. Adversus hunc furo- rem nemo potest muniri ulla, quamvis magna praestantia virtutis sine agnitione et imitatione Christi. Sed Christi humilitatem vero corde ali- quo modo intuentes, reprimere se quoque pos- sunt, ne intumescant. David agnoscens se pol- lutum esse adulterio, caede, et ingentibus scan- dalis motae seditionis, stupratarum coniugum, factarum innumerabilium caedium; abiicit se, et cogitur fateri se miserum et horribiliter deforma- tum esse, sic de suis quisque sordibus cogitet. Sed iam ad hanc imaginem confer Christum, quan- ta humilitas est, quod iacet Christus coram patre prostratus, iram sustinens, quasi ipse meis, tuis, et Davidis sceleribus pollusisset, hanc tantam de- formitatem in sese transtulit. Haec non est re- thorica et inanis amplificatio, sed vere talis dolor Christi fuit, derivans in sese iram Dei, ac si ipse admisisset haec nostra delicta. Quis autem potest magnitudinem humilitatis huius enarrare, quod subiicit filius Dei, tanquam reum tantarum tur- pitudinum. Hanc humilitatem, cum filius Dei praestet, cum nostra probra in se derivat, pudeat nos, quod nolumus exiguas opinionis nostrae ia- cturas pati, sed efferimus nos quasi vertice coe- lum tangentes, et blandimur ipsi nobis, quasi antecellamus omnibus sapientia et virtute.

Tertius morbus affinis est ambitioni, scili- cet impatientia. Multi iniuriis irritati labun- tur cupiditate vindictae, ut discordias excitent. Ut Coriolanus irritatus iniusta condemnatione, bellum patriae intulit. Ita in Ecclesia saepe acci- dit, ut boni viri ac iniuste laesi, dolore iniuriae postea iniusta certamina moverint. Difficile est irato et ardenti cupiditate vindictae, cohibere se, quo minus extra metas erumpat. Sed haec sunt piorum exercitia, non solum iustas molestias, sed etiam iniurias perferre. Propter has causas hoc arbitror proprie Christi mandatum dici, quia nemo potest haec facere, nisi et intelligens Evangelium, et aliquo modo has singulares in Christo virtutes imitans, scilicet, humilitatem et patientiam, de quibus ipse inquit: Discite a me, quia mitis sum et humilis corde.

## 15:18
If the world hates you, know, etc.

He adds consolations from his own example: The servant is not greater than his Lord: I endured hatreds and dangers. Know, therefore, that these must also be sustained and tolerated by us, and let not your spirits be broken, even if not everyone embraces the Gospel; not everyone embraced it when I was teaching; imitate my course, and do not let yourselves be deterred either by dangers, or by the contempt of the Gospel, or by the multitude of adversaries.

Latin:

Si mundus vos odit, scitote, etc.

Addit consolationes a suo exemplo: Non est servus maior Domino suo: Ego sustinui odia et pericula. Scitote igitur et nobis sustinenda et to- leranda esse, nec frangantur animi vestri, etiamsi non omnes amplectentur Evangelium; nec me do- cente omnes amplexi sunt, meum cursum imite- mini, nec deterreri vos sinatis aut periculis, aut contemtu Evangelii, aut multitudine adversan- tium.

## 15:22
If I had not come, and had spoken.

Here they inquire about the sins of ignorance. Are those who have fallen through ignorance guilty before God, or are they rejected sinners, when Christ expressly says: If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin. Are Socrates, Xenophon, Plato, Scipio, and countless others excused, who did not rightly call upon God, being ignorant of the word of God? I answer: They are not excused, just as Christ affirms in the chapter immediately following, that the Holy Spirit will convict this sin, that the world does not believe in the Son of God. But you will say: What kind of hardness, or tyranny, is it to demand obedience, and not show what must be done? First, regarding the law, the answer is easy: Everyone knows the law, as Paul says, Rom. 1. Therefore, knowing it, they violated the law. Next, regarding the promise, this must be answered: God immediately at the beginning in Paradise handed down the promise concerning reconciliation, and concerning the Christ who was to come. He afterwards propagated this with certain and illustrious testimonies, and from time to time restored it, and always wished it to be known to all. And therefore he also always preserved some famous Church, in which the public ministry would sound the voice of the Gospel, which would be heard in the whole world. They are therefore guilty and wretched heathens, who have neglected or despised the ministry of the Gospel concerning the promised mediator.

Since, therefore, Christ says here: If I had not come and spoken to them, he is speaking of the universal revelation of the Gospel, made from the beginning of the world. I judge this to be a simple explanation of this saying. If the secret counsel of God concerning reconciliation had not been brought forth from the bosom of the eternal Father by the voice of the Son preaching from the beginning, men ignorant of the Gospel would not be guilty. Now, all who are ignorant are horribly guilty, because it has been revealed, and the revelation has been often repeated with illustrious testimonies, and the more illustrious the revelation is (such as it was then, when Christ himself, having assumed human nature, preached), the more grievous is the sin of those who despise and oppose it. Augustine answers thus: They would not have this sin, namely of blasphemy, unless they were to condemn the Gospel while knowing it to be the voice of God.

Latin:

Si non venissem, et locutus fuissem.

Hic quaerunt de peccatis ignorantiae. An ignorantia lapsi, sint rei coram Deo, seu pecca- tores abiecti, cum Christus expresse dicat: Si non venissem et dixissem eis, peccatum non haberent. Suntne excusati Socrates, Xenophon, Plato, Scipio, et alii innumerabiles, qui non recte in- vocarunt Deum, ignari verbi Dei? Respondeo: Non sunt excusati, sicut mox sequenti capite af- firmat Christus, Spiritum sanctum accusaturum esse hoc peccatum, quod mundus non credat in filium Dei. Sed dices: Quae est ita durities, seu tyrannis, postulare obedientiam, nec monstrare quid agendum sit? Primum de lege facilis est re- sponsio: Legem omnes norunt, sicut Paulus in- quit, Rom. 1. Scientes igitur violarunt legem. Deinde de promissione hoc respondendum est: Deus initio statim in Paradiso tradidit promissio- nem de reconciliatione, et de Christo futuro. Hanc certis et illustribus testimoniis postea pro- pagavit, et subinde instauravit, ac semper omni- bus voluit notam esse. Ideoque et semper Eccle- siam aliquam celebrem servavit, in qua ministe- rium publicum sonaret vocem Evangelii, quae ex- audiretur toto orbe terrarum. Sunt igitur rei et abiecti ethnici, qui neglexerunt, aut contemse- runt ministerium Evangelii de promisso media- tore.

Cum igitur Christus hic dicit: Si non venis- sem et dixissem eis, loquitur de universa revela- tione Evangelii, facta ab initio mundi. Hanc iudico simplicem explicationem esse huius dicti. Si non prolatum esset arcanum Dei consilium de reconciliatione ex sinu aeterni patris, voce filii concionantis ab initio, non essent rei homines ignorati Evangelii. Nunc horribiliter rei sunt omnes ignari, quia et revelatum est, et saepe re- petita est revelatio illustribus testimoniis, et quo illustrior est revelatio: (qualis fuit tunc, cum ipse Christus assumta humana natura concionatus est) eo gravius peccatum est contemnentium et adversantium. Augustinus sic respondet: Non haberent hoc peccatum, scilicet blasphemiae, nisi scientes Evangelium Dei vocem esse, tamen damnarent.

## 15:23
He who hates me, hates my Father also.

If even above in chapter 5 he said: He who does not honor the Son, does not honor the Father. These two sentences must be observed most diligently. For they show the distinction between true religion and fictitious ones, and between true invocation and false. Jews and Mahometans boast that they invoke the one and true God, the creator of heaven and earth, and of men and of all other creatures. Indeed, even the minds of Plato and similar men thought of some one God as the creator of universal nature. But these sayings of Christ reject that Jewish, Mahometan, and Heathen thought, who deny that this one who sent his Son Jesus Christ is truly the God who is the creator. They do not acknowledge, they do not invoke the true God, but they carve for themselves a new idol of God, and they stray from the true God. Let us therefore hold to the distinction of religions, and let us not concede to the Jews and Mahometans that the God who is the creator of heaven and earth is worshipped by them, but they imagine him to be a God who is about to send another Messiah, or who sent Mahomet. And it is most certain that Mahomet was sent by the devil, because the doctrine of Mahomet is recent, fighting against the Prophets and Apostles, as is manifest. Wherefore it is certain that it is impious and diabolical.

Always also in invocation, when calling upon God, let us think of this God the creator of heaven and earth, who sent his Son our Lord Jesus Christ, and through him revealed himself by giving the Gospel. Thus, let us first think of which God, where, and how revealed we are addressing, then let us also set before ourselves the promises in which he affirms that he will hear those who invoke him, on account of the Son the mediator. It behooves us to bring these thoughts and this faith to prayer. And such invocation distinguishes the true Church from the Heathens, Jews, and Turks who invoke, and it is effective.

And in Psalm 16 the Church is thus distinguished from other nations. True and effective invocation is also distinguished from false and damned invocation, when it is said: To the saints who are in the earth, and to the wonderful, all my will is in them, that is, I, Christ, perpetually love the righteous, that is, the assembly that hears me, I provide for them by this my passion, all my labors, all my offices are destined for this, that they may bring help to them. We foolishly think that Christ sits somewhere idle, and is blessed in himself. Here he cries out that he is solicitous for his assembly, that he labors, intercedes, rules it, defends and preserves it. On the contrary, he adds that he damns the libations and invocations of others who do not wish to hear him. I will not pour out, he says, their libations, nor will I take their names upon my lips, that is, I will not name them, I will not intercede for them before the Father.
