Harum tantarum miseriarum cogitatione mo- veamur, ne simus securi, nec obliviscamur mi- narum Christi, et in hac cogitatione invocemus filium Dei, qui vicit, ut nos iuvaret, ac in no- stris periculis opem nobis ferret, et illum dirum hostem vinceret, fide et invocatione, in nostris aerumnis confugiamus ad filium Dei propugna- torem nostrum, quod si faciemus, experiemur nos vere iuvari, ac liberari. Nisi iudicatus, id est, condemnatus esset diabolus, ita videlicet, ne possit grassari, ut cupit, membra Ecclesiae sin- gula tam horrendis malis implicarentur, ut elu- ctari non possent, sed quia reprimitur a filio Dei, ideo emergunt, ut Adam lapsus restitutus est, et postea in multis ingentibus doloribus erectus: et David ex tot peccatis et scandalis evasit. Haec exempla intueamur, et ad ea conferamus nostra pericula, et miserias inexplicabiles humanis con- siliis, et hanc consolationem nobis proponamus, iudicatus et condemnatus est diabolus, ne vincat filium Dei, et confugientes ad eum. Invocemus igitur filium Dei, et defensionem et liberationem petamus, nec putemus hanc invocationem irritam esse, sed ardeat fides, et expectet auxilium Chri- sti, quod cum faciemus, revera experiemur libe- rationem.

Haec exercitia fidei usu discenda sunt, sed plerunque homines impliciti periculis, cum hu- manis consiliis destituuntur, et vident se non iuvari causis secundis, et iis modis, quos humana ratio prospicere potest, languefacti amittunt fidem, et ducunt invocationem inane murmur esse, et tandem, vel in furores epicureos incidunt, vel dolore oppressi pereunt, sicut Saul et Iudas. Ad- versus has tristissimas tentationes consolatur nos Chrisus in hoc textu. Quare hoc dictum infiga- mus animis, et assidue cogitemus. Haec medi- tatio illustrabit hanc Christi concionem magis quam ullae prolixae enarrationes. Etsi hoc quo- que prodest commonefieri auditorem, ut ad sua pericula conferat consolationem, et opponat eam diaboli telis ignitis, qui hoc praecipue molitur, ut impellat languefactos animos, ut ruant in con- temtum Dei, aut in desperationem. Adversus haec extrema mala simus intenti, et praemunia- mus nos his Christi promissionibus toties repetitis.

## 16:12
I still have many things to say to you.

Having entered into the thought of the greatest things, which are immense and cannot be fully comprehended by the human mind, Christ breaks off his discourse, out of pity for our infirmity, which indeed he openly deplores, and immediately adds a consolation, saying that he is going to send another teacher, the Holy Spirit. Nor do I wish in these most weighty sentences to refute at length the most insipid nonsense of hypocrites, who with these words defend human traditions: There remain many things to be said, which you cannot bear now; these, they say, were revealed later. Which ones? The doctrine concerning the distinction of foods, of garments, concerning sacrifice for the dead, and many other absurdities. Let a brief refutation be held. It was said above in chapter 14: He will teach you all things, and will bring to your remembrance those things which I have said to you. The Holy Spirit does not bring a new doctrine, not yet handed down by Christ, but kindles a light in hearts, so that they may assent to the Gospel, which the voice of Christ has already sounded, and here it is said: He will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears, he will speak. It is most unworthy not to attribute greater things to the Holy Spirit than the absurdities of human traditions. Therefore I leave this discussion, and I only remind the reader to consider that the Holy Spirit was promised for the beginning of wisdom in hearts, placed far above and outside the grasp of human reason, and the word of Christ and the light kindled in hearts by the Holy Spirit must agree, as they truly do agree in all the members of Christ, even if in one there is more light, in another less.

But because the knowledge of these things is immense, namely how great things sin and the wrath of God are, and this victim the Son of God deriving the wrath into himself, and how great the glory of the reigning Christ is, how great the power of the devil, what kind of struggles of Christ and the devil, these such great things were not yet perceived, he says, by the Apostles, nay rather all men in all times from Adam onwards have gradually progressed in this knowledge, and we ought to ask for the Holy Spirit with ardent vows, that he may instruct us with his light, just as the Prophet incessantly cries: Deal with thy servant according to thy mercy, and teach me thy statutes. Likewise: I am thy servant, give me understanding. These most ardent petitions speak of great matters, not of the absurdities of human traditions.

Latin:

Adhuc multa habeo dicere vobis.

Ingressus in maximarum rerum cogitatio- nem Christus, quae sunt immensae, nec possunt prorsus comprehendi ab humana mente, abrum- pit sermonem, miseratione nostrae infirmitatis, quam quidem aperte deplorat, et statim subiicit consolationem, ait se missurum esse, et alium doctorem Spiritum sanctum. Nec volo in his gravissimis sententiis prolixe refutare insulsissi- mas naenias hypocritarum, qui hisce verbis de- fendunt humanas traditiones: Restant multa di- cenda, quae non potestis modo portare, haec, inquiunt, postea revelata sunt. Quaenam? Doctrina de discrimine ciborum, vestium, de sacrificio pro mortuis, et aliae multae ineptiae. Teneatur brevis refutatio. Supra dictum est cap. 14.: Ille docebit vos omnia, et rediget vobis in memoriam ea quae dixi vobis. Spiritus sanctus non affert novam doctrinam, nondum traditam a Christo, sed accendit lucem in cordibus, ut assentiantur Evangelio, quod iam sonuit vox Christi, et hic dicitur: Non loquetur a sese, sed quae audierit, loquetur. Indignissimum est, non maiora tribuere Spiritui sancto, quam ineptias humanarum traditionum. Ideo relinquo hanc disputationem, ac tantum commonefacio lectorem, ut cogitet Spiritum sanctum promissum esse ad incoandam in cordibus sapientiam, longe positam supra et extra captum humanae rationis, et oportet congruere verbum Christi, et lucem accensam in cordibus a Spiritu sancto, ut revera congruunt in omnibus Christi membris, etsi in alio plus, in alio minus lucis est.

Quia autem harum rerum cognitio immensa est, videlicet quantae res sint peccatum et ira Dei, et haec victima filius Dei in se derivans iram, et quanta gloria sit regnantis Christi, quanta potentia diaboli, qualia certamina Christi et diaboli, has tantas res nondum percipi, inquit, ab Apostolis, imo omnes omnibus temporibus inde usque ab Adam paulatim in hac cognitione profecerunt, et nos ardentibus votis petere Spiritum sanctum debemus, ut erudiat nos sua luce, sicut assidue clamat Propheta: Fac cum servo tuo secundum misericordiam tuam, et iustificationes tuas doce me. Item: Servus tuus sum, da mihi intellectum. Hae ardentissimae petitiones de rebus magnis loquuntur, non de ineptiis traditionum humanarum.

## 16:13
He will lead you into all truth.

The Greek narrative should be observed in this place, because it testifies more clearly than the Latin reading that the Holy Spirit is a person. For unless he wished to signify a person, he would not have said ἐκεῖνος, τὸ πνεῦμα, but would have been content with the neuter gender. This brief annotation is not to be neglected. Then indeed the descriptions of the Holy Spirit, handed down above, are repeated here. Let these be understood both concerning the ministry of the Gospel publicly and privately concerning the light in the hearts of individuals, as was said above in similar places: The Holy Spirit governs the ministry of the Gospel, and from time to time kindles light again in some teachers, just as Isaiah also says in chapter 59: This is my covenant with them, says the Lord, my spirit, which is in thee, and my words which I have put in thy mouth, shall not depart out of thy mouth, nor out of the mouth of thy seed, says the Lord, from henceforth and for ever. Here he promises that the ministry will remain perpetually, in which the Gospel will sound, although at times more, at times less clearly, but yet it will remain, and from time to time it will be restored, and the Holy Spirit will govern the minds of some teachers, and will be effective through the ministry, just as Christ also says concerning teachers, Matt. 10: It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you. These most sweet consolations confirm us, so that we may know that those teaching the Gospel are helped by the Holy Spirit.

Then also privately the Holy Spirit bends the hearts of those hearing the Gospel to the truth, so that they may rightly acknowledge and call upon God, and rightly understand the doctrine of the Gospel concerning God, concerning Christ, concerning grace, concerning justice, and other necessary things, just as it is said in Zech. 12: I will pour upon the house of David the spirit of grace and the spirit of supplications, that is, by whose moving the hearts of individuals, they experience consolation, and acknowledge themselves to be in grace, and to be received, and are impelled to invocation.

Let us consider these huge goods, so that we may learn to understand and desire these consolations, and these salutary motions of true invocation. When these things happen in us, minds are governed so that kinds of doctrines may also be judged rightly, and may be distinguished from law, from philosophy, and from human opinions and cults, therefore Paul says 1 Cor. 2: The spiritual man examines, or judges, all things, and 1 John 2: The anointing teaches you concerning all things, and it is true, and is not a lie. There exist everywhere many sayings which preach about these benefits of the Holy Spirit in the same way, as it is said here: He will lead you into all truth. It is a great and salutary thing not to err in the judgment of doctrine, and in the counsels of private life, or of government, just as others have hallucinated in the interpretation of scripture more furiously, like the Pharisees and Heretics, others more stupidly, like Origen, Thomas, and many such writers, and our age, which has seen the horrible insanity of the Anabaptists.

other examples are to be considered, so that from the region we may learn to magnify the benefit of the Holy Spirit, and to ask that He may govern us with His true light, and Christ commanded that this be asked, and added a promise, saying: How much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him. I pray Thee therefore, living and almighty God, eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, creator and preserver of all things, and helper, with Thy Son our Lord Jesus Christ, Thy λόγῳ and image, and the Holy Spirit poured out upon the Apostles, the Paraclete, wise, good, merciful, judge, strong, chaste, truthful and most free: Have mercy on us for the sake of Jesus Christ Thy Son our Lord, crucified for us and resurrected, whom Thou didst will to be a victim for us, καὶ μεσίτην, καὶ ἱκέτην, and kindle, rule, and sanctify our hearts with Thy Holy Spirit, that we may truly acknowledge, invoke, and fear Thee, truly believe in Thee, give thanks, and obey Thee; do not allow the light of the Gospel to be extinguished in us by the deceits of the devil; rule us with counsel in all matters, because Thy Son promised that Thou wouldst give the Holy Spirit to those who ask, as it is written: How much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him.

For He will not speak on His own authority.

He meets many questions. Since another teacher is promised, the question is: Is He going to bring another doctrine, other articles, not handed down by Christ? Christ answers: Nay, He will teach exactly the same thing that I teach, nor will He bring other or new articles not handed down by me, but the doctrine of the eternal Father, mine, and the Holy Spirit's is the same. This answer of Christ is to be observed, so that it may be opposed to those who try to defend the sales of Masses, and the invocations of the dead, and many other errors under this pretext, that although they were not handed down in the Gospel, yet they were received afterwards, with the Holy Spirit moving minds.

Moreover, there is a twofold refutation. The first: All who wish to be seen to embrace the Gospel are forced to admit that dogmas conflicting with those which have already been handed down by Christ are not to be received. But when we condemn the errors of our adversaries, we show that they conflict with certain dogmas handed down by Christ. The immutable counsel of God proposed by Christ is certain, by which we are taught that sins are remitted on account of the Mediator through faith, and not on account of any works of ours, or worship devised by us. Since, therefore, against this voice of the Gospel the Monks affirm that sins are remitted on account of the sacrifices of the Mass, or their own vows, they openly conflict with the Gospel. Against this clear refutation they cite in vain that dream which they invent about dogmas revealed to the Church, and not handed down by the voice of the Gospel.

The second refutation is this: it is a customary saying that the Church does not beget articles of faith, but receives them from God through a certain and unambiguous word. Therefore, it is not necessary that opinions be received in the Church as articles of faith which are proposed without certain testimony of Scripture, even if they do not manifestly conflict with the sayings of prophetic or apostolic Scripture, as the old narrative is in the Church that Zechariah, the father of the Baptist, was killed on account of his confession concerning Christ, and that mention of this history is made in Matthew twenty-third; nor does this narrative conflict with the Gospel, but yet it is not an article of faith. Furthermore, it is true that we learn articles of faith from the Church, but we do not believe on account of the Church, as the Church teaches us that the person is signified by this word λόγος, John 1, but faith and invocation must rest upon divine testimony, because a creature cannot hold a firm opinion concerning the essence and will of God without divine revelation. We seek, therefore, in the prophetic and apostolic writings for testimonies which are not ambiguous. Confirmed by these, we bring true knowledge of God to invocation. These things are easily understood by the pious. There remains here another question, namely, concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, whether He proceeds from the Father alone. I said above that we embrace the opinion of the Latin Church, that the Holy Spirit proceeds simultaneously from the eternal Father and from the Son. A sufficiently firm testimony stands here: He will receive from mine. The Holy Spirit is therefore something of the essence of the Son, or even ὁμοούσιον to the Son. This proof is sufficiently firm for a pious mind, which does not seek cavils to undermine the text. And those things agree with this, that Christ Himself in John 20: He breathes the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles. This breath proceeds not from the Father alone, but also from the Son. Moreover, a confirmation is added in this place: All things that the Father has are mine. This voice, equating the Son to the Father, should be diligently observed, nor is there any doubt that the power is equal, since the Son is thus omnipotent, by nature God, wherefore He is also ὁμοούσιον to the Father. Hence it follows that the Holy Spirit proceeds from both. Nor do I wish to dispute at greater length concerning these mysteries, which must be thought upon with reverence, and one must not linger in speculation, but the benefits should be considered. How great is the love of the Son of God towards us, how great is the humility, that while He is God by nature, He casts Himself down, and puts on this nature of ours, He makes a covenant with us, the most intimate of all, namely by the union of nature, and becomes a victim for us. What a great benefit it is that God pours His Spirit into our hearts, whose essence is divine, and makes us, as Peter says, partakers of the divine nature. Let us acknowledge these such great benefits, and let us proclaim them with thanks, and in turn let us submit ourselves to God, that we may show that we are truly thankful to God, and let us truly pray that the Holy Spirit may kindle this gratitude in us.

Latin:

Ducet vos in omnem veritatem.

Graeca narratio hoc loco observetur, quia testatur magis perspicue, quam Latina lectio, Spiritum sanctum esse personam. Nisi enim personam vellet significare, non dixisset ἐκεῖνος, τὸ πνεῦμα, sed fuisset contentus genere neutro. Haec brevis annotatio non est negligenda. Deinde vero repetuntur hic descriptiones Spiritus sancti, supra traditae. Hae et de ministerio Evangelii publice et privatim de luce in cordi- bus singulorum intelligantur, ut supra in simi- libus locis dictum est: Spiritus sanctus gubernat ministerium Evangelii, et subinde rursus lucem in aliquibus doctoribus accendit, sicut et Esaias inquit cap. 59.: Hoc foedus meum cum eis, dicit Dominus, spiritus meus, qui est in te, et verba mea quae posui in ore tuo, non recedent ab ore tuo, nec ab ore seminis tui, dicit Domi- nus, deinceps et in sempiternum. Hic pro- mittit perpetuo mansurum esse ministerium, in quo Evangelium sonabit, etsi alias magis, alias minus perspicue, sed tamen mansurum est, et subinde restituetur, et Spiritus sanctus gubernabit mentes aliquorum docentium, et erit efficax per ministerium, sic et Christus inquit de doctoribus, Matth. 10: Non vos estis qui loqui- mini, sed Spiritus Patris vestri est, qui loquitur in vobis. Hae dulcissimae consolationes con- firmant nos, ut sciamus docentes Evangelium iuvari a Spiritu sancto.

Deinde et privatim Spiritus sanctus flectit corda audientium Evangelium ad veritatem, ut Deum recte agnoscant et invocent, et recte intelli- gant doctrinam Evangelii de Deo, de Christo, de gratia, de iusticia, et aliis rebus necessariis, sicut Zach. 12. dicitur: Effundam super domum David spiritum gratiae et spiritum precum, id est, quo movente singulorum corda, experiun- tur consolationem, et agnoscunt se esse in gratia, ac recipi, et impelluntur ad invocationem.

Haec ingentia bona consideremus, ut disca- mus intelligere et optare has consolationes, et hos salutares motus verae invocationis. Haec cum fiunt in nobis, reguntur mentes ut dextre etiam genera doctrinarum diiudicentur, ac discer- natur a lege, a philosophia, et ab humanis opi- nionibus et cultibus, ideo Paulus inquit 1. Co- rinth. 2.: Spiritualis omnia examinat, seu diiu- dicat, et 1. Ioan. 2.: Unctio docet vos de omni- bus, et vera est, et non est mendacium. Extant passim multa dicta, quae de his beneficiis Spiritus sancti eodem modo concionantur, ut hic dicitur: Ducet vos in omnem veritatem. Magna et salutaris res est, non aberrare in iudi- cio doctrinae, et in consiliis privatae vitae, aut gubernationis, sicut hallucinati sunt in interpre- tatione scripturae alii furiosius, ut Pharisaei et Haeretici, alii stolidius, ut Origenes, Thomas, et multi tales scriptores, et nostra aetas, quam horrendam insaniam vidit Anabaptistarum.

lia exempla consideranda sunt, ut e regione bene- ficium S. sancti magnifacere discamus, ac petere, ut vera luce sua nos gubernet, idque peti iussit Christus, et promissionem addidit inquiens: Quanto magis pater vester coelestis dabit Spiri- tum sanctum petentibus. Te igitur oro vive et omnipotens Deus, aeterne pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, conditor omnium rerum et conser- vator, et opitulator, cum filio tuo Domino nostro Iesu Christo, λόγῳ et imagine tua, et Spiritu sancto effuso in Apostolos, paracleto, sapiens, bone, misericors, iudex, fortis, caste, verax et liberrime: Miserere nostri propter Iesum Chri- stum filium tuum Dominum nostrum crucifixum pro nobis, et resuscitatum, quem voluisti pro nobis esse victimam, καὶ μεσίτην, καὶ ἱκέτην, et accende, rege, sanctifica corda nostra Spiritu sancto tuo, ut te vere agnoscamus, invocemus, metuamus, tibi vere credamus, gratias agamus, et obediamus, ne sinas praestigiis diaboli extingui in nobis lucem Evangelii, rege nos consilio in omnibus negotiis, quia filius tuus promisit, te petentibus daturum esse Spiritum sanctum, sicut scriptum est: Quanto magis pater vester coelestis dabit Spiritum sanctum petentibus se.

Non enim loquetur a seipso.

Multis quaestionibus occurrit. Cum alius doctor promittatur, quaestio est: An aliam do- ctrinam, alios articulos allaturus sit, non tradi- tos a Christo? Respondet Christus: Imo idem prorsus docebit, quod ego doceo, nec alios arti- culos, nec novos afferet a me non traditos, sed eadem est doctrina aeterni patris, mea, et Spiri- tus sancti. Haec responsio Christi observanda est, ut opponatur illis, qui Missae venditiones, et invocationes mortuorum, et multos errores alios defendere conantur hoc praetextu, quod quanquam non sint traditi in Evangelio, tamen postea sint recepti, movente mentes Spiritu sancto.

Est autem duplex refutatio. Prior: Fateri coguntur omnes, qui videri volunt amplecti Evan- gelium, non recipienda esse dogmata pugnantia cum his, quae iam tradita sunt a Christo. Nos autem cum improbamus errores adversariorum, hoc ostendimus, pugnare eos cum certis dogma- tibus a Christo traditis. Certum est propositum a Christo consilium Dei immutabile, quo docemur remitti peccata propter mediatorem fide, et non propter ulla nostra opera, aut cultus a nobis excogitatos. Cum igitur contra hanc Evangelii vocem Monachi affirmant remitti peccata, propter sacrificia Missae, aut sua vota, aperte pugnant cum Evangelio. Contra hanc perspicuam refutationem frustra citant illud somnium, quod fingunt de dogmatibus revelatis Ecclesiae, et non traditis voce Evangelii.

Secunda refutatio haec est, usitatum dictum est, Ecclesia non gignit articulos fidei, sed accipit eos a Deo per verbum certum, et non ambiguum. Non igitur necesse est recipi opiniones in Ecclesia tanquam articulos fidei, quae sine testimonio certo scripturae proponuntur, etiamsi non manifeste pugnant cum dictis scripturae propheticae, seu apostolicae, ut vetus narratio est in Ecclesia, Zachariam Baptistae patrem interfectum esse propter confessionem de Christo, ac mentionem eius historiae fieri, Matthaei vicesimo tertio nec pugnat haec narratio cum Evangelio, sed tamen non est articulus fidei. Caeterum illud verum est, discimus ab Ecclesia articulos fidei, sed non credimus propter Ecclesiam, ut Ecclesia docet nos, significari personam hac voce λόγος, Ioan. 1. sed fidem et invocationem oportet niti testimonio divino, quia de Dei essentia et voluntate non potest creatura sine revelatione divina firmam sententiam tenere. Quaerimus igitur in scriptis propheticis et apostolicis testimonia, quae non sunt ambigua. His confirmati, veram agnitionem Dei ad invocationem afferimus. Haec facile intelliguntur a piis. Restat hic et alia quaestio, scilicet de processione Spiritus sancti, an a solo patre procedat. Dixi supra, nos amplecti sententiam Latinae Ecclesiae, Spiritum sanctum procedere simul ab aeterno patre et a filio. Testimonium hic satis firmum extat: Ex meo accipiet. Est igitur Spiritus sanctus aliquid essentiae filii, seu etiam filio ὁμοούσιον. Haec probatio satis firma est piae menti, quae non quaerit cavillationes ad labefactandum textum. Et huc congruunt illa, quod Christus ipse Ioan. 20.: Afflat Spiritum sanctum Apostolis. Hic flatus non a solo patre, sed etiam a filio procedit. Additur autem et confirmatio hoc loco: Omnia quae pater habet, mea sunt. Haec vox aequans filium patri diligenter observetur, nec dubium est potentiam aequari, cum filius sic omnipotens, natura Deus est, quare et patri ὁμοούσιος est. Hinc sequitur, et ab utroque procedere Spiritum sanctum. Nec volo prolixius de his arcanis disputare, quae re- verenter cogitanda sunt, nec immorandum est speculationi, sed beneficia considerentur. Quan- tus amor est filii Dei erga nos, quanta humilitas, quod cum sit natura Deus, abiicit se, et induit hanc nostram naturam, facit foedus nobiscum omnium arctissimum, scilicet copulatione natu- rae, et fit victima pro nobis. Quantum bene- ficium est, quod Deus effundit in corda nostra spiritum suum, cuius est essentia divina, et efficit nos, ut Petrus inquit, socios naturae divinae. Haec tanta beneficia agnoscamus, et grati praedi- cemus, et vicissim nos Deo subiiciamus, ut osten- damus nos vere Deo gratos esse, et vere oremus, ut Spiritus sanctus accendat in nobis hanc grati- tudinem.

## 16:16
A little while and you will not see me.

Previously He preached at length concerning the ministry, now He inserts a consolation, by which He signifies that He is about to suffer, but He expressly affirms that He will return to them shortly. Although, however, He had often predicted the same things concerning His passion, yet they were so fascinated by the opinion concerning the political empire of the Messiah, that they did not understand these sermons concerning the passion. Therefore they question Him, and confess that they do not know what He is saying. These examples warn first that the darkness is to be deplored, because at that time in the Church of God the understanding of the promises concerning Christ was so extinguished that they foolishly dreamed only of a civil empire. It is necessary that there were some who felt rightly, as were Zacharias, Simeon, Joseph, the Baptist, Mary, Elizabeth, Anna, and many others. For always some Church remains that feels rightly, even if it is small and dispersed, and the multitude is far greater, contaminated by many foul errors, which holds the government. Since, however, at that time, and often otherwise, great errors were publicly handed down by the governors, and received by the greatest multitude, let us know that in this last age also the pontiffs, and the greatest part of the learned and of the people, could and can err, and let us not be moved by the authority of rank, or of the multitude, but let us seek the truth in the word of God, just as the Prophets often preach concerning the same matter. But there is a most sweet passage in Isaiah 8, where first Isaiah prays that God may preserve pure doctrine in some. Seal the law, he says, in my disciples, that is, I see that horrible darkness and forgetfulness of doctrine are about to follow, as has happened at other times; then in the time of the Pharisees and Sadducees, and I am in the greatest pain and mourning on account of the Church. But I pray Thee, O God, do not allow the true doctrine handed down by Thee to be utterly extinguished, but preserve it enclosed in the minds of my disciples, that they may transmit it uncorrupted to posterity. He signifies, however, that the doctrine is to remain only among those who are disciples of the Prophets, that is, who hear, embrace, and retain this word handed down by God through the Prophets. Let us all often think upon this prayer of Isaiah, and join our vows to it, let us ask that He may seal His law in us also, and confirm our minds, that the truth may shine in us, and through our ministry reach posterity uncorrupted. There follows, however, a description of the event: Behold, I and my children, whom God has given me for a sign in Israel. This saying is a promise and a consolation, which affirms that there will be some assembly of the Church for posterity, but small and hated by the powerful. Then the commandment is expressly added, where the true doctrine handed down by God is to be sought, namely not in the common persuasion of princes and the multitude, as now a great multitude of Monks is cited, but in the word which God handed down by certain testimonies through the Prophets, to the law and to the testimony, he says: Whoever will not embrace that word, there will be no morning light for them. I have reviewed these things briefly, that we may consider the times and miseries of the Church, and learn where the truth is to be sought.

Secondly, the example of the Apostles shows that there are many in the Church who are weak, who nevertheless are chosen and tolerated by God. We all have need of this consolation. For we all carry around with us both some sins and errors. But those who retain the foundation of the faith, and do not persevere in errors or transgressions against their conscience, but are teachable, and begin amendment, these remain in grace, just as it is also most sweetly said, at Rom. 14: God has received him, where Paul affirms that even the weak person pleases God.

Thirdly, this sermon warns that the Church in this life is subject to the cross, as is often said elsewhere: And this doctrine is proper to the Church, unknown to philosophy, whence the calamities of the whole human race are, why the Church is most harshly exercised, and what true and firm consolation it has set before it. These things have been said elsewhere, but yet they must be repeated from time to time. When it is asked whence they are The calamities of the whole human race, philosophy says, arise partly from matter, partly from human errors and human will, as they say the cause of death is the nature of matter. They say Pompey brought calamity upon himself by error, because he thought the defense of the Republic was just, and he generally knew that the established power would be victorious. But a perverse will drove Catiline to destruction, because although he understood the danger, he nevertheless stirred up sedition. Philosophy recounts these causes, which, even if they are proximate and concurrent causes, are nevertheless other than the prior and more powerful ones. The first and chief cause of death and all punishments is sin, which is born with us, originating from the fall of Adam, and the tyranny of the devil, who horribly impels weak nature into crimes and punishments.

Then, however, in the Church many causes concur, since sin remains in this life in the saints, death and other calamities remain, so that, being warned of the wrath of God, we may acknowledge sin and seek help, and also so that, the flames of vices being repressed, true faith, invocation, and other virtues may be kindled in us, as it is said in the Psalm: It is good for me that you have humbled me, that I might learn your justifications. There are also other causes, which are recounted elsewhere in a complete explanation of this passage.

Finally, philosophy sees the destruction of nature and other calamities, but it cannot propose a firm consolation; it only warns us not to increase the sense of evils which cannot be avoided, by adding moreover a greater sadness of mind, as Socrates, when he cannot escape death, acts wisely because he resists grief, as if breaking its force in some way, but he does not see the outcome of evil and the restoration of a better life. Wherefore, in great evils, philosophical consolation does not help minds at all, and all human wisdom is a funeral song, as was signified in Matthew 9: When the flute players were hired for the funeral of the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, who sing funeral melodies.

But the Christian doctrine alone shows the help and presence of God in all afflictions, and moreover the restoration of eternal life. This showing of help and liberation is a true and effective consolation. Therefore, Christ preaches about it not only often elsewhere, but also in this place: You will grieve, but your sadness will be turned into joy. This is not the voice of philosophy or of any human wisdom.

Indeed, not even of the law, but of the Gospel alone, and in this struggle the differences of doctrines become clear; when in true sorrows we seek consolations from everywhere, and by experience itself we find that we are not helped by human thoughts, finally the pious mind, running to the voice of the Gospel as to a fountain of living water, begins to find rest, as it is said in the Psalm: Your word will give me life.

Whatever you ask, he will give you, etc.

Before, he predicted that afflictions would follow, and added a promise concerning liberation. Now he adds two sayings which pertain to consolation and are an approach to liberation, namely concerning the true knowledge of the will of God, and concerning prayer. Unless these two shine in afflictions, minds cannot find rest, as Cato, Brutus, and the like, because they are ignorant of the will of God, judge that they are neglected or cast off by God. Thus they rush into eternal despair and into hatred of God. Jeremiah, however, even though he sees his country falling, yet knows that the Church of God is not deserted. Confirmed by this knowledge, he endures present miseries, for he understands their causes, and that there will be an end to them, and he knows of the restoration of the Church. The first saying in this place, therefore, speaks of the knowledge of the will of God. On that day you will not ask me anything, that is, after the resurrection your eyes will be witnesses that I live. You will therefore be confirmed, so that you do not doubt concerning my life. Then, when you have received the Holy Spirit, you will understand what my kingdom is, what are the causes of the afflictions of the Church, and how I am going to gather, preserve, and liberate the Church. You will discern the righteousness of faith and political righteousness, you will cast away the Pharisaic dreams concerning the civil empire of the Messiah, finally you will know all things necessary for eternal salvation. This certain knowledge of the Gospel is the source of the chief consolations.

To this knowledge let prayer be added. There is, therefore, a repeated promise, about which it has been spoken several times above. And it must be diligently observed that an oath has been added: Amen, amen, I say to you. Let this great asseveration rouse us, so that we may believe the promise and more ardently seek help. But as often as this promise is expounded, the five precepts of prayer, about which it was spoken above, must be repeated: First, which God is to be invoked, for the invocation of the Church must be separated from the invocation of the heathen, the Mohammedan, and other impious nations. Second, the commandments should be considered, which command us to pray. For the human mind, especially when wounded by the recognition of its own sin, flees from God, nor does it dare to ask for good things. Against this trepidation, first the commandments, then the promises, and the doctrine of faith should be set. Thirdly, therefore, we look upon the promises, which affirm that God truly wills to give eternal and present good things. Fourthly, let faith be kindled, which determines that we are received and heard on account of Christ, just as he adds here explicitly: Whatever you ask the Father in my name, that is, by naming me, by proposing me to the Father as propitiator and intercessor, that is: Let your faith truly expect good things, and let it rely not on your own dignity, not on any other intercessors, but let it rely on me as propitiator, and indeed ask by name in this way: Eternal God, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on us, hear us, and help us on account of your Son our Lord Jesus Christ, whom you have appointed as propitiator, as I have often reviewed the form elsewhere. Fifthly, let the thing to be asked for be reviewed in prayer, because prayer asking for nothing, or not giving thanks for benefits, is cold tautology. I have run through these briefly, because they have been stated more copiously elsewhere. But why does he say in this place:

Latin:

Modicum et non videbitis me.

Antea de ministerio prolixe concionatus est, nunc inserit consolationem, qua significat se pas- surum esse, sed expresse affirmat se brevi ad eos rediturum esse. Quanquam autem saepe prae- dixerat eadem de sua passione, tamen ita fasci- nati fuerunt opinione de imperio Messiae politico, ut has conciones de passione non intellexerint. Ideo eum interpellant, et fatentur se nescire, quid dicat. Haec exempla monent primum deploran- dam esse caliginem, quod tunc in Ecclesia Dei intellectus promissionum de Christo adeo extin- ctus fuit, ut stulte tantum civile imperium somnia- rent. Fuisse aliquos recte sentientes necesse est, ut fuerunt Zacharias, Simeon, Ioseph, Baptista, Maria, Elizabeth, Anna, et alii multi. Semper enim aliqua Ecclesia manet recte sentiens, etiamsi exigua et dispersa est, et longe maior est multi- tudo multis tetris erroribus contaminata, quae gubernationem tenet. Cum autem illo tempore, et saepe alias magni errores publice a gubernato- ribus traditi sunt, et a maxima multitudine re- cepti, sciamus et hac postrema aetate potuisse, et posse errare pontifices, et maximam doctorum et populi partem, et non moveamur autoritate gradus, aut multitudinis, sed quaeramus verita- tem in verbo Dei, sicut eadem de re saepe con- cionantur Prophetae. Sed locus est dulcissimus Esaiae 8. ubi primum precatur Esaias, ut Deus servet puram doctrinam in aliquibus. Obsigna legem, inquit, in discipulis meis, id est, video horrendas tenebras, et doctrinae oblivionem se- cuturam esse, ut accidit cum alias; tum Phari- saeorum et Sadducaeorum tempore, et maximo in dolore et luctu sum propter Ecclesiam. Sed te Deus oro, ne sinas prorsus extingui veram do- ctrinam a te traditam, sed inclusam in mentes meorum discipulorum serves, ut incorruptam transmittant ad posteros. Significat autem do- ctrinam mansuram esse apud illos tantum, qui sunt discipuli Prophetarum, id est, qui hoc ver- bum traditum a Deo per Prophetas audiunt, am- plectuntur, et retinent. Hanc precationem Esaiae omnes saepe cogitemus, et ad eam vota nostra ad- iungamus, petamus, ut in nobis quoque legem suam obsignet, et confirmet mentes nostras, ut veritas in nobis luceat, et nostro ministerio ad posteros incorrupta perveniat. Sequitur autem descriptio eventus: Ecce, ego et pueri mei, quos dedit mihi Deus in portentum Israël. Hoc di- ctum promissio et consolatio est, quae affirmat aliquem fore coetum Ecclesiae ad posteros, sed exiguum et invisum potentibus. Deinde expresse additur praeceptum, ubi vera doctrina a Deo tra- dita, quaerenda sit, videlicet non in vulgari per- suasione principum et multitudinis, ut nunc cita- tur magna multitudo Monachorum, sed in verbo, quod Deus certis testimoniis per Prophetas tradi- dit, ad legem et ad testimonium, inquit: Id ver- bum qui non amplectentur, non erit eis matutina lux. Haec breviter recensui, ut tempora et mi- serias Ecclesiae consideremus, et discamus, ubi quaerenda sit veritas.

Secundo exemplum Apostolorum ostendit multos in Ecclesia esse infirmos, qui tamen sunt electi et a Deo tolerantur. Hac consolatione omnibus nobis opus est. Omnes enim et peccata aliqua, et errores nobiscum circumferimus. Sed qui retinent fundamentum fidei, et non perseve- rant in erroribus, aut delictis contra conscien- tiam, sed sunt dociles, et emendationem incoant, hi manent in gratia, sicut et dulcissime dictum est, ad Rom. 14.: Deus eum assumsit, ubi affir- mat Paulus etiam infirmum Deo placere.

Tertio monet haec concio Ecclesiam in hac vita subiectam esse cruci, ut alias saepe dicitur: Estque propria Ecclesiae haec doctrina ignota phi- losophiae, unde sint calamitates universi generis humani, cur Ecclesia durissime exerceatur, et quam habeat propositam veram et firmam conso- lationem. Haec alias dicta sunt, sed tamen sub- inde sunt repetenda. Cum quaeritur unde sint calamitates universi generis humani, philosophia dicit, eas partim a materia oriri, partim ab erro- ribus humanis et voluntate humana, ut mortis causam dicunt esse materiae naturam. Pompeium dicunt errore sibi calamitatem accersivisse, quia putabat defensionem Reipub. iustam esse, et ple- runque sciebat ordinariam potestatem esse victri- cem. Catilinam vero prava voluntas impulit in exitium, quia quanquam intelligeret periculum, tamen seditionem movit. Has causas philosophia recitat, quae etiamsi sunt propinquae, et concur- rentes causae, tamen aliae sunt priores et potiores. Causa mortis et omnium poenarum prima et prae- cipua est peccatum, quod nobiscum nascitur, or- tum a lapsu Adae, et tyrannis diaboli horribiliter infirmam naturam impellentis in scelera et in poenas.

Deinde vero in Ecclesia causae multae con- currunt, cum maneat peccatum in hac vita in san- ctis, manent mors et aliae calamitates, ut admo- niti de ira Dei, agnoscamus peccatum, et quae- ramus auxilium, item ut flammis vitiorum re- pressis, accendantur in nobis vera fides, invoca- tio, et aliae virtutes, ut in Psalm. dicitur: Bo- num mihi quod humiliasti me, ut discerem iusti- ficationes tuas. Sunt et aliae causae, quae in in- tegra explicatione huius loci alibi recensentur.

Postremo philosophia videt naturae interi- tum et alias calamitates, sed proponere consola- tionem firmam non potest, tantum monet, ne augeamus malorum sensum, quae vitari non pos- sunt, addita insuper maiore animi moestitia, ut Socrates cum effugere mortem non possit, sapien- ter facit, quod repugnat dolori, quasi vim eius aliquo modo frangens, exitum autem mali ac re- stitutionem vitae melioris non videt. Quare in magnis malis philosophica consolatio nihil iuvat mentes, et tota sapientia humana est cantus fune- bris, ut significatum est, Matth. 9.: Cum con- ducti sunt ad funus filiae Archisynagogi tibicines, qui funebres modos canunt.

At sola Christiana doctrina ostendit auxilium et praesentiam Dei in omnibus aerumnis, et in- super vitae aeternae restitutionem. Haec auxilii et liberationis ostensio est vera et efficax consola- tio. Ideo de ea cum saepe alias, tum hoc loco etiam Christus concionatur: Vos dolebitis, sed tristitia vertetur in gaudium. Haec non est vox philosophiae, aut ullius humanae sapientiae.

Imo ne legis quidem, sed solius Evangelii, et in hoc agone discrimina doctrinarum fiunt illustria, in veris doloribus cum undique quaerimus conso- lationes, et re ipsa experimur nos non iuvari hu- manis cogitationibus, tandem pia mens decurrens ad vocem Evangelii, tanquam ad fontem aquae vivae, incipit acquiescere, sicut in Psalmo dici- tur: Eloquium tuum vivificabit me.

Quicquid petetis, dabit vobis, etc.

Antea praedixit secuturas esse afflictiones, et addidit promissionem de liberatione. Nunc ad- iungit duo dicta, quae ad consolationem perti- nent, et sunt aditus ad liberationem, scilicet de vera noticia voluntatis Dei, et de precatione. Haec duo nisi luceant in afflictionibus, non pos- sunt mentes acquiescere, ut Cato, Brutus, et si- miles, quia ignorant voluntatem Dei, iudicant se negligi, aut abiici a Deo. Ita ruunt in aeternam desperationem, et in odium Dei. Ieremias vero etsi videt ruentem patriam, tamen scit non deseri Ecclesiam Dei. Hac noticia confirmatus perfert praesentes miserias, intelligit enim earum causas, et finem fore earum, et instaurationem Ecclesiae novit. Primum igitur dictum hoc loco de noticia voluntatis Dei loquitur. Illo die me non interro- gabitis quicquam, id est, post resurrectionem oculi vestri erunt testes me vivere. Eritis igitur confirmati, ut non dubitetis de mea vita. Deinde cum acceperitis Spiritum sanctum, intelligetis, quale sit meum regnum, quae sint causae afflictio- num Ecclesiae, et quomodo sim collecturus, ser- vaturus et liberaturus Ecclesiam. Discernetis iusticiam fidei, et politicam, abiicietis somnia pharisaica de civili imperio Messiae, denique scietis omnia necessaria ad salutem aeternam. Haec certa noticia Evangelii fons est praecipuarum consolationum.

Ad hanc noticiam accedat precatio. Est igi- tur repetita promissio, de qua supra aliquoties dictum est. Et diligenter observandum est, quod additum est iusiurandum: Amen amen dico vo- bis. Haec tanta asseveratio exuscitet nos, ut pro- missioni credamus, et ardentius petamus auxilium. Quoties autem haec promissio exponitur, repe- tenda sunt quinque praecepta precationis, de qui- bus supra dictum est: Primum quis Deus invo- cetur, segreganda est enim invocatio Ecclesiae ab Ethnica, Mahometica, et aliarum impiarum gen- tium invocatione. Secundo mandata cogitentur, quae iubent precari. Nam mens humana, prae- sertim saucia agnitione peccati sui, fugit Deum, nec audet bona petere. Huic trepidationi pri- mum mandata, deinde promissiones, et doctrina de fide opponantur. Tertio igitur promissiones intuemur, quae affirmant Deum vere velle bona aeterna et praesentia dare. Quarto accendatur fides, quae statuit nos propter Christum recipi et exaudiri, sicut hic diserte addit: Quicquid pe- tieritis patrem in nomine meo, id est, me nomi- nato, me proponentes patri, tanquam placato- rem et intercessorem, id est: Fides vestra vere expectet bona, et nitatur non vestra dignitate, non ullis aliis intercessoribus, sed nitatur me pro- piciatore, et quidem nominatim ita petite: Deus aeterne, pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, miserere nostri, exaudi, et iuva nos propter filium tuum Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, quem con- stituisti propiciatorem, ut saepe alibi formam re- censui. Quinto recenseatur in precatione res pe- tenda, quia precatio nihil petens, aut non agens gratias pro beneficiis, est frigida ταυτολογία. Haec breviter percurri, quia alibi copiosius dicta sunt. Sed cur dicit hoc loco:

## 16:23
Hitherto you have asked nothing in my name.

I answer, here a most serious matter is handed down, namely the distinction between carnal confidence and true faith, shining in a heart destitute of carnal supports. Hitherto, he says, you have trusted in my visible presence, just as the soldiers of David trusted in the presence of this their leader: Therefore you have asked for nothing in my name, that is, by faith truly invoking God on account of me as propitiator; but henceforth this light of true faith invoking on account of me as propitiator will be kindled in you. There is therefore an emphasis in this addition: In my name, that is, you have not asked with faith, which would look upon me as propitiator while I am absent, but you have trusted in a carnal manner in visible defense in this familiar association.

Latin:

Hactenus non petiistis quicquam in nomine meo.

Respondeo, hic tradi rem gravissimam, vi- delicet discrimen fiduciae carnalis, et verae fidei, lucentis in corde destituto carnalibus praesidiis. Hactenus inquit, estis confisi praesentia mea visi- bili, ut milites Davidis confidebant huius sui du- cis praesentia: Propterea nihil petiistis in meo nomine, id est, fide vera invocante Deum pro- pter me propiciatorem; sed deinceps accendetur in vobis haec lux verae fidei invocantis propter me propiciatorem. Est ergo emphasis in hac addi- tione: In nomine meo, id est, non petiistis fide, quae me absente propiciatorem intueretur, sed carnali more confisi estis visibili defensione in hac familiari consuetudine.

## 16:24
Ask and you shall receive, that your joy may be full.

He repeats the commandment concerning prayer, as often elsewhere, and adds a promise. Then, he says: Your joy will be perfect, that is, not hypocritical, not feigned, but true, lasting, eternal. Faith asking rests in the promise, and expects help and mitigation.

This very resting is a part of eternal joy. Then, when events show that evils are mitigated, the heart rejoices more, and determines that prayers are truly heard, that God is present and regards us. Thus eternal joy grows in the heart. Concerning this joy it is said to the Philippians 4: The peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, shall guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus, that is, the joy resting in God, which is kindled by faith, and is true consolation, by which the Holy Spirit sustains us in death itself, and provides life for us, and is placed above and outside of human judgments. David experiences this consolation in his exile: Pompey or Saul does not experience it.

Latin:

Petite et accipietis, ut gaudium vestrum sit plenum.

Repetit mandatum de precatione, ut saepe alias, et addit promissionem. Tunc inquit: Gaudium vestrum erit perfectum, id est, non hypocriticum, non simulatum, sed verum, man- surum, aeternum. Fides petens acquiescit in promissione, et expectat auxilium et mitigationem.

Hoc ipsum acquiescere est pars gaudii aeterni. Deinde cum eventus ostendunt mitigari mala, magis laetatur cor, et statuit preces vere exaudiri, Deum adesse et respicere nos. Ita crescit gau- dium aeternum in corde. De hoc gaudio dicitur ad Philip. 4.: Pax Dei superans omnem sensum, custodiat corda vestra, et cogitationes vestras in Christo Iesu, id est, laetitia acquiescens in Deo, quae accenditur fide, et est vera consolatio, qua Spiritus sanctus in ipsa morte nos sustentat, et vitam nobis praebet, et supra et extra iudicia humana posita est. David hanc consolationem in exilio suo experitur: Pompeius, aut Saul non experitur.

## 16:25
The hour comes, when I will no longer speak in parables.

Is it an antithesis? Hitherto he says that he has spoken obscure sentences, or proverbs, as the text says. Afterwards he says: I will not speak in proverbs, but I will announce openly concerning the Father. Is the previous discourse obscure, ambiguous, uncertain? I answer: Both this discourse which Christ has held until now, and the whole sum of the doctrine of the Gospel, has been handed down in certain and clear words. There is therefore no obscurity, as far as the discourse itself pertains, but there is obscurity, as far as the minds that are still duller and darkened pertain, just as the Sun is most luminous by itself, but the sharpness of our eyes is too weak to be able to gaze upon such brightness. Christ has discoursed concerning the ministry of the Gospel, concerning the remission of sins, concerning the efficacy of the Holy Spirit, concerning the beginning of eternal life, concerning the cross, concerning the faith by which souls are to be sustained, destitute of all human supports. These things are all clear to us now reading the discourse. But the Apostles had their minds occupied with the persuasion concerning an earthly empire, which greatly hindered the understanding of these discourses, but afterwards, the Holy Spirit having been given, those sweet dreams concerning an empire vanished. Therefore he says here: That afterwards he would speak plainly with them. But the following antithesis is more obscure.

Latin:

Venit hora, cum non amplius loquar in parabolis.

Antithesis est? Hactenus ait se obscuras sen- tentias, seu proverbia, ut textus inquit, locutum esse. Postea inquit: Non loquar proverbia, sed palam de patre annunciabo. An sermo superior est obscurus, ambiguus, incertus? Respondeo: Et haec concio quam hactenus habuit Christus, et tota summa doctrinae Evangelii certa et perspi- cuis verbis tradita est. Non est igitur obscuritas, quod ad ipsam concionem attinet, sed est obscu- ritas, quod ad ipsam concionem attinet, sed est obscuritas, quod ad mentes adhuc hebetiores et caligantes attinet, ut Sol per sese lucidissimus est, sed acies nostrorum oculorum infirmior est, quam ut fulgorem tantum contueri possit. Christus concionatus est de ministerio Evangelii, de remis- sione peccatorum, de efficacia Spiritus sancti, de incoatione vitae aeternae, de cruce, de fide, qua sustentandi sunt animi, destituti omnibus prae- sidiis humanis. Haec nobis iam legentibus con- cionem, omnia perspicua sunt. At Apostoli ha- bebant occupatas mentes persuasione de imperio mundano, quae valde impediebat intellectum ha- rum concionum, sed postea dato Spiritu sancto, evanuerunt illa dulcia somnia de imperio. Ideo hic dicit: Postea se plane cum eis locuturum esse. Sed sequens antithesis obscurior est.

## 16:26
In that day you will ask in my name.

The first member is clear: In that day you will ask in my name, that is: Hitherto indeed, relying on visible association, you have had carnal security, but henceforth you will ask with true faith, which looks upon me as absent as propitiator, you will wander over the whole world without protection, you will be an object of hatred not only to tyrants, but even to the wise. Could such wanderers gather a Church? Nay, he says: Your labor will not be in vain, and you will have a defense: For you will ask in my name, that is, in reliance upon me, wherefore the Father will certainly hear you, will save, defend, and help you.

But why does he add: I do not say to you that I will ask the Father for you, for the Father himself loves you. This statement must be softened by interpretation, because it is the chief and proper office of Christ to be a priest and to pray for us assiduously, as it is often written in Rom. 9: Who is at the right hand of the Father, and intercedes for us. The explanation, however, is easy for one who judges rightly and not captiously. Christ meets the immense weakness of men, who, especially when looking upon their sins in great sorrows, do not dare to approach God, do not dare to ask, or to expect help, or the mitigation of their miseries. This trepidation and flight Christ reproves, and draws us back, hesitating, to himself. Nay, he says: I will not pray alone, thus understood the exclusive is true, that is, I want you yourselves to approach the Father with me, I your priest will go before you, I will carry your prayers to the Father, but yet I also want you to pray, nor let the sight of your weakness deter you, for even if you are weak, yet the Father loves you with a true and fatherly love because of me, as my members.

Because you have loved me, etc.

He explains the reason why they are loved by the Father, because he says: You have loved me and believed that I was sent by the Father into this world. Here let these two points be observed, of which one has been very often repeated, that the elect are loved not because of their own dignity, but because they are joined to Christ by faith, as it is said in Ephes. 1: He loved us because of the beloved. Secondly, let us hold this statement, so that it may be opposed to temptations concerning election, in which we are tormented as to whether we are elect, and why men are chosen: let this be the one, simple, and brief answer, which may be an anchor for the imperiled soul in those waves of temptation: Because you have loved me and believed that I was sent by the Father. This voice draws us back to Christ and to the Gospel, and affirms that all are so loved, if they themselves embrace the Gospel with true faith, and call upon this God who has revealed himself in the Gospel and sent his Son. He does not want us to seek other causes of election outside the word of God, and with the Son omitted, but he has simply bound the Church to this one head, namely, to Christ. Here he is to be acknowledged, heard, and embraced by faith. If one repenting believes that he is received because of this mediator, and finally perseveres in this faith, he is without any doubt elect. As often, therefore, as we are tormented about election, having rejected other disputes which are taken from human reason or from the law, let us return to this statement: We are therefore elect and received because we believe in the Son. Let us hold this consolation, and oppose it to many other inextricable labyrinths, which do not heal fearful minds, but rather overturn them.

Latin:

In illa die petetis in nomine meo.

Prius membrum perspicuum est: In illa die in nomine meo petetis, id est: Hactenus quidem freti consuetudine visibili, carnalem securitatem habuistis, sed deinceps vera fide, quae me ab- sentem tanquam propiciatorem intuetur, petetis, vagabimini toto orbe terrarum sine praesidiis, eritis in odio non solum tyrannis, sed etiam sapientibus. Talesne errones possent Ecclesiam colligere? Imo inquit: Labor vester non erit inanis, et defensionem habebitis: Petetis enim in nomine meo, id est, fiducia mei, quare certo vos pater exaudiet, servabit, defendet et iuvabit.

Sed cur addit: Non dico vobis, quod ego rogaturus sim patrem pro vobis, ipse enim pater diligit vos. Hoc dictum necesse est leniri interpretatione, quia praecipuum et proprium Christi officium est, esse sacerdotem, et pro nobis assidue deprecari, sicut saepe scriptum est ad Rom. 9.: Qui est ad dextram patris, et intercedit pro nobis. Facilis est autem explicatio, dextre et non calumniose iudicanti. Occurrit Christus ingenti imbecillitati hominum, qui praesertim in magnis doloribus intuentes sua peccata, non audent ad Deum accedere, non audent petere, aut expectare auxilium, aut mitigationem miseriarum. Hanc trepidationem et fugam reprehendit Christus, et retrahit nos dubitantes ad sese. Imo inquit: Non solus orabo, sic intellecta exclusiva vera est, id est, volo vos ipsos mecum ad patrem accedere, ego vester sacerdos praeibo vobis, perferam vestra vota ad patrem, sed tamen et vos precari volo, nec deterreat vos conspectus imbecillitatis vestrae, etsi enim infirmi estis, tamen diligit vos pater vero et paterno amore propter me, ut membra mea.

Quia me dilexistis, etc.

Exponit causam, quare diligantur a patre, quia inquit: Me dilexistis et credidistis, quod ego a patre in hunc mundum missus sim. Hic hae duae sententiae observentur, quarum altera saepissime repetita est, diligi electos non propter propriam dignitatem, sed quia fide copulati sunt Christo, sicut ad Ephes. 1. dicitur: Dilexit nos propter dilectum. Secundo teneamus hoc dictum, ut tentationibus de electione opponatur, in quibus angimur, utrum simus electi, et cur eligantur homines: una, simplex et brevis responsio haec sit, quae in illis fluctibus tentationum ancora sit periclitantis animae: Quia me dilexistis et credidistis, quod a patre missus sim. Retrahit nos haec vox ad Christum et ad Evangelium, et affirmat ita diligi omnes, si ipsi amplectantur vera fide Evangelium, et hunc Deum invocent, qui se in Evangelio patefecit, et misit filium suum. Non vult nos alias causas electionis extra verbum Dei, et omisso filio, quaerere, sed simpliciter alligavit Ecclesiam ad hoc unum caput, scilicet, ad Christum. Hic agnoscendus, audiendus, et fide amplectendus est. Si agens poenitentiam, credit se propter hunc mediatorem recipi, et in hac fide tandem perseverat, sine ulla dubitatione electus est. Quoties igitur de electione angimur, reiectis aliis disputationibus, quae ex humana ratione, aut ex lege sumuntur, redeamus ad hoc dictum: Ideo sumus electi et recepti, quia credimus in filium. Hanc consolationem teneamus, et opponamus aliis multis inextricabilibus labyrinthis, qui pavidas mentes non sanant, sed potius evertunt.

## 16:33
In the world you will have tribulation.

At the end, as the disciples are questioning him, he predicts their trepidation, and again adds a general admonition concerning the cross, and consolation: In the world you will have affliction, these words refute the persuasion which was fixed in the minds of the Jewish people concerning the worldly kingdom of the Messiah: Lay aside, he says, the error, I will save you, I will gather, and I will preserve for myself a Church in this world, while kings rage, and empires are everywhere in turmoil, in which the ministers of the Gospel and the Church will feel great miseries. But do not be broken in spirit, do not think yourselves neglected or deserted by me. I promise you help and victory, because I have overcome the world, that is, I have come to destroy the works of the devil, I have abolished sin and death. I will give you the Holy Spirit, so that you may be able to endure punishments, and I will repress many of the furies of your enemies. Finally, I will adorn you with eternal life, joy, and glory in the fellowship of God. He repeated this chief consolation at the end, in which, having predicted miseries, he added two arguments which most greatly confirm the minds, he promises help, and he promises eternal liberation.

Latin:

In mundo pressuram habebitis.

In fine interpellantibus discipulis praedicit eorum trepidationem, et rursus addit generalem commonefactionem de cruce, et consolationem: In mundo afflictionem habebitis, haec verba refutant persuasionem, quae de regno mundano Messiae infixa erat Iudaici populi animis: Deponite, inquit, errorem, servabo vos, colligam, et servabo mihi Ecclesiam in hoc mundo, saevientibus regibus, et passim tumultuantibus imperiis, in quibus ministri Evangelii et Ecclesia magnas aerumnas sentient. Sed vos non frangamini animis, non putate vos a me neglectos aut desertos esse. Promitto vobis auxilium et victoriam, quia ego vici mundum, id est, ego veni, ut destruam opera diaboli, delevi peccatum et mortem. Dabo vobis Spiritum sanctum, ut perferre supplicia possitis, et multos furores hostium vestrorum reprimam. Denique ornabo vos aeterna vita, laetitia et gloria in consuetudine Dei. Hanc praecipuam consolationem in fine repetivit, in qua cum praedixisset aerumnas, addidit duo argumenta, quae maxime confirmant animos, pollicetur auxilium, et promittit liberationem aeternam.

## 17:1 Argument
Chapter XVII.

Latin:

Caput XVII.

## 17:1
Jesus spoke these things.

In the three preceding chapters he has preached to the Apostles about the ministry of the Gospel, about the sum of the doctrine of the Gospel, about the mission of the Holy Spirit, concerning his presence, concerning the effects of the Gospel, concerning the cross, concerning the consolations which must be opposed to the most atrocious terrors by which the world attempts to destroy the Gospel. Now an apostrophe is made to the eternal Father, and since it is the final part of this discourse, to the doctrine and exhortations recited above, there is now added a most grave and most sweet prayer to be learned by heart and often pondered with great intention of mind.

But first he prays for himself, afterwards for the whole Church, and concerning this he asks for four principal things for the Church: the preservation of true doctrine, the concord of the Church, the application of his sacrifice, and the last and highest good, that the Church may be adorned with Christ, with life, joy, and eternal glory.

Many profane people, when they read these discourses or prayers, think them to be, like those of a disturbed man, empty complaints. But the pious and attentive reader sees that doctrine concerning the greatest matters has been delivered beforehand, and here he recognizes that the principal gifts which are most necessary for the Church are being asked for. What else would the dying David ask for than that the purity of heavenly doctrine be preserved in this Church which he had ruled, and the concord of his posterity? Christ also asks for these sinews of a good state in this life, but he adds two things which it befits Christ himself, as priest and author of eternal life, to ask for, namely that this sacrifice of his be received for the universal Church, and that eternal life be given to the whole Church. This sum of the prayer must first be pondered briefly, then the members should be viewed in order.

But some ask why Christ asks for these things, since he says elsewhere that he himself will lay down his life and take it up again; why does he ask for what is in his own power? Furthermore, since he knows the outcome, why is he now distressed, as if in a doubtful matter? I touch upon these questions unwillingly. For they arise from idle and profane minds, but I will answer briefly. To the first: The times must be distinguished in the history of Christ. At this time of the passion, the divine nature in him rested, as Irenaeus says, and he himself truly sustained not only the natural fear of death and certain other sorrows, because he foresaw the destruction of the Jewish nation, and likewise because he saw a great part of the human race heaping up the wrath of God, having despised this so great a benefit, namely the sacrifice of the Son of God, but also another far greater and ineffable sorrow, because he truly felt the wrath of God against the sins of the human race, which was being poured out upon him, as if he himself had polluted himself with my sins, your sins, David's sins, and the sins of all the elect; he lay before God, feeling the wrath against sins.

Although these things are ineffable, yet they have been signified somewhat when it is said: Christ was made a curse. Likewise, God placed upon him the iniquities of us all, nor let us think these were feigned; they were true and immense sorrows which he sustained, as I said before, with the divine nature resting and obeying the eternal Father, and in this very sacrifice Christ is the high priest of the universal Church of the elect. The whole Church sustains immense sorrows, but the high priest Christ sustains greater ones, and he begins the prayer so that the rest of the Church may also call upon him and be heard. These things are described also in the Epistle to the Hebrews: We do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our infirmity, but one tempted in all things according to the likeness, without sin. As often, therefore, as we begin our prayers, let us think of this high priest, the Son of God, standing before the eternal Father, truly being affected by our sorrow, groaning with us, as a loving father groans with his children oppressed by a great calamity, and carrying our prayers to the eternal Father. These things certainly must be pondered while praying, etc.

To the second question the answer is easier; although Christ knows the outcome, yet at the same time he also knows his own infirmity, and the greater the wisdom is, the more he understands what a great thing the wrath of God is, and he knows it cannot be sustained without divine aid. Therefore he asks for both aid and liberation.

Latin:

Haec locutus est Iesus.

Tribus superioribus capitibus concionatus est ad Apostolos, de ministerio Evangelii, de summa doctrinae Evangelii, de missione Spiritus sancti, de sua praesentia, de effectibus Evangelii, de cruce, de consolationibus, quae opponendae sunt atrocissimis terroribus, quibus mundus delere Evangelium conatur. Nunc fit apostrophe ad aeternum patrem, et cum sit postrema pars huius concionis, doctrina et adhortationibus supra recitatis, nunc adiicitur gravissima et dulcissima precatio ediscenda, et saepe magna intentione animi cogitanda.

Primum autem de seipso precatur, postea de tota Ecclesia, et de hac petit quatuor res praecipuas Ecclesiae. Conservationem verae doctrinae, concordiam Ecclesiae, applicationem sui sacrificii, et ultimum ac summum bonum, ut Ecclesia cum Christo ornetur, vita, laetitia, et gloria aeterna.

Multi profani cum legunt has conciones aut precationes, putant esse, ut hominis perturbati, inanes querelas. Sed pius et attentus lector videt antea de maximis rebus doctrinam esse traditam, et hic agnoscit peti praecipua dona quae maxime necessaria sunt Ecclesiae. Quid David moriens aliud peteret, quam servari puritatem doctrinae coelestis in hac Ecclesia quam rexerat, et concordiam suae posteritatis. Hos nervos boni status in hac vita et Christus petit, sed duas res addit, quas proprie ipsum Christum sacerdotem et autorem vitae aeternae petere decet, videlicet ut hoc suum sacrificium pro universa Ecclesia recipiatur, et ut toti Ecclesiae detur vita aeterna. Haec summa precationis primum breviter cogitanda est, deinde membra ordine aspiciantur.

Quaerunt autem aliqui cur Christus haec petat, cum alibi dicat, seipsum depositurum esse animam suam, et rursus sumturum eam, cur petit, quod in sua potestate est? Deinde cum sciat eventum, cur nunc angitur, quasi in re dubia? Has quaestiones invitus attingo. Oriuntur enim ab otiosis et profanis mentibus, sed breviter respondebo. Ad primam: Tempora discernenda sunt in historia Christi. Hoc tempore passionis natura divina in eo quievit, ut loquitur Irenaeus, et ipse vere sustinuit non modo naturalem mortis metum, et alios quosdam dolores, quod praevidit gentis Iudaicae interitum, item quod vidit magnam partem generis humani cumulare iram Dei, contemto hoc tanto beneficio, scilicet sacrificio filii Dei, sed etiam alium longe maiorem et inenarrabilem dolorem, quod videlicet sensit iram Dei adversus peccata generis humani, quae in ipsum effundebatur, sic quasi ipse sese polluisset meis, tuis, Davidis, et omnium electorum pec- catis, iacuit coram Deo, sentiens iram adversus peccata.

Haec etiamsi sunt inenarrabilia, tamen si- gnificata sunt aliquantulum, cum dicitur: Chri- stun factum esse maledictum. Item, posuit Deus in eo iniquitates omnium nostrum, nec putemus haec fuisse simulata, veri et ingentes dolores fue- runt, quos sustinuit, ut antea dixi, quiescente divina natura, et obediente aeterno patri, et in hoc ipso sacrificio Christus sit pontifex Ecclesiae universae electorum. Tota Ecclesia sustinet in- gentes dolores, sed summus sacerdos Christus sus- tinet maiores, et incoat precationem, ut et reli- qua Ecclesia invocet et exaudiatur. Haec descri- pta sunt et in Epistola ad Ebraeos: Non habemus pontificem, qui non possit compati infirmitati nostrae, sed tentatum per omnia secundum simi- litudinem sine peccato. Quoties igitur nostras precationes incipimus, cogitemus hunc summum sacerdotem filium Dei, stantem coram aeterno pa- tre, vere affici nostro dolore, gemere nobiscum, ut pater φιλόστοργος gemit cum liberis magna ca- lamitate oppressis, et nostras preces perferre ad aeternum patrem. Haec certe inter precandum cogitanda sunt, etc.

Ad secundam quaestionem facilior est re- sponsio, etiamsi scit eventum Christus, tamen si- mul et infirmitatem suam novit, et quo maior est sapientia, eo magis intelligit, quanta res sit ira Dei, et novit eam sustineri sine divino auxilio non posse. Ideo et auxilium et liberationem petit.

## 17:1
With eyes lifted to heaven.

Beginning the prayer, he lifts his eyes to heaven. This very gesture signifies singular and immense movements of the breast and mind. Then follows the address: Father. This very word, a witness of mutual love between the Son and the Father, stirs up ardent affections in both. Afterwards follows the description of the danger: The hour has come, that is, now the greatest of all agonies is pressing, such as none of the fathers sustained, just as he cries out in the Psalm: In you our fathers hoped, they hoped and you delivered them. But I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people. Glorify your Son, that is, do not allow me to succumb in this agony, but help struggling, and deliver, and restore me to that glory which I had with you in the beginning, before the world was created, and as above in the invocation of the Father, so here in the invocation of the Son there is a reminder of mutual love. There follows the final cause, why he asks for help and deliverance, that your Son also may glorify you, that is: This agony was ordained by you for this purpose, that by this obedience of mine your justice might be satisfied, your most just wrath might be appeased, sin might be blotted out, and my inheritance, namely the Church, might be redeemed by my blood, to celebrate you forever. He recounts this final cause of glorification, that all that you have given him, he may give them eternal life.

Latin:

Sublatis oculis in coelum.

Incoans precationem, oculos in coelum tol- lit. Hic ipse gestus singulares et ingentes motus pectoris et animi significat. Deinde sequitur com- pellatio: Pater. Haec ipsa vox testis mutui amo- ris inter filium et patrem, ciet in utroque arden- tes affectus. Postea sequitur descriptio periculi: Venit hora, id est, iam instat agon omnium ma- ximus, qualem nemo patrum sustinuit, sicut in Psalmo clamitat: In te speraverunt patres nostri, speraverunt et liberasti eos. Ego autem sum ver- mis et non homo, opprobrium hominum et ab- iectio plebis. Glorifica filium tuum, id est, non sinas me succumbere in hoc agone, sed adiuva luctantem, et libera, ac me in eam gloriam resti- tue, quam apud te initio habui, antequam mun- dus conderetur, et ut supra in appellatione Patris, ita hic in appellatione Filii commonefactio est mu- tui amoris. Sequitur causa finalis, cur petat au- xilium et liberationem, ut et Filius tuus te glori- ficet, id est: Hic agon ideo a te ordinatus est, ut hac mea obedientia satisfiat iusticiae tuae, ira iu- stissima fiat placata, deleatur peccatum, et tibi haereditas mea, videlicet Ecclesia meo sanguine redimatur, celebratura te in aeternum. Hanc causam finalem glorificationis recenset, ut omne quod dedisti ei, det eis vitam aeternam.

## 17:2
And this is eternal life.

This saying is among the most important of the entire evangelical narrative, containing the sum of the Gospel, which is to be so fixed in the mind that it is thought upon very often, and opposed to the law, philosophy, ethnic wisdom, Jewish and Mahometan furies, and all human opinions about the blessed life, and the forms of worship which men have devised outside the Gospel. But first, a wonderful definition of eternal life is recited here, calling it the knowledge of the true God and of Christ; that it may be understood of the future life, and of the beginning of eternal life in this present life; concerning the future, it is most customary to say that it is the sight of God, or the vision of God, and it is rightly said so. For when the human mind shall behold God favoring it face to face, an ineffable joy will be kindled, as Augustine learnedly said of the blessed: They will rejoice as much as they will love, they will love as much as they will know. But they will behold God showing himself with immense mercy, and revealing his wisdom, and filling us with light, wisdom, justice, life, and eternal joy.

But the saying of Christ in this place does not speak only of the future life, although the sight in the future life is unlike the sight in this life. Then, as it is said in 1 John 3: We shall see him as he is: now, resting by faith in the word, we behold him, that is, we think of that God by faith who sent his Son our Lord Jesus Christ, born of the Virgin Mary, crucified and resurrected, and through him delivered to us the promise of the Gospel; let the mind, thinking of God who sends, behold this crucified and resurrected one, just as he himself binds us to himself. John 14: He who sees me, sees the Father. There is, therefore, a beginning of eternal life in this life, by faith to acknowledge this eternal God, who sent his Son Jesus Christ, to be appeased through the Son, and to call upon him, to seek and to expect consolation in all tribulations. This consolation in true anguish is a foretaste of eternal life, of which it is spoken here, and of which Paul says in Romans 8: You have received the spirit of adoption of sons, by which we cry Abba Father, and 2 Corinthians 3: The Spirit gives life, that is, consoles terrified minds, and kindles in them a new life, light, that is, wisdom and justice. These things happen by faith, when hearts acknowledge the mercy and help of God, and rest in God by faith on account of the mediator.

To this pertain many sayings, which all preach about this one and the same thing, as Matthew 11: Come to me all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. John 7: If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. He who believes in me, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly. John 8: If anyone keeps my word, he shall not taste death. Let all these sayings, and similar ones, be in view, and let them teach our minds that by faith we truly receive the remission of sins, and are reconciled to God, and that by faith eternal life is begun in us, that is, that light and new justice are kindled, as has been said. This sentence teaches the same: This is eternal life, that they may know you the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.

Furthermore, it is discussed here concerning the syntax of the words; it seems to be very simple. This is eternal life, that they may know you to be the only true God, and that they may know Jesus to be the Christ. For customarily in the scriptures, Christ is a name of office, just as if he were saying that Jesus is the mediator. For he wishes to inculcate the sentence often repeated: No one comes to the Father except through the Son; one wanders from the true God unless this God is invoked, who is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and God does not hear unless we approach with confidence in the mediator Jesus Christ. This syntax illustrates this principal doctrine of the Gospel, which teaches who is the true God, and what is his will, and how he wishes to be invoked and to hear. Nor does it follow on that account that the Son is not God, because he says: You only, for this particle does not exclude the Son or the Holy Spirit, but the fictitious deities of all nations, and just as elsewhere when Christ says: The Father is greater than I, no distinction is proposed between the persons according to divinity, but according to the present calling or mission of Christ. Thus here is recited the distinction between the humility of Christ, the mediator, serving in this mission, and the whole divinity reigning in secret majesty.

There is an entirely similar form, Matt. 19: Why do you call me good? No one is good except one, God. Here also a distinction is proposed between Christ the minister and the invisible majesty. These are very simple: but because the Arians were corrupting this saying, and twisting it to confirm their own frenzies, another syntax was handed down by those who were refuting the Arians: This is eternal life, that they may know you, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent, to be the only true God. Here, however, the question concerning the Holy Spirit remains, therefore I do not strongly advocate this syntax, as if someone wishes to use it, yet it will be necessary to include the Holy Spirit also. And soon follow illustrious testimonies concerning the divinity of the Son.

I have glorified you on earth, and now glorify me.

He repeats the prayer he has begun, Glorify me, and alleges the cause, namely, the very counsel of God or the divine ordination. Thus you ordained these highest matters, and the greatest of all, you willed to reveal yourself by sending the Son, you willed the human race to be redeemed, you willed me to become the victim and the propitiator. Behold, I have obeyed, and I obey; now in turn, according to your ordination, glorify me, help me, that I may not succumb in this agony, and restore to me the eternal glory which I had with you before the world was created. This saying speaks expressly concerning the divinity of the Son of God, for if he was before the foundation of the world, he is not a creature. Let students therefore remember this saying, and count it among the testimonies concerning the divinity of the Son. He then proceeds to explain by what things he has glorified the Father, namely, because he has delivered to the Apostles the Gospel brought forth from the secret bosom of the Father, has instituted the ministry of the Gospel, and has added wondrous testimonies, the raising of the dead, and other things which convince all creatures, so that they are forced to confess that this doctrine delivered by this preacher, Jesus, is true. These words, therefore, placed in this passage, show the dignity of the ministry of the Gospel, when Christ says that God is glorified by the preaching of the Gospel.

I pray for them.

He soon attaches a prayer for the Apostles and for the whole Church, which prayer he will later repeat and increase. Now let this sad distinction be briefly considered: I do not pray for the world; he calls the world all those who stubbornly oppose the Gospel; concerning these he also says in the Psalm: I will not take their names upon my lips. What greater misery can happen to any creature than to be excluded from the prayer of Christ, to be cursed by God, and to be subject to the eternal wrath of God? These greatest evils are signified by this exclusion.

Then is added the praise of the Church, which is the sweetest consolation of all who embrace and profess the Gospel, for thus he says: I have been glorified in them, that is, who embrace my word and carry it around among all men.
