I ask that these guardians of my word be kept by you; I affirm that these are yours. By this consolation let the Church and pious teachers confirm themselves, and hope for defense from God, even if tyrants everywhere in the whole world try to destroy the Gospel; let us know that we are defended not by ourselves, not by the kings of the world, but by God. They are yours, says Christ, namely those in whom I have been glorified, that is, who embrace my Gospel and faithfully scatter it among the peoples. Let this last particle be diligently looked at, so that we may know of whom the promise speaks. And let not disputes about election be inserted here, but let us know it is expressly said concerning those who glorify Christ, that is, concerning the Churches embracing and sounding forth the Gospel.

He also signifies their dangers by a single very brief appellation, when he says: They are in the world, that is, they will live in this confusion of men, in which there are very many impious and cruel ones, such as tyrants, many fanatics, heretics, many fickle and perfidious ones, who all are instruments of the devil incited to destroy the knowledge of God and to dissipate the Church. Then in the Church itself there are great and deplorable infirmities; therefore, there are dangers on all sides for pious governors, which cannot all be ruled by human wisdom, just as the Prophet says: I know, O Lord, that the way of man is not in himself, nor is it in man to direct his steps. Therefore, here too Christ prays for us, that we may be preserved in this great variety of dangers, and often elsewhere help is promised, as in Isaiah 46: I will carry the aging Church, I have made, I will carry, and I will save it.

Latin:

Haec autem est vita aeterna.

Hoc dictum inter praecipua est universae evangelicae narrationis, complectens summam Evangelii, quod ita est affigendum animo, ut saepissime cogitetur, et opponendum legi, phi- losophiae, ethnicae sapientiae, Iudaicis et Ma- hometicis furoribus, et omnibus humanis opinio- nibus de vita beata, et cultibus, quos excogita- runt homines extra Evangelium. Primum autem hic miranda definitio vitae aeternae recitatur, vo- cat agnitionem veri Dei et Christi; quod intelli- gatur de vita futura, et de incoatione vitae aeter- nae in hac praesenti vita, de futura usitatissimum est dici eam esse conspectum Dei, seu visionem Dei, et recte ita dicitur. Cum enim mens humana Deum faventem coram aspiciet, accendetur in- enarrabilis laeticia, ut erudite dixit Augustinus de beatis: Tantum gaudebunt, quantum amabunt, tantum amabunt, quantum cognoscent. Intue- buntur autem Deum ostendentem se immensa mi- sericordia, et patefacientem sapientiam suam, et luce, sapientia, iusticia, vita, et laetitia aeterna nos implentem.

Sed dictum Christi hoc loco non tantum de futura vita loquitur, etsi conspectus in futura vita dissimilis est conspectui in hac vita. Tunc, ut 1. Ioannis 3. dicitur: Aspiciemus eum, qualis est: nunc fide acquiescentes in verbo eum intuemur, id est, cogitamus illum Deum fide, qui misit filium suum Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, natum ex Maria virgine, crucifixum et resusci- tatum, et per eum promissionem Evangelii nobis tradidit, in hunc crucifixum et resuscitatum in- tueatur mens de Deo mittente cogitans, sicut ipse nos ad sese alligat. Ioannis 14.: Qui me videt, videt patrem. Est ergo incoatio vitae aeternae in hac vita, fide hunc aeternum Deum, qui misit filium Iesum Christum, agnoscere placatum esse per filium, et eum invocare, petere et expectare consolationem in omnibus aerumnis. Haec con- solatio in veris angoribus est gustus vitae aeter- nae, de quo hic dicitur, et de quo Paulus, Ro- man. octavo: Accepistis spiritum adoptionis filio- rum, quo clamamus Abba pater, et 2. Corinth. 3.: Spiritus vivificat, id est, consolatur perterrefactas mentes, et accendit in eis novam vitam, lucem, id est, sapientiam et iusticiam. Haec fiunt fide, cum corda agnoscunt Dei misericordiam et auxi- lium, et in Deo fide propter mediatorem acquie- scunt.

Huc pertinent multa dicta, quae omnia de hac una et eadem re concionantur, ut Matth. 11.: Venite ad me omnes qui laboratis et onerati estis, et ego reficiam vos. Ioann. 7.: Si quis sitit, ve- niat ad me et bibat. Qui credit in me, flumina aquae vivae fluent de ventre eius. Ioann. 8.: Si quis sermonem meum servat, non gustabit mor- tem. Haec dicta omnia, et similia sint in con- spectu, et doceant mentes nostras fide nos vere accipere remissionem peccatorum, et reconciliari Deo, et fide incoari in nobis vitam aeternam, id est, accendi lucem et iusticiam novam, ut dictum est. Idem docet haec sententia: Haec est vita aeterna, ut agnoscant te solum verum Deum, et quem misisti Iesum Christum.

Caeterum de verborum syntaxi hic disseritur, simplicissima esse videtur. Haec est vita aeterna, ut agnoscant te solum esse verum Deum, et agno- scant Iesum esse Christum. Nam usitate in scri- pturis Christus est officii nomen, perinde ac si diceret Iesum esse mediatorem. Vult enim in- culcare sententiam saepe repetitam: Nemo venit ad patrem, nisi per filium, deerratur a vero Deo, nisi hic Deus invocetur, qui est pater Domini no- stri Iesu Christi, et non exaudit Deus, nisi acce- damus fiducia mediatoris Iesu Christi. Hanc principalem Evangelii doctrinam, quae tradit quis sit verus Deus, et quae sit eius voluntas, quo- modo velit invocari et exaudire, illustrat haec syntaxis. Nec propterea sequitur filium non esse Deum, quia dicit: Te solum, nam haec particula non excludit filium aut Spiritum sanctum, sed numina commentitia omnium gentium, et sicut alibi cum Christus inquit: Pater maior me est, non proponitur discrimen inter personas secun- dum divinitatem, sed secundum praesentem vo- cationem seu missionem Christi. Ita hic recitatur discrimen Christi humilitati, mediatoris, servien- tis in hac missione, et totius divinitatis regnantis in arcana maiestate.

Similis omnino forma est, Matth. 19.: Quid me vocas bonum, nemo bonus est nisi unus Deus. Hic quoque discrimen proponitur inter Christum ministrum, et invisibilem maiestatem. Haec sunt simplicissima: sed quia Ariani hoc dictum cor- rumpebant, et ad suos furores confirmandos de- torquebant, alia syntaxis ab iis, qui Arianos re- futabant, tradita est: Haec est vita aeterna, ut agnoscant te, et quem misisti Iesum Christum, esse solum verum Deum. Hic tamen quaestio de Spiritu sancto reliqua est, ideo hanc syntaxin non valde propugno, quasi quis volet uti, tamen Spiritum sanctum etiam complecti oportebit. Ac mox sequuntur testimonia de filii divinitate illu- stria.

Ego glorificavi te super terram, et nunc glorifica me.

Repetit institutam precationem, Glorifica me, et allegat causam, scilicet, ipsum consilium Dei seu ordinationem divinam. Sic ordinasti has res summas, et omnium maximas, voluisti te pate- facere misso filio, voluisti redimi genus huma- num, voluisti me fieri victimam et placatorem. Ecce obedivi, et obedio, nunc vicissim iuxta tuam ordinationem me glorificato, adiuva me, ne succumbam in hoc agone, et restitue mihi glo- riam aeternam, quam apud te habui, antequam mundus conderetur. Hoc dictum expresse de filii Dei divinitate concionatur, nam si fuit ante mundi conditionem, non est creatura. Memine- rint igitur studiosi hoc dictum, et inter testimo- nia de divinitate filii recenseant. Pergit deinde explicare, quibus rebus glorificaverit patrem, sci- licet, quia Evangelium ex arcano sinu patris pro- latum tradiderit Apostolis, instituerit ministe- rium Evangelii, et addiderit testimonia miranda, resuscitationes mortuorum, et alia quae convin- cunt omnes creaturas, ut fateri cogantur hanc doctrinam ab hoc concionatore Iesu traditam, ve- ram esse. Haec igitur verba hoc loco posita, ostendunt dignitatem ministerii Evangelii, cum ait Christus, glorificari Deum praedicatione Evan- gelii.

Ego pro ipsis rogo.

Attexit mox precationem pro Apostolis et pro tota Ecclesia, quam precationem postea repetet et augebit. Nunc breviter hoc triste discrimen consideretur: Non pro mundo oro, vocat mundum omnes, qui pertinaciter Evangelio adversantur, de his et in Psalmo inquit: Non assumam nomina eorum super labia mea. Quae maior miseria ulli creaturae accidere potest, quam exclusam esse a deprecatione Christi, maledictam a Deo, et aeternae irae Dei subiectam esse? Haec summa mala significantur hac exclusione.

Deinde additur laudatio Ecclesiae, quae est dulcissima consolatio omnium amplectentium et profitentium Evangelium, sic enim ait: Ego glorificatus sum in eis, id est, qui meum sermonem amplectuntur et circumferunt apud omnes homines. Hos mei sermonis custodes a te servari peto, hos esse tuos affirmo. Hac se consolatione Ecclesiae, et doctores pii confirment, et sperent defensionem a Deo, etiamsi tyranni passim in toto orbe terrarum delere Evangelium conantur, sciamus nos non a nobis, non a regibus mundi, sed a Deo defendi. Tui sunt, inquit Christus, illi scilicet, in quibus glorificatus sum, id est, qui meum Evangelium amplectuntur, et fideliter spargunt in populos. Haec postrema particula diligenter aspiciatur, ut sciamus, de quibus loquatur promissio. Nec inserantur huc disputationes de electione, sed sciamus diserte dici de glorificantibus Christum, id est, de Ecclesiis amplectentibus, et sonantibus Evangelium.

Pericula etiam eorum unica brevissima appellatione significat, cum ait: Illi in mundo sunt, id est, vivent in hac confusione hominum, in qua plurimi sunt impii et crudeles, ut tyranni, multi fanatici, haeretici, multi leves, et perfidiosi, qui omnes sunt organa diaboli incitata, ut noticiam Dei deleant, et Ecclesiam dissipent. Deinde in ipsa Ecclesia magnae, et deplorandae infirmitates sunt, undique igitur pericula sunt piis gubernatoribus, quae regi non possunt omnia sapientia humana, sicut dicit Propheta: Scio Domine, non est hominis via eius, nec viri est dirigere gressus suos. Ideo et hic Christus pro nobis precatur, ut in hac tanta varietate periculorum servemur, et saepe alias promittitur auxilium, ut Esaiae 46.: Ego senescentem Ecclesiam gestabo, ego feci, ego portabo, et salvabo eam.

## 17:11
Holy Father, keep them in your name.

I said above that there are three principal parts of the prayer, which speak of the highest matters, which are the nerves constituting and preserving the Church. The first is that the truth, that is, the light of the Gospel, may not be extinguished. The second, that concord may remain among the teachers. The third is the application of the sacrifice, that God, on account of this sacrifice of Christ, may remit sins for all, and give eternal life to those who flee to Christ by faith. Let us diligently consider these three parts, and let us not seek idle speculations, but let us look upon the very life of men, and let us attend to what are the highest goods and the highest evils. Solomon, about to die, if he is anxious about the Republic, certainly asks for these things especially, that the light of doctrine and the Church of God may remain. Then that the sons who are to succeed, and other governors, may be in concord.

And the first petition is always about doctrine, the next about concord, as in the Lord's Prayer we ask at the beginning: Hallowed be thy name, that is, may the true knowledge of God shine and be preserved, so here he says: Holy Father, keep them in your name, that is, on account of your name, or the acknowledgment of you, so that the knowledge of you, your doctrine, the invocation of you may remain, this is, first of all I ask that your doctrine may not be extinguished, but that there may always be a Church, that there may always be teachers who rightly teach the Gospel, so that the true God may be acknowledged and invoked. May this always be the highest care in the hearts of all, may this be the first petition, that the light of true doctrine may not be extinguished, as the Psalms so often cry out. Psalm 115: Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory, for your mercy and your truth, lest the nations say: Where is their God? This petition is afterwards repeated several times, as happens, with an ardent movement of the soul.

But immediately another is inserted concerning concord. No one is ignorant that in every government concord is a necessary thing, but there is the greatest need in the Church for the consensus of doctrine, and for the true mutual benevolence of the teachers themselves. For when the consensus of doctrine is disturbed, one departs from the one true opinion, and infinite errors are feigned. But often the consensus of doctrine is disturbed on account of private discords, as Arius, out of hatred for Alexander the Bishop, spread blasphemies against the Son of God. Since, therefore, the concord of those who rightly teach is most necessary for the Church, this petition is also repeated several times. And below it is expressly said: That they may be one in us.

He does not ask only this, that they may be in concord, just as often in the government of the Republic two great men have been in concord, such as Augustus and Agrippa, Epaminondas and Pelopidas, but he says by name: That they may be one in us, that is, first let the minds of Peter and John be joined to God, let them be bound to the one true God, and let them embrace one doctrine. Then, joined through one God and one doctrine, let them agree among themselves. These things were said very significantly by Christ, for concord does not remain for very long unless they tend toward one end with a similar will. For when teachers begin to ζυγομαχεῖν, and one seeks one end, another seeks the favor of other kings, and their wills are not similar, but they dare to depart from the delivered Gospel, and some feign one opinion and others another, as it is evident that concord is disturbed in many ways. Foreseeing these great evils, Christ prays so ardently, and frequently repeats the same petition.

Latin:

Pater sancte, serva eos in nomine tuo.

Dixi supra precationis tria esse membra praecipua, quae de rebus summis loquuntur, quae sunt nervi constituentes et servantes Eccle- siam. Primum est, ut veritas, id est, lux Evan- gelii non extinguatur. Secundum, ut maneat in- ter doctores concordia. Tertium est applicatio sacrificii, ut Deus propter hoc Christi sacrificium omnibus remittat peccata, et det vitam aeternam fide confugientibus ad Christum. Haec tria mem- bra diligenter consideremus, et non quaeramus otiosas speculationes, sed ipsam vitam hominum intueamur, et quae sint summa bona, et summa mala attendamus. Salomon moriturus, si angi- tur de Repub. certe haec praecipue petit, ut lux doctrinae et Ecclesia Dei maneat. Deinde ut filii successuri, et alii gubernatores sint concordes.

Ac semper prima petitio est de doctrina, proxima de concordia, ut in oratione dominica initio petimus: Sanctificetur nomen tuum, id est, vera noticia Dei luceat et servetur, ita hic ait: Pater sancte, serva eos in nomine tuo, id est, propter nomen tuum, seu agnitionem tui, ut no- ticia tui, doctrina tua, invocatio tui maneat, hoc est, primum omnium peto, ut doctrina tua non extinguatur, sed semper sit Ecclesia, semper sint doctores, qui recte doceant Evangelium, ut agno- scatur et invocetur verus Deus. Haec in omnium pectoribus semper sit summa cura, haec sit prima petitio, ne extinguatur lux verae doctrinae, ut Psalmi toties clamant. Psalm. 115.: Non nobis Domine, non nobis, sed nomini tuo da gloriam, propter misericordiam tuam, et veritatem tuam, ne quando dicant gentes: Ubi est Deus eorum? Haec petitio postea aliquoties, ut fit, ardente motu animi repetitur.

Statim autem inseritur altera de concordia. Nemo ignorat in omni gubernatione rem necessa- riam esse concordiam, sed multo maxime opus est Ecclesiae consensu doctrinae, et ipsorum do- centium mutua inter se vera benevolentia. Nam doctrinae consensu turbato, disceditur ab una vera sententia, et finguntur infiniti errores. Saepe autem doctrinae consensus propter privatas dis- cordias turbatur, ut Arius odio Alexandri Epi- scopi sparsit blasphemias contra filium Dei. Cum igitur maxime necessaria sit Ecclesiae concordia recte docentium, aliquoties et haec petitio inge- minatur. Et infra diserte dicitur: In nobis unum sint.

Non hoc petit tantum, ut sint concordes, sicut saepe in gubernatione Reipub. duo magni viri concordes fuerunt, ut Augustus et Agrippa, Epaminondas et Pelopidas, sed nominatim dicit: In nobis unum sint, id est, prius mentes Petri et Ioannis sint copulatae Deo, uni vero Deo sint al- ligatae, et unam doctrinam amplectantur. Deinde copulatae per unum Deum et unam doctrinam inter sese congruant. Haec valde significanter a Christo dicta sunt, nam nec manet plurimum concordia, nisi ad unum finem simili voluntate tendant. Cum enim incipiunt doctores ζυγομα- χεῖν, et alius alium finem expetit, alius quaerit aliorum regum, favorem, nec voluntates sunt si- miles, sed audent discedere ab Evangelio tradito, et fingunt alii alias opiniones, ut constat multis modis concordiam turbari. Haec magna mala prospiciens Christus, tam ardenter orat, et ean- dem petitionem crebro ingeminat.

## 17:13
That they may have my joy fulfilled.

These things, he says, I pray, that they may know that they have full consolation, that is, true, not failing the hearts in the greatest dangers, that is, let them know that you will be present for them, and will certainly gather and preserve the Church, even with all empires resisting, and that our labors will not be in vain. But above it was declared what he calls perfect or full joy, namely, true and firm consolation, unlike human consolations. The matter will be better understood from the antithesis: Saul sustains himself with human consolations, he sees that he still excels in strength, and is in possession of the kingdom, and has a son who is well-deserving. He reasons, therefore, that David can easily be excluded. But human consolations finally fail him. But David, driven into exile and deprived of all human supports, retains this firm consolation, he knows that he has the remission of sins, he knows that he has a propitious God, and he rests in him, he knows that he will not perish. This consolation in great mourning is nevertheless called full, because it is firm. Let it be understood, therefore, as full or perfect not in quantity, but in firmness.

I will add, for the sake of declaring the antithesis, a verse of Virgil from the sixth Aeneid: For you know how we spent the last night among false joys. This verse contains an image of the whole life of the ungodly, and of all the comforts which they seek. The whole life is a night full of darkness, in ignorance of the true God and of the permanent goods; they seek false joys, that is, those which cannot refresh the soul in the midst of great and true sorrows. When Pompey was defeated, no pleasures or hopes of aid soothe his grief, and if he has any hopes, they quickly vanish. But on the contrary, when the city of Jerusalem was surrounded by a huge army by Sennacherib, who had previously conquered and scattered the ten tribes, yet Hezekiah retains firm consolation; he knows that God will be present to His Church, he rests in this consolation, therefore he does not have false and fleeting joys. To the pious who understand the exercises of faith and invocation, this antithesis is not obscure.

Latin:

Ut habeant gaudium meum plenum.'

Haec inquit precor, ut sciant se consolatio- nem plenam, id est, veram, non destituentem corda in maximis periculis habere, id est, sciant te sibi affuturum esse, et certo collecturum et ser- vaturum esse Ecclesiam, etiam repugnantibus omnibus imperiis, nec labores nostros inanes fore. Supra autem declaratum est, quid vocet perfectum seu plenum gaudium, videlicet veram et firmam consolationem, dissimilem humanis consolationibus. Ex antithesi res melius intel- ligetur: Saul humanis consolationibus se susten- tat, videt adhuc se viribus antecellere, et esse in possessione regni, et habere filium bene meritum. Ratiocinatur igitur Davidem facile excludi posse. Sed humanae consolationes tandem eum desti- tuunt. Ad David pulsus in exilium, ac destitutus omnibus humanis praesidiis, retinet hanc firmam consolationem, scit se habere remissionem pecca- torum, scit se habere Deum propicium, ac in eo acquiescit, scit se non periturum esse. Haec con- solatio in luctu ingenti, tamen dicitur plena, quia est firma. Intelligatur ergo plena seu perfecta non quantitate, sed firmitate.

Addam declarandae antithesis causa versicu- lum Virgilii sexto Aeneid.: Namque ut supre- mam falsa inter gaudia noctem, egerimus, nosti. Hic versiculus imaginem continet totius vitae im- piorum, et omnium solatiorum, quae expetunt. Tota vita nox est plena tenebrarum, in ignora- tione veri Dei, et permanentium bonorum, quae- runt aptem falsa gaudia, id est, quae in magnis et veris doloribus non possunt recreare animos. Pompeio victo non leniunt dolorem ullae volupta- tes, aut ullae spes auxiliorum, et si quas habet spes, cito evanescunt. At econtra cum urbs Ie- rosolyma ab ingenti exercitu circumdata est a Sennaherib, qui antea decem tribus vicerat et dissipaverat, tamen Ezechias retinet firmam con- solationem, scit Deum affuturum esse Ecclesiae suae, in hac consolatione acquiescit, non igitur habet falsa et fugacia gaudia. Piis qui fidei exer- citia et invocationem intelligunt, haec antithesis non est obscura.

## 17:15
I do not ask that you take them out of the world.

This saying also testifies that God wills that at all times in this mortal life, in which there is a sad confusion of men and empires, there should always be some true Church pleasing to God. Let us therefore take two consolations from this petition: The first, that since it is certain that the Church of God will remain, we should always know that God is effective through the Gospel, that God is present with us, and that the promises are always valid and are being fulfilled, and that those who believe the Gospel are members of the Church of God and heirs of eternal life, and that the ministry of the Gospel is always effective, just as Christ promises: Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.

The second consolation is that defense is promised against all kinds of furies by which the Church is attacked. If God had soon taken the Apostles out of this life and adorned them with eternal glory, that would indeed be an admirable liberation, but this is much more wonderful, that He preserves the Church at all times as if standing in the Red Sea between waves and enemies; empires are for the most part hostile to the Gospel, and often rage with immense cruelty against all the members of the Church. Furthermore, the greatest part of men despise and hate the true doctrine about God; the devil inflames many, even in the very assembly of the Church, to sow disturbances of dogmas, or to contend with ambitions and other desires. Hence arise huge struggles, and the prudent see that the Church is at all times involved in such dangers, as if it were standing constantly between heaps of water in the Red Sea, nor can those dangers be ruled by any human wisdom, nor can any human strength sustain them. But let the pious sustain themselves with this consolation, that they know we are helped and defended by God, just as is requested here: Keep them from the evil one.

Thus also Isaiah says concerning the journey of Moses through the Red Sea: Who led Moses by his right hand, with his glorious arm. Likewise: The Spirit of the Lord was his guide, etc. In this way it is certain that the Church is always led through huge dangers, as if through waves, by God Himself, and by this faith and invocation of God such great things, which far exceed our strength, must be sustained. Often, therefore, thinking about our dangers, let us remember this prayer of the Son of God, which was both recited and heard at that time, and is constantly repeated before the eternal Father. For the Son of God remains a constant intercessor, and His intercession is not in vain, but He constantly obtains for us help, defense, and liberation. To the thought of this prayer let us add the promises, as in Isaiah 46: I will carry you even in old age, I have made, I will bear, I will save.

Sanctify them in your truth; your word is truth.

He repeats more expressly the prayer concerning the truth of doctrine, that God may preserve the Gospel, and the true and pure sense of the Gospel in the Apostles, and subsequently in the ministry, just as Isaiah also prays in chapter 8: Seal the law among my disciples, that is, I see that the saddest darkness is going to follow among the people of God, and that many are going to reject the doctrine concerning the Messiah, concerning faith, concerning true invocation, concerning true worship, and will receive ethnic opinions concerning the worldly empire of the Messiah, concerning the heaping up of sacrifices. But I pray to you, O God, preserve the word which you have handed down to the Prophets in the minds of those who hear, learn, and embrace the prophetic doctrine, and indeed preserve it sealed, lest they pour it out, either the word itself or its native sense, just as the Sadducees did not even receive the letter of the Prophets. The Pharisees wanted to seem to retain the letter, but they attached false interpretations, as is still customary among Jews and heretics.

However, it must be diligently observed that He asks by name for the doctrine to be preserved in the disciples, that is, in those who are learning. He therefore requires study and knowledge of the letter; He wants us to be hearers of the Prophets. In that assembly of those learning and embracing the prophetic writings, there will be some retaining the light of doctrine and the native meaning, not among the Sadducees or others, who neither read nor learn the Prophets. Wherefore let us love study, let us listen to pious and expert interpreters, let us compare the testimonies of doctrine, let us ask for our minds to be ruled and kindled by the Holy Spirit. These are the duties of disciples, and this study is happy, and shows the truth, as it is written in Proverbs 2: If you will incline your heart to wisdom, you will find it. Now weigh the words of Christ's prayer diligently, and daily gather yourself to this our priest, and with the same words ask with your whole heart. Sanctify them in your truth, that is, preserve the Gospel and the true meaning in the minds of those calling upon you, and by the very acknowledgment of the Gospel sanctify us, that is, do not allow the knowledge to be idle, but kindle minds and hearts, so that the fear of God, faith, and love may truly burn in us, and that we may truly be, not without God, like the Gentiles and all other impious people, but be governed by you, serve you, and invite others to the true acknowledgment of you and true invocation. For holy is opposed to profane, and signifies that which is properly dedicated to the uses of God, or when it is said of a man, in whom God dwells, and begins eternal life. Therefore, at the same time in this prayer it is asked that we may be temples of God, and that God may be effective in us through the Gospel. And let this saying be recounted among the testimonies which teach about the efficacy of the evangelical ministry. And he alludes with the word of sanctification to the customary expression in Moses, about sanctifying priests, that is, separating them from the profane and properly dedicating them to God.

Moreover, Christ adds expressly what truth is, so that fanatical spirits may be refuted, who boast that they too are teachers of truth, nay, that they have divine inspirations, as Marcion, the Manichaeans, the Enthusiasts, Mahomet, and many others have boasted. But let this saying be opposed to all these: Your word is truth; that doctrine alone, handed down through Christ and commended to the Apostles, is the truth about God. Outside of this, the doctrines of all sects about God are diabolical frenzies; they do not show God, they do not sanctify minds. Let students therefore remember this saying, because it distinguishes the Church from all other sects, and condemns all opinions about God alien to the Gospel, and it agrees with this saying: If anyone teaches another Gospel, let him be anathema.

Consolation mixed with prayer is the most effective of all. It is certain that the Son of God was not sent in vain, since God has produced so many manifest testimonies to show that this teacher was sent by God, that He approves this doctrine, and that He will truly give the good things which the Gospel promises. Now, however, Christ says that He is sending the Apostles in the same way as He Himself was sent. Therefore they will not be sent in vain, they will not be useless bawlers, they will not be disturbers of polities, as atheistic men judge concerning the ministers of the Gospel; nay, in such infirmity of those teaching, in such confusion of the Church, the minds of all men are troubled, and they ask whether the voice of the Gospel benefits the human race, or whether it is truly only an imposture, whether Paul benefits more, or Phocylides, or Theognis, or Aesop. Then, because they see polities being disturbed by dissension about religion, many are also deterred from the profession of the Gospel, as if it were only a torch of discords.

Against these false judgments of human reason, testimonies about the efficacy and dignity of the ministry must be collected. Here and below the Son of God expressly affirms that He is sending the Apostles in the same way as He Himself was sent by the Father, and above He affirms several times that their ministry will be effective, as in chapter 14 it is said with the most serious asseveration: Amen, amen I say to you, he who believes in me, the works that I do, he will do, and he will do greater things than these. And chapter 15: I chose you that you might bear fruit, and your fruit might remain. And Paul says: The Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes. With these and similar testimonies let us confirm our minds, so that they may most firmly establish that the ministry of the Gospel is effective, that it begins eternal life in all who do penance and truly believe the Gospel, and that it governs many dangers of the present life. It is therefore profitable to teach, to hear, to learn, to embrace the Gospel, even if atheistic men want to see what it profits, nay, they judge the voice of the Gospel to be an empty fable, or an imposture, or a torch of seditions.

And this prayer of Christ pertains not only to the Apostles, but to all who rightly perform the ministry, nay, to all who embrace the Gospel, as Christ soon adds: I pray not for them only, but for those who will believe in me through their word,

Therefore, let us each apply this saying to ourselves: The Gospel will be effective in you yourself when you learn and embrace it; it will be effective in some portion of the people who hear it, even if many will furiously despise it, or, burning with hatred, will attempt to destroy it, and great and manifold will be the distractions of men and the disturbances of empires. Amidst these sad spectacles, however, let us hold fast to this voice: Just as the eternal Father sent his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, and the Son sent the Apostles, so that the Gospel might truly be effective, so now too God sends pastors and teachers; he wills that the voice of the Gospel be effective now too, even if the accidents of the mission differ—as Paul was called in one way, Timothy in another—yet the substantial element is always the same and remains the same, namely, that the Gospel should be effective. The huge confusion of human affairs often disturbs weak minds, so that they think all things are rolled and agitated by chance; but you, looking upon the Church and the schools sounding the voice of the Gospel, consider—nay, God is certainly present to his Church, he governs and preserves the remnants, he sends pastors and teachers, just as he sent the Son, the Prophets, and the Apostles.

Latin:

Non rogo, ut tollas eos de mundo.

Testatur et hoc dictum velle Deum, ut omni tempore in hac mortali vita, in qua tristis confu- sio est hominum et imperiorum, semper aliqua sit Ecclesia vera Deo placens. Duas igitur con- solationes ex hac petitione sumamus: Alteram, quod cum certum sit mansuram esse Dei Eccle- siam, semper sciamus Deum efficacem esse per Evangelium, Deum nobis adesse, et promissio- nes semper ratas esse et fieri, et esse membra Ec- clesiae Dei, et haeredes vitae aeternae eos, qui credunt Evangelio, et ministerium Evangelii sem- per esse efficax, sicut promittit Christus: Ecce ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus usque ad con- summationem seculi.

Altera consolatio est, quod defensio promit- titur adversus omnis generis furores, quibus Ec- clesia oppugnatur. Si Deus mox abduxisset Apo- stolos ex hac vita, et ornasset eos aeterna gloria, esset ea quidem liberatio admiranda, sed haec multo mirabilior est, quod Ecclesiam omni tem- pore velut in mari rubro stantem inter fluctus et hostes servat, imperia plerumque sunt inimica Evangelio, et saepe immani crudelitate grassan- tur adversus omnia membra Ecclesiae. Praeterea maxima pars hominum contemnit, et odit veram de Deo doctrinam, inflammat diabolus multos, et in ipso Ecclesiae coetu, ut serant conturbatio- nes dogmatum, aut certent ambitionibus et aliis cupiditatibus. Hinc existunt ingentia certamina, ac prudentes vident, Ecclesiam omnibus tempo- ribus in talibus periculis versari, ac si staret assidue inter aquarum cumulos in mari rubro, nec ulla humana sapientia regi illa pericula pos- sunt, nec sustinere ea ullum robur humanum potest. Sed pii hac se consolatione sustentent, quod sciunt iuvari ac defendi nos a Deo, sicut hic petitur: Serva eos a malo.

Sic et Esaias dicit de itinere Mosi per mare rubrum: Qui eduxit dextra Mosen, brachio ma- iestatis suae. Item: Spiritus Domini ductor eius fuit, etc. Hoc modo semper duci Ecclesiam per ingentia pericula, tanquam per undas ab ipso Deo certum est, et hac fide et invocatione Dei res tan- tae, quae longe superant vires nostras, sustinen- dae sunt. Saepe igitur cogitantes de nostris peri- culis, hanc precationem filii Dei recordemur, quae et tunc recitata et exaudita est, et assidue coram aeterno patre repetitur. Manet enim filius Dei intercessor assiduus, nec irrita est eius inter- cessio, sed impetrat nobis assidue auxilium, de- fensionem et liberationem. Ad cogitationem huius precationis adiungamus et promissiones, ut Esaiae 46.: Ego vos etiam in senecta gestabo, ego feci, ego feram, ego salvabo.

Santifica eos in veritate tua, sermo tuus est veritas.

Repetit expressius precationem de doctrinae veritate, ut Deus Evangelium, et veram ac puram Evangelii sententiam in Apostolis, et deinceps in ministerio servet, sicut et Esaias precatur cap. 8.: Obsigna legem in discipulis meis, id est, video tristissimas tenebras in populo Dei secuturas esse, et multos abiecturos esse doctrinam de Messia, de fide, de vera invocatione, de veris cultibus et re- cepturos ethnicas opiniones de imperio mundano Messiae, de cumulandis sacrificiis. Sed te Deus oro, verbum quod Prophetis tradidisti, serva in mentibus eorum, qui propheticam doctrinam au- diunt, discunt, et amplectuntur, et quidem serva obsignatam, ne effundant, aut verbum ipsum, aut nativam sententiam, sicut Sadducaei, ne li- teram quidem Prophetarum recipiebant. Phari- saei videri volebant retinere literam, sed inter- pretationes falsas affingebant, ut adhuc Iudaeis et haereticis usitatum est.

Diligenter autem observandum est, quod no- minatim petit servari doctrinam in discipulis, id est, in discentibus. Requirit igitur studium et cognitionem literae, vult nos auditores esse Pro- phetarum. In eo coetu discentium et amplecten- tium prophetica scripta, erunt aliqui retinentes lucem doctrinae et nativam sententiam, non inter Sadducaeos aut alios, qui nec legunt nec discunt Prophetas. Quare amemus studium, audiamus pios et peritos interpretes, conferamus testimonia doctrinae, petamus mentes nostras regi et ac- cendi a Spiritu sancto. Haec sunt discipulorum officia, et hoc studium est felix, et monstrat veri- tatem, sicut scriptum est Proverb. 2.: Si inclina- bis cor tuum ad sapientiam, invenies eam. Nunc verba precationis Christi diligenter expende, et quotidie te ad hunc nostrum sacerdotem aggre- gato, et iisdem verbis toto corde petito. Sancti- fica eos in veritate tua, id est, serva Evangelium et veram sententiam in mentibus invocantium te, et ipsa agnitione Evangelii sanctifica nos, id est, Non sinas esse otiosam noticiam, sed accende mentes et corda, ut vere ardeant in nobis timor Dei, fides, dilectio, et vere simus, non sine Deo, sicut Ethnici, et omnes alii impii, sed a te guber- nemur, tibi serviamus, et invitemus alios ad veram agnitionem tui et veram invocationem. Sanctum enim opponitur profano, et significat id, quod est proprie dicatum usibus Dei, seu cum de homine dicitur, in quo habitat Deus, et incoat vitam aeternam, Simul igitur in hac precatione petitur, ut simus templa Dei, et Deus sit efficax in nobis per Evangelium. Et hoc dictum inter testimonia recenseatur, quae docent de efficacia ministerii evangelici. Et alludit verbo sancti- ficationis ad usitatam locutionem in Mose, de sanctificandis sacerdotibus, id est, segregandis a profanis et proprie dicandis Deo.

Addit autem Christus expresse, quid sit ve- ritas, ut refutari fanatici spiritus possint, qui gloriantur se quoque veritatis doctores esse, imo se habere divinos afflatus, ut Marcion, Mani- chaei, Enthusiastae, Mahometus, et alii multi gloriati sunt. Sed his omnibus opponatur hoc dictum, Sermo tuus est veritas, illa sola doctrina per Christum tradita, et commendata Apostolis, est veritas de Deo. Extra hanc omnium sectarum doctrinae de Deo, sunt furores diabolici, non monstrant Deum, non sanctificant mentes. Me- minerint igitur studiosi hoc dictum, quia discer- nit Ecclesiam ab omnibus aliis sectis, et damnat omnes opiniones de Deo, alienas ab Evangelio, et congruit cum hoc dicto: Si quis aliud Evan- gelium docet, anathema sit.

Consolatio precationi mixta, est omnium effi- cacissima. Certum est filium Dei non frustra mis- sum esse, cum Deus tot manifesta testimonia edi- derit, ut ostenderet, hunc doctorem a Deo mis- sum esse, se approbare hanc doctrinam, et vere daturum bona, quae promittit Evangelium. Nunc autem dicit Christus, se eodem modo Apostolos mittere, sicut ipse missus est. Non igitur frustra mittentur, non erunt inutiles vociferatores, non erunt turbatores politiarum, sicut de ministris Evangelii homines atheoi iudicant, imo in tanta infirmitate docentium, in tanta confusione Eccle- siae, omnium hominum animi anguntur, et quae- runt an prosit generi humano vox Evangelii, an vero tantum sit impostura, utrum plus prosit Pau- lus, an Phocylides, aut Theognis, aut Aesopus. Deinde quia vident turbari politias, dissensione de religione, multi etiam deterrentur ab Evan- gelii professione, quasi sit tantum fax discor- diarum.

Adversus haec falsa iudicia humanae rationis colligenda sunt testimonia de ministerii efficacia et dignitate. Hic et infra filius Dei expresse affir- mat, se mittere Apostolos eodem modo, sicut ipse a patre missus est, et supra aliquoties affirmat ministerium eorum efficax fore, ut cap. 14. dici- tur cum gravissima asseveratione: Amen, amen dico vobis, qui credit in me, opera quae ego fa- cio, ille faciet, et maiora his faciet. Et cap. 15.: Elegi vos ut fructum faciatis, et fructus vester maneat. Et Paulus inquit: Evangelium est po- tentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti. His et si- milibus testimoniis confirmemus mentes nostras, ut firmissime statuant ministerium Evangelii esse efficax, incoare vitam aeternam in omnibus qui agunt poenitentiam, et vere credunt Evangelio, et multa pericula vitae praesentis gubernare. Prodest igitur docere, audire, discere, amplecti Evangelium, etiamsi homines ἄθεοι videre volunt quid prosit, imo iudicant vocem Evangelii esse inanem fabulam, aut imposturam, aut facem se- ditionum.

Nec tantum ad Apostolos haec precatio Chri- sti pertinet, sed ad omnes recte fungentes mini- sterio, imo ad omnes amplectentes Evangelium, sicut mox subiicit Christus: Oro non pro eis tan- tum, sed pro credituris per verbum eorum in me,

Ergo singuli ad nos ipsos accommodemus hoc dictum: Erit efficax Evangelium in te ipso, cum disces et amplecteris, erit efficax in aliqua parte hominum audientium, etiamsi multi furenter contemnent, aut ardentes odiis delere conabuntur, et magnae et multiplices fient hominum distractiones, et imperiorum perturbationes. Inter haec tristia spectacula, tamen hanc vocem teneamus: Sicut aeternus pater misit filium suum Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, et filius misit Apostolos, ut vere esset efficax Evangelium, ita nunc quoque Deus mittit pastores et doctores, vult nunc quoque efficacem esse Evangelii vocem, etiamsi accidentia missionis differunt, ut aliter vocatus est Paulus, aliter Timotheus, tamen substantiale semper est, et manet idem, scilicet ut Evangelium sit efficax. Ingens confusio rerum humanarum saepe perturbat imbecilles animos, ut cogitent omnia casu volvi et agitari, sed tu intuens Ecclesiam, et scholas, sonantes vocem Evangelii, cogita, imo Deus certo adest Ecclesiae suae, gubernat et servat reliquias, mittit pastores et doctores, sicut misit Filium, Prophetas et Apostolos.

## 17:19
And for them I sanctify myself.

Always in every life one must think about the application of the sacrifice of Christ and his intercession for us. For thus we shall rightly think about Christ as mediator and priest, when, namely, we also behold him interceding for us too and applying the sacrifice for us. For it pertains to the office of a priest not only to offer something, but that the mind should approach praying for him for whom the sacrifice is made, and testifying that it performs this obedience for him. Therefore, here the Son of God sets forth the words of application, which are the chief words of the whole Gospel, sounding from the first promise even unto all eternity; nay, they are the revelation of that secret deliberation of the eternal Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, in which, immediately after the fall of Adam and Eve, the Son was the intercessor for the human race and the appeaser of the just and immense wrath of God.

He repeats this discourse in this great and ineffable agony, saying: I sanctify myself for them. As often as you begin to say prayers, as often as you seek the remission of sins or other goods, let your mind first behold that priest, and let these words of application be repeated in your ears, tongue, and heart, so that you may truly conclude that the Son of God was made a victim for you too, and that he himself interceded for you and applied his sacrifice for you. Nor indeed is the intercession of the Son of God empty, nor is the sacrifice useless: by this doctrine faith is to be aroused in every invocation and in the whole of life.

The word 'I sanctify' in this place is without any doubt taken from priests and victims. For it was said of both, and the whole preparation, slaughter, and offering of a victim was called sanctification. Thus Christ says here: I sanctify myself, that is, I separate myself from the whole human race, so that I may become a host dedicated to God, and I offer myself to be slaughtered, and I offer myself to you, that is, on account of your will I sustain this slaughter, I declare my obedience to you, I am not moved by any unjust desire of my own; and properly, sanctification is the obedient will itself, as it is said in Hebrews 6: He was heard because of his reverence, that is, the obedience rendered to God, so that he himself might be honored. And Psalm 40: In the head of the book it is written of me, that I should do your will. My God, I have willed, and your law is in the midst of my heart, that is, you did not want other victims to be offered, but you wanted me to obey you; I willingly comply with this secret decree of yours.

But let us most faithfully remember these words of application: For them. Likewise: I pray not for them only, but for those who will believe through their word. Here Christ openly affirms that his sacrifice is valid not only for the Apostles, but for all who will embrace the Gospel; he does not lead us to speculations of election, but points to the Church, for which he affirms he is made a victim, and expressly says that his sacrifice is profitable to you and to all others who believe in his Gospel; thus in Psalm 16 he applies his sacrifice: To the saints who are in the earth, all my will is in them, that is, I suffer these things on account of the saints on earth, and these I truly love.

But here let us know concerning the application that it must be received by faith; Christ applies it for all, but he says by name: To those who will believe, that is, he wills that his sacrifice be profitable to you in such a way, if you conclude by faith that the fruit of this sacrifice pertains to you. If you conclude that on account of this very sacrifice the wrath of God is truly appeased for you, that you are truly received, heard, and saved. Therefore Paul says, Romans 3: We are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God has set forth as a propitiator through faith in his blood. Thus he says: He is a propitiator for you, when you believe that for the sake of his death God is appeased toward you.

Let us remember this doctrine of application perpetually and with the greatest care, and both parts have been neglected by many writers; they do not warn where Christ applied his sacrifice for us, and where he performed the chief duty of a priest, for it is the proper office of a high priest to apply his sacrifice. Afterward, they have handed down much less how individuals ought to apply the fruit of the sacrifice to themselves; here they have invented applications through Masses and other works, against which errors minds must be most diligently fortified, and the doctrine of faith must be learned, by which God wills that each one apply this sacrifice to himself, as I cited before from Paul, where he says: Christ was set forth as a propitiator through faith in his blood, that is, by faith we must establish that Christ died for us, and that we have been washed by his blood.

After he spoke of the application, he repeats the prayer concerning the effects: That they may be one in us, and that they may be where I am, and may see my glory. Therefore, he again asks for three things, as above. First, that the truth and light of doctrine may remain in the Church. Then, that it may be harmonious. Third, that eternal glory may be given, and that the sons may be co-heirs. The first petition is repeated in this particle, that they may be one in us, that is, first that they may agree with us, and be enlightened by our light and truth. He does not desire the concord of a human assembly, as the Spartan state is harmonious against the Athenians, but he desires first that the minds of all be joined with God through the Gospel. But after men are joined with God, then he desires that the concord of doctrine be retained, and he forbids the Church to be disturbed. Finally, he asks for eternal glory for us. Concerning these highest goods, Christ prays in this final struggle with a most ardent heart and most ardent words, and the same sentiments are repeated again and again, as happens in great emotions.

Moreover, at the end there are words of most burning love toward the eternal Father and toward us, which also contain testimony concerning the divine nature in Christ; for when he says: Because you loved me before the foundation of the world, he affirms the same thing that he said above: Glorify me, Father, with yourself with the eternal glory which I had with you before this world was. The Son of God existed before this world, and was loved with an eternal love before the world, therefore he is not a creature. Now, since that love in the will of the eternal Father is true and not feigned, and yet the Son was sent for our sake so that he might become a victim, and he assumed human nature, and we are loved for his sake, it is necessary that there be a true and immense love toward us, the magnitude of which no creature can sufficiently express. It is necessary, however, that this great love be often thought of by us in some part during prayer itself, and that our minds be kindled by faith and gratitude. For we think in vain about the love of God unless this faith is added, namely, that by confidence in his love for the sake of the Son we establish that we ourselves are received, heard, and saved. Let this doctrine of application always be in sight, and let it be practiced daily in prayer, in all business, and in dangers.

Latin:

Et pro ipsis me sanctifico.

Semper in omni vita cogitandum est de applicatione sacrificii Christi, et intercessione pro nobis. Sic enim recte de mediatore et sacerdote Christi cogitabimus, cum videlicet etiam intuebimur eum pro nobis quoque intercedentem, et pro nobis applicantem sacrificium. Nam ad officium sacerdotis pertinet non solum offerre aliquid, sed mens accedat orans pro eo, pro quo fit sacrificium et testificans se pro illo hanc obedientiam praestare. Ideo hic Dei filius ponit verba applicationis, quae sunt praecipua verba totius Evangelii, sonantis inde usque a prima promissione ad omnem aeternitatem, imo sunt revelatio illius arcanae deliberationis aeterni patris, et filii, et Spiritus sancti, in qua statim post lapsum Adae et Evae, filius fuit deprecator pro genere humano et placator iustae et ingentis irae Dei.

Hunc sermonem in hoc magno et ineffabili agone repetit, inquiens: Ego sanctifico me pro eis. Quoties incipis preces dicere, quoties petis remissionem peccatorum, aut alia bona, primum illum sacerdotem mens intueatur, et in auribus tuis, lingua et pectore haec verba applicationis repetantur, ut statuas vere pro te quoque filium Dei factum esse victimam, et ipsum quidem pro te intercessisse, et pro te sacrificium suum applicasse. Nec vero inanis est filii Dei intercessio, non est inutile sacrificium: hac doctrina exuscitanda est fides in omni invocatione et in tota vita.

Verbum sanctifico, hoc loco sine ulla dubi- tatione a sacerdotibus et victimis sumtum est. Nam de utrisque dicebatur, ac tota praeparatio, mactatio, et oblatio victimae vocabatur sanctifica- tio. Sic Christus hic inquit: Ego me sanctifico, id est, segrego me ex toto genere humano, ut fiam hostia Deo dicata, et me praebeo mactandum, et tibi me offero, id est, propter tuam voluntatem sustineo hanc mactationem, tibi obedientiam meam declaro, non aliqua iniusta mea cupiditate moveor, ac proprie santificatio est ipsa voluntas obediens, ut dicitur ad Hebraeos 6.: Exauditus est propter reverentiam, id est, obedientiam praestitam Deo, ut ipse honore afficeretur. Et Psalm. 40.: In capite libri scriptum est de me, ut facerem voluntatem tuam. Deus meus, volui, et lex tua in medio cordis mei, id est, alias victi- mas offerri noluisti, sed me voluisti tibi obedire, huic tuo arcano decreto volens obtempero.

Fidelissime autem haec verba applicationis meminerimus: Pro eis. Item: Oro non pro eis tantum, sed pro credituris per verbum eorum. Hic palam affirmat Christus valere suum sacrifi- cium, non tantum pro Apostolis, sed pro omni- bus, qui Evangelium amplectentur, non deducit nos ad speculationes electionis, sed monstrat Ecclesiam, pro qua affirmat se fieri victimam, et expresse inquit, tibi, et omnibus aliis prodesse suum sacrificium, qui suo Evangelio credunt, sic in Psalm. 16. applicat suum sacrificium: Sanctis, qui sunt in terra, omnis voluntas mea in eis, id est, haec patior propter sanctos in terra, et hos vere diligo,

Sed hic sciamus de applicatione, oportere eam accipi fide, Christus pro omnibus applicat, sed nominatim dicit: Credituris, id est, ita vult tibi prodesse suum sacrificium, si fide statuas, huius sacrificii fructum ad te pertinere. Si sta- tuas propter hoc ipsum sacrificium vere tibi pla- catam esse iram Dei, te vere recipi, exaudiri, et salvari. Ideo Paulus inquit, Rom. 3.: Iustifica- mur gratis ipsius gratia per redemtionem, quae est in Christo Iesu, quem proposuit Deus propi- ciatorem per fidem in sanguine suo. Sic inquit: Tibi est propiciator, cum credis, quod propter ipsius mortem tibi Deus placatus sit.

Hanc doctrinam applicationis perpetuo et summa cura meminerimus, ac utraque pars a mul- tis scriptoribus neglecta est, non monent, ubi Christus pro nobis applicaverit suum sacrificium, et ubi praecipuo munere sacerdotis functus sit, nam proprium summi sacerdotis officium est, ap- plicare suum sacrificium. Postea multo minus tradiderunt, quomodo singuli sacrificii fructum sibi applicare debeant, hic finxerunt applicationes per Missas et alia opera, adversus quos errores diligentissime muniendae sunt mentes, et discenda est doctrina de fide, qua sibi unumquemque Deus vult hoc sacrificium applicare, ut antea ex Paulo citavi, ubi ait: Christum positum propiciatorem per fidem in sanguine ipsius, id est, fide statuen- dum pro nobis Christum mortuum esse, et nos sanguine eius ablutos esse.

Postquam de applicatione dixit, repetit pre- cationem de effectibus: Ut unum sint in nobis, et ut ibi sint ubi ego sum, et videant gloriam meam. Rursus igitur tria petit, ut supra. Pri- mum, ut doctrinae veritas et lux in Ecclesia ma- neat. Deinde, ut sit concors. Tertio, ut donetur aeterna gloria, et sint cohaeredes filii. Prima petitio in hac particula repetitur, ut sint unum in nobis, id est, primum consentiant nobiscum, sint illustrati nostra luce et veritate. Non vult concordiam coetus humani, ut est concors civitas Spartana contra Athenienses, sed vult prius co- pulatas esse omnium mentes cum Deo per Evan- gelium. Postquam autem cum Deo copulati sunt homines, tunc vult retineri concordiam doctrinae, et vetat turbari Ecclesiam. Postremo petit nobis aeternam gloriam. De his summis bonis in hoc ultimo agone Christus ardentissimo pectore, et ardentissimis verbis precatur, et eaedem senten- tiae subinde repetuntur, ut fit in magnis affe- ctibus.

Sunt autem in fine flagrantissimi amoris ver- ba erga aeternum patrem, et erga nos, quae etiam testimonium continent de natura divina in Chri- sto, cum enim inquit: Quia dilexisti me ante conditionem mundi, affirmat idem, quod supra dixit: Glorifica me pater apud te aeterna gloria, quam habui apud te, antequam hic mundus esset. Fuit filius Dei ante hunc mundum, et aeterno amore dilectus est ante mundum, ergo non est creatura. Iam cum ille amor in voluntate aeterni patris verus et non simulatus sit, et tamen filius propter nos missus sit, ut fieret victima, et assumserit humanam naturam, et nos propter eum diligamur, necesse est verum et ingentem amorem esse erga nos, cuius magnitudinem nulla creatura eloqui satis potest. Necesse est tamen hunc tantum amorem saepe a nobis aliqua ex parte cogitari in ipsa invocatione, et accendi mentes fide et gratitudine. Frustra enim cogitamus de dilectione Dei, nisi haec fides accedat, videlicet, ut fiducia dilectionis propter filium statuamus nos ipsos recipi, exaudiri, et salvari. Haec doctrina de applicatione semper sit in conspectu, et quotidie exerceatur in invocatione, in omnibus negotiis, et periculis.

## 18:1 Argument
Chapter XVIII.

Latin:

Caput XVIII.

## 18:1
When Jesus had said these things, he went out.

As often as it is spoken of the passion of the Son of God, it is useful for the more unlearned to be reminded of this triple meditation on the passion. The first is pedagogical: to recite, to hear, and to think about the history with moderate attention, and with a certain zeal for learning and for exciting repentance and faith in ourselves. This meditation is not to be despised if it is without superstition; indeed, it is necessary that the history be learned and repeated from time to time, and the thought of the history is the beginning of ardent spiritual movements which please God. And just as the Church often sets forth the history, so individual men must be accustomed to read and hear it often, and to distribute and consider all parts of the history diligently, so that it becomes most familiarly known. For by this very thought spiritual movements are kindled in the heart, according to that: Faith is from hearing, hearing through the word of God; nor should the reading be cold or unlearned, but the causes of the divine counsel should be thought upon, insofar as they have been revealed in the word of God, the very series of the history, the effects, the application, and the whole government of the Church from the beginning.

For the causes of the passion of Christ are the object that moved the will of the Son of God: sin and the most sad damnation of the human race, which the Son of God did not wish to perish entirely.

The impulsive cause is the Father's love and the intercession of the Son praying for us; concerning this cause the Son says: God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son for the world. The final cause, that to a great part of the human race justice and eternal glory might be rendered, and that God might have an eternal Church, by which He would be acknowledged and celebrated, as it is said in Psalm 22: My praise is of thee, in the great congregation I will praise thee, I will pay my vows before them that fear God.

The efficient cause for the sake of a good end, the will of the Son of God and His person, willing this obedience, on account of the secret counsel of the eternal Father, whose wrath could not be appeased by any other sacrifice. By this will, Christ Himself is the priest, offering Himself to the eternal Father for us.

The matter of the passion, in which, that is, the subject, is the Son of God Himself, and let the principal parts be distributed, which felt the pain; the nerves of the body felt the torments which the laceration brought, the heart fled from death, and a part of the torments of the body penetrated to the heart, but the greater torments were of the soul, which also made the heart and the whole body languish. For the soul by natural inclination abhorred death, and as in other brave men, minds are always more tormented by the cause of miseries than by the miseries themselves, just as the thought of guilt exercised David much more than the misery of exile itself. So in the soul of Christ, the cause of the passion stirred up huge pains, namely, that Christ knew that God was angry at the sins of the human race, and that the wrath had been derived onto Him, as if He Himself had polluted Himself with such great crimes. This secret and ineffable pain arising from the cause of the passion, men do not understand. Here the soul of Christ struggled, not only with the torments of the body and with death, but much more with the wrath of God; the Son of God grieved that God was horribly offended and treated with contumely, and He acknowledged that the wrath had been derived onto Him; He also grieved that a great part of the human race, not having understood or having despised this benefit of God, namely the death of the Son of God, rushes into eternal destruction. But this consolation overcame these pains, that He willingly obeyed the Father, and awaited the help of God and liberation, as will be said in its place in the history, and we have said certain things above about the pains and struggle of Christ.

The instrumental and external cause, not congruent with the end which God had established, are the devils and the Jews, and their satellites, who, burning with fury and hatred of God and of all the Prophets, even attempted to destroy Christ.

The effect, the appeasement of the wrath of God, so that the justice of God might be satisfied. For the wrath was not cast away rashly, but God willed that a λύτρον be rendered, because every law binds either to obedience or to punishment. Then follow many other effects, the reconciliation of God and men, the donation of justice, of the Holy Spirit and of eternal life, the destruction of the works of the devil, of sin and of death.

The application contains the doctrine of repentance and faith. First, let the true and horrible wrath of God against our sins be considered. For since He willed the Son to become a victim for the human race, it is certain that there is a huge and not feigned wrath. There are many most sad testimonies of the wrath of God against sins, such as death and infinite other calamities of men. But this testimony far surpasses all, that in that secret divine counsel it was decreed that the Son of God should become a victim.

The application of the passion is therefore, first, to truly tremble at the recognition of the wrath of God against our sins, as He Himself says, Luke 23: Weep not for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children. Then let another application of faith follow, which may establish that the eternal and immutable command of God is that we believe that for our sake the Son of God was made a victim, and that we are received by God when we believe that our sins are remitted to us for His sake. By this faith, eternal life is begun in hearts, because this consolation frees them from terrors, and begins a new light and life.

To pedagogical meditation, then, this doctrine also pertains, that namely our application ought to be followed by thanksgiving, preaching, confession, and imitation in the cross. To this let there be added also the doctrine concerning the priesthood of Christ, of which it is written: Thou art a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek. For Christ is truly the high priest, to whom this definition applies. A priest is a person who has a divine promise, so that he can certainly establish that he is heard, called by divine command, so that he may teach the Gospel, and pray, and sacrifice for others. These most properly and primarily belong to the Son of God, who has the promise by which He certainly knows that He is heard, according to that: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased, and 1 Timothy 2: One mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus. And this Son brought forth the secret decree concerning reconciliation from the bosom of the eternal Father, as it is said in John 1: The only begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, He has declared it, and John 17: I have delivered unto them thy word. But that He prays for us, the words openly testify, John 17: I pray not for them alone, but for all who shall believe through their word in me, and it is written in Isa. ch. 53: He bore the sins of many, and prayed for the transgressors. Finally, he also offered a sacrifice for us, his own death, and indeed he applied that sacrifice for us, as he says expressly in John 17: For them I sanctify myself, that they also may be sanctified in the truth, and Matt. 20: The Son of man came to give his life as a ransom for all. But this application must be apprehended by faith, as I said above, and it is written in Acts 10: To him all the prophets bear witness, that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name. This statement demands that we receive the benefit of Christ by faith, that is, that we truly determine that forgiveness is given to us on account of the sacrifice and intercession of this mediator. The thought of this whole doctrine is a certain pedagogy, but yet not to be despised, if it is done without superstition. For through these thoughts spiritual movements are kindled.

There is therefore a second meditation, which is properly called spiritual, and is salutary, to truly tremble in our hearts with the knowledge of the wrath of God against our sins, and to discern this wrath poured out upon the Son of God, as Paul says in Rom. 8, that it is necessary for us to be made like the image of the Son of God. And in Rom. 6: We have been grafted into the likeness of his death. Likewise: Our old man was crucified together with him, that the body of sin might be abolished. Yet let not terrors only remain, but it is necessary that consolation and vivification should follow. Therefore, in this spiritual meditation, a new light and joy should also be felt, when faith determines that the wrath of God has been appeased through the Son, and that on account of the Son sins are forgiven us, and righteousness and life are restored to us, as it is written in Rom. 6: So it is necessary for us to be grafted into the likeness of Christ's resurrection. 2 Cor.: Through whom you were also raised together through faith, of the efficacy of God. And in Phil. 3: That I may be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which is from the law, but that which is through faith in Christ, which is the righteousness from God through faith, that I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings.

This second meditation must be diligently distinguished from the third, which is exemplary; the second apprehends Christ as propitiator and savior, and the price and cause of our reconciliation, righteousness, and eternal life, but the third, which is exemplary, looks upon Christ as a teacher, by whose examples we may be consoled, and whom we may strive to imitate, just as we propose to ourselves the examples of David. We see that Christ, Abel, David, and other saints sustained horrible hardships. Let us know, therefore, that it is the will of God that the Church be subject to the cross, and that we are not cast away, even if we suffer hard things; let us also imitate the invocation which they exercised on the cross, their tolerance, hope, and other virtues. This exemplary meditation is pious, if the second is not lacking. For he does not rightly acknowledge Christ who thinks he was only a teacher, like Moses, or that examples are only to be sought from him, as from David or similar ones.

But those rightly instructed in the Gospel, and understanding the second meditation, can derive from it the sweetest consolation and useful admonitions. For in this very history of the passion of Christ, images are proposed of almost everything that happens to the Church. The persons here are saints, firm and weak, many kinds of enemies, hypocrites, tyrants, priests, princes, the common people, various dangers, manifest violence, hidden snares, betrayal, the flight of friends, sarcasms in calamity. On the other hand, however, are the struggles, consolations, and wondrous deliverances of the saints, and the most sorrowful punishments of the impious, such as Judas. Finally, this history is as it were a prophecy, signifying for the Church of all times similar calamities, consolations, and deliverances. The consideration of these examples can instruct, confirm, and console the pious.

History.

I shall distribute the history into several acts, and so that the reading may be more clear, I will note the times at the beginning. It is certain that Christ was crucified on the 8th of the Kalends of April, that is, on the 25th of March, as the calculation of months is now used, in the 18th year of Tiberius, and Christ had already entered his 34th year. And although the calculation of the preceding days cannot be determined with certainty, yet this moderate distribution brings some light to the history.

On the 14th of March, it seems he began his journey from the desert, where John had baptized, from where to Jericho is a distance of two German miles, on which journey he healed the blind man. On the 15th he stayed with Zacchaeus. On the 16th he made the journey from Jericho to Bethany. For Jericho is distant from Jerusalem a little more than four of our miles.

On the 17th of March Lazarus is raised before Palm Sunday. On the 18th perhaps he stayed in Bethany.

The 19th, supper with Lazarus in Bethany on the Sabbath. The 20th, Palm Sunday. The 21st, he cursed the fig tree, and held most sharp sermons in the temple, which are extant in Matthew. The 22nd, supper in Bethany in the house of Simon the leper. The 23rd, the pact of Judas. The 24th, the day of unleavened bread, the eating of the lamb, and the institution of the Lord's Supper. And it was the true day of the Mosaic Passover from the evening of that day until the next day according to the Mosaic reckoning. Wherefore Christ both ate the lamb on the legitimate day, and was crucified on the true day of the Passover. The 25th, the crucifixion. The 26th, he was in the sepulchre. The 27th, the resurrection.

From this table it can be observed on what day Christ ate the lamb, and then began his agony at the Mount of Olives; the Mount of Olives was near Jerusalem on that side where the city faced the east, and it is often celebrated, as in 2 Kings 15 in the flight of David. And although they dispute about the name Cedron, nevertheless it is consistent that it is the same appellation which is in the same history of David. Christ therefore goes out by the same way by which David, once oppressed by great sorrow and mourning, had fled, stripped now not only of his kingdom, but of that excellent glory of virtue which he had had: but much sadder is the journey of Christ, who goes out to a far more difficult struggle.

Let the first act, therefore, be the struggle and the deeds done in the garden, which are narrated more copiously by the other Evangelists. Matthew begins that narration with terrors: Jesus began to be sorrowful, and to be vehemently distressed in mind, and Christ says: My soul is sorrowful even unto death; amidst these sorrows he prays, and the struggle is so great that a bloody sweat breaks out, and an angel is also sent to him to strengthen him. When profane men read these things, they wonder why such great sadness existed in a brave man, when Socrates, nay sometimes even girls, like the daughter of Hercules in Euripides, are said to have approached and sustained death with greater tranquility of mind; but let the Church consider the causes and the difference between the death of Christ and that of other men. It is common to all men, when the mind foresees death, that the soul and heart dread torments and death. Because nature universally flees its own destruction, and desires to be preserved and to remain unharmed. Thus also Socrates and Cicero truly grieve, although they govern their external gestures with some moderation, yet the sorrow is enclosed in the soul and in the heart, which can be described sufficiently by no one's speech. And in this depravity of nature, not only is there a certain natural flight from death in Cicero, but also vicious affections are added; he is angry with God, he wonders why this excellent nature should be burdened with such great evils, he parts with the pleasures of life with difficulty. Thus in others, other inordinate motions are added. But in Christ, although there is a natural flight from death and sorrow, yet these are not inordinate. But afterwards there are horrible sorrows, the magnitude of which neither men nor any angels can express. Christ knows that God is truly and horribly angry at sins, and that this wrath has been derived onto himself. He lies therefore prostrate before God, grieving that he is guilty, as if he had contaminated himself with the horrible filth with which the most base worshippers of idols, murderers, and those polluted by lusts have contaminated themselves throughout the whole world. For these sins of ours he is the intercessor, and he struggles with the wrath of God, so that as an intercessor he always derives a portion of the wrath onto himself, who seems to relieve the wicked and to be less angry at filth than he ought to be, just as Joab is blamed for patronizing Absalom; but this sorrow and struggle of the Son of God far surpasses all the thoughts of all angels and men.

Other causes of most sad mourning also approached, namely that he saw his own nation was about to perish, likewise that he saw the greatest part of the human race would be ungrateful for this benefit; he also saw the eternal destruction of such a great multitude, and he deplored it with great sadness. Let us consider these things when we read this saying: He began to be sorrowful and to be distressed in mind, and let us each know that our sins were transferred onto Christ and increased his sorrows.

Moreover, above we replied to the objections, which must be briefly repeated here. The first is, in many other men and girls there was not as much sorrow at the approach of death as there was in Christ. Why therefore does he himself, when he has the highest perfection of virtues, dread it so much? I answer: No creature can sustain the magnitude of the wrath of God; the Son of God therefore bore the punishment, so that the rest might not bear it; therefore in Lawrence and others greater cheerfulness is seen, because the principal causes of sorrow are not in them as they are in Christ. Blessed are they whose sins are covered, says the Psalm. Lawrence is therefore more cheerful, because since the wrath of God has been derived onto Christ, Lawrence is spared, so that he does not see it. Christ struggled and was λύτρον, so that we might be spared; wherefore the Psalm says: If you, O Lord, should mark iniquities, Lord, who shall stand?

Second objection: Not to obey God with all one's strength is a sin; in Christ there is some flight from death: How then is it said that obedience was entire in him without sin? I answer briefly: Although this struggle cannot be described in words, yet this must be retained, which is said in Heb. 4, that Christ was tempted in all things, according to the likeness, without sin. And first, the laceration of the body and nerves laterally brings pain without sin. There is also in the heart and will a natural sadness fleeing death, which in Christ was without vice, because every nature burdened beyond its strength groans and shudders at the magnitude of the burden. Cicero grieved, but inordinately, doubting whether there is providence, or if he thought there was providence, being angry at God because a more just cause was being defeated. Such a confusion of doubts and blasphemies was not in Christ. Furthermore, even if there is another greater pain in Christ, as I said, the sense of the wrath of God, yet this is without indignation and blasphemy against God; Christ subjects himself to the will of the Father with true reverence, as it is said in Heb.: He was heard because of his reverence, that is, because of an obedience not feigned, but sprung from true reverence, by which the Son willingly subjected himself to the eternal Father with huge love for the human race. Would that the thought of this such great love might be kindled in us a little. The Son assumed the human race, and calls himself our brother, and truly burns with brotherly love. For nothing is feigned or fictitious in Christ, and he is moved by this such great love, that he subjects himself to horrendous torments and the wrath of God for us. Let us therefore rouse ourselves by the thought of this love, so that trust in his mercy toward us may be kindled, and we too may be moved by some sense of gratitude, so that we may study more to obey God.

Third objection: Contradictory things cannot be in the same subject. Since, however, Christ was always blessed, it follows that he was in excellent joy. How then is there such consternation at the same time? I answer: Although others distinguish parts or powers in Christ, and attribute joy to some, pain to others, yet a simpler answer is to distinguish the times. This was a time in which blessedness or glory did not shine in the Son as at other times. For now, with the divine nature resting and not exerting its power, he lies humiliated, and as is said in a most sad voice in Isaiah: Stricken by God. These three arguments having been considered, pious minds thinking about the struggle of Christ are in some way reminded what the causes of that pain were. And let individuals contemplate this struggle in their own great pains. When we do this, not only will the consternation of Christ be able to be understood better, but we shall also take consolation from his example and victory; the Son of God bore such horrendous tortures, let us bear them too. Sustaining, however, he interceded for us, and obtained for us mitigation and liberation, as he says: O death, I will be thy death. By this faith let us raise ourselves in our consternations; this experience will illustrate this doctrine.

Now let us consider the persons in the first act in order. Christ feels huge torments, he struggles with these, and sustains himself with prayers, and experiences consolation, for an angel is also sent to strengthen him. In this struggle he truly becomes a victim, or the Lamb of God sustaining our sins. For then the wrath of God is poured out upon him, and such indeed is the head of the Church. What meanwhile does the Church say? The apostles neither understand the magnitude of the pains of Christ, nor are they greatly anguished in their souls, nay, they are even overcome by sleep. But Christ rebukes them because they are not more vigilant and intent, and commands them to pray to God, lest they be oppressed by temptation. This passage universally depicts the security and negligence of a great part of the Church, not yet feeling miseries, even when others are struggling with huge calamities. Here Christ warns, so that we may know that the danger is common, and we may ask to be helped, ruled, and confirmed, lest either secure minds fall into Epicurean contempt, or, oppressed by the weight of calamities, be overturned by despair, like Eli, Saul, and countless others. Always, however, there are some in the Church who truly acknowledge the will of God concerning sin and the mediator Christ, and understand the pains of Christ, and feel in some way similar pains, and await liberation, as from there even from the beginning the saddest laments of Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, etc., are recounted. At the very time of the passion, Mary understood why the Son was suffering, and was a companion of his pains, and with constant faith awaited liberation.

On the other hand, the persons waging war on Christ, who are the principal causes of the contests, are the devils, the impious priests and their teachers, and from the very company of Christ, the traitors: then the political magistrates, and the greatest part of the people, and others have other causes. The devils burn simply with hatred

of God and Christ, and so that they may act against God, they rage most atrociously against all members of the Church: Impious priests and teachers oppose the Gospel, because it taxes false opinions and fictitious cults. Moreover, most men hate rebuke, either from natural pride, because we love and please ourselves, or fearing for their power and gain. In traitors like Doeg, Alcimus, and Judas, many causes converge: diabolical hatred, desire for revenge, hope of power and profit. Political magistrates fear changes of kingdoms, and those who have great advantages from impious priests collude with them; many are even openly Epicureans.

Such causes also inflame the people: Epicurean contempt of God, superstition, hope of leisure, profit, and the benevolence of the powerful. It is profitable to consider these and similar causes, which irritate minds against Christ, so that weak spirits may be fortified against them, and the wicked may be more sharply refuted and rebuked.

We are still narrating the history of the first act in the garden, and we have spoken about the struggle and prayer of Christ, and about the persons. The rest of the history in that place contains this: the rebuke of the Apostles, of which it has been spoken, and the exhortation to pray, which let us diligently propose to ourselves: Watch and pray, he says, that you may not enter into temptation.
