Moreover, they join to him Simon the Cyrenian, perhaps met on the way, whom they compel to help Christ; afterwards, two robbers are also added to be crucified together. The name Golgotha signifies either a heap, that is, a place raised up, whether by stones or by sods, or the very skull of a human head, which is written elsewhere in the Hebrew text as Golgotha. But since I cannot recount all the members at greater length, I will now speak only of the allegory of Simon the Cyrenian, since that example, which seems to contain a small circumstance, has been so diligently recited. Moreover, this Simon signifies that there are always some in the afflictions of the Church, whether princes, or teachers, or other pious men, who bear a part of the cross; just as now, when kings in their anger attempt to destroy the Gospel and kill the teachers, some princes and governors in courts and cities sustain great dangers and hardships in the defense of the churches and of those who teach; indeed, even our scholastic order truly bears a part of the cross, and it is agreed that the name Simeon signifies a hearer. Students learning the Gospel are likewise involved in dangers; many pious scholars now sustain great miseries because of the Gospel, but God will render rewards to them, just as He rendered them to this Simeon. For He later called his sons, Alexander and Rufus, to the ministry of the Gospel.

The third passage is the address of Christ to the women who, wailing, accompany Christ carrying the cross. For not only is the atrocity of the punishment to be considered, but also the causes and the words of Christ spoken in the meantime, which contain a most ample doctrine. It is, however, an address of repentance, first reproving the women who do not yet understand why Christ sustains this agony, then predicting the horrible punishments which are going to oppress both this people and all the impious; thirdly, making a comparison of the afflictions of the Church and of the impious. And the two former members are sufficiently clear; the women, with the common affection of mediocre people, were deploring the calamity of Christ for his own sake. They did not know the causes, namely, that Christ was suffering for our sins. Moreover, it is necessary that this doctrine be delivered and inculcated to all men: that God is truly angry at our sins, that because of our sins punishments are to be feared, and that our evils must be acknowledged and deplored. Again, however, it must be known that our evils are taken away through Christ. But it is foolishness, as it is said, to be wise abroad—that is, being ignorant of one's own evils, to deplore the evils of others, such as those of Priam or Hector, and yet This folly is common to the greatest part of men. Hence those sayings: Physician, heal thyself. Likewise: ἄλλων ἰατρὸς αὐτὸς ἕλκεσι βρύων. Likewise: I hate the wise man who is not wise for himself. Let us first acknowledge our miseries, and let us learn what remedies God has handed down to us.

Nor are the most sorrowful discourses concerning the punishments of the impious obscure, of which mention is made here: then they shall say to the mountains, Fall upon us. Here let us consider not only the destruction of Jerusalem, but also similar examples of all times, which show that things often happen to men that are sadder than death itself; as for parents it is much sadder than death to see the cruel tortures of their children; death is therefore sought, so that punishments may be ended; how great, therefore, is the evil after this life, when they cannot even be ended by death? Christ warns not only these women of this, but the whole human race. And the chief cause of so many horrible spectacles in this life is because God wishes His wrath against sins to be seen; He wishes us to be reminded, as Psalm 39 says: For iniquities Thou dost correct man; let us therefore contemplate our own calamities and those of others, so that the fear of God may be stirred up in us.

In the third member it is said: If they do this in the green wood, what shall be done in the dry? That is, if the green and fruitful tree is uprooted, what shall become of the dry and barren one? By this figure this comparison is signified, since the members of God, who bear fruits pleasing to God, such as Abel, Jeremiah, the Baptist, endure great calamities, what shall become of the impious? This discourse of Christ agrees with the saying of Solomon, Prov. 11: If the righteous in the earth receives, how much more the impious and the sinner? To which these words are added in 1 Pet. 4: Judgment begins from the house of God. Here, however, human reason protests, being offended by this very confusion, that it goes ill with the good and well with the bad; minds argue that all things are carried by chance, and that human affairs are not ruled by providence, or that the government is unjust: philosophy cannot sufficiently explain this dispute, which does not know the first sources of human miseries, but these are shown in the doctrine of the Church. When therefore reason argues thus: It ought to go well with the righteous, and ill with the unrighteous: Jeremiah, the Baptist, are righteous, therefore it ought to go well with them. Here the Church answers, first concerning the major premise; the major premise is most true, for it is the law of God, as the first commandment testifies, and it is indeed so true that God compensates righteousness, or obedience, not only with perishing goods, but with eternal ones, so that they may be firm and non-perishing rewards. But the Gospel teaches in what order this distribution is made, which at the same time affirms that all men are subject to death and other calamities, because we all carry sin about with us. Now therefore the minor premise must be answered: Jeremiah, the Baptist, and the like are righteous, namely by imputation on account of the Son of God the mediator, but they are not yet righteous in total newness; nay, a great and sad darkness, and many diseases, still cling to the hearts of all the saints in this life. But God is truly angry at sin, and He wishes this wrath to be understood especially by the Church. Therefore He presses the Church in this life more than the rest of the dregs of men; afterwards many other causes also accrue, namely that He wishes these very afflictions of the saints to be testimonies concerning eternal life. For since God testifies that He approves of Paul in this life, when through him He raises the dead, and yet allows him to be killed by a most filthy tyrant, it is necessary that a judgment remain afterwards, in which God will show that He has not forgotten Paul, and that He prefers Paul to the most foul tyrant. But this doctrine concerning the causes has been recited more copiously elsewhere; now I return to the text. Christ warns the women concerning the wrath of God against the sins of all men, and testifies that they are also punished. But that He Himself suffers, it happens because He is the mediator and intercessor, who has derived into Himself the wrath of God against our sins, as the Baptist says: Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world.

The fourth place is the crucifixion itself, where it is to be observed first of all the saying which Paul cites and illustrates in Gal. 3: Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree, which words are taken from chapter 12 of Deut., where it is expressly added: Cursed by God is he who hangs on a tree; thus Scripture does not speak of punishments elsewhere. For punishments themselves do not make men guilty, that is, God is not angry at men on account of punishments, but on account of sins. Why therefore does God speak so atrociously concerning this punishment? I think it is said only on account of the death of Christ, so that it may be understood that the curse to which the human race was subject was derived into Him, that is, that He endured the punishment owed to the justice of God, and thus paid the λύτρον for us. Furthermore, how sad an appellation it is to be called cursed by God, that cannot be explained in words, but let us learn by pious meditation, when we read the complaints in the Psalms and elsewhere. Likewise when we ourselves in some way look upon our sins and dread them, fearing truly that we are cast away by God into eternal damnation. Although David grieved that he was cast out of his kingdom by his son, whom he loved dearly, that a rebellion had been stirred up, and that he was stripped of the glory of wisdom and justice which he had possessed, yet these sorrows were not the greatest. Another much greater sadness tormented him, because he saw that his own transgression was the cause of such great crimes and scandals, in which many who had been holy perished horribly. Here he judged himself to be the plague of the Church and of the people of God, and he felt a mass of sins so great that he acknowledged he could not bear it; he feared, therefore, that he had been cast away by God, like Saul or other tyrants who were vessels of the wrath of God. These sorrows of David in some way declare the atrocity of this description, when it is said that Christ was made a curse, but these things are not understood by profane or secure minds. Therefore let us also look upon our sins, and let us tremble at the thought of the wrath of God and of horrible punishments; thus it will come to pass that we may in some way understand this doctrine; indeed, this dread and this sorrow is the true meditation on the passion of Christ.

Fifth point: There are many sayings of Christ on the cross, but the principal sermon is to the thief, and the spectacle itself is remarkable. The two thieves are an image of the whole human race, which is entirely subject to death, but a part is liberated through Christ, and a part remains in death. Let us think that the whole human race hangs there, so that in truth we all, by various calamities and death, represent that very appearance of the thieves. But that the impious thief, in the midst of his punishment, nevertheless plays and mocks Christ with poisonous ironies, is a manifest madness, to play insolently in such great torture and in death itself; but his insanity signifies the similar security of all the impious in the whole human race. Nero plays securely and mocks God, nor does he feel that he is in the midst of hell and most sad miseries.

On the other hand, the other thief acknowledges his transgression and the cause of his punishment; he is not secure, he does not play like that mocker, but he judges that he is being punished by God, and furthermore he fears eternal punishments, for he says clearly: We are punished justly. Therefore he is tormented with great sorrows and dreads, but meanwhile, when he thinks who this just man is, who was called the Messiah, who is now a companion in punishment, he seeks true consolations, and perhaps these thoughts of his are kindled when he sees God signify by wondrous prodigies that He is a spectator of this punishment, and that He will be the judge. For this conversation is held when already at midday the light of the sun has been extinguished, as appears from the narrative of Luke. He acknowledges, therefore, that this just man is the Messiah, and first he openly distinguishes him from himself, the other companion in punishment, and affirms that he has done nothing wrong. Then he addresses him, and making mention of his future kingdom, he shows who he believes in, namely that this man, even if he now hangs on the cross and is about to die, yet will not perish, but will live, and will give life to others who call upon him. Finally, he understands the doctrine concerning the Messiah more correctly than all the Pharisees. He acknowledges in his life that the Church is on the cross, but that it will have life, justice, and eternal glory through this Lord. He asks, therefore, for these goods from him, saying: Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom. These are the words of a faith that has already struggled out of sorrows, death, and dreads, and that understands the sum of the doctrine of the Gospel. Christ, however, answers, as if pronouncing absolution, and receiving him into the Church, and indeed adding an oath: Amen I say to you, today you will be with me in Paradise, that is, in the place of the blessed Church, which has new and eternal light, wisdom, justice, and glory.

This is the order of the conversation, which we know is recited for many reasons. In the beginning, it testifies that God preserves the Church, and always raises up some confessors, even then when enemies triumph and think it has been destroyed. At that time the Church had been scattered, Christ himself hangs on the cross and dies, his mother is hindered by grief and sadness from speaking much, the Apostles flee. At such a time, in such great dissipation, the sun and the splitting rocks begin to preach, and this thief becomes an Apostle, preaching from on high to the whole human race.

Secondly, the conversion and salvation of this thief is an image of the conversion and salvation of individual elect persons. Do not think that you will enter eternal life in any other way than this thief enters it. Do not imagine that you bring merits to God, but we are all guilty of the wrath of God and of eternal death, like this thief, as Paul says, Romans 3: That every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may be guilty before God. You should propose this thief to your mind in contrition, faith, absolution, cross, and good works. Examples of all these parts are here set forth. Contrition is the acknowledgment of sin, because the thief says that he is justly punished, and he grieves that he has offended God, and he feels the wrath of God, being moved by this very punishment, and indeed he publicly confesses his sin, and proclaims the judgment of God to be just. All these things pertain to contrition, like those words of Daniel 9: To Thee, O Lord, is justice, but to us confusion of face.

His faith is most clearly shown by the petition: Remember me, Lord, when Thou shalt come into Thy kingdom. For he truly understands this companion in punishment, although he is now about to die, to be nevertheless the Messiah taking away sins and death, and redeeming the human race by this death of His, just as he could have remembered some sayings from Isaiah: he asks therefore from Him for the remission of sins and eternal life. And so that his faith may be confirmed, he hears the sweetest absolution: Today thou shalt be with me in paradise. Now see in him obedience begun. For it is said unlearnedly that there were no good works of this thief after his conversion; it is true, he cannot ask for the remission of sins on account of any good works, and therefore it is proposed to us, so that it may teach us about gratuitous reconciliation, but once converted he has great virtues. Contrition itself and sorrow on account of sin, and confession attributing justice to God, are good works, and testimonies of the love of God kindled in him. Then faith itself is a good work, with which it is necessary that the love of God, and many good works, be joined. There is added also an understanding of the doctrine concerning the cross and patience; he knows now that the human race has been plunged into death and calamities on account of sin, and yet that men are not rejected on account of calamities, but that God demands this obedience, and receives those who flee to Him, and sustains them with the Holy Spirit. And now in this very consolation, when his heart was lifted up by faith, he says this very sentence, which is in Isaiah in the last chapter, which affirms that God dwells with the contrite. He learned therefore this wisdom of the Gospel not shown in the law, and placed far above and outside of philosophy and the grasp of human reason, and now hanging in body on the cross and dying, he nevertheless truly lives an eternal life, he rejoices in the acknowledgment of God and the Messiah, and he offers to God this obedience by true tolerance, and awaits the new kingdom of the Messiah in paradise. He far surpasses, therefore, in wisdom and virtues, not only the Pharisees, but even the Apostles.

Finally, he also has external good works, the confession of his sin, and of the just judgment of God, the invocation of Christ, and the rebuke of the adversary. For to refute those who speak evil of the Gospel is a work commanded in these sentences, Luke 9: Whoever shall be ashamed of me and of my words, of him shall the Son of man be ashamed. And Psalm 118: And I spoke of Thy testimonies in the sight of kings, and was not ashamed. The example, however, pertains to all men, so that they may learn that it is a necessary work to profess the faith, and to declare it by the refutation of blasphemies.

Although, therefore, profane and powerful men are offended by such refutations, yet let us know that this duty is necessary, and truly pleases God, and let us remember this consolation in the schools, which incur the hatred of the powerful most of all, on account of such refutations.

The sixth, the final part, is the epitasis, most terrible of all. Here now, with the sun darkened against the order of nature, and hard rocks rent without any human force, and the dead coming forth having received life divinely, the Son of God dies amidst cries and prayers: since the whole nature of things is moved, heaven and earth, it is to be lamented that we are so hard that we do not tremble at the thought of such a great event. Let us pray therefore to God, that He may kindle our minds, so that we may in some way consider the will of God, that He willed His Son to become a victim, and this sacrifice as the greatest of all, and understand that in this very sad punishment the wrath of God against our sins is shown, and again mercy is proposed. Because this death is a propitiation for us. In this thought let us truly be terrified by the acknowledgment of the wrath of God, and again let us be lifted up in our terrors by faith, and let us give thanks that by this sacrifice of His Son, God, being appeased, has received us. These things have been said several times above, but now in the final agony of Christ they must be repeated most of all, which cannot be read and thought upon by the pious without some consternation of mind.

Concerning this eclipse of the sun, it is known that it happened at the time of the opposition of the moon and the sun, because the Jewish people celebrate the Passover in the middle of the lunar month. Since, however, it is certain that in the customary order of nature eclipses of the sun happen only in the conjunction of the moon and the sun, it is manifest that this eclipse of the sun happened entirely against the order of nature. It was therefore a testimony of God signifying that He was a spectator of this slaughter, and that He would be an avenger. It was signified also that light was snatched away from all the enemies of Christ, and that they would be in horrible and eternal darkness and punishments. But not the very laceration of the body, not the horrible suspension on the cross, so strike the minds thinking about the passion of Christ, as this sad cry: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?

What kind of complaint is this in the Son of God? Does it indicate that he is deserted and cast away? These words are taken from Psalm 22, which must be considered in its entirety if we wish in any way to think how sad this sentence is. I have said above several times about the sorrows of Christ, and about their causes, or objects. First, it is natural and common to all that the laceration of the body brings pain; thus also Lawrence suffered, but when joy is felt in the heart because of the presence and favor of God, one is less tormented by those external pains. Secondly, it is natural and common to all to flee death with horrible consternation, but this consternation too is overwhelmed by the joy of the heart, which determines that we please God, and it looks upon eternal life and does not doubt that it is already passing to the sight of God and the fellowship of Christ and all the saints. Here Paul cries out: I desire to be dissolved, and Stephen rejoices, seeing Jesus standing at the right hand of God.

Why therefore is the pain of Christ greater? Because he himself is pressed by another horrible object, which Lawrence and Stephen do not feel, and which Christ bore for this reason, because we cannot bear it. For he himself feels not only the lacerations of the body and that natural flight from death, but he feels peculiar terrors, by which GOD shows him wrath against our sins, just as sometimes in true contrition the pious feel horrible dreads, or confusions, or consternations, as if they were cast away by God, concerning which dreads Hezekiah says: As a lion he has crushed all my bones. And David says: For your arrows are fixed in me, you have confirmed your hand upon me: There is no peace to my bones from the face of my sins.

But that this pain may be recognized by us in some way, let us either look upon our own sins ourselves, or let us think of David oppressed by horrible pain, when he recognizes that he had provided the cause for these such great sins and scandals which followed his fall: Because of my sin, he says, God being angry, permitted the sedition to be moved, and indeed by my son; the sedition was followed by the defilement of my wives, and much slaughter in the whole kingdom, and many other crimes which accompany internal discords, and innumerable souls were oppressed by the eternal wrath of God because of the sedition. Many saints died of sadness because of the scandal. Many saints also by the contagion of the sedition shook off the Holy Spirit, and were oppressed by the eternal wrath of God, nor is there any doubt that some of David's wives were extinguished by grief. Looking at this such great mass of evils, David thinks that he is a plague to the Church of God, and a vessel of wrath, and perhaps eternally cast away by God.

In such pain there is some image of the sorrows of Christ. For as David sustains terrors because of his own sins, so the Son of God sustains terrors because of our sins, as if he himself had polluted himself with so many of our crimes: for he derives into himself the wrath of God, which otherwise was going to oppress us. And this such great matter is signified by many sayings. Isaiah says: That he was struck by God, by which description he signifies that Christ was not only lacerated by human cruelty. Lawrence is burned, nor is he tormented in his heart as if cast away by God. Another thing is much sadder, to judge oneself to be cast away by God as a vessel of wrath. Thus struggling with himself on the cross, Christ utters this saddest voice: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? As if he were saying, I do not lament because of the laceration of the body, or because of death, but because of another far sadder evil, that you forsake me, that I do not feel in my heart the joy which other saints feel, whom you console. Nay, I feel that you are horribly angry at the sins of the human race, for which I am now guilty, I say before you: It would not be most bitter for me to be disapproved by the judgments of the world, but to feel your wrath is sad. And although the magnitude of the sorrows of Christ cannot be either explained by human words or comprehended by thought, yet it is necessary for the pious to consider them in some way, so that we may learn of the wrath of God against sins, and in some way celebrate the magnitude of the burden which Christ sustained for us. And since God repeats these things often through the Prophets and Apostles, he certainly wants this doctrine to sound in the Church. Therefore let us excite our minds to the thought of these greatest things, and let us pray to God that he may kindle light in our hearts, so that we may understand this agony of Christ, and this such great benefit more and more, and give thanks for it.

The seventh topic is about the mother commended to John. For as to many other parts of this history, because they are less obscure, I will not add an interpretation, so that all may understand that by the sarcasms are signified the audacity and furies of the hypocrites and Epicureans, who at all times most proudly mock Christ, the Gospel, and the Church. By the division of the garments, both the heretics tearing apart the Gospel and variously mocking the words of Christ, and indeed also other impious men, such as Julian and his like, who seized the resources of the Church, by which it was then necessary for ministers to be fed, but omitting these, I will speak about the mother commended to John.

First, let us here think about the faith and fortitude of the mother; this fortitude far exceeds human strength, because the mother is present as a spectator of such torments of her son, and is not extinguished by grief. Nor is it credible that any mother in the whole human race could have endured, or can endure, such a spectacle. It is necessary, therefore, that there was in her a great light and a great strength of faith. She remembered the conception, she knew the predictions of the Prophets concerning the sacrifice of the Messiah, and she understood them better than the Apostles; she thought of the resurrected Lazarus and other examples. Therefore, she knew that this sacrifice of her son was happening by the singular and ineffable counsel of God, and was a λύτρον for the whole human race. Nor did she mourn the sins of the human race less than the death of her son himself, but in these sorrows she knew that God must be obeyed, and she awaited the resuscitation of her son. In these good objects of yours, that is, in the will of God and the resuscitation, as she looked with faith, the magnitude of her grief was somewhat softened. Let us, however, remember this example in our own afflictions, so that we too may learn to show obedience and faith.

Secondly, let this type be considered: just as Christ commended his mother to John, so he commends the Church to all the pious, and especially to teachers and governors. There are always many and great sorrows for the Church, that is, for the pious and the weak, for it is torn by dissensions of dogmas and feels the cruelty of tyrants. Here, let pious teachers heal those who are wavering or erring, let them fortify the inexperienced, confirm the weak, and unfold obscure and intricate questions, lest men, entangled by doubts, fall into despair. Let pious princes also hear the Son of God preaching on the very cross, so that by their duties they may cherish, protect, and help Mother Church. Concerning this matter, precepts are often given, as in Psalm 41: Blessed is he who considers the needy and the poor; the Lord will deliver him in the day of evil. Let us compare this precept of the Psalm to this image, in which shines the φιλοστοργία of Christ, not only toward his mother but also toward the universal Church. For on our account this public commendation is made at such a time, and Christ truly loves the whole Church as his mother, from which he assumed human nature, which is a manifest and certain testimony of his immense love toward us.

The eighth topic is the burial of Christ, concerning which the time should be especially considered. Christ is in the sepulcher for the whole Sabbath. Although the type of the old Sabbath signifies many things, yet it also signified this rest of the Son of God in the sepulcher. For then God truly rested in a wonderful way, when that human nature, to which the divine is united, most truly dies. For as Peter says: Christ suffered in the flesh, but yet in the meantime the divine nature united to the human rested, so that it could suffer and die as human, as Irenaeus says: That is, he did not exert his powers, but obeyed the eternal Father in this humility. For it is true, and the Church has always taught it so, that the divine nature did not depart from the body of Christ, nor from his soul, even after death. Therefore Damascenus says: What the λόγος once assumed, he never afterwards dismissed, nor was the divine nature of the Son of God ever separated from the body or from the soul of Christ after the assumption, and yet this person, who is Christ, truly died, because the soul was separated from the body, as the text says, Matt. 27: Crying with a loud voice, he expired. In the meantime, the divine nature united to both the body and the soul rested. This secret wisdom will have to be learned in eternal life; now, as it is handed down in the Word, it must be embraced by faith, nor can it be either comprehended by human thought or explained in words. But this admirable rest in death and the sepulcher is the obedience decreed in the secret counsel of God, which was both the cause and the signification of the future resurrection, and for us this admirable rest, that is, obedience, merited reconciliation and eternal life, and it made our death, which would have been a damned thing, now a rest, pleasing to God, and a journey to eternal life. Without Christ, dead men would have lain, and do lie, in hell, but those dying in Christ have lain and do lie in the sepulcher of Christ. Indeed, we all, immediately after conversion to God has taken place in this life, lie in the sepulcher of Christ, we suffer this carnal nature to be mortified, and by faith we await the resurrection. This doctrine is set forth in the burial of Christ. But it is mocked by the idle and the Epicureans, nor can it be understood except by those who in great sorrows seek consolation, and recognize that they are being laid not into hell, but into the sepulcher of Christ, in which they know that this rest is pleasing to God, and that it is the way to eternal life. Therefore I will not add a longer explanation, because these things must be learned in true sorrows, but nevertheless it is useful for the pious to be reminded.

Here also the question is raised concerning the article of the descent into hell, what that descent is. First, some understand the descent into hell before death, the very humiliation by which Christ sustained the horrible sense of the wrath of God against our sins. Some understand death and burial itself, but let us simply believe that Christ truly resurrected the fathers, as Peter says, and preached to the spirits who were in prison. I understand this meeting with the fathers according to the saying of Peter to be the descent into hell, nor do I wish to dispute these things curiously, but let the modest and pious think upon certain mysteries concerning the wondrous death and resurrection of Christ, which the resurrected fathers beheld, signified in the saying of Peter, which are not more plainly recounted.

Latin:

Caput XIX.

Actus quartus fere ab horae sextae initio ex- ordiens, continet horas tres, et aliquanto amplius. Nam Christus hora nona mortuus est, cumque fuerint horae καιρικαὶ usitatae eo tempore sextam sciamus esse meridianam horam, deinde vero no- nam, quae nobis est a meridie tertia. Continen- tur autem in hoc actu condemnatio facta a Pilato, supplicium Christi, dicta eius in cruce, mors et sepultura. Saepe autem iam dictum est, magni- tudinem harum rerum non posse ullius oratione, aut ullis voluminibus exponi, sed assidue in omni vita repetendam esse cogitationem huius mirandi consilii Dei, et sacrificii Christi, et beneficii, propter quod filius Dei victima factus est, breviter tamen recitabo aliquas partes.

Primus locus est: Pilatus metuens, ne apud Caesarem accusaretur, contra conscientiam condemnat Christum, cum quidem prius multis signis ostendat se hanc ipsam condemnationem improbare, ait se hunc Iesum dimissurum esse, ut solebant in festo aliquem captivum dimittere, Sed Iudaei anteferunt latronem, et seditionis autorem, lavat et manus, et ait se innocentem esse, quod signum erat laesae conscientiae, nam revera sciebat se non esse innocentem: Faciens enim scelus, et consentiens, eandem poenam merentur. De hoc loco non dicam plura, sed hic caecitatem esse furorem Regum, Principum, et potentum omnium deploremus, qui simili modo saeviunt in Ecclesiam, incitati ab impiis sacerdotibus. Et quanquam volunt derivare culpam in sacerdotes, dicunt se oportere sequi autoritatem Ecclesiae, tamen revera sunt et erunt rei coram Deo, quia non solis sacerdotibus mandatum est, ut sciant Evangelium, sed omnibus hominibus dictum est de Christo: Hunc audite, et nominatim regibus dictum est: Et nunc reges intelligite, erudimini qui iudicatis terram.

Nomen Gabbatha significat locum eminentem a vocabulo Gaba, quod est altitudo, et allegoria monet eminentia et summa imperia belligerari cum Deo, et in Christum et Ecclesiam saevire, sicut plerumque factum esse horribiliter tota mundi historia ostendit. Hic quoque tristissima voce Iudaei seipsos condemnant, dicentes: Se nullum habere Regem nisi Caesarem, palam negant Messiam, et vaticinantur se habituros Caesarem, id est, non Messiam salvatorem, sed Caesarem Titum, qui aliquanto post totam Iudaicam politiam magna crudelitate deleturus est. Significat autem Caesar idem quod crudelis, palam etiam clamitant: Sit sanguis eius super nos et filios nostros. Cohorrescere omnes pios necesse est, hanc vocem audientes, aut cogitantes: cum autem hunc tantum furorem huius populi consideramus, excitemur, ut veris et ardentibus votis petamus, ut a Deo gubernemur, ne in similem amentiam et furorem ruamus.

Secundus locus est. Milites educunt Christum, et imponunt ei crucem. Adiungunt autem ei Simonem Cyrenaeum, forte in via oblatum, quem cogunt ut adiuvet Christum, postea addun- tur et duo latrones una crucifigendi. Nomen Gol- gatha significat vel acervum, id est, locum exci- tatum, seu lapidibus, seu cespitibus: vel ipsam calvam cranii, seu capitis humani, quod alibi in textu Hebraeo scribitur Golgatha. Cum autem omnia membra longius enarrare non possim, nunc tantum de Simonis Cyrenaei allegoria dicam, cum id exemplum, quod videtur exiguam circumstan- tiam continere, tam diligenter recitatum sit. Si- gnificat autem hic Simon semper in afflictionibus Ecclesiae aliquos esse, cum principes, tum docto- res, tum alios homines pios, qui partem crucis gestant, ut nunc, cum reges irati delere Evange- lium, et interficere doctores conantur, aliqui prin- cipes et gubernatores, in aulis et civitatibus magna pericula et aerumnas sustinent, in defensione Ec- clesiarum et docentium: imo etiam noster ordo scholasticus vere partem crucis gestat, et constat nomine Simeon significari auditorem. Studiosi discentes Evangelium simul implicantur periculis, multi nunc pii scholastici magnas miserias susti- nent propter Evangelium, sed Deus reddet eis praemia, sicut et huic Simeoni reddidit. Nam filios eius Alexandrum et Rufum postea ad munus Evangelii vocavit.

Tertius locus est concio Christi ad mulieres, quae eiulantes comitantur Christum gestantem crucem. Non enim tantum atrocitas supplicii con- sideranda est, sed etiam causae, et sermones Chri- sti interim habiti, qui amplissimam doctrinam con- tinent. Est autem concio poenitentiae, primum reprehendens mulieres nondum intelligentes, cur Christus hunc agonem sustineat, deinde horribiles poenas praedicens, quae et hunc populum et om- nes impios oppressurae sunt: tertio collationem faciens afflictionum Ecclesiae et impiorum. Ac duo priora membra satis perspicua sunt, mulieres communi mediocrium hominum στοργῇ deplora- bant Christi calamitatem propter ipsum. Non no- rant causas, videlicet pati Christum propter nostra peccata. Necesse est autem omnibus hominibus hanc doctrinam tradi et inculcari, nostris peccatis Deum vere irasci, propter nostra peccata metuen- das esse poenas, nostra mala agnoscenda et deplo- randa esse. Rursus autem sciendum, tolli nostra mala per Christum. Stultitia est autem, ut dici- tur, foris sapere, id est, ignorantem propria mala, deplorare aliena, ut Priami aut Hectoris, et tamen haec stultitia communis est maximae parti homi- num. Hinc illa sunt: Medice cura te ipsum. Item: ἄλλων ἰατρὸς αὐτὸς ἕλκεσι βρύων. Item: Odi sapientem, qui sibi non sapit. Primum nostras miserias agnoscamus, et discamus, quae remedia Deus nobis tradiderit.

Nec obscurae sunt tristissimae conciones de poenis impiorum, quarum hic fit mentio: tunc dicent montibus, Cadite super nos. Hic non solum Ierosolymorum excidium cogitemus, sed etiam similia exempla omnium temporum, quae ostendunt saepe accidere hominibus tristiora morte ipsa, ut parentibus multo tristius morte est videre saeva supplicia natorum, expetitur igitur mors, ut finiantur poenae, quantum igitur mali est post hanc vitam, cumne morte quidem finiri possunt? haec monet Christus non tantum has mulieres, sed totum genus humanum. Ac praecipua tot spectaculorum horribilium in hac vita causa est, quia Deus vult conspici iram suam adversus pec- cata, vult nos commonefieri, ut Psalmus 39. in- quit: Propter iniquitates corripis homines, in- tueamur ergo nostras et alienas calamitates, ut timor Dei in nobis excitetur.

In tertio membro dicitur: Si in viridi ligno hoc faciunt, in arido quid fiet? id est, si viridis et foecunda arbor extirpatur, quid fiet de arida et sterili? Qua figura significatur haec collatio, cum membra Dei, quae fructus Deo placentes ferunt, ut Abel, Ieremias, Baptista, sustineant magnas calamitates, quid fiet de impiis? Congruit haec Christi concio cum dicto Salomonis, Prov. 11.: Si iustus in terra recipit, quanto magis impius et peccator? Ad quae 1. Pet. 4. adduntur haec verba: Iudicium a domo Dei incipit. Hic autem reclamat humana ratio, offendi se hac ipsa con- fusione, quod bonis male sit, et malis bene, dis- putant mentes aut casu omnia ferri, nec regi res humanas providentia, aut gubernationem in- iustam esse: hanc disputationem philosophia non satis explicare potest, quae non novit primos fon- tes humanarum miseriarum, sed hi monstrantur in doctrina Ecclesiae. Cum ergo sic argumenta- tur ratio: Iustis bene esse debet, iniustis male: Ieremias, Baptista, sunt iusti, ergo bene esse eis debeat. Hic respondet Ecclesia, primum de maiore, verissima est maior, est enim lex Dei, ut primum praeceptum testatur, et quidem adeo vera est, ut Deus non tantum perituris bonis compenset iusticiam, seu obedientiam, sed aeter- nis, ut sint firma, et non pereuntia praemia. Sed quo ordine fiat haec distributio, Evangelium docet, quod simul affirmat omnes homines morti, et aliis calamitatibus subiectos esse, quia omnes circumferimus peccatum. Nunc igitur ad mino- rem respondendum est: Ieremias, Baptista, et similes sunt iusti, scilicet imputatione propter filium Dei mediatorem, sed nondum sunt iusti tota novitate, imo magna et tristis caligo, et multi morbi adhuc in cordibus omnium sanctorum in hac vita haerent. Vere autem irascitur Deus pec- cato, et hanc iram praecipue ab Ecclesia vult in- telligi. Ideo premit Ecclesiam in hac vita magis, quam reliquam hominum fecem, postea accedunt et aliae plures causae, videlicet quod vult has ip- sas sanctorum afflictiones testimonia esse de vita aeterna. Cum enim Deus testetur se approbare Paulum in hac vita, cum per eum resuscitat mor- tuos, et tamen sinat eum interfici ab inquinatis- simo tyranno, necesse est postea restare iudi- cium, in quo Deus ostendet se non oblitum esse Pauli, et anteferre Paulum teterrimo tyranno. Sed haec doctrina de causis alibi copiosius reci- tata est, nunc ad textum redeo. Christus admo- net mulieres de ira Dei adversus peccata omnium hominum, ac testatur etiam puniri. Quod vero ipse patitur, ideo fit, quia ipse est mediator et intercessor, quid in sese derivavit iram Dei ad- versus nostra peccata, sicut Baptista inquit: Ecce agnus Dei, qui tollit peccata mundi.

Quartus locus est ipsa crucifixio, ubi in pri- mis observandum est dictum, quod citat et il- lustrat Paulus Gal. 3.: Maledictus omnis qui pen- det in ligno, quae verba ex cap. 12. Deut. sumta sunt, ubi expresse additum est: Maledictus a Deo, qui pendet in ligno, sic alibi de poenis non loquitur scriptura. Nam poenae ipsae non fa- ciunt homines reos, id est, propter poenas non irascitur Deus hominibus, sed propter peccata. Cur igitur de hac poena tam atrociter loquitur Deus? Existimo tantum propter mortem Christi hoc dictum esse, ut intelligatur in hunc deriva- tam esse maledictionem, cui genus humanum subiectum fuit, id est, hunc sustinuisse poenam debitam iusticiae Dei, et ita pro nobis persolvisse λύτρον. Caeterum quam tristis appellatio sit dici maledictum a Deo, id non potest verbis ex- plicari, sed discamus pia meditatione, cum que- relas in Psalmis et alibi legimus. Item cum ipsi aliquo modo nostra peccata aspicimus ac expa- vescimus, metuentes vere nos a Deo abiici in aeternam damnationem. Etsi dolebat David se ex regno eiici a filio, quem valde diligebat, motam esse seditionem, et se exui gloria sapientiae et iusticiae, quam habuerat, tamen hi dolores non erant summi. Alia multo maior moestitia excruciabat eum, quod videbat suum delictum causam esse tantorum scelerum et scandalorum, in quibus multi, qui fuerant sancti, horribiliter perierunt. Hic sese iudicabat esse pestem Ecclesiae et populi Dei, et molem peccatorum tantam sentiebat, ut agnosceret se non posse eam sustinere, metuebat igitur se abiectum esse a Deo, ut Saulem aut alios tyrannos, qui fuerunt vasa irae Dei. Hi dolores Davidis aliquo modo declarant atrocitatem huius descriptionis, cum dicitur Christus factus esse maledictum, sed haec a profanis aut securis mentibus non intelliguntur. Ideo et nos peccata nostra aspiciamus, et cogitatione irae Dei, et horribilium poenarum expavescamus, ita fiet, ut aliquo modo hanc doctrinam intelligamus, imo hic pavor et hic dolor est vera meditatio passionis Christi.

Quintus locus: Multa sunt dicta Christi in cruce, sed concio praecipua est ad latronem, et spectaculum ipsum est insigne. Latrones duo sunt imago totius generis humani, quod totum est morti subiectum, sed pars liberatur per Christum, pars manet in morte. Ita totum genus humanum ibi pendere cogitemus, ut revera omnes variis calamitatibus et morte illam ipsam speciem latronum referimus. Quod autem impius latro medio supplicio tamen ludit, et Christum venenatis ironiis subsannat, manifestus furor est in tanto cruciatu et ipsa morte petulanter ludere, sed huius amentia significat similem esse omnium impiorum securitatem in toto genere humano. Nero secure ludit et deridet Deum, nec sentit se in mediis inferis et tristissimis miseriis esse.

Econtra alter latro agnoscit delictum suum et causam poenae, non est securus, non ludit, ut ille subsannator, sed iudicat se a Deo puniri, et insuper metuit aeternas poenas, clare enim dicit: Nos iuste plectimur. Magnis igitur doloribus et pavoribus excruciatur, sed interim cum cogitat quis sit hic vir iustus, qui dictus est Messias, qui nunc est supplicii socius, quaerit veras consolationes, et fortassis accenduntur hae eius cogitationes, cum videt Deum mirandis prodigiis significare se spectatorem esse huius supplicii, et fore se iudicem. Nam hoc colloquium habetur, cum iam medio die solis lumen extinctum est, ut ex Lucae narratione apparet. Agnoscit igitur hunc iustum virum esse Messiam, et primum palam discernit eum a se, altero socio supplicii, affirmat eum nihil mali fecisse. Deinde ipsum alloquitur, ac faciens mentionem futuri ipsius regni, ostendit, qui credat, videlicet hunc vi- rum, etiamsi nunc pendeat in cruce ac moriturus sit, tamen non interiturum esse, sed victurum, et vitam aliis ipsum invocantibus daturum esse. Denique rectius intelligit doctrinam de Messia, quam omnes Pharisaei. Agnoscit in vita Eccle- siam in cruce esse, sed habituram per hunc Do- minum vitam, iusticiam, et gloriam aeternam. Petit igitur ab eo haec bona, inquiens: Memento mei Domine, cum veneris in regnum tuum. Haec sunt verba fidei eluctatae iam ex doloribus, morte, pavoribus, et intelligentis summam do- ctrinae Evangelii. Respondet autem Christus, tan- quam pronuncians absolutionem, et eum recipiens in Ecclesiam, et quidem iusiurandum addens: Amen dico tibi, hodie mecum eris in Paradiso, id est, in loco Ecclesiae beatae, quae novam et aeternam lucem, sapientiam, iusticiam et glo- riam habet.

Hic est ordo colloquii, quod sciamus propter multas causas recitari. Principio testatur Deum servare Ecclesiam, et semper aliquos excitare confessores, etiam tunc cum hostes triumphant, et putant deletam esse. Tunc dissipata erat Ec- clesia, Christus ipse pendet in cruce ac moritur, mater luctu et moestitia impeditur, ne multa lo- quatur, Apostoli diffugiunt. Tali tempore in tanta dissipatione incipiunt concionari sol et sco- puli hiscentes, et fit Apostolus hic latro, de sublimi concionans toti generi humano.

Secundo, conversio et salvatio huius latro- nis imago est conversionis et salvationis singulo- rum electorum. Non putes te aliter ingressurum esse vitam aeternam, quem hic latro ingreditur. Non fingas te afferre merita ad Deum, sed sumus rei irae Dei, et mortis aeternae omnes, ut hic latro, sicut Paulus inquit, Roman 3.: Ut omne os obturetur, et reus sit totus mundus Deo. Hunc latronem menti tuae proponas in contri- tione, fide, absolutione, cruce, et bonis operi- bus. Harum partium omnium exempla hic pro- posita sunt. Contritio est agnitio peccati, quod ait latro se iuste puniri, et dolet se Deum offen- disse, et sentit iram Dei, hac ipsa poena commo- nefactus, et quidem publice fatetur peccatum suum, et praedicat iudicium Dei iustum esse. Haec omnia pertinent ad contritionem, ut illae voces Danielis 9.: Tibi Domine iusticia, nobis autem confusio faciei.

Fidem eius clarissime ostendit petitio: Me- mento mei Domine, quando venies in regnum tuum. Vere enim intelligit hunc socium suppli- cii, quanquam iam moriturum, tamen esse Mes- siam tollentem peccata et mortem, et redimentem genus humanum hac sua morte, sicut ex Esaia potuit aliqua dicta meminisse: petit igitur ab eo remissionem peccatorum et vitam aeternam. Et ut fides eius confirmetur, audit dulcissimam ab- solutionem: Hodie mecum eris in paradiso. Iam vide in eo incoatam obedientiam. Inerudite enim dicitur nulla fuisse bona opera huius latronis post conversionem, verum est, non potest petere re- missionem peccatorum propter ulla bona opera, ideoquae proponitur nobis, ut doceat nos de gra- tuita reconciliatione, sed iam conversus habet magnas virtutes. Contritio ipsa et dolor propter peccatum, et confessio tribuens Deo iusticiam, sunt bona opera, et testimonia accensae in eo di- lectionis Dei. Deinde fides ipsa bonum opus est, cum quo necesse est dilectionem Dei, et multa bona opera coniuncta esse. Accedit et intellectus doctrinae de cruce et patientia, scit iam genus humanum propter peccatum in mortem et calami- tates mersum esse, nec tamen propter calamita- tes reiici homines, sed Deum postulare hanc obe- dientiam, et recipere confugientes, et Spiritu sancto sustentare. Et iam in ipsa consolatione, cum cor fide erigeretur, dicit hanc ipsam senten- tiam, quae est apud Esaiam capite ultimo, quae affirmat Deum habitare cum contritis. Didicit igitur hanc Evangelii sapientiam non monstratam in lege, et longe positam supra et extra philoso- phiam et captum humanae rationis, et iam cor- pore pendens in cruce ac moriens, tamen vere vivit vita aeterna, laetatur agnitione Dei et Mes- siae, et praestat Deo hanc obedientiam vera tole- rantia, et expectat novum Messiae regnum in paradiso. Longe igitur superat sapientia et virtutibus, non solum Pharisaeos, sed etiam Apostolos.

Postremo et externa bona opera habet, con- fessionem peccati sui, et iusti iudicii Dei, invo- cationem Christi, et obiurgationem adversarii. Nam refutare maledicentes Evangelio, est opus praeceptum in his sententiis, Lucae 9.: Quem mei pudebit et meorum sermonum, hunc confun- det filius hominis. Et Psalm. 118.: Et loquebar de testimoniis tuis in conspectu regum, et non confundebar. Pertinet autem exemplum ad omnes homines, ut discant opus necessarium esse profi- teri fidem, et eam declarare refutatione blasphe- miarum.

Etsi igitur homines profani et potentes tali- bus refutationibus offenduntur, tamen sciamus hoc officium necessarium esse, et vere placere Deo, et hanc consolationem nos in scholis memi- nerimus, quae plurimum incurrunt in odia po- tentum, propter tales refutationes.

Sextus, postrema pars est epitasis omnium maxime terribilis. Hic iam obscurato Sole contra naturae ordinem, et dura saxa sine ulla vi hu- mana rumpuntur, et mortui divinitus vita recepta prodeunt, filius Dei inter clamores et preces mo- ritur: cum tota rerum natura moveatur, coelum et terra, dolendum est nos adeo duros esse, ut tantae rei cogitatione non contremiscamus. Ore- mus igitur Deum, ut nostras mentes accendat, ut aliquo modo voluntatem Dei, quod filium victi- mam fieri voluit, et hoc sacrificium omnium sum- mum consideremus, et intelligamus in hac ipsa tam tristi poena ostendi iram Dei, adversus nostra peccata, et rursus proponi misericordiam. Quia haec mors est propiciatio pro nobis. In hac co- gitatione vere expavescamus agnitione irae Dei, et rursus in pavoribus erigamur fide, et agamus gratias, quod hoc sacrificio filii Deus placatus nos recepit. Haec supra aliquoties dicta sunt, sed nunc in extremo agone Christi maxime repetenda sunt, qui legi et cogitari a piis sine aliqua animi consternatione non potest.

De hac Eclipsi Solis notum est eam factam esse tempore oppositionis Lunae et Solis, quia populus Iudaicus celebrat Pascha in medio mense lunari. Cum autem certum sit usitato ordine naturae eclipses Solis tantum in coniunctione Lu- nae et Solis fieri, manifestum est hanc eclipsin So- lis prorsus contra naturae ordinem factam esse. Fuit igitur testimonium Dei significantis se specta- torem esse huius necis, et se vindicem fore. Si- gnificatum est etiam omnibus hostibus Christi lu- cem eripi, et futuros eos in horrendis et aeter- nis tenebris et poenis. Sed non ipsa laceratio corporis, non hor- renda suspensio in cruce, sic feriunt animos co- gitantes de passione Christi, sicut hic tristis clamor: Deus Deus meus, quare dereliquis me?

Qualis est haec querela in filio Dei? An indicat se desertum et abiectum esse? Haec verba ex Psal. 22. sumta sunt, qui totus considerandus est, si aliquo modo volumus cogitare, quam tri- stis sit haec sententia. Dixi autem supra aliquo- ties de doloribus Christi, et de eorum causis, sive obiectis. Primum naturale et commune est omnibus, quod laceratio corporis affert dolorem, sic etiam Laurentius dolebat, sed cum in corde sentitur laetitiae propter Dei praesentiam et favo- rem, minus excruciatur illis externis doloribus. Secundo, naturale et commune est omnibus hor- ribili consternatione fugere mortem, sed obruitur haec etiam consternatio laetitia cordis, quod statuit nos Deo placere, et intuetur vitam aeternam et non dubitat se iam Dei conspectum, et consuetudinem Christi et omnium sanctorum transire. Hic cla- mat Paulus: Cupio dissolvi, et Stephanus laetatur, videns Iesum stantem ad dextram Dei.

Cur igitur maior dolor est Christi? Quia ipse alio obiecto horribili premitur, quod non sen- tiunt Laurentius et Stephanus, quodque Chri- stus ideo tulit, quia nos ferre non possumus. Ipse enim sentit non possumus. Ipse enim sen- tit non tantum lacerationes corporis, et illam naturalem mortis fugam, sed sentit peculiares terrores, quibus ostendit ipsi DEUS iram ad- versus peccata nostra, sicut aliquando in vera contritione sentiunt pii horribiles pavores, seu confusiones, seu consternationes, quasi abiician- tur a Deo, de quibus pavoribus inquit Ezechias: Sicut leo contrivit omnia ossa mea. Et David in- quit: Quoniam sagittae tuae infixae sunt mihi confirmasti super mea manum tuam: Non est pax ossibus meis a facie peccatorum meorum.

At ut aliquo modo hic dolor a nobis agno- scatur, aut propria peccata aspiciamus ipsi, aut cogitemus Davidem horribili dolore oppressum, cum agnoscit se causam praebuisse his tantis pec- catis et scandalis, quae lapsum ipsius secuta sunt: Propter meum peccatum, inquit, Deus iratus, permisit moveri seditionem, et quidem a meo filio, seditionem secuta est coniugum mearum contaminatio, et multa caedes in toto regno, et alia multa scelera quae comitantur intestinas dis- cordias, et innumerabiles animae oppressae sunt aeterna ira Dei propter seditionem. Multi sancti propter scandalum moesticia mortui sunt. Multi sancti etiam contagio seditionis excusserunt Spiri- tum sanctum, et oppressi sunt aeterna ira Dei, nec dubium est aliquas Davidis coniuges moerore extinctas esse. Hanc tantam molem malorum in- tuens David, cogitat se pestem esse Ecclesiae Dei, et vas irae, et fortassis in aeternum abiectum a Deo.

In tali dolore aliqua imago est dolorum Chri- sti. Nam ut David sustinet terrores propter pro- pria peccata, ita filius Dei sustinet terrores pro- pter nostra peccata, quasi ipse se tot nostris sce- leribus polluisset : derivat enim in sese iram Dei, quae alioqui nos opressura erat. Estque significata haec tanta res multis dictis. Esaias in- quit: Percussum esse a Deo, qua descriptione significat non tantum humana saevitia lacera- tum esse Christum. Uritur Laurentius, nec ex- cruciatur in corde tanquam a Deo abiectus. Alia res multo tristior est, iudicare se a Deo tanquam vas irae abiectum esse. Ita luctans secum Chri- stus in cruce, edit hanc tristissimam vocem: Deus meus, Deus meus, quare dereliquisti me? quasi dicat, non lamentor propter corporis lace- rationem, aut propter mortem, sed propter aliud longe tristius malum, quod tu me relinquis, quod non sentio in corde laetitiam, quam sentiunt alii sancti, quos consolaris. Imo sentio te hor- ribiliter irasci peccatis generis humani, propter quae ego nunc reus sum, coram te inquam: Non esset mihi acerbissimum mundi iudiciis impro- bari, sed tuam iram sentire triste est. Etsi autem non potest magnitudo dolorum Christi, aut ver- bis homanis exponi, aut cogitatione compre- hendi, tamen necesse est pios aliquo modo eos considerare, ut discamus iram Dei adversus pec- cata, et aliquo modo celebremus magnitudinem oneris, quod pro nobis Christus sustinuit. Et cum Deus haec per Prophetas et Apostolos saepe repetat, vult certe sonare hanc doctrina in Eccle- sia. Ideo excitemus mentes ad harum maximarum rerum cogitationem, et oremus Deum, ut lucem in cordibus nostris accendat, ut hunc Christi agonem, et hoc tantum beneficium magis magis- que intelligamus, et pro eo gratias agamus.

Septimus locus de matre commendata Io- hanni. Nam multis aliis partibus huius historiae, quia minus obscurae sunt, non addam interpreta- tionem, ut omnes intelligunt per sarcasmos signi- ficari audaciam et furores hypocritarum et Epicu- reorum, omni tempore superbissime deridentium Christum, Evangelium, et Ecclesiam. Per di- visionem vestium, tum haereticos dilacerantes Evangelium, et varie ludentes dictis Christi, tum vero etiam alios impios, ut Iulianum, et similes, qui facultates Ecclesiae, quibus ministros tunc ali necesse erat, rapuerunt, sed his omissis, di- cam de matre commendata Iohanni.

Primum hic cogitemus de fide et fortitudine matris, longe superat robur humanum haec for- titudo, quod adest mater spectatrix talium sup- pliciorum filii, et non extinguitur dolore. Nec credibile est ullam matrem in toto genere hu- mano tale spectaculum perferre potuisse, aut posse. Necesse est igitur in ea magnam lucem, et magnum robur fidei fuisse. Meminerat con- ceptum, norat Prophetarum praedictiones de sa- crificio Messiae, et melius eas intelligebat quam Apostoli, cogitabat resuscitatum Lazarum, et alia exempla. Ideo sciebat hoc sacrificium filii sin- gulari et inenarrabili consilio Dei fieri, et esse λύτρον pro toto genere humano. Nec minus lu- gebat generis humani peccata, quam ipsius filii mortem, sed in his doloribus obediendum esse Deo norat, et expectabat resuscitationem filii. In haec tuo bona obiecta, id est, in voluntatem Dei et resuscitationem intuenti fide, aliquantulum leniebatur magnitudo doloris. Meminerimus autem hoc exemplum in nostris afflictionibus, ut obedientiam et fidem praestare nos quoque discamus.

Secundo typus hic consideretur, sicut Chri- stus matrem Iohanni commendavit, ita Eccle- siam omnibus piis, et praecipue doctoribus et gu- bernatoribus commendat. Semper multi et magni dolores sunt Ecclesiae, id est piorum et imbecil- lium, nam et dissidiis dogmatum laceratur, et sentit tyrannorum saevitiam. Hic pii doctores sanent ambigentes, aut errantes, praemuniant im- peritos, confirment imbecilles, evolvant obscu- ras et intricatas quaestiones, ne homines im- pliciti dubitationibus incidant in desperationes. Audiant et pii principes filium Dei in ipsa cruce concionantem, ut suis officiis matrem Ecclesiam foveant, tueantur, iuvent. De hac re saepe tra- duntur praecepta, ut Psalm. 41.: Beatus qui intelligit super egenum et pauperem, in die mala liberabit eum Dominus. Hoc praeceptum Psalmi conferamus ad hanc imaginem, in qua lucet φιλοστοργία Christi, non solum erga matrem, sed etiam erga universam Ecclesiam. Nam propter nos fit haec publica commendatio tali tempore, et Christus revera diligit ut matrem totam Ecclesiam, ex qua assumsit naturam humanam, quod est manifestum et certum testimonium ingentis amoris erga nos.

Octavus locus est sepultura Christi, de qua praecipue tempus consideretur. Christus toto sabbato est in sepulcro. Etsi typus sabbati veteris multa significat, tamen etiam hanc quietem filii Dei in sepulcro significavit. Tunc enim vere quievit Deus mirabili modo, cum illa natura humana, cui unita est divina, verissime moritur. Nam ut Petrus inquit: Christus passus est carne, sed tamen interea divina natura humanae unita quievit, ut pati et mori humana posset, sicut inquit Irenaeus: Hoc est, non exeruit suas vires, sed obedivit aeterno patri in hac humilitate. Verum est enim, et semper ita docuit Ecclesia, naturam divinam nec a corpore Christi, nec ab anima discessisse, etiam post mortem. Ideo Damascenus inquit: Quod semel assumsit λόγος, nunquam postea dimisit, nec a corpore, nec ab anima Christi unquam separata est divina natura filii Dei post assumtionem, et tamen revera haec persona, quae est Christus, mortua est, quia anima a corpore separata est, sicut textus inquit, Matth. 27.: Clamans voce magna, expiravit. Interea quievit natura divina unita et corpori et animae. Haec arcana sapientia in vita aeterna discenda erit, nunc ut traditur in verbo, amplectenda est fide, nec potest aut cogitatione humana comprehendi, aut explicari verbis. Sed haec admiranda quies in morte et sepulcro, est obedientia in arcano Dei consilio decreta, quae et causa fuit et significatio futurae resurrectionis, et nobis haec miranda quies, id est, obedientia meruit reconciliationem et vitam aeternam, et nostram mortem, quae fuisset res damnata, fecit iam quietem, Deo placentem, et iter ad vitam aeternam. Sine Christo mortui homines iacuissent, et iacent in inferno, sed morientes in Christo iacuerunt et iacent in sepulcro Christi. Imo nos omnes statim postquam in hac vita facta est conversio ad Deum, iacemus in sepulcro Christi, patimur hanc carnalem naturam mortificari, et fide expectamus resurrectionem. Haec doctrina proposita est in sepultura Christi. Sed ab otio- sis et Epicureis ridetur, nec intelligi potest, nisi ab iis, qui in magnis doloribus quaerunt conso- lationem, et agnoscunt se condi non in infer- num, sed in Christi sepulcrum, in quo sciunt placere Deo hanc quietem, eamque iter esse ad vitam aeternam. Ideo non addam longiorem enarrationem, quia haec in veris doloribus discenda sunt, sed tamen commonefieri pios utile est.

Hic etiam quaeritur de articulo descensus ad inferos, quid sit ille descensus. Primum ante mortem intelligunt aliqui descensum ad inferos, ipsam humiliationem, qua Christus horribilem sensum irae Dei adversus peccata nostra sustinuit. Aliqui ipsam mortem et sepulturam intelligunt, sed nos simpliciter sentiamus Christum revera resuscitasse patres, ut Petrus dicit, praedicasse spiritibus, qui erant in carcere. Hunc congres- sum cum patribus iuxta Petri dictum intelligo descensum ad inferos, nec curiose haec disputare volo, sed modesti et pii cogitent arcana quaedam de miranda morte et resurrectione Christi, quam spectarunt et patres resuscitati, significari in dicto Petri, quae non sunt planius recitata.

## 20:1 Argument
Chapter XX.

And on the first day of the week.

The fifth act of this history concerning the death and resurrection of Christ contains the glorious outcome of such great struggles that preceded it. For now is narrated the resurrection of the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, who after death on the third day was resurrected by divine power and lived again, human nature being entirely restored in him and mortality put off. Here, however, there is a discussion about the three days, to which I briefly reply: that it is a synecdoche, that is, even if the individual days of this three-day period are not complete, yet the body lay in the sepulcher for some part of each. For it was taken down from the cross after the ninth hour καίρικὴν, which for us is the third. Therefore, for some part of the sixth day the body was in the sepulcher. Then the following day is the space from evening to evening, and this day is complete. For he wished, undoubtedly because of a singular significance, to rest for the entire Sabbath.

The third day begins in the evening after the afternoon of the Sabbath, and the body was in the sepulcher that evening and night, and at the time of dawn, which followed that night, so also a good part of the third day is included. Let this brief accommodation suffice: For light-minded men are not to be heard, who invent bitter quibbles about the calculation of the three days.

Let us rather speak of the glory and efficacy of the resurrection itself, which is excellently depicted by antithesis. The women come to the monument to anoint the dead body. This duty signifies the worship of the law and the entire justice of the law, as the disciples of some Prophet, thinking well of the dead and judging that he was unjustly killed, show their love toward the dead. Thus those women only think that this teacher of theirs is dead, and they strive to honor him with this duty, which nevertheless would only be a certain useless watering of the dead. Such is the worship of the law; discipline labors with mediocre diligence to perform certain duties, but these serve this mortal life in some way, and do not take away death, and it is a more illustrious image adapted to doctrine. The law without the Gospel preaches only to this miserable and dead person, and discipline in some way restrains these dead limbs.

Compare now this part of the antithesis to the efficacy of the resurrected Son of God. Here he is no longer to be anointed, but to be worshiped in another way; he has lived again so that, sin being deleted and death deleted, he may restore to us justice and life, and he wishes to be recognized as the giver of justice and life, and he testifies that the eternal Father has ordained that we receive these goods on account of this mediator, and through this mediator by faith. This faith God wishes us to bring to this resurrected Lord. The end of the duties that perform rites for the dead is now here; that very resurrected Messiah restores justice to us, not that discipline which preserves dead nature, but another justice, which is light and eternal life.

This antithesis therefore being considered, let us learn why the Son of God rose again, what the efficacy of the resurrection is, where he now is, what kind of kingdom this living Messiah has; but as often elsewhere, so also in Romans 4, Paul preaches about the efficacy of the resurrection, comparing death and resurrection: He was delivered, he says, for our offenses, and was raised for our justification, that is, death is a sacrifice, by which the Son, sustaining the punishment of the law and turning away from himself the wrath of the Father against our sins, merits for us the remission of sins. But the resurrection begins the immortal life in Christ, by which, already living, he reigns at the right hand of the Father, and is effective, sends and governs the ministers of the Gospel, gives the Holy Spirit to those hearing and embracing the Gospel, intercedes for us, and gives the remission of sins, hears us when we call upon him, defends and preserves his Church, drives away devils, and their instruments, tyrants, fanatical spirits, and other impious ones, finally raises the dead, and gives eternal life to those in whom justice has been begun in this life by faith, and casts into eternal punishments all who persevere in the contempt of God. All these wonderful works are effects of the resurrection, which we should learn to apply to ourselves by faith; whenever hearts truly dismayed by the sight of their sins struggle with diffidence and despair, let us know that it is the eternal and immutable command of God that we flee to the resurrected Son of God, sitting at the right hand of the eternal Father, and believe that we are received and heard. For this reason he rose again, that he might hear, that he might be effective, that he might help this miserable mass of the human race, which he has joined to himself by an eternal covenant. The Lord is not dead and idle, as minds without the light of the Gospel imagine, but he is truly a helper and savior, truly he still cries out: Come to me all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. How difficult a thing it is in true sorrows to excite this faith, experience shows, and yet it is necessary that these struggles be learned, and that faith be confirmed in them, to look upon the resurrected Son of God and the present Church, just as if we were seeing him with the eyes of the body, and embracing him joined to us. But in order that this faith may be excited, it is necessary that the doctrine be acknowledged concerning faith, by which the remission of sins is received freely for Christ's sake. For as long as opinions taken from the law cling to minds, that we are not received, not heard, unless there are enough merits, the mind cannot be raised by true consolation, and by a true understanding of the benefits of the resurrection.

Latin:

Caput XX.

Una autem die sabbati.

Quintus actus historiae huius de morte et re- surrectione Christi continet gloriosum exitum tantorum agonum, qui praecesserunt. Nunc enim narratur resurrectio filii Dei Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui post mortem die tertio divina potentia resuscitatus revixit, integre restituta in ipso natura humana et exuta mortalitate. Hic autem disseritur de triduo, de quo breviter re- spondeo: Synecdochen esse, hoc est, etsi non sint integri singuli dies huius tridui, tamen parte ali- qua singulorum iacuit corpus in sepulcro. Depo- situm est enim a cruce post horam nonam καί- ρικὴν, quae nobis est tertia. Parte igitur aliqua diei sextae corpus fuit in sepulcro, Deinde se- quens dies spatium est a vespera ad vesperam, et hic dies integer est. Voluit enim haud dubie propter singularem significationem integro sab- bato quiescere.

Tertius dies incoatur vespere post meridiem sabbati, fuitque corpus in sepulcro eo vespere et nocte, et aurorae tempore, quae noctem illam secuta est, ita et bona pars tertii diei etiam com- prehenditur. Haec brevis accommodatio suffi- ciat: Non enim audiendi sunt homines leves, qui cavillationes acerbas de tridui computatione com- miniscuntur.

Potius de ipsa resurrectionis gloria et effica- cia dicamus, quae egregie pingitur antithesi. Mulieres veniunt ad monumentum, ut ungant mortuum corpus. Hoc officium significat cultum legis et universam iusticiam legis, ut discipuli alicuius Prophetae, bene sentientes de mortuo, et iudicantes iniuste interfectum esse ostendunt suum amorem erga mortuum. Sic illae mulieres tantum cogitant hunc suum doctorem mortuum esse, et hoc officio ornare eum student, quod tamen tantum esset inutilis quaedam mortui riga- tio. Talis est cultus legis, disciplina mediocri diligentia laborat, ut praestet aliqua officia, sed haec utcunque serviunt huic mortali vitae, et non tollunt mortem, estque imago illustrior accom- modata ad doctrinam. Lex sine Evangelio tan- tum huic miserae et mortuae concionatur, et ut- cunque disciplina coërcet haec mortua membra.

Hanc partem antithesis confer iam ad effica- ciam resuscitati filii Dei. Hic iam non ungendus est, sed alio modo colendus, revixit ut deleto pec- cato, deleta morte nobis reddat iusticiam et vitam, et vult agnosci dator iusticiae et vitae, et testatur aeternum patrem constituisse, ut haec bona propter hunc mediatorem, et per hunc me- diatorem fide accipiamus. Hanc fidem vult nos afferre Deus ad hunc resuscitatum Dominum. Finis est iam officiorum, quae mortuos perfun- dunt, ille ipse resuscitatus Messias, iusticiam nobis reddit, non illam mortuae naturae serva- tricem disciplinam, sed aliam iusticiam, quae est lux et vita aeterna.

Hac igitur antithesi considerata, discamus quare resurrexerit filius Dei, quae sit efficacia re- surrectionis, ubi nunc sit, quale regnum sit huius viventis Messiae, ut autem saepe alias, ita et Rom. 4. concionatur Paulus de efficacia resur- rectionis, conferens mortem et resurrectionem: Traditus est, inquit, propter delicta nostra, et resuscitatus est propter iusticiam nostram, id est, mors est sacrificium, quo filius sustinens poenam legis, et se derivans iram patris adversus nostra peccata, meretur nobis remissionem peccatorum. Sed resurrectio incoat vitam immortalem in Chri- sto, qua iam vivens regnat ad dextram patris, et est efficax, mittit et gubernat Evangelii ministros, dat Spiritum sanctum audientibus et amplectenti- bus Evangelium, intercedit pro nobis, et dat remissionem peccatorum, exaudit nos invocan- tes, defendit et servat Ecclesiam suam, depellit diabolos, et eius organa, tyrannos, fanaticos spiritus, et alios impios, denique resuscitat mortuos, et dat vitam aeternam iis, in quibus fide in hac vita incoata est iusticia, et coniicit in aeternas poenas omnes qui perseverant in con- temtu Dei. Haec admiranda opera omnia sunt effectus resurrectionis, quos fide nobis appli- care discamus, quandocunque corda vere con- sternata conspectu peccatorum luctantur cum dif- fidentia et desperatione, sciamus aeternum et im- mutabile mandatum Dei esse, ut confugiamus ad filium Dei resuscitatum, sedentem ad dextram aeterni patris, et credamus nos recipi et exau- diri. Ideo resurrexit, ut exaudiat, ut sit effi- cax, ut iuvet hanc miseram massam generis hu- mani, quam sibi copulavit aeterno foedere. Non est mortuus et otiosus Dominus, ut fingunt men- tes sine luce Evangelii, sed vere est opitulator et salvator, vere adhuc clamat: Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis et onerati estis, et ego refi- ciam vos. Quam difficilis res sit in veris dolori- bus excitare hanc fidem, experientia monstrat, et tamen necesse est disci haec certamina, et in eis confirmari fidem, intueri in filium Dei re- suscitatum et Ecclesiam praesentem, perinde ac si oculis corporis eum cerneremus, et adiunctum nobis complecteremur. Ut autem haec fides ex- citari possit, necesse est doctrinam agnosci de fide, qua gratis propter Christum accipitur re- missio peccatorum. Donec enim haerent in men- tibus opiniones ex lege sumtae, non recipi nos, non exaudiri, nisi satis sit meritorum, non potest mens erigi vera consolatione, et vero in- tellectu beneficiorum resurrectionis.

## 20:11
But Mary stood outside.

Especially concerning the resurrection these things are to be considered. First, the history of the resurrection itself. Second, the effects, namely, that through the resurrected Christ, and for his sake, justice and eternal life are rendered, as has been said. Third, the application which is made in this life through faith, by which we believe that we are truly received for the sake of this resurrected Lord, and we believe that he is an assiduous intercessor for us, and that we are helped and defended by him. And since this faith is the beginning of eternal life in us, it is necessary that it grow daily in invocation during the dangers and actions of this life.

Fourth, illustrious testimonies, namely of all who saw Christ and others who were resurrected. For there was a manifest and most sweet familiarity, for 40 days of Christ and many resurrected ones, with Mary the mother of Christ, the Apostles, and five hundred brethren. Nor at any time from the beginning of the human race was such glory seen by men still living in this mortal flesh, as the saints saw in those 40 days. For he wished to remain and be seen among his own for so many days, so that their minds might be confirmed concerning the resurrection, and they might certainly conclude that Christ had truly revived, and that it was not an empty specter that was observed, that he had often sat for whole days with Mary, those first matrons, Eve, Sarah, Rachel, Leah and others, and that they had spoken individually about the dangers of their age and divine liberations, nay even about the Son of God often seen long ago by the first parents, and about that glory of eternal life, with which they now saw themselves to be endowed and adorned. They often embraced Mary as a daughter, and congratulated her that she was the mother of the Son of God, and gave thanks that she had endured together with him the immense sorrows in the passion of her son. There is therefore the testimony of the resurrection, the consensus and assertion of so many men, who during these 40 days were familiar with Christ and the other resurrected saints. Then the testimony of these is confirmed by all the miracles which were afterwards done in the Church through the Apostles and other witnesses. Fifth, let the sayings of the Prophets concerning the resurrection be considered, which Luke says Christ explained on the way to Emmaus. Sixth, let the infirmity of the Apostles be considered, who not only doubted greatly before the resurrection, but even afterwards could scarcely be confirmed, and yet in this infirmity they were not cast away, because they eagerly heard the doctrine and testimonies. Let us think often and much upon this example, when we look upon our own infirmity, and let us give thanks to God, because he receives the infirm. But let us also know that it behooves us to be teachable, to hear and meditate upon the Gospel, and in true exercises to increase faith more and more. I have briefly reviewed these six chapters, so that the principal points of the doctrine concerning the resurrection may be more in view are such, the thought of which is useful for nourishing faith and for the exercises of faith. I will not recite the individual manifestations, the individual conversations, but I will excerpt the more obscure sayings from the principal ones. The first manifestation was made to the women, because just as through them death first pervaded the human race, so Christ wished to show them first the restoration of eternal life, and Christ brings aid to the weaker ones first, so that we may know that he truly loves the humble and the weak, according to that saying: 'A bruised reed he will not break.' But why does he say: 'Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father'? It is certainly a marvelous speech. But this seems to be the meaning of the precept: The woman is rebuked because she seeks with human desire the embrace of Christ, and dreams that he has revived so that he may live again among friends, as before, and gladden himself with visible presence; she does not yet know that the presence of the invisible Christ is henceforth to be acknowledged by faith.

Latin:

Stabat autem Maria foris.

Praecipue de resurrectione haec consideranda sunt. Primum ipsa historia resurrectionis. Se- cundo effectus, scilicet, quod per Christum re- suscitatum, et propter eum redduntur iusticia et vita aeterna, ut dictum est. Tertio applicatio quae fit in hac vita per fidem, qua credimus vere nos recipi propter hunc resuscitatum Dominum, et credimus eum esse assiduum intercessorem pro nobis, et nos iuvari ab eo et defendi. Et cum haec fides sit incoatio vitae aeternae in nobis, ne- cesse est eam in invocatione in periculis et actio- nibus huius vitae quotidie crescere.

Quarto illustria testimonia, videlicet omnium qui viderunt Christum et alios resuscitatos. Fuit enim manifesta et dulcissima familiaritas, per dies 40 Christi et multorum resuscitatorum, cum Maria matre Christi, Apostolis, et quin- gentis fratribus. Nec ullo unquam tempore a principio generis humani tanta gloria conspecta est ab hominibus in hac carne mortali adhuc vi- ventibus, quantam viderunt sancti illis 40 die- bus. Voluit enim per tot dies inter suos com- morari et conspici, ut confirmarentur eorum mentes de resurrectione, ac certo statuerent vere revixisse Christum, nec observatum esse inane spectrum, saepe assedisse totos dies apud Ma- riam, primas illas matronas, Evam, Saram, Ra- hel, Leam et alias, et singulas de suae aetatis pe- riculis et divinis liberationibus locutas esse, imo ettiam de filio Dei saepe olim conspecto a primis parentibus, et de illa gloria aeternae vitae, qua iam se videbant donatas et ornatas esse. Saepe complexae sunt Mariam tanquam filiam, eique gratulatae sunt quod mater esset filii Dei, et gra- tias egerunt quod in filii passione ingentes dolores una sustinuisset. Est igitur testimonium resur- rectionis, consensus et asseveratio tot hominum, qui his 40 diebus familiares fuerunt Christo et aliis resuscitatis sanctis. Deinde horum testimo- nium confirmatur omnibus miraculis, quae postea in Ecclesia per Apostoles et alios testes facta sunt. Quinto considerentur dicta Prophetarum de resurrectione, quae ait Lucas, Christum in via ad Emaus enarrasse. Sexto consideretur Aposto- lorum infirmitas, qui non solum ante resurre- ctionem valde dubitaverunt, sed etiam postea vix confirmari potuerunt, et tamen in hac infirmi- tate non abiiciebantur, quia doctrinam et testi- monia avide audiebant. Hoc exemplum saepe multumque cogitemus, cum nostram infirmita- tem intuemur, et agamus Deo gratias, quod re- cipit infirmos. Sed sciamus etiam oportere nos dociles esse, audire et meditari Evangelium, et in veris exercitiis magis magisque accedere fidem. Haec sex capita breviter recensui, ut praecipui loci doctrinae de resurrectione magis in conspectu sint, quorum cogitatio ad alendam fidem, et ad exercitia fidei utilis est. Non recitabo singulas ostensiones, singula colloquia, sed obscuriora dicta ex praecipuis excerpam. Prima ostensio facta est mulieribus, quia ut per eas mors primum pervasit in genus humanum, ita Christus voluit eis primum ostendere restitutionem vitae aeternae, et languidioribus prius opem fert Christus, ut sciamus eum humilia et imbecillia vere diligere, iuxta illud: 'Calamum quassatum non confringet. Quare autem dicit? Ne me tangas, quia nondum ascendi ad patrem meum, sane miranda oratio est. Sed haec videtur esse sententia praecepti: Reprehenditur mulier, quod desiderio humano expetit complexum Christi, et somniat eum revixisse, ut rursus inter amicos vivat, ut antea, et praesentia visibili se exhilaret, nondum scit fide praesentiam invisibilis Christi deinceps agnoscendam esse.

## 20:17
For I have not yet ascended to my Father.

There are two interpretations which in some way explain this connection. This one is customary: I forbid bodily contact, because I shall ascend to the Father, and you will no longer enjoy this visible association, with which you have mixed many human affections. You were rejoicing in my presence, like children at the sight of sweet parents, who knew that you were safer under my patronage, but now I will give you the Holy Spirit when I have ascended to the Father, so that you may embrace me in another way; I will be present among you, but you will perceive me by faith, and you will embrace me by faith, not with childish affections as before.
