This customary interpretation makes an antithesis between bodily contact, which took place in visible association, and faith embracing Christ, because he is no longer seen by the eyes of the body.

But the other interpretation, as it seems to me, is simpler, which makes an antithesis of two contacts, or visible conversations. Now he says: I forbid contact, because you foolishly dream of an association such as it was before, which was not yet eternal life, but there will be another association, for the sake of which I was sent, and now I have revived, namely eternal life with the Father; there you will see me and the Father face to face with your eyes, and you will embrace me. Therefore, think of that time of new contact; now omit childish embraces and affections for us; thus the connection seems to be elegant: Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father, as if he were to say:

You will then touch me when I have ascended to the Father, namely, when I have brought you and the rest of the Church to the Father. Another kingdom, another life remains to be given to you, in which you will enjoy the association of the Father and of me, and what follows squares with this meaning.

Latin:

Nondum enim ascendi ad patrem meum.

Duae sunt interpretationes, quae utcunque declarant hanc connexionem. Usitata haec est: Prohibeo contrectationem corporalem, quia ascendam ad patrem, nec fruemini deinceps hac visibili consuetudine, cui vos multum humanorum affectuum miscuistis. Laetabamini mea praesentia, ut pueri dulcium parentum conspectu, qui sciebatis vos meo patrocinio tutiores esse, sed nunc dabo vobis Spiritum sanctum, cum ascendero ad patrem, ut me alio modo complectamini, ero praesens inter vos, sed fide me cernetis, et fide complectemini, non affectibus puerilibus ut antea. Haec usitata interpretatio facit antithesin contrectationis corporalis, quae fiebat in consuetudine visibili, et fidei complectentis Christum, quia iam non cernitur oculis corporis.

Altera vero interpretatio, ut mihi videtur, simplicior est, quae facit antithesin duarum contrectationum, seu visibilium conversationum. Nunc inquit: Prohibeo contrectationem, quia stulta somnias consuetudinem, qualis antea fuit, quae nondum erat vita aeterna, sed alia erit consuetudo, propter quam missus sum, et nunc revixi, scilicet vita aeterna apud patrem, ibi me et patrem cernes oculis coram, et complecteris. Illud igitur tempus novae contrectationis cogita, nunc nos pueriles complexus et affectus omitte, sic videtur esse concinna connexio: Ne tangas me, quia nondum ascendi ad patrem, quasi dicat:

Tunc contrectabis me, cum ascendero ad patrem, videlicet, cum te, et reliquam Ecclesiam adduxero ad patrem. Aliud regnum, alia vita restat vobis danda, in qua fruemini patris consuetudine et mea, et ad hanc sententiam quadrant quae sequuntur.

## 20:17
I ascend to my Father, and your Father.

As if he were to say, expect another kingdom, another association, conversation, and contact. But what these consolations are, must be learned in the assiduous exercises of faith and hope; he promises eternal association with God; looking to this, and hoping for it, let us meanwhile endure labors and hardships, and at the same time let us know that our Messiah is now with us, and is to be embraced by faith, even if he cannot be seen by the eyes of the body, nor touched by hands; he is present, however, to govern and help us.

Latin:

Ascendo ad patrem meum, et patrem vestrum.

Quasi dicat, aliud regnum, aliam consuetudinem, conversationem et contrectationem expectato. Qualis autem hae sint consolationes, discendum est in assiduis exercitiis fidei et spei, promittit aeternam consuetudinem cum Deo, hanc intuentes, ac sperantes, interim sustineamus labores et aerumnas, et simul sciamus nunc nobiscum esse Messiam nostrum, et fide amplectendum, etiamsi nec cerni corporis oculis, contrectari manibus potest, adest tamen, ut nos gubernet et iuvet.

## 20:21
As the Father has sent me.

Many testimonies of the resurrection are narrated by the writers of the evangelical history, which it is useful to remember, but now I will briefly run through these which are in the narrative of John. On the first evening of that day on which Christ had risen, he came to the whole assembly of the Apostles, who were together in Jerusalem, and when he had greeted them, and had shown them his hands and side, in the same conversation he begins to preach to them about their own ministry, he gives them the Holy Spirit, and adds a command concerning the remission of sins, that is, he explains to them the sum of the Gospel. A few things must be said in order about these three parts.

First, let us know that here the ministry of the Gospel is confirmed, and the efficacy of God is promised through the voice of all who teach the uncorrupted Gospel: As the Father sent me, and was efficacious through me, called and gathered an eternal Church: so I send you, I will be efficacious through you, I will call and gather an eternal Church. This statement agrees with that saying: 'He who hears you, hears me.' Let us hold this doctrine and consolation, and truly establish that God is efficacious through the voice of the Gospel and wishes that we sustain ourselves with the promises of the Gospel, as if he himself were addressing us from heaven with his own voice. This consolation is to be often inculcated and thought upon.

Then the same statement affirms that the Apostles are not sent to occupy empires with arms. And it distinguishes the ministry of the Gospel from empires. For it is expressly said: As the Father sent me, but it is certain that Christ was sent without arms and royal armies. Thirdly, consolation is delivered for teachers and learners, namely that, just as the Father was present with Christ, so he will certainly be present with the rest who perform the ministry of the Gospel. Fourthly, the necessity of serving the ministry of the Gospel is to be learned from this saying, and the opinion of monks and the like is to be censured, who think it is worship of God or wisdom to flee public administration and hide themselves in corners, according to that saying: live in obscurity. But when the Son of God came forth from his secret seat to teach and to provide testimonies of his doctrine, to become a victim, and sent the Apostles to gather a Church from all nations, even though this could not be done without great tumults, therefore he commands us also, that when called we should perform our ministries, and not hide ourselves in corners. These consolations are useful to the pious, because these thoughts often clamor against us: why did you come into this battle line? why have you allowed yourself to be burdened with such a mass of dangers and miseries? why do you not flee from these miseries? or finally, who helps you? Against all these temptations let us oppose these consolations: As the Father has sent me, so I send you. Likewise: Whoever has confessed me before men, him I will confess before my heavenly Father.

Latin:

Sicut misit me pater.

Multa testimonia resurrectionis narrantur a scriptoribus historiae evangelicae, quae meminisse utile est, sed nunc breviter haec quae sunt in narratione Ioannis, percurram. Primo vespere eius diei, quo resurrexerat Christus, venit ad totum coetum Apostolorum, qui una erant Ierosolymae, et cum salutasset eos, et manus et latus ostendisset, in eodem colloquio incipit eis concionari de ipsorum ministerio, dat eis Spiritum sanctum, et addit mandatum de remissione peccatorum, id est, summam Evangelii eis exponit. De his tribus membris ordine pauca dicenda sunt.

Primum sciamus hic confirmari ministerium Evangelii, et promitti efficaciam Dei per vocem omnium docentium Evangelium incorruptum: Sicut misit me pater, et fuit per me efficax, vocavit et collegit aeternam Ecclesiam: ita ego mitto vos, ero per vos efficax, vocabo et colligam aeternam Ecclesiam. Haec sententia congruit cum illo dicto: Qui vos audit, me audit, Hanc doctrinam et consolationem teneamus, ac vere statuamus Deum efficacem esse per vocem Evangelii et velle ut promissionibus Evangelii nos sustentemus, quasi ipse nos sua voce de coelo alloqueretur. Haec consolatio saepe inculcanda et cogitanda est.

Deinde idem dictum affirmat, Apostolos non mitti, ut imperia armis occupent. Et discernit ministerium Evangelii ab imperiis. Expresse enim dicitur: Sicut misit me pater, constat autem Christum missum esse sine armis et regiis exer- citibus. Tertio, consolatio pro doctoribus et discenti- bus traditur, quod videlicet, sicut adfuit Christo pater, ita certo adfuturus sit reliquis fungentibus ministerio Evangelii. Quarto, necessitas serviendi ministerio Evan- gelii ex hoc dicto discenda est, et taxanda mona- chorum, et similium opinio, qui putant cultum Dei aut sapientiam esse, fugere publicam admini- strationem, et abdere se in latebras, iuxta illud: λάθε βιώσας. Cum autem filius Dei ex sua ar- cana sede prodierit, ut doceret, et ederet testi- monia doctrinae, ut fieret victima, et miserit Apo- stolos, ut ex omnibus gentibus colligeret Eccle- siam, etiamsi hoc sine magnis tumultibus fieri non poterat, ideo nobis quoque praecipit, ut vocati fungamur ministeriis, nec abdamus nos in late- bras. Hae consolationes piis utiles sunt, quia saepe nobis obstrepunt hae cogitationes, cur in hanc aciem venisti? cur tanta mole periculorum et miseriarum te onerari passus es? cur non fugis ex his miseriis? vel tandem, quis iuvat te? Ad- versus has tentationes omnes opponamus has con- solationes: Sicut misit me pater, sic mitto vos. Item: Qui me confessus fuerit coram hominibus, eum confitebor coram patre meo coelesti.

## 20:22
He breathed on them.

In brief words a most weighty history is recounted, which both testifies that Christ is God by nature, and signifies what the Holy Spirit is like, and that he is the governor of the evangelical ministry. First, to give the Holy Spirit, who begins eternal life, light, and eternal justice, is truly and properly of God. Here Christ by his own breath gives the Holy Spirit from himself, therefore he is truly and by nature God. Secondly, it teaches what he is like by the word he breathed. Although the divine nature cannot be perceived, yet God, distinguishing the persons and taking images from the properties of man, shows in some way what the divine nature is like, and what the distinctions of the persons are. And since God uses words which we understand in some way, he wants us to recognize and invoke God in this way, and to distinguish him from fictitious deities. The Son is called the Word and the image of the Father; it is signified, therefore, that the Son is born from the thought of the Father contemplating himself and begetting his own image, just as in man an image of the thing thought of is begotten by thought: Thus in human thought it is in some way shadowed forth what the generation of the Son is like, and that he is the image. And because God uses words taken from human nature, he wants us to think of this likeness, so that the distinctions of the persons may be considered in some way. Great, however, is the dignity of human nature, that God has established these pictures of his own nature in us.

Thus also the name of Spirit indicates in some way whence he proceeds, and what the Holy Spirit is like. And in this example of Christ the matter is more illustrious, as in the mind of man there are thoughts and images of things which we think of: so in the heart there are spirits, that is, breath and motions, as we experience in love, anger, and other affections, where the heart pours forth spirits with great motion. As therefore the Son of God is an image begotten from the mind: so the Spirit is from the will of the Father and the Son, whether love or the ardor of love and breath, by which the Father and Son mutually embrace each other, and by which they embrace angels and men. Therefore also in this history Christ bestows the Holy Spirit with his breath, because he proceeds from the will, and the heart in Christ is joined with the will, in which love toward us burns.

In this likeness or picture many things are learned. First, the distinction of generation and spiration in the divinity is shown in some way. Generation is properly from the mind, spiration is from the will. Next, it is signified why the Son is called the image, because the mind begets images. Likewise, the Son is the Word, because he is the image; it is also signified the magnitude of the love of God toward those to whom the Holy Spirit is given. Because as the spirit poured out from our heart in a kiss is a messenger of true love, and a transfusion of our nature, so let us know that it is true, not feigned love, when God transfuses the Spirit from himself into us, as he says in Joel: I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh. We are warned likewise what a wonderful likeness of the divine nature there is in man. And how great an evil it is to contaminate these images or likenesses of God in human nature, and to tear them away from God. These and many other things the pious can think about in this place, considering that the Holy Spirit is given by the very breath. And this must be known, that with the breath, or blowing, or emission of the bodily spirit from the breast of Christ, there was in reality at the same time the Holy Spirit himself, the third person of the divinity, so that these things truly agree: I will pour out of my Spirit. I have briefly reviewed these things, so that readers may be invited to pious thought about these such great matters.

Latin:

Insufflavit in eos.

Brevibus verbis historia gravissima recitatur, quae et testatur Christum natura Deum esse, et significat qualis sit Spiritus sanctus, et quod sit ministerii evangelici gubernator. Primum dare Spiritum sanctum, qui vitam aeternam, lucem, et iusticiam aeternam incoat, est vere et proprie Dei. Hic Christus suo afflatu dat Spiritum san- ctum ex sese, ergo vere et natura Deus est. Se- cundo, qualis sit, docet verbum inhalavit. Etsi perspici divina natura non potest, tamen Deus discernens personas, et sumens imagines a pro- prietatibus hominis, aliquo modo ostendit, qualis sit natura divina, et qualia sint discrimina per- sonarum. Et cum vocabulis utatur Deus, quae aliquo modo intelligimus, vult nos ita agnoscere et invocare Deum, et cum discernere a commen- titiis numinibus. Filius vocatur λόγος et imago patris, significatur ergo, nasci filium cogitatione patris sese intuentis, et gignentis sui imaginem, sicut in homine cogitatione gignitur imago rei cogitatae: Ita in humana cogitatione aliquo modo adumbratur, qualis sit generatio filii, et quod sit imago. Et quia Deus vocabulis utitur sumtis ex humana natura, vult nos hanc similitudinem co- gitare, ut aliquo modo discrimina personarum considerentur. Magna est autem dignitas huma- nae naturae, quod Deus has picturas suae naturae in nobis condidit.

Sic et nomen Spiritus indicat aliquo modo, unde procedat, et qualis sit Spiritus sanctus. Et in hoc Christi exemplo res est illustrior, ut in mente hominis sunt cogitationes et imagines re- rum, quas cogitamus: sic in corde sunt spiritus, id est, halitus, et motus, ut in amore, ira et aliis affectibus experimur, ubi cor magno motu fundit spiritus. Ut igitur filius Dei est imago a mente genita: ita spiritus est a voluntate patris et filii, seu amor seu amoris ardor et halitus, quo se pater et filius mutuo complectuntur, et quo angelos et homines complectuntur. Ideo et in hac historia Christus halitu largitur Spiritum sanctum, quia a voluntate spiritus procedit, et cum voluntate cor in Christo copulatum est, in quo ardet amor erga nos.

In hac similitudine, seu pictura multa di- scuntur. Primum aliquo modo monstratur dis- crimen generationis, et spirationis in divinitate. Generatio est proprie a mente, spiratio est a vo- luntate. Deinde significatur, cur filius vocetur imago, quia mens gignit imagines. Item λόγος est filius, quia est imago, significatur etiam ma- gnitudo amoris Dei erga eos, quibus datur Spiritus sanctus. Quia ut spiritus ex nostro corde effusus in osculo nuncius est veri amoris, et transfusio naturae nostrae, ita sciamus verum, non simula- tum amorem esse, cum Deus in nos spiritum ex sese transfundit, sicut in Ioele dicit: Effundam de spiritu meo super omnem carnem. Admone- mur item quam miranda similitudo sit divinae naturae in homine. Et quantum malum, has Dei imagines, seu similitudines in natura humana contaminare, et a Deo avellere. Haec et alia multa pii hoc loco cogitare possunt considerantes dari Spiritum sanctum ipso halitu. Estque hoc sciendum, cum halitu, seu flatu, seu emissione spiritus corporalis ex pectore Christi, revera simul fuisse ipsum Spiritum sanctum, personam ter- tiam divinitatis, ut haec vere congruant: Effun- dam de spiritu meo. Haec breviter recensui, ut lectores invitentur ad piam de his tantis rebus cogitationem.

## 20:23
Whose sins you shall forgive.

I said that three things are especially to be considered in this place: the calling to the ministry of the Gospel, the gift of the Holy Spirit, and the sum of the Gospel. These are joined together in the Church: the ministry, the Holy Spirit, and the remission of sins. And when we hear the remission of sins named, let us at the same time embrace the gift of the Holy Spirit, of eternal life, and all the promises proper to the Gospel, that having been received by God we are heard, helped, and defended by God. In short, all the benefits of the Gospel are comprehended by the appellation of the remission of sins. Now therefore he delivers the sum of the Gospel to the disciples, when he explains this will of God to them, that God truly takes away and blots out the sins of all to whom, by the voice and ministry of those teaching the Gospel, remission is made. Here let each one think for himself of the distinction between the Law and the Gospel, and thus this passage will become clearer. For the Law is the doctrine of God's precepts, commanding what sort of persons we ought to be, and what we ought to do and omit, and demanding entire obedience, and denouncing the wrath of God and eternal punishments to all who do not perform entire obedience. But the Gospel is the preaching of repentance, and a promise exhibiting on account of Christ the free remission of sins, reconciliation, and the imputation of righteousness, the gift of the Holy Spirit and of eternal life, and these promises ought to be received by faith. Since therefore these kinds of doctrine differ very widely, as has often been said, one must be most diligent to take care that they are not confused. And since Christ here gives commands concerning the remission of sins, let us understand a free remission, as is often declared by Paul.

Secondly, let us know that this very ministry of the Gospel is the ministry of the Spirit, that is, that God is truly efficacious through this ministry, truly gives the Holy Spirit through the voice and acknowledgment of the Gospel, and truly draws and moves hearts so that we may become heirs of eternal life. And although it seems very strange to human wisdom that such great things are effected through the word, and that no other visions of God are to be sought in this life, yet let it be most certain to us that these things are thus effected through the word; therefore it is written: The Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to everyone that believeth. Likewise 1 Corinthians 3: The Gospel is the ministry of the Spirit. To this let the words of Christ recited in this place be added: Whose sins you shall forgive, they shall be forgiven them. Here he affirms clearly that sin is taken away through the voice of the Gospel which the minister sounds, that is, God truly approves it, and through it gives the Holy Spirit. It is necessary to have these testimonies concerning the presence and efficacy of God through the ministry most familiarly known, so that we ourselves may both find rest in praying and look upon this God who has revealed himself in this word. And let us know that no other visions of God are to be sought, and that the frenzies of the Enthusiasts are to be execrated, who, omitting the word, fashion for themselves speculations and inspirations, and wander away from God.

Thirdly, it is disputed here concerning private absolution, whether this also is approved by this testimony. I answer briefly: The ministry of the Gospel is the announcement of the remission of sins, which is offered to all who believe in Christ. This announcement can be made either in general for many, as in a sermon where the hearer, raising himself up in true repentance by the voice of the Gospel, receives by faith certainly the remission of sins and the Holy Spirit, just as Cornelius and others received the Holy Spirit in a public sermon. Or it can be made privately, when remission is announced to individuals who ask for it, just as Christ absolved the woman in the house of the leper. And Paul absolved, and commanded to be absolved, the incestuous person. Therefore it is most certain that private absolution is the voice of the Gospel, confirmed also by this very saying: Whose sins you shall forgive, etc. It is therefore manifest that it has always been in the Church, for Peter of Alexandria also cites the custom of the earlier Church against the frenzies of Meletius and the Cathari, which always received the lapsed by private absolution; nay, the Prophets also, understanding the Gospel, administered it even in the Old Testament, as Nathan announces to David the remission of sins by private absolution, and Daniel to the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar.

But those ignorant of the Gospel shout that it belongs to God alone to forgive sins. This cavil is most insipid, because just as in baptism the minister receives a man in the place of Christ, and truly forgives sins as one acting in the stead of Christ, so in the announcement of the Gospel the minister does nothing by his own or human authority, but pronounces a sentence commended to him by God. Nor do they understand what the ministry of the Gospel is, who, because of that most insipid cavil, abolish private absolution.

Latin:

Quorum remiseritis peccata.

Dixi tria in hoc loco praecipue consideranda esse, vocationem ad ministerium Evangelii, do- nationem Spiritus sancti, et summam Evangelii. Haec coniuncta sunt in Ecclesia, ministerium, Spiritus sanctus, et remissio peccatorum. Et cum audimus nominari remissionem peccatorum, simul complectamur donationem Spiritus sancti, vitae aeternae, et omnes promissiones proprias Evangelii, quod recepti a Deo exaudiamur, iuve- mur, et defendamur a Deo. Denique omnia be- neficia Evangelii comprehenduntur appellatione remissionis peccatorum. Nunc igitur summam Evangelii tradit discipulis, cum hanc voluntatem Dei eis exponit, Deum vere auferre, et delere peccata omnium, quibus voce, et ministerio do- centium Evangelium, fit remissio. Hic legis et Evangelii discrimen apud se quisque cogitet, ita hic locus fiet illustrior. Lex enim est doctrina praeceptorum Dei, praecipiens quales nos esse, et quae facere, et omittere oporteat, et postulans integram obedientiam, ac denuncians iram Dei, et aeternas poenas omnibus, qui non praestant in- tegram obedientiam. At Evangelium est praedi- catio poenitentiae, et promissio exhibens propter Christum gratis remissionem peccatorum, recon- ciliationem et imputationem iustitiae, donatio- nem Spiritus sancti et vitae aeternae, et has pro- missiones fide accipi oportet. Cum igitur longis- sime differant haec doctrinae genera, ut saepe dictum est, diligentissime cavendum est, ne con- fundantur. Cumque Christus hic det mandata de remissione peccatorum, intelligamus gratuitam remissionem, ut saepe a Paulo declaratur.

Secundo sciamus hoc ipsum ministerii Evan- gelii, esse ministerium spiritus, id est, Deum vere efficacem esse per hoc ministerium, vere dare Spiritum sanctum, per vocem et agnitionem Evangelii, vere trahere et movere corda, ut fia- mus haeredes vitae aeternae. Etsi autem huma- nae sapientiae valde mirum videtur, res tantas effici per verbum, et non postulandos esse in hac vita alios contuitus Dei, tamen nobis certissimum sit haec ita effici per verbum, ideo scriptum est: Evangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni cre- denti. Item 1. Corinth. 3.: Evangelium est mini- sterium spiritus. Huc adiungantur et verba Chri- sti hoc loco recitata: Quorum remiseritis peccata, remittentur eis. Hic affirmat clare auferri pec- catum per vocem Evangelii, quam sonat minister, id est, Deus vere eam approbat, et per eam dat Spiritum sanctum. Haec testimonia de praesentia et efficacia Dei per ministerium, necesse est habere familiarissime nota, ut et nos ipsi in invocando acquiescamus, et hunc Deum intueamur, qui se in hoc verbo patefecit. Et sciamus non quaeren- dos esse alios contuitus Dei, et execrandos esse furores Enthusiastarum, qui omisso verbo, sibi ipsi fingunt speculationes et afflatus, et aberrant a Deo.

Tertio disputatur hic de privata absolutione, an haec quoque approbata sit hoc testimonio. Breviter respondeo: Ministerium Evangelii est annunciatio remissionis peccatorum, quae offer- tur omnibus credentibus in Christum. Haec an- nunciatio potest fieri, aut in genere pro multis, ut in concione ubi audiens, et in vera poenitentia se erigens voce Evangelii, fide accipit certo remis- sionem peccatorum et Spiritum sanctum, sicut Cor- nelius et alii in publica concione accipiebant Spiritum sanctum. Aut potest fieri privatim, cum singulis petentibus annunciatur remissio, ut Chri- stus absolvit mulierem in domo leprosi. Et Pau- lus absolvit, et iubet absolvi incestum. Itaque certissimum est, privatam absolutionem esse Evan- gelii vocem, confirmatam et hoc ipso dicto: Quo- rum remiseritis peccata, etc. Semper igitur fuisse eam in Ecclesia manifestum est, nam et Petrus Alexandrinus citat morem Ecclesiae superioris, contra furores Meletii et Catharorum, quae lap- sos privata absolutione semper recepit, imo Pro- phetae eam etiam in veteri testamento, intelligen- tes Evangelium, administrarunt, ut Nathan pri- vata absolutione annunciat Davidi remissionem peccatorum, Daniel regi Babylonico Nabucho- donosor.

Sed ignari Evangelii, vociferantur solius Dei esse remittere peccata. Haec cavillatio est insul- sissima, quia ut in baptismo minister loco Christi recipit hominem, et vere remittit peccata tanquam gerens vice Christi, ita in annunciatione Evange- lii, nihil sua aut humana autoritate agit minister, sed pronunciat sententiam a Deo ipsi commenda- tam. Nec intelligunt, quid sit ministerium Evan- gelii, qui propter illam insulsissimam cavillatio- nem abolent privatam absolutionem.

## 20:24
But Thomas, one of the twelve.

Many accounts of the testimonies are omitted in the recitation of John, which exist in the histories of Luke and others, which we also shall omit here, and I shall speak briefly about this very history of Thomas. I also omit the curious discussion about the scars of the wounds, whether these remain in the resurrected body, and I only answer that Christ showed himself because, out of his great goodness, he wished to heal the great doubt of the weak disciple. There are, however, three main points in this history: First, the great weakness and doubt in the Apostles. Second, the confession of the confirmed Apostle, asserting that Christ is God. Third, the doctrine concerning faith, that God is rightly invoked when we behold him only by faith through the word, and we acknowledge and call upon this God, who revealed himself through the Gospel, and by sending his Son, crucified and resurrected, even if other illuminations or new revelations do not approach.

those hearers who say in John 6: This is a hard saying.

Latin:

Thomas autem unus ex duodecim.

Multae narrationes testimoniorum omittuntur in recitatione Iohannis, quae extant in historiis Lucae et aliorum, quas et nos hic omittemus, et de hac ipsa historia Thomae breviter dicam. Omitto etiam curiosam disputationem, de cica- tricibus vulnerum, an hae maneant in corpore resuscilato, ac tantum respondeo, Christum osten- disse se, quia pro sua magna bonitate voluit ma- gnam dubitationem infirmi discipuli sanare. Tres autem hi loci praecipui sunt in hac historia: Pri- mus, magna infirmitas et dubitatio in Apostolis. Secundus, confessio confirmati Apostoli, asseve- rans Christum esse Deum. Tertius, doctrina de fide, quod recte invocetur Deus, cum tantum fide per verbum eum intuemur, et agnoscimus et com- pellamus hunc Deum, qui se per Evangelium, et misso filio crucifixo et resuscitato patefecit, etiamsi non accedunt aliae illuminationes, aut novae re- velationes.

illi auditores, qui Ioannis 6. dicunt: Durus est hic sermo.

## 20:28
My Lord and my God.

Concerning the second point. After Christ showed himself, and with great goodness healed the disciple's weakness, exhibiting himself to be touched, the hearer is now confirmed, and such a light is kindled in him that he professes this Messiah to be God. For let us understand the word God properly in this place, since the testimonies of John 1 and elsewhere agree, and let us not make the appellation ambiguous. I think, however, that by the custom of the Prophets two names are joined, Lord and God, because since in the Church the invocation and calling upon the true God must be distinguished from the fictitious deities of the heathens, the Prophets address this God, revealed in Israel through the word handed down to the Fathers and Prophets, by a certain name not used by the nations, and they join these appellations, Jehovah our God, as in Psalm 20: But we will call upon the name of Jehovah our God, as if he were saying, of this one God, who is truly God, the creator of all things, who revealed himself in this people and gave promises, truly hears, helps, and saves.

Latin:

Dominus meus et Deus meus.

De secundo loco. Postquam Christus osten- dit se, et magna bonitate sanavit discipuli infir- mitatem, sese exhibens contrectandum, iam con- firmatur auditor, et tanta lux in eo accenditur, ut profiteatur hunc Messiam esse Deum. Intelli- gamus enim vocabulum Dei proprie hoc loco, cum testimonia Ioannis 1. et alibi congruant, nec fa- ciamus appellationem ambiguam. Arbitror antem consuetudine Prophetarum iungi duo nomina, Domini et Dei, quia cum in Ecclesia oporteat discerni invocationem et compellationem veri Dei a commentitiis ethnicorum numinibus, Pro- phetae hunc Deum, patefactum in Israël per ver- bum traditum Patribus et Prophetis, certo no- mine, non usitato gentibus alloquuntur, et iun- gunt has appellationes Iehova Deus noster, ut in Psalm. 20.: Nos autem in nomine Iehova Dei nostri invocabimus, quasi dicat, huius unius Dei, qui vere Deus est, conditor omnium rerum, qui se patefecit in hoc populo, et dedit promissiones, vere exaudit, iuvat, et salvat.

## 20:29
Blessed are those who, when they have not seen, believe.

It was said above that in this place is handed down the most necessary doctrine concerning the acknowledgment and invocation of God: For anxious minds ask what they should invoke, how we invoke the true God more than Plato or Xenophon, who also think they are invoking one eternal mind, the maker and preserver of the world and of the human race. They ask the same, whether it is enough to address God in this way, looking upon him who revealed himself through the Gospel, and how we ought to decide concerning his will, and whether it is enough to acquiesce in the word of God. For human minds would prefer to see before them a visible form of God, so that by certainly beholding it they would know they are not straying from God. They would also prefer to hear consolations face to face, just as Moses beholds a visible form and receives from the clear voice of God the sentences handed down concerning individual matters. Thus we also desire to see and hear God face to face and familiarly. It is necessary for pious minds to be rightly instructed concerning these questions.

The monks answer briefly that one must always doubt concerning all these questions, whether it is enough to invoke God in this way, addressing this God who revealed himself through the Gospel, or whether

Concerning this article, it is very necessary for all who invoke him to be instructed, because weak minds argue with themselves which God they are addressing, how they ought to distinguish him from heathen and fictitious deities, and whether it is enough to behold him recognized by faith through the word, but I shall briefly finish the first two points.

Examples of doubts and weaknesses in the Apostles are proposed to us for two reasons. The first is that we may acknowledge that sins truly remain in the regenerate in this life, and that we may truly grieve that we carry about such darkness and weakness, and not exalt ourselves as if there were no vice in us, and as if God unjustly burdened us with punishments, just as hypocrites rage against the judgment of God. The second reason is that when we see the Apostles, although weak, were received and healed, we may know that we also are truly received and healed; therefore Paul says in Romans 14 concerning the weak: For God has received him. This consolation is pleasing and necessary for the pious.

But let us know that there are two kinds of weak people. The teachable, these are received and healed, namely by hearing the Gospel and curbing and taking captive their own thoughts into the obedience of Christ. Others, however, are unteachable, who stubbornly prefer their own thoughts to the Gospel. These are not received, but are cast out among the enemies of the Gospel. Just as they themselves declare that they are enemies, and depart from Christ, so that he may hear us, whether one ought to acquiesce in the promises. To all these things, in the manner of the heathen, the Monks and Mahometans reply that one must doubt. On the contrary, however, the Enthusiasts and Anabaptists, when they see that this doubt is heathen, command us to ask that a visible appearance be shown to us. But the error of both is to be detested, and the true and firm doctrine concerning faith is to be sought, and it must be learned what faith is.

Thus, therefore, I reply: First, that a visible appearance of God is not to be sought, nor is it to be doubted whether we rightly call upon God, but we call upon God truly and rightly when the mind addresses that God who has revealed Himself by the given Gospel and by the sending of His Son, our Lord Jesus Christ. This invocation distinguishes the Xenophontic from the Pauline, and it pleases God, and that it is sufficient to invoke Him thus, this saying teaches: Blessed are they who, when they have not seen, yet believe, and all sayings concerning faith agree with this doctrine. Rom. 5: By faith we approach God, and Rom. 10: The word is near in your mouth. It leads us only to this word, in this it wishes God to be thought of, and by this faith to be addressed, nor does it require anything else. Then, concerning the will, it matters a great deal that this be held most firmly, that one must acquiesce in the promises, just as if new voices were sounding from heaven amidst thunder and lightning, as on Mount Sinai. But although it is difficult for us to acquiesce in this way, and there is a great struggle of the heart debating whether this is truly the will of God toward you also, which He has delivered in the promise, as when He says: Come to me all you who labor, and I will refresh you, nevertheless the mind must be confirmed by the sayings concerning faith, Rom. 5: Justified by faith we have peace, and by similar sayings.

Nor are other illuminations outside the Gospel to be sought or demanded. This necessary and salutary doctrine concerning recognition and invocation is delivered in this saying: Blessed are they who, not seeing, believe, and the meaning of this saying will become more clear, and its usefulness will become more illustrious, if we think upon it often while invoking.

Latin:

Beati, qui cum non viderint, credunt.

Dictum est supra hoc in loco tradi doctrinam maxime necessariam de agnitione et invocatione Dei: Quaerunt enim anxiae mentes, quid invo- cent, quomodo magis invocemus nos verum Deum, quam Plato aut Xenophon, qui etiam cogitant se invocare unam mentem aeternam, opificem et servatricem mundi, et generis humani. Quae- runt idem, an satis sit sic alloqui Deum, intuen- tes hunc, qui se per Evangelium patefecit, et quo- modo de voluntate eius statuere debeamus, et an satis sit acquiescere in verbo Dei. Mallent enim humanae mentes coram cernere visibilem speciem Dei, quam certo intuentes scirent se non aberrare a Deo. Mallent et consolationes audire coram, ut Moyses intuetur visibilem speciem, et de sin- gulis negotiis accipit clara voce Dei traditas sen- tentias. Sic nos etiam coram et familiariter vi- dere et audire Deum cupimus. De his quaestio- nibus recte erudiri pias mentes necesse est.

Monachi breviter respondent, semper de omnibus his quaestionibus dubitandum esse, an satis sit sic invocare Deum, alloquentes hunc Deum, qui se per Evangelium patefecit, an vero

De hoc articulo valde necesse est omnes invo- cantes erudiri, quia disputant secum infirmae mentes, quem Deum alloquantur, quomodo eum discernere debeant ab ethnicis et commentitiis nu- minibus, et an satis sit eum intueri fide agnitum per verbum, sed priores duos locos breviter ab- solvam.

Exempla dubitationum et infirmitatum in Apostolis proponuntur nobis propter duas causas. Prior est, ut agnoscamus vere peccata reliqua esse in renatis in hac vita, et vere doleamus nos cir- cumferre tantam caliginem et infirmitatem, nec efferamus nos quasi nihil in nobis vitii sit, et quasi Deus iniuste nos oneret poenis, sicut hypo- critae fremunt adversus iudicium Dei. Altera causa est, ut cum videmus Apostolos quanquam infirmos, receptos et sanatos esse, sciamus et nos vere recipi et sanari, ideo Paulus ad Rom. 14. inquit de infirmo: Deus enim eum assumsit. Haec consolatio piis grata et necessaria est.

Sed sciamus duplices esse infirmos. Dociles, hi recipiuntur et sanantur, videlicet audientes Evangelium, et suas cogitationes frenantes et ca- ptivantes in obsequium Christi. Alii vero sunt in- dociles, qui pertinaciter anteferunt Evangelio suas cogitationes. Hi non recipiuntur, sed abii- ciuntur inter hostes Evangelii. Sicut et ipsi se declarant esse hostes, et discedunt a Christo, ut nos exaudiat, an aequiescendum sit in promissio- nibus. Ad haec omnia ethnico more respondent Monachi et Mahometistae, dubitandum esse. Econ- tra vero Enthusiastae et Anabaptistae, cum vi- deant hanc dubitationem ethnicam esse, iubent petere, ut visibilis species nobis ostendatur. Sed error utrorumque detestandus est, et quaerenda vera et firma doctrina de fide, et discendum quid sit fides.

Sic igitur respondeo: Primum non petendam esse speciem Dei visibilem, nec dubitandum esse an recte Deum invocemus, sed tunc vere et recte Deum invocamus, cum mens alloquitur illum Deum, qui se patefecit dato Evangelio, et misso filio Domino nostro Iesu Christo. Haec invocatio discernit Xenophonteam et Paulinam, et placet Deo, et quod satis sit sic invocare, docet hoc dictum: Beati qui cum non viderint, tamen cre- dunt, et congruunt ad hanc doctrinam omnia dicta de fide. Rom. 5.: Fide accedimus ad Deum, et Rom. 10.: Prope est verbum in ore tuo. Tan- tum nos ad hoc verbum deducit, in hoc vult co- gitari Deum, et hac fide eum compellari, nec aliud requirit. Deinde de voluntate plurimum refert hoc firmissime teneri, acquiescendum esse in promissionibus, perinde ac si novae voces de coelo inter tonitrua et fulmina ut in monte Sina, sonarent. Etsi autem difficile est nobis sic acquie- scere, et magna lucta est cordis disputantis, an vere haec sit voluntas Dei erga te quoque, quam in promissione tradidit, ut cum dicit: Venite ad me omnes qui laboratis, et ego reficiam vos, tamen confirmanda est mens dictis de fide, Rom. 5.: Iu- stificati fide pacem habemus, et similibus dictis.

Nec aliae illuminationes extra Evangelium quaerendae aut poscendae sunt. Haec necessaria et salutaris doctrina de agnitione et invocatione traditur in hoc dicto: Beati qui non videntes cre- dunt, et magis perspicua fiet huius dicti sententia, et fiet illustrior utilitas, si eam saepe cogitabimus inter invocandum.

## 21:1 Argument
Chapter XXI.

In the last chapter he narrates several deeds in which Christ showed Himself most clearly to the Apostles after the resurrection. Let us often repeat all the collected testimonies to confirm our faith. Then, since there are some sermons in almost every one, containing notable doctrine, let us contemplate these also. In this history which is recited here, there are three principal points: The first concerning the ministry, a command is given to the ministers that they should love Christ and feed the Church. The second concerning the distinction between discipline and the cross. The third concerning vocation, that each should obey his own vocation, and not abandon his own, or be broken in spirit, even if he sees another called differently.

Concerning the first point, namely concerning the commands which are given to the Apostles, that they should love Christ and feed the flock, let us know that a rule is delivered here, containing the principal virtues of all who teach in the Church. The first is that they should love Christ, that is, acknowledge and by true faith invoke Christ, and love His doctrine, and not love their own power, wealth, and pleasures more than Christ. Unless this foundation exists in a teacher or governor, he will neither defend the doctrine constantly, nor will he faithfully administer the other parts of the ministry, as many, out of ambition and desire for vengeance, have scattered and are scattering false dogmas, because they love their own glory more than Christ and the truth of the Gospel, and now it is manifest that the monks, for the sake of gain, defend the impious cults of the dead, and their Masses, and other superstitions. That, therefore, teachers may provide integrity and faith in the ministry of the Gospel, Christ first demands love in them. These things are plain and clear, because no one faithfully serves any master unless he loves him.

But as for the arguments taken from this passage concerning the primacy of the Roman pontiff, the briefest reply of the pious is: even if by divine right the Roman bishop were the highest, yet it would be necessary to dissent from him, since he defends dogmas conflicting with the Gospel, and idols, as Paul says: If any angel from heaven shall preach another Gospel, let him be anathema. But it is manifest that atrocious errors and idols are defended by the Roman bishop and his satellites. Thus Jeremiah, and Zechariah, and others dissented from their pontiffs, even though it was manifest that the Levitical Pontiff was by divine right superior to the other priests. By this reply, let the pious first confirm themselves in the controversies of these times.

Then it is easy to reply to the vicious connections, to Peter specifically it is said: Feed my sheep, therefore he is placed before the other Apostles. The consequence must be denied. For elsewhere common commands are given to all, as in the last chapter of Luke, and above in John: Whose sins you shall remit, they will be remitted. Nor is that conjecture firm, Peter loves more, therefore greater power is attributed to him. For there can be greater love in a private person without power than in a governor; in short, the ministry of the Gospel is a mandate of teaching the Gospel and administering the sacraments, it is not a power similar to political power. and peace, according to certain laws, by bodily force, and it has a certain people, whom it compels to obedience, and it can pass new laws congruent to reason, useful to its empire. But the minister of the Gospel does not have such power, he does not have the authority of passing new laws outside the Gospel, nor of compelling other ministers by force or excommunication to laws passed outside the Gospel.

Therefore, the power of any bishop is not to be imagined as similar to the power of kings, as they imagine concerning the Roman pontiff. Let this be enough to have warned briefly concerning this question.

Concerning the second point, namely, concerning the distinction between discipline and the cross. When you were younger, says Christ, you girded yourself, etc. As often elsewhere, so also in this conversation Christ censures the foolish persuasion of Peter, who was expecting now after the resurrection of Christ that golden empire, by which the Jews thought that, having subdued the nations, they would possess supreme power and wealth. Nay, he says, now will be the beginning of huge afflictions. Before you girded yourself, now others will gird you. In this place, let rational discipline be distinguished from the cross. Discipline is the diligence of governing external morals, according to the commands of God, that is, girding oneself in whatever way. Although God commands this discipline, as it is said: The law is good if one uses it lawfully. Likewise: He who takes the sword will perish by the sword, yet it is only an external work, which can exist even in the impious. But the cross is called an affliction, not sought by our will, but either arisen from tyrants attempting to destroy the Gospel, or following the common infirmity of human nature subject to diseases, poverty, infamy, and other sorrows, not sought by our will. It is tolerated, however, on account of the obedience owed to God, and to that obedience are added faith, hope, and invocation. The tolerance of such afflictions in the saints is called sacrifice and mortification, and it is a far greater and more difficult thing than pedagogical discipline, of which it was spoken before: When you were younger, you girded yourself.

Christ therefore warns Peter to put aside that sweet dream of power and wealth, and to prepare himself for the cross. But it has often been said elsewhere that in the Church of God alone exists the true doctrine concerning the cross, and firm consolation. The Gentiles and others ignorant of the Gospel neither know the causes, whence are such great calamities of such excellent human nature, nor do they know effective remedies truly healing the sorrows of the heart. But the Gospel shows both the causes and the remedies, and the entire doctrine concerning this point has often been recited elsewhere, which certainly all ought always to have in sight, so that they may hold true consolations in great sorrows.

Latin:

Caput XXI.

In postremo capite narrat plura facta, in quibus Christus se post resurrectionem Apostolis claris- sime ostendit. Nos omnia testimonia collecta, saepe repetamus ad confirmandam fidem nostram. De- inde cum fere in singulis conciones aliquae sint, insignem doctrinam continentes, has quoque con- templemur. In hac historia quae hic recitatur, tres sunt loci praecipui: Primus de ministerio datur mandatum ministris, ut diligant Christum, et pascant Ecclesiam. Secundus de discrimine disciplinae et crucis. Tertius de vocatione, ut suae quisque vocationi obtemperet, nec relinquat suam, aut frangatur animo, etiamsi alium aliter vocari videt.

De primo loco, videlicet de mandatis, quae dantur Apostolis, ut diligant Christum, et pascant gregem, sciamus hic regulam tradi, continentem praecipuas virtutes omnium docentium in Ecclesia. Prior est, ut diligant Christum, id est agnoscant, et vera fide invocent Christum, et diligant eius doctrinam, nec magis ament suam potentiam, opes, voluptates, quam Christum. Hoc fundamentum nisi sit in doctore seu gubernatore, nec doctrinam constanter defendet, nec caeteras partes ministerii fideliter administrabit, ut multi ambitione et cupiditate vindictae, sparserunt et spargunt falsa dogmata, quia magis amant gloriam suam, quam Christum et veritatem Evangelii, et nunc manifestum est monachos, propter quaestum tueri impios cultus mortuorum, et suas Missas, et alias superstitiones. Ut igitur doctores integritatem et fidem in ministerio Evangelii praestent, prius in eis Christus dilectionem flagitat. Haec plana et perspicua sunt, quia nemo fideliter servit ulli domino, nisi diligat eum.

Quod autem ex hoc loco sumta sunt argumenta de primatu Romani pontificis, brevissima responsio est piorum: etiamsi iure divino Romanus episcopus esset summus, tamen necesse esset ab eo dissentire, cum defendat dogmata pugnantia cum Evangelio, et idola, ut Paulus inquit: Si quis angelus de coelo aliud Evangelium praedicabit, anathema sit. Manifestum est autem atroces errores et idola defendi a Romano episcopo, et eius satellitibus. Ita Ieremias, et Zacharias, et alii dissenserunt a suis pontificibus, tametsi manifestum erat Leviticum Pontificem iure divino superiorem esse caeteris sacerdotibus. Hac responsione primum pii se confirment in horum temporum controversiis.

Deinde facile est respondere ad vitiosas connexiones, ad Petrum nominatim dicitur: Pasce oves meas, ergo caeteris Apostolis anteponitur. Neganda est consequentia. Nam alibi communia mandata dantur omnibus, ut Lucae ultimo, et supra in Iohanne: Quorum remiseritis peccata, remittentur. Nec coniectura illa firma est, Petrus plus diligit, ergo ei tribuitur maior potestas. Potest enim sine potestate maior dilectio esse in privato, quam in gubernatore, denique ministerium Evangelii est mandatum docendi Evangelii et administrandi sacramenta, non est potestas similis politicae. Nam potestas politica habet mandatum tuendi disciplinam et pacem, iuxta certas leges, vi corporali, et habet certum populum, quem cogit ad obedientiam, et potest ferre novas leges congruentes rationi, utiles suo imperio. Non est autem ministro Evangelii talis potestas, non habet autoritatem ferendi novas leges extra Evangelium, nec vi aut excommunicatione cogendi alios ministros ad leges extra Evangelium latas.

Non est igitur fingenda potestas alicuius episcopi similis regum potestati, ut de Romano pontifice fingunt. Haec satis sit de hac quaestione breviter monuisse.

De secundo loco, scilicet de discrimine disciplinae et crucis. Cum esses iunior, inquit Christus, cingebas te ipse, etc. Ut saepe alias, ita et in hoc colloquio taxat Christus stultam persuasionem Petri, qui expectabat iam post resurrectionem Christi illud aureum imperium, quo putabant Iudaei se domitis gentibus summam potentiam et opes possessuros esse. Imo, inquit, nunc initium erit ingentium afflictionum. Antea cingebas te ipse, nunc alii cingent. In hoc loco discernatur disciplina rationalis a cruce. Disciplina est diligentia regendi externos mores, iuxta mandata Dei, hoc est, utcunque seipsum cingere. Etsi autem hanc disciplinam Deus praecipit, ut dicitur: Lex est bona legitime utenti. Item: Qui gladium acceperit, gladio peribit, tamen tantum est externum opus, quod etiam in impiis esse potest. Sed crux dicitur afflictio, non accersita nostra voluntate, sed aut orta a tyrannis conantibus delere Evangelium, aut sequens communem infirmitatem naturae hominum obnoxiae morbis, paupertati, infamiae, et aliis doloribus, non accersitis nostra voluntate. Toleratur autem propter obedientiam Deo debitam, et ad eam obedientiam accedunt fides, spes, et invocatio. Talium afflictionum tolerantia in sanctis vocatur sacrificium et mortificatio, et longe maior et difficilior res est, quam disciplina paedagogica, de qua prius dictum est: Cum esses iunior, cingebas teipsum.

Praemonet igitur Christus Petrum, ut de- ponas illud dulce somnium de potentia et opibus, et se praeparet ad crucem. Saepe autem alias dictum est, in sola Ecclesia Dei extare doctrinam veram de cruce, et firmam consolationem. Eth- nici et alii ignorantes Evangelium, nec causas no- runt, unde sint tantae calamitates, tam praestan- tis naturae hominum, nec norunt efficacia reme- dia vere sanantia dolores cordis. Sed Evange- lium et causas ostendit, et remedia, ac saepe alias integra doctrina de hoc loco recitata est, quam certe oportet omnes semper in conspectu habere, ut teneant in magnis doloribus veras consolationes.

## 21:22
If I want him to remain, etc.

I said that in the third point is contained a doctrine most worthy of memory concerning vocation, since there are diverse gifts in the Church, and diverse vocations, so that we may not be broken by despair, or inflamed by envy on account of others excelling, or by perverse imitation or κακοζηλίᾳ, or πολυπραγμοσύνῃ, having deserted our own vocation, rush into others; these things extend widely in life, as examples show. We, because our gifts are not equal to the gifts of the Prophets and Apostles, are tormented and doubt whether we please God, whether God wishes to be present to our course. This weakness must be cast out, and one must serve with firm faith, even if our gifts are meager. Furthermore, Cain, Saul, are inflamed by envy. This evil is customary not only in the Church, but also in other gatherings of men. Pompey grieves that Julius is growing, and that he himself is considered as inferior, therefore he is more easily impelled to move civil war, and as in empires seditions and civil wars in all ages have arisen from envy and the desire for revenge: so often in the Church false opinions have been moved, and great dissipations have been made, so that the envious might remove others growing in position, and shake them from their height. Thus Arius, grieving that another was preferred to him in the election of a Bishop, moved the contest concerning the Son of God. And this age of ours has seen examples of some, who it is certain were incited only by envy to move or defend false opinions to undermine the authority of those who were thought to excel. Since therefore it is a very common evil to envy those who are better, and often horrible fires of the Church and of empires arise from thence, one must learn what this evil is, what are its seeds, what the connected plagues are, so that we may resist all these diseases with greater prudence. The seed is pride, as in Saul, Pompey, and the like, who wish to excel everyone. Then follows envy, which attempts to remove an equal or one who is rising: then, so that an antagonist may be moved from his place, an opportunity is sought to crush him, either by fabricated calumnies, as Saul pretends that David is invading the kingdom, or arms are openly taken up. All these vices are condemned by God: pride, envy, injury. It is difficult, however, for sharp natures to restrain these impulses, but an illustrious example of one alien to pride and envy is Jonathan; let us propose him to ourselves, let us imitate him. He is first of all humble, because through the fear of God he acknowledges his own weakness, nor does he covet the kingdom; indeed, he knows that there is nothing greater in human life than the governance, especially of the people of God. He knows also that this very kingdom is a gift of God, and is not to be invaded by any man, but that he is to have it to whom God would deliver it by His counsel, just as He had delivered it to his father Saul: then he is not envious, after he sees that David has been called by God to this governance; he does not strive to move him from his place, but yields to him, and submits himself to him, and rejoices that another more excellent has been chosen, whose governance he saw would be happier than the governance of the previous time, which Saul and he himself had held. Finally, he does not inflict injuries upon David, but truly loves, venerates, and defends him against his father. And he does this for many reasons: he knows that he owes love to David, he knows that he is now subject to him as king, he knows also that for the sake of public utility concord must be maintained, and that the king who has been called by God must be helped. Let us diligently consider these virtues of Jonathan, and if we ever see the seeds of emulation arising, let us repress our impulses through the fear and invocation of God. Thus Christ recalls Peter to the consideration of his own vocation: Follow me, who am calling, and do not contend with emulation or spite against another, if you think someone is outstripping you, etc. The third member is about perverse imitation, κακοζηλίᾳ, and the confusion of ministers; many saw the examples of the Prophets, who sacrificed in different places. They imitated this against the rule, and thought they were performing a singular worship to God because the Prophets sacrificed in that way, but the imitation was of an external shadow, and not of the prophetic spirit. Thus in all times many have sinned in the Church through perverse imitation. The Jews slaughtered their children, abusing the example of Abraham; many deserted their spouses and magistracies, and withdrew into deserts through perverse imitation. Thus through perverse imitation the abuses of the Lord's Supper grew, Masses were accumulated, and the selling of them followed. Finally, as perverse imitation is dangerous and often pernicious in all things, so in matters of worship one must especially beware that foolish imitation does not beget or confirm errors.

Often also ministries are confused by emulation; Bishops, having omitted their ecclesiastical duty, have wished to be equal to princes, and often preachers wish to govern the political affairs of courts or cities, and teachers of letters, when they see that disputes about religion are more plausible than the doctrine of the inferior arts, suddenly become Theologians. This ambition is very pernicious to the Church and to the whole of human life; therefore it must be restrained, and the rule must always be held: If I want him to be greater, what is that to you? Follow me. Let each one understand his own vocation and serve in it, and adorn it, whether it be humble or arduous, as it is commonly said: You have obtained Sparta, adorn it. Let us know that this goal is surrounded not only by human wisdom, but much more by divine precepts, because Peter expressly commands that we should not be ἀλλοτριοεπίσκοποι, and Paul most learnedly says, 1. Thess. 4.: We exhort you, brothers, to excel more and to take singular care to be quiet and to do your own things. He used very significant words. Ambition invites profane men to break out beyond their vocations, as Antony is not content with the partnership of the empire with Octavius, but wishes to reign alone with his partner oppressed: or they stir up unnecessary things, even if they do not seem to covet superior vocations, as C. Gracchus disturbed the Republic with many new laws, agrarian, judicial, and others. For there is a vicious ambition, a desire for glory, which is not sought in order, when, namely, the applause of anyone at all is sought, by attempting actions beyond one's strength or outside one's vocation, through reliance on one's own wisdom or one's own powers. The Holy Spirit often condemns this vicious ambition, as in Rom. 12.: For I say through the grace that has been given to me, to all who are among you, not to think of themselves more highly than they ought, but to think modestly of themselves, as God has distributed to each the measure of faith. And in Gal. 6.: If anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself.

Since therefore this foolish ambition is an evil common to many, and is thought by many to be greatness of soul, Paul opposes a contrary ambition, that is, a contrary manner of seeking glory, and he retains the name of ambition, φιλοτιμίας, which is indeed common to both vice and virtue, even in the ancient manner of speaking, but he retained the same name, which was more plausible and pleasing among the ambitious, so that the admonition might be more illustrious, as if he were saying, let ambition or the desire for glory be indeed a very noble thing, nor do I blame glory or the desire for glory, but let it be rightly ordered: Glory is the approval of a conscience judging rightly, and of others judging rightly. This approval is to be sought, but a conscience judging rightly does not approve the impulses of those who undertake things beyond their strength or outside their calling, through a foolish confidence in themselves. No one judging rightly praises Antony or C. Gracchus or the like, but the conscience of one judging rightly approves a will serving its calling and containing itself within these bounds on account of the will of God, and because it sees that human infirmity cannot sustain the burden of government. Such was the will of Jonathan, who willingly entrusted the kingdom to David. He wants such a φιλοτιμίαν in us, contrary to that with which profane minds burn, which stir up many unnecessary things, or even break out beyond their calling. But you, be quiet, he says, that is, do not stir up unnecessary things, and do your own works, that is, let each one perform the duties of his own calling. How necessary this whole doctrine concerning the curbing of ambition and πολυπραγμοσύνη is in the Church of God and in all government is by no means obscure. For often churches and empires have been overturned by ambition, often by πολυπραγμοσύνη. It is therefore useful for men to be forewarned, so that they may learn to restrain erring impulses, and guide their counsels by the commandments of God, by the fear of God and faith, and by the invocation of God, as it is written: Commit your life to God, and he himself will act.

The End.

Latin:

Si eum volo manere, etc.

Dixi in tertio loco contineri doctrinam dignissimam memoria de vocatione, cum diversa sint in Ecclesia dona, et diversae vocationes, ne aut desperatione frangamur, aut invidentia in- cendamur, propter alios antecellentes, aut prava imitatione seu κακοζηλίᾳ, aut πολυπραγμοσύνῃ, deserta nostra vocatione, in alienas irruamus, haec late patent in vita, ut exempla ostendunt. Nos quia nostra dona non sunt paria Propheta- rum et Apostolorum donis, angimur et dubita- mus, an Deo placeamus, an Deus velit adesse nostro curriculo. Haec imbecillitas eiicienda est, et serviendum firma fide, etiamsi dona nostra sunt exigua. Praeterea Cain, Saul, incendun- tur invidentia. Hoc malum usitatum est non so- lum in Ecclesia, sed etiam in aliis hominum coe- tibus. Pompeius dolet crescere Iulium, et se quasi inferiorem duci, ideo facilius impellitur ad movendum bellum civile, ac ut in imperiis sedi- tiones et bella civilia omnibus aetatibus ex invidia et cupiditate vindictae orta sunt: ita saepe in Ec- clesia motae sunt falsae opiniones, et magnae dis- sipationes factae sunt, ut invidi alios crescentes loco moverent, et ex fastigio excuterent. Sic Arius dolens alium sibi praelatum esse in ele- ctione Episcopi, movit certamen de filio Dei. Et haec nostra aetas vidit exempla aliquorum, quos constat tantum livore incitatos esse, ut moverent, aut propugnarent falsas opiniones ad labefactan- dam eorum autoritatem, qui antecellere existima- bantur. Cum igitur valde commune malum sit, invidere melioribus, et saepe horrenda incendia Ecclesiae, et imperiorum inde oriantur, discen- dum est, quale sit hoc malum, quae sint semina, quae sint coniunctae pestes, ut maiore prudentia repugnemus omnibus his morbis. Semen est superbia, ut in Saule, Pompeio, et similibus, qui volunt antecellere omnibus. Deinde sequitur invidentia, quae removere parem, aut crescentem conatur: deinde ut antagonista loco moveatur, quaeritur occasio eius premendi, seu confictis calumniis, ut fingit Saul Davidem invadere regnum, se palam arma capiuntur. Haec vitia omnia damnata sunt a Deo, superbia, invidentia, iniuria. Difficile est autem acrib. naturis frenare hos impetus, sed exemplum illustri alieni a superbia et invidentia est Ionathan, hunc nobis proponamus, hunc imitemur. Hic primum est humilis, quia timore Dei agnoscit suam infirmitatem, nec appetit regnum, imo scit nihil esse maius in hominum vita, quam gubernationem praesertim populi Dei. Scit etiam hoc ipsum regnum Dei donum esse, nec invadendum esse ab ullo homine, sed hunc habiturum esse, cui Deus suo consilio traditurus esset, sicut patri Saul tradiderat: deinde non est invidus, postquam videt Davidem a Deo ad hanc gubernationem vocatum esse, non studet eum loco movere, sed cedit ei, et sese ei subiicit, et gaudet alium praestantiorem electum esse, cuius gubernationem videbat futuram feliciorem gubernatione proximi temporis, quam Saul et ipse tenuerant. Postremo nec iniuriis afficit Davidem, sed eum vere diligit, veneratur, et defendit adversus patrem. Idque propter multas causas facit, scit se debere Davidi dilectionem, scit se ei nunc subiectum esse, ut regi, scit etiam propter publicam utilitatem concordiam tuendam esse, et eum regem qui a Deo vocatus est, adiuvandum esse. Has Ionathae virtutes diligenter consideremus, et nostros impetus, si quando aemulationum semina oriri videmus, timore et invocatione Dei reprimamus. Ita Christus revocat Petrum ad considerationem propriae vocationis: Tu me sequere vocantem, nec certato aemulatione aut livore cum alio, si quem tibi praecurrere existimas, etc. Tertium membrum est de prava imitatione, κακοζηλίᾳ et confusione ministrorum, viderunt multi exempla Prophetarum, qui diversis locis sacrificarunt. Id imitati sunt contra regulam, et putabant se cultum Deo singularem praestare, quia Prophetae ita sacrificarunt, sed imitatio erat umbrae externae, et non prophetici spiritus. Ita omnibus temporibus multi peccarunt in Ecclesia, prava imita- tione. Iudaei mactarunt filios abusi exemplo Abrahae, multi deseruerunt coniuges et magistra- tus, et concesserunt in eremos prava imitatione. Sic prava imitatione creverunt abusus coenae Do- mini, cumulatae sunt Missae, et secutae vendi- tiones earum. Denique ut in omnibus rebus prava imitatio periculosa, et saepe perniciosa est, ita maxime in cultibus cavendum est, ne stulta imitatio gignat, aut confirmet errores.

Saepe etiam aemulatione ministeria confun- duntur, Episcopi omisso munere ecclesiastico, voluerunt pares esse principibus, et saepe con- cionatores volunt regere politica negotia aularum, aut civitatum, et doctores literarum, cum vident disputationes de religione plausibiliores esse, quam doctrinam inferiorum artium, fiunt subito Theologi. Haec ambitio valde perniciosa est Ec- clesiae et universae vitae humanae, ideo fre- nanda est, et semper tenenda regula: Si illum volo maiorem esse, quid a te, tu me sequere. Suam quisque vocationem intelligat et in ea ser- viat, eamque ornet, sive sit humilis, sive ar- dua, sicut usitate dictum est: Spartam nactus es, hanc orna. Hanc metam non tantum humana sapientia, sed multo magis divinis praeceptis circumdatam nobis esse sciamus, quia Petrus ex- presse praecipit, ne simus ἀλλοτριοεπίσκοποι, et Paulus eruditissime inquit, 1. Thess. 4.: Horta- mur vos fratres antecellere magis et singulari stu- dio curare ut quiescatis et agatis propria. Valde significantibus verbis usus est. Profanos homi- nes ambitio invitat, ut extra vocationes erumpant, ut Antonius non contentus est societate imperii cum Octavio, sed solus vult regnare oppresso so- cio: aut moveant non necessaria, etiamsi supe- riores vocationes non videntur appetere, ut C. Gracchus multis novis legibus latis turbabat Rempubl. Agraria, iudiciali, et aliis. Est enim vitiosa ambitio, cupiditas gloriae, quae non ap- petitur ordine, cum videlicet quaeritur applau- sus qualiumcunque, tentatis actionibus supra vi- res aut extra vocationem, fiducia propriae sapien- tiae, aut suarum virium. Hanc vitiosam ambi- tionem saepe damnat Spiritus sanctus, ut ad Rom. 12.: Dico autem per gratiam, quae mihi data est, omnibus, qui sunt inter vos, ne sen- tiant de se supra quam oportet, sed sentiant de se modeste, ut cuique distribuit Deus mensuram fidei. Et ad Galat. 6.: Si quis putat, se aliquid esse, cum nihil sit, seipsum decipit.

Cum igitur haec stulta ambitio malum sit pluribus usitatum, et a multis putatur esse animi magnitudo, Paulus contrariam ambitionem oppo- nit, id est, contrarium modum quaerendae gloriae, et retinet nomen ambitionis, φιλοτιμίας, quod est quidem commune ad vitium et virtutem, etiam veteri more loquendi, sed tamen ideo, ut esset illustrior admonitio, nomen idem retinuit, quod erat apud ambitiosos plausibilius et gratius, quasi dicat, sit sane praeclarum quiddam ambitio seu gloriae cupiditas, nec vitupero gloriam, aut glo- riae cupiditatem, sed sit recte ordinata: Gloria est approbatio conscientiae recte iudicantis, et alio- rum recte iudicantium. Haec approbatio appe- tenda est, sed conscientia recte iudicans non ap- probat impetus eorum qui suscipiunt res supra vires aut extra vocationem, stulta sui fiducia. Nemo recte iudicans laudat Antonium aut C. Grac- chum aut similes, sed conscientia recte iudican- tis approbat voluntatem servientem vocationi et intra has metas se continentem propter volunta- tem Dei, et quia videt, infirmitatem humanam non posse molem gubernationis sustinere. Qua- lis fuit voluntas Ionathae, ultro credentis re- gnum Davidi. Talem vult esse φιλοτιμίαν in nobis contrariam illi, qua ardent profanae men- tes, quae multa movent non necessaria, aut erumpunt etiam extra vocationem. At vos quiescite, inquit, id est, non movete non ne- cessaria, et facite proprias operas, id est, facite officia sua quisque vocationis. Haec tota do- ctrina de frenanda ambitione et πολυπραγ- μοσύνη quam necessaria sit in Ecclesia Dei et in omni gubernatione nequaquam obscurum est. Saepe enim Ecclesiae et imperia ambitione, saepe πολυπραγμοσύνη eversa sunt. Praemo- neri igitur homines utile est, ut errantes impe- tus coërcere discant, et regant consilia manda- tis Dei, timore Dei et fide, invocatione Dei, sicut scriptum est: Commenda Deo vitam tuam, et ipse faciet.

Finis.

# Romans

## 1:1 Introduction
Sixteen years after the Commentaries of Melanchthon on the Epistle to the Romans had seen the light, having passed by, Melanchthon worked out and published a new exposition of the same epistle, inscribed to Ulricus Mordeisen. (See the dedicatory epistle above, Vol. VIII, p. 737.) Exposition of the Epistles of Paul written to the Romans, edited by Phil. Melanchthon. A.D. 1556. (At the end:) Wittenberg, from the printing office of Vitus Creutzer, at the expense of Conrad Rhuel.

1 Alphabet, 8 sheets, 8. Repeated ibid. and by the same in the year 1558. 1 Alphabet, 9 sheets — and again: Epistles of Paul — — Wittenberg, executed by Io. Lufft. 1561. 1 Alphabet, 9 sheets, 8. In the works of Melanchthon edited by Peucer, Vol. IV, p. 35–209. EXPOSITION OF THE EPISTLES OF PAUL WRITTEN TO THE ROMANS, EDITED BY PHIL. MELANCHTHON IN THE YEAR 1556. Argument of the Epistle. God wills that the Son be acknowledged as mediator, nor does He will to liberate men from sin and eternal death in any other way than in the invocation of the Son, just as He says in the second Psalm: Kiss the Son, blessed are all who trust in Him.

And the voice of the Father, sounding from heaven, is this: This is my beloved Son, hear him. And the Son says: No one comes to the Father except through the Son. Likewise: This is eternal life, that they may know you, the true God, and whom you have sent, Jesus Christ. It is necessary, therefore, that the benefits proper to the Son of God be rightly perceived in the Church, that is, the remission of sins, reconciliation, the gift of the Holy Spirit, of righteousness, and of eternal life.

And in order that the Son of God be rightly acknowledged, it is necessary on the other hand to understand what an evil Sin is, and to discern the difference between philosophy, the Law, and the Gospel, between the righteousness of faith and the righteousness of works, which is whatever human diligence there may be in performing the law.

It is also necessary to know what kind of assembly the Church of God is in this life. The knowledge of these greatest of things is the wisdom proper to the Church, revealed in the promises and the voice of the Gospel, from the very beginning, from the first promise promulgated to our first parents, and often repeated thereafter. For since this doctrine is outside human judgment, men from time to time lose the true light concerning the mediator and the righteousness of faith, and they slip into human opinions, which imagine that our discipline is the remission of sins and that men are righteous by such discipline, that is, acceptable to God and heirs of eternal life, and they forget the mediator.

Thus a great part in Israel always felt, and finally the Pharisees openly taught with great contention that men merit the remission of sins and are righteous by that discipline and the diligence of performing the law.

Then they imagined that the Messiah would come to establish a political empire in this mortal life more justly and tranquilly. But God from time to time rebuked these errors, having sent Prophets and pious teachers, and having sent the Son and the Apostles. Similar errors, however, wander through the human race in all times. Thus the Heathens, who did not wish to appear atheists, used to pretend that they merited the remission of sins by their sacrifices and were righteous by discipline.

Thus for a long time the Sacrificers and Monks taught that they merited the remission of sins by the sacrifice of the Mass and other works, and were righteous by such discipline. It is always necessary that these errors be refuted in the Church, and that the doctrine concerning [the Son of God and His benefits be illustrated]. the Son of God and his benefits.

These things are done with the greatest clarity in the Epistle of Paul to the Romans.

Because when the Pharisees and many others at that time were defending their errors about the justice of the law most fiercely, and were not acknowledging the Son of God and the justice of faith, it was necessary that a clear refutation be opposed to them.

Yet this Epistle is not to be applied only to that time, but it is always necessary that the Son of God be rightly acknowledged, and the justice of faith be understood, and the distinction between the Law and the Gospel.

Therefore, this Epistle preaches to the Church, even until the final judgment, just as the same things were handed down before by the Prophets, in which exist most severe sermons against those pharisaical shadows, and many were killed by the Priests and Pharisees because of these rebukes.

Indeed, Paul, although he affirms that he received the doctrine by the revelation of the Son of God, as he says expressly to the Galatians: yet he cites the testimonies of the Prophets, to show that there is one perpetual voice of the Gospel in the Church, concerning the benefits of the Son of God, concerning the mode of reconciliation, concerning justice, concerning true worship, concerning the true Church, and concerning the judgment of God.

But this Epistle of Paul is the more clear because it contains an express antithesis of contrary opinions, and argues in order, as an artisan does, and it is almost a method of doctrine, which is proper to the Church, because it explains the principal matters so accurately: the benefits of the mediator, the distinction between the Law and the Gospel, the distinction between the justice of faith and the justice of works, the doctrine concerning the true Church, and concerning true worship.

It is necessary, therefore, that this Epistle be most familiarly known to all, and the greatest vigilance must be applied, so that its meaning may be retained uncorrupted.

But before I speak of the corruptions, I will first recite the summary of the doctrine concerning justification, so that the comparison may be clearer afterwards.

Summary of the doctrine handed down in the prophetic and apostolic writings, concerning justification before God.

In the beginning, I will recite two examples, which for this reason should always be in sight, not only because they illustrate this whole doctrine, but also so that they may remind us ourselves of repentance and true consolation.

When Adam, after the fall, is rebuked by God, he trembles horribly, because, when God himself accuses the creature with his own voice, let us not think that the conversation is idle, but God is a consuming fire, as it is written.

Adam therefore lies prostrate before God, knowing nothing but the law, from which he rightly reasons that he is perpetually condemned.

For he thinks thus: The justice of God is immutable, to punish and to cast away the disobedient.

I did not obey, and I was horribly ungrateful to God, when he had loved this nature so much that he had infused his greatest gifts into it, and had made it his own image; I destroyed this work of God, and I cast away such great gifts and shook off God dwelling in me: Therefore it is necessary that I, in turn, be cast away.

In this judgment and true agony, there was no such thought in Adam that he could merit the remission of sins, and could take away sin, but he truly felt the wrath of God, and that he was displeasing to God, and he truly felt that he could be helped by the aid of no creature, and the argument taken from the law was true, nor could it have been solved by any creature.

But the Son of God becomes the intercessor, and transfers the punishment onto himself by a wonderful and ineffable counsel.

For it is most true that the justice of God is immutable, and that God is truly and horribly angry at sins.

I have sinned, therefore I shall be punished.

Here the Son of God answers: Either Adam will be punished, or another, with me interceding, namely, I myself, having assumed human nature, whose punishment will be an equivalent price for the human race, I shall pay.

Concerning this admirable deliberation, we shall consider the wisdom, justice, and mercy of God in eternal life.

Nor are our punishments in this life a price that appeases the wrath of God, but they are only signs and reminders, so that we may think that God is truly angry at sins.

And so Adam, still ignorant of the promise, and hearing the divine accusation, struggles with death and sees no help anywhere.

Although he had begun to tremble before, covering a part of his body with fig leaves, yet he had not yet been in such pain, he had not yet felt the wrath of God in this way: but afterwards, when God speaks, he recognizes that sins are not covered by those fig leaves.

Finally, however, he hears the consolation, when the promise, brought forth from the secret counsel of God, is promulgated, which affirms that the seed of the woman will come, by which sin is to be taken away again.

Adam therefore understands that he is received, and is raised up by faith in this promise, and because of this seed he determines that he now pleases God, even though he was far more deformed than he had been before the fall.

By this faith, therefore, he receives the remission of sins, and thence he is just before God, he approaches God, calls, and is vivified by the Son of God through the Holy Spirit, having heard the promise, he begins again to obey, so that he does not act against his conscience. [He knows him as] the propitiator.

He determines, therefore, that he too is... received on account of him, and he knows that this worship and this honor must be rendered to God, so that he may believe the promise, and neither accuse God of lying, nor fall away from God, nor despise the mediator. Let this image of the conversion of Adam, and how, having heard the promise, he is raised up by faith, and is righteous, that is, accepted by God, and afterwards begins again to obey, always be in view, because in the same way conversion and consolation happen in others.
