But the doctrine of faith is more illustrious in the first example, in which it is necessary that there were horrible sorrows, and because Adam understood more the magnitude of the fall, who knew what he had been, and because he thought it was an incurable evil, since the promise had not yet been given, and because he knew of the rejection of the demons.

But we read that great history with too idle minds, in which so many things concur, of which some show the immense wrath of God, others the immense magnitude of his mercy. For that God receives fallen men, when his justice is immutable, and that he receives them in such a way that the Son becomes a victim, these wondrous counsels far surpass the wisdom of all creatures. And yet God wills that we consider his justice and mercy in some way in this life, so that true fear, true faith, invocation, gratitude, love, and other virtues may be kindled in us.

Let another example be the conversion of David after his fall, in which these two motions are also seen, immense dread, and then consolation.

For when he is rebuked by the Prophet Nathan, concerning the stolen wife of another, and concerning the death of her husband, horrible dreads arise in David, such as he often describes: There is no peace in my bones from the sight of my sins etc. He recognizes the wrath of God against sin, he grieves therefore, because he offended God, he fears that he will be cast away by God, just as he had seen before that Saul was horribly cast away.

Finally, he fears eternal and present punishments, and he can no longer gather merits, he sees that his own virtues or former deeds cannot be opposed to the wrath of God, and he would be extinguished by the magnitude of his sorrow, if consolation did not approach: You shall not die, the Lord has taken away your sin.

Having heard this absolution, faith is again kindled in him, by which, apprehending the absolution, he begins to behold the mercy of God, and he thinks now of the other promises, and rests in the mediator, and recognizes that men are received through immense mercy on account of the high priest, interceding for us, whom he himself names a Priest according to the order of Melchizedek. He knows this one to be the mediator and propitiator. He determines, therefore, that he too is received on account of him, and he knows that this worship and this honor must be rendered to God, so that he may believe the promise, and neither accuse God of lying, nor fall away from God, nor despise the mediator. Looking into these examples and similar ones, we will more easily understand the doctrine of Justification, especially if it will not be merely a cold thought of an idle mind, but if we too seriously tremble at the remembrance of our sins, and seek consolation.

Let us know, therefore, that this is the doctrine of the Gospel, about which Paul preaches in this Epistle.

He argues against sin, just as it is written: The Holy Spirit will convict the world of sin, and he proposes consolation, namely, the promise of the remission of sins, and reconciliation to be given on account of the Son of God, and he affirms that those who believe in those dreads, that sins are remitted to them on account of the Son the mediator, freely, that they are truly received, and receive the remission of sins, and together with the remission of sins the Holy Spirit is given, who helps the struggling conscience, and sustaining itself by faith, and at the same time kindles other virtues, namely the invocation of God, and confirms the will, so that it submits itself to God, has the fear of God, love and a good purpose, just as it is clearly said in Galatians 3:

That we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.

This will of God, concerning reconciliation on account of the Son, is not known to men by natural light, as the law is, but by immense goodness, the Son interceding, it was made manifest by the voice of God in the beginning in the promises, and afterwards illustrated by the Prophets, by the Son himself and the Apostles.

Although this doctrine has been clearly handed down in the Prophets and Apostles, yet it has been variously obscured in the world from time to time.

The younger ones must therefore be warned to retain the native meaning of the Gospel.

It is most certain that Paul means this, We are justified by faith freely, that is, on account of the Son of God, and not on account of our dignity, or any merits of ours do we receive the remission of sins, and reconciliation and the imputation of justice, when we believe the Gospel, and by faith determine that these benefits are given to us on account of the Son of God, and indeed this faith believes all the articles of faith, and refers the others to this very article: The remission of sins, concerning which article it is not only to be believed in general, that sins are remitted to some others, just as even the demons believe, but it is to be believed in truth for yourself. PHILIP MELANCHTHON'S EXEGETICAL WRITINGS.

803

804

that the remission of sins is given.

With this faith we are raised up, and at the same time, as I have said, the Son of God quickens the believer, and gives the Holy Spirit, and we receive the remission of sins, and we are righteous, that is, accepted by God unto eternal life on account of the Mediator, even though there are still in us remnants of sin and great infirmity.

That this is the plain and native meaning of Paul is not in doubt, as we shall declare more fully later.

And we retain in this interpretation the propriety of Paul's words, and we are hearers of Paul, we do not attach other meanings to Paul's discourse, and it appears that this our interpretation is native and true, when all the members of Paul's disputation are compared.

Likewise, when the sermons of the Prophets and of Christ are compared.

Likewise, when the testimony of the catholic Church of God is compared, that is, of all men who understand the exercises of repentance and invocation, and have learned that one must acquiesce by faith in the Son of God.

Such have always been, are, and will be many in the Church, in whom the true meaning of the Gospel shines.

And although writers have sometimes spoken improperly, yet we see that many agree with this meaning, such as Augustine, Prosper, Ambrose, Basil, Bernard, Tauler, and others.

And so we do not despise the judgment and testimony of the Church, so that we may appeal to pious minds throughout the whole world who understand the exercises of repentance.

But although in the corruptions of this saying: "We are justified by faith," others have spoken differently, yet the cause of error is the same for all, and all construct the same false meaning.

All understand by faith only the knowledge of history, and they understand "righteous" philosophically, as having the virtues themselves, as when we say, "the water is heated," that is, heat is transfused into the water.

In this way, since they err concerning the words, they then attach alien interpretations, which, however, all in sum mean this: that in this proposition there is a synecdoche, "we are justified by faith," that is, we are justified by faith and other virtues, or we are prepared by faith, so that afterwards we may be righteous by other virtues.

The Monks have spoken thus: "by formed faith, namely, by love, we are righteous," which they understood thus: "on account of love we are righteous."

Others have interpreted it thus: "by faith, that is, by works commanded by God, we are righteous," not by the works of human traditions.

Others pervert it in this way: "by faith, that is, by interior worship, not by external works, we are righteous."

All these interpretations mean this: Man is righteous, that is, accepted by God unto eternal life on account of his own virtues and works.

And some relate this more absurdly, others omit certain absurdities.

The Monks say that men merit the remission of sins by their own virtues and works; they say that the righteous satisfy the law, as Malvenda says, therefore a man is called righteous because he pays the debt to God.

And they add further: Since no one knows when he has enough works, they command one to always doubt whether one is in grace, and they call this doubt pious.

Thus they utterly remove faith, and delete the voice of the Gospel, and the consolation which God has revealed by His immense goodness, and wishes to exist in the Church.

Now let the studious see whether these interpretations agree with the entire disputation of Paul.

Likewise, whether they agree with the perpetual prophetic and apostolic meaning.

It is manifest, however, that these three members are the chief ones of Paul's disputation.

First, he affirms clearly and without any ambiguity that men do not satisfy the law of God, nor are they righteous by the law, but that all are guilty and under sin, as is clearly said in Chapter 3: "That every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may be guilty before God."

He concluded all under sin, that He might have mercy on all.

Secondly, he affirms that men are received on account of the Mediator, freely, and he wishes it to be understood that for this very cause the Messiah was sent, that He might be the propitiator, and take away sin and death, not that He might establish the empires of the world, as the Pharisees dreamed.

Thirdly, he affirms that reconciliation must be received by faith, and that it must be established by faith that we are not received and pleasing to God on account of the Mediator, and that one must not remain in doubt.

Now since it is manifest that these three members were handed down by Paul, it is certain that interpretations conflicting with these three members are false.

Nor is the refutation difficult for those holding these foundations which I have reviewed.

Because the particle "Freely" expressly removes our merits, and leads us to the merits of the Son of God, and God wishes the Son to be acknowledged, and this honor to be attributed to Him, that we may confess Him to be the Propitiator and Mediator.

Wherefore it is manifest that the monks err when they teach that men merit the remission of sins by their own works or virtues. They were also, when they understand faith only as knowledge of history, and command men to always remain in doubt, because Paul manifestly says, It is necessary that the promise be received by faith. He speaks, therefore, of the faith by which we also embrace the other articles of faith, and assent to the promise, and determine that the promised benefit is exhibited to us, with which faith there is a trust resting in the mercy promised on account of the Son, or resting in the Son, approaching to God, invoking and crying Abba Father etc. Item, he who remains in doubt does not determine for himself that the Son of God is his mediator. He does not, therefore, attribute to him the due honor.

But another question is agitated here: after a man has been converted, and spiritual newness, or, as others speak, love, has already been kindled in him, they say that he is righteous after conversion by this newness or love, that is, that his person is accepted by God and he is an heir of eternal life on account of love; and the monks formerly accumulated these things, saying that this newness is a merit of eternal life by condignity, that is, a price on account of which eternal life is owed, and they declaim that the gift of God in the converted is not to be diminished, since conversion is made for this reason, that a man may be made righteous from unrighteous, and since love is righteousness, they shout that it is absurd to deny that a man is righteous on account of it, just as a wall is called white on account of whiteness, and they accommodate many sayings to this. He who does righteousness is righteous. Item: Not the hearers of the law, but the doers are righteous. Item: Those who are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God, etc.

But since it is necessary that the simple truth of the Gospel be held, and that due honor always be attributed to the mediator, and that firm consolation of conscience be retained, and that hearts be rightly governed in every invocation, the converted must be taught how one ought to think about the righteousness of faith even after conversion.

The true doctrine and the perpetual consensus of the Church, handed down through the Prophets and Apostles, is that even after conversion it must be determined that the person is righteous, that is, accepted by God for eternal life, on account of the mediator, by faith alone, through mercy, not on account of one's own dignity of virtues, qualities, or works etc. For although virtues are begun, yet at the same time many impurities still cling to the converted, nor does the Son of God thereafter cease to be mediator. Therefore it must be determined that by faith we are pleasing on account of him, not on account of our own dignity: the mediator always remains as a covering, embracing us, and covering our impurities, and on account of him the eternal Father certainly receives us.

To this pertain these sayings: No living man shall be justified in thy sight.

Item, 1 John 1: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves etc.

And 1 Corinthians 4: I am conscious of nothing, yet I am not justified in this.

And Exod. 34: Before thee the innocent is not innocent.

Item 1 Cor. 1: He who boasts, let him boast in the Lord.

Therefore this proposition is always true: In conversion and after conversion in this life, by faith on account of the Son of God, the person is righteous, that is, accepted by God through mercy, not on account of one's own dignity, by faith alone.

And yet it is an eternal and immovable truth that it is necessary that in the converted there be a begun love, and in the will a good purpose, and the beginnings of new obedience, according to that: He who does not love, remains in death. And yet above all these things the mediator must be placed; him one must apprehend by faith, and let this faith shine forth in every invocation.

But one's own unworthiness always clamors against the one invoking: What do you ask, what do you expect from God, when you are unworthy, deserving of punishment, and still carry around many impurities? Against this thought this doctrine must be exercised daily, that you may know the voice of the Gospel to be eternal and immovable, so that, converted to God, you may determine that you are certainly received on account of the Son, and heard through mercy, freely, not on account of your own dignity, just as Daniel also prays: Hear us O Lord, not on account of our righteousness, but through mercy on account of the Lord. All the pious understand that this consolation is necessary.

But the adversaries, feigning that the converted is righteous on account of new love, remove the mediator, and attribute no more to him than that he merited for us the beginnings of those qualities, or that he is the cause of that change in us; afterwards they bury him, and say not a word about his intercession and about the imputation of righteousness.

Because truly a man looking at his own qualities finds many impurities, they not only extinguish true consolation and faith in invocation, but also command one to doubt. Nor do they say more about righteousness than what Plato said, that it is an excellent or heroic virtue when hearts are not only ruled by human diligence, but are also kindled by divine motion or inspiration.

That is truly said, and consideration is appropriate to nature and the divine work of philosophy, but it is not yet enough for the conscience asking whether it pleases God, and the voice of the Gospel adds more; it says the convert is received on account of the Son of God, and is gifted with the Holy Spirit, and although there are already in him the beginnings of new virtues, yet it says the person henceforth also pleases [God], and is just by imputation on account of the mediator through faith, not on account of his own purity, since the remnants of sin still cling to us: and that by this faith one must approach God, because we are received on account of the mediator.

In order for Paul to illustrate this, he cites the first statement in Genesis concerning faith, and proposes the notable example of Abraham himself. For at the same time he wishes to show this, that the doctrine of faith, which was then being renewed by the voice of the Gospel, is not new, but is the perpetual consensus of the true Church. Therefore he begins from that first statement. Although, therefore, there are many excellent virtues in Abraham, yet he says, Righteousness is imputed to him, that is, he is certainly received, and pleases [God] through mercy, when he acquiesces in the promise by faith, not on account of his own virtues. And he declares this sentiment in more words, and specifically says: Faith is imputed to him for righteousness, so that we may know that faith is not just knowledge, which is a preparation for righteousness, but is this very thing, by which, acquiescing in the promise, we are received and made alive, according to that: But what I now live, I live in the faith of the Son of God.

From this recitation, the argument of Paul is understood, and it can certainly be judged what the native sentiment is, and the sources appear, from which firm arguments can be taken to refute corruptions, whether Origenist or recent. We follow the uncorrupted speech of Paul, we acknowledge that we ought to be disciples of the divine voice, and to retain the literal sense [τὸ ῥητὸν] rightly and piously, not to bring to Paul a philosophy-born understanding [διάνοιαν], which fights with Paul, and corrupts the series of his disputation.

But as I said above, testimonies are not lacking for our interpretation: thus I now repeat that admonition, even if Ambrose, Augustine, Bernard, speak more properly in some places and less in others, because many are and have been negligent in speaking, yet it can be understood sufficiently, by comparing their statements, that their perpetual sentiment agrees with our interpretation.

Furthermore, there is also the clear and most weighty testimony of the Church, namely, the experience of all the pious and experienced. Those who understand the exercises of repentance and invocation, these confess that one must acquiesce in the mediator.

Therefore, as the doctrine concerning repentance is most well-known: God affirms by oath that He wills that we be converted and live. Thus let us learn here, both how conversion is made, and how reconciliation is made, and let us often contemplate the examples which I recited above, of Adam and David.

Conversion does not happen as long as a man remains secure, and retaining the purpose of acting against the law of God, lives in contempt of divine judgment. For the sentiment is expressed: The works of the flesh are manifest, adultery etc. on account of these the wrath of God comes upon the disobedient.

Therefore contrition is necessary. That is, it is necessary that there exist in our hearts fears, on account of the wrath of God against sin, and one must grieve that we have sinned, that is, that God has been offended by us. In these fears and sorrows, when you seek remission, and truly believe, that sin is remitted to you, and that You are received on account of the Son of God, freely, not on account of your dignity or merits, and by this faith and consolation you sustain your fearful heart, your sins are certainly remitted to you, and God receives you into grace, and at the same time gives the Holy Spirit, who is received in this very consolation, when we stir up faith with the thought of the promise.

And these causes concur: The Word of God, and the Holy Spirit in the thought of the Word of God, helping the mind and the will. Item: Mind and Will. And with the Holy Spirit given, faith is more and more kindled, and overcomes fears, and cries Abba Father, invokes God, and with mercy acknowledged, now subjects us to God.

Thus the love of God and a good purpose are begun. And the Holy Spirit kindles motions appropriate to the divine will, which is expressed in the law of God. Therefore it is said: I will put my law in their hearts etc.

Thus spiritual newness is always necessarily joined with the remission of sins and reconciliation. And faith is that very thing, which is the beginning of newness, and by which we are made alive to eternal life, according to that: The just shall live by his faith.

Explanation of certain arguments.

It is absolutely impossible for a man to be just by knowledge alone: Faith is only knowledge, Therefore it is impossible for a man to be just by faith alone.

By this imagination, many who are not unlearned are moved, so that they greatly abhor this proposition, "We are justified by faith," but the truest and firmest answer is that the minor premise must be denied. For in this proposition of Paul, "Being justified by faith, we have peace," and in similar sayings, faith by no means signifies only knowledge, such as is in the devils, which knowledge increases terrors, flight, and consternation. For the fear of judgment and punishments is more atrocious and greater in demons for this reason, because they understand more the magnitude and atrocity of their crimes against God and against the Son of God, and they know more the magnitude of the wrath of God, and they determine more certainly that God is a judge: but faith, of which Paul speaks, has entirely contrary effects; it heals terrors and brings us to God, joined to the Mediator, because it is not only knowledge of history, but it is an assent by which you embrace the promises, so that you determine that sin is remitted to You by name, and that you are received; and with this assent there is necessarily at the same time a trust resting in the Mediator, which is in the will, and it approaches God joyfully, with the Mediator leading, and calls upon Him. That Paul speaks of this faith is most manifest, where he says: "Being justified by faith we have peace." And Eph. 3: "In whom we have boldness to access confidently through faith in him." From this we shall take this definition of faith.

Faith is an assent by which we assent to every word of God delivered to us, and to the promise of reconciliation, and it is a trust resting in the Mediator, crying: Abba Father.

But faith or trust differs from hope, because hope is the expectation of future liberation: but faith receives the present benefit, namely, the remission of sins in the present, and reconciliation and the imputation of righteousness.

We know, however, that the monks, fascinated by their own imaginations, furiously reject this interpretation, but it is to be lamented that the Church has almost forgotten its own language, since there are such contentions about the word "faith." The testimony of Paul in Rom. 4 is clear and most firm, that faith is the trust by which we receive the promise. But after it has been spoken about the true meaning of the word, then also students must be warned of this. This argument arises from a philosophical or legal imagination, that we are righteous because of our own quality. Therefore it asks, where is that quality? But it has been said so often in this proposition: "We are righteous by faith," that it is not said that we are righteous because of our own quality, but because of the Mediator, and this must be apprehended by faith, and justification signifies the remission of sins, reconciliation, the imputation of righteousness, that is, acceptance unto eternal life, with which acceptance the gift of the Holy Spirit is conjoined.

Second argument. "He who does not love remains in death": Therefore we are not righteous by faith alone. The antecedent, as it sounds, is simply most true. For all these things must be in the convert: contrition, faith, love, good purpose, obedience, which is the righteousness of a good conscience.

But in the argument, the consequence must be denied. For it does not follow: The righteousness of a good conscience is present at the same time, Therefore because of it the person is righteous, that is, accepted in the judgment of God, as Paul most clearly says: "I am conscious of nothing against myself, yet I am not hereby justified."

It is a good thing, or a virtue, to give alms. But the person, in whom there is still much filth, is not accepted in the judgment of God because of such virtues, but through mercy because of the Mediator, as it is said: "In thy sight shall no man living be justified," etc. Likewise: "He who glories, let him glory in the Lord." And yet the truth of that saying remains unmoved: "Because he who does not love remains in death," in whom it is necessary that many virtues be present at the same time.

Third argument.

Love is righteousness: Therefore we are righteous by love.

The consequence is valid and in the place of conjugates. As when we say: Whiteness is a color, Therefore the wall is colored white by whiteness. The consequence is valid in conjugates, if there is no ambiguity, as if here righteousness is understood as a virtue, this proposition is true: love is righteousness, that is, a beautiful and excellent virtue. Therefore we are righteous by love, that is, possessing this virtue.

But it is one thing to speak of the righteousness of the Person, another of the righteousness of works or virtues. The righteousness of the person is the imputation of righteousness or acceptance in the judgment of God, which is done because of the Mediator by faith alone. But the righteousness of works are virtues in us, and good works, which are indeed very good things, but it is another thing, because of which the person pleases, which does not yet satisfy the law of God, and still carries around many impurities and infirmities.

With this distinction between the justice of the person and of works considered, much light is added to this whole doctrine. Now, consider again these connected terms: Love is justice, that is, virtue; therefore, by love we are just. If "just" here signifies that the person is accepted before God, the consequence will not hold because of ambiguity, just as if you were to say: Love of country is justice; therefore, Cicero, because of his love of country, is just before God. It is manifest that the consequence does not hold here because of the ambiguity.

The fourth argument.

The medium by which is not the end to which. Faith is the medium by which we receive the remission of sins: Therefore, faith is not justice, but the thing by which we receive it. I concede the whole, speaking most properly, because it is true that by faith it is received, that is, justice is applied to us, that is, the imputation of justice, because we are not just and accepted because of our own qualities, but because of the Son of God, the mediator, whom, however, it is necessary to behold and apprehend by faith.

Then this very faith is the beginning of all virtues, which are kindled in us, and which ought to be in the converted. The fifth argument.

To be justified is to be made just from being unjust: We are made just, that is, already changed in ourselves by faith, hope, and love: Therefore, not by faith alone. First, to the major premise, so that the proper description of the word may be maintained. There is ambiguity in the major premise: to be justified is to be made just from being unjust; the adversaries understand this only in this way: just, that is, another, clothed with new qualities. That is not enough, but it must be understood as just, that is, reconciled to God by the remission of sins having been made, and accepted by God.

Then, however, it must be added: clothed with new qualities. This interpretation of the word must be diligently considered, so that this specious cavil may be answered skillfully: now that the interpretation of the word has been established, let the major premise be answered.

The major premise is true regarding the change in us. But it is not true regarding the remission of sins and the acceptance of the person. It is true that many virtues must be kindled at the same time, but nevertheless, the person is just, that is, having the remission of sins and accepted by God, by faith, because of the mediator, not because of one's own virtues. With these explanations considered, other similar deceptions can also be easily judged and refuted, and I have provided explanations of many objections elsewhere.

Furthermore, for the understanding of both this controversy and the Pauline Epistle, it is necessary that the distinction between Law and Gospel be known rightly and truly. Likewise, the proper and true meanings of the words justification, Grace, Faith, etc., and the prophetic and apostolic phrase must be understood without corruptions.

An exposition of some words.

The Law of God is doctrine consenting with the eternal and immovable norm of the divine mind, commanding what we ought not to be, and what we ought to do and omit, and condemning all who do not provide complete obedience to the Law of God. This definition is taken from these words of Moses: Cursed is he who does not remain in all things which are written in the law.

And it is necessary that this distinction exist and be retained in the Church.

By human judgment, it is thought that the divine law is satisfied, and others as well, when external obedience is provided. But the judgment of God and of the divine law is different, namely, that the order should correspond with the divine mind and will, not only in external deeds but also in the whole nature of man.

Because man was so created that he is the image of God, and the law is implanted in human minds, so that the order in the whole nature of man would correspond with the order of the divine mind. But because after the fall the nature of man does not correspond with that eternal norm in the divine mind, God is truly angry at this interior depravity, not only at external offenses, but also at the interior depravity.

Although the law was previously implanted in minds, yet God promulgated it with an express voice, because after the fall it began to be more obscure to human minds. God therefore wished to renew it, and issued illustrious testimonies, so that we might know that the knowledge implanted in minds is a light handed down by God, and to what extent human minds correspond with the judgment of God.

Likewise, so that the judgment of God against interior and exterior sins might exist. For the very voice of the law expressly testifies that complete obedience is demanded.

As the words say: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your strength.

Likewise: You shall not covet. This understanding of the law must be preserved in the Church.

Therefore also

Matthew 5. This interpretation is proposed, so that it may be a doctrine of repentance, and with sin acknowledged, a mediator may be sought.

Just as the Pharisees of old imagined that they were satisfying the law of God only by external discipline, and afterwards attached many errors to it, that by this discipline men merited the remission of sins, and likewise, that they were righteous before God by this discipline, and there was complete silence about a mediator.

So often in the Church similar errors have wandered far; thus the Pelagians and recent writers, Thomas, Scotus, and the like, have imagined that men satisfy the law of God by this discipline, and merit the remission of sins, and are righteous before God by this discipline.

These impious imaginations have obscured both the law and the benefits of the Son of God.

It is necessary to warn of this at the beginning regarding the understanding of the law, just as Paul in 2 Corinthians 3 distinguishes the Pharisaic understanding of the law from the true understanding.

Human wisdom looks upon the veiled face of Moses, that is, it deems external discipline to be the fulfillment of the law. But when hearts are indicated in true repentance through the evangelical Ministry, in some way the face of Moses is uncovered, and the judgment of God against sins is known, signified by the rays scattered from the face of Moses.

Of Sin.

Paul often uses the name of Sin for the whole root and the evil fruits, but for the sake of teaching, the distinction between Original and Actual sin has been rightly and usefully handed down.

And it is absolutely necessary for the Church to know that sin does not only signify vicious actions, as the word seems to sound to grammarians, or as Philosophers or political laws speak of vicious actions or habits, but the Hebrew phrase names Sin any evil whatsoever that fights against the law of God, and makes one guilty before God.

Therefore, it embraces not only vicious actions, but also the root, namely, original evil, the description of which will be recited below.

Now a general definition, suitable to both original and actual sin, can be established as follows.

Sin is a defect, or an inclination, or an action, fighting against the law of God, offending God, and deserving eternal punishments, unless remission has been made on account of the Son of God.

But this definition is also taken from the saying of Moses: Cursed is he who does not remain in all things which are written in the law.

But afterwards, the distinction between original and actual sin will be explained more copiously.

For now, this brief admonition is recited, lest the younger ones, in the political manner, think that only external offenses are called sins, but that they may know that there are great interior evils: to doubt whether God cares for human affairs, whether He is truly angry at the sins of all, whether He truly receives all who perform repentance.

Likewise, to be without the fear of God, without faith and without trust, without the love of God, without invocation, to imagine that secondary and adverse things happen, or in adversity to be angry at God, and to flee Him.

Likewise, to be stubborn in heart against the law of God, and to burn with the many flames of wandering desires.

This great confusion of evils in man must be acknowledged and deplored, and it must be known that many more evils are comprehended under the name of sin in the Church than in philosophy and political doctrine.

But the monks have corrupted even this word, because they deny that original evil in the reborn is an evil fighting against the law of God, etc.

Of Grace.

The name of Grace has been greatly obscured, since the monks have used it only for an infused habit, and hence darkness has followed in the entire doctrine of Grace, Justice, and Faith.

It must be known, therefore, that Grace signifies gratuitous mercy, or the remission of sins, and acceptance, granted on account of the Son, with which, however, is joined the gift of the Holy Spirit, kindling new light and new virtues in the heart of the man to whom sins are remitted.

Paul uses two appellations to distinguish these two: gratuitous acceptance and the new virtues kindled in us.

Rom. 5.: Much more the grace of God, and the gift through grace, through Jesus Christ, abounds unto many.

Thus, when it is said: You are not under the law, but under grace, it is not enough to be understood thus, that you are governed by an infused habit, but it is necessary first to hold this sweetest consolation: you are under grace, that is, you have the remission of sins, and you are accepted by God on account of the mediator, freely, even if there are still in you remnants of sin, great infirmity, and much filth.

Of Justification.

Justice, when we speak of the Justice of the law, signifies virtues in us, and Just is the same as having those virtues.

Since these are philosophical and legal, Thomas and the like have understood these words only in this way as qualities, and they have interpreted the word 'to justify' as 'to infuse virtues,' as if they were saying, 'to make warm' signifies 'to infuse heat.'

Although it is necessary that new virtues be kindled in us, as has often been said already, yet the phrasing in these appellations is different.

For the Gospel speaks of justice differently than the Law or Philosophy. When your mind is troubled as to whether you are just, it is not primarily asked what qualities are in the heart. Indeed, you even perceive that there is great impurity of heart, but this is what is asked: whether you are accepted by God, whether God has received you, whether He has forgiven your sins. Therefore, the principal meaning of the word 'Just' in this question is 'accepted by God unto eternal life.' Hence also the word 'to justify' signifies 'to absolve from sins,' and 'to account or pronounce just,' that is, 'accepted,' just as is often the case in forensic speech, even if the Hebrews spoke in such a way, as if they were to say, 'The Roman people justified Scipio, who was accused by the Tribune,' that is, 'pronounced him just.' When, therefore, it is asked whether we are justified by faith, it is not asked whether faith alone is in the heart, but whether God has received us, whether He has forgiven our sins, whether we are accepted on account of the Son of God, not on account of our own qualities.

And yet, when faith is kindled, by which we acknowledge the Son of God and embrace the promise, it is necessary that many virtues be present at the same time. For trust, resting in God and raising up hearts in true terrors, is by no means without love, without invocation, without fear, and it is a movement that cries out, as Paul says: Abba, Father. Afterwards, when it is said concerning Works, what the use of the words 'just' and 'to be justified' is, one not unskilled in grammar will easily judge, as when it is said: 'Not the hearers of the law, but the doers are justified,' that is, 'are pronounced as having that justice of the law.'

On the word Faith.

Although the adversaries contend most stubbornly and without any end that 'faith' signifies only knowledge, yet it is a certain and immovable truth in this saying: 'The just shall live by his faith.' Likewise: 'We are justified by faith,' and in similar passages, by the name of Faith is embraced both the knowledge of all the articles of faith and the trust resting in the promise, which itself is also comprehended in the articles of the Creed, namely: 'I believe in the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the body, and life everlasting.' For it is necessary to refer the earlier articles to these benefits.

And Paul, in Romans 4, manifestly affirms that he is speaking of that faith which embraces the promise. This, however, is the trust by which the mind rests in the Son of God, determining that sins are forgiven not only to certain others, but to You yourself. Let this definition therefore be held for the sake of teaching: Faith is the assent by which we assent to the word of God handed down to us, and thus also to the promise of reconciliation: and it is trust, resting in the Son of God, according to the promise.

Latin:

Sedecim annis, postquam Commentarii Mel. in Epist. ad Rom. lucem viderant, praeterlapsis, Melanthon novam enarrationem eiusdem epistolae elaboravit et edidit, Ulrico Mordeisen inscriptam. (Vid. epist. nuncupat. supra Vol. VIII. p. 737.) Epistolae Pauli scriptae ad Romanos Enarratio, edita a Phil. Melanthone. A. 1556. (In fine:) Witebergae ex offic. typographica Viti Creutzeri, sumptibus Conradi Rhuel.

1 Alph. 8 pl. 8. Repetita ibid. et apud eundem anno 1558. 1 Alph. 9 pl. — et iterum: Epistolae Pauli — — Viteberg. execut. Io. Lufft. 1561. 1 Alph. 9 pl. 8. In opp. Melanchonis a Peucero editis Tom. IV. p. 35–209. EPISTOLAE PAULI SCRIPTAE AD ROMANOS ENARRATIO EDITA A PHIL. MELANTHONE ANNO M. D. LVI. Argumentum Epistolae. Deus vult agnosci filium mediatorem, nec vult aliter liberare homines a peccato et a morte aeterna, nisi in invocatione filii, sicut in secundo Psalmo dicit: Osculamini filium, Beati omnes, qui confidunt in eo.

Et patris vox, sonans de coelo haec est: Hic est filius meus dilectus, hunc audite. Et filius inquit: Nemo venit ad patrem, nisi per filium. Item: Haec est vita aeterna, ut agnoscant te Deum verum, et quem misisti, lesum esse Christum. Necesse est igitur, in Ecclesia recte conspici beneficia filii Dei propria, id est, remissionem peccatorum, reconciliationem, donationem Spiritus sancti, iusticiae, et vitae aeternae.

Et ut filius Dei recte agnoscatur, necesse est econtra intelligi, quale malum sit Peccatum, et cerui discrimen inter philosophiam, legem et Evangelium, inter iusticiam fidei et iusticiam operum, quae est qualiscunque diligentia humana, faciendi legem.

Necesse est etiam scire, qualis coetus sit Ecclesia Dei in hac vita. Harum maximarum rerum cognitio, sapientia est Ecclesiae propria, patefacta in promissionibus et voce Evangelii, inde usque ab initio, a promulgata prima promissione ad primos parentes, et saepe deinde repetita. Cum enim haec doctrina sit extra iudicia humana, subinde homines amittunt veram lucem de mediatore, et de iusticia fidei, et delabuntur ad opiniones humanas, quae imaginantur, nostram disciplinam remissionem peccatorum et homines tali disciplina iustos esse, id est, acceptos Deo, et haeredes vitae aeternae, et obliviscuntur mediatorem.

Ita magna pars in Israël semper sensit, et postremo Pharisaei palam magna contentione docuerunt, homines mereri remissionem peccatorum, et iustos esse illa disciplina, et diligentia faciendae legis.

Deinde finxerunt, Messiam venturum esse, ut politicum imperium in hac mortali vita iustius et tranquillius constitueret. Sed hos errores subinde taxavit Deus, missis Prophetis et piis doctoribus, misso filio et Apostolis. Vagantur autem similes errores in genere humano omnibus temporibus.

Sic fingebant Ethnici, qui non volebant videri athei, se mereri suis sacrificiis remissionem peccatorum, et esse iustos disciplina. Sic longo tempore Sacrificuli et Monachi docuerunt se mereri remissionem peccatorum sacrificio Missae et aliis operibus, et tali disciplina iustos esse. Hos errores refutari in Ecclesia semper necessarium est, et contra illustrari doctrinam de filio Dei et eius beneficiis.

Haec fiunt summa perspicuitate in Epistola Pauli ad Romanos.

Quia cum Pharisaei et multi alii tunc acerrime defenderent suos errores de iusticia legis, et non agnoscerent filium Dei et iusticiam fidei, necesse fuit opponi perspicuam refutationem.

Nec tamen tantum ad illud tempus haec Epistola accommodanda est, sed semper necesse est, recte agnosci filium Dei, et intelligi iusticiam fidei, et discrimen legis et Evangelii.

Concionatur ergo haec Epistola Ecclesiae, usque ad extremum iudicium, sicut res eaedem antea a Prophetis traditae sunt, in quibus extant severissimae conciones contra illas pharisaicas tenebras, et multi propter has reprehensiones a Sacerdotibus et Pharisaeis interfecti sunt.

Imo Paulus, cum quidem affirmet, se doctrinam accepisse revelante filio Dei, ut ad Galatas expresse inquit: tamen citat testimonia Prophetarum, ut ostendat, unam perpetuam vocem Evangelii in Ecclesia esse, de beneficiis filii Dei, de modo reconciliationis, de iusticia, de veris cultibus, de vera Ecclesia, et de iudicio Dei.

Sed haec Epistola Pauli eo magis perspicua est, quia continet expressam antithesin contrariarum sententiarum, et ordine disputat, ut facit artifex, ac propemodum methodus est doctrinae, quae Ecclesiae propria est, quia principales materias tam accurate exponit, beneficia mediatoris, discrimen legis et Evangelii, discrimen iusticiae fidei, et iusticiae operum, doctrinam de vera Ecclesia, et de veris cultibus.

Necesse est igitur, hanc Epistolam familiarissime notam esse omnibus, et summa vigilantia adhibenda est, ut eius sententia retineatur incorrupta.

Sed antequam de corruptelis dicam, prius recitabo summam doctrinae de iustificatione, ut postea collatio magis perspicua sit.

Summa doctrinae in scriptis propheticis et apostolicis traditae, de iustificatione coram Deo.

Principio recitabo duo exempla, quae ideo semper in conspectu sint, non solum quia totam hanc doctrinam illustrant, sed etiam, ut nos ipsos de poenitentia et de vera consolatione commonefaciant.

Cum Adam post lapsum a Deo arguitur, horribiliter expavescit, quia, cum Deus ipse sua voce accusat creaturam, non existimemus, otiosum esse colloquium, sed Deus est ignis consumens, ut scriptum est.

Iacet igitur Adam prostratus coram Deo, nihil nisi legem sciens, ex qua recte ratiocinatur, se perpetuo damnatum esse.

Sic enim cogitat: Iusticia Dei immutabilis est, punire, et abiicere inobedientes.

Ego non obtemperavi, et fui horribiliter ingratus Deo, cum adeo dilexerit hanc naturam, ut in eam transfuderit sua summa dona, et fecerit eam imaginem suam, Ego et destruxi hoc opus Dei, et abieci tanta dona et excussi habitantem in me Deum: Ergo necesse est, me vicissim abiici.

In hoc iudicio ac vero agone nulla talis in Adam cogitatio erat, se posse mereri remissionem peccatorum, ac posse tollere peccatum, sed vere sentiebat iram Dei, et se displicere Deo, et vere sentiebat, se nullius creaturae ope iuvari posse, et argumentum ex lege sumtum verum erat, nec potuisset ab ulla creatura solvi.

Sed filius Dei fit deprecator, et poenam in sese transfert mirabili et inenarrabili consilio.

Verissimum est enim, iusticiam Dei immutabilem esse, ac Deum vere et horribiliter irasci peccatis.

Ego peccavi, Ergo puniar.

Hic respondet filius Dei: Vel Adam punietur, vel alius me deprecante, scilicet, ego ipse assumta natura humana, cuius poena erit aequivalens pretium pro genere humano, persolvam.

De hac admiranda deliberatione, sapientiam, iusticiam et misericordiam Dei considerabimus in vita aeterna.

Nec nostrae poenae in hac vita sunt pretium placans iram Dei, sed tantum sunt signa et commonefactiones, ut cogitemus, Deum vere irasci peccatis.

Itaque Adam ignarus adhuc promissionis, et audiens accusationem divinam, luctatur cum morte et nihil usquam auxilii videt.

Etsi autem antea trepidare coeperat, foliis fici tegens partem corporis, tamen nondum in tanto dolore fuerat, nondum sic senserat iram Dei: postea vero loquente Deo agnoscit istis foliis fici non tegi peccata.

Tandem vero audit consolationem, cum promissio, ex arcano consilio Dei prolata, promulgatur, quae affirmat, semen mulieris venturum esse, quo rursus tollendum sit peccatum.

Recipi igitur se Adam intelligit, et erigitur fide huius promissionis, et propter hoc semen statuit, se iam placere Deo, etiamsi longe deformior erat, quam fuerat ante lapsum.

Hac itaque fide accipit remissionem peccatorum, et deinde iustus est coram Deo, accedit ad Deum, invocat, et vivificat per filium Dei Spiritu sancto, audita promissione, incipit rursus obedire, ita, ne contra conscientiam faciat. placatorem.

Statuit igitur, se quoque propter eum recipi, et scit hunc cultum et hunc honorem Deo praestandum... esse, ut promissioni credat, nec accuset Deum mendacii, nec deficiat a Deo, nec contemnat mediatorem. Haec imago conversionis Adae, et quomodo audita promissione erigatur fide, et sit iustus, id est, acceptus Deo, et postea rursus incipiat obedire, semper sit in conspectu, quia eodem modo fiunt conversio et consolatio in caeteris.

Sed doctrina de fide illustrior est in primo exemplo, in quo necesse est fuisse horribiles dolores, et quia magnitudinem lapsus magis intellexit Adam, qui sciebat, qualis fuerat, et quia insanabile malum esse cogitabat, cum promissio nondum edita esset, et quia reiectionem daemonum norat.

Sed nos nimis otiosis animis illam tantam historiam legimus, in qua tam multa concurrunt, quorum alia iram Dei ingentem, alia immensam magnitudinem misericordiae ostendunt. Quod enim recipit Deus homines lapsos, cum iusticiae eius sit immutabilis, et quod sic recipit, ut filius fiat victima, haec miranda consilia longe superant omnium creaturarum sapientiam. Et tamen vult Deus, ut suam iusticiam et misericordiam aliquo modo in hac vita consideremus, ut accendantur in nobis verus timor, vera fides, invocatio, gratitudo, dilectio, et caeterae virtutes.

Alterum exemplum sit conversio Davidis post lapsum, in qua etiam conspiciuntur hi duo motus, ingens pavor, et deinde consolatio.

Nam cum a Propheta Nathan arguitur, de rapta coniuge alterius, et de nece mariti, exsistunt in Davide horrendi pavores, quales saepe describit: Non est pax ossibus meis a conspectu peccatorum meorum etc. Agnoscit iram Dei adversus peccatum, dolet propterea, quod offendit Deum, metuit se abiici a Deo, sicut ante viderat horribiliter abiici Saulem.

Denique metuit aeternas et praesentes poenas, nec iam colligere merita potest, videt irae Dei non posse opponi suas virtutes, aut priora facta, et extingueretur magnitudine doloris, nisi accederet consolatio: Non morieris, Dominus abstulit peccatum tuum.

Hac audita absolutione rursus accenditur in eo fides, qua apprehendens absolutionem, incipit intueri misericordiam Dei, et cogitat iam caeteras promissiones, et in mediatore acquiescit, ac agnoscit homines recipi per immensam misericordiam propter summum sacerdotem, interpellantem pro nobis, quem ipse nominat Sacerdotem secundum ordinem Melchizedech. Hunc scit esse mediatorem et placatorem. Statuit igitur, se quoque propter eum recipi, et scit hunc cultum et hunc honorem Deo praestandum esse, ut promissioni credat, nec accuset Deum mendacii, nec deficiat a Deo, nec contemnat mediatorem. In haec exempla et similia intuentes facilius intelligemus doctrinam de Iustificatione, praesertim si non erit tantum frigida otiosi animi cogitatio, sed si nos quoque serio expavescimus recordatione nostrorum delictorum, et quaerimus consolationem.

Sciamus igitur, hanc esse doctrinam Evangelii, de qua Paulus in hac Epistola concionatur.

Arguit peccatum, sicut scriptum est: Spiritus sanctus arguet mundum de peccato, et proponit consolationem, videlicet, promissionem de remissione peccatorum, et reconciliatione donanda propter filium Dei, et affirmat eos, qui in illis pavoribus credunt, sibi remitti peccata propter filium mediatorem, gratis, vere recipi, et accipere remissionem peccatorum, et simul cum remissione peccatorum datur Spiritus sanctus, qui adiuvat luctantem conscientiam, et sustentantem se fide, et simul accendit caeteras virtutes, scilicet invocationem Dei, et confirmat voluntatem, ut se subiiciat Deo, habeat timorem Dei, dilectionem et bonum propositum, sicut clare dicitur ad Gala.

3.: Ut promissionem spiritus accipiamus per fidem.

Haec voluntas Dei, de reconciliatione propter filium, non est nota hominibus naturali luce, sicut lex, sed immensa bonitate intercedente filio, patefacta est voce Dei initio in promissionibus, et postea illustrata per Prophetas, per ipsum filium et Apostolos.

Quanquam autem perspicue tradita est haec doctrina in Prophetis et Apostolis, tamen subinde in mundo varie obscurata est.

Monendi sunt igitur iuniores, ut nativam Evangelii sententiam retineant.

Certissimum est, Paulum hoc velle, Fide iustificamur gratis, id est, propter filium Dei, et non propter nostram dignitatem, aut ulla nostra merita accipimus remissionem peccatorum, et reconciliationem et imputationem iusticiae, cum credimus Evangelio, et fide statuimus, haec beneficia nobis propter filium Dei dari, et quidem credit haec fides omnibus articulis fidei, et refert caeteros ad hunc ipsum articulum: Remissionem peccatorum, de quo articulo non tantum in genere credendum est, quibusdam aliis remitti, sicut et daemones credunt, sed revera tibi ipsi credendum. das donari remissionem peccatorum.

Cum hac fide erigimur, simul, ut dixi, filius Dei vivificat credentem, et donat Spiritum sanctum, et nos accipimus remissionem peccatorum, et sumus iusti, id est, accepti Deo ad vitam aeternam propter mediatorem, etiamsi sunt in nobis adhuc reliquiae peccati, et magna infirmitas.

Hanc esse planam et nativam sententiam Pauli non dubium est, ut postea copiosius declarabimus.

Ac retinemus nos in hac interpretatione proprietatem verborum Pauli, et auditores sumus Pauli, non affingimus alia significata sermoni Paulino, et hanc nostram interpretationem nativam et veram esse apparet, collatis omnibus membris Paulinae disputationis.

Item, collatis Prophetarum et Christi concionibus.

Item, collato testimonio Ecclesiae catholicae Dei, id est, omnium hominum, qui intelligunt exercitia poenitentiae et invocationis, et didicerunt acquiescendum esse fide in filio Dei.

Tales semper fuerunt, sunt et erunt multi in Ecclesia, in quibus lucet vera Evangelii sententia.

Et quanquam scriptores interdum improprie loquuti sunt, tamen conguere cum hac sententia multos videmus, ut Augustinum, Prosperum, Ambrosium, Basilium, Bernardum, Taulerum, et alios.

Adeoque non contemnimus Ecclesiae iudicium ac testimonium, ut ad pias mentes toto orbe terrarum, intelligentes exercitia poenitentiae, provocemus.

Etsi autem in corruptelis huius dicti: Fide iustificamur, alii aliter loquuti sunt, tamen eadem est causa erroris omnibus, et eandem sententiam falsam omnes extruunt.

Omnes intelligunt fide tantum significari noticiam historiae, et iustum intelligunt philosophice, habentem ipsas virtutes, ut cum dicimus, aqua calefacta est, id est, calor transfusus est in aquam.

Hoc modo cum de vocabulis errent, affingunt deinde alienas interpretationes, quae tamen omnes in summa hoc volunt, in hac propositione synecdochen esse, fide iustificamur, id est, fide et caeteris virtutibus iustificamur, seu fide praeparamur, ut postea aliis virtutibus iusti simus.

Monachi sic loquuti sunt, fide formata, scilicet, dilectione iusti sumus, quod sic intellexerunt, propter dilectionem iusti sumus.

Alii sic interpretati sunt, fide, id est, operibus a Deo mandatis, iusti sumus, non operibus traditionum humanarum.

Alii hoc modo depravant, fide, id est, interiore cultu, non externis operibus iusti sumus.

Hae interpretationes omnes hoc volunt: Homo est iustus, id est, Deo acceptus ad vitam aeternam propter proprias virtutes et opera.

Et hoc alii enarrant absurdius, alii quaedam absurda omittunt.

Monachi dicunt, homines mereri remissionem peccatorum suis virtutibus et operibus, dicunt iustos satisfacere legi, ut Malvenda inquit, ideo hominem dici iustum, quia Deo persolvat debitum.

Et addunt amplius: Cum nemo sciat, quando satis operum habeat, iubent semper dubitare an sis in gratia, et hanc dubitationem dicunt piam esse.

Ita prorsus removent fidem, et delent vocem Evangelii, et consolationem, quam Deus immensa bonitate patefecit, et vult in Ecclesia extare.

Nunc videant studiosi, an hae interpretationes congruant cum integra disputatione Pauli.

Item, an congruant cum perpetua sententia prophetica et apostolica.

Manifestum est autem, haec tria membra praecipua esse Paulinae disputationis.

Primum perspicue et sine ulla ambiguitate affirmat, homines non satisfacere legi Dei, nec lege iustos esse, sed omnes reos et sub peccato esse, ut Capite 3. perspicue dicitur: Ut omne os obturetur, et totus mundus reus sit coram Deo.

Conclusit omnes sub peccatum, ut Omnium misereatur.

Secundo affirmat, recipi homines propter mediatorem, gratis, et vult intelligi, propter hanc ipsam causam missum esse Messiam, ut sit placator, et tollat peccatum et mortem, non ut imperia mundi constituat, sicut somniabant Pharisaei.

Tertio affirmat, oportere fide accipi reconciliationem, et fide statuendum esse, non receptos esse, et placere Deo propter mediatorem, nec manendum esse in dubitatione.

Iam cum manifestum sit, haec tria membra a Paulo tradita esse, constat interpretationes pugnantes cum his tribus membris falsas esse.

Nec difficilis est refutatio, tenentibus haec fundamenta, quae recensui.

Quia particula Gratis expresse tollit nostra merita, et deducit nos ad merita filii Dei, et vult Deus agnosci filium, et hunc ei honorem tribui, ut fateamur, esse Propiciatorem et Mediatorem.

Quare manifestum est, errare monachos, cum docent, homines suis operibus aut virtutibus mereri remissionem peccatorum.

 Erant etiam, cum fidem intelligunt tantum noticiam historiae, et iubent homines semper manere in dubitatione, quia Paulus manifeste inquit, Oportet promissionem fide accipi. Loquitur igitur de fide, qua et caeteros articulos fidei amplectimur, et assentimur promissioni, et statuimus, promissum beneficium nobis exhiberi, cum qua fide est fiducia acquiescens in misericordia promissa propter filium, seu acquiescens in filio, accedens ad Deum, invocans et clamans Abba Pater etc. Item, qui manet in dubitatione, non statuit sibi mediatorem esse filium Dei. Non igitur tribuit ei debitum honorem.

Sed altera quaestio hic agitatur, postquam homo conversus est, et iam accensa est in eo novitas spiritualis, seu, ut alii loquuntur, dilectio, dicunt eum iustum esse post conversionem hac novitate seu dilectione, id est, personam acceptam esse Deo et haeredem vitae aeternae propter dilectionem, et haec cumularunt antea monachi, dixerunt hanc novitatem esse meritum vitae aeternae de condigno, id est, pretium propter quod debeatur vita aeterna, et declamitant non esse extenuandum donum Dei in conversis, cum ideo fiat conversio, ut homo ex iniusto fiat iustus, et cum dilectio sit iustitia, vociferantur absurdum esse negare hominem propter eam iustum esse, cum tamen propter albedinem paries dicatur albus, et huc accommodant multa dicta. Qui facit iustitiam iustus est. Item: Non auditores legis, sed factores iusti sunt. Item: Qui spiritu Dei aguntur, hi sunt filii Dei, etc.

Cum autem necesse sit teneri simplicem veritatem Evangelii, et mediatori semper tribui debitum honorem, et retineri conscientiae firmam consolationem, et recte gubernari corda in omni invocatione, docendi sunt conversi, quomodo de iusticia fidei etiam post conversionem sentiendum sit.

Vera doctrina est et perpetuus Ecclesiae consensus per Prophetas et Apostolos traditus, etiam post conversionem statuendum esse, iustam esse personam, id est, acceptam Deo ad vitam aeternam, propter mediatorem, sola fide, per misericordiam, non propter propriam dignitatem virtutum, qualitatum aut operum etc. Etsi enim sunt incoatae virtutes, tamen simul adhuc multae sordes haerent in converso, nec filius Dei postea desinit esse mediator. Ideo statuendum est, fide nos propter ipsum placere, non propter nostram dignitatem: semper manet mediator velut umbraculum, amplectens nos, et tegens nostras sordes, et propter ipsum nos certo recipit aeternus pater.

Huc pertinent haec dicta: Non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens.

Item, 1. Ioh. 1.: Si dicimus, quod peccatum non habemus, nos ipsos decipimus etc.

Et 1. Corinth. 4.: Nil mihi conscius sum, sed in hoc non iustificatus sum.

Et Exod. 34.: Coram te innocens non est innocens.

Item 1. Corint. 1.: Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur.

Semper igitur vera est haec propositio: In conversione et post conversionem in hac vita fide propter filium Dei persona est iusta, id est, accepta Deo per misericordiam, non propter propriam dignitatem, sola fide.

Et tamen aeterna et immota veritas est, quod oportet in converso incoatam esse dilectionem, et in voluntate bonum propositum esse, et novae obedientiae initia, iuxta illud: Qui non diligit, manet in morte. Et tamen supra haec omnia collocandus est mediator, hunc fide apprehendi oportet, et haec fides praeluceat in omni invocatione.

Semper autem obstrepit invocanti propria indignitas: Quid petis, quid expectas a Deo, cum sis indignus, meritus poenam, et adhuc circumferas multum sordium? Contra hanc cogitationem quotidie haec doctrina exercenda est, scias vocem Evangelii aeternam et immotam esse, ut conversus ad Deum statuas te propter filium certo recipi, et exaudiri per misericordiam, gratis, non propter propriam dignitatem, sicut et Daniel orat: Exaudi nos Domine, non propter iusticiam nostram, sed per misericordiam propter Dominum. Hanc consolationem necessariam esse omnes pii intelligunt.

Sed adversarii, fingentes conversum iustum esse propter novam dilectionem, removent mediatorem, nec plus ei tribuunt, quam quod nobis initia illarum qualitatum meruit, seu quod sit causa illius mutationis in nobis, postea eum sepe liunt, et de eius intercessione, et de imputatione iusticiae nullum verbum dicunt.

Quia vero homo intuens suas qualitates multum sordium invenit, non solum consolationem veram et fidem in invocatione extinguunt, sed etiam dubitare iubent. Nec plus dicunt de iusticia, quam quantum Plato dixit, tunc esse excellentem seu heroicam virtutem, quando pectora non tantum diligentia humana reguntur, sed etiam divino motu seu afflatu accenduntur.

Id vere dicitur, et consideratio est naturae et operis divini conveniens philosophiae, sed nondum satis est conscientiae quaerenti an Deo placeat, et vox Evangelii plus addit, dicit conversum recipi propter filium Dei, et donari Spiritu sancto, et quanquam iam in... eo initia sunt novarum virtutum, tamen dicit personam deinceps etiam placere, et imputatione iustam esse propter mediatorem fide, non propter propriam munditiem, cum haereant adhuc in nobis reliquiae peccati: et hac fide accedendum esse ad Deum, quod propter mediatorem recepti simus.

Haec ut illustret Paulus, citat primum dictum in Genesi de fide, et proponit exemplum insigne ipsum Abraham. Simul enim et hoc vult ostendere, doctrinam de fide, quae tunc voce Evangelii renovabatur, non novam esse, sed perpetuum verae Ecclesiae consensum esse. Ideo ab illo primo dicto orditur. Quanquam igitur multae excellentes virtutes sunt in Abraham, tamen dicit, Imputari ei iusticiam, id est, certo eum recipi, et placere per misericordiam, cum fide acquiescit in promissione, non propter suas virtutes. Et hanc sententiam declarat pluribus verbis, et nominatim inquit: Fides ei imputatur ad iusticiam, ut sciamus fidem non tantum noticiam esse, quae sit praeparatio ad iusticiam, sed esse hoc ipsum, quo acquiescentes in promissione recipimur et vivificamur, iuxta illud: Quod autem nunc vivo, in fide filii Dei vivo.

Ex hac recitatione et argumentum Pauli intelligitur, et certo iudicari potest, quae sit nativa sententia, et fontes apparent, unde sumi possunt firma argumenta ad refutandas corruptelas, seu Origenicas seu recentes. Nos sermonem Pauli sequimur incorruptum, agnoscimus nos discipulos divinae vocis esse debere, ac τὸ ῥητὸν dextre et pie retinere, non afferre Paulum διάνοιαν in philosophia natam, quae pugnat cum Paulo, et seriem disputationis eius corrumpit.

Ut autem supra dixi, nostrae interpretationi non deesse testimonia: ita nunc repeto eam commonefactionem, etiamsi Ambrosius, Augustinus, Bernhardus, alibi magis, alibi minus proprie loquuntur, quia multi sunt et fuerunt negligentes in dicendo, tamen satis intelligi potest, collatis eorum dictis, perpetuam eorum sententiam congruere cum nostra interpretatione.

Deinde et perspicuum et gravissimum testimonium est Ecclesiae, videlicet, experientia omnium piorum et peritorum. Qui intelligunt exercitia poenitentiae et invocationis, hi fatentur, acquiescendum esse in mediatore.

Ut igitur de poenitentia notissima est doctrina: Iureiurando Deus affirmat, se velle, ut convertamur et vivamus. Ita hic discamus, et quomodo fiat conversio, et quomodo fiat reconciliatio, et exempla, quae supra recitavi, Adae et Davidis, saepe intueamur.

Non fit conversio, donec manet homo securus, et retinens propositum faciendi contra legem Dei, vivit in contemptu iudicii divini. Expressa est enim sententia: Manifesta sunt opera carnis, adulterium etc. propter haec venit ira Dei super inobedientes.

Ideo necessaria est contritio. Id est, oportet existere in nostris cordibus pavores, propter iram Dei adversus peccatum, et dolendum est, nos peccasse, id est, Deum a nobis offensum esse. In his pavoribus et doloribus cum petis remissionem, et vere credis, Tibi remitti peccatum, et Te recipi propter filium Dei, gratis, non propter tuam dignitatem aut merita, et hac fide et consolatione cor pavidum sustentas, certo remittuntur tibi peccata, et Deus te recipit in gratiam, et simul dat Spiritum sanctum, qui accipitur in hac ipsa consolatione, cum cogitatione promissionis fidem excuscitamus.

Et concurrunt hae causae: Verbum Dei, et Spiritus sanctus in cogitatione verbi Dei, adiuvans mentem et voluntatem. Item: Mens et Voluntas. Et dato Spiritu sancto fides magis magisque accenditur, et vincit pavores, et clamat Abba Pater, invocat Deum, et agnita misericordia iam subiicit nos Deo.

Ita incoantur dilectio Dei, et bonum propositum. Et Spiritus sanctus accendit motus convenientes voluntati divinae, quae expressa est in lege Dei. Ideo dictum est: Dabo legem meam in corda eorum etc.

Ita semper necessario coniuncta est cum remissione peccatorum et reconciliatione novitas spiritualis. Et fides est illa ipsa res, quae est initium novitatis, et qua vivificamur ad vitam aeternam, iuxta illud: Iustus fide sua vivet.

Argumentorum quorundam explicatio.

Prorsus impossibile est, sola noticia hominem istum esse: Fides est tantum noticia, Ergo impossibile est, hominem sola fide iustum esse.

Hac imaginatione moventur praecipue multi non indocti, ut valde abhorreant ab hac propositione, Fide iustificamur, sed verissima et firmissima responsio est, negandum esse minorem. Nam in hac propositione apud Paulum, fide iustificati pacem habemus, et in dictis similibus, fides nequaquam significat tantum noticiam, qualis est in diabolis, quae noticia auget pavores, fugam et consternationem. Ideo enim metus iudicii et poenarum atrocior et maior est in daemonibus, quia magis intelligunt magnitudinem et atrocitatem suorum scelerum adversus Deum et adversus filium Dei, et magis norunt magnitudinem irae Dei, et certius statuunt, Deum iudicem esse: sed fides, de qua Paulus loquitur, prorsus contrarios effectus habet, sanat pavores et adducit nos ad Deum adiunctos mediatori, quia non est tantum noticia historiae, sed est assensus, quo amplecteris promissiones, ita ut nominatim Tibi peccatum remitti, et te recipi statuas, et cum hoc assensu necessario simul est fiducia acquiescens in mediatore, quae est in voluntate, et laeta accedit ad Deum ducente mediatore, et invocat. De hac fide loqui Paulum manifestissimum est, qua inquit: Iustificati fide pacem habemus. Et Ephe. 3.: Per quem audemus accedere confidenter per fidem eius. Inde hanc fidei definitionem sumemus.

Fides est assensus, quo omni verbo Dei nobis tradito, ac promissioni reconciliationis assentimur, et est fiducia acquiescens in mediatore, clamans: Abba Pater.

Differt autem fides seu fiducia a spe, quia spes est expectatio futurae liberationis: at fides accipit praesens beneficium, scilicet remissionem peccatorum in praesentia, et reconciliationem ac imputationem iusticiae.

Scimus autem monachos fascinatos suis imaginationibus furenter reiicere hanc interpretationem, sed dolendum est, Ecclesiam quasi linguae suae oblitam esse, cum de vocabulo fidei tanta sint certamina. Perspicuum et firmissimum est testimonium Pauli Rom. 4., Fidem esse fiduciam, qua accipimus promissionem. Postquam autem de vera significatione vocabuli dictum est, deinde et hoc monendi sunt studiosi. Hoc argumentum oritur ex imaginatione philosophica seu legali, quod iusti simus propter nostram qualitatem. Ideo quaerit, ubi sit illa qualitas. Toties autem iam dictum est in hac propositione: Fide sumus iusti, non hoc dici, nos propter nostram qualitatem iustos esse, sed propter mediatorem, et hunc fide apprehendi opportet, et iustificatio significat remissionem peccatorum, reconciliationem, imputationem iusticiae, id est, acceptationem ad vitam aeternam, cum qua acceptatione coniuncta est donatio Spiritus sancti.

Secundum argumentum. Qui non diligit, manet in morte: Igitur non sola fide sumus iusti. Antecedens simpliciter ut sonat verissimum est. Nam haec omnia oportet in converso esse, contritionem, fidem, dilectionem, bonum propositum, obedientiam, quae est iusticia bonae conscientiae.

Sed in argumento consequentia neganda est. Non enim sequitur: Iusticia bonae conscientiae est simul, Ergo propter eam persona est iusta, id est, accepta in iudicio Dei, sicut clarissime inquit Paulus: Nihil mihi conscius sum, sed in hoc non iustificatus sum.

Bona res est, seu virtus dare Eleemosynas. Sed persona, in qua adhuc multum est sordium, non propter tales virtutes in iudicio Dei accepta est, sed per misericordiam propter mediatorem, ut dicitur: Non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo etc. Item: Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur. Et tamen manet dicti illius immota veritas: Quia non diligit, manet in morte, qui simul esse necesse est multas virtutes.

Tertium argumentum.

Dilectio est iusticia: Ergo dilectione sumus iusti.

Valet consequentia et loco coniugatorum. Ut cum dicimus: Albedo est color, Ergo paries albus albedine est coloratus. Valet conscientia in coniugatis, si nulla sit ambiguitas, ut si hic iusticia intelligatur virtus, vera est propositio haec dilectio est iusticia, id est, pulcra et excellens virtus. Ergo dilectione sumus iusti, id est, habentes hanc virtutem.

Sed aliud est loqui de iusticia Personae, aliud de iusticia operum seu virtutum. Iusticia personae est imputatio iusticiae seu acceptatio in iudicio Dei, quae fit propter mediatorem sola fide. At iusticia operum virtutes sunt in nobis, et bona opera, quae sunt quidem res valde bonae, sed aliud est, propter quod persona placet, quae nondum fatisfacit legi Dei, et adhuc multas sordes et infirmitates circumfert.

Hoc discrimine de iusticia personae et operum considerato, multum lucis accedit universae huic doctrinae. Iam rursus consideres haec coniugata, Dilectio est iusticia, id est, virtus, Ergo dilectione sumus iusti, hic si iusti significet personam acceptam esse coram Deo, non valebit consequentia propter ambiguitatem, ut si dicas: Amor patriae est iusticia, Ergo Cicero propter amorem patriae est iustus coram Deo. Manifestum est hic non valere consequentiam propter ambiguitatem.

Quartum argumentum.

Medium quo non est terminus ad quem, Fides est medium quo accipimus remissionem peccatorum: Igitur fides non est iusticia, sed res qua accipimus eam. Concedo totum, propriissime loquendo, quia verum est, fide accipi, id est, applicari nobis iusticiam, id est, imputationem iusticiae, quia non sumus iusti et accepti propter nostras qualitates, sed propter filium Dei mediatorem, quem tamen necesse est fide intueri et apprehendere.

Deinde haec ipsa fides initium est virtutum omnium, quae in nobis accenduntur, et quas esse in conversis oportet. Quintum argumentum.

Iustificari ex iniusto iustum fieri: Efficimur iusti, id est, mutati iam in nobis fide, spe, et dilectione: Ergo non sola fide. Primum ad maiorem, ut descriptio vocabuli propria teneatur. Ambiguitas est in maiore, iustificari est ex iniusto iustum fieri: haec intelligunt adversarii tantum hoc modo, iustum, id est, alium, indutum novis qualitatibus. Id non satis est, sed intelligi oportet iustum, id est, reconciliatum Deo facta remissione peccatorum, et acceptum Deo.

Deinde vero addendum est, indutum novis qualitatibus. Haec vocabuli interpretatio diligenter consideranda est, ut ad hanc speciosam cavillationem dextre responderi possit: iam vocabuli interpretatione constituta respondeatur ad maiorem.

Maior est vera de mutatione in nobis. Sed non est vera de remissione peccatorum, et acceptatione personae. Verum est, multas virtutes simul accendi oportere, sed tamen persona iusta est, id est, habens remissionem peccatorum, et accepta Deo, fide, propter mediatorem, non propter proprias virtutes. His explicationibus consideratis aliae similes praestigiae etiam facile iudicari et refutari possunt, et alibi multarum obiectionum explicationes tradidi.

Caeterum ad intellectum et controversiae huius et Epistolae Paulinae, necesse est recte et vere cognosci discrimen legis et Evangelii. Item proprias et veras significationes vocabulorum iustificationis, Gratiae, Fidei, etc. et phrasis propheticae et apostolicae sine corruptelis intelligenda est.

Enarratio aliquot vocabulorum.

Lex Dei est doctrina consentiens cum aeterna et immota norma mentis divinae, praecipiens quales non esse, et quae facere et omittere oporteat, et damnans omnes, qui non praestant integram obedientiam legi Dei. Haec definitio sumta est ex his verbis Moisi: Maledictus, qui non manet in omnibus, quae scripta sunt in lege.

Ac necesse est in Ecclesia extare et retineri hoc discrimen.

Humano iudicio existimatur satisfactum esse legi divinae, et aliis, quando externa obedientia praestatur. Sed iudicium Dei et legis divinae aliud est, videlicet, ut ordo non solum in externis factis, sed etiam in tota hominis natura congruat cum mente et voluntate divina.

Quia homo ita conditus est, ut sit imago Dei, et lex insita est mentibus humanis, ut ordo in tota natura hominis, congrueret cum ordine mentis divinae. Quia vero post lapsum non congruit natura hominis cum illa aeterna norma in mente divina, Deus vere irascitur huic depravatione interiori non tantum externis delictis, sed etiam interiori depravationi.

Quanquam autem lex antea insita fuit mentibus, tamen Deus expressa voce eam promulgavit, quia mentibus humanis post lapsum coepit obscurior esse. Voluit igitur Deus eam renovare, et edidit illustria testimonia, ut sciamus noticiam mentibus insitam lumen esse a Deo traditum, et quatenus mentes humanae cum iudicio Dei congruant.

Item ut extet iudicium Dei adsersus peccata interiora et exteriora. Nam ipsa vox legis expresse testatur, postulari integram obedientiam.

Sicut verba dicunt: Diligas Dominum Deum tuum ex tota corde, ex tota anima, ex omnibus viribus.

Item: Non concupiscas. Hunc intellectum legis necesse est in Ecclesia conservari.

Ideo et

Matth. 5. haec interpretatio proponitur, ut sit doctrina poenitentiae, et agnito peccato quaeratur mediator.

Sicut autem Pharisaei olim tantum disciplinam externam satisfacere legi Dei imaginabantur, et postea multos errores affingebant, hac disciplina homines mereri remissionem peccatorum, item, iustos esse hac disciplina coram Deo et de mediatore prorsus silentium erat.

Ita saepe in Ecclesia similes errores late vagati sunt, sic Pelagiani et recentes scriptores, Thomas, Scotus et similes finxerunt, homines legi Dei satisfacere hac disciplina, et mereri remissionem peccatorum, et iustos esse coram Deo hac disciplina.

Hae impiae imaginationes et legem et beneficia filii Dei obscuraverunt.

Haec initio monere de intellectu legis necesse est, sicut et Paulus 2. Corinth 3. discernit pharisaicum intellectum legis a vero intellectu.

Sapientia humana intuetur faciem Moisi velatam, id est, externam disciplinam existimat esse legis impletionem. Sed quando indicantur corda in vera poenitentia per evangelicum Ministerium, aliquo modo retegitur facies Moisi, et cognoscitur iudicium Dei adversus peccata, significatum radiis sparsis ex facie Moisi.

De Peccato.

Peccati nomine Paulus saepe utitur pro tota radice et malis fructibus, sed docendi causa recte et utiliter tradita est distinctio peccati Originalis et Actualis.

Ac prorsus ac Ecclesia necesse est scire, peccatum non tantum significare vitiosas actiones, ut grammaticis videtur sonare vocabulum, seu ut de vitiosis actionibus aut habitibus loquuntur Philosophi, aut leges politicae, sed Ebraea phrasis nominat Peccatum malum quodcunque pugnans cum legi Dei, et reum coram Deo.

Complectitur ergo non tantum vitiosas actiones, sed etiam radicem, scilicet, malum originale, cuius descriptio infra recitanda erit.

Nunc generalis definitio, conveniens et originali et actuali peccato, constitui talis potest.

Peccatum est defectus, vel inclinatio, vel actio, pugnans cum lege Dei, offendens Deum, et commerens aeternas poenas, nisi facta sit remissio propter filium Dei.

Sumitur autem et haec definitio ex dicto Moisi: Maledictus qui non manet in omnibus, quae scripta sunt in lege.

Postea autem copiosius explicabitur distinctio peccati originalis et actualis.

Nunc enim haec brevis admonitio recitatur, ne iuniores politico more tantum putent externa delicta nominari peccata, sed ut sciant, magna interiora mala esse, dubitare, an curet Deus humana, an vere irascatur omnium peccatis, an vere recipiat omnes agentes poenitentiam.

Item, esse sine timore Dei, sine fide et sine fiducia, sine dilectione Dei, sine invocatione, fingere secundas et adversas res accidere, vel in adversis irasci Deo, et fugere eum.

Item, corde contumacem esse adversus legem Dei, et ardere multis flammis errantium cupiditatum.

Haec magna confusio malorum in homine agnoscenda et deploranda est, et sciendum, multo plura mala peccati nomine comprehendi in Ecclesia, quam in philosophia et politica doctrina.

Monachi vero et hoc vocabulum corruperunt, quia negant, malum originale in renatis esse malum pugnans cum lege Dei, etc.

De Gratia.

Nomen Gratiae valde obscuratum est, cum monachi tantum usurparunt pro habitu infuso, et hinc tenebrae sequutae sunt in universa doctrina de Gratia, Iusticia, et Fide.

Sciendum est igitur, Gratiam significare gratuitam misericordiam, seu remissionem peccatorum, et acceptationem, donatam propter filium, cum qua tamen coniuncta est donatio Spiritus sancti, accendentis novam lucem, et novas virtutes in corde hominis, cui remittuntur peccata.

Utitur Paulus duabus appellationibus, ut discernat haec duo: gratuitatam acceptationem et novas virtutes in nobis accensas.

Rom. 5.: Multo magis gratia Dei, et donum per gratiam, per Iesum Christum in multos exuberant.

Sic cum dicitur: Non estis sub lege, sed sub gratia, non satis est sic intelligi, gubernamini habitu infuso, sed necesse est, prius hanc dulcissimam consolationem tenere: estis sub gratia, id est, habetis remissionem peccatorum, et accepti estis Deo propter mediatorem, gratis, etiamsi adhuc in vobis reliquae sunt peccati, magna infirmitas, et multum sordium.

De Iustificatione.

Iusticia, cum de legis Iusticia loquimur, significat virtutes in nobis, et Iustus idem quod habens illas virtutes.

Haec cum philosophica et legalia sint, Thomas et similes tantum hoc modo intellexerunt haec vocabula de qualitatibus, et verbum iustificare interpretati sunt, infundere virtutes, ut si dicerent, Calefacere significat infundere calorem.

Etsi autem necesse est novas virtutes in nobis accendi, ut saepe iam dictum est, tamen phrasis in his appellationibus alia est. Nam Evangelium aliter de iusticia loquitur, quam Lex aut Philosophia. Cum tua mens angitur, an sis iustus, non hoc principaliter quaeritur, quae sint in corde qualitates. Imo vero cernis etiam, magnam esse immunditiem cordis, sed hoc quaeritur, an sis acceptus Deo, an Deus te receperit, an remiserit tibi peccata.

Est igitur principalis significatio vocabuli Iustus in hac quaestione, acceptus Deo ad vitam aeternam. Inde et verbum iustificare significat absolvere a peccatis, et iustum, id est, acceptum reputare seu pronunciare, sicut plerunque in forensi sermone etiamsi loquuti sunt Ebraei, ut si dicerent, Populus Romanus iustificavit Scipionem accusatum a Tribuno, id est, pronunciavit iustum. Cum igitur quaeritur, an fide iustificemur, non hoc quaeritur, an sola fides in corde sit, sed an receperit nos Deus, an remiserit peccata, an simus accepti propter filium Dei, non propter qualitates nostras.

Et tamen cum accensa est fides, qua agnoscimus filium Dei, et promissionem amplectimur, necesse est multas virtutes simul esse. Nam fiducia acquiescens in Deo, et erigens corda in veris pavoribus, nequaquam est sine dilectione, sine invocatione, sine timore, et est motus clamans, ut Paulus inquit: Abba Pater. Postea, cum de Operibus dicitur, quis sit usus verborum, iustus et iustificari, non rudis grammaticae facile iudicabit, ut cum dicitur: Non auditores legis, sed factores iustificantur, id est, pronunciantur habentes illam legis iusticiam.

De vocabulo Fidei.

Etsi pertinacissime et sine ullo fine contendunt adversarii, fide tantum significari noticiam, tamen certa et immota veritas est, in hoc dicto: Iustus fide sua vivet.
