Item: Fide iustificamur, et similibus, nomine Fidei complecti et noticiam omnium articulorum fidei, et fiduciam acquiescentem in promissione, quae et ipsa comprehenditur in articulis Symboli, scilicet: Credo remissionem peccatorum, carnis resurrectionem, et vitam aeternam.

Necesse est enim priores articulos ad haec beneficia referre. Et Paulus Rom. 4. manifeste affirmat, se de ea fide loqui, quae promissionem amplectitur. Haec autem est fiducia, qua acquiescit mens in filio Dei, statuens non tantum aliis quibusdam, sed Tibi ipsi remitti peccata. Teneatur ergo docendi causa haec definitio: Fides est assensus, quo verbo Dei nobis tradito, atque ita promissioni reconciliationis etiam assentimur: et est fiducia, acquiescens in filio Dei, iuxta promissionem.

## 1:1 Disposition of Romans: Argument
This book appeared first: The arrangement of the discourse in the Epistle of Paul to the Romans, by the author Philipp Melanchthon. Hagenau by Jo. Secerius. 1529. 8vo. 2 1/2 sheets. It is inscribed to Hermann, Count of New Aquila. (See the Epistle above Vol. I. p. 1043.) The booklet was reprinted:

1) The arrangement of the discourse in the Epistle of Paul to the Romans. By the author Phil. Melan., likewise the same Epistle of Paul to the Romans rendered in heroic verse by Berthram Damianus of Brunswick (without indication of place) 1529. 8vo. 11 sheets.

2) Arrangement of the discourse — — — Hagenau by Jo. Secerius, in the year 1530, month of September. 8vo.

3) Arrangement — — Wittenberg by Jos. Clug. 1530. 5 1/2 sheets. 8vo. (enlarged by Melanchthon.)

4) Arrangement — — — (without indication of place and bookseller) 1539. 8vo. Repeated also in the Works of Melanchthon, Basel, Vol. II, p. 355, and in the Works of Melanchthon edited at Wittenberg by Peucer, Vol. IV, p. 3, from which we have drawn it here.

THE ARRANGEMENT OF THE DISCOURSE IN THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS BY THE AUTHOR PHILIPP MELANCHTHON.

The Argument of the Epistle of Paul to the Romans.

It is very useful in the reading of the whole of Scripture to observe that there is a twofold righteousness. The one is political—for so we shall call it for the sake of teaching—when human reason produces good, or civil, works. And human reason sees no other righteousness at all. Therefore, it judges that such works are sufficient before God for justification. And it thinks there is no other worship of God except to perform those civil works: not to steal, not to kill, not to lie, not to commit adultery, to obey magistrates, to moderate pleasures. And by such works it determines that the wrath of God is appeased. Meanwhile, it does not see the impurity of the human heart, which is devoid of the fear of God, of trust toward God, and has concupiscence and evil affections of every kind. Therefore, there has always been dissension between the pious and the world. The pious teach a certain other righteousness besides that hypocrisy of works. The world, on the contrary, defends the hypocrisy of works in such a way that it teaches that those works appease the wrath of God and justify before God. But the Gospel shows a far different righteousness, which is called the righteousness of faith. For the Gospel teaches that Christ the Son of God was given for us, and that righteousness before God is to believe that our sins are forgiven us on account of Christ, or that on account of Christ we are received into the grace of the Father. Meanwhile, it convicts our sins, and condemns not only external offenses but also the impurity of the heart. It shows that the human heart is empty of the fear of God, empty of trust toward God. It shows the baseness of the concupiscence burning in our members. Therefore, it denies that we can appease the wrath of God by the hypocrisy of our works, and it shows us another righteousness, entirely hidden and unknown to the world, namely that which Paul calls the righteousness of faith. And this is conceived in this way. When sins are convicted by the Word, and our hearts are terrified, if in these terrors we have believed that our sins are forgiven us, and that we are received into the grace of the Father on account of Christ, according to the Gospel. That faith raises up and consoles terrified minds. That faith is truly righteousness before God. That faith appeases the wrath of God. No works of ours can appease it. And when we have conceived faith, we now truly know that we are a care to God, that we are defended by God, we dare to call upon God, and to seek and expect help. Nor does this faith come without a struggle. In all our life it behooves us to contend with our incredulity, and to raise up the hesitating conscience by the Word and by faith. This matter is entirely unknown to the world, which sees no righteousness except political, wherefore the greatest part of men derides and condemns this doctrine without understanding it. And human philosophers, if any wish to appear not to abhor Christian piety, nevertheless dream that the Gospel teaches nothing else except political justice, just as the ethics of Aristotle teach, or Cato, or Phocylides. These men cavil at and evade the sentences of Scripture concerning the justice of faith in various ways. But holy men know that for terrified minds there is no firm consolation proposed, except in faith. Our works cannot render the conscience tranquil, as David testifies: You shall not enter into judgment with your servant. Since, therefore, there is such a great disagreement of human reason with the Gospel, Paul wrote the Epistle to the Romans, in which he has embraced this controversy, so that he might teach not only the Romans, but all the Churches, concerning the chief point of Christian doctrine. For unless this point is known, it cannot be understood why Christ came. Paul therefore wished to propose it as a method of the Gospel. Now, men who are moderately literate are not ignorant of how much it contributes in every doctrine to maintain a method. The whole of Christian doctrine revolves around this point, how we may be justified before God, or what Christian justice is. This definition is the head and sum of the entire Christian doctrine, wherefore he undertook to reveal and illustrate this definition. Let this be enough to have said in this place concerning the counsel of Paul and the argument of the Epistle.

This Epistle pertains properly to the didactic genus, because its end is to teach us what justice before God is. It can, however, be referred to the judicial genus, because this also is accommodated to teaching. The status of the Epistle is definitive. For the justice of God is defined in this way. The justice of God is to believe that on account of Christ we are received into the grace of the Father, without our merits, etc. He calls this justice of God by his own phrase, by which God reckons us just, or by which we are just before God, for it is opposed to carnal or human justice, which is so called from the efficient cause, by which the flesh justifies itself, or makes itself just.

And because the best kind of interpreting is to show the οἰκονομίαν of the discourse, we have annotated the series of all the points, propositions, and arguments, so that the genuine meaning of Paul may be discerned, and it may be understood how the individual members of the disputation agree among themselves. For consciences must be so fortified that they certainly know the sentence of Scripture concerning such great matters, so that they may have firm and certain defenses to which they may betake themselves in temptations.

Points of the exordium.

The exordium contains the points by which goodwill is customarily captured.

Goodwill.

In the former there is affection, joined with a commendation of the Romans: I give thanks to God that you believe. In the latter place he offers them his service: I desired to set out to you, that I might teach you, but I have been hindered. And there is added a binding epiphonema drawn from a general sentence concerning the office of the Apostle: I am a debtor to Greeks and Barbarians, to the wise and to the unwise. For good bishops, desiring to teach all according to their strength, ought to help and adapt themselves to the capacity of those learning. The weak are to be treated in one way, those who appear to be stronger in another.

Attention.

There is also added a point of attention from the dignity of the Gospel: I am not ashamed of the Gospel, even though the world may hate or despise it. A confirmation or αἰτιολογία follows this sentence, because the Gospel is the power of God, that is, through the Gospel God is efficacious, moves hearts to believe, and imputes that faith for justice. And there is added a proof of that reason from the definition of the Gospel, for the Gospel teaches justice, which justifies before God. Dialecticians teach that the head of the art is to define correctly, and to diligently inculcate the definition to the learner. Here, therefore, let the reader remember what the Gospel is, what it contains in sum, and what the proper and chief point of the Gospel is. Thus it will be able to be easily understood how it differs from the law, how it differs from philosophy. For the Gospel reveals the justice of faith, that those who believe they are received into grace on account of Christ are held to be just before God. The law teaches a certain other justice, philosophy hands down the civility of morals, therefore they are far distant from the Gospel. Although a proposition is placed below, and the status of the whole disputation is demonstrated in somewhat more words, yet even here in the exordium he inserts into the brief words the sum of the disputation, as if proposing it, that the Gospel reveals justice, namely that to believe in Christ justifies and pacifies hearts.

Proposition.

Faith is righteousness. The Prophet's testimony is added: The just shall live by faith.

Elaboration and repetition of the proposition.

Because he will explain in more words the principal proposition, which he just touched upon lightly, a certain proposition is therefore placed before it, through which he makes a step toward the principal one. It is, however, taken as if from the contrary. Men by nature are not righteous, nor can they be justified by their works. To this he then opposes the principal proposition: Men are justified by faith. He proposes the former with these words. The Gospel argues that all men are impious, or contemners of God and sinners. For the Gospel preaches repentance, wherefore it argues sins immediately at the beginning.

Subjoined to this general proposition is a rhetorical distribution, which divides the proposition into members. The Gentiles are accused, and the Jews. These members are treated in order; the Gentiles did not glorify God. He amplifies from the effects, for the fruits of impiety are later recounted by a heap, that those who do not glorify God are delivered into a reprobate mind, so that they rush into various sins, become adulterers, murderers, thieves.

Latin:

Prodiit hic liber primum: Dispositio orationis in Epist. Pauli ad Romanos, auctore Philippo Mel. Haganoae per Jo. Secerium. 1529. 8. 2 1/2 pl. Inscripta est Hermanno, Comiti Novae Aquilae. (Epist. vid. supra Vol. I. p. 1043.) Recusus est libellus:

1) Dispositio orationis in Epist. Pauli ad Romanos. Autore Phil. Melan., item eiusdem Pauli ad Rom. Epistola versu heroico reddita per Berthramum Damianum Brunovicanum (s. ind. loci) 1529. 8. 11 pl.

2) Disposit. orat. — — — Haganoae apud Jo. Secerium, anno 1530. m. Septb. 8.

3) Dispositio — — Witebergae apud Jos. Clug. 1530. 5 1/2 pl. 8. (aucta a Melanthone.)

4) Dispositio — — — (sine ind. loci et bibliop.) 1539. 8. Repetita etiam in Operibus Melanth. Basil. T. II, p. 355. et in Opp. Mel. Witebergae a Peucero editis T. IV. p. 3., unde illam hic hausimus.

DISPOSITIO ORATIONIS IN EPISTOLA PAULI AD ROMANOS AUCOTRE PHILIPPO MELANCHTHONE.

Argumentum Epistolae Pauli ad Romanos.

Valde prodest in universae scripturae lectione observare, quod duplex sit iusticia. Altera est politica, sic enim docendi causa vocabimus, cum opera bona, seu civilia, ratio humana efficit. Nec videt aliam iusticiam ullam humana ratio. Itaque iudicat eiusmodi opera sufficere coram Deo ad iustificationem. Nec cultum Dei alium ullum existimat, nisi opera illa civilia praestare, non furari, non occidere, non mentiri, non moe- chari, obtemperare magistratibus, moderari vo- luptates. Et talibus operibus statuit placari iram Dei. Interea non videt immunditiem cordis hu- mani, quod vacat metu Dei, fiducia erga Deum, et habet concupiscentiam et omnis generis malos affectus. Semper igitur dissensio fuit piis cum mundo. Pii aliam quandam iusticiam praeter illam hypocrisin operum docent. Mundus contra ita defendit hypocrisin operum, ut doceat illa opera placare iram Dei, et iustificare coram Deo. At Evangelium longe aliam iusticiam ostendit, quae vocatur iusticia fidei. Nam Evangelium do- cet Christum filium Dei pro nobis datum esse, et iusticiam coram Deo esse, credere quod pec- cata nostra propter Christum nobis condonentur, seu quod propter Christum recipiamur in gratiam patris. Interea arguit nostra peccata, et non tantum externa delicta, sed etiam immunditiem cordis damnat. Ostendit humanum cor vacuum esse metu Dei, vacuum fiducia erga Deum. Osten- dit turpitudinem concupiscentiae flagrantis in membris nostris. Itaque negat nos posse pla- care iram Dei hypocrisi nostrorum operum, et aliam iusticiam prorsus arcanam et incognitam mundo nobis monstrat, videlicet eam, quam Pau- lus vocat iusticiam fidei. Atque haec ita conci- pitur. Cum verbo arguuntur peccata, et perter- refiunt corda nostra, si in his terroribus credide- rimus nobis ignosci peccata, et in gratiam patris nos recipi propter Christum, iuxta Evangelium. Ea fides erigit et consolatur perterrefactas mentes. Ea fides est vere iusticia coram Deo. Ea fides placat iram Dei. Nulla nostra opera placare pos- sunt. Et cum fidem concepimus, iam vere sci- mus Deo nos curae esse, nos a Deo defendi, au- demus invocare Deum, et petere et expectare auxilium. Nec sine certamine contingit haec fides. In omni vita dimicare nos oportet cum in- credulitate nostra, et haesitantem conscientiam verbo et fide erigere. Haec res prorsus est ignota mundo, qui nullam iusticiam videt, nisi politi- cam, quare maxima pars hominum hanc doctri- nam irridet ac damnat non intellectam. Et ho- mines philosophi, si qui volunt videri non ab- horrere a Christiana pietate, tamen somniant Evangelium nihil docere aliud, nisi politicam iusticiam, sicut Aristotelis ethica docent, aut Cato, aut Phocylides. Hi sententias scripturae de iusticia fidei, varie cavillantur et eludunt. At sancti viri norunt territis mentibus nullam esse propositam firmam consolationem, nisi in fide. Opera nostra non possunt conscientiam red- dere tranquillam, sicut testatur David: Non ingredieris in iudicium cum servo tuo. Cum ita- que tanta sit dissensio rationi humanae cum Evangelio, Paulus scripsit epistolam ad Roma- nos, in qua hanc controversiam complexus est, ut de loco praecipuo Christianae doctrinae non tantum Romanos, sed omnes Ecclesias doceret. Nam nisi hoc loco cognito, non potest intelligi, cur venerit Christus. Voluit igitur Paulus tan- quam methodum Evangelii proponere. Quan- tum autem conducat in omni doctrina methodum tenere, non ignorant homines mediocriter literati. Tota doctrina Christiana versatur circa hunc lo- cum, quomodo coram Deo iustificemur, seu quid sit iusticia Christiana. Haec definitio caput et summa est universae doctrinae Christianae, quare hanc definitionem patefaciendam et illustrandam suscepit. Haec satis sit hoc loco de consilio Pauli, et de argumento Epistolae dixisse.

Propriae pertinet haec Epistola ad genus di- dacticum, quia finis eius est, ut doceat nos, quid sit iusticia coram Deo. Potest tamen ad iudiciale genus referri, quia hoc quoque ad do- cendum accommodatum est. Status Epistolae fini- tivus est. Nam iusticia Dei definitur hoc modo. Iusticia Dei est credere, quod propter Christum recipiamur in gratiam patris, sine nostris meri- tis, etc. Vocat autem sua phrasi iusticiam Dei hanc, qua Deus reputat nos iustos, seu qua nos sumus iusti coram Deo, opponitur enim car- nali seu humanae iusticiae, quae sic appellatur ab efficiente causa, qua caro se iustificat, aut iustam efficit.

Et quia optimum interpretandi genus est οἰκονομίαν orationis ostendere, seriem omnium locorum, propositionum et argumentorum anno- tavimus, ut genuina sententia Pauli cerni possit, et intelligi quomodo consentiant inter se singula membra disputationis. Nam conscientiae ita mu- niendae sunt, ut certo sciant sententiam scriptu- rae de tantis rebus, ut firma et certa praesidia habeant, ad quae in tentationibus se recipiant.

Loci exordii.

Exordium continet locos, quibus benevo- lentia de more captatur.

Benevolentia.

In priore affectus est, coniunctus cum prae- conio Romanorum: Ago gratias Deo, quod cre- ditis. Posteriore loco officium defert illis: Cu- piebam ad vos proficisci, ut vos docerem, sed sum impeditus. Et subiectum est legans epipho- nema ex generali sententia ex officio Apostoli du- ctum: Graecis et Barbaris sapientibus et insi- pientibus debitor sum. Nam boni Episcopi pro viribus iuxta omnes discere cupientes, adiuvare debent, et attemperare se captui discentium. Ali- ter tractandi sint imbecilles, aliter isti quos ap- paret esse firmiores.

Attentio.

Est et additus locus attentionis ab Evangelii dignitate: Non pudet me Evangelii, tametsi mundus oderit, aut aspernetur. Quam senten- tiam confirmatio seu αἰτιολογία sequitur, quia Evangelium est potentia Dei, id est, per Evan- gelium Deus est efficax, movet corda ad creden- dum, et eam fidem imputat pro iusticia. Et ad- dita est eius rationis comprobatio ex definitione Evangelii, nam Evangelium docet iusticiam, quae coram Deo iustificat. Dialectici caput artis esse docent, recte definire, ac definitionem dili- genter inculcare discenti. Hic igitur meminerit lector quid Evangelium sit, quid in summa con- tineat, quis proprius ac praecipuus Evangelii locus sit. Ita facile intelligi poterit, quomodo a lege, quomodo a philosophia differat. Nam Evangelium patefacit iusticiam fidei, quod coram Deo iusti habeantur, qui credunt se propter Chri- stum in gratiam recipi. Lex aliam quandam iusti- ciam docet, philosophia civilitatem morum tra- dit, procul igitur ab Evangelio distant. Quan- quam autem infra ponatur propositio, et totius disputationis status aliquanto pluribus verbis de- monstretur, tamen et hic exordio summam dis- putationis, velut proponens, brevibus verbis in- seruit, quod Evangelium patefaciat iusticiam, nempe quod credere in Christum, iustificet et pacificet corda.

Propositio.

Fides est iusticia. Additum est Prophetae testimonium: Iustus ex fide vivet.

Propositionis expolitio, et repetitio.

Quia pluribus verbis principalem propositio- nem, quam modo leviter attigit, explicabit, ideo praeponitur quaedam propositio, per quam gra- dum ad principalem facit. Est autem velut ex contrario sumta. Homines natura non sunt iusti, nec possunt operibus suis iustificari. Huic deinde opponit principalem propositionem: Fide iustifi- cantur homines. Priorem his verbis proponit. Evangelium arguit omnes homines quod sint im- pii, seu contemtores Dei et peccatores. Nam Evangelium praedicat poenitentiam, quare statim initio arguit peccata.

Huic generali propositioni est subiecta rhe- torica distributio, quae partitur propositionem in membra. Gentes accusantur et Iudaei. Haec membra ordine tractantur, Gentes non glorifica- verunt Deum. Amplificat ab effectibus, nam im- pietatis fructus postea per congeriem recensentur, qui non glorificant Deum traduntur in reprobum sensum, ut ruant in varia peccata, fiant moechi, homicidae, fures.

## 1:1 Argument
Chapter I.

Paul, a servant of Christ, called to be an Apostle. The superscription, as is done in Epistles, is placed in front. And for great reasons, the mention of office and doctrine is inserted. It is necessary in the Church that vocations or teachers be discerned.

And just as it is necessary to believe God Himself, speaking with His own voice in Paradise, or to Abraham, or to Moses, and just as it is necessary to believe the Son of God Himself, speaking with His own voice, and that very divine voice is valid, firm, and immutable: so it is necessary to believe the Prophets and Apostles, because they do not themselves generate a new kind of doctrine, but receive certain commands from God, these they sound forth, and God adds testimonies so that they do not err, just as Moses repeatedly uses this opening: 'The Lord God spoke,' etc. Thus, therefore, they are to be heard, just as the voice of God sounding from heaven and confirmed by illustrious testimonies.

And it is necessary that all men assent to them, and it is not permitted for any creature to change their doctrine.

Then, indeed, other teachers must receive the voice from the Prophets and Apostles, and sound this one thing, and when they sound this, they teach rightly. But many depart from this voice, and by inventing other things of their own, they err. It must be known, therefore, that it is not necessary to believe Bishops or other teachers, besides God, the Prophets, and the Apostles, except insofar as they recite that very voice of God, of the Prophets, and of the Apostles.

And let the distinctions be learnedly held.

A Prophet among the people of Israel is a person called immediately by God to teach and illustrate the Gospel, having the testimony that he does not err, and sent to govern certain political counsels, such as Moses, Samuel, Elijah, Elisha, Isaiah, Jeremiah, etc.

An Apostle is a person, immediately called by God, to teach the Gospel, having testimony that he does not err, nor yet is he sent to rule the councils of political government. He has, however, a universal calling, so that he may teach in any place whatsoever. A Bishop is a person, called by men, to teach the Gospel, in a certain place, who does not have testimonies that he does not err: but he can err and slip, when indeed he departs from the prophetic and apostolic voice. This distinction being considered, we understand that there are many reasons why mention is made of the office.

First, it is necessary to know that Paul does not wander by his own private counsel, but was called and sent by God. Second, that he carries around a doctrine not devised by himself, but commended to him divinely, which indeed is the admirable decree of the divinity, concerning the liberation of the human race from sin and from death through the Son. Third, that we may know that nothing of error is mixed into this doctrine. Fourth, that he is to be believed, as the voice of God sounding from heaven, and that faith may acquiesce in his sermons, and certainly determine that this is the immovable will of God which he proposes. It is necessary to consider these things, both for our consolation and to prohibit the horrible audacity of changing the doctrine. Because God, in His immense mercy, has revealed that decree of His, which it is permitted to no creature to change.

Latin:

Caput I.

Paulius servus Christi vocatus Apostolus. Epigrapha, ut fit in Epistolis, praeposita est. Et propter magnas causas inserta est mentio officii et doctrinae. Necesse est in Ecclesia discerni vocationes seu doctores.

Ac sicut Deo ipsi, sua voce concionanti in Paradiso, vel ad Abraham, aut Moisen, et sicut ipsi filio Dei sua voce concionanti, credi necesse est, et illa ipsa vox divina rata, firma et immutabilis est: sic Prophetis et Apostolis credi necesse est, quia non gignunt ipsi novum genus doctrinae, sed accipiunt certa mandata a Deo, haec sonant, et addit testimonia Deus, quod non errent, sicut Moises subinde repetit hoc exordium: Locutus est Dominus Deus etc. Sic igitur audiendi sunt, sicut vox Dei sonans de coelo, et confirmata illustribus testimoniis.

Et necesse est, eis omnes homines assentiri, et nulli creaturae licet eorum doctrinam mutare.

Deinde vero a Prophetis et Apostolis alii doctores accipere vocem debent, et hanc unam sonare, et hanc cum sonant, recte docent. Sed multi ab hac voce discedunt, et alia de suo affingentes errant. Sciendum est igitur, Episcopis vel doctoribus aliis, praeter Deum, Prophetas et Apostolos, non necessario credendum esse, nisi quatenus illam ipsam vocem Dei, Prophetarum et Apostolorum recitant.

Ac erudite teneantur discrimina.

Propheta in populo Israël, est persona immediate a Deo vocata ad docendum et illustrandum Evangelium, habens testimonium, quod non erret, et missa ad gubernanda aliqua politica consilia, ut Moises, Samuel, Elias, Elisaeus, Esaias, Ieremias etc.

Apostolus est persona, immediate a Deo vocata, ad docendum Evangelium, habens testimonium quod non erret, neque tamen missa est, ut regat consilia gubernationis politicae. Habet autem vocationem universalem, ut quocunque loco docere possit. Episcopus est persona, vocata per homines, ad docendum Evangelium, in loco certo, quae non habet testimonia, quod non erret: sed errare et labi potest, cum videlicet a voce prophetica et apostolica discedit. Hoc discrimine considerato, intelligimus multas causas esse, cur mentio fiat officii.

Primum sciri necesse est, non vagari Paulum suo privato consilio, sed a Deo vocatum missum esse. Secundo circumferre eum doctrinam, non ab ipso excogitatam, sed commendatam ei divinitus, quae quidem est admirandum decretum divinitatis, de liberatione generis humani a peccato et a morte per filium. Tertio, ut sciamus, nihil erroris admixtum esse huic doctrinae. Quarto, ut ei credatur, tanquam voci Dei, de coelo sonanti, et acquiescat fides in eius concionibus, et certo statuat, hanc esse voluntatem immotam Dei, quam proponit. Haec considerare necesse est, et ad consolationem nostram, et ad prohibendam horribilem audaciam mutandae doctrinae. Quia Deus immensa misericordia decretum illud suum patefecit, quod nulli creaturae mutare licet.

## 1:1
Set apart for the Gospel of God.

In the description of the office he now recites what the Office is, namely, the duty of teaching the Gospel, which he then defines, so that he may distinguish it from the law.

But first, let the word 'Set apart' be observed, which signifies that he was chosen with a certain segregation for divine use, not common to the rest of the multitude, just as it is said of victims, that they are set apart, that is, chosen for this use, so that they may be sacrificed to God. Thus also in Numbers chapter 8, it is said that the Levites are set apart from the rest of the multitude for divine uses. And a notable image is proposed in the victims. The ministers of the Gospel are similar to victims, and the chief victim is the high priest, the Son of God. The metaphor therefore signifies that the Apostles are not called to power, not to wealth, not to delights, but to huge dangers and struggles, as he says in Psalm 43: For thy sake we are killed all the day long, and are counted as sheep for the slaughter.

Here it is necessary to think of a comparison. The callings of Moses, Joshua, Samuel, Elijah, Elisha, how glorious were they? These, by manifest testimonies of God, established and ruled empires. This matter is glorious in the judgments of men, because present benefits strike the eyes. But the appearance in the apostolic calling is far different. They wander as miserable vagabonds, without certain lodgings, they are killed by most cruel punishments. And although the appearance is different, yet God adorns them too with testimonies, so that we may be certain of the doctrine.

But here is the sweetest consolation, which he delivers in 2 Corinthians, let it be thought of often and diligently. Since there was great glory of the Old Testament in the leading out from Egypt, in the promulgation of the law, in the perpetual defense of that polity, trust that God will also be present to the Church, and will defend it among calamities, and afterwards will adorn it with huge glory. This comparison is to be thought of often to console us, so that we may confirm this sentiment in our minds, that the Son of God is truly present with the Church, just as He says: Behold, I am with you always, even unto the end of the world. There will therefore always be a ministry of the Gospel, there will be some assemblies somewhere, and some lodgings of doctrine even against the gates of hell. With this hope let us seek and expect the defense of the Church, and let us not cast away the studies of doctrine etc. Let us gather ourselves to that assembly in which the voice of the Gospel sounds.

Latin:

Segregatus in Evangelium Dei.

In descriptione officii iam recitat, quodnam sit Officium, scilicet, munus docendi Evangelii, quod deinde definit, ut discernat a lege.

Primum autem observetur vocabulum Segregatus, quod significat, delectum esse cum quadam segregatione ad divinum usum, non communem reliquae multitudini, sicut et de victimis dicitur, segregari eas, id est, eligi ad hunc usum, ut Deo mactentur. Sic et in Numeris capite 8. dicitur, Levitas segregari a reliqua multitudine ad divinos usus. Et imago insignis proponitur in victimis. Ministri Evangelii sunt similes victimis, et praecipua victima est summus sacerdos, filius Dei. Significat igitur metaphora, Apostolos non ad imperium, non ad opes, non ad delicias vocari, sed ad ingentia pericula et certamina, ut Psalmo 43. inquit: Propter te mortificamur tota die, et sicut oves occisionis aestimati sumus.

Hic necesse est cogitari collationem. Vocationes Moisi, Iosuae, Samuelis, Eliae, Elisaei, quam gloriosae fuerunt? Hi manifestis testimoniis Dei imperia constituerunt et rexerunt. Haec res gloriosa est hominum iudiciis, quia beneficia praesentia incurrunt in oculos. Sed species in vocatione apostolica longe dissimilis est. Vagantur ut errones miseri, sine certis hospitiis, interficiuntur crudelissimis suppliciis. Etsi autem dissimilis species est, tamen Deus et ipsos testimoniis ornat, ut certi simus de doctrina.

Hic autem dulcissima consolatio, quam tradit in 2. ad Corinth. saepe et diligenter cogitetur. Cum magna fuerit gloria veteris Testamenti in eductione ex Aegypto, in promulgatione legis, in defensione perpetua illius politiae, confidite et Ecclesiae Deum adfuturum esse, et eam inter calamitates defensurum, et postea ingenti gloria ornaturum esse. Haec collatio ad nos consolandos saepe cogitanda est, ut confirmemus hanc sententiam in mentibus nostris, quod filius Dei vere adsit Ecclesiae, sic ut dicit: Ecce, ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus, usque ad consummationem seculi. Erit igitur semper ministerium Evangelii, erunt alicubi aliqui coetus, et aliqua doctrinae hospitia etiam invitis portis inferorum. Hac spe petamus et expectemus Ecclesiae defensionem, et non abiiciamus doctrinae studia etc. Aggregemus nos ad eum coetum, in quo sonat vox Evangelii.

## 1:1
In the Gospel of God.

Especially in the Church it is necessary that there exist an illustrious distinction between the law and the Gospel. For unless this distinction shines forth in the whole doctrine, great darkness and pernicious errors follow. And because it is spoken of elsewhere copiously concerning this distinction, indeed this very Epistle to the Romans especially shows the distinction, here the reader must be briefly warned.

But let the younger ones know, that it is spoken especially of the moral law, which we usually call the Decalogue. Some knowledge of the moral law is born with us, as of numbers. And let the younger ones consider here the usual doctrine concerning principles. But the Gospel is a doctrine, by no means known to the nature of men, or to any creature, without divine revelation, because it is a decree of the secret counsel of the divinity, concerning the Son interceding for the human race, concerning sending the Son, so that He might become a victim, concerning announcing gratuitous remission through the Son, concerning granting justice, and eternal life etc.

This neither angels nor men could know the decree, unless God himself promulgated it.

Let this, therefore, be the definition. The Gospel is the preaching of repentance and the promise, the knowledge of which is not born with men, but was brought forth and revealed from the secret counsel of the eternal Father, out of immense goodness, in which God promises, for the sake of the Son, freely, the remission of sins, reconciliation, the Holy Spirit, righteousness, and eternal life to those who believe in the Son. This definition is taken both from this very inscription and, subsequently, from the clear members of the principal disputation in this Epistle.

As below in Chapter 3, when it is said: Now without the law the righteousness of God is manifested. Likewise: We are justified freely by faith, for the sake of the Son, etc. And because the same things will have to be repeated below, let it now suffice to have warned the younger ones to always keep in view the distinction between the law and the Gospel, lest posterity slide into the pernicious error of those who have imagined that there are three laws: Natural, Mosaic, and Evangelical, and have overwhelmed the doctrine concerning free remission and many articles of the Gospel.

Which he promised before by his Prophets in the holy scriptures.

He meets an objection: It is true without any doubt that the principal article of doctrine in the Church must be known at all times: You bring a new doctrine, therefore it is not necessary for the Church. To this argument Paul responds immediately here in the vestibule, and constantly asserts that this doctrine, concerning the remission of sins, concerning righteousness and eternal life, to be given for the sake of the Son, is by no means new, but that the promise was revealed by God immediately at the beginning of the Church, and subsequently propagated by the voice of the Prophets with illustrious divine testimonies.

And indeed he leads us to the prophetic writings themselves. To these the Church is bound, just as it is said elsewhere that the Church is built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, etc.

Here again the younger ones must be warned about the distinction between the law and the Gospel.

There is one moral law, and it is eternal for all times, which this corrupt human nature could not satisfy at any time, nor can it satisfy. Wherefore the Fathers and Prophets did not have the remission of sins, nor were they righteous before God, that is, accepted for eternal life, because of the law, but because of the mediator through faith. For there is one promise of the remission of sins and of eternal life for all times, published at the beginning in these words: The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent, and then more and more illustrated by the voice of the Prophets. Wherefore in one and the same way all the saints from the beginning receive the remission of sins and eternal life by faith, that is, by trust in the mediator, whom the promise points out, according to that: To him all the Prophets bear witness, that through his name all who believe in him receive the remission of sins.

Concerning his Son, who was born of the seed of David, according to the flesh. And who was declared to be the Son of God in power, that is, omnipotent.

Here Paul discourses concerning the two natures in the Messiah. Concerning the human nature, which the Son, coeternal with the Father, the Word (λόγος), assumed from the seed of David, that is, from the virgin Mary. But concerning the divine nature he adds: Who was declared to be the Son of God.

For he refutes the most common error of the Jews, who even then impiously thought and still so clamor, that there would be only a human nature in the Messiah. Paul, on the contrary, names the Messiah the Son of God, powerful according to nature, or omnipotent and life-giving. And he makes use of a remarkable word, ὁρισθέντος, which signifies that it is certainly known, as if he were saying: Concerning the Son, who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh, and who is certainly known to be the omnipotent Son of God.

For ὁρίζεσθαι signifies to be most certainly defined, to be comprehended and known without any doubt: which word the more recent version renders however it may: Who was declared. The ancient version obscured it entirely: Who was predestined, and provides an occasion for extraneous disputations.

Therefore the true interpretation is: whom it is most certainly known to be the Son of God. For Paul is speaking, not of predestination in the divine mind, but of the most certain manifestation of the Son of God to the whole human race.

For we are convinced that this Messiah is omnipotent, because he both rose from the dead and raised the dead, etc. In power.

Let the younger ones diligently consider the phrase: Because he was declared to be the Son of God in power, that is, powerful. But this particle is opposed the former. Born from the seed of David according to the flesh, that is, according to human nature, subject to death, without sin, etc. The rest are opposed to the delusions of the Jews, who expected a Messiah powerful in arms, victories, opulence, and the empires of the world. But Paul says, he is powerful according to the sanctifying Spirit, that is, because he gives the Holy Spirit, and takes away sin and death, and restores justice and eternal life. But all these things are proper to divine power. Therefore, the Son is by nature omnipotent. Thus he says he is known through his own resurrection, and through all miracles, through the raising of the dead, and others, and through the gift of the Holy Spirit, who has testified of him by illustrious miracles.

Grace and peace. Grace usually signifies relatively the gratuitous remission of sins, and reconciliation or gratuitous acceptance on account of the Son of God, with which is joined vivification through the Son, and the gift of the Holy Spirit. Peace is used in the Hebrew manner just as salvation is among us. It signifies the very gift of the Holy Spirit, and many effects, namely, peace of conscience, faith, hope, invocation, divine aid in governance, and success in one's calling, and in all parts of life. From God our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ. Usually he joins the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ. First, to warn that the Son is also by nature God, from whom these goods are to be sought and received. Second, to warn that these goods are given on account of the Son, according to that: Whatever you ask the Father in my name, I will do. Third, to warn that God must be acknowledged in such a way that the mind and address are directed to this true God, who revealed himself by sending the Son, according to that: No one can come to the Father except through the Son. Let us consider the ineffable goodness of God, who, since the essence of God is invisible, always added some testimony to his word, by which the true God might be distinguished from fictitious deities. But the chief testimony is that he sent the Son, whom, having assumed human nature, we ought to contemplate with the mind, and by faith establish that the true divine essence, the creator of heaven and earth, and of men and other creatures, is the Father of this our Lord Jesus Christ, and this Son is Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the eternal Father and the Son. And in invocation, the revelations are to be thought of, such as occurred at the baptism of Christ.

Exordium.

Before he institutes the disputation, in the customary manner in orations, he places an exordium, whose first proposition is Thanksgiving, as it is most customary to begin with thanksgivings and prayers. And the thanksgiving is followed by another neighboring proposition, namely: And I myself have often determined to come to you, that I might teach and confirm you. Then follows the adversative: But when I was hindered, etc. Fourth follows the αἰτιολογία (aetiology), taken from his own office. Because I am a debtor to the wise and the unwise. Fifth, the Occupatio, by which he meets a hidden objection: Even though I know that the profession of the Gospel is both despised and hated by the wise of the world, yet I am not ashamed of this doctrine. There he adds an asseveration contrary to the judgments of the world, and affirms that thus the eternal Church is gathered to God through the ministry of the Gospel, and adds the principal proposition of the Epistle: The just shall live by his faith.

To whom I serve in my spirit. He distinguishes Levitical worship from interior worship, and from the preaching of the Gospel and confession, just as Christ also says in John 4: True worshipers will worship the Father in Spirit and Truth, that is, by the motion of the heart kindled by the Holy Spirit, and in truth, that is, by the true knowledge of God and trust in the Son, according to the word handed down by God, just as it is said elsewhere: Father, sanctify them in truth, thy word is truth. For he signifies that sanctification is not in other Sects and opinions, but that the Gospel must be acknowledged and held incorrupt. Therefore, he names here also the worship of God, to teach, to learn, and to confess the Gospel, as he says below: I sacrifice the Gospel. These sayings affirm that the labor of teaching and learning pleases God. And although the dangers of those teaching and learning are great, yet let us not abandon these studies, broken by terrors, and let us determine that God will be present with us, and that our labors will not be in vain, and that God will preserve some congregations, invoking him, who may be guardians of the doctrine. Many testimonies pertain to this.

Psalm 1: His leaves shall not wither. And John 16: In this is glorified my Father, that you may bear much fruit, and be my disciples.

Item Isaiah 51: I have put my words in your mouth, and I will protect you with my hand, that you may plant the heavens. These consolations are often to be pondered, lest we cast away the studies of doctrine.

I am a debtor to the Greeks and to the barbarians, to the wise and to the unwise.

This voice seems most arrogant to the impious and to those ignorant of what the Gospel is, who thought it a great impudence to promise this wisdom, which had been unknown to the wisest men who established Republics many centuries ago.

But we in the Church know that the promise concerning the redemption and restoration of the human race must be distinguished from political and philosophical wisdom.

And unless God himself had revealed the promise, no creature could know it.

But the promise was first delivered by the voice of God himself, concerning the Son, and often afterwards, when it had been deleted either by oblivion or obscured by errors, it was again illustrated by the immense goodness of God through new revelations by the Fathers, Prophets, the Son of God, the Apostles, and pious teachers.

And indeed, God wills that it be heard by the whole human race, and that the Son be acknowledged by the whole human race, according to that: Hear him.

Therefore Paul here embraces all men, he says that he preaches to all, to the wise and to the unwise, because he does not bring political or philosophical wisdom, but the promise brought forth from the secret bosom of God, which God wills to be heard by the whole human race.

But let both here think of their duty, teachers and disciples, both are debtors.

Teachers, that they may teach; Auditors, indeed, that they may hear and learn.

Hither pertain many sayings which command teachers to teach faithfully, and to guard the purity of doctrine uncorrupted, that they may consult for the firm and the infirm, etc.

Item, other mandates which command the rest to hear and learn the Gospel, according to that: Hear him.

Item: Seek first the kingdom of God.

Item: He who will not hear, I will be an avenger.

Item: And now, O Kings, understand, kiss the Son, lest he be angry.

Item: He who does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be Anathema, Maran atha, that is, the Lord comes.

For I am not ashamed of the Gospel.

This is a place of attention, and it answers the judgments of enemies.

And it is an aetiologia (causal explanation) taken from the true dignity and efficacy of the Gospel.

But that this brief assertion: I am not ashamed of the Gospel, may be understood, the judgments must be considered, the bitterness of which is then more visible when, with controversies stirred up, the wills of men are laid bare.

Profane wise men consider political tranquility to be the highest good.

Since they do not want this to be disturbed by any novelty, they most bitterly hate the new doctrine concerning God, as a torch of seditions and horrible discords, and they take care that teachers and auditors be removed, as seditious persons and enemies of the fatherland.

Then others, not profane, but fascinated by superstition, burn with much more truculent hatreds, because they think they have more causes to fight, as they themselves speak, for the glory of God, for the unity of the Church, and for political peace.

For they accuse pious teachers in the reprehension of vicious cults, because they impede the honors due to God from being attributed.

Then they complain that the Church is being distracted and peace disturbed.

And the dispute concerning the law of Moses was more difficult then, because it seemed a supreme crime to abolish cults instituted by God.

Just as even now many vociferate that it is a supreme crime not to make an offering in the mass.

Therefore they execrate those who dissent as heretics, schismatics, and seditious, and they think it is a duty pleasing to God to kill us, as pests of the human race, or as katharmata kai alastoras (scum and avenging spirits).

Against these most bitter judgments, Paul says with great strength of faith: I am not ashamed of the Gospel.

Thus it is said in Isaiah 51: Do not fear the reproaches of men.

But how great a burden it is to sustain such virulent judgments, and such bitterness of hatreds, experience shows, and it is difficult to so confirm minds, lest, broken by such judgments, calumnies, hatreds, terrors, and punishments, they cast away the profession of the Gospel.

For it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth.

From the sources of principal doctrine is taken the reason concerning the dignity and efficacy of the Gospel, as if he were saying: The Gospel is not an empty fable, as profane men judge.

Nay, it is even more powerful than the law, because it is that voice through which God is truly efficacious in the human race, gathers to himself an eternal Church, truly takes away sin and death, gives the Holy Spirit, renders to us righteousness and eternal life.

These highest goods neither by human wisdom, nor are they given through the law, but through this voice of the Gospel.

Let us remember, however, that in this saying, testimony is set forth concerning the efficacy of the ministry of the Gospel.

Since eyes do not perceive God, the mind asks what He is, and where God is, whom it wishes to address... and to invoke, and how the true God is to be distinguished from fictitious deities, what His will is, whether and why He hears prayer. To all these questions, this saying responds: The Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes, that is, God has bound Himself to the voice of the Gospel; thus He wishes to be known, that this is truly God, who revealed Himself by sending His Son, and delivered the promise proposed in the Gospel. By this thought, He wishes to be distinguished from fictitious deities, He wishes His will to be known, why He wishes to hear prayer, and by the contemplated promise, He wishes you to believe and acquiesce, as if you were seeing and hearing God Himself comforting you. And when we believe in this way, God is truly efficacious in us.

This is the efficacy of the ministry described in many sayings. Rom. 1: The Gospel is the power of God, that is, the instrument through which God is efficacious unto salvation in those who believe. It is not an idle voice, or an empty sound, but an instrument of God, when we assent and receive it by faith. Likewise, Romans 10 it is said: Faith comes from hearing. And 2 Corinth. 3: The Gospel is the ministry of the Spirit. And Galatians 3: That we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith. Matth. 10: He who hears you, hears me. Eph. 4: For the perfecting of the saints, for the edifying of the body of Christ. Rom. 15: That through the consolation of the scriptures we might have hope. All these sayings testify that God is efficacious when we contemplate the Gospel and assent to it. Nor should this efficacy be understood as if we were speaking of heating: Fire is efficacious in straw, even if the straw does nothing. Thus the Manichaeans, Enthusiasts, and Anabaptists dreamed that illuminations occurred in a mind that was entirely idle, and they thought that they would only then be willing to believe when they first felt that new light within themselves. These imaginations must be exploded, and it must be known that we ought to hear the Gospel, contemplate it, embrace it with assent, and resist doubt. When we do this, at the same time the Holy Spirit is efficacious in that very consolation and in this struggle. These things must be learned in experience and daily invocation.

To everyone who believes. There is also a universal particle to be considered, To everyone who believes. And below, this universal must often be spoken of, lest faith be disturbed by this human imagination, which attributes partiality (προσωποληψίαν) to God: God receives certain others, He does not receive you. Against this imagination of particularity, the universal saying must be opposed, which Paul repeats often. Let us therefore include ourselves also in the universal promise, and let us determine that it pertains to us as well, so that we may attribute to God the praise of truth, and keep many universal sayings in readiness: Come to me all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.

Latin:

In Evangelium Dei.

Praecipue in Ecclesia extare necesse est illustre discrimen legis et Evangelii. Nisi enim in universa doctrina praeluceat hoc discrimen, sequuntur magnae tenebrae et perniciosi errores. Et quia alibi copiose de hoc discrimine dicitur, imo haec ipsa Epistola ad Romanos praecipue monstrat discrimen, hic breviter monendus est lector.

Sciant autem iuniores, praecipue dici de lege morali, quam usitate vocamus Decalogum. Nascitur nobiscum aliqua legis moralis notitia, ut numerorum. Et considerent hic iuniores doctrinam usitatam de principiis. Evangelium vero doctrina est, nequaquam naturae hominum, aut ulli creaturae nota, sine revelatione divina, quia decretum est arcani consilii divinitatis, de filio deprecante pro genere humano, de mittendo filio, ut fieret victima, de annuncianda gratuita remissione propter filium, de donanda iustitia, et vita aeterna etc.

Hoc decretum neque angeli, neque homines nosse poterant, nisi Deo ipso promulgante.

Sit igitur haec definitio. Evangelium est praedicatio poenitentiae, et promissio, cuius noticia non nascitur cum hominibus, sed ex arcano consilio aeterni patris, immensa bonitate, prolata et patefacta est, in qua promittit Deus propter filium, gratis, remissionem peccatorum, reconciliationem, Spiritum sanctum, iusticiam et vitam aeternam, credentibus in filium. Haec definitio sumitur et ex hac ipsa epigraphe, et deinceps ex perspicuis membris praecipuae disputationis in hac Epistola.

Ut infra Capite 3. cum dicitur. Nunc sine lege manifestata est iusticia Dei. Item: Gratis iustificamur fide, propter filium etc. Et quia infra res eaedem repetendae erunt, nunc satis sit iuniores monuisse, ut semper in conspectu habeant discrimen legis et Evangelii, ne delabatur posteritas in perniciosum errorem eorum, qui finxerunt, tres esse leges: Naturalem, Mosaicam, et Evangelicam, et obruerunt doctrinam de gratuita remissione, et de multis articulis Evangelii.

Quod antea promisit per Prophetas in scripturis sanctis.

Occurrit obiectioni: Sine ulla dubitatione verum est, articulum doctrinae in Ecclesia principalem, oportere omnibus temporibus notum esse: Tu adfers novam doctrinam, Non est igitur necessaria Ecclesiae. Huic argumento statim hic in vestibulo respondet Paulus, et constanter asseverat, hanc doctrinam, de remissione peccatorum, de iusticia et vita aeterna, donanda propter filium, nequaquam novam esse, sed statim initio Ecclesiae patefactam esse promissionem a Deo, et deinceps voce Prophetarum illustribus testimoniis divinis propagatam esse.

Et quidem deducit nos ad ipsa scripta prophetica. Ad haec alligata est Ecclesia, sicut alias dicitur, Ecclesiam extructam esse super fundamentum Apostolorum et Prophetarum etc.

Hic rursus admonendi sunt iuniores, de discrimine legis et Evangelii.

Una est lex moralis, et aeterna omnium temporum, cui nullo tempore haec corrupta hominum natura satisfacere potuit, neque satisfacere potest. Quare Patres et Prophetae non habebant remissionem peccatorum, neque erant iusti coram Deo, id est, accepti ad vitam aeternam, propter legem, sed propter mediatorem fide. Una est enim et promissio remissionis peccatorum et vitae aeternae omnium temporum, edita initio his verbis: Semen mulieris conculcabit caput serpentis, et deinde magis magisque illustrata voce Prophetarum. Quare uno et eodem modo omnes sancti ab initio accipiunt remissionem peccatorum et vitam aeternam fide, id est, fiducia mediatoris, quem promissio monstrat, iuxta illud: Huic omnes Prophetae perhibent testimonium, accipere remissionem peccatorum per nomen eius, Omnes qui credunt in eum.

De filio suo, qui natus est ex semine David, secundum carnem. Et qui declaratus est, esse filius Dei potens, id est, omnipotens.

Hic Paulus concionatur de duabus naturis in Messia. De natura humana, quam assumsit filius coaeternus patri λόγος ex semine David, id est, ex virgine Maria. De natura divina autem addit: Qui declaratus est, esse filius Dei.

Refutat enim vulgatissimum errorum Iudaeorum, qui et tunc impie cogitabant et adhuc ita clamitant, in Messia tantum humanam naturam fore. Paulus contra nominat Messiam filium Dei, secundum naturam potentem, seu omnipotentem et vivificatricem. Et est usus insigni verbo, ὁρισθέντος, quod significat, certo cognitum esse, quasi dicat: De filio, qui natus est ex semine David secundum carnem, et quem certo cognitum est, esse filium Dei omnipotentem.

Nam ὁρίζεσθαι significat, certissime definiri, sine ulla dubitatione comprehendi et cognosci: quam vocem utcunque reddit recentior versio: Qui declaratus est. Antiqua versio prorsus obscuravit: Qui praedestinatus est, et praebet occasionem alienis disputationibus.

Est igitur vera interpretatio: quem certissime cognitum est, esse filium Dei. Loquitur enim Paulus, non de praedestinatione in mente divina, sed de certissima manifestatione filii Dei in toto genere humano.

Convincimur enim, hunc Messiam esse omnipotentem, quia et resurrexit a mortuis, et resuscitavit mortuos etc. In potentia.

Iuniores diligenter considerent phrasin: Quia declaratus est, esse filius Dei in potentia, id est, potens. Opponitur autem haec particula priori. Natus ex semine David secundum carnem, id est, secundum naturam humanam, obnoxiam morti, sine peccato etc. Reliqua opponuntur deliriis Iudaeorum, qui expectabant Messiam potentem armis, victoriis, opulentia, imperiis mundi. At Paulus inquit, potentem esse secundum Spiritum sanctificantem, id est, quia dat Spiritum sanctum, et aufert peccatum et mortem, et reddit iusticiam et vitam aeternam. Haec autem omnia propria sunt divinae potentiae. Est igitur filius natura omnipotens. Sic ait cognitum esse per ipsius resurrectionem, et per omnia miracula, per resuscitationem mortuorum, et alia, et per donationem Spiritus sancti, qui de eo illustribus miraculis testificatus est.

Gratia et pax. Gratia usitate significat relative remissionem peccatorum gratuitam, et reconciliationem seu acceptationem gratuitam propter filium Dei, cum qua coniuncta est vivificatio per filium, et donatio Spiritus sancti. Pax Ebraico more prorsus usurpatur sicut apud nos salus. Significat autem ipsam donationem Spiritus sancti, et effectus multos, scilicet pacem conscientiae, fidem, spem, invocationem, auxilium divinum in gubernatione, et successus in vocatione, et in omnibus vitae partibus. A Deo patre nostro, et Domino Iesu Christo. Usitate coniungit patrem, et Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum. Primum, ut moneat, filium quoque natura Deum esse, a quo petenda et accipienda sint haec bona. Secundo, ut moneat, dari haec bona propter filium, iuxta illud: Quidquid petieritis patrem in nomine meo, faciam. Tertio, ut moneat, sic oportere agnosci Deum, ut sit directa mens et compellatio ad hunc verum Deum, qui se patefecit misso filio, iuxta illud: Nemo potest venire ad patrem, nisi per filium. Cogitemus autem inenarrabilem bonitatem Dei, qui cum essentia Dei sit invisibilis, semper aliquod testimonium suo verbo addidit, quo discerneretur verus Deus a commentitiis numinibus. Sed praecipuum testimonium est, quod filium misit, quem assumta humana natura, mente intueri nos oportet, et fide statuere, veram essentiam divinam conditricem coeli et terrae, et hominum et aliarum creaturarum, esse patrem huius Domini nostri Iesu Christi, et hunc filium Iesum Christum, et Spiritum sanctum, procedentem ab aeterno patre et filio. Et in invocatione patefactiones cogitandae sunt, qualis facta est in baptismo Christi.

Exordium.

Antequam instituit disputationem, usitato more in orationibus, exordium praeponit, cuius prima propositio est Gratulatio, sicut usitatissimum est, a gratulationibus et a precationibus ordiri. Et gratulationem sequitur alia vicina propositio, videlicet: Et ipse ad vos proficisci saepe constitui, ut vos docerem et confirmarem. Deinde sequitur adversativa: Sed cum impeditus etc. Quarto sequitur αἰτιολογία, sumta ex proprio officio. Quia debitor sum sapientibus et insipientibus. Quinto, Occupatio, qua occurrit tectae obiectioni: Etiamsi scio professionem Evangelii et despectam et invisam esse sapientibus mundi, tamen me non pudet huius doctrinae. Ibi addit asseverationem contrariam iudiciis mundi, et affirmat, sic colligi aeternam Ecclesiam Deo per ministerium Evangelii, et addit propositionem principalem Epistolae: Iustus fide sua vivet.

Cui servio in Spiritu meo. Discernit cultus Leviticos ab interiore cultu, et a praedicatione Evangelii et confessione, sicut et Christus inquit Ioan. 4.: Veri adoratores adorabunt patrem in Spiritu et Veritate, id est, motu cordis accenso per Spiritum sanctum, et in veritate, id est, vera agnitione Dei et fiducia filii, iuxta verbum a Deo traditum, sicut et alibi dicitur: Pater sanctifica eos in veritate, sermo tuus est veritas. Significat enim, non esse sanctificationem in aliis Sectis et opinionibus, sed oportere agnosci Evangelium, et teneri incorruptum. Nominat igitur et hic cultum Dei, docere, discere et confiteri Evangelium, sicut infra inquit: Sacrifico Evangelium. Haec dicta affirmant, Deo placere laborem docendi et discendi. Et quanquam magna sunt pericula docentium et discentium, tamen non abiiciamus haec studia, fracti terroribus, et statuamus, Deum nobis adfuturum esse, nec labores nostros irritos fore, et Deum servaturum esse aliquos coetus, ipsum invocantes, qui sint custodes doctrinae.

Huc pertinent multa testimonia. Psalm. 1.: Folia eius non defluent. Et Iohan. 16.: In hoc glorificatur pater meus, ut fructum copiosum feratis, et sitis mei discipuli.

Item Esaiae 51.: Posui verba mea in ore tuo, et manu mea protegam te, ut plantes coelos. Hae consolationes saepe cogitandae sunt, ne studia doctrinae abiiciamus.

Graecis et barbaris, sapientibus et insipientibus debitor sum.

Haec vox impiis et ignorantibus quid sit Evangelium, arrogantissima esse videtur, qui cogitabant magnam impudentiam esse, hunc errorem promittere sapientiam, quae fuerit ignota sapientissimis hominibus, qui ante multa secula Respublicas constituerunt.

Sed nos in Ecclesia scimus, promissionem de redemtione et restitutione generis humani, discernendam esse a sapientia politica et philosophica.

Ac nisi Deus ipse promissionem patefecisset, nulla eam creatura scire posset.

Primum autem ipsius Dei voce tradita est promissio, de filio, et saepe postea, cum vel oblivione deleta esset, vel erroribus obscurata, rursus immensa bonitate Dei novis revelationibus illustrata est per Patres, Prophetas, filium Dei, Apostolos, et pios doctores.

Et quidem vult Deus exaudiri eam a toto genere humano, et agnosci filium a toto genere humano, iuxta illud: Hunc audite.

Ideo Paulus hic omnes homines complectitur, ait se Omnibus concionari, sapientibus et insipientibus, quia non adfert politicam aut philosophicam sapientiam, sed promissionem prolatam ex arcano sinu Dei, quam vult Deus exaudiri a toto genere humano.

Utrique autem hic de officio suo cogitent, doctores et discipuli, utrique sunt debitores.

Doctores, ut doceant, Auditores vero, ut audiant et discant.

Huc pertinent plurima dicta, quae praecipiunt doctoribus, ut fideliter doceant, et tueantur puritatem doctrinae incorruptam, ut consulant firmis et infirmis etc.

Item, alia mandata, quae caeteris praecipiunt, ut audiant et discant Evangelium, iuxta illud: Hunc audite.

Item: Primum quaerite regnum Dei.

Item: Qui non audierit, ego ultor ero.

Item: Et nunc Reges intelligite, Osculamini filium, ne quando irascatur.

Item: Qui non diligit Dominum Iesum Christum, sit Anathema, Maran atha, id est, Dominus venit.

Non enim pudet me Evangelii.

Locus est attentionis, et respondet iudiciis hostium.

Et est αἰτιολογία sumta ex vera dignitate et efficacia Evangelii.

Ut autem haec brevis asseveratio: Non pudet me Evangelii, intelligatur, consideranda sunt iudicia, quorum acerbitas tunc magis conspicitur, quando motis controversiis voluntates hominum patefiunt.

Sapientes profani summum bonum esse ducunt, tranquillitatem politicam.

Hanc cum nolunt turbari ulla novitate, acerbissime oderunt novam doctrinam de Deo, tanquam facem seditionum et horribilium discordiarum, et tolli curant doctores et auditores, tanquam seditiosos et hostes patriae.

Deinde alii non profani, sed fascinati superstitione, ardent multo truculentioribus odiis, quia plures causas habere se existimant, ut dimicent, sicut ipsi loquuntur de gloria Dei, de unitate Ecclesiae, et de pace politica.

Accusant enim pios doctores in reprehensione vitiosorum cultuum, quod impediant, quo minus Deo debiti honores tribuantur.

Deinde quaeruntur, distrahi Ecclesiam, et turbari pacem.

Ac de lege Moisi difficilior disputatio tunc erat, quia summum scelus videbatur abolere cultus a Deo institutos.

Sicut et nunc multi summum scelus esse vociferantur, non facere oblationem in missa.

Ideo execrantur dissentientes tanquam haereticos, schismaticos et seditiosos, et existimant, Deo gratum officium esse, interficere nos, tanquam pestes generis humani, seu tanquam καθάρματα καὶ ἀλάστορας.

Adversuss haec acerbissima iudicia magno robore fidei inquit Paulus: Non pudet me Evangelii.

Sic Esaiae 51. dicitur: Non timete probra hominum.

Quantum autem sit onus, sustinere tam virulenta iudicia, et tantum odiorum acerbitatem, experientia ostendit, estque difficile ita confirmare animos, ne fracti talibus iudiciis, calumniis, odiis, terroribus, suppliciis, abiiciant Evangelii professionem.

Potentia enim Dei est ad salutem omni credenti.

Ex fontibus principalis doctrinae sumitur ratio, de dignitate et efficacia Evangelii, quasi dicat: Non est inanis fabula Evangelium, ut profani homines iudicant.

Imo etiam potentius est,... quam lex, quia est illa vox, per quam Deus vere est efficax in genere humano, colligit sibi aeternam Ecclesiam, vere tollit peccatum et mortem, dat Spiritum sanctum, reddit nobis iusticiam et vitam aeternam.

Haec summa bona nec per humanam sapientiam, nec per legem dantur, sed per hanc Evangelii vocem.

Meminerimus autem, in hoc dicto testimonium proponi, de efficacia ministerii Evangelii.

Cum oculi non cernant Deum, quaerit mens, quid sit, et ubi sit Deus, quem alloqui... et invocare vult, et quomodo sit discernendus verus Deus a commentitiis numinibus, quae sit voluntas eius, an et cur exaudiat. De his quaestionibus omnibus respondet hoc dictum: Evangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti, id est, Deus alligavit se ad vocem Evangelii, sic vult agnosci, hunc vere Deum esse, qui se patefecit misso filio, et tradidit promissionem in Evangelio propositam. Hac cogitatione vult discerni a commentitiis numinibus, vult agnosci voluntatem suam, cur velit exaudire, et cogitata promissione vult te credere et acquiescere, ac si videres et audires ipsum Deum te consolantem. Et cum sic credimus, vere Deus efficax est in nobis.

Haec est efficacia ministerii describitur in multis dictis. Rom. 1.: Evangelium est potentia Dei, id est, instrumentum, per quod Deus est efficax ad salutem in credentibus. Non est otiosa vox, aut inanis sonitus, sed instrumentum Dei, cum assentimur, et fide accipimus. Item, Romanos 10. dicitur: Fides ex auditu est. Et 2. Corinth. 3.: Evangelium est ministerium spiritus. Et Galatas 3.: Ut promissionem spiritus accipiamus per fidem. Matth. 10.: Qui vos audit, me audit. Eph. 4.: Ut perficiantur sancti, ad aedificationem corporis Christi. Rom. 15.: Ut per consolationem scripturarum spem habeamus. Haec dicta omnia testantur, Deum efficacem esse, cum Evangelium cogitamus, et ei assentimur. Nec enim ita intelligatur haec efficacia, ut si de calefactione loqueremur: Ignis est efficax in stramine, etiamsi stramen nihil agit. Sic Manichaei, Enthusiastae, Anabaptistae somniabant, fieri illuminationes in mente prorsus otiosa, et cogitabant, tunc demum se velle credere, cum prius sentirent in se illud novum lumen. Hae imaginationes explodendae sunt, et sciendum est, oportere nos audire Evangelium, cogitare, et assensu amplecti, et repugnare dubitationi. Hoc cum facimus, simul Spiritus sanctus est efficax in ipsa consolatione et in hac lucta. Haec in experientiae et quotidiana invocatione discenda sunt.

Omni credenti. Est et particula universalis consideranda, Omni credenti. Ac infra saepe de hac universali dicendum erit, ne turbetur fides hac humana imaginatione, quae Deo tribuit προσωποληψίαν: Deus alios quosdam recipit, Te non recipit. Huic imaginationi particularitatis opponendum est dictum universale, quod saepe repetit Paulus. Includamus igitur nos quoque in universalem promissionem, et pertinere eam ad nos quoque statuamus, ut Deo laudem veritatis tribuamus, et teneamus dicta universalia multa in promptu: Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis et onerati estis, et ego reficiam vos.

## 1:17
For the righteousness of God is revealed in it.

Previously, as in a place of attention, he made mention of the dignity and efficacy of the Gospel. Here he illustrates the same member, and specifically says how the Gospel is profitable for salvation, because it reveals the wonderful decree of God concerning the justification of man, that is, concerning liberation from sin, and the gift of righteousness and eternal life. And thus, at the end of the exordium, he recites the proposition of this Epistle, and (so to speak) the state of the whole case, which he will expound, and at the same time distinguishes the law and the Gospel, and the righteousness of the law from the righteousness of faith.

But so that the phrase may be rightly understood, the younger ones must be warned that the righteousness of God in this place, and often elsewhere, is said not to be that by which He Himself is just, as we say, The justice of a judge is to punish a thief, but that by which God pronounces us to be just, and which God gives to us through faith, when for the sake of His Son He receives us and pronounces us just, that is, absolved or liberated from sin, and received into grace, and sanctifies us by the Holy Spirit unto eternal life. Nor without a singular cause did he use the word "revealing," as if to say: In the Gospel, the secret decree of God is made manifest, namely, that He wishes in immense mercy, for the sake of His Son the intercessor, to receive freely, and to send the Son, that He might become a victim, and take away sin and death, and render righteousness and eternal life to All who truly believe that they are freely received for the sake of the Son. This decree no creature could perceive, but it was revealed and promulgated by the voice of God Himself, and it is a different voice than the voice of the law concerning righteousness. For the righteousness of the law is to do the law, or, as the Philosophers they say, universal justice is our obedience according to all laws.

This definition describes the justice of the law, which neither brings the remission of sins, nor removes sin or death. Therefore Paul says that another justice is proposed in the promises or the voice of the Gospel, just as he also says below: Now the justice of God has been manifested, without the law. This justice, that is, the free remission of sins on account of the Son, and acceptance before God, with which is joined the gift of the Holy Spirit and the inheritance of eternal life, is given not on account of the law or the justice of the law, etc.

From faith to faith. Let us be content with the common explanation: From imperfect faith to a more ardent and firmer one.

Because in invocation and daily dangers, a firmer assent is made, and we determine more that we are in God's care, that we are accepted, that we are heard and protected by God; we determine more firmly that God truly gathers to Himself an eternal Church by the voice of the Gospel, and that we are truly members of that eternal Church, and that God is present with us, even if we are pressed by horrible calamities. Others interpret it: From the faith of the fathers before the resurrection of Christ, into the faith of the saints after the resurrection, because the whole Church in all times, from Adam onwards, is justified and saved in the same way, namely by trust in the mediator, not on account of the fulfillment of the law.

And yet this distinction must be considered. They recognized the coming Messiah; we know that He has been exhibited. He adds to the proposition concerning the justice of faith a testimony from Habakkuk, which he also cites elsewhere, and clearly in Galatians, he opposes it to the justice of the law, saying: That no one is justified by the law is manifest, because the just lives by faith.

But the law is not of faith, but he who has done these things shall live in them, etc. In this antithesis, Paul says clearly that no one is justified by the law. Thus, therefore, he feels that the one who believes is just by faith, that is, that he is accepted by God and is made alive. And this very ἀντίθεσις (antithesis) in Paul refutes the calumnious interpretations devised against Paul's sentiment, such as this one: Namely, that the just man pleases God afterwards by works, when faith is added, that is, a profession of doctrine.

This corruption fights against Paul himself, because he prefaces that no one is justified by the law. But here it is necessary to establish what the word Faith signifies, about which it has been said often above and elsewhere. For it does not signify only knowledge or a profession of doctrine, but trust, by which we receive the promise and rest in the mercy of God, which is shown in the promise: and that faith is understood in this way in the very narrative of Habakkuk is manifest.

For he speaks of the expectation of the Messiah, and of liberation through the Messiah. This, therefore, is what he feels: The just man by faith, that is, by trust in the mercy promised on account of the Messiah, will not be oppressed by despair, will not fall into eternal destruction, but will be sustained by this true consolation, and the expectation will not fail him, but God will save the believer. Here again, certain crafty men stir up new tumults, crying that Paul twists foreign sayings to his own cause.

Posterity is promised to Abraham, they say: Just as victory to Gideon. What has this to do with the remission of sins, or with justice? It is necessary that pious minds be rightly instructed concerning this specious criticism. And first, let all the pious know that always in faith, although bodily benefits are sought, faith must shine forth, which receives the remission of sins, and reconciliation or the imputation of justice.

David cannot seek or expect victory until his mind thinks that God is angry, and trembling and fleeing, he does not dare to expect help. It is necessary, therefore, that trust in mercy precede, and indeed all bodily promises are given and are valid on account of the principal promise concerning the Messiah, because all good things are given on account of the mediator interceding for us. And the fathers universally referred all promises to that first and principal one.

They sought and expected all necessary things on account of the Messiah, on account of whom they knew themselves to be the people and Church of God. Thus, in the Lord's Prayer, the petitions for bodily and spiritual benefits are expressly joined. When we ask for bread, the conscience soon objects: Why do you ask, when you are unworthy?

Therefore, an express petition is added: Forgive us our debts, etc. Therefore, let this faith always shine forth, determining concerning the remission of sins, and let this necessary doctrine be exercised in daily invocation. God wills to be worshipped in this way by petition, hope, and expectation of spiritual and bodily goods, and indeed He wills that in the petition for bodily things, faith should simultaneously shine, which determines concerning the remission of sins.

The Prophets fought against the hypocrites concerning this worship. But although the external affairs of Abraham and Gideon, of David fighting, and of the woman in labor: yet faith is similar.

And the principal object of faith is always God, who in the promise revealed His will. Each approaches God, receiving reconciliation on account of the promised mediator. Then, indeed, he asks for and expects help in his bodily pain. Thus, in the Epistle to the Hebrews, many examples of faith are gathered, where, although the external affairs are dissimilar, faith nevertheless looks to the same principal promise, as has been said. Wherefore it is not to be imagined that Paul cites foreign sayings, as if David did not believe in reconciliation, but only in victory.

This admonition will be the more perspicuous if we think of it in daily invocation. Moreover, it is also true that the sayings which Paul cites speak specifically of the Messiah. Habakkuk clearly preaches of the coming liberator, and Abraham knew the promise previously given to the fathers, and hears these sayings, which signify reconciliation: I will bless thee. Item: I will be thy protector, namely on account of the mediator, of whom it was afterwards expressly said: In thy seed shall all nations be blessed.

The wrath of God is revealed against all ungodliness.

There is one and the same voice of the Gospel in all times, from the very first sermon made in Paradise, when the first parents were rebuked and received. The voice of the Gospel always rebukes sin, and afterwards adds consolation, namely the promise of gratuitous reconciliation on account of the mediator. Thus, in Paradise, the Son of God Himself preaches. Thus the Prophets, thus the Baptist, thus the Son of God cries out: Repent, and believe the Gospel. Thus the Lord commands the Apostles to teach: Preach repentance in my name, and the remission of sins.

And this consideration is profitable to those who are learning. For the doctrine becomes more perspicuous when we understand that the same voice always sounds in the Church from those who teach rightly.

As, therefore, in Paradise sin is first rebuked, and as Isaiah begins from a great and terrible exordium: Hear, O heaven, and earth, Woe to the sinful nation, they have forsaken the Lord, they have blasphemed the holy One of Israel. So here the narrative begins from a most sad condemnation: The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness. In the beginning, therefore, he rebukes sin, as is done in the preaching of repentance. Afterwards he adds consolation.

And because Paul institutes a disputation, he will deliver two principal propositions in this narrative, of which the former is this: God, in the ministry of the Gospel, in all times rebukes all men in this infirmity of nature, and affirms that all are under sin, that is, guilty of sin and eternal punishment, and that they cannot be freed from sin and from eternal wrath by their own justice or law.

He dwells on this proposition through two heads, which will be the more perspicuous to us if we propose to ourselves the doctrine of repentance or conversion, if we think of the wrath of God against our sins, if, having shaken off foul security, we truly tremble at the thought of judgment and the wrath of God, which He indeed declares by horrible punishments, wandering through the whole human race. He declares it also by the voice of the ministry, as the Lord also says: The Holy Spirit will rebuke the world of sin.

But the greatest part of men, secure and raging, indulges itself, having shaken off the fear of judgment and divine wrath: therefore these sad divine sermons fly past their ears, and although they are not obscure, yet they seem the colder because our hearts are not affected by a sense of the wrath of God. They can, however, without long narration, be properly and rightly understood by all the pious who know the exercises of repentance. I have said these things, therefore, so that the younger may consider why the narrative is thus begun with the preaching of repentance, and whither Paul tends.

For afterwards he adds the second proposition or consolation: We certainly receive the remission of sins and the gift of gratuitous reconciliation on account of the mediator, and we are reputed just, on account of the Son of God, freely, by faith. He will arrive at this second proposition in the third Chapter, which is the principal status of the disputation in this Epistle, as we shall say more copiously in its proper place.

Against all ungodliness, of those who hold the truth in unrighteousness.

That is, all men are rebuked in this corruption of nature. For although they know the law of God, yet they hold the knowledge captive in unrighteousness, that is, they do not obey it.

It is a brief saying, but it contains a most atrocious accusation, and paints two parts in man: True knowledge, which is wisdom, congruent with the wisdom of God, namely the knowledge of the law.

Then, indeed, he says that this very divine wisdom is oppressed by the horrible contumacy of human nature, that is, even if the knowledge of the law shines in the knowing part, divinely implanted, which affirm that God exists, that He is about to judge, and teaching what kind He is, namely wise, good, truthful, just, chaste: yet in hearts there is such an aversion from God, that they do not truly fear, do not truly love God, do not truly trust in Him, do not truly call upon Him: nay, they usually despise this judge with manifest furies.

In order that these things may become clearer, here the childish doctrine must be recalled, which distinguishes notions from appetites, and it must be seen what powers are the domiciles of the notion, whence these notions are, and what kind they are: and why they remain in human nature, where the contumacy of nature is.
