Let the juniors know, therefore, that the notion of the Law was divinely implanted in human minds at creation, just as the notion of numbers is implanted in us, and it is in the knowing part, with which the Will and Heart used to agree before the fall.

But this harmony was disturbed in the fall, and the Will and Heart no longer burn with the love of God.

And yet God willed that the notion should remain, so that a testimony about God might exist in nature, and that we might recognize sin, and that we might confess that we are justly punished by God.

Finally, also, that discipline might be governed by this notion.

Let it also be considered what a horrible misery human nature is: this disturbance of the most beautiful order, when now the will and heart, with God the ruler expelled, despise the creator, and as is said below, when now the sense of the flesh is enmity against God.

Nor can the magnitude of sin in the nature of man be described in sadder or more atrocious words, than by this very Pauline saying.

Here also the doctrine of the Church must be recalled, which distinguishes what kind of freedom of the will remains in man, and what kind has been lost.

For in order that discipline might be able to be governed, God willed this freedom to remain, so that the locomotive [faculty] might obey the command of the will.

But good actions toward God in the heart do not happen without conversion to the son of God, and without the help of the Holy Spirit.

This doctrine is handed down more copiously elsewhere, which, since it is necessary for this narration, must be repeated here by reflection.

For insofar as God can be known, God is known.

This is an exposition of the proposition recited before, by which all men are generally argued, because they hold the truth in injustice, that is, they do not obey the law of God.

He adds, therefore, what that Truth is, which he has thus named.

It is the notion, he says, of God, and the other notions, which are called Natural Laws, which all are a testimony about God, and teach what kind God is, and that He is about to judge.

But because he accuses both Gentiles and Jews, he makes mention of the law of nature, or the natural notion of God.

Where the juniors must be warned that we, indeed, in the Church, in order to confirm our assent, ought to look in order at all the histories in which God revealed Himself, such as the miracles done in the exodus from Egypt, the resurrections of the dead, and others, and in the reflection of these, simultaneously to embrace this, that this very one is truly God the creator, who revealed Himself there, and let us give thanks to God for these testimonies.

When we have considered these revelations, then it is also profitable to think about the natural notion, and to seek testimonies in nature, some of which are very illustrious, and convince human minds, so that they conclude that this world did not exist by chance, when they look at the most beautiful order of the bodies of the sky, and of the Elements.

Likewise the order in the notions of numbers, and in others, and especially in the distinction of honorable and base things: which could not be at all, if we had not sprung from such a nature, which itself understands this distinction.

Likewise, in the conservation of species.

Likewise, in political society, and in the regular punishments of atrocious crimes.

All these things collected confirm us about providence.

But it is to be lamented that there is such darkness of the human mind, that nevertheless the assent is very languid, and is easily shaken off.

Therefore God added other manifest revelations and miracles.

Let us join the reflection of these to these physical things.

Now I return to the words of the text.

This is the syntax: The invisible things of God, namely His eternal power and divinity, are seen from the workmanship of the world, perceived from the works, that is, from the order and art of the works.

But when he names divinity, he understands such an essence, namely eternal, the creator of things, omnipotent, wise, truthful, just, good, beneficent, chaste, free, distinguishing rightly done things and crimes, and punishing offenses.

He wants such an essence to be understood when he names divinity.

And let us remember in this place, that the natural notion of God is the notion of the law, and not the evangelical promise, concerning gratuitous remission on account of the son.

For this promise is by no means implanted in human minds at creation, but I. afterwards promulgated by a new and singular revelation, and it must be distinguished from the law, as has often been said.

However, mention is made here of the law of nature, concerning which, as we think upon it, let us embrace the whole, that is, let us know that it is said and is true that there is a God, and that He wishes to be worshipped by the observation of the distinction between honorable and base things. Here also let the younger students repeat the philosophical doctrine concerning principles, so that they may hold a clear definition of the law of nature.

The law of nature is the knowledge of practical principles and of the conclusions which are built up from them by necessary consequence, implanted in the minds of men by God, and congruent with the eternal norm of the divine mind, so that it shows both that there is a God, and what He is like, and that He commands the distinction between honorable and base things to be kept, and that He is about to judge and punish those who do not keep it.

But Paul added explicitly: God manifested it to them, that is, a twofold light has been implanted in human minds. A simple knowledge, that there is a God, and reasoning, which seeks testimonies in the order of created things.

That they may be without excuse.

Here it must be known for what causes God willed that a remnant of the knowledge of the law should remain in man, the first of which is that there might exist a testimony about God within us. The second, that it might accuse and condemn sins. The third, that it might govern discipline.

Afterwards, the reborn also have need of the knowledge of the Decalogue, so that they may know what worship is pleasing to God.

They did not glorify Him.

First, it accuses impiety.

And here all sins that fight against the first Table must be embraced, the catalog of which is to be taken from the narration of the Decalogue. And let us most diligently think upon the doctrine concerning the first table, how God wishes to be acknowledged and invoked: How ethnic invocation differs from true invocation. What is Fear, what is Faith, what is the trust that approaches God in invocation, what is Hope, what are true acts of worship, how they can be performed, and how they are pleasing.

It is necessary to embrace all these things, so that it may be understood what it is to glorify God.

For to glorify is to attribute glory to Him, that is, to acknowledge and confess that He is truly God, wise, truthful, good, just, chaste, free, omnipotent, the creator of the world, not idle, punishing the impious, and hearing and helping those who flee to the mediator. And when we think thus of God, it pertains to glorification to fear Him, to believe Him, to love Him, to invoke Him, and to obey Him in the acts of worship which He has commanded.

But let us each learn in the exercises of the fear of God, and of invocation, what this glorification is.

And these descriptions become clearer when the antithesis is considered.

The atheists (ἄθεοι) do not attribute glory to God. Nor do the worshippers of idols, who with audacity imagine a crowd of Gods. Nor those who invoke dead men. Nor those who imagine God to be something other than as He has manifested Himself, like the Mahometans and the impious Jews, and the heretics. Nor those who remain in perpetual doubt. Nor those who rush into crimes against their conscience in impious security. Nor those who invoke without the knowledge of the mediator, and without true faith. Nor those who devise acts of worship against the command of God. Nor those who despise or persecute the Gospel. Finally, as I said before, let the catalog be taken from the narration of the Decalogue.

Now think, in the whole human race, how horribly multiple furies rage against the first table.

Let us also acknowledge our own infirmities, because fear and faith, and other virtues, are much more languid than they ought to be, etc.

To give thanks is a part of glorification, namely to acknowledge that God is not idle, but truly cares for us, hears us, helps those who invoke Him rightly, and to celebrate this goodness, and to submit ourselves reverently to God and to love Him.

God gave them up.

I said that the first accusation was of sins which fight against the first Table.

Then follows the accusation of crimes against the second table.

Because when hearts are not governed by God, there follow also foul crimes against the second table, just as Paul signifies here, that blindness is the punishment of impiety: and Paul says expressly in Ephesians 2, that the Devil is effective in the impious. And it is said of Judas: Satan entered into him. Item: he who commits sin is of the devil. Item, Luke 11: They entered and dwell there.

These horrendous discourses show how great is the misery of man, who is without repentance, and without the invocation of God; here he rushes by his own infirmity into various external crimes, and is impelled by the devil, so that he moves many things pernicious to many.

So that although there was great genius, great wisdom and virtue in Saul, Pericles, Alcibiades, Cato, Julius, Brutus and other innumerable men: yet even so, manifestly They committed many crimes willingly, and, driven by devils, they approved of foul furies against God and against the actions of human life, and they set in motion affairs destructive to themselves and others. Saul was consumed by the glory of David. While he indulges in this emotion willingly and of his own accord, the devil approaches, who increases these flames, keeps Saul in poisonous thoughts, incites slanderers who bring tales to the king, and incites him, already burning with anger and hatred, to kill the priests. Let such examples be considered, and let them be compared with those sayings which I have recited, namely with this sad description of Judas: Satan entered into him.

Nor are there lacking examples in any times. Often a brother is killed by a brother. Often a mother kills the infant whom she has brought forth in recent birth. These foul events arise from the devil, who oppresses secure men, and those living without the invocation of God.

Let us therefore be terrified, and let us remember the saying of the Son of God: Pray, that you may not enter into temptation. Let us ask the Holy Spirit, for Christ's sake, to govern our minds, wills, and hearts, to kindle in us the true light concerning God, fear, faith, and other virtues, just as the Prophet cries out: Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within my bowels, etc. And let the promise be in our sight: How much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him. Likewise: No one shall snatch my sheep from my hands.

We have said, however, that the effective and properly so-called causes of evil actions are the will of the delinquents and of the devils, as was said concerning Saul. Therefore, it is necessary for the younger students to be warned about the phrase in this place: He delivered them into the desires of their hearts, that is, he permitted them to rush by their own will, or driven by the devil. For this meaning of permission is most common in the words of the Hebrews. As in the Lord's Prayer: Lead us not into temptation, that is, do not allow us to be oppressed by temptation. And in the one hundred and fourth Psalm: He changed their hearts, so that they hated his people, that is, he permitted them to be changed. For God was not the cause of the hatred in Pharaoh against the Israelites.

This simple and true grammatical interpretation removes the labyrinths of many questions. And the most true sentiment, which exists in Hosea, is to be held: From yourself is your destruction, in me alone is your help. God neither wills, nor approves, nor effects sin. This true sentiment must be most firmly retained.

Explanation of the following words.

It is a heap of words which signify sins, and Paul has gathered many, so that he might remind the reader what kind of furies rage in the human race. And this table is almost a mirror of the life of the impious. In some, however, other vices and crimes are more visible. Let the younger students know, however, that an excellent enumeration of virtues can be instituted according to the order of the precepts of the Decalogue. In the same way, the species of vices can be clearly distributed.

And it behooves the learned to know the distributions or species of virtues and vices, about which it has also been spoken in the Gentiles in its proper place. Ἀδικία, Injustice, signifies universal injustice, as we speak in philosophy, that is, disobedience violating all laws. As Catiline is ἄδικος, that is, he neither fears God, nor cares for human duties, he kills citizens, is incestuous, rapacious, seditious. Πορνεία, Fornication, and it embraces all contaminations fighting against the sixth commandment. Πονηρία, Depravity, and it signifies more than κακία. For κακία is also a general name for vice, and signifies sins of commission and omission, of negligence and petulance.

But πονηρία signifies the desire to do harm, and petulance. As Antony is κακὸς, a glutton, a drunkard, negligent. But Domitian is πονηρὸς, desirous of doing harm, to whom this very thing is a pleasure, to harm others even gratuitously. Πλεονεξία signifies avarice, and embraces all vices and crimes fighting against the seventh commandment: You shall not steal.

Now consider how various are the frauds, and how various are the unjust pursuits of gain in the whole human race, thefts, robberies, usury, swindling, mendacity, extortion, impostures, and other things of this kind. Κακοήθεια, malevolence, fights against the fifth and eighth commandments, that is, it is opposed to justice, Candor, and Truth. As, Tiberius is full of poison and malevolence, κακοήθης μὴ καθαρὸν. For Plutarch opposes these to each other.

A connected vice to malevolence is Detraction; this reveals malevolence, artfully depraving things rightly done, and certainly not done with a bad intention. As, Lentulus, Cato, and others barked at Scipio, who deserved very well of his country, out of mere malevolence. There exist verses of Menander, in which are described a certain class of men, by whom the powerful are especially corrupted: "Life is most pleased by the wicked, and the flatterer fares best of all, the slanderer second, the malicious man speaks third." He assigns the first place to the Flatterer. For he is the most pleasant. Next is the informer, or whisperer, who gains favor by carrying tales and constructing calumnies.

The third place is held by the malicious man, who knows how to allude to the Lord's affections, to interpret deeds done with good intent in a different way, and to kindle hatreds. "God-hated," whether taken actively or passively, signifies those who are openly insulting toward God, such as the atheists who are many in all times, who do not even hide their furies, just as Mezentius in Virgil, Sennacherib and Rabshakeh in the history of Isaiah.

Antiochus in the history of the Maccabees, and very many similar tyrants, who openly profess that they are enemies of God. He calls them "inventors of evils," meaning inventors of new crimes and new authors of evil examples, just as Lamech was the first to depart from the true institution of marriage and at the same time had several wives, and introduced this vicious custom into the world, against the order initially instituted by God.

Such are they, who in courts devise new pretexts for unjust plunder, or who invent causes for occupying the property of others. Likewise Merchants, who devise new frauds, change the just prices of currency, find new increments of usury, and new pretexts.

Finally, this evil is widespread; many new frauds and many tricks are devised to excuse crimes in many affairs of life. "Senseless," furious, who blind against the judgment of common sense rush headlong into all crimes, and by their own manifest madness bring destruction upon themselves, like Catiline, Thomas Müntzer, who ragingly stirred up sedition in Thuringia, and ordered the multitude, which had flocked together in a reckless gathering, to take up arms to destroy neighboring Princes and to plunder the wealth of the rich.

Likewise, the Scoundrel of Münster in Westphalia, who called himself the King of the temple of God. The Prophets often say that this madness is a punishment for impiety, as in Isaiah 19.

He has mingled among them a spirit of giddiness, namely, as if pouring it into a cup.

Thus Pharaoh, Saul, and countless others destroyed themselves and others with manifest fury.

And both are lacking in such men: A good conscience and moderate counsel.

"Faithless," not keeping pacts in honest promises, contracts, or treaties, and either failing without any excuse, or sophistically evading promises.

As the Thracians, having agreed to a thirty-day truce, would ravage the fields at night, because they had agreed to a truce of days, not of nights.

And examples of treachery are so frequent that the saying of Virgil is on everyone's lips: Faith is nowhere safe.

Likewise: "Avoid those you believe to be faithful, and you will be safe." And that saying of Epicharmus: "Be sober and remember to distrust; these are the joints of the mind." "Without natural affection," who cast off natural affections toward parents, offspring, brothers, or those who have deserved well.

For "natural affections" are good affections, because God so created hearts, especially in humans, that by a certain wonderful natural fire they love their kin as a part of their own nature.

Indeed, in a mother, breasts were added to the chest for these reasons: First, so that the milk might be better cooked by the heat of the heart. Then, so that from the heart also spirit and love might be transfused into the fetus, and mutual love might perpetually burn between parents and children. For in beasts, the memory of parents and offspring is extinguished.

And let students learn in this place that the error of the Stoics, who wish all affections to be removed from nature, must be fled and exploded. For the divine law clearly protests against it, which says: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart."

Likewise: "You shall love your neighbor as yourself."

And indeed, that there is true and ardent love in the eternal Father toward the Son, His own voice testifies when He says: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased."

And in God toward us humans there is true love, as it is written: "So God loved the world, etc." That there is a great fire of love toward us in the Son the mediator is most certain. And the "natural affections" of humans are impressed so that they may be reminders of the love of the eternal Father toward the Son and toward us.

God therefore wills that there be in us affections consistent with His law.

And there are some good affections in natures that are not monstrous, which, even if they have some contagion on account of the common depravity of nature, nevertheless God approves of them and wills them to be rightly governed.

He wills that a husband love his spouse, parents love their children, a brother his brother, the beneficiary his benefactor; He wills that humans be joined and associated among themselves by such bonds. For as it is wont to be said, "The Good is by its nature conservative, congregative, and communicative." to be preservative, congregative, and communicative; thus God is also truly a lover of the congregation and communication of benefits.

He wills that men be joined together by many bonds: by marriage, by love toward their children (as toward a part of their own nature), by the care of educating children, by the communication of benefits, and by the understanding of justice, which commands that benefits be returned in exchange for benefits. And by these bonds and this communication, He wills that nature be preserved. Thus, the reason is seen why the στοργαί [natural affections] are impressed upon men.

And all this wisdom concerning the goodness of God is comprehended in this sweetest saying: God is love, and he who abides in love, abides in God, and God in him.

And these sayings are near: God is good, and, God is love, that is, truly loving His own image, the intelligent nature. For this latter saying conforms more to intelligent natures. Now consider, since the στοργαὶ [natural affections] are truly the works of God, and reflect the goodness of God, and are things ordered in nature, what a dire depravation there is in the devils, who have cast away the στοργὰς [natural affections], and in many men, who, having extinguished this natural love and bond of association, wage war with God and with the nature of the human race.

Such is Cain, such are Atreus and Thyestes, such is Medea, who kills her own children. But since nature in man, not yet entirely furious, still feels natural inclinations in some part, there is no doubt that Cain and his like are impelled by devils, who, having extinguished natural benevolence, can exercise cruelty toward their kin and toward a part of their own nature. And of such also the saying is true: Satan entered into their hearts. Therefore, considering how dire and hideous these crimes are, and whence they arise, let us pray with great care to God the eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the φιλόστοργον [affectionate] creator of the human race, that for the sake of His Son, whom He loves with ardent benevolence, He may guard and rule our hearts by His Holy Spirit, and drive away from us the conspiring devils, His enemies.

Let us also wisely resist the very beginnings and sparks of such hatreds ourselves, lest the devil be invited. Many crimes of this kind are rampant among men, privately and publicly, some more, some less atrocious, just as Cain is more ἄστοργος [unaffectionate] than Esau.

There are also ἄστοργοι [unaffectionate] seditious men, who disturb the Church or the fatherland without necessary causes, because they are the causes of huge sorrows, and of the death of many good men, old men, matrons, and boys. And once public affairs are moved, peace, discipline, laws, and religion cannot easily be restored afterward. "Ασπονδοι [implacable] are those who cannot be appeased, just as Saul could not be appeased by any duty, so that he might lay aside the unjust hatred with which he burned against David, who had deserved well of the fatherland and of him. This stubbornness of hatred in livid and savage men is not rare. Ἀνελεήμονες [unmerciful], immisericordes: this appellation comprehends more than cruelty.

He is cruel who harms another atrociously, without just cause, or inflicts a greater punishment than is proportionate to the offense. As the host of Augustus was cruel, who wanted to throw his servant to the lampreys because he had broken a crystal cup. But he is unmerciful who is not only cruel, but also who, when there is a probable reason, does not mitigate a just severity. For it is justice to harm no one without cause. It is also justice to preserve equality in punishments: but mercy is primarily just, it does not harm the innocent. Then, by a probable reason, it also mitigates a just punishment. Thus God is merciful, and as the Psalm says: He does not kindle all His wrath. I have added this grammatical explanation of certain words, so that the younger students may become accustomed to diligence in considering the propriety of words and in distributing virtues and vices.

Let them look, however, as I have often said elsewhere, to the Decalogue. Those who know the law of God. Here he adds a rule concerning natural laws or natural notions, which are named the Law of nature.

For in order to convict men in this accusation, he proposes to them those natural notions. These, he says, accuse you, which indeed God did not want to be entirely extinguished in the nature of men, so that they might be testimonies concerning God and the judgment of God, and so that we might know for certain, being admonished by this voice of nature, that God is truly and horribly angry with all who act against these notions, divinely implanted in us. Let the younger students consider Paul's sermon. These notions, which we call Laws of nature or the law of nature, he expressly names here the Law of God. Let us know, therefore, what is most true, that the laws of nature are divine law: for it is a light founded by God in our minds, and it most truly conforms with the Decalogue and other sayings in the law of Moses, in which the law of nature has been repeated. For there are most grave causes, on account of which God, by an express voice, repeated this very law previously implanted in minds at creation, and added illustrious testimonies, and commanded it to be written.

For after the depravity of human nature, there is darkness in minds, and many doubts. And gradually evil examples increased the darkness. But I have often spoken elsewhere about these matters. And let the younger ones learn what the Law of nature truly is, and let them hold to the rule handed down by the ancients: The violation of the law of nature is a mortal sin, just as the violation of divine law.

That those who do such things are worthy of death. It is a truly wonderful statement that he says, that men naturally understand that all who violate the laws of nature are worthy of death.

But Paul is not speaking of political government, which only punishes external deeds: but rather of the judgment proper in each person's conscience, looking toward God. And he looks much deeper into the minds of men than even the Epicureans or hypocrites, who, secure and drunk on pleasures, have not experienced the true terrors of conscience.

Saul does not judge himself to be worthy of death when, against the command of Samuel, he spares the captive king. But then conscience recognizes that any sin is worthy of death when it looks toward God, and feels the wrath of God, and considers what a great evil the neglect of God is, or contumacy against God.

In this judgment, minds see that sin is not only a deformity dissenting from the harmony of nature, but something guilty and condemned before God, and that this guilty nature, on account of the contempt of God, is worthy of horrendous punishments and destruction. When Adam tasted the apple against the command, he thought that this deed was not of great moment.

He had not yet experienced these horrendous terrors of conscience which oppress this miserable nature with death. But afterwards, rebuked by God, he recognized that sin was the neglect or contempt of God, he felt that God was angry, he was terrified, and he would have been extinguished by the magnitude of the pain, had he not been recalled from death by a divine promise. The Law, says Paul, is the power of sin.

Thus the law of nature in the minds of men indicates and condemns sin. And in true terrors it shows that God is angry at all sins, external and internal. Paul speaks here of this judgment of one's own conscience, and condemns not only external offenses, but also the entire internal impurity, aversion from God, doubts about God, blind security, and contempt of God, and all depraved inclinations, and wandering desires.

Therefore he accuses not only those who do them, but also, as he names here, συνευδοκοῦντας [those who consent/take pleasure in], that is, those who see similar vices in their own nature, and do not abhor them, nor grieve, when they are tickled by these their own vices. But other affections erupt in others.

Atticus is not incestuous, he did not commit murder with his hands, but nevertheless he doubts whether God cares for human affairs, whether He punishes, whether He hears men; he rejoices that the fear of divine judgment is removed from him by academic disputations, he seeks his own tranquility without the recognition of God, and he himself feels that he has many impulses that wander from the law of nature. For Paul names here συνευδοκοῦντας, not as we say in the forum, those who consent, who manifestly aid or defend the crimes of others: but those who in their own nature are tickled by similar inclinations, even if they do not bring them forth.

For εὐδοκεῖν generally is to be of a benevolent mind toward something, as εὐδοκεῖ ξένῳ, that is, he is of a benevolent mind toward a guest, it is not with an alien will. εὐδοκεῖ λεγομένοις, he receives what is said. Atticus συνευδοκεῖ φιλοσόφοις καταγελῶσι τῶν πιστευόντων, εἶναι τιμωρίας τινὰς ἀνθρώπων μετὰ θάνατον [Atticus takes pleasure in philosophers who mock those who believe that there are certain punishments for men after death]. From such examples the meaning of the word can be sufficiently understood.

Latin:

Iustitia enim Dei revelatur in eo.

Antea, ut in loco attentionis, mentionem, fecit dignitatis et efficaciae Evangelii. Hic idem membrum illustrat, et nominatim dicit, quomodo prosit Evangelium ad salutem, quia patefacit mirandum decretum Dei iustificatione hominis, hoc est, de liberatione a peccato, et de donatione iustitiae et vitae aeternae. Atque ita in fine exordii recitat propositionem huius Epistolae, et (uti ita dicam) statum totius causae, quam exponet, et simul discernit legem et Evangelium, et iustitiam legis, a iustitia fidei.

Ut autem phrasis dextre intelligatur, monendi sunt iuniores, iustitiam Dei hoc loco, et saepe alias dici, non qua ipse istus est, ut dicimus, Iustitia iudicis puniri latronem, sed qua Deus nos pronunciat esse iustos, et quam Deus donat nobis per fidem, cum propter filium nos recipit, et pronunciat nos iustos, id est, absolutos seu liberatos a peccato, et receptos in gratiam, et sanctificat nos Spiritu sancto ad vitam aeternam. Nec sine singulari causa usus est verbo Revelandi, quasi dicat: In Evangelio arcanum decretum Dei patefit, quod videlicet velit genus humanum immensa misericordia propter filium deprecatorem gratis recipere, ac mittere filium, ut fiat victima, et tollere peccatum et mortem, ac reddere iustitiam et vitam aeternam Omnibus, qui vere credent, se propter filium gratis recipi. Hoc decretum nulla creatura cernere poterat, sed ipsius Dei voce patefactum et promulgatum est, et alia vox est, quam vox legis de iustitia. Nam iustitia legis est, facere legem, seu, ut Philosophi dicunt, iusticia universalis est obedientia nostra iuxta omnes leges.

Haec definitio describit legis iusticiam, quae neque adfert remissionem peccatorum, neque tollit peccatum aut mortem. Ideo Paulus dicit, aliam iusticiam in promissionibus seu voce Evangelii proponi, sicut et infra inquit: Nunc iusticia Dei manifestata est, sine lege. Haec iusticia, id est, remissio peccatorum propter filium gratuita, et acceptatio coram Deo, cum qua conjuncta est donatio Spiritus sancti et haereditas vitae aeternae, datur non propter legem aut legis iusticiam etc.

Ex fide in fidem. Simus contenti vulgari enarratione: Fide imperfecta in ardentiorem et firmiorem.

Quia in invocatione et quotidianis periculis fiat assensio firmior, et magis statuamus, nos Deo curae esse, nos receptos esse, nos exaudiri et protegi a Deo, statuamus firmius Deum vere sibi colligere aeternam Ecclesiam voce Evangelii, et nos vere membra esse illius aeternae Ecclesiae, et nobis adesse Deum, etiamsi horribilibus aerumnis premimur. Alii interpretantur: Ex fide patrum ante resurrectionem Christi, in fidem sanctorum post resurrectionem, quia tota Ecclesia omnibus temporibus, inde usque ab Adam, eodem modo iustificatur et salvatur, scilicet fiducia mediatoris, non propter impletionem legis.

Et tamen hoc discrimen considerandum est. Illi venturum Messiam agnoscebant, nos exhibitum esse scimus. Addit propositioni de iusticia fidei testimonium ex Abacuc, quod et alibi citat, ac perspicue in Galatis, opponit iusticiae legis, inquiens: Quod autem lege nemo iustificetur, manifestum est, quia iustus fide vivit.

Lex autem non est ex fide, sed qui fecerit ea, vivet in eis etc. In hanc antithesi Paulus diserte inquit, neminem lege iustificari. Sic igitur sentit, credentem fide iustum, id est, acceptum Deo esse, et vivificari. Et haec ipsa ἀντίθεσις in Paulo refutat calumniosas interpretationes, excogitatas contra Pauli sententiam, qualis haec est: Iustus scilicet operibus postea placet, cum accedit fides, id est, professio doctrinae.

Haec corruptela pugnat cum ipso Paulo, quia praefatur, nemo lege iustificatur. Sed hic necesse est constitui, quid significet vocabulum Fides, de quo supra et alibi saepe dictum est. Non enim tantum noticiam, seu professionem doctrinae significat, sed fiduciam, qua promissionem accipimus et acquiescimus in misericordia Dei, quae in promissione ostensa est: et sic intelligi fidem in ipsa narratione Abacuc manifestum est.

Loquitur enim de expectatione Messiae, et liberationis per Messiam. Hoc igitur sentit: Iustus fide, id est, fiducia misericordiae propter Messiam promissae, non opprimetur desperatione, non ruet in aeternum exitium, sed sustentabitur hac vera consolatione, nec fallet eum expectatio, sed Deus credentem servabit. Hic rursus astuti quidam novos tumultus excitant, clamant Paulum aliena dicta ad suam causam detorquere.

Abrahae promittitur posteritas, inquiunt: Sicut Gedeoni victoria. Quid haec ad remissionem peccatorum, seu ad iusticiam? De hac speciosa reprehensione necesse est pias mentes recte erudiri. Ac primum sciant omnes pii, semper in fide, quanquam corporalia beneficia petuntur, oportere praelucere fidem, quae accipit remissionem peccatorum, et reconciliationem seu imputationem iusticiae.

David non potest petere vel expectare victoriam, donec mens existimat irasci Deum, et trepida ac fugitans non audet expectare auxilium. Necesse est igitur praecedere fiduciam misericordiae, et quidem promissiones corporales omnes propter principale promissionem de Messia et datae sunt et valent, quia propter mediatorem intercedentem pro nobis dantur omnia bona. Ac patres universaliter omnes promissiones ad primam illam et praecipuam referebant.

Petebant et expectabant necessaria omnia propter Messiam, propter quem et populum et Ecclesiam Dei se esse sciebant. Ita in precatione Dominica expresse copulatae sunt petitiones corporalium et spiritualium beneficiorum. Cum petimus panem, mox conscientia obstrepit: Cur petis, cum sis indignus?

Addita est igitur ex pressa petitio: Remitte nobis debita nostra etc. Semper igitur praeluceat haec fides, statuens de remissione peccatorum, et in quotidiana invocatione haec necessaria doctrina exerceatur. Vult Deus sic coli petitione, spe et expectatione spiritualium et corporalium bonorum, et quidem vult in petitione corporalium simul lucere fidem, quae statuit de remissione peccatorum.

De hoc cultu pugnabant Prophetae cum hypocritis. Etsi autem differunt negotia externa Abrahae et Gedeonis, Davidis praeliantis, et mulieris parturientis: tamen fides similis est.

Et principale obiectum fidei semper est Deus, qui in promissione patefecit voluntatem suam. Uterque accedit ad Deum accipiens reconciliationem propter promissum mediatorem. Deinde vero petit et expectat auxilium in suo corporali dolore. Sic in Epistola ad Ebraeos multa exempla de fide coacervantur, ubi etsi dissimilia sunt externa negotia, fides tamen eandem principalem promissionem, ut dictum est, intuetur. Quare non imaginandum est, Paulum aliena dicta citare, quasi David non credideret de reconciliatione, sed tantum de victoria.

Haec admonitio necessaria magis perspicua erit, si eam cogitabimus in quotidiana invocatione. Caeterum et hoc verum est, dicta quae citat Paulus, nominatim de Messia loqui. Abacuc manifeste concionatur de venturo liberatore, et Abraham norat promissionem antea datam patribus, et audit haec dicta, quae reconciliationem significant: Benedicam tibi. Item: Ero protector tuus, scilicet propter mediatorem, de quo postea expresse dictum est: In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes.

Revelatur ira Dei super omnem impietatem.

Una et eadem vox est Evangelii omnibus temporibus, inde usque a prima concione in Paradiso facta, cum arguerentur et reciperentur primi parentes. Semper vox Evangelii arguit peccatum, et postea addit consolationem, videlicet promissionem reconciliationis gratuitae propter mediatorem. Sic in Paradiso ipse filius Dei concionatur. Sic Prophetae, sic Baptista, sic filius Dei clamitat: Agite poenitentiam, et credite Evangelio. Sic Apostolis Dominus praecipit docere: Praedicate poenitentiam in nomine meo, et remissionem peccatorum.

Ac discentibus prodest haec consideratio. Magis enim fit perspicua doctrina, cum intelligimus, semper eandem vocem recte docentes in Ecclesia sonare.

Ut igitur in Paradiso primum arguitur peccatum, et ut Esaias orditur a grandi et terribili exordio: Audite coelum et terra, Vae genti peccatrici, dereliquerunt Dominum, blasphemarunt sanctum Israël. Ita hic narratio incoatur a tristissima condemnatione: Revelatur ira Dei de coelo super omnem impietatem. Initio igitur arguit peccatum, ut fit in praedicatione poenitentiae. Postea addit consolationem.

Et quia Paulus disputationem instituit, tradet duas propositiones in hac narratione praecipuas, quarum prior haec est: Deus in ministerio Evangelii omnibus temporibus arguit omnes homines, in hac naturae infirmitate, et affirmat omnes sub peccato esse, id est, reos peccati et aeternae poenae, nec posse liberari a peccato, et ab aeterna ira per propriam iusticiam seu legem.

In hac propositione commoratur per duo capita, quae nobis ita magis perspicua erit, si nobis ipsis doctrinam de poenitentia seu conversione proponemus, si iram Dei adversus nostra peccata cogitabimus, si excussa tetra securitate vere expavescemus cogitatione iudicii et irae Dei, quam quidem declarat horribilibus poenis, vagantibus per totum genus humanum. Declarat et voce ministerii, ut et Dominus inquit: Spiritus sanctus arguet mundum de peccato.

Sed maxima pars hominum secura et furens indulget sibi, excusso metu iudicii et irae divinae: ideo hae tristes conciones divinae praetervolant aures, et quanquam non sunt obscurae, tamen eo videntur frigidiores, quia pectora nostra non adficiuntur sensu irae Dei. Possunt autem sine longa enarratione proprie et recte intelligi ab omnibus piis, qui norunt exercitia poenitentiae. Haec ideo dixi, ut iuniores considerent, quare sic incoata sit narratio a praedicatione poenitentiae, et quo tendat Paulus.

Postea enim addit alteram propositionem seu consolationem: Certo accipimus remissionem peccatorum et reconciliationis gratuitae propter mediatorem, et reputamur iusti, propter filium Dei, gratis, fide. Ad hanc secundam propositionem in tertio Capite perveniet, quae principalis status est disputationis in hac Epistola, ut suo loco copiosius dicemus.

Super omnem impietatem, veritatem in iniusticia detinentium.

Id est, omnes homines arguuntur in hac corruptione naturae. Etsi enim norunt legem Dei, tamen noticiam in iniusticia captivam detinent, id est, non obtemperant ei.

Breve dictum est, sed atrocissimam accusationem continet, et duas partes in homine pingit: Noticias veras, quae sunt sapientia, congruens cum sapientia Dei, videlicet legis noticia.

Deinde vero hanc ipsam divinam sapientiam inquit oppressam esse horribili contumacia naturae humanae, id est, etiamsi lucent in parte cognoscente noticiae legis, quidem divinitus insitae, quae affirmant, quod sit Deus, quod sit iudicaturus, et docens qualis sit, videlicet sapiens, bonus, verax, iustus, castus: tamen in cordibus talis est aversio a Deo, ut non vere timeant, non vere diligant Deum non vere confidant ei, non vere invocent: imo plerumque manifestis furoribus hunc iudicem contemnant.

Haec ut fiant planiora, hic recordanda est puerilis doctrina, quae discernit noticias ab appetitionibus, et videndum, quae potentiae sint domicilia noticiae, unde sint hae noticiae, et quales: et cur in natura humana reliquae sint, ubi sit contumacia naturae.

Sciant igitur iuniores, Legis noticiam divinitus insitam esse mentibus humanis in creatione, sicut numerorum noticia nobis insita est, estque in parte cognoscente, cum qua ante lapsum congruebat Voluntas et Cor.

Sed haec harmonia in lapsu turbata est, nec iam ardent Voluntas et Cor dilectione Dei.

Et tamen voluit Deus reliquam esse noticiam, ut extet in natura testimonium de Deo, et ut agnoscamus peccatum, et ut fateamur, nos iuste a Deo puniri.

Postremo etiam, ut hac noticia regatur disciplina.

Cogitetur etiam, quam horribilis miseria sit naturae humanae: haec turbatio pulcerrimi ordinis, cum iam voluntas et cor expulso Deo rectore, contemnunt conditorem, et ut infra dicitur, cum iam sensus carnis inimicitia sit adversus Deum.

Nec potest tristioribus aut atrocioribus verbis magnitudo peccati in natura hominis describi, iam hoc ipso Paulino dicto.

Hic etiam recordanda est doctrina Ecclesiae, quae discernit, qualis libertas voluntatis in homine reliqua sit, qualis amissa sit.

Ut enim disciplina regi possit, Deus hanc libertatem voluit reliquam esse, ut locomotiva obtemperet imperio voluntatis.

Sed actiones bonae erga Deum in corde, non fiunt sine conversione ad filium Dei, et sine auxilio Spiritus sancti.

Haec doctrina alibi copiosius traditur, quae cum ad hanc enarrationem necessaria sit, hic cogitatione repetenda est.

Quatenus enim Deus cognosci potest, notus est Deus.

Expositio est propositionis antea recitatae, qua generaliter arguuntur omnes homines, quod veritatem in iniusticia detineant, id est, non obtemperent legi Dei.

Addit igitur, quae sit illa Veritas, quam sic nominavit.

Est noticia, inquit, de Deo, et ceterae noticiae, quae vocantur Leges Naturales, quae omnes sunt testimonium de Deo, et docent, quales sit Deus, et quod iudicaturus sit.

Quia autem et Gentes et Iudaeos accusat, facit mentionem legis naturae, seu noticiae naturalis de Deo.

Ubi iuniores monendi sunt, nos quidem in Ecclesia, ut confirmemus assensionem nostram, intueri debere ordine omnes historias, in quibus se patefecit Deus, ut miracula facta in exitu ex Aegypto, resuscitationes mortuorum, et alia, et in horum cogitatione simul hoc complecti, hunc ipsum vere Deum esse conditorem, qui se ibi patefecit, et Deo pro his testimoniis gratias agamus.

Has patefactiones cum consideravimus, deinde prodest etiam cogitare de noticia naturali, et quaerere testimonia in natura, quorum aliqua valde illustria sunt, et convincunt humanas mentes, ut statuant, hunc mundum non extitisse casu, cum intuentur pulcerrimum ordinem corporum coeli, et Elementorum.

Item ordinem in noticiis numerorum, et aliis, ac praesertim in discrimine honestorum et turpium: quod nullum esse posset, si non a tali natura orti essemus, quae ipsa intelligat hoc discrimen.

Item, in conservatione specierum.

Item, in politica societate, et regularibus poenis atrocium delictorum.

Haec omnia collecta confirmant nos de providentia.

Sed dolendum est, tantam caliginem esse mentis humanae, ut tamen assensio valde languida sit, et facile excutiatur.

Ideo Deus addidit alias manifestas patefactiones et miracula.

Horum cogitationem adiungamus ad haec physica.

Nunc ad verba textus redeo.

Syntaxin haec est: Invisibilia Dei, videlicet aeterna potentia, et divinitas eius, conspiciuntur ab opificio mundi, animadversa ex operibus, id est, ex ordine et arte operum.

Cum autem nominat divinitatem, intelligit talem essentiam, videlicet aeternam, conditricem rerum, omnipotentem, sapientem, veracem, iustam, bonam, beneficam, castam, liberam, discernentem recte facta et scelera, et punientem delicta.

Talem essentiam vult intelligi, cum nominat divinitatem.

Ac meminerimus hoc loco, noticiam naturalem de Deo esse legis noticiam, et non promissionem evangelicam, de gratuita remissione propter filium.

Nam haec promissio nequaquam insita est in creatione mentibus humanis, sed I. postea nova et singulari patefactione promulgata est, et a lege discernenda est, ut saepe dictum est.

Fit autem hic mentio legis naturae, de qua cogitantes totam complectamur, id est, sciamus simul dici et esse Deum, et quod coli velit observatione discriminis honestorum et turpium. Hic etiam repetant iuniores doctrinam philosophicam de principiis, ut perspicuam definitionem legis naturae teneant.

Lex naturae et noticia principiorum practicorum et conclusionum, quae inde necessaria consequentia extruuntur, insita mentibus hominum a Deo, et congruens cum aeterna norma mentis divinae, ut ostendat, et esse Deum, et qualis sit, et quod praecipiat servari discrimen honestorum et turpium, et quod iudicaturus sit, ac puniturus eos qui non servant.

Addidit autem Paulus diserte: Deus eis manifestavit, id est, duplex lumen inditum est humanis mentibus. Noticia simplex, quod sit Deus, et ratiocinatio, quaerens testimonia in ordine creaturarum.

Ut sint inexcusabiles.

Hic sciendum est, propter quas causas Deus in homine voluerit reliquam esse legis noticiam, quarum prima est, ut extet testimonium de Deo in nobis. Secunda, ut accuset et damnet peccata. Tertia, ut regat disciplinam.

Postea renatis etiam opus est cognitione Decalogi, ut sciant, qui cultus Deo placeant.

Non glorificaverunt.

Primum accusat impietatem.

Et complectendas sunt hic omnia peccata pugnantia cum prima Tabula, quorum catalogus sumatur ex enarratione Decalogi. Et diligentissime cogitemus doctrinam de prima tabula, quomodo velit agnosci et invocari Deus: Quid differat invocatio ethnica ab invocatione vera. Quid sit Timor, quid Fides, quid fiducia accedens ad Deum in invocatione, quid Spes, qui sint veri cultus, quomodo fieri possint, et quomodo placeant.

Haec omnia necesse est complecti, ut intelligatur, quid sit glorificare Deum.

Est enim glorificare, tribuere ei gloriam, id est, agnoscere et fateri, quod vere sit Deus, sapiens, verax, bonus, iustus, castus, liber, omnipotens, conditor mundi, non otiosus, puniens impios, et exaudiens ac iuvans eos, qui ad mediatorem confugiunt. Et cum sic de Deo sentimus, ad glorificationem pertinet, timere eum, credere ei, diligere eum, invocare eum, et obedire ei in cultibus, quos praecepit.

Discamus autem singuli in exercitiis timoris Dei, et invocationis, quid sit haec glorificatio.

Ac fiunt hae descriptiones illustriores considerata antithesi.

Non tribuunt Deo gloriam ἄθεοι. Nec cultores idolorum, qui fingunt horribilia audacia turbam Deorum. Nec qui invocant homines mortuos. Nec qui aliud fingunt esse Deum, quam sicut se patefecit, ut Mahometistae et Iudaei impii, et haeretici. Nec qui manent in perpetua dubitatione. Nec qui impia securitate ruunt in scelera contra conscientiam. Nec qui invocant sine agnitione mediatoris, et sine vera fide. Nec qui excogitant cultus contra mandatum Dei. Nec qui contemnunt aut persequuntur Evangelium. Denique ut ante dixi, catalogus sumatur ex enarratione Decalogi.

Iam cogita, in toto genere humano, quam horribiliter grassentur multiplices furores contra primam tabulam.

Agnoscamus et infirmitates nostras, quia timor et fides, et aliae virtutes, multo sunt languidiores, quam esse debent etc.

Gratias agere est pars glorificationis, videlicet agnoscere, quod non sit otiosus Deus, sed vere nos curet, exaudiat, iuvet recte invocantes, et hanc bonitatem celebrare, et nos Deo reverenter subiicere et eum diligere.

Tradidit eos Deus.

Dixi primam accusationem fuisse peccatorum, quae pugnant cum prima Tabula.

Deinde sequitur accusatio scelerum contra secundam tabulam.

Quia quando corda non reguntur a Deo, sequuntur etiam tetra delicta contra secundam tabulam, sicut hic Paulus significat, coecitatem poenam esse impietatis: et expresse inquit Paulus ad Ephesios secundo, Diabolum efficacem esse in impiis. Et de Iuda dicitur: Intravit in eum Satanas. Item: qui facit peccatum, ex diabolo est. Item, Lucae 11.: Ingressi habitant ibi.

Hae horrendae conciones ostendunt, quanta sit miseria hominis, qui est sine poenitentia, et sine invocatione Dei, hic et sua infirmitate ruit in varia delicta externa, et a diabolo impellitur, ut multa moveat perniciosa multis.

Ut quanquam fuit magnum ingenium, magna sapientia et virtus in Saule, Pericle, Alcibiade, Catone, Iulio, Bruto et aliis innumerabilibus: tamen et manifeste sta scelera multa volentes perpetrarunt, et impulsi a diabolis tetros furores de Deo, et de actionibus vitae humanae adprobaverunt, et moverunt negotia, exitiosas sibi et aliis. Saul urebatur gloria Davidis. Huic adfectui dum indulget volens et sua sponte, accedit diabolus, qui has flammas auget, retinet Saulem in cogitationibus venenatis, incitat calumniatores, qui fabellas ad regem adferunt, ardentem iam ira et odio incitat, ut interficiat sacerdotes. Talia exempla considerentur, et cum illis dictis, quae recitavi, conferantur, videlicet cum hac tristi descriptione Iudae: Satanas intravit in eum.

Nec desunt exempla ullis temporibus. Saepe frater a fratre interficitur. Saepe mater necat infantem, quem recenti partu edidit. Hi tetri eventus a diabolo oriuntur, qui securos homines, et sine invocatione Dei viventes, opprimit.

Expavescamus igitur, et dictum filii Dei meminerimus: Orate, ne intretis in tentationem. Petamus a Spiritu sancto propter Christum gubernari mentes, voluntates et corda nostra, accendi in nobis veram de Deo lucem, timorem, fidem, et alias virtutes, sicut clamat Propheta: Cor mundum crea in me Deus, et spiritum rectum innova in visceribus meis etc. Et sit in conspectu promissio: Quanto magis pater vester coelestis dabit Spiritum sanctum petentibus. Item: Nemo rapiet oves meas ex manibus meis.

Diximus autem, causas malarum actionum efficaces et proprie dictas, esse voluntatem delinquentium et diabolorum, ut de Saule dictum est. Ideo de phrasi hoc loco moneri iuniores necesse est: Tradidit eos in desideria cordium, id est, permisit eos ruere sua voluntate, aut impulsos a diabolo. Nam haec significatio permissionis usitatissima est in verbis Ebraeorum. Ut in precatione Dominica: Ne inducas nos in tentationem, id est, non sinas nos opprimi tentatione. Et in Psalmo centesimo quarto: Mutavit corda eorum, ut odissent populum eius, id est, mutari permisit. Deus enim non fuit causa odii in Pharaone adversus Israëlitas.

Haec simplex et vera grammatica interpretatio labyrinthos multarum quaestionum tollit. Estque tenenda verissima sententia, quae extat apud Hoseam: Ex te perditio tua, Tantum in me auxilium tuum. Nec vult, nec adprobat, nec efficit peccatum Deus. Haec vera sententia firmissime retinenda est.

Enarratio vocabulorum sequentium.

Acervus est vocabulorum, quae significant peccata, et multa congessit Paulus, ut lectorem commonefaciat, quales furores in genere humano grassentur. Et haec tabella fere speculum est vitae impiorum. In aliis autem alia vitiae et scelera magis conspiciuntur. Sciant autem iuniores, optimam enumerationem virtutum iuxta ordinem praeceptorum Decalogi institui posse. Ad eundem modum perspicue distribui possunt species vitiorum.

Et eruditos decet nosse distributiones seu species virtutum ac vitiorum, de quibus et in Ethnicis suo loco dictum est. Ἀδικία, Iniusticia, significat universalem iniusticiam, ut in philosophia loquimur, id est, inobedientiam violantem omnes leges. Ut Catilina est ἄδικος, id est, nec Deum metuit, nec curat humana officia, interficit cives, est incestus, rapax, seditiosus. Πορνεία, Scortatio, et complectitur omnes contaminationes pugnantes cum sexto praecepto. Πονηρία, Pravitas, et significat plus, quam κακία. Nam κακία etiam generale nomen est vitii, et significat peccata commissionis et omissionis, negligentiae et petulantiae.

At πονηρία significat cupiditatem nocendi, et petulantiam. Ut Antonius est κακὸς, helluo, ebriosus, negligens. At Domitianus est πονηρὸς, cupidus nocendi, cui hoc ipsum voluptati est, aliis etiam gratis nocere. Πλεονεξία significat avariciam, et complectitur omnia vitia et scelera pugnantia cum praecepto septimo: Non furtum facies.

Iam cogita, quam variae fraudes, et varia sint iniusta aucupia lucri in toto genere humano, furta, rapinae usurae, stellionatus, mendicitas, concussionis, imposturae, et huiusmodi alia. Κακοήθεια, malevolentia, pugnat cum praecepto quinto et octavo, id est, opposita est iusticiae, Candori et Veritati. Ut, Tiberius est plenus veneni et malevolentiae, κακοήθης μὴ καθαρὸν. Haec enim inter se Plutarchus opponit.

Coniunctum vitium est malevolentiae Obtrectatio, haec patefacit malevolentiam, arte depravans recte facta, et certe non malo studio facta. Ut, Scipionem optime meritum de patria allatrabant Lentulus, Cato et alii, sola malevolentia. Extant versiculi Menandri, in quibus describuntur gradus quidam hominum, quibus praecipue delibantur potentes: ὁ βίος μάλιστα τοῖς πονηροῖς ἥδεται, πράττει δ᾽ ὁ κόλαξ ἄριστα πάντων, δεύτερα ὁ συκοφάντης, ὁ κακοήθης τρίτα λέγει. Primum locum tribuit Adsentatori. Nam hic dulcissimus est. Proximus est delator, seu susurro, qui init gratiam perferendis fabellis, ac instruendis calumniis.

Tertium locum habet κακοήθης, qui novit alludere ad Domini adfectus, bono studio facta secus interpretari, odia incendere. Θεοστυγεῖς sive active sive passive accipitur, significat palam contumeliosos adversus Deum, quales sunt ἄθεοι omnibus temporibus multi, qui ne quidem dissimulant suos furores, sicut Mezentius apud Virgilium, Sennacherib et Rapsaces in historia Esaiae.

Antiochus in historia Maccabaeorum, et similes tyranni plurimi, qui aperte profitentur, se esse hostes Dei. Ἐφευρετὰς κακῶν nominat inventores novorum scelerum, et novos autores malorum exemplorum, ut Lamech primus discessit a vera coniugii institutione, et simul plures uxores habuit, et hunc vitiosum morem in mundum invexit, contra ordinem initio a Deo institutum.

Tales sunt, qui in aulis excogitant novos praetextus iniustarum expilationum, aut qui fingunt causas occupandi aliena. Item Mercatores, qui novas imposturas excogitant, mutant iusta pretia monetae, inveniunt nova usurarum incrementa, et novos praetextus.

Denique late patet hoc malum, multae novae fraudes, et multae praestigiae excogitantur ad excusanda scelera in multis vitae negotiis. Ἀσύνετοι, furiosi, qui coeci contra iudicium communis sensus ruunt praecipites in omnia scelera, et sibi ipsis manifesta amentia accersunt exitium, ut Catilina, Thomas Monetarius, qui furens movit seditionem in Turingia, et multitudinem, quae temerario concursu confluxerat, arma capere iussit ad delendos vicinos Principes, ad diripiendas locupletum facultates.

Item, Nebulo Monasteriensis in Westvalia, qui se nominabat Regem templi Dei. Hanc amentiam saepe dicunt Prophetae poenam esse impietatis, ut Esaiae 19.

Miscuit inter eos spiritum vertiginis, videlicet, tanquam infundens in poculum.

Sic Pharao, Saul et alii innumerabiles manifesto furore se et alios perdiderunt.

Ac utrunque talibus deest: Bona conscientia, et moderatum consilium.

Ἀσύνθετοι non servantes pacta in promissionibus honestis, contractibus aut foederibus, et aut sine ulla excusatione fallentes, aut sophistice eludentes promissa.

Ut Thraces pacti triginta dierum indutias noctu populabantur agros, quia dierum non noctium indutias pacti essent.

Ac adeo crebra sunt perfidiae exempla, ut dictum Virgilii omnibus in ore sit: Nusquam tuta fides.

Item: Quos credis fidos, effuge, tutus eris. Et illud Epicharmi: νῆφε καὶ μέμνησο ἀπιστεῖν, ἄρθρα ταῦτα φρενῶν. Ἄστοργοι, qui naturales adfectus erga parentes, sobolem, fratres, aut bene meritos exuunt.

Nam στοργαὶ sunt boni adfectus, quia Deus ita condidit corda, praesertim in hominibus, ut mirabili quodam naturali incendio ament cognatos tanquam suae naturae partem.

Imo in matre ubera pectori addita sunt, propter has causas: Primum, ut lac melius coquatur calore cordis. Deinde, ut a corde etiam spiritus et amor transfundatur in foetum, et mutuus amor perpetuo flagret inter parentes et natos. Nam in bestiis extinguitur memoria parentum et sobolis.

Ac discant in hoc loco studiosi, fugiendum et explodendum esse Stoicorum errorem, qui omnes adfectus tolli volunt ex natura. Manifeste enim reclamat lex divina, quae dicit: Diligas Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde.

Item: Diligas proximum, sicut te ipsum.

Et quidem in aeterno patre verum et ardentem amorem esse erga filium, ipsius vox testatur, cum inquit: Hic est filius meus dilectus, quo delector.

Et in Deo erga nos homines verus amor est, ut scriptum est: Sic Deus dilexit mundum etc. In filio mediatore magnum esse incendium amoris erga nos certissimum est. Suntque impressae στοργαὶ hominum naturae, ut sint commonefactiones de amore aeterni patris erga filium, et erga nos.

Vult igitur Deus, esse in nobis adfectus congruentes suae legi.

Et sunt aliqui boni adfectus in naturis non monstrosis, qui etiamsi propter communem naturae depravationem aliquid habent contagii, tamen Deus eos adprobat, et vult eos recte gubernari.

Vult ut maritus amet coniugem, parentes ament natos, frater fratrem, adfectus beneficio benefactorem, vult homines talibus vinculis inter sese coniunctos et consociatos esse. Ut enim dici solet, Bonum natura sui conservativum et congregativum et communicativum. servativum et congregativum et communicativum esse, ita Deus et vere amans est congregationis et communicationis beneficiorum.

Vult homines inter se multis vinculis copulatos esse, coniugio, amore erga natos, tanquam erga partem propriae naturae, cura educandi natos, communicatione beneficiorum, intellectu iusticiae, quae pro beneficiis iubet vicissim beneficia reddere. Et his vinculis et hac communicatione vult conservari naturam. Ita causa conspicitur, cur impressae sint hominibus στοργαί.

Estque tota haec sapientia de bonitate Dei comprehensa in hoc dulcissimo dicto: Deus est dilectio, et qui in dilectione manet, in Deo manet, et Deus in eo.

Et vicina sunt haec dicta: Deus est bonus, et, Deus est dilectio, id est, vere diligens suam effigiem, naturam intelligentem. Nam hoc posterius dictum magis ad naturas intelligentes congruit. Iam cogita, cum στοργαὶ sint vere opera Dei, et referant Dei bonitatem, et sint res in natura ordinatae, quam dira depravatio sit in diabolis, qui abiecerunt στοργὰς, et in multis hominibus, qui hoc naturali amore et vinculo consociationis extincto, bellum gerunt cum Deo et cum natura generis humani.

Talis est Cain, tales sunt Atreus et Thyestes, talis est Medea, quae filios suos interficit. Cum autem natura in homine, nondum prorsus furioso, tamen aliqua ex parte naturales inclinationes sentiat, non dubium est a diabolis impelli Cain et similes, qui extincta naturali benevolentia, saevitiam in cognatos et naturae suae partem exercere possunt. Et de talibus quoque verum est dictum: Satanas intravit in corda eorum. Considerantes igitur, quam dira et tetra sint haec scelera, et unde oriantur, magna cura Deum aeternum patrem Domini nostri Iesu Christi, conditorem φιλόστοργον generis humani, oremus, ut propter filium, quem ardenti benevolentia diligit, corda nostra Spiritu suo sancto custodiat et regat, ac depellat a nobis insidiatores diabolos, hostes suos.

Primis etiam initiis ac scintillis talium odiorum sapienter repugnemus ipsi, ne diabolus invitetur. Multa grassantur scelera huius generis inter homines, privatim et publice, alia magis, alia minus atrocia, ut magis est ἄστοργος Cain, quam Esau.

Sunt etiam ἄστοργοι homines seditiosi, qui Ecclesiam aut patriam sine necessariis causis turbant, quia causae sunt ingentium dolorum, et mortis multorum bonorum hominum, senum, matronarum, puerorum. Et semel motis Rebuspublicis non facile postea pax, disciplina, leges, religio restitui possunt. "Ασπονδοι sunt implacabiles, sicut Saul nullo officio placari potuit, ut deponeret iniustum odium, quo ardebat adversus Davidem, bene de patria et de ipso meritum. Haec pertinacia odiorum in hominibus lividis et saevis non rara est. Ἀνελεήμονες, immisericordes: haec appellatio plura comprehendit, quam crudelitas.

Crudelis est, qui laedit alium atrociter, sine causa iusta, aut poena maiore adficit, quam pro modo delicti. Ut crudelis erat Augusti hospes, qui servum obiicere murenis voluit, quia fregerat poculum crystallinum. Sed immisericors est non solum crudelis, sed etiam qui cum probabilis ratio est, non mitigat iustam asperitatem. Nam iusticia est, neminem laedere sine causa. Est et in poenis servare aequalitatem: misericordia vero primum iusta est, non laedit insontes. Deinde probabili ratione etiam iustam poenam mitigat. Ita Deus misericors est, et ut Psalmus inquit: Non accendit totam iram suam. Hanc grammaticam enarrationem quarundam vocum addidi, ut iuniores adsuefiant ad diligentiam in consideranda proprietate verborum et in distribuendis virtutibus et vitiis.

Intueantur autem, ut saepe alias dixi, Decalogum. Scientes ius Dei. Hic addit regulam de legibus naturalibus sen noticiis naturalibus, quae nominantur Ius naturae.

Ut enim in hac accusatione convincat homines, proponit eis naturales illas noticias. Hae inquit, accusant vos, quas quidem ideo in hominum natura Deus non voluit prorsus extingui, ut essent testimonia de Deo et de iudicio Dei, et certo sciremus, hac voce naturae comonefacti, Deum vere et horribiliter irasci omnibus facientibus contra has noticias, divinitus nobis insitas. Considerent autem iuniores Pauli sermonem. Has noticias, quas vocamus Leges naturae seu ius naturae, expresse hic nominat Ius Dei. Sciamus igitur, quod verissimum est, leges naturae esse ius divinum: est enim lux a Deo in mentibus nostris condita, et verissime congruit cum Decalogo et aliis dictis in lege Moisi, in quibus repetitum est ius naturae. Sunt enim gravissimae causae, propter quas Deus expressa voce hanc ipsam legem antea in creatione mentibus insitam, repetivit, et testimonia illustria addidit, et scribi eam iussit.

Nam post naturae humanae depravationem in mentibus est caligo, et multum dubitationum. Et paulatim mala exempla augebant caliginem. Sed de his materiis alibi saepe dixi, Et discant iuniores, quid vere sit Lex naturae, et teneant regulam a veteribus traditam: Violatio iuris naturae est peccatum mortale, sicut violatio iuris divini.

Quod talia facientes digni morte sint. Mira profecto sententia est, quod ait, homines naturaliter intelligere, dignos morte esse omnes, qui violant leges naturae.

Sed Paulus non loquitur de politica gubernatione, quae tantum externa facta punit: Verum de iudicio proprio in cuiusque conscientia, intuente Deum. Ac multo altius introspicit mentes hominum, quam vel Epicurei, vel hypocritae, qui securi et ebrii voluptatibus, non sunt experti veros pavores conscientiae.

Non iudicat Saul, se morte dignum esse, cum contra mandatum Samuelis parcit regi captivo. Sed tunc agnoscit conscientia, quodlibet peccatum morte dignum esse, cum intuetur Deum, et sentit iram Dei, et reputat, quantum malum sit neglectio Dei, vel contumacia adversus Deum.

In hoc iudicio vident mentes, peccatum esse non tantum deformitatem dissentientem ab harmonia naturae, sed quiddam reum, et damnatum coram Deo, et hanc sontem naturam propter contemptum Dei dignam esse horrendis poenis et destructione. Adam cum gustaret pomum contra mandatum, existimabat, id factum non magni momenti esse.

Nondum hos horrendos terrores conscientiae expertus erat, qui hanc miseram naturam opprimunt morte. Postea vero obiurgatus a Deo, agnovit peccatum esse neglectionem seu contemptum Dei, sensit irasci Deum, expavit, et extinctus esset magnitudine doloris, nisi divina promissione ex morte revocatus esset. Lex, inquit Paulus, est potentia peccati.

Ita lex naturae in mentibus hominum indicat et damnat peccatum. Et in veris pavoribus ostendit, Deum irasci omnibus peccatis, externis et interioribus, De hoc vero iudicio propriae conscientiae loquitur hic Paulus, ac damnat non solum externa delicta, sed etiam universam immunditiem interiorem, aversionem a Deo, dubitationes de Deo, coecam securitatem, et contemptum Dei, et omnes pravas inclinationes, et errantes cupiditates.

Ideo accusat non solum facientes, sed etiam, ut hic nominat, συνευδοκοῦντας, id est, qui in sua natura similia vitia cernunt, et ab eis non abhorrent, nec dolent, cum titillantur his suis vitiis. Erumpunt autem alii adfectus in aliis.

Atticus non est incestus, non fecit caedem manibus, sed tamen dubitat, an Deus curet humana, an puniat, an exaudiat homines, gaudet sibi eximi metum indicii divini academicis disputationibus, quaerit suam tranquillitatem sine agnitione Dei, et sentit ipse, se habere multos motus aberrantes a lege naturae. Nominat enim Paulus hic συνευδοκοῦντας, non ut in foro dicimus, consentientes, qui manifeste adiuvant aut defendunt aliorum scelera: sed eos, qui in sua natura titillantur similibus inclinationibus, etiamsi eas non proferunt.

Nam εὐδοκεῖν generaliter est, benevolo animo esse erga aliquid, ut εὐδοκεῖ ξένῳ, id est, est benevolo animo erga hospitem, non est aliena voluntate. εὐδοκεῖ λεγομένοις, recipit dicta. Atticus συνευδοκεῖ φιλοσόφοις καταγελῶσι τῶν πιστευόντων, εἶναι τιμωρίας τινὰς ἀνθρώπων μετὰ θάνατον. Ex talibus exemplis verbi significatio satis intelligi potest.

## 2:1 Disposition of Romans: Argument
Chapter II.

An objection is inserted in this place by the way, as to why Paul seems to depart from the established proposition. But let the reader diligently consider where Paul returns to the subject, so that he may observe the perpetual order of the disputation. And as if ignoring the digressions into which the Apostle sometimes wanders for a little while, let him remember the principal members of the disputation, and take pains to connect and join them correctly. The meaning of the objection is this: How do you argue that all men are sinners, when many among the Gentiles have lived honestly, such as Socrates, Aristides, Cato, Pomponius Atticus, and the Jews also perform the works of the law? The voice of the Gospel therefore seems unjust, that all are sinners, that without the Gospel no one is justified. Paul answers that those who did honest works were nevertheless hypocrites. But the Gospel argues not only external offenses, but much more, impure hearts. And the occasion for the objection is taken from that sentiment, that they are guilty not only who do [the deeds], but who, even if they do not do them, yet consent, that is, have impure affections in their heart.

In our times, some similarly dispute against those who defend the righteousness of faith. They deny that all men by nature are under sin, and contend that they can be justified by good works. These require only an external and civil righteousness. But the Gospel shows that hearts are impious, without faith, without the fear of God; therefore, the Gospel reveals a certain other righteousness.

To this rebuke an exhortation is added, by which he also calls hypocrites to repentance. And just as we use threats in persuasive passages, so Paul added a threat. To the incredulous, wrath, etc. And an amplification is added from the persons, that Jews and Gentiles are judged equally, because those who sin without the law perish without the law, and those who sin in the law will be judged through the law.

A correction follows; when he had previously said that the Gentiles sin without the law, he corrects and interprets that statement, that the Gentiles have the law written in their hearts. And he defines that law as being the judgment of conscience, which either excuses or accuses works. This passage teaches most clearly what the law of nature is, which they call such in the schools. For it is that natural judgment of the mind which either approves or disapproves of works.

But behold, you, O Jew.

He returns to the established distribution, and completes the second member, that the Jews are impious, even though they perform the works of the law. And he amplifies this member through a heap of many vices, and through antitheses, in which he signifies that they perform the works of the law outwardly, and yet have unclean hearts.

Latin:

Caput II.

Obiter hoc loco inseritur occupatio, quare Paulus discedere ab instituta propositione vide- tur. Diligenter autem consideret lector, ubi Paulus ad propositum redeat, ut perpetuum ordi- nem disputationis observet. Et tanquam dissimu- lans egressiones, in quas nonnunquam paulisper expaciatur Apostolus, me minerit principalia dis- putationis membra, et det operam, ut illa recte connectat et coagmentet. Est autem occupationis sententia. Quomodo arguis omnes homines, cum multi apud Gentes honeste vixerint, ut Socrates, Aristides, Cato, Pomponius Atticus, Iudaei etiam legis opera faciunt. Videtur igitur iniusta Evangelii vox, quod omnes sint peccatores, quod sine Evangelio nemo sit iustificatus. Paulus respondet, eos qui honesta opera fecerunt, ta- men fuisse hypocritas. Evangelium autem ar- guit, non tantum externa delicta, sed multo magis impura corda. Et sumta est occasio oc- cupationis ex illa sententia, reos esse non tan- tum qui faciunt, sed qui etiamsi non faciant, ta- men consentiunt, id est, in corde impuros ad- fectus habent.

Nostris temporibus quidam similiter dispu- tant adversus eos, qui fidei iusticiam defendunt. Negant omnes homines natura sub peccato esse, et contendunt quod bonis operibus iustificari queant. Hi tantum externam et civilem iusticiam requirunt. At Evangelium ostendit corda esse impia, sine fide, sine timore Dei, propterea aliam quandam iusticiam patefacit Evangelium.

Huic obiurgationi — addita est adhortatio, qua etiam hypocritas vocat ad poenitentiam. Et sicut in locis suasoriis utimur comminationibus, ita Paulus adiecit comminationem. Incredulis ira etc. Et a personis amplificatio accedit, Iu- daeos et Gentes pariter iudicari, quia qui sine lege peccant, sine lege pereunt, qui in lege peccant, per legem iudicabuntur.

Sequitur correctio, cum ante dixisset, Gen- tes sine lege peccare, corrigit et interpretatur id dictum, Gentes habere legem in cordibus scri- ptam. Et definit eam legem, conscientiae iudi- cium esse, quae vel excusat vel accusat opera. Hic locus planissime docet, quid sit lex naturae, quam sic vocant in scholis. Est enim iudicium illud naturale mentis, quod vel probat vel impro- bat opera.

Ecce autem tu Iudaeus.

Redit ad institutam distributionem, ad al- terum membrum absolvit, quod Iudaei sint im- pii, tametsi opera legis faciant. Et amplificat hoc membrum per congeriem multorum vitio- rum, et per antitheses, in quibus significat il- los foris facere legis opera, et tamen corda im- munda habere.

## 2:1 Argument
Chapter II.

At the beginning of the second Chapter he adds a conclusion, properly pertaining to this accusation of internal vices.

Therefore even you, who judge, that is, who although you do not commit external crimes, yet in mind and heart have similar impurity, you are guilty before God. It is a complete syllogism.

At the end of the previous chapter the major premise is recited: All are worthy of death, both those who commit external crimes, and indeed others who carry around false opinions about God in their mind, and have very many vicious inclinations in their heart. The minor follows in the second chapter: You who judge another, you do the same things, that is, you who honestly govern external actions, and judge that only those who are polluted by external offenses are displeasing to God, and you do not condemn yourself, but judge yourself to be just before God on account of honest external actions, you nevertheless do the same things, that is, you have similar vices in mind and heart: You doubt whether God cares for human affairs, whether He puniat, whether he hears men, you have also other wandering desires.

This is the meaning of this saying: You do the same, namely, with the interior motions of the mind.

Because it is most well-known that the principal causes of actions are the mind, the will, and the Heart.

Therefore, the conclusion follows: Therefore, since you do the same, you are inexcusable, whoever you are who judges, that is, you condemn others, who are contaminated by external crimes, [but] you do not condemn yourself, who have a similar interior depravity.

And this conclusion is an accusation of all who think themselves to be righteous before God on account of civil morals, when they know that their minds are full of doubts and errors, and their hearts burn with many vicious desires.

But Paul adds a confirmation: The judgment of God is according to truth, that is, it judges not only the external shadow of actions, but the minds and the source of actions.

If in the minds there does not shine a true opinion about God, if the wills are turned away from God, and they love themselves more than God, certainly they do not obey the law of God, which says: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, etc.

But you think, O man.

He interweaves a brief exhortation, by which he calls all to repentance, and teaches why God delays punishments, namely, to grant us space for conversion.

Individuals, in whatever fall, become guilty of eternal death, and could justly be killed by God: but the immense goodness of God, because He does not want the whole human race to perish, grants space to the miserable, so that they may return to the way, according to that: I live, says the Lord, I do not want the death of the sinner, etc.

To this pertains the parable of the fig tree, Luke 13.

It is to be lamented, however, that human nature is of such foul depravity that this very delay, for which it ought to give thanks, confirms [its] manifold impiety.

For men care less about the judgment of God because punishments are delayed, even though this very delay is very short.

Therefore, in addition, crimes are added to crimes.

Paul accuses this pernicious security in a brief saying, but nevertheless with harsh words; he says that men despise the goodness and tolerance of God.

Likewise, [that they] heap up wrath for themselves.

He will render to each according to his works.

Let us leave aside all the sophistries of sophists, and let us recognize the phrasing of the law.

He will render to each according to his works, that is, He will afflict the unjust with punishment, [and] He will give good things to the just.

Concerning the unjust, it is manifest that punishments are owed for their deeds, and on account of their deeds.

Concerning the just, it must be known from the Gospel how they are just.

And since it is necessary that faith be in us, as the Gospel teaches, this very mention of faith, which relies not on our dignity, but on the mercy promised on account of the mediator, shows that eternal life is given on account of the Son of God.

And yet, because faith is a virtue in us, the law speaks in its own way as if of our own virtue.

For there is no respect of persons with God.

As Paul says in this place to the Romans: There is no respect of persons with God: so also in Acts chapter 10 it is written: God is no respecter of persons.

And elsewhere this saying is often repeated, as in Isaiah 42 concerning the Messiah: Do not accept a person, etc.

It signifies, however, generally, not to accept a person, to make a judgment about a matter, without discrimination of accidents, which are foreign to the matter.

As Torquatus judges only the matter, condemning his son, and does not obscure the matter on account of kinship.

Respect of persons is usually described: It is to give equal things to unequals, or unequal things to equals.

But the opinion, prohibiting προσωποληψίαν [respect of persons], arises from the fountains of justice.

Justice is equality, but ordered according to some measure.

As a Judge is then just, when he equally keeps the measure, punishes the guilty, and defends the innocent, and does not depart from the measure on account of other accidents in men.

And to act against this measure is inequality, which is unjust and tyranny.

Therefore, when it is said: With God there is no respect of persons, the praise of justice and equality is attributed to Him, of which this is the measure.

God universally judges sin in man, and universally accepts all who flee to the mediator.

He has established this measure by His most wise and most just counsel, and He wants it to be immovable.

And to imagine that He does not keep this equality is to attribute to Him προσωποληψίαν.

Therefore Paul also says: God wants all men to be saved, that is, He is equal to all, according to the measure which He instituted.

And as far as His own will is concerned, He wants to save All men, but many by their own fault do not accept the offered benefit, etc.

This is a great and necessary consolation, because in the minds of all men there is great trepidation, because of this imagination, which feigns inequality in God.

Men often cry out: Even if God receives some, yet you are not in that number, nor written in those fatal tablets. Could not so powerful a Lord cast away whom He would?

However, the voice of the promises must be set against this, in which God wills His will to be acknowledged.

And the promise is universal. Nor are there contradictory wills in God, because God is truthful. Therefore, it is necessary that we obey the promise, and with firm faith establish that this is truly the will of God, which He shows in the promise, and that God is truly equal to all, according to the measure which He instituted by His own voice.

I have said these things briefly, so that the younger ones may observe this saying with greater care, and accommodate it both to nourishing fear and to their own consolation. Not that they should be moved by sophistical contentions, but that we may learn to look upon the revealed will of God, to acquiesce in it, and to reverently give thanks to Him for the immense benefit of the given promise, etc.

As many as have sinned without law, shall perish without law.

Here it is necessary that this saying be understood as without a written or promulgated law: because afterwards he expressly adds a correction: Nay, even the Gentiles had a law, that is, a natural knowledge, discerning between honest and base things.

For he says: They are a law unto themselves, and there is in them a conscience accusing and excusing. Therefore, there is in them a natural knowledge, discerning honest and base things, which in reality is the law of God, agreeing with the Decalogue.

Here again, let the students observe that the law of nature is described and approved, and let them rightly learn what the law of nature is, as I have said above and often elsewhere with practical demonstrations.

And this is a notable description, namely that he says the knowledge is accusing and excusing.

For it signifies the divine light, which God therefore infused into human minds, so that He Himself might be acknowledged, and sin in us might be argued. Just as murderers feel horrible terrors, even when they are in safety, and fear no magistrates.

Augustinus in this place disputes too anxiously about many members.

He answers those who cite the saying against the justice of faith: The doers of the law are justified.

But the proper and clear answer is, this description is of the justice of the law, which in no way hinders other sayings about the justice of faith.

Because it is true that the justice of the law is to do the law, not only to hear it. For in this place Paul properly deals with this, that justice is not knowledge or profession, as many men flattering themselves imagine, but is obedience in the will.
