This general saying on the justice of the law hinders absolutely nothing of those things which are said afterwards about the justice of faith. Let there only be dexterity in interpretation, so that right sayings are not corrupted.

Afterwards, Augustinus disputes, Did the Gentiles do the law, and did they do it by nature?

Paul only wishes to reason this, that in the Gentiles there is a knowledge of the law, which he reasons from there, because many did only by natural judgment as much as the Jews by the written law: And honest and base things are judged in their consciences.

This follows, if only discipline and external deeds are considered.

Scipio did not touch the spouse of another, because he knew adultery to be base, and to be punished by God.

He therefore did the work of the law, and Paul does not say that the Gentiles did the law, but those things which are of the law, that is, some works of the law.

And the word Nature here signifies the same as natural knowledge, showing the distinction between honest and base things.

This is the simple and native opinion, which the reader should embrace, having rejected the corruptions which Pelagius and others feigned.

And what Paul says, The work written in their hearts, signifies that these natural knowledges are gifts attributed to nature, and born with us, just as the knowledges of numbers are attributed to nature, and are born with us.

Behold, you who are called a Jew.

Before he accused the Gentiles, now he accuses the Jews, so that he may arrive at this equalization: That all men in this depravity of nature are under sin, and are not freed by the law from sin and from the wrath of God, as is said below: He concluded all under sin.

But let this rebuke be accepted in such a way that you understand that not only external offenses are accused, but also hypocrisy, and the trust in one's own justice, such as was the arrogance in the Jews, because of their title and profession.

And Paul speaks of the Jews, insofar as they were without the true recognition of the Messiah, who even if they excelled in discipline, yet were forced to confess that they had vicious hearts, and that they were not removed from those diseases by the law, or by ceremonies, or by sacrifices.

He adds also a rebuke of the vainest persuasion, by which they feigned that they were just because of their title or profession and ceremonies.

And he hands down the rule, that external ceremonies are valid in such a way, if the hearts agree with the law of God. Circumcision is profitable, if you observe the law.

Here it must be observed that these false persuasions about ceremonies are always wandering in the world, either that they merit the remission of sins, or that they are acts of worship and please God, even without the righteousness of the heart: and as is commonly said, ex opere operato [by the work performed], just as the monks have impudently written concerning the offering in the mass. Therefore, in all ages in the Church, some have censured this error, as in Psalm 50: "I will not reprove you for your sacrifices." And Jeremiah 7: "I did not command them concerning burnt offerings, but I commanded this word: Hear my voice, and I will be your God."

It has been said often elsewhere, in what order ceremonies are pleasing, and I have pictured a ship, and in the ship a book, and upon the book a chalice standing, that is: First, the promise concerning the Son of God must be heard, and it must be established by faith that you are accepted on account of him. This faith begins new obedience, love in the heart, hope, invocation, and other virtues. Then follow the ceremonies, as signs that remind us of the promise, or exercises of external ministry, of invocation, of thanksgiving, etc., as has been said more copiously elsewhere.

But from this, the fiercest struggles always have been and will be in the Church. Hypocrites rage furiously when the opinion of merit is taken away from ceremonies. As the Jews shouted: "If we are not righteous by the law, why was the law given?" Paul answers this question immediately, and the explanation is necessary, because this question is agitated in all times: "If our diligence does not merit the remission of sins, why is discipline demanded?" Likewise: "If we are not righteous on account of our own virtues, why is license not granted to our desires?"

Therefore, at the beginning of the third Chapter, Paul raises this question: "What then does the Jew have, by which he excels? Why was the law given? Why was the polity of Moses established? Why are we called the people of God, if we are not righteous by this observance?" Concerning these questions, it is necessary that true and clear doctrine exist in the Church, and that those foul delusions be rejected, which invented three laws: the first of Nature, the second of Moses, the third Evangelical, and that at any time men were righteous by the observance of their own law. Against these pernicious errors, it must be known, as is often said, that there is one eternal moral law, which accuses sin in all, at all times: and that the fathers were not righteous by the law, but by the faith of the mediator, whom they acknowledged from the promise.

Latin:

Caput II.

In secundi Capitis initio addit conclusionem, proprie pertinentem ad hanc accusationem interiorum vitiorum.

Ergo et tu, qui iudicas, id est, qui quanquam non facis externa scelera, sed tamen in mente et corde similem habes immunditiam, reus es coram Deo. Syllogismus integer est.

In fine prioris capitis recitatur maior: Digni morte sunt omnes, cum externa scelera facientes, tum vero alii, qui falsas opiniones de Deo in mente circumferunt, et habent vitiosas inclinationes in corde plurimas. Sequitur minor in secundo capite: Tu qui iudicas alterum, facis eadem, id est, qui regis honeste externas actiones, et iudicas eos tantum displicere ...Deo, qui externis delictis polluti sunt, nec damnas teipsum, sed iudicas te instum esse coram Deo propter externas actiones honestas, facis tamen eadem, id est, habes similia vitia in mente et corde: Dubitas an Deus curet humana, an puniat, an exaudiat homines, habes et alias errantes cupiditates.

Haec est sententia huius dicti: Eadem facis, scilicet interioribus animi motibus.

Quia notissimum est principales causas actionum esse mentem, voluntatem et Cor.

Accedit igitur... conclusio: Ergo, cum eadem facias, inexcusabilis es quisquis iudicas, id est, alios damnas, externis delictis contaminatos, Te non damnas, qui similem habes interiorem pravitatem.

Estque haec conclusio accusatio omnium, qui se propter civiles mores arbitrantur iustos esse coram Deo, cum sciant, mentes plenas esse dubitationum et errorum, et corda multis vitiosis cupiditatibus ardere.

Addit autem Paulus confirmationem: Iudicium Dei secundum veritatem est, id est, iudicat non solum externam umbram actionum, sed mentes et fontem actionum.

Si in mentibus non lucet vera de Deo sententia, si voluntates aversae sunt a Deo, et sese plus amant, quam Deum, certe non obtemperant legi Dei, quae inquit: Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde etc.

Existimas autem o homo.

Intertexit brevem adhortationem, qua omnes vocat ad poenitentiam, ac docet, quare Deus differat poenas, videlicet, ut spatium nobis concedat ad conversionem.

Singuli, in quocunque lapsu, rei fiunt mortis aeternae, et iuste possent a Deo interfici: sed immensa bonitas Dei, quia non vult totum genus humanum perire, concedit spatium miseris, ut in viam redeant, iuxta illud: Vivo ego, dicit Dominus, nolo mortem peccatoris etc.

Huc pertinet parabola de ficu, Lucae 13.

Dolendum est autem, tam tetram pravitatem esse humanae naturae, ut haec ipsa mora, pro qua gratias agere debebat, confirmet multiplicem impietatem.

Levius enim curant homines iudicium Dei, propterea quod poenae differantur, etsi haec ipsa mora valde brevis est.

Insuper igitur scelera sceleribus adduntur.

Hanc perniciosam securitatem Paulus brevi quidem dicto, sed tamen atrocibus verbis accusat, dicit homines contemnere bonitatem et tolerantiam Dei.

Item, sibi cumulare iram.

Reddet unicuique iuxta opera sua.

Relinquamus omnes praestigias sophismatum, et agnoscamus phrasin legis.

Reddet unicuique iuxta opera sua, id est, iniustos afficiet poena, iustis dabit bona.

De iniustis manifestum est, deberi poenas pro ipsorum factis, et propter ipsorum facta.

De iustis ex Evangelio sciendum est, quomodo sint iusti.

Et cum fidem opporteat esse in nobis, sicut Evangelium docet, haec ipsa mentio fidei, quae nititur non nostra dignitate, sed misericordia promissa propter mediatorem, ostendit, dari vitam aeternam propter filium Dei.

Et tamen quia fides virtus est in nobis, lex suo more tanquam de nostra virtute loquitur.

Non est enim acceptio personarum apud Deum.

Ut hoc loco ad Romanos inquit Paulus: Non est acceptio personarum apud Deum: ita et in Actis capite 10. scriptum est: Non est personae acceptor Deus.

Et alibi saepe repetitur hoc dictum, ut Esaiae 42. de Messia: Non accipite personam etc.

Significat autem generaliter, non accipere personam, facere iudicium de re, sine discrimine accidentium, quae a re aliena sunt.

Ut Torquatus de sola re iudicat condemnans filium, nec obruit rem propter cognationem.

Usitate describitur acceptio personarum: Est dare aequalia inaequalibus, vel inaequalia aequalibus.

Oritur autem sententia, prohibens προσωποληψίαν, ex fontibus iusticiae.

Iusticia est aequalitas, sed ordinata secundum mensuram aliquam.

Ut Iudex tunc est iustus, cum aequaliter mensuram servat, punit sontes, et defendit innocentes, nec discedit a mensura propter alia accidentia in hominibus.

Et contra hanc mensuram facere, inaequalitas est, quae est iniusta et tyrannis.

Ideo cum dicitur: Apud Deum non est acceptio personarum, tribuitur ei laus iusticiae et aequalitatis, cuius haec mensura est.

Universaliter iudicatur Deus peccato in homine, et universaliter accipit omnes ad mediatorem confugientes.

Hanc mensuram suo sapientissimo et iustissimo consilio sanxit, et vult immotam esse.

Ac fingere, quod non servet hanc aequalitatem, est tribuere ei προσωποληψίαν.

Ideo et Paulus inquit: Deus vult omnes homines salvos fieri, id est, aequalis est omnibus, iuxta mensuram ...quam instituit.

Et quod ad ipsius voluntatem attinet, vult Omnes homines salvos facere, sed multi sua culpa oblatum beneficium non accipiunt etc.

Haec est magna et necessaria consolatio, quia in omnium hominum mentibus magna est trepidatio, propter hanc imaginationem, quae fingit in Deo inaequalitatem.

Saepe clamant homines: Etiam si Deus aliquos recipit, tamen tu non es in illo numero, nec scriptus in illis tabulis fatalibus. Tam potens Dominus non posset abiicere quos... vellet?

Opponenda est autem vox promissionum, in qua Deus vult agnosci suam voluntatem.

Et promissio est universalis. Nec sunt in Deo contradictoriae voluntates, quia Deus est verax. Ideo necesse est nos obedire promissioni, et firma fide statuere, vere hanc esse voluntatem Dei, quam ostendit in promissione, et vere Deum aequalem esse omnibus, juxta mensuram, quam sua voce instituit.

Haec dixi breviter, ut iuniores hoc dictum maiore cura observent, et ad timorem alendum, et ad consolationem suam accommodent. Non, ut moveantur sophistica certamina, sed discamus intueri voluntatem Dei patefactam, in ea acquiescere, et ei reverenter gratias agere pro immenso beneficio donatae promissionis etc.

Qui sine lege peccaverunt, sine lege peribunt.

Hic necesse est intelligi hoc dictum, sine scripta lege aut promulgata: quia postea expresse addit correctionem: Imo et Gentes habuerunt legem, hoc est, noticiam naturalem, discernentem honesta et turpia.

Ait enim: Sibi ipsis sunt lex, et est in eis conscientia accusans et excusans. Ergo est in eis naturalis noticia, discernens honesta et turpia, quae re ipsa est lex Dei, congruens cum Decalogo.

Hic rursus observent studiosi describi et approbari legem naturae, et recte discant, quae sit lex naturae, ut supra, et alibi saepe demonstrationibus practicis dixi.

Et haec insignis descriptio est, quod videlicet ait, noticiam esse accusantem et excusantem.

Significat enim lucem divinam, quam Deus ideo transfudit in humanas mentes, ut ipse agnoscatur, et peccatum in nobis arguatur. Sicut homicidae sentiunt horribiles pavores, etiam cum sunt in tuto, et nullos magistratus metuunt.

Augustinus hoc loco de multis membris nimis anxie disputat.

Respondet iis, qui contra iusticiam fidei citant dictum: Factores legis iustificantur.

Sed propria et perspicua responsio est, haec descriptio est iusticiae legis, quae nihil impedit alia dicta de iusticia fidei.

Quia verum est, iusticiam legis esse, facere legem, non tantum audire. Nam hoc loco Paulus hoc proprie agit, iusticiam non esse noticiam seu professionem, ut multi homines sibi blandientes imaginantur, sed esse obedientiam in voluntate.

Hoc generale dictum in iusticia legis, prorsus nihil impedit ea, quae postea dicuntur de iusticia fidei. Adsit tantum in interpretatione dexteritas, non corrumpantur recte dicta.

Postea disputat Augustinus, An Gentes legem fecerint, et an natura fecerint?

Paulus tantum hoc ratiocinari vult, in Gentibus esse noticiam legis quod inde ratiocinatur, quia multi tantum fecerint indicio naturali, quantum Iudaei lege scripta: Et diiudicari in conscientiis honesta et turpia.

Hoc sequitur, si tantum disciplina et externa facta considerentur.

Scipio non attigit sponsam alterius, quia sciebat adulterium turpe esse, et a Deo puniri.

Fecit igitur opus legis, et Paulus non dicit, Gentes legem fecisse, sed ea quae sunt legis, id est, aliqua legis opera.

Et vocabulum Natura hic significat idem quod naturali noticia, monstrante discrimen honestorum et turpium.

Haec est simplex et nativa sententia, quam lector amplectatur reiectis corruptelis, quas finxit Pelagius et caeteri.

Et quod inquit Paulus, Opus scriptum in cordibus, significat has noticias naturales dona esse attributa naturae, et nobiscum nascentia, sicut noticiae numerorum naturae attributae sunt, et nobiscum nascuntur.

Ecce tu, qui Iudaeus nominaris.

Antea Gentes accusavit, nunc accusat Iudaeos, ut perveniat ad hanc exaequationem: Omnes homines in hac depravatione naturae sub peccato esse, nec lege liberari a peccato et ab ira Dei, ut infra dicitur: Conclusit Omnes sub peccatum.

Sic autem accipiatur haec obiurgatio, ut intelligas, non tantum externa delicta accusari, sed etiam hypocrisin, et fiduciam propriae iusticiae, qualis erat arrogantia in Iudaeis, propter titulum et professionem.

Et loquitur Paulus de Iudaeis, quatenus erant sine vera agnitione Messiae, qui etiamsi excellebant disciplina, tamen fateri cogebantur, se habere corda vitiosa, nec lege, vel ceremoniis, vel sacrificiis eos morbos tolli.

Addit autem et reprehensionem vanissimae persuasionis, qua fingebant, se propter titulum seu professionem et ceremonias iustos esse.

Et regulam tradit, Valere externas ceremonias ita, si corda congruant cum lege Dei. Circumcisio prodest, si legem observes.

Hic observandum est, semper in mundo vagari has falsas persuasiones de ceremoniiis, vel quod mereantur remissionem peccatorum, vel quod sint cultus, et Deo placeant, etiam sine iusticia cordis: et ut vulgo dicitur, ex opere operato, sicut de oblatione in missa impudenter scripserunt monachi. Omnibus igitur aetatibus in Ecclesia aliqui taxaverunt hunc errorem, ut Psalmo 50.: Non in sacrificiis tuis arguam te. Et Ieremiae 7.: Non praecepi eis de holocaustis, sed hoc verbum praecepi: Audite vocem meam, et ero vobis Deus.

Dictum est autem alias saepe, quo ordine placeant ceremoniae, et pinxi navim, et in navi librum, et supra librum stare calicem, id est: Primum audienda est promissio de filio Dei, et fide statuendum, te recipi propter eum. Haec fides incoat novam obedientiam, in corde dilectionem, spem, invocationem, et alias virtutes. Deinde accedunt ceremoniae, ut signa, quae de promissione nos commonefaciant, vel exercitiae externi ministerii, invocationis, gratiarum actionis etc., ut alibi copiosius dictum est.

Sed hinc asperrima certamina semper in Ecclesia et fuerunt et erunt. Hypocritae furenter irascuntur, cum detrahitur ceremoniis opinio meriti. Ut Iudaei vociferabantur: Si non sumus iusti lege, cur data est lex? Huic quaestioni mox respondet Paulus, et necessaria est explicatio, quia omnibus temporibus haec quaestio agitatur: Si nostra diligentia non meretur remissionem peccatorum, cur disciplina flagitatur? Item: Si non sumus iusti propter nostras virtutes, cur non conceditur licentia cupiditatibus?

Ideo initio tertii Capitis movet hanc quaestionem Paulus: Quid igitur habet Iudaeus, quo antecellat? Quare lex data est? Quare politia Moisi constituta est? Quare dicimur populus Dei, si non sumus iusti hac observatione? De his quaestionibus necesse est in Ecclesia extare veram et perspicuam doctrinam, et illa tetra deliramenta reiici, quae finxerunt tres leges: Primam Naturae, secundam Moisi, tertiam Evangelicam, et quolibet tempore homines suae legis observatione iustos fuisse. Adversus hos perniciosos errores sciendum, ut saepe dicitur, Unam esse aeternam legem moralem, quae accusat peccatum in omnibus, omni tempore: nec patres fuisse iustos lege, sed fide mediatoris, quem ex promissione agnoscebant.

## 3:1 Disposition of Romans: Argument
Chapter III.

Here, however, a great and difficult question arises. For since he condemns Jews and Gentiles alike, it is necessary to ask what the law contributes, and why the Jews are called the people of God. If the law does not justify, why was it given? If the Jews do not excel the Gentiles, why are they called the people of God? Is there no difference between Jews and Gentiles? This question is therefore inserted in a few words. To which he responds in two ways: And what you might find surprising, the responses seem to conflict with one another. First he says that the Jews excel the Gentiles by much. Then, as if retracting the previous statement, he says, the Jews excel the Gentiles in nothing.

But we shall understand that these opinions do not conflict with one another if we consider where the Jews excel and where they do not. They excel, he says, as far as the promises are concerned. For it is something to have the word, and for the promises to pertain to them. Otherwise, the Jews do not excel at all as far as merit is concerned. For one is not justified by his own worship or by the works of the law. Yet he does not yet sufficiently explain this question, why the law was given; he only touches upon it incidentally and in passing, and signifies that the Jews were separated from the Gentiles, not so that they might merit righteousness by that worship, but because it was necessary that there exist some certain people in whom the promises concerning Christ might be revealed, in whom testimonies concerning the word of God might exist manifest and certain; below, in Cap. 5 and Cap. 7, he will explain more fully that the law was not given so that it might justify.

Incidental questions of another kind are also inserted. If the promises pertain to the Jews, why did so few believe? He repeats this question below in chapter 9. Now he omits it as if it were untimely and hastens to the principal proposition, lest he seem to have forgotten his purpose. And indeed it is prudence to see how, having wandered for a little while, he returns to the purpose.

Here, therefore, he recurs to the members of the distribution, and as ought to be done in an epilogue or conclusion, he joins both members: All men, both Jews and Gentiles, are under sin, that is, they are guilty of eternal death, they truly have sin, contempt of God, and concupiscence. Nor can we be freed from sin or eternal death by our works or by the law. He adds testimonies from the Psalm and elsewhere. And at the end, a certain interpretation of the proposition is added, so that we may understand that not only the openly wicked are accused, but also those very ones who attempt to merit justification by good works. Therefore he says: By the works of the law shall no flesh be justified. It is necessary to remember this sentence in particular, because some attempt to interpret this passage of Paul civilly, and argue that Paul does not mean that all men by nature are under sin, but only that he is accusing those whose morals are openly evil. And because there is a great multitude of this kind, they say that he uses a synecdoche and argues against all, when meanwhile some are good, whose morals cannot be reproved, such as Pomponius Atticus or Aristides; these they contend are justified by the powers of nature and by works. But Paul refutes this calumny, and lest anyone be able to invent a synecdoche, he expressly rejects the exception and recalls that part of men to the universal proposition: All are under sin. And so that the matter might be clearer, he does not speak of persons, but of the thing which seems to provide an exception. By the works of the law, he says, no one is justified. The Apostle could not speak more properly. And in such propriety of speech, they nevertheless seek something to cavil at. This very thing, he says, which you except, I include, I accuse, I condemn. Therefore, they fabricate a synecdoche against Paul's sentence in this place. But the error arises from the fact that they dream that there is no sin in Pomponius Atticus and those like him. And they call only civil morals the righteousness of God, and they do not also require the knowledge of God, faith or trust toward God; in short, they are content with the works of the second table, of the first table οὐδεὶς λόγος. They do not perceive that there are sins in Atticus: ignorance of God, distrust in God, being devoid of the fear of God, trusting in one's own prudence, etc.

There follows a very brief occupation concerning the use of the law. For it is necessary for a reader who is not foolish to have this question come to mind. But if the works of the law do not justify, why then was the law given? It seems extremely absurd to give a law if the works of the law do not justify. Paul answers and sets forth a new and unheard-of sentence to the world. The law was given so that through it sin might be known, so that it might argue sin, not so that it might abolish it. Furthermore, to know sin is to be truly terrified by the sight of sin. For they do not yet know sin who do not tremble; for they do not yet truly feel within themselves that God, being offended, is angry. But sin is that which offends God, and at which God is incensed. But he will teach the reader about the use of the law copiously below.

The status of the whole Epistle.

Now at last he arrives at the principal proposition, which is the status of this whole Epistle. But just as an architect has the whole form of a building enclosed in his mind, and sees how all the parts agree among themselves, so we, in reading grave disputations, ought to embrace in our mind the series of all propositions and arguments. Above all, however, it is necessary to remember the status, which contains the sum of the matter, to which all arguments are referred as to a head. And just as those who shoot direct their weapon at a certain target, so every thought of the mind must be directed toward the goal, as if toward a target. Therefore, in this Epistle, this passage is to be observed above all; this is the principal proposition of the whole case, this is the definition of Christian righteousness: that righteousness is to believe that for Christ's sake we are received into the favor of the Father, that Christ is the redeemer and propitiatory, that for his sake we are justified freely, without our merits, if we believe.

The proposition is clothed in somewhat more words. For circumstances are added. This righteousness, which is revealed in the Gospel, was also preached of old by the Prophets. Likewise, from the contrary: Christ appeared without the law.

This particle also is to be greatly observed among the notable sentences of this Epistle, that the righteousness of God has been revealed without the law. He teaches, however, that Christ did not come to bring the law, so that we might merit righteousness through our works, but that he came to justify those who believe freely, without our merits. I remember the scholastics anxiously asking what laws, besides the decalogue previously revealed, Christ brought. But no new law is to be sought. Here Paul manifestly separates the law from the Gospel and teaches that Christ brings righteousness freely without our merits, that Christ is not a legislator, but a redeemer. The law was given through Moses; through Christ, the remission of sins and the Holy Spirit are given. A circumstance is also added regarding to whom the righteousness revealed in the Gospel pertains. For he says 'unto all, and upon all' who believe, and he repeats the first proposition: all have sinned, and all are void of the glory of God, that is, the knowledge of God, trust toward God. He also took an ornament from the types. Christ is set forth to be a propitiatory, but through faith, as if he were saying that Christ is that true propitiatory through whom access to the Father is opened. Just as God had promised at the propitiatory in the tabernacle that he would hear the vows and prayers of the high priest: but I cease to recite all the circumstances of the proposition. For I am not writing a commentary. However, let the reader remember the sum of the proposition and grasp it in a dialectical manner. Righteousness before God is to believe that for Christ's sake righteousness and the remission of sins are given to us without our merits. And this is the definition of Christian righteousness. For so we shall call it for the sake of teaching, since Paul calls it the righteousness of God, namely, that by which we are righteous before God, or by which God deems us righteous. These things will be understood more clearly when human righteousness or civil righteousness is also defined, which is gathered by our own powers and works, and when a comparison of the definitions is made. But what great consolations are proposed in this place to terrified consciences, no human voice can explain according to its worth. Even if works are lacking, let us nevertheless believe that we are received into favor by the Father for Christ's sake freely. For this righteousness is revealed without the law; it is blasphemy against Christ and a profanation of the propitiatory not to accept consolation, not to be lifted up when righteousness is offered through Christ, but to despair because good works are lacking to us. It is also blasphemy to choose works with this hope and opinion, that we might be justified through them. To this sentiment follows an amplification: boasting is excluded.

The amplification of the proposition is taken from the final cause. If the works of the law justified, the end of works would be to merit favor. The end would also be trust in ourselves or boasting. Now, the cause ceasing, as they say, the effect ceases: justification is taken away from our works. Therefore, trust in ourselves and boasting are taken away from us. John does not deserve to be justified more than Magdalene because John lived continuously. And here, incidentally, the proposition is repeated: We reckon that a man is justified by faith, and he excludes the contrary, without the works of the law. In this manner, he strips trust from our works and satisfactions. For trust in ourselves would follow as an end if works justified.

A brief objection is added: Do we abolish the law? For to all sane men, when they hear that we do not merit righteousness by works, that John does not merit righteousness more than Magdalene, it must come to mind that it is permitted to live basely, that the law is abolished in such a way that license to sin is granted. Paul briefly answers this objection, for the same question will be treated copiously below. Nay, he says, we do not abolish the law, but we fulfill it, because the law requires righteousness from us before God. But he who believes in Christ is already righteous before God; he therefore has the end of the law, even though sin still clings to the flesh. And yet the same person now truly acknowledges God, truly feels that God is present with us, saving and defending those who believe. This is the fulfillment of the first table. Likewise, he conceives good affections of every kind, thus he obeys the second table, for the Spirit is given holy, who produces new movements in souls and new works.

Latin:

Caput III.

Hic vero magna difficilisque quaestio exori- tur. Nam cum pariter condemnet Iudaeos ac gentes, necesse est quaerere, quid conducat lex, cur Iudaei populus Dei vocentur. Si lex non iu- stificat, quare lata est? Si Iudaei non praestant gentibus, quare vocantur populus Dei? Nihilne inter Iudaeos ac gentes interest? Inseritur igitur paucis verbis haec quaestio. Ad quam bifariam respondet: Et quod mireris, videntur respon- siones inter se pugnare. Primum ait, Iudaeos multum praestare gentibus. Deinde velut retra- ctans proximam sententiam inquit, Iudaei nihil praestant gentibus.

Sed intelligemus has sententias non pugnare inter se, si consideraverimus ubi praestent Iu- daei, ubi non praestent. Excellunt, inquit, quod ad promissiones attinet. Nam est aliquid habere verbum, ac promissiones ad eos pertinere. Cae- terum nihil excellunt Iudaei, quod ad meritum attinet. Non enim iustificatur suo cultu, aut operibus legis. Nondum tamen satis explicat hanc quaestionem, cur lata sit lex, tantum obi- ter et in transcursu attingit, et significat Iudaeos a gentibus separatos esse, non ut isto cultu me- rerentur iusticiam, sed quia oportuit existere cer- tum aliquem populum, in quo promissiones de Christo revelarentur, in quo testimonia de verbo Dei manifesta et certa extarent, infra Cap. 5. et Cap. 7. latius exponet, quod lex non sit lata, ut iustificet.

Obiter etiam quaestiones aliae quaedam in- seruntur. Si promissiones pertinent ad Iudaeos, cur tam pauci crediderunt? Hanc quaestionem infra in cap. 9. repetit. Nunc velut intempesti- vam omittit ac properat ad principalem proposi- tionem, ne videatur oblitus instituti sui. Ac sane prudentia est videre quomodo paulisper eva- gatus redeat ad propositum.

Hic ergo recurrit ad membra distributionis, et ut in Epilogo seu conclusione fieri debet, con- iungit utrumque membrum: Omnes homines tum Iudaei, tum gentes sunt sub paccato, id est, sunt rei mortis aeternae, habent vere peccatum, contemtum Dei, et concupiscentiam. Nec pos- sumus a peccato, aut aeterna morte liberari no- stris operibus, aut lege. Addit testimonia ex Psalmo et aliunde. Et in fine est addita proposi- tionis interpretatio quaedam, ut intelligamus non tantum aperte flagitiosos accusari, sed etiam illos ipsos, qui bonis operibus conantur mereri iusti- ficationem. Ideo inquit: Ex operibus legis non iustificatur omnis caro. Hanc sententiam in pri- mis oportet meminisse, quia nonnulli hunc Pauli locum civiliter interpretari conantur, et dispu- tant Paulum non hoc velle, quod omnes homines natura sint sub peccato, sed tantum accusare illos, quorum mores aperte mali sunt. Et quia magna huiusmodi multitudo est, aiunt eum sy- necdoche uti, et omnes arguere, cum interim ali- qui boni sint, quorum mores non possint repre- hendi, ut Pomponius Atticus, Aristides hos con- tendunt naturae viribus et operibus iustificari. Sed Paulus hanc calumniam refutat, ac ne quis synecdochen comminisci posset, exceptionem di- serte repudiat, et illam hominum partem revocat ad universalem propositionem: Omnes sunt sub peccato. Et quo clarior esset res, non de perso- nis loquitur, sed de re, quae exceptionem vide- tur parere. Ex operibus legis, inquit, nemo iustificatur. Non poterat magis proprie loqui Apostolus. Et in tanta proprietate sermonis, ta- men quaerunt isti quod cavillentur. Hoc ipsum, inquit, quod excipis ego complector, ego accuso, ego damno. Itaque contra Pauli sententiam hoc loco synecdochen confingunt. Sed error inde oritur, quod somniant in Pomponio Attico et si- milibus non esse peccatum. Et iusticiam Dei vo- cant tantum civiles mores, non etiam requirunt noticiam Dei, fidem seu fiduciam erga Deum, bre- viter operibus secundae tabulae contenti sunt, primae tabulae οὐδεὶς λόγος. Non sentiunt pec- cata esse in Attico, ignorationem Dei, diffidere Deo, vacare metu Dei, confidere propria pru- dentia etc.

Accedit brevissima occupatio de usu legis. Necesse est enim lectori non stulto in mentem ve- nire hanc quaestionem. Quod si legis opera non iustificant, cur igitur lata est lex? videtur extreme absurdum, legem ferre, si legis opera non iustifi- cant. Paulus respondet et novam ac inauditam mundo sententiam ponit. Lex lata est, ut per eam cognoscatur peccatum, ut arguat peccatum, non ut aboleat. Porro cognoscere peccatum est vere terreri conspectu peccati. Nondum enim no- runt peccatum, qui non expavescunt: nondum enim apud se vere sentiunt, quod Deus offensus irascatur. At peccatum est, quod offendit Deum, et cui Deus succenset. Sed de usu legis infra co- piose docebit lectorem.

Status totius Epistolae.

Nunc demum pervenit ad principalem pro- positionem, quae est huius totius Epistolae status. Ut autem architectus totam aedificii formam in animo inclusam habet, et videt quomodo omnes inter se partes consentiant. Ita nos in legendis gravibus disputationibus, omnium propositionum atque argumentorum seriem oportet animo com- plecti. In primis autem meminisse statum necesse est, qui continet negotii summam, ad quem omnia argumenta tanquam ad caput referuntur. Et quem- admodum illi, qui iaculantur ad certum scopum dirigunt telum, ita omnis animi cogitatio ad sta- tum, velut ad scopum dirigenda est. Proinde in hac Epistola inprimis observandus est hic locus, haec principalis est totius causae propositio, haec definitio est Christianae iusticiae, quod iusticia sit credere, quod propter Christum in gratiam patris recipiamur, quod Christus sit redemtor et propiciatorium, quod propter eum gratis, sine nostris meritis iustificemur, si credamus.

Propositio aliquanto pluribus verbis vestita est. Accedunt enim circumstantiae. Haec iu- sticia quae patefit in Evangelio, olim et a Prophe- tis praedicata est. Item ex contrario. Christus apparuit sine lege.

Est et haec particula inter insignes huius Epistolae sententias magnopere observanda, quod sine lege revelata sit iusticia Dei. Docet autem non venisse Christum, ut legem ferret, ut per nostra opera mereremur iusticiam: sed venisse, ut gratis sine nostris meritis credentes iustificaret. Memini scholasticos anxie quaerere, quas leges praeter decalogum antea revelatum, Christus tu- lerit. Atqui nulla nova lex quaerenda est. Hic manifeste Paulus separat ab Evangelio legem, ac docet Christum adferre iusticiam gratis sine no- stris meritis, Christum non esse legislatorem, sed redemtorem. Lex per Moisen data est, per Chri- stum donatur remissio peccatorum et Spiritus san- ctus. Addita est circumstantia etiam, ad quos pertineat iusticia revelata in Evangelio. Ait enim in omnes, et super omnes credentes, et repetit primam propositionem, omnes peccaverunt, et omnes sunt vacui gloria Dei, id est, noticia Dei, fiducia erga Deum. Sumsit ornamentum etiam ex typis. Christus est propositus, ut sit propi- ciatorium, sed per fidem, quasi dicat, Christum esse verum illud propiciatorium, per quod patet aditus ad patrem. Sicut apud propiciatorium in tabernaculo promiserat Deus, se auditurum esse vota et preces pontificis: sed cesso omnes propo- sitionis circumstantias recitare. Non enim scribo commentarium. Caeterum meminerit lector pro- positionis summam, et eam dialectico more com- prehendat. Iusticia coram Deo est, credere quod propter Christum donetur nobis sine nostris meritis iusticia, et remissio peccatorum. Atque haec definitio est iusticiae Christianae. Sic enim docendi causa vocabimus, cum Paulus vocet iu- sticiam Dei, scilicet, qua nos coram Deo iusti sumus, seu qua nos Deus reputat iustos. Clarius haec intelligentur cum definietur etiam humana iusticia seu civilis iusticia, quae colligitur nostris viribus et operibus, et cum fiet comparatio defi- nitionum. Quantae autem consolationes in hoc loco territis conscientiis propositae sint, nulla vox humana pro dignitate explicare potest. Etiamsi desint opera, tamen credamus nos propter Chri- stum a patre in gratiam recipi gratis. Nam haec iusticia sine lege patefit, blasphemia est in Chri- stum, et propiciatorii prophanatio, non accipere consolationem, non erigi, oblata per Christum iusticia, sed desperare, quia desint nobis opera bona. Est et blasphemia eligere opera hac spe et opinione, ut per ea iustificemur. In hanc sen- tentiam sequitur amplificatio, exclusa est glo- riatio.

Sumta est autem amplificatio propositionis ex finali causa. Si opera legis iustificarent, finis operum esset mereri gratiam. Esset et fiducia no- stri seu gloriatio finis. Nunc cessante causa, ut aiunt, cessat effectus: operibus nostris adimitur iustificatio. Ergo adimitur nobis fiducia nostri, et gloriatio. Non ideo magis meretur iustificari Ioannes quam Magdalena, quia Ioannes conti- nenter vixit. Atque hic obiter repetitur propo- sitio: Arbitramur hominem iustificari fide, et ex- cludit contrarium, sine operibus legis. Ad hunc modum detrahit fiduciam nostris operibus et sa- tisfactionibus. Sequeretur enim fiducia nostri, tanquam finis, opera si iustificarent.

Brevis occupatio addita est: Num abolemus legem? Nam omnibus sanis hominibus, cum au- diunt non mereri nos operibus iusticiam, non magis Ioannem mereri iusticiam, quam Magdale- nam: necesse est in mentem venire, quod liceat turpiter vivere, quod lex ita aboleatur, ut pec- candi licentia concedatur. Paulus breviter re- spondet ad hanc obiectionem, nam infra eadem quaestio copiose tractabitur. Imo inquit, non abo- lemus legem, sed perficimus, quia lex requirit a nobis iusticiam coram Deo. At qui in Christum credit, iam est iustus coram Deo, habet ergo le- gis finem, tametsi peccatum adhuc in carne hae- reat. Et tamen idem vere iam agnoscit Deum, vere sentit Deum nobis adesse, servare ac defen- dere credentes. Haec primae tabulae impletio est. Item concipit omnis generis bonos affectus, ita secundae tabulae obedit, datur enim Spiritus sanctus, qui novos motus in animis et nova opera parit.

## 3:1 Argument
Chapter III. In what, therefore, does he excel the Jews?

A question is inserted incidentally. And the occasion must be diligently observed, which I have recounted. For from there this question arises. Since the Jews do not merit remission, nor are they righteous by the law, why was the Law given? And in what do they excel the Gentiles, from where they are rather the people of God than the Gentiles?

He answers this question in two ways. For he retains his proposition, that the Jews do not merit the remission of sins, nor are they righteous by the law. But he narrates other causes why that most beautiful polity was established, and whence Israel is the people of God. And first he says that the descendants of Abraham are the people of God, because the promise was handed down to them, and it certainly pertains to them. Therefore, they are the people of God on account of the promise, and not on account of the law. And the chief benefit is the promise of the Messiah, not the polity or the promulgation of the law. But yet, even afterwards, a huge benefit was the very constitution of the polity, which served the promise, because God willed there to be a certain place, a certain nation and family, in which he would reveal himself, where he would issue and repeat promises, and show the testimonies of the promise, where there would be some public assembly invoking the true God, and testifying concerning the true God, where the Messiah would be born, would be seen, would teach, would issue testimonies of his doctrine, would become a victim, would be resurrected from the dead, where the testimonies of the resurrection would be seen.

God willed there to be a certain seat for these greatest things, and known and trustworthy witnesses. This is the principal cause why that polity was established, and many benefits concur. There, very many examples of the presence of God, of wrath and mercy, were seen. There, many wondrous defenses and liberations were made. How glorious was the continuous succession of Prophets, of Samuel, David, Elijah, Elisha, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, and those following? And this was most pleasing to good minds, that there was a certain seat of the Church, a certain and perpetual school of true doctrine. What a degree would it now be for good minds to know that these strongholds were to remain for posterity for a long time, and that the seat of the Church and of doctrine was to remain here?

All sane people understand that these things are the greatest.

PAUL'S EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS. CHAPTER III. The years are from the exodus out of Egypt up to the resurrection of Christ, 1545. That the Church and the seat of doctrine remained in the same footprint for so long was a huge good. For these reasons, the elders understood that the Mosaic polity had been established. For in order for the people to be certain, it was necessary that they be distinguished from other nations by political bonds and rites. And in the rites, elegance of exercises and signs that were types of the promise were added. Therefore, Paul in the first promise prefers the Jews far above the Gentiles. He says that they had been adorned with the most ample benefits above others, which we have already recited very briefly.

And there are significant weights to the words. He says that they excel much and in all ways, because it is most true that there was a great amplitude of benefits, of which I spoke, the chief of which he says here is this: That to this family, that is, to the descendants of Abraham, the promise of the Messiah was handed down. Where he also used a significant word, the Promises were commended to them, or entrusted, that is, they themselves were made guardians of the promises. And it was a huge prerogative that the promise should sound in this family. And there are always some true members of the eternal Church there, where the voice of the promise sounds, just as it is often said elsewhere, that in the assembly of the called there are always some elect.

But immediately another response must be added. The Jews did not excel as far as merit is concerned, that is, they neither deserved the remission of sins, nor were they just by the law before God, but those who were reconciled to God were received by faith on account of the promised Messiah, and by faith they were just.

Latin:

Caput III. Qua igitur re antecellit Iudaeis?

Obiter inserta est quaestio. Et occasio diligenter observanda est, quam recitavi. Inde enim oritur haec quaestio. Cum Iudaei non mereantur remissionem, nec sint iusti lege, cur data est Lex? et qua re antecellunt Gentibus, unde potius ipsi sint populus Dei, quam Gentes.

De hac quaestione dupliciter respondet. Retinet enim suam propositionem, quod Iudaei non mereantur remissionem peccatorum, nec sint iusti lege. Sed causas alias narrat, cur pulcerrima illa politia constituta sit, et unde sit Israëli populus Dei. Ac primum ait, posteros Abrahae esse populus Dei, quia promissio ipsis tradita est, et certo ad eos pertinet. Sunt igitur populus Dei propter promissionem, et non propter legem. Ac praecipuum beneficium est, promissio Messiae, non politia seu legis promulgatio. Sed tamen et postea ingens beneficium fuit ipsa politiae constitutio, quae servivit promissioni, quia voluit Deus certum locum, certam nationem et familiam esse, in qua se patefaceret, ubi promissiones ederet et repeteret, et ostenderet promissionis testimonia, ubi publicus aliquis coetus esset invocans verum Deum, et testificans de vero Deo, ubi Messias nasceretur, conspiceretur, doceret, ederet testimonia doctrinae, fieret victima, resuscitaretur ex mortuis, ubi conspicerentur testimonia resurrectionis.

Harum maximarum rerum Deus certam sedem, et notos ac fide dignos testes esse voluit. Haec est principalis causa, cur politia illa constituta sit, et multa beneficia concurrunt. Ibi exempla plurima praesentiae Dei, irae et misericordiae conspecta sunt. Ibi multae mirandae defensiones et liberationes factae sunt. Quam gloriosa fuit continua Prophetarum successio, Samuelis, Davidis, Eliae, Elisaei, Esaiae, Ieremiae, Danielis et sequentium? Gratissimum et hoc fuit, bonis mentibus, certam esse Ecclesiae sedem, certam et perpetuam scholam verae doctrinae. Quam gradum nunc bonus mentibus esset, scire ad posteros diu haec oppida mansura esse, et hic Ecclesiae et doctrinae sedem mansuram esse?

Has res esse maximas omnes sani intelligunt.

PAULI AD ROMANOS. CAP. III. Anni sunt ab exitu ex Aegypto usque ad resurrectionem Christi 1545. Tam diu in eodem vestigio mansisse Ecclesiam et doctrinae sedem, fuit ingens bonum. Propter has causas intelligebant seniores politiam Mosaicam constitutam esse. Nam ut certus esset populus, discerni eum politicis vinculis et ritibus ab aliis gentibus oportuit. Et in ritibus elegantia exercitia, et signa quae essent typi promissionis addita sunt. Itaque Paulus in prima promissione longe antefert Iudaeos Gentibus. Dicit, eos amplissimis beneficiis prae aliis ornatos fuisse, quae iam brevissime recitavimus.

Et sunt insignia verborum pondera. Dicit, multum et omnibus modis antecellere, quia verissimum est, magnam fuisse amplitudinem beneficiorum, de quibus dixi, quorum praecipuum ipse hic esse inquit: Quod huic familiae, id est, posteris Abrahae, tradita est promissio Messiae. Ubi etiam insigni verbo usus est, Promissiones sunt commendatae eis, seu creditae, id est, ipsi facti sunt custodes promissionum. Et fuit ingens praerogativa, sonare in hac familia promissionem. Et semper ibi aliqua sunt vera membra aeternae Ecclesiae, ubi vox promissionis sonat, sicut alias saepe dicitur, In coetu vocatorum semper aliquos esse electos.

Sed statim adiungenda est et altera responsio. Non antecelluerunt Iudaei, quod ad meritum attinet, id est, nec merebantur remissionem peccatorum, nec erant iusti lege coram Deo, sed illi, qui Deo reconciliati sunt, fide propter promissam Messiam recepti sunt, et fide iusti erant.

## 3:2
What then, even if some did not believe.

He inserts other questions, as happens in difficult controversies. When he had said that the promise of grace was handed down to Abraham and his descendants, he asks whether it is valid, since there are and have been so many impious people who have spurned it? He answers that the promise is valid, even if very many do not believe.

Consider, however, that here a necessary consolation is proposed to us, against a common temptation, which strongly attacks faith with this argument: Since so many others perish, do you think you are received by God ahead of many? Here Paul opposes the promise of God with examples, and an immovable argument, that God is truthful. Let us therefore establish most certainly that the promise is valid for all who believe, as is said below. Therefore, it is by faith freely, so that the promise may be firm.

However, sayings from the Psalms are cited here, so that the antithesis may increase clarity. God is truthful, but every man is a liar. For God keeps his promises, even to the unworthy, on account of his truth and goodness. Every man is a liar, that is, either doubting entirely, or struggling with many doubts, neither fearing greatly, nor believing God firmly. For even in the saints, the remnants of these vices remain.

Latin:

Quid enim, etiamsi aliqui non crediderunt.

Inserit et alias quaestiones, ut fit in difficilibus controversiis. Cum dixisset, promissionem gratiae traditam esse Abrahae et eius posteris, quaerit, an rata sit, cum tam multi sint et fuerint impii, qui eam aspernati sunt? Respondet, promissionem ratam esse, etiamsi plurimi non credunt.

Consideres autem, hic necessariam consolationem nobis proponi, contra vulgarem tentationem, quae valde oppugnat fidem hoc argumento: Cum alii tam multi pereant, num te putes a Deo prae multis recipi? Hic exemplis Paulus opponit promissionem Dei, et immotum argumentum, quod Deus sit verax. Statuamus igitur certissime ratam esse promissionem omnibus credentibus, ut infra dicitur. Ideo ex fide gratis, ut firma sit promissio.

Citantur autem hic dicta ex Psalmis, ut antithesis augeat perspicuitatem. Deus est verax, omnis autem homo mendax. Servat enim Deus promissa, etiam indignis, propter suam veritatem et bonitatem. Omnis homo mendax, id est, vel prorsus dubitans, vel multis dubitationibus conflictans, nec valde timens, nec firmiter credens Deo. Nam et in sanctis horum vitiorum reliquiae maneant.

## 3:4
That you may be justified, and may win when you are judged.

He adds another testimony, which takes away from us the dignity or glory of justice and merits. This verse contains both the necessary doctrine concerning the confession of our unworthiness, and the sweetest consolation. I am only a sinner before you, or something guilty and worthy of punishment, which I confess, so that you may be pronounced just when you punish, and may win when you are judged, that is, when hypocrites judge you: just as almost all men in their clamors think that God is either unjust or cruel, and that he burdens this weak nature with excessively great miseries. Many also rage, when they have been well-deserving, like Saul, or have defended more just causes, like Cato, and yet they are oppressed by calamities, just as Pompey, Cato, and Brutus questioned providence.

But Daniel cries out: To you, O Lord, is justice, but to us confusion of face. And Job says: I know truly that a man cannot be justified compared to God, etc. Even if he kills me, I will hope in him. Nevertheless, I will argue my ways in his sight, and he himself will be my savior, and no hypocrite will come into his sight, that is, he who wants to approach by his own justice. And the Emperor Maurice says: You are just, O Lord, and your judgment is right.

When therefore, says David: That you may win when you are judged, he looks at the hypocrites accusing God of injustice or cruelty, and shows that the confession of the Church attributes the praise of Justice to God, and therefore performs obedience in some voluntary way in punishments, according to that: Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God. Item: Pray without anger and without hesitation.

These things concerning the doctrine of confession in this verse are to be considered first. Afterwards, let it be learned and 54 consolation. We confess that we are unworthy and guilty, and yet we are received on account of the promise. Thus we attribute to God the praise of Truth, which hypocrites do not attribute to Him, but think that they are neglected because they do not bring enough merits. But you should know that one must approach God with the confidence of a mediator, according to the promise. Even if you bring great sins and great uncleanness, grace nevertheless abounds over the transgression, and the truthful God, who promised that He would receive us freely on account of the mediator, prevails. Both sentiments regarding confession and consolation become illustrious in words of sorrow and true repentance. But if our injustice commends the justice of God, what shall we say?

Other objections follow, of which this is the sentiment: When men hear that our works and this diligence of whatever kind in governing our morals do not merit the remission of sins, but that sins are remitted freely, and that not only the frugal but also the prodigal son is received, they object with these absurdities: If this great and heavy labor of governing morals does not merit remission, let us rather loosen the reins to our desires, especially if the glory of mercy becomes more illustrious. Because those polluted with great sins are received, as the reception of the prodigal son shows. This profane objection was not only opposed to the doctrine of Grace at that time, but these arguments disturb human reason in all ages. And it is to be lamented that even good men become more negligent in restraining themselves, when the opinion of merit is taken away from that diligence. But since these profane objections are merely calumnies, and the pious know that license to sin is not granted on that account, Paul breaks off these questions with a brief and sad rebuke: Whose condemnation is just, namely of those who by such calumnies obscure the immense mercy of God, etc.

But below in chapter 6, he will respond to this objection. Meanwhile, it is enough to know that license to sin is not granted, but that God is truly and horribly angry at sins. And therefore we are received freely, so that sin may be destroyed, not so that it may be confirmed. These things will be explained more copiously below. Now Paul returns to the principal subject.

What then excels? Another and principal negative response is that the Jews do not merit the remission of sins by their works, nor are they just before God, nor do they please God on account of their works.

And a universal proposition is added, collected from the two preceding ones: All men in this depravity of nature are by nature under sin, that is, they are guilty of the wrath of God and eternal punishment, and are so captive that they cannot be liberated from it by their own merits, or by the observation of the law. For the phrase must be understood: To be under sin is to be a captive of sin. And he speaks of all, except our Lord Jesus Christ. He speaks of all others, and even of the saints, insofar as their nature is considered, and they are not understood to be reconciled through mercy. But may this equalization always admonish us, that the proud are accused and terrified. On the contrary, consolation is proposed to the terrified, because the amplitude of mercy is seen, when this discourse affirms that we are truly received freely, on account of the mediator, although we are unworthy and polluted by sins. He confirms the proposition with cited testimonies, in which not only external transgressions are accused, but also internal ones. There is none that understands nor seeks after God, that is, hearts in this depravity of nature are full of darkness and doubts about God, What He is, How He wishes to be known?

Whether He cares, Whether He hears us? They do not truly fear wrath and judgment, they are full of distrust, they seek human protections without order, they love themselves more than God, etc. Innumerable men think with horrible audacity that it is a game of wits to generate their own certain opinions about God, as the Stoics feigned one thing, the Idolaters another, the Heretics another. In short, there always has been, and will be, a horrible confusion of opinions about God. The divine voice often and most justly accuses these shadows in the nature of men, about which these sayings also discourse, in which there is great atrocity of words: With their tongues they have dealt deceitfully, the poison of asps is under their lips. But it must be most diligently observed that he repeats the universal proposition, with a notable figure and emphasis of words, so that every mouth may be stopped, and the whole world may be guilty before God. Let us fix this universal proposition in our minds, and let us acknowledge that we ourselves are guilty, and let us oppose it to the Pelagians and monks, and the like, who feign that man merits remission by his works, or is just by his own merits.

Let us also acknowledge, truly that it is the will of God that we believe we are received on account of the mediator, although we are unworthy and polluted by sins. With this consolation we sustain ourselves, and let us exercise this faith in true repentance and invocation.

Latin:

Ut iu iustificeris, ut vincas cum iudicaris.

Addit aliud testimonium, quod detrahit nobis dignitatem seu gloriam iustitiae et meritorum. Continet autem hic versus et doctrinam necessariam de confessione nostrae indignitatis, et dulcissimam consolationem. Tibi tantum sum peccator, seu quiddam reum et dignum poena, quod fateor, ut tu iustus pronuncieris cum punis, et vincas cum iudicaris, id est, cum te hypocritae iudicant: sicut fere omnes homines in clamitatibus cogitant, Deum vel iniustum vel crudelem esse, et hanc imbecillem naturam nimis magnis aerumnis onerare. Multi etiam fremunt, cum sint benemeriti, ut Saul, vel causas iustiores defenderint, ut Cato, et tamen se opprimi calamitatibus, sicut Pompeius, Cato, Brutus, de providentia quaesti sunt.

Sed Daniel clamitat: Tibi Domine iusticia, nobis autem confusio faciei nostrae. Et Iob inquit: Vere scio, quod non iustificetur homo comparatus Deo etc. Etiamsi occiderit me, in eo sperabo. Veruntamen vias meas in conspectu eius arguam, et ipse erit salvator meus, nec veniet in conspectu eius omnis hypocrita, id est, qui vult accedere sua iusticia. Et imperator Mauricius inquit: Iustus es Domine, et rectum iudicium tuum.

Cum igitur inquit David: Ut vincas cum iudicaris, intuetur hypocritas accusantes Deum iniusticiae vel crudelitatis, et ostendit, Ecclesiae confessionem Deo tribuere laudem Iusticiae, et propterea obedientiam aliquo modo voluntariam in poenis praestare, iuxta illud: Humiliamini sub potenti manu Dei. Item: Orate sine ira et sine haesitatione.

Haec de doctrina confessionis in hoc versu primum consideranda sunt. Postea discatur et 54 consolatio. Fatemur nos indignos et reos esse, et recipi tamen propter promissionem. Ita Deo laudem Veritatis tribuimus, quam hypocritae non tribuunt ei, sed cogitant se negligi, quia non satis meritorum afferunt. Tu vero scias accedendum esse ad Deum fiducia mediatoris, iuxta promissionem. Etiamsi affers magna peccata et magnam immunditiem, exuberat tamen gratia supra delictum, et vincit Deus verax, qui promisit, se recepturum nos gratis propter mediatorem. Utraque sententia de confessione et consolatione fit illustris in verbis doloribus et vera poenitentia. Si autem iniusticia nostra commendat iusticiam Dei, quid dicemus?

Sequuntur aliae obiectiones, quarum haec est sententia: Cum audiunt homines, nostra opera et hanc qualemcunque diligentiam regendi mores, non mereri remissionem peccatorum, sed gratis remitti peccata, nec solum frugalem, sed etiam filium prodigum recipi, obiiciunt haec absurda: Si hic magnus et gravis labor regendi mores non meretur remissionem, laxemus potius frenos cupiditatibus, praesertim si gloria misericordiae fit illustrior. Quia polluti magnis peccatis recipiuntur, ut ostendit receptio filii prodigi. Haec profana obiectio non tunc solum opponebatur doctrinae de Gratia, sed omnibus temporibus haec argumenta turbant humanam rationem. Et dolendum est, bonos etiam fieri negligentiores in seipsis frenandis, cum opinio meriti detracta est illi diligentiae. Cum autem hae profanae obiectiones tantum sint calumniae, et pii sciant, non propterea concedi licentiam peccandi, abrumpit Paulus has quaestiones, opposita brevi et tristi obiurgatione: Quorum damnatio iusta est, videlicet eorum, qui talibus calumniis immensam misericordiam Dei obscurant etc.

Infra autem cap. 6. respondebit ad hanc obiectionem. Interea satis est sciri, non concedi licentiam peccandi, sed Deum vere et horribiliter irasci peccatis. Ideo autem recipi nos gratis, ut deleatur peccatum, non ut confirmetur. Haec infra copiosius exponentur.

Nunc redit Paulus ad principale institutum. Quid igitur praecellit.

Altera et principalis responsio negativa est, Iudaei non merentur remissionem peccatorum suis operibus, nec sunt iusti coram Deo, nec placent Deo propter sua opera. Et additur universalis propositio, collecta ex duabus praecedentibus: Omnes homines in hac naturae depravatione secundum naturam sunt sub peccato, id est, sunt rei irae Dei et poenae aeternae, et ita captivi, ut non possint ab eo liberari propriis meritis, seu observatione legis. Cognoscenda est enim phrasis: Sub peccato esse, est captivum peccati esse. Ac loquitur de omnibus, excepto Domino nostro Iesu Christo. De aliis omnibus loquitur, ac de sanctis etiam, quatenus natura eorum consideratur, nec intelliguntur per misericordiam reconciliati. Semper autem haec exaequatio nos admoneat, accusari superbos et perterrefieri. Econtra vero consolationem proponi perterrefactis, quia conspicitur amplitudo misericordiae, cum affirmat haec concio, vere recipi nos gratis, propter mediatorem, quanquam indigni simus, et polluti peccatis. Confirmat autem propositionem citatis testimoniis, in quibus accusantur non tantum externa delicta, sed etiam interiora.

Non est intelligens nec requirens Deum, id est, corda in hac pravitate naturae plena sunt caliginis et dubitationum de Deo, Quid sit, Quomodo velit agnosci? An curet, An exaudiat nos? Non vere timent iram et indicium, sunt plena diffidentiae, quaerunt praesidia humana sine ordine, sese amant plus quam Deum etc. Innumirabiles homines horribili audacia ludum ingeniorum esse putant, gignere suas quasdam opiniones de Deo, ut aliud fingebant Stoici, aliud Idolatrae, aliud Haeretici. Denique semper fuit, et erit horribilis confusio opinionum de Deo. Has tenebras in natura hominum saepe et iustissime accusat vox divina, de quibus et haec dicta concionantur, in quibus magna est verborum atrocitas: Linguis suis dolose agebant, Venenum aspidum sub labiis eorum. Diligentissime autem observandum est, quod repetit universalem propositionem, insigni figura et verborum emphasi, ut omne os obturetur, et reus sit totus mundus Deo.

Hanc universalem propositionem infigamus animis, et ut nos ipsos reos esse agnoscamus, et ut opponamus eam Pelagianis et monachis, et similibus, fingentibus, hominem mereri remissionem suis operibus, aut iustum esse propriis meritis. Agnoscamus etiam, vere voluntatem Dei esse, ut nos propter mediatorem recipi credamus, quanquam sumus indigni et polluti peccatis. Hac nos consolatione sustenemus, et hanc fidem in vera poenitentia et invocatione exerceamus.

## 3:20
Because by the works of the law no flesh is justified.

A manifest assertion it is, that the works of the law do not merit the remission of sins, nor are men on account of them just before God, that is, accepted unto eternal life. But others have eluded this statement in other ways. Many have said that Paul speaks only of Ceremonies, not of moral works. No one shall be justified by the works of the law, namely, the ceremonial ones. But this evasion is false, because Paul speaks of all parts of the law, as he takes an example below from the moral law: Thou shalt not covet. Nay, men do not satisfy the moral law in the least.

Others elude it thus, they say it is a synecdoche, which accuses many, not all. There are few, they say, because few obey the law. Meanwhile, however, some are just, such as Pomponius Atticus, Fabius, Scipio, because they obey the law. This synecdoche Paul himself clearly refutes, because he explicitly not only accuses persons, but strips justice from the works themselves, as if he were saying: I speak of these very things, who do the works of the law, I deny that these are just on account of these works.

Let therefore the so often repeated sentences be gathered, which expressly affirm the same, that men do not merit the remission of sins by their own works, nor are they just before God on account of this or that observation of the law, and let the false opinions of Pelagius and the monks be constantly rejected, which have corrupted the doctrine of the Church, and have feigned that men merit the remission of sins, and are just by this discipline, or by whatever fulfillment of the law that men can perform.

But Paul explicitly adds these words: Before God, that he may warn that he speaks of the judgment of God, not of human judgment. The wrath of God is not taken away by our works, nor does this our justice merit the remission of sins, nor does it satisfy the law of God, just as the Psalm also says: In thy sight shall no man living be justified.

Latin:

Propterea quod ex operibus legis non iustificatur omnis caro.

Manifesta asseveratio est, opera legis non mereri remissionem peccatorum, nec propter ea homines iustos esse coram Deo, id est, acceptos ad vitam aeternam. Eluserunt autem hoc dictum alii aliter. Multi dixerunt, Paulum loqui tantum de Ceremoniis, non de moralibus operibus. Nemo iustificabitur ex operibus legis scilicet ceremonialibus. Sed haec elusio falsa est, quia Paulus de omnibus partibus legis loquitur, ut infra sumit exemplum ex lege morali: Non concupisces. Imo legi morali minime satisfaciunt homines.

Alii sic eludunt, dicunt synecdochen esse, quae accuset plurimos, non omnes. Pauci sunt, inquiunt, quia pauci obtemperant legi. Interea tamen aliqui iusti sunt, ut Pomponius Atticus, Fabius, Scipio, quia legi obtemperant. Hanc synecdochen perspicue refutat ipse Paulus, quia diserte non solum personas accusat, sed ipsis operibus detrahit iusticiam, quasi dicat: De his ipsis loquor, qui faciunt opera legis, hos nego iustos esse propter haec opera.

Colligantur ergo toties repetitae sententiae, quae idem expresse affirmant, non mereri homines remissionem peccatorum propriis operibus, nec iustos esse propter hanc qualemcunque legis observationem coram Deo, et constanter reiiciantur Pelagii et monachorum falsae opiniones, quae doctrinam Ecclesiae corruperunt, et finxerunt homines mereri remissionem peccatorum, et iustos esse hac disciplina, seu qualicunque legis impletione, quam efficere homines possunt.

Diserte autem addit Paulus haec verba: Coram Deo, ut moneat se de iudicio Dei loqui, non de humano iudicio. Non tollitur ira Dei nostris operibus, nec meretur remissionem peccatorum haec nostra iusticia, nec satisfacit legi Dei, sicut et Psalmus inquit: Non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens.

## 3:20
For by the law is the knowledge of sin.

An objection is briefly inserted concerning the use of the law, of which he will speak copiously later in chapter 7. For it could be asked: If the law does not profit unto justice, why was it given? Certainly, lawmakers propose laws for this reason, that citizens may become better, and those who obey, they name just, that is, they approve.

To this question he responds: Nay, he says, the divine law exists, that it may be a testimony of the judgment of God, showing what sins are in the human race.

This wisdom is unlike political wisdom, because it is true that in empires laws are established, not only that they may show sins, but that they may take them away, namely, external crimes. But the divine law prohibits interior uncleanness. This it judges and accuses before God, it does not take it away. Therefore these Pauline sayings are by no means to be mixed with political wisdom. A far different matter is treated here, namely, Whether the wrath of God is taken away by our works, or by the law.

It must be known, however, that there are three uses of the law, which we customarily distinguish thus to instruct the younger ones.

The first use is political or pedagogical, which is the knowledge of the law, ruling the external members either by fear or by whatever habituation, so that external actions do not fight against the law: as because a citizen thinks of the commandment, Thou shalt not kill, and fears the punishment, by this thought he stirs the nerves, so that the hands may be restrained, lest they kill an enemy, even if he hates him. We often say that this discipline or locomotive government is necessary even in the unregenerate, and the human will has in some way the freedom to stir the nerves, so that they may move or restrain the members, as these things are copiously declared in physical doctrine. Achilles can command his nerves, so that his hands may return the sword to the scabbard. And this discipline is a thought in the mind and brain, which commands the nerves, so that the external members may be moved thus. Nor is it the justice of the heart, nor is it the fulfillment of the law, but the letter, namely, a thought as if painted in the brain, thus ruling the external members. But we clearly affirm that this discipline neither merits the remission of sins, nor is it justice before God. And we say it is necessary for this reason: because it is necessary to obey God, who also commands this discipline to all. Furthermore, it is necessary for avoiding bodily punishments in this life. But Paul does not speak of this use in this Epistle. Elsewhere he indicates this use, when he says: The law is good if one uses it lawfully. And these things are often copiously declared elsewhere.

The second use is spiritual Judgment, of which Paul says: The law is spiritual, that is, the judgment if the hearts agree with the Law of God. Circumcision profits, if you observe the Law. Here it must be observed that these false persuasions about ceremonies are always vagrant in the world, either that they merit the remission of sins, or that they are acts of worship, and please God, even without the righteousness of the heart: and as is commonly said, ex opere operato [by the work performed], just as the monks impudently wrote concerning the oblation in the mass.

Therefore, in all ages in the Church, some have censured this error, as in Psalm 50: "I will not reprove you for your sacrifices."

And Jeremiah 7: "I did not command them concerning burnt offerings, but I commanded this word: Hear my voice, and I will be your God." It has been said often elsewhere, in what order ceremonies please, and I pictured a ship, and in the ship a book, and upon the book a chalice, that is: First, the promise concerning the Son of God must be heard, and by faith it must be established that you are accepted through him. This faith begins new obedience, in the heart love, hope, invocation, and other virtues.

Then the ceremonies follow, as signs, which remind us of the promise, or exercises of external ministry, of invocation, of thanksgiving, etc., as has been said more copiously elsewhere. But from this, the harshest struggles always have been and will be in the Church.

Hypocrites rage furiously when the opinion of merit is taken away from ceremonies. As the Jews shouted: If we are not righteous by the Law, why was the Law given?

To this question Paul soon responds, and the explanation is necessary, because this question is agitated in all times: If our diligence does not merit the remission of sins, why is discipline demanded?

Item: If we are not righteous because of our own virtues, why is license not granted to our desires? Therefore, at the beginning of the third Chapter, Paul moves this question: What then does the Jew have, by which he excels?

Why was the Law given? Why was the polity of Moses established? Why are we called the people of God, if we are not righteous by this observation? Concerning these questions, it is necessary that true and clear doctrine exist in the Church, and that those foul ravings be rejected, which invented three laws: the first of Nature, the second of Moses, the third Evangelical, and that at any time men were righteous by the observation of their own law.

Against these pernicious errors, it must be known, as is often said, that there is one eternal moral law, which accuses sin in all, at all times: and that the fathers were not righteous by the law, but by faith in the mediator, whom they acknowledged from the promise.

Chapter III.

By what then does he excel the Jews?

An incidental question is inserted. And the occasion must be diligently observed, which I have recited. For from there this question arises. Since the Jews do not merit remission, nor are they righteous by the Law, why was the Law given? And by what do they excel the Gentiles, whence they are rather the people of God than the Gentiles.

He responds to this question in two ways.

He retains his proposition, that the Jews do not merit the remission of sins, nor are they righteous by the Law. But he narrates other causes, why that most beautiful polity was established, and whence Israel is the people of God.

And first he says, that the descendants of Abraham are the people of God, because the promise was handed down to them, and it certainly pertains to them. They are therefore the people of God because of the promise, and not because of the law. And the chief benefit is the promise of the Messiah, not the polity or the promulgation of the law.

But yet afterward, a huge benefit was the very constitution of the polity, which served the promise, because God wanted a certain place, a certain nation and family to exist, in which he would reveal himself, where he would issue and repeat promises, and show the testimonies of the promise, where some public assembly would exist invoking the true God, and testifying of the true God, where the Messiah would be born, would be seen, would teach, would issue testimonies of doctrine, would become a victim, would be raised from the dead, where the testimonies of the resurrection would be seen. Of these greatest things, God wanted a certain seat, and known and trustworthy witnesses to exist.

This is the principal cause, why that polity was established, and many benefits concur. There many examples of the presence of God, of wrath and mercy were seen. There many wondrous defenses and deliverances were made.

How glorious was the continuous succession of Prophets, Samuel, David, Elijah, Elisha, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel and those following? And this was most pleasing to good minds, that there was a certain seat of the Church, a certain and perpetual school of true doctrine.

What a step it would be now for good minds, to know that these strongholds would remain for posterity for a long time, and that here the seat of the Church and doctrine would remain?

All sane men understand that these things are the greatest.

CHAP. III. The years from the exodus out of Egypt until the resurrection of Christ are 1545. That the Church and the seat of doctrine remained in the same track for so long was a huge good. For these reasons, the elders understood that the Mosaic polity had been established. For in order that the people might be certain, it was necessary that they be distinguished from other nations by political bonds and rites. And in the rites, exercises of elegance, and signs which were types of the promise, were added. Therefore, Paul in the first promise prefers the Jews far above the Gentiles. He says that they were adorned with the most ample benefits above others, which we have already recited very briefly.

And there are significant weights to the words. He says that they excel much and in all ways, because it is most true that there was a great amplitude of benefits, of which I spoke, the chief of which he says here is this: That to this family, that is, to the descendants of Abraham, the promise of the Messiah was handed down. Where he also used a significant word, the Promises were commended to them, or entrusted, that is, they themselves were made guardians of the promises. And it was a huge prerogative that the promise should sound in this family. And there are always there some true members of the eternal Church, where the voice of the promise sounds, just as it is often said elsewhere, that in the assembly of the called there are always some elect.

But immediately another response must be added. The Jews did not excel as far as merit is concerned, that is, they neither deserved the remission of sins, nor were they righteous by the law before God, but those who were reconciled to God were received by faith on account of the promised Messiah, and by faith they were righteous.

Latin:

Per legem enim agnitio peccati.

Occupatio est breviter inserta de usu legis, de quo postea cap. 7. copiose dicet. Poterat enim quaeri: Si non prodest lex ad iustitiam, cur data est? Certe legumlatores ideo proponunt leges, ut Cives faciant meliores, et eos qui obediunt, nominant iustos, id est, approbant.

Huic quaestioni respondet: Imo, inquit, lex divina extat, ut sit testimonium iudicii Dei, monstrans quae sint peccata in genere humano.

Haec sapientia dissimilis est politicae sapientiae, quia verum est in imperiis condi leges, non solum ut monstrent peccata, sed ut tollant, videlicet externa scelera. Sed lex divina prohibet interiorem immunditiem. Hanc iudicat et accusat coram Deo, non tollit. Ideo haec Paulina dicta nequaquam miscenda sunt politicae sapientiae. Longe alia res hic agitur, scilicet, An ira Dei nostris operibus, seu lege tollatur.

Sciendum est autem tres esse legis usus, quos usitate sic discernimus ad commonefaciendos iuniores.

Primus usus est politicus seu paedagogicus, qui est noticia legis, regens seu metu seu qualicunque adsuefactione externa membra, ut actiones externae non pugnent cum lege: ut quia cogitat civis praeceptum, Non occides, et metuit poenam, hac cogitatione ciet nervos, ut manus reprimant, ne interficiant inimicum, etiam si odit. Hanc disciplinam seu locomotivae gubernationem necessariam esse etiam in non renatis, saepe dicimus, et humana voluntas aliquo modo libertatem habet ciendi nervos, ut moveant aut reprimant membra, ut haec in doctrina physica copiose declarantur. Achilles potest imperare nervis, ut manus recondant gladium in vaginam. Et haec disciplina est cogitatio in mente et cerebro, quae nervis imperat, ut externa membra sic cieant. Nec est iusticia cordis, nec est impletio legis, sed litera, videlicet, cogitatio quasi picta in cerebro, sic regens externa membra. Clare autem affirmamus, hanc disciplinam nec mereri remissionem peccatorum, nec iusticiam coram Deo esse. Ideo autem dicimus esse necessariam: quia necesse est Deo obedire, qui et hanc disciplinam omnibus praecipit. Deinde necessaria est ad vitandas poenas corporales in hac vita. Sed de hoc usu Paulus in hac Epistola non loquitur. Alibi hunc usum indicat, cum ait: Lex est bona legitime utenti. Et sunt haec alibi saepe copiose declarata.

Secundus usus est Iudicium spirituale, de quo inquit Paulus: Lex spiritualis est, id est, iudicium si corda congruant cum lege Dei. Circumcisio prodest, si legem observes. Hic observandum est, semper in mundo vagari has falsas persuasiones de ceremoniis, vel quod mereantur remissionem peccatorum, vel quod sint cultus, et Deo placeant, etiam sine iusticia cordis: et ut vulgo dicitur, ex opere operato, sicut de oblatione in missa impudenter scripserunt monachi.

Omnibus igitur aetatibus in Ecclesia aliqui taxaverunt hunc errorem, ut Psalmo 50.: Non in sacrificiis tuis arguam te.

Et Ieremiae 7.: Non praecepi eis de holocaustis, sed hoc verbum praecepi: Audite vocem meam, et ero vobis Deus. Dictum est autem alias saepe, quo ordine placeant ceremoniae, et pinxi navim, et in navi librum, et supra librum stare calicem, id est: Primum audienda est promissio de filio Dei, et fide statuendum, te recipi propter eum. Haec fides incohat novam obedientiam, in corde dilectionem, spem, invocationem, et alias virtutes.

Deinde accedunt ceremoniae, ut signa, quae de promissione nos commonefaciant, vel exercitiae externi ministerii, invocationis, gratiarum actionis etc., ut alibi copiosius dictum est. Sed hinc asperrima certamina semper in Ecclesia et fuerunt et erunt.

Hypocritae furenter irascuntur, cum detrahitur ceremoniis opinio meriti. Ut Iudaei vociferabantur: Si non sumus iusti lege, cur data est lex?

Huic quaestioni mox respondet Paulus, et necessaria est explicatio, quia omnibus temporibus haec quaestio agitatur: Si nostra diligentia non meretur remissionem peccatorum, cur disciplina flagitatur?

Item: Si non sumus iusti propter nostras virtutes, cur non conceditur licentia cupiditatibus? Ideo initio tertii Capitis movet hanc quaestionem Paulus: Quid igitur habet Iudaeus, quo antecellat?

Quare lex data est? Quare politia Moisi constituta est? Quare dicimur populus Dei, si non sumus iusti hac observatione?
