De his quaestionibus necesse est in Ecclesia extare veram et perspicuam doctrinam, et illa tetra deliramenta reiici, quae finxerunt tres leges: Primam Naturae, secundam Moisi, tertiam Evangelicam, et quolibet tempore homines suae legis observatione iustos fuisse.

Adversus hos perniciosos errores sciendum, ut saepe dicitur, Unam esse aeternam legem moralem, quae accusat peccatum in omnibus, omni tempore: nec patres fuisse iustos lege, sed fide mediatoris, quem ex promissione agnoscebant.

Caput III.

Qua igitur re antecellit Iudaeis?

Obiter inserta est quaestio. Et occasio diligenter observanda est, quam recitavi. Inde enim oritur haec quaestio. Cum Iudaei non mereantur remissionem, nec sint iusti lege, cur data est Lex? et qua re antecellunt Gentibus, unde potius ipsi sint populus Dei, quam Gentes.

De hac quaestione dupliciter respondet.

Retinet enim suam propositionem, quod Iudaei non mereantur remissionem peccatorum, nec sint iusti lege. Sed causas alias narrat, cur pulcerrima illa politia constituta sit, et unde sit Israël populus Dei.

Ac primum ait, posteros Abrahae esse populus Dei, quia promissio ipsis tradita est, et certo ad eos pertinet. Sunt igitur populus Dei propter promissionem, et non propter legem. Ac praecipuum beneficium est, promissio Messiae, non politia seu legis promulgatio.

Sed tamen et postea ingens beneficium fuit ipsa politiae constitutio, quae servivit promissioni, quia voluit Deus certum locum, certam nationem et familiam esse, in qua se patefaceret, ubi promissiones ederet et repeteret, et ostenderet promissionis testimonia, ubi publicus aliquis coetus esset invocans verum Deum, et testificans de vero Deo, ubi Messias nasceretur, conspiceretur, doceret, ederet testimonia doctrinae, fieret victima, resuscitaretur ex mortuis, ubi conspicerentur testimonia resurrectionis. Harum maximarum rerum Deus certam sedem, et notos ac fide dignos testes esse voluit.

Haec est principalis causa, cur politia illa constituta sit, et multa beneficia concurrunt. Ibi exempla plurima praesentiae Dei, irae et misericordiae conspecta sunt. Ibi multae mirandae defensiones et liberationes factae sunt.

Quam gloriosa fuit continua Prophetarum successio, Samuelis, Davidis, Eliae, Elisaei, Esaiae, Ieremiae, Danielis et sequentium? Gratissimum et hoc fuit, bonis mentibus, certam esse Ecclesiae sedem, certam et perpetuam scholam verae doctrinae.

Quam gradum nunc bonus mentibus esset, scire ad posteros diu haec oppida mansura esse, et hic Ecclesiae et doctrinae sedem mansuram esse?

Has res esse maximas omnes sani intelligunt.

CAP. III. Anni sunt ab exitu ex Aegypto usque ad resurrectionem Christi 1545. Tam diu in eodem vestigio mansisse Ecclesiam et doctrinae sedem, fuit ingens bonum. Propter has causas intelligebant seniores politiam Mosaicam constitutam esse. Nam ut certus esset populus, discerni eum politicis vinculis et ritibus ab aliis gentibus oportuit. Et in ritibus elegantia exercitia, et signa quae essent typi promissionis addita sunt. Itaque Paulus in prima promissione longe antefert Iudaeos Gentibus. Dicit, eos amplissimis beneficiis prae aliis ornatos fuisse, quae iam brevissime recitavimus.

Et sunt insignia verborum pondera. Dicit, multum et omnibus modis antecellere, quia verissimum est, magnam fuisse amplitudinem beneficiorum, de quibus dixi, quorum praecipuum ipse hic esse inquit: Quod huic familiae, id est, posteris Abrahae, tradita est promissio Messiae. Ubi etiam insigni verbo usus est, Promissiones sunt commendatae eis, seu creditae, id est, ipsi facti sunt custodes promissionum. Et fuit ingens praerogativa, sonare in hac familia promissionem. Et semper ibi aliqua sunt vera membra aeternae Ecclesiae, ubi vox promissionis sonat, sicut alias saepe dicitur, In coetu vocatorum semper aliquos esse electos.

Sed statim adiungenda est et altera responsio. Non antecelluerunt Iudaei, quod ad meritum attinet, id est, nec merebantur remissionem peccatorum, nec erant iusti lege coram Deo, sed illi, qui Deo reconciliati sunt, fide propter promissam Messiam recepti sunt, et fide iusti erant.

## 4:1 Disposition of Romans: Argument
Confirmation. Chapter IV.

In every dispute, a confirmation ought to follow the proposition, in which the arguments that give assurance to the proposition are set forth. And Paul followed this custom of teachers. Thus, therefore, this chapter ought to be read so that it is not torn away from the proposition: for it is always necessary for the proposition to be kept before the eyes, so that by dialectical custom it may be joined with the arguments and conclude them. For Paul used a brief style of speech, wherefore you will scarcely ever find a complete syllogism in him; he has frequent and dense enthymemes, which cannot be immediately discerned by a reader who is not very attentive, unless they are distinguished and explained in the dialectical manner.

He begins the confirmation, however, with a certain anticipation, so as to pave a way for himself to the example of Abraham. For the Jews felt that Abraham had merited righteousness by circumcision and other good works. For when circumcision is named, the whole cult ought to be understood, and among these also moral works. Therefore, he affirms in no obscure words that Abraham did not have praise before God on account of the righteousness of the flesh, that is, on account of honest works which nature accomplishes by its own powers. Before men, civil righteousness justifies, not before God.

The first argument is drawn from example; Abraham is the father of the people of God, in whom the form of justification has been proposed. Furthermore, Abraham was justified by faith, therefore others also are justified by faith, not by works. And a testimony from Genesis is added: Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness. He gathers the definition from the words of scripture. For in the sacred writings, the testimonies of scripture are of the greatest value. Nor can one judge concerning the will of God, except from the word of God. Therefore, it is fitting that scripture be alleged and that it be shown through it that God declares faith to be our righteousness, which is pleasing to Him. Certain βέβηλοι cavil at this passage and argue that Paul abuses the testimony of Genesis because he twists it to faith in Christ, since there is no mention of Christ there, but of posterity. But those calumniators understand nothing of faith, except the knowledge of history. But scripture calls faith that which believes God to be appeased and propitious, which trusts in the help of God, which dares to expect and ask for help from God. Such was the faith of Abraham. And that faith always embraces the knowledge of Christ, that the Father receives us into grace, not on account of our merits, but on account of Christ. And Abraham knew that the promised seed was he in whom the nations would be blessed. Therefore, when the faith of the Fathers which they exercised in bodily goods is praised, yet the trust in the grace and mercy of God ought always to be joined to it. For how can those who do not feel that they have a God who is propitious and appeased expect bodily goods from God? But all the fathers knew that they were received into grace by God on account of the promised Christ; they knew that the wrath of God is not appeased by our merits or works. As often, therefore, as the name of faith is used here, it ought to be understood not only as the knowledge of history that Christ suffered, but also as the knowledge of the cause, why Christ suffered. For that also pertains to history. Demons and impious men also know that Christ suffered, but they do not believe that the Father is appeased toward them on account of Christ, and that they are loved and defended by God. But I return to Paul's argumentation.

After he reviewed the words of Genesis, he begins to urge the emphasis of the word, to reckon, and defines imputation as being gratuitous. Thus, from that passage of Genesis, new arguments are born while he interprets and amplifies it. That imputation is gratuitous, he shows from a Psalm. Therefore, the second argument will be drawn from the Psalm: Justification is the remission of sins: Therefore, justification does not happen from our works. Likewise, justification is that sins are not reckoned: Therefore, justification is not from our works.

The reason for the consequence is because it is necessary that all works be of such a kind that they could be reckoned as sins, since justification is nothing other than that sins are not reckoned. Even if someone has good works, yet he will be righteous in this way, if sin is not reckoned, according to David's definition. Therefore, those very good works are of such a kind that they can be reckoned as sins. There is a wonderful subtlety in this argument, and it contributes greatly to consoling and raising up terrified minds to understand this definition of justification, that justification is properly the remission of sins. Nor can these things be understood except in true terrors and true repentance, where it is easy to feel how no work of ours sustains us and consoles us against the judgment of God.

The third argument is taken from the order of cause and effect. Abraham was justified before circumcision, therefore circumcision does not justify. For the cause is prior to the effect.

And in order to satisfy the silent thought of the reader, he adds what the use of circumcision is. It is a sign, he says, of the righteousness of faith. From this we learn what the use of the sacraments is. Just as faith is conceived by the word, so it is raised up and confirmed by signs. As Augustine says clearly: A sacrament is a visible word, teaching that the use of the word and the sacrament is the same.

The fourth argument is drawn from the nature of causes. Righteousness was promised to Abraham, without the law. For the law is later: Therefore the law does not justify. But this argument is not treated here, but in the Galatians.

The fifth argument is from the final cause. In vain is righteousness promised, if we ourselves can effect it, but it is promised by God, therefore we cannot effect righteousness.

The sixth argument is drawn from the nature of relatives: Every promise is received by faith, righteousness is a promise, therefore righteousness is to be received by faith.

This argument must be diligently observed for treating promises in the whole of scripture, so that we may know everywhere that faith is required where promises are given. And let us know that faith is not to be placed in our works, but in the word and truth of God. It appears also from this passage that Paul calls faith not only knowledge of history, but much more the faith that assents to the promise of God. Augustine treated this passage somewhere aptly, and rightly perceived the Apostle's meaning. The seventh argument is taken from contrary effects. Law produces wrath. Therefore it does not produce grace. The antecedent can be declared by a sorites, which Paul institutes but does not complete. When the law is violated, it accuses and disturbs the conscience. A disturbed conscience flees and fears the judgment of God. Therefore it hates God. Paul, in his custom, only placed the antecedent of the enthymeme. The law produces wrath, he does not add the consequent. But the discourse would have more light if such mutilated and hanging arguments were not sometimes left behind. Wherefore good craftsmen employ composition and periods to complete arguments. Furthermore, the meaning of these words is: The law produces wrath, that is, terrors of conscience, despair, and hatred of God. From this it can easily be understood that the law does not justify, since it produces despair and hatred of God, not peace of conscience and love of God. The conclusion of the confirmation is: Therefore it is by faith, so that the promise may be firm according to grace. Here he incidentally brings back to the reader's memory the sixth argument, that the promise would not be firm if the conscience had to look to works. For the conscience will always be in doubt whether it has a propitious God. For it will always doubt whether these works, which it has performed, are sufficient, if indeed it has performed any works in which it sees no fault. Therefore the conscience will not have firm consolation against despair, unless it sustains itself by the naked promise of God. To this it is absurd, when God has promised, not to trust in the truth of God more than in our own works. Paul has encompassed these sentiments very briefly when he says, so that the promise may be firm.

After the conclusion, he amplifies the instituted example of Abraham, from which almost all the arguments were born. And he adorns the faith of Abraham with a most weighty encomium, so that in this image he may show how faith is exercised concerning things placed outside the sight of reason, and above nature.

Finally, he accommodates the example to us, according to the precepts of art, saying that these things were written about Abraham for our sake, and that the form of justification was shown in him.

Latin:

Confirmatio. Cap. IV.

In omni disputatione propositionem sequi de- bet confirmatio, in qua exponuntur argumenta, quae propositioni fidem faciunt. Et hanc docen- tium consuetudinem Paulus secutus est. Sic igi- tur hoc caput legi debet, ut non divellatur a pro- positione: semper enim oportet propositionem ob oculos versari, ut dialectica consuetudine cum ar- gumentis coniungatur, eaque claudat. Nam Pau- lus brevi genere orationis usus est, quare vix un- quam reperias apud eum integrum syllogismum, habet crebra et densa enthymemata, quae a lectore parum attento non statim cerni possunt, nisi dia- lectico more distinguantur et explicentur.

Est autem exorsus confirmationem a quadam occupatione, ut viam sibi sterneret ad Abrahae exemplum. Iudaei enim sentiebant Abraham cir- cumsisione et aliis bonis operibus meritum esse iusticiam. Nam cum circumsisio nominatur, to- tus cultus intelligi debet, et in his etiam opera moralia. Itaque neutiquam obscuris verbis affir- mat, Abraham non habuisse laudem coram Deo propter iusticiam carnis, id est, propter honesta opera, quae natura suis viribus efficit. Coram hominibus iustificat civilis iusticia, non coram Deo.

Primum argumentum ab exemplo ductum est, Abraham pater est populi Dei, in quo forma iustificationis proposita est. Porro Abraham fide iustificatus est, igitur et caeteri fide iustificantur, non operibus. Et accedit testimonium ex genesi: Credidit Abraham Deo, et reputatum est ei ad iu- sticiam. Definitionem colligit ex verbis scriptu- rae. Nam in sacris literis plurimum valent testi- monia scripturae. Nec de voluntate Dei iudicari potest, nisi ex verbo Dei. Ideo convenit allegari scripturam et per eam ostendi, quod Deus pro- nunciet fidem esse iusticiam nostram, quae ipsi placeat. Quidam βέβηλοι cavillantur hunc locum, et disputant Paulum abuti Genesis testimonio, quia detorqueat ad fidem in Christum, cum illic non fiat Christi mentio, sed posteritatis. Sed illi calumniatores nihil intelligunt fidem esse, nisi historiae noticiam. At scriptura vocat fidem, quae credit Deum esse placatum, propicium, quae confidit auxilio Dei, quae audet expectare et po- scere auxilium a Deo. Talis erat Abrahae fides. Et semper ista fides complectitur Christi noticiam, quod pater nos recipiat in gratiam, non propter nostra merita, sed propter Christum. Et norat Abraham promissum semen esse, in quo benedi- ceretur gentibus. Itaque cum laudatur fides Pa- trum quam in corporalibus bonis exercuerunt, ta- men semper coniungi debet fiducia gratiae ac mi- sericordiae Dei. Quomodo enim possunt corpo- ralia bona a Deo expectare isti, qui non sentiunt se habere Deum propicium ac placatum. Norant autem patres omnes se recipi in gratiam a Deo propter promissum Christum, sciebant non pla- cari iram Dei nostris meritis aut operibus. Quo- ties igitur hic fidei nomen usurpatur, intelligi de- bet, non tantum historiae noticia quod Christus passus sit, sed etiam causae cognitio, cur sit pas- sus Christus. Nam id quoque ad historiam per- tinet. Norunt daemones etiam et impii homines Christum passum esse, sed non credunt sibi pa- trem propter Christum placatum esse, se diligi ac defendi a Deo. Sed redeo ad Pauli argumenta- tionem.

Postquam recensuit verba Genesis, incipit urgere emphasin vocis, imputare, et definit im- putationem esse gratuitam. Ita ex illo loco Gene- sis nova argumenta nascuntur, dum eum inter- pretatur, et amplificat. Quod autem imputatio sit gratuita, ostendit ex Psalmo. Erit igitur se- cundum argumentum ex Psalmo ductum: Iustificatio est remissio peccatorum: Ergo iustificatio non contingit ex nostris operibus. Item, iustificatio est, non imputari peccata: Ergo iustificatio non est ex nostris operibus.

Consequentiae ratio est, quia necesse est omnia opera eiusmodi esse, quae pro peccatis im- putari possent, siquidem nihil est aliud iustifica- tio, quam non imputari peccata. Etiamsi bona opera habeat quispiam, tamen ita iustus erit, si non imputetur peccatum, iuxta Davidis definitio- nem. Ergo illa ipsa bona opera sunt eiusmodi, ut pro peccatis imputari possint. Mira huius ar- gumenti subtilitas est, et ad consolandas et eri- gendas territas mentes magnopere conducit, intel- ligere hanc iustificationis definitionem, quod iu- stificatio proprie sit remissio peccatorum. Nec intelligi ista possunt, nisi in veris pavoribus et vera poenitentia, ubi facile est sentire, quomodo nullum opus nostrum sustentet nos et consoletur adversus iudicium Dei.

Tertium argumentum sumtum est ex ordine causae et effectus. Abraham iustificatus est ante circumcisionem, Ergo circumcisio non iustificat. Nam causa prior est effectu.

Et ut cogitationi lectoris tacitae satisfaciat, addit quis sit usus circumcisionis. Est signum, inquit, iusticiae fidei. Hinc discimus, quis sit usus sacramentorum. Sicut verbo fides concipitur, ita signis erigitur et confirmatur. Ut praeclare Augustinus ait: Sacramentum est verbum visibile, docens eundem usum esse verbi et sacramenti.

Quartum argumentum ductum est ex causarum natura. Iusticia est promissa Abrahae, sine lege. Nam lex postea est: Ergo lex non iustificat. Verum hoc argumentum non pertractatur hic, sed in Galatis.

Quintum argumentum est ex causa finali, Frustra promittitur iusticia, si nos ipsi possumus eam efficere, Sed est promissa a Deo, Ergo nos non possumus efficere iusticiam.

Sextum argumentum ex natura relativorum ductum est: Omnis promissio fide accipitur, Iusticia est promissa, Ergo iusticia est fide accipienda.

Hoc argumentum diligenter observandum est ad tractandas promissiones in universa scriptura, ut ubique sciamus fidem requiri, ubi promissiones dantur. Et sciamus fidem non in opera nostra, sed in verbum et veritatem Dei collocandam esse. Adparet etiam ex hoc loco Paulum vocare fidem, non tantum historiae noticiam, sed multo magis fidem quae assentitur promissioni Dei. Augustinus hunc locum alicubi dextre tractavit, et recte perspexit Apostoli sententiam. Septimum argumentum ex contrariis effectibus sumtum est. Lex iram parit. Non igitur parit gratiam. Antecedens declarari per soriten potest, quem Paulus instituit, sed non absolvit. Lex cum violatur accusat et perturbat conscientiam. Perturbata conscientia fugit ac timet iudicium Dei. Odit igitur Deum. Paulus suo more tantum antecedens enthymematis posuit. Lex iram efficit, consequens non addit. Plus autem lucis haberet oratio, si non interdum relinquerentur huiusmodi mutila argumenta, et pendentia. Quare boni artifices compositionem et periodos adhibent, ad absolvenda argumenta. Porro sententia horum verborum est. Lex iram efficit, id est terrores conscientiae, desperationem, et odium Dei. Hinc facile intelligi potest, quod lex non iustificet, siquidem desperationem et odium Dei, non pacem conscientiae, et amorem Dei gignit. Conclusio confirmationis est. Ideo ex fide, ut secundum gratiam firma sit promissio. Hic obiter lectori in memoriam redigit sextum argumentum, promissionem non futuram firmam, si conscientia debeat ad opera respicere. Semper enim ambiget conscientia, an habeat propicium Deum. Semper enim dubitabit, utrum haec opera, quae effecit, sufficiant, si tamen opera aliqua effecerit, in quibus nihil videt vitii. Proinde non habebit conscientia firmam consolationem adversus desperationem, nisi nuda promissione Dei sustentet se. Ad hoc absurdum est, cum Deus promiserit, non confidere veritate Dei magis, quam nostris operibus. Has sententias brevissime complexus est Paulus, cum inquit, ut sit firma promissio.

Post conclusionem amplificat institutum exemplum Abrahem, ex quo propemodum omnia argumenta nata sunt. Et fidem Abrahae gravissimo encomio ornat, ut in hac imagine ostendat, quomodo fides versetur circa res positas extra conspectum rationis, et supra naturam.

Postremo exemplum ad nos accommodat, iuxta artis praecepta, inquiens nostra causa haec scripta esse de Abraham, et formam iustificationis in illo ostensam esse.

## 4:3
What then, even if some did not believe.

He inserts other questions, as happens in difficult controversies. When he had said that the promise of grace was handed down to Abraham and his descendants, he asks, is it valid, since there are and have been so many impious people who have spurned it? He answers that the promise is valid, even if very many do not believe.

Consider, however, that here a necessary consolation is proposed to us, against a common temptation, which strongly attacks faith with this argument: Since so many others perish, do you think you are received by God ahead of so many? Here Paul opposes the promise of God to these examples, and an immovable argument, that God is truthful. Let us therefore conclude most certainly that the promise is valid for all who believe, as is said below. Therefore, it is by faith, freely, so that the promise may be firm.

But the sayings from the Psalms are cited here, so that the antithesis may increase clarity. God is truthful, but every man is a liar. For God keeps his promises, even to the unworthy, on account of his truth and goodness. Every man is a liar, that is, either doubting altogether, or struggling with many doubts, neither fearing greatly, nor believing God firmly. For even in the saints, the remnants of these vices remain.

That you may be justified, and may win when you are judged.

He adds another testimony, which takes away from us the dignity or glory of righteousness and merits. This verse contains both the necessary doctrine concerning the confession of our unworthiness, and the sweetest consolation. I am only a sinner to you, or something guilty and worthy of punishment, which I confess, so that you may be pronounced righteous when you punish, and may win when you are judged, that is, when hypocrites judge you: just as almost all men in their clamors think that God is either unjust or cruel, and that he burdens this weak nature with excessively great miseries. Many also rage, when they have been well-deserving, like Saul, or have defended more just causes, like Cato, and yet they are oppressed by calamities, just as Pompey, Cato, and Brutus were; concerning providence there is a question.

But Daniel cries out: To you, O Lord, righteousness, but to us confusion of face. And Job says: Truly I know that man is not justified compared with God, etc. Even if he should kill me, in him will I hope. Nevertheless I will argue my ways before him, and he himself shall be my savior, and no hypocrite shall come into his sight, that is, one who wishes to approach by his own righteousness. And the emperor Maurice says: You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is right.

When therefore David says: That you may win when you are judged, he looks at the hypocrites accusing God of injustice or cruelty, and shows that the confession of the Church attributes to God the praise of Righteousness, and therefore offers obedience in some way voluntarily in punishments, according to that: Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God. Item: Pray without anger and without hesitation.

These things concerning the doctrine of confession in this verse are to be considered first. Afterwards, let it be learned also spiritual, by which God shows wrath against sin, judges, and terrifies hearts, of which use it is said: The Law works wrath. Item: The sting of death is sin, the power of sin is the Law. This use is in some way learned in true conversion and contrition, as when David says: There is no peace in my bones because of my sins. Item Ezechias [Isaiah]: As a lion he has crushed all my bones. Regarding this use, Paul also says here: Through the Law is the knowledge of sin, and below in the seventh chapter he declares this at length.

Nor should the sentences regarding this spiritual judgment be confused with political wisdom, which has its own goals, which also ought to be rightly known. The third use is in the reborn, to teach and testify what God himself is, namely wise, truthful, beneficent, just, equal, chaste, demanding conformity in us, and what kind of worship and what works are pleasing to him. But how the begun obedience is pleasing to believers on account of the mediator, will be said later.

Now, however, without the Law the righteousness of God has been manifested.

So that the explanation may be clearer later, I will first refute Osiander's error. Osiander understands the righteousness of God as God himself dwelling in the reborn and moving him so that he does just things. Thus, in reality, he teaches that a man is just by newness and works. But for the effect, he names the cause, God himself. And although he mixes many things, and obscures some things as if deliberately with ambiguous wrappings, and with a certain grandiloquence of his own, in which there are many wonders of words, he thunders: Yet the sum of his dogma, and the status, and, if I may say so, the citadel is that a man is just by newness and works, just as the Baptists also contend.

But first, consider what evil there is in that imagination.

In true sorrows and in the sense of the wrath of God, a man does not seek what kind of newness is in him; rather, he perceives his own uncleanness and the mass of sin, according to the saying: No living man shall be justified in thy sight.

Here the voice of the Gospel teaches everywhere that it is first necessary to receive the remission of sins and reconciliation by faith on account of the mediator, freely, not on account of our own dignity, and thus it is necessary for men to approach God by trust in the mediator.

And let there be illustrious testimonies in sight, as Acts 10: To him all the prophets bear witness, that through his name they receive the remission of sins, etc. And Daniel: Not in our righteousness. Ephes. 3: Through whom we have boldness to approach confidently through faith in him. 1 John 1: The blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from all sin. Rom. 5: Justified by his blood. Item: Reconciled by his death. Psalm 6: Deliver my soul, and save me for thy mercy's sake. Psalm 31: Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. I said I will confess, etc.

These and similar sayings show that we in this life bring sins to God, and wish for God, so that we may be certain that we are received and are pleasing to God on account of the Son, the mediator, not on account of our own dignity or newness.

Thus all the Prophets approach God, and looking at their sayings, you will be certain that you do not err in approaching God in this way. Osiander destroys this doctrine and consolation, denying that a man is just by faith on account of the mediator, but contending that a man is just on account of God dwelling within, or, as he himself speaks, essential righteousness, which makes us do just things.

Furthermore, if he feigns, as he speaks, that Nero has remission, but is damned because he does not have essential righteousness, it is a horrible impiety. For the distraction of remission and justification manifestly fights against Scripture, according to the saying: He who does not believe in the Son, the wrath of God remains upon him.

Thinking about this forewarning regarding Osiander's error, we will later more easily understand the terms.

When, therefore, Paul says here: Without the Law the righteousness of God has been manifested, he understands the righteousness promised on account of the mediator, by which God receives us and pronounces us just on account of the Son. At the same time, however, he makes believers alive through the Son, and frees them from eternal death, and faith relies on the obedience of the mediator, not on the indwelling, or essential righteousness, which makes us do just things: indeed, the obedience of the mediator is to be preferred infinitely to the actions which are done in the reborn.

It is manifest that in political discourse the word...

'righteousness' has these two meanings. Otherwise, it signifies universal righteousness, which is obedience toward all laws, or congruence with all laws, which are rays of the wisdom of God discerning right and not right.

As when

Aristides is named just, it is understood as a man guilty of no crime, but obedient to all laws in external discipline. Thus it is commonly said of universal justice. * Justice in itself contains all virtues.* And in Horace: The man just and tenacious of purpose, neither the face of the threatening tyrant shakes his solid mind, if the broken ruins of the city should fall upon him, he will strike them unafraid. Otherwise it signifies particular justice, which is to observe equality in contracts, as Mecaenas is just in transactions, even if he does not observe moderation in pleasures. These are the significations convenient to the law, wherefore both Prophets and Apostles, when they speak of works in the manner of the law, fall into these significations, as the Psalm speaks of universal justice: I have done judgment and justice, and John: He who does justice is just.

Sometimes it is said of particular justice, as Psalm 7: Judge me, O Lord, according to my justice, namely particular, that is, according to this just cause, in which Saul falsely accuses me, that I am seditious, and wish to cast him out of the kingdom, You be witness, that I do not have this injustice.

It is another thing to speak of the justice of a person before God, that is, of the acceptance of a person: but a Person just or accepted by faith, is afterwards said to have a good conscience, and to seek from God help and defense in a good cause. Here it can be understood how much it matters that the word 'justice' be rightly understood there as particular justice. Genesis 30: Tomorrow my justice will answer for me, namely particular, because I justly demand my wages.

Matthew 3: It becomes us to fulfill all justice, namely particular to each one's own vocation, I mine, you yours. There is also that legal definition, embracing universal and particular justice: justice is the communion of God with equality.

The first part speaks of the newness, by which God shines in the reborn, and kindles faith, fear, and other virtues. The second part speaks of the works of the second table, which preaches about equality toward one's neighbor, as it is said: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. Item: What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another. But let equality be understood as ordained by the law of God, according to these sayings: You shall not commit adultery, You shall not steal.

But think of David, who when he is rebuked by Nathan, feeling the wrath of God, and seeing the huge mass of sins, adultery, homicide, and horrible scandals, flees from God, and struggles with death. Here he does not dispute what virtues he has, and sees that he does not have essential justice. Of this struggle Paul speaks, following: All have sinned, that is, all are guilty, and lack the glory of God, that is, the light of God shining in incorrupt nature, or they lack God himself, showing himself and kindling ardent love, and other motions congruent to the law, without any sin.

For when Paul names the Glory of God, he speaks of that light: and it does not displease me to embrace both effect and cause, as when it is said: God will be all in all. But Paul says that all are unclean and guilty before God. Since therefore David in this sense of the wrath of God seeks justice, what does the promise and voice of the Gospel offer? It does not say he is just by the fulfillment of the law, but shows the benefits of the mediator, the remission of sins and gratuitous reconciliation, or the imputation of justice on account of the mediator, with which at the same time vivification occurs, when he believes he is received on account of the obedience of the mediator.

By whatever words therefore you wish to use, it is necessary to embrace the remission of sins, reconciliation, or the imputation of justice on account of the mediator. For Paul uses these words expressly, and David seeks, not what virtues dwell in him, or what kind of inhabitation of essential justice is in him, but how he may receive the remission of sins and reconciliation, how he may please, and be accepted by God. It is necessary to embrace these relations, in whatever words you may finally wish to use.

When therefore we shall consider true conversion, we will more easily understand what Paul names Justice, or Justification. There is no doubt that it is taught in this place how a man is just before God, when nevertheless our nature is unclean, oppressed by a mass of sins, and guilty. Here Paul says in Romans 3: We are justified freely, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as a propitiator through his blood.

Item Romans 5: Justified by his blood. Item: Reconciled to God through the death of his son.

Since therefore justification is the acceptance of the remission of sins and of reconciliation, or of acceptance before God, through faith in the mediator, in which simultaneously occurs vivification through the Son: it is necessary to embrace all the benefits of the Messiah, and remission is not to be torn away from present conversion, as Osiander feigns, that sins were remitted to Nero, but that he is condemned because he does not have essential justice.

I shudder to report these things, and I grieve greatly that such discourses must be repeated, against which these sentences must be held: To Him all the Prophets bear witness, that all who believe in Him receive remission of sins, etc. Item: He who does not believe in the Son, the wrath of God remains upon him. Therefore, remission of sins is not to be torn away from justification.

Since, therefore, Paul names justice in this place, saying: The justice of God has appeared without the law, it is manifest that all the benefits of the mediator must be embraced: the remission of sins, reconciliation, or the imputation of justice, and vivification. For Paul speaks of justice promised on account of the mediator.

Rom. 4. Paul names the imputation of justice, for he wishes justice, which is our fulfillment of the law, to be distinguished from this justice, which is acceptance on account of the mediator, since we do not have the complete fulfillment of the law.

For it is manifest that by the word 'imputation' a relation is signified, just as that word is used elsewhere, which is placed there in Genesis, signifying a thought, Genesis 50: You thought evil against me, but the Lord thought this for good. This thought is acceptance, which is announced by the voice of the Gospel and received by faith. And that the word 'imputation' is to be understood relatively, Paul shows immediately in the same place, saying: David says that the blessedness of the man is that to whom God imputes justice without works, and he adds: Blessed are they whose iniquities are remitted, that is, the Person is thus received, bringing to God not his own justice, or essential justice, but in the sense of the wrath of God against sins, fleeing to the mediator, and believing that on account of the mediator sins are remitted to him, and justice is imputed, and as it were, we are the justice of the mediator. This is the simple sentiment of the Psalm and of Paul.

Since, therefore, Paul says in this place: The justice of God is manifested, the phrase is not to be understood concerning His essential justice, as if you were to say: The justice of the judge Aurelian is seen in the punishment of the soldier who had violated a hostess by force. This legal phrase does not pertain here, but in this place, the justice of God is to be understood most simply as the justice promised on account of the mediator.

This form of speaking seems to me indeed most simple, so that it is the justice of God by which God justifies us, or by which He pronounces us just, that is, accepted for eternal life, which justice is received with faith, and simultaneously vivification occurs, according to these sayings: The just shall live by his faith. Item: Being justified by faith we have peace. Item: He who has the Son, has life. For to have the Son is to receive by faith the remission of sins, reconciliation, and the imputation of justice on account of the mediator, and to be vivified through Him.

Without the law. How do these things agree: The justice of God is manifested without the law, when the law itself is wisdom and justice in God, revealed to us, and demanding conformity? How, therefore, can it be manifested without the law? Certainly, essential justice is not without the law, but is in itself the very wisdom and justice of the law in God.

Therefore, these words also refute Osiander: Justice without the law. Because here is understood the justice promised on account of the mediator, and imputed to us, even if the justice of the law is not in us, and we are very unlike the law.

David cries out: Every living person shall not be justified in Thy sight. He sees that he is unlike the law, but that he is received and is just, that is, accepted on account of the mediator. Therefore, the promise of grace, or of the Gospel, announces another justice, which is not the justice of the law, nor is it given on account of the law, nor on account of our works, nor on account of our qualities and virtues.

Origen sticks at this point, nor can he struggle free, arguing how the justice of the Gospel is manifested without the law: but error in the beginning then begets many other errors.

There is the densest darkness in human minds concerning the law of God, concerning sin. Men imagine that the law of God is satisfied by some external discipline, and that sins are only external crimes. And so, since Origen does not consider what a great thing the law of God is, how far this miserable nature is from that conformity with God of which the law preaches, and how great an evil sin is, and does not rightly distinguish the law and the Gospel, he slips into hallucinations, that the Gospel is a new law, and that the justice of the Gospel is works, which are commanded in legal sayings, which are recited here and there by Christ and the Apostles.

These imaginations are entirely alien to Paul, who for this reason distinguishes the justice of God from the law, because this nature cannot have the justice of the law, that is, its complete fulfillment, as is said below: The flesh cannot even be subject to the law of God. Therefore, another justice has been manifested in the promise of grace, namely, remission and reconciliation, or the imputation of justice and vivification on account of the mediator, and through him. And these goods are given freely to one who believes in the mediator, not on account of the law: and without the law, because this nature of men in this life is unlike the law, nor does reconciliation depend on this condition: If we fulfill the law: just as legal promises depend on the condition of the fulfilled law, He who has done them shall live in them.

The Church does not beget a new doctrine, but in its ministry it is the propagator of the voice received from God, and it wishes neither to add anything nor to mutilate it. But since it is a disciple of the divine voice, it ought also to retain the native meaning of the words and the phrase. It is, however, a common sophistry in all corruptions to attach alien meanings to prophetic and apostolic sayings.

As Samosatenus interprets λόγον (the Word) as a purpose or decree in God, concerning the saving of men, not as λόγον ὑφιστάμενον (the Word subsisting), who has assumed human nature.

Pelagius interpreted grace as the law itself, because it is also a benefit of God.

Origenes, and many others, in the saying: The justice of God has been revealed without the law, made a pernicious mutilation: Without the law, namely, the ceremonial and judicial, nor does he interpret Paul concerning the whole law, when indeed he speaks manifestly about all parts of the law: The justice of God has been revealed without the law, namely, the moral, ceremonial, and judicial.

Now Osiander pours out darkness, interpreting the justice of God as essential justice, which is in God, or which is God himself. It is known, however, that this justice has been revealed in the law, which was given for this reason, that it might be a testimony of what God is, and what kind he is, that he wishes us to be conformable to him, and that he destroys all who are not conformable.

Afterwards the Osiandrists add more, for they posit the justice of God to be tropical justice. Likewise, that Christ justifies by accident. These impious voices are to be execrated.

And the refutation must be held, as when they say, God alone is good: Therefore God alone is justice. I respond to the antecedent: God alone is good, namely, by origin, perfection, and cause, that is, the fountain of goodness, perfectly good, and the cause of good in creatures. Then, however, this proposition is also true: God saw all things that he had made, and they were very good, that is, conformable to the wisdom of God, each in its own degree, just as they were created by God.

And it must by no means be said that the obedience of Christ is only tropically justice, for it is the highest conformity in mind and will with the eternal Father, as it is said in Psalm 39: My God, I have willed, and your law is in the midst of my heart. This willing in the Son, by which he subjects himself to the eternal Father, honoring him with greater humility than any creature, and loving him most perfectly, is truly named justice, Rom. 5, not by any figure or abuse of the name.

And it is a horrible lie to say that Christ justifies by accident, since it is a predication of a proper effect from a proper cause, as when I say: Fire warms, or heat warms.

Elsewhere it is said in Paul: God is just, and justifying him who is of the faith of Jesus, that is, truly condemning sin in all men, justifying him who is of the faith of Jesus, that is, receiving those who believe in the Son on account of his obedience.

Here both are named as a cause in itself and immutable, God justifies, as the efficient cause. And the obedience of the Son is the impulsive cause in itself. And these things could be said more subtly, but I avoid excessive subtlety, and I warn the younger ones to speak reverently about such great matters.

A cause by accident is such that without it the thing could have happened, as when you say that fever is a cause by accident of temperance, for even before the fever, thought and will could have restrained the hands: but the obedience of Christ is so ordered by the immutable decree of God, that in this way, and not otherwise, reconciliation is made. It is not, therefore, a cause by accident.

Another. Mercy justifies, Mercy is the essence of God: Therefore the essence of God justifies.

I respond, I concede the whole περὶ πρώτου αἰτίου (concerning the first cause), as when Paul says: It is God who justifies.

For it is most true that God is the efficient cause of justification, who both receives us and gives us life. But the question is about the impulsive or formal cause, namely, whether this proposition is true: We are righteous, that is, accepted by the essence of God. Or whether that one is true: We are righteous, that is, accepted by the obedience of the mediator. Here Paul's saying is manifest: By the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.

Therefore, the efficient cause and the primary cause (καὶ πρῶτον αἴτιον) is God receiving us. The impulsive or formal cause is the obedience of the mediator.

Moreover, the argument can be easily declared and refuted by the commemoration of other properties of God.

Essence is omnipotence, Likewise, God is a consuming fire: Therefore, a consuming fire justifies, if indeed essence justifies. One must concede the argument concerning the efficient cause, because the same God, who is omnipotent and just, punishing the unjust, justifies. But the question remains concerning the impulsive or formal cause, whom and how He justifies. This example shows the confusion of causes in these deceptions.

Another. Righteousness is that which makes us do righteous things, The divine essence makes us do righteous things: Therefore, the divine essence is our righteousness.

I answer most simply, and without contention. I concede the whole, speaking legally. But in this life we are not righteous by the obedience of the law: therefore, in the revealed promise there is another righteousness, namely, reconciliation, or acceptance on account of the Son. Wherefore the Osiandrian definition is only legal. And here Osiander's error is manifestly seen, for the source of many confusions is an error in definition.

It is necessary, therefore, to oppose the legal definition with another, proper to the Gospel.

Righteousness is the remission of sins, and imputation on account of the obedience of the Son of God, through faith, by which we believe that we are accepted by God on account of the Son. At the same time, however, in this consolation, when we are given life through the Son, the Holy Spirit is given for the beginning of obedience, which will be consummated in eternal life.

Now, therefore, you may repeat the argument, with the major premise refuted by another definition: Righteousness according to the Gospel is the acceptance of the remission of sins and the imputation of righteousness through faith; this remission and imputation occurs on account of the obedience of the Son, not on account of the essence of the Father, or of the Holy Spirit; therefore, on account of the obedience of the Son we are righteous.

Another. Daniel says: Everlasting righteousness shall be brought in. God alone is eternal: Therefore, God alone is righteousness.

I answer briefly: If you retain in the word 'Eternal' the same meaning of 'without beginning and without end', I concede the whole argument, that God alone is eternal and essential righteousness. But Daniel speaks of righteousness given to men, who are not without beginning. And I interpret Daniel most simply, when he names everlasting righteousness, as referring to the consummated benefit of Christ, just as Isaiah speaks of the consummated benefit when he says in Chapter 45: In the Lord shall all the seed of Israel be justified. And in the same chapter: Israel is saved in the Lord, with an eternal salvation. In these sayings Isaiah embraces all the benefits of Christ, and yet it is necessary to distinguish the imputation of righteousness in this life, and the consummation of righteousness in eternal life.

Nor will I object if someone understands everlasting righteousness as the very person of Christ, God and man, just as Jeremiah spoke: His name shall be called Jehovah, our righteousness. Where also by the word 'righteousness' he comprehends all benefits. In this life, on account of the obedience of Christ, we have the remission of sins, and the imputation of righteousness, and through Christ the beginning of newness and eternal life, and vivification unto eternal life. And then, through Him, the resurrection, righteousness, and eternal life: this simple interpretation is true, and let us not be delighted by the deceptions of cavils, such as are endlessly fashioned by sophistic minds.

Another. Daniel names everlasting righteousness. Remission of sins is not eternal, as they say: Therefore, it is not righteousness.

I answer. I deny the minor premise, because the remission of sins is to be understood as the reconciliation in all eternity, in which even sin is so remitted that it is entirely blotted out, as it is said: O death, I will be thy death; O hell, I will be thy plague.

Although, as I said before, it is more elegant to interpret "everlasting righteousness" as the completed benefit, by which both remission and eternal life are comprehended.

And indeed, Daniel at the same time expressly names the remission of sins there with these words: "Transgression shall be finished, sin shall be sealed up," that is, it shall be closed, so that it may not accuse us, "and propitiation shall be made for iniquity." And then it follows: "Everlasting righteousness shall be brought in," which signifies that the remission of which he had spoken before is not only a good of the present life, but is the beginning of eternal salvation and life.

He speaks, therefore, of a completed benefit. And it is manifest that the name of "eternal righteousness" is opposed to the righteousness of works, which ceases with this bodily life.

"Having testimony in the Law and the Prophets." We have said that the righteousness of God in this place is necessarily understood as that which is promised on account of the mediator: that this is now manifestly preached in the Gospel.

But it could be objected: Since there has always been a Church, it is necessary that this righteousness was known both to the Fathers and the Prophets: and the rule is true, "Everything that is first is most true." To meet this objection, or anticipation, he inserts these words, by which he affirms not only that this righteousness promised on account of the mediator was known, but that for this reason all the Prophets were sent, and their calling confirmed by illustrious miracles, so that they might be witnesses of this promise, as Peter says: "To Him all the Prophets bear witness."

The emphasis, therefore, in this place should be considered in the word "testimony," and from there let us look at the doctrine, callings, and miracles of the Fathers and Prophets from the very beginning. First, the promise was published to Adam: "The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent."

Afterwards to Abraham: "In your seed shall all nations be blessed." And Jacob says: "The scepter shall not depart from Judah, until Shiloh comes, and to him shall the gathering of the nations be." And Deut. 18: "I will raise up for them a Prophet from among their brethren, like unto you." Then in the Psalms and the writings of all the Prophets there are more clear testimonies, as in Isaiah 53: "The knowledge of my righteous servant shall justify many."

And Daniel 9: "Everlasting righteousness shall be brought in, and transgression shall be finished, and propitiation shall be made for sin, and the Holy of Holies shall be anointed." It is manifest, therefore, that it is rightly said by Paul that there exist MELANTH.

OPER. VOL. XV. testimonies concerning this righteousness, which the Messiah will bring.

But why does he say: "In the Law"?

Osiander does not want the book of Moses and the writings of the Prophets to be understood, but strictly the Law: let it be so, indeed. For the sacrifices in the Law also signified the sacrifice of the Son of God, and Paul says: "Christ is the end of the Law," which is said not only of the ceremonies, but of the moral law as well.

Therefore the moral law was promulgated so that it might convict sin, and show that all men are, as Paul says: "He has shut up all under sin." The law is, therefore, a testimony that we are not righteous by the law.

Wherefore it is necessary that there be a mediator and propitiator, on account of whom the remission of sins is given. And since the law is not frustrated, it is necessary that nature be restored, so that the law may be fulfilled.

Thus Christ is the end of the law, namely, by giving reconciliation after the law shows wrath, because God does not want us to remain in death, according to the saying: "As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner." Christ is also the restorer of the law, when He resurrects and gives eternal life, in which God will be all in all.

At the same time, however, Paul refutes the foolish and pernicious error of those who have imagined that, in order in the human race, there were three laws: the Law of nature, the Mosaic, and the evangelical.

And that men were saved at any time by the works of the laws of their own time. These foolish imaginations arose from the fact that the distinction between Law and Gospel was unknown. It is necessary, therefore, that the voice of Paul be most well-known: "The righteousness of God," namely, promised on account of the mediator, "is manifested without the law," but it has prophetic testimonies at all times, namely, in the promise of grace, delivered to Adam and Abraham.

But just as there is one and the same wisdom in God discerning right and not right, so in all eternity there is the same moral law, which has been repeated in the Church at all times, and did not begin to be taught for the first time when it was recited on Mount Sinai amidst great miracles.

Again, it must also be known that there is a single promise of grace, which was brought forth from the bosom of the eternal Father through the Son immediately when Adam and Eve were received: "The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent." This promise was afterwards repeated and illustrated by the voice of the Prophets and in the Gospel.

Nor were the fathers righteous on account of the law, but by faith alone in the promised mercy on account of the mediator, as Peter expressly says in the Acts: "By the grace 55 of our Lord Jesus Christ we believe to be saved, just as they also. And the Lord says: Abraham saw my day, and was glad.

Latin:

Quid enim, etiamsi aliqui non crediderunt.

Inserit et alias quaestiones, ut fit in difficilibus controversiis. Cum dixisset, promissionem gratiae traditam esse Abrahae et eius posteris, quaerit, an rata sit, cum tam multi sint et fuerint impii, qui eam aspernati sunt? Respondet, promissionem ratam esse, etiamsi plurimi non credunt.

Consideres autem, hic necessariam consolationem nobis proponi, contra vulgarem tentationem, quae valde oppugnat fidem hoc argumento: Cum alii tam multi pereant, num te putes a Deo prae tam multis recipi? Hic exemplis Paulus opponit promissionem Dei, et immotum argumentum, quod Deus sit verax. Statuamus igitur certissime ratam esse promissionem omnibus credentibus, ut infra dicitur. Ideo ex fide gratis, ut firma sit promissio.

Citantur autem hic dicta ex Psalmis, ut antithesis augeat perspicuitatem. Deus est verax, omnis autem homo mendax. Servat enim Deus promissa, etiam indignis, propter suam veritatem et bonitatem. Omnis homo mendax, id est, vel prorsus dubitans, vel multis dubitationibus conflictans, nec valde timens, nec firmiter credens Deo. Nam et in sanctis horum vitiorum reliquiae maneant.

Ut iu iustificeris, ut vincas cum iudicaris.

Addit aliud testimonium, quod detrahit nobis dignitatem seu gloriam iustitiae et meritorum. Continet autem hic versus et doctrinam necessariam de confessione nostrae indignitatis, et dulcissimam consolationem. Tibi tantum sum peccator, seu quiddam reum et dignum poena, quod fateor, ut tu iustus pronuncieris cum punis, et vincas cum iudicaris, id est, cum te hypocritae indicant: sicut fere omnes homines in clamitatibus cogitant, Deum vel iniustum vel crudelem esse, et hanc imbecillem naturam nimis magnis aerumnis onerare. Multi etiam fremunt, cum sint benemeriti, ut Saul, vel causas iustiores defenderint, ut Cato, et tamen se opprimi calamitatibus, sicut Pompeius, Cato, Brutus, de providentia quaesti sunt.

Sed Daniel clamitat: Tibi Domine iustitia, nobis autem confusio faciei nostrae. Et Iob inquit: Vere scio, quod non iustificetur homo comparatus Deo etc. Etiamsi occiderit me, in eo sperabo. Veruntamen vias meas in conspectu eius arguam, et ipse erit salvator meus, nec veniet in conspectu eius omnis hypocrita, id est, qui vult accedere sua iustitia. Et imperator Mauritius inquit: Iustus es Domine, et rectum iudicium tuum.

Cum igitur inquit David: Ut vincas cum iudicaris, intuetur hypocritas accusantes Deum iniusticiae vel crudelitatis, et ostendit, Ecclesiae confessionem Deo tribuere laudem Iustitiae, et propterea obedientiam aliquo modo voluntariam in poenis praestare, iuxta illud: Humiliamini sub potenti manu Dei. Item: Orate sine ira et sine haesitatione.

Haec de doctrina confessionis in hoc versu primum consideranda sunt. Postea discatur et spirituale, quo Deus ostendit iram adversus peccatum, iudicat et perterrefacit corda, de quo usu dicitur: Lex iram efficit. Item: Aculeus mortis peccatum est, Potentia peccati lex est. Hic usus aliquo modo discitur in vera conversione et contritione, ut cum David inquit: Non est pax ossibus meis a facie peccatorum meorum. Item Ezechias [Esaias]: Sicut leo contrivit omnia ossa mea. De hoc usu et hic ait Paulus: Per legem cognitio peccati, et infra Capite septimo haec prolixe declarat.

Nec sunt confundendae sententiae de hoc spirituali iudicio, cum politica sapientia, quae habet suas metas, quas etiam recte cognosci oportet. Tertius usus est in renatis docere et testificari, qualis sit ipse Deus, videlicet sapiens, verax, beneficus, iustus, aequalis, castus, postulans conformitatem in nobis, et quales cultus, quae opera ipsi placeant. Quomodo autem placeat incoata obedientia propter mediatorem in credentibus, postea dicetur.

Nunc vero sine lege iusticia Dei manifestata est.

Ut postea planior sit enarratio, primum refutabo Osiandri errorem. Osiander intelligit iusticiam Dei ipsum Deum habitantem in renato, et moventem eum, ut iusta faciat. Ita re ipsa docet hominem novitate et operibus iustum esse. Sed pro effectu nominat causam, ipsum Deum. Etsi autem multa miscet, et quaedam velut consulto ambiguis involucris obscurat, et sua quadam grandiloquentia, in qua multa sunt θαύματα ῥημάτων, tonat: Summa tamen dogmatis eius, et status, et ut ita dicam, arx est, hominem esse novitate et operibus iustum, sicut et Paptistae contendunt.

Primum autem consideres, quid mali sit in ista imaginatione.

In veris doloribus et sensu irae Dei quaerit homo, non qualis sit in ipso novitas sit, imo cernit suam immunditiem, et molem peccati, iuxta dictum: Non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens.

Hic docet ubique vox Evangelii, primum oportere accipi remissionem peccatorum et reconciliationem fide propter mediatorem, gratis, non propter nostram dignitatem, et sic oportere homines accedere ad Deum fiducia mediatoris.

Et sint in conspectu illustria testimonia, ut Acto. 10.: Huic omnes Prophetae testimonium perhibent, remissionem peccatorum accipere per nomen eius etc. Et Daniel: Non in iusticia nostra. Ephes. 3.: Per quem audemus accedere confidenter per fidem in ipsum. 1. Iohan. 1.: Sanguis Iesu Christi purificat nos ab omni peccato. Rom. 5.: Iustificati sanguine eius. Item: Reconciliati per mortem eius.

Psalm. 6.: Eripe animam meam, et salvum me fac propter misericordiam tuam. Psalm. 31.: Beati quorum remissae sunt iniquitates, et quorum tecta sunt peccata. Dixi confitebor etc. Haec et similia dicta ostendunt nos in hac vita afferre ad Deum peccata, et velle Deum, ut certo statuamus, nos propter filium mediatorem recipi et placere Deo, non propter propriam dignitatem aut novitatem.

Sic accedunt ad Deum omnes Prophetae, quorum dicta intuens, certus eris, te non errare, sic accedentem ad Deum. Hanc doctrinam et consolationem obruit Osiander, negans hominem iustum esse fide propter mediatorem, sed contendens hominem iustum esse propter Deum inhabitantem, seu, ut ipse loquitur, iusticiam essentialem, quae efficit nos iusta facere.

Praeterea, si fingit, ut loquitur, Neronem habere remissionem, sed ideo damnatum esse, quia non habet iusticiam essentialem, horribilis impietas est. Nam distractio remissionis et iustificationis manifeste pugnat cum scriptura, iuxta dictum: Qui non credit in filium, ira Dei manet super eum.

Hanc praemonitionem de Osiandri errore cogitantes, postea facilius intelligemus vocabula.

Cum igitur Paulus hic dicit: Sine lege iusticia Dei manifestata est, intelligit iusticiam promissam propter mediatorem, qua nos Deus recipit, et iustos pronunciat propter filium. Simul autem credentes per filium vivificat, et a morte aeterna liberat, et nititur fides obedientia mediatoris, non inhabitatione, seu iusticia essentiali, efficiente nos iusta facere: imo obedientia mediatoris in infinitum anteferenda est actionibus, quae fiunt in renato.

Manifestum est in politicis sermonibus vocabulum iusticiae habere has duas significationes.

Alias significat iusticiam universalem, quae est obedientia erga omnes leges, seu congruentia cum omnibus legibus, quae sunt radii sapientiae Dei discernentis recta et non recta.

Ut cum

Aristides nominatur iustus, intelligitur vir nullius criminis reus, sed obediens omnibus legibus in externa disciplina. Sic usitate dicitur de iusticia universali. * Iusticia in sese virtutes continet omnes.* Et apud Horatium: Iustum et tenacem propositi virum, Non vultus instantis tyranni mente quatit solida, Si fractus illabatur urbis, impavidum ferient ruinae. Alias significat iusticiam particularem, quae est aequalitatem in contractibus servare, ut Mecaenas in eintionibus iustus est, etiamsi in voluptatibus non servat modum. Hae sunt significationes legi convenientes, quare et Prophetae et Apostoli, cum legis more de operibus loquuntur, incurrunt in has significationes, ut Psalmus de universali loquitur: Feci iudicium et iusticiam, et Ioannes: Qui facit iusticiam, iustus est.

Interdum de particulari iusticia dicitur, ut Psalm. 7.: Iudica me Domine secundum iusticiam meam, scilicet particularem, hoc est, secundum hanc causam iustam, in qua Saul me falso criminatur, quod sim seditiosus, et velim eum ex regno excutere, Tu sis testis, me non habere hanc iniusticiam.

Aliud est loqui de iusticia personae coram Deo, id est, de acceptatione personae: sed Persona fide iusta seu accepta, postea dicitur habere bonam conscientiam, et petere a Deo auxilium et defensionem in causa bona. Hic intelligi potest, quantum referat vocabulum iusticiae ibi recte intelligi de particulari iusticia. Genesis 30.: Cras respondebit mihi iusticia mea, scilicet particularis, quod iuste mercedem postulem.

Matth. 3.: Decet nos implere omnem iusticiam, scilicet particularem suae cuiusque vocationis, me meam, te tuam. Est et illa legalis definitio, complectens universale et particularem iusticiam: δικαιοσύνη ἐστὶ κοινωνία Θεοῦ μετ' ἰσότητος.

Prior pars loquitur de novitate, qua Deus lucet in renatis, et accendit fidem, timorem, et alias virtutes. Secunda pars loquitur de operibus secundae tabulae, quae concionatur de aequalitate erga proximum, ut dicitur: Diligas proximum tuum sicut te ipsum. Item: Quod tibi non vis fieri, alteri ne feceris. Sed intelligatur aequalitas ordinata lege Dei, iuxta haec dicta: Non moechaberis, Non furtum facies.

Sed cogita Davidem, qui cum obiurgatur a Nathan, sentiens iram Dei, et videns ingentem molem peccatorum, adulterii, homicidii, et horribilium scandalorum, fugit Deum, et luctatur cum morte. Hic non disputat, quas virtutes habeat, et videt se non habere iusticiam essentialem. De hoc agone loquitur Paulus, insequens: Omnes peccaverunt, id est, omnes sunt rei, et carent gloria Dei, id est, luce Dei fulgente in natura incorrupta, seu ipso Deo carent, ostendente se et accendente ardentem dilectionem, et alios motus legi congruentes, sine ullo peccato.

Cum enim Paulus nominat Gloriam Dei, loquitur de illa luce: et mihi non displicet effectum et causam complecti, ut cum dicitur: Erit Deus omnia in omnibus. Inquit autem Paulus, omnes esse immundos et reos coram Deo. Cum igitur David in hoc sensu irae Dei quaerit iusticiam, quid offert promissio et vox Evangelii? Non ait eum iustum esse impletione legis, sed monstrat beneficia mediatoris, remissionem peccatorum et reconciliationem gratuitam, seu imputationem iusticiae propter mediatorem, cum qua simul fit vivificatio, cum credit se propter obedientiam mediatoris recipi.

Quibuscunque igitur verbis uti velis, necesse est complecti remissionem peccatorum, reconciliationem, seu imputationem iusticiae propter mediatorem. Nam his verbis expresse utitur Paulus, et quaerit David, non quae virtutes in eo habitent, aut qualis sit inhabitatio in ipso iusticiae essentialis, sed quomodo accipiat remissionem peccatorum et reconciliationem, quomodo placeat, et sit acceptus Deo. Has relationes necesse est complecti, quibuscunque tandem verbis uti voles.

Cum igitur considerabimus veram conversionem, facilius intelligemus, quid Paulus nominet Iusticiam, seu Iustificationem. Nihil dubium est, doceri hoc loco, quomodo homo sit iustus coram Deo, cum tamen nostra natura sit immunda, oppressa mole peccatorum, et rea. Hic inquit Paulus Rom. 3.: Iustificamur gratis, per redemptionem, quae est in Christo Iesu, quem proposuit Deus propitiatorem per sanguinem ipsius.

Item Rom. 5.: Iustificati sanguine eius. Item: Reconciliati Deo per mortem filii.

Cum igitur iustificatio sit acceptio remissionis peccatorum et reconciliationis, seu acceptationis coram Deo, per fidem in mediatorem, in qua simul fit vivificatio per filium: complecti omnia beneficia Messiae necesse est, nec divellenda est remissio a praesenti conversione, sicut Osiander fingit, Neroni remissa esse peccata, sed damuari eum, quia non habeat iusticiam essentialem.

Horresco haec referens, et valde doleo, tales sermones repetendos esse, contra quos tenendae sunt hae sententiae: Huic omnes Prophetae testimonium perhibent, accipere remissionem peccatorum per nomen eius, omnes qui credunt in eum etc. Item: Qui non credit in filium, manet ira Dei super eum. Non igitur divellenda est remissio peccatorum a iustificatione.

Cum igitur nominat Paulus hoc loco iusticiam, inquiens: Sine lege iusticia Dei apparuit, manifestum est, complectenda esse omnia beneficia mediatoris, remissionem peccatorum, reconciliationem, seu imputationem iusticiae et vivificationem. Loquitur enim Paulus de iusticia propter mediatorem promissa.

Rom. 4. Nominat Paulus imputationem iusticiae, vult enim discerni iusticiam, quae est nostra legis impletio, ab hac iusticia, quae est acceptatio propter mediatorem, cum non habeamus integram legis impletionem.

Manifestum enim, vocabulo imputationis significari relationem, ut alibi usitate vox illa, quae ibi in Genesi ponitur, cogitationem significat, Genesis 50.: Vos cogitastis adversus me malum, Dominus cogitavit hoc ad bonum. Haec cogitatio est acceptatio, quae voce Evangelii annunciatur, et fide accipitur. Et relative intelligendum esse vocabulum imputationis, ostendit mox eodem loco Paulus, dicens: David dicit beatitudinem hominis esse, cui Deus imputat iusticiam sine operibus, et addit: Beati quorum remissae sunt iniquitates, id est, Persona sic recipitur afferens ad Deum non propriam iusticiam, aut iusticiam essentialem, sed in sensu irae Dei contra peccata confugiens ad mediatorem, et credens propter mediatorem sibi remitti peccata, et imputari iusticiam, et quasi vestri nos iusticia mediatoris. Haec est simplex Psalmi et Pauli sententia.

Cum igitur Paulus hoc loco inquit: Iusticia Dei manifestatur, non intelligenda est phrasis de iusticia eius essentiali, ut si dicas: Iusticia iudicis Aureliani cernitur in poena militis, qui vi stupraverat hospitam. Haec phrasis legalis huc non pertinet, sed hoc loco iusticia Dei simplicissime intelligatur iusticia promissa propter mediatorem.

Haec forma loquendi mihi quidem simplicissima videtur, ut sit iusticia Dei, qua Deus nos iustificat, seu qua nos iustos pronunciat, id est, acceptos ad vitam aeternam, quae iusticia cum fide accipitur, simul fit vivificatio, iuxta haec dicta: Iustus ex fide sua vivet. Item: Iustificati fide pacem habemus. Item: Qui habet filium, habet vitam. Nam habere filium, est fide accipere remissionem peccatorum, reconciliationem, et imputationem iusticiae, propter mediatorem, et vivificari per eum.

Sine lege. Quomodo haec congruunt: Iusticia Dei sine lege manifestata est, cum lex re ipsa sit sapientia et iusticia in Deo, nobis patefacta, et postulans conformitatem? Quomodo igitur manifestari potest sine lege? Certe iusticia essentialis non est sine lege, sed est re ipsa sapientia et iusticia legis in Deo.

Refutant igitur Osiandrum et haec verba: Iusticia sine lege. Quia hic intelligitur iusticia promissa propter mediatorem, et imputata nobis, etiamsi legis iusticia non est in nobis, et legi valde dissimiles sumus.

David clamat: Non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens. Videt se dissimilem esse legi, recipi autem se et iustum, id est, acceptum esse propter mediatorem. Annunciat igitur promissio gratiae, seu Evangelii iusticiam aliam, quae non est iusticia legis, nec datur propter legem, nec propter nostra opera, nec propter qualitates et virtutes nostras.

Haeret in hoc loco Origenes, nec potest eluctari, disputans, quomodo iusticia Evangelii manifestata sit sine lege: sed error in principio parit deinde alios multos errores.

Densissimae tenebrae sunt in mentibus humanis de lege Dei, de peccato. Imaginantur homines legi Dei satisfieri qualicunque externa disciplina, et peccata tantum esse externa scelera. Itaque cum non consideret Origenes, quanta res sit lex Dei, quam procul absit haec misera natura ab illa conformitate cum Deo, de qua lex concionatur, et quantum malum sit peccatum, nec recte discernat legem et Evangelium, delabitur ad hallucinationes, Evangelium esse novam legem, et iusticiam Evangelii esse opera, quae praecipiuntur in dictis legalibus, quae passim recitantur a Christo et Apostolis.

Hae imaginationes prorsus alienae sunt a Paulo, qui ideo discernit iusticiam Dei a lege, quia legis iusticiam, id est, impletionem integram haec natura non potest habere, sicut infra dicitur: Caro legi Dei ne potest quidem subiici. Alia igitur iusticia in promissione gratiae manifestata est, scilicet remissio et reconciliatio, seu imputatio iusticiae et vivificatio propter mediatorem, et per eum. Ac haec bona dantur gratis credenti in mediatorem, non propter legem: et sine lege, quia haec natura hominum in hac vita dissimilis est legi, nec pendet reconciliatio ex hac conditione: Si nos legem impleamus: sicut legales promissiones pendent ex conditione impletae legis, Qui fecerit ea, vivet in eis.

Ecclesia non gignit novam doctrinam, sed in ministerio propagatrix est vocis acceptae a Deo, nec addere quidquam, nec mutilare eam velit. Cum autem sit discipula vocis divinae, retinere etiam debet nativam significationem verborum et phrasis. Usitata est autem sophistica in omnibus corruptelis, affingere dictis propheticis et apostolicis alienas significationes.

Ut Samosatenus λόγον interpretatur propositum seu decretum in Deo, de salvandis hominibus, non λόγον ὑφιστάμενον, qui adsumserit humanam naturam.

Pelagius gratiam interpretabatur ipsam legem, quia etiam beneficium Dei est.

Origenes, et alii multi in dicto: Iusticia Dei revelata est sine lege, fecit perniciosam mutilationem: Sine lege, scilicet ceremoniali et iudicali, nec interpretatur Paulum de tota lege, cum quidem manifeste loquatur de omnibus partibus legis: Iusticia Dei sine lege revelata est, scilicet morali, ceremoniali et iudiciali.

Nunc Osiander offundit caliginem, interpretans iusticiam Dei, iusticiam essentialem, quae est in Deo, seu quae est ipse Deus. Notum est autem hanc iusticiam in lege revelatam esse, quae ideo tradita est, ut sit testimonium, quod sit Deus, et qualis sit, quod velit nos sibi esse conformes, et destruat omnes non conformes.

Postea addunt Osiandrici amplius, ponunt enim iusticiam Dei, esse iusticiam tropicam. Item, Christum iustificare per accidens. Hae impiae voces execrandae sunt.

Et tenenda est refutatio, ut cum dicant, Solus Deus est bonus: Ergo solus Deus est iusticia. Respondeo ad antecedens: Solus Deus est honus, scilicet origine, perfectione et causa, id est, fons bonitatis, perfecte bonus, et causa boni in creaturis. Deinde vera est tamen et haec propositio: Vidit Deus omnia quae fecerat, et erant valde bona, id est, conformia sapientiae Dei, singula suo gradu, sicut condita erant a Deo.

Ac nequaquam dicendum est, Obedientiam Christi tantum tropice iusticiam esse, est enim conformitas summa in mente et voluntate cum aeterno patre, sicut Psalm. 39. dicitur: Deus meus volui, et lex tua in medio cordis mei. Hoc velle in filio, quo se subiicit aeterno patri, honorans eum maiore humilitate, quam ulla creatura, et perfectissime diligens eum, nominatur vere iusticia, Rom. 5., non aliqua figura, seu nominis abusu.

Et horribile mendacium est dicere, Christum per accidens iustificare, cum sit praedicatio proprii effectus de propria causa, ut cum dico: Ignis calefacit, seu calor calefacit.

Alibi dicitur in Paulo: Deus est iustus, et iustificans eum, qui est ex fide Iesu, id est, vere damnans peccatum in omnibus hominibus, iustificans eum, qui est ex fide Iesu, id est, recipiens credentes in filium propter eius obedientiam.

Hic utraque per se causa et immutabilis nominatur, Deus iustificat, ut causa efficiens. Et obedientia filii est impulsiva per se causa. Et possent haec dici subtilius, sed fugio nimiam subtilitatem, et moneo iuniores, ut reverenter de tantis rebus loquantur.

Causa per accidens talis est, sine qua res fieri poterat, ut cum dicis, febrim causam per accidens esse temperantiae, poterant etiam ante febrim sine ea frenare manus cogitatio et voluntas: at Christi obedientia sic ordinata est immutabili decreto Dei, ut hoc modo, et non aliter fiat reconciliatio. Non est igitur causa per accidens.

Aliud. Misericordia iustificat, Misericordia est essentia Dei: Ergo essentia Dei iustificat.

Respondeo, Concedo totum περὶ πρώτου αἰ-τίου, ut cum Paulus dicit: Deus est qui iustificat.

Verissimum est enim, Deum esse efficientem causam iustificationis, qui et recipit nos, et vivificat. Sed quaestio est de causa impulsiva, seu formali, ut, an haec propositio sit vera: Sumus iusti, id est, accepti essentia Dei. Aut an illa sit vera: Sumus iusti, id est, accepti obedientia mediatoris. Hic manifestum est Pauli dictum: Propter unius obedientiam iusti constituentur multi.

Est ergo efficiens causa καὶ πρῶτον αἴτιον Deus recipiens nos. Causa impulsiva seu formalis est obedientia mediatoris.

Declarari autem et refutari argumentum facile potest, commemoratione aliarum proprietatum Dei.

Essentia est omnipotentia, Item, Deus est ignis consumens: Ergo ignis consumens iustificat, siquidem essentia iustificat. Concedendum est argumentum de causa efficiente, Quia idem Deus, qui est omnipotens et iustus, puniens iniustos, iustificat. Sed manet quaestio de causa impulsiva seu formali, quos et quomodo iustificet. Hoc exemplum ostendit confusionem causarum in istis praestigiis.

Aliud. Iusticia est, quod facit nos iusta facere, Essentia divina facit nos iusta facere: Ergo essentia divina est nostra iusticia.

Respondeo simplicissime, et sine contentione. Concedo totum, legaliter loquendo. Sed in hac vita non sumus iusti obedientia legis: ideo in promissione revelata est alia iusticia, scilicet reconciliatio, seu acceptatio propter filium. Quare definitio Osiandrica tantum legalis est. Ac manifeste conspicitur hic Osiandri error, fons enim multarum confusionum est error in definitione.

Necesse est igitur opponi definitioni legali aliam propriam Evangelii.

Iusticia est remissio peccatorum, et imputatio propter obedientiam filii Dei, per fidem, qua credimus nos propter filium Deo acceptos esse. Simul autem in hac consolatione, cum vivificamur per filium, datur Spiritus sanctus ad incoandam obedientiam, quae erit consummata in vita aeterna.

Iam igitur repetas argumentum, refutata maiore per aliam definitionem: Iusticia secundum Evangelium est acceptio remissionis peccatorum et imputationis iusticiae per fidem, haec remissio et imputatio fit propter obedientiam filii, non propter essentiam patris, aut Spiritus sancti, Ergo propter obedientiam filii sumus iusti.

Aliud. Daniel inquit: Adducetur iusticia sempiterna. Solus Deus est aeternus: Ergo solus Deus est iusticia.

Respondeo breviter: Si retines in vocabulo Aeternus eandem significationem sine principio et sine fine, concedo totum argumentum, Solum Deum esse aeternam et essentialem iusticiam. Sed Daniel loquitur de iusticia donata hominibus, qui non sunt sine principio. Et simplicissime interpretor Danielem, cum nominat iusticiam sempiternam, de consummato beneficio Christi, ut Esaias de consummato beneficio loquitur, cum ait Cap. 45.: In Domino iustificabitur omne semen Israël. Et in eodem capite: Israël salvatus est in Domino, salute aeterna. In his dictis complectitur Esaias omnia Christi beneficia, et tamen discerni oportet imputationem iusticiae in hac vita, et consummationem iusticiae in vita aeterna.

Nec repugnabo, si quis iusticiam sempiternam intelligat ipsam personam Christi, Deum et hominem, sicut Ieremias locutus est: Vocabitur nomen eius Iehova, iusticia nostra. Ubi etiam vocabulo iusticiae comprehendit omnia beneficia. In hac vita propter obedientiam Christi habemus remissionem peccatorum, et imputationem iusticiae, et per Christum incoationem novitatis et vitae aeternae, et vivificationem ad vitam aeternam. Et deinde, per eum, resuscitationem, iusticiam, et vitam aeternam: haec simplex interpretatio vera est, nec delectemur praestigiis cavillationum, quales sine fine a sophisticis ingeniis finguntur.

Aliud. Daniel nominat iusticiam sempiternam. Remissio peccatorum non est aeterna, ut isti dicunt: Ergo non est iusticia.

Respondeo. Nego minorem, quia remissio peccatorum intelligenda est de reconciliatione in tota aeternate, in qua et peccatum ita remissum est, ut totum deleatur, sicut dicitur: O mors, ero mors tua, et o inferne ero pestis tua.

Quanquam ut antea dixi, concinnius est interpretari iusticiam sempiternam de consummato beneficio, quo comprehenduntur et remissio, et vita aeterna.

Et quidem Daniel simul ibi expresse nominat remissionem peccatorum his verbis: Praevaricatio finietur, peccatum obsignabitur, id est, claudetur, ne nos accuset, et propitiatio fiet pro iniquitate. Ac deinde sequitur: Adducetur iusticia sempiterna, quae significat remissionem, de qua prius dixerat, non tantum esse praesentis vitae bonum, sed initium esse aeternae salutis et vitae.

Loquitur ergo de consummato beneficio. Ac manifestum est, nomen aeternae iusticiae opponi iusticiae operum, quae desinit cum hac corporali vita.

Testimonium habens in lege et Prophetis. Diximus iusticiam Dei hoc loco necessario intelligi promissam propter mediatorem: hanc sit nunc in Evangelio manifeste praedicari.

Sed posset obiici: Cum semper fuerit Ecclesia, necesse est hanc iusticiam et Patribus et Prophetis notam fuisse: et regula vera est, Primum quodque verissimum est. Huic obiectioni, ut occurrat, vel occupationi, inserit haec verba, quibus adfirmat non solum notam fuisse hanc iusticiam promissam propter mediatorem, sed ideo Prophetas omnes missos esse, et confirmatam eorum vocationem illustribus miraculis, ut de hac promissione testes essent, sicut Petrus inquit: Huic omnes Prophetas testimonium perhibent.
