Emphasis igitur in hoc loco in vocabulo testimonii consideretur, et inde usque ab initio Patrum et Prophetarum doctrinam vocationes et miracula intueamur. Primum ad Adam edita est promissio: Semen mulieris conculcabit caput serpentis.

Postea ad Abraham: In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes. Et Iacob inquit: Non auferetur sceptrum a Iuda, donec venerit Siloh, et ad hunc gentes congregabuntur. Et Deut. 18.: Prophetam suscitabo eis ex fratribus meis, similem tui. Deinde in Psalmis et omnium Prophetarum scriptis magis perspicua testimonia sunt, ut Esaiae 53.: Agnitio servi mei iusti iustificabit multos.

Et Danielis 9.: Adducetur iusticia sempiterna et finietur praevaricatio, et fiet propitiatio pro peccato, et ungetur Sanctus Sanctorum. Manifestum est igitur recte dici a Paulo, extare MELANTH.

OPER. VOL. XV. testimonia de hac iusticia, quam adducet Messias.

Sed cur dicit: In lege?

Osiander non vult intelligi librum Moisi et scripta Prophetarum, sed proprie legem: sit ita sane. Nam et victimae in lege significabant victimam filium Dei, et Paulus inquit: Finis legis est Christus, quod non de ceremoniis tantum dicitur, sed de lege morali quoque.

Ideo lex moralis promulgata est, ut arguat peccatum, et ostendat omnes homines esse, ut Paulus inquit: Conclusit omnes sub peccatum. Est igitur lex testimonium, quod non simus iusti legi.

Quare necesse est esse mediatorem et propitiatorem, propter quem detur remissio peccatorum. Et cum lex non sit frustrata, necesse est restitui naturam, ut fiat lex.

Ita Christus est finis legis, scilicet, dans reconciliationem, postquam lex iram ostendit, quia Deus non vult nos in morte manere, iuxta dictum: Vivo ego, dicit Dominus, nolo mortem peccatoris. Est et restitutor legis Christus, cum resuscitat et dat vitam aeternam, in qua Deus erit omnia in omnibus.

Simul autem refutat Paulus stultum et perniciosum errorem illorum, qui finxerunt, ordine in genere humano tres fuisse leges, Legem naturae, Mosaicam et evangelicam.

Et homines salvatos esse quolibet tempore operibus legum sui temporis. Hae stultae imaginationes inde ortae sunt, quod discrimen legis et Evangelii ignotum fuit. Necesse est igitur, notissimam esse vocem Pauli, Iusticia Dei, videlicet promissa propter mediatorem, sine lege manifestata est, sed testimonia habet prophetica omnibus temporibus, videlicet in promissione gratiae, tradita Adae et Abrahae.

Sicut autem una et eadem est sapientia in Deo discernens recta, et non recta. Sic in omni aeternitate eadem est lex moralis, quae in Ecclesia omnibus temporibus repetita est, non tunc primum doceri coepit, cum in monte Sinai inter magna miracula recitata est.

Rursus etiam sciendum est, unicum esse promissionem gratiae, quae statim, cum Adam et Eva reciperentur, prolata est ex sinu aeterni patris pro filium: Semen mulieris conculcabit caput serpentis. Haec promissio postea voce Prophetarum et in Evangelio repetita et illustrata est.

Nec patres fuerunt iusti propter legem, sed sola fide promissae misericordiae propter mediatorem, sicut expresse inquit Petrus in Actis: Per gratiam 55 Domini nostri Iesu Christi credimus salvari, sicut et illi. Et Dominus inquit: Abraham vidit diem meum, et laetatus est.

## 4:5
The righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ unto all, and upon all.

In any disputation, it is necessary to be most intent upon the state of the controversy and the principal proposition. Let the younger students know, therefore, that in this place the principal proposition concerning justification is being delivered. Paul, however, incidentally repeats another antecedent proposition recited a little earlier: The whole world is guilty before God. Thus he says here: All have sinned, and lack the glory of God, where exactly the same thing is said that was said before: That all men born in this depravity of nature have sin, and are guilty before God. And that they are neither made nor are righteous by the law, just as the Psalm says: He shall not be justified in thy sight, etc.

Thus it is said here: All have sinned, that is, they have sin, and are guilty (let it be noted that this is a Hebrew phrase). And they lack the glory of God, that is, God himself shining in them, who truly is glory, that is, light, wisdom, righteousness, eternal life, and eternal joy. And communicating himself to the blessed, he causes his own light, wisdom, righteousness, eternal life, and joy to shine in them, as it is said: God shall be all in all. This interpretation fits in this place, because it is affirmed here that in us there is not that righteousness which is glory before God, that is, the best thing, for which God would love a man and not destroy him.

Let glory, therefore, be understood as either God himself communicating himself to us, or conformity with God shining in us. For this perishing life and this righteousness of works, however great it is, is not glory before God, that is, such a thing for which God would love a man and not destroy him. Even if the righteousness of Solon or Aristides is an excellent glory before men, yet it does not grant him eternal life. The disputations of others concerning this phrase are long: They lack the glory of God, but the meaning is not obscure. Paul affirms that this righteousness is missing in human nature, which is complete conformity with God, without sin and without death.

But the universal particle must be diligently observed in both propositions, in the preaching of repentance and the promise of grace: All men born in this corruption of nature are condemned, as he says: All lack the glory of God, he does not want the universal particle [to be ignored].

The righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ unto all, and upon all. The righteousness of God, that is, which God promised on account of the mediator, unknown to reason, which is not the righteousness of the law, or of works, but is the remission of sins and reconciliation, and the imputation of righteousness, or acceptance on account of the mediator's obedience, with which reconciliation is joined vivification, which is done through the son of God himself, when we apprehend the word of the Gospel by faith. He says this righteousness is offered to all, just as he often inculcates the universal elsewhere.

Chap. 10. God is rich unto all, whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.

And Chap. 11. God hath concluded all under sin etc. And the Lord says: Come unto me all ye that labor and are heavy laden etc.

Likewise: God will have all men to be saved. And Isaiah. 42.: He shall not accept a person. 53.: God hath laid on him the iniquities of us all. Let us hold these universal sayings concerning the promise and oppose them to the temptation concerning particularity, when minds dispute whether they are in the number of the elect? Let us be led from this disputation to the revealed will of God in the Gospel, and let us believe the express word of God, and let us include ourselves in the universal promise, let us know that it pertains to us also, let us know that the son of God is a truthful messenger, through whom the promise was brought forth from the bosom of the eternal father, and let us not imagine contradictory wills in God concerning the same matter, because God is truthful.

Let us hold this consolation taken from the express word, and let us not entangle ourselves in the inextricable labyrinths of disputations, which overturn faith, and much more let us struggle with our own weakness, and oppose to it the universal promise, to which we may assent, and at the same time ask to be confirmed, just as he says: I believe Lord, but help my unbelief, and let us not indulge our own diffidence. It is manifest that this admonition is useful.

We are justified, however, Freely. This whole period, which follows, is the principal proposition and state in this disputation of Paul, and many circumstances are interwoven here.

But let the phrase "We are justified" be noted, that is, from being guilty we are pronounced not guilty, we are gifted with the remission of sins, by reconciliation or the imputation of righteousness, with which is joined vivification, which is done through the Son of God himself, when we receive the vocal word with faith, with which the Son of God is truly efficacious, as it is said: The Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to everyone that believeth.

For although it is necessary to retain in the term of justification the relation, namely the remission of sins and reconciliation, or the imputation of righteousness, on account of the mediator, yet it must be known that vivification by faith happens at the same time, when the Son speaks consolation in the hearts through the vocal word, and shows this to be the will of the eternal Father, and gives the Holy Spirit, as it is most sweetly said in Isaiah 38, where true conversion is described. When Hezekiah had spoken of terrors or contrition: As a lion he hath broken all my bones: afterwards he adds concerning consolation, Thou shalt correct me and vivify me, but thou hast delivered my soul, that it should not perish, Thou hast cast all my sins behind thy back.

Thus the divine voice in scripture preaches universally concerning conversion, and joins two motions, terrors and consolation, which is done by faith, that is, by the recognition and trust in the Son of God, according to the saying: The knowledge of my righteous servant shall justify many.

Nor do we imagine a justification that is an idle thought about remission, but we say these motions are done divinely in man, when sin is rebuked by the voice of the ministry, which teaches what sins are, by mention of the law and the Gospel rebuking unbelief, according to the saying: The Holy Spirit will rebuke the world of sin, because they believe not in me: men feel the wrath of God. And in this sense of the wrath of God, when the voice of the Gospel shows the Son as mediator, and offers the remission of sins, by this voice the Son of God gathering the Church is at the same time immediately efficacious, so that hearts begin to believe, and sustain themselves, having recognized the mercy promised on account of the Son, in that consolation he vivifies hearts, lest they be oppressed by the sorrows of the infernal regions.

Thus let us look at true conversion, or repentance, and transfer Paul's doctrine to use, in which it will become more illustrious.

At the same time, let the phrase also be considered. Although there are many motions in conversion, yet the word to be justified signifies without doubt to receive remission, reconciliation, and the imputation of righteousness.

and we are at the same time vivified. Thus Hezekiah joined these two: Thou hast cast all my sins behind thy back.

Therefore Hezekiah joined these two: Thou hast cast all my sins behind thy back. This was said concerning remission, reconciliation, and the imputation of righteousness; that he said concerning vivification: Thou hast delivered my soul, that it should not perish. There follows the exclusive particle, Gratis (freely), which excludes our merits, and yet the cause of reconciliation is soon added, namely, by his grace, that is, by mercy, as he says to the Ephesians: Beloved in the beloved. And afterwards it follows, that justice was tempered by a wonderful counsel of mercy, God remits through mercy, but in such a way that he still wishes the order of justice to be preserved.

Every law obliges, either to obedience or to punishment. After, therefore, men were made guilty, the Son offers himself for the punishment, which is valid for others, because he himself is both innocent and truly loved. This wonderful counsel and temperament of mercy and justice we shall contemplate in all eternity in God, and we shall hear the Son of God teaching us about it, and we shall celebrate this wonderful covenant, the union of the divine and human nature, and we shall give thanks to God. Yet it is necessary that these thoughts be begun in this life. Let us constantly consider what a great thing it is that a divine person humbles himself and assumes the mass of our nature, how great the love is in the Son towards us, how great the mercy of the eternal Father, that he sends the Son, how precious this obedience is in the Son, which is to be preferred to the horrible crimes of all men, according to the saying: Grace abounds above the offense. One must think of the causes why the Son was sent, and why the divine and human nature were joined in the Messiah, and that the Messiah is not only a victim, but that the Son was sent from the beginning, that he might gather the Church, and be efficacious in it, as he says: I give unto them eternal life. Item: No one knows the Father, except the Son, and he to whom the Son will wish to reveal him.

But let the causes of the union of the divine and human nature be in sight.

1. Unless the decree had been made that the Son should assume the mass of the human race, the whole human nature would soon have been utterly destroyed.

But it was preserved, so that this Son might be born, and then believers inserted into him might be vivified again through him.

2. Since the human race had sinned, it was fitting that someone in the human race should pay the penalty.

Therefore the Son as intercessor assumed human nature, as it is said in the second Psalm: Ask of me, and I will give thee the nations for thine inheritance.

3. No creature's strength is such that it could have sustained such wrath; therefore, this Redeemer is God.

4. In order that the price might be equal, the Redeemer is God; therefore, it must be considered that the merit of the Son, the Mediator, infinitely and far surpasses all the sins of all people.

5. A creature is not a life-giver, but as it is written in the first chapter of John: In Him was life; therefore, this Redeemer is omnipotent, so that He may conquer death and restore life to human nature: just as in the beginning, in creation, the Word (λόγος) was immediately the life-giver, so also now He is the life-giver.

6. This Mediator constantly intercedes for the Church, and the Son sees the secret heart of the Father, as He says: No one knows the Father, except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal Him.

This Savior is constantly present with the Church, hears it, saves, protects, and restores eternal life, as He says: I give them eternal life. I am the vine, you are the branches; without Me you can do nothing. Likewise: He sits at the right hand of the eternal Father, giving gifts to men. These, however, are the properties of an omnipotent nature.

These things must be attentively considered in daily prayer, just as in the prophetic writings the invocation of the Messiah is an illustrious and firm testimony, which shows Him to be God by nature and omnipotent, according to the sayings, Psalm 72: And all the kings of the earth shall worship Him. And in Jeremiah: They shall call Him, The Lord our righteousness, that is, they shall invoke Him, and in the invocation they shall confess that He is the Lord our righteousness. Thus He calls us to Himself: Come to Me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will refresh you.

When, therefore, mention is made of the particle 'Freely' (Gratis), let us first know that all our merits are excluded, and that merit is taken away not only from ceremonial works, but also from the works of the Decalogue, and at the same time let us know that the merit of the Son of God is established, for the sake of which alone all who believe in the Son are received in conversion, and it is so great that it far surpasses all the sins of all people. Therefore, just as the thief on the cross, the sinful woman, Manasseh, and others are received freely by faith on account of the Mediator, and are simultaneously made alive through the Son by the gift of the Holy Spirit, and become heirs of eternal life: so also Joseph and Daniel are received freely by faith through mercy on account of the Mediator, and are simultaneously made alive through the Son by the gift of the Holy Spirit, and become heirs of eternal life.

This equalization must also be opposed to pride, as it is said: Let the whole world be guilty before God, and the consolation is firm for all, because in some way they feel the weight of their sins. Therefore the Lord says in Luke 5: I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.

To this also pertain the parables of the prodigal son, and of the sheep that had been lost, and this saying: There is greater joy in heaven over one sinner.

1 Timothy 1: This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptance, that Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners, etc.

However, these four causes should always be in view, for which it is necessary to retain the exclusive particle.

The first, which is the principal one, is that the due honor may be attributed to the Son of God: that His obedience alone is the price and merit for the sins of men, not the works of any man. Therefore it is said in Psalm 39: Burnt offering and sin offering You did not require. Then I said: Behold, I come; in the scroll of the book it is written of me, that I should do Your will. Likewise, by one offering He has perfected those who are being sanctified.

The second cause is that consciences may have firm consolation: because, if the remission of sins depended on the condition of our dignity, it would become uncertain; therefore Paul says: Therefore it is of faith, Freely, so that the promise might be firm.

The third cause is that prayer may be made in the confidence of the Son of God, not in the confidence of our own merits, according to these sayings: How shall they call on Him in whom they have not believed? Likewise: Whatever you ask the Father in My name, that is, in the acknowledgment and confidence of Me, He will give you. For as long as hearts flee from God and retain wrath and rage against Him, true prayer does not occur.

The fourth cause is that the distinction between the Law and the Gospel may be in view. The Law has its promises, but by no means free ones, as it is said: For he who does these things shall live by them. But the particle, 'Freely on account of the Son of God,' clearly distinguishes the Gospel from the Law.

These simplest elements of doctrine must be most familiarly known to all in the Church. Wherefore, since Paul has expressly placed the particle 'Freely' in this passage, we have briefly repeated this sentiment. And to the same effect it is said in our Churches: We are justified by faith alone, that is, by the acknowledgment and confidence of the Son of God alone, establishing that through him are given to us the remission of sins, and reconciliation and vivification through him, by the gift of the Holy Spirit, and the inheritance of eternal life.

It is most certain, however, that by the gift of the Holy Spirit many virtues are begun at once, according to the saying: I will pour out upon the house of David a spirit of grace and of supplications.

And yet the proposition is true: By faith alone is Paul righteous, because he is pleasing through the mediator by faith, not on account of his own dignity or newness.

The particle, therefore, 'Gratis' (freely), does not exclude other virtues, lest they be present, but it excludes the condition of merit or of our dignity, as we customarily say: Even if many virtues are present at once, yet they are not the causes, or the merit of the remission of sins, or of justification and acceptance unto eternal life.

These things, rightly understood, illustrate the promise and the benefits of Christ, and bring consolation to the pious, and kindle true invocation, by which we approach God with the confidence of the son of the mediator.

Here the younger ones must be warned about the corruption of the word 'Grace,' which the monks have interpreted as infused qualities, as they themselves speak, when here without any doubt it signifies gratuitous mercy.

And in its own place elsewhere, the use of the word has been spoken of more at length.

Through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.

Since he had said before that mercy is gratuitous, he soon adds a commemoration of the mediator, so that we may understand that our merits are excluded, and not the merit of the Son of God, but that in that arcane decree concerning the restoration of the human race, the justice of mercy was tempered by a wondrous counsel.

It is of immense mercy that the divinity does not wish the human race to perish for all eternity, just as in all eternity he cast away the devils: but yet, so that the justice of God might also be satisfied for our sin, a penalty was ordained, which is the obedience of the innocent mediator: this is the merit and the price, on account of which our sins are remitted, and we are pleasing to God or are accepted, when it is applied to us by faith, as Paul says shortly about faith.

And four works of immense mercy concur, namely, that we are received on account of the son, and that the son is sent most freely so that we might be received, he is constituted mediator and propitiator, and the same son is efficacious, he brings forth the Gospel, gathers the Church, vivifies believers, and afterwards resurrects them to eternal life.

We shall contemplate the causes of these wondrous counsels and works, and their movement in all eternity, in God: now, as infants and sucklings, however much the beginnings of this doctrine are to be pondered, the immense benefits of God are to be acknowledged, and received by faith, and thanks are to be given to God who sends the son, and to the son who suffered for us and was resurrected, and who gathers the eternal Church, and we pray that we may be taught and confirmed, let us cry out assiduously: I believe, Lord, but bring help to my weakness.

And let the argument of our first parents be repeated often in thought, who after the fall, before the promise was issued, reasoned thus in the sense of the wrath of God: The justice of God is immutable, We are guilty: Therefore destruction is immutable.

No creature knew the solution to this argument, but the Son of God, interceding for us and offering himself to the penalty, brings forth and shows the solution to this argument, and teaches how mercy and justice agree.

These things are to be pondered piously and reverently, that we may consider how great an evil sin is: and again, that we may magnify the benefits of God.

Whom God set forth as a propitiator through faith in his blood.

Let it be understood, therefore, in the appellation of propitiator, offering his merits for us, and paying the penalty, and applying his merits to us, just as the Lord himself says: I sanctify myself for them.

This property, proper to this person, who alone has been constituted to be mediator, is comprehended in all these appellations of mediator, high priest, propitiator, and redeemer, and this honor is not to be transferred to any other men or angels, and this whole doctrine becomes more illustrious, when the definition of the high priest, which is handed down in the Epistle to the Hebrews, is brought to bear here.

The high priest, and Son of God, sent immediately by the eternal father, and ordained to bring forth the Gospel and to offer his own death, so that it might be the appeasement of the father's wrath, and the price to be paid for others to divine justice, and always interceding for us, and having the promise that he is certainly heard. This definition, and the whole doctrine concerning the priesthood of Christ, is full of the sweetest consolations, and is to be pondered daily.

Paul, however, added in this place with a singular purpose this clause: Whom he set forth as a propitiator through faith in his blood. For here he teaches us about application.

Even the Papists say that the Son of God is mediator, redeemer, and propitiator, but they afterwards destroy this very thing, because they utterly omit any mention of faith; nay, they command you to doubt whether these benefits of the Son of God pertain to you, namely, whether you are in a state of grace, and they speak only thus: Christ merited the first grace, that is, the occasion of meriting, just as if a father of a family were appeased toward a servant by some friend, but afterwards the servant pleases him by his own duties, and there is no further business there for that friend. Thus the Papists bury Christ, when they imagine that a man is afterwards righteous by his own virtues, not by faith, not by mercy on account of the Son of God, by imputed righteousness.

But when Paul names faith here, he opposes it to doubt; he wants doubt to be overcome, he wants application to be made by faith, he wants you to firmly establish that on account of this propitiator, or on account of his obedience, we receive the remission of sins, reconciliation, or acceptance, with righteousness imputed on account of the blood of the mediator, that is, his obedience granted to us, just as on account of it we are righteous, that is, pleasing and accepted to God. Thus the Son always remains for us a propitiator, on account of whom we are pleasing, not on account of our own virtues, which cannot be opposed to the wrath of God.

Joseph, Elijah, Elisha, and Daniel have excellent virtues and divine actions in themselves, but they do not oppose these virtues and divine actions to the judgment of God, but they flee to the mediator and the promised mercy, and they determine that they are pleasing to God through mercy on account of the mediator, as it is said in the Psalm: Turn, O Lord, and deliver me for thy mercy's sake, make me safe. And Daniel says: We do not present our supplications before thee for our righteousness, but for the Lord's sake through mercy.

For the demonstration of his righteousness for the remission of sins. That is, that he might declare his righteousness in the remission of sins, and it follows afterwards that he is righteous and the justifier of him who is of the faith of Jesus.

And Paul presently declares how he wishes the word 'righteousness' to be understood, when he says, that he might be righteous, and the justifier of him who is of the faith of Jesus, that is, in the Gospel the righteousness of God is declared, that he himself is righteous, not we, and that he justly condemns sin in all, as he says, that the whole world may be guilty before God. Item: Against thee only have I sinned and done evil before thee, that thou mightest be justified in thy words, and overcome when thou art judged.

God therefore declares himself to be righteous and condemning sins, then he also declares this, that he himself justifies, nor can we ourselves justify by the works of the law. He justifies, however, in this way himself, namely by the remission of sins.

He defines justification therefore as below, when he cites the saying: Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven. Justification is the acceptance of the remission of sins, or of reconciliation through faith, by which the Son of God comforts us, showing the mercy of the eternal Father in the voice of the Gospel, and delivering us from eternal death, he makes us alive, and gives the Holy Spirit, and makes us heirs of eternal life. As John says: He who has the Son, has life.

With this definition considered, it can be understood that the remission of sins and vivification are not torn apart, but that these have a correlative relationship: for thus remission is made, when it is received by faith, pondered by the voice of the Gospel. And with this faith looking upon the obedience of the Son of God, the Son himself, the λόγος (Word) of the eternal Father, makes alive those who believe and dwells in them, confirming their hearts with the Holy Spirit. Yet this vivification or this indwelling does not happen unless faith shines forth, which relies on the obedience of the Son of God.

But why does he say: Of past sins? Here some respond that this clause was added so that we might know that in the Gospel a license to sin is not granted, but that we might know that sins are remitted in those who perform repentance, in whom sin ceases to reign.

And the Novatians abused this place: since it does not follow from there that if the lapsed are converted again, their offenses are not remitted: for as often as remission is made, it is a remission of past sins. But in this place the remission of sins is understood not only of actual offenses, but of the remission of actual sins and original sin, which, though remitted, the disease remains in this life.

But Paul opposes this clause, 'of past sins', to the Law, as if he were to say: Not even the law abolished sin, but it precedes until it is taken away by the acknowledgment and faith of the Messiah, as he will say afterwards: Until the law, sin was in the world, that is, even when the law was given, sin and death nevertheless remained. It is taken away, however, by acknowledgment and faith. sons of God in two ways: by imputation, namely in this life, because the guilt is removed, and the person is made just, that is, accepted by faith on account of the mediator. And in reality, renewal begins in the heart through the Son and the Holy Spirit, which later will be complete in the resurrection.

Where then is the boasting? He adds an epiphonema from the comparison of the contrary. Since this statement is true, that men are made just by faith before God. It follows that there is no boasting of ours, that is, that we do not have our own justice, or the fulfillment of the law, or merit.

And this very antithesis is a clear confirmation of our interpretation. If we were just by the fulfillment of the law, we would have glory and merit, but these sayings expressly take this glory and merit away from us, Psalm 142: No one living will be justified in your sight. And Job: I know truly that no man is just before God. And Paul said: All lack the glory of God. Likewise, so that the whole world may be guilty before God. Therefore, the antithesis is clear: Therefore, since we are just by mercy alone, we do not have the glory of our own justice in the judgment of God.

But it has often been said already that these propositions are to be understood correlatively: we are just by mercy on account of the Son of God, that is, by trust in mercy on account of the mediator. As Romans 4 connects promise and faith correlatively: Therefore it is by faith, freely, so that the promise may be firm: Paul therefore says that boasting is excluded by the law of faith, that is, the doctrine of faith, which affirms that we are just through mercy on account of the mediator, and rests in God on account of the mediator, not on account of our own dignity. He therefore excludes our own dignity and merit.

That this is the native and simplest explanation, congruent with the entire prophetic scripture, there is no doubt. Thus Daniel prays: Hear us not on account of our own justice, but through mercy on account of the Lord, and David says: Save me on account of your mercy. Thus let us approach God daily in invocation with trust in the mediator, not with trust in our own dignity or essential justice.

Let these things also be noted as correctly said by the writers; Augustine says: The certainty of all trust ought to be in the precious blood of Christ. And Basil says in his sermon on humility, page 388: But the Apostle says: Let him who boasts, boast in the Lord, saying that Christ is for us wisdom from God, justice, and sanctification and redemption, just as it is written: Let him who boasts, boast in the Lord. For this is perfect and complete boasting in God, when one is not even exalted on account of his own justice, but acknowledges that he lacks true justice, and is justified by faith in Christ alone.

These things agree with this saying: Boasting is excluded by the doctrine of faith. He opposes this to the law of works, which is the doctrine commanding complete obedience, and teaching that justice is to have complete obedience, just as he says below in chapter 10. Moses describes the justice which is from the law: he who does these things will live in them.

He therefore names the law of works, the doctrine of the law, that is, the law itself so properly called, of which it is said elsewhere: The law brings about wrath. But that people willingly used the name of law, wherefore it is often used generally for doctrine, or for the word of God, as in the whole of Psalm 118: Blessed are the blameless in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. Likewise: Great peace have those who love your law, and there is no scandal to them.

We assert therefore that a man is justified by faith without works. To the epiphonema he adds a Conclusion, in which he briefly repeats the sum of the proposition, and again inculcates the Exclusive.

For repetitions conduce to this, so that the reader may know that that particle did not slip out of the speaker's mouth by chance, but that he wills this seriously and with deliberation, which he inculcates so often. Nor is there obscurity in the saying of Paul, but the propriety of the words is to be retained. It is childish that some dispute about the word 'we reckon' (arbitramur): for in Greek λογίζομαι signifies an asseveration gathered from the preceding connection.

Faith signifies the assent by which we embrace the promise of grace, which is offered in the Gospel on account of the mediator, and it is trust in the promised mercy, as this explanation of the word has often been handed down: as Paul in Ephesians four explains one word with many: Through whom we dare to approach in trust through faith in him, as the Psalm also speaks: Blessed are all who trust in him. To be justified signifies to receive the remission of sins and reconciliation, and the imputation of justice or acceptance, with which at the same time is the efficacious Son of God, he speaks consolation by the voice of the Gospel in the mind, and shows the will of the Father, and vivifies the believer, and pours the Holy Spirit into the heart, just as it is said in 1 John 4: In this we know that we remain in Him and He in us, because He gives us of His Spirit. we know that we remain in Him and He in us, because He gives us of His Spirit.

The meaning of the proposition is therefore: We assert that man receives the remission of sins, reconciliation, and the imputation of righteousness, through the Son of God, the mediator, by mercy freely, not because of the law, or our virtues, or works. And this mercy must be received by faith: since the words of Paul beget this simple sentiment, let us be disciples of the divine word, and let us retain the native understanding of the words.

It means nothing to the monks to be justified by faith, because they understand faith only as knowledge, such as exists even in devils.

They therefore invent this synecdoche, that we are justified by faith, namely, formed [faith]; they say that doctrine is the beginning, but afterwards man is righteous by love, that is, by the obedience which he renders to the law. Therefore they add this particle to Paul, that man is justified by faith, namely, formed by love. And by this dream they explain the appellation. As when the soul is infused into the body the body lives, so they say that knowledge becomes alive when the remaining obedience is added. This imagination is a total corruption: for faith is not called alive because of love.

For it is a divine movement, by which the heart is freed from terrors, and rests in God, having acknowledged mercy because of the mediator, ceases to flee from God, and cries Abba Father, nor does it receive life from love, which follows, but it is the cause of love. For God is loved because the mercy promised because of the Son has been acknowledged, who, praying for us, says: Let Thy love be in them, with which Thou lovest me. Monks have restricted the Exclusive 'without works' in this way: Without works, namely, the ceremonial and forensic [works] of Moses.

And meanwhile they retain this proposition, that moral works merit remission, [and] that man is righteous before God because of moral works. This whole corruption of the monks must be rejected, and this true sentiment must be constantly retained, which Paul repeats so often when he uses the exclusive, 'Freely': namely, that men neither merit the remission of sins by their own moral works or others, nor are they righteous before God because of good moral works, or because of their own virtues, neither before renovation, nor after renovation in this life, nor do they have in this life the complete obedience of the decalogue.

Therefore it was said above: Let the whole world be guilty before God. And it is said in the Psalm: No living man shall be justified in Thy sight. And Job says in Chapter 9: I know truly that no man is righteous before God. These clear confessions are not to be corrupted in this way. Man is not righteous before God by ceremonies, but he is righteous because he has the perfect obedience of the decalogue.

In such an imagination, it would be a manifest lie. For it is necessary to confess that all men born in this impurity of nature do not have in themselves the perfect obedience of the decalogue.

The Gospel therefore shows the mediator and mercy, and affirms that men are righteous, that is, having the remission of sins, and pleasing to God because of the mediator through mercy, Freely, by faith, that is, by the trust of mercy resting in God because of the mediator.

Therefore, against the corruption of the monks, who exclude only ceremonies, the particle 'Freely' must be opposed, which testifies that moral works do not merit the remission of sins: for neither would reconciliation be free, nor would it be certain for us, if it depended on the condition of having fulfilled the decalogue.

Wherefore Paul also says afterwards: Therefore by faith freely, that the promise may be firm.

Then also the express confession of not having fulfilled the decalogue should be opposed to the corruption of the monks: No living man shall be justified in Thy sight. This confession being posited, it is manifest that reconciliation is given because of the mediator, not because of our virtues, and is received by faith.

This is the meaning of the Exclusive in our Churches also, when we say that man is justified by faith alone. Here also the Osiandrian corruption must be refuted, which is similar to the synecdoche of the monks, [that] we are justified by faith preparatorily, as if you were to say: Motion warms, namely preparatorily, but afterwards we are warm by heat.

Thus Osiander contends it should be said: We are justified by faith, that is, faith prepares us, so that afterwards we may be righteous by another thing, namely, by newness. But although newness follows, and it is true that man becomes the temple of God and that God dwells in the converted or reborn, yet this consolation must be retained, that the converted or reborn are righteous by faith freely, because of the obedience of the mediator, not because of the following newness or essential righteousness, but because of the mediator.

It is necessary that this consolation be retained in this saying: The righteous shall live by his faith.

Let us look at the true struggle of the conscience in conversion, and subsequently in the great conflict, and let us consider what is the true consolation. Here [are] the most certain [things].

[it] is to establish all the Prophets and all the saints, that they please God through mercy, and that this mercy is promised and certain on account of the mediator, and that faith relies on the obedience of the mediator, not on essential justice. These things are manifest also from this saying to the Ephesians: Through him we have access in confidence through faith in him. And although it is true that in that consolation vivification occurs, and that God kindles new actions in man, yet the believer infinitely prefers the obedience of the mediator to these actions of God, which already occur in the reborn. These things are clear to one considering the distinction between the Law and the Gospel, and the consolations in true conversion.

Latin:

Iusticia Dei per fidem Iesu Christi in omnes, et super omnes.

In qualibet disputatione necesse est maxime intentum esse in controversiae statum et principalem propositionem. Sciant igitur iuniores, hoc loco tradi principalem propositionem de iustificatione. Obiter autem repetit Paulus aliam antecedentem propositionem paulo ante recitatam: Totus mundus est reus Deo. Ita hic inquit: Omnes peccaverunt, et carent gloria Dei, ubi prorsus idem dicitur, quod ante dictum est: Omnes homines natos in hac depravatione naturae habere peccatum, et reos esse coram Deo. Et neque fieri neque esse iustos lege, sicut Psalmus inquit: Non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo etc.

Ita hic dicitur: Omnes peccaverunt, id est, habent peccatum, et sunt rei (Nota sit enim phrasis Ebraea). Et carent gloria Dei, id est, Deo ipso lucente in eis, qui vere est gloria, id est, lux, sapientia, iustitia, vita aeterna et laetitia aeterna. Et communicans se se beatis, facit ut in eis luceat ipsius lux, sapientia, iustitia, vita aeterna et laetitia, sicut dicitur: Deus erit omnia in omnibus. Haec interpretatio hoc loco quadrat, quia hic affirmatur, quod in nobis non sit illa iustitia, quae est gloria coram Deo, id est, res optima, propter quam Deus hominem diligeret, et non destrueret.

Intelligatur ergo gloria, vel ipse Deus se se nobis communicans, vel conformitas cum Deo lucente in nobis. Nam haec interitura vita et haec iustitia operum, quantacunque est, non est gloria coram Deo, id est, res talis, propter quam Deus diligat hominem, et non destruat. Etiamsi est excellens gloria coram hominibus iustitia Solonis, aut Aristidis, tamen non tribuit ei vitam aeternam. Longae sunt disputationes aliorum de hac phrasi: Carent gloria Dei, sed sententia non est obscura. Paulus affirmat deesse hanc iustitiam in hominum natura, quae est integra conformitas cum Deo, sine peccato et sine morte.

Diligenter autem observanda est universalis particula in utraque propositione, in praedicatione poenitentiae et promissione gratiae: Damnantur omnes homines nati in hac corruptione naturae, ut inquit: Omnes carent gloria Dei, non vult particulam universalem.

Iusticia Dei per fidem Iesu Christi in omnes, et super omnes. Iusticia Dei, id est, quam Deus promisit propter mediatorem ignotam rationi, quae non est iustitia legis, seu operum, sed est remissio peccatorum et reconciliatio, et imputatio iustitiae, seu acceptatio propter mediatoris obedientiam, cum qua reconciliatione coniuncta est vivificatio, quae fit per ipsum filium Dei, cum fide apprehendimus verbum Evangelii. Hanc iustitiam ait offerri omnibus, sicut alibi saepe inculcat universale.

Cap. 10. Dives Deus in omnes, qui invocaverit nomen Domini, salvus erit.

Et Cap. 11. Conclusit Deus omnes sub peccatum etc. Et Dominus inquit: Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis et onerati estis etc.

Item: Deus vult omnes homines salvos fieri. Et Esai. 42.: Non accipiet personam. 53.: Posuit Deus in eo iniquitates omnium nostrum. Haec universalia dicta de promissione teneamus et opponamus tentationi de particularitate, cum disputant mentes, an sint in numero electorum? ab hac disputatione ad revelatam Dei voluntatem in Evangelio deducamur, et credamus expresso verbo Dei, et nos in universalem promissionem includamus, sciamus eam ad nos quoque pertinere, sciamus filium Dei veracem nuncium esse, per quem prolata est promissio ex sinu aeterni patris, nec fingamus de eadem re contradictorias voluntates in Deo, quia Deus verax est.

Hanc consolationem sumtam ex verbo expresso teneamus, nec nos ipsos inextricabilibus labyrinthis disputationum implicemus, quae fidem evertunt, ac multo magis luctemur cum nostra imbecillitate, et ei promissionem universalem opponamus, cui assentiamur, et simul petamus nos confirmari, sicut ille inquit: Credo Domine, sed opem fer imbecillitati meae, nec indulgeamus nostrae diffidentiae. Hanc admonitionem utilem esse manifestum est.

Iustificamur autem Gratis. Haec tota periodus, quae sequitur, est principalis propositio et status in hac disputatione Pauli, ac multae circumstantiae hic intexuntur.

Sit autem nota phrasis Iustificamur, id est, ex reis pronunciamur non rei, donamur remissione peccatorum, reconciliatione seu imputatione iusticiae, cum qua coniuncta est vivificatio, quae fit per ipsum filium Dei, cum fide verbum vocale accipimus, cum quo vere est efficax filius Dei, ut dicitur: Evangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti.

Etsi enim necesse est retineri in vocabulo iustificationis relationem, scilicet remissionem peccatorum et reconciliationem, seu imputationem iusticiae, propter mediatorem, tamen sciri oportet simul fieri vivificationem fide, cum filius dicit consolationem in cordibus per verbum vocale, et ostendit hanc esse voluntatem aeterni patris, et dat Spiritum sanctum, sicut Esai. 38. dulcissime dicitur, ubi vera conversio describitur. Cum dixisset Ezechias de terroribus seu contritione: Sicut leo contrivit omnia ossa mea: postea addit de consolatione, Corripies me et vivificabis me, tu autem eruisti animam meam, ut non periret, Proiecisti post tergum tuum omnia peccata mea.

Ita universaliter de conversione concionatur vox divina in scriptura, et duos motus coniungit, Pavores et consolationem, quae fit fide, id est, agnitione et fiducia filii Dei, iuxta dictum: Noticia servi mei iusti iustificabit multos.

Nec fingimus iustificationem, quae sit otiosa cogitatio de remissione, sed dicimus hos motus divinitus fieri in homine, cum arguitur peccatum voce ministerii, quod docet, quae sint peccata, mentione legis et Evangelii arguentis incredulitatem, iuxta dictum: Spiritus sanctus arguet mundum de peccato, quod non credunt in me: sentiunt homines iram Dei. Et in hoc sensu irae Dei, cum vox Evangelii ostendit filium mediatorem, et offert remissionem peccatorum, hac voce filius Dei colligens Ecclesiam simul immediate est efficax, ut corda incipiant credere, et se sustentent, agnita misericordia propter filium promissa, in ea consolatione vivificat corda, ne opprimantur doloribus inferorum.

Ita aspiciamus veram conversionem, seu poenitentiam, et Pauli doctrinam ad usum transferamus, in quo fiet illustrior.

Simul autem et phrasis consideretur. Quanquam sunt in conversione plures motus, tamen vocabulum iustificari, significat haud dubie accipere remissionem, reconciliationem, ac imputationem iusticiae.

Hanc autem cum accipimus, simul vivificamur. Ideo Ezechias haec duo coniunxit: Proiecisti post tergum omnia peccata mea.

Hoc de remissione, reconciliatione, et imputatione iusticiae dictum est, illud de vivificatione dixit: Eripuisti animam meam, ne periret. Sequitur particula exclusiva, Gratis, quae excludit nostra merita, et tamen causa reconciliationis mox addita est, scilicet, per gratiam ipsius, id est, per misericordiam, ut ad Ephesios inquit: Dilecti in dilecto. Et postea sequitur, mirando consilio temperatam esse misericordiae iusticiam, Remittit Deus per misericordiam, sed ita, ut servari tamen ordinem iusticiae velit.

Omnis lex obligat, vel ad obedientiam, vel ad poenam. Postquam igitur homines facti sunt rei, offert se filius ad poenam, quae valet pro aliis, quia ipse et innocens est et vere diligitur. Hoc mirandum consilium et temperamentum misericordiae et iusticiae in tota aeternitate contemplabimur in Deo, et de eo filium Dei nos docentem audiemus, et celebrabimus hoc mirandum foedus, copulationem divinae et humanae naturae, et Deo gratias agemus. Incoari tamen has cogitationes in hac vita necesse est. Assiduo consideremus, quanta res sit, quod divina persona se demittit, et assumit massam nostrae naturae, quantus amor sit in filio erga nos, quanta misericordia aeterni patris, quod filium mittit, quam pretiosa sit haec obedientia in filio, quae horribilibus sceleribus omnium hominum anteferenda est, iuxta dictum: Gratia exuberat supra delictum. Cogitandae sunt causae, quare filius missus sit, et quare copulatae sint in Messia natura divina et humana, et quod Messias non tantum sit victima, sed quod filius missus sit ab initio, ut Ecclesiam colliga, et in ea sit efficax, sicut inquit: Ego vitam aeternam do eis. Item: Nemo novit patrem, nisi filius, et cui filius volet revelare.

Sint autem in conspectu causae copulationis divinae et humanae naturae.

1. Nisi factum esset decretum, ut filius assumeret massam generis humani, tota natura humana mox funditus deleta esset.

Servata est autem, ut hic filius nasceretur, et deinde inserti ei credentes rursus per eum vivificarentur.

2. Cum genus humanum peccaverit, congruebat, ut poenam lueret aliquis in genere humano.

Ideo filius intercessor assumsit humanam naturam, ut Psalmo secundo dicitur: Postula a me, et dabo tibi gentes haereditatem tuam.

3. Nullius creaturae robur tantum est, ut sustinere tantam iram potuerit, ideo hic Redemtor Deus est.

4. Ut pretium esset aequale, redemtor est Deus, ideo cogitandum est meritum filii mediatoris in infinitum longe antecellere omnibus omnium peccatis.

5. Creatura non est vivificatrix, sed ut Ioannis primo scriptum est: In ipso erat vita ideo hic redemtor est omnipotens, ut vincat mortem, et restituat humanae naturae vitam: sicut initio in creatione λόγος immediate fuit vivificator, ita et nunc est vivificator.

6. Hic mediator assidue interpellat pro Ecclesia, filius autem videt arcanum pectus patris, sicut inquit: Nemo novit patrem, nisi filius, et cui filius volet revelare.

Hic salvator assidue adest Ecclesiae, exaudit eam, servat, protegit, reddit vitam aeternam, sicut inquit: Ego vitam aeternam do eis. Ego sum vitis, vos palmites, sine me nihil potestis facere. Item: Sedet ad dextram aeterni patris dans dona hominibus. Haec autem sunt propriae omnipotentis naturae.

Haec attente consideranda sunt in quotidiana invocatione, ut in propheticis scriptis invocatio Messiae est illustre et firmum testimonium, quod ostendit eum esse natura Deum et omnipotentem, iuxta dicta, Psal. 72.: Et adorabunt eum omnes reges terrae. Et apud Ieremiam: Vocabunt eum, Deus iusticia nostra, id est, invocabunt, et in invocatione confitebuntur esse Deum iusticiam nostram. Sic ipse nos ad sese vocat: Venite ad me omnes qui laboratis et onerati estis, et ego reficiam vos.

Cum igitur fit mentio particulae Gratis, primum sciamus excludi omnia merita nostra, et non solum opera ceremonialia, sed etiam operibus decalogi detrahi meritum, et simul sciamus constitutum esse meritum filii Dei, propter quod solum recipiuntur omnes in conversione, qui credunt in filium, et id tam magnum est, ut longe vincat omnia omnium peccata. Ut igitur latro in cruce, mulier peccatrix, Manasses, et alii, propter mediatorem gratis recipiuntur fide, et simul vivificantur per filium dato Spiritu sancto, et fiunt haeredes vitae aeternae: sic et Ioseph et Daniel Gratis per misericordiam propter mediatorem recipiuntur fide, et simul vivificantur per filium dato Spiritu sancto, et fiunt haeredes vitae aeternae.

Haec exaequatio et opponenda est superbiae, sicut dicitur: Totus mundus reus sit Deo, et consolatio firma est omnibus, quia aliquo modo sentiunt molem suorum peccatorum. Ideo Dominus inquit Lucae 5.: Non veni vocare iustos, sed peccatores ad poenitentiam.

Huc pertinet et parabolae de filio prodigo, item de ove quae fuerat amissa, et hoc dictum: Maius gaudium est coelo de uno peccatore.

1. Timoth. 1. Certus est sermo, et omni acceptione dignus, quod Iesus Christus venerit in mundum, peccatores salvos facere etc.

Semper autem in conspectu sint hae quatuor causae, propter quas necesse est retinere exclusivam.

Prima, quae est principalis, ut debitus honos filio Dei tribuatur: quod sola ipsius obedientia sit pretium et meritum pro peccatis hominum, non ullius hominis opera. Ideo dictum est in Psalmo 39.: Holocaustum et hostiam pro peccato non postulasti. Tunc dixi: Ecce venio, in capite libri scriptum est de me, ut faciam voluntatem tuam. Item, unica oblatione consummavit sanctos.

Secunda causa, ut conscientiae habeant firmam consolationem: quia, si remissio peccatorum penderet ex conditione nostrae dignitatis, fieret incerta, inquit igitur Paulus: Ideo ex fide, Gratis, ut sit firma promissio.

Tertia causa, ut possit invocatio fieri fiducia filii Dei, non fiducia nostrorum meritorum, iuxta haec dicta: Quomodo invocabunt, nisi credent. Item: Quicquid petieritis patrem in nomine meo, id est, id agnitione et fiducia mei, dabit vobis. Donec enim corda fugiunt Deum, et retinent iram et fremitus adversus eum, non fit vera invocatio.

Quarta causa, ut sit conspectus discrimen legis et Evangelii. Habet lex suas promissiones, sed nequaquam gratuitas, ut dicitur: Quia fecerit ea, vivet in eis. At particula, Gratis propter filium Dei, manifeste discernit Evangelium a lege.

Haec simplicissima elementa doctrinae in Ecclesia necesse est omnibus familiarissime nota esse. Quare, cum hoc loco Paulus expresse particulam Gratis posuerit, breviter hanc sententiam repetivimus. Et in eandem sententiam dicitur in Ecclesiis nostris: Sola fide iustificamur, id est, agnitione et fiducia solius filii Dei statuente, quod propter eum nobis dentur remissio peccatorum, et reconciliatio et vivificatio per ipsum, dato Spiritu sancto, et haereditas vitae aeternae.

Certissimum ast autem, dato Spiritu sancto multas virtutes simul incoari, iuxta dictum: Effundam super domum David spiritum gratiae et precum.

Et tamen propositio vera est: Sola fide Paulus est iustus, quia propter mediatorem placet fide, non propter propriam dignitatem seu novitatem.

Particula ergo, Gratis, non excludit caeteras virtutes, ne adsint, sed excludit conditionem meriti seu dignitatis nostrae, ut usitate dicimus: Etiamsi multae virtutes simul sunt, tamen non sunt causae, vel meritum remissionis peccatorum, seu iustificationis et acceptationis ad vitam aeternam.

Haec recte intellecta illustrant promissionem et beneficia Christi, et afferunt piis consolationem, et accendunt veram invocationem, qua accedimus ad Deum fiducia filii mediatoris.

Hic iuniores monendi sunt de corruptela vocabuli Gratiae, quod interpretati sunt monachi de qualitatibus infusis, ut ipsi loquuntur, cum hic sine ulla dubitatione significet gratuitam misericordiam.

Ac suo loco alibi de usu vocabuli proxilius dictum est.

Per redemptionem, quae est in Christo Iesu.

Cum antea dixisset, gratuitam esse misericordiam, mox addit commemorationem de mediatore, ut intelligamus excludi nostra merita, et non meritum filii Dei, sed in illo arcano decreto de generis humani restitutione mirando consilio temperatam esse misericordiae iusticiam.

Immensae misericordiae est, quod divinitas non vult perire in totam aeternitatem genus humanum, sicut in tota aeternitate abiecit diabolos: sed tamen ut iusticiae quoque Dei satisfieret pro nostro peccato, ordinata est poena, quae est obedientia mediatoris innocentis: haec est meritum et pretium, propter quod et peccata nostra remittuntur, et nos Deo placemus seu accepti sumus, cum fide nobis applicatur, ut mox Paulus de fide dicit.

Et quatuor opera immensae misericordiae concurrunt, videlicet, quod recipimur propter filium, et ut recipi possimus liberrime mittitur filius, constituitur mediator et propiciator, et idem filius efficax est, profert Evangelium, colligit Ecclesiam, vivificat credentes, postea resuscitat ad vitam aeternam.

Horum mirabilium consiliorum, et operum causas, et motum in tota aeternitate contemplabimur in Deo: nunc, ut infantes et lactentes, utcunque initia huius doctrinae cogitanda sunt, agnoscenda ingentia beneficia Dei, et accipienda fide, et gratiae agendae sunt Deo mittenti filium, et filio passo pro nobis et resuscitato, ac colligentia aeternam Ecclesiam, et doceri et confirmari nos petamus, clamemus assidue: Credo Domine, sed opem fer imbecillitati meae.

Ac saepe repetatur cogitatione argumentum primorum parentum, qui post lapsum ante editam promissionem in sensu irae Dei sic ratiocinabantur: Iusticia Dei est immutabilis, Nos sumus rei: Ergo destructio est immutabilis.

Huius argumenti solutionem nulla creatura norat, sed filius Dei intercedens pro nobis, et sese offerens ad poenam, profert et ostendit huius argumenti solutionem, et docet quomodo congruant misericordia et iusticia.

Haec pie et reverenter cogitanda sunt, Ut quantum malum sit peccatum, consideremus: rursus etiam, ut beneficia Dei magnificiamus.

Quem constituit Deus propiciatorem per fidem in sanguine eius.

Intelligatur ergo in appellatione propiciatoris, offerens pro nobis sua merita, et persolvens poenam, et applicans sua merita nobis, sicut ipse Dominus inquit: Ego me pro eis sanctifico.

Haec proprietas propria huius personae, quae sola constituta est, ut sit mediatrix, comprehenditur in omnibus his appellationibus mediatoris, summi sacerdotis, propiciatoris et redemptoris, nec transferendus est hic honos in ullos alios homines aut angelos, et tota haec doctrina fit illistrior, collata huc definitione summi sacerdotis, quae traditur in Epistola ad Ebraeos.

Summus sacerdos, et filius Dei, immediate ab aeterno patre missus, et ordinatus ad proferendum Evangelium et ad offerendam suam mortem, ut esset placatio irae patris, et pretium pro aliis persolvendum iusticiae divinae, et semper intercedens pro nobis, et habens promissionem, quod certo exaudiatur. Hæc definitio, et tota doctrina de sacerdotio Christi, plena est dulcissimarum consolationum, et quotidie cogitanda.

Addidit autem Paulus hoc loco singulari consilio hanc particulam: Quem posuit propiciatorem per fidem in sanguine ipsius. Hic enim de applicatione nos docet.

Dicunt et Papistæ, filium Dei mediatorem, redemtorem et propiciatorem esse, sed hoc ipsum postea delent, quia prorsus omittunt mentionem fidei, imo iubent te dubitare, an hæc beneficia filii Dei ad te pertineant, videlicet, an sis in gratia, ac tantum sic loquuntur: Christus meruit primam gratiam, id est, occasionem merendi, ut si paterfamilias sit servo placatus ab amico aliquo, postea autem servus placeat suis officiis, nihil deinde ibi negotii est illi amico. Sic Papistæ sepeliunt Christum, cum fingunt hominem postea propriis virtutibus iustum esse, non fide, non misericordia propter filium Dei, imputata iustitia.

At cum Paulus nominat hic fidem, opponit eam dubitationi, vult vinci dubitationem, vult applicationem fieri fide, vult te firmiter statuere, quod propter hunc propiciatorem, seu propter eius obedientiam accipimus remissionem peccatorum, reconciliationem, seu acceptationem, imputata iustitia propter sanguinem mediatoris, scilicet, donata nobis ipsius obedientia, sicut propter eam simus iusti, id est, placentes et accepti Deo. Ita semper manet nobis filius propiciator, propter quem placemus, non propter nostras virtutes, quæ non possunt opponi iræ Dei.

Habent excellentes virtutes et divinas actiones in sese, Ioseph, Elias, Elisaeus, Daniel, sed has virtutes et actiones divinas non opponunt iudicio Dei, sed confugiunt ad mediatorem et promissam misericordiam, et statuunt se placere Deo, per misericordiam propter mediatorem, sicut in Psalmo dicitur: Convertere Domine, et eripe me propter misericordiam tuam, salvum me fac. Et Daniel inquit: Non in iustitia nostra exaudi nos, sed propter Dominum per misericordiam.

Ad ostensionem iusticiae suae propter remissionem peccatorum. Id est, ut declaret suam iusticiam in remissione peccatorum, et sequitur postea, quod sit iustus et iustificans eum: qui est ex fide Iesu.

Ac Paulus mox declarat, quomodo velit intelligi vocabulum iusticiae, cum ait, ut sit iustus, et iustificans eum, qui est ex fide Iesu, id est, in Evangelio declaratur iusticia Dei, quod ipse sit iustus, non nos, et iuste damnet peccatum in omnibus, sicut inquit, ut totus mundus reus sit Deo. Item: Tibi soli sum peccator et malum coram te feci, iustificeris in sermonibus tuis, et vincas cum iudicaris.

Declarat ergo Deus sese esse iustum et damnantem peccata, deinde et hoc declarat, quod ipse iustificet, nec ipsi nos iustificare possumus operibus legis. Iustificet autem hoc modo ipse, scilicet remissione peccatorum.

Definit igitur iustificationem ut infra, cum citat dictum: Beati quorum remissæ sunt iniquitates. Iustificatio est acceptio remissionis peccatorum, seu reconciliationis per fidem, qua filius Dei consolatur nos, ostendens misericordiam æterni patris in voce Evangelii, et liberans ex morte æterna vivificat nos, et dat Spiritum sanctum, ac facit nos hæredes vitæ æternæ. Sicut Iohannes inquit: Qui habet filium, habet vitam.

Hac definitione considerata intelligi potest, non divelli remissionem peccatorum, et vivificationem, sed hæc correlative se habere: sic enim fit remissio, cum fide accipitur, cogitata voce Evangelii. Et hac fide intuente obedientiam filii Dei, ipse filius λόγος æterni patris, vivificat credentes et habitat in eis, Spiritu sancto confirmans corda. Neque tamen fit vivificatio aut hæc inhabitatio, nisi præluceat fides, qui nititur obedientia filii Dei.

Sed cur inquit: Præcedentium peccatorum? Hic respondent quidam hanc particulam adiectam esse, ut sciamus in Evangelio non concedi licentiam peccandi, sed sciamus peccata remitti in his, qui agunt poenitentiam, in quibus peccatum desinit regnare.

Ac Novatiani hoc loco abusi sunt: cum non sequatur inde, Lapsis si rursus convertantur, non remitti delicta: quotiescunque enim fit remissio, fit præcedentium peccatorum remissio. Sed hoc loco remissio peccatorum non tantum de actualibus delictis intelligitur, sed de remissione actualium peccatorum et originalis, quo remisso in hac vita tamen morbus manet.

Sed Paulus opponit hanc particulam Præcedentium peccatorum, Legi, quasi dicat: Ne lex quidem abolevit peccatum, sed id præcedit donec agnitione et fiducia Messiae tollitur, sicut postea dicet: Usque ad legem peccatum fuit in mundo, id est, etiam cum lex lata est, manserunt tamen peccatum et mors. Tollitur autem agnitione et fiducia. filii Dei dupliciter, imputatione, scilicet in hac vita, quia reatus tollitur, et persona fit iusta, id est, accepta fide propter mediatorem. Et re ipsa incipit renovatio in corde per filium et Spiritum sanctum, quae postea erit integra in resurrectione.

Ubi est igitur gloriatio? Addit epiphonema ex collatione contrarii. Cum vera sit haec sententia, homines iustos esse fide coram Deo. Sequitur nullam esse gloriationem nostram, id est, nos non habere propriam iusticiam, seu legis impletionem seu meritum.

Estque perspicua confirmatio nostrae interpretationis, haec ipsa antithesis. Si essemus iusti impletione legis, haberemus gloriam et meritum, sed hanc gloriam et meritum expresse detrahunt nobis haec dicta, Psalm 142.: Non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens. Et Iob: Vere scio, quod non sit homo iustus coram Deo. Et Paulus dixit: Omnes carent gloria Dei. Item, ut totus mundus reus sit Deo. Est igitur perspicua antithesis: Ergo cum simus iusti sola misericordia, non habemus gloriam propriae iusticiae, in iudicio Dei.

Saepe autem iam dictum est, has propositiones correlative intelligendas esse, per misericordiam propter filium Dei sumus iusti, id est, fiducia misericordiae propter mediatorem. Ut Romanorum 4. correlative connectit promissionem et fidem: Ideo ex fide gratis, ut sit firma promissio: inquit igitur Paulus, exclusivam esse gloriationem lege fidei, id est, doctrina de fide, quae affirmat nos per misericordiam propter mediatorem iustos esse, et acquiescit in Deo propter mediatorem, non propter propriam dignitatem. Excludit ergo propriam dignitatem et meritum.

Hanc esse nativam et simplicissimam enarrationem congruentem universae propheticae scripturae, nihil dubium est. Sic orat Daniel: Exaudi nos non propter nostram iusticiam, sed per misericordiam propter Dominum, et David inquit: Salvum me fac propter misericordiam tuam. Sic accedamus ad Deum quotidie in invocatione fiducia mediatoris, non fiducia nostrae dignitatis aut iusticiae essentialis.

Nota sint et haec recte dicta scriptorum, Augustinus inquit: Totius fiduciae certitudo debet in pretioso sanguine Christi. Et Basilius inquit in concione de humilitate, pag. 388.: Dicit autem Apostolus: Qui gloriatur in Domino glorietur, dicens, quod Christus nobis sit sapientia a Deo, iusticia, et sanctificatio et redemtio, sicut scriptum est: Qui gloriatur in Domino glorietur. Haec enim perfecta et integra gloriatio in Deo, quando ne quidem propter suam iusticiam aliquis extollitur, sed agnoscit sese carere vera iusticia, sola autem fide in Christum iustificari.

Haec congruunt cum hoc dicto: Exclusa est gloriatio per doctrinam de fide. Hanc opponit legi operum, quae est doctrina praecipiens integram obedientiam, et docens iusticiam esse, habere integram obedientiam, sicut infra inquit capite 10. Moises describit iusticiam, quae ex lege est, qui fecerit ea, vivet in eis.

Nominat ergo legem operum, doctrinam legis, id est, ipsam legem sic proprie dictam, de qua alibi dicitur: Lex iram efficit. Libenter autem usa est illa gens nomine legis, quare saepe generaliter pro doctrina, seu pro verbo Dei usurpatur, ut in toto Psal. 118.: Beati immaculati in via, qui ambulant in lege Domini. Item: Pax multa diligentibus legem tuam, et non est eis scandalum.

Adseveramus igitur fide iustificari hominem sine operibus. Epiphonemati adiecit Conclusionem, in qua breviter repetit summam propositionis, et iterum inculcat Exclusivam. Nam ad hoc repetitiones conducunt, ut sciat lector non obiter eam particulam dicenti excidisse, sed serio et re deliberata velle eum hoc, quod toties inculcat.

Nec obscuritas est in dicto Pauli, sed verborum proprietas retineatur. Puerile est, quod quidam disputant de verbo arbitramur: nam Graece λογίζομαι significat asseverationem collectam ex praecedenti copulatione. Fides significat assensionem, qua amplectimur promissionem gratiae, quae in Evangelio propter mediatorem offertur, et est fiducia promissae misericordiae, ut haec vocabulu enarratio saepe tradita est: ut Ephesios quarto Paulus enarrat unum vocabulum multis: Per quem audemus accedere in fiducia per fidem eius, ut et Psalmus loquitur: Beati omnes qui confidunt in eo.

Iustificari significat accipere remissionem peccatorum et reconciliationem, et imputationem iusticiae ...seu acceptationem, cum qua simul est efficax filius Dei, dicit consolationem voce Evangelii in mente, et ostendit voluntatem patris, et vivificat credentem, ac effundit Spiritum sanctum in cor, sicut 1. Iohan. 4. dicitur: In hoc cognoscimus, quod in ipso manemus et ipse in nobis, quia de spiritu suo dat nobis.

Est igitur sententia propositionis: Asseveramus hominem accipere remissionem peccatorum, reconciliationem, et imputationem iusticiae, propter filium Dei mediatorem per misericordiam gratis, non propter legem, seu nostras virtutes, seu opera. Et hanc misericordiam accipi oportet fide: hanc simplicem sententiam cum verba Pauli gignant, simus discipuli sermonis divini, et retineamus nativum intellectum verborum.

Nihil significat monachis fide iustificari, quia fidem intelligunt tantum noticiam, qualis est et in diabolis.

Adfingunt igitur hanc synecdochen, fide iustificamur, scilicet formata, dicunt doctrinam initium esse, sed postea hominem esse iustum dilectione, id est, obedientia quam legi praestat. Ideo addunt Paulo hanc particulam, fide homo iustificatur, scilicet formata per dilectionem. Et hoc somnio declarant appellationem. Ut cum anima corpori infunditur vivit corpus, sic dicunt noticiam fieri vivam, cum accedit reliqua obedientia. Haec imaginatio prorsus corruptela est: nam fides non dicitur viva propter dilectionem.

Est enim motus divinus, quo cor expavoribus liberatur, et acquiescit in Deo, agnita misericordia propter mediatorem, desinit fugere Deum, et clamat Abba Pater, nec accipit vitam a dilectione, quae sequitur, sed est causa dilectionis. Ideo enim diligitur Deus, quia misericordia propter filium promissa agnita est, qui pro nobis orans, inquit: Sit dilectio tua in eis, qua me diligis. Monachi Exclusivam sine operibus sic restrinxerunt: Sine operibus, videlicet ceremonialibus et forensibus Moisi.

Et interea retinent hanc propositionem, opera moralia mereri remissionem, hominem iustum esse propter opera moralia coram Deo. Haec tota corruptela monachorum reiicienda est, et constanter haec vera sententia retinenda est, quam toties Paulus repetit, cum utitur exclusiva, Gratis: videlicet, homines nec mereri remissionem peccatorum propriis operibus moralibus aut aliis, nec coram Deo iustos esse propter bona opera moralia, seu propter virtutes proprias, neque ante renovationem, neque post renovationem in hac vita, nec habere in hac vita integram obedientiam decalogi.

Ideo supra dictum est: Totus mundus reus sit Deo. Et in Psalmo dicitur: Non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens. Et Iob inquit Cap. 9.: Vere scio, quod non sit homo iustus coram Deo. Hae perspicuae confessiones non sic corrumpendae sunt.

Non est homo iustus coram Deo ceremoniis, sed est iustus, quia habet perfectam obedientiam decalogi. In tali imaginatione manifestum esset mendacium.

Necesse est enim fateri omnes homines natos in hac naturae immunditie, non habere se perfectam obedientiam decalogi. Ostendit igitur Evangelium, mediatorem et misericordiam, ac adfirmat homines iustos esse, id est, habentes remissionem peccatorum, et placentes Deo propter mediatorem per misericordiam, Gratis, fide, id est, fiducia misericordiae acquiescente in Deo propter mediatorem.

Itaque adversus corruptelam monachorum, qui tantum ceremonias excludunt, opponenda est particula Gratis, quae testatur nec moralia opera mereri remissionem peccatorum: nam reconciliationeque gratuita, neque certa nobis esset, si penderet ex conditione impleti decalogi.

Quare et postea inquit Paulus: Ideo ex fide gratis, ut sit firma promissio.

Deinde et expressa confessio non impleti decalogi opponatur corruptelae monachorum: Non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens. Hac confessione posita, manifestum est reconciliationem dari propter mediatorem, non propter nostras virtutes, et accipi eam fide.

Haec est sententia Exclusivae in nostris Ecclesiis etiam, cum dicimus hominem iustificari sola fide. Hic et corruptela Osiandrica refutanda est, quae est similis synecdochae monachorum, iustificamur fide praeparative, ut si dicas: Motus calefacit, scilicet praeparative, sed postea calore sumus calidi. Sic contendit Osiander dici: Fide iustificamur, id est, fides praeparat nos, ut postea alia re simus iusti, scilicet novitate.

Quam autem novitas sequitur, et verum est, hominem fieri templum Dei et habitare Deum in conversis seu renatis, tamen retinenda est haec consolatio, quod conversi seu renati sint iusti fide gratis, propter obedientiam mediatoris, non propter sequentem novitatem aut iusticiam essentialem, sed propter mediatorem.

Hanc consolationem retineri necesse est in hoc dicto: Iustus fide sua vivet. Intueamur verum agonem conscientiae in conversione, et deinceps in magna lucta, et cogitemus quae sit vera consolatio.

Hic certissimi.

mum est omnes Prophetas et omnes sanctos statuere, quod per misericordiam Deo placeant, et hanc misericordiam promissam et certam esse propter mediatorem, et fidem niti obedientia mediatoris, non iusticia essentiali. Haec manifesta sunt etiam ex hoc dicto ad Ephesios: Per ipsum audemus accedere in fiducia per fidem in ipsum. Et quanquam verum est, in ea consolatione fieri vivificationem, et Deum accendere novas actiones in homine, tamen credens in infinitum antefert obedientiam mediatoris his actionibus Dei, quae iam in renato fiunt. Haec sunt perspicua consideranti discrimen legis et Evangelii, et consolationes in vera conversione.

## 4:14
Do we then abolish the Law?

God forbid.

Why, he asks, is the Law established, when the polity of Moses has already been utterly destroyed by the horrible wrath of God? Is this not abolishing the Law? And the decree of the Apostles, which is recited in Acts chapter 15, in which it is expressly pronounced that the Mosaic Ceremonies are not the justice about which the Gospel preaches, nor are they necessary things in the Church of the Son of God, was made and issued before Paul wrote this Epistle to the Romans, because that decree was made before Paul crossed into Europe. And this Epistle was written by Paul when he was in the city of Corinth.

But the explanation is easy for one considering these sayings: Christ is the end of the Law. Likewise: I did not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it. The whole Law signifies Christ, as is manifest, that the victims were types and shadows of the victim to come, whose obedience God, by a wondrous counsel, willed to be the price for us. But when the true victim is exhibited, that which the types had signified is exhibited, namely, reconciliation and justice through the mediator, which is received by the recognition and confidence of the mediator. It can easily be understood that Christ is the end of the ceremonies, because certainly the types are on account of the signified victim. And the whole polity is a shadow of the eternal kingdom or the eternal Church. When, therefore, the Messiah exhibits the eternal kingdom, the shadow yields to the thing signified. And indeed all the miracles of the defense and preservation of that polity are testimonies of the coming Messiah.

But I omit these parts of the Law. For it is spoken of here especially concerning the moral law, because it speaks of the law which signifies justice and convicts of sin. Christ is the end also of the moral law, because the Moral Law is a horrible testimony and judgment in the nature of men against sin, and it convicts the guilty nature, it does not liberate: it testifies, therefore, that there is need of a mediator, and it signifies the justice which the mediator brings.

We understand all these things less in this darkness of ours, because human minds have too childish dreams about the moral law; we think it is some kind of bridle governing external gestures, and we rage against this bond, and we would rather wander with opinions and desires without any boundaries. We do not sufficiently recognize these most sad evils in the nature of men: afterwards we imagine that some external discipline is the fulfillment of the law and justice. Since, therefore, we do not think enough about what the Law of God is, and why it is implanted in the nature of men, why it has been repeated by the voice of God, and that the nature of men was created for it, and is restored to it through the Son of God, and how unlike the law the nature of men is: on account of this darkness of ours, the sayings of Paul seem obscure to us, and sometimes it happens in Explanations, that which is said in the proverb, so that it sounds: One thing the Foot, another the Lyre.

Let us not imagine the moral law to be a decree similar to the Spartan law about the iron coin, which not only could be changed and abolished, but was also easily and conveniently changed.

But let us know the Law of God, which is named moral, to be the eternal and immovable wisdom and norm of justice revealed in God to the rational creature, and demanding that the rational creature be conformable to God, and destroying all who are not conformable. This eternal wisdom of God is by no means abolished in the Gospel.

And just as the nature of men was created by a wondrous counsel for this wisdom and conformity with God, so God wills us to be restored to this very light and conformity through the Son. Therefore Christ is said to be the end of the Law. And here Paul says: By faith we establish the Law, which I interpret thus concerning the moral law. But although I judge our interpretation to be true, and congruent with Paul, yet I confess that I cannot sufficiently explain the amplitude of the apostolic wisdom.

I know that Augustine often uses this explanation: Through faith the Law is established, that is, help is obtained, so that you may be able to obey the Law. This explanation is very thin and mutilated. Although it is true, that there is given

Holy Spirit is given in consolation, in which by faith we acquiesce in the mediator, and such motions are kindled by the Holy Spirit, as he himself is: yet this begun obedience in us is still far from the perfection of the law. Osiander rightly says that God dwells in believers, but at the same time there is still a great mass of sin in men. Then when God shall be all in all, that is, when he shall shine in the blessed, in whom there shall be no sin, there we shall understand what the fulfilling of the law is, there we shall be righteous with God shining in us. But in this life, in such infirmity, we so approach God that we flee to the mercy promised on account of the mediator, and are covered by the mediator, just as in Isaiah the mediator is named a Shelter. And Paul says: Through him we have access in confidence, through faith in him.

Thus, therefore, for the sake of teaching, I say that the law is established by faith in three ways. First, by the confession of the truth, that the law of God is justly judging and condemning us, and that our righteousness does not merit reconciliation, nor is it the fulfilling of the law. Secondly, by the imputation of righteousness on account of the mediator. For because by faith we acknowledge the mediator, and believe that for his sake the remission of sins and reconciliation are given to us, and that we are reputed righteous on account of his obedience, we are righteous and accepted by God in this life on account of the obedience of the Son, by faith. The law is therefore established, because we acknowledge that the law is not an empty murmur, but that a penalty had to be paid for the human race, and that this payment has been given to us.

But it is a rule that laws are established and confirmed by penalty. And although obedience is begun in this life, yet we are still far from the perfection of the law, but we are reputed righteous, that is, having the remission of sins and reconciliation on account of the mediator by faith: thus we have that which the law signified, that the wrath of God is not taken away by our fulfilling, and reconciliation made, but that the mediator's obedience is given to believers. Thus it is said in Rom. 5: Justified by his blood, we shall be saved through him from wrath.

Thirdly, the law is established by faith, according to the saying to the Galatians: We by the Spirit from faith wait for the hope of righteousness, that is, those reconciled by faith shall have the entire righteousness signified in the law. For it is most certain that in the law is signified not only the beginning, which happens in this life, but is signified the perfect conformity with God, which shall be, when God shall be all in all, that is, when he shall communicate himself to us in the clearest light, and shall vivify us with eternal life, and his wisdom, righteousness, and joy shall shine in us, and there shall in no way be remnants of sin in us at the same time. We look upon this consummated benefit, when it is said: I came not to destroy the law, but to fulfill, Item: Jehovah our righteousness. And at the same time let us know that in this life believers have the beginnings of eternal life, according to the saying: He who has the Son, has life.

Let this be understood in order, both of the beginning, and of eternal life in that heavenly Church. But he has the Son in this life, whoever in true conversion believes that he has, on account of the obedience of the mediator, the remission of sins, reconciliation, and the imputation of righteousness. When he is raised up by this consolation, the Son of the eternal Father is immediately effective by the voice of the Gospel, and vivifies the believer, and pours the Holy Spirit into the heart, by which joy acquiescing in God, the love of God, and true invocation are kindled.
