These are the beginnings of eternal life: thus the Lord also preaches, saying: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him, and make our dwelling with him. First, the Son commands himself to be heard, and the voice of the Gospel to be received. Thus he begins the healing from the voice of the Gospel.

But the Father loves the believer; see the propriety of the expression. Although we are not yet without sin in this life, yet the believer is loved by God, he is righteous, because the Father receives him through mercy on account of the Son the mediator, and imputes righteousness to him. But that our nature also may be restored, this happens at the same time: We will come to him, and make our dwelling with him.

The eternal Father sent the Son to bring forth the voice of the Gospel, arcane and unknown to all creatures, and through this Son he immediately gathers the Church by the voice of the Gospel. This Son is immediately effective, when consolation is made by the voice of the Gospel, the Word (λόγος) is truly present, and shows the Father, as he says: No one knows the Father, except the Son, and he to whom the Son will choose to reveal him. And then at the same time the Father and the Son pour the Holy Spirit into the heart of the believer: for the Holy Spirit is given through the Son, when consolation is made with the voice of the Gospel. And let the opinion of Athanasius be noted: In whomever the Holy Spirit is said to be, he is there through the Word.

Wherefore also below mention is made of both persons, in the 8th chapter of Romans: If indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. Item: If Christ is in you. And he himself says: I am the vine, you are the branches, He who remains in me, and I in Truly, therefore, the Word, the Son of God, is present in the believer, and is effective through the voice of the Gospel. Thus it is also said in the third chapter to the Ephesians: That Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith. Paul embraces all these immense benefits of the mediator when he says, "We establish the law by faith," namely, both by the imputation of righteousness and the presence of God in believers, who even in this life kindles a new light and new motions in the hearts, and afterwards gives eternal life, in which the righteousness of God, signified in the law, will be whole in us, which is described by these words in the law: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, etc."

And in daily invocation we reflect upon these greatest matters, upon all the benefits of the Son of God in order: that He was sent to gather an eternal Church, that He is truly present and effective through the voice of the Gospel, that for His sake the eternal Father receives us, and is simultaneously present in us, and wills to have mercy on us and truly gives the Holy Spirit through the Son, so that He may govern us. When we ask for these benefits, then that which Paul says here comes to pass: "We establish the law by faith," because this true invocation is the beginning of new obedience. At the same time, let us consider the common doctrine, that a person is righteous by faith on account of the mediator in this life, even if our nature is still very unlike the law of God. This faith must shine before new obedience. Next, it must also be known how new obedience is both begun and pleasing to God. It is begun because God truly dwells in the heart of the believer, and it is pleasing to God because the person is pleasing solely by faith on account of the mediator, and believes that this very obedience is pleasing to God, not because it satisfies the law, but on account of the mediator, who is the high priest constantly interceding for us. Although, therefore, because of the immense infirmity of our nature in this life, this begun obedience is very languid and squalid, yet in that way, as has been said, it is pleasing to God, and is named Righteousness and Sacrifice.

This whole doctrine becomes more clear when it is piously considered in daily invocation, in true sorrows and exercises of conversion, in which the very groans of the pious refute even the furies of the Monks and Antinomians. The Monks do not understand faith as anything other than a knowledge of history, and they command men to always doubt whether they are pleasing to God. Afterwards, they pretend that their works are the fulfillment of the law and merits of eternal life, and they accumulate many errors, the falsity of which is seen in those very sorrows of the pious.

The Antinomians are also refuted, for the pious feel that they are judged by the law of God, they feel in public and private punishments the just wrath of God, which is the execution of the law, and they confess the same thing that the Prophet says: "Because of iniquity you punish men." They do not think that the law, the judgment of God, and the wrath of God are empty words. Let us therefore look in the Pauline reading for true conversion, not what the Epicureans, who are Antinomians, most audaciously invent, nor what the monks simulate, who boast that they obey or even satisfy the law of God, nay, that they are even perfect, when in truth their minds are Epicurean and they deride God, and turn this simulation to gain. Even more impudent is the Cynic in Austria, who recently renewed in his writings errors about perfection: he names the mendicancy of the monks perfection, which he knows to be a snare artificially instituted, not so much to feed the belly as to seek power.

But You, Son of God, Lord Jesus Christ, who truly gather an eternal Church by the voice of the Gospel, I pray that You may illuminate Your truth and repress all the furies of the impious. You see how great is the madness and the power of the enemies of the truth; I humbly beseech You for the sake of Your glory, that You may illuminate Your truth, and govern us, and in us kindle and increase Your light, and blot out the lies and blasphemies which many, with Cyclopean profanity, both speak against You and attempt to defend.

But as Paul says in this place, "by faith we establish the law," so the Lord says: "I have not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it." The Greek phrase is λύειν νόμον, which means not only to commit an offense against the law, but to abolish the law itself, as when we say: "Cicero the Consul abolished the agrarian law." Therefore, our Lord Jesus Christ affirms that He did not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it.

He fulfills it, however, in four ways. First, by His own obedience, which is whole. Second, by deriving upon Himself the punishment which we owed to the law. For God so wills His law, which is eternal wisdom and the norm of righteousness in Himself, to be valid, that although He receives men through mercy, yet justice is so coupled that He willed that the law be satisfied and the punishment paid for us. Here let the Antinomians consider, if they are not Epicureans, what the law is, and why God willed it to be valid, when not the human race would be accepted, unless the Son paid the penalty for us. We shall contemplate this wondrous counsel, the authority of the law, the tempering of justice and mercy, and the magnitude of love in the Son of God toward us, and in the eternal Father toward the Son and toward us, in that eternal academy. Now, however, God wishes us to learn the first elements of this wisdom. I confess that my speech regarding the magnitude of such great things is far weaker than it ought to be, but yet with whatever clamor I signify my indignation against Hypocrites, Monks, and Antinomians, who speak scurrilously about the law of God.

But when the Lord signifies that He pays the penalty of the law of God for us, He simultaneously embraces the doctrine concerning the remission of sins and reconciliation, and the imputation of justice. For because He pays the penalty for us, and appeases the wrath of the eternal Father for us, there are granted to believers, on account of His own sacrifice, the remission of sins, reconciliation, the imputation of justice, vivification through the Son and the Holy Spirit, and the donation of eternal life.

Thirdly, the Son of God fulfills the law by effectuation or restoration in us. For God so wishes the law to be valid that He sent the Son, that He might both pay the penalty for us, and restore in us obedience or conformity with Himself, which is indeed begun in this life. But in the heavenly Church it will be complete, when God shall be all in all the blessed. Fourthly, the Son of God fulfills the moral law by teaching, or sanctioning, or repeating the decalogue. For although He was not sent to be the founder of the law, for the law was previously implanted in rational creatures at the beginning, and afterwards was always divinely repeated in the Church, and indeed in the Church of God alone has the law always been retained without corruptions: yet He Himself repeats it, and testifies that this is the judgment of God, arguing against sins, and showing true worship, and He expounds it, and cleanses the Pharisaical filth, with which hypocrites corrupt the law both then and in all times.

Chapter IV.

What then shall we say that Abraham our father found according to the flesh? In the fourth chapter, the confirmation of the proposition is begun, taken from the example of Abraham and the first saying, in which mention is expressly made of the justice of faith. For Paul wishes to show that the doctrine proposed in the Gospel is not unknown to the ancient Church, of the Prophets and Fathers, but that there is one perpetual and consenting voice of the Fathers, Prophets, Christ, and the Apostles, just as the Lord Himself says: Abraham saw my day, and was glad. Although this entire confirmation is born from that saying, "Abraham believed God" etc.: yet because the explanation of the circumstances generates many arguments, we shall distribute it into these five arguments, which may be in view, and so that they may confirm us in the doctrine, and in daily invocation and consolation may stir up faith, because invocation cannot happen unless this faith shines forth, that we are received and heard on account of the Son, and indeed on account of the obedience of the Son.

First argument. Abraham was not righteous on account of works before God, but by faith, Therefore neither are others righteous on account of works, but by faith. The consequence is valid: Because Abraham is proposed as an example of the doctrine. The antecedent is proved from the saying: Abraham believed God.

Second. Justification is the imputation of justice, by which God through mercy receives and vivifies us, Therefore we are not righteous by our own works or merits.

Third. Justification is the remission of sins, by which God receives and vivifies us on account of the mediator, and through Him, Therefore we are not righteous by our own works or merits.

Fourth. Abraham is righteous by faith before circumcision, Therefore he is not righteous by circumcision.

Fifth. It is necessary that the promise of grace or reconciliation be certain.

A promise hanging on the condition of the law becomes uncertain, because the law works wrath, Therefore the promise of grace does not hang on the condition of the law, but is given freely, and is to be received by faith. ENARRATION ON THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS, CHAP. IV. For if Abraham [was justified] by works etc. The first express assertion in the text to be considered is that Paul openly affirms that Abraham was not righteous before God on account of his works, just as it was said above: By the works of the law shall no flesh be justified.

And there is no doubt that Paul includes moral works: for Abraham also preceded the polity of Moses by four hundred and thirty years or thereabouts.

Next, let the accommodation of the saying be considered: Abraham believed God, and it was imputed to him for righteousness.

Elsewhere he cites these sayings: The just shall live by his faith. Item: He who believes in him shall not be confounded. Here, however, he recites the first saying, in which mention of faith is expressly made.

For he wishes also to show by this that he is not now bringing in a doctrine unknown to the Church of the Fathers and Prophets, but that the same doctrine concerning righteousness has always existed in the true Church.

But in order that the accommodation may be rightly understood, the cavils that are opposed to it must be refuted, of which this is the first.

The first cavil of the adversaries.

The adversaries say that Paul misuses this saying, because it is said there concerning faith expecting posterity. But the Gospel speaks of faith acknowledging Christ crucified and resurrected, and receiving the remission of sins. Therefore, Moses speaks of one faith, and Paul of another.

I answer: Concerning all the examples in which faith is praised, such as Gideon, David, they believe that God will be present with them as they fight: even when an external thing is sought and expected, it is always necessary that this faith shine forth, by which reconciliation is received on account of the mediator, according to the saying: No one can come to the father except through the son.

Item Rom. 5: Through him we have access by faith. Therefore, the first and principal object of faith is always God not being angry, but receiving us on account of the son, and the first struggle is, Whether God is willing to receive you.

And since we now believe him to be propitious, we afterwards expect other benefits from him. Gideon and David could not ask for or expect victories from God unless they first believed that they were accepted and pleasing to God. But they know from the promise that men are received through mercy on account of the mediator, according to the saying: In thy seed shall all nations be blessed. And just as it is certain that the Church is gathered on account of the son, so the saints know that the promises of bodily goods were handed down on account of the son, because they are necessary for the Church.

Therefore 2 Cor. 7 it is said:

All promises are ratified in Christ. Let the objects of faith therefore be distinguished: the first and principal is God propitious on account of the mediator; afterwards other external objects can be added.

As Abraham seeks protection among impious nations, he seeks posterity and the preservation of the Church. Finally, in daily invocation we embrace many things, but all the saints approach God in one and the same way, namely, believing God to be propitious on account of the mediator, just as the Lord himself says: Whatever you ask the father in my name, he will give to you. Now let the words of the text be considered.

In chapter 12 of Genesis, the Lord says: I will bless thee.

Item: In thee shall all nations be blessed.

Afterwards in chapter 15 it is said: Fear not, I am thy protector and thy reward exceeding great. In these most sweet promises, reconciliation is manifestly shown, and Abraham knew the first promise: The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent.

And indeed he knew this promise was already restricted to his own posterity, because it had been said: In thee shall all nations be blessed. He receives, therefore, at once both the promise of reconciliation and of the blessed seed and of posterity, that is, of the Church to be propagated.

That he receives these promises with faith is manifest, [and that] it is the same faith of Abraham and of Paul, and of all the saints in the true Church, receiving reconciliation on account of the mediator.

Therefore the Lord also says: Abraham saw my day, that is, he recognized the mediator in the promise and by trust in the mediator received the remission of sins, and was freed from the underworld and from the wrath of God. Abraham believed God etc.

This answer is true and firm, just as experience testifies in the hearts of all the pious.

The same text in Moses shows what he names Faith there, namely, not just knowledge about God, such as is in the devils, or in the Gentiles, that God exists, that he is the creator of the world, wise, truthful, just, chaste, demanding obedience congruent to his own wisdom and will, and judging and punishing the disobedient, just as Latomus of Louvain says, [that] there was no other [faith] in Abraham’s faith, just as the knowledge of it was in Cicero or in Xenophon.

But this text in Moses had previously recited the promises: In you shall all nations be blessed. Likewise: Do not fear, I am your protector, etc. Since, therefore, he says, Abraham believed, it is necessary for this to be referred to the preceding promises: for faith is also to assent to every word of God revealed.

Wherefore it follows necessarily and manifestly that the faith of Abraham was not only knowledge of history, but also knowledge and assent, by which he embraced the promises. Moses and Paul do not speak of a mutilated faith, which is only knowledge of history, but of this faith, which is knowledge of history and of the promises, and is assent and trust, by which we embrace the promise, and hearts acquiesce in the promised mediator, or in God promising on account of the mediator. Therefore, Paul also soon in this chapter couples promise and faith, so that he may show that he is speaking of that faith which receives the promise, by which God, on account of the mediator, promises to all believers the remission of sins, reconciliation, the imputation of righteousness, sanctification through the Holy Spirit, and eternal life.

Since, therefore, it is clear what Moses and Paul name Faith, the refutation of the cavils which are objected is manifest, such as: Demons believe and are not righteous, therefore men are not justified by faith. Likewise: No nature is righteous by knowledge alone, Faith is only knowledge, therefore no one is righteous by faith. Likewise: Faith is a work, Therefore: We are righteous by works. The explanation of these objections declares the term Faith, nor do we invent tricks or subtleties, but we illustrate the native meaning of the word in the discourse of the Prophets and Apostles. There is, therefore, a response to the first objection.

Demons believe, but with a mutilated faith, that is, they hold the knowledge of history, and they know that the Son of God will punish all devils with a horrible judgment, but they by no means embrace the promises, they do not conclude that sins are remitted to them: therefore they furiously hate God and Christ, and they feel punishments, and they fear sadder torments. Paul does not speak of this faith when he says, Being justified by faith we have peace toward God: but of the faith which is not only knowledge of history, but also embraces the promise, and is trust acquiescing in the mediator. Therefore, the definition customary among us is: Faith is to assent to every word of God delivered to us, and thus to the promise of grace, and it is trust acquiescing in the promise, that is, in God promising on account of the mediator.

Second argument. No nature is righteous by knowledge alone, Faith is only knowledge, Therefore: We are not righteous by faith alone. I answer simply: I deny the minor premise.

For as it was said before, the faith which assents to the promise is not only knowledge, but is at the same time trust, which is a motion kindled by the Holy Spirit, by which the will and heart are enlivened and gladdened, so that they may acquiesce in God on account of the mediator: as when David hears the absolution: The Lord has taken away your sin, there is not only in him knowledge of this proposition, but the will and heart, this good having been shown, emerge again from the highest sorrows and from the depths. As it is said: Being justified by faith we have peace. And Hezekiah says: But you have delivered my soul so that it would not perish, you have cast all my sins behind your back. Thus Paul shows what motions faith embraces when he says: Through him we dare to approach in trust through faith in him. There he shows that trust and approach to God are included in this faith, of which he speaks, and it is necessary that these be included, because it is said of that faith which assents to the promise. There is, therefore, also trust in the will and heart acquiescing in the promise, that is, in God promising on account of the mediator.

The third argument.

We are justified by faith, Faith is a work, Therefore: We are justified by works. I answer: There is a simple and true explanation, which all who are moderately learned in our Churches have always used, namely these propositions: By faith we have the remission of sins, By faith we are justified.

By no means is it to be understood thus, that on account of this work in us, namely to believe, or on account of the dignity of this work, men have remission or are justified. For Paul universally intends this, that men have remission freely on account of the mediator, and are accepted by God, not on account of the dignity of any work in us, whether it be done by our own powers, or by God moving the hearts. These works also are kindled by God in us, the love of God, patience, chastity. But just as we do not have remission on account of these works, so neither on account of faith, insofar as it is a quality, or a work in us, but because by faith we acknowledge the mediator, and his benefits must be applied to us by faith, through the thought-out voice of the Gospel. I answer, therefore, to the major premise, as we customarily say: We are justified by faith, this proposition is to be understood correlatively, as if it were said, We are justified by mercy on account of the mediator, whom, however, it is necessary to acknowledge by faith, and his benefits must be applied in us by faith.

The meaning in the major premise is therefore: On account of Christ we have remission and s. men freely through the mediator have remission, and are accepted by God, not because of the dignity of any work in us, whether it be done by our own powers, or by God moving our hearts.

These works also are kindled in us by God: love of God, patience, chastity. But just as we do not have remission because of these works, so neither because of faith, insofar as it is a quality or a work in us, but because by faith we acknowledge the mediator, and it is necessary that his benefits be applied to us by faith, as thought of by the voice of the Gospel.

I answer therefore to the major premise, as we customarily say: By faith we are justified.

This proposition must be understood correlatively, as if it were said: We are justified by mercy through the mediator, whom, however, it is necessary to acknowledge by faith, and his benefits to be applied to us by faith. The meaning in the major premise is therefore: Because of Christ we have remission and are righteous, that is, accepted. Therefore, the conclusion does not follow that we are righteous because of works.

Thus, when it is said in Isaiah: "The knowledge of my righteous servant shall justify many": let it not be understood that believers are pleasing because of the dignity of faith, but the Prophet speaks thus because it is necessary to acknowledge the mediator and that his benefits be applied to him by faith.

For he had said before: "By his stripes we are healed."

These things have been said briefly so that the word "Faith," or "he believed," might be clear.

Now the other words follow: "Righteousness was imputed to him": for so the Hebrews read, that is, righteousness was thought of or decreed for this man, who was previously guilty, that is, the remission of sins, and divine acceptance, and the inheritance of eternal life and righteousness, when he believes the promise.

And Paul cites this saying because it expresses first how righteousness is decreed to a man without condition.

For in the law there are only conditional propositions: "Cursed is he who does not remain in all things," etc.

He adds, therefore, a declaration that the imputation is gratuitous, namely, that God thinks or decrees this believer to be righteous by His mercy, even if there is not in him the fulfillment of the law, which God would approve by debt, if it were present. He says, therefore: "Reward is given by debt," that is, where there is the actual fulfillment of the law, God, who is such, approves it out of His righteousness.

Here let the juniors learn that the words "Debt" and "Merit" are correlative.

When the monks said: "The contrite man has merits of condignity," they meant that this obedience is righteousness, which God receives by debt, etc. Therefore, just as Paul here rejects debt, so let us know that the merit of the remission of sins and of eternal life is rejected.

Latin:

An igitur legem abolemus?

Absit.

Cur inquit stabiliri legem, cum iam politia Moisi funditus deleta sit horribili irae Dei? An hoc non est abolere legem? Et decretum Apostolorum, quod recitatur in Actis capite 15. in quo expresse pronunciatur, Ceremonias Mosaicas non esse iusticiam, de qua concionatur Evangelium, nec res necessarias esse in Ecclesia filii Dei, factum et editum est antequam Paulus hanc Epistolam ad Romanos scripsit, quia decretum illud factum est priusquam Paulus in Europam traiecit. Et haec Epistola scripta est a Paulo, cum in urbe Corintho esset.

Sed facilis est explicatio consideranti haec dicta: Christus est finis legis. Item: Non veni solvere legem, sed implere. Tota lex significat Christum, ut manifestum est, victimas fuisse typos et umbras venturae victimae, cuius obedientiam mirando consilio Deus voluit esse pretium pro nobis. Exhibita autem vera victima, exhibetur id quod significaverant typi, scilicet reconciliatio et iusticia per mediatorem, quae agnitione et fiducia mediatoris accipitur. Facile intelligi potest, Christum finem esse ceremoniarum, quia certe typi sunt propter significatam victimam. Et tota politia umbra est aeterni regni seu aeternae Ecclesiae. Cum igitur Messias exhibet aeternum regnum, cedit umbra rei significatae. Et quidem omnia miracula defensionis et conservationis illius politiae sunt testimonia de venturo Messia.

Sed has partes legis omitto. Praecipue enim de lege morali hic dicitur, quia loquitur de lege, quae significat iusticiam et arguit peccatum. Christus est finis etiam legis moralis, quia Lex Moralis est horribile testimonium et iudicium in natura hominum adversus peccatum, et arguit ream naturam, non liberat: testatur ergo opus esse mediatore, et significat iusticiam, quam mediator adfert.

Haec omnia minus intelligimus in hac nostra caligine, quia de lege morali humanae mentes nimis puerilia somnia habent, cogitamus qualecunque frenum esse regens externos gestus, et fremimus adversus hoc vinculum, et mallemus vagari opinionibus et cupiditatibus sine ullis metis. Haec tristissima mala in hominum natura non satis agnoscimus: postea fingimus qualemcunque externam disciplinam esse legis impletionem et iusticiam. Cum igitur non satis cogitemus, quid sit lex Dei, et quare naturae hominum insita sit, quare voce Dei repetita sit, et quod ad eam condita sit natura hominum, et ad eam restituatur per filium Dei, et quam dissimilis sit legi natura hominum: propter hanc nostram caliginem dicta Pauli vidententur nobis obscura, et interdum accidit in Enarrationibus, id quod in proverbio dicitur, ut sonet: Aliud Pes, aliud Cithara.

Non imaginemur legem moralem esse decretum simile Spartanae legi de ferreo numo, quod non solum mutari et aboleri potuit, sed etiam facile et commode mutatum est.

Sed sciamus legem Dei, quae nominatur moralis, esse aeternam et immotam sapientiam et normam iusticiae in Deo patefactam rationali creaturae, et postulantem, ut rationalis creatura sit conformis Deo, et destruentem omnes non conformes. Haec aeterna sapientia Dei nequaquam aboletur in Evangelio.

Et sicut hominum natura mirando consilio ad hanc sapientiam et conformitatem cum Deo condita est, ita vult Deus restitui nos ad hanc ipsam lucem et conformitatem per filium. Ideo Christus dicitur esse finis legis. Et hic Paulus inquit: Fide legem stabilimus, quod de lege morali sic interpretor. Etsi autem iudico nostram interpretationem veram esse, et congruentem cum Paulo, tamen fateor me amplitudinem sapientiae apostolicae non satis explicare posse. Deploro gemens meam caliginem, et doleo in hac barbarie vitae impediri etiam cogitationes de tantis rebus.

Scio Augustinum hac enarratione saepe uti: Per fidem lex stabilitur, id est, impetratur auxilium, ut legi obedire possis. Haec enarratio valde tenuis et mutila est. Etsi verum est, dari

Spiritum sanctum in consolatione, in qua fide acquiescimus in mediatore, et accendi motus tales a Spiritu sancto, qualis ipse est: tamen haec incoata obedientia in nobis adhuc procul abest a perfectione legis. Recte dicit Osiander, Deum habitare... in credentibus, sed simul adhuc in hominibus magna moles est peccati. Tunc cum Deus erit omnia in omnibus, id est, cum fulgebit in beatis, in quibus non erit peccatum, ibi intelligemus quid sit legis impletio, ibi erimus iusti Deo fulgente in nobis. Sed in hac vita in tanta infirmitate sic accedimus ad Deum, ut ad misericordiam propter mediatorem promissam confugiamus, et tegamur a mediatore, sicut in Esaia nominatur mediator Umbraculum. Et Paulus inquit: Per hunc audemus accedere in fiducia, per fidem in ipsum.

Sic igitur utcunque docendi causa dico, legem stabiliri fide tripliciter. Primum, confessione veritatis, quod sit lex Dei iuste iudicans et damnans nos, et quod nostra iusticia non mereatur reconciliationem, nec sit legis impletio. Secundo, imputatione iusticiae propter mediatorem. Quia enim fide agnoscimus mediatorem, et credimus nobis propter eum dari remissionem peccatorum et reconciliationem, et nos reputari iustos propter ipsius obedientiam, sumus iusti et accepti Deo in hac vita propter obedientiam filii, fide. Stabilitur ergo lex, quia agnoscimus legem non esse inane murmur, sed poenam pro genere humano fuisse persolvendam, et hanc persolutionem nobis donatam esse.

Regula est autem stabiliri et confirmari leges poena. Et quanquam in hac vita incoatur obedientia, tamen adhuc procul absumus a perfectione legis, sed reputamur iusti, id est, habentes remissionem peccatorum et reconciliationem propter mediatorem fide: sic habemus hoc quod lex significabat, non nostra impletione tolli iram Dei, et fieri reconciliationem, sed mediatoris obedientiam donari credentibus. Sic Rom. 5. dicitur: Iustificati sanguine eius, salvabimur per eum ab ira.

Tertio, stabilitur lex fide, iuxta dictum ad Galatas: Nos spiritu ex fide spem iusticiae expectamus, id est, reconciliati fide habebunt integram iusticiam in lege significatam. Certissimum est enim in lege non tantum significari incoationem, quae fit in hac vita, sed significari perfectam conformitatem cum Deo, quae erit, cum Deus erit omnia in omnibus, id est, cum sese nobis communicabit in clarissima luce, et vivificabit nos vita aeterna, et fulgebunt in nobis ipsius sapientia, iusticia et laetitia, et nequaquam simul erunt in nobis reliquiae peccati. Hoc consummatum beneficium intuemur, cum dicitur: Non veni solvere legem, sed implere, Item: Iehova iusticia nostra. Et simul sciamus in hac vita credentes habere initia aeternae vitae, iuxta dictum: Qui habet filium, habet vitam.

Id intelligatur ordine, et de initio, et de vita aeterna in illa coelesti Ecclesia. Habet autem filium in hac vita, quisquis in vera conversione, credit se propter obedientiam mediatoris habere remissionem peccatorum, reconciliationem et imputationem iusticiae. Hac consolatione cum erigitur, filius aeterni patris immediate est efficax voce Evangelii, et vivificat credentem, et effundit in cor Spiritum sanctum, quo laetitia acquiescens in Deo, dilectio Dei et vera invocatio accenduntur. Haec sunt initia vitae aeternae: sic concionatur et Dominus, inquiens: Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum servabit, et pater meus diliget eum, et veniemus ad eum, et mansionem apud eum faciemus. Primum iubet filius se audiri, et accipi vocem Evangelii. Ita orditur sanationem a voce Evangelii.

Credentem autem diligit pater, vide proprietatem orationis. Etsi nondum in hac vita sine peccato sumus, tamen credens diligitur a Deo, est iustus, quia pater eum per misericordiam propter filium mediatorem recipit, et imputat ei iusticiam. Ut autem et natura nostra restituatur, simul hoc fit: Veniemus ad eum, et mansionem apud eum faciemus.

Aeternus pater misit filium ad proferendam vocem Evangelii arcanam et ignotam omnibus creaturis, Et per hunc filium immediate colligit Ecclesiam voce Evangelii. Hic filius immediate est efficax, cum fit consolatio voce Evangelii vere adest λόγος, et ostendit patrem, sicut inquit: Nemo novit patrem, nisi filius, et cui filius volet revelare. Et tunc simul pater et filius effundunt Spiritum sanctum in cor credentis: dantur enim Spiritus sanctus per filium, cum voce Evangelii fit consolatio. Et nota sit sententia Athanasii, In quocunque dicitur esse Spiritus sanctus, ibi est per Verbum.

Quare et infra fit utriusque personae mentio, Romanorum 8. capite: Siquidem spiritus Dei habitat in vobis. Item: Si Christus est in vobis. Et ipse inquit: Ego sum vitis, vos palmites, Qui manet in me, et Ego in Vere ergo λόγος filius Dei adest in credente, et est efficax voce Evangelii. Sic et ad Ephesios tertio dictum est: Ut habitet Christus per fidem in cordibus vestris. Haec immensa beneficia mediatoris omnia complectitur Paulus, cum inquit, Legem fide stabilimus, videlicet et imputatione iusticiae et praesentia Dei in credentibus, qui et in hac vita accendit novam lucem, et novos motus in cordibus, et postea dat vitam aeternam, in qua iusticia Dei, significata in lege, erit in nobis integra, quae describitur his verbis in lege: Diligas Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde, ex tota anima etc.

Ac in quotidiana invocatione cogimus de his maximis rebus, de omnibus beneficiis filii Dei ordine, quod missus sit, ut colligat aeternam Ecclesiam, quod vere adsit et sit efficax voce Evangelii, quod propter eum aeternus pater recipiat nos, et simul adsit in nobis, et velit nobis misereri et vere per filium det Spiritum sanctum, ut gubernet nos. Haec beneficia cum petimus, tunc fit hoc quod Paulus hic inquit: Legem fide stabilimus, quia haec vera invocatio est initium novae obedientiae. Simul autem cogitemus communem doctrinam, quod persona sit iusta fide propter mediatorem in hac vita, etiamsi adhuc natura nostra valde dissimilis est legi Dei. Hanc fidem praelucere oportet novae obedientiae. Deinde sciendum est etiam, quomodo et incoëtur et placeat Deo nova obedientia. Incoatur, quia vere habitat Deus in corde credentis, et placet Deo, quia persona propter mediatorem sola fide placet, et credit hanc ipsam obedientiam Deo placere, non quia legi satisfaciat, sed propter mediatorem, qui est summus sacerdos adsidue pro nobis interpellans. Quanquam igitur propter ingentem infirmitatem nostrae naturae in hac vita, haec incoata obedientia valde languida et squalida est, tamen illo modo, ut dictum est, placet Deo, et nominatur Iusticia et Sacrificium.

Fit magis perspicua haec tota doctrina, cum pie cogitatur in quotidiana invocatione, in veris doloribus et exercitiis conversionis, in quibus ipsi gemitus piorum refutant etiam furores Monachorum et Antinomorum. Monachi fidem non intelligunt aliud, nisi noticiam historiae, et iubent homines semper dubitare an placeant Deo. Postea fingunt opera sua esse impletionem legis et merita vitae aeternae, et multos errores cumulant, quorum falsitas conspicitur in illis ipsis doloribus piorum.

Refutantur et Antinomi, sentiunt enim pii se iudicari lege Dei, sentiunt in poenis publicis et privatis iram Dei iustam, quae est legis executio, et fatentur idem quod Propheta inquit: Propter iniquitatem corripis homines. Non cogitant legem, iudicium Dei, iram Dei, inania vocabula esse. Intueamur ergo in lectione Paulina veram conversionem, non quid audacissime fingant Epicurei, qui sunt Antinomi, nec quid simulent monachi, qui iactitant se legi Dei obtemperare aut etiam satisfacere, imo et perfectos esse, cum re vera mentes sint Epicureae et derideant Deum, et hanc simulationem ad quaestum conferant. Magis est impudeus etiam Cynicus in Austria, qui recens renovavit scriptis errores de perfectione: nominat perfectionem monachorum mendicitatem, quam scit aucupium esse artificiose institutum, non tam ad pascendum ventrem, quam ad potentiam quaerendam.

Sed te fili Dei Domine Iesu Christe, qui vere colligis aeternam Ecclesiam voce Evangelii, oro, ut veritatem tuam illustres et reprimas omnes impiorum furores. Tu vides quanta sit et rabies, et potentia hostium veritatis, te supplex obtestor propter tuam gloriam, ut veritatem tuam illustres, et nos gubernes, et in nobis accendas et augeas lucem tuam, et deleas mendacia et blasphemias, quas cyclopica prophanitate contra te multi et dicunt et defendere conantur.

Ut autem hoc loco Paulus inquit, fide legem stabilimus, ita inquit Dominus: Non veni solvere legem, sed implere. Graeca phrasis est λύειν νόμον, quod significat, non tantum delictum admittere contra legem, sed ipsam legem abolere, ut cum dicimus: Cicero Consul abolevit legem agrariam. Affirmat igitur Dominus noster Iesus Christus, se non venisse ut legem aboleat, sed ut impleat.

Impleat autem quatuor modis. Primum propria obedientia quae est integra. Secundo derivando in sese poenam, quam nos legi debuimus. Adeo enim vult Deus ratam esse legem suam, quae est aeterna sapientia et norma iusticiae in ipso, ut quanquam per misericordiam recipit homines, tamen ita sit copulata iusticia, ut legi satisfieri et persolvi poenam pro nobis voluerit. Hic cogitent Antinomi, si non sunt Epicurei, quid sit lex, et quare voluerit Deus esse ratam, cum non receptum sit genus humanum, nisi filius pro nobis poenam solveret. Hoc mirandum consilium, legis auctoritatem, iusticiae et misericordiae temperamentum, et magnitudinem amoris in filio Deo erga nos, et in aeterno patre erga filium et erga nos, in illa aeterna academia contemplabimur. Nunc tamen vult Deus nos huius sapientiae prima elementa discere. Fateor de tantarum rerum magnitudine meam orationem longe tenuiorem esse, quam esse debebat, sed tamen qualicunque clamore significo indignationem adversus Hypocritas, Monachos, et Antinomos, qui de lege Dei scurriliter loquuntur.

Cum autem significat Dominus se pro nobis legi Dei poenam persolvere simul complectitur doctrinam de remissione peccatorum et de reconciliatione, de imputatione iusticiae. Quia enim poenam pro nobis persolvit, et nobis placat iram aeterni patris, donantur credentibus propter ipsius sacrificium, remissio peccatorum, reconciliatio, imputatio iusticiae, vivificatio per filium et Spiritum sanctum, et donatio vitae aeternae.

Tertio, implet filius Dei legem effectione seu restitutione in nobis. Adeo enim vult Deus ratam esse legem, ut ideo filium miserit, ut et poenam pro nobis lueret, et restituat in nobis obedientiam seu conformitatem cum ipso, quae quidem in hac vita incoatur. Sed in Ecclesia coelesti erit integra, cum Deus erit omnia in omnibus beatis. Quarto, implet filius Dei legem moralem, docendo, seu sanciendo, seu repetendo decalogum. Etsi enim non est missus, ut sit legis conditor, nam lex antea initio fuit insita rationalibus creaturis, et postea semper in Ecclesia divinitus repetita est, et quidem in sola Dei Ecclesia semper lex sine corruptelis retenta est: tamen ipse eam repetit, et testatur hoc esse iudicium Dei, arguens peccata, et ostendens veros cultos, et eam enarrat, et detergit pharisaicas sordes, quibus legem et tunc et omnibus temporibus hypocritae corrumpunt.

Caput IV.

Quid ergo dicemus invenisse Abraham patrem nostrum secundum carnem? In quarto capite incoatur confirmatio propositionis, sumta ex exemplo Abrahae et primo dicto, in quo expresse fit mentio iusticiae fidei. Vult enim Paulus ostendere doctrinam in Evangelio proponi non ignotam veteri Ecclesiae, Prophetarum et Patrum, sed unam perpetuam et consentientem vocem esse Patrum, Prophetarum, Christi et Apostolorum, sicut ipse Dominus inquit: Abraham vidit diem meum, et laetatus est. Etsi autem haec confirmatio tota nascitur ex dicto illo, Credidit Abraham Deo etc.: tamen quia circumstantiarum explicatio gignit multa argumenta, distribuemus eam in haec quinque argumenta, quae sint in conspectu, et ut nos de doctrina confirment, et in quotidiana invocatione et consolatione exuscitent fidem, quia non potest fieri invocatio, nisi praeluceat haec fides, quod recipiamur et exaudiamur propter filium, et quidem propter obedientiam filii.

Primum argumentum. Abraham non fuit iustus propter opera coram Deo, sed fide, Ergo nec caeteri sunt iusti propter opera, sed fide. Valet consequentia: Quia Abraham ut exemplum doctrinae proponitur. Antecedens probatur ex dicto: Credidit Abraham Deo.

Secundum. Iustificatio est imputatio iusticiae, qua Deus per misericordiam nos recipit et vivificat, Non igitur sumus iusti nostris operibus aut meritis.

Tertium. Iustificatio est remissio peccatorum, qua Deus nos recipit et vivificat propter mediatorem, et per eum, Igitur non sumus iusti nostris operibus aut meritis.

Quartum. Abraham est fide iustus ante circumcisionem, Ergo non est iustus circumcisione.

Quintum. Oportet promissionem gratiae seu reconciliationis esse certam.

Promissio pendens ex conditione legis fit incerta, quia lex iram efficit, Igitur promissio gratiae non pendet ex conditione legis, sed gratis datur, et fide accipienda est. 3. ENARRATIO EPIST. PAULI AD ROMANOS, CAP. IV. Si enim Abraham ex operibus etc. Primum expressa asseveratio in textu consideranda est, quod aperte affirmat Paulus Abraham non fuisse iustum coram Deo propter opera sua, sicut et supra dictum est: Ex operibus legis non iustificabitur omnis caro.

Et nihil dubium est complecti Paulum opera moralia: nam et Abraham antecessit politiam Moisi annis quadrigentis et triginta vel circiter.

Deinde consideretur accommodatio dicti: Credidit Abraham Deo, et imputatum est ei ad iusticiam.

Alibi citat haec dicta: Iustus sua vivet. Item: Qui credit in eum, non confundetur. Hic autem recitat primum dictum, in quo expresse fit mentio fidei.

Vult enim et hoc ostendere, non afferi nunc doctrinam ignotam Ecclesiae Patrum et Prophetarum, sed eandem in vera Ecclesia doctrinam de iusticia semper fuisse.

Ut autem accomodatio recte intelligatur, cavillationes refutandae sunt, quae opponuntur, quarum prima haec est.

Prima cavillatio adversariorum.

Adversarii dicunt, Paulum abuti hoc dicto, quia ibi dicitur de fide expectante posteritatem. At Evangelium loquitur de fide agnoscente Christum crucifixum et resuscitatum, et accipiente remissionem peccatorum, Ergo de alia fide Moises, de alia Paulus loquitur.

Respondeo: De omnibus exemplis in quibus laudatur fides, ut Gedeon, David, credunt Deum ipsis praeliantibus affuturum esse: etiam cum res externa petitur et expectatur, semper tamen oportet praelucere hanc fidem, qua accipitur reconciliatio propter mediatorem, iuxta dictum: Nemo potest venire ad patrem nisi per filium.

Item Rom. 5.: Per hunc habemus accessum fide. Semper igitur primum et principale obiectum fidei est Deus non irascens, sed propter filium nos recipiens, et prima lucta est, An Deus velit te recipere.

Cumque iam credimus eum esse propicium, postea expectamus ab eo caetera beneficia. Gedeon, David non possent a Deo petere vel expectare victorias, nisi prius crederent se receptos esse et placere Deo. Sciunt autem ex promissione, quod recipiantur homines per misericordiam propter mediatorem, iuxta dictum: In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes. Et sicut certum est Ecclesiam colligi propter filium, ita norunt sancti et promissiones bonorum corporalium traditas esse propter filium, quia Ecclesiae necessaria sunt.

Ideo 2. Corinth. 7. dicitur:

Omnes promissiones in Christo ratae sunt.

Discernantur ergo obiecta fidei: primum et principale est Deus propicius propter mediatorem, postea possunt accedere alia externa obiecta. Ut Abraham petit protectionem inter impias gentes, petit posteritatem et conservationem Ecclesiae. Denique in quotidiana invocatione singuli multa complectimur, sed uno et eodem modo ad Deum accedunt omnes sancti, scilicet, Credentes Deum esse propicium propter mediatorem, sicut ipse Dominus inquit: Quicquid petieritis patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis.

Iam considerentur verba textus.

In capite 12. Gene. dicit Dominus: Benedicam tibi. Item: In te benedicentur omnes gentes.

Postea in capite 15. dicitur: Noli timere, ego protector tuus et magna merces valde. In his dulcissimis promissionibus manifeste ostenditur reconciliatio, et norat Abraham primam promissionem: Semen mulieris conteret caput serpentis.

Et quidem sciebat hanc promissionem, iam restringi ad suam posteritatem, quia dictum erat: In te benedicentur omnes gentes.

Accipit igitur simul et promissionem reconciliationis et semini benedicti et posteritatis, id est, propagandae Ecclesiae. Has promissiones cum fide accipiat manifestum est, eandem esse fidem Abrahae et Pauli, et omnium sanctorum in vera Ecclesia accipientem reconciliationem propter mediatorem.

Ideo et Dominus inquit: Vidit Abraham diem meum id est, agnovit in promissione mediatorem et fiducia mediatoris accepit remissionem peccatorum, et liberatus est ab inferis et ab ira Dei.

Credidit Abraham Deo etc. Haec responsio vera et firma est, sicut et experientia testatur in omnium piorum cordibus.

Idem textus in Moise ostendit, quid ibi nominet Fidem, videlicet non tantum noticiam te Deo, qualis est in diabolis, vel in Ethnicis, quod sit Deus, quod sit conditor mundi, sapiens, verax, iustus, castus, postulans obedientiam congruentem ipsius sapientiae et voluntati, et iudicans ac puniens inobedientes, sicut Latomus Lovaniensis inquit, Non aliam fuisse in Abraham fidem, quam qualis fuit noticia in Cicerone aut in Xenophonte.

Sed hic textus in Moise antea recitavit promissiones: In te benedicentur omnes gentes. Item: Noli timere, ego protector tuus etc. Cum igitur inquit, Credidit Abraham, necesse est hoc referri ad praecedentes promissiones: nam et fides est assentiri omni verbo Dei patefacto.

Quare necessario et manifeste sequitur fidem Abrahae non tantum fuisse noticiam historiae, sed etiam noticiam et assensum, quo promissiones amplexus est. Non loquuntur Moises et Paulus de mutilata fide, quae est tantum noticia historiae, sed de hac fide, quae est historiae et promissionum noticia, et est assensus ac fiducia, qua promissionem amplectimur, et corda acquiescunt in mediatore promisso, seu in Deo promittente propter mediatorem. Ideo et Paulus mox in hoc capite promissionem et fidem copulat, ut ostendat se de ea fide loqui, quae promissionem accipit, qua Deus propter mediatorem omnibus credentibus promittit remissionem peccatorum, reconciliationem, imputationem iusticiae, sanctificationem per Spiritum sanctum et vitam aeternam.

Cum igitur perspicuum sit, quid Moises et Paulus nominent Fidem, refutatio cavillationum, quae obiiciuntur manifesta est, quales sunt, Daemones credunt et non sunt iusti, Non igitur iustificantur homines fide. Item: Nulla natura est iusta sola noticia, Fides est tantum noticia, Nemo igitur fide iustus est. Item: Fides est opus, Ergo: Operibus iusti sumus. Harum obiectionum explicatio declarat vocabulum Fidei, nec fingimus praestigias aut subtilitates, sed illustramus nativam vocabuli significationem in sermone Prophetarum et Apostolorum, Est igitur responsio ad primam obiectionem.

Daemones credunt, sed mutilata fide, id est, tenent noticiam historiae, et sciunt filium Dei horribili indicio puniturum esse omnes diabolos, nequaquam autem amplectuntur promissiones, non statuunt sibi remitti peccata: ideo furenter oderunt Deum et Christum, et sentiunt poenas, et metuunt tristiores cruciatus. De hac fide non loquitur Paulus, cum inquit, Iustificati fide pacem habemus erga Deum: sed de fide, quae non solum est noticia historiae, sed etiam promissionem amplectitur, et est fiducia acquiescens in mediatore. Ideo usitata apud nos definitio est: Fides est assentiri omni verbo Dei nobis tradito, atque ita promissioni gratiae, et est fiducia acquiescens in promissione, id est, in Deo promittente propter mediatorem.

Secundum argumentum. Nulla natura est iusta sola noticia, Fides est tantum noticia, Ergo: Non sola fide sumus iusti. Respondeo simpliciter: Nego minorem.

Nam ut antea dictum est Fides quae assentitur promissioni non est tantum noticia, sed est simul fiducia, quae est motus a Spiritu sancto accensus, quo voluntas et cor vivificantur et laetificantur, ut acquiescant in Deo propter mediatorem: ut cum audit David absolutionem: Dominus abstulit peccatum tuum, non tantum in eo noticia est huius propositionis, sed voluntas et cor ostenso hoc bono rursus ex summis doloribus et ex inferis emergunt. Sicut dicitur: Iustificati fide pacem habemus. Et Ezechias inquit: Tu autem eruisti animam meam ut non periret, proiecisisti post tergum tuum omnia peccata mea. Sic ostendit Paulus, quos motus complectatur fides, cum inquit: Per hunc audemus accedere in fiducia per fidem ipsius. Ibi ostendit fiduciam et accessum ad Deum in hac fide comprehendi, de qua loquitur, Et necesse est haec comprehendi, quia de ea fide dicitur, quae assentitur promissioni. Est igitur et fiducia in voluntate et corde acquiescens in promissione, id est, in Deo promittente propter mediatorem.

Tertium argumentum.

Fide iustificamur, Fides est opus, Ergo: Operibus iustificamur. Respondeo: Simplex et vera explicatio est, qua omnes mediocriter docti in nostris Ecclesiis semper usi sunt, videlicet has propositiones: Fide habemus remissionem peccatorum, Fide iustificamur.

Nequaquam sic intelligi, propter hoc opus in nobis, scilicet credere, seu propter dignitatem huius operis, habere homines remissionem aut iustificari. Nam Paulus universaliter hoc vult, homines gratis propter mediatorem habere remissionem, et esse acceptos Deo, non propter ullius operis dignitatem in nobis, sive fiat nostris viribus, sive Deo movente corda. Sunt et haec opera a Deo in nobis accensa, dilectio Dei, patientia, castitas. Sicut autem non habemus remissionem propter haec opera, ita nec propter fidem, quatenus est qualitas, seu opus in nobis, sed quia fide agnoscimus mediatorem, et beneficia eius adplicari nobis oportet fide, cogitata voce Evangelii. Respondeo igitur ad maiorem, sicut usitate dicimus: Fide iustificamur, Haec propositio correlative intelligenda est, quasi dicatur, Per misericordiam propter mediatorem iustificamur, quem tamen fide agnosci et adplicari in nobis eius beneficia fide oportet.

Est ergo sententia in maiore: Propter Christum habemus remissionem et s. mines gratis propter mediatorem habere remissionem, et esse acceptos Deo, non propter ullius operis dignitatem in nobis, sive fiat nostris viribus, sive Deo movente corda.

Sunt et haec opera a Deo in nobis accensa, dilectio Dei, patientia, castitas. Sicut autem non habemus remissionem propter haec opera, ita nec propter fidem, quatenus est qualitas, seu opus in nobis, sed quia fide agnoscimus mediatorem, et beneficia eius adplicari nobis oportet fide, cogitata voce Evangelii.

Respondeo igitur ad maiorem, sicut usitate dicimus: Fide iustificamur.

Haec propositio correlative intelligenda est, quasi dicatur, Per misericordiam propter mediatorem iustificamur, quem tamen fide agnosci et adplicari nobis eius beneficia fide oportet. Est ergo sententia in maiore: Propter Christum habemus remissionem et sumus iusti, id est, accepti. Non igitur sequitur conclusio, quod propter opera simus iusti.

Sic cum in Esaia dicitur: Noticia servi mei iusti, iustificabit multos: non intelligatur, credentes propter dignitatem fidei placere, sed ideo sic loquitur Propheta, quia agnosci mediatorem et fide adplicari ei eius beneficia oportet.

Antea enim dixerat: Livore eius sanati sumus.

Haec breviter dicta sunt, ut vocabulum Fides, seu credidit, sit perspicuum.

Nunc sequuntur cetera vocabula, Imputata est ei iusticia: sic enim Hebraei legunt, id est, Cogitata seu decreta est huic, qui antea reus erat, iusticia, id est, remissio peccatorum, et acceptatio divina et haereditas aeternae vitae et iusticiae, cum credit promissioni.

Ac citat Paulus hoc dictum, quia primum expresse dicit, Quomodo homini decernatur iusticia sine conditione.

In lege enim tantum conditionales propositiones sunt: Maledictus qui non manet in omnibus etc.

Addit igitur declarationem, quod imputatio sit gratuita, videlicet quod Deus hunc credentem cogitet seu decernat esse iustum sua misericordia, etiamsi non est in eo impletio legis, quam Deus adprobaret ex debito, si adesset, inquit igitur: Merces datur ex debito, id est, Ubi est reipsa legis impletio, Deus, qui est talis, approbat eam ex sua iusticia.

Hic discant iuniores vocabula Debiti et Meriti correlativa esse.

Cum monachi dixerunt: Contritus habet merita de condigno, hoc voluerunt, hanc obedientiam esse iusticiam, quam recipiat Deus ex debito etc. Ut igitur hic Paulus reicit debitum, ita sciamus reici meritum remissionis peccatorum et vitae aeternae.

## 4:16
Therefore it is of faith, that the promise may be firm according to grace.

This is the conclusion of the syllogism, which, since it is a clear assertion about free reconciliation on account of the Son of God through faith, should be most well-known not only for the sake of doctrine, but also for the sake of consolation, and should always be in sight. God wills the promise of reconciliation to be valid and firm for us on account of his truth, and on account of the mediator the Son, not on account of any merits of ours. And he wills the promise to be received by faith, and our hearts to rest in him on account of the mediator.

This is the highest consolation in true sorrows, and in this consolation these sayings are understood: Being justified by faith we have peace. Likewise: Those who believe in him shall not be confounded. And Jonah 2: Those who do not flee to mercy, follow vanities. Likewise Eph. 3: Through whom we dare to approach confidently through faith in Jesus Christ. And Heb. 4: Having this high priest, etc.

Let a heap of such testimonies be held, so that we may confirm ourselves in doctrine, and know that we must truly approach God in this way, and that men are truly received in this way, when in true sorrows they sustain themselves with the promise, and believe that they are received on account of the Son of God, and are righteous, that is, accepted, and let us exercise this consolation in daily invocation. In these exercises this sentence will be more illustrious: Therefore it is of faith freely, that the promise may be firm: and I add no other interpretation, but let the native meaning be taken from the words themselves.

These consolations must be held against many errors. Monks say that one must remain in doubt, and they say: You will be pleasing thus, if you have fulfilled the law. Osiander says thus: You are righteous thus, when essential righteousness impels you to do good, he bids you seek what kind of impulses are in you. But Paul leads you to the Son of God the mediator and to the promise, according to the sayings: Through him we dare to approach through faith, etc. Likewise: Those who do not flee to mercy, follow vanities.

Then follows an amplification, which, when it shows what kind of faith Abraham’s was, teaches much about the nature of faith, and in the end adds the principal application, affirming that the saying written in Genesis was not for Abraham’s sake only, but also for our sake, so that we may know that it is for us too. to be considered righteousness for those believing in the mediator, and that it is a common doctrine, and pertains to the whole Church. Now let the particles be considered concerning the nature of faith: He believed against hope in hope, that is, against the objects of hope, on account of which reason despairs; he leaned upon the invisible object, God, shown in the promise, just as faith is the evidence of things not seen. Moses believes that he will escape, although the enemy presses and he is hemmed in by mountains and the sea. The Baptist believes that he will live, even if he is killed. Everywhere there are great confusions of the human race, and many vices, we ask therefore: Is there and where is the Church? But it must be established by faith, that there is some Church of God, and that it will not utterly perish among these ruins of the world.

He did not doubt through unbelief.

Here he expressly shows that faith and doubt fight among themselves, and that one must struggle out of doubt. Faith is weak, but yet it is faith in that man in Mark, who says: I believe, Lord, but help my unbelief. Thus it is necessary to struggle out of doubt by faith, otherwise peace, or joy, would not follow faith. This particle is repeated in the expression: He was certain.

This certainty is to assent to the word of God and the promise, and not to be torn away on account of contrary things, which reason shows: as reason says, it is impossible for the people to escape through the waters, but Moses, assenting to the divine promise, retains certainty.

Stand, he says, and you shall see the great works of God. Added here is the particle: Giving glory to God. This is a notable proclamation of faith. To give glory to God is truly to acknowledge and celebrate that He is God, and that He is wise, truthful, good, just, omnipotent, an avenger, merciful, acting freely, the creator of the whole fabric of the world, preserving things, loving and caring for the human race, and on account of His Son gathering an eternal Church in the human race, hearing and helping those who call upon Him with trust in the Son, communicating Himself to us, and giving us the Holy Spirit and eternal life. This whole copulative is comprehended in this saying: Giving glory to God.

These things are made illustrious by antithesis.

Epicureans do not give glory to God, because they say that He is nothing or cares for nothing, etc. The devils, and Saul, Judas, and the like know that God exists, and that He is the creator and avenger, and they feel His wrath, but with horrible gnashing they hate Him, and treat Him with insults, because He is unequal in a tyrannical manner. But David, Hezekiah, Daniel, and other saints truly give glory to God, according to that copulative recited above. They not only confess that God exists, and that He is the creator and avenger, but they also acknowledge and confess that He is good and merciful, receiving, hearing, and saving those who call upon Him on account of the Son.

Where this faith shines in the heart, glory is truly given to God, and His presence is felt, and the heart is sustained by trust in divine aid.

But where this faith does not shine in the heart, man is either secure in the Epicurean manner, or like an academic, full of doubts, and is not a dwelling of God, or feeling wrath, he horribly flees from God. Neither calls upon God, neither expects help from God, therefore they do not give Him the glory of goodness, but treat Him with insult. From this antithesis it is understood in some way that it is a horrible sin not to believe in the remission of sins, and not to call upon God, because the glory due to God is not given.

Let hearts therefore be excited to true conversion, and let them be raised by faith receiving the benefits of the mediator, and let them ask for faith and true invocation to be increased.

The Prophets often preach about this glory, as in Jeremiah 13: Give glory to the Lord your God before darkness comes, that is, Believe in Him according to all the articles of faith, be converted and call upon Him. And Malachi 2: If you will not hear, and if you will not lay it to heart, to give glory to my name, says the Lord of hosts, I will send poverty upon you.

He was delivered for our sins, and rose again for our righteousness.

Paul distinguishes the merit of Christ and the distribution of the merit. The whole obedience of Christ is the price for our sins and the propitiation, by which the wrath of God is appeased. But Christ lives again, and because He is the victor of death, and so that He may reign and apply His merits to us, and render to us life and eternal righteousness, just as it is said in Hosea 13: O death, I will be thy death, and O hell, I will be thy plague. And Isaiah 25: Death is swallowed up forever.

And although the merit of Christ is one thing, and the application to us is another, yet this application happens simultaneously and at the same time, when a man is converted to God, and is raised by faith and the knowledge of the Son of God, so that at the same time there occurs the remission of sins, justification, reconciliation, and the gift of the Holy Spirit, according to these sayings, John 3: He who does not believe, the wrath of God remains upon him. Acts 10: That all who believe in him receive remission of sins through his name. And Galatians ...3: That we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith, etc. For although the merit preceded, yet it was so ordained from the beginning that it would then be applied to individuals when they received it by faith.

Nor must it be imagined that the sins of Nero were remitted, but only that this was lacking to him, that he is not righteous. The devil devised this distraction to diminish the magnitude of sin and to confirm security. Wherefore, let us be fortified against such furies by clear divine testimonies.

But when Paul says: He rose again for our righteousness, understand the consummated benefit, that is, for the remission of sins, reconciliation, vivification, and justification, life, righteousness, and eternal joy. As Daniel also speaks, saying: Sin shall be blotted out and everlasting righteousness shall be brought in.

Latin:

Ideo ex fide, ut secundum gratiam firma sit promissio.

Haec est syllogismi conclusio, quae cum sit perspicua asseveratio de gratuita reconciliatione propter filium Dei per fidem, non solum doctrinae causa, sed etiam propter consolationem sit notissima, et semper in conspectu sit. Deus promissionem reconciliationis vult nobis ratam et firmam esse propter suam veritatem, et propter mediatorem filium, non propter nostra merita ulla. Ac vult accipi promissionem fide, et acquiescere corda nostra in ipso propter mediatorem.

Haec est summa consolatio in veris doloribus, et in hac consolatione intelliguntur haec dicta: Iustificati fide pacem habemus. Item: Qui credunt in eum, non confundentur. Et Ionae 2.: Qui non confugiunt ad misericordiam, sectantur vana. Item Ephes. 3.: Per quem audemus accedere confidenter per fidem Iesu Christi. Et Hebr. 4.: Hunc habentes pontificem etc.

Talium testimoniorum acervus teneatur, ut et de doctrina nos confirmemus, ac sciamus vere sic ad Deum accedendum esse, et vere sic recipi homines, cum in veris doloribus sustentant se promissione, et credunt se propter filium Dei recipi, et iustos, id est, acceptos esse, et hanc consolationem in quotidiana invocatione exerceamus. In his exercitiis erit illustrior et haec sententia: Ideo ex fide gratis, ut sit firma promissio: nec aliam interpretationem addo, sed nativa sententia ex ipsis verbis sumatur.

Haec consolationes tenendae sunt contra multos errores. Monachi dicunt manendum esse in dubitatione, et dicunt: Ita placebis, si legem impleveris. Osiander sic dicit: Ita es iustus, cum iusticia essentialis impellit te ad bene operandum, iubet te quaerere quales in te sint impulsiones. Sed Paulus deducit te ad filium Dei mediatorem et ad promissionem, iuxta dicta: Per hunc audemus accedere per fidem etc. Item: Qui non confugiunt ad misericordiam, sectantur vana.

Deinde sequitur amplificatio, quae cum ostendit qualis fuerit fides Abrahae, multa docet de natura fidei, et in fine addit principalem applicationem, affirmat dictum in Genesi scriptum esse, non propter Abraham tantum, sed etiam propter nos, ut sciamus nobis quoque . putari iusticiam credentibus in mediatorem, et communem doctrinam esse, et ad totam Ecclesiam pertinere. Iam particulae considerentur de natura fidei: Credidit contra spem in spem, id est, contra obiecta spei, propter quae ratio desperat, Innixus est obiecto invisibili Deo monstrato in promissione, sicut fides est ἔλεγχος non adparentium. Moises credit, se evasurum esse, quanquam hostis instat et interclusus est montibus et mari. Baptista credit se victurum esse, etiamsi interficitur. Ubique magnae sunt confusiones generis humani, et multum vitiorum, quaerimus igitur: An sit et ubi sit Ecclesia? sed fide statuendum est, et esse aliquam Dei Ecclesiam, et inter has ruinas mundi non prorsus interituram esse.

Non dubitavit diffidentia.

Hic expresse ostendit fidem et dubitationem inter se pugnare, et eluctandum esse ex dubitatione. Languida fides, sed tamen fides est in illo apud Marcum, qui inquit: Credo Domine, sed opem fert diffidentiae meae. Ita eluctari fidem ex dubitatione necesse est, alioquin non sequeretur fidem pax, seu laetitia. Repetita est haec particula in dictione: Certus fuit.

Haec certitudo est assentiri verbo Dei et promissioni, nec avelli propter contraria, quae ratio ostendit: ut ratio dicit, populo impossibile est per aquas evadere, sed Moises assentiens promissioni divinae retinet certitudinem.

State, inquit, et videbitis magnalia Dei. Additur hic particula: Dans gloriam Deo. Hoc insigne praeconium fidei est. Gloriam Deo tribuere, est vere agnoscere et celebrare, quod sit Deus, et quod sit sapiens, verax, bonus, iustus, omnipotens, vindex, misericors, agens liberum, conditor totius opificii mundi, conservans res, diligens et curans genus humanum, et propter filium colligens aeternam Ecclesiam in genere humano, exaudiens et iuvans invocantes fiducia filii, communicans nobis seipsum, et dans nobis Spiritum sanctum et vitam aeternam. Haec tota copulativa comprehenditur in hoc dicto: Dans gloriam Deo.

Fiunt autem haec illustria antithesi.

Epicurei non tribuunt gloriam Deo, quia dicunt, eum nihil esse aut nihil curare etc. Diaboli, et Saul, Iudas et similes esse norunt Deum, et conditorem ac vindicem esse, et sentiunt eius iram, sed horribili fremitu eum oderunt, et contumeliis afficiunt, quod sit inaequalis more tyrannico. David vero, Ezechias, Daniel, et alii sancti vere tribuunt gloriam Deo, iuxta illam copulativam supra recitatam. Non solum fatentur esse Deum, et conditorem ac vindicem, sed etiam agnoscunt et fatentur bonum et misericordem esse, recipientem, exaudientem et salvantem invocantes ipsum propter filium.

Ubi haec fides lucet in corde, vere tribuitur Deo gloria, et sentitur eius praesentia, et sustentatur cor fiducia auxilii divini.

Ubi vero haec fides non lucet in corde, homo aut securus est more Epicureo, vel academico, plenus dubitationum, et non est domicilium Dei, aut sentiens iram horribiliter fugit Deum. Neutri invocant Deum, neutri expectant auxilium a Deo, ideo non tribuunt ei gloriam bonitatis, sed afficiunt eum contumelia. Ex hac antithesi aliquo modo intelligitur horrenda peccata esse, non credere remissionem peccatorum, et non invocare Deum, quia non tribuitur gloria Deo debita.

Excitentur ergo corda ad veram conversionem, et erigantur fide accipiente beneficia mediatoris, et petant augeri fidem et veram invocationem.

De hac gloria saepe concionantur Prophetae, ut Ieremiae 13.: Date Domino Deo vestro gloriam antequam fient tenebrae, id est, Credite ei iuxta omnes articulos fidei, Convertimini et invocate eum. Et Malachiae 2.: Si nolueritis audire, et si nolueritis ponere super cor, ut detis gloriam nomini meo, ait Dominus exercituum, mittam in vos egestatem.

Traditus est propter peccata nostra, et resurrexit propter iusticiam nostram.

Discernit Paulus meritum Christi et distributionem meriti. Tota obedientia Christi est pretium pro nostris peccatis et propiciatio, qua placatur ira Dei. Reviviscit autem Christus, et quia est victor mortis, et ut regnet ac nobis merita adplicet, ac reddat nobis vitam et iusticiam aeternam, sicut Oseae 13. dicitur: O mors, ero mors tua, et inferne ero pestis tua. Et Esaiae 25.: Absorpta est mors in perpetuum.

Et quanquam aliud est meritum Christi, et aliud adplicatio ad nos, tamen haec adplicatio ita fit simul et eodem tempore, cum homo convertitur ad Deum, et fide ac agnitione filii Dei erigitur, ut simul fiant remissio peccatorum, iustificatio, reconciliatio, et donatio Spiritus sancti, iuxta haec dicta, Iohannes 3.: Qui non credit, manet ira Dei super eum. Acto. 10.: Remissionem peccatorum accipere per nomen eius omnes, qui credunt in eum. Et Galat. 3.: Ut promissionem spiritus accipiamus per fidem etc.

Quanquam enim praecessit meritum, tamen ita ordinatum fuit ab initio, ut tunc singulis adplicaretur, cum fide acciperent. Nec imaginandum est, peccata Neronis remissa esse, sed tantum hoc ei deesse, quod non sit iustus. Hanc distractionem excogitavit diabolus, ut peccati magnitudinem extenuaret, et confirmaret securitatem. Quare contra tales furores muniti simus divinis testimoniis perspicuis.

Cum autem inquit Paulus: Resurrexit propter iusticiam nostram, intellige consummatum beneficium, id est, propter remissionem peccatorum, reconciliationem, vivificationem et iustificationem, vitam, iusticiam et laetitiam aeternam. Sicut et Daniel loquitur, inquiens: Peccatum delebitur et adducetur iusticia sempiterna.

## 4:19
Paul's counsel must be diligently considered.

He cites the saying in Genesis about faith because there the assertion is made expressly and without condition, and it is revealed by an express testimony that the believer is righteous. He opposes this to the law, as if he were saying: Nowhere do we read that anyone is pronounced righteous because he fulfilled the law, but the law always accuses men; therefore, we are not righteous by the law.

This consolation spoken to Abraham must therefore be retained, that he is righteous by faith.

Paul dwells, however, on the declaration of imputation, to show that it is gratuitous, and that it is the remission of sins, and reconciliation, or acceptance because of the mediator.

He adds, therefore, the sayings of the Psalm: "Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven," etc. "Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin," etc. Paul recites the antecedent, but a more clear accommodation will be made when the consequent is attached, namely: Since no one is otherwise blessed, that is, righteous or accepted by God, unless sins are remitted, covered, and not imputed, it follows manifestly that no one in this depraved nature satisfies the law, that no one is righteous by the law, and that sins cling to all, because they are remitted to the believer because of the mediator.

Let that Psalm be entirely well-known, because it contains necessary doctrine and the sweetest consolation.

For since we have learned, both from that Psalm and from this entire doctrine of Paul, that only in this way and no other does a man become righteous, that is, accepted by God, when he believes that his sins are remitted to him because of the mediator, freely, and that God wills this His mercy to be acknowledged, and the benefits of the Son to be seen, as He cries out, "Kiss the Son, blessed are all who trust in Him": a most ample consolation is proposed to us, which sustains us in conversion, so that we may not be submerged in desperation and destruction, but may approach God by this faith.

The words in the Psalm are clear.

First, the remission of sins is named, which is to cease to be angry at sins, whether past or present.

Next, for sins to be covered is for the mediator to be a shelter, so that the wrath of God may not be poured out upon us.

And it is properly said: "Sin is covered," which still exists in the regenerate.

For although there is sin, and it is worthy of eternal punishment, yet we are covered through the Son of God, as it is said: "You are not under the law, but under grace."

And although the Psalm understands sins to be covered with respect to eternal punishment, yet let us know that they are thus also covered with respect to corporal punishment, according to the sayings: "The mercy of the Lord, that we are not consumed." For God wills the Church to be surviving. That sins are not imputed is understood also concerning past and present ones, and it is not to think, not to decree, that that believer is to be punished with eternal punishment, although he previously sinned, and there are still stains in him. The Latins would say, "Not to reproach them, not to accuse the man as guilty of eternal punishment." But here the customary objection must be recited, why Paul cites the saying about remission, and does not add the sayings about works, "Blessed are the meek, blessed are the merciful." I answer: Because the sayings about the praises of works are always synecdoches. For they are praised in those who are reconciled by faith, according to the sayings, Rom. 14: "Everything that is not of faith is sin." Rom. 3: "We establish the law" although, as regards eternal punishment, yet let us know that they are also covered in this way, as regards bodily punishment, according to the words: The mercy of the Lord, that we are not consumed.

For God wills that the Church should survive. That sins are not imputed is understood also of past and present sins, and it is not to think, not to decree, that that believer is to be punished with eternal punishment, although he sinned before, and there are still stains in him. The Latins would say, Not to reproach them, not to accuse a man as guilty of eternal punishment.

But here a common objection must be recited, why Paul cites the saying about remission, and does not add the sayings about works, Blessed are the meek, Blessed are the merciful.

I answer: Because the sayings about the praises of works are always synecdoches.

For in these are praised those who are reconciled by faith, according to the sayings, Rom. 14.: Everything that is not of faith is sin. Rom.

3.: We establish the law by faith. Universally, therefore, in the praises of works, let faith be understood first as shining forth, which receives the remission of sins, and reconciliation freely on account of the mediator.

Therefore these sayings are not cited in this place, because good works follow in the justified, they do not justify. But Paul here does not ask how works are done or please afterwards, but how a person is made just, that is, accepted by God, namely by the remission of sins.

Therefore he cites the sayings about remission, which are not synecdoches, because we are received freely on account of the Son, and this remission precedes good works.

Addenda This admonition must also be added.

Osiander interprets these words: Righteousness was imputed to him in this way, that is, divinity was transfused into him.

But although it is most true that in the remission of sins a renewal takes place, when, upon hearing the voice of the Gospel in a terrified heart, the Son of God says this consolation, Thy sins are forgiven thee, and gives the Holy Spirit: yet it is one thing to speak of that renewal, another of the cause on account of which a person first receives the remission of sins and becomes accepted, or of the manner in which we approach God.

But as it is said below, By the obedience of one shall many be made righteous: so let us understand here that the obedience of the mediator is imputed to us, on account of whom we have the remission of sins and acceptance.

Therefore also here Paul, citing the Psalm: Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven etc.

Shows that he is speaking of the imputation by which sins are forgiven us on account of the mediator, and by which the person is accepted. Therefore he also says afterwards: Faith is imputed to him for righteousness, but on account of the mediator, and that faith which relies on the mediator, seeking and receiving the remission of sins.

And the Prophets teach universally in this way, that one must approach God by trust in mercy on account of the mediator, as Daniel says: Not in our righteousness, but in thy mercy on account of the Lord, hear us.

And Psalm 6.: Save me for thy mercy's sake. And Exod.: The Lord God, merciful and gracious.

And Rom. 5.: Through him we have access to God. Likewise: No one comes to the father, except through the son.

And yet it is true, as we have said so often, that at the same time in this remission the Son of God gives us of his Spirit, but the merit of Christ must not be obscured, nor are minds to be led away from this unique consolation proposed in the Gospel, which affirms that believers are received and please God on account of the mediator, as he said above: Whom he set forth as a propitiator by faith.

But let this admonition be retained against many cavils, since in the word righteousness it must be confessed that this is a relation of acceptance, it is necessary to understand us to be righteous, that is, accepted on account of the mediator God and man, and not to understand righteousness only of divinity.

It was imputed to him in uncircumcision.

The fourth argument.

Righteousness was imputed before circumcision, Therefore circumcision is not the cause on account of which Abraham is righteous.

The consequence is manifest, because an effect does not precede its cause in time. But Abraham was circumcised in the 99th year of his age, when he had previously been called from Haran at 75. There are therefore 24 years from that calling to circumcision.

In this argument is contained the doctrine concerning signs or sacraments, as we commonly name them, and the doctrine concerning good works.

Abraham is not righteous on account of a work, which indeed had been commanded by God: therefore neither are we righteous on account of works, but good works please God in those who are already righteous by faith, even if the remnants of sin still cling to them, as is said more fully elsewhere.

Now let us speak of the Sacraments.

Paul has used a remarkable word, he names this rite a seal of the righteousness of faith.

Here let learners first consider what are the common judgments of men concerning with such rites.

Men think such rites are either signs of an external profession, or of a distinction among men, just as the Toga distinguished the Roman from the Greeks, or that they are merely allegories of our works. Thus the Anabaptists teach universally that the anabaptism which they have is a distinction of their assembly from other men: then that it is an allegory of patience, which reminds them of being immersed as if into waves. They say the Lord's Supper is a covenant of mutual benevolence, just as a common table has always been a sign of friendship among all nations. Such are human interpretations of the Sacraments: although they will have their place later, yet another principal interpretation must be held first, and the principal ends must be considered.

But two principal ends always precede.

The first, that the sacraments are part of the public ministry, because God wills that the Church be gathered by an external ministry, and wills it to be a visible congregation. Thus baptism is part of the ministry, by which the Church is visibly gathered, and the external invocation of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit sounds forth. The Lord's Supper is the nerve of the public congregation, in which God wills the whole doctrine of the Gospel to sound forth publicly, as it is written: As often as you meet, you shall announce the death of the Lord until He comes. The second end is that which pertains privately to individuals, that the sacraments are signs not only toward men, but toward God, and are as it were testimonies or pledges of the promise of grace.
