So that when faith is excited by the Holy Spirit with the word, this external testimony is added as a sign, and indeed one applying the general promise to individuals, that is, testifying that the promise pertains to individuals. Paul therefore calls circumcision a seal of the righteousness of faith, because it was a testimony in the body of Abraham handed down by God, reminding him of the promise and showing that the promise pertained to him. But just as Abraham was confirmed by receiving this new sign from heaven, so we must be confirmed in the use of the sacraments, as if we were receiving a new voice or sign from heaven, and know that the promise is applied to us. But custom causes those testimonies of God handed down to us to be cared for more lightly.

Let us therefore rightly think about the use of the sacraments, and know that they are seals, that is, reminders of the promise and testimonies of the application, that the promise truly pertains to you, and faith, looking at the promise, may conclude that we are truly received and heard by God on account of the mediator. These things become more illustrious in the true exercises of conversion and in true consolation. And because it requires faith in the use of the sacraments, it is manifest that the wretched impiety is condemned, which feigns that those works merit remission by the work performed (ex opere operato).

If they, who are heirs by the law, the promise is void etc.

The fifth argument.

No promise depending on the condition of the law is valid and certain for us, The promise of grace must be valid and certain, Therefore: The promise of grace does not depend on the condition of the law, but is gratuitous and to be received by faith. This argument is taken from the fountains of the whole ecclesiastical doctrine, and is the foundation and the bond (συνέχον) of the whole controversy, and shows the distinction between the law and the Gospel.

It will be more illustrious when the first example is considered.

When Adam and Eve fell, they could not reason otherwise from the law, except that they were already cast out for all eternity, and the whole human race had already perished, unless God, by issuing a promise, had drawn them back from death, and by this promise of grace had founded the Church: thus we know that God wills to gather for Himself an eternal Church in the human race, because beyond the law He issued an admirable promise, concerning the mediator, concerning the gratuitous remission of sins, concerning reconciliation, and concerning eternal life. Let these beginnings of the Church be considered, so that the promise may be made more conspicuous and it may be thought how the Church has always been gathered, and what thing has made the distinction between the Church and the Gentiles.

Both know the law, and the law accuses both, but the promise of grace makes the distinction, for always and only there has been and will be the true Church of God, where the promise and the understanding of the promise of grace remains, as Paul says: No other foundation can be laid, besides that which is laid, which is Christ Jesus. Let those first examples of Adam and Evetherefore be in sight.

They clearly understood the major proposition, No promise depending on the condition of the law is valid and certain for us. They themselves knew the law, but after the fall they understood that they were judged to be not liberated from sin by the law, and subsequently all the holy fathers understood that they were accused by the law, because the law does not only demand external discipline, but is a sad judgment of God, by which God shows us the huge evils in our hearts, and oppresses men with terror and pain, in which they flee from God with a horrible trembling, as it is said: God is a consuming fire.

Item: There is no peace in my bones, etc. He therefore adds a confirmation to the major proposition: The law produces wrath, that is, because this depraved nature by no means agrees with the law. Therefore the law always accuses us, produces wrath, that is, terrors, sad tremblings in the heart, and deadly pains in the sense of the judgment and wrath of God, as it is said elsewhere: The sting of death is sin, but the power of sin is the law, that is, the true recognition of sin: as when Nathan rebukes David, God through that rebuke judges David as if by his own thunderbolt, and shows him the magnitude of sin.

The same is said below: The law kills, etc. From these sayings the major proposition can be understood in some way, which will be declared below in the seventh chapter.

The confirmation of the minor is illustrated from the major.

For since the law does not announce the remission of sins, but rather always accuses, it can be sufficiently understood that men could not have been saved, unless a clear and gratuitous promise had been issued concerning the remission of sins, and concerning the restitution of justice and eternal life.

Just as Adam and Eve reasoned that they were going to perish, and would have perished, had not God in his immense mercy restored life to them through a new reconciliation, and restored it by the promise issued concerning the seed. Therefore the Lord says: God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten son, etc. This most ample promise was issued at the intercession of the son, by the immense goodness of God, not because of the law or the merits of any men, and God confirmed it with many miracles and by an oath, according to these sayings: The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent.

Item: As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, etc. There is therefore a certain and ratified promise concerning the mission of the son, and concerning his benefits because of the truth of God, not because of any dignity of men.

Here it is useful for the younger ones to be warned about the error which the monks have taught and do teach, and which the Synod of Trent established, namely, that everyone ought always to doubt whether their sins have been remitted to them, and whether they please God, and this doubt they call pious.

This pernicious error deletes the promise of the Gospel, and fights against this whole doctrine of Paul, and snatches away the highest consolation from the pious.

The doctrine of the Church does not leave men in doubt on either side. These most true sentences must therefore be held. Whoever perseveres in sins against conscience, let him certainly conclude that he is guilty of the wrath of God and eternal punishment, according to these sayings: Those who do such things shall not possess the kingdom of God.

Item: He who commits sin is of the devil. On the contrary, whoever is converted to God by true repentance, ought to apprehend the promise by faith, and conclude truly that sins are remitted to him, and that he subsequently pleases God because of the mediator, not because of his own dignity, and that he is vivified and sanctified by the son of God through the Holy Spirit, as it is said: He himself gives us of his spirit. And although in this our infirmity a great doubt still clings in individuals, yet it is necessary that the doubt be overcome by faith, otherwise the heart does not struggle out from the pains of the infernal regions.

Therefore Paul says: Being justified by faith we have peace. Item: Through him we have access to God by faith. Item: Let us approach with confidence to the throne of grace. Item: Everyone who believes in the son has eternal life. Item: He who does not believe in him, accuses him of lying. Not to want to believe the promise of God given because of the son, is to pretend that sin and the kingdom of the devil are more powerful than the son of God, and it fights against this saying: Grace abounds above the offense.

This doctrine must be opposed to the impious decree of the Synod of Trent, and to the pernicious ravings of the monks, and must be thought of daily in every invocation.

Item in the creed: I believe in the remission of sins. From these it is clear that the Church is distinguished from other nations by the knowledge of the promise concerning the mediator and his benefits, as Paul says: No other foundation can be laid, besides that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ.

Therefore there is no Church of God where there is no knowledge of the mediator and his benefits, even if there is some knowledge of the law there, because neither the remission of sins, nor true invocation can take place, unless the promise concerning gratuitous reconciliation because of the mediator is apprehended by faith.

CAP. IV. This text also shows that faith is understood here not as knowledge of the law, because Paul expressly preaches about the promise, which was issued for this very reason, because no one is righteous by the law.

And because such faith is required, which receives the promise, it is manifest that faith is understood as that which is assent to the promise, in which mercy is shown promised on account of the mediator; this mercy being shown, the heart rests in the confidence of the mediator, and thus receives remission and is freed from the pains of hell. Thus it is also said in Acts: To him all the Prophets bear witness, etc.

Furthermore, it is manifest that Paul speaks of that faith which brings peace and joy to the heart, as when he says: Being justified by faith we have peace. Likewise: He who believes in him shall not be confounded.

But knowledge of history in devils and other impious people horribly increases terrors, because the devils know that the Son of God is the judge, whom they most proudly hate, and that he will show their malice before the whole celestial Church, and that they will certainly be in eternal punishments: therefore they grieve and rage all the more.

It is necessary, therefore, that Paul be understood not only of knowledge of history, but of this faith, which assents to the promise, and indeed receives it in such a way that you believe for yourself that the benefits of the mediator are given to you. And because faith relates correlatively to the promise and to the mediator, it must be known that this proposition: We are justified by faith, is to be understood correlatively, for this proposition: On account of the Son of God the mediator through mercy, freely, we receive the remission of sins and reconciliation by faith, not on account of the dignity of our work, which is named faith, and yet faith is the medium by which we apprehend the mediator and rest in him. All these things must be considered, so that the proposition: We are justified by faith, may be understood as Paul speaks.

Osiander has another imagination: We are justified by faith, that is, we apprehend God himself, so that he may be in us, and be effective; and then he says that we are righteous, because we have righteousness, namely God moving us, so that we may act righteously.

These things are said about the subsequent newness, not about the acceptance of the remission of sins and reconciliation, and about the consolation, which must always shine before newness. For first the conscience asks whether it has the remission of sins and reconciliation, and it receives this by faith looking upon the mediator God and man, as it has been said: Through him we have access, etc.

Latin:

Consilium Pauli diligenter considerandum est.

Ideo citat dictum in Genesi de fide, quia ibi expresse et sine conditione fit asseveratio, et revelatur expresso testimonio, quod credens sit iustus. Hoc opponit legi, quasi dicat: Nusquam legimus pronunciari aliquem iustum, quia legem implevit, sed lex semper accusat homines, Ergo non sumus lege iusti.

Retinenda est igitur haec consolatio Abrahae dicta, quod sit iustus fide.

Commoratur autem Paulus in declaratione imputationis, ut ostendat gratuitam esse, et esse eam remissionem peccatorum, et reconciliationem, seu acceptationem propter mediatorem.

Adiungit igitur dicta Psalmi: Beati quorum remissae sunt iniquitates etc. Beatus vir, cui non imputavit Dominus peccatum etc. Recitat Paulus antecedens, sed fiet accommodatio magis perspicua, cum consequens attexitur, videlicet: Cum nemo aliter sit beatus, id est, iustus seu acceptus Deo, nisi peccata remittantur, tegantur et non imputentur, manifeste sequitur, neminem in hac depravata natura satisfacere legi, neminem lege iustum esse, et in omnibus haerere peccata, quia propter mediatorem remittuntur credenti.

Sit autem Psalmus ille totus notissimus, quia doctrinam necessariam et dulcissimam consolationem continet.

Cum enim didicimus et ex eo Psalmo, et ex hac integra Pauli doctrina, quod hoc modo tantum et non aliter homo fiat iustus, id est, acceptus Deo, cum credit sibi remitti peccata propter mediatorem, gratis, et quod velit Deus hanc suam misericordiam agnosci, et conspici beneficia filii, sicut clamat, Osculamini filium, Beati omnes qui confidunt in eo: amplissima consolatio nobis proponitur, quae sustentat nos in conversione, ne mergamur in desperationem et exitium, sed accedamus ad Deum hac fide.

Vocabula in Psalmo sunt perspicua.

Primum nominatur remissio peccatorum, quae est desinere irasci peccatis, seu praeteritis seu praesentibus.

Deinde tegi peccata est mediatorem esse umbraculum, ne effundatur in nos ira Dei.

Et proprie dicitur: Tegi peccatum, quod adhuc adest in renatis.

Etsi enim est peccatum, et dignum aeterna poena, tamen tegimur per filium Dei, sicut dicitur: Non estis sub lege, sed sub gratia.

Et quanquam intelligit Psalmus tegi pec cata, quo ad poenam aeternam, tamen sciamus sic etiam ea tegi, quo ad poenam corporalem, iuxta dicta: Misericordia Domini, quod non consumti sumus.

Vult enim Deus superstitem esse Ecclesiam. Non imputari peccata intelligitur etiam et de praeteritis et de praesentibus, et est non cogitare, non decernere, quod ille credens sit puniendus aeterna poena, quanquam antea deliquit, et adhuc sunt in eo sordes. Latini dicerent, Non exprobrare ea, non accusare hominem tanquam reum poenae aeternae.

Sed hic usitata obiectio recitanda est, quare Paulus citat dictum de remissione, et non adiungit dicta de operibus, Beati mites, Beati misericordes.

Respondeo: Quia semper dicta de laudibus operum sunt synecdochae.

Laudantur enim in his, qui sunt reconciliati fide, iuxta dicta, Rom. 14.: Omne quod non est ex fide peccatum est. Rom.

3.: Legem stabilimus fide. Universaliter igitur in laudibus operum prius intelligatur fides praelucens, quae accipit remissionem peccatorum, et reconciliationem gratis propter mediatorem.

Ideo haec dicta hoc loco non citantur, quia bona opera sequuntur in iustificatis, non iustificant. Paulus autem hic quaerit non quomodo postea opera fiant aut placeant, sed quomodo persona fiat iusta, id est, accepta Deo, videlicet remissione peccatorum.

Ideo dicta de remissione citat, quae non sunt synecdochae, quia gratis propter filium recipimur, et haec remissio antecedit bona opera.

Addenda est et haec admonitio.

Osiander interpretatur haec verba: Imputata est ei iusticia hoc modo, id est, transfusa est in eum divinitas.

Etsi autem verissimum est, in remissione peccatorum fieri renovationem, cum audita voce Evangelii in corde perterrefacto filius Dei hanc consolationem dicit, Remittuntur tibi peccata, Et dat Spiritum sanctum: tamen aliud est loqui de illa renovatione, aliud de causa, propter quam persona prius accipit remissionem peccatorum, et fit accepta, seu de modo quo accedimus ad Deum.

Sicut autem infra dicitur, Propter obedientiam unius constituuntur iusti multi: ita hic intelligamus imputari nobis obedientiam mediatoris, propter quem habemus remissionem peccatorum et acceptationem.

Ideo et hic Paulus citans Psalmum: Beati quorum remissae sunt iniquitates etc.

Ostendit se loqui de imputatione, qua nobis propter mediatorem peccata remittuntur, et qua persona accepta est. Ideo et postea dicit: Fides imputatur ei ad iusticiam, sed propter mediatorem, et illa fides, quae nititur mediatore petens et accipiens remissionem peccatorum.

Ac universaliter sic docent Prophetae, Accedendum esse ad Deum fiducia misericordiae propter mediatorem, sicut Daniel inquit: Non in iusticia nostra, sed in misericordia tua propter Dominum exaudi nos.

Et Psalmo 6.: Salvum me fac propter misericordiam tuam. Et Exod.: Dominator Dominus Deus misericors.

Et Rom. 5.: Per hunc habemus accessum ad Deum. Item: Nemo pervenit ad patrem, nisi per filium.

Et tamen verum est, ut toties diximus, Simul in hac remissione filium Dei dare nobis de spiritu suo, sed non obscurandum est meritum Christi, nec abducendae sunt mentes ab hac unica consolatione in Evangelio proposita, quae affirmat, recipi et placere credentes propter mediatorem, sicut supra dixit: Quem posuit propiciatorem fide.

Retineatur autem adversus multas cavillationes haec admonitio, cum in vocabulo iusticiae fatendum sit, esse hanc relationem acceptationis, necesse est intelligi nos iustos, id est, acceptos esse propter mediatorem Deum et hominem, et non intelligi iusticiam tantum de divinitate.

Imputatum est ei in praeputio.

Quartum argumentum.

Iusticia imputata est ante circumcisionem, Ergo circumcisio non est causa, propter quam Abraham est iustus.

Consequentia manifesta est, quia effectus non antecedit causam tempore. Circumcisus est autem Abraham anno aetatis suae 99., cum antea vocatus esset ex Haran 75. Sunt ergo anni ab ea vocatione ad circumcisionem 24.

In hoc argumento continetur doctrina de signis seu sacramentis, ut usitate nomiuamus, et doctrina de bonis operibus.

Abraham non est iustus propter opus, quod quidem a Deo mandatum erat: ergo nec nos sumus iusti propter opera, sed placent Deo bona opera in his, qui iam fide iusti sunt, etiamsi haerent adhuc in eis reliquiae peccati, ut alibi copiosius dicitur.

Nunc de Sacramentis dicamus.

Paulus insigni verbo usus est, nominat hunc ritum sigillum iusticiae fidei.

Hic primum considerent discentes, quae sint usitata hominum iudicia de talibus ritibus.

Homines existimant tales ritus aut esse signa professionis externae, seu distinctionis inter homines, sicut Toga discernebat Romanum a Graecis, aut esse allegorias tantum de nostris operibus. Sic Anabaptistae universaliter docent anabaptismum, quem habent, esse distinctionem sui coetus a caeteris hominibus: deinde esse allegoriam de patientia, quae commonefaciat eos velut in fluctus mergi. Coenam Domini dicunt esse foedus mutuae benevolentiae, sicut semper apud omnes gentes communis mensa fuit signum amicitiae. Tales sunt humanae interpretationes de Sacramentis: quibus etsi postea suus locus erit, tamen alia principalis interpretatio prius tenenda est, et considerandi sunt fines principales.

Semper autem antecedunt duo principales fines.

Prior, quod sacramenta sunt pars publici ministerii, quia vult Deus colligi Ecclesiam externo ministerio, et vult eam esse congregationem visibilem. Sic baptismus est pars ministerii, quo visibiliter colligitur Ecclesia, et sonat externa invocatio Patris, Filii et Spiritus sancti. Coena Domini est nervus publicae congregationis, in qua vult Deus publice sonare totam doctrinam Evangelii, ut scriptum est: Quotiescunque convenientis, mortem Domini annuntiabitis donec venerit. Secundus finis est privatim ad singulos pertinens, quod sacramenta sunt signa non tantum erga homines, sed erga Deum, et sunt tanquam testimonia seu pignora promissionis gratiae.

Ut cum verbo excitatur fides per Spiritum sanctum, accedit hoc externum testimonium tanquam signum, et quidem adplicans generalem promissionem ad singulos, id est, testificans promissionem ad singulos pertinere. Nominat igitur Paulus circumcisionem sigillum iusticiae fidei, quia erat testificatio in corpore Abrahae a Deo tradita, commonefaciens eum de promissione et ostendens promissionem ad ipsum pertinere. Sicut autem Abraham confirmabatur accepto hoc novo signo de coelo, sic nos in usu sacramentorum confirmari oportet, quasi novam vocem aut signum ex coelo acciperemus, et scire nobis applicari promissionem. Sed consuetudo facit, ut illa testimonia Dei nobis tradita levius curentur.

Recte igitur cogitemus de usu sacramentorum, et sciamus esse sigilla, id est, commonefactiones de promissione et testificationes de applicatione, quod videlicet promissio vere ad te pertineat, et fides intuens promissionem, statuat vere nos recipi et exaudiri a Deo propter mediatorem. Haec in veris exercitiis conversionis et in vera consolatione fiunt illustriora. Et quia requirit in usu sacramentorum fidem, manifestum est, damnari tetram impietatem, quae fingit illa opera mereri remissionem ex opere operato.

Si hi, qui ex lege sunt haeredes, irrita est promissio etc.

Quinta argumentum.

Nulla promissio pendens ex conditione legis est nobis rata et certa, Promissionem gratiae oportet esse ratam et certam, Ergo: Promissio gratiae non pendet ex conditione legis, sed est gratuita et accipienda fide. Hoc argumentum sumturn est ex fontibus totius doctrinae ecclesiasticae, et est fundamentum ac συνέχον totius controversiae, et ostendit discrimen legis et Evangelii.

Erit autem illustrius considerato primo exemplo.

Cum Adam et Eva lapsi sunt, non poterant aliter ratiocinari ex lege, nisi se iam in tota aeternitate abiectos esse, et totum genus humanum iam perierat, nisi Deus edita promissione retraxisset eos ex morte, et hac promissione gratiae condidisset Ecclesiam: ita scimus Deum velle sibi in genere humano colligere aeternam Ecclesiam, quia praeter legem edidit admirandam promissionem, de mediatore, de remissione peccatorum gratuita, de reconliliatione, et de vita aeterna. Haec initia Ecclesiae considerentur, ut fiat conspectior promissio et cogitetur quomodo semper Ecclesia collecta sit, et quae res fecerit discrimen inter Ecclesiam et Ethnicos.

Norunt legem utrique, et utrosque lex accusat, sed promissio gratiae facit discrimen, semper enim tantum ibi fuit, et est erit vera Dei Ecclesia, ubi manet promissio et intellectus promissionis gratiae, sicut Paulus inquit: Fundamentum aliud poni non potest, praeter id quod positum est, quod est Christus Iesus. Sint igitur in conspectu illa prima exempla Adae et Evae.

Hi perspicue intellexerunt maiorem propositionem, Nulla promissio pendens ex conditione legis, est nobis rata et certa, Ipsi norant legem, sed post lapsum intelligebant se iudicari a lege non liberari a peccato, et deinceps omnes sancti patres intellexerunt se lege accusari, quia lex non tantum externam disciplinam postulat, sed est triste iudicium Dei, quo Deus ostendit nobis ingentia mala in nostris cordibus, et opprimit homines terrore et dolore, in quo fugiunt Deum horribili fremitu, sicut dicitur: Deus est ignis consumens.

Item: Non est pax ossibus meis etc. Addit igitur confirmationem maiori propositioni: Lex iram efficit, id est, quia haec depravata natura nequaquam congruit cum lege. Ideo semper accusat nos lex, efficit iram, id est, pavores, tristes fremitus in corde, et exitiosos dolores in sensu iudicii et irae Dei, sicut alibi dicitur: Aculeus mortis peccatum est, potentia vero peccati lex est, id est, vera agnitio peccati: ut cum Nathan obiurgat Davidem, Deus per illam obiurgationem tanquam suo fulmine iudicat Davidem, et ostendit ei magnitudinem peccati.

Idem infra dicitur: Lex occidit etc. Ex his dictis utcunque intelligi maior propositio potest, quae infra declarabitur in capite septimo.

Confirmatio minoris illustratur ex maiore.

Quia enim lex non annunciat remissionem peccatorum, imo semper accusat, satis intelligi potest, non potuisse homines salvos fieri, nisi edita perspicua et gratuita promissione de remissione peccatorum, et de restitutione iusticiae et vitae aeternae.

Sicut Adam et Eva ratiocinabantur se perituros esse, et periissent, nisi Deus immensa misericordia nova reconciliatione reddidisset eis vitam, et reddidit promissione edita de semine. Ideo inquit Dominus: Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut filium suum unigenitum dederit etc. Haec amplissima promissio edita est deprecante filio, immensa bonitate Dei, non propter legem aut merita ullorum hominum, et confirmavit eam Deus multis miraculis et iureiurando, iuxta haec dicta: Iuravit Dominus, et non poenitebit eum.

Item: Vivo ego, dicit Dominus, nolo mortem peccatoris etc. Est igitur certa et rata promissio de filii missione, et de beneficiis eius propter veritatem Dei, non propter ullam hominum dignitatem.

Hic utile est moneri iuniores de errore, quem monachi docuerunt et docent, et Synodus Tridentina stabilivit, videlicet, Unumquemlibet semper debere dubitare, an sibi remissa sint peccata, et an Deo placeat, et hanc dubitationem dicunt piam esse.

Hic perniciosus error delet promissionem Evangelii, et pugnat cum hac tota doctrina Pauli, et summam consolationem piis eripit.

Doctrina Ecclesiae in neutra parte relinquit homines in dubitatione. Tenendae sunt igitur hae verissimae sententiae. Qui perseverat in delictis contra conscientiam, is certo statuat se reum esse irae Dei et aeternae poenae, iuxta haec dicta: Talia facientes, non possidebunt regnum Dei.

Item: Qui facit peccatum, ex diabolo est. Contra vero, quisquis convertitur ad Deum vera poenitentia, debet apprehendere fide promissionem, et statuere vere sibi remitti peccata, et se deinceps placere Deo propter mediatorem, non propter propriam dignitatem, et se vivificari et sanctificari a filio Dei per Spiritum sanctum, sicut dicitur: Ipse dat nobis de spiritu suo. Et quanquam in hac nostra infirmitate semper in singulis haeret adhuc magna dubitatio, tamen vinci dubitationem fide necesse est, alioqui cor non eluctatur ex doloribus inferorum.

Ideo Paulus inquit: Iustificati fide pacem habemus. Item: Per hunc habemus accessum ad Deum fide. Item: Accedamus cum fiducia ad thronum gratiae. Item: Omnis qui credit in filium, habet vitam aeternam. Item: Qui non credit in eum, arguit eum mendacii. Non velle credere promissioni Dei propter filium traditae, est fingere peccatum et regnum diaboli potentius esse filio Dei, et pugnat cum hoc dicto: Gratia exuberat supra delictum.

Haec doctrina opponenda est impio decreto Synodi Tridentinae, et perniciosis monachorum deliramentis, et cogitanda est quotidie in omni invocatione.

Item in symbolo: Credo remissionem peccatorum. Ex his perspicuum est Ecclesiam discerni a caeteris gentibus, noticia promissionis de mediatore et eius beneficiis, sicut Paulus inquit: Fundamentum aliud poni non potest, praeter id quod positum est, quod est Iesus Christus.

Non est igitur Ecclesia Dei, ubi non est noticia mediatoris et beneficiorum eius, etiamsi est ibi aliqua legis noticia, quia nec remissio peccatorum, nec vera invocatio fieri potest, nisi fide apprehendatur promissio de gratuita reconciliatione propter mediatorem.

CAP. IV. Hic textus etiam ostendit fidem hic intelligi non noticiam legis, quia expresse concionatur Paulus de promissione, quae hanc ipsam ob causam edita est, quia nemo lege iustus est.

Et quia talis fides postulatur, quae promissionem accipit, manifestum est intelligi fidem, quae est assentiri promissioni, in qua ostenditur misericordia propter mediatorem promissa, hac misericordia ostensa acquiescit cor fiducia mediatoris, et sic accipit remissionem et liberatur ex doloribus inferorum. Sic et in Actis dicitur: Huic omnes Prophetae testimonium etc.

Praeterea manifestum est Paulum loqui de ea fide, quae affert pacem et laeticiam cordi, ut cum inquit: Iustificati fide pacem habemus. Item: Qui credit in eum, non confundetur.

At noticia historiae in diabolis et aliis impiis horribiliter angent terrores, quia enim sciunt diaboli filium Dei iudicem esse, quem ipsi superbissime oderunt, et coram tota Ecclesia coelesti ostensurum esse malitiam ipsorum, et se in poenis aeternis certo futuros esse: ideo magis dolent et fremunt.

Necesse est igitur Paulum intelligi non tantum de noticia historiae, sed de hac fide, quae assentitur promissioni, et quidem sic eam accipit, ut tibi ipsi credas dari beneficia mediatoris. Et quia fides correlative se habet ad promissionem et ad mediatorem, sciendum est hanc propositionem: Fide iustificamur, correlative intelligendam esse, pro hac propositione: Propter filium Dei mediatorem per misericordiam, Gratis, accipimus remissionem peccatorum et reconciliationem fide, non propter dignitatem nostri operis, quod nominatur fides, et tamen fides est medium, quo apprehendimus mediatorem et in eo acquiescimus. Haec omnia consideranda sunt, ut propositio: Fide iustificamur, sic intelligatur, ut Paulus loquitur.

Osiandri alia est imaginatio: Fide iustificamur, id est, apprehendimus Deum ipsum, ut sit in nobis, et sit efficax; et deinde dicit nos iustos esse, quia habemus iusticiam, scilicet Deum moventem nos, ut iuste agamus.

Haec dicuntur de novitate sequenti, non de acceptione remissionis peccatorum et reconciliationis, et de consolatione, quam semper praelucere novitati oportet. Primum enim quaerit conscientia, an habeat remissionem peccatorum et reconciliationem, et hanc accipit fide intuente mediatorem Deum et hominem, sicut dictum est: Per hunc habemus accessum etc.

## 5:1 Disposition of Romans: Argument
Cap. V. Epilogus.

In every disputation the principal members are the Proposition and the confirmation. Upon which the reader must always fix his eyes and mind. Wherefore, let the eyes hasten to contemplate the remaining parts, so that they may nevertheless often look back to the superior members. Moreover, the Epilogue is made with wonderful art. First, the proposition is repeated, afterwards it is amplified by the effects of faith.

For faith produces tranquility of conscience, and raises one up in all terrors and afflictions. state of conscience, and raises it up in all terrors and afflictions.

Thirdly, consolation is added. It is a repetition of the proposition.

Latin:

Cap. V. Epilogus.

In omni disputatione praecipua membra sunt, Propositio, et confirmatio. In quem lectorem semper oportet oculos atque animum defigere. Quare ad reliquas partes contemplandas, ita properent oculi, ut tamen ad superiora membra saepe respiciant. Est autem Epilogus mira arte factus. Primum repetitur propositio, postea amplificatur ab effectibus fidei.

Efficit enim fides tranquilli- tatem conscientiae, et erigit in omnibus pavoribus et afflictionibus.

Tertio addita est consolatio. Propositionis repetitio est.

## 5:1 Disposition of Romans
Justified by faith.

Effect of faith is peace toward God, or joy of conscience.

Therefore it follows: We have peace toward God through our Lord Jesus Christ.

He proceeds to commemorate the effects; this faith sustains and consoles us in afflictions.

And here he makes a rhetorical gradation, or as the Greeks call it, a κλίμαξ (climax), so that it may be seen more clearly where faith is to be exercised. κλίμαξ.

Tribulation [produces] patience.

Patience [produces] probation.

Probation produces hope.

Hope , however, does not disappoint.

In the previous degrees he sets forth the cause why God afflicts, namely, not to destroy, but so that we may have an occasion for exercising faith, and so that faith, or hope, may be hardened and confirmed in these things.

For there is no need to subtly tear faith away from hope, for they are related affections.

He adds the efficient cause of faith, for the Holy Spirit poured into the saints produces faith, so that they may feel that they are loved by God.

Then follows consolation, taken from the amplification of God’s love toward us.

For despairing consciences doubt the love of God toward us.

These Paul raises up by the amplification of God’s love.

And they are enthymemes drawn from the greater.

If we were received into grace when we were still sinners, how much more shall we, now justified, be saved?

This enthymeme is repeated.

And there are inserted amplifications from the kind of death.

No one dies willingly when he owes [a debt].

But Christ died for us, to whom He owed nothing.

Thus far the question, "What is Christian justice," has been agitated, and the contention, as rhetoricians call it, has been completed.

For the confirmation, which is the principal part in a contention, has been treated, and an Epilogue has been added to close the disputation.

Now he will institute as it were a new book, for the contention being finished, he begins to explain the simple terms which are the principal ones in this controversy.

And this is, to speak in the Aristotelian manner, a methodical analysis (ἀνάλυσις μεθοδική).

Above he set forth the proposition that all are under sin.

Now he dissolves the members of the proposition and teaches whence sin is and what the effects of sin are.

He teaches likewise what the effects of the law are.

Likewise, what grace is.

And these are the principal topics of Christian doctrine; he who does not hold them cannot understand either what the Gospel is or why Christ appeared.

Let the reader therefore diligently remember that the former part of the Epistle was a certain contention.

But this which follows pertains to that part of Dialectic which defines simple terms, and is as it were a new book, which nevertheless will bring some light to the contention completed above.

Latin:

Iustificati ex fide.

Effectus fidei, pax est erga Deum, seu gaudium conscientiae.

Ideo sequitur: Pacem habemus erga Deum per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum.

Pergit effectus commemorare, haec fides sustentat et consolatur nos in afflictionibus.

Et hic facit rhetoricam gradationem, seu ut Graeci vocant κλίμακα, ut clarius cerni possit, ubi fides exercenda sit. κλίμαξ.

Tribulatio patientiam.

Patientia probationem.

Probatio spem efficit.

Spes autem non confundit.

In prioribus gradibus ponit causam, cur Deus adfligat, scilicet, non ut perdat, sed ut occasionem habeamus exercendae fidei, et ut in his duretur et confirmetur fides, seu spes.

Nihil enim opus est fidem a spe subtiliter divellere, sunt enim cognati affectus.

Addit causam efficientem fidei, nam Spiritus sanctus effusus in sanctos efficit fidem, ut sentiant se a Deo diligi.

Deinde consolatio sequitur, ab amplificatione amoris Dei erga nos sumta.

Nam desperabundae conscientiae dubitant de amore Dei erga nos.

Has erigit Paulus, amplificatione amoris Dei.

Et sunt enthymemata ex maiore ducta.

Si recepti sumus in gratiam, cum adhuc peccatores essemus, quanto magis iustificati nunc servabimur?

Hoc enthymema repetitur.

Et sunt insertae amplificationes ex genere mortis.

Nemo cum debet, libenter moritur.

At Christus mortuus est pro nobis, quibus nihil debebat.

Hactenus quaestio, Quid sit iusticia Christiana, agitata est, et absoluta contentio, quam sic vocant rhetores.

Nam confirmatio, quae est in contentione praecipua pars, pertractata est, et additus Epilogus, qui clauderet disputationem.

Nunc veluti novum librum instituet, nam finita contentione, incipit simplices voces explicare, quae in hac controversia praecipuae sunt.

Estque haec, ut Aristotelico more dicam, ἀνάλυσις μεθοδική.

Supra posuit propositionem, omnes esse sub peccato.

Nunc dissolvit membra propositionis, et docet unde sit peccatum et qui effectus peccati.

Docet item, qui sint legis effectus.

Item, quid sit gratia.

Atque hi sunt praecipui loci doctrinae Christianae, quos qui non tenet, non potest intelligere vel quid sit Evangelium, vel cur apparuerit Christus.

Diligenter igitur meminerit lector, superiorem Epistolae partem fuisse quandam contentionem.

Hanc vero quae sequitur, pertinere ad eam Dialecticae partem, quae simplices voces definit, ac veluti novum librum esse, qui tamen aliquid lucis afferet contentioni supra absolutae.

## 5:1 Argument
Chapter V.

Therefore being justified by faith we have peace with God, etc.

The beginning of the fifth chapter is an epilogue, in which the principal proposition is repeated most briefly, and a necessary amplification is added concerning the effects of reconciliation, namely, concerning the consummation of the benefit of Christ. For what would it profit to have received the remission of sins if eternal life and righteousness did not follow?

Therefore he now discourses on these benefits which follow faith, and at the same time answers the objection of all men: Why do you boast that you are the Church of God, that you are righteous and dear to God, when you are the most miserable of all men, without power, without defense, scattered, wandering in uncertain dwellings, and in many ways wretched?

To these objections he answers: I confess, he says, that the Church of God is by a certain counsel subjected to the cross, but yet it is the heir of eternal life, righteousness, and joy; this we certainly expect amidst these miseries, and he adds arguments of consolation, taken from the testimonies of God's love toward us in the Son himself, and from the testimony of the Holy Spirit, in the consolation of our hearts amidst these very miseries.

This is the sum of the epilogue. Afterward, he institutes another part, which is as it were a method concerning the principal articles of doctrine which are proper to the Church, namely, concerning sin, whence it is, what it is, and what kind it is.

Then, what is the use of the law. Thirdly, what is grace, and what is the amplitude of grace.

Now let the propriety of the words of the text be diligently considered: Justified by faith, that is, absolved from sins, and reconciled and accepted by God through faith, namely, that which relies on the mediator Christ, God and man, we have peace toward God, that is, we feel consolation by faith itself, by which we are freed from the wrath of God and the horrendous pains of the infernal regions, of which Hezekiah says: As a lion he crushed all my bones.

Paul therefore speaks of the consolation by which hearts are freed from those pains and are vivified, as he said above: The just shall live by his faith, and below: They who believe in him shall not be confounded.

And Psalm 2: Blessed are all who trust in him. And Psalm 118: Be mindful of thy word to thy servant, in which thou hast given me hope, this has comforted me in my humility, because thy word vivifies me.

And Psalm 129: My soul has waited in his word, my soul has hoped in the Lord, etc. In the hope of the glory of God, etc.

It is a manifest assertion that those justified by faith are pleasing to God on account of the mediator, and are heirs of eternal life.

It is necessary to hold this doctrine and consolation concerning the consummated benefit: let us not think, even if I have now turned to God and the remission of sins has been announced to me, that it is nevertheless uncertain afterward whether I am pleasing to God, since there is such great infirmity, and whether I am an heir of eternal life.

Against these doubts he delivers here a clear doctrine and consolation, affirming that those who are turned to God are pleasing to God on account of the mediator by faith, and on account of him are certainly heirs of eternal life, not on account of their own dignity. As it is also said in John 3: God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, that everyone who believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.

And 1 John 5: He who has the Son has life. And in Romans 8: Whom he justifies, them he also glorifies.

So he says here: Through Christ we have access to God into grace, that is, gratuitous acceptance, in which we stand, namely, retaining faith: We are and henceforth accepted, and we glory in the hope of the glory of God, that is, we rejoice and determine that God is about to adorn us with His eternal glory, that is, with eternal life and the communication of Himself, namely, of His light, wisdom, justice..., and eternal joy. And let the phrase be observed: The glory of God, namely, insofar as He communicates it to us and makes us like Himself, as John speaks. Moreover, to glory signifies to rejoice and to determine that something is glorious for us, that is, that it is a good or salutary thing. Thus we rejoice in the hope of future glory, and we consider that glory to be true salvation and liberation. Here also let the definition of hope be held: Hope is the certain expectation of eternal life, to be given freely on account of the mediator, and of the mitigation of present calamities, according to the counsel of God.

Indeed, we even glory in afflictions.

It is the judgment of the Law and of reason that it should go well with the righteous. That is true, but it must be understood according to the declaration of the Gospel, which teaches how men become righteous, when they are to receive rewards, and why they are subject to the cross in this life. But the world, ignorant of these things, judges from the most sorrowful spectacles of the miseries of the Church that it is neglected by God. Against this judgment, God confirms us in the whole doctrine of the Church, as in Psalm 33: Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the Lord will deliver them out of them all. And Paul says here: We glory in afflictions, we rejoice and determine that they are not signs of the wrath of God, but good things, as the Psalm says: It is good for me that You have humbled me, that I might learn Your justifications, etc. Paul weaves in this necessary commemoration of afflictions so that he may meet the human objection: If we are righteous and dear to God, why are we in such great miseries?

He answers briefly: These miseries are exercises of faith and hope; they are not signs of the wrath of God against us.

Now, let the entire doctrine be added here: why is the whole human race subject to death and other calamities? And then, why is the Church more miserable than other men?

The first cause of death and common calamities in the whole human race is the fall of our first parents and the sin that we bring with us at birth. Then, punishments are accumulated daily by actual transgressions, and the furies of the devils are added, who exercise horrible cruelty upon this miserable and deserted nature because they are murderers. But why is the Church more miserable?

Here, first, the common causes must be repeated, because we are all born with sin. But God wills that in the Church, wrath against sin—which the world carelessly despises—be especially understood. Therefore, the Church is exercised more harshly so that it may be reminded of the wrath of God.

To this pertain the *dokimasiai* , according to the saying: The son whom He loves, He chastises.

Second, the Devil, out of hatred for Christ, tries to rage more atrociously against the Church.

Third, there are very many actual sins in the Church, such as David's adultery and Manasseh's idolatry. God also punishes these with atrocious penalties in this life, as in other men. To this pertain the *timoriai* .

Fourth, punishments in confession are testimonies that the saints truly feel as they teach.

They are also testimonies that show another judgment remains: for since God previously showed Himself to be present to Paul as he raised the dead, and then allowed him to be killed by Nero, He signifies that there will be a distinction afterward between Paul and Nero.

Fifth, because God wills that the excellent members in the Church be made conformable to the Son of God.

Sixth, God wills that His presence be seen in the human race, and especially in the Church, so that the Epicureans may be refuted. Therefore, the Church does not have protection like the empires of the world, and many things happen to the saints that are inextricable by human counsel, as Jeremiah says: I know, O Lord, that a man's way is not his own. Likewise: When we do not know what should be done, our eyes are lifted to You, O Lord: such as the fall of Adam, the selling of Joseph, the exile of David, the sickness of King Nebuchadnezzar, etc.

Therefore, the presence of God is seen when the saints are delivered in such a way that it is necessary for them and others to confess that they have been saved divinely.

Thus Moses prays in Numbers, Chapter 14: That the Egyptians may hear that You, O Lord, are in this people. And 1 Kings 17, David says: That all the earth may know that the Lord is God in Israel. And Jeremiah 14: But You, O Lord, are in us, and Your name is called upon us; do not forsake us. Let these causes, why the Church is subject to the cross, always be in sight, and let us know that God demands obedience in punishments and in the cross, according to the saying: Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God. Likewise: Be subject to God, and hope in Him.

Next, let us add consolations, some of which arise from these causes which I have recounted.

For in order that we may both desire obedience—which desire is a virtue called Patience—and joyfully await the outcome, it is necessary to see some good things in adversities, namely the good will of God, the presence of God, the help of God, and a good end. When we discern these good things in adversities, we begin in some way to desire this obedience for God's sake, and we are not only in pain, but we are quickened by faith and hope, and in some way we joyfully await the outcome. For consolation ought to produce some joy, however small, in the heart.

Let the distinction between philosophical and theological consolations be in view.

Philosophical topics are: 1. Necessity. 2. The dignity of virtue. 3. A good conscience. 4. Examples. 5. The utility of others, as in military service. 6. Comparison of events.

Theological topics are: 1. Necessity, namely, the law and justice of God. 2. The dignity of virtue. 3. A good conscience. 4. Remission of sins and reconciliation. 5. Recognition of the presence of God and divine help. 6. Hope of mitigation and final liberation, and invocation. 7. Examples. 8. The utility of others. 9. Comparison of events. Having considered the common doctrine concerning Patience and consolations, the gradation in the text will be better understood.

Tribulation, namely, this whole burden of miseries in the Church, produces patience, specifically in those who discern the good will of God and the presence of God in adversities, and are uplifted by faith and hope: as in David in exile, not in the Epicureans or in Saul: these, since they see only evils, are not patient.

Therefore, in order for there to be patience, it is necessary that the doctrine concerning the causes why the Church is subject to afflictions should shine forth. Likewise faith, which receives reconciliation and discerns the presence of God, and hope, which awaits help and liberation. And let the distinction between philosophical and Christian patience be held.

Philosophical patience is not to act against justice or other virtues when broken by pain, as Cato acts against justice, because he committed suicide on account of pain. Aristides tolerates injuries patiently, and in order that the pain may be in some way alleviated, he seeks other causes from those which I have recounted: the chief of which is a good conscience, and this kind of patience can exist without the hope of help and liberation. But Christian patience is not only to do nothing against God when broken by pain, as Saul does, but it is in some way to desire obedience, through the recognition of the good will of God and the presence of God, and by this faith and hope of divine help and liberation to have a heart quickened by the Word of God, so that there is some joy diminishing the pain: as David in exile desires in some way obedience for God's sake, and although he carries about an immense pain, yet he feels his heart quickened by the Word, so that there is some joy diminishing the pain.

Latin:

Caput V.

Iustificati ergo fide pacem habemus apud Deum etc.

Initium Capitis quinti est epilogus, in quo brevissime repetita est principalis propositio, et additur amplificatio necessaria de effectibus reconciliationis, videlicet de consummatione beneficii Christi. Quid enim prodesset accepisse remissionem peccatorum, si non sequeretur vita et iusticia aeterna?

Ideo iam de his beneficiis concionatur, quae fidem sequuntur, et simul respondet obiectioni omnium hominum: Quid gloriamini vos esse Ecclesiam Dei, vos iustos et Deo caros esse, cum sitis omnium hominum miserrimi, sine imperio, sine defensione, dissipati, vagantes incertis sedibus, et multis modis aerumnosi? Ad has obiectiones respondet: Fateor, inquit, Ecclesiam Dei certo consilio subiectam esse cruci, sed tamen est haeres aeternae vitae, iusticiae et Laetitiae, hanc certo expectamus inter has aerumnas, et addit argumenta consolationis, sumta ex testimoniis amoris Dei erga nos in ipso filio, et ex testimonio Spiritus sancti, in consolatione cordium nostrorum inter ipsas aerumnas.

Haec est epilogus summa. Postea instituit aliam partem, quae est tanquam methodus de praecipuis articulis doctrinae, quae propria est Ecclesiae, videlicet de peccato, unde sit, quid sit, et quale sit.

Deinde quis sit usus legis. Tertio quid sit gratia, et quae sit gratiae amplitudo.

Nunc diligenter consideretur proprietas verborum textus: Iustificati fide, id est, absolutia peccatis, et reconciliati ac accepti Deo per fidem, scilicet, quae nititur mediatore Christo Deo et homine, pacem habemus erga Deum, id est, consolationem ipsa fide sentimus, qua liberamur ab ira Dei et horrendis doloribus inferorum, de quibus dicit Ezechias: Sicut leo contrivit omnia ossa mea. Loquitur ergo Paulus de consolatione, qua corda liberantur ab illis doloribus et vivificantur, sicut supra inquit: Iustus fide sua vivet, et infra: Qui credunt in eum, non confundentur.

Et Psalm. 2.: Beati omnes qui confidunt in eo.

Et Psalm. 118.: Memor esto verbi tui servo tuo, in quo mihi spem dedisti, Haec me consolata est in humilitate mea, Quia eloquium tuum vivificat me.

Et Psalm. 129.: Sustinuit anima mea in verbo eius, speravit anima mea in Domino etc.

In spe gloriae Dei etc. Manifesta asseveratio est, quod iustificati fide placeant Deo propter mediatorem, et sint haeredes vitae aeternae.

Hanc doctrinam et consolationem de consummato beneficio tenere necesse est: ne cogitemus, etsi iam conversus sum ad Deum, et annunciata est mihi remissio peccatorum, tamen postea incertum est, an placeam Deo, cum tanta sit infirmitas, et an sim haeres aeterni vitae. Adversus has dubitationes perspicuam doctrinam et consolationem hic tradit, affirmat conversos ad Deum, placere Deo propter mediatorem fide, et propter eum certo haeredes esse vitae aeternae, non propter propriam dignitatem.

Sicut et Ioan. 3. dicitur: Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut filium unigenitum dederit, ut omnis qui credit in eum non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam.

Et 1. Ioan.

5.: Qui habet filium,... habet vitam. Et Romanorum octavo: Quos iustificat eosdem et glorificat.

Ita hic inquit: Per Christum habemus accessum ad Deum in gratiam, id est, gratuitam acceptationem, in qua stamus, scilicet, retinentes fidem: Sumus et deinceps accepti, et gloriamur spe gloriae Dei, id est, laetamur et statuimus, quod Deus sit nos gloria sua aeterna ornaturus, id est, vita aeterna et communicatione sui ipsius, videlicet suae lucis, sapientiae, iustitiae et laetitiae aeternae. Et phrasis observetur: Gloria Dei, scilicet, quatenus eam nobis communicat, et facit nos similes sibi, ut Ioannes loquitur. Significat autem gloriari, laetari, et statuere aliquid nobis gloriosum esse, id est, rem bonam seu salutarem esse. Ita laetamur spe venturae gloriae, et ducimus illam gloriam esse veram salutem et liberationem. Hic et definitio spei teneatur: Spes est certa expectatio aeternae vitae, Gratis dandae propter mediatorem, et mitigationis praesentium calamitatum, iuxta consilium Dei.

Imo etiam gloriamur in afflictionibus.

Legis et rationis iudicium est, Iustis debet bene esse, Id verum est, sed intelligendum est iuxta Evangelii declarationem, quod docet, quomodo homines fiant iusti, et quando sint accepturi praemia, et cur in hac vita subiecti sint cruci. Sed mundus haec ignorans, iudicat ex tristissimis spectaculis miseriarum Ecclesiae, negligi eam a Deo. Adversus hoc iudicium confirmat nos Deus in tota doctrina Ecclesiae, ut Psalm. 33.: Multae tribulationes iustorum, sed ex omnibus his liberabit eos Dominus. Et Paulus hic inquit: Gloriamur in afflictionibus, Laetamur et statuimus eas esse non signa irae Dei, sed res bonas, ut Psalmus inquit: Bonum mihi quod humiliasti me, ut discerem iustificationes tuas etc. Intexit autem Paulus hanc necessariam commemorationem de afflictionibus, ut occurrat humanae obiectioni: Si sumus iusti et cari Deo, cur sumus in tantis aerumnis?

Respondet autem breviter: Hae aerumnae sunt exercitia fidei et spei, non sunt signa irae Dei adversus nos.

Iam huc adiungatur integra doctrina, quare totum genus humanum sit subiectum morti et aliis calamitatibus? Deinde quare Ecclesia magis aerumnosa sit, quam alii homines.

Prima causa est mortis et communium calamitatum in toto genere humano, lapsus primorum parentum, et peccatum quod nascentes afferimus. Deinde cumulantur poenae actualibus delictis quotidie, et accedunt furores diabolorum, qui in hanc miseram et desertam naturam exercent horribilem saevitiam, quia sunt homicidae. Sed quare Ecclesia magis est aerumnosa.

Hic primum repetendae sunt communes causae, quia omnes nascimur cum peccato. Vult autem Deus in Ecclesia praecipue intelligi iram adversus peccatum, quod mundus securus contemnit. Exercetur ergo Ecclesia durius, ut commonefiat de ira Dei.

Huc pertinentδοκιμασίαι , iuxta dictum: Filium quem diligit, castigat.

Secunda, Diabolus odio Christi atrocius saevire conatur in Ecclesiam.

Tertia, Valde multa sunt et actualia delicta in Ecclesia, ut Davidis adulterium, Manassae idolatria. Haec etiam Deus punit atrocibus poenis in hac vita, ut in aliis hominibus. Huc pertinent τιμωρίαι .

Quarta, Supplicia in confessione sunt testimonia, quod sancti vere sic sentiant sicut docent.

Sunt item testimonia, quae ostendunt restare aliud iudicium: quia enim Deus antea ostendit se Paulo adesse resuscitanti mortuos, et deinde finit eum interfici a Nerone, significat postea discrimen fore inter Paulum et Neronem.

Quinta, Quia vult Deus excellentiam membra in Ecclesia fieri conformia filio Dei.

Sexta, Vult Deus conspici suam praesentiam in genere humano, et praesertim in Ecclesia, ut refutentur Epicurei. Ideo non habet Ecclesia defensionem ut imperia mundi, et accidunt sanctis, multa inextricabilia humano consilio, sicut inquit Ieremias: Scio Domine, quod non sit hominis via eius. Item: Cum nescimus quid agendum sit, oculi nostri ad te Domine tolluntur: ut lapsus Adae, venditio Ioseph, Davidis exilium, morbus regis Nabuchodonosor etc.

Conspicitur igitur praesentia Dei, cum sic liberantur sancti, ut fateri ipsos et alios necesse sit, divinitus servatos esse.

Sic orat Moises in numeris Cap. 14.: Ut audiant Aegyptii, quod tu Domine sis in hoc populo. Et 1. Reg. 17. inquit David: Ut sciat omnis terra, quod est Dominus Deus in Israël. Et Ieremiae 14.: Tu autem in nobis es Domine, et nomen tuum invocatum est super nos, ne derelinquas nos. Hae causae, quare Ecclesia cruci subiecta sit, semper sint in conspectu, et sciamus Deum postulare obedientiam in poenis, et in cruce, iuxta dictum: Humiliamini sub potenti manu Dei. Item: Subditus esto Deo, et spera in eo.

Deinde et consolationes adiungamus, quarum aliquae et ex his causis, quas recensui, oriuntur.

Ut enim et velimus obedientiam, quod velle est virtus, quae nominatur Patientia, et laeti expectemus exitum, necesse est in adversis videre aliquas res bonas, scilicet voluntatem Dei bonam, praesentiam Dei, auxilium Dei, bonum finem. Cum haec bona cernimus in adversis, incipimus aliquomodo velle hanc obedientiam propter Deum, et non tantum sumus in dolore, sed fide et spe vivificamur, et aliquomodo laeti expectamus exitum. Nam consolatio debet aliquam laetitiam, quantulacunque est, in corde efficere.

Iam sit in conspectu discrimen consolationum philosophicarum et theologicarum.

Loci philosophici sunt: 1. Necessitas. 2. Dignitas virtutis. 3. Bona conscientia. 4. Exempla. 5. Utilitas aliorum, ut in militia. 6. Collatio eventuum. Loci theologici sunt:

1. Necessitas, videlicet, lex et iusticia Dei. 2. Dignitas virtutis. 3. Bona conscientia. 4. Remissio peccatorum et reconciliatio. 5. Agnitio praesentiae Dei et auxilii divini. 6. Spes mitigationis et liberationis finalis, et invocatio. 7. Exempla. 8. Utilitas aliorum. 9. Collatio eventuum. Considerata autem communi doctrina de Patientia et consolationibus, gradatio in textu melius intelligetur.

Tribulatio videlicet, totum hoc onus miseriarum in Ecclesia patientiam efficit, videlicet in his, qui cernunt bonam voluntatem Dei, et praesentiam Dei in adversis, et fide et spe erecti sunt: ut in Davide exulante, non in Epicureis aut in Saule: hi cum tantum videant mala, non sunt patientes.

Ut igitur sit patientia, necesse est, ut praeluceat doctrina de causis, quare Ecclesia subiecta sit aerumnis. Item fides, quae accipit reconciliationem et cernit praesentiam Dei, et spes quae expectat auxilium et liberationem. Ac teneatur discrimen philosophicae et Christianae patientiae.

Philosophica patientia est non facere contra iusticiam aut alias virtutes fractos dolore, ut Cato facit contra iusticiam, quia propter dolorem sibi conscivit mortem. Aristidis tolerat iniurias patienter, et ut dolor aliquomodo leniatur, quaerit alias causas ex his, quas recensui: quarum praecipua est, Bona conscientia, et haec qualiscunque patientia potest esse sine spe auxilii et liberationis. Sed patientia Christiana est, non solum nihil contra Deum facere fractos dolore, ut facit Saul, sed est aliquomodo velle obedientiam, agnitione bonae voluntatis Dei et praesentiae Dei, et hac fide et spe auxilii divini et liberationis habere cor vivificatum verbo Dei, ita, ut aliqua sit laetitia minuens dolorem: ut David in exilio vult aliquomodo obedientiam propter Deum, et quanquam ingentem dolorem circumfert, tamen sentit verbo vivificari cor, ut aliqua sit laetitia minuens dolorem.

## 5:4
Patience [produces] probation.

That is, patience effects an exploration, which shows that faith is not feigned, but true, living, and ardent. Affliction shows both to others and to ourselves that faith is not feigned.

And there is no need for a declaration concerning the testimony of others.

When others see wise old men preferring to be killed rather than to cast away their confession, they reason that they truly feel what they profess, for sane men would not want to suffer such sad things for empty fables.

But it is more that, when we do not fail in afflictions, we ourselves feel the increments and consolation, the motions of the Holy Spirit and the presence of God, just as Paul says: The Spirit intercedes for us with groanings that cannot be uttered.

Item: You have received the spirit of adoption of sons, crying Abba, Father, which gives testimony to our spirit. And Nahum, first chapter: The Lord is good and comforting in the day of tribulation, and caring for those who hope in Him. Isaiah 28: Whom shall He teach knowledge?

Those weaned from the milk. Item: Vexation shall give understanding. Item: God shall instruct him in judgment and shall teach him.

Ecclesiasticus 80: He who has not been tempted, what does he know? Proof of hope.

That is: In that exercise, faith and hope are confirmed. Faith and hope are neighboring movements, and they are always joined, and yet there is some distinction of objects. Faith is the movement apprehending the word of God, and God himself, and in the present receiving reconciliation. Thus, consolation and joy occur when this present good is apprehended. But hope is the certain expectation of eternal life, on account of the mediator of the promise, and the expectation of future mitigation in this life, according to the counsel of God.

Thus says Isaiah: In silence and hope shall be your strength. First, he commands silence, that is, this obedience, which is not to be angry at God in afflictions, and not to seek forbidden protections, but with faith shining forth and acknowledging the will of God and the presence of God, to bend the hearts in some way toward obedience, so that they may be willing to endure afflictions. Then he commands hope, which looks toward the coming liberation, or mitigation. Thus he says: You will be saved by being silent and hoping, you will be strong, you will stand firm, you will have good outcomes, according to those sayings: Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.

Psalm 9: And let those who know your name hope in you, because you do not abandon those who seek you, O Lord. Hope does not put to shame.

It is a Hebrew phrase: Hope does not put to shame, that is, it does not frustrate the one hoping, for thus the word to confound or to put to shame is often used for to frustrate. It is, however, an assertion and consolation to be opposed to profane judgments, which think that the sayings about the coming judgment, and the promise of salvation, and the threats of punishments after this life are empty fables. Against these human judgments, God has issued his own voice and illustrious testimonies, affirming that the dead will rise again, and that a judgment will follow after this life, in which he will give life, wisdom, justice, joy, and eternal life to those who believe in the Son.

But he will cast the impious into eternal torments. And Christ, by his resurrection and the resurrection of many, showed that these things will certainly come to pass. To these testimonies, let this saying be added: Hope is not frustrated, namely for those believing in the Son.

But here, in individual cases, the conscience disputes, The promise pertains to the worthy: But I am unworthy, etc. Wherefore, even if the promise has been made, and it is commanded that we hope, yet perhaps the promise does not pertain to me. Against this objection, it is necessary to know the distinction between the Law and the Gospel, and to know the doctrine concerning the exclusive particle, "Freely." This is the climax of the struggle: Does God wish to remit sins for us, and does he wish to give us eternal salvation when we are unworthy?

Here it is necessary to know the proper voice of the Gospel. On account of the Son of God, the remission of sins, reconciliation, or justification, the gift of the Holy Spirit, and eternal life are given to you freely, although we are unworthy; the command of God is immutable, that we believe this, according to the saying: Therefore it is by faith freely, so that the promise may be firm. Because the love of God has been poured into our hearts. The reasoning of the consequence seems obscure: Hope does not put to shame, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts.

The consequence would seem less obscure if it said: Hope does not put to shame, because the promise is certain and ratified: for this reasoning is taken from the proximate object of hope, which is known from the promise. In reality, however, Paul says the same thing, but adds something, for the meaning is: Hope does not put to shame, because God certainly loves us, and we apprehend this love by the very movement of faith, by which the Holy Spirit is simultaneously efficacious, and raises up hearts in true sorrows, with consolation and joy, and thus the Holy Spirit is a pledge, and gives testimony to our spirit.

Therefore, "the love of God" in this place signifies the love with which God loves us, as below: Who shall separate us from the love of God? namely, with which he loves us. And at the same time it is true that then, in the heart, our love toward God is kindled in turn.

Here many questions are raised: Is love the Holy Spirit himself substantially, and is no created love of God to be posited in man? Likewise, is the knowledge, which is faith, the Son of God himself, the Word, and is no created knowledge of the promise to be posited in man?

These questions were raised in the past, and are now being renewed by Osiander: As if someone were to imagine, that a righteous man is changed in nothing in himself, but is only a dwelling place of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit dwelling there, just as when water is poured into a cask, no change occurs to the cask.

Regarding these questions, I respond by proposing the example of the first conversion. When Adam heard God speaking, he simultaneously hears outside himself the vocal promise, which the Son utters, and that same Son of God is then present in the heart of man, and causes the illustrious knowledge and assent to shine in the mind, in which knowledge Adam understands that he is received by God, and recognizes the will of the eternal Father, and simultaneously the Son pours the Holy Spirit into the heart of Adam, by which Adam feels life and joy. Here in the mind there is not only the Son, but also created knowledge and assent, by which Adam understands the Word and believes, and in the heart there is not only the uncreated Holy Spirit, but also joy kindled by the Holy Spirit, because the Word and the Holy Spirit are not there as water in a cask, but man is reborn, and has kindled created knowledge, and motions or affections created by the Holy Spirit, just as it is said to the Galatians: The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, faith, etc.

2 Corinthians 3 it is said: We, beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord. A secure reason does not discern the wrath of God against sins, it does not discern the presence of God in consolation, or joy in God. But in true conversion, man feels the wrath of God and joy in God.

There, with unveiled face, he discerns the glory of God, that is, he discerns in the Word the judgment and mercy of God, and with the Word shining in the mind, the mind and heart are transformed into a similar glory, that is, they now have knowledge and motions congruent with the Word, and these things happen when, upon hearing the Word, the Spirit of God kindles new motions in us.

Paul would not say, "We are transformed into the same image," if only the divinity were there, and no created knowledge or love. Likewise, Rom. 8: The Holy Spirit gives testimony to our spirit. Therefore, we also have knowledge and affections congruent with the Holy Spirit in true consolation. Although, therefore, knowledge, fears, and joys are excited in us, nevertheless the distinction between the cause and the effects must be maintained, as 1 John 3 it is said: We shall be like him.

Therefore, a change also happens in us, and we learn how it happens, in true conversion, in sorrows and consolation. Let us hold to this simple and true opinion, and let us not be disturbed by the deceits of sophisms, which are opposed.

Christ, when we were still weak, etc. There follows an amplification, which collects signs and testimonies that God loves us, but this is the highest and ineffable benefit, namely, that He gave His Son for us, and indeed willed this very thing to be a certain pledge of true and immutable love, etc.

Scarcely for a righteous man will one die. He amplifies this love with a double comparison: Scarcely for a righteous thing does one die, that is, even when we must die, yet we meet death unwillingly, as a thief dies unwillingly, even if he owes death to the laws. Understand, therefore, the words of Paul: For a righteous thing, that is, for a righteous matter, or a righteous cause, or a debt.

For a good thing one might dare to die. Another comparison is: For a good thing one might dare to die, that is, for a good and pleasant thing, that is, incited by desire or the opinion of great utility for our own, we more easily undertake dangers, as a brave man goes to death for the defense of his spouse, children, or dignity.

From these two propositions he argues, and amplifies the love of God and Christ toward us, from a comparison of causes. It is necessary that he be moved by a great force of love who does good to another with his own pain, when he owes nothing to him, and receives no utility from it, because even those who owe punishment to the laws, yet die unwillingly.

Others perhaps, if any go to death, are moved by some opinion of great utility for their own, or by their own glory. But Christ died for us, when He owed us nothing, nor was He moved by any utility of His own. Therefore, it is necessary that there be an immense and ineffable force of love in Him toward us.

These things agree with the saying: God so loved the world that He gave His only-begotten Son for us. And the Lord asks: So may Thy love be in them, with which Thou lovest me.

Latin:

Patientia probationem.

Id est, patientia efficit explorationem, quae ostendit fidem non esse simulatam, sed veram, vivam et ardentem. Ostendit autem afflictio et aliis et nobis ipsis, fidem non simulatam esse.

Ac de aliorum testimonio non est opus declaratione.

Cum alii vident, senes sapientes malle interfici, quam abiicere confessionem, ratiocinantur eos vere hoc sentire, quod profitentur, nam sani homines non vellent tam tristia pati propter inanes fabulas.

Plus autem est, quod cum non deficimus in afflictionibus, nos ipsi sentimus incrementa et consolationem, motus Spiritus sancti et praesentiam Dei, sicut Paulus inquit: Spiritus interpellat pro nobis gemitibus inenarrabilibus.

Item: Accepistis spiritum adoptionis filiorum clamantem Abba Pater, qui dat testimonium spiritui nostro. Et Nahum primo: Bonus Dominus et confortans in die tribulationis, et curans sperantes in ipsum. Esaiae 28.: Quem docebit scientiam?

Ablactatos a lacte. Item: Vexatio dabit intellectum. Item: Erudiet eum in iudicio Deus et docebit eum. Ecclesiast.

80.: Qui non est tentatus, qualia scit? Probatio spem.

Id est: In illo exercitio fides et spes confirmantur. Sunt autem vicini motus fides et spes, et semper coniuncti sunt, et tamen aliquod est discrimen obiectorum. Fides est motus apprehendens verbum Dei, et Deum ipsum, et in praesentia accipiens reconciliationem. Ita fit consolatio et laetitia cum hoc praesens bonum apprehenditur. Sed spes est certa expectatio vitae aeternae, propter mediatorem promissae, et expectatio futurae mitigationis in hac vita, iuxta consilium Dei.

Sic inquit Esaias: In silentio et spe erit fortitudo vestra. Primum praecipit silentium, id est, hanc obedientiam, quae est non irasci Deo in afflictionibus, et non quaerere inconcessa praesidia, sed praelucente fide et agnoscente voluntatem Dei et praesentiam Dei, flectere corda aliquo modo ad obedientiam, ut velint perferre afflictiones. Deinde spem praecipit, quae intuetur venturam liberationem, seu mitigationem. Ita inquit: Silentes et sperantes servabimini, eritis fortes, consistetis, habebitis bonos eventus, iuxta illa dicta: Omnis qui credit in eum, non confundetur.

Psal. 9.: Et sperent in te, qui noverunt nomen tuum, quia non derelinquis quaerentes te Domine.

Spes non confundit. Phrasis Hebraica est: Spes non confundit, id est, non frustratur sperantem, sic enim saepe verbum confundere seu pudefacere usurpatur pro frustrari. Est autem asseveratio et consolatio opponenda prophanis iudiciis, quae existimant dicta de venturo iudicio, et promissione salutis, et minas poenarum post hanc vitam esse inanes fabulas.

Contra haec humana iudicia edidit Deus suam vocem et testimonia illustria affirmat mortuos revicturos esse, et secuturum esse iudicium post hanc vitam, in quo credentibus in filium dabit vitam, sapientiam, iusticiam, laetitiam, et vitam aeternam. Impios vero abiiciet in aeternos cruciatus. Et Christus sua resurrectione et multorum resurrectione haec certo eventura esse ostendit.

Ad haec testimonia adiungatur hoc dictum, Spes non frustratur, scilicet credentes in filium. Sed hic in singulis conscientia disputat, Promissio pertinet ad dignos: Ego autem sum indignus etc. Quare etiamsi promissio facta est, et mandatum est, ut speremus, tamen fortassis promissio nihil ad me attinet.

Adversus hanc obiectionem necesse est nosse discrimen legis et Evangelii, et scire doctrinam de particula exclusiva, Gratis. Haec est epitasis certaminis, An Deus velit nobis remittere peccata, et an velit nobis dare aeternam salutem cum simus indigni? Hic necesse est nosse vocem Evangelii propriam. Propter filium Dei gratis tibi donantur remissio peccatorum, reconciliatio, seu iustificatio, donatio Spiritus sancti, et vitae aeternae, quanquam sumus indigni, mandatum Dei immutabile est, ut hoc credamus, iuxta dictum: Ideo ex fide gratis, ut sit firma promissio.

Quia dilectio Dei effusa est in corda nostra. Videtur obscura esse ratio consequentiae, Spes non confundit, quia dilectio Dei effusa est in corda nostra.

Minus videretur obscura consequentia, si sic diceret: Spes non confundit, quia promissio est certa et rata: nam haec ratio sumitur ex proximo obiecto spei, quod notum est ex promissione. Reipsa vero idem dicit Paulus, sed addit aliquid, Est enim sententia: Spes non confundit, quia Deus certo nos diligit, et hanc dilectionem apprehendimus ipso motu fidei, quo simul Spiritus sanctus est efficax, et erigit corda in veris doloribus, consolatione et laetitia, atque ita Spiritus sanctus est arrabo, et dat testimonium spiritui nostro.

Significat igitur dilectio Dei hoc loco dilectionem, qua nos diligit Deus, ut infra: Quis separabit nos a dilectione Dei? scilicet, qua nos diligit. Et simul verum est, tunc in corde vicissim accendi dilectionem nostram erga Deum.

Hic multae quaestiones moventur, An dilectio sit ipse Spiritus sanctus substantialiter, Et nulla sit ponenda dilectio Dei creata in homine? Item, An noticia, quae est fides, sit ipse filius Dei, Verbum, Et nulla sit ponenda noticia promissionis creata in homine? Hae quaestiones et olim motae sunt, et nunc ab Osiandro renovantur: Ut si quis imaginetur, hominem iustum nihil in seipso mutatum esse, sed tantum esse domicilium habitantis ibi Patris, Filii et Spiritus sancti, ut cum in dolium infunditur aqua, nulla fit dolii mutatio.

De his quaestionibus respondeo proposito exemplo primae conversionis. Cum Adam audiret Deum loquentem, simul foris audit promissionem vocalem, quam sonat filius, et ille idem filius Dei in corde hominis tunc adest, et facit, ut luceat illustris noticia et assensio in mente, in qua noticia intelligit Adam se a Deo recipi, et agnosci aeterni patris voluntatem, et simul effundit filius Spiritum sanctum in cor Adae, quo sentit Adam vitam et laetitiam. Hic in mente non tantum est filius, sed etiam creata noticia et assensio, qua Adam intelligit verbum et credit, et in corde non tantum est increatus Spiritus sanctus, sed etiam laetitia accensa per Spiritum sanctum, quia Verbum et Spiritus sanctus non sunt ibi, ut in dolio aqua, sed homo renascitur, et habet accensam noticiam creatam, et motus seu affectus a Spiritu sancto creatos, sicut ad Galatas dicitur: Fructus spiritus est dilectio, gaudium, pax, fides etc.

2. Corinth. 3. dicitur: Nos retecta facie gloriam Domini intuentes, in eandem imaginem transformamur a gloria in gloriam, tanquam a spiritu Domini.

Ratio secura non cernit iram Dei adversus peccata, non cernit praesentiam Dei in consolatione, seu laetitiam in Deo. Sed in vera conversione sentit homo iram Dei et laetitiam in Deo. Ibi retecta facie cernit gloriam Dei, id est, cernit in verbo iudicium et misericordiam Dei, et verbo lucente in mente transformantur mens et cor in similem gloriam, id est, habent iam noticias et motus congruentes cum verbo, et haec fiunt, cum audito verbo spiritus Dei accendit novos motus in nobis.

Non diceret Paulus, Nos in eandem imaginem transformari, si tantum ibi esset divinitas, et nulla creata noticia vel dilectio. Item, Rom. 8.: Spiritus sanctus dat testimonium spiritui nostro. Ergo et nos habemus noticias et affectus congruentes cum Spiritu sancto in vera consolatione.

Quanquam igitur noticiae, pavores, laetitiae excitantur in nobis, tamen discrimen inter causam et effectus tenendum est, ut 1. Iohan. 3. dicitur: Erimus ei similes. Fit igitur et in nobis mutatio, et quomodo fiat, in vera conversione, in doloribus et consolatione discimus.

Hanc simplicem et veram sententiam teneamus, et non turbemur praestigiis sophismatum, quae opponuntur. Christus cum adhuc essemus infirmi etc. Sequitur amplificatio, quae colligit signa et testimonia, quod Deus diligat nos, sed hoc summum et ineffabile beneficium, scilicet, quod dedit filium pro nobis, et quidem voluit hunc ipsum esse certum pignus verae et immutabilis dilectionis etc.

Vix pro iusto aliquis moritur. Hunc amorem amplificat duplici collatione: Vix pro iusta re aliquis moritur, id est, etiam cum debemus mori, tamen inviti oppetimus mortem, ut latro invitus moritur, etiamsi debet mortem legibus. Intelligas igitur verba Pauli: Pro iusta, id est, pro re iusta, seu causa iusta, seu debito.

Pro bono ausit aliquis mori. Altera collatio est: Pro bono ausit aliquis mori, id est, pro bona et suavi re, id est, incitati cupiditate aut opinione magnae utilitatis nostrorum facilius suscipimus pericula, ut vir fortis adit mortem pro defensione coniugis, liberorum aut dignitatis.

Ex his duabus propositionibus argumentatur, et amplificat amorem Dei et Christi erga nos, a collatione causarum. Necesse est hunc magna vi amoris moveri, qui bene facit alteri cum suo dolore, cum nihil ei debeat, et nihil inde accipiat utilitatis, quia etiam qui debent poenam legibus, tamen inviti moriuntur.

Alii fortassis, si qui mortem adeunt, moventur opinione aliqua magnae utilitatis suorum, aut sua gloria. At Christus pro nobis mortuus est, cum nobis non deberet, nec aliqua sua utilitate moveretur. Ergo necesse est ingentem et ineffabilem vim esse amoris in ipso erga nos.

Haec congruunt cum dicto: Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut filium unigenitum daret pro nobis. Et Dominus petit: Sic dilectio tua in eis, qua me diligis.

## 5:8
God commends his love to us.

Having commemorated the love, he returns to that part of the epilogue which he had established concerning salvation, or concerning the consummation of the benefit of the Son of God. Since God has received us through Christ with immense mercy, when we were unjust, how much more will he give eternal salvation, since we are now justified as righteous by the blood of Christ. It is necessary to add this doctrine concerning the consummation of the benefit, because what would it profit to have been received, if eternal life did not follow. These things are clear.

Let us know, however, that the sweetest consolation is also handed down against the immense weakness which remains in those who have been justified in this life. For he affirms that these are certainly heirs of eternal life: although the remnants of sin cling to us, yet we have been justified by the blood of Christ, that is, let us hold to this consolation, that we are reconciled, that is, that we are pleasing to God on account of the mediator, although we are unworthy and weak, and it is expressly said: Justified by his blood, that is, by the obedience of Christ, as it is said below: By the obedience of one, many are constituted righteous. And he himself interprets here the word 'justified' by the word 'reconciled', so that we may know that in the word 'righteous' it is necessary to understand a relation, namely, reconciliation or acceptance, which happens on account of the mediator, God and man.

And yet it is true, as it is said below: Through Christ grace and the gift are given: When we apprehend reconciliation by faith, we are made alive through the Son, as he himself says: I give them eternal life. Item: He who has the Son, has life. Item: He gives us of his Spirit.

But it is necessary to set forth that consolation which establishes that we, on account of the mediator, God and man, are received and are pleasing, as he says here: Justified by his blood. Those glorying in God. Not glorying in ourselves, that is, not attributing to ourselves that our virtues, our newness, our merits are the cause of such a great benefit, but God on account of the Son gives freely, both reconciliation and eternal life.
