As he says elsewhere: He who glories, let him glory in the Lord. Item: Rejoicing I will rejoice in the Lord, because he has clothed me with the garments of righteousness, and has clothed me with the garment of salvation.

But let these sayings also be opposed to our weakness, and let us establish that the benefit, the donation of eternal life on account of the mediator, is certain, even if the remnants of sin still cling to us, according to the saying: There is now no condemnation to those who walk in Christ Jesus. As through one man sin entered into the world etc.

The former part of the Epistle explained the proposition, that men are justified by faith on account of the Son of God the mediator, not on account of the law, or on account of our works, and added a confirmation to the proposition.

Now, as if beginning a new book, he institutes an analysis, in which he explains individual words, namely of sin, of the Law, of Grace, and copiously teaches the Church whence sin is, and what its effects are. Then, what is the principal effect of the law. Afterwards, whence grace is, what it is, and what benefits it embraces.

What the Law is.

The moral law is the eternal and immovable wisdom and norm of righteousness in God, revealed to men, infused into us by a similar light in creation, and afterwards promulgated in the Decalogue, so that we may know what God is, and what kind he is, and may discern him from evil natures, and understand that we ought to be conformable to him, obligating all rational creatures, so that they may be such as that wisdom of God commands them to be, demanding entire obedience, and denouncing the eternal wrath of God to all who are not such according to entire obedience, unless remission is made on account of the Son.

This definition is taken from the words of the Decalogue, Exod. 20, and from the fourth chapter of Deut.: This is your wisdom and understanding etc. Item: God is a consuming fire. Item: Cursed is everyone who does not remain in all things which are written in the law.

But let the Ceremonial and Forensic laws be prudently distinguished from the moral law. For because God established the polity of Israel, so that there might be a certain place in which Christ would be born from a certain lineage, and where he would be seen, would teach, would give testimonies, would be revealed, and would take refuge, ceremonial and forensic laws were added for a certain time, because human society in this civil custom cannot exist without order and without judgments. But he willed

God [ordained] these external works to be exercises of internal justice in the hearts.

Latin:

Commendat autem Deus nobis suum amorem.

Commemorata dilectione redit ad illam partem epilogi, quam instituerat de salvatione, seu de consummatione beneficii filii Dei. Cum Deus nos propter Christum immensa misericordia receperit, cum essemus iniusti, quanto magis aeternam salutem dabit, postquam nunc iustificati sumus iusti sanguine Christi. Hanc doctrinam de consummatione beneficii necesse est addi, quia quid prodesset receptos esse, si non sequeretur aeterna solus. Haec perspicua sunt.

Sciamus autem et dulcissimam consolationem tradi adversus ingentem imbecillitatem, quae reliqua est in his, qui iustificati sunt in hac vita. Affirmat enim hos certo haeredes vitae aeternae: quanquam haerent in nobis reliquiae peccati, tamen iustificati sumus sanguine Christi, id est, teneamus hanc consolationem, nos esse reconciliatos, id est, placere Deo propter mediatorem, quanquam sumus indigni et infirmi, et expresse dicitur: Iustificati sanguine, id est, obedientia Christi, sicut infra dicitur: Per unius obedientiam iusti constituuntur multi. Et interpretatur ipse hic vocabulum iustificati, vocabulo reconciliati, ut sciamus in vocabulo, Iusti, oportere intelligi relationem, videlicet reconciliationem seu acceptationem, quae fit propter mediatorem Deum et hominem.

Et tamen verum est, sicut infra dicitur: Per Christum dari gratiam et donum: Cum fide reconciliationem apprehendimus, vivificari nos per filium, sicut ipse inquit: Ego vitam aeternam do eis. Item: Qui habet filium, habet vitam. Item: Dat nobis de Spiritu suo.

Sed praeclucere illam consolationem oportet, quae statuit nos propter mediatorem Deum et hominem, recipi et placere, sicut hic inquit: Iustificati sanguine. Gloriantes in Deo. Non gloriantes in nobis ipsis, hoc est, non tribuentes nobis, quod nostrae virtutes, nostra novitas, nostra merita sint causa huius tanti beneficii, sed Deus propter filium dat Gratis, et reconciliationem et vitam aeternam. Sicut alibi inquit: Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur. Item: Gaudens gaudebo in Domino, quod vestimentis iusticiae induit me, et vestimento salutis vestivit me.

Opponantur autem et haec dicta nostrae infirmitati, et statuamus certum esse beneficium, donationem vitae aeternae propter mediatorem, etiamsi adhuc haerent in nobis reliquiae peccati, iuxta dictum: Nulla nunc damnatio est his, qui in Christo Iesu ambulant. Sicut per unum hominem peccatum in mundum intravit etc.

Superior pars Epistolae exposuit propositionem, iustificari homines fide propter filium Dei mediatorem, non propter legem, aut propter nostra opera, et propositioni addidit confirmationem.

Nunc velut novum librum incoans iustituit ἀνάλυσιν, in qua exponit singula vocabula, videlicet peccati, Legis, Gratiae, et copiose docet Ecclesiam, unde sit peccatum, et qui sint eius effectus. Deinde quis sit effectus principalis legis. Postea unde sit gratia, quid sit, et quae beneficia complectatur.

Quid sit Lex.

Lex moralis est aeterna et immota sapientia et norma iusticiae in Deo, patefacta hominibus, transfusa in nos simili luce in creatione, et postea promulgata in Decalogo, ut sciamus quod sit Deus, et qualis sit, et discernamus eum a malis naturis, et intelligamus nos oportere ei conformes esse, omnes creaturas rationales obligans, ut sint tales, quales illa sapientia Dei esse praecipit, postulans integram obedientiam, et denuncians aeternam iram Dei omnibus, qui non sunt tales iuxta integram obedientiam, nisi fiat remissio propter filium.

Haec definitio sumitur ex verbis Decalogi Exod. 20. et ex Capite quarto Deut.: Haec est sapientia vestra et intellectus etc. Item: Deus ignis consumens est. Item: Maledictus omnis qui non manet in omnibus, quae in lege scripta sunt.

Prudenter autem discernantur a lege morali Ceremoniales et Forenses. Quia enim Deus constituit politiam Israël, ut certus locus esset, in quo ex certa stirpe nasceretur Christus, et ubi conspiceretur, doceret, ederet testimonia, patefetur, et refugeret, sunt additae leges ceremoniales et forenses ad certum tempus, quia societas humana in hac civili consuetudine non potest esse sine ordine et sine iudiciis. Voluit autem

Deus haec externa opera esse exercitia interioris iustitiae in cordibus.

## 5:12 Disposition of Romans
Through sin, death pervaded all men.

Aetiology.

Because all have sinned.

Circumstance of time.

Even when the law had been given, sin and death nevertheless remained in the world, nor did the law abolish sin and death.

Circumstance, to whom.

Death rages against those also who have not committed actual sins, as we call them.

This passage testifies that all men are born with sin.

That they now call original sin; Paul did not add the surname, although he speaks without doubt of original sin.

But he aptly embraces both original sin and its fruits under the same name.

Afterward, holy men were compelled to distinguish the appellations of original and actual sin, when the impious Pelagians twisted the name of sin only to actual crimes, not to the disease of nature, just as certain profane teachers in our age philosophize.

Whence grace.

Latin:

Per peccatum mors pervasit ad omnes homines.

Αἰτιολογία.

Quia omnes peccaverunt.

Circumstantia quam diu.

Etiam cum lex data esset, tamen manserunt peccatum et mors in mundo, nec abolevit lex peccatum et mortem.

Circumstantia, ad quos.

Mors saevit in illos etiam, qui non admiserunt actualia peccata, ut vocamus.

Hic locus testatur omnes homines nasci cum peccato.

Id nunc vocant peccatum originis, Paulus non addidit cognomen, tametsi de peccato originis haud dubie loquitur.

Sed apte eodem nomine peccatum originis et fructus complectitur.

Postea sancti viri coacti sunt discernere appellationes, peccati originalis et actualis, cum impii Pelagiani nomen peccati detorquerent tantum ad actualia flagitia, non ad naturae morbum, sicut nostra aetate quidam prophani doctores philosophantur.

Unde gratia.

## 5:14 Disposition of Romans
Sin was propagated through Adam into all his descendants.

Effect of sin.

Latin:

Peccatum per Adam propagatum est in omnes posteros.

Effectus peccati.

## 5:15 Disposition of Romans
Grace, and the gift through grace, by one Jesus Christ, abounds in many.

The name grace signifies the remission of sins, or, to explain it grammatically, favor.

The gift through grace signifies the Holy Spirit, who is poured into the hearts of those to whom sins are remitted, who sanctifies and vivifies and [creates] a new creates a creature.

As often as mention is made of grace, Scripture embraces these two things: the remission of sins and the gift of the Holy Spirit, as will be clearly stated again below in the eighth chapter. Therefore, they are mistaken who argue that some are in a state of grace even if they do not possess the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

Gratia, et donum per gratiam, per unum Iesum Christum exuberat in multos.

Nomen gratia significat remissionem peccatorum, seu ut grammatice exponam, favorem.

Donum per gratiam significat Spiritum sanctum, qui effunditur in corda eorum, quibus peccata remittuntur, qui sanctificat et vivificat et novam creaturam gignit.

Quoties gratiae mentio fit, haec duo complectitur scriptura, remissionem peccatorum, et donationem Spiritus sancti, ut infra rursus in octavo capite clare dicetur. Errant igitur qui disputant aliquos in gratia esse tametsi Spiritum sanctum non habeant.

## 5:16 Disposition of Romans
Comparison of Sin, Law, and Grace.

Here he begins to speak of the cause of sin: Therefore as through one man, etc.

And he delivers these sentences in order.

Cause of sin.

Latin:

Comparatio Peccati, Legis et Gratiae.

Hic incipit de causa peccati dicere: Propterea sicut per unum hominem etc.

Et ordine has sententias tradit.

Causa peccati.

## 5:16 Disposition of Romans
Comparison of sin and grace.

Grace is far more abundant than sin, because grace abolishes many sins, both original and actual, however atrocious they may be. And even though sin may cling to the saints, yet the magnitude of grace overcomes it, and sin does not reign and kill them; great consolation is placed in this passage. For since grace is more abundant than sin, we must feel that there are no sins so atrocious that the amplitude of grace does not surpass them.

The effects of grace.

Grace not only abolishes sin, but also death. If by the transgression of one Adam death reigned, much more will those who receive the overflowing grace and the gift of righteousness reign in life through one Jesus Christ. Observe in the particle, the "much more" (αὔξησιν) of grace, that it surpasses the power and magnitude of sin.

Concerning the law.

Why was the law given? For human reason judges that laws are made for the purpose of prohibiting sins. But Paul pronounces quite differently concerning the law: "Through the law sin abounded." He will declare this opinion somewhat later in the 7th chapter. And because it seems very absurd, he now immediately mitigates the things that can be objected, which, however, so that they may be more easily understood, we shall first speak briefly about the office of the law.

There are two offices of the law: The first is to restrain the impious. For God wills that the wicked be contained by political justice, so that they do not do harm: Paul speaks of this effect of the law to Timothy, where he says that the law is laid down for the unjust. But this discipline is not righteousness before God, but pertains only to the state and the magistrates. And all laws made by men, written by those who hold the republics, and even by the philosophers, must be understood only as this external discipline, which indeed is necessary, even though it is not righteousness before God. Nor should Paul be understood in this way, when he says that sin is increased by the law, as if he did not want the impious and carnal to be restrained outwardly, or as if he felt that men are incited to admit more crimes outwardly.

The second office of the law is to show sin and to terrify consciences.

When this happens, hearts naturally grow angry at the judgment of God and conceive hatred of God. Thus the law increases sin, as Paul will explain below. He therefore denies that external discipline is righteousness, and teaches that the law, for the most part, only terrifies consciences and kills.

Just as he writes to the Corinthians: "The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law."

Hence those questions arise in the sixth chapter.

Digression.

Chapter VI.

VI. Since the opinion already posited concerning the law and works seems very absurd, human reason protests.

If good works are of no use for justification, we shall therefore indulge our nature and sin. It will be enough to believe in Christ. Thus, in the end, grace will become much more abundant, because if we continue to sin, it will abolish more sins. Exactly the same things are objected now to those who defend the righteousness of faith. For Paul prudently saw how this doctrine abhors the judgment of reason.

Certain profane men think Paul was so dull that he did not see that he was saying things little consistent with reason, and they invent wondrous hyperboles to remedy his speech, so that it does not dissent from human judgment. But he saw that he was delivering things alien to the judgment of reason, and so that no one could suspect that these opinions escaped him inadvertently (λεληθότως) and with little consideration, he agitates the argument of reason, and rhetorizes at length, and responds not only to the calumnies of that age, but of all times.

First objection.

Objection. If good works do not merit justification, let us therefore continue to sin.

Response: It is taken from two places. From the final cause, and from the efficient cause. From the final cause, an inversion is made.

Nay, you have been justified so that you may work well. As if one were to argue in this way:

Labor is of no use to a sick man, therefore, even when cured, I shall do nothing. One must respond by inversion from the final cause: Nay, you have been cured so that you may labor thereafter. He immediately adds the efficient cause, where, since there is an antithesis, there are two members of the sentence. I shall include the whole of Paul's opinion in two syllogisms.

Negative Syllogism. The dead nature is not effective: The old nature in you is dead. For the old man was crucified with Christ: Therefore the old nature in you ought not to be effective.

Affirmative Syllogism.

The new nature ought to have new fruits: You are not only dead, but also made alive with Christ, that you may walk in new life: Therefore you ought to bring forth new fruits and work well.

It is an epilogue. Therefore let not sin reign.

It contains an exhortation, for persuasive passages are sometimes mixed into the disputations. The proposition of the epilogue is: Let not sin reign, etc. An αἰτιολογία (etiology) is added from the possible, or the easy, because sin will not have dominion over you.

Therefore you can now work well. The meaning of the antecedent is this: You already have certain consciences concerning God's benevolence: You know for certain that God is present with you, and that He helps you. Sin does not deter you, because it has been forgiven.

It has no power over these, to drag them to evil works, because they are governed by the Holy Spirit. Christ is stronger than sin.

Paul proves this antecedent with these words: You are not under the law, but under grace, therefore sin will not have dominion over you. The reason for the consequence would be obscure if he only said, you are not under the law. Now because he adds: But under grace, it is easy to understand: for to be under grace is to have God appeased, a defender, a helper. He will not allow us to be conquered by sin.

Second objection. And yet, because a new and seemingly absurd expression escapes him: You are not under the law, he therefore lingers a little while in softening it, before he returns from the digression to the subject.

All wise men, all who hold public offices, all sane men judge with great consensus that the human race must perish unless it is restrained by laws. Therefore this tribunitian expression: You are not under the law, seems unworthy of a good man, and seditious and utterly intolerable. Paul satisfies the reader excellently.

But I also thought the reader should be warned in passing that Paul is speaking here of the law, insofar as we attempt to earn righteousness before God by it. He says nothing here about the state, which he adorned with the highest praises below. For the Gospel in no way dissipates states, but rather strongly fortifies them, and commands that civil ordinances be religiously observed. It only teaches this, that we are not justified by that civil righteousness before God.

But I come to Paul's response.

What do you say, Paul? If we are not under the law, do you therefore give license to sin? For thus the world understands the abrogation of the law. In this place the Dialectician requires a definition, what the abrogation of the law is, whether it is to grant license to sin. Paul denies that license to sin is granted.

But he adds a refutation of the objection taken not from the definition, but from the circumstance: To whom the law has been abrogated. For privileges do not pertain to all, but to certain persons. Thus liberty pertains not to the impious, but to the just.

Meanwhile, it is the will of God that the impious be restrained, and be enclosed by the law as if by a prison. From the circumstance, To whom.

Everyone obeys him, whose servant he is: You are servants of righteousness: Therefore you ought to obey righteousness. He confirms the minor from the nature of opposites. You have ceased to be servants of sin: Therefore you are servants of righteousness.

As if one were to argue: Darkness has been driven away, therefore there is light.

The rest of the discourse in this chapter is an elaboration of the minor. For he declares in many words how they were servants of sin, what the fruits of sin were, what punishments follow sin. Likewise what fruits they ought now to produce, after they have acknowledged Christ.

But there is an inserted correction: I speak as a man.

For Paul sees that a definition is desired, what the abrogation of the law is: He sees that he is only using a persuasive argument, when a longer disputation is required. But in order to temper himself to the capacity of the reader, he deliberately avoids a more subtle disputation. And yet meanwhile in this persuasive argument he urges this, that the law is abrogated only for the justified.

And he indicates, for it is not to grant license to sin, but to have righteousness, the remission of sins, to have a conscience before God that is appeased and tranquil, whence it happens that, not being deterred, they do not flee from and hate God, but love Him and expect all good things from Him, and eagerly obey Him.

Conversely, to be under the law is to be restrained by the law, to be accused and condemned: But it hates judgment and the flesh [fears] punishment, therefore it also hates God. Thus for Paul it is the same thing to be under the law, to be in the flesh, to be a slave of sin. But at the beginning of the seventh chapter the circumstance, 'Quibus' [to whom], will be treated more clearly. For the argument above pertains more to persuasive topics. This which follows is more dialectical.

Latin:

Comparatio peccati et gratiae.

Longe uberior est gratia, quam peccatum, quia gratia abolet multa peccata, tum originale tum actualia, quantumvis atrocia. Et tametsi peccatum haereat in sanctis, tamen vincit gratiae magnitudo, nec peccatum regnet, et occidat eos, magna consolatio in hoc loco posita est. Nam cum uberior sit gratia, quam peccatum, sentire debemus, nulla tam atrocia esse peccata, quae non superet amplitudo gratiae.

Effectus gratiae.

Gratia non modo peccatum abolet, sed etiam mortem. Si unius Adae delicto mors regnavit, multo magis regnabunt in vita per unum Iesum Christum illi, qui exuberantem gratiam et donum iusticiae accipiunt. Observa in particula, multo magis αὔξησιν gratiae, quod superet peccati vim et magnitudinem.

De lege.

Cur lata est lex? nam ratio humana iudicat leges ideo ferri, ut prohibeant peccata. Sed Paulus longe aliter pronunciat de lege: Per legem abundavit peccatum. Hanc sententiam aliquanto post declarabit in 7. capite. Et quomodo valde absurda videtur, nunc statim mitigat ea quae obiici possunt, quae tamen, ut facilius intelligantur, nos antea breviter de legis officio dicemus.

Legis duo sunt officia: Primum est cohercere impios. Vult enim Deus politica iusticia contineri malos, ne noceant: de hoc effectu legis loquitur Paulus ad Timotheum, ubi ait, legem iniustis positam esse. Neque vero haec disciplina est iusticia coram Deo, sed tantum ad politiam ac magistratus pertinet. Et omnes leges latae ab hominibus, ab his qui tenent respublicas scriptae etiam a Philosophis, tantum de hac externa disciplina intelligi debent, quae quidem est necessaria, tametsi non est iusticia coram Deo. Nec Paulus sic intelligi debet, cum ait, lege augeri peccatum, quasi nolit coherceri foris impios et carnales, aut sentiat incitari homines, ut plura delicta foris admittant.

Alterum officium legis est ostendere peccatum, et terrere conscientias.

Hoc cum fit, corda naturaliter irascuntur iudicio Dei, et concipiunt odium Dei. Sic lex auget peccatum, ut infra exponet Paulus. Negat itaque disciplinam externam esse iusticiam, et docet legem ut plurimum efficiat, tantum terrere conscientias, et occidere.

Sicut ad Corinthos scribit: Aculeus mortis peccatum est, potentia vero peccati lex.

Hinc quaestiones illae oriuntur in cap. sexto.

Digressio.

Cap.

VI. Cum sententia iam posita de lege et operibus valde absurda videatur, reclamat humana ratio.

Si nihil prosunt bona opera ad iustificationem, indulgebimus igitur genio, et peccabimus. Satis erit credere in Christum. Ita tandem fiet multo locupletior gratia, quia si pergimus peccare, plura peccata abolebit. Prorsus eadem obiiciuntur et nunc istis, qui defendunt iusticiam fidei. Prudenter enim vidit Paulus, quomodo abhorreat haec doctrina a iudicio rationis.

Quidam prophani homines Paulum adeo putant crassum fuisse, ut non viderit se parum consentanea rationi dicere, et miras hyperbolas comminiscuntur, ut medeantur eius orationi, ne dissentiat ab humano iudicio. Ille vero et vidit se aliena a iudicio rationis tradere, et ne quis suspicari posset, has sententias ei λεληθότως et parum animadvertentie excidere, agitat argumentum rationis, et prolixe rhetoricatur, et non tantum illius seculi, sed omnium temporum calumniis respondet.

Prima occupatio.

Obiectio. Si bona opera non merentur iustificationem, pergamus igitur peccare.

Responsio sumitur ex duobus locis. Ex causa finali, et ex causa efficiente. Ex causa finali fit inversio.

Imo ideo iustificati estis, ut bene operemini. Ut si quis hoc modo argumentetur.

Labor non prodest aegroto, Ergo etiam curatus nihil agam. Respondendum erit per inversionem ex causa finali: Imo ideo curatus es, ut deinceps labores. Statim subiicit causam efficientem, ubi quoniam est antithesis, ideo duo membra sunt sententiae. Ego duobus syllogismis includam totam Pauli sententiam.

Syllogismus negativus. Mortua natura non est efficax: Vetus natura in vobis est mortua. Nam vetus homo crucifixus est cum Christo: Ergo vetus natura in vobis non debet esse efficax.

Syllogismus affirmativus.

Nova natura debet habere novos fructus: Vos non tantum mortui estis, sed etiam vivificati cum Christo, ut in nova vita ambuletis: Ergo debetis novos fructus afferre et bene operari.

Epilogus est. Non ergo regnet peccatum.

Continet autem adhortationem, miscentur enim disputationibus interdum loci suasorii. Propositio est epilogi: Non regnet peccatum etc. Αἰτιολογία addita est a possibili, seu facili, quia peccatum non dominabitur vobis. Ergo potestis iam bene operari.

Antecedentis sententia est. Habetis iam conscientias certas de Dei benevolentia: Certo scitis Deum vobis adesse, vos adiuvare. Non absterret vos peccatum, quia condonatum est.

Ad haec non habet vires, ut ad mala opera rapiat eos, quia Spiritu sancto gubernantur. Fortior est Christus, quam peccatum.

Paulus probat hoc antecedens his verbis: Non estis sub lege, sed sub gratia, Ergo peccatum non dominabitur vobis. Consequentiae ratio esset obscura, si tantum diceret, non estis sub lege. Nunc quia addit: Sed sub gratia, facilis est intellectu: nam sub gratia esse, est habere Deum placatum, defensorem, adiutorem. Is non sinet nos a peccato vinci.

Secunda occupatio. Et tamen, quia excidit ei nova vox et absurda in speciem: Non estis sub lege, ideo paulisper in ea mollienda commoratur, priusquam a digressione ad institutum redeat.

Omnes sapientes viri, omnes qui tenent respublicas, omnes sani homines magno consensu iudicant humanum genus interire oportere, nisi legibus contineretur. Itaque haec tribunitia vox: Non estis sub lege, videtur indigna esse bono viro, et seditiosa et prorsus intolerabilis. Paulus egregie satisfacit lectori.

Sed ego quoque obiter duxi lectorem monendum esse, Paulum hic loqui de lege, quatenus ea conamur mereri iusticiam coram Deo. De politia nihil hic dicit, quam infra amplissimis laudibus ornavit. Nam Evangelium nullo modo dissipat politias, sed maxime munit eas, et praecipit civiles ordinationes religiose servare. Tantum hoc docet, non iustificari nos illa civili iusticia coram Deo.

Sed venio ad Pauli responsionem.

Quid ais Paule? Si non sumus sub lege, ergo licentiam das peccandi? Sic enim mundus intelligit legis abrogationem. Hoc loco Dialecticus requirit definitionem, quid sit legis abrogatio, utrum sit concedere licentiam peccandi. Paulus negat concedi licentiam peccandi.

Sed addit confutationem obiectionis sumtam non ex definitione, verum ex circumstantia: Quibus sit abrogata lex. Privilegia enim non ad omnes pertinent, sed ad certas personas. Ita libertas pertinet non ad impios, sed ad iustos.

Interea voluntas Dei est, ut impii coërceantur, et sint lege tanquam carcere septi. Ex circumstantia, Quibus.

Unusquisque obtemperat illi, cuius est servus: Vos estis servi iusticiae: Ergo debitis iusticiae obtemperare. Minorem confirmat ex natura oppositorum. Vos desiistis esse servi peccati: Ergo estis servi iusticiae.

Ut si quis argumentetur: Tenebrae pulsae sunt, ergo lux est.

Reliqua oratio in hoc capite est minoris expolitio. Nam multis verbis declarat, quomodo fuerint servi peccati, quales fuerint peccati fructus, quae poenae peccatum sequantur. Item quales nunc parere fructus debeant, postquam agnoverunt Christum.

Est autem insita quaedam correctio: Humanum dico.

Videt enim Paulus desiderari definitionem, quid sit legis abrogatio: Videt se tantum suasorio argumento uti, cum longior disputatio requiratur. Sed ut temperet se ad captum lectoris, consulto fugit subtiliorem disputationem. Et tamen interim in hoc suasorio argumento urget hoc, quod solis iustificatis lex sit abrogata.

Et subindicat, non est enim concedere peccandi licentiam, sed habere iusticiam, remissionem peccatorum, habere conscientiam coram Deo pacatam et tranquillam, unde fit, ne absterriti Deum fugiant et oderint, sed diligant et ab eo expectent omnia bona, et ei cupide obtemperent.

Contra esse sub lege, est a lege coërceri, accusari et condemnari: Odit autem iudicium et poenam caro, ergo et Deum odit. Itaque Paulo idem est, esse sub lege, esse in carne, esse ser- vum peccati. Sed initio Capitis septimi clarius tractabitur circumstantia, Quibus. Nam superius argumen- tum magis ad suasorios locos pertinet. Hoc quod sequitur, magis dialecticum est.

## 5:16
What is sin?

A brief and concise definition of sin is found in John. Sin is not to conform with the law of God. Ἁμαρτία ἐστὶν ἀνομία (Sin is lawlessness). Let it be understood, however, in this description also this, that on account of this lawlessness man is guilty of the wrath of God.

This definition is rightly established, since privations are understood in this way when they are compared to a norm. John, therefore, learnedly describes sin by a comparison with the law, and leads us to the norm.

This definition of sin is common to original and actual [sin]: but because profane men have contended that there is no such thing as original sin, it was necessary to establish proper appellations and descriptions.

Original sin is guilt on account of the fall of the first parents and the depravity that followed the fall of the first parents in all who are propagated according to nature, which depravity is a manifold darkness in the mind concerning God, and concupiscence resisting the law of God, and therefore it is not only a punishment, but truly sin, on account of which men are born guilty of eternal wrath, unless they are reborn through the Son of God.

The Vulgate definition of Anselm says exactly the same thing as ours, just as he himself explained it copiously. Original sin is the lack of original justice, which ought to have been present. For original justice would have been not only acceptance, but also the integrity of the powers, or rectitude, in which man would have been a temple of God, and there would have been congruence in all powers with the law of God. The cause of original sin is the devil and the will of the first parents, which, since it was free, turned itself away from the word of God, and did not retain obedience toward God. Therefore, because the first parents had received gifts for the whole human race, and their persons represented the whole posterity, the posterity becomes guilty on account of their fall, and because they themselves lose the first gifts, such [people] are born afterwards as these are with the gifts lost, that is, they bring darkness concerning God and aversion from God, and they are not a temple of God, wherefore they have neither divine light, that is, firm assent concerning God, nor divine motions, nor can their powers conform with the law of God.

Now think also of the magnitude of the fall and of the misery of our nature.

In the first fall there are many transgressions.

First, there is doubt concerning the word of God.

Second, the loss of faith. For they do not believe God threatening punishment, but fascinated by the specious promise of the devil, they cease to fear punishment, and they burn with that desire for greater glory: You shall be as Gods.

The third sin, therefore, is curiosity, to depart from the word, and to seek another wisdom.

Fourth, pride, by which they wish to magnify themselves.

Fifth, contempt of God, when they violate a commandment against conscience.

Sixth, that they prefer the devil to God.

Seventh, ingratitude, because they expel the spirit of God dwelling in them.

Eighth, the murder of themselves and of all posterity, and that this fall is the first gateway of all the crimes and miseries of posterity.

Such a heap of huge transgressions was in this fall, about which, for many reasons, one must think most diligently. The magnitude of our misery is indeed seen in the effects of the first fall.

Effects.

Monks have said that this evil, which is customarily called vicious concupiscence, is not sin, is not sin, but only a punishment, and they called it the 'fomes' [tinder]. We say that that vicious concupiscence is both a punishment in guilty nature and a sin.

The second punishment is death and all the calamities of the human race.

The third punishment is that this weak nature is subject to the tyranny of the devil, who both tries to destroy men with bodily evils, and drives them to sins of every kind, to blasphemies, heresies, murders, lusts, and other things, as it is expressly said: Satan entered into him.

Philosophers have wondered whence there is so much, not only of calamities but also of crimes, in the so excellent nature of the human race; when indeed it is according to nature to do right, as Quintilian says: It is more wonderful that more men are bad than few are good, when to do right is according to nature. But only the doctrine of the Church of God shows the cause, namely, original sin. And the magnitude of original sin is declared especially by these words of Paul, which follow in the eighth Chapter: The mind of the flesh is enmity against God, for it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be.

The mind of the flesh signifies both opinions about God and affections, such as are in this human nature, not reborn by the light of the Gospel and the Holy Spirit. Great and sad evils are doubts about God, about providence, about the judgment of God, about divine threats and promises, about the presence of God in the conservation and sustenance of things, the ignorance of the Son of God, as it is written: The Holy Spirit will convict the world of sin, because they do not believe in me. Afterwards there are in the will and heart an aversion from God, not having the fear of God, not burning with faith and love, and there are innumerable wandering motions, like the tides in the Syrtes, unjust loves, unjust hatreds, ambitions, the desire for vengeance.

This whole confusion Paul calls the mind of the flesh, and these great evils, he says, are enmity against God. Nothing could be said more atrocious, and yet it is said most properly, and he adds an explanation, when he says, these evils fight against the law. Thus the whole definition of sin is comprehended, Sin is whatever fights against the law of God, on account of which the person is also guilty, unless remission is made on account of the Son.

Here guilt is expressly signified by the word Enmity. A similar description is found in Jeremiah Chap. 17: The heart is perverse above all things, and miserable, that is, full of sorrows. By the former word is signified guilt, because perversity is an aversion from God, or not to agree with God, or not to agree with God, and this guilt is the cause of condemnation and punishments, in which sins are increased, as Saul, Judas in punishments become more furious, and feel horrendous pains. Such prophetic and apostolic sayings are brief, but they are to be pondered with pious thought, and the magnitude of our misery is to be thought upon, and God reveals his wrath even in these sayings, and shows it in the mass of calamities of the human race, in death, diseases, famine, wars, devastations and other miseries.

Let us therefore acknowledge the wrath of God, and flee to the mediator. Let us also tax the blindness of those who contend that these defects in man are not, properly speaking, sins, just as the Tridentine Synod impiously played with ambiguities.

By one man sin entered into the world. This part of the Epistle, as I said above, is an analysis, in which the words Sin, Law, and Grace are declared.

And Paul embraces under one name of sin, original evil and actual transgressions. The Church, however, later distinguished these species by name, because it was a work of new appellation, when Pelagius contended that Paul was speaking only of actual transgressions and of the example of Adam.

But Paul affirms that sin entered by propagation, For he says expressly: Because of the disobedience of one, others are sinners. Item: Because of the transgression of one, condemnation passed into all. There is therefore some propagated sin, the punishment of which is death even in those who do not have actual transgressions, as in infants.

For if there were no propagation of sin, Paul could not say that others have sin on account of Adam. He says therefore expressly: Death passed into all, because all have sinned, that is, all have sin, namely, propagated depravity and guilt.

For the Hebrew phrase is to be considered, in which words do not only signify actions, but often something habitual. They have sinned, that is, they have sins, and in the word Sin are understood depravity and guilt, because here Paul embraces both.

Until the law sin. He does not only mean this, that sin was in the world before the law was promulgated, but he also adds this here, that sin was not abolished by the Law.

Therefore let this saying be understood inclusively: Until the law sin was in the world, that is, even when the law of Moses was promulgated, yet sin remained. Thus he briefly admonishes that sin and death are not taken away by the Law, because external justice, which men imitating the law perform in some way, does not liberate from sin, nor is it the beginning of eternal life, but is some kind of external restraint.

Meanwhile, there remain in man most sad doubts about God, aversion from God, and manifold uncleanness of the heart: and when the conscience is convicted, and seeks justification in the law, then the law has its principal effect, it accuses and condemns all, and overwhelms them with horrendous sorrows, as Paul says later: The law kills etc. and is the ministry of death. It follows therefore concerning the effect of the law: But sin is not imputed, where is not law, that is, Where there is no law, sin is not acknowledged, nor is it accused in us ourselves.

For Paul speaks of the judgment of our conscience. But there has always been a moral law accusing sins. Here, however, mention is made of the promulgation, because then God sanctioned the law with manifest testimonies, and showed that natural knowledge is truly a ray of His wisdom, and a judgment against sin.

But it is manifest that when the law was promulgated, and the Mosaic polity established, sin and death did not cease.

Death reigned from Adam even unto Moses. This saying should be understood inclusively: even after Moses received the law, and this polity was established, yet death did not cease: and he adds, that death reigned over those who did not sin according to the likeness of the transgression of Adam, that is, even infants are subject to death, although they do not have actual sins.

For Paul calls an actual sin a transgression. He says this, however, to confirm the first proposition, that sin is propagated from Adam. For since the only cause of the death of men is sin, and infants are subject to death, it is manifest that there is sin in infants, namely, propagated depravity and guilt.

Who is the figure of him that was to come.

Thus far he has discoursed concerning original sin, and affirmed that there is a certain sin in the propagation of human nature, which is also the root of actual sins, and that it is not abolished by the law.

Now an antithesis is added concerning the Messiah, and concerning the benefits which He properly brings to the human race, of which Daniel also says: Transgression shall be finished, and sin shall be sealed up, and propitiation shall be made for iniquity, and everlasting righteousness shall be brought in, and the Vision and Prophecy shall be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies shall be anointed.

Thus the Prophets expressly affirm that the Messiah brings eternal blessings. Therefore, this antithesis is instituted.

There are two supreme persons in the human race, Adam and Christ, God and man, of whom each merited for others, but opposite things. As therefore he spoke before of the cause of sin, of its effect and propagation, so now he will show the cause of grace, its effect and propagation. But the things are dissimilar, and the mode of propagation, therefore he immediately adds: But not as the offense, so also is the free gift, that is, the things are dissimilar, and there are other dissimilarities.

But this agrees, that each merited for others.

Latin:

Quid est peccatum?

Brevis et concinna definitio est peccati apud Iohannem. Peccatum est non congruere cum lege Dei. Ἁμαρτία ἐστὶν ἀνομία. Intelligatur autem in hac descriptione et hoc, quod propter hanc ἀνομίαν homo sit reus irae Dei.

Recte autem constituta est haec definitio, qui privationes ita intelliguntur, cum ad normam conferuntur. Iohannes igitur erudite describit peccatum collatione legis, et deducit nos ad normam.

Est autem communis haec definitio peccati originali et actuali: sed quia homines prophani contenderunt nihil esse peccatum originale, necesse fuit proprias appellationes et descriptiones constituere.

Peccatum originis est reatus propter lapsum primorum parentum et pravitatem secutam lapsum primorum parentum in omnibus propagatis secundum naturam, quae pravitas est multiplex caligo in mente de Deo, et concupiscentia repugnans legi Dei, et propterea non tantum poena est, sed vere peccatum, propter quod et rei sunt aeternae irae homines nascentes, nisi renascantur per filium Dei.

Vulgata Anselmi definitio prorsus idem dicit quod nostra, sicut et ipse eam copiose enarravit. Peccatum originis est carentia iustitiae originalis, quae debebat inesse. Nam iustitia originalis fuisset non tantum acceptatio, sed etiam integritas virium, seu rectitudo, in qua fuisset homo templum Dei, et fuisset congruentia in omnibus viribus cum lege Dei. Causa peccati originalis est diabolus et voluntas primorum parentum, quae cum esset libera, per sese avertit se a verbo Dei, nec retinuit obedientiam erga Deum. Ideo, quia dona acceperant primi parentes pro toto genere humano, et personae eorum repraesentabant totam posteritatem, fit rea posteritas propter eorum lapsum, et quia ipsi amittunt prima dona, tales postea gignuntur, quales isti sunt amissis donis, id est, afferunt tenebras de Deo et aversionem a Deo, et non sunt templum Dei, quare nec lucem divinam, id est, firmam assensionem de Deo, nec motus divinos habent, nec vires possunt congruere cum lege Dei.

Iam cogita et de lapsus magnitudine et de miseria nostrae naturae.

In primo lapsu multa sunt delicta.

Primum, est dubitatio de verbo Dei.

Secundum, amissio fidei. Non enim credunt Deo minitanti poenam, sed fascinati speciosa promissione diaboli, desinunt metuere poenam, et ardent illa cupiditate maioris gloriae: Eritis sicut Dii.

Tertium igitur peccatum, est curiositas, discedere a verbo, et quaerere aliam sapientiam.

Quartum, superbia, qua volunt sese magnificare.

Quintum, contemtus Dei, cum violant mandatum contra conscientiam.

Sextum, quod anteferunt diabolum Deo.

Septimum, ingratitudo, quod expellunt spiritum Dei in ipsis habitantem.

Octavum, homicidium sui et totius posteritatis, et quod hic lapsus est prima ianua omnium scelerum et miseriarum posteritatis.

Tantus acervus ingentium delictorum fuit in hoc lapsu, de quo propter multas causas diligentissime cogitandum est. Magnitudo vero miseriae nostrae conspicitur in effectibus primi lapsus.

Effectus.

Monachi dixerunt hoc malum, quod usitate vitiosa concupiscentia nominatur, non esse peccatum, non esse peccatum, sed tantum poenam, et nominarunt fomitem. Nos dicimus, illam vitiosam concupiscentiam, et poenam in rea natura, et peccatum esse.

Secunda poena est mors et omnes calamitates generis humani.

Tertia poena est, quod haec infirma natura subiecta est tyrannidi diaboli, qui et corporalibus malis conatur perdere homines, et impellit eos ad peccata omnis generis, ad blasphemias, haereses, caedes, libidines et alia, sicut expresse dictum est: Intravit in eum Satanas.

Philosophi mirati sunt, unde in tam praestanti natura generis humani tantum sit, non modo calamitatum, sed etiam scelerum; cum quidem secundum naturam sit recte facere, ut Quintilian. ait: Magis mirum est plures homines esse malos, quam paucos bonos, cum recte facere sit secundum naturam. Sed sola doctrina Ecclesiae Dei monstrat causam, scilicet, peccatum originis. Ac magnitudo mali originalis praecipue declaratur his verbis Pauli, quae sequuntur in octavo Capite: Sensus carnis inimicitia est adversus Deum, lege enim Dei non subiicitur, ac ne potest quidem subiici.

Sensus carnis significat et opiniones de Deo et affectus, quales sunt in hac humana natura, non renata luce Evangelii et Spiritu sancto. Magna et tristia mala sunt dubitationes de Deo, de providentia, de iudicio Dei, de minis et promissionibus divinis, de praesentia Dei in conservatione et sustentatione rerum, ignoratio filii Dei, sicut scriptum est: Spiritus sanctus arguet mundum de peccato, quod non credunt in me. Postea sunt in voluntate et corde aversio a Deo, non habere timorem Dei, non ardere fide et dilectione, et sunt errantes motus innumerabiles, sicut aestus in Syrtibus, amores iniusti, odia iniusta, ambitiones, cupiditas vindictae.

Hanc totam confusionem nominat Paulus Sensum carnis, et haec magna mala, ait, inimicitiam esse adversus Deum. Nihil potuit dici atrocius, et tamen propriissime dictum est, et addit explicationem, cum inquit, haec mala pugnare cum lege. Ita tota peccati definitio comprehenditur, Peccatum est quicquid pugnat cum lege Dei, propter quod et persona rea est, nisi fiat remissio propter filium.

Hic reatus expresse significatur vocabulo Inimicitiae. Similis descriptio est apud Ieremiam Cap. 17. : Perversum est cor super omnia, et aerumnosum, id est, plenum doloribus. Priore vocabulo significatur culpa, quia perversitas est aversio a Deo, seu non congruere cum Deo, seu non congruere cum Deo, et haec culpa causa est condemnationis et poenarum, in quibus augentur peccata, ut Saul, Iudas in poenis fiunt magis furiosi, et sentiunt horrendos dolores. Talia dicta prophetica et apostolica brevia sunt, sed pia cogitatione evolvenda sunt, et magnitudo nostrae miseriae cogitanda est, ac iram suam Deus et in his dictis patefacit, et ostendit in mole calamitatum generis humani, in morte, morbis, fame, bellis, vastationibus et aliis aerumnis.

Agnoscamus igitur iram Dei, et confugiamus ad mediatorem. Taxemus etiam coecitatem eorum, qui contendunt hos defectus in homine non esse proprie loquendo peccata, sicut Tridentina Synodus impie lusit ambiguitatibus.

Per unum hominem peccatum intravit in mundum. Haec pars Epistolae, ut supra dixi, ἀνάλυσις est, in qua declarantur vocabula Peccati, Legis, et Gratiae.

Et complectitur Paulus uno nomine peccati, malum originale et actualia delicta. Ecclesia autem postea nominatim distinxit has species, quia fuit opus nova appellatione, cum Pelagius contenderet, loqui Paulum tantum de actualibus delictis et de exemplo Adae.

At Paulus affirmat, intrasse peccatum propagatione, Expresse enim inquit: Propter inobedientiam unius peccatores sunt alii. Item: Propter unius delictum condemnatio pervasit in omnes. Est ergo aliquod propagatum peccatum, cuius poena est mors etiam in his, qui non habent actualia delicta, ut in infantibus.

Nam si nulla esset propagatio peccati, non posset dicere Paulus, caeteros propter Adam habere peccatum. Expresse igitur dicit: Mors pervasit in omnes, quia omnes peccaverunt, id est, omnes habent peccatum, scilicet pravitatem propagatam et reatum.

Phrasis enim Ebraea consideranda est, in qua verba non tantum significant actiones, sed saepe aliquid habituale. Peccaverunt, id est, habent peccata, et in vocabulo Peccati intelligantur pravitas et reatus, quia hic Paulus utrunque complectitur.

Usque ad legem peccatum. Non solum hoc vult, peccatum fuisse in mundo ante promulgatam legem, sed etiam illud hic attexit, Lege non esse abolitum peccatum.

Ideo inclusive intelligatur hoc dictum: Usque ad legem peccatum erat in mundo, id est, etiam cum lex Moisi promulgata est, tamen mansit peccatum. Ita breviter admonet, Lege non tolli peccatum et mortem, quia externa iustitia, quam utcunque praestant homines legem imitantes, non liberat a peccato, nec est incoatio vitae aeternae, sed est qualecunque frenum externum.

Interea manent in homine tristissimae dubitationes de Deo, aversio a Deo, et multiplex immundities cordis: et cum arguitur conscientia, et quaerit iustificationem in lege, tunc lex habet praecipuum effectum, accusat et condemnat omnes, et obruit horrendis doloribus, sicut postea inquit Paulus: Lex occidit etc. et est ministerium mortis. Sequitur ergo de effectu legis: Sed peccatum non reputatur, ubi non est lex, id est, Ubi non est lex, non agnoscitur, non accusatur peccatum in nobis ipsis.

Loquitur enim Paulus de iudicio nostrae conscientiae. Semper autem fuit moralis lex accusans peccata. Hic autem fit mentio promulgationis, quia tunc Deus manifestis testimoniis sanxit legem, et ostendit naturalem noticiam, vere radium esse suae sapientiae, et iudicium adversus peccatum.

Manifestum est autem promulgata lege, et constituta politia Mosaica, tamen non cessasse peccatum et mortem.

Mors regnavit ab Adam usque ad Moisen. Inclusive et hoc dictum intelligatur: etiam postquam Moises accepit legem, et haec politia constituta est, tamen mors non cessavit: et addit, mortem regnasse in eos, qui non peccaverunt secundum similitudinem transgressionis Adae, id est, etiam infantes morti subiecti sunt, quanquam non habent actualia delicta.

Nam Paulus actuale delictum nominat transgressionem. Ideo autem hoc dicit, ut primam propositionem confirmet, quod sit peccatum propagatum ab Adam. Cum enim causa mortis hominum sola sit peccatum, et infantes subiecti sint morti, manifestum est et in infantibus peccatum esse, scilicet pravitatem propagatam et reatum.

Qui est forma futuri.

Hactenus de peccato originis concionatus est, et affirmavit esse quoddam peccatum in natura hominum propagatione, quod et radix est actualium delictorum, et non esse abolitum lege.

Nunc antithesis additur de Messia, et de beneficiis quae ipse proprie affert generi humano, de quibus et Daniel inquit: Finietur praevaricatio, et obsignabitur peccatum et fiet propiciatio pro iniquitate, et adducetur iusticia sempiterna, et implebitur Visio et Prophetia, et ungetur Sanctus Sanctorum.

Ita Prophetae expresse affirmant, Messiam afferre aeterna bona. Instituitur ergo hic antithesis.

Duae sunt summae personae in genere humano, Adam et Christus, Deus et homo, quarum utraque meruit aliis, sed res contrarias. Ut igitur antea de causa peccati, de effectu et propagatione dixit, ita nunc ostendet causam gratiae effectus et propagationem. Sunt autem res dissimiles, et modus propagationis, ideo statim addit: Sed non ut delictum sic et donum, id est, res sunt dissimiles, et sunt aliae dissimilitudines.

Hoc autem congruit, quod uterque aliis meruit.

## 5:16
Of Grace.

It must be most diligently observed that Paul joins Grace and the Gift, just as it is said in John: Grace and Truth came by Christ. The word Grace signifies gratuitous mercy, therefore here it signifies most truly the remission of sins, and gratuitous acceptance on account of the Son of God. The gift by grace signifies not only the donation of the Holy Spirit in this life, but the entire benefit of Christ, namely, vivification and sanctification in this life, which happens when we are vivified in true consolation by the Word and the Holy Spirit, and then eternal life, in which God is all in all, and our nature will be without sin.

But the first comparison is made concerning the mode of merit. In this, Adam and Christ agree in that each merited for others; Adam merited guilt for others, Christ merited reconciliation, righteousness, and eternal life for others.

This comparison illustrates the doctrine of imputation. Just as on account of Adam others are guilty, so on account of Christ believers are reconciled, or accepted, not on account of their own dignity.

Afterwards Paul adds a correction concerning the diversity of things, saying: But not as the offense, so also is the free gift, that is, there are many things dissimilar in this comparison.

First, the things are most diverse, Sin and Grace, eternal death and eternal life. Secondly, there is a difference in the mode of propagation. From Adam, guilty nature is propagated, having sin and being subject to death: and on the contrary, from Christ, reconciliation is given; this is not propagated by carnal generation, but is received by faith, John 1: He gave them power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name, which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God.

John 3: Except a man be born again of water and of the Spirit, etc.

This dissimilarity of propagation must be diligently observed, on account of the Anabaptists, who invent prodigious ravings.

Some say outright that there was never any original sin: others pretend that after the resurrection of Christ entirely that no one born has original sin.

Against those fanatical opinions, those sentences cited from John fortify us, and one must consider how great is the insanity of the Anabaptists. If there were no original sin, all men would live without sin and without death. Since this is manifestly false, it is necessary that the cause remains, namely original sin.

A third dissimilarity is of great moment. If Sin and Grace had equal power, how would grace save, especially when Sin and Death are felt: it was therefore necessary in this antithesis to show that grace is far more powerful than sin, and is victorious, just as the voice of the Son of God says: O Death, I will be your death, and O Hell, I will be your plague.

Paul therefore illustrates this dissimilarity when he later says: Grace overcomes sin. It overcomes, however, in two ways, both by imputation and by effect. It overcomes by imputation, because God deems those righteous who apprehend grace by faith, even if they in reality still have the remnants of sin. Then it also overcomes by effect, because in those very people, however infirm, God nevertheless dwells and new motions exist in them, which resist sin, and by faith the pains of hell are overcome, according to the saying: Being justified by faith we have peace. Likewise, those same people, although the body is destroyed because of the remnants of sin, are nevertheless resurrected to eternal life. It is necessary that these things be known, so that the benefit of Christ may be understood, and we may know that grace is victorious.

The Law entered that the offense might abound. He affirms that by the law sin was neither deleted, nor death abolished; rather, he says that sin was increased, which he declares later, because indeed the conscience, accused by the law, flees from God, and in those horrendous pains, it is more angry at God, sin becomes much more atrocious, and there becomes a confusion of many horrible sins, by which man rushes into eternal destruction, as is seen in Saul and Judas. He repeats this doctrine concerning the effect of the law several times in this Epistle. It must be known, however, that he is not speaking of the political use of the law, but of this principal use, which is to judge and condemn hearts before God, and to be a ministry by which God pours out His wrath against men, just as was said above: The Law works wrath.

But where sin abounded, Grace did much more abound. Here is proposed a necessary doctrine in this antithesis, and a most sweet consolation, namely, that Grace is victorious and far more powerful than sin; therefore he says: Grace did much more abound.

I said before, however, that the consideration of this dissimilarity in this antithesis is very necessary: for if sin and Grace had equal power, and grace did not conquer, what help would it bring? Therefore, a mediator was given to us, so that he might delete sin and death, and restore to us righteousness and life, and be the victor, just as the promise says: The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent, 1 John 3: For this purpose the Son of God appeared, that he might destroy the works of the devil. And it is certain that this very sentence has been repeated most often. Let us therefore hold fast to Paul's saying, which is remarkable for its brevity and the weight of its words, and let us accommodate it to use, where in true consolation this discourse becomes more illustrious and sweeter to us.

David, considering the magnitude of his falls, opposes this doctrine: Blessed are all who trust in him, and he attributes this glory to the Son of God, so that he may believe Him to be more powerful than sin and the kingdom of the devil. Thus he struggled out of death and out of hell.

Again, however, I admonish that Grace is more powerful in two ways: by imputation and by effect. First by imputation, because God deems those who believe in the Son righteous, even if the remnants of sin still cling to them, as he says below: You are no longer under the law. And Rom. 8: There is now no condemnation to those who walk in Christ Jesus, and in the Psalm: Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. Then Grace overcomes by effect, because the Son of God himself vivifies hearts, and delivers them from hell, and by the Holy Spirit takes away pains and restores joy and life to the heart, according to the saying: Being justified by faith we have peace.

Likewise, because it excites good motions and represses sin. Finally, it also resurrects the dead to eternal life. One must also observe the word 'Reign'. Where there is not grace and faith, sin reigns unto death, that is, it is not only the cause of bodily death, but it is the cause of that death which is the sense of the eternal wrath of God, and eternal condemnation, as in Saul and Judas.

But where there is Grace and faith, although there are in man remnants of sin and death corporal, yet they do not reign, because even if the body is destroyed, yet the pains of the lower world are not felt, but the spirit lives on account of righteousness, as he says below in chapter 8: And afterwards man is resurrected to eternal light, wisdom, righteousness, and joy. Thus he says here: Grace reigns through righteousness, that is, gratuitous mercy reigns and conquers, by which we are also reputed righteous, and are gifted with new light, wisdom, and righteousness through Jesus Christ. For here Paul embraces both imputation and vivification, by which the Son of God himself is effective in us.

Latin:

De Gratia.

Diligentissime observandum est, Paulum coniungere Gratiam et Donum, sicut et in Iohanne dicitur: Per Christum Gratia et Veritas facta est. Vocabulum Gratiae significat gratuitam misericordiam, ideo hic significat verissime remissionem peccatorum, et gratuitam acceptationem propter filium Dei. Donum per gratiam significat non tantum in hac vita donationem Spiritus sancti, sed integrum beneficium Christi, scilicet vivificationem et sanctificationem in hac vita, quae fit, cum in vera consolatione verbo et Spiritu sancto vivificamur, et deinde vitam aeternam, in qua Deus est omnia in omnibus, et natura nostra erit sine peccato.

Primum autem collatio fit de modo meriti. In hac ita congruunt Adam et Christus, quod uterque aliis meruit, Adam meruit aliis reatum, Christus meruit aliis reconciliationem, iusticiam et vitam aeternam.

Haec collatio illustrat doctrinam de imputatione. Sicut propter Adam alii sunt rei, ita propter Christum credentes sunt reconciliati, seu accepti, non propter propriam dignitatem.

Postea addit Paulus correctionem de rerum diversitate, inquiens: Sed non sicut delictum sic et donum, id est, multa sunt dissimilia in hac collatione.

Primum, res sunt diversissimae, Peccatum et Gratia, mors aeterna et vita aeterna. Secundo, differentia est in modo propagationis. Ab Adam propagatur natura rea, habens peccatum et morti obnoxia: et contra a Christo donatur reconciliatio, haec non propagatur generatione carnali, sed fide accipitur, Iohannes 1.: Dedit eis potestatem filios Dei fieri, iis qui credent in eum, qui non ex sanguinibus, sed ex Deo nati sunt.

Iohan. 3.: Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua et spiritu etc.

Haec dissimilitudo propagationis diligenter observanda est, propter Anabaptistas, qui prodigiosa deliramenta comminiscuntur.

Alii prorsus dicunt nullum fuisse unquam peccatum originis: alii fingunt post resurrectionem Christi prorsus neminem nascentem habere peccatum originis.

Adversus illas fanaticas opiniones muniunt nos illae sententiae citatae ex Iohanne, et cogitandum est, quanta sit insania Anabaptistarum. Si nullum esset peccatum originis, omnes homines viverent sine peccato et sine morte. Quod cum sit manifeste falsum, necesse est manere causam, scilicet peccatum originis.

Tertia dissimilitudo magni momenti est. Si parem vim haberent Peccatum et Gratia, quomodo gratia salvaret, praesertim cum Peccatum et Mors sentiantur: necesse fuit igitur in hac antithesi ostendere gratiam longe potentiorem esse peccato, et victricem esse, sicut inquit vox filii Dei: O Mors, ero mors tua, et o Inferne, ero pestis tua.

Illustrat igitur Paulus hanc dissimilitudinem, cum postea inquit: Gratia superat peccatum. Superat autem dupliciter, et imputatione et effectu. Imputatione superat, quia Deus reputat eos iustos, qui apprehendunt fide gratiam, etiamsi reipsa adhuc habent reliquias peccati. Deinde etiam effectu superat, quia in illis ipsis quanquam infirmis, tamen habitat Deus et existunt in eis novi motus, qui resistunt peccato, et fide vincuntur dolores inferorum, iuxta dictum: Iustificati fide pacem habemus. Item, illi ipsi, quanquam corpus destruitur propter reliquias peccati, tamen resuscitantur ad vitam aeternam. Haec sciri necesse est, ut beneficium Christi intelligatur, et sciamus gratiam victricem esse.

Lex subintravit ut abundaret delictum. Affirmat lege neque deletum esse peccatum, neque abolitam mortem, imo peccatum auctum esse inquit, quod postea declarat, quia enim conscientia accusata lege fugit Deum, et in illis horrendis doloribus, magis irascitur Deo, peccatum fit multo atrocius, et fit multorum horribilium peccatorum confusio, qua ruit homo in aeternum exitium, ut in Saule et Iuda conspicitur. Hanc doctrinam de legis effectu aliquoties in hac Epistola repetit. Sciendum est autem, loqui eum non de politico usu legis, sed de hoc principali usu, qui est iudicare et condemnare corda coram Deo, et esse ministerium, quo Deus iram suam effundit adversus homines, sicut supra dictum est: Lex iram efficit.

Ubi autem abundavit peccatum, ibi excelluit Gratia. Hic proponitur doctrina necessaria in hac antithesi, et dulcissima consolatio, videlicet, Gratiam victricem esse et longe potentiorem peccato, ideo inquit: Superexcelluit Gratia.

Dixi autem antea, valde necessariam esse considerationem huius dissimilitudinis in hac antithesi: quia si parem vim haberent peccatum et Gratia, nec vinceret gratia, quid afferret auxilii? Ideo autem donatus est nobis mediator, ut deleat peccatum et mortem, et restituat nobis iusticiam et vitam, et sit victor, sicut promissio inquit: Semen mulieris conculcabit caput serpentis, 1. Iohan. 3.: Ad hoc apparuit filius Dei, ut destruat opera diaboli. Et constat hanc ipsam sententiam saepissime repetitam esse. Teneamus ergo Pauli dictum, quod propter brevitatem et verborum pondera insigne est, et ad usum accomodemus, ubi in vera consolatione hae concio nobis fit illustior et dulcior.

David considerans magnitudinem suorum lapsuum, opponit hanc doctrinam: Beati omnes qui confident in eum, et filio Dei hanc gloriam tribuit, ut credat potentiorem esse peccato et regno diaboli. Ita eluctatus est ex morte et ex infernis.

Iterum autem admoneo, Gratiam potentiorem esse dupliciter: Imputatione et effectu. Primum imputatione, quia Deus reputat iustos credentes in filium, etiam si adhuc haerent in eis reliquiae peccati, ut infra inquit: Iam non estis sub lege. Et Rom. 8.: Nulla nunc condemnatio est his, qui in Christo Iesu ambulant, Et in Psalmo: Beati quorum remissae sunt iniquitates, et quorum tecta sunt peccata. Deinde superat Gratia effectu, quia ipse filius Dei vivificat corda, et liberat ea ex inferis, ac Spiritu sancto tollit dolores et reddit laetitiam et vitam cordi, iuxta dictum: Iustificati fide pacem habemus.

Item, quia excitat bonos motus et reprimit peccatum. Denique et resusciat mortuos ad vitam aeternam. Observandum est et verbum Regnare, Ubi non est gratia et fides, peccatum regnat ad mortem, id est, non est tantum causa mortis corporalis, sed est causa eius mortis, quae est sensus aeternae irae Dei, et aeterna condemnatio, ut in Saul et Iuda.

Sed ubi est Gratia et fides, quanquam sunt in homine reliquiae peccati et mors corporalis, tamen non regnant, quia etiam si corpus destruitur, tamen non sentiuntur dolores inferorum, sed spiritus vivit propter iusticiam, ut infra inquit capite 8.: Et postea resusciatur homo ad aeternam lucem, sapientiam, iusticiam et laetitiam. Ita hic inquit: Gratia regnat per iusticiam, id est, misericordia gratuita regnat et vincit, qua et iusti reputamur, et donamur nova luce, sapientia et iusticia per Iesum Christum. Utrunque enim hic complectitur Paulus et imputationem et vivificationem, qua ipse filius Dei in nobis est efficax.

## 6:1 Argument
Chapter VI. What then shall we say?

Before Paul weaves together the begun collation of sin, law, and Grace, he inserts objections, because a great tumult of questions arises here: If we are not righteous by the law and our own works, but by mercy on account of the mediator, why is there a need to do good works?

This objection becomes more clear if the controversies of our time are considered. For the adversaries object to us with the very same absurdities: If we are not righteous on account of works, why does it matter to do good works? Indeed, the weakness of our nature is so great that individuals relax their intention and care for doing good works, once the doctrine of imputation is heard. But the knowledge of mercy ought to inflame us more to do good works: for doubt is an arcane and deep rumbling, which horribly weakens souls in prayer and all actions. But the customary answer to the question is: If we are not righteous on account of works, is there therefore no need to do good works?

Answer: I deny the consequence, and the reason is that in this argument there is a fallacy of 'non-cause as cause'.

For there are other great and necessary causes for doing good, even if works do not justify. Justification is given on account of the mediator through faith, that is, on account of the Son of God we receive the remission of sins, and are reputed righteous, that is, accepted by God freely. For it is necessary that the due honor be attributed to the Son, and it is necessary that the consolation be firm and certain.

But the application of this benefit occurs through faith, by which hearts are simultaneously regenerated, because then the Son of God vivifies hearts through the Gospel, and gives the Holy Spirit. Thus, in the mind and heart, Regeneration is begun by receiving the word, that is, the Consolation, which the Son speaks in the heart and by receiving the Holy Spirit, who kindles new motions in the heart. So says Peter: You have been reborn, not of corruptible seed, but through the living word of God, and remaining forever. And to Titus 3: According to his mercy he saved us through the washing of regeneration, and the renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our savior. And in Zechariah 11: I will pour out upon the house of David a spirit of grace and prayers.

Therefore, the necessary causes for doing good must be considered: and it is rustic to understand necessity as coercion. The obedience of the angels is necessary, that is, so ordered by God, and yet it is spontaneous, not extorted by coercion or terrors.

Therefore, the causes for doing good are: Impulsive, Efficient, and Final. Impulsive, because the order of God remains unmoved, so that the creature may obey God: of this cause Paul speaks below when he says: We are debtors.

Efficient, of which he speaks here, is the Holy Spirit, who kindles such motions as he himself is.

Hence Paul constructs two arguments.

Dead nature is not effective:

The old nature has begun to die, because when it convicts sin in conversion, there in the sense of the wrath of God, the mortification of the old nature truly occurs, as it is said: As a Lion he has crushed all my bones.

Therefore it is not effective.

Item, A living and reigning nature is effective.

Now the Spirit reigns in the heart: therefore it is effective. For the Holy Spirit kindles such motions as he himself is, according to the saying: I will put my law in their hearts.

These arguments Paul recites here.

Final causes are many and great. The Son of God by no means suffered for this reason, nor does he give the remission of sins for this reason, that he might confirm sin and the horrible furies in the human race, but that he might destroy sin and death, and restore righteousness and eternal life: and therefore he wills us to be made conformable to his death and resurrection.

And to this very end, the death of the body remains even for the elect and the sanctified, so that the mass of sin may be utterly destroyed, and yet he wills that light, righteousness, and eternal life be begun in this life, and he gives.

remission of sins, so that at the same time by this faith, by which remission is received, life may be begun, and it may be the victor over sin and the terrors of death. This victory is the beginning of conformity with the resurrection of Christ. Moreover, this victory is this very thing in us, which is called the newness of the Spirit, and it is not merely a human thought, like the diligence of governing discipline in Pomponius Atticus: but the Son of God himself is effective through the voice of the Gospel in the hearts of believers, and makes them conformable to his resurrection, when he vivifies them and draws them back from the pains of the underworld, and at the same time gives them the Holy Spirit, who kindles new motions in them congruent with God, that is, joy and love toward God. Thus sin is conquered in us through the Son of God, as he himself says: I am the vine, you are the branches; he who remains in me and I in him, will bear much fruit, because without me you can do nothing, etc. 2 Corinthians 15: Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.

The same is said, when it is said by others, that new obedience is to retain the previously granted remission and reconciliation, the Holy Spirit, and faith. And the whole matter becomes clear if the doctrine of repentance or conversion is compared to this, and it is useful in doctrines to see where the same things are named by different words, lest the unwary think of different things: just as the Anabaptists, when they hear these words, mortification and vivification, imagine things different from repentance or conversion: afterwards they invent that mortification is feigned gestures of humility, contempt of political order, of marriage, the sharing of goods, lack of natural affection [ἀστοργίαν], etc. Then they imagine their own certain illuminations and ecstasies [ἐκστάσεις] as vivification. Paul himself warns men about these fanatical imaginations, so that they may prudently judge those grand words and the simulation of holiness, lest they be deceived.

We speak of things known in the Church and in the exercises of the pious. That which is usually called contrition is here called Mortification, and it signifies true terrors and pains in the heart recognizing the wrath of God against sins, concerning which pains it was said: As a lion he crushed my bones. And in such mortification men rush into eternal destruction, like Saul and Judas, when faith does not approach.

Paul speaks, however, of the mortification by which we are conformable to the death of Christ, namely, with which faith is present, by which we are simultaneously sustained and vivified through Christ. Vivification is the other part of conversion, namely faith, of which it is said: The just shall live by his faith.

For in this consolation the Son of God vivifies the heart, and gives the Holy Spirit, who kindles new motions in the heart, according to the saying: You have received the spirit of adoption of sons, crying Abba Father. Item: I will pour out upon the house of David a spirit of grace and prayers.

These motions are called and are new obedience. This comparison of the words of repentance or conversion is useful to the people against Anabaptist and similar ravings. And let the true, simple, and clear doctrine of repentance or conversion always be in sight, and let it be exercised in daily invocation, as the Psalms teach: O Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury. Have mercy on me, O God. And from the depths: who also speak of mortification and vivification, of which Paul also speaks here. Let the phrases also be rightly understood: Old man and new man, Flesh and Spirit.

Old man signifies not only a part of man, the senses and the appetites of the senses, but also the reason and the will: and not only do the appetites of the senses fight against the law of God, but also in the reason or the thinking part there is ignorance of God, doubts about providence, ignorance of the Messiah, and manifold darkness. Then in the will there is aversion from God. The will is without the fear of God, without love, trust, hope, without joy in God, it loves and hates against the commandments of God: these vices are in the higher part. Therefore Paul, describing a man without the Holy Spirit, 1 Corinthians 2, says: The animal [natural] man does not perceive the things that are of the spirit of God. And he calls the whole man not reborn by the word and spirit, ψυχικόν [natural/soulish], just as elsewhere he calls this whole man Flesh.

He is called a new man, insofar as he has new light, and new motions kindled by the word and the Holy Spirit, namely the knowledge of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, true faith and trust in Christ, the fear of God, invocation, love, joy acquiescing in God, hope, and other motions of the Holy Spirit. Of this newness Paul speaks in 2 Corinthians 2: Now with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, we are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord, that is, with faith we discern the glory of the Lord, namely, himself Christ, showing us the mercy of the eternal Father, by which being known we approach God, we do not flee as Saul did, but we truly acknowledge God to be good and present, that we are received and saved by Him on account of the Son; in this light of the Son we are also transformed, that is, we receive the rays scattered into us through the Son by the gift of the Holy Spirit, namely the knowledge of God and new impulses, which the Holy Spirit kindles and confirms when the voice of the Gospel is heard.

Nor does "newness" signify the thoughts and impulses of reason without the Holy Spirit, nor does "spirit" signify reason, but the third person of the divinity, which the eternal Father gives through the Son into our hearts.

However, the newness of man will be complete in the heavenly Church, in which God will be all in all, that is, He will shine in us in such a way that He is openly beheld, not through the ministry of the Gospel, and He will stir all impulses, in such a way that there is no sin in us at the same time.

But in this life the same reborn man is Old and New, that is, Paul is new because God dwells in him, and illuminates him with His word and sanctifies him with the Holy Spirit, and the mind and heart receive some rays of divine light and impulses of the Holy Spirit.

For Paul feels invocation, confidence, and joy in God: to that extent he is new, and this newness ought to reign.

But not yet in this life is the nature of Paul entirely without sin and without death; to that extent he is the old man, but this oldness is being mortified, it does not reign.

Latin:

Cap. VI. Quid igitur dicemus?

Priusquam Paulus incoatam collationem peccati, legis et Gratiae pertexit, inserit occupationes, quia magnus tumultus quaestionum hic oritur: Si non sumus iusti lege et operibus nostris, sed per misericordiam propter mediatorem, quorsum opus est bene operari?

Haec obiectio fit magis perspicua, si nostri temporis controversiae considerentur. Nam prorsus eadem absurda nobis adversarii obiiciunt: Si propter opera non sumus iusti, quorsum attinet bene operari. Imo tanta est infirmitas naturae nostrae, ut singuli remittant intentionem et curam bene operandi, audita doctrina de imputatione. At cognitio misericordiae magis accendere nos ad bene operandum deberet: nam dubitatio est arcanus et profundus fremitus, qui horribiliter languefacit animos in invocatione et omnibus actionibus. Usitata autem responsio est ad quaestionem: Si non sumus iusti propter opera, non igitur opus est bene operari?

Responsio: Nego consequentiam, et ratio est, quia in hoc argumento fallacia est secundum non causam, ut causam.

Sunt enim aliae magnae et necessariae causae bene operandi, etiamsi opera non iustificant. Donatur iustificatio propter mediatorem per fidem, id est, propter filium Dei accipimus remissionem peccatorum, et reputamur iusti, id est, accepti Deo gratis. Oportet enim tribui filio debitum honorem, et oportet consolationem esse firmam et certam.

Fit autem huius beneficii applicatio per fidem, qua simul corda regenerantur, quia tunc filius Dei per Evangelium vivificat corda, et dat Spiritum sanctum. Ita in mente et corde incoatur Regeneratio accepto verbo, id est, Consolatione, quam dicit filius in corde et accepto Spiritu sancto, qui novos motus accendit in corde. Sic ait Petrus: Renati estis, non semine corruptibili, sed per sermonem viventem Dei, et manentem in secula. Et ad Titum 3.: Secundum misericordiam salvavit nos per lavacrum regenerationis, et renovationem Spiritus sancti, quem effudit super nos opulenter per Iesum Christum salvatorem nostrum. Et Zachariae 11.: Effundam super domum David spiritum gratiae et precum.

Considerandae sunt igitur causae bene operandi necessariae: et agreste est intelligere necessitatem coactionem. Angelorum obedientia est necessaria, id est, sic ordinata a Deo, et tamen est spontanea, non extorta coactione vel terroribus.

Sunt igitur causae bene operandi, Impulsiva, Efficiens, Finales. Impulsiva, quia manet ordo Dei immotus, ut creatura obediat Deo: de hac causa loquitur Paulus infra cum inquit: Debitores sumus.

Efficiens, de qua hic loquitur, est Spiritus sanctus, qui tales motus accendit, qualis ipse est.

Hinc duo argumenta extruit Paulus.

Natura mortua non sit efficax:

Vetus natura coepit mori, quia cum in conversione arguit peccatum, ibi in sensu irae Dei revera fit mortificatio veteris naturae, ut dicitur: Sicut Leo contrivit omnia ossa mea.

Non igitur sit efficax.

Item, Viva et regnans natura sit efficax.

Iam regnat in corde Spiritus: sit igitur efficax. Nam Spiritus sanctus accendit tales motus, qualis ipse est, iuxta dictum: Dabo legem meam in corda eorum.

Haec argumenta recitat hic Paulus.

Causae finales sunt multae et magnae. Filius Dei nequaquam ideo passus est, nec ideo dat remissionem peccatorum, ut confirmet peccatum, et horribiles furores in genere humano, sed ut deleat peccatum et mortem, et restituat iusticiam et vitam aeternam: ideoque vult nos fieri conformes suae mortis et resurrectionis.

Et ad hunc ipsum finem manet mors corporis etiam electorum et sanctificatorum, ut massa peccati prorsus destruatur, et tamen ea vult incoari in hac vita lucem, iusticiam et vitam aeternam, et dat.

remissionem peccatorum, ut simul hac fide, qua accipitur remissio, incoëtur vita, et sit victrix peccati et terrorum mortis. Haec victoria est initium conformitatis cum resurrectione Christi.
