Est autem haec victoria hoc ipsum in nobis, quod vocatur novitas Spiritus, et non est tantum cogitatio humana, sicut diligentia regendi disciplinam in Pomponio Attico: sed ipse filius Dei est efficax per vocem Evangelii in cordibus credentium, et facit eos suae resurrectioni conformes, cum vivificat eos et retrahit ex doloribus inferorum, ac simul dat eis Spiritum sanctum, qui accendit novos motus in eis congruentes cum Deo, id est, laetitiam et amorem erga Deum. Ita vincitur peccatum in nobis per filium Dei, ut et ipse inquit: Ego sum vitis, vos palmites, qui manet in me et ego in eo, feret fructum multum, quia sine me nihil potestis facere etc. 2. Corinth. 15.: Gratia Deo, qui dat nobis victoriam per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum.

Idem dicitur, cum ab aliis dicitur, nova obedientia est retinere antea donatam remissionem et reconciliationem, Spiritum sanctum et fidem. Ac tota res fit perspicua, si conferatur huc doctrina de poenitentia seu conversione, et est utile in doctrinis videre, ubi res eaedem diversis vocabulis nominentur, ne incauti res diversas cogitent: sicut Anabaptistae, cum audiunt haec vocabula, mortificationem et vivificationem, fingunt res diversas a poenitentia seu conversione: postea comminiscuntur mortificationem esse simulatos gestus humilitatis, contemtum ordinis politici, coniugii, rerum communicationem, ἀστοργίαν etc. Deinde vivificationem fingunt suas quasdam illuminationes et ἐκστάσεις. De his fanaticis imaginationibus Paulus ipse praemonet homines, ut prudenter iudicent illa grandia verba et simulationem sanctitatis, ne decipiantur. Nos loquimur de rebus notis in Ecclesia et in exercitiis piorum.

Hoc quod usitate nominatur contritio, id hic nominatur Mortificatio, et significat veros pavores et dolores in corde agnoscente iram Dei adversus peccata, de quibus doloribus dictum est: Sicut leo contrivit ossa mea. Et in tali mortificatione ruunt homines in aeternum exitium, sicut Saul et Iudas, quando non accedit fides.

Loquitur autem Paulus de mortificatione, qua morti Christi conformes sumus, videlicet, cum qua fides est, qua simul per Christum sustentamur et vivificamur. Est autem vivificatio altera pars conversionis, scilicet fides, de qua dicitur: Iustus fide sua vivet.

Nam in hac consolatione filius Dei vivificat cor, et dat Spiritum sanctum, qui accendit novos motus in corde, iuxta dictum: Accepistis spiritum adoptionis filiorum clamantem Abba Pater. Item: Effundam super domum David spiritum gratiae et precum.

Hi motus dicuntur et sunt nova obedientia. Haec collatio vocabulorum poenitentiae seu conversionis est utilis populo contra anabaptistica et similia deliramenta. Et semper sit in conspectu vera, simplex et perspicua doctrina de poenitentia, seu conversione, et exerceatur in quotidiana invocatione, sicut docent Psalmi: Domine ne in furore tuo arguas me. Miserere mei Deus. Et de profundis: qui et de mortificatione et de vivificatione loquuntur, de quibus et hic Paulus loquitur. Recte intelligantur et phrases: Vetus homo et novus homo, Caro et Spiritus.

Vetus homo significat non tantum partem hominis, sensus et appetitiones sensuum, sed etiam rationem et voluntatem: nec solum appetitiones sensuum pugnant cum lege Dei, sed etiam in ratione seu parte cogitante sunt ignoratio Dei, dubitationes de providentia, ignoratio Messiae, et multiplex caligo. Deinde in voluntate est aversio a Deo. Voluntas est sine timore Dei, sine amore, fiducia, spe, sine laetitia in Deo, amat, odit contra mandata Dei: haec vitia sunt in superiore parte. Ideo Paulus describens hominem sine Spiritu sancto 1. Corinth. 2. inquit: Animalis homo non percipit ea, quae sunt spiritus Dei. Ac totum hominem non renatum verbo et spiritu, nominat ψυχικόν, sicut alibi totum hunc hominem nominat Carnem.

Novus homo dicitur, quatenus habet novam lucem, ac novos motus accensos per verbum et Spiritum sanctum, videlicet agnitionem Dei et Domini nostri Iesu Christi, veram fidem et fiduciam in Christum, timorem Dei, invocationem, dilectionem, laetitiam acquiescentem in Deo, spem et alios motus Spiritus sancti. De hac novitate loquitur Paulus 2. Corinth. 2.: Nunc intecta facie gloriam Domini intuentes, in eandem imaginem transformamur a fulgore in fulgorem, tanquam a Domini spiritu, id est, cum fide cernimus fulgorem Domini, videlicet, ipsum Christum, ostendentem nobis misericordiam aeterni patris, qua agnita accedimus ad Deum, non fugimus ut Saul, sed vere agnoscimus Deum esse bonum et praesentem, nos recipi et servari ab eo propter filium, in hac filii luce nos quoque transformamur, id est, accipimus radios per filium in nos sparsos dato Spiritu sancto, videlicet noticiam Dei et novos motus, quos accendit et confirmat Spiritus sanctus audita voce Evangelii.

Nec significat novitas, cogitationes et motus rationis sine Spiritu sancto, nec significat spiritus rationem, sed tertiam personam divinitatis, quam aeternus pater dat per filium in corda nostra.

Erit autem novitas hominis integra in Ecclesia coelesti, in qua erit Deus omnia in omnibus, id est, sic fulgebit in nobis, ut palam conspiciatur, non per ministerium Evangelii, et ciebit omnes motus, ita, ut non sit simul in nobis peccatum.

At in hac vita idem homo renatus, est Vetus et Novus, id est, Paulus est novus, quia in eo habitat Deus, et illustrat eum verbo suo et sanctificat Spiritu sancto, et mens et cor accipiunt aliquos radios lucis divinae et motus Spiritus sancti.

Sentit enim Paulus invocationem, fiduciam, laetitiam in Deo: eatenus est novus, et haec novitas regnare debet.

Sed nondum in hac vita natura Pauli prorsus est sine peccato et sine morte, eatenus est vetus homo, sed haec vetustas mortificatur, non regnat.

## 6:2
We who have died to sin, how, etc.

The first argument is taken from the efficient causes.

A dead nature is not effective.

In us the old nature, which is a mass of sin, is dead, that is, it has begun to be mortified, and it does not reign: Therefore it is not effective.

He proves the minor premise, because through baptism we have been baptized into the death of Christ and buried with him: because baptism is a testimony by which we are immersed as if into the blood of Christ, so that we may be washed and receive the remission of sins.

But remission is effected in such a way that, on account of the death and resurrection of Christ, sin is also actually abolished in us, because the Son, through the Gospel and the gift of the Holy Spirit, convicts hearts of sin, and in turn vivifies, and kindles new light and new impulses in us.

Baptism is the testimony and pledge of this remission or reconciliation and of the efficacy of Christ in us, and when mortification and vivification have thus been begun, we are buried together with Christ.

Moreover, the mass of sin is buried in two ways: First, by imputation, because the remnants of sin are remitted to us.

Secondly, as far as the effect is concerned, because this mass, after it began to be mortified, ceased to be effective, that is, it does not reign.

Nor does Paul speak only of mortification, but he adds an argument concerning vivification: for unless life were to approach and conquer, there would be no liberation.

Therefore it was also said above: Grace abounds over the offense.

Likewise: Grace reigns through righteousness unto eternal life.

From there he argues thus: A living nature is effective.

We have been vivified through Christ, who for this reason assumed this mass, that he might also restore life to us: and this vivification is begun in this life, when the Son of God through the Gospel and the Holy Spirit consoles hearts, and frees us from eternal death, according to the saying: Having been justified by faith we have peace.

Likewise: O death, I will be your death, and O hell, I will be your hell, etc.

But because this life, which is restored through the Son by the gift of the Holy Spirit, is such as the Holy Spirit himself is, let the actions be congruent with the Holy Spirit.

As it is said elsewhere: We, beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, are transformed into the same image, etc.

Thus the necessity of doing good is shown from the efficient and final cause.

Included in these is also the necessity of duty, because this order is immovable, that the rational creature should obey God: and nature is restored so that it may return to this obedience.

This order Paul calls duty.

Latin:

Qui mortui sumus peccato, quomodo etc.

Primum argumentum sumtum a causis efficientibus.

Mortua natura non sit efficax.

In nobis vetus natura, quae est massa peccati est mortua, id est, coepit mortificari, nec regnat: Ergo non sit efficax.

Minorem probat, quia per baptismum sumus in mortem Christi baptizati et consepulti eum eo: quia baptismus est testimonium quo mergimur tanquam in sanguinem Christi, ut abluamur et accipiamus remissionem peccatorum.

Ita autem fit remissio, ut propter mortem et resurrectionem Christi etiam re ipsa in nobis aboleatur peccatum, quia filius per Evangelium dato Spiritu sancto arguit corda de peccato, et rursus vivificat, et accendit novam lucem et novos motus in nobis.

Huius remissionis seu reconciliationis et efficaciae Christi in nobis testimonium et pignus est baptismus, et cum sic incoata est mortificatio et vivificatio, sepelimur una cum Christo.

Est autem massa peccati sepulta dupliciter: Primum imputatione, quia remittuntur nobis reliquiae peccati.

Secundo, quod ad effectum attinet, quia haec massa postquam mortificari coepit, desiit esse efficax, id est, non regnat.

Nec tantum de mortificatione loquitur Paulus, sed addit argumentum de vivificatione: nisi enim accederet vita et vinceret, nulla esset liberatio.

Ideo et supra dictum est: Gratia exuberat supra delictum.

Item: Regnat gratia per iusticiam ad vitam aeternam.

Inde sic argumentatur: Viva natura est efficax.

Nos vivificati sumus per Christum, qui ideo assumsit hanc massam, ut nobis quoque vitam redderet: et haec vivificatio incoatur in hac vita, cum filius Dei per Euangelium et Spiritum sanctum consolatur corda, et liberat nos ex morte aeterna, iuxta dictum: Iustificati fide pacem habemus.

Item: O mors ero mors tua, et o inferne ero infernus tuus etc.

Quia vero haec vita, quae restituitur per filium dato Spiritu sancto, est talis, qualis est ipse Spiritus sanctus, sint actiones congruentes Spiritui sancto.

Ut alibi dicitur: Nos retecta facie gloriam Domini speculantes transformamur in eandem imaginem etc.

Ita necessitas bene operandi ex causa efficiente, et finali ostenditur.

In his comprehensa est et necessitas debiti, quia hic ordo immotus est, ut creatura rationalis Deo obediat: et restituitur natura, ut ad hanc obedientiam redeat.

Hunc ordinem nominat Paulus debitum.

## 6:7
He who has died has been justified from sins.

Many quibbles are stirred up concerning this saying.

He who has died has been justified from sin; Judas has died; Therefore: He has been justified.

I answer most simply: This saying speaks of the actual sins of this life, as it is said "a dead man does not bite," that is, he who has died now does nothing in this life: as one strangled ceases to steal.

Or you may say: He who has been crucified with Christ has died and been justified from sin. Others respond more cleverly: He who is dead has been justified, that is, he has been subjected to a just punishment. But he who does not suffer punishment willingly is not just. For just as obedience is justice when it is voluntary, so he who sustains punishment is just when he sustains it willingly, just as the Son of God willingly sustained punishment for us. His obedience was therefore justice. But let us be content with the former simple explanation: a dead man does not bite.

Furthermore, let us know this: that devils and all the damned commit horrible sins throughout all eternity, because they are angry with God without end, etc. Christ says that the devil is a murderer and a liar. Thinking of these horrible furies, let us be more terrified by the thought of eternal punishments.

Latin:

Qui mortuus est, iustificatus est a peccatis.

De hoc dicto multae cavillationes agitantur.

Mortuus iustificatus est a peccato, Iudas est mortuus, Igitur: Iustificatus est.

Respondeo simplicissime: Dictum hoc loquitur de actualibus peccatis huius vitae, ut dicitur νεκρὸς οὐ δάκνει, id est, qui mortuus est, iam nihil agit in hac vita: ut strangulatus desinit furari.

Vel dicas: Mortuus iustificatus est a peccato, qui est crucifixus cum Christo. Alii argutius respondent: Qui mortuus est, iustificatus est, id est, iusta poena adfectus est. Sed qui poenam non patitur volens, non est iustus. Ut enim obedientia tunc est iusticia, cum est voluntaria, ita sustinens poenam tunc est iustus, cum volens sustinet, sicut filius Dei pro nobis volens sustinuit poenam. Fuit igitur obedientia eius iusticia. Sed simus contenti priore simplici explicatione νεκρὸς οὐ δάκνει.

Caeterum hoc sciamus, diabolos et omnes damnatos in omni aeternitate horribilia peccata facere, quia sine fine irascuntur Deo etc. Christus ait, diabolum esse homicidam et mendacem. De his horribilibus furoribus cogitantes, magis expavescamus cogitatione aeternarum poenarum.

## 6:12
Let not sin reign in your mortal body.

This is the conclusion of the response which he opposed to the objection recited earlier.

He says explicitly, however: Let not sin reign, so that he may signify that in this life the vicious nature has not been entirely extinguished, as if he were saying: Sin remains in nature in this life, but let it not reign, that is, let it not obey vicious affections, just as he also says below: If by the Spirit you mortify the deeds of the flesh, you shall live. These passages and similar ones show the distinction between the sin that remains in the saints and those sins on account of which a man ceases to be in grace and which cast out the Holy Spirit. It is necessary for this distinction to be known and observed in the Church.

The rule, however, delivered below is in 1 Timothy 1: Wage the good warfare, holding faith and a good conscience. From this rule, let the distinction be established.

When a man assents to error in one or more articles of faith, whether knowingly or deceived, he loses the Holy Spirit, according to the saying: He who does not believe is already judged. Likewise: The Spirit will take from what is mine. Likewise: No other foundation can be laid than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ. And although there is darkness in all saints in this life, and the articles of faith are not sufficiently understood, and assent is weaker, or even stubble is built upon true doctrine: yet this weakness differs from the subversion of an article of faith, or from a contrary assertion, as Samosatenus and Arius destroyed the article concerning the divinity of the Son, and many assented to them, whose error grieved and cast out the Holy Spirit. Because there is no Spirit in the heart except through the true voice of doctrine, the saying: Sanctify them in the truth, the word is truth.

Furthermore, a man violating the commandments of God against his conscience loses the Holy Spirit, and again becomes guilty of the wrath of God, and falls into eternal destruction if conversion does not take place. 1 Corinthians 6: Fornicators, adulterers, will not possess the kingdom of God. And with the Holy Spirit cast out, sin is said to reign, because it effects its own proper result, namely, that a man falls into eternal punishments: therefore, the more upright age calls it mortal.

This rule having been established, let us then know that in the reborn in this life there are still many and great sins, even if true faith and a good conscience, that is, a good purpose, shine in the mind, as Paul says in Romans 7: I find another law in my members captivating me in the law of sin, that is, there are some diseases, darkness, and many sad doubts about God: likewise, there is not in the heart as much fear, love, and trust in God as there ought to be, and there are many wandering flames of desires, ignorance, and many omissions. These are indeed sins in their own kind, but the reborn, who grieve on account of this impurity and resist it, and by faith on account of the mediator believe that they are forgiven and covered, retain the Holy Spirit and faith, and remain in grace: therefore this sin is called sin not reigning, namely in the reborn, who resist and retain faith, as is said below in the eighth chapter: There is now no condemnation to those who walk in Christ Jesus. And here the sweetest consolation is delivered, Sin does not have dominion over you, For you are not under the law, but under grace, as if he were saying: Because you are under grace, that is, under gratuitous reconciliation on account of the Son, therefore the law no longer accuses you, does not condemn you, and the remnants of sin in you are covered by a shelter, namely by the mediator Christ, etc.

It is necessary to hold this doctrine concerning the distinction of sins for many and most serious reasons. What then, shall we sin because we are not under the law, etc.? He meets the objection concerning liberty: for in political custom, the abrogation of laws is understood in such a way that it is afterwards permitted to act against the law. Just as we also act against the laws concerning ceremonies, we eat swine's flesh, etc.

CHAP. VI. The question is therefore, is liberation from the law understood in the same way regarding ceremonial, forensic, and moral laws? I answer: As far as justification and condemnation are concerned, liberation is understood in the same way regarding all of them, that is, just as eating swine's flesh does not merit the remission of sins, and is not righteousness by which you are accepted before God, so neither do the works of the decalogue merit remission, nor are they righteousness by which a person is accepted before God: but as far as obedience is concerned, there is a distinction between ceremonial, forensic, and moral laws. By no means does the debt of obedience remain in ceremonial laws, as it does in moral ones, because the Mosaic polity was established by a singular counsel, so that it would last only until the Messiah should preach there, bear witness, offer sacrifice, rise from the dead, and thence send the Apostles. Therefore, the ceremonial and forensic laws, which are the very Polity or the nerves of the polity, have collapsed at the same time. But the moral law is the eternal and immovable wisdom in God and the norm of righteousness, the radius of which was implanted in the rational creature, so that we might be conformable to God, and this order is eternal, that the rational creature should be conformable to God. Therefore, God never wills sin. For although He receives man with immense mercy on account of the Son, yet He does not will sin: but He remits it, because the penalty has been paid through the Son, and He receives us in such a way that He simultaneously restores conformity with God, and God communicates Himself to us in all eternity. Thus, in this place, Paul also argues from the final or formal cause, although he has used political similitudes, which he himself confesses to be rather crude.

Now you are servants of righteousness: Therefore, let your works be righteous. That is, the final cause of reconciliation is that eternal conformity with God be restored, therefore let your actions be conformable. Likewise, by the act of divorce, a woman belongs to the later husband, not the former. Thus we are now Christ's and conformable to Christ, who is the image of the eternal Father, and He came to restore in us the image of God. But when it is said thus: We are free from the moral law, as far as condemnation is concerned, this is by no means understood of those who are not converted to God, nor are they vivified by faith through the Son of God, because of them it is said: He who does not believe is already judged. Likewise: The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law, but thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, only those are liberated from this judgment of the moral law, that is, from condemnation, who have been justified by faith, of whom it was said above: Being justified by faith we have peace. Likewise below: There is now no condemnation to those who walk in Christ Jesus. Likewise: You are not under the law, but under grace. Likewise: He who has the Son has life, He who does not have the Son of God does not have life, Likewise, if the Son shall have made you free, you shall be truly free.

But it is objected: The law is eternal and immovable, Therefore, condemnation necessarily remains where sin remains. I answer: Every law obligates, either to obedience or to voluntary penalty. But since the penalty has been derived onto the Son, the law has been satisfied, just as He Himself says: I did not come to destroy the law, but to fulfill it. And because the innocent and willing Son suffers, that payment of the penalty is applied, and it is given to us. But this very penalty shows that God does not will nor approve of sin, but that men are received on account of the ransom (λύτρα) which the Son gave, and are received in such a way that the order and law remain in the divine mind, which does not will sin, and receives us to restore obedience.

These things are to be thought upon often with pious meditation, both so that the doctrine may become more illustrious, and that true consolations may be rightly understood, etc.

And let the sayings of the Prophets be compared. Isaiah

Chap. 52: You have been sold for nothing, you shall not be redeemed with silver, that is, when the devil deceived you with his promises, You have been sold for nothing, that is, you did not receive those promises, You shall be as Gods: but rather you have been burdened with all evils. But the seller ought to receive something of value for the thing sold: That was not done when you were sold to the devil.

Again, redemption shall also be made, not with your price, but the Son shall pay the ransom (λύτρα).

Isaiah 43: You have made me serve in your sins, You have made me labor in your iniquities, I myself blot out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins.

Isaiah 53: He shall lay down his soul as an offering for sin.

Let the sweetest formulas of speaking be observed in this chapter: Offer your members as weapons

of righteousness. He names the members, as we have said elsewhere, the powers and organs in man, namely the mind and the will, the heart, the locomotive [faculty], and the senses. Let these be weapons incited by the Holy Spirit. Just as the heart of Joseph burned with the Holy Spirit when he resisted the adulteress: and because he names weapons, he wants us not to be sluggish.

Latin:

Non regnet peccatum in mortali corpore.

Conclusio est responsionis, quam opposuit obiectioni antea recitatae.

Diserte autem dicit: Non regnet peccatum, ut significet in hac vita non prorsus extinctam esse vitiosam naturam, quasi dicat: Reliquum est peccatum in natura in hac vita, sed non regnet, id est, non obtemperet vitiis affectibus, sicut et infra dicit: Si actiones carnis spiritu mortificabitis, vivetis. Hi loci et similes ostendunt discrimen peccati, quod in sanctis reliquum est, et illorum peccatorum, propter quae homo desinit esse in gratia, et quae excutiunt Spiritum sanctum. Hoc discrimen in Ecclesia cognosci et conspici necessarium est.

Regula autem infra tradita est, 1. Timoth. 1.: Milita bonam militiam, retinens fidem et bonam conscientiam. Ex hac regula constituatur discrimen.

Cum assentitur homo errori in uno vel pluribus articulis fidei, sive sciens sive deceptus, amittit Spiritum sanctum, iuxta dictum: Qui non credit, iam iudicatus est. Item: Spiritus de meo accipiet. Item: Fundamentum aliud poni non potest, praeter id quod positum est, quod est Iesus Christus. Etsi autem in omnibus sanctis in hac vita caligo est, nec satis intelliguntur articuli fidei, et assensio est languidior, aut etiam extruuntur stipulae supra veram doctrinam: tamen haec imbecillitas differt ab eversione articuli fidei, seu ab asseveratione contraria, ut Samosatenus, Arius, delebant articulum de divinitate filii, et multi eis assentiebantur, quorum error contristavit et excussit Spiritum sanctum. Quia non est spiritus in corde, nisi per veram vocem doctrinae, dictum: Sanctifica eos in veritate, sermo est veritas.

Praeterea homo violans mandata Dei cor conscientiam, amittit Spiritum sanctum, et rursus fit reus irae Dei, et ruit in aeternum exitium si non fiat conversio. 1. Corint. 6.: Scortatores, adulteri, non possidebunt regnum Dei. Et excusso Spiritu sancto Peccatum dicitur regnare peccatum, quia efficit proprium effectum, scilicet, ut homo ruat in aeternas poenas: ideo rectior aetas nominat mortale.

Constituta hac regula, deinde sciamus Renatis in hac vita tamen adhuc multa et magna peccata esse, etiam si lucet in mente et vera fides et conscientia bona est, id est, bonum propositum, ut Paulus Rom. 7. inquit: Invenio aliam legem in membris captivantem me in lege peccati, id est, aliqui sunt morbi, caligo et multae tristes dubitationes de Deo: item, in corde non est tantus timor, dilectio, fiducia Dei, ut esse debebat, et sunt multae errantes flammae cupiditatum, ignorantiae et omissiones multae. Haec sunt vero suo genere peccata, sed Renati, qui dolent propter hanc immunditiem et resistunt ei, et fide propter mediatorem credunt ea remitti ac tegi, retinent Spiritum sanctum et fidem, ac manent in gratia: ideo hoc peccatum nominatur peccatum non regnans, videlicet in renatis, qui resistunt et retinent fidem, sicut infra dicitur octavo cap.: Nulla condemnatio est nunc his, qui in Christo Iesu ambulant. Et hic traditur dulcissima consolatio, Peccatum non dominatur vobis, Non enim estis sub lege, sed sub gratia, quasi dicat: Quia estis sub gratia, id est, sub gratuita reconciliatione propter filium, ideo lex iam non accusat vos, non damnat vos, et reliquiae peccati in vobis teguntur per umbraculum, videlicet per mediatorem Christum etc.

Hanc doctrinam de discrimine peccatorum tenere necesse est, propter multas et gravissimas causas. Quid igitur, num peccabimus, quia non sumus sub lege etc.? Occurrit obiectioni de libertate: nam in politica consuetudine intelligitur abrogatio legum sic, ut postea concedatur facere contra legem. Sicut etiam contra leges de ceremoniis facimus, vescimur carne suilla etc.

CAP. VI. Quaestio est igitur, an eodem modo intelligatur liberatio a lege de ceremonialibus, forensibus et moralibus legibus? Respondeo: Quod ad iustificationem et condemnationem attinet, eodem modo de omnibus intelligitur liberatio, id est, sicut non esui illa carne non meretur remissionem peccatorum, et non est iustitia, qua coram Deo sis accepta, sic nec opera decalogi merentur remissionem, nec sunt iustitia, qua coram Deo persona sit accepta: sed quod ad obedientiam attinet, discrimen est legum ceremonialium, forensium et moralium. Nequaquam manet debitum obedientiae in ceremonialibus, sicut in moralibus, quia politia Mosaica singulari consilio constituta est, ut duraret tantum, donec Messias ibi concionaretur, ederet testimonia, offerret sacrificium, resurgeret ex morte, et inde mitteret Apostolos. Simul igitur collapsae sunt leges ceremoniales et forenses, quae sunt ipsa Politia seu nervi politiae. Sed lex moralis est aeterna et immota sapientia in Deo et norma iustitiae, cuius radius creaturae rationali insitus fuit, ut essemus conformes Deo, et hic ordo aeternus est, ut creatura rationalis sit conformis Deo. Nunquam igitur vult Deus peccatum. Quanquam enim recipit hominem immensa misericordia propter filium, tamen non vult peccatum: sed remittit, quia poena per filium persoluta est, et ita nos recipit, ut simul conformitatem cum Deo restituat, et Deus nobis in tota aeternitate sese communicet. Ita et hoc loco Paulus argumentatur a causa finali seu formali, quanquam similitudinibus politicis usus est, quas ipse fatetur rudiores esse.

Iam estis servi iustitiae: Ergo sint opera iusta. Id est, causa finalis reconciliationis est, ut restituatur aeterna conformitas cum Deo, sint igitur actiones conformes. Item, facto divortio mulier est posterioris viri, non prioris. Sic sumus iam Christi et conformes Christo, qui est imago aeterni patris, et venit ut restituat in nobis imaginem Dei. Cum autem sic dicitur: Sumus liberi a lege morali, quod ad condemnationem attinet, id nequaquam intelligitur de his, qui non sunt conversi ad Deum, nec fide sunt vivificati per filium Dei, quia de his dictum est: Qui non credit, iam iudicatus est. Item: Aculeus mortis peccatum est, potentia vero peccati lex est, Deo autem sit gratia, qui dat nobis victoriam per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum. Tantum igitur illi ab hoc iudicio legis moralis, id est, a condemnatione liberati sunt, qui iustificati sunt fide, de quibus supra dictum est: Iustificati fide pacem habemus. Item infra: Nulla nunc damnatio est his, qui in Christo Iesu ambulant. Item: Non estis sub lege, sed sub gratia. Item: Qui habet filium, habet vitam, Qui non habet filium Dei, non habet vitam, Item, si vos filius liberaverit, vere liberi eritis.

Obiicitur autem: Lex est aeterna et immota, Ergo necessario manet condemnatio, ubi manet peccatum. Respondeo: Omnis lex obligat, vel ad obedientiam, vel ad poenam voluntariam. Cum autem derivata sit poena in filium, legi satisfactum est, sicut ipse inquit: Non veni solvere legem, sed implere. Et quia filius innocens et volens patitur, applicatur illa persolutio poenae, et donatur nobis. Ostendit autem haec ipsa poena, Deum non velle nec approbare peccatum, sed recipi homines propter λύτρα, quae filius dedit, et ita recipi, ut maneat ordo et lex in mente divina, quae non vult peccatum, et recipit nos ad restituendam obedientiam.

Haec pia meditatione saepe cogitanda sunt, et ut doctrina fiat illustrior, et verae consolationes recte intelligantur etc.

Et conferantur dicta Prophetarum. Esaiae

Cap. 52.: Gratis venundati estis, non argento redimimini, id est, cum diabolus vos decepit in suis promissis, Gratis venundati estis, id est, non accepistis illa promissa, Eritis sicut Dii: sed potius omnibus malis onerati estis. Vendens autem debet aliquid boni recipere pro re vendita: Id non factum est, cum vos venditi estis diabolo.

Rursus etiam fiet redemtio non vestro pretio, sed filius persolvet λύτρα.

Esaiae 43.: In peccatis tuis servire me fecisti, Laborare me fecisti in iniquitatibus tuis, Ego ipse deleo delicta tua propter me, et peccatorum tuorum non recordabor.

Esaiae 53.: Ponet animam suam hostiam pro peccato.

Observentur in hoc capite et dulcissimae formulae loquendi: Praebete membra vestra arma

iusticiae. Membra nominat, ut alias diximus Potentias et organa in homine, videlicet men- tem et voluntatem, cor, locomotivam et sensus. Haec sint arma incitata a Spiritu sancto. Sicut cor Ioseph ardebat Spiritu sancto, cum resisteret adulterae: et quia nominat arma, vult nos non esse segnes.

## 6:23
The wages of sin is death.

Let the antithesis be observed. Concerning sin he says: The wages of sin is death, that is, sin deserves death. But eternal life is the gift of God through and because of Christ Jesus, because the remission of sins, reconciliation, and the inheritance of eternal life are received simultaneously by grace through faith, according to the sayings: God so loved the world that everyone who believes in the Son should not perish, but have eternal life.

Rom. 5: Having been justified by his blood, we shall be saved by him from wrath. Likewise: How much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved in his life. Likewise: He who has the Son has life. Likewise: No living person shall be justified in your sight.

And it is useful to remember the saying of Bernard, who says: It is necessary to believe that you have the remission of sins only through grace, not because of your merits, and it is necessary for you to believe that it is remitted to you. So also it is necessary to believe that eternal life is given freely because of Christ, not because of your merits. Augustine torments himself as to how eternal life is both a gift and a reward, but the true explanation is this. Properly it is a gift, because the only cause for which eternal life is given is Christ, and because of him it is given freely to the believer at conversion, according to the oath: As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, etc. Then, since it was given for another reason, it happens to it that it is also a compensation or reward for labors, just as an inheritance is given because one is a son, and yet it happens to the inheritance afterwards that it is a compensation for duties, if you have performed any.

This is the true and simple explanation. Furthermore, let us also know this, that the phrase of the law must be interpreted according to the Gospel, as was said above in Chapter 2: He will give to each one according to his works.

Latin:

Stipendium peccati mors est.

Antithesis observetur. De peccato inquit: Stipendium peccati mors est, id est, peccatum meretur mortem. Sed vita aeterna est donum Dei per et propter Christum Iesum, quia simul accipiuntur Gratis, fide remissio peccatorum, re- conciliatio et haereditas vitae aeternae, iuxta di- cta: Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut omnis qui cre- dit in filium, non pereat, sed habeat vitam ae- ternam.

Rom. 5.: Iustificati sanguine ipsius salvabi- mur per eum ab ira. Item: Quanto magis recon- ciliati salvabimur in vita eius. Item: Qui habet filium, habet vitam. Item: Non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens.

Ac utile est meminisse dictum Bernardi, qui inquit: Necesse est credere, quod tantum per gratiam, non propter merita tua habeas remissio- nem peccatorum, et credere te necesse est, tibi remitti. Sic etiam necesse est credere, quod gra- tis donetur vita aeterna propter Christum, non propter tua merita. Augustinus torquet se, quo- modo vita aeterna et donum sit et merces, sed vera explicatio est. Proprie donum est, quia sola causa, propter quam datur vita aeterna, est Christus, et propter hunc gratis datur credenti in conversione, iuxta iusiurandum: Vivo ego, dicit Dominus, nolo mortem peccatoris etc. Deinde cum propter aliud data sit, accidit ei, ut sit etiam compensatio seu merces laborum, sicut datur haereditas, quia filius est, et tamen postea accidit haereditati, ut sit compensatio officiorum, si qua praestiteris.

Haec est vera et simplex explicatio. Deinde et hoc sciamus, phrasin legis enarrandam esse iuxta Evangelium, ut supra Cap. 2. dictum est: Dabit unicuique iuxta opera sua.

## 7:1 Disposition of Romans: Argument
Chapter VII.

Those who first divided the chapters followed the number of verses more than the subject matter. But the reader must take care not to tear apart things that are connected through lack of thought. The beginning of this chapter pertains to the previous digression and contains the second response, by which the objection concerning the license to sin is satisfied. If we are not under the law, therefore a license to sin is granted. The refutation was established above; now a second reason is added.

Only the dead have ceased to be under the law: therefore the law is abrogated for you in such a way, if you are mortified in Christ.

He declares the antecedent with a certain example. Now this is the antecedent: The law dominates the living. The example: A woman is bound to her husband as long as the husband lives.

And because there are two parts in the example, two enthymemes are made. Just as a woman, if she has married another after her former husband is dead, remains legally with the latter. So you, exempted from the former servitude and brought into the power of Christ, remain legally with Christ. Augustine sweats greatly here in adapting the similitude to the cause, but it is easy to see how it fits. It is a comparison of servitude. Just as a woman is bound to one husband, so we are bound to our sinful nature while it lives. If a woman has married another after her husband is dead, she will be bound to the latter. Thus Paul wishes to show that we, exempted from the former servitude, are bound to Christ. Nor indeed is it necessary for all parts in a similitude to correspond exactly.

Paul embraces the consequent of both enthymemes, saying thus: 'Therefore, brothers, you also have been mortified to the law through the body of Christ,' this pertains to the first antecedent, 'so that you may be of another,' etc. Then he repeats the same consequences, but with an amplification taken from the cause, what the law effects in the living flesh. In this place he signifies to the reader what the abrogation of the law is, or what it is not to be under the law. For those living in the flesh, there is a need for the law so that they may be restrained. But yet in these same people the law excites the affections of sins, hatred of God, and despair. Where, therefore, the sinful nature is mortified, to what end is there a need for the law, which either restrains or accuses? Therefore, to be under the law is to be restrained by the law, to be condemned, and to be incited to hatred of God and despair. And the abrogation of the law is not to grant a license to sin, but to free from condemnation and to take away the hatred of God, and to take away despair. That happens when the remission of sins is granted. But that [remission] happens when the flesh is mortified in Christ, and mortification occurs when, with sin recognized, minds are terrified, which, when they apprehend the remission of sins through faith, again conceive consolation and the Holy Spirit, who begets a new life. And this is the end of the digression.

On the effect of the law.

What then shall we say? Is the law sin? Here Paul returns to the established method, or to the comparison established above in the fifth chapter. And let the reader remember, as if the digression were set aside, that this passage concerning the effect of the law is to be joined with that method.

And so that the passage might become more illustrious and conspicuous, he began with a question. Is the law sin? As if he were saying, it was said above that sin is increased by the law: likewise, I just said that the law excites the affections of sins. Therefore the law seems to be some evil thing. He answers, denying that the law is evil. And he submits what the proper effect of the law is, namely, to show sin.

Then he adds a rhetorical transfer, that the law does not increase sin by itself. For the blame is transferred from the law to the vice of our nature, and to sin itself. For when the law shows sin, nature, angered by the judgment of God, begins to be angry at God and to despair.

He institutes, moreover, a prosopographia. For it was necessary to propose a person, in whom he might show the effects of the law and of sin. And so he proposes his own example, and weaves a certain narrative, in which it can be discerned what the law accomplishes.

I was living at one time without the law, that is, I was a secure hypocrite: I dreamed that I was fulfilling the law excellently.

Afterwards comes the law, for then it is truly law, when it is not written on walls, but when it accuses, when it terrifies. Here sin revived, that is, as I saw myself condemned by the law, here nature began to be angry at the judgment of God etc. Conclusion of the translation. The law is good, but it is the fault of sin and corrupted nature that it does not justify, but only terrifies, and confuses, and incites to despair. And this happens so that the baseness and magnitude of sin may be seen, so that we may see that we have need of another justice than the justice of the law. Objection. How does the law increase sin, since it restrains, since many who obey the law live honestly. It is a timely objection, and very necessary for rightly understanding this dispute. The law, he says, is spiritual, that is, the law of God is not merely political, as men dream, but it requires affections, and judges affections. Let it restrain the political law outwardly, and these are satisfied when one lives civilly, when honest works are done for appearance. But the law of God is not satisfied by external works. For the law requires the knowledge of God, the fear of God, trust toward God, chaste hearts, loving one's neighbor. Pomponius Atticus, or that Pharisee in Luke, does not satisfy the law of God, even though they diligently perform the works of the law. For their hearts are empty of the fear of God, trust toward God, love of God, and similar affections. Origen explains it ridiculously. The law is spiritual, that is, allegorical, since Paul above set forth an example from the Decalogue: Thou shalt not covet. It seems to me to contribute greatly to clarity if it is explained by comparison. The law is spiritual, that is, it is not merely political, for spirit signifies affections, or spiritual motions, which are carried toward God. But Origen and his lovers, when they hear mention of the law being made, understand nothing but political [matters]. When they dispute whether it is possible by the powers of nature to do the law, they only dream that it is asked about theft, about murder, about adultery. The first table never comes to mind. But let the Christian reader know that Paul is not disputing here about polity. Another matter is being treated, namely, about justice before God. The question is primarily about the first table, and about the motions of the heart toward God. Let men be ashamed, who wish to be called Christians, to so forget the decalogue that when they dispute about the justice of God, they require nothing but the second table, and political works. I have said these things so that the reader may more diligently observe what Paul calls the law, and why he says it is spiritual. Nor are we now refuting Origen's interpretations for the first time, but the greatest men in the ancient Church condemned his writings. For thus Epiphanius writes about him: And as for whatever was said in homilies, and through introductions regarding the habits and natures of animals and other things, he was carried along in the middle, often narrating things gracefully; but as for whatever he dogmatized regarding doctrines, and concerning faith and higher contemplation, he is found to be the most absurd of all those before him and after him.

But I am carnal, sold under sin, that is, a slave, or captive of sin. This is the comparison of our nature with the law. The law is spiritual, it requires spiritual motions, knowledge of God, trust toward God, obedience, patience in afflictions. But our nature is carnal, understanding only carnal things, desiring only carnal things, despising God, holding the judgment of God in hatred, seeking carnal protections for life, placing trust in one's own powers, justice, wisdom, in riches.

In the remaining part of the narrative, Paul describes how he still struggles with sin. For he wishes to show that sin so clings to carnal nature that not even those who are once reborn cast it off entirely.

Latin:

Caput VII.

Qui primi distinxerunt capita, magis secuti sunt numerum versuum, quam materias. Sed lectori videndum est, ne res cohaerentes impru- dens divellat. Initium huius capitis ad proxi- mam digressionem pertinet, et continet alteram responsionem, qua satisfit obiectioni, de licentia peccandi. Si non sumus sub lege, Ergo conce- ditur licentia peccandi. Confutatio supra insti- tuta est, nunc additur altera ratio.

Tantum mortui desierunt esse sub lege: Ergo ita vobis abrogata est lex, si estis mor- tificati in Christo.

Antecedens declarat exemplo quodam. Est autem hoc antecedens: Lex dominatur vivis. Exemplum: Mulier alligata est marito, tantis- per dum vivit maritus.

Et quia in exemplo duae sunt partes, duo fiunt enthymemata. Sicut mulier si mortuo ma- rito priore, nupserit alteri, iure manet apud po- steriorem. Ita vos exemti servituti priori et re- dacti in potestatem Christi, iure apud Christum manetis. Augustinus valde sudat hic in accomo- danda similitudine ad causam, sed facile est vi- dere, quomodo conveniat. Servitutis compara- tio est. Sicut mulier uno marito alligata est, sic nos naturae peccatrici dum vivit alligati su- mus. Si mulier mortuo marito alteri nupserit, posteriori erit alligata. Ita vult Paulus ostendere nos exemtos a priore servitute, Christo alligatos esse. Neque vero necesse est in similitudine omnes partes ad unguem congruere.

Paulus utriusque enthymematis consequens complectitur, sic inquiens: Itaque fratres et vos mortificati estis legi per corpus Christi, hoc ad primum antecedens pertinet, ut sitis alte- rius etc. Deinde repetit eadem consequentia, sed cum amplificatione, sumta ex causa, quid lex efficiat in carne viva. Quo loco significat lectori, quid sit legis abrogatio, seu quid sit non esse sub lege. Viventibus in carne opus est lege, ut coërceantur. Sed tamen in iisdem lex exuscitat affectus peccatorum, odium Dei et desperatio- nem. Ubi ergo peccatrix natura est mortificata, quorsum opus est lege, quae vel coërceat, vel ac- cuset? Est ergo esse sub lege, coërceri a lege, condemnari, et incitari ad odium Dei et despe- rationem. Et legis abrogatio est non concedere licentiam peccandi, sed liberare a damnatione et auferre odium Dei, ac auferre desperationem. Id fit, cum donatur remissio peccatorum. Illa vero contingit carne mortificata in Christo, et fit mortificatio, cum cognito peccato perterre- fiunt animi, qui cum apprehendant remissio- nem peccatorum per fidem, iterum concipiunt consolationem et Spiritum sanctum, qui novam vitam gignit. Et hic est digressionis finis.

De legis effectu.

Quid igitur dicemus? Estne lex peccatum? Hic redit Paulus ad institutam methodum, seu ad comparationem iustitutam supra in quinto Ca- pite. Et meminerit lector tanquam dissimulata digressione, hunc locum de legis effectu coniuu- gendum esse cum illa methodo.

Et ut fieret illustrior ac conspectior locus, coepit ab interrogatione. Estne lex peccatum? quasi dicat, supra dictum est, peccatum augeri lege: item, modo dixi, quod lex exuscitet affectus peccatorum. Videtur igitur lex malum quiddam esse. Respondet, negans legem malam esse. Et subiicit, quis sit proprius effectus legis, vide- licet ostendere peccatum.

Deinde addit rhetoricam translationem, quod lex non augeat peccatum per sese. Trans- fertur enim culpa a lege, in naturae nostrae vi- tium, et in ipsum peccatum. Cum enim lex ostendit peccatum, natura irata iudicio Dei, in- cipit irasci Deo et desperare.

Instituit autem προσωπογραφίαν. Erat enim opus proponere personam, in qua ostenderet ef- fectus legis et peccati. Itaque suum exemplum proponit, et narrationem quandam texit, in qua cerni potest, quid efficiat lex.

Ego vivebam aliquando sine lege, id est, ego eram securus hypocrita: somniabam me legem egregie perficere.

Postea venit lex, tunc enim est vere lex, cum non in parietibus scripta est, sed cum accu- sat, cum terret. Hic peccatum revixit, id est, ut vidi me damnari a lege, hic coepit natura irasci iudicio Dei etc. Conclusio translationis. Lex est bona, sed peccati et vitiatae naturae culpa est, quod non iustificat, tantum terret, et confundit, et incitat ad desperandum. Et hoc ideo fit, ut conspici peccati turpitudo ac magnitudo possit, ut videa- mus, nobis alia iusticia opus esse, quam legis iusticia. Occupatio. Quomodo auget lex peccatum, cum coerceat, cum multi legi obtemperantes ho- neste vivant. Tempestiva occupatio est, et ad hanc disputationem recte intelligendam valde ne- cessaria. Lex, inquit, spiritualis est, id est, lex Dei non est politica tantum, sicut somniant ho- mines, sed requirit affectus, et iudicat affectus. Politicae legis foris coerceat, et his satisfit, cum civiliter vivitur, cum honesta opera in speciem fiunt. Sed legi Dei non satisfit per externa opera. Lex enim requirit noticiam Dei, timorem Dei, fiduciam erga Deum, corda casta, amantia proxi- mi. Non satisfacit lege Dei Pomponius Atticus, aut Pharisaeus ille in Luca, tametsi legis opera diligenter perficiant. Corda enim sunt vacua metu Dei, fiducia erga Deum, amore Dei et si- milibus affectibus. Origenes ridicule exponit. Lex est spiritua- lis, id est, allegorica, cum Paulus supra ex De- calogo posuerit exemplum: Non concupisces. Mihi videtur valde conducere ad perspicuitatem, si per collationem exponatur. Lex est spiritualis, id est, non est tantum politica, spiritus enim significat affectus, seu motus spirituales, qui ad Deum feruntur. Sed Origenes et eius amatores cum audiunt legis mentionem fieri, nihil intelli- gunt, nisi politica. Cum disputant, Utrum pos- sibile sit naturae viribus legem facere, tantum somniant quaeri de furto, de caede, de adulterio. Primae tabulae nunquam venit in mentem. Sed lector Christianus sciat, Paulum non disputare hic de politia. Alia res agitur, videlicet de iusti- cia coram Deo. De prima tabula praecipua est quaestio, et de motibus cordis erga Deum. Pu- deat homines, qui Christiani dici volunt, sic oblivisci decalogi, ut cum de iusticia Dei dispu- tant, nihil requirant, nisi secundam tabulam, et politica opera. Haec dixi, ut diligentius ob- servet lector, quid Paulus vocet legem, et cur dicat esse spiritualem. Neque nos nunc Orige- nis interpretationes primi refellimus, sed maximi viri in Ecclesia veteri damnaverunt eius scripta. Sic einim scribit de eo Epiphanius: καὶ ὅσα μὲν ἐν προσομιλίαις, καὶ διὰ τῶν προοιμίων εἰς ἤθη τε καὶ εἰς φύσεις ζώων τε καὶ τῶν ἄλλων εἴρηται, μέσος φερόμενος, πολλάκις χαρίεντα διηγήσατο, ὅσα δὲ εἰς δόγματα ἐδογμάτισε, καὶ περὶ πίστεως καὶ μείζονος θεωρίας, τῶν πάντων ἀτοπώτατα τῶν πρὸ αὐτοῦ, καὶ μετ’ αὐτὸν εὑρίσκεται.

Ego autem sum carnalis venundatus sub pec- catum, id est, mancipium, seu captivus peccati. Haec est collatio nostrae naturae cum lege. Lex est spiritualis, requirit motus spirituales, noti- ciam Dei, fiduciam erga Deum, obedientiam, patientiam in afflictionibus. At natura nostra carnalis est, carnalia tantum intelligens, tantum appetens carnalia, contemnens Deum, odio ha- bens iudicium Dei, quaerens praesidia vitae car- nalia, collocans fiduciam in propriis viribus, iu- sticia, sapientia, in opibus.

In reliqua parte narrationis describit Paulus, quomodo etiamnum. decertet cum peccato. Vult enim ostendere, quod peccatum ita haereat in natura carnali, ut nec renati semel universum exuant.

## 7:1 Argument
Chapter VII.

Just as he previously used the analogy of servitude, so now he depicts with the analogy of a second marriage the obedience which must be rendered to God, and the application is not difficult. As a woman, upon the death of her former husband, belongs to a second, so we, having been freed from the law of the former Lord, namely from the condemnation that terrifies and drives hearts to doubt, distrust, and raging against God: we are now another's, namely God's, in whom we rejoice, to whom we approach by faith through Christ, through whom we live, and because we are now his own, obedience is to be rendered to him.

It was said above, however, that these arguments are taken from final causes. The Son of God came to destroy the works of the devil, not to confirm sin, but so that, with sin and death utterly destroyed, righteousness and eternal life might be restored in us, etc.

Latin:

Caput VII.

Sicut antea similitudine servitutis usus est, ita nunc similitudine secundi coniugii pingit obe- dientiam, quae Deo praestanda est, nec difficilis est accommodatio. Ut mulier mortuo priore ma- rito propria est secundi, sic nos liberati a lege prioris Domini, videlicet a condemnatione per- terrefaciente et impellente corda ad dubitationem, diffidentiam, et fremitum contra Deum: iam su- mus alterius, scilicet Dei, in quo laetamur, ad quem accedimus fide per Christum, per hunc vi- vimus, et quia iam sumus eius proprii, praeste- tur ei obedientia.

Dictum est autem supra, haec argumenta a causis finalibus sumta esse. Venit filius Dei, ut destruat opera diaboli, non ut confirmet pecca- tum, sed ut prorsus deleto peccato et morte re- stituantur in nobis iusticia et vita aeterna etc.

## 7:4
Since you are dead to the law through the body of Christ.

This is the conclusion of the preceding exhortation, in which Paul applies the analogy of the new marriage to us, who are now another's, namely Christ's, after the condemnation has been removed: and he says it was removed through the body of Christ, namely through the victim Christ, who satisfied the law for us.

Latin:

Cum sitis mortui legi per corpus Christi.

Conclusio est superioris adhortationis, in qua Paulus accommodat similitudinem de novo coniugio ad nos, qui iam sumus alterius, scili- cet Christi, postquam condemnatio sublata est: et ait sublatam esse per corpus Christi, videlicet per victimam Christum, qui pro nobis legi sa- tisfecit.

## 7:5
When we were in the flesh.

He appends an antithesis to the conclusion, in which he narrates what the former servitude under the law was like, and what the newness is now after we have been freed from the law. Such was the servitude, that the law not only did not delete sin, but even increased and armed it, so that it might kill us. And the particle must be diligently observed: The passions of sins, which are through the law, were effective unto death.

Of which passions and of which sins does he speak? I answer: He speaks of doubt, distrust, indignation, flight, and raging against God, such as are the waves in Saul or in Judas. Where this doubt overcomes hearts, they do not call upon God, they do not seek nor expect help from him, they seek safeguards against the commandments of God. Finally, many interior and exterior sins concur, and unless a man is drawn back from this doubt and consternation, he rushes into eternal death. Therefore he says: The passions of sins, which are through the law, that is, doubt, distrust, flight, raging against God were effective, and would have driven us into eternal death, had we not been freed by the acknowledgment and trust of the Son.

Here the impious doctrine of the monks must be most severely censured, which says that doubt is not a sin, and does not show the consolation proposed in the Gospel, which commands us to overcome doubt by faith, as it is said in Rom. 4: Therefore it is of faith, that the promise might be firm. Rom. 5. chap.: Being justified by faith we have peace. John 16: The Holy Spirit will convict the world of sin, because they do not believe in me. These and similar sayings must be opposed to doubt, so that by the recognition of the Son of God, faith may be kindled and hearts may revive and rejoice in God, just as Hezekiah says: You have delivered my soul, that I might not perish, you have cast my sins behind your back.

After this consolation, man serves in the newness of the spirit, that is, in the beginnings of eternal life, and in the motions which the Holy Spirit kindles, who is substantial love and joy, and the eternal Father and Son join us to themselves by this their Spirit, who excites such love and joy in us as He Himself is.

But that sorrow precedes this joy, in which we recognize sin, and feel the wrath of God against sin.

Of this sorrow he says: Dead to the law, by which we were held captive. What then shall we say, Is the law sin?

After the digression, he returns to the comparison established above, concerning sin, law, and grace: and especially here he preaches about the use of the law, so that he may correct these two opinions which cling not only in the Jews, but universally in all souls.

For all imagine that the discipline which a man can perform in any way satisfies the law of God, and is righteousness before God, nor does reason see the magnitude of sin in human nature. But on the contrary, Paul here affirms that no one in this depravity of nature can satisfy the law of God, and that men are by no means righteous by the law, but that by it the wrath of God against sin is shown. And the thing itself shows that Paul is not here wrangling about ceremonies, but is preaching about the decalogue, about interior evils, about darkness in the human mind, about doubt, about the neglect of God, and about the manifold contumacy in the human heart against God, and about the horrible judgment and wrath of God against these interior evils.

Therefore he cites the law from the decalogue: You shall not covet, by which appellation he signifies this whole disorder (ἀταξίαν), of which he says below: The mind of the flesh is enmity against God. And Jeremiah says: The heart of man is perverse toward all things and miserable. There is another political wisdom concerning the law, concerning justice, and concerning offenses.

In political life, the law governs external acts, or, as we commonly say, the locomotive [faculty], and external discipline is called political justice, and only external crimes are punished, but Paul says: The law is spiritual, that is, not political only, but it demands spiritual motions, that is, those congruent with God in mind and heart, true light concerning God and ardent love of God.

And the law is a ministry, by which God horribly shows His wrath against sins in all men who do not agree with God, according to the saying about spiritual judgment: God is a consuming fire. God wants this doctrine concerning the law and sin, which Paul recites here, to be seen and known in the Church, He wants it to be understood what sin is, He wants it to be known that external discipline does not satisfy the law of God, and is not righteousness before God, so that we may flee to the Son of God, and learn this doctrine, of which it is said in Isaiah: The knowledge of my servant shall justify many.

The sum, however, of this narration in Paul is that we are not righteous by the law, as has often been said already, and Paul recites an example of the use of the law, proposing himself, as he speaks of himself now converted to God, and in his own person as an Apostle, he signifies that the same things happen in other living members of the Church, just as the examples of the universal Church are the conversion of David, Hezekiah, and others.

But that the example may be made clear, let us posit three degrees of men.

One is that of the carnal, who live securely, whether as Epicureans or as Pharisees, and have no true terrors of conscience.

Such a kind of life he calls here living without the law, namely, judging or accusing, because the law in them does not yet have its principal effect, to show and accuse sin. For the law is then truly called Law, when it is truly understood in the mind, and judges and accuses the hearts, not when the tablets hang on the walls. The second degree is that of those who are oppressed by terrors and torments of conscience, like Judas and Saul.

Because these do not hear the voice of the Gospel, they succumb in these terrors and feel themselves damned, therefore he says here: When the law came, sin revived, that is, it began to be effective, and oppressed me with horrible terror, and I died.

For if Paul had not heard the voice of the Gospel, he too would have perished in these terrors.

The third degree is of those who are raised up in terrors by the voice of the Gospel, as was said above: Being justified by faith we have peace. Item: He that hath the Son, hath life. These degrees being considered, this narrative of Paul can be rightly and properly understood, which Origen and others have greatly corrupted with foreign interpretations.

Now, in the text, a question is raised for the sake of explanation: Whether the law is an evil thing, since it increases sin, because in the accusation the hearts flee from God, and horribly rage against him. Paul answers by way of translation: That the law is the ministry of death, does not happen by the fault of the law, but because of our sin.

For since this depraved nature is not conformable to the law, but full of darkness and doubts, and is without fear, without love, without trust in God, and is an unspeakable stubbornness, finally since it is without God, when the wrath of God is shown through the law, it cannot sustain it, but flees, and would wish itself or God to be reduced to nothing, as it is written in Luke 23: You shall say to the mountains, fall upon us. Paul says, therefore, that the effect of the law is to show and accuse sin: afterwards the guilty nature rages against God.

Paul cites the law: Thou shalt not covet, so that he may signify that not only external sins are condemned, but also internal ones. And by the name of concupiscence are understood all the erring inclinations in this miserable nature, and the total aversion from God. Paul adds, therefore, concerning the cause in itself: Sin, having taken occasion by the law, that is, being accused by the law, provoked all concupiscence, or corrupted it, that is, it made it rage more atrociously against God, as in Judas, Saul, and the like: as it is also said afterwards: Sin by the law becomes exceedingly sinful, that is, the guilt is felt in horrible pain and in raging.

Without the law sin was dead. To be sure, without the law judging and accusing, there are not those terrors, raging, and indignation against God.

Then he begins to propose himself for the sake of example: where three degrees are to be considered, which I have recounted. I once lived without the law, that is, I was secure, when I was a Pharisee, and I dreamed that I was righteous by the law, I did not yet feel the judgment of the law and the wrath of God. Such is the greatest part of men, secure for a long time, until at last they are overwhelmed by the judgment of God.

This security and the threatening of judgment are described immediately in the first sermon in Genesis 4: Thy sin shall rest, until it is revealed. For it signifies that in the whole human race there will be security, but yet afterwards all men and individuals are overwhelmed at another time by the judgment of God, because God is a consuming fire against sin.

Zephaniah 1: It shall be in that time, I will search Jerusalem with lamps, and I will visit those who are sunk in their filth, who say in their hearts, God will not do good nor evil, and their house shall be desolate, etc. Ecclesiastes 8: It shall not be well with the wicked. And the last chapter: God will bring all into judgment. Psalm 58: Truly there is a God judging men on earth. And 62: Thou renderest to every man according to his works.

When the law came, sin revived. When the law came, that is, with the heart now accusing, so that I might feel the wrath of God against my uncleanness, hypocrisy, and security, there sin revived, that is: It became more restless, and was in itself the cause of terrors, flight, and indignation against God, and this very consternation is death: therefore it is added.

But I died, as he says to the Corinthians: The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.

And in this Chapter: Sin becomes exceedingly sinful, that is, very guilty, that is, in true terrors and in the sense of the wrath of God, the magnitude of sin is discerned in some way, which secure and idle men lightly care about, and especially hypocrites, inflated and swollen with this persuasion, that they excel others in virtue, and have served the human race usefully, such men, drunk with admiration of themselves, do not discern their own uncleanness.

Against this hypocrisy, the following things in the text are said.

We know that the law is spiritual. This saying has been most insipidly corrupted by Origen and the others who have followed him, who dreamed that this is only said, The law is spiritual, that is, allegorical in ceremonies.

Paul is doing something far different here, and he means exactly this, The divine law is spiritual, that is, not only political wisdom, or discipline restraining the locomotive [faculty], as laws in

OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS.

CHAP. VII. of empires. Let not men by any means think that they satisfy the law of God, even if they have an irreproachable external discipline.

But the divine law is wisdom in God, and the norm of justice revealed to us, by which God wills that our hearts should live by the spirit, that is, that they should have light and spiritual motions congruent with God, firm assent, and ardent love toward God, etc.

And again, the Law of God is a spiritual judgment, that is, not merely external, but such a one in which God Himself, who is spirit and a consuming fire, causes by the voice of the law that men should feel the divine wrath against sin, concerning which sense of wrath Job says: The arrows of the Lord are in me, and the terrors of God war against me.

Psalm. 50: Our God shall come, and shall not keep silence; a fire shall blaze before Him.

In such terrors we learn that the law of God is a spiritual judgment, not merely a political restraint. But I am carnal, sold under sin. He himself interprets what he calls the carnal nature, namely, the whole man sold under sin, that is, a slave of sin and death, just as this antithesis is also illustrated below: The sense of the flesh is death.

Likewise: It is enmity against God, etc.

But as by the appellation of spirit is understood the Holy Spirit Himself, and the congruent motions kindled by the Holy Spirit in the saints, life, light, and joy acquiescing in God, the flame of love toward God, so conversely let the flesh and the sense of the flesh be understood concerning the whole unregenerate man.

And not only in the appetite of the senses and in the heart is there contumacy against God, namely, unjust fires of loves, hatreds, and vengeance, but also in the higher part, namely, in the intellect of the unregenerate man, there are darkness and a great chaos of doubts about God, and the will is without fear, without love of God, without joy acquiescing in God, either despising God or fleeing Him with horrible trembling, and is without God vivifying, gladdening, and governing.

Such a man without God is called Flesh according to all the powers of the soul: and let there be in sight the doctrine concerning the distinction of the powers of the soul.

But first Paul narrates what the carnal nature is like according to itself, because he says: I am sold under sin, that is, snatched into slavery: for the phrase is taken from captives who were sold and were slaves.

Thus he says that the carnal nature according to itself is a slave of sin and death, and can neither lay aside depravity and death, nor draw back justice and life by itself, but the Son of God regenerates man by the voice of the Gospel and the Holy Spirit.

Although, however, the beginnings of new light and spiritual motions are kindled in the regenerate, yet in this mortal life the remnants of the former disease still cling to the carnal nature.

There follows, therefore, a struggle, in which the Word and the Holy Spirit mortify those remnants: this struggle Paul will soon describe.

But when he uses the word Sold, he looks to the saying of Isaiah 52: You have been sold for nothing, you shall be redeemed without silver.

Where God objects injustice to the devil, as if He were to say: I will act by a just order.

The devil snatched you from me by fraud, and he neither paid me a price, nor gave you the promises.

It is just, therefore, in turn, that I recover my own property, without a price being given to the robber.

For just as a thing is not to be bought back from a thief or robber, but is restored to the Lord without a price by a just judge: so God recovers the human race, paying nothing to the unjust and wicked robber, the devil.

He said, therefore: You have been sold for nothing, that is, you have been unjustly dragged into slavery by the fraud of the devil, and no price was paid to God, nor were promises given to men.

Therefore, again, you are redeemed for nothing; I will not give a price to the Devil, and I will receive you by my mercy, since he cannot give me a price.

But the following narrative of this chapter shows, when Paul says, You have been sold under sin, he understands original sin, not merely imputation, as many monks have understood, but the very depravity of human nature, that is, darkness and doubts in the intellect, and the aversion of the will from God, contempt and trembling against God, and the contumacy of the heart, and that all powers are without God vivifying, gladdening, and governing: as he says afterwards: I see another law in my members. I delight in the law of God according to the inner man, etc. In this narrative is described the contest which is in the Regenerate, in whom the Son of God by the voice of the Gospel kindles light and the beginnings of faith, and the Holy Spirit consoles the heart, so that it may begin to rejoice in God. and has motions congruent with God, or the law of God. This light, however, and these divine motions are hindered by our carnal nature, in which there is much darkness and contrary motions, just as light can be seen less clearly in a darker lantern. God wishes these remnants of sin to be acknowledged and deplored; He does not wish them to be extenuated, as the monks have extenuated them, who said that the reborn are righteous by this new obedience of theirs, and said that it is the fulfillment of the law, and they exaggerated these things so much that they said those works were merits of eternal life by worthiness. Against these errors, these testimonies, handed down everywhere in the prophetic and apostolic writings, must be held, which show that in the reborn in this life there is great darkness and remaining doubts, and that hearts do not burn so with love and joy in God, with gratitude toward Him and patience, as they ought, and that these evils are sins, that is, evils fighting against the law, on account of which man would be worthy of eternal punishments if they were not remitted to the believer on account of the mediator.

Therefore, Moses also says: Before you, the innocent is not innocent. And Job ch. 9: Truly I know that there is no man righteous before God, namely, by the proper fulfillment of the law. And again in the same chapter: I fear all my pains, because I know that you do not find the innocent. And in the Psalm: No one living shall be justified in your sight. Item: Blessed are they whose iniquities are remitted, etc. Item: For this, every saint shall pray to you in an opportune time. Similar to these confessions of the Prophets is this complaint of Paul: and the Prophets and Apostles represent the whole Church in this confession.

Let this narrative about the Reborn be understood, therefore, and let us know that the interpretation of the monks is false and to be rejected, who said that in this place Paul is speaking about a man not yet converted; that this is false is shown by the text itself, which says: I delight in the law of God according to the inner man. But a man not yet reborn does not delight in the law of God. For although there is in a man not yet reborn a knowledge of the law, yet the will and heart do not delight in the law of God, but are either entirely without the fear of God, or they rage against Him. And Paul names the inner man insofar as a man is Reborn, namely, insofar as the beginnings of faith shine in the mind, will, and heart, and through the Holy Spirit these motions are kindled: the fear of God, love, joy in God, etc. Paul adds, however, a splendid antithesis illustrated by figures taken from warfare: I find another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and taking me captive to the law of sin, which is in my members. By the word Law, let governance be understood here generally, as if he were saying: One thing is that which governs the inner man, namely, the Word and the Holy Spirit: another is that which governs the carnal nature, namely, blind doubts and impulses turned away from God, wandering flames of desires, impatience in the cross, etc. These evils, he says, are in my members, and they are not light diseases, but they hinder, weaken, and accuse me in a constant warfare.

Latin:

Cum essemus in carne.

Attexit conclusioni antithesin, in qua nar- rat qualis fuerit prior servitus sub lege, et qualis sit nunc novitas postquam a lege liberati sumus. Talis erat servitus, ut lex non solum non dele- verit peccatum, sed etiam auxerit et armaverit, ut nos occideret. Ac diligenter observanda est particula: Affectus peccatorum, qui per legem sunt, erant efficaces ad mortem.

De quibus affectibus et de quibus peccatis loquitur? Respondeo: Loquitur de dubitatione, diffidentia, indignatione, fuga et fremitu adver- sus Deum, quales sunt fluctus in Saule aut in Iuda. Ubi haec dubitatio vincit corda, non in- vocant Deum, non petunt nec expectant ab eo auxilium, quaerunt praesidia contra mandata Dei. Denique multa peccata interiora et exteriora concurrunt, et nisi homo retrahatur ex hac du- bitatione et consternatione, ruit in mortem ae- ternam. Ideo dicit: Affectus peccatorum, qui sunt per legem, id est, dubitatio, diffidentia, fuga, fremitus adversus Deum erant efficaces, et impulissent nos in mortem aeternam, nisi libe- rati essemus agnitione et fiducia filii.

Hic severissime taxanda est impia doctrina monachorum, quae ait, dubitationem non esse peccatum, et non ostendit consolationem in Evangelio propositam, quae iubet vincere dubitationem fide, ut dicitur Rom. 4.: Ideo ex fide, ut sit firma promissio. Rom. 5. cap.: Iustificati fide pacem habemus. Iohannis 16.: Spiritus sanctus arguet mundum de peccato, quod non credunt in me. Haec et similia dicta opponenda sunt dubitationi, ut agnitione filii Dei accendatur fides et reviviscant corda et laetentur in Deo, sicut inquit Ezechias: Tu eruisti animam meam, ut non perirem, proiecisti post tergum peccata mea.

Post hanc consolationem homo servit in novitate spiritus, id est, in vitae aeternae initiis, et motibus quos accendit Spiritus sanctus, qui est amor et laetitia substantialis, et copulant nos sibi aeternus pater et filius hoc suo spiritu, qui talem amorem et laetitiam excusitat in nobis, qualis est ipse.

Praecedit autem hanc laetitiam dolor ille, in quo agnoscimus peccatum, et sentimus iram Dei adversus peccatum.

De hoc dolore inquit: Mortui legi, qua captivi tenebamur. Quid igitur dicemus, Num lex peccatum est?

Post digressionem redit ad collationem supra institutam, de peccato, lege et gratia: ac praecipue hic concionatur de usu legis, ut has duas opiniones non tantum in Iudaeis, sed universaliter in omnibus animis haerentes emendet.

Omnes enim imaginantur disciplinam, quam homo utcunque praestare potest, satisfacere legi Dei, et esse iusticiam coram Deo, nec videt ratio magnitudinem peccati in natura humana. Contra vero Paulus hic affirmat, neminem in hac naturae depravatione legi Dei satisfacere posse, et homines nequaquam iustos esse lege, sed ab ea ostendi iram Dei adversus peccatum. Ac res ipsa ostendit Paulum hic non rixari de ceremoniis, sed concionari de decalogo, de interioribus malis, de tenebris in mente humana, de dubitatione, de neglectione Dei, et multiplici contumacia in corde humano adversus Deum, et de horribili iudicio et ira Dei adversus haec interiora mala.

Ideo citat legem ex decalogo: Non concupisces, qua appellatione significat hanc totam ἀταξίαν, de qua infra dicit: Sensus carnis inimicitia est adversus Deum. Et Ieremias inquit: Perversum est cor hominis erga omnia et aerumnosum. Alia est sapientia politica de lege, de iusticia, et de delictis.

In vita politica lex regit externa facta, seu, ut dicimus usitate Locomotivam, et disciplina externa nominatur iusticia politica, et tantum externa scelera puniuntur, sed Paulus inquit: Lex spiritualis, id est, non politica tantum, sed postulat motus spirituales, id est, congruentes cum Deo in mente et corde, veram lucem de Deo et ardentem dilectionem Dei.

Et ministerium est lex, quo Deus horribiliter ostendit iram suam contra peccata in omnibus hominibus, qui non congruunt cum Deo, iuxta dictum de spirituali iudicio: Deus est ignis consumens. Hanc doctrinam de lege et de peccato, quam hic Paulus recitat, vult Deus conspici et notam esse in Ecclesia, vult intelligi quid sit peccatum, vult sciri externam disciplinam non satisfacere legi Dei, et non esse iusticiam coram Deo, ut confugiamus ad filium Dei, et discamus hanc doctrinam, de qua dicitur in Esaia: Noticia servi mei iustificabit multos.

Summa autem huius narrationis apud Paulum est, quod non simus lege iusti, ut saepe iam dictum est, et Paulus exemplum de usu legis recitat, se ipsum proponens, ut loquitur de se converso iam ad Deum, et sua persona tanquam Apostoli, significat eadem fieri in aliis vivis membris Ecclesiae, sicut exempla universae Ecclesiae sunt, conversio Davidis, Ezechiae et aliorum.

Ut autem exemplum fiat illustre, ponamus tres hominum gradus.

Unus est carnalium, qui vivunt securi, seu ut Epicurei, seu ut Pharisaei, nec habent veros pavores conscientiae.

Tale vitae genus nominat hic vivere sine lege, scilicet iudicante seu accusante, quia lex in illis nondum habet principalem effectum, ut ostendat et accuset peccatum. Lex enim tunc vere Lex dicitur, cum in mente vere intelligitur, et iudicat et accusat corda, non cum tabulae pendent in parietibus. Secundus gradus est eorum, qui opprimuntur terroribus et cruciatibus conscientiae, sicut Iudas et Saul.

Hi quia non audiunt vocem Evangelii, succumbunt in his terroribus et sentiunt se damnari, ideo hic inquit: Veniente lege peccatum revixit, id est, coepit esse efficax, et horribili terrore me oppressit, et ego mortuus sum.

Nisi enim Paulus audivisset vocem Evangelii, ipse quoque periisset in his terroribus.

Tertius gradus est illorum, qui in terroribus eriguntur voce Evangelii, sicut supra dictum est: Iustificati fide pacem habemus. Item: Qui habet Christum, habet vitam. His gradibus consideratis haec narratio Pauli recte et proprie intelligi poterit, quam peregrinis interpretationibus Origenes et alii valde corruperunt.

Est autem in textu declarandi causa instituta quaestio, Num lex sit res mala, cum augeat peccatum, quia in accusatione corda fugiunt Deum, et horribiliter fremunt adversus eum. Respondet Paulus per translationem: Quod lex est ministerium mortis, non fit legis vitio, sed propter nostrum peccatum.

Cum enim haec depravata natura non sit conformis legi, sed plena tenebrarum et dubitationum, et sit sine timore, sine dilectione, sine fiducia Dei, et sit inenarrabilis contumacia, denique cum sit sine Deo, quando per legem ostenditur ira Dei, non potest eam sustinere, sed fugit, et vellet se aut Deum in nihilum redigi, sicut scriptum est Lucae 23.: Dicetis montibus, cadite super nos. Ait ergo Paulus, Effectum legis esse ostendere et accusare peccatum: postea natura rea fremit adversus Deum.

Paulus citat legem: Non concupisces, ut significet non tantum externa peccata damnari, sed etiam interiora. Et nomine concupiscentiae intelligantur omnes errantes inclinationes in hac misera natura, et tota aversio a Deo. Addit igitur Paulus de per se causa: Peccatum occasione accepta per legem, id est, lege accusatum, irritavit omnem concupiscentiam, seu corrupit, id est, fecit eam atrocius frementem adversus Deum, ut in Iuda, Saul, et similibus: ut et postea dicitur: Peccatum per legem fit excellenter peccatum, id est, reatus sentitur in horribili dolore in fremitu.

Sine lege peccatum erat mortuum. Scilicet, sine lege iudicante et accusante non sunt illi terrores, fremitus et indignatio adversus Deum.

Deinde incipit sese exempli causa proponere: ubi tres gradus considerentur, quos recensui. Ego aliquando sine lege vixi, id est, fui securus, cum essem Pharisaeus, et somniam me lege iustum esse, nondum sentiebam iudicium legis et iram Dei. Talis est maxima pars hominum, secura longo tempore, donec tandem iudicio Dei obruitur.
