Haec securitas et comminatio iudicii describuntur statim in prima concione Genesis 4.: Peccatum tuum quiescet, donec revelabitur. Significat enim in toto genere humano futuram esse securitatem, sed tamen postea omnes homines et singulos alios alio tempore obrui iudicio Dei, quia Deus est ignis consumens adversus peccatum.

Sopho. 1.: Erit in tempore illo, scrutabor Ierusalem lucernis, et visitabo mersos in feces suas, qui dicunt in cordibus, non faciet Deus bene nec male, et erit domus eorum deserta etc. Ecclesiast. 8.: Non erit bene impio. Et cap. ultimo: Cunctos adducet Deus in iudicium. Psalm. 58.: Utique est Deus iudicans homines in terra. Et 62.: Tu reddis unicuique iuxta opera sua.

Veniente lege peccatum revixit. Veniente lege, id est, iam accusante cor, ut sentirem iram Dei adversus immunditiem meam, hypocrisin et securitatem, ibi peccatum revixit, id est: Factum est inquietius, et fuit per se causa pavorum, fugae, et indignationis adversus Deum, et haec ipsa consternatio est mors: ideo additum est.

Ego autem mortuus sum, Sicut ad Corinth.

inquit: Aculeus mortis peccatum est, potentia vero peccati lex est. Et in hoc Capite: Peccatum fit excellenter peccatum, id est, valde reum, hoc est, in veris pavoribus et sensu irae Dei cernitur aliquo modo peccati magnitudo, quam securi et otiosi homines leviter curant, et praesertim hypocritae inflati et tumentes hac persuasione, quod antecellant aliis virtute, et utiliter servierint humano generi, tales ebrii admiratione sui, non cernunt immunditiem suam.

Adversus hanc hypocrisin dicuntur et sequentia in textu.

Scimus quod lex spiritualis sit. Hoc dictum insulsissime depravatum est ab Origene et caeteris, qui eum secuti sunt, qui somniarunt tantum hoc dici, Lex est spiritualis, id est, allegorica in ceremoniis.

Longe aliud hic agit Paulus, et prorsus hoc sentit, Lex divina est spiritualis, id est, non tantum politica sapientia, vel disciplina frenans locomotivam, sicut leges in

PAULI AD ROMANOS.

CAP. VII. imperiis. Nequaquam existiment homines se legi Dei satisfacere, etiamsi habent externam disciplinam inculpatam.

Sed lex divina est sapientia in Deo, et norma iustitiae nobis patefacta, qua vult Deus ut corda nostra vivant spiritu, id est, habeant lucem et motus spirituales congruentes cum Deo, firmam assensionem et ardentem amorem erga Deum etc.

Et rursus, Lex Dei est iudicium spirituale, id est, non externum tantum, sed tale, in quo Deus ipse, qui est spiritus et ignis consumens, facit voce legis, ut sentiant homines iram divinam adversus peccatum, de quo sensu irae inquit Iob.: Sagittae Domini in me, et terrores Dei militant contra me.

Psalm. 50.: Veniet Deus noster, et non silebit, in conspectu eius exardescet ignis.

In talibus pauoribus discimus legem Dei esse spirituale iudicium, non tantum politicum frenum. Ego autem carnalis sum, venundatus sub peccatum. Interpretatur ipse quid nominet carnalem naturam, scilicet, totum hominem venundatum sub peccatum, id est, servum peccati et mortis, sicut et infra haec antithesis illustratur: Sensus carnis mors est.

Item: Inimicitia est adversus Deum etc.

Ut autem appellatione spiritus intelligitur ipse Spiritus sanctus, et a Spiritu sancto accensi congruentes motus in sanctis, vita, lux, et laetitia acquiescens in Deo, flamma dilectionis erga Deum, sic e regione caro sensus carnis intelligantur, de toto homine non renato.

Nec solum in appetitu sensuum et in corde est contumacia contra Deum, videlicet, iniusta incendia amorum, odiorum, vindictae, sed etiam in superiore parte, videlicet, in intellectu hominis non renati sunt tenebrae et magnum chaos dubitationum de Deo, et voluntas est sine timore, sine dilectione Dei, sine laetitia acquiescente in Deo aut contemnens Deum, aut horribili fremitu fugiens eum, et est sine Deo vivificante, laetificante et gubernante.

Talis homo sine Deo dicitur Caro secundum omnes animae potentias: et in conspectu sit doctrina de distinctione potentiarum animae.

Primum autem narrat Paulus qualis sit natura carnalis secundum sese, quia inquit: Venundatus sum sub peccatum, id est, raptus in servitutem: Phrasis enim sumta est a captivis, qui vendebantur et erant servi.

Ita inquit, naturam carnalem secundum sese servam peccati et mortis esse, nec posse deponere pravitatem et mortem, nec retrahere per sese iustitiam et vitam, sed filius Dei voce Evangelii et Spiritu sancto regenerat hominem.

Quanquam autem initia novae lucis et motuum spiritualium in renatis accenduntur, tamen in hac mortali vita haerent adhuc in natura carnali reliquiae prioris morbi.

Sequitur ergo lucta, in qua verbum et Spiritus sanctus mortificant reliquias illas: hanc luctam mox describet Paulus.

Cum autem utitur vocabulo Venundatus, intuetur dictum Esaiae 52.: Gratis venundati estis, sine argento redimemini.

Ubi Deus obiicit diabolo iniustitiam, quasi dicat: Agam iusto ordine.

Diabolus vos fraude mihi eripuit, et neque mihi solvit pretium, neque vobis dedit promissa.

Iustum est igitur vicissim, me rem meam recuperare, non dato pretio praedoni.

Sicut enim a fure aut praedone res non rursus emenda est, sed sine pretio per iudicem iustum restituitur Domino: ita Deus recuperat genus humanum, nihil solvens iniusto et scelerato praedoni diabolo.

Dixit igitur: Gratis venundati estis, id est, iniuste in servitutem pertracti estis fraude diaboli, nec Deo solutum est pretium, neque hominibus data promissa.

Rursus igitur gratis redimemini, non dabo pretium Diabolo, et vos recipiam mea misericordia, cum mihi pretium non possit dare.

Ostendit autem sequens narratio huius capitis, cum inquit Paulus, Venundati estis sub peccatum, intelligit peccatum originale, non tantum imputationem, sicut multi monachi intellexerunt, sed ipsam naturae humanae depravationem, id est, tenebras et dubitationes in intellectu, et aversionem voluntatis a Deo, contemtum et fremitum adversus Deum, et cordis contumaciam, Et quod vires omnes sunt sine Deo vivificante, laetificante et gubernante: sicut postea inquit: Video aliam legem in membris meis. Condelector lege Dei secundum interiorem hominem etc. In hac narratione describitur certamen, quod est in Renatis, in quibus filius Dei voce Evangelii accendit lucem et initia fidei, et Spiritus sanctus consolatur cor, ut incipiat laetari in Deo, et habeat motus congruentes cum Deo, seu lege Dei. Haec lux tamen et hi motus divini impediuntur a nostra carnali natura, in qua multum caliginis est, et contrariorum motuum, sicut minus conspici potest lumen in laterna obscuriore. Has peccati reliquias vult agnosci et deplorari Deus, non vult extenuari, sicut monachi extenuaverunt, qui dixerunt, Renatos iustos esse hac sua nova obedientia, et dixerunt, esse legis impletionem, et haec ita exaggeraverunt, ut dixerint, illa opera esse merita vitae aeternae de condigno. Adversus hos errores tenenda sunt haec testimonia passim tradita in scriptis propheticis et apostolicis, quae ostendunt in renatis in hac vita magnam caliginem et dubitationes reliquas esse, et corda non sic ardere dilectione et laetitia in Deo, gratitudine erga eum et patientia, sicut debebant, et haec mala esse peccata, id est, mala pugnantia cum lege, propter quae homo dignus esset poenis aeternis, si non remitterentur propter mediatorem credenti.

Ideo et Moises inquit: Coram te innocens non est innocens. Et Iob cap. 9.: Vere scio quod non est homo iustus coram Deo, scilicet, propria legis impletione. Et rursus eodem cap.: Timeo omnes dolores meos, quia scio, quod non invenis innocentem. Et in Psalmo: Non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens. Item: Beati quorum remissae sunt iniquitates etc. Item: Pro hoc orabit ad te omnis sanctus in tempore oportuno. His confessionibus Prophetarum similis est et haec Pauli querela: et repraesentant Prophetae et Apostoli totam Ecclesiam in hac confessione.

Intelligatur ergo haec narratio de Renatis, et sciamus monachorum interpretationem falsam et reiiciendam esse, qui dixerunt, hoc loco Paulum de homine nondum converso loqui, id falsum esse ostenditur ex ipso textu, qui dicit: Delector lege Dei secundum interiorem hominem. At homo nondum renatus non delectatur lege Dei. Etsi enim est in homine nondum renato noticia legis, tamen voluntas et cor non delectantur lege Dei, sed sunt aut prorsus sine timore Dei, aut fremunt adversus eum. Et nominat Paulus interiorem hominem, quatenus homo Renatus est, videlicet, quatenus luceat in mente, voluntate et corde initia fidei, et per Spiritum sanctum accensi sunt motus isti, timor Dei, dilectio, laetitia in Deo etc. Addit autem Paulus splendidam antithesin illustratam figuris a militia sumtis: Invenio aliam legem in membris meis, militantem contra legem mentis meae, et rapientem me captivum legi peccati, quae est in membris meis. Vocabulo Legis generaliter hic intelligatur gubernatio, quasi dicat: Aliud est gubernans interiorem hominem, scilicet verbum et Spiritus sanctus: aliud est gubernans carnalem naturam, scilicet coecae dubitationes et impetus aversi a Deo, errantes flammae cupiditatum, impatientia in cruce etc. Haec mala, inquit, sunt in membris meis, et non sunt leves morbi, sed adsidua militia impediunt, languefaciunt et accusant me.

## 7:25 Disposition of Romans
Of grace and the effect of grace.

Latin:

De gratiae et effectu gratiae.

## 8:1 Disposition of Romans: Argument
Chapter VIII.

Thus far he has spoken of the effect of the law, and showed that the law does not justify, but only terrifies consciences, and begets hatred of God, and despair. Likewise, he showed how sin clings to nature. Now he speaks of the power of grace.

Proposition: There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh, but according to the spirit. I said above that grace comprises two things: the remission of sins, or the favor of God, and the gift of the Holy Spirit. Here, therefore, Paul joins these two. First, he says there is no condemnation. He does not say there is no sin, for he signifies that sin is present in the saints, but that it is forgiven on account of faith in Christ. Secondly, that sin is also overcome by the Holy Spirit, who is given to believers.

There follows either the reason, or the exposition of the proposition, concerning the effect of the Holy Spirit. Because the law of the spirit of life in Christ Jesus frees me from the law of sin and death, that is, the governance of the Holy Spirit, who gives life, who is conceived by faith in Christ, does not allow sin and death to rule. Although sin and death are present, they do not rule. Sin cannot drive to despair, death cannot absorb, because the Holy Spirit, who is conceived by faith in Christ, sustains, consoles, and gives life in those terrors. In the word 'law' here there is a μετάληψις: for it signifies not some writing, but governance, for he adds, 'the law of the spirit of life,' that is, the governance which is done through the life-giving spirit.

Αἰτιολογία from the contrary.

Since the law could not be done because of the weakness of the flesh, God sent his son, who would make satisfaction for sin, so that the justification of the law might be fulfilled in us, and the Holy Spirit might be given.

Amplification through contention or Antithesis of natural powers, and the efficacy of the Holy Spirit. First Antithesis.

Those who are according to the flesh, savor, love, and seek carnal wisdom, justice, tranquility, pleasures, and wealth. They trust in carnal things, human prudence, justice, powers, and wealth. For there are three degrees of things which the flesh seeks. The first is of honest things, of human wisdom and justice. The second is of useful things, of glory, wealth, power, and tranquility. The third is of pleasures.

Those who are according to the spirit, savor spiritual things, that is, they know the will of God, they trust in God, they rejoice to obey the will of God in the cross, etc. For 'spirit' signifies the Holy Spirit, who is poured out into those who believe. And 'spiritual things' signify not those things which reason produces, but new motions, in which God is apprehended, who, since he is spirit, is discerned by the spirit. 'Flesh' signifies the whole nature of man, reason with sense and appetite, λόγον and ὁρμὴν. And they dissent entirely from Paul who dream that 'spirit' signifies reason, and make a certain human philosophy out of the Gospel, requiring nothing beyond the works of reason. There are many arguments in this chapter which confirm that 'spirit' does not signify reason. For Paul says a little later: 'You are not in the flesh, but in the spirit, if indeed the spirit of God dwells in you.' Likewise, if anyone does not have the spirit of Christ, he is not of Christ. Therefore, he who does not have the spirit of Christ, even if he uses reason, and even if he follows philosophy, is not yet just before God. Nor indeed does the 'spirit of Christ' signify our reason, but the Holy Spirit, for below he testifies that he is speaking about the spirit which the saints receive. But it is not the place here to pursue this dispute; I only wished to warn the reader to reject profane glosses. For this whole chapter of Paul has been wickedly contaminated by Origen and others, who, as if sworn to the words of Origen, ὑπερασπίζουσι τῆς φιλοσοφίας αὐτοῦ: but the untimely philosophy of these men, while they attribute justification to the powers of reason, arises from the fact that they think nothing is required in man except civil works. And these they see to be in some way in the power of reason. Thus they forget the first table, which commands concerning the fear of God and trust in God and other spiritual affections. But Paul speaks about the whole law and about justice before God, not about politics. Now philosophy itself cries out that reason can determine nothing about the will of God, that it cannot trust except in present things, etc. But I return to the Pauline Antithesis.

Second Antithesis.

The sense of the flesh is death; understand this concerning knowledge and appetite, although good rational knowledge about morals, although good works effected by reason, are death; they do not sustain, they do not give life in the judgment of God.

The sense of the spirit is life and peace; understand this concerning knowledge and affections. To truly know God, to truly trust in God, gives life, and renders the conscience peaceful, and is eternal life, as Christ says: 'This is eternal life, that they may know you the true God and Jesus whom you have sent to be Christ.'

Reason of the Antithesis.

The mind of the flesh is enmity against God, for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can it be subject to the law of God. It is a manifest sentence that the natural powers of man cannot fulfill the law of God. Here I again admonish the reader of the first table, to which if we look, it will be easily understood what Paul says, that the mind of the flesh is enmity against God. For reason determines nothing concerning the will of God, does not fear God, does not trust in God, but he trusts in present things, in human wisdom, in human justice, in riches, in strength.

Apostrophe to the Readers.

Those who are in the flesh cannot please God, but you are not in the flesh, but in the spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. By merely changing the person, he repeats the antithesis and declares that he calls it spirit, not some part of reason, but the Holy Spirit, who is God by nature, given to believers so that He may beget the knowledge of God in them, and beget new motions and a new life. And he calls it now the spirit of God, now the spirit of Christ, to signify that Christ also is God by nature, because He bestows the Holy Spirit. Moreover, this change of person is a kind of peroration, which follows immediately, παρασκευή.

Peroration or Conclusion.

Therefore, brothers, we are debtors not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. This is the end of the method in which he explained the effects of sin, law, and grace. Now, after he has taught the reader about the principal points of Christian doctrine, he adds a peroration, but one taken from the persuasive genre. For the listener must always first be taught what the matter is. Afterwards, he must be urged to transfer the doctrine to use. Moreover, this peroration is hortatory at the beginning, then consolatory.

Latin:

Caput VIII.

Hactenus de legis effectu dixit, et ostendit, quod lex non iustificet, tantum perterrefaciat conscientias, et pariat odium Dei, et desperatio- nem. Item ostendit quomodo peccatum haereat in natura. Nunc de gratiae vi loquitur.

Propositio: Nulla condemnatio his, qui in Christo Iesu, non secundum carnem ambulant, sed secundum spiritum. Dixi supra gratiam duo complecti, remissionem peccatorum, seu favo- rem Dei, et donationem Spiritus sancti. Hic igitur coniungit haec duo Paulus. Primum ait non esse condemnationem. Non dicit, non est peccatum, significat enim adesse peccatum in sanctis, sed remitti propter fidem in Christum. Secundo, id peccatum etiam vinci Spiritu sancto, qui donatur credentibus.

Sequitur seu ratio, seu expolitio propsitio- nis, de effectu Spiritus sancti. Quia lex spiritus vitae in Christo Iesu libe- rat me a lege peccati et mortis, id est, guberna- tio Spiritus sancti, qui vivificat, qui fide in Chri- stum concipitur, non sinit dominari peccatum et mortem. Tametsi adsint peccatum et mors, ta- men non dominantur. Peccatum non potest adi- gere ad desperationem, mors non potest absor- bere, quia Spiritus sanctus, qui fide in Christum concipitur, sustentat, consolatur, et vivificat in illis terroribus. In vocabulo legis hic μετάληψις est: significat enim non scripturam aliquam, sed gubernationem, addit enim, lex spiritus vitae, id est, gubernatio, quae fit per spiritum vivi- ficantem.

Αἰτιολογία ex contrario.

Cum lex fieri non posset propter carnis im- becillitatem, Deus misit filium suum, qui satis- faceret pro peccato, ut iustificatio legis implere- tur in nobis, et daretur Spiritus sanctus.

Amplificatio per contentionem seu Antithesin naturalium virium, et ef- ficaciae Spiritus sancti. Prima Antithesis.

Qui secundum carnem sunt, carnalia sapiunt, amant, quaerunt carnalem sapientiam, iusticiam, tranquillitatem, voluptates, opes. Confidunt rebus carnalibus, humana prudentia, iusticia, viribus, opibus. Tres enim gradus sunt rerum, quas expetit caro. Primus est rerum honesta- rum, sapientiae et iusticiae humanae. Secundus est rerum utilium, gloriae, opum, potentiae et tranquillitatis. Tertius est voluptatum.

Qui secundum spiritum sunt, sapiunt spiri- tualia, id est, norunt voluntatem Dei, confi- dunt Deo, gaudent obtemperare voluntati Dei in cruce etc. Spiritus enim significat Spiritum san- ctum, qui effunditur in eos qui credunt. Et Spi- ritualia significant non ea, quae ratio efficit, sed novos motus, in quibus apprehenditur Deus, qui cum sit spiritus, spiritu cernitur. Caro signifi- cat totam hominis naturam, rationem cum sensu et appetitu, λόγον et ὁρμὴν. Et prorsus a Paulo dissentiunt, qui somniant Spiritum significare ra- tionem, et ex Evangelio philosophiam quandam humanam faciunt, nihil praeter rationis opera requirentes. Multa sunt argumenta in hoc capite, quae confirmant quod spiritus non significet ra- tionem. Nam Paulus aliquanto post ait: Vos in carne non estis, sed in spiritu, siquidem spiritus Dei habitat in vobis. Item, si quis spiritum Christi non habet, is non est Christi, Ergo qui spiritum Christi non habet, etiamsi ratione uti- tur, etiamsi philosophiam sequitur, nondum ta- men iustus est coram Deo. Neque vero spiritus Christi significat rationem nostram, sed Spiritum sanctum, infra enim testatur se loqui de spiritu, quem accipiunt sancti. Sed non est huius loci persequi hanc disputationem, tantum monere lectorem volui, ut prophana glossemata repudiet. Nam hoc totum caput Pauli sceleste contamina- tum est ab Origene et aliis, cui tanquam iurati in verba Origenis ὑπερασπίζουσι τῆς φιλοσοφίας αὐτοῦ: sed horum intempestiva philosophia, dum tribuunt iustificationem viribus rationis, inde ori- tur, quod nihil requiri putant in homine, nisi civilia opera. Et haec vident aliquo modo in potestate rationis esse. Sic obliviscuntur primae tabulae, quae de timore Dei et fiducia in Deum et aliis spiritualibus affectibus praecipit. At Pau- lus de tota lege et de iusticia coram Deo, non de politia loquitur. Iam philosophia ipsa clami- tat, quod ratio nihil possit de Dei voluntate sta- tuere, quod non possit confidere, nisi rebus prae- sentibus etc. Sed redeo ad Paulinam Antithesin.

Secunda Antithesis.

Sensus carnis mors est, de noticia et appe- titu intellige, quamvis bona noticia rationalis de moribus, quamvis bona opera ratione effecta, sunt mors, non sustenant, non vivificant in iu- dicio Dei.

Sensus spiritus vita est et pax, intellige de noticia et affectibus. Vero nosse Deum, vere confidere Deo, vivificat, et reddit pacatam con- scientiam, et est vita aeterna, ut Christus ait: Haec est vita aeterna, ut noscant te Deum verum et quem misisti Iesum esse Christum.

Ratio Antithesis.

Sensus carnis inimicicia est adversus Deum, qui legi Dei non subditur, neque enim potest legi Dei subiici. Manifesta sententia est, quod natu- rales hominis vires non possint legem Dei facere. Hic iterum admoneo lectorem primae tabulae, ad quam si respexerimus, facile intelligi poterit hoc quod ait Paulus, sensum carnis inimicitiam esse adversus Deum. Ratio enim nihil statuit de vo- luntate Dei, non timet Deum, non confidit Deo, sed confidit rebus praesentibus, humana sapientia, humana iusticia, opibus, viribus.

Apostrophe ad Lectores.

Qui in carne sunt Deo placere non possunt, vos autem non estis in carne, sed spiritu, siqui- dem spiritus Dei habitat in vobis. Tantum mu- tata persona repetit antithesin, et declarat se spiritum vocare, non aliquam rationis partem, sed Spiritum sanctum, qui natura Deus est, do- natum credentibus, ut gignat noticiam Dei in eis, gignat novos motus et novam vitam. Et vocat nunc spiritum Dei, nunc spiritum Christi, ut significet et Christum natura Deum esse, quia largitur Spiritum sanctum. Est autem haec per- sonae mutatio quaedam perorationis, quae mox sequitur, παρασκευή.

Peroratio seu Conclusio.

Ergo fratres debitores sumus non carni, ut secundum carnem vivamus. Hic finis est metho- di, in qua explicavit peccati, legis et gratiae ef- fectus. Nunc postquam lectorem de praecipuis locis doctrinae Christianae docuit, addit perora- tionem, sed ex suasorio genere sumtam. Sem- per enim primum docendus est auditor, quid res sit. Postea incitandus est, ut doctrinam ad usum transferat. Est autem haec peroratio initio adhor- toria, deinde consolatoria.

## 8:1 Argument
Chapter VIII.

There is therefore now no condemnation to those who walk in Christ Jesus, etc.

It was said above that a comparison of Sin, Law, and Grace had been instituted. Now he returns to the description of grace, and it is a consolation added to the previous complaint. For since he had said before that sin still clings to the saints in this life. The question is common to all saints, how are they righteous? That is, accepted by God and heirs of eternal life, when they still feel sins, their own doubts, and it is necessary to confess that all good motions are very languid—the fear of God, love, faith, hope—and meanwhile many wandering flames of desires are at the same time in their hearts. To this common question of all the saints, he responds with a clear asseveration: There is now no condemnation to those who walk in Christ Jesus not according to the flesh, but according to the spirit. He said the same above: Being justified by faith we have peace, etc. Item: You are not under the law, but under grace. He interprets, however, the word Grace by the removal of its contrary: There is now no condemnation: because the word Grace is a relative name, that is, a gratuitous acceptance, which is said more plainly, No condemnation: nor does he say, There is now no sin. And this is the meaning: Those justified by faith are pleasing to God on account of the mediator Son, and are heirs of eternal life, even if sins cling to them, namely, vicious concupiscence and evil effects, if nevertheless they are in Christ Jesus, and walk according to the spirit.

that is, if there be in them a conversion to God, and faith comforting their hearts by the recognition of the Son of God, which faith indeed is the motion of the Holy Spirit, who afterwards governs and sanctifies the reborn, so that they may resist depraved affections. This is the principal proposition in this chapter, containing doctrine and consolation for the Church necessary at all times. This has always been, is, and will be the question in the minds of all the saints: how do you please God, when you still feel many impurities? The Pharisees and monks taught men to please God by their own merits, and by sacrifices, by Masses. Thus they confirmed the confidence of their own dignity in those who are still secure, and led men to sacrifices, where vain confidence from sacrifices made idols. Afterwards, having disturbed their security, they ordered men to remain in doubt. These things are simply heathen, and remaining in doubt, one is finally oppressed by despair, and with a horrible roar rushes into eternal destruction. But the voice of the Gospel forbids doubt and commands that we believe in the Son of God, and it cries out and affirms that those who believe in the Son please God, even if the remnants of sin cling to the converted: this necessary doctrine and consolation is proposed here.

Wherefore let this testimony of Paul always be in sight. It must be observed, however, that he says expressly: To those walking in Christ according to the spirit, not according to the flesh.

He does not promise consolation to those who are without repentance, who, secure and raging, persevere in wickedness against their conscience, of whom it will be said later: If you live according to the flesh, you shall die. Item: He who commits sin is of the devil. Item: Those who do such things shall not possess the kingdom of God. But of those he says: There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, and are ruled by the Holy Spirit.

He names two persons: Christ the mediator, because first it is necessary for the converted to recognize Christ by faith, and through this propitiator to receive remission and reconciliation, and to become his members. But when hearts are raised up by the recognition of the mediator and by faith, the Holy Spirit is simultaneously poured into the hearts, so that he may kindle such motions as he himself is, according to the saying: I will pour out upon the house of David the spirit of grace and of supplications. Item, 2 Corinthians 3: We are transformed into the same image, as by the Spirit of the Lord. For the law of the spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set me free etc. Previously the proposition was delivered: There is now no condemnation for those who walk in Christ Jesus etc.

Now follows the declaration of this proposition: We are set free through Christ, where mention is made at the same time of the merit of Christ and of his efficacy. Here he discourses on the merit of Christ, when he names him a sacrifice for sin, and says that because of this sacrifice sin was condemned. Concerning the efficacy of Christ in believers it is said: The law of the spirit of life in Christ, that is, the vivification which is done through Christ, having given the Holy Spirit, has set me free, as is said in Galatians second: I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me.

He dwells on this declaration by positing an antithesis: The law could not set us free from sin and death, but the Son of God was sent, so that we might be set free through him. Therefore, the particle concerning the law must first be considered attentively.

And the grammatical syntax must be correctly explained. The series of this is: Since it was impossible for the law, namely, to take away sin, for the reason that through the flesh the law could not be fulfilled, God sent his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and as a sacrifice for sin condemned sin in the flesh, so that the requirement of the law might be fulfilled. Here let the express assertion be considered first, that it was impossible for the law to take away sin or to justify men, and he adds, because the law could not be fulfilled through the flesh.

He explained this sentiment more prolixly in the seventh chapter; now he repeats it with a brief assertion, which may be in sight for refuting the Pelagians and Monks and the like, who imagined that the law of God discourses only on external discipline: afterwards they affirm that men can satisfy the law of God, and by this discipline be just before God.

The divine voice in the Church condemns this blindness; therefore it was said above in chapter 8: By the works of the law shall no flesh be justified before God. After this assertion follows the saying concerning the merit of Christ: God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, that is, he sent the Son, who assumed the true nature of man, and indeed a passible one, but without sin: therefore he used these words, He sent the Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, because in reality he was without sin, and yet [subject to] sorrows and was subject to death, similarly, so that we miserable humans full of sin [might be redeemed].

Here let the common doctrine regarding the assumption of human nature be held.

Next, let the phrase be observed: God condemned our sin in the flesh for sin, that is, by Christ as a host [sacrifice], offered for sin: for the phrase περὶ ἁμαρτίας [concerning sin] signifies a host for sin. Thus in Leviticus the Greek reading always speaks, and in the same way in the Greek reading of Isaiah it is said: ἐὰν δῶται περὶ ἁμαρτίας ἡ ψυχὴ αὐτοῦ ὄψεται σπέρμα μακρόβιον [if he shall give his soul for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed]. In the Hebrew text the preposition is not added, but it reads thus: Because he shall put his soul as sin, he shall see a long-lived seed. But from the Greek reading of Leviticus the phrase περὶ ἁμαρτίας is most well-known. Elsewhere Paul omitted the preposition: Him who knew no sin, he made sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in him.

Thus Galatians 3: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us. These formulas of speaking signify the same thing, namely, a Host for sin, which elsewhere is named sin, elsewhere a curse, just as the Greeks said κάθαρμα [expiatory sacrifice/offscouring], the Latins piaculum [atonement/sin-offering], and by these atrocious words a most sad punishment, and so to speak, the magnitude of the guilt is signified.

For the sentiment is that this victim was guilty for us, and sustained the horrendous wrath of God, as if he himself had committed all our sins, mine and yours, just as Isaiah says there: The Lord hath laid on him the iniquities of us all. Psalm 39. In the Greek version the phrase περὶ ἁμαρτίας is placed thus absolutely, as in this passage of Paul: Burnt offerings and for sin thou hast not required, which you should understand thus: Thou hast not required burnt offerings and victims for sin. In the Hebrew text of the Psalm the preposition is not added, which however is often added in Leviticus.

Latin:

Caput VIII.

Nulla igitur nunc condemnatio est iis, qui in Christo Iesu ambulant etc.

Dictum est supra, institutam esse collationem Peccati, Legis et Gratiae. Nunc redit ad descriptionem gratiae, et est consolatio addita superiori querelae. Cum enim antea dixerit adhuc haerere peccatum in sanctis in hac vita. Quaestio est communis omnium sanctorum, quomodo sint iusti? Id est, Deo accepti et haeredes vitae externae, cum adhuc sentiant peccata, suas dubitationes, et fateri necesse sit omnes bonos motus valde languidos esse, timorem Dei, dilectionem, fidem, spem, et interea multas errantes flammas cupiditatum simul esse in cordibus. Huic communi quaestioni omnium sanctorum respondet perspicua asseveratione: Nulla nunc condemnatio est his, qui in Christo Iesu non secundum carnem, sed secundum spiritum ambulant. Idem supra dixit: Iustificati fide pacem habemus etc. Item: Non estis sub lege, sed sub gratia. Interpretatur autem vocabulum Gratiae, remotione contrarii: Nulla nunc condemnatio est: quia vocabulum Gratiae est nomen relativum, id est, gratuita acceptatio, quod planius dicitur, Nulla condemnatio: nec dicit, Nullum nunc peccatum est. Et haec est sententia: Iustificati fide placent Deo propter filium mediatorem, et sunt haeredes vitae aeternae, etiamsi in eis haerent peccata, videlicet, vitiosa concupiscentia et pravi effectus, si tamen sint in Christo Iesu, et ambulent secundum spiritum

Christo Iesu, et ambulant secundum spiritum, id est, si sint in eis conversio ad Deum, et fides consolans corda agnitione filii Dei, quae quidem fides est motus Spiritus sancti, qui postea gubernat et sanctificat renatos, ut repugnent pravis adfectibus. Haec est propositio principalis in hoc capite, continens doctrinam et consolationem Ecclesiae necessariam omnibus temporibus. Semper haec fuit, est, et erit quaestio in omnium sanctorum animis, quomodo places Deo, cum sentias adhuc multum sordium. Pharisaei et monachi docuerunt homines placere propter propria merita, et propter sacrificia, propter Missas. Ita fiduciam propriae dignitatis in his, qui adhuc securi sunt, confirmaverunt, et deduxerunt homines ad sacrificia, ubi inanis fiducia ex sacrificiis fecit idola. Postea turbata securitate iusserunt homines manere in dubitatione. Haec simpliciter sunt ethnica, et manens in dubitatione, tandem opprimitur desperatione, et horribili fremitu ruit in aeternum exitium. Sed vox Evangelii prohibet dubitationem et praecipit, ut credamus in filium Dei, et clamat at ca affirmat credentes in filium Deo placere, etiamsi haerent in conversis reliquiae peccati: haec necessaria doctrina et consolatio hic proponitur.

Quare hoc testimonium Pauli semper sit in conspectu. Observandum est autem, quod expresse inquit: Ambulantibus in Christo secundum spiritum, non secundum carnem.

Non promittit consolationem his, qui sunt sine poenitentia, qui securi et furentes perseverant in sceleribus contra conscientiam, de quibus postea dicetur: Si secundum carnem vivetis, moriemini. Item: Qui facit peccatum, ex diabolo est. Item: Qui talia faciunt, regnum Dei non possidebunt. Sed de illis inquit: Nulla damnatio est, qui sunt in Christo Iesu, et reguntur Spiritu sancto.

Nominat duas personas: Christum mediatorem, quia primum oportet conversos agnoscere Christum fide, et propter hunc propiciatorem accipere remissionem et reconciliationem, et fieri eius membra. Cum autem agnitione mediatoris et fide eriguntur corda, simul effunditur Spiritus sanctus in corda, ut tales motus accendat, qualis est ipse, iuxta dictum: Effundam super domum David spiritum gratiae et precum. Item, 2. Corinth. 3.: Nos in eandem imaginem transformamur, tanquam a Domini spiritu. Quia lex spiritus vitae in Christo Iesu liberavit me etc. Antea propositio tradita est: Nulla nunc condemnatio est his, qui in Christo Iesu ambulant etc.

Nunc sequitur declaratio huius propositionis: Per Christum liberati sumus, ubi simul fit mentio meriti Christi et efficaciae. Hic de merito Christi concionatur, cum nominat eum hostiam pro peccato, et ait, propter hanc hostiam damnatum esse peccatum. De efficacia Christi in credentibus dicitur: Lex spiritus vitae in Christo, id est, vivificatio, quae fit per Christum, dato Spiritu sancto liberavit me, ut Galat. secundo dicitur: Vivo autem non iam ego, vivit autem in me Christus.

Huic declarationi immoratur posita antithesi, Lex non potuit nos liberare a peccato et a morte, sed filius Dei missus est, ut per ipsum liberemur. Primum ergo attente consideranda est particula de lege.

Et grammatica Syntaxis recte explicanda est. Huius haec est series: Cum esset impossibile legi, scilicet, tollere peccatum, eo quod per carnem lex non poterat fieri, Deus misit filium suum in similitudine carnis peccati, et hostia pro peccato damnavit peccatum in carne, ut ius legis impleatur. Hic expressa asseveratio primum consideretur, Quod legi fuerit impossibile tollere peccatum seu iustificare homines, et addit, quia lex non poterat fieri per carnem.

Hanc sententiam in cap. septimo prolixius exposuit, nunc brevi asseveratione repetit, quae sit in conspectu ad refutandos Pelagianos et Monachos et similes, qui finxerunt legem Dei tantum de externa disciplina concionari: postea affirmant homines posse legi Dei satisfacere, et hac disciplina iustos esse coram Deo.

Hanc coecitatem vox divina in Ecclesia damnat, ideo supra dictum est cap. 8.: Ex operibus legis non iustificabitur omnis caro coram Deo. Post hanc adseverationem sequitur dictum de merito Christi: Misit Deus filium suum in similitudine carnis peccati, id est, misit filium, qui assumsit veram hominis naturam, et quidem passibilem, sed sine peccato: ideo usus est his verbis, Misit filium in similitudine carnis peccati, quia reipsa sine peccato fuit, et tamen doloribus et morti subiectus est, similiter, ut nos miseri homines pleni peccato.

Hic communis doctrina teneatur de assumtione naturae humanae.

Deinde phrasis observetur: Deus damnavit peccatum nostrum in carne pro peccato, id est, hostia Christo, oblata pro peccato: nam phrasis περὶ ἁμαρτίας significat hostiam pro peccato. Sic in Levitico Graeca lectio semper loquitur, et eodem modo in Graeca lectione Esaiae dicitur: ἐὰν δῶται περὶ ἁμαρτίας ἡ ψυχὴ αὐτοῦ ὄψεται σπέρμα μακρόβιον. In textu Hebraeo non additur praepositio, sed sic legitur: Quia ponet peccatum animam suam, videbit semen longaevum. Sed ex Levitici Graeca lectione phrasis περὶ ἁμαρτίας notissima est. Alibi Paulus omisit praepositionem: Eum qui non norat peccatum, pro nobis fecit peccatum, ut nos fieremus iusticia Dei in ipso.

Sic Galat. 3.: Christus redemit nos a maledictione legis, factus pro nobis maledictum. Hae formulae loquendi idem significant, videlicet, Hostia pro peccato, quae alibi nominatur peccatum, alibi maledictum, sicut Graeci dixerunt κάθαρμα, Latini piaculum, et his atrocibus verbis tristissima poena, et ut ita dicam, magnitudo reatus significatur.

Est enim sententia, hac victimam pro nobis fuisse ream, et horrendam iram Dei sustinuisse, quasi ipse omnia nostra, mea et tua scelera fecisset, sicut ibi Esai. inquit: Posuit Dominus in eum iniquitates omnium nostrum. Psalmo 39. In Graeca versione phrasis περὶ ἁμαρτίας sic absolute ponitur, ut in hoc loco Pauli: Holocausta et pro peccato non postulasti, quod sic intelligas, Non postulasti holocausta et victimas pro peccato. In textu Hebraeo Psalmi non est addita praepositio, quae tamen in Levitico saepe addita est.

## 8:3
He condemned sin in the flesh.

Namely, our sin: and let the emphasis be observed in the verb, condemned. For just as a judge condemning a murderer first pronounces him guilty, afterwards executes him, so God, condemning sin, when the innocent son was made a victim, first took away from sin the authority to accuse us, afterwards he destroys it entirely, when he restores to us eternal life and complete righteousness.

But he says the law is preached for this reason, that it might be fulfilled in us, that is, that we might then be righteous. For the Son of God does not suffer for this reason, that sin might afterwards remain, and that the horrendous furies of men might be confirmed; the Son of God does not hang on the cross for this reason, that David might have license to snatch another's wife and kill her husband, but that sin might be destroyed, and that we might henceforth be righteous. But as often as it is spoken of the fulfillment of the law in this life, as when Paul says: Through faith the law is established. Item: The law of God is made [effective] through grace.

It is necessary to embrace both, namely, imputation and the beginning of newness, which afterwards will be complete. The law is fulfilled, first by imputation, because on account of the mediator we are reckoned righteous, and we are accepted on account of him, even if we are not yet such as the law commands us to be: But he who has Christ by faith, has the end of the law. Then it is true that newness is also begun, congruent with the law, because the Son of God vivifies hearts in that true consolation, and pours into them the Holy Spirit, by whom we are transformed into his own image, are assimilated to him by a new light, and have such motions as the Holy Spirit is. Such things, however, the law commands: but this newness in this life is only begun, afterwards it will be complete, when God shall be all in all.

In exactly the same way Paul speaks to the Corinthians: Him who knew no sin, he made sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in him. It is a comparison of two greatest things, extreme misery and supreme glory, or the highest good. Extreme misery is to be guilty of the wrath of God, and to sustain the sense of the wrath of God. On the contrary, the highest good is the righteousness of God. But such a permutation has been made: the Son sustains that which is most miserable, namely the sense of the wrath of God, and bestows upon us that which is best, namely the righteousness of God.

And the particle 'in him' must be diligently observed: because both on account of him we are reckoned righteous, and he is the person immediately gathering the Church through the Gospel, vivifying believers, and bestowing the Holy Spirit. And although this vivification and newness is most truly the work of God, nevertheless the obedience of the Son of God is to be preferred infinitely to these very actions which happen in you: therefore in this life it is necessary to believe that we are righteous, that is, that we please God on account of the mediator, God and man, not on account of our newness.

CHAPTER. VIII. The mind of the flesh is enmity against God.

There is a long and illustrious antithesis between the nature of unregenerate man and regeneration or vivification, which occurs in conversion, when the Son of God himself consoles us with the voice of the Gospel, and by giving the Holy Spirit, kindles in you a new light and the beginnings of eternal life. Let this splendid antithesis always be in sight, because it clearly refutes the Pharisaic and Pelagian dreams, which imagine that men can satisfy the law of God by natural powers, and that by this discipline, whatever it may be, they can merit the remission of sins and be righteous before God.

Against this blindness, the most sorrowful sermons are placed here, concerning the infirmity of human nature, and they expressly assert that men in this life cannot satisfy the law of God. For he says, The flesh cannot be subject to the law of God. Likewise, The mind of the flesh is enmity against God. What could be said more sad and atrocious than that in this miserable nature of men, there is not only disobedience, but also indignation and rage against God.

But since the monks, following the Pharisaic and Pelagian doctrine, have attached false interpretations to these words, it is necessary to admonish the younger ones concerning the discourse.

It is customary for Paul to call the flesh the whole nature of unregenerate man, namely, not only the appetites of the senses or affections, but also the higher part, namely the intellect and the will, as we name them in the schools. And let the distribution of the powers of the soul be noted here.

Therefore Paul calls the mind of the flesh not only the appetites or affections in the heart, such as loves, hatreds, joy, sadness, the fires of lusts, anger, but also in the higher part, the darkness and doubts about God, about providence, and about the word of God. Likewise, in the will, aversion from God, distrust, blind security, contempt of the judgment of God, indignation and rage against God. All these he calls φρόνημα σαρκὸς (mind of the flesh), and the name φρόνημα includes thoughts and affections.

The word Spirit here signifies the Holy Spirit, God, and the motions which are kindled in the regenerate heart by the Holy Spirit. Thus, that flesh and spirit are distinguished in this place is manifest. For he says: He who does not have the Spirit of Christ, this one is not his. This admonition concerning the words is necessary to avoid many corruptions. For some, hallucinating, have said that Flesh and Spirit are distinguished here just as affections and reason are distinguished in philosophy. This pernicious error must be censured: for all that which philosophy calls affections and reason, Paul here calls Flesh and φρόνημα σαρκὸς.

But they object, Why does he say the mind of the flesh is enmity against God, when nevertheless there are many good notions in man, such as numbers and the laws of nature, likewise, good affections, such as natural affections (στοργαὶ)? I answer: Paul speaks principally of thoughts about God, such as they are in the unregenerate mind, in which at the same time there is a great confusion of doubts: then also about affections toward God, such as they are in the will and heart of the regenerate. In those who are secure there is contempt of the judgment of God: in those who are terrified, as in Saul, Judas, there is indignation and rage against God, and there is manifold obstinacy in the heart against the law of God, nor are the στοργαὶ governed by order. Paul preaches concerning these interior evils, when he says, The flesh cannot be subject to the law of God.

And in this place the necessary doctrine concerning the distinction between external discipline and interior obedience must be held: for even after the fall of the first parents this liberty of the will remains in man, that he is able to govern the locomotive power, that is, the external gestures of the members. Still such is the nature of the nerves, fashioned by a marvelous art of God, that they can obey thought and will, because God wills that the external members be bridled and restrained by human diligence, and he wills that in some way the distinction between an agent free and not free be understood, so that we may know God to be the most free agent. Nor does Paul speak of these external gestures when he says, The flesh cannot be subject to the law of God, but he speaks of interior obedience, because in man faith ought to shine forth, believing with firm assent the threatenings and promises of God, and rightly acknowledging the Son of God, and there ought to be in the heart conformity with God, burning love of God, true fear. Finally, the heart ought to be the temple of God, without any perverse inclination, and without perverse motions; but unregenerate man cannot so much as begin this interior obedience. Concerning these interior darknesses and doubts and evil inclinations it is said: The flesh cannot be subject to the law of God. If anyone does not have the spirit of Christ, this one is not his.

These words clearly refute the Pelagians and Monks, who said that men not reborn can satisfy the law of God, and by this discipline merit the remission of sins, and on account of it be righteous and please God. These impious dreams must be condemned in the Church, according to the sayings: Who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God. And in this place: he who does not have the spirit of Christ, is not his. Item: Without me you can do nothing.

It is to be observed that in this place the Spirit of Christ is explicitly named.

First, so that it may be understood that the spirit is not reason, but the Holy Spirit, who is the third person of the divinity. Then, so that we may be admonished as to how the Holy Spirit is given, because he is not given without the knowledge of the Son of God, and without the thought of the Gospel, but then is most truly poured into hearts, when in true conversion minds terrified are raised up by the voice of the Gospel, and by faith begin to acknowledge the Son of God, and to acquiesce in the consolation proposed through the Gospel, and to rejoice in God on account of the mediator, as it is said to the Galatians: That we might receive the promise of the spirit through faith. However, as often as we think about justification, let us look at the three persons, let us acknowledge the Son, the mediator, God and man constituted as propitiator, on account of whom we are received, and let us know that we are received at the same time by the eternal Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and that we are vivified by the Son, when with the given voice of the Gospel the Son speaks consolation in us, and shows the Father, and pours out the Holy Spirit gladdening the believing heart. Therefore it is said in John 14: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him, and we will make our dwelling with him.

For the Father and the Son breathe the Holy Spirit into the heart.

And here Paul says elsewhere, If Christ is in you: elsewhere he says, If the spirit of Christ dwells in you. For the Son also, who is the λόγος (Word), is present to the Church, is Emmanuel, and is effective in it, makes manifest the Gospel, and by the voice of the Gospel shows the Father, speaks consolation, and gives the Holy Spirit.

Therefore Athanasius says: Whenever it is said that the Holy Spirit is in a man, he is in him through the word. And he speaks of the Son.

But let the difference be noted: It is one thing for God to be everywhere: another for him to dwell in the Church.

To be everywhere is said of the universal presence, by which the whole divinity preserves the substances of creatures, of which it is said in Jeremiah 23: Do I not fill heaven and earth? But for God to dwell in the Church is, through the Son, by the voice of the Gospel, to kindle true knowledge of God and to console the heart, and through the Holy Spirit to rule the heart, so that it may have motions pleasing to him, and the beginnings of righteousness and eternal salvation.

Let the words of Athanasius also be noted concerning the divine nature in Christ, in the book on the incarnation of the Word: The λόγος (Word) is not in the body in such a way that he is not elsewhere, nor does he move the body in such a way that he is absent from other creatures, but in a wondrous way, while he is the λόγος, he is comprehended by no one, but he himself comprehends all things, and while he is in every creature, yet he is a different substance from the creatures. Our souls, even if they think of things outside the body, do not move them: for they do not agitate the sun, although they see that it is moved: the λόγος is not like this, in the assumed nature, for he is not included, but he himself contains the body, and at the same time is in the bosom of the eternal Father, and is present to creatures. [The] body is dead because of sin.

An objection occurs: Why, when believers are righteous and children of God, are they still subject to death and other calamities, and indeed are burdened more harshly than other men?

He answers briefly: Although in the soul there is begun light and eternal life through the Word and the Holy Spirit, yet sin still clings in the carnal mass, therefore it is necessary that the carnal mass be destroyed, so that afterwards in the resurrection we may be clothed with a body thoroughly purified, just as it is written to the Corinthians: We shall be clothed upon, if indeed we shall not be found naked. Thus he answers the argument of reason:

The righteous man ought to be well: The Church is righteous, Therefore the Church ought to be well. I answer first to the minor: The Church is righteous, this is true, by imputation, not yet by consummation.

Since therefore sin still clings in the reborn in this life, there follows the destruction of the body, because God wills that sin be thoroughly destroyed. Then let it be answered also to the major: To the righteous it ought to be well: the saying is legal and true, but it is to be understood according to the declaration made manifest in the Gospel, which teaches that God wills the Church to be gathered in this life, and wills it to be subject to the cross, because although he receives believers, and to sanctify it begins, yet sin still clings in the carnal mass. Afterwards, God in the resurrection will clothe those who have believed, with the body completely purified, and He will be all in all, that is, He will fill them with His light and justice, so that there may be no sin in them.

Fratres debitores sumus. Up to this point, he has delivered the doctrine concerning justification, and the comparison of the law, of sin, and of grace.

Now he adds the doctrine concerning new obedience: for it is necessary that this part of the doctrine also exist in the Church, so that it may be known what kind of obedience exists in the reborn in this life, and what kind of sin it is, on account of which they fall from grace and lose the Holy Spirit and the faith by which hearts are quickened, according to the saying: Being justified by faith, we have peace. Therefore, Paul establishes the proposition: We are debtors, so that we may not obey the flesh. And first, observe the designation, We are debtors. He opposes this word to those who poorly understand evangelical liberty, which frees the reborn so that they may not be condemned by the law, but does not free them so that they may not obey.

For the eternal and immutable order remains, that we should obey God. Some foolish people criticize these forms of speaking: New obedience is owed. Likewise, new obedience is necessary. And they say that coercion or obedience extorted by fear is meant. This interpretation is not native to the words of debt and necessity. For these words signify an immutable order, they do not properly signify coercion, which is done by the fear of punishments. New obedience is necessary for that very reason, because this is the eternal order, that the creature should willingly obey God. Afterwards, he teaches what kind of obedience it is: for since in the reborn in this life there remain remnants of sin and great filth, it is necessary that degrees be discerned, what kind of sins are in the reborn, and what kind are not, just as he also distinguished above between reigning and non-reigning sin. For that the reborn can again lose grace and the Holy Spirit is manifest from the words in Matthew 12: Finding the house swept, the evil spirit returns. And 2 Peter 2: When they had escaped the pollutions of the world, they return to their vomit, etc. Adam and Eve were elect, and yet in the fall they become guilty of eternal wrath. And in Deuteronomy it is said concerning Aaron: God was very angry against Aaron, so as to destroy him. It is necessary, therefore, to discern what kind of sins remain in the reborn, what kind grieve and expel the Holy Spirit, on account of which a man again becomes guilty of eternal wrath, and falls into eternal punishments, unless he is again converted to God.

There are, however, customary designations, mortal and venial sin.

Mortal is named every sin in the non-reborn: likewise such a sin, on account of which the reborn loses grace and the Holy Spirit, and again becomes guilty of eternal wrath.

The definition of sin is simple and brief in the Epistle of John, when he says: ἁμαρτία ἐστὶν ἀνομία, that is, sin is whatever is against the law.

This description must be understood correctly, and let us know that every sin in the non-reborn is mortal: that is, what Paul names reigning sin, that is, the non-reborn are actually guilty of eternal punishment on account of all sins, original and actual, interior and exterior, and unless they are converted to God, they fall into eternal destruction.

When, therefore, it is said, Sin is whatever is against the law of God, the guilt is simultaneously included, namely that the non-reborn are actually guilty of eternal punishment. This guilt is expressed in these words: Cursed is he who does not remain in all things which are written in the law of God. Likewise: He who does not believe, the wrath of God remains upon him.

Afterwards, concerning the reborn, it must be known that there are two degrees of sins. One is non-reigning sin, which is named venial, which is original evil, many defects and depraved inclinations and doubts, sins of ignorance and omission, depraved affections, but in those who are reborn, and retain faith and the fear of God by the help of the Holy Spirit, and resist depraved affections, and do not fall against their conscience. Such sins cling in the reborn in this life, and are in reality sins, evils fighting against the law, and on account of them a man would be guilty of eternal punishment, unless reconciliation had been given by faith on account of the mediator. Thus, those who are reborn are not actually guilty. Therefore it was said above: There is now no condemnation to those who walk in Christ Jesus. Likewise: For this, every saint will pray at an opportune time. Such sins do not shake off faith and the Holy Spirit in those who grieve on account of this filth, and believe that they are forgiven on account of the mediator, and do not indulge in them against their conscience.

Another degree of sins is error in the foundation; likewise a fall against conscience, as when David, knowing and willing, seizes another man's wife, and refers her to the glory of God; he does not wish to alienate the wills of men from the doctrine by scandal.

Therefore, it is not only a repression of the locomotive faculty that happens here, but there is true light in the mind, and the Holy Spirit assimilates the heart to the word of God shining in the mind.

Because of such sins, a man again loses grace, the Holy Spirit, and faith, and becomes actually guilty of eternal punishment, and unless conversion occurs, he rushes into eternal destruction, just as Saul is condemned, who, although he had previously pleased God, nevertheless rushed against his conscience, and is not again converted to God.

David is again converted to God, and becomes an heir of eternal life.

These degrees are clearly discerned in the Church, and let there be an illustrious distinction between sin that reigns and sin that does not reign.

Paul embraces this doctrine in the saying: Wage a good warfare, keeping faith and a good conscience.

Item, 1 Corinthians 6: Do not err; fornicators, adulterers, idolaters will not possess the kingdom of God.

From these sayings, let a declaration be taken in this place.

If you live according to the flesh, you will die, that is: If you admit false opinions and indulge in depraved affections, you will again be guilty of eternal punishment, you will lose grace and the Holy Spirit.

I call these sins lapses against conscience and error in the foundation, as when the pious, who had thought rightly, embrace impious dogmas, whether by error or knowingly: as many, who had previously thought rightly, embraced the Arian impiety.

Of all these it is said: Do not err; fornicators, adulterers, idolaters, murderers will not possess the kingdom of God.

But concerning the other degree it is said: If you mortify the actions of the flesh by the Spirit, you will live.

He admits that there are actions of the flesh in the reborn, that is, carnal affections and opinions not congruent with the Holy Spirit.

He commands these evils to be mortified by the Spirit, that is, he commands that the reborn be intent and vigilant, lest they approve of false opinions.

Item, he commands that they resist depraved affections, and not rush against their conscience.

Therefore, Paul here commands that the actions of the flesh be mortified by the Spirit, and he makes mention of mortification, because in that struggle he wants us to acknowledge our infirmity, and to grieve because of these stains, and by faith to seek the remission even of these stains.

Of these, Paul says: Those who mortify the actions of the flesh by the Spirit, retain life, that is, they retain grace, the Holy Spirit, faith comforting the hearts, and they remain heirs of eternal life, just as he said above: There is now no condemnation for those who walk in Christ Jesus.

Both must be acknowledged: both that there are sins in the reborn, for which they ought truly to tremble and grieve, and again the magnitude of God's mercy must be acknowledged, that He receives believers for the sake of the Son freely, and affirms that He wills that obedience be begun in us, and that it pleases Him, although very mutilated and languid, if nevertheless the reborn resist vicious affections, and grieve that they have such stains, and by faith seek remission.

Concerning this obedience, it is said in Romans 14: He who in these serves Christ, pleases God well, and is approved by men.

Thus, there are simultaneously true humility, acknowledging one's own infirmity and truly grieving because of these remnants of sin, and on the other hand, consolation and joy in God, which is trust acquiescing for the sake of the mediator: according to the saying: Being justified by faith, we have peace.

But let the distinction between offenses against conscience and offenses not against conscience always be in sight.

Those who are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God.

Previously he set forth the proposition, We are debtors, and asserted that new obedience is necessary, and added arguments from punishments and the retention of grace and eternal life.

Now he adds an argument from the efficient cause and from the possible.

As is the efficient, so let the effect be: In true conversion, hearts are raised by the Holy Spirit through faith: Therefore, let the motions be congruent with the Holy Spirit.

This doctrine concerning the gift of the Holy Spirit has often been repeated already, and must often be pondered for the sake of consolation, so that invocation may be kindled.

This doctrine concerning the gift of the Holy Spirit has already been repeated often, and it must be pondered often for the sake of consolation, so that invocation may be kindled.

Since the infirmity of men is great, and the devil goes about like a roaring lion, that he may devour as many as possible, let us flee to these safeguards and to these consolations, that Emanuel, the Son of God, is the guardian of the Church, as he says: No one shall snatch my sheep from my hands, and he governs, confirms, teaches, and consoles us with the Holy Spirit, and he wills that these benefits be sought, and promises them to those who ask, as it is written: Without me you can do nothing.

Ask, and you shall receive. How much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask. Item: Without your divine power there is nothing in man, nothing is harmless. The Spirit helps our infirmity.

Let such sentences be in sight, so that they may rouse us to invocation, and let us learn this doctrine and the exercises of faith in daily troubles, where in true consolation we shall experience the presence of the Holy Spirit.

However, let the word 'leads' be observed in this place. The Holy Spirit is not idle; he moves minds and leads, namely, those not resisting: for it is not coercion, such that the will cannot resist. God draws, but he draws the willing, therefore he says: He will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask. Item: Offer your members as weapons of righteousness.

Latin:

Damnavit peccatum in carne.

Scilicet nostra: et emphasis observetur in verbo, damnavit. Ut enim iudex damnans homicidam, primum pronunciat eum reum esse, postea interficit eum, sic Deus damnans peccatum, cum filius innocens sit factus victima, primum eripuit peccato autoritatem nos accusandi, postea omnino delet, cum reddit nobis aeternam vitam et iusticiam integram.

Ait autem ideo concionatur lex, in nobis impleatur, id est, ut deinde iusti simus. Non enim ideo patitur filius Dei, ut peccatum postea maneat, et ut horrendi furores hominum confirmentur, non ideo pendet in cruce filius Dei, ut David licentiam habeat rapiendi alterius coniugem, et interficiendi maritum, sed ut deleatur peccatum, et deinceps iusti simus. Quoties autem dicitur de impletione legis in hac vita, ut cum ait Paulus: Per fidem stabilitur lex. Item: Lex Dei fit per gratiam.

Necesse est utrunque complecti, videlicet imputationem et incoationem novitatis, quae postea erit integra. Lex impletur, primum imputatione, quia propter mediatorem reputamur iusti, et sumus accepti propter ipsum, etiamsi nondum sumus tales, quales lex esse praecipit: Habens autem Christum fide, habet finem legis. Deinde verum est, tunc et incoari novitatem congruentem cum lege, quia filius Dei vivificat corda in illa vera consolatione, et effundit in ea Spiritum sanctum, quo transformamur in ipsius imaginem, assimilamur ipsi nova luce, et habemus tales motus, qualis est Spiritus sanctus. Tales autem praecipit lex: sed haec novitas in hac vita tantum incoatur, postea erit integra, cum erit Deus omnia in omnibus.

Prorsus eodem modo loquitur Paulus ad Corinthios: Eum qui non norat peccatum, fecit peccatum pro nobis, ut nos fieremus iusticia Dei in ipso. Collatio est duarum maximarum rerum, extremae miseriae et summae gloriae, seu summi boni. Extrema miseria est reum esse irae Dei, et sensum irae Dei sustinere. Econtra summum bonum est iusticia Dei. Talis autem permutatio facta est, Filius sustinet id, quod est miserrimum, scilicet sensum irae Dei, et nobis donat id, quod optimum est, scilicet iusticiam Dei.

Ac diligenter observanda est particula, in ipso: quia et propter ipsum reputamur iusti, et ipse est persona immediate colligens Ecclesiam per Evangelium, vivificans credentes, et donans Spiritum sanctum. Etsi autem haec vivificatio et novitas verissime opus Dei est, tamen obedientia filii Dei in infinitum anteferenda est his ipsis actionibus, quae in te fiunt: ideo in hac vita necesse est credere nos iustos esse, id est, placere Deo propter mediatorem Deum et hominem, non propter novitatem nostram.

CAP. VIII. Sensus carnis inimicitia est adversus Deum.

Longa et illustris antithesis est naturae hominis non renatae, et regenerationis seu vivificationis, quae fit in conversione, cum ipse filius Dei voce Evangelii consolatur nos, et dato Spiritu sancto, accendit in vobis novam lucem et initia vitae aeternae. Haec splendida antithesis semper sit in conspectu, quia perspicue refutat Pharisaica et Pelagiana somnia, quae fingunt homines viribus naturalibus posse legi Dei satisfacere, et hanc qualemcunque disciplinam mereri remissionem peccatorum, et esse iusticiam coram Deo.

Contra hanc coecitatem tristissima conciones hic ponuntur, de humanae naturae infirmitate, et expresse asseverant homines in hac vita non posse legi Dei satisfacere. Ait enim, Caro non potest esse subdita lege Dei. Item, Sensus carnis inimicitia est adversus Deum. Quid potuit dici tristius et atrocius, quam in hac misera natura hominum, non solum esse inobedientiam, sed etiam indignationem et fremitum adversus Deum.

Cum autem monachi sequentes Pharisaicam et Pelagianam doctrinam affinxerint vocabulis falsas interpretationes, necesse est moneri iuniores de sermone.

Usitatum est Paulo nominare carnem totam naturam hominis non renati, videlicet, non solum appetitiones sensuum seu affectus, sed etiam partem superiorem, videlicet intellectum et voluntatem, ut in scholis nominamus. Et nota sit hic distributio potentiarum animae.

Sensum igitur carnis nominat Paulus, non tantum appetitiones seu affectus in corde, ut amores, odia, laetitiam, tristitiam, incendia libidinum, iram, sed etiam in superiore parte caliginem et dubitationes de Deo, de providentia et de verbo Dei. Item, in voluntate aversionem a Deo, diffidentiam, coecam securitatem, contemptum iudicii Dei, indignationem et fremitus adversus Deum. Haec omnia nominat φρόνημα σαρκὸς, ac nomen φρόνημα complectitur cogitationes et affectus.

Vocabulum vero Spiritus hic significat Spiritum sanctum Deum, et motus, qui accenduntur in corde renato a Spiritu sancto. Sic discerni carnem et spiritum, hoc loco manifestum est. Ait enim: Qui spiritum Christi non habet, hic non est ipsius. Haec admonitio de vocabulis necessaria est ad vitandas multas corruptelas. Aliqui enim hallucinantes dixerunt, hic distingui Carnem et Spiritum, sicut in philosophia distinguuntur affectus et ratio. Hunc perniciosum errorem taxari necesse est: nam totum hoc, quod philosophia nominat affectus et rationem, id Paulus hic nominat Carnem et φρόνημα σαρκὸς.

Sed obiiciunt, Cur ait sensum carnis inimicitiam esse adversus Deum, cum tamen in homine sint multae bonae noticiae, ut numeri et leges naturae, item, boni affectus, ut στοργαὶ? Respondeo: Loquitur Paulus principaliter de cogitationibus de Deo, quales sunt in mente non renata, in qua simul magna confusio est dubitationum: deinde et de affectibus erga Deum, quales sunt in voluntate et corde de renato. In securis est contemptus iudicii Dei: in perterrefactis, ut in Saul, Iuda, est indignatio et fremitus adversus Deum, et est multiplex contumacia in corde contra legem Dei, nec στοργαὶ reguntur ordine. De his interioribus malis concionatur Paulus, cum ait, Carnem non posse subiici legi Dei.

Ac tenenda est hoc loco doctrina necessaria de distinctione externae disciplinae et interioris obedientiae: nam etiam post lapsum primorum parentum haec libertas voluntatis in homine reliqua est, posse regere locomotivam, id est, externos membrorum gestus. Adhuc talis est natura nervorum, mirabili arte a Deo condita, ut obedire cogitationi et voluntati possint, quia Deus vult externa membra frenari, et coërceri humana diligentia, et vult aliquo modo intelligi discrimen inter agens liberum et non liberum, ut sciamus Deum esse agens liberrimum. Nec de his externis gestibus loquitur Paulus cum ait, Carnem non posse legi Dei subiici, sed loquitur de interiore obedientia, quia in homine debebat lucere fides, firma assensione credens comminationibus et promissionibus Dei, et recte agnoscens filium Dei, et in corde debebat esse conformitas cum Deo, ardens dilectio Dei, verus timor. Denique cor debebat esse templum Dei, sine ulla prava inclinatione, et sine pravis motibus, sed homo non renatus hanc interiorem obedientiam ne quidem incoare potest. De his interioribus tenebris et dubitationibus et malis inclinationibus dicitur: Caro non potest subiici legi Dei. Si quis spiritum Christi non habet, hic non est ipsius.

Haec verba perspicue refutant Pelagianos et Monachos, qui dixerunt, homines non renatos posse lege Dei satisfacere, et hac disciplina mereri remissionem peccatorum, et propter eam iustos esse et placere Deo. Haec impia somnia necesse est in Ecclesia damnari, iuxta dicta: Qui non ex sanguinibus, neque ex voluntate carnis, neque ex voluntate viri, sed ex Deo nati sunt. Et hoc loco: qui non habet spiritum Christi, non est ipsius. Item: Sine me nihil potestis facere.

Observandum est diserte hoc loco nominari Spiritum Christi.

Primum, ut intelligatur spiritus non ratio, sed Spiritus sanctus, qui est tertia persona divinitatis. Deinde, ut admoneamur, quomodo detur Spiritus sanctus, quia non datur sine agnitione filii Dei, et sine cogitatione Evangelii, sed tunc verissime effunditur in corda, quando in vera conversione mentes perterrefactae eriguntur voce Evangelii, et fide incipiunt agnoscere filium Dei, et acquiescere in consolatione per Evangelium proposita, et laetari in Deo propter mediatorem, ut ad Galatas dicitur: Ut accipiamus promissionem spiritus per fidem. Quoties autem de iustificatione cogitamus, intueamur tres personas, agnoscamus filium mediatorem Deum et hominem constitutum propitiatorem, propter quem recipimur, et sciamus nos simul recipi ab aeterno Patre, Filio et Spiritu sancto, et vivificari nos per filium, cum data voce Evangelii filius consolationem in nobis dicit, et patrem ostendit, et effundit Spiritum sanctum laetificantem cor credens. Ideo dicitur Iohannis 14.: Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum servabit, et pater meus diligit eum, et veniemus ad eum, et mansionem apud eum faciemus.

Spirant enim pater et filius Spiritum sanctum in cor, Et hic Paulus alias inquit, Si Christus in vobis est: alias inquit, Si spiritus Christi habitat in vobis.

Nam et filius, qui est λόγος, adest Ecclesiae, est Emanuel, et est in ea efficax, patefacit Evangelium, et voce Evangelii ostendit patrem, dicit consolationem, et dat Spiritum sanctum. Ideo inquit Athanasius: Quandocunque dicitur Spiritus sanctus in homine esse, est in eo per verbum.

Et de filio loquitur. Nota sit autem differentia, Aliud est Deum esse ubique: aliud habitare eum in Ecclesia.

Esse ubique dicitur de universali praesentia, qua tota divinitas substantias creaturarum conservat, de qua Ieremiae 23. dicitur: Non ne coelum et terram ego impleo.

Sed Deum habitare in Ecclesia, est per filium voce Evangelii veram Dei noticiam accendere et consolari cor, et per Spiritum sanctum regere cor, ut habeat motus ipsi placentes, et initia iusticiae et salutis aeternae. Nota sint etiam verba Athanasii de natura divina in Christo, in libro de incarnatione verbi: Non ita est in corpore λόγος, ut alibi non sit, nec ita movet corpus, ut desit aliis creaturis, sed mirando modo, cum λόγος sit, a nullo comprehenditur, sed ipse comprehendit omnia, et cum in omni creatura sit, tamen alia substantia est a creaturis.

Animae nostrae etsi cogitant res extra corpus, eas non movent: non enim agitant solem, quanquam moveri eum cernunt: non sic est λόγος, in assumta natura, non enim inclusus est, sed ipse continet corpus, et simul est in sinu aeterni patris, et adest creaturis. Corpus mortuum est propter peccatum.

Occurrit obiectioni, Quare, cum credentes sint iusti et filii Dei, adhuc tamen subiecti sunt morti et aliis calamitatibus et quidem durius onerati sunt quam alii homines.

Respondet breviter: Quanquam in anima incoata est lux et vita aeterna per verbum et Spiritum sanctum, tamen adhuc in massa carnali haeret peccatum, ideo destrui massam carnalem oportet, ut postea in resuscitatione induamur corpore prorsus purificato, sicut ad Corinth. scriptum est: Superinduemur, si tamen non nudi reperiemur. Ita respondet ad argumentum rationis:

Iustus debet bene esse: Ecclesia est iusta, Ergo Ecclesiae debet bene esse. Respondeo primum ad minorem: Ecclesia est iusta, hoc verum est, imputatione, nondum consummatione.

Cum igitur adhuc in renatis in hac vita haereat peccatum, sequitur destructio corporis, quia Deus vult peccatum prorsus destrui. Deinde respondeatur et ad maiorem: Iustis debet bene esse: dictum est legale et verum, sed intelligendum est iuxta declarationem in Evangelio patefactam, quae docet velle Deum Ecclesiam in hac vita colligi, et velle subiectam esse cruci, quia quanquam credentes recipit, et sanctificare incipit, tamen adhuc haeret peccatum in massa carnali. Postea Deus in resuscitatione vestiet illos qui crediderunt, corpore prorsus purificato, et erit omnia in omnibus, id est, implebit eos sua luce et iusticia, ut non sit in eis peccatum.

Fratres debitores sumus. Hactenus tradidit doctrinam de iustificatione, et collationem legis, peccati et gratiae.

Nunc addit doctrinam de nova obedientia: nam et hanc partem doctrina in Ecclesia extare necesse est, ut sciatur, qualis sit obedientia in renatis in hac vita, et quale sit peccatum, propter quod excidunt a gratia, et amittunt Spiritum sanctum et fidem, qua vivificantur corda, iuxta dictum: Iustificati fide pacem habemus. Instituit igitur Paulus propositionem: Debitores sumus, ne obediamus carni. Ac primum observes appellationem, Debitores sumus. Hanc vocem opponit male intelligentibus libertatem evangelicam, quae liberat renatos, ne condemnentur a lege, non liberat ne obediant.

Manet enim aeternus et immutabilis ordo, ut Deo obediamus. Aliqui inepti reprehendunt has formas loquendi: Nova obedientia est debita. Item, nova obedientia est necessaria. Et dicunt intelligi coactionem seu obedientiam metu extortam. Haec interpretatio non est nativa in verbis debiti et necessitatis. Significant enim haec verba ordinem immutabilem, non significant proprie coactionem, quae fit metu poenarum. Nova obedientia eo ipso est necessaria, quia hic est ordo aeternus, ut creatura Deo volens obediat. Postea docet qualis sit obedientia: cum enim in renatis in hac vita maneant reliquiae peccati et magnae sordes, necesse est discerni gradus, qualia peccata sint in renatis, qualia non sint, sicut et supra distinxit peccatum regnans et non regnans. Nam renatos posse rursus amittere gratiam et Spiritum sanctum, manifestum est ex dictis Matth. 12.: Inveniens domum mundatam, nequam spiritus redit. Et 2. Petri 2.: Cum effugissent inquinamenta mundi, redeunt ad vomitum etc. Adam et Eva erant electi, et tamen in lapsu fiunt rei aeternae irae. Et in Deuteronomio de Aharon dicitur: Adversus Aharon valde iratus est Deus, ut deleret eum. Necesse est igitur discerni, qualia peccata maneant in renatis, qualia contristent et expellant Spiritum sanctum, propter quae homo rursus fit reus aeternae irae, et ruit in aeternas poenas, nisi rursus convertatur ad Deum.

Sunt autem usitatae appellationes, peccatum mortale et veniale.

Mortale nominatur omne peccatum in non renato: item tale peccatum, propter quod renatus amittit gratiam et Spiritum sanctum, et iterum fit reus aeternae irae.

Definitio peccati simplex et brevis extat in Epistola Iohannis, cum inquit: ἁμαρτία ἐστὶν ἀνομία, id est, peccatum est quicquid contra legem est.

Haec descriptio dextre intelligenda est, et sciarnus omne peccatum in non renatis mortale esse: id est, quod Paulus nominat peccatum regnans, id est, non renati sunt actu rei poenae aeternae propter omnia peccata, originalia et actualia, interiora et exteriora, et nisi convertantur ad Deum, ruunt in aeternum exitium.

Cum igitur dicitur, Peccatum est quicquid est contra legem Dei, simul comprehendatur reatus, quod videlicet non renati sint actu rei poenae aeternae. Hic reatus expressus est in his verbis: Maledictus qui non manet in omnibus, quae sunt scripta in lege Dei. Item: Qui non credit, manet ira Dei super eum.

Postea de renatis sciendum est, duos esse gradus peccatorum. Aliud est peccatum non regnans, quod nominatur veniale, quod est malum originale, multi defectus et pravae inclinationes et dubitationes, peccata ignorantiae et omissionis, pravi affectus, sed in his qui sunt renati, et retinent fidem et timorem Dei auxilio Spiritus sancti, et repugnant pravis affectibus, nec ruunt contra conscientiam. Talia peccata in renatis in hac vita haerent, et sunt reipsa peccata, mala pugnantia cum lege, et propter ea homo esset reus aeternae poenae, nisi fide propter mediatorem donata esset reconciliatio. Ita non sunt actu rei, qui sunt renati. Ideo supra dictum est: Nulla nunc condemnatio est his, qui Christo Iesu ambulant. Item: Pro hoc orabit ad omnis sanctus in tempore oportuno. Talia peccata non excutiunt fidem et Spiritum sanctum in his, qui dolent propter has sordes, et credunt sibi eas remitti propter mediatorem, nec indulgent eis contra conscientiam.

Alius gradus est peccatorum error in fundamento; item lapsus contra conscientiam, ut cum David sciens et volens rapit alterius coniugem, et refert eam ad gloriam Dei, non vult scandalo alienare voluntates hominum a doctrina.

Non igitur tantum hic repressio fit locomotivae, sed in mente vera lux est, et Spiritus sanctus adsimilat cor verbo Dei lucenti in mente.

Propter talia peccata homo rursus amittit gratiam, Spiritum sanctum et fidem, et fit actu reus aeternae poenae, et nisi fiat conversio ruit in aeternum exitium, sicut Saul damnatur, qui quanquam placuerat antea Deo, ruit tamen contra conscientiam, nec rursus convertitur ad Deum.

David rursus convertitur ad Deum, et fit haeres vitae aeternae.

Hi gradus perspicue discernuntur in Ecclesia, et sit illustre discrimen peccati regnantis et non regnantis.
