Hanc doctrinam complectitur Paulus in dicto: Milita bonam militiam retinens fidem et bonam conscientiam.

Item, 1 Corinth.

6.: Ne erretis, scortatores, adulteri, idolatrae regnum Dei non possidebunt.

Ex his dictis sumatur declaratio in hoc loco.

Si secundum carnem vixeritis, moriemini, id est: Si admittetis falsas opiniones et indulgebitis pravis affectibus, rursus eritis rei aeternae poenae, amittetis gratiam et Spiritum sanctum.

Haec peccata nomino lapsus contra conscientiam et errorem in fundamento, ut cum pii, qui recta sentierant, amplectuntur impia dogmata, seu errore seu scientes: ut multi, qui antea recte senserant amplexi sunt Arianam impietatem.

De his omnibus dicitur: Nolite errare, scortatores, adulteri, idolatrae, homicidae, non possidebunt regnum Dei.

De altero gradu autem dicitur: Si actiones carnis spiritu mortificabitis, vivetis.

Fatetur esse in renatis actiones carnis, id est, affectus carnales et opiniones non congruentes cum Spiritu sancto.

Haec mala iubet mortificari spiritu, id est, inbet ut renati sint intenti et vigilantes, ne adprobent falsas opiniones.

Item, iubet, ut repugnent pravis affectibus, nec ruant contra conscientiam.

Ideo Paulus hic iubet spiritu mortificari actiones carnis, et facit mentionem mortificationis, quia in illa lucta vult nos agnoscere nostram infirmitatem, et dolere propter has sordes et fide petere remissionem etiam harum sordium.

De his inquit Paulus: Qui mortificant actiones carnis spiritu, retinere eos vitam, id est, retinere gratiam, Spiritum sanctum, fidem consolantem corda, et manere eos haeredes vitae aeternae, sicut supra dixit: Nulla nunc condemnatio est his, qui in Christo Iesu ambulant.

Utrunque agnoscendum est, et quod sint in renatis peccata, propter quae vere expavescere et dolere debent, et rursus agnoscenda est magnitudo misericordiae Dei, quod recipit credentes propter filium gratis, et affirmat se velle, ut in nobis obedientia incoëtur, et placere eam sibi quanquam valde mutilam et languidam, si tamen renati repugnent vitiosis affectibus, ac doleant se habere tales sordes, et fide petant remissionem.

De hac obedientia dicitur Roma 14.: Qui in his servit Christo, bene placet Deo, et probatus est hominibus.

Ita simul sunt et vera humilitas, agnoscens propriam infirmitatem, et vere dolens propter has reliquias peccati, et econtra consolatio ac laetitia in Deo, quae est fiducia acquiescens propter mediatorem: iuxta dictum: Iustificati fide pacem habemus.

Semper autem sit in conspectu discrimen inter delicta contra conscientiam, et delicta non contra conscientiam.

Qui spiritu Dei ducuntur, hi sunt filii Dei.

Antea posuit propositionem, Debitores sumus, et asseveravit novam obedientiam necessariam esse, et addidit argumenta a poenis et retentione gratiae et vitae aeternae.

Nunc addit argumentum a causa efficiente et a possibili.

Qualis est efficiens, talis sit effectus: In vera conversione Spiritu sancto eriguntur corda per fidem: Sint igitur motus congruentes Spiritu sancto.

Haec doctrina de donatione Spiritus sancti saepe iam repetita est, et saepe cogitanda est consolationis causa, ut accendatur invocatio.

enim ingens sit infirmitas hominum, et diabolus tanquam leo rugiens circumeat, ut quam plurimos devoret, confugiamus ad haec praesidia et ad has consolationes, quod filios Dei Emanuel est custos Ecclesiae, sicut inquit: Nemo rapiet oves meas ex manibus meis, et gubernat, confirmat, docet et consolatur nos Spiritu sancto, et vult haec beneficia peti, et promittit ea petentibus, sicut scriptum est: Sine me nihil potestis facere.

Petite, et accipietis. Quanto magis pater vester coelestis dabit Spiritum sanctum petentibus. Item: Sine tuo numine nihil est in homine, nihil est innoxium. Spiritus opitulatur infirmitati nostrae.

Tales sententiae sint in conspectu, ut exuscitent nos ad invocationem, es discamus hanc doctrinam et exercitia fidei in quotidianis aerumnis, ubi in vera consolatione experiemur praesentiam Spiritus sancti.

Observetur autem hoc loco verbum Ducit. Non est otiosus Spiritus sanctus, movet mentes et ducit, videlicet, non repugnantes: non enim coactio, ut voluntas non possit repugnare. Trahit Deus, sed volentem trahit, ideo inquit: Dabit Spiritum sanctum petentibus. Item: Praebete membra vestra arma iusticiae.

## 8:12 Disposition of Romans
Proposition. We are debtors not to the flesh.

The argument is drawn from reward and punishment: rewards and punishments in persuasive causes pertain to the topic of utility. The dialectician adapts this to the final cause: If anyone here should cavil that one must do good, not for fear of punishment, but because of the will of God, I will answer him nothing, except that these subtleties are untimely in so grave a cause. The saints discern the wrath of God in punishments, and grace in rewards.

The second argument is taken from the efficient cause, and in persuasive speeches it can be referred to the topic of the possible.

By the Holy Spirit mortify the actions of the flesh, because the Holy Spirit has been given to you so that you may be governed by Him. Paul sets forth the major and minor premises; he does not add the conclusion, which a prudent reader can easily attach. For Paul is hastening to consolation, as we shall see.

The children of God are led by the Holy Spirit; you have been made children of God, having received the Holy Spirit, therefore it will be necessary for you also to be led and governed by the Holy Spirit. Hypocrites, by reason, restrain coarser desires in some way and provide a certain simulation of civil duties. But the Holy Spirit slaughters the contempt of God, trust in present things, and similar plagues.

Consolation.

To the minor premise he attaches a κλίμακα or gradation, by which he arrives at consolation. If we are children, we are also heirs. If we are heirs of God, we are co-heirs of Christ. If we are co-heirs of Christ, therefore it is fitting to suffer similarly, so that we may be glorified similarly. Thus, this is the proposition in the consolation: If we suffer together: If the proposition were not bound to the argument, the form would be more childish: It is necessary for us to suffer together with Christ. I. The argument is drawn from rewards, because the most ample rewards will befall us. And he amplifies the rewards by comparison. Present afflictions in no way correspond to the magnitude of the rewards and the glory which will be revealed then when Christ returns to renew the whole universe of things. From this circumstance of time, a new argument is born for him. II. The argument is taken from the example of the universe of things. The whole creation awaits renewal, meanwhile it suffers with us, therefore let us not be burdened to await redemption. There is, moreover, a most grave πάθος, which attributes to the nature of things a sense of the greatest matter, which human reason in no way comprehends. For it signifies that the nature of things grieves for this reason, because meanwhile the devil and the impious abuse the world. And it indicates that it will come to pass that the nature of things shall be freed from this abuse. See, therefore, how reason and the Holy Spirit derive diverse arguments from the same thing. The Epicureans reason thus: The impious fare well, therefore God does not care for human affairs: Paul reasons to the contrary. It is not possible that this whole nature of things was created for abuse. The impious now abuse the world, therefore it is necessary that when the world is freed, the impious must pay the penalty. III. From the example of the Apostles: We who have received the first fruits of the Holy Spirit, are distressed, and we struggle with the world, with despair and the devil, therefore do not cast away your hope in afflictions or temptations. IV. From the definition of hope. It is derived, however, from the formal cause, that is, from the mode of salvation, and the syllogism is complete. Hope is of those things which are not seen, You have been saved by hope, Therefore it is fitting to await the promised goods. Perhaps the conscience feels sin, diffidence, and other evils. Let it know, therefore, that perfect justice and other goods are still to be awaited. V. From the help of the Holy Spirit in persuasive causes, it is referred to the topic of the possible. The Holy Spirit helps the weak, Therefore He will not allow you to succumb. Even if the flesh bears afflictions with difficulty, hangs with difficulty upon the help of God, and would prefer to have present aids etc., nevertheless the Holy Spirit causes us to obey the will of God and to await liberation from Him. This is also a most serious πάθος: He intercedes with inexpressible groanings. VI. From the will of God. It is taken, however, from the object, or the efficient cause. And it is an argument most proper to this business, because the cause of fear and despair is that God seems to be angry and to desert. Here, therefore, the contrary cause, the contrary object is proposed. The conclusion is placed in the first position, afflictions work together for good. The reason follows from the will of God. Those whom God called, these He wills to be made similar to the image of His Son: The Son was glorified through the cross: Therefore He will glorify you also through the cross. He shows the will of the Father in the image of the Son. And afterwards he adds an amplification of the good will of God collected from many signs, which, so that it might have some movement, adds frequent interrogations. For the passage is full of the most ardent affections, by which, looking into the image of Christ and the magnitude of mercy, the mind of Paul was moved. What shall we say to these things? ἀδύνατον is, that is, we can say nothing that consoles more effectively. What shall we say further, what besides shall we require? than His own benevolence and love toward us? He loves us, a sign, because He gave His Son for us all. Amplification. With Him He has given all things, victory against the devil, sin, and death. The remaining signs follow. God justifies us, Christ sits at the right hand of God and intercedes for us. Conclusion: Therefore we shall conquer in afflictions, because God loves us. For the love of God toward us is greater than to allow us to succumb or perish. There are degrees in the interrogations, so that the sound of the speech might be fuller: who is against us, who will accuse, who will condemn, who will separate us from the love of God toward us? What oratorical virtue is finally lacking in this place, the arguments are taken from the proper topics. For it is of singular prudence to see which are the proper topics in a case and which teach the auditor most perfectly, and which the auditor most requires. But the topics of definitions and causes are the most proper. Objects are the causes of the affections, and they stir the motions of the mind, wherefore he treats here copiously the argument taken from the object. The cause of fear and diffidence in the minds of men is the object, that the will of God is proposed to us as alienated. Paul teaches to the contrary, that it is not alienated, that afflictions are not signs of wrath, but rather of grace. And this object increases the terrors: we feel nothing but sin and death. Justice and eternal life are not yet felt. Paul answers by concession from the mode of salvation, so that he may teach that these terrors and the sense of sin do not shake off justice and salvation. For we have been saved by hope. The terrors and aids lift [the spirit], likewise the commemoration of the outcome and the rewards. For in this way we argue in persuasive speeches from the easy and the useful. Paul therefore saw what was most profitable in the case, and he adorned these with excellent figures, proposed an example of the nature of things, and added amplifications where it was most necessary. For the whole matter is placed in this, that the will of God be proposed to us not alienated, so that we may truly establish that we are loved by God, that He cares for us, that He has not cast us away: therefore he amplifies the love of God toward us with many words. The end of the method.

Latin:

Propositio. Debitores sumus non carni.

Ratio ducitur a praemio et poena: Pertinent autem praemia et poenae in suasoris causis ad lo- cum utilitatis. Dialecticus ad finalem causam accommodat: Si quis hic cavilletur, benefacien- dum esse, non metu poenae, sed propter vo- luntatem Dei, huic nihil respondebo, nisi has argutias in tam gravi causa, intempestivas esse. Sancti in poenis iram Dei cernunt, in praemiis gratiam.

Secunda ratio sumta est ex causa efficien- te, et potest in suasoriis ad locum a possibili referri.

Spiritu sancto mortificate actiones carnis, quia Spiritus sanctus est vobis datus, ut ab eo gubernemini. Paulus ponit maiorem et minorem, conclusionem non addit, quam prudens lector facile potest attexere. Properat enim Paulus ad consolationem, ut videbimus.

Filii Dei aguntur Spiritu sancto; Vos estis facti filii Dei, accepto Spiritu sancto, Ergo oportebit et vos agi ac gubernari a Spi- ritu sancto. Hypocritae ratione coërcent aliquo modo cu- piditates crassiores, et quandam simulationem civilium officiorum praestant. At Spiritus sanctus iugulat contemtum Dei, fiduciam rerum praesen- tium et similes pestes.

Consolatio.

Minori attexit κλίμακα seu gradationem, qua pervenit ad consolationem. Si sumus filii, sumus etiam haeredes. Si sumus haeredes Dei, sumus cohaeredes Christi. Si sumus cohaeredes Christi, ergo similiter pati convenit, ut similiter glorificemur. Est itaque haec propositio in consolatione: Si una patimur: Si non esset illigata propositio argumento, forma esset magis puerilis: Oportet nos una pati cum Christo. I. Ratio ducitur a praemiis, quia amplissi- ma praemia contingent. Et amplificat praemia collatione. Nullo modo respondent praesentes afflictiones magnitudini praemiorum et gloriae, quae revelabitur tunc cum redierit Christus ad renovandam totam rerum universitatem. Ex haec circumstantia temporis nascitur ei nova ratio. II. Ratio, ab exemplo universitatis rerum sumitur. Tota creatura expectat renovationem, interea nobiscum patitur, Ergo et nos non gra- vemur expectare redemtionem. Est autem gra- vissimum πάθος, quod naturae rerum tribuit rei maximae sensum, quem humana ratio nullo modo comprehendit. Significat enim ideo dolere rerum naturam, quia interea diabolus et impii abutun- tur mundo. Et subindicat futurum, ut hoc abusu liberetur natura rerum. Vide igitur quomodo diversa argumenta ex eadem re ducant ratio et Spiritus sanctus. Epicurei sic ratiocinantur: Impii bene habent, Ergo Deus non curat humana: Paulus contra ratiocinatur. Non est possibile, hanc totam rerum naturam ad abusum conditam esse. Impii nunc abutuntur mundo, Ergo ne- cesse liberato mundo, impios dare poenas. III. Ab exemplo Apostolorum: Nos qui accepimus primitias Spiritus sancti, angimur, et cum mundo, cum desperatione et diabolo decer- tamus, Ergo nec vos abiicite spem, in afflictio- nibus aut tentationibus. IV. A definitione spei. Ducitur autem ex causa formali, hoc est, ex modo salvationis, et Syllogismus integer est. Spes est earum rerum, quae non videntur, Vos estis spe salvi facti, Ergo expectare convenit promissa bona. Fortasse sen- tit conscientia peccatum, diffidentiam et alia mala. Sciat igitur adhuc expectandam esse perfectam iusticiam, et alia bona. V. Ab auxilio Spiritus sancti in suasoriis causis refertur ad locum a possibili. Spiritus sanctus adiuvat infirmos, Ergo non sinet vos suc- cumbere. Etiamsi caro aegre ferat afflictiones, aegre pendeat ab auxilio Dei, malit habere prae- sentia auxilia etc., tamen Spiritus sanctus facit, ut obtemperemus voluntati Dei, et ab eo expectemus liberationem. Est et hoc gravissimum πάθος: Interpellat gemitibus inenarrabilibus. VI. A voluntate Dei. Sumitur autem ab obiecto, seu causa efficiente. Et est argumentum maxime proprium huic negotio, quia causa pavo- ris ac desperationis est, quod videtur Deus irasci ac deserere. Hic igitur contraria causa, contra- rium obiectum proponitur. Conclusio primo loco ponitur, afflictiones ad bonum cooperantur. Se- quitur ratio ex voluntate Dei. Quos vocavit Deus, hos vult similes fieri imaginis filii sui: Filius est per crucem glorificatus: Ergo et vos per crucem glorificabit. Vo- luntatem patris in imagine filii ostendit. Et po- stea addit amplificationem bonae voluntatis Dei ex multis signis collectam, quae ut motum haberet aliquem, crebras interrogationes addit. Plenus enim locus est ardentissimis affectibus, quibus intuens in imaginem Christi et magnitudinem mi- sericordiae, commotus est animus Pauli. Quid dicemus ad haec? ἀδύνατον est, id est, nihil possumus dicere quod efficacius conso- letur. Quid dicemus amplius, quid praeterea requiremus? quam ipsius benevolentiam et amo- rem erga nos? Amat nos, signum, quia dedit filium pro nobis omnibus. Amplificatio. Omnia cum illo donavit, victo- riam adversus diabolum, peccatum et mortem. Sequuntur reliqua signa. Deus iustificat nos, Christus sedet ad dextram Dei et pro nobis inter- pellat. Conclusio: Ergo vincemus in afflictioni- bus, quia Deus diligit nos. Nam amor Dei erga nos maior est, quam ut sinat nos succumbere aut perire. Gradus sunt in interrogationibus, ut so- nus orationis esset plenior: quis contra nos, quis accusabit, quis condemnabit, quis separabit nos ab amore Dei erga nos? Quae tandem oratoria virtus deest in hoc loco, argumenta sumta sunt ex propriis locis. Est enim singularis prudentiae, videre qui sint in causa loci proprii et qui perfectissime docent au- ditorem, quosque maxime requirit auditor. Sunt autem definitionum et causarum loci maxime pro- prii. Obiecta sunt causae affectuum, et cient motus animi, quare hic copiose tractat argumen- tum ab obiecto sumtum. Causa pavoris et diffi- dentiae est, in animis hominum, obiectum, quod voluntas Dei proponitur nobis abalienata. Pau- lus contra docet, non esse abalienatam, afflictio- nes non esse irae signa, sed magis gratiae. Auget terrores et hoc obiectum: nihil nisi peccatum et mortem sentimus. Nondum sentiun- tur iusticia, vita aeterna. Paulus respondet per concessionem ex modo salvationis, ut doceat hos terrores, et peccati sensum, non excutere iusti- ciam et salutem. Spe enim salvati sumus. Levant terrores et auxilia, item commemo- ratio de exitu et praemiis. Nam hoc modo in suasoriis a facili et utili argumentamur. Vidit igitur Paulus, quid maxime prodesset in causa, et haec egregiis figuris ornavit, proposuit exem- plum naturae rerum, addidit amplificationes, ubi maxime oportuit. Nam tota res in eo posita est, ut proponatur nobis voluntas Dei non alienata, ut possimus vere statuere, quod diligamur a Deo, quod curet nos, quod non abiecerit nos: ideo amorem Dei erga nos multis verbis amplificat. Finis methodi.

## 8:15
For you have not received the spirit of slavery.

Afterwards are described the motions which the Holy Spirit stirs up. You have not received the spirit of slavery, or as he says to Timothy, the spirit of timidity, that is, men not having consolation through the Gospel and the Holy Spirit, when any troubles come, they succumb to sorrow, they pine away and by despair rush into eternal destruction, like Saul, Achitophel. These consternations he calls the spirit of slavery, or of timidity. But where hearts are sustained by the voice of the Gospel and the Holy Spirit, there is felt in sorrow a mitigation and strength, as it is said: Being justified by faith we have peace.

Item: Everyone who trusts in the Lord shall not be confounded. Item: Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved. Item: Come to me all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Item: He who has the Son, has life. In this we know that we remain in him, and he in us, because he gives us of his Spirit.

Moreover, the immediate effects of the Holy Spirit are trust and joy in the heart, with the voice of the Gospel shining forth, and invocation, by which we now approach God erected by faith, we do not flee, we do not rage against him, the love of God, hope, the will for obedience, etc.

All these motions he comprehends, when he says that we, having received the Holy Spirit, cry out Abba Father.

Joint heirs of Christ, if indeed we suffer together.

The proper doctrine of the Church is the assertion of the coming judgment and of the eternal punishments of the impious, and of the eternal glory of the true Church, which Christ earned for us by his obedience, and gives to us himself: because although the resurrection is done by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit together, yet it is done immediately through the Son, and through the Son the visible judgment is made. For the impious will not see the divinity, but they will see the Son, as it is said in Matt. 26: Then all the tribes of the earth will lament, and they will see the Son of Man coming into the world. Concerning this visible judgment it is said: He has given all judgment to the Son. This assertion concerning eternal punishments, and concerning eternal glory, God wills to be known to the Church, so that we may know that we are called not only to the cross and confusion in this life, but to liberation, by which the Church will live in all eternity, and will joyfully enjoy the sight of God, and will discern the righteousness of God in the distinction between the blessed and the damned.

This doctrine and consolation Paul repeats here, since he had spoken before of the remission of sins, of faith, of renovation or new obedience. For it is necessary that this end be known, and at the same time be known that no one is saved after this life, unless in this mortal life the remission of sins has been accepted by faith, and sanctification begun. 2 Cor. 5: We shall be clothed upon, if however we are not found naked. John 3: Unless one is born again of water and the spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven. Item: I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live.

This condition is to be understood not of the merit of our works, but of the necessity of conversion in this life, and this very conversion is a perpetual struggle with the devils and with the flesh. Nor

It is necessary to bear many hardships, therefore our patience is a merit of eternal life. For obedience is owed because of the order sanctioned by God, not because it is a price: And the remission of sins, the Holy Spirit, and the inheritance of eternal life are given to the believer, freely, on account of the Son.

Here again let the causes be considered, for which God wills the Church in this mortal life to be subject to the cross; we often recite these, therefore I will note them briefly here.

The first is, because sin remains in this miserable nature even after conversion, therefore death and other calamities remain.

The second cause is, the Devils rage more rabidly against the Church than against other men, Gene. 3.: I will put enmities etc.

Third, the Church has many actual sins, as Aaron, David, Manasseh, and many others. Therefore punishments follow, because God also in this life wishes examples of his judgment to be seen, according to the saying: You chasten the sons of men for iniquities. He also wishes to recall us to conversion on account of these punishments, 1. Corinthians 11.: When we are judged, we are chastened by the Lord, that we may not be condemned with this world.

Psalm 118: It is good for me that you have humbled me, that I may learn your justifications.

Isaiah 28: Vexation gives understanding.

Fourth, even the saints would become more negligent and proud if they were not exercised by the cross: therefore Paul says, 2. Corinth. 1.: We had the answer of death in ourselves, that we should not be confident in ourselves.

Fifth, God allows things to happen that are inextricable to human counsel, so that his presence may be seen in the Church, when he delivers in wondrous ways, and faith, invocation, and other virtues may be exercised, as Numbers 14.: That the Egyptians may hear, that you O Lord are in this people.

And 1. Kings 17: That all the earth may know that the Lord is God in Israel.

Sixth, God wills the death of the Baptist, Paul, and the like to be testimonies that another judgment remains. Also, that they themselves may seriously feel that the doctrine is true and not feigned. Also, that they profess it for the glory of God, not for their own pleasures or utilities. For because God previously gave a testimony to Paul, by which he showed that he cared for him, when he does not defend him in death against Nero, it is necessary that a judgment remains afterwards, in which he will show that he approves of Paul, not Nero.

Seventh, it is fitting that we become similar to the image of the Son of God. It was a certain order and wisdom, if men had not fallen, for them to live without death and without miseries. Now there is another wisdom; God wills us to acknowledge him to be just, and us, immersed in sin, to humbly confess that we are guilty, and justly to sustain the destruction of this depraved nature, as Daniel says: To you O Lord is justice, but to us confusion of face.

The Son, however, is sent, who, when he sustains punishment though innocent, his passion becomes a λύτρον for others, and he himself becomes a victor and struggles out of death: the same Son of God is effective in us, who justly sustain punishment. Our death, however, is by no means a λύτρον, but is a just punishment and a reminder of the judgment of God. We shall, however, be like the Son of God when he restores life to us: meanwhile, God wills that we be in some way like him both in death and in miseries, so that he may remind us of his judgment against sin.

Finally, the wisdom of the cross is manifold and inexhaustible, concerning which the counsel of God must be pondered throughout the whole of life, and this saying should always be in sight: Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, mighty, that is, to press down and to liberate.

Philosophy neither shows the principal causes of human calamities, nor does it sufficiently provide consolations, but in the Church alone has God revealed his will, both concerning punishments and concerning liberations.

On consolations.

Having considered, however, the causes on account of which the Church is subjected to the cross, let us afterwards look at the consolations, just as when diseases are known, remedies are then provided. Nothing, however, soothes pain unless some reason for good is perceived in it.

Although others may distribute the topics of philosophical consolations differently, yet for the sake of teaching, they are six in number, which are: 1. Necessity, 2. The dignity of virtue to be preferred to pain, 3. A good conscience, 4. Examples, 5. Final causes, such as fighting for one's country, 6. Comparison of events, such as it is better to be hindered by sickness than to come to evil company. I omit, however, a longer declaration, because for those moderately instructed, the consideration is not difficult. In the Church, I recite the same places of consolation, but I add others properly evangelical. For philosophical ones arise from the doctrine of the law. They are not, therefore, to be neglected, but yet it is necessary to add the evangelical ones. And Paul, in this consolation, takes arguments also from the law, as he does when he speaks of Necessity and examples.

These, therefore, are the places:

1. Necessity, because it is necessary to obey God, according to the saying: Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, and this obedience becomes a sacrifice. 2. The dignity of virtue is to be preferred to pain, for the law also commands this, lest, broken by pain, we do unjust things. 3. A good conscience. 4. The promise of the remission of sins and of reconciliation. 5. The promise of divine aid, of mitigation, and of the presence of God in the very miseries. 6. The promise of final liberation and of eternal salvation, as Job says: Even if He slays me, I will hope in Him. 7. The examples of the Son of God and of the universal Church. 8. Final causes, because we are afflicted not that we may perish, but that we may be recalled to repentance. Also, that the fear of God, faith, and invocation may grow in us. Also, that God may be celebrated in confession. 9. A comparison of events, as it was better for Jonathan to die than to become at some time an enemy of David.

We contemplate this brief summary of the doctrine concerning the cross and concerning consolations also in this most splendid discourse of Paul, in which the first argument is taken from the outcome of afflictions, and from the final liberation and eternal salvation. For this is the chief argument: The mind seeing the good, namely eternal salvation, rejoices, and is less moved by present pain, which it knows to be a brief journey. And this chief argument is often repeated in this very discourse of Paul, which he recites at the beginning with these words: I reckon that the afflictions of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come. For the expectation of the creature etc.

The second argument is taken from the example of the world. It is a customary place of consolations to propose examples of those similarly afflicted, because equality seems to be a certain justice, namely, that no one should desire extraordinary things, and wish to enjoy greater comforts than others who are perhaps more worthy; therefore Elias says: I am not better than my fathers. Thus Paul argues here: Common miseries are to be borne: The whole nature of things is now subject to corruption and the abuse of the impious, and it groans with us, but it awaits liberation. Therefore, let us also bear our part of common miseries, and let us await liberation.

In this prosopopoeia, let us consider what kind of πάθος (pathos) this is, and what a sweet argument it continues: he says the nature of things groans. Although heaven and earth are without sense, yet the corruption and the horrendous abuse of things in the world are most sad spectacles, and there is pain in the saints looking upon this deformity, and thinking of the causes: he transfers this pain to the very nature of things in this prosopopoeia. The walls did not grieve for the profaned temple of Jerusalem, but the Maccabees and other saints grieved, seeing this deformity of the land, the insults to God, the slaughter of citizens, of matrons, of boys and girls, the exiles and other calamities. In such examples, let it be considered what kind of prosopopoeia this is.

Then there is a clear refutation of the Epicureans in this argument. Thus Epicurus argues: Where there is no order, there is no providence of God. In the world there is no order, because often it is better for the evil than for the good. Therefore the world is not ruled by providence.

Paul argues against this: Since nature is most beautifully ordered, and yet there is now manifold abuse, it is necessary that there be causes for both things. The cause of order is God, but the cause of abuses is sin, and yet God did not create this most beautiful work in vain. Therefore, this abuse will not be perpetual. Present calamity is a testimony of future liberation. For it is by no means to be thought that this most beautiful workmanship of the world was created only for those confusions for all eternity.

Although we cannot fully exhaust the wisdom and sorrows of Paul in this very argument, let us nevertheless think something about these matters: let us contemplate the abuse, not as the Epicureans do, but let us deplore the causes, namely sins, and let us look at both, namely the most beautiful order of many things established in nature by God, and then the confusion of order which occurred because of sin, and let us think, since the world was not created for eternal abuse, that a liberation will follow at some time, and that God will reveal His judgment.

But we ourselves, who have the beginnings of the Spirit, etc.

The third argument is taken from the example of the Apostles.

We who have more excellent gifts are afflicted, we struggle with the conscience of past falls and the remaining impurity, with the terrors of the devil, with our own infirmity, with dangers and persecutions, and we await liberation.

Latin:

Non enim accepistis spiritum servitutis.

Postea describuntur motus, quos ciet Spiritus sanctus. Non accepistis spiritum servitutis, seu ut ad Timotheum inquit, Spiritum timiditatis, id est, homines non habentes consolationem per Evangelium et Spiritum sanctum, cum veniunt aerumnae quaecunque, succumbunt dolori, contabescunt et desperatione ruunt in aeternum exitium, ut Saul, Achitophel. Has consternationes nominat Spiritum servitutis, seu timiditatis. Ubi vero corda sustentantur voce Evangelii et Spiritu sancto, ibi sentitur in dolore mitigatio et robur, sicut dicitur: Iustificati fide pacem habemus.

Item: Omnis qui confidit in Domino, non confundetur. Item: Omnis qui invocaverit nomen Domini, salvus erit. Item: Venite ad me omnes qui laboratis et onerati estis, et ego reficiam vos. Item: Qui habet filium, habet vitam. In hoc cognoscimus quod in eo manemus, et ipse in nobis, quia de spiritu suo dat nobis

Sunt autem effectus immediati Spiritus sancti, fiducia et laetitia in corde praelucente voce Evangelii, invocatio, qua iam accedimus ad Deum erecti fide, non fugimus, non fremimus adversus eum, dilectio Dei, spes, velle obedientiam etc.

Hos motus omnes comprehendit, cum inquit, nos accepto Spiritu sancto clamare Abba Pater.

Cohaeredes Christi, siquidem una patimur.

Propria doctrina est Ecclesiae, asseveratio de venturo iudicio et de poenis aeternis impiorum, et de gloria aeterna verae Ecclesiae, quam meruit nobis Christus sua obedientia, et donat nobis ipse: quia etsi resuscitatio fit a Patre, Filio et a Spiritu sancto simul, tamen fit immediate per filium, et per filium fit visibile iudicium. Impii enim non videbunt divinitatem, sed filium videbunt, ut Matth. 26. dicitur: Tunc plangent omnes tribus terrae, et videbunt filium hominis venientem in mundum. De hoc visibili iudicio dicitur: Dedit omne iudicium filio. Hanc asseverationem de aeternis poenis, et de gloria aeterna, vult Deus Ecclesiae notam esse, ut sciamus nos vocari non tantum ad crucem et confusionem in hac vita, sed ad liberationem, qua in tota aeternitate vivet Ecclesia, et laeta fruetur conspectu Dei, et cernet iusticiam Dei in discrimine beatorum et damnatorum.

Hanc doctrinam et consolationem hic repetit Paulus, cum antea dixerit de remissione peccatorum, de fide, de renovatione seu nova obedientia. Necesse est enim hunc finem sciri, et simul sciri, neminem salvum fieri post hanc vitam, nisi in hac vita mortali remissio peccatorum fide accepta sit, et incoata sanctificatio 2. Corinth. 5.: Superinduemur, si tamen non nudi reperiemur. Iohan. 3.: Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua et spiritu, non intrabit in regnum coelorum. Item: Vivo ego, dicit Dominus, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed ut convertatur et vivat. Iuramentum postulat conversionem. Item, Apocal. 2.: Esto fidelis usque ad mortem, et dabo tibi coronam vitae. Item: Beati mortui, qui in Domino moriuntur. Matth. 22.: Amice quare intrasti, non habens vestem nuptialem. Psal. 23.: Mors impii mala. Ideo Paulus hoc loco inquit: Glorificabimur: et addit, Siquidem una patimur.

Haec conditio intelligatur non de merito nostrorum operum, sed de necessitate conversionis in hac vita, et haec ipsa conversio est perpetuum certamen cum diabolis et cum carnes. Nec

Necesse est ferre multas aerumnas, Ergo patientia nostra est meritum vitae ae- ternae. Debetur enim obedientia propter ordi- nem a Deo sancitum, non quia sit pretium: Ac donantur credenti remissio peccatorum, Spiritus sanctus, et haereditas vitae aeternae, Gratis, pro- pter filium.

Hic rursus considerentur causae, propter quas Deus vult Ecclesiam in hac mortali vita sub- iectam esse cruci, has saepe recitamus: ideo hic breviter eas annotabo.

Prima est, quia manet peccatum in hac mi- sera natura etiam post conversionem, manent igitur mors et aliae calamitates.

Secunda causa est, Diaboli rabiosius sae- viunt in Ecclesiam, quam in alios homines, Gene. 3.: Ponam inimicitias etc.

Tertia, Habet Ecclesia multa actualia pec- cata, ut Aaron, David, Manasse, et alii pluri- mi. Sequuntur ergo poenae, quia Deus etiam in hac vita vult conspici exempla iudicii sui, iuxta dictum: Propter iniquitates corripis filios homi- num. Vult item nos propter has poenas revocare ad conversionem, 1. Corinthiorum 11.: Cum iudi- camur, a Domino corripimur, ne cum hoc mundo damnemur.

Psalm. 118.: Bonum mihi, quod humiliasti me, ut discam iustificationes tuas.

Esaiae 28.: Vexatio dat intellectum.

Quarta, Etiam sancti fierent negligentiores et superbi, si non exercerntur cruce: ideo Pau- lus inquit, 2. Corinth. 1.: Responsum mortis in nobis habuimus, ut non simus confidentes in no- bis ipsis.

Quinta, Sinit Deus accidere inextricabilia humano consilio, ut conspiciatur praesentia eius in Ecclesia, cum mirandis modis liberat, et exer- ceantur fides, invocatio et aliae virtutes, ut Nu- meri 14.: Ut audiant Aegypti, quod tu Domine sis in hoc populo.

Et 1. Reg. 17. Ut sciat omnis terra, quod sit Dominus Deus in Israël.

Sexta, Vult Deus mortem Baptistae, Pauli, et similium testimonia esse, quod restet aliud iu- dicium. Item, quod ipsi serio sentiant, doctri- nam veram esse et non commentitiam. Item, quod eam profiteantur propter gloriam Dei, non propter suas voluptates aut utilitates. Quia enim Deus antea dedit testimonium Paulo, quo osten- dit sibi eum curae esse, cum eum non defendat in morte contra Neronem, necesse est postea re- stare judicium, in quo ostendet se adprobare Paulum, non Neronem.

Septima, Oportet nos similes fieri imaginis filii Dei. Erat ordinatum quiddam et sapientia, si homines non essent lapsi, vivere eos sine mor- te et sine miseriis. Nunc alia sapientia est, vult Deus nos agnoscere ipsum esse iustum, et nos mersos in peccatum, humiliter fateri nos esse reos, et iuste sustinere destructionem huius de- pravatae naturae, sicut inquit Daniel: Tibi Do- mine iusticia, nobis autem confusio faciei.

Mittitur autem filius, qui cum innocens poe- nam sustinet, fit eius passio λύτρον pro aliis, et ipse fit victor et eluctatur ex morte: idem filius Dei est efficax in nobis, qui iuste poenam susti- nemus. Nequaquam tamen nostra mors est λύ- τρον, sed est iusta poena et commonefactio de iu- dicio Dei. Erimus autem similes filio Dei, cum vitam nobis reddet: interea vult nos Deus aliquo modo et in morte et in miseriis ei similes esse, ut commonefaciat nos de iudicio suo adversus peccatum.

Denique multiplex et inexhausta crucis sa- pientia est, de qua consilium Dei in tota vita cogitandum est, et semper sit in conspectu hoc dictum: Humiliamini sub potenti manu Dei, po- tenti videlicet, ad premendum et ad liberandum.

Philosophia nec causas principales calamita- tum humanarum ostendit, nec sufficienter con- solationes tradit, sed in sola Ecclesia patefecit Deus voluntatem suam, et de poenis et de libe- rationibus.

De consolationibus.

Consideratis autem causis, propter quas Ec- clesia cruci subiecta est, postea consolationes in- tueamur, sicut cognitis morbis deinde remedia traduntur. Nihil autem lenit dolorem, nisi ali- qua boni ratio in eo conspiciatur.

Etsi autem alii aliter distribuere locos philo- sophicarum consolationum possint, tamen utcun- que docendi causa sex numero, qui sunt: 1. Necessitas, 2. Dignitas virtutis anteferenda dolori, 3. Bona conscientia, 4. Exempla, 5. Causae finales, ut pugnare pro patria, 6. Collatio eventuum, ut melius est morbo im- pediri, quam venire ad malum sodalitium. Omitto autem longiorem declarationem, quia mediocriter institutis non est difficilis consideratio. In Ecclesia eosdem locos consolationum recito, sed addo alios proprie evangelicos. Nam philosophici ex legis doctrina oriuntur. Non sunt igitur negligendi, sed tamen addi evangelicos oportet. Et Paulus in hac consolatione ex lege etiam sumit argumenta, ut cum de Necessitate et exemplis dicit.

Sunt igitur hi loci:

1. Necessitas, quia Deo necesse est obedire, iuxta dictum: Humiliamini sub potenti manu Dei, et haec obedientia fit sacrificium. 2. Dignitatis virtutis anteferenda dolori, nam hoc quoque lex praecipit, ne fracti dolore iniusta faciamus. 3. Bona conscientia. 4. Promissio remissionis peccatorum et reconciliationis. 5. Promissio auxilii divini, mitigationis ac praesentiae Dei in ipsis aerumnis. 6. Promissio liberationis finalis et aeternae salutis, sicut Iob inquit: Etiam si occidet me, sperabo in eo. 7. Exempla filii Dei et universae Ecclesiae. 8. Causae finales, quia affligimur non ut pereamus, sed ut revocemur ad poenitentiam. Item, ut crescant in nobis timor Dei, fides, invocatio. Item, ut in confessione celebretur Deus. 9. Collatio eventuum, ut melius fuit Ionathae mori, quam fieri aliquando hostem Davidis.

Hanc brevem summam doctrinae de cruce et de consolationibus intuemur etiam in hac splendidissima Pauli concione, in qua primum argumentum sumtum est ab exitu afflictionum, et finali liberatione et aeterna salute. Nam hoc argumentum praecipuum est: Mens videns bonum, scilicet aeternam salutem laetatur, et minus movetur praesenti dolore, quem scit breve iter esse. Ac saepe repetitur hoc praecipuum argumentum in hac ipsa Pauli concione, quod initio recitat his verbis: Decerno afflictiones huius temporis, non esse pares venturae gloriae. Nam expectatio creaturae etc.

Secundum argumentum ab exemplo mundi sumtum est. Usitatus locus est consolationum proponere exempla similiter afflictorum, quia aequalitas videtur esse quaedam iustitia, videlicet, ne quis appetat extraordinaria, et velit frui maioribus commodis, quam alii fortassis digniores, ideo inquit Elias: Non sum melior patribus meis. Ita hic argumentatur Paulus: Ferendae sunt communes miseriae: Tota rerum natura nunc subiecta est cortioni et abusui impiorum, et gemit nobiscum, sed expectat liberationem. Ergo et nos feramus partem communium miseriarum, et expectemus liberationem.

In hac prosopopoeia consideremus, quale sit hoc πάθος, et quam dulce argumentum continuat: ait gemere naturam rerum. Etsi autem coelum et terra sunt sine sensu, tamen corruptio et horrendi abusus rerum in mundo sunt tristissima spectacula, et dolor est in sanctis aspicientibus hanc deformitatem, et cogitantibus causas: hunc dolorem transfert ad ipsam rerum naturam in hac prosopopoeia. Non dolebant muri prophanato templo Ierosolymae, sed dolebant Maccabaei et alii sancti, videntes hanc terram deformitatem, contumelias Dei, neces civium, matronarum, puerorum et puellarum exilia et alias calamitates. In talibus exemplis consideretur, qualis sit haec prosopopoeia.

Deinde perspicua refutatio est Epicureorum in hoc argumento. Sic argumentatur Epicurus: Ubi non est ordo, ibi non est providentia Dei. In mundo non est ordo, quia saepe malis melius est quam bonis. Ergo non regitur mundus providentia.

Paulus contra argumentatur: Cum natura sit pulcerrime ordinata, et tamen iam sit multiplex abusus, necesse est utriusque rei causas esse. Ordinis causa Deus est, sed abusuum causa peccatum est, nec tamen Deus frustra condidit hoc pulcerrimum opus. Non igitur perpetuus erit hic abusus. Calamitas praesens testimonium est futurae liberationis. Quia nequaquam existimandum est, hoc pulcerrimum mundi opificium tantum ad illas confusiones in omnem aeternitatem conditum esse.

Quanquam autem sapientiam et dolores Pauli in hoc ipso argumento non prorsus exhaurire possumus, tamen cogitemus aliquid de his rebus: intuemur abusum non ut Epicurei, sed deploremus causas, scilicet peccata, et aspiciamus utrunque, videlicet pulcerrimum ordinem multarum rerum in natura conditum a Deo, et deinde confusionem ordinis, quae accessit propter peccatum, et cogitemus, cum non conditus sit mundus ad aeternum abusum, secuturam esse aliquando liberationem, et Deum patefacturum esse iudicium suum.

Sed et nos ipsi, qui initia spiritus habemus etc.

Tertium argumentum sumtum est ab exemplo Apostolorum.

Nos qui excellentiora dona habemus affligimur, luctamur cum conscientia lapsuum praeteritorum et reliqua immunditie, cum terroribus diaboli, cum nostra infirmitate, cum periculis et persecutionibus, et expectamus liberationem.

## 8:24
For by hope we are saved.

The fourth argument is from the order and time of liberation.

We are liberated in such a way that the inheritance is still to be hoped for, to be possessed afterwards, and so that I may say: Now we have the right to the thing, not yet the thing itself.

For thus God gathers the eternal Church, and not otherwise. He wills that we be reborn in this life through the Gospel, and He wills that the Church in this life be subject to the cross: afterwards in eternal life there will be complete newness and joy.

Paul therefore understands salvation in this place as that final and complete liberation: which must be said for this reason, so that a sophistical captious argument may be answered.

Latin:

Spe enim salvati sumus.

Quartum argumentum ab ordine et tempore liberationis.

Sic liberati sumus, ut adhuc speranda sit haereditas, postea possidenda, et ut ita dicam: Nunc habemus ius ad rem, nondum in re.

Sic enim Deus colligit Ecclesiam aeternam, et non aliter. Vult nos in hac vita per Evangelium renasci, et vult Ecclesiam in hac vita subiectam esse cruci: postea in vita aeterna erit integra novitas et laetitia.

Intelligit ergo Paulus hoc loco salvationem, illam ultimam et integram liberationem: quod ideo dicendum est, ut sophisticae captionis respondeatur.

## 8:24
By hope we are saved: Therefore we are not saved by faith alone.

I answer: I deny the consequence, because there is ambiguity in the word 'Saved'. When he says: 'By hope we are saved', he does not understand the word 'Saved' as referring to those reconciled, but he understands it as referring to those liberated from all miseries.

When I say: 'By hope we are liberated', time is understood, and grammatically this is signified, that complete liberation is still awaited. When it is said: 'By faith we are justified', the cause is shown, namely the mercy promised because of the Son of God, which must be received by faith.

Although faith and hope are related virtues, and can by no means be torn apart, yet because Paul makes some distinction, when he says: 'These three, Faith, Hope, Love', let them be held as distinct descriptions in some way.

Faith is to assent to every word of God delivered to us, and thus to the promise of grace, and it is a trust resting in God because of the mediator, not because of our own virtues or works, and moving hearts so that they approach God, and call upon Him and cry 'Abba Father'.

Hope is the certain expectation of eternal salvation to be given freely because of the mediator, and it is the expectation of the mitigation of punishments in this life, according to the counsel of God.

Faith and hope differ, however, because faith in the present receives the remission of sins, and reconciliation, or the imputation of righteousness because of the mediator, and brings peace, that is, joy to the heart that has felt true terrors, as it is said: 'Being justified by faith we have peace with God.'

And by this faith, struggling out of the sorrows of the lower regions, we approach God, we rightly acknowledge Him and call upon Him, as it is said to the Ephesians: 'Through Him we have boldness to approach in trust through faith in Him.' Thus faith receives in the present reconciliation, the earnest of future goods, namely the Holy Spirit, and it is an apprehensive and quieting virtue.

But hope is the expectation of future liberation, which expectation is preceded by the knowledge of the promise and assent, and the trust receiving reconciliation, as David, having heard the promise, was uplifted, and afterwards began to hope for liberation.

Love is obedience according to the commands of God, with faith shining forth with true joy in God, because it is said in 1 John 5: 'This is the love of God, that we keep His commandments.'

By patience we await, etc.

I said the fourth argument is taken from the order and time of liberation. First, the inheritance is to be hoped for, but afterwards to be possessed. Now he dwells on the description of hope, he says that hope is of a future good, not yet present..., therefore he says: 'Hope that is seen is not hope': where the phrase should be rightly understood. He adds patience to hope, however, because meanwhile in this life great agonies must be endured, just as he also predicts: God 3. EXPOSITION OF PAUL'S EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS. CHAP. VIII. 966 precepts patience, and [ he] affirms that [he] will help us.

These are the predictions: 2 Tim. 3: All who want to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution. And Psalm 33: Many are ...the tribulations of the righteous. And Jeremiah 12: I have given my beloved soul into the hands of her enemies.

These, however, are the precepts of patience: Matt. 16: If anyone wishes to follow me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. 1 Peter last: Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God. 1 Cor. 10: Do not murmur. 1 Tim. 6: Pursue righteousness, patience, etc. Psalm 37: Be subject to God, and pray to him. In Isaiah: In silence and hope shall be your strength. These are the promises: Psalm 90: I am with him in tribulation, I will deliver him and glorify him. Psalm 49: Call upon me in the day of tribulation, and I will deliver you.

Let such sayings, predictions, precepts, and promises be in sight, so that doctrine and consolation in hardships may be sought from them, as has been said above regarding places of consolation.

But someone objects: Since such is its nature, [and] all who feel torment cannot but grieve, and become angry at causes, and seek deliverances, others otherwise, why then do you call it Patience? Is it an empty name? I answer: Philosophical patience is a perfection in adversity, which commands one to bear [it] with reason, so that one may somehow moderate external gestures, lest you act broken by pain against some virtue, as Cato acts against justice, being conscious of his own death. Medea, angry, kills her children for Jason, and many seek deliverances by illicit means, or consult Magi, or make unjust covenants; and because philosophical patience often does not show deliverance, therefore it remains interior pain, and thus it grows, so that it extinguishes the man: there patience is an empty name.

But Christian patience is to wish to obey God in those things which he commands to be borne, and to do nothing against the commandments of God, and at the same time to discern the presence of God in torment, and to hope for help and deliverance, and to rejoice in God, because we discern good things, namely God himself present to the afflicted, as help and deliverance. Such patience is not an empty name, because joy is felt, which overcomes pains.

Just as therefore David in his hardships feels true joy in God, as he says in Psalm 114: The pains of death, and the anguish of hell have found me, and I will call upon the name of the Lord, O Lord deliver my soul. Afterwards follows the voice of joy: Turn, O my soul, into thy rest, for the Lord hath delivered my soul from death. Also Psalm 93: According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, thy consolations have gladdened my soul. And when this joy is actually felt, it can be understood that this patience is not an empty name, but rather that this joy is patience, and yet there is a struggle of pains and consolation, and in others more, in others less, joy is felt: just as the struggle is described in this same Chapter 8 to the Romans: The Spirit helps our infirmity.

And very often in the Psalms, as Psalm 41: As the hart panteth after the fountains of water, so my soul panteth after thee, O God, Why art thou sad, O my soul, and why dost thou hope in God, etc. And this is the illustrious distinction of philosophical and Christian patience, that Christian patience in some way wants obedience for the sake of God, and is always joined with faith and the hope of divine help, which are the cause of joy. But in Palamedes, Socrates, Dionysius, Phocion, patience is not the hope of divine help, but is any external moderation of gestures, because the interior pain is less, when the conscience is not wounded, according to the saying: It is a crime for great evils to be absent.

The Spirit helps our infirmity. The fifth argument is taken from divine help. For since he had spoken of patience and had established that there are great hardships of the Church, and difficult struggles, he adds an argument of help, which is most effective for confirming the pious: for he shows good things and [things] mitigating pains.

Here it must be known, therefore, that the Church is exercised, so that in sorrows we may think of the causes of affliction, and of the promise of help and deliverance, as it is said in Isaiah 28: Vexation gives understanding. Item: God does an alien work, so that He may do His own work, that is, He allows the Church to be afflicted, so that He may show Himself to be a liberator, etc.

In that contemplation of the promises and in prayer, the Holy Spirit is given, and His efficacy is felt, as is said concerning the promises in Psalm 5: My soul waited in His word. And it must be known that the Holy Spirit is given in this way, namely, in the contemplation of the promise and in prayer. Just as the Lord also says: How much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him. The rest in the text of Paul describe the magnitude of the sorrows and the struggle: We do not know what we should pray for, etc., but the Spirit intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings, that is, the weak nature would prefer not to suffer, but the Holy Spirit bends the will and the hearts, so that in some way we may desire obedience, and He incites us to invocation, which is pleasing to God, just as David preferred not to perish in exile, and yet says: Let Him do what is good before Him.

And Job: Even if He kills me, I will hope in Him. Here it is asked: By what distinction is Christ elsewhere called the intercessor for us, while here the Holy Spirit is called the intercessor?

I answer: Christ is the intercessor because He is the redeemer, and by His merit He appeases the wrath of the eternal Father.

But the Holy Spirit is the intercessor in that He moves us to invocation, according to the saying: You have received the Spirit, by whom we cry Abba Father. Item, Zech. 11: I will pour out upon the house of David a spirit of grace and of prayers. The Son is the intercessor because He is the redeemer, who paid the price so that He might satisfy the justice of God, and the wrath of God might be appeased.

But the Holy Spirit intercedes after the wrath has been appeased through the Son, in such a way that He kindles invocation in us, according to the saying: I will pour out upon the house of David a spirit of grace and of prayers, that is, the Spirit testifying in consolation through the Gospel that God receives us and is propitious to us, and kindling us to invocation and gladdening our hearts with acquiescence in God, etc. We know, however, that for those who love God, all things work together for good.

The sixth argument is a repetition of the first and principal argument, which is taken from the outcome of afflictions, as if he were saying: Since the liberation is certain and the future outcomes will be most joyful, endure the hardships of a short time: and the causes and the example of Christ are interwoven.

We seek the fellowship of the eternal Church.

And thus God gathers the Church, and then glorifies it, and not otherwise. So that we may arrive at the goal, let us also bear the labors of this necessary journey, according to the saying: He who seeks the end, let him not flee the means to the end.

Moreover, the example of the Son of God is proposed, which is a most illustrious testimony in both respects, namely, of the immense wrath of God against our sins, and of the love of God toward us, and of the liberation of the Church.

It is necessary that there be immense wrath, since no one is a redeemer except the Son. And it is necessary that there be great love toward us, since the Son was given for us. And the liberation is certain, since the Son promises that He will so liberate the Church that we ourselves may be most like Him in all eternity. Just as He says: I give them eternal life, etc.

And in the Psalm: God has anointed you because of your companions. He reminds us of these greatest matters by the proposed example of the Son.

Here again, the causes must be considered why the Church is subjected to the cross, which we have recited several times above.

Those whom He chose, them He also called. He adds a most splendid amplification concerning the conservation of the Church in such great deformity, and in these confusions and ruins of kingdoms, as if he were saying: Although all things threaten destruction, yet know that the Church is a care to God, and that it will not perish.

He begins, therefore, from election, so that He may remind us of the eternal counsel of God, and of the conservation of the Church, as if he were saying: Know that the Church is chosen because of the Son, as it is said in the Psalm: The lines have fallen to me in pleasant places.

There will always be some inheritance of the Son of God in the human race. And this chosen Church is gathered by preaching, and becomes righteous, and will be adorned with eternal glory. Soon, therefore, He warns where the elect are to be sought, namely, in the assembly of the called.

Therefore He says: Those whom He chose, them He also called. Let us hold to this consolation, and let us not imagine that the elect are to be sought outside the assembly of the called, but let us know that they are in the assembly of the called, which is the visible Church, in which the voice of the Gospel sounds uncorrupted; there the Son of God is efficacious through the Gospel.

As it is written:

The Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth. And it is the commandment of God, that individuals join themselves to this assembly of the called, according to the sayings: He that heareth you, heareth me; He that gathereth not with me, scattereth. Item, Psalm 83: Blessed are they that dwell in thy house, O Lord. This whole doctrine is briefly comprehended here, which is to be thought upon as often as we recite the article: I believe there is a catholic Church, that is, I believe God will always preserve the Church, and I also join myself to it; in this are all the elect who retain faith and a good conscience.

If God be for us, who can be against us? He amplifies at the end the certainty of grace and liberation, by mentioning the pledge given, namely the redeemer and intercessor, and at the same time refutes objections.

For two terrible arguments come into view, which impel men to doubt. The sight of our own impurity, which clings to all, even those who do not have sins against conscience: for conscience always disputes. God does not hear sinners, I am a sinner: Therefore I am not in grace. Then the sight of external miseries, about which we reason. It ought to be well with the righteous. The Church is most afflicted and not only small, but also deformed by domestic wounds. Who would have thought in the time of Herod in Judea alone, which was full of calamities and civil wars, that there was a Church, and that God did not care more for Augustus and the Roman senators, who excelled in wisdom, virtue, power, and other ornaments?

These two arguments do not lightly shake the minds of all men. And by the former argument, the monks were so moved that they taught that in this life one must always doubt whether we are in grace, and they approve of this doubt, and say it is humility. Against this foul error, the voice of the Gospel most constantly teaches that doubt must be overcome by faith, so that those converted to God may conclude that their sins are truly forgiven them for the sake of the Son, and that for his sake they are pleasing to God, although there still cling to us not sins against conscience, but defects and depraved inclinations and the flames of depraved affections, which we nevertheless resist.

This doctrine concerning the overcoming of doubt, and this necessary consolation, has been often repeated above, where you may consider these testimonies. Rom. 4: Therefore it is of faith, that the promise might be firm, as if he said: To the unbeliever the promise is an empty sound, and it is the eternal and immovable commandment of God that we hear the Son, as the heavenly Father says: Hear him. Item in the Psalm: Kiss the Son.

They treat him with contempt who do not grant him this honor, that they believe that for his sake sins are forgiven them. To this add other illustrious testimonies:

Acts 10: To him all the Prophets bear witness, that through his name all who believe in him receive remission of sins. Rom. 5: Being justified by faith we have peace. But this peace is opposed to doubt.

And Eph. 3: Through whom we have boldness to approach in confidence through faith in him. Item, Heb. 4: Let us approach with confidence to the throne of grace.

Let us know, therefore, that it is the commandment of God and the proper voice of the Gospel that we believe that our sins are forgiven us in conversion, and that we are in grace for the sake of the Son, and that doubt must be overcome by this faith. And although this victory is weak, yet it ought to grow continually, both repentance and this victory, as he says: I believe, Lord, but help my unbelief.

But the arguments which are opposed to this certainty have been explained often elsewhere. God does not hear sinners, namely, those who do not convert to God, but persevere in wickedness against conscience, or defend errors against the foundation, that is, against the articles of faith.

This saying of Solomon is also cited: No man knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred: But the answer is brief and most firm. Solomon is speaking of the judgment of men, which is taken from events in this life, namely from prosperous or adverse things.

As Ahab should not think he is pleasing to God because of his victories, David let him not think himself rejected because of exile.

But let him be judged by the will of God from His word.

Thus the saying of Solomon agrees with our opinion, not with the false imagination of the monks. *Who shall accuse the elect?

It is God who justifies.* This is a response to the argument recited earlier.

For when the conscience objects in the converted, since many impurities still cling to us, and many sins of ignorance and omission, how can I not doubt?

Here Paul answers that faith relies on the merit and intercession of the Son of God, not on our dignity, and mention is made of both things, merit and intercession.

He shows the merit when he says: He who did not spare His own Son, but delivered Him up for us all, how shall He not with Him freely give us all things?

Item: Who shall accuse the elect?

It is God who justifies, that is, who receives believers and pronounces them to be righteous, that is, they themselves are pleasing because they are covered by the righteousness of the Son through the Son.

Afterwards he speaks of intercession: Who also makes intercession for us.

Here the doctrine of the priesthood of Christ must be held, of which it was said: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.

This consideration of the priesthood of Christ contains the most ample doctrine and the sweetest consolation.

But first, let the definition be noted.

The high priest is a person immediately sent by God to announce the Gospel, and immediately bringing it forth from the bosom of the eternal Father, and sent to offer a sacrifice, so that by the penalty paid for us the wrath of God might be appeased, and constantly praying for us, and having the testimony that he is heard, and preserving the ministry of the Gospel in the Church, and perpetually gathering the Church by the voice of the Gospel and blessing it, giving the remission of sins, the Holy Spirit, and eternal life.

The Epistle to the Hebrews shows that all these members are contained in the definition of the high priest.

And this high priest is not typical, but is Christ, God and man: for the name of the office pertains to the person, who is God and man.

For the sake of consolation, however, the consideration of both things is necessary, namely, of the sacrifice or merit, and of the intercession.

This person offers a sacrifice, that is, His entire obedience and humiliation even unto the resurrection, so that He might pay the penalty for us; He Himself applies this offering to the Church with His own words, saying: I sanctify Myself for them.

And it is said to the Hebrews, Chap.

1: By which will we have been sanctified, through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.

Item: By one offering He has perfected us.

Therefore, this consolation, which is proposed in the merit of Christ, or sacrifice, is first made in sight, namely, that in conversion believers are truly received and are pleasing to God because of this victim, even if the remnants of sin still cling to the converted.

Therefore, doubt must be overcome, because the doubter argues whether the merit of Christ suffices, or prefers his own sins to the merit of Christ, contrary to the saying: Grace abounds over the offense.

Therefore he says here: Who shall accuse the elect, since it is God who justifies, as if he were saying: Even if the remnants of sin cling to the converted, yet God justifies them because of the Son.

But concerning intercession, let us know that the application of the merit of Christ to us happens at all times, before the eternal Father through the mediator Himself, who prays for us.

Thus merit and intercession are joined.

Merit is the obedience of Christ satisfying the justice of God to appease His wrath.

Intercession is the constant application for us, as it is said in Hebrews 7: Always living, that He may intercede for them.

And in this place in Romans 8: Who is at the right hand of God, who also makes intercession for us, that is, who reigns with the Father, and sees the heart of the Father, and in that secret counsel intercedes for us, and carries our groans to the Father, who receives us because of the Son, according to the saying: Whatever you ask the Father in My name, He will give you.

Let this consolation always be in sight.

Even if we are very weak and unworthy, yet we are pleasing, because this Son by His merit appeases the Father, and always intercedes for us, and covers us with the application of His merit, lest the great divine wrath be poured out upon us.

Let the saying be accommodated here: You are a priest forever.

Item, the whole prayer said before the agony, which is the perpetual voice of the mediator at all times.

The words of application are: I sanctify Myself for them, that is, I offer Myself.

Item: I pray not for them alone, but for those who will believe through their word, that they may be one in us.

Item: That the love

in them is, by which you love me.

This intercessor, however, the eternal Father certainly hears, according to the saying: Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as an inheritance.

Latin:

Spe salvati sumus: Ergo non sola fide salvamur.

Respondeo: Nego consequentiam, quia ambiguitas est in vocabulo Salvati. Cum dicit: Spe salvati sumus, non intelligit vocabulum Salvati pro reconciliatis, sed intelligit de liberatis ab omnibus miseriis. Et aliud est loqui de tempore integrae liberationis, aliud de causa iustificationis.

Cum dico: Spe liberati sumus, tempus intelligitur, et grammatice hoc significatur, Integra liberatio adhuc expectatur. Cum dicitur: Fide iustificamur, monstratur causa scilicet misericordia promissa propter filium Dei, quam fide oportet accipi.

Quanquam autem fides et spes sunt cognatae virtutes, et nequaquam divelli possunt, tamen quia Paulus aliquod discrimen facit, cum inquit: Tria haec, Fides, Spes, Dilectio, teneantur utcunque distinctae descriptiones.

Fides est assentiri omni verbo Dei nobis tradito, atque ita promissioni gratiae, et est fiducia acquiescens in Deo propter mediatorem, non propter nostras virtutes aut opera, et movens corda, ut accedant ad Deum, et eum invocent et clament Abba Pater.

Spes est certa expectatio salutis aeternae propter mediatorem gratis donandae, et est expectatio mitigationis poenarum in hac vita, iuxta consilium Dei.

Differunt autem fides et spes, quia fides in praesentia accipit remissionem peccatorum, et reconciliationem, seu imputationem iusticiae propter mediatorem, et adfert pacem, id est, laetitiam cordi, quod sensit veros pavores, ut dicitur: Iustificati fide pacem habemus apud Deum.

Et hac fide ex doloribus inferorum eluctantes accedimus ad Deum, recte eum agnoscimus et invocamus, ut ad Ephes. dicitur: Per hunc audemus accedere in fiducia per fidem eius. Ita fides accipit in praesentia reconciliationem, arrabonem futurorum bonorum, videlicet Spiritum sanctum, et est virtus apprehensiva et quietativa.

Sed spes est expectatio futurae liberationis, quam expectationem antecedunt noticia promissionis et assensus, et fiducia accipiens reconciliationem, ut David audita promissione erectus, postea incipit sperare liberationem.

Dilectio est obedientia secundum mandata Dei, praelucente fide cum vera laetitia in Deo, quia 1 Iohan. 5. dicitur: Haec est dilectio Dei, mandata eius servare.

Per patientiam expectamus etc.

Dixi quartum argumentum sumtum esse ab ordine et tempore liberationis. Primum spe expectanda est haereditas, postea vero possidenda. Nunc in descriptione spei commoratur, dicit, spem esse futuri boni, nondum praesentis, ideo inquit: Spes quae videtur non est spes: ubi phrasis recte intelligatur. Adiungit autem spei patientiam, quia interea in hac vita magni agones perferendi sunt sicut et praedicit: Deus 3. EXPOSITION OF PAUL'S EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS. CHAP. VIII. 966 praecipit patientiam, et affirmat se nobis opitulaturum esse.

Praedictionem hae sunt: 2. Tim. 3.: Omnes qui pie volunt vivere in Christo persecutionem patientur. Et ...Psalm. 33.: Multae tribulationes iustorum. Et Ieremiae 12.: Dedi animam meam dilectam in manus inimicorum eius.

Praecepta vero de patientio haec sunt: Matth. 16.: Si quis vult me sequi, abneget seipsum, et tollat crucem suam, et sequatur me. 1. Petri ultimo: Humiliamini sub potenti manu Dei. 1. Corinth. 10.: Ne murmuretis. 1. Timoth. 6.: Sectare iusticiam patientiam etc. Psalm. 37.: Subditus esto Deo, et ora eum.

Apud Esaiam: In silentio et spe erit fortitudo vestra. Promissiones sunt hae: Psalm. 90.: Cum ipso sum in tribulatione, eripiam eum et glorificabo eum. Psalm. 49.: Invoca me in die tribulationis, et eripiam te. Talia dicta, praedictionem, praecepta et promissiones sint in conspectu, ut inde doctrina et consolatio in aerumnis petantur, ut supra de locis consolationum dictum est.

Sed obiiciet aliquis: Cum talis sit natura, ut omnes, qui sentiunt cruciatus, non possint non dolere, et irascantur causis, et quaerant liberationes, alii aliter, quid igitur nominas Patientiam? estne inane nomen? Respondeo: Philosophica patientia est in adversis perferendis, quae iubet ratio ferre, utcunque velle obedire rationi sic, ut externos gestus modereris, ne fractus dolore facias contra aliquam virtutem, ut Cato facit contra iusticiam sibi consciscens mortem. Medea irata Iasoni interficit natos, et multi quaerunt liberationes illicitis modis, ut qui Magos consulunt, aut qui iniusta foedera faciunt: et quia philosophica patientia saepe non ostendit liberationem, ideo in iniustis manet interior dolor, et ita crescit, ut extinguat hominem: ibi fit patientia inane nomen.

At patientia Christiana est velle obedire Deo in his, quae iubet ferre, et nihil facere contra mandata Dei, et simul cernere praesentiam Dei in cruciatu, et sperare auxilium et liberationem, ac laetari in Deo, quia cernimus res bonas, scilicet Deum ipsum praesentem afflictis, auxilium ac liberationem. Talis patientia non est inane nomen, quia sentitur vera laetitia, quae vincit dolores.

Sicut igitur David in suis aerumnis sentit veram laetitiam in Deo, ut cum inquit Psalm. 114.: Circumdederunt me dolores mortis, et angustiae inferni invenerunt me, Et nomen Domini invocabo, O Domine libera animam meam. Postea sequitur vox laetitiae: Convertere anima mea in requiem tuam, quia Dominus eripuit animam meam a morte. Item Psalm. 93.: Secundum multitudinem dolorum meorum in corde meo consolationes laetificaverunt animam meam. Cumque haec laetitia reipsa sentiatur, intelligi potest hanc patientiam non esse inane nomen, imo reipsa patientiam esse hanc laetitiam, et tamen lucta est dolorum et consolationum, et alias magis, alias minus sentitur laetitia: sicut lucta describitur in hoc ipso Capite 8. ad Rom.: Spiritus opem fert infirmitati nostrae.

Et saepissime in Palmis, ut Psalm. 41.: Quemadmodum desiderat cervus ad fontes aquarum, sic desiderat anima mea ad te Deus, Quare tristis es anima mea, spera in Deo, etc. Et hoc illustre discrimen est patientiae philosophicae et Christianae, quod Christiana patientia aliquo modo vult obedientiam propter Deum, et semper est coniuncta cum fide et spe auxilii divini, quae sunt causa laetitiae. Sed in Palamedis, Socratis, Dionis, Phocionis patentia non est spes auxilii divini, sed est qualiscunque externa gestuum moderatio, quia interior dolor minor est, cum conscientia non est saucia, iuxta dictum: Est aliquid magnis crimen abesse malis.

Spiritus adiuvat infirmitatem nostram. Quintum argumentum sumtum est ab auxilio divino. Cum enim de patientia et spe dixerit, et constet magnas Ecclesiae aerumnas esse, et difficilimos agones, addit argumentum de auxilio, quod ad confirmandos pios efficacissimum est: ostenditur enim res bona et dolores mitigans.

Hic sciendum est, ideo exerceri Ecclesiam, ut in doloribus cogitemus de causis afflictionum, et de promissione auxilii et liberationis, ut Esaiae 28. dicitur: Vexatio dat intellectum. Item: Alienum opus facit Deus, ut faciat proprium opus, id est, sinit affligi Ecclesiam, ut ostendat se esse liberatorem etc.

In ea cogitatione promissionum et in precatione datur Spiritus sanctus, et sentitur eius efficacia, ut de promissionibus dicitur in Psalmo 5.: Sustinuit anima mea in verbo eius. Ac sciendum est, sic dari Spiritum sanctum, videlicet, in cogitatione promissionis et in precatione. Sicut et Dominus inquit: Quanto magis pater vester coelestis dabit Spiritum sanctum petentibus. Caetera in textu Pauli describunt magnitudinem dolorum et luctae: Nescimus quid petamus etc., sed Spiritus interpellat pro nobis gemitibus inenarrabilibus, id est, infirma natura mallet non pati, sed Spiritus sanctus flectit voluntatem et corda, ut aliquo modo velimus obedientiam, et incitat ad invocationem, quae Deo placet, sicut David malebat non perire in exilio, et tamen dicit: Faciat quod bonum est coram ipso.

Et Iob: Etiam si occidet me, sperabo in eo. Hic quaeritur: Quo discrimine alibi Christus dicatur interpellator pro nobis, hic vero Spiritus sanctus dicatur interpellator.

Respondeo: Christus est interpellator, quia est redemtor, et suo merito placans iram aeterni patris.

Sed Spiritus sanctus est interpellator in quantum nos movet ad invocationem, iuxta dictum: Accepistis spiritum, quo clamamus Abba Pater. Item, Zach. 11.: Effundam super domum David spiritum gratiae et precum. Filius est interpellator, quia est redemtor, qui persolvit pretium, ut satisfieret iusticiae Dei, et placaretur ira Dei.

Sed Spiritus sanctus interpellat post placatam iram per filium, sic, ut accendat in nobis invocationem, iuxta dictum: Effundam super domum David spiritum gratiae et precum, id est, Spiritum testificantem in consolatione per Evangelium, quod Deus nos recipiat, et sit nobis propicius, et accendentem nos ad invocationem et laetificantem corda acquiescentia in Deo etc. Scimus autem, quod diligentibus Deum, omnia cooperantur ad bonum.

Sextum argumentum repetitio est primi et praecipui argumenti, quod ab exitu afflictionum sumitur, quasi dicat: Cum certa sit liberatio et exitus futuri sint laetissimi, Tolerate exigui temporis aerumnas: et intexuntur causae et exemplum Christi.

Expetimus societatem aeternae Ecclesiae.

Sic autem Deus Ecclesiam colligit, et deinde glorificat, ac non aliter. Ut igitur ad metam veniamus, etiam huius necessarii itineris labores feramus, iuxta dictum: Qui finem expetit, non fugiat media ad finem.

Proponitur autem exemplum filii Dei, quod in utramque partem est maxime illustre testimonium, videlicet ingentis irae Dei adversus nostra peccata, et amoris Dei erga nos, et liberationis Ecclesiae.

Necesse est ingentem iram esse, cum nemo sit redemtor nisi filius. Et necesse est magnum amorem erga nos esse, cum filius pro nobis datus sit. Et certa est liberatio, cum filius promittat se Ecclesiam sic liberaturum esse, ut ipsi in tota aeternitate similes simus. Sicut ait: Ego vitam aeternam do eis etc.

Et in Psalm.: Unxit te Deus propter consortes tuos. De his maximis rebus commonefacit nos proposito exemplo filii.

Hic rursus cogitandae sunt causae, quare Ecclesia subiecta sit cruci, quas supra aliquoties recitavimus.

Quos elegit, hos et vocavit. Attexit splendidissimam amplificationem de conservatione Ecclesiae in hac tanta deformitate, et in his confusionibus et ruinis regnorum, quasi dicat: Quanquam omnia minantur interitum, tamen scitote Ecclesiam curae esse Deo, et non interituram esse.

Orditur igitur ab electione, ut nos commonefaciat de perpetuo consilio Dei, et de conservatione Ecclesiae, quasi dicat: Scitote esse Ecclesiam electam propter filium, sicut in Psalmo dicitur: Funes ceciderunt mihi in praeclaris.

Semper aliqua haereditas erit filii Dei in genere humano. Et haec electa Ecclesia praedicatione colligitur, et fit iusta, et ornabitur aeterna gloria. Mox igitur monet, ubi electi quaerendi sint, scilicet in coetu vocatorum.

Ideo inquit: Quos elegit, hos et vocavit. Hanc consolationem teneamus, nec fingamus electos quaerendos esse extra coetum vocatorum, sit sciamus eos esse in coetu vocatorum, qui est visibilis Ecclesia, in qua sonat vox Evangelii incorrupta, ibi filius Dei est efficax per Evangelium.

Sicut scriptum est:

Evangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti. Et mandatum Dei est, ut singuli se ad hunc coetum vocatorum adiungant, iuxta dicta: Qui vos audit, me audit, Qui non colligit mecum, dissipat. Item, Psalm. 83.: Beati qui habitant in domo tua Domine. Haec tota doctrina hic breviter comprehensa est, quae cogitanda est, quoties recitamus articulum: Credo esse Ecclesiam catholicam, id est, Credo Deum semper conservaturum esse Ecclesiam, et me quoque ad eam adiungo, in hac sunt electi omnes qui retinent fidem et bonam conscientiam.

Si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? Amplificat in fine certitudinem gratiae et liberationis, mentione dati pignoris, scilicet redemptoris et intercessoris, et simul refutat obiectiones.

Duo enim terribilia argumenta incurrunt in oculos, quae impellunt homines ad dubitandum. Conspectus nostrae immunditiae, quae haeret in omnibus, etiam non habentibus delicta contra conscientiam: semper enim disputat conscientia. Deus peccatores non exaudit, Ego sum peccator: Non igitur sum in gratia. Deinde conspectus externarum aerumnarum, de quibus sit ratiocinamur. Iustis debebat bene esse. Ecclesia est afflictissima et non solum exigua, sed etiam deformis domesticis vulneribus.
