Quis existimaret tempore Herodis in sola Iudaea, quae erat plena calamitatum et civilium bellorum fuisse Ecclesiam, et non magis Deo curae esse Augustum et senatores Romanos antecellentes sapientia, virtute, imperio, et aliis ornamentis.

Haec duo argumenta non leviter concutiunt omnium hominum animos. Ac priori argumento sic moti sunt monachi, ut docuerint in hac vita semper dubitandum esse, an simus in gratia, et hanc dubitationem approbent, et dicant esse humilitatem. Adversus hunc tetrum errorem constantissime docet vox Evangelii, vincendam esse fide dubitationem, sic, ut conversi ad Deum statuant, vere sibi remitti peccata propter filium, et propter eum se placere Deo, quanquam adhuc haerent in nobis non peccata contra conscientiam, sed defectus et pravae inclinationes et flammae pravorum affectuum, quibus tamen repugnamus.

Haec doctrina de vincenda dubitatione, et haec necessaria consolatio saepe repetita est supra, ubi consideres haec testimonia. Rom. 4.: Ideo ex fide, ut sit firma promissio, quasi dicat: Non credenti promissio est inanis sonitus, et mandatum aeternum, et immotum Dei est, ut audiamus filium, ut inquit coelestis pater: Hunc audite. Item in Psalmo: Osculamini filium.

Hunc contumelia afficiunt, qui non tribuunt ei hunc honorem, ut credant sibi propter ipsum remitti peccata. Huc adde alia illustria testimonia: Acto.

10.: Huic omnes Prophetae testimonium perhibent, remissionem peccatorum accipere per nomen eius omnes qui credunt in eum. Rom. 5.: Iustificati fide pacem habemus. Opposita est autem haec pax dubitationi.

Et Ephe. 3.: Per quem audemus accedere in fiducia per fidem eius. Item, Ebrae. 4.: Accedamus cum fiducia ad thronum gratiae.

Sciamus igitur mandatum Dei et propriam Evangelii vocem esse, ut credamus nobis remitti peccata in conversione, et conversos esse in gratia propter filium, et vincendam esse dubitationem hac fide. Et quanquam haec victoria languida est, tamen adsidue crescere et poenitentiam et hanc victoriam oportet, sicut inquit ille: Credo Domine, sed opem fer imbecillitati meae.

Saepe autem alibi explicata sunt argumenta, quae opponuntur contra hanc certitudinem. Peccatores Deus non exaudit, scilicet, qui non convertuntur ad Deum, sed perseverant in sceleribus contra conscientiam, aut defendunt errores contra fundamentum, id est, contra articulos fidei.

Citatur et hoc dictum Salomonis: Nemo scit an odio, aut amore dignus sit: Est autem brevis responsio, et firmissima. Loquitur Salomon de iudicio hominum, quod ex eventibus sumitur in hac vita, videlicet ex rebus secundis aut adversis.

Ut Achab non existimet se placere Deo propter victorias, David non existimet se reiectum esse propter exilium.

Sed de valuntate Dei ex verbo eius iudicetur.

Ita dictum Salomonis congruit ad nostram sententiam, non ad falsam imaginationem monachorum. Quis accusabit electos, Deus est qui iustificat. Responsio est ad argumentum antea recitatum.

Cum enim obiicit conscientia in conversis, cum adhuc haereant in nobis multae sordes, et multa peccata ignorantiae et omissionis, quomodo possum non dubitare.

Hic respondet Paulus fidem niti merito et intercessione filii Dei, non nostra dignitate, et fit utriusque rei mentio, meriti et intercessionis.

Meritum ostendit cum ait: Qui proprio filio non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit eum, quomodo non omnia cum eo nobis donet.

Item: Quis accusabit electos, Deus est qui iustificat, id est, qui recipit credentes, et pronunciat eos esse iustos, id est, ipsi placentes propter filium tectos iusticia filii.

Postea de intercessione loquitur: Qui et interpellat pro nobis.

Hic tenenda est doctrina de sacerdotio Christi, de quo dictum est: Tu es sacerdos in aeternum secundum ordinem Melchizedec.

Continet autem haec consideratio de sacerdotio Christi amplissimam doctrinam et dulcissimam consolationem.

Primum vero nota sit definitio.

Summus sacerdos est persona immediate missa a Deo ad annunciandum Evangelium, et immediate proferens id ex sinu aeterni patris, ac missa ad offerendum sacrificium, ut persoluta poena pro nobis placaretur ira Dei, et assidue orans pro nobis, ac habens testimonium quod exaudiatur, et conservans ministerium Evangelii in Ecclesia, et perpetuo colligens Ecclesiam voce Evangelii et benedicens, dans remissionem peccatorum, Spiritum sanctum et vitam aeternam.

Haec membra omnia contineri in definitione summi sacerdotis, ostendit Epistola ad Ebraeos.

Et hic summus sacerdos non est typicus, sed est Christus Deus et homo: nam officii nomen ad personam pertinet, quae est Deus et homo.

Ad consolationem vero consideratio utriusque rei necessaria est, scilicet sacrificii seu meriti, et intercessionis.

Haec persona offert sacrificium, id est, universam obedientiam suam et humiliationem usque ad resurrectionem, ut poenam pro nobis persolvat, hanc oblationem ipse suis verbis pro Ecclesia applicat inquiens: Ego pro eis sanctifico me.

Et ad Ebraeos dicitur Cap.

1.: Qua voluntate sanctificati sumus, per oblationem corporis Iesu Christi semel.

Item: Una oblatione consummavit nos.

Primum igitur fit in conspectu haec consolatio quae proponitur in merito Christi, seu sacrificio, videlicet, quod in conversione vere recipiantur et placeant Deo credentes propter hanc victimam, etiam si adhuc haerent in conversis reliquiae peccati.

Vincenda est igitur dubitatio, quia dubitans disputat, an meritum Christi sufficiat, aut antefert sua peccata merito Christi contradictum: Gratia exuberat supra delictum.

Ideo hic inquit: Quis accusabit electos, cum Deus sit, qui iustificat, quasi dicat: Etiamsi haerent in conversis reliquiae peccati, tamen eos iustificat Deus propter filium.

De intercessione vero sciamus applicationem meriti Christi ad nos fieri omni tempore, coram aeterno patre per ipsum mediatorem deprecantem pro nobis.

Sic coniuncta sunt meritum et intercessio.

Meritum est obedientia Christi satisfaciens iusticiae Dei ad placandam iram.

Intercessio est assidua applicatio pro nobis, sicut Ebrae.

7. dicitur: Semper vivens, ut intercedat pro eis.

Et hoc loco ad Rom.

8.: Qui est ad dextram Dei, qui et interpellat pro nobis, id est, qui regnat cum patre, et videt pectus patris, et in illo arcano consilio pro nobis intercedit, et nostros gemitus ad patrem perfert, qui propter filium nos recipit, iuxta dictum: Quicquid petieritis patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis.

Haec consolatio semper in conspectu sit.

Etiamsi valde infirmi et indigni sumus, tamen placemus, quia hic filius merito suo placat patrem, et semper pro nobis intercedit, et tegit nos applicatione meriti sui, ne in nos effundatur ingens ira divina.

Huc accommodetur et dictum: Tu es sacerdos in aeternum.

Item, tota precatio ante agonem dicta, quae est perpetua vox mediatoris omni tempore.

Verba applicationis sunt: Ego me pro eis sanctifico, id est, offero.

Item: Oro non pro ipsis tantum, sed pro credituris per verbum eorum, ut unum sint in nobis.

Item: Ut dilectio

tua in eis sit, qua me diligis.

Hunc deprecatorem autem certo exaudit aeternus pater, iuxta dictum: Postula a me, et dabo tibi gentes haereditatem.

## 8:35
Who shall separate us from the love of God?

This is the conclusion of the whole consolation. Since God loves us on account of the merit and intercession of the Son, it is most certain that He will preserve the Church, even if it is weak and is attacked by the horrible furies of devils and the impious.

Some, however, dispute here: can an elect person lose the love by which he loves God?

This question is foreign to this place. It has been said elsewhere, however, that the elect can fall, just as Adam, Eve, Aaron, and David fell.

Paul, however, speaks here of the love by which God loves the universal Church, and he speaks of the preservation of the universal Church.

Then also of the individual members, who truly are members of the Church through faith.

This love is revealed in the promise, which affirms that God will always gather the Church, which in all eternity will enjoy His life, light, justice, and joy, according to the saying: The gates of hell shall not prevail against it.

The promise also affirms that those who are converted and inserted into Christ by true faith are loved by God, as it is said in John 14: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, etc. He speaks here of this certainty of faith, by which we know the preservation of the universal Church to be certain: we also certainly know that individuals persevering in faith will be saved.

He adds, therefore, the Church will be preserved, even if there will be great struggles and it will be attacked in various ways—by the sweetness of life, the fear of death, the snares of devils, the terrors of tyrants, and of armies: for he calls tyrants ἀρχὰς (principalities), and armies δυνάμεις (powers), namely, the whole host of persecutors.

It is attacked both by present allurements and terrors, and by the hope of future tranquility and the fear of dangers. By 'height' I understand, in general, the wisdom of heretics and other impious people. By 'depth,' the common furies of the mob.

Against all these, the Church is confirmed through the Son of God and the Holy Spirit, so that it may gloriously conquer, as it is said in the Psalm: Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babes you have perfected praise for yourself. Item: No one shall snatch my sheep from my hands.

Latin:

Quis separabit nos a dilectione Dei?

Conclusio est totius consolationis. Cum Deus diligat nos propter meritum et intercessionem filii, certissimum est servaturum esse Ecclesiam, etiamsi est infirma, et horribilibus furoribus diabolorum et impiorum oppugnatur.

Disputant autem hic aliqui, an possit electus amittere dilectionem qua Deum diligit?

Haec quaestio aliena est ab hoc loco. Dictum est autem alibi, electos posse labi, sicut lapsi sunt Adam, Eva, Aaron, David.

Paulus autem hic loquitur de dilectione, qua Deus universam Ecclesiam diligit, et loquitur de conservatione universae Ecclesiae.

Deinde etiam de singulis membris, quae revera per fidem sunt Ecclesiae membra.

Haec dilectio in promissione revelata est, quae affirmat Deum semper collecturum esse Ecclesiam, quae in tota aeternitate fruetur eius vita, luce, iusticia et laetitia, iuxta dictum: Portae inferorum non praevalebunt adversus eam.

Adfirmat item promissio, conversos qui vera fide inseruntur Christo, diligia Deo, ut Ioh. 14. dicitur: Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum servabit etc. De hac certitudine fidei hic loquitur, qua conservationem universae Ecclesiae scimus certam esse: certo etiam scimus singulos perseverantes in fide salvos fore.

Addit igitur, Servabitur Ecclesia, etiamsi erunt magna certamina et oppugnabitur variis modis, dulcedine vitae, metu mortis, insidiis diabolorum, terroribus tyrannorum, et exercituum: nam tyrannos nominat ἀρχὰς, exercitus autem δυνάμεις, videlicet tota agmina persequentium.

Oppugnatur et praesentibus illecebris, et terroribus, et spe futurae tranquillitatis et metu periculorum. Altitudinem intelligo in genere sapientiam haereticorum et aliorum impiorum. Profunditatem, communes vulgi furores.

Adversus haec omnia confirmatur Ecclesia per filium Dei et Spiritum sanctum, ut gloriose vincat, sicut in Psalmo dicitur: Ex ore infantium et lactentium perfecisti tibi laudem. Item: Nemo rapiet oves meas ex manibus meis.

## 9:1 Disposition of Romans: Argument
Chapter IX.

Paul could have stopped. He completes that whole doctrine of justification and has treated those topics in which is the sum of the Gospel, and which it behooves us to hold above all. But because here a question arises concerning Election, he wished to touch upon this also: for it is asked, if our works merit nothing, why God chooses some and does not choose others. And this question was being agitated most at that time by the Ju- as those who had the worship of God, who boasted that they deserved righteousness.

And so they argued that the promises concerning Christ were not fulfilled, because salvation and the Holy Spirit had not reached them, who had the worship of God, who seemed to deserve righteousness.

Paul therefore begins from a complaint, and deplores the defection of the Jews.

Afterwards he teaches that our merits are not the cause of election.

The complaint is: I speak the truth, etc.

I grieve vehemently that the Jews are perishing, and I would have wished to redeem them by my own destruction.

Here he immediately adds a correction, Not that the word of God has failed, that is, the Jews are not so cast off that none can be saved, so that the promises made to that people are void.

Nay, the promises are most firm, wherefore there is no doubt that salvation pertains to this people.

Then follows the principal Proposition of this disputation.

Not all who are of Israel are Israel, nor are all children, because they are the seed of Abraham.

But in Isaac shall your seed be called, that is, the children of the flesh are not the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted for the seed.

This is the proposition, but implicated in the first proof, as is wont to be done.

But below, the proposition is repeated several times in the conclusions and epilogues.

For a conclusion is nothing but a repetition of the status.

And this is the meaning of the proposition: The children of God are made by election, not by nature, or by our merits.

Concerning Predestination.

I. But in order that it may appear that this is the perpetual sentiment of scripture, he draws arguments from as far back as the first election, where the posterity of Abraham was separated from the remaining nations.

And this is the first argument.

Scripture says: In Isaac shall your seed be called.

Therefore they are children of God only because they are chosen by God.

If nature or merits made children of God, what need would there be for promises?

Since therefore the promise brings it about that some become children, therefore it is not a matter of our own powers.

Or if it is in the power of nature to become children, why is Isaac chosen, while the Chaldeans, Egyptians, or others are not chosen, who lived no less civilly according to nature than Abraham, Isaac?

As if one were to reason, why did He call us to the Gospel, and not call Alexander the Macedonian, Augustus, Socrates, Pomponius Atticus, who certainly lived no less civilly than we do.

Here it is necessary to cast the cause back upon the will of God.

II. Argument.

Jacob is chosen, Esau is rejected, before they had done anything good or evil.

Hence Paul makes a conclusion, which manifestly denies that our merits are the cause of election.

Therefore works were not the cause, but the will of the caller.

I will not add here how some cavil at these things.

Let the reader only remember this, if works to be followed in life were the cause of election, it was not permitted for Paul to say, not of works.

Objection. Paul saw that this sentiment concerning election was abhorrent to the judgment of reason: therefore he objects with an argument taken from reason, for which there was no need, if Paul had thought that our merits were the cause of election.

For let someone say: If David and Saul deserve nothing in themselves, therefore God is unjust, who chooses this one, and does not choose that one.

This inequality and προσωποληψία (respect of persons) does not seem to fall into the best nature of God.

If the merits of all are equal, why are the rewards not equal or the punishments equal?

Equality is most fitting for a judge, for so the Greeks say: ἶσα πόλεμον οὐ ποιεῖ (equality does not make war).

Paul mitigates this objection in this way.

God does not render equal things to equals: Therefore it seems to be injustice.

In this argument the major premise must be distinguished.

Justice is to render equal things, when a debt is paid.

For in giving, there is no need to give equal things to equals.

The minor does not cohere with the major, for the major speaks of debt.

The minor speaks of benefits, which are given freely, God does not render equal things, namely, because He gives salvation to some.

Then justice could be accused, if God owed this benefit to all, but because He does not owe it, it is not injustice that He liberates some, it is rather mercy, as if a prince were to exempt some condemned persons from punishment, it will be clemency.

Meanwhile, it is not [injustice] if He does not exempt the remaining similarly condemned persons from punishment.

Paul therefore dilutes the objection by translation, to choose is of mercy, it is not a debt.

Therefore justice cannot be accused.

And he cites the place of Exodus, to show that the benefit is given freely, election is not a debt: I will have mercy, etc.

He adds an Epilogue, in which he places the principal proposition of this disputation.

For in epilogues propositions are repeated, nay sometimes The proposition having been concealed at the beginning, it is clearly set forth first in the conclusion: This is what was done here. Therefore it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy. We do not deserve to be chosen by our will or running, that is, by our works, but it is a benefit of the mercy of God freely given. He cites another testimony, by which he proves that it is not of our own powers to deserve salvation. For this purpose I have raised you up, etc. The consequence is, Therefore He has mercy on whom He wills, and whom He wills He hardens, that is, justification is not of our own powers, but of the mercy of God; when God does not show mercy, men persist in impiety.

Second objection. He inserts an objection again, for it seems extremely absurd to say that justification is not of our own powers. If we cannot be justified unless mercy happens to us, and God does not impart mercy to all, why then does God accuse us? He is inclement who demands impossibilities, who punishes men when it seems that fault is absent, because they cannot do good.

He answers nothing to this objection, but repudiates it as unworthy; they call this figure apodioxis, when we do not wish to answer a difficult argument, and, so that we may seem to pass over it deliberately, we reject it as untimely or unworthy. Thus here Paul signifies that the objection is unworthy; he says we ought not to expostulate with God, because it is permitted to God to use His creatures according to His will. He adds the similitude of the clay and the potter, so that the reason for the repudiated objection might become clearer, namely, that God owes us nothing, wherefore we ought not to accuse Him and, as it were, summon Him to court. There is in this place an antapodoton, because the construction does not seem absolute. If God, willing to show His wrath, endured the vessels, etc. The circumlocution will be complete if it is repeated from the above: it is not for you to criticize His counsel.

Here he begins to recite testimonies concerning the calling of the Gentiles and the defection of the Jews. For I said above that the Jews had disputed that the promises pertained to them, not to the Gentiles, and that they themselves deserved grace by their own worship. But this scandal moved the weak even more, that so few of the Jews believed. And so they argued that this was not the Christ whom the Apostles preached, because the promises concerning Christ were to reach the whole people, or at least the greatest part of the people. Now, only a few, and indeed the lowest of men, boasted that they had obtained such magnificent promises. This event did not seem to correspond to such great promises, which they thought a few were seizing, as if by sedition, when they pertained to the whole people.

Paul therefore collects testimonies concerning the calling of the Gentiles and the defection of the Jews, and incidentally again detracts honor from merits. Chapter X. Above he began to speak of the rejection of the Jews; in this place he will finish it, and in the two following chapters: he institutes nothing new here, therefore, but continues to speak of the defection of the Jews, and a little later he will recite more testimonies. But the holy man cannot remember such a great calamity, or such great wrath of God, without the most bitter pain of soul; therefore he adds affection, and also shows the Jews the cause of their error, so that, this being removed, he might draw some to Christ. At the beginning there is ethos, or affection: I wish the best for the Jews, and I pray for them. He removes the cause of the error; they think that righteousness before God is their own works. Nor indeed can human reason judge otherwise than that our works, and indeed those commanded by God, render God appeased.

Incidentally, in this place, a comparison of the righteousness of the law and the righteousness of faith is inserted. And the comparison is taken from the definitions. For when he had said that the Jews attributed too much to the righteousness of the law, it was useful to add the definitions of the righteousness of the law and the righteousness of faith. He defines the righteousness of the law from the words of Leviticus: He who shall do these things shall live in them. He defines the righteousness of faith from the words of Deuteronomy: The righteousness of faith is to have the word in the heart and in the mouth, the word, I say, which we preach concerning Christ.

Others treat this comparison differently. I judge that the state of the comparison is placed in these members: To do, and To have the Word in the heart. I think these members of the definitions are opposed to one another. For he wishes to propose a notable difference between them, and to teach explicitly that works are not the righteousness of God, so that the error of the Jews may be understood to be clearly rebuked. The righteousness of the law is to do, that is, to perform external works with reason imitating the law. But the righteousness of faith is, To have the word in the heart and in the mouth, as if he were saying: You dream that the righteousness of God is your works, but we [have] a far different one. we deliver justice: for works do not justify us before God. There is another kind of justice, by which we are justified before God, namely, to believe in Christ; whoever apprehends this, he has the end of the law, that is, the sum of the law; this is, he is righteous before God, he has satisfied God.

He has elegantly adorned the definition by the contrary. Justice is, not to say in the heart, who shall ascend into heaven, or who shall descend into the abyss? These figures contain human reasonings, and depict the incredulous heart.

For reason argues in this way: I cannot ascend into heaven and see the will of God before me, therefore I will not believe that I am a care to God, I will not assent that God looks upon us, that God is appeased toward us in this way according to the word. Nor do I descend into the abyss, that is, I have not seen how the dead live, how they can return to life. Therefore I will not assent that anyone can revive, or be liberated from death. For reason draws arguments from those things which it comprehends by sense. This impiety of the heart adheres to all men by nature. He therefore opposes the contrary, to have the word in the heart, that is, to truly assent that this word, which the Apostles preach, is true, that on account of Christ we are received into the grace of the Father, that on account of Christ justice and life happen, that on account of Christ we are truly a care to God, that we are defended by God and saved.

Epiphonema, with the heart one believes unto justice, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.

The effect of faith is repeated, namely, that faith justifies, not works. And a testimony from the Prophet is added: Everyone who believes shall not be put to shame. Another testimony is also cited: Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved. In his own manner he connects a gradation, by which he declares the mode of justification, and the cause of faith, or how faith is conceived.

Dialecticians teach that a sorites is concerned with causes and effects. A sorites is akin to a gradation. Therefore Paul, when he wished to show the cause of faith, instituted a gradation in this way. No one calls upon Him, unless he believes: No one believes, unless he has heard the word: The word cannot be heard, unless it is preached.

The word cannot be preached, unless they are sent by God who preach. And he recites the testimony, in which the Prophet predicted that it would come to pass that they would be sent, who would scatter the new word into the world, in which grace and peace are announced, not wrath. For the law previously showed the wrath of God. Here the Prophet prophesies of another word, which preaches the remission of sins, and freely offers justice to those who believe. He teaches that faith happens in this way, if we hear the word of God, and that preached by a human voice.

Therefore the efficient cause of faith is the word, by which God impels and moves hearts to believe. Without the word, the Holy Spirit does not happen. And that he might commend the ministry of the word of God, he added the mission also. Many and great utilities the pious reader can glean from this chapter.

Above, a very clear definition of faith is set forth, in which it can be discerned what faith is. For the nature and power of faith is very clearly depicted, when those doubts of the impious mind are refuted. Who ascends into heaven? By what way is the return open for the dead to life? For it is faith, which certainly determines concerning the will of God, that we are a care to God, that God forgives us according to this word, that we are covered and defended and saved by God. Likewise, he separates the justice of faith from the justice of the law, and attributes justification to faith alone, and clearly takes it away from the other kind.

Then the gradation concerning the mode of justification, or concerning the cause of faith, is greatly to be observed against fanatical men, who despise the ministry of the word, who, having omitted the word, require new illuminations, who by their own speculations attempt to comprehend God, who dream that the Holy Spirit is conceived or works in us through our speculations without the word of God, who dream that the Holy Spirit is conceived through preparations of certain works. Such heretics were formerly enthusiasts [ἐνθουσιασταί], and many others.

And in our times there are Anabaptists, and others who despise the ministry of the word, and dream that the Holy Spirit is given without the word of God. Therefore this passage is publicly useful for retaining the ministry of the word of God. It is also useful privately in the temptations of the pious.

For the mind hangs with difficulty upon the word alone, and requires other consolations, illuminations, it does not dare to sustain itself by the word alone. Therefore, so that we may know that no other consolations are to be required, he bids us to look to the word, and to feel that this is undoubtedly the will of God to help us, which is ...shown in the word. And lest any other illumination be required, he testifies that he speaks of the word preached by a human voice, of the corporal word, which is read, which sounds in the ears. Therefore Moses says eloquently:

The word which is in your mouth. And Paul: The word which we preach. Likewise, he joins hearing, preaching, and mission. And the Prophet praises the feet, so that he may testify that he praises the word preached by the voice of those who are sent by God. These feet are contaminated and spat upon by those who deny that the Word and the Sacraments are useful for comforting and confirming consciences. But perhaps it is appropriate to treat these things in a commentary, not in this work; however, the reader had to be admonished in passing, lest he neglectfully pass over such great matters placed in this location.

Afterwards, he returns to the defection of the Jews, when he says: But not all obey the Gospel, and he adds testimonies which prophesy about the ruin of the Jews. For since the small number of believers offends the weak, it is necessary to oppose the scriptures against that scandal, so that they may know that it happens by the judgment of God.

Latin:

Caput IX.

Poterat desinere Paulus. Absolvit eam to- tam iustificationis doctrinam et pertractavit eos locos, in quibus est Evangelii summa, quosque in primis tenere nos oportet. Sed quia hic quae- stio oritur de Electione, voluit hanc quoque at- tingere: quaeritur enim, si nostra opera nihil me- rentur, cur eligit Deus alios, alios non eligit. Et hanc quaestionem maxime agitabant tunc Iu- Iudaei, ut qui cultum Dei habebant, qui gloriabantur se mereri iusticiam.

Itaque disputabant promissiones de Christo non esse impletas, quia non contigisset ipsis salus et Spiritus sanctus, qui cultum Dei habebant, qui iusticiam mereri videbantur.

Paulus igitur a querela orditur, et deplorat Iudaeorum defectionem.

Postea docet, nostra merita non esse causam electionis.

Querela est: Veritatem dico etc.

Vehementer doleo quod Iudaei pereunt, ac optarim meo interitu eos redimere.

Hic statim subiicit correctionem, Non quod exciderit sermo Dei, id est, non sic sunt abiecti Iudaei, ut nulli queant servari, ut promissiones factae illi populo irritae sint.

Imo firmissimae sunt promissiones, quare non dubium est, quin ad hunc populum pertineat salus.

Deinde sequitur Propositio principalis huius disputationis.

Non omnes qui sunt ex Israël, sunt Israël, neque omnes sunt filii, ideo quia sunt Abrahae semen.

Sed in Isaac vocabitur tibi semen, hoc est, filii carnis non sunt filii Dei, sed filii promissionis reputantur in semen.

Haec est propositio, sed implicata primae probationi, quemadmodum fieri solet.

Infra autem aliquoties in conclusionibus et epilogis repetitur propositio.

Conclusio enim nihil est, nisi repetitio status.

Est autem haec sententia propositionis: Filii Dei fiunt electione, non natura, aut meritis nostris.

De Praedestinatione.

I. Ut autem appareat hanc perpetuam esse scripturae sententiam, ducit argumenta inde usque a prima electione, ubi Abrahae posteritas a reliquis gentibus separata est.

Et est primum argumentum.

Scriptura inquit: In Isaac vocabitur semen.

Ergo filii Dei tantum sunt, quia a Deo eliguntur.

Si natura aut merita facerent filios Dei, quid opus esset promissionibus?

Cum igitur promissio efficiat, ut aliqui fiant filii, ergo non est res nostrarum virium.

Aut si est penes naturam fieri filios, quare Isaac eligitur, Chaldaei, Aegyptii aut alii non eliguntur, qui non minus civiliter vivebant iuxta naturam, quam Abraham, Isaac?

Ut si quis ratiocinetur, cur nos ad Evangelium vocavit, non vocavit Alexandrum Macedonem, Augustum, Socratem, Pomponium Atticum, qui certe non minus civiliter vivebant quam nos.

Hic necesse est causam reiicere in voluntatem Dei.

II. Argumentum.

Iacob electus est, Esau repudiatur, priusquam aliquid boni aut mali fecissent.

Hinc Paulus conclusionem efficit, quae manifeste negat merita nostra causam electionis esse.

Ergo opera non erant causa, sed voluntas vocantis.

Non addam hic quomodo cavillentur ista nonnulli.

Tantum hoc meminerit lector, si opera secura in vita erant causa electionis, non licuit dicere Paulo, non ex operibus.

Occupatio. Vidit Paulus hanc de electione sententiam abhorrere a iudicio rationis: ideo argumentum a ratione sumtum obiicit, quo nihil opus erat, si Paulus sensisset merita nostra causam electionis esse.

Dicat enim aliquis: Si David et Saul iuxta nihil merentur, iniquus igitur est Deus, qui hunc eligit, illum non eligit.

Non videtur haec inaequalitas et προσωποληψία in optimam naturam Dei cadere.

Si merita omnium paria sunt, cur non sunt paria praemia aut pares poenae?

Iudicem maxime decet aequalitas, sic enim inquiunt Graeci: ἶσα πόλεμον οὐ ποιεῖ.

Paulus mitigat hanc obiectionem hoc modo.

Deus non reddit paria paribus: Igitur videtur esse iniusticia.

In hoc argumento maior distinguenda erit.

Iusticia est reddere paria, cum debitum solvitur.

Nam in donando nihil opus est paria dare paribus.

Minor non cohaeret cum maiore, maior enim loquitur de debito.

Minor loquitur de beneficiis, quae gratis donantur, Deus non reddit paria, scilicet, quia quibusdam donat salutem.

Tunc accusari iusticia posset, si Deus deberet hoc beneficium omnibus, sed quia non debet, non est iniusticia, quod aliquos liberat, misericordia magis est, ut si princeps eximat poenae aliquos condemnatos, clementia erit.

Interim non est si reliquos similiter condemnatos, non eximat poenae.

Diluit igitur Paulus obiectionem per translationem, eligere est misericordiae, non est debitum.

Igitur accusari iusticia non potest.

Et citat locum Exodi, ut ostendat gratis donatum beneficium esse, electionem non debitum: Miserebor etc.

Addit Epilogum, in quo ponit principalem propositionem huius disputationis.

Nam in epilogis repetuntur propositiones, imo interdum initio dissimulata propositio, primum in conclusione clare ponitur: Id hic factum est. Igitur non est volentis, neque currentis, sed miserentis Dei. Non nos meremur eligi voluntate aut cursu, hoc est, operibus nostris, sed beneficium est misericordiae Dei gratis donatum. Citat aliud testimonium, quo probat non esse nostrarum virium, mereri salutem. In hoc excitavi te etc. consequens est, Ergo cuius vult miseretur, et quem vult indurat, id est, non est nostrarum virium iustificatio, sed misericordiae Dei, cum non miseretur Deus, perseverant in impietate homines.

Secunda occupatio. Iterum inserit obiectionem, videtur enim extreme absurdum, dicere, quod non sit nostrarum virium iustificatio. Si nos non possumus iustificari, nisi contingat misericordia. Et misericordiam Deus non impertit omnibus, Cur igitur accusat nos Deus? Inclemens est, qui impossibilia exigit, qui punit homines cum videatur culpa abesse, quia non possunt benefacere.

Nihil respondet ad hanc obiectionem, sed repudiat eam veluti indignam, hanc figuram vocant ἀποδίωξιν, cum argumento difficili nolumus respondere, et, ut videamur consulta praeterire, reiiciamus tanquam intempestivum, aut indignum. Ita hic Paulus significat indignam esse obiectionem, ait nos non debere expostulare cum Deo, quia Deo liceat uti creaturis pro arbitrio. Addit de luto et figulo similitudinem, ut fiat clarior ratio repudiatae obiectionis, videlicet quod nihil debeat nobis Deus, quare non debeamus eum accusare, et tanquam in ius vocare. Est in hoc loco ἀνταποδότον, quia non videtur absoluta constructio. Si Deus volens ostendere iram, toleravit vasa etc. Circumductio ita erit integra, si repetatur ex superiore, non est tuum reprehendere eius consilium.

Hic incipit recitare testimonia de vocatione gentium, et de defectione Iudaeorum. Supra enim dixi Iudaeos disputasse, quod ad ipsos pertinerent promissiones, non ad gentes, quod ipsi cultu suo mererentur gratiam. Sed hoc scandalum multo etiam magis movit imbecilles, quod tam pauci ex Iudaeis crediderunt. Itaque disputabant hunc non esse Christum, quem praedicabant Apostoli, quia promissiones de Christo ad universum populum, aut certe ad maximam populi partem perventurae essent. Nunc paucos tantum et quidem infimos homines gloriari se adeptos esse tam magnifica promissa. Non videbatur respondere hic eventus tantis promissionibus, quas ad universum populum pertinentes, paucos tanquam per seditionem invadere existimabant.

Colligit igitur Paulus testimonia de vocatione gentium, et de defectione Iudaeorum et obiter meritis rursus detrahit honorem. Caput X. Supra coepit de reiectione Iudaeorum dicere, in hoc loco consumet et duo sequentia capita: nihil igitur novi hic instituit, sed pergit dicere de Iudaeorum defectione, et aliquanto post testimonia plura recitabit. Sed non potest vir sanctus tantae calamitatis meminisse, seu irae Dei tantae, sine acerbissimo dolore animi, ideo addit affectus, causam etiam erroris ostendit Iudaeis, ut hac sublata, aliquos ad Christum pertrahat. Initio ἦθος est, seu affectus, Ego optime volo Iudaeis, et pro eis oro. Causam erroris tollit, putant iusticiam coram Deo esse opera sua. Neque sane potest aliter humana ratio iudicare, quam quod opera nostra et quidem a Deo mandata, reddant Deum placatum.

Obiter hoc loco inseritur collatio iusticia legis et iusticiae fidei. Et sumta est collatio ex definitionibus. Nam cum dixisset Iudaeos nimium tribuere iusticiae legis, profuit addere definitiones iusticiae legis et iusticiae fidei. Iusticiam legis definit ex verbis Levitici: Qui fecerit ea, vivet in eis. Iusticiam fidei definit ex verbis Deuteronomii: Iusticia fidei est, habere verbum in corde et ore, verbum inquam quod praedicamus de Christo.

Alii aliter tractant hanc collationem. Ego collationis statum positum esse iudico in his membris: Facere, et Verbum habere in corde. Haec membra definitionum opponi inter se arbitror. Vult enim insignem differentiam earum proponere, et diserte docere, quod opera non sint iusticia Dei, ut errorem Iudaeorum clare reprehendere intelligatur. Iusticia legis est facere, id est, externa opera ratione imitante legem efficere. At iusticia fidei est, Habere verbum in corde et ore, quasi dicat: Vos somniatis iusticiam Dei esse opera vestra, Nos vero longe aliam iusticiam tradimus: non enim instificant opera nostra coram Deo. Alia quaedam iusticia est, qua coram Deo iustificamur, nempe, credere in Christum, hunc quisquis apprehendit, is habet finem legis, id est, summam legis, hoc est, est iustus coram Deo, satisfecit Deo.

Eleganter autem ornavit definitionem ex contrario. Iusticia est, non dicere in corde, quis ascendet in coelum, aut quis descendet in abyssum? hae figurae continent rationes humanas, et depingunt cor incredulum.

Nam ratio argumentatur hoc modo: Non possum ascendere in coelum et coram videre voluntatem Dei, ergo non credam me Deo curae esse, non assentiar Deum nos respicere, Deum nobis hoc modo placari iuxta verbum. Nec descendi in abyssum, hoc est, non vidi quomodo mortui degant, quomodo redire ad vitam possint. Igitur non assentiar quenquam reviviscere posse, aut a morte liberari. Ratio enim ducit argumenta ex his, quae sensu comprehendit. Haec impietas cordis haeret in omnibus hominibus natura. Opponit igitur contrarium, habere verbum in corde, id est, vere assentiri, quod hoc verbum, quod praedicant Apostoli, verum sit, quod propter Christum recipiamur in gratiam patris, quod propter Christum contingat iusticia, vita, propter Christum vere simus Deo curae, quod defendamur a Deo et servemur.

Epiphonema, corde creditur ad iusticiam, et ore fit confessio ad salutem.

Repetitur autem effectus fidei, scilicet, quod fides iustificet, non opera. Et additur testimonium ex Propheta: Omnis qui crediderit non pudefiet. Citatur et aliud testimonium: Omnis qui invocaverit nomen Domini, salvus erit. Suo more annectit gradationem, qua declarat modum iustificationis, et fidei causam, seu quomodo fides concipiatur.

Dialectici tradunt soriten versari in causis et effectibus. Est autem sorites gradationi affinis. Ideo Paulus, cum vellet ostendere fidei causam, instituit gradationem hoc modo. Nemo invocat, nisi credat: Nemo credit, nisi audiverit verbum: Non potest audiri verbum, nisi praedicetur.

Non potest praedicari verbum, nisi mittantur a Deo qui praedicent. Et recitat testimonium, in quo Propheta praedixit futurum esse, ut mittantur, qui novum verbum spargant in mundum, in quo annuncientur gratia et pax, non ira. Nam lex antea iram Dei ostendit. Hic de alio verbo vaticinatur Propheta, quod praedicat remissionem peccatorum, et gratis offert iusticiam credentibus. Docet autem fidem sic contingere, si audiamus verbum Dei, et quidam humana voce praedicatum.

Est igitur causa efficiens fidei verbum, quo impellit et movet Deus corda ad credendum. Sine verbo non contingit Spiritus sanctus. Et ut ministerium verbi Dei commendaret, addidit missionem quoque. Multas ac magnas utilitates decerpere pius lector ex hoc capite potest.

Supra valde clara ponitur definitio fidei, in qua cerni potest, quid sit fides. Natura enim et vis fidei valde clare depingitur, cum dubitationes illae mentis impiae reprehenduntur. Quis ascendit in coelum? Qua via patet reditus mortuis ad vitam? Est enim fides, quae certo statuit de voluntate Dei, Deo nos curae esse, Deum nobis ignoscere iuxta hoc verbum, tegi et defendi et servari nos a Deo. Item separat iusticiam fidei a iusticia legis, et soli fidei tribuit iustificationem, alteri generi clare adimit.

Deinde gradatio de modo iustificationis, seu de fidei causa magnopere observanda est contra fanaticos homines, qui contemnunt ministerium verbi, qui, omisso verbo, novas illuminationes requirunt, qui suis speculationibus conantur Deum comprehendere, qui somniant Spiritum sanctum concipi aut operari in nobis per nostras speculationes sine verbo Dei, qui somniant Spiritum sanctum concipi per praeparationes certorum operum. Tales haeretici fuerunt olim ἐνθουσιασταί, et alii multi.

Et nostris temporibus sunt Anabaptistae, et alii qui ministerium verbi contemnunt, et somniant Spiritum sanctum dari sine verbo Dei. Itaque publice prodest hic locus ad retinendum ministerium verbi Dei. Prodest et privatim in tentationibus piorum.

Nam aegre pendet mens a solo verbo, et requirit alias consolationes, illuminationes, non audet se tantum verbo sustentare. Ut igitur sciamus non esse alias consolationes requirendas, iubet nos ad verbum respicere, ac sentire, quod haud dubie... haec sit Dei voluntas iuvandi nos, quae in verbo ostenditur. Et ne requireret alia illuminatio, testatur se loqui de verbo praedicato humana voce, de corporali verbo, quod legitur, quod personat in auribus, Ideo diserte ait Moses:

Verbum quod est in ore tuo. Et Paulus: Verbum quod praedicamus. Item, coniungit auditum, praedicationem, et missionem. Et Propheta pedes laudat, ut testetur se laudare verbum praedicatum voce istorum, qui mittuntur a Deo. Hos pedes contaminant... et conspuunt isti, qui negant Verbum et Sacramenta prodesse ad consolandas et confirmandas conscientias. Sed haec fortasse convenit in commentario tractare, non in hoc opere, fuit tamen obiter admonendus lector, ne res tantas hoc loco positas negligenter praeteriret.

Postea redit ad Iudaeorum defectionem, cum ait: Sed non omnes obediunt Evangelio, et addit testimonia, quae vaticinantur de Iudaeorum ruina. Nam cum offendat imbecilles paucitas credentium, opus est adversus id scandalum opponere scripturas, ut iudico Dei id accidere sciant.

## 9:1 Argument
Chapter IX.

A completely new discussion is instituted concerning the Church, or the people of God, and concerning the calling of the Gentiles.

For although it is necessary to interweave somewhere the distinction between the law and the justice of faith, yet the principal question here is, what is the Church of God, or who is the people of God.

For the Jews also used to oppose the Apostles with the authority of the Church, and they argued in this way. Since the Church does not err, and we, who are the principal part of the people—the ordinary priests, teachers, governors, and the greater multitude excelling in virtue and authority—are the Church, and we dissent from you. It is not credible that you think rightly, you who introduce a new kind of doctrine into the Church, unknown to our fathers: nay, contrary to the law, because you abolish the law given by God with illustrious testimonies, and you do this, being few and seditious men, as the thing itself shows, because you overturn this most beautiful polity, which alone in the human race was established by the voice of God, and was preserved and often restored by mighty miracles.

These specious arguments the Jews used to oppose, which cannot be refuted by any human wisdom, but they are refuted by divine testimonies, namely, by prophetic sayings and miracles. Now the Papists oppose similar things, but because it is established that they are fighting about laws and rites handed down by human authority, their arguments are weaker. The Jews were fighting about the divine law.

Always, however, all moderate men are moved by the name and appearance of the Church, and one must not rashly depart from the most ancient consensus of those whose authority is approved. Paul says that the Church is the house of God, the pillar and seat of truth. The Lord says: If he will not hear the Church, let him be to you as a Gentile. Samson says: If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have found it.

Since, however, men are moved by the name of the Church, it is necessary to ask which is the true Church of God, because always even diverse and dissenting peoples usurp this glorious title, as now Christians, Jews, and Mahometans fight among themselves over this title. Indeed, in this very multitude which is called Christian, there are dissensions.

Paul therefore answers and teaches what the Church is, where it is, and how it is to be recognized.

That there is some visible Church of God is manifest from many testimonies. For when Christ says: Tell it to the Church, He leads us to a visible assembly. And the Psalm says: Their sound has gone out into all the earth. God wills the voice of the Gospel to be heard, He wills the Son to be acknowledged, therefore He always gathers some assembly, at times more, at times less frequent, which can be seen and heard among the human race, and in this assembly the foundation is retained, at times more, at times less pure, but yet idols are not defended. And always in this assembly there are some elect, that is, heirs of eternal life, even if at the same time many who are not holy and not elect are mixed in with them, who nevertheless do not dissent from the holy ones regarding doctrine in external profession, as the parable of the net teaches, in which there are good and bad fish.

Nor are the elect to be sought outside the assembly of the called, according to the saying: Whom He chose, them He also called. Likewise: My sheep hear my voice. But wherever there are, whether among these or elsewhere, those who oppose the foundation, that is, the articles of faith, it is certain that these are outside the Church, and are rejected and condemned, according to the sayings of John 3: He who does not believe in the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God will remain upon him. And 1 Corinthians 3: No one can lay another foundation besides that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ.

Since, therefore, there is some true visible Church, let us hold to this definition. The visible Church is a visible assembly of those embracing the Gospel without corruptions, and rightly using the Sacraments, in which assembly the Son of God is effective through the ministry of the Gospel, and regenerates many by the given Holy Spirit.

And there are in that assembly many who are not holy, but yet who consent to the doctrine. And the command is immutable, pertaining to all men, that individuals should become members and citizens of this true Church, wherever they are in the world, among their own or among strangers, joined in such a way, namely, that they acknowledge and confess that assembly to be the true Church of God, and that there be a similar confession of doctrine, and a similar invocation of God, and a similar use of the Sacraments, and a will to help and not to destroy that assembly. Nor is it necessary that there be a similarity of human traditions, nor is it necessary that all be included under one political empire.

That individuals ought to become members of the true Church, these sayings testify: Whom He chose, them He also called. Psalm 26: One thing I have asked of the Lord, this I will seek, that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, that I may see the will of the Lord, and visit His temple. Psalm 83: Blessed are they who dwell in Thy house, O Lord. Psalm 91: Planted in the house of the Lord, they shall flourish in the courts of the house of our God. Psalm 35: I will wash my hands among the innocent, and I will go around Thy altar, O Lord. I have loved the beauty of Thy house, and the place of the habitation of Thy glory. Psalm 121: Pray for the things that are for the peace of Jerusalem. And happiness to those who love Thee, for the sake of the house of the Lord our God, I have sought Thy good things. Hebrews 10: Not forsaking our congregation. 1 Corinthians 1: Let there be no schisms among you, but be joined together in the same doctrine and the same will. Matthew 12: He who does not gather with me, scatters. These and similar sayings command association, and order individuals to become members of the true Church, and forbid being partners of the enemies of the Gospel, or wanderers, who for this reason flee the society of the Church, so that they may be able to wander more in their opinions.

But so that the true Church may be recognized, let these three primary external signs that strike the senses be proposed. The pure voice of the doctrine of the Gospel. The legitimate use of the Sacraments. And the conjunction of the Church with pastors, namely obedience in those things which pertain to the ministry according to the Gospel, that is, that some do not separate themselves from the common congregation, and either wander without a ministry, or, despising the rightly constituted Church, establish private conventicles etc.

This is the first thing necessary to be known about the visible Church, because in this only are the elect, for whose sake this visible assembly is gathered and preserved by God.

But here the question is asked about the cause of election, where the first conspicuous answer is about rejection.

The cause of rejection is perseverance in sins, according to these sayings: He who does not believe in the Son is already judged.

Likewise: He who does not believe in the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God will remain upon [him].

IX. him. Psalm 2: Kiss the son, lest his anger kindle, and you perish in the way. But concerning the cause of election, it must be known that the mercy of God, who for the sake of the Son gathers an inheritance among the human race, is the cause of election, not our merits. Therefore it is said in Hosea: Thy destruction is from thyself, but thy help is through me. And Rom. 11: If it were of works, it would no longer be grace, as it is manifest that the promise was issued from the beginning by the gratuitous mercy of God for the sake of the Son, and that the Church is gathered and restored, just as it is said in Psalm 2: Ask of me, and I will give thee the nations for an inheritance. Psalm 15: Thou sustainest my inheritance, the lines have fallen to me in pleasant places, and my inheritance is excellent to me. And Ephes.

There are, however, two questions which horribly torment the minds of those thinking about election. The first is the question of dignity or merit. When we think thus: if I were worthy, sufficiently pure, or well-deserving, I would also establish myself as an heir of the eternal benefits which God promised. This imagination arises from the law, which demands dignity and merits. Here, therefore, it is necessary to hold to the voice of the Gospel concerning gratuitous mercy. For this very reason the voice of the Gospel concerning gratuitous reconciliation for the sake of the Son was revealed, that it might meet that question of merit, and heal us in this difficult struggle, asserting that we are certainly received for the sake of the mediator gratuitously, not because of our own dignity. And let there be in sight some clear testimonies, as Rom. 4: Therefore it is of faith gratuitously, that the promise may be firm. And to Titus 3: Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us.

The other question is about particularity. For because we hear that mercy is the cause of election, and yet that few are elected, we are even more distressed: we dispute whether God is equal, whether there is respect of persons (προσωποληψία) with him, why he does not have mercy on all.

Against this cruel temptation must be opposed the most firm doctrine, which affirms that the promise of grace is universal, and asserts that God, for the sake of the mediator, and gratuitously, promises the remission of sins and salvation to all who are terrified.

Here let the universal sayings be noted, and let us know that we must determine the will of God from the revealed word, and that we must not invent contradictions to the will that has been handed down, so that it may show the will of God to be true and not feigned, and the true messenger is the Son of God, who brings forth the Gospel from the bosom of the Father, just as he is named in Isaiah, Counselor, because he brings forth this decree of salvation.

This Son says: Come unto me all ye that labor and are heavy laden, and I will refresh you.

John 3: So God loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life.

Rom. 3: The righteousness of God by the faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all them that believe.

Rom. 10: The same Lord of all, is rich unto all that call upon him.

Rom. 11: God hath concluded all in unbelief, that he might have mercy upon all.

1 Tim. 2: God will have all men to be saved.

Rom. 2: There is no respect of persons with God.

Isaiah 53: All we like sheep have gone astray, and the Lord hath laid on him the iniquities of us all.

And it is most manifest that the command of God is universal and immutable, that all should believe in the Son, according to the saying: Hear him. And Psalm: Blessed are all they that trust in him.

From these most manifest testimonies and similar ones, let us most firmly establish that both proclamations are universal: the proclamation of repentance, which convicts sin in all, and commands that all be converted: and the promise of grace, to offer grace to all who are terrified, and to command that they believe in the Son of God.

When, therefore, election is spoken of, let these three admonitions always be in sight. First, one must judge concerning the will of God from his own word, and we approach God with the word shining before us, according to the saying: Thy word is a lamp unto my feet. But the first great consolation is this, that we know for certain from the word of God that God, by his immense mercy for the sake of the Son, always gathers the Church in the human race, and indeed by the voice of the Gospel, and in that assembly which teaches, learns, and embraces the Gospel, and does not defend idols or other corruptions against the foundation, it is certain that there are some elect, according to these sayings: Behold, I am with you always, even unto the end of the world.

Item: My sheep hear my voice. And these sayings testify that there are always some elect, Matth. 14.: In the coming of the son of man there will be two in the field, one will be taken, the other will be left. Item: For the sake of the elect these days will be shortened. Nor are the elect to be sought outside the assembly of the called, but Paul’s saying must be retained: Whom he chose, these he also called. Item, Iohan. 8.: He who is of God, hears the word of God. And for the sake of such a Church, some polities are preserved, although great dissipations and devastations of nations occur everywhere.

Second admonition.

But you will say, this consolation is useful in that I know the Church is preserved for others, but perhaps it is of no use to me, and how can I know who the elect are? I answer: This general consolation is useful to you also, because you ought to believe that the Church is preserved for you too, and the command of God is eternal and immovable, that you also should hear the son, repent, and believe that you are received by God for the sake of the mediator; when you are such a one departing from this life, it is certain that you are in the number of the elect, as it is written: Whom he justifies, these he also glorifies. Item: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord. Item, Apocal. 2.: Be faithful unto death, and I will give you a crown. Item, 2. Corinth. 5.: We shall be clothed upon, if indeed we are not found naked. Thus, as often as we think about election, we look upon the revealed word of God, the calling, the command about hearing the Gospel, about repentance and faith. Because all who are to be saved are elected for the sake of the son of God, and they are elected in such a way that they acknowledge the son, flee to him, and it is of these fleeing to him that he speaks when he says: No one shall snatch my sheep from my hands. Thus we are sheep, when we hear his voice, according to the preceding saying: My sheep hear my voice.

Third admonition.

Since it has been said that one must necessarily judge concerning the will of God from the word delivered by him, not from human imaginations, this rule must also be held: That contradictory wills are not to be posited in God, because God is truthful. Since, therefore, the promise is universal and gratuitous, and it is manifest that the divine command is eternal and immovable, that we should believe in the son, let us obey this command, and let us include ourselves also in the universal promise: (Come unto me all) and let us determine that it pertains to us. Those who sustain themselves with this faith when departing from this life feel the consolation which is the beginning of eternal life, according to the saying: This is eternal life, that they may know you the true God etc. Such are in the number of the elect. But the trembling mind objects: I cannot believe, unless God grants faith. I answer: It is true that men are drawn by God, but they are drawn through the voice of the Gospel, to which God wants you to assent, and at the same time to seek help, as it is written: How much more will he give the Holy Spirit to those who ask. Therefore, do not resist the Gospel, do not indulge in diffidence, do not think, as the enthusiasts dream, that a violent motion must be awaited by which God might snatch you even while you are resisting and again rushing into crimes, but assent to the divine voice, and at the same time ask for help, like that man in Mark: I believe Lord, but help my weakness. When this is done, it is certain that you are being drawn and helped by God, as he swears: As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he may be converted and live. To this sentiment also these sayings belong: God draws, but he draws the willing.

Item: Only be willing, and God anticipates, as Basil says in his sermon on the prodigal son, to whom, as he returns, the father proceeds to meet him and falls upon his neck. We say these things to console those who are in the Church, and who understand themselves to be called by the voice of the Gospel, and who wish to be converted. But if any, without repentance, raise curious questions, it is in vain to dispute with such. That nations lived for a long time in ignorance, or that even now many nations are completely ignorant of the Gospel, the fault is not God’s, but of the men themselves. Because God has always had, and has, a Church in the human race, and he places it as a fortress in a high place, which men ought to hear, but at all times there are many impious ones who do not wish to hear the voice of the son of God, of whom it is said: Kiss the son.

Item: Hear him. Therefore, the impiety of men is to be accused: but let us know that the voice of the son of God must be heard. Now I come to the text.

But I said above why he raises the question about the Church here, because the Jews were arguing that, since they are the Church, they do not err. Paul replies that one must discern

EXPOSITION OF THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. CHAP. IX. [To distinguish] the elect Church from another multitude, which has the title and boasts of carnal propagation, or ordinary succession in external government.

Know, therefore, that this is the sum of this disputation. Paul wishes the true Church to be discerned from the false, and thus he speaks of the effect of election. Therefore he says: Not all who are from Israel, that is, not all propagated from Israel by carnal propagation, or reigning in ordinary succession, are the true Church: because the Church is not gathered by carnal propagation or the succession of Bishops, but by the calling through the Gospel, and by regeneration, in which the Son of God vivifies hearts by the Holy Spirit, as it is said in John 1: Who were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.

Paul, however, opposes a common argument of reason. If Jacob and Esau are equals: why is not each elected, since justice gives equal things to equals?

Paul answers: When a debt is paid, justice gives equal things to equals, but in donation and gratuitous mercy, he is not unjust who gives a benefit not owed to one, and does not give it to another, just as the parable of those hired into the vineyard teaches. God is not unjust in choosing Nebuchadnezzar and not choosing Sennacherib, since both are unworthy.

He confirms this answer with the saying about mercy: I will have mercy on whom I have mercy. Afterwards he says, whom he wills he hardens: where note the Hebrew phrase, in which active verbs often signify permission: he hardens, that is, he allows to be hard, and does not convert him. And by no means is it to be reasoned from this that God wills and effects sins, or forces wills to sin, because it is said: You are not a God who wills impiety.

The Stoic frenzies about necessity must also be removed. Pharaoh, willing, burns with anger and desire, and obeys the devils inciting him: and the cause of rejection is in Pharaoh himself. God, however, allows such things to happen, because he wants the distinction between justice and injustice to be seen in all eternity, and he wants his horrible wrath against the impious to be discerned; therefore he allows some angels and men to fall and rage, so that in punishment, in this life and in all eternity, the distinction between justice and injustice may be seen.

The phrase in the word, He endured the vessels of wrath, also signifies in Greek usage the same as he tolerated. Let us be content with this exposition, and with the Stoic frenzies removed, let us know that the cause of rejection is sin in the impious. Then let us know that the mercy of God on account of the Son is the cause of election, just as it is said here: It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy. Item, Ephes. 1: We are beloved in the Son, and grace is therefore certain to us, because we are received freely on account of the Son, but yet it behooves us to hear the Gospel and not to resist, and he who assents is drawn willingly, just as here also the will is required (but merit is removed) when he says: It is not of him who wills. And it was said above: God draws, but he draws the willing. And let this unmoved and immutable mandate of God always be in sight, which commands that we hear the Son: let us obey this mandate, and let us know that grace abounds over the offense.

Who are you, who argue with God?

He breaks off the question, and although he confesses that many have been rejected, yet he does not say this, that the cause of rejection is not in them. At the same time, however, he commands us to hear the Gospel, and to obey God who calls, and not to be broken, or to fall away from God on account of the example of the multitude, but to give thanks, because he calls all. He draws, however, those who hear the Gospel and do not resist, just as he speaks expressly afterwards about the calling of all and the contumacy of many: All day long I have stretched out my hands to a contumacious and contradicting people. Here he names the cause of reprobation. By no means, therefore, is the similitude of the clay and the potter to be understood as if it said this, that the impious do nothing: for the opinion must be held most firmly that God is not the cause of sin, but that similitude agrees only to this extent, that out of one mass of the human race God both converts many and rejects the contumacious.

Latin:

Caput IX.

Prorsus nova disputatio instituitur de Ecclesia, seu populo Dei, et de vocatione gentium.

Etsi enim necesse est, intexi alicubi discrimen legis et iusticiae fidei, tamen hic principalis quaestio est, quae sit Ecclesia Dei, seu quis sit populus Dei.

Nam et Iudaei opponebant Apostolis autoritatem Ecclesiae, et argumentabantur hoc modo. Cum Ecclesia non erret, Et nos, qui sumus praecipua pars populi, ordinarii sacerdotes, doctores, gubernatores, et maior multitudo antecellens virtute et autoritate, simus Ecclesia, et dissentiamus a vobis. Non est credibile vos recte sentire, qui novum doctrinae genus invehitis in Ecclesiam, ignotum patribus nostris: imo contrarium legi, quia legem a Deo illustribus testimoniis latam aboletis, Idque facitis pauci et seditiosi homines, ut res ipsa ostendit, quia hanc pulcherrimam politiam, quae sola in genere humano voce Dei constituta est, et ingentibus miraculis conservata et saepe restituta est, vos evertitis.

Haec speciosa argumenta opponebant Iudaei, quae nulla humana sapientia refutari possunt, sed refutantur testimoniis divinis, videlicet dictis propheticis et miraculis. Nunc similia opponunt Papistae, sed quia constat eos dimicare de legibus et ritibus humana autoritate traditis, argumenta eorum languidiora sunt. Iudaei dimicabant de lege divina.

Semper tamen Ecclesiae nomine et specie moventur omnes homines moderati, nec temere discedendum est a vetustissimo consensu eorum, quorum probatur autoritas. Paulus inquit, Ecclesiam esse domum Dei, columnam et sedem veritatis. Dominus inquit: Si non audierit Ecclesiam, sit tibi sicut Ethnicus. Samson ait: Si non arassetis mea vitula, non invenissetis.

Cum autem Ecclesiae nomine moveantur homines, necesse est quaerere quae sit vera Dei Ecclesia, quia semper etiam diversi et dissentientes populi hunc gloriosum titulum usurpant, ut nunc de hoc titulo pugnant inter se Christiani, Iudaei et Mahometistae. Imo in hac ipsa multitudine quae nominatur Christiana, sunt dissensiones.

Respondet igitur Paulus et docet, quae sit Ecclesia et ubi sit, et quomodo sit agnoscenda.

Esse autem aliquam visibilem Ecclesiam Dei manifestum est ex multis testimoniis. Cum enim inquit Christus: Dic Ecclesiae, deducit nos ad visibilem coetum. Et Psalmus ait: In omnem terram exiit sonus eorum. Vult Deus audiri vocem Evangelii, vult agnosci filium, ideo semper aliquem coetum alias magis alias minus frequentem colligit, qui conspici et exaudiri possit in genere humano, et in hoc coetu retinetur fundamentum, alias magis alias minus purum, sed tamen non defenduntur idola. Ac semper in hoc coetu sunt electi aliqui, id est, haeredes aeternae vitae, etiam si simul his admixti sunt multi non sancti et non electi, qui tamen de doctrina in externa professione a sanctis non dissentiunt, ut docet similitudo de sagena, in qua sunt boni et mali pisces.

Nec quaerendi sunt electi extra coetum vocatorum, iuxta dictum: Quos elegit, hos et vocavit. Item: Oves meae vocem meam audiunt. Ubicunque autem sunt sive inter hos, sive alibi, qui oppugnant fundamentum, id est, articulos fidei, hos esse extra Ecclesiam, et reiectos et damnatos certum est, iuxta dicta Iohannis 3.: Qui non credit in filium, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manebit super eum.

Et 1. Corinth. 3.: Fundamentum aliud ponere nemo potest, praeter id quod positum est, quod est Iesus Christus.

Cum igitur sit aliqua vera Ecclesia visibilis, teneamus hanc definitionem. Ecclesia visibilis est coetus visibilis amplectentium Evangelium sine corruptelis, et recte utentium Sacramentis, in quo coetu filius Dei est efficax per ministerium Evangelii, et multos regenerat dato Spiritu sancto. Suntque in eo coetu multi non sancti, sed tamen de doctrina consentientes. Ac mandatum est immutabile, pertinens ad omnes homines, ut singuli fiant membra et cives huius verae Ecclesiae, ubicunque sunt in mundo apud suos aut alienos, ita adiuncti, videlicet ut agnoscant et fateantur eum coetum esse veram Dei Ecclesiam, et similis sit confessio doctrinae, et similis invocatio Dei, et similis usus Sacramentorum, et voluntas iuvandi et non perdendi eum coetum.

Nec necesse est similitudinem esse humanarum traditionum, nec necesse est omnes uni politico imperio inclusos esse. Quod autem oporteat singulos fieri membra verae Ecclesiae, testantur haec dicta: Quos elegit, hos et vocavit. Psalm. 26.: Unum petii a Domino, hoc requiram, ut inhabitem in domo Domini omnibus diebus vitae meae, ut videam voluntatem Domini, et visitem templum eius. Psalm. 83.: Beati qui habitant in domo tua Domine. Psalm. 91.: Plantati in domo Domini, in atriis domus Dei nostri florebunt. Psalm. 35.: Lavabo inter innocentes manus meas, et circundabo altare tuum Domine. Dilexi decorum domus tuae, et locum habitationis gloriae tuae.

Psalm. 121.: Rogate quae ad pacem sunt Ierusalem. Et felicitas diligentibus te, propter domum Domini Dei nostri, quaesivi bona tua. Ebraeos 10.: Non relinquentes congregationem nostram.

1 Corinth. 1.: Non sint inter vos schismata, sed sitis coagmentati eadem doctrina et eadem voluntate. Matth. 12.: Qui non congregat mecum, dispergit. Haec et similia dicta praecipiunt de consociatione, et iubent singulos fieri membra verae Ecclesiae, et vetant esse socios hostium Evangelii, seu errones, qui ideo fugiunt Ecclesiae societatem, ut magis vagari opinionibus possint.

Ut autem agnosci vera Ecclesia possit, haec tria praecipua signa externa in sensus incurrentia proposita sint. Pura vox doctrinae Evangelii. Legitimus usus Sacramentorum. Et coniunctio Ecclesiae cum pastoribus, videlicet obedientia in his, quae ad ministerium iuxta Evangelium pertinent, hoc est, ne aliqui seiungant se a communi congregatione, et aut vagentur sine ministerio, aut fastidientes Ecclesiam recte constitutam, instituant privata conventicula etc.

Haec primum de Ecclesia visibili sciri necesse est, quia in hac tantum sunt electi, propter quos et hic visibilis coetus a Deo colligitur et conservatur.

Hic autem quaeritur de causa electionis, ubi primum conspicua responsio est de reiectione. Causa reiectionis est perseverantia in peccatis, iuxta haec dicta: Qui non credit in filium, iam iudicatus est. Item: Qui non credit in filium, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manebit super.

CAP. IX. eum. Psalm. 2.: Osculamini filium, ne exardescat ira eius, et pereatis in via. Sed de causa electionis sciendum est, misericordiam Dei, qui propter filium colligit haereditatem in genere humano, causam esse electionis, non nostra merita. Ideo dictum est in Osea: Perditio tua ex te est, sed auxilium tuum per me est. Et Rom. 11.: Si ex operibus, iam non esset gratia, ut manifestum est gratuita misericordia Dei propter filium initio editam esse promissionem, et colligi et restitui Ecclesiam, sicut Psalm. 2. dicitur: Postula a me, et dabo tibi gentes haereditatem. Psalm. 15.: Tu sustentas haereditatem meam, Funes ceciderunt mihi in praeclaris, et haereditas mea praeclara est mihi. Et Ephes. 1.: Dilexit nos in dilecto.

Duae sunt autem quaestiones, quae horribiliter excruciant animos cogitantes de electione. Prior est quaestio de dignitate seu merito. Cum sic cogitamus, si essem dignus, satis purus, aut bene meritus, statuerem me quoque haeredem esse beneficiorum aeternorum, quae Deus promisit. Haec imaginatio a lege oritur, quae postulat dignitatem et merita. Hic igitur necesse est tenere vocem Evangelii de gratuita misericordia. Hanc ipsam ob causam vox Evangelii de gratuita reconciliatione propter filium revelata est, ut occurrat illi quaestioni de merito, et sanet nos in hoc difficili agone, asseverans certo recipi nos propter mediatorem gratis, non propter nostram dignitatem. Et sint in conspectu aliqua perspicua testimonia, ut Rom. 4.: Ideo ex fide gratis, ut sit firma promissio. Et ad Titum 3.: Non ex operibus iusticiae, quae fecimus nos, sed secundum misericordiam suam salvavit nos.

Altera quaestio est de particularitate. Quia enim audimus misericordiam esse causam electionis, et tamen paucos electos esse, magis etiam angimur: disputamus an sit Deus aequalis, an sit apud eum προσωποληψία, cur non omnium misereatur.

Huic saevae tentationi opponenda est firmissima doctrina, quae affirmat promissionem gratiae universalem esse, et asseverat Deum propter mediatorem, et gratis, omnibus perterrefactis promittere remissionem peccatorum et salutem.

Hic nota sint dicta universalia, et sciamus de voluntate Dei ex verbo revelato statuendum esse, nec fingendas esse contradictorias voluntati tradita est, ut ostendat voluntatem Dei veram et non simulatam, et verax nuncius est filius Dei, qui Evangelium profert ex sinu patris, sicut nominatur apud Esaiam, Consiliarius, quia hoc decretum salutis profert.

Hic filius inquit: Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis et onerati estis, et ego reficiam vos.

Iohan. 3.: Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut filium suum unigenitum dederit, ut omnis qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam.

Rom. 3.: Iusticia Dei per fidem Iesu Christi in omnes et super omnes credentes.

Rom. 10.: Idem Dominus omnium, dives in omnes qui invocant eum.

Rom. 11.: Conclusit Deus omnes sub inobedientiam, ut omnium misereatur.

1. Timoth. 2.: Deus vult omnes homines salvos fieri.

Rom. 2.: Non est acceptio personarum apud Deum.

Esaiae 53.: Omnes nos quasi oves erravimus, et posuit Dominus in eum iniquitates omnium nostrum.

Et manifestissimum est, mandatum Dei universale et immutabile esse, ut omnes credant filio, iuxta dictum: Hunc audite. Et Psalm.: Beati omnes qui confidunt in eo.

Ex his manifestissimis testimoniis et similibus firmissime statuamus utramque concionem universalem esse, concionem poenitentiae, quae arguit peccatum in omnibus, et praecipit ut omnes convertantur: et promissionem gratiae omnibus perterrefactis offerre gratiam, et praecipere ut credant in filium Dei.

Cum igitur de electione dicitur, semper hae tres admonitiones sint in conspectu. Prima iudicandum est de voluntate Dei ex ipsius verbo, et accedimus ad Deum praelucente verbo, iuxta dictum: Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum. Magna autem consolatio primum haec est, quod certo scimus ex verbo Dei. Deum immensa misericordia propter filium semper colligere Ecclesiam in genere humano, et quidem voce Evangelii, et in eo coetu, qui docet, discit et amplectitur Evangelium, et non defendit idola aut alias corruptelas contra fundamentum, certum est esse aliquos electos, iuxta haec dicta: Ecce ego vobiscum sum usque ad consummationem seculi.

Item: Oves meae vocem meam audiunt. Ac semper esse aliquos electos testantur haec dicta, Matth. 14.: In adventu filii hominis duo erunt in agro, unus assumetur, alter relinquetur. Item: Propter electos abbreviabuntur hi dies. Nec sunt electi extra coetum vocatorum quaerendi, sed retinendum est dictum Pauli: Quos elegit, hos et vocavit. Item, Iohan. 8.: Qui est ex Deo, verbum Dei audit. Et propter talem Ecclesiam servantur aliquae politiae, quanquam passim fiunt magnae gentium dissipationes et vastationes.

Secunda admonitio.

Sed dices, haec consolatio eo prodest, quod scio aliis servari Ecclesiam, fortassis autem mihi id nihil prodest, et quomodo sciam qui sint electi? Respondeo: Tibi quoque haec generalis consolatio prodest, quia credere debes tibi quoque servari Ecclesiam, et mandatum Dei aeternum et immotum est, ut tu quoque audias filium, agas poenitentiam et credas te recipi a Deo propter mediatorem, talis cum es discedens ex hac vita, certum est te in numero electorum esse, sicut scriptum est: Quos iustificat, eosdem et glorificat. Item: Beati mortui, qui in Domino moriuntur. Item, Apocal. 2.: Esto fidelis usque ad mortem, et dabo tibi coronam. Item, 2. Corinth. 5.: Superinduemur, si tamen non nudi reperiemur. Sic quoties cogitamus de electione, intuemur verbum Dei revelatum, vocationem, mandatum de audiendo Evangelio, de poenitentia et de fide. Quia omnes salvandi propter filium Dei electi sunt, et ita sunt electi, ut agnoscant filium, ad eum confugiant, et de his confugientibus ad ipsum loquitur, cum ait: Nemo rapiet oves meas ex manibus meis. Sic sumus oves, cum vocem eius audimus, iuxta praecedens dictum: Oves meae vocem meam audiunt.

Tertia admonitio.

Cum dictum sit, necessario iudicandum esse de voluntate Dei ex verbo ab ipso tradito, non ex imaginationibus humanis, tenenda est etiam haec regula: Non esse ponendas contradictorias voluntates in Deo, quia Deus verax est. Cum igitur promissio sit universalis et gratuita, et manifestum sit, mandatum divinum aeternum et immotum esse, ut filio credamus, obtemperemus huic mandato, et includamus nos quoque in promissionem universalem: (Venite ad me omnes) et eam ad nos pertinere statuamus. Hac fide qui se sustentant discedentes ex hac vita, sentiunt consolationem, quae est initium vitae aeternae, iuxta dictum: Haec est vita aeterna, ut agnoscant te Deum verum etc. Tales sunt in numero electorum. Sed obiicit trepida mens: Non possum credere, nisi Deo fidem accendente. Respondeo: Verum est homines a Deo trahi, sed trahuntur per vocem Evangelii, cui vult te Deus assentiri, et simul petere auxilium, sicut scriptum est: Quanto magis dabit Spiritum sanctum petentibus. Non igitur repugnes Evangelio, non indulgeas diffidentiae, non cogites, ut somniant enthusiastae, expectandum esse violentum motum, quo te rapiat Deus etiam repugnantem, et iterum ruentem in scelera, sed assentiaris voci divinae, et simul petito auxilium, sicut ille apud Marcum: Credo Domine, sed opem fer imbecillitati meae. Hoc cum fit, certum est te a Deo trahi et adiuvari, sicut iurat: Vivo ego, dicit Dominus, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed ut convertatur et vivat. In hanc sententiam et haec dicta sunt: Deus trahit, sed volentem trahit.

Item: Tantum velis, et Deus praeoccurrit, ut Basilius dicit in concione de filio prodigo, cui redeunti pater obviam procedit et involat in complexum. Haec dicimus ad consolandos eos, qui sunt in Ecclesia, et se intelligunt vocari voce Evangelii, et volunt converti. Si qui autem sine poenitentia movent curiosas quaestiones, cum talibus frustra disputatur. Quod autem longo tempore gentes in ignorantia vixerunt, aut nunc quoque multae gentes prorsus ignorant Evangelium, culpa est non Dei, sed ipsorum hominum. Quia Deus semper in genere humano habuit, et habet Ecclesiam, et velut arcem in excelso loco collocat, quam audire homines debebant, sed omnibus temporibus multi sunt impii, qui audire vocem filii Dei non volunt, de quibus dictum est: Osculamini filium.

Item: Hunc audite. Accusanda est igitur hominum impietas: nos vero sciamus audiendam esse vocem filii Dei. Nunc ad textum venio.

Supra autem dixi, quare hic quaestionem de Ecclesia moveat, quia Iudaei disputabant, se cum sint Ecclesia, non errare. Respondet Paulus, discernendam esse

3. ENARRATIO EPIST. PAULI AD ROMANOS. CAP. IX. Ecclesiam electam ab alia multitudine, quae titulum habet et iactitat propagationem carnalem, seu ordinariam successionem in externa gubernatione. Scias igitur hanc esse huius disputationis summam. Vult Paulus discerni veram Ecclesiam a falsa, atque ita de effectu electionis loquitur.

Ideo inquit: Non omnes qui sunt ex Israël, id est, non omnes propagati ab Israël propagatione carnali, aut regnantes in successione ordinaria sunt vera Ecclesia: quia Ecclesia non colligitur propagatione carnali aut successione Episcoporum, sed vocatione per Evangelium, et regeneratione, in qua filius Dei vivificat corda Spiritu sancto, ut Iohan. 1. dicitur: Qui non ex sanguinibus, neque ex voluntate carnis, neque ex voluntate viri, sed ex Deo nati sunt.

Opponit autem Paulus commune argumentum rationis. Si pares sunt Iacob et Esau: cur non uterque eligitur, quia iusticia dat aequalia aequalibus?
