Respondet Paulus: Cum solvitur debitum, iusticia dat aequalia aequalibus, sed in donatione et gratuita misericordia non est iniustus, qui dat alicui non debitum beneficium, alteri non dat, sicut docet et parabola de conductis in vineam. Non est iniustus Deus eligens Nabuchodonosor, et non eligens Sennacherib, cum uterque sit indignus. Hanc responsionem confirmat dicto de misericordia: Misereor cuius misereor.

Postea ait, quem vult indurat: ubi nota sit Ebraea phrasis, in qua verba activa saepe permissionem significant: indurat, id est, sinit esse durum, nec convertit eum. Ac nequaquam inde ratiocinandum est, Deum velle et efficere peccata, aut cogere voluntates ad peccandum, quia dictum est: Non Deus volens impietatem tu es.

Removendi sunt et Stoici furores de necessitate. Pharao volens ardet ira et cupiditate, et obtemperat diabolis eum incitantibus: estque in ipso Pharaone causa reiectionis. Sinit autem Deus talia fieri, quia vult conspici discrimen in omni aeternitate inter iusticiam et iniusticiam, et vult cerni horribilem iram suam adversus impios, ideo sinit labi et furere aliquos angelos et homines, ut in poena conspiciatur in hac vita, et in tota aeternitate, discrimen inter iusticiam et iniusticiam.

Phrasis in verbo, Tulit vasa irae, etiam Graeca consuetudine significat idem quod toleravit. Hac enarratione simus contenti, et remotis stoicis furoribus, sciamus causam reiectionis peccatum esse in impiis. Deinde sciamus misericordiam Dei propter filium causam esse electionis, sicut hic dicitur: Non est volentis, nec currentis, sed Dei miserentis. Item, Ephes. 1.: Sumus dilecti in filio, et gratia ideo nobis certa est, quia gratis propter filium recipimur, sed tamen audire nos Evangelium oportet et non repugnare, ac assentiens trahitur volens, sicut et hic quoque requiritur voluntas (sed meritum tollitur) cum ait: Non est volentis. Et supra dictum est: Trahit Deus, sed volentem trahit. Et semper in conspectu sit hoc immotum et immutabile mandatum Dei, quod praecipit, ut audiamus filium: huic mandato obtemperemus, et sciamus gratiam exuberare supra delictum.

Tu qui es, qui litigas cum Deo?

Abrumpit quaestionem, et quanquam fatetur multos reiectos esse, tamen non hoc dicit, non esse causam reiectiones in ipsis. Simul autem iubet nos audire Evangelium, et obtemperare Deo vocanti, et non frangi, aut deficere a Deo propter exemplum multitudinis, sed agere gratias, quod omnes vocat. Trahit autem audientes Evangelium, et non repugnantes, sicut postea de omnium vocatione et multorum contumacia expresse loquitur: Tota die expandi manus meas ad populum contumacem, et contradicentem. Hic nominat causam reprobationis. Nequaquam igitur sic intelligenda est similitudo de luto et figulo, quasi hoc dicat, nihil agere impios: firmissime enim tenenda est sententia, quod Deus non sit causa peccati, sed similitudo illa eatenus congruit, quod ex una massa generis humani Deus et convertit multos, et contumaces reiicit.

## 9:28
The word consuming and abbreviating.

After he has delivered this sweetest consolation, that there is always some Church elected on account of the Son, as it is said in Psalm 16: You are the one who sustains my inheritance for me. He now adds testimonies about the destruction of the Jewish polity and about the gathering of the Church from the Jews and the Gentiles. In Hosea it is said: I will call them who are not my people, that they may be my people.

And in Isaiah it is said, Chapter 10: Even if the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved, that is, even if there be a great multitude of the people of Israel, yet the greater part shall horribly perish, the polity being destroyed, and only a remnant, that is, a small part, shall be converted to God.

For thus the Prophet declares himself: The Lord will make a consummation and predefinition in the midst of the earth, that is, He will make an end of the polity of Israel at the appointed time, and then the pre-defined consummation will overflow with justice, that is, in that destruction of the polity, justice will be most liberally given to the Jews and the Gentiles, namely: The Son of God Himself and His benefits, the remission of sins, reconciliation, new and eternal justice and life to be given through the Son, to those sanctified by the voice of the Gospel and the Holy Spirit, just as Daniel says, Chapter 9: Propitiation shall be made for sin, iniquity shall be blotted out, and everlasting justice shall be brought in, and the Holy of Holies shall be anointed, and the people shall cease to be, and the people of the Prince to come, namely Titus, shall destroy the city and the temple.

These words of Daniel agree with the aforementioned Isaiah. Let us therefore retain this interpretation, which is true, native, simple, and clear.

And although the reading taken in Paul and the Greek translation of the Prophets is more obscure, yet the meaning truly agrees with the Hebrew reading. The Lord will make a shortened word, that is, a thing or business shortened, or an abbreviation, that is, an end of the polity of Israel, and then God, making this abbreviation, or end of the polity, will cause justice to overflow, that is, then He will exhibit the Messiah and His benefits.

However, the sweet metaphor in the word 'overflows' is to be observed, which signifies a large and gratuitous justice given by the immense goodness of God for the sake of the mediator, freely. Being reminded, therefore, by this sweet metaphor, let us think of the amplitude of grace, so that faith and invocation may be kindled, and the declaration is to be taken from the preceding [passages] concerning gratuitous reconciliation and the universal promise.

Israel, by pursuing the law of justice, did not arrive at justice. Here he expressly places the cause of reprobation, because the impious do not wish to believe the Gospel; therefore I said above that the similitude of the Clay is not to be taken as if there were no cause for reprobation in the very will of men: for he says that many in Israel perish because, by pursuing the law of justice, they stubbornly retain this opinion, that by their own works and cults they merit the remission of sins, and are just, that is, accepted by God, and heirs of eternal life because of these shadows, that is, because of moral works, not because of the Messiah.

Thus let the phrase be understood: To pursue the law from works. At the end is added a most sweet testimony: Everyone who believes in him shall not be confounded, that is, shall not be frustrated.

For it is a customary phrase, 'to be confounded,' for 'to be frustrated,' although in Isaiah chapter 28, the word in Hebrew signifies haste, trepidation, consternation, or flight.

But Paul rendered the meaning according to the saying in Psalm 2: Blessed are all who trust in him.

And there are many similar sayings. Let us learn the meaning of this saying in our daily consolations, and let us know that here both the Messiah and the particle 'Gratis' are comprehended.

Faith looks upon the Messiah, and most firmly establishes that we are received 'Gratis' for His sake, not because of our own dignity, and that we are heirs of eternal life. Chapter X. He institutes nothing new, but repeats the former opinion concerning the cause of the defection of the Jews, and the cause for which they oppose the Gospel.

Latin:

Verbum consummans et abbrevians.

Postquam hanc dulcissimam consolationem tradidit, quod semper aliqua sit Ecclesia electa propter filium, sicut Psalm. 16. dicitur: Tu es, qui sustentas haereditatem meam mihi. Addit nunc testimonia de destructione politiae Iudaicae et de collectione Ecclesiae ex Iudaeis et Gentibus. In Osea dicitur: Vocabo eos qui non sunt populus, ut sint meus populus.

Et apud Esaiam dicitur Cap. 10.: Etiamsi erit numerus filiorum Israël ut arena maris, reliquiae salvae erunt, id est, etsi magna multitudo erit populi Israël, tamen maior pars horribiliter peritura est deleta politia, et tantum reliquiae, id est, exigua pars convertetur ad Deum.

Sic enim declarat se Propheta: Consummationem et praefinitionem faciet Dominus in medio terrae, id est, faciet finem constituto tempore politiae Israël, et tunc consummatio praefinita exundabit iusticiam, id est, in illo interitu politiae largissime donabitur iusticia Iudaeis et Gentibus, videlicet: Ipse filius Dei et eius beneficia, remissio peccatorum, reconciliatio, nova et aeterna iusticia et vita donanda per filium, sanctificatis voce Evangelii et Spiritu sancto, prorsus ut Daniel inquit, Cap. 9.: Fiet propiciatio pro peccato, delebitur iniquitas et adducetur iusticia sempiterna, et ungetur Sanctus sanctorum, et populus desinet esse, et civitatem et templum delebit populus Ducis venturi, scilicet Titus.

Haec Danielis verba congruunt cum Esai. dicto. Hanc igitur interpretationem veram, nativam, simplicem et perspicuam retineamus.

Et quanquam lectio in Paulo sumta et translatione Graeca Prophetarum obscurior est, tamen sententia re vera cum Ebraea lectione congruit. Verbum abbreviatum faciet Dominus, id est, rem seu negotium abbreviatum, seu abbreviationem, id est, finem politiae Israël, et tunc faciens Deus hanc abbreviationem, seu finem politiae, exundabit iusticiam, id est, tunc exhibebit Messiam et eius beneficia.

Observanda est autem dulcis metaphora in verbo Exundat, quod significat largam et gratuitam iusticiam donatam immensa bonitate Dei propter mediatorem gratis. Commonefacti igitur hac dulci metaphora, cogitemus amplitudinem gratiae, ut fides et invocatio accendantur, et sumenda est declaratio ex superioribus de gratuita reconciliatione, et universali promissione.

Israël sectando legem iusticiae, ad iusticiam non pervenit. Hic expresse ponit causam reprobationis, quia impii non volunt credere Evangelio, ideo supra dixi similitudinem de Luto non sic accipiendam esse, quasi non sit in ipsa hominum voluntate causa reprobationis: ait enim, ideo multos in Israël perire, quia sectando legem iusticiae pertinaciter retineant hanc opinionem, quod suis operibus et cultibus mereantur remissionem peccatorum, et sint iusti, id est, accepti Deo, et haeredes vitae aeternae propter has umbras, id est, propter opera moralia, non propter Messiam.

Sic intelligatur phrasis: Sectari legem ex operibus. In fine additum est dulcissimum testimonium: Omnis qui credit in eum, non confundetur, id est, non frustrabitur.

Est enim usitata phrasis, confundi, pro frustrari, Quanquam apud Esaiam cap. 28. Verbum est in Ebraeo, quod significat festinationem, trepidationem, consternationem, seu fugam.

Sed Paulus sententiam reddidit, iuxta dictum in 2. Psalm.: Beati omnes qui confidunt in eo.

Et sunt similia dicta multa. Discamus autem huius dicti sententiam in quotidianis consolationibus, et sciamus hic comprehendi, et Messiam, et particulam Gratis.

Fides intuetur Messiam, et firmissime statuat Gratis propter ipsum, non propter dignitatem nostram nos recipi, et esse haeredes vitae aeternae. Caput X.

## 10:1 Argument
Therefore they war (he says) against the Gospel, because they do not want the justice of the law to be diminished, nor do they understand that the justice of the Gospel is something else: they even fight for their own polity, which they see being dissolved by the preaching of the Gospel.

Just as now Bishops and Monks fight for their own ceremonies, so that the status and splendor of their polity may be preserved. He adds, however, a complaint about the destruction of the nation, as above, and attributes to them zeal, that is, study or an ardent will, or fervor, which seems good to them, but is not good, because it is joined with errors: and there are errors in the principal articles of faith, concerning the merits of Christ, the kingdom, and the offices, whence comes the remission of sins, what sin is, and what true justice is. Moreover, a grave threat is added against the defenders of impious opinions concerning the justice of the law, when he says:

Moreover, a grave threat is added against the defenders of impious opinions concerning the justice of the law, when he says: to subject them to the righteousness of God. Clearly, therefore, he condemns all who oppose the true doctrine of the righteousness of faith.

Again, the younger ones must be warned about the phrase. The righteousness of God does not signify in this place an essential righteousness in God, but it signifies the righteousness by which God, for the sake of the Son, accounts us righteous, that is, accounts us accepted through faith. And when this happens, it is simultaneously true that those who believe are vivified through the Son of God, and are sanctified by the Holy Spirit, as he says: I give eternal life to them. And in John it is said: He who has the Son, has life. Likewise: He gives of His Spirit to us. The end of the law is Christ for righteousness to everyone who believes, etc.

Here he institutes a comparison between the righteousness of the law and the righteousness of the Gospel, and defines both, and proposes a sentiment opposed to the Jewish imaginations about the law, as if he were saying: The Jews think that the law is satisfied by external obedience, and by this external discipline they dream that they are righteous before God, like the Pharisee in Luke 18. Nor do they understand that the Messiah is the end of the law, that is, that He was promised so that He might take away sin, which the law only shows and convicts, but does not take away.

Therefore, the sweetest sentiment must be considered: Christ is the end of the law, that is, the fulfillment or consummation of the law, granting that which the law commands, taking away sin and death, and restoring eternal righteousness and life, as Daniel says: Sin will be finished, and wickedness will be blotted out, propitiation will be made, and everlasting righteousness will be brought in. These good things will be consummated after the resurrection; now in this life, liberation from sin happens by imputation and by beginning, that is, he who believes in Christ is righteous, first by imputation, that is, having the remission of sins and reconciliation, and is accepted, or pleasing to God through faith on account of Christ's obedience and intercession. But at the same time, a new righteousness and life is begun, because the Son in this consolation vivifies hearts and sanctifies them, the Holy Spirit having been given, as was said above: He who has the Son, has life, and: He gives of His Spirit to you. But this newness will be complete in eternal life.

For Moses writes: He who has done them, shall live in them.

In this antithesis, some have imagined that the state of this comparison is in these words: He shall live in them, that is, that double rewards are conferred for works. That the works of reason have bodily rewards, but good works born of the Holy Spirit have eternal rewards. This interpretation is foreign to Paul's sentiment.

For it is not a comparison of rewards that is being made, but it is spoken of formally, as to what the righteousness of the law is in reality, and conversely, what the righteousness of the Gospel is.

Therefore, the state of the comparison is in these two words, To do and To believe. The righteousness of the law is to do the law, that is, to perform perfect obedience according to the law. Thus he says the righteousness of the law is described by Moses, when he says: He who does them shall live in them, as if he were saying: The righteousness of the law is this very obedience, by which truly and entirely all things that the law commands would be done in an uncorrupted nature, or it is an entire conformity with the law in us, namely, an ardent and perfect love of God and neighbor, without any vicious concupiscence. This definition of the righteousness of the law also agrees with this saying: Cursed is he who does not remain in all things which are written in the law. To do all things, or to remain in all things, that is, to be conformable to the law by entire obedience without any sin. This is named the righteousness of the law described in the saying of Moses: He who has done them, shall live in them.

But it has often been said above that this entire obedience cannot exist in this depraved nature.

For it is expressly said in Romans 8: The mind of the flesh cannot be subject to the law of God, and Romans 3: By the works of the law no flesh will be justified. Since, therefore, no one is righteous before God by the law in this mortal nature, the Gospel preaches of another righteousness, which is to believe in the Son of God, as John says: He who believes in the Son, has life.

Do not say in your heart, Who will ascend into heaven.

Paul borrows the description of faith from the saying of Moses, and does not twist it to a different or foreign sentiment. For Moses also truly describes and demands faith in the same place, but in Moses it is a general saying about the word and about faith, which Paul adapts to this word about Christ, who is the end of the law, and of whom the promises spoke, having been handed down before the law.

Let us therefore first look at the saying of Moses, who depicts the impiety of the human heart with illustrious figures, because even though it thinks there is a God, nevertheless it disputes whether God cares for us: and although it is moved by the fear of punishments, so that he thinks crimes are punished by some order of nature, yet he can affirm absolutely nothing about salvation without the revealed word, but wanders in darkness, and denies that men are heard, especially in present calamity, denies that God is reconciled, and that calamities are mitigated, and that eternal life and eternal joy are given.

It is manifest that these doubts cling in the minds of men according to the judgment of reason: therefore the law taxes them and demands faith.

"Do not say in your heart, who shall ascend into heaven etc." That is, do not be an Epicurean, do not think that there is no God, or that it is unknown whether there is a God and what He is like, or whether He cares for human affairs; do not think that God is hidden in such a way that He does not wish to be known, but think that He has truly come forth from His secret seat in immense goodness, and has revealed Himself by His word, and is such as He affirms Himself to be in the law and in the promise, namely wise, truthful, beneficent, just, chaste, punishing the contrary, merciful on account of the mediator.

Therefore Moses says, "Look to the Word, which is near in your mouth." Thus Moses leads us away from the chaos of the thoughts of human reason to the revealed word, and according to this word he wants us to know God, not to wander in thoughts, as the Gentiles and all the impious wander, as the poems sound: "O Jupiter, whatever you are, whether this heaven, or the mind which is carried in heaven, although I have long been invoking idle helpers": as Hecuba says in Euripides.

Many such things are read among the poets, who depict the hearts of all the impious.

And in Crete they write that there was a statue of Jove without ears, which the sculptor, fashioning it thus, showed that he felt this, that men are not heard by God etc. Against these impious thoughts Moses opposes this necessary admonition, that we should think about the essence and will of God as He reveals Himself in His word, and he affirms that God is thus rightly known and apprehended.

It is certain that this very doctrine has been most often repeated in many sermons of Christ, the Prophets, and the Apostles, as in Numbers, ch. 15: "Let them remember all the commandments of the Lord, and not follow their own thoughts, and their eyes which go whoring etc."

Psalm 1 and Ps.

118: "Your word is a lamp to my feet etc."

Also in Psalm 130: "My soul has waited in His word."

And Isaiah 8: "To the law and to the testimony, if they do not speak according to this word, there will be no morning light for them etc." 1 Cor.

1: "Since the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God to save those who believe through the foolish preaching."

And Coloss. 3: "Let the word of God dwell in you abundantly in all wisdom."

Also John 14: "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word." By such many testimonies let us confirm and fortify ourselves, lest weak minds slip into speculations about God outside the revealed word, just as Eve slips, and countless others.

But after the opinion of Moses is clear, now let us consider the Pauline accommodation.

Moses says generally: "Do not say in your heart, who ascends into heaven, but the word is near," that is, do not be an Epicurean, do not judge about God from the speculations of reason, but embrace the revealed word of God. Paul accommodates this general admonition to this word also concerning the mediator, which indeed Moses also embraced, even if he does not expressly name the mediator there, but speaks of every word of God.

Therefore the Apostle, illustrating the saying of Moses, expressly names the mediator.

Do not say in your heart, Who shall ascend into heaven.

That is, first, do not be an Epicurean. Then, do not doubt that this is the will of God, which He has revealed by so many illustrious testimonies, which He added to the promise and preaching of the Gospel, namely, that the Son has been appointed mediator and, having been resurrected, reigns, so that He may gather the Church, give it the remission of sins, be present to the voice of the Gospel in the Church, speak consolation in the heart through the Gospel, give life, and give the Holy Spirit.

If you do not believe these things, you deny that He reigns, that is, you drag Him down as if from heaven; so he adds: "Who shall descend into the abyss," that is, who knows what remains after death, or how it can be thought that men are to live again from death, and do not think that Christ lies extinct, nor that He is the victor of death, but rather know that the true voice is: "O death, I will be your death."

Christ shows by His resurrection and by those raised that He will return life to men, and will judge all men. NARRATION OF THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. CHAP. X. [having] raised others, that He would restore life to men, and would judge all men.

This simple narration shows that Paul has neatly accommodated the general saying about the word and faith to this word, and to faith in the Mediator. And those indeed, who rightly understood the law, knew that the Mediator was signified in the law, and that the promise of grace concerning the Mediator was published immediately at the beginning, and that obedience could not be begun, unless faith shines in the heart, receiving reconciliation, and approaching God by trust in the Mediator.

Near is the word in thy mouth.

Previously He forbade doubts: Do not say, Who shall ascend into heaven etc. Now He adds an asseveration, and expressly leads us to the word handed down by God, and that He speaks of the revealed word, which we receive with our ears and thoughts, it is manifest, because He says: The word which is in thy mouth.

Afterwards He says: How shall they preach, unless they have been sent?

And it is true that the Son of God Himself, the λόγος [Word], is present to this vocal word, and is effective through the voice in hearts, and reigns in the Church, as it is said elsewhere: The Gospel is the power of God unto salvation etc.

Item: I give eternal life to them etc. Item: Sanctify them in the truth, thy word is truth. With the heart one believes unto righteousness.

Now He completes the antithesis of the righteousness of the law and the righteousness of faith, where the definitions on both sides are to be prudently considered.

The righteousness of the law is to do the law, as He said above.

This discourse is νομικός [legal], and political custom and philosophy concerning universal righteousness imitate this discourse, as Theognis also says: Righteousness in itself contains all virtues.

However, the distinction between the righteousness of the law and the righteousness of faith must be understood. But the righteousness of faith is to believe in this Christ, the Son of God, crucified and resurrected, not idle, but reigning, through whom and by whom we who believe truly receive the remission of sins, reconciliation, or the imputation of righteousness, vivification, and the gift of the Holy Spirit and eternal life.

For Paul comprehends this when he says: If you have confessed this Jesus to be Lord, that is, reigning, gathering the Church, and effective through the voice of the eternal Son, if you believe with your heart that God has raised Him, namely for this reason, that He might be the victor of death, and restore to us righteousness and eternal life.

And by this faith, he says, a man is righteous, when he says: With the heart one believes unto righteousness, that is, by believing with the heart one is righteous, having the remission of sins, and pleasing God freely on account of the Mediator.

The thief on the cross, receiving remission and reconciliation, is righteous, pleases God, and is vivified, even if he did not do the law before, nor afterwards, as long as he lived in the body, he has the complete fulfillment of the law: even if there was a beginning of obedience.

Thus, having posited the antithesis of the definitions of the Righteousness of the law and the Righteousness of faith, Paul shows the distinction.

Everyone who believes in Him shall not be confounded.

Paul adds a testimony taken from Isaiah Chapter 28, where the sweetest promise concerning the Messiah is expressly repeated: Behold, I will lay in Sion a tried stone, a corner stone, precious in the foundation, he who believes in Him shall not tremble.

He uses a similar metaphor in the Psalm: The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the head of the corner.

Paul explains this metaphor to the Ephesians.

Item, when he says: No other foundation can be laid, besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus.

He carries the Church by merit and efficacy, He redeemed her by His death, and is the Mediator and intercessor for us, offering His merits, and is effective in the Church, He Himself is present to her, and vivifies her by the voice of the Gospel and the Holy Spirit.

But how the benefits of the Messiah are applied to us, he teaches when he says: He who believes in Him shall not tremble.

These things agree with many other similar sayings, Psalm 2: Blessed are all who trust in Him.

And Paul here adds the universal particle, just as it is also posited in the Psalm.

But I have often said that the consideration of the Universal particle is necessary, so that everyone may include himself in the universal promise, and not imagine in God any προσωποληψίαν [respect of persons], or contradictory wills, and the Universal [particle] is repeated soon after several times, Rich unto all who call upon Him.

And the Lord says: Come unto me all etc.

It is, however, an eternal command, that all should believe in Him.

Latin:

Nihil novi instituit, sed repetit priorem sententiam de causa defectionis Iudaeorum, et de causa, propter quam Evangelio adversantur. Ideo belligerantur (inquit) cum Evangelio, quia nolunt extenuari iusticiam legis, nec intelligunt aliud esse iusticiam Evangelii: dimicant etiam de sua politia, quam praedicatione Evangelii vident dissolvi.

Sicut nunc Episcopi et Monachi dimicant de suis ceremoniis, ut status et splendor suae politiae conserventur. Addit autem querelam de gentis interitu, ut supra, et tribuit eis zelum, id est, studium seu ardentem voluntatem, seu fervorem, qui ipsis bonus videtur, sed non est bonus, quia cum erroribus coniunctus est: et sunt errores in articulis fidei praecipuis, de Christi meritis, regno et officiis, unde sit remissio peccatorum, quid sit peccatum, quae sit vera iusticia.

Est autem gravis comminatio addita adversus defensores impiarum opinionum de iusticia legis, cum inquit: on subijci eos iusticiae Dei. Perspicue igitur damnat omnes adversantes verae doctrinae de iusticia fidei.

Rursus autem monendi sunt iuniores de phrasi. Iusticia Dei non significat hoc loco iusticiam essentialem in Deo, sed significat iusticiam, qua nos Deus propter filium reputat iustos, id est, nos acceptos fide. Et hoc cum fit, simul verum est, vivificari credentes per filium Dei, et sanctificari eos Spiritu sancto, sicut inquit: Ego vitam aeternam do eis. Et in Iohanne dicitur: Qui habet filium, habet vitam. Item: De spiritu suo dat nobis. Finis legis est Christus ad iusticiam omni credenti etc.

Hic instituit collationem iusticiae legis et iusticiae Evangelii, et utramque definit, ac proponit sententiam oppositam Iudaicis imaginationibus de lege, quasi dicat: Iudaei cogitant legi satisfieri externa obedientia, et hac externa disciplina somniant se iustos esse coram Deo, ut Pharisaeus Lucae 18. Nec intelligunt Messiam esse finem legis, hoc est, promissum esse, ut tollat peccatum, quod lex tantum ostendit et arguit, non tollit.

Consideranda est igitur dulcissima sententia: Christus est finis legis, id est, impletio seu consummatio legis, donans id, quod lex praecipit, tollens peccatum et mortem, et restituens aeternam iusticiam et vitam, sicut Daniel inquit: Finietur peccatum, et delebitur pravitas, fiet propiciatio et adducetur iusticia sempiterna. Haec bona erunt consummata post resurrectionem, nunc in hac vita liberatio a peccato fit imputatione et incoatione, id est, qui credit in Christum, est iustus, primum imputatione, id est, habens remissionem peccatorum et reconciliationem, et acceptus, seu placens Deo per fidem propter Christi obedientiam et intercessionem. Simul autem incoatur nova iusticia et vita, quia filius in hac consolatione vivificat corda et sanctificat ea, dato Spiritu sancto, ut supra dictum est: Qui habet filium, habet vitam, et: De spiritu suo dat vobis. Sed haec novitas erit integra in vita aeterna.

Moises enim scribit: Qui fecerit ea, vivet in eis.

In hac antithesi quidam imaginati sunt, statum collationis huius esse in his verbis: Vivet in eis, hoc est, penes praemia conferri duplicia opera. Opera rationis habere praemia corporalia, sed bona opera orta a Spiritu sancto habere praemia aeterna. Haec interpretatio aliena est a sententia Pauli.

Non enim fit collatio praemiorum, sed de formali dicitur, quid re ipsa sit iusticia legis, et contra, quid sit iusticia Evangelii.

Est igitur status collationis in his duobus verbis, Facere et Credere. Iusticia legis est facere legem, hoc est, praestare perfectam obedientiam iuxta legem. Sic ait describi a Moisi iusticiam legis, cum inquit: Faciens ea vivet in eis, quasi dicat: Iusticia legis est haec ipsa obedientia, qua vere et integre omnia quae lex praecipit, fierent in natura integra, seu est integra in nobis conformitas cum lege, videlicet ardens et perfecta dilectio Dei et proximi, sine ulla vitiosa concupiscentia. Haec definitio iusticiae legis etiam ad hoc dictum congruit: Maledictus qui non manet in omnibus, quae sunt scripta in lege. Facere omnia, seu manere in omnibus, id est, esse conformem legi integra obedientia sine ullo peccato. Haec nominatur iusticia legis descripta in dicto Moisi: Qui fecerit ea, vivet in eis.

Supra autem saepe dictum est, hanc integram obedientiam non posse in hac depravata natura esse.

Expresse enim dicitur Rom. 8.: Sensus carnis non potest legi Dei subijci, et Rom. 3.: Ex operibus legis non iustificabitur omnis caro. Cum igitur lege nemo sit iustus coram Deo in hac mortali natura, Evangelium concionatur de alia iusticia, quae est credere in filium Dei, sicut Iohannes inquit: Qui credit in filium, habet vitam.

Ne dixeris in corde tuo, Quis ascendet in coelum.

Paulus mutuatur descriptionem fidei ex dicto Moisi, nec detorquet illud ad diversam, aut peregrinam sententiam. Nam et Moises ibidem vere describit et postulat fidem, sed in Moisi generale dictum est de verbo et de fide, quod Paulus accommodat ad hoc verbum de Christo, qui est finis legis, et... de quo promissiones loquuntur ante legem traditae.

Primum igitur dictum Moisi inspiciamus, qui illustribus figuris impietatem humani cordis depingit, quod etiamsi cogitat esse Deum, tamen disputat, an Deus curet nos: et quanquam exemplis poenarum movetur, ut cogitet puniri scelera ordine aliquo naturae, tamen de salvatione prorsus nihil adfirmare potest sine verbo revelato, sed vagatur in tenebris, et negat exaudiri homines, praesertim in praesenti calamitate, negat reconciliari Deum, et mitigare calamitates, et dare vitam aeternam et laetitiam aeternam.

Has dubitationes in hominum animis iuxta rationis iudicium haerere manifestum est: ideo lex eas taxat et postulat fidem.

Ne dixeris in corde tuo, quis ascendet in coelum etc. Id est, ne sis Epicureus, ne cogites nihil esse Deum, aut nesciri an sit Deus et qualis sit, an curet humana, ne cogites Deum sic latere, ut non velit agnosci, sed cogites eum vere ex arcana sede immensa bonitate prodiisse, et se verbo suo patefecisse, et talem esse, qualia se velle affirmat in lege et in promissione, videlicet sapientem, veracem, beneficum, iustum, castum, punientem contraria, misericordem propter mediatorem.

Ideo inquit Moises, Verbum intuere, quod prope est in ore tuo. Ita abducit nos Moises a Chao cogitationum humanae rationis ad patefactum verbum, et iuxta hoc verbum vult nos agnoscere Deum, non vagari cogitationibus, sicut vagantur Ethnici et omnes impii, ut sonant Poëmata: O Iupiter quicquid es, sive hoc coelum, sive mens, quae vehitur in coelo, quanquam diu iam invoco adiutores ignavos: ut Hecuba dicit apud Euripidem.

Talia leguntur multa apud poëtas, qui pingunt omnium impiorum corda.

Et in Creta scribunt fuisse Iovis statum sine auribus, quam statuarius sic fabricans, ostendit se esse hoc sentire, homines non exaudiri a Deo etc. His impiis cogitationibus opponit Moises hanc necessariam commonefactionem, ut sic de essentia et voluntate Dei sentiamus, sicut se in verbo suo patefacit, et affirmat sic recte agnosci et apprehendi Deum.

Hanc ipsam doctrinam constat saepissime repetitam esse in multis concionibus Christi, Prophetarum et Apostolorum, ut in Nume. cap. 15.: Recordentur omnium mandatorum Domini, nec sequantur cogitationes suas, et oculos scortantes etc.

Psalm. 1. et Ps.

118.: Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum etc.

Item in Psalm. 130.: Sustinuit anima mea in verbo eius.

Et Esaiae 8.: Ad legem et ad testimonium si non dixerint iuxta verbum hoc, non erit eis matutina lux etc.

1 Cor. 1.: Cum Deum sapientem non nosset mundus per sapientiam, placuit Deo salvos facere credentes per stultam concionem.

Et Coloss. 3.: Sermo Dei habitet in vobis abunde in omni sapientia.

Item Iohannis 14.: Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum servabit. Talibus testimoniis multis confirmemus et muniamus nos, ne labantur infirmae mentes ad speculationes de Deo extra patefactum verbum, sicut labitur Eva, et alii innumerabiles.

Postquam autem perspicue est Moisi sententia, nunc consideremus Paulinam accommodationem.

Moises generaliter inquit: Ne dixeris in corde, quis ascendit in coelum, sed prope est verbum, id est, ne sis Epicureus, ne iudica ex speculationibus rationis de Deo, sed amplectere verbum Dei patefactum. Hanc generalem admonitionem accommodat Paulus ad hoc verbum etiam de mediatore, quod quidem et Moises complectebatur, etsi ibi non expresse nominat mediatorem, sed de omni verbo Dei loquitur.

Igitur Apostolus illustrans dictum Moisi expresse nominat mediatorem.

Ne dixeris in corde tuo, Quis ascendet in coelum.

Id est, primum ne sis Epicureus. Deinde ne dubites, quin haec sit voluntas Dei, quam revelavit tot illustribus testimoniis, quae addidit promissioni et praedicationi Evangelii, videlicet, filium constitutum esse mediatorem et resuscitatum regnare, ut colligat Ecclesiam, det ei remissionem peccatorum, adsit voci Evangelii in Ecclesia, dicat consolationem in corde per Evangelium, vivificet, et det Spiritum sanctum.

Haec si non credis, negas eum regnare, hoc est, eum velut de coelo detrahere, ita addit: Quis descendet in abyssum, id est, quis scit quid post mortem restet, aut quomodo existimari potest revicturos esse homines ex morte, nec cogites Christum iacere extinctum, nec victorem esse mortis, imo scias veram esse vocem: O mors ero mors tua.

Ostendit Christus resurrectione sua et resuscitatis aliis, se redditurum esse vitam hominibus, et iudicaturum esse omnes homines. ENARRATIO EPIST. PAULI AD ROMANOS. CAP. X. suscitatis aliis, se redditurum esse vitam hominibus, et iudicaturum esse omnes homines.

Haec simplex enarratio ostendit Paulum concinne accommodasse generale dictum de verbo et fide ad hoc verbum, et ad fidem de mediatore. Ac illi quidem, qui recte intelligebant legem, sciebant in lege significari mediatorem, et statim initio editam esse promissionem gratiae de mediatore, nec posse incoari obedientiam, nisi in corde praeluceat fide accipiens reconciliationem, et accedens ad Deum fiducia mediatoris.

Prope est verbum in ore tuo.

Antea prohibuit dubitationes: Ne dixeris, Quis ascendet in coelum etc. Nunc addit adseverationem, et expresse deducit nos ad verbum a Deo traditum, et loqui eum de verbo patefacto, quod auribus et cogitationibus accipimus, manifestum est, quia inquit: Verbum quod est in ore tuo.

Postea inquit: Quomodo praedicabunt, nisi missi fuerint.

Ac verum est huic verbo vocali adesse ipsum filium Dei λόγον, et per vocem in cordibus efficacem esse, et regnare in Ecclesia, sicut alibi dicitur: Evangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem etc.

Item: Ego vitam aeternam do eis etc. Item: Sanctifica eos in veritate, sermo tuus est veritas. Corde creditur ad iusticiam.

Nunc absolvit antithesin iusticia legis et iusticiae fidei, ubi definitiones utrinque prudenter considerandae sunt.

Iusticia legis est facere legem, ut supra dixit.

Hic sermo est νομικός, et imitantur hunc sermonem politica consuetudo et philosophia de iusticia universali, ut Theognis quoque dicit: Iusticia in sese virtutes continet omnes.

Intelligendum est autem discrimen inter iusticiam legis et iusticiam fidei. Sed iusticia fidei est credere in hunc Christum filium Dei crucifixum et resuscitatum, non otiosum, sed regnantem, propter quem et per quem vere accipimus credentes remissionem peccatorum, reconciliationem, seu imputationem iusticiae, vivificationem, et donationem Spiritus sancti et vitae aeternae.

Haec enim comprehendit Paulus cum ait: Si confessus fueris hunc Iesum esse Dominum, id est regnantem, colligentem Ecclesiam, eë efficacem per vocem filii aeterni, si corde credes, quod Deus eum resuscitaverit, videlicet ideo, ut sit victor mortis, et nobis restituat iusticiam et vitam aeternam.

Et hac fide inquit hominem esse iustum, cum ait: Corde creditur ad iusticiam, id est, corde credens est iustus, habens remissionem peccatorum, et placens Deo propter mediatorem gratis.

Latro in cruce accipiens remissionem et reconciliationem est iustus, placet Deo et vivificatur, etiamsi nec antea fecit legem, neque postea, donec in corpore vixit, habet integram legis impletionem: etiamsi fuit incoatio obedientiae.

Ita posita antithesi definitionum Iusticiae legis et Iusticiae fidei, Paulus discrimen ostendit.

Omnis qui credit in eum, non confundetur.

Addit Paulus testimonium sumtum ex Esaiae Capite 28., ubi dulcissima promissio de Messia expresse repetita est: Ecce, ego ponam in Sion lapidem probatum, angularem, pretiosum in fundamento, qui credit in eo, non trepidabit.

Utitur metaphora simili in Psalmo: Lapidem quem reprobaverunt aedificantes, hic factus est in caput anguli.

Hanc metaphoram enarrat Paulus ad Ephes.

Item, cum inquit: Aliud fundamentum poni non potest, praeter id quod positum est, quod est Christus Iesus.

Hic gestat Ecclesiam merito et efficacia, hic redemit eam sua morte, et est mediator et intercessor pro nobis, offerens sua merita, et est efficax in Ecclesia, ipse adest ei, et vivificat eam voce Evangelii et Spiritu sancto.

Quomodo autem beneficia Messiae nobis applicentur, docet cum inquit: Qui credit in eum, non trepidabit.

Haec congruunt cum aliis multis similibus dictis, Psalmo 2.: Beati omnes qui confidunt in eo.

Et Paulus hic universalem particulam addit, sicut et in Psalmo posita est.

Saepe autem dixi, necessariam esse considerationem particulae Universalis, ut unusquisque se in promissionem universalem includat, nec fingat in Deo προσωποληψίαν, aut contradictorias voluntates, ac mox repetita est aliquoties Universalis, Dives in omnes quo invocant eum.

Et Dominus inquit: Venite ad me omnes etc.

Est autem mandatum aeternum, ut omnes credant in eum.

## 10:14
How shall they call on him in whom they have not believed?

In this gradation, a most copious doctrine is contained. The first member teaches that in invocation, faith and the contemplation of the divine promise are necessary. Here, the whole doctrine must be considered concerning invocation, and concerning the distinction between Christian and ethnic invocation.

For they address something that is not God, and they fashion various idols, just as Hecuba says in Euripides: O Jupiter, whoever you are, whether this heaven, or the mind in heaven, although I have long invoked idle helpers.

Afterward, concerning the will, they do not know whether or why they are heard, because the Gentiles are ignorant of the mediator and the promise: but the true Church of God thinks rightly about the Essence, because it addresses the true God, who revealed Himself by sending His Son, by giving the voice of the Gospel, and by providing illustrious testimonies. Then it knows the promises, and approaches God with the confidence of the mediator. Therefore it says: How shall they call on him in whom they have not believed?

Latin:

Quomodo invocabunt si non credent?

In hac gradatione copiosissima doctrina continetur. Primum membrum docet in invocatione necessariam esse fidem, et cogitationem promissionis divinae. Hic tota doctrina cogitanda est de invocatione, et de discrimine invocationis Christianae et ethnicae.

Errat enim ethnica praecipue dupliciter, de Essentia et de voluntate Dei. Alloquitur enim aliquid, quod non est Deus, et fingit varia idola, sicut ait Hecuba apud Euripidem: O Iupiter, quicquid es, sive hoc coelum, sive mens in coelo, quanquam diu iam ignavos opitulatores invoco.

Postea de voluntate nesciunt, An et cur exaudiantur, quia Ethnici ignorant mediatorem et promissionem: sed vera Ecclesia Dei recte cogitat de Essentia, quia alloquitur verum Deum, qui se patefecit misso filio, data voce Evangelii, et editis illustribus testimoniis. Deinde scit promissiones, et accedit ad Deum fiducia mediatoris. Ideo dicit: Quomodo invocabunt si non credent?

## 10:14
How shall they hear without a preacher?

This saying manifestly shows that Paul affirms this: that God, through the voice of the Gospel sounding in the ministry and contemplated by the hearer or reader, is efficacious, if faith is kindled, with God moving the heart through this very voice. Therefore, the error of Stenckfeld and similar Enthusiasts is to be condemned, because they lead men away from the voice of doctrine to speculations, which they call illuminations outside the written word, and they destroy the exercises of faith, because God wills that we contemplate this very word issued by the voice of Christ, the Prophets, and the Apostles, and He wills that we assent to this written word just as if we were hearing a new voice of God sounding from heaven. Therefore, Paul also says elsewhere: That through the consolation of the scriptures we might have hope. These exercises of faith must be learned in daily invocation, in which we feel our hearts resting in God, with our contemplation raised to the divine promises.

But since we know that the ministry of the Gospel is necessary, let us the more venerate and defend the ministers of the Gospel. Here, this also must be considered: since the knowledge of the written doctrine is necessary, it is certain that the labors of those learning and those teaching are pleasing to God. Wherefore, let us love the studies of doctrine more. Let us also add invocation, being reminded by doctrine, so that the Son of God, who is the λόγος (Word) of the eternal Father, may rule our judgments, and not allow us to wander from His word, and may kindle true light in our hearts.

Paul cites the most sweet saying of Isaiah from chapter 52: How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the Gospel of peace. He speaks also of the saying concerning the voice sounding in the ministry, and teaches that the Church is gathered in this way, namely, by the voice of the Gospel. The metaphor of the feet signifies the runner or messenger, and he says these are beautiful and lovely, because they bring the most joyful promise of grace and eternal life.

But these most sweet praises are opposed by the judgments of the enemies of the Gospel; they do not say the feet of the Apostles are beautiful, but they shout that the Apostles are the torches of dissension and the plagues of the human race.

But when Isaiah says that they bring the Gospel, and also peace and good things, he signifies that the kingdom of Christ is administered by the word, not by corporal arms, and he distinguishes this word from the law: The Law denounces wrath, but in the Gospel, peace and other good things are offered, that is, liberation from sins, from death, from the wrath of God, and the restitution of righteousness, eternal life, and eternal joy in God.

Latin:

Quomodo audient sine praedicante?

Hoc dictum manifeste ostendit, Paulum hoc affirmare, Deum per vocem Evangelii sonantem in ministerio cogitatam ab audiente, seu legente, efficacem esse, si accendi fidem, Deo per hanc ipsam vocem movente cor. Ideo damnandus est error Stenckfeldii et similium Enthusiastarum, qui abducunt homines a voce doctrinae ad speculationes, quas nominant illuminationes extra scriptum verbum, et delent exercitia fidei, quia vult Deus cogitare hoc ipsum verbum editum voce Christi, Prophetarum et Apostolorum, et huic scripto verbo sic nos vult assentiri, ac si audiremus novam vocem Dei de coelo sonantem. Ideo et alibi Paulus inquit: Ut per consolationem scripturarum spem habeamus. Haec exercitia fidei in quotidiana invocatione discenda sunt, in qua sentimus acquiescere corda in Deo, erecta cogitatione promissionum divinarum.

Cum autem sciamus ministerium Evangelii necessarium esse, magis veneremur et tueamur Evangelii ministros. Hic et hoc cogitandum est, Cum necessaria sit scriptae doctrinae cognitio, certum est labores discentium et docentium Deo placere, Quare magis amemus doctrinae studia. Adiungamus autem et invocationem, commonefacti a doctrina, ut filius Dei, qui est λόγος aeterni patris, regat iudicia, et non sinat nos aberrare a suo verbo, et accendat veram lucem in cordibus nostris.

Citat autem Paulus dulcissimum dictum Esaiae ex cap. 52.: Quam speciosi pedes Evangelizantium pacem. Loquitur et dictum de voce sonante in ministerio, et docet sic colligi Ecclesiam, scilicet voce Evangelii. Metaphora pedum significat cursorem seu nuncium, et hos ait formosos et amabiles esse, quia adferunt laetissimam promissionem gratiae et vitae aeternae.

Opponantur autem hae dulcissimae laudationes iudiciis inimicorum Evangelii, hi non aiunt pedes Apostolorum formosos esse, sed vociferantur Apostolas esse faces dissidiorum et pestes generis humani.

Cum autem Esaias inquit, afferre eos Evangelium, item pacem et bona, significat regnum Christi verbo administrari non armis corporalibus, et discernit hoc verbum a lege: Lex iram denunciat, sed in Evangelio offeruntur pax et alia bona, id est, liberatio a peccatis, a morte, ab ira Dei, et restitutio iusticiae, vitae aeternae et laetitiae aeternae in Deo.

## 11:1 Disposition of Romans: Argument
Chapter XI.

This is a correction, in which he mitigates those things which were said about the ruin of the Jews, and consoles them, lest they despair and think that all have been cast away.

Proposition. God has not cast away his people.

I. Argument from his own example. I am an Israelite, and yet I have believed; therefore, the people are not cast away.

II. Derived from the opinion of Elijah. Just as in the times of Elijah there were chosen remnants, that is, a small part of the people: so also at this time remnants will be snatched away and saved, that is, a small and lowly part of the people.

He adds, however, an amplification concerning the cause of election, that our merits are not the cause of election. And Paul made an enthymeme that is purely rhetorical. This is how they mostly call an argumentation which consists of disjunctives. If justification happens by merits, it is not by grace. If it happens by grace, it cannot happen by merits. But it is by grace, therefore we cannot earn it. He concludes, therefore, that the elect attain justification. He amplifies with an antithesis: The others, however, have been made blind, they have a spirit of compunction, that is, an angry and embittered mind. They hate the Gospel because they think that their own polity is being dissipated by the Gospel; they take it indignantly that their justice and wisdom are condemned by the Gospel, just as now those people bitterly hate us, who think that the opinion of their own wisdom and holiness is being detracted from.

Proposition repeated. Have they fallen in such a way that the whole nation is to perish? No.

And a reason is added from the final cause, They have fallen in some part, so that the Gentiles might be received to provoke the Jews: Therefore, they have not fallen for that reason, that this whole nation should be cast away.

The antecedent of the argument is cleverly inverted, so that from this another reason may be gathered, which shows that the Jews are not cast away. The fall of the Jews was not in itself the cause why he called the Gentiles. But rather the safety of the Jews was in itself the cause of the calling of the Gentiles: Therefore, the Jews are not cast away.

The antecedent is proven from the final cause of the calling of the Gentiles. The Gentiles were received so that they might provoke the Jews to believe in Christ: Therefore, there remain Jews who are to come to Christ. For what need would there be to provoke, if the whole people were cast away? Thus, from the word of provoking, which is in the testimony of Moses, he reasons that the rest are chosen among the people of the Jews.

But so that the inversion may be better understood, I will write down an example.

Need is not the cause of labor. Hope of sustenance is rather the cause of labor.

For a dialectician does not stop at privation, but seeks the ultimate cause, which it is fitting for a certain thing to be.

Thus, the fall of the Jews did not compel the Gentiles to be received. But the safety of the Jews compelled the Gentiles to be received, because, clearly, there were remnants chosen in this people. He therefore calls the fullness (πλήρωμα) the safety of the people, who are thus far safe, insofar as they have remnants chosen at whatever time. He calls the loss (ἥττημα) insofar as they have those to be damned.

He adds an apostrophe to the Gentiles: I say to you, etc. Here he amplifies the nearest argument with his own example. I also, he says, labor more at this, that I may draw the Gentiles to Christ, so that I may provoke the Jews by my example and that of the Gentiles. For when the Jews saw that the Gospel was effective among the Gentiles, they were compelled to acknowledge that this was the Christ whom the Apostles were preaching, especially since there were also prophecies extant about Christ, that the Gentiles would adhere to him. And he repeats the inversion... begun above. If their casting away were the reconciliation of the world, it would be just as if life were taken from death. For ironically he wishes to signify an absurdity, as if he were saying, It would be absurd to feel, that the rejection of the Jews had been profitable. It would be the same as if someone were to say that death is profitable. We will use our own example. It is absurd to say that poverty is profitable; it is more fitting that we say that the hope of managing a matter well is profitable. Thus, the fall of the Jews was not profitable in itself. Another cause must be sought, which was profitable, namely, the will to save the nation.

IV. Argument, from the promises pertaining to the nation.

The firstfruits are holy, therefore the lump is holy. The root is holy, therefore the branches are holy, that is, the promise was made to the fathers, therefore it pertains to their posterity.

There follows an exhortation to the Gentiles, not to despise the Jews, nor to think that the Gentiles are preferred because they were better than the Jews, or to arrogate to themselves any praise of merit. The proposition has an antithesis. Do not be proud, but fear. The reason is from the greater. If God did not spare the Jews, who were the peculiar people of God, much less will He spare you, if you have cast away the fear of Him.

He inserts by the way a prophecy, by which he proves that the Jews are not rejected, because there are remnants in that people who are elect, who will eventually believe in Christ, while the Gospel is preached among the Gentiles. And he confirms by the testimony of Isaiah that the remnants are elect. Christ will take away the sins of Jacob, therefore it is necessary that some of the descendants of Jacob be converted to Christ.

Conclusion. The Jews are enemies, as far as the present state is concerned, so that through that occasion the Gentiles might be called. But they are friends according to election. The reason is that the gifts of God and the promises of God are not changed. But the Jews have the promises, therefore they have also the elect.

Epiphonema. God has concluded all in unbelief, that He might have mercy on all. In this epiphonema he gathers that the causes of the Jews and the Gentiles are equal, so that He might take away from both the glory of merit.

Moreover, a most abundant consolation is proposed in this sentence. When we discern sin, we interpret it as a sign of wrath and damnation. When David considers his adultery, he judges himself to have fallen, because he is rejected by God. But Paul changes this meaning of sin. Sin admonishes of mercy. Therefore David fell, not because he was rejected, but so that the glory of the mercy of God might become more illustrious, and that he might not attribute honor to merits.

This sentence has almost a similar use to that one: I live, I do not desire the death of the sinner. Where God testifies by an oath that He wills to forgive. But it is necessary that we believe God, and indeed Him swearing. Thus in this sentence mercy is promised to all. And lest sin should deter anyone, he signifies that this pertains to the glory of mercy, not to wrath, because we have been concluded under sin, if however we believe in Christ.

Finally, an exclamation, or rather an admiration, is added.

For the Apostle admires the counsel of God, that He calls to the Gospel a small part of men, that He calls those who do not excel in talents or wisdom. But he forbids searching into the causes, and commands to yield to the wisdom of God, and takes away honor from merits.

Thus far the doctrine concerning justification has been delivered and the proposition agitated, that we are justified by faith, not by our works. But let the reader remember that this is the chief place of the Gospel, without which it cannot be understood why Christ came. For He came not to bring the law, so that we might merit righteousness by certain works, but so that He might freely grant righteousness and the Holy Spirit to those who believe. And this doctrine concerning justification ought properly to be called the Gospel, and prudently discerned from the law. And because this place is nowhere as well illustrated as in this Epistle, effort must be given so that we make it as familiar to us as possible.

Furthermore, as an architect is accustomed to embrace the form of the whole building in his mind, so we ought to include the idea of the whole writing in our mind, so that we may thoroughly perceive the Apostle's sentiment. For that matter, it will contribute much in so long a disputation to know the series of all the parts and sentiments, wherefore I hope this my labor will be profitable to studious youths.

But we must always look into this Epistle: we must always have this sentiment placed before our eyes, that we are justified by faith in Christ before the Father. For the conscience will not be able to be at peace unless it holds this sentiment. As often as we pray, we must first look into this Epistle, so that we may lift ourselves up and know that we are heard, if we believe in Christ not because of our merits.

For unless we look to this, our sins deter us, so that we dare not expect anything from God.

Formerly this Epistle was read in such a way that that long preceding disputation was thought to pertain nothing to our times: but it was said to have been written because of the quarrels of those times concerning the ceremonies of the Jews. But let us know that, just as the Gospel pertains to all ages, so this Epistle pertains to all ages, which explains the chief place of the Gospel.

It is, however, the custom of Paul here, that at the beginning he delivers the doctrine of justification, which happens through faith. Afterwards he adds precepts concerning morals. For although works do not justify, yet since we live in the body, this life cannot be passed without works, and faith ought to exercise itself so as to show itself in the cross and good works.

There follows, therefore, as it were a new book, containing law more than Gospel. And because the doctrine of the law is not unknown to human reason, therefore many sentences are found in Hesiod, Phocylides, and others, similar to those which are in Paul.

Nor should it be thought for that reason that there is no difference between Christ's doctrine and philosophy. For philosophy can deliver law or precepts concerning morals in some part. But human reason does not know at all the Gospel, that we are justified freely before God, when we believe that we are received into grace by the Father on account of Christ.

But what the law effects, has been said above. And yet when the Apostles deliver precepts concerning morals, they deliver them far differently than the Philosophers. For they sprinkle many sentences about the will of God, and about the benefits of Christ. To these they teach that in these snares of the devil, we cannot govern our morals, unless we are governed by the spirit of Christ and resist the devil by faith.

Latin:

Caput XI.

Correctio est, in qua mitigat ea, quae de ruina Iudaeorum dicta sunt, et consolatur, ne desperent, ac putent omnes abiectos esse.

Propositio. Non abiecit Deus populum suum.

I. Ratio ab exemplo proprio. Ego sum Israëli-ta, et tamen credidi, Ergo non est abiectus populus.

II. Ex sententia Eliae ducta. Sicut Eliae temporibus reliquiae electae erant, hoc est, exigua pars populi: sic et hoc tempore reliquiae eripientur ac salvabuntur, hoc est, exigua et infima pars populi.

Addit autem amplificationem de causa electionis, quod merita nostra non sint electionis causa. Et fecit Paulus enthymema prorsus rhetoricum. Sic maxime vocant argumentationem, quae constat ex disiunctivis. Si contingit iustificatio meritis, non est gratia. Si contingit per gratiam, non potest contingere meritis. Sed est gratia, Ergo non possumus mereri. Concludit igitur electos consequi iustificationem. Amplificat antithesi, Caeteri autem sunt caeci facti, habent spiritum compunctionis, id est, iratum et exacerbatum animum. Oderunt Evangelium, quia arbitrantur Evangelio dissipari ipsorum politiam, indigne ferunt ab Evangelio iusticiam et sapientiam eorum damnari, sicut nunc acerbe oderunt nos isti, qui sibi sapientiae et sanctitatis opinionem detrahi putant.

Propositio repetitur. Num ita lapsi sunt, ut tota gens sit peritura? Non.

Et additur ratio ex causa finali, Lapsi sunt aliqua ex parte, ut reciperentur gentes ad provocandos Iudaeos: Ergo non sunt ideo lapsi, ut haec tota gens abiiceretur.

Antecedens argumenti callide invertitur, ut hinc alia ratio colligatur, quae ostendat Iudaeos non esse abiectos. Lapsus Iudaeorum non fuit per se causa, cur vocarent gentes. Sed magis incolumitas Iudaeorum fuit per se causa vocationis gentium: Ergo Iudaei non sunt abiecti.

Antecedens probatur ex causa finali vocationis gentium. Gentes receptae sunt, ut provocent Iudaeos ad credendum christo: Ergo restant Iudaei venturi ad Christum. Quid enim opus esset provocare, si totus populus abiectus esset? Ita ex verbo provocandi, quod est in testimonio Mosi, ratiocinatur reliquos esse electos in populo Iudaeorum.

Sed ut inversio melius intelligi possit, ascribam exemplum.

Inopia non est causa laboris. Spes victus magis est causa laboris.

Dialecticus enim non resistit in privatione, sed quaerit ultimam causam, quam convenit certam rem esse.

Sic lapsus Iudaeorum non coëgit, ut gentes reciperentur. Sed incolumitas Iudaeorum coëgit, ut gentes reciperentur, quod videlicet reliqui erant in hoc populo electi. Vocat igitur πλήρωμα incolumitatem populi, qui eatenus est incolumis adhuc, quatenus reliquos habet electos quocunque tempore. Vocat ἥττημα quatenus habet damnandos.

Addit ἀποστροφὴν ad gentes: Vobis dico etc. Hic proximum argumentum amplificat suo exemplo. Ego etiam, inquit, hoc magis laboro, ut gentes ad Christum pertraham, ut provocem et meo et gentium exemplo Iudaeos. Nam cum videbant Iudaei Evangelium inter gentes efficax esse, cogebantur agnoscere, hunc esse Christum, quem Apostoli praedicabant, praesertim cum de Christo etiam extarent prophetiae, quod gentes ei adhaesurae essent. Et repetit inversionem supra incoatam. Si abiectio eorum esset reconciliatio mundi, id perinde esset, ac si vita ex morte sumeretur. Nam εἰρωνικῶς absurditatem vult significare, quasi dicat, Absurdum esset sentire, quod abiectio Iudaeorum profuisset. Id perinde esset, ac si quis diceret, mortem prodesse. Nos utemur nostro exemplo. Absurdum est dicere, inopiam prodesse, magis convenit ut dicamus, spem rei bene gerendae prodesse. Ita Iudaeorum casus non profuit per se. Alia causa quaerenda est, quae profuerit, videlicet voluntas servandae gentis.

IV. Argumentum, ex promissionibus ad gentem pertinentibus.

Primitiae sunt sanctae, Igitur et massa sancta est. Radix est sancta, Igitur et rami sunt sanctae, id est, promissio patribus facta est, Igitur ad eorum posteritatem pertinet.

Sequitur adhortatio ad gentes, ne contemnant Iudaeos, neve putent gentes praelatas esse, quia meliores fuerint Iudaeis, aut arrogent sibi aliquam meriti laudem. Propositio habet antithesin. Ne sis superbus, sed time. Ratio ex maiore. Si non pepercit Deus Iudaeis, qui erant peculiaris populus Dei, multo minus tibi parcet, si abieceris timorem ipsius.

Inserit obiter vaticinium, quo probat non esse abiectos Iudaeos, quia sint reliqui in eo populo electi, qui subinde sint credituri in Christum, dum Evangelium inter gentes praedicatur. Et confirmat Esaiae testimonio, quod reliqui sint electi. Christus delebit peccata Iacob, Ergo necesse est aliquos posteros Iacob converti ad Christum.

Conclusio. Iudaei sunt inimici, quod ad praesentem statum attinet, ut per eam occasionem gentes vocentur. At sunt amici secundum electionem. Ratio, quia dona Dei et promissiones Dei non mutantur. At Iudaei habent promissiones, habent igitur et electos.

Epiphonema. Conclusit Deus omnes in incredulitatem, ut omnium misereatur. In hoc epiphonemate colligit pares esse causas Iudaeorum et gentium, ut utrisque adimat gloriam meriti.

Caeterum uberrima consolatio proponitur in hac sententia. Cum cernimus peccatum, interpretamur signum irae ac damnationis esse. David cum considerat adulterium suum, iudicat se lapsum esse, quia sit abiectus a Deo. At Paulus mutat hanc peccati significationem. Peccatum admonet misericordiae. Ideo lapsus est David, non quia abiectus erat, sed ut gloria misericordiae Dei fieret illustrior, neve tribueret honorem meritis.

Propemodum habet similem usum haec sententia, ut illa: Vivo ego, nolo mortem peccatoris. Ubi iureiurando testatur Deus, se velle ignoscere. Necesse est autem, ut Deo, et quidem iuranti, credamus. Ita in hac sententia promittitur omnibus misericordia. Et ne quem absterreret peccatum, significat hoc ad gloriam misericordiae pertinere, non ad iram, quod sub peccatum conclusi sumus, si tamen Christo credimus.

Postremo adiecta est exclamatio, seu potius admiratio.

Nam Apostolus miratur Dei consilium, quod exiguam partem hominum, quod hos qui non praestant ingeniis aut sapientia ad Evangelium vocat. Vetat autem scrutari causas, et iubet cedere sapientiae Dei, ac detrahit honorem meritis.

Hactenus doctrina de iustificatione tradita est et agitata propositio, quod iustificemur fide, non operibus nostris. Meminerit autem lector hunc esse praecipuum Evangelii locum, sine quo intelligi non potest, cur venerit Christus. Venit enim non ut legem ferret, ut certis operibus iusticiam mereremur, sed ut donaret gratis iusticiam et Spiritum sanctum credentibus. Et Evangelium proprie vocari debet, haec de iustificatione doctrina, et prudenter a lege discerni. Et quia hic locus nusquam perinde illustratus, ut in hac Epistola danda est opera, ut eam nobis quam familiarissimam faciamus.

Porro ut architectus totius formam aedificii in animo complecti solet, ita nos totius scripti tanquam ideam, quandam in animum includere debemus, ut Apostoli sententiam penitus perspiciamus. Ad eam rem multum conducet in tam longa disputatione nosse seriem omnium partium ac sententiarum, quare spero hanc meam operam studiosis iuvenibus profuturam esse.

Semper autem in hanc Epistolam intueri nos oportet: semper oportet habere positam ob oculos hanc sententiam, quod fide in Christum iustificemur coram patre. Non enim poterit conscientia pacata esse, nisi teneat hanc sententiam. Quoties orabimus, primum in hanc Epistolam intuendum est, ut erigamus nos ac sciamus nos exaudiri, si credimus in Christum non propter merita nostra.

Nam nisi huc respicimus, absterrent nos peccata nostra, ut neque expectare quidquam a Deo audeamus.

Olim ita legebatur haec Epistola, ut illa tam longa disputatio superior nihil ad nostra tempora pertinere putaretur: sed dicebatur esse scripta propter rixas illorum temporum de Iudaeorum ceremoniis. Nos vero sciamus, ut Evangelium ad omnes aetates pertinet, ita hanc Epistolam ad omnes aetates pertinere, quae praecipuum Evangelii locum explicat.

Est autem hic mos Paulo, ut initio tradat doctrinam iustificationis, quae contigit per fidem. Postea subiiciat praecepta de moribus. Quanquam enim non iustificant opera, tamen quoniam in corpore degimus, sine operibus haec vita transigi non potest, et fides debet se exercere ut ostendere in cruce et bonis operibus.

Sequitur igitur tanquam novus liber, continens legem magis, quam Evangelium. Et quia legis doctrina non ignota est humanae rationi, ideo multae sententiae reperiuntur in Hesiodo, Phocylide et aliis, similes his quae sunt apud Paulum.

Neque ideo putandum est nihil interesse inter Christi doctrinam et philosophiam. Legem enim seu praecepta de moribus potest philosophia aliqua ex parte tradere. At Evangelium prorsus non novit humana ratio, quod gratis coram Deo iustificemur, cum credimus nos in gratiam a patre propter Christum recipi.

Quid autem efficiat lex, supra dictum est. Et tamen Apostoli cum tradunt praecepta de moribus, longe aliter tradunt, quam Philosophi. Multas enim sententias aspergunt de voluntate Dei, et de Christi beneficiis. Ad haec docent in his insidiis diaboli, non posse nos mores regere, nisi spiritu Christi gubernemur et fide resistamus diabolo.

## 11:1 Argument
Chapter XI.

At the beginning, he mitigates the complaint raised above concerning the defection of the Jews. For although the polity is destroyed, as Daniel predicted, and they cease to be a people: yet the promise of the Gospel still pertains to the Israelites, which is offered to all nations, according to the saying: In thy seed shall all nations be blessed. Many Israelites, therefore, will still acknowledge the true Messiah, and will receive His benefits.

And first, he argues from his own example: I am an Israelite, and I acknowledge this true Messiah, and I have been gifted with His benefits of the remission of sins, and with vivification, when I felt myself liberated from the wrath of God, and I have become an heir of eternal life, and I have the earnest of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, the promise still pertains to the Israelites, but this hinders many, because they do not understand the promise of the Messiah concerning eternal goods, and they bear it ill that the polity is destroyed and the righteousness of the law is diminished. Just as now the papists fret that their authority, power, and status are being undermined. He describes this bitterness of hatreds and this fretting when he says: God has given them the spirit of compunction, that is, sorrow mixed with most bitter hatred, just as Saul grieves and burns with hatred for David.

XI. First, it is necessary here to consider diligently the distinction between the Mosaic polity and the promises concerning the Messiah, by which the eternal Church is gathered.

Let the causes also be considered, why the Jewish polity was destroyed.

First, that God might show His wrath against the enemies of Christ.

Second, that He might show that the promises of the Messiah are to be understood as concerning eternal goods.

Third, that He might show that the works of the law are not righteousness.

Fourth, that the prerogative of the Israelite nation might be taken away.

Fifth, that the destruction of that polity might testify that the Messiah had appeared, because it was expressly predicted that the Messiah would preach in the second temple, and would come while that polity was standing.

Paul therefore distinguishes in this place the polity from the collection of the Church, and affirms that the promise concerning the Messiah still pertains to the Israelites, even if the kingdom is destroyed. Here, therefore, amidst the ruins of kingdoms, it is necessary to know that the Church of God will nevertheless remain, just as the Lord Himself says, that the destructions of kingdoms are to come, but that in the meantime He will preserve the Church, as He says: Behold, I am with you even unto the consummation of the age.

Item: Those days shall be shortened for the sake of the elect.

Item: It shall be as in the days of Noah, one shall be taken, and the other left, etc.

And in Isaiah 59, He affirms that the Church will always remain: This is my covenant with them, says the Lord, My Spirit, which is in you, and my words, which I have put in your mouth, shall not depart from your mouth, nor from the mouth of your seed from henceforth and forever.

Item: Do this until I come.

Secondly, it is necessary also to consider what and where the Church is, namely, this multitude is the Church, even if it is in different empires, which embraces the incorrupt doctrine of the Gospel, according to the saying: My sheep hear my voice. Item: Father, sanctify them in truth, your word is truth.

Thirdly, consolation must also be held. For when we look at impious kingdoms, their power and great victories, and the multitude of the impious, minds are troubled, so that they dispute whether all things happen by chance, or whether those who flourish most in power and excel the rest are more pleasing to God.

Against these spectacles, God warns us, and affirms that the Church is small, and that it is only that which embraces the incorrupt doctrine of the Gospel, even if another part of the human race excels in power and multitude, etc.

He wants us not to depart from the word of God, moved by the multitude or power of others: therefore it is said in Isaiah 1: Unless the Lord had left us a seed, we would have been made as Sodom.

Isaiah 34: As when a few grapes remain in the gleaning, so shall they be in the land, lifting up their voice and praising the Lord.

Isaiah 65: As in a sterile vintage, where a grape shall have been found, it shall be said, The blessing of the Lord.

And Christ says: Many are called, few are chosen. And yet these few are many, as is signified in this place from the saying to Elijah: I have left for myself seven thousand, which have not bowed the knee to Baal.

This necessary doctrine is contained in the beginning of this chapter, namely, concerning the distinction of the polity, and the promise of eternal goods, and concerning the Church, what and of what kind it is.

Have they so stumbled that they should fall?

The proposition established above is repeated: The Jews have not so stumbled that in the whole nation there is no one to be saved. The reasoning is shrewdly thought out, nor is the meaning obscure, for the argument is taken from the final cause, in this way: The Gentiles were received, so that the Jews might be provoked to believe, when they see the Gospel to be effective among the Gentiles, as it is written in Moses: I will provoke you not by a nation. Therefore, it is necessary that there be some remaining among the Jews who are to believe: for why would there be a need for the Jews to be provoked, if none were to believe? The consequence follows thus: Your ruin profited the Gentiles, but not simply ruin, but much more your fullness, that is, the part that is safe and about to believe, which was to be provoked by the example of the Gentiles: therefore there are some remaining among the Jews to be converted. This remaining part he calls the Fullness, that is, the complement of the entire Church to be converted from the seed of Abraham.

Let us be content with this simplest explanation, and I leave the long disputes of others in this place to the consideration and judgment of the elders.

And so afterwards an amplification is added: If the rejection of the Jews profited, how glorious will be the restoration, which is to be as it were a resurrection from the dead. tution, which is to be a future resurrection, as it were, from the dead.

He signifies, therefore, that the greater remaining part was rejected because it was bewitched by the persuasion that they were the people of God and the Church, on account of their lineage, law, ceremonies, and merit: nor did they understand the Church to be anything other than this Jewish polity.

But now these, who are received, will learn that the polity is one thing, the Church another, the promise of bodily goods one thing, the promise of grace and eternal life another.

They will learn that for the whole Church, Gentiles and Jews, as if they were dead, righteousness and eternal life are rendered on account of the Messiah, and through him, not on account of the law or the merits of men.

Concerning these great matters, Paul preaches here; it is necessary that this doctrine always be in sight: that the Church of God is one thing, and polities, or the kingdoms of the world, whether Jewish or pontifical, are another: because the Son of God, who is the head of the Church, gathers it by the voice of the Gospel everywhere from diverse empires, and sanctifies it with his holy Spirit, and begins in them eternal righteousness and life in the heart.

Meanwhile, in this life, in civil custom, he allows his members to use the laws of the empires in which they live, which are congruent with reason, just as he allows them to use the different spaces of days and nights, etc.

And indeed, the true gathering of the Church happens in such a way, as a restoration of life from death, that is, All are under sin and guilty of the wrath of God, and they do not become heirs of eternal life on account of the law or their own merits, but freely on account of the Son through faith.

This doctrine and consolation is repeated in these words, in which he dwells afterwards, and at the end adds an epiphonema: He has concluded all under sin, that he might have mercy on all, as if he were saying: He argues for sin, not that he might destroy, but that, with sin acknowledged, we might believe in the promise and acknowledge the Son, just as it is said in the oath: As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he might be converted and live.

Latin:

Caput XI.

Initio mitigat querelam supra positam de defectione Iudaeorum. Quanquam enim politia destruitur, sisut praedixit Daniel, desinet esse populus: tamen promissio Evangelii adhuc ad Israëlitas pertinet, quae omnibus gentibus offertur, iuxta dictum: In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes. Multi igitur Israëlitae adhuc agnoscent verum Messiam, et beneficia eius accipient.

Ac primum a suo exemplo argumentatur: Ego sum Israëlita, et agnosco hunc verum Messiam, et donatus sum eius beneficiis remissione peccatorum, et vivificatione, cum sensi me liberari ab ira Dei, et factus sum haeres vitae aeternae, et habeo arrabonem Spiritum sanctum.

Ergo adhuc ad Israëlitas promissio pertinet, sed hoc multos impedit, quod non intelligunt promisionem Messiae de bonis aeternis, et aegre ferunt politiam destrui, et extenuari iusticiam legis. Sicut nunc fremunt pontificii suam autoritatem, potentiam et statum labefactari. Hanc acerbitatem odiorum, et hunc fremitum describit, cum inquit: Dedit eis spiritum compunctionis, id est, dolorem mixtum acerbissimo odio, sicut dolet Saul et ardet odio Davidis.

CAP. XI. Primum autem hic necesse est diligenter considerare discrimen inter politiam Mosaicam et promissiones de Messia, quibus aeterna Ecclesia colligitur.

Causae etiam considerentur, cur deleta sit politia Iudaica.

Prima, ut Deus ostenderet iram adversus hostes Christi.

Secunda, ut ostenderet promissiones Messiae intelligendas esse de bonis aeternis.

Tertia, ut ostenderet opera legis non esse iusticiam.

Quarta, ut praerogativa gentis Israëliticae tolleretur.

Quinta, ut deletio eius politiae testetur apparuisse Messiam, quia expressa praedictum fuit Messiam in secundo templo concionaturum esse, et venturum stante illa politia.

Discernit igitur Paulus hoc loco politiam a collectione Ecclesiae, et adfirmat promissionem de Messia adhuc pertinere ad Israëlitas, etiam si regnum deletum est. Hic igitur inter ruinas regnorum necesse est scire, tamen Ecclesiam Dei mansuram esse, sicut Dominus ipse inquit, venturas esse regnorum destructiones, sed interea se Ecclesiam servaturum esse, sicut inquit: Ecce ego vobiscum sum usque ad consummationem seculi.

Item: Isti dies abbreviabuntur propter electos.

Item: Erit sicut in diebus Noae, unus assumetur, et alter relinquetur etc.

Et Esaiae 59. affirmat semper mansuram esse Ecclesiam: Hoc est foedus meum cum eis, dicit Dominus, Spiritus meus, qui est in te, et verba mea, quae posui in ore tuo, non recedent ab ore tuo, et de ore seminis tui deinceps et usque in sempiternum.

Item: Hoc facite-donec veniam.

Secundo, necesse est etiam cogitare quae sit et ubi sit Ecclesia, videlicet, haec multitudo est Ecclesia, etiam si est in dissimilibus imperiis, quae amplectitur incorruptam doctrinam Evangelii, iuxta dictum: Oves meae vocem meam audiunt. Item: Pater sanctifica eos in veritate, sermo tuus est veritas.

Tertio, tenenda est etiam consolatio. Cum enim aspicimus regna impia potentiam ac magnas victorias eorum, et multitudinem impiorum, turbantur animi, ut disputent, an casu omnia fiant, aut an illi potius Deo placeant, qui maxime florent potentia et antecellunt caeteris.

Contra haec spectacula praemonet nos Deus, et affirmat Ecclesiam exiguam esse, et eam tantum esse, quae incorruptam doctrinam Evangelii amplectitur, etiam si alia pars generis humani antecellit potentia et multitudine etc.
