Vult nos non discedere a verbo Dei motos seu multitudine seu potentia aliorum: ideo Esaia 1. dicitur: Nisi Dominus reliquisset nobis semen, sicut Sodoma facti essemus.

Esaiae 34.: Ut cum paucae uvae reliquae sunt in racematione, sic erunt in terra levantes vocem et laudantes Dominum.

Esaiae 65.: Ut in sterili vindemia, ubi inventa fuerit uva, dicetur, Benedictio Domini.

Et Christus inquit: Multi vocati, pauci electi. Et tamen hi pauci multi sunt, sicut hoc loco significatur ex dicto ad Eliam: Reliqui mihi septem millia, quae non adoraverunt Baal.

Haec necessaria doctrina in principio huius capitis continentur, scilicet de discrimine politiae, et promissionis de bonis aeternis, et de Ecclesia, quae et qualis sit.

Num ita impegerunt, ut caderent?

Propositio supra instituta repetitur: Non sic impegerunt Iudaei, ut in tota gente nemo sit salvandus. Ratio argute cogitata est, nec est obscura sententia, sumtum est enim argumentum ex causa finali, hoc modo: Gentes receptae sunt, ut Iudaei provocentur ad credendum, cum videbunt Evangelium in Gentibus efficax esse, sicut in Mose scriptum est: Provocabo vos non in gente. Igitur necesse est aliquos esse reliquos inter Iudaeos, qui credituri sunt: quorsum enim opus esse provocari Iudaeos, si nulli credituri essent? Consequens sic attexit: Ruina vestra profuit gentibus, sed non simpliciter ruina, Verum multo magis plenitudo vestra, id est, pars incolumis creditura, quae provocanda fuit gentium exemplo: sunt ergo reliqui inter Iudaeos convertendi. Hanc reliquam partem nominat Plenitudinem, id est, complementum integrae Ecclesiae convertendae ex semine Abrahae.

Hac simplicissima explicatione contenti simus, et longas aliorum disputationes hoc loco relinquo considerationi et indicio seniorum.

Sic et postea amplificatio additur: Si abiectio Iudaeorum profuit, quam gloriosa erit restitutio, quae est futura quasi resurrectio ex mortuis. tutionem, quae est futura quasi resurrectio ex mortuis.

Significat autem ideo reliquam maiorem partem reiectam esse, quia fuit fascinata persuasione, se esse populum Dei et Ecclesiam, propter genus, legem, ceremonias, et meritum: nec aliud intellexerunt esse Ecclesiam, nisi hanc politiam Judaicam.

Nunc vero hi, qui recipiuntur, discent, aliud esse politiam, aliud Ecclesiam, aliud promissionem bonorum corporalium, aliud promissionem gratiae et vitae aeternae.

Discent toti Ecclesiae, Gentibus et Judaeis, velut mortuis, reddi iusticiam et vitam aeternam propter Messiam, et per eum non propter legem aut merita hominum.

De his tantis rebus hic concionatur Paulus, semper in conspectu esse oportet hanc doctrinam, aliud esse Ecclesiam Dei, aliud politias, seu regna mundi, sive Judaicum, sive pontificium: quia filius Dei, qui est caput Ecclesiae, colligit eam voce Evangelii passim ex diversis imperiis, et sanctificat eam Spiritu suo sancto, incoat in eis aeternam iusticiam et vitam in corde.

Interea in hac vita in civili consuetudine sinit sua membra uti legibus imperiorum, in quibus vivunt, congruentibus cum ratione, sicut sinit eos uti dissimilibus spatiis dierum et noctium etc.

Et quidem vera collectio Ecclesiae sic fit, ut restitutio vitae ex morte, id est, Omnes sunt sub peccato et rei irae Dei, nec propter legem aut merita propria fiunt haeredes vitae aeternae, sed gratis propter filium fide.

Haec doctrina et consolatio in his verbis repetita est, in qua postea commoratur, et in fine addit epiphonema: Conclusit omnes sub peccatum, ut omnium misereatur, quasi dicat: Arguit peccatum, non ut perdat, sed ut agnito peccato credamus promissioni, et agnoscamus filium, sicut in iuramento dicitur: Vivo ego, dicit Dominus, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed ut convertatur et vivat.

## 11:25
I do not want you to be ignorant, etc.

Paul prophesies concerning the ruin of the Church of the Gentiles.

The outcome shows this.

Immediately after the disciples of the Apostles, horrible sects arose, and as greater lacerations gradually occurred, Mahomet found the minds of many prepared for a kind of doctrine that was plausible and political, by which the Gospel is utterly destroyed.

Thus, in all of Africa and in a great part of Asia, the Churches were utterly destroyed.

And in Europe, the Papacy established manifold idolatry, invocations of dead men, the profanation of the Lord's Supper in the Mass, and in the carrying about [of the host].

Likewise, satisfactions and Monasticism.

Likewise, it extinguished the doctrine concerning the offices of the persons of the Divinity, and concerning justification.

And now the Pontiffs openly exercise cruelty against those who embrace the purity of the Gospel.

Paul predicts this desertion in the greatest part of the human race here, and yet, among these ruins, God preserves some remnants, lest the whole human race be born in vain and only for destruction.

Let us consider these things, and let us look around with greater care as to what and where the Church is, and let us join ourselves to it.

Paul also adds a prophecy concerning the conversion of the Jews, which I understand in this way: that it will be the case that, from time to time until the end of the world, some from among the Jews will be converted.

He preaches the saying of Isaiah concerning the advent of the Messiah.

When he was born of a virgin, then he taught openly, gave testimonies, was made a victim, rose again, sent the Holy Spirit, and began the preaching of the Gospel.

But let the whole discourse of Isaiah in chapter 59 be noted, because it contains the sweetest doctrine concerning the benefits of Christ and concerning the Church; he shows what the true Church is, and affirms that there will always be some: The redeemer will come from Zion, where the emphasis of the word should be noted: he is a Redeemer, who, having given a price, frees another.

And he will turn away iniquities from Jacob: therefore Christ is sent, that he might truly blot out the sins of all who believe in him.

And let the entire benefit be considered; he restored life and eternal righteousness, just as Daniel also speaks.

Then Isaiah adds a discourse there concerning the Church: This is my covenant with them, says the Lord, my spirit, which is in you, and my words, which I have put in your mouth, shall not depart from your mouth, and from the mouth of your seed, now and forever, that is, this is the true Church, in which the word given to Isaiah concerning the redeemer taking away sin sounds, and in it, believers are certainly sanctified by the Holy Spirit.

He affirms that such a Church will always remain, although at times it is more, at times less frequent: and because the light of doctrine often becomes more obscure, the Son of God from time to time restores it, just as the Moon at different times receives light from the Sun in different ways.

Let this description of the Church in Isaiah be most well-known to all.

God has concluded all under sin, that He might have mercy on all.

This is an epiphonema, in which is placed the equalization of the Gentiles and the Jews, and the confidence in the merits of Christ is taken away. He exhorts all to repentance, then equally proposes consolation to all who perform repentance. And it is a most welcome doctrine in both members.

For to be concluded under sin is not to be understood idly, but it embraces guilt, dread, judgment, and the punishments of sin, as if he were saying: All are guilty, all will be subject to the judgment of God, to death and afflictions, just as David was concluded under sin when he was driven into exile, when he was tormented with horrible pains, according to the saying: God is a consuming fire. He argues, however, for sin, not so that men may be left in sin and destruction, but so that they may be liberated through the Son.

Here, therefore, consolation is immediately added: That He might have mercy on all. Gratuitous reconciliation is promised, which is to be opposed to the temptation concerning merit, or concerning dignity: and the promise is universal; let us oppose this universal particle to the temptation concerning particularity, and let us not be troubled by the disputations of the Stoics and Manichaeans; let us know that the Son of God Himself brings forth this universal promise (Come to me all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you) from the bosom of the eternal Father; let us not imagine contradictory wills in God, but let us believe the Son of God sent for this very purpose, that you may be a messenger, a witness, a pledge, and a sealer of the divine promise, just as He says: So God loved the world, that everyone who believes in Him should not perish.

O the depth of the riches.

An exclamation is added, by which he breaks off the disputation, because although God is equal, and immediately at the beginning issued the promise concerning the Mediator, and willed it to be known to all posterity, and for all posterity to remain in the true knowledge and invocation of God, and most often repeated the voice of the promise, and again gathered the Church: yet after a huge multitude had subsequently forgotten the promise, and horrible furies followed. Human reason asks many things: why such a great multitude in all ages perishes, why so few are saved: Why the Church is a dissipated and oppressed assembly, without a certain empire and without beautiful order: Why the impious multitude excels in empires, glory, wealth, and many excellent virtues, wisdom, and fortitude: why it is permitted for the devils to rage with such madness against this weak human nature. These and many other things exercise human thoughts, but Paul in this exclamation signifies that not all the counsels of God can be comprehended by human reasonings, but that the revealed word of God is to be embraced, and one must not fall away from it, and these huge benefits which He offers are to be received and retained with free minds, and His goodness and the justice of God are to be celebrated.

Afterwards, in that eternal school, we shall learn the causes of the divine counsels, just as it has been most often commanded: Your word is a lamp to my feet. Item: To the law and to the testimony, if they do not speak according to this word: There will be no morning light for them. Item: This is my beloved Son, hear him. Let us obey these precepts, and let us not allow our minds to wander with curiosity, which, entangled in the labyrinths of disputations, are oppressed by doubt, which plunges innumerable people into eternal destruction, just as Julian and many others perished.

Let us also understand the snares of the devils, who impel curious minds to move empty disputations. Against these, let us fortify ourselves with both doctrine and the invocation of God, just as the Prophet cries out: Deal with your servant according to your mercy, and teach me your justifications. Item: Pray, that you may not enter into temptation. And certainly there ought to be a limit to disputations, just as Paul commands: Let us not be wise beyond what it is proper to be wise, but let us be wise in such a way that we modestly remain within the rule which God has handed down.

Latin:

Nolo vos ignorare etc.

Vaticinatur Paulus de ruina Ecclesiae gentium.

Id eventus ostendit.

Statim post discipulos Apostolorum exortae sunt horribiles sectae, et cum paulatim dilacerationes maiores fierent, invenit Mahometus praeparatos multorum animos ad genus doctrinae plausibile et politicum, quo prorsus deletur Evangelium.

Ita in tota Aphrica et in magna parte Asiae prorsus Ecclesiae deletae sunt.

Et in Europa Papatus constituit multiplicem idolatriam, invocationes hominum mortuorum, profanationem coenae Domini in Missa, et in circumgestatione.

Item, satisfactiones et Monachatus.

Item, extinxit doctrinam de officiis personarum Divinitatis, et de iustificatione.

Et nunc palam exercent Pontifices saevitiam in eos, qui puritatem Evangelii amplectuntur.

Hanc desertionem in maxima parte generis humani praedicit hic Paulus, et tamen inter has ruinas servat Deus reliquias aliquas, ne totum genus humanum frustra et tantum ad exitium nascatur.

Haec consideremus, et maiore cura circumspiciamus, quae et ubi sit Ecclesia, et nos ad eam adiungamus.

Addit etiam Paulus vaticinium de conversione Iudaeorum, quod sic intelligo, futurum esse, ut subinde usque ad finem mundi aliqui ex Iudaeis convertantur.

Essaiae dictum concionatur de adventu Messiae.

Cum ex virgine natus est, tunc palam docuit, edidit testimonia, factus est victima, resurrexit, misit Spiritum sanctum, et incoavit Evangelii praedicationem.

Nota sit autem tota concio Esaiae in capite 59., quia continet dulcissimam doctrinam de beneficiis Christi et de Ecclesia, ostendit quid sit vera Ecclesia, et affirmat semper aliquam futuram esse: Veniet ex Sion redemtor, ubi vocabuli emphasis nota sit, Redemtor est, qui dato pretio alium liberat.

Et avertet iniquitates a Iacob: ideo mittitur Christus, ut revera deleat peccata omnium, qui credunt in eum.

Et cogitetur integrum beneficium, restituit vitam et iusticiam aeternam, sicut et Daniel loquitur.

Deinde ibi Esaias addit concionem de Ecclesiae: Hoc est foedus meum cum eis, dicit Dominus, spiritus meus, qui est in te, et verba mea, quae posui in ore tuo, non recedent ab ore tuo, et ab ore seminis tui, nunc et usque in sempiternum, id est, haec est vera Ecclesia, in qua sonat verbum datum Esaiae de redemtore tollente peccatum, et in ea certo sanctificantur credentes Spiritu sancto.

Talem Ecclesiam semper mansuram esse affirmat, quanquam alias magis, alias minus frequens est: et quia saepe lux doctrinae fit obscurior, filius Dei subinde eam restituit, sicut Luna alias aliter lumen a Sole accipit.

Haec descriptio Ecclesiae apud Esaiam omnibus notissima sit.

Conclusit Deus omnes sub peccatum, ut omnium misereatur.

Epiphonema est, in quo ponitur exaequatio Gentium et Iudaeorum, et detrahitur fiducia meritorum Christi. Hortatur omnes ad poenitentiam, deinde aequaliter proponit omnibus agentibus poenitentiam consolationem. Estque gratissima doctrina in utroque membro.

Nam concludi sub peccatum non est otiose intelligendum, sed complectitur reatum, pavorem, iudicium et poenas peccati, quasi dicat: Omnes rei sunt, omnes erunt subiiciendi iudicio Dei, morti et afflictionibus, ut David erat conclusus sub peccatum, cum pelleretur in exilium, cum horribilibus doloribus excruciaretur, iuxta dictum: Deus ignis consumens est. Arguit autem peccatum, non ut relinquantur homines in peccato et exitio, sed ut per filium liberentur.

Hic igitur mox consolatio addita est: Ut omnium misereatur. Promittitur gratuita reconciliatio, quae opponenda est tentationi de merito, seu de dignitate: et promissio universalis est, hanc particulam universalem opponamus tentationi de particularitate, nec turbemur Stoicis et Manichaeis disputationibus, sciamus ipsum filium Dei hanc promissionem universalem (Venite ad me omnes qui laboratis et onerati estis, ego reficiam vos) proferre ex sinu aeterni patris, non fingamus in Deo contradictorias voluntates, sed credamus filio Dei misso ad hoc ipsum, ut sis nuncius, testis, pignus, et obsignator divinae promissionis, sicut inquit: Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut omnis qui credit in eum non pereat.

O altitudo divitiarum.

Exclamatio addita est, qua abrumpit disputationem, quia quanquam Deus est aequalis, et statim initio edidit promissionem de mediatore, et voluit omnibus posteris notam esse, et omnes posteros manere in vera agnitione et invocatione Dei, et saepissime repetivit vocem promissionis, et rursus collegit Ecclesiam: tamen postquam ingens multitudo subinde oblita est promissionis, et secuti sunt horrendi furores. Multa quaerit humana ratio, quare tanta multitudo omnibus seculis pereat, cur tam pauci fiant salvi: Cur Ecclesia sit dissipatus et oppressus coetus, sine certo imperio et sine pulcro ordine: Cur impia multitudo antecellat imperiis, gloria, opibus, multis excellentibus virtutibus, sapientiae et fortitudine: quare in hanc imbecillem naturam humanam tanta rabie grassari diabolis permittatur. Haec et alia multa exercent humanas cogitationes, sed Paulus in hac exclamatione significat, non omnia consilia Dei humanis ratiocinationibus comprehendi posse, sed amplectendum esse verbum Dei revelatum, nec ab eo deficiendum esse, et gratis mentibus haec beneficia ingentia, quae offert, accipienda et retinenda esse, et ipsius bonitatem et iusticiam Dei celebrandam esse.

Postea in illa aeterna schola causas consiliorum divinorum discemus, sicut saepissime praeceptum est: Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum. Item: Ad legem et ad testimonium, si non dixerint iuxta verbum hoc: Non erit eis matutina lux. Item: Hic est filius meus dilectus, hunc audite. His praeceptis obtemperemus, nec sinamus vagari mentes curiositate, quae implicatae labyrinthis disputationum opprimuntur dubitatione, quae mergit innumerabiles in aeternum exitium, sicut Iulianus et alii multi perierunt.

Insidias etiam diabolorum intelligamus, qui curiosas mentes impellunt ad inanes disputationes movendas. Adversus has et doctrina et invocatione Dei nos muniamus, sicut clamat Propheta: Fac cum servo tuo secundum misericordiam tuam, et iustificationes tuas doce me. Item: Orate, ne intretis in tentationem. Et certe modum esse disputationum oportet, sicut praecipit Paulus: Ne sapiamus praeter quam oportet sapere, sed sapiamus ita, ut modeste intra regulam, quam Deus tradidit, maneamus.

## 12:1 Disposition of Romans: Argument
Chapter XII.

We have placed the former part of the Epistle in the judicial genus, for it is occupied in teaching. The following chapters, which are as it were an appendix to that disputation, pertain to the suasory genus, because they contain precepts concerning morals.

Nor is there need here to inquire subtly into the reason of the disposition. For the members do not cohere in the same way as in a disputation, but the individual precepts are new propositions, or if one prefers this, new books. And yet if anyone in such a heap desires to hold some method or reason, so as to bring them into a few chapters, and to embrace all the precepts in order, he can, and he has the example of Paul, who contracts everything into the second table of the decalogue.

For the doctrine of faith, in which the superior part of the Epistle is consumed, pertains to the first table. Nor indeed can any method concerning morals be conceived more exact than the decalogue is. We, however, will also divide the precepts, according to the kinds of life. For as one is private life, another public, or as the Philosophers call it political, so there are double precepts here.

In the twelfth chapter he recites precepts pertaining more to private life. The following chapter pertains to political life, for it teaches us about the magistrate. Chapter 14 warns about scandals, lest we offend weak brothers by our liberty. In the remaining two chapters he promises, as is done in epistles, his duty to the Romans, and adds salutations.

There is a general proposition embracing the cross and good works. Present your bodies a living sacrifice to God, and rational worship etc. Here you see precepts are delivered differently by the Philosophers, differently by the Apostles.

For Paul, inserting an amplification into the proposition, requires faith also. For he signifies that works and afflictions ought to be sacrifices. But they are not sacrifices among the impious. But among those who believe that our afflictions and works please God, because we are members of Christ, and that both our afflictions and our works are governed by God.

And λογικὴ λατρεία (rational worship) is opposed not only to animal victims, but also to all human exercises and works, which are without the fear of God and without trust. For λογικὸν does not signify man, as they describe man in the schools, a rational animal, but it signifies one who thinks, so that it is λογικὴ λατρεία, in which God is thought of, or discerned, or apprehended through the word. ἄλογος (irrational) latria is when hearts do not feel the fear of God, are not raised by faith, do not know God, even if they perform excellent works of natural effort, while in the meantime they doubt whether God regards us, whether He hears etc.

Then he recounts the precepts, in which not without great cause he placed in the first place that each should serve his own vocation, and teach nothing without the word of God, and undertake nothing without the command of God. Afterwards various duties of charity are commemorated, and at the end he forbids revenge.

Where the reader should remember that private revenge is forbidden. For the Gospel does not forbid legitimate revenge. which is exercised by the magistrates, but approves of it, and adorns it with the most ample praises, as the next chapter will show.

Latin:

Caput XII.

Superiorem Epistolae partem collocavimus in genere iudiciali, versatur enim in docendo. Sequentia capita, quae sunt velut appendix illius disputationis, pertinent ad genus suasorium, quia continent praecepta de moribus.

Nec opus est hic subtiliter quaerere rationem dispositionis. Non enim perinde cohaerent membra, ut in disputatione, sed singula praecepta, novae propositiones sunt, aut si quis hoc mavult, novi libri. Et tamen si quis in tanto acervo, methodum aliquam aut rationem tenere cupit, ut in pauca capita conferre, et ordine complecti omnia praecepta, possit, is habet Pauli exemplum, qui contrahit omnia in secundam tabulam decalogi.

Nam doctrina fidei, in qua superior Epistolae pars consumitur, pertinet ad primam tabulam. Neque sane methodus de moribus ulla magis exacta concipi potest, quam decalogus est. Nos tamen etiam partiemur praecepta, iuxta vitae genera. Ut enim alia est privata vita, alia publica, seu ut Philosophi appellant politica, ita duplicia hic praecepta sunt.

In duodecimo capite recitat praecepta magis ad privatam vitam pertinentia. Sequens caput ad politicam vitam pertinet, docet enim nos de magistratu. Caput 14. de scandalis admonet, ne offendamus libertate nostra imbecilles fratres. In reliquis duobus capitibus pollicetur, ut fit in epistolis, officium suum Romanis, et adscribit salutationes.

Propositio generalis est complectens crucem et bona opera. Praebete corpora vestra hostiam Deo, et cultum rationalem etc. Hic vides aliter tradi praecepta a Philosophis, aliter ab Apostolis.

Nam Paulus inserens amplificationem propositioni, fidem etiam requirit. Significat enim opera et afflictiones debere hostias esse. Non sunt autem hostiae apud impios. Sed apud hos qui credunt Deo placere afflictiones nostras et opera, quia Christi membra sumus, et gubernari a Deo, tum afflictiones nostras, tum opera.

Et λογικὴ λατρεία opponitur non modo pecuinis victimis, sed etiam omnibus humanis exercitiis et operibus, quae sunt sine timore Dei et sine fiducia. Nam λογικὸν non significat hominem, ut in scholis hominem describunt, animal rationale, sed significat cogitantem, ut sit λογικὴ λατρεία, in qua cogitatur, seu cernitur, seu apprehenditur Deus per verbum ἄλογος latria, cum corda non sentiant timorem Dei, non eriguntur fide, non norunt Deum, etiam si egregia opera praestent conaturationis, cum interim dubitent, an respiciat nos Deus, an exaudiat etc.

Deinde recenset praecepta, in quibus non sine magna causa primo loco posuit, ut suae quisque vocationi serviat, et nihil sine verbo Dei doceat, nihil suscipiat sine mandato Dei. Postea commemorantur varia officia caritatis, et ad extremum prohibet vindictam.

Ubi meminerit lector, privatam vindictam prohiberi. Nam Evangelium non prohibet vindictam legitimam. quae a magistratibus exercetur, sed approbat eam, et amplissimis laudibus ornat, ut ostendet proximum caput.

## 12:1 Argument
Chapter XII.

It is customary for Paul first to deliver the voice of the Gospel concerning the promise of grace, concerning reconciliation, concerning justification on account of the Son and through Him. Afterwards he adds the doctrine concerning good works, or new obedience, or precepts, which are an explanation of the Decalogue. Here, however, let the sum of the doctrine concerning good works be noted, which, for the sake of teaching, we distribute in some way into these five questions.

The first is: What works are to be done? Answer: Precepts from God, both internal and external, according to the saying in Ezekiel: Walk in my precepts, and the sum comprehended in the Decalogue. is, which must be rightly understood, according to the interpretations handed down in the prophetic and apostolic writings.

For works not commanded by God are not the worship of God, according to the saying: In vain do they worship me with the commandments of men. Therefore, the worship of God is a work commanded by God, done in the recognition of the mediator and in true faith, related to this end, that honor may be rendered to God, namely, due obedience, and that by this very obedience we may testify that we feel that this is truly the God whom we invoke, and who commanded himself to be worshipped by this obedience.

Second question: How can they be done?

Response: With the recognition and trust of the mediator shining before us, and the mediator vivifying us through the Gospel, and pouring the Holy Spirit into us, because love of God and joy in God cannot exist unless mercy and reconciliation have first been apprehended by faith on account of the mediator.

In this consolation, the divinity dwells in the heart, because the eternal Father, through the Son who consoles by the voice of the Gospel, is truly effective there: and the Holy Spirit is given by the Father and the Son, kindling joy and invocation, according to the sayings: I will pour out the spirit of grace and of prayers. Item: We will come to him and make our abode with him.

Item, 2 Corinthians 3: Looking upon the glory of the Lord, we are transformed into the same image, that is, looking upon the λόγον [Word], who is the image of the eternal Father, and in consolation shows the presence and goodness of God, we are made similar to his image, with the Holy Spirit kindling our hearts. Thus then the Son is Emmanuel, through him the divinity is present to us, vivifies, protects, governs, carries us, rules our counsels and events, just as he says: I am the vine, you are the branches, without me you can do nothing.

Third question: How does new obedience please?

Response: It pleases by faith on account of the Son of God.

We declare these words in this way. First, it must be believed that the Person is reconciled and righteous, that is, accepted by God freely on account of Christ by faith alone, by which the imputation of righteousness is apprehended, of which it is said: Abraham believed God, and it was imputed to him for righteousness.

Secondly: Let us acknowledge and truly grieve that we still have many stains, and are far from the perfection of the law, according to the sayings: No one living shall be justified in your sight. Item: Not in our righteousness, but through your mercy hear us on account of the Lord.

Thirdly: And yet at the same time let us know that God demands begun obedience, and that in the reborn it pleases God by faith on account of Christ, who is also the propitiator, offering his obedience for us: and now he always intercedes for us, and carries our groans to the eternal Father. Therefore Peter says: Offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God on account of Christ, namely, both the propitiator, and the one now interceding for us, just as he said: I pray that your love, with which you love me, may be in them.

Fourth question: For what causes are good works to be done?

Response: The first and clear cause is duty, that is, the eternal and immovable Order in the divine mind, that a rational creature should obey God; this order is called Duty, Rom.

8: We are debtors, and the necessity of debt. But although the Antinomians and many fanatical men rage and shout against this necessity and the common appellation of debt, yet they are manifestly refuted by the sayings of Christ and Paul: We have done what we ought to have done. Item: Unless your righteousness exceeds the righteousness of the Pharisees and Scribes, you will not enter into the kingdom of heaven.

Second Necessity, which is the formal [cause] of conversion and regeneration. For in the oath the copulative sentence is: As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he may be converted and live.

Conversion is necessary, and when it does not happen, man is not vivified by faith through the Holy Spirit. Because it is manifest that the Holy Spirit is not in those who persevere in crimes against conscience, according to the saying: Those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God.

And the formal [cause] of regeneration is the beginning of new and eternal life, which is new and eternal light, wisdom and righteousness and the renewal of the image of God in us, which happens as God communicates himself to us, when the Son consoles hearts by the voice of the Gospel, and pours the Holy Spirit into them. Thirdly, the Necessity of retaining faith, because the Holy Spirit is grieved and cast out when sins are committed against conscience.

But although it is most true that new obedience is necessary on account of these true causes which have been stated, yet this voice of Paul must always be retained: The gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ, because good works do not merit the remission of sins, nor justification, nor eternal life.

Then other causes should be considered, for which good works are to be done, namely dignity. Also, rewards and the necessity of avoiding punishments. Dignity is that God receives new obedience, even if it is weak, on account of the mediator, as I said before, and calls them sacrifices, and it is the fruit of the Holy Spirit, because God always wishes there to be some in the human race to whom He may communicate Himself, and by whom in turn He may be rightly acknowledged and invoked.

Finally, rewards and the necessity of avoiding punishments should also be considered, because it is most certain that crimes against conscience attract punishments in this life, even if there is no conversion after this life, according to the saying of Psalm 38: Because of iniquities you chastise the sons of men. And although good works do not merit eternal life, yet they have certain rewards of their own in this life and after this life, according to the counsel of God, nor are legal promises void in the reconciled, as: Give, and it shall be given to you. Also, Matt. 10: Whoever shall have given a drink of water to one of the least of mine on account of doctrine, shall not lose his reward.

And it is very necessary to know the distinction between the promise of grace and the promises of temporal goods. The promise of grace is received freely by faith alone on account of the mediator, and is always valid for all who in conversion sustain themselves by faith, even when all bodily goods are lost, according to the saying of Job: Even if he kills me, I will hope in him. But the promises of temporal goods, although they are also valid on account of the Son of God, and are of no use unless faith shines forth, which receives grace, yet they are added to good works, and especially on account of these five causes.

The first is: That they may be testimonies of providence. For God wishes it to be known that bodily goods are things created by Him, and not scattered by chance, but are also given and preserved by Him for the Church, according to the saying: He is your life, and the length of your days. Also, Psalm 36: In the days of famine they shall be satisfied, etc. The rich have hungered, but to him who fears the Lord no good thing shall be lacking.

The second: That they may be testimonies that God wishes to preserve the Church in this life, wherefore Paul says, 1 Tim. 4: Piety has promises of the present life and of the future. For because God wishes in His immense goodness to gather the Church on account of the Son, He preserves this order of nature for so long, and makes the earth fruitful, so that He may feed the Church in this life, and since He feeds others on account of the Church, we ought especially to be grateful.

The third cause is: Because God wishes bodily necessity also to be a reminder of faith, invocation, hope, and thanksgiving, therefore He issued promises, so that we might know that this petition is not void, and indeed He wishes these very goods also to be sought and expected by faith, and in this petition and expectation faith, hope, and patience to grow.

The fourth cause is: That they may be reminders of the promise of grace, because faith, which acknowledges the Son and receives reconciliation, must always shine forth in the petition for bodily things. And indeed on account of the Son other promises have been issued and are valid. All these are comprehended in the saying: Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you.

The fifth cause is: Because God wishes both to be known, that the Church is subjected to the cross, and yet among these very dangers is miraculously preserved in this life, so that the entire admirable preservation of the Church, and all the wonderful liberations, may be testimonies of the presence of God in the Church, as is said in Numbers ch. 14: That the Egyptians may know that you, O Lord, are in this people. Joshua 3: You shall know that the Lord God is in your midst. 1 Kings 17: That all the earth may know that God is in Israel. Isaiah 37: And now, O Lord our God, save us from the hand of Sennacherib, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the Lord.

Let these causes concerning bodily promises be often pondered, so that faith may be confirmed in many ways, and invocation and thanksgiving may be kindled, and we may know that truly in this life common calamities are therefore softened, so that the Church may be preserved, and for the good works of the saints many public and private rewards are given, even in the dangers of this life, as it is said in Isaiah 33: Bread is given to him, his waters are faithful, and they shall irrigate the land, they shall see the King in his beauty.

And the saints acknowledge that even in bodily benefits they are far surpassed by the liberality of God in their own good deeds, even if they merit anything. Therefore James says: I am less than all your mercies.

The fifth question concerning the distinction of sins.

It is necessary for men to be warned about the distinction of sins, lest when they hear that there are remaining sins in the saints in this life, they might dream with horrible madness that those who persevere in crimes against conscience please God. Since therefore it is asked, what sins are there [sins] in the saints in this life? First I answer: By no means are there sins in the saints, or lapses against conscience, that is, when they, who have been saints, knowingly and willingly violate the law of God, as David seizing another man's wife; these grieve and cast out the Holy Spirit, and cease to be saints, and again become guilty of the wrath of God and eternal death, until they are again converted, according to these sayings, 1 Corinthians 6:

Do not err, fornicators, idolaters, adulterers etc. shall not possess the kingdom of God. And Galatians

5: The works of the flesh are manifest, adultery, murder etc. those who do such things shall not possess the kingdom of God. Item: Those failing from the foundation, that is, casting away some article of faith, whether they understand it or do not understand it, but are deceived by impostures, these also cease to be saints, and cast out the Holy Spirit, and become guilty of eternal wrath, as many fell away to the Arians, and many now also who for some time thought rightly, cast away the truth.

These degrees of sins are to be considered most diligently, which are commonly named mortal or reigning sins. Most firmly, therefore, the rule against the Antinomians must be held: Fight the good fight, keeping faith and a good conscience.

What sins, therefore, remain in the saints in this life?

I answer: Much darkness and doubt, many omissions and vicious affections, which evils, however, the saints resist, lest they fall against conscience, and they believe they are covered on account of the Son of God.

Let this darkness and uncleanness in man not be thought to be a light evil, on account of which it is said: No one living shall be justified in thy sight. And yet the Son of God is a shelter for believers.

Therefore, although this uncleanness is in the saints, yet the persons are pleasing on account of the Son of God, receiving by faith the imputation of righteousness, according to the sayings: Blessed are they whose sins are covered. Item: For this shall every saint pray to thee.

Item: If you mortify the actions of the flesh by the spirit, you shall live. And it is customary to name these sins venial, or not reigning.

These five questions must always be repeated in the doctrine of good works; now let us look at Paul's most learned sermon.

In the beginning, he hands down a general precept about restraining the body according to all moral precepts: Offer your bodies a living sacrifice, and perform a rational service, so that the newness and image of God may grow in the mind, just as he says elsewhere in Ephesians

4: Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who according to God was created in righteousness and true holiness. He opposes, however, obedience according to moral precepts to Levitical worships, therefore he says: Offer a living sacrifice and rational service.

He names it a living sacrifice, because God for this reason restored eternal life, so that in all eternity we might be living with him, and he himself might communicate himself to us. God created rational creatures, angels and men, so that they might be creatures to whom he communicates himself and his highest goods, life, light, wisdom, and righteousness, and from them in turn he requires conformity, and the recognition and celebration of this goodness.

This conformity with God, and the recognition and celebration of the goodness of God, are the true and eternal worship of God, which are begun in this life, and afterwards will be complete: and the same worship is named λογικὴ λατρεία [logical service], that is, the service of the mind, in which the mind by faith, or in the presence of God, beholds him, and truly feels fear and joy in God, according to the saying: True worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth, that is, the Holy Spirit kindling true and ardent motions, fear, trust, love, and joy. In truth, that is, in the true recognition of God, which is made by the word shining in the heart, through which the Son shows the will of the Father.

One must therefore oppose λογικὴ λατρεία, not only to the slaughtering of cattle, but universally to the most vain imagination of those who say that some external or rational works, even in the unregenerate, please God ex opere operato [by the work performed], without a good motion of the user, just as the Papists wrote, that the Mass merits for others ex opere operato, even if the priest is an adulterer, or as they said, that honest moral works even in the unregenerate merit grace. These false imaginations the Prophets often tax, as Psalm 49: Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, Psalm 50: You will not delight in burnt offerings. Hosea

6: I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and knowledge more than burnt offerings.

Finally, this sermon is most often repeated, and the sum is comprised in these sayings: True worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth. Item: No one comes to the Father except through the Son.

From this whole doctrine let an explanation be taken of what λογικὴ λατρεία is, and from thence let a definition be taken.

NARRATION OF THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. CHAP. XII. The worship of God is a work commanded by God, performed in true knowledge and fear of God, and true trust in the Son, to this end, that obedience and honor be rendered to God, that is, that by this work we testify that this is the true God whom we thus worship; as the chastity of Joseph is the worship of God, because in the mind of Joseph there is true knowledge of God, fear and trust in the Mediator, and the work is referred to this end, that it may show that this is truly the God whom we thus worship, and how He wills to be worshipped.

Chastity in Scipio is without the light of God and the knowledge of the Mediator, therefore it is not the worship of God.

But someone might ask: Since God demands living sacrifices, and a perpetual worship of the mind, for what purpose did He institute the slaughtering of cattle and other ceremonies?

I answer: That the ministry of teaching the word of God might be preserved, for which work two things are necessary: teachers and a congregation.

Therefore, signs were instituted, which were also meant to be reminders added to the doctrine, and the nerves of the congregation, and many ceremonies were instituted so that from them the teachers might be fed, such as the offering of firstfruits, tithes, and cattle.

These ends must be understood in ceremonial worships or sacrifices.

But as we have defined worship, so in the same way sacrifice in general can be defined.

Sacrifice is a work, commanded by God, performed in true knowledge, fear of God, and faith, to this end, that obedience be rendered to God, and by this work a testimony be shown, that this is the true God to whom this obedience is rendered.

Add, when we speak of the sacrifices of men, that it is performed with trust in the Mediator.

There are, however, two species of sacrifice according to the general definition: Propitiatory and eucharistic (εὐχαριστικὸν).

Propitiatory is one, namely the obedience of Christ alone, which merits for others the remission of sins and reconciliation.

For the Levitical [sacrifices], which were called propitiations, and [sacrifices] for sin, were only types; they by no means merited the remission of sins.

Therefore it is written: It was impossible for the blood of bulls to take away sins.

All other things, when they are done rightly, are eucharistic (εὐχαριστικὰ), whether they be ceremonies or other good works, as it is said: A sacrifice to God is a broken spirit; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, Thou wilt not despise.

This nature was not created to be idle, but so that God might communicate to us His light, wisdom, justice, and joy in all eternity, and in turn God wills to be celebrated in this life, and after this life: therefore it is necessary that there be some actions, the end of all of which is the celebration of God.

All these in this life and after this life are in reality sacrifices of praise, or eucharistic (εὐχαριστικὰ), and a rational service (λογικὴ λατρεία).

Osiander's partition makes three members: Typical, propitiatory, and the threptikon (θρεπτήριον), by which the priests were fed.

This distribution does not displease me, but it is more convenient to name it eucharistic (εὐχαριστικὸν), so that all sacrifices of the spirit and ceremonies may be included.

It is necessary that these distinctions exist, so that the sacrifice of the Son of God may be discerned from the sacrifices of all other men.

For the others are by no means hilastika (ἱλαστικὰ), or propitiatory, that is, they do not merit the remission of sins and reconciliation: and many errors have crept into the Church, because the word 'Sacrifice' was not rightly understood.

Wherefore it is necessary that the younger ones be admonished about this distinction.

Having known these foundations, it can be understood what Paul calls rational service (λογικὴν λατρείαν), and this is holy, that is, truly dedicated to God, not profane, like the virtues in the Gentiles, in whom the true knowledge of God and the Mediator does not shine: it is also pleasing to God, as was said above, how good works please God, namely those commanded by God and performed in the knowledge of the Mediator and trust in the Son.

Do not imitate the ways of this world.

As he previously instituted a general proposition concerning obedience according to all the commandments: Offer a rational service (λογικὴν λατρείαν), so now he repeats it according to all the commandments: Let us not have affections similar to those of the worldly, but new affections conformable to God.

For when he forbids imitating the ways of the world, he does not disparage the things whose use God has ordained; he does not forbid the use of food, marriage, governments, judgments, contracts, and other ordinances of God, but he forbids vicious affections, therefore he says: The ways, that is, the motions of the minds, should not be similar to the worldly, so that contrary to the ordinance of God the impious may crave pleasures, seek wealth and power by unjust means, contend with ambition, burn with unjust hatreds, and disturb the Church and polities with private desires.

These vices reign in the greater part of the human race, of which part of the human race, contrary to those converted to God, the appellation of 'the world' is often used, as in 1 John 2: Everything that is in the world, is the lust of the flesh and the lust of the eyes.

He commands, however, to be renewed in mind, that is, he commands us to have other notions of God, to rightly acknowledge God, and with firm assent to embrace the universal doctrine, and to have in the heart affections conformable to God, true fear, trust, joy in God, hope, love, patience, chastity, and other virtues.

Therefore he adds: That you may know what is the good will of God.

He interprets most simply what he said before, Be renewed in mind: for he speaks of the will of God revealed in precepts, comminations, and promises, as if he were saying: Rightly acknowledge God, and rightly acknowledge his will, made manifest by immense goodness in the Law and the Gospel, and let interior and exterior obedience agree with the word of God. As because the three men in Babylon know the good will of God, that is, that it is the command of God not to invoke idols, they obey God, and are not broken by the fear of punishment, but prefer the command of God to their own life. This is the simple explanation of this saying.

I say to you through the grace which has been given to me.

Before, he set forth a general proposition concerning all virtues, or concerning universal obedience. Now he approaches special virtues, and because among those which pertain to ministry or to government, there are two especially: Obedience in one's calling, and justice keeping bounds in judging. Concerning these two virtues he discourses at the beginning. For just as in political government, meddlesomeness (πολυπραγμοσύνη) is very pernicious, when private men thrust themselves into affairs and hinder ordinary governors: or when busybodies, who are in charge, do the work of others: so do restless men harm the Church, who, incited either by foolish zeal or by hatreds, either burst forth outside their calling and attempt to reform many things in doctrine or rites which it would have been better not to change: or, on the other hand, teachers of the Church lay down laws for magistrates concerning civil affairs, and have one foot in the Curia and the other in the Church, as Aristophanes said of Cleon, that he had one foot in the camp and the other in the assembly.

Now the virtue of the third commandment is obedience in one's calling. The meddler or busybody fights against the third commandment and against the saying of Paul: Do your own things. Another evil is Arrogance in judging about unknown things; this also Paul prohibits in this place, when he forbids thinking more highly than one ought: and he commands to think modestly, and delivers the norm that prophecies should be analogous to the faith, that is, that narrations and judgments should agree with the faith.

It is known, however, that no one ought to take upon himself a judgment about that which he does not know; therefore it is written in Deuteronomy 17: When it has been announced, you shall hear and inquire well, and when it has been found true and certain, let punishment follow.

And the same sentiment has been often repeated in divine commands. And in Matthew 5 it is said: If a blind man is a guide to a blind man, both fall into the pit. Syracides chapter 11: Before you hear, do not answer. And yet it is most common for those fascinated by persuasion to judge without knowing the sources, against whom it is also said in Exodus: You shall not follow the crowd in judging. Reason also teaches the same: And no one can teach what he knows little of. And Plato says: Not by the multitude to judge, but by knowledge (οὐ πλήθει δικάζειν ἀλλ᾽ ἐπιστήμῃ). To this also pertain those things: Let each one exercise the art he has learned. For being a carpenter, you were not doing wood-working (τέκτων γὰρ ὢν, ἔπραττες οὐ ξυλουργικά).

Admonished by such sentiments, let us be more circumspect in judging, and let us seek the sources, and let us not be self-opinionated (ἰδιοβουλεύοντες), but let us willingly confer our thoughts with the judgments of other experts, as is commanded in 1 Corinthians 15. And in the first place, let us hold the rule, That prophecy should be analogous to the faith, that is, that narrations and judgments should agree with the foundation, that is, with the Law and the Gospel and the symbols. It is necessary that this norm be known and followed, according to the saying: If anyone teaches another Gospel, let him be anathema. It is necessary, therefore, first to know the uncorrupted Gospel, according to the saying: Be instructed, you who judge the earth.

Now consider what horrendous furies have arisen in all times from interpretations fighting against the faith, such as the corruptions of Ebion, Cerinthus, and Samosatenus, who denied that there is a divine nature in Christ. And both Samosatenus and Servetus, by cunning interpretation, perverted the text in John: In the beginning was the word. Item: The Manichaeans and similar foul monsters invented things against the Law and the Gospel, as in our time the Anabaptists.

In all times there have been some similar to the Pharisees, who took away the distinction between the Law and the Gospel, and invented that men merit the remission of sins and are righteous by external discipline, just as the Pharisee in Luke 18 dreams.

Such was the imagination of Pelagius, the Papists, and the Monks, in which there is a great chaos of errors. They destroy the whole doctrine of the justice of faith, they feign that men merit the remission of sins, and are just by their own works. Afterwards they add: Because no one knows when he has enough works, one must doubt whether one is in grace. These are by no means analogous to faith.

They are also manifestly idolatrous, the Invocation of the dead, because it is written, You shall adore the Lord your God. Item, the Adoration of the bread in the carrying about. Item, the Fictitious offering in the Mass for the dead. Nor was it to be believed by the deceitful spirits who asked for Masses to be celebrated for the dead.

Nor are those things analogous to faith which they feign concerning vows, satisfactions, and other human rites, which they say are necessary worships of God, and merit the remission of sins.

Nor are the Anabaptist ravings analogous to faith, which are partly pharisaical, partly the furies of Manichaeus, destroying the political order.

I have added this brief catalog, so that the younger may think more diligently about this rule. Let prophecy be analogous to faith, and let them be circumspect in judging doctrine and in judging interpretations, and let them fortify themselves with the investigation of true doctrine and with prayer.

Then follows in the text a long accumulation of many precepts concerning mutual love, beneficence, diligence in invocation, patience, prayer, humility, the restraining of the desire for private vengeance, etc. These mandates are distributed into the decalogue, and it is not difficult to see to which chapter of the decalogue each pertains, just as we often warn elsewhere that the doctrine concerning virtues is to be distributed into the decalogue.

Latin:

Caput XII.

Usitatum est Paulo primum tradere vocem Evangelii de promissione gratiae de reconciliatione, de iustificatione propter filium et per eum. Postea addit doctrinam de bonis operibus, seu nova obedientia, seu praecepta, quae sunt explicatio Decalogi. Hic autem nota sit summa doctrinae, de bonis operibus, quam docendi causa utcunque distribuimus in has quinque quaestiones.

Prima est: Quae opera facienda sunt? Responsio: Praecepta a Deo interiora et exteriora, iuxta dictum in Ezechiele: In praeceptis meis ambulate, ac summa in Decalogo comprehensa. est, quem recte intelligi oportet, iuxta enarrationes traditas in propheticis et apostolicis scriptis.

Nam opera non mandata a Deo non sunt cultus Dei, iuxta dictum: Frustra colunt me mandatis hominum. Est igitur cultus Dei opus a Deo mandatum, factum in agnitione mediatoris et vera fide, relatum ad hunc finem, ut Deo praestetur honos, videlicet, debita obedientia, et ut hac ipsa obedientia testemur nos sentire hunc vere esse Deum, quem invocamus, et qui hac obedientia coli se praecepit.

Secunda quaestio: Quomodo fieri possunt?

Responsio: Praelucente agnitione et fiducia mediatoris, et vivificante nos mediatore per Evangelium, et effundente in nos Spiritum sanctum, quia dilectio Dei et laetitia in Deo nulla esse potest, nisi prius fide apprehensa sit misericordia et reconciliatio propter mediatorem.

In hac consolatione divinitas habitat in corde, quia aeternus pater per filium consolantem voce Evangelii, vere est ibi efficax: et datur a patre et filio Spiritus sanctus, accendens laetitiam et invocationem, iuxta dicta: Effundam spiritum gratiae et precum. Item: Veniemus ad eum et mansionem apud eum faciemus.

Item, 2. Corinth. 3.: Intuentes gloriam Domini, transformamur ad eandem imaginem, id est, intuentes λόγον, qui est imago aeterni patris, et in consolatione ostendit praesentiam et bonitatem Dei, efficimur similes eius imaginis, Spiritu sancto accendente corda. Ita tunc filius est Emanuel, per eum adest nobis divinitas, vivificat, protegit, gubernat, gestat nos, regit consilia et eventus, sicut dicit: Ego sum vitis, vos palmites, sine me nihil potestis facere.

Tertia quaestio: Quomodo placet nova obedientia?

Responsio: Placet fide propter filium Dei.

Haec verba declaramus hoc modo. Primum credendum est, Personam reconciliatam et iustam esse, id est, acceptam Deo gratis propter Christum sola fide, qua apprehenditur imputatio iusticiae, de qua dicitur: Credidit Abraham Deo, et imputatum est ei ad iusticiam.

Secundo: Agnoscamus et vere doleamus nos adhuc multum sordium habere, et procul abesse a perfectione legis, iuxta dicta: Non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens. Item: Non in iusticia nostra, sed per misericordiam tuam exaudi nos propter Dominum.

Tertio: Et tamen simul sciamus Deum postulare inchoatam obedientiam, et in renatis eam placere Deo fide propter Christum, qui et propiciator est, offerens suam obedientiam pro nobis: et nunc semper interpellat pro nobis, et nostros gemitus ad aeternum patrem perfert. Ideo Petrus inquit: Offerte hostias spirituales acceptas Deo propter Christum, scilicet, et propiciatorem, et nunc pro nobis interpellantem, sicut dixit: Oro, ut dilectio tua, quam me diligis, sit in eis.

Quarta quaestio: Propter quas causas facienda sunt bona opera?

Responsio: Prima et perspicua causa est debitum, id est, Ordo aeternus et immotus in mente divina, ut creatura rationalis Deo obediat, hic ordo dicitur Debitum, Rom. 8.: Debitores sumus, et necessitas debiti.

Etsi autem furenter Antinomi et multi fanatici homines vociferantur contra hanc necessitatem et communem appellationem debiti, tamen manifeste refutantur dictis Christi et Pauli: Quod debuimus fecimus. Item: Nisi iusticia vestra antecellit iusticiae Pharisaeorum et Scribarum, non intrabitis in regnum coelorum.

Secunda Necessitas, quae est formale conversionis et regenerationis. Nam in iuramento copulativa oratio est: Vivo ego, dicit Dominus, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed ut convertatur et vivat.

Conversio necessaria est, quae cum non fit, non vivificatur homo fide per Spiritum sanctum. Quia manifestum est Spiritum sanctum non esse in his, qui perseverant in sceleribus contra conscientiam, iuxta dictum: Qui faciunt talia, regnum Dei non possidebunt.

Et formale regenerationis est incoatio novae et aeternae vitae, quae est nova et aeterna lux, sapientia et iusticia et renovatio imaginis Dei in nobis, quae fit Deo se nobis communicante, cum filius voce Evangelii consolatur corda, et effundit in ea Spiritum sanctum. Tertio, Necessitas retinendae fidei, quia Spiritus sanctus contristatur et excutitur, cum fiunt delicta contra conscientiam.

Quanquam autem verissimum est, novam obedientiam necessariam esse propter has veras causas, quae dictae sunt, tamen semper retinenda est haec vox Pauli: Donum Dei est vita aeterna per Iesum Christum, quia bona opera neque remissionem peccatorum, neque iustificationem, neque vitam aeternam merentur.

Deinde et aliae causae considerentur, propter quas bona opera facienda sunt, scilicet dignitas. Item, praemia et necessitas vitandi poenas. Dignitas est quod Deus novam obedientiam, etsi est infirma, recipit propter mediatorem, ut antea dixi, et nominat sacrificia, et est fructus Spiritus sancti, quia semper vult Deus aliquos esse in genere humano, quibus sese communicet, et a quibus vicissim recte agnoscatur et invocetur.

Postremo etiam praemia et necessitas vitandi poenas considerentur, quia certissimum est scelera contra conscientiam attrahere poenas in hac vita, etsi non fiat conversio post hanc vitam, iuxta dictum Psalmi 38.: Propter iniquitates corripis filios hominum. Et quanquam bona opera non merentur vitam aeternam, tamen habent sua quaedam praemia in hac vita et post hanc vitam, iuxta consilium Dei, nec sunt irritae legales promissiones in reconciliatis, ut: Date, et dabitur vobis. Item, Matth. 10.: Qui dederit potum aquae uni ex minimis meorum propter doctrinam, non perdet mercedem suam.

Ac valde necessarium est scire discrimen inter promissionem gratiae et promissiones bonorum temporalium. Promissio gratiae propter mediatorem gratis sola fide accipitur, et semper rata est omnibus, qui in conversione sustentant se fide, etiam amissis omnibus bonis corporalibus, iuxta dictum Iob: Etiamsi occidet me, sperabo in eum. Sed promissiones bonorum temporalium, quanquam etiam ratae sunt propter filium Dei, et non prosunt nisi praelucente fide, quae accipit gratiam, tamen additae sunt bonis operibus, et praecipue propter has quinque causas.

Prima est: Ut sint testimonia providentiae. Vult enim sciri Deus et bona corporalia res esse ab ipso creatas, et non casu spargi, sed ab ipso etiam Ecclesiae dari et conservari, iuxta dictum: Ipse est vita tua, et longitudo dierum tuorum. Item, Psalm. 36.: In diebus famis saturabuntur etc. Divites esurierunt, timenti autem Dominum non deerit ullum bonum.

Secunda: Ut sint testimonia, quod velit Deus in hac vita servare Ecclesiam, quare Paulus inquit, 1. Timoth. 4.: Pietas habet promissiones praesentis vitae et futurae. Quia enim vult Deus immensa bonitate colligere Ecclesiam propter filium, tantisper servat hunc ordinem naturae, foecundat terram, ut alat Ecclesiam in hac vita, et cum propter Ecclesiam caeteros pascat, nos praecipue gratos esse oportebat.

Tertia causa est: Quia vult Deus et necessitatem corporalem esse commonefactionem de fide, invocatione, spe et gratiarum actione, ideo promissiones edidit, ut sciamus hanc petitionem non esse irritam, et quidem vult haec ipsa bona etiam fide peti et expectari, et in hac petitione et expectatione fidem, spem, patientiam crescere.

Quarta causa est: Ut sint commonefactiones de promissione gratiae, quia fidem, quae agnoscit filium, et accipit reconciliationem oportet semper praelucere in petitione corporalium rerum. Et quidem propter filium caeterae promissiones editae et ratae sunt. Haec omnia comprehenduntur in dicto: Quidquid petieritis patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis.

Quinta causa est: Quia vult utrumque sciri Deus, et subiectam esse Ecclesiam cruci, et inter ipsa pericula tamen mirabiliter servari in hac vita, ut universa admiranda conservatio Ecclesiae, et omnes mirandae liberationes sint testimonia praesentiae Dei in Ecclesia, ut dicitur in Numeris cap. 14.: Ut sciant Aegyptii, quod tu Domine sis in hoc populo. Iosua 3.: Scietis, quod Dominus Deus in medio vestri sit. 1. Regum 17.: Ut sciat omnis terra, quod sit Deus in Israël. Esaiae 37.: Et nunc Domine Deus noster salva nos de manu Sennacherib, ut cognoscant omnia regna terrae, quod tu solus sis Dominus.

Hae causae de promissionibus corporalibus saepe cogitentur, ut fides multipliciter confirmetur, et accendantur invocatio et gratiarum actio, et sciamus vere in hac vita ideo leniri communes calamitates, ut servetur Ecclesia, et pro bonis operibus sanctorum dari multa praemia publica et privata, etiam in huius vitae periculis, sicut Esaiae 33. dicitur: Panis ei datus est, aquae eius fideles sunt, et rigabunt terram, Regem in decore suo videbunt.

Et agnoscunt sancti etiam in corporalibus beneficiis longe superari liberalitate Dei ipsorum benefacta, etiam si quid merentur. Ideo dicit Iacobus: Minor sum cunctis miserationibus tuis.

Quinta quaestio de discrimine peccatorum.

Necesse est moneri homines de discrimine peccatorum, ne cum audiunt reliqua esse peccata in sanctis in hac vita, horribili furore somnient perseverantes in sceleribus contra conscientiam placere Deo. Cum igitur quaeritur, quae peccata sint in sanctis in hac vita? Primum respondeo: Nequaquam sunt in sanctis peccata, seu lapsus contra conscientiam, id est, Cum illi, qui fuerunt sancti scientes et volentes violant legem Dei, ut David rapiens alterius conjugem, hi contristant et excutiunt Spiritum sanctum, et desinunt esse sancti, ac rursus fiunt rei irae Dei et mortis aeternae, donec rursus convertuntur, iuxta haec dicta, 1.

Corinth 6.: Ne erretis, scortatores, idolatrae, adulteri etc. regnum Dei non possidebunt. Et Galat.

5.: Manifesta sunt opera carnis, adulterium, caedes etc. talia facientes regnum Dei non possidebunt. Item: Deficientes a fundamento, id est, aliquem articulum fidei abiicientes, sive eum intelligant, sive non intelligant, sed decipiantur praestigiis, hi quoque desinunt esse sancti, et excutiunt Spiritum sanctum, et fiunt rei aeternae irae, ut multi deficiebant ad Arianos, multi nunc quoque qui aliquandiu recte senserunt, abiiciunt veritatem.

Hi gradus peccatorum diligentissime considerandi sunt, qui nominantur usitate peccata mortalia seu regnantia. Firmissime igitur tenenda est regula contra Antinomos: Milita bonam militiam, retinens fidem et bonam conscientiam.

Quae igitur peccata reliqua sunt in sanctis in hac vita?

Respondeo: Multum caliginis et dubitationum, multae omissiones et vitiosi affectus, quibus malis tamen sancti repugnant, ne ruant contra conscientiam, et credunt ea tegi propter filium Dei.

Haec caligo et immundities in homine non existimetur leve malum esse, propter quam dictum est: Non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens. Et tamen filius Dei umbraculum est credentibus.

Ideo quanquam haec immundities est in sanctis, tamen placent personae propter filium Dei, fide accipientes imputationem iusticiae, iuxta dicta: Beati quorum tecta sunt peccata. Item: Pro hoc orabit ad te omnis sanctus.

Item: Si actiones carnis spiritu mortificabitis, vivetis. Et usitatum est, haec peccata nominare venialia, seu non regnantia.

Hae quinque quaestiones semper repetendae sunt in doctrina de bonis operibus, nunc aspiciamus eruditissimam Pauli concionem.

Initio generale praeceptum tradit de coërcendo corpore iuxta omnia praecepta moralia: Offerte corpora hostiam vivam, et praestate cultum rationalem, ut novitas et imago Dei in mente crescat, sicut alibi inquit Ephe.

4.: Renovamini spiritu mentis vestrae, et induite novum hominem, qui secundum Deum creatus erat in iusticia et sanctitate vera. Opponit autem obedientiam iuxta praecepta moralia cultibus Leviticis, ideo inquit: Offerte hostiam vivam et cultum rationalem.

Nominat vivam hostiam, quia Deus ideo restituit vitam aeternam, ut in tota aeternitate simus vivi cum ipso, et ipse sese communicet nobis. Deus condidit rationales creaturas, angelos et homines, ut essent creaturae, quibus sese et sua summa bona, vitam, lucem, sapientiam et iusticiam communicet, et ab his vicissim requirit conformatem, et huius bonitatis agnitionem et celebrationem.

Haec conformitas cum Deo, et agnitio ac celebratio bonitatis Dei, sunt veri et aeterni cultus Dei, qui in hac vita incoantur, postea erunt integri: et iidem cultus nominantur λογικὴ λατρεία, id est, cultus mentis, in quo mens fide, aut coram intuetur Deum, et vere sentit timorem et laetitiam in Deo, iuxta dictum: Veri adoratores adorabunt patrem in spiritu et veritate, id est, Spiritu sancto accendente veros et ardentes motus, timorem, fiduciam, dilectionem et laetitiam. Veritate, id est, vera agnitione Dei, quae fit verbo lucente in corde, per quod filius ostendit voluntatem patris.

Opponenda est igitur λογικὴ λατρεία, non tantum mactationibus pecorum, sed universaliter vanissimae imaginationi eorum, qui dicunt, aliqua opera externa aut rationalia, etiam in non renatis, placere Deo ex opere operato, sine bono motu utentis, sicut Papistae scripserunt, Missam mereri aliis ex opere operato, etiamsi Sacrificulus sit adulter, aut sicut dixerunt, opera moralia honesta etiam in non renatis mereri gratiam. Has falsas imaginationes saepe taxant Prophetae, ut Psalm 49.: Nunquid manducabo carnes taurorum, Psalm 50.: Holocausted non delectaberis.

Oseae. 6.: Misericordiam volo, non sacrificium, et scientiam magis quam holocausta.

Denique saepissime repetita est haec concio, et summa comprehensa est in his dictis: Veri adoratores adorabunt patrem in spiritu et veritate. Item: Nemo venit ad patrem nisi per filium.

Ex hac tota doctrina sumatur enarratio, quid sit λογικὴ λατρεία, inde et definitio sumatur.

3. ENARRATIO EPIST. PAULI AD ROMANOS. CAP. XII. Cultus Dei est opus a Deo mandatum, factum in vera agnitione et timore Dei, et vera fiducia filii, hoc fine, ut Deo praestetur obedientia, et honos, id est, ut hoc opere testemur, hunc verum Deum esse, quem sic colimus, ut castitas Ioseph est cultus Dei, quia in mente Ioseph sunt vera agnitio Dei, timor et fiducia mediatoris, et opus refertur ad hunc finem, ut ostendat hunc vere Deum esse quem sic colimus, et quomodo velit coli.

Castitas in Scipione est sine luce Dei et agnitione mediatoris, ideo non est cultus Dei.

Quaerat autem aliquis: Cum Deus postulet vivas hostias, et perpetuum cultum mentis, ad quem usum instituit mactationes pecudum, et alias ceremonias?

Respondeo: Ut conservetur ministerium docendi verbum Dei, ad quod opus est duabus rebus: docentibus et congregatione.

Sunt ergo instituta signa, quae et commonefactiones essent additae doctrinae, et nervi congregationis, et multae ceremoniae institutae sunt, ut inde doctores alerentur, ut oblatio primitiarum, decimarum et pecudum.

Hos fines intelligi oportet in cultibus seu sacrificiis ceremonialibus.

Ut autem cultum definivimus, ita eodem modo sacrificium in genere definiri potest.

Sacrificium est opus, mandatum a Deo, factum in vera agnitione, timore Dei et fide, hoc fine, ut Deo praestetur obedientia, et hoc opere ostendatur testimonium, quod hic sit verus Deus, cui praestetur haec obedientia.

Adde, cum de sacrificiis hominum loquimur, factum fiducia mediatoris.

Sunt autem sacrificii species iuxta generalem definitionem duae: Propiciatorium et εὐχαριστικὸν.

Propiciatorium est unum, videlicet solius Christi obedientia, quae meretur aliis remissionem peccatorum et reconciliationem.

Nam Levitica, quae nominabantur propiciationes, et pro peccato, erant tantum typi, nequaquam merebantur remissionem peccatorum.

Ideo scriptum est: Impossibile fuit sanguine taurorum tolli peccata.

Caetera omnia, cum recte fiunt, sunt εὐχαριστικὰ, sive sint cemoriae, sive alia bona opera, sicut dicitur: Sacrificium Deo spiritus contribulatus, cor contritum et humiliatum Deus non despicies.

Non est condita haec natura, ut sit otiosa, sed ut Deus communicet nobis suam lucem, sapientiam, iusticiam et laetitiam in tota aeternitate, et vicissim vult Deus celebrari in hac vita, et post hanc vitam: ideo necesse est actiones aliquas esse, quarum omnium finis sit celebratio Dei.

Hae omnes in hac vita et post hanc vitam sunt reipsa sacrificia laudis, seu εὐχαριστικὰ, καὶ λογικὴ λατρεία.

Osiandri partitio tria membra facit: Typicum, propiciatorium et θρεπτήριον, quo alebantur sacerdotes.

Haec distributio mihi non displicet, sed commodius est nominare εὐχαριστικὸν, ut comprehendantur omnia sacrificia spiritus, et ceremoniae.

Has distinctiones necesse est extare, ut discernantur sacrificium filii Dei ab omnium aliorum hominum sacrificiis.

Nam caetera nequaquam sunt ἱλαστικὰ, seu propiciatoria, id est, non merentur remissionem peccatorum et reconciliationem: ac multi errores irrepserunt in Ecclesiam, non recte intellecto vocabulo Sacrificii.

Quare necesse est iuniores de hac distinctione admoneri.

Cognitis his fundamentis intelligi potest, quid Paulus nominet λογικὴν λατρείαν, et haec est sancta, id est, vere dedicata Deo, non prophana, ut virtutes in Ethnicis, in quibus non lucet vera agnitio Dei et mediatoris: est et Deo placens, ut supra dictum est, quomodo bona opera placeant Deo, scilicet mandata a Deo et facta in agnitione mediatoris et fiducia filii.

Ne imitemini gestus huius mundi.

Ut antea instituit generalem propositionem de obedientia secundum omnia praecepta: Offerte λογικὴν λατρείαν, ita nunc eam repetit iuxta omnia praecepta: Ne habemus affectus similes mundanorum, sed novos affectus Deo conformes.

Nam cum vetat imitari gestus mundi, non vituperat res, quarum usum Deus ordinavit, non vetat usum ciborum, coniugii, imperiorum, indiciorum, contractuum, et aliarum ordinationum Dei, sed prohibet vitiosos affectus, ideo inquit: Gestus, id est, motus animorum non sint similes mundanis, ut contra ordinationem Dei adpetant impii voluptates, quaerunt opes et potentiam iniustis modis, certant ambitione, ardent iniustis odiis, turbant Ecclesiam et politias privatis cupiditatibus.

Haec vitia regnant in maxima parte generis humani, de qua parte generis humani contraria conversis ad Deum, saepe usurpatur adpellatio mundi, ut 1. Iohannis 2.: Omne quod est in mundo, est concupiscentia carnis et concupiscentia oculorum.

Iubet autem renovari mente, id est, iubet nos habere alias noticias de Deo recte agnoscere Deum, et firma assensione universam doctrinam amplecti, et in corde habere affectus conformes Deo, verum timorem, fiduciam, laetitiam in Deo, spem, dilectionem, patientiam, castitatem, et alias virtutes.

Ideo addit: Ut agnoscatis, quae sit voluntas Dei bona.

Simplicissime interpretatur, quod antea dixit, Renovamini mente: loquitur enim de voluntate Dei revelata in praeceptis, comminationibus et promissionibus, quasi dicat: Recte agnoscite Deum, et recte agnoscite voluntatem eius immensa bonitate patefactam in lege et Evangelio, et congruat obedientia interior et exterior cum verbo Dei. Ut quia sciunt tres viri in Babylone bonam voluntatem Dei, id est, mandatum Dei esse, non invocare idola, obediunt Deo, nec franguntur metu poenae, sed anteferunt mandatum Dei suae vitae. Haec est simplex enarratio huius dicti.

Dico vobis per gratiam, quae data est mihi.

Antea posuit generalem propositionem de omnibus virtutibus, seu de universali obedientia. Nunc accedit ad speciales virtutes, et quia inter eas, quae ad ministerium, seu ad gubernationem pertinent, Duae sunt praecipue: Obedientia in vocatione, et iusticia servans metas in iudicando. De his duabus virtutibus initio concionatur. Ut enim in politica gubernatione valde perniciosa est πολυπραγμοσύνη, cum privati homines ingerunt se negotiis, et impediunt ordinarios gubernatores: aut cum ardeliones, qui praesunt, agunt aliena: sic Ecclesiae nocent inquieti homines, qui vel stulto zelo, vel odiis incitati, aut extra vocationem erumpunt, et multa reformare in doctrina aut ritibus conantur, quae melius erat non mutari: aut e regione doctores Ecclesiae leges ferunt magistratibus de civilibus negotiis, et habent alterum pedem in Curia, alterum in Ecclesia, ut de Cleone Aristophanes dicebat, Habere eum alterum pedem in castris, alterum in concione.

Est autem virtus tertii praecepti obedientia in vocatione. Polypragmon seu ardelio pugnat cum tertio praecepto et cum dicto Pauli: Propria faciatis. Alterum malum est Arrogantia in iudicando de ignotis, id quoque prohibet hoc loco Paulus, cum vetat sapere praeter quam oportet: et iubet modeste sapere, et tradit normam, ut prophetiae sint analogae fidei, id est, ut enarrationes et iudicia congruant cum fide.

Notum est autem, neminem sibi debere iudicium sumere de eo, quod nesciat, ideo scriptum Deuteron. 17.: Cum fuerit nunciatum, audias et bene inquiri, et cum fuerit verum et certum, poena sequatur.

Et eadem sententia saepe repetita est in mandatis divinis. Et Matth. 5. dicitur: Caeco si caecus dux fuerit, ambo in foveam cadunt. Syracides cap. 11.: Priusquam audieris, ne respondeas. Et tamen usitatissimum est, fascinatos persuasione iudicare non cognitis fontibus, contra quos et in Exodo dicitur: Non sequaris turbam in iudicando. Idem et ratio docet: Quodque parum novit nemo docere potest. Et Plato inquit: οὐ πλήθει δικάζειν ἀλλ᾽ ἐπιστήμῃ. Huc et illa pertinent: Quam quisque artem didicit, hanc exerceat. τέκτων γὰρ ὢν, ἔπραττες οὐ ξυλουργικά.

Talibus sententiis commonefacti, simus in iudicando circumspectiores, et fontes quaeramus, et non simus ἰδιοβουλεύοντες, sed libenter conferamus nostras cogitationes cum aliorum peritorum iudiciis, ut 1 Corinth. 15. praecipitur. Et in primis teneamus regulam, Ut prophetia sit analoga fidei, id est, ut enarrationes et iudicia congruant cum fundamento, id est, cum lege et Evangelio et symbolis. Hanc normam sciri et sciri et sequi necesse est, iuxta dictum: Si quis aliud Evangelium docet, anathema sit. Necesse est igitur, prius nosse incorruptum Evangelium, iuxta dictum: Erudimini qui iudicatis terram.

Iam considera quam horrendi furores omnibus temporibus orti sint ab interpretationibus pugnantibus cum fide, ut corruptelae Ebionis, Cerinthi, Samosateni, qui negaverunt in Christo esse naturam divinam. Et Samosatenus et Servetus astuta interpretatione depraverunt textum in Iohanne: In principio erat verbum. Item: Manichaei et similes tetra portenta contra legem et Evangelium finxerunt, ut nostro tempore Anabaptistae.

Omnibus temporibus fuerunt similes aliqui Pharisaeis, qui sustulerunt discrimen legis et Evangelii, et finxerunt homines mereri remissionem peccatorum et iustos esse externa disciplina, sicut somniat Pharisaeus Lucae 18.

Talis fuit imaginatio Pelagii, Papistarum et Monachorum, in qua magnum chaos est errorum. Delent totam doctrinam de iusticia fidei, fingunt homines mereri remissionem peccatorum, et iustos esse propriis operibus. Postea addunt: Quia nemo scit, quando satis operum habeat, dubitandum esse, an sis in gratia. Haec nequaquam sunt ἀνάλογα fidei.

Sunt et manifeste idolatrica, Invocatio mortuorum, quia scriptum est, Dominum Deum tuum adorabis. Item, Adoratio panis in circumgestatione. Item, Ficticia oblatio in Missa pro mortuis. Nec fuit credendum fallacibus spiritibus, qui petiverunt celebrari Missas pro mortuis. Quia scriptum est Esaiae 8.: Non a mortuis require veritatem, sed ad legem et ad testimonium.

Nec sunt ἀνάλογα fidei ea, quae de votis, de satisfactionibus et aliis ritibus humanis fingunt, quos dicunt esse cultus Dei necessarios, et mereri remissionem peccatorum.

Nec sunt ἀνάλογα fidei anabaptistica deliramenta, quae sint partim pharisaica, partim furores Manichaei, delentes politicum ordinem.

Hunc brevem catalogum addidi, ut iuniores diligentius cogitent de hac regula. Prophetia sit analoga fidei, et sint circumspecti in iudicanda doctrina et iudicandis interpretationibus, et muniant se inquisitione verae doctrinae et precatione.

Deinde sequitur in textu longa coacervatio multorum praeceptorum de dilectione mutua, de beneficentia, de diligentia in invocatione, de patientia, de precatione, de humilitate, de reprimenda cupiditate privatae vindictae etc. Haec mandata distribuantur in decalogum, nec difficile est videre, ad quod caput decalogi singula pertineant, sicut alias saepe monemus doctrinam de virtutibus in decalogum distribuendam esse.

## 13:1 Disposition of Romans: Argument
Chapter XIII.

Proposition.

Let everyone obey his own magistrate. He adds reasons drawn from the dignity of the magistrate, and from the punishment which avenges the contempt of the magistrate.

Here again it appears that Paul delivers precepts concerning morals differently than the Philosophers do. For he teaches us concerning the will of God, that the politeia (civil government) is a divine ordinance, just as the changes of the seasons, winter, summer, day, night, and these perpetual courses and motions of the stars, are both founded by God and are preserved. Thus God has ordained and preserves the politeia in the world, the magistrates and the laws.

There have been many fanatical men even in our own times, who have contended that it is not lawful for a Christian to hold the office of magistrate, because the Gospel often forbids vengeance. And so they have felt that the magistracy is robbery and unjust force. Against this impious and seditious opinion, Paul fortifies us, and teaches that the magistracy is a divine ordinance, or a good work of God; wherefore it happens that those who hold the magistracy are performing a lawful and honest office.

No one can express in words how great are the benefits this doctrine brings, both to magistrates and to subjects.

For magistrates can perform their office with a good conscience, when they know that their way of life and their administration are pleasing to God. And they dare to expect and ask for help from God, since they hold his place, so that he may defend and govern his ministers. No armies, no fortresses, can better protect princes in so many dangers and snares of the devil than this trust in divine help.

Furthermore, no reason moves the minds of men more effectively to obey the magistrate than if they know that he is a minister of God, and that he is to be venerated, just as other sacred things, and that this obedience is rendered not to men, but to God.

As we have honor for sacred ceremonies, because they have been commended to us by the word of God, and certain benefits of God are exhibited to us through them: so pious minds have honor for the magistrate, because he is commended by the word of God, and they recognize the benefits of God, justice, and tranquility coming to us through them. Besides this, they understand that the magistrate cannot be oppressed by human force, because they know he is defended by God. And because punishment or vengeance is the work of God, they do not doubt that the seditious will pay the penalty, even if the forces of the magistrate seem to be lacking for punishment. In this way, this doctrine of Paul fosters reverence toward magistrates and laws.

What similar thing is read in Plato's Republic?

Paul teaches that laws and magistrates are an ordinance of God. Plato condemns the present form of the republic, invents a new politeia, and, saying nothing consistent with the judgment of human reason, speaks insults against kings, like a buffoon.
