And there exist books written by some in these recent years, where they falsely mock princes, and often even the way of life is censured, as if it were fighting against the Gospel.

And all men are moved by nature, when they consider the vices of princes, when they look upon the changes of kingdoms, to suspect that empires are established and retained by human violence without the counsel of God. Against scandals of this kind, this passage of Paul must be opposed, so that it may accustom us to fear and magnify the magistrate from the heart. And I would wish that those who teach the Gospel would treat and illustrate this passage diligently and assiduously.

Furthermore, that vengeance is forbidden in some places, that must be understood only of private vengeance.

For here magistrates are expressly excepted; vengeance is called divine, which magistrates exercise, so that we may know that political administration is truly the work of God. There is also emphasis in the word: They are ordained.

For ordination signifies the form of government, that is, laws, judgments, punishments, contracts: therefore it approves not only of the magistrate, but also of the laws and the whole form of the republic, namely marriages, the division of property, contracts, and judgments. It embraces all these things, so that we may know that we can use civil affairs with a good conscience, just as we do food, clothing, air, and light. And surely we should not think that civil ordinances, laws, contracts, judgments, and magistrates are less necessary for bodily life than food is, or the air which we breathe.

Wherefore, the Anabaptists and others, who vituperate public laws, who condemn judgments, who dream of piety, and how easy it is to err here, are waging war not with the magistrates, but with the whole of human nature. Wherefore I have thought it necessary to warn the reader, that he should fortify his heart in this place against . such fanatical opinions, which the devil sows, so that he may render the Gospel hateful, and so that by stirred-up seditions he may dissipate Churches and republics.

Christian doctrine was for this reason hateful to great men among the Gentiles, because they judged that by the prohibition of vengeance, magistrates and judgments were being removed from the republic, that impunity was being granted to the wicked and the criminal, and that the bonds of peace and civil society were being severed. To these things they thought that in the Gospel a certain Platonic community of goods was being commanded, which utterly abhors the nature of the human race.

Here our people labor in refuting.

Some respond that these precepts pertain to the perfect, so that they may not exercise vengeance, so that they may share their goods; they invent circles, some of the imperfect, others of the perfect, but these things do not satisfy the adversaries.

And as long as the opinion clings in the Church that perfection consists in works of this kind, there is never a lack of material for tumults.

For fanatical men arise who disapprove of the office of magistrates, who condemn the civil custom of life. Such opinions, scattered among the ignorant, disturb the consciences of many and stir up the greatest commotions.

Wherefore it is useful to root out these errors from the minds of men.

This will be done if men are rightly taught about the justice of faith, that perfection does not consist in external observations of life, but in fear and faith, that it is permitted in the external custom of life to use all civil things, just as food, air, and similar natural things, because Christ delivers eternal justice, which is attained through faith.

Meanwhile, he does not abolish civil duties, but highly approves and requires them, and wishes us to serve politically ordained structures religiously. When men have known what the kingdom of Christ is, and what the difference is between the kingdom of Christ and the kingdom of the world or πολιτείαν [polity], and that the Gospel most severely commands that honor be held for authority, that we obey from the heart and with the fear of God, this matter will be of the greatest use for retaining public peace and the dignity of magistrates.

Furthermore, this Epistle of Paul teaches us copiously about both kingdoms, what the kingdom of Christ is, and what is to be thought about the polity. And someone might be able to divide the Epistle in this way, that in the former part he teaches us about the kingdom of Christ, in the latter he teaches about the polity.

Formerly both topics lay in the doctrine of the Monks, buried in more than Cimmerian darkness.

Now, by the grace of God, they have been revealed and illustrated again.

But to what end the sentences about vengeance pertain, we have often said elsewhere.

For they are most effective for confirming magistrates. Christ repeats the same thing so often, so that the disciples may learn that magistrates are not to be violated.

For he prohibits vengeance to those who are not in the magistracy, and who were dreaming of a new kingdom of the world. Just as even now the Jews hope that they will possess the empire of the whole world.

Christ wished to remove this error from the disciples, which is why he so often forbids taking revenge.

But we have spoken of these sentences elsewhere.

Therefore, when you look upon the magistrate, when you look upon the fasces, when you look upon the signs of empire, when you hear laws recited, when you see judgment being exercised, or men contracting among themselves by law, remember that these are the ordinance of God, which, unless it were preserved by God, could not stand against the cruelty of the devil, who, since he is a murderer, assiduously incites the wicked to disturb this most beautiful harmony of the human race.

Therefore, give thanks to God, who, just as he ordained the perpetual course of the sun, so he ordained the πολιτείαν [polity], and pray that he may retain tranquility, and govern the minds of princes, so that they may rule rightly and happily.

If there is any vice in princes, let us accuse ourselves, who, since we are ungrateful to God, and by despising the magistrate corrupt this benefit, are not worthy of those to whom more useful princes have fallen.

For what the Poet says: Whatever madness kings commit, the Greeks pay the price, is truly said: but that is truer, that princes are often afflicted because of our sins.

But let someone say: Since Paul approves the polities of the Gentiles, should a Christian also use the laws of the Milesians or Sybarites, concerning the prostitution of new brides, etc.?

Paul saw that this could be objected, therefore he also added about the office of the magistrate, and about the laws, what kind they ought to be.

They ought to honor good work, and punish crimes. But what are good works, the law of nature judges: Therefore Paul concedes that we use the laws of the Gentiles which are consonant with reason.

It is a confusion of the divine ordinance to approve of manifest turpitude.

But it is not the purpose of this work to explain the individual particles of the text, for they are very rich.

The conclusion is with Paul.

Therefore it is necessary to obey, not only because of wrath, but because of conscience, that is, to speak briefly, if you can XIII. 1. ANNOTATIONS ON THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. to escape a robber, you commit no sin, but even if you can escape the punishment of the magistrate, nevertheless you ought not to reject the authority; this is what he says, not on account of wrath only, but on account of conscience.

And indeed he says, It is necessary to obey.

But just as individuals should obey the magistrates, so also they should obey their laws. Let those obey the Roman laws whose magistrate uses Roman law. Let those obey the Saxon laws whose magistrate uses Saxon law.

Let each one use the laws of his own magistrate in contracting business. Theologians dispute superstitiously about which contracts are to be approved, since that matter does not pertain to the judgment of Theologians, but to the cognizance of the magistrate.

It is permitted to use all contracts which the magistrate approves, or which the laws approve, just as it is permitted to use other political ordinances. And just as a magistrate ought not to be a misanthrope (μισάνθρωπος), but to grant much to the times, and to bend laws toward equity, so in judging contracts, one is not to seek for exact justice (ἀκριβοδίκαιον), and to bind consciences to some one most exact form.

And it is very profitable for consoling consciences to hold this general rule, that just as it is permitted for a Christian to use other political ordinances, so in contracts it is sufficient to follow the received laws or the judgment of the magistrate. This the Theologian ought to teach, just as he ought to teach that it is permitted for the sick to use medicine, and that they ought to have regard for the body.

That does not pertain to the Theologian, which medicines are to be given to those laboring with fever or pleurisy. For these arts are subject to the judgment of reason, and have certain experts; they are not taught in the Gospel. Thus political (πολιτικά) affairs are subject to the judgment of reason, and indeed of the magistrate; they are not taught in the Gospel.

In Strabo I see φόρος (tribute) called a certain revenue from possessions, which is paid to magistrates, but τέλος (tax), a toll, or an imposed tribute, and it seems Paul wished to include ordinary burdens.

Epilogue of the precepts.

He contracts the precepts into the decalogue, and the second table of the decalogue into the precept concerning the love of one's neighbor. You shall love your neighbor etc.

He adds to the exhortation an argument taken from the debt of the new revelation of the word, which he compares to light. From that metaphor he draws an argument.

Those things are to be done which are becoming in the light.

Latin:

Caput XIII.

Propositio.

Unusquisque obediat suo magistratui. Rationes addit ductas ex dignitate magistratus, et ex poena quae ulciscitur contemtum magistratus.

Hic rursus apparet Paulum aliter tradere praecepta de moribus, quam tradunt Philosophi. Docet enim nos de voluntate Dei, quod πολιτεία sit ordinatio divina, sicut vices temporum, hyems, aestas, dies, nox et hi perpetui cursus ac motus siderum, a Deo, et conditi sunt, et conservantur. Ita ordinavit Deus et conservat πολιτείαν in mundo, magistratus et leges.

Multi fuerunt fanatici homines etiam nostris temporibus, qui contenderunt non licere Christiano gerere magistratum, quia Evangelium saepe prohibeat vindictam. Itaque magistratum senserunt latrocinium ac iniustam vim esse. Adversus hanc impiam ac seditiosam opinionem munit nos Paulus, ac docet magistratum, esse ordinationem divinam, seu opus Dei bonum, quare fit, ut hi qui gerunt magistratum, tractent officium licitum et honestum.

Nemo verbis consequi potest quantas afferat utilitates, tum magistratibus, tum subditis haec doctrina.

Nam magistratus bona conscientia suum officium facere possunt, cum sciunt, suum vitae genus, suam procurationem Deo placere. Et audent a Deo expectare ac petere auxilium, quoniam ipsius gerunt vicem, ut defendat et gubernet suos ministros. Nulli exercitus, nullae arces, magis munire principes in tot periculis et insidiis diaboli queunt, quam haec fiducia auxilii divini.

Deinde nulla ratio efficacius movet animos hominum, ut magistratui pareant, quam si sciant Dei ministrum esse, et venerandum esse, ut alias res sacras, et hanc obedientiam non hominibus, sed Deo praestari.

Ut sacris ceremoniis honorem habemus, quia verbo Dei nobis commendatae sunt, et certa beneficia Dei nobis per eas exhibentur: ita magistratui habent honorem piae mentes, quia verbo Dei commendatus est, et agnoscunt beneficia Dei, ius, et tranquillitatem per illos nobis contingere. Ad haec intelligunt non posse humana vi magistratum opprimi, quia sciunt eum a Deo defendi. Et quia poena seu vindicta opus Dei est, nihil dubitant quin seditiosi poenas daturi sint, etiam si vires magistratui ad puniendum deesse videantur. Ad hunc modum alit reverentiam erga magistratus et leges haec Pauli doctrina.

Quid simile in Platonis republica legitur?

Paulus docet leges et magistratus ordinationem Dei esse. Plato damnat praesentem reipublicae formam, fingit novam πολιτείαν, et nihil congruentem ad rationis humanae iudicium, dicit convicia regibus, tanquam scurra. Et extant quorundam libri scripti his proximis annis, ubi falso irrident principes, saepe etiam vitae genus taxatur, tanquam pugnans cum Evangelio.

Et natura moventur omnes homines, cum vitia principum considerant, cum regnorum mutationes intuentur, ut suspicentur humana violentia sine consilio Dei imperia et constitui et retineri. Adversus huiusmodi scandala opponendus est hic Pauli locus, ut assuefaciat nos, ut ex animo magistratus vereamur, et magnificiamus. Et optarim hos qui docent Evangelium, hunc locum diligenter et sedulo tractare et illustrare.

Caeterum quod vindicta alicubi prohibetur, id tantum de vindicta privata intelligi debet.

Nam hic diserte excipiuntur magistratus, vindicta appellatur divina, quam exercent magistratus, ut sciamus vere opus Dei esse administrationem politicam. Est et emphasis in voce: Ordinatae sunt.

Nam ordinatio significat formam imperii, hoc est, leges, iudicia, poenas, contractus: proinde adprobat non tantum magistratus, sed leges etiam et totam formam reipublicae, scilicet coniugia, rerum divisionem, contractus, iudicia. Haec omnia complectitur, ut sciamus nos civilibus rebus bona conscientia uti posse, sicut victu, vestitu, aere, luce. Neque sane minus ad vitam corporalem existimemus necessarias esse civiles ordinationes, leges, contractus, iudicia, magistratus, quam victus est, aut aër quem haurimus.

Quare non cum magistratibus, sed cum tota natura humana bellum gerunt Anabaptistae et alii, qui publicas leges vituperant, qui damnant iudicia, qui somniant pietatem, et quam proclive sit hic errare. Quare duxi monendum esse lectorem, ut hoc loco muniat pectus adversus. fanaticas opiniones, quas serit diabolus, ut Evangelium reddat invisum, et ut excitatis seditionibus dissipet Ecclesias et respublicas.

Doctrina Christiana hoc nomine fuit invisa magnis viris inter Ethnicos, quod vindicta prohibita iudicabant magistratus et iudicia e repub. tolli, impunitatem improbis et facinorosis concedi, et vincula pacis et civilis societatis rescindi. Ad haec putabant in Evangelio Platonicam quandam communicationem facultatum praecipi, quae prorsus a natura humani generis abhorret.

Hic nostri laborant in confutando.

Nonnulli respondent haec praecepta ad perfectos pertinere, ne vindictam exerceant, ut communicent facultates, fingunt circulos, alios imperfectorum, alios perfectorum, sed haec non satisfaciunt adversariis.

Et donec haeret in Ecclesia opinio, quod perfectio sit in huiusmodi operibus, nunquam deest materia tumultuum.

Exoriuntur enim fanatici homines, qui improbant magistratuum officium, qui damnant civilem vitae consuetudinem. Tales opiniones sparsae in imperitos, multorum conscientias perturbant, et maximos motus cient.

Quare utile est hos errores radicitus ex animis hominum evellere.

Id ita fiet, si recte doceantur homines de iusticia fidei, quod perfectio non sit in externis vitae observationibus, sed in timore ac fide, quod liceat in externa consuetudine vitae uti omnibus civilibus rebus, sicut victu aëre, et similibus rebus naturalibus, quod Christus iusticiam aeternam tradat, quae contingit per fidem.

Interea non aboleat civilia officia, sed maxime probet et requirat ea, et velit nos religiose servire politicis ordinationibus. Cum cognoverint homines, quid sit regnum Christi, et quid intersit inter regnum Christi, et regnum mundi seu πολιτείαν, et quod Evangelium severissime praecipiat, ut honos habeatur potestati, ut ex animo et cum timore Dei obtemperemus, ea res plurimum ad retinendam publicam pacem, et dignitatem magistratuum profuerit.

Porro haec Epistolae Pauli copiose nos de utroque regno docet, quit sit regnum Christi, et quid de politia sentiendum sit. Ac possit aliquis hoc modo partiri Epistolam, quod in priore parte doceat nos de regno Christi, in posteriore doceat de politia.

Olim uterque locus in doctrina Monachorum iacuit obrutus plusquam Cimmeriis tenebris.

Nunc Dei beneficio iterum patefacti et illustrati sunt.

Quorsum autem pertineant sententiae de vindicta, saepe alias diximus.

Maxime enim ad confirmandos magistratus valent. Toties idem repetit Christus, ut discant discipuli non esse violandos magistratus.

Prohibet enim illis vindictam, qui non sunt in magistratu, quique somniabant novum regnum mundi. Sicut adhuc Iudaei sperant se imperio orbis terrarum potituros esse.

Hunc errorem voluit Christus eximere discipulis, quare toties vetat ulcisci.

Sed de his sententiis alibi diximus.

Itaque cum magistratum, cum fasces, cum imperii signa intueris, cum audis leges recitare, cum vides exerceri iudicium, aut lege homines inter se contrahere, memineris haec esse Dei ordinationem, quam nisi a Deo conservaretur, non posset consistere adversus diaboli saevitiam, qui cum sit homicida, assidue incitat improbos ad perturbandam hanc pulcerrimam harmoniam humani generis.

Itaque agas gratias Deo, qui ut perpetuum solis cursum, ita πολιτείαν, ordinavit, et ores ut tranquillitatem retineat, et gubernet animos principum, ut recte et feliciter imperent.

Si quid est vitii in principibus, nos accusemus, qui cum Deo simus ingrati, et contemto magistratu hoc beneficium corrumpamus, non sumus digni quibus contigerint utiliores principes.

Nam quod Poëta inquit: Quicquid delirant reges, plectuntur Achivi, vere dictum est: sed illud est verius, principes saepe affligi propter nostra peccata.

Verum dicat aliquis: Cum probat Paulus gentium politias, uteturne Christianus etiam Milesiorum aut Sybaritarum legibus, de prostituendis novis nuptis etc.

Vidit Paulus hoc obiici posse, propterea etiam addidit de officio magistratus, et de legibus, quales esse debeant.

Debent autem bonum opus honore afficere, et punire flagitia. Quae vero sint bona opera, lex naturae iudicat: Ergo concedit Paulus, ut gentium legibus utamur, quae sunt consentaneae rationi.

Confusio ordinationis divinae est, probare manifestam turpitudinem.

Sed non est huius instituti explicare singulas particulas textus, sunt enim uberrimae.

Conclusio apud Paulum est.

Ideo necesse est obedire, non tantum propter iram, sed propter conscientiam, hoc est, ut breviter dicam, si potes XIII. 1. ANNOTATIONES IN EPIST. PAULI AD ROMANOS. effugere latronem, nihil peccas, sed etiam si possis effugere poenam magistratus, tamen non debes detrectare imperium, hoc est quod ait, non propter iram tantum, sed propter conscientiam.

Et quidem ait, Necesse est obedire.

Sicut autem magistratibus, ita et legibus suis singuli pareant. Romanis legibus pareant isti, quorum magistratus Romano iure utitur. Saxonicis legibus pareant isti, quorum magistratus Saxonico iure utitur.

Unusquisque utatur sui magistratus legibus in contrahendis rebus. Theologi superstitiose disputant, qui contractus sint probandi, cum ea res ad Theologorum iudicium non pertineat, sed ad magistratus cognitionem.

Licet uti contractibus omnibus, quos magistratus approbat, seu quos leges approbant, sicut uti licet aliis politicis ordinationibus. Et ut magistratus non debet esse μισάνθρωπος, sed multa concedere temporibus, et leges ad aequitatem flectere, ita in iudicandis contractibus, non est quaerendum ἀκριβοδίκαιον, et alligandae conscientiae ad unam aliquam exactissimam formam.

Ac valde prodest ad conscientias consolandas tenere hanc generalem regulam, quod ut aliis politicis ordinationibus licet uti Christiano, ita in contractibus satis est recepta iura seu iudicium magistratus sequi. Hoc docere Theologus debet, quemadmodum docere debet, quod aegrotis liceat uti medicina, quod debeant honorem habere corpori.

Illud ad Theologum non pertinet, quae pharmaca danda sint laborantibus febri, aut pleuritide. Nam hae artes subiectae sunt iudicio rationis, et habent certos artifices, non docentur in Evangelio. Sic negotia πολιτικά subiecta sunt iudicio rationis, et quidem magistratus, non docentur in Evangelio.

Apud Strabonem video φόρον appellari certum reditum ex possessionibus, qui penditur magistratibus, τέλος autem, vectigal, seu tributum superindictum, ac videtur Paulus ordinaria onera voluisse complecti.

Epilogus praeceptorum.

Contrahit praecepta in decalogum, et decalogi secundam tabulam in praeceptum de dilectione proximi. Diliges proximum etc.

Addit adhortationi argumentum ex debito sumtum a nova revelatione verbi, quam luci comparat. Ex ea metaphora ducit argumentum.

Ea sunt agenda, in quae luce decent.

## 13:1 Argument
Chapter XIII.

In the previous chapter he recounted precepts concerning private morals. Now he adds the doctrine concerning political life. For although the Gospel preaches concerning reconciliation with God and eternal justice, and does not bring laws specifically concerning successions, contracts, the form of judgments, or the distinction of actions—for God has commended these to the counsel of the political magistrate, just as the Gospel does not teach specifically the art of medicine or architecture—nevertheless, in general, it is necessary that the word of God, or divine testimony, exist concerning the use of these external and corporal things, for two reasons. First, so that we may know that this very order is the work of God and a testimony of God's wisdom among us; second, so that we may know that the use is granted to the pious. Because it is necessary that our works have testimony from the word of God, as it is said in 1 Timothy 4: The creature is sanctified by the word and prayer.

It is also useful to know the struggles of the Church of all times. But there have always been fanatic men who condemned the political order, and stirred up great confusions, one after another. They wanted to bring about a Platonic community of goods, as Marcion, Carpocrates, and others did of old, whom Irenaeus refutes.

In the town of Pepusa in Phrygia, certain fanatics began such a kingdom as the Anabaptists in our time tried to establish in the city of Münster, and they named the town the new Jerusalem, which they would have more correctly named empousan (a phantom). But it was destroyed, and Montanus and Maximilla, the leaders of the faction, strangled themselves.

In our time, Anabaptists still wander about, who condemn magistrates, the distinction of dominions, contracts, judgments, and many others have been and are who deny that Roman laws should be used. Against these furies, let us know that the Church is fortified by this thirteenth chapter of Paul to the Romans, which for that reason ought to be most known to all, lest any, deceived by the hypocrisy of fanatic men, be entangled in false and seditious opinions.

First, therefore, let this rule be clearly and constantly held: The Gospel is the voice concerning the remission of sins and reconciliation with God through the mediator, and concerning light, justice, and eternal life in the hearts. Meanwhile, just as it allows bodies to use different spaces of days in different places, so it allows the use of different forms of polities, provided they agree with reason.

This rule has often been expressly handed down, as in Colossians 3: Put on the new man, who is renewed in knowledge after the image of him who created him, where there is no Greek, nor Jew, nor circumcision, nor uncircumcision, nor barbarian, nor Scythian, nor slave, nor free, but Christ is all in all. This illustrious distinction of the Gospel and are they in the saints in this life?

First I answer: By no means are there sins in the saints, or lapses against conscience, that is, when those who have been saints, knowingly and willingly violate the law of God, as David did when he seized another man's wife; these grieve and cast out the Holy Spirit, and cease to be saints, and again become subject to the wrath of God and eternal death, until they are converted again, according to these sayings: 1 Corinthians 6:

Do not be deceived, fornicators, idolaters, adulterers, etc., shall not inherit the kingdom of God. And Galatians 5:

The works of the flesh are manifest, adultery, murder, etc.; those who do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God. Item: Those who fall away from the foundation, that is, those who reject any article of faith, whether they understand it or not, but are deceived by illusions, these also cease to be saints, and cast out the Holy Spirit, and become subject to eternal wrath, as many fell away to the Arians, and many now also, who for a time thought rightly, reject the truth.

These degrees of sins are to be considered most diligently, which are commonly called mortal or reigning sins.

Therefore, the rule against the Antinomians must be held most firmly: Fight the good fight, keeping faith and a good conscience. What sins, then, remain in the saints in this life?

I answer: Much darkness and doubt, many omissions and vicious affections, which evils, however, the saints resist, so that they do not fall against their conscience, and they believe that these are covered on account of the Son of God. This darkness and impurity in man should not be considered a light evil, on account of which it is said: No one living shall be justified in your sight.

And yet the Son of God is a shelter for believers. Therefore, although this impurity is in the saints, yet the persons are pleasing on account of the Son of God, receiving by faith the imputation of righteousness, according to the sayings: Blessed are they whose sins are covered.

Item: For this, every saint shall pray to you. Item: If you mortify the actions of the flesh by the Spirit, you shall live.

And it is customary to call these sins venial, or not reigning. These five questions must always be repeated in the doctrine of good works; now let us look at Paul's most learned sermon.

At the beginning, he delivers a general precept about subduing the body according to all moral precepts: Offer your bodies as a living sacrifice, and perform a rational service, so that the newness and image of God may grow in the mind, just as he says elsewhere in Ephesians 4:

Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who was created according to God in true righteousness and holiness. He opposes, however, obedience according to moral precepts to the Levitical cults; therefore he says: Offer a living sacrifice and a rational service.

He calls it a living sacrifice, because God restored eternal life for this reason, that in all eternity we might be alive with Him, and He Himself might communicate Himself to us. God created rational creatures, angels and men, so that they might be creatures to whom He communicates Himself and His highest goods—life, light, wisdom, and righteousness—and from them in turn He requires conformity, and the recognition and celebration of this goodness.

This conformity with God, and the recognition and celebration of the goodness of God, are the true and eternal worship of God, which are begun in this life and will later be complete: and the same worship is called λογικὴ λατρεία [rational service], that is, the worship of the mind, in which the mind by faith, or in the presence of God, beholds Him, and truly feels fear and joy in God, according to the saying: True worshipers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth, that is, with the Holy Spirit kindling true and ardent motions, fear, trust, love, and joy. In truth, that is, in the true recognition of God, which happens by the Word shining in the heart, through which the Son shows the will of the Father. Therefore, λογικὴ λατρεία [rational service] must be opposed not only to the slaughtering of cattle, but universally to the most vain imagination of those who say that some external or rational works, even in the unregenerate, please God ex opere operato [by the work performed], without a good motion of the user, just as the Papists wrote that the Mass merits for others ex opere operato, even if the priest is an adulterer, or as they said, that honest moral works even in the unregenerate merit grace.

The Prophets often tax these false imaginations, as in Psalm 49: Shall I eat the flesh of bulls? Psalm 50: You will not delight in burnt offerings.

Hosea 6: I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and knowledge more than burnt offerings. Finally, this sermon is repeated most often, and the sum is contained in these sayings: True worshipers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth.

Item: No one comes to the Father except through the Son. From this whole doctrine, let the exposition be taken of what λογικὴ λατρεία [rational service] is, and from that, let the definition be taken.

The worship of God is a work commanded by God, performed in true knowledge and fear of God, and true trust in the Son, to this end, that obedience and honor be rendered to God, that is, that by this work we testify that this is the true God whom we thus worship; just as the chastity of Joseph is the worship of God, because in Joseph's mind there is true knowledge of God, fear, and trust in the Mediator, and the work is referred to this end, that it may show that this is truly the God whom we thus worship, and how He wills to be worshipped. Chastity in Scipio is without the light of God and the knowledge of the Mediator, therefore it is not the worship of God.

But someone might ask: Since God demands living sacrifices, and the perpetual worship of the mind, for what purpose did He institute the slaughter of cattle and other ceremonies?

I answer: So that the ministry of teaching the Word of God might be preserved, for which work two things are necessary: teachers and a congregation.

Therefore, signs were instituted, which were also added as reminders of the doctrine, and as the sinews of the congregation, and many ceremonies were instituted so that teachers might be supported thereby, such as the offering of firstfruits, tithes, and cattle.

These ends must be understood in ceremonial worships or sacrifices.

But as we have defined worship, so in the same way sacrifice in general can be defined.

Sacrifice is a work, commanded by God, performed in true knowledge, fear of God, and faith, to this end, that obedience be rendered to God, and by this work a testimony be shown, that this is the true God to whom this obedience is rendered.

Add, when we speak of the sacrifices of men, that it is performed with trust in the Mediator.

There are, however, two species of sacrifice according to the general definition: Propitiatory and eucharistic (εὐχαριστικόν).

Propitiatory is one, namely the obedience of Christ alone, which merits for others the remission of sins and reconciliation.

For the Levitical [sacrifices], which were called propitiations, and [sacrifices] for sin, were only types; they by no means merited the remission of sins.

Therefore it is written: It was impossible for the blood of bulls to take away sins.

All other things, when they are done rightly, are eucharistic (εὐχαριστικά), whether they be ceremonies or other good works, as it is said: A sacrifice to God is a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise.

This nature was not created to be idle, but so that God might communicate to us His light, wisdom, justice, and joy in all eternity, and in turn God wills to be celebrated in this life and after this life: therefore it is necessary that there be some actions, the end of all of which is the celebration of God.

All these in this life and after this life are in reality sacrifices of praise, or eucharistic (εὐχαριστικά), and a spiritual service (λογικὴ λατρεία).

Osiander's partition makes three members: Typical, propitiatory, and nutritive (θρεπτήριον), by which the priests were fed.

This distribution does not displease me, but it is more convenient to name it eucharistic (εὐχαριστικόν), so that all sacrifices of the spirit and ceremonies may be included.

It is necessary that these distinctions exist, so that the sacrifice of the Son of God may be distinguished from the sacrifices of all other men.

For the others are by no means expiatory (ἱλαστικά), or propitiatory, that is, they do not merit the remission of sins and reconciliation: and many errors have crept into the Church, because the word 'Sacrifice' was not rightly understood.

Wherefore it is necessary that the younger ones be admonished about this distinction.

Having known these foundations, it can be understood what Paul calls 'spiritual service' (λογικὴν λατρείαν), and this is holy, that is, truly dedicated to God, not profane, like the virtues in the Heathens, in whom the true knowledge of God and the Mediator does not shine: it is also pleasing to God, as was said above, how good works please God, namely, those commanded by God and performed in the knowledge of the Mediator and trust in the Son.

Do not be conformed to the ways of this world.

As he previously instituted a general proposition concerning obedience according to all the commandments: Offer a 'spiritual service' (λογικὴν λατρείαν), so now he repeats it according to all the commandments: Let us not have affections similar to those of the worldly, but new affections conformed to God.

For when he forbids imitating the ways of the world, he does not disparage the things whose use God has ordained; he does not forbid the use of food, marriage, governments, judgments, contracts, and other ordinances of God, but he forbids vicious affections; therefore he says: 'Ways', that is, the motions of the mind, should not be similar to the worldly, as the impious, contrary to the ordinance of God, covet pleasures, seek wealth and power by unjust means, contend with ambition, burn with unjust hatreds, and disturb the Church and polities with private desires.

These vices reign in the greatest part of the human race, for which part of the human race, contrary to those converted to God, the term 'world' is often used, as in 1 John 2:

Everything that is of political life always be in sight. Afterwards, let the dignity of political life also be considered, as described both in this chapter and in many prophetic testimonies. Let every soul be subject to the authorities that are over it.

At the beginning, he delivers the precept simply and clearly, that each one should obey his own magistrate. For the particle (that are over it) is not added idly, but excludes foreign magistrates. For it is not necessary for a citizen of Lübeck to obey the Parisian magistrate. Likewise, Paul removes the doubt of consciences if there is an obscure contention about the title, so that although the English king writes that he is king of France, yet it is not necessary for the citizens of the French kingdom to obey the English king.

Then he adds the reason for the precept: Since empires are an order divinely instituted, which is truly the work of God, God is angry with those who disturb this order. It is necessary, therefore, to obey for the sake of conscience.

Here, let the word 'Ordination' be diligently considered. For when human judgments look upon the confusion and vices in empires, they do not conclude that government is the work of God, but that it is established partly by human cunning, partly by force, and that empires are retained. And many things are disputed among philosophers concerning the causes.

But let us distinguish the political order from the persons and from the vices which the persons mix in. For the order itself is the knowledge of divine law, and the rank of those who rule and are ruled, and the laws passed by the true authority of magistrates, marriages, contracts, judgments, punishments, defense, legitimate militia, legitimate tributes, discipline in peace, studies of the sciences and other honest arts. This whole order in the human race is the work of God, just as the order of celestial motions and the fertility of the earth. And it is not only permissively from God, but God by His own wisdom and voice instituted this order, and as much of the order as remains, He Himself effectively preserves. Meanwhile, it is true that devils, and many instruments of devils—tyrants, seditious persons, and other wicked men—multiply to disturb this order, and mix in many confusions and many vices, just as wolves tear a part of a flock, and yet the faithful shepherd defends the remaining troop: so, as much of the order as remains in human society is preserved by the immense goodness of God Himself.

This article of faith must therefore be held: The political order is truly the work of God, and a good thing, and is a testimony of the wisdom, justice, and goodness of God toward men, and of His presence among men. For the law and judgments show wisdom; equality in contracts and the execution of punishments show justice: the wonderful preservation of the whole of human society amidst such great dangers shows goodness and presence. Likewise, the execution of punishments, which manifestly surpasses human strength, of which the Lord says: He who takes the sword shall perish by the sword.

Let testimonies therefore be added which affirm that the political order is the work of God.

Daniel 2: God transfers kingdoms and establishes them, that is, He causes them to flourish and endure. Proverbs 16: The balance and scales are the judgments of the Lord, and all the stones of the bag.

Psalm 126: Unless the Lord guards the city, he who guards it watches in vain.

God is the guardian and preserver of the political order, therefore He approves of it. Psalm 143: You who give salvation to kings. These words testify that governors are helped by God.

Proverbs 8: By me kings reign, and judges decree what is just.

2 Chronicles 20: You do not exercise the judgment of man, but of the Lord.

Psalm 81: I said, You are gods, that is, having offices commanded by God, so that they may be the voice of the law of God, and executors of the law of God. Isaiah 1: Seek judgment, help the oppressed, defend the widow.

God commands political offices to each according to his vocation.

There is no doubt, therefore, that the political order is approved by Him. And many sayings exist in the Prophets to this effect, which specifically command political offices. Luke 3: The Baptist preaches to the publicans and soldiers, and delivers express political precepts.

Therefore, he approves of the function itself, when he teaches how it is to be administered, so that they do not demand more than is established: Do not extort from anyone, nor falsely accuse. This whole sermon approves of the political state, judgments, and the militia, and distinguishes from the order the vices or confusions which human malice mixes in.

And the futile, empty, and insipid cavil of the Anabaptists is to be rejected, who say that the Baptist permitted these things to the imperfect, and that Christ later taught otherwise.

For the sermons of Christ and the Baptist do not conflict at all.

I have recited the testimonies congruent with the text of Paul, which it is very profitable to ponder often, and at the same time to weigh the causes for which God revealed this doctrine. For He wishes it to be known what the works of God are, and He wishes them to be distinguished from diabolical furies. He wishes to confirm in us obedience and reverence toward the order, which is a divine work and a huge benefit. He also wishes to kindle us to prayer and thanksgiving.

But you should remember that in the text of Paul, order is distinguished from confusions. Therefore, Paul used the word Order. Magistrate is the minister of God, an avenger for wrath etc.

After Paul said in general that the political order is the work of God, he adds a complete definition of the magistrate, so that he may distinguish order and the magistrate from robberies. Magistrate is the minister of God, for our good, an avenger to defend those who do right, and to punish delinquents with the sword, that is, with corporal punishments. This definition is complete, and even better than the Aristotelian one: The magistrate is the guardian of the law, for Paul adds the efficient cause, namely, that he is instituted by God. And in the final cause he adds the illustrious clause, "For your good," where he distinguishes the magistrate from robbery. For a robber does not foster an honest society, and tyrants are like robbers. But the magistrate defends the just, and punishes those who rush contumaciously into crimes, and fosters the common society, just like a father of a family. Therefore it was said by the Persian leader in Xenophon: A good prince differs nothing from a good father.

But in this definition it is asked: Whence do we know what things are rightly done? I answer: Paul here omits a longer declaration, and therefore he speaks generally, so that he approves the laws of all nations concerning civil affairs, if however they agree with the law of nature.

Here therefore let this be the rule: That Christians are not bound to the Mosaic polity, but it is permitted to them to use the laws of their own nations, which agree with reason, that is, with the law of nature, or the decalogue rightly understood, indeed just as a Christian owes obedience to the present laws that are congruent with the decalogue. It is permitted, therefore, to hang thieves, it is permitted to divide inheritances by our laws: because the Gospel does not establish a new worldly polity, but preaches about justice and eternal life, which is begun in hearts through the Son of God by the voice of the Gospel in true conversion. Meanwhile, it allows bodies to use different polities, just as different spans of days.

Therefore it is necessary to obey, not only because of wrath, but also because of conscience.

Following the definition is the conclusion, in which he repeats the precept concerning obedience, and adds a necessary declaration, so that the Church may know what kind of obligation it is, and what kind of sin it is to be unwilling to obey legitimate empires. And many writers agitate this argument, "The magistrate can punish no one with eternal punishment." "Therefore, one violating the law of the magistrates is not bound to eternal punishments." The consequence must be denied, because one violating the laws of the magistrates is bound to eternal punishment because of the command of God, just as one violating the commands of parents is bound to eternal punishment, even if parents cannot punish anyone with eternal punishment.

But God Himself is angry at those who violate the order sanctioned by Him, and He is the guardian of His own order: therefore He Himself executes the punishment. And the words of Paul must be considered most diligently. It is necessary to obey, not only because of wrath, that is, because of the punishments with which the magistrate can punish the guilty, but also because of conscience, namely, lest one become guilty of eternal punishment in those who do not wish to obey legitimate empires. Let us know, therefore, that it is truly a mortal sin, that is, offending God and making a man guilty of eternal punishment, to be unwilling to obey legitimate empires.

Thus he declares the necessity, so that it may be understood concerning the obligation of conscience and concerning eternal punishments, namely, unless conversion occurs. Now let all men consider with what severity God Himself has fortified magistrates and the whole political order, since Paul expressly affirms that the conscience becomes guilty before God, that is, that the disobedient are deserted by God, become captives of the devil, and are cast into eternal punishments, unless conversion occurs. And atrocious contumacy is also punished divinely in this life, as Solomon says: "Do not associate with the seditious, because their destruction will come quickly."

And in Ecclesiastes he says: "They will not escape in the day of war": just as the entire history of the world shows that the seditious have been oppressed by horrible things. punishments. No human power, no armies fortify empires more than this most severe law of God: It is necessary to obey for the sake of conscience, of which law God himself is the executor.

These things must be diligently thought upon, both by the people and by the masters. For masters also, when they become tyrants, that is, when they violate justice, they themselves tear apart the divine ordinance, and they are divinely caught in punishments. Therefore, a guilty conscience is formed in them as well, so that the whole Psalm: God stood in the assembly of the Gods, judging the Gods, accuses tyrants and threatens them with punishments. And this address has been repeated often.

Isaiah 3: The Lord will come to judgment against the Princes and Elders of the people.

Micah 3: Hear, O Princes, etc., because of you Zion shall be plowed as a field, and Jerusalem shall be a heap of stones.

Zechariah 11: My fury is kindled against the shepherds.

Here, however, one must answer briefly regarding two questions. The former is this: We are freed from the law, therefore conscience is not harmed by the violation of political laws.

I answer briefly to the antecedent: Believers in the mediator are freed from the law, as far as justification is concerned, that is, another thing is proposed by which they are righteous before God, namely the mediator who frees souls from eternal death, raised up by faith. Meanwhile, however, the proper duties of the body remain in this bodily life, which are a different thing than eternal reconciliation, righteousness, and the life of the spirit. But because God gathers the Church in this way, and not otherwise, namely by the preaching of the Gospel in this life, He wills us for the time being, as far as bodies are concerned, to be subject to the laws of bodies, of food, of drink, of political order. For similarly, food, drink, marriage, the education of offspring, political society, and the defense of bodies are necessary things for the body, and it is written: Honor must be had for the body. And yet these things are not that eternal righteousness, of which Daniel says: Eternal righteousness shall be brought in, etc. which in reality is the freedom of the spirit and liberation from the law.

This simple answer can be easily understood regarding the distinction between eternal light and righteousness in the heart and bodily life, and as long as we live in this mortal body. Elsewhere, however, it has been spoken of more copiously regarding liberation from the law, and the common answer can be rightly adapted here: We are free from the moral law as far as justification is concerned, but not as far as obedience is concerned. For liberation from the law itself is regeneration unto new obedience.

Another argument.

And from the same sources let answers be taken to this saying: The law is not laid down for the just, namely, so that by the law one might be just before God, or as far as eternal righteousness is concerned. But the law is laid down for the just as far as bodily life is concerned, namely the laws of food, drink, and political society.

Add also another answer: For the just, insofar as he is such, the law is not laid down, that is, the law does not condemn the just man who retains righteousness. But when he ceases to be just, violating the commands of God against his conscience, the law condemns him again.

Another objection.

Why does the conscience become guilty when acting against the laws of civil magistrates, and not become guilty when acting against the traditions of Bishops?

I answer: The reason for the diversity is this. God expressly sanctioned this liberty in the Church by the voice of the Gospel, so that neither should Bishops establish traditions with an opinion of necessity, nor should the Church receive them as such. Therefore, it is expressly said in Colossians 3: Let no one judge you in food, drink, etc. And to the Galatians: Stand fast in the liberty to which you have been called. But concerning political power, it is expressly said: It is necessary to obey for the sake of conscience. God wills that a distinction be seen between the kingdom of Christ and the empires of the world; He wills it to be known that the kingdom of Christ is gathered only by the voice of the Gospel. He does not will human traditions to be attached, which obscure or oppress the light of the Gospel. Meanwhile, He simultaneously wills it to be known that bodies are subject to political order, and that kings are armed with the power of establishing laws for the honest defense of bodies, for which new laws are sometimes necessary.

Furthermore, civil magistrates and Bishops sin equally when they establish laws conflicting with divine commands, or prescribe new forms of worship. Such laws are not to be obeyed, just as the Israelites did not obey the law of Nebuchadnezzar, which commanded them to worship the statue.

However, some ask: Is greater reverence owed to civil power than to the pastors of the Church, since it has been said: He who rejects you, rejects me

Item: Obey those who are set over you. Item: Those who rule well are worthy of double honor.

Regarding this question and these sayings, I answer clearly.

It is most certain that these do not constitute for Bishops or Pastors a kingdom outside the Gospel, nor do they grant them the power to establish their own laws, just as God has armed kings with the authority to establish laws concerning political affairs.

But at the same time, it must be known that obedience is owed to pastors who teach correctly in those things which are proper to the evangelical ministry, because it is most certain that all who are unwilling to obey the divine mandates, which the voice of the pastor sounds, sin mortally.

Item: Those unwilling to obey in the jurisdiction which is proper to the Gospel.

As when Ambrose kept the emperor Theodosius, and Basil kept the emperor Valens, from communion.

To whom you owe honor, give honor etc.

Previously he spoke in general about obedience, now he recites the degrees of internal and external duties: Honor, Fear, Tributes, Taxes.

Here the weights of the words should be considered.

Honor is in the soul a knowledge approving something on account of the command of God, and because God communicates to him His wisdom and justice: or because he is an instrument of the wisdom and justice of God, and it is to love that according to the order sanctioned by God.

Honor toward magistrates is, therefore, a knowledge which recognizes and confesses that the political order is the work of God, and is preserved by God, and that the magistrate is the guardian of the law of God, and in that guardianship the presence of God is seen in the human race, and the wisdom and justice of God shine forth.

And it is to love the order and the persons, having the προαίρεσιν (choice/intent) of doing rightly, who are instruments of the divine order, and so to love, that we subject ourselves to that high station according to the precepts of God.

Item, to ask of God that He Himself be the guardian of this His order, and that He rule those to whom He has handed over authority.

This knowledge and approval in the mind, and in the will love, subjection, and prayer for the empires are properly honor.

Then, the eternal signs of honor, what they are, is known, as bowing the knees signifies the subjection of oneself in the will.

Regarding the duties of the magistrate, Paul encompasses the sum when he says that he is a minister of God, to punish those who do evil.

And the sum can be comprehended in this definition: The magistrate is the guardian of the law, namely of both tables in external discipline.

Let all magistrates look upon this definition, and think that it is the norm of all government. Φόρος (Phóros) signifies ordinary tributes from lands. Τέλος (Télos) signifies those things which are paid from goods brought in from elsewhere.

Because there is need for guards to prevent robbery on the roads.

Now, what the manner of tributes ought to be, the words of John show: Be content with your wages.

And let princes know that they also are subject to the divine law: You shall not steal.

And let them observe the distinction of ownerships, let them know that some things are the property of the citizens, others their own, as the history of the vineyard of Naboth shows.

But the βουλῑμίαι (insatiable hungers) of kings and princes are often not content with legitimate pensions.

Hence are the old complaints: ταμίαι λαμίαι (treasurers are gluttons).

And Nazianzen says: With Briarean hands, governors snatch from the resources of the people.

Render to all their due.

In the end, he returns to the general precepts which pertain to all, and repeats the sum of the doctrine concerning good works, about which he proposes the decalogue: because it is necessary that faith and works be ruled by the expressed word of God, according to these sayings: Your word is a lamp to my feet.

Item in Ezekiel 20: Walk in my precepts.

Item in Numbers: Let not your eyes go whoring, that you may walk according to your own thoughts etc.

Item, In vain they worship me with the commandments of men.

And Matt.

5: I have not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it.

It is necessary, therefore, that the decalogue be proposed in the Church, and that it be expounded just as Christ, the Prophets, and the Apostles expound it, and always in the Church from the beginning of the world there has been the same doctrine of the decalogue.

Furthermore, how the doctrine concerning liberation from the law is to be understood has been said above, and in the following chapter the same explanation will be repeated.

Now let the legal sayings in this place be considered: Pay to all their due.

By this word he encompasses all duties necessary in society.

He commands that not only obedience be rendered to superiors, but also due duties to others, to parents, to a spouse, to children, to the family.

He commands also in contracts that to everyone the things owed and the money owed be exhibited, according to the precept of the decalogue: You shall not steal.

Psalm 27 says: The wicked borrows and does not pay back, but the just man shows mercy and gives.

And the decalogue is repeated here for this reason, that we may know the whole the doctrine of good works recited in these two chapters and elsewhere, is contained in the Decalogue.

Again, let the repetition concerning debt be considered: Owe no man anything, except mutual love.

Let there be known to all a distinction full of erudition concerning obligations.

Some things are owed by natural obligation, not civil, that is, for the performance of which the magistrate does not compel a man with his punishments, as he who receives a benefit, in turn owes gratitude of spirit by natural obligation.

Those in danger in the waters, those present ought to help, if they can; the rich man ought to have helped the present Lazarus, but the magistrate does not punish such omissions, he only indicates atrocious external crimes. And natural obligation is divine, according to the commandment: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. Likewise, Prov. 21: He who stops his ear to the cry of the poor, will himself also cry out, and will not be heard. Likewise: Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor.

Another is divine obligation, or Natural and Civil, that is, on account of which the magistrate also compels men to perform external works, or to give external things, price or wages, because if this compensation were removed, the society of the human race would be utterly dissipated.

Paul, however, speaks here of both obligations.

He wants debts owed by civil obligation to be given, according to the commandment: You shall not commit theft. And it is known that it is a manifest baseness not to perform what is owed by divine and civil obligation.

The Persians, as Herodotus writes, judged it dishonest even to be in debt: which, however, I understand of those not paying at the convenient time. For thus says Herodotus: They consider it most shameful to lie, and then to be in debt, because they think a debtor often lies.

When therefore Paul says, Owe no man anything, he wants those things to be performed which are owed by civil obligation, so that we are thus freed from civil obligation, after we have given or done what was owed. Meanwhile, however, the divine and natural obligation is perpetual, which is the perpetual love of the neighbor.

And although we shall better understand what is ardent and ordered love in eternal life, yet now it must be begun, as John says: He who does not love, remains in death. And a description of whatever kind must be held.

Osiander names love God himself; of this form of speaking it is said elsewhere.

Paul understands love to be owed to the neighbor, which is an affection that is kindled in the converted by the Holy Spirit. We owe this affection to the neighbor, of which affection Paul speaks here and in 1 Cor. 13. And to the Galatians: The fruit of the spirit is love, etc.

This love, therefore, is to rejoice in God in true faith, and to obey all the commandments of God, and for his sake to love the neighbor, and to wish to do him good according to the commandments of God, wherever it is possible.

To this love man is always obligated by God, according to the saying: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and your neighbor as yourself.

Most eruditely, therefore, Paul distinguished obligation here. He commands that we perform what is owed by civil obligation; these being given, the civil obligation ceases, therefore he says: Owe no man anything, that is, perform what is owed by civil obligation, thus this obligation ceases. But you shall owe love, that is, the natural and divine obligation always remains, for love in the heart and for many external duties, not owed by civil obligation. As the rich man did not owe Lazarus by civil obligation: but yet he owed by natural and divine obligation love in the heart, and external benefits, which he could then perform.

Latin:

Caput XIII.

In priori capite recitavit praecepta de privatis moribus. Nunc addit doctrinam de vita politica. Quanquam enim Evangelium concionatur de reconciliatione cum Deo et de aeterna iusticia, nec fert leges in specie de successionibus, de contractibus, de forma iudiciorum, de distinctione actionum, commendavit enim haec Deus consilio politici magistratus, sicut non docet Evangelium in specie artem medicam, aut architectonicam: tamen in genere necesse est de usu harum externarum et corporalium rerum extare verbum Dei, seu testimonium divinum, propter duas causas. Primum ut sciamus hunc ipsum ordinem esse opus Dei, et testimonium sapientiae Dei inter nos: deinde ut sciamus usum concessum esse piis. Quia oportet opera nostra testimonium habere ex verbo Dei, ut 1 Timoth. 4. dicitur: Sanctificatur creatura per verbum et orationem.

Utile est et nosse certamina Ecclesiae omnium temporum. Semper autem fuerunt fanatici homines, qui damnaverunt ordinem politicum, et magnas confusiones alii alias excitarunt. Voluerunt efficere Platonicam communicationem facultatum, ut olim Marcion, Carpocrates, et alii, quos refutat Irenaeus.

In oppido Phrygiae Pepusa fanatici quidam tale regnum incoarunt, quale nostro tempore Anabaptistae in urbe Monasteriensi conati sunt constituere, et oppidum nominarunt novam Ierosolymam, quod rectius nominassent ἐμποῦσαν. Sed deletum est, et Montanus et Maximilla duces factionis sese strangularunt.

Nostro tempore adhuc vagantur Anabaptistae, qui damnant magistratus, distinctionem dominiorum, contractus, iudicia, et multi alii fuerunt et sunt, qui negant utendum esse Romanis legibus. Contra hos furores sciamus Ecclesiam praemunitam esse hoc tertiodecimo capite Pauli ad Romanos, quod ideo notissimum omnibus esse debet, ne qui hypocrisi fanaticorum hominum decepti implicentur falsis et seditiosis opinionibus.

Primum igitur perspicue et constanter teneatur haec regula: Evangelium est vox de remissione peccatorum et de reconciliatione cum Deo propter mediatorem, et de luce, iusticia et vita aeterna in cordibus. Interea sicut corpora sinit uti diversis dierum spatiis in diversis locis, ita sinit uti diversis formis politiarum, modo cum ratione congruant.

Haec regula saepe expresse tradita est, ut Coloss. 3.: Induite novum hominem, qui renovatur agnitione ad imaginem eius, qui condidit eum, ubi non est Graecus, nec Iudaeus, nec circumcisio, nec praeputium, nec barbarus, nec Scytha, nec servus, nec liber, sed omnia in omnibus est Christus. Hoc illustre discrimen Evangelii et sint in sanctis in hac vita?

Primum respondeo: Nequaquam sunt in sanctis peccata, seu lapsus contra conscientiam, id est, Cum illi, qui fuerunt sancti scientes et volentes violant legem Dei, ut David rapiens alterius coniugem, hi contristant et excutiunt Spiritum sanctum, et desinunt esse sancti, ac rursus fiunt rei irae Dei et mortis aeternae, donec rursus convertuntur, iuxta haec dicta, 1.

Corinth 6.: Ne erretis, scortatores, idolatrae, adulteri etc. regnum Dei non possidebunt. Et Galat.

5.: Manifesta sunt opera carnis, adulterium, caedes etc. talia facientes regnum Dei non possidebunt. Item: Deficientes a fundamento, id est, aliquem articulum fidei abiicientes, sive eum intelligant, sive non intelligant, sed decipiantur praestigiis, hi quoque desinunt esse sancti, et excutiunt Spiritum sanctum, et fiunt rei aeternae irae, ut multi deficiebant ad Arianos, multi nunc quoque qui aliquandiu recte senserunt, abiiciunt veritatem.

Hi gradus peccatorum diligentissime considerandi sunt, qui nominantur usitate peccata mortalia seu regnantia.

Firmissime igitur tenenda est regula contra Antinomos: Milita bonam militiam, retinens fidem et bonam conscientiam. Quae igitur peccata reliqua sunt in sanctis in hac vita?

Respondeo: Multum caliginis et dubitationum, multae omissiones et vitiosi affectus, quibus malis tamen sancti repugnant, ne ruant contra conscientiam, et credunt ea tegi propter filium Dei. Haec caligo et immundities in homine non existimetur leve malum esse, propter quam dictum est: Non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens.

Et tamen filius Dei umbraculum est credentibus. Ideo quanquam haec immundities est in sanctis, tamen placent personae propter filium Dei, fide accipientes imputationem iusticiae, iuxta dicta: Beati quorum tecta sunt peccata.

Item: Pro hoc orabit ad te omnis sanctus. Item: Si actiones carnis spiritu mortificabitis, vivetis.

Et usitatum est, haec peccata nominare venialia, seu non regnantia. Hae quinque quaestiones semper repetendae sunt in doctrina de bonis operibus, nunc aspiciamus eruditissimam Pauli concionem.

Initio generale praeceptum tradit de coercendo corpore iuxta omnia praecepta moralia: Offerte corpora hostiam vivam, et praestate cultum rationale, ut novitas et imago Dei in mente crescat, sicut alibi inquit Ephe.

4.: Renovamini spiritu mentis vestrae, et induite novum hominem, qui secundum Deum creatus erat in iusticia et sanctitate vera. Opponit autem obedientiam iuxta praecepta moralia cultibus Leviticis, ideo inquit: Offerte hostiam vivam et cultum rationale.

Nominat vivam hostiam, quia Deus ideo restituit vitam aeternam, ut in tota aeternitate simus vivi cum ipso, et ipse sese communicet nobis. Deus condidit rationales creaturas, angelos et homines, ut essent creaturae, quibus sese et sua summa bona, vitam, lucem, sapientiam et iusticiam communicet, et ab his vicissim requirit conformatem, et huius bonitatis agnitionem et celebrationem.

Haec conformitas cum Deo, et agnitio ac celebratio bonitatis Dei, sunt veri et aeterni cultus Dei, qui in hac vita incoantur, postea erunt integri: et iidem cultus nominantur λογικὴ λατρεία, id est, cultus mentis, in quo mens fide, aut coram intuetur Deum, et vere sentit timorem et laetitiam in Deo, iuxta dictum: Veri adoratores adorabunt patrem in spiritu et veritate, id est, Spiritu sancto accendente veros et ardentes motus, timorem, fiduciam, dilectionem et laetitiam. Veritate, id est, vera agnitione Dei, quae fit verbo lucente in corde, per quod filius ostendit voluntatem patris. Opponenda est igitur λογικὴ λατρεία, non tantum mactationibus pecorum, sed universaliter vanissimae imaginationi eorum, qui dicunt, aliqua opera externa aut rationalia, etiam in non renatis, placere Deo ex opere operato, sine bono motu utentis, sicut Papistae scripserunt, Missam mereri aliis ex opere operato, etiamsi Sacrificulus sit adulter, aut sicut dixerunt, opera moralia honesta etiam in non renatis mereri gratiam.

Has falsas imaginationes saepe taxant Prophetae, ut Psalm 49.: Nunquid manducabo carnes taurorum. Psalm 50.: Holocaustis non delectaberis.

Oseae. 6.: Misericordiam volo, non sacrificium, et scientiam magis quam holocausta. Denique saepissime repetita est haec concio, et summa comprehensa est in his dictis: Veri adoratores adorabunt patrem in spiritu et veritate.

Item: Nemo venit ad patrem nisi per filium. Ex hac tota doctrina sumatur enarratio, quid sit λογικὴ λατρεία, inde et definitio sumatur.

Cultus Dei est opus a Deo mandatum, factum in vera agnitione et timore Dei, et vera fiducia filii, hoc fine, ut Deo praestetur obedientia, et honos, id est, ut hoc opere testemur, hunc verum Deum esse quem sic colimus, ut castitas Ioseph est cultus Dei, quia in mente Ioseph sunt vera agnitio Dei, timor et fiducia mediatoris, et opus refertur ad hunc finem, ut ostendat hunc vere Deum esse quem sic colimus, et quomodo velit coli. Castitas in Scipione est sine luce Dei et agnitione mediatoris, ideo non est cultus Dei.

Quaerat autem aliquis: Cum Deus postulet vivas hostias, et perpetuum cultum mentis, ad quem usum instituit mactationes pecudum, et alias ceremonias?

Respondeo: Ut conservetur ministerium docendi verbum Dei, ad quod opus est duabus rebus: docentibus et congregatione.

Sunt ergo instituta signa, quae et commonefactiones essent additae doctrinae, et nervi congregationis, et multae ceremoniae instituta sunt, ut inde doctores alerentur, ut oblatio primitiarum, decimarum et pecudum.

Hos fines intelligi oportet in cultibus seu sacrificiis ceremonialibus.

Ut autem cultum definivimus, ita eodem modo sacrificium in genere definiri potest.

Sacrificium est opus, mandatum a Deo, factum in vera agnitione, timore Dei et fide, hoc fine, ut Deo praestetur obedientia, et hoc opere ostendatur testimonium, quod hic sit verus Deus, cui praestetur haec obedientia.

Adde, cum de sacrificiis hominum loquimur, factum fiducia mediatoris.

Sunt autem sacrificii species iuxta generalem definitionem duae: Propiciatorium et εὐχαριστικόν.

Propiciatorium est unum, videlicet solius Christi obedientia, quae meretur aliis remissionem peccatorum et reconciliationem.

Nam Levitica, quae nominabantur propiciationes, et pro peccato, erant tantum typi, nequaquam merebantur remissionem peccatorum.

Ideo scriptum est: Impossibile fuit sanguine taurorum tolli peccata.

Caetera omnia, cum recte fiunt, sunt εὐχαριστικά, sive sint cemoriae, sive alia bona opera, sicut dicitur: Sacrificium Deo spiritus contribulatus, cor contritum et humiliatum Deus non despicies.

Non est condita haec natura, ut sit otiosa, sed ut Deus communicet nobis suam lucem, sapientiam, iusticiam et laetitiam in tota aeternitate, et vicissim vult Deus celebrari in hac vita, et post hanc vitam: ideo necesse est actiones aliquas esse, quarum omnium finis sit celebratio Dei.

Hae omnes in hac vita et post hanc vitam sunt reipsa sacrificia laudis, seu εὐχαριστικά, καὶ λογικὴ λατρεία.

Osiandri partitio tria membra facit: Typicum, propiciatorium et θρεπτήριον, quo alebantur sacerdotes.

Haec distributio mihi non displicet, sed commodius est nominare εὐχαριστικόν, ut comprehendantur omnia sacrificia spiritus, et ceremoniae.

Has distinctiones necesse est extare, ut discernantur sacrificium filii Dei ab omnium aliorum hominum sacrificiis.

Nam caetera nequaquam sunt ἱλαστικά, seu propiciatoria, id est, non merentur remissionem peccatorum et reconciliationem: ac multi errores irrepserunt in Ecclesiam, non recte intellecto vocabulo Sacrificii.

Quare necesse est iuniores de hac distinctione admoneri.

Cognitis his fundamentis intelligi potest, quid Paulus nominet λογικὴν λατρείαν, et haec est sancta, id est, vere didicata Deo, non prophana, ut virtutes in Ethnicis, in quibus non lucet vera agnitio Dei et mediatoris: est et Deo placens, ut supra dictum est, quomodo bona opera placeant Deo, scilicet mandata a Deo et facta in agnitione mediatoris et fiducia filii.

Ne imitemini gestus huius mundi.

Ut antea instituit generalem propositionem de obedientia secundum omnia praecepta: Offerte λογικὴν λατρείαν, ita nunc eam repetit iuxta omnia praecepta: Ne habemus affectus similes mundanorum, sed novos affectus Deo conformes.

Nam cum vetat imitari gestus mundi, non vituperat res, quarum usum Deus ordinavit, non vetat usum ciborum, coniugii, imperiorum, iudiciorum, contractuum, et aliarum ordinationum Dei, sed prohibet vitiosos affectus, ideo inquit: Gestus, id est, motus animorum non sint similes mundanis, ut contra ordinationem Dei adpetunt impii voluptates, quaerunt opes et potentiam iniustis modis, certant ambitione, ardent iniustis odiis, turbant Ecclesiam et politias privatis cupiditatibus.

Haec vitia regnant in maxima parte generis humani, de qua parte generis humani contraria conversis ad Deum, saepe usurpatur adpelatio mundi, ut 1.

Iohannis 2.: Omne quod est vitae politicae semper in conspectu sit. Postea etiam vitae politicae dignitas consideretur descripta et in hoc capite, et in multis testimoniis propheticis. Omnis anima potestatibus, quae praesunt, subdita sit.

Initio simpliciter et perspicue tradit praeceptum, ut suo quisque magistratui obediat. Nam particula (Quae praesunt) non est otiose addita, sed excludit alienos magistratus. Non enim necesse est civem Lubecensem obedire magistratui Parisiensi. Tollit item Paulus dubitationem conscientiarum, si sit obscura contentio de titulo, nt quanquam rex Anglicus scribit se regem Franciae: tamen non necesse est cives regni Gallici obedire regi Anglico.

Deinde addit rationem praecepti: Cum imperia sint ordo divinitus institutus, qui vere est opus Dei, irascitur Deus turbantibus hunc ordinem. Necesse est igitur obedire propter conscientiam.

Hic diligenter consideretur vocabulum Ordinatio. Nam humana iudicia cum intuentur confusionem et vitia in imperiis, non statuunt gubernationem opus Dei esse, sed partim calliditate humana, partim robore constituta esse, et retineri imperia. Et multa de causis apud Philosophos disputantur.

Sed nos discernamus ordinem politicum a personis et a vitiis, quae miscent personae. Est enim ordo ipse legis divinae noticia, et gradus eorum, qui regunt, et reguntur, et leges latae vera autoritate magistratuum, coniugia, contractus, iudicia, poenae, defensio, legitima militia, legitima tributa, disciplina in pace, studia doctrinarum et aliarum honestarum artium. Hic totus ordo in genere humano est opus Dei, sicut ordo motuum coelestium, et terrae foecunditas. Nec tantum permissive a Deo, sed Deus sua sapientia et voce instituit hunc ordinem, et quantum superest ordinis, conservat ipse efficaciter. Interea verum est, quod diaboli, et multa organa diabolorum tyranni, seditiosi, et alii scelerati homines multipliciter turbant hunc ordinem, et multas confusiones et multa vitia miscent, sicut lupi aliquam gregis partem lacerant, et tamen pastor fidelis defendit reliquum agmen: ita quantum ordinis reliquum est in societate humana, conservatur immensa bonitate ab ipso Deo.

Tenendus est igitur hic articulus fidei: Ordo politicus est revera opus Dei, et res bona, et est testimonium sapientiae, iusticiae Dei et bonitatis erga homines, et praesentiae eius inter homines. Lex enim et iudicia ostendunt sapientiam, aequalitas in contractibus, et executio poenarum ostendunt iusticiam: Bonitatem et praesentiam ostendit miranda conservatio totius societatis humanae inter tanta pericula. Item, poenarum executio manifeste superans vires humanas, de qua dicit Dominus: Qui gladium acceperit, gladio peribit.

Addantur ergo testimonia, quae adfirmant ordinem politicum esse opus Dei.

Danielis 2.: Deus transfert regna et constituit, id est, efficit ut floreant et durent. Proverb. 16.: Libra et pondus iudicia Domini sunt, et omnes lapides lancis.

Psalm. 126.: Nisi Dominus custodierit civitatem, frustra vigilat qui custodit eam.

Custos et conservator est Deus ordinis politici, ergo eum adprobat. Psalm. 143.: Qui das salutem regibus. Haec verba adiuvari gubernatores a Deo testantur.

Proverb. 8.: Per me reges regnant, et iudices iusta decernunt.

2. Paralip. 20.: Non hominis exercetis iudicium, sed Domini.

Psalm. 81.: Ego dixi, Dii estis, id est, habentes officia mandata a Deo, ut sint vox legis Dei, et executores legis Dei. Esaiae 1.: Quaerite iudicium, subvenite oppresso, defendite viduam.

Praecipit Deus politica officia cuique pro sua vocatione.

Non dubium est igitur adprobari ab eo politicum ordinem. Et in hanc sententiam multa dicta apud Prophetas extant, quae nominatim politica officia praecipiunt. Lucae 3.: Baptista publicanis et militibus concionatur, ac tradit expresse praecepta politica.

Ergo ipsam functionem adprobat, cum doceat quomodo sit administranda, ne plus quam constitutum est postulent: Neminem concutiatis, neque calumniemini. Haec tota concio politicum statum, iudicia, militiam adprobat, et discernit ab ordine vitia seu confusiones, quas humana malitia admiscet.

Et futilis, ieiuna et insulsa cavillatio Anabaptistarum explodenda est, qui dicunt, Baptistam haec imperfectis permisisse, Christum postea aliter docuisse.

Nequaquam enim pugnant Christi et Baptistae conciones.

Recitavi testimonia congruentia cum textu Pauli, quae valde prodest saepe cogitari, et simul causas expendere, propter quas Deus hanc doctrinam patefecit. Vult enim sciri, quae sint Dei opera, et vult ea discerni a furoribus diabolicis. Vult in nobis obedientiam et reverentiam erga ordinem, qui est opus divinum et ingens beneficium, confirmare. Vult etiam nos accendere ad precationem et gratiarum actionem.

Memineris autem diserte in textu Pauli discerni ordinem a confusionibus. Ideo usus est Paulus vocabulo Ordinis. Magistratus est minister Dei, vindex ad iram etc.

Postquam in genere dixit Paulus, ordinem politicum esse opus Dei, addit definitionem magistratus integram, ut discernat ordinem et magistratum a latrociniis. Magistratus est minister Dei, nobis ad bonum, vindex ad defendendos recte facientes, et puniendos delinquentes gladio, id est, poenis corporalibus. Haec definitio est integra, et melior etiam quam Aristotelica: Magistratus est custos legis, Paulus enim addit efficientem causam, scilicet, quod sit institutus a Deo. Et in causa finali addit illustrem particulam, Tibi in bonum, ubi discernit magistratum a latrocinio. Nam latro non fovet honestam societatem, et tyranni sunt latronum similes. Sed magistratus defendit iustos, et punit contumaciter ruentes in scelera, et fovet communem societatem, sicut paterfamilias. Ideo dictum est a duce Persico in Xenophonte: Nihil differt bonus princeps a patre bono.

Sed in hac definitione quaeritur: Unde scimus, quae sint recte facta? Respondeo: Paulus hic omittit longiorem declarationem, et ideo generaliter loquitur, ut leges omnium gentium adprobet de civilibus negotiis, si tamen consentiant cum lege naturae.

Hic igitur nota sit regula: Christianos non esse alligatos ad politiam Mosaicam, sed licere eis uti legibus suarum gentium, quae consentiunt cum ratione, id est, cum lege naturae, seu decalogo recte intellecto, imo sicut debet Christianus obedientiam praesentibus legibus cum decalogo congruentibus. Licet igitur fures suspendere, licet haereditates dividere nostris legibus: quia Evangelium non constituit novam politiam mundanam, sed concionatur de iusticia et vita aeterna, quae in cordibus incoatur per filium Dei voce Evangelii in vera conversione. Interea sinit corpora uti diversis politiis, sicut diversis dierum spatiis.

Ideo necesse est obedire, non solum propter iram, sed etiam propter conscientiam.

Definitionem sequitur conclusio, in qua repetit praeceptum de obedientia, et addit necessariam declarationem, ut sciat Ecclesia, qualis obligatio sit, et quale peccatum sit nolle obedire legitimis imperiis. Ac multi scriptores hoc argumentum agitant, Magistratus neminem potest poena aeterna adficere. Ergo violans legem magistratuum, non est obligatus ad poenas aeternas. Neganda est consequentia, Quia violans leges magistratuum obligatur ad poenam aeternam propter mandatum Dei, sicut violans mandata parentum, obligatur ad poenam aeternam, etiamsi parentes neminem possunt adficere poena aeterna.

Sed Deus ipse irascitur violantibus ordinem ab ipso sancitum, et est custos sui ordinis: ideo poenam ipse exequitur. Ac verba Pauli diligentissime consideranda sunt. Necesse est obedire, non solum propter iram, id est, propter supplicia, quibus magistratus potest sontes adficere, sed etiam propter conscientiam, scilicet, ne fiat rea aeternae poenae in his, qui nolunt obedire legitimis imperiis. Sciamus igitur vere peccatum mortale esse, id est, Deum offendens et faciens hominem reum aeternae poenae, nolle obedire legitimis imperiis.

Sic declarat necessitatem, ut intelligatur de obligatione conscientiae et de aeternis poenis, videlicet, nisi fiat conversio. Iam considerent omnes homines, quanta severitate Deus ipse muniverit magistratus et totum politicum ordinem, cum expresse Paulus adfirmet, conscientiam ream fieri coram Deo, hoc est, inobedientes deseri a Deo, fieri captivos diaboli, et abiici in aeternas poenas, nisi fiat conversio. Et atrox contumacia etiam divinitus in hac vita punitur, sicut Salomon inquit: Cum seditiosis ne commiscearis, quia cito veniet eorum iuteritus.

Et in Ecclesiastae inquit: Non effugient in die belli: sicut universa mundi historia ostendit, seditiosos oppressos esse horribilibus. poenis. Nulla potentia humana, nulli exercitus magis muniunt imperia, quam haec severissima lex Dei: Necesse est obedire propter conscien- tiam, cuius legis ipse Deus executor est.

Haec diligenter cogitanda sunt, et a populo et a dominis. Nam et domini, cum fiunt ty- ranni, id est, cum violant iusticiam, lacerant et ipsi ordinationem divinam, et divinitus haerent in poenis. Fit igitur in ipsis quoque rea con- scientia, ut totus Psalmus: Deus stetit in syna- goga Deorum Deos iudicans, accusat tyrannos, minatur eis poenas. Et saepe repetita est haec concio.

Esaiae 3.: Dominus ad iudicium veniet ad- versus Principes et Seniores populi.

Micheae 3.: Audite Principes etc. propter vos Sion quasi ager arabitur et Ierosolyma erit acervus lapidum.

Zachariae 11.: Super pastores iratus est fu- ror meus.

Hic autem breviter de duabus quaestionibus respondendum est. Prior haec est: Sumus liberati a lege, Ergo non laeditur conscientia violatione le- gum politicarum.

Respondeo breviter ad antecedens: Creden- tes in mediatorem sunt liberati a lege, quod ad iustificationem attinet, id est, proposita est alia res, qua sunt iusti coram Deo, scilicet mediator qui liberat animas ex morte aeterna erectas fide. Interea manent tamen in hac vita corporali pro- pria officia corporis, quae sunt alia res quam re- conciliatio aeterna, iusticia, et vita spiritus. Quia autem sic colligit Deus Ecclesiam, et non aliter, videlicet praedicatione Evangelii in hac vita, vult nos tantisper, quod ad corpora attinet, sub- iectos esse legibus corporum, cibi, potus, poli- tici ordinis.
