Similiter enim res necessariae sunt corpori cibus, potus, coniugium, educatio sobo- lis, politica societas, defensio corporum, et scri- ptum est: Habendum esse honorem corpori. Et tamen hae res non sunt illa aeterna iusticia, de qua dicit Daniel: Iusticia aeterna adducetur etc. quae reipsa est libertas spiritus et liberatio a lege.

Haec simplex responsio facile intelligi potest de discrimine aeternae lucis et iusticiae in corde et vitae corporalis, et donec in hoc mortali corpore vivimus. Alibi autem copiosius dictum est de liberatione a lege, et recte accommodari huc potest communis responsio: Sumus liberi a lege morali, quod ad iustificationem attinet, sed non quod ad obedientiam attinet. Nam ipsa liberatio a lege regeneratio est ad novam obedientiam.

Aliud argumentum.

Et iisdem fontibus sumantur responsiones ad hoc dictum: Iusto non est lex posita, scilicet, ut lege iustus sit coram Deo, seu quod ad aeternam iusticiam attinet. Sed iusto est lex posita, quod ad vitam corporalem attinet, videlicet leges cibi, potus, politicae societatis.

Adde et alteram responsionem: Iusto in quantum tali non est lex posita, id est, lex non damnat iustum retinentem iusticiam. Sed cum desinit esse iustus, contra conscientiam violans mandata Dei, lex rursus eum damnat.

Alia obiectio.

Cur fit rea conscientia faciens contra leges magistratuum civilium, et non fit rea faciens contra traditiones Episcoporum?

Respondeo: Ratio diversitatis est. Deus ex- presse voce Evangelii sanxit hanc libertatem in Ecclesia, ut nec Episcopi condant traditiones cum opinione necessitatis, nec Ecclesia eas sic acci- piat. Ideo Colos. 3. expresse dictum est: Nemo vos arguat in cibo, potu etc. Et ad Galatas: State in libertate, ad quam vocati estis. Sed de poli- tica potestate expresse dictum est: Necesse est obedire propter conscientiam. Vult Deus con- spici discrimen inter regnum Christi et imperia mundi, vult sciri tantum voce Evangelii colligi regnum Christi. Non vult adfingi traditiones humanas, quae obscurant vel opprimunt lucem Evangelii. Interea simul vult sciri, corpora sub- iecta esse politico ordini, et reges armatos esse potestate condendi leges, ad honestam defensio- nem corporum, ad quam opus est interdum novis legibus.

Caeterum pariter peccant magistratus civilis et Episcopi, quando condunt leges pugnantes cum mandatis divinis, aut praecipiunt novos cultus. Talibus legibus non est obediendum, sicut nec Israëlitae obediebant legi Nabuchodonosor, prae- cipienti adorare statuam.

Interrogant autem aliqui: Maiorne reveren- tia debetur potestati civili, quam pastoribus Ec- clesiae, cum dictum sit: Qui vos spernit, me

Item: Obedite praepositis vestris. Item: Qui bene praesunt, duplici honore digni sunt.

De hac interrogatione et his dictis plane respondeo.

Certissimum est haec non constituere Episcopis aut Pastoribus regnum extra Evangelium, nec tribuere eis potestatem proprias leges condendi, sicut reges Deus armavit autoritate condendi leges de politicis negotiis.

Sed simul hoc sciendum est, pastoribus recte docentibus deberi obedientiam in his, quae sunt propria ministerii evangelici, quia certissimum est peccare mortaliter omnes nolentes obedire mandatis divinis, quae sonat vox pastoris.

Item: Nolentes obedire in iurisdictione, quae est propria Evangelii.

Ut cum Ambrosius Theodosium imperatorem, et Basilius Valentem imperatorem arcent a communione.

Cui honorem debitis, tribuite honorem etc.

Antea in genere dixit de obedientia, nunc gradus recitat interna et externa officia, Honorem, Timorem, Tributa, Vectigalia.

Hic pondera vocabulorum considerentur.

Honos est in anima noticia adprobans aliquid propter mandatum Dei, et quia Deus ei communicat sapientiam suam et iusticiam: aut quia est organum sapientiae et iusticiae Dei, et est diligere illud iuxta ordinem a Deo sancitum.

Est igitur honos erga magistratus noticia, quae agnoscit et fatetur, ordinem politicum esse opus Dei, et conservari a Deo, et magistratum esse custodem legis Dei, et in ea custodia conspici praesentiam Dei in genere humano, et lucere sapientiam et iusticiam Dei.

Et est diligere ordinem et personas, habentes προαίρεσιν recte faciendi, quae sunt organa divini ordinis, et sic diligere, ut nos illi fastigio subiiciamus iuxta praecepta Dei.

Item, petere a Deo, ut ipse sit custos huius sui ordinis, et regat eos, quibus tradidit imperium.

Haec noticia et approbatio in mente, et in voluntate dilectio, subiectio et precatio pro imperiis sunt proprie honos.

Deinde signa aeterna honoris quae sint notum est, ut flectere genua significat subiectionem sui in voluntate.

De officiis magistratus complexus est Paulus summam, cum ait, esse ministrum Dei, ut puniat malefacientes.

Et summa comprehendi potest in hac definitione: Magistratus est custos legis, videlicet utriusque tabulae in externa disciplina.

Hanc definitionem intueantur omnes magistratus, et cogitent esse normam totius gubernationis. Φόρος significat ordinaria tributa ex fundis. Τέλος significat ea, quae penduntur et rebus aliunde advectis.

Quia praesidiis opus est ad prohibenda latrocinia in viis.

Iam qui debebat esse modus tributorum, ostendunt verba Iohannis: Estote contenti stipendiis vestris.

Et sciant principes se quoque subiectos esse legi divinae: Non furtum facies.

Et servent distinctionem dominiorum, sciant alia esse civium propria, alia ipsorum, ut ostendit historia de vinea Nabot.

Sed βουλῑμίαι regum et principum saepe non sunt contentae legitimis pensionibus.

Hinc sunt querelae veteres: ταμίαι λαμίαι.

Et Nazianzenus inquit: Briarei manibus rapere gubernatores ex populi facultatibus.

Reddite omnibus debitum.

In fine redit ad generalia praecepta, quae ad omnes pertinent, ac repetit summam doctrinae de bonis operibus, de qua proponit decalogum: quia necesse est fidem et opera regi expresso verbo Dei, iuxta haec dicta: Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum.

Item in Ezechiele 20.: In praeceptis meis ambulate.

Item in Numeris: Non fornicentur oculi vestri, ut ambuletis secundum cogitationes vestras etc.

Item, Frustra me colunt mandatis hominum.

Et Matth.

5.: Non veni solvere legem, sed implere.

Necesse est igitur in Ecclesia proponi decalogum, et eum enarrari sicut enarrant Christus, Prophetae et Apostoli, et semper in Ecclesia inde usque a principio mundi fuit eadem decalogi doctrina.

Caeterum quomodo intelligenda sit doctrina de liberatione a lege, supra dictum est, et sequenti capite eadem explicatio repetetur.

Nunc considerentur dicta legalia hoc loco: Persolvite omnibus debitum.

Hac voce complectitur omnia officia in societate necessaria.

Iubet praestari non solum obedientiam superioribus, sed etiam caeteris debita officia, parentibus, coniugi, liberis, familiae.

Iubet item in contractibus cuicunque res debitas et pecuniam debitam exhiberi, iuxta praeceptum decalogi: Non furtum facies.

Psalmus 27. inquit: Impius mutuo sumit, et non reddit, iustus autem miseretur et largitur.

Ac repetitur ideo hic decalogus, ut sciamus totam doctrinam de bonis operibus recitatam his duobus capitibus et alibi, comprehensam esse in decalogo.

Rursus etiam consideretur repetitio de bito: Nemini quidquam debeatis nisi mutuam dilectionem.

Nota sit omnibus distinctio plena eruditionis de obligationibus.

Alia debentur obligatione naturali, non civili, id est, ad quae praestanda magistratus suis poenis non cogit hominem, ut is qui accipit beneficium, vicissim debet animi gratitudinem obligatione naturali. Sed magistratus non nisi in paucis gradibus punit ingratos.

Periclitanti in aquis debent opitulari alii praesentes, si possunt, Dives praesenti Lazaro debebat opitulari, sed magistratus tales omissiones non punit, tantum atrocia externa scelera indicat. Ac naturalis obligatio est divina, iuxta praeceptum: Diligas proximum tuum sicut teipsum. Item, Proverb. 21.: Obstruens aurem ad clamorem pauperis, vicissim clamabit, et non exaudietur. Item: Beatus qui intelligit super egenum et pauperem.

Alia est obligatio divina, seu Naturalis et Civilis, id est, propter quam et magistratus cogit homines facere externas operas, aut dare res externas, pretium aut merces, quia hac compensatione sublata, prorsus dissiparetur societas generis humani.

Paulus autem de utraque obligatione hic loquitur.

Debita obligatione civili vult dari, iuxta praeceptum: Non furtum facies. Et notum est, manifestam turpitudinem esse non praestare debita obligatione divina et civili.

Persae, ut scribit Herodotus, inhonestum esse iudicabant ipsum etiam debere: quod tamen intelligo de non solventibus convenienti tempore. Sic enim ait Herodotus: Turpissimum ducunt mentiri, deinde vero debere, quia existimant debitorem saepe mentire.

Cum igitur inquit Paulus, Nemini quidquam debeatis, vult ea praestari, quae civili obligatione debentur, ut ita liberemur a civili obligatione, posteaquam debita dedimus aut fecimus. Interea tamen perpetua est obligatio divina et naturalis, quae est perpetua dilectio proximi.

Etsi autem quid sit ardens et ordinata dilectio in vita aeterna melius intelligemus, tamen nunc incoari eam oportet, sicut Iohannes inquit: Qui non diligit, manet in morte. Et descriptio qualiscunque tenenda est.

Osiander dilectionem nominat ipsum Deum, de hac forma loquendi alibi dicitur.

Paulus dilectionem deberi proximo intelligit, quae est affectus, qui in conversis accenditur a Spiritu sancto. Hunc affectum debemus proximo, de quo affectu Paulus hic et 1. Corinth. 13. loquitur. Et ad Galat.: Fructus spiritus dilectio etc.

Est igitur haec dilectio, in vera fide laetari in Deo, et obedire omnibus mandatis Dei, et propter eum diligere proximum, ac velle ei benefacere iuxta praecepta Dei, ubicunque est possibile.

Ad hanc dilectionem homo semper obligatus est a Deo, iuxta dictum: Diligas Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde, et proximum tuum sicut teipsum.

Eruditissime igitur distinxit hic Paulus obligationem. Praecipit, ut debita civili obligatione praestemus, his datis, cessat obligatio civili, ideo dicit: Nemini quicquam debeatis, id est, praestate debita obligatione civili, ita cessat haec obligatio. Sed dilectionem debebitis, id est, manet semper obligatio naturalis et divina, ad dilectionem in corde et ad multa externa officia, non debita civili obligatione. Ut Lazaro non debebat dives civili obligatione: sed tamen debebat naturali et divina obligatione dilectionem in corde, et externa beneficia, quae tunc praestare poterat.

## 13:10
Love is the fulfilling of the law.

Paul speaks properly, and as an expert, because it is true that in the law is commanded ordered love toward God and men, and this embraces universal obedience, as it is written: You shall love God with all your heart, and your neighbor as yourself.

But here let the juniors learn to judge this argument: The fulfilling of the law is justice, Love is the fulfilling of the law: Therefore, love is justice.

I answer: I concede the whole concerning legal justice, if the words are rightly understood. Because it is most true that the integral or perfect fulfillment of the law is justice, it is also true that perfect love is the fulfillment of the law: but No man has perfect love, nor perfect fulfillment of the law, except the mediator, our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, other men are not righteous before God by law or by love, but because of the mediator, by faith, freely, the person is received and is pleasing. Afterwards, new obedience is also pleasing, although it is far from perfection, and is languid, mutilated, beggarly, and sordid, as has often been said above.

Let the answer therefore be brief: Love is the fulfillment of the law. Likewise, It is justice, if that is understood of the idea, not of such love as exists in men in this life. Let this be enough to have pointed out.

Moreover, Paul adds in this place a repetition of the decalogue, and the doctrine concerning love, because it is necessary in this life that obedience be begun, according to all moral precepts, just as it is written: If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments, namely, just as the Gospel teaches that we are received on account of the Son, and that obedience is begun by faith, just as Paul says: By faith the law is established.

It is now the hour for us to awake from sleep.

The exhortation is taken from the time because of the opportunities, as if he were saying: Now, by His immense goodness, God has revealed the Gospel to us, to the Gentiles and to the Jews, whereas before you were in darkness, and He calls you. Let us acknowledge this highest benefit, and let us not despise so great a gift, but let us eagerly embrace it, and obey God.

The Lord proposes the same exhortation, because the light of the Gospel is not seen in the same way at all times: Walk, says the Lord, while you have the light, lest darkness overwhelm you. As in Judea, the calling having been spurned, greater darkness followed, and great furies, confusions of opinions, and discords of Princes, by which they drew upon themselves ultimate destruction: so it happens at other times. And now many abuse the pretext of liberty, and turn the grace of God into wantonness, as Peter speaks. Therefore, dissensions of opinions follow, and other calamities, wars, and confusions of empires. And 2 Corinthians 6, Paul says: Behold, now is the acceptable time. For he warns that we should not neglect the benefits offered, nor abuse them impiously.

He calls ignorance of the Gospel sleep, and acknowledgment the vigils. And because the labors and struggles belong to those who are awake, he commands them to put on the armor of light, namely, the knowledge of true doctrine, invocation, tolerance, and new obedience, as the description of the armor stands in the last chapter of Ephesians, taken from the 59th chapter of Isaiah.

Latin:

Dilectio est impletio legis.

Proprie loquitur Paulus, et ut artifex, quia verum est, in lege praecipi ordinatam dilectionem erga Deum et homines, et haec complectitur universalem obedientiam, sicut scriptum est: Diliges Deum ex toto corde, et proximum sicut teipsum.

Hic autem discant iuniores hoc argumentum iudicare: Impletio legis est iusticia, Dilectio est impletio legis: Ergo, dilectio est iusticia.

Respondeo: Concedo totum de iusticia legali, si vocabula recte intelligantur. Quia verissimum est, integram seu perfectam impletionem legis esse iusticiam, verum est etiam, perfectam dilectionem esse impletionem legis: sed neque perfectam dilectionem, neque perfectam legis impletionem ullus homo habet, excepto mediatore, Domino nostro Iesu Christo. Ideo caeteri homines nec lege, nec dilectione sunt iusti coram Deo, sed propter mediatorem fide, gratis, persona recipitur et placet. Postea placet et nova obedientia, quamvis procul abest a perfectione, et est languida, mutila, mendica et sordida, ut supra saepe dictum est.

Sit igitur brevis responsio: Dilectio est impletio legis. Item, Est iusticia, si id intelligatur de idea, non de tali dilectione, qualis est in hominibus in hac vita. Haec satis sit monuisse.

Addit autem Paulus hoc loco repetitionem decalogi, et doctrinam de dilectione, quia necesse est in hac vita incoari obedientiam, iuxta omnia praecepta moralia, sicut scriptum est: Si vis ingredi in vitam, serva mandata, scilicet, sicut Evangelium docet propter filium nos recipi, et fide incoari obedientiam, sicut Paulus inquit: Per fidem lex stabilitur.

Iam hora est, nos ex sommo expergisci.

Adhortatio est a tempore sumta propter occasiones, quasi dicat: Iam immensa bonitate Deus nobis patefecit Evangelium Gentibus et Iudaeis, cum antea in tenebris essetis, et vos vocat. Id summum beneficium agnoscamus, nec tantum munus adspernemur, sed avide amplectamur, et Deo obediamus.

Eandem adhortationem proponit Dominus, quia non omnibus temporibus similiter conspicitur lux Evangelii: Ambulate, inquit Dominus, dum lucem habetis, ne tenebrae vos obruant. Ut in Iudaea, spreta vocatione, secutae sunt maiores tenebrae, et magni furores, confusiones opinionum, et Principum discordiae, quibus attraxerunt ultimum exitium: ita fit et aliis temporibus. Et nunc multi abutuntur praetextu libertatis, et vertunt gratiam Dei in petulantiam, ut Petrus loquitur. Ideo sequuntur dissidia opinionum, et aliae calamitates, bella et confusiones imperiorum. Et 2. Corinth. 6. Paulus inquit: Ecce nunc tempus acceptum. Monet enim, ne oblata beneficia negligamus, nec eis impie abutamur.

Somnum nominat ignorantiam Evangelii, Vigilias agnitionem. Et quia vigilantium sunt labores et certamina, iubet sumere arma lucis, scilicet verae doctrinae cognitionem, invocationem, tolerantiam, novam obedientiam, ut extat descriptio armorum, ad Ephesios ultimo, sumta ex 59. cap. Esaiae.

## 13:11
Salvation is nearer than when we believed.

Salvation, that is, Christ Himself exhibited, and the preaching of the Gospel among the Gentiles are said to be nearer, because before this, the preaching had not been commonly spread among the Gentiles. Even fewer Jews understood what the kingdom of Christ would be like. Now he says: All things are more illustrious than then when we believed, namely, concerning these future benefits, which were then known to many fewer. He signifies, therefore, that the objects are now nearer, that is, more known: he does not say this, that men are saved now in one way, and that the fathers were saved in another. For both the fathers and subsequently other men are saved by faith. There is only this difference, that the fathers believed in the Lord who was to come, we in the One who has been exhibited.

Not in the luxury of banquets and drunkenness. Κῶμος signifies a banquet of companions instituted for pleasures and games, whence Comedy is named.

For luxury and drunkenness are censured, not the necessary use of food and drink, therefore he adds below: Provide for the flesh, not for lusts. He wants the body to be cared for, but without luxury, lest pious thoughts, invocation, and the exercises of other virtues be hindered, etc. Just as Peter also says: Be modest and sober for prayer.

Let the younger ones consider the phrase: Make no provision for the flesh. For here Augustine seeks a foreign interpretation, that they should not follow carnal counsels, so that it could be said to a miser, do not seek wealth by usury through carnal counsel: and to one desirous of domination it could be said, Do not invade the kingdom by illicit means. But the phrase signifies something else. Paul commands to care for the body, but to have regard for the flesh or body, that is, to consider what the safety of the body demands, but in a just manner and order. Thus Demosthenes says: ποιεῖσθαι πρόνοιαν ἑορτῆς, that is, to have regard for the festival.

Latin:

Propior est salus quam tum cum credebamus.

Salus, id est, ipse Christus exhibitus, et Evangelii praedicatio inter Gentes dicuntur propius adesse, quia antea non fuit communis praedicatio inter Gentes sparsa. Pauciores etiam Iudaei intelligebant, quale futurum esset regnum Christi. Iam inquit: Omnia sunt magis illustria, quam tunc cum credebamus, scilicet de venturis his beneficiis, quae tunc multo paucioribus nota erant. Significat igitur, obiecta nunc propiora esse, id est, notiora: non hoc dicit, aliter nunc salvari homines, aliter patres salvatos esse. Nam utrique patres et deinceps alii homines fide salvantur. Tantum hoc discrimen est, quod patres de venturo Domino credebant, nos de exhibito.

Non in luxu conviviorum et ebrietate. Κῶμος significat convivium sodalium ad voluptates et ludos institutum, unde Comoedia dicta est.

Luxus enim et ebrietas taxantur, non usus cibi et potus necessarius, ideo infra addit: Curate carnem, non ad cupiditates. Vult curari corpus, sed sine luxu, ne impediantur piae cogitationes, invocatio, et aliarum virtutum exercitia etc. Sicut et Petrus inquit: Sitis modesti et sobrii ad precationem.

Iuniores considerent phrasin: Providentiam carnis ne facite. Hic enim peregrinam interpretationem quaerit Augustinus, Ne sequantur carnalia consilia, ut dici posset avaro, ne carnali consilio quaerat opes per usuras: et cupido dominationis dici posset, Ne invadas regnum illicitis modis. Sed phrasis aliud significat. Iubet Paulus curare corpus, sed habere rationem carnis seu corporis, id est, considerare quid corporis incolumitas postulet, sed iusto modo et ordine. Sic Demosthenes inquit: ποιεῖσθαι πρόνοιαν ἑορτῆς, id est, habere rationem festi.

## 13:14
Put on Christ.

This figure of speech does not only signify imitation, as if you were to say to an angry Prince, May you put on the mind of Augustus in repressing anger, that is, may you imitate his clemency. But there are other much more important significations in this place, of which mention is made in the 61st chapter of Isaiah: I will rejoice greatly in the Lord, and my soul shall exult in my God, because He has clothed me with the garments of salvation, and has covered me with the robe of justice, and it is as a Bridegroom adorned in priestly attire, and as a Bride adorned with her ornaments. We are clothed by the Son of God in two ways. First, by His merit or obedience, which merits for us the remission of sins, so that our sins are covered as if with a clean garment, and we are reconciled and righteous, that is, accepted by God through the imputed justice of the Son, just as it is also said in the Psalm: Blessed are they whose sins are covered, etc. And Isaiah 4: There will be a shade against the heat. Then we are also clothed by the efficacious presence of the Son of God ...in believers. For when we receive consolation by faith, we are vivified by God in this order: the λόγος is present and efficacious by the voice of the Gospel, and shows the Father's mercy, and vivifies hearts, and the Holy Spirit is poured into hearts, so that may rejoice, and my soul shall exult in my God, because he has clothed me with the garments of salvation, and with the garment of justice he has surrounded me, and he is as a Bridegroom in priestly attire, and as a Bride adorned with her ornaments.

We are clothed by the Son of God in two ways. First, by his own merit or obedience, which merits for us the remission of sins, so that our sins may be covered as with a clean garment, and we may be reconciled and just, that is, accepted by God through the imputed justice of the Son, as it is also said in the Psalm: Blessed are they whose sins are covered etc. And Isaiah 4: There shall be a shelter against the heat.

Then we are clothed also by the efficacious presence of the Son of God in believers. For when by faith we receive consolation, we are vivified by God in this order: the λόγος (Word) is present and efficacious by the voice of the Gospel, and shows the Father's mercy, and vivifies hearts, and the Holy Spirit is poured out into hearts, so that they may rejoice in God, who is known through the Word, and they may be turned to invocation, and faith may be firm, and hearts may be made like the λόγος, who is the image of God, as it is said in 2 Corinthians 3: We are transformed into his likeness etc.

Of this clothing it is said in John 14: We will come to him, and we will make our abode with him.

So therefore says Isaiah: I will rejoice in my God etc., that is, I confess that liberation is not the work of our own powers, but of God's.

And this God Messiah clothes me with his merits, and with his efficacious presence, by which I become a temple and dwelling of God, and this clothing is begun in this life, but will be perfected in eternal life.

He adds, moreover, what kind of clothing this is. It is the Bridegroom's, namely the Messiah's priestly attire, that is, the passion, or obedience in the passion, and the fortitude of having overcome death and restored life, and the ministry of the Gospel, by which he is efficacious, and clothes his bride with a similar attire. Now the bride, the Church, is clothed with a similar attire, by the passion in this life, and by the vivification which is done through the Messiah, and it is now begun, and in eternal life it will be consummated, when the bride will be like Christ, that is, she will be entirely without sin and without death, and God will shine in her, vivifying and suffusing her with his light, wisdom, justice and joy, so that she may be conformable to God.

The phrase, therefore, is most sweet to observe, that he says the attire of Christ the Bridegroom is priestly. For it signifies the voice of the Gospel, the passion of Christ, the intercession for us, the victories and the efficacy in us, as it is said in the Psalm: Thou art a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.

So it was said to the Galatians: Whoever of you have been baptized, have put on Christ. Where it is manifest that Paul is not speaking properly of imitation, but of the Son of God himself clothing us with his benefits. So therefore let it be understood, you have put on Christ, namely, by his justice being imputed to us: then also by the accepted presence of the divinity, which is efficacious in us. Now Christ is put on whenever by faith consolation is made in conversion and invocation, when the mind is sustained by the true thought of the promise, in which, on account of the Son of God, are given the remission of sins, and reconciliation.

So also this saying to the Romans is understood: Put on Christ, as if he were saying: By word and faith receive the benefits of Christ, the imputed justice and efficacy of the Son of God, ask that he may govern you, and do not resist him.

With this interpretation we are first confirmed, which distinguishes the Son of God from other teachers and examples, then there can be added the interpretation concerning example. Imitate Christ, as an example in virtues, which ought to be common to all, namely in the care of teaching the Gospel, constancy of confession, humility, patience in enduring injuries, as if I were to say to a Prince: Put on the spirit of Augustus in the moderation of anger.

Latin:

Induite Christum.

Haec figura sermonis non tantum significat imitationem, ut si dicas Principi irato, Induas animum Augusti in reprimenda ira, id est, imiteris eius clementiam. Sed aliae multo potiores significationes sunt hoc loco, quarum fit mentio in capite 61. Esaiae: Gaudens gaudebo in Domino, et exultabit anima mea in Deo meo, quia induit me vestimentis salutis, et vestimento iusticiae circumdedit me, et est velut Sponsus in sacerdotali ornatum, et sicut Sponsa decorata suis ornamentis. Vestimur a filio Dei dupliciter. Primum ipsius merito seu obedientia, quae meretur nobis remissionem peccatorum, ut tegantur nostra peccata tanquam munda veste, ac simus reconciliati et iusti, id est, accepti Deo imputata filii iusticia, sicut et in Psalmo dicitur: Beati quorum tecta sunt peccata etc. Et Esaiae 4.: Erit umbraculum contra aestum. Deinde vestimur et efficaci praesentia filii Dei ...in credentibus. Cum enim fide accipimus consolationem, vivificamur a Deo hoc ordine: λόγος est praesens et efficax voce Evangelii, et monstrat patris misericordiam, et vivificat corda, et effunditur Spiritus sanctus in corda, ut laetemino, et exultabit anima mea in Deo meo, quia induit me vestimentis salutis, et vestimento iusticiae circumdedit me, et est velut Sponsus in sacerdotali ornatu, et sicut Sponsa decorata suis ornamentis.

Vestimur a filio Dei dupliciter. Primum ipsius merito seu obedientia, quae meretur nobis remissionem peccatorum, ut tegantur nostra peccata tanquam munda veste, ac simus reconciliati et iusti, id est, accepti Deo imputata filii iusticia, sicut et in Psalmo dicitur: Beati quorum tecta sunt peccata etc. Et Esaiae 4.: Erit umbraculum contra aestum.

Deinde vestimur et efficaci praesentia filii Dei in credentibus. Cum enim fide accipimus consolationem, vivificamur a Deo hoc ordine: λόγος est praesens et efficax voce Evangelii, et monstrat patris misericordiam, et vivificat corda, et effunditur Spiritus sanctus in corda, ut laetentur in Deo, qui est agnitus per verbum, et flectantur ad invocationem, et fides sit firma, et adsimilentur corda λόγῳ, qui est imago Dei, sicut 2. Corinth. 3. dicitur: Transformamur ad similitudinem eius etc.

De hoc vestitu dicitur Iohannis 14.: Veniemus ad eum, et mansionem apud eum faciemus.

Sic igitur inquit Esaias: Gaudebo in Deo meo etc., id est, fateor liberationem non esse opus nostrarum virium, sed Dei, Et hic Deus Messias vestit me suis meritis, et suo efficaci praesentia, qua fio templum et domicilium Dei, et hic vestitus incoatur in hac vita, sed perficietur in vita aeterna.

Addit autem amplius, qualis sit hic vestitus.

Est Sponsi, scilicet Messiae sacerdotalis ornatus, id est, passio, vel obedientia in passione, et fortitudo superata morte et restituta vita, et ministerium Evangelii, quo est efficax, et suam sponsam simili ornatu vestit. Est autem sponsa Ecclesia simili ornatu vestita, passione in hac vita, et vivificatione quae fit per Messiam, et nunc incoatur, et in vita aeterna consummata erit, cum sponsa erit similis Christo, id est, erit prorsus sine peccato et sine morte, et fulgebit in ea Deus vivificans et perfundens eam sua luce, sapientia, iusticia et laetitia, ut sit conformis Deo.

Phrasis igitur dulcissima observelur, quod ait, Christi sponsi ornatum esse sacerdotalem. Significat enim vocem Evangelii, passionem Christi, deprecationem pro nobis, victorias et efficaciam in nobis, sicut in Psalmo dicitur: Tu es sacerdos in aeternum secundum ordinem Melchisedech. Sic ad Galatas dictum est: Quicunque baptizati estis, Christum induistis.

Ubi manifestum est, non loqui Paulum proprie de imitatione, sed de filio Dei ipso nos vestiente suis beneficiis. Sic ergo intelligatur, Christum induistis, scilicet, imputata nobis ipsius iusticia: deinde et accepta praesentia divinitatis, quae in nobis est efficax. Sic autem induitur Christus, quandocunque fide fit consolatio in conversione et invocatione, cum mens sustentatur vera cogitatione promissionis, in qua propter filium Dei dantur remissio peccatorum, et reconciliatio.

Sic et hoc dictum ad Romanos intelligitur: Induamini Christum, quasi dicat: Verbo et fide accipite beneficia Christi, imputatam iusticiam et efficaciam filii Dei, petite ut vos gubernet, nec repugnate ei. Cum hac interpretatione primum confirmati sumus, quae discernit filium Dei ab aliis doctoribus et exemplis, deinde potest addi interpretatio de exemplo.

Imitemini Christum, ut exemplum in virtutibus, quae debent esse communes omnibus, videlicet in cura docendi Evangelii, constantia confessionis, humilitate, patientia in tolerandis iniuriis, ut si dicam Principi: Induito animum Augusti in moderatione iracundiae.

## 14:1 Disposition of Romans: Argument
Chapter XIV. He exhorts to tolerate the weak in faith; and to raise them up little by little, so that they may become stronger.

He exhorts also the weaker ones, not to judge rashly concerning the stronger ones.

Proposition.

Help the weak in faith, so that he may not be left ambiguous in faith. To the exposition of the proposition pertains: Let each one be certain in his own mind, that is, nothing is to be done with an ambiguous conscience.

For when you doubt whether that which you undertake pleases God, and yet you undertake it, that certainly is to despise God. In the same vein at the end he adds a maxim (γνώμην): Everything that is not of faith is sin.

Latin:

Caput XIV. Hortatur tolerare imbecilles in fide; et eos paulatim erigere, ut fiant firmiores.

Hortatur et infirmiores, ne temere iudicent de firmioribus.

Propositio.

Infirmum in fide adiuvate, ne relinquatur in fide ambiguus. Ad expositionem propositionis pertinet: Unusquisque in sua sententia certus sit, id est, nihil faciendum ambigua conscientia.

Nam cum dubitas, utrum Deo placeat id quod suscipis, et suscipis tamen, id certe est contemnere Deum. In eandem sententiam in fine addit γνώμην: Omne quod non est ex fide, peccatum est.

## 14:1 Argument
Chapter XIV.

Above we said that the doctrine of works was begun in the twelfth chapter. The order, therefore, of these legal exhortations should be considered. The twelfth chapter is as it were ethical, concerning the virtues common to all. The thirteenth is political. The fourteenth is ἱερατικὸν (priestly) concerning ceremonies.

For these are the three principal kinds of works in the conversation of men, for because this mortal life cannot be without ceremonies, that is, an order distinguishing the ranks of persons, the times of public assemblies and readings, or of childish exercises, it was necessary for the Church to be admonished concerning their use.

For error concerning ceremonies begets many huge inconveniences. First, the doctrine of the Gospel concerning faith and the benefits of Christ is obscured, when the opinion creeps in, that those rites merit the remission of sins, or that on account of them a man is just, as

The Pharisees imagined regarding their sacrifices and rites. Secondly, the light concerning the distinction between external shadows and the newness of the spirit is extinguished, by which those converted to God are made temples of God.

But when the opinion creeps in that monastic rites, celibacy, the flight from common labors in political life, and distinctions of foods are worship of God and perfection, the true forms of worship, which ought to be in the heart—fear, faith, patience, hope, conjugal chastity, and other fruits of the spirit—are obscured. Thirdly, the doctrine concerning the distinction of works is destroyed, when Ceremonies are preferred to works commanded by God, just as monks preferred their rites to marriage and political duties. Fourthly, the opinion of Necessity creeps in, which is a dangerous torture-chamber for consciences; for when the observance of human rites is thought to be necessary, minds occupied with this great care are hindered in other necessary matters, nor yet do they always observe all the rites. And when they pretend that these are sins, prayer is hindered; furthermore, it is a sin itself to think that such works are worship of God, and that omission is a sin. Fifthly, the opinion of necessity begets incurable discords, just as there were once dissensions concerning the Passover. Sixthly, the power of establishing traditions is falsely attributed to Bishops, with the opinion of worship or necessity, as often as the true use of traditions is ignored.

Since, therefore, the error concerning Traditions produces many inconveniences, it is necessary that there exist in the Church a doctrine concerning their use that is rightly explained and clear.

But first, let the doctrine concerning Christian liberty be noted, regarding which we usually make four degrees in this life for the sake of teaching.

The first is liberation from sin and the wrath of God, and eternal damnation on account of the mediator, namely the Remission of sins and reconciliation, and justification or the gratuitous imputation of righteousness on account of the mediator. The second is joined with the first regarding the effect, namely Vivification in us, which is done through the son of God vivifying hearts, and freeing them from the pains of the lower world, by the gift of the Holy Spirit: and then the constant presence of the divinity in those who call upon Him, ruling, protecting, helping, and saving them by many wondrous liberations, just as Daniel is saved among the lions. These are the principal degrees, and the glorious liberty, about which one must think daily in prayer, and of these degrees it is especially said: If the son shall have made you free, you shall be truly free. The third degree is liberation from the polity of Moses, namely from Mosaic ceremonies and the forensic laws of Moses: because the kingdom of Christ is the restoration of eternal life and eternal righteousness, with sin and death abolished. This kingdom begins, however, when the son is first sent, revealing the promise: The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent. This son is then always effective through the ministry of the Gospel, and moves and confirms believers by the Holy Spirit: and this person, God and man, is the head of the Church, and through this person the resurrection of the dead happens immediately, just as Paul says in 1.

Corinthians 15: After death [came] through man, also through man comes the resurrection of the dead. Likewise, the Lord says: He has given all judgment to the son.

The kingdom of the Messiah is therefore far different from political kingdoms, and it is gathered in this life from diverse nations, where there are diverse polities, just as Paul says in Colossians 2: Put on the new man, who is renewed unto knowledge according to the image of him who created him, where there is no Greek, nor Jew, nor slave, nor free, but all and in all is Christ, that is, giving all good things by his merit, namely the remission of sins and reconciliation, and at the same time effecting in believers new light, righteousness, and life. This distinction between the kingdom of Christ and the polities of the world must first be considered, afterwards it must be considered why the polity of Moses was instituted for a time, which lasted 1582 years.

For there are that many years from the exodus from Egypt to the final destruction of Jerusalem under Titus. For God wanted there to be a certain seat for that people, in whom He wanted the Messiah to be born, to preach openly, to suffer, to rise again from death, and to show testimonies. In order for these things to be certain, God wanted the nation and polity to be distinct from other nations. Afterwards, once the Messiah was exhibited, this polity was abolished, so that it might be known that the kingdom of Christ is one thing, and the Mosaic polity another.

From these sources it can be understood that we are not bound to the ceremonies and positive law of Moses, but that individuals in their own polities can use laws congruent with reason, which the polity of that [nation] has sanctioned.

ordinary authority regarding political affairs, just as we use the different spans of days.

The fourth degree is liberation from human traditions in the Church, as Paul says, Colossians 2: Let no one judge you in food, drink, or the turns of festivals. Item: Which are according to the commandments and traditions of men.

And from the same source this liberty arises, from which arises liberation from Mosaic ceremonies. Since Christ's obedience is the merit for the remission of sins, no human works, and much less the slaughtering of beasts, or rites of satisfaction, or fasts in the Church merit the remission of sins. Item: Since the kingdom of Christ is life, light, wisdom, and eternal justice in hearts, which is begun in this life through Him by the ministry of the Gospel, and by the gift of the Holy Spirit, it is not the observance of external rites of the slaughtering of beasts, or of fasts, or of clothing. Therefore Paul says: our citizenship (πολίτευμα) is in heaven, that is, the kingdom of Christ is not an external and perishing polity, but a new light in the soul that will endure for all eternity.

With this source considered, these degrees of liberty can be more correctly understood.

Afterwards, it is necessary to know the distinctions of traditions which have been made in the Church by human authority (for we are not now speaking of political laws, which were made for the defense of bodily society and honest peace in empires, but of ecclesiastical rites), of which there are three degrees. First.

Some traditions by themselves conflict with the commandments of God, such as the edict of Nebuchadnezzar, which commanded that the statue be worshipped. Such traditions are the invocation of the dead, the worship of statues, Papist Masses, Papist satisfactions. Item, the law of celibacy, because it cannot be observed without sin. Regarding all these traditions, it is necessary to hold the rule: One must obey God rather than men. It is therefore necessary to abolish such laws and rites simply.

The second degree is of rites which, although they are of things whose use does not by itself conflict with the commandments of God, yet their observance becomes impious when the opinion of worship or necessity is added, such as the distinction of foods, clothing, and times. In these, it is necessary to censure false opinions and to show what are true and necessary forms of worship. And those rites themselves can be utterly abolished which do not contribute to good order, such as the foolish rites of the distinction of foods, since the observance indeed obscures the doctrine.

The third degree is of rites which do not conflict with the commandments of God, and are useful for good order, and are done without the opinion of worship and necessity. For because the rational nature understands order and knows the causes for which order is to be loved, it is commanded that in the Church also all things be done in order and decently, as Paul says. Therefore, the Church, even in the times of the early Fathers, always distinguished feast days accommodated to histories, and so we distinguish readings and chants. God commanded the paschal lamb to be eaten at that very time when the Son was to be the victim on the cross. Thus the distinction of time was accommodated to the future history.

There was at Athens a certain insolent man, Cynesias, who was accustomed to celebrate festivals contrary to public ones; if anyone were to exercise such insolence in the Church, he would by no means follow the saying of Paul: Let all things be done in order and decently in the Church. Therefore, some such rites useful for order can be retained: and the distinction of times is a reminder of history. But always let the rule be in sight: that to that observance, the opinion of worship and necessity is by no means to be added, nor is it to be thought that those who omit such rites without scandal are sinning. This doctrine is taught by Paul in the following chapter.

Concerning scandal.

The word 'Scandal' they say comes from σκάζω, which means 'I limp', or from σκάμβον, which is 'curved', as is said in the proverb: a curved stick (σκάμβον ξύλον) is never straight (οὐδέποτε ὀρθὸν γίνεσθαι). For 'scandal' properly signifies a trap in instruments by which wolves, or foxes, or mice are caught. And Hesychius expressly says: σκάνδαλον is that which is in snares (τὸ ἐν μνάγραις). And the commentary on Aristophanes says: σκανδάληθρα are the curved pieces of wood in traps. Rightly, therefore, the name σκάνδαλον is rendered by the word 'snare' (tendicula): from there the Church transferred the name to ambushes, or snares, namely, perverse dogmas and perverse examples, which catch men just as snares catch beasts.

However, usually and for the sake of teaching, offenses are distinguished. Pharisaic offense is called the indignation in the impious, who are offended by true doctrine and by examples approved by God, because they bear with difficulty the undermining of their power or the hindrance of their gain. As when the Pharisees are offended by Christ censuring the gain in the temple and the false opinions concerning sacrifices. Concerning this offense it is said in Matthew 15

The Pharisees, hearing this discourse, were scandalized. Hence the name is used, 'Pharisaic scandal,' for a Pharisaic offense.

However, the rule must be held: It is necessary to obey God rather than men. Item: Whoever shall have confessed me before men, I also will confess him before my Father in heaven. Wherefore it is necessary to teach the truth and to perform the commands of God, even if tyrants rage and tumult and disturb empires. And let not the minds of those who teach rightly and do rightly languish because of Pharisaic offense, just as Christ says: Let them alone, they are blind, and leaders of the blind.

This consolation against Pharisaic offenses must be held first. Nor can it indeed happen that moderate men do not grieve when they see, upon errors being censured, dissensions arise and empires disturbed. But yet the first commandment: You shall have no other gods, is most necessary, to be preferred to our life, to the tranquility of the fatherland, and to all bodily goods. This consolation the Lord often repeats: Whoever loves father or mother more than me, is not worthy of me.

And in Deuteronomy 33, in the blessing of the tribe of Levi: Who said to his father and mother, I know you not, these keep your law, bless O Lord them, strike the backs of his enemies, and let those who hate them not rise up.

There, consolation is added, so that the pious may not languish because of Pharisaic judgments, hatreds, and cruelty. And to all of us at this time, this admonition concerning Pharisaic scandals is also necessary. Because the impious cry out that public tranquility is disturbed by the propagation of our doctrine, by the marriage of priests, and by the censure of cults, which they impiously defend. Therefore, against the unjust judgments of the world, let us confirm ourselves with divine commands: Flee from idols. And especially let us be moved by this thunderbolt: Whoever shall have spoken blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, it shall not be forgiven him.

By no means, therefore, are the enemies of the Gospel to be helped.

Another scandal, properly so called, which is named 'Datum' [a stumbling block], concerning which the Lord says: Woe to the world because of scandals, is impious doctrine, or an impious example, which others imitating become worse. All ages are full of examples: because there are always many impious people who either beget or confirm depraved dogmas. Item: Those who give evil counsel. Item: Those who by their examples draw others into a society of crimes, as Catiline moving an unjust war: or to imitation, as many imitate examples of lusts, gluttony, rapine, and usury. Since such deeds are in themselves horrendous sins, they become the more atrocious because they draw many with them and tear them away from God, and are the seeds of other subsequent crimes. Just as the fall of David first polluted a holy matron, then impelled him to depraved counsels concerning killing her husband, afterwards punishments followed, in which Absalom and a great part of the people offended God in many ways.

Because in sedition there are innumerable crimes, as the saying of Thucydides is known: ἐν στάσει πᾶσα ἰδέα κακοῦ ἐστὶ [in sedition every form of evil exists]. Often, therefore, let us think about this kind of scandal with a most sad discourse: Woe to the world because of scandals, and let us know that it encompasses huge confusions in the whole human race, false dogmas, public and private examples harmful to morals, the beginnings of unjust dissensions and wars, depraved associations: let us be more circumspect in teaching, in giving counsel, and in all actions, according to the saying: Watch and pray, that you enter not into temptation.

Item: All that you do, do for the glory of God, and do not offend the Church.

Another degree is of avoiding scandal in the use of indifferent things, either among docile weaklings, or among stubborn hypocritical adversaries. It is, however, among docile weaklings to use liberty in such a way that sudden novelty does not deter them from the doctrine: Or if they are invited, not yet confirmed, they might afterwards fall into dangerous doubts: as the pastor of a certain Church, who had taught with great contention that the use of meats was permitted, afterwards, falling ill, ordered it to be requested of the Church that at least then, in the fast, they should abstain, lest he himself be the author of a changed ancient custom. Concerning this third kind, Paul here warns that it must be judged prudently how the use of liberty is to be moderated, concerning which it was said above, and there are two rules: Docile weaklings are not to be disturbed by sudden novelty, as is said here: Him that is weak in the faith receive, etc.

But on the contrary, against stubborn adversaries, examples of the doctrine concerning liberty are to be used, just as the Apostles violated Pharisaic traditions, etc.

Let each one be certain in his own mind.

That is, let nothing be done with a doubting conscience: but let the conscience be confirmed by the word of God. This doctrine is very necessary, that nothing is to be done against conscience, and likewise that nothing is to be done with a doubting conscience. And below this doctrine is repeated: Everything that is not of faith is sin.

The Papists explain this saying only legally, namely, Whatever fights against the law is sin: which is rightly said, but it does not yet render the complete sentiment of Paul. For it is not enough that deeds agree with the law, but it is necessary that the knowledge of Christ shine forth, and that one govern all obedience with the trust of a son of God, so that we may know both which deeds please, and how they please. Now deeds that agree with the law please when the person pleases by righteous faith, freely on account of the mediator, and then he knows that obedience begun is required, and that it pleases on account of the mediator although it does not satisfy the law.

Here it is necessary to censure the foul error of the Papists, who teach that one must always doubt whether one is reconciled, and that this doubt is not a sin. Against this error must be opposed this saying of Paul: Everything that is not of faith is sin.

The word πληροφορεῖσθαι signifies to be certain, as in Isocrates: πληροφορηθεὶς ἐμ' ἐξαρνὸν εἶναι, that is, when he was certain that I was denying. Thus Paul used this word exactly, Rom. 4, concerning Abraham: When he was certain that God was able to make a barren mother fruitful. And in Luke chapter 1 and Colossians 2, πληροφορία signifies certainty, as if you were to say: Full assent.

But someone might say: You boast gloriously that you please God, when yet this natural darkness always feels doubts and distrust? I answer: It is true that doubts and distrust cling to the minds of men in this depravity of nature: but for this very reason God has published the voice of the law and the Gospel. He wants us to be certain about both things, about wrath and about grace. He wants it to be known for certain that God truly and horribly condemns those not converted to the Son, just as it is written in John 3: He who does not believe in the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him. He wants, in turn, also that reconciliation granted on account of the Son to those who believe be known to us for certain by His immense goodness.

For this very reason the promise concerning the Son and concerning grace was published immediately from the beginning, when it was unknown to all creatures, therefore the Lord says: God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son, that everyone who believes in Him should not perish, but have eternal life. And He wants this promise to be known, and rightly understood, and received by faith. For to what purpose would it pertain to be revealed, if it were not to be received by faith? Thus therefore Paul says: Therefore it is by faith, freely, so that the promise may be firm. Why was an oath added, if not so that the consolation might be certain for us? As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live. Let there be, therefore, conversion in us, and let the free promise be apprehended by faith, so that we may hold onto consolation against despair and the pains of hell. Therefore, concerning both things it is said in Mark 1: Repent, and believe the Gospel.

Although, however, doubt clings to all men in this depravity of nature: yet let converted minds resist this doubt and oppose to it the voice of the promise, and let such faith be kindled that believes, not only that the remission of sins is given to others, but to you yourself also, and with this faith approach God, and struggle out of doubt, so that you may be able to call upon God. Paul speaks of this faith, which raises up and consoles the heart in true sorrows, when he says: Being justified by faith we have peace. Likewise, Eph. 3: Through whom we dare to approach in confidence through faith in Him.

Elsewhere the saying of Solomon has often been explained, which the monks impiously cite to confirm doubt: No one knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred, because similar things happen to the just and the unjust, namely in this life. That saying simply means this: that one must judge concerning the will of God from His word, not from favorable or adverse things in this life. Let not Ahab think that he pleases God because he has a flourishing kingdom and is a victor: nor let David think that he is cast off by God because he has been driven from his kingdom, but let each judge from the word of God: therefore Solomon's sentiment agrees entirely with us, because it leads us to the word of God.

The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness, joy, and peace in the Holy Spirit. In these things, serving Christ, he pleases God, and is approved by men.

…A most common hypocrisy is that about which the Lord preaches, Matt. 23, saying: Woe to Woe to you, scribes and hypocrites, who strain at a gnat and swallow a camel. Namely, when divine precepts, and indeed the most important ones, are neglected, some retain certain ceremonies and rites handed down by men, and they feel that these external observations are righteousness before God and necessary acts of worship of God, and they think that neglecting them is impiety, and with this opinion they most fiercely defend their rites and exercise cruelty against others who think rightly.

But just as it is necessary in all things to distinguish the necessary from the unnecessary, so in the Church it is most necessary to distinguish the foundation from the stubble, as Paul says: 'No other foundation can be laid than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ.' Likewise Psalm 50: 'If I am hungry, I will not tell you; call upon me in the day of trouble, etc.' And Jeremiah 7: 'I did not speak to them concerning burnt offerings, but this I commanded them: hear me.' And Ecclesiastes 4: 'Obedience is better than the sacrifices of fools, for they do not know how much evil they do.' The examples show of what great sins this complaint speaks.

A great part of men think that the offering in the Mass is the chief act of worship, and they trust most in that worship, although there is a horrible idolomania there. These do not understand how much evil they do. Therefore, Paul opposes a rule from the definition of the kingdom of God: 'The kingdom of God is not food and drink,' that is, not an external observation in foods and clothes, 'but is righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.' By these appellations he includes all necessary acts of worship of God, as elsewhere: 'Fight the good fight, keeping faith and a good conscience.'

Hosea also delivers a similar sentiment: 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.' Zechariah says: 'Love truth and peace.' Thus, the divine voice everywhere warns the Church about the distinction between true acts of worship and false acts of worship.

But as Daniel says elsewhere that the Messiah would bring everlasting righteousness, so here let righteousness be understood concerning the whole benefit of the Son of God, which is begun in this life by faith, that is, trust in the Mediator, by which we are righteous, that is, accepted by God, by which also the Son of God gives life to believers, and shows the Father, and gives the Holy Spirit, so that a new obedience may be begun, which will later be complete in eternal life, when God will be all in all. Therefore, the kingdom of God is in reality eternal righteousness, as Daniel names it, that is, such a life restored through the Son, by faith, which then becomes complete obedience after the resurrection.

Peace signifies reconciliation with God, as Paul says elsewhere: 'Having been justified, we have peace with God,' that is, having faith we are already reconciled, freed from wrath and condemnation, and we are pleasing to God. This peace is accompanied by joy in the heart resting in God, and this he names joy in the Holy Spirit, that is, which is kindled by the Holy Spirit, who is love and substantial joy. Therefore, he kindles such motions as he himself is. But since he kindles motions consistent with all the precepts of God, Paul here includes begun obedience, according to all the precepts of God, joy in invocation, in the love of God, thanksgiving and confession, obedience in the love of neighbor, chastity, and other virtues, as he enumerates the fruits of the Spirit, Galatians 5 and elsewhere.

Concerning these true acts of worship he says later: 'He who serves Christ in these is pleasing to God and approved by men.' Here let us remember that a testimony is delivered which expressly affirms that the good works of the reborn are pleasing to God, as will be said more copiously in its own place. Peter says: 'Offer spiritual sacrifices pleasing to God through Jesus Christ.'

Secondly, he says by name: 'He who serves Christ,' to signify that he is speaking of those works which are done in the knowledge and trust of the Mediator.

Thirdly, he also wants obedience to be referred to this end, that it be performed not for our own glory, or for the belly, but for the Son of God himself, namely, because we feel that this honor is owed to him, and by this honor we show that we confess that he is God and Savior, and we celebrate him. Finally, let us include here the universal doctrine in which he explains how good works are pleasing to God.

But why does he add: 'He is approved by men,' when nevertheless in most men there is a horrible bitterness of hatred against the saints, so that many are most cruelly killed who are nevertheless adorned with divine testimonies, such as the Son of God himself, who had raised the dead, Abel, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and others?

I answer: Paul speaks of the judgments of the Church. The saints always have true testimonies in the Church. As the son of Sirach says in chapter 44: 'The Church will declare their praise.' And God himself says: 'I will bless those who bless you.' But let Paul weave the tyranny of certain arrogant ones tyranny of certain arrogant ones, who think they will do what they imagine is granted to them, and do not want their liberty to be hindered, even if they know that the minds and eyes of good men are offended by untimely examples, and that scandals follow, either because of imitation or because of the alienation of wills from the Gospel.

Therefore, 1 Corinthians 10, the same rule is handed down: Whatever you do, do it to the glory of God, and do not be a scandal to the Church.

It is desired, therefore, that the judgments of the Church be regarded; for this reason, it is often commanded that one's reputation be defended, as Syracides 41 says: Take care of a good name, for it excels many treasures: and let the verse be known: It is light, nor does the glory of honor stimulate it.

Latin:

Caput XIV.

Supra diximus incoatam esse doctrinam operum in capite duodecimo. Ordo igitur consideretur harum legalium concionum. Caput duodecimum est velut ethicum de communibus omnium virtutibus. Tertiumdecimum est politicum. Decimumquartum est ἱερατικὸν de ceremoniis.

Sunt enim haec tria genera praecipua operum in conversatione hominum, quia enim haec vita mortalis non potest carere ceremoniis, id est, ordine distinguente gradus personarum, tempora publicorum congressuum et lectionum, aut exercitiorum puerilium, necesse fuit Ecclesiam de usu earum fidmoneri. Nam error de ceremoniis parit multa ingentia incommoda.

Primum, obscuratur doctrina Evangelii de fide et beneficiis Christi, cum obrepit opinio, quod ritus illi mereantur remissionem peccatorum, aut quod propter eos homo sit iustus, sicut

Pharisaei de suis sacrificiis et ritibus imaginabantur. Secundo, extinguitur lux de discrimine umbrarum externarum et novitatis spiritus, qua conversi ad Deum efficiuntur templa Dei.

Cum autem obrepit opinio, ritus monasticos, coelibatum, fugam laborum communium in vita politica, discrimina ciborum, esse cultus Dei et perfectionem, obscurantur veri cultus, qui debent esse in corde, timor, fides, patientia, spes, castitas coniugalis, et alii fructus spiritus. Tertio, deletur doctrina de distinctione operum, cum Ceremoniae anteferuntur operibus a Deo mandatis, ut monachi praetulerunt suos ritus coningio et officiis politicis. Quarto, obrepit opinio Necessitatis, quae est periculosa carnificina conscientiarum, cum enim observatio humanorum rituum necessaria esse putatur, mentes occupatae hac tanta cura, impediuntur in aliis necessariis rebus, nec tamen omnes ritus semper observant. Et cum fingunt esse peccata, impeditur invocatio, deinde hoc ipsum est peccatum, existimare quod talia opera sint cultus Dei, et quod omissio sit peccatum. Quinto, opinio necessitatis gignit discordias insanabiles, sicut olim de Paschate fuerunt dissensiones. Sexto, falso tribuitur Episcopis potestas condendi traditiones, cum opinione cultus aut necessitatis, quoties ignoratur verus usus traditionum.

Cum igitur error de Traditionibus multa incommoda pariat, necesse est in Ecclesia extare doctrinam de usu earum recte explicatam et perspicuam.

Primum autem nota sit doctrina de libertate Christiana, de qua usitate, docendi causa, quatuor gradus in hac vita facimus.

Primus est liberatio a peccato et ira Dei, et damnatione aeterna propter mediatorem, videlicet Remissio peccatorum et reconciliatio, ac iustificatio seu imputatio iusticiae gratuita propter mediatorem. Secundus coniunctus est cum primo de effectione, videlicet Vivificatio in nobis, quae fit per filium Dei vivificantem corda, et liberantem ex doloribus inferorum, donato Spiritu sancto: et deinde adsidua praesentia divinitatis in invocantibus, regens, protegens, adiuvans, multis mirandis liberationibus servans eos, ut cum servatur Daniel inter leones. Hi sunt praecipui gradus, et gloriosa libertas, de qua in invocatione quotidie cogitandum est, et de his gradibus praecipue dicitur: Si vos filius liberaverit, vere liberi eritis. Tertius gradus est liberatio a politia Moisi, videlicet a ceremoniis Mosaicis et legibus forensibus Moisi: quia Christi regnum est restitutio vitae aeternae et iusticiae aeternae, abolito peccato et morte. Incoatur autem hoc regnum, quando primum filius mittitur, patefaciens promissionem: Semen mulieris conculcabit caput serpentis. Hic filius deinde semper est efficax per ministerium Evangelii, et Spiritus sancto movet et confirmat credentes: et haec persona, Deus et homo, est caput Ecclesiae, et per hanc personam immediate fit resuscitatio mortuorum, sicut Paulus inquit 1.

Corinth. 15.: Postquam per hominem mors, etiam per hominem fit resuscitatio mortuorum. Item, Dominus inquit: Omne iudicium dedit filio.

Est igitur Messiae regnum longe aliud, quam politica regna, et colligitur in hac vita ex diversis gentibus, ubi sunt diversae politiae, sicut inquit Paulus Colos. 2.: Induite novum hominem, qui renovatur ad agnitionem secundum imaginem eius, qui condidit eum, ubi non est Graecus, nec Iudaeus, nec servus, nec liber, sed omnia et in omnibus Christus, id est, dans omnia bona suo merito, scilicet remissionem peccatorum et reconciliationem, et simul efficiens in credentibus novam lucem, iusticiam et vitam. Haec distinctio regni Christi et politiarum mundi primum cogitanda est, postea cogitandum, quare ad tempus fuerit instituta politia Moisi, quae duravit annos 1582.

Tot enim sunt anni ab exitu ex Aegypto ad ultimam destructionem Ierosolymae sub Tito. Voluit enim Deus certam esse sedem illius populi, in quo voluit nasci Messiam, palam concionari, pati, reviviscere ex morte, testimonia ostendere. Haec ut certa essent, voluit Deus distinctam esse gentem et politiam a caeteris gentibus. Postea postquam exhibitus est Messias, deleta est haec politia, ut sciatur, aliud esse regnum Christi, aliud politiam Mosaicam.

Ex his fontibus intelligi potest, nos non alligatos esse ad ceremonias et ius positivum Moisi, sed singulos in suis politiis uti posse legibus cum ratione congruentibus, quas sanxit eius politiae.

ordinaria autoritas de negotiis politicis, sicut dissimilibus dierum spatiis utimur.

Quartus gradus est liberatio a traditionibus humanis in Ecclesia, ut Paulus inquit, Colos. 2.: Nemo vos iudicet in cibo, potu, vicibus festorum. Item: Quae sunt secundum mandata et traditiones hominum.

Et ex eodem fonte haec libertas oritur, ex quo oritur liberatio a ceremoniis Mosaicis. Cum Christi obedientia sit meritum remissionis peccatorum, nulla humana opera, ac multo minus mactationes pecudum, aut ritus satisfactionum, aut ieiunia in Ecclesia merentur remissionem peccatum. Item: Cum regnum Christi sit vita, lux, sapientia et iusticia aeterna in cordibus, quae incoatur in hac vita per ipsum ministerio Evangelii, et donato Spiritu sancto, non est observatio externorum rituum mactationis pecudum, aut ieiuniorum, aut vestitus. Ideo Paulus inquit: πολίτευμα nostrum in coelis est, id est, regnum Christi non est externa et interitura politia, sed nova lux in anima duratura in tota aeternitate.

Hoc fonte considerato, rectius intelligi possunt hi gradus libertatis.

Postea necesse est scire discrimina traditionum, quae in Ecclesia factae sunt humana autoritate, (non enim iam loquimur de legibus politicis, quae ad defensionem societatis corporalis et honestam pacem in imperiis factae sunt, sed de ritibus ecclesiasticis) horum tres sunt gradus. Primus.

Aliquae traditiones per sese pugnant cum praeceptis Dei, ut edictum Nabuchodonosor, quod iubebat adorari statuam. Tales traditiones sunt invocatio mortuorum, adoratio statuarum, Missae papisticae, satisfactiones papisticae. Item, lex de coelibatu, quia sine peccatis non potest observari. De his traditionibus omnibus necesse est tenere regulam: Oportet Deo magis obedire quam hominibus. Necesse est igitur tales leges et ritus simpliciter abolere.

Secundus gradus est rituum, qui etsi sunt rerum, quarum usus per sese non pugnant cum praeceptis Dei, tamen observatio fit impia, cum additur opinio cultus aut necessitatis, ut discrimen ciborum, vestitus, temporum. In his necesse est taxare falsas opiniones, et ostendere qui sint veri et necessarii cultus. Ac prorsus aboleri possunt ipsi ritus, qui non prosunt ad bonum ordinem, ut stulti ritus discriminis ciborum, cum quidem et doctrinam obscuret observatio.

Tertius gradus est rituum, qui non pugnant cum praeceptis Dei, et sunt utiles ad bonum ordinem, et fiunt sine opinione cultus et necessitatis. Quia enim natura rationalis intelligit ordinem, et scit causas, propter quas ordo amandus est, praecipitur ut et in Ecclesia omnia ordine et decenter fiant, sicut inquit Paulus. Semper igitur Ecclesia etiam primorum Patrum temporibus distinxit festos dies accommodatos historiis, sic et lectiones et cantilenas distinguimus. Deus mandavit agnum paschalem eo ipso tempore edi, quo in cruce filius victima futurus erat. Sic ad historiam futuram accommodata est temporis distinctio.

Fuit Athenis quidam petulans homo Cynesias, qui solitus est contraria festa publicis celebrare, si quis talem petulantiam in Ecclesia exerceret, nequaquam sequeretur dictum Pauli: Omnia fiant ordine et decenter in Ecclesia. Possunt igitur aliqui tales ritus ordini utiles retineri: et temporum distinctio commonefactio est de historia. Sed semper in conspectu sit regula, Illi observationi nequaquam addendam esse opinionem cultus et necessitatis, nec cogitandum esse, peccare eos, qui sine scandalo tales ritus omittunt. Haec doctrina traditur a Paulo in capite sequenti.

De scandalo.

Vocabulum Scandali dicunt esse a σκάζω, quod significat claudico, vel a σκάμβον, quod est curvo, ut in proverbio dicitur: σκάμβον ξύλον οὐδέποτε ὀρθὸν γίνεσθαι. Significat enim scandalum proprie tigillum in instrumentis, quibus capiuntur lupi, aut vulpes, aut mures. Et Hesychius expresse inquit: σκάνδαλον τὸ ἐν μνάγραις. Et commentarius Aristophanis inquit: σκανδάληθρα sunt curva ligna in decipulis. Recte igitur redditur nomen σκάνδαλον vocabulo tendiculae: inde Ecclesia nomen transtulit ad insidias, seu tendiculas, videlicet prava dogmata et prava exempla, quae capiunt homines, sicut tendiculae bestias.

Usitate autem et docendi causa offensiones discernuntur. Offensio pharisaica dicitur indignatio in impiis, qui offenduntur vera doctrina, et exemplis a Deo adprobatis, quia aegre ferunt labefactari suam potentiam, aut impediri quaestum. Ut cum Pharisaei offenduntur, taxante Christo quaestum in templo, et falsas opiniones de sacrificiis. De hac offensione dicitur Matth. 15

Pharisaei audientes sermonem hunc, scandalizabantur. Inde nomen usurpatur pharisaicum scandalum pro pharisaica offensione.

Tenenda est autem regula: Oportet Deo magis obedire quam hominibus. Item: Qui me confessus fuerit coram hominibus, confitebor et ego eum coram patre meo coelesti. Quare necesse est vera docere, et facere mandata a Deo, etiamsi fremant et tumultuentur, et turbent imperia tyranni. Nec languefiant animi recte docentes, et recta facientes offensione pharisaica, sicut Christus inquit: Omitte eos, coeci sunt, et duces coecorum.

Hanc consolationem adversus pharisaicas offensiones primum tenere necesse est. Nec fieri quidem potest, quin moderti homines doleant, cum vident, taxatis erroribus, oriri dissidia, et turbari imperia. Sed tamen primum praeceptum: Non habebis deos alienos, maxime necessarium est, anteferendum vitae nostrae, tranquillitati patriae et omnibus bonis corporalibus. Hanc consolationem saepe repetit Dominus: Si quis diligit patrem aut matrem plus quam me, non est me dignus.

Et Deutero. 33. in benedictione tribus Leviticae: Qui dixerit patri suo et matri suae, nescio vos, hi custodiunt legem tuam, benedic Domine eis, percute dorsa inimicorum eius, et qui oderunt eos, non consurgant.

Ibi addita est consolatio, ne languefiant pii propter pharisaica iudicia, odia et saevitiam. Ac nobis omnibus hoc tempore etiam necessaria est haec admonitio de pharisaicis scandalis. Quia impii vociferantur turbari publicam tranquillitatem propagatione nostrae doctrinae, coningio sacerdotum et reprehensione cultuum, quos impie defendunt. Itaque adversus iniusta iudicia mundi confirmemus nos mandatis divinis: Fugite idola. Ac praecipue hoc fulmine moveamur: Si quis dixerit blasphemiam contra Spiritum sanctum, non remittetur ei.

Nequaquam igitur adiuvandi sunt hostes Evangelii.

Aliud scandalum proprie sic dictum, quod nominatur Datum, de quo inquit Dominus: Vae mundo a scandalis, est impia doctrina, seu impium exemplum, quod alii imitantes fiunt deteriores. Plenae sunt exemplorum omnes aetates: quia semper multi impii sunt, qui prava dogmata vel gignunt vel confirmant. Item: Qui dant mala consilia. Item: Qui exemplis trahunt alios ad societatem scelerum, ut Catilina movens iniustum bellum: vel ad imitationem, ut multi libidinum, helluationum, rapinarum, usurarum exempla imitantur. Talia facta cum per sese sint horrenda peccata, fiunt eo atrociora, qui plures secum trahunt et a Deo avellunt, et sunt semina aliorum sequentium scelerum. Sicut lapsus Davidis primum polluit sanctam matronam, deinde impulit illum ad prava consilia de viro interficiendo, postea secutae sunt poenae, in quibus Absolon et magna pars populi multipliciter offenderunt Deum.

Quia in seditione sunt innumerabilia scelera, ut notum est dictum Thucydidis: ἐν στάσει πᾶσα ἰδέα κακοῦ ἐστὶ. Saepe igitur de hoc genere scandalorum cogitemus tristissimam concionem: Vae mundo a scandalis, et sciamus eam complecti ingentes confusiones in toto genere humano, falsa dogmata, exempla publica et privata nocentia moribus, initia iniusta dissidiorum et bellorum, prava sodalitia: simus circumspectiores in docendo, in consiliis dandis et in omnibus actionibus, iuxta dictum: Vigilate et orate, ne intretis in tentationem.

Item: Omnia quae facitis, ad gloriam Dei facite, et ne offendatis Ecclesiam.

Alius gradus est scandali vitandi in usu rerum indifferentium, vel apud infirmos dociles, vel apud pertinaces adversarios hypocritas. Est autem apud infirmos dociles sic uti libertate, ut subita novitas deterreat eos a doctrina: Aut si invitentur nondum confirmati, postea incidant in periculosas dubitationes: ut pastor cuiusdam Ecclesiae, qui cum magna contentione docuerat, carnium usum concessum esse, postea aegrotans iussit peti ab Ecclesia, ut saltem tunc in ieiunio abstinerent, ne ipse esset autor mutatae vetustae consuetudinis. De hoc tertio genere Paulus hic monet prudenter iudicandum esse, quomodo moderandus sit usus libertatis, de qua supra dictum est, et regulae sunt duae: Infirmi dociles non turbentur subita novitate, sicut hic dicitur: Infirmum in fide assumite etc.

Sed contra adversarios pertinaces exemplis doctrinae de libertate utendum est, ut Apostoli violabant traditiones pharisaicas etc.

Vnusquisque in sua mente certus sit.

Id est, nihil fiat dubitante conscientia: sit autem conscientia confirmata verbo Dei. Haec doctrina valde necessaria est, Nihil faciendum esse contra conscientiam, Nihil item faciendum esse dubitante conscientia. Et infra repetita est haec doctrina: Omne quod non est ex fide, pec- catum est.

Id dictum Papistae tantum enarrant legaliter, videlicet, Quicquid pugnat cum lege, peccatum est: quod recte dicitur, sed nondum reddit inte- gram Pauli sententiam. Non enim satis est, facta cum lege congruere, sed oportet praelucere agni- tionem Christi, et totam obedientiam regi fiducia filii Dei, ita, ut et sciamus, quae facta placeant, et quomodo placeant. Placent autem facta con- gruentia cum lege, cum persona placet iusta fide, gratis propter mediatorem, et deinde scit obe- dientiam incoatam requiri, et placere eam pro- pter mediatorem quanquam legi non fatisfacit.

Hic necesse est taxari tetrum errorem Papi- starum, qui docent, semper dubitandum esse, an sis reconciliatus, et hanc dubitationem non esse peccatum. Huic errori opponendum est hoc di- ctum Pauli: Omne quod non est ex fide, pec- catum est.

Verbum πληροφορεῖσθαι significat certum esse, ut apud Isocratem πληροφορηθεὶς ἐμ' ἐξαρ- νὸν εἶναι, id est, cum certus esset me negare. Sic prorsus usus est eo verbo Paulus, Rom. 4. de Abraham: Cum certus esset, Deum posse steri- lem matrem foecundam facere. Et Lucae capite 1. et Colos. 2. πληροφορία significat certitudinem, quasi dicas: Plenam assensionem.

Sed dicat aliquis: Gloriose iactatis, vos Deo placere, cum tamen haec naturalis caligo semper sentiat dubitationes et diffidentiam? Respondeo: Verum est, dubitationes et diffidentiam haerere in animis hominum in hac depravatione naturae: sed hanc ipsam ob causam Deus edidit vocem legis et Evangelii. Vult nos de utraque re, de ira et de gratia certos esse. Vult certo sciri, Deum vere et horribiliter condemnare non conversos ad filium, sicut scriptum est Ioh. 3.: Qui non cre- dit in filium, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei ma- net super eum. Vult rursus etiam immensa boni- tate nobis certo notam esse reconciliationem do- natam propter filium credentibus.

Hanc ipsam ob causam edita est promissio de filio, et de gratia statim ab initio, cum ignota esset omnibus creaturis, ido inquit Dominus: Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut filium unigenitum de- derit, ut omnis qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam. Et hanc promissio- nem vult notam esse, et recte intelligi, et fide accipi. Quorsum enim attineret revelatam esse, si non esset fide accipienda. Sic igitur inquit Pau- lus: Ideo ex fide, gratis, ut sit firma promissio. Quare additum est iuramentum, nisi ideo, ut nobis consolatio certa sit. Vivo ego, dicit Do- minus, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed ut conver- tatur et vivat. Sit igitur in nobis conversio, et fide apprehendatur gratuita promissio, ut conso- lationem teneamus contra desperationem et dolo- res inferorum. Ideo de utraque re dicitur Mar- ci 1.: Agite poenitentiam, et credite Evangelio.

Quanquam autem haeret dubitatio in omni- bus hominibus in hac depravatione naturae: tamen huic dubitationi mentes conversae repu- gnent et opponant vocem promissionis, et accen- datur talis fides, quae credat, non tantum aliis dari remissionem peccatorum, sed tibi ipsi quo- que, et hac fide accedas ad Deum, et elucteris ex dubitatione, ut possis invocare Deum. De hac fide erigente et consolante corde in veris dolori- bus loquitur Paulus, cum ait: Iustificati fide pacem habemus. Item, Ephes. 3.: Per quem audemus accedere in fiducia per fidem eius.

Alibi saepe enarratum est dictum Salomonis, quod impie citant monachi ad confirmandam du- bitationem: Nemo scit, an amore vel odio dignus sit, quia iustis et iniustis similia accidunt, vide- licet in hac vita. Id dictum simpliciter hoc vult, de voluntate Dei iudicandum esse ex verbo ipsius, non ex rebus secundis aut adversis in hac vita. Achab non existimet se Deo placere, quia habet florens regnum, et est victor: nec David existimet se abiectum esse a Deo, quia est pulsus regno, sed uterque ex verbo Dei iudicet: prorsus igitur congruit Salomonis sententia nobiscum, quia deducit nos ad verbum Dei.

Regnum Dei non est esca et potus, sed iusticia, gaudium et pax in Spiritu sancto. In his ser- viens Christo, placet Deo, et probatus est hominibus.

Usitatissima hypocrisis est, de qua concio- natur Dominus, Matth. 23. inquiens: Vae vo- bis scribae et hypocritae, qui colatis culicem, et devoratis camelum. Cum videlicet neglectis prae- ceptis divinis, et quidem praecipuis, aliqui reti- nent ceremonias aliquas, et ritus ab hominibus traditos, et eas externas observationes sentiunt esse iusticiam coram Deo, et necessarios cultus Dei, et neglectionem cogitant esse impietatem, et hac opinione acerrime defendunt suos ritus, et crudelitatem exercent adversus alios recte sen- tientes.

Ut autem in omnibus rebus necesse est dis- cernere necessaria a non necessariis, ita in Eccle- sia maxime necessarium est discernere fundamen- tum a stipulis, sicut inquit Paulus: Fundamen- tum aliud poni non potest, praeter id quod posi- tum est, quod est Christus Iesus. Item Psal. 50.: Si esuriero, non dicam tibi, Invoca me in die tribulationis etc. Et Ieremiae 7.: Non praecepi eis de holocaustis, sed hoc praecepi, audite me. Et Ecclesiastae 4.: Melior est obedientia quam victimae stultorum, quia nesciunt, quantum fa- ciant mali. Haec querela de quantis peccatis lo- quatur ostendunt exempla.

Magna pars hominum cogitat oblationem in Missa praecipuum cultum esse, et eo cultu maxime confidit, cum ibi horrenda idolomania sit. Hi non intelligunt, quantum faciant mali. Opponit igitur Paulus regulam ex definitione regni Dei: Regnum Dei non est esca et potus, id est, non externa observatio in cibis et vestibus, sed est iusticia, pax et gaudium in Spiritu sancto. His appellationibus comprehendit omnes necessarios cultus Dei, ut alibi: Milita bonam militiam, re- tinens fidem et bonam conscientiam.

Tradit et Oseas similem sententiam: Mise- ricordiam volo, non sacrificium, agnitionem Dei magis quam holocausta. Zacharias inquit: Di- ligite veritatem et pacem. Ita passim vox divina monet Ecclesiam de discrimine verorum cul- tuum et falsorum cultuum.

Ut autem alibi Daniel inquit: Messiam alla- turum esse iusticiam sempiternam, ita hic intel- ligatur iusticia de toto beneficio filii Dei, quod in hac vita incoatur fide, id est fiducia mediatoris, qua sumus iusti, id est, accepti Deo, qua et filius Dei vivificat credentes, et ostendit patrem, dat Spiritum sanctum, ut incoëtur nova obedientia, quae postea erit integra in vita aeterna, cum erit Deus omnia in omnibus. Est igitur reipsa regnum Dei iusticia aeterna, ut Daniel nominat, id est, talis vita reddita per filium, fide, quae deinde fit integra obedientia post resurrectionem.
