Pax significat reconciliationem cum Deo, sicut alibi inquit Paulus: Iustificati pacem habe- mus apud Deum, id est, habentes fidem iam su- mus reconciliati, liberati ab ira et a damnatione, et placemus Deo. Hanc pacem comitatur laetitia in corde acquiescens in Deo, et hanc nominat laetitiam in Spiritu sancto, id est, quae accen- ditur a Spiritu sancto, qui est amor et laeti- tia substantialis. Ideo tales motus accendit, qua- lis est ipse. Cum autem accendat motus con- gruentes omnibus praeceptis Dei, complectitur hic Paulus incoatam obedientiam, iuxta omnia prae- cepta Dei, laetitiam in invocatione, in dilectione Dei, gratiarum actionem et confessionem, obe- dientiam in dilectione proximi, castitate et aliis virtutibus, sicut enumerat fructus spiritus, Ga- lat. 5. et alibi.

De his veris cultibus postea dicit: Qui in his servit Christo, placet Deo, et probatus est homi- nibus. Hic meminerimus tradi testimonium, quod expresse adfirmat bona opera renatorum placere Deo, sicut suo loco copiosius dicetur. Petrus inquit: Offerte hostias spirituales placen- tes Deo per Iesum Christum.

Secundo, nominatim inquit: Qui servit Christo, ut significet, se de his operibus loqui, quae fiunt in agnitione et fiducia mediatoris.

Tertio, vult et ad hunc finem referri obe- dientiam, ut praestetur non propter nostram glo- riam, aut propter ventrem, sed propter ipsum filium Dei, scilicet, quia sentimus ei hunc honorem de- beri, et hoc honore ostendimus, nos fateri, quod hic sit Deus et salvator, et eum celebramus. De- nique hic complectamur universam doctrinam, in qua exponit quomodo bona opera Deo placent.

Sed quare addit: Est probatus hominibus, cum tamen in plurimis hominibus horribilis acerbitas sit odii adversus sanctos, ut multi cru- delissime interficiuntur, qui tamen sunt ornati testimoniis divinis, ut ipse filius Dei, qui resus- citaverat mortuos, Abel, Esaias, Ieremias et alii?

Respondeo: Paulus loquitur de iudiciis Ec- clesiae, Semper habent sancti testimonia vera in Ecclesia. Sicut Syracides cap. 44. inquit: Lau- dem ipsorum nunciabit Ecclesia. Et Deus ipse inquit: Benedicam benedicentibus tibi. Texat autem Paulus quorundam arrogantium tyranni- tyrannidem, qui cogitant se facturos esse, quod imaginantur ipsis concessum esse, et nolle impediri suam libertatem, etiamsi sciant intempestivis exemplis bonorum hominum animos et oculos offendi, et sequi scandala, vel propter imitationem vel propter alienationem voluntatum ab Evangelio.

Ideo 1. Corinth. 10. eadem regula traditur: Quicquid facitis, facite ad gloriam Dei, et non sitis scandalo Ecclesiae.

Vult igitur respici iudicia Ecclesiae, ideo et de tuenda fama saepe praecipitur, ut Syracides 41.: Cura de bono nomine, antecellit enim multis thesauris: et sit notus versiculus: Levis est, nec illum stimulat gloriae decus.

## 15:1 Disposition of Romans: Argument
Chapter XV. At the beginning it contains the conclusion of the previous exhortation.

He adds a reason from example, just as Christ bore our errors, so let us bear the weakness of our brothers. Amplification.

What things were written, were written for our instruction, that we might have hope through the consolation of the scriptures. He seems to have added this sentence at the end on purpose, to admonish us concerning the dignity of the ministry of the word, so that we might know that other illuminations are not to be sought, but that by this word, which stands written, minds are to be raised up and consoled.

Let us therefore establish that such promises in scripture pertain to us: Call upon me in the day of tribulation, and I will deliver you etc. An epilogue is also added, which gathers that the Gospel pertains to the Jews and the Gentiles.

For this was also a part of the controversy, as appears above, whether the Gospel pertains to those who do not observe the law. And here testimonies are cited concerning the calling of the Gentiles.

Next he ascribes certain things concerning his own office, he warns also, that they should not receive a doctrine repugnant to this doctrine of his. And he indicates by what art evil teachers create a deception, namely through 'chrestologies' (χρηστολογίας) and 'eulogies' (εὐλογίας).

The Greeks call 'chrestologies' smooth speeches, such as those of people promising kindly and flatterers: they call 'euloga' (εὔλογα) plausible things, which are not said rashly, but have reasons that are likely in appearance, just as impious doctrine is accustomed to collect plausible arguments of reason.

Thus by twin arts the impious teachers deceive, they flatter the desires of the people, as once the monks did. chi promised riches to the worshippers of Anna, they promised heaven to those putting on the cowl, and now the Anabaptists commend themselves to the common people with a wonderful appearance of humility, they condemn all magistrates, all public laws, all doctrine.

Since the common people hate these things by nature, they bring great momentum to impelling minds.

But the other part imposes even upon the more prudent because they bring forward learned thoughts, which do not recoil from the judgment of reason, as when they teach that our works satisfy for sins, that the justice of God is nothing but this simulation of civil works.

These things are defended by arguments born in reason, but let us follow the admonition of Paul, and let us receive no dogmas against scripture.

For in the judgment of God, the human mind cannot stand without the word of God.

May Christ stir our hearts, that we may truly acknowledge him, and may he bring the scattered Churches into a pious and perpetual concord.

Amen.

Latin:

Caput XV. Initio conclusionem proximae adhortationis continet.

Addit rationem ab exemplo, sicut Christus tulit nostra errata, sic nos fratrum imbecillitatem feramus. Amplificatio.

Quae scripta sunt, ad nostram doctrinam scripta sunt, ut spem habeamus per consolationem scripturarum. Consulto videtur in fine adiecisse hanc sententiam, ut admoneret nos de dignitate ministerii verbi, ut sciremus non esse alias illuminationes requirendas, sed hoc verbo, quod scriptum extat, erigendas mentes et consolandas esse.

Vere igitur ad nos pertinere statuamus huiusmodi promissiones in scriptura: Invoca me in die tribulationis, et eripiam te etc. Additus est et epilogus, qui colligit Evangelium ad Iudaeos ac gentes pertinere.

Fuit enim et haec controversiae pars, ut supra apparet, utrum Evangelium pertineat ad hos, qui legem non observant. Et citantur hic testimonia de vocatione gentium.

Deinceps ascribit quaedam de officio suo, monet etiam, ne recipiant doctrinam repugnantem huic suae doctrinae. Et indicat, qua arte mali doctores fucum faciant, nempe per χρηστολογίας et εὐλογίας.

Graeci vocant χρηστολογίας blandos sermones, ut sunt benigne pollicentium et assentatorum: εὔλογα vocant probabilia, quae non temere dicuntur, sed habent rationes in speciem versimiles sicut solet impia doctrina rationis argumenta plausibilia colligere.

Ita geminis artibus fallunt impii doctores, assentantur cupiditatibus populi, ut olim monachorum. chi pollicebantur divitias cultoribus Annae, promittebant coelum induentibus cucullum, et nunc Anabaptistae mira specie humilitatis se commendant vulgo, damnant omnes magistratus, omnia publica iura, omnem doctrinam.

Haec cum natura vulgus oderit, magnum momentum adferunt ad impellendos animos.

Sed altera pars imponit etiam prudentioribus quod afferunt erudite cogitata, quae non abhorrent a iudicio rationis, ut cum docent, quod opera nostra satisfaciant pro peccatis, quod iusticia Dei nihil sit nisi haec civilium operum simulatio.

Haec defenduntur argumentis in ratione natis, sed nos sequamur Pauli admonitionem, et nulla dogmata recipiamus contra scripturam.

Nam in iudicio Dei non potest humana mens consistere sine verbo Dei.

Christus excitet corda nostra, ut vere agnoscamus ipsum, et dissipatas Ecclesias redigat in concordiam piam et perpetuam.

Amen.

## 15:1 Argument
Chapter XV.

Since he shows by the example of Christ that the weak are to be tolerated, and has recited the saying of the Psalm, he soon adds a general admonition concerning the use of the Scriptures.

He commands that we hold onto hope through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures.

Paul repeats in this place the customary precept, namely, that minds are to be bound to the word of God revealed and comprehended in the prophetic and apostolic writings: and that one is not to judge concerning the essence and will of God according to human imaginations, without the word of God.

Likewise, in our sorrows, the promises are to be looked upon, and it is to be established that they pertain to us as well, even if they address all in general.

Many sow Stoic and enthusiastic opinions, and lead minds to this doubt: Since God has written a catalog of the elect, the promise of grace pertains to these; perhaps it does not pertain to you, since you do not know if you are in that catalog.

Against this doubt, this manifest rule must be opposed: Both proclamations are universal, the preaching of repentance and the promise of grace.

God accuses all because of sins, and offers to all who will believe the remission of sins freely, because of the Son, and He sent the Son so that He might bring forth this secret decree.

Nor are contradictory wills to be imagined in God.

Nor is it to be thought: Perhaps He wills something else concerning you than what the promise sounds.

From this imagination, minds are to be recalled to the promise itself, and it is to be most constantly established that the Son was sent for this reason, that He might show this will of the eternal Father, and that He is a truthful messenger.

Thus, when we sustain ourselves with the promise, at the same time the Son of God is efficacious, and in order He speaks consolation by the very voice of the Gospel, and shows the Father's will, because He says: No one knows the Father, except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal Him.

This whole doctrine, which commands one to begin from the revealed word, and not to wander outside the word, and to seek illuminations or raptures, must be held against many fanatics, Stoics, Manichaeans, Enthusiasts, and Anabaptists, who entangle themselves and others in doubts, having abandoned the word and cast off faith.

Nor do we attribute magical power to the word, but we say that God wills to be known in this order, and not otherwise, and wills that we apply consideration, and at the same time in that very consideration the Son is efficacious, according to the saying: Faith is from hearing, and hearing through the word of God.

Clearly, therefore, Paul says: Through the consolation of the Scriptures, so that we may understand Him to speak of the external word, whether heard or read.

Here Stenkefeldius laughs, and says that the thought of the written or heard word is only the occupation of the external man, as was abstaining from swine's flesh: he does not want it to be an instrument by which the Son of God Himself is efficacious.

But let us oppose these clear sayings of Paul: The Gospel is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes.

Likewise: The Gospel is the ministry of the Spirit, that is, by which, when men sustain themselves, the Son of God Himself is efficacious, and pours the Holy Spirit into their hearts.

But because mention is made of consolation, patience is also named, so that it may be signified that the Church in this life is always subject to the cross, and he warns that the causes are to be considered why it is subject to huge calamities.

He warns also what kind of obedience is necessary under the cross, and how the Church differs from the empires of the world.

The Church, however, does not speak only of calamities, as the Philosophers do, but also of liberation.

Therefore, Paul joins patience, consolation, and hope: therefore, philosophical and Christian patience differ in their objects and end.

Philosophical patience is to obey reason in enduring adversities, which reason commands one to endure, and often it is without any hope of liberation or help, just as in Socrates there is neither hope of help in the present, nor certain hope of liberation after death.

Yet he endures the punishment in such a way that he is not driven by pain to do an external work against justice or modesty.

Cato, against justice, commits suicide. cero [being] oppressed by pain acts against modesty etc. Socrates, although he is calm on the outside, nevertheless in his heart has sad groanings, and waves of doubt concerning providence. But Christian patience is to obey God in adversities, which God commands to be borne, and always mixed with this obedience is the hope of divine help or trust in the divine presence, and the hope of liberation, by which hope the heart, being raised up, rejoices in some way in God. This joy is not in philosophical patience, which is full of groaning in the heart, even if on the outside it does not add tragic gestures.

Now consider, against what calamities, death, diseases, poverty, the hatreds of tyrants and hypocrites, the factions of the most poisonous Sophists, exiles, slanders, punishments, what does Paul oppose? Namely, the scriptures. Here not only tyrants laugh, but also Stenkefeldius and similar enthusiasts.

Will you remove or alleviate death, diseases, tyrants, or punishments with letters and syllables? I answer: Do not understand these things magically concerning the figures, but concerning the contemplation of this very word, in which God has revealed Himself, which He willed to be committed to letters, in the contemplation of which the Son of God is present at the same time, and speaks consolation in the heart of the believer, and kindles faith, hope, joy, and invocation.

We conquer, therefore, by the conquering Son of God, recognized through the word; therefore it is said in the Psalm: My soul waited in His word, My soul hoped in the Lord. Likewise, Psalm 118: My soul has melted in anguish, confirm me by Thy word. Thus Paul joins the scriptures and hope, so that we may know that we are led from the scriptures, by the contemplation of the word in which God has revealed Himself, to God Himself, whom hope, recognized by the word, looks upon.

This whole doctrine becomes more illustrious in true sorrows and true invocation. Therefore, receive one another, just as Christ also received us. This is the conclusion of the admonition concerning the use of ceremonies and concerning concord.

Again, however, testimonies are added concerning the calling of the Gentiles, so that both those converted from the Gentiles may be confirmed, and the Jews may think more studiously concerning the kingdom of Christ. Let them know that it is not a Mosaic polity, but another kingdom, in which eternal goods are restored to believers, whether they be in ethnic polities or in the Mosaic polity, just as it is said to the Philippians: our πολίτευμα (citizenship/commonwealth) is in the heavens, that is, the true light; by which we rightly recognize God and rightly invoke Him; the beginning of justice and eternal life are heavenly things, nor do they hinder that bodies in this life should be in diverse polities. Moreover, the saying of Isaiah is cited, which is most notable, which also contains the sum of the doctrine of the Gospel, and is a testimony concerning the passion and resurrection of Christ.

And in that day there shall be a root of Jesse, which shall stand, to be a sign to the peoples; to it the Gentiles shall flee, and His rest shall be glory. Paul takes the words as they are read in the Greek interpretation, which was in use at that time. However, the meaning does not differ: He shall be raised up, to rule over the Gentiles; in Him the Gentiles shall hope. For they are the same things, to be a banner of the people, and to be a leader.

Here, first, let the definition be held. The kingdom of Christ is that the Son of God was sent to the Church in the beginning, the promise having been brought forth, and to gather and preserve the Church, and then, human nature having been assumed after the resurrection, to have been exalted, and now this person, who is God and Man, to preserve and restore the ministry of the Gospel, and to gather and vivify the Church by the word and the given Holy Spirit, and to protect it miraculously against devils and tyrants, and after this life to resurrect it, and to give eternal salvation.

Which benefits, although they are actions of the divine nature, nevertheless are done by the Son in the assumed nature, and are now common actions of this person, who is Jesus Christ, just as the first promise also says: The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent. And to the Corinthians Paul says: Death shall be destroyed through the man Christ. Thus He is also named the head of the Church, perfecting all things in all. For although vivification is proper to the divine nature, nevertheless it is done by the Son in the assumed nature. Thus this person is the head of the Church. Moreover, the same kingdom, which is named the Kingdom of God, likewise the eternal Kingdom of Christ, Paul distinguishes thus to the Corinthians, when he says: He shall deliver the kingdom to God and the Father.

So that we may understand the kingdom to be the same, but the mode to differ. In this life it is properly called the kingdom of Christ: because through the ministry of the Gospel God is effective immediately through this second person, who is the λόγος (Word), who immediately brought forth the Gospel from the bosom of the eternal Father, and it is immediately efficacious in ministry, as he says: No one knows the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him. God is therefore apprehended by the word, and the essence of the divinity is not yet seen openly.

But let each particular phrase in the said Isaiah be carefully considered: In him shall the Gentiles hope. Paul presses the designation of the Gentiles, and cites among the testimonies that affirm that the Gospel pertains not only to those who were born of the seed of Jacob. Then the word hoping is set in opposition to damnation, and it comprises the sum of the promises, namely, that the Son of God is sent to crush the head of the serpent. Likewise, that he may destroy the kingdom of the devil, blot out sin and death, and restore righteousness and eternal life. These gifts are given on account of the Son of God, and through him to those who believe in him. Therefore he says: They shall hope in him, namely, that they may receive these good things, just as it is also said in the Psalm: Blessed are all who trust in him. It is therefore a kingdom of consolation, not of damnation. And the worship proper to this kingdom is faith, hope, confession, thanksgiving, invocation, the propagation of the Gospel. For by the word hoping all these are comprised: faith, hope, invocation, and the neighboring impulses. And in invocation let faith, hope, invocation, and thanksgiving be kindled and confirmed concerning this kingdom.

It is added moreover: “His death will be glory.” By this it is signified that the Messiah will rise again from death, and thus abolish death, not only in his own body, but in all who believe in him, and will render to them righteousness and eternal life. The death of Alexander is not glory, but the end of all of Alexander’s actions. For the divine voice does not name glory as spectacles or fame, which is not perceived by the one being celebrated, as when Alexander’s corpse is led with great pomp from Babylon and placed in Egypt on a golden throne: but it names the actions of the living person as glory. Just as Christ rises again after death, and, living, gathers the eternal Church, truly he intercedes for it continually before the Father in the secret counsel of divinity, he is present, he preserves the ministry of the Gospel proclaimed. from the bosom of the eternal Father, and immediately in the ministry is effective by the voice of the Gospel, giving gifts to men, that is, vivifying believers, giving the Holy Spirit, and raising men from death, and restoring to us righteousness and eternal life, defending also the Church miraculously in this life, since He is Emmanuel and the head of the Church, perfecting all things in the saints.

These actions are true glory, not the shadows of spectacles, or empty fame. I am certain etc.

Having finished the whole admonition concerning ceremonies, he adds a mitigation in the oratorical manner, in case any who are too fierce or morose might think themselves to have been rebuked too harshly.

For some, being more fierce, bear it ill that their liberty is restricted; others, being morose, bear it ill that customary ceremonies are neglected.

He therefore placates both, attributing to them the praise of goodness and learning, and asking that they take this admonition in good part, since they are placid, candid, not easily irritable, and are intelligent.

For among the candid and intelligent there is a place for knowing and forgiving, as it is truly said, "How sweet is kindness tempered with understanding." Others, being unlearned and irascible, are easily irritated, and once irritated are implacable, as it is said: "Nothing is ever more unjust than an ignorant man." And Solomon says: "The wrath of a fool is a heavy burden." Thus he softens both, when he says they should be placid, not irascible, not morose, and furthermore rightly learned: for such people take free admonition in good part. Because of the grace which has been given to me. And to placate the readers, and to increase the authority of the admonition, the mention of his office and of the miracles which he adds is conducive, as if he were saying: I am moved by the office of an Apostle, that I may teach and remind you, and God has provided testimonies to my doctrine.

Wherefore you should listen to me placidly, and assent to me without doubt.

Here it must be considered again what the apostolic authority is: namely, that it is certain that the Apostle's doctrine is divine, and that it must be believed, just as the voice of God sounding from heaven immediately among manifest miracles, as the decalogue was promulgated, and it has often been spoken of copiously elsewhere concerning apostolic authority.

He adorns the ministry with the word of sacrifice, saying that he is a minister sacrificing the Gospel.

This is a new form of speech, but learned, taken XIII. 8. NARRATION ON THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. CHAP. XV. from the collation and interpretation of the Levitical sacrifices.

It has been said elsewhere that there is a distinction between the polity of Moses and the eternal Church, which is gathered by the voice of the promise concerning the Son of God, and why the polity of Moses was established, and what sacrifices are, and what the distinction is between signs and true sacrifices, because the law in this life ordains both. It ordains signs, by which men testify that this is the true God whom they invoke, and by these rites they distinguish Him from fictitious deities. It also ordains other interior and exterior sacrifices, in which God Himself communicates with us and is efficacious, because it is necessary that there be some things joining us with God. Such are the sacrifices: the true knowledge of God shining in the mind, and the total newness by which man becomes the temple of God, and by which God communicates Himself to us, and in turn man celebrates God. For thus God communicates Himself to a rational creature when He is rightly acknowledged, because He is the light shining in the saints. Celebration in this life is done by teaching, confessing, invocation, thanksgiving, conformity of heart, and joy in God. These are begun in this life, and besides the fact that the mode of teaching in the ministry is not such in eternal life, all other things remain the same, namely confession, thanksgiving, conformity of heart, and joy in God. In these very actions God communicates Himself in all eternity, when He shall be all in all.

It is written therefore in Hosea 4: Take away all iniquity, and do good to us, and we will render the calves of our lips, that is, You, Messiah, give benefits according to Your promise, grace and eternal life, and we will render sacrifices, not signs, but true sacrifices, the ministry of teaching, invocation, confession, thanksgiving, joyful obedience in the heart.

Thus Paul says here: That he sacrifices the Gospel of Christ, that is, by teaching he performs true worship to God. And Paul does both; he himself offers to God when he teaches, that is, he celebrates God and attributes honor to Him. At the same time, he prepares other victims, that is, the hearers, so that they too may offer true worship to God. Just as there were two distinct offices of the Levites and the Priests. The Levites, as butchers, slaughtered the cattle and prepared the victims, but the Priests offered them. Now the same Paul both offers himself and prepares others, because by his voice others are converted to God.

Therefore, it is added here concerning the sacrifice of the hearers.

So that the offering of the Gentiles may be made acceptable to God, that is, so that the Gentiles themselves may become victims, and offer eternal sacrifices to God—true faith, true invocation, confession, thanksgiving, conformity with God, and joy with Him in all eternity—and not offer to fictitious deities, Bacchus, Venus, etc.

Let this whole passage of Paul be better known and more welcome, because it is a testimony concerning the ministry of the Gospel.

First, he consoles those who teach and those who learn, affirming that this labor is pleasing to God, when it is called a sacrifice, by which appellation is signified the excellence of works, namely that the work is good and pleasing to God, and such that God judges that honor is attributed to Him by it. Let the following sayings be applied here: We will offer the calves of our lips. Item, Isaiah 61: You shall be called Priests of the Lord, ministers of our God. And Psalm 118: Let the voluntary offerings of my mouth be pleasing to You, that is, the sacrifices of teaching and invoking, and also of learning, are pleasing to You. Let the hearers also learn to feel reverently concerning the ministry of the Gospel when they hear these praises, as it has often been commanded.

And 1 Thessalonians 5 it is said: I beseech you, brethren, that you esteem them highly who are over you in the Lord, because of their ministry.

1 Timothy 5: The presbyters who rule well are worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in word and doctrine. Double, he says, that is, in reverence and in sustenance. Sustenance includes defense, but reverence includes obedience in those things which are proper to the ministry for God's sake, to whom honor is first due: and when with obedience is joined an honorable opinion, which understands that we are subject to the ministry for God's sake, and love and a will that prefers the ministry to other affairs of life.

Let us know, however, the primary reason why doctrine and the ministry ought to be heard and preserved, because thus God gathers the Church, and not otherwise, namely by the voice and thought of the written Gospel, when it is heard or read, as it is said in Romans 10: How shall they believe without a preacher? Item: The Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes. 2 Corinthians 3: The Gospel is the ministry of the spirit, that is, God is efficacious by the thought of the Gospel heard or read, and converts hearts in the thought of the Gospel. The error of Schwenckfeld is to be utterly execrated, who writes expressly that God is not effective through the knowledge of the Gospel heard or read, and he invents other illuminations outside the Gospel, and without the Gospel.

Such frenzies were once those of Marcion, the Manichaeans, and the Enthusiasts, and the erring Anabaptists circulate similar portents.

Let good minds know, however, that it is commanded that we learn and meditate upon the word of God, according to the saying: Hear Him. Item: Kiss the Son.

And let us know for certain that God is effective through the meditation of this written Gospel, as it is said in Romans 10: Faith comes by hearing.

Item: Father, sanctify them in the truth; thy word is truth. Now, however, I am setting out for Jerusalem, that we may serve the saints.

Since he spoke earlier of his office, he narrates in passing his travels, and signifies his benevolence toward the Church that was at Rome, and gives them hope of his arrival.

Now, however, he says that he is setting out for Judea, to bring money to the needy saints, which the Churches in Macedonia and Achaia had contributed, so that they might bring aid to the needy in the famine.

For it is very well known in the history of the Emperor Claudius that at that time there was a great famine in Asia, Greece, and Italy for several years, and that many men were extinguished by famine everywhere.

Concerning that famine, it is said in the Acts, chapter eleven: and Eusebius writes that a modius of wheat was sold for six drachmae.

And in the sixth chapter of the Apocalypse, famine is numbered among the punishments, in which he says it will come to pass that a choenix is to be bought for a denarius.

Now the common price of a modius in average years was three or four sestertii, as Cicero writes, that the price of a modius by law was three sestertii, that is, twenty-four of our Misnian coins.

Now if a modius in the famine was bought for six drachmae, the price increased fivefold, since in average years the customary price was a drachma, or thereabouts.

There were, however, eight choenices in a modius: and a choenix was the flour for one day.

Therefore, in average years, the flour for one day was four Misnian coins: that much flour was bought in the famine for a denarius, that is, thirty-two Misnian coins.

The price had therefore increased sevenfold.

The consideration of these computations is useful, both for understanding history and for this observation, as to what order was in the diet appropriate to man.

And it appears from this that there was such frugality and temperance, which nevertheless was consistent with nature, and that food was not sordidly given to servants.

There were, however, especially in Judea, great calamities for those who embraced the Gospel.

For many were being killed, very many were being driven from their own possessions, and were being forced into exile.

To these miseries was then added a common famine throughout all Asia and Europe.

So that, therefore, poor families might be helped somewhere, Paul collected money in Greece and elsewhere, which he brought to Judea.

It is useful to consider these circumstances of the times, and the hardships of the Church, and the cares of the Apostles in helping the poor, and in fostering the benevolence of the Churches.

At the same time, however, he weaves in here an admonition concerning the wages due to the ministers of the Gospel, concerning which, however, he preaches more copiously in the first to the Corinthians, chapter 9, where he says expressly: So the Lord has ordained, that those who preach the Gospel should have their living from the Gospel.

And many arguments are added.

Who serves as a soldier at his own expense? where he used the term ὀψώνιον (opsonion).

For thus were stipends customarily named, because to soldiers in the provinces, in place of a stipend, grain, meat, wine, oil, fruit, and figs were given.

Because the Romans, occupied with the provinces, at the beginning only imposed this burden, that they should pay tithes to the empire, as Appian writes.

Thence, to the garrisons were given things born of the earth, the name of which, ὀψώνιον, was used for a stipend.

Now ὄψον (opson) is from ἕψω (hepsō), which is to boil, and from the verb ὀνοῦμαι (onoumai), which is to buy: for it signifies the foods which are added besides bread, most of which are cooked by boiling.

Since, however, God in His immense goodness gathers the eternal Church by the voice of doctrine, and not otherwise, and most severely commands that the doctrine be preserved, for which to happen, it is necessary that there be assemblies of those teaching and learning.

And indeed the Son of God Himself, sent by the eternal Father, that through Him the Church might be gathered, preserves both the doctrine by His power, and institutes the ministry of teaching, and in all times has raised up teachers, and raises them up, whom He wills to be organs sounding the voice of the Gospel, by which He bends the hearts of those not resisting the Gospel to the true invocation of God and to eternal salvation, and in this great militia, to those faithfully serving, that is, to Pastors and Doctors, He wills that a living be given.

This precept has been often repeated, and most ample promises of rewards have been added, which is most certain is to be given both in this life and after this life to the pious, who are beneficent toward faithful teachers. And illustrious examples are recounted in the prophetic histories, nor are examples lacking in our own age.

Matt. 10: Whoever gives a cup of water to one of these little ones, because of the doctrine, Amen I say to you, he shall have his reward. 1 Cor. 9: Thus the Lord has ordained, that those who teach the Gospel, should live from the Gospel. Prov. 3: Honor the Lord with your substance, and with the first fruits of all your produce, and your barns will be filled with plenty, and your wine presses will overflow with new wine. Sirach 7: With all your soul fear God, and hold his priests in honor, and give them their portions, which the law commands to be given, the first fruits and the offerings, so that God may in turn bless you. Isaiah 49: Kings shall be your foster fathers and queens your nursing mothers, that is, let Princes and Republics take care that the ministers of the Gospel have sustenance and protection.

To these precepts and to these promises, examples are added. God showed kindness to the hosts of Abraham. In Egypt, God showed kindness to the midwives, who did not kill the infants of the Israelites. He nourished the Sareptan hostess of Elijah in a miraculous way, and adorned her with her son restored from death. Obadiah hid the Prophets in a cave, and provided them with food. The royal Eunuch helped the captive Jeremiah, to whom safety is promised in the destruction of Jerusalem, and the Egyptian king Apries, the killer of Jeremiah, was strangled by the prefect Amasis.

Let us therefore be moved both by the precepts of God, and by the examples of rewards and promises, so that we may piously exercise beneficence in this matter.

But although tyrants and other profane men shout that these exhortations concerning beneficence toward the ministers of the Gospel are traps of avarice, and that these sermons are like the sermons of wolves, which they pretend are given to geese: yet we look to the will of God, and we know that he most severely commands the preservation of the evangelical ministry. God also always turns the hearts of some men toward this beneficence. Just as Sergius the Proconsul, Onesiphorus, and others everywhere provide hospitality to Paul.

Even on the ship, Paul is heard as a shipmaster and chief navigator by the centurion, the soldiers, and the sailors, and they embrace him with singular benevolence.

Let us also consider the customs of this time. There are some Princes and private men who are beneficent in this matter, who bring help to those who teach and those who learn.

But very many Kings, Princes, and Bishops, defenders of idols, exercise horrible cruelty against the ministers of the Gospel. I remember a man excellent in talent, erudition, and piety, Henry of Zutphen, who in Dithmarschen, because he taught correctly, was cruelly killed: nor was there any other cause for his death. There was at Tübingen Johannes Croesus, Doctor of Theology, a most modest man and a student of true doctrine, who was later subjected to the ultimate punishment in Tillingen. Nor could any crime be charged against him, other than that he, a priest, had preferred to live chastely in marriage than to pollute himself in various ways in celibacy.

And I could recount a long catalog of such outstanding men, who were killed as innocents solely because of their confession of the truth. Nor is there an end to the cruelty in Italy, France, Britain, Belgium, and elsewhere.

This cruelty is undoubtedly followed by new punishments and great changes of empires.

But gradually both Princes and wealthy private men, who had wanted the doctrine of the Gospel to be preserved and propagated, formerly assigned revenues to the Churches, which in the beginning were distributed into four parts. From the first part, salaries and food were given to the ministers of the Gospel, the Pastors, and their colleagues, who taught publicly in the churches. The second part was for those teaching in Schools and for poor scholars. From the third part, the poverty of the needy was provided for, who because of sickness could not seek their sustenance by their own labors. The fourth part was contributed to buildings and the salaries of messengers.

Now Bishops and Abbots enjoy those riches, and neglect the ministry of the Gospel and the studies of doctrine, just as it was predicted in the Epistle of Jude: They will gorge themselves on your alms.

Let us deplore these evils, and meanwhile in our own Churches let us urge pious governors to take care that the revenues of the Churches are piously allocated, and especially that they provide sustenance for the families of pastors who teach correctly, and bring help to poor scholars. Governors owe these duties to the Churches, according to the saying of Isaiah: Kings shall be your foster fathers, and queens your nursing mothers.

That saying, when in the inspection

Frederick Myconius, Justus Menius, and I had read out in letters written to the most excellent Prince, the Elector Duke of Saxony, John, in which we asked that moderate annual pensions be assigned to the Churches from certain estates that we had named. The most excellent Prince was so delighted with this proposal that he himself immediately examined Isaiah, and, having read the entire chapter, he replied joyfully that he would always keep this proposal in mind, and he generously donated those revenues to the Churches of which we had written, and ordered that the donation be promptly confirmed by public letters.

In the last chapter greetings are appended, and then an admonition that opinions conflicting with this rule which he handed down are not to be accepted, as he says elsewhere: If anyone teaches another Gospel, let him be anathema.

Concerning greetings, although I shall not say much, nevertheless it has seemed good to give this warning. This long list of names shows what kind of church it was. For although we do not read here the names of many kings and princes, nevertheless it is evident that there was a company of honorable men, and many honorable families. Such is the church scattered through different regions, agreeing on the Gospel, rightly acknowledging and invoking God and our Lord Jesus Christ, even if it has neither empires of the world, nor is it contained by the soldiers of a single kingdom, as the church was then gathered, not only in the Roman Empire, but also in the kingdom of the Parthians and elsewhere. Altogether mournful is the appearance of the church in this life, because it is not contained within one and the same empire, nor does it have sure political defenses, but is like a scholastic band scattered through different regions without power, without resources, without arms, without a king, in short, as it seems, without order. This deformity alienates the minds of kings and the powerful, but let us know that in this life such a company is the church. And yet in the meantime let us look around, what sort of men they are, what sort of families, which bear testimony concerning the doctrine. For it is not an army of Cyclopes or Centaurs, but there is some order, and there are pursuits of doctrine and examples of virtues. And there are some honorable families, and there is some union of those who think rightly, so that although in Judea there were different sects, which fought among themselves, Pha- Fridericus Myconius of the churches, and Iustus [and I] were of the Pharisees and Sadducees.

And King Herod and the courtly crowd were atheists, yet there were churches of these families, of Zacharias, of Simeon, of Joseph, of Zebedee, and many others.

And these agreed on doctrine, and with the same voice they invoked and celebrated God, and they maintained their union; they did not fight among themselves like the Cadmean brothers, or the Centaurs and Lapiths.

When, therefore, we read Paul's salutations, let us imagine the Church being depicted for us; let us know that there was some honest visible assembly, and that there were many honest families, and that in them there was the light of doctrine, and true invocation of God, and mutual benevolence and a zeal for maintaining union.

For God wishes the Church to shine through faith and other virtues; He does not wish teachers to sow unnecessary cavils or sophistries out of ambition to disturb pious consensus, but He wishes candor to be applied in judging.

He does not wish the people to be distracted into diverse factions on account of private hatreds, but He wishes us to be mindful of this saying: God is love; he who abides in love, abides in God, and God in him.

To this zeal for maintaining union pertain these examples of salutations, about which it is necessary for good minds to think much, both for the glory of God and for the utility of the Church.

Through flatteries and blessings etc.

He commands us to beware, lest being deceived we receive corruptions of true doctrine.

He names two artifices, however, by which hypocrites capture the minds of men: χρηστολογίας (smooth speech) and εὐλογίας (blessings).

χρηστολογίαι signify smooth speeches in general, and flatteries are of one kind in manners, and another in the dogmas themselves, which allude to the judgments and affections of those whose company is sought.

In manners, the simulation of humility and patience is pleasing to men, because, since we are proud by nature, we love more those who seem to cast themselves below us.

It is also customary to increase admiration by boasting of conversations with God, or enthusiasms, or simulated ecstasy, or the seeing of specters.

These artifices the monks knew of old, and now many impostors carry them about.

In the city of Münster there was a certain scoundrel who often in public streets and in the crowd of men would suddenly fall, and lying for some time would lift his eyes to heaven and produce strange gestures: afterwards he would bring forth certain mandates to the people, as if they were oracles delivered in a conversation with God.

Many such impostures are read of in Mahometan [texts] and Manichaean histories.

But since such gestures are simulated by design, so that the simulation is easily detected, they are worthy of hatred, because they are manifest lies. But when the devil thus stirs up the members of the ignorant, as to what they are doing, the tricks and diabolical snares must be understood and detested.

But in the dogmas themselves there are many more flatteries (κολακεῖαι).

I think these are properly called here 'kind-sounding words' (χρηστολογίας). But examples are everywhere to be seen. The speech was pleasing to the rustics at the time of the sedition, when turbulent teachers shouted that Christian liberty exists, and that one need not pay legitimate taxes to lords and magistrates. A pleasing dogma attracts many lazy Anabaptists, when they hear that they can enjoy the property of others there. Thus, many were attracted by the kitchen to the monasteries. Now also there is the pleasing dogma of the Antinomians, who say that those who persevere in sins against their conscience still please God, if in the meantime they pretend to believe in the Gospel. Finally, the matter is widely evident; flatteries please, because we love ourselves and favor our own vices, therefore we are delighted by those who adopt our affections and praise us.

Nor is it difficult to consider what opinions and what men those people approve, whom everyone serves, and to adorn the same opinions and the same men, but to disparage the contrary. And the verse is known: 'Indeed, the master's cook must have a gullet.'

And since this simulation brings wealth and power, it is customary in courts and in Churches.

How many, against their conscience, adore and defend foul idols, and praise and assist the unjust cruelty which is exercised against the innocent, so that they may grow in the favor of princes or the people. In Isaiah chapter 30, both are most gravely accused, both the people, who do not want to hear anything but flatterers, and the teachers themselves who serve the desires of their masters: 'Speak to us pleasing things, see errors for us.' The fact itself shows that these evils have always been and are customary in the world.

Therefore, Paul warns that we should beware, lest we be deceived by 'kind-sounding words' (χρηστολογίαις), and thus he names artificial flatteries, which pertain to a vice fighting against the truth, namely, all flatteries simulated for the sake of deceiving.

But 'blessings' (εὐλογίαι) in the Hebrew phrase signify benedictions, that is, good imprecations and sweet promises, just as monks promise the salvation of souls for the sacrifices of the Mass, as they call them.

By this artifice, the invocation of dead men has been confirmed, so that riches were promised to those invoking Anna, victories to George, and to others is attributed the healing of other diseases.

The Pope condemns all who oppose the idols and pontifical errors: and now the monks incite kings and princes against the truth with these promises, if they suppress this doctrine, which sounds in our Churches, that God will give them huge rewards, victories, and new kingdoms and other worlds. I judge that such promises are properly called here 'blessings' (εὐλογίας).

These are worth more than simple flatteries, because an assertion about the presence of God, about rewards and punishments, is added.

By this assertion, even absurd dogmas are often confirmed, which do not flatter reason, because there are certain monstrous minds that beget and defend, whether by ambition or only by the perversity of nature, opinions fighting against the judgments of all sane people.

I know such a one to be Thammer, who still wanders about everywhere, who contended that he who had sworn that he would commit an unjust murder, ought to commit that murder. Afterwards, he defended Stoic necessity, and affirmed that all things happen necessarily, both good and evil.

And when it was objected that God is not the cause of sin, he replied that God is not bound by his own law, but like a tyrant does whatever he wants. I shudder while reciting these frenzies, therefore I will not add more examples, but those who defend such absurdities, when arguments fail them, resort to the thunderbolts of execrations, and curse those who are learning.

But concerning such execrations or unjust curses, the saying of Psalm 108 must be held: 'They will curse, and you will bless.' Let us, however, fortify ourselves against all corruptions of doctrine with these two things: diligence in learning correctly, and ardent prayer.

Concerning the former, Paul says: 'Attend to reading, doctrine, and consolation.' And to the Colossians: 'Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom, and teach and admonish one another.'

Let these two most grave admonitions always be in sight, and be diligently considered.

Paul names reading first, because the doctrine of the Church is unlike philosophical doctrines.

The beginning of Arithmetic is not from reading, but from the natural knowledge of numbers, but the decree concerning the Son of God: and concerning reconciliation and the restitution of eternal life, it was unknown to all creatures before the revelation, in which the Son of God himself brought forth the promise of grace from the bosom of the eternal Father.

But this afterwards he willed it to be written by the Prophets.

Paul therefore begins the doctrine of the Church from reading, then the reading must be illustrated by doctrine, that is, the words must be explained: what God, what the Son of God, what the Law, what sin, what the remission of sin, grace, justice, the Gospel, the Church, the polities, and eternal life signify. It is necessary that these be set forth in an order accommodated to teaching. He also names consolation, because the end of doctrine in the Church is consolation, namely, that by which, being reconciled to God through trust in the Mediator, we are made temples of God and receive the beginnings of eternal life, to which we shall be resurrected from death, and then God will be all in all the blessed, communicating to us Himself, His light, wisdom, justice, and joy in eternity.

Philosophy, which is a particle of divine law, does not show such an end of life; it sees and deplores the immense calamities of the human race, and exhorts men to modesty, just as Plato says: Philosophy is the meditation of death [μελέτησιν θανάτου]. But the voice of the Gospel is: Everyone who believes in the Son has eternal life.

God wills it to be known that the Son was sent, so that He might gather an eternal Church, and that He is always present to the Church; He wills that help, defense, and then restoration from death be sought and expected from the Son. He wills that faith and invocation be exercised and the voice of the Gospel be propagated, so that the whole human race might not have been created in vain, but that a great part might be the eternal Church, which recognizes Him in this life, and to which He communicates His goodness in all eternity. Therefore, Paul has encompassed the greatest matters in that brief saying: the distinction of doctrine, which is proper to the Church, and rational wisdom or philosophy.

Likewise, the beginning and end of doctrine, and at the same time he exhorts us to learning, and binds us to these certain writings handed down through the Prophets and Apostles. He also refutes Stenkefeld and other enthusiasts, who lead men away from reading and command them to fly into heaven with human thoughts, and overwhelm the true exercises of faith that contemplates the divine voice. Let us therefore be moved by Paul's saying, and let us rouse ourselves to reading. Another sentence also commends to us the care of reading and learning with these exaggerations: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom.

It is necessary that the sources of doctrine be correctly learned, because heretics do not treat the word of Christ wisely, as the Anabaptists, condemning the political order, the distinction of masters, the magistrate, and judgments, foolishly and furiously corrupt the sayings of the Gospel. Therefore, studies of doctrine are necessary. But in this place I do not add a longer explanation; I only beseech all who fear God that they love the reading of the divine books, both for the glory of God and for their own salvation.

Moreover, let the invocation of God be added, and let groans and vows be mingled with reading and thought, and let us ask to be instructed by the Son of God, who is the Word [λόγος] of the eternal Father, just as He commanded us to ask this: Pray, that you may not enter into temptation. And indeed He Himself prays assiduously for the Church, as He says: Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth. Let us join our own vows to the prayer of this our supreme Priest. Therefore, You, Son of God, Lord Jesus Christ, crucified for us and resurrected, Word and eternal image of the eternal Father [λόγε καὶ εἰκὼν ἀΐδιε ἀϊδίου πατρὸς], sitting at the right hand of the eternal Father, I humbly pray that You give gifts to men, that You teach and govern us, and protect the Churches of these regions, Amen.

Latin:

Caput XV.

Cum Christi exemplo ostendit infirmos tolerandos esse, et dictum Psalmi recitavit, mox addit generalem admonitionem de usu scripturarum.

Iubet, ut per patientiam et scripturarum consolationem spem teneamus.

Repetit hoc loco Paulus usitatum praeceptum, videlicet, alligandas esse mentes ad verbum Dei revelatum et comprehensum in scriptis propheticis et apostolicis: et non iudicandum esse de essentia et voluntate Dei, iuxta imaginationes humanas, sine verbo Dei.

Item, in nostris doloribus intuendas esse promissiones et statuendum, eas ad nos quoque pertinere, etiamsi in genere omnes alloquuntur.

Multi serunt stoicas et enthusiasticas opiniones, et deducunt mentes ad hanc dubitationem: Cum scripserit Deus catalogum electorum, ad hos pertinet promissio gratiae, fortassis ad te non pertinet, cum nescias an sis in eo catalogo.

Adversus hanc dubitationem haec manifesta regula opponenda est: Utraque concio est universalis, praedicatio poenitentiae, et promissio gratiae.

Accusat Deus omnes propter peccata, et offert omnibus credituris remissionem Gratis, propter filium, ac misit filium, ut hoc arcanum decretum proferat.

Nec sunt in Deo fingendae contradictoriae voluntates.

Nec cogitandum est. Fortassis aliud vult de te, quam sonat promissio.

Ab hac imaginatione revocandae sunt mentes ad ipsam promissionem, et constantissime statuendum est, Filium ideo missum esse, ut hunc voluntatem aeterni patris ostendat, et veracem nuncium esse.

Sic cum promissione nos sustentamus, simul filius Dei est efficax, et in orde dicit consolationem ipsa Evangelii voce, et patris voluntatem ostendit, quia dicit: Nemo novit patrem, nisi filius, et cui filius volet revelare.

Haec tota doctrina, quae iubet a verbo revelato ordiri, nec extra verbum vagari, et quaerere illuminationes, seu raptus, tenenda est contra multos fanaticos, Stoicos, Manichaeos, Enthusiastas et Anabaptistas, qui se et alios implicant dubitationibus, relicto verbo et excussa fide.

Nec tribuimus vim magicam verbo, sed dicimus Deum velle hoc ordine cognosci, et non aliter, et velle nos adhibere considerationem, et simul in ipsa consideratione filium efficacem esse, iuxta dictum: Fides ex auditu est, auditus per verbum Dei.

Diserte igitur inquit Paulus: Per consolationem scripturarum, ut intelligamus eum loqui de verbo externo, seu audito, seu lecto.

Hic ridet Stenkefeldius, et dicit cogitationem verbi scripti seu auditi tantum esse externi hominis occupationem, ut fuit abstinere a suilla carne: non vult esse instrumentum, quo filius Dei ipse est efficax.

Sed nos haec perspicua dicta Pauli opponamus: Evangelium est potentia Dei salutem omni credenti.

Item: Evangelium est ministerium spiritus, id est, quo, cum homines se sustentant, filius Dei ipse est efficax, et effundit Spiritum sanctum in corda.

Quia vero mentio fit consolationis, nominatur etiam patientia, ut significetur, Ecclesiam in hac vita semper cruci subiectam esse, et monet, causas cogitandas esse, quare sit subiecta ingentibus aerumnis.

Monet item, Qualis obedientia in cruce necessaria sit, et quomodo differat Ecclesia ab imperiis mundi.

Ecclesia autem non tantum de aerumnis loquitur, ut Philosophi, sed etiam de liberatione.

Ideo Paulus coniungit patientiam, consolationem et spem: differunt igitur patientia philosophica et Christiana obiectis et fine.

Patientia philosophica, est obedire rationi in perferendis adversis, quae ratio iubet ferre, et saepe est sine ulla spe liberationis aut auxilii, sicut in Socrate nec spes auxilii in praesentia est, nec spes liberationis certa post mortem.

Fert autem supplicium sic, ne impellatur dolore, ut opus externum contra iustitiam aut modestiam faciat.

Cato contra iustitiam sibi mortem consciscit. cero oppressus dolore facit contra modestiam etc. Socrates etsi foris est placidus, tamen in corde habet tristes fremitus, et fluctus dubitationum de providentia. Sed patientia Christiana est obedire Deo in adversis, quae Deus iubet ferre, et semper huic obedientiae mixta est spes auxilii divini seu fiducia praesentiae divinae, et spes liberationis, qua spe erectum cor laetatur aliquo modo in Deo. Haec laetitia non est in philosophica patientia, quae est plena fremitus in corde, etiamsi foris non addit tragicos gestus.

Iam cogita, quantis calamitatibus, morti, morbis, inopiae, odiis tyrannorum et hypocritarum, factionibus venenatissimorum Sophistarum, exiliis calumniis, suppliciis, quid opponat Paulus, videlicet scripturas. Hic rident non solum tyranni, sed etiam Stenkefeldius, et similes enthusiastae. Num literis et syllabis mortem, morbos, tyrannos, aut supplicia tolles aut lenies?

Respondeo: Non haec intelligas magice de figuris, sed de cogitatione huius ipsius verbi, in quo se Deus patefecit, quod voluit literis mandari, in cuius cogitatione filius Dei simul adest, et dicit consolationem in corde credentis, et accendit fidem, spem, laetitiam et invocationem. Vincimus igitur vincente filio Dei agnito per verbum, ideo in Psalm. dicitur: Sustinuit anima mea in verbo eius, Speravit anima mea in Domino.

Item, Psalm. 118.: Liquefacta est anima mea in angustia, confirma me verbo tuo. Sic coniungit Paulus scripturas et spem, ut sciamus, nos a scripturis cogitatione verbi, in quo se Deus patefecit, deduci ad ipsum Deum, quem spes intuetur agnitum verbo.

Haec tota doctrina fit illustrior in veris doloribus et vera invocatione. Ideo assumite vos, sicut et Christus assumsit nos. Conclusio est admonitionis de usu ceremoniarum, et de concordia.

Rursus autem adduntur testimonia de vocatione Gentium, ut et conversi ex Gentibus confirmentur, et Iudaei studiosius cogitent de regno Christi, Sciant non esse politiam Mosaicam, sed alium regnum, in quo bona aeterna credentibus restituuntur, sive sint in politiis ethnicis, sive in Mosaica politia, sicut ad Philippenses dicitur: πολίτευμα nostrum in coelis est, id est, vera lux; qua Deum recte agnoscimus et recte invocamus, incoatio iusticiae et vitae aeternae sunt res coelestes, nec impediunt, quo minus corpora in hac vita sint in diversis politiis. Citatur autem dictum Esaiae maxime insigne, quod et summam doctrinae Evangelii continet, et testimonium est de passione et resurrectione Christi.

Et erit illo die radix Iessae, quae stabit, ut sit signum populis, ad eam Gentes confugient, et erit requies eius gloria. Paulus sumit verba, ut leguntur in Graeca interpretatione, quae illo tempore usitata fuit. Nihil autem discrepat sententia: Erigetur, ut imperet Gentibus, in eo Gentes sperabunt. Eadem enim sunt, esse vexillum populi, et esse ducem. Hic primum teneatur definitio.

Regnum Christi, est filium Dei missum esse ad Ecclesiam initio, prolata promissione, et colligere ac servare Ecclesiam, et deinde adsumta humana natura post resurrectionem exaltatum esse, et iam hanc personam, quae est Deus et Homo, servare et restituere ministerium Evangelii, et colligere ac vivificare Ecclesiam verbo et dato Spiritu sancto, et protegere eam mirabiliter contra diabolos et tyrannos, et post hanc vitam resuscitare eam, et dare aeternam salutem. Quae beneficia, quanquam sunt actiones divinae naturae, tamen fiunt a filio in natura adsumta, et sunt iam actiones communes huius personae, quae est Iesus Christus, sicut et prima promissio inquit: Semen mulieris conculcabit caput serpentis.

Et ad Corinthios inquit Paulus: Mors delebitur per hominem Christum. Sic etiam nominatur caput Ecclesiae, omnia in omnibus perficiens. Etsi enim vivificatio est propria divinae naturae, tamen fit a filio in natura adsumta. Ita haec persona est caput Ecclesiae. Idem autem regnum, quod nominatur Regnum Dei, item Regnum aeternum Christi, Paulus ita discernit ad Corinthios, cum ait: Tradet regnum Deo et patri.

Ut intelligamus regnum idem esse, sed modum differre. In hac vita dicitur proprie regnum Christi: quia per ministerium Evangelii Deus efficax est immediate per hanc secundam personam, quae est λόγος, quae immediate protulit Evangelium ex sinu aeterni patris, et immediate in ministerio est efficax, sicut inquit: Nemo novit patrem nisi filius, et cui filius volet revelare. Apprehenditur ergo Deus verbo, et nondum conspicitur palam essentia divinitatis.

Diligenter autem singulæ particulæ in dicto Esaiaæ considerentur: In ipso Gentes sperabunt. Paulus urget adpellationem Gentium, ac citat inter testimonia, quæ adfirmant Evangelium non tantum ad eos pertinere, qui nati sunt ex semine Iacob. Deinde verbum sperandi opponatur damnationi, et comprehendatur summa promissionum, videlicet, mitti filium Dei, ut caput serpentis conterat. Item, ut destruæt regnum diaboli, deleat peccatum et mortem, et restituat iusticiam et vitam æternam. Hæc dona dantur propter filium Dei, et per eum credentibus in ipsum. Ideo inquit: Sperabunt in eum, videlicet, ut hæc bona accipiant, sicut et in Psalmo dicitur: Beati omnes qui confidunt in eo. Est ergo regnum consolationis, non damnationis. Et cultus proprii huius regni sunt, fides, spes, confessio, gratiarum actio, invocatio, propagatio Evangelii. Nam vocabulo sperandi omnia hæc comprehenduntur, fides, spes, invocatio et vicini motus. Et in invocatione accendantur et confirmenur de hoc regno, fides, spes, invocatio et gratiarum actio.

Additur autem: Mors eius erit gloria. Ubi significat, Messiam revicturum esse ex morte, atque ita aboliturum esse mortem, non tantum in proprio corpore, sed in omnibus credentibus in eum, ac redditurum eis iusticiam et vitam æternam. Alexandri mors non est gloria, sed finis est iam omnium actionum Alexandri. Nominat enim vox divina gloriam non spectacula aut famam, quam non sentit is qui celebratur, ut Alexandri cadaver magna pompa ducitur ex Babylone in Ægyptum collocatum in auream sellam: sed nominat gloriam viventis personæ actiones. Ut Christus post mortem reviviscit, et vivens colligit æternam Ecclesiam, vere deprecatur pro ea assidue apud patrem in arcano consilio divinitatis, adest, servat ministerium Evangelii prolati ex sinu aeterni patris, et immediate in ministerio est efficax voce Evangelii, dans dona hominibus, id est, vivificans credentes, dans Spiritum sanctum, et resuscitans homines ex morte, et restituens nobis iusticiam et vitam aeternam, defendens etiam Ecclesiam mirabiliter in hac vita, cum sit Emmanuel et caput Ecclesiae, omnia perficiens in sanctis.

Hae actiones sunt vera gloria, non umbrae spectaculorum, aut inanis fama. Certus sum etc.

Finita tota admonitione de ceremoniis, addit oratorio more mitigationem, si qui praeferoces aut morosi se durins obiurgatos esse existimarent.

Nam aliqui ferociores aegre ferunt libertatem restringi, alii morosi aegre ferunt usitatas ceremonias negligi, placat igitur utrosque, tribuens eis laudem bonitatis et eruditionis, ac petens, ut et hanc admonitionem boni consulant, cum sint placidi, candidi, non facile irritabiles, et sint intelligentes.

Nam apud candidos et intelligentes est cognoscendi et ignoscendi locus, sicut vere dicitur, ὡς ἡδὺ συνέσει χρηστότης κεκραμένη.

Alii indocti et iracundi facile irritantur, et semel irritati sunt implacabiles, ut dicitur: Imperito homine nunquam quidquam iniustius. Et Salomon inquit: Iram stulti magnum onus esse. Ita lenit utrosque, cum ait, placidos, non iracundos, non morosos esse, et praeterea recte doctos esse: tales enim liberam admonitionem boni consulant. Propter gratiam quae data est mihi. Et ad placandos lectores, et ad augendam auctoritatem admonitionis conducit mentio officii et miraculorum quam addit, quasi dicat: Moveor Apostoli officio, ut vos doceam et commonefaciam, et Deus tribuit testimonia meae doctrinae.

Quare me placide audiatis, et mihi assentiamini sine dubitatione.

Hic considerandum est rursus, qualis sit auctoritas apostolica: quod videlicet certum sit, Apostoli doctrinam esse divinam, et ei credendum esse, sicut voci Dei de coelo sonanti immediate inter manifesta miracula, sicut decalogus promulgatus est, et saepe alibi de apostolica autoritate copiosus dictum est.

Ornat autem ministerium vocabulo sacrificii, ait se ministrum esse sacrificantem Evangelium.

Nova haec forma sermonis est, sed erudita, sumta XIII. 8. ENARRATIO EPIST. PAULI AD ROMANOS. CAP. XV. ex collatione et interpretatione sacrificiorum Leviticorum.

Dictum est autem alibi, quod sit discrimen politiae Moisi et aeternae Ecclesiae, quae voce promissionis de filio Dei colligitur, et quare politia Moisi constituta sit, et quid sint sacrificia, quod sit discrimen inter signa et vera sacrificia, quia lex in hac vita ordinat utraque. Ordinat signa, quibus homines testantur hunc esse verum Deum quem invocant, et his ritibus discernunt eum a commentitiis numinibus. Ordinat autem et alia interiora et externa sacrificia, in quibus sese Deus ipse nobis communicat et est efficax, quia oportet aliquas res esse copulantes nos cum Deo. Talia sunt sacrificia, vera agnitio Dei lucens in mente, et tota novitas, qua homo fit templum Dei, et qua sese Deus nobis communicat, et vicissim homo celebrat Deum. Sic enim Deus se communicat rationali creaturae, cum recte agnoscitur, quia est lux lucens in sanctis. Fit autem celebratio in hac vita docendo, confitendo, invocatione, gratiarum actione, conformitate cordis et laetitia in Deo. Haec incoantur in hac vita, et praeterquam quod modus docendi in ministerio non est talis in vita aeterna, caetera omnia manent eadem, scilicet confessio, gratiarum actio, conformitas cordis et laetitia in Deo. In his ipsis actionibus sese communicat Deus in tota aeternitate, cum erit omnia in omnibus.

Scriptum est igitur Oseae 4.: Omnem aufer iniquitatem, et benefac nobis, et reddemus vitulos labiorum nostrorum, id est, tu Messia, da beneficia iuxta promissionem tuam, gratiam et vitam aeternam, et reddemus sacrificia, non signa, sed vera sacrificia, ministerium docendi, invocationem, confessionem, gratiarum actionem, laetam obedientiam in corde.

Ita hic Paulus inquit: Se sacrificare Evangelium Christi, id est, docendo praestare Deo verum cultum. Et facit Paulus utrumque, ipse offert Deo cum docet, id est, celebrat Deum et tribuit ei honorem. Simul autem praeparat alias hostias, id est, auditores, ut hi quoque offerant Deo veros cultus. Sicut duo erant officia distincta Levitarum et Sacerdotum. Levitae ceu lanii mactabant pecudes, praeparabant hostias, Sacerdotes autem offerebant. Nunc idem Paulus et offert ipse, et praeparat alios, quia voce eius alii ad Deum convertuntur.

Ideo hic additur de sacrificio auditorum.

Ut oblatio gentium fiat accepta Deo, id est, ut et Gentes ipsae fiant hostiae, et aeterna sacrificia Deo offerant, veram fidem, veram invocationem, confessionem, gratiarum actionem, conformitatem cum Deo et laetitiam cum eo in tota aeternitate, non offerant commentitiis numinibus, Baccho, Veneri etc.

Sit autem hic totus locus Pauli notior et gratior, quia testimonium est de ministerio Evangelii.

Primum consolatur docentes et discentes, affirmans placere Deo hunc laborem, cum nominatur sacrificium, qua appellatione significatur excellentia operum, quod videlicet opus sit bonum Deo placens, et tale, quo iudicat Deus sibi honorem tribui. Huc accommodentur dicta: Offeremus vitulos labiorum. Item, Esaiae 61.: Vos Sacerdotes Domini vocabimini, ministri Dei nostri. Et Psalm. 118.: Voluntaria oris meis beneplaceant tibi, id est, sacrificia docendi et invocandi, item discendi, placent tibi. Discant et auditores reverenter sentire de ministerio Evangelii, cum has laudes audiunt, sicut saepe praeceptum est.

Et 1. Thessal. 5. dicitur: Oro vos fratres, ut excellenter diligatis eos, qui praesunt vobis in Domino, propter ministerium ipsorum.

1. Timoth. 5.: Presbyteri, qui bene praesunt, duplici honore digni sunt, praecipue qui laborant in sermone et doctrina. Duplici, inquit, id est, reverentia et victu. Complectitur autem victus defensionem, reverentia vero obedientiam in his, quae sunt propria ministerii propter Deum, cui honos primum debetur: et cum obedientia sit coniuncta honorifica opinio, quae intelligat nos ministerio propter Deum subiectos esse, et dilectio et voluntas anteferens ministerium aliis negotiis vitae.

Sciamus autem praecipuam causam esse, propter quam doctrinam et ministerium oportet audiri et conservari, quia sic Deus colligit Ecclesiam, et non aliter, scilicet voce et cogitatione scripti Evangelii, cum auditur aut legitur, ut Rom. 10. dicitur: Quomodo credent sine praedicante. Item: Evangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti. 2. Corinth. 3.: Evangelium est ministerium spiritus, id est, Deus est efficax cogitatione Evangelii auditi aut lecti, et convertit corda in cogitatione Evangelii. Ac prorsus execrandus est error Stenkefeldii, qui expresse scribit, Deum non esse efficacem per cognitionem Evangelii auditi aut lecti, ac fingit alias illuminationes extra Evangelium, et sine Evangelio.

Tales furores olim Marcionis, Manichaeorum et Enthusiastarum fuerunt, et errones Anabaptistae similia portenta circumferunt.

Sciant autem bonae mentes praecipi, ut discamus et cogitemus verbum Dei, iuxta dictum: Hunc audite. Item: Osculamini filium.

Et certo sciamus Deum per huius scripti Evangelii cogitationem efficacem esse, ut dicitur Roman. 10.: Fides ex auditu est. Item: Pater sanctifica eos in veritate, sermo tuus est veritas.

Nunc autem proficiscor Ierosolymam, ut serviamus sanctis.

Cum antea de suo officio dixerit, obiter narrat et peregrinationes suas, et benevolentiam suam erga Ecclesiam, quae Romae fuit, significat, et spem eis adventus sui facit.

Nunc vero ait, in Iudaeam se proficisci, ut sanctis egentibus adferat pecuniam, quam in Macedonia et Achaia contulerant Ecclesiae, ut egentibus in fame opem ferrent.

Notissimum est enim in historia Claudii imperatoris in Asia, Graecia et Italia eo tempore magnam sterilitatem aliquot annorum fuisse, et multos homines passim fame extinctos esse.

De ea fame in Actis dicitur cap. undecimo: et Eusebius scribit modium tritici sex drachmis venditum esse.

Et in sexto capite Apocalypsis inter poenas numeratur fames, in qua futurum dicit, ut choenix denario sit emendus.

Fuit autem commune pretium modii mediocribus annis, tres aut quatuor sestertii, ut Cicero scribit, modii pretium lege fuisse tres sestertios, id est, nostrates numos Misnicos quatuor et viginti.

Iam si modius in fame emtus est sex drachmis crevit pretium quintuplo, cum mediocribus annis usitatum pretium esset drachma, aut circiter.

Erant autem in modio octo choenices: et choenix erat unius diei farina.

Fuit igitur mediocribus annis farina unius diei pro quatuor Misnicis numis: tantum farinae in fame emebatur denario, hoc est, numis Misnicis triginta duobus.

Creverat igitur pretium septuplo.

Harum computationum consideratio utilis est, et ad intelligendam historiam, et ad hanc animadversionem, qui ordo fuerit in victu congruens homini.

Et adparet inde, frugalitatem et temperantiam tantam fuisse, quae tamen naturae congrueret, et victum non sordide datum esse servis.

Erant autem praecipue in Iudaea magnae calamitates eorum, qui Evangelium amplectebantur.

Multi enim interficiebantur, plurimi ex possessionibus propriis excutiebantur, cogebantur exulare.

Ad has miserias tunc accessit communis fames in tota Asia et Europa.

Ut igitur alicubi pauperes familiae iuvarentur, Paulus in Graecia et alibi pecuniam collegit, quam in Iudaeam attulit.

Has temporum circumstantias et Ecclesiae aerumnas, et Apostolorum curas in iuvandis pauperibus, et alenda benevolentia Ecclesiarum considerare utile est.

Simul autem intexit hic admonitionem de mercede debita ministris Evangelii, de qua tamen concionatur copiosius primae ad Corinth.

9., ubi expresse inquit: Sic Dominus ordinavit, ut hi qui Evangelium docent, ex Evangelio victum habeant. Et adduntur multa argumenta.

Quis militat suis stipendiis? ubi usus est nomine ὀψώνιον.

Sic enim usitate stipendia nominabantur, quia militibus in provinciis stipendii loco, frumentum, carnes, vinum, oleum, poma, fici dabantur.

Quia Romani occupati provinciis initio tantum hoc onus indicebant, ut decimas imperio penderent, ut scribit Appianus.

Inde praesidiis dabantur res terra natae, quarum nomen ὀψώνιον pro stipendio usurpatum est.

Est autem ὄψον ab ἕψω, quod est elixo, et a verbo ὀνοῦμαι, quod est emo: significat enim escas, quae praeter panem adduntur, quarum pleraque elixatione coquuntur.

Cum autem Deus immensa bonitate colligat aeternam Ecclesiam voce doctrinae, et non aliter, et severissime praecipit conservari doctrinam, quod ut fiat, necesse est esse docentium et discentium coetus.

Et quidem ipse filius Dei missus ab aeterno patre, ut per eum Ecclesia colligatur, sua potentia et doctrinam servat, et instituit ministerium docendi, et omnibus temporibus excutavit doctores, et exuscitat, quos vult esse organa sonantia vocem Evangelii, qua flectit corda non repugnantium Evangelio ad veram Dei invocationem et ad aeternam salutem, et in hac tanta militia fideliter servientibus, id est, Pastoribus et Doctoribus vult dari victum.

Hoc praeceptum saepe repetitum est, et additae sunt promissiones amplissimae praemiorum, quae certissimum est tribui et in hac vita et post hanc vitam piis, qui benefici sunt erga fideles doctores. Et exempla illustria recitantur in historiis propheticis, nec desunt exempla nostrae aetati.

Matth. 10.: Qui dederit potum aquae uni ex minimis istorum, propter doctrinam, Amen dico vobis, habebit mercedem. 1. Corinth. 9.: Sic ordinavit Dominus, ut hi, qui docent Evangelium, ex Evangelio vivant. Proverb. 3.: Honora Dominum de tua substantia, et de primitiis omnium frugum tuarum, et implebuntur horrea tua saturitate, et musto exundabunt torcularia tua. Syracidae 7.: Tota anima tua reverere Deum, et honore adficito sacerdotes eius, et des eis partes, quas lex dari praecipit, primitias et hostias, ut tibi vicissim Deus benedicat. Esaiae 49.: Reges erunt nutritores tui et reginae nutrices, id est, Principes et Respublicae curent, ut ministri Evangelii habeant victum et defensionem.

Ad haec praecepta et ad has promissiones exempla addantur. Deus benefecit hospitibus Abrahae. In Aegypto Deus benefecit obstetricibus, quae non interfecerunt infantes Israëlitarum. Sareptanam hospitam Eliae mirando modo aluit, et ornavit restituto filio ex morte. Abdias abdidit Prophetas in specum, et eis cibum praebuit. Ieremiae captivo opitulatus est regius Eunuchus, cui promittitur incolumitas in excidio Ierosolymae, Et rex Aegyptius Apryes interfector Ieremiae strangulatus est ab Amasi praefecto.

Moveamur ergo et praeceptis Dei, et promissionibus praemiorum et promissionum exemplis, ut in hoc genere beneficentiam pie exerceamus.

Etsi autem tyranni et alii prophani homines vociferantur, has adhortationes de beneficentia erga ministros Evangelii esse aucupia avariciae, et similes esse has conciones luporum concionibus, quas habere finguntur ad anseres: tamen nos voluntatem Dei intuemur, et sciamus eum severissime praecipere conservationem ministerii evangelici. Semper etiam Deus aliquorum hominum pectora ad hanc beneficentiam flectit. Sicut Paulo praebent hospitium Sergius Proconsul, Onesiphorus, et passim alii.

In navi etiam Paulus velut navarchus et praecipuus gubernator auditur a centurione, militibus et nautis, et hi singulari eum benevolentia complectuntur.

Consideremus autem et huius temporis mores. Sunt aliqui Principes et privati homines benefici in hoc genere, qui docentibus et discentibus opem ferunt.

Sed plurimi Reges, Principes, Episcopi defensores idolorum, horribilem saevitiam in ministros Evangelii exercent. Memini virum excellentem ingenio, eruditione et pietate, Henricum Sutphaniensem, qui in Ditmarsia, quia recte docebat, crudeliter interfectus est: nec alia fuit ulla causa necis eius. Fuit Tubingae Johannes Croesus Theologiae Doctor, vir modestissimus et studiosus verae doctrinae, qui postea in Tillingen adfectus est ultimo supplicio. Nec ullum crimen ei obiici potuit, quam quod sacerdos in coniugio caste vivere maluerat, quam in coelibatu se varie polluere.

Et possem longum catalogum recensere talium praestantium virorum, qui innocentes tantum propter veritatis confessionem interfecti sunt. Nec saevitiae finis est in Italia, Gallia, Britannia, Belgico et alibi.

Hanc crudelitatem haud dubie sequuntur novae poenae et magnae mutationes imperiorum.

Paulatim vero et Principes et privati homines locupletes, qui voluerant doctrinam Evangelii conservari et propagari, attribuerunt olim Ecclesiis reditus, qui initio in quatuor partes distributi fuerunt. Ex prima parte dabantur mercedes et alimenta ministris Evangelii, Pastoribus, eorum collegis, qui publice in templis docebant. Secunda pars erat docentium in Scholis et panperum scholasticorum. Ex tertia parte consulebatur inopiae egentium, qui propter morbos non poterant laboribus suis victum quaerere. Quarta pars conferebatur in aedificationes et mercedes nunciorum.

Nunc Episcopi et Abbates fruuntur illis opibus, et negligunt ministerium Evangelii et studia doctrinae, sicut praedictum est in Epistola Iudae: Helluabuntur de eleemosynis vestris.

Haec mala deploremus, et interea in nostris Ecclesiis hortemur pios gubernatores, ut reditus Ecclesiarum pie collocari curent, ac praesertim ut victum praebeant familiis pastorum recte docentium, et opem ferant pauperibus scholasticis. Haec officia gubernatores debent Ecclesiis, iuxta dictum Esaiae: Reges erunt nutritores tui, et reginae nutrices.

Id dictum cum in inspectione

Ecclesiarum Fridericus Myconius, et Iustus Menius et ego recitassemus in literis scriptis ad optimum Principem Ducem Saxoniae Electorem Ioannem, in quibus petebamus annuas pensiones mediocres ex certis fundis, quos nominaveramus, attribui Ecclesiis, ita delectatus est optimus Princeps hac sententia, ut statim Esaiam ipse inspexerit, et lecto toto capite laetus responderit, se semper huius sententiae memorem fore, et reditus illos Ecclesiis, de quibus scripseramus, liberaliter donaverit, et iusserit donationem publicis literis mox confirmari.

In postremo capite adscriptae sunt salutationes, et deinde admonitio, ne recipiantur opiniones pugnantes cum hac norma quam tradidit, sicut alibi inquit: Si quis aliud Evangelium docet, anathema sit.

De salutationibus, etsi non multa dicam, tamen hoc monere visum est. Haec longa nomenclatura ostendit, qualis fuerit Ecclesia. Etsi enim hic non legimus multorum Regum et Principum nomina, tamen adparet fuisse coetum honestorum hominum, et multas honestas familias. Talis est Ecclesia sparsa in diversas regiones, consentiens de Evangelio, recte agnoscens et invocans Deum et Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, etiamsi nec habet imperia mundi, nec continetur unius regni militibus, ut tunc colligebatur Ecclesia, non tantum in Romano imperio, sed etiam in regno Parthorum et alibi. Est omnino moesta species Ecclesiae in hac vita, quod non continetur unico et eodem imperio, nec habet certa praesidia politica, sed est velut agmen scholasticum sparsum in diversas regiones sine potentia, sine opibus, sine armis, sine rege, denique ut videtur, sine ordine. Haec deformitas alienat animos regum et potentum, sed sciamus in hac vita talem coetum esse Ecclesiam. Et tamen interea circumspiciamus, quales sint homines, quales familiae, quae testimonium dicunt de doctrina. Non est enim Cyclopum aut Centaurorum exercitus, sed aliquis ordo est, et sunt studia doctrinae et exempla virtutum. Et sunt aliquae honestae familiae, et recte sententium aliqua coniunctio est, ut quamvis in Iudaea diversae sectae erant, quae inter se dimicabant, Pha- Ecclesiarum Fridericus Myconius, et Iustus Merisaei et Zadducaei.
