Et rex Herodes et aulica turba erant Athei, tamen erant Ecclesiae hae familiae, Zachariae Simeonis, Ioseph, Zebedaei, et multae aliae.

Et hae de doctrina consentiebant, et eadem voce Deum invocabant et celebrabant, et coniunctionem suam tuebantur, non dimicabant inter sese ut Cadmaei fratres, aut Centauri et Lapithae.

Cum igitur Pauli salutationes legimus, Ecclesiam pingi nobis existimemus, sciamus aliquem honestum coetum visibilem, et honestas familias multas fuisse, et in eis doctrinae lucem fuisse, et veram Dei invocationem, et mutuam benevolentiam et studium tuendae coniunctionis.

Vult enim Deus per fidem et caeteras virtutes Ecclesiam fulgere, non vult doctores ambitione cavillationes non necessarias, aut sophismata serere ad turbandum pium consensum, sed vult candorem in iudicando adhiberi.

Non vult propter privata odia distrahi populum in diversas factiones, sed vult nos dicti huius memores esse: Deus dilectio est, Qui manet in dilectione, in Deo manet, et Deus in eo.

Ad hoc studium tuendae coniunctionis pertinent haec exempla salutationum, de quo multa cogitare bonas mentes et propter gloriam Dei, et propter Ecclesiae utilitatem necesse est.

Per blanditias et benedictiones etc.

Iubet cavere, ne decepti recipiant corruptelas verae doctrinae.

Duo autem artificia nominat, quibus hypocritae capiunt hominum animos, χρηστολογίας et εὐλογίας.

Significant autem χρηστολογίαι blandos sermones in genere, et blanditiae aliae sunt in moribus, aliae in ipsis dogmatibus, quae alludunt ad iudicia et adfectus eorum, quorum societas quaeritur.

In moribus simulatio humilitatis et patientiae grata est hominibus, quia cum simus natura superbi, magis amamus eos, qui videntur sese infra nos abiicere.

Usitatum est etiam augere admirationem iactandis colloquiis cum Deo, seu enthusiasmis, seu simulanda ecstasi, seu videndis spectris.

Haec artificia et olim norant monachi, et nunc multi impostores circumferunt.

In urbe Monasteriensi fuit quidam Nebulo, qui saepe in publicis viis et hominum frequentia subito lapsus est, et aliquandiu iacens oculos in coelum sustulit, et miros gestus edidit: postea protulit certa mandata ad populum, quasi oracula tradita in colloquio Dei.

Tales imposturae multae leguntur in Mahometicis et Manichaei historiis.

Cum autem tales gestus de industria simulati sunt, ut facile deprehenditur simulatio, digni sunt odio, quia sunt manifesta mendacia. Cum vero diaboli sic cient membra ignorantium, quid agant, praestigiae et insidiae diabolicae intelligendae et detestandae sunt.

Sed in ipsis dogmatibus multo plures sunt κολακεῖαι.

Has existimo hic proprie nominari χρηστολογίας. Sunt autem ubique obvia exempla. Grata erat oratio Rusticis tempore seditionis, cum turbulenti doctores vociferentur Christianam libertatem esse, non pendere legitima tributa dominis et magistratibus. Ad Anabaptistas multos ignavos attrahit blandum dogma, cum audiunt se ibi alienis facultatibus frui posse. Ita multos culinae attraxerunt ad monasteria. Nunc quoque blandum dogma est Antinomorum, qui dicunt perseverantes in delictis contra conscientiam, tamen Deo placere, si interea fingant se credere Evangelio. Denique late patet res, Placent assentationes, quia amamus nos ipsos et vitiis nostris favemus, delectamur ergo iis, qui adfectus nostros adsumunt, et nos laudant.

Nec difficile est considerare, quas opiniones, quos homines illi probent, quibus quisque servit, et easdem opiniones et eosdem homines ornare, contraria vero vituperare. Et notus est versus: Nempe cocus domini debet habere gulam.

Cumque opes et potentiam haec simulatio adferat, usitata est in aulis et in Ecclesiis, Quam multi contra conscientiam tetra idola adorant et defendunt, et iniustam saevitiam, quae exercetur contra innocentes, laudant et adiuvant, ut Principum aut populi favore crescant.

Apud Esaiam cap. 30. gravissime accusantur utrique, et populus, qui non vult audire nisi adsentatores, et ipsi doctores qui cupiditatibus dominorum serviunt, Loquimini nobis placentia, videte nobis errores. Haec mala semper in mundo usitata fuisse et esse res ipsa ostendit.

Monet igitur Paulus, ut caveamus, ne decipiamur χρηστολογίαις, et sic nominat artificiosas adsentationes, quae pertinent ad vitium pugnans cum veritate, videlicet ad blanditias omnes decipiendi causa simulatas.

Sed εὐλογίαι Ebraea phrasi significant benedictiones, id est, bonas imprecationes et dulces promissiones, ut monachi promittunt salutem animarum pro sacrificiis Missae, ut nominant. Hoc artificio confirmata est invocatio mortuorum hominum, ut invocantibus Annam promissae sunt divitiae, Georgium victoriae, et aliis attribuitur aliorum morborum sanatio.

Papa damnat omnes, qui adversantur idolis et erroribus pontificiis: et nunc monachi incendunt reges et principes contra veritatem his promissionibus, si opprimant hanc doctrinam, quae sonat in Ecclesiis nostris, Deum daturum esse ipsis ingentia praemia, victorias et nova regna et mundos alios.

Tales promissiones hic nominari proprie εὐλογίας iudico.

Hae plus valent quam simplices blanditiae, quia additur adseveratio de praesentia Dei, de praemiis et de poenis. Hac adseveratione etiam absurda dogmata saepe confirmantur, quae non blandiuntur rationi, quia sunt quaedam monstrosa ingenia, quae gignunt et defendunt, seu ambitione, seu tantum naturae perversitate opiniones pugnantes cum omnium sanorum iudiciis.

Talem novi esse Thammerum, qui adhuc passim vagatur, qui contendebat eum, qui iurasset se facturum esse iniustam caedem, oportere eam caedem facere.

Postea defendebat stoicam necessitatem, adfirmabat omnia necessario fieri, bona et mala. Et cum obiiceretur, Deum non esse causam peccati, ille respondit, Deum non teneri sua lege, sed velut tyrannum facere quicquid vellet.

Cohorresco hos furores recitans, non igitur addam plura exempla, sed qui talia absurda defendunt, cum desunt eis argumenta, decurrunt ad fulmina execrationum, maledicunt discentibus.

Sed de talibus execrationibus seu maledictionibus iniustis tenendum est dictum Psalmi 108.: Maledicent illi, et tu benedices. Praemuniamus autem nos adversus omnes corruptelas doctrinae his duabus rebus.

Diligentia recte discendi, et ardenti precatione. De priore modo inquit Paulus: Attende lectioni, doctrinae et consolationi.

Et ad Colossenses: Sermo Christi habitet in vobis opulenter in omni sapientia, et docete et emendate vos mutuo. Hae duae gravissimae admonitiones semper in conspectu sint, et diligenter considerentur.

Primum nominat Paulus lectionem, quia doctrina Ecclesiae dissimilis est philosophicis doctrinis.

Initium Arithmeticae non est a lectione, sed a noticia naturali numerorum, sed decretum de filio Dei: et de reconciliatione et restitutione vitae aeternae, omnibus creaturis ignotum fuit ante patefactionem, in qua ipse filius Dei promissionem gratiae ex sinu aeterni patris protulit.

Hanc autem postea per Prophetas scribi voluit.

Orditur ergo Paulus Ecclesiae doctrinam a lectione, deinde lectio illustranda est doctrina, id est, vocabula enarranda sunt, quid Deus, quid filius Dei, quid lex, quid peccatum, quid remissio peccati, gratia, iusticia, Evangelium, Ecclesia, politiae, vita aeterna, significant. Haec ordine ad docendum accommodato exponi necesse est. Nominat et consolationem, quia finis doctrinae in Ecclesia est consolatio, videlicet, qua reconciliati Deo fiducia mediatoris, efficimur templa Dei et accipimus initia vitae aeternae, ad quam resuscitabimur ex morte, et erit tunc Deus omnia in omnibus beatis, communicans nobis sese, suam lucem, sapientiam, iusticiam et laetitiam in aeternitate.

Talem vitae exitum non ostendit philosophia, quae est particula legis divinae, et videt ac deplorat ingentes calamitates generis humani, et hortatur homines ad modestiam, sicut Plato inquit: Philosophiam esse μελέτησιν θανάτου. Sed vox Evangelii est: Omnis qui credit in filium, habet vitam aeternam.

Vult sciri Deus filium missum esse, ut colligat aeternam Ecclesiam, et semper eum adesse Ecclesiae, vult peti et expectari a filio auxilium, defensionem, et deinde restitutionem ex morte. Vult fidem et invocationem exerceri et propagari vocem Evangelii, ne totum genus humanum frustra conditum sit, sed pars magna sit aeterna Ecclesia, quae ipsum in hac vita agnoscat, et cui in tota aeternitate bonitatem suam communicet. Res igitur maximas Paulus in illo brevi dicto complexus est, distinctionem doctrinae, quae est Ecclesiae propria, et sapientiae rationalis seu philosophiae.

Item doctrinae initium et finem, Et simul hortatur nos ad discendum, et alligat nos ad haec certa scripta per Prophetas et Apostolos tradita. Refutat etiam Stenkefeldium et alios enthusiastas, qui abducunt homines a lectione, et iubent volitare in coelum humanis cogitationibus, et vera exercitia fidei intuentis vocem divinam, obruunt. Moveamur igitur Pauli dicto, nos ad lectionem excsitemus. Altera sententia etiam legendi et discendi curam nobis commendat his exaggerationibus: Sermo Christi habitet in vobis opulenter in omni sapientia.

Necesse est fontes doctrinae recte disci, quia haeretici non tractant sermonem Christi sapienter, ut Anabaptistae damnantes ordinem politicum, distinctionem dominorum, magistratus et iudicia, insipienter et furenter corrumpunt dicta Evangelii. Necessaria sunt igitur doctrinae studia. Sed hoc loco non addo longiorem explicationem, tantum obtestor omnes timentes Deum, ut ament lectionem divinorum librorum, et propter gloriam Dei, et propter propriam salutem.

Accedat autem invocatio Dei, ac lectioni et cogitationi misceantur gemitus et vota, et petamus nos a filio Dei, qui est λόγος aeterni patris, erudiri, sicut hoc petere iussit: Orate, ne intretis in tentationem. Et quidem ipse pro Ecclesia assidue precatur, sicut inquit: Sanctifica eos in veritate, sermo tuus est veritas. Ad huius summi Sacerdotis nostri precationem adiungamus et nostra vota. Te igitur fili Dei Domine Iesu Christe, crucifixe pro nobis et resuscitate, λόγε καὶ εἰκὼν ἀΐδιε ἀϊδίου πατρὸς, sedens ad dextram aeterni patris, ut des dona hominibus, supplex oro, ut nos doceas et gubernes, et harum regionum Ecclesias protegas, Amen.

# 1 Corinthians

## 1:1 Argument
COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE

OF PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS.

Melanchthon wrote this commentary in the year 1551 and gave it to Paulus Eberus, his student and colleague, so that he might dictate it privately to his students, to whom he was accustomed to give a grammatical explanation of the Epistles of Paul during the spare hours of feast days. — After the death of Melanchthon, Eberus published this commentary and dedicated it to Wolfgang, Count Palatine.

It appeared, therefore, as: "A brief and useful Commentary on the first epistle of Paul to the Corinthians, and on some chapters of the second, written by Philipp Melanchthon. Wittenberg, 1561. 1 Alphabet 8vo." — It is read in the works of Melanchthon, Wittenberg, Vol. IV, p. 210. To the most illustrious Prince and Lord, D. Wolfgang, Count Palatine on the Rhine, Duke of Bavaria, Count of Veldenz and Zweibrücken. To his most clement Lord: Paulus Eberus of Kitzingen, Pastor of the Church of Wittenberg, sends greetings. For a long time I hesitated whether I should publish this little commentary on the Epistle to the Corinthians—which the Reverend and incomparable man of virtue and learning, Lord Philipp Melanchthon, my Preceptor and Father of pious memory, wrote for this purpose ten years ago, after I had undertaken the grammatical explanation of the Epistles of Paul in my own home, so that I might dictate it privately to my students, which I did—or whether I should suppress and hide it entirely, since it is both too meager to satisfy those who require long and declamatory expositions of individual sayings, and furthermore it is also incomplete, explaining barely three chapters of the second Epistle.

But the primary cause of my hesitation was the perversity of this age, which has finally proceeded to such a degree of moroseness and iniquity that almost nothing can now be written or said so sincerely that it does not incur the criticism, and often even the condemnation, of certain sciolists. This license, gaining strength daily through impunity itself, and indeed not only received by some with applause but even confirmed in some places with payment and rewards, will yet cause great harm to the Church, if it has not already inflicted a most sad and almost incurable wound upon it.

It rightly deters good men, who are averse to the spirit of quarreling, from publicly communicating any of their own studies with such danger, even though those studies might contain more doctrine and consolation than the pugnacious and biting writings of certain people, which only make a vehement attack on others and strive with every effort to overturn the opinions of others: yet they teach nothing or very little about the true Foundations and what ought to be firmly held regarding the matter at hand. If you remove from them the insults and other pigments drawn from the most bitter invectives, or rather from the circles of buffoons, you will find them to be bare and entirely empty.

This anxiety of mine, and the fear of such criticisms, has hitherto made me more hesitant to publish this useful work, which, however, the persistent urging of many pious and learned men finally overcame and shook out of me. They had read this commentary and reproached me for continuing, in my desire to avoid the unjust and malicious cavils of the wicked—which no one, however cautious, could ever have escaped, nor should anyone conscious of his own rectitude care about—to defraud men who love piety and truth of the reading of this much-sought-after and expected Commentary, which, even if it were brief, nevertheless explained the principal matters so clearly that, among the works of other learned men longer and more accurate commentaries will undoubtedly also have their place and their praise among those who are intelligent and judge rightly.

I have been impelled by these and many other arguments, so that, neglecting the incursions of those who, in this unhappy age, lie in wait like ἐφεδρεύοντες [those lying in ambush] over the writings of others, seeking for themselves a name and applause through the disparagement of those who are superior, I might publish this little commentary at this time, however imperfect it may be. This, indeed, would have been done more seasonably, more safely, and more usefully while Philip himself was still alive, whose presence and authority could have more effectively commended this writing to the Reader.

Nor did I ever notice that he himself abhorred the publication of this work of his. But because I always had the hope that what is still missing from the explanation of the second Epistle would eventually be added by the author, I deliberately delayed the publication: But since, as was said above, Philip had initiated this writing for me while I was privately explaining some of Paul's Epistles, and the pestilential plague of 1552 had disrupted these private exercises of ours, as well as our public works, forcing us to withdraw to Torgau, and such restless times followed thereafter, and we were both hindered by so many journeys, the commentary could not be completed by the author while he lived.

It seemed, however, to be the opinion of many that it is better for it to be published mutilated than to be suppressed entirely.

For they said that these very fragments would be welcome to many, as they excellently illustrate the entire first Epistle and three chapters of the second in this very brevity. Those who are intelligent know, however, that among all of Paul's Epistles, those which were written to the Corinthians, and especially the first, are more obscure due to the variety of the causes he treats and the questions upon which Paul pronounces, and that they require a learned exposition. Although I confess that this can be taken from the most learned lucubrations of others, yet I would dare to affirm that the pious reader will be helped not a little by the reading of this writing toward a more correct understanding of Paul's disputations and responses, and if nothing else, he will certainly approve of the brevity of this commentary, which cuts off all idle and untimely declamations.

How necessary and useful the reading of the Epistle, especially the first to the Corinthians, is to the pious at this time, is experienced by those who, looking upon this most sad face of the Church, are moved with serious grief and seek mitigation for their sorrow from the word of God.

For who is there, endowed with a sound mind, to whom both religion and eternal salvation are a care, who would not shudder, looking upon these present wounds and dangers of the Church? For to say nothing now of the enemies of the Son of God, the Turks and others, who openly wage war against the Church and threaten its destruction: in that assembly which professes the name of Christ and bears the title of Church, the greatest and most powerful part, flourishing in wisdom, dignity, wealth, and the glory of ordinary succession, most bitterly opposes the pure doctrine of the Gospel, and since it is polluted with manifold idolatry, it cannot bear to have its impiety taxed, so that it strives to stabilize it by the exquisite cruelty of punishments, and to destroy utterly the true understanding of heavenly doctrine, nay, to wrest from the hands of the pious every use of the prophetic and apostolic writings.

By these persecutors of the truth, who falsely arrogate to themselves the title of Church, the remaining small multitude is oppressed, which embraces the uncorrupted voice of God and retains the legitimate use of the Sacraments, itself unarmed, weak, dispersed, yet having its little nests and defenders somewhere. Where and under whom it may celebrate safe gatherings in public, which, since it is truly the Church and the people of God, in whom there are undoubtedly many who are reborn, and the dwellings of God, destined to live with Him in eternal communion, yet the whole assembly is so deformed by so many and such great confusions and scandals that it appears to be nothing less than what it professes.

For if you look at the teachers, you see some corrupting doctrine through ambition, or emulation, or curiosity, and boldly spreading false dogmas, or stubbornly defending them; some sowing and fostering unnecessary conflicts with implacable hatreds; some bending, feigning, and refashioning religion to the whim and desires of Lords or assemblies, whose favor they value more than the glory of God and the propagation of the truth; and some, indeed, destroying again by the license of morals and the turpitude of life all that they had truly built up by teaching.

These blemishes, seen in the order of those who profess heavenly doctrine, cannot but sadden the pious and render many more alienated from the study of the Gospel.

Again, if you turn your eyes to the hearers, you will see the most foul abuse of religion and Christian liberty, the contempt and neglect of the holy ministry, the profanity of disputations, the plundering of the goods of the Church, the ingratitude toward faithful ministers of the Word, the relaxation of discipline, the unbridled stubbornness of youth, and a crop of other vices growing more abundant every day, which, when one looks upon these evils, one cannot but be vehemently struck in spirit, and sometimes shaken by the waves of doubt, wondering whether this assembly can be a Church, in which there are so many distractions, confusions, and enormous vices.

This pain is increased for the pious when they see that by these scandals and distractions of the true Church, the Papists are confirmed and strengthened on one side, so that they may seize pretexts from them, by which they excuse their own parricides, and cover their own Idolomania more speciously, and draw back some weak ones from the acknowledged truth to their own impiety.

On the other side, the fanatical spirits and sectarians, so that they may more effectively spread their pestiferous errors and sell them more plausibly to the common people, by pointing out the vices, dissensions, and profanity of this party, which alone boasts of the possession of uncorrupted doctrine.

In this miserable appearance, and the extreme deformity of the Church in this last old age of the world, when the minds of the pious are undoubtedly horribly tormented, they must be fortified with true consolations, so that they may also consider the causes whence these evils arise, lest they impute them to the Word of God and its most holy ministry, but believe them to be cast upon the Church by the devil through men who are fickle, proud, curious, profane, and secure.

Then let them know that the Son of God, and his Apostles themselves, predicted these very evils, and indeed warned more cumulatively that they were to come about the last times of the world, and yet at the same time promised the perpetuity of the Church, against which no gates of hell shall prevail.

But the most effective remedy, in my judgment, against these doubts about the Church, arising from the sight of present confusions and evils, is taken from the writings of the Apostles and especially Paul, who depicts the Churches of his own time in such a way that it is clear they were not only not without infirmity and blemishes, but were also deformed by foul scandals and confusions.

For, to say nothing now of the Churches of the Galatians, which after the departure of the divine Paul, from whom they had received the sincere doctrine of the Gospel, had been so troubled by Pseudo-apostles, and were falling away entirely to Jewish superstition, and were persuaded that the observation of the law and ceremonies was so necessary that without it, however much one believed in the Son of God, one could not attain salvation: in the Corinthian Church, in which for so long both Paul and Apollos, and other men outstanding in spirit and piety, had sincerely taught the Gospel, what enormities, what foul scandals existed, both Epistles written to the Corinthians clearly show.

For from the responses of Paul it appears that even among the teachers there were emulations and contentions about eminence, which others wished to be valued by the dignity of the Preceptors, that is, the Apostles, by whom each had been instructed, and to whom they had been familiar: others, because of the excellence of the gifts with which they had been adorned, were either preferred to others by the hearers, or wished themselves to be preferred, which emulations among the teachers, as happens, were followed by factions, schisms, quarrels, mutual condemnations, and hostile hatreds among the hearers.

And when they began to dispute more acutely about doctrine than to embrace it seriously with true faith, and to show it effective by the pious governance of morals and the study of virtues, they loosened the reins to their desires; some, according to the customs and affections and artifices of the Heathens, litigated before heathen judges; some relapsed into the previously accustomed obscene pleasures of the body: some were present at heathen sacrifices and feasts, with grave offense to weak Christians, and confirmation of heathen idolatry; some, abusing Christian liberty, believed themselves so loosed from all bonds of the law that they thought it permissible for them to have their stepmother as their wife: some, out of superstition, fled from marriage altogether, as a forbidden kind of life; some thought they ought to abstain entirely from their spouses in marriage; some persuaded others to desert spouses who did not agree on religion, and to marry others from the number of believers.

There was immoderate curiosity in others, abolishing now this, now that rite, which nature however had sanctioned, and instituting something new; the profanation of the most holy Supper of the Lord had invaded the Church, and the abuse was so great that it brought down public punishments: some preferred to use the variety of spiritual gifts for ostentation, and for the contempt and oppression of other mediocre ones, rather than for the edification and utility of the hearers: some light and profane minds had proceeded to such a pitch of audacity that they attempted to undermine the foundation of our faith in a way, and disputed that the promised resurrection of the dead was to be understood allegorically. to be about the amendment of morals, and conversion in this life, and that one should not expect a true resurrection of these bodies, reduced to ashes, for eternal life and communion with God.

That these errors and vices of that Church were indeed neither small nor trivial, but so great that they vehemently disturbed Paul and many other pious men, and most foully deformed the Church, and not a little hindered the course of the Gospel, is apparent from the responses of Paul, who with such spirit, emotion, and vehemence even censures and condemns, and strives to correct those scandals.

If, therefore, that first Church, which had the Apostles themselves as Doctors, called immediately by Christ, and confirming the certainty of both their doctrine and their vocation by the testimonies of inimitable miracles, could not be immune and free from these enormous and foul errors and scandals, which undoubtedly disturbed and miserably tormented the souls of the pious: with what face do either the assenters to the Pontiffs, or the fanatical error-mongers among us, who truly can boast by the benefit of God that the incorrupt doctrine of the Gospel sounds in our temples and schools, dare to seek and demand such a Church as consists of mere angels, has no stain, no infirmity, no dissensions, no disputes, no lapses and other scandals, when they know that the author of these evils is the devil, the father of lies, dissensions, murders, and horrible lapses, and that he has not yet been utterly destroyed, nor does he sleep or rest, but goes about like a roaring and famished lion, and indeed rages more furiously around this last age of the world, sensing that the time of judgment is approaching, and is full of eternal damnation and the punishment of inestimable and infinitely increasing torments. Let them also know that the nature of men after the fall is miserably corrupted, and with the age of the world itself having become more languid to the extreme, it is now more easily driven by devils to curiosity, ambition, envy, pride, the desire for vengeance, hatreds, and profanity, from which affections arise then all those plagues by which we experience the Church to be disturbed, the course and efficacy of the Gospel to be hindered, the weak to be alienated, and even the pious and strong to be dismayed and tormented.

We do not patronize errors, vices, and scandals, whose authors we know must undergo grave judgment and pay horrible penalties, according to the most grave warning of Christ, Matt. 18: Woe to that man by whom the scandal comes. And Paul in Gal. 5: He who disturbs you shall bear the judgment, whoever he is. But we say with Christ nevertheless: It is necessary that scandals come, which in Luke ch. 17 is said with greater vehemence: It is impossible that scandals should not come.

And Paul depicts the men of the present age with illustrious and true, as experience testifies, but very sad colors, 2 Tim. 3, when he warns his Timothy: Know this, that in the last days grievous times shall come. For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy, without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good, traitors, heady, highminded, lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God; having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof.

That Paul speaks of those who are in the Church, and expressly includes the Doctors as well, is manifest from the fact that he says there are some among them who creep into houses under the pretext of communicating doctrine, and especially insinuate themselves into women in the gynaecea, and into the houses of other powerful men, whose minds, when they have once occupied them with false doctrine, they understand afterwards that they will also easily have the zeal and defense of their husbands.

Since such are the men of this last age of the world, and since the fury of the devil has erupted to extreme bitterness, it should seem strange to no one that scandals, dissensions, and other foul crimes exist where the purer doctrine of the Gospel is taught, which the devil hates and desires to be extinguished, since things similar to these, or certainly not much lighter, existed in the times of the Apostles in the first Church, that more sedate, and firmer and more vigorous age of the world, which we might oppose both to the fanatical spirits of the Anabaptists and Stenckfeldians, and to the perfidious apostates who now kiss the feet of the Pontiff (indignation had almost expressed another word to me), whose entire power and dignity they previously publicly condemned from the pulpit in these very Churches, and cursed with dire imprecations.

Because of this necessary consolation, the reading of both the Epistles of Paul to the Corinthians and also of this little commentary, which contains most grave admonitions concerning many parts of heavenly doctrine, ought to be most commendable and welcome to the pious at this time, which is not only to be expected, but I doubt not that pious and learned men will testify, and from this very writing, however brief, will both recognize and admire the author's piety, the felicity of his genius, the rectitude of his judgment, the constancy of his confession, his kindness and facility in communicating sound doctrine, and his other immense gifts, by which he shone while alive, and served the Church of God usefully, seeking nothing for himself, courting no favors of Kings and potentates, or the applause of the crowd, or the accession of honors, or heaps of wealth—of which virtues he has left very many most trustworthy witnesses of every rank, among whom it has seemed fitting especially to name your Highness, Most Illustrious Prince, who always loved Master Philippus, of whom I now speak, perhaps (as I suppose) unknown to you by face, with a sincere and constant love, on account of admiration for his gifts and the excellence of his virtues; of which an eyewitness (αὐτόπτης), and a most trustworthy informant to your Highness beyond innumerable others, could be, and without doubt was, Doctor Huldericus Sizingerus, your Highness's Chancellor—a man most excellent in learning, virtue, prudence, and faithfulness. For this reason I especially wished to offer this little book of Master Philippus to your Highness, so that, having read it through, and having come to know his sincerity in doctrine and his faithfulness in communicating it, you might take up the patronage of this so great a man, who, as if he had been scourged too little by his own foster-sons and pupils while he lived, cannot even find rest now that he is dead: for some of those whom he long nourished at his own table, with whom he shared not only doctrine publicly but also privately whatever counsels and secrets he had and could give, to whom he would even have given his own heart, torn from his breast, had it been possible, now rage against his bloodless body in the tomb, with such zeal for vengeance and such bitterness, that I believe, if the wretched and now putrefying corpse of Philippus were set before them, they would rush upon it with their teeth like dogs, and tear his flesh to pieces. For what else can you think, if you read the writing which a certain man recently spread among the people for the sake of defending his own doctrine and fame, as he wishes to appear? Against what injury, indeed, does he defend himself? Or what injury to a most faithful Teacher, nay, a most affectionate [εὐστοργοτάτου] and kind Father, can be so atrocious that it deserves such bitterness, that his dead corpse, almost dug up from the tomb, should be so cruelly lacerated? Philippus wrote, having been secretly asked for counsel by the Prince Elector, under whose dominion he was born, a few things about the Lord's Supper, more to persuade how the quarrels that had arisen about it at Heidelberg, and were publicly heaped up from the pulpit by the mutual insults of the preachers, might be quieted and settled, than to pronounce on the controversy itself, indicating a form of speaking from Paul, which it would be safest to use in the meantime, until it should be decided about the whole controversy in a Synod.

In that little page written to one person, written secretly, not written for this, that it should be published, and yet published against the will of the author, and indeed only after his death, mention is made of D. Heshusius, a little too ungraciously, such that his authority is postponed to the highest and most ancient writers in the Church. This is that injury, this deed of the Father so atrocious, that it utterly abolishes and extinguishes the memory of all benefits received, privately and publicly bestowed, and of all virtues, and inflames the mind with such a desire for vengeance, that it cannot be satisfied in this way of most atrocious and contumelious defense. But if he did not wish to have regard for his own reputation, which it is certain is somewhat diminished among the intelligent by this great harshness, which he used against the dead, against one who deserved so well, against a Teacher, nay, a parent: it was most equitable to spare his most honest and now most afflicted family, by whom he was affected with many benefits, to spare this School, dwelling in most bitter grief on account of its bereavement, to spare the wretched youth, languishing with desire for their lost rector of studies, to spare the Church and posterity, and finally to spare God, whom Philippus served with a good conscience, so as not to deform the doctrine, and the morals and actions of this man, as if he had played the knave in heavenly doctrine, and had written blasphemies, or spoken against the Son of God, nor to tear him apart with other insults, resting in the sepulcher, nay, in the bosom and embrace of the Son of God, the judge and avenger of all crimes, and especially of ingratitude, enjoying the joyful sight and conversation of God.

Whether this be the Spirit of God, to debauch in such great bitterness, let others judge. Paul, 2 Timothy 2, certainly instructs his ministers otherwise, when he says: "And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient, in meekness instructing those that oppose themselves," etc.

But I hope that your Highness and all others who are preeminent in piety, modesty, prudence, and virtue, who are lovers of letters, students of truth, and concerned for posterity, and who are solicitous for the conservation and propagation of uncorrupted doctrine, will not be moved by the invectives of such a few, so as to cease to love, magnify, and follow with grateful memory this man, whom so many useful monuments, so many labors exhausted for the sake of public utility, such a harmony and constancy of the highest virtues, and so many merits toward many privately and all publicly have commended to us.

Indeed, I hope that this bitterness of theirs will provide many with a reason to value him more, to study his writings more diligently, and to separate themselves as far as possible from this ungrateful cohort.

I hope that God himself will also one day bear witness to the truth, when he will examine with fire what each of the builders has built upon the solid foundation, which is our only Lord Jesus Christ, and him crucified, and resurrected, and reigning at the right hand of the Father, who alone gives suitable and salutary ministers, and does not allow their labors to be in vain, nor ever to be dissolved, because it is from him.

We know that Philip built upon this foundation, together with Luther and after Luther, in good faith, an entire Body of doctrine, with a good and clear method, and that he strove to avoid all useless and dangerous disputations, and also abstained by his own counsel from unnecessary flagellations and condemnations of others, and at the same time illustrated with writings and voice all the remaining arts which are necessary for the explanation of heavenly doctrine.

Let these lucubrations be compared with the papers of others who seem to themselves to be wiser than the rest, and to have labored and accomplished the most in the Church, but who are now occupied with how they may carp at the writings of this man, and render them suspect and hateful to others, and the difference will truly be seen to be far more evident than that which is between gold and stubble, which these people, however, claim are built upon the same foundation, and they wish them to be equal to the gold of Luther and far preferred to the silver of Philip.

But as it has been said, fire will test the work of each one, on that day when the Lord will judge the structure of his workmen, which time modest men should patiently await, and not rashly and precipitately applaud the pompous and artificially painted clamors of those people, which are disguised with a wonderful zeal for defending the truth.

Therefore, I send to you, most Illustrious Prince Palatine, this little book to be joined to the other useful monuments of Philip, with this intention: that just as you once embraced Philip with your own judgment, as a minister of God and a useful instrument, with a love that was not courtly, and loved him even to the end, so you may also defend and protect his fame and authority, even now that he is dead, against the unworthy bites of such men.

Furthermore, I also commend to your Highness the most honorable family of this man, which, twice bereaved this year, has received the most grievous causes of double mourning in a short time, that is, in an interval of nine months, with the death of a man most preeminent in wisdom, erudition, and virtue, Lord D.

Georgius Sabinus, son-in-law of Lord Philip and father of many children, to whom, just as to his father-in-law, he left very little of his own, beyond the fame of erudition and virtue, and monuments of excellence of genius, and the studies of good men, for whose orphans it is most equitable that the munificence of princes should provide, which God will compensate with most generous rewards, as Syracides testifies: Be merciful to orphans as a father, and for a man to their mother, and you will be as a son of the Most High, and he will love you more than your mother.

To that God who has been revealed by the most true and certain testimonies, the eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the creator and preserver of the human race, I humbly commend your Highness with all your own, and I wish from my heart that this coming year may be happy and tranquil.

Given at Wittenberg, on the Kalends of January, in the year 1561.

ARGUMENT AND BRIEF EXPLANATION OF THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS, WRITTEN BY PHILIP MELANCHTHON.

The First Epistle to the Corinthians is not one continuous disputation, like the Epistle to the Romans, but gathers together many dissimilar matters: the whole body, however, pertains to the Persuasive genus, because there are rebukes, admonitions, and precepts concerning various affairs, and here and there are interspersed sermons, which are doctrines pertaining to the Didactic genus.

But in order that Paul's purpose may be understood, the occasion for writing should first be considered.

When he had left the Church gathered in Corinth, rightly instructed in the whole doctrine of the Gospel, concerning the benefits of the Son of God, concerning faith, concerning the use of liberty, concerning marriage, concerning the Sacraments, concerning the resurrection of the dead, and concerning other articles, and many there excelled in gifts: immediately there, as in a Greek city, Pride and Curiosity gave birth to dissensions.

Some, baptized by others, retained some of their rites, from whom they had been baptized.

Others, more bashful, were unwilling to go when invited to their Gentile kinsmen, when there were customary gatherings of families, in which they used to sacrifice first, and afterwards eat of the victim.

Others, more free, would go: one took so much liberty for himself that he took his stepmother.

Some instituted a private Lord's Supper, neglecting the common one.

Some, elated by the gift of tongues, despised others, and among these very ones, who were adorned with this gift, there were self-loves (φιλαυτίαι) and rivalries.

Some, bold and curious, disputed against the resurrection of the dead.

Such was the confusion of that time, certainly not light, nor less than many have been in our own time.

And yet all these Corinthians were greatly puffed up with a persuasion of holiness, and were pleased with themselves, admired themselves, and judged themselves to be inspired by the Holy Spirit, when yet there was much vanity, pride, Greek levity, and curiosity in them.

They had returned to these vices, even though they had had the Holy Spirit, and some still had the beginnings, which, however, they were gradually extinguishing, as they indulged their own affections and follies.

This age has seen many similar examples, therefore these things are easy to understand.

Paul, therefore, in the first chapter, at the beginning, rebukes the hearers because they are stirring up dissensions.

Then, in order to pull up the root of the dissensions, he reprehends the admiration of one's own wisdom, and curiosity, peculiar to light minds, as if he were now preaching to Servetus, Campanus, and the like.

He therefore weaves in this common topic: One must not judge of God from human wisdom, but minds must be recalled within this boundary, namely, to the Word, in which God has revealed Himself, and let not minds wander outside this boundary with our speculations, and play at their own discretion.

God in His immense mercy revealed Himself, gave the Gospel, instituted the ministry of the Gospel; God willed that it be heard, and that we be enclosed within it.

Having thus entered into this topic, he preaches what is the principal and necessary doctrine, and adds the doctrine concerning the dignity of the ministry.

There is, therefore, a most grave sermon against human wisdom in the first and second chapters, recalling us to the Word of God and divine revelations.

How great the necessity of this precept is, the rude and unskilled do not consider.

But the petulance of the human mind is horrendous, which, how audaciously it fashions opinions about God and worship, the whole history of the world from the very first beginnings of idols shows.

Human minds seek neat opinions, and those congruent with reason, and they flee the absurd, as Samosatenus, Mahomet, and Pelagius did.

Others, raging in another way, fashion monstrous things, as those who slaughtered human victims, the Egyptians who worshipped serpents and cats, the Manichaeans who fashioned two eternal, warring deities.

Paul therefore forbids the generating of doctrine about God from one's own imaginations, and leads us to the Gospel, and teaches that God must be acknowledged just as He has revealed Himself, and that in every thought and invocation this God must be looked upon, who revealed Himself by giving this Gospel and sending His Son, just as the Son Himself says: He who sees me, sees also the Father. In the third chapter, he first says that ministers teach the same Gospel, and that God is equally effective through the voice of the Gospel, in whatever language it may sound.

He therefore condemns the arrogance of those who prefer themselves to others, as if their ministry were more effective than that of others, as the Pontiffs invented regarding indulgences, that they remit more sins than others, or indeed that they lead souls out of purgatory.

At the same time, however, this passage testifies that God is effective through the evangelical ministry, as is said in Rom. 1: The Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes. Afterwards, he adds a precept about retaining the principal doctrine of the Gospel, and hands down a very useful rule: The foundation must be retained, that is, the articles of faith, and the Church of God is there, where the foundation is retained.

Meanwhile, however, in this infirmity of men, some teach more purely, others less so. For which reason all ages in this life retain some flaws, that is, some inconvenient opinions. This is the meaning of these words: No other foundation can be laid than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ.

But another builds upon the foundation gold, silver, gems, another wood, stubble etc., that is, one illuminates the articles of faith with true and clear doctrine, says why the Son of God is called λόγος (the Word), what original sin is, what the difference is between the Law and the Promises, how the remission of sins is given to man, what Grace is, what Faith is, what works are pleasing to God, what the differences are between reigning and non-reigning sin.

Others, however, build stubble upon the foundation, just as writers immediately in the beginning obscured the doctrine of the Justice of faith, and increased ceremonies, and bound them to be peculiar cults, were harsher than they ought to have been in commanding celibacy, and mixed in some still modest invocation of the dead: Pray for me, Saint Peter.

Many such stubble [opinions] are forgiven in all ages to those who retain the foundation. A useful admonition is therefore proposed in this chapter, namely, that we may know where the Church is, namely, where the foundation is retained.

Nor are they members of the Church who stubbornly defend idols, and stubbornly condemn any article of faith. Then, so that we may know that some inconvenient opinions remain in the true Church, which are to be amended by the more learned, and that weak members are not to be condemned on account of them, if only they allow themselves to be taught, and if stubbornness is absent. Therefore he says: The day will declare it, namely, not only of the final judgment, but at any time, when doctrine is illuminated, as now the day declares the invocation of the dead to be false and a fabrication.

And what he adds: To be revealed in fire, signifies temptations, as Bernard and Bonaventure learn in true temptation to acquiesce in the trust of the Son of God, not in their own works. Thus fire, that is, temptations and many struggles, purge and restore doctrine. In the same third chapter after the middle, when he says: Do you not know that you are the temple of God? he returns to the extenuation of human wisdom in judging the will of God, and sharply rebukes those swelling with the persuasion of wisdom, who, namely, by human judgment wish to embrace what is neat and flee what is absurd.

But what is more absurd to human judgment than that the Son of God should be crucified? Wherefore also innumerable men have abhorred the Gospel, moved by this absurdity, which many have also agitated in their writings, such as Lucian, Julian, and others. Therefore Paul says here: Since you are the temple of God, in which, namely, the Holy Spirit already dwells with true light, see that you do not extinguish this light by bringing in human opinions, and thus corrupt the temple of God, just as Julian, casting away true doctrine, became an organ of the devil from being a temple of God.

How many today fall away from the Gospel, moved by human wisdom either in the judgment of dogmas or on account of scandals.

It is human wisdom when they argue that nothing should be changed in the rite of the Mass, because the people are held by this cult, and if it is lost, the people will become entirely profane.

It is human wisdom that some command peace to be preferred to true doctrine, and they use this cause as a pretext: Because if there are wars, devastations will follow, in which doctrine will be destroyed. And it would be better that some gaudy religion be retained than none at all. These human counsels all fight against the command of God: You shall have no other gods.

How great are the frenzies of many today, who invent reconciliations of dogmas or 'ἐπιεικείας' (moderations), and corrupt the truth? Finally, daily examples are in sight for all ages. For there are many and horrible sins of human wisdom, not judging rightly concerning God. Therefore Paul preaches here so harshly against it, and commands those who seem wise to themselves in this world, that is, following the judgments of human reason, to become fools, that is, to acknowledge that this wisdom is not the wisdom of the Gospel: but that one must judge concerning the essence and will of God from His own revelation, and as he writes to the same Corinthians in the second Epistle, that it is necessary for reason to be led captive to obey Christ.

Latin:

COMMENTARIUS IN EPIST.

PAULI AD CORINTHIOS.

Hunc commentarium Melanthon anno 1551. scripsit et dedit Paulo Ebero, discipulo suo ac collegae, ut eum privatim auditoribus suis dictaret, quibus succisivis horis dierum festorum explicationem grammaticam epistolarum Pauli dare solebat. — Post obitum Melanthonis Eberus hunc commentarium edidit, eumque Wolfgango Comiti Palatino dicavit.

Prodiit igitur: „Brevis et utilis Commentarius in priorem epistolam Pauli ad Corinthios, et in aliquot capita secundae, scriptus a Philippo Melanchone. Witeb. 1561. 1 Alph. 8.“ — Legitur in opp. Melanth. Witeberg. T. IV. p. 210. Clarissimo Principi ac Domino, D. Wolfgango Comiti Palatino ad Rhenum, Duci Bavariae, Comiti Valentiae et Bipontii. Domino suo clementissimo: Paulus Eberus Kittinghensis, Pastor Ecclesiae Vitebergensis, S. D. Diu dubitavi, utrum hunc commentariolum Epistolae ad Corinthios, quem Reverendus et incomparabilis virtutis et eruditionis vir Dominus Philippus Melanthon, Praeceptor noster et Pater piae memoriae, mihi ante annos decem post susceptam domi meae explicationem Grammaticam Epistolarum Pauli, succisivis horis dierum Festorum in hunc usum scripsit, ut eum privatim auditoribus meis dictarem, quod feci, in publicum emitterem: an vero prorsus supprimerem et occultarem, cum et exilior sit, quam qui requirentibus prolixas et declamatorias singulorum dictorum enarrationes, satisfacere queat, et praeterea etiam mutilus sit, vix tria secundae Epistolae capita explicans.

Praecipuam vero dubitandi causam mihi praebuit huius seculi perversitas, quae eo morositatis et iniquitatis processit tandem, ut nihil tam sincere scribi aut dici fere iam possit, quod non in aliquorum sciolorum reprehensionem, saepe etiam condemnationem incurrat, quae sane licentia, ipsa impunitate indies vires acquirens, imo ab aliquibus non modo cum applausu excepta, verum etiam mercede et praemiis alicubi confirmata, magnum adhuc malum dabit Ecclesiae, si non iam ante tristissimum, et propemodum insanabile vulnus eidem inflixit.

Bonos certe, et rixandi studio alienos merito absterret, ne quid suarum lucubrationum cum tanto periculo publice communicent, quae tamen plus fortassis et doctrinae et consolationis continerent, quam ista pugnacia et mordacia quorundam scripta, quae in alios tantum impetum vehementem faciunt, et alienas sententias omni conatu evertere nituntur: de veris autem Fundamentis, et quid de re integra firmiter sentiendum sit, aut nihil aut parum docent, ex quibus si convicia et alia exacerbissimis invectivis, vel scurrarum potius circulis accersita pigmenta sustuleris, nuda ea et inania prorsus deprehendes.

Haec me solicitudo, et metus talium reprehensionum hactenus cunctantiorem fecit ad editionem huius utilis scripti, quem tamen tandem vicit et excussit mihi assidua flagitatio multorum piorum et eruditorum hominum, qui hunc commentarium perlegerant, obiurgantium me, quod studio vitandi iniquorum iniustas et malitiosas cavillationes, quas neque effugere quisquam quantusvis cautus unquam potuisset, neque sibi conscius recti curare deberet, pergerem pietatis et veritatis amantes viros fraudare lectione huius du expetiti et expectati Commentarii, qui etsi brevis esset, tamen res praecipuas ita perspicue explicaret, ut inter aliorum eruditorum hominum prolixiores et accuratiores commentarios etiam suum locum et suam laudem haud dubie apud intelligentes et recte iudicantes sit habiturus.

Talibus et pluribus aliis argumentis impulsus sum, ut neglectis eorum incursationibus, qui alienis scriptis hoc infelici seculo quasi ἐφεδρεύοντες, obtrectatione praestantiorum qualicunque, nomen sibi et applausum quaerunt, hoc tempore hunc quamvis imperfectum commentariolum publicarem, quod sane factum fuisset et tempestivius et tutius, et utilius adhuc ipso Philippo vivente, cuius praesentis autoritas efficacius commendare hoc scriptum Lectori potuisset.

Neque ego quidem animadverti unquam, ipsum abhorrere ab editione huius sui operis. Sed quia mihi semper spes erat, fore, ut id, quod explicationi secundae Epistolae adhuc deest, aliquando ab autore adiiceretur, distuli consulto editionem: Verum cum, ut supra dictum est, Philippus mihi privatim explicanti aliquibus Epistolas Paulinas, hanc scriptionem instituisset, et haec privata exercitia nostra, sicut et publicas operas, interturbasset lues pestilis 1552. cogens nos Torgam secedere, talia postea tempora et tam inquieta consecuta sunt, tot profectionibus partim ipse, partim ambo impediti fuimus, ut commentarius ab autore, dum vixit, compleri nequiverit.

Visum tamen est plurimis consultum, ut potius mutilus edatur, quam prorsus supprimatur.

Fore enim aiebant haec ipsa fragmenta grata multis, quae priorem Epistolam totam, et secundae tria capita in hac ipsa brevitate egregie illustrent. Sciunt autem intelligentes, inter omnes Pauli Epistolas, has quae ad Corinthios scriptae sunt, ac praesertim priorem, propter causarum quas tractat, et quaestionum de quibus pronunciat Paulus, varietatem, obscuriores esse, et requirere eruditam enarrationem, quam etsi fateor ex aliorum doctissimis lucubrationibus sumi posse, tamen affirmare ausim, pium lectorem etiam huius scripti lectione ad rectius intelligendas Pauli disputationes et responsiones nonnihil adiutum iri, et si nihil aliud, certe vel brevitatem huius commentarii, omnes otiosas, ac intempestivas declamationes praecidentem, probaturum esse.

Quam autem sic hoc tempore piis necessaria et utilis lectio Epistolae praesertim prioris ad Corinthios, experiuntur illi, qui intuentes hanc tristissimam faciem Ecclesiae, serio dolore commoventur, et suae moestitiae ex verbo Dei mitigationem quaerunt.

Quis vero est sana mente praeditus, cui et religio et aeterna salus curae est, qui non cohorrescat, aspiciens haec praesentia vulnera et pericula Ecclesiae? Ut enim nihil iam dicamus de hostibus Filii Dei, Turcis et aliis, qui ex professo Ecclesiae bellum inferunt, et excidium minantur: in eo coetu, qui Christi nomen profitetur, et titulum Ecclesiae gerit, maxima et potentissima pars, florens sapientia, dignitate, opibus, et gloria ordinariae successionis, purae doctrinae Evangelii acerrime adversatur, et cum sit polluta multiplici idolatria, adeo ferre non potest taxari suam impietatem, ut exquisita suppliciorum immanitate eam stabilire, et delere funditus verum intellectum doctrinae coelestis, imo omnem usum propheticorum et apostolicorum scriptorum piis ex manibus extorquere conetur.

Ab his persecutoribus veritatis, falso sibi titulum Ecclesiae arrogantibus, premitur reliqua exigua multitudo, quae vocem Dei incorruptam amplectitur, et legitimum Sacramentorum usum retinet, ipsa inermis, imbecilla, dispersa, alicubi tamen nidulos suos et defensores habens, Ubi et sub quibus tutos congressus in publico celebret, quae cum vere sit Ecclesia et populus Dei, in quo haud dubie multi sunt renati, et domicilia Dei, cum ipso victuri in aeterna consuetudine, tamen tot et tantis confusionibus et scandalis deformatur totus coetus, ut nihil videatur minus esse, quam quod profitetur.

Nam si ad docentes respicias, videas quosdam vel ambitione, vel aemulatione, vel curiositate doctrinam corrumpere, et falsa dogmata audacter spargere, aut pertinaciter tueri, aliquos non necessaria certamina serere et fovere implacabilibus odiis, Aliquos religionem inflectere, fingere ac refingere ad nutum et cupiditates vel Dominorum, vel coetuum, quorum gratiam pluris faciunt, quam gloriam Dei et veritatis propagationem, Aliquos vero universum id, quod vere docendo extruxerunt, morum licentia, et turpitudine vitae rursus destruere.

Hi naevi conspecti in ordine profitentium doctrinam coelestem, non possunt non contristare pios, et multos ab Evangelii studio reddere alieniores.

Rursus si ad auditores oculos convertas, videbis religionis et libertatis Christianae foedissimum abusum, contemptum et neglectum sancti ministerii, disputationum profanitatem, direptionem bonorum Ecclesiae, ingratitudinem erga fideles ministros Verbi, disciplinae laxationem, effrenem contumaciam iuventutis, et aliorum vitiorum segetem indies uberrimam succrescentem, quae mala intuens, non potest non vehementer animo percelli, et interdum quassari fluctibus dubitationum, ambigens, an hic coetus possit esse Ecclesia, in quo tantum sic distractionum, confusionum, et enormium vitiorum.

Augetur hic dolor piis, cum vident his scandalis et distractionibus verae Ecclesiae confirmari et roborari in una parte Pontificios, ut inde praetextus arripiant, quibus et parricidia sua excusent, et Idolomaniam suam speciosius tegant, et aliquos imbecilles ab agnita veritate ad suam impietatem retrahant.

In altera parte fanaticos spiritus, et sectarios, ut suos errores pestiferos spargere efficacius et venditare vulgo plausibilius possint, monstratis vitiis, dissidiis, et profanitate huius partis, quae de possessione incorruptae doctrinae sola gloriatur.

Hac miserabili specie, et summa deformitate Ecclesiae in hac postrema senecta mundi, cum piorum animi haud dubie horribiliter excrucientur, muniendi sunt veris consolationibus, ut et causas considerent, unde haec mala existant, ne ea verbo Dei et sanctissimo ministerio illius imputent, sed credant aspergi Ecclesiae a diabolo per homines leves, superbos, curiosos, profanos et securos.

Deinde sciant filium Dei, et ipsius Apostolos, haec ipsa mala praedixisse, et quidem ventura cumulatius praemonuisse circa postrema tempora mundi, et tamen simul promisisse perpetuitatem Ecclesiae, adversus quam nullae portae inferorum sint praevaliturae.

Omnium autem efficacissimum, meo quidem iudicio, remedium adversus has dubitationes de Ecclesia, ortas ex conspectu praesentium confusionum et malorum, sumitur ex Apostolorum ac praecipue Pauli scriptis, ita pingentis sui temporis Ecclesias, ut constet eas non modo sine infirmitate et naevis non fuisse, sed etiam deformatas fuisse tetris scandalis et confusionibus.

Ut enim nunc nihil dicam de Ecclesiis Galatarum, quae post discessum divi Pauli, a quo sinceram Evangelii doctrinam acceperant, a Pseudoapostolis ita turbatae fuerant, et totae ad Iudaicam superstitionem reciderent, et persuasae essent, legis ac ceremoniarum observationem ita necessariam esse, ut sine illa, quantumvis credens in filium Dei, salutem consequi non posset: in Ecclesia Corinthiaca, in qua tamdiu et Paulus et Apollos, et alii praestantes spiritu et pietate viri, Evangelium sincere docuerant, quantae enormitates, quam foeda scandala extiterint, ambae Epistolae ad Corinthios scriptae perspicue ostendunt.

Nam ex responsis Pauli apparet, et inter doctores fuisse aemulationes et certamina de eminentia, quam alii aestimari volebant a Praeceptorum, hoc est, Apostolorum dignitate, a quibus singuli instituti, et quibus familiares fuerant: alii propter donorum excellentiam, quibus ornati fuerant, caeteris vel praeferebantur ab auditoribus, vel ipsi sese anteferri volebant, quas aemulationes inter doctores, ut fit, sequebantur factiones, schismata, rixae, mutuae condemnationes, et hostilia odia in auditoribus.

Cumque inciperent magis acute disputare de doctrina, quam eam vera fide serio amplecti, et morum pia gubernatione et virtutum studio efficacem ostendere, laxabant frenos cupiditatibus, aliqui more et affectibus et artificiis Ethnicorum litigabant coram iudicibus ethnicis, relabebantur aliqui ad consuetas prius corporis voluptates obscoenas: aderant aliqui sacrificiis et epulis ethnicis, cum gravi offensione imbecillium Christianorum, et confirmatione idolatriae ethnicae, aliqui abutentes libertate Christiana, ita se omnibus legis vinculis solutum credebat, ut putaret sibi licere novercam suam uxorem habere: aliqui superstitione coniugium prorsus fugiebant, tanquam vitae genus prohibitum, aliqui in matrimonio abstinendum sibi prorsus a coniugibus esse censebant, aliqui coniuges de religione non consentientes deserere, et alias ducere ex numero credentium suadebant.

Erat curiositas in aliis immodica, iam hunc, iam alium ritum, quem natura tamen sanxerat, abolens, et novi aliquid instituens, invaserat in Ecclesiam Coenae sacratissimae Domini profanatio, et abusus tantus, ut poenas publicas accerseret: aliqui donorum spiritualium varietate ad ostentationem, et aliorum mediocrium contemptum et oppressionem uti malebant, quam ad aedificationem et utilitatem auditorum: aliqua levia et profana ingenia eo audaciae processerant, ut fundamentum quodammodo fidei nostrae subruere conarententur, et disputarent resurrectionem mortuorum promissam, allegorice intelligendam. esse de emendatione morum, et conversione in hac vita, non esse expectandam veram resuscitationem horum corporum, in cineres redactorum, ad aeternam vitam et consuetudinem cum Deo.

Haec profecto et errata et vitia illius Ecclesiae nec parva, nec frivola, sed tanta fuisse, ut et Paulum multosque alios pios vehementer conturbarint, et Ecclesiam foedissime deformarint, et Evangelii cursum non parum impedierint, apparet ex responsionibus Pauli, tanto spiritu, commotione, vehementia etiam taxantis et damnantis, et corrigere studentis illa scandala.

Si igitur illa prima Ecclesia, quae Doctores habuit ipsos Apostolos, immediate a Christo vocatos, et miraculorum inimitabilium testimoniis certitudinem et doctrina suae et vocationis confirmantes, non potuit esse immunis et libera ab enormibus et foedis his erroribus et scandalis, turbantibus haud dubie, et misere excruciantibus piorum animos: qua fronte, vel Pontificum assentatores, vel fanatici errores, apud nos, qui vere Dei beneficio gloriari possumus, incorruptam Evangelii doctrinam in nostris templis et scholis sonare, quaerere et postulare audent talem Ecclesiam, quae meris constet angelis, nihil habeat labis, nihil infirmitatis, nihil dissensionum, nihil disputationum, nihil etiam lapsuum et scandalorum aliorum, cum sciant autorem horum malorum diabolum patrem mendaciorum, dissidiorum, caedium, et horribilium lapsuum, nec dum funditus deletum esse, nec dormire aut interquiescere, sed circumire more rugientis et famelici leonis, et quidem circa postremam aetatem mundi grassari furentius, sentientem accedere tempus iudicii, et aeternae damnationis, et supplicii inaestimabilium et in infinitum augendorum tormentorum pleni. Sciant etiam hominum naturam post lapsum misere corruptam, et cum aetate mundi etiam ipsam languidiorem factam ad extremum, facilius nunc a diabolis impelli ad curiositatem, ambitionem, invidiam, superbiam, cupiditatem vindictae, odia, et profanitatem, ex quibus adfectibus oriuntur deinde omnes illae pestes, quibus Ecclesiam turbari, et Evangelii cursum et efficaciam impediri, et imbecilles alienari, pios etiam et fortes consternari et excruciari experimur.

Non patrocinamur erroribus, vitiis et scandalis, quorum autoribus scimus grave iudicium subeundum, et horribiles poenas solvendas esse, iuxta gravissimam Christi comminationem, Matth. 18.: Vae homini illi, per quem venit scandalum. Et Pauli Galat. 5.: Qui conturbat vos, portabit iudicium, quicunque est. Sed dicimus cum Christo tamen: Necesse esse, ut veniant scandala, quod in Lucae 17. cap. maiore cum vehementia dicitur: Impossibile esse, ut non veniant scandala.

Et Paulus illustribus quidem et veris, ut experientia testatur, sed admodum tristibus coloribus praesentis seculi homines depingit, 2. Timoth. 3. cum Timotheum suum praemonet: τοῦτο γίνωσκε, ὅτι ἐν ἐσχάταις ἡμέραις ἐνστήσονται καιροὶ χαλεποί. ἔσονται γὰρ οἱ ἄνθρωποι φίλαυτοι, φιλάργυροι, ἀλαζόνες, ὑπερήφανοι, βλάσφημοι, γονεῦσιν ἀπειθεῖς, ἀχάριστοι, ἀνόσιοι, ἄστοργοι, ἄσπονδοι, διάβολοι, ἀκρατεῖς, ἀνήμεροι, ἀφιλάγαθοι, προδόται, προπετεῖς, τετυφωμένοι, φιλήδονοι μᾶλλον ἢ φιλόθεοι, ἔχοντες μόρφωσιν εὐσεβείας, τὴν δὲ δύναμιν αὐτῆς ἠρνημένοι.

Loqui autem Paulum de iis, qui in Ecclesia sunt, et expresse complecti simul Doctores, ex eo manifestum est, quod dicit de iis aliquos esse, qui irrepant praetextu communicandae doctrinae in domos, et maxime se insinuent mulieribus in gynaeceis, et aliorum potentum domibus, quarum animos cum occuparunt semel doctrina falsa, intellegunt postea se etiam facile studia et defensionem maritorum habituros esse.

Tales cum sint homines huius postremae aetatis mundi, et cum furor diaboli ad extremam acerbitatem eruperit, mirum videri nemini debet, ibi existere scandala, dissensiones, et alia tetra facinora, ubi purior Evangelii doctrina traditur, quam odit et extinctam cupit diabolus, cum similia his, aut certe non multo leviora extiterint Apostolorum temporibus in prima Ecclesia, illa sedatiore, et firmiore et vegetiore aetate mundi, quae opponamus et fanaticis spiritibus Anabaptistis et Stenckfeldianis, et perfidis apostatis, qui nunc Pontificis pedes (indignatio pene aliud mihi verbum expresserat) osculantur, cuius prius universam potentiam et dignitatem de suggesto in his ipsis Ecclesiis publice damnarunt, et diris devoverunt.

Propter hanc necessariam consolationem commendatissima et gratissima hoc tempore piis esse debet lectio cum Epistolarum Pauli ad Corinthios, tum etiam huius commentarioli, qui de multis partibus doctrinae coelestis gravissimas commonefactiones continet, id quod non dubito testaturos esse pios et eruditos viros, et ex hoc ipso quoque quantumvis brevi scripto, et cognituros et admiraturos esse autoris pietatem, ingenii felicitatem, iudicii rectitudinem, confessionis constantiam, in communicanda sana doctrina benignitatem et facilitatem, et alia ipsius ingentia dona, quibus claruit vivus, et Ecclesiae Dei utiliter servivit, nihil sibi quaerens, nullos captans vel Regum ac potentum favores, vel vulgi applausus, vel dignitatum accessiones, vel opum cumulos, quarum virtutum testes reliquit plurimos omnium ordinum viros fide dignissimos, inter quos praecipue appellare visum est Celsitudinem tuam, Illustrissime Princeps, quae Dominum Philippum, de quo nunc ago, fortassis (ut existimo) de facie ignotum, sincero ac constanti amore semper dilexit, propter admirationem donorum et praestantiam virtutum ipsius, quarum αὐτόπτης, et fide dignissimus index praeter innumeros alios tuae Celsitudini esse potuit, et fuit haud dubie, vir eruditione, virtute, prudentia ac fide praestantissimus, Doctor Huldericus Sizingerus, Celsitudinis tuae Cancellarius. Ea de causa hunc Domini Philippi libellum tuae Celsitudini offerre potissimum volui, ut perlecto eo, et cognita sinceritate in doctrina, et in communicatione fida, patrocinium suscipiat huius tanti viri, qui quasi parum a suis alumnis et discipulis esset flagellatus dum viveret, etiam mortuus conquiescere non potest, quin ex iis, quos in sua mensa diu aluit, quibus cum non modo publice doctrinam, sed privatim etiam quae habuit et potuit, consilia, et secreta sua communicavit, quibus etiam cor suum, si licuisset, ex pectore exemtum impertivisset, aliqui in exangue corpus sepulti saeviant, vindictae studio tanto, et acerbitate tanta, ut credam, si coram ipsis miserum et iam putrescens cadaver Philippi expositum sit, eos dentibus more canum irruituros, et frustulatim carnem eius laceraturos esse.

Quid enim aliud censeas, si legas scriptum, quod recens quidam suae doctrinae et famae tuendae causa, ut videri vult, in vulgus sparsit? Adversus quam iniuriam vero se se defendit? Aut quae potest esse Praeceptoris fidissimi, imo Patris εὐστοργοτάτου et benignissimi, iniuria tam atrox, quae tantam mereatur acerbitatem, ut eius mortui cadaver propemodum et tumulo refossum ita crudeliter laceretur? Scripsit Philippus secreto rogatus consilium Principe Electore, sub cuius ditione natus est, paucula de Coena Domini, magis ut rixas de illa Edelbergae ortas, et publice de suggesto mutuis concionatorum conviciis cumulatas, suaderet quomodo sopiri et dirimi, quam ut de ipsa controversia pronuntiaret, indicans formam loquendi ex Paulo, qua tutissimum esset uti interea, donec de tota controversia in Synodo statueretur. In illa pagella ad unum scripta, secreto scripta, non in hoc scripta, ut vulgaretur, et tamen contra voluntatem autoris, et quidem post mortem demum publicata, fit mentio D. Heshusii paulo inclementior talis, ut eius autoritas summis in Ecclesia et antiquissimis scriptoribus postponatur. Haec est iniuria illa, hoc facinus Patris tam atrox, ut omnium acceptorum beneficiorum privatim et publice praestitorum, omnium virtutum memoriam penitus aboleat et extinguat, et animum cupiditate vindictae tanta accendat, ut ea, nisi hoc modo defensionis atrocissimae et contumeliosissimae satiari non possit.

Sed si non voluit habere rationem sua existimationis, quam certum est apud intelligentes nonnihil minui hac tanta asperitate, qua usus est in mortuum, in optime meritum, in Praeceptorem, imo in parentem: aequissimum erat parcere ipsius honestissimae et nunc adflictissimae familiae, a qua multis est affectus beneficiis parcere huic Scholae, versanti in acerbissimo luctu propter orbitatem, parcere miserae inventuti, desiderio amissis rectoris studiorum languenti, parcere Ecclesiae et posteritati, parcere denique Deo, cui cum bona conscientia servivit Philippus, ne ita deformaret et doctrinam, et mores et actiones huius viri, quasi veteratorie luserit in doctrina coelesti, et blasphemias scripserit, aut dixerit in filium Dei, neve aliis conviciis enm proscinderet, in sepulcro quiescentem, imo in sinu et complexu filii Dei iudicis et vindicis omnium scelerum, et inprimis ingratitudinis, perfruentem laeto conspectu et colloquio Dei. An hic sit Spiritus Dei, debacchari in talem tanta acerbitate, iudicent alii. Paulus 2. Timoth. 2. certe suos ministros aliter instruit, cum inquit: δοῦλον δὲ κυρίου οὐ δεῖ μάχεσθαι, ἀλλ’ ἤπιον εἶναι πρὸς ΠΑΝΤΑΣ, διδακτικὸν, ἀνεξικακὸν ἐν πρᾳότητι, παιδεύοντα τοὺς ἀντιδιατιθεμένους, etc.

Sed spero tuam Celsitudinem et omnes alios pietate, modestia, prudentia et virtute praestantes, literarum amantes, veritatis studiosos, posteritatis curam agentes, de conservatione et propagatione doctrinae incorruptae sollicitos, non moveri eiusmodi paucorum invectivis, ut desinant amare, magnificere, et grata memoria prosequi hunc virum, quem tot utilia monumenta, tanti labores exhausti publicae utilitatis causa, tantus summarum virtutum concentus et constantia, tot in multos privatim, et omnes publice merita nobis commendarunt.

Imo spero hanc istorum acerbitatem multis causam praebituram, ut pluris eum faciat, eiusque scripta studiosius cognoscant, et ab hac ingrata cohorte se quam longissime seiungant.

Spero Deum quoque ipsum veritati aliquando testimonium praebiturum, quando igne examinabit, quid aedificantium quisque extruxeris super fundamentum solidum, quod est unicus Dominus noster Iesus Christus, et hic crucifixus, et resuscitatus, et regnans ad dexteram patris, qui solus dat idoneos et salutares ministros, et ipsorum labores non sinit esse irritos, nec dissolvi unquam, quod ex ipso est.

Super hoc fundamento scimus extruxisse Philippum, una cum Lutherero et post Lutherum optima fide, integrum Corpus doctrinae, bona et perspicua methodo, studio vitasse omnes inutiles et periculosas disputationes, et abstinuisse etiam suo consilio a non necessariis flagellationibus et damnationibus aliorum, et simul illustrasse scriptis et voce omnes reliquas artes, quae ad explicationem doctrinae coelestis necessariae sunt.

Hae lucubrationes conferantur cum aliorum chartis, qui sibi videntur prae caeteris sapere, et plurimum laborasse, et effecisse in Ecclesia, nunc vero occupati sunt in eo, quomodo huius viri scripta carpant, ac suspecta et invisa aliis reddant, et vere conspicietur discrimen longe evidentius, quam inter aurum et stipulas est, quas tamen isti super eodem fundamento, ut iactitant, extructas, aequari auro Lutheri, et longe praeferri argento Philippi volunt.

Sed ut dictum est, ignis arguet uniuscuiusque opus, eo die, quo Dominus iudicabit Fabrorum suorum structuram, quod tempus patienter exspectent homines modesti, nec temere ac praecipitanter applaudant istorum pomposis et artificiose pictis et miro zelo veritatis tuendae fucatis clamoribus.

Hunc igitur libellum caeteris utilibus monumentis Philippi adiungendum, ad te mitto, Illustrissime Princeps Palatine, eo consilio, ut sicut Philippum semel tuo iudicio, ut Dei ministrum et utile organum, amore non aulico complexus, ad extremum usque dilexisti, ita eius mortui etiam famam et autoritatem contra talium hominum indignos morsus tuearis et protegas.

Deinde etiam commendo tuae Celsitudini huius viri honestissimam familiam, quae hoc anno dupliciter orbata, gemini luctus gravissimas causas brevi, hoc est, novem mensium intervallo accepit, mortuo viro sapientia, eruditione et virtute praestantissimo, Domino D.

Georgio Sabino, genero Domini Philippi et multorum liberorum patre, quibus, sicut et socer, suis, praeter famam eruditionis et virtutis, et excellentia ingenii monumenta, et bonorum virorum studia, parum admodum reliquit, quorum amborum orphanis principum munificentia subveniri aequissimum est, quam Deus largissimis praemiis compensabit, sicut testatur Syracides: Esto pupillis misericors ut pater, et pro viro matri illorum, et eris tu velut filius altissimi obediens, et diliget te magis, quam mater tua.

Ei verissimo et certissimis testimoniis patefacto Deo, aeterno Patri Domini nostri Iesu Christi, conditori generis humani et conservatori, Celsitudinem tuam cum omnibus suis supplex commendo, et hunc ineuntem annum felicem et tranquillum ex animo opto.

Data Vitebergae. Calendis Ianuarii Anno M.D. LXI.

ARGUMENTUM ET BREVIS EXPLICATIO PRIORIS EPISTOLAE AD CORINTHIOS, SCRIPTA A PHILIPPO MELANTHONE.

Prima Epistola ad Corinthios non est una perpetua disputatio, ut Epistola ad Romanos, sed multas dissimiles materias coacervat: totum tamen corpus ad genus Suasorium pertinet, quia sunt obiurgationes, commonefactiones, praecepta de diversis negotiis, et intertextae sunt alicubi conciones, quae sunt doctrinae pertinentes ad genus Didascalicon.

Ut autem consilium Pauli intelligatur, occasio scribendi primum consideretur.

Cum Ecclesiam in Corintho collectam reliquisset recte eruditam de universa doctrina Evangelii, de beneficiis filii Dei, de fide, de usu libertatis, de coniugio, de Sacramentis, de resurrectione mortuorum, et de aliis articulis, et multi ibi antecellerent donis: statim ibi, ut in Graeca civitate, Superbia et Curiositas pepererunt dissidia.

Alii ab aliis baptisati retinebant aliquos ritus eorum, a quibus baptisati erant.

Alii verecundiores, nolebant accedere ad cognatos Ethnicos invitati, cum familiarum usitati conventus essent, in quibus prius sacrificabant, et postea ex victima comedebant.

Alii liberiores, accedebant: aliquis tantum libertatis sibi sumsit, ut duceret novercam.

Aliqui instituebant Coenam Domini peculiarem, neglecta communi.

Aliqui elati dono linguarum, contemnebant alios, et inter hos ipsos, qui ornati erant hoc dono, erant φιλαυτίαι et aemulationes.

Aliqui audaces et curiosi disputabant contra resurrectionem mortuorum.

Talis erat eius temporis confusio profecto non levis, nec minor, quam fuerunt multae nostro tempore.

Et tamen omnes hi Corinthii valde tumebant persuasione sanctitatis, et sibi placebant, sese mirabantur, et se afflatos esse Spiritu sancto iudicabant, cum tamen multum in eis esset vanitatis, superbiae, Graecae levitatis et curiositatis.

Ad haec vitia redierant, etiamsi habuerant Spiritum sanctum, et aliqui adhuc habebant initia, quae tamen paulatim extinguebant, cum suis affectibus et ineptiis indulgerent.

Multa vidit haec aetas exempla similia, ideo haec facilia sunt intellectu.

Paulus igitur in primo capite initio obiurgat auditores, quod excitent dissidia.

Deinde ut radicem dissidiorum evellat, reprehendit admirationem propriae sapientiae, et curiositatem, propriam levibus ingeniis, ut si nunc concionaretur Serveto, Campano et similibus.

Intexit igitur hunc locum communem: Non est iudicandum de Deo ex humana sapientia, sed revocandae sunt mentes intra hanc metam, videlicet, ad Verbum, in quo se patefecit Deus, nec extra hanc metam nostris speculationibus evagentur ingenia, et ludant suo arbitrio.

Deus immensa misericordia se patefecit, dedit Evangelium, instituit ministerium Evangelii, illud audiri, et intra illud nos concludi Deus voluit.

Ita ingressus in hunc locum concionatur, quae sit principalis et necessaria doctrina, et addit doctrinam de ministerii dignitate.

Est igitur gravissima concio contra humanam sapientiam in primo et secundo capite, revocans nos ad Verbum Dei et patefactiones divinas.

Huius praecepti necessitas quanta sit, rudes et imperiti non considerant.

Sed petulantia humanae mentis horrenda est, quae quam audacter fingat opiniones de Deo, et cultus, tota mundi historia inde usque a primis idolorum initiis ostendit.

Quaerunt humanae mentes concinnas opiniones, et cum ratione congruentes, et fugiunt absurda, ut Samosatenus, Mahomet, Pelagius fecerunt.

Alii alio modo furentes fingunt portentosa, ut qui humanas hostias mactarunt, Aegyptii, qui serpentes et feles coluerunt, Manichaei, qui duo aeterna pugnantia numina finxerunt.

Vetat igitur Paulus gignere doctrinam de Deo propriis imaginationibus, et deducit nos ad Evangelium, ac docet, agnoscendum esse Deum sicut se patefecit, et in omni cogitatione et invocatione hunc Deum intuendum esse, qui se patefecit dato hoc Evangelio, et misso filio, sicut filius ipse dicit: Qui videt me, videt et patrem. In tertio capite primum ait, ministros idem Evangelium docere, et Dum pariter efficacem esse per vocem Evangelii, cuiuscunque lingua sonet.

Damnat igitur arrogantiam eorum, qui se aliis anteferunt, quasi suum ministerium sit efficacius, quam aliorum, ut finxerunt Pontifices de indulgentiis, se plura peccata remittere, quam alios, imo se educere animas ex purgatorio.

Simul autem testatur hic locus, Deum esse efficacem per ministerium evangelicum, ut Rom. 1. dicitur: Evangelium potentia Dei est ad salutem omni credenti. Postea addit praeceptum de doctrina principali Evangelii retinenda, et regulam valde utilem tradit: Retinendum esse fundamentum, id est, articulos fidei, et ibi Ecclesiam Dei esse, ubi fundamentum retinetur.

Interea tamen in hac infirmitate hominum alios magis alios minus pure docere. Quam ob causam omnes aetates in hac vita aliquos naevos, hoc est, aliquas incommodas opiniones retinent. Haec est sententia horum verborum: Fundamentum aliud poni non potest, praeter id quod positum est, quod est Iesus Christus.

Sed alius supra fundamentum extruit aurum, argentum, gemmas, alius ligna, stipulas etc., id est, alius illustrat articulos fidei vera et perspicua doctrina, dicit, cur filius Dei vocetur λόγος, quid sit peccatum Originis, quid intersit inter Legem et Promissiones, quomodo detur homini remissio peccatorum, quid sit Gratia, quid Fides, quae opera placeant Deo, quae sint discrimina peccati regnantis et non regnantis.
