Alii vero stipulas supra fundamentum extruunt, ut statim initio scriptores obscuraverunt doctrinam de Iusticia fidei, et auxerunt ceremonias, et vinxerunt esse peculiares cultus, fuerunt duriores quam oportuit in praecipiendo coelibatu, miscuerunt aliquam adhuc verecundam invocationem mortuorum: Ora pro me sancte Petre.

Tales stipulae multae omnibus aetatibus condonantur retinentibus fundamentum. Utilis igitur admonitio in hoc capite proponitur, videlicet, ut sciamus ubi sit Ecclesia, videlicet, ubi fundamentum retinetur.

Nec sunt Ecclesiae membra, qui idola pertinaciter defendunt, et aliquem articulum fidei pertinaciter damnant. Deinde ut sciamus in vera Ecclesia manere aliquas incommodas opiniones, quae ab eruditioribus emendandae sunt, nec propter eas imbecillia membra damnanda sunt, si tamen doceri sinant, et absit pervicacia. Ideo inquit: Dies declarabit, videlicet, non tantum extremi iudicii, sed quocunque tempore, cum doctrina illustratur, ut nunc dies declarat invocationem mortuorum falsam et commentitiam esse.

Et quod addit: In igne revelari, significat tentationes, ut Bernardus, Bonaventura in vera tentatione discunt acquiescere fiducia filii Dei, non suorum operum. Ita ignis, id est, tentationes et multa certamina purgant et instant doctrinam. In eodem tertio capite post medium, cum ait: Non scitis vos templum Dei esse? redit ad extenuationem humanae sapientiae in iudicanda voluntate Dei, et acriter obiurgat tumentes persuasione sapientiae, qui videlicet humano iudicio volunt amplecti concinna, et fugere absurda.

Quid autem absurdius humano iudicio, quam filium Dei crucifigi? Quare et innumerabiles homines abhorruerunt ab Evangelio, moti hac absurditate, quam et exagitaverunt multi scriptis, ut Lucianus, Iulianus, et alii. Ideo Paulus hic ait: Cum sitis templum Dei, in quo scilicet vera luce Spiritus sanctus iam habitat, videte ne hanc lucem extinguatis accersitis humanis opinionibus, et ita corrumpatis templum Dei, sicut Iulianus abiiciens veram doctrinam, ex Dei templo factus est organum diaboli.

Quam multi deficiunt hodie hodie ab Evangelio moti humana sapientia vel in iudicio dogmatum, vel propter scandala.

Humana sapientia est, cum disputant, nihil mutandum esse in ritu Missae, quia populus hoc cultu tenetur, quo amisso, populus omnio fiet prophanus.

Humana sapientia est, quod iubent aliqui pacem anteferre verae doctrinae, et praetexunt hanc causam: Quia si erunt bella, sequentur vastationes, in quibus delebitur doctrina. Et melius esset, aliquam fucosam religionem retineri, quam nullam. Haec humana consilia omnia pugnant cum mandato Dei: Non habebis deos alienos.

Quanti furores sunt hodie multorum, qui dogmatum conciliationes aut ἐπιεικείας fingunt, et veritatem corrumpunt? Denique quotidiana exempla sunt in conspe- ctu omnibus aetatibus. Multa enim et horrenda peccata sunt humanae sapientiae, non recte iudi- cantis de Deo. Ideo tam aspere adversus eam hic concionatur Paulus, et iubet eos, qui videntur sibi sapientes in hoc mundo, id est, sequentes humanae rationis iudicia, ut fiant stulti, id est, agnoscant hanc sapientiam non esse sapientiam Evangelii : sed de Dei essentia et voluntate ex ipsius patefactione iudicandum esse, et sicut iisdem Corinthiis in secunda Epistola scribit, oportere captivam duci rationem ad obediendum Christo.

## 4:1 Argument
Chapter IV.

In the fourth chapter, after he previously rebuked everyone in general, following human wisdom and departing from the goal of the Gospel, he now preaches to the ministers by name, and makes them equal in power and efficacy as far as the ministry is concerned, and at the same time teaches what sort they ought to be, namely, faithful. And he briefly signifies here that the ministry is effective through Christ, not by human strength. But let the minister be faithful, that is, let him rightly understand and rightly teach the doctrine, let him not have affected ignorance, nor be negligent, as for many centuries bishops in almost the whole world understood the doctrine, nor did they care for it to be taught rightly. From which negligence this horrible disturbance of the whole world especially arises now.

Moreover, a necessary rule is proposed here for governing the consciences of all in private life, and in any administration whatsoever. For conscience asks: How shall I satisfy my duty, when the difficulty is greatest? And many things, which were to be done, cannot be foreseen? And often events do not respond to good counsels? Just as Josiah errs, moving an unhappy war.

A most sweet consolation is proposed here: It is enough to be faithful, that is, with a good conscience to teach and do rightly what you judge to be right, with mediocre diligence, deliberated with a good conscience. But let faith be added, by which we are righteous, that is, by which the person is pleasing and we ask that God may govern us. Let this rule shine before all the actions of life.

At the same time, however, the doctrine concerning justification is inserted here, that we are righteous by faith, on account of Christ, not on account of the righteousness of our conscience, although this also ought to be present, but many sins of ignorance and omission remain, and many vicious affections, which evils are forgiven to the believer on account of the mediator.

Then he rebukes those preferring themselves to others either by power, or by the efficacy of the ministry, or on account of other causes: even if they are ministers rightly doing their duty, afterwards he commands the judgment to be left to God, as to who may excel privately: that is not of our judgment. But let us judge concerning the doctrine of individuals.

And again follows a most harsh rebuke of those who prefer themselves to others, where he proposes the example of the Apostles, which itself contains a remarkable consolation. He says that the Apostles are so ruled by the will of God that they are subject to the cross before the rest of the Church, that they are spectacles to Angels and Men, nay rather are led to be καθάρματα and περιψήματα.

These are the saddest of all appellations, signifying the most bitter hatreds of men. For κάθαρμα and περίψημα signify the same as piaculum to the Latins, that is, such a thing which, unless it be removed, might pollute whole nations, and provoke the wrath of God against whole nations. As Oedipus is a piaculum or κάθαρμα, because he took his mother as wife. Thus the Hebrews said a curse. And there are many similar words among the Greeks, such as:

ἀποτρόπαιος.

προστρόπαιος.

Polluted, pollution.

Accursed. Execrable.

Cursed.

Subject to the curse.

Held by the curse.

Utterly destroyed, untimely destroyed.

Destructive to all.

Abomination.

Sinful or impious.

Accursed. Guilt or pollution.

Avenging spirit or wretch.

Murderer or one haunted by a crime.

Accursed.

Anathema.

A means of purification.

A stain.

A scapegoat.

An offscouring.

Unholy.

Cursed.

An ill-omened man.

Held by pollutions.

A purified man.

A sorcerer.

Cast away.

He who is for the purification of the city.

Opposite to these are. Pure.

Accursed.

Holy.

From this example of the Apostles, let the chief Doctors now also learn not to be inflamed by a desire for glory or power, but to excel others in tolerance and a zeal for humility.

In the same chapter, when he now leaves behind the general admonition concerning human wisdom, and sets out to censure certain specific faults of the Corinthians, he prefaces that he will return, if he can, and will personally chastise the pride of certain ones who admire themselves, who either abuse their liberty or spread corruptions of doctrine. And he adds a useful sentiment: that the Kingdom of God is not the chatter of disputations and games of wit, as the Stoics, Epicureans, and Academics then contended with subtleties, and as there was and will be much of useless disputations in the Church: but that it is power, that is, the efficacy of God, initiating in the heart true fear and true trust.

Where these things are, there is a right judgment of the mind in distinguishing necessary doctrine from unnecessary disputations, as a pious Doctor speaks of the true knowledge of God, of true invocation, of repentance, of faith, of good works, of eternal glory, and of eternal punishments. Another wrangler seeks some madness from the ancient Stoics, which he mixes with the Gospel, contends that all things happen by necessity, or that there ought to be no affections in man: or he invents from Plato purifications of souls after death, which are to be freed by sacrifices: or he invents Accidents without a subject in the change of bread in the Lord's Supper: or he invents that the Mosaic polity ought to be received in the Church. Finally, there are infinite frenzies of disputations, which only seek materials about which they may wrangle, and do not have the true exercises of Repentance, Faith, Invocation, and the Cross, in which true light is kindled. This is the sum of the fourth chapter.

Latin:

Caput IV.

In capite quarto, postquam antea in genere omnes obiurgavit, humanam sapientiam sequen- tes ac discedentes a meta Evangelii, nunc nomi- natim ministris concionatur, et eos, quo ad mi- nisterium attinet, facit aequales potestate et effi- cacia, et simul docet, quales esse oporteat, sci- cet fideles. Ac breviter hic significat ministerium esse efficax per Christum, non humanis viribus. Sed minister sit fidelis, id est, recte intelligat et recte doceat doctrinam, non habeat affectatam ignorantiam, nec sit negligens, ut multis seculis Episcopi fere in toto orbe terrarum, intellexerunt doctrinam, nec recte doceri curaverunt. Ex qua negligentia praecipue nunc existit haec horrenda perturbatio orbis terrarum.

Proponitur autem hic regula necessaria ad gubernandas omnium conscientias in vita privata, et quacunque administratione. Quaerit enim conscientia: Quomodo satisfaciam officio meo, cum difficultas sit maxima? et multa, quae erant facienda, prospici non possint? Et saepe bonis consiliis non respondeant eventus? Sicut errat Iosias, movens bellum infelix.

Consolatio hic dulcissima proponitur: Satis est esse fidelem, id est, bona conscientia recte docere et facere, quae recta esse iudicas, re me- diocri diligentia, bona conscientia deliberata. Accedat autem fides, qua sumus iusti, id est, qua persona placet et petimus, ut Deus nos gubernet. Haec regula praeluceat omnibus vitae actionibus.

Simul autem hic inseritur doctrina de iusti- ficatione, quod simus iusti fide, propter Chri- stum, non propter iusticiam nostrae conscientiae, quanquam adesse et hanc oportet, sed multa re- liqua sunt peccata ignorantiae et omissionis, et multi vitiosi affectus, quae mala condonantur credenti propter mediatorem.

Deinde obiurgat sese aliis praeferentes vel potestate, vel efficacia ministerii, vel propter alias causas: etsi sunt ministri recte facientes officium, postea Deo iudicium relinqui iubet, qui privatim antecellant: id non est nostri iudicii. Sed nos de doctrina singulorum iudicemus.

Et sequitur rursus asperrima obiurgatio eorum, qui se praeferunt aliis, ubi proponit exemplum Apostolorum, quod ipsum continet consolationem insignem. Ait Apostolos volun- tate Dei ita regi, ut prae reliqua Ecclesia subiecti sint cruci, sint spectacula Angelis et Hominibus, imo ducantur esse καθάρματα et περιψήματα.

Hae sunt appellationes omnium tristissimae, significantes acerbissima odia hominum. Nam κάθαρμα et περίψημα significat idem quod pia- culum Latinis, id est, rem talem, quae nisi tolla- tur, totas gentes polluat, et iram Dei adversus totas gentes irritet. Ut Oedipus est piaculum seu κάθαρμα, quia matrem duxit uxorem. Sic He- braei maledictum dicebant. Et multa sunt simi- lia vocabula apud Graecos, ut:

ἀποτρόπαιος.

προστρόπαιος.

μιαρὸς, μίασμα.

κατάρατος. ἐπάρατος.

ἀραῖος.

τῇ ἀρᾷ ἔνοχος.

Ex hoc exemplo Apostolorum discant nunc quoque praecipui Doctores, ne cupiditate gloriae aut potentiae accendantur, sed antecellant aliis tolerantia, et studio humilitatis.

In eodem capite, cum iam relinquit gene- ralem admonitionem de sapientia humana, et in specie delicta quaedam Corinthiorum taxare insti- tuit, praefatur se rediturum esse, si possit, et superbiam quorundam sese admirantium, qui aut libertate abutuntur, aut spargunt corruptelas dogmatum, coram castigaturum esse. Et attexit utilem sententiam: Regnum Dei non esse garru- litatem disputationum, et ludos ingenii, ut tunc Stoici, Epicurei, Academici, certabant argutiis, et in Ecclesia multum fuit et erit disputationum inutilium: sed esse potentiam, id est, efficaciam Dei, incoantis in corde verum timorem et veram fiduciam.

Haec ubi sunt, rectum iudicium est mentis, in discernenda necessaria doctrina a non necessa- riis disputationibus, ut pius Doctor dicit de vera agnitione Dei, de vera invocatione, de poeniten- tia, de fide, de bonis operibus, de aeterna glo- ria et aeternis poenis. Alius rixator quaerit ex veteribus Stoicis aliquod deliramentum, quod miscet Evangelio, contendit omnia necessario fieri, aut nullos debere in homine affectus esse: aut fingit ex Platone animarum purgationes post mortem, quae liberandae sint sacrificiis: aut fin- git Accidentia sine subiecto in mutatione panis in Coena Domini: aut fingit in Ecclesia oportere recipi politiam Mosaicam. Denique infiniti furo- res sunt disputationum, qui tantum quaerunt materias, de quibus rixentur, non habent vera exercitia Poenitentiae, Fidei, Invocationis, Cru- cis, in quibus vera lux accenditur. Haec est summa quarti capitis.

## 5:1 Argument
Chapter V.

In the fifth chapter he now specifically accuses the abuse of liberty, namely concerning him who had taken his stepmother. It is an altogether foul example. For even the Heathens disapproved of such unions, as when the father Seleucus yielded his stepmother Stratonice, the daughter of Demetrius, to his son Antiochus. And Theseus devotes his son Hippolytus to curses, having been accused because he had solicited his stepmother Phaedra to lewdness.

And since the Church in the time of the Apostles was deformed by such blemishes, let us consider that many foul examples can happen also in other times, and let us not on that account fall away from God, but let us deplore our infirmity and the snares of the devil, and let governors strive to correct them.

But when the Corinthians thought, having heard the doctrine of Christian liberty, that even the laws of marriage were relaxed, Paul recalls them from this error and teaches that moral and natural precepts are eternal and immutable. Divine laws, which prohibit the union of certain persons or degrees, are laws sanctioned in nature, which God wills to be valid and perpetual. Wherefore God says that the Canaanites were to be punished and destroyed on account of incestuous lusts, even though at that time, when they were contaminating their bodies with such crimes, the law had not yet been promulgated through Moses: because God willed that this be the light of nature, and immediately in the beginning He prohibited to parents the union with their offspring, when He says: A man shall leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife.

Furthermore, the doctrine concerning liberty is handed down elsewhere in its entirety, and later it will have to be spoken of again. Now let the doctrine concerning Excommunication be added.

Concerning Excommunication.

Paul casts out of the Church the incestuous man, whose crime was manifest. By this example he shows how those guilty of manifest crimes are to be punished in the Church: and when later in the second Epistle he narrates that this incestuous man, after conversion, was rightly received into the Church, he proposes an illustrious testimony against the Novatians, which shows that for those who have fallen and are doing repentance, sins are truly forgiven, and they are to be received into the Church, concerning which article it will have to be spoken in its own place. Now let the doctrine concerning Excommunication be considered, in which first one must know the distinction between the evangelical ministry and political power. And since there are many parts of that distinction, I will now speak only of the doctrine of punishments.

Political power coerces and punishes with bodily force, and visits the contumacious with capital punishment.

But the ministry of the Gospel coerces and punishes only with the word, but in that order which Christ recites in Matthew chapter 18. First, let him who has offended be admonished, if he does not obey. Afterwards, let him be cast out of the Church by public sentence, as it is said there: Tell To the Church, that is, to the chief ministers and those who are joined in the investigations.

This custom was not first instituted by the Messiah, but is an old habit of the Levitical priests, who in their place protected discipline with such judgments, even though political power had other judgments and other punishments, which, as is usual, was more negligent in protecting discipline. Nor shall I speak at greater length about this passage. I only add this, that this sinew of discipline must not be neglected.

But as to what he says: 'I deliver him to Satan for the vexation of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved,' it must truly be understood in this way: that excommunication in the Church is not an empty scarecrow, but an effective and divine thunderbolt, and that punishments follow in the body and in worldly goods, by which those who are chastised are recalled to repentance, just as it is said concerning the most ancient excommunication to Abraham: 'I will curse those who curse you.' And when Ambrose had punished the scribe of Stilicho with such a sentence, the mind of the scribe was moved for some time, by which sickness he was admonished, afterwards he amended himself, and was received back into the Church by Ambrose.

Latin:

Caput V.

In quinto capite iam in specie accusat ab- usum libertatis, scilicet de eo, qui novercam duxerat. Est omnino tetrum exemplum. Nam et Ethnici improbarunt tales commixtiones, ut cum pater Seleucus filio Antiocho cessit nover- cam Stratonicen Demetrii filiam. Et Theseus diris devovet filium Hippolytum, accusatum, quod solicitasset novercam Phaedram ad stuprum.

Cumque Apostolorum tempore Ecclesia de- formata sit talibus naevis, cogitemus etiam aliis temporibus posse multa tetra exempla accidere, nec propterea deficiamus a Deo, sed deploremus infirmitatem nostram, et diaboli insidias, et gu- bernatores corrigere ea studeant.

Cum autem Corinthii putarent audita doctri- na libertatis Christianae, etiam leges coniugii laxantas esse, Paulus revocat eos ab hoc errore, et docet, praecepta moralia et naturalia aeterna et immota esse. Leges divinae, quae prohibent commixtionem certarum personarum seu gra- duum, sunt leges sancitae in natura, quas Deus vult ratas et perpetuas esse. Quare Deus inquit: Cananaeos propter incestas libidines puniri et de- leri, etiamsi tunc, cum illi corpora sua talibus sceleribus contaminarent, lex nondum per Moy- sen promulgata esset: quia Deus naturae lucem hanc esse voluit, et statim initio parentibus pro- hibuit commixtionem cum natis, cum ait: Relin- quet homo patrem et matrem, et adhaerebit uxori suae.

Caeterum doctrina de libertate alias inte- gre traditur, et postea rursus de ea dicendum erit. Nunc addatur doctrina de Excommuni- catione.

De Excommunicatione.

Incestum, cuius delictum fuit manifestum, Paulus eiicit ex Ecclesia. Hoc exemplo ostendit, quomodo puniendi sint in Ecclesia rei manifesto- rum scelerum: et cum postea in secunda Epistola narrat hunc incestum, post conversionem, in Ecclesiam recte receptum esse, illustre testimo- nium proponit contra Novatianos, quod ostendit, lapsis agentibus poenitentiam vere remitti peccata, eosque in Ecclesiam recipiendos esse, de quo articulo dicendum erit suo loco. Nunc doctrina de Excommunicatione consideretur, in qua pri- mum sciendum est discrimen ministerii evange- lici, et potestatis politicae. Cumque eius discri- minis multae partes sint, nunc tantum de poena- rum doctrina dicam.

Potestas politica coërcet et punit vi corpo- rali, et contumaces capitali supplicio afficit.

Sed ministerium Evangelii coërcet et punit tantum verbo, sed eo ordine, quem Christus Matth. capite 18. recitat. Primum moneatur is, qui deliquit, si non obtemperat. Postea eiiciatur ex Ecclesia publica sententia, ut ibi dicitur: Dic Ecclesiae, id est, praecipuis ministris et iis, qui in cognitionibus adiunguntur.

Haec consuetudo non primum instituta est a Messia, sed est vetus mos sacerdotum Leviti- corum, qui suo loco disciplinam talibus iudiciis tutati sunt, etiamsi potestas politica alia iudicia et alias poenas habebat, quae ut solet, in disci- plina tuenda negligentior erat. Nec dicam pro- lixius de hoc loco. Tantum illud addo, hunc nervum disciplinae non negligendum esse.

Quod vero ait. Trado eum Satanae ad vexa- tionem carnis, ut spiritus salvus fiat, vere ita sentiendum est, Excommunicationem in Eccle- sia non esse inane terriculamentum, sed efficax et divinum fulmen, et sequi poenas in corpore et rebus, quibus castigati ad poenitentiam revocan- tur, sicut de vetustissima excommunicatione di- citur ad Abraham: Maledicam maledicentibus tibi. Et cum Ambrosius scribam Stilliconis tali sententia puniisset, Scribae mota est mens per aliquod tempus, quo morbo admonitus, postea se emendavit, et ab Ambrosio rursus in Eccle- siam receptus est.

## 5:7
Concerning the Passover.

In order to show that this judgment must necessarily be retained in the Church, Paul adds a comparison: 'As in the Jewish Passover the leaven had to be removed, so let us remove the leaven from the Church.' Then, in the explanation of the type of the Passover, he dwells for a while, and warns that the eating of the lamb was instituted so that the death of the Messiah might be signified. And the whole allegory of the Passover is to be explained more fully elsewhere. Here, let the words in the text be observed.

Let us celebrate the feast with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth: he opposes truth to lies and false opinions, and calls truth the acknowledgment and confession of the true doctrine concerning God. He opposes sincerity to hypocrisy, and to false invocation without fear, faith, and constancy. And he calls sincerity not painted virtues, but fear, faith, invocation, and constancy of faith.

Latin:

De Paschate.

Ut ostendat Paulus hoc iudicium necessario in Ecclesia retinendum esse, addit similitudinem: Ut in Paschate Iudaico fermentum tollendum fuit, sic nos ex Ecclesia fermentum tollamus. Deinde in enarratione typi Paschatis aliquantisper com- moratur, monet institutum esse esum agni, ut mors Messiae significaretur. Ac tota Paschatis allegoria alias copiosius enarranda est. Hic vo- cabula in textu observentur.

Celebremus festum in azymis sinceritatis et veritatis: veritatem opponit mendaciis et falsis opinionibus, et vocat veritatem verae doctrinae de Deo agnitionem et confessionem. Sinceritatem opponit hypocrisi, falsae invocatione sine Ti- more, Fide, Constantia. Et vocat sinceritatem, non fucatas virtutes, Timorem, Fidem, Invo- cationem, Constantiam fidei.

## 6:1 Argument
Chapter VI.

Concerning lawsuits.

Above he censured the abuse of liberty and lusts; now he rebukes those litigating who, since they contend out of hatred or avarice, violate the commandments of the Decalogue: 'You shall not kill,' or 'You shall not steal.' For he does not condemn judgments, or any part of the judicial process, or forensic disputation. For these political ordinances are good things, ordained and approved divinely, just as it is most clearly handed down in Romans 13. And Jehoshaphat says: 'You exercise the judgment of the Lord.' But forensic disputation is one thing, and hatred or avarice in a litigant is another. And just as saints can rightly use marriage, so they can rightly use the courts, just as it is clearly said in Romans 13: 'The magistrate is for the honor of the good.' Therefore, a saint can bring a case into court without a wicked affection. And in that matter, many virtues are contained.

1. Reverence toward laws and magistrates, because he permits judgment to them, yielding from his own opinion.

2. Love of justice, because he does not covet what belongs to another, but as if stripping himself of his own property, he leaves it to the power of the judge and the laws, so that they may attribute it by their sentence to whomever it shall seem fit: a greedy mind does not do this.

3. Love of truth, because he suffers reasons to be compared and judged.

4. Love of public peace, because he prefers that his own property be attributed to another by a judge, rather than that public peace be disturbed.

These virtues are in a holy litigant.

It is certain, therefore, that litigants are rebuked by Paul on account of hatreds and avarice, likewise, on account of scandal, because they not only litigated before Gentiles, but also mixed in the affections and deceits and calumnies of the Gentiles. This is manifest from the text, because he says: You do injury to others, you defraud. Thus let that which he says be understood: ἥττημα is in you. He does not mean that the very questioning of the forum is ἥττημα, but injustice, of which forensic contention is a sign. κρίματα ἔχετε, therefore ἥττημα is not the having of κρίματα itself, but ἀδικεῖν is ἥττημα. Wherefore let κρίματα ἔχειν not be understood as the subject to ἥττημα, but as part of an enthymeme, because from that sign he reasons that there are depraved desires in them.

The word ἥττημα is also softer than ἁμαρτία, that is, something condemned, and it signifies to succumb to some affection, as we say: ἥττων ὀργῆς, ἥττων ἔρωτος.

Μὴ πλανᾶσθε. Do not err.

On the abuse of liberty, and on fornication.

It must often be considered what kind of world the Apostles found, not only because it is profitable consideration for understanding the sermons of the Apostles, but also because the manifest turpitudes of that time show more clearly how great the misery of the human race is than the vices of the present age, which, even if they are many and great, are nevertheless more concealed. A comparison, however, also reminds us of our own vices.

A large part of mankind is always entirely atheistic. But at that time many openly taught that there was no providence. The rest of the multitude horribly worshipped idols, and some devised one thing, others another, daily.

Then against the second Table...

not only were customary, but also permitted, were various vague lusts. Intercourse, whether of a married man or a bachelor with a woman who had prostituted her body, was not reproved at all. Indeed, in the Comedies of Plautus, fathers and sons love the same women. Very many openly and with impunity even abused the sex, concerning which turpitude, even if antiquity had had severe laws, nevertheless those had already fallen silent for many centuries in Greece, Asia, and Italy.

Against the fifth commandment, the custom of gladiators was also accepted.

Against the seventh, usury was openly permitted.

But those frenzies against the first commandment, and against the sixth, raged much more widely and are more foul.

Since the world was such, God nevertheless, out of that most filthy mire, by His immense mercy gathered a Church for Himself, which example contains the most ample consolation, which Paul also proposes here, admonishing us concerning the remission of sins, when he says: And such were some of you, but you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of Christ and the Holy Spirit. It is very profitable to remember these words, both for the sake of consolation and for the sake of the doctrine, by which they speak learnedly concerning justification, affirming that we have been received on account of Christ and gifted with the Holy Spirit.

Then, since the corruption of morals was such, it can easily be judged how difficult it was to tear out from the minds of the Gentiles so many false opinions that had been confirmed. And especially the custom with prostituted women was most accepted, confirmed not only by time and the common examples of all, but also by the sweetness of associations and banquets and the charm of games and comedies. Therefore, such a long sermon is instituted here against fornication. And lest there be ambiguity in the word, he expressly says that he disapproves of the custom with a prostituted woman, not only other, fouler lusts.

But first he hands down a rule against the abuse of liberty. Because they were relaxing the doctrine of liberty too much, and transferring it to a license not granted by God, therefore this rule is handed down: Evangelical liberty does not permit moral commandments to be violated. He expressly hands down this rule in the seventh chapter: Circumcision is nothing... but the keeping of the commandments of God. Because the New Testament exhibits righteousness and eternal life, which is the very interior and exterior fulfillment of moral commandments, consistent with the eternal and immovable will of God expressed in the moral commandments. Therefore, he here reproves errors concerning liberty, and by name prohibits offenses conflicting with the first, sixth, seventh, and eighth commandments. For the fifth commandment concerning homicide was otherwise known, and is added elsewhere.

And he manifestly affirms that those who persevere in such violation of moral commandments against conscience are not heirs of eternal life: Do not err, he says, for fornicators will not be heirs of the kingdom of God. And so that the sermon may be understood not as concerning past offenses, but as concerning perseverance, he adds an explanation: Such were you, but you were washed. Let us fix these words in our minds, because, as I said, they contain the sweetest doctrine and consolation.

The distinction between Necessary things and indifferent things.

All things are lawful for me, namely ἀδιάφορα. And those things are ἀδιάφορα which are not commanded by the moral law. Because the moral law is the very eternal law in the divine mind and the will of the Holy Spirit in the reborn, who begins an eternal obedience, agreeable to the divine will, according to that saying: I will put my law in their hearts. Ceremonies, however, are external observations, which are exercises of this mortal life, they are not the interior and perpetual righteousness of the heart.

Then follows the correction: But let no thing bring me into bondage, that is, those things are permitted which do not draw back into bondage a conscience torn away from God, just as the adultery of David draws back into bondage his conscience torn away from God. For this is bondage, to become guilty before God, with the Holy Spirit cast off, and, our conscience condemning us, not to be able to call upon God, because we have fallen knowingly and willingly against his will. This slavery of conscience and this guilt, he calls being reduced to slavery. He denies, therefore, that such things are permitted as make the conscience guilty, that is, which drive out the Holy Spirit. But such are those things which fight against the moral law, because the will of the Holy Spirit is the same as that of the moral law, which is the eternal and immovable wisdom of God. Now the rest, which follow, are plainer: Food for the belly, and the belly for foods, God will destroy both this and that, that is, foods and the belly serving mortal life are things that will perish, nor do they pertain to the righteousness of the spirit or the conscience, nor are they beginnings of light or eternal righteousness in the mind, nor do they hinder the Holy Spirit: therefore they are indifferent. These things are permitted. But fornication is different, which is a contamination of persons against the will of God, and therefore tears the consciences of two away from God, and makes them guilty. Therefore Paul says: But let the body serve not fornication, but the Lord, that is, the belly was created for foods suitable to nature without distinction. But the body or person is ordained to serve God, who has forbidden wandering lusts, and is horribly angry at them. Therefore, since the person ought now to be God's own, let it not make confusions of lusts, with the order of God despised, as Nero, the Ptolemies, and a huge multitude of men did. But the reading of Paul will be clearer if you understand σῶμα as the person, as the Greeks used to speak, and Paul wishes to speak about the ordered use of the person. The foundation, however, of the dissimilarity concerning foods and wandering intercourse is this, that he affirms those things which are of the moral law to be necessary, because the moral law is the very eternal law in the divine mind, and the will of the Holy Spirit, who begins an obedience similar to the divine will, as I said above. But the confusion of lusts fights horribly against the will of God.

Latin:

Caput VI.

De litibus.

Supra abusum libertatis et libidines taxavit, nunc obiurgat litigantes, qui cum certent odiis aut avaricia, violant praecepta decalogi: Non oc- cides, aut: Non furaberis. Non enim damnat iudicia, aut ullam iudiciorum partem, aut dispu- tationem forensem. Nam hae ordinationes poli- ticae sunt res bonae, ordinatae et approbatae divinitus, sicut Roman. 13. clarissime traditum est. Et Iosaphat inquit: Iudicium Domini exer- cetis. Aliud est autem disputatio forensis, aliud odium aut avaricia in litigatore. Ac ut sancti recte uti possunt coniugio, sic recte uti possunt iudiciis, sicut clare dicitur Roma. 13.: Magistra- tus est honori bonis. Potest igitur sanctus deferre causam in iudicium sine pravo affectu. Et in ea re multae insunt virtutes.

1. Reverentia erga leges et magistratus, quia iudicium illis permittit, cedens de sua sententia.

2. Amor iusticiae, quod non appetit alie- num, sed quasi exuens rem suam, potestati iudi- cis et legum relinquit, ut attribuant sua senten- tia, cui videbitur: Hoc non facit animus pleo- necticus.

3. Amor veritatis, quod patitur conferri ra- tiones et iudicari.

4. Amor pacis publicae, quod mavult a iu- dice suum alteri attribui, quam turbari pacem publicam.

Hae vertutes sunt in litigatore sancto.

Certum est igitur a Paulo obiurgari litigan- tes propter odia et avariciam, item, propter scan- dalum, quod non modo litigabant coram Ethni- cis, sed etiam Ethnicorum affectus et praestigias et calumnias miscebant. Hoc manifestum est ex textu, quia dicit: Vos iniuriam facitis aliis, vos defraudatis. Sic intelligatur quod dicit: ἥττημα est in vobis. Non vult ipsam dubitationem fori, esse ἥττημα, sed iniusticiam, cuius signum est forensis contentio. κρίματα ἔχετε, ergo est ἥτ- τημα non ipsum κρίματα ἔχειν, sed ἀδικεῖν est ἥττημα. Quare κρίματα ἔχειν non intelligatur ut subiectum ad ἥττημα, sed ut pars enthyme- matis, quia ab eo signo ratiocinatur in eis esse pravas cupiditates.

Est et vocabulum ἥττημα mollius, quam ἁμαρτία, id est, quiddam damnatum, et signi- ficat succumbere affectui alicui, ut dicimus: ἥτ- των ὀργῆς, ἥττων ἔρωτος.

Μὴ πλανᾶσθε. Ne erretis.

De abusu libertatis, et de scortatione.

Saepe cogitandum est, qualem invenerint mundum Apostoli, non solum quia prodest ea consideratio ad intelligendas conciones Apostolorum, sed etiam quia eius temporis manifestae turpitudines magis ostendunt, quanta sit miseria generis humani, quam praesentis aetatis vitia, quae etiamsi sunt multa et magna, tamen magis teguntur. Collatio tamen et nos de nostris vitiis commonefacit.

Semper magna pars hominum prorsus est athea. Sed tunc multi palam docebant nullam esse providentiam. Reliqua multitudo horribiliter colebat idola, et alii alia quotidie excogitabant.

Deinde contra secundam Tabulam .....

...... cautam non so- lum usitatae, sed etiam concessae erant vagae libidines multiplices. Concubitus seu mariti seu coelibis cum ea, quae corpus prostituerat, prorsus non reprehendebatur. Imo in Plaudi Comoediis patres et filii easdem amant. Plurimi palam impune etiam sexu abutebantur, de qua turpitudine etiamsi vetustas habuerat severas leges, tamen illae iam in Graecia, Asia et Italia, multis seculis conticuerant.

Contra quintum praeceptum recepta erat et gladiatorum consuetudo.

Contra septimum concessae palam erant usurae.

Sed illi furores contra primum praeceptum, et contra sextum, multo latius grassabantur, et magis tetri sunt.

Talis cum esset mundus, tamen Deus ex illa turpissima colluvie, immensa misericordia Ecclesiam sibi collegit, quod exemplum continet amplissimam consolationem, quam et hic Paulus proponit, admonens nos de remissione peccatorum, cum ait: Et haec quidem aliqui fuistis, sed abluti estis, sanctificati estis, iustificati estis in nomine Christi et Spiritu sancto. Quae verba meminisse valde prodest, et propter consolationem et propter doctrinam, qua de iustificatione erudite loquuntur, affirmant nos receptos esse propter Christum, et donatos Spiritu sancto.

Deinde cum talis fuerit morum corruptio, facile iudicari potest, quam difficile fuerit, tot falsas opiniones confirmatas in Ethnicis, ex eorum animis evellere. Ac praecipue consuetudo cum mulieribus prostitutis receptissima erat, confirmata non solum temporibus, et communibus omnium exemplis, sed etiam sodalitiorum et conviviorum suavitate et ludorum et comoediarum venustate. Ideo tam prolixa concio hic con- tra scortationem instituitur. Et ne sit ambiguitas in vocabulo, diserte dicit se improbare consuetu- dinem cum muliere prostituta, non tantum alias libidines turpiores.

Primum autem regulam tradit contra abu- sum libertatis. Quia enim doctrinam de liber- tate nimium laxabant, et transferebant ad licen- tiam non concessam a Deo, ideo haec regula tra- ditur: Libertas evangelica non concedit violari praecepta moralia. Hanc regulam capite septimo expresse tradit: Circumcisio nihil est ... est, sed observatio mandatorum Dei. Quia novum Testamentum exhibet iusticiam et vitam aeternam, quae est ipsa interior et exterior impletio moralium praeceptorum, conveniens cum aeterna et immota voluntate Dei expressa in praeceptis moralibus. Ideo hic errores de liber- tate reprehendit, et nominatim prohibet delicta pugnantia cum primo praecepto, sexto, septimo et octavo. Nam praeceptum quintum de homi- cidio alioqui notum erat, et alibi additur.

Et manifeste affirmat, non esse haeredes vitae aeternae, qui perseverant in tali violatione moralium praeceptorum contra conscientiam: Nolite errare, inquit, scortatores enim non erunt haeredes regni Dei. Ac ut intelligatur concio non de praeteritis delictis, sed de perseverantia, explicationem addit: Haec fuistis, sed abluti estis. Haec verba infigamus animis, quia, ut dixi, do- ctrinam et consolationem dulcissimam continent.

Discrimen inter Necessaria et ἀδιάφορα.

Omnia mihi licent, scilicet ἀδιάφορα. Et sunt ἀδιάφορα, quae non sunt praecepta lege morali. Quia lex moralis est ipsa aeterna lex in mente divina et voluntas Spiritus sancti in rena- tis, qui aeternam obedientiam incóat, convenien- tem voluntati divinae, iuxta illud: Dabo legem meam in corda eorum. Ceremoniae vero sunt observationes externae, quae sunt exercitia istius vitae mortalis, non sunt iustitia interior et per- petua cordis.

Deinde sequitur correctio: Sed nulla res me redigat in servitutem, id est, illa sunt concessa, quae non retrahunt in servitutem conscientiam avulsam a Deo, ut adulterium Davidis in servi- tutem retrahit eius conscientiam avulsam a Deo. Est enim haec servitus, fieri reum coram Deo, excusso Spiritu sancto, et damnante nos conscien- tia, non posse invocare Deum, quia contra eius voluntatem scientes et volentes lapsi sumus. Hanc conscientiae servitutem et hunc reatum, hic vo- cat redigi in servitutem. Negat ergo concessa esse talia, quae ream faciunt conscientiam, id est, quae excutiunt Spiritum sanctum. Talia autem sunt, quae pugnant cum lege morali, quia ea- dem est voluntas Spiritus sancti, et legis mora- lis, quae est aeterna et immota sapientia Dei. Nunc caetera, quae sequuntur, planiora sunt: Esca ventri, et venter escis, Deus hunc et hanc destruet, id est, cibi et venter serviens vitae mortali sunt res periturae, nec pertinent ad iu- sticiam spiritus aut conscientiam, nec sunt lucis aut iusticiae aeternae initia in mente, nec impe- diunt Spiritum sanctum: ideo sunt adiaphora. Haec concessa sunt. Sed scortatio dissimilis est, quae est perso- narum contaminatio contra voluntatem Dei, ac propterea duorum conscientias a Deo avellit, et reas facit. Ideo Paulus dicit: Corpus autem non scortationi, sed Domino serviat, id est, venter creatus est ad cibos naturae convenientes sine dis- crimine. Sed corpus seu persona ordinata est, ut Deo serviat, qui vagas libidines prohibuit, et horribiliter eis irascitur. Ideo cum persona iam propria Dei esse debeat, non faciat libidinum confusiones, spreto ordine Dei, sicut fecerunt Nero, Ptolemaei, et ingens multitudo hominum. Erit autem magis dilucida lectio Pauli, si σῶμα intelligas de persona, ut olim loquebantur Graeci, et vult Paulus de usu ordinato perso- nae loqui. Fundamentum autem dissimilitudinis de ci- bis et de vago concubitu, hoc est, quod ea, quae sunt legis moralis, affirmat esse necessaria, quia lex moralis est ipsa lex aeterna in mente divina, et voluntas Spiritus sancti, qui obedientiam in- coat similem voluntati divinae, ut supra dixi. Pugnat autem horribiliter cum voluntate Dei libi- dinum confusio.

## 6:16
On the saying: They shall be two into one flesh.

From the saying of Genesis: They shall be two into one flesh, Paul takes an argument from a similarity, which I will recite later. For it is necessary first to hold the proper and native meaning of that saying, which many unlearned people think was placed idly, as if it only says this, which is known to all, that the nature of men was so founded that the human race is to be propagated from the union of Male and Female. And although that brief discourse also embraces that meaning, yet it simultaneously contains precepts about the manner of generation, that is, it sanctioned laws about marriage and the prohibition of wandering lusts, and proposes a true, complete, and learned definition of marriage.

For when he commands the male and female to be joined, he prohibits other mixtures fighting against this order of nature.

When he says: Two, he prohibits wandering lusts. He wants one male to be bound to one female, and he wants one female to be bound to one male. Such was the first institution of nature, from which human infirmity later departed a little, with God tolerating it, when polygamy was received, yet in such a way that several women were joined to one man, not several men to one woman.

Finally, he also wants that union of male and female to be perpetual and indissoluble, when he says: They shall be into one flesh, that is, inseparably joined. For unity signifies the bond of perpetual union, and prohibits divorces, such as are now Turkish, and were once those of almost all nations, indeed even of the Jews. But yet Moses also relaxed this particle a little, with God tolerating it, because of the huge infirmity of men after the fall. For this law in Genesis is a description of a most beautiful society, such as would have been in an uncorrupted nature, and ought to have been. And Christ reminds the Church of this first form in Matthew 19, as we shall say later in the seventh chapter.

I add nothing to that discourse in Genesis, but this meaning, which I have recited, is true, simple, and proper to that place, which if anyone will consider, he will understand that that saying was not placed idly, but discourses on the greatest matters, and from this is constructed the definition of marriage, which we shall recite in the seventh chapter.

Now that the native meaning is understood, let the argument of Paul be considered, who transfers the saying of Genesis to the spiritual marriage of the Son of God and the Church, as he does also in the Epistle to the Ephesians: You are joined to the Son of God, and made his members. Therefore do not be members of harlots wandering and straying from the Son of God. A husband and spouse can to be members of the Son of God at the same time, because that union is approved by God. And both spouses can be members of the Son of God, indeed they are as it were one member. Nor does the husband wander away or get torn from the Son of God by having intimacy with his spouse, because that intimacy is approved by God, and does not break the unity. But when lust wanders against the commandment of God, then the person is torn from the Son of God, and is polluted, and becomes a member of a harlot and an instrument of the devil, just as Nero or the Ptolemies wander horribly.

From this explanation it can be understood in some way how Paul transferred the saying in Genesis to spiritual marriage. However, the accommodation which I have reviewed seems obscure to a rude reader. But yet if anyone will consider it attentively, he will recognize that Paul intended what I have recited. For he wishes in sum that the order established by God should not be disturbed. This is the order, that spouses, who are members of Christ, should not wander with lusts, which when they do, they cease to be members of Christ, and become polluted members of harlots and instruments of the devil.

Nor do all the particles from the saying of Genesis fit Paul's argument. For the particle 'One' understood properly, as in Genesis, does not fit, namely concerning inseparability. But the other particle fits concerning the commixture, 'Anthony becomes the flesh of Cleopatra.' Here that ordered unity of which Genesis speaks does not remain.

Ὁ δὲ πορνεύων, εἰς τὸ ἴδιον σῶμα ἁμαρτάνει. He who commits fornication sins against his own body.

He exaggerates the offense from the object. Cato sins more by killing himself than if he had killed another. Thus, since all fornication pollutes one's own body, that is, for an alien use, against the order instituted by God, and destroys the temple of God in yourself, it should not be considered a light sin.

But what he says, that other sins are committed outside one's own body, that should be understood concerning the kinds of offenses which are more frequent. Murderers generally rage against others; those who commit suicide are rarer: these also sin against their own body. But Paul's saying should be accepted with a certain candor, concerning those things which happen more often.

But why does he say that it is done outside the body, when individual sinners burn with depraved affections in their own body, and employ organs, just as Clodius commits murder with his own hand?

I said above that a comparison of objects is being made, not of formal causes or organs. For in any sin a double destruction occurs: the first in the sinner, by which he turns himself away from God and becomes guilty of eternal wrath and death. As Cain first destroys himself. The second destruction is of the object. As when Cain kills his brother. Thus in fornication the first destruction is in the will and heart wandering from God. Afterwards, destruction follows of the objects, which here are one's own body and the body of another person. But just as one's own body is the object of this crime, so generally afterwards punishments cling to one's own body, namely savage diseases, or because of the abuse of seed, punishments rage against the children, as after David's adultery follows the incestuous rape of his daughter, then the tragic deaths of his sons. Just as punishments generally rage in that thing by which one sins, and as it is said in the book of Wisdom: By what things a man sins, by the same he is punished. This happens so that we may know that punishments do not happen by chance, but are truly the avengers of certain crimes. Likewise, so that we may know that we are being reminded by God concerning those very offenses, so that we may return to repentance.

But why is the abuse of one's own body a greater offense? To that I answer: Because we ought to govern ourselves with greater care than others, and more drive sin away from ourselves than from others, just as this itself is easier. And in wandering lusts the consciences of many are torn from God. David polluted his own conscience and that of the adulteress. Therefore these sins are by no means to be considered light.

Latin:

De dicto: Erunt duo in carnem unam.

Ex dicto Genesis: Erunt duo in carnem unam, sumit Paulus argumentum a similitudine, quod postea recitabo. Necesse est enim prius teneri propriam et nativam sententiam eius dicti, quod multi indocti putant otiose positum esse, quasi tantum hoc dicat, quod omnibus notum est, ita conditam esse naturam hominum, ut ex Maris et Foeminae coniunctione genus humanum propa- gandum sit. Etsi autem eam sententiam comple- ctitur etiam illa brevis concio, tamen simul con- tinet praecepta de modo generationis, hoc est, sanxit leges de coniugio et prohibitione vagarum libidinum, et veram, integram et eruditam defi- nitionem coniugii proponit.

Cum enim praecipit iungi marem et foemi- nam, prohibet alias commixtiones cum hoc or- dine naturae pugnantes.

Cum ait: Duo, prohibet vagas libidines. Unum marem vult alligatum esse ad unam foemi- nam, et unam foeminam vult alligatam esse ad unum marem. Talis fuit prima naturae institu- tio, a qua postea aliquantulum discessit humana infirmitas, tolerante Deo, quando recepta est πο- λυγαμία, ita tamen, ut uni viro adiungerentur plures mulieres, non uni mulieri plures viri.

Postremo vult etiam coniunctionem illam maris et foeminae perpetuam et indissolubilem esse, cum ait: Erunt in carnem unam, id est, inseparabiliter iuncti. Unitas enim significat Vin- culum perpetuae coniunctionis, et prohibet di- vortia, qualia nunc sunt Turcica, et fuerunt olim omnium fere gentium, imo et Iudaeorum. Sed tamen et Moyses aliquantulum laxavit hanc par- ticulam, tolerante Deo, propter ingentem infir- mitatem hominum post lapsum. Nam haec lex in Genesi descriptio est pulcerrimae societatis, qualis in natura integra fuisset, et esse debebat. Et Christus Ecclesiam de hac prima forma com- monefacit Matth. 19. ut postea dicemus in capite septimo.

Nihil affingo concioni illi in Genesi, sed haec sententia, quam recitavi, vera, simplex et propria est eius loci, quam si quis considerabit, intelliget illud dictum non otiose positum esse, sed de rebus maximis concionari, et hinc extrui definitionem coniugii, quam in capite septimo recitabimus.

Nunc intellecta nativa sententia considere- tur argumentum Pauli, qui transfert dictum Ge- nesis ad coniugium spirituale filii Dei et Eccle- siae, ut facit etiam in Epistola ad Ephesios: Iuncti estis filio Dei, et facti membra eius. Ergo non sitis membra scortorum vagantia et aber- rantia a filio Dei. Maritus et coniunx possunt esse membra filii Dei simul, quia ea coniunctio approbata est a Deo. Et coniuges ambo possunt esse membra filii Dei, imo sunt velut unum membrum. Nec aberrat nec avellitur a filio Dei maritus, habens consuetudinem cum coniuge, quia ea consuetudo est approbata a Deo, et non rumpit unitatem. Sed cum vagatur libido contra praeceptum Dei, tunc avellitur persona a filio Dei, et polluitur, et fit membrum scorti et orga- num diaboli, sicut Nero aut Ptolemaei horribi- liter vagantur.

Ex hac enarratione utcunque intelligi potest, quomodo Paulus transtulerit dictum in Genesi ad spirituale coniugium. Videtur autem obscura rudi lectori accommodatio, quam recensui. Sed tamen si quis eam attente considerabit, agnoscet Paulum hoc voluisse, quod recitavi. Vult enim in summa, ordinem a Deo constitutum non con- turbandum esse. Hic est ordo, ut coniuges, qui sunt membra Christi, non vagentur libidinibus, quod cum faciunt, desinunt esse membra Christi, et fiunt membra polluta scortorum et organa diaboli.

Nec ex dicto Genesis omnes particulae con- gruunt ad Pauli argumentum. Nam particula Unum proprie intellecta, ut in Genesi, non congruit, scilicet de Inseparabilitate. Sed altera particula congruit de commixtione, Antonius fit caro Cleopatrae. Hic non manet illa unitas or- dinata, de qua loquitur Genesis.

Ὁ δὲ πορνεύων, εἰς τὸ ἴδιον σῶμα ἁμαρτάνει. Fornicans in proprium corpus peccat.

Exaggerat delictum ex obiecto. Plus peccat Cato, sese interficiens, quam si alium interfecis- set. Ita cum omnis scortatio polluat proprium corpus, id est, ad usum alienum, contra ordi- nem a Deo institutum, et destruat templum Dei in te ipso, non ducatur esse leve peccatum.

Quod vero inquit, caetera peccata extra pro- prium corpus fieri, id intelligatur de generibus delictorum, quae sunt frequentiora. Homicidae plerunque in alios saeviunt, rariores sunt, qui sibi mortem consciscunt: hi quoque in suum corpus peccant. Sed Pauli dictum cum quo- dam candore accipiatur, de iis, quae saepius ac- cidunt.

Sed cur dicit, Extra corpus fieri, cum sin- guli peccantes ardeant pravis affectibus in corpore suo, et organa adhibeant, ut Clodius sua manu caedem facit?

Dixi supra, Obiectorum collationem fieri, non causarum formalium, aut organorum. Nam in quolibet peccato duplex fit destructio, prior in peccante, qua se avertit ipse a Deo, et fit reus aeternae irae et mortis. Ut Cain primum ipse sese destruit. Altera destructio est obiecti. Ut cum Cain interficit fratrem. Ita in scortatione prima destructio est in voluntate et corde aber- rante a Deo. Postea destructio sequitur obiecto- rum, quae hic sunt corpus proprium et corpus alterius personae. Ut autem corpus proprium obiectum est huius sceleris, ita plerunque postea haerent poenae in proprio corpore, videlicet saevi morbi, aut quia seminis abusus est, grassantur poenae in liberos, ut post Davidis adulterium sequitur incestum stuprum filiae, deinde filiorum tragici interitus. Sicut plerunque poenae in ea re grassantur, qua peccatur, et ut in libro Sa- pientiae dicitur: Per quae quis peccat, per eadem punitur. Id eo fit, ut sciamus poenas non acci- dere casu, sed vere esse certorum scelerum vin- dices. Item, ut sciamus nos a Deo commone- fieri de illi ipsis delictis, ut redeamus ad poeni- tentiam.

Quare autem maius delictum est proprii cor- poris abusus? Ad id respondo: Quia maiore cura nos ipsos regere debemus, quam alios, et magis a nobis depellere peccatum, quam ab aliis, sicut hoc ipsum facilius est. Et in vagis libidinibus multorum conscientiae a Deo avelluntur. David suam et adulterae conscientiam polluit. Ideo haec peccata nequaquam levia ducenda sunt.

## 7:1 Argument
Concerning the seventh chapter.

In the seventh chapter a doctrine very necessary for the whole Church is handed down concerning marriage, which we shall recite in order.

The occasion for these responses, however, should be considered at the beginning.

There was great confusion of lusts among the Gentiles, and divorces were frequent. Wherefore some, as happens, in the new zeal of received doctrine and conversion, were dissuading marriage altogether. Others were making divorces under the pretext of religion. Paul therefore responds, and delivers some necessary rules, which I will recite in order: first by a definition of marriage, as it was instituted in Genesis 2.

Marriage is the indissoluble union of one man and one woman, who can be lawfully joined, instituted by God for the sake of procreation and to avoid wandering lusts.

The words of this chapter confirm this definition, that it is an indissoluble union; these words bear witness: 'I command, not I, but the Lord, that the wife not depart from her husband, and that the husband not dismiss his wife.' That this end also pleases God, that a wife be taken, if not for the sake of offspring, yet to avoid wandering lusts, this also is expressly said here, and the doctrine and consolation is necessary for the pious: 'For the sake of avoiding fornication, let each one have his own wife.'

The rules follow. First. Marriage is not only not to be prohibited, but it is even necessary for those who are not fit for continence. As Paul says: 'It is better to marry than to suffer burning.' This rule is set against the superstitious, who, when they saw the wandering lusts of the Gentiles, fled from marriage itself with a new zeal for chastity, and disapproved of it, which superstition greatly exercised the Church at that time. Therefore, both Paul and the disciples of the Apostles opposed most serious judgments, which must also now be opposed to the papal law and the doctrine of the monks. For Ignatius wrote thus: 'Impose the yoke of virginity on no one. For it is a dangerous possession and difficult to retain when it is commanded by force. Grant marriage to the younger ones before they are corrupted by the habit of prostitutes.' These are the words: παρθενίας ζύγον μηδενὶ ἐπιτίδει. ἐπισφαλὲς γὰρ τὸ κτῆμα καὶ δυσφύλακτον, ὅταν κατὰ ἀνάγκην γένηται. Grant marriage to the younger ones, before they are corrupted into harlots.

And here Paul commands everyone to consider his own strengths, or his own gifts, and to judge whether he is fit for celibacy or not. Therefore he says: 'Each one has his own gift from God, one in this way, another in that.' This admonition, repeated twice, signifies the Apostle's concern, which foresaw the great destruction of souls that would follow from the imprudence of those who were rashly about to burden themselves with celibacy.

Then follow the rules concerning marriage itself, but in the Schools it is spoken of first regarding betrothal, which persons can be joined, and when a contract is valid.

The prohibition concerning persons exists in Leviticus 18. That prohibition is divine, and it binds all nations as a law of nature, because God sanctioned this reverence for kindred blood in nature, so that mixtures with those nearest of kin might not occur, and He horribly punishes incestuous lusts, as is said there concerning the Canaanites, and the examples of the punishments of Oedipus and the Egyptian kings show the wrath of God.

Afterwards, it must be considered which degrees, added by probable reasoning, should be observed in rightly instituted Churches.

Concerning the contract, antiquity also preserved this, which is honest, pious, and more accommodating for resolving controversies of betrothals, that betrothals made without the clear and express consent of parents be judged void. Wherefore it is said in the Institutes: 'Let them have the consent of the parents, under whose power they are.' For both civil and natural reason persuade that this ought to be done, to such an extent that the command of the parents ought to precede. And Ambrose, in the history of Rebecca, wishes the consent of the parents to be present, and says that it is so honest and agreeable to nature that even the Poets taught the same. And he cites the saying of Euripides, in whose Andromache, when Orestes seeks the marriage of Hermione, she replies that this matter pertains to the judgment of the father. These are the verses: Νυμφευμάτων μὲν τῶν ἐμῶν πατὴρ ἐμὸς, μέριμναν ἕξει, κ’ οὐκ ἐμὸν κρίνειν τάδε.

The words of Paul in this chapter agree with this ancient custom: 'He who gives her in marriage does well.' For these words signify that one must bargain concerning marriages with the consent of the parents. If the law of Moses has spoken: 'When you take a wife for your son.'

Let the Churches now also follow this ancient custom, omitting the recent law, which has produced inextricable labyrinths in judging secret betrothals.

But yet where parents are too harsh, pious magistrates should interpose their authority: just as ancient laws also prescribe.

There is also a distinction between betrothals for the future and for the present, which may be taken from the longer writings of others. One may withdraw from betrothals for the future, unless intercourse has occurred. But betrothals for the present are already in reality a marriage or wedlock, because consent makes a marriage. Nor will I dispute more subtly about this distinction. For I do not recount these things, so that more quarrels let us sow, but so that the more unlearned may hold the principal rules of this contract.

Regarding an honest and possible condition added, let this rule also be held, as when it is said: I will marry you, if you give me one hundred. Such a condition hinders the marriage if it is not fulfilled. But such conditions are abolished by sexual intercourse. I omit, however, the disputes concerning dishonest and impossible conditions, because in common life they are rarer examples.

Thus far I have recited the principal disputes concerning the contract. Now let the rules concerning conjugal duties and the accidents in marriage be added. Paul in the text makes mention of the conjugal duty, which he adorns with an honest appellation, naming it due benevolence. From this let the rule be taken: That the conjugal duty is a just work, and that superstitious opinions are to be condemned which falsely pretend that this work displeases God, when it has been founded and instituted by God in a certain order.

From these words: The husband does not have power over his own body, some also reason that πολυγαμίαν is disapproved, concerning which I spoke briefly above: That the society of one husband and one wife was first instituted. From this order a weaker nature later departed, which the law shows insofar as God permitted it, but the Gospel reminds us of the first institution.

The second rule prohibits common divorces, which, as they are now among the Turks, so they were then among the Jews and Gentiles without any discrimination at all, as one pleased.

Christ, Matt. 19, and Paul in this place restrict this license, and they will have marriage to be a perpetual and indissoluble union. Therefore he says: Not I, but the Lord commands, that a wife should not be separated from her husband, and that a husband should not desert his wife. God wills this rule to be kept in the Church. But divorces happen there also, not by the will of the pious, but by the fault of the other spouse. And only two cases have been expressed: one by Christ, the other by Paul.

The person who has committed adultery breaks the covenant of marriage. In that case, although reconciliation is to be attempted, nevertheless the innocent person cannot be forced to receive back the defiled one.

When therefore the innocent one seeks to be pronounced divorced, the judge condemns the guilty one, who broke the covenant of marriage, and pronounces the innocent person to be free, who, since he is completely freed from the guilty one, can contract another marriage. Such a divorce is not made by any desire of the innocent one, but by the fault of the other, who has already dissolved the bond of marriage. It can therefore be easily understood that this divorce is unlike the Jewish or Roman ones. Cato willingly yields Marcia to Hortensius. Agrippa willingly dismisses Marcella, intending to marry Julia, the daughter of Augustus. Tiberius Nero willingly yields Livia to Augustus. The other case was expressed by Paul, when one of the spouses truly deserts the spouse living without crime, so that the will of the deserter can be judged from the causes of flight and time and wanderings, and other circumstances, as Ulysses is not a deserter. Theseus, leaving Ariadne, is a deserter. Demophoon is a deserter of Phyllis, the Thracian woman, who had been his spouse. In this case also the Apostle says that the innocent person who has been deserted is freed. In the same way, therefore, as above, the deserter is sought, as much as can be done, and reconciliation is attempted, which if it does not proceed, the judge pronounces the deserted one to be free. And it is manifest that in this case also the deserted one does not dissolve the marriage by his own will, but the covenant was previously broken by the perfidy of the deserter. The text of Matt. 19 and in this chapter speaks openly of these two cases. Although, however, recent Canons admit that divorces are granted in these cases, yet they then prohibit marriage to the innocent person. Concerning this question, the opinions of the ancients are also dissimilar. But there are examples in Justin and Jerome which show that the first Church granted marriage to the innocent person: and I judge that to be just and pious, and agreeable to the sayings of Christ and Paul. For when a divorce is made, it is necessary to understand a divorce which is a divorce in actual fact, not in empty name, that is, in which the innocent person is truly free and can contract another marriage, just as the law of Moses itself understands the term of divorce. When therefore Christ, in the case of which it has been spoken, grants a divorce, it is necessary that such a true and not feigned divorce be understood. And that antiquity judged thus appears from Justin, who, as Eusebius recites, narrates that an honest and pious woman made a divorce with an adulterous and obscene husband, as was done then. And Jerome excuses Fabiola, because after a divorce was made with her first husband, an adulterer, she has married a second time, where he says concerning the former husband: The former husband had had such great vices that not even a harlot and a vile slave could have endured them.

Although, therefore, recent Canons are harsher due to a certain superstition, nevertheless the reformed Churches rightly grant marriage to the innocent person. The guilty person is left to the political judge, who ought to punish or remove them.

It has been spoken of two cases, the examples of which being frequent, it is useful to know what is to be judged.

Now let us speak of the question which we see here was proposed to Paul, and which the Canons show was afterwards very often agitated in the Church. For it was asked: Whether it is lawful for a pious husband to retain an impious spouse, or one who worships idols, and conversely: whether it is lawful for a pious woman to remain in the marriage of an impious man, or one who worships idols.

It was not a light question. For the law of Moses also forbids having a spouse remaining in an impious profession. And it is manifest from the dissension concerning the worship of God that most atrocious discords arise, because since the dissension is about a great matter, there is a greater fire of spirits in conversations, and greater pain. And the pious hear many things said contumeliously, on account of which they are affected with greater pain than if death were to be faced. Wills, therefore, cannot but be alienated.

For the customary rites of families existed, to which all relatives used to gather. And these meetings were bonds of mutual benevolence and of the discipline of the younger ones. If the head of the family came here without a spouse and children, or the mother of the family without a husband, or there was some distraction of the children, the meeting was already less pleasant. Finally, in daily life, very many offenses arise from such great dissension concerning God. But especially the dissimilar upbringing of children produces discords, as we see examples daily in this age.

There is no doubt, therefore, that there was great doubt among the prudent concerning this question, as afterwards even the Canons did not decree in the same way.

But Paul with singular wisdom judges that these marriages are not to be torn apart, because the justice of the Gospel is the justice of the heart, and eternal, not hindering the laws of political life: therefore, in the meantime, he wishes other civil covenants to be kept. Just as, therefore, the Church can exist under atheist kings, so a pious spouse can remain in the family of an impious spouse. Furthermore, why should such marriages be torn apart, when among those who are called members of the Church there are always some impious spouses? Nabal was impious, Abigail pious. And it contributes more to public peace not to tear spouses apart. But the counsels of governors should always be συμβιβαστικὰ (conciliatory), and as much as possible, they should follow those things which join the wills of citizens, just as that Platonic saying, if it is understood rightly, advises: ὅτι δεῖ ἓν ποιεῖν τὴν πόλιν (that one must make the city one).

Finally, the consideration of scandal also had to be taken into account. If the Gospel had torn apart marriage, how much more would all moderate men have abhorred it.

Paul therefore answers that marriages are not to be torn apart on account of dissimilar opinions concerning God, provided only that the impious person does not cast off the other, and he adds a consolation or reason: The unbelieving husband is sanctified by the believing wife, concerning which saying various interpretations have been fabricated. But this is the true and native one. Just as he says elsewhere that food is sanctified, for that which is a holy use, that is, granted by God to believers: so here he speaks, that the use of a spouse is holy and granted by God. When a pious person holds the doctrine of the Gospel, and determines that he is righteous by faith on account of the mediator, and that the Church is scattered into this confusion of the human race among the wicked, and yet that political society is to be retained so that the Church may be gathered, and that invocation and love are to be exercised by political duties: he rightly and piously uses an ethnic spouse, and that custom is pleasing to God. Just as Esther piously used the marriage of Ahasuerus. And Monica, the mother of Augustine, piously used the marriage of an ethnic husband, and the sister of Constantine the marriage of Licinius. And this opinion agrees with that saying of Paul: To the pure all things are pure.

A later age tore apart the marriages of those dissenting concerning God, and Augustine adds a sophism: It is permitted to dismiss an adulteress, therefore it will be permitted to dismiss one who worships idols, since the worship of idols is also called adultery. But let us omit these disputes of the moderns, which exist in the title concerning divorces, and in Gratian in cause 28, and rather let us follow the doctrine of Paul, which proposes a consolation wholesome to the pious at all times. Always For there are many marriages in which there are disagreements about God and about invocation.

Moreover, there exists a law of Theodosius in the Code which allows divorces to take place, not only on account of adultery and desertion, but also on account of cruelty and plots laid against one's life. One may inquire about these causes, and the Canons have established something regarding dangers to life. Although I do not wish for the bond of marriage to be loosened further, yet since divine law has granted divorce on account of the impious and the untamable, a wise magistrate, dispensing justice to the impious and the untamable, could provide for the conscience and life of a pious person out of that law. For it appears that that law of Theodosius was passed with serious deliberation. For since previously divorces were taking place without serious causes, as it pleased anyone in the Turkish manner, and were taking place without the matter being judged, Theodosius wished by this law to restrain that pagan license, and he lists the causes by name for which alone he wishes divorce to be granted, and he forbids them from taking place without the matter being judged. But the fact that more causes are named than two, there was some reason for the counsel in them that is not to be blamed. But these things are to be commended to the judgment of wise Magistrates and Pastors, who should also inquire from what source one should provide for him who, on account of leprosy, is forced to lack the intimacy of a spouse.

Otherwise your children would be unclean. Ἐπεὶ ἄρα τὰ τέκνα ὑμῶν ἀκάθαρτα ἐστὶν, νῦν δὲ ἅγια ἐστὶν.

The Septuagint translation speaks thus: it calls ἀκάθαρτα unclean, that is, prohibited, just as we say that swine's flesh is unclean by the law of Moses, that is, prohibited, or that a woman who has just given birth is unclean, that is, one whose touch is prohibited.

The connection of the argument, however, is this: If the marital intimacy were not pleasing, your children would be illegitimate, and to that extent unclean, ἀκάθαρτοι. But your children are not illegitimate: therefore, marital intimacy is pleasing to God.

How, however, illegitimate children were unclean in a special way, the law of Deut. 23 shows: A מַמְזֵר shall not enter into the assembly of the Lord, even to the tenth generation, that is, let him be admitted to no function in the Church.

Let this, therefore, be the simplest meaning: The children born are not illegitimate, and are not to be excluded, as the law of Moses excluded them: Therefore, marital intimacy is also pleasing to God.

But as for the fact that the Anabaptists reason from this passage that there is no original sin, and that holy ones are born from holy ones, that is, that the offspring is not guilty and is without the stain of origin: these things cannot be derived from this text, and they are refuted clearly in other places. In John 1 and John 3 it is clearly said that no one is an heir of eternal life unless reborn of the Holy Spirit. These testimonies must be opposed to the Anabaptists.

Why, therefore, does Paul here call infants holy? The simplest explanation is regarding the uncleanness of which the law of Moses speaks: They are not illegitimate children to be excluded from the Church.

Then, if anyone should contend that more is being said, let it be understood as said of those who have been inserted into the Church of God, either through baptism or through the invocation of the Son of God over them, because both are certain: that the Apostles began the baptism of infants, and that believing women no longer used pagan invocation and purification of infants, as among the nations some rites always remained by which newly born offspring were commended to God, as the γενέθλια indicate, which everyone celebrated.

There is no doubt, therefore, that women who had just given birth, who knew the true invocation, also commended their offspring to the true God; indeed, some who were born were baptized, some were brought to the Church for common prayer. Such were inserted into the Church, and in them the Holy Spirit was effective. Therefore, the saying pertains to them: Of such is the kingdom of heaven.

Paul therefore affirms that both the cohabitation of a pious spouse with a heathen husband and the procreation of children are pleasing to God, because on account of the faith of one spouse the cohabitation is purity, and those procreated are pure: nay, those born even become holy by the invocation of a pious mother or a pious father. Let us consider that there was a great ardor of faith in that first Church, and that the pious vehemently abhorred idols. Therefore it is highly consistent that heathen rites, by which infants were purified, were immediately added.

Ἡ περιτομὴ οὐδέν ἐστι. Circumcision is nothing.

In this part of the chapter he distinguishes Morals and Ceremonies, and the Degrees of political life, just as this distinction has been repeated often elsewhere, as in Galatians 5: in Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith, which is effective through love.

Good moral works are necessary in the same way for all. These he calls commandments in this place. And let the reader remember this saying for the refutation of the Antinomians, who imagine that in the Church there are no commandments, no law. But moral works are necessary because they are the justice of the heart, agreeing with the divine mind, of which our reborn Mind and Will ought to be the image, according to that: I will put my law in their hearts.

But the Levitical ceremonies, which were instituted for a time in the Mosaic polity, do not pertain to us at all.

- Then the ranks of political life, Lord, Servant, Rich, Poor, and the like, are ἀδιάφορα, and can exist in both good and evil. But let this be observed, that each one should obey his own calling. Likewise, that we do not abuse these ranks. Let the one who is weeping not succumb to grief, failing away from God. Let the one who is joyful not be puffed up, so that, having forgotten God, he indulges in desires, as happens in prosperous affairs, as it is said: Minds are usually wanton in prosperous affairs.

Finally, therefore, he adds: The fashion of this world passes away, that is, worldly behavior, the various ranks of life, lordships, servitudes, contracts.

Observe also here that contracts and the ownership of things are approved, since he approves of buying. Concerning all these things, the judgment is easy for those who know that the justice, about which the Gospel preaches, is a new and perpetual light, justice, and life in the hearts. Meanwhile, however, in this civil custom, one must use the political ordinances of those places where we live, if, however, they agree with the law of nature.

Latin:

De Capite septimo.

In capite septimo doctrina valde necessaria toti Ecclesiae traditur de coniugio, quam ordine recitabimus.

Occasio autem harum responsionum initio consideretur.

Magna apud Ethnicos confusio fuit libidi- num, et crebra fuerunt divortia. Quare alii, ut fit, in novo studio acceptae doctrinae et conver- sionis, prorsus dissuadebant coniugia. Alii prae- textu religionis divortia faciebant. Respondet igitur Paulus, et aliquot necessarias regulas tra- dit, quas ordine recitabo: primum definitione coniugii constituta, sicut institutum est Genesis 2.

Coniugium est unius maris et unius foeminae, quae legitime iungi possunt, coniunctio indissolubilis, instituta a Deo, propter generationem, et ad vitandas vagas libidines.

Hanc definitionem verba huius capitis confirmant, quod sit coniunctio indissolubilis, testantur haec verba: Praecipio non ego, sed Dominus, mulierem a viro non discedere, et viro, mulierem non dimittere. Quod hic finis etiam Deo placeat, ut ducatur uxor, si non prolis causa, tamen ad vitandas vagas libidines, id quoque hic expresse dicitur, et doctrina ac consolatio piis necessaria est: Vitandae scortationis causa, unusquisque suam habeat uxorem.

Sequuntur regulae. Prima. Coniugium non solum non prohibendum est, sed etiam iis, qui non sunt idonei ad continentiam, necessarium est. Sicut inquit Paulus: Melius est ducere uxorem quam incendia pati. Haec regula contra superstitiosos posita est, qui cum vagas libidines Ethnicorum viderent, novo studio castitatis etiam coniugium fugiebant, et improbabant, quae superstitio Ecclesiam tunc valde exercuit. Ideo et Paulus et Apostolorum discipuli gravissimas sententias opposuerunt, quae et nunc legi pontificiae, et doctrinae monachorum opponendae sunt. Sic enim scripsit Ignatius: Virginitatis iugum nemini imponito. Periculosa est enim possessio et difficulter retinetur, quando coactis imperatur. Iunioribus concede coniugium, priusquam corrumpantur consuetudine prostitutarum. Verba haec sunt: παρθενίας ζύγον μηδενὶ ἐπιτίδει. ἐπισφαλὲς γὰρ τὸ κτῆμα καὶ δυσφύλακτον, ὅταν κατὰ ἀνάγκην γένηται. τοῖς νεωτέροις ἐπίτρεπε γαμεῖν, πρὶν διαφθαρῶσιν εἰς ἑταίρας.

Et hic Paulus unumquemque iubet suas vires, seu dona sua considerare, ac iudicare, an idoneus sit ad coelibatum, aut non sit. Ideo inquit: Unusquisque proprium donum habet a Deo, alius sic, alius aliter. Haec admonitio bis repetita significat Apostoli solicitudinem, quae praevidit secuturam magnam perniciem animarum ex imprudentia eorum, qui se temere oneraturi erant coelibatu.

Deinde sequuntur regulae de ipso coniugio, sed in Scholis prius desponsatione dicitur, quae personae coniungi possint, et quando contractus valeat.

Prohibitio de personis extat Levit. 18.
