Ea prohibitio divina est, et obligat omnes gentes, tanquam ius naturae, quia Deus hanc reveren- tiam cognati sanguinis in natura sanxit, ne fiant commixtiones cum promiximis, et horribiliter punit incestas libidines, ut ibi de Cananaeis dici- tur, et exempla poenarum Oedipi et Aegyptio- rum regum iram Dei ostendunt.

Postea qui gradus probabili ratione additi in Ecclesiis recte institutis serventur, consideran- dum est.

De contractu et hoc servavit vetustas, quod honestum, pium, et ad explicandas controver- sias desponsationum accommodatius est, ut de- sponsationes sine perspicuo et expresso consensu parentum factae iudicentur irritae. Quare in In- stitutionibus dicitur: Consensum parentum ha- beant, quorum sunt in potestate. Nam hoc fieri debere et civilis et naturalis ratio suadet, in tan- tum, ut iussus parentum praecedere debeat. Et Ambrosius in historia Rebeccaevult accedere con- sensum parentum, idque ait adeo honestum et naturae consentaneum esse, ut etiam Poëtae idem docuerint. Et citat dictum Euripidis, apud quem in Andromache, cum Orestes petit coniugium Hermiones, haec respondet, Eam rem pertinere ad arbitrium patris. Versus hi sunt: Νυμφευμάτων μὲν τῶν ἐμῶν πατὴρ ἐμὸς, μέριμναν ἕξει, κ’ οὐκ ἐμὸν κρίνειν τάδε.

Cum hoc veteri more congruunt verba Pauli in hoc capite: Qui elocat, recte facit. Nam haec verba significant, consensu parentum de coniu- giis paciscendum esse. Si lex Moysi locuta est: Cum duces filio uxorem.

Hanc vetustam consuetudinem nunc quoque sequantur Ecclesiae, omissa recenti lege, quae inextricabiles labyrinthos peperit in diiudicandis arcanis desponsationibus.

Sed tamen ubi duriores sunt parentes, pii magistratus suam autoritatem interponant: sicut etiam vetustae leges praecipiunt.

Discrimen etiam est inter sponsalia de fu- turo et de praesenti, quod sumatur ex aliorum longioribus scriptis. A sponsalibus de futuro recedi potest, nisi accesserit concubitus. Sed sponsalia de praesenti sunt iam re ipsa matrimo- nium seu coniugium, quia consensus facit con- iugium. Nec de hoc discrimine subtilius dispu- tabo. Non enim haec recenseo, ut plus rixarum seramus, sed ut rudiores teneant praecipuas re- gulas huius contractus.

De conditione honesta et possibili adiecta etiam haec regula teneatur, ut cum dicitur: Du- cam te, si dabis mihi centum. Talis conditio impedir coniugium, si non impleatur. Sed tales conditiones concubitu abolentur. Omitto autem disputationes de conditionibus inhonestis et im- possibilibus, quia in communi vita exempla ra- riora sunt.

Hactenus de contractu praecipuas disputatio- nes recitavi. Nunc addantur regulae de officiis coniugalibus et de accidentibus in coniugio. Paulus in textu mentionem facit officii coniugalis, quod honesta appellatione ornat, nominans debi- tam benevolentiam. Hinc regula sumatur: Offi- cium coniugale opus iustum esse, et superstitio- sas opiniones damnandas, quae falso fingunt id opus displicere Deo, cum sit conditum, et certo ordine institutum a Deo.

Ex his verbis: Vir non habet potestatem sui corporis, aliqui etiam ratiocinantur improbari πολυγαμίαν, de qua supra breviter dixi: Pir- mum institutam esse societatem unius maris et unis foeminae. Ab hoc ordine postea infirmior natura discessit, quod quatenus permiserit Deus, lex ostendit, sed Evangelium nos de prima in- stitutione commonefacit.

Secunda regula prohibet vulgaria divortia, quae ut nunc apud Turcas, ita tunc apud Iudaeos et Ethnicos sine discrimine prorsus, ut libuit, fiebant.

Hanc licentiam restringunt Christus, Matth. 19. et hoc loco Paulus, et volunt coniugium esse per- petuam et indissolubilem coniunctionem. Ideo in- quit: Non ego, sed Dominus praecipit, ne uxor a marito separetur, et ne maritus uxorem dese- rat. Hanc regulam in Ecclesia vult Deus servari. Sed accidunt ibi quoque divortia non voluntate piorum, sed alterius coniugis delicto. Et tan- tum duo casus expressi sunt: alter a Christo, alter a Paulo.

Persona quae admisit adulterium, rumpit foedus coniugii. In eo casu etsi reconciliatio ten- tanda est, tamen cogi innocens persona non potest, ut pollutam recipiat.

Cum igitur petit innocens pronunciari de di- vortio, iudex damnat nocentem, quae rupit foe- dus coniugii, et pronunciat innocentem personam liberam esse, quae cum sit prorsus liberata a no- cente, potest aliud coniugium contrahere. Tale divortium non fit cupiditate aliqua in- nocentis, sed alterius delicto, quae iam vincu- culum coniugii dissolvit. Facile igitur intelligi potest, hoc divortium Iudaicis aut Romanis dis- simile esse. Cato cedit volens Martiam Horten- sio. Agrippa volens dimittit Marcellam, ductu- rus Iuliam Augusti filiam. Tiberius Nero volens cedit Liviam Augusto. Alter casus a Paulo expressus est, cum con- iugem sine crimine viventem, alter coniugum re vera deserit, ita ut voluntas deserentis ex causis fugae et tempore et errationibus, et aliis circum- stantiis iudicari possit, ut Ulysses non est deser- tor. Theseus relinquens Ariadnen, est desertor. Demophoon desertor est Phyllidis mulieris Thra- ciae, quae fuerat coniunx. In hoc casu etiam Apostolus dicit, personam innocentem desertam, liberatam esse. Eodem igitur modo ut supra inquiritur deserens, quan- tum fieri potest, et reconciliatio tentatur, quae si non procedit, iudex pronunciat desertam esse liberam. Ac manifestum est et in hoc casu de- sertam non dissolvere coniugium sua voluntate, sed foedus antea ruptum est perfidia desertoris. De his duobus casibus aperte loquitur tex- tus Matth. 19. et in hoc capite. Quanquam autem Canones recentes fatentur, divortia concedi in his casibus, tamen deinde personae innocenti prohibent coniugium. De hac quaestione dissimiles sunt etiam veterum senten- tiae. Sed exempla sunt apud Iustinum et Hiero- nymum, quae ostendunt, primam Ecclesiam con- cessisse coniugium innocenti personae: idque sentio iustum et pium esse, et consentaneum di- ctis Christi et Pauli. Cum enim fiat divortium, necesse est intelligi divortium, quod re ipsa, non inani appellatione sit divortium, hoc est, in quo vere persona innocens libera sit, et pos- sit aliud coniugium contrahere, sicut ipsa lex Moysi intelligit vocabulum divortii. Cum igi- tur Christus in casu, de quo dictum est, con- cedat divortium, necesse est tale verum et non commentitium divortium intelligi. Et sic iudi- casse antiquitatem ex Iustino apparet, qui, ut re- citat Eusebius, narrat mulierem honestam et piam cum marito adultero et obscoeno divortium fe- cisse, ut tunc fiebat. Et Hieronymus Fabiolam excusat, quod divortio facto cum primo marito adultero, nupserit secundo, ubi de priore marito dicit: Tanta prior maritus vitia habuerat, ut ne scortum quidem et vile mancipium ea sustinere potuisset.

Etsi igitur superstitione quadam recentes Canones duriores sunt, tamen Ecclesiae emen- datae recte concedunt coniugium personae inno- centi. Persona nocens iudici politico relinquitur, qui eam punire, aut tollere debebat.

Dictum est de duobus casibus, quorum exem- pla cum sint crebra, prodest scire, quid iudican- dum sit.

Nunc dicamus de quaestione, quam et Paulo propositam esse hic videmus, et postea saepissime agitatam esse in Ecclesia, ostendunt Canones. Quaerebatur enim: An liceat marito pio retinere coniugem impiam, seu idola colentem, et contra: an liceat mulieri piae manere in coniugio viri im- pii, seu idola colentis.

Non fuit levis quaestio. Nam et lex Moysi prohibet habere coniugem manentem in profes- sione impia. Et manifestum est ex dissensione de cultu Dei oriri atrocissimas discordias, quia cum de re magna sit dissensio, maius est incen- dium animorum in colloquiis, et maior dolor. Et multa contumeliose dicta pii audiunt, propter quae maiore dolore afficiuntur, quam si mors op- petenda esset. Non possunt igitur non alienari voluntates.

Erant enim usitata familiarum sacra, ad quae cognati omnes conveniebant. Et hi congressus vincula erant mutuae benevolentiae, et discipli- nae iuniorum. Huc si paterfamilias veniebat sine coniuge et liberis, aut materfamilias sine marito, aut liberorum aliqua distractio erat, iam congres- sus erat insuavior. Denique in quotidiana con- suetudine plurimae offensiones oriuntur ex tanta dissensione de Deo. Praecipue vero institutio liberorum dissimilis parit discordias, ut exempla videmus hac aetate quotidiana.

Non dubium est igitur, magnam de hac quaestione dubitationem inter prudentes fuisse, ut postea etiam Canones non eodem modo decre- verunt.

Sed Paulus sapientia singulari iudicat, non esse divellenda haec coniugia, quia iusticia Evan- gelii est iusticia cordis, et aeterna, non impe- diens leges vitae politicae: ideo interea vult alia foedera civilia servari. Sicut igitur potest Eccle- sia esse sub atheis regibus, sic potest pia con- iunx manere in familia coniugis impii. Deinde cur talia coniugia divellerentur, cum semper inter hos, qui dicuntur membra Ecclesiae, ali- qui sint coniuges impii? Nabal erat impius, Abi- gail pia. Et magis ad publicam pacem conducit, non distrahere coniuges. Semper autem guber- natorum consilia sint συμβιβαστικὰ, et quan- tum fieri potest, ea magis sequantur, quae con- iungunt voluntates civium, sicut et Platonicum illud, si dextre intelligatur, monet: ὅτι δεῖ ἓν ποιεῖν τὴν πόλιν.

Postremo scandali etiam ratio habenda fuit. Si Evangelium divulsisset coniugium, quanto magis ab eo omnes moderati homines abhor- ruissent.

Respondet igitur Paulus, Coniugia propter dissimiles sententias de Deo, non divellenda esse, si modo persona impia non abiiciat alteram, et con- solationem addit seu rationem: Sanctificatur vir infidelis per mulierem fidelem, de quo dicto va- riae interpretationes confictae sunt. Sed vera et nativa haec est. Sicut alias inquit, Cibum sancti- ficari, pro eo quod est usum sanctum, hoc est, a Deo concessum esse credentibus: ita hic loqui- tur, Usum coniugis sanctum et a Deo conces- sum esse. Cum pius tenet doctrinam Evangelii, et statuit se fide iustum esse propter mediato- rem, et Ecclesiam esse sparsam in hanc con- fusionem generis humani inter malos, et tamen politicam societatem retinendam esse, ut colligi Ecclesia possit, et invocationem et dilectionem politicis officiis exercendam esse: recte et pie coniuge ethnica utitur, et consuetudo illa Deo placet. Sicut Esther pie utebatur coniugio Ass- veri. Et Monica Augustini mater pie utebatur coniugio mariti ethnici, et soror Constantini coniugio Licinii. Et congruit haec sententia cum illo Pauli dicto: Omnia munda mundis.

Posterior aetas divulsit coniugia dissentien- tium de Deo, ac addit Augustinus sophisma: Li- cet adulteram dimittere, Licebit igitur colentem idola dimittere, cum idolorum cultus etiam vo- cetur adulterium. Verum has recentiorum dis- putationes, quae extant in titulo de divortiis, et apud Gratianum in causa 28. omittamus, et po- tius Pauli doctrinam sequamur, quae consolatio- nem proponit omni tempore piis salutarem. Sem- per enim multa sunt coniugia, in quibus de Deo et de invocatione dissensiones sunt.

Extat autem lex Theodosii in Codice, quae fieri divortia concedit, non tantum propter adul- teria et desertionem, sed etiam propter saevitiam et insidias vitae structas. De his causis quaeri potest, et Canones de vitae periculis aliquid sta- tuerunt. Etsi autem nolo magis laxari vinculum coniugii, tamen cum lex divina divortium pro- pter impios et indomitos concesserit, sapiens ma- gistratus dicens ius impiis et indomitis, posset conscientiae et vitae pii hominis ex ea lege consu- lere. Apparet enim illam Theodosii legem gravi consilio latam esse. Cum enim antea fierent di- vortia sine gravibus causis, ut cuilibet libebat more Turcico, et fierent re non iudicata, Theo- dosius hac lege illam ethnicam licentiam astrin- gere voluit, et causas nominatim recenset, pro- pter quas solas concedi vult divortium, et vetat ea fieri re non iudicata. Quod autem plures cau- sae nominantur quam duae, eis consilii aliqua ratio fuit non vituperanda. Sed haec iudicio sa- pientum Magistratum et Pastorum commendanda sunt, qui etiam quaerant, ex quo fonte consu- lendum sit illi, qui propter lepram carere con- suetudine coniugis cogitur.

Alioqui filii vestri essent immundi. Ἐπεὶ ἄρα τὰ τέκνα ὑμῶν ἀκάθαρτα ἐστὶν, νῦν δὲ ἅγια ἐστὶν.

Interpretatio Septuaginta sic loquitur: ἀκά- θαρτα vocat immunda, id est, prohibita, ut di- cimus, suillam carnem lege Moysi immundam esse, hoc est, prohibitam aut puerperam im- mundam esse, hoc est, cuius contrectatio prohi- bita est.

Connexio autem argumenti haec est. Si non placeret consuetudo coniugalis, filii vestri essent Spurii, et eatenus immundi, ἀκάθαρτοι. At filii vestri non sunt spurii: ergo consuetudo coniu- galis Deo placet.

Quomodo autem spurii peculiari modo fue- rint immundi, ostendit lex Deut. 23.: Non ingredi- tur מַמְזֵר in Ecclesiam Domini, usque ad deci- mam generationem, id est, ad nullam functio- nem in Ecclesia admittatur.

Sit igitur haec simplicissima sententia: Nati non sunt spurii, et non arcendi, ut lex Moysi arcebat: Igitur et consuetudo coniugalis pla- cet Deo.

Quod vero ex hoc loco Anabaptistae ratioci- nantur, nihil esse peccatum originis, et ex san- ctis nasci sanctos, id est, foetum non reum, et sine labe originis: haec non possunt ex hoc textu effici, et refutantur in aliis locis perspicue. Io- han. 1. et Iohan. 3. clare dicitur, neminem esse haeredem vitae aeternae, nisi renatum ex Spiritu sancto. Haec testimonia opponenda sunt Ana- baptistis.

Cur igitur Paulus hic vocat infantes sanctos? Simplicissima est enarratio de immunditia, de qua lex Moysi dicit: Non sunt spurii arcendi ab Ecclesia.

Deinde si quis contendat, plus dici, intel- ligatur dictum de his, qui inserti sunt Ecclesiae Dei, vel per baptismum, vel per invocationem filii Dei, super eos, quia utrunque certum est, Apostolos incoasse baptismum infantum, et mu- lieres credentes non amplius usas esse ethnica in- vocatione et lustratione infantum, ut semper inter gentes etiam ritus aliqui manserunt, quibus recens editi foetus Deo commendati sunt, γενέθ- λια indicant, quae omnes celebrabant.

Non dubium est igitur puerperas, quae veram invocationem norant, etiam vero Deo commen- dasse sobolem, imo aliqui nati baptizabantur, aliqui ad Ecclesiam adferebantur propter commu- nem precationem. Tales sunt inserti Ecclesiae, et in eis fuit efficax Spiritus sanctus. Ideo ad eos pertinet dictum: Talium est regnum coelorum.

Affirmat igitur Paulus, et consuetudinem piae coniugis cum ethnico marito, et liberorum procreationem Deo placere, quia propter fidem alterius coniugis concubitus sit mundities, et pro- creati mundi: imo nati etiam fiant sancti invo- catione piae matris aut pii patris. Cogitemus magnum ardorem fidei in illa prima Ecclesia fuisse, et pios vehementer abhorruisse ab idolis. Ideo valde consentaneum est, ethnicos ritus, qui- bus infantes lustrabantur, statim adiectos esse.

Ἡ περιτομὴ οὐδέν ἐστι. Circumcisio nihil est.

In hac parte capitis discernit Moralia et Ce- remonias, et Gradus vitae politicae, sicut saepe alias repetitum est hoc discrimen, ut ad Galatas 5. in Christo Iesu nec circumcisio aliquid valet, nec praeputium, sed fides, quae per dilectionem est efficax.

Bona opera moralia eodem modo necessa- ria sunt in omnibus. Haec vocat in hoc loco mandata. Et meminerit lector hoc dictum ad refutandos Antinomos, qui fingunt, in Ecclesia nulla esse mandata, nullam legem. Ideo autem moralia necessaria sunt, quia sunt iusticia cordis, congruens cum mente divina, cuius imago esse nostra Mens et Voluntas renata debet, iuxta illud: Dabo legem meam in corda eorum.

At ceremoniae leviticae nihil ad nos perti- nent, quae ad tempus in politia Mosaica institu- tae fuerunt.

- Deinde gradus vitae politicae, Dominus, Servus, Dives, Pauper, et similes, sunt ἀδιά- φορα, et possunt in bonis et malis esse. Verum hoc servetur, ut suae quisque vocationi obtem- peret. Item, ne abutamur his gradibus. Plo- rans, non succumbat dolori, deficiens a Deo. Laetus non efferatur, ut oblitus Dei indulgeat cupiditatibus, ut fit in rebus sesundis, ut dicitur: Luxuriant animi rebus plerunque secundis.

Tandem igitur addit: Praeterit figura huius mundi, id est, gestus mundani, varii gradus vi- tae, dominia, servitutes, contractus.

Observa etiam hic approbari contractus et rerum dominia, cum approbat emptionem. De his omnibus facile est iudicium iis, qui norunt iusticiam, de qua concionatur Evangelium, esse novam et perpetuam lucem, iusticiam, et vitam in cordibus. Interea tamen in hac consuetudine civili utendum esse politicis ordinationibus eorum locorum, ubi vivimus, si tamen congruant cum lege naturae.

## 8:1 Argument
Chapter VIII.

Περὶ δὲ τῶν εἰδωλοθύτων οἴδαμεν.

At the beginning, let the custom be considered, which the Gentiles received from their fathers, and which they retained even after the true doctrine was lost.

When a sacrifice was made on feast days, a part of the victim was burned, a part belonged to the Priests, and a part was common to the head of the household and the others who had given the victims. And there were many peculiar sacrifices of certain families, in which relatives frequently gathered, and brought parts of the victims from the shrine into their homes, just as the old man in Aristophanes in the Plutus brings a part of the victim home. Some also feasted at the shrines together with the Priests. It is credible, however, that some who had already cast off the worship of idols were nevertheless called by their relatives to the feasts. And it could hardly happen that a pious wife would not be present at the feast of an ethnic husband.

In such cases we see that Paul used some ἐπιεικείᾳ and permitted that those nearby should be present not at the sacrifices, but at the feasts. Some, however, as happens, relaxed that permission too much, and ate the meat of the victims by a bad example, that is, they invited others who were weaker so that they too would eat, whose consciences were afterwards troubled. For they condemned themselves, as if they were confirming an impious custom. Whenever, however, a conscience condemns itself, it judges that it is acting against God. Wherefore faith is shaken, and invocation is hindered.

Now, therefore, Paul restricts that permission, and here he preaches only about Scandal; afterwards, he restricts it again in general, because however much it may be excused, there is still something of evil in the example. For the custom of those worshipping idols will be confirmed.

But here mention is made by name of this scandal, that the learned were moving the weaker ones to eat, and the consciences of these were afterwards wounded, just as various cases have happened in our time, where by the imitation of liberty, even in rightly done things, weak consciences have been greatly troubled.

Paul therefore rebukes the learned who are pleased with themselves, and those who are bold in unnecessary matters, as many are for the sake of showing off their erudition and wisdom. And he repeats here the rule handed down in Romans 14: He teaches that necessary things must be done: But in non-necessary things, which are only permitted, that moderation must be observed, so that our examples do not harm the consciences of others, or undermine common concord, just as the rule of the Jurisconsults rightly teaches: What does not harm you, and benefits another, that is to be performed. It is therefore just to restrict liberty for the sake of the salvation of others, just as one who is robust on a journey hastens less for the sake of weak companions.

This rule, which warns that a distinction must be maintained between necessary and non-necessary things, has great use in the whole of life, and restrains many vices, πολυπραγμοσύνην, arrogance, and others.

This is the summary of the chapter, which I have reviewed. Furthermore, many sayings are inserted, which contain excellent doctrine: Knowledge puffs up, Love builds up. This saying warns that knowledge is not a virtue, nor a work pleasing to God without the obedience of the will, as philosophy also teaches, that knowledge is not a virtue. But it is necessary that the conversion of the will to God should follow, by which the will is subjected to God, and possesses προαίρεσιν, or, as they commonly say, a good purpose of doing rightly, according to that: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart.

There exists here also a testimony concerning the true God revealed in the mission of the Son, crucified and resurrected, distinguishing Him from all other deities which are thought of or worshipped outside of this God. For the meaning of this testimony is exclusive, that besides this revealed God there is no other eternal deity. Therefore, it leads us in the knowledge of God to this one, who revealed Himself by giving promises, performing miracles, and sending His Son. He wants us to look to Him while praying, and He wants us to separate our invocation from that of the heathens and others. Therefore He spoke thus: There is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, as if He were saying: I wish the fictitious gods of the nations to be excluded from divinity, and I affirm that there is one God; whom truly, and where is He to be acknowledged? This one, I say, who is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and who revealed Himself by sending His Son. Thinking therefore of God, look to this Father and Son. For He attributes divinity also to the Son, when He says: Through whom are all things. Nor does He exclude the Holy Spirit, but, as I said, the exclusive is opposed to all fictitious deities, just as it is often said in the Prophets, as in Isaiah 44: Besides me there is no God, says Jehovah the King of Israel, that is, besides me revealed in Israel.

Latin:

Caput VIII.

Περὶ δὲ τῶν εἰδωλοθύτων οἴδαμεν.

Initio mos consideretur, quam acceptum a patribus Ethnici, postea etiam amissa vera do- ctrina retinuerunt.

Cum in diebus festis sacrificium fiebat, pars victimae incendebatur, pars erat propria Sacerdo- tum, pars communis patrifamilias et caeteris, qui victimas dederant. Et erant multa peculiaria cer- tarum familiarum sacrificia, in quibus cognati frequentes conveniebant, et a sacello victimae partes in suas domos afferebant, ut senex apud Aristophanem in Pluto victimae partem domum affert. Aliqui etiam ad sacella una cum Sacer- dotibus convivabantur. Credibile est autem, ali- quos, qui iam abiecerant cultum idolorum, tamen a cognatis ad convivia vocatos esse. Et vix fieri potuit, quin mariti ethnici convivio interesset uxor pia.

In talibus casibus videmus Paulum aliqua ἐπιεικείᾳ usum esse ac permisisse, ut proximi in- teressent non sacrificiis, sed conviviis. Aliqui autem, ut fit, illam permissionem nimium laxa- bant, et victimarum carne vescebantur malo exem- plo, id est, invitabant alios imbecilliores, ut ipsi quoque vescerentur, quorum conscientiae postea turbabantur. Damnabant enim sese, quasi consuetudinem impiam confirmarent. Quando- cunque autem conscientia sese damnat, iudicat se contra Deum facere. Quare fides excutitur, et impeditur invocatio.

Nunc igitur Paulus illam permissionem astringit, et hic tantum de Scandalo concionatur, postea rursus in genere astringit, quia quoquo modo excusetur, tamen aliquid in exemplo mali est. Nam consuetudo colentium idola confir- mabitur.

Sed hic nominatim fit mentio huius scandali, quod eruditi movebant imbecilliores, ut vesceren- tur, et horum postea sauciebantur conscientiae, ut varii casus nostro tempore acciderunt, ubi imi- tatione libertatis etiam in recte factis imbecilles conscientiae valde turbatae sunt.

Obiurgat igitur Paulus doctos sibi placentes, et audaces in rebus non necessariis, ut sunt multi propter ostentationem suae eruditionis et sapien- tiae. Et regulam Roman. 14. traditam, hic re- petit: Docet necessaria facienda esse: In non ne- cessariis vero, quae tantum licita sunt, eam mo- derationem servandam esse, ne exempla nostra laedant aliorum conscientias, aut labefactent com- munem concordiam, sicut regula Iurisconsulto- rum recte docet: Quod tibi non nocet, et alteri prodest, id praestandum est. Iustum est igitur astringere libertatem propter aliorum salutem, ut itinere faciendo robustus minus properat propter imbecilles comites.

Haec regula, quae monet servandum esse discrimen inter necessaria et non necessaria, ma- gnum usum habet in universa vita, et coërcet multa vitia, πολυπραγμοσύνην, arrogantiam, et alia.

Haec est summa capitis, quam recensui. Caeterum dicta multa inserta sunt, doctrinam exi- miam continent: Scientia inflat, Dilectio aedifi- cat. Hoc dictum monet, Cognitionem non esse virtutem, nec opus placens Deo sine obedientia voluntatis, ut etiam philosophia docet, Cogni- tionem non esse virtutem. Sed necesse est acce- dere voluntatis conversionem ad Deum, qua vo- luntas Deo subiicitur, et habet προαίρεσιν, seu, ut loquuntur usitate, bonum propositum recte faciendi, iuxta illud: Diligas Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo.

Extat hic etiam testimonium de vero Deo patefacto in missione filii, crucifixi et resusci- tati, discernendo ab omnibus aliis numinibus, quae extra hunc Deum cogitantur aut coluntur. Nam huius testimonii sententia exclusiva est, praeter hunc patefactum Deum nihil aliud esse numen aeternum. Deducit igitur nos in agni- tione Dei ad hunc unum, qui se patefecit datis promissionibus, editis miraculis, et misso filio. In hunc vult nos intueri invocantes, et vult nos separare invocationem nostram ab ethnica, et aliis. Ideo sic locutus est: Unus est Deus, Pater, ex quo sunt omnia, et unus Dominus Iesus Chri- stus, quasi dicat: Volo excludi a divinitate, gen- tium commentitios Deos, et affirmo unum esse Deum, quem vero, et ubi agnoscendum? Hunc inquam, qui est pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, et qui se patefecit misso filio. Cogitans igitur Deum, intuere hunc patrem filium. Tribuit enim et filio divinitatem, cum inquit: Per quem sunt omnia. Nec excludit Spiritum sanctum, sed, ut dixi, exclusiva opponitur omnibus commentitiis numinibus, sicut plerunque in Prophetis dicitur, ut Esaiae 44.: Praeter me non est Deus, dicit Iehova rex Israël, id est, praeter me patefactum in Israël.

## 9:1 Argument
New chapter.

The first and longer part is consumed in this precept: that a living is owed to those who teach the Gospel, and he confirms this precept with many examples, and with a Mosaic allegory and the command of Christ.

This is the Mosaic allegory: You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain. He elegantly transfers this image of rites to be observed among cattle to men who perform works: As it is necessary for the herd to be fed, so much more is it necessary for the man whose labors we enjoy to be fed.

But what he says: Is it for oxen that God is concerned? does not remove providence, but says only this: That laws are not written for the sake of oxen, but for the sake of the discipline of men, namely, that men may learn just duties.

Paul adds, however, that he did not use this right, to ask that he be fed by the Corinthians, lest the malevolent should deform the Gospel with this calumny, that a doctrine was being peddled which was a means for teachers to seek money, and to avoid calumnies, he says that he even tolerates many things which it was not necessary to bear, where by his own example he teaches that a leader ought both to do necessary things, and to endure not only the cruelty of tyrants, which he cannot repel: but also the injuries of friends, with whom although he could contend, yet he forgives them for the sake of common tranquility, lest wills be alienated which can be retained and advanced. Therefore πάντα στέγομεν, which signifies either to sustain an imposed burden, as columns sustain a roof, or to contain, as a vessel contains a congius of wine. But the former meaning of bearing a burden is more appropriate here. I not only tolerate the cruelty of Nero and the Pharisees, but I also sustain another burden, namely the moroseness and ingratitude of the brethren, and I conceal my own pain. He teaches therefore by his illustrious example that ἐπιείκειαν (forbearance) is necessary for a leader, tolerating the infirmities and injuries of many people. Just as he says later: I have become all things to all men. And that saying is often cited against excessive severity, which exists in the Greek Epistles: Know that you are imitating instruments, which are discordant when too loose, but break when too tight. And the same is true of servants. For relaxation produces discord in discipline, but tension produces a dissolution of nature. And in this one must understand that a measure in all things is best.

The Holy Spirit often commands concerning this very equity, as in Ecclesiastes 7: Do not be righteous too much. And Paul says of himself: I am a debtor to the wise and the unwise, that is, I ought to adapt myself to the capacity of the weak, and not immediately demand perfection harshly. And 1 Thessalonians 2: As a nursing mother I cherished infants. Let us obey these exhortations concerning equity, and tolerate the infirmities of friends for the sake of public concord, as it is commonly said: You should know the habits of a friend, not hate them. Paul repeats this sentiment in this chapter, and afterwards a few times, meanwhile however he retains the regu- lation, that it is necessary to do necessary things. Therefore he says: Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel. And this very statement testifies that obedience to the commandments is necessary, and not something ἀδιάφορον, as the Antinomians imagine.

Πᾶς δὲ ὁ ἀγωνιζόμενος. But everyone who competes.

After he previously said many things about the equity adjusting ἀδιάφορα to the utility of those among whom we live: now he adds a general rule necessary in all life, which contains the doctrine of Diligence, which is prudence in looking toward the end, and the means to the end, and the intention of the mind in preparing and maintaining those means. And this rule is: So run, that you may look toward the goal, and the means and that goal leading rightly. This admonition is also proposed in Ethics, and although it is necessary in the whole of life, yet often through our foolishness or depraved desires we act against it, and run as if outside the path. It is necessary that these errors be understood, so that they may be avoided. Let virtue therefore be Diligence, as I have said, deliberation about the end and the means, and a certain contention of the will, and constancy in maintaining the means.

The opposite vices are: Sloth and πολυπραγμοσύνη arising from various causes, from a restless nature, from stubbornness, from ambition, from avarice, from the desire to dominate, from emulation and similar diseases.

Scipio in his course looks toward this end, that the fatherland may be blessed, he chooses the means, the labors of military service and legitimate commands, and he does not covet power against the laws, or any extraordinary advantages, nay, so that he may not disturb the fatherland, he yields to turbulent citizens, and accepts injuries.

Pericles has the same end proposed, that the fatherland may be blessed, and excel the rest of Greece: but he does not rightly choose the means, and he sins by unjust stubbornness, when he proposes harsher edicts against the Aeginetans, and irritates the Lacedaemonians.

Alcibiades, Pompey, and many others, err concerning the end and the means. They want themselves to be the highest, not the fatherland to be blessed, and by many contrary counsels they bring destruction upon themselves. Alcibiades now sides with the citizens, now with the Lacedaemonians, now he is a friend to Tissaphernes, now to Pharnabazus.

Now let us compare examples in the Church: for Jeremiah, the Baptist, Paul, the goal is proposed, that the doctrine be purely propagated, for the sake of the glory of God, and that they themselves may be saved. For this end they choose the means, they sustain the labors of teaching, where they can, they invite listeners with good examples, they confirm the teachable, they tolerate the more ignorant, they restrain all desires, so that they may neither deform the doctrine, nor disturb the Church, nor offend God.

On the other hand, Carlstadt, although he has the end proposed that the doctrine of the Gospel be purely propagated, yet he often errs concerning the means, he makes a tumult about articles either false or unnecessary, he condemns all forensic offices and Roman laws, he fights about Stoic necessity, he often yields to his own desires, to anger, to ambition, to avarice, and he alienates listeners, and offends God. Although therefore he has an ill-considered zeal, yet he does not arrive at the goal.

They sin more, who look toward neither a just end, nor rightly seek the means, like Münzer, the Anabaptist king, the Pontiffs, who do not seek this, that the doctrine be rightly propagated, or that the Church be blessed, but that they may prepare for themselves power or wealth, or defend them, or that they may safely enjoy pleasures, and they resort to many contrary and impious counsels.

Now it is easy to understand the text: All run, but one receives the prize, namely he who has directed his mind, counsels, and will to the just end, which he names below: Do all things for the glory of God, and be not a scandal to the Church, that is, he who especially wants this, that God be truly invoked, that the Church be blessed. And he rightly chooses the means, he rightly teaches necessary things, he restrains private desires. And thus Paul runs: ὡς οὐκ ἀδήλως, not with blind impulse, without thought of the end, not without prudence choosing salutary means, not with ill-considered zeal, as we have seen many run in these years, not bad men, but not rightly choosing the means, like Hutten and others.

Οὕτως πυκτεύω. Thus I fight.

As the former similitude is taken from a wandering course, so this one is taken from a pugilist, who does not strike his antagonist, but, missing, strikes his gauntlet into the neighboring air. But the meaning is the same. For this similitude also signifies those who either tumultuously act without any proposed end, as many fanatics, or other light men: or even if they look upon a true end, yet they either neglect the means, or do not rightly apply them. Such, when they labor in vain, are said to beat the air themselves. As in public government teachers beat the air, who contend about unnecessary and uncertain things, while meanwhile they leave behind necessary things, as those who litigate about the form of a garment in the Liturgy: or in private life monks sought many useless rites. As Carthusian abstinence from meat or malevolence, and yet to profess a zeal for religion, is also beating the air. These images of the race and the contest of boxers depict diligence looking toward the end and the means, because it behooves the runner to look at the goal, the boxer to strike the antagonist. And let both see the means necessary for their own contest. Now therefore he speaks about the means, he says he restrains vicious desires, ambition, the desire for revenge, avarice, the fires of lusts. He has used, however, significant words: It is much more to ὑπωπιάζειν than to restrain. For ὑπώπια signifies swellings arisen from blows. Hence is ὑπωπιάζω, I beat the body so harshly that the bruised parts swell and become livid, both of which happen because by the striking the blood is shaken out from its own vessels and gathers around the struck place, where, deprived of its own heat, it becomes pus. Although a distinction is handed down between these, ὑπώπιον a spot, ὑπόπυον purulent, and πελιώματα bruises, nevertheless they are related, just as the effects are joined, namely putrefaction and the pallor or lividness of the skin. Paul therefore signifies the hard repressions of the affections, which are done with some pain. As tolerance in dissembling detraction, and in bearing injuries, which represses the desire for glory or revenge, cannot be performed without a sharp sense of pain, as Juvenal says: But revenge is a good, sweeter than life itself. Someone powerful in authority criticizes a sentiment rightly handed down by you, and seems to detract something from your authority; it is often profitable to dissemble this injury, but it cannot be done without pain. Thus other more ardent affections are not repressed without pain, Anger, Love. If you are inflamed with an unjust love, custom must be avoided, the eyes must be governed, the mind must be turned away by some labor or study, which demands assiduity or intention. All these he calls to beat the body harshly, and to bring into servitude, that is, to compel, so that the heart, eyes, tongue, and other members may easily obey the judgment of the mind. He says he does these things, lest he lose the inheritance of eternal life. Here again he admonishes that new obedience is necessary, and is not something ἀδιάφορον.

Since, however, some have cited this passage to confirm the exercises of monks, a few things must also be said about that accommodation.

Paul speaks in general about the necessary and serious repression of desires, he does not speak about Ceremonies and Simulation. As Tetzel does not therefore repress ambition because he wears the sordid garment of monks. Thus he does not therefore repress the flames of love because he does not eat meat on the sixth day. True and serious diligence in curbing vicious desires is always necessary. As temperance is always necessary, the fasting of certain days is not necessary, but should be left to the judgment of each person. He speaks, however, about necessary virtues and their serious exercises, about repressing ambition, φιλονεικίᾳ, irascibility, emulation, avarice, about extinguishing the fires of lusts, and other evils.

Latin:

Caput novum.

Prima pars et longior consumitur in hoc praecepto: Docentibus Evangelium deberi vi- ctum, idque praeceptum confirmat multis exem- plis, et allegoria Mosaica et mandato Christi.

Allegoria Mosaica haec est: Non ligabis os bovi trituranti. Hanc imaginem ritus servandi in armento eleganter transfert ad homines, qui fa- ciunt operas: Ut necesse est armentum pasci, ita multo magis hominem, cuius laboribus fruimur ali necesse est.

Quod autem inquit: Num boves Deo curae sunt? non tollit providentiam, sed hoc tantum dicit: Non scribi leges boum causa, sed disci- plinae hominum causa, videlicet, ut homines discant iusta officia.

Addit autem Paulus, se hoc iure non usum esse, ut ali se a Corinthiis peteret, ne malevoli hac calumnia Evangelium deformarent, circum- ferri doctrinam, quae doctoribus aucupium esset quaerendae pecuniae, et ut vitet calumnias, ait se etiam multa tolerare, quae non necesse erat ferri, ubi suo exemplo docet, gubernatorem opor- tere et necessaria facere, et perferre non solum saevitiam tyrannorum, quam depellere non po- test: sed etiam iniurias amicorum, quibus cum adversari posset, tamen eos condonet communi tranquillitati, ne alienentur voluntates, quae re- tineri et provehi possunt. Ideo πάντα στέγομεν, quod significat, aut onus impositum sustinere, ut columnae sustinent fastigium, aut capere, ut vas capit congium vini. Sed prior significatio de onere ferendo hic est accommodatior. Non so- lum tolero saevitiam Neronis et Pharisaeorum, sed etiam sustineo aliud onus, scilicet fratrum moro- sitates et ingratitudinem, et meum dolorem dis- simulo. Docet igitur exemplo suo illustri, ne- cessariam esse gubernatori ἐπιείκειαν, multos multorum infirmitates et iniurias tolerantem. Si- cut postea dicit: Omnibus omnia factus sum. Et saepe citatur dictum illud contra nimiam severi- tatem, quod extat in Graecis Epistolis: ἴσθι μι- μουμένη τὰ ὄργανα, ἃ διαφωνεῖ μᾶλλον ἀνει- μένα, ἐκρήττεται δὲ μᾶλλον ἐπιτεινόμενα. καὶ γὰρ ἐπὶ τῶν θεραπαινῶν ταυτόν. ἡ μὲν γὰρ ἄνε- σις διαφωνίαν ἐμποιοῦσα τῆς πειθαρχείας, ἡ δὲ ἐπίτασις τῆς ἀνάγκης, διάλυσιν τῆς φύσεως. καὶ ἐπὶ τούτου δεῖ νοεῖν, μέτρον ἐπὶ πᾶσιν ἄρι- στον.

De hac ipsa aequitate saepe praecipit Spiri- tus sanctus, ut Ecclesiastae 7.: Ne sis iustus ni- mis. Et Paulus de sese inquit: Sapientibus et insipientibus debitor sum, id est, attemperare me ad captum imbecillium debeo, nec statim acerbe perfectionem postulare. Et 1. Thesal. 2.: Ut nutricula fovi infantes. His concionibus de aequitate obtemperemus, et amicorum infirmita- tes toleremus publicae concordiae causa, ut usi- tate dicitur: Mores amici noveris, non oderis. Hanc sententiam in hoc capite, et postea aliquo- ties repetit Paulus, interim tamen retinet regu- lam, oportere necessaria facere. Ideo dicit: Vae mihi, si non evangelizavero. Et hoc ipsum di- ctum testatur, obedientiam praeceptorum neces- sariam esse, et non quiddam ἀδιάφορον, ut An- tinomi fingunt.

Πᾶς δὲ ὁ ἀγωνιζόμενος. Omnis autem qui certat.

Postquam antea multa dixit de aequitate at- temperante ἀδιάφορα ad utilitatem eorum, inter quos vivimus: nunc generalem regulam in omni vita necessariam addit, quae continet doctrinam de Diligentia, quae est prudentia in prospiciendo fine, et mediis ad finem, et intentio animi in mediis illis parandis tuendis. Estque haec re- gula: Sic curras, ut metam prospicias, et media et eam metam recte ducentia. Haec commone- factio etiam in Ethicis proponitur, et cum in tota vita necessaria sit, tamen saepe stultitia nostra aut pravis cupiditatibus contra eam facimus, et quasi extra viam currimus. Hos errores intelligi necesse est, ut caveri possint. Sit igitur virtus Diligentia, ut dixi, deliberatio de fine et de mediis, et quaedam voluntatis contentio, et con- stantia in tuendis mediis.

Vitia opposita sunt: Ignavia et πολυπραγ- μοσύνη orta ex variis causis, ex natura inquieta, ex pertinacia, ex ambitione, ex avaricia, ex cu- piditate dominandi, ex aemulatione et similibus morbis.

Scipio in suo cursu hunc finem intuetur, ut patria sit beata, eligit media, labores militiae et legitima imperia, et non concupiscit potentiam contra leges, aut ulla extraordinaria commoda, imo ne turbet patriam, cedit turbulentis civibus, et iniurias accipit.

Habet eundem finem propositum Pericles, ut beata sit patria, et antecellat reliquae Graeciae: sed medio non recte eligit, et peccat iniusta per- tinacia, cum duriora edicta proponit adversus Aeginetas, et irritat Lacedaemonios.

Alcibiades, Pompeius, et multi alii, de fine et de mediis errant. Se volunt summos esse, non beatam patriam, et multis contrariis consiliis ipsi sibi exitium accersunt. Alcibiades nunc cum ci- vibus, nunc cum Lacedaemoniis sentit, nunc Tissapherni, nunc Pharnabazo amicus est.

Iam conferamus exempla in Ecclesia: Iere- miae, Baptistae, Paulo, meta proposita est, ut doctrina pure propagetur, propter gloriam Dei, et ut ipsi salvi fiant. Ad hunc finem eligunt me- dia, sustinent labores docendi, ubi possunt, in- vitant bonis exemplis auditores, confirmant doci- les, tolerant rudiores, frenant omnes cupiditates, ne aut doctrinam deforment, aut turbent Eccle- siam, aut Deum offendant.

Econtra Carolostadius etsi finem propositum habet, ut doctrina Evangelii pure propagetur, tamen de mediis saepe errat, tumultuatur de arti- culis aut falsis, aut non necessariis, damnat om- nia forensia officia et leges Romanas, pugnat de necessitate stoica, saepe obsequitur suis cupidi- tatibus, iracundiae, ambitioni, avariciae, et alienat auditores, et offendit Deum. Etsi igitur studium habet inconsultum, tamen ad metam non pervenit.

Plus peccant, qui nec finem iustum intuen- tur, nec media recte quaerunt, ut Monetarius, rex anabaptisticus, Pontifices, qui non hoc quae- runt, ut doctrina recte propagetur, aut ut Eccle- sia beata sit, sed ut ipsi potentiam aut opes sibi parent, aut defendant, aut ut voluptatibus tuto fruantur, et ad multa contraria et impia consilia decurrunt.

Iam facile est intelligere textum: Omnes currunt, sed unus accipit praemium, scilicet qui direxit mentem, consilia, et voluntatem ad iu- stum finem, quem infra nominat: Omnia ad gloriam Dei facite, et non sitis scandalo Ecclesiae, id est, qui praecipue hoc vult, ut Deus vere in- vocetur, ut Ecclesia beata sit. Et media recte eligit, recte docet necessaria, frenat cupiditates privatas. Et sic currit Paulus: ὡς οὐκ ἀδήλως, non coeco impetu, sine cogitatione finis, non sine prudentia eligente media salutaria, non in- consulto studio, ut currere his annis multos vidi- mus, non malos homines, sed media non recte eligentes, ut Huttenum et alios.

Οὕτως πυκτεύω. Sic pugno.

Ut prior similitudo a vago cursu sumta est, ita haec sumitur a pugile, qui non ferit antago- nistam, sed aberrans, caestum incutit vicinio aëri. Sed sententia eadem est. Significat enim et haec similitudo eos, qui aut nullo fine propo- sito tumultuantur, ut multi fanatici, at alii leves homines: aut etiamsi verum finem intuentur, tamen media vel negligunt, vel non recte adhi- bent. Tales cum frustra laborent, dicuntur et ipsi aërem verberare. Ut in publica gubernatione aërem verberant doctores, qui de non necessariis et incertis dimicant, cum interea relinquant ne- cessaria, ut qui litigant de forma vestis in Litur- gia: aut in privata vita monachi quaerebant multos inutiles ritus. Ut abstinentia carthusiana a carne, prorsus est aërem verberare. Rursus laxare frenum ambitioni, aut male- volentiae, et tamen prae se ferre studium religio- nis, etiam est aërem verberare. Hae imagines cursus, et pugilum certamen, pingunt diligentiam prospicientem finem et media, quia cursorem oportet intueri metam, Pugil feriat antagonistam. Et uterque videat media, suo certamini ne- cessaria. Iam igitur de mediis loquitur, dicit se fre- nare vitiosas cupiditates, ambitionem, cupidita- tem vindictae, avariciam, incendia libidinum. Usus est autem insignibus verbis: Multo plus est ὑπωπιάζειν, quam frenare. Nam ὑπώπια signi- ficat tumores ortos ex plagis. Inde est ὑπωπιάζω, adeo duriter tundo corpus, ut partes quassatae tumescant, et fiant lividae, quorum utrumque eo fit, quia percussione sanguis ex propriis vasis ex- cutitur, et circa locum ictum concurrit, ubi de- stitutus suo calore fit pus. Etsi discrimen tradi- tur inter haec, ὑπώπιον macula, ὑπόπυον puru- lentum, et πελιώματα livores, tamen vicina sunt, situt effectus coniuncti sunt, scilicet putre- factio, et cutis pallor seu livor. Significat igitur Paulus duras repressiones affectuum, quae cum aliquo dolore fiunt. Ut tolerantia in dissimu- landa obtrectatione, et in ferendis iniuriis, quae reprimit gloriae aut vindictae cupiditatem, non potest praestari sine acri sensu doloris, ut inquit Iuvenalis: At vindicta bonum est, vita iucundius ipsa. Reprehendit aliquis valens autoritate sententiam a te recte traditam, et videtur aliquid de tua auto- ritate detrahere, hanc iniuriam saepe prodest dis- simulare, sed sine dolore id fieri non potest. Ita caeteri affectus ardentiores non sine dolore repri- muntur, Ira, Amor. Si es incensus iniusto amo- re, vitanda est consuetudo, oculi regendi, aver- tenda mens est labore aliquo seu studio, quod assiduitatem aut intentionem flagitat. Haec om- nia vocat duriter tundere corpus, et in servitu- tem redigere, id est, cogere, ut mentis iudicio facile obtemperent cor oculi, lingua et caetera membra. Haec se facere inquit, ne amittat hae- reditatem vitae aeternae. Hic rursus admonet, novam obedientiam necessariam esse, nec esse quiddam ἀδιάφορον.

Cum autem nonnulli hunc locum citarint ad confirmanda monachorum exercitia, pauca etiam de ea accommodatione dicenda sunt.

Paulus in genere loquitur de necessaria et seria cupiditatum repressione, non loquitur de Ceremoniis et Simulatione. Ut non ideo reprimit ambitionem Tecelius, quia sordidam vestem mo- nachorum gerit. Sic non ideo reprimit flammas amoris, quia non comedit carnes die sexto. Vera ac seria diligentia coërcendi vitiosas cupiditates semper est necessaria. Ut temperantia semper est necessaria, inedia certorum dierum non est necessaria, sed suo cuiusque iudicio relinquatur. Loquitur autem de virtutibus necessariis et se- riis earum exercitiis, de reprimenda ambitione, φιλονεικίᾳ, iracundia, aemulatione, avaricia, de extinguendis incendiis libidinum, et aliis malis.

## 10:1 Argument
Chapter ten.

After he has entered into this admonition about the diligence of doing good, he now attaches a long sermon, in which he compares the times, falls, and punishments of the Church, so that he may excite us to the zeal of retaining justice, and to avoiding falls. And this is the sentiment: As the fathers perished rushing against conscience, so also you will perish, if you admit similar falls. Therefore with great care and vigilance retain the justice given to you. This is the sum of the argument.

First, therefore, he teaches that in the reconciled, new obedience is necessary, as has often been said.

Secondly, he warns that in all times the Church of God is similar, namely an assembly in which the ministry of the Gospel sounds forth concerning the mediator, and through which many reconciled become heirs of eternal life. And although the voice of the ministry is the same, yet the external signs differ, as Circumcision and Baptism. For they are changed, so that the novelty of the sign may be a reminder of the new restoration of doctrine. There are also dissimilar polities at different times. But the troubles are similar and the ranks of men, some persevere in faith, others fall, and in these Some who have fallen are converted again, as Aaron, David: some who have fallen perish, as Saul, Korah, Dathan and others. He wishes us to contemplate this image of the ancient Church.

From this, thirdly, we learn that those who are truly reconciled can fall, and again lose the Holy Spirit, grace, and faith, because he says clearly here that all were baptized, that is, received by external testimonies, with the cloud covering the people and the waters standing in the sea. These miracles were sacraments, testifying that this people was received. And Paul makes both a type of baptism.

But as to what he says: that they were baptized into Moses, let it be understood that they were baptized by the ministry of Moses, because it is necessary to know that the Word which we embrace has been delivered by divine authority. Therefore Moses is named in that Church, who had been called by illustrious testimonies.

And all ate the same spiritual food, and drank the same spiritual drink.

Here he clearly affirms that believers in the Church of Moses were truly reconciled and reborn by the Holy Spirit. For he interprets the drink: They drank from the spiritual Rock accompanying them, and the Rock was Christ. Here he affirms that the Son of God was present with the people and gave them drink, not only to their bodies, flowing from the rock, but also to their minds, a spiritual drink, namely the Holy Spirit. For he says expressly that the Rock going with them was Christ. It is necessary to remember this testimony, so that we may know that the Son of God has always been present with the Church, is present, and will be present, just as he himself says: My Father is working until now, and I am working. Likewise: I am with you until the end of the age. He calls him the Rock, however, alluding to the mountain ridges toward which they made their journey, from which a river of water burst forth, with the Messiah himself, who was present, pouring out those fountains. Moreover, Christ is the rock pouring out fountains by which eternal life is rendered to us.

᾿Αλλὰ οὐκ ἐν τοῖς πλείοσιν αὐτῶν εὐδόκησεν ὁ θεὸς. But God was not well pleased with most of them.

Since he had said before that all were received, namely the believers, when those huge miracles had been displayed by which God had testified that this people was truly His Church. Now he adds another statement about those who fell, that many, namely those who fell, did not please God, namely because of the offenses which followed afterward, as Paul subsequently recounts certain offenses.

But let the phrase be understood simply: Many displeased God, namely because of their falls. For εὐδοκεῖν is to be well-disposed toward someone, or to take delight in someone, as εὐδόκησε τῷ ξένῳ, he was well-disposed toward the guest. Thus also let that be accepted: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. For the Father affirms that he both loves the Son and rejoices in this Son, and when we think of these things, let Stoic imaginations about God be cast away, and let us establish that, just as there are affections (στοργαὶ) in humans toward their children and parents, so there is truly love and joy in the eternal Father and Son, even if we do not know how these burn in the divine nature. That they exist, however, there is no doubt, and the affections (στοργαὶ) in us are traces of the divine love toward the Son, implanted in us so that they may in some way remind us of God, what He is like, and how He is affected toward His Son and toward His creatures.

These things are to be observed concerning the word εὐδοκεῖν, about which various interpretations are handed down by others.

In the recounting of the offenses, he proposes the examples of the people of Israel and their punishments, so that he may signify that similar sins are constantly wandering about in the Church, and that similar punishments follow.

Although, however, many things are contained universally in one offense, or many things are coupled to one: yet the kinds are distinguished, because there are dissimilar occasions which mix some deeds with other sins, which otherwise concur.

In all the offenses of the people in the desert there is horrible ingratitude, distrust, impatience, or murmuring against God. But at other times other falls are added. And here these kinds are named in order.

I. Intemperance.

II. Idolatry.

III. Fornication.

IV. To tempt God.

V. And murmuring.

Paul, however, looks at the histories of the people of Israel, as I have said, because at the same time he reminds us of the punishments.

Concerning intemperance, there exists a history in Moses in Numbers chapter 11, where the people, already loathing the manna, crave meat: nor is the eating of meat censured, but the loathing of the present gift. And many sins concur, as I have said: the ingratitude of the people, who, when they had been led out by God by such great miracles from Egypt, and already knew that he was being led into the land promised to the Fathers, where God was about to establish a most beautiful polity as a certain seat of the Church: now they remember neither God nor the miracles, but broken by the weariness of the journeys they are angry at Moses, they complain that they were led out of Egypt by human counsel and by his own tyranny. They are also disobedient, as their impatience shows, because they refuse to bear the moderate labor of the journeys. And although there is a moderate supply of food, and they do not labor with hunger, for they enjoy Manna, they are not content with this gift of God, but crave delicacies.

God punishes this intemperance, when indeed other sins are also added. And similar sins occur from time to time in the Church, as now, because we experience difficulties in domestic affairs, and the hatreds and contempt of the powerful against us on account of the profession of the Gospel, many crave that sweet leisure and splendor which they had before the amendment of doctrine. Indeed, some abuse the Gospel to increase intemperance and avarice, and for ostentation and the amplification of splendor. Punishments have therefore followed, wars and other calamities.

Secondly, the adoration of Idols is named. And the words are taken from Moses, chapter 32 of Exodus, where the idle and secure people order an idol to be fashioned. And there is no doubt that the people of Israel fashioned the calf in imitation of the Egyptians, because the Egyptians worshipped Apis in the form of a bull, on account of agriculture. And often men relapse into accustomed idols. But here it should be considered especially how great is the misery of men, that after so many miracles the people nevertheless receive the worship of an idol, which they knew had been condemned by God, and that Aaron assents.

He narrates the cause: The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play. That is, in luxury and in idleness men call upon God more coldly, and with greater audacity invent opinions about God, as often happens in the Church. Samosatenus, Arius, and the like, when they lived in great security, petulantly devised new opinions: and in these recent years many frenzies of opinions have arisen. And those very people, who previously shouted most vehemently against ceremonies, now restore the Mass, in which they know there is a manifest idol.

Thirdly, concerning Whoredom, Paul looks at the history in Numbers chapter 25.

Fourthly, he names the sin: To tempt Christ, an example of which is in the history in Numbers chapter 21, where mention is made of the serpents, and in Exodus 17 Moses used these words: Why do you tempt the Lord?

Although this sin, to tempt God, is very atrocious and often happens, yet because it is more obscure, we will add an explanation by comparison in this way.

Murmuring and tempting God differ. For murmuring is of impatience, which is disobedience angry at God in hardships or punishments. We understand this disobedience in some way, because such groanings and indignations often exist even in the saints, as in Job, Jeremiah, and others.

But tempting God adds another greater sin. It is not only to be angry at God, but also to add besides either a negation or a correction, by reliance on one's own wisdom, as in Exodus they add a negation: Is the Lord among us, or not? Where they contradict manifest miracles as if they had been deceived, and this whole leading out, full of miraculous testimonies of God, had been an imposture.

In Numbers chapter 14 they add a horrible correction from their own wisdom; they want to elect a new leader, by whom they may be led back into Egypt. Afterwards, having been restrained in some way, they want to proceed and fight with the enemies, when indeed God was then prohibiting it. Thus human wisdom often sins; what God commands, it does not want to do, and it seeks other things, which He prohibits. Ahaz does not want to obey the voice of Isaiah, in which God promises him help. Afterwards he seeks the help of impious kings, which are pernicious to himself and to the kingdom. Isaiah says: In silence and hope shall be your strength. But many, on account of impatience and diffidence, seek unjust remedies. Such corrections are tempting God.

This interpretation agrees with the sentence, Matthew 4, where when the devil was the persuader that Christ, omitting the steps, should cast himself down from the pinnacle of the temple through the air, Christ answered: You shall not tempt the Lord your God. For it is clear that this is what Christ wants: corrections of the divine ordinance are not to be made by human curiosity, but a man knowing the command and ordinance of God should remain reverently within these bounds, and give thanks to God, and obey Him. As when we know the command and ordinance of God to be that a man should nourish his life with food and drink, as is written in the first and second chapters of the book of Genesis, one would commit a sin of this kind, that is, he would tempt God, if anyone did not want to use food and drink.

Thus, without any doubt, those who, having abandoned the divine ordinance of marriage, seek celibacy, and indeed pretend that this work is an excellent worship of God, sin and tempt God.

Thus also in Acts chapter 15, Peter says: Why do you tempt God, by placing a yoke upon the necks of the disciples? Here is a manifest correction. They know from the Gospel that sins are forgiven, and men are reconciled, reckoned righteous, sanctified, and become heirs of eternal life on account of the Son of God freely, by faith, not on account of the ceremonies of Moses; they know that the end of the Mosaic polity has come; they know that the promise of Grace pertains to the Israelites and to the Gentiles. They also know that it is by no means permitted for man to institute forms of worship, as it is written: In vain do they worship me with the commandments of men. Although they know all these things, yet some, by human wisdom, wish to establish and amplify the Mosaic polity; they think it is beautiful for the Churches of the Gentiles to imitate the fountain, for the rites to be similar, and for this Pedagogy to be more honorable, just as the ingenious among those converted from the Jews, and those who love their fatherland, were able to devise many elegant arguments according to their own imagination. Such corrections, arising from human wisdom against the wisdom of God already revealed to the Church, Peter calls tempting God.

Thus, he who, having heard the Gospel concerning the free remission of sins on account of the mediator, does not wish to acquiesce, but runs into the desert, devises Monasticism, or similar works, tempts God. Such corrections are altogether a tempting of God.

These examples do not obscurely declare this appellation, tempting God, and it must be known that this sin is not a lapse of ignorance, but of one who knows, who out of deliberate choice, trusting in his own wisdom, righteousness, or strength, departs from the divine command and ordinance, as if contending with God by his own wisdom or strength, namely, either denying that God exists, or denying the works of God, when he has been otherwise convinced, or correcting the ordinance of God with human counsels. The Israelites deny that they were led out by God, and they contradict the manifest testimonies of God, for the reason that not all events respond to their own imaginations. They sin, therefore, by impatience, because they do not wish to obey God, and then they add a new and more atrocious sin: they deny that it is the work of God, of which they had been convinced by most certain miracles; they deny that Moses was a leader appointed by God, but they shout that he is an impostor.

Such sins often happen privately and publicly, in worship, actions, and doctrine. Regarding worship, the examples are manifest: monks, having abandoned the way ordained by God, pretend that their own vows are better forms of worship, and that they merit the remission of sins, and are perfection. Regarding actions, the way is ordained by God, that Pastors should rightly teach the Gospel, and not seek empires, nor stir up wars under the pretext of the evangelical ministry, as the Roman Pontiffs have done and do, and as Struthio and Münzer brought forth new laws, and stirred up seditions, and dreamed that they wished to establish a beautiful state. Regarding doctrine, curiosity has examples in all times. For many always depart from the word of God, and seek either more elegant opinions, or more subtle ones, just as Samosatenus corrupts the saying of John: In the beginning was the word. Monks corrupted the saying: We are justified by faith, namely, formed [faith].

᾿Απώλοντο ὑπὸ τοῦ ὀλοθρευτοῦ.

The text in Numbers chapter 14 says: That all the scouts except Joshua and Caleb were killed by divine sudden death before the people, and it is consistent that many other seditious ones were destroyed at the same time. These things were done through an angel, whom he calls the destroyer. And I believe the appellation was taken from the 12th chapter of Exodus, where it is said: He will not allow the destroyer מַשְׁחִית to enter, with which word the text also uses in the history of Sodom, and it signifies properly the destroyer, one who loses and deletes something. Therefore, in Hebrews chapter eleven, he used the same word concerning the angel going through Egypt. Moreover, God executes punishments even through holy angels, as is manifestly said in the history of Sodom.

Ταῦτα δὲ πάντα τύποι συνέβαινον ἐκείνοις.

Why, he says, Types, when these punishments were not figures, but manifest punishments of crimes? Likewise: Why does he say, that they happened to them as types? I answer: The word, them, does not need to be referred to the types, but to the word, Happened. These punishments overwhelmed them, that is, among them these things were done.

But why does he name Types?

Either he speaks of types generally as examples, or because all bodily punishments are types, that is, signs of eternal punishments, which follow, unless conversion to God takes place. Because bodily punishments are primarily ordained for this purpose, that they may be reminders of the justice and wrath of God, afterwards they are also ordained for this, that they may be useful for peace among men.

Therefore Paul wishes to say this: Those punishments, which history recounts, were figures signifying that God is truly angry at similar sins in the Church at all times, and that eternal punishments will follow, unless conversion takes place, just as the divine voice universally teaches that bodily punishments are reminders of repentance, as Paul says below: When we are judged, we are chastened by the Lord, that we may not be condemned with this world. Likewise: Vexation gives understanding.

Ὥστε ὁ δοκῶν ἑστάναι, βλεπέτω μὴ πέσῃ. Therefore let him who thinks he stands, see that he does not fall.

A useful admonition is that in which this must first be considered, that the reborn can fall, and lose grace and the Holy Spirit, as Christ says manifestly in the parable in Matthew 12. And there are manifest examples, Adam, Aaron, Saul, David, and some repent, like Adam, Aaron, David, some persevere without repentance in their furies, and rush into eternal destruction.

However, the Anabaptists are in an uproar about this question in many ways. Some deny that the elect can fall, some deny that they pour out the Holy Spirit even if they fall, some say that Saul and others were not elect, although they had true faith.

But let us oppose to all these this common saying of Paul: Let him who stands, see that he does not fall. That the elect can fall and lose grace and the Holy Spirit is testified to by the saddest examples of Adam and Aaron, of whom it is said in Deuteronomy chapter 9: The Lord was very angry with Aaron, and wished to destroy him. And there are very many sad and atrocious falls of very many saints, such as David, Solomon, Peter, and others, from which, however, being recalled through repentance, they are raised up by faith, and are again gifted with grace and the Holy Spirit, and become heirs of eternal life.

And Christ, knowing the immense weakness of men, commands to forgive seventy times seven, Matthew 18.

Therefore the errors of the Cathari are to be exploded, and the falls of the saints are not to be extenuated, but rather the whole doctrine of repentance is to be known and exercised.

But that in some, who had the beginnings of faith, who have afterwards fallen and do not return, that faith, before it is cast off, is true, the saying of Peter testifies in 2 Peter 2: They capture them with enticements, who had truly escaped, τοὺς ὄντως ἀποφυγόντας. Likewise: For when these, who had escaped the contaminations of the world in the knowledge of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, are again entangled in the same and succumb, the last things become worse for them than the first.

And Matthew 12, the Lord expressly says that the unclean spirit had been cast out, and the house swept and garnished. There is no doubt that this is said of one truly justified. And Saul was truly just, because the text says: The Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul. Nor would such be called fallen if they had never been just. Let us be content with this brief admonition in this place.

Πειρασμὸς ὑμᾶς οὐκ εἴληφεν, εἰ μὴ ἀνθρώπινος. Temptation has not apprehended you, except human.

Let the antithesis of human and diabolical temptation be considered. And Paul mitigates the rebuke of the Corinthians, so that he may console them, lest, broken by despair, they fall away from God entirely.

Although, however, the sin which he recounted above concerning the incestuous man who had relations with his stepmother was atrocious, and others had committed other sins, they were contending with rivalry and hatreds: nevertheless, he wishes these sins to be distinguished from blasphemies, just as John distinguishes sins unto death from sins not unto death.

Diabolical temptation is when Satan enters into the heart, or, as is said in Luke, when Satan snatches the Word of God from the heart of man, such as Epicurean contempt of God, as in Rabshakeh, or hatred and anger against God, as in Saul, or the attacking of the truth, or the rabid defense of an impious dogma. Such were the temptations of Cain, Saul, Judas, Samosatenus, Arius, and the like, ignited by the devil impelling their minds and strengthening the darkness, and as it is written concerning Judas, the devil having entered into their hearts.

Although, however, this huge evil cannot be grasped by the judgment of reason, how great a misery it is for the devil to rule in the heart of man: nevertheless, since the statements in the prophetic and apostolic narratives are manifest, let all men be terrified by the thought of such a great evil, and let them pray that the Son

of God may drive away the devils, according to that saying: No one shall snatch my sheep from my hands.

Human temptation is doubt, or error, or a fall arising from human infirmity, with the madness not yet so confirmed that the mind is Epicurean, so that there follows a persecution of the acknowledged truth or hatred of God. David's fall was very sad, and the devil laid snares for him not lightly, but yet he could not drive him to Epicurean contempt or hatred of God, as he drove Saul.

Perhaps Paul in this very description looks at the distinction between the first crime of the devil and the first fall of men. The crime of the devil was blasphemy, because since he knew God more closely, and was not driven by anything else, by his own counsel and will he proudly despised God and the Son of God.

But the first parents fell, having been driven by another source.

But although it is very difficult for men to judge these things, yet the distinction must be considered in some way, and it must be thought how various and horrible falls are curable and incurable, and minds must be stirred to the fear of God and to invocation, just as Peter commands: Be sober, and watch, because your adversary, the devil, goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour, whom resist, strong in the faith.

Latin:

Caput decimum.

Postquam ingressus est in hanc commone- factionem de diligentia bene operandi, iam at- texit longam concionem, in qua confert Eccle- siae tempora, lapsus et poenas, ut nos excitet ad studium retinendae iusticiae, et ad cavendos lapsus. Estque haec sententia: Ut patres perie- runt ruentes contra conscientiam, ita et vos per- ibitis, si similes lapsus admittetis. Igitur ma- gna cura et vigilantia retinete iusticiam vobis do- natam. Haec est argumenti summa.

Primum igitur docet, in reconciliatis novam obedientiam necessariam esse, ut saepe di- ctum est.

Secundo monet, omnibus temporibus esse Ecclesiam Dei similem, scilicet coetum, in quo sonat ministerium Evangelii de mediatore, et per quod multi reconciliati fiunt haeredes vitae aeter- nae. Et quanquam vox ministerii eadem est, ta- men externa signa differunt, ut Circumcisio et Baptismus. Mutantur enim, ut novitas signi sit commonefactrix de nova instauratione doctrinae. Sunt etiam dissimiles politiae diversis temporibus. Sed aerumnae sunt similes et gradus hominum, alii perseverant in fide, alii labuntur, et in his aliqui lapsi rursus convertuntur, ut Aaron, David: aliqui lapsi pereunt, ut Saul, Chore, Dathan et alii. Hanc imaginem Ecclesiae veteris vult nos intueri.

Hinc tertio discimus vere reconciliatos posse labi, et rursus amittere Spiritum sanctum, gratiam et fidem, quia hic clare dicit, Omnes baptizatos esse, id est, receptos externis testimoniis, nube tegente populum, et undis stantibus in mari. Haec miracula fuerunt sacramenta, testificantia hunc populum recipi. Et Paulus utrunque facit typum baptismi.

Quod autem inquit: In Moysen baptizatos esse, intelligatur, ministerio Moysi baptizatos esse, quia necesse est scire, Verbum, quod amplectimur, divina autoritate traditum esse. Ideo nominatur in ea Ecclesia Moyses, qui illustribus testimoniis vocatus erat.

Et omnes eundem cibum spiritualem manducarunt, et eundem potum spiritualem biberunt.

Hic clare affirmat credentes in Ecclesia Moysi vere reconciliatos esse, et a Spiritu sancto renatos. Interpretatur enim potum: Biberunt ex spirituali comitante eos Petra, Petra autem erat Christus. Hic affirmat, filium Dei affuisse populo, et dedisse potum, non modo corporibus, fluentem ex rupe, sed etiam mentibus spiritualem, scilicet Spiritum sanctum. Expresse enim inquit, Petram una euntem fuisse Christum. Hoc testimonium necesse est meminisse, ut sciamus semper Ecclesiae interfuisse, interesse, et interfuturum esse filium Dei, sicut ipse dicit: Pater meus usque modo operatur, et ego operor. Item: Maneo vobiscum usque ad consummationem seculi. Nominat autem eum Petram, alludens ad iuga montium, ad quae iter fecerunt, ex quibus flumen aquae erupit, ipso Messia fundente eos fontes, qui aderat. Est autem Christus rupes fundens fontes, quibus redditur nobis vita aeterna.

᾿Αλλὰ οὐκ ἐν τοῖς πλείοσιν αὐτῶν εὐδόκησεν ὁ θεὸς. Sed non in pluribus eorum beneplacitum erat Deo.

Cum antea dixisset, receptos esse omnes, scilicet credentes, cum illa ingentia miracula exhibita essent, quibus Deus testificatus fuerat vere hunc populum Ecclesiam suam esse. Nunc addit alteram sententiam de lapsis, multos, scilicet lapsos non placuisse Deo, scilicet propter delicta, quae postea secuta sunt, ut deinceps Paulus delicta quaedam recitat.

At phrasis simpliciter intelligatur: Multi displicuerunt Deo, scilicet propter lapsus. Nam εὐδοκεῖν est bene affici erga aliquem, seu delectari aliquo, ut εὐδόκησε τῷ ξένῳ, bene afficiebatur erga hospitem. Sic et illud accipiatur: Hic est filius meus dilectus, quo delector. Affirmat enim pater, se et amare filium, et laetari hoc filio, quae cum cogitamus, abiiciantur stoicae imaginationes de Deo, et statuamus, ut in hominibus sunt στοργαὶ erga natos et parentes, ita vere esse in patre aeterno et filio amorem, laetitiam, etiamsi nescimus, quomodo haec in divina natura flagrent. Esse tamen, non dubium est, et στοργαὶ in nobis sunt vestigia divini amoris erga filium, nobis insita, ut aliquo modo commonefaciant nos de Deo, qualis sit, et quomodo erga filium et erga suas creaturas affectus sit.

Haec de vocabulo εὐδοκεῖν observanda sunt, de quo variae interpretationes ab aliis traduntur.

In recitatione delictorum exempla populi Israël et poenas proponit, ut significet, similia peccata subinde vagari in Ecclesia, et sequi poenas similes.

Etsi autem universaliter in uno delicto multa insunt, seu uni multa copulata sunt: tamen genera discernuntur, quia dissimiles occasiones sunt, quae miscent alias alia facta caeteris peccatis, quae alioqui concurrunt.

In omnibus delictis populi in deserto sunt horrenda ingratitudo, diffidentia, impatientia seu fremitus adversus Deum. Sed alias accedunt alii lapsus. Et hic nominantur ordine haec genera.

I. Intemperantia.

II. Idolorum cultus.

III. Scortatio.

IV. Tentare Deum.

V. Et murmuratio.

Intuetur autem Paulus historias populi Israël, ut dixi, quia simul nos de poenis commonefacit.

De Intemperantia extat historia apud Moysen in Numeris capite 11., ubi populus fastidiens iam Manna adpetit carnes: nec esus carnium taxatur, sed fastidium praesentis doni. Et concurrunt multa peccata ut dixi: Ingratitudo populi, qui cum a Deo tantis miraculis eductus esset ex Aegypto, et sciret iam se in terram promissam Patribus duci, ubi pulcerrimam politiam tan- quam sedem Ecclesiae certam Deus conditurus erat: nunc nec Deum nec miracula recordantur, sed taedio itinerum fracti irascuntur Moysi, quae- runtur se humano consilio, et ipsius tyrannide ex Aegypto eductos esse. Sunt et inobedientes, ut ostendit impatientia, quia mediocrem laborem itinerum recusant ferre. Cumque mediocris co- pia sit victus, nec laborent fame, fruuntur enim Manna, non contenti sunt hoc dono Dei, sed ap- petunt delicias.

Hanc intemperantiam, cum quidem et alia peccata accedunt, punit Deus. Et similia peccata subinde in Ecclesia accedunt, ut nunc, quia dif- ficultates in re familiari, et potentum adversus nos odia et contemtum experimur propter pro- fessionem Evangelii, multi appetunt suave illud otium et splendorem, quem habuerunt ante emendationem doctrinae. Imo aliqui abutuntur Evangelio ad augendam intemperantiam et avari- ciam, et ad ostentationem et splendoris ampli- ficationem. Secutae sunt igitur poenae, bella et aliae calamitates.

Secundo nominatur adoratio Idolorum. Et verba sumuntur ex Moyse capite 32. Exodi, ubi populus otiosus et securus iubet fabricari idolum. Nec dubium est populum Israël imitatione Aegy- ptiorum fabricasse vitulum, quia Aegyptii colue- runt Apin specie tauri, propter agriculturam. Et saepe homines ad usitata idola relabuntur. Praecipue vero hic consideretur, quanta sit ho- minum miseria, quod post tanta miracula popu- lus tamen recipit idoli cultum, quem sciebat a Deo damnatum esse, et quod Aaron assentitur.

Causam vero narrat: Sedit populus mandu- care et bibere, et surrexit ludere. Id est, in luxu et in otio homines frigidius invocant Deum, et maiore audacia fingunt opiniones de Deo, ut saepe accidit in Ecclesia. Samosatenus, Arius et similes, cum in magna securitate viverent, novas opiniones petulanter excogitarunt: et his proximis annis multi furores opinionum extite- runt. Et illi ipsi, qui antea vehementissime vo- ciferati sunt contra ceremonias, nunc restituunt Missam, in qua sciunt manifestum idolum esse.

Tertio de Scortatione intuetur Paulus histo- riam in Numeris cap. 25.

Quarto nominat peccatum: Tentare Chri- stum, cuius exemplum est in historia in Numeris cap. 21., ubi fit mentio serpentum, et Exodi 17. usus est Moyses his verbis: Cur tentatis Do- minum?

Etsi autem hoc peccatum, tentare Deum, valde atrox est, et saepe accidit, tamen quia obscurius est, declarationem addemus ex colla- tione hoc modo.

Differunt Murmuratio et tentare Deum. Murmuratio enim est impatientiae, quae est inobedientia irascens Deo in aerumnis aut poenis. Hanc inobedientiam intelligimus utcunque, quia saepe et in sanctis existunt tales fremitus et indi- gnationes, ut in Iob, Ieremia et aliis.

Sed tentare Deum addit aliud peccatum ma- ius. Non tantum est irasci Deo, sed etiam insu- per addere vel negationem, vel correctionem, fiducia propriae sapientiae, ut in Exodo addunt negationem: Estne Dominus inter nos, an non? Ubi contradicunt manifestis miraculis quasi de- cepti sint, et tota haec eductio, plena mirabilium testimoniorum Dei, fuerit impostura.

In Numeris capite 14. addunt correctionem horrendam ex sua sapientia, volunt novum du- cem eligere, a quo reducantur in Aegyptum. Postea utcunque repressi, volunt pergere et prae- liari cum hostibus, cum quidem tunc Deus pro- hiberet. Ita saepe humana sapientia peccat, quae iubet Deus, non vult facere, et quaerit alia, quae prohibet. Achas non vult parere voci Esaiae, in qua Deus promittit ei auxilium. Po- stea quaerit impiorum regum auxilia, quae sunt ipsi et regno perniciosa. Esaias dicit: In silen- tio et spe fortitudo vestra. Sed multi propter im- patientiam et diffidentiam quaerunt remedia in- iusta. Tales correctiones sunt tentare Deum.

Haec interpretatio congruit cum sententia, Matth. 4., ubi cum diabolus esset suasor, ut Christus omissis gradibus deiiceret se de fastigio templi per aërem, respondit Christus: Non ten- tabis Dominum Deum tuum. Perspicuum est enim hoc velle Christum: non sunt faciendae correctiones ordinationis divinae humana curiosi- tate, sed homo sciens mandatum et ordinationem Dei manere inter has metas reverenter debet, et Deo gratias agere, et ei obedire.
