Ut cum scia- mus mandatum et ordinationem Dei esse, ut ho- mo vitam cibo et potu foveat, ut in primo et secundo capite libri 1. Moysi scriptum est, Fa- ceret peccatum huius generis, id est, tentaret Deum, si quis nollet uti cibo et potu.

Sic sine ulla dubitatione peccant et tentant Deum, qui omissa divina ordinatione coniugii, quaerunt coelibatum, et quidem fingunt, id opus esse excellentem cultum Dei.

Sic et in Actis cap. 15. inquit Petrus: Quid tentatis Deum, imponentes iugum super cervices discipulorum? Hic manifesta est correctio. Sciunt ex Evangelio remitti peccata, et reconciliari homines, reputari iustos, sanctificari, et fieri haeredes vitae aeternae propter filium Dei gratis, fide, non propter ceremonias Moysi, sciunt finem esse politiae Mosaicae, sciunt promissionem Gratiae pertinere ad Israëlitas et ad Gentes. Sciunt etiam nequaquàm homini licere cultus instituere, sicut scriptum est: Frustra colunt me mandatis hominum. Quanquam autem haec omnia norunt, tamen aliqui humana sapientia volunt stabilire et amplificare politiam Mosaicam, cogitant pulcrum esse, Ecclesias gentium imitari fontem, esse similes ritus, et hanc Paedagogiam esse honestiorem, sicut ingeniosi inter conversos ex Iudaeis, et amantes patriam pro sua imaginatione multa concinna argumenta excogitare poterant. Tales correctiones ortas a sapientia humana contra sapientiam Dei iam Ecclesiae patefactam, nominat Petrus tentare Deum.

Sic tentat Deum is, qui audito Evangelio de remissione peccatorum gratuita propter mediatorem, non vult acquiescere, sed currit in eremum, excogitat Monachatum, aut similia opera. Tales correctiones prorsus sunt tentare Deum.

Haec exempla non obscure declarant hanc appellationem, tentare Deum, ac sciendum est, id peccatum esse non ignorantiae lapsum, sed scientis, qui ἐκ προαιρέσεως fiducia suae sapientiae, iusticiae, aut virium, discedit a mandato et ordinatione divina, tanquam certans cum Deo, sapientia aut viribus propriis, videlicet, aut negans esse Deum, aut opera Dei, cum sit aliter convictus, aut corrigens ordinationem Dei humanis consiliis. Negant Israëlitae, se a Deo eductos esse, et contradicunt manifestis testimoniis Dei, propterea quia non omnes eventus respondent ipsorum imaginationibus. Peccant igitur impatientia, quia Deo nolunt obedire, et deinde addunt novum et atrocius peccatum, negant esse opus Dei, de quo convicti erant certissimis miraculis, negant Moysen esse ducem a Deo constitutum, sed vociferantur eum esse impostorem.

Talia peccata saepe accidunt privatim et publice, in cultibus, actionibus et doctrina. De cultibus exempla manifesta sunt, monachi relicta via a Deo ordinata, fingunt sua vota meliores cultus esse, et mereri remissionem peccatorum, et esse perfectionem. De actionibus via ordinata est a Deo, ut Pastores recte doceant Evangelium, nec quaerant imperia, nec moveant bella praetextu ministerii evangelici, sicut Romani Pontifices fecerunt et faciunt, et sicut Struthio et Monetarius ferebant novas leges, et movebant seditiones, ac somniabant se pulcrum statum velle constituere. De doctrina curiositas omnibus temporibus habet exempla. Semper enim multi discedunt a verbo Dei, et quaerunt vel concinniores opiniones, vel argutiores, ut Samosatenus corrumpit dictum Iohannis: In principio erat verbum. Monachi corruperunt dictum: Fide iustificamur, scilicet formata.

᾿Απώλοντο ὑπὸ τοῦ ὀλοθρευτοῦ.

Textus in Numeris capite 14. inquit: Exploratores omnes praeter Iosuam et Caleb subita nece coram populo divinitus interfectos esse, et consentaneum est, multos seditiosos alios simul extinctos esse. Haec facta sunt per angelum, quem nominat ὀλοθρευτὴν. Et sumtam esse appellationem existimo ex 12. capite Exodi, ubi dicitur: Non sinet ingredi percussorem מַשְׁחִית, quo verbo et in historia de Sodomis textus utitur, et significat proprie ὀλοθρευτὴς perdentem et delentem aliquid. Ideo ad Ebraeos undecimo usus est eodem verbo de angelo eunte per Aegyptum. Exequitur autem Deus poenas etiam per sanctos angelos, ut in historia de Sodomis manifeste dicitur.

Ταῦτα δὲ πάντα τύποι συνέβαινον ἐκείνοις.

Cur inquit, Typi, cum hae poenae non fuerint figurae, sed manifesta supplicia scelerum? Item: Cur dicit, ipsis accidisse ut typos? Respondeo: Vocabulum, Ipsis, non est necesse referre ad typos, sed ad verbum, Acciderunt. Hae poenae obruerunt ipsos, id est, inter ipsos haec facta sunt.

Sed cur nominat Typos?

Vel generaliter dicit typos pro exemplis, vel quia omnes corporales poenae sunt typi, id est, signa aeternarum poenarum, quae sequuntur, nisi fiat conversio ad Deum. Quia corporales poenae principaliter ad hoc ordinatae sunt, ut sint commonefactiones de iusticia et ira Dei, postea etiam sunt ad hoc ordinatae, ut prosint ad pacem inter homines.

Hoc igitur vult dicere Paulus: Illae poenae, quas recitat historia, fuerunt figurae significantes, Deum vere irasci similibus peccatis in Ecclesia omnibus temporibus, et aeternas poenas secuturas esse, nisi fiat conversio, sicut universaliter docet vox divina, corporales poenas esse commonefactiones de poenitentia, ut infra Paulus inquit: Cum iudicamur, a Domino corripimur, ne cum hoc mundo damnemur. Item: Vexatio dat intellectum.

Ὥστε ὁ δοκῶν ἑστάναι, βλεπέτω μὴ πέσῃ. Ideo qui se existimat stare, videat ne cadat.

Admonitio utilis est, in qua primum hoc considerandum est renatos posse labi, et amittere gratiam et Spiritum sanctum, ut manifeste inquit Christus in parabola Matth. 12. Et exempla manifesta sunt, Adam, Aaron, Saul, David, et aliqui resipiscunt, ut Adam, Aaron, David, aliqui sine poenitentia perseverant in suis furoribus, et ruunt in aeternum exitium.

Tumultuantur autem de hac quaestione Anabaptistae multis modis. Aliqui negant electos labi posse, aliqui negant eos effundere Spiritum sanctum, etiamsi labantur, aliqui dicunt Saulem et alios non electos, quanquam habere veram fidem.

Sed his omnibus opponamus hoc commune dictum Pauli: Qui stat, videat ne cadat. Electos posse labi et amittere 'gratiam et Spiritum sanctum, testantur tristissima exempla Adae et Aaronis, de quo dicitur Deut. 9. capite: Adversus Aaron valde iratus est Dominus, et voluit conterere eum. Et sunt valde multi plurimorum sanctorum tristes et atroces lapsus, ut Davidis, Salomonis, Petri et aliorum, ex quibus tamen revocati per poenitentiam fide eriguntur, et rursus donantur gratia et Spiritu sancto, et fiunt haeredes vitae aeternae.

Et Christus sciens ingentem imbecillitatem hominum, iubet remittere septuagies septies, Matth. 18.

Itaque explodendi sunt errores Catharorum, et non sunt extenuandi sanctorum lapsus, sed potius doctrina tota de poenitentia cognoscenda et exercenda est.

Quod autem in aliquibus, qui initia fidei habuerunt, est postea lapsi non redeunt, fides illa, priusquam excutitur, vera sit, dictum Pe- tri testatur 2. Pet. 2.: Illecebris capiunt eos, qui vere effugerant, τοὺς ὄντως ἀποφυγόντας. Item: Cum enim hi, qui effugerant contaminationes mundi in agnitione Domini et servatoris Iesu Christi, rursus iisdem implicati succumbunt, fiunt eis postrema deteriora prioribus.

Et Matth. 12. Dominus expresse dicit, Ex- pulsum fuisse immundum spiritum, et domum purgatam et ornatam. Haec de vere iustificato dici, non dubium est. Et Saul vere iustus fuit, quia textus dicit: Spiritus Domini recessit a Saul. Nec tales dicerentur lapsi, si nunquam iusti fuis- sent. Hac brevi admonitione hoc loco contenti simus.

Πειρασμὸς ὑμᾶς οὐκ εἴληφεν, εἰ μὴ ἀνθρώπινος. Tentatio vos non apprehendit, nisi humana.

Antithesis cogitetur tentationis humanae et diabolicae. Ac mitigat Paulus obiurgationem Corinthiorum, ut eos consoletur, ne fracti despe- ratione prorsus a Deo deficiant.

Quanquam autem erat atrox peccatum, quod supra recitavit de incesto, qui cum noverca con- suetudinem habuit, et alii alia peccata admise- rant, certabant aemulatione et odiis: tamen vult haec peccata discerni a blasphemiis, sicut Iohan- nes discernit peccata ad mortem a peccatis non ad mortem.

Tentatio diabolica est, quando Satanas in cor ingreditur, vel, sicut in Luca dicitur, quando Satanas rapit Verbum Dei ex corde hominis, ut Epicureus contemtus Dei, ut in Rabsace, aut odium et ira adversus Deum, ut in Saule, seu oppugnatio veritatis, seu rabiosa propugnatio impii dogmatis. Tales fuerunt tentationes Cain, Saul, Iudae, Samosateni, Arii, et similium, accensae diabolo impellente mentes, et confir- mante tenebras, et sicut de Iuda scriptum est, Diabolo ingresso in corda eorum.

Etsi autem hoc ingens malum non compre- hendi potest indicio rationis, quanta miseria sit, dominari diabolum in corde hominis: tamen cum manifesta sint dicta in narrationibus pro- pheticis et apostolicis, expavescant omnes homi- nes, cogitatione tanti mali, et petant, ut filius

Dei depellat diabolos, juxta istud dictum: Nemo rapiet oves meas ex manibus meis.

Tentatio humana est dubitatio, vel error vel lapsus ab humana infirmitate ortus, nondum ita confirmato furore, ut mens sit Epicurea, ut accedat persecutio agnitae veritatis aut odium Dei. Valde tristis lapsus fuit Davidis, et diabolus ei non leviter insidiatus est, sed tamen non potuit eum impellere ad Epicureum comtemtum vel odium Dei, ut Saulem impulit.

Fortassis intuetur Paulus in hac ipsa descri- ptione discrimen primi sceleris diaboli, et primi lapsus hominum. Scelus diaboli fuit blasphemia, quia cum propius nosset Deum, et non aliunde impelleretur, suo consilio et arbitrio superbe con- temsit Deum et filium Dei.

Sed primi parentes aliunde impulsi ceci- derunt.

Etsi autem hominibus valde difficile est ista diiudicare, tamen utcunque discrimen conside- randum est, et cogitandum, quam varii et hor- rendi lapsus sint sanabiles et insanabiles, et ex- citandae mentes sunt ad timorem Dei, et ad in- vocationem, sicut praecipit Petrus: Sobrii estote, et vigilate quia adversarius vester, diabolus, tan- quam leo rugiens circumit, quaerens quem devo- ret, cui resistite fortes in fide.

## 10:13
Πιστὸς δ’ ὁ θεὸς ὃς οὐκ ἐάσει. But God is faithful, who will not allow, etc.

Before, he delivered a most severe admonition that we should be vigilant and resist the allurements of desires and the devil. Now he adds consolation concerning divine protection and the help of God. And it is an argument from the possible: Since you both ought to and can resist wicked allurements, do not be slothful. But you can conquer, because God both wards off greater dangers and helps you in your struggles. Therefore he says: God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but will even with the temptation provide a way out, so that you may be able to conquer.

Faithful means beneficent and truthful. He pities our infirmity and has promised help. Therefore he is truly present with us, just as he protected and helped Abraham in the dangers of his wife, and Joseph tempted by the adulteress and afterwards cast into prison, and Moses in his entire governance against Pharaoh and the seditious, so that he would neither be oppressed by enemies nor, broken by despair, fall away from God. And all the pious experience this presence of God at all times, just as David cries out in Psalm 27: The Lord is my helper and my protector, in him my heart has hoped, and I have been helped. And Psalm 90: I am with him in tribulation, I will deliver him and glorify him. And Psalm 144: The Lord lifts up all who are falling, and raises up all who are bowed down.

These and similar sayings most appropriately agree with the saying of Paul in this place.

But since so many, overcome by the devil and their own infirmity, fall into destruction, as the greatest part of the people in the desert, and the parable of the seed in Matthew 13 signifies that very many fall away from God: How does it agree with these sayings that such a multitude is not protected?

I answer: There are always two parts in the Church. One having the beginnings of fear and faith, which although it is weak, yet has the exercises of Repentance and Invocation, and retains the fear of God and faith, of which part it is said: To him who has, it shall be given. Likewise Psalm 144: The Lord is near to all who call upon him, to all who call upon him in truth. Likewise: How much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask? Likewise, Isaiah 66: To whom shall I look, except to the one who is contrite in spirit and trembles at my words.

The other part is secure without the exercises of repentance and invocation, drunk with pleasures, or with admiration and confidence in its own wisdom and justice, like Saul, Ahithophel, Absalom, and countless others. These are overcome by the devil because they are without the fear of God, without the agitation of their own infirmity, without sorrow, nor do they seek the help of God. Therefore let them not accuse God that they are not protected, but themselves, because they themselves by their own madness ward off God, according to those sayings: From him who does not have, even what he has shall be taken away. Likewise, Matthew 12: And coming, he finds the house empty. Then he takes seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and the last state becomes worse than the first. And 2 Peter 2: If after they have escaped the pollutions of the world, they are again entangled in them, the latter state becomes worse than the former.

From these and similar testimonies it is manifest that the saying in Paul is to be understood of those who have the exercises of repentance and invocation: God is faithful, and will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able to bear. You, namely, not raging with security, but having the exercises of repentance and invocation, just as Solomon also says: Blessed is he who is always fearful. And in Zechariah 1 it is said: Turn ye unto me, and I will turn unto you. And in Isaiah 1: cease to do evil, and learn to do well. If your sins be as scarlet, you shall be white as snow. These, therefore, God protects, these He sustains as if with an underlying hand, so that they, wavering or slipping, may not fall into destruction. And in their temptations He governs the outcome, and gives peaceful exits, as is said here: He gives with the temptation an exit or deliverance, so that they may be able to overcome.

But concerning the secure, who do not have the exercises of repentance, it is said in Proverbs, chapter one: Because I have called and you have refused, and have neglected my rebukes, I also will laugh in your destruction.

This distinction having been considered, let us correct our security, and let us stir up invocation. Thus let us know that the sweetest consolation is set before us in these words of Paul.

Φεύγετε ἀπὸ τῆς εἰδωλολατρίας.

He returns to special admonitions, and first he generally prohibits that they be polluted by any contagions of the worship of idols, that is, that they do not approach ethnic sacrifices, likewise that they do not knowingly come into banquets in which it was customary to eat a portion of the consecrated meats. For certain families had their own particular sacrifices, and feast days, in which kinsmen would invite kinsmen.

But it was an impious and foul confusion to profess the acknowledgment of the true God, and either to take part in the sacrifices of idols, or in banquets where a consecrated portion was set forth as if by a certain religion.

He prohibits this confusion from happening, just as now also it is a foul confusion to take part in a procession in which bread is adored, and to understand that the bread in that procession is an idol. Let other similar examples be considered here.

But when mention is made of banquets, Paul makes an antithesis between the Supper of the Lord and the sacrifices and banquets of the heathens, and expressly says that such a confusion of the table of Christ and the table of demons is not to be made. This is the summary of this passage. Now let us consider the words of Paul in order.

Latin:

Πιστὸς δ’ ὁ θεὸς ὃς οὐκ ἐάσει. Fidelis autem Deus est, qui non sinet, etc.

Antea tradidit severissimam admonitionem, ut simus vigilantes, et illecebris cupiditatum ac diabolo repugnemus. Nunc consolationem de protectione divina, et auxilio Dei addit. Et est argumentum a possibili: Cum et debeatis et pos- sitis repugnare pravis illecebris, non sitis ignavi. Potestis autem vincere, quia Deus et pericula maiora arcet, et vobis in vestris certaminibus opitulatur. Ideo inquit: Fidelis Deus, qui non sinet vos tentari, supra quam ferre potestis, imo et cum tentatione dabit eventum, ut vincere possitis.

Fidelis est beneficus et verax. Miseretur infirmitatis nostrae, et promisit auxilium. Ideo vere nobis adest, sicut protexit et adiuvit Abra- ham in periculis uxoris, et Ioseph tentatum ab adultera, et postea coniectum in carcerem, et Moysen in tota gubernatione adversus Pharaonem et seditiosos, ne vel opprimeretur ab hostibus, vel fractus desperatione a Deo deficeret. Et expe- riuntur omnes pii hanc praesentiam Dei omnibus temporibus, sicut clamat David Psalmo 27.: Dominus adiutor meus et protector meus, in ipso speravit cor meum, et adiutus sum. Et Psalm. 90.: Cum ipso sum in tribulatione, eripiam eum et glorificabo eum. Et Psalmo 144.: Allevat Dominus omnes, qui corruunt, et erigit omnes elisos.

Haec et similia dicta propriissime congruunt cum dicto Pauli in hoc loco.

Sed cum tam multi superati a diabolo et sua infirmitate, ruant in exitium, ut maxima pars populi in deserto, et parabola de semine Matth. 13. significat plurimos deficere a Deo: Quomodo congruit ad haec dicta, quod tanta multitudo non protegitur?

Respondeo: Semper in Ecclesia duae sunt partes. Una habens initia timoris et fidei, quae quanquam infirma est, tamen habet exercitia Poenitentiae et Invocationis, et retinet timorem Dei et fidem, de qua parte dicitur: Habenti dabitur. Item Psalmo 144.: Prope est Dominus omnibus invocantibus eum, omnibus invocantibus eum in veritate. Item: Quanto magis pater vester coelestis dabit Spiritum sanctum petentibus? Item, Esaiae 66.: Ad quem respiciam, nisi ad contritum spiritu et trementem sermones meos.

Altera pars est secura sine exercitiis poenitentiae et invocationis, ebria voluptatibus, aut admiratione et fiducia suae sapientiae et iusticiae, ut Saul, Achitophel, Absolon, et alii innumerabiles. Hi superantur a diabolo, quia sunt sine timore Dei, sine agitatione infirmitatis suae, sine dolore, nec expetunt auxilium Dei. Non igitur accusent Deum, quod non proteguntur, sed seipsos, quia ipsi suo furore arcent Deum, iuxta illa dicta: A non habente etiam id quod habet, auferetur. Item, Matth. 12.: Et veniens, invenit domum otiosam. Tunc alios septem spiritus assumit nequiores se, et fiunt novissima peiora prioribus. Et 2. Pet. 2.: Si cum effugeritis contaminationes mundi, rursus eis implicabimini, fiunt posteriora deteriora prioribus.

Ex his et similibus testimoniis manifestum est, dictum in Paulo intelligendum esse de his, qui habent exercitia poenitentiae et invocationem: Fidelis est Deus, nec sinet nos tentari, supra quam ferre potestis. Vos videlicet, non furentes securitate, sed habentes exercitia poenitentiae et invocationis, sicut et Salomon inquit: Beatus qui semper est pavidus. Et Zachar. 1. dicitur: Convertimini ad me, et ego convertar ad vos. Et Esaiae 1.: Desi- nite mala facere, et discite bene facere. Si fue- rint peccata vestra sicut coccinum, eritis candidi sicut nix. Hos igitur protegit Deus, hos susten- tat velut subiecta manu, ut nutantes aut labentes non ruant in exitium. Et in horum tentationibus regit eventus, et dat placidos exitus, sicut hic di- citur: Dat cum tentatione exitum seu liberatio- nem, ut vincere possint.

Sed de securis, qui non habent exercitia poenitentiae, dicitur Proverb. primo: Quia vo- cavi et renuistis, et increpationes meas neglexistis, ego quoque in exitio vestro ridebo.

Hac distinctione considerata securitatem cor- rigamus, et invocationem exuscitemus. Ita no- bis dulcissimam consolationem in his dictis Pauli propositam esse sciamus.

Φεύγετε ἀπὸ τῆς εἰδωλολατρίας.

Redit ad speciales admonitiones, ac primum generaliter prohibet, ne polluantur ullis conta- giis cultus idolorum, id est, ne accedant ad sa- crificia ethnica, item ne scientes veniant in con- vivia, in quibus usitatum erat, vesci parte car- nium consecrata. Habebant enim certae familiae sua quaedam sacrificia, et dies festos, in quibus cognati cognatos vocabant.

Erat autem impia et tetra confusio, profiteri agnitionem veri Dei, et vel interesse sacrificiis idolorum, vel conviviis, ubi pars consecrata quasi religione quadam proponebatur.

Hanc confusionem fieri prohibet, sicut nunc quoque tetra confusio est, interesse pompae, in qua panis adoratur, et intelligere, panem in ea pompa esse idolum. Considerentur hic et alia similia exempla.

Cum autem fiat mentio conviviorum, Pau- lus antithesin facit Coenae Domini, et sacrificio- rum ac conviviorum ethnicorum, et expresse in- quit, non faciendam esse talem confusionem mensae Christi et mensae daemonum. Haec est summa huius loci. Nunc verba Pauli ordine consideremus.

## 10:16
Τὸ ποτήριον τῆς εὐλογίας, ὃ εὐλογοῦμεν: The cup of blessing, which we bless, etc.

It is manifest that Paul is speaking about the Supper of the Lord. It is therefore the cup of blessing, the cup by which the blood of Christ is taken, as the words concerning the institution of the Supper in Matthew, Mark, Luke, and below in chapter 11, sound.

He names it, however, the cup of blessing, and adds: Which we bless, so that he may distinguish this cup from a profane drink, which is drained for the sake of thirst, since this drink is drained not for the irrigation of our body, but so that it may be a reminder of the blood of Christ shed for us.

So that these things may be understood more clearly, let the use of the word to bless be considered, which either signifies to give thanks, as when it is said in Psalm 33: I will bless the Lord at all times. And David in 1 Kings 25: Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who sent you today to meet me.

Either it signifies to pray for good things: or when God blesses, it signifies to do good, because God by speaking brings it about, as it is written in Genesis 48: Jacob blessed his sons, that is, he prayed well for them. And afterwards in the same place: May God bless these boys, that is, by speaking may He do good to them, may He give them good things. Likewise: The blessing of the Lord makes rich, that is, God by speaking increases good things, and guards possessions.

These are the principal meanings of the word to bless, the examples of which are obvious everywhere, and in reading one must prudently judge which is the simple and native meaning.

Moreover, the words εὐλογήσας and εὐχαριστήσας are used interchangeably in Matthew and Mark concerning the Lord's Supper. And the word εὐχαριστήσας shows that the Lord wishes a thanksgiving to be made at the supper. Therefore the simplest explanation will be: The cup of blessing, that is, the cup of thanksgiving, from which we who drink may give thanks to God, and to our Lord Jesus Christ, because we have been redeemed by the blood of Christ, that is, let us acknowledge and celebrate this benefit, and with true faith let us determine that we are received, and for the immense mercy and wondrous plan of redemption let us reverently give thanks, and let there be true gratitude, by which hearts submit themselves to God, and truly call upon Him. I omit the other interpretations.

Thus what follows: The cup which we bless, that is, over which we say the words handed down by the Lord, likewise the thanksgiving and the prayer, all of which together are the rite distinguishing this supper from a profane supper, which feeds our body. For this supper was not instituted for this physical use, but has another end.

An interpretation used by others is, which we bless, that is, which we consecrate. This interpretation, if rightly understood, is not to be blamed. We consecrate, that is, we add sacred words and thanksgiving, so that the use may not be profane or physical, but may be a consolation to the soul. But the mass-priests say, we consecrate, that is, we make a change of substance by the power of the words.

Moreover, Christ is present in His Sacrament, not because the priest makes a change there, or because there is a force in the words changing things, but because He most freely wills to be present at the rite which He instituted, just as the Holy Spirit is most freely present in baptizing.

Is it not the communion of the blood of Christ?

That is, it is that external visible thing by which the blood of the Lord is exhibited to us.

Thus the bread which we break is that external visible thing by which we are made partners and members of the body of Christ. Just as it is said: The Gospel is the power of God, that is, that thing or instrument by which God is effective.

A more recent age of monks invented transubstantiation, which they named with such a new term, concerning which, before I speak, certain things must be said about the nature of the Sacraments.

I shall begin, however, from the very beginning.

The Church of God is gathered by the voice of the promise from the very beginning, soon after the first promise was issued, by which Adam and Eve were received: and God always added external signs to the promise. And not much is written about the signs before the flood. But nevertheless, the very burning of the lamb was a sign.

Then when the promise was renewed and restricted to the posterity of Abraham, a sign was added, namely circumcision.

And subsequently in the Levitical ceremonies there were many signs, the slaughtering of the Paschal lamb. And finally after the advent of the Messiah, Baptism and the Supper of the Lord.

Thus the Church has always been constituted by the voice of the promise and the Sacraments, and distinguished from other nations, and the Fathers and Prophets, and their pious and learned hearers, understood the doctrine concerning the promise of grace and faith, and the true use of the signs. But a great multitude in all ages has always forgotten the doctrine concerning the promise and the righteousness of faith, and has corrupted the use of the signs in many ways.

Others turned the signs into divinities or gods, as the Chaldeans and Persians imagined fire to be God Himself, because they had heard that victims were burned by fire having fallen from heaven.

Others have imagined that rites are works which merit the remission of sins. And with this opinion they have heaped up those works, and have devised not only new ceremonies, but also new divinities and new Gods.

Thus the Pharisees thought that they merited remission by their sacrifices, and they ordered the people to perform slaughters often, so that in this way sins might be blotted out.

These errors have wandered through the human race in all ages.

Thus the Papists carry around bread, and affirm that it is God. And concerning the Mass, concerning monastic rites, they have said that these works merit the remission of sins. And the people, fascinated by this persuasion, have taken care to heap up such ceremonies with great expense.

It is necessary that these foul errors be censured in the Church. And we see the Prophets condemning these frenzies with the most grave and harsh sermons, as in Psalm 49: I will not rebuke you for your sacrifices. And Isaiah 1. And Jeremiah 7: I did not command concerning burnt offerings, where certainly to the Jews the Prophet seemed to fight expressly with the law. And Hosea 6: I desire mercy, not sacrifice: and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.

Finally, such sermons are met with everywhere in the Prophets. I have indicated these passages only so that the younger generation may consider those ancient struggles, and recognize that they are similar to the present ones.

But with the abuses rejected, let there exist in the Church a pure and whole doctrine concerning the righteousness of faith, that man receives the remission of sins, and is reckoned righteous by faith on account of the Son of God freely, not on account of his own worthiness, works, or virtues.

Next, it must be known that there are two primary ends of the Sacraments. The one is that they may be signs of the Promise. The other, that they may be signs of Confession, and distinguish the Church of God from other nations. As circumcision was primarily a sign of the promise. For the promise makes mention of the seed. Therefore in that part the sign was instituted. And thus it is a testimony concerning the will of God toward us, just as the promise itself. And rightly says Augustine: A sacrament is a visible word, that is, it warns of the same thing that the promise does, but it meets the eyes, when the promise is to be received by the ears, and the mind, looking upon the sign, should be reminded of the will of God toward us, that is, of the promise, and should conclude that it itself is accepted according to the promise. And faith should rely upon the mediator himself, not upon this work or sign.

Moreover, God added such signs to the promises, so that the memory of the promises might be firmer and more lasting, because spectacles that strike the eyes move the mind more, and are more easily retained, than bare words.

The second end is that they may be signs of confession and of the distinction of the Church. But this end should not be considered the first or the only one, as the Anabaptists imagined, that Baptism was only a rite invented to distinguish the Church from other men. Rather, the primary end is that it should be a sign of the will of God toward us, namely of the promise; it reminds us that we are certainly immersed into the death of the Son of God, and that on account of him and through him our sins are washed away.

Then other ends follow. And certain signs are properly the nerves of public assemblies, because God always willed the voice of the Gospel to be heard among the human race, and therefore, so that the voice of the Gospel could be spread widely, he willed the Church to be heard and seen, and he instituted honorable public assemblies for the sake of propagating doctrine, and he preserves these by his immense goodness in all ages, despite the raging of the devils. And so that such congregations might be held with greater gravity, he added ceremonies, as panegyric rites, which would be the bonds and nerves of those assemblies.

Let these most grave and most true causes of public rites be considered, and let the imaginations that invent idols and merit be removed far away.

Then also let this most true sentiment be held: that nothing has the nature of a Sacrament outside of its instituted use, because Sacraments are actions ordered in the Church in a certain way. When a rite is changed, or transferred outside of the instituted order to other uses, it is not a Sacrament, but a superstitious action, or an idol; as if a baptism were performed to remove leprosy, such an immersion would not be a Sacrament, just as the circumcision of the Jews at this time, nor does Mahometan circumcision in any way have the nature of a Sacrament.

Thus the bread which is carried around in no way has the nature of a Sacrament, and its adoration is entirely the adoration of an idol, just like the adoration of the Chaldean or Persian fire, which they imagined to be God, and named Oromasda, that is, the sacred light. So also in the papistic oblation, the adoration is the adoration of an idol, because that cult was invented outside of the institution. When pious minds think of this so foul a profanation and idolomania, they cannot but grieve horribly.

And it is very consistent that Daniel speaks of this very idol when he says, 'He shall honor the god Maozim with gold and silver.' Nor is the name Maozim far from the name Missa, which name is also related to the name Mazon, which signifies food. But let us pray to the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, with constant groans, that for the sake of his glory he may remove all idols and all errors from the Church, and kindle true invocation in our minds.

Abuses therefore being removed, let us speak of the true use. The action is recited by Matthew, Mark, Luke, and Paul, which should be done just as it is described there. And let the first end be that this reception may be for us as a pledge, by which, being confirmed, we believe that we truly are and are becoming members of the Son of God, and have been washed by the blood of the Son of God. And thus let us conclude that the remission of sins is most certainly given to us, not on account of this reception, but on account of the Son of God, who was a victim for us, and now reigns, gathers, and sanctifies the Church. Thus the application of the benefits of Christ becomes proper, by faith, and by one's own reception, not by the alien oblation of a priest, because it is manifest that the reception of individuals was instituted, as it is said: Take, eat. Nor should this spectacle be thought to be similar to the tragedy of Hercules or Theseus, as profane men imagine, where a remembrance of the dead and absent is made; but the Son of God lives and reigns, and wills to be present in the Sacrament in this instituted use, and joins us to himself as members, and without any doubt he is efficacious there in those who receive by faith, and sustain themselves with this consolation.

Afterwards there are other ends of this whole action.

That first one is what I said: That faith may be stirred up, applying the benefits to us. Just as Abraham by the thought of circumcision stirred up his faith, and rejoiced in the promise of the seed.

Second, thanksgiving, because the remembrance of a benefit ought at the same time to kindle gratitude. Hence is the customary term εὐχαριστία. And Cyprian embraces both ends, affirming that the benefits of Christ must be received, and in turn thanks must be given: Piety gives thanks to the bestower of so great a benefit for what has been given and what has been forgiven. The third end is, that it may be the sinew of the public congregation, in which God wills the voice of the evangelical Ministry to sound and be preserved. Therefore he says: As often as you shall do this, you shall proclaim the death of the Lord. And God has always willed that there be honest and public assemblies of the Church, and by his goodness he preserves and protects them.

The fourth end, that in the public assembly there may be a testimony of confession, because God wills that through this reception it be seen what doctrine and what assemblies we approve.

The fifth end, that it may be a sign of mutual love and as it were of a covenant, just as it was most customary to ratify covenants by eating together in sacrifices.

But so many ends must be prudently distinguished, and the principal one must always be retained, lest the use of the ceremony be corrupted.

Do I therefore say that an idol is anything?

This is a refutation of the subtle excuse by which some defended their license: Since an idol is nothing, it is permitted to use things as they are by nature, just as Rachel had carried away with her the golden idols of her father, so that she might have travel money, not that she might worship them.

Paul refutes this cunning evasion: Even if an idol is nothing in reality, nevertheless it is necessary that the opinion and worship among the Gentiles be openly censured. For the frenzies of those who either devise or establish idols are great and foul sins, which it is necessary to oppose, because it has been said: You shall have no other gods.

Those, however, who are present at either the sacrifices or the banquets of those sacrificing to idols, confirm their opinion, since they do not show that they abhor such sacrifices. Just as now, if any accompany lords in the carrying about of the bread, they seem not to disapprove of that adoration, which certainly conflicts with the command: You shall not adore other gods.

The example of Rachel differs much from the banquets of the Corinthians. For when Rachel takes away the statues, by this very act she shows that she does not want them to be worshipped by her father, nor does she worship them herself, but she is going to collect the gold for travel money, just as Irene, daughter of the emperor Licinius, destroyed the golden statues in her father's chapel. But the familiarity of the Corinthians with those sacrificing was similar to collusion. It is, however, most certain that God wills the worship and confirmation of idols to be avoided.

Paul's meaning is not obscure, but it will become more clear when we transfer it to the examples of those who in our age are present at the carrying about of the bread, or at the worship of idols in the invocation of the dead, or at funeral Masses and the like.

Πάντα μοὶ ἔξεστιν, ἀλλὰ οὐ, etc. All things are lawful for me, etc.

He refutes another objection taken from the doctrine concerning Christian liberty: Christian liberty removes distinctions of foods. Why therefore do you forbid me at the banquets of friends these foods, which I know to be a good creature of God, and not changed by foolish consecrations, just as gold, from which sacred cups are made, is not changed?

Paul responds, adding a restriction to the general doctrine concerning liberty: Although all things are lawful, namely in this category, which are called indifferent, as in the use of food, drink, and days, nevertheless this restriction concerning scandal must be added: Do not use your liberty where it confirms the worship of idols, or where it leads the consciences of the weak into doubt, but serve the utility of others.

Afterwards, Paul again adds a confirmation of the doctrine of liberty. Eat everything that is sold in the meat market, not inquiring for conscience' sake, because the earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof. Nothing is said in these passages about the political distinction of things. Christian liberty does not grant that dominions be disturbed, and the spouses or cattle of others be seized. Because God wills this civil society to be ruled by political ordinances. It is not spoken here of civil society, but of the conscience of individuals toward God, in the use of their own property. This is the question: whether it is a sin before God to eat the flesh of a hare, which is rightfully yours. Here Paul answers that it is not a sin. And he adapts a saying from the Psalm: The earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof.

In the Psalm, there is no doubt that this is the simplest meaning: Since he addresses kings, 'Lift up your heads, O ye gates,' etc. At the beginning he places an antithesis: 'The earth is the Lord's,' as if he were saying: It is not the earth of kings and princes, but of God. It is your duty to obey Him, and so to use the earth as it pleases the Lord: and indeed the Lord wills to gather a Church from the whole earth. This is the native meaning. Paul took a general one concerning creation, of which mention is also made shortly after: 'He has founded it upon the seas,' the Lord created the earth, and the things born in it, and indeed He created it so that the Church might enjoy it, and they are good things. And with a good conscience Adam was to use all appropriate things. This dominion is now restored to the Church; the Church can now use a good conscience for all appropriate things. For the bonds of the law have been removed, and things were created for this reason, that the Church might enjoy them.

Latin:

Τὸ ποτήριον τῆς εὐλογίας, ὃ εὐλογοῦμεν: Calix benedictionis, quem benedicimus, etc.

Manifestum est loqui Paulum de Coena Do- mini. Est igitur Calix benedictionis, calix, quo sumitur sanguis Christi, sicut sonant verba de in- stitutione Coenae apud Matthaeum, Marcum, Lu- cam, et infra cap. 11.

Nominat autem Calicem benedictionis, et addit: Quem benedicimus, ut discernat hunc ca- licem a profano potu, qui hauritur sitis causa, cum hic potus hauriatur non propter corporis nostri rigationem, sed ut sit commonefactio de sanguine Christi pro nobis effuso.

Haec ut planius intelligantur, consideretur usus vocabuli benedicere, quod aut significat gra- tias agere, ut cum dicitur, Psalmo 33.: Benedi- cam Domino omni tempore. Et David 1. Reg. 25.: Benedictus Dominus Deus Israël, qui misit te hodie in occursum mihi.

Aut significat bona precari: aut cum Deus benedicit, significat benefacere, quia Deus di- cendo efficit, ut Genesis 48. scriptum est: Bene- dixit Iacob filiis, id est, bene precatus est. Et postea in eodem loco: Benedicat Deus pueris istis, id est, dicendo benefaciat eis, det eis bona. Item: Benedictio Domini divites facit, id est, Deus bona dicendo auget, et custodit facultates.

Hae sunt praecipuae significationes verbi Be- nedicere, quarum exempla ubique obvia sunt, et in lectione prudenter iudicandum est, quae sit simplex et nativa significatio.

Promiscue autem usurpata sunt in Matthaeo et Marco de Coena Domini verba εὐλογήσας et εὐχαριστήσας. Et verbum εὐχαριστήσας osten- dit, Dominum velle in coena fieri gratiarum actio- nem. Itaque simplicissima erit enarratio: Calix benedictionis, id est, calix gratiarum actionis, ex quo bibentes agamus gratias Deo, et Domino nostro Iesu Christo, quod sanguine Christi re- demti simus, id est, agnoscamus et celebremus hoc beneficium, et vera fide statuamus, nos re- cipi, et pro immensa misericordia et mirando con- silio redemtionis reverenter agamus gratias, et sit vera gratitudo, qua corda se Deo subiiciant, et vere eum invocent. Caeteras interpretationes omitto.

Ita quod sequitur: Quem benedicimus, id est, apud quem dicimus verba tradita a Domino, item gratiarum actionem et precationem, quae omnia simul sunt ritus discernens hanc coenam a profana coena, quae pascit corpus nostrum. Nam haec coena non est ad hunc physicum usum insti- tuta, sed habet alium finem.

Usitata est aliis interpretatio, quem bene- dicimus, id est, quem consecramus. Haec interpretatio dextre intellecta, non vi- tuperanda est. Consecramus, id est, addimus sacra verba et gratiarum actionem, ne sit usus profanus seu physicus, sed sit consolatio ani- mae. Sed sacrificuli dicunt, consecramus, id est, facimus virtute verborum mutationem sub- stantiae.

Adest autem Christus suo Sacramento, non quia sacerdos faciat ibi mutationem, aut quia sit vis in verbis mutans res, sed quia liberrime vult adesse ritui quem instituit, sicut Spiritus san- ctus liberrime adest in baptisando.

Οὐχὶ κοινωνία τοῦ αἵματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐστὶν.

Id est, est illa res externa visibilis, qua san- guis Domini nobis exhibetur.

Sic panis quem frangimus, est illa res externa visibilis, qua efficimur socii et membra corporis Christi. Sicut dicitur: Evangelium est potentia Dei, id est, illa res seu instrumentum, quo Deus est efficax.

Recentior aetas monachorum finxit trans- substantionem, quam ita novo nomine nuncupa- runt, de qua priusquam dico, quaedam de ra- tione Sacramentorum dicenda sunt.

Exordiar autem a primo initio.

Ecclesia Dei colligitur voce promissionis inde usque ab initio, mox post editam primam pro- missionem, qua recepti sunt Adam et Eva: ac semper addidit promissioni Deus externa signa. Ac de signis ante diluvium non multa scripta sunt. Sed tamen signum erat ipsa agni inflam- matio.

Deinde cum promissio renovata est, et re- stricta ad posteritatem Abrahae, additum est si- gnum, scilicet circumcisio.

Et deinceps in ceremoniis Leviticis multa si- gna fuerunt, mactatio agni Pascatos. Et postre- mo post adventum Messiae, Baptismus et Coena Domini.

Ita Ecclesia semper voce promissionis et Sa- cramentis constituta est, et a caeteris gentibus distincta, et Patres et Prophetae, et eorum audi- tores pii et eruditi intellexerunt doctrinam de promissione gratiae et fide, et vero usu signo- rum. Sed magna multitudo semper omnibus aetatibus oblita est doctrinae de promissione et de justicia fidei, et signorum usum multis modis de- pravavit.

Alii signa verterunt in numina seu Deos, ut Chaldaei et Persae ignem finxerunt esse ipsum Deum, quia audierant igni delapso ex coelo in- censas esse victimas.

Alii finxerunt ritus esse opera, quae mere- rentur remissionem peccatorum. Et hac opinione cumularunt illa opera, et non solum novas cere- monias, sed etiam nova numina et novos Deos excogitaverunt.

Sic Pharisaei putabant se mereri remissio- nem suis sacrificiis, et iubebant populum saepe facere mactationes, ut hoc modo peccata de- lerentur.

Hi errores vagati sunt in genere humano om- nibus aetatibus.

Ita circumferunt Papistae panem, et affir- mant esse Deum. Et de Missa, de monasticis ritibus dixerunt, haec opera mereri remissionem peccatorum. Et populus hac persuasione fascina- tus, magna pecunia cumulari tales ceremonias curavit.

Hos tetros errores necesse est in in Ecclesia taxari. Et videmus Prophetas gravissimis et asperrimis concionibus hos furores damnare, ut Psalm. 49.: Non in sacrificiis tuis arguam te. Et Iesaiae 1. Et Ierem. 7.: Non praecepi de holo- caustis, ubi certe Iudaeis videbatur Propheta ex- presse pugnare cum lege. Et Oseae 6.: Miseri- cordiam volo, non sacrificium: et agnitionem Dei magis quam holocausta.

Denique passim in Prophetis obviae sunt ta- les conciones. Haec vero loca tantum eo indi- cavi, ut illa vetera certamina iuniores conside- rent, et agnoscant similia esse praesentium.

Reiectis vero abusibus, extet in Ecclesia do- ctrina pura et integra de iusticia fidei, quod homo accipiat remissionem peccatorum, et reputetur iustus fide propter filium Dei gratis, non pro- pter propriam dignitatem, opera, aut virtutes.

Deinde sciendum est, duos esse potiores fines Sacramentorum. Alter est, ut sint signa Promissionis. Alter, ut sint signa Confessionis, et distinguant Ecclesiam Dei a caeteris gentibus. Ut circumcisio primum erat signum promissionis. Nam promissio facit mentionem seminis. Igitur in ea parte signum institutum est. Atque ita testimonium est de voluntate Dei erga nos, sicut ipsa promissio. Et recte inquit Augustinus: Sa- cramentum est verbum visibile, id est, idem mo- net quod promissio, sed incurrit in oculos, cum promissio accipienda sit auribus, et mens intuens signum, commonefiat de voluntate Dei erga nos, hoc est, de promissione, et statuat se iuxta pro- missionem receptum esse. Et nitatur fides ipso mediatore, non hoc opere aut signo.

Addidit autem Deus talia signa promissioni- bus, ut firmior et durabilior memoria esset pro- missionum, quia spectacula incurrentia in oculos magis movent animos, et facilius retinentur, quam nuda dicta.

Alter finis est, ut sint signa confessionis et distinctionis Ecclesiae. Sed hic finis nec primus nec solus esse ducatur, ut Anabaptistae fingebant, Baptismum tantum fuisse ritum inventum, ut discerneret Ecclesiam ab aliis hominibus. Imo prior finis est, ut sit signum voluntatis Dei erga nos, videlicet promissionis, monet certo nos mergi in mortem filii Dei, et propter eum ac per eum ablui peccata nostra.

Deinde accedunt alii fines. Et quaedam signa proprie sunt nervi publicorum congressuum, quia semper Deus voluit exaudiri vocem Evange- lii in genere humano, ac propterea ut late spargi vox Evangelii posset, voluit audiri et conspici Ecclesiam, et honestos congressus publicos do- ctrinae propagandae causa instituit, et hos im- mensa bonitate omnibus aetatibus servat, fremen- tibus diabolis. Et ut tales congregationes fierent maiore gravitate, ceremonias addidit, tanquam ritus panegyricos, quae essent vincula et nervi illorum congressuum.

Hae gravissimae et verissimae causae rituum publicorum considerentur, et procul removeantur imaginationes, quae fingunt idola et meritum.

Deinde et haec sententia verissima teneatur, nihil habere rationem Sacramenti extra usum in- stitutum, quia Sacramenta sunt actiones in Ec- clesia ordinatae certo modo. Cum ritus mutatur, aut extra institutum ordinem transfertur ad alios usus, non est Sacramentum, sed actio supersti- tiosa, aut idolum, ut si baptisatio fieret ad tol- lendam lepram, talis mersio non esset Sacramen- tum, sicut circumcisio Iudaeorum hoc tempore, nec Mahometica circumcisio ullo modo rationem habet Sacramenti.

Ita panis, qui circumgestatur, nullo modo rationem habet Sacramenti, et adoratio prorsus est idoli adoratio, sicut adoratio ignis Chaldaici aut Persici, quem fingebant esse Deum, et nomi- nabant Oromasda, id est, sacrum lumen. Sic et in papistica oblatione adoratio est idoli adoratio, quia cultus ille extra institutionem confictus est. Hanc tam tetram profanationem et idolomaniam cum piae mentes cogitant, non possunt non horribiliter dolere.

Et valde consentaneum est, Danielem de hoc ipso idolo loqui, cum inquit, Colet Deum Maozim auro et argento. Nec nomen Maozim procul abest a nomina Missa, quod nomen etiam affine est nomini Mazon, quod Cibum significat. Sed filium Dei Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum assiduis gemitibus oremus, ut propter suam gloriam omnia idola et omnes errores ex Ecclesia tollat, et in mentibus nostris veram invocationem accendat.

Remotis igitur abusibus dicamus de vero usu. Actio recitatur a Matthaeo, Marco, Luca et Paulo, quae sic fiat, sicut ibi describitur. Et sit primus finis, ut haec sumtio sit nobis tanquam pignus, quo confirmati credamus vere nos esse et fieri membra filii Dei, et ablutos esse sanguine filii Dei. Atque ita statuamus nobis certissime dari remissionem peccatorum, non propter hanc sumtionem, sed propter filium Dei, qui fuit victima pro nobis, et nunc regnat, colligit et sanctificat Ecclesiam. Ita fit applicatio beneficiorum Christi propria, fide, et sumtione propria, non aliena oblatione sacerdotis, quia manifestum est, institutam esse sumtionem singulorum, sicut dicitur: Accipite, manducate. Nec existimetur hoc spectaculum esse simile tragoediae Herculis aut Thesei, ut profani homines imaginantur, ubi mortuorum et absentium recordatio fit, sed vivit filius Dei et regnat, et vult adesse Sacramento in hoc usu instituto, et nos sibi tanquam membra copulat, et sine ulla dubitatione ibi efficax est in iis, qui fide sumunt, et hac consolatione se sustentant.

Postea sunt alii fines huius totius actionis.

Primus ille est, quem dixi, Ut fides exuscitetur, applicans nobis beneficia. Sicut Abraham cogitatione circumcisionis exuscitabat fidem, laetabatur promissione seminis.

Secundus, Gratiarum actio, quia beneficii recordatio simul accendere gratitudinem debet. Hinc est usitata appellatio εὐχαριστία. Et Cyprianus complectitur utrunque finem, adfirmat accipienda esse beneficia Christi, et vicissim agendas esse gratias: Pietas inter data et condonata tanti beneficii largitori gratias agit. Tertius finis est, Ut sit nervus publicae congregationis, in qua vult Deus sonare et conservari vocem Ministerii evangelici. Ideo dicit: Quotiescunque facietis, mortem Domini annunciabitis. Ac semper voluit Deus honestos et publicos Ecclesiae congressus esse, et eos sua bonitate conservat et tuetur.

Quartus finis, Ut in publico congressu sit testimonium confessionis, quia vult Deus per hanc sumtionem conspici, quam doctrinam, quos coetus approbemus.

Quintus finis, Ut sit mutuae dilectionis et quasi foederis signum, sicut usitatissimum fuit sancire foedera simul edendo in sacrificiis.

Sed prudenter discernendi sunt tot fines, ac semper principalis retinendus est, ne de pravetur usus ceremoniae.

Num igitur dico, quod idolum aliquid sit?

Refutatio est argutae excusationis, qua defendebant aliqui suam licentiam: Cum idolum nihil sit, licet rebus uti, quales sunt natura, ut Rahel idola patris aurea secum avexerat, ut viaticum haberet, non ut coleret.

Hanc callidam elusionem Paulus refutat: Etsi nihil est reipsa idolum, tamen necesse est opinionem et cultum in Ethnicis aperte taxari. Nam horum furores, qui idola vel excogitant vel stabiliunt, sunt magna et tetra peccata, quibus adversari necesse est, quia dictum est: Non habebis Deos alienos.

Illi autem, qui intersunt vel sacrificiis vel conviviis sacrificantium idolis, confirmant eorum opinionem, cum non ostendant se abhorrere a talibus sacrificiis. Sicut nunc, si qui comitantur dominos in circumgestatione panis, videntur illam adorationem non improbare, quae certe pugnat cum dicto: Non adorabis Deos alienos.

Multum differt exemplum Rahel a Corinthiorum conviviis. Nam cum Rahel aufert statuas, hoc ipso ostendit, se nolle eas a patre coli, nec ipsa colit, sed aurum in viaticum collatura est, sicut Irene filia imperatoris Licinii statuas aureas in sacello patris destruxit. At familiaritas Corinthiorum cum sacrificantibus similis erat collusioni. Certissimum est autem, velle Deum vitari idolorum cultus et confirmationem.

Non obscura est Pauli sententia, sed fiet magis perspicua, cum transferemus eam ad exempla eorum, qui nostra aetate intersunt circumgesta- tioni panis, aut idolorum cultibus in invocatione mortuorum, aut Missis funebríbus et similibus.

Πάντα μοὶ ἔξεστιν, ἀλλὰ οὐ, etc. Omnia mihi licent, etc.

Refutat aliam obiectionem ex doctrina de libertate Christiana sumtam: Libertas Christiana tollit discrimina ciborum. Cur igitur interdicis mihi in amicorum conviviis his cibis, quos scio creaturam Dei bonam esse, nec mutari per stul- tas consecrationes, sicut aurum, ex quo facta sunt sacra pocula, non mutatur?

Respondet Paulus, addens restrictionem ad generalem doctrinam de libertate: Quanquam licent omnia, scilicet in hoc genere, quae dicun- tur media, ut in usu cibi, potus dierum, tamen addenda est haec restrictio de scandalo: Non uta- ris libertate, ubi confirmat cultum idolorum, aut ubi adducit conscientias imbecillium in dubitatio- nem, sed servias utilitati aliorum.

Postea rursus addit Paulus confirmationem doctrinae libertatis. Omne quod in macello ven- ditur, comedite, non inquirentes propter con- scientiam, quia Domini est terra et plenitudo eius. Nihil in his locis dicitur de distinctione politica rerum. Libertas Christiana non conce- dit conturbari dominia, et rapi aliorum coniuges aut pecudes. Quia hanc civilem societatem vult Deus regi politicis ordinationibus. Non de civili societate hic dicitur, sed de conscientia singulo- rum erga Deum, in usu rerum propriarum. Hoc quaeritur, an sit peccatum coram Deo, vesci carne leporis, qui iure tuus set. Hic respondet Pau- lus, non esse peccatum. Et accomodat dictum ex Psalmo: Domini est terra et plenitudo eius.

In Psalmo non dubium est hanc simpli- cissimam esse sententiam: Cum alloquatur re- ges, Attollite portae capita vestra etc. Ini- tio praeponit antithesin: Domini est terra, quasi dicat: Non est Regum et Principum, sed Dei. Vestrum est ei obedire, et sic uti terra, ut placet Domino: et quidem vult Do- minus ex tota terra colligere Ecclesiam. Haec est nativa sententia. Paulus generalem sumsit de creatione, cuius etiam mox fit mentio: Ipse super maria fundavit eam, Dominus condidit terram, et res nascentes in ea, et quidem condidit, ut frueretur Ecclesia, et sunt res bonae. Et bona conscientia omnibus convenientibus rebus usurus erat Adam. Hoc dominium nunc redditur Ecclesiae, Omnibus convenientibus rebus bona conscientia nunc Ecclesia uti potest. Nam vincula legis remota sunt, et res ideo conditae sunt, ut eis Ecclesia fruatur.

## 10:29
But I say conscience, etc. But I say conscience, etc.

It is a forensic term, ἀνακρίνοντες, which means examining, questioning, or inquiring, just as litigants or witnesses are examined in courts of law. Paul, therefore, as a prudent monitor, in order to cut off the occasions for many questions, prefers that the interrogations be omitted. For if any were eating in ignorance, there would not have been a dispute, but ignorance excused them all equally.

Moreover, a most useful admonition concerning indifferent things has been added, so that at whatever time we use them or do not use them, we may not wound the consciences of others. For such is the nature of men that some are disturbed either by ignorance or by infirmity and are led into doubt; others, indeed, out of peevishness, take it ill that something is done against their opinions and against their custom. Afterwards, faith and invocation languish, both from doubt and from indignation. And from these small offenses follow great and pernicious discords and defections.

Therefore, whether infirmity, or peevishness, or malice is the cause of dissensions, Paul, as a wise monitor, advises that the occasions for such conflicts be avoided, and he prefers that the learned not use their liberty, lest they irritate the spectators, whoever they may be, whether infirm, or foolish, or peevish. Paul's admonition is altogether wisely thought out, as his argument will show later in the conclusion, which he opposes to the objection of those who wish to be considered more learned. These oppose these words to the peevish: Why is my liberty judged by another's conscience? Why do the peevish take upon themselves the judgment of us, and despise us because of the use of a permitted thing, because of clothing or the order of hymns? (For these words are to be read mimetically.)

Although Paul even taxes the peevish with this very objection, yet as a wise monitor, he prefers that the wise yield to the infirmity and peevishness of others. And he hands down a rule which shows the highest ends of all deliberations, the consideration of which ought to govern all actions in the whole of life.

The first and highest end of all creatures, especially intelligent ones, is that they do all things to illustrate the knowledge of God, and to adorn his glory, and to confirm invocation. This end is contained in the first commandment, and the law of nature shows it in some way. And the Son of God says: Let your light shine, that your heavenly Father may be glorified. So here he says: Do all things for the glory of God.

Then follows the second rule: Do not offend the Church of God. After that first care for the glory of God, let the next care be, not what is pleasant to us or seems beautiful, but what fosters common concord and does not disturb invocation. Such circumspection is necessary not only in the Church but also in civil life, just as Plato says: That the ends of all laws ought to be these two, that citizens be honest and friends among themselves.

These rules, taken from the fountains of wisdom, must be diligently thought upon in all the actions of life. And a man, considering by what things common concord is either fostered or disturbed, understands that the force of these rules is very great.

Latin:

Συνείδησιν δὲ λέγω, etc. Conscientiam autem dico, etc.

Vocabulum est forense, ἀνακρίνοντες, quod significat scrutantes, interrogantes seu inquirentes, sicut in iudiciis examinantur litigatores aut testes. Paulus igitur tanquam prudens monitor, ut occasiones multarum quaestionum praecidat, mavult omitti interrogationes. Nam si qui vescerentur inscii, non erat futura disputatio, sed ignorantia pariter omnes excusabat.

Addita est autem utilissima admonitio de rebus mediis, ut quocunque tempore sic eis utamur aut non utamur, ne alienas conscientias sauciemus. Talis est enim natura hominum, ut aliqui aut inscitia aut infirmitate turbentur, et in dubitationem adducantur: aliqui vero morositate aegre ferant fieri aliquid contra suas opiniones et contra suam consuetudinem. Postea languefiunt fides et invocatio tum dubitatione, tum indignatione. Et sequuntur ex his parvis offensionibus magnae et perniciosœ discordiae et defectiones.

Sive igitur infirmitas, sive morositas, sive malitia causa est dissensionum, Paulus ut sapiens monitor suadet vitari occasiones talium dissidiorum, et mavult doctos non uti sua libertate, ne spectatores irritent qualescunque sunt, seu infirmi, seu stulti, seu morosi. Est omnino sapienter cogitata Pauli admonitio, ut postea in conclusione ostendet eius argumentum, quod opponit obiectioni eorům, qui volunt perhiberi doctiores. Hi opponunt morosis haec dicta: Quare libertas mea iudicatur ab aliena conscientia? Quare morosi sumunt sibi iudicium de nobis, et nos contemnant propter usum rei concessae, propter vestem aut ordinem cantionum? (Nam haec verba μιμητικῶς legenda sunt.)

Etsi autem Paulus hac ipsa obiectione etiam taxat morosos, tamen ut sapiens monitor, potius vult sapientes alienae infirmitati et morositati cedere. Et regulam tradit, quae monstrat summos fines omnium deliberationum, quorum consideratio omnes actiones in tota vita regere debet.

Primus et summus finis est omnium creaturarum, praesertim intelligentium, ut omnia faciant ad illustrandam noticiam Dei, et ornandam eius gloriam, et confirmandam invocationem. Hic finis in primo praecepto continetur, et lex naturae aliquo modo eum monstrat. Et filius Dei inquit: Luceat lux vestra, ut glorificetur pater vester coelestis. Ita hic inquit: Omnia ad gloriam Dei facite.

Deinde sequitur altera regula: Non offendite Ecclesiam Dei. Post illam primam curam de gloria Dei, sit proxima cura, non quod nobis suave est, aut pulcrum videtur, sed quod fovet communem concordiam, et non turbat invocationem. Talis circumspectio necessaria non est solum in Ecclesia, sed etiam in vita civili, sicut Plato inquit: Omnium legum fines esse oportere hos duos, ut cives honesti sint, et inter sese amici.

Hae regulae ex fontibus sapientiae sumtae, diligenter cogitandae sunt in omnibus vitae actionibus. Et homo considerans, quibus rebus vel foveatur vel turbetur communis concordia, intelligit harum regularum vim maximam esse.

## 11:1 Argument
Chapter eleven.

The first admonition in this chapter is that we follow one norm of doctrine and worship handed down by our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore the Apostle says: Be imitators of me, just as I am of Christ. He by no means wants other doctrine or worship to be received, except that which he received as handed down by Christ. And he praises the hearers because they retain the doctrine and rites just as he handed them down. And the term παραδόσεις should be understood concerning the doctrine and the principal rites, the testimonies of which exist in the apostolic writings. And the use of rites should be understood according to the doctrine of the Apostles, without superstition.

Although the occasion of the question concerning unveiled women cannot be known at this time, especially since in these regions the custom is now different: yet it appears that that question arose from discussions about liberty. Some, by the old custom, came to the public congregation veiled, just as Jewish and Roman women walked; others, more free, walked unveiled. And it is credible that this liberty, which perhaps was an imitation of ethnic women, as can be judged from the comedies, displeased the more severe. Therefore Paul approves a stricter rite, and seeks reasons in the very order instituted at creation, just as in moral matters a rule must be observed, so that we may follow the order of nature suitable according to creation. Let a man abstain from a menstruating woman, let him abstain from a woman who has just given birth, because of the weakness of nature. Thus he argues here: By nature a woman is adorned with longer hair, so that she may be covered. And it is shameful and alien to nature for a woman to be seen without any hair. Therefore, he says, let her be covered.

From this suitability of nature an argument is taken, and Paul wants that to be done which is more honorable, because it is more in agreement with nature, just as we now say that it is more honorable in a public gathering to be dressed in modest clothing, which covers the buttocks, because it is in agreement with nature to cover those parts.

And the voice is very worthy of consideration and memory, when he says: Does not nature itself teach you? Here let us know that the law of nature must be considered in morals. For he says expressly: Does not nature teach you? He does not want us to follow the desires or affections of this depraved nature, but he wants it to be understood what nature teaches, that is, he wants the law or the notions showing the order to be looked at. This distinction must be considered most diligently. And often in morals this rule can be proposed: In contracts observe equality, because nature teaches that this equality is justice pleasing to God, and necessary for common society, and unless equality is observed, one part is exhausted and perishes. And many examples could be recited. But let it be enough that the reader has been warned to observe this rule concerning nature teaching. And yet it must be known that Paul is speaking about morals and about the law, not about the promise of the Gospel or other matters placed outside the view of human reason. Indeed, even in these moral matters let us know that we are also surrounded by boundaries through the express law of God, because reason in some affairs, especially in this depravity of nature, wanders too far, as Lamech dared to take more wives, and then the Egyptians took sisters. Although therefore it must be considered what nature teaches, nevertheless God for that reason also handed down the law, so that he might put reins on wandering reason. Therefore the express law of God is to be preferred.

Let these things be said in summary about this question, about which however Paul himself shows that he does not want these things to be understood superstitiously; he does not make this custom of veiling a form of worship, nor a necessary work: but he wants contentions to be avoided, and he advises what is more honorable.

Latin:

Caput undecimum.

Prima admonitio est in hoc capite, ut unam normam doctrinae et cultuum traditam a Domino nostro Iesu Christo sequamur. Ideo Apostolus inquit: Imitatores mei estote, sicut ego sum Christi. Nequaquam vult doctrinam aut cultus alios recipi, nisi quos accepit traditos a Christo. Et laudat auditores, quod retineant doctrinam et ritus, sicut ipse tradidit. Et vocabulum παραδόσεις intelligatur de doctrina et ritibus praecipuis, quorum testimonia extant in scriptis apostolicis. Et rituum usus intelligatur iuxta doctrinam Apostolorum, sine superstitione.

Etsi autem occasio quaestionis de mulieribus non velatis, sciri hoc tempore non potest, praesertim cum in his regionibus alia nunc sit consuetudo: tamen adparet ortam esse eam quaestionem ex sermonibus de libertate. Aliae veteri more veniebant in publicam congregationem velatae, sicut Iudaicae et Romanae mulieres incedebant: aliae liberiores incedebant non velatae. Et credibile est, severioribus displicuisse hanc libertatem, quae fortassis imitatio erat ethnicarum mulierum, ut ex comoediis iudicari potest. Igitur Paulus ritum severiorem adprobat, et quaerit rationes in ipso ordine in creatione instituto, sicut in moralibus regula servanda est, ut ordinem naturae convenientem iuxta creationem sequamur. Abstineat vir a muliere menstrua, abstineat a puerpera, propter naturae debilitatem. Ita hic argumentatur: Natura mulier ornata est prolixiore coma, ut sit tecta. Et turpe et alienum a natura est, mulierem conspici sine ulla coma. Ergo inquit, sit tecta.

Ab hac convenientia naturae sumitur argumentum, et vult Paulus fieri id, quod est honestius, quia naturae magis congruit, sicut nos nunc dicimus, honestius esse in publico congressu vestitum esse mediocri veste, quae nates tegit, quia naturae congruit eas partes tegere.

Et vox valde digna est consideratione et memoria, cum ait: An non docet vos natura? Hic sciamus in moribus considerandum esse legem naturae. Diserte enim dicit: An non docet vos natura? non vult nos cupiditates seu affectus huius depravatae naturae sequi, sed vult intelligi, quid doceat natura, id est, legem seu noticias monstrantes ordinem vult aspici. Hoc discrimen diligentissime considerandum est. Et saepe in moribus haec regula proponi potest: In contractibus servato aequalitatem, quia natura docet hanc aequalitatem iusticiam esse Deo placentem, et necessariam communi societati, et nisi servetur aequalitas, exhauriri unam partem et interire. Ac multa exempla recitari possent. Sed satis sit monitum esse lectorem, ut hanc regulam observet, de natura docente. Et tamen sciendum est, loqui Paulum de moribus et de lege, non de promissione Evangelii aut aliis materiis extra conspectum rationis humanae positis. Imo et in his moralibus sciamus etiam nobis circumdatas esse metas per expressam legem Dei, quia ratio in aliquibus negotiis, praesertim in haec naturae depravatione vagatur longius, ut Lamech ausus est plures uxores ducere, et deinde Aegyptii duxerunt sorores. Etsi igitur considerandum est, quid doceat natura, tamen Deus ideo legem quoque tradidit, ut vagabundae rationi frenos iniiceret. Anteferenda est igitur lex Dei expressa.

Haec in summa de hac quaestione dicta sint, de qua tamen Paulus ipse ostendit, se non velle haec superstitiose intelligi, non facit cultum, non opus necessarium, hanc velandi consuetu- dinem: sed vult contentiones vitari, et monet, quid sit honestius.

## 11:3
The head of the man is Christ.

We have recited the principal sentence in this admonition: Be imitators of me, just as I am of Christ. He wants us to embrace the doctrine handed down by the Son of God, and that absolutely nothing be received against the judgment of the Gospel.

Then in the question about veiling women he uses two arguments, which are not to be taken superstitiously. And in the latter there is greater clarity. For nature added long hair to a woman, and it signifies that she should be covered more, because she ought to come less into the sight of the people. Such hair was not added to a man, because a man must be seen in government, in battle, in the Senate, in speaking. Therefore let the woman be veiled. It is an oratorical enthymeme, and rightly taken from signs in nature and natural judgment. And sane men do not gainsay this argument so aptly taken from nature.

The other argument is more obscure, which when it is taken rightly and without cavils, agrees with this question, and contains useful doctrine. He makes degrees: God is the head of Christ. Christ is the head of the man. The man is the head of the woman. Here a caviller will object: Nay, Christ is also the head of the woman, just as it is most certain that women and men are equally heirs of eternal life, and are equally received by faith because of the mediator. And it is written: In Christ there is neither male nor female, nor is there partiality. But I answer thus truly and rightly. Paul is not speaking here about the remission of sins of both, but about ministries. Thus without any sophistry the order in the recited degrees agrees. God is the head of Christ, it is not said concerning essence, but concerning ministries. The Son as mediator receives a ministry from the counsel of the divinity, as he often says: The Father sent me. Mention is made here not of the arcane essence, but of the ministry, to which the Son was sent in a singular way. Then it agrees: Christ is the head of the man. It is most certain that the man in the whole human race first receives the ministry of teaching and governing the public assembly: since indeed God wills that there always be public gatherings and that the voice of those teaching in the public assembly be heard by the whole human race, as it has been said: In the great Church I will praise you. It is therefore regular that this glory belongs to the man, to teach and rule the public assembly, and polities, and that the woman is properly the economic governor, as Homer says: λόγος δ' ἄνδρεσσι μελήσει.

in a similar office, because God willed this very creation to be a type of the Church born from the Son.

Without any doubt, the nearest image of the eternal Father is the Son, that is, He is an intelligent nature, having rays of the essence, wisdom, justice, and life of the eternal Father transfused into Himself, and He is the glory of the Father, that is, showing and celebrating the Father among the human race.

The economic order therefore follows: The man is the head of the woman, that is, the man first receives the ministry of teaching and ruling, then he attributes a part to the woman in the household. The mother teaches and rules the offspring, just as Rebecca teaches her son Jacob. This interpretation is true, plain, and clear. And the man in the public assembly is a teacher, and a governor, and a warrior. He ought to be seen: therefore he should not be veiled. The woman does not teach in the public assembly, nor is she a political governor nor a warrior: therefore in the public assembly she should be veiled. These things fit aptly, because an orator, a governor, a leader, ought to be seen in battle, just as at home in economic government the mother of the family ought to be seen.

Then, just as a rib is taken from Adam, whence, as it is written there, Eve is built: so the Church is taken from the very body of the Son of God, that is, from the nature of the companion of the Son of God redeemed by Him. And this is the image of the Lord, an intelligent nature, receiving from Him immediately the word, the knowledge of God, wisdom and justice, and is the glory celebrating Him. And because she is bone of His bones, and flesh of His flesh, there is a wonderful mutual fire of love between this Lord and the Church.

This type illustrates the saying of Paul, indeed the whole doctrine concerning Creation. As Christ is the image of the eternal Father: so the man is the nearest image of God or Christ, that is, an intelligent nature, adorned with the knowledge of God and justice, and ordered to public ministry, to celebrate God.

These sayings are therefore clear: A man standing in a public assembly veiled in public prayer, or a sermon, dishonors his head, that is, he does not keep the order, he does not wish to be seen, just as Christ offers Himself to be seen.

A leader who does not wish to be seen is despised by the army. And it always was and is customary for leaders to have singular signs in battle, so that they can be perceived and recognized.

Thus the action of an orator, if he were to speak veiled, would be ridiculous. For action is dominated by the face and the eyes. Rightly therefore it is written: He dishonors his head, himself and Christ.

Afterwards, also, since the woman is taken from the man, she is the nearest image and glory of the man, but yet at the same time coupled to God, because things which are equal or similar to a third are equal or similar among themselves. And so the woman is also an intelligent nature, adorned with the knowledge of God and justice, and ordered to a certain ministry, but narrower than the ministry of the man, namely to the instruction and economic government. And yet with similar wisdom and justice they invoke and celebrate God. And therefore with a wonderful fire the man loves the woman, and the woman the man, because the woman is taken from the man, and is similar, that is, an intelligent nature, adorned with similar knowledge of God, wisdom, and justice. And knowledge and similarity kindle love, which is then perfect when they are coupled in God, just as in the beginning before the fall Male and Female were equally coupled in God. From these sources are to be taken the true and wonderful arguments of the association of male and female, and of marriage, and of mutual love. A man does not love a statue in this way, because it is neither related, nor is it similar, that is, it is not an intelligent thing, nor adorned with similar wisdom and justice, and similar ministry. But the woman is related, and is similar, that is, she is an intelligent thing, adorned with similar knowledge

On the other hand, the woman dishonors her head if she is not veiled, because she also does not keep the order, and a member is interwoven from another argument: Nature has covered her with hair.

Latin:

Viri caput est Christus.

Recitavimus praecipuam in hac admonitione sententiam: Imitatores mei estote, sicut ego sum Christi. Vult nos amplecti doctrinam a filio Dei traditam, et prorsus nihil recipi contra Evangelii sententiam.

Deinde in quaestione de velandis mulieribus utitur duobus argumentis, quae non superstitiose accipienda sunt. Et in altero perspicuitas maior est. Nam natura comam prolixam mulieri addidit, et significat magis eam tegendam esse, quia minus debet venire in conspectum populi. Viro non est addita talis coma, quia virum in gubernatione, in acie, in Senatu, in dicendo conspici oportet. Ergo mulier sit velata. Enthymema oratorium est, et a signis in natura et iudicio naturali recte sumtum. Et homines sani huic argumento tam apte sumto ex natura, non refragantur.

Alterum argumentum obscurius est, quod cum dextre et sine cavillationibus accipitur, congruit ad hanc quaestionem, et doctrinam continet utilem. Gradus facit: Deus est caput Christi. Christus est caput viri. Vir est caput mulieris. Hic cavillator obiiciet: Imo Christus et mulieris caput est, sicut certissimum est, mulieres et viros pariter haeredes esse vitae aeternae, et pariter recipi fide propter mediatorem. Et scriptum est: In Christo nec mas est nec foemina, nec προσωποληψία est. Sed vere et dextre sic respondeo. Paulus non loquitur hic de remissione peccatorum utriusque, sed de ministeriis. Ita sine ulla sophistica congruit ordo in gradibus recitatis. Deus est caput Christi, non de essentia dicitur, sed de ministeriis. Filius mediator accipit ministerium a consilio divinitatis, sicut saepe inquit: Pater misit me. Fit hic mentio non arcanae essentiae, sed ministerii, ad quod filius singulari modo missus est. Deinde congruit: Christus est caput viri. Certissimum est, virum in toto genere humano primum accipere ministerium docendi et gubernandi publicum coetum: cum quidem velit Deus semper esse publicos congressus et vocem docentium in publico coetu exaudiri a toto genere humano, sicut dictum est: In Ecclesia magna laudabo te. Est igitur regulare hoc, viri esse hanc gloriam, do- cere et regere coetum publicum, et politias, et mulierem proprie gubernatricem oeconomicam esse, sicut inquit Homerus: λόγος δ' ἄνδρεσσι μελήσει.

in simili officio, quia voluit Deus hanc ipsam creationem typum esse Ecclesiae nascentis ex filio.

Sine ulla dubitatione proxima imago est aeterni patris, filius, id est, est natura intelli- gens, habens radios in se transfusos essentiae, sapientiae, iusticiae et vitae aeterni patris, et est gloria patris, id est, ostendens et celebrans patrem in genere humano.

Sequitur ergo gradus oeconomicus: Vir est caput mulieris, id est, vir prius accipit ministe- rium docendi et regendi, deinde partem attribuit mulieri in oeconomia. Mater docet et regit so- bolem, sicut Rebecca docet filium Iacob. Haec interpretatio vera, plana et perspicua est. Et vir in publico coetu doctor est, et gubernator et praeliator. Hunc conspici oportet: ideo non sit velatus. Mulier non docet in publico congressu, nec est gubernatrix politica nec praeliatrix: ideo in publico conventu sit velata. Haec apte con- gruunt, quia oratorem, gubernatorem, ducem, in acie conspici oportet, sicut et domi in oeco- nomica gubernatione matremfamilias conspici oportet.

Deinde sicut ex Adam sumitur costa, unde, ut ibi scriptum est, aedificatur Eva: ita sumitur Ecclesia ex ipso corpore filii Dei, id est, ex na- tura socia filii Dei redemta per ipsum. Et haec est imago domini, natura intelligens, accipiens ab ipso immediate verbum, agnitionem Dei, sa- pientiam et iusticiam, et est gloria celebrans eum. Et quia est os ex ossibus eius, et caro ex carne, mirabile incendium est amoris mutuum inter hunc dominum et inter Ecclesiam.

Hic typus illustrat dictum Pauli, imo totam doctrinam de Creatione. Ut Christus est imago aeterni patris: ita vir est proxima imago Dei seu Christi, id est, natura intelligens, ornata agni- tione Dei et iusticia, et ordinata ad publicum ministerium, ad celebrandum Deum.

Sunt ergo perspicua haec dicta: Vir in pu- blico congressu stans velatus in precatione pu- blica, aut concione, deformat caput, id est, non servat ordinem, non vult conspici, sicut Christus se praebet conspiciendum.
