Dux qui non vult conspici, spernitur ab exercitu. Et semper fuit et est usitatum, duces habere singularia signa in acie, ut cerni et agno- sci possint.

Sic oratoris actio, si diceret velatus, ridicula esset. Actio enim dominatur in vultu et in ocu- lis. Recte igitur scriptum est: Deformat caput, se et Christum.

Postea et mulier cum sit ex viro sumta, proxime est imago et gloria viri, sed tamen simul copulata Deo, quia quae uni tertio aequalia seu similia sunt, inter sese sunt aequalia seu similia. Itaque et mulier est natura intelligens, ornata agnitione Dei et iusticia, et ordinata ad certum ministerium, sed angustius ministerio viri, scili- cet ad institutionem et gubernationem oecono- micam. Et tamen simili sapientia et iusticia in- vocant et celebrant Deum. Ideoque mirando in- cendio diligit vir mulierem, et mulier virum, quia mulier ex viro sumta est, et est similis, id est, natura intelligens, ornata simili agnitione Dei, sapientia et iusticia. Et amorem accen- dunt cognitio et similitudo, quae tunc perfecta est, cum copulati sunt in Deo, sicut et initio ante lapsum Mas et Foemina pariter in Deo co- pulati erant. Ex his fontibus sumenda sunt vera et miranda argumenta consociationis maris et foeminae, et coniugii, et amoris mutui. Non sic amat vir statuam, quia nec cognata est, nec similis est, id est, non est res intelligens, nec ornata simili sapientia et iusticia, ac simili mini- sterio. Sed mulier est cognata, et est similis, id est, est res intelligens, ornata simili agnitione

Econtra mulier deformat caput, si non sit velata, quia etiam non servat ordinem, et intexi- tur membrum ex altero argumento: Natura eam texit coma.

## 11:7
Man is the image and glory of God.

Is not woman also the image of God? It is most true that the human race, male and female, was so created that they are intelligent, eternal natures, acknowledging God, adorned with justice, and placed in the world so that they might celebrate God with certain duties and hand down the knowledge of Him to those born from them. Thus, both are the image and temple of God; both are an intelligent nature, adorned with the knowledge of God and justice.

But yet there are degrees. Man is prior to woman, and woman was created from him by a wondrous plan, and yet she is similar to man, and serving in her own place

of God and justice, and serving in the same ministry, although a narrower one, and a partner of generation, and a helper to the husband in many duties and dangers of life. And therefore she is also the glory of the man, because she is a kinswoman, similar, a partner of generation, and a helper in life. The wisdom and goodness of this wondrous order, now after the fall, can neither be understood nor told in words, just as it will be able to be understood and told when we shall consider these counsels of God in that eternal fellowship of God, for which we have been created and redeemed without any doubt.

But Paul touched upon the greatest matters briefly, and did not wish to rhetoricate childishly, but preached most gravely concerning the wondrous covenant and order of God, of Christ, of the husband and the wife. I, having indicated the sum of the matter as best I could, exhort the reader to apply pious meditation to these greatest matters.

Συνερχομένων ὑμῶν ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ, ἀκούω σχίσματα ἐν ὑμῖν ὑπάρχειν. When you come together in the Church, I hear that there are schisms among you.

It was said above that God wills that honest public assemblies take place, in which the voice of the Gospel may sound, and that the Lord's Supper is the sinew of our assemblies, because God wills that the Church be seen and heard, so that the Son may be acknowledged in the whole human race, and the benefits which are given to the human race on account of the Son may be known. Paul therefore ordains these public assemblies here. And how he ordains them, and how a more recent age has departed from this form of Paul, we shall say later.

The reader must first be admonished concerning this saying: It must be that there are heresies. Let the doctrine be known also by other most manifest testimonies, that God is not the cause of sin, nor does He will, nor approve, nor effect, nor aid sins, according to that: You are not a God who wills impiety. Nor are there contradictory wills in God, because He is truthful. And in John 8 it is said: When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own.

From these foundations, which are most true and most firm, let the interpretation of the saying be taken: It must be that there are heresies. For necessity is by no means to be understood otherwise than as a necessity of consequence, namely, because since the devil, burning with hatred for the Son of God, does not cease to disturb the Churches, and easily impels light minds, the causes of horrible dissensions do not cease. Thus it follows that many heresies arise, even though God truly is angry at these furies, and it is by no means necessary for human wills to be implicated in them. But the pious, calling upon God and seeking the truth, can avoid them, just as Paul here also signifies that there are distinctions of wills: By such signs, he says, the sincere are distinguished from the feigned. The sincere love the truth and constantly retain it. Others, light, or ambitious, or greedy, are easily impelled to embrace new dogmas.

Let us be content with this true admonition concerning the saying of Paul in this place. Now let us see how he ordains the Lord's Supper.

First, he wishes it to be common, and prohibits particular suppers in one place. There was therefore one common supper, and not the offering of one. Wherefore it is manifest that the custom of the private Mass, born later, is disapproved by this testimony.

Afterwards he wishes a sermon to be added. Therefore he says: As often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the death of the Lord.

Thirdly, he wishes all to bring repentance, and prohibits eating by those who persevere in sins against conscience. Therefore he says: He who eats unworthily is guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. Likewise: Let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of the bread and drink of the cup. For since this supper is named, and is a rite of the New Testament, that is, of the new promise sealed by the death of the Son of God, and is a testimony of the remission of sins, and sins are not remitted to one persevering in sins against conscience and despising the remission, it is manifest that this testimony of remission is despised by such persons.

Therefore let good minds know what it is to eat unworthily, and what kind of examination is required.

He eats worthily who, thinking of the death of the Son of God, acknowledges the wrath of God against our sins, and performs repentance, and at the same time acknowledges that the wrath of God is appeased and sins are remitted on account of the Son, and that this wondrous promise of God is the New Testament, confirmed by the death of the Son of God, and, raised up by this consolation, believes that he is received and is pleasing to God, and establishes this rite as a testimony of this divine benefit.

This examination is therefore also required: Whether there is in us an evil purpose, whether there is repentance, whether there is faith, by which we may determine that our sins are remitted to us, and whether, uplifted by this consolation, we may approach the mediator.

Furthermore, let the common doctrine be known, which sins are in the saints in this life, which are not. Dignity should not be understood in such a way that there are no sins in us, but that sins against conscience ought to be put away.

Fourthly, let the punishment be considered. Paul clearly says here that many are sick and many are dead because of the abuse of the Supper. Therefore, negligence is punished even in the saints, but much more will all those be punished with present and eternal punishments who have turned the Lord's Supper into a horrible worship of idols, and who, for the sake of gain, have invented a sacrifice for the living and the dead. The magnitude of these greatest crimes will be seen after this life. And there we shall recognize that these crimes were the causes of many calamities in this life. We pray, however, with ardent groans to the Son of God, that He Himself may heal these great wounds of the Church.

Now let us consider the words.

In the text it is: Which is broken for you. In the narrative according to Luke it is written: Which is given for you, that is, which is a victim for the human race. Therefore, others here interpret 'broken' as 'lacerated'. I do not criticize that. But it seems simpler that 'breaking' should be understood as distribution, just as the Hebrews spoke: Break your bread to the hungry. And this word came into Paul's mind because of the custom of distribution, especially since he wishes the Supper to be common.

Τοῦτο τὸ ποτήριον ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη ἐστὶν. This is the Chalice, which is the new Testament in my blood.

This narrative in Luke is set down in the same words. But these words are added: Which is poured out for you. The syntax in Matthew and Mark is different. This is my blood of the new Testament: nor should the difference be subtly sought. Both readings are to be understood in the same way: This is the chalice of the new Testament, that is, the rite and pledge or seal of the new Testament. For 'Testament' principally and properly signifies the very promise of the remission of sins, of the Holy Spirit, of righteousness, and of eternal life. Then these benefits are the things given by this Testament, that is, by this Promise. And external rites are added, which are the signs and pledges of this promise: Baptism and the Lord's Supper. Therefore Matthew said: This is my blood of the new Testament.

But since Luke and Paul say: This is the chalice, the new Testament, it is a metonymy, as if I were to say: The fasces are the Roman empire. Let us be content with this brief admonition concerning the syntax in this place.

Then a consideration is very necessary, why mention of the new Testament was expressly made here, and indeed in that narrative where mention is made of blood.

A testament is the promise of one who is about to die. Therefore this word was used concerning the promise of the Son of God giving His benefits, so that it might signify the coming death, as it is written to the Hebrews. This particle was therefore expressly added to this narrative, which speaks of the shedding of blood. And the types of the blood of victims in the old Testament, which were all signs of this future death, are to be opposed to it.

Now also the antithesis of the old and new Testament is to be considered. The old Testament is the promise of a polity, with an obligation to keep the law delivered through Moses, which polity was established so that in it the promise concerning the Messiah might be preserved, and there the Messiah might be exhibited, for whose sake there was also always some Church of the elect there.

But the new Testament is the promise of eternal goods, of the remission of sins, of the Holy Spirit, of righteousness, and of eternal life, which are exhibited freely for the sake of the Messiah, not for the sake of the law.

The Lord therefore affirms that these goods are now being exhibited, and that this chalice is the pledge of this exhibition. Great consolation is therefore proposed to the universal Church. When this chalice is exhibited, know for certain that eternal goods are being exhibited, on account of the blood of the Son of God shed in His death. Nor does the work of any man merit those eternal goods bequeathed on account of the Son's death. This rite, therefore, is not a sacrifice that merits these goods for the one performing it and for others, but it testifies that they are exhibited, and they ought to be received by faith, which relies upon the sacrifice of the Son of God Himself, not upon any of our merits.

This most ample doctrine is comprised in this appellation of the New Testament, which we cannot here embrace in its entirety: I only briefly advise that the sources of this doctrine must be sought, as often as we think about the Lord's Supper, and as often as we approach it.

It is a manifest refutation of the Sacrificers and the Anabaptists. Since it is a rite of the new promis- sion, which is free, is not a sacrifice that merits for others. Likewise, since it is a rite of the Testament, it testifies that legacies are exhibited to us by the Son, and it is a pledge of the will of God toward us, not merely a ceremony of mutual love among guests, as the Anabaptists say.

This passage is also significant, because he commands that this rite be observed until Christ comes. These words are a clear testimony that God will always preserve the Church in this life until the resurrection of the dead, the public ministry of the Sacraments, public assemblies, and some shelters for the churches. These sweet consolations are contained in this brief passage.

Ἔνοχος ἔσται τοῦ σώματος καὶ αἵματος. He shall be guilty of the body and blood.

He describes the magnitude of the sin in the abuse of the Lord's Supper when he says that those who abuse it are guilty of the body and blood, that is, they treat the body and blood of the Lord with contempt, just as the robbers who crucified the Lord treated him with contempt. And there are degrees. There is contempt when the profane receive it out of custom, without repentance and without faith seeking remission. But there is greater contempt when it is pretended that the use is a sacrifice that merits for others. Likewise, when it is turned into profit and changed into an idol. Because of these horrible sins, whole nations are punished with many huge calamities, wars, and devastations, and those who do not repent will be oppressed with eternal punishments. Let us pray, however, to the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, that he may free his Church from all errors and idols, and kindle the light of truth, true invocation, and true worship.

Εἰ γὰρ ἑαυτοὺς διεκρίνομεν, οὐκ ἂν ἐκρινόμεθα. If we were judging ourselves, we would not be judged.

Monks have transferred this sentence to satisfactions. But the whole passage is clearly about repentance. At the same time, guilt and eternal punishment are freely remitted on account of the Son of God, according to that: O death, I will be your death, and your plague, O hell. Likewise: He who believes in the Son has eternal life.

Then it is also true that present punishments are mitigated or removed on account of total repentance, as the history of Jonah testifies. And in Isaiah chapter 1 it is said: If your sins are as scarlet, you shall be white as snow. For since God wishes to preserve the Church in this life, although it is full of misery, he mitigates punishments so that some people may survive, that the generation and education of offspring may be preserved, and the public ministry of the Gospel, and that there may be shelters for the Church in the state and the household. And let us know that punishments are mitigated for this end, so that the Church may not be utterly destroyed in this life. And looking to this end, let us ask for mitigation, just as the Church prays in the Psalm: Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory. The dead will not praise you, O Lord.

Then Paul delivers a general doctrine concerning afflictions: When we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined, so that we may not be condemned with this world. In the Church, it is necessary to know the causes why human nature, although it excels all living creatures, is subject to death and such great miseries, and then, why this part, which is the Church of God, is even more burdened.

Philosophers say that some evils arise from matter, some from our errors and wills. They speak of proximate causes. But why is the matter of man subject to corruption? Why is there such darkness in the human mind? Why is there such stubbornness in the wills and the heart? Here, the voice of God alone in the Church shows the principal cause, which narrates that sin is the cause of death and other miseries in the whole human race, as it is written in Genesis. And Paul says: Through sin, death.

Furthermore, since God wishes his wrath against sins to be seen in the Church, and wishes us to be reminded of repentance and of the promises, he exercises the Church even more. And there are many other causes, which are recited in their proper place. But the most common is this one, which Paul recites in this place, of which the Psalm also speaks: It is good for me that you have humbled me, that I may learn your justifications. From these fountains are drawn the principal consolations, of which it is spoken more copiously elsewhere. Here I will only add a comparison of philosophical and Christian consolations, which it is useful to have in view.

There are five places of philosophical consolations.

I. Necessity.

II. Virtue is to be preferred to pain.

III. A good conscience.

IV. Examples.

V. Final causes.

The first topic is necessity. For since an evil cannot be changed, we increase our pain in vain by resisting, as it is said: μὴ πρὸς κέντρα λακτίζειν.

The second, because reason and the law of nature command that virtue be preferred to pain, let us not do anything dishonestly, broken by pain, as Cato does unjustly, who brings death upon himself because of pain.

The third, a great relief is a good conscience, as it is said: It is something for great evils to be free of crime: because Palamedes, Socrates, Camillus, and the like suffer less, because their conscience is not wounded. On the contrary, Judas and the like suffer more, because they are tormented within and without, and the Furies of conscience bring much greater torments than any external laceration of the body.

The fourth, examples soothe pain to some extent because they show the sad misfortunes of honest men, that calamity itself is not a disgrace. However, those things are borne more easily which seem to be without disgrace, as Cicero bears exile more easily because he knows that in the same republic the best men were previously expelled, such as Camillus, Rutilius, and others even killed, such as Antonius the orator and others.

The fifth, a good final cause diminishes pain, as when our calamity benefits others, as Codrus seeks death for his country.

These consolations, although they soothe minds to some extent, nevertheless leave them in death, nor do they show life and liberation from miseries. Therefore, let Christian consolations be opposed to these languid consolations, some of whose topics taken from the law of God agree with philosophical ones, but some are proper to the Gospel.

The first is Necessity, namely the law of God, which has sanctioned punishments. Therefore it is also said: Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God.

The second, Virtue is to be preferred to pain. This consolation is also taken from the law, because the divine law commands that we do not act against justice when broken by pain, as Cato violated the law: You shall not kill.

The third, A good conscience. This topic is also taken from the divine law, because the divine law also commands pain on account of crimes, and concerning a good conscience it is written: A secure mind is a continual feast.

The fourth, Recognition of the mercy and presence of God, and of divine help. This consolation is proper to the Gospel, in which it is certain that the remission of sins, and of eternal punishment, and the help of God in this life have been promised. David, driven into exile, remembers his fall, but nevertheless sustains himself and rests in God, because he knows that his sins and eternal punishments are remitted to him. He knows that he has been received by God, and that he is now heard and protected by God, as Isaiah says: God dwelling with a contrite and humble spirit, and to revive the spirit of the humble. This consolation ought to be the chief one in every pain, as those rightly instructed in the Gospel know.

Fifth, the hope of liberation or mitigation, and finally of eternal salvation. This consolation is joined with the previous one. When hearts, uplifted by the remission of sins, find rest in God and firmly determine that they are heard by God, they know now that liberation from eternal death has been promised; they know also that God wills to bring aid in the present, and either to remove afflictions entirely or to mitigate them. These two consolations truly overcome sorrow, because as long as the mind looks only at afflictions and death or destruction, sorrow prevails. But when a good thing is set before it, namely a God who is propitious and willing to bring aid and to mitigate present miseries, and finally to liberate from all evils—this object, which is a good thing, is the cause of joy. Therefore, sorrow is overcome when the mind contemplates these good objects. Job overcomes his sorrows because he knows that the final liberation is set before him, as he says: 'Even if he slays me, yet will I hope in him'; and yet he expects mitigation in the present as well. Palamedes and Socrates, although they grieve less because their conscience is not wounded, yet see nothing but destruction. But the Baptist and Stephen contemplate the life to come in the sweetest fellowship of the eternal Church. They already possess this good by hope. And hope is the cause of gladness, as is said in the verse about Stephen: 'He went on, rejoicing in spirit, and by his hope lightened his losses,' that is, he was joyful, both because he willingly obeyed God and because he was already by hope a citizen of the heavenly Church.

Sixth, examples in the Church also soften sorrow more than among the heathens, because in the Church the reasons are known why one is subject to the cross: and we know that not only destruction, but liberation is set before us. And the examples are more illustrious. Since the Son of God, since other principal members The Churches have sustained huge hardships by the certain counsel of God, which shows to the Church that we should not wish to be separated from the rest of society in afflictions and liberations. And it would be inequality and pride if we wished it to be better for us than for the Son of God, than for Abel, Jeremiah, the Baptist, and the like. And here let the causes of afflictions be noted. Because of the sin born with us, death has been imposed upon the human race universally, and diseases and many other hardships. Next, individual afflictions are sometimes punishments for certain offenses, like David's exile: sometimes exercises, like Joseph's prison: sometimes testimonies of confession and immortality, like the deaths of Abel, the Baptist, and Stephen. And when we propose examples to ourselves, the causes must be considered at the same time. As in other doctrines, it is not enough to look at examples, but the reasons and distinctions of the examples must also be considered. And concerning examples rightly accommodated, that old saying can be spoken: κοινὸν ναυάγιον πᾶσι παραμύθιον. Seventh, final causes. This is the most common final cause: It is good for me that you have humbled me, that I might learn your justifications. God afflicts not to destroy, but to either draw men back to repentance, as David, Uzziah, and Manasseh are afflicted: or to exercise and confirm his own, as Joseph, Daniel, and the like are afflicted, and Paul makes mention of this cause in this place: When we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord, that we may not be condemned with this world. There are also other causes in the Church, of which I have already spoken. Grief is also softened when we know by our confession that others are confirmed, of which cause Paul speaks to the Philippians 2, when he says that he rejoices that he is being poured out, so that they may be confirmed in the sacrifice and ministry of faith. This brief admonition concerning the comparison of consolations brings some light to this passage of Paul. And let readers contemplate in their minds those things which are said more copiously elsewhere concerning the cross.

Latin:

Vir est imago et gloria Dei.

An non et mulier est imago Dei? Verissi- mum est, ita conditum esse genus humanum ma- rem et foeminam, ut sint naturae intelligentes, aeternae, agnoscentes Deum, ornatae iusticia, et collocatae in mundum, ut certis officiis celebrent Deum, et eius noticiam tradant nascentibus ex ipsis. Ita uterque est imago et templum Dei, uterque est natura intelligens, ornata agnitione Dei et iusticia.

Sed tamen gradus sunt. Vir est prior mu- liere, et mulier mirando consilio ex ipso condita est, et tamen similis viro, et serviens suo loco

Dei et iusticia, et serviens in eodem ministerio, quanquam angustiore, et socia generationis, et opulatrix viro in multis vitae officiis et periculis. Ideoque et gloria viri est, quia est cognata, similis, socia generationis, et opulatrix in vita. Huius mirandi ordinis sapientia et bonitas, nunc post lapsum nec intelligi, nec verbis enarrari potest, sicut intelligi et enarrari poterit, cum haec consilia Dei considerabimus in illa aeterna consuetudine Dei, ad quam sine ulla dubitatione conditi et redemti sumus.

At Paulus res maximas breviter attigit, nec voluit tantum pueriliter rhetoricari, sed gravissime concionatus est de mirando foedere et ordine Dei, Christi, maris et foeminae. Ego summa rei utcunque indicata, lectorem adhortor, ut de his rebus maximis piam meditationem adhibeat.

Συνερχομένων ὑμῶν ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ, ἀκούω σχίσματα ἐν ὑμῖν ὑπάρχειν. Convenientibus vobis in Ecclesia, audio schismata inter vos esse.

Dictum est supra, Deum velle, ut fiant honesti congressus publici, in quibus sonet vox Evangelii, et nervum nostrorum congressuum esse coenam Domini, quia vult Deus Ecclesiam conspici et audiri, ut filius in toto genere humano agnoscatur, et nota sint beneficia, quae propter filium generi humano donantur. Hos igitur publicos congressus hic ordinat Paulus. Et quomodo eos ordinet, et quomodo discesserit ab hac forma Pauli recensior aetas, postea dicemus.

Prius admonendus est lector de hoc dicto: Oportet haereses esse. Nota sit doctrina et aliis manifestissimis testimoniis, Deum non esse causam peccati, nec velle nec adprobare, nec efficere nec adiuvare peccata, iuxta illud: Deus non volens impietatem tu es. Nec in Deo sunt contradictoriae voluntates, quia verax est. Et Iohannis 8. dicitur: Cum mendacium loquitur, ex propriis loquitur.

Ex his fundamentis, quae sunt verissima et firmissima, sumatur interpretatio dicti: Oportet haereses esse. Nequaquam enim intelligenda est necessitas aliter, nisi de necessitate consequentiae, scilicet, quia cum diabolus ardens odio filii Dei, non desinat turbare Ecclesias, et levia ingenia facile impellat, non cessant causae horribilium dissidiorum. Ita sequitur, ut multae oriantur haereses, etiamsi Deus vere his furo- ribus irascitur, et nequaquam necesse est volun- tates humanas eis implicari. Sed pii invocantes Deum, et veritatem quaerentes, possunt eas vi- tare, sicut hic quoque significat Paulus discri- mina voluntatum esse: Talibus signis, inquit, discernuntur sinceri a fucatis. Sinceri amant veritatem et constanter eam retinent. Alii leves, aut ambitiosi aut avari facile impelluntur, ut nova dogmata amplectantur.

Hac vera admonitione de dicto Pauli hoc loco contenti simus. Nunc videamus quomodo coenam Domini ordinet.

Primum vult esse communem, et prohibet particulares coenas in uno loco. Fuit igitur una communis coena, et non unius oblatio. Quare hoc testimonio improbari consuetudinem priva- tae Missae postea natam, manifestum est.

Postea vult addi concionem. Ideo inquit: Quoties editis panem hunc, et hoc poculum bi- betis, mortem Domini annunciate.

Tertio vult omnes adferre poenitentiam, et prohibet manducationem fieri ab iis, qui perseve- rant in delictis contra conscientiam. Ideo inquit: Qui indigne manducat, reus est corporis et san- guinis Domini. Item: Probet homo seipsum, et sic de pane manducet, et de poculo bibat. Cum enim haec coena nominetur, et sit ritus novi Te- stamenti, id est, novae promissionis obsignatae morte filii Dei, et sit testimonium remissionis peccatorum, nec remittantur peccata perseve- ranti in delictis contra conscientiam, et contem- nenti remissionem, manifestum est, contemni hoc testimonium remissionis a talibus.

Itaque sciant bonae mentes, quid sit indigne manducare, et qualis exploratio requiratur.

Digne manducat, qui mortem filii Dei cogi- tans, agnoscit iram Dei adversus nostra peccata, et agit poenitentiam, et simul agnoscit placatam esse iram Dei, et remitti peccata propter filium, et hanc mirandam promissionem Dei esse novum Testamentum, confirmatum morte filii Dei, et hac consolatione erectus, credit se recipi, et placere Deo, et hunc ritum statuit testimonium esse huius beneficii divini.

Requiritur ergo et haec scrutatio: An sit in nobis malum propositum, an sit poenitentia, an sit fides, qua remitti nobis peccata nostra statua- mus, et an hac consolatione erecti ad mediatorem accedamus.

Caeterum nota sit doctrina communis, quae peccata sint in sanctis in hac vita, quae non sint. Non sic intelligatur dignitas, quod nulla sint in nobis peccata, sed quod oporteat deponi peccata contra conscientiam.

Quarto poena consideretur. Manifeste hic dicit Paulus, multos aegrotare, et multos mor- tuos esse propter abusum coenae. Ergo etiam in sanctis punitur negligentia, multo magis vero punientur praesentibus et aeternis poenis omnes illi, qui coenam Domini verterunt in horrendum cultum idolorum, et qui quaestus causa finxerunt sacrificium, pro vivis et mortuis. Horum maxi- morum scelerum magnitudo conspicietur post hanc vitam. Et ibi agnoscemus, haec scelera multa- rum calamitatum in hac vita causas fuisse. Ora- mus autem ardentibus gemitibus filium Dei, ut ipse his magnis vulneribus Ecclesiae medeatur.

Nunc verba consideremus.

In textu est: Quod pro vobis frangitur. In narratione apud Lucam scriptum est: Quod pro vobis datur, id est, quod est victima pro genere humano. Ideo et hic alia interpretantur, fran- gitur pro laceratur. Id non reprehendo. Sed simplicius videtur fractionem intelligendam esse distributionem, sicut Ebraei loquebantur: Fran- ge esurienti panem tuum. Et hoc verbum Paulo in mentem venit propter morem distributionis, praesertim cum velit esse coenam communem.

Τοῦτο τὸ ποτήριον ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη ἐστὶν. Hic est Calix, qui est novum Testamentum in meo sanguine.

Haec narratio apud Lucam iisdem verbis po- sita est. Sed addita sunt haec verba: Qui pro vobis effunditur. Syntaxis apud Matthaeum et Marcum alia est. Hic est sanguis meus novi Te- stamenti: nec subtiliter quaerenda est differentia. Eodem modo utraque lectio intelligenda est: Hic est calix novi Testamenti, id est, ritus et pignus seu sigillum novi Testamenti. Nam Testamentum principaliter et proprie significat ipsam promis- sionem remissionis peccatorum, Spiritus sancti, iusticiae, et vitae aeternae. Deinde haec bene- ficia sunt res donatae hoc Testamento, id est, hac Promissione. Et accedunt externi ritus, qui sunt huius promissionis signa et pignora: Ba- ptismus et Coena Domini. Ideo Matthaeus dixit: Hic est sanguis meus novi Testamenti.

Cum autem Lucas et Paulus dicant: Hic est calix, novum Testamentum, μετωνυμία est, ut si dicam: Fasces sunt imperium Romanum. Hac brevi admonitione de Syntaxi hoc loco contenti simus.

Deinde valde necessaria est consideratio, cur hic expresse facta sit mentio novi Testamenti, et quidem in ea narratione, ubi fit mentio san- guinis.

Testamentum est promissio morituri. Ideo usurpata est haec vox de promissione filii Dei do- nantis sua beneficia, ut significaretur ventura mors, sicut ad Ebraeos scriptum est. Addita est igitur haec particula diserte huic narrationi, quae de fundendo sanguine loquitur. Et opponendi sunt typi sanguinis victimarum in veteri Testa- mento, qui omnes fuerunt signa huius futurae mortis.

Iam et antithesis consideranda est veteris et novi Testamenti. Vetus Testamentum est pro- missio politiae, cum obligatione ad servandam legem per Moysen traditam, quae politia consti- tuta est, ut in ea conservaretur promissio de Messia, et ibi Messias exhiberetur, propter quem et semper ibi aliqua electorum Ecclesia fuit.

Sed novum Testamentum est promissio bo- norum aeternorum, remissionis peccatorum, Spi- ritus sancti, iusticiae et vitae aeternae, quae propter Messiam Gratis exhibentur, non propter legem.

Affirmat igitur Dominus, iam haec bona exhi- beri, et hunc calicem huius exhibitionis pignus esse. Magna igitur consolatio universae Ecclesiae pro- ponitur. Exhibito hoc calice, scias certo exhi- beri bona aeterna, propter sanguinem filii Dei effusum in ipsius morte. Nec opus ullius homi- nis meretur illa aeterna bona legata propter filii mortem. Non igitur hic ritus sacrificium est, quod mereatur facienti et aliis haec bona, sed testatur ea exhiberi, et fide ea accipi oportet, quae nititur ipsius filii Dei sacrificio, non ullis nostris meritis.

Haec amplissima doctrina comprehensa est in hac appellatione novi Testamenti, quam hic integram complecti non possumus: tantum bre- viter admoneo, huius doctrinae fontes requiren- dos esse, quoties de coena Domini cogitamus, et quoties ad eam accedimus.

Manifesta refutatio est Sacrificulorum et Anabaptistarum. Cum sit ritus novae promis- sionis, quae est gratuita, non est sacrificium, quod aliis mereatur, Item, cum sit ritus Testa- menti, nobis exhiberi legata a filio testatur, et pignus est voluntatis Dei erga nos, non tantum est ceremonia mutuae dilectionis inter convivas, ut Anabaptistae dicunt.

Est et haec particula insignis, quod hunc ritum servare iubet, donec Christus venerit. Haec verba sunt perspicuum testimonium, Deum sem- per in hac vita usque ad resuscitationem mortuo- rum servaturum esse Ecclesiam, publicum mini- nisterium Sacramentorum, publicos congressus, et aliqua Ecclesiarum hospitia. Hae dulces con- solationes in hac brevi particula continentur.

Ἔνοχος ἔσται τοῦ σώματος καὶ αἵματος. Reus erit corporis et sanguinis.

Magnitudinem peccati in abusu coenae Do- mini describit, cum ait, abutentes reos esse cor- poris et sanguinis, id est, contumelia afficere corpus et sanguinem Domini, sicut latrones cru- cifigentes Dominum contumelia eum afficiebant. Et gradus sunt. Contumeliae sunt, cum profani accipiunt propter consuetudinem, sine poeniten- tia et sine fide petente remissionem. Sed maio- res contumeliae sunt, cum fingitur usus esse sa- crificium, quod mereatur aliis. Item, cum con- fertur in quaestum, et mutatur in idolum. Pro- pter haec horrenda peccata multis ingentibus calamitatibus, bellis et vastationibus totae gentes puniuntur, et hi qui non agunt poenitentiam, op- primentur aeternis poenis. Oremus autem filium Dei Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, ut Ec- clesiam suam liberet ab omnibus erroribus et ido- lis, et lumen veritatis, veram invocationem, et veros cultus accendat.

Εἰ γὰρ ἑαυτοὺς διεκρίνομεν, οὐκ ἂν ἐκρινόμεθα. Si nos ipsos iudicaremus, non iudicaremur.

Hanc sententiam monachi ad satisfactiones transtulerunt. Sed manifesta concio est tota poe- nitentia. Simul culpa et poena aeterna propter filium Dei Gratis remittuntur, iuxta illud: O mors ero mors tua, et pestis tua o inferne. Item: Qui credit in filium, habet vitam aeternam.

Deinde verum et hoc est, praesentes poenas propter totam poenitentiam mitigari vel tolli, ut testatur historia Ionae. Et Esaiae 1. cap. dicitur: Si peccata vestra fuerint ut coccinum, eritis can- didi sicut nix. Cum enim velit Deus in hac vita, quanquam aerumnosa, servare Ecclesiam, mitigat poenas, ut aliqui homines sint superstites, conservetur generatio et educatio sobolis, et ministerium Evangelii publicum, et sint Ecclesiae hospitia politiae et oeconomiae. Et sciamus propter hunc finem mitigari poenas, ne Ecclesia funditus in hac vita deleatur. Et hunc finem intuentes, petamus mitigationem, sicut precatur Ecclesia in Psalmo: Non nobis Domine, non nobis, sed nomini tuo da gloriam, Non mortui laudabunt te Domine.

Deinde Paulus generalem doctrinam de afflictionibus tradit: Cum iudicamur a Domino corripimur, ne cum hoc mundo damnemur. In Ecclesia necesse est sciri causas, quare natura humana, cum antecellat omnibus animantibus, subiecta sit morti et tantis aerumnis, ac deinde, quare haec pars, quae est Ecclesia Dei, magis etiam onerata sit.

Philosophi dicunt, mala quaedam oriri a materia, quaedam a nostris erroribus et voluntatibus. Hi loquuntur de propinquis causis. Sed cur materia hominis obnoxia est corruptioni? Cur tanta caligo in mente humana? cur in voluntatibus et corde tanta contumacia est? Hic principalem causam sola vox Dei in Ecclesia monstrat, quae narrat peccatum esse causam mortis et aliarum miseriarum in toto genere humano, ut in Genesi scriptum est. Et Paulus inquit: Per peccatum mors.

Praeterea cum Deus velit in Ecclesia conspici suam iram adversus peccata, et velit nos commonefieri de poenitentia et de promissionibus, magis etiam exercet Ecclesiam. Et sunt aliae plures causae, quae suo loco recitantur. Communissima est autem haec, quam Paulus hoc loco recitat, de qua et Psalm. loquitur: Bonum mihi quod humiliasti me, ut discam iustificationes tuas. Ex his fontibus sumuntur praecipuae consolationes, de quibus alibi copiosius dicitur. Hic tantum adscribam collationem philosophicarum consolationum, et Christianarum, quam habere in conspectu utile est.

Philosophicarum consolationum loci sunt quinque.

I. Necessitas.

II. Virtus anteferenda dolori.

III. Bona conscientia.

IV. Exempla.

V. Causae finales.

Primus locus est necessitas. Cum enim mutari malum non potest, frustra augemus dolorem repugnando, sicut dicitur: μὴ πρὸς κέντρα λακτίζειν.

Secundus, quia ratio et lex naturae iubent anteferre virtutem dolori, non faciamus aliquid inhoneste, fracti dolore, ut Cato iniuste facit, quod sibi mortem consciscit propter dolorem.

Tertius, magna levatio est bona conscientia, ut dicitur: Est aliquid magnis crimen abesse malis: quia minus dolent Palamedes, Socrates, Camillus et similes, quia conscientia non est saucia. Econtra Iudas et similes magis dolent, quia intus et foris cruciantur, et conscientiae Erinnyes multo maiores cruciatus afferunt, quam ulla externa corporis laceratio.

Quartus, Exempla ideo utcunque leniunt dolorem, quia honestorum tristes casus ostendunt, ipsam calamitatem non esse turpitudinem. Feruntur autem facilius ea, quae videntur esse sine turpitudine, ut facilius fert exilium Cicero, quia scit in eadem republica antea viros optimos expulsos esse, ut Camillum, Rutilium, alios etiam interfectos, ut Antonium oratorem et alios.

Quintus, Causa finalis bona minuit dolorem, ut quando aliis prodest nostra calamitas, ut Codrus appetit mortem pro patria.

Hae consolationes, etsi utcunque deliniunt animos, tamen relinquunt eos in morte, nec ostendunt vitam et liberationem ex miseriis. Ideo his languidis consolationibus opponantur Christianae, quarum loci aliqui sumti ex lege Dei congruunt cum philosophicis, sed aliqui sunt proprii Evangelii.

Primus est Necessitas, videlicet lex Dei, quae sanxit poenas. Ideo etiam dictum est: Humiliamini sub potenti manu Dei.

Secundus, Virtus anteferenda dolori. Sumitur et haec consolatio ex lege, quia lex divina praecipit, ne fracti dolore contra iusticiam faciamus, ut Cato violavit legem: Non occidas.

Tertius, Bona conscientia. Sumitur et hic locus ex lege divina, quia et lex divina praecipit dolorem propter scelera, et de bona conscientia scriptum est: Secura mens iuge convivium.

Quartus, Agnitio misericordiae et praesentiae Dei, et auxilii divini. Haec consolatio propria est Evangelii, in quo certum est promissam esse remissionem peccatorum, et poenae aeternae, et auxilium Dei in hac vita. David pulsus in exilium meminit sui lapsus, sed tamen sustentat se, et acquiescit in Deo, quia scit sibi remitti peccata et poenas aeternas. Scit se a Deo rece- ptum esse, et se a Deo exaudiri iam et protegi, sicut Esaias inquit: Deus habitans cum contrito et humiliato spiritu, et vivificet spiritum humi- lium. Praecipuam oportet esse hanc consolatio- nem in omni dolore, ut recte instituti in Evange- lio norunt.

Quintus, Spes liberationis aut mitigationis, et tandem aeternae salutis. Haec consolatio cum proxima coniuncta est. Cum corda erecta remis- sione peccatorum acquiescunt in Deo, et certo statuunt, se exaudiri a Deo, norunt iam promis- sam esse liberationem ab aeterna morte, sciunt etiam Deum velle in praesentia opem ferre, et vel prorsus tollere aerumnas, vel mitigare. Hae duae consolationes vere superant dolorem, quia donec mens tantum intuetur aerumnas, et mor- tem seu interitum, vincit dolor. Sed quando ob- iectum est res bona, videlicet Deus propicius et volens opem ferre, et mitigare praesentes mise- rias, et tandem liberare ab omnibus malis. Hoc obiectum, quod est res bona, causa est gaudii. Tunc igitur vincitur dolor, cum haec bona ob- iecta mens intuetur. Iob vincit dolores suos, quia scit propositam esse ultimam liberationem, sicut inquit: Etiamsi occidet me, tamen sperabo in eo: et tamen expectat in praesentia quoque mi- tigationem. Palamedes, Socrates, etsi minus dolent, quia conscientia non est sauciata, tamen nihil nisi interitum cernunt. Sed Baptista, Ste- phanus intuentur venturam vitam in dulcissima consuetudine aeternae Ecclesiae. Hoc bonum spe iam possident. Et spes laetitiae causa est, sicut in versu de Stephano dicitur: Ibat ovans animis, et spe sua damna levabat, id est, laetus, et quia libenter Deo obediebat, et quia iam spe Ecclesiae coelestis civis erat.

Sextus, Exempla in Ecclesia etiam magis leniunt dolorem, quam apud Ethnicos, quia in Ecclesia causae notae sunt, quare subiecta sit cruci: et scimus non tantum interitum, sed libe- rationem propositam esse. Et exempla sunt illu- striora. Cum filius Dei, cum alia praecipua membra Ecclesiae sustinuerint ingentes aerumnas certo con- silio Dei, quod Ecclesiae ostendit, non velimus nos seiungi a reliqua societate in afflictionibus et liberationibus. Et inqualitas ac superbia esset, si vellemus nobis melius esse, quam filio Dei, quam Abel, Ieremiae, Baptistae et similibus. Et hic causae afflictionum notae sint. Pro- pter peccatum nobiscum nascens generi humano universaliter mos imposita est, et morbi et aliae multae aerumnae. Deinde singulares afflictiones, sunt alias poenae certorum delictorum, ut Davi- dis exilium: alias exercitia, ut carcer Ioseph: alias testimonia confessionis et immortalitatis, ut neces Abel, Baptistae, Stephani. Et cum exem- pla nobis proponimus, simul considerandae sunt causae. Ut in aliis doctrinis non satis est exem- pla intueri, sed etiam considerari oportet exem- plorum rationes et discrimina. Et de exemplis recte accommodatis dici potest illud vetus dictum: κοινὸν ναυάγιον πᾶσι παραμύθιον. Septimus, Causae finales. Communissima causa finalis haec est: Bonum mihi, quod humi- liasti me, ut discerem iustificationes tuas. Affli- git Deus non ut perdat, sed ut vel retrahat ho- mines ad poenitentiam, ut affliguntur David, Osias, Manasses: vel exerceat et confirmet suos, ut affliguntur Ioseph, Daniel et similes, et Pau- lus huius causae mentionem facit hoc loco: Cum iudicamur, a Domino corripimur, ne cum hoc mundo damnemur. Sunt et in Ecclesia aliae causae, de quibus iam dixi. Lenitur etiam dolor, quando nostra confes- sione scimus alios confirmari, de qua causa lo- quitur Paulus ad Philippenses 2. cum inquit, Se laetari, quod immoletur, ut ipsi in sacrificio et ministerio fidei confirmentur. Haec brevis admo- nitio de collatione consolationum, aliquid lucis adfert huic loco Pauli. Et lectores mente in- tueantur ea, quae de cruce alibi copiosius di- cuntur.

## 12:1 Argument
Chapter twelve.

Great is the infirmity of human nature, great is the dissimilarity of natures. Wherefore even in a small society, rivalries, dissensions, lapses, and offenses easily arise, just as Demosthenes says that errors and contentions are the common diseases of all cities, and happen necessarily: κοινὰ καὶ

ἀναγκαῖα ἁμαρτήματα πολιτικὰ, ἀγνοίας καὶ φιλονεικείας. Thus in the Corinthian Church, lapses and other inconveniences had occurred. There were dissensions concerning doctrine, there was incest, abuse of liberty, some were approaching feasts in the sacrifices of the Gentiles, some were raising questions about the divorces of non-believers, some were disturbing the order of the Lord's Supper. Some were unwilling to contribute to the support of faithful ministers. He has endeavored to remedy these offenses thus far in this Epistle. Nor is there one perpetual argument, as the thing itself shows: and let the reader consider the diverse occasions.

In this following part he writes about two matters: Concerning the order of readings and interpretations in public assembly, and concerning the resurrection of the dead. The Greek nation delighted in the gift of tongues, and many were showing off their eloquence in public assembly. From there, rivalries also arose. Paul therefore preaches in general about the use of gifts, and afterwards adds precepts about the order of readings and interpretations, useful for all ages. Indeed, even the form of judgments in Synods is to be taken from here.

Latin:

Caput duodecimum.

Magna infirmitas est naturae humanae, magna naturarum dissimilitudo. Quare etiam in parva societate facile existunt aemulationes, dissidia, lapsus et offensiones, sicut Demothenes ait, Er- rores et contentiones communes morbos esse om- nium civitatum, et necessario accidere: κοινὰ καὶ

ἀναγκαῖα ἁμαρτήματα πολιτικὰ, ἀγνοίας καὶ φιλονεικείας. Ita in Ecclesia Corinthia acciderant lapsus et alia incommoda. Erant dissensiones de doctrina, incestus erat abusus libertate, aliqui accedebant ad convivia in Ethnicorum sacrificiis, movebant aliqui quaestiones de divortiis non cre- dentium, quidam turbabant ordinem coenae Do- mini. Quidam nolebant conferre ad alendos fide- les ministros. His offensionibus hactenus in hac Epistola mederi studuit. Nec est unum perpe- tuum argumentum, ut res ipsa ostendit: et lector diversas occasiones consideret.

In hac sequenti parte de duabus materiis scribit: De ordine lectionum et interpretationum in publico congressu, et de resurrectione mortuo- rum. Graeca natio delectabatur dono linguarum, et multi in publico congressu suam eloquentiam ostentabant. Inde etiam aemulationes orieban- tur. Paulus igitur in genere concionatur de usu donorum, et postea addit praecepta de or- dine lectionum et interpretationum, utilia omni- bus aetatibus. Imo et forma iudiciorum in Syn- odis hinc sumenda est.

## 12:2
Οἴδατε ὅτι ὅτε ἔθνη ἦτε. You know that when you were Gentiles.

Before he speaks about the diverse gifts of individuals, he first warns that one common, chief gift ought to be in all, and that it is to be sought in individuals above other gifts, and maintained, namely the Holy Spirit confessing that Jesus is Lord, just as he also said above, that there is one foundation, Jesus Christ.

He says this foundation is necessary in all, that all ought to abhor idols, and that there ought to be true invocation of God and acknowledgment of the mediator in all. This he commands all to maintain at the beginning, lest they rush, as they did before when they were not ruled by the light of the Gospel and the Holy Spirit, to mute idols wherever they were driven.

Here therefore he warns of many things, he shows that the blindness of all men who are not ruled by the light of the Gospel and by the Holy Spirit is horrible, as examples show. The Gentiles were daily devising new cults; the Athenians in the war of Xerxes instituted sacrifices to Boreas, they said he was friendly to them because he had once begotten children from Orithyia. Prostitutes in that very city of Corinth made a common vow for the safety of Greece. Finally, there was no end to such madnesses. And similar things happened and they are still done, where one runs to statues, and the dead and various idols are invoked.

He therefore delivers the same rule, making the antithesis in a twofold way, because usually wickedness can be more clearly seen: No one having the Holy Spirit, he says, calls Jesus Anathema. It is most certain that those who either openly curse the Son of God, or in any way provide a sign of contempt and hatred, are not members of the Church of God: and these things can easily be detected, because after hatred has flared up in persecution, a huge and not obscure fire is made. Judas does not hide his hatred for long. For the instigator, the devil, approaches, as it is written: Satan entered into his heart. Immediately, therefore, great furies occur, as is seen in Julian, Arius, and in the history of these recent times: when once hatred has flared up, a huge fury is made, as in Eccius, Latomus, and Hofmeister, who even while raging showed signs of their despair before death. And a monk in Berlin, whom many here knew, while cursing in the very sermon, suddenly collapsed and was extinguished immediately afterwards.

The Apostle therefore wishes the enemies of Christ to be distinguished from the rest, and he shows a sign by which they can be distinguished without any ambiguity. And at the same time he warns that we should avoid such lapses, and tremble at the thought of the horrible punishment, lest we fall, like Judas, Arius, Latomus, Hofmeister, and the like.

The other part in the antithesis seems more obscure, when he says: No one can confess that Jesus is Lord, except in the Holy Spirit. For someone will object about the innumerable hypocrites, monks, and the like, who also want to appear to worship Jesus. And he himself says elsewhere: Not everyone who says to me Lord, Lord, will enter the kingdom of heaven. But the explanation is easy.

Paul speaks of a persevering confession, and in the whole doctrine. Hypocrites fail quickly, and when their errors are rebuked, they become the most bitter enemies of the Gospel, as we now see happening in Bishops, Monks, and Mass-priests. Nor can hypocrisy ever remain hidden for long.

Therefore, just as hatred against Christ and curses are the most certain signs of a mind that is impious and captive to the devil, so on the contrary, the testimonies of the Holy Spirit are the invocation of Christ—not fleeing from him, but willingly approaching him and resting in him—and love for the whole doctrine, and a zeal for learning, and constancy in confession. These things most correctly agree with this saying: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him. And the conscience of each person can judge concerning their own invocation. Furthermore, others can also perceive the strength of spirit in confession, and there are many signs by which hypocrisy can be distinguished from true faith.

Διαιρέσεις δὲ χαρισμάτων εἰσί. There are divisions of gifts.

Before, he spoke of the common gift, which must be in all true members of the Church, namely, of the true invocation of God and the acknowledgment of the Son of God, and of fleeing from idols.

Now he speaks of other gifts, which are added, in some one, in others another. Such as the gift of tongues; the gift of healing. And at the beginning he prefaces that these also are given by God, so that they may be testimonies of the Holy Spirit, and be of benefit to the Church. However, let the distinctions of the names be observed. He calls these endowments χαρίσματα, διακονίας, and ἐνεργήματα. Διακονίαι are those which immediately serve the utility of others, such as healings. Thus, there are διακονίαι of singular success in military matters or government. As Samson and Solomon excelled in διακονίᾳ.

The name ἐνεργήματα signifies other wondrous effects, such as raising the dead, likewise killing by a word, just as Peter recalled a woman to life in Joppa, and killed Ananias with a word.

The general term is χαρίσματα, such as prophecy, the prediction of future events, as Agabus.

But as to what he says: The same God is he who works all things in all, it is manifest that this is said here only concerning good actions in the Church. Therefore, this sentence is not to be twisted toward the Stoic ravings, which imagine God to be the cause of evil and good actions alike.

But as to the fact that here the names πνεῦμα, κύριος, θεὸς are accommodated to the three persons, that also pleased Luther.

Λόγος σοφίας.

Σοφία and γνῶσις differ.

Σοφία is the knowledge of the whole doctrine concerning God, and the experience of terrors in contrition, and of the consolations of faith, illuminating doctrine, and judging dogmas. As those who have experienced it, David, Hezekiah, Paul, understand the saying: We are justified by faith, differently. Origen understands it differently.

Γνῶσις is the prudence that gives counsel in matters to be done, as in Solomon judging whose the dead infant was, there was γνῶσις. There was γνῶσις when Paul indicated where he would observe Jewish rites and where he would not, when he gave counsel concerning marriages. In Zechariah dissuading that war be moved against the Romans, although they were seizing the didrachma from the temple.

Πίστις is a general gift of faith for performing miracles, whether in one's own dangers or those of others, as it was πίστις that is written in Acts chapter 27: The ship and the whole company of those sailing together are saved because of the faith of Paul. And the following words show that the name πίστις is general, because he says: If I have all faith, so that I move mountains.

What the gifts of healings signify is clear.

I said above that Ἐνεργήματα are excellent effects, such as the raising of the dead.

Prophecy in this place is the prediction of future events, as we said concerning Agabus. Below there will also be the correct and right interpretation of sermons which have been divinely delivered in the Prophets and Apostles.

Next is added διάκρισις πνευμάτων, the discernment of both dogmas and spirits, just as at the beginning the first authors and propagators of the Anabaptist superstition cast a great appearance of religion before the eyes of men, boasted of singular revelations, and narrated what kind of motions they felt in their heart. This new appearance among many, as among Karlstadt, begat admiration for them. But Luther immediately noticed the deception, because they did not teach the doctrine of the righteousness of faith, but exalted their own wisdom and their own exercises. And in the city of Münster in Westphalia, before the manifest crimes of the Anabaptists had broken out, Hermann von dem Busche, a noble man and poet, most sharply opposed them at the beginning, when they began to make a segregation of the pure Church from the rest, whose morals they were criticizing.

Γένη γλωσσῶν is to know many diverse languages.

Ἑρμηνεία γλωσσῶν is the faculty of teaching, and of explaining intricate controversies in order and clearly. So that although Reuchlin knows many languages, he could not have explained the controversy concerning the righteousness of faith or the power of Bishops as Luther did.

Afterwards Paul adds the precept that this diversity of gifts should be brought to the common utility. And he repeats the ranks.

Apostles are those who are called immediately by Christ to teach the Gospel, and have testimonies that they do not err in doctrine, and have a universal calling so that they can teach everywhere, and they are not called to political government, like Samuel, Elisha, Jeremiah.

Prophets here are interpreters who are instructed with a singular gift for the restoration of doctrine, like Augustine in his time, Luther in our time.

Doctors are those who receive doctrine from these, and faithfully hand it on to others without corruptions; they are not Apostles or the first restorers of collapsed doctrine, but are as it were δεύτερα λέγοντες, agreeing with the voice of the Apostles and Prophets.

He calls Δυνάμεις the same thing as ἐνεργήματα above.

᾿Αντιλήψεις, aids, deliverances from great dangers, as Paul delivers those sailing with him. Isaiah delivers Jerusalem from a siege. James the Bishop delivers Nisibis, when it was being besieged by the Persian king, as the tripartite history narrates. And many similar examples are read.

Κυβερνήσεις, that is, governances, such as the offices of Deacons, of magistrates.

Latin:

Οἴδατε ὅτι ὅτε ἔθνη ἦτε. Scitis quod quando gentiles eratis.

Antequam dicit de singulorum donis diver- sis, primum monet unum commune donum prae- cipuum in omnibus esse oportere, et id prae cae- teris donis quaerendum esse in singulis, et tuen- dum, videlicet Spiritum sanctum confitentem Iesum esse Dominum, sicut et supra dixit, uni- cum esse fundamentum, Iesum Christum.

Hoc fundamentum ait necessarium esse in omnibus, oportere omnes abhorrere ab idolis, et oportere in omnibus veram invocationem Dei, et agnitionem mediatoris esse. Id initio iubet omnes tueri, ne ruant, sicut antea cum non re- gerentur luce Evangelii et Spiritu sancto, ad muta idola quocunque impellebantur.

Hic igitur multa monet, ostendit horrendam esse coecitatem omnium hominum, qui non re- guntur luce Evangelii et a Spiritu sancto, sicut exempla ostendunt. Ethnici quotidie novos cul- tus excogitabant, Athenienses bello Xerxis insti- tuerunt sacrificia Boreae, dicebant esse ipsis ami- cum, quia olim ex Orithyia genuisset filios. Me- retrices in illa ipsa urbe Corintho pro salute Grae- ciae commune votum fecerunt. Denique nullus fuit finis talium furorum. Et similia acciderunt et adhuc fiunt, ubi curritur ad statuas, et invo- cantur mortui et varia idola.

Tradit igitur regulam eandem, dupliciter faciens antithesin, quia plerunque scelus magis conspici potest: Nemo habens Spiritum sanctum, dicit, Anathema Iesum. Certissimum est, vel palam maledicentes filio Dei, vel quoquo modo praebentes significationem contemtus et odii, non esse membra Ecclesiae Dei: et facile haec depre- hendi possunt, quia postquam exarsit odium in persecutione, fit ingens et non obscurum incen- dium. Non diu occultat odium Iudas. Nam ac- cedit impulsor diabolus, sicut scriptum est: Sa- tanas intravit in cor eius. Statim igitur fiunt magni furores, ut in Iuliano, Ario, et in horum recentium temporum historia conspicitur: cum semel exarsit odium, fit ingens furor, ut in Ec- cio, Latomo, Hofmeistero, qui etiam furentes ante mortem suae desperationis signa ostenderunt. Et Berlini monachus, quem hic multi noverunt, inter maledicendum in ipsa concione subito col- lapsus, statim postea extinctus est.

Vult igitur Apostolus discerni hostes Christi a caeteris, et signum monstrat, quo discerni sine ulla ambiguitate possunt. Et simul monet, ut tales lapsus vitemus, et horrendae poenae cogi- tatione expavescamus, ne ruamus, sicut Iudas, Arius, Latomus, Hofmeisterus et similes.

Altera pars in antithesi videtur obscurior, cum ait: Nemo potest fateri Iesum esse Domi- num, nisi in Spiritu sancto. Obiiciet enim ali- quis innumerabiles hypocritas, monachos et si- miles, qui etiam videri volunt Iesum adorare. Et ipse alibi inquit: Non omnis qui dicit mihi Domine Domine, intrabit in regnum coelorum. Sed explicatio facilis est.

Paulus loquitur de confessione perseveranti, et in tota doctrina. Hypocritae cito deficiunt, et cum reprehenduntur ipsorum errores, fiunt acer- bissimi hostes Evangelii, ut nunc in Episcopis, Monachis, et Sacrificulis fieri cernimus. Nec unquam hypocrisis diu latere potest.

Ut igitur odium adversus Christum, et ma- ledicta sunt certissima signa mentis impiae et ca- ptivae diabolis, ita econtra Spiritus sancti testi- monia sunt, invocatio Christi, non fugitans, sed libenter ad eum accedens, et in eo acquiescens, et amor totius doctrinae, et studium discendi, et constantia in confessione. Haec rectissime con- gruunt ad hoc dictum: Si quis diligit me, sermo- nem meum servabit, et pater meus diliget eum, et veniemus ad eum, et mansionem apud eum faciemus. Ac potest uniuscuiusque conscientia iudicare de propria invocatione. Deinde et alii cernere robur animi in confessione possunt, et multa signa sunt, quibus hypocrisis a vera fide discerni potest.

Διαιρέσεις δὲ χαρισμάτων εἰσί. Divisiones donorum sunt.

Antea dixit de communi dono, quod in om- nibus veris membris Ecclesiae esse oportet, scili- cet de vera invocatione Dei et agnitione filii Dei, et de fugiendis idolis.

Nunc dicit de aliis donis, quae accedunt, in aliis alia. Ut de dono linguarum; de dono sana- tionis. Et initio praefatur, haec quoque dari a Deo, ut sint testimonia Spiritus sancti, et pro- sint Ecclesiae. Observentur autem discrimina nominum. Vocat has dotes χαρίσματα διακονίας et ἐνεργήματα. Διακονίαι sunt, quae imme- diate serviunt aliorum utilitati, ut sanationes. Ita sunt διακονίαι singularis felicitas in re mili- tari aut gubernatione. Ut Samson et Salomon excelluerunt διακονίᾳ.

Nomen ἐνεργήματα significat alias miran- das effectiones, ut resuscitare mortuos, item verbo occidere, sicut Petrus revocavit in vitam mulie- rem in Ioppe, occidit verbo Ananiam.

Generale est χαρίσματα, ut prophetia, prae- dictio futurorum, ut Agabus.

Quod autem dicit: Idem Deus est, qui effi- cit omnia in omnibus, manifestum est hic tan- tum dici de bonis actionibus in Ecclesia. Non igitur detorquenda est haec sententia ad stoica deliramenta, quae fingunt Deum causam esse pa- riter malarum et bonarum actionum.

Quod vero hic ad tres personas accommo- data sunt nomina, πνεῦμα, κύριος, θεὸς, id et Luthero placebat.

Λόγος σοφίας.

Σοφία et γνῶσις differunt.

Σοφία est cognitio totius doctrinae de Deo, et experientia terrorum in contritione, et conso- lationum fidei, illustrans doctrinam, et diiudi- cans dogmata. Ut experti, David, Ezechias, Paulus, aliter intelligunt dictum: Fide iustifica- mur. Aliter intelligit Origenes.

Γνῶσις est prudentia dans consilia in rebus agendis, ut in Salomone iudicante, cuius esset infans mortuus, erat γνῶσις. Erat γνῶσις, quando Paulus indicabat, ubi servaret ritus Iudaicos, ubi non servaret, quando dabat consilia de coniugiis. In Zacharia dissuadente, ne bellum moveretur contra Romanos, quanquam eripiebant templo didrachmum.

Πίστις generale donum fide faciendi miracula, vel in propriis periculis vel alienis, ut πίστις fuit, quod in Actis capite 27. scriptum est: Servatur navis et totus coetus simul navigantium propter fidem Pauli. Et verba sequentia ostendunt nomen πίστις generale esse, quia dicit: Si habuero omnem fidem, ut montes transferam.

Donationes sanationum quid significent, perspicuum est.

Ἐνεργήματα dixi supra effectiones excellentes esse, qualis est resuscitatio mortuorum.

Prophetia hoc loco est praedictio futurorum, ut diximus de Agabo. Infra etiam erit recta et dextra interpretatio concionum, quae sunt divinitus traditae in Prophetis et Apostolis.

Proxime additur διάκρισις πνευμάτων, diiudicatio et dogmatum et spirituum, ut initio primi autores et propagatores anabaptisticae superstitionis magnam speciem religionis offundebant oculis hominum, iactitabant singulares revelationes, et narrabant quales in corde motus sentirent. Haec nova species apud multos, ut apud Carolostadium, pariebat eis admirationem. Sed Lutherus statim animadvertit fucum, quia non docebant doctrinam de iusticia fidei, sed efferebant suam sapientiam et sua exercitia. Et in urbe Monasteriensi in Westphalia, priusquam erupissent manifesta scelera Anabaptistarum, acerrime adversatus est eis initio Hermannus Buschius, vir nobilis et poëta, cum segregationem facere inciperent Ecclesiae pura a reliquis, quorum mores reprehendebant.

Γένη γλωσσῶν est nosse multas diversas linguas.

Ἑρμηνεία γλωσσῶν est facultas docendi, et ordine ac plane exponendi controversias intricatas. Ut quanquam Capnio novit multas linguas, tamen non potuisset controversiam de iusticia fidei, aut potestate Episcoporum exponere, ut Lutherus.

Postea addit Paulus praeceptum, ut haec di- versitas donorum conferatur ad communem utili- tatem. Et repetit gradus.

Apostoli sunt, qui immediate a Christo ad docendum Evangelium vocati sunt, et testimonia habent, quod non errent in doctrina, et habent universalem vocationem, ut docere ubique pos- sint, nec sunt vocati ad politicam gubernationem, ut Samuel, Elisaeus, Ieremias.

Prophetae hic sunt interpretes, qui ad in- stauratiouem doctrinae singulari dono instructi sunt, ut Augustinus suo tempore, Lutherus no- stro tempore.

Doctores sunt, qui doctrinam ab his acci- piunt, et aliis fideliter tradunt sine corruptelis, non sunt Apostoli, aut primi instauratores col- lapsae doctrinae, sed tanquam δεύτερα λέγον- τες, consentientia cum Apostolorum et Prophe- tarum voce.

Δυνάμεις nominat idem quod supra ἐνερ- γήματα.

᾿Αντιλήψεις, auxilia, liberationes ex magnis periculis, ut Paulus liberat simul navigantes. Esaias liberat obsidione Ierosolymam. Iacobus Episcopus Nisibin, cum oppugnaretur a rege Per- sico, ut narrat historia tripartita. Et multa simi- lia exempla leguntur.

Κυβερνήσεις, id est, gubernationes, ut officia Diaconorum, magistratuum.

## 13:1 Argument
Chapter thirteen.

A universal rule is to be held in all deliberations and actions: Necessary things are to be preferred to non-necessary things. Now those things are necessary which are properly demanded by the commandments of God, namely the true knowledge of God, Faith, Fear, true Invocation, Love of neighbor. Therefore it is said in Matt. 19: If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.

Matt. 22: Which is the greatest commandment in the law? You shall love the Lord your God. But the second is like to this: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.

And 1 Timothy 1 it is said: The sum of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and faith unfeigned. Likewise: Fight the good fight, having faith and a good conscience. And in the last chapter of Matthew: Teaching them to observe all things, whatsoever I have commanded you. And in the last chapter of Ecclesiastes: Fear God, and keep his commandments. This pertains to all men. Micah 5: I will show thee, O man, what is good, and what the Lord requireth of thee: To do judgment, and to love mercy, and to walk solicitous with thy God. And Ezekiel 20: Walk in my statutes. And the negative sayings are more illustrious. In the first Epistle of John, chapter 3: Everyone who hateth his brother is a murderer. And you know that no murderer hath eternal life abiding in himself. And in the same chapter is expressly recited the true and artificially constituted definition of sin: ἁμαρτία ἐστὶν ἀνομία, sin is not obeying the law. For it is privatively opposed to the definition of universal justice: τὸ δίκαιον νόμιμον, as Plato, Xenophon, and Aristotle speak. Justice is the obedience due to all laws. And Galatians 5: The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, benignity, goodness, faith, mildness, continency. Against such there is no law. Where he also delivers a norm, namely the law, and approves actions congruent to this norm, and condemns the contrary, as he says in the same place: The works of the flesh are manifest, which are fornication, uncleanness, idolatry, they who do such things shall not obtain the kingdom of God. These rules having therefore been established: that necessary things must be done, and that precepts are by divine law, it follows clearly that love of neighbor is necessary, and to be preferred to gifts, which are ornaments not necessary to individuals, just as it is not necessary for individuals to know many languages. Paul usefully inserts this admonition concerning necessity here, taxing those who relaxed liberty in such a way that they thought they did not sin, even when they knowingly acted against the commandments of God. They preach therefore most severely concerning necessity: If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not love, I am become as sounding brass. And if I should have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not love, I am nothing. Here there are great contentions concerning justification. Since love is necessary, why do we not say that men are just by love? I answer: The cause of justification is one thing, that which is necessary as an effect following justification is another. As if I should say: The cause of life is one thing, that which is necessary in a living being as a following effect is another. As motion in a living being is necessary, not as the cause of life, but as a following effect. This example adds some light to this declaration: It is most manifest that contrition, love, and a good purpose are not the causes of justification, that is, of the remission of sins and the imputation of justice, and the donation of the Holy Spirit and eternal life. But the efficient cause, namely the justifying cause, is God on account of the merit of the Son alone. Faith, however, is the instrument by which the application is made. For by faith are received the remission of sins, the imputation of justice, the donation of the Holy Spirit, and of eternal life.

But after the Holy Spirit has been received, there are now in the reborn such motions as the Holy Spirit is. And if anyone feigns that the Holy Spirit is in someone, and that love is not there, he feigns contradictory things, as if someone were to feign that water is in something, and that there is no moisture.

Love is therefore necessary in the reborn, as an effect necessarily following. As we say that motion is necessarily in a living being, which nevertheless is not the cause of life. These things are clear to those who judge rightly and not calumniously.

But some cry out much more vehemently. Since Paul says, Even if I have all faith, I am nothing: he denies that a man is just, even if faith is present, yet love does not approach. Nor is any other argument more specious opposed against the exclusive: We are justified by faith alone.

The usual answer is that Paul is speaking of the gift of miracles, not of justifying faith. But here it is asked again, whether the gift can be in those who are not just, who cast off the Holy Spirit?

This perversity of men is greatly to be deplored and detested, that when the truth has been shown, they nevertheless do not acquiesce, nor do they give thanks to God, nor do they transfer it to use, but seek cavils without end. Whether gifts remain in some part or do not remain, the proposition is true: If I have not love, I am nothing. Because no one is just on account of the gift of miracles. And it is consistent that some gifts remain in hypocrites, as is said in Matthew: In thy name we have done many mighty works.

But in whatever way the word of faith is understood here, Paul's [statement] is absolutely true and immovable Prayer: Without love I am nothing. For it is necessary that in the reconciled or righteous person, that is, in him who is accepted by God, there be love. As has been said above: The Holy Spirit stirs such motions as He Himself is. Nor does Paul’s statement mean anything other than that of John: He who does not love remains in death. The prayer is true, because in the reconciled person there is conversion and begun obedience, according to that saying: As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live. Here in the oath itself mention is made of conversion. And the sayings are most well-known: I will put my law in their hearts. Likewise: Those who are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God. There is no doubt, therefore, that these sayings of Paul and John, which affirm that love is necessary, demand love as an effect which follows faith, and it is not the cause or merit of the remission of sins or of justification. Since these things are most manifest to those rightly instructed, I will not be more prolix. The rest in this chapter are grammatical.

Ἡ ἀγάπη μακροθυμεῖ.

Previously he said that in the reconciled love is necessary, which is to love one's neighbor for God's sake according to the commandments of God. Now he reviews the works of love, so that those who love may be distinguished from those who do not love. And Paul began with a work more well-known than the others, namely, the remission of vengeance. Vices are always more conspicuous. Therefore, let the explanation be taken from the contrary. The desire for vengeance manifestly fights with love, when, namely, someone thinking himself to have been harmed, burns with hatred and anger, and wishes to harm those by whom he thinks himself to have been harmed. Just as huge civil wars arose from the desire for vengeance between Marius and Sulla. The remission of vengeance calmed wars, as when Thrasybulus established an ἀμνηστίαν (amnesty). Scipio yielded to the Tribunes, so that greater disturbances might not arise in the republic. Maximilian, the victor, made peace with the Venetians, so that he would not attract the Turks. Arius, out of the pain of rejection in the election of a Bishop, later stirred up the struggle concerning the Son of God. And we ourselves have seen in these years certain ones inflamed by the desire for vengeance spreading new dogmas and stirring up the republic.

To repress this emotion is a great virtue, which is here named μακροθυμία, that is, patience. As David, when he indeed had great causes for removing Saul, nevertheless endures injuries, and is an illustrious example of this saying: Love is patient, that is, not desirous of vengeance. Moreover, this patience is a virtue pertaining to the commandment: You shall not kill. And it is justice, or equity near to justice, sparing others, even if it seems to be a cause of harm, yet for the sake of God and the public safety, as David spares many seditious citizens, so that the public calamity may be mitigated.

Χρηστεύεται.

It is kind or beneficial. To repress vengeance, when you seem to have been harmed, is patience, and is either justice or equity near to justice. But kindness or beneficence is, in addition, to do good either to friends or to enemies. Others have translated it as gentleness, which is not to be easily irritated. But that is clear, when one does good even to enemies, as Camillus is not alienated from the citizens by the pain of injury, but does good to them, and returns for the liberation of the fatherland, although unjustly expelled. Joseph does good to his brothers, although they had tried to destroy him.

Ἡ ἀγάπη οὐ ζηλοῖ.

It is not envious or jealous. Emulation is to wish to remove another, not because he has harmed, but because we are pained that he excels us. As Cain, Saul, Korah, Dathan, Abiram, and indeed even Aaron and his sister are inflamed by emulation. That evil arises most directly from pride, which first accompanies the love of ourselves. For we each wish to excel others, and to be like God, as the serpent says to Eve. Therefore we try to remove those who seem to be preferred. This vice is named Emulation and Envy. Hence those sayings: All the care for the men, who should be the commander. Likewise Cicero, It is the stain of the age to envy virtue.

Ἡ ἀγάπη οὐ περπερεύεται. It does not act insidiously.

Next to emulation and envy is to act insidiously, which is to drive out or remove others by artifice, just as Pericles by artifice expelled Cimon. And Aeschines tried to expel Demosthenes, and it is customary not only for courtiers, but also for public speakers, to find τέχνας (arts/tricks) for extruding colleagues, as Maximus by artifice extruded Gregory of Nazianzus. The Greeks use the word περπεροὶ concerning the Cecropians, who, since they were robbers, with singular cunning oppressed travelers. Wherefore the meaning of the word includes petulance and insidious plots. The name Perperi exists in the explanation of Proverbs in Erasmus: Do not fall into Melampygus.

Latin:

Caput tredecimum.

Universalis regula tenenda est in omnibus deliberationibus et actionibus: Necessaria ante- ferenda sunt non necessariis. Sunt autem neces- saria, quae praeceptis Dei proprie flagitantur, videlicet vera agnitio Dei, Fides, Timor, vera Invocatio, Dilectio proximi. Ideo dictum est Matth. 19. : Si vis in vitam ingredi, serva mandata.

Matth. 22.: Quod est mandatum maximum in lege? Diligas Dominum Deum tuum. Secun- dum autem simile huic: Diligas proximum sicut te ipsum.

Et 1. ad Timoth. 1. dicitur: Summa man- dati est, dilectio ex corde puro, conscientia bona, et fide non ficta. Item: Milita bonam militiam, habens fidem et bonam conscientiam. Et Matth. ultimo: Docentes eos servare om- nia, quae mandavi vobis. Et in capite ultimo Ecclesiastae: Deum time, et mandata eius servato. Hoc ad omnes homines pertinet. Micheae 5.: Indicabo o homo quid sit bo- num, et quid Dominus postulet abs te: Facere iudicium et diligere misericordiam, et solicitum ambulare coram Deo tuo. Et Ezechielis 20.: In praeceptis meis ambu- late. Ac magis illustria sunt dicta negativa. In prima Epistola Iohannis capite 3.: Om- nis qui odit fratrem, homicida est. Et scitis, quod omnis homicida non habet vitam aeternam in se manentem. Et eodem capite expresse recitatur vera et artificiose constituta definitio peccati: ἁμαρτία ἐστὶν ἀνομία, peccatum est non obedire legi. Est enim privative opposita definitioni iusticiae universalis: τὸ δίκαιον νόμιμον, ut Plato, Xeno- phon et Aristoteles loquuntur. Iusticia est obe- dientia legibus omnibus debita. Et Galat. 5.: Fructus spiritus, dilectio, gau- dium, pax, patientia, benignitas, bonitas, fides, mansuetudo, continentia. Contra talia enim non est lex. Ubi etiam normam tradit, scilicet legem, et adprobat actiones congruentes ad hanc normam, et damnat contrarias, ut eodem loco dicit: Ma- nifestae sunt actiones carnis, adulterium, scorta- tio, idolorum cultus, talia agentes regnum Dei non possidebunt. Constitutis igitur his regulis: Necessaria fa- cienda esse, et praecepta lege divina, necessaria esse: perspicue sequitur, dilectionem proximi necessariam esse, et anteferendam donis, quae sunt ornamenta non singulis necessaria, ut non necesse est singulos scire multas linguas. Hanc admonitionem de necessitate utiliter hic inserit Paulus, taxans eos, qui libertatem ita laxabant, ut arbitrarentur se non peccare, etiam cum scientes faciebant contra mandata Dei. Seve- rissime igitur concionantur de necessitate: Si lin- guis hominum et angelorum loquar, dilectionem autem non habeam, sum aes sonans. Etsi om- nem fidem habeam, ita aut montes transferam, dilectionem autem non habeam, nihil sum. Hic magnae contentiones sunt, de iustifica- tione, Cum necessaria sit dilectio, cur non di- cimus homines dilectione justos esse? Respon- deo: Aliud est causa iustificationis, aliud est ne- cessarium, ut effectus sequens iustificationem. Ut si dicam: Aliud est vitae causa, aliud est neces- sarium in vivente, ut effectus sequens. Ut mo- tus in vivente necessarius est, non ut vitae causa, sed ut effectus sequens. Hoc exemplum aliquid lucis addit huic declarationi: Manifestissimum est, contritionem, dilectionem, bonum proposi- tum non esse causas iustificationis, id est, remis- sionis peccatorum et imputationis iusticiae, et do- nationis Spiritus sancti et vitae aeternae. Sed causa efficiens, videlicet iustificans, est Deus propter solius filii meritum. Fides autem est in- strumentum, quo fit applicatio. Nam fide acci- piuntur remissio peccatorum, imputatio iusticiae, donatio Spiritus sancti, et vitae aeternae.

Postquam autem acceptus est Spiritus san- ctus, iam in renatis sunt motus tales, quales est Spiritus sanctus. Et si quis fingit in aliquo Spi- ritum sanctum esse, et non esse ibi dilectionem, pugnantia fingit, ut si quis fingeret in aliquo aquam esse, et nihil humoris esse.

Necessaria est igitur dilectio in renatis, ut effectus necessario sequens. Ut in vivente dici- mus necessario motum esse, qui tamen non est vitae causa. Haec perspicua sunt dextre et non calumniose iudicantibus.
