Sed vociferantur aliqui multo vehementius. Cum Paulus dicat, Etiamsi omnem fidem habeam, nihil sum: negat hominem iustum esse, etiamsi adsit fides, nec tamen accedat dilectio. Nec aliud argumentum speciosius opponitur contra exclusi- vam: Sola fide iustificamur.

Usitata responsio est, Paulum loqui de dono miraculorum, non de fide iustificante. Sed hic rursus quaeritur, an donum possit esse in his, qui non sunt iusti, qui excutiunt Spiritum sanctum?

Valde deploranda et detestanda est haec ho- minum perversitas, quod monstrata veritate, ta- men non acquiescunt, nec Deo gratias agunt, nec transferunt eam ad usum, sed quaerunt cavilla- tiones sine fine. Sive dona manent aliqua ex parte, sive non manent, vera est propositio: Si dilectionem non habeam, nihil sum. Quia nemo est iustus propter donum miraculorum. Et con- sentaneum est, aliqua dona manere in hypo- critis, ut in Matthaeo dicitur: In nomine tuo multas virtutes fecimus.

Caeterum quocunque modo vocabulum fidei hic intelligitur, prorsus vera et immota est Pauli oratio: Sine dilectione nihil sum. Oportet enim in reconciliato seu iusto, id est, in eo, qui acceptus est Deo, esse dilectionem. Ut supra dictum est: Spiritus sanctus tales motus ciet, qualis est ipse. Nec aliud vult Pauli dictum, quam illud Iohannis: Qui non diligit, manet in morte. Vera est oratio, quia in reconciliato est conversio et incoata obedientia, iuxta illud: Vivo ego, dicit Dominus, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed ut convertatur et vivat. Hic in ipso iuramento fit mentio conversionis. Et notissima sunt dicta: Dabo legem meam in corda eorum. Item: Qui spiritu Dei aguntur, hi sunt filii Dei. Non dubium est igitur, haec dicta Pauli et Iohannis, quae affirmant necessariam esse dilectionem, postulare dilectionem, ut effectum, qui sequitur fidem, nec est causa aut meritum remissionis peccatorum aut iustificationis. Haec cum manifestissima sint recte institutis, non ero prolixior. Caetera in hoc capite grammatica sunt.

Ἡ ἀγάπη μακροθυμεῖ.

Antea dixit, in reconciliatis necessariam esse dilectionem, quae est, propter Deum iuxta mandata Dei diligere proximum. Nunc recenset opera dilectionis, ut discerni possint diligentes a non diligentibus. Et exorsus est Paulus ab opere notiore caeteris, videlicet a remissione vindictae. Semper conspectiora sunt vitia. Ideo ex contrario sumatur declaratio. Cupiditas vindictae manifeste pugnat cum dilectione, cum videlicet aliquis putans se laesum esse, ardet odio et ira, et vult illis nocere, a quibus se laesum esse existimat. Ut civilia bella ingentia ex cupiditate vindictae inter Marium et Syllam orta sunt. Remissio vindictae sedavit bella, ut cum Thrasibulus sanxit ἀμνηστίαν. Scipio cessit Tribunis, ne maiores motus in republica orirentur. Maximilianus victor fecit pacem cum Venetis, ne attraheret Turcos. Arius dolore repulsae in electione Episcopi, movit postea certamen de filio Dei. Et vidimus ipsi his annis quosdam inflammatos cupiditate vindictae nova dogmata spargere et movere rempublicam.

Hunc affectum reprimere magna virtus est, quae hic nominatur μακροθυμία, id est, patientia. Ut David, cum quidem magnas causas haberet tollendi Saulem, tamen iniurias perfert, et est illustre exemplum huius dicti: Dilectio est patiens, id est, non cupida vindictae. Est autem haec patientia virtus pertinens ad praeceptum: Non occides. Et est iusticia, aut vicina iusticiae aequitas, aliis, etiamsi videatur esse nocendi causa, tamen propter Deum et salutem publicam parcens, ut David parcit multis civibus seditiosis, ut calamitas publica mitigetur.

Χρηστεύεται.

Benigna est seu benefica. Reprimere vin- dictam, cum videaris laesus, patientia est, et est vel iusticia, vel aequitas vicina iusticiae. Se be- nignitas seu beneficentia insuper est benefacere seu amicis seu inimicis. Lenitatem alii verterunt, quae est non facile irritari. Sed id perspicuum est, cum benefit etiam inimicis, ut Camillus non alie- natur a civibus dolore iniuriae, sed benefacit eis, et redit ad patriae liberationem, quanquam iniuste expulsus. Ioseph benefacit fratribus, quanquam perdere eum conati fuerant.

Ἡ ἀγάπη οὐ ζηλοῖ.

Non est aemulatrix seu invida. Aemulatio est velle alium tollere, non quia laesit, sed quia dolemus eum nobis antecellere. Ut Cain, Saul, Chore, Dathan, Abiron, imo et Aaron et soror accenduntur aemulatione. Id malum proxime oritur ex superbia, quae amorem nostri prima comitatur. Singuli enim volumus antecellere aliis, et esse Dei similes, ut inquit serpens ad Evam. Ideo tollere eos conamur, qui videntur anteferri. Hoc vitium nominatur Aemulatio et Invidentia. Hinc illa dicta sunt: Omnis cura viris, uter esset induperator. Item Cicero, Labes est seculi, invidere virtuti.

Ἡ ἀγάπη οὐ περπερεύεται. Non agit insidiose.

Aemulationi et invidentiae proximum est in- sidiari, quod est arte alios pellere aut tollere, sicut Pericles arte expulit Cimonem. Et Aschines co- nabatur expellere Demosthenem, et usitatum est non solum aulicis, sed et concionatoribus, inve- nire τέχνας ad extrudendos collegas, ut Maximus arte extrudit Gregorium Nazianzenum. Graeci usurpant vocabulum περπεροὶ de Cecropibus, qui cum essent latrones, singulari astutia viato- res opprimebant. Quare vocabuli significatio pe- tulantiam et insidias complectitur. Nomen Per- peri extat in explicatione Proverb. apud Eras- mum: In Melampygum ne incidas.

## 13:4
Οὐ φυσιοῦται. It is not puffed up.

If you consider the order of vices, the first is Pride, that is, admiration of self, preferring oneself to others, since in this depravity of nature men love themselves most, admire their own gifts, and demand to be magnified and honored by others, and wish to be like Gods, as the serpent said to Eve. From this pride follow hatreds against those who seem to obscure us. And when we try to repel them, great contentions and dissensions arise. This order of vices can be easily understood. But Paul previously spoke of those manifest vices which can be more observed and which arise from pride, of the desire for vengeance, of moroseness, which is the opposite of gentleness, and of treachery. Now he speaks of the root. He says that love is not puffed up, that is, that it is alien to pride and the haughtiness that despises others and exercises a kind of kingdom over others, which is a tyrannical evil, even when cruelty does not accompany it: yet to endure one who is despising and lifting himself too much above his colleagues, and acting as if he were reigning, is burdensome. And it is more burdensome when insults against others are added, as when the Roman Bishop Alexander III placed his foot on the neck of the Emperor Frederick. Within our memory there was the notable pride of the Cardinal of York in England, who, although he was the son of a butcher, walked in the middle between the Emperor Charles V and the English King Henry, placing his hand on the shoulder of each. In such a gesture this evil can be recognized in some way. But it is proper to love to subject oneself to others, and to confer gifts for the utility of others, and to conduct oneself as a minister and inferior to others, just as the Son of God took on the form of a servant. And there was very little pride in Cyrus and in Scipio, who even towards the lowest strove to be obliging, nor did they offer any sign that they preferred themselves to others. They strive to excel by labors and virtue, not by haughtiness.

Οὐκ ἀσχημονεῖ.

Many unseemly gestures accompany pride, of which mention is made here. The first is vain ostentation, as Philip of Macedon ordered his statue to be carried among the statues of the Gods. Alexander walked as if he were Jupiter Ammon. The Roman Bishops are carried adorned with a triple crown, and a horse precedes them carrying the consecrated bread, just as fire was carried before the Persian kings, so that adoration might be made at the same time.

And there are many other unseemly gestures of the Roman Pontiff, such as that he offers his feet to be kissed.

It would be long to recite the differences of deformed gestures, some of which are properly full of buffoonery, such as the French dances of the Cardinals. Others arise from anger, from emulation, hatreds, the desire for vengeance, such as insults, detractions, disdain, calumnious accusations, the cruelty of punishments, as the defender of Arian impiety, Gregory the Bishop of Alexandria, ordered virgins to be led naked to punishments who retained the confession of true doctrine; he also sent in a cohort of cavalry to kill men who had gathered in another temple. And there are many such tyrannical examples of all ages. Faber, the Bishop of Vienna, ordered Grynacus, who had spoken to him peacefully, to be sought immediately by lictors to be led to prison, after he had heard his monstrous errors in a sermon delivered at the assembly at Speyer in the year 1529. Finally, the deformity of gestures can be judged moderately in the highest and the lowest.

Οὐ ζητεῖ τὸ ἑαυτῆς.

That is, it is not πλεονεκτικὴ (covetous), but loves equality, nor does it crave extraordinary advantages, nor does it burden others with labors, but rather transfers more of the burdens onto itself, because inequality, which snatches advantages from others, alienates wills, as it is said: ἴσα πόλεμον οὐ ποιεῖ (equality does not make war).

Therefore Cyrus studiously, although he sustains the greatest part of the labor, nevertheless reverently treats King Cyaxares with honor, as his lord, and orders him to be treated with honor by others.

Οὐ παροξύνεται.

That is, first, he does not allow himself to be provoked by false or frivolous accusations, indeed, not even on account of true causes does he become overly angry. Now it is established that, very often, pernicious divisions of wills are caused by false accusations and slanders, from which discord in the republic and wars subsequently follow. And the most grave saying of Solomon is well known: Slander disturbs the wise man, and breaks the strength of his heart. Moreover, Slander is one of the chief plagues of the court, concerning which a certain person said of Alexander's Κόλαξ μήδιος: Slander boldly, because something always sticks.

Concerning anger also and the desire for vengeance, it has been spoken of above. And we see commonwealths shaken when governors loosen the reins of anger and the desire for vengeance, so that they may destroy those with whom they are enraged. Hence the saying of James is most true: The wrath of man does not work the righteousness of God. And against those who are tenacious of offenses, let the sayings be opposed: Forgive and it shall be forgiven you, which is excellently recited in the verses of Nazianzen: If you know you are a debtor, also lend gentleness, for pity is weighed by pity and by God. The Attic decree also pertains to this: not to harbor resentment.

It does not think evil. That is, not suspicious.

Moreover, it is a great ruin of common life to be suspicious, and a vice that loves calumnies. For suspicion fights against both truth and candor. Truth believes only what is certain and explored. Candor interprets ambiguous things in the better part. Suspicion often assents to false, and for the most part uncertain, things: It is therefore a vice worthy of hatred, and since it breeds distractions of wills, it must be avoided with great care. Claudian praises Theodosius because he was not suspicious.

It does not rejoice in injustice.

That is, it is without epichairekakia (rejoicing in the misfortune of others). Moreover, epichairekakia is a vice most proper to the devil, to rejoice in the unjust calamity of good men, as Shimei rejoices in the calamity of David, and harasses him with poisonous sarcasms. Fulvia so rejoiced in the death of Cicero that she pierced with needles the tongue taken from the head of the slain man. And in the Belgian lands, the images of the captured Duke and his sons were publicly subjected to insult, and now many adversaries rejoice in our calamity. In this vice many things concur: Injustice and cruelty. For it was of justice to wish good things for the good. And it is mercy to be affected with grief in the calamity of mediocre men, and to soothe their troubles in some way, as Theseus says in Euripides: It is not shameful for humans to share in the evils of others. Likewise: For if I, being a human, do not serve the fortunes of a human, I shall not appear to be wise.

But it rejoices in the truth.

To be unwilling to approve the truth out of hatred for a person, which you nevertheless silently approve, or to criticize it under some pretext, is a most common vice, as we have seen certain people, solely out of hatred for the person of Luther and out of party zeal, condemn true causes and men who think rightly, even though in reality they thought otherwise. This vice is prosopolepsia, to judge unjustly about matters because of a person. But Justice and Truth are opposed to this vice, which virtues approve what is true and just, and condemn what is unjust and false without any respect of persons, and without any foreign affections. Just as Jonathan constantly approved the cause of David against his father. Aristides approved the counsel of Themistocles, although there was emulation between them. Sempronius, although an enemy of the Scipios, nevertheless freed Scipio Asiaticus when he was being led to prison.

It bears all things.

There follow four virtues most necessary in government. The first is epieikeia (equity), which is to mitigate something from the highest law, to bear some weaknesses of those who are curable, just as spouses and friends ought to cover over with this epieikeia some things that offend among themselves, as it is commonly said: You should know the character of a friend, not hate it. Nor is it possible for colleagues to maintain concord among themselves without this virtue. And to the same sentiment he said above in chapter nine: we bear all things. But what the measure of this virtue is, is said elsewhere. The infirmities of character are to be dissembled and tolerated, not enormous vices or corruptions of the truth.

Candor follows: It believes all things.

Epieikeia is near to candor. For as epieikeia remits something from the bitterness of the law, so candor interprets ambiguous things in the better part, and is not diffident, not suspicious, not envious. Nor does it believe, because of light and frivolous suspicions, that another is plotting against it or contriving some evil, until it has true arguments, as Alexander refused to distrust the physician Philip, whose loyalty was well-known to him, even though Parmenion had warned that there was danger from him. Truth and Candor are virtues in the middle: the extremes are to be entirely incautious, and the opposite is Diffidence, which, without probable reason, yet distrusts everyone out of a certain malevolence of nature, like Dionysius the tyrant, Alexander of Pherae. Between these, the middle virtue is to consider the wills of men, and to trust and distrust based on probable reason. Thus this virtue retains its boundaries, and obeys this saying: remember to distrust, so that it may not be incautious, and so that it may not forget the saying: Cursed is he who trusts in man.

It hopes all things.

The third virtue is leniency hoping for amendment, which virtue is a step that in government one must often approach before others. As David tolerates the ways of Joab, even though he does certain things too irascibly, David interprets certain things as candor demands in a better light. Finally, even when this old leader Joab had killed the outstanding men Abner and Amasa, David nevertheless does not hasten to punishment, but still hopes he will be faithful. But with the habit confirmed, impiety is not easily changed. As therefore Joab was always restless and turbulent, so at the end he showed a specimen of a restless nature, having spurned the authority of David, he attempts seditiously to make Adonijah king at his own whim. Wherefore he is killed afterwards.

Alexander for a long time spares Philotas, the son of Parmenion, who spoke insultingly about him. Finally, when signs of a conspiracy are brought forward, he orders him to be killed. Thus also Dion, when he had long tolerated the injuries of his associate Heraclides, finally permitted him to be killed. And Augustus [did the same to] Cornelius Gallus.

But the most illustrious example of all is the leniency in God, who for a long time tolerates many great sins of ours, which He does not ignore, but tolerates them for this reason, that He may grant us space for repentance, as is said in the parable of the fig tree, Luke 13, and Romans 2.

It endures all things.

Patience is necessary in all these steps. Many great sorrows must be endured on account of the injuries and faults of others in government. And certain leniency (ἐπιείκεια) of those who are better can be healed, as Fabius corrects the errors of Minucius. He names this tolerance in the last place, however, both because it is mixed with the previous steps, and because sometimes this patience must be retained even when we see that colleagues are incurable, and there is no hope of amendment, as Jonathan with great sorrow tolerates the furies of his father, whom he sees can no longer be healed. This particle is not leniency (ἐπιείκεια) softening or excusing the crimes of the father, but he tolerates them with great sorrow, and expects a change from God.

Love never fails.

Some have interpreted it thus: Love does not fall away, that is, it is not frustrated, it is not a useless virtue. Other gifts are often useless to the one having them or to others, as eloquence often harms the orator and the people. But Paul speaks of perpetuity. Love remains in those who are heirs of eternal life in all eternity, and as was said above: Virtue is necessary in all things. Of other gifts, such as the gift of healing, there is no use after this life. But love must be eternal, because that eternal justice will be the fulfillment of the law, which, as is known, commands love. And what would eternal life be like in the fellowship of God and the Church, without love? Indeed, the sorrows among the infernal will be a horrible indignation against God and the whole Church, and a hatred of God and the Church, which we ought to shudder at even now while thinking of it.

Most gravely, therefore, Paul warns that we should look upon eternity, and exercise this virtue, which must shine in us in all eternity.

But whether there be prophecies, they shall be done away with.

He dwells on the comparison of virtues, and on the declaration of the previous statement, by which he signifies that love is necessary, and will endure perpetually, and is to be preferred to virtues and gifts which serve the Church in this fleetingness of life, and will cease afterwards.

Prophecies, he says, will cease, which is true, whether you understand prophecies concerning the ministry of interpretation, or concerning the predictions of future events. For in eternal life, as he says afterwards, we shall look face to face upon God, the fountain of wisdom, and we shall see the events. Prophecies now are: The dead will rise again, the Church will be adorned with perpetual glory, the impious will be cast into eternal punishments. The knowledge of these greatest things will be much more illustrious after the events.

The gift of tongues will also cease, because individual nations will not have their own languages as they do now, not understood by others. This does not need explanation.

Knowledge or science will also cease, that is, obscure knowledge, or as we say, abstractive, concerning many parts of ecclesiastical and natural doctrine, concerning God, concerning spiritual essence, concerning the soul, concerning the nature of celestial bodies, finally concerning many things, concerning the wonderful union of the divine and human nature, because then we shall behold God, the Son of God, and the angels face to face, and we shall perceive our own and other substances, and with God we shall contemplate the idea of such great things, we shall learn the causes of the divine counsel. Ἐκ μέρους γὰρ γινώσκομεν. This is a correction. For when he had said that knowledge would cease, it could immediately be objected: Why then do we learn much here about God, about the Son of God, about the soul, and about other things, if this knowledge is to be utterly destroyed? Do we not learn true beginnings here, and do we not think of and address the same God whom we shall also see and address afterwards? If the knowledge of this time is to be extinguished, why was it said: This is eternal life, that they may know you the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent? Does not the Lord wish for knowledge to be begun in this life, which will endure in all eternity? Likewise, why does Daniel say: Those who are learned shall shine like the stars, if the light kindled in this life is to be extinguished equally in all? These things could be objected, and from this misunderstood saying of Paul, many have taken up absurd disputations. Paul therefore adds a correction or interpretation: [2] He says that the prior knowledge will not be utterly destroyed, but the imperfection will be cast away, and from knowledge that is obscure, shadowy, and mixed with doubts, it will become illustrious and immovable, and to use known terms, from abstractive it will become intuitive, full of light and splendor. As if someone who had somehow seen someone in the twilight, afterwards beholds him more clearly in bright light. He says therefore: We know in part, that is, imperfectly, obscurely, languidly. In the same way, let what he says be understood: We prophesy in part, that is, we understand both interpretations and predictions imperfectly and obscurely. We know that the Son of God will return our bodies to us. This is a prophecy, but a very obscure one. For no one can conceive how members so often dissipated into vapors and into other bodies for five thousand years since then are to return again to their own bodies. I omit other examples. [3] He says that he had spoken before of this imperfection and obscurity when he said that prophecies and our knowledge would cease. But the beginnings of doctrine will remain in us, which are now greater in some, smaller in others. And the sentence will be true: Those who are learned shall shine like the stars, as we shall say again below. I know now what the city of Rome is like; I have seen pictures, I have some sort of obscure image of the city in my mind. This knowledge is not destroyed when I come to Rome and contemplate all the buildings and the site of the city in person, but since it is a begun knowledge of the same thing that I had previously thought of as absent, it becomes more perfect, just as the same light in the air that was in the twilight remains in the air, but more light is added when the sun has now been raised higher above the earth. He declares this comparison of imperfection and perfection with other examples and similitudes: When I was a child, I spoke as a child. Ὅτε ἤμεν νήπιος, ὡς νήπιος ἐλάλουν.

It is a manifest example, which shows that those goods which are present before are not destroyed: but that imperfection is cast away, and more strength is added to the prior goods. As when one who is a little older begins to speak correctly after the babbling of tender age, he does not lose the prior movements of the tongue, but now has them easier and clearer.

Latin:

Οὐ φυσιοῦται. Non inflatur.

Si ordinem vitiorum consideres, primum est Superbia, id est, admiratio sui, praeferens sese caeteris, qui in hac depravatione naturae ho- mines sese plurimum amant, sua dona mirantur, et se ab aliis magnifieri et coli postulant, et vo- lunt esse sicut Dii, ut inquit serpens ad Evam. Ex hac superbia sequuntur odia adversus eos, qui videntur nos obscurare. Et cum hos repellere conamur, magnae contentiones et dissidia oriun- tur. Hic ordo vitiorum facile intelligi potest. Prius autem Paulus de illis manifestis vitiis locu- tus est, quae magis conspici possunt, et ex su- perbia oriuntur, de cupiditate vindictae, de mo- rositate, quae est opposita lenitati, et de insidiis. Nunc de radice loquitur. Ait dilectionem non inflari, id est, alienam esse a superbia et fastu despiciente alios, et quasi regnum in alios exer- cente, qui est malum tyrannicum, etiam cum praeterea non accedit saevitia: tamen ferre de- spicientem et evehentem sese nimium supra col- legas, et quasi regnum gerentem, molestum est. Et molestius est, cum accedunt contumeliae ad- versus alios, ut cum Romanus Episcopus Alexan- der tertius Friderici Imperatoris collo pedem im- posuit. Fuit nostra memoria insignis superbia Cardinalis Eboracensis in Anglia, qui cum esset lanii filius, medius incessit inter Carolum V. Imperatorem, et Henricum regem Anglicum, utriusque humero manum imponens. In tali gestu utcunque agnosci hoc malum potest. Est autem proprium dilectionis subiicere sese aliis, et dona ad aliorum utilitatem conferre, et se tan- quam ministrum et inferiorem aliis gerere, ut filius Dei formam servi induit. Et minimum fuit superbiae in Cyro et in Scipione, qui etiam erga infimos studuerunt esse officiosi, nec praebuerunt significationem, quod se aliis anteferrent. La- boribus et virtute student antecellere, non fastu.

Οὐκ ἀσχημονεῖ.

Superbiam multi indecori gestus comitantur, quorum hic fit mentio. Primus est inanis osten- tatio, ut Philippus Macedo iussit suam statuam gestari inter Deorum statuas. Alexander inces- sit velut Iupiter Hammon. Episcopi Romani ge- stantur corona triplici ornati, et praecedit equus gestans panem consecratum, sicut ignis veheba- tur ante Persicos reges, ut simul fieret adoratio.

Et multi sunt alii indecori gestus Romani Pontificis, ut quod praebet pedes osculandos.

Longum esset differentias gestuum deformium recitare, quorum alii proprie pleni sunt scurrilitatis, ut gallicae saltationes Cardinalium. Alii oriuntur ab ira, ab aemulatione, odiis, cupiditate vindictae, ut convicia, obtrectationes, fastidia, calumniosae delationes, crudelitas suppliciorum, ut defensor Arianae impietatis Gregorius Episcopus Alexandrinus iussit virgines duci nudas ad supplicia, quae retinebant confessionem verae doctrinae, immisit et equitum cohortem ad interficiendos homines, qui in alio templo convenerant. Et multa sunt talia tyrannica exempla omnium aetatum. Faber Episcopus Viennensis Grynacum, qui placide eum allocutus fuerat, auditis monstrosis erroribus in concione habita in conventu Spirensi, Anno 1529. statim per lictores quaeri iussit, ut in carcerem duceretur. Denique mediocriter iudicari potest gestuum deformitas in summis et infimis.

Οὐ ζητεῖ τὸ ἑαυτῆς.

Id est, non est πλεονεκτικὴ, sed amat aequalitatem, nec appetit extraordinaria commoda, nec alios onerat laboribus, sed potius in sese plus onerum transfert, quia in aequalitas, quae aliis eripit commoda, voluntates alienat, ut dicitur: ἴσα πόλεμον οὐ ποιεῖ.

Ideo studiose Cyrus, etsi plurimum laboris sustinet, tamen regem Cyaxarem reverenter honore adficit, tanquam dominum, et iubet eum ab aliis honore adfici.

Οὐ παροξύνεται.

Id est, primum non sinit se irritari falsis aut frivolis delationibus, imo nec propter veras causas vehementius irascitur. Primum autem constat, saepissime falsis criminationibus et calumniis fieri perniciosas distractiones voluntatum, unde postea discordiae in republica et bella sequuntur. Et notum est dictum Salomonis gravissimum: Calumnia conturbat sapientem, et frangit robur cordis eius. Est autem Calumnia una ex pestibus aulicis praecipua, de qua dixit quidam Alexandri Κόλαξ μήδιος: Calumniare audacter, quia semper aliud haeret.

De ira etiam et cupiditate vindictae supra dictum est. Ac videmus moveri respub. cum gu- bernatoses laxant frenos irae et cupiditati vin- dictae, ut tollant eos, quibus succensent. Ideo verissimum et dictum Iacobi: Ira viri non ope- ratur iusticiam Dei. Et contra tenaces offensio- num opponantur dicta: Remittite et remittetur vobis, quod versibus Nazianzeni egregie recitatur: Εἰδ᾽ οἶδας ὄφλων καὶ πρόχρησον τὸ πρᾷον, Οἴκτῳ γὰρ οἶκτος καὶ θεῷ σταθμίζεται. Huc et decretum Atticum pertinet: μὴ μνη- σικακεῖν.

Οὐ λογίζεται τὸ κακὸν. Id est, non suspicax.

Est autem pernicies magna vitae communis esse suspicacem, et vitium amori calumniarum. Pugnat enim et suspicio cum veritate et candore. Veritas tantum credit certa et explorata. Candor ambigua interpretatur in meliorem partem. Su- spicio saepe falsis, et plerunque incertis assenti- tur: Est igitur vitium dignum odio, et cum pa- riat distractiones voluntatum, magna cura vitan- dum est. Claudianus laudat Theodosium, quod non fuerat suspicax.

Οὐ χαίρει ἐπὶ τῇ ἀδικίᾳ.

Id est, est sine ἐπιχαιρεκακίᾳ. Est autem ἐπιχαιρεκακίᾳ vitium maxime proprium diabolo, laetari in calamitate iniusta bonorum, ut Semei laetatur in calamitate Davidis, et eum venenatis sarcasmis exagitat. Fulvia adeo laetata est nece Ciceronis, ut linguam exemptam ex interfecti ca- pite aciculis confoderit, Et in Belgico imagines captivi Ducis et filiorum, publice contumelia ad- fectae sunt, et nunc multi adversarii laetantur nostra calamitate. In hoc vitio multa concur- runt: Iniusticia et crudelitas. Nam iusticiae erat bonis bona optare. Et misericordia est, dolore affici in calamitate mediocrium hominum, et lenire aliquo modo aerumnas, ut Theseus inquit apud Euripidem: οὐκ αἰσχρὸν ἀνθρώποισιν ἀλ- λοίλων κακά. Item: εἰ μὴ γὰρ ὢν ἄνθρωπος ἀνθρώπου τύχαις ὑπηρετήσω, οὐ φανήσομαι φρονῶν.

Συγχαίρει δὲ τῇ ἀληθείᾳ.

Odio personae nolle adprobare veritatem, quam tamen tacite probas, aut specie aliqua re- prehendere, usitatissimum vitium est, ut vidi- mus quosdam tantum odio personae Lutheri et studio partium damnasse veras causas, et homi- nes recte sentientes, cum reipsa aliter sentirent. Hoc vitium est προσωποληψία, propter personam iniuste de rebus iudicare. Sed huic vitio oppo- nuntur Iusticia et Veritas, quae virtutes vera et iusta adprobant, et damnant iniusta et falsa sine ullo personarum respectu, et sine ullis peregrinis affectibus. Sicut Ionathas constanter approbavit causam Davidis contra patrem. Aristides proba- vit consilium Themistoclis, quanquam inter eos aemulatio erat. Sempronius quanquam inimicus Scipionum, tamen Scipionem Asiaticum libera- vit, cum in carcerem duceretur.

Πάντα στέγει.

Sequuntur virtutes quatuor maxime neces- sariae in gubernatione. Prima est ἐπιείκεια, quae est mitigare aliquid ex summo iure, ferre aliquas imbecillitates eorum, qui sunt sanabiles, sicut coniuges et amicos oportet inter sese hac ἐπιεικείᾳ aliqua, quae offendunt, obruere, ut usitate dicitur: Mores amici noveris, non oderis. Nec possibile est collegas sine hac virtute concordiam inter sese tueri. Et in eandem sententiam supra capite nono dixit: πάντα στέγομεν. Qui sit autem mo- dus huius virtutis, alibi dicitur. Dissimulandae et tolerandae sunt morum infirmitates, non vitia enormia, aut corruptelae veritatis.

Sequitur Candor: Πάντα πιστεύει.

Ἐπιείκεια vicina est candori. Ut enim re- mittit ἐπιείκεια aliquid ex acerbitate iuris: ita candor interpretatur ambigua in meliorem par- tem, et non est diffidens, non suspicax, non lividus. Nec propter leves et frivolas suspicio- nes credit alium sibi insidiari aut aliquid mali moliri, donec argumenta vera habet, ut Alexan- der noluit diffidere medico Philippo, cuius ei fides perspecta erat, tametsi Parmenio monuerat ab eo periculum esse. Veritas et Candor virtutes sunt in medio: extrema sunt, esse prorsus in- cautum, et contrarium Diffidentia, quae sine probabili ratione, tamen omnibus diffidit qua- dam naturae malevolentia, sicut Dionysius ty- rannus, Alexander Phereus. Inter haec media virtus est, considerare voluntates hominum, et probabili ratione confidere ac diffidere. Ita haec virtus retinet metas, et obtemperat huic dicto: μέμνησο ἀπιστεῖν, ne sit incauta, et ne oblivi- scatur dicti: Maledictus qui confidit in homine.

Πάντα ἐλπίζει.

Tertia virtus est lenitas sperans emendatio- nem, quae virtus gradus est, quem in guberna- tione saepe ad priores accedere oportet. Ut Da- vid tolerat mores Ioab, etsi quaedam facit iracun- dius, quaedam ut candor postulat, in meliorem partem David interpretatur. Tandem etiam cum praestantes viros Abner et Amasam hic vetus dux Ioab interfecisset, tamen David non properat ad poenam, sed adhuc sperat eum fidelem fore. Sed consuetudine confirmata, impietas non facile mu- tatur. Ut igitur semper Ioab fuit inquietus et turbulentus, ita ad extremum naturae inquietae specimen ostendit, spreta autoritate Davidis, conatur seditiose regem creare Adoniam suo ar- bitrio. Quare postea interficitur.

Alexander diu parcit Philotae filio Parme- nionis, contumeliose de ipso loquenti. Tandem cum proferuntur signa coniurationis, eum inter- fici iubet. Sic et Dion, cum Heraclidis socii in- iurias diu tolerasset, tandem eum interfici permi- sit. Et Augustus Cornelium Gallum.

Sed omnium maxime illustre exemplum est lenitas in Deo, qui diu multa magna peccata no- stra tolerat, quae non ignorat, sed eo tolerat, ut spatium nobis ad poenitentiam concedat, ut in parabola de ficu, Lucae 13. dicitur et Roman. 2.

Πάντα ὑπομένει.

Patientia in omnibus his gradibus necessaria est. Multi magni dolores perferendi sunt propter iniurias et delicta aliorum in gubernatione. Et quaedam ἐπιείκεια eorum, qui sunt meliores, sa- nari possunt, ut Fabius corrigit errata Minutii. Ideo autem postremo loco nominat hanc toleran- tiam, et quia superioribus gradibus mixta est, et quia aliquando haec patientia retinenda est, etiam cum videmus insanabiles esse collegas, et non est spes emendationis, ut Ionathas magno cum dolore tolerat patris furores, quem videt iam sanari non posse. Haec particula non est ἐπιεί- κεια leniens vel excusans scelera patris, sed ma- gno cum dolore ea tolerat, et a Deo mutationem expectat.

Ἡ ἀγάπη οὐδέποτε ἐκπίπτει.

Quidam sic interpretati sunt: Dilectio non excidit, id est, non frustratur, non est inutilis virtus. Caetera dona saepe inutilia sunt habenti vel aliis, ut eloquentia saepe nocet oratori et populo. Sed Paulus de perpetuitate loquitur. Dilectio manet in iis, qui sunt haeredes vitae aeternae in omni aeternitate, et ut supra dictum est: Virtus est necessaria in omnibus. Aliorum donorum, ut doni sanationis, non est usus post hanc vitam. Dilectionem vero aeternam esse oportet, quia illa aeterna iusticia erit legis im- pletio, quae, ut notum est, praecipit dilectio- nem. Et qualis esset aeterna vita in consuetu- dine Dei et Ecclesiae, sine dilectione? Imo do- lores apud inferos erunt horribilis indignatio ad- versus Deum et totam Ecclesiam, et odium Dei et Ecclesiae, quod nunc quoque cogitantes expa- vescere debemus.

Gravissime igitur monet Paulus, ut aeterni- tatem intueamur, et hanc virtutem exerceamus, quam in omni aeternitate in nobis fulgere oportet.

Εἴτε δὲ προφητεῖαι καταργηθήσονται.

Commoratur in collatione virtutum, et in declaratione proximi dicti, quo significat dilectio- nem necessariam, et perpetuo duraturam, ante- ferendam esse virtutibus et donis, quae in hac fugacitate vitae serviunt Ecclesiae, et postea ces- satura sunt.

Prophetiae, inquit, cessabunt, quod verum est, sive intelligas prophetias de ministerio in- terpretationis, sive de praedictionibus futurorum eventuum. Nam in vita aeterna, ut postea dicit, coram intuebimur fontem sapientiae Deum, et videbimus eventus. Prophetiae nunc sunt: Mor- tui reviviscent, Ecclesia ornabitur perpetua glo- ria, impii abiicientur in aeternas poenas. Ha- rum maximarum rerum noticia post eventus multo erit illustrior.

Cessabit et donum linguarum, quia non ut nunc suas linguas habebunt singulae gentes, non intellectas ab aliis. Hoc non indiget de- claratione.

Cessabit et cognitio seu scientia, id est, no- ticia obscura, seu ut loquimur abstractiva, de multis partibus doctrinae ecclesiasticae et natura- lis, de Deo, de spirituali essentia, de anima, de natura coelestium corporum, denique de multis rebus, de miranda copulatione divinae et huma- nae naturae, quia tunc coram aspiciemus Deum, filium Dei, angelos, et perspiciemus nostras et alias substantias, et cum Deo intuebimur ideam tantarum rerum, causas consilii divini disce- mus. Ἐκ μέρους γὰρ γινώσκομεν. Correctio est. Nam cum dixisset cessaturam esse cognitionem, statim obiici potuit: Quid igi- tur hic de Deo, de filio Dei, de anima, et de aliis rebus multa discimus, si haec noticia peni- tus delebitur. An non hic initia vera discimus, et eundem Deum cogitamus et alloquimur, quem et postea cernemus et alloquimur? Si extingue- tur huius temporis noticia, cur dictum est: Haec est vita aeterna, ut agnoscant te Deum verum, et quem misisti Iesum esse Christum? Nonne vult Dominus in hac vita incoari agnitionem, duraturam in omni aeternitate? Item, Cur in- quit Daniel: Docti fulgebunt ut stellae, si pari- ter in omnibus extinguetur lux in hac vita accensa? Haec obiici poterant, et ex hoc dicto Pauli male intellecto, multi absurdas disputationes sumserunt. Addit igitur Paulus correctionem seu interpretationem: Non inquit penitus dele- bitur prior noticia, sed imperfectio abiicietur, et ex noticia obscura, umbratili, ac mixta dubita- tionibus fiet illustris et immota, et ut vocabulis notis utamur, ex abstractiva fiet intuitiva, plena lucis et splendoris. Ut si quis aliquem in crepu- sculo utcunque conspectum, postea in clara luce manifestius intuetur. Inquit igitur: Ex parte cognoscimus, id est, imperfecte, obscure, languide. Eodem modo intelligatur quod inquit: Ex parte prophetamus, id est, imperfecte et obscure intelligimus tum in- terpretationes, tum praedictiones. Scimus filium Dei redditurum esse nobis corpora nostra. Haec prophetia est, sed valde obscura. Nemo enim cogitare potest, quomodo toties dissipata membra in halitus, et in alia corpora inde usque a quin- que millibus annorum rursus ad sua corpora re- ditura sint. Omitto exempla alia. De hac im- perfectione et obscuritate se antea locutum esse inquit, cum diceret, cessaturas esse prophetias et nostram cognitionem. Sed manebunt in nobis initia doctrinae, quae nunc sunt in aliis maiora, in aliis minora. Et vera erit sententia: Docti fulgebunt ut stellae, ut infra rursus dicemus. Scio iam qualis sit urbs Roma, vidi picturas, habeo qualemcunque obscuram imaginem urbis in mente. Haec noticia non deletur, cum Ro- mam venio, et omnia aedificia ac situm urbis coram contemplor, sed cum sit incoata noticia eiusdem rei, quam prius absentem cogitaveram, fit perfectior, ut eadem lux in aëre, quae fuit in crepusculo, manet in aëre, sed plus lucis accedit, cum sol iam supra terram altius evectus est. Hanc collationem imperfectionis et perfectionis declarat aliis exemplis et similitudinibus: Cum essem infans, ut infans loquebar. Ὅτε ἤμεν νήπιος, ὡς νήπιος ἐλάλουν.

Manifestum exemplum est, quod ostendit, non deleri ea bona, quae prius adsunt: sed im- perfectionem abiici, ac bonis prioribus addi plus roboris. Ut cum post tenerae aetatis balbutiem recte loqui grandiusculus incipit, non amittit priores linguae motus, sed habet iam faciliores et planiores.

## 13:12
We see now through a mirror, in a riddle.

He does not say this, that knowledge in this life, taken from the word of God, is uncertain, but although it is most certain, yet it is obscure, and by no means as illustrious as that light will be in the heavenly communion. It is already most certain to us by faith that in the Son of God our Lord Jesus Christ there are two natures, divine and human, and the invocation looking upon the Son of God confesses him to be omnipotent, but it establishes this according to the word. This knowledge is still obscure and similar to a riddle. For the word is as it were a wrapping of that secret and wonderful thing which we shall behold face to face in the heavenly life.

Thus now the word concerning the resurrection is as it were a riddle, that is, a wrapping of an event that will follow afterwards, which will then be clearly seen. Thus faith, awaiting the promised liberation, sees the event wrapped in the word as in a riddle.

The leading out from Egypt was promised to the Israelites. Moses sees this in the word, and although faith is firm, yet he does not see what kind it is, or when it is to be.

Such examples somehow show that the word is aptly named a riddle, as a wrapping. For a riddle signifies a speech covertly signifying something else.

…But what does he name a mirror, or seeing through a mirror? There are two things, the object and the vision itself. The riddle is the object, as the word showing consolation, namely: Do not fear Abram, I am your protector. But the very sense of consolation, which the Holy Spirit kindles in the heart of the believing Abraham, and is a light and joy not unknown to the pious, is this mirror, through which they behold God showing himself in that word or enigma. Thus also in 2 Corinthians 3 it is said: Beholding the glory of the Lord, that is, looking upon God in that light, and consolation kindled through the Gospel and through the Holy Spirit.

But this knowledge is not yet so illustrious as the intuitive knowledge in the heavenly fellowship, which he here calls Seeing face to face, that is, to discern the substance and will of God in person without that darkness, and in Him the causes of divine works.

Now I know in part, but then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known.

He rightly used the word ἐπιγνώσομαι, because it signifies to know certainly a thing previously known or thought of in some way, when it afterwards comes into view, from that prior idea of whatever kind; the Latins call this Agnoscere (to recognize). Now we think, however obscurely, what God is, what the soul is, but afterwards we shall know Him more clearly, and we shall understand that He corresponds to the prior thought. He warns, however, that the knowledge will be very clear, because it will be such as it is in God looking upon us, that is, clear and certain without any darkness and ambiguity.

Moreover, from this passage this consolation also must be taken in invocation in this life. We grieve that we do not see God more clearly, and in invocation we would willingly, as it were, embrace Him with our arms. But let us be content with this thought, however it may be, beholding God in the word and His testimonies, according to those sayings: Blessed are they who believe, when they have not seen. Likewise: Being justified by faith we have peace. Intuitive knowledge does not yet shine in us, but let us acquiesce by faith in the enigma, namely in the word.

But now faith, hope, love remain.

Paul proposes this very consolation, and in this life commands us to apprehend God by faith and hope. Moreover, from this passage is taken the customary enumeration of the three virtues, which are called Theological. Nor is the enumeration inconsistent: for many other virtues can be included in these members.

In any enumeration of virtues, the first and preceding thing is knowledge. Because there is no desire for the unknown. Therefore, the first commandment also begins from the knowledge of God: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt. God is named first there, and is distinguished from all creatures and fictitious deities. Thus Paul learnedly says here that faith is a necessary virtue, namely knowledge, and indeed such as is faith, that is, assent, by which we embrace the word of God concerning things not falling into sense, nor grasped by reason.

This knowledge is either of history, or of laws and threats, or of promises. When we embrace laws and threats with true assent, fear arises. But when we embrace promises, there arises trust acquiescing in God, and quickening hearts. This virtue is properly called Faith, because we then finally approach God, when mercy promised on account of the Son has been apprehended. Concerning this faith it is said to the Ephesians 3: Through whom we have confidence, and we dare to approach through faith in Him. This faith embraces all the articles of faith, and it is not only knowledge, but it is trust, by which the heart acquiesces in the Son of God, and in God, according to the promise. Because when in true terrors you so embrace the article, I believe the remission of sins, that you also include yourself in the universal promise, and determine that your sins are remitted to you, it is most certain that trust and joy acquiescing in God follow in the heart, as experience shows in true consolation, in which we rightly learn what faith is, and at the same time we recognize that we ought to acquiesce by faith in the word of God, and not seek other illuminations. Experience also shows that this admonition is necessary.

Hope is the certain expectation of eternal life, on account of the Son of God, according to the promise expressed in the Gospel, and it is the expectation of the mitigation of punishments or calamities in this life, according to the counsel of God. But since the adversaries of true doctrine say that the distinctions of the virtues, of faith and hope, are not kept by us, it is necessary that the younger be warned about the true difference. Faith receives a present benefit, namely the remission of sins and reconciliation, as is most certain from the saying: Being justified by faith we have peace. But hope looks to and expects future liberation. This doctrine is clear. But they ask: Why do we affirm that faith and hope are virtues in the Church, when faith is nevertheless knowledge? Furthermore, even if it is said to be trust, one can still wonder how it is a virtue. Likewise, why is hope a virtue, when it is most common in life that men, incited by hope, are deceived and rush into the greatest calamities, as it has been said: Good hope is often deceived by its own augury. And Pindar says: Hopes are the dreams of the waking. And the saying of Epictetus is very worthy of memory: As with feet, so with hope, one must walk toward what is possible, ὥσπερ τοῖς σκέλεσι, οὕτως καὶ ἐλπίσι πρὸς τὰ δυνατὰ δεῖ βαδίζειν.

I answer: Faith and hope are undoubtedly virtues, because they are obedience, which God demands be rendered to His command. The divine voice is manifest: Hear Him. Likewise: This is the will of my Father, that everyone who believes in the Son may have eternal life. Faith, therefore, is a virtue because it obeys God, and when it is an assent embracing all the articles of faith and the promise of grace, and joined with it is trust resting in God. Known also are the many precepts concerning hope in 1 Peter 1: Firmly hope for the grace that will be exhibited to us when Jesus Christ is revealed, namely in the judgment. And in the same chapter: That your faith and hope may be in God. And Romans 5: Hope does not disappoint. And Rom. 8: By hope we have been saved. Hope is therefore a virtue, which obeys the word of God.

And from here let the answer be taken to the objections recited above concerning fallacious hope: The divine voice commands hope regarding those things which He has promised, and the promise of eternal life on account of the Son is certain and immovable. It does not command Pompey to hope for victory, even if he himself is moved by this imagination of his. The cause commands the gods to hope for better outcomes, because it is the judgment of God which cause is more just. And God often punishes men on account of prior offenses, even if they have a just cause in the present matter, as He was punishing the Israelites fighting with the tribe of Benjamin, and often otherwise. Therefore, that hope is fallacious which is not governed by the divine promise.

But the hope of eternal life and the hope of the mitigation of punishments and calamities in this life are governed by the divine promise, where also this doctrine must be held: Even if present calamities are not removed, nor seem to be mitigated, yet the hope of eternal life must always be retained, according to the saying of Job: Even if He kills me, I will hope in Him, yet I will argue my ways before Him, and He Himself will be my savior, and all hypocrites will not come to Him, that is, even if calamities are not removed in this life, yet let all who turn to God retain the hope of eternal life.

We experience, however, that our spirits become very faint in punishments, and we doubt whether eternal salvation is to be hoped for and expected, when we now feel the wrath of God in punishments and seem to be cast away. Against this most sad doubt, it is necessary to keep in view firm consolations, of which this is the first and chief, that God wills us to turn to Him at any time, and He most certainly receives those who have turned on account of the Son freely, because this promise is always true and immovable: God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son, that everyone who believes in Him may not perish, but have eternal life. And Ezekiel 38: As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he may turn and live. Likewise: On whatever day the wicked shall have turned, he shall not fall in his wickedness. Matt. 19: How often shall I forgive: Seventy times seven. Luke 15: There is joy among the angels over one sinner doing penance. And there the conversion of the prodigal son is recited.

The second consolation is: For this very reason God punishes, that He may draw us back to repentance, and give eternal life to those who have turned, not that He may destroy us. 1 Cor. 11: When we are judged by the Lord, we are chastened, that we may not be condemned with this world. And in the Psalm: It is good for me that You have humbled me, that I might learn Your justifications. Isaiah 28: Vexation gives understanding. Isaiah 66: To whom shall I look, except to the miserable and contrite in spirit, and trembling at My words. Micah last: I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against Him. Here he speaks expressly of punishment, and confesses sin. Afterward he adds a consolation, in which he narrates that he retains faith and hope: When I shall sit in darkness, the Lord is my light. To these sayings add the voice of the Son of God, which contains the most ample and certain consolation: Come to Me all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. And Rom. 8: There is a long discourse about retaining hope in the greatest sorrows and torments. By hope we have been saved. But hope that is seen is not hope.

Let us hold these sayings and similar ones, lest on account of the punishments by which God reminds us in this life of His wrath, we cast away the hope of eternal life. And let us know that this hope is by no means vain, because it is commanded by the divine voice. Although, however, present punishments in this life are often not entirely removed, because God for many reasons wishes the Church to be subjected to the cross, nevertheless a mitigation is also promised, which happens at other times in other ways. And since it has been promised divinely, this hope is also not in vain. Nahum 1: The Lord is good, and strengthening in the day of trouble, and knowing them that hope in him. Joel 2: Turn to the Lord your God, for he is good, and merciful, and mitigating the punishment. Hosea 11: I will not execute the fierceness of my anger. And Luke 21: Pray that you may be able to escape the things that are to come. And there are illustrious examples of the mitigation of punishments: the sparing of Nineveh, the restoration of David to the kingdom, the healing of Hezekiah, the restoration of Manasseh, and there is no doubt that such mitigations happen daily in the whole Church, as Psalm 77 says: And he did not kindle all his anger. Jeremiah in Lamentations chapter 3: It is of the Lord's mercies that we are not consumed. And elsewhere chapter 46: I will make an end of all the nations whither I have driven thee, but I will not make an end of thee, but I will correct thee in judgment, and will not leave thee, as thou seemest innocent, to be innocent. And Habakkuk 3: O Lord, in wrath remember mercy. Let us often think of these and similar sayings, so that we may both more ardently seek the mitigation of public and private punishments, and acknowledge the immense mercy of God, because it most truly softens punishments and sustains us, and let us give thanks to him. It is manifest that this reminder concerning faith and hope is most useful. And so that the invocation may be more ardent, it must be thought of often. It is established, however, from these things which I have said, that faith and hope are rightly called virtues, because they are obedience which is ruled by the word of God, and they are the chief worship, as the Psalm says: Sacrifice the sacrifice of righteousness, and hope in the Lord. Nor are these virtues known to the Philosophers, because they are only shown by the voice of God, which also teaches how they are to be governed. By faith we receive the remission of sins, by Hope we certainly expect eternal life, not because of our merits, but because of the Son of God freely. It is necessary that these things be done thus, because in the Gospel God has revealed this will of his by most certain testimonies. And this wisdom is placed far outside of philosophy. Nor does philosophy place faith and hope among the virtues, since they are not governed by certain and firm knowledge of principles, experience, or demonstration, but it judges it to be folly to assent to uncertain things. As when Antonius hopes for victory because he is better equipped than Augustus. But the Church is certain because of the divine promise, and believes against hope in hope, that is, it believes and hopes where even the opposite appears to natural judgment. As it is said in Psalm 71: He delivered the poor, who had no helper. And Psalm 26: My father and my mother have forsaken me, but the Lord hath taken me up. And although other virtues, such as fear or reverence, obedience in afflictions owed to God, which is a part of justice and is named tolerance or patience, are rightly comprehended in love, as I shall say presently: nevertheless it must be known that faith and hope shine forth above these and the others. So that this may be clear, let a comparison be made of philosophical and Christian patience, and of the consolations of both kinds. Philosophical patience is to obey reason in some way in bearing adversities, so that you do nothing against justice or other virtues. As Cato, killing himself, acts against justice. But Socrates violates neither justice nor modesty, when he seeks death without sedition and without any deformity. Nor is hope included in philosophical patience, but Palamedes obeys reason, even when all hopes of safety in this life, and afterwards, are extinguished. But Christian patience is to obey the divine command in tolerating adversities, so that you do not do anything against the commands of God, so that you are not angry at God, but by faith acknowledge him to be propitious to you, and hope for help, mitigation, or liberation, and by this faith and hope soften the pain. You see here in the definition that faith and hope are added, just as above the most severe commands were recited concerning both virtues, according to that: Without faith it is impossible to please God. Likewise, Peter: Hope firmly for the grace that will be exhibited to you when Jesus Christ will be revealed. Therefore, pain is softened in Christian patience because then the good objects are seen by faith and hope. The Baptist knows that he is dear to God, and that God is present in this very struggle, and he sees that this death is a journey to the heavenly Church. Palamedes, Socrates, Theramenes, or those like them do not see these things. However, pain is not truly alleviated as long as the mind contemplates only sad objects. But what objects should be proposed for the comforting of souls in philosophy, and what in the Gospel, has been said above. And it is very profitable to always remember that comparison of causes.

᾿Αγάπη, these three, but the greatest of these is love.

There follows a description of love, by which all antiquity embraced universal obedience, the love of God and of men for the sake of God, and according to the order instituted by God, just as Paul says in Romans 13: Love is the fulfilling of the law. And in First John 5: This is the love of God, that we keep His commandments. Moved by these words, antiquity used the name of love, just as we otherwise use the name of universal justice. I recite these things for this reason, both so that the words of the writers may be more clear to readers, and so that the ineptitudes of moderns may be repudiated, who contend in this text of Paul that only the love of neighbor and duties toward the neighbor are spoken of, not the love of God. It is a great blindness to tear these virtues apart, because the love of neighbor is not ordered unless it is ruled by the love of God, that is, unless there is such a will, and there are such duties, as God ordains in His commandments. Likewise, unless it is referred to this end, that obedience be rendered to God, and we be joined in God, just as the Lord says: That they may be one in us. Let us know, therefore, that the love of God and neighbor is one virtue, which has degrees, but yet it both begins from God, and refers the lower degrees to God as to the principal end. Abraham loves God. Afterward he also loves Hagar, but he values God more, at whose command he sends away the handmaid Hagar.

It is, however, difficult for us in this great hardness of hearts to provide an illustrious definition of love. For if hearts were burning with the sense of the love of God, just as lovers feel the fires of love between themselves, it would be less obscure what is called Love. And indeed such true fires toward God ought to be in the heart, but because they are very languid, even if there are any, the description is more obscure.

But yet let us establish this description, such as it is: The love of God and neighbor is, after the mercy of God given on account of the Son has been apprehended by true faith, to submit the heart in turn to God, and to do His commandments, with a certain joy acquiescing in Him. As because Lawrence knows that he pleases God, he in turn obeys Him in confession and other duties, and with joy acquiesces in God, although the body feels great torments. This joy is the effect and indication of love, as it is often written, as in Acts 5: The Apostles went from the presence of the council rejoicing that they had been counted worthy to suffer shame for the Lord. Ordinary men can feel this joy to some extent. Sometimes, however, more ardent sudden flames of love are kindled in the hearts of the pious, which we should leave to each one's own experience. Let this suffice to have advised concerning the description of love.

Paul adds to the enumeration, These three, as if signifying that he had named the principal virtues, which is true. For since love is universal justice, as can easily be understood, there is no need afterward for a longer enumeration, but let the decalogue be looked at, and let the duties of love be considered according to the individual commandments. Thus if anyone wishes to make a distribution of the virtues, he will recite them concisely according to the commandments. It is necessary, however, for faith and hope to shine forth: which are virtues sprung from the promise of the Gospel: then love is the beginning of the law.

According to the first table, the love of God embraces filial fear of God, that is, true reverence for God, confession, thanksgiving, patience in the troubles of confession, and the zeal to preserve the evangelical ministry.

In the second table, in the fourth commandment, love of spouse, offspring, parents, benefactors, and magistrates, for the sake of God.

In the fifth commandment, justice, which takes care not to harm the body of another, likewise the meekness that bridles anger and the desire for revenge, likewise beneficence.

In the seventh commandment, justice abstaining from the property of others, and liberality helping the needy. That all these are duties of the love of neighbor is clear, because they are the bonds of the association of the human race, which is mutual benevolence.

In the sixth commandment, Chastity.

In the eighth place Truth, virtues are necessary, even if they were not of benefit to one's neighbor. And yet these also benefit the common society in many ways.

From this consideration it can be judged that the other virtues are included under the designation of love.

But why does he say: The greatest among these is love? I answer most simply: Since the virtues among themselves are compared according to their essence, it is most true that the love of God far excels all others. Just as the law also names the greatest virtue: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart. Concerning which commandment, since the Lord himself says: This is the first and great commandment, it is signified that the virtue of which he speaks is the chief one. And in eternal life, the sense of God's love toward us, and in turn our love toward God, will be the highest degree of blessedness. And love always embraces knowledge, which indeed in eternal life will be much more illustrious, not obscure, as the knowledge of faith is now.

of Paul in this place correctly to explain, and to answer many other objections in this article.

I will add this too, that it is a common answer: Love is the greatest, namely with regard to actions among men, because almost all the actions of the commandments of the second Table are works of love. But I omit this answer, although it is true, as I said above, that the love of one's neighbor is a virtue simply necessary for individuals; the gifts of miracles are not necessary for individuals. And it is of this faith, which is the gift of miracles, that Paul speaks especially here, as he shows immediately at the beginning in the following chapter: Pursue love, yet desire spiritual gifts. He wants individuals to pursue, that is, to desire love, which is a virtue simply necessary for individuals. Then he wants the other gifts, which benefit the Church and are motions and testimonies of the Holy Spirit, to be magnified, even if it is not necessary for them to be given to individuals.

However, I will not dispute more subtly about the comparison of these virtues. Let us know that both are a flame kindled by the Holy Spirit, namely true faith and true love. Therefore, both are to be magnified, even if one excels the other.

But an argument must be explained here, which some oppose against the statement, We are justified by faith:

The greatest virtue justifies more. Love is the greatest virtue: Therefore, love justifies more.

Latin:

Videmus iam per speculum, in aenigmate.

Non hoc dicit, incertam esse cognitionem in hac vita, sumtam ex verbo Dei, sed quan- quam sit certissima, tamen obscura est, et ne- quaquam ita illustris, ut erit lux illa in consue- tudine coelesti. Certissimum iam nobis est fide, in filio Dei Domino nostro Iesu Christo duas esse naturas, divinam et humanam, et invocatio in- tuens filium Dei fatetur eum esse omnipotentem, sed hoc statuit iuxta verbum. Haec cognitio est adhuc obscura et similis aenigmati. Verbum enim est velut involucrum illius arcanae et mi- randae rei, quam in vita coelesti coram aspi- ciemus.

Ita nunc verbum de resurrectione est velut aenigma, id est, involucrum eventus postea se- cuturi, qui tunc clare conspicietur. Ita fides expectans promissam liberationem cernit eventum involutum verbo tanquam aenigmate.

Israëlitis promissa est eductio ex Aegypto. Hanc cernit Moyses in verbo, et quanquam fides est firma, tamen qualis, aut quando sit futura non cernit.

Talia exempla utcunque ostendunt, verbum apte nominari aenigma, tanquam involucrum. Significat enim aenigma sermonem tecte aliud significantem.

Sed quid nominat speculum, seu videre per speculum? Duo sunt, obiectum et ipsa visio. Aenigma est obiectum, ut verbum monstrans consolationem, videlicet: Noli timere Abram, ego protector tuus. Ipse vero sensus consolationis, quem accendit Spiritus sanctus in corde Abraham credenti, et est lux et laetitia non ignota piis, est hoc speculum, per quod intuentur Deum in illo verbo seu aenigmate se ostendentem. Ita et 2. Corinth. 3. dicitur: Speculantes gloriam Domini, id est, intuentes Deum in illa luce, et consolatione accensa per Evangelium et per Spiritum sanctum.

Sed haec noticia nondum adeo illustris est, ut intuitiva in coelesti consuetudine, quam hic nominat Videre facie ad faciem, id est, coram sine caligine illa cernere Dei substantiam et voluntatem, et in eo causas divinorum operum.

Ἄρτι γινώσκω ἐκ μέρους, τότε δὲ ἐπιγνώσομαι, καθὼς καὶ ἐπεγνώσθην.

Recte usus est verbo ἐπιγνώσομαι, quia significat rem antea utcunque notam seu cogitatam, cum postea venit in conspectum, ex illa priore qualicunque idea certo cognoscere, id Latini nominant Agnoscere. Nunc utcunque obscure cogitamus, quid sit Deus, quid sit anima, sed postea clarius eum cognoscemus, et congruere eum ad priorem cogitationem intelligemus. Monet autem valde perspicuam noticiam fore, quia talis erit, qualis est in Deo nos intuente, id est, clara et certa sine ulla caligine et ambiguitate.

Caeterum ex hoc loco etiam haec consolatio sumenda est in invocatione in hac vita. Dolemus, quod non clarius cernimus Deum, et in invocatione libenter quasi complecti eum brachiis vellemus. Sed simus contenti hac qualicunque cogitatione intuente Deum in verbo et eius testimoniis, iuxta illa dicta: Beati qui credunt, cum non viderint. Item: Iustificati fide pacem habemus. Nondum fulget in nobis intuitiva noticia, sed acquiescamus fide in aenigmate, videlicet in verbo.

Νυνὶ δὲ μένει πίστις, ἐλπὶς, ἀγάπη.

Hanc ipsam consolationem proponit Paulus, in hac vita iubet adprehendere Deum fide et spe. Caeterum ex hoc loco sumta est usitata enumeratio trium virtutum, quae nominantur Theologicae. Nec inconcinna est enumeratio: nam virtutes aliae multae in haec membra includi possunt.

In quacunque enumeratione virtutum prima res et praecedens est cognitio. Quia ignoti nulla cupido. Ideo et primum praeceptum ab agni- tione Dei orditur: Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus, qui te eduxi de terra Aegypti. Primum ibi no- minatur Deus, et discernitur ab omnibus creatu- ris et commentitiis numinibus. Ita erudite hic ait Paulus, necessariam virtutem esse fidem, vide- licet cognitionem, et quidem talem, quae sit fides, id est, assensio, qua verbum Dei amplectimur de rebus non incurrentibus in sensum, nec ra- tione deprehensis.

Haec cognitio aut est historiae, aut legum et comminationum, aut promissionum. Cum vera adsensione leges et comminationes ample- ctimur, oritur timor. Cum autem promissio- nes amplectimur, oritur fiducia acquiescens in Deo, et vivificans corda. Haec virtus proprie nominatur Fides, quia tunc demum accedimus ad Deum, cum apprehensa est misericordia propter filium promissa. De hac fide dicitur ad Ephe- sios 3.: Per quem habemus fiduciam, et audemus accedere per fidem eius. Complectitur autem haec fides omnes articulos fidei, nec tantum no- ticia est, sed est fiducia, qua cor acquiescit in filio Dei, et in Deo, iuxta promissionem. Quia cum in veris pavoribus articulum, Credo remis- sionem peccatorum, ita amplecteris, ut de quo- que includas in promissionem universalem, et statuas tibi remitti peccata, certissimum est in corde sequi fiduciam et laetitiam acquiescentem in Deo, ut experientia in vera consolatione osten- dit, in qua recte discimus, quid sit fides, et simul agnoscimus, oportere nos fide acquiescere in verbo Dei, nec quaerere alias illuminationes. Hanc admonitionem necessariam esse, etiam ostendit experientia.

Spes est expectatio vitae aeternae certa, pro- pter filium Dei, iuxta promissionem in Evangelio expressam, et est expectatio mitigationis poena- rum seu calamitatum in hac vita, iuxta consilium Dei. Cum autem dicant adversarii verae doctri- nae, non servari a nobis discrimina virtutum, fidei et spei, moneri iuniores de vera differentia necesse est. Fides accipit praesens beneficium, scilicet remissionem peccatorum et reconciliatio- nem, ut certissimum est ex dicto: Iustificati fide pacem habemus. At spes futuram liberationem intuetur, et expectat. Haec doctrina perspi- cua est. Sed quaerunt: Cur affirmemus in Ecclesia fidem et spem virtutes esse, cum tamen fides sit noticia? Deinde etiamsi fiducia esse dicatur, tamen mirari aliquis potest, quomodo sit virtus. Item, cur spes sit virtus, cum in vita usitatissi- mum sit, spe incitatos homines decipi, et ruere in maximas calamitates, ut dictum est: Fallitur augurio spes bona saepe suo. Et Pindarus inquit: Spes somnia esse vigilantium. Et dictum est Epicteti valde dignum memoria: Ut pedibus, ita spe accedenda sunt possibilia, ὥσπερ τοῖς σκέλεσι, οὕτως καὶ ἐλπίσι πρὸς τὰ δυνατὰ δεῖ βαδίζειν.

Respondeo: Fides et spes sunt haud dubie virtutes, quia sunt obedientia, quam postulat Deus praestari suo mandato. Vox divina mani- festa est: Hunc audite. Item: Haec est voluntas patris mei, ut omnis qui credit in filium, habeat vitam aeternam. Fides igitur virtus est, quia Deo obtemperat, et cum est assensio amplectens omnes articulos fidei ac promissionem gratiae, et cum ea coniuncta est fiducia in Deo acquiescens. Nota sunt et de spe plurima praecepta 1. Petri 1.: Firmiter sperate gratiam, quae nobis exhibebitur, cum Iesus Christus revelabitur, videlicet in iu- dicio. Et in eodem capite: Ut fides vestra et spes sit in Deum. Et Roman. 5.: Spes non confundit. Et Rom. 8.: Spe salvi facti sumus. Est igitur vir- tus spes, quae verbo Dei obtemperat.

Et hinc sumatur responsio ad obiectiones supra recitatas de spe fallaci: Vox divina praeci- pit spem de iis rebus, quas promisit, ac vitae aeternae promissio propter filium certa et immota est. Non praecipit Pompeio sperare victoriam, etiamsi ipse hac sua imaginatione movetur. Causa iubet superos melior sperare secundos, quia iu- dicium Dei est, utra causa sit iustior. Et saepe Deus punit homines propter priora delicta, etiamsi in praesenti negotio iustam causam ha- bent, ut puniebat Israëlitas pugnantes cum tribu Beniamin, et saepe alias. Est igitur fallax spes, quae non regitur promissione divina.

Reguntur autem promissione divina spes vitae aeternae, et spes mitigationis poenarum et calamitatum in hac vita, ubi et doctrina tenenda est: Etiamsi praesentes calamitates non tolluntur, nec mitigari videntur, tamen semper retinenda est spes vitae aeternae, iuxta dictum Iob: Etiamsi occidet me, sperabo in eum, veruntamen vias meas coram eo arguam, et ipse erit mihi salvator, et non venient ad eum omnes hypocritae, id est, etiamsi in hac vita non tollentur calamitates, tamen spem vitae aeternae retineant omnes, qui ad Deum convertuntur.

Experimur autem valde languefieri animos in poenis, et dubitare, an sit speranda et expe- ctanda salus aeterna, cum nunc sentimus iram Dei in poenis, et abiici videmur. Adversus hanc tristissimam dubitationem necesse est tenere in conspectu firmas consolationes, quarum haec prima et praecipua est, quod Deus vult nos quocunque tempore ad se converti, et conversos certissime recipit propter filium Gratis, quia haec promissio semper vera et immota est: Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut filium suum unigenitum de- derit, ut Omnis, qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam. Et Ezechielis 38.: Vivo ego, dicit Dominus, nolo mortem peccato- ris, sed ut convertatur et vivat. Item: In qua- cunque die conversus fuerit impius, non corruet in impietate. Matth. 19.: Quoties remittam: Septuagies septies. Lucae 15.: Gaudium est an- gelis de uno peccatore poenitentiam agente. Et ibi recitatur conversio filii prodigi.

Altera consolatio est: Hanc ipsam ob cau- sam punit Deus, ut nos retrahat ad poenitentiam, et conversis det vitam aeternam, non ut perdat nos. 1. Cor. 11.: Cum iudicamur a Domino cor- ripimur, ne cum hoc mundo damnemur. Et in Psalmo: Bonum mihi quod humiliasti me, ut discerem iustificationes tuas. Esaiae 28.: Vexa- tio dat intellectum. Esaiae 66.: Ad quem re- spiciam, nisi ad miserum et contritum spiritu, et trementem sermones meos. Micheae ultimo: Iram Domini portabo, quia peccavi ei. Hic ex- presse de poena loquitur, et confitetur peccatum. Postea addit consolationem, in qua narrat se fidem et spem retinere: Cum sedebo in tenebris, Dominus lux mea est. His dictis adde vocem filii Dei, quae continet amplissimam et certissi- mam consolationem: Venite ad me Omnes, qui laboratis et onerati estis, et ego reficiam vos. Et Rom. 8.: Longa est concio de spe retinenda in summis doloribus et cruciatibus. Spe salvi facti sumus. Spes autem, quae videtur, non est spes.

Haec dicta et similia teneamus, ne propter poenas, quibus Deus in hac vita nos de ira sua commonefacit, spem vitae aeternae abiiciamus. Et sciamus hanc spem nequaquam esse irritam, quia praecipitur voce divina. Quanquam autem praesentes poenae in hac vita saepe non prorsus tolluntur, quia Deus propter multas causas vult Ecclesiam cruci subiectam esse, tamen et mitiga- tio promissa est, quae fit alias aliter. Cumque promissa sit divinitus, haec spes etiam non est irrita. Nahum primo: Bonus est Dominus, et confortans in tribulatione, et respiciens sperantes in ipsum. Ioëlis 2.: Convertimini ad Dominum Deum vestrum, quia bonus est, et misericors, et miti- gans poenam. Osea 11.: Non faciam furorem irae meae. Et Lucae 21.: Orate, ut possitis effugere ventura mala. Et illustria exempla sunt mitigationis poena- rum, servata Ninive, restitutio Davidis in re- gnum, sanatio Ezechiae, reductio Manassae, et non dubium est, tales mitigationes in tota Eccle- sia quotidie fieri, sicut Psalm. 77. dicit: Et non accendit totam iram suam. Ieremias in Threnis capite 3.: Misericordiae Domini quod non consumti sumus. Et alibi capite 46.: Consumam cunctas gen- tes, ad quas eieci te, te vero non consumam, sed castigabo te in iudicio, et ostendam te, quae vi- deris innocens, non innocentem esse. Et Abacuc 3.: Domine in ira misericordiae recorderis. Haec et similia dicta saepe cogitemus, ut et ardentius petamus mitigationem poenarum publi- carum et privatarum, et agnoscamus immensam Dei misericordiam, quod verissime lenit poenas, et nos sustentat, et ei gratias agamus. Hanc commonefactionem de fide et spe utilis- simam esse manifestum est. Et ut sit ardentior invocatio, saepe cogitanda est. Constat autem ex his, quae dixi, recte nun- cupari fidem et spem virtutes, quia sunt obedien- tia, quae regitur verbo Dei, et sunt cultus prae- cipui, ut Psalm. inquit: Sacrificate sacrificium iusticiae, et sperate in Domino. Nec sunt Phi- losophis notae hae virtutes, quia tantum mon- strantur voce Dei, quae docet etiam, quomodo regendae sint. Fide accipimus remissionem pec- catorum, Spe expectamus certo vitam aeternam, non propter nostra merita, sed propter filium Dei Gratis. Haec ita fieri oportet, quia in Evan- gelio Deus hanc suam voluntatem certissimis te- stimoniis patefecit. Ac procul extra philoso- phiam haec sapientia posita est. Nec philosophia fidem et spem inter virtutes ponit, cum non re- guntur certa et firma noticia principiorum, expe- rientia aut demonstratione, sed iudicat stultitiam esse assentiri incertis. Ut cum sperat Antonius victoriam, quia instructior est Augusto. Sed Ecclesia certa est propter promissionem divinam, et credit praeter spem in spem, in est, credit et sperat, ubi etiam diversum iudicio natu- rali apparet. Ut Psalmo 71. dicitur: Liberavit pauperem, cui non erat adiutor. Et Psalm. 26.: Pater et mater dereliquerunt me, Dominus autem suscepit me. Etsi autem caeterae virtutes, ut timor vel reverentia, obedientia in afflictionibus Deo de- bita, quae est pars iusticiae, et nominatur tole- rantia vel patientia, recte comprehenduntur in dilectione, ut mox dicam: tamen sciendum est, et his et caeteris fidem et spem praelucere. Quod ut fiat perspicuum, fiat collatio patientiae philo- sophicae et Christianae, et consolationum utrius- que generis. Philosophica patientia est utcunque obedire rationi in ferendis adversis, ita ut nihil contra iusticiam aut alias virtutes facias. Ut Cato se ipsum interficiens contra iusticiam facit. At So- crates nec iusticiam nec modestiam violat, cum sine seditione et sine deformitate ulla mortem op- petit. Nec in philosophica patientia spes inclusa est, sed Palamedes rationi obtemperat, etiam cum spes omnes salutis in hac vita, et postea ex- tinctae sunt. At Christiana patientia est, obedire man- dato divino in tolerandis adversis, ita, ne facias aliquid contra mandata Dei, ne Deo irascaris, sed fide agnoscas eum tibi propicium esse, et speres auxilium, mitigationem aut liberationem, et hac fide et spe lenias dolorem. Cernis hic in definitione addi fidem et spem, sicut supra de utraque virtute mandata severis- sima recitata sunt, iuxta illud: Sine fide impos- sibile est placere Deo. Item, Petrus: Firmiter sperate gratiam, quae vobis exhibebitur, cum Iesus Christus revelabitur. Ideo autem in Chri- stiana patientia lenitur dolor, quia tunc obiecta bona, fide et spe cernuntur. Baptista scit se Deo carum esse, et Deum adesse in hoc ipso agone, et videt hanc mortem esse iter ad coelestem Ecclesiam. Haec non vi- dent Palamedes, Socrates, Theramenes, aut si- miles. Non autem vere lenitur dolor, donec tan- tum tristia obiecta mens intuetur. Quae autem obiecta ad consolandos animos proponantur in philosophia, quae in Evangelio, supra dictum est. Et valde prodest collationem illam causa- rum semper meminisse.

᾿Αγάπη, τὰ τρία ταῦτα, μείζων δὲ τούτων ἡ ἀγάπη.

Sequitur descriptio dilectionis, qua universa antiquitas complexa est obedientiam universalem, dilectionem Dei et hominum propter Deum, et iuxta ordinem a Deo institutum, sicut Paulus in- quit Roma 13.: Dilectio est impletio legis. Et primae Iohannis 5.: Haec est dilectio Dei, ut mandata eius servemus. His dictis mota antiqui- tas, nomine dilectionis usa est, sicut alioqui uti- mur nomine iusticiae universalis. Haec ideo re- cito, et ut dicta scriptorum magis perspicua sint legentibus, et ut recentium ineptiae repudientur, qui in hoc textu Pauli contendunt tantum de di- lectione proximi et officiis erga proximum dici, non de dilectione Dei. Magna coecitas est, has virtutes divellere, quia dilectio proximi non est ordinata, nisi regatur dilectione Dei, id est, nisi sit talis voluntas, et sint talia officia, qualia Deus in suis praeceptis ordinat. Item, Nisi ad hunc finem referatur, ut Deo praestetur obedientia, et simus in Deo copulati, sicut Dominus inquit: Ut unum sint in nobis. Sciamus igitur unam esse virtutem dilectionem Dei et proximi, quae gra- dus habet, sed tamen et orditur a Deo, et refert inferiores gradus ad Deum tanquam ad principa- lem finem. Abraham diligit Deum. Postea et Agar diligit, sed pluris facit Deum, quo iubente, dimittit ancillam Agar.

Difficile est autem nobis in hac tanta duritie cordium tradere illustrem definitionem dilectio- nis. Si enim arderent corda sensu amoris Dei, sicut amantes incendia amoris inter sese sentiunt, minus obscurum esset quid nominetur Dilectio. Ac profecto talia vera incendia erga Deum in corde esse deberent, sed quia valde languida sunt, etiam si qua sunt, obscurior est descriptio.

Sed tamen constituamus hanc qualemcunque descriptionem: Dilectio Dei et proximi est, post- quam vera fide apprehensa est misericordia Dei propter filium donata, vicissim subiicere cor Deo, et facere mandata eius, cum quadam laetitia ac- quiescente ipso. Ut quia scit Laurentius se Deo placere, vicissim ei obtemperat in confessione et aliis officiis, et laetitia acquiescit in Deo, quan- quam corpus sentit magnos cruciatus. Haec lae- titia est effectus et indicium dilectionis, sicut saepe scriptum est, ut Actorum 5.: Ibant Apo- stoli a conspectu synedrii gaudentes, quod contu- melia affecti essent propter Dominum.
