Hanc laeti- tiam utcunque sentire mediocres homines possunt. Interdum vero in cordibus piorum accenduntur subitae flammae dilectionis ardentiores, quas suae cuiusque experientiae relinquamus. Haec de descriptione dilectionis monuisse satis sit.

Addit autem Paulus enumerationi, Tria haec, quasi significans, se praecipuas virtutes nominasse, quod verum est. Nam cum dilectio sit iusticia universalis, ut facile intelligi potest, non est postea opus longiore enumeratione, sed aspiciatur decalogus, et considerentur dilectio- nis officia iuxta singula praecepta. Ita si quis volet distributionem virtutum facere, iuxta prae- cepta concinne eas recitabit. Necesse est autem praelucere fidem et spem: quae sunt virtutes or- tae ex promissione Evangelii: deinde dilectio est incoatio legis.

Iuxta primam tabulam dilectio Dei comple- ctitur timorem filialem Dei, id est, veram reve- rentiam Dei, confessionem, gratiarum actio- nem, patientiam in aerumnis confessionis, stu- dium conservandi ministerii evangelici.

In secunda tabula in quarto praecepto amo- rem coniugis, sobolis, parentum, beneficiorum, magistratum, propter Deum.

In quinto praecepto iusticiam, quae cavet, ne laedat corpus alterius, item mansuetudinem frenatricem irae et cupiditatis vindictae, item beneficentiam.

In septimo praecepto iusticiam abstinentem a rebus alienis, et liberalitatem iuvantem egenos. Haec omnia esse officia dilectionis proximi per- spicuum est, quia sunt vincula consociationis ge- neris humani, quae est mutua benevolentia.

In sexto praecepto Castitas.

In octavo Veritas, virtutes sunt necessariae, etiamsi non prodessent proximis. Et tamen hae quoque multipliciter prosunt societati communi.

Ex hac consideratione iudicari potest, ad- pellatione dilectionis virtutes caeteras compre- hendi.

Sed cur inquit: Maxima inter has dilectio? Repondeo simplicissime: Cum virtutes inter sese conferuntur iuxta suam essentiam, verissimum est, dilectionem Dei longe omnibus aliis antecel- lere. Sicut lex etiam summam virtutem nomi- nat: Diligas Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo. De quo praecepto cum Dominus ipse dicat: Hoc est primum et magnum mandatum, signifi- catur, et virtutem, de qua loquitur, praecipuam esse. Et in vita aeterna sensus amoris Dei erga nos, et vicissim noster amor erga Deum erit sum- mus gradus beatitudinis. Et semper amor com- plectitur noticiam, quae quidem in vita aeterna erit multo illustrior, non obscura, ut nunc est fidei noticia.

Pauli hoc loco recte explicare, et multis aliis ob- iectionibus in hoc articulo respondere.

Addam et hoc, usitatam responsionem esse: Dilectio est maxima, scilicet quo ad actiones inter homines, quia fere omnes actiones prae- ceptorum secundae Tabulae sunt opera dilectio- nis. Sed hanc responsionem omitto, etsi verum est, ut supra dixi, dilectionem proximi virtutem simpliciter necessariam esse singulis, dona mira-, culorum non sunt singulis necessaria. Et de hac fide, quae est donum miraculorum, praecipue hic Paulus loquitur, ut mox initio in sequenti capite ostendit: Sectamini dilectionem, suscipite vero spiritualia. Vult singulos sectari, id est, appetere dilectionem, quae est virtus simpliciter necessaria singulis. Deinde vult dona caetera, quae prosunt Ecclesiae, et sunt motus et testimo- nia Spiritus sancti, magnificari, etiamsi non est necesse singulis ea dari.

Non disputabo autem subtilius de collatione harum virtutum. Utramque sciamus esse flam- mam a Spiritu sancto accensam, scilicet veram fidem et veram dilectionem. Ideo utraque ma- gnifacienda est, etiamsi altera antecellit.

Sed argumentum hic explicandum est, quod opponunt aliqui contra dictum, Fide iustifi- camur:

Maxima virtus potius iustificat. Dilectio est maxima virtus: Igitur dilectio potius iustificat.

## 14:1 Argument
Chapter XIV.

Διώκετε τὴν ἀγάπην, ζηλοῦτε δὲ τὰ πνευματικά.

It was said above that the distinction must be considered between what is necessary for individuals and other gifts, which, even if they benefit the Church, are nevertheless not given to all, as the gifts of Joseph and Daniel are excellent, and benefit the whole Church, and are illustrious testimonies of the presence of God in the Church. But yet such great ornaments are not bestowed upon all. He indicates this distinction here when he says: Pursue love, that is, this is such a thing as you individuals ought to seek and possess. But admire the gifts of the spirit, magnify them, and acknowledge them to be benefits of God, and testimonies of doctrine, and give thanks to God for this revelation. And as it is said in Ephesians 4: He gives some as Prophets, others as Apostles, know that the ministries and gifts of individuals are not similar. Therefore, concerning these he used the word ζηλοῦτε, that is, admire them and magnify them, and let each one perform his ministry in his own place, and serve the Church with his own gift. However, Paul's prudence must be considered. The Corinthians were becoming more insolent through their zeal for gifts, and were neglecting love. Now, when they hear that love is preferred, lest they neglect the study and exercises of the gifts, he assigns a convenient place to each kind.

I answer: The major premise would be true if we were righteous by the fulfillment of the law. But because we are not righteous by the law, and another righteousness is shown in the promise, namely that we are righteous on account of the Son of God, with his righteousness imputed to us: faith is named, which apprehends the mediator; whether this virtue is greater or lesser than love, that does not pertain to the matter. For we are not righteous on account of our own qualities, but on account of the Son of God. And yet it is true that when the Son of God is apprehended by faith, hearts are quickened, and the Son of God is truly effective in us, and kindles by the Holy Spirit a new light, love, and other virtues, which are the begun fulfillment of the law. And yet because there are still remnants of sin in this miserable nature, the person is righteous, that is, accepted by God on account of the mediator interceding for us before the eternal Father, and with the righteousness of the mediator imputed to us, he is not righteous on account of his own dignity. Rightly, therefore, do we speak of both, of renewal and of imputation: It is necessary for renewal to take place. And the Son of God is in us, and is effective. And yet this consolation is necessary for all, that on account of the Son of God himself we certainly please God, by faith, not on account of our own dignity. Those who consider these fountains of this doctrine can also [understand] the statement

Then, omitting the rest, he speaks of that passage whose primary use is in teaching.

Μᾶλλον δὲ ἵνα προφητεύητε.

It is certain that prophecy in this chapter signifies the exposition of some read or recited passage, just as Luther, expounding Paul to the Romans or to the Galatians, uses the gift of prophecy. To speak with a tongue is to be able to utter diverse languages. When some displayed that miracle in a public congregation—because, as Greeks were otherwise fond of eloquence, so they were more delighted by the knowledge of many languages than other nations, and loved this study, and recited praises or prayers in diverse languages as it were—Paul draws them back to the study of exposition. And especially in a public congregation, merely to sound diverse languages without exposition was of no use. Paul, however, wishes those speaking in a public assembly not to institute a theatrical display, as was customary among the Gentiles to recite poems or panegyrics in spectacles, but to serve the utility of those learning, and to kindle pious affections and invocation.

And here an old custom must be considered. A passage having been read in the books of the Prophets in the synagogues, several spoke about it in order, as in Luke 4 the Lord recites a passage from Isaiah, and in Acts chapter 13 a place for speaking is given to Paul. Yet there were not confused shouts, as in the voting of the common people, but a place for speaking was given by him who presided over the synagogue, as is said in the Acts. And here there is a distinction between those sitting and the rest of the multitude, as was said concerning judgments: The leaders sit, while the crowd stands. Thus Paul here orders several to speak in order without tumult, and to expound the read passages.

Λαλεῖ οἰκοδομὴν καὶ παράκλησιν καὶ παρα- μυθίαν.

He dwells on the instituted admonition. Speaking with a tongue, that is, saying praises, thanksgiving, or prayer in various languages, or in a foreign language, does not speak to men, that is, it does not teach the people. But in spirit, that is, by a spiritual gift by which he is kindled with the affections of the heart, he speaks things that are indeed good, but yet not understood by others. But he who prophesies, that is, expounds, speaks those things which contribute to edification, exhortation, and consolation.

It is customary for Paul to divide the kinds of sermons into these three species, which are the principal ones. The first species is didactic. For it is necessary at the beginning to hand down the doctrine concerning the articles of faith and concerning the distinction between Law and Gospel, and other principal members of doctrine.

Another species is exhortation to repentance and to good works, which also includes rebuke, and is similar to persuasive materials in Rhetoric.

The third species is consolation, which is taken principally from the Gospel, because the foundation in all true and effective consolation is the acknowledgment of the remission of sins and of reconciliation with God on account of the Son, as was said above concerning consolations.

In the same way Paul distributes the kinds of doctrines in the first Epistle to Timothy 4: Be diligent in reading, consolation, and doctrine. This statement agrees entirely with these words which are recited in this Epistle to the Corinthians, and he wisely teaches what are the principal kinds of sermons in the Church, that there ought to be a plan in teaching, and to what ends every speech should be referred.

First, mention is made of reading, where the distinction between doctrine in the Church and other arts must be considered. We do not begin Arithmetic or other parts of philosophy from reading, but we bring with us to the description of the arts the beginnings born with us, such as counting and other things, but the doctrine of the Church must be learned in a far different way. It is necessary to begin from reading. Because since the articles of faith concerning the three persons of the divinity and concerning the two natures in the Redeemer born of the Virgin Mary, concerning the Church, concerning the gratuitous remission of sins, concerning the resurrection of the dead, and other articles of the Gospel are by no means known by nature, it is necessary that they be known only from divine revelation, which God, in His immense goodness, willed to be committed to writing after our first parents through the Prophets, and then through the Apostles. Therefore he first leads us to the reading, that is, he wills that the prophetic and apostolic books be read in the Church, which he wills to be the fountains of doctrine and the norm, so that no opinions dissenting from this norm may be received, just as he himself says: If anyone teaches another Gospel, let him be anathema. Therefore, let this be the first duty of the preacher, that he read the prophetic and apostolic books to the people, and take pains that they be read, and warn that the rule of doctrine is contained in them. The second duty of the preacher is to teach. There is, however, one simple way of teaching: to explain the type of discourse in a reading, and then to show the order of the things that are proposed, and to distinguish the parts, and by a certain method of the arts to add definitions and comparisons. As in the beginning of the book of Moses, it is necessary to warn the reader where the Creation is spoken of, and where the Fall of our first parents is spoken of.

Afterwards, it is necessary to distinguish justice and sin, then the law and the promise. Finally, all sane people understand that in teaching, it is necessary to employ Grammar, Arithmetic, Dialectic, and the aids of other arts. It is necessary that the articles of faith be proposed to the people in order, that the Law and the Gospel be distinguished, sin and the redeemer, philosophical justice and the other justice, which is either imputed to us on account of the Son, or is restored in us.

It is necessary to distinguish the Church and Empires, the Old and New Testament, divine and human laws, eternal punishments and eternal rewards.

Paul calls the explanation of these things in the Corinthians Edification. And let the preacher understand what matters are principal and necessary for edification, that is, for confirming faith in all articles. Let him repeat these, omitting foreign disputes, just as he commands to Timothy that things useful for edification be chosen. These two types, reading and the explanation of doctrine, pertain to the didactic genre.

The third genre is Consolation. The end of doctrine in the Church is not only knowledge, nor only our actions, but God has revealed himself and delivered the Gospel so that he might free us from sin and eternal death, and the end is that, with sin and death abolished, enjoying the communication of the wisdom, justice, and joy of God, we may live with him in all eternity, and in turn celebrate him. Therefore, the final genre is consolation.

Therefore, after the preacher has proposed the reading and the doctrine, let him show how it should be applied to consolation, and for this effect, let him finally refer the discourse. And let these steps be considered.

First, faith must be raised up, that is, trust in mercy, by which, when we rest in God, peace and joy follow, as it is written: Being justified by faith we have peace. And the next steps are Invocation, Hope, and Thanksgiving. For we know that invocation is by no means in vain. Therefore, sorrows are softened by the hope of the mitigation of calamities, or of the liberation which we seek and expect. And thanksgiving is kindled when we acknowledge the benefits of God in order, however we may. First the remission of sins, then help, and the presence of the Son of God sustaining us, afterwards the mitigation of calamities or liberation.

Soon he repeats the same types of sermons: If, having returned to you, I were only to sound my prayers or hymns in various tongues, what would I profit you, unless a sermon also came by revelation, or knowledge, or prophecy, or doctrine?

He calls doctrine reading, and the recitation of dogmas, as was said above. Prophecy, the explanation of both reading and dogmas. And these two parts pertain partly to the didactic genre, partly to the other genre, which he called consolation. Knowledge is an admonition concerning morals and external governance, as was said above in the twelfth chapter, such as concerning the election and power of the ministers of the Gospel, concerning the distinction of laws, which are abolished, which are perpetual, concerning the use of liberty, concerning the judgments of the Church, concerning marriage, concerning the use of political affairs, and similar matters.

He calls revelation the singular testimonies exhibited to the doctrine itself, just as he says to the Galatians: I did not receive the Gospel from man, nor did any man teach me, but I received it by the revelation of Jesus Christ. Predictions also pertain here, just as he prophesies concerning the last times of the Church to the Thessalonians and to Timothy. Likewise, judgments concerning fanatical teachers, such as many who were wandering about at that time, and were boasting of certain illuminations of theirs, and were deceiving and troubling the Churches with various tricks, as in Acts chapter 13. In Cyprus he punishes Elymas with blindness, and he narrates to Timothy that he had delivered Hymenaeus and Alexander to Satan, so that they might cease to spread blasphemies.

We also saw in our time, long before the peasant sedition, a fanatical man, Nicolaus Stork, born in Zwickau, wandering about in these religions, who narrated that angels had often spoken with him in visible form, and had predicted to him that he would be the leader of the restoration of the Churches. He spoke, however, about worship in the manner of enthusiasts; he said that justice was a new and heavenly light in hearts, and new motions or inspirations. And he did not rightly speak concerning faith and consolation in true terrors, in which hearts sustain themselves by the imputation of the righteousness of the Son of God. Exaggerating, however, those enthusiasms, he diminished the use of the Sacraments, and rejected human traditions entirely, nor did the admiration of sublime and unknown things move few to embrace his opinions, many of whom we could name. Now, among his chief admirers was Thomas Müntzer, who later was the author and leader of the sedition in Thuringia, by which sedition being suppressed, Müntzer was put to death, in which they relate that he was of a very broken spirit. And not long after, his master, Nicolaus Stork, died a fugitive in the Munich hospital in Bavaria. Thus the outcome refuted the frenzies of these men. But long before, Luther had condemned that very faction both in person and in public writings. Such deceptions of the devil cannot be judged without a singular gift of God. Wherefore we also include such judgments here under the name of revelation.

Ὅμως τὰ ἄψυχα φωνὴν διδόντα.

By many comparisons he shows that it is not profitable to recite prayers or readings in an assembly in foreign languages without explanation. Just as it is of no use for a trumpet to give sounds not understood by soldiers.

These comparisons are not obscure, therefore I do not add an explanation. But the reader must be admonished to fix this often-repeated sentiment in his heart: Magnify the gifts, so that you may be richer and better instructed for the edification of the Church. Likewise: Let all things be done for the edification of the Church. Let us follow this precept in teaching; let us not show off our talents with the subtlety of disputes about unnecessary matters. Let us not court the applause and favor of princes or the multitude, fawning either upon their perverse judgments or their depraved desires, but let minds and speech be governed by this rule: Let all things be done for edification, that is, let necessary materials be chosen, let the articles of faith be correctly explained, let the entire body of doctrine be correctly proposed. And after the doctrine has been recited, let the sermon always be referred to these ends, so that in the hearers there may be excited the fear of God, and then faith, raising up terrified minds and kindling invocation and thanksgiving. Let us always keep these goals in view when preaching.

Ἐὰν γὰρ προσεύχομαι γλώσσῃ, τὸ πνεῦμα μου προσεύχεται.

He dwells on the comparison he has instituted. Although it is a pious work to say a prayer in any language, nevertheless the utility of the Church must also be served, and an explanation must be added. When I recite a prayer in a foreign language, my spirit prays, that is, the affection kindled by the spiritual gift. For he speaks not of simulated readings or chants, such as hired hypocrites now sound in temples, but of the serious prayer of the pious. But my mind is without fruit, that is, the mind, which in this pious meditation has thought of good sentiments, the knowledge of which would profit others, does not impart them to the assembly.

He says, therefore, that he will recite a prayer or Psalm both with the spirit and with the mind, that is, that he will, if the occasion arises, compose a prayer or hymn in various languages, but will nevertheless add an explanation useful to the rest of the assembly.

He illustrates the argument which he has instituted from the useless. If you say a public prayer in a foreign language, how can the hearers at the end add the customary clause, by which they signify that they are asking for the same things, and that the vows of the whole Church are joined, namely, when it is said in the customary manner Amen, which word it appears from chapter 27 of Deuteronomy that the Church used in this way in the time of Moses, when the people responding testified that they were asking for the same things, where these words are often repeated: And let all the people say, Amen. That the Greek translates as καὶ ἐροῦσι πᾶς ὁ λαὸς: γένοιτο. For to the grammarians it is, Truly, that is, let it be ratified and firm, let it come to pass what we ask, nor do we think these vows of ours to be an empty murmur, as the heathens indeed shout to God, but doubt what they are invoking: likewise whether any deities regard men, or whether they hear and care for their groans and tears. In these doubts their cries are dissipated in vain into the air, and they are entirely, as Seneca says: Empty rumors, and vain words, And like a tale to an anxious dream.

Opposed to this heathen opinion is the confession of the Church, when it says Amen. Because it is an asseveration, as if it were saying: May these vows be true and ratified, and we believe them to be ratified. We know that He wishes to be worshipped and invoked by this faith, by which we believe that on account of the mediator our groans are truly regarded, and our prayers are heard, and we certainly obtain either deliverances or mitigations. Let this suffice to be noted here concerning the term. For the complete doctrine concerning prayer is delivered elsewhere, and it is fitting that it be most familiarly known to all, so that it may be in sight during daily invocation, and that you yourself may always add this assertion of yours when the prayer is finished: I believe, O Lord, that these my vows are received by you on account of the Son, the mediator, but bring aid to my weakness. I know that you desire this honor to be attributed to you, that we believe you are truly moved by care for us, and that we are heard, and that your promises are not empty sounds. In this exercise of ours we learn why antiquity always added to prayers, Amen. And observe the perpetual custom of the Church: There was always some one person in the assembly who reverently recited the public prayer with his own voice. Afterwards, either the people, or one person in the name of the people, responded Amen. What need is there, someone may say? I answer: God wills that there be consensus in the Church in doctrine, faith, invocation, and petition: He also wills that public and honorable assemblies be held, and in these He wills to be invoked by the consenting hearts of the pious, according to the promise of Matthew 18: If two of you shall agree on earth, concerning any matter that they shall ask, it shall be done for them. Therefore this custom has been preserved, so that the people might add this signification of their consensus. And Paul wills that it be added. He says therefore concerning the one responding: How will he who fills the place of the unlearned say Amen, if he does not understand you? ἀναπληρῶν τόπον τοῦ ἰδιώτου, he is called the one responding, as if completing the prayer recited by another, afterwards fulfilling it with the expressed consensus of the people. To this very custom many other sayings also correspond, as in Psalm 117, where he first names the house of Aaron, and commands it to give thanks and celebrate God: let the house of Aaron now say, the Lord is good, and his mercy is forever. Let the priest be the leader of the public prayer, and as it were lead the people with his own voice. Afterwards, therefore, it was added: Let all who fear the Lord now say, the Lord is good, and his mercy is forever.

Brethren, do not become children in mind, but be infants in malice, yet be mature in mind.

He inserts a general admonition, that they may judge rightly concerning the use of gifts. The gifts were not exhibited for the sake of an empty spectacle, as those seem to think who only show off the gift of tongues by reciting a hymn in a foreign language, which the assembly does not understand. This admonition extends widely.

Sacrifices in Israel were instituted for certain uses. But the priests transferred them to pomp or gain. The Lord's Supper was instituted for a certain use, namely for the consolation of consciences. Afterwards it was horribly profaned, and in a great part of the human race it is celebrated as a spectacle, or for the sake of gain. Churches contended about the day of Passover, and often about other unnecessary questions. Concerning this whole class, Paul warns that we should not be caught like children by spectacles and rites, but that we should wisely govern our actions, and look to the causes, and assign to each thing its own place. And he repeats the rule here often: Let all things be done for edification. Consider why the gift of tongues was attributed to the Church, not as an empty spectacle, but so that it might benefit those places where the use of foreign languages is necessary. But in your Church let the reading be recited in a language understood by the people, and let an exposition useful to the hearers be proposed concerning some part of doctrine.

Ἐν νόμῳ γέγραπται, ὅτι ἐν ἑτερογλώσσοις.

There are three causes for which the gift of tongues was attributed to the Church. The first and principal one, so that the Gospel could be propagated quickly among many nations, whose language is not one.

The second, so that this very gift might be a testimony of the Holy Spirit, and of the presence of God in the Church, just like other great miracles.

The third, so that it might be a sign and testimony that other nations are also to be called to the fellowship of the Gospel.

Isaiah signifies this in chapter 28, from where these words are cited. And although various meanings are sought in Isaiah, nevertheless he undoubtedly also embraces this one which Paul recites, that it would come to pass that the Gospel would be spread among many nations in diverse languages, which would be displeasing to this people, and that the people would then pay the penalty for having despised the divine voice. Isaiah in a long narrative censures the blindness of the Church, which was fascinated by false opinions and traditions. All tables are filled with vomit, that is, the Church is almost everywhere drunk and delirious with great errors, and after the return from Babylon the Pharisees and Sadducees arose, whose frenzies Isaiah also accuses. Thus, after the Apostles, heresies spread in the Church, then the traditions of the Popes, Monks, and Sophists, concerning the sacrifice of the Mass, concerning the adoration of the bread, concerning the invocation of the dead, concerning doubt, concerning the righteousness of works, concerning celibacy, and other foolish ceremonies, the light of the Gospel having been extinguished.

After this rebuke, Isaiah adds an antithesis: Whom shall he teach knowledge? Those weaned from the milk, those drawn from the breasts, that is, those chastened and not drunk with the pleasures and opinions which this blind nature has brought forth, and which they learned among the Pharisees from childhood, just as he says shortly after in the same chapter: Vexation gives understanding.

Afterwards follows a Mimesis, which recites their traditions: Command, command again, wait, wait again, a little here, as if he were saying: They accumulate commands and glosses. But these glosses will be their destruction. He adds, therefore: They mock me with their traditions or ironies. I in turn will speak to them in a language that will displease, or a mocking one, and I will call the Gentiles to the fellowship of the Church in diverse languages, and I will destroy their polity. This is the simplest explanation. In the Hebrew it is read: With mocking lips, and he will speak to this people in another language. Where the antithesis should be considered, as if he were saying: Now they mock my word, and my language is foreign or barbaric to them: I in turn will speak to them in a truly foreign language, which will then be unpleasant to them, I will gather the Gentiles to the fellowship of the Church, this polity having been destroyed.

From this simple recitation it is manifest that Paul rightly cited this saying, and from it showed that the gift of tongues is a sign of the preaching of the Gospel. In the Greek version of Isaiah it is read: διὰ φαυλισμὸν χειλέων, διὰ γλώσσης ἑτέρας, etc. For he rendered לעגֵי as φαυλισμὸν, which signifies mocking. Then also another word is added in the Hebrew and in the Greek, namely, another language, which agrees with Paul's sentiment.

Ὡστε αἱ γλῶσσαι εἰς σημεῖον εἰσὶν, οὐ τοῖς πιστεύουσιν, ἀλλὰ τοῖς ἀπίστοις.

It was said above that the gift of tongues was attributed to the Church so that the Gospel could be propagated among the nations. At the same time, however, it was a testimony of the presence of God, like other miracles. Here, therefore, Paul says that the variety of tongues is a sign not for believers, but for unbelievers, namely, so that moved by this miracle, they, like others, might be invited to the Gospel. Nor is there need for a longer explanation on this point.

Afterwards he says that prophecy is profitable to believers. The meaning is clear. He says that interpretation is profitable to the whole assembly, in which many did not understand foreign languages. When these hear in their own language an explanation of some prophetic discourse concerning the sum of doctrine, they are instructed and stirred up to fear, faith, hope, invocation, thanksgiving, tolerance, and to other virtues. Just as Paul teaches and confirms believers, citing and explaining the saying from Genesis: Abraham believed God, and it was imputed to him for righteousness. And in the Epistle to the Hebrews, believers are instructed by the explanation of the saying concerning the priesthood of the Son of God: You are a Priest forever, etc. The explanation of this testimony showed the reasons why the Levitical or typical priesthood ceased after the Messiah was exhibited. And he taught what the priesthood of the Son of God is, by which the wrath of God against sin is truly appeased, and the remission of sin is announced, and sin and death are abolished, just as it is written there: By one offering he has perfected forever those who are sanctified. Finally, at all times the pious are instructed and confirmed by such explanations, which he here calls Prophecies. This gift, therefore, he wishes to be exercised more in a Church of one language, where if those ignorant of foreign languages should come into the assembly, and only hear foreign sounds there, they might wonder what was being done, since that recitation brings no utility to the people, just as on the day of Dionysius in the Würzburg Church songs written in Latin letters are sung in Greek, not understood even by those singing them. These childish ineptitudes neither befit the gravity of the Church, nor profit those singing or the people. This example in some way illustrates these words: Will they not say that you are insane? Why then did he say earlier that the variety of tongues is profitable as a miracle? It is true, it is profitable as a miracle among those where the use of foreign languages exists. But here he speaks of an assembly of one language, in which the Church already gathered needs constant explanation. In such an assembly it is inept to display foreign languages.

Εἰσέλθῃ δέ τις ἄπιστος ἢ ἰδιώτης, ἐλέγχεται ὑπὸ πάντων.

I have already said that Paul is speaking about an assembly of one language, in which a discourse by one explaining the chief articles of doctrine in the Church is profitable both to an unbeliever who understands the language and to a believer, as it is consistent that this very often happened, that modest men from among the Gentiles came with friends to the assemblies of the Church, pagan wives with husbands already professing the Gospel, or brothers with brothers, sons with parents. Some of these, when they heard the worship of idols and the great darkness of the pagans being censured, were certainly moved. And it is manifest that the Church was gathered in this way little by little. A hymn composed in a foreign language would have profited such people nothing. To this effect Paul says here: If an unbeliever enters, as when the servants of Cornelius the Centurion hear Peter preaching. Or an unlearned person, that is, a rude one, who has begun to hear the doctrine of the Catechism for the first time: Such people, he says, are reproved and convinced by all, and the secrets of their hearts are made manifest, that is, the doctrine being heard, censuring pagan vices, Epicurean opinions, or the worship of idols, lusts, and other crimes, and showing the manifestation of the true God, they are converted to God, and acknowledge that the Church is truly the assembly of God, and that this doctrine is not fictitious. And the highest praise of the Church is described in these very brief words: He acknowledges and confesses that God is truly among you, ἀπαγγέλλων, ὅτι ὁ θεὸς ὄντως ἐν ὑμῖν ἐστί. Here let the histories concerning the gathering of the Church be recalled. The enemies of the Gospel spoke evil of the meetings of Christians, as Tertullian and others write. Friends of the believers were brought along so that they might be spectators and report what was being done there. Many of these, when they heard the excellent doctrine and saw the most honorable examples, were moved so that they themselves also embraced the Gospel.

And there are four arguments used in Justin Martyr, who writes to the Emperor Marcus Antoninus, and in others, by which they refute the pagans, which it is most useful for everyone to keep in view.

First: It is a manifest absurdity and manifest madness for pagans to embrace Epicurean opinions, or to approve the worship of idols and many gods, or to approve wicked lusts. These vices can be refuted by natural demonstrations, which are often to be pondered by the pious, and the refutation has moved many pagans to seek another doctrine.

Second argument: That which greatly confirms good minds, and which Justin urges most, is taken from antiquity. Because it is manifest that the history of the Church is older than the histories of all pagans. The series of times and empires shows that the Israelites and their fathers existed before the monarchies, before the Assyrian, Persian, Greek, and Roman. And many traces among the nations provide testimonies to the antiquity of the Church. The Greeks confess that they originated from Japheth, the Persians from Elam. And there are many similar things. Nor are there any writings extant in the whole human race that show a continuous series of years from the beginnings of things, except for the history of the Church alone. Let us therefore hold to the excellent rule of Tertullian: Whatever is first is most true.

Third argument: Constant miracles, the raising of the dead, and others, which the devil can by no means imitate. And I include among the miracles the predictions concerning the monarchies, in Moses, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Daniel. That miracle is an illustrious testimony at any time after the event. When many saw in the time of the Roman Empire that the succession of monarchies had been such as the Prophets had predicted, they confessed both that this doctrine was handed down from God, and that God governs such changes of empires, and that the human race is divinely preserved.

Let us also propose the same argument to ourselves, so that we may embrace the doctrine of the Church with the firmest assent.

And this is also a constant miracle, that the Church cannot be destroyed, although in all ages the highest kings, and those excelling in glory and power, have attempted to oppress it, such as Pharaoh, Nebuchadnezzar, Antiochus, many Roman emperors, and afterwards the Turks and others. The perpetuity of the Church among such great waves is therefore an illustrious testimony, which shows that it is preserved by God.

Fourth argument is taken from the very nature of the doctrine. No nation has a law more honorable and more rightly in agreement with natural judgment. All philosophy confesses its own imperfection, because it sees that true notions shine in reason, and yet that there is the greatest discord of human powers; it is ignorant of whence this is, nor can it show remedies.

It sees that many absurdities follow if souls are not immortal: and yet it doubts concerning immortality.

Philosophy can by no means affirm that even good men, such as Palamedes or Socrates, are heard in their calamities.

No nation outside the Church has a certain and express doctrine concerning the remission of sins, concerning the presence of God with those who truly call upon Him, and concerning eternal life, and concerning the manner in which eternal life is certainly received, since no one satisfies the law, and no one is without sin.

When these four arguments are joined together, they move men who are not Cyclopean. And when afterwards the sense of the judgment of God is added in the acknowledgment of sins, and consolation and vivification in the heart, once the Son of God is acknowledged, in these movements the Holy Spirit draws and confirms hearts, so that they now confess themselves to be convinced, and begin to assent more firmly to the Gospel. These things happen in this way in all who understand the exercises of repentance, and Paul speaks of this confirmation when he says, 2 Cor. 1: But it is God who confirms us in Christ, who also has anointed and sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts. And Rom. 8: The Spirit gives testimony to our spirit, that we are the children of God. And 1 John 2: The anointing teaches you of all things. And Heb. 11: Faith is called ἔλεγχος, because in this way, as I have said, minds are convinced; and assent is made firm. Thus also in this chapter Paul says: That some, having heard the sum of the doctrine in the assembly of the Church, and having made a comparison with heathen errors, are drawn by the Holy Spirit, and inclined to embrace the Gospel. Such, he says, confess that God is truly in the Church, that is, they feel themselves to be drawn by God, terrified, and again raised up and vivified, and they confess the doctrine to be true, and embrace it.

This narrative shows how the Church was both gathered and increased, when the Gentiles came to hear the doctrine. And in the same way the Church is gathered at all times.

Πάντα πρὸς οἰκοδομὴν γινέσθω.

He repeats the precept, which he also delivered above, that teachers should consider what is profitable for the Church, namely, for acknowledging the necessary doctrine concerning individual articles. Then for inclining minds to repentance, for correcting profane security. Afterwards for the consolation of the pious, for exciting faith, invocation, hope, and joy in God, for an ardent zeal for true obedience. These and similar things he embraces with the word edification, alluding to the construction of a building.

On the contrary, recitations that are not understood do not edify, that is, they do not help the Church. Curious questions and labyrinths also destroy as if a building, which entangle minds with doubts, and beget hatred of the doctrine, as if it were uncertain and ambiguous.

Here he warns that order must be kept in teaching. And at the same time he appoints judges, which is very worthy of consideration. He does not want license to be granted in the Church to scatter any opinions whatsoever, but he wants doctrine to be judged. Here is contained the order of synods and judgments concerning doctrine, of which these four things are to be considered:

I. What persons are judges of doctrine in the Church.

II. What is the norm, according to which judgment must be made.

III. How the judgment is to be valid.

IV. What is the execution.

Regarding the first question, it is one thing to speak of the norm, another of persons. Concerning the norm, there is no doubt that the norm is simply the heads of doctrine handed down in the prophetic and apostolic writings, and comprised in the symbols. And this norm is as the supreme judge. But because the question is now about persons, just as Paul also speaks of persons, and in this life in the refutation of errors, in the congregation, it is necessary for some persons by their voice and their testimony to oppose those who err. Therefore the dispute is, who those persons are. Paul says: Let those sitting judge, that is, all the hearers, not as in a sedition, without order, but each in his own place, as Paul says later: Let all things be done in order. Likewise: God is not the author of ἀκαταστασίας. So also it is written in Matt. 18: Tell the Church. These words are not understood of an impious assembly, which dominates in the Church with the titles of Bishops, and yet is an enemy of true doctrine, but of an assembly which does not falsely hold the name of the Church, such as were the assemblies then gathered by Paul. In this assembly let opinions be stated in order by the teachers and elders, just as it is said in Acts chapter 15: The Apostles and elders were gathered together, that they might consider this matter. Afterwards in establishing the decree, not the Apostles or elders alone take to themselves an ὀλιγαρχικὴν power, but the consent of the whole Church is added, according to these words: Then it seemed good to the Apostles and Presbyters with the whole Church. And afterwards it is said again: The Apostles and Presbyters and brethren. The Holy Spirit did not wish to establish a tyrannical or oligarchic power in the Church, but wished the pious to be heard even in the lower ranks, just as Paul says here: You can all speak one by one, that all may learn. Likewise: If a revelation is made to someone sitting by, let the first be silent. Likewise, 1 Thessalonians 5: Do not quench the Spirit, do not despise prophecies. Test all things, hold fast to what is good. In this way, for the sake of refuting Samosatenus, Gregory of Neocaesarea and others gathered from afar by private study for the glory of God. And such are always the judgments of the true Church, whenever the Churches are moderately restored, as we, having employed other pious and learned men, have often refuted and condemned the Anabaptists in this way. Basil speaks of such a non-tyrannical judgment, saying: Ἀλλά εἰσιν ἐπίσκοποι, κληθῶσι εἰς ἀκρόασιν. Ἐστὶ κλῆρος κατὰ πᾶσαν τοῦ θεοῦ παροικίαν, συναχθήτωσαν οἱ δοκιμώτατοι, λεγέτω μετὰ παῥῥησίας ὁ βουλόμενος, ἵνα ἔλεγχος ᾖ τὸ γιγνόμενον, καὶ μὴ λοιδορία.

The second question is about the norm according to which one must judge. Here there is no doubt that the norm is the prophetic and apostolic books themselves and the symbols, in which the principal articles proposed in the prophetic and apostolic books are briefly comprised. And when some delusion fights against a clear article delivered in the prophetic or apostolic books, or the symbols, the judgment is manifest according to this rule: If anyone teaches another Gospel, let him be anathema, just as the Manichaean furies, likewise the Pelagians, fought against clear articles.

But here the Sophists object that there are many obscure and ambiguous sayings in the prophetic and apostolic books. Wherefore they contend that the voice of the judge is to be preferred to the prophetic and apostolic books. Under this pretext, some prefer synods, others the Pope, to these books, just as in any kingdom, when obscurity or ambiguity is detected in the laws, the voice of the king explaining what was said obscurely or ambiguously is preferred. And in empires it is necessary to acquiesce in that explanation, otherwise there would be no end to lawsuits. The Sophists transfer this political example to the judgments of the Church.

But it must be answered: Concerning necessary doctrine, there is no ambiguity in the prophetic and apostolic books and in the symbols, if they are understood without cavil and dexterously, having inspected the perpetual series of narratives and the members agreeing with themselves, as ought to be done in any interpretation. Therefore 2 Corinthians 4 is said: If our Gospel is veiled, it is veiled in those who are perishing.

Likewise, since it is expressly commanded: You shall add nothing, you shall take nothing away, and in Numbers chapter 15:

Let them not follow their own thoughts, but let them be mindful of the commandments of God: It follows that there is no ambiguity to which an interpretation can be added by human judgment.

Although, however, there is no ambiguity in the prophetic and apostolic writings concerning the law, the promises, and the necessary articles, yet because in contentions even plainly spoken things are transformed into many meanings by diverse interpretations, it is profitable to hear the testimonies of the purer Church on some matters, and to compare them to the sources; when we see that these agree more with the sources, we are much confirmed by these very testimonies. For although Samosatenus astutely disputes the saying of John ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, that the person is not understood by the name λόγος, yet when we read the opinions of Irenaeus, Gregory of Neocaesarea, and other approved interpreters, these testimonies are useful for teaching and confirming us. For God preserves the ministry in the Church for this reason, as is written in Ephesians 4, that we may not be carried about by various winds of doctrine, but that there may be some witnesses of true doctrine without ambiguity. And He commanded the teaching and admonishing Church to be heard, just as Samson says: If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have found it. And to Peter He says: And you, when you have turned, strengthen your brothers.

The true Church is therefore to be heard as a teacher and monitor, but let faith rest upon the word of God. Being admonished therefore by the Church, let us compare its testimonies to the sources. And it is a pleasing confirmation to a good mind to know that it does not depart from the consensus of the true Church, and to invoke God with one spirit and one voice with the true Church, as is said in Psalm 21: In the midst of the Church I will praise you. Likewise, Psalm 110: I will confess to you, O Lord, in the council and congregation of the righteous. And in the sources, from the whole series of narratives, a single and native meaning can usually be found. Thus also now we are helped in many controversies by the ancient and more sincere Church. It is manifest that in the first Church there were no private Masses. When we compare this custom to the sayings of Paul, we see it agree with this saying, 1 Corinthians 11: When you come together for the Lord's supper, wait for one another. Concerning the baptism of infants, Augustine also cites the custom of the first Church. And Origen expressly says so in the 6th chapter to the Romans. And so the Church also received the tradition from the Apostles, even to give baptism to little ones. And that agrees more with the sayings in scripture. It is certain that the promises to little ones, who are in the Church, pertain, not to others outside the Church. Wherefore they are to be inserted into the Church through baptism. There are therefore norms of judgment, the prophetic and apostolic writings and the symbols. And in some controversies we are aided by the testimonies of the true Church. And the true Church must be rightly distinguished from the unlearned rabble. One must also look at the perpetual opinion of the learned; mutilated sayings are not to be excerpted and sophistically distorted against the perpetual opinion of the authors. For no one always speaks sufficiently circumspectly, clearly, and properly. After it has been spoken about the norm of judgment, now this also is asked. If those who err do not wish to be convinced, how are they to be restrained? For if they are not restrained, there will be no end to dissensions. Here it must be known that the outcome of judgments in the Church is different from the outcome in political judgments, just as the authority of those judging is also different. When political judges have pronounced on an ambiguous question, they ought to restrain the contumacious with arms, so that there may be an end to lawsuits and dissensions. Because in civil matters, since they are subject to reason, the magistrate has the authority to pronounce on an ambiguous question with probable reason, and God has armed them with this authority, so that He wills their interpretations to be valid and received. Controversies can therefore be entirely removed. But in the Church, judges do not have royal or praetorian power, nor ought they afterwards to restrain the condemned with arms. And when there is a great power and multitude of those who err, if they do not wish to be convinced, even if the true Church excommunicates them, nevertheless discord remains, just as even if the Apostles condemned the synagogue, nevertheless the discord was not extinguished until God Himself was the executor of the Apostles' sentence and destroyed the synagogue. And for the most part, great dissensions in the Church have been resolved in this way, not by human strength. Let us add this also concerning synods. When we speak of judgments in the Church, it must always be considered which assemblies are truly the Church of God. We by no means make judges of doctrine the assembly of those who are openly enemies of the doctrine of the Gospel, just as the synagogue, which had condemned Christ and afterwards the Apostles and Stephen, was neither the Church of God nor could it be a judge: so now their bishops, satellites, monks, and others, who are openly enemies of the Gospel and daily show by many prejudices that they had condemned the Gospel long before, can by no means be judges. Concerning all these, let the rule be held: If anyone teaches another Gospel, let him be anathema. The Apostle proposes this admonition and consolation; he does not want us to provoke the judgments of these people, but to avoid them as anathemas. And although many are moved by their titles and authority, nevertheless he proposes a most serious consolation to us when he names them anathemas. Let us not be moved by their thunderbolts, but let us know that it is written in Psalm 109: They will curse, and you will bless. But those things which have been said about judgments in the Church should be understood concerning churches sounding the voice of the Gospel, as Paul speaks about the Corinthian assembly. For controversies can arise even in such a Church, as in Acts chapter 15, where the pious mixed with hypocrites raise a question about ceremonies. Let it suffice to have said this much about synods, which rightly square with this commemoration of Paul, because here he in some way ordains such judgments.

Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others judge.

It is manifest from the narrative of Luke 4 and from the Acts that there was a most honorable order of speakers in public gatherings in the synagogues. Nor were there promiscuous clamors of the mob, such as there were in Rome during the tribunician suffrages, nor was it a tyranny: but the elders spoke their opinions in their place, and if anyone wished to add something modestly, it was granted, according to the rule: Do not extinguish the spirit, test all things, hold fast to what is good. And the judgment was in the hands of the Church concerning the opinions of individuals, which, when it approved someone's interpretation, another did not shout down, nor did he stir up a contest. Therefore he says here: If it has been revealed to one sitting, let the first be silent.

And so that tyranny may be prohibited, he says expressly: You can all interpret, with order preserved by each. This saying contains a very useful consolation concerning vocation. It is manifest that those who are in the ministry, in temples and in schools, ought, because of the very place to which they have been called, to state their opinions, nor can that saying be objected to them: They were running, and I did not send them.

But why do others write or teach who have not been called to a public place? If these write or teach true things, they have here an express concession: you can all interpret. And there exists a common precept Col. 3: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom, and teach and admonish one another. It is absolutely a command to all that they should learn, and for the sake of learning, a comparison of opinions in teaching, hearing, and disputing is necessary, just as he says here: Teach and admonish one another. Likewise, parents and teachers have an express command, as in Deuteronomy 11: Teach your children, that they may meditate upon them. And Psalm 77: And he established testimonies in Jacob, and set a law in Israel, which he commanded our fathers, that they should make them known to their children. And Ephesians 6: Bring up your children in the discipline and instruction of the Lord. Parents and teachers therefore have their own calling, and are compelled by divine command to teach. And when parents and teachers neglect this part of their duty, they sin gravely, and offend God. Let them fortify themselves with this thought, when it is objected to them: They ran, and I did not send them. Nay, parents and teachers are sent and called, so that in their own place they may rightly teach the doctrine concerning God. And let them not meanwhile disturb the calling of others.

Furthermore, a general command is given to all, that each individual should show their confession, which those who rightly teach and write do more clearly than others. And let the sayings concerning confession be in sight, Matthew 10: Everyone who will confess me before men, I also will confess him before my heavenly Father. And this command concerning confession compels the pious in the assembly, of which Paul speaks, to state their opinion when they hear others err in interpretation. But Paul wishes all things to be done in order, and peacefully, not with seditious and turbulent clamors. Therefore it follows: God is not the author of ἀκαταστασίας (confusion), but of peace.

Moreover, it pertains to good order that when some in the Church recite their interpretations, the elders and the more learned should hear them, and be judges, and show what they approve and what they reject. Therefore he says here: Let the others judge. And at the end of the first Epistle to the Thessalonians it is said: Prove all things, hold fast that which is good. God wishes there to be judges in the Church of the controversies which are stirred up from time to time. And it was said above whose duty it is primarily to convene the others, and to hear the learned teachers who fear God. The example of that matter is to be followed which is proposed in the Acts, where it is written in chapter 15: The Apostles and elders were gathered together to consider this matter. Thus also in this Church and Academy we have often settled controversies, whether they arose here or elsewhere. Thus the Church of Antioch condemned the impious dogma of Samosatenus, although the author was a Bishop. Thus the Alexandrian Church refuted Meletius, who denied that those who had lapsed after baptism should be received, and it likewise refuted Arius. And ancient examples are read everywhere. Nor are recent ones lacking to this age. For wherever the true Church of God is, there are some who judge rightly, of whom it is written, 1 John 2: The anointing teaches you concerning all things, and it is true, and is no lie. The sentiment of the foundation remains uncorrupted in some, from which it is possible to judge rightly concerning necessary matters. The rest concerning synods and judgments has been said above.

And let this admonition of Paul be the more known and acceptable to all, because although the mention is brief, yet it shows that there ought to be judgments in the Church, and it prohibits both: tyranny and the seditious clamors of the mob. And it establishes a form similar to an Aristocracy. He wishes many who are learned and fear God to be heard. You can, he says, all speak your opinions in order. He also prohibits contumacy, when he says: If it be revealed to one sitting by, let the first be silent. After it was pronounced by the most upright judgment of the Apostles that the Mosaic rites were to be omitted, the others ought to have obeyed this opinion. And many did obey, but yet certain others, being stubborn, retained their opinion, just as for a long time afterwards many retained the Mosaic rites.

Paul also refutes the objection of the fanatical spirits, saying: The spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets. As if he were to say: There are some who boast of zeal, and singular divine raptures, or ἐμφωτισμοὺς (illuminations), just as Marcion and many Anabaptists have boasted. These shout that they are divinely impelled to contradict. But let pious judges discern the spirits; if they contradict a certain sentiment of the Gospel, it is most manifest that they are fanatics and liars, and that those who shout that they cannot be silent are either lying, or are being violently impelled by devils, just as the inspired prophetesses used to prophesy at Delphi. And it is useful to consider this distinction between good spirits and fanatics, such as the pagan seers also were. Fanatics and Pagans do not understand their own prophecies, and they utter them while being violently impelled by the devil or inspired in such a way that they cannot be silent. Often also they pour forth only ambiguities, as Virgil says in the 6th Aeneid:

He rages, if the prophet can shake off the great God from his breast, so much the more does he weary his rabid mouth, taming his wild heart. And again: He sings horrendous riddles, and bellows in the cave, wrapping truth in obscurities. For just as the devils sometimes utter sounds and oracles through statues, so they scatter predictions through their prophets, which the prophets themselves neither understand nor can keep silent, as was said through the statue to the Spartan leader Pausanias: Go near to justice, for pride is a great evil to men. And in Hesse before the war, a dog uttered several continuous words. Histories are full of such examples.

But the Prophets in the Church, teaching or explaining the articles of faith, who are governed by the light of the Holy Spirit, understand their own words, and do not pour them out under compulsion, such that they cannot restrain themselves. And when they hear better things, they yield. Certainly, they do not stubbornly resist the truth.

We have heard, however, the Anabaptists themselves, even when they were refuted, yet rabidly crying out against the truth concerning original sin, the dignity of the political order, and similar manifest matters, so that the evidence of the truth might show that they are agitated by devils. It is profitable to consider such examples, so that spirits may be discerned, as in 1

John

4 it is said: Test the spirits, whether they are from God.

Let your women keep silence in the churches.

This passage is not obscure.

For it is known among all nations, whose government was not entirely barbaric, that the duties of men and women were distinct, and that men ruled wars and political affairs in public assemblies of the people, just as Homer says of both: War shall be the concern of men. And speech shall be the concern of men. Women, however, were to manage domestic economic affairs at home, and were not accustomed to preach in the public assemblies of men.

This honorable custom Paul wishes to be preserved also in the Church, and he wishes it to be done in public government in accordance with the law of God, and with true human judgments according to right reason.

He does not want barbaric confusions to occur in the Church; he does not want a Semiramis or a Zenobia to become Bishops. For although there are many holy and wise matrons, yet these public offices do not befit this sex, and the example is dangerous.

Paul finally flares up, looking at those ineptitudes of the Corinthians, in which he saw signs of Greek vanity, curiosity, ostentation, and garrulity. The men competed in ostentation, when some would compose and recite hymns in one language, others in another: The women, out of curiosity, also wanted to recite hymns or dispute in public. Paul therefore grieved that so much foolishness and ineptitude remained among the saints, and he adds a harsh rebuke.

You indulge yourselves too much, O Greeks; you think the doctrine of the Gospel and these gifts of God were brought from heaven so that you might show off your talents with these materials, and transfer them to games, spectacles, and comedies, just as you play with the Trojan history and the like. Far be this vanity from the Church.

Think rather how great these things are: the revelation of God, whom you previously did not know; what the justice and wrath of God is against your sins and those of others. Grieve that you have horribly irritated God with Epicurean furies or the invocation of idols, with lusts, and other crimes. Again, also consider what a plan it is that God delivers you through his Son from eternal punishments, that he shows his light to you, that he restores justice and eternal life. For these gifts, give thanks to him, celebrate him, and show your gratitude by true obedience.

Let consolations, invocations, and thanksgivings be mixed with true sorrows. Let not secure minds play with the ostentation of gifts, as if you had received reeds, like Hesiod from the Muses, or flutes, like Marsyas from Pallas. Remove these games from the Church, which nevertheless will be introduced into it some time later.

The learned will compete in disputations, they will show off their talents, they will most audaciously give birth to new dogmas, they will establish empires under the pretext of ministry, they will compete with ambition, avarice, hatreds, and the desire for vengeance. From these evils, wars, dissipations of the human race, and devastations will arise. Suppress the beginnings of such great evils now.

Let us now, in this old age of the world, consider from what beginnings greater evils have followed later, and let us grieve that, always in the Church, even when times are happier, there is still much weakness, and let us pray to the Son of God that he may heal public and private diseases, and preserve the remnants of his Church.

But let all things be done decently and in order. At the end, he adds a general rule: Let all things be done with decorum and in order, that is, let all actions conform to the law of God and to natural judgment. so that gatherings may be honorable and increase reverence for religion. Here it is disputed concerning rites in the Church, concerning the order of days and readings, and concerning other exercises, whether they are worship, whether they are necessary things, or whether they are to be observed for the sake of order only, without snares for the conscience. This dispute, since it has been sufficiently explained elsewhere, I omit.

Latin:

Caput XIV.

Διώκετε τὴν ἀγάπην, ζηλοῦτε δὲ τὰ πνευ- ματικά.

Dictum est supra, considerandum esse dis- crimen inter necessaria singulis, et inter alia dona, quae etiamsi prosunt Ecclesiae, tamen non dantur omnibus, ut dona Ioseph et Danielis sunt excellentia, et universae Ecclesiae prosunt, et sunt illustria testimonia de praesentia Dei in Ec- clesia. Sed tamen non omnibus tanta ornamenta tribuuntur. Id discrimen hic indicat, cum ait: Sectamini dilectionem, id est, haec talis est, quam expetere et possidere vos singulos oportet. Sed dona spiritus admiramini, magnifacite, et agnoscite beneficia Dei esse, et doctrinae testimo- nia, et Deo pro hac patefactione gratias agite. Et sicut ad Ephes. 4. dicitur: Dat alios Prophe- tas, alios Apostolos, scitote non similia esse mi- nisteria et dona singulorum. Ideo de his usus est verbo ζηλοῦτε, id est, admiramini ea et ma- gnifacite, et suo loco quisque suo ministerio fun- gatur, et suo dono serviat Ecclesiae. Conside- randa est autem Pauli prudentia. Corinthii stu- dio donorum fiebant insolentiores, et negligebant dilectionem. Nunc cum audiant anteferri dile- ctionem, ne studium et exercitia donorum negli- gant, tribuit utrique generi locum convenientem.

Respondeo: Maior vera esset, si iusti esse- mus impletione legis. Sed quia lege non sumus iusti, et in promissione ostenditur alia iusticia, scilicet quod propter filium Dei iusti simus, im- putata nobis ipsius iusticia: nominatur fides, quae adprehendit mediatorem, sive haec virtus sit maior, sive minor dilectione, id ad rem non per- tinet. Non enim sumus iusti propter nostras qua- litates, sed propter filium Dei. Et tamen verum est, quod cum fide apprehenditur filius Dei, corda vivificantur, et filius Dei vere in nobis efficax est, et accendit Spiritu sancto novam lucem, dilectio- nem et caeteras virtutes, quae sunt incoata im- pletio legis. Et tamen quia adhuc in hac misera natura sunt reliquiae peccati, persona est iusta, id est, accepta Deo propter mediatorem pro no- bis interpellantem apud aeternum patrem, et im- putata nobis iusticia mediatoris, non est iusta propter propriam dignitatem. Recte igitur de utroque dicimus, de renovatione et de imputa- tione: Necesse est fieri renovationem. Et filius Dei est in nobis, et ex efficax. Et tamen haec consolatio omnibus necessaria est, quod propter ipsum filium Dei certo placeamus Deo, fide, non propter dignitatem nostram. Qui hos fontes huius doctrinae considerant, possunt et dictum

Deinde omissis caeteris, loquitur de eo loco, cuius praecipuus usus est in docendo.

Μᾶλλον δὲ ἵνα προφητεύητε.

Certum est phrophetiam in hoc capite signi- ficare sententiae alicuius lectae seu recitatae enar- rationem, ut Lutherus enarrans Paulum ad Ro- manos aut ad Galatas, prophetiae dono utitur. Lingua loqui, est diversas linguas posse so- nare. Id miraculum cum ostentarent aliqui in publica congregatione, quia ut alioqui Graeci homines amarunt eloquentiam, ita magis delecta- bantur cognitione multarum linguarum, quam caeterae gentes et hoc studium amabant, et tan- quam laudes seu precationes diversis linguis reci- tabant: Paulus retrahit eos ad studium enarratio- nis. Et praesertim in publica congregatione tan- tum sonare diversas linguas, sine enarratione, nulla utilitas erat. Vult autem Paulus dicentes in publico coetu non theatricam ostentationem instituere, ut apud Ethnicos fuit usitatum reci- tare Poëmata aut Panegyricos in spectaculis: sed servire utilitati discentium, et accendi pios affe- ctus et invocationem.

Et hic vetus mos considerandus est. Lecta aliqua sententia in libris Prophetarum in Syna- gogis, plures ordine de ea dicebant, ut Lucae 4. Dominus recitat sententiam ex Esaia, et in Actis cap. 13. Paulo datur locus dicendi. Nec tamen erant promiscui clamores, ut in vulgi suffraga- tionibus, sed dabatur locus dicendi ab eo, qui praeerat Synagogae, ut in Actis dicitur. Et hic discrimen est inter sedentes et reliquam multitu- dinem, ut de iudiciis dictum est: Considere duces, ut vulgi stante corrona. Ita Paulus hic plures ordine sine tumultu iubet dicere, et enarrare lectas sententias.

Λαλεῖ οἰκοδομὴν καὶ παράκλησιν καὶ παρα- μυθίαν.

Commoratur in instituta admonitione. Lo- quens lingua, id est, dicens laudes, gratiarum actionem seu precationem variis linguis, aut pe- regrina lingua, non hominibus loquitur, id est, non docet populum. Sed spiritu, id est, dono spirituali, quo cordis affectibus accensus est, lo- quitur bona quidem, sed tamen non intellecta cae- teris. Sed prophetans, id est, enarrans, loqui- tur ea, quae praesunt ad aedificationem, adhor- tationem et consolationem.

Usitatum est Paulo, genera concionum par- tiri in has tres species, quae sunt praecipuae. Prima species est διδασκαλικὴ. Oportet enim initio doctrinam de articulis fidei et de distin- ctione Legis et Evangelii, et aliis membris do- ctrinae principalibus tradere.

Alia species est adhortatio ad poenitentiam et ad bona opera, quae et obiurgationem comple- ctitur, et similis est suasoriis materiis in Rhe- toricis.

Tertia species est consolatio, quae praecipue sumitur ex Evangelio, quia fundamentum in omni vera et efficaci consolatione est, agnitio remissio- nis peccatorum, et reconciliationis cum Deo pro- pter filium, ut supra de consolationibus di- ctum est.

Eodem modo Paulus distribuit genera doctri- narum in priore Epistola ad Timoth. 4.: Assi- duus esto in lectione, consolatione et doctrina. Hoc dictum prorsus congruit cum his verbis, quae recitantur in hac Epistola ad Corinthios, et sa- pienter docet, quae sint praecipua genera con- cionum in Ecclesia, quod esse consilium in do- cendo oporteat, et ad quos fines referenda sit omnis oratio.

Primum fit mentio lectionis, ubi conside- randum est discrimen doctrinae in Ecclesia, et artium caeterarum. Non ordimur Arithmeticam aut alias philosophiae partes a lectione, sed affe- rimus ad artium descriptionem initia nobiscum nata, ut numerationem et alia, sed doctrina Ec- clesiae longe aliter discenda est. Ordiri necesse est a lectione. Quia cum articuli fidei de tribus personis divinitatis et de duabus naturis in re- demtore nato ex Maria virgine, de Ecclesia, de gratuita remissione peccatorum, de resurrectione mortuorum, et alii articuli Evangelii nequaquam natura noti sint: necesse est eos cognosci tantum ex patefactione divina, quam Deus immensa bo- nitate post primos parentes literis mandari voluit per Prophetas, ac deinde per Apostolos. Ideo nos primum ad lectionem deducit, id est, vult in Ecclesia legi libros propheticos et apostolicos, quos vult esse fontes doctrinae, et normam, ne recipiantur ullae opiniones ab hac norma dissen- tientes, sicut ipse dicit: Si quis aliud Evange- lium docet, anathema sit. Itaque sit hoc pri- mum concionatoris munus, ut libros propheticos et apostolicos populi legat, et legi curet, et mo- neat regulam doctrinae in his contineri. Secundum officium concionatoris est Docere. Est autem una simplex via docendi, in lectione genus sermonis enarrare, et deinde monstrare or- dinem rerum, quae proponuntur, et membra di- stinguere, et via quadam artium addere defini- tiones et collationes. Ut in principio libri Moysi necesse est monere lectorem, ubi de Creatione, ubi de Lapsu primorum parentum dicatur.

Postea discerni oportet iusticiam et pecca- tum, deinde legem et promissionem. Denique sani omnes intelligunt, in docendo adhiberi opor- tere Gramaticen, Numerationem, Dialecticen, et aliarum artium adminicula. Necesse est articu- los fidei ordine populo proponi, discerni Legem et Evangelium, peccatum et redemtorem, iusti- ciam philosophicam et aliam iusticiam, quae aut propter filium nobis imputatur, aut in nobis restituitur.

Discerni oportet Ecclesiam et Imperia, Ve- tus et Novum Testamentum, leges divinas et hu- manas, aeternas poenas et aeterna praemia.

Harum rerum enarrationem in Corinthiis nominat Paulus Aedificationem. Et intelligat concionator, quae materiae sint principales ac ne- cessariae ad aedificationem, id est, ad confirman- dam fidem in omnibus articulis. Has repetat, omissis peregrinis disputationibus, sicut iubet ad Timotheum eligi utilia ad aedificationem. Perti- nent autem haec duo genera lectio et doctrinae explicatio ad genus didascalicon.

Tertium genus est Consolatio. Non est finis doctrinae in Ecclesia tantum scientia, nec tan- tum actiones nostrae, sed Deus se patefecit et Evangelium tradidit, ut liberet nos à peccato et aeterna morte, et finis est, ut abolito peccato et morte, fruentes communicatione sapientiae, iusti- ciae et laetitiae Dei, in omni aeternitate apud eum vivamus, et vicissim eum celebremus. Est igitur genus extremum consolatio.

Postquam igitur concionator proposuit lectio- nem et doctrinam, ostendat quomodo applicanda sit ad consolationem, et ad hunc effectum postre- mo orationem referat. Et gradus hic conside- rentur.

Primum erigenda est fides, id est, fiducia misericordiae, qua cum in Deo acquiescimus, se- quitur pax et gaudium, ut scriptum est: Iustifi- cati fide pacem habemus. Et proximi gradus sunt Invocatio, Spes et Gratiarum actio. Scimus enim invocationem nequaquam irritam esse. Leniun- tur ergo dolores spe mitigationis calamitatum, aut liberationis, quam petimus et expectamus. Et gratiarum actio accenditur, cum ordine beneficia Dei utcunque agnoscimus. Primum remissionem peccatorum, deinde auxilium, et praesentiam filii Dei nos sustentantis, postea mitigationem cala- mitatum vel liberationem.

Mox repetit eadem genera concionum: Si reversus ad vos tantum variis linguis sonarem meas precationes aut hymnos, quid prodessem vobis, nisi et concio accederet ex revelatione, vel scientia, vel prophetia, vel doctrina?

Nominat doctrinam lectionem, et dogma- tum recitationem, ut supra dictum est. Prophe- tiam enarrationem et lectionis et dogmatum. Et haec duo membra partim ad genus didascalicon, partim ad alterum genus pertinent, quod nuncu- pavit consolationem. Scientia est admonitio de moribus et de externa gubernatione, ut supra ca- pite duodecimo dictum est, ut de electione et de potestate ministrorum Evangelii, de legum dis- crimine, quae sint abolitae, quae sint perpetuae, de usu libertatis, de iudiciis Ecclesiae, de con- iugio, de usu rerum politicarum, et similibus negotiis.

Revelationem vero nominat singularia testi- monia doctrinae ipsi exhibita, sicut ad Galat. in- quit: Non ab homine accepi Evangelium, nec me quisquam hominum docuit, sed accepi revelante Iesu Christo. Pertinent huc et praedictiones, sicut de postremis Ecclesiae temporibus vaticina- tur ad Thessalonicenses et ad Timoth. Item iu- dicia de fanaticis doctoribus, quales tunc quoque multi vagabuntur, et iactitabant suas quasdam illuminationes, ac variis praestigiis fallebant et turbabant Ecclesias, ut in Actis capite 13. In Cypro Elymam punit coecitate, et narrat ad Ti- motheum, se Hymenaeum et Alexandrum tra- didisse Satanae, ut desinerent spargere blas- phemias.

Vidimus et nostro tempore multo ante sedi- tionem rusticanam fanaticum hominem Nicolaum Stork, natum Cygneae, vagari in his religioni- bus, qui narrabat, saepe angelos visibili specie secum locutos esse, et ipsi praedixisse, fore eum ducem instaurationis Ecclesiarum. Loquebatur autem de cultibus more enthusiastarum, dicebat iusticiam esse in cordibus novam et coelestem lucem, et novos motus seu afflatus. Nec recte de fide et consolatione in veris pavoribus loquebatur, in quibus corda se sustentant imputatione iusti- ciae filii Dei. Exaggerans vero illos enthusias- mos, extenuabat usum Sacramentorum, et tradi- tiones humanas prorsus reiiciebat, nec paucos admiratio rerum sublimium et ignotarum move- bat, ut eius sententias amplecterentur, quorum multos nominare possemus. Fuit autem inter praecipuos eius admiratores Thomas Monetarius, qui postea seditionis in Thuringia autor et dux fuit, qua seditione oppressa Monetarius supplicio affectus est, in quo valde fracto animo fuisse eum narrant. Nec multo post eius Magister Nicolaus Stork fugitivus in Xenodochio Monachensi, in Bavaria mortuus est. Ita eventus refutavit ho- rum furores. Sed multo ante Lutherus illam ipsam factionem coram et publicis scriptis dam- naverat. Tales praestigiae diaboli non iudicari possunt sine singulari dono Dei. Quare et talia iudicia nomine revelationis hic complectimur.

Ὅμως τὰ ἄψυχα φωνὴν διδόντα.

Multis similitudinibus ostendit, non pro- desse in coetu peregrinis linguis recitare preces aut lectiones sine enarratione. Ut nihil prodest tuba edere sonos non intellectos militibus.

Non sunt obscurae hae similitudines, ideo non addo declarationem. Sed lector admonen- dus est, ut hanc sententiam saepe repetitam in- figat pectori: Magnifacite dona, ut ad aedificatio- nem Ecclesiae sitis locupletiores et instructiores. Item: Omnia ad aedificationem Ecclesiae fiant. Hoc praeceptum in docendo sequamur, non osten- temus ingenia subtilitate disputationum de rebus non necessariis. Non captemus plausus et studia principum aut multitudinis, blandientis aut per- versis eorum iudiciis, aut pravis cupiditatibus, sed regantur mentes et oratio hac regula: Omnia fiant ad aedificationem, id est, eligantur materiae necessariae, recte enarrentur articuli fidei, recte proponatur integrum doctrinae corpus. Et post- quam doctrina recitata est, semper ad hos fines referatur concio, ut in auditoribus excitentur ti- mor Dei, ac deinde fides, erigens perterrefactas mentes et accendens invocationem et gratiarum actionem. Has metas in concionando semper intueamur.

Ἐὰν γὰρ προσεύχομαι γλώσσῃ, τὸ πνεῦμα μου προσεύχεται.

Commoratur in instituta collatione. Etsi pium opus est, precationem dicere quacunque lingua, tamen utilitati Ecclesiae etiam servien- dum est, et addenda enarratio. Cum lingua peregrina recito precationem, spiritus meus orat, id est, affectus dono spirituali accensus. Loqui- tur enim non de simulatis lectionibus aut cantile- nis, quales nunc sonant conducticii hypocritae in templis, sed de seria precatione piorum. Sed mens mea sine fructu est, id est, mens, quae in hac pia meditatione cogitavit bonas sententias, quarum cognitio prodesset aliis, non impertit eas coetui.

Inquit igitur se et spiritu precationem seu Psalmum recitaturum esse, et mente, id est, se si ita sit occasio, variis linguis precationem seu hymnum compositurum esse, sed tamen additu- rum enarrationem utilem reliquo coetui.

Illustrat argumentum, quod instituit, ab inutili. Si publicam precationem dicas lingua peregrina, quomodo possunt auditores in fine usitatam clausulam addere, qua signisans se eadem petere, et coniuncta esse vota universae Ecclesiae, videlicet, cum dicitur usitato more Amen, qua voce et Moysi tempore hoc modo usam esse Ecclesiam, cum populus respondens testabatur se eadem petere, apparet ex capite 27. Deutero., ubi saepe repetita sunt haec verba: Et dicat omnis populus, Amen. Id Graecus vertit καὶ ἐροῦσι πᾶς ὁ λαὸς: γένοιτο. Grammaticis enim est, Verum, id est, ratum et firmum sit, eveniat quod petimus, nec existimamus haec nostra vota inane murmur esse, ut Ethnici vociferantur quidem ad Deum, sed dubitant quid invocent: item an ulla numina respiciant homines, an ipso- rum gemitus et lacrimas audiant et curent. In his dubitationibus eorum clamores irriti dissipan- tur in auras, et prorsus sunt, ut Seneca inquit: Rumores vacui, verbaque inania, Et par solicito fabula somnio.

Huic ethnicae opinioni opposita est confes- sio Ecclesiae, cum ait Amen. Quia est asseve- ratio, quasi dicat: Vera et rata sint haec vota, et esse rata credimus. Scimus eum velle hac fide coli et invocari, qua credimus propter mediato- rem vere nostros gemitus respici, et nostras pre- ces exaudiri, et certo impetrare vel liberationes vel mitigationes. Haec de vocabulo satis sit hic monere. Nam doctrina integra de precatione alibi traditur, et familiarissime notam esse omnibus oportet, ut in quotidiana invocatione sit in conspectu, et sem- per addas ipse hanc tuam asseverationem finita precatione: Credo Domine, haec mea vota pro- pter filium mediatorem a te recipi, sed opem fer meae imbecillitati. Scio de velle hunc honorem tibi tribui, ut credamus te vere affici cura nostri, et nos exaudiri, nec promissiones tuas inanes sonos esse. In hoc nostro exercitio discimus, quare antiquitas semper addiderit precationibus, Amen.
