Ac vide morem Ecclesiae perpetuum: Sem- per fuit unus aliquis in coetu, qui sua voce reve- renter recitavit publicam precationem. Postea vel populus, vel unus nomine populi respondit Amen. Quid opus est, dicat aliquis? Respon- deo: Vult Deus consensum esse Ecclesiae in do- ctrina, fide, invocatione et petitione: vult et pu- blicos ac honestos congressus fieri, et in his vult consentientibus piorum pectoribus invocari, iuxta promissionem Matthaei 18.: Si duo ex vobis con- senserint in terra, de omni negotio quod petent, fiet eis. Ideo servatus est hic mos, ut populus adderet hanc significationem sui consensus. Et Paulus vult eam addi. Ait igitur de respondente: Quomodo implens locum idiotae, dicet Amen, si te non intelliget? ἀναπληρῶν τόπον τοῦ ἰδιώ- του, dicitur respondens, quasi precationem ab alio recitatam, postea complens expresso consensu populi. Ad hunc ipsum morem et multa alia dicta congruunt, ut Psalmo 117. prius nominat domum Aaron, et hanc iubet gratias agere et celebrare Deum: dicat nunc domus Aaron, bo- nus est Dominus, et in seculum misericordia eius. Sit sacerdos ἔξαρχος publicae precationis, et quasi praeeat populo sua voce. Postea igitur ad- ditum est: Dicant nunc omnes qui timent Do- minum, bonus est Dominus, et in seculum mi- sericordia eius.

Fratres, ne pueri fiatis mente, sed sitis infan- tes malitia, integri vero sitis mente.

Inserit generalem admonitionem, ut recte iudicent de usu donorum. Non inanis specta- culi causa dona exhibita sunt, sicut videntur illi cogitare, qui tantum ostentant donum linguarum recitando hymnum peregrina lingua, quem coe- tus non intelligit. Haec admonitio late patet.

Sacrificia in Israël instituta erant ad certos usus. At sacerdotes transtulerunt ea ad pompam aut quaestum. Coena Domini ad usum certum, videlicet ad consolationem conscientiarum instituta est. Postea horribiliter prophanata est, et in magna parte generis humani celebratur ut spectaculum, aut quaestus causa. Certarunt Ecclesiae de die Paschatos, et saepe de aliis non necessariis quaestionibus. De hoc toto genere monet Paulus, ut non velut pueri spectaculis et ritibus capiamur, sed sapienter regamus actiones, et causas intueamur, et suum cuique locum tribuamus. Et regulam hic saepe repetit: Omnia ad aedificationem fiant. Cogitate quare donum linguarum attributum sit Ecclesiae, non ut inane spectaculum, sed ut prosit iis locis, ubi peregrinae linguae usus necessarius est. Sed in vestra Ecclesia recitetur lectio lingua intellecta populo, et enarratio utilis audientibus proponatur de aliqua doctrinae parte.

Ἐν νόμῳ γέγραπται, ὅτι ἐν ἑτερογλώσσοις.

Causae tres sunt, propter quas donum linguarum Ecclesiae attributum est. Prima et principalis, ut propagari Evangelium cito in multis gentibus posset, quarum non est una lingua.

Secunda, ut hoc ipsum donum esset testimonium Spiritus sancti, et praesentiae Dei in Ecclesia, sicut alia magna miracula.

Tertia, ut esse signum et testimonium, caeteras gentes etiam ad Evangelii societatem vocandas esse.

Haec significat Esaias capite 28., unde haec verba citantur. Etsi autem sententiae variae quaeruntur apud Esaiam, tamen haud dubie et hanc complectitur quam recitat Paulus, fore, ut Evangelium spargatur in multas gentes diversis linguis, quod displiciturum sit huic populo, et populum tunc poenas daturum esse contemtae vocis divinae. Esaias longa narratione taxat coecitatem Ecclesiae fascinatae falsis opinionibus et traditionibus. Omnes mensae repletae sunt vomitu, id est, fere ubique ebria et delira est Ecclesia magnis erroribus, et post reditum ex Babylone Pharisaei et Saducaei exorti sunt, quorum furores etiam accusat Esaias. Ita post Apostolos in Ecclesia grassatae sunt haereses, deinde Pontificum, Monachorum, et Sophistarum traditiones, de sacrificio Missae, de adoratione panis, de invocatione mortuorum, de dubitatione, de iusticia operum, de coelibatu, et aliis stultis cere- moniis, extincta luce Evangelii.

Post hanc reprehensionem addit Esaias an- tithesin: Quem docebit scientiam? ablactatos a lacte, avulsos ab uberibus, id est, castigatos et non ebrios voluptatibus et opinionibus, quas peperit haec coeca natura, et quas didicerunt inter Pharisaeos a pueritia, sicut in eodem capite mox inquit: Vexatio dat intellectum.

Postea sequitur Mimesis, quae recitat eorum traditiones: Manda remanda, expecta re expecta, modicum ibi, quasi dicat: Ipsi mandata et glos- sas cumulant. Sed hae glossae erunt eis exitio. Addit igitur: Me derident suis vel traditionibus vel ironiis. Ego vicissim loquar eis lingua, quae displicebit, seu derisoria, et vocabo gentes ad societatem Ecclesiae diversis linguis, et delebo ipsorum politiam. Haec est simplicissima enar- ratio. In Hebraico legitur: Labiis subsannatoriis, et alia lingua loquetur ad hunc populum. Ubi antithesis consideretur, quasi dicat: Nunc ipsi meum verbum derident, et mea lingua ipsis pe- regrina est seu barbara: Ego vicissim loquar eis lingua vere peregrina, quae tunc eis ingrata erit, colligam gentes ad societatem Ecclesiae deleta hac politia.

Ex hac simplici recitatione manifestum est, Paulum recte citasse hoc dictum, et inde osten- dere donum linguarum signum esse praedicationis Evangelii. In Graeca versione Esaiae legitur: διὰ φαυλισμὸν χειλέων, διὰ γλώσσης ἑτέρας, etc. Reddidit enim לעגֵי φαυλισμὸν, quod signi- ficat subsannationem. Deinde et altera vox ad- ditur in Ebraeo et in Graeco, videlicet alia lin- gua, quod convenit ad Pauli sententiam.

Ὡστε αἱ γλῶσσαι εἰς σημεῖον εἰσὶν, οὐ τοῖς πιστεύουσιν, ἀλλὰ τοῖς ἀπίστοις.

Dictum est supra, donum linguarum Eccle- siae attributum esse, ut Evangelium inter gentes propagari posset. Simul autem fuit testimonium praesentiae Dei, ut alia miracula. Hic igitur Paulus inquit, linguarum varietatem signum esse non credentibus, sed incredulis, videlicet, ut moti hoc miraculo, sicut caeteri invitentur ad Evangelium. Nec opus est longiore enarratione in hoc membro.

Postea prophetiam ait prodesse credentibus. Manifesta sententia est, Ait interpretationem toti coetui prodesse, in quo multi peregrinas linguas non intelligebant. Hi cum audiunt sua lingua enarrationem alicuius propheticae concionis de summa doctrinae, erudiuntur et exuscitantur ad timorem, fidem, spem, invocationem, gratiarum actionem, tolerantiam, et ad alias virtutes. Si- cut Paulus docet et confirmat credentes, citans et enarrans dictum ex Genesi: Credidit Abraham Deo, et imputatum est ei ad iusticiam. Et in Epistola ad Ebraeos erudiuntur credentes, enar- ratione dicti de saserdotio filii Dei: Tu es Sacer- dos in aeternum, etc. Huius testimonii explica- tio ostendebat causas, cur Sacerdotium Leviti- cum seu typicum post exhibitum Messiam desine- ret. Et docebat, quale sit sacerdotium filii Dei, quo vere placatur ira Dei adversus peccatum, et annunciatur remissio peccati, et abolentur pec- catum et mors, sicut ibi scriptum est: Una obla- tione consummavit in perpetuum eos, qui sancti- ficantur. Denique omnibus temporibus pii eru- diuntur et confirmantur talibus enarrationibus, quas hic nominat Prophetias. Hoc igitur donum in Ecclesia unius linguae magis vult exerceri, ubi si veniant in coetum ignari peregrinarum lin- guarum, et tantum audiant ibi peregrinos sonos, mirari possent, quid ageretur, cum illa recita- tio nullam populo utilitatem adferat, sicut in die Dionysii in Ecclesia Wirtzburgensi canuntur Graece cantilenae scriptae latinis literis, nec ipsis quidem canentibus intellectae. Hae pueri- les ineptiae nec gravitati Ecclesiae conveniunt, nec prosunt canentibus aut populo. Hoc exem- plum utcunque illustrat haec verba: Nonne di- cent vos insanire? Cur igitur antea dixit, pro- desse linguarum varietatem tanquam miraculum? Verum est, prodesse ut miraculum apud eos, ubi usus est peregrinarum linguarum. Sed hic lo- quitur de coetu unius linguae, in quo iam Ec- clesia collecta indiget assidua enarratione. In tali coetu ineptum est ostentare peregrinas lin- guas.

Εἰσέλθῃ δέ τις ἄπιστος ἢ ἰδιώτης, ἐλέγχεται ὑπὸ πάντων.

Dixi iam loqui Paulum de coetu unius lin- guae, in quo et infideli intelligenti linguam, et fideli prodest concio enarrantis praecipuos articu- los doctrinae in Ecclesia, ut consentaneum est saepissime hoc accidisse, ut homines modesti ex Ethnicis accesserint cum amicis ad conciones Ec- clesiae, uxores ethnicae cum maritis iam Evan- gelium profitentibus, aut fratres cum fratribus, filii cum parentibus. Horum aliqui cum audie- bant taxari idolorum cultus, et magnas tenebras Ethnicorum, certe flectebantur. Et sic paulatim collectam esse Ecclesiam manifestum est. Tali- bus nihil profuisset hymnus peregrina lingua compositus. In hanc sententiam hic Paulus in- quit: Si ingrediatur infidelis, ut cum ministri Cornelii Centurionis audiunt Petrum concionan- tem. Aut Idiota, id est, rudis, qui primum ce- pit Catechismi doctrinam audire: Tales, ait, argui et convinci ab omnibus, et occulta cordium pate- fieri, id est, audita doctrina, taxante ethnica vitia, Epicureas opiniones, aut cultus idolorum, libidines et alia scelera, et monstrante veri Dei patefactionem, converti eos ad Deum, et agno- scere Ecclesiam vere esse coetum Dei, et hanc doctrinam non esse commentitiam. Et summa laus Ecclesiae his brevissimis verbis describitur: Agnoscit et fatetur vere Deum inter vos esse, ἀπαγγέλλων, ὅτι ὁ θεὸς ὄντως ἐν ὑμῖν ἐστί. Hic retro cogitentur historiae de collectione Ec- clesiae. Hostes Evangelii male loquebantur de congressibus Christianorum, ut scribit Tertullia- nus, et alii. Adducti sunt amici credentium, ut spectatores essent, et narrarent, quid ibi age- retur. Horum multi cum et audirent optimam doctrinam, et honestissima exempla cernerent, movebantur, ut et ipsi Evangelium amplecte- rentur.

Et usitata sunt in Iustino Martyre, qui scri- bit ad Marcum Antoninum imperatorem, et in aliis argumenta quatuor, quibus refutant Eth- nicos, quae in conspectu habere singulos utilis- simum est.

Primum: Manifesta absurditas et manifestus furor est Ethnicorum, Epicureas opiniones am- plecti, aut probare cultus idolorum, et multos Deos, aut probare nefarias libidines. Haec vitia demonstrationibus naturalibus refutari possunt, quae saepe a piis cogitandae sunt, et refutatio multos Ethnicos movit, ut aliam doctrinam quae- rerent.

Secundum argumentum: Quod bonas men- tes valde confirmat, et quod Iustinus maxime ur- get, sumtum est ab antiquitate. Quia manife- stum est, historiam Ecclesiae antiquiorem esse omnium Ethnicorum historiis. Series temporum et imperiorum ostendit, Israëlitas et patres eorum ante monarchias fuisse, ante Assyriam, Persi- cam, Graecam et Romanam. Et multa vestigia apud gentes testimonia praebent antiquitati Eccle- siae. Graeci fatentur se ortos esse ab Iapeto, Persae ab Elam. Et similia multa sunt. Nec ulla in toto genere humano extant scripta, quae a rerum initiis continuam seriem annorum mon- strent, nisi sola historia Ecclesiae. Teneamus igitur regulam Tertulliani optimam: Primum quodque verissimum est.

Tertium argumentum: Miracula assidua, resuscitatio mortuorum et alia, quae nequaquam potest imitari diabolus. Ac recenseo inter mira- cula praedictiones de monarchiis, in Moyse, Esaia, Ieremia et Daniele. Id miraculum est illustre testimonium quocunque tempore post eventum. Cum viderent multi tempore Romani imperii talem fuisse successionem monarchiarum, qualem Prophetae praedixerant, fatebantur et hanc doctrinam a Deo traditam esse, et Deum regere tales imperiorum mutationes, et divinitus conservari genus humanum.

Idem argumentum nobis quoque propona- mus, ut firmissima assensione doctrinam Eccle- siae amplectamur.

Est et hoc miraculum assiduum, quod non deleri potest Ecclesia, cum omnibus seculis sum- mi reges, et antecellentes gloria et potentia, op- primere eam conati sint, ut Pharao, Nabugdo- nosor, Antiochus, Romani imperatores multi, postea Turci et alii. Est igitur perpetuitas Ec- clesiae inter tantos fluctus illustre testimonium, quod ostendit, conservari eam a Deo.

Quartum argumentum sumitur ab ipso ge- nere doctrinae. Nulla gens habet legem hone- stioremt et rectius convenientem iudicio naturali. Tota philosophia fatetur imperfectionem suam, quod videt in ratione lucere veras noticias, et tamen dissidium esse maximum virium humana- rum, id unde sit ignorat, nec remedia ostendere potest.

Videt absurda multa sequi, si animae non sint immortales: et tamen dubitat de immorta- litate.

Nequaquam potest affirmare philosophia, exaudiri etiam bonos, ut Palamedem aut Socra- tem, in calamitatibus.

Nulla gens extra Ecclesiam habet certam et expressam doctrinam de remissione peccatorum, de praesentia Dei apud vere invocantes, et de vita aeterna, et de modo, quo accipitur vita aeterna certo, cum nemo legi satisfaciat, et nemo sit sine peccato.

Cum haec quatuor argumenta simul coniun- guntur, movent homines non Cyclopicos. Et cum postea accedit sensus iudicii Dei in agnitione peccatorum, et consolatio ac vivificatio in corde, agnito filio Dei, in his motibus Spiritus sanctus trahit et confirmat corda, ut iam convinci se fa- teantur, et Evangelio assentiri firmius incipiant. Haec ita fiunt in omnibus, qui exercitia poeni- tentiae intelligunt, et de hac confirmatione loqui- tur Paulus, cum ait, 2. Corinth. 1.: Deus est autem, qui confirmat nos in Christum, qui et unxit et obsignavit nos, et dedit arrabonem spiri- tus in corda nostra. Et Roman. 8.: Spiritus dat testimonium spiritui nostro, quod simus filii Dei. Et 1. Iohan. 2.: Unctio docet vos de omnibus. Et Hebr. 11.: Fides nominatur ἔλεγχος, quod hoc modo, ut dixi, convincantur mentes; et firma fiat assentio. Ita et in hoc capite inquit Paulus: Ali- quos audita summa doctrinae in congressu Eccle- siae, et facta collatione ad ethnicos errores, trahi a Spiritu sancto, et flecti ad amplectendum Evan- gelium. Tales inquit fateri, quod vere Deus sit in Ecclesia, id est, sentiunt se a Deo trahi, ter- reri, et rursus erigi ac vivificari, et fatentur do- ctrinam veram esse, et amplectuntur eam.

Haec narratio ostendit, quomodo et collecta et aucta sit Ecclesia, cum veniebant Ethnici ad audiendam doctrinam. Et eodem modo colligi- tur Ecclesia omnibus temporibus.

Πάντα πρὸς οἰκοδομὴν γινέσθω.

Repetit praeceptum, quod et supra tradidit, ut considerent doctores, quid Ecclesiae prosit, videlicet, ad agnoscendam necessariam doctrinam de singulis articulis. Deinde ad flectendos animos ad poenitentiam, ad corrigendam profanam se- curitatem. Postea ad consolationem piorum, ad excitandam fidem, invocationem, spem et lae- titiam in Deo, ad ardens studium verae obedien- tiae. Haec et similia complectitur verbo aedifica- tionis, alludens ad extructionem aedificii.

Contra non aedificant, id est, non iuvant Ecclesiam recitationes non intellectae. Destruunt etiam tanquam aedificium curiosae quaestiones et labyrinthi, quae mentes implicant dubitationibus, et pariunt odium doctrinae, tanquam incertae et ambiguae.

Hic monet, ordinem servandum esse in docendo. Et simul iudices constituit, quod valde dignum est consideratione. Non vult in Ecclesia concedi licentiam spargendi quaslibet opiniones, sed vult iudicari doctrinam. Hic continetur ordo synodorum et iudiciorum de doctrina, de quibus haec quatuor consideranda sunt:

I. Quae personae sint iudices de doctrina in Ecclesia.

II. Quae sit norma, iuxta quam iudicandum est.

III. Quomodo iudicatum valeat.

IV. Quae sit executio.

De prima quaestione, aliud est loqui de norma, aliud de personis. De norma non dubium est, simpliciter normam esse capita doctrinae tradita in scriptis propheticis et apostolicis, et comprehensa in symbolis. Et haec norma est tanquam summus iudex. Sed quia iam de personis quaeritur, ut et Paulus de personis loquitur, et in hac vita in refutatione errorum, in congregatione, personas aliquas oportet sua voce et suo testimonio adversari errantibus. Ideo disputatio est, quae sint illae personae. Paulus inquit: Sedentes iudicent, id est, omnes auditores, non ut in seditione, sine ordine, sed suo quisque loco, ut postea inquit Paulus: Omnia fiant ordine. Item: Deus non est autor ἀκαταστασίας. Ita et Matth. 18. scriptum est: Dic Ecclesiae. Haec verba non intelliguntur de impio coetu, qui dominatur in Ecclesia titulis Episcoporum, et tamen est hostis vera doctrinae, sed de coetu, qui non falso tenet nomen Ecclesiae, quales erant coetus tunc a Paulo collecti. In hoc coetu ordine dicantur sententiae a docentibus et senioribus, sicut in Actis capite 15. dicitur: Congregati sunt Apostoli et seniores, ut considerarent hanc causam. Postea in condendo decreto, non soli Apostoli aut seniores sumunt sibi potestatem ὀλιγαρχικὴν, sed totius Ecclesiae consensus accedit, iuxta haec verba: Tunc visum est Apostolis et Presbyteris cum tota Ecclesia. Et postea rursus dicitur: Apostoli et Presbyteri et fratres. Non voluit Spiritus sanctus in Ecclesia tyrannicam aut oligarchicam potestatem constituere, sed audiri pios voluit etiam in gradibus inferioribus, sicut hic inquit Paulus: Potestis singuli dicere, ut omnes discant. Item: Si fuerit sedenti revela- tum, taceat prior. Item, 1. Thessalonicens. 5.: Spiritum ne extinguite, prophetias ne contem- nite. Omnia probate, quod bonum est, tenete. Hoc modo ad refutandum Samosatenum privato studio propter gloriam Dei convenerunt procul Gregorius Neocaesariensis et alii. Ac talia sem- per sunt verae Ecclesiae iudicia, quandocunque sunt Ecclesiae mediocriter restitutae, ut nos ad- hibitis aliis piis ac eruditis viris, hoc modo saepe Anabaptistas refutavimus ac damnavimus. De tali iudicio non tyrannico Basilius loquitur, in- quiens: Ἀλλά εἰσιν ἐπίσκοποι, κληθῶσι εἰς ἀκρόα- σιν. Ἐστὶ κλῆρος κατὰ πᾶσαν τοῦ θεοῦ παροι- κίαν, συναχθήτωσαν οἱ δοκιμώτατοι, λεγέτω μετὰ παῥῥησίας ὁ βουλόμενος, ἵνα ἔλεγχος ᾖ τὸ γιγνόμενον, καὶ μὴ λοιδορία.

Secunda quaestio est de norma, iuxta quam iudicandum est. Hic non dubium est normam esse ipsos libros propheticos et apostolicos et symbola, in quibus praecipui articuli propositi in libris propheticis et apostolicis breviter com- prehensi sunt. Et cum deliramentum aliquod pugnat cum perspicuo articulo tradito in libris propheticis aut apostolicis, aut symbolis, mani- festa est diiudicatio iuxta hanc regulam: Si quis aliud Evangelium docet, anathema sit, ut Mani- chai furores, item Pelagiani cum perspicuis arti- culis pugnabant.

Sed hic obiiciunt Sophistae, multa esse dicta obscura et ambigua in libris propheticis et aposto- licis. Quare vocem iudicis contendunt anteferen- dam esse libris propheticis et apostolicis. Hoc praetextu alii synodos, alii Papam anteferunt his libris, sicut in quolibet regno, cum in legibus deprehenditur obscuritas aut ambiguitas, antefer- tur vox regis explicans obscure vel ambigue di- ctum. Et in imperiis necesse est acquiescere in ea explicatione, alioqui nullus finis esset litium. Hoc exemplum politicum transferunt Sophistae ad iudicia Ecclesiae.

Sed respondendum est: De doctrina neces- saria, nulla est ambiguitas in libris propheticis et apostolicis et in symbolis, si sine cavillatione et dextre intelligantur, inspecta perpetua narratio- num serie, et secum consentientibus membris, ut in quacunque interpretatione fieri debet. Ideo 2. Corinth. 4. dicitur: Si velatum est Evangelium nostrum, in his qui pereunt, velatum est.

Item cum expresse praeceptum sit: Nihil ad- das, nihil detrahas, et in Numeris capite 15.:

Non sequantur cogitationes suas, sed sint memo- res praeceptorum Dei: Sequitur non esse ambi- guitatem, cui humano iudicio possit addi inter- pretatio.

Etsi autem de lege, et de promissionibus et de articulis necessariis, non est ambiguitas in scriptis propheticis et apostolicis, tamen quia in contentionibus etiam plane dicta diversis inter- pretationibus transformantur in plures sententias, prodest audire testimonia purioris Ecclesiae in aliquibus materiis, et ea conferre ad fontes, quae cum videmus magis congruere cum fontibus, mul- tum confirmamur et his ipsis testimoniis. Ut quanquam Samosatenus astute disputat in dicto Iohannis ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, non intelligi per- sonam nomine λόγος, tamen cum legimus Irenaei, Gregorii Neocaesariensis, et aliorum probatorum interpretum sententias, prosunt haec testimonia ad nos docendos et confirmandos. Ideo enim Deus ministerium in Ecclesia servat, ut Ephes. 4. scriptum est, Ne circumferamur variis doctrina- rum ventis, sed sint aliqui testes verae doctrinae sine ambiguitate. Et iussit audiri Ecclesiam do- ctricem et monitricem, sicut inquit Samson: Nisi arassetis mea vitula, non invenissetis. Et ad Pe- trum inquit: Et tu conversus confirma fratres tuos.

Audienda est igitur vera Ecclesia ut doctrix et monitrix, sed fides nitatur verbo Dei. Com- monefacti igitur ab Ecclesia conferamus testimo- nia eius ad fontes. Et grata confirmatio est bo- nae menti, scire se non discedere a consensu ve- rae Ecclesiae, et uno spiritu et una voce Deum invocare cum vera Ecclesia, sicut Psalmo 21. di- citur: In medio Ecclesiae laudabo te. Item, Psalmo 110.: Confitebor tibi Domine in concilio et congregatione iustorum. Et in fontibus ex tota narrationum serie unica et nativa sententia plerunque inveniri potest. Sic et nunc adiuva- mur in multis controversiis a veteri et sinceriori Ecclesia. Manifestum est in prima Ecclesia non fuisse privatas Missas. Hunc morem cum ad Pauli dicta conferimus, videmus eum congruere cum hoc dicto, 1. Corinth. 11.: Cum convenitis ad coenam Domini, expectate caeteros. De ba- ptismo infantum etiam Augustinus citat primae Ecclesiae consuetudinem. Et Origenes expresse inquit 6. capite ad Romanos. Itaque et Ecclesia ab Apostolis traditionem accepit, etiam parvulis dare baptismum. Et id magis congruit cum di- ctis in scriptura. Certum est promissiones ad parvulos, qui sunt in Ecclesia, pertinere, non ad alios extra Ecclesiam. Quare inserendi sunt Ecclesiae per baptismum. Sunt igitur normae iudicii scripta prophe- tica et apostolica et symbola. Et in aliquibus controversiis adiuvamur testimoniis verae Eccle- siae. Ac recte discernenda est vera Ecclesia ab indocta colluvie. Videnda etiam perpetua eru- ditorum sententia, non excerpenda sunt mutila dicta, et sophistice detorquenda contra perpetuam autorum sententiam. Nemo enim semper satis circumspecte, diserte et proprie loquitur. Postquam de norma iudicii dictum est, iam et hoc quaeritur. Si non convinci velint erran- tes, quomodo compescendi sint? Nam si non compescantur, non erit finis dissidiorum. Hic sciendum est, eventum iudiciorum in Ecclesia dissimilem esse eventui in iudiciis politi- cis, sicut et iudicantium autoritas dissimilis est. Cum iudices politici pronunciarunt in quae- stione ambigua, contumaces armis compescere debent, ut sit finis litium et dissidiorum. Quia in materiis civilibus cum sint subiectae rationi, ma- gistratus autoritatem habet probabili ratione pro- nunciandi de ambigua quaestione, et armavit Deus eos hac autoritate, ut eorum interpretatio- nes valere et recipi velit. Possunt igitur prorsus tolli controversiae. Sed in Ecclesia iudices non habent potesta- tem regiam seu praetoriam, nec postea armis com- pescere condemnatos debent. Et cum magna po- tentia et multitudo est errantium, si nolint con- vinci, etiamsi vera Ecclesia eos excommunicat, tamen haeret discordia, ut etiamsi Apostoli dam- nabant synagogam, tamen non extincta est dis- cordia, donec Deus ipse fuit executor sententiae Apostolorum, et synagogam delevit. Ac plerun- que hoc modo solutae sunt magnae dissensiones in Ecclesia, non humanis viribus. Addamus et hoc de synodis. Cum de iudi- ciis in Ecclesia loquimur, semper considerandum est, qui coetus vere sint Ecclesia Dei. Nequa- quam facimus iudices de doctrina coetum eorum, qui palam sunt hostes doctrinae Evangelii, ut synagoga, quae Christum et postea Apostolos et Stephanum damnaverat, nec Ecclesia Dei erat, nec iudex esse poterat: ita nunc iudices esse ne- quaquam poterunt Episcopi eorum satellites, mo- nachi, et alii, qui palam sunt hostes Evangelii, et multis praeiudiciis quotidie ostendunt, se multo ante damnasse Evangelium. De his omnibus re- gula teneatur: Si quis aliud Evangelium docet, anathema sit. Hanc admonitionem et consolatio- nem proponit Apostolus, non vult nos ad horum iudicia provocare, sed vitari eos tanquam ana- themata. Et quanquam titulis et autoritate eo- rum multi moventur: tamen gravissimam conso- lationem nobis proponit, cum eos nominat ana- themata. Non moveamur eorum fulminibus, sed sciamus in Psalm. 108. scriptum esse: Maledi- cent illi, et tu benedices. Sed ea, quae de iudi- ciis in Ecclesia dicta sunt, intelligantur de Ec- clesiis sonantibus vocem Evangelii, ut Paulus de coetu Corinthio loquitur. Possunt enim et in tali Ecclesia oriri controversiae, ut in Actis capite 15. movent quaestionem de ceremoniis pii admixti hypocritis. Haec de synodis iam dixisse satis sit, quae ad hanc Pauli commemorationem recte quadrant, quia hic aliquo modo iudicia talia ordinat.

Prophetae duo vel tres loquantur, et caeteri iudicent.

Manifestum est ex narratione Lucae 4 et ex Actis, fuisse honestissimum ordinem dicentium in publicis congressibus in synagogis. Nec pro- miscui clamores erant vulgi, quales fuerunt Ro- mae in suffragationibus tribunitiis, nec tyrannis erat: sed seniores suo loco dixerunt sententias, ac si quis modeste addere aliquid voluit, fuit con- cessum, iuxta regulam: Nolite extinguere spiri- tus, omnia probate, quod bonum est, tenete. Et iudicium erat penes Ecclesiam, de singulorum sententiis, quae cum probabat alicuius interpre- tationem, alius non obstrepebat, nec movebat certamen. Ideo hic inquit: Si fuerit sedenti re- velatum, taceat prior.

Et ut sit prohibita tyrannis, expresse inquit: Potestis omnes interpretari, servato per singulos ordine. Hoc dictum valde utilem consolationem continet de vocatione. Manifestum est, eos qui sunt in ministerio, in templis et in scholis, oportere propter locum ipsum, ad quem vocati sunt, di- cere sententias, nec his obiici dictum illud potest: Curabant, et non mittebam eos.

Sed cur alii scribunt aut docent, qui non sunt ad locum publicum vocati? Hi si vera scri- bunt aut docent, habent hic expressam concessio- nem, potestis omnes interpretari. Et extat com- mune praeceptum Colos. 3.: Sermo Christi habi- tet inter vos abunde in omni sapientia, et docete et commonefacite vos mutuo. Prorsus mandatum est omnibus ut discant, et ad discendum collatio sententiarum in docendo, audiendo et disputando necessaria est, sicut hic inquit: Docete et com- monefacite vos mutuo. Item, Parentes et pae- dagogi habent expressum mandatum, ut Deut: undecimo: Docete filios vestros, ut illa mediten- tur. Et Psalm. 77.: Et statuit testimonia in Ia- cob, et legem posuit in Israël, quam praecepit patribus nostris, ut notam faciant eam filiis suis. Et Ephes 6.: Educate filios in disciplina et do- ctrina Domini. Habent igitur parentes et pae- dagogi suam vocationem, et mandato divino co- guntur docere. Et cum hanc officii partem ne- gligunt parentes ac paedagogi, graviter peccant, et Deum offendunt. Hac se cogitatione muniant, cum eis obiicitur: Currebant, et non mittebam eos. Imo parentes et paedagogi missi et vocati sunt, ut suo loco doctrinam de Deo recte doceant. Nec interea turbent aliorum vocationem.

Praeterea generale mandatum est omnibus traditum, ut suam confessionem singuli osten- dant, quod magis perspicue faciunt hi, qui recte docent et scribunt, quam alii. Ac dicta de con- fessione sint in conspectu, Matth. 10.: Omnis qui confitebitur me coram hominibus, confitebor et ego eum coram patre coelesti. Et hoc manda- tum de confessione cogit pios in congressu, de quo Paulus loquitur, dicere sententiam, cum audiunt alios in interpretatione errare. Sed omnia vult Paulus fieri ordine, et placide, non seditio- sis et turbulentis clamoribus. Ideo sequitur: Deus non est autor ἀκαταστασίας, sed pacis.

Pertinet autem ad bonum ordinem hoc quo- que, ut cum aliqui in Ecclesia recitant suas inter- pretationes, audiant eas seniores et doctiores, et sint iudices, ostendant quid adprobent, et quid reiiciant. Ideo hic inquit: Caeteri iudicent. Et in fine prioris Epistolae ad Thessalonicenses di- citur: Omnia probate, quod bonum est, tenete. Vult Deus in Ecclesia iudices esse controversia- rum, quae subinde moventur. Et dictum est supra, quorum sit officium praecipuum convocare caeteros, et audire doctores eruditos, et timentes Deum. Eius rei exemplum sequendum est, quod in Actis proponitur, ubi scriptum est capite 15.: Congregati sunt Apostoli et seniores considerare hunc sermonem. Ita et in hac Ecclesia et Aca- demia saepe controversias diremimus, hic aut alibi ortas. Sic Ecclesia Antiochena damnavit impium dogma Samosateni, quanquam autor erat Episcopus. Sic Alexandrina Ecclesia refutavit Meletium, qui negabat lapsos post baptismum recipiendos esse, refutavit item Arium. Ac vetera exempla passim leguntur. Nec desunt huic aetati recentia. Ubicunque enim est vera Ecclesia Dei, ibi sunt aliqui recte iudicantes, de quibus scriptum est, 1. Iohan. 2.: Unctio vos docet de omnibus, et vera est, et non est mendacium. Manet in aliquibus fundamenti sententia incorrupta, ex quo de rebus necessariis recte iudicari potest. Caetera de synodis et iudiciis supra dicta sunt.

Et haec Pauli admonitio eo sit omnibus notior et gratior, quia quanquam commemoratio brevis est, tamen ostendit, oportere iudicia in Ecclesia esse, et prohibet utrunque: Tyrannidem, et seditiosos vulgi clamores. Ac formam similem Aristocratiae constituit. Vult audiri multos eruditos et timentes Deum. Potestis inquit ordine omnes dicere sententias. Prohibet et contumaciam, cum ait: Si fuerit sedenti revelatum, taceat prior. Postquam rectissimo iudicio Apostolorum pronunciatum est, omittendos esse ritus Mosaicos, huic sententiae caeteri obedire debebant. Et multi obtemperaverunt, sed tamen alii quidam pertinaces retinuerunt suam opinionem, ut longo tempore postea multi ritus Mosaicos retinuerunt.

Obiectionem etiam fanaticorum spirituum refutat Paulus inquiens: Spiritus Prophetarum Prophetis subditi sunt. Quasi dicat: Sunt quidam, qui iactant zelum, et singulares raptus divinos, seu ἐμφωτισμοὺς, sicut Marcion et multi Anabaptistae iactarunt. Hi vociferantur se divinitus impelli ad contradicendum. Sed pii iudices discernant spiritus, si contradicunt certae Evangelii sententiae, manifestissimum est fanaticos et mendaces esse, et vel mentiri illos, qui vociferantur, se non posse tacere, vel a diabolis violenter impelli, sicut afflatae fatidicae mulieres Delphis vaticinabantur. Estque utile conciderare hoc discrimen inter bonos spiritus et fanaticos, quales et ethnici vates fuerunt. Fanatici et Ethnici non intelligunt sua vaticinia, et sonant ea violenter impulsi a diabolo seu afflati ita, ut tacere non possint. Saepe etiam tantum ambigua fundunt, ut Virgilius inquit in 6. Aeneid.:

Bacchatur, vates magnum si pectore possit Excussisse Deum, tanto magis ille fatigat Os rabidum, fera corda domans. Et rursus: Horrendas canit ambages, antroque remugit Obscuris vera involvens. Sicut enim diaboli interdum per statuas edunt sonos et oracula, ita per suos vates spargunt praedictiones, quas nec intelligunt ipsi vates, nec reticere possunt, ut per statuam dictum fuit duci Spartano Pausaniae: Στεῖχε δίκης ἆσσον, μάλα τοι κακὸν ἀνδράσιν ὕβρις. Et in Hassia ante bellum Canis edidit aliquot continuata verba. Talium exemplorum historiae plenae sunt.

Sed Prophetae in Ecclesia docentes aut enarrantes articulos fidei, qui reguntur luce Spiritus sancti intelligunt sua dicta, et non fundunt ea coacti, sic, ut non possint se reprimere. Et cum audiunt meliora, cedunt. Certe non pertinaciter repugnant veritati.

Audivimus autem ipsi Anabaptistas etiam cum convincerentur, tamen rabiose reclamare veritati de peccato originis, de dignitate ordinis politici, et similibus manifestis rebus, ut evidentia veritatis ostenderet, eos agitari a diabolis. Talia exempla considerari prodest, ut spiritus discernantur, ut 1.

Iohan.

4. dicitur: Explorate spiritus, an ex Deo sint.

Αἱ γυναῖκες ὑμῶν ἐν ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις σιγάτωσαν.

Haec particula non est obscura.

Notum est enim apud omnes gentes, quarum gubernatio non prorsus barbarica fuit, distincta fuisse virorum et mulierum officia, et viros rexisse bella et politica negotia in publicis populi conventibus, sicut Homerus utrunque dicit: πόλεμος δ' ἀνδρεσσι μελήσει. Et λόγος δ' ἀνδρεσσι μελήσει. Mulieres vero domi oeconomica negotia curasse, et non solitas in publicis virorum conventibus concionari.

Hunc honestum morem vult Paulus et in Ecclesia servari, et vult in gubernatione publica fieri congruentia legi Dei, et veris iudiciis humanis secundum rectam rationem.

Non vult barbaricas confusiones in Ecclesia fieri, non vult Semiramidem aut Zenobiam fieri Episcopos. Etsi enim sunt multae sanctae et sapientes matronae, tamen haec publica officia non conveniunt huic sexui, et exemplum periculosum est.

Escandescit tandem Paulus intuens illas ineptias Corinthiorum, in quibus Graecae vanitatis, curiositatis, ostentationis et garrulitatis signa videbat. Viri ostentatione certabant, cum alii alia lingua componerent et recitarent hymnos: Mulieres curiositate, quae et ipse in publico recitare hymnos vel disputare volebant. Dolebat igitur Paulus in sanctis tantum stultitiae et ineptiarum manere, et addit asperam increpationem.

Nimium vobis indulgetis homines Graeci, putatis doctrinam Evangelii et haec dona Dei de coelo allata esse, ut his materiis ostentetis ingenia, et transferatis eas ad ludos, spectacula, comoedias, sicut luditis de historia Troiana et similibus. Absit haec ab Ecclesia vanitas.

Cogitate potius, quantae res sint, patefactio Dei, quem antea ignorastis, quae sit iustitia et ira Dei adversus peccata vestra et aliorum. Dolete vos horribiliter irritasse Deum Epicureis furoribus aut idolorum invocatione, libidinibus, et aliis sceleribus. Rursus etiam considerate, quale consilium sit, quod vos liberat Deus per filium ex aeternis poenis, quod suam lucem vobis ostendit, quod reddit iusticiam et vitam aeternam. Pro his donis agite gratias ipsi, celebrate ipsum, et gratitudinem vera obedientia ostendite.

Sint mixtae veris doloribus consolationes, invocationes, gratiarum actiones. Non ludant animi securi, ostentatione donorum, quasi accepissetis calamos, ut Hesiodus, a Musis, aut Tibias, et Marsyas, a Pallade. Hos ludos removete ab Ecclesia, qui tamen aliquanto post in eam invehentur.

Certabunt docti disputationibus, ostentabunt ingenia, audacissime nova dogmata gignent, constituent imperia praetextu ministerii, certabunt ambitione, avaritia, odiis, cupiditate vindictae. Ex his malis bella, dissipationes generis humani et vastationes orientur. Tantorum malorum initia iam compescite.

Nos iam in hac senecta mundi cogitemus, ex qualibus initiis postea maiora mala secuta sint, et doleamus, semper in Ecclesia, etiam tempora sunt feliciora, tamen multum imbecillitatis esse, et filium Dei oremus, ut publicis et privatis morbis medeatur, et reliquias suae Ecclesiae servet.

Omnia autem decenter et ordine fiant. In fine regulam generalem addit: Omnia decore et ordine fiant, id est, congruant omnes actiones ad legem Dei, et ad naturale iudicium, ut sint congressus honesti, et augeant reverentiam religionis. Hic disputatur de ritibus in Ecclesia, de ordine dierum et lectionum, et de aliis exercitiis, an sint cultus, an sint res necessariae, an vero ordinis causa tantum sine laqueis conscientiae observanda. Hanc disputationem, cum alibi satis explicata sit, omitto.

## 15:1 Argument
Chapter XV.

In this chapter there stands a long and clear confirmation of the article concerning the resurrection of the dead, and doctrine concerning certain other most serious topics is inserted. But first, let us marvel here and acknowledge the weakness of the Church. Even then, when many were still living who had seen Christ resurrected, and others who had been resurrected at that time, who knew that many had been resurrected by Christ and the Apostles: nevertheless, doubts arose concerning this chief article. Some deceivers feigned that the resurrection of the dead was allegorical and signified the amendment of morals. And some denied that life was restored to bodies, even if souls were to flutter about as survivors for some time, as the Stoics taught. Some, similar to the Epicureans and Sadducees, felt that bodies and souls were extinguished at the same time, and that souls were neither survivors nor was life restored to bodies.

Paul therefore opposes these frenzies with testimony, namely the resurrection of Christ, and narrates that Christ was seen by a great multitude after the resurrection. Christ rose again, however, for this reason: that he might also restore life to all of us after death in the same way as he himself revived in the body, and that he might abolish death. These things have been said quite clearly in the text.

Ὅτ᾿ ἂν παραδῷ τὴν βασιλείαν τῷ θεῷ καὶ πατρί.

It may seem strange why Paul speaks in such a way, as if he distinguishes the kingdom of Christ and the kingdom of the Father, when nevertheless it is said so often that the kingdom of Christ is an eternal kingdom, as it is said in Luke 1: And of his kingdom there will be no end. But I explain these things thus.

He calls the kingdom of the Father that state in which, with the whole work of Christ the mediator now completed, after the resurrection, we shall see the divinity face to face immediately, and the divinity will immediately grant us its light, wisdom, justice, and eternal joy. Before the Church arrives at this state, Christ the mediator, God and man, still exercises certain works necessary for the consummation of the Church, because these are always the proper works of the mediator: to be the high Priest, to intercede for the Church, to preserve the ministry of the Gospel, to give the Holy Spirit, to gather the Church through the Gospel, and at the same time to be effective in those receiving the Gospel by giving the Holy Spirit, by imputing his justice to them, and by overshadowing them, likewise by snatching believers from eternal death, likewise by driving away devils, by resurrecting the dead. These things are done immediately through this mediator the Son, even if the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are effective at the same time, yet the immediate action is that of this mediator, to whom the Father has handed over such a kingdom, so that through him the Church may be gathered and saved immediately in this way, and be brought to God, whose light it may afterwards enjoy immediately face to face.

This declaration, such as it is, illustrates the doctrine concerning the kingdom of Christ and shows that it is the will of God that faith should immediately behold and apprehend the mediator himself, and through him be brought to the eternal Father, just as he says in John 14: No one comes to the Father except through the Son. And let us exercise this doctrine in prayer; let us know that we are received and heard on account of the Son, and are as it were brought to the Father through him, and that he intercedes for us, and thus the Father and the Son together breathe the Holy Spirit into our hearts, as it is said: We will come to him and make our dwelling with him.

Now let the sayings of the ancient promises also be considered: The seed of the woman will crush the head of the serpent. Likewise: In your seed shall all nations be blessed. Likewise: A child is born to us, the father of the future age, etc. Does not the whole divinity crush the head of the serpent and bless us? I answer: The texts speak expressly of the seed of the woman, of the seed of Abraham, of the child born of a virgin.

Although, therefore, the whole divinity crushes the head of the serpent, yet it is done immediately through the mediator, and it is the merit proper to the mediator, by which the justice of God is satisfied. Furthermore, the very action by which the Church is gathered through the ministry, and is sanctified by the Holy Spirit being given, and the saints are snatched from eternal death, is immediately the work of the Son, as it is expressly said in John 17: You have given him power over all flesh, so that all that you have given him, he may give them eternal life. Christ the King has these actions until he brings the resurrected Church to the Father, that is, until the divinity immediately shows itself to the Church. Then he will offer the kingdom to the Father, that is, he will show that these actions are complete. And then he will reign simultaneously as God, immediately showing the divinity to us, no longer having the actions of an intercessor, or of one gathering the Church through ministry.

When he will abolish every principality.

Some have understood this concerning the empires of the world, and the power of the devils, just as it is said in Daniel chapter two and seven concerning the destruction of empires. And although we also embrace this opinion, yet I understand generally that both the empires of the world, and the power of the devils, and the ministries of the angels and the Church are abolished. Indeed, even the aids of food, drink, and other creatures, because then God will show himself immediately, and will vivify the blessed, immediately pouring into them his light, wisdom, justice, and joy. In this opinion it is also said afterwards: God will be all in all, namely, not ruling through the ministry of the Gospel, but immediately showing himself, vivifying, and pouring into the blessed his wonderful light, wisdom, justice, and joy.

Latin:

Caput XV.

In hoc capite longa et perspicua confirmatio extat articuli de resurrectione mortuorum, ac inseritur doctrina de aliis quibusdam locis gravissimis. Primum autem hic miremur, et agnoscamus imbecillitatem Ecclesiae. Tunc quoque, cum viverent adhuc multi, qui viderant Christum resuscitatum, et alios, qui tunc resuscitati fuerant, qui sciebant multos a Christo et Apostolis resuscitatos esse: tamen ortae sunt dubitationes de hoc praecipuo articulo. Finxerunt aliqui praestigiatores, allegoricam esse resuscitationem mortuorum, et significare emendationem morum. Et aliqui negaverunt corporibus reddi vitam, etiamsi aliquandiu superstites volitarent animae, ut Stoici docebant. Aliqui Epicureorum et Sadducaeorum similes, senserunt simul extingui corpora et animas, et nec superstites esse animas, nec restitui vitam corporibus.

Opponit igitur Paulus his furoribus testimonium, videlicet resurrectionem Christi, et narrat, a magna multitudine Christum post resurrectionem conspectum esse. Resurrexit autem ideo Christus, ut et nobis omnibus post mortem restituat vitam eodem modo, sicut ipse in corpore revixit, et aboleat mortem. Haec in textu satis perspicue dicta sunt.

Ὅτ᾿ ἂν παραδῷ τὴν βασιλείαν τῷ θεῷ καὶ πατρί.

Mirum videri potest, quare Paulus ita loquatur, quasi discernat regnum Christi et regnum patris, cum tamen toties dicatur, regnum Christi esse regnum aeternum, ut Lucae 1. dicitur: Et regni eius non erit finis. Sic autem haec declaro.

Regnum patris nominat illum statum, in quo iam completo toto opere Christi mediatoris, post resuscitationem, coram videbimus divinitatem immediate, et divinitas nobis immediate concedet suam lucem, sapientiam, iusticiam et laetitiam aeternam. Antequam ad hunc statum perveniat Ecclesia, adhuc Christus mediator Deus et homo exercet certa opera necessaria ad consummatio- nem Ecclesiae, quia semper mediatoris propria opera haec sunt: esse summum Sacerdotem, de- precari pro Ecclesia, conservare ministerium Evangelii, dare Spiritum sanctum, colligere Ec- clesiam per Evangelium, et simul in accipienti- bus Evangelium esse efficacem dando Spiritum sanctum, imputando illis suam iusticiam, et obumbrando eos, item eripiendo credentes ex aeterna morte, item depellendo diabolos, resu- citando mortuos. Haec fiunt immediate per hunc mediatorem filium, etiamsi simul sunt effi- caces, pater, filius et Spiritus sanctus, tamen actio immediata est huius mediatoris, cui pater hoc tale regnum tradidit, ut per ipsum imme- diate sic colligatur et salvetur Ecclesia, et addu- catur ad Deum, cuius luce postea immediate co- ram fruatur.

Haec qualiscunque declaratio illustrat doctri- nam de regno Christi, et ostendit, voluntatem Dei esse, ut fides immediate ipsum mediatorem intueatur et apprehendat, et per eum ad aeter- num patrem adducatur, sicut inquit, Ioan. 14.: Nemo venit ad patrem, nisi per filium. Ac in precatione hanc doctrinam exerceamus, sciamus propter filium nos recipi et exaudiri, et per ipsum quasi adduci ad patrem, et deprecari eum pro nobis, et sic simul patrem et filium spirare Spi- ritum sanctum in corda nostra, sicut dicitur: Veniemus ad eum, et mansionem apud eum fa- ciemus.

Iam considerentur et veterum promissionum dicta: Semen mulieris conteret caput serpentis. Item: In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes. Item: Parvulus datus est nobis, pater futuri se- culi etc. An non tota divinitas conterit caput serpentis, et benedicit nobis? Respondeo: Tex- tus expresse dicunt de semine mulieris, de se- mine Abrahae, de parvulo nato ex virgine.

Quanquam igitur tota divinitas conterit ca- put serpentis, tamen id fit immediate per media- torem, et meritum est proprium mediatoris, quo satisfit iusticiae Dei. Deinde et ipsa actio, qua colligitur Ecclesia per ministerium, et sanctifica- tur dato Spiritu sancto, et eripiuntur sancti ex aeterna morte, est immediate opus filii, sicut expresse dicitur, Iohan. 17.: Dedisti ei potesta- tem omnis carnis, ut omne, quod dedisti ei, det eis vitam aeternam. Has actiones habet rex Christus, donec ad- ducet resuscitatam Ecclesiam ad patrem, id est, donec divinitas immediate se ostendet Ecclesiae. Tunc offeret regnum patri, id est, ostendet has actiones completas esse. Et deinde simul regna- bit ut Deus, immediate divinitatem nobis osten- dens, non habens iam actiones deprecatoris, aut colligentis Ecclesiam per ministerium.

Quando abolebit omnem principatum.

Aliqui intellexerunt de imperiis mundi, et de potentia diabolorum, sicut Danielis secundo et septimo de interitu imperiorum dicitur. Etsi autem et hanc sententiam complectimur, tamen generaliter intelligo aboleri et imperia mundi, et potentiam diabolorum, et ministeria angelorum et Ecclesiae. Imo et auxilia cibi, potus, et alia- rum creaturarum, quia tunc Deus se ostendet immediate, et vivificabit beatos, immediate ef- fundens in eos suam lucem, sapientiam, iusti- ciam et laetitiam. In hanc sententiam et postea dicitur: Deus erit omnia in omnibus, scilicet, non per ministerium Evangelii regens, sed im- mediate se ostendens, vivificans, et effundens in beatos suam mirandam lucem, sapientiam, iu- sticiam et laetitiam.

## 15:29
Ἐπεὶ τὶ ποιήσουσιν οἱ βαπτιζόμενοι ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν. Otherwise what will they do, who are baptized for the dead.

It is evident now, even when infants are baptized, that the articles of the symbol, as they call it, are recited. That example was taken from the early Church, in which it was instituted with the best counsel that a very plain profession of the individual articles should be made. And some write that those to be baptized were brought to the bones of the dead, and there professed the article concerning the resurrection of the dead, and being asked whether they believed that these very ones would live again, whose bones they were looking at there, they answered that it would come to pass that life would be restored to these very ones.

Although this rite was not universal, yet everyone everywhere in baptism very plainly professed that they believed in the resurrection of the dead with the firmest faith. Although many interpretations are handed down concerning this passage, yet it is very consistent that this simple interpretation is native and true: βαπτιζόμενοι ὑπὲρ τῶν

νεκρῶν, that is, βαπτιζόμενοι ἐξομολογοῦντες ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν. They are baptized for the dead, that is, professing concerning the dead. For the preposition ὑπὲρ contains this meaning of profession, it does not signify substitution, ἀντὶ. It is not necessary to reason from this that some were initiated into baptism through a proxy person. For there it would have had to be said ἀντὶ νεκρῶν. These things, to those considering the use of the Greek language, are most manifest, as ὑπὲρ ἄλλου ἀπολογοῦμαι, not ἀντὶ ἄλλου. I could also recite other interpretations: but I will be content with this one, because there is no doubt that the profession of the symbol was made everywhere in baptism.

Τὶ καὶ ἡμεῖς κινδυνεύομεν.

The argument concerning the resurrection is taken from present hardships. If another life did not remain, there would be no distinction between the just and the unjust, and the just would foolishly endure such labors and such hardships in life: but they endure them with the certain hope of future tranquility. Therefore the Church truly feels that another life remains. He inserts, however, an admonition that they should avoid corrupt conversations, and the verse is worthy of memory:

Φθείρουσιν ἤθη χρησθ᾽ ὁμιλίαι κακαί. And it is said in Aeschylus: Οὐδὲν κάκιον κακῆς ὁμιλίας.

Ἀλλ᾿ ἐρεῖ τις πῶς ἐγείρονται οἱ νεκροί. But someone will say, how do they rise?

One must believe the divine voice, even if we do not know how God is going to effect those things which he promises, or predicts that he will do, just as it was necessary to believe Moses, that the struck rock would pour forth great rivers of water. But human diffidence is accustomed to ask about the manner in which God is going to effect his miracles. But here he represses those asking, opposing a familiar example in nature: Since you do not know how a stalk, and many ears, and grains arise from a dead grain, why do you ask the manner of the resurrection? At the same time, however, he signifies that from the small dust particles left behind, the whole body is nevertheless built up again, just as a huge tree arises from a kernel.

It is an animal body.

A ψυχικὸν body signifies living by a life which is nourished by food and drink, and has the actions of all powers, even the nutritive. The form of speaking is taken from Genesis: Adam became a living soul living, namely by this life, which has the functions of all the powers of the soul, even the nutritive. He calls such a body also χοῖκὸν, as if you were to say, earthen, from χοῦς, which signified a pot, because it still has a terrestrial and mutable nature. But he calls the other body, such as it will be after the resurrection, spiritual, not because the prior matter is not restored, or because it has been reduced to nothing, but because, once restored, it now lives a spiritual life, that is, not by the functions of the nutritive power, nor is it mutable and mortal, like the earthen one, but it is infused with spirit, and lives in another way than before, it is luminous, pure, not mutable, not mortal, having the actions of the rational soul, of the senses, of the appetites, of locomotion, which all burn with the Holy Spirit, just as when a flame is made from the matter of a lamp, ignited by fire. Thus also this mass of ours, ignited by the spirit of Christ, becomes spiritual. Therefore he says that this man is heavenly, that is, ignited by the spirit of Christ, and now similar to Christ.

Ὅτι σὰρξ καὶ αἷμα βασιλείαν θεοῦ κληρονομῆ- σαι οὐ δύνανται. Because flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God.

There is an article in the creed: I believe in the resurrection of the dead, by which we affirm that individual men will rise again from death, the elect to eternal salvation, the impious to eternal torments, as the Son of God says expressly in the fifth chapter of John: All who are in the graves will hear his voice and will come forth, those who have done good, to the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment. And Romans 14 it is said: We shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ. Likewise: Each one of us will give an account for himself to God. 2 Corinthians 5: We must all be manifested before the judgment seat of Christ, that each one may receive what he has done in the body.

In the former Epistle to the Thessalonians in chapter 4: The dead who are in Christ will rise first, then we who are alive, who are left, shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord. And 2 Peter 3: The day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night, in which the heavens will pass away with a roar, but the elements will be dissolved by fire, and the earth, and the things that are in it, will be burned up. Since all these things will be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in holy conduct and godliness, waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God.

Since, therefore, the sayings of the Son of God and the Apostles expressly affirm that all men will rise again, it also follows that the same ones who lived in this life, who are flesh and blood, will rise again. And he says expressly in Job chapter 19: I know that my redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth. And again I shall be surrounded by my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God, whom I myself shall see, and my eyes shall behold, and not another.

These illustrious testimonies must be held against those who invent Pythagorean migrations of souls, or μετεμψυχώσεις, and against others who invent that not all will rise again, nor will bodies be restored, when Job expressly says: Whom I myself shall see, and my eyes shall behold, and not another.

Why therefore does Paul say in this place: Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God? I answer: Paul himself here affirms both, that the same men will rise again, and yet that it will come to pass that this very matter, which had previously been mortal, will then become immortal. This explanation has been repeated often. The mortal must put on immortality. Therefore the substance of flesh and blood remains, but another property has been attributed to it through the Son of God. Thus, therefore, the speech is to be understood: Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God, namely, without change, such as this mortal flesh is. Soon therefore it follows: Πάντες μὲν οὐ κοιμηθησόμεθα, πάντες δὲ ἀλλαγα- σόμεθαι.

We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed. The text shows that this following declaration was added, lest ambiguity in the previous words should cause some inconvenience. There were, however, diverse readings in this text. But let us retain the Greek, which is customary and most simple, the meaning of which agrees with the saying in the Epistle to the Thessalonians, it affirms that some will not die, who will then be alive, when the Son of God shows himself to the whole human race: these will be those who meet the coming Christ. Therefore it is not μετεμψύχωσις, and individuals will meet Christ in their own bodies.

But nevertheless a change of property will take place, so that suddenly these bodies, which previously were mortal, may be endowed with this property, that henceforth they may be immortal.

Then shall come to pass the word that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory. Then shall come to pass the word that is written: Death is swallowed up in victory, etc.

It is very useful here to advise the reader whence these sayings have been taken, and what is read in the sources, and what the variety of interpretations is. It must be known, therefore, that these sayings are cited from two Prophets. It is most certain that the former sentence is taken from chapter 25 of Isaiah, where a long discourse and a clear testimony stands, which ought to be most well-known to all, concerning the abolishing of death and the restoring of eternal life. In the Hebrew reading are these words: בִּלַּע הַמָּוֶת לָנֶצַח which, according to grammar, are most simply rendered thus: He devours death unto victory, or forever. He devours, namely the Lord, whom he names before in the same discourse. Jerome renders it with these words: He will cast down death forever. This interpretation does not differ in the thing itself from the other. The Greek reading in the books commonly used for Isaiah contains these words: death has swallowed up, having prevailed, as if he were saying, previously death, prevailing or victorious, had devoured men, but then the Lord took away the tear from every face. If this reading existed in the time of Paul, it is very credible that he deliberately rendered this sentence otherwise, so that he might amend the former interpretation. And because passive forms are fuller, he rendered the verb passively, it is swallowed up.

Furthermore, the most common phrase is לָנֶצַח for the end or for victory, and at other times it signifies time, at other times manner, that is, either forever or entirely, as if you were to say, the matter being thoroughly overcome, so that there is an end to it. Paul says: ἐς νῖκος, that is, unto victory, so that the sentence is: Death is swallowed up, or the Lord has devoured death unto victory, that is, entirely, so that it is thoroughly overcome, or it is swallowed up forever. In Psalm 9: The enemies have failed, their swords unto the end לָנֶצַח, that is, utterly, and often otherwise. These interpretations by no means disagree.

But having known the grammar, let us transfer this most sweet discourse to use in fierce pains, and being erected by so illustrious a testimony, let us more firmly establish that sin and death have been truly devoured and destroyed by the Son of God the victor, and let us not rush into destruction at the sight of sin and death. Perhaps the Greek reading of Isaiah was once different, κατέπιεν θάνατον ὁ ἰσχύσας, the victor Lord devoured death. Ambrose reads: Death is swallowed up unto contention, but he erred, thinking it was written νεῖκος with a diphthong, which signifies contention. But there is another noun, νῗκος, which signifies victory. For in that signification Paul also uses the word νῗκος later: Thanks be to Him who gave us the victory. Where it would be most alien to read, who gave us contention. Nor is there any doubt that Paul wished to render the word Nezah.

But that the saying of Isaiah may become more illustrious and sweeter, that whole discourse of Isaiah 25 is to be read and pondered often.

There follows another saying taken from chapter 13 of Hosea, which Jerome interprets thus: I will be thy death, O death, thy bite will I be, O hell. Nor is the sentence obscure, but disputes have been stirred up concerning the grammar and the emphasis of the words. For it is certain that it is predicted here also that it will come to pass that death shall be abolished by the Messiah, and eternal life restored. He therefore joined the testimonies of the two Prophets, because they affirm exactly the same thing. The prior dispute is about the words, Where and I will be. Jerome rendered אהי I will be, and relates that the same interpretation is found in Symmachus. But commonly among the Greeks, both the fifth edition and Aquila interpret it as Where: the Pauline reading agrees with these.

If you read I will be, you embrace the person of the victor: I the Messiah, who am Jehovah, will be the plague of death, that is, destroying or abolishing death by my resurrection, just as he also said before: Destruction is from thee, but in me is help. In order, therefore, that the person of the victor may be comprehended, some prefer the reading I will be.

Furthermore, the assertion is fuller when he says: I will be thy death, O death, although the use of the word אהי is ambiguous, yet grammarians know that according to analogy it is more likely to be the future I will be.

Others, to whom the interrogation Where pleases, are moved by the fact that they willingly accommodate the words plague and pestilence to death and to hell. They prefer it to be said that the plague of death and the pestilence of hell have been destroyed, rather than that Christ is said to be the plague of death. For they wish the emphasis to be illustrated. Death is not a natural evil, like the rotting of an apple. But with death or the destruction of man there is a horrible sense of the wrath of God. In order, therefore, that we may understand that both have been abolished, both death and the sense of the wrath of God, they approve the interrogation, which couples both, and gloriously as if in the triumphal song he affirms that death and the powers of death have been extinguished. And he shows that Paul intended this by his reading and the exposition which he adds: Where is death, your sting? And afterwards he says that sin is this sting, because when sin is shown, men are extinguished by the sense of the wrath of God, as it is said in Psalm 89: and in your wrath we have failed. Likewise, Isaiah 38: Like a lion he has crushed all my bones. He says these huge pains and the flight in death arise from sin and the law showing sin, as experience shows. Therefore he says sin is the sting of death. And in the words of Hosea he places κέντρον, which in the Greek version is placed in the other member: ποῦ τὸ κέντρον σοῦ ᾅδη; In the former member they have used this word δίκη: ποῦ ἡ δίκη σοῦ ϑάνατε; Where is your judgment, O death, or accusation, or the punishment with which you afflict us? This agrees with the opinion of Paul, that not only is death abolished, that is, destruction itself, but the accusation or punishment as well, that is, the sense of the wrath of God. I have recited these things briefly, so that the emphasis in each reading may be considered. In the sum of the sentence there is no ambiguity. For each reading teaches that the Messiah will restore righteousness and eternal life to believers, with sin, death, and the underworld abolished.

Paul adds, however, a brief repetition of his doctrine concerning the law. The sting of death is sin, but the power of sin is the law. He is by no means speaking here of the political use of the law, but as in Romans 7, of that most sad judgment in which God, by the thought of the law, shows his wrath against sins. As David is terrified when he is rebuked by the voice of Nathan. And Paul says of himself, Romans 7: Sin, that it might become exceedingly sinful, that is, guilty, through the good, worked death in me. This whole doctrine has been repeated often in the writings of Paul. And it must be opposed to the Pharisaic dreams of those who imagine that men merit the remission of sins by the law, when the law is only a judgment by which God shows his horrible wrath against sin in us.

Here, however, Paul adds an antithesis: Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ, as if he were saying: When we are terrified by the law, let us know that this alone is the true and effective consolation proposed to us, of which it is said in John: God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten son, that everyone who believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life. In these terrors, let us establish by faith that on account of the Son of God who suffered, was resurrected, and reigns, sins are certainly remitted to us, his righteousness is imputed to us, and we are made righteous and heirs of eternal life. By this faith we overcome the terrors of sin and death through the Son of God, as it is said in Romans 5: Being justified by faith, we have peace with God. And indeed in this very consolation the Holy Spirit is given, who effects peace, that is, the joy of the heart, and the beginning of eternal life, according to the saying: I will pour out upon the house of David a spirit of grace and of supplications, that is, that they will feel that they are in grace, and liberated from terrors and eternal death, and they will now be able to truly rejoice in God and call upon him, as it is said in Romans 8: You have received the spirit of adoption of sons, by which we cry Abba Father. It is necessary for this consolation to be made known to all in the exercises of repentance, and those who understand it see how foul are the errors of the monks, who imagine that men merit remission by their works, and command them to remain in doubt. These furies fight even against this triumphal proclamation which Paul recites here: Thanks be to God who gives the victory through Jesus Christ.

Ἑδραῖοι γίνεσθε, ἀμετακίνητοι. Be firm, etc.

After he refuted the furies of those who had scattered false opinions about the resurrection, he adds at the end a brief exhortation, in which he commands that they should constantly retain the entire doctrine handed down by the Apostles, and not admit corruptions in any article.

He adds, however, also a most sweet consolation: Your labor is not in vain in the Lord. Let this sentence always be in the sight of us all: first, that we may soothe private sorrows with this hope, that after this life we shall certainly be in the fellowship of the eternal Church, in which God will communicate to us his wisdom, goodness, and joy.

Then, that we may oppose this assertion to this sorrow which we have, when many do not seem to profit from our labors, that some are nevertheless improved, and that our voice and our diligence are in some way useful for gathering and preserving the Church. We have great need of this consolation. Because when a man thinks that his that labors are entirely vain, and do not benefit others, the will would be deterred, so that it might entirely abandon the works begun. To this temptation must be opposed this most sweet sentiment: Your labor is not in vain in the Lord, that is, God himself will bring it about that our labors may benefit some, and may aid the preservation of the Church, even if a great multitude is furiously despising God, and disturbing the Church and the common society of life.

Let us therefore follow this rule often repeated in divine sermons: Let us obey the command of God, which prescribes the works of our calling, and let us hope that God will govern the outcomes, according to the saying: Commit your way to the Lord, and hope in him, and he will act. And concerning success, let these testimonies be noted, John 15: He who remains in me, and I in him, he will bear much fruit. Likewise: I have placed you, that you may go, and bear fruit, and your fruit may remain. And Psalm 1: His leaf will not fall, and all things whatsoever he does will prosper. And Isaiah 55: My word, which will go forth from my mouth, will not return to me empty. And Isaiah 65: My elect will not labor in vain. To this may be added also the notable consolations recited in Ecclesiastes chapter 11: In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening let not your hand cease, because you do not know which will grow more. And in the same place he proposes an illustrious picture. Those things which are scattered upon the waters seem to perish. But Solomon commands that we scatter bread, that is, doctrine, as if upon the waters, and he affirms that we will nevertheless after some time receive the fruit of that labor. Let us therefore obey these commands: Be instant in season, out of season, argue, rebuke, exhort. And let us firmly establish that the Son of God himself will be effective in this his ministry, as he says: I will be with you even to the consummation of the age. Even if few will profit, and the doctrine seems as if scattered upon the waters, yet some will always profit, as he says: He who remains in me, and I in him, he will bear much fruit. And there will always be some true Church, even if it will be small, as he says in Isaiah 65, that it will be like a vintage, in which a few grapes, but pleasing ones, are found. We understand that this whole consolation is necessary for each of us in this duty of teaching. Therefore let us often think upon this saying of Paul, and other congruent testimonies, and let us not, broken by grief or desperation, omit the duties of our calling.

It is certain that it was the custom even in Israel, that when the people had gathered on feast days, each would contribute something to the needs of the needy through the liberality of others. The Apostles handed down this custom also to the Churches. And at the time when Paul wrote this Epistle, many in Judea were being expelled from their possessions. And at the same time, in the time of Claudius, there was a famine in the East so severe that a modius of grain was sold for six drachmas. But let the example be considered, which advises that in public gatherings of the Church this pious kind of liberality be exercised, and that each contribute something. And histories show that the ancient Church was very dutiful in this kind.

If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema.

The other sayings in this chapter have no obscurity. But Paul added with his own hand a most grave sentiment, which ought to be most known to all: If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema Maran atha. He condemns both the manifest enemies of the Gospel, and the hypocrites, who under the pretext of religion seek their own power or other advantages, and bend the Gospel to the desires of men, and mix in corruptions; against all such he pronounces this voice of divine judgment, and sends it like a thunderbolt, as John the Baptist says: He who believes in the Son has eternal life, but he who does not believe in the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God will remain upon him. And concerning hypocrites and evil teachers there exist often-repeated threats, as in Matthew 25: And he will cast the useless servant into the darkness that is outside. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

But first he says, Let him be anathema, that is, something condemned, just as the use of this word is known in the Church, as to the Galatians: If anyone teaches another Gospel, let him be anathema. And the reason for the etymology may be taken from the law concerning consecrated things, which it was necessary to remove and destroy.

But he adds the foreign words Maran atha, which words are placed as a recitation, and are to be attached by grammatical apposition to the nearest word, as if he were saying: Let him be anathema, that is, let him be condemned by this very saddest sentence, which are the words of the curse: Maran atha, that is, our Lord comes, namely, to punish, and to declare the most sorrowful wrath, which you previously despised. These are therefore a true imprecation of punishment, as if it were said: Εὗρε θεὸς τὸν ἄλιτρον.

Or as Psalm 57 says: The righteous shall rejoice when he sees the vengeance, he shall wash his hands in the blood of the sinner, and man shall say, surely there is a reward for the righteous, surely there is a judge on earth. Such is the assertion concerning the coming judgment, and concerning the punishment in these words: Our Lord comes.

Moreover, the Syriac or Chaldean language is related to Hebrew, because neighboring nations retained the Hebrew language from their fathers, but gradually corrupted it, as is wont to happen, yet the traces can be recognized. Mar or Mara signifies Lord, as in the Targum, Proverbs chapter 25 and Amos 1. It is consistent, however, that the name Mara is from the word מוֹרֶה which signifies Teacher, or from the word מוֹרָא which signifies terrible. And the origins are known: יוֹרֶה he taught, and יָרֵא he feared. And in the life of Hilarion it is read that in his age there was still an idol in Syria called Maras. It was customary for new idols and cults to attribute new names, which seemed to signify something greater. As after the first cult, in which God was named יְהוָה אֱלוֹהַ, wicked men, who abandoned the old doctrine and cult, named God בַּעַל, a possessor, δεσπότην. Afterwards, the neighbors devised another more terrible name, Maran, that is, our terrible one. Thus, when there is a departure from true doctrine and true cults, superstition fashions both new names and opinions and other rites. Mara was therefore a name used in Syria. The appendix n, or na, is our; Atha, he comes. They affirm that this is the native interpretation of the word Maran atha, and they write that it is often used in Jewish narrations. Therefore it is a wonder why the learned man Burgensis devised another etymology, who for Maran atha made Meherem motha, and says the Apostle wished to name a most atrocious species of condemnation: He who does not love Christ, let him be not a common anathema, but Meherem, that is, a thing destroyed and devastated, and such an anathema that it is necessary to be killed; therefore he thinks Motha was added, as if he were saying: Anathema destined for devastation and death, because not all consecrated things were killed. I have recited this etymology of Burgensis so that it might not be unknown to the younger ones, not because I approve of it, since it appears to be far-fetched. Let us embrace the other, which Jerome also hands down, and which they say agrees with the language of the commentaries. Maran atha, that is, our Lord comes. And let the reader know that these words are placed narratively as a formula by which a judge has invoked punishments or curses. This final clause contains a most grave threat against all enemies of the Gospel and hypocrites, and especially against corrupters of doctrine. Therefore, let us seek the truth with sincere hearts, and let us pray to the Son of God himself, our Lord Jesus Christ, that he may govern us with his Holy Spirit.

ARGUMENT OF THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS.

Let the distinction between Law and Gospel always be in view, and let us know that not only the histories of the travels of Paul and moral precepts are to be sought in his writings, but a far different wisdom concerning the Son of God, and concerning his benefits, concerning the remission of sins, concerning the wonderful gathering of the Church, and concerning eternal life. But nevertheless, for those who have rightly learned the doctrine of the Church, it is also useful to know the times and the series of history. Therefore, in order that we may consider at what time Paul first came to Corinth, and when afterwards he wrote the Epistles to the churches of that place, I shall distribute the years in some order.

Years from the conversion of Paul.

Year of Christ. Year after conversion.

35. 1. Year of Paul's conversion, Year from the birth of Christ 35.

36. 2. Paul went into Arabia.

39. 5. He went into Tarsus, Acts 9.

42. 8. Barnabas led Paul from Tarsus to Antioch, Acts 13.

44. 10. He went into Cyprus, Acts 13. Where Sergius the proconsul was a hearer.

45. 11. Having set out into Perga and Iconium, Acts 14, and neighboring cities.

51. 17. The Synod of Jerusalem, at which Paul was present.

52. 18. He returned into Iconium and Lystra, where he joined Timothy to himself, and crossed into Macedonia, and was at Corinth.

Year of Christ. Year after conversion.

55. 21. He returned to Asia, and was for two years in Ephesus.

58. 24. Paul returned to Macedonia, having first traveled through Phrygia and the borders of the Galatians. And when he had come into Macedonia, just as he says here that he crossed over from Troas, he wrote both Epistles to the Corinthians at Philippi at no long interval. Afterwards he returned to Asia, and came to Mytilene, likewise to Samos and Miletus.

64. 30. Around this time Paul made his final journey to Jerusalem, from there he was sent to Rome as a captive.

66. 32. Paul, sent to Rome, was for two years in a rented house, Acts last chapter. Concerning the remaining time it is not written, but nevertheless it is consistent that he remained at Rome until the penultimate year of Nero, in which he was killed, because no other journeys of Paul are read of after he came to Rome. And that remaining time is short.

69. 35. Paul killed by Nero in the 13th year of Nero.

70. 36. The fourteenth year of Nero, in which Nero committed suicide there. I have added this brief recitation, in which the principal journeys are recounted. For all things cannot certainly be distributed into individual years. And it appears that in later years, in the time of Claudius and then of Nero, he often traveled through the same places of Asia and Greece.

We see, however, that in the former Epistle he encompassed many matters, because it happens thus: once a Church is established, a lasting tranquility does not remain, but it is disturbed by the snares of the devil and the vanity of human minds. Thus, when dissensions had arisen at Corinth, and many questions were raised—concerning marriage, the use of evangelical liberty, the custom with a stepmother, feasts among friends returning from sacrifices, the resurrection, and others—Paul responded gravely to each question and showed that he was affected by great sorrow on account of the scandals. Since, therefore, the Corinthians responded and showed signs of amendment, Paul now responds more gently, and first excuses himself for not coming to them now, saying that he will come at a less sad time.

In the second chapter he orders the fallen one to be received, who had had a custom with his stepmother. That example is to be observed against the Novatians, because it manifestly teaches that those who have fallen from sin are to be absolved and received.

In the third chapter he preaches generally about the efficacy of the evangelical ministry, about the distinction between the Law and the Gospel, and about the cross.

This commemoration was especially necessary, and is always necessary in the Church. For just as formerly, before the advent of the Messiah, many Jews who had lived among the Gentiles, such as Daniel and others, had joined listeners to themselves—some rightly handing down the doctrine concerning the Messiah, others preaching only about the external discipline of the Law—so in Paul's time many Jews still had listeners among the Gentiles, whom, however, they taught only about the external discipline of the Law. These, when they heard from Paul that the Messiah had come, and that the Jewish polity was about to perish, and that men do not merit the remission of sins by the Law, and are not righteous by the Law. They execrated this new doctrine, which conflicted with the opinions they themselves had previously handed down, when they had taught the Gentiles that the Messiah would come, who would unite all nations in the whole world under one empire, and would bring it about that in the same way, namely by the Law of Moses, they would call upon the true God, with idols abolished. Many Pseudo-apostles confirmed this same opinion. But when Paul taught otherwise, the Jews everywhere opposed him and stirred up their own listeners against him. And besides, the other Gentiles abhorred this new kind of doctrine and did not want their idols to be censured.

He therefore opposes to the clamors of the Jews and the Pseudo-apostles this long sermon about the distinction between the Law and the Gospel, and about the efficacy of the evangelical ministry, and about the cross, as if he were saying: Although the Jews previously taught you about the Law, and condemned idols, and preached in some way about the discipline of the Law, nevertheless the Gospel is a different doctrine; it shows that the remission of sins is given, not on account of the Law, but on account of the Messiah, and at the same time it pours the Holy Spirit into the hearts of believers, and eternal righteousness and life are begun, and eternal goods are already exhibited, the shadows of which were proposed in the Law. And these things are truly done by the voice of our ministry, to which God adds testimonies with manifest miracles, although we are subject to the cross, and we cannot destroy the nations as Moses and Joshua occupied Canaan, and as the Jews think the Messiah will subdue the nations with arms.

With this occasion of Paul's disputations considered, it can be understood why he instituted these sermons, and what he wishes to teach. Therefore, in the third chapter, he proposes this most memorable sentence: The Law is the letter and the ministry of death, but the Gospel is the ministry of the spirit.
