This voice was new to the Jews, who had previously taught the Gentiles something about discipline, just as it was often unknown in the Church, and now monks and the like abhor it. But just as in the time of the Prophets there were always some who were illustrators of this doctrine, so this is the proper voice of the Apostles: to show the distinction between the Law and the Gospel, and by His immense goodness God from time to time renews this distinction in the Church. This light was extinguished by the interpretations of Origen, who feigned that men are righteous by the Law, that is, by moral discipline, and interpreted the letter only as external ceremonies, and the spirit as allegories. Afterwards, Augustine censured the error that had been widely scattered and showed that the letter is both the ceremonies and the moral works which are done by human diligence, not by the Holy Spirit vivifying hearts in true terrors. But the spirit is the Holy Spirit Himself, vivifying hearts in true terrors, and beginning in us righteousness and eternal life, and providing in reality those goods which are signified in the Law.

Thus, after Augustine, there were some, and recently Luther, who renewed that distinction between the Law and the Gospel, and between the letter and the spirit.

Paul dwells on this distinction from the beginning of the third chapter up to the sixth chapter, and he mixes doctrine and consolations, which indeed follow necessarily from the doctrine.

The first distinction of the ministry of the Law and the evangelical ministry is taken from their immediate effects. The ministry of the Law, without the voice of the Gospel, is only a ministry of death, that is, it is either political discipline, which is external government and a bridle for the locomotive power, as we call it: or it is judgment, by which God shows in the heart of man his horrible wrath against sin, concerning which judgment it is said in Isaiah 38: As a lion he crushed all my bones. And Paul says in Romans 3: Through the law comes the knowledge of sin. Likewise: The law brings about wrath, because God willed that this knowledge remain in man after the fall, so that through it external discipline might be governed, and then that it might be the voice of the sentence by which God shows wrath and condemnation. It is manifest, however, that not only is sin and death not taken away by that judgment and sense of the wrath of God, but also that this very sense of the wrath of God is terrors and sorrows more sad than the death of the body itself, and the beginning of eternal punishments, unless man is liberated by the voice of the Gospel through the Son of God, as it is written: The sting of death is sin, the power of sin is the law. Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. Furthermore, external discipline neither takes away sins, nor merits the remission of sins, nor is it the fulfillment of the law.

But the Gospel is the ministry of the spirit, as is said here in the third chapter, that is, the voice by which God remits sins to the believer on account of the Son, and gives the Holy Spirit, by whom hearts are raised up in that sense of the wrath of God and in terrors, and are snatched from the sorrows of the underworld, and feel peace and joy in God, and the beginnings of eternal life.

The second distinction is from the further things and the modes that accompany them. With the law promulgated, the polity of Moses is established, and glorious bodily liberations are added, the leading out from Egypt, and many admirable victories, the repression of the course of the sun, and other things falling into the eyes of many nations, and which were profitable to the whole multitude, to the saints and the non-saints.

The promulgation of the Gospel, however, does not have a similar political glory, nor does it establish a worldly polity, but it gathers other listeners elsewhere in different polities, and it is a ministry by which justice and eternal life are begun in them. Meanwhile, however, in this mortal life, the listeners remain subject to the cross and to huge miseries. By this appearance, however, the minds of men are greatly alienated from the Gospel. For it seems most absurd that these scattered men, without a polity, without a certain seat, without a certain empire, without defenses, who are killed here and there by anyone at all, should be the people of God. Nor is it consistent, when Moses established such a beautiful polity, that the Messiah should hand over no certain lodging to his own.

These absurdities always move all men. But Paul responds that by the ministry of the Gospel, goods are brought that are by no means about to perish, as political ones perish: but eternal ones, and he says that testimonies are also added to this voice, such as the resurrections of the dead and other miracles. And he consoles the Church with a most sweet argument taken from the lesser.

Since there was great glory and preservation of the polity which was instituted in the promulgation of the law, which nevertheless was a thing about to perish: the Church will undoubtedly also be preserved, and its glory will be greater, even if these things happen differently.

After these comparisons of the Law and the Gospel, since by this ministry of the Messiah a political kingdom is not established, as the Jews dreamed, and the Church is gathered in different empires and in persecution: it is necessary for the Church to be taught about the cross and about the coming liberation in eternal life. Paul therefore adds in chapters 4 and 5 sermons about the cross and about eternal life: and he inserts notable sentences about the other members of the Gospel, such as this one at the end of the 5th chapter, which is as it were an epilogue of the preceding: We act as ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us, and we pray in the name of Christ: Be reconciled to God. For him who did not know sin, he made sin for us, so that we might become the justice of God in him. Although the whole reading is full of necessary doctrine, nevertheless this sentence is especially worthy of consideration, because it both illustrates the dignity of the ministry and afterwards preaches about the redeemer with most splendid figures. There are two appellations here, one of sin, the other of the justice of God. Nothing, however, can be named sadder than sin, because it is an evil to which God horribly is angry, and that which is horribly condemned by God. Again, nothing is more glorious and better than the justice of God, that is, something pleasing to God, and agreeing with the will of God, and living by the light and eternal life divinely given. Consider therefore in this place the exchange. The Son of God is without sin, as it is said here, He knew no sin, that is, he does not have, he does not want any evil fighting against the will of God, but he is also just in essence, and he has then perfect obedience, by which he subjects himself to the eternal Father, having assumed human nature, and by this obedience he satisfies the law, and pays the λύτρα for us, as he himself names it, Matt. 20. Although therefore the justice of God, that is, the divine light and rectitude and perfect obedience is in the Son, yet he himself is made sin for us, that is, something guilty before God, and the wrath of God is poured out upon him. For although the human race is received by God through mercy, yet it was also necessary that divine justice be satisfied, and an ineffable union of mercy and justice was made. Thus the human race was received, if someone in the human race would pay the penalty. But in order for the penalty to be valid for others, it was necessary for this redeemer to be without sin. And therefore he is called a redeemer, because he pays the price for us. He is made sin therefore, that is, something guilty, he feels the horrendous wrath of the eternal Father, against the sins of all, as if he himself had defiled himself with your and my and everyone's sins. No creature can sufficiently understand the magnitude of this pain. But on the contrary, he grants to you and to all believers that which is highest in heaven. Since he himself is just by the justice of God, he grants that to us, first by imputation and beginning, afterwards also by consummation. We who in reality are unclean and guilty of sin, are covered through the Son, we are pronounced not guilty, but just, God justifying, that is, accepting us, and at the same time renewing and vivifying us. Nothing greater can be said or thought. Thus he says, Isaiah ch. 61: I will rejoice greatly in the Lord, and my soul will exult in my God. Because he has clothed me with the garments of salvation, and has surrounded me with the robe of justice, and he himself is like a bridegroom in priestly attire, and we like a bride adorned with jewels. First he says that he rejoices not in the powers of our nature, or the help of any creature, but I will rejoice, he says, in the Lord my God. I will rejoice that I have been reconciled to God, and that I have been freed from the highest evils by the work of God himself, and now live in him with eternal life. He has clothed me, he says, with the garment of justice, that is, he covers me with the remission of sins, and the imputation of justice, nay even with the effectuation of a new and eternal justice. He himself surrounds me as with a garment with his justice, which is imputed to me, and at the same time begins a new and eternal justice in me. He clothes me also with salvation, that is, eternal life, and other gifts in this life and after this life. And he himself is like a bridegroom in priestly attire. The Son of God is the bridegroom of the Church, he truly loves and preserves her. He embraces her, however, in priestly attire: first because he himself is the high priest, offering himself for us, prostrate before the Father, praying for his miserable bride: then also, having been resurrected, joining her to himself, and adorning her with the Holy Spirit, and always interceding for her, instituting and preserving the ministry, protecting and saving her.

She herself also stands by the bridegroom, adorned with similar ornaments, agreeing with this bridegroom, outwardly with the cross, inwardly with the remission of sins, the Holy Spirit, the imputation of justice, and then eternal justice and life, addicted to this one bridegroom, not defiled by any idols, burning with love for this bridegroom, and through him brought to the eternal Father, and joyful in all eternity celebrating God, enjoying his light, wisdom, justice, and life. These are those eternal nuptials, to which this bride, adorned by the bridegroom, is led. By the comparison of such sayings, this passage of Paul becomes more illustrious.

In the sixth chapter, after he has previously recited the doctrine of the Gospel, he adds an exhortation that we should retain and exercise the gifts that have been begun, and he mixes in consolations. By name, however, he prohibits the confusion of religions. He commands that they avoid the worship of idols and the sacrifices which were made to idols. It was, however, the custom to prepare feasts from sacrificed meat, to which whole families were summoned. He prohibits these contagions, just as it is now necessary for the pious to flee the profanation of the Lord's Supper in the papal Mass, the adorations of the bread in the carrying about, the invocations of the dead, as will be said more copiously in the exposition.

In the seventh chapter he repeats the former exhortation, that we should avoid idols. And immediately afterwards he softens their pain, which the indignation of Paul had brought upon them, where the wonderful solicitude of the Apostle is observed.

He does not wish to leave in their minds any suspicion of an embittered spirit, but wishes them to know for certain that the offense has been thoroughly wiped away, so that their goodwill may be firmer, and so that dissensions may not arise, which would happen if silent resentments remained behind. He inserts, moreover, the necessary doctrine concerning conversion or repentance, that it is a part of the ministry in the Church to rebuke sins, and that it is necessary for sorrows to arise in conversion. This whole sentiment is to be referred to the common doctrine concerning Contrition, of which it is said: As a lion he has crushed all my bones. And Isaiah 66: To whom shall I look? except to him who is humble and contrite in spirit etc. And Psalm 50: A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit, a contrite and humbled heart you will not despise. Likewise, Deut. 4: God is a consuming fire.

God wishes sins to be acknowledged in some way, and His wrath against sins. He does not wish it to be neglected, and He condemns secure and iron hearts, as in Jeremiah chapter 8: They knew not how to blush. Isa. 48: Your forehead is of bronze. And Zechariah: They have set their heart like adamant. And Paul says to the Ephesians that the impious are ἀπηλγηκότας, that is, without pain, secure, despising the judgment of God. These most sorrowful discourses are to be observed, so that we may know that contrition is necessary, which they name in this way, namely, true terrors and sorrows on account of the wrath of God against our sins.

In the eighth and in the ninth he exhorts the Corinthians to help the Churches in the East by the collection of alms, which were in need of the liberality of others, and because many pious people were being driven out of their possessions, and because then in the time of the emperor Claudius the famine was so savage that the price of a modius was 6 drachmae, when in usual years it was one drachma, so that if the price of a medimnus in Leipzig is the usual half-Joachim, then it would have been sold for three Joachims. Such a difficulty existed in Germany in the year 1517.

There are, however, many notable sayings in this exhortation. Mention is made of equality. Here, equality should not be understood by arithmetic proportion: nor let us imagine that Paul is teaching a Platonic community of goods, or a Spartan equalization of faculties, as the Anabaptists have imagined. For it is most certain that external polities are not established in the Gospel, but that a distinction of things and legitimate governments are approved, as will be said more fully in its proper place. But Paul speaks of an equality not of dominion and possession, but of use in the voluntary communication of a generous man toward the needy, according to the saying:

Let your fountains be dispersed abroad, and remain you the master of them. This whole collection is voluntary, nor is it necessary to adapt it precisely to arithmetic or geometric or harmonic proportion. It is manifest that it is wicked to make equality by arithmetic proportion, so that Isaac does not possess more in number than Ishmael. Nor is equality by geometric proportion necessary. It is not necessary for a Consul to have twice as much as another citizen: or for a Consul to contribute twice as much as another citizen. That collection seems to correspond more with harmonic proportion, in which there is equality neither of proportions nor of differences, but as the greatest term stands to the minimum, so the difference of the greatest and the middle stands to the difference of the middle and the minimum, as: 3, 4, 6. The number six is double to three. Therefore also the difference of the middle and the minimum, which is unity. Thus are Lucullus 6, Atticus 4, and the needy exile Cicero 3. If Lucullus gives two talents to the exile, let Atticus give one.

But yet because it is a voluntary collection, it is not necessary to be bound to these chains. But Paul himself testifies several times that he does not demand this collection in such a way that he is thought to be compelling anyone, but that he speaks of voluntary liberality. Therefore he does not establish a new Platonic or Anabaptist polity.

In the ninth chapter he reminds them of the divine promise, just as it is said in the Gospel of Luke 6: Give, and it shall be given to you. Here the distinction of promises must be held. One is the proper promise of the Gospel of reconciliation, by which the remission of sins and the imputation of righteousness are offered freely only on account of the Son of God.

Others are legal, which are valid among the reconciled. For God wishes to give also certain rewards of His own for the good works of the reconciled, just as the widow of Zarephath is fed, because she was liberal toward Elijah. Let us attribute truth to God, and let us hope for and seek these rewards, and by this hope let us also stir ourselves to do good.

In the tenth chapter, 11. 12. he adds a refutation of the Pseudo-apostles, who were spreading Jewish opinions, and were attempting to impose Jewish ceremonies upon the Gentiles, and were dreaming that the kingdom of the Messiah would be such that the Jewish polity would be extended to the whole world. These were also alleging the examples of other Apostles, who were still using ancestral rites in Judea and the vicinity.

Paul, however, opposes not only the recitation of his own labors, but also divine testimonies, by which his doctrine was confirmed by God. Among these testimonies he recounts a singular revelation of divinity shown to him, he says he was caught up into the third heaven, which I understand to be said in the manner of the Hebrews, who call even this air under the moon heaven. The lowest heaven will therefore be the air: the second, all the spheres by which the lights, planets, and stars are carried: the third, the secret seat of God, in this was divinity shown to Paul. Nor is there need to inquire curiously about this singular revelation, what it was like, just as we cannot know how God showed himself to Moses in the rock. For although many pious minds sometimes have clearer light in consolations, yet the revelations made to the Fathers, Prophets, and Apostles are more illustrious, and we know that it behooves us to acquiesce by faith in the word, as it is written: Blessed are they who believe and do not see. And what it is to acquiesce by faith, experience teaches, when great pains are alleviated by faith and hope, as Paul says: Justified by faith we have peace. Nor must it be asked what kind of pains were in Paul, who is here named σκόλοψ in the flesh, only let the foolish opinion be cast away, which imagines there were fires of lusts. I believe, however, they were singular terrors, such as are often described in the Psalms, as when David says: There is no peace for my bones. And various are the struggles of faith concerning many parts of doctrine, concerning the dangers of the Church, and concerning private salvation, in which minds are greatly tormented. Such torments he signifies when he names σκόλοπα, that is, a stake or a very sharp pole, because it was an ancient punishment to impale a man on a pole, which they called ἀνασκολοπίζειν, which is now also customary among the Turks: for it does not signify light annoyances.

And there Paul recounts a most sweet consolation. He says that to him asking, the answer was, My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is perfected in infirmity: other infirmities remain in others. But let this consolation always be in sight: Grace abounds above the offense. This consolation he proposes here, reciting these words: My grace is sufficient for you. Then the presence of God and help to the infirm is shown. The presence of God becomes more conspicuous when he defends Daniel among the lions, than if he were to cover him among barbarian men, whom he might seem to be able to sway by his own counsel. Thus to the whole people returning from Babylon the presence of God becomes more conspicuous, when the unwarlike multitude is defended, which had neither garrisons nor walls, than when before the exile it had walls and armies. And God allows evils inextricable by human counsels to happen to us, so that, destitute of other aids, we may flee to him, and being liberated, we may confess that we have been saved divinely, as is said in the Psalm: Father and mother have forsaken me, but the Lord has taken me up. Item: You will be a helper to the orphan. Item, Psalm 59: Will you not go forth, O God, in our mighty works, give us help from tribulation. And, vain is the salvation of man.

In the last chapter he adds a threat: If I come, he says, and see that you have not been amended, I will use the power of the spirit to punish some. For he signifies that he will imprecate diseases upon some, death upon others, just as by the voice of Peter Ananias was killed, Acts 5. And Acts 13, Elymas the sorcerer lost his sight by the imprecation of Paul. But Paul mitigates this threat, because he says that he wishes first to know the causes with witnesses heard.

He also adds a memorable saying, which is often cited against tyranny: Power has been given to me not for destruction, but for edification, that is, the Lord wants us to use power, not to indulge private affections, as tyrants abuse power, but he wants us to use it for the salvation of others: first he desires individuals to be amended, and to omit punishment, then if punishment is necessary for chastising some, let the example benefit the others.

Thus far the argument of the second Epistle to the Corinthians has been recited. For the individual parts will be able to be understood more easily if the reader will first consider the summaries of the matters and the sequence, and will note what the occasions are, why he institutes other matters elsewhere. Now we will add a brief explanation to the speech of Paul itself.

Latin:

Ἐπεὶ τὶ ποιήσουσιν οἱ βαπτιζόμενοι ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν. Alioqui quid facient, qui baptisantur qui mortuis.

Constat nunc, etiam cum infantes bapti- zantur, tamen recitari articulos symboli, ut vo- cant. Id exemplum sumtum est a prima Eccle- sia, in qua optimo consilio institutum fuit, ut fieret planissima professio singulorum articulo- rum. Et scribunt quidam, adductos esse bapti- zandos ad ossa mortuorum, et ibi professos esse articulum de resurrectione mortuorum, et inter- rogatos, an crederent hos ipsos revicturos esse, quorum ibi ossa intuerentur, respondisse, futu- rum, ut his ipsis vita restituatur.

Quanquam autem hic ritus non fuit univer- salis, tamen omnes in baptismo ubique planissi- me professi sunt, se firmissima fide resurrectio- nem mortuorum credere. Etsi multae interpre- tationes de hoc loco traduntur, tamen valde con- sentaneum est, hanc simplicem interpretationem nativam et veram esse: βαπτιζόμενοι ὑπὲρ τῶν

νεκρῶν, id est, βαπτιζόμενοι ἐξομολογοῦντες ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν. Baptisantur pro mortuis, id est, profitentes de mortuis. Nam praepositio ὑπὲρ hanc significationem professionis continet, non significat vices, ἀντὶ. Non hoc inde ratio- cinari necesse est, aliquos per vicariam personam baptismo initiatos esse. Ibi enim dicendum fuis- set ἀντὶ νεκρῶν. Haec utcunque consideranti- bus Graecae linguae usum, manifestissima sunt, ut ὑπὲρ ἄλλου ἀπολογοῦμαι, non ἀντὶ ἄλλου. Possem et alias recitare interpretationes: sed hac contentus ero, quia non dubium est, in baptismo ubique factam esse professionem symboli.

Τὶ καὶ ἡμεῖς κινδυνεύομεν.

Argumentum de resurrectione sumtum a praesentibus aerumnis. Si non restaret alia vita, non esset discrimen inter iustos et iniustos, et iusti stulte sustinerent in vita tantos labores et tantas aerumnas: sustinent autem certa spe futu- rae tranquillitatis. Igitur Ecclesia vere sentit restare aliam vitam. Inserit autem admonitio- nem, ut vitent prava colloquia, et versus est me- moria dignus:

Φθείρουσιν ἤθη χρησθ᾽ ὁμιλίαι κακαί. Et apud Aeschylum dicitur: Οὐδὲν κάκιον κακῆς ὁμιλίας.

Ἀλλ᾿ ἐρεῖ τις πῶς ἐγείρονται οἱ νεκροί. Sed dicet aliquis, quomodo surgunt?

Voci divinae credendum est, etiamsi non scimus, quomodo effecturus sit Deus ea, quae promittit, aut praedicit se facturum esse, sicut Moysen credere oportuit, petram percussam ef- fusuram esse magna flumina aquarum. Sed hu- mana diffidentia interrogare solet de modo, quo Deus sua miracula effecturus est. Reprimit au- tem hic interrogantes, opponens familiare exem- plum in natura: Cum non scias, quomodo ex grano mortuo exoriantur culmus, et multae spi- cae, et grana, cur quaeris modum resurrectionis? Simul autem significat, ex parvis pulvisculis re- lictis, tamen totum corpus rursus aedificari, sicut ex nucleo ingens arbor oritur.

Est corpus animale.

Corpus ψυχικὸν significat vivens vita, quae alitur cibo et potu, et habet actiones omnium potentiarum, etiam nutritivae. Forma loquendi ex Genesi sumta est: Factus est Adam in animam viventem, hac videlicet vita, quae habet functio- nes omnium potentiarum animae, etiam nutriti- vae. Tale corpus nominat et χοῖκὸν, quasi di- cas, testaceam, a χοῦς, quod ollam significabat, quia adhuc terrestrem et mutabilem naturam ha- bet. Aliud autem corpus, quale erit post resur- rectionem, nominat spirituale, non quod prior materia non restituatur, seu quod sit redacta in nihilum, sed quod restituta vivat iam vita spi- rituali, id est, non functionibus potentiae nutri- tivae, nec sit mutabilis et mortalis, sicut testa- cea, sed sit perfusa spiritu, et alio modo vivat quam antea, sit lucida, pura, non mutabilis, non mortalis, habens actiones animae rationalis, sensuum, adpetitionum, locomotivae, quae om- nes ardent Spiritu sancto, ut cum ex materia lychni fit flamma, accensa ab igni. Ita et haec nostra massa accensa a spiritu Christi fit spiri- tualis. Ideo dicit hunc hominem coelestem esse, id est, accensum spiritu Christi, et similem iam Christo.

Ὅτι σὰρξ καὶ αἷμα βασιλείαν θεοῦ κληρονομῆ- σαι οὐ δύνανται. Quia caro et sanguis regnum Dei haereditare non possunt.

Articulus est in symbolo: Credo resurrectio- nem mortuorum, quo adfirmamus singulos ho- mines resurrecturos esse ex morte, electos ad sa- lutem aeternam, impios ad cruciatus aeternos, ut expresse dicit filius Dei in capite Iohannis quinto: Omnes qui in monumentis sunt, audient vocem eius et procedent, qui bona fecerunt, in resur- rectionem vitae, qui vero mala egerunt, in resur- rectionem iudicii. Et Roman. 14. dicitur: Om- nes stabimus ante tribunal Christi. Item: Unus- quisque nostrum pro se rationem reddet Deo. 2. Corinth. 5.: Omnes nos manifestari oportet coram tribunali Christi, ut reportet unusquisque ea, quae gessit in corpore.

In priore Epistola ad Thessalonicenses in capite 4.: Mortui, qui in Christo sunt, resurgent primum, deinde nos qui vivimus, qui reliqui sumus, simul cum eis rapiemur in nubibus, in occursum Domini. Et 2. Petri 3.: Veniet dies Domini, sicut fur in nocte, in qua coeli cum so- nitu transibunt, elementa vero incendio solven- tur, et terra, et quae sunt in ea, comburentur. Haec omnia cum dissolventur, quales oportet vos esse in sancta conversatione et pietate, expectan- tes et festinantes, ut in die Dei praesto sitis.

Cum igitur expresse adfirment dicta filii Dei et Apostolorum, omnes homines resurrecturos esse, hoc quoque sequitur, eosdem qui vixerunt in hac vita, qui sunt caro et sanguis, resurrectu- ros esse. Et expresse inquit Iob capite 19.: Scio quod redemtor meus vivit, et in novissimo die de terra surrecturus sum. Et rursus circumdabor pelle mea, et in carne mea videbo Deum, quem visurus sum ego ipse, et oculi mei conspecturi sunt, et non alius.

Haec illustria testimonia tenenda sunt contra eos, qui fingunt Pythagoricas migrationes anima- rum, seu μετεμψυχώσεις, et contra alios, qui fingunt, non omnes resurrecturos esse, nec re- stitui corpora, cum Iob expresse dicat: Quem vi- surus sum ego ipse, et oculi mei conspecturi sunt, et non alius.

Cur igitur Paulus hoc loco dicit: Caro et sanguis regnum Dei possidere non possunt. Re- spondeo: Paulus ipse hic utrunque adfirmat, eos- dem homines resurrecturos esse, et tamen futu- rum esse, ut haec ipsa materia, quae antea fuerat mortalis, tunc fiat immortalis. Haec enarratio saepe repetita est. Oportet mortale induere im- mortalitatem. Itaque manet substantia carnis et sanguinis, sed proprietas alia ei per filium Dei attributa est. Sic igitur intelligenda est oratio: Caro et sanguis regnum Dei non possidebunt, scilicet, sine mutatione, qualis est haec mortalis caro. Mox ergo sequitur: Πάντες μὲν οὐ κοιμηθησόμεθα, πάντες δὲ ἀλλαγα- σόμεθαι.

Omnes quidem non dormiemus, sed omnes mutabimur. Textus ostendit hanc sequentem de- clarationem additam esse, ne ambiguitas in prio- ribus verbis aliquid incommodi pareret. Fuerunt autem lectiones diversae in hoc textu. Sed reti- neamus Graecam usitatam et simplicissimam, cu- ius sententia congruit cum dicto in Epistola ad Thessalonicenses, adfirmat aliquos non moritu- ros esse, qui tunc vivent, cum se filius Dei osten- det toti generi humano: hi erunt obvii venienti Christo. Non igitur est μετεμψύχωσις, et sin- guli in suis corporibus occurrent Christo.

Sed tamen fiet mutatio proprietatis, ut subito haec corpora, quae prius fuerunt mor- talia, donentur hac proprietate, ut deinceps sint immortalia.

Τότε γενήσεται ὁ λόγος ὁ γεγραμμένος, κατε- πόθη ὁ θάνατος εἰς νῖκος. Tunc fiet verbum dictum: Absorpta est mors in victoria, etc.

Valde prodest hic monere lectorem, unde haec dicta sumta sint, et quid legatur in fontibus, et quae sit interpretationum varietas. Sciendum est igitur, haec dicta ex duobus Prophetis citata esse. Priorem sententiam ex capite 25. Esaiae sumtam esse certissimum est, ubi longa concio et perspicuum testimonium extat, quod oportet om- nibus esse notissimum, de abolenda morte, et restituenda aeterna vita. In lectione Ebraea sunt haec verba: בִּלַּע הַמָּוֶת לָנֶצַח quae iuxta Grammaticam simplicissime sic redduntur: De- vorat mortem ad victoriam, seu in sempiternum. Devorat, videlicet Dominus, quem antea in eadem concione nominat. Hieronymus reddit his verbis: Praecipitabit mortem in sempiternum. Haec interpretatio re ipsa non dissentit ab altera. Graeca lectio in libris usitatis apud Esaiam con- tinet haec verba: κατέπιεν ὁ θάνατος ἰσχύσας, quasi dicat, antea devoraverant homines mors praevalens seu victrix, sed deinde abstulit Do- minus lacrimam ab omni facie. Si haec lectio tempore Pauli extabat, valde credibile est, con- sulto eum aliter reddidisse hanc sententiam, ut priorem interpretationem emendaret. Et quia passiva sunt pleniora, verbum reddidit passive, absorpta est.

Deinde phrasis usitatissima est לָנֶצַח ad finem vel ad victoriam, et alias tempus, alias mo- dum significat, id est, vel in sempiternum vel omnino, quasi dicas, re penitus superata, ut eius finis sit. Paulus inquit: ἐς νῖκος, id est, ad victoriam, ut sit sententia: Absorpta est mors, vel Dominus devoravit mortem ad victoriam, id est, omnino, ita ut sit penitus victa, vel ab- sorpta est in sempiternum. Psalmo 9.: Inimici defecerunt frameae in finem לָנֶצַח, id est, pror- sus, et saepe alias. Hae interpretationes nequa- quam dissentiunt.

Cognita autem Grammatica, hanc dulcissi- mam concionem transferamus ad usum in feris doloribus, et tam illustri testimonio erecti, fir- mius statuamus, peccatum et mortem vere devo- rata et deleta esse per filium Dei victorem, nec ruamus in exitium conspectu peccati et mortis. Fortassis lectio Graeca Esaiae olim alia fuit, κα- τέπιεν θάνατον ὁ ἰσχύσας, devoravit mortem victor Dominus. Ambrosius legit: Absorpta est mors ad contentionem, sed erravit, existimans scriptum esse νεῖκος cum diphthongo, quod significat contentionem. Aliud autem nomen est νῗκος, quod significat victoriam. In ea enim significatione Paulus et postea utitur voce νῗκος: Gratia qui dedit nobis victoriam. Ubi alienissimum esset legere, qui dedit nobis contentionem. Nec dubium est Paulum voluisse reddere verbum Nezah.

Ut autem Esaiae dictum illustrius et dulcius fiat, tota illa concio Esaiae 25. saepe legenda et cogitanda est.

Sequitur alterum dictum sumtum ex capite Hoseae 13., quod Hieronymus sic interpretatur: Ero mors tua o mors, morsus tuus ero inferne. Nec obscura est sententia, sed de Grammatica et emphasi verborum disputationes motae sunt. Certum est enim hic quoque praedici, futurum esse, ut mors aboleatur per Messiam, et vita aeterna restituatur. Coniunxit igitur duorum Prophetarum testimonia, quia prorsus idem affirmant. Prior disputatio est de vocabulis, Ubi et Ero. Hieronymus reddidit אהי ero, et narrat eandem interpretationem esse apud Symmachum. Sed usitate apud Graecos, et quinta editio et Aquila interpretantur Ubi: cum his congruit Paulina lectio.

Si legas Ero, complecteris personam victoris: Ego Messias, qui sum Iehova, ero pestis mortis, id est, delens seu abolens mortem mea resurrectione, sicut et antea dixit: Perditio ex te est, at in me auxilium est. Ut igitur persona victoris comprehendatur, aliqui magis amant lectionem Ero.

Deinde asseveratio plenior est, cum dicit: Ero mors tua o mors, quanquam vocabuli אהי usus est ambiguus, tamen Grammatici norunt iuxta analogiam magis esse futurum Ero.

Alii quibus placet interrogatio Ubi, moventur eo, quod libenter vocabula pestis et luis accomodant ad mortem, et ad infernum. Malunt dici pestem mortis et luem inferorum deletam, quam dici Christum esse pestem mortis. Volunt enim illustrari emphasin. Mors non est malum naturale, sicut putrefactio pomi. Sed cum morte seu interitu hominis est horribilis sensus irae Dei. Ut igitur intelligamus utrunque abolitum esse, et mortem et sensum irae Dei, probant interrogationem, quae copulat utrunque, Et gloriose velut in carmine ἐπινικίῳ affirmat mortem et vires mor- tis extinctas esse. Idque voluisse Paulum osten- dit eius lectio et enarratio quam addit: Ubi est mors aculeus tuus? Et postea inquit, peccatum esse hunc aculeum, quia cum peccatum osten- ditur, sensu irae Dei homines extinguuntur, ut Psalmo 89. dicitur: Posuisti iniquitates nostras in conspectu tuo, et in ira tua defecimus. Item, Esaiae 38.: Sicut leo contrivit omnia ossa mea. Hos ingentes dolores, et fugam in morte dicit oriri a peccato et lege ostendente peccatum, ut experientia ostendit. Ideo dicit peccatum esse aculeum mortis. Et in verbis Oseae ponit κέν- τρον, quod in Graeca versione in altero membro ponitur: ποῦ τὸ κέντρον σοῦ ᾅδη; In priore membro sunt usi hanc voce δίκη: ποῦ ἡ δίκη σοῦ ϑάνατε; Ubi est iudicium tuum mors, vel accu- satio, vel poena, qua nos afficis? Id congruit cum sententia Pauli, Non tantum aboleri mor- tem, id est, ipsum interitum, sed accusationem seu poenam quoque, id est, sensum irae Dei. Haec breviter recitavi, ut quae sit emphasis in utraque lectione consideretur. In summa sen- tentiae non est ambiguitas. Nam utraque lectio docet, Messiam credentibus redditurum esse iu- sticiam et vitam aeternam, abolitis peccato, morte et inferis.

Addit autem Paulus brevem repetitionem doctrinae suae de lege. Aculeus mortis peccatum est, potentia vero peccati lex est. Nequaquam hic loquitur de politico usu legis, sed ut Roman. 7. de illo tristissimo iudicio, in quo Deus cogita- tione legis ostendit iram suam adversus peccata. Ut David expavescit, cum obiurgatur voce Na- than. Et de se inquit Paulus, Roman. 7.: Pec- catum ut fiet excellenter peccatum, id est, reum, per bonum, in me effecit mortem. Haec tota doctrina saepe repetita est in Pauli scriptis. Et opponenda est somniis pharisaicis, qui fingunt homines lege mereri remissionem peccatorum, cum lex tantum sit iudicium, quod Deus hor- rendam iram suam adversus peccatum in nobis ostendit.

Hic autem addit Paulus antithesin: Gratia Deo, qui dat nobis victoriam per Dominum no- strum Iesum Christum, quasi dicat: Cum lege perterrefacti sumus, sciamus hanc solam veram et efficacem consolationem nobis propositam esse, de qua dicitur in Iohanne: Sic Deus dilexit mun- dum, ut filium suum unigenitum daret, ut omnis qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam. In his terroribus fide statuamus propter filium Dei passum, resuscitatum et regnantem certo nobis remitti peccata, imputari nobis ipsius iusticiam, nos fieri iustos et haeredes vitae aeternae. Hac fide vincimus per filium Dei terrores peccati et mortis, ut Roman. 5. dicitur: Iustificati fide pacem habemus apud Deum. Et quidem in hac ipsa consolatione datur Spiritus sanctus, qui efficit pacem, id est, laetitiam cordis, et initium vitae aeternae, iuxta dictum: Effundam super domum David spiritum gratiae et precum, id est, quod sentient se esse in gratia, et liberatos ex pavoribus et morte aeterna, et poterunt iam vere laetari in Deo et eum invocare, sicut Roman. 8. dicitur: Accepistis spiritum adoptionis filiorum, quo clamamus Abba pater. Hanc consolationem necesse est omnibus, in exercitiis poenitentiae notam fieri, quam qui intelligunt, vident, quam tetri sint errores monachorum, qui fingunt homines mereri remissionem suis operibus, et iubent manere in dubitatione. Hi furores pugnant etiam cum hoc triumphali praeconio, quod hic recitat Paulus: Gratia Deo qui dat victoriam per Iesum Christum.

Ἑδραῖοι γίνεσθε, ἀμετακίνητοι. Firmi estote etc.

Postquam refutavit furores eorum, qui de resurrectione falsas opiniones sparserant, addit in fine brevem adhortationem, in qua praecipit, ut constanter retineant integram doctrinam ab Apostolis traditam, nec admittant corruptelas in ullo articulo.

Addit autem et consolationem dulcissimam: Labor vester non est inanis in Domino. Haec sententia nobis omnibus semper in conspectu sit: primum ut leniamus dolores privatos hac spe, quod post hanc vitam certo simus futuri in consuetudine aeternae Ecclesiae, in qua Deus nobis communicabit sapientiam, bonitatem et laetitiam suam.

Deinde ut huic dolori, quem habemus, cum non videntur multi proficere ex nostris laboribus, opponamus hanc asseverationem, aliquos tamen emendari, et ad colligendam et ad conservandam Ecclesiam aliquo modo nostram vocem et nostram sedulitatem prodesse. Hac consolatione nobis valde opus est. Quia eum homo existimat, suos labores prorsus inanes esse, nec prodesse aliis, voluntas deterreretur, ut prorsus abiiciat incoatas operas. Huic tentationi opponendae est haec dulcissima sententia: Labor vester non est inanis in Domino, id est, Deus ipse efficiet, ut labores nostri aliquibus prosint, et iuvent conservatio- nem Ecclesiae, etiamsi magna multitudo est fu- renter contemnens Deum, et turbans Ecclesiam et communem vitae societatem.

Sequamur ergo hanc regulam saepe repeti- tam in concionibus divinis: Obtemperemus man- dato Dei, quod praecipit operas vocationis, et speremus Deum gubernaturum esse eventus, iuxta dictum: Commenda Deo viam tuam, et spera in eo, et ipse faciet. Et de successu haec testimo- nia nota sint, Iohan. 15.: Qui manet in me, et ego in eo, hic feret fructum copiosum. Item: Posui vos, ut eatis, et fructum feratis, et fructus vester maneat. Et Psalm. 1.: Folium eius non defluet, et omnia quaecunque faciet, prospera- buntur. Et Esaiae 55.: Verbum meum, quod egredietur de ore meo, non redibit ad me va- cuum. Et Esaiae 65.: Electi mei non laborabunt frustra. Huc addantur et insignes consolationes recitatae in Ecclesiaste capite 11.: Mane semina semen tuum, et vespere ne cesset manus tua, quia nescis utrum magis oriatur. Et ibidem picturam illustrem proponit. Videntur perire ea, quae in aquam sparguntur. At Salomon iubet, ut panes, id est, doctrinam tanquam in aquas spargamus, et affirmat nos tamen post aliquod tempus re- cepturos fructum eius laboris. Obediamus igi- tur his mandatis: Insta opportune, importune, argue, increpa, adhortare. Et certo statuamus, ipsum filium Dei in hoc suo ministerio effi- cacem fore, sicut inquit: Ego ero vobiscum usque ad consummationem seculi. Etiamsi pauci proficient, et videtur tanquam in aquas spargi doctrina, tamen semper aliqui proficient, sicut inquit: Qui manet in me, et ego in eo, ille feret fructum copiosum. Et semper aliqua erit vera Ecclesia, etiamsi erit exigua, ut Esaiae 65. ait, similem fore vindemiae, in qua paucae uvae, sed gratae reperiantur. Hanc totam consolationem singuli nobis in hoc docendi munere necessariam esse intelligimus. Ideo hoc dictum Pauli, et cae- tera congruentia testimonia saepe cogitemus, nec fracti dolore aut desperatione officia vocationis omittamus.

Certum est morem fuisse etiam in Israël, ut cum in diebus festis populus convenisset, singuli aliquid conferrent ad usus egentium aliena libera- litate. Hunc morem Apostoli tradiderunt etiam Ecclesiis. Et eo tempore, quo Paulus hanc Epi- stolam scripsit, multi in Iudaea expellebantur ex possessionibus. Et simul Claudii tempore prae- cipue in Oriente fames tam saeva fuit, ut modius frumenti sex drachmis venderetur. Exemplum autem consideretur, quod monet, ut in publicis congressibus Ecclesiae hoc pium genus liberalita- tis exerceatur, et singuli aliquid conferant. Ac historiae ostendunt, veterem Ecclesiam in hoc genere valde officiosam fuisse.

Εἴ τις οὐ φιλεῖ τὸν κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν, ἤτω ἀνάθεμα.

Caetera dicta in hoc capite nihil obscuritatis habent. Adscripsit autem Paulus sua manu gra- vissimam sententiam, quae omnibus notissima esse debet: Si quis non diligit Dominum Iesum Christum, sit anathema Maran atha. Damnat utrosque et manifestos hostes Evangelii, et hypo- critas, qui praetextu religionis quaerunt suam potentiam aut alia commoda, et inflectunt Evan- gelion ad hominum cupiditates, et miscent cor- ruptelas, adversus tales omnes hanc vocem iudi- cii dvini pronunciat, et tanquam fulmen mittit, ut Iohannes Baptista inquit: Qui credit in filium, habet vitam aeternam, qui autem non credit filio, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manebit super eum. Et de hypocritis et malis doctoribus extant comminationes saepe repetitae, ut Matth. 25.: Et inutilem servum eiiciet in tenebras quae foris sunt. Ibi erit fletus et stridor dentium.

Primum autem dicit, Sit anathema, id est, quiddam damnatum, sicut huius vocabuli usus in Ecclesia notus est, ut ad Galatas: Si quis aliud Evangelium docet, anathema sit. Et ratio ety- mologiae sumatur ex lege de consecratis, quae tolli et interfici oportuit.

Addit autem peregrina vocabula Maran atha, quae verba recitative ponuntur, et grammatica ad- positione attexenda sunt dictioni proximae, quasi dicat: Sit anathema, id est, sit damnatus hac ipsa tristissima sententia, quae sunt verba ana- thematis: Maran atha, id est, Dominus noster venit, scilicet, ad puniendum, et ad declaran- dam tristissimam iram, quam antea contemsisti. Sunt igitur haec vera imprecatio poenae, ut si diceretur: Εὗρε θεὸς τὸν ἄλιτρον.

Vel sicut Psalmus 57. inquit: Laetabitur iustus, cum viderit vindictam, manus suas lavabit in san- guine peccatoris, et dicet homo, utique est fru- ctus iusto, utique est iudicans in terra. Talis est asseveratio de venturo iudicio, et de poena in his verbis: Dominus noster venit.

Est autem sermo Syriacus seu Chaldaicus affinis Ebraico, quia vicinae gentes linguam Ebraeam a patribus retinuerunt, sed paulatim depravarunt, ut fieri solet, vestigia tamen agnosci possunt. Mar seu Mara significat Dominum, ut in Thargum, Proverb. cap. 25. et Amos 1. Con- sentaneum est autem nomen, Mara esse a dictione מוֹרֶה quod significat Doctorem, vel a dictione מוֹרָא quod significat terribilem. Et notae sunt origines יוֹרֶה docuit, et יָרֵא timuit. Et in vita Hilarionis legitur, illius aetate adhuc idolum fuisse in Syria Maras. Fuit autem usitatum no- vis idolis et cultibus tribuere nova nomina, quae videbantur maiorem significare. Ut post primum cultum, in quo Deus nominabatur יְהוָה אֱלוֹהַ impii homines, qui veterem doctri- nam et cultum reliquerunt, nominarunt Deum בַּעַל possessorem, δεσπότην. Postea vicini aliud terribilius nomen excogitarunt, Maran, id est, terribilis noster. Ita cum discessum est a vera doctrina, et veris cultibus, superstitio et nomina nova et opiniones, et ritus alios fingit. Fuit igitur Mara nomen usitatum in Syria. Appen- dix n, vel na, est noster Atha, venit. Hanc esse nativam interpretationem vocabuli Maran atha affirmant, et saepe usurpari in Iudaicis enar- rationibus scribunt. Ideo mirum est, cur Bur- gensis vir doctus aliam etymologiam excogita- verit, qui pro Maran atha fecit Meherem motha, et dicit Apostolum voluisse atrocissimam speciem condemnationis nominare: Qui non diligit Chri- stum, sit non vulgare anathema, sed Meherem, id est, res deleta sua vastata, et tale anathema, quod occidi necesse sit, ideo additum esse exi- stimat Motha, quasi dicat: Anathema vasta- tioni et morti destinatum, quia non omnia con- secrata interficiebantur. Hanc etymologiam Bur- gensis ideo recitavi, ne sit ignota iunioribus, non quod eam probem, cum adpareat longius accersi- tam esse. Amplectamur autem alteram, quam et Hieronymus tradit, et cum sermone commen- tariorum congruere aiunt. Maran atha, id est, Dominus noster venit. Et sciat lector haec verba recitative poni tanquam formulam, qua iudex poenas seu diras imprecatus est. Continet autem haec postrema clausula gravissimam comminatio- nem adversus omnes hostes Evangelii et hypocri- tas, ac praesertim doctrinae corruptores. Ideo sinceris pectoribus quaeramus veritatem, et ipsum filium Dei Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum oremus, us nos Spirito suo sancto gubernet.

SECUNDAE EPISTOLAE AD CORINTHIOS, ARGUMENTUM.

Semper in conspectu sit discrimen Legis et Evan- gelii, et sciamus non tantum historias peregrina- tionum Pauli et praecepta moralia in eius scriptis quaerenda esse, sed longe aliam sapientiam de filio Dei, et de eius beneficiis, de remissione pec- catorum, de miranda collectione Ecclesiae, et de vita aeterna. Sed tamen iis, qui doctrinam Ecclesiae recte didicerunt, utile est etiam tem- pora et seriem historiae nosse. Ut igitur consi- deremus, quo tempore primum venerit Paulus Corinthum, et quando postea scripserit Epistolas ad Ecclesias eius loci, ordine utcunque distribuam annos.

Anni a conversione Pauli.

Anno Christi. An. post con- versionem.

35. 1. Annus Pauli conversionis, Annus a natali Christi 35.

36. 2. Ivit Paulus in Arabiam.

39. 5. Ivit in Tarsum, Acto. 9.

42. 8. Barnabas ex Tarso duxit Paulum Antiochiam, Acto. 13.

44. 10. Ivit in Cyprum, Act. 13. Ubi auditor fuit Sergius proconsul.

45. 11. Profectus in Pergen et Iconium Act. 14. et vicinas urbes.

51. 17. Synodus Ierosolymae, cui Paulus interfuit.

52. 18. Rediit in Iconium et Lystram, ubi Timotheum sibi adiunxit, et traiecit in Macedoniam, et fuit Corinthi.

Anno Christi. An. post con- versionem.

55. 21. Rediit in Asiam, et fuit biennio in Epheso.

58. 24. Rediit Paulus in Macedoniam, prius peragrata Phrygia et finibus Ga- latarum. Cumque venisset in Macedoniam, sicut hic inquit se ex Troade traiecisse, scripsit in Philippis utranque Epistolam ad Corinthios non longo inter- vallo. Postea rediit in Asiam, ac venit Mytilenen, item in Sa- mum et Miletum.

64. 30. Circa hoc tempus fecit Paulus iter postremum Ierosolymam, inde missus est Romam captivus.

66. 32. Paulus Romam missus, fuit bien- nium in domo conducta Acto. ult. De reliquo tempore non scribi- tur, sed tamen consentaneum est, eum Romae mansisse usque ad annum penultimum Neronis, quo interfectus est, quia non le- guntur alia Pauli itinera, post- quam Romam venit. Et illud reliquum tempus breve est.

69. 35. Interfectus Paulus a Nerone anno 13. Neronis.

70. 36. Decimus quartus Neronis, quo Nero ibi conscivit mortem. Hanc brevem recitationem addidi, in qua praecipua itinera recensentur. Nam omnia certo in singulos annos distribui non possunt. Ac ad- paret annis posterioribus Claudii ac deinde Nero- nis tempore saepe eadem Asiae et Graeciae loca pervagatum esse.

Videmus autem in priore Epistola multas materias complexum esse, quia ita fit, constituta Ecclesia, non diuturna tranquillitas manet, sed diaboli insidiis et vanitate ingeniorum turbatur. Ita cum Corinthi orta essent dissidia, et multae quaestiones motae, de coniugio, de usu libertatis evangelicae, de consuetudine cum noverca, de conviviis apud amicos redeuntes ex sacrificiis, de resurrectione et aliae; Paulus graviter ad singulas quaestiones respondit, et ostendit se magno dolore affici propter scandala. Cum igitur Corinthii re- sponderent, et signa emendationis ostenderent, Paulus nunc respondet lenius, ac primum excusat se, quod nunc non accedat ad eos, inquiens se venturum esse tempore minus tristi.

In secundo capite iubet recipi lapsum, qui consuetudinem habuerat cum noverca. Id exem- plum observandum est contra Novatianos, quia manifeste docet lapsos a peccato absolvendos et recipiendos esse.

In tertio capite generaliter concionatur de efficacia ministerii evangelici, et de discrimine legis et Evangelii, et de cruce.

Haec commemoratio praecipue necessaria fuit, et semper in Ecclesia necessaria est. Ut enim olim ante adventum Messiae Iudaei multi, qui inter gentes vixerant, ut Daniel et alii, ad- iunxerant sibi auditores, alii recte tradentes do- ctrinam de Messia, alii tantum de externa disci- plina legis concionantes: ita Pauli tempore multi Iudaei adhuc inter gentes auditores habebant, quos tamen tantum de externa disciplina legis docebant. Hi cum audirent a Pauli doceri Mes- siam venisse, et politiam Iudaicam interituram esse, et homines non mereri remissionem peccatorum lege, non esse iustos lege. Execrabantur hanc novam doctrinam, pugnantem cum opinionibus, quas antea tradiderant ipsi, cum docuissent Eth- nicos, venturum Messiam, qui uno imperio om- nes gentes in toto orbe terrarum coniuncturus es- set, et perfecturus, ut eodem modo, videlicet lege Moysi, verum Deum, idolis abolitis, invo- carent. Eandem opinionem multi Pseudoapo- stoli confirmabant. Cum autem Paulus aliter doceret, Iudaei passim ei adversabantur, et suos auditores contra eum concitabant. Et alioqui Ethnici caeteri abhorrebant a novo genere doctrinae, et nolebant idola taxari.

Opponit igitur clamoribus Iudaeorum et Pseudoapostolorum hanc longam concionem de discrimine legis et Evangelii, et de efficacia ministerii evangelici, et de cruce, quasi dicat: Etsi antea Iudaei vos docuerunt de lege, et idola damnaverunt, et utcunque de disciplina legis concionati sunt: tamen Evangelium alia doctrina est, ostendit donari remissionem peccatorum, non propter legem, sed propter Messiam, et simul effundit Spiritum sanctum in corda credentium, et incoari aeternam iusticiam et vitam, et exhiberi iam bona aeterna, quorum umbrae in lege propositae fuerunt. Et haec revera fiunt voce nostri ministerii, cui Deus testimonia addit manifestis miraculis, quanquam subiecti sumus cruci, et non possumus delere gentes, ut Moyses et Iosua occupabant Cananaeam, et ut Iudaei existimant, Messiam armis domiturum esse gentes.

Hac occasione disputationum Pauli considerata, intelligi potest, quare has conciones instituerit, et quid velit docere. Ideo in tertio capite hanc maxime memorabilem sententiam proponit: Lex est litera et ministerium mortis, sed Evangelium est ministerium spiritus. Haec vox nova erat Iudaeis, qui antea gentes utcunque de disciplina docuerant, sicut et saepe in Ecclesia fuit ignota, et nunc monachi et similes ab ea abhorrent. Ut autem Prophetarum tempore semper aliqui fuerunt huius doctrinae illustratores: ita haec propria vox est Apostolorum, ostendere discrimen legis et Evangelii, et immensa bonitate Deus subinde in Ecclesia renovat hoc discrimen. Extincta fuit haec lux interpretationibus Origenis, qui finxit homines iustos esse lege, id est, disciplina morali, et literam tantum interpretatus est, ceremonias externas, et spiritum, allegorias. Postea Augustinus errorem late sparsum taxavit et ostendit, literam esse, et ceremonias et opera moralia, quae fiunt humana diligentia, non Spiritu sancto vivificante corda in veris pavoribus. Spiritum vero esse ipsum Spiritum sanctum, vivificantem corda in veris pavoribus, et incoantem in nobis iusticiam et vitam aeternam, et illa bona re ipsa praestantem, quae significantur in lege.

Ita post Augustinum aliqui fuerunt, et re- cens Lutherus, qui discrimen illud legis et Evangelii, et literae ac spiritus renovarunt.

Commoratur in hoc discrimine Paulus a ter- tii capitis initio usque ad sextum caput, et miscet doctrinam et consolationes, quae quidem ex do- ctrina necessario sequuntur.

Primum discrimen ministerii legis et mini- sterii evangelici sumitur a proximis effectibus. Ministerium legis, sine voce Evangelii, est tantum ministerium mortis, id est, aut est politica disci- plina, quae est externa gubernatio et frenum po- tentiae locomotivae, ut nominamus: aut est iu- dicium, quo Deus ostendit in corde hominis hor- rendam iram adversus peccatum, de quo iudicio dicitur Esaiae 38.: Sicut leo contrivit omnia ossa mea. Et Paulus Rom. 3. ait: Per legem cognitio peccati. Item: Lex iram efficit, quia Deus hanc noticiam in homine post lapsum vo- luit reliquam esse, ut per eam regatur externa disciplina, et deinde ut sit vox sententiae, qua Deus monstret iram et condemnationem. Mani- festum est autem, non solum non tolli peccatum et mortem, iudicio illo et sensu irae Dei, sed etiam hunc ipsum sensum irae Dei esse pavores, et dolores tristiores ipsa morte corporis, et ini- tium aeternarum poenarum, nisi voce Evangelii per filium Dei homo liberetur, sicut scriptum est: Aculeus mortis peccatum est, Potentia peccati lex. Gratia autem Deo, qui dat nobis victoriam per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum. Prae- terea disciplina externa nec tollit peccata, nec meretur remissionem peccatorum, nec est imple- tio legis.

Sed Evangelium est ministerium spiritus, ut hic in capite tertio dicitur, id est, vox, qua Deus credenti remittit peccata propter filium, et dat Spiritum sanctum, quo corda in illo sensu irae Dei et in pavoribus eriguntur, et ex dolori- bus inferorum eripiuntur, et sentiunt pacem et laetitiam in Deo, et initia vitae aeternae.

Alterum discrimen est ab ulterioribus, et modis, qui accedunt. Lege promulgata, consti- tuitur politia Moysi, et adduntur gloriosae libe- rationes corporales, eductio ex Aegypto, et mul- tae admirandae victoriae, repressio cursus solis, et alia incurrentia in oculos multarum gentium, et quae proderant universae multitudini, sanctis et non sanctis.

Evangelii vero promulgatio non habet simi- lem politicam gloriam, nec constituit politiam mundanam, sed colligit alibi alios auditores in diversis politiis, et est ministerium, quo in eis incoantur iusticia et vita aeterna. Interea vero in hac mortali vita manent auditores subiecti cruci, et ingentibus aerumnis. Hac specie autem valde alienantur animi hominum ab Evangelio. Absurdissimum enim videtur, hos dispersos ho- mines sine politia, sine certa sede, sine certo imperio, sine praesidiis, qui passim a quibusli- bet interficiuntur, esse populum Dei. Nec con- sentaneum est, cum Moyses tam pulcram poli- tiam constituerit, Messiam nullum certum hospi- tium suis tradere.

Haec absurda semper omnes homines mo- vent. Sed Paulus respondet, Ministerio Evan- gelii afferri bona nequaquam peritura, ut intereunt politica: sed aeterna, et ait, huic voci etiam addi testimonia, ut resuscitationes mortuorum, et alia miracula. Et consolatur Ecclesiam dulcissimo argumento ex minore sumto.

Cum fuerit magna gloria et conservatio poli- tiae, quae in promulgatione legis instituta est, quae tamen fuit res interitura: conservabitur haud dubie etiam Ecclesia, et erit maior eius gloria, etiamsi dissimiliter haec fiunt.

Post has collationes legis et Evangelii, cum hoc ministerio Messiae non constituatur regnum politicum, ut Iudaei somniarunt, et Ecclesia in diversis imperiis et in persecutione colligatur: necesse est doceri Ecclesiam de cruce, et de ven- tura liberatione in vita aeterna. Addit igitur Paulus in capite 4 et 5. conciones de cruce, et de vita aeterna: et inserit insignes sententias de cae- teris Evangelii membris, qualis haec est in fine 5. capitis, quae est tanquam epilogus superiorum: De Christo legatione fungimur, tanquam Deo ad- hortante per nos, et precamur nomine Christi: Reconciliamini Deo. Eum enim, qui non novit peccatum pro nobis fecit peccatum, ut nos fiamus iusticia Deo in ipso. Etsi autem tota lectio plena est doctrinae necessariae, tamen haec sententia praecipue digna est consideratione, quia et mini- sterii dignitatem illustrat, et postea splendidissimis figuris concionatur de redemtore. Duae sunt hic adpellationes, altera peccati, altera iusticiae Dei. Nihil autem tristius nominari potest, quam pec- catum, quia est malum, cui Deus horribiliter irascitur, et quod horribiliter damnatum est a Deo. Rursus nihil gloriosius et melius est, quam iusticia Dei, id est, quiddam placens Deo, et con- gruens cum voluntate Dei, et vivens luce et vita aeterna divinitus donata. Considera igitur hoc loco permutationem. Filius Dei est sine peccato, sicut hic dicitur, Non novit peccatum, id est, non habet, non vult ullum malum pugnans cum voluntate Dei, sed et essentia est iustus, et habet deinde obedientiam perfectam, qua se subiicit aeterno patri assumta humana natura, et hac obedientia legi satisfacit, et solvit λύτρα pro nobis, sicut ipse nominat, Matth. 20. Quanquam igitur iusticia Dei, id est, lux et rectitudo divina et perfecta obedientia est in filio, tamen ipse fit pro nobis peccatum, id est, quiddam reum coram Deo, et ira Dei in ipsum effunditur. Etsi enim genus humanum per mi- sericordiam a Deo recipitur, tamen etiam iusti- ciae divinae satisfieri oportuit, ac inenarrabilis copulatio misericordiae et iusticiae facta est. Ita receptum est genus humanum, si poenam solve- ret aliquis in genere humano. Sed ut valeret poena pro aliis, hunc redemtorem oportuit esse sine peccato. Ideoque redemtor dicitur, quia pretium pro nobis persolvit. Fit igitur peccatum, id est, reum quiddam, sentit horrendam iram aeterni patris, contra omnium peccata, quasi ipse se tuis et meis et omnium peccatis polluisset. Huius doloris magnitudinem nulla creatura satis intelligere potest. Contra vero tibi et omnibus credentibus tri- buit id, quod in coelo summum est. Cum ipse sit iustus iusticia Dei, id nobis tribuit, primum imputatione et incoatione, postea etiam consum- matione. Nos qui reipsa sumus immundi et rei peccati, tegimur per filium, pronunciamur non rei, sed iusti, Deo iustificante, id est, acceptante nos, et simul renovante et vivificante. Nihil maius dici aut cogitari potest. Ita inquit, Esaias cap. 61.: Gaudens gaudebo in Domino, et exul- tabit anima mea in Deo meo. Quia induit me vestimentis salutis, et indumento iusticiae cir- cumdedit, et est ipse sicut sponsus in sacerdotali ornatu, et nos sicut sponsa ornata monilibus. Primum inquit se laetari non viribus naturae no- strae, aut ullius creaturae auxilio, sed gaudebo inquit in Domino Deo meo. Gaudebo me re- conciliatum esse Deo, et me ipsius Dei opera a summis malis liberatum esse, et iam in eo vivere vita aeterna. Induit me, inquit, vestimento iusticiae, id est, tegit me remissione peccatorum, et imputatione iusticiae, imo et effectione novae et aeternae iusticiae. Ipse tanquam vestem mihi circumdat suam iusticiam, quae mihi imputatur, et simul novam et aeternam iusticiam in me incoat. Vestit me etiam salute, id est, vita aeterna, et aliis donis in hac vita et post hanc vitam. Et ipse est sicut sponsus in sacerdotali ornatu. Filius Dei est sponsus Ecclesiae, vere eam diligit et servat. Amplectitur autem eam in sacerdotali ornatu: primum quia ipse est summus sacerdos, offerens seipsum pro nobis, prostratus coram patre, deprecans pro misera sponsa: deinde etiam resuscitatus adiungens eam sibi, et ornans eam Spiritu sancto, et semper pro ea intercedens, instituens et conservans ministerium, protegens et salvans eam.

Astat et ipsa apud sponsum, decorata similibus ornamentis, congruentibus huic sponso, foris cruce, intus remissione peccatorum, Spiritu sancto, imputatione iusticiae, et deinde aeterna iusticia et vita, huic uni sponso addicta, non polluta, ullis idolis, ardens dilectione huius sponsi, et per ipsum adducta ad aeternum patrem, et laeta in omni aeternitate celebrans Deum, fruens eius luce, sapientia, iusticia, et vita. Hae sunt illae aeternae nuptiae, ad quas haec sponsa ornata a sponso ducitur. Talium dictorum collatione fit illustrior hic locus Pauli.

In sexto capite, postquam antea doctrinam Evangelii recitavit, addit adhortationem, ut incoata dona retineamus et exerceamus, et miscet consolationes. Nominatim vero prohibet confusiones religionum. Iubet ut vitent idolorum cultus et sacrificia, quae idolis fiebant. Fuit autem mos, ex sacrificata carne convivia instruere, ad quae familiae totae convocabantur. Haec contagia prohibet, sicut nunc necesse est pios fugere profanationem coenae Domini in Missa pontificia, adorationes panis in circumgestatione, invocationes mortuorum, ut in enarratione copiosius dicetur.

In septimo capite repetit priorem adhortationem, ut vitemus idola. Et statim postea lenit eorum dolorem, quem attulerat eis indignatio Pauli, ubi mira solicitudo Apostoli conspicitur.

Non vult relinquere in animis eorum ullam suspi- cionem animi exulcerati, sed vult illos certo scire, penitus deletam esse offensionem, ut sit firmior benevolentia, et ne dissidia oriantur, quod fieret, si simultates tacitae manerent reliquae. Inserit autem necessariam doctrinam de conversione seu poenitentia, partem esse ministerii in Ecclesia ar- guere peccata, et oportere in conversione dolo- res oriri. Haec tota sententia referenda est ad communem doctrinam de Contritione, de qua di- citur: Sicut leo contrivit omnia ossa mea. Et Esaiae 66.: Ad quem respiciam? nisi ad humi- liatum et contritum spiritu etc. Et Psalmo 50.: Sacrificium Deo spiritus contribulatus, cor con- tritum et humiliatum non despicies. Item, Deut. 4.: Deus ignis consumens est.

Vult Deus aliquo modo agnosci peccata, et iram suam adversus peccata. Non vult eam ne- gligi, et damnat secura et ferrea corda, ut apud Ieremiam cap. 8.: Erubescere nescierunt. Esa. 48.: Frons tua aenea. Et Zachar.: Posuerunt cor suum velut adamantem. Et Paulus ad Ephesios ait, impios esse ἀπηλγηκότας, id est, sine do- lore, securos, contemnentes iudicium Dei. Hae tristissimae conciones observandae sunt, ut scia- mus necessariam esse contritionem, quam sic no- minant, scilicet veros pavores et dolores propter iram Dei adversus nostra peccata.

In octavo et in nono adhortatur Corinthios, ut collatione eleemosynae iuvent Ecclesias in Orien- te, quae indigebant aliena liberalitate, et quia multi pii ex suis possessionibus expellebantur, et quia tunc Claudii imperatoris tempore fames adeo saeva erat, ut modii pretium fuerint 6 drach- mae, cum usitatis annis esset una drachma, ut si Lipsici medimni pretium sit usitatum dimidius Ioachimicus, tunc venditus esset trib. Ioachimicis. Talis difficultas fuit in Germania anno 1517.

Multa sunt autem dicta insignia in hac ad- hortatione. Fit mentio aequalitatis. Hic non intelligatur aequalitas ἀναλογίᾳ arithmetica: nec fingamus Paulum docere Platonicam rerum com- munionem, aut Spartanam exaequationem facul- tatum, ut Anabaptistae finxerunt. Certissimum est enim in Evangelio non constitui politias ex- ternas, sed adprobari rerum distinctionem, et legitima imperia, ut suo loco copiosius dicetur. Sed loquitur Paulus de aequalitate non dominii et possessionis, sed usus in communicatione volun- taria hominis benefici erga egentes, iuxta dictum:

Fontes tui deriventur foras, et tu Dominus eorum maneto. Tota haec collatio voluntaria est, nec necesse est praecise eam ad arithmeticam vel geo- metricam vel harmonicam proportionem accom- modare. Manifestum est sceleratum esse, facere aequalitatem proportione arithmetica, ut non plus numero possideat Isaac, quam Ismael. Nec necessaria est aequalitas proportione geometrica. Non necesse est Consulem duplo plus habere, quam alium civem: aut Consulem duplo plus conferre, quam alium civem. Magis congruere illa collatio cum harmonica proportione videtur, in qua nec proportionum, nec differentiarum aequalitas est, sed sicut se habet maximus terminus ad minimum, ita se habet differentia maximi et medii ad diffe- rentiam medii et minimi, ut: 3, 4, 6. Senarius est duplus ad tria. Ergo et differentiam medii et minimi, quae est unitas. Ita sunt Lucullus 6, Atticus 4, et Cicero exul egens 3. Si Lucullus dat duo talenta exulanti, det Atticus unum.

Sed tamen quia voluntaria collatio est, non necesse est ad haec vincula astringi. At Paulus ipse aliquoties testatur, se non postulare hanc colla- tionem ita, ut cogere ullum existimetur, sed se de voluntaria liberalitate loqui. Non igitur novam politiam Platonicam vel anabaptisticam constituit.

In capite nono commonefacit eos promissio- nis divinae, sicut in Evangelio dicitur Lucae 6.: Date, et dabitur vobis. Hic tenendum est discri- men promissionum. Alia est propria Evangelii promissio reconciliationis, qua tantum propter filium Dei gratis exhibentur remissio peccatorum et imputatio iusticiae.

Aliae sunt legales, quae valent in reconcilia- tis. Vult enim Deus pro bonis operibus recon- ciliatorum etiam sua quaedam praemia dare, ut vidua Sareptana alitur, quia fuit liberalis erga Eliam. Tribuamus Deo veritatem, et speremus ac petamus haec praemia, et hac spe et nos ad benefaciendum excitemus.

In decimo capite, 11. 12. addit refutationem Pseudoapostolorum, qui spargebant Iudaicas opi- niones, et gentibus imponere ceremonias Iudai- cas conabantur, ac somniabant, imperium Mes- siae tale fore, in quo politia Iudaica in totum mundum proferretur. Hi et aliorum Apostolo- rum exempla allegabant, qui adhuc in Iudaea et vicina patriis ritibus utebantur.

Opponit autem Paulus non solum recitatio- nem suorum laborum, sed etiam testimonia di- vina, quibus a Deo ipsius doctrina confirmata est. Inter haec testimonia recitat singularem patefa- ctionem divinitatis ipsi ostensam, ait se raptum esse in tertium coelum, quod intelligo dictum esse Hebraeorum more, qui coelum nominant etiam hunc aërem sub luna. Erit igitur imum coelum aër: secundum, orbes omnes, quibus vehuntur lumina, planetae et stellae: tertium, arcana sedes Dei, in hac ostensa est divinitas Paulo. Nec opus est curiose quaeri de hac sin- gulari ostensione, qualis fuerit, sicut nec scire possumus, quo modo se Moysi Deus in rupe osten- derit. Etsi enim multae piae mentes interdum clariorem lucem in consolationibus habent, tamen ostensiones factae Patribus, Prophetis et Aposto- lis, illustriores sunt, et nos scimus oportere nos fide acquiescere in verbo, sicut scriptum est: Beati qui credunt et non vident. Et quid hoc sit fide acquiescere, experientia docet, cum magni dolo- res fide et spe leniuntur, ut dicit Paulus: Iustifi- cati fide pacem habemus. Neque hoc quaeren- dum est, quales in Paulo fuerint dolores, qui hic nominatur σκόλοψ in carne, tantum stulta opinio abiiciatur, quae fingit fuisse incendia libidinum. Existimo autem fuisse singulares terrores, quales saepe describuntur in Psalmis, ut cum David inquit: Non est pax ossibus meis. Et variae sunt luctae fidei de multis doctrinae partibus, de Ecclesiae periculis, et de privata salute, in quibus animi valde cruciantur. Tales cruciatus significat, cum nominat σκόλοπα, id est, sudem seu palum prae- acutum, quia vetus supplicium fuit hominem configere palo, quod nominabant ἀνασκολοπίζειν, quod nunc quoque Turcis usitatum est: non enim leves molestias significat.

Et recenset ibi Paulus dulcissimam consola- tionem. Ait sibi petenti responsum esse, Sufficit tibi gratia mea, nam potentia mea in infirmitate perficitur: manent in aliis aliae imbecillitates. Semper autem in conspectu sit haec consolatio: Exuberat gratia supra delictum. Hanc consola- tionem hic proponit, recitans haec verba: Suffi- cit tibi gratia mea. Deinde praesentia Dei et auxilium infirmis ostenditur. Fit conspectior Dei praesentia, cum defendit Danielem inter leones, quam si inter barbaros homines eum tegeret, quos videretur ipse suo consilio posse flectere. Sic toti populo redeunti ex Babylone fit conspe- ctior praesentia Dei, cum defenditur imbellis multitudo, quae praesidia, nec moenia habebat, quam cum ante exilium haberet moenia et exerci- tus. Et sinit Deus accidere nobis inextricabilia mala humanis consiliis, ut destituti aliis auxiliis confugiamus ad ipsum, et liberati, fateamur nos divinitus servatos esse, ut in Psalm. dicitur: Pater et mater dereliquerunt me, Dominus autem sus- cepit me. Item: Orphano tu eris adiutor. Item, Psalm. 59.: Non egredieris Deus in virtutibus nostris, da nobis auxilium de tribulatione. Et, vana salus hominis.

In ultimo capite addit comminationem: Si venero, inquit, ac videro vos non esse emenda- tos, utar potentia spiritus ad puniendos aliquos. Significat enim se aliquibus imprecaturnm esse morbos, aliquibus mortem, sicut Petri voce in- terfectus est Ananias, Act. 5. Et Act. 13. Ely- mas magus visum amisit imprecatione Pauli. Sed mitigat Paulus hanc comminationem, quia ait, se prius velle auditis testibus causas cognoscere.

Addit etiam dictum memorabile, quod saepe citatur contra tyrannidem: Data est mihi potestas non ad destructionem, sed ad aedificationem, id est, vult nos Dominus uti potestate, non ut pri- vatis affectibus morem geramus, ut tyranni abu- tuntur potestate, sed vult nos ea uti ad aliorum salutem: primum singulos emendari cupit, et poenam omittere, deinde si poena necessaria est castigandis aliquibus, prosit exemplum caeteris.

Hactenus argumentum Epistolae secundae ad Corinthios recitatum est. Facilius enim sin- gulae partes intelligi poterunt, si lector primum considerabit summas rerum et seriem, et ani- madvertet, quae sint occasiones, cur alibi alias materias instituat. Nunc addemus brevem enar- rationem ipsi orationi Pauli.

# 2 Corinthians

## 1:1 Argument
SECOND EPISTLE Chapter one

IN the first and second chapter he excuses himself, because he did not return to Corinth immediately, as he had shown hope. He begins, however, with thanksgiving, as happens very often, because words of affection are familiar to introductions. Then he narrates that he was in great danger in Asia, and asks to be helped by the prayers of the Church, so that more people may celebrate the benefit of God, and give thanks to God. These are the beginnings of the first chapter.

Concerning the inscription and greeting I will say nothing now, because the exposition has been repeated often elsewhere.

In the introduction he gives thanks to God, because He helps him in afflictions. And he says this is done for the sake of the Church. Here a copious doctrine is contained, why the Church is subjected to the cross, and that it is certain that God is present to it in afflictions, as is said in Isaiah, that God dwells in the afflicted, namely in those who turn to God, and by faith receive the remission of sins, and seek and expect help, according to the saying: As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he may turn and live.

This doctrine concerning the law judging sin, and concerning consolation in afflictions, which is proposed in the Gospel, recited at length elsewhere, is to be repeated here in the mind. And especially let this comparison be considered: The law says: God is a consuming fire. He says here: I give thanks to the Father of mercies, and the God of all consolation. He affirms that God truly hears the afflicted, who, having turned, seek and expect help.

Here, however, he adds a singular final cause pertaining to teachers. Therefore teachers are more exercised by afflictions, and are delivered more gloriously, so that the Church, beholding their examples, may be confirmed in both things, in enduring hardships, and in faith discerning the presence of God, and seeking and expecting mitigation or liberation. Therefore he says thus: Consoling us in all affliction, so that we ourselves may be able to console others with the same consolation with which we are raised up, that is, with this assertion, that God is certainly present to us, and brings aid. Likewise: Whether we are troubled, we are afflicted for this reason, that the example of pa-

a and second.

tience and liberation may profit you, and you may be raised up by faith in similar calamities. Whether we are raised up by consolation, this also happens for your sake. Thus he says elsewhere: Be a pattern of the faithful in faith, in spirit etc.

Latin:

EPISTOLAE SECUND Caput primum

IN primo et secundo capite excusat se, quod non rediit Corinthum statim, sicut spem ostenderat. Orditur autem a gratiarum actione, ut fit saepis- sime, quia exordiis familiaria sunt verba affe- ctuum. Deinde narrat se in magno periculo in Asia fuisse, et petit se iuvari Ecclesiae precibus, ut plures celebrent beneficium Dei, et Deo gratias agant. Haec sunt initia primi capitis.

De inscriptione et salutatione nihil iam di- cam, quia enarratio alias saepe repetita est.

In exordio agit Deo gratias, quod in affli- ctionibus ipsi opitulatur. Et hoc ait fieri Eccle- siae causa. Hic copiosa doctrina continetur, quare Ecclesia subiecta sit cruci, et quod certum sit, adesse ei Deum in afflictionibus, sicut apud Esaiam dicitur, Habitare Deum in afflictis, scili- cet iis, qui ad Deum convertuntur, et fide ac- cipiunt remissionem peccatorum, et petunt et ex- pectant auxilium, iuxta dictum: Vivo ego, dicit Dominus, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed ut con- vertatur et vivat.

Haec doctrina de lege iudicante peccatum, et de consolatione in afflictionibus, quae in Evan- gelio proponitur, alibi prolixe recitata, hic mente repetenda est. Et praecipue consideretur haec collatio: Lex dicit: Deus est ignis consumens. Hic ait: Gratias ago patri miserationum, et Deo omnis consolationis. Affirmat Deum vere exau- dire afflictos, qui conversi petunt et expectant auxilium.

Hic autem singularem causam finalem addit pertinentem ad doctores. Ideo doctores magis exercentur afflictionibus, et liberantur gloriosius, ut Ecclesia intuens eorum exempla confirmetur in utraque re, in perferendis aerumnis, et in fide cernente praesentiam Dei, et petente et expe- ctante mitigationem aut liberationem. Ideo sic ait: Consolans nos in omni afflictione, ut possi- mus ipsi consolari alios eadem consolatione, qua nos erigimur, id est, hac asseveratione, quod Deus certo nobis adsit, et opem ferat. Item: Sive tribulamur, ideo affligimur, ut exemplum pa-

a et secundum.

tientiae et liberatio vobis prosit, et vos erigamini fide in similibus calamitatibus. Sive consolatione erigimur, fit hoc quoque vestra causa. Sic alibi inquit: Sis typus fidelium in fide, in spiritu etc.

## 1:8
For we do not want you to be ignorant.

After the thanksgiving, with which he begins the Epistle, he adds a narrative about his danger, which he says was so great that it could not be saved by any human aid. Here concerning the final cause he adds a memorable sentence. Therefore the Church is burdened with such hardships, from which it cannot escape by human counsels, so that in the liberation the presence of God may be seen, and faith in us may be confirmed. David is forced to confess that he was not restored to the kingdom by human aid. In such examples these sermons are to be learned: Vain is the salvation of man. Likewise: Your destruction is from yourself, O Israel, only in me is your help. Likewise: Father and mother have forsaken me, but the Lord has taken me up. Likewise, Psalm 71: He has delivered the poor, for whom there was no helper. Likewise, Psalm 124: Those who trust in the Lord, shall not be moved, like Mount Zion. Jeremiah in Lamentations chapter three: The mercies of the Lord, that we are not consumed, because his mercies do not fail. They return in the morning, and great is your mercy: the Lord is my portion, therefore I will wait for him. The Lord is good to those who hope in him.

He asks, however, to be helped by the prayers of the Church, and adds a notable admonition concerning thanksgiving. Once a benefit is given, God demands thanksgiving, as he says in the Psalm: Call upon me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me. So he says here, that thanks may be given by many for us from many persons.

Do these sayings mean the same thing? Through many, and from many persons? I do not think they mean the same. First, this is clear when he says: Through many. For he wishes thanks to be given to God by the voice of many people, and divine deliverances to be celebrated by many. But why does he say, from many persons? Here he signifies several reasons for celebrating the benefit.

As if several persons were speaking in some history.

Others may celebrate Paul's liberation for this reason, because it is useful to the Church that such a teacher should survive for a long time. Others may celebrate, because it is a glorious example, and it confirms many, so that they may more firmly conclude that this teacher was sent by God, and may more firmly embrace the doctrine. Others may celebrate, because they are moved by this example, so that they themselves also may dare to seek and expect liberations, just as in the Psalm an example is proposed for this reason, so that others also may flee to God: This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him.

For this is our boasting, the testimony of our conscience.

Here he institutes that part of the narrative in which he excuses himself for not having returned to Corinth, although he had indeed given them hope of a return.

And afterwards he says several times in this Epistle: that the confirmations of his ministry were many miracles, which showed him not to be an impostor, but a minister pleasing to God, and rightly performing his ministry, not lying in wait for the property of others, not seeking power, not forming factions to stir up seditions.

Now he begins only with the purity of his conscience: Although I have not yet returned, nevertheless I do not want you to suspect otherwise of me, as if I had not returned because I could not defend my doctrine against the Pseudo-apostles, or that I am ashamed of my course among you, or that I have sought something elsewhere.

But I affirm that I perform my ministry with a clear conscience, both among you and elsewhere, that I am not an impostor, but truly carry around the uncorrupted voice of the Gospel, and that I do not serve any private greed.

For he embraces an assertion both about doctrine and about private morals.

Therefore he says: This is our boasting, the testimony of our conscience, that in the simplicity and sincerity of God, not in carnal wisdom, but in the Grace of God I have conducted myself in the world.

That is, I affirm with a clear conscience that I neither corrupt the doctrine, nor astutely bend it to anyone's affections, nor serve any private greed.

Let us take examples from recent histories.

They do a favor to kings, who seek deceits, as to how they may bend the doctrine of the Church to the state, which pleases them, who artfully paint the Mass, or other rites. Many do a favor, who increase their power under the pretext of religion, and arm the people against those whom they try to shake off. These artifices are neither unknown nor unusual.

Thus there were those at that time who astutely adjusted the doctrine to the senses and wills of their own factions.

He denies that he did this, and calls carnal wisdom all such human counsels, whether for corrupting the doctrine, or for bending it in any way, so that it might appear more consistent to human reason, or be more accommodated to establishing the power of the factious.

He calls the purity of doctrine sincerity, just as he says to Titus: in teaching, incorruptness [ἀδιαφθορίαν].

He calls simplicity the uprightness of his will, not serving any private greed, or the affections of any factious people.

Very many examples could be taken from the histories of all times.

Many, both formerly and now, have openly corrupted the doctrine of the righteousness of faith, because it does not seem consistent to reason.

For however much human minds know the law, and judge righteousness to be obedience according to the law, and can in some way perform discipline.
