By this they pretend to merit the remission of sins and eternal life, and they are ignorant of the Messiah, nor do they discern the interior sins in their hearts, the darkness and doubts about God, and the disorder [ἀταξίαν] in the heart.

In this darkness of the human mind, men are prone to trust in their own righteousness, and they seek merits in themselves, and institute various exercises, as if they were the worship of God.

Therefore, from time to time in the Church, the light of the doctrine concerning the righteousness of faith has been greatly obscured, just as in the writings of Thomas and similar ones there is complete silence about the righteousness of faith, and the distinction between the law and the Gospel is confounded.

Such imaginations born in human reason Paul calls carnal wisdom, and thus other articles of faith have been corrupted, while consistency with reason is sought, or servitude to the affections of men, as at that time Ebion denied that the Messiah was the son of God, and many contended that Mosaic ceremonies should not be omitted, lest the most beautiful Israelite polity be dissolved.

From these examples it can be moderately understood what Paul intends here, when he affirms that he has taught sincerely, and has not corrupted the doctrine with human opinions or affections.

Question concerning the boasting of the conscience The question concerning the boasting of the conscience has been treated often elsewhere. Yet, nevertheless, the younger students must be briefly warned here also about these statements, which seem to disagree: 1 Corinthians 1: "Let no flesh boast before him." But it is said otherwise, 2 Corinthians 1: "Our boasting is the testimony of our conscience." The former prohibits boasting in anything of our own: the latter admits it, if there is no wound of conscience. But these statements, when placed in their proper order, do not disagree at all. Let no one boast, namely, of justification before God; that is, let no one think that he is righteous before God by any of his own virtues, just as Paul says elsewhere in exactly the same sense: "I am conscious of nothing against myself, yet I am not justified by this." But after we have been received by mercy through faith, the righteousness of a good conscience is also pleasing to God, and it is necessary to defend it, and it must be opposed to calumnies, because the lies of calumniators must by no means be confirmed.

For the divine voice says: "You shall not bear false witness." Hence also the disputation in the book of Job can be understood. He confesses that he is not righteous before God, and says in chapter nine: "I know truly that a man cannot be justified before God." Likewise: "It is God, whose wrath no one can resist." But he affirms that he has no wound of conscience, just as his friends were accusing him.

"I have not taught false things, my governance was not tyrannical, I am not polluted by adulteries." Therefore he says in chapter 27: "My justification, which I have begun to hold, I will not desert. For my heart does not reproach me in all my life." For as many as are the promises of God, in him they are Yes and Amen. He has not yet recounted the reason why he did not return to Corinth, but only says that it should not be attributed to fickleness that he delayed his journey. But he adds a sign, which shows that he is not vain and fickle, because he says: "You have known me to have been truthful in my ministry, and that my doctrine was effective among you, that you received the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and that God testified by many miracles that I am by no means an impostor." In this sense he says: "God is faithful, that our word among you was not 'yes and no,' but truthful and effective in God." Then he adds a general statement, that divine promises are valid and firm.

After he has delivered the general statement about divine promises, he adds an example concerning himself and the Corinthian Church: Since the promises are valid, and it is certain in the Gospel that these good things are promised—reconciliation, the Holy Spirit, and the inheritance of eternal life—it is not to be thought that our sermons are merely empty thelktēria (charms), just as fables are told to children about the Fortunate Isles or the Elysian fields; but it is most certain that we receive the good things promised in the Gospel, and you already feel in your heart the beginnings of a new light, and the Holy Spirit, who is the pledge and earnest, who shows certainly that God is with us, and that he will give us eternal life.

When this series of members is considered, the speech will be more perspicuous, and the magnitude of the things of which he speaks is more clearly seen. Let the younger students know that the word arrabo (earnest) is made from the Hebrew עֵרָבוֹן, which signifies "he pledged" or "he gave surety." Hence arrabo is said properly in purchases of something given for this purpose, that it may be a testimony of a confirmed purchase.

Thus is the outpouring of the Holy Spirit into the hearts of believers, which they feel in true consolation, and it is a testimony of reconciliation and of the presence of God, and of the future inheritance of eternal life. Just as it is said in Romans 8: "The Spirit himself testifies with our spirit that we are children of God; and if children, then also heirs." So also it is said in Zechariah: "I will pour out upon the house of David a spirit of grace and of supplications." He names the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son, raising us up in true terrors, and vivifying hearts with true consolation, which consolation we, feeling, dare to approach God and call upon him. Therefore, he is later named the spirit of supplications.

But I call God as a witness. Here, finally, with an oath added, he recounts the reason why he did not return to Corinth, because if he had come, he would have punished some more harshly. But when he had understood that they were in great grief on account of the rebuke which he wrote in the former Epistle, he did not wish to increase their sadness with harsher examples, if, having returned, he had struck some with the thunderbolt of his spirit, as Peter struck Ananias. Here it appears how great a fire there was in apostolic indignation and zeal. He signifies, therefore, that he did not return to Corinth for this reason, lest that indignation be inflamed even more in their presence. Just as otherwise prudent people, when they feel they are becoming angry, avoid the company of those with whom they are angry.

However, one must observe in this place the example of an oath, which shows that it is permitted for Christians to swear, as is said more fully elsewhere.

From this, however, it can be surmised that there were great causes for this indignation. Undoubtedly, some fanatical and proud Pseudo-apostles with their faction had greatly disturbed the Church of Corinth. But nevertheless, Paul represses his anger. Wherefore, having soon recited the reason why he did not come, he weaves in an occupation, so that he may meet a tacit objection. For some less modest persons could have said: Why do you threaten us? What kind of authority do you assume over us? We did not embrace the Gospel so that you might exercise tyranny over us; if such dangerous servitude must be borne, let us rather return to the Gentiles. He meets this objection in this way: I do not assume authority over you. I do not seek power or wealth, but I am a minister of your salvation, and he says this more gently, of your joy; I follow the rule handed down to me by God, who by this ministry of ours calls you to salvation, in which I only do those things, according to the rule handed down by God, which are salutary for you. And these things, as long as you stand in faith, will be pleasing to you.

Now here the distinction between political power and evangelical ministry should be considered, as is often said elsewhere. Political power restrains and punishes the unwilling by bodily force, as the Romans, after Capua was recovered, tied the Capuan senators to a stake and struck them with an axe against their will: but ecclesiastical power does nothing by bodily force; it does not have weapons and an army. These things are explained more fully elsewhere.

Latin:

Non enim volumus vos ignorare.

Post gratiarum actionem, qua incoat Epistolam, addit narrationem de suo periculo, quod ait fuisse tantum, ut nulla humana ope servari potuerit. Hic de causa finali addit memorabilem sententiam. Ideo Ecclesia talibus aerumnis oneratur, ex quibus eluctari humanis consiliis non potest, ut in liberatione conspiciatur praesentia Dei, et fides in nobis confirmetur. David fateri cogitur, se non humana ope in regnum restitutum esse. In talibus exemplis discendae sunt hae conciones: Vana salus hominis. Item: Perditio tua ex te Israël, tantum in me auxilium tuum. Item: Pater et mater dereliquerunt me, Dominus autem suscepit me. Item, Psalm. 71.: Liberavit pauperem, cui non erat adiutor. Item, Psalm. 124.: Qui confidunt in Domino, sicut mons Sion non commovebitur. Ieremias in Threnis capite tertio: Misericordiae Domini, quod non consumti sumus, qui non deficiunt miserationes eius. Mane redit, et magna est misericordia tua: pars mea Dominus, propterea expectabo eum. Bonus est Dominus sperantibus in eum.

Petit autem se iuvari precibus Ecclesiae, et addit insignem admonitionem de gratiarum actione. Dato beneficio postulat Deus gratiarum actionem, ut in Psalm. dicit: Invoca me in die tribulationis, et eripiam te, et glorificabis me. Ita hic inquit, ut gratiae agantur per multos pro nobis ex multis personis.

Idemne significant haec dicta? Per multos, et ex multis personis? Non existimo idem significare. Primum hoc perspicuum est cum ait: Per multos. Vult enim multorum hominum voce Deo gratias agi, et liberationes divinas a multis celebrari. Sed cur ait, a multis personis? Hic plures causas significat celebrandi beneficii.

Ut si plures personae in historia aliqua loquerentur.

Alii celebrent liberationem Pauli propter hanc causam, quia utile est Ecclesiae diu superstitem esse talem doctorem. Alii celebrent, quia gloriosum exemplum est, et confirmat multos, ut firmius statuant, hunc doctorem a Deo missum esse, ac firmius amplectantur doctrinam. Alii celebrent, quia moventur hoc exemplo, ut ipsi quoque ausint petere et expectare liberationes, sicut in Psalmo ob hanc causam exemplum proponitur, ut alii quoque confugiant ad Deum: Iste pauper clamavit, et Dominus exaudivit eum.

Gloriatio enim nostra haec est, testimonium conscientiae nostrae.

Hic instituit eam partem narrationis, in qua se excusat, quod non rediit Corinthum, cum quidem spem reditus ei fecisset.

Ac postea aliquoties in hac Epistola inquit: Ministerii sui confirmationes esse multa miracula, quae ostendebant ipsum non esse impostorem, sed ministrum Deo placentem, et recte fungentem suo ministerio, non insidiantem alienis facultatibus non potentiam quaerentem, non factiones constituentem ad movendas seditiones.

Nunc orditur tantum a puritate suae conscientiae: Etsi nondum redii, tamen nolo vos de me secus suspicari, quasi eo non redierim, quia non possim tueri doctrinam meam contra Pseudoapostolos, aut pudeat me cursus mei apud vos, aut alibi aliquid captarim.

Sed affirmo me optima conscientia, et apud vos et alibi fungi ministerio, me non esse impostorem, sed vere circumferre incorruptam vocem Evangelii, nec me servire ulli privatae cupiditati.

Complectitur enim asseverationem et de doctrina, et de privatis moribus.

Ideo inquit: Haec est gloriatio nostra, testimonium conscientiae nostrae, quod in simplicitate et sinceritate Dei, non in sapientia carnali, sed in Gratia Dei versatus sim in mundo.

Id est, affirmo optima conscientia, me nec corrumpere doctrinam, nec astute inflectere ad cuiusque affectus, nec me privatae ulli cupiditati servire.

Sumamus exempla ex recentibus historiis.

Gratum faciunt regibus, qui quaerunt fucos, quomodo doctrinam Ecclesiae inflectant ad statum, qui ipsis placet, qui arte pignunt Missam, aut alios ritus. Gratum faciunt multi, qui angent potentiam eorum, praetextu religionis, et armant populum contra eos, quos excutere conantur. Haec artificia nec ignota nec usitata sunt.

Ita tunc erant, qui doctrinam ad suarum factionum sensus et voluntates astute attemperabant.

Haec se fecisse negat, et sapientiam carnalem nominat omnia talia consilia humana, vel corrumpendae doctrinae, vel quoquo modo inflectendae, ut aut rationi humanae magis concinna videatur, aut magis accommodata sit constituendae factiosorum potentiae.

Puritatem vero doctrinae nominat sinceritatem, sicut ad Titum ait: ἐν τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ ἀδιαφθορίαν.

Simplicitatem nominat suae voluntatis rectitudinem, non servientis ulli privatae cupiditati, aut ullorum factiosorum affectibus.

Exempla plurima ex omnium temporum historiis sumi possent.

Multi et olim et nunc palam corruperunt doctrinam de iusticia fidei, quia non videtur concinna rationi.

Utcunque enim norunt humanae mentes legem, et iudicant iusticiam esse obedientiam secundum legem, et possunt aliquo modo praestare disciplinam.

Hac fingunt se mereri remissionem peccatorum et vitam aeternam, et ignorant Messiam, nec cernunt interiora peccata in cordibus, tenebras et dubitationes de Deo, et ἀταξίαν in corde.

In hac caligine humanae mentis homines proni sunt ad fiduciam suae iusticiae, et quaerunt merita in seipsis, et varia exercitia instituunt, tanquam cultus Dei.

Ideo subinde in Ecclesia lux doctrinae de iusticia fidei valde obscurata est, sicut in scriptis Thomae et similium prorsus silentium est de iusticia fidei, et confunditur discrimen legis et Evangelii.

Tales imaginationes natas in ratione humana Paulus nominat sapientiam carnalem, sic et alii articuli fidei corrupti sunt, dum quaeritur concinnitas cum ratione, aut servitus affectibus hominum, ut tunc Ebion negabat Messiam esse filium Dei, et multi contendebant, non esse omittendas ceremonias Mosaicas, ne pulcherrima politia Israëlítica dissolveretur.

Ex his exemplis mediocriter intelligi potest, quid Paulus hic velit, cum affirmat, se sincere docuisse, nec corrupisse doctrinam opinionibus aut affectibus humanis.

Quaestio de gloriatione conscientiae Quaestio de gloriatione conscientiae alias saepe tractata est. Sed tamen breviter hic quoque monendi sunt iuniores de his sententiis, quae discrepare videntur, 1. Corinth. 1.: Non glorietur omnis caro coram eo. Aliter vero dicitur, 2. Corinth. 1.: Gloriatio nostra est testimonium conscientiae nostrae. Altera prohibet gloriationem in ulla re nostra: altera admittit, si nullum sit vulnus conscientiae. Sed nequaquam discrepant hae sententiae suo ordine collocatae. Nemo glorietur, scilicet de iustificatione coram Deo, id est, nemo cogitet se iustum esse ullis virtutibus suis coram Deo, sicut et alibi inquit Paulus prorsus eadem sententia: Nihil mihi conscius sum, sed in hoc non iustificatus sum.

Postquam autem fide per misericordiam recepti sumus, placet etiam Deo quoque iusticia bonae conscientiae, et necesse est eam tueri, et calumniis opponenda est, quia nequaquam confirmanda sunt calumniatorum mendacia. Ait enim vox divina: Non dices falsum testimonium. Hinc et disputatio in libro Iob intelligi potest. Fatetur se non esse iustum coram Deo, et inquit capite nono: Vere scio, quod non iustificetur homo coram Deo. Item: Deus est, cuius irae nemo resistere potest. Sed affirmat se nullum habere vulnus conscientiae, sicut eum accusabant sui amici.

Non docui falsa, mea gubernatio non fuit tyrannica, non sum pollutus adulteriis. Ideo inquit capite 27.: Iustificationem meam, quam coepi tenere, non deseram. Neque enim reprehendit me cor meum in omni vita mea. Quotquot enim promissiones Dei in ipso sunt Etiam et Amen. Nondum recitavit causam, cur non redierit Corinthum, sed tantum ait, non esse levitati tribuendum, quod iter distulit. Addit autem signum, quod ostendit, se non esse vanum et levem, quia inquit: Cognovistis me in ministerio meo fuisse veracem, et doctrinam in vobis efficacem fuisse, Vos dona Spiritus sancti accepisse, et multis miraculis Deum testificatum esse, me nequaquam esse impostorem.

In hanc sententiam inquit: Fidelis est Deus, quod sermo noster apud vos non fuit etiam et non, sed verax et effiax in Deo. Deinde addit generalem sententiam, promissiones divinas ratas et firmas esse. Postquam vero tradidit generalem sententiam de promissionibus divinis, addit exemplum de sese et de Ecclesia Corinthia: Cum promissiones sint ratae, et in Evangelio certum sit promissa esse haec bona, reconciliationem et Spiritum sanctum, et haereditatem vitae aeternae, non existimandum est, nostras conciones tantum esse inania θελκτήρια, sicut pueris narrantur fabellae de fortunatis Insulis aut de campo Elysio, sed certissimum est, nos bona promissa in Evangelio accipere, et iam sentitis in corde initia novae lucis, et Spiritum sanctum, qui est pignus et arrabo, qui ostendit certe Deum nobiscum esse, et nobis daturum esse vitam aeternam.

Haec serie membrorum considerata, oratio magis perspicua erit, et magnitudo rerum de quibus loquitur, magis conspicitur. Sciant iuniores vocabulum arrabo factum esse ex Ebraeo עֵרָבוֹן quod significat spopondit, seu fideiussit. Inde arrabo dicitur proprie in emtionibus aliquid datum ad hoc, ut sit testimonium confirmatae emtionis.

Ita effusio Spiritus sancti in corda credentium, quam sentiunt in vera consolatione, et testimonium reconciliationis et praesentiae Dei, et venturae haereditatis vitae aeternae. Sicut Roma. 8. dicitur: Ipse spiritus testificatur cum spiritu nostro, quod simul filii Dei, Si autem filii, etiam haeredes sumus. Sic et apud Zachariam dicitur: Effundam super domum David spiritum gratiae et precum. Nominat Spiritum sanctum procedentem a patre et filio, erigentem nos in veris pavoribus, et vera consolatione vivificantem corda, quam consolationem sentientes audemus accedere ad Deum et eum invocare.

Ideo postea nominatur spiritus precum. Ἐγὼ δὲ μάρτυρα τὸν Θεὸν ἐπικαλοῦμαι. Hic tandem iuramento addito recitat causam, cur non redierit Corinthum, quia si venisset aliquos durius castigasset. Cum autem intellexisset, eos magno in dolore esse propter obiurgationem, quam in priore Epistola scripsit, noluit eis augere moestitiam durioribus exemplis, si reversus aliquos fulmine spiritus sui interfecisset, ut Petrus Ananiam interfecit. Hic apparet, quantum incendium fuerit in apostolica indignatione et zelo. Significat igitur, ideo se non rediisse Corinthum, ne ea indignatio coram magis inflammaretur. sicut alioqui prudentes cum sentiunt se irasci, vitant congressus eorum, quibus irascuntur.

Observandum est autem hoc loco exemplum iuramenti, quod ostendit, concessum esse Chri- stianis iurare, ut alibi copiosius dicitur.

Inde autem existimari potest, fuisse magnas causas huius indignationis, Haud dubie aliqui fanatici et superbi Pseudoapostoli cum sua factione valde turbaverant Ecclesiam Corinthi. Sed ta- men Paulus iram reprimit. Quare mox recitata causa, cur non venerit, intexit occupationem, ut occurrat tacitae obiectioni. Poterant enim aliqui minus verecundi dicere: Quid minitaris nobis? Quale imperium tibi sumis? non ideo amplexi sumus Evangelium, ut tu in nos tyrannidem exerceas, si tam periculosa servitus ferenda est, potius ad Ethnicos redeamus. Huic obiectioni occurrit hoc modo: Non mihi sumo in vos impe- rium. Non quaero potentiam aut opes, sed mi- nister sum salutis vestrae, idque dicit blandius, gaudii vestri, sequor regulam mihi a Deo tradi- tam, qui hoc nostro ministerio vocat vos ad salu- tem, in quo tantum ea ago, iuxta regulam a Deo traditam, quae vobis salutaria sunt. Et haec do- nec fide statis, vobis grata erunt.

Iam hic discrimen politicae potestatis, et ministerii evangelici consideretur, ut alias saepe dicitur. Potestas politica vi corporali coërcet, et punit invitos, ut Romani recepta Capua Senato- res Capuanos ad palum deligatos securi percusse- runt invitos: sed potestas ecclesiastica nihil agit vi corporali, non habet arma et exercitum. Haec alibi copiosius enarrantur.

## 2:1 Argument
Chapter II.

I determined within myself.

The beginning of the second chapter pertains to the end of the previous one. For he narrates in many words why he did not return, namely, lest some severity might increase his sadness. And he mitigates the rebuke written in the former Epistle, repeatedly renewing the commemoration of his benevolence toward them, and in turn the respect of the Corinthians toward him. He says that he is writing while weeping.

Afterward, he adds an express absolution of the man previously condemned on account of an incestuous relationship with his stepmother, who had returned to repentance. And first, it must be known here that this example is recited among the illustrious testimonies which confirm that those who have lapsed after baptism can return to repentance, and that those who return are to be received.

He joins, however, his own judgment with the voice of that Church: To whom you forgive, I also forgive. Thus he wished the order of judgments to be preserved, not that any should be armed to pronounce judgment without investigation, as is often done by the Roman pontiffs. Thus let the following words also be understood: When I forgive others, I forgive for your sake, that is, I did not use a harsher punishment than moderate chastisement, which would not kill the guilty party, lest I bring greater grief to you and alienate your minds from the Gospel. And now I absolve him completely, and I wish him to be raised up by true consolation, lest diabolical snares in this grief drive him into desperation and destruction. I know, he says, the thoughts of the enemies; I know that the devils lie in wait for the Church and are intent on the opportunity to press those who are weighed down by sadness. Nor do I add a longer narration here. For it is enough to remind the reader to observe the example regarding the manner of condemning the lapsed, and regarding the receiving of the converted; a longer doctrine concerning conversion is recited elsewhere.

᾿Αλλὰ ἀποταξάμενος αὐτοῖς, ἐξῆλθον εἰς μακεδονίαν.

He narrates his journeys, and it appears in these narrations that he often traveled through Asia Minor, and sailed from there into Europe several times. The word ἀποταξάμενος signifies this, indicating a departure from others, as in Luke 9. It is also used in Acts chapter 18. Moreover, there is this emphasis in the word: to arrange with others what pertains to a departure. Therefore, ἀποτάξασθαι τῇ κληρονομίᾳ is also a legal term, to cede an inheritance, to judge, to profess that one does not wish to hear of an inheritance. And Cyril said: εἰς νοῦν μὴ λαβόντες τὴν σύνταξιν χριστοῦ, καὶ τὴν ἀπόταξιν τοῦ διαβόλου, Not considering that they were joined by a covenant with Christ, and had renounced the devil.

To Him who leads us in triumph in Christ.

…The Apostle gives thanks to God, because although he is exercised everywhere by more hardships and struggles, nevertheless he is preserved, and has a place for teaching, and gathers some assembly, just as it is now a wonder that, with popes and kings so opposing, God nevertheless preserves somewhere both the ministry of the Gospel and the Churches. For that benefit let us also give thanks to God, and let us consider that these are the victories and triumphs of the Son of God, suppressing the devils and their instruments.

They say the word θριαμβεύειν is derived from θρίον, that is, a fig leaf, because they say that in olden times victors were crowned with fig leaves, because victory is sweet. Ἄμβη is a margin or extremity, as a crown placed upon the head or other ornaments. But there is a different meaning in the construction. Here he says: I give thanks to God who is conquering and triumphing in us through Christ. Here a person joined to the one triumphing is signified. In Colossians the accusative signifies a hostile person; he leads the devils in triumph.

Latin:

Caput II.

Decrevi apud meipsum.

Initium secundi capitis pertinet ad finem proximi. Narrat enim pluribus verbis, cur non redierit, videlicet ne eius moestitiam severitas aliqua augeret. Et mitigat obiurgationem in priore Epistola scriptam, subinde repetens com- memorationem suae erga nos ipsos benevolentiae, et vicissim Corinthiorum erga ipsum observan- tiam. Ait se lacrimantem scribere.

Postea addit expressam absolutionem homi- nis antea damnati propter incestam consuetudi- nem cum noverca, qui ad poenitentiam redierat. Ac primum hic sciendum est, hoc exemplum in- ter illustria testimonia recitari, quae confirmant lapsos post baptismum redire ad poenitentiam posse, et redeuntes recipiendos esse.

Coniungit autem suam sententiam cum illius Ecclesiae voce: Cui ignoscitis, et ego ignosco. Ita voluit ordinem iudiciorum servari, non armari ullos, ut sine cognitione pronunciarent, sicut saepe fit a Romanis pontificibus. Sic intelliga- tur et sequentia verba: Ego cum ignosco aliis, ignosco vestra causa, id est, non sum usus poena duriore, quam mediocri castigatione, quae non interficeret sontem, ne vobis maiorem dolorem afferrem, et vestros animos ab Evangelio aliena- rem. Et nunc absolvo eum prorsus, et consola- tione vera erigi volo, ne diabolicae insidiae in hoc dolore eum impellant in desperationem et in exi- tium. Novi, inquit, cogitationes hostium, scio diabolos insidiari Ecclesiae, et intentos esse in occasionein, ut oppressos moestitia, urgeant. Nec addo hic longiorem enarrationem. Satis est enim commonefacere lectorem, ut exemplum observet de modo condemnandi lapsos, et de re- cipiendis conversis longior doctrina de conver- sione alibi recitatur.

᾿Αλλὰ ἀποταξάμενος αὐτοῖς, ἐξῆλθον εἰς μακε- δονίαν.

Narrat itinera sua, ac adparet in his narra- tionibus saepe pervagatum esse minorem Asiam, et aliquoties inde in Europam navigasse. Ver- bum ἀποταξάμενος significat, indicans disces- sum aliis, sicut Lucae 9. Usurpatur et in Actis capite 18. Est autem in verbo haec emphasis, ordinare apud alios, quae ad discessum pertinent. Est igitur et forense verbum ἀποτάξασθαι τῇ κλη- ρονομίᾳ, cedere haereditate, iudicare, profiteri se nolle haereditatem audire. Et Cyrillus dixit: εἰς νοῦν μὴ λαβόντες τὴν σύνταξιν χριστοῦ, καὶ τὴν ἀπόταξιν τοῦ διαβόλου, Non cogitantes se foedere coniunctos esse cum Christo, et renun- ciasse diabolo.

Τῷ θριαμβεύοντι ἡμᾶς ἐν τῷ χριστῷ.

Agit gratias Apostolus Deo, quod quan- quam magis aerumnis et certaminibus passim exerceatur, tamen servetur, et habeat docendi locum, et colligat aliquem coetum, sicut nunc mirum est, adeo adversantibus pontificibus et regibus, tamen Deum alicubi et ministerium Evangelii et Ecclesias servare. Pro eo beneficio nos quoque Deo gratias agamus, et cogitemus esse victorias et triumphos filii Dei, reprimentis dia- bolos et eorum organa.

Verbum θριαμβεύειν aiunt factum esse a θρίον, id est, folium fici, quia dicunt, olim victo- res coronatos esse foliis ficorum, quia victoria est dulcis. Ἄμβη est margo vel extremitas, ut co- rona imposita capiti aut caeteris ornamentis. Est autem dissimilis significatio in constructione. Hic inquit: Ago gratias Deo vincenti et trium- phanti in nobis per Christum. Hic persona con- iuncta triumphanti significatur. In Colossensi- bus accusativus significat personam hostilem, du- cit in triumpho diabolos.

## 2:15
We are a sweet savor to God.

The metaphor is taken from the custom of those offering incense, which exhales fragrant fumes. And just as those vapors are dissipated, so our sermons are scattered among the human race, and they are salutary to those who receive them with faith, but to others who despise them, they announce the wrath of God. But he says expressly: We are the sweet savor of Christ, that is, our sermons are vapors scattered by Christ, and from him, which are pleasing to God. And so that the accommodation may be clearer, paint in your mind the image of Christ as the high priest before the eternal Father offering incense that is widely fragrant and exhaling fumes. He interprets these vapors to be the voice of the Gospel, which is scattered by Christ the high priest through them, and it is effective because it is issued by Christ himself; it is not a human invention, as will be spoken of immediately and at length regarding the efficacy of the ministry in the next chapter, where he says that the Gospel is the ministry of the spirit and of life. For he wishes to show the difference between the law and the Gospel, and he refutes the Pseudo-apostles, who said many futile things about the law, attempted to preserve the polity of Moses, and pretended that men are righteous by the law; they did not understand that in the Gospel the polity of this mortal life is not established, but the Son of God is offered, who remits and abolishes sin and death, and restores eternal righteousness and life, as will be spoken of more copiously later.

And for these things who is sufficient?

He inserts a brief commemoration of his faithfulness; later he will speak of efficacy. And there are two propositions, both of which it is necessary to hold. The former is this: It is certain that the ministry of the Gospel is effective not by any human power, but by divine, as will be said later. Here someone might say: It matters nothing, therefore, by whom or how they are taught, if human power does nothing? He answers this objection with the second proposition, which is recited here: Even though the efficacy is divine, nevertheless it behooves us to be faithful in teaching, that is, to deliver the voice of the Gospel uncorrupted, just as he says in the former Epistle: This is required, that we be faithful. Thus he says here: I affirm that I am faithful, that I teach the doctrine delivered by God without corruptions, and with Christ himself as witness and spectator of my course and helping me. I do not mix depraved dogmas with the truth, just as tavern-keepers corrupt wines. I do not bend the truth to the affections of the Jews, who dream of a political kingdom, nor to the judgments of reason, which thinks that sin is taken away by the law, and understands neither the law nor the righteousness of the Gospel correctly. From this commemoration of his faithfulness he returns to the other proposition concerning efficacy, and concerning the difference between the law and the Gospel.

Latin:

Bonus odor sumus Deo.

Sumta est metaphora a consuetudine offe- rentium accensa thura, quae fumos fragrantes ex- halant. Ac ut illi halitus dissipantur, sic no- strae conciones in genere humano sparguntur, et salutares sunt iis, qui eas fide accipiunt, aliis vero, qui aspernantur, annunciant iram Dei. Diserte autem inquit: Sumus bonus odor Chri- sti, id est, conciones nostrae sunt halitus sparsi a Christo, et de ipso, qui sunt grati Deo. Ac ut accommodatio sit illustrior, pinge in mente imaginem Christi tanquam summi sacerdotis co- ram aeterno patre offerentis accensa thura late fragrantia et exhalantia fumos. Hos halitus in- terpretatur esse vocem Evangelii, quae a Chri- sto summo sacerdote per ipsos spargitur, et est efficax, quia ab ipso Christo editur, non est ho- minum inventum, ut de efficacia ministerii statim prolixe dicetur in capite proximo, ubi ait, Evan- gelium esse ministerium spiritus et vitae. Vult enim ostendere discrimen legis et Evangelii, et refutat Pseudoapostolos, qui multa futiliter de lege dicebant, conabantur politiam Moysi conser- vare, et fingebant homines lege iustos esse, non intelligebant, in Evangelio non constitui poli- tiam huius vitae mortalis, sed offerri filium Dei, qui remittit et abolet peccatum et mortem, et re- stituit aeternam iusticiam et vitam, ut postea co- piosius dicetur.

Et ad haec quis sufficiens est?

Inserit brevem commemorationem de sua fidelitate, postea de efficacia loquetur. Ac duae sunt sententiae, quas tenere ambas necesse est. Prior haec est: Certum est, ministerium Evan- gelii efficax esse non potentia ulla humana, sed divina, ut postea dicetur. Hic dicat aliquis: Nihil igitur refert, a qui- bus aut quomodo doceantur, si humana potentia nihil agit? Huic obiectioni respondet altera sen- tentia, quae hic recitatur: Etiamsi efficacia est divina, tamen nos oportet fideles esse in docendo, id est, vocem Evangelii incorruptam tradere, sicut in priore Epistola dicit: Hoc requiritur, ut fideles simus. Ita hic inquit: Affirmo me fide- lem esse, docere sine corruptelis traditam a Deo doctrinam, et ipso teste et spectante meum cur- sum et iuvante Christo. Non misceo veritati prava dogmata, sicut caupones vina corrumpunt. Non inflecto veritatem ad affectus Iudaeorum, qui somniant regnum politicum, non ad iudicia rationis, quae putat lege tolli peccatum, et nec legem nec iusticiam Evangelii recte intelligit. Ab hac commemoratione de sua fidelitate redit ad alteram sententiam de efficacia, et de discri- mine legis et Evangelii.

## 3:1 Argument
Chapter III.

Concerning his whole ministry, concerning faithfulness and efficacy, he appeals at the beginning to their own testimony: You know that my ministry was effective among you, because you both saw miracles, and you yourselves were adorned with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, the gift of healing, and the gift of tongues; you also felt in your hearts conversion and consolation. Therefore I am not an impostor, nor is the doctrine an empty fable. In this preface he makes mention of the efficient cause, where there is a manifest assertion, which affirms that the ministry of the Gospel is effective, not by human strengths, but by God himself converting and vivifying hearts. This testimony must be opposed to many errors. Others dream that the Gospel is an idle narration, and that it effects nothing anywhere, and they think that the labor of teaching and learning the Gospel is empty, and that there is no Church. Many sayings in this place and elsewhere must be opposed to this pernicious error. But the principal ones are: John 20: As the Father has sent me, so I send you. It is manifest, however, that the Son's ministry was effective. It is therefore also effective thereafter through others, called by him or by his command. John 15: I chose you and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit, and your fruit may remain. Luke 10: He who hears you, hears me. Romans 1: The Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth. Isaiah 55: My word that shall go forth from my mouth, shall not return to me void, but shall accomplish all that I will. Isaiah 51: I have put my words in thy mouth, and with the shadow of my hand I will protect thee, that thou mayest plant the heavens. John 17: I pray not for these only, but also for them who shall believe in me through their word.

all thoughts, good intentions, efforts, and habits of human powers, without the Holy Spirit kindling true fear of God, and true trust and invocation of the Son of God, by which hearts are freed from true sorrows. He calls all these the letter, that is, painted imitations in the mind and external members, which are not divine life and motion. Thus he speaks of the letter in Romans 2: Circumcision of the heart in the spirit, not in the letter. And Romans 7: Let us serve in newness of spirit, and not in the oldness of the letter.

Let these and similar testimonies be before our eyes, so that we may firmly establish that the Church is truly gathered by God, whenever and wherever the voice of the Gospel sounds uncorrupted, and that that ministry is truly effective. It is clear that this confirmation is necessary for us all, which illustrates the article of the creed: I believe in the holy catholic Church, the communion of saints.

The Spirit most truly signifies in this place the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the eternal Father and the Son, our Lord Jesus Christ. For when, by the voice of the Gospel received through the Son, who is the Word of the eternal Father, we are reconciled to the eternal Father, the Holy Spirit is at the same time poured into our hearts by the eternal Father and the Son, and the divinity truly dwells in us, frees us from the sorrows of the underworld, and quickens us, and begins a new light and wisdom, and motions in harmony with God, as manifest testimonies affirm.

Moreover, there is an illustrious testimony placed in this passage, of which I shall speak later. Since the promulgation of the law was not empty, but had its effects, the constitution of the Mosaic polity, and many testimonies of the presence of God: How much more will the voice of the Gospel be effective, and truly bring the eternal goods which it promises, since it is for the sake of this ministry that all the former things were done. For what would the polity profit the dead fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who never saw it? Therefore they expected other, greater goods. But we shall speak of these words in the text later.

Galatians 4: God sent the spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying Abba, Father.

And in Acts chapter 2: Exalted by the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured forth this, which you now see and hear.

And John 14: He will give you another paraclete, that he may remain with you forever, the spirit of truth.

Others dream: Even if the Gospel is not an empty fable, yet it is only law, and by this discipline men are righteous, which they perform by human powers, with nature somehow imitating the law.

And Zechariah 12: I will pour out upon the house of David the spirit of grace and of prayers. Although it is a brief description, yet it shows why the Holy Spirit is given, and what the difference is between the righteousness of the New Testament and the law, by which we either rush into death condemned, or somehow perform the discipline. For it is for this reason that the Holy Spirit is given through the Gospel, that first the hearts may feel that they are in grace, and may acknowledge the Son of God, through whom and for whose sake the remission of sins is given, just as he himself says in John 16: He shall glorify me. With the Holy Spirit kindling the hearts, the benefits of the mediator are acknowledged, and we are quickened by true trust in the mercy promised for the sake of the mediator. And at the same time the presence of God is felt, and true invocation is made. And because the Holy Spirit himself is the divine mover, and the law of God is not fulfilled otherwise, neither in angels nor in men, unless God himself shines in them and moves them, there are already in the saints the beginnings of eternal life and eternal righteousness, just as it is also said shortly in this third chapter: We

To this false imagination, against which he always contends with the pseudo-apostles, he opposes the following antithesis: God made us ministers not of the letter, but of the spirit: for the letter kills, but the spirit gives life.

Here first let the designations be distinguished. Origen and many others, like the Pseudo-apostles, thought the Gospel was a moral law, and one more convenient than the Mosaic was, because it is more expeditious and does not burden the nations with ceremonies, and Origen understands the letter as ceremonies, and the spirit as allegorical interpretation. These Origenian ravings are false and are to be rejected. And it must be known that the letter is said to be every doctrine of the law and the Gospel, the understanding of the letter historical or according to the propriety of the speech and allegories, finally beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, we are transformed into the same image from glory to glory by the Spirit of the Lord, that is, we truly feeling the judgment and wrath of God against sins, and again feeling consolation when the promise is heard and the mediator is acknowledged, we discern the glory of the Lord, judgment and life we are made partakers of this light and life, and this glory, that is, the light of righteousness and life, grows in the converted, with the Spirit of our Lord Jesus Christ shining in them, through whom the Holy Spirit is given.

Finally, the comparison of the letter and the spirit becomes clear when one considers in any way what eternal righteousness and life will be like after the resurrection, when God will be all in all. Here there will be complete righteousness with God himself dwelling and shining in us. Compare to that eternal life and light the righteousness of some Pharisee, who is either secure, as long as he does not feel the judgment of God, or rushes into despair and the pains of hell when he feels the wrath of God, like Saul. In such a man the heart is without God and without life, and there are horrible roarings against God, according to that saying: The heart of man is perverse and miserable.

Latin:

Caput III.

De toto suo ministerio, de fidelitate et de efficacia provocat initio ad testimonium ipsorum: Vos scitis meum ministerium fuisse efficax inter vos, quia et miracula vidistis, et vos ipsi ornati estis donis Spiritus sancti, dono curationis, et dono linguarum, sensistis et in cordibus vestris conversionem et consolationem. Ergo non sum impostor, nec doctrina inanis fabula est. In hac praefatione facit mentionem causae efficientis, ubi manifesta asseveratio est, quae af- firmat, ministerium Evangelii esse efficax, non humanis viribus, sed Deo ipso convertente et vi- vificante corda. Hoc testimonium opponendum est multis erroribus, Alii somniant in Evange- lium esse otiosam narrationem, et nihil efficere usquam, et cogitant inanem esse laborem do- cendi et discendi Evangelii, et nullam esse Ec- clesiam. Huic pernicioso errori opponenda sunt multa dicta hoc loco et alibi. Sunt autem prae- cipua: Iohannis 20.: Sicut misit me pater, sic ego mitto vos. Manifestum est autem, filii mi- nisterium fuisse efficax. Est igitur et deinceps efficax per alios, ab ipso aut mandato ipsius vo- catos. Iohannis 15.: Ego elegi vos et posui vos, ut vos eatis et fructum feratis, et fructus vester maneat. Lucae 10.: Qui vos audit, me audit Roma 1.: Evangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti. Esaiae 55.: Verbum meum quod egredietur de ore meo, non redibit ad me vacuum, sed efficiet omnia, quae volo. Esaiae 51.: Po- sui verba mea in ore tuo, et umbra manus meae protegam te, ut plantes coelos. Iohannis 17.: Non pro his tantum oro, sed etiam pro iis, qui credituri sunt per Verbum eorum in me.

omnes cogitationes, bonas intentiones, conatus et assuefactiones humanarum virium, sine Spi- ritu sancto accendente verum timorem Dei, et veram fiduciam et invocationem filii Dei, qua corda liberantur ex veris doloribus. Haec omnia nominat literam, id est, pictas imitationes in mente et externis membris, quae non sunt vita et motus divini. Sic loquitur de litera Roma 2.: Circumcisio cordis spiritu non litera. Et Roma 7.: Serviamus in novitate spiritus, non in vetustate literae.

Haec et similia testimonia sint nobis in con- spectu, ut certo statuamus, vere colligi Eccle- siam Deo, quandocunque et ubicunque sonat vox Evangelii incorrupta, et id ministerium vere esse efficax. Hanc confirmationem nobis omnibus necessariam esse perspicuum est, quae illustrat articulum symboli: Credo esse Ecclesiam catho- licam, sanctorum communionem.

Spiritus significat verissime hoc loco Spiri- tum sanctum, procedentem ab aeterno patre et filio Domino nostro Iesu Christo. Cum enim voce Evangelii accepta per filium, qui est Ver- bum aeterni patris, reconciliamur aeterno patri, simul ab aeterno patre et filio effunditur in corda nostra Spiritus sanctus, et vere habitat in nobis divinitas, liberat nos ex doloribus inferorum, et vivificat nos, incoat novam lucem et sapientiam, et motus cum Deo congruentes, ut manifesta testi- monia adfirmant.

Est autem illustre testimonium hoc loco po- situm, de quo postea dicam. Cum promulgatio legis non fuerit inanis, sed habuerit suos ef- fectus, constitutionem politiae Mosaicae, et multa testimonia praesentiae Dei: Quanto ma- gis vox Evangelii erit efficax, et vere adferet aeterna bona, quae promittit, cum propter hoc ministerium priora omnia facta sint. Quid enim prodesset politia mortuis patribus Abrahae, Isaac, Iacob, qui eam nunquam viderunt? Alia igitur maiora bona expectarunt. Sed de his ver- bis in textu postea dicemus.

Galatas quarto: Misit Deus spiritum filii sui in corda nostra, clamantem Abba pater.

Et in Actis capite secundo: Dextra Dei exal- tatus, promissionem sancti Spiritus accipiens a pa- tre effudit eum, quem nunc vos videtis et auditis.

Et Iohannis 14.: Dabit vobis alium paracle- tum, ut maneat vobiscum in sempiternum, spiri- tum veritatis.

Alii somniant: Etiamsi non est inanis fa- bula Evangelium, tamen est tantum lex, et hac disciplina homines sunt iusti, quam praestant viribus humanis, naturae utcunque imitantibus legem.

Et Zachariae 12.: Effundam super domum David spiritum gratiae et precum. Etsi brevis descriptio est, tamen ostendit, quare detur Spi- ritus sanctus, et quid intersit inter iusticiam novi Testamenti et legem, qua vel condemnati ruimus in mortem, vet utcunque praestamus disciplinam. Ideo enim per Evangelium datur Spiritus sanctus, ut primum corda sentiant se esse in gratia, et agnoscant filium Dei, per quem et propter quem datur remissio peccatorum, sicut ipse inquit Io- han. 16.: Ipse me glorificabit. Spiritu sancto accendente corda, beneficia mediatoris agnoscun- tur, et vera fiducia misericordiae propter media- torem promissae vivificamur. Ac simul praesen- tia Dei sentitur, et fit vera invocatio. Et quia ipse Spiritus sanctus est motor divinus, et lex Dei non fit aliter, nec in angelis nec in hominibus, nisi ipso Deo in eis lucente et eos movente, iam sunt in sanctis initia aeternae vitae et iustitiae aeternae, sicut et mox dicitur in hoc capite tertio: Nos

Huic falsae imaginationi, de qua cum Pseu- doapostolis semper dimicat, opponit sequentem antithesin: Deus fecit nos ministros non literae, sed spiritus: litera enim occidit, sed spiritus vivificat.

Hic primum adpellationes discernantur. Origenes et multi alii, sicut Pseudoapostoli, co- gitarunt Evangelium legem moralem, et eo commodiorem, quam fuit Mosaica, quia est ex- peditior, nec onerat gentes ceremoniis, Et li- teram intelligit Origines ceremonias, spiritum interpretationem allegoricam. Haec Origenica deliramenta falsa et explodenda sunt. Et scien- dum est, literam dici omnem doctrinam legis et Evangelii, intellectum literae historicum seu juxta sermonis proprietatem et allegorias, denique revelata facie gloriam Domini speculantes, in ean- dem imaginem transformamur a gloria in glo- riam Domini spiritu, id est, nos vere sentientes iudicium et iram Dei adversus peccata, et rursus sentientes audita promissione et agnito mediatore consolationem, cernimus gloriam Domini, iudi- cium et vitam, et transformamur in eandem ima- ginem, id est, huius lucis et vitae participes effi- cimur, et haec gloria, id est, lux iusticia et vita crescunt in conversis, lucente in eis spiritu Do- mini nostri Iesu Christi, per quem datur Spiri- tus sanctus.

Denique collatio literae et spiritus ita fit illu- stris, cum cogitatur utcunque, qualis sit post re- surrectionem futura aeterna iusticia et vita, cum Deus erit omnia in omnibus. Hic integra iusticia erit Deo ipsi in nobis palam habitante et lutente. Ad illam aeternam vitam et lucem confer iusti- ciam Pharisaei alicuius, qui aut securus est, do- nec non sentit iudicium Dei, aut ruit in despera- tionem et dolores inferorum, cum sentit iram Dei, ut Saul. In tali viro cor est sine Deo et sine vita, et sunt horrendi fremitus adversus Deum, iuxta illud dictum: Cor hominis perver- sum et aerumnosum.

## 3:8
If the ministration of death was glorious, much more shall the ministration of the spirit be glorious.

The minds of all men are greatly tormented by the sad appearance of the Church. The Apostles by no means constitute the Church with such glory as Moses did the polity. They wander about like vagabonds, and since there are such great dissipations, the efforts of the Apostles seem to be vain. The minds of individuals are also shaken by doubt, whether the voice of the Gospel is effective in them, whether it is true, whether there is any Church, whether God hears us, since only a few men, and as it were seditious ones, embrace the Gospel, and these are oppressed by tyranny and many miseries, nor is the multitude associated under a certain government.

Against this most serious temptation he opposes a most sweet consolation: God was effective in establishing the shadow: Therefore He will be much more effective now that the Messiah Himself has been exhibited.

But the appellations must be diligently considered. He calls the promulgation of the law the ministration of death and condemnation, as has often been said elsewhere, that by the Law one is only accused, and sin is not taken away in this miserable nature. But he calls the Gospel the ministration of the spirit and of righteousness, because it is certain that by the voice of the Gospel the Son of God in those who

Up to this point Philip has woven his commentary; believe it to be effective, who when they recognize in true terrors that they receive by faith the remission of sins, the Holy Spirit quickens them, and effects in their hearts joy in God, and motions corresponding to the will of God, as it is said in Zechariah: I will pour upon the house of David the spirit of grace and of supplications, that is, the Holy Spirit, by whom hearts may recognize themselves in grace, and who may kindle true invocation and other virtues. Therefore Paul later calls the Gospel in this place the ministration of righteousness, where again the antithesis must be considered. The Law arms sin, as it is said elsewhere: The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. But the Gospel is the ministration of righteousness, because it both shows how the remission of sins is given, and how we are righteous, and heirs of eternal life, and through this very voice the Son of God is effective, and moves hearts by His Holy Spirit, so that they may receive by faith the benefits offered. He calls all these things righteousness: The remission of sins and reconciliation, which is made by faith on account of the Son of God, and the Son of God Himself imputing to us His righteousness, and quickening us by the Holy Spirit, and kindling new motions corresponding to God, as is said above, 1 Cor. 1: Of Him you are in Christ Jesus, who is made unto us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption.

Finally, Paul also adds a comparison: Indeed, such is the excellence of the glory of the Gospel, that the promulgation of the law, which contains many terrible examples, such as the punishments of Pharaoh, and others of many, is not to be called glorious, if it is compared to the eternal goods which the Gospel brings, and which will be openly seen after the resurrection. The following words indicate that this is the meaning. Since the law, which nevertheless was to perish, was adorned with such glory, how much more glorious and effective will the Gospel be, which does not bring shadows, but eternal things? This whole discourse is a consolation, so that we may know that the Gospel is certainly effective, and that in this way an eternal Church is truly gathered by God, even if to human judgments it seems strange that such great things are effected in this way by the voice of miserable men, especially when no certain polity is established, and the whole Church is a dissipated multitude. Against these scandals this consolation has been instituted. Therefore he soon says: Having therefore such hope, we use great boldness.

Latin:

Cum ministerium mortis fuerit gloriosum, multo magis ministerium spiritus erit gloriosum.

Valde excruciantur omnium hominum animi tristi specie Ecclesiae. Nequaquam tali gloria constituunt Apostoli Ecclesiam, ut Moyses poli- tiam. Vagantur, ut errones, et cum tantae sint dissipationes, videntur conatus Apostolorum ina- nes esse. Concutiuntur etiam dubitatione singu- lorum animi, an vox Evangelii in ipsis sit efficax, an sit vera, an sit aliqua Ecclesia, an exaudiat nos Deus, cum tantum pauci homines, ac velut seditiosi amplectantur Evangelium, et hi sint op- pressi tyrannide et multis aerumnis, nec sit con- sociata multitudo certo imperio.

Adversus hanc gravissimam tentationem op- ponit dulcissimam consolationem: Deus fuit effi- cax in constituenda umbra: Ergo multo magis erit efficax nunc exhibito ipso Messia.

Diligenter autem considerandae sunt appel- lationes. Promulgationem legis nominat ministe- rium mortis et condemnationis, sicut alias saepe dictum est, Lege tantum accusari, non tolli pec- catum in hac misera natura. Evangelium vero nominat ministerium spiritus et iusticiae, quia certum est voce Evangelii filium Dei in his, qui

Huc usque pertexuit Philippus commentari credunt efficacem esse, qui cum in veris terro- ribus agnoscunt se fide accipere remissionem pec- catorum, vivificat eos Spiritus sanctus, et efficit in cordibus laetitiam in Deo, et motus congruen- tes voluntati Dei, sicut in Zacharia dictum est: Effundam super domum David spiritum gratiae et precum, id est, Spiritum sanctum, quo corda agnoscant se sese in gratia, et qui accendat veram invocationem et caeteras virtutes. Ideo postea nominat Paulus hoc loco Evangelium ministe- rium iusticiae, ubi rursus antithesis consideranda est. Lex armat peccatum, ut alibi dictum est: Aculeus mortis peccatum est, potentia autem pec- cati lex est. Sed Evangelium est ministerium iu- sticiae, quia et ostendit, quomodo detur remissio peccatorum, et quomodo simus iusti, et haeredes vitae aeternae, et per hanc ipsam vocem filius Dei est efficax, et movet corda Spiritu suo sancto, ut fide accipiant beneficia oblata. Nominat autem iusticiam haec omnia: Remissionem peccatorum et reconciliationem, quae fit fide propter filium Dei, et ipsum filium Dei imputantem nobis suam iusticiam, et vivificantem nos Spiritu sancto, et novos motus congruentes Deo accendentem, sicut supra dicitur, 1. Cor. 1.: Ex ipso vos estis per Christum Iesum, qui factus est nobis sapientia a Deo, iusticia et sanctitas et redemtio.

Tandem et collationem addit Paulus: Imo tanta est excellentia gloriae Evangelii, ut pro- mulgatio legis, quae multa exempla terribilia con- tinet, ut poenas Pharaonis, et alias multorum, non sit dicenda gloriosa, si ad bona aeterna con- feratur, qua affert Evangelium, et quae post re- surrectionem palam conspicientur. Hanc esse sen- tentiam sequentia indicant. Cum lex, quae tamen interitura erat, tanta gloria ornata sit, quanto magis Evangelium erit gloriosum et efficax, quod non affert umbras, sed res aeternas? Haec tota oratio consolatio est, ut sciamus Evangelium certo efficax esse, et vere sic Deo colligi aeternam Ec- clesiam, etiamsi humanis iudiciis videtur mirum, hoc modo voce miserorum hominum res tantas ef- fici, praesertim cum non constituatur certa poli- tia, et tota Ecclesia sit dissipata multitudo. Ad- versus haec scandala instituta est consolatio. Ideo mox inquit: Habentes igitur talem spem, magna libertate utimur.

## 3:14
The same veil remains in the election of the Old Testament.

Having explained the terms Letter and Spirit, Paul adapts the type concerning the veiled face of Moses. This prophetic and apostolic interpretation was unknown to the Pharisees and Pseudo-apostles, who understood neither the law nor the promises. But first, the history must be known, which is recited in Exodus 34, where it is said that Moses' face radiated a brightness so that it could not be looked upon by the people, and therefore when he spoke to the people, he covered his face with a veil, which, however, he removed when entering to the Lord and speaking with Him. The Apostle here explains the significance of this history, which is handed down nowhere else. It is manifest that the whole human nature by natural powers without regeneration, even when it learns and imitates the law, nevertheless only performs certain external gestures of the law, just as Saul retains in some way the profession of the one God, revealed in this people, but the heart is full of doubts, it does not conclude that it is received and heard by God, it feels itself dying, and in death it does not feel consolation and life. Then there are other most bitter motions fighting against God. Finally, all men who are not profane know by their own experience that human powers can only in some way govern the locomotive, or external gestures. But when God shows His wrath against sin, which is described in the law, hearts flee, and are oppressed by the magnitude of the wrath, and roar against God and rush into death. And so both are signified. The people look upon the veiled face, that is, they hear and imitate in some way the external works of the law, and this imitation is political and pharisaical judgment, but the nature of men cannot bear the brightness of Moses, that is, the judgment and wrath of God against sins, which is described by the law of God, the nature of men can by no means tolerate. As it is said here: The law is the ministry of death. And experience testifies that men without evangelical consolation rush into eternal despair and death.

This doctrine is often repeated by Paul, as in Romans 4: The law works wrath. Likewise, Romans 7: Sin through the law kills me. Likewise, 1 Corinthians 15: The sting of death is sin, but the power of sin is the law. Paul repeats this so often to show that men are not made righteous by the law.

But what is said in Exodus, that Moses removed the veil when entering to God and speaking with Him, and was filled with divine light: it is signified that there is another righteousness, by which we are accepted by God, and by which we can sustain God, namely when the Son speaking in us communicates His light to us. Thus the veil is drawn from the law, and hypocrisy is taken away, and there are in us the righteousness and life which the law describes but does not exhibit, but the Son of God does exhibit. Therefore Paul says here: The veil is abolished through Christ. This sentence is to be understood concerning true conversion. In true sorrows we acknowledge that peace and life are not rendered to consciences through good works. We acknowledge also that we are far from the perfection of the law, but that true consolation, which is the beginning of eternal life, is rendered to consciences when we acknowledge the Son of God and are sustained by His promise, as David revives, hearing and embracing by faith this voice: The Lord has taken away your sin. For then, the mercy of God being acknowledged, he is quickened through the Son of God, and approaches God, calls upon Him, and has the beginnings of true obedience according to these sayings: You have received the spirit of adoption of sons, by which we cry Abba Father. And all the sayings that speak of true conversion and of eternal life and righteousness pertain to this in those who are converted, as in Jeremiah 31: I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts.

Paul therefore explains this saying, how the veil is abolished through Christ, because he soon discourses about conversion, saying: When Israel shall have turned to the Lord, the veil is taken away. We learn this doctrine in some measure in true conversion and consolation. Nor is it enough here to speak of the allegories of the ceremonies. For this comparison speaks of the moral law, or of judgment and wrath against sin, and of consolation.

It has been spoken of the letter, of the spirit, of the distinction of external discipline, which looks upon the veiled face of Moses, and of the sense of judgment and the wrath of God, and of consolation. These interpretations having been considered, the continuous series of this chapter will now be clearer. And it is very profitable to keep this consolation, which is recited here, in view, and to think upon it often.

Latin:

Idem velum in electione veteris Testamenti manet.

Enarratis vocabulis Literae et Spiritus, ac- commodat Paulus typum de facie Moysi velata. Haec interpretatio prophetica et apostolica Pha- risaeis et Pseudoapostolis ignota fuit, qui nec legem nec promissiones intellexerunt. Primum autem historiam oportet notam esse, quae recita- tur Exodi 34 ubi dicitur, Mosi faciem sparsisse fulgorem, ut aspici a populo non posset, ac pro- pterea cum loqueretur ad populum, texisse eum faciem velamine, quod tamen ingrediens ad Domi- num et loquens cum eo amovit. Huius historiae significationem, quae nusquam alibi traditur, Apostolus hic exponit. Manifestum est totam naturam humanam viribus naturalibus sini rege- neratione, etiam cum discit et imitatur legem, tamen tantum qualescunque externos gestus legis facere, ut Saul retinet utcunque professionem de unico Deo, in hoc populo patefacto, sed cor est plenum dubitationibus, non statuit se recipi et exaudiri a Deo, sentit se mori, et in morte non sentit consolationem et vitam. Deinde sunt alii acerrimi motus pugnantes cum Deo. Denique omnes homines non profani sua experientia no- runt, humanas vires tantum utcunque regere posse locomotivam, seu externos gestus. Cum autem Deus ostendit iram suam contra peccatum, quae describitur in lege, fugiunt corda, et ma- gnitudine irae opprimuntur, et fremunt adversus Deum et ruunt in mortem. Itaque utrunque significatur. Populus intuetur faciem velatam, id est, legis externa opera utcunque audit et imi- tatur, et haec imitatio est iudicia politica, et pha- risaica, sed fulgorem Moysi ferre natura homi- num non potest, id est, iudicium et iram Dei ad- versus peccata, quae describitur lege Dei, nequa- quam potest natura hominum tolerare. Sicut hic dicitur: Lex est ministerium mortis. Et experientia testatur, homines sine consolatione evangelica ruere in aeternam desperationem et mortem.

Haec doctrina saepe apud Paulum repetita est, ut Rom. 4.: Lex iram efficit. Item, Rom. 7.: Peccatum per legem occidit me. Item, 1. Co- rinth. 15.: Aculeus mortis peccatum est, poten- tia vero peccati lex. Haec toties repetit Paulus, ut ostendat homines non fieri iustos lege.

Quod vero dicitur in Exodo, Moysen amovisse velamen ingredientem ad Deum, et lo- quentem cum eo, et completum esse luce divina: significatum est, aliam esse iusticiam, qua Deo sumus accepti, et qua Deum sustinere possumus, scilicet quando filius loquens in nobis, communi- cat nobis lucem suam. Ita velum legi detrahitur, et tollitur hypocrisis, et sunt in nobis iusticia et vita, quam lex describit, sed non exhibet, verum filius Dei exhibet. Ideo hic inquit Paulus: Ve- lum aboleri per Christum. Haec sententia de vera conversione intelligenda est. In veris doloribus agnoscimus non reddi pacem conscientiis et vitam per bona opera. Agnoscimus et procul nos a per- fectione legis abesse, sed ita reddi conscientiis veram consolationem, quae est initium vitae aeter- nae, cum filium Dei agnoscimus, et promissione ipsius sustentamur, ut David reviviscit, audiens et fide amplectens hanc vocem: Dominus abstulit peccatum tuum. Tunc enim agnita misericordia Dei, vivificatur per filium Dei, et ad Deum acce- dit, invocat eum, et habet initia verae obedien- tiae iuxta haec dicta: Accepistis spiritum ado- ptionis filiorum, quo clamamus Abba pater. Et pertinent huc dicta omnia, quae loquuntur de vera conversione, et de vita ac iusticia aeterna in conversis, ut Ieremiae 31.: Dabo legem meam in visceribus eorum, et in corde eorum scribam eam.

Declarat igitur Paulus hoc dictum, quomodo velum aboleatur per Christum, quia mox concio- natur de conversione, inquiens: Cum conversus fuerit Israël ad Dominum, aufertur velamen. Hanc doctrinam utcunque in vera conversione et consolatione discimus. Nec satis est hic de alle- goriis ceremoniarum dicere. Loquitur enim haec collatio de lege morali, seu de iudicio et ira ad- versus peccatum, et de consolatione.

Dictum est de litera, de spiritu, de discri- mine externae disciplinae, quae velatam Moysi faciem intuetur, et de sensu iudicii ac irae Dei, et de consolatione. His interpretationibus consi- deratis, iam continua series huius capitis erit pla- nior. Ac valde prodest hanc consolationem, quae hic recitatur, in conspectu tenere, et saepe cogitare.

# Philippians

## 1:1 Argument
ARGUMENT OF PAUL'S EPISTLE TO THE PHILIPPIANS.

Blessed Strobelius in his booklet: Von Melanthons Verdiensten um die heil. Schrift (Nuremberg and Altdorf 1773), recorded that Georg Major, a disciple of Melanchthon, prefixed to his own exposition of the Epistle to the Philippians an Argument of the Epistle dictated in the school at Wittenberg by Ph. Melanchthon. Major's book is titled: Enarratio Epist. Pauli scriptae ad Philippenses. Autore Georgio Maiore. Witeb. 1554. 8. I did not happen to see that book, but it is reprinted in the works of Georg Major, Vol. I, Wittenberg 1569, Folio, where it is read on page 731, from which I copied that argument. However, in the works of Major, nothing is read about the fact that Melanchthon dictated the argument.

Latin:

ARGUMENTUM EPISTOLAE PAULI AD PHILIPPENSES.

Beatus Strobelius in libello: Von Melanthons Verdiensten um die heil. Schrift (Norimb. et Alt. 1773), commemoravit, Georgium Maiorem, Melanthonis discipulum enarrationi suae Epistolae ad Philipp. praeposuisse Argumentum Epistolae in schola Viteb. dictatum a Ph. Melanthone. Liber Maioris est inscriptus: Enarratio Epist. Pauli scriptae ad Philippenses. Autore Georgio Maiore. Witeb. 1554. 8. Illum librum videre mihi non contigit, sed est recusns in Georgii Maioris operibus, T. I. Witeb. 1569. Fol. ubi legitur pag. 731, unde illud argumentum descripsi. In operibus Maioris autem nihil legitur de eo, quod Melanthon argumentum dictaverit.

## 1:1
ARGUMENT OF THE EPISTLE (TO THE PHILIPPIANS).

Philippi was a town situated on the extreme borders between Thrace and Macedonia, not far from the very well-known river Strymon on the shore of the Strymonic Gulf, which nevertheless is attributed to Macedonia. By its ancient name it was called Krenides, as if you were to say 'of the fountains,' where the gold veins were so rich that Philip, king of Macedonia, received from there more than a thousand talents, that is, more than six hundred thousand crowns annually.

I do not find what its name is now, but they call the neighboring Pydna 'Chytra,' from the pots, as I suppose. Such is the inconstancy of human affairs that in those very regions which were most adorned with cities, a multitude of men, and civil discipline, and for some time the true knowledge of God, there are now again solitudes or only the huts and stables of barbarian men, because on account of the many and great crimes of men, nations are grieved, and, as the divine voice says, the earth is struck with a curse.

They say that formerly that town was founded by the Thasians and the veins were sought out; for the Thasians also had rich veins of gold and silver on their own island.

Therefore, lest a similar desolation happen in Germany, let us be firm in true doctrine and more ardent in prayer and other pious duties.

But when Philip, the father of Alexander, had captured the town of Krenides, he abolished the old name and subsequently named it Philippi, where also the gold Philippei were made.

It is enough to have said these things about the name.

Concerning the calling of Paul into Macedonia, that he might teach the Gospel there.

These things concerning both names are recounted by Diodorus Siculus and by Stephanus, who cites Archemidor. And Ptolemy, Stephanus, the History of Brutus, and the Narrative in the Acts of the Apostles recount it among the towns of Macedonia, and indeed in the Acts it is said to have been a Roman Colony. There also Antony and Octavius routed the army of Brutus.

How Paul crossed into Europe from Troas, and first approached the city of Philippi, is read in Acts chapter 16. An angel seen at night in the appearance of a Macedonian man called Paul into Macedonia, where first must be recognized the immense goodness of God, who by his mercy for the sake of his son gathers an eternal Church, not only not having merits, but also entirely ignorant and not desiring this great benefit. There was in those places total darkness concerning God; no one had heard the voice of the Gospel, no one desired it. And yet God, through an angel, summons teachers, and the seeds of the Gospel are scattered widely through Macedonia and Greece, and God shows undoubted testimonies of the doctrine by illustrious miracles. Let us acknowledge this immense mercy of God, and let us give thanks to God, because He sent Paul and gathers a Church for Himself among us by the voice of the Gospel. Let there also be care to retain this great benefit, because it is written: to him who has, it will be given, and from him who does not have, that which he has will be taken away. And let the desolation of those regions, where once there were most flourishing Churches, remind us of the wrath of God and of the horrible punishments which follow contumacy, such as was also in Judea, of which the Lord says: how often I wanted to gather you, and you would not. Considering these ancient examples in the whole world, in Asia, Syria, Egypt, Africa, then also in Europe, in Thrace, Illyricum, Greece, I cannot but shudder, thinking of the just and immense wrath of God, and fearing similar devastations in the rest of Europe. Then in the same history this also is worthy of consideration. God could have taught the Gospel in Macedonia through that very angel, but He calls Paul; He wants men to perform this great ministry, in which God is effective, and He gives righteousness and eternal life to those who hear and do not resist. Through these firm and weak vessels He wants to destroy the power of the devil. These things must be considered, so that we may willingly hear the voice of the ministry, even if it seems absurd that wretched men should speak of the presence of God, of eternal salvation, and of other most important matters. Thirdly, because there was a great crowd in that town on account of the metal veins and the right of a Colony, it is consistent that Paul preferred to set out there for that reason, and since he himself was a Roman citizen, born in the Colony of Tarsus, he hoped that he would be safer there. But these reasons being omitted, let us know that the more important cause was the mercy of God, who thus directed the journeys of Paul, and willed that the seeds of the Gospel be scattered there immediately. He therefore adds illustrious testimonies of the new doctrine. The woman Lydia with her whole family embraces

the Gospel, and her house becomes a lodging for Paul and the Church. A demon is cast out of a fortune-telling girl. Paul and Silas, thrown into prison, are freed by a singular miracle. The jailer with his family receives the Gospel. These are the beginnings of the Church in that place, which, know that it grew, appears from the epistle which he later writes to them, in which he praises both their faith and their liberality.

And God wants such histories to exist for many reasons. God wants it to be known that the Gospel was entrusted by Himself to certain men, and He adds illustrious testimonies; He wants it to be known whence this doctrine was received, through whom and in what way it was propagated, so that it may be distinguished from superstitions, which for the most part have crept secretly into the world, and have been accumulated little by little in such a way that their beginnings are scarcely known, just as it cannot be sufficiently known how the Bacchanalia or Lupercalia first arose. In the Church, however, the manifestations of God and the revelations of the promise have always been made by manifest and illustrious testimonies, as the liberation in the flood was a testimony concerning the preaching of Noah, in the calling of Abraham the generation of a son from a mother who was old and barren, concerning Moses the leading out from Egypt, concerning Samuel, David, Elijah, Elisha, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, their own miracles witnessed by whole nations testify at individual times. Thus later the resurrection of the dead and other miracles were testimonies concerning the doctrine of the Son of God and the Apostles. Therefore, so that the Church may know for certain that the voice of the Gospel has been delivered by God, such testimonies were exhibited, and this history was written.

I have recited these historical matters because the sweetest epistle written to the Church which was gathered in Philippi, at the first entrance to Europe, is more pleasing to one considering both the place and the mutual benevolence between Paul and that Church. How great is the praise, because he names them his joy and crown, where the Apostle adorns the hearers with such a great proclamation, it can be sufficiently estimated that the Church also faithfully preserved the purity of the doctrine, and was without scandals.

On the argument of the Epistle.

Now I will recite the argument of the epistle. We see that it is not a long writing nor that any continuous disputation has been instituted, but, as written to friends, a brief exhortation and admonition.

In the first chapter, after he has prayed well for them at the beginning, he narrates that he is held captive at Rome, and yet meanwhile on various occasions the name of Christ is becoming more known, and the Gospel is being propagated, and the Church is growing. Such narrations are customary in epistles, as everyone knows.

In the second chapter, an exhortation is instituted to maintain consensus in doctrine and to retain concord, which is more often disturbed by ambition than by other causes. Therefore, he opposes to ambition the example of the Son of God, who humbled himself for our sake and endured not only the common miseries of men, but even a shameful death. Here is inserted the doctrine concerning the two natures in the Messiah, born of the virgin Mary, as we shall say later.

Then immediately follows a notable sentence concerning the efficacy of God in the members of the Church, containing most ample doctrine and consolation: It is God who works in you, both to will and to perform, so that some things may become pleasing to Him. Here he condemns the Pharisaic opinions, which imagined that the law is fulfilled by human works and that sin is taken away by that discipline. For he affirms on the contrary that God is efficacious in conversion and thereafter, and that these eternal goods are effected by God, and that sin and death are taken away, not by human wisdom and discipline, but by God regenerating us, as is said in John 3, and as it was predicted in the Prophets concerning this wonderful liberation from sin, as is said in Joel: I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh. Likewise: I will pour out upon the house of David the spirit of grace and of supplications.

And consolation follows. Soon when the Church began to be gathered, huge struggles were stirred up; when idols are condemned, the defenders of idols begin to rage against the Church, which, because it is small, seems in vain to oppose itself to supreme empires. Therefore, many, weakened by despair, cast away these struggles. But Paul adds consolation; nay, he says, you do not cry out in vain, but God will be with you and will give success and good outcomes. The power of the world will not destroy the Church. Paul proposes this sweetest consolation in this saying, which in this great infirmity of ours should always be in our sight in the greatest dangers: when God calls us to the Gospel, and kindles the beginnings of faith in us, He does not begin these things in vain, but He also wills to perfect the benefits begun. And the final cause is added, so that some things may become pleasing to God, that is, God does not will the whole human race to have been created in vain, but He wills there always to be some part of the human race which does things pleasing to Him, and to which He may afterwards communicate His goodness in all eternity, while meanwhile the greatest part of the human race rushes furiously against the will of God. There are many Epicureans openly insulting against God, many worshippers of idols fascinated by devils, who with monstrous rage oppose the Gospel, many others polluted by lusts and other crimes. In such great confusion of the human race, nevertheless God preserves some assembly which truly celebrates Him, and has done right and salutary things, so that although in the Babylonian kingdom there are very many impious princes and peoples, nevertheless there Daniel and the Church joined to Daniel teach Darius and Cyrus and many others about the true God, and celebrate God with confession and other duties of virtues, and God mitigates many things in the whole government of the kingdom on their account. And so some things pleasing to God come to pass in that empire.

This is the native meaning of the Pauline saying in this place. And those horrid and false interpretations are to be removed, which transform the saying into a Stoic sentence, as if Paul meant that good and evil things happen by fatal necessity. This imagination does not agree with Paul's saying, which is a sweetest consolation to those who, called to the knowledge of God, have the beginnings of faith and invocation, and seek help. To these, help is promised in this place. And more below concerning untimely interpretations. Now I have added these only for the sake of inviting the reader, so that he may consider the chief lights of the Epistle.

In the third chapter he warns the Church not to be deceived by impostors, where immediately is interwoven a notable passage concerning the distinction between the righteousness of the Law and of the Gospel. Here, as we shall say copiously later, it is necessary first to understand the appellations, what he calls the righteousness of the law, and then what he calls the righteousness of faith. And he does not only call the righteousness of the law obedience in ceremonies, but also obedience in moral works, as much as can be performed by men in this miserable and depraved nature. Comparing this mutilated and defiled righteousness to the righteousness of faith or of the Gospel, he says that he judges it to be loss and σκύβαλα in comparison to that other. The word σκύβαλα signifies dung, as if κυσὶ βαλλόμενα, that is, thrown to the dogs. This notable disparagement brings great consolation to the pious and to those who rightly understand it. For in truth there is an infinite difference between the justice of the law and of faith, even though these things also have the commandments of God, and discipline and good works are necessary in their own place. But the recognition of the Son of God and of the mercy of God, and liberation from eternal death and the gift of justice and eternal life, is a far different matter.

He then dwells on the complaints about the deceivers who were corrupting the doctrine, and signifies that the Jews, fascinated by the persuasion concerning the preservation of their polity, were wandering and sowing such great contentions about the law, on account of which a decree had been made at Jerusalem, which is recited in Acts chapter 15. To these he opposes the statement: our πολίτευμα is in heaven, that is, the voice of the Gospel does not establish a polity or empire in this mortal life, as the Jews dream that the Messiah will reign once the nations have been subdued, and will govern all provinces with a just and tranquil empire according to the law of Moses.
