He wishes this whole dream to be cast aside, and for it to be known that by the Gospel a worldly empire is by no means established, but that in us a true recognition of God, justice, and eternal life is begun, and after the resurrection of the dead, the Church, as if in one city, is to be the measure in eternal fellowship before God, where it will enjoy His wisdom and goodness without end. This heavenly polity, he says, is restored through the Son of God by the voice of the Gospel and the Holy Spirit. He wishes us to await this with true faith, hope, confession, and by enduring punishments in confession, and to propagate the true recognition and invocation of God in this life, not to take up arms so that we may establish new empires, as did Münzer in Thuringia and Schappeler in Swabia and later the furious men in the city of Münster and Westphalia. The comparison of these examples illustrates the statement of Paul.

The fourth chapter contains general admonitions to constancy in the confession of doctrine, to invocation, and to the duties of the other virtues, the chief of which he has encompassed in this accumulation: furthermore, brothers, whatever things are true, consistent with gravity, just, chaste, friendly, and praiseworthy, think on virtue and praise as you have learned and do these things. He names truth at the beginning, because it is necessary before all other virtues to hold the true knowledge of doctrine and faith. Truth is therefore a firm assent and confession concerning true and uncorrupted doctrine and a clear refutation of errors, just as Athanasius is truthful, because he perpetually retains the assent and profession of true doctrine, and is not broken by flatteries, hatreds, terrors, exiles, and other afflictions, so that he might omit his confession. Conversely, however, Hosius, although he was not an enemy of true doctrine, nevertheless yielded to the Arians at the Synod of Sirmium.

Secondly, he names gravity, σεμνότητα, which is a virtue diligent in teaching and in every action, necessary and consistent with modesty and constancy, and it fights against futility, vanity, virulence, scurrility, and arrogance in gesture and speech. He wishes the teacher not to be futile and bickering about unnecessary matters, as either fools or factious men do, and those burning with hatred, as are many entirely futile questions: whether it is necessary to use leavened bread in the Lord's Supper; likewise, whether it is necessary to administer the Lord's Supper in the evening, just as the Lord Himself first administered it, and other similar ones.

Scurrility is that which Bishops and Canons do when they play, gorge themselves, and rail, like the most frivolous men among the common people.

By justice in this place I understand particular justice, giving to each his own, the violation of which is a great sin, which indeed even political magistrates punish.

Chastity is a virtue which forbids all wandering lusts and preserves the order divinely instituted, either by pure virginity or in lawful marriage.

When he names friendly things, he demands equity, that is ἐπιείκειαν, remitting something from the bitterness of the highest law, and pardoning private offenses for the sake of public tranquility, as David, returning after the sedition, swears that he will kill no one, 2 Samuel 19. Let a good governor understand what things invite the benevolence of men, such as beneficence, as Cyrus says in the second book of Xenophon: that those whom we wish to be allies must be hunted by doing good and speaking well.

Sixthly, he names praiseworthy things, εὔφημα, that is, to show modesty for the sake of avoiding scandal and not to disturb the common congregation and association without necessary causes, as those abusing liberty often alienate the wills of modest men, just as those did who, under the pretext of the Gospel

God wishes to invite men to the acknowledgment of the Gospel by good examples, not to be deterred by petulance, as it is written: let your light shine before men, that your heavenly Father may be glorified, Item 1 Corinthians 10: do all things for the glory of God, and be without offense to others. And the contrary rebuke is written in Ezekiel: because of you the name of God is evil spoken of among the nations. Nor is it difficult for men of moderate understanding to judge which actions are necessary, and which is unnecessary petulance. But as scandals conflict with the second commandment of the decalogue, because either the name of God and doctrine are falsely used as a pretext for private desires, or dishonest deeds alienate wills from doctrine: so the virtue which he names here, to do εὔφημα, is a work of the second commandment, and is modesty, which strives to avoid scandals, of which Paul also says elsewhere: he who serves Christ in these things, pleases God and is approved by men.

In all actions this end must be looked to, whether it invites men to celebrate God and to foster the association of the true Church, or whether it disturbs the society of the Church, and alienates the wills of pious men who judge rightly from the doctrine, as Paul says: do all things for the glory of God, and be without offense to others.

If there is any virtue.

At the end he adds general names, in which both a repetition of the above is contained, and it is signified, so that they may understand that other virtues are also included, which are not expressly named here, such as patience, temperance, frugality, liberality, although they can be included in those appellations which have been recited. But the most correct and most clear declaration of virtues is to distribute the works of the decalogue in order, from which this definition can be established: Virtue is to do things consistent with the decalogue, that is, with the moral laws which have been divinely handed down to the whole human race. God does not wish men to live without a certain norm of actions, and to wander where blind desires lead, but immediately at creation he implanted in human minds an eternal and immovable distinction between good and evil actions. He later repeated this often with his own voice. He wishes actions to conform to this norm. Therefore the most correct and most clear definition of virtue in the Church is this: Virtue is to do things consistent with the decalogue, according to the interpretation of the Gospel, just as the definition of sin is recited by John from the opposite: ἡ ἁμαρτία ἐστὲν ἀνομία, that is, sin is not to obey the law of God. Learned men can easily understand that this description is most appropriate, because in the definitions of actions a comparison of knowledge must be made, namely of the divine immovable norms to the actions. Therefore good actions, that is, virtues, are those which conform with the norm, but on the other hand, evil actions are those which deviate from that norm and conflict with it.

If there is any praise.

Afterwards Paul says: if there is any praise. I said before, in all actions, this end must be looked to, that men may be invited to the doctrine. Nor can the variety of examples be briefly comprehended, others alienate the wills of men in other ways. Therefore he commands that we ourselves prudently consider what is becoming, and what is profitable for preserving and fostering the Church. Therefore, so that he may not omit anything, he commands them to recall the whole doctrine heard before, when he says: think on these things, which you have both received and learned etc.

This enumeration of virtues in this chapter is notable, and as the sum of the doctrine concerning virtues it ought to be familiarly known to all. Afterwards, as happens in letters, he adds customary things about his own person, he gives thanks that they sent supplies to Rome for him as a captive, in which narrative he wisely does both, he wishes to be held neither as a beggar or greedy, nor as ungrateful. For both are unjust. For justice is not wishing to burden or plunder others. There is also justice in being grateful for a benefit. Paul performs both, he narrates that he did not ask for this benefit from them, and he describes his own modesty with notable words. I can, he says, be content, I can also bear a humble lot or abjection, again I can also bear prosperous things; but afterwards he adds: with the help of Christ. He used a Greek word, I have been initiated in all things, μεμύημαι. For μυεῖσθαι is the proper word of the priests which signified to be consecrated to certain ceremonies, whence our word is: weihen. Paul therefore transferred a word customary for priests to the hardships of teachers, whom it especially behooves to be prepared for all contingencies, and skillfully to bear both fortunes rightly, not to grow insolent in favorable circumstances, nor to fall away from God on account of adverse ones. This strength in teachers is also demanded by the words of Moses, in the descriptions of the tribes in Deut. 33: who said to his father and his mother, I know you not etc. They keep thy word and thy covenant etc. To such precepts the example of Paul proposed in this place is appropriate.

But after he refuted the suspicion of avarice, he then narrates that he accepts the gift with a grateful mind, and praises their former liberality, because he had also experienced their benevolence before, of which, however, he speaks in such a way as to signify that a reward is owed to teachers, just as he also says elsewhere in Rom. 15: they are debtors to them. Thus he says here: no

church communicated with me concerning the account of giving and receiving, but you only. He signifies therefore that in return for doctrine given, rewards must be given, as is most true. Since, however, there were gold mines in that place, it is consistent that there were many who, as they had previously dedicated many things to idols, so afterwards, when the true doctrine concerning God and the Redeemer had shone upon them, contributed something to assist the ministry of the Gospel.

Paul used here the word ἀπέχω, which was customary in contracts, where he who had received a debt confessed that he had received it, ἀπέχω, that is, I have received the debt paid in full, whence is the name ἀποχή for a receipt of a debt received.

I have said these things in the recitation of the argument, so that afterwards the notable subject matters may be observed more diligently.

Glory to God.

Latin:

ARGUMENTUM EPISTOLAE (AD PHILIPPENSES).

Φίλιπποι oppidum fuit situm in extremis finibus inter Thraciam et Macedoniam, non pro- cul a fluvio notissimo Strymone in littore sinus Strymonici, quod tamen Macedoniae attributum est. Veteri appellatione nominatum est Κρηνίδης, quasi dicas fontanae, ubi venae aureae adeo lo- cupletes fuerunt, ut rex Macedoniae Philippus inde plus mille talentis, id est, plus sexcentis millibus coronatorum quotannis acceperit.

Nunc quae sit appellatio non invenio, Pyd- nam vero vicinam nominant Χύτραν, ab ollis, ut opinor. Talis est rerum humanarum incon- stantia ut in illis ipsis regionibus, quae fuerunt ornatissimae urbibus, hominum frequentia et ci- vili disciplina et aliquandiu vera Dei agnitione, nunc rursus sint solitudines aut tantum barbaro- rum hominum tuguria et stabula, quia propter multa et magna hominum scelera gentes dolentur, et, ut vox divina dicit, terra feritur anathemate.

Olim ainnt a Thassiis id oppidum conditum et venas inquisitas esse; nam et Thassii in sua insula uberes venas auri et argenti habuerunt.

Ne igitur similis vastitas fiat in Germania, simus in vera doctrina firmi et in inovocatione et aliis piis officiis ardentiores.

Cum autem Philippus, Alexandri pater, op- pidum Κρηνίδας coepisset, vetus nomen abolevit, et deinceps nominavit Philippos, ubi et aurei Philippei facti sunt.

Haec de nomine dixisse satis est.

De vocatione Pauli in Macedoniam, ut ibi Evangelium doceret.

Haec de utraque appellatione recitantur a Diodoro Siculo et a Stephano, qui citat Arche- midorum. Ac Ptolemaeus, Stephanus, Histo- ria Bruti et Narratio in Actis Apostolicis recen- sent inter oppida Macedoniae, et quidem in Actis dicitur fuisse Romana Colonia. Ibi et Bruti exer- citum profligarunt Antonius et Octavius.

Quomodo Paulus in Europam ex Troade tra- iecerit, et primum accesserit ad urbem Philippos, legitur in Actis cap. 16. Angelus noctu specie viri Macedonis conspectus vocavit Paulum in Mace- doniam, ubi primum agnoscenda est immensa bo- nitas Dei, qui sua misericordia propter filium colligit aeternam Ecclesiam, non solum non ha- bentem merita, sed etiam prorsus ignorantem et non optantem hoc tantum beneficium. Erant in illis locis prorsus tenebrae de Deo, nemo audie- rat vocem Evangelii, nemo optabat. Et tamen Deus per angelum accersit doctores et semina Evangelii, late per Macedoniam et Graeciam spar- guntur, et ostendit Deus non dubia testimonia doctrinae illustribus miraculis. Hanc immensam misericordiam Dei agnoscamus, et Deo gratias agamus, quod misit Paulum et Evangelii voce Ecclesiam sibi inter nos colligit. Sit etiam cura hoc tantum beneficium reti- nendi, quia scriptum est: habenti dabitur, et a non habenti id, quod habet, auferetur. Et illa- rum regionum solitudo, ubi quondam florentis- simae Ecclesiae fuerunt, nos commonefaciat de ira Dei et de horrendis poenis, quae sequuntur con- tumaciam, qualis et in Iudaea fuit, de qua dicit Dominus: quoties volui te congregare, et no- luisti. Haec vetera exempla in toto orbe terrarum, in Asia, Syria, Aegypto, Africa, deinde et in Europa, in Thracia, Illyrico, Graecia conside- rans, non possum non expavescere, cogitans iu- stum et ingentem iram Dei, et metuens similes vastationes in reliqua Europa. Deinde in eadem historia et hoc dignum est consideratione. Poterat Deus per illum ipsum angelum docere Evangelium in Macedonia, sed vocat Paulum, vult homines fungi hoc tanto mi- nisterio, in quo Deus est efficax, et dat iusticiam et vitam aeternam audientibus et non repugnanti- bus. Per haec vasa firma et languida vult diaboli potentiam destruere. Haec consideranda sunt, ut libenter audia- mus vocem ministerii, etiamsi videtur absurdum, homines aerumnosos, de praesentia Dei, de aeterna salute et aliis maximis rebus loqui. Tertio, quia magna frequentia fuit in illo oppido propter venas metallicas et propter ius Coloniae, consentaneum est, Paulum propter eam causam eo proficisci maluisse, et cum ipse civis Romanus esset, natus in Colonia Tarso, speravit, ubi se tutiorem fore. Sed his causis omissis, sciamus potiorem causam fuisse miseri- cordiam Dei, qui ita rexit itinera Pauli, et voluit ibi statim sparsi Evangelii semina. Addit igitur illustria testimonia novae doctri- nae. Mulier Lydia cum tota familia amplectitur

Evangelium, et eius domus fit hospitium Pauli et Ecclesiae. Eiicitur daemonium ex puella fa- tidica. Coniecti in carcerem Paulus et Silas sin- gulari miraculo liberantur. Custos carceris cum sua familia recipit Evangelium. Haec sunt ini- tia Ecclesiae in eo loco, quam scito crevisse, ap- paret ex epistola, quam postea ad eos scribit, in qua et fidem et liberalitatem eorum praedicat.

Et vult Deus extare tales historias propter multas causas. Vult Deus sciri, a sese Evange- lium certis hominibus commendatum esse, et ad- dit illustria testimonia; vult sciri, unde accepta sit haec doctrina, per quos et quo modo propa- gata sit, ut dicerni possit a superstitionibus, quae plerunque clam irrepserunt in mundum, et pau- latim cumulatae sunt ita, ut vix sciantur initia, ut quomodo Bacchanalia aut Lupercalia primum orta sint, non satis sciri potest. In Ecclesia vero semper manifestis et illustribus testimoniis factae sunt patefactiones Dei, et revelationes promis- sionis, ut de praedicatione Nohae testimonium fuit liberatio in diluvio, in vocatione Abrahae ge- neratio filii ex matre anu et sterili, de Mose eductio ex Aegypto, de Samuele, Davide, Elia, Eliseo, Esaia, Ieremia, Daniele testantur singu- lis temporibus sua miracula conspecta totis genti- bus. Ita postea resuscitatio mortuorum et alia miracula fuerunt testimonia de doctrina filii Dei et Apostolorum. Ut igitur certo sciat Ecclesia, vocem Evangelii a Deo traditam esse talia testi- monia exhibita sunt, et haec historia scripta est.

Haec historica recitavi quia gratior est dul- cissima epistola scripta ad Ecclesiam, quae in Phi- lippis, in primo Europae aditu, collecta est, con- sideranti et locum et mutuam benevolentiam inter Paulum et illam Ecclesiam. Quanta laus est, quod nominat eos cum gaudium et coronam suam, ubi auditores hoc tanto praeconio ornat Aposto- lus, existimari satis potest, Ecclesiam etiam fideliter conservasse doctrinae puritatem, et sine scandalis fuisse.

De argumento Epistolae.

Nunc argumentum epistolae recitabo. Vi- demus non longum scriptum esse nec perpetuam aliquam disputationem institutam esse, sed, ut ad amicos scriptam, brevem hortationem et ad- monitionem.

In primo capite, postquam initio eos bene precatus est, narrat, se Romae captivum retineri, et tamen interea variis occasionibus nomen Chri- sti fieri magis notum, et propagari Evangelium, et crescere Ecclesiam. Tales narrationes usita- tae sunt in epistolis, ut omnes norunt.

In secundo capite instituitur adhortatio ad tuendum consensum in doctrina et ad retinendam concordiam, quae ambitione saepius turbatur, quam aliis causis. Ideo opponit ambitioni exem- plum filii Dei, qui sese propter nos abiecit et sustinuit non solum communes hominum aeru- mnas, sed etiam contumeliosam mortem. Hic in- seritur doctrina de duabus naturis in Messia, nato ex virgine Maria, ut postea dicemus.

Deinde statim sequitur insignis sententia de efficacia Dei in membris Ecclesiae, continens amplissimam doctrinam et consolationem: Deus est qui efficit in vobis, ut velitis et ut perficia- tis, ut aliqua ei grata fiant. Hic damnat Phari- saicas opiniones, quae fingebant legem impleri humanis operibus et disciplina illa tolli peccatum. Contra enim affirmat Deum efficacem esse in con- versione et deinceps, et haec aeterna bona effici a Deo, tolli peccatum et mortem, non humana sapientia et disciplina, sed Deo nos regenerante, sicut Iohan. 3. dicitur, et sicut in Prophetis prae- dictum est de hac miranda liberatione a peccato, ut in Ioël dicitur: effundam de spiritu meo super omnem carnem, Item: effundam super domum David spiritum gratiae et precum.

Et sequitur consolatio. Mox ubi coepit Ec- clesia colligi certamina ingentia moventur, cum idola damnantur, defensores idolorum saevire in Ecclesiam incipiunt, quae quia est exigua, frustra videtur se opponere summis imperiis. Ideo multi desperatione languefacti abiiciunt haec cer- tamina. Sed Paulus consolationem addit, imo, inquit, non frustra clamatis, sed Deus vobis ad- erit et successus et bonos eventus dabit. Non de- lebit Ecclesiam potentia mundi. Hanc dulcissi- mam consolationem Paulus in hoc dicto proponit, quae in hac tanta infirmitate nostra in maximis periculis semper nobis in conspectu sit: cum Deus vocet nos ad Evangelium, et initia fidei in nobis accendat, non frustra haec inchoat, sed vult etiam inchoata beneficia perficere. Et causa finalis addi- tur, ut aliqua grata Deo fiant, id est, Deus non vult universum genus humanum frustra conditum esse, sed vult semper aliquam esse partem gene- ris humani, quae ipsi grata faciat, et cui postea in omni aeternitate suam bonitatem communicet, cum interea maxima pars generis humani furen- ter contra voluntatem Dei ruat. Multi sunt Epi- curaei palam contumeliosi contra Deum, multi cultores idolorum fascinati a diabolis, qui im- mani rabie Evangelio repugnant, multi alii pol- luti libidinibus et aliis sceleribus. In tanta con- fusione generis humani, tamen Deus servat coe- tum aliquem, qui ipsum vere celebrat, et recta et salutaria fecit, ut quanquam in regno Babylo- nico plurimi sunt principes et populi impii, tamen ibi Daniel et Ecclesia adiuncta Danieli, Darium et Cyrum et multos alios docent de vero Deo, et celebrant Deum confessione et aliis virtutum offi- ciis, et multa in tota gubernatione regni Deus propter eos mitigat. Itaque fiunt aliqua grata Deo in illo imperio.

Haec est nativa sententiam dicti Paulini hoc loco. Ac removendae sunt horridae et fal- sae interpretationes, quae transformant dictum in Stoicam sententiam, quasi velit Paulus, bona et mala fieri necessitate fatali. Haec imaginatio non congruit ad Pauli dictum, quod est consola- tio dulcissima iis, qui vocati ad agnitionem Dei, initia fidei et invocationis habent, et auxilium petunt. His hoc loco promittitur auxilium. Ac infra plura de intempestivis interpretationibus. Nunc tantum haec adieci invitandi lectoris causa, ut consideret praecipua Epistolae lumina.

In tertio capite monet Ecclesiam, ne deci- piatur ab impostoribus, ubi statim intexitur insignis locus de discrimine iusticiae Legis et Evangelii. Hic, ut postea copiose dice- mus necesse est, primum adpellationes intel- ligi, quid nominet iusticiam legis, et deinde quid nominet iusticiam fidei. Nec tantum nominat iusticiam legis obedientiam in cere- moniis, sed etiam obedientiam in operibus mo- ralibus, quanta in hominibus in hac misera et depravata natura praestari potest. Hanc mutilam et inquinatam iusticiam conferens ad iusticiam fidei seu Evangelii, dicit eam se iudicare damna et σκύβαλα prae illa altera. Vocabulum σκύ- βαλα significat stercora, quasi κυσὶ βαλλόμενα, id est, obiecta canibus. Haec insignis extenua- tio magnam consolationem piis et recte intelli- gentibus eam adfert Nam revera infinitum dis- crimen est inter iusticiam legis et fidei, etiamsi hae res etiam mandata Dei habent, et suo loco necessariae sunt disciplina et bona opera. Sed longe alia res est agnitio filii Dei et misericordiae Dei, et liberatio ex morte aeterna et donatio iu- sticiae et vitae aeternae.

Commoratur deinde in querelis de praesti- giatonibus, qui doctrinam corrumpebant, et si- gnificat Iudaeos fascinatos persuasione de conser- vatione suae politiae vagari et tanta certamina de lege serere, propter quae decretum Hieroso- lymis factum fuerat, quod recitatur in Actis cap. 15. His opponit dictum: nostrum πολίτευμα in coelis est, id est, vox Evangelii non constituit politiam aut imperium in hac mortali vita, sicut Iudaei somniant, Messiam domitis gentibus re- gnaturum esse, et omnes provincias iusto et tran- quillo imperio gubernaturum esse iuxta legem Moysi. Hoc totum somnium vult abiici, et sciri per Evangelium nequaquam constitui mundanum imperium, sed inchoari in nobis veram agnitio- nem Dei, iusticiam et vitam aeternam et post re- suscitationem mortuorum Ecclesiam tanquam in una civitate in aeterna consuetudine mensuram esse apud Deum, ubi fruetur eius sapientia et bo- nitate sine fine. Hanc coelestem politiam, inquit, per filium Dei voce Evangelii et Spiritu sancto re- stitui. Hanc nos vult expectare vera fide, spe, confessione et tolerandis suppliciis in confessione, et veram Dei agnitionem et invocationem in hac vita propagare, non capere arma, ut nova impe- ria constituamus, sicut fecerunt Monetarius in Turingia et Schaplerus in Suevia et postea furiosi homines in urbe Monasteriensi et Westphalia. Horum exemplorum collatio illustrat dictum Pauli.

Quartum caput continet generales admoni- tiones ad constantiam in confessione doctrinae, ad invocationem et ad caeterarum virtutum offi- cia, quarum praecipuas complexus est hac coacer- vatione: caeterum, fratres, quae sunt vera, gra- vitati convenientia, iusta, casta, amicabilia et laudabilia, virtutem et laudem cogitate sicut di- dicistis et haec facite. Nominat initio veritatem, quia necesse est ante caeteras virtutes omnes te- nere verum doctrinae noticiam et fidem. Est igi- tur veritas firma assensio et confessio de vera et incorrupta doctrina et perspicua refutatio erro- rum, ut Athanasius est verax, quia perpetuo re- tinet adsensionem et professionem verae doctri- nae, nec frangitur blanditiis, odiis, terroribus, exiliis et aliis adflictionibus, ut confessionem omittat. Contra vero Hosius, etsi non fuit hostis verae doctrinae, tamen cedit Arianis in Synodo Sirmiensi.

Secundo nominat gravitatem σεμνότητα, quae est virtus diligens in docendo et in omni actione necessaria et convenientia *) modestiae et constantiae et pugnat cum futilitate, vanitate, virulentia, scurrilitate, arrogantia, in gestu et sermonibus. Vult doctorem non esse futilem et de rebus non necessariis rixantem, ut fa- ciunt aut fatui aut factiosi et ardentes odiis, ut sunt multae prorsus futiles quaestiones: an ne- cesse sit in coena Domini uti pane fermentato; item, an necesse sit, administrare coenam Do- mini vespere, sicut primum administravit ipse Dominus, et aliae similes.

Scurrilitas est, quod Episcopi et Canonici ludunt, helluantur, conviciantur, ut levissimi ho- mines in vulgo.

Iusticiam hoc loco intelligo particularem iu- sticiam, suum cuique tribuentem, cuius violatio est magnum peccatum, quod quidem et politici magistratus puniunt.

Castitas est virtus, quae omnes vagas libidi- nes vetat, et servat ordinem divinitus institutum, vel virginitate pura, vel in coniugio legitimo.

Cum nominat amicabilia, postulat aequita- tem, id est ἐπιείκειαν, aliquid remittentem de acerbitate summi iuris, et condonantem privatas offensiones publicae tranquillitati, ut David post seditionem rediens iurat, se neminem interfe- cturum esse, 2. Reg. 19. Intelligat bonus gu- bernator, quae res invitent benevolentiam homi- num, ut beneficentia, ut in secundo libro Cyrus inquit apud Xenophontem: quos volumus esse socios, venandos esse benefaciendo et benedi- cendo.

Sexto nominat laudabilia, εὔφημα, id est, scandali vitandi causa modestiam praestare et non turbare communem congregationem et con- sociationem sine necessariis causis, ut abutentes libertate saepe alienant voluntates modestorum hominum, sicut illi fecerunt, qui praetextu Evan-

Reg. 19. Intelligat bonus gu- bernator, quae res invitent benevolentiam homi- num, ut beneficentia, ut in secundo libro Cyrus inquit apud Xenophontem: quos volumus esse socios, venandos esse benefaciendo et benedi- cendo.

Sexto nominat laudabilia, εὔφημα, id est, scandali vitandi causa modestiam praestare et non turbare communem congregationem et con- sociationem sine necessariis causis, ut abutentes libertate saepe alienant voluntates modestorum hominum, sicut illi fecerunt, qui praetextu Evan- gelicae libertatis plures uxores simul habuerunt, Item, novos titulos sibi tribuerunt, ut rex Mona- steriensis, qui se nominabat regem in templo Dei, Item, qui Turcas induxerunt in Europam et postea in Pannoniam.

Vult Deus bonis exemplis invitare homines ad agnitionem Evangelii, non petulantia deter- reri, sicut scriptum est: luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, ut glorificetur pater vester coelestis, Item 1. Corinth. 10.: omnia ad gloriam Dei facite, et sine offensione aliis estote. Et contraria ob- iurgatio apud Ezechielem scripta est: propter vos male audit nomen Dei inter gentes. Nec dif- ficile est iudicare mediocribus hominibus, quae actiones necessariae sint, quae sit petulantia non necessaria. Ut autem scandala pugnant cum se- cundo praecepto decalogi, quia vel falso praetexi- tur nomen Dei et doctrina privatis cupiditatibus, vel facta inhonesta alienant voluntates a doctrina: ita virtus, quam hic nominat, facere εὔφημα, opus est secundi praecepti, et est modestia, quae studet vitare scandala, de qua et alibi Paulus inquit: qui in his servit Christo, placet Deo et probatus est hominibus.

In omnibus actionibus hic finis prospicien- dus est, an invitet homines ad celebrandum Deum et ad fovendam verae Ecclesiae consociationem, an vero turbet Ecclesiae societatem, et voluntates piorum recte iudicantium a doctrina alienet, sicut Paulus ait: omnia id gloriam Dei facite, et sine offensione aliis estote.

Si quis virtus.

In fine addit generalia nomina, in quibus et repetitio superiorum continetur, et significatur, ut intelligant comprehendi etiam virtutes caeteras, quae hic non expresse nominatae sunt, ut patien- tia, temperantia, frugalitas, liberalitas, tametsi adpellationibus illis, quae recitatae sunt, includi possunt. Sed rectissima et maxime perspicua et declaratio virtutum est, ordine distribuere opera decalogi, unde constitui haec definitio potest: Virtus est facere convenientia decalogo, id est, legibus moralibus, quae divinitus toti humano generi traditae sunt. Non vult Deus vivere ho- mines sine certa norma actionum, et vagari quo trahunt caecae cupiditates, sed statim in crea- tione indidit humanis mentibus discrimen aeter- num et immotum bonarum et malarum actionum. Id postea voce sua saepe repetivit. Ad hanc nor- mam vult congruere actiones. Ideo rectissima et maxime perspicua definitio virtutis in Ecclesia haec est, Virtus est facere congruentia decalogo, iuxta enarrationem Evangelii, sicut e regione de- finitio peccati a Iohanne recitatur: ἡ ἁμαρτία ἐστὲν ἀνομία, id est, peccatum est non obedire legi Dei. Hanc descriptionem convenientissimam esse, docti facile intelligere possunt, Quia in de- finitionibus actionum oportet fieri collationem noticiae, ut videlicet normae divinae immotae ad actiones. Sunt igitur bonae actiones, id est, virtutes, quae congruunt cum norma, contra an- tem malae actiones sunt, quae aberrant ab illa norma, et cum ea pugnant.

Si qua laus.

Postea inquit Paulus: si qua laus. Dixi autea, in omnibus actionibus, hunc finem pro- spiciendum esse, ut homines invitentur ad doctri- nam. Nec potest breviter comprehendi varietas exemplorum, alii aliis modis alienant voluntates hominum. Ideo iubet, ut nos ipsi prudenter consideremus, quid deceat, et quid prosit ad conservandam et fovendam Ecclesiam. Ne igitur aliquid omittat, iubet eos totam doctrinam recor- dari antea auditam, cum inquit: haec ergo cogi- tate, quae et accepistis et didicistis etc.

Haec enumeratio virtutum in hoc capite in- signis est, et ut summa doctrinae de virtutibus familiariter omnibus nota esse debet. Postea, ut fit in epistolis, addit usitata de sua persona, agit gratias, quod Romam captivo sumptus mise- runt, in qua narratione sapienter utrumque facit, nec petax seu avarus, nec ingratus perhiberi vult. Utrumque enim iniustum est. Nam iusticia est non velle onerare aut expilare alios. Est et iu- sticia gratum esse pro beneficio. Paulus utrum- que praestat, narrat se non petivisse ab eis hoc beneficium, et insignibus verbis modestiam suam describit. Possum, inquit, contentus esse, pos- sum etiam ferre humilem sortem seu abiectionem, rursus etiam possum res secundas ferre; sed po- stea addit: iuvante Christo. Usus est verbo graeco, in omnibus initiatus sum, μεμύημαι. Est enim μυεῖσθαι proprium verbum sacerdo- tum quod significabat ad certas ceremonias con- secrari, unde nostrum vocabulum est: weihen. Transtulit igitur Paulus verbum usitatum sacer- dotibus ad aerumnas docentium, quos praecipue oportet paratos esse ad omnes casus, et scite utramque fortunam recte ferre, non insolescere in rebus secundis, nec propter adversas a Deo deficere. Hoc robur in docentibus postulant et Moysi dicta, in descriptionibus tribuum Deut. 33.: qui dixit patri suo et matri suae, nescio vos etc. Hi custodiunt eloquium tuum et pactum tuum etc. Ad talia praecepta congruit exemplum Pauli hoc loco propositum.

Posteaquam autem suspicionem avaritiae re- futavit, deinde narrat, se grato animo accipere munus, et laudat veterem eorum liberalitatem, quia et antea expertus sit eorum benevolentiam, de qua tamen ita loquitur, ut significat, docenti- bus mercedem deberi, sicut et alibi inquit Rom. 15.: debitores ipsis sunt. Ita hic inquit: nulla

Ecclesia mihi communicavit iuxta rationem Dati et Accepti, nisi vos soli. Significat igitur pro data doctrina vicissim dandas esse mercedes, sicut verissimum est. Cum autem venae auri in illo loco fuerint, consentaneum est, multos fuisse, qui et antea idolis multa dedicarunt, ita postea cum illuxisset eis vera de Deo et de Redemptore doctrina, contulisse aliquid ad iuvandum ministerium Evangelii.

Usus est Paulus hic verbo ἀπέχω, quod fuit usitatum in contractibus, ubi fatebatur is, qui debitum acceperat, se recepisse, ἀπέχω, id est, recepi persolutum debitum, unde est nomen ἀποχή pro testimonio accepti debiti.

Haec in argumenti recitatione dixi, ut postea insignes materiae diligentius observantur.

Θεῷ δόξα.

# Colossians

## 1:1 Argument
PHIL. MEL. EXPOSITION OF PAUL'S EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS.

We have two books in which Melanchthon interpreted Paul's Epistle to the Colossians, the former of which is inscribed: Scholia on the Ep. to the Coloss., the latter: Exposition of the Ep. to the Coloss. —

Melanchthon published the Scholia in the year 1527, and dedicated them to Drachstadius. We have provided the dedicatory epistle, which is read only in the first Secerian edition, in Epistles Vol. I. p. 873. The book is inscribed:

1) Scholia on the Epist. of Paul to the Colossians by Phil. Melanch. at Hagenau by Joann. Secerius. In the year M. D. XXVII. in the month of August. (At the end: in the month of September.) 9 sheets 8vo. — Due to the negligence of Secerius there are many typographical errors in this first edition, as Melanchthon himself testified in Epist. Vol. I. p. 1007. — What Melanchthon wrote at chapter 7, 8, concerning true and false philosophy, these were also reprinted separately: Phil. Mel. on the passage to the Coloss. 'see that no one deceives you through philosophy' recently edited. Basel 1527.

2) German version: Exposition of the Epistle to the Colossians by Philipp Mel., translated into German by Johann Agricola Eysleben. Wittenberg 1527. 8vo.

3) Ph. Mel. Scholia on the Ep. to the Coloss. revised by the author. Wittenberg 1528. 8vo.

4) The Epistle of St. Paul to the Colossians with the commentaries of Phil. Melanchthon now finally revised and enriched by him in many places. Hagenau 1529. by Jo. Secerius. 12 sheets 8vo.

5) Scholia on the Ep. of Paul to the Coloss. again revised by the author Phil. Mel. Wittenberg at the house of Joseph Clug. M. D. XXXIV. 8vo.

6) The Epistle of Paul to the Coloss. with the comment. [Scholia?] of Phil. Mel., which have now most recently been revised and enriched by the author himself, and that in very many places. Hagenau by Val. Kobianus, in the month of August. 1534. 12 sheets 8vo.

7) Scholia — — — Wittenberg 1545. 14 sheets 8vo.

8) Scholia — — — Hall in Swabia 1545. 8vo.

We did not wish to insert these scholia into the Works, since Melanchthon explained everything more accurately in the exposition of this Epistle, and Peucer did not repeat the scholia in the works of Melanchthon. However, the exposition of this Epistle did not appear in the year MDLVI, as is read in the works due to a typographical error, but in the year MDLIX, inscribed thus:

Philipp Melanchthon, Enarratio of the Epistle of Paul to the Colossians. Wittenberg, 1559. 9 sheets, 8vo.

Again, Phil. Melanchthon, Enarratio of the Epistle of Paul to the Colossians. Added is a response to the calumnies of Staphylus and Avio, Frankfurt, 1559. 10 sheets, 8vo.

Likewise in the Works of Melanchthon, Wittenberg, Vol. IV, p. 324 et seqq.

We have provided the preface to Herluf Trolle in the Letters, Vol. IX, p. 745. We have provided the book itself according to the text in the Wittenberg Works.

EXPOSITION OF THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE COLOSSIANS.

Colossae was a town near the river Lycus and the Maeander on the border of Lydia in the region of Laodicea, celebrated by Herodotus, Xenophon, and Strabo. I believe it was omitted by Ptolemy because, as Eutropius writes, Colossae and Laodicea were submerged by an earthquake in the year after Paul's death. Thus, after God had gathered out His Church, the impious and the worshippers of idols were punished.

Since, therefore, the location of this town is known, those who transfer this name to the Rhodians are foolish, because the Colossus of the Sun, celebrated by many, was there. The location is known so that the punishment may be considered, which I said followed after Paul's death. Nor is there any need to ask whence the town was so named: for perhaps there were great statues there as well. For a Colossus is properly a truncated statue, from κόλον, that is, mutilated, and ὄσσε, that is, eyes. Or the name is Henetic, from mud, whence in Pannonia the same name belongs to a famous town. But omitting these follies, let us rather consider the argument and utility of the Epistle.

In the first chapter, the proper doctrine of the Gospel concerning the Person and Benefits of Christ, and concerning the righteousness of faith, and the gift of eternal life, is recited. For there exists here an illustrious testimony concerning the divinity of the Son: All things were created through Him, He is before all things, and all things consist through Him. For since he affirms that all things were created through this Christ, through whom he says we have remission through His blood, it is necessary to confess that in this Christ there are two natures, the divine, λόγον, and the assumed human nature. Because the world was not created through a human nature. The Λόγος, therefore, through whom creation is made, is not a vanishing thing, but a subsisting one. He is called the image of the eternal Father, just as among the Hebrews the ἀπαύγασμα of glory and the character of the Father's substance. Glory in the Mosaic phrase signifies light. He therefore names the Son ἀπαύγασμα, just as in the creed He is called Light from Light, so that thought in us or speech reveals the mind, or, to use this likeness for what it is worth, just as rays are scattered from the Sun. In John, the Son is named λόγος; here He is named εἰκὼν. These two appellations are proper to the Son, and distinguish Him from the Father and the Holy Spirit.

Let the word Image be understood as the whole, living, and substantial image of the eternal Father, which we recognize to the extent that the Father has been revealed through the Son by the voice of doctrine, as being Creator, wise, truthful, good, just, judge, merciful, most free, remitting sins, and restoring righteousness and life through the Mediator. We understand the word λόγος more clearly when we think that the Son is called λόγος because He is the person immediately bringing forth the Gospel from the bosom of the eternal Father, and immediately preserving the ministry, speaking to us, sustaining the Church, just as Wisdom says in Solomon: Playing in the world and my delights are with the sons of men. Which description is to be observed. For it is a testimony concerning the mission to the Church, from that time even from the first revelation of the promise. And what can be thought of as sweeter than that the Son of God affirms that He delights in the company of men. Here, however, let the doctrine concerning the three persons, which is treated more copiously in its own place, be recalled to mind.

Afterwards, in the first chapter, he speaks of the benefits of the Son, and names Him Head of the Church, which pertains to the person who is God and Man. Because the properties of both natures concur in the appellation of head. Christ is head by merit, because He Himself merited salvation for the whole human race: He is also head by Efficacy, because He was truly sent from the beginning to the Church, and is efficacious in it according to His divine nature, just as this very description is declared in the Epistle to the Ephesians: He gave Him as head of the Church, which is His whole body, who perfects all things in all. Just as He Himself says: I am the vine, you are the branches, without me you can do nothing. He Himself sustains and preserves the Church, He Himself gives gifts to the Church, teachers, pastors, through whom He is effective.

Afterwards, in the first chapter, he speaks about the application of the benefits of Christ, when he says: If you remain firm in the faith. Then he adds certain things about the ministry of the Gospel and about the cross. Thus you see that the principal members of the doctrine are briefly comprised in the first chapter, namely, the doctrine concerning the person of Christ, concerning the two natures, concerning the benefits, concerning the application of the benefits through faith, concerning the ministry of the Gospel and the Cross.

Moreover, he has used a remarkable figure concerning the Cross: I fill up what is lacking in the afflictions, etc., namely, not as it pertains to the merit of the leader, but as it pertains to the fellowship of the warfare, which is not yet completed, but lasts until the end of the ministry. The merit of the leader Christ is whole and sufficient for all subjects. We, however, are soldiers in the same ministry, the end of which is not yet. Thus, one after another, the afflictions of the succeeding soldiers are added to the afflictions of the leader, which are lacking to the leader for so long as the end of the ministry in the gathering of the universal Church is not yet reached, even though the merit of the leader and the battles of the soldiers differ. By these words Paul's statement is explained most simply: I fill up what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ, etc., not as it pertains to merit, which is most full and belongs to Christ alone, but as it pertains to the fellowship of the warfare, in which soldiers succeeding one another must in turn suffer afflictions similar to those of the leader. Because the devils hate the leader, the doctrine, and the soldiers, and it could be said that the form of the afflictions is similar, but the final causes are dissimilar; Christ is the propitiator and teacher, Paul is only a teacher.

The Papists impiously distort the statement to refer to the merits of the saints, and they pretend that the afflictions of the saints merit remission for themselves and others. This interpretation is false according to the statement in Romans 5: The grace and the gift through the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abounded to many. 1 John 2: He himself is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only, but for the sins of the whole world. And to the Hebrews: By one offering he has perfected the saints.

In the second chapter, like a prudent physician, when he has provided healthy remedies, Paul warns that the opposites must be avoided, and he gives instructions about avoiding the snares and corruptions of doctrine. See to it, he says, that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deception according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world. For the word Element is not understood as the natural philosophers speak, but generally concerning an external order, whence the name in Greek is στοῖχος.

Moreover, he adds a remarkable reason why we must be on guard not to be deceived by human imaginations and traditions. Because, he says, you have been made complete in Christ. This completion is to be understood in two ways: first, by imputation, that is, that those who are converted are righteous by faith on account of the mediator, that is, reconciled and accepted by God, even though a huge infirmity still clings to them in this life, as it is said in Romans 5: Justified by his blood. Secondly, by renewal, which is begun in this life and becomes whole in eternal life. And this renewal happens on account of Christ, because in him dwells all the fullness of the divinity bodily. All the fullness, namely, with regard to the gifts or effective properties, that is, life, omnipotence, infinite wisdom and justice, which gifts he communicates to men, showing them light and consolation by the voice of the Gospel, and giving the Holy Spirit, as if he were saying: In angels and men there are particular gifts, there is no omnipotence, there is no infinite wisdom and justice, but this fullness belongs to the Son, who indeed dwells bodily, that is, personally, in the assumed nature, not separably, not only effectively: as God is in David separably and effectively, but in such a way that he is one person or one ὑφιστάμενον, that is, that the two natures, divine and human, are inseparably joined by a hypostatic union, by which the human nature is borne by the λόγος, much like how the soul and body of a man are one ὑφιστάμενον, the body is borne by the soul, or as a shoot grafted onto a tree is borne by it, although this similarity is further removed. But yet this depicts in some way that the human nature has been saved: because the Son assumed the mass, and we, grafted into this mass, are saved, because we receive from the fullness of the Son, we are pleasing on account of him, and we are vivified immediately through him, just as he says: I am the vine, you are the branches. The eternal Father sent the Son, through whom the promise is revealed, and this Son gathers the Church, is the redeemer, and by the voice of the promise speaks consolation into hearts, and gives the Holy Spirit. Thus, since all the fullness of the divinity dwells in him, he is effective in us, and we receive from his fullness eternal life, wisdom, and eternal justice.

Afterwards, the commemoration of the benefits of Christ, of liberation from sin and from death, was repeated, and an illustrious image of the triumph of Christ was inserted, in which the figures of the words were taken from the triumphs of kings, in which the spoils of enemies were carried before the triumphal chariot. Then the captive enemies were led bound before the victor. Thus he says most sweetly here, that the spoils are carried before him hanging on the cross, namely, the handwritings of our sins blotted out. How can the remission of sins and reconciliation be painted more illustriously than in this very image? In which it is said that the accusation was blotted out, and carried on the cross of Christ? Because the Son, the Redeemer, satisfied the eternal Father for us, and took away the accusation. The bound devils are also led, so that we may know that, although the Church is weak, yet it is defended by the victor Christ amidst the snares of devils and the furies of tyrants and heretics. As it is also said in John: The Son of God appeared, that he might destroy the works of the devil.

Afterwards Paul returns to the admonition concerning avoiding the corruptions of doctrine, and by name he sets forth this assertion, that it is not a sin to violate the ceremonial laws of Moses and human traditions concerning foods, feasts, and similar external rites, which are not the righteousness of the heart, and he paints the deceits by which impostors astutely scatter false dogmas, namely, the artificial simulation of humility, poverty, and patience, by which they wish to appear to have cast off the common desires of pleasures, riches, and glory above other men: then the boasting of heavenly conversations with God and the angels. Our age has seen examples of both kinds, and here is a notable word: Let no one rule you badly in the contest. Brabeutes is from rhabdos, that is, a rod; hence is the word katabrabeuein, to rule a contestant badly, or to deceive, to move the goal, or in any way to place an impediment in the way.

In the third chapter, since he had previously recited the summary of the doctrine concerning the benefits of the Mediator, and the admonitions concerning avoiding the corruptions of doctrine, he adds precepts concerning good works, both interior and exterior, concerning the exercises of renewal.

In these there is also a notable precept concerning the zeal for learning and teaching, which is to be the more loved because such sayings, which commend reading, are testimonies against Stencfeld and other fanatics, who lead men away from the reading of doctrine and the ministry, and at the same time they testify that reading and studies are pleasing to God, and that God is effective through the contemplation of the written word: which, when the pious know, they may the more love the studies of reading and learning. Let this saying therefore be most familiarly known: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom, and teach and admonish one another. Richly, he says, let it dwell. Therefore let it be read often and much, let judgments be compared. When he says, Teach and admonish one another: let there be therefore studies of doctrine, let invocation be mingled, just as it is said elsewhere: How much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask. He uses, however, the word Dwelling, so that he may signify assiduity, namely, that the doctrine may be familiarly known, just as those are known who dwell with us. At the same time, however, let us know this, wherever in true conversion to God doctrine is contemplated by faith, in that heart God himself most certainly dwells at the same time, that is, He is present by His essence and efficacy, He is truly present, and is effective. John 14: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him, and make our abode with him. And Ephesians, third chapter: That Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts. Colossians, first chapter: He himself is the head of the Church, perfecting all things in all. For the Son, by the voice of the Gospel speaking consolation, shows in the mind the presence and mercy of the Father. Thus the Father and the Son are present, and the Father and the Son breathe the Holy Spirit into the heart of the believer, so that joy, invocation, eternal life, and all the fruits of the Spirit may be kindled. Thus the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are together. These things are to be thought of piously and rightly, and let there be thanks for the emphasis on the word Dwelling. He commands, however, that the word of God dwell in us in all wisdom. This admonition is inserted concerning diligence, which has two extremes, Sloth and Sophistry. The word of God does not dwell in unlearned mass-priests, who read or sing without understanding and without art; it does not dwell in Sophists, Heretics, and Superstitious people, who sow curious disputes or pernicious opinions, as are the most vain sophisms of the monks, whether God could have assumed a non-rational nature, whether accidents exist without a subject in the Sacrament, whether it is permitted to consecrate leavened bread, and the blasphemies of Samosatenus, the Manichaeans, Arius, Servetus, and other heretics. Likewise the papistical darkness, that men are righteous by the proper fulfillment of the law, that man should always doubt whether he is in grace, that dead men are to be invoked, that souls are liberated from purgatory through Masses, that no one can be a Bishop unless confirmed by the Pope, that the Pope holds both swords, that the vows of monks are Christian perfection. Likewise, Anabaptist delusions, that a Platonic community of goods is necessary, that oaths, judicial proceedings, holding magistracies, legitimate warfare, and pleading cases in court are illicit by their nature, that it is not permitted to use Roman law, that tithes are to be given only to priests. Afterwards, there was a huge chaos of superstitious traditions inextricable to fearful consciences; concerning the enumeration of sins in private confession, concerning satisfactions, concerning indulgences, concerning the prohibition of marriage, concerning fasts and other infinite superstitions.

Such examples must be pondered, so that we may consider why it is said: Let the word of God dwell in you with wisdom, that is, let there be true diligence in learning, let the members of doctrine be rightly distinguished and let comparison illustrate the truth, let there not be idle recitation βαττολογία, and let the sophistic deceits of all heretics be entirely removed. However, the rectitude of judgment cannot be retained without the care of learning, and without the invocation of God, wherefore it is also said in Psalm 46: Sing wisely. And concerning prayer it is said, in Psalm 118: Deal with thy servant according to thy mercy, and teach me thy justifications.

In the same chapter is also contained this notable sentence: Charity is the bond of perfection. Here some stir up idle disputes about perfection, when the grammatical explanation is plain.

Perfection here signifies joining together, as in a building beams are joined and joined together, not torn apart, not shaken, the work does not collapse. He speaks here of this perfection, that is, joining together, by which the body of the Church coheres, the strong and the weak agree, the learned use ἐπιείκεια toward the more unlearned who are teachable: The bond of this perfection, that is, of this conjunction, is charity, as in the Senate, even if Scipio and Fabius sometimes disagree, yet no distraction of the Republic arises from it. Because since they look to the same thing, that is, they tend toward the same principal end, that the Republic may be safe, since they are friends, one yields to the other. Thus their friendship is the bond of the concord of the empire. Conversely, Marius and Sulla neither tend toward one end, nor are they friends. Therefore they tear the Republic apart.

Thus in the Church the learned and the good sometimes disagree in their judgments, and yet one tolerates and listens to the other. But when minds are ulcerated, then even things rightly said are depraved by malice and ill-will. Afterwards a pretext is sought, an occasion for quarreling is sought everywhere, just as Solomon says: He who wishes to desert a friend, seeks an occasion. These things do not happen where there is charity. Therefore Paul calls charity the bond of perfection, that is, of common concord. And he does not speak of the private perfection of any person, but of the integrity of the whole body of the Church.

Furthermore, let the use of the word Perfect be observed. Elsewhere, a thing is called perfect in substance, as we call a boy a perfect human being, that is, in substance. Elsewhere, perfect in quantity or degrees, as when we say: No one has perfect obedience according to the law of God. He speaks of the perfection of degrees.

Paul uses the same name in two ways in Philippians chapter three. Let us who are perfect think otherwise. Here he names those perfect who retain faith and a good conscience without corruptions, which we call perfect in substance. Thus it is said to Abraham: Be perfect. Afterwards Paul says that he is not perfect, that is, that he does not have all the degrees of obedience, which we call perfect in degrees.

Often perfect signifies the same as not feigned, as Christ says: That your joy may be perfect, that is, not feigned, not hypocritical. God so consoles us by the voice of the Gospel and the Holy Spirit that joy is felt in the heart and life is restored. Philosophical consolations do not bring life and joy to the heart. Thus also Peter says: Hope perfectly, that is, let not your hope be feigned.

In the saying of Christ: If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all things etc., and follow me, the simplest explanation is to interpret perfect as meaning not feignedly, not hypocritically. For when the young man had boasted that he had satisfied the command of God, the Lord adds, in order to uncover his hypocrisy: Therefore; so that you may show that you keep the commandments not hypocritically, and seek the glory of God, follow me in the ministry. But when he refuses to follow, his boasting is refuted. For he shows that he is not perfect, that is, sincere without hypocrisy. But let a second explanation also be added: Perfection is by no means a work better than the works of the Decalogue. Because no obedience is better, according to these sayings: I desire mercy and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God, not burnt offerings. Likewise: In vain they worship me with the commandments of men. Likewise: Obedience is better than the sacrifices of fools. Therefore, let perfection in this place be understood as concerning the commanded work, namely, Follow me, and let it be understood as perfect not by degrees, but by substance, as when it is said to Abraham: Be perfect, namely, retaining faith and a good conscience. To this pertains that everyone should obey his own calling. David is called to the kingdom, this young man is called to the ministry of the Gospel. These interpretations of the word Perfect must be held, to refute the ravings of the monks, who called works not commanded by God, hypocritical poverty, and other hypocrisies, Perfection.

that he be acknowledged as impartial. Likewise, he is angry at sin in all, and receives all who flee to the Son. He wishes these rules to be most firm.

This doctrine is useful for confirming the fear of God, and for confirming faith; let not David flatter himself, thinking that God will not punish his adultery because he has deserved well. Nor let Aaron, Manasseh, Nebuchadnezzar, Peter, or the thief on the cross despair because they have many great offenses, but let them hold to the rule: Grace abounds over the offense, and: Before God there is no respect of persons.

Moreover, God wishes to be judged concerning His Essence and Will from the word in which He has revealed Himself. Impartiality is therefore to be attributed to Him, just as He so often affirms: There is no προσωποληψία in God.

Let us hold this consolation against the temptation concerning particularity. For there are two principal temptations, one concerning Dignity, the other concerning Particularity. For first we tremble and doubt that we are received, because we are unworthy, and we perceive a great mass of sins, against which the wrath of God is most certainly denounced in the law, according to the saying: God is a consuming fire. Against this temptation, the particle Freely must be opposed. Likewise this sentence: Grace abounds over sin.

There is, however, a twofold abandonment of possessions: one is necessary on account of confession or vocation. In such abandonment, obedience is a work commanded by God, namely, to prefer the profession or vocation to life and possessions. Therefore, it is a good work and a worship of God in the believer. The other is an unnecessary abandonment, that is, which is done neither for the sake of confession nor for the sake of vocation, such as the Cynic abandonment of possessions, as when Crates left his possessions so that he would not be hindered in his Cynic philosophy, who afterwards, uncalled, would approach any banquets whatsoever. This abandonment is not a good work, and when superstition or seeking of glory is added, it is a sin.

But although it is difficult to struggle out of this temptation, yet the other temptation concerning particularity again harshly torments the mind, when, namely, we dispute whether we are in the number of the elect, and very many in this very doubt become more languid. Why do you labor, if you are not in the number of the elect? Against this most sad consternation, let the universal promises be opposed, and the universal and highest command, that we should hear the Son, and these sayings concerning the impartiality of God: There is no προσωποληψία in God.

In the same chapter he says: Before God there is no respect of persons, which he names by the Greek compound προσωποληψίαν. It is, however, a word made from the Hebrew of Deuteronomy 10: The Lord your God does not accept a person. In Hebrew, face, that is, he does not prefer the external appearance to the case. For it signifies to judge a case impartially, without regard for other accidents outside the case. What therefore the Greeks named πρόσωπον, in Hebrew is face, that is, appearance. But the Apostles often repeat this saying from Deuteronomy, Romans 2 and in Acts chapter 10.

Both proclamations are universal. God accuses all on account of sins, He wishes all to repent and flee to the Son. Nor is there any doubt that all men owe obedience to this highest command: Hear the Son. And the Son says: Repent and believe the Gospel. Nor must it be imagined that the Son, when He says: Come to me all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you etc., is not a truthful messenger. Erected by these consolations, let us resist doubt, and let us establish that God is impartial, and that we too are truly received when fleeing to the Son, just as it is written: Everyone who believes in him shall not be put to shame. Let the description therefore be held. Respect of persons is to give unequal things to equals, or equal things to unequals. The Greeks simply name it inequality and tyranny, according to the verse: It grants pardon to the crows, it vexes the doves with censure.

But God often commands that a judge be impartial, as in the first chapter of Deuteronomy, and He wishes Himself to be

let it be given. Item: God is rich toward all and over all, Item: Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved. To this consolation let these sayings be applied: There is no προσωποληψία

with God, and let faith be confirmed in the invocation of the divine promises and commandments, which command that one believe in the Son of God.

THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE COLOSSIANS Chapter one.

Latin:

PHIL. MEL. ENARRATIO EPISTOLAE PAULI AD COLOSSENSES.

Duos habemus libros, quibus Melanthon interpretatus est Epistolam Pauli ad Colossenses, quorum prior inscriptus est: Scholia in Ep. ad Coloss., posterior: Enarratio Ep. ad Coloss. —

Scholia edidit Melanthon anno 1527, eaque dicavit Drachstadio. Epistolam nuncupatoriam, quae non nisi in prima editione Seceriana legitur, dedimus in Epistolis Vol. I. p. 873. Liber inscriptus est:

1) Scholia in Epist. Pauli ad Colossenses Phil. Melanch. Haganoae per Joann. Secerium. Anno M. D. XXVII. mense Augusto. (In fine: mense Septembr.) 9 pl. 8. — Negligentia Secerii multa errata typographica sunt in hac prima editione, ut Melanthon ipse in Epist. Vol. I. p. 1007. testatus est. — Quae Melanthon ad cap. 7, 8. scripsit de philosophia vera et falsa, ea etiam separatim recusa sunt: Phil. Mel. in locum ad Coloss. videte ne quis vos decipiat per philosophiam dissent. recens edita. Ba- sileae 1527.

2) Versio germanica: Auslegung der Epistel an die Kolosser durch Philipp Mel., gedeudscht durch Johann Agri- cola Eysleben. Wittenberg 1527. 8.

3) Ph. Mel. Scholia in Ep. ad Coloss. recognita ab autore. Witeb. 1528. 8.

4) S. Pauli ad Colossenses Epistola cum commentariis Phil. Melanchthonis iam ultimo ab ipso multis in locis recognitis ac locupletatis. Hagan. 1529. per Jo. Secerium. 12 pl. 8.

5) Scholia in Ep. Pauli ad Coloss. iterum ab auctore recognita Phil. Mel. Witeb. apud Joseph Clug. M. D. XXXIV. 8.

6) Epistola Pauli ad Coloss. cum comment. [Scholiis?] Phil. Mel., quae iam novissime ab authore ipso re- cognita sunt ac locupletata, idque quam plurimis in locis. Hagan. per Val. Kobianum, mense Au- gusto. 1534. 12 pl. 8.

7) Scholia — — — Witeb. 1545. 14 pl. 8.

8) Scholia — — — Halae Suev. 1545. 8.

Haec scholia Operibus inserere noluimus, quum Melanthon omnia accuratius exposuerit in enarratione huius Epistolae, neque Peucerus scholia in operibus Melanth. repetierit. Enarratio huius Epistolae autem non anno MDLVI. prodiit, ut in operibus ex errore typographico legitur, sed anno MDLIX. sic inscripta:

Philippi Mel. Enarratio Epistolae Pauli ad Colossenses. Viteb. 1559. 9 pl. 8.

Iterum Phil. Mel. Enarratio Epist. Pauli ad Coloss. Addita est responsio ad calumnias Staphyli et Avii, Francof. 1559. 10 pl. 8.

Item in Opp. Melanth. Witteb. T. IV. p. 324 sqq.

Praefationem ad Herlufum Troll dedimus in Epistolis Vol. IX. p. 745. Librum ipsum dedimus secundum textum in Opp. Witeb.

ENARRATIO EPISTOLAE PAULI AD COLOSSENSES.

OPpidum fuit Colossae vicinum amni Lyco et Meandro in confinio Lydiae e regione Laodiceae, celebratum ab Herodoto et a Xenophonte, et a Strabone. Ideo autem a Ptolemaeo omissum exi- stimo, quia anno post Pauli mortem, ut scribit Eutropius, terrae motu submersae sunt Colossae et Laodicea. Sic postquam Deus excerpsit suam Ecclesiam, deinde impii et idolorum cultores pu- niti sunt.

Cum igitur huius oppidi locus notus sit, in- epti sunt, qui transferunt hoc nomen ad Rhodios, quia ibi fuerit Colossus Solis a multis celebratus. Locus ideo notus sit, ut poena consideretur, quam dixi secutam esse post Pauli mortem. Nec opus est quaerere unde sic nominatum sit oppi- dum: fortasse enim ibi quoque magnae statuae fuerunt. Nam Colossus proprie est truncata sta- tua, a κόλον, id est, mutilum, et ὄσσε, id est, oculi. Vel appellatio Heneta est a luto, unde in Pannonia idem est nomen oppido celebri. Sed his ineptiis omissis argumentum potius et utilita- tem Epistolae consideremus.

In primo capite recitatur doctrina Evangelii propria de Persona et Beneficiis Christi, et de Iu- sticia fidei, et donatione vitae aeternae. Extat enim hic illustre testimonium de divinitate filii: Omnia per eum condita sunt, ipse est ante om- nia, et omnia per eum consistunt. Cum enim affirmat per hunc Christum, per quem dicit nos habere remissionem per sanguinem eius, omnia condita esse, necesse est fateri, in hoc Christo duas naturas esse, divinam, λόγον et naturam humanam assumtam. Quia mundus non est crea- tus per naturam humanam. Λόγος igitur, per quem fit creatio, non est res evanescens, sed sub- sistens. Hic autem vocatur imago aeterni patris, sicut apud Hebraeos ἀπαύγασμα gloriae et cha- racter substantiae patris. Gloria phrasi Mosaica lucem significat. Nominat igitur filium ἀπαύ- γασμα, ut in symbolo Lumen de Lumine dici- tur, ut cogitatio in nobis seu sermo ostendit men- tem, seu, ut hac qualicunque similitudine uta- mur, sicut radii a Sole sparguntur. In Iohanne filius nominatur λόγος, hic nominatur εἰκὼν. Hae tuae appellationes sunt filii propriae, et dis- cernunt eum a Patre et Spiritu sancto.

Intelligatur autem vocabulum Imago integra, viva et substantialis imago aeterni patris, quam nos eatenus agnoscimus, quatenus per filium pater voce doctrinae patefactus est, quod sit crea- tor, sapiens, verax, bonus, iustus, iudex, mi- sericors, liberrimus, remittens peccata, resti- tuens iusticiam, et vitam per mediatorem. Nos vocabulum λόγος planius intelligimus, cum cogi- tamus filium ideo dici λόγον, quia sit persona immediate proferens Evangelium ex sinu aeterni patris, et immediate conservans ministerium, al- loquens nos, sustentans Ecclesiam, sicut dicit in Salomone Sapientia: Ludens in orbe terrae et de- lectationes meae cum filiis hominum. Quae de- scriptio observanda est. Est enim testimonium de missione ad Ecclesiam, inde usque a prima patefactione promissionis. Et quid cogitari dul- cius potest, quam quod filius Dei affirmat, se de- lectari consuetudine hominum. Hic autem mente repetatur doctrina de tribus personis, quae suo loco copiosius traditur.

Postea in primo capite dicit de beneficiis filii, et nominat eum Caput Ecclesiae, quod ad personam, quae est Deus et Homo, pertinet. Quia utriusque naturae proprietates concurrunt in ap- pellatione capitis. Christus est caput merito, quia ipse meruit toti generi humano salutem: est et caput Efficacia, quia revera missus est ab initio ad Ecclesiam, et est in ea efficax secundum na- turam divinam, sicut declaratur haec ipsa descri- ptio in Epistola ad Ephesios: Dedit eum caput Ecclesiae, quae est corpus eius integrum, qui omnia in omnibus perficit. Sicut et ipse dicit: Ego sum vitis, vos palmites, sine me nihil po- testis facere. Ipse sustentat et conservat Eccle- siam, ipse dat dona Ecclesiae, doctores, pasto- res, per quos est efficax.

Postea in primo capite de applicatione bene- ficiorum Christi loquitur, cum ait: Si in fide ma- netis firmi. Deinde quaedam addit de ministerio Evangelii et de cruce. Ita cernis ordine membra doctrinae praecipua breviter in primo capite com- prehensa esse, videlicet, doctrinam de persona Christi, de duabus naturis, de beneficiis, de ap- plicatione beneficiorum per fidem, de ministerio Evangelii et de Cruce.

Est autem insigni figura usus de Cruce: Im- pleo quod deest afflictionibus etc., videlicet, non quod ad meritum ducis attinet, sed quod ad mi- litiae societatem attinet, quae nondum completa est, sed durat usque ad finem ministerii. Ducis Christi meritum integrum est et sufficiens pro omnibus subditis. Nos autem sumus milites in eodem ministerio, cuius nondum finis est. Ita subinde ad afflictiones ducis accedunt succeden- tium militum afflictiones, quae tantisper desunt duci, donec finis est ministerii in collectione uni- versae Ecclesiae, etiamsi differunt meritum du- cis et praelia militum. His verbis simplicissime enarretur Pauli dictum: Impleo quod deest af- flictionibus Christi etc., non quod ad meritum, quod plenissimum est solius Christi, sed quod ad militiae societatem attinet, in quo subinde milites succedentes oportet similia pati afflictio- num ducis. Quia diaboli oderunt ducem, do- ctrinam et milites, ac dici posset, formam affli- ctionum esse similem, causas finales dissimiles esse, Christus est propiciator et doctor, Paulus tantum est doctor.

Papistae impie detorquent dictum ad merita sanctorum, et fingunt adflictiones sanctorum me- reri remissionem ipsis et aliis. Haec interpreta- tio falsa est iuxta dictum, Roman. 5.: Gratia et donum per gratiam unius hominis Iesu Christi exuberavit in multos. 1. Iohan. 2.: Ipse et pro- piciatio pro nostris peccatis, et non pro nostris tantum, sed pro totius mundi peccatis. Et ad Hebraeos: Una oblatione consummavit sanctos.

In secundo capite, ut prudens medi- cus, cum tradidit salubria, monet vitanda esse contraria, praecipit Paulus de vitandis insidiis et corruptelis doctrinae. Videte, inquit, ne quis vos depraedetur per philosophiam et inanem de- ceptionem secundum traditionem hominum, se- cundum elementa mundi. Nam vocabulum Elementum non intelligitur, ut Physici loquuntur, sed generaliter de externo ordine, unde Graecis est nomen στοῖχος.

Addit autem insignem causam, quare cavendum sit, ne decipiamur humanis imaginationibus et traditionibus. Quia, inquit, in Christo consummati estis. Haec consummatio dupliciter intelligenda est, primum imputatione, quod, scilicet, conversi propter mediatorem sint iusti fide, id est, reconciliati et accepti Deo, etiamsi in eis in hac vita adhuc haeret ingens infirmitas, ut Roma. 5. dicitur: Iustificati sanguine ipsius. Secundo renovatione, quae incoatur in hac et fit integra in vita aeterna. Fitque haec renovatio propter Christum ideo, quia in eo habitat omnis plenitudo divinitatis corporaliter. Omnis plenitudo, videlicet, quo ad dona seu proprietates efficaces, id est, vitam, omnipotentiam, infinitam sapientiam et iusticiam, quae dona communicat hominibus, ostendens ipsis lucem et consolationem voce Evangelii, et dans Spiritum sanctum, quasi dicat: In angelis et hominibus sunt particularia dona, non est omnipotentia, non est infinita sapientia et iusticia, sed haec plenitudo filii est, qui quidem corporaliter, hoc est, personaliter habitat in natura assumta, non separabiliter, non tantum effective: ut Deus est in Davide separabiliter, et effective, sed ita, ut sit una persona seu ὑφιστάμενον unum, id est, ut sint inseparabiliter copulatae duae naturae, divina et humana, unione hypostatica, qua gestatur natura humana a λόγῳ, propemodum, ut anima et corpus hominis sint unum ὑφιστάμενον, corpus gestatur ab anima, vel, ut surculus insertus arbori ab ea gestatur, etsi haec similitudo longius abest. Sed tamen hoc utcunque pingit, naturam humanam servatam esse: quia filius massam assumsit, et nos huic massae inserti servamur, quia ex plenitudine filii accipimus, placemus propter ipsum et vivificamur immediate per eum, sicut inquit: Ego sum vitis, vos palmites. Aeternus pater misit filium, per quem patefit promissio, et hic filius colligit Ecclesiam, est redemtor, et voce promissionis dicit consolationem in cordibus, et dat Spiritum sanctum. Sic cum in eo habitet omnis plenitudo divinitatis, est efficax in nobis, et accipimus ex eius plenitudine vitam aeternam, sapientiam et iusticiam aeternam.

Postea repetita est commemoratio beneficio- rum Christi, liberationis a peccato et a morte, et inserta est illustris imago triumphi Christi, in qua figurae verborum sumtae sunt a regum trium- phis, in quibus spolia hostium anteferebantur currvi triumphali. Deinde captivi hostes ligati ducebantur ante victorem. Ita hic dulcissime in- quit, spolia praeferri pendentia in cruce, videli- cet, chirographa peccatorum nostrorum deleta. Quomodo pingi potest illustrius remissio peccato- rum et reconciliatio, quam in hac ipsa imagine? in qua dicitur accusatio deleta esse, et gestari in cruce Christi? Quia filius redemtor pro nobis satisfecit aeterno patri, et sustulit accusationem. Ducuntur et vincti diaboli, ut sciamus, quan- quam infirma est Ecclesia, tamen a victore Chri- sto inter insidias diabolorum et furores tyranno- rum et haereticorum defendi eam a victore Chri- sto. Sicut et in Iohanne dicitur: Apparuit filius Dei, ut destruat opera diaboli.

Redit postea Paulus ad admonitionem de vi- tandis corruptelis doctrinae, et nominatim ponit hanc asseverationem, quod non sit peccatum violare leges ceremoniales Moysi et traditiones humanas de cibis, festis et similibus externis riti- bus, qui non sunt iusticia cordis, et pingit prae- stigias, quibus astute impostores spargunt falsa dogmata, videlicet, artificiosam simulationem hu- militatis, paupertatis et patientiae, qua videri volunt supra caeteros homines exuisse communes cupiditates, voluptatum, opum et gloriae: deinde iactantiam colloquiorum coelestium cum Deo et angelis. Utriusque modi vidit exempla nostra aetas, et est hic insigne verbum: Nemo vos male regat in certamine. Βραβευτὴς est a ῥάβδος, id est, virga, hinc est verbum καταβραβεύειν, male regere certantem, seu decipere, metam trans- ferre, aut quocunque modo impedimentum ob- iicere.

In tertio capite, cum antea recitaverit summam doctrinae de beneficiis mediatoris, et admonitiones de vitandis corruptelis doctrinae, addit praecepta de bonis operibus interioribus et exterioribus, de exercitiis renovationis.

In his etiam praeceptum est insigne de stu- dio discendi et docendi, quod eo magis amandum est, quia talia dicta, quae lectionem commendant, testimonia sunt contra Stencfeldium et alios fana- ticos, qui abducunt homines a lectione doctrinae et ministerio, et simul testantur lectionem et stu- dia Deo placere, Deum per cogitationem verbi scripti efficacem esse: quod cum sciunt pii, magis ament legendi et discendi studia. Sit igitur familiarissime notum hoc dictum: Sermo Christi habitet in vobis copiose in omni sapientia, et docete et emendate vos mutuo. Copiose, inquit, habitet. Ergo saepe multumque legatur, conferantur iudicia. Cum inquit, Docete et emendate vos mutuo: sint igitur studia doctrinae, misceatur invocatio, sicut alibi dicitur: Quanto magis pater vester coelestis dabit Spiritum sanctum petentibus. Utitur autem verbo Habitandi, ut significet assiduitatem, videlicet, ut doctrina familiariter nota sit, sicut hi noti sunt, qui nobiscum habitant. Simul autem hoc sciamus, ubicunque in vera conversione ad Deum fide cogitatur doctrina, in eo corde certissime simul habitat Deus ipse, id est, est praesens sua essentia et efficacia, vere adest, et est efficax. Iohan. 14.: Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum servabit, et pater meus diliget eum, et veniemus ad eum, et mansionem apud eum faciemus. Et Ephesios tertio: Ut habitet Christus per fidem in cordibus vestris. Colossenses primo: Ipse est caput Ecclesiae perficiens omnia in omnibus. Nam filius voce Evangelii dicens consolationem in mente ostendit praesentiam et misericordiam patris. Sic adsunt pater et filius, et pater ac filius spirant Spiritum sanctum in cor credentis, ut laetitia, invocatio, vita aeterna et omnes fructus spiritus accendantur. Sic simul sunt Pater, Filius, et Spiritus sanctus. Haec pie et recte cogitanda sunt, et grata sit emphasis in verbo Habitandi. Iubet autem, ut habitet in nobis sermo Dei in omni sapientia. Haec admonitio inseritur de diligentia, quae habet duo extrema, Ignaviam et Sophisticen. Non habitat sermo Dei in sacrificulis indoctis, qui legunt aut canunt sine intellectu et sine arte, non habitat in Sophistis, Haereticis et Superstitiosis, qui curiosas disputationes aut perniciosas opiniones serunt, ut vanissima sophismata sunt monachorum, an Deus potuisset assumere naturam non rationalem, an accidentia sint sine subiecto in Sacramento, an liceat consecrare fermentatum panem, et blasphemiae sunt Samosateni, Manichaeorum, Arii, Serveti, et aliorum haereticorum. Item tenebrae papisticae, quod homines sint iusti propria legis impletione, quod homo semper dubitate debeat, an sit in gratia, quod mortui homines sint invocandi, quod per Missas liberentur animae ex purgatorio, quod nemo pos- sit esse Episcopus nisi a Papa confirmatus, quod Papa habeat utrunque gladium, quod vota mona- chorum sint perfectio Christiana. Item deliria anabaptistica, quod necessaria sit Platonica com- munio facultatum, quod sint res illicitae suo ge- nere iuramenta, iudicia, gerere magistratus, le- gitima militia, dicere causas in foro, quod non liceat uti iure Romano, quod solis sacerdotibus tribuendae sint decimae. Postea ingens chaos fuit traditionum superstitiosarum inextricabilium pavidis conscientiis; de enumeratione delictorum in privata confessione, de satisfactionibus, de indulgentiis, de prohibitione coniugii, de ieiuniis et aliis infinitis superstitionibus.

Talia exempla cogitanda sunt, ut considere- mus, quare dicatur: Habitet in vobis sermo Dei cum sapientia, hoc est, sit vera diligentia in discendo, recte distinguantur membra doctrinae et collatio illustret veritatem, non sit recitatio otiosa βαττολογία, et omnino removeantur so- phisticae praestigiae omnium haereticorum. Non potest autem rectitudo iudicii retineri sine cura discendi, et sine invocatione Dei, quare et Psal- mo 46. dictum est: Psallite sapienter. Et de precatione dicitur, Psalmo 118.: Fac cum servo tuo secundum misericordiam tuam, et iustifica- tiones tuas doce me.

In eodem capite continetur et haec insignis sententia: Dilectio est vinculum perfectionis. Hic aliqui otiosas disputationes de perfectione movent, cum grammatica explicatio sit plana.

Perfectio significat hic coagmentationem, ut in aedificio coniunctae et coagmentatae sunt tra- bes, non divulsae, non excussae, non corruit opus. De hac perfectione, hoc est, coagmenta- tione hic loquitur, qua cohaeret corpus Ecclesiae, congruunt firmi et infirmi, docti utuntur ἐπιεί- κειᾳ erga rudiores dociles: Huius perfectionis, id est, coniunctionis vinculum est dilectio, ut in Senatu, etiamsi quando dissentiunt Scipio et Fa- bius, tamen non oritur inde distractio Reipub. Quia cum illi idem spectent, hoc est, ad eundem principalem finem tendant, ut salva sit Respub., cum sint amici, alter alteri cedit. Ita amicitia ipsorum vinculum est concordiae imperii. Con- tra Marius et Sylla nec ad unum finem tendunt, nec sunt amici. Ideo dilacerant Rempublicam.

Sic in Ecclesia docti ac boni iudiciis aliquando dissentiunt, et tamen alter alterum tolerat et audit. Sed quando mentes sunt exulceratae, tunc etiam recte dicta livore et malevolentia depravantur. Postea quaeritur praetextus, quaeritur ubique rixandi occasio, sicut Salomo inquit: Qui vult deserere amicum, quaerit occasionem. Haec non accidunt ubi est dilectio. Ideo Paulus nominat dilectionem Vinculum perfectionis, hoc est, communis concordiae. Ac non loquitur de perfectione privata ullius personae, sed de integritate universi corporis Ecclesiae.

Caeterum observetur usus vocabuli Perfectus. Alibi perfectum dicitur substantia, ut Puerum dicimus perfectum hominem, hoc est, substantia. Alibi perfectum quantitate seu gradibus, ut cum dicimus: Nemo habet perfectam obedientiam iuxta legem Dei, Loquitur de perfectione graduum.

Paulus eodem nomine dupliciter utitur Philippenses tertio. Qui perfecti sumus, aliter sentiamus. Hic nominat perfectos, retinentes fidem et bonam conscientiam sine corruptelis, quod nominamus Perfectum substantia. Sic ad Abraham dicitur: Esto perfectus.
