Postea inquit Paulus se non perfectum esse, hoc est, non habere se omnes gradus obedientiae, quod nominamus perfectum gradibus.

Saepe perfectum significat idem quod non simulatum, ut Christus inquit: Gaudium vestrum sit perfectum, hoc est, non simulatum, non hypocriticum, Deus voce Evangelii, Spiritu sancto sic consolatur nos, ut laetitia in corde sentiatur et vita restituatur. Philosophicae consolationes non adferunt vitam et laetitiam cordis. Sic et Petrus inquit: Perfecte sperate, hoc est, non sit spes simulata.

In dicto Christi: Si vis perfectus esse, vade, vende omnia etc., et sequere me, simplicissima enarratio est, interpretari perfectum, pro non simulate, non hypocritice. Cum enim adolescens gloriatus esset se mandato Deo satisfecisse, subiicit Dominus, ut retegat hypocrisin eius: Ergo; ut ostendas te mandata non hypocritice servare, et gloriam Dei quaerere, me sequaris in ministerio. Cum autem ille recuset sequi, refutatur eius iactantia. Ostendit enim se non esse perfectum, hoc est, sincerum sine hypocrisi. Sed addatur et altera enarratio: Nequaquam perfectio est opus melius operibus Decalogi. Quia nulla est melior obedientia, iuxta haec dicta: Miseri- cordiam volo non sacrificium, et scientiam Do- mini, non holocausta. Item: Frustra colunt me mandatis hominum. Item: Melior est obedien- tia quam victimae stultorum. Ergo perfectio hoc loco intelligatur de opere praecepto, scilicet, Se- quere me, et intelligatur perfectum non gradibus, sed substantia, ut cum dicitur ad Abraham: Esto perfectus, scilicet, retinens fidem et bonam con- scientiam. Ad hanc pertinet, obedire quemque suae vocationi. David vocatur ad regnum, hic adolescens vocatur ad ministerium Evangelii. Hae interpretationes vocabuli Perfectus tenendae sunt, ad refutanda deliria monachorum, qui opera non mandata a Deo, hypocriticam pau- pertatem et alias hypocryses nominarunt Per- fectionem.

que agnosci aequalem. Item irascitur peccato in omnibus, et omnes recipit confugientes ad filium. Has regulas vult esse firmissimas.

Haec doctrina utilis est ad confirmandum ti- morem Dei, et ad confirmandam fidem, non blan- diatur sibi David cogitans Deum non esse punitu- rum adulterium ipsius, quia praeclare meritus sit. Nec desperent Aaron, Manasses, Nabucho- donosor, Petrus, latro in cruce, quia multa ma- gna delicta habent, sed teneant regulam: Gratia exuberat supra delictum, et: Coram Deo non est personarum acceptio.

Vult autem Deus de Essentia et Voluntate sua iudicari ex verbo, in quo se patefecit. Tri- buenda est igitur ei aequalitas, sicut toties affir- mat: Non est in Deo προσωποληψία.

Hanc consolationem teneamus contra tenta- tionem de particularitate. Duae sunt enim prae- cipuae tentationes, altera de Dignitate, altera de Particularitate. Primum enim trepidamus et du- bitamus nos recipi, quia sumus indigni, et cer- nimus magnam peccatorum molem, adversus quae ira Dei in lege certissime denunciatur, iuxta di- ctum: Deus ignis consumens est. Adversus hanc tentationem opponenda est particula Gratis. Item haec sententia: Gratia exuberat supra peccatum.

Duplex est autem desertio facultatum: alia necessaria propter confessionem aut vocationem. In tali desertione obedientia est opus a Deo prae- ceptum, scilicet, anteferre professionem seu vo- cationem vitae et facultatibus. Ideo est opus bo- num et cultus Dei in credente. Alia est desertio non necessaria, hoc est, quae neque propter con- fessionem, neque propter vocationem fit, qualis est cynica desertio facultatum, ut cum Crates suas possessiones reliquit, ne impediretur in sua cynica philosophia, qui postea non vocatus ad quaecunque convivia accedebat. Haec desertio non est opus bonum, et cum accedit superstitio aut captatio, peccatum est.

Etsi autem difficile est eluctari ex hac tenta- tione, tamen altera tentatio de particularitate rur- sus duriter excruciat animum, cum, videlicet, disputamus an simus in numero electorum, et plurimi in hac ipsa dubitatione fiunt languidio- res. Quid laboras, si non es in numero electo- rum. Huic consternationi tristissimae opponan- tur promissiones universales, et mandatum uni- versale et summum, ut audiamus filium, et haec dicta de aequalitate Dei: Non est προσωποληψία in Deo.

In eodem capite inquit: Coram Deo non est acceptio personarum, quam nominat Graeca compositione προσωποληψίαν. Est autem voca- bulum ex Hebraeo factum Deuteronomii 10.: Do- minus Deus vester personam non accipit. He- braice faciem, hoc est, externam speciem non antefert causae. Significat enim de causa aequa- liter iudicare, sine respectu aliorum accidentium extra causam. Quod igitur Graeci nominarunt πρόσωπον, in Hebraeo est facies, hoc est, spe- cies. Saepe autem Apostoli repetunt hoc dictum ex Deuteronomio, Rom. 2. et in Actis capite 10.

Utraque concio est universalis. Accusat Deus omnes propter peccata, vult omnes agere poenitentiam et confugere ad filium. Nec du- bium est omnes homines huic summo praecepto debere obedientiam: Audite filium. Et filius in- quit: Poenitentiam agite et credite Evangelio. Nec fingendum est, filium, cum inquit: Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis et onerati estis, ego reficiam vos etc., non esse veracem legatum. His erecti consolationibus, repugnemus dubitationi, et statuamus Deum aequalem esse, et vere nos quoque recipi confugientes ad filium, sicut scri- ptum est: Omnis qui credit in eum, non confun- Teneatur igitur descriptio. Personarum ac- ceptio est dare inaequalia aequalibus, aut aequa- lia inaequalibus. Graeci simpliciter nominant inaequalitatem et tyrannidem, iuxta versum: Dat veniam corvis, vexat censura columbas.

Saepe autem praecipit Deus ut iudex sit aequalis, ut Deuteronomii primo, et vult se quo-

detur. Item: Dives Deus in omnes et super omnes, Item: Omnis qui invocaverit nomen Domini salvus erit. Ad hanc consolationem adhibeantur haec dicta: Non est προσωποληψία

apud Deum, et confirmetur fides in invocatione promissionibus et mandatis divinis, quae praecipiunt credi filio Dei.

EPISTOLAE PAULI AD COLOSSENSES Caput primum.

## 1:1
Paul, an Apostle of Jesus Christ.

In the title, mention is made of his office. Because it is necessary in the Church to know from where doctrine has been received. Because the Gospel is not wisdom known to reason, but is divinely revealed at the beginning through the Son of God himself, with illustrious testimonies and divine miracles added.

Afterwards it was repeated in many divine manifestations, and miracles were added. And therefore the Son himself, the Prophets, and the Apostles were sent, and the propagation of the Gospel was entrusted to the Church, and the differences of callings must be considered.

For a Prophet is a person called immediately by God to illustrate the promise concerning Christ, and he has divine testimonies that he does not err, and he was sent to some part of the political government, in which miracles are shown.

An Apostle is a person called immediately by God to teach the Gospel, and he has divine testimonies that he does not err, nor was he sent to a political government.

A Bishop, or Pastor, or Doctor is a person called by God mediately through the Church, or those to whom the Church entrusts this, to teach the Gospel written by the Prophets and Apostles, nor does he have any other testimony that he does not err, except the prophetic and apostolic writings themselves; when he dissents from these, he errs, just as the lapses of many, some greater, some lesser, have occurred, are occurring, and will occur.

It is necessary to consider these distinctions of callings because of political men, who ask why one should believe Paul more than Bishops, who have ordinary authority, whereas Paul seems to wander as a vagabond. Here it must be known that the Apostles were sent by a singular calling immediately by God, and have divine testimonies that they do not err, and that their voice is to be believed, just as the voice of God sounding immediately from heaven: and it is necessary for this to be commemorated to the Church, that they were immediately called by God, and that they bring forth not a doctrine invented by themselves, but one handed down through the Son of God, who is in the bosom of the eternal Father, and who first brought forth the Gospel. Therefore the Prophets so often repeat: Thus says the Lord. And Paul in many words in the first chapter to the Galatians makes mention of his calling.

This consolation is also necessary, that we know that God truly wills to be effective through the Gospel even when those teach who are called by the Church: just as Paul commands Titus, and likewise Timothy, to appoint Presbyters, to entrust the Gospel to those fit to teach. Because the Son is immediately effective, whether the Gospel is announced through Prophets, or through Apostles, or through Pastors.

Grace and peace from God.

Grace signifies gratuitous reconciliation and acceptance on account of the mediator, with which, however, is joined vivification, which is brought about through the Son, kindled by the true knowledge of God through the Gospel in the mind, and by the Holy Spirit poured into the hearts, just as it is said in Romans 8: He who does not have the Spirit of Christ is not His. Therefore, Paul joins these two, grace and the gift by grace, where he understands grace relatively concerning reconciliation and acceptance on account of the Son, just as it is said elsewhere: Beloved in the Beloved. But he understands the gift, without any doubt, as the bestowed benefits which are in us, namely, that we are made temples of God, and are gifted with eternal life. And indeed let the gift be understood not only of the beginning, but of the whole consummation of the benefits of Christ.

The Hebrews use the word Peace just as we use the word Salvation or Joy. Therefore, in this place, it signifies first joy in God, then the good state of the Church, and privately the gifts of God necessary for individuals in sanctification, life, and vocations. Likewise, tranquil governments, success in administration. This grammatical explanation of the word Peace, how widely it extends, must be considered, as when it is said in the Psalm: Pray for the things that are for the peace of Jerusalem.

Latin:

Paulus Apostolus Iesu Christi.

In titulo fit officii mentio. Quia necesse est in Ecclesia sciri, unde doctrina accepta sit. Quia Evangelium non est sapientia rationi nota, sed est divinitus revelatum initio per ipsum filium Dei, additis illustribus testimoniis et miraculis divinis.

Postea repetitum est in multis patefactionibus divinis, et addita sunt miracula. Ideoque missi sunt filius ipse, Prophetae et Apostoli, et Ecclesiae mandata est propagatio Evangelii, et vocationum differentiae considerandae sunt.

Est enim Propheta persona immediate vocata a Deo ad illustrandam promissionem de Christo, et habet testimonia divina, quod non erret, et missus est ad aliquam partem politicae gubernationis, in qua ostenduntur miracula.

Apostolus est persona immediate vocata a Deo ad docendum Evangelium, et habet testimonia divina, quod non erret, nec missus est ad politicam gubernationem.

Episcopus, seu Pastor, seu Doctor est persona vocata a Deo mediate per Ecclesiam, aut eos quibus hoc Ecclesia commendat, ad docendum Evangelium scriptum per Prophetas et Apostolos, nec habet aliud testimonium, quod non erret, nisi ipsa scripta prophetica et apostolica, ab his cum dissentit, errat, sicut multorum lapsus alii maiores, alii minores acciderunt, accidunt et accident.

Has distinctiones vocationum necesse est considerare propter homines politicos, qui interrogant, cur magis credendum sit Paulo quam Episcopis, qui habent ordinariam potestatem, Paulus autem videtur vagari ut erro. Hic scien- dum est, Apostolos singulari vocatione immediate a Deo missos esse, et habere divina testimonia quod non errent, et eorum voci credendum esse, sicut voci Dei immediate de coelo sonanti: et necesse est Ecclesiae hoc commemorari, quod sint immediate vocati a Deo, et perferant non a se inventam doctrinam, sed traditam per filium Dei, qui est in sinu aeterni patris, et primus protulit Evangelium. Ideo toties repetunt Prophetae: Haec dicit Dominus. Et Paulus multis verbis ad Galatas primo mentionem facit suae vocationis.

Necessaria est et haec consolatio, quod scimus Deum vere velle efficacem esse per Evangelium etiam cum hi docent, qui sunt ab Ecclesia vocati: sicut Paulus praecipit Tito, item Timotheo, ut constituant Presbyteros, ut commendent Evangelium idoneis ad docendum. Quia filius immediate efficax est, sive per Prophetas sive per Apostolos, sive per Pastores annuncietur Evangelium.

Gratia et pax a Deo.

Gratia, significat gratuitam reconciliationem et acceptationem propter mediatorem, cum qua tamen est coniuncta vivificatio, quae fit per filium accensa vera agnitione Dei per Evangelium in mente, et effuso Spiritu sancto in corda, sicut Roman. 8. dicitur: Qui spiritum Christi non habet, non est eius. Ideo Paulus haec duo coniungit, Gratiam et donum per gratiam, ubi gratiam intelligit relative de reconciliatione et acceptatione propter filium, sicut alibi dicitur: Dilecti in dilecto. Donum vero intelligit sine ulla dubitatione donata beneficia, quae sunt in nobis, scilicet, quod efficimur templa Dei, et donamur vita aeterna. Et quidem intelligatur donum non de incoatione tantum, sed de tota consumma- tione beneficiorum Christi.

Vocabulo Pacis Hebraei utuntur sicut nos vocabulo Salutis seu Laetitiae. Significat igitur hoc loco primum laetitiam in Deo, deinde bonum statum Ecclesiae, et privatim dona Dei singulis necessaria in sanctificatione, vita et vocationibus. Item, tranquilla imperia, successus in guberna- tione. Haec grammatica explicatio vocabuli Pa- cis quam late pateat cogitandum ist, ut cum in Psalmo dicitur: Rogate quae ad pacem sunt Ie- rusalem.

## 1:3
From God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

When he joins the eternal Father and Christ, let us consider these two things, the omnipotence of the Son and his intercession; when he says that grace and the gift are given at the same time by the Father and the Son, he signifies that the Son is also God by nature. And let us add here these sayings: My Father works until now, and I work. Likewise: May God Almighty bless these boys, and the angel who delivered me from all evils. Likewise: All things consist through him.

Secondly, let us consider that mention is also made of the Son so that we may be admonished concerning the mediator; all good things which are given to the Church are given on account of the mediator, who both offered his own sacrifice for us and always intercedes for us. Here the common doctrine concerning the distinction between true and false invocation is repeated. Let us learn to separate our invocation from the Heathen, Turkish, and Papistical, and let us daily in our invocation consider whom we are addressing, where and by what testimonies he has been revealed, and why we are heard.

We usually distinguish Christian invocation from that of other peoples. The Heathens and Mahometans err concerning the Essence and will of God; they deny that this is truly God, the creator of heaven and earth, and of men, who revealed himself by sending our Lord Jesus Christ, and gave testimonies of himself in the Church, and who is thus revealed in the Church, that the divinity is the eternal Father, and λόγος, the Son of the eternal Father always sent to the Church, and the Holy Spirit gladdening and confirming it. But the Heathens wander, not knowing whom they invoke, just as Hecuba says in Euripides: O Jupiter, whatever you are, whether this heaven or the mind in heaven. Then they err concerning the Will, because they do not know if or why he hears, and they invoke in perpetual doubt, just as the Papists also teach.

But we in the Church, when invoking, let us first consider concerning the Essence that this is the true God, the creator, who revealed himself by sending our Lord Jesus Christ, and who teaches us in the Church that the divinity is the eternal Father, and λόγος, the Son always sent to the Church, and the Holy Spirit gladdening and confirming hearts. Let us contemplate these three persons together in our mind, and let us know that good things are given by them together, because actions toward the outside are common to the three persons, according to these sayings: All things were made through him. Likewise: All things consist through him. Likewise: By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power.

Then let us also consider concerning the Will, that God wishes to be invoked not with doubt, of which it is said in the Poet: I agree that there is a God, but I doubt whether he cares for human affairs: but that he wishes us to believe that he truly wishes to hear us on account of the Son, the mediator, God and man, and that he wishes mention of the Son to be made, as it is said: Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give to you. He commands that it be asked in the name of the mediator, because the confidence that the invocation is not in vain rests upon the mediator.

Wherefore, in invocation, one must always think of the Son in both ways. First, as the giver of good things with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Secondly, again as the mediator or intercessor. Because he says clearly thus: Whatever you ask the Father in my name, this he will give you. In Rom. 8 it is said: Who sits at the right hand of the Father, that he may intercede for us. And in Hebrews 7: Always living, that he may intercede for them. It is commanded that we believe we are heard, according to the saying: How shall they invoke, if they do not believe? Likewise: Pray without anger and hesitation. Faith ought to rest not on our own dignity, but on the mediator. Therefore, it is necessary to acknowledge and address the Son as mediator.

But as for the objection of the saying in John 16: I do not say to you that I will pray for you, the grammatical and true answer is that Christ's prayer is not excluded, just as a leader might say: I do not say that I will fight, but you will fight with me. Here it appears sufficiently in the latter member that it is an affirmative statement, just as in the same place he says: On that day you will ask in my name. He wishes, therefore, even now to be acknowledged as mediator and intercessor. There is therefore no exclusion of the intercession of Christ, but it is a correction of the error concerning the omission of our prayer, or an admonition that our prayer should be joined. Now consider what a sweet command it is, which orders that we also should approach God, that we should join our vows and our sighs to his intercession; he wants you also to pray, nor does he want us to be slothful or idle soldiers, but he wants us also to approach God, just as a leader wants his soldiers to fight together, etc. Let us be content with this grammatical and true answer, and let us remember that a most sweet consolation is set before us, which affirms that our prayers are both heard and that we are loved together with the Son for his sake, just as it is said in the same place: The Father himself loves you. Let us not allow this most sweet consolation to be corrupted by poisonous sophistry.

The exordium contains thanksgiving and prayer, just as in exordia the words of affections, congratulations, complaints, etc., are most welcome and customary. And the sum of the thought is: I give thanks to God, because he called you to the knowledge of the Son and kindled your hearts, so that you might believe the Gospel, and I pray that he may confirm you. Paul says this in more words, in which, when the phrase is considered, there is no obscurity. And the thought is taken from the common doctrine, that the Gospel is a wisdom not known to reason, but the immense mercy of God revealed through the Son. Likewise, that reason does not receive this wonderful wisdom by faith, unless the Son himself shows it, kindling and confirming minds and hearts, so that we may assent and retain our assent and faith, just as Paul says to the Galatians: That we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.

What is the image of God, etc.

That in Christ born of a virgin there are two natures, the λόγον, and the human nature, the narrative in John expressly affirms: And the Word was made flesh, and that the λόγον is not an evanescent sound, as many have astutely caviled, but is ὑφιστάμενον, that very narrative in John shows.

But let us hold to the illustrious confirmations which may be considered in daily invocation. I judge that invocation is a firm testimony, by which the fathers address this Lord as one doing something. They feel, therefore, that he is an ὑφιστάμενον, living, intelligent, and effective with the Father, just as Jacob says: May God bless these boys, and the angel who delivered me from all evils. Here, without any doubt, the angel is understood as the person sent: the person blessing or delivering is not an angel, who is a creature, and Paul expressly says that Christ was with the fathers in the desert, and he himself says: Before Abraham was born, I am. And in this place to the Colossians, Paul says that all things were created and are sustained through Christ. But creatures were not created through human nature, and yet in this man Christ is the creating nature. Therefore the λόγος is not an evanescent sound.

The confirmation is also illustrious in the sayings concerning Omnipotence, when he says: I give them eternal life. Likewise: I am the vine, you are the branches, without me you can do nothing. And 1 John 4: In this we know that we remain in him, and he in us, because he gives us of his Spirit. A finite nature cannot give the Holy Spirit. There is therefore, before the assumption of human nature, a person sent, who is called the λόγος and the Image of the eternal Father, as in Heb. 1 he is expressly named the ἀπαύγασμα of glory, that is, of the paternal light, wisdom, and justice, and the Image of the paternal substance. In the same place it is also affirmed that through him, who is the image of the eternal Father, all things were created and are sustained. Since this creating nature is in the man Christ, it is necessary that it not be an evanescent sound. For otherwise it would not be in the man Christ, if it were an evanescent sound.

He is called the Image, however, because the Father, contemplating himself in this thought of himself, begets his own image, and when this substantial image then shines in the human nature of Christ, who perfectly acknowledges the eternal Father, and is perfectly just, and like to God because of the substantial image shining in him: Christ is called God and man, the image of the eternal Father.

But when the Son is called the image of the eternal Father, let us think not only of the secret collation of the Father and the Son, but of the manifestation toward us. Such is the Father as the Son announces him to be, and speech is the image of the mind. Therefore it is said: No one has ever seen God, but the Son who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him to us. Likewise: No one knows the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son wishes to reveal him. Thus, therefore, let us acknowledge God, just as he has been manifested through this Son, namely, wise, truthful, good, beneficent, just, a judge, chaste, omnipotent, most free. And although he is immutably just, yet he is one who forgives sins and restores justice and eternal life for the sake of the Son and through him. Let us know this to be truly the will of God, nor let us imagine contradictory opinions in him.

Secondly, the name of Image reminds us to discern the true God from all fictitious deities. The invisible divinity proposes this visible son to you, and commands you to invoke this true God, who sent this redeemer, and added testimonies to him, and truly dwells in that redeemer, as he says: He who sees me, sees the father.

Thirdly, it must be known that this image of God was sent to us, so that we in turn might become the image of God through him, that is, so that the knowledge of God might shine in us, kindled through the son, by which we are again made conformable to God, as it is said in 2 Corinthians 3: Acknowledging God through the voice of the Gospel, we are transformed into the same image, that is, a Light similar to the Word is kindled in you. Athanasius says: It was fitting for the son to assume human nature, so that man might be restored through the essential image of God, having been created to be a created image of God. Because through the word, by which the divinity is revealed, the image is restored.

These things must be thought upon reverently and piously, and learned in true invocation, in which the mind ought to behold God revealed through this son, and distinguish true invocation from ethnic invocation.

I omit the deceits of Samosatenus and Arius and their like, who caviled: An image is the shadow of another thing, etc. This very text refutes such sophistries, when it says later: That all things were created and preserved through the son. And it is said to the Hebrews, The Character of his Substance, namely, a substantial Image.

Latin:

A Deo patre nostro et Domino Iesu Christo.

Cum coniungit aeternum patrem et Chri- stum, duo haec consideremus, Omnipotentiam filii et intercessiouem, cum ait dari gratiam et donum simul a patre et filio, significat filium etiam natura Deum esse. Et huc adiungamus haec dicta: Pater meus usque modo operatur, et ego operor. Item: Benedicat his pueris Deus om- nipotens, et angelus qui eripuit me ex omnibus malis. Item: Omnia per eum consistunt.

Secundo consideremus, etiam eo fieri men- tionem filii, ut admoneamur de mediatore, omnia bona, quae dantur Ecclesiae, dantur propter me- diatorem, qui et sacrificium suum pro nobis ob- tulit, et semper intercedit pro nobis. Hic repe- tatur communis doctrina de discrimine verae et falsae invocationis. Discamus seiungere nostram iuvocationem ab Ethnica, Turcica et Papistica, et quotidie in invocatione cogitemus, quem Deum alloquamur, ubi et quibus testimoniis patefactum, et quare exaudiamur.

Usitate autem discernimus invocationem Christianam ab aliis populis. Errant Ethnici et Mahometistae de Essentia et voluntate Dei, ne- gant hunc vere esse Deum, creatorem coeli et terrae, et hominum, qui se patefecit misso Do- mino nostro Iesu Christo, et testimonia de se in Ecclesia dedit, et qui sic revelatus est in Ecclesia, quod divinitas sit aeternus pater, et λόγος, filius aeterni patris semper missus ad Ecclesiam, et Spi- ritus sanctus laetificans et confirmans eam. Sed vagantur Ethnici nescientes quid invocent, sicut Hecuba apud Euripidem inquit: O Iupiter quic- quid es, sive hoc coelum sive mens in coelo. Deinde de Voluntate errant, quod nesciunt, an et cur exaudiat, et invocant in dubitatione perpetua, sicut et Papistae docent.

At nos in Ecclesia invocantes primum de Essentia cogitemus hunc esse verum Deum, creatorem, qui se patefecit misso Domino nostro Iesu Christo, et qui docet nos in Ecclesia divinitatem esse aeternum patrem, et λόγον, filium semper ad Ecclesiam missum, et Spiritum sanctum laetificantem et confirmantem corda. Has tres personas simul mente intueamur, et sciamus simul ab eis dari bona, quia actiones ad extra sunt communes tribus personis, iuxta haec dicta: Omnia per ipsum facta sunt. Item: Omnia per ipsum consistunt. Item: Verbo Domini coeli firmati sunt, et spiritu oris eius omnis virtus eorum.

Deinde et de Voluntate cogitemus, velle Deum invocari non cum dubitatione, de qua apud Poëtam dicitur: Esse Deum assentior, sed an curet humana dubito: sed velle nos credere, quod vere velit nos exaudire propter filium mediatorem Deum et hominem, velle mentionem filii fieri, sicut dicitur: Quicquid petieritis patrem in nomine meo, dabit nobis. Iubet peti nomine mediatoris, quia fiducia, quod non sit irrita invocatio, nititur mediatore.

Quare semper in invocatione utroque modo cogitandum est de filio. Primum tanquam de datore bonorum cum Patre et Spiritu sancto. Secundo rursus tanquam de mediatore seu intercessore. Quia clare sic dicit: Quicquid petieritis patrem in nomine meo, hoc dabit vobis. Rom. 8. dicitur: Qui sedet ad dextram patris, ut interpellet pro nobis. Et Hebrae 7.: Semper vivens, ut interpellet pro eis. Mandatum est ut credamus nos exaudiri, iuxta dictum: Quomodo invocabunt, si non credunt? Item: Orate sine ira et haesitatione. Niti fides debet non nostra dignitate, sed mediatore. Ergo necesse est filium ut mediatorem agnoscere et alloqui.

Quod vero obiicitur dictum Iohan. 16.: Non dico vobis, quod ego precaturus sim pro vobis, grammatica et vera responsio est, non excludi Christi precationem, ut sit dux dicat: Non dico me praeliaturum esse, sed vos mecum praeliabimini. Hic satis apparet in posteriore membro affirmativam sententiam esse, sicut et eodem loco inquit: In illo die in nomine meo petetis. Vult ergo nunc quoque agnosci, quod sit mediator et intercessor. Non est igitur exclusio in- tercessionis Christi, sed est correctio erroris de omissione nostrae precationis, seu admonitio ut adiungatur nostra precatio. Iam cogita quam dulce mandatum sit, quod praecipit, ut nos quo- que accedamus ad Deum, ut nos ad ipsius inter- cessionem adiungamus nostra vota et nostros ge- mitus, vult te quoque precari, nec vult nos igna- vos aut otiosos milites esse, sed vult ut ipsi quo- que accedamus ad Deum, sicut dux vult milites simul praeliari etc. Hac grammatica et vera re- sponsione contenti simus, et meminerimus dul- cissimam consolationem nobis propositam esse, quae affirmat, et audiri nostras preces et simul cum filio diligi propter ipsum, sicut eodem loco dicitur: Ipse pater diligit vos. Hanc dulcissimam consolationem non sinamus corrumpi venenata sophistica.

Exordium continet gratiarum actionem et precationem, sicut in exordiis maxime grata et usitata sunt verba affectuum, gratulationum, que- relarum etc. Estque summa sententiae: Deo gra- tias ago, quod vos ad agnitionem filii vocavit et accendit corda vestra, ut Evangelio credatis, et oro ut vos confirmet. Haec Paulus pluribus ver- bis dicit, in quibus phrasi considerata nihil est obscuritatis. Estque sumta sententia ex communi doctrina, quod Evangelium sit sapientia non nota rationi, sed immensa misericordia Dei revelata per filium. Item, quod hanc mirandam sapien- tiam ratio non accipiat fide, nisi filio ipso mon- strante, mentes et corda accendente et confir- mante, ut assentiamur et retineamus assensionem et fidem, sicut Paulus inquit ad Galatas: Ut promissionem spiritus accipiamus per fidem.

Quid est imago Dei, etc.

In Christo nato ex virgine esse duas naturas, λόγον, et naturam humanam, expresse affirmat narratio in Iohanne: Et Verbum caro factum est, et λόγον non esse sonum evanescentem, sicut multi astute cavillati sunt, sed esse ὑφιστάμενον, illa ipsa narratio in Iohanne ostendit.

Sed teneamus illustres confirmationes, quae cogitentur in quotidiana invocatione. Iudico fir- mum testimonium esse invocationem, qua patres alloquuntur hunc Dominum, ut agentem aliquid. Sentiunt igitur esse ὑφιστάμενον vivum, intelli- gentem, et cum patre efficacem, sicut ait Iacob: Benedicat his pueris Deus, et angelus qui eripuit me ex omnibus malis. Hic sine ulla dubitatione angelus intelligitur persona missa: persona bene- dicens aut liberans non est angelus, qui est crea- tura, et Paulus expresse dicit Christum fuisse apud patres in deserto, et ipse inquit: Antequam Abraham natus est, ego sum. Et hoc loco ad Co- lossenes inquit Paulus, per Christum omnia condita esse et conservari. Non sunt autem con- ditae creaturae per naturam humanam, et tamen in hoc homine Christo est natura conditrix. Ergo λόγος non est sonus evanescens.

Confirmatio est etiam illustris in dictis de Omnipotentia, cum inquit: Ego vitam aeternam do eis. Item: Ego sum vitis, vos palmites, sine me nihil potestis facere. Et 1. Iohan. 4.: In hoc scimus, quod in eo manemus, et ipse in nobis, quia de spiritu suo dat nobis. Natura finita non potest dare Spiritum sanctum. Est ergo ante as- sumtionem naturae humanae persona missa, quae λόγος et Imago aeterni patris dicitur, ut Hebr. 1. expresse nominatur ἀπαύγασμα gloriae, hoc est, lucis paternae, sapientiae et iusticiae, et Imago substantiae paternae. Ibidem etiam affirmatur, per hunc, qui est imago aeterni patris, omnia condita esse et sustentari. Haec natura conditrix cum sit in homine Christo, necesse est non esse evanescentem sonum. Alioqui enim non esset in homine Christo, si esset sonus evanescens.

Dicitur autem Imago, quia pater sese intuens hac cogitatione sui gignit imaginem suam, et cum haec imago substantialis deinde fulgeat in natura humana Christi, qui perfecte agnoscit aeternum patrem, et perfecte iustus est, et similis Deo propter imaginem substantialem in ipso fulgen- tem: dicitur Christus Deus et homo imago aeterni patris.

Cum autem dicitur Filius imago aeterni pa- tris, cogitemus non solum de arcana patris et filii collatione, sed de patefactione erga nos. Talis est pater, qualem esse filius annunciat, et sermo est imago mentis. Ideo dicitur: Deum nemo vi- dit unquam, sed filius qui est in sinu patris, ipse enarravit nobis. Item: Nemo novit patrem nisi filius, et cui volet filius revelare. Sic igitur agno- scamus Deum, sicut per hunc filium patefactus est, scilicet, sapientem, veracem, bonum, be- neficum, iustum, iudicem, castum, omnipoten- tem, liberrimum. Et quanquam immutabiliter iustus est, tamen remittentem peccata et redden- tem iusticiam et vitam aeternam propter filium et per eum. Hanc sciamus vere voluntatem Dei esse, nec imaginemur in eo contradictorias senten- tias.

Secundo nomen Imaginis commonefacit nos de discernendo vero Deo ab omnibus commenti- tiis numinibus. Proponit tibi invisibilis divini- tas hunc filium visibilem, et iubet te invocare hunc verum Deum, qui misit hunc redemtorem, et addidit ei testimonia, et vere in isto redem- tore habitat, sicut inquit: Qui videt me, videt patrem.

Tertio sciendum est hanc Dei imaginem ad nos missam esse, ut nos rursus per eum fiamus imago Dei, hoc est, ut luceat in nobis agnitio Dei, per filium accensa, qua rursus efficimur con- formes Deo, sicut 2. Corinth. 3. dicitur: Agno- scentes Deum per vocem Evangelii, transforma- mur in eandem imaginem, hoc est, Lux similis verbo in vobis accenditur. Athanasius dicit: Congruebat filium assumere naturam humanam, ut per imaginem Dei essentialem homo restitue- retur, conditus ut esset imago Dei creata. Quia per verbum, quo divinitas patefit, restituitur imago.

Haec reverenter et pie cogitanda sunt, et in vera invocatione discenda, in qua mens intueri debet Deum patefactum per hunc filium, et discer- nere veram invocationem ab ethnica.

Omitto praestigias Samosateni et Arii et si- milium, qui cavillati sunt: Imago est umbra alte- rius rei, etc. Tales sycophantias hic ipse textus refutat, cum postea inquit: Per filium omnia esse condita et conservata. Et ad Hebraeos dicitur Character Substantiae, videlicet, substantialis Imago.

## 1:15
The firstborn of every creature etc.

The simplest explanation is concerning his dignity. Firstborn, that is, lord of all creatures, according to these words in the eighth Psalm: You have put all things under his feet. And in the last chapter of Matthew: All power is given to me in heaven and in earth. And here it is said: All things were created in him, that is, on account of him, that is, so that God might reveal himself in this son, and show his love toward the human race in this wonderful union of divine and human nature.

And since the Church is gathered immediately through this son, his power is also immediate over all creatures. The son, for the sake of the gathering of the Church, immediately preserves heaven and earth, the human race, the ministry of the Gospel, defends the Church against the rage of devils, against tyrants and against fanatic furies, and is the judge, he punishes and will punish the impious, meanwhile he simultaneously prays for us to the eternal father, and is effective by the voice of the Gospel, so that some may be converted, he forgives sins to those who believe, he hears, protects, softens punishments, mitigates many things in the order of nature, feeds us, helps and saves those who invoke him, as he says: Come to me all you who labor and are burdened. Likewise: No one shall snatch my sheep from my hands. Without me you can do nothing. He sits at the right hand of the eternal father, giving gifts to men, he himself is the head of the Church, perfecting all things in all.

These things must be thought upon concerning the right of primogeniture, that is, concerning the dominion of Christ, and transferred to consolation and to invocation, so that it may not be thought to be an idle dominion, but truly effective in creatures and in us. Those who care neither for his judgment nor his help think this presence of the son of God and this dominion are empty fables. An illustrious testimony is added here concerning the omnipotent nature in the son: In this visible son is the λόγος, through whom all things were created. Therefore the λόγος is not a created, vanishing sound, but is ὑφιστάμενος and omnipotent.

Latin:

Primogenitus universae creaturae etc.

Simplicissima enarratio est de dignitate. Pri- mogenitus, hoc est, dominus omnium creatura- rum, iuxta haec dicta Psalmo octavo: Omnia subiecisti sub pedibus eius. Et Matthaei ultimo: Data est mihi omnis potestas in coelo et in terra. Et hic dicitur: In eum omnia sunt condita, hoc est, propter eum, id est, ut in hoc filio se pate- faciat Deus, et ostendat in hac miranda copula- tione divinae et humanae naturae suum amorem erga genus humanum.

Et cum per hunc filium immediate colligatur Ecclesia, potestas eius est etiam immediata supra omnes creaturas. Filius propter collectionem Ec- clesiae immediate servat coelum et terram, genus humanum, ministerium Evangelii, defendit Ec- clesiam contra rabiem diabolorum, contra tyran- nos et contra fanaticos furores, et est iudex, pu- nit et puniet impios, interea simul orat pro no- bis aeternum patrem, et est efficax voce Evangelii, ut aliqui convertantur, remittit peccata credenti- bus, exaudit, protegit, lenit poenas, multa mi- tigat in ordine naturae, pascit nos, iuvat et sal- vat invocantes ipsum, sicut inquit: Venite ad me omnes qui laboratis et onerati estis. Item: Nemo rapiet oves meas ex manibus meis. Sine me nihil potestis facere. Sedet ad dexteram aeterni patris, dans dona hominibus, ipse est caput Ecclesiae, perficiens omnia in omnibus.

Haec de iure primogeniturae, hoc est, de do- minio Christi cogitanda sunt, et ad consolationem et ad invocationem transferenda, ne cogitetur esse otiosa dominatio, sed vere efficax in creaturis et in nobis. Hanc praesentiam filii Dei et hoc do- minium putant inanes fabulas esse illi, qui nec cu- rant iudicium ipsius nec auxilium. Additur hic illustre testimonium de omnipotente natura in filio: In hoc visibili filio est λόγος, per quem om- nia condita sunt. Ergo λόγος non est sonus crea- tus evanescens, sed est ὑφιστάμενος et omni- potens.

## 1:16
Thrones or dominions etc.

By thrones, dominions, principalities and powers, antiquity understands angels; we understand all empires and the order of creatures, polities, economies, marriage, laws, and government in heaven and on earth. Certainly, it wants to say that all creatures were both created and ordered through this son, even if devils and men later departed from that order.

That the son is God by nature, manifest testimonies are placed here, because it is said: That all things were created through him, and most sweetly he adds here: He is before all things. When this is said, it is necessary to understand that there is in him a nature which existed before the assumption of human nature. Hence it follows clearly that the λόγος is not a vanishing sound, since it is said of Christ, That he is before all things.

This phrase, however, is well known, that all things were created through the Son. For although all actions toward the outside are common to the three persons, yet each person has his own property, and the saying of Augustine is harmonious.

The Son acts through himself, not from himself; the Father wills the creation and the whole order of things, and expresses this will through the Word, by whose speaking things are made and distinguished in order, as it is written in Genesis: The Lord said: Let us make man to our image and likeness. And by the Holy Spirit creating at the same time, things are cherished, just as it is written in Genesis: The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters, or was cherishing the water.

It must be diligently considered that, wherever mention of creation is made, the presence of God in the preservation of substances must be understood at the same time, according to these sayings: In him we live, and move, and are. Deut. 30: He is your life and the length of your days. Nor should creation be understood as the building of a ship, from which the architect departs after he has constructed it, but the substances of things would perish if they were not also subsequently preserved by God, whom we should know, however, to be present to the creature most freely, to help, to adorn, to moderate, or by deserting it to destroy nature by his most free will. Therefore he says here: All things consist through him. And Hebrews 1: Upholding all things by the word of his power.

But why does he say: All things were created in him? This is, this Son is the final cause why God created all things. Because this union of the divine and human nature is the highest work of God, as he says: Yet once more I will move heaven and earth, and in this union of the divine and human nature the manifold wisdom of God is seen, and his immense love toward the human race. There will be wisdom to be learned in all eternity, to see in this Son the movement of this union and to see the causes, and what kind of wisdom the law is, and what the cause is why the Son was appointed to be the price for the law, what kind of mission the Son has for gathering the Church, what kind of works there were in every liberation. This whole wisdom is seen in that consideration of the Son, whose beginnings God wills to be learned in this life, according to the saying: Out of the mouth of infants and of sucklings you have perfected praise.

Latin:

Throni sive dominationes etc.

Thronos, dominationes, principatus et po- testates intelligit vetustas angelos, nos omnia im- peria et ordinem creaturarum, politiarum, oeco- nomiarum, coniugii, legum, gubernationem in coelo et in terra intelligimus. Certe hoc vult di- cere omnes creaturas et creatas et ordinatas esse per hunc filium, etiamsi postea ab illo ordine discesserunt diaboli et homines.

Quod filius sit natura Deus, manifesta hic testimonia posita sunt, quia dicitur: Omnia per ipsum esse condita, et dulcissime hic addit: Ipse est ante omnia. Hoc cum dicitur, necesse est in- telligi in eo naturam esse, quae fuerit ante as- sumtionem humanae naturae. Hinc perspicue sequitur, λόγον non esse sonum evanescentem, cum de Christo dicitur, Quod sit ante omnia.

Nota est autem haec phrasis, per filium om- nia condita esse. Etsi enim omnes actiones ad extra sunt communes tribus personis, tamen sua cuiusque personae est proprietas, et dictum Augu- stini concinnum est.

Agit filius per se, non a se, pater vult crea- tionem et totum ordinem rerum, et exprimit hanc voluntatem per verbum, quo dicente res fiunt et ordine distinguuntur, ut in Genesi scriptum est: Dixit Dominus: Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram. Et Spiritu sancto si- mul creante foventur res, sicut in Genesi scri- ptum est: Spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas, seu fovebat aquam.

Diligenter considerandum est, ubicunque fit creationis mentio, simul intelligendam esse prae- sentiam Dei in conservatione substantiarum, iuxta haec dicta: In ipso vivimus, sumus et movemur. Deuteron. 30.: Ipse est vita tua et longitudo dierum tuorum. Nec sic intelligatur creatio, ut fabricatio navis, a qua discedit architectus postquam eam extruxit, sed substantiae rerum interirent, nisi deinceps quoque conservarentur a Deo, quem ta- men sciamus adesse creaturae liberrime, iuvare, ornare, moderari, aut deserendo destruere natu- ram liberrima voluntate. Ideo dicit hic: Omnia per eum consistunt. Et Hebraeos 1.: Ferens om- nia verbo potentiae suae.

Sed quare dicit: Omnia in ipsum condita sunt? Hoc est, hic filius est causa finalis, quare Deus omnia condiderit. Quia haec copulatio di- vinae et humanae naturae est summum opus Dei, sicut inquit: Adhuc semel et movebo coelum et terram, et in hac copulatione divinae et humanae naturae conspicitur multiplex sapientia Dei, et immensus amor erga genus humanum. Erit sa- pientia in tota aeternitate discenda, in hoc filio videre motum huius copulationis et causas videre, et qualis sapientia sit lex, et quae causa sit, cur filius constitutus sit, ut sit pretium pro lege, qualis sit filii missio ad colligendam Ecclesiam, qualia fuerint opera in omni liberatione. Haec tota sapientia conspicitur in illa consideratione filii, cuius vult Deus initia in hac vita disci, iuxta dictum: Ex ore infantium et lactentium perfe- cisti laudem.

## 1:18
And he is the head of the body of the Church.

Writers in book 3 of the Sentences, distinction 13, expressly confess that the name of head is attributed to the whole person, Christ, and that other properties belong to him according to his human nature, others according to his divine nature. Moreover, he is head by efficacy, by perfection, by merit, and by order.

First, by Efficacy, because this person was properly sent so that the eternal Father might immediately gather the Church through him. This person brings forth the Gospel at the beginning, is present to the Church, and sustains and protects it immediately. A likeness can be thought of. Just as the head in any man sends down nerves and animal spirit into the rest of the body, which are the cause of sense and motion: so the Son of God sustains and teaches us, as is said to the Ephesians, To fill all in all. Likewise: No one knows the Father except the Son. Likewise: I give them eternal life. And although this efficacy is of the head, yet it is attributed to the person, because he is efficacious in this assumed nature, as is said in 1 Corinthians 15: By man came death, and by man the resurrection of the dead. Many actions are done by the ministry of the assumed nature, as when he will judge the resurrected visibly. Moreover, there is also his efficacy of the assumed nature, which excels all creatures in power, drives away devils, and protects the Church, and does many things powerfully which befit the head.

Secondly, he is called head by Perfection, not only according to his divine nature, but also according to his human, because the human nature in Christ excels all angels in wisdom.

Thirdly, he is head by Merit, according to his human nature, by which, with most perfect obedience, he merited the redemption and eternal salvation of the Church; it is just that he be superior in the whole Church.

Fourthly, by Order, because of his mission, as John says: He is before me. Because this person was sent to the Church at the beginning, so that he might bring forth the Gospel from the bosom of the eternal Father.

It is commonly said that Christ is named Head because he excels in dignity. But let it be understood not as an idle dignity, but rather all these things are included: Efficacy, Perfection of the divine nature and the human nature, Merit, and Order.

Moreover, let the saying to the Ephesians be added: He is the head of the Church, filling all in all, and as he himself says: I am the vine, you are the branches. Likewise: Of his fullness we have all received. Therefore he says here: In him dwells all the fullness of the divinity, namely of gifts, of wisdom, of justice, and not only so that he himself is adorned with this excellence for his own sake, but also so that he may be efficacious in others, as is said in the Psalm: God your God has anointed you with the oil of gladness because of your fellows, and this sentence will be repeated below, where it is to be explained more copiously.

Latin:

Et ipse est caput corporis Ecclesiae.

Expresse fatentur scriptores libro 3. sentent. distinctione 13. nomen capitis tribui toti perso- nae, Christo, et alias proprietates competere ei secundum humanam naturam, alias secundum divinam naturam. Est autem caput efficacia, perfectione, merito, et ordine.

Primum Efficacia, quia haec persona pro- prie missa est, ut immediate per eam aeternus pater colligat Ecclesiam. Haec persona initio profert Evangelium, adest Ecclesiae, et eam sus- tentat, et protegit immediate. Similitudo cogi- tari potest. Sicut caput in quolibet homine demit- tit nervos et spiritum animalem in reliquum cor- pus, qui sunt causa sensus et motus: ita filius Dei sustentat et docet nos, sicut dicitur ad Ephe- sios, Perficere omnia in omnibus. Item: Nemo novit patrem nisi filius. Item: Ego vitam aeter- nam do eis. Etsi autem haec efficacia est capitis, tamen personae tribuitur, quia efficax est in hac assumta natura, ut 1. Corinth. 15. dicitur: Per hominem mors, et per hominem resuscitatio mor- tuorum. Multae actiones fiunt ministerio assum- tae naturae, ut cum iudicabit resuscitatos visibi- liter. Est autem et sua efficacia assumtae naturae, quae antecellit omnibus creaturis potentia, depel- lit diabolos, et protegit Ecclesiam, et multa po- tenter agit, quae capiti congruunt.

Secundo caput Perfectione sic dicitur, non solum secundum divinam naturam, sed etiam iuxta humanam, quia natura humana in Christo antecellit sapientia omnibus angelis.

Tertio est caput Merito, iuxta humanam naturam, qua cum perfectissima obedientia me- ruerit Ecclesiae redemtionem et salutem aeter- nam, iustum est eum superiorem esse in universa Ecclesia.

Quarto, Ordine propter missionem, sicut Iohannes inquit: Prior me est. Quia haec per- sona ad Ecclesiam initio missa est, ut proferat Evangelium ex sinu aeterni patris.

Usitate dicitur, Christum nominari Caput, quia dignitate antecellit. Sed intelligatur non otiosa dignitas, verum haec omnia comprehen- duntur, Efficacia, Perfectio naturae divinae et naturae humanae, Meritum et Ordo.

Adiungatur autem dictum ad Ephesios: Ipse est caput Ecclesiae, omnia in omnibus perficiens, et sicut ipse inquit: Ego sum vitis, vos estis pal- mites. Item: Ex plenitudine eius omnes accepi- mus. Ideo hic inquit: In ipso habitat omnis ple- nitudo divinitatis, videlicet donorum, sapientiae, iusticiae, nec tantum sic, ut ipse pro sese orna- tus sit hac excellentia, sed etiam ut sit efficax in aliis, sicut in Psalmo dicitur: Unxit te Deus tuus oleo laetitiae propter consortes tuos, et re- petetur haec sententia infra, ubi copiosius est enarranda.

## 1:20
And through him to reconcile all things to himself, having made peace through the blood of his cross etc.

In the Ephesians it is most sweetly said, to gather together in one all things in heaven and on earth. They were conformed to the one head, God, and all rational creatures were joined to him, before the fall of the devils and of men. Afterwards, let it be considered what a sad rupture this is, in which the devils in horrible fury are angry with God throughout all eternity, and afflict him with insults, in themselves and in the human race as much as they can, as is shown by the blasphemies, murders, lusts, and other crimes to which the devils drive miserable men, only so that they may afflict God with insult. But in order that the human race may again be coupled with the head, God, a mediator has been appointed, who is the head of the Church, joining us to the head, God. Thus in heaven and on earth that rupture is healed, as is said afterwards: Making peace in heaven and on earth, namely between God and man, and he repeats it several times: Through the blood, through the death, through the body of Christ, that he might bring and present you holy, and unblameable, and unreproveable in his sight.

Let these words be opposed to the papistic errors, which imagine that men merit the remission of sins on account of discipline, and that they are righteous by their own fulfillment of the law. Paul on the contrary affirms that we are reconciled by the blood and death of the Son of God, that is, by his total obedience. Let there also be added from other places the particle Freely, which expressly excludes our merits.

The order of the words shows what things happen in the justification of a man before God. Therefore the Son was sent, that he might reveal this wonderful decree, that God wills the Son to be a victim, and on account of him forgives sins, restores righteousness and eternal life, hears, and wonderfully rules and protects. And in true sorrows the first and highest struggle is whether God forgives you your sins, and whether he receives you. Of this struggle it is said: Being justified by faith we have peace. And when the imputation of righteousness and the remission of sins is apprehended by faith, at the same time in this very consolation the Son of God through the Gospel shows the mercy and presence of the eternal Father, and the Holy Spirit is given by the Father and the Son, by whom the heart is drawn to assent to the Gospel, is gladdened, confirmed, vivified, and freed from the sorrows of the underworld, as Hezekiah says: You have delivered my soul, that it should not perish, you have cast all my sins behind your back. The assertion therefore concerning the remission of sins and the imputation of righteousness is recited in this place with these words: You who were enemies, he has reconciled, and indeed he adds: By the body, by the death of his flesh etc., so that he may signify that we are pleasing to God and accepted on account of the obedience of the Son, as it is said in Romans 5: By the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.

Nor are minds to be led away from this consolation by Osiandrian speculations, which say that men are righteous before God on account of an essential righteousness, and not through the mercy of imputed righteousness.

Latin:

Et per eum cuncta reconciliare erga se pacifica- tis per sanguinem crucis eius etc.

In Ephesiis dulcissime dicitur, redigere ad unum caput omnia in coelo et in terra. Fuerunt uni capiti Deo conformes, et adiunctae omnes rales creaturae, ante lapsum diabolorum et hominum. Postea cogitetur quam tristis avulsio sit, in qua diaboli horribili furore in tota aeter- nitate irascuntur Deo, et contumeliis eum affi- ciunt, in seipsis et in genere humano quantum- cunque possunt, ut ostendunt blasphemiae, cae- des, libidines et alia scelera, ad quae diaboli im- pellunt miseros homines, tantum ut contumelia Deum afficiant. Ut autem rursus cum capite Deo copuletur genus humanum, mediator constitutus est, qui est caput Ecclesiae, adiungens nos capiti Deo. Sic in coelo et in terra sanatur illa avulsio, sicut postea dicitur: Faciens pacem in coelo et in terra, videlicet inter Deum et hominem, et ali- quoties repetit: Per sanguinem, per mortem, per corpus Christi, ut adducat et sistat vos san- ctos, inculpatos et non accusandos coram eo.

Haec verba opponantur erroribus papisticis, qui fingunt homines mereri remissionem pecca- torum propter disciplinam, et iustos esse propria impletione legis. Paulus contra affirmat, san- guine et morte filii Dei, id est, obedientia tota nos reconciliari. Addatur autem et ex aliis locis particula Gratis, quae expresse excludit nostra merita.

Ordo autem verborum ostendit, quae res fiant in iustificatione hominis coram Deo. Ideo Filius missus est, ut hoc mirandum decretum pa- tefaciat, quod Deus velit filium esse victimam, et propter eum remittat peccata, restituat iusti- ciam et vitam aeternam, exaudiat et mirabiliter regat et protegat. Et in veris doloribus primum et summum certamen est, an Deus tibi remittat peccata, et an te recipiat. De hac lucta dicitur: Iustificati fide pacem habemus. Cumque appre- henditur fide imputatio iusticiae et remissio pec- catorum, simul in hac ipsa consolatione filius Dei per Evangelium ostendit misericordiam et prae- sentiam aeterni patris, et datur Spiritus sanctus a Patre et Filio, quo cor ad assentiendum Evan- gelio trahitur, laetificatur, confirmatur, vivifi- catur, et ex doloribus inferorum liberatur, sicut Ezechias inquit: Tu eruisti animam meam, ne periret, proiecasti post tergum tuum omnia peccata mea. Asseveratio igitur de remissione peccato- rum et imputatione iusticiae recitatur hoc loco his verbis: Vos qui eratis inimici, reconciliavit, et quidem addit: Corpore, morte carnis etc., ut significet nos propter obedientiam filii placere Deo, et acceptos esse, sicut Roman. 5. dicitur: Propter unius obedientiam iusti constituentur multi.

Nec abducendae sunt mentes ab hac conso- latione Osiandricis speculationibus, quae dicunt, homines iustos esse coram Deo propter iusticiam essentialem, et non per misericordiam imputata iusticia.

## 1:22
That he might present you holy etc.

Then let the remaining words also be considered, That he might present you holy, unblameable, unreproveable. Let these words be understood in this life as follows: Holy, that is, converted to God. For holiness signifies the very working of God in us, by which a man is both justified by faith and is now a dwelling place of God.

The following word, Unblameable, is used for that which is said in Genesis: Be perfect. And in the Psalm, undefiled, namely by imputation and by beginning, as when he says: As you are unleavened. Therefore he soon adds again the word ἀνέγκλητοι, which signifies Unreproveable, and here he adds: In his sight, which must necessarily be understood of imputation in this life, as Paul says: There is now no condemnation to those who walk in Christ Jesus. Therefore, although in this life many great stains, ignorances, doubts, wandering flames etc. cling to us, nevertheless by imputation we are righteous and ἀνέγκλητοι on account of the mediator, as it is said in Romans 5: Being justified by faith we have peace with God, through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom also we have access by faith into this grace, wherein we stand. This faith, however, relies in reality upon the obedience of the mediator.

In this way let the weights of the words be examined, and in eternal life holiness will be consummated, and we shall be altogether undefiled. For God will be all in all the blessed, that is, there will be no sin there in the saints as in this life.

Latin:

Ut exhiberet vos sanctos etc.

Deinde et reliqua verba considerentur, Ut sistat vos sanctos, inculpatos, non accusandos, Haec verba in hac vita sic intelligantur, Sanctos, id est, conversos ad Deum. Nam sanctitas signi- ficat ipsam effectionem Dei in nobis, qua homo et iustificatur fide, et iam est domicilium Dei.

Sequens vocabulum, Inculpatos, est usurpa- tum pro eo, quod in Genesi dicitur: Perfectus esto. Et in Psalmo, immaculatum, videlicet imputatione et incoatione, ut cum inquit: Sicut estis azymi. Ideo mox rursus addit vocabulum ἀνέγκλητοι, quod significat Non accusandos, et hic addit: Coram Deo, quod necesse est intelligi de imputatione in hac vita, sicut Paulus inquit: Nulla nunc est condemnatio his, qui in Christo Iesu ambulant. Ideo etsi in hac vita haerent in nobis multae magnae sordes, ignorantiae, dubi- tationes, errantes flammae etc.: tamen imputa- tione iusti sumus et ἀνέγκλητοι propter mediato- rem, ut Roman. 5. dicitur: Iustificati fide pacem habemus apud Deum, per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, per quem et accessum habemus fide in gratiam hanc, in qua stamus. Haec fides autem re ipsa nititur obedientia mediatoris.

Hoc modo diligenter pondera verborum exa- minentur, ac in vita aeterna erit consummata sanctitas, et erimus prorsus immaculati. Erit enim Deus omnia in omnibus beatis, hoc est, non erit ibi peccatum in sanctis ut in hac vita.

## 1:23
If indeed you continue in the faith grounded and settled etc.

He has spoken before both of the person of the Son of God and of His benefits, now he adds the doctrine concerning the appeal, in what way we may receive and retain those eternal benefits, namely by faith. This very doctrine is explained more fully in the words of Paul in the Epistle to the Romans, where it is illustrated by an antithesis: By the works of the law shall no flesh be justified. Likewise: That the whole world may be guilty before God, But being justified by faith we have peace. Let this antithesis always be in sight. In the true struggle and judgment of God, let all men in this depraved nature acknowledge this prayer: Enter not into judgment with thy servant, for in thy sight shall no living man be justified. Likewise Job 19: Truly, I know that a man is not just before God. And on the other hand, let us contemplate this true consolation, that God in his immense wisdom and goodness sent his son, and willed him to become a victim, and wills thus and not otherwise to remit sins, and to restore in us righteousness and life, and to vivify men by faith, when they believe that they are received and justified freely for the sake of the mediator son, not for the sake of any of our virtues and works, just as Paul sets this forth more prolixly in the Epistle to the Romans.

And Faith signifies not a knowledge of history, such as exists even in the devils, but an assent by which we embrace the promise. Paul connects faith and promise correlatively in Rom. 4, and explains the term in Eph. 3: Through whom we have boldness to approach in confidence, which is through faith in him. And that faith ought to be understood as confidence in the mercy promised for Christ's sake, the antithesis itself shows, since it is most certain that men are not just before God for the sake of their own virtues and works, but through mercy, as the Psalm says: Save me for thy mercy's sake: It follows necessarily that faith is to be understood as confidence in the mercy promised for the sake of the son. Because mercy cannot be apprehended otherwise than by faith, and nothing could be asserted about mercy unless a promise had been issued that the son has been given to us, just as Paul says: We are beloved in the beloved. Thus from the antithesis itself it is most firmly shown that faith is to be understood as confidence in the mercy promised for the sake of the son, and in this way we embrace all the articles of faith or of the creed.

And let the younger ones know that the same thing is signified by these propositions: We are justified by faith, and, We are justified through the mercy promised for the sake of the son. For they are correlative propositions, and the truth of each proposition is immovable, as they are called propositions true in themselves, not by accident.

And to say that Christ justifies by accident is an execrable blasphemy. But when the proposition, We are justified by faith, is rightly understood, it is easy to refute the Osiandrian imagination. Since the universal scripture teaches that in the judgment of God a man is made just through mercy, that is, pleasing and acceptable to God, it is manifest that the other proposition dissents: Man is just because God moves him to do just things, as Osiander contends, and he defines righteousness: Righteousness is that which moves men to do just things.

But although it is true that when a man is received by faith, that is, by confidence in mercy, God is at the same time effective in the believer: nevertheless that subsequent newness is not that for which the person is accepted, but faith, that is, confidence in mercy, must always shine forth, according to the sayings: Being justified by faith we have peace.

Do not be moved away from the hope of the Gospel etc., of which I Paul am a minister etc.

He often repeats the mention of the ministry, so that we may know that his voice is to be believed, just as the voice of God sounding from heaven, as Moses and the Prophets say: The Lord has spoken these things. For it is necessary that the Church be certain whence the doctrine which the Apostles carry about was received, and it is necessary to know that the doctrine of the law is one thing, and that of the Gospel is another, which preaches about promises that are outside and above the intellect of all creatures, and were brought forth from the bosom of the eternal father through the son. And God has provided testimonies of the Gospel at all times ever since the first revelation. All these things are to be considered when Paul commemorates the dignity of his ministry.

I rejoice in my afflictions, and I fill up what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ etc.

But reason is offended by the appearance of the Cross both in the teachers and in the whole Church. Therefore he confirms the Church by the mention of his own afflictions, as if he were saying: Even though we Apostles and the Church are subject to the cross, nevertheless know that the voice of the Gospel is true, and that the Church is truly gathered in this way, and that it will be under the cross among the empires of the world until the final judgment, and yet is miraculously preserved through the son of God, according to the sayings: Whoever wishes to follow me, let him take up his cross, and follow me. Likewise: All who wish to live piously in Christ, will suffer persecution. But what he says, that he fills up those things which are lacking in the afflictions of Christ, is to be understood not of merit, but of the likeness of the afflictions, which as a member of the body of Christ he sustains. And because he sustains them in his ministry, he says: For his body, namely, that my ministry may serve the Church in teaching, not that the afflictions of the Apostles are a merit of reconciliation. But the common rule remains concerning the likeness of afflictions: We must be made conformable to the image of the Son of God. And for what causes the Son was sent, that he might be made a victim, it must be known, and the mission of the Son must be distinguished from the rest of the Church, which for other causes is subjected to the cross. The passion of Christ alone is λύτρον, but the afflictions of the Church are either τιμωρίαι, or δοκιμασίαι, or μαρτύρια.

Latin:

Siquidem permanetis in fide fundati ac stabi- les etc.

Antea et de persona filii Dei et de beneficiis dixit, nunc addit doctrinam de appellatione, quo- modo illa beneficia aeterna accipiamus et retinea- mus, scilicet fide. Exponitur autem haec ipsa doctrina copiosius Pauli verbis in Epistola ad Romanos, ubi antithesi illustratur: Ex operibus legis non iustificabitur omnis caro. Item: Ut to- tus mundus sit reus Deo, Sed fide iustificati pa- cem habemus. Haec antithesis semper in con- spectu sit. In vero agone et iudicio Dei omnes homines in hac depravata natura agnoscant hanc concionem: Non intres in iudicium cum servo tuo, quia non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo om- nis vivens. Item Iob. 19.: Vere, scio quod non sit homo iustus coram Deo. Et econtra intuea- mur hanc veram consolationem, quod immensa sapientia et bonitate Deus miserit filium, et vo- luerit eum fieri victimam, et velit sic et non ali- ter remittere peccata, et restituere in nobis iusti- ciam et vitam, et vivificare homines fide, cum credunt se propter filium mediatorem gratis recipi et iustificari, non propter ullas nostras virtutes et opera, sicut haec Paulus in Epistola ad Romanos prolixius tradit.

Ac significat Fides non noticiam historiae, qualis et in diabolis est, sed assensum quo am- plectimur promissionem. Paulus correlative con- nectit fidem et promissionem Rom. 4., et enarrat vocabulum Ephes. 3.: Per quem audemus acce- dere in fiducia, quae est per fidem ipsius. Et fidem oportere intelligi fiduciam misericordiae propter Christum promissae, ostendit ipsa anti- thesis, cum certissimum sit homines propter pro- prias virtutes et opera non esse iustos coram Deo, sed per misericordiam, ut Psalmus inquit: Sal- vum me fac propter misericordiam tuam: Sequitur necessario, fidem intelligendam esse fiduciam mi- sericordiae propter filium promissae. Quia mi- sericordia aliter apprehendi non potest, nisi fide, et asseverari de misericordia nihil posset, nisi promissio edita esset, quod filius nobis donatus est, sicut Paulus inquit: Sumus dilecti in dilecto. Ita ex ipsa antithesi firmissime ostenditur, fidem intelligendam esse fiduciam misericordiae propter filium promissae, et ita complectimur omnes arti- culos fidei seu symboli.

Ac sciant iuniores idem significari his pro- positionibus: Fide iustificamur, et, Per miseri- cordiam propter filium promissum iustificamur. Sunt enim correlativae propositiones, et utrius- que propositionis veritas immota est, ut nomi- nantur propositiones verae per se, non per ac- cidens.

Ac dicere Christum per accidens iustificare, execranda est blasphemia. Cum autem proposi- tio, Fide iustificamur, recte intelligitur, facile est Osiandricam imaginationem refutare. Cum uni- versa scriptura doceat in iudicio Dei hominem per misericordiam fieri iustum, hoc est, placen- tem et acceptum Deo, manifestum est alteram propositionem dissentire: Homo est iustus, quia Deus movet eum ad iusta facienda, sicut Osiander contendit, et definit iusticiam: Iusticia est quae movet homines ad iusta faciendum.

Etsi autem verum est, cum fide recipitur ho- mo, hoc est, fiducia misericordiae, simul Deum efficacem esse in credente: tamen illa sequens novitas non est id, propter quod persona accepta est, sed semper oportet praelucere fidem, id est, fiduciam misericordiae, iuxta dicta: Iustificati fide pacem habemus.

Ne dimoveamini a spe Evangelii etc., cuius ego Paulus sum minister etc.

Saepe repetit mentionem ministerii, ut scia- mus voci eius credendum esse, sicut voci Dei de coelo sonanti, sicut Moses et Prophetae di- cunt: Haec locutus est Dominus. Necesse est enim Ecclesiam certam esse, unde accepta sit doctrina, quam Apostoli circumferunt, et sciri necesse est, aliam esse doctrinam legis, aliam Evangelii, quod concionatur de promissionibus, quae sunt extra et supra intellectum omnium creaturarum, et sunt ex sinu aeterni patris pro- latae per filium. Et tradidit Deus testimonia Evangelii omnibus temporibus inde usque a pri- ma revelatione. Haec omnia consideranda sunt, quando ministerii sui dignitatem Paulus com- memorat.

Gaudeo in afflictionibus meis, et impleo quod deest afflictionibus Christi etc.

Offenditur autem ratio specie Crucis et in docentibus et in tota Ecclesia. Ideo confirmat Ecclesiam mentione afflictionum suarum, quasi dicat: Etiamsi sumus subiecti cruci nos Apostoli et Ecclesia, tamen scitote veram vocem esse Evan- gelii, et vere sic colligi Ecclesiam, et eam usque ad novissimum indicium inter imperia mundi sub cruce futuram esse, et tamen mirabiliter per filium Dei conservari, iuxta dicta: Qui vult me sequi, tollat crucem suam, et sequatur me. Item: Omnes qui pie vivere volent in Christo, perse- cutionem patientur. Quod autem dicit, se im- plere ea, quae desunt afflictionibus Christi, in- telligatur non de merito, sed de similitudine af- flictionum, quas ut membrum corporis Christi sustinet. Et quia in ministerio sustinet, dicit: Pro corpore eius, videlicet, ut ministerium meum serviat Ecclesiae in docendo, non quod afflictio- nes Apostolorum sint meritum reconciliationis. Sed manet communis regula de similitudine af- flictionum: Oportet nos fieri conformes imaginis filii Dei. Et propter quas causas filius missus sit, ut fieret victima, sciendum est, et distin- guenda missio filii a reliqua Ecclesia, quae pro- pter alias causas cruci subiecta est. Solius Chri- sti passio est λύτρον, afflictiones vero Ecclesiae sunt aut τιμωρίαι, aut δοκιμασίαι, aut μαρ- τύρια.

## 2:1 Argument
Chapter two.

There is an admonition concerning the avoiding of corruptions of doctrine, and first he has used notable words, συμβιβασθέντες ἐν ἀγάπῃ, that is, harmoniously joined together, united, coupled in love. Πληροφορία signifies Certainty, above to the Romans: Let every man be certain in his own mind. So here he says that he confirms the Church, so that the certainty of faith may be firmer in them, because faith is not an ambiguous imagination similar to academic disputations, but there must be certainty, as is said in the definition: Faith is ἔλεγχος of things not apparent: and the saying is known: He who does not believe in the Son is already judged. Likewise: He who does not believe in the Son, the wrath of God remains upon him. Faith is not, however, doubt, even if the beginnings of faith are weak, yet it is necessary for firmness to grow, as he asks: I believe Lord, bring help to my weakness.

Latin:

Caput secundum.

Admonitio est de vitandis corruptelis doctri- nae, ac primum insignibus vocabulis usus est, συμβιβασθέντες ἐν ἀγάπῃ, hoc est, concinne coagmentati, coniuncti, copulati in dilectione. Πληροφορία significat Certitudinem, supra ad Romanos: Unusquisque certus sit in sua sen- tentia. Ita hic dicit, se confirmare Ecclesiam, ut certitudo fidei sit in ipsis firmior, quia fides non est imaginatio ambigua similis academicarum disputationum, sed oportet esse certitudinem, sicut dicitur in definitione: Fides est ἔλεγχος non apparentium: et notum est dictum: Qui non cre- dit in filium, iam iudicatus est. Item: Qui non credit in filium, manet ira Dei super eum. Non est autem dubitatio Fides, etiamsi initia fidei lan- guida sunt, crescere tamen firmitatem oportet, sicut ille petit: Credo Domine, opem fer imbe- cillitati meae.

## 2:8
Beware lest anyone seduce you through philosophy etc.

Before, in summary, he gave instructions about avoiding corruptions, now he recounts some species, the confusion of philosophy and the Gospel, human ordinances, feigned enthusiasms, and counterfeit miracles. To these modes almost all impostures can be reduced, as Samosatenus, Mahomet, Servetus, Thammerus seek philosophical harmony, they dispute that λόγον is only a vanishing voice. Pelagius and the monks say that man can satisfy the law of God, and that discipline is the perfect fulfillment of the law and righteousness, by which a man is righteous before God, that is, pleasing to God and accepted for eternal life. These are philosophical, and harmony is sought.

The second mode of impostures is without erudition, namely the false accommodation of external rites and gestures, which nevertheless first arose from the fact that it is necessary in life to have order and some exercises. To these, men afterwards attach the opinion of righteousness and merit, and of the worship of God, just as the name superstition was made from this, because it is immoderate assiduity in rites. To this pertain the rites of monks, distinctions of foods, celibacy, βαττολογίαι, and the superstitions of all nations. Whence also many idols have arisen and been accumulated, soldiers seek a deity by a certain rite, which may help in war: women seek help in childbirth, therefore statues of Juno, Anna etc. have been devised.

In these two modes reason sins, seeking God without the word, either by disputing within, or by wrongly accommodating gestures and works without.

The third mode is either impudently feigned vanity, or diabolical illusion. For many falsely boast of enthusiasms, as very many Anabaptists sell themselves with these lies: or they are diabolical prestiges, as also many false miracles are done by devils, and often specters offer themselves to the eyes of men. There is, however, in this place the word συλαγω- γῶν, which signifies to lead away a captive as booty. For σκῦλα signifies Spoils, thence is σῦλα with one letter worn away. He commands therefore to beware, lest we be deceived by those modes, concerning which he warns us, and at the same time he signifies that the deceived are also held ensnared as captives, and not easily liberated, as he says elsewhere, that the minds of the impious are held captive by the devil.

But concerning the first mode, let the younger ones know that true philosophy remaining within its own bounds is not condemned, but the confusion of doctrines is condemned, when philosophy is taught for the Gospel, which is revealed and is beyond human grasp, or when the Gospel is transformed into philosophy, as the Pelagians and monks crudely do, who feigned that men could satisfy the law of God, and that this discipline, such as it is, is the perfect fulfillment of the law, and merits the remission of sins, and is righteousness, by which a man is righteous before God, pleasing to God and accepted for eternal life. These things are falsely constructed from philosophy, which does not speak of eternal justice, of eternal life, nor of the remission of sins, but of the direction of locomotion in external gestures. It is therefore necessary to know the distinctions of doctrines, and the rule must be held 1 Tim. 4: Every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected which is taken with thanksgiving: for it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer. That there are certain true natural notions implanted in the minds of men at creation, which are norms of truth and certainty, such as those of numbers, order, figures, natural laws concerning morals, and physical principles, from which many arts are constructed, is manifest, and indeed Paul calls natural laws the truth of God, and says the law is written in hearts. And it is manifest that numbering, writing, reading, architecture, the medical art are approved by God, and concerning the architect it is said Exod. 31: God filled him with this wisdom. And God both instituted and showed the learned account of the year, and God commands to count. That languages are a gift of the Holy Spirit the history of the Apostles shows, and concerning the medical art it is said Sirach 38: God gave knowledge to men, that he might be glorified in his marvelous works, that is, that the singular efficacy in individual remedies might be a testimony concerning the providence of God, that things were founded for the uses of men. Let us therefore acknowledge that the arts constructed from notions which are implanted in the minds of men at creation are good things and gifts of God, and indeed let us know that they are reminders and testimonies concerning God, because they show that God is wise, and indeed the law of nature testifies that there is a God, and teaches what kind he is, distinguishes him from evil natures, and testifies that he is a judge. Therefore Plato says most sweetly: That a grateful report about God is scattered in the arts. And Solomon says: That the eye may see and the ear may hear, God makes both, that is, the light in the eyes and in the mind is a creature of God, and much more the excellent light in excellent craftsmen. Thinking therefore first about the arts, let us acknowledge and celebrate God, the fountain of wisdom. Then let us use the arts, because they rule the whole bodily life, as he commanded, and for them let us give thanks to God. If any blame the arts, they are furious, and they harm the life of men, and they offer insult to God the author. I name philosophy or the arts as the notions of principles and demonstrations, not any dreams or sophistic deceits and corruptions, such as many have scattered, like the Epicureans, Stoics, Pyrrhonians, Cynics, and others.

Then this also must be known, that the arts which have arisen from natural light have their own goals, and judge concerning those things about which human minds can be convinced, according to criteria.
