But besides the arts which have arisen from natural light, God has revealed the Gospel by singular testimonies, concerning his essence and will, and specifically concerning the Son and the promise of grace, just as 1 Cor. 1 it is said: When the world did not know God in wisdom through wisdom, it pleased God through foolish preaching to save those who believe. Therefore concerning the essence and will of God it must be determined according to the Gospel, not according to philosophy.

This distinction of doctrines must be understood, and its own place must be assigned to each, and Paul condemns the confusion of this distinction, he does not blame true notions, which are a light founded by God, if they are rightly accommodated.

The second mode of impostures can be understood more easily, because it revolves around external gestures, which strike the eyes, as when in the desert Moses was absent for a longer time from the sight of the people, the multitude gathers, and demands to be instituted in a certain worship. Aaron therefore, in the Egyptian manner, sets up a calf. There they sacrifice, and the people sing hymns divided into choirs. Thus all men without the light of the word of God fashion for themselves deities and external gestures. The heathens in the dangers of war used to set up a statue of Mars, and added rites, such as the songs of the Salii. Women because of the dangers of childbirth used to set up a statue of Juno, and there they sacrificed in a certain way. These things were so accumulated that the slaughter of men was added, because men wanted to punish themselves in a notable way, so that they might merit pardon.

This opinion of merit among all Nations increased ceremonies, and the mockeries of the devil were added, which drove men to manifest indecencies, and the games of wits were also added. In Argos, so that marriages might be happy, a statue of Juno was worshipped holding a pomegranate in her left hand, to which a cuckoo flew, and they feigned that Jupiter first came to Juno in the form of a cuckoo. Thus horribly do human minds without the light of the word and without the Holy Spirit offer insults to the true God, just as in the Church rites have been depraved, and gestures accumulated in the heathen manner, statues have been set up, and there has been a running to them as if to deities, the bread is carried around and adored, since it can have no reason for being a Sacrament outside of its instituted use, hermits and monks chose singular works, and feigned that they merit the remission of sins and eternal life, just as other men have feigned that their fasts and other exercises are worship of God and merits: mass-priests sell their masses as a chief merit. Against these insults to God it is necessary to hold to the doctrine by which God commands true worship and condemns false.

Therefore, let the rules of Ezekiel 20 be held: Walk in my statutes, not in the statutes of your fathers. Likewise: This is my beloved son, hear him. John 14: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my father will love him, and we will come to him, and make our dwelling with him. Matthew 15: In vain do they worship me with the commandments of men.

Here let the whole doctrine concerning true worship and commandments be repeated. The worship of God is a work commanded by God, done in the acknowledgment of our Lord Jesus Christ and in faith, the principal end of which work is that through it honor may be attributed to God, that is, that you show that the true God wishes to be worshipped in this way, and that this is the true God and judge whom you worship thus and not otherwise, and that you testify that this obedience is owed to this true God; as the chastity of Joseph is worship, because it is a work commanded by God, and is done with the illumination of the mediator and the faith of the promised mercy, and by this work he attributes honor to God, that is, he shows that the true God wishes to be worshipped thus, and that this is the true God whom he worships thus, and he testifies that this obedience is owed to him.

This definition is taken from the sayings which I have already recited: Walk in my statutes. Likewise: Hear him.

From this definition of the worship of God it is manifest that works not commanded by God are not the worship of God, whether they are commanded in human traditions or chosen by private judgment. He names here, however, the elements of the world, not as physicists speak, but the word signifies an arrangement from στοῖχος, which is a series, and he understands worldly arrangements, distinct rites, such as we use in this world, that is, in this bodily life, namely, ranks of persons, order in food, clothing, days, or similar things.

The third kind of impostures is that of fictitious enthusiasms, which are either entirely feigned and invented, as are most Anabaptists and Schwenkfeldians, or are diabolical illusions, as were the frenzies of many fanatical men, the Pepusians and others. Schwenkfeld feigns that God communicates himself without a medium, that is, without the thought of the divine word. Thus the devil astutely leads men away from the word revealed by divine testimonies, so that afterwards men may play with feigning opinions, worships, idols, and a confusion of works, as happened among the heathens: and with the divine word abandoned, faith is absolutely nothing, which is the apprehension of God by the thought of the written word, as Paul says: Faith comes from hearing, and hearing from the word of God. In conversion, let sorrow arise from the thought of the word, which convicts of sin. Again, also in consolation, let the mind contemplate the divine promises, and when the heart is sustained by the thought of the word, true faith is kindled. Thus the son of God is efficacious, giving us of his spirit, nor is it to be imagined that faith is first in the heart, and afterwards the thought of doctrine first approaches, which would be an exercise of the external man or a testimony concerning an inner light, as Schwenkfeld speaks. These things must be diligently considered, lest illuminations or enthusiasms be sought without the word of God.

Latin:

Videte ne quis seducat vos per philoso- phiam etc.

Ante in summa praecepit de cavendis cor- ruptelis, nunc species aliquas recenset, confusio- nem philosophiae et Evangelii, ordinationes hu- manas, fictos enthusiasmos et ementita miracula. Ad hos modos fere reduci possunt omnes impo- sturae, ut Samosatenus, Mahometus, Servetus, Thammerus quaerunt philosophicam concinnita- tem, disputant λόγον esse tantum vocem evane- scentem. Pelagius et monachi dicunt hominem posse satisfacere legi Dei, et disciplinam esse per- fectam impletionem legis et iusticiam, qua homo coram Deo iustus sit, hoc est, placens Deo et ac- ceptus ad vitam aeternam. Haec sunt philoso- phica, et quaeritur concinnitas.

Secundus modus imposturarum est sine eru- ditione, videlicet externorum rituum et gestuum falsa accommodatio, qui tamen primum inde orti sunt, quod necesse est in vita esse ordinem et aliqua exercitia. His postea affingunt homines opinionem iusticiae et meriti, et cultus Dei, si- cut nomen superstitionem inde factum est, quod sit immodica assiduitas in ritibus. Huc pertinent ritus monachorum, discrimina ciborum, coeli- batus, βαττολογίαι, et omnium gentium super- stitiones. Unde et multa idola orta et cumulata sunt, milites quaerunt numen certo ritu, quod opituletur in bello: mulieres quaerunt auxilium in partu, ideo statuae Iunonis, Annae etc. exco- gitatae sunt.

In his duobus modis peccat ratio, quaerens Deum sine verbo, aut intus disputando, aut foris male accommodando gestus et opera.

Tertius modus est aut impudenter simulata vanitas, aut diabolica illusio. Multi enim falso iactitant enthusiasmos, ut Anabaptistae plurimi his mendaciis se venditant: aut sunt praestigiae diabolicae, ut et multa falsa miracula a diabolis fiunt, et saepe spectra sese oculis hominum offe- runt. Est autem hoc loco vocabulum συλαγω- γῶν, quod significat captivum adducere tanquam praedam. Nam σκῦλα significant Spolia, inde est σῦλα una litera detrita. Iubet igitur cavere, ne decipiamur illis modis, de quibus nos monet, et simul significat deceptos et simul irretitos velut captivos teneri, nec facile liberari, sicut alibi inquit, a diabolo mentes impiorum captivas teneri.

De primo autem modo sciant iuniores non damnari veram philosophiam manentem intra suas metas, sed damnari confusionem doctrina- rum, cum philosophia docetur pro Evangelio, quod est revelatum et est extra captum huma- num, seu cum Evangelium transformatur in phi- losophiam, ut crasse faciunt Pelagiani et mona- chi, qui finxerunt homines posse legi Dei satis- facere, et hanc qualemcunque disciplinam esse perfectam impletionem legis, et mereri remis- sionem peccatorum, et esse iusticiam, qua homo sit iustus coram Deo, placens Deo et acceptus ad vitam aeternam. Haec falso extruuntur ex phi- losophia, quae non loquitur de aeterna iusticia, de aeterna vita, nec de remissione peccatorum, sed de rectione locomotivae in externis gestibus. Necesse igitur est scire discrimina doctrina- rum, ac regula tenenda est 1. Timoth. 4.: Om- nis creatura Dei bona est, et nihil reiiciendum quod cum gratiarum actione sumitur: sanctifica- tur enim per verbum Dei et precationem. Esse autem noticias naturales quasdam veras in crea- tione mentibus hominum insitas, quae sunt nor- mae veritatis et certitudinis, ut numerorum, or- dinis, figurarum, legum naturalium de moribus, et physica principia, ex quibus extruuntur mul- tae artes manifestum est, et quidem Paulus no- minat leges naturales veritatem Dei, et ait legem scriptam esse in cordibus. Et manifestum est a Deo probari numerationem, scriptionem, lectio- nem, architectonicam, artem medicam, et de architecto dicitur Exod. 31.: Deus implevit eum hac sapientia. Et anni rationem eruditam Deus et instituit et ostendit, et numerare Deus iubet. Linguas esse donum Spiritus sancti historia Apo- stolorum ostendit, et de arte medica dicitur Sy- racidae 38.: Deus dedit hominibus scientiam, ut glorificetur in mirabilibus suis, hoc est, ut sin- gularis efficacia in singulis remediis sit testimo- nium de providentia Dei, quod ad usus hominum res conditae sint. Agnoscamus igitur artes extructas ex noticiis, quae in creatione hominum mentibus insitae sunt, esse res bonas et Dei dona, et quidem scia- mus esse commonefactiones et testimonia de Deo, quia ostendunt Deum esse sapientem, et quidem lex naturae testatur esse Deum, et docet qualis sit, discernit eum a malis naturis, et testatur vin- dicem esse. Ideo dulcissime inquit Plato: Gra- tam de Deo famam in artibus sparsam esse. Et Salomon inquit: Ut oculus videat et auris audiat, Deus facit utrunque, hoc est, lumen in oculis et in mente creatura Dei est, et multo magis ex- cellens lumen in excellentibus artificibus. Primum ergo cogitantes de artibus, fontem sapientiae Deum agnoscamus et celebremus. Deinde artibus, quia totam vitam corporalem re- gunt, utamur sicut iussit, et pro eis gratias Deo agamus. Si qui vituperant artes, furiosi sunt, et nocent hominum vitae, et Deum autorem con- tumelia afficiunt. Nomino autem philosophiam seu artes noticias principiorum et demonstrationes, non quaelibet somnia aut sophisticas praestigias et corruptelas, quales multi sparserunt, ut Epi- curei, Stoici, Pyrrhonii, Cynici et alii.

Deinde hoc quoque sciendum est, artes ex luce naturali ortas habere suas metas, et iudicare de his, de quibus mentes humanae convinci pos- sunt, iuxta κριτήρια.

Sed praeter artes ex luce naturali ortas Deus singularibus testimoniis Evangelium reve- lavit, de sua essentia et voluntate, ac nominatim de filio et de promissione gratiae, sicut 1. Co- rinth. 1. dicitur: Cum mundus non nosset Deum in sapientia per sapientiam, placuit Deo per stul- tam praedicationem salvos facere credentes. Ideo de essentia et voluntate Dei statuendum est, iuxta Evangelium, non iuxta philosophiam.

Hoc discrimen doctrinarum intelligi necesse est, et suus cuique locus tribuendus est, et huius discriminis confusionem damnat Paulus, non vi- tuperat veras noticias, quae sunt lumen a Deo conditum, si recte accommodentur.

Secundus modus imposturarum facilius in- telligi potest, quia circa externos gestus versatur, qui incurrunt in oculos, ut cum in deserto Mo- ses diutius abesset a conspectu populi, concurrit multitudo, et postulat institui certum cultum. Aaron igitur Aegyptio more vitulum collocat. Ibi sacrificant, et populus canit hymnos distribu- tus in choros. Ita omnes homines sine luce verbi Dei fingunt sibi numina et externos gestus. Eth- nici in periculis belli collocabant statuam Martis, et addebant ritus, ut Saliorum carmina. Mulie- res propter pericula partus collocabant statuam Iunonis, et ibi certo modo sacrificabant. Haec ita cumulata sunt, ut accesserint mactationes ho- minum, quia homines sese punire insigni modo volebant, ut veniam mererentur.

Haec opinio meriti apud omnes Gentes auxit ceremonias, et accesserunt diaboli ludibria, quae impulerunt homines ad manifestas turpitudines, accesserunt et ludi ingeniorum. In Argis ut es- sent foelicia coniugia, colebatur statua Iunonis tenens in sinistra pomum punicum, ad quod ad- volabat cuculus, et finxerunt Iovem specie cu- culi primum ad Iunonem venisse. Ita horribili- ter humanae mentes sine luce verbi et sine Spi- ritu sancto contumeliis verum Deum afficiunt, sicut in Ecclesia ritus depravati sunt, et cumulati gestus ethnico more, collocatae sunt statuae, et ad eas velut ad numina concursum est, circum- gestatur panis et adoratur, cum nihil possit habere rationem Sacramenti extra institutum usum, ele- gerunt singularia oper a Eremitae et monachi, et finxerunt ea mereri remissionem peccatorum et vitam aeternam, sicut et alii homines finxerunt cultus Dei et merita esse sua ieiunia et alia exer- citia: sacrificuli vendunt suas missas tanquam praecipuum meritum. Adversus has contumelias Dei necesse est tenere doctrinam, qua Deus prae- cipit veros cultus et damnat falsos.

Regulae igitur teneantur Ezechiel. 20.: In praeceptis meis ambulate, non in praeceptis pa- trum vestrorum. Item: Hic est filius meus di- lectus, hunc audite. Iohan. 14.: Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum servabit, et pater meus dili- get eum, et veniemus ad eum, et mansionem apud eum faciemus. Matthaei 15.: Frustra me colunt mandatis hominum.

Hic repetatur tota doctrina de veris cultibus et de mandatis. Cultus Dei est opus mandatum a Deo, factum in agnitione Domini nostri Iesu Christi et fide, cuius operis principalis finis est, ut per ipsum honos Deo tribuatur, hoc est, ut ostendas verum Deum velle coli hoc modo, et hunc esse verum Deum et iudicem, quem sic colis et non aliter, et testeris huic vero Deo hanc obe- dientiam deberi, ut castitas Ioseph est cultus, quia est opus a Deo mandatum, et fit praelucente agitatione mediatoris, et fide promissae miseri- cordiae, et hoc opere tribuit honorem Deo, id est, ostendit verum Deum sic velle coli, et hunc esse verum Deum, quem sic colit, eique deberi hanc obedientiam testatur.

Haec definitio sumta est ex dictis 'quae iam recitavi: In praeceptis meis ambulate. Item: Hunc audite.

Ex hac definitione cultus Dei manifestum est, opera non mandata a Deo non esse cultus Dei, sive sint mandata in humanis traditionibus, sive sint electa privato arbitrio. Nominat autem hic Elementa mundi, non ut Physici loquuntur, sed vocabulum significat ordinationem a στοῖχος, quod est series, et intelligit ordinationes munda- nas, ritus distinctos, qualibus in hoc mundo, hoc est, hac vita corporali utimur, videlicet, gradus personarum, ordinem in cibo, vestitu, diebus aut similibus.

Tertium genus imposturarum est ficticii en- thusiasmi, qui aut sunt prorsus simulati et emen- titi, ut Anabaptistici plerique et Stencfeldiani, aut sunt illusiones diabolicae, ut fuerunt multorum fanaticorum hominum, Pepusianorum et aliorum furores. Fingit Stencfeldius Deum sese communicare sine medio, id est, sine verbi divini cogitatione. Ita astute diabolus abducit homines a verbo pate- facto divinis testimoniis, ut postea ludant homi- nes fingendis opinionibus, cultibus, idolis et confusione operum, sicut apud Ethnicos accidit: et relicto verbo divino prorsus nihil est fides, quae est apprehensio Dei cogitatione scripti verbi, sicut Paulus inquit: Fides ex auditu est, auditus ex verbo Dei. In conversione dolor oriatur cogitatione verbi, quod arguit peccatum. Rursus etiam in conso- latione mens intueatur promissiones divinas, cum- que cor sustentatur cogitatione verbi, vera fides accenditur. Sic filius Dei efficax est, dans nobis de suo spiritu, nec imaginandum est fidem prius esse in corde, et postea primum accedere cogita- tionem doctrinae, quae sit exercitium externi ho- minis seu testimonium de luce interiore, sicut loquitur Stencfeldius. Haec necesse est diligen- ter considerari, ne quaerantur illuminationes seu enthusiasmi sine verbo Dei.

## 2:9
In him dwells all the fullness of the divinity bodily, etc.

The word 'bodily' signifies properly in this place what we usually call 'personally,' and is opposed to a separable indwelling, as God dwells in the blessed or in the saints in this life, but in such a way that he is efficacious there, and the divinity is separable.

Let four modes of the presence of God be considered here.

The first mode is universal presence, by which for the conservation of substances, God is thus present to all creatures, good and evil, so that he preserves their substances, for as long as they are preserved, as Pharaoh is destroyed when God ceases to preserve his substance. Concerning this universal presence it is said in Jeremiah 23: Do I not fill heaven and earth, says the Lord. And let the verse be known: Enter, praesenter, Deus hic et ubique potenter.

The second mode of presence is called special, by which God is in the blessed, namely, in such a way that he not only preserves their substances, but communicates himself to them, filling them with his light and justice, and quickening them with eternal life, and is immediately beheld by them. And although he does not depart from them, yet he is present only by association, and in reality is separable. Concerning this mode it is said: God will be all in all, namely in the blessed, that is, he will be in them in such a way that sin is not present at the same time.

The third mode is also called special presence, by which he is in the saints in this life, as in David, by which presence God not only preserves their substances, but also effects in them a new light and motions pleasing to himself, and is beheld immediately, as in eternal life, but through the word. That this presence is separable is manifest, according to the saying about those returning to their vomit.

The fourth mode of presence is personal union, by which, namely, the second person of the divinity assumed human nature, not only inseparably, but in such a way that it is one complete ὑφιστάμενον [subsistence] with that human nature, and the λόγος [Word] assuming human nature in much the same way as in other men a complete ὑφιστάμενον [subsistence] is made by the union of soul and body. Athanasius, Cyril, and Justin used this comparison.

Thus, therefore, let 'to dwell bodily' be understood in this place, so that personal union may be distinguished from other modes of presence, just as it is said: The Word was made flesh. But what he says: The fullness of the divinity, distinguishes the Son from other blessed ones in this way. In others there are particular gifts, as in Moses, Elijah. In the Son, however, is the substance, which is the second person of the divinity, of immense perfection, omnipotent, and effective in others, as John says: From his fullness we have all received. Therefore, let not the text be understood as if the three persons assumed human nature, but that the fullness is opposed to the particular gifts of the saints.

In him you are made complete etc.

This sentiment is also very significant, and is opposed to the imagination seeking righteousness through works, whether of the divine law or of traditions, concerning which imagination I spoke before: Let no one deceive you through human traditions. And it is an antithesis. By the law of God you are not made complete, that is, neither righteous before God, nor freed from death, nor gifted with eternal life, much less by human traditions. But in Christ you are made complete, namely, both by the imputation and restoration of righteousness and eternal life, which is begun in us in this life, and is exhibited complete after this life. This effect is brought about because of the mediator and through him. Therefore it is explicitly said: In Christ you are made complete, not by the merits of any creature, not by the law, not by traditions. And this consolation must always be held in this life, that although there are still remnants of sin and great filth in us, yet in Christ we are made complete by imputation, as it is said in Romans 5: Being justified by faith we have peace with God. Romans 6: You are not under the law but under grace. Romans 8: There is now no condemnation for those who walk in Christ Jesus. Likewise: Who shall accuse the elect? It is God who justifies. Likewise: Christ is at the right hand of the Father interceding for us. Job 13: Even if he kills me, I will hope in him. Nevertheless, I will argue my ways, and he is for me for salvation. Because every hypocrite will not enter before him. 1 John 5: He who has the Son has life. John 3: So God loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son etc. And John 17: May the love with which you love me be in them. With these most ample and sweetest consolations let us confirm ourselves in invocation, and let us join them to the saying: In him you are made complete.

In whom also you were circumcised with a circumcision not made by hand etc.

He explains the previous clause, In him you are made complete, with an added antithesis. By the law you were not made complete, but the law was a type, the thing exhibited was through Christ. Circumcision signified the casting off of the body of sins and regeneration; these things you now have through Christ. He interprets, therefore, the circumcision and repeats the benefits of Christ, in which he again embraces both, the imputation of righteousness and the renewal, which is done in this life in conversion, and he embraces two modes, mortification and vivification. Concerning mortification he says: You are buried with him through baptism. Concerning vivification he says: You are raised with him through faith in his efficacy. But since these words Mortification and Vivification have been distorted from their true understanding to the hypocrisy of external gestures by monks and fanatical men, let the true meaning be considered.

But as in all arts and affairs diligence is necessary, to see where the same things are expressed by several appellations, and to correctly join the appellations: so in this place let us know

Paul speaks of true conversion to God, which the Church usually calls Repentance, the parts of which we say are Contrition, Faith, and new Obedience. Contrition is signified here by these words: To put off the body of sins, to be mortified and buried together with Christ. Therefore, true terrors and sorrows are signified, such as are in conversion when, in the acknowledgment of sins, the wrath of God is felt, as it is said: As a lion he has crushed all my bones. For although the degrees of sorrows are not similar in all things, nevertheless it is not doubtful that some contrition is necessary in conversion, as it is said in Isaiah 66: To whom shall I look, except to him who is contrite and humbled in spirit, and who trembles at my words. And these terrors and sorrows are then mortification and burial with Christ, when at the same time there are the beginnings of faith, which causes hearts to grieve that they have offended God, so that they do not rage against him, but flee to him on account of the mediator. Thus he says here: You are buried with Christ, namely in this life; now this nature lies in sorrows and on the cross, it does not reign with the furies of doubts and false opinions and depraved desires, such evils as reign in the ungodly.

And the comparison of the burial of Christ to the present life of all the pious in the Church must be diligently considered. The Church lies in this life under the cross and sorrows, as Christ in the sepulcher, awaiting complete newness.

But that we usually place faith in the second part of conversion is taken from the passages of Paul in Romans 6 and here, where vivification is added to mortification, which is done by faith, according to the saying: The just shall live by his faith. For one must not remain in death and eternal flight, but we are converted for this reason, that we may live, according to the saying: I live, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live. But vivification occurs, as has already been said, by Faith which apprehends the remission of sins and reconciliation. And mention of faith is made by name in the doctrine of conversion or repentance, so that the horrible lie of the Papists may be taxed, who say that one must remain in doubt, and they completely overwhelm with silence this faith, by which it must be established that to you in conversion sin is truly remitted, and you are truly reckoned just, endowed with the Holy Spirit and the inheritance of eternal life.

He attributes our vivification, however, to the resurrection of Christ, saying: You have been raised together through faith, he has vivified you together with him.

Because Christ, having been raised, reigns in such a way that he gathers an eternal Church by the voice of the Gospel, is effective in it, vivifies it, gives the Holy Spirit, and miraculously protects and preserves it amidst the horrible confusions and darkness of the human race. And he says expressly that this vivification is done by faith, and he signifies that this faith is a movement divinely kindled when he says that Faith is the efficacy of God, that is, that by which God is effective. Afterward, Paul repeats the same sentiment about conversion in more words: You were dead, he says, because of sins and the uncircumcision, that is, because of the unclean and guilty nature, such as is propagated by carnal generation. He calls such an unclean and guilty nature having original sin the Uncircumcision.

But now you have been vivified, with the remission of all sins given and the handwriting, etc., blotted out.

In these words he embraces both the imputation of righteousness and vivification. For that which he says, that all sins have been remitted freely, pertains to the imputation of righteousness. Then he adds that the handwriting has been blotted out, that is, the sentence of condemnation, which is the conclusion from the divine law. Therefore he adds that the handwriting was against us through decrees, that is, through the law. Thus he distinguishes the handwriting from the law as a conclusion from the preceding propositions. For the judgment of conscience is an entire practical syllogism drawn from the law, approving what is in accordance with the law and condemning the contrary, and there follows in the order divinely established, after the condemnation, sorrow and an avenger, which grows as God judges and destroys the guilty nature, as in David the judgment of conscience is this syllogism: God casts the adulterer and murderer into eternal punishments. David is an adulterer and murderer, and worse than that, because he is more ungrateful to God than others, since he had been adorned with huge gifts. Hence follows the conclusion from the law: Therefore David is rejected by God.

This conclusion is named the Handwriting, that is, the sentence in the mind and heart as if written by the law and the acknowledgment of the fall, and at the same time a huge sorrow is imprinted, which grows when a singular sense of the wrath of God judging and destroying the guilty nature through the law approaches, as it is said: The sting of death is sin, the power of sin is the law. Romans 4: The law works wrath. Likewise: As a lion he has crushed all my bones. And in Psalm 37: There is no peace in my bones because of my sins. Psalm 114:

The sorrows of death surrounded me etc. Job 9: God, whose wrath no one can resist. This sad judgment, by which God strikes guilty nature through the law, he here calls the handwriting contrary to us through the law.

At the same time, vivification occurs in the deletion of the handwriting. For when remission and imputation are received by faith, in that consolation occurs vivification, in which the Son of God by the voice of the Gospel effectively vivifies hearts, and pours the Holy Spirit into them, as it is said in 1 John 5: This life is in his Son; he who has the Son has life; he who does not have the Son of God does not have life. For then, instead of doubt, assent shines in the mind, receiving the promise, and instead of the sense of the wrath of God and terrors, there are in the heart trust and joy resting in God on account of the mediator, which joy is the life of the spirit, of which Paul says: The spirit lives because of righteousness. Let us know, therefore, that Paul is not speaking of feigned enthusiasms, or of Stencfeldian and Anabaptist grimness, but of true conversion or repentance. Thus, when the words of Paul are accommodated to consolation in true conversion, they become clear.

How sweet a consolation it is to contemplate this very picture of the triumph! The victor is the Son of God who crushed the head of the serpent, that is, he destroyed the kingdom and power of the devil, sin, and eternal death, namely in believers. The liberated Church follows and will follow him as a conqueror throughout all eternity, and the spoils are carried, as was done in triumphs, namely our handwritings hanging on the cross. These have now been deleted for those who believe in the mediator, who by his blood, that is, by his entire obedience, deleted the handwritings of the law, so that they might lose the right of accusing, as it is said in 1 John 1: The blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from all sin. Let us often think of this very picture in invocation, so that faith may be kindled and confirmed.

But also that the devils are led as if in a spectacle, stripped of their principality and power, namely, so that they do not destroy those who believe in the Son by their snares, as it is said: No one shall snatch my sheep from my hands.

At the end, however, he adds the particle: Triumphing through himself; this is said in distinction to human victories. For men in corporal battles do not win without the help of soldiers. But the Son of God, without the help of any creature, crushed the head of the serpent; this one person is the redeemer and by his own power conquers the devils, takes away sin and death.

Let no one therefore judge you in food and drink, or in part of a feast day etc.

This conclusion is the antithesis of the preceding, since righteousness is to have remission and reconciliation on account of the Son, and to be vivified through the Son to eternal life; it follows that distinctions of foods and days and similar rites are not righteousness, which neither take away sin nor death, nor are they eternal things. Wherefore, the omissions of such rites are not sins either.

An assertion is therefore expressly placed here, which affirms that the observation of such rites is not righteousness, and their omissions are not sins. And since this whole passage is most clear, it ought to be most well-known to all for confirming minds in this doctrine concerning human traditions, which has been restored divinely in our Churches, namely that their observation is not righteousness, and that their omission is not a sin. For Paul speaks not only of Mosaic ceremonies, but in general of all, of Mosaic ones and of those devised by Bishops and by other men, just as the saying of Christ is general: In vain they worship me with the commandments of men. And below, Paul expressly includes in this rule the commandments and traditions of men: Let no one judge you, that is, condemn you on account of the omission of such rites, in foods, drink, part of a feast day, that is, turns of feasts, as the Greek phrase ἐν μέρει signifies by turns.

Let the whole doctrine concerning human traditions be repeated here, as it is taught in our Churches, and let it be considered what kind of blindness it was when the observation of human traditions was thought to be the worship of God, and indeed necessary, and what kind of torture it was for the conscience that imagined the omissions of such rites to be sins.

The books of Gerson are extant, in which ἐπιείκεια (equity) is sought, and it is disputed that some traditions were made for the sake of necessity, others for the sake of ornament; other σοφὰ φάρμακα (wise remedies) are sought so that the false exacerbation may be mitigated. But just as Alexander did not solve the Gordian knot by long untying, but suddenly cut it with his sword, so this rule of Paul most briefly removes all those bonds of consciences, when it affirms that neither is observation righteousness, nor is omission sin. He speaks, however, of the Mosaic ceremonies, that they were shadows at that time, since they were instituted not by human authority, but by divine, that is, they were by no means merits for the remission of sins, nor righteousness before God, but were signs reminding men of the promise and of the coming Messiah. But the body is Christ, that is, the thing signified and exhibited, namely, that the obedience of Christ alone is the merit of the remission of sins and of eternal righteousness and life and λύτρον, and a propitiation for us, and that he himself, the mediator, is the giver of righteousness and eternal life, as it is said in Daniel: Everlasting righteousness shall be brought in, etc. This antithesis is copiously expressed in the Epistle to the Hebrews concerning the distinction between the priesthood of Aaron and the priesthood of Christ, where it is said that the sacrifices of Aaron were only ἀντίτυπα of the sacrifice of Christ, just as Paul here calls them shadows. But concerning the sacrifice of Christ he says: By which will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.

The Prophets themselves often repeat this doctrine concerning the understanding of the sacrifices, and they teach that there is one and the same doctrine of justification at all times. The Fathers before Moses and after him were righteous before God by faith alone, that is, by trust in the mediator, that is, they received the remission of sins, the imputation of righteousness, vivification through the Holy Spirit, and eternal life, as it is said in Acts 15: We believe that we are saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, just as they are, etc.

What, therefore, were so many sacrifices and so many ceremonies? I answer: They were a distinction of that polity from the Gentiles. Because God, in His immense goodness, willed that the polity in which Christ would be born, would teach, would provide testimonies of His doctrine, would become a victim, would rise again from death, and would show the testimonies of the resurrection, and in which the doctrine would be preserved by the sending of Prophets, should be known and observed. And so that this polity could be more observed, it was placed between the most famous empires, the Babylonian and the Egyptian. And because He willed this polity to be a school of doctrine and the seat of the Church, He Himself instituted by His own voice external exercises, which would be pictures of the doctrine, so that they might remind the people of the promise and of the mediator, and move many Gentiles to seek the cause of the distinction of the polity. Therefore, the Prophets often censure the Pharisaic opinion, who falsely pretended that these rites were merit and righteousness, as the Psalm says: You will not delight in burnt offerings. And Isaiah: He who offers a sheep is like one who strangles a dog.

Let no one deceive you by a feigned humility, etc.

The Greeks call those βαυκοπανούργους who feign modesty or humility, and by this simulation lay snares, so that they may be thought not to seek wealth, glory, or pleasures for themselves, but to be as it were demigods. This is the art of impostors in the Church. But so that simulation may be distinguished from virtue, let the definition of virtue be known, which is called ταπεινοφροσύνη, for which the common name is Humility.

But so that the matter may become clearer by antithesis, and since vices are better known, Pride is defined first, in which many vices concur, as there are many appellations which do not signify only a single virtue or a single vice. Pride is, for one not discerning his own infirmity or sins, and falsely attributing great virtues to himself, to be secure, and to fear neither God nor punishments, and by trust in one's own virtues to break out beyond the bounds of one's vocation, to move toward or desire things greater than one's vocation, and to despise others, as if they were not useful instruments, and to be angry at God and men when they are hindered from reigning. Thus the beginning of pride is a lie, which is followed by security, then the audacity of breaking out beyond one's vocation, as Alexander dreams that he is God, then, secure, he breaks out beyond his vocation, despises laws, and kills righteous men. Samosatenus, arrogating to himself great wisdom, neglecting the word of God, and neither fearing God, and trusting in the applause of the people, is carried beyond the bounds, and sows an opinion pleasing to the multitude, and fortifies himself with a faction, so that he may oppress those who oppose him and hold the kingdom, even if outwardly he feigns that he is not contending for his own excellence, but for the truth, preferring others to himself in appearance, and does not wish to seem to desire pleasure or power.

Now let the contrary examples of true humility be looked at, from which a definition may afterwards be constituted. For in true humility there are together truth, rightly judging concerning infirmity. Then the fear of God and sorrow on account of infirmity and sin, then the care of remaining within one's vocation, as in Jonathan there is truth rightly judging that no man is equal to the kingdom, and that a king is constituted by God, especially in Israel. Then there are in him fear of God and the care of remaining within the bounds of one's calling, he serves in his place, and gives thanks to God, because He adorns him with glorious testimonies, he submits himself to David, to whom he sees God has handed over the kingdom, and he is not angry with God, even when he later falls into calamity. Let this therefore be the definition.

True humility is for one who judges truly concerning his own infirmity to fear God, and to be affected with sorrow on account of his own infirmity and sin, and it is to serve God in one's calling with faith and trust in divine help, not to despise others, but to judge that God makes others also useful instruments, and to attribute honor to them for God's sake, and not to be angry with God or men when punishments come from God. This definition is taken from these sayings, Prov. 16: An abomination before God is every proud heart. Rom. 12: Not seeking high things, but content with humble things. Philip. 2: In humility consider others as excelling yourselves, just as Christ, when He was in the form of God, did not snatch at equality with God, that is, He did not use it outside of His calling. And Peter says: God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. Sirach: The greater you are, the more you humble yourself, and you will find grace before the Lord.

Since therefore Paul says: Let no one deceive you desiring in humility, let it be understood as feigning humility, as if he were saying, desiring to deceive in humility. Such is the nature of men, ὅμοιον ὁμοίῳ φίλον, equals or inferiors are loved, and it is pleasing to no one to be despised. For it is just to attribute to each his own place by geometric proportion. Since therefore someone exalts himself above others, and especially when he presses others, so that he as it were thrusts them from their place, he comes into hatred: finally all men are captured by flattery. They are therefore pleasing who submit themselves to others and artfully flatter, and bend themselves to the affections of those whom they wish to please. Therefore men are easily captured by that theatricality, which artfully imitates humbler gestures, it even produces admiration to appear not to desire pleasures and wealth, because if they were without avarice and without foolish ambition, they would have an excellent virtue.

Experience however shows that these deceptions, that is, gestures of humility or modesty, are used by impostors who scatter perverse dogmas. Such hypocrites have always been, are, and will be in the human race. Therefore also in Matthew an admonition is handed down about guarding against such ensnarers, who have the appearance of sheep, but inwardly are ravenous wolves. Paul also names another kind of deception, falsely boasting of inspirations, Enthusiasms, illuminations, conversations with angels, and seeing visions offered divinely. Just as in the city of Münster the Anabaptists falsely boasted of inspirations, and individual ages have examples. Paul expressly accuses them of lying, he says they walk proudly in those things which they have not seen. It is a Greek phrase, which signifies an elation of mind by a proud gait, as, ἐπιβατεύων τοῦ Σμέρδεως ὀνόματι, that is, acting proudly in the name of Smerdis. It is said therefore that they proudly boast of most vain lies, that they have inspirations or conversations of angels, which they do not have. Just as I have known many who falsely boasted that they had inspirations, which they did not have. The word θρησκεία is superstition, as if τερασκεία, that is, to practice something prodigious, as if τέρατα ἀσκεῖν. Suidas says it is as if θεὸν δέρκειν, to see God. But because the people admire such ones, whom they think to be familiar with God, and superstitious people seek a similar familiarity, therefore many assent to them, whether they teach true or false things. Often therefore the admonition about guarding against these deceptions of the enthusiasts has been repeated, and Paul here says that they are vainly puffed up by the persuasion of their flesh, that is, they swell with a false imagination concerning their own wisdom and justice, that is to be proud and to exalt oneself above others, and to pretend that they are like the Prophets. But so that snares may be guarded against, it is necessary that there be some norm. For judgment is difficult, as is also said in the old verse: χαλεπὸν νόον ἴδμεναι ἀνδρὸς. Likewise: κιβδήλου δ’ ἀνδρὸς γνῶναι χαλεπώτερον οὐδὲν. The norm is however expressed universally in these sayings: If anyone teaches another Gospel, let him be anathema. Likewise: No one can lay a foundation, besides that which is laid, which is Christ Jesus. He shows this norm here also when he says: Not holding the head, namely Christ, who through the voice of the Gospel is effective, and gathers the Church not through other doctrines. Therefore he adds here expressly about the head, so that the gathering of the Church may be understood and the Gospel or the integrity of doctrines may be comprehended. He says therefore: From which head Christ the whole body, that is, the Church, is joined together and grows through joints and ligaments, and becomes such a body, in which God will be all in all in eternity. He understands, however, the joints and ligaments to be the consensus in the same true doctrine, by which consensus the members of the Church are joined, and the Son of God is effective, gathering the Church with one and the same voice of the Gospel, as he says: I am the vine, you are the branches. And it is an antithesis opposed to the enthusiasts, of whom he spoke earlier, as if to say: They boast that they are the dwellings of God and have enthusiasms, but they lie openly, because they are neither members of the Church, nor does God dwell in impostors who invent a kind of doctrine contrary to the Gospel. But God dwells in those who are joined to the head, Christ, and are members of the Church retaining the same voice of the Gospel uncorrupted.

The Anabaptists boast that they have wondrous enthusiasms, but it is certain that they are impostors: because they manifestly depart from the head, Christ, and from the doctrine of the Gospel, and are enemies of the true Church and of true doctrine; they pretend that they are righteous by their own feigned inspirations and their own patience, and they call the desertion of political order, etc., patience. Those who retain such great errors, fighting against the Gospel, are neither temples of God nor members of the Church, but are outside those ligaments of which Paul speaks here.

If you have died with Christ to the elements of the world, why, as though living in the world, do you make decrees: Do not touch, do not handle, do not taste, etc.

At the beginning, the younger ones must be warned that these words, 'Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle,' are said μιμητικῶς, or recitatively, not dispositively; that is, Paul is reciting examples of foreign laws, such as hypocrites establish: Do not taste meat on the sixth day, etc. He did not insert these words as if enacting laws, as monks have foolishly interpreted, not understanding the figure of speech. He adds, however: 'Which are all to perish with use,' just as garments and cups are worn out by constant use, and foods are consumed by use. For he wishes to say that newness in the reborn is eternal light and life, kindled through the Son by the voice of the Gospel and the Holy Spirit, and the Son of God and the Holy Spirit are eternal things. Therefore, the righteousness of the Gospel is not a thing or the observation of a thing that is consumed by use, like foods or garments. And the word ἀπόχρησις does not signify abuse, which is κατάχρησις, but ἀπόχρησις signifies the assiduity of use or sufficiency in use, as innumerable examples show, as in Plato's 2nd Republic. Ἀποχρῇ, that is, it suffices to say that God is the author of such great goods.

According to the commandments and doctrines of men, which have a show of wisdom in superstition, etc.

So that it may be known that in these sermons of Paul, not only Mosaic ceremonies are rejected, but also other rites which are instituted by human authority, whether by Bishops, or by Monks, or by other men. Therefore, he expressly names and rejects here the precepts and doctrines of men, and superstitions, which he calls ἐθελοθρησκείας, that is, rites devised without the command of God, or exercises or bodily vexations not commanded by God, as some have imposed upon themselves fasting for three days or more. Hermits hid themselves in solitude, even leaving their families. Monks instituted celibacy and other rites. It has always been customary in the world to invent cults, and from there proceeded the audacity of men, so that they even invented new deities with various devised cults, just as soldiers invented Mars, and women Juno, Venus, and other idols. God binds us, however, in the first commandment of the Decalogue to the one true God, who revealed himself by this very word which he handed down through the Prophets and through the Son, and he very often condemns all other invocations, as when he says: You shall have no other gods. Likewise: You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him only. And Isaiah 44: Thus says the Lord the King of Israel: Besides me there is no God. And he wants us in invocation to address this true God, and to separate our invocation from the invocations of other nations. It is also said expressly about cults in Isaiah 29: In vain they worship me with the commandments of men. And Ezekiel 20: Do not walk in the statutes of your fathers, walk in my statutes, and know that I am the Lord your God. And in Numbers 15: Let them not follow their own thoughts and whorish eyes, that is, looking toward various deities, but mindful of the commandments of the Lord, let them do them, and be holy to their God; I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.

May these illustrious and express testimonies be most known to all, so that we may know that works not commanded by God are not cults of God, and let the definition be noted, namely: The cult of God is a work commanded by God, done in faith, the principal end of which is that we attribute this honor to God, that is, that by this obedience we testify that this is the true God whom we thus worship, and that he wishes to be worshipped in this way.

But why, says Paul, do human traditions have the appearance of human wisdom or pretexts, which seem wisely thought out, when in many rites there is manifest cruelty or baseness, as in the slaughter of men, in the Bacchanalia, in acts of lewdness, and likewise many manifest lies, as in the adoration of statues, or in the adoration of bread in the carrying about, which they pretend is God? I answer: Steps are taken gradually toward more absurd things, but the beginnings and seeds are less observed, as it is said: Given one absurdity, many follow. For the devils increase their furies in the impious. Paul therefore speaks of many things which have less absurdity, as in the beginning it was established for the sake of utility, that there should be three principal Bishops, the Roman, the Constantinopolitan, and the Alexandrian, each of whom should have the authority of convening synods of neighbors, and that an appeal should be made to them by the neighbors. This triumvirate was established by human law, and at that time utility moved the synods. But afterwards the Roman Pope tyrannically attached many things, that he is by divine law the highest of Bishops, that he has the power of establishing dogmas and worship, that he has both swords, and finally, as happens in courts, many jugglers amplified the pontifical authority without measure. A few years ago monks wrote that the offering in the Mass merits the remission of sins ex opere operato. Since that is manifestly absurd, they now cover it with art and speak more modestly, and yet they retain the nerve of idolatry, and they accumulate many things alien to the matter concerning sacrifices and the κακοζηλίᾳ of Levitical sacrifices, which are adorned with words, as is true of sophistry, what Euripides says in the Hippolytus: οἱ καλοὶ λίαν λόγοι overturn well-ordered cities. Therefore Paul says here that traditions have the appearance or pretext of wisdom. For thus I interpret λόγον, as if you were to say, Words not the thing, as the Greeks customarily say concerning false pretexts: λόγος ἐστὶ καὶ πρόφασις, that is, they are words not the thing, one thing is shown, another is done, as when Emperor Charles pretended that he was waging war against our people not for the sake of religion, λόγος ἦν καὶ πρόφασις, they were words and a pretext. Thus Plutarch speaks in the Eumenes. But in order that one may answer sophistical tricks aptly and clearly, both are necessary: to know the sources of those doctrines from which the material of the dispute is taken, and not to be ignorant of dialectic, as when the Papists defend human traditions, it is λόγος καὶ πρόφασις.

It is necessary that there be order in the Church, as Paul says: Let all things be done decently and in order in the Church. Therefore pastors can establish decrees.

I answer to the consequence: They can, for the sake of good order, with the consent of the Church, make some distinctions of readings or festivals, but without the opinion of worship and without the opinion of necessity. The Papists, however, add false opinions of worship and necessity. It is necessary to tax and remove these false opinions, which are added to the Pauline saying against the rule which forbids there to be more in the conclusion than in the premises.

The grandiloquence of Osiander is also an appearance of wisdom, which overwhelms the doctrine of the Gospel concerning the righteousness of faith. We affirm that in this miserable nature of men great sins and great filth remain, even if the reborn person, having received the remission of sins through faith, has been made a temple of God, and the Son truly kindles in him a new light by the voice of the Gospel, and, the Holy Spirit having been given, stirs up new motions in the heart. Therefore, in this life, one must always hold to the consolation that the reborn are righteous, that is, accepted by God on account of the mediator through mercy by faith alone, just as David says: No living person shall be justified in your sight. Here Osiander opposes a magnificent appearance of wisdom. God alone is righteousness, therefore he who has God has righteousness. Thus he leads men away from the sight of the mediator, and destroys faith, that is, trust in mercy, and teaches men to trust in their own newness, which God effects.

Osiander's imagination is therefore a corruption, and it is not a λογομαχία, but in reality the doctrine of the Gospel is removed from sight, and those θαύματα ῥημάτων move men, Essential righteousness, and this appearance of wisdom: God alone is righteousness, which is true concerning His eternal and immense righteousness judging, saving, and damning, concerning the source and perfection of righteousness. And at the same time the proposition is true: The obedience of the Son is righteousness, which is the price for us, and is established so that it may be that righteousness on account of which we are righteous and accepted. When therefore it is added: He who has God has righteousness, you should understand it insofar as he has it, as if you were to say: God alone is strength, therefore he who has strength has God. I concede it insofar as he has it, as Alexander fighting bravely is armed by God, but he is not righteous on that account. Thus newness is the work of God, and the reborn person has God, but in such a way that he first receives imputed righteousness on account of the Son through faith. In this way, first the person is accepted, afterwards the novelty which God effects is righteousness, insofar as it is the work of God. But at the same time, many sins still remain in us; therefore, the person is accepted for another reason, namely, for the sake of the obedience of the mediator, which is also righteousness, and indeed that righteousness for the sake of which we are accepted by faith. In this example, you should consider how much darkness that species of wisdom casts, and how difficult its explanation is. But one must strive in good causes, so that we may hold firm confirmations, and as far as possible, solve objections clearly, and be mindful of the Aristotelian saying: Πολλοὶ πλέξαντες εὖ, κακῶς λύουσι.

Latin:

In ipso habitat omnis plenitudo divinitatis corporaliter etc.

Vocabulum Corporaliter significat proprie idem hoc loco, quod usitate dicimus Personaliter, et post oppositum inhabitationi separabili, ut ha- bitat Deus in beatis vel in sanctis in hac vita, sed ita, ut sit ibi efficax, et sit separabilis di- vinitas.

Considerentur autem hic quatuor modi prae- sentiae Dei.

Primus modus est praesentia universalis, quo ad conservationem substantiarum, qua sic adest Deus omnibus creaturis bonis et malis, ut con- servet earum substantias, tantisper donec conser- vantur, ut Pharao destruitur cum Deus desinit servare substantiam. De hac universali praesen- tia dicitur Hieremiae 28.: Coelum et terram ego impleo, dicit Dominus. Et notus sit versus: Enter, praesenter, Deus hic et ubique potenter.

Secundus modus praesentiae nominatur spe- cialis, qua Deus est in beatis, scilicet, ita ut non tantum servet substantias, sed sese eis communi- cet, complens eos sua luce et iusticia, et vivifi- cans eos vita aeterna, et immediate conspicitur ab eis. Et quanquam non discedit ab eis, tamen adest tantum societate, et reipsa est separabilis. De hoc modo dicitur: Deus erit omnia in omni- bus, scilicet in beatis, id est, sic erit in eis, ut non sit simul peccatum.

Tertius modus nominatur etiam specialis praesentia, qua est in sanctis in hac vita, ut in Davide, qua praesentia non tantum servat Deus eorum substantias, sed etiam efficit in eis novam lucem et motus sibi placentes, et conspicitur im- mediate, ut in vita aeterna, sed per verbum. Hanc praesentiam separabilem esse manifestum est, iuxta dictum de redeuntibus ad vomitum.

Quartus modus praesentiae est unio persona- lis, qua scilicet secunda persona divinitatis as- sumsit humanam naturam, non solum insepara- biliter, sed ita, ut sit unum completum ὑφιστά- μενον illa natura humana, et λόγος assumens hu- manam naturam propemodum, ut in caeteris hominibus copulatione animae et corporis fit unum completum ὑφιστάμενον. Hac similitu- dine usi sunt Athanasius, Cyrillus et Iustinus.

Sic igitur intelligatur hoc loco inhabitare corporaliter, ut discernatur unio personalis ab aliis modis praesentiae, sicut dicitur: Verbum caro factum est. Quod autem inquit: Plenitudo divinitatis, discernit et hoc modo filium ab aliis beatis. In aliis sunt particularia dona, ut in Moise, Helia. In filio autem est substantia, quae est secunda persona divinitatis, immensae per- fectionis, omnipotens, et efficax in aliis, ut Io- hannes inquit: Ex plenitudine eius omnes acce- pimus. Non igitur sic intelligatur textus, quod tres personae assumserint humanam naturam, sed plenitudo sit opposita particularibus donis san- ctorum.

In ipso estis consummati etc.

Est et haec sententia valde insignis, et op- ponitur imaginationi quaerenti iusticiam operibus, seu legis divinae, seu traditionum, de qua ima- ginatione antea dixi: Nemo vos decipiat per tra- ditiones humanas. Estque antithesis. Lege Dei non estis consummati, id est, nec iusti coram Deo, nec liberati a morte, nec donati vita aeter- na, multo minus traditionibus humanis. Sed in Christo consummati estis, scilicet, et imputa- tione et restitutione iusticiae et vitae aeternae, quae in nobis incoatur in hac vita, et exhibetur consummata post hanc vitam. Fit autem haec effectio propter mediatorem et per eum. Ideo nominatim dicitur: In Christo consummati estis, non meritis ullius creaturae, non lege, non tra- ditionibus. Ac semper in hac vita tenenda est haec consolatio, quod quanquam sunt in nobis adhuc reliquiae peccati et magnae sordes, tamen in Christo simus consummati imputatione, ut ad Romanos 5. dicitur: Iustificati fide pacem habe- mus apud Deum. Roman. 6.: Non estis sub lege sed sub gratia. Roma. 8.: Nulla nunc est condemnatio his qui in Christo Iesu ambulant. Item: Quis accusabit electos? Deus est qui iusti- ficat. Item: Christus est in dextera patris inter- pellans pro nobis. Iob. 13.: Etiamsi occidet me, sperabo in eum. Veruntamen vias meas ego ar- guam, et ipse est mihi ad salutem. Quia non in- trabit coram eo omnis hypocrita. 1. Iohan. 5.: Qui habet filium, habet vitam. Ioh. 3.: Sic Deus dilexit mundum, u filium suum unigenitum da- ret etc. Et Ioh. 17.: Sit dilectio in eis qua me di- ligis. His amplissimis et dulcissimis consolatio- nibus confirmemus nos in invocatione, et adiun- gamus eas ad dictum: In ipso consummati estis.

In quo et circumcisi estis circumcisione non manu facta etc.

Declarat superiorem particulam, In ipso consummati estis, addita antithesi. Lege non eratis consummati, sed lex erat typus, Res ex- hibita est per Christum. Circumcisio significabat abiectionem corporis peccatorum et regeneratio- nem, has res iam habetis per Christum. Inter- pretatur ergo Circumcisionem et repetit beneficia Christi, in quibus rursus utrunque complectitur, imputationem iusticiae et renovationem, quae in hac vita fit in conversione, et duos modos com- plectitur, mortificationem et vivificationem. De mortificatione dicit: Estis consepulti cum eo per baptismum. De vivificatione inquit: Estis re- suscitati cum eo per fidem efficacia eius. Cum autem haec vocabula Mortificatio et Vivificatio a vero intellectu ad hypocrisin externorum gestuum a monachis et fanaticis hominibus detorta sint, consideretur vera significatio.

Ut autem in omnibus artibus et negotiis di- ligentia necessaria est, videre ubi res eaedem pluribus appellationibus efferantur, et recte con- iungere appellationes: ita in hoc loco sciamus

Paulus loqui de vera conversione ad Deum, quam usitate nominat Ecclesia Poenitentiam, cuius has partes esse dicimus Contritionem, Fidem et novam Obedientiam. Contritio hic significatur his ver- bis: Exuere corpus peccatorum, mortificari et consepeliri cum Christo. Significantur ergo veri pavores et dolores, quales sunt in conversione cum in agnitione peccatorum sentitur ira Dei, sicut dicitur: Sicut leo contrivit omnia ossa mea. Quanquam enim non sunt similes in omnibus do- lorum gradus, tamen in conversione aliquam con- tritionem necessariam esse non dubium est, ut Iesaiae 66. dicitur: Ad quem respiciam nisi ad contritum et humiliatum spiritu, et trementem sermones meos. Et hi pavores et dolores tunc sunt, mortificari et sepeliri cum Christo, cum si- mul sunt initia fidei, quae facit ut doleant corda se offendisse Deum, ut non fremant adversus eum, sed confugiunt ad eum propter mediato- rem. Ita hic dicit: Estis sepulti cum Christo, scilicet in hac vita, nunc iacet haec natura in doloribus et in cruce, non regnat furoribus du- bitationum et falsarum opinionum et pravarum cupiditatum, qualia mala regnant in impiis.

Estque diligenter consideranda collatio se- pulturae Christi ad praesentem vitam omnium piorum in Ecclesia. Iacet in hac vita Ecclesia sub cruce et doloribus, ut Christus in sepulcro, expectans integram novitatem.

Quod autem in secunda parte conversionis usitate ponimus fidem, id sumitur ex locis Pauli Rom. 6. et hinc, ubi mortificationi additur vivi- ficatio, quae fit fide, iuxta dictum: Iustus fide sua vivet. Non enim manendum est in morte et aeterna fuga, sed ideo convertimur ut vivamus, iuxta dictum: Vivo ego, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed ut convertatur et vivat. Fit autem vivificatio, sicut iam dictum est, Fide quae apprehendit re- missionem peccatorum et reconciliationem. Et fit nominatim mentio fidei in doctrina conversio- nis seu poenitentiae, ut taxetur horribile menda- cium Papistarum, qui dicunt manendum esse in dubitatione, et omnino silentio obruunt hanc fidem, qua statuendum est, tibi in conversione vere re- mitti peccatum, et te vere reputari iustum, do- nari Spiritu sancto et haereditate vitae aeternae.

Attribuit autem vivificationem nostri resur- rectioni Christi, inquiens: Simul resuscitati estis per fidem, simul vivificavit vos cum eo.

Quia Christus resuscitatus sic regnat, ut colligat aeternam Ecclesiam voce Evangelii, sit in ea efficax, vivificet eam, det Spiritum sanctum, et mirabiliter protegat ac servet eam inter horribiles confusiones et tenebras generis humani. Ac expresse dicit, fieri hanc vivificationem fide, et hanc fidem esse motum divinitus accensum significat, cum ait, Fidem esse efficaciam Dei, id est, qua Deus est efficax. Postea pluribus verbis eandem sententiam de conversione Paulus repetit: Eratis mortui, inquit, propter peccata et praeputium, id est, propter naturam immundam et ream, qualis propagata est generatione carnali. Talem naturam immundam et ream habentem peccatum originis nominat Praeputium.

At nunc vivificati estis data remissione omnium peccatorum et deleto chirographo etc.

In his verbis et imputationem iusticiae et vivificationem complectitur. Nam ad imputationem iusticiae pertinet id quod ait, omnia peccata remissa esse gratis. Deinde addit, deletum esse chirographum, id est, sententiam condemnationis, quae est conclusio ex lege divina. Ideo addit, Chirographum contra nos fuisse per decreta, id est, per legem. Sic discernit chirographum a lege tanquam conclusionem a praecedentibus propositionibus. Nam iudicium conscientiae est integer syllogismus practicus ex lege ductus, approbans convenientia cum lege, et condemnans contraria, et sequitur ordine divinitus condito condemnationem dolor et vindex, qui crescit Deo iudicante et destruente naturam ream, ut in Davide iudicium conscientiae est hic syllogismus: Moechum et homicidam Deus abiicit in aeternas poenas. David est moechus et homicida, et eo deterior, quia magis ingratus est Deo quam alii, cum fuisset ornatus ingentibus donis. Hinc sequitur conclusio ex lege: Ergo David est reiectus a Deo.

Haec conclusio nominatur Chirographum, id est, sententia in mente et corde tanquam scripta lege et agnitione lapsus, ac simul imprimitur ingens dolor, qui crescit, cum accedit singularis sensus irae Dei iudicantis et destruentis naturam ream per legem, sicut dicitur: Aculeus mortis peccatum est, potentia peccati lex. Roma. 4.: Lex iram efficit. Item: Sicut leo contrivit omnia ossa mea. Et Psalmo 37.: Non est pax ossibus meis a facie peccatorum meorum. Psalmo 114.:

Circumdederunt me dolores mortis etc. Iob. 9.: Deus cuius irae nemo resistere potest. Hoc triste iudicium, quo Deus per legem percutit ream na- turam, hic nominat Chirographum contrarium per legem.

Simul et vivificatio fit in deletione chiro- graphi. Quia cum remissio et imputatio accipiun- tur fide, in ea consolatione fit vivificatio, in qua filius Dei voce Evangelii efficaciter vivificat corda, et effundit in ea Spiritum sanctum, sicut 1. Io- han. 5. dicitur: Haec vita in filio eius est, qui habet filium, habet vitam, qui non habet filium Dei, vitam non habet. Tunc enim pro dubita- tione in mente lucet assensio accipiens promissio- nem, et pro sensu irae Dei et terroribus sunt in corde fiducia et laetitia acquiescens in Deo propter mediatorem, quae laetitia est vita spiritus, de qua Paulus inquit: Spiritus vivit propter iusticiam. Sciamus igitur Paulum loqui non de simulatis enthusiasmis, seu Stencfeldiana et Anabaptistica torvitate, sed de vera conversione seu poeni- tentia. Ita cum verba Pauli ad consolatio- nem in vera conversione accommodantur, fiunt perspicua.

Quam dulcis consolatio est, intueri hanc ipsam picturam triumphi? Victor est filius Dei qui contrivit caput serpentis, id est, delevit re- gnum et potentiam diaboli, peccatum et mortem aeternam, scilicet in credentibus. Hunc tan- quam triumphantem sequitur et sequetur in tota aeternitate Ecclesia liberata, et gestantur ut fie- bat in triumphis spolia, videlicet chirographa nostra pendentia in cruce. Haec iam deleta sunt credentibus in mediatorem, qui sanguine suo, id est, tota obedientia sua delevit chirographa legis, ut amitterent ius accusandi, ut 1. Iohan. 1. dici- tur: Sanguis Iesu Christi purificat nos ab omni peccato. Hanc ipsam picturam saepe in invocatione cogitemus, ut fides accendatur et confirmetur.

At etiam diabolos duci tanquam in specta- culo, exutos principatu et potestate, scilicet, ne perdant insidiis credentes in filium, sicut dicitur: Nemo rapiet oves meas ex manibus meis.

In fine autem addit particulam: Triumphans per sese, id ad differentiam victoriarum humana- rum dicitur. Homines enim in corporalibus prae- liis non vincunt sine auxiliis militum. At filius Dei sine auxilio ullius creaturae contrivit caput serpentis, haec una persona est redemtrix et pro- pria potentia vincit diabolos, tollit peccatum et mortem.

Nemo igitur vos iudicet in cibo et potu, aut in parte diei festi etc.

Haec conclusio antithesis est antecedentium, cum iusticia sit habere remissionem et reconciliationem propter filium, et vivificari per filium ad vitam aeternam, sequitur non esse iusticiam discrimina ciborum et dierum et similes ritus, qui neque peccatum neque mortem tollunt, neque sunt res aeternae. Quare nec peccata sunt talium rituum omissiones.

Expresse igitur hic asseveratio ponitur, quae affirmat talium rituum observationem non esse iusticiam, et omissiones eorum non esse peccata. Cumque hic totus locus maxime perspicuus sit, notissimum esse omnibus oportet ad confirmandas mentes in hac doctrina de traditionibus humanis, quae in Ecclesiis nostris restituta est divinitus, quod videlicet earum observatio non sit iusticia, et quod earum omissio non sit peccatum. Loquitur enim Paulus non solum de Mosaicis ceremoniis, sed in genere de omnibus, de Mosaicis et de excogitatis ab Episcopis et ab aliis hominibus, sicut dictum Christi generale est: Frustra colunt me mandatis hominum Et infra Paulus expresse comprehendit in hac regula mandata et traditiones hominum: Nemo vos iudicet, id est, condemnet propter omissionem talium rituum, in cibis, potu, parte diei festi, id est, vicibus festorum, ut Graeca phrasis ἐν μέρει significat per vices.

Repetatur autem hic tota doctrina de traditionibus humanis, sicut in nostris Ecclesiis traditur, et cogitetur qualis coecitas fuerit, cum observatio humanarum traditionum putaretur esse cultus Dei, et quidem necessarius, et qualis carnificina fuerit opinio, quae fingebat omissiones talium rituum esse peccata.

Extant libri Gersonis, in quibus quaeritur ἐπιείκεια, et disputatur, alias traditiones factas esse necessitatis causa, alias factas ornatus causa, quaeruntur et alia σοφὰ φάρμακα, ut mitigetur falsa exacerbatio. Sed ut Alexander Gordium nodum non longa extricatione solvit, sed subito dissecuit gladio, ita haec Pauli regula brevissime omnia illa vincula conscientiarum tollit, cum affirmat, nec observationem iusticiam esse, nec omissionem peccatum. Dicit autem de ceremoniis Mosaicis, tunc eas fuisse umbras, cum institutae sunt non hu- mana autoritate, sed divina, id est, nequaquam fuisse merita remissionis peccatorum, neque iusti- ciam coram Deo, sed fuisse signa commonefacien- tia homines de promissione et de venturo Messia. Corpus autem esse Christum, id est, rem signifi- catam et exhibitam, videlicet solam obedientiam Christi esse meritum remissionis peccatorum et aeternae iusticiae et vitae et λύτρον, ac propicia- tionem pro nobis, et ipsum mediatorem esse da- torem iusticiae et vitae aeternae, sicut in Daniele dicitur: Adducetur iusticia sempiterna etc. Haec antithesis in Epistola ad Hebraeos copiose expri- mitur de discrimine sacerdotii Aaron et sacerdotii Christi, ubi dicitur, Sacrificia Aaron tantum fuisse ἀντίτυπα sacrificii Christi, sicut hic Paulus Umbras nominat. Sed de sacrificio Christi in- quit: Qua voluntate sanctificati sumus per obla- tionem corporis Iesu Christi semel.

Hanc doctrinam de intellectu sacrificiorum saepe repetunt ipsi Prophetae, ac docent unam et eandem esse doctrinam de iustificatione omnibus temporibus. Patres ante Mosen et post eum sola fide, id est, fiducia mediatoris coram Deo iustos fuisse, id est, accepisse remissionem peccatorum, imputationem iusticiae, vivificationem per Spiri- tum sanctum et vitam aeternam, sicut Actor. 15. dicitur: Per gratiam Domini nostri Iesu Christi credimus salvari, sicut et illi, etc.

Quid igitur erant tot sacrificia et tot cere- moniae? Respondeo: Erant distinctio illius po- litiae ab ethnicis. Quia voluit Deus immensa bonitate notam esse, et conspici politiam, in qua Christus nasceretur, doceret, ederet testimonia suae doctrinae, fieret victima, resurgeret ex morte, et ostenderet resurrectionis testimonia, et in qua conservaretur doctrina missis Prophetis. Ac ut magis conspici haec politia posset, inter clarissima imperia Babylonium et Aegyptium in- teriecta fuit. Et quia hanc politiam voluit esse doctrinae scholam et sedem Ecclesiae, instituit ipse sua voce exercitia externa, quae essent pictu- rae doctrinae, ut populum commonefacerent de promissione et de mediatore, et moverent multos Ethnicos ad quaerendam causam distinctionis po- litiae. Saepe igitur Prophetae taxant pharisai- cam opinionem, qui falso fingebant hos ritus esse meritum et iusticiam, sicut Psalmus inquit: Ho- sti- locaustis non delectaberis. Et Iesaias: Offerens ovem similis est strangulanti canem.

Nemo vos decipiat simulata humilitate etc.

Graeci nominant βαυκοπανούργους, qui simulant modestiam seu humilitatem, et hac si- mulatione struunt insidias, ut existimentur sibi non quaerere opes, gloriam aut voluptates, sed veluti semidei esse. Haec est ars impostorum in Ecclesia. Ut autem simulatio a virtute discerni possit, nota sit definitio virtutis, quae nominatur ταπεινοφροσύνη, pro qua usitatum nomen est Humilitas.

Ut autem res fiat illustrior antithesi, et cum vitia notiora sint, prius Superbia definitur, in qua multa vitia concurrunt, ut sunt multa ap- pellationes, quae non tantum unicam virtutem aut unicum vitium significant. Superbia est non cernentem propriam infirmitatem aut pec- cata, et sibi magnas virtutes falso tribuentem, securum esse, nec Deum nec poenas timere, et fiducia propriarum virtutum erumpere extra me- tas vocationis, movere seu appetere maiora vo- catione, et despicere alios, quasi non sint or- gana utilia, et irasci Deo et hominibus cum im- pediuntur quo minus regnent. Ita initium su- perbiae est mendacium, quod sequitur securitas, deinde audacia erumpendi extra vocationem, ut Alexander somniat se Deum esse, deinde securus extra vocationem erumpit, contemnit leges, in- terficit viros iustos. Samosatenus arrogans sibi magnam sapientiam, negligens verbum Dei, nec metuens Deum, et confidens applausu populi extra metas effertur, et serit opinionem gratam multi- tudini, et munit se factione, ut adversantes op- primat et regnum teneat, etiamsi foris simulat, se non de sua antecellentia dimicare, sed de veri- tate alios in speciem sibi praeferens, non vult vi- deri appetere voluptatem aut potentiam.

Iam contraria exempla verae humilitatis aspiciantur, ex quibus postea definitio constitua- tur. Nam in vera humilitate simul sunt veri- tas recte iudicans de infirmitate. Deinde timor Dei et dolor propter infirmitatem et peccatum, deinde cura manendi intra vocationem, ut in Io- natha est veritas recte iudicans nullum hominem esse parem regno, et a Deo regem constitui, praesertim in Israël. Deinde sunt in eo timor Dei et cura manendi intra metas vocationis, ser- vit suo loco, et Deo gratias agit, quod eum glo- riosis testimoniis ornat, subiicit se Davidi, cui videt Deum tradidisse regnum, et non irascitur Deo, etiam cum postea in calamitatem incidit. Sit igitur haec definitio.

Vera humilitas est vere iudicantem de pro- pria infirmitate timere Deum, et dolore affici propter propriam infirmitatem et peccatum, et est in vocatione Deo servire fide et fiducia auxilii divini, non despicere alios, sed iudicare Deum, alios quoque utilia organa facere, et eis propter Deum honorem tribuere, et non irasci Deo aut ho- minibus, cum divinitus poenae veniunt. Haec defi- nitio sumitur ex his dictis, Proverb. 16.: Abomina- tio coram Deo omne cor superbum. Rom. 12.: Non alta expetentes, sed humilibus contenti. Philip. 2.: In humilitate mutua sentite, alios antecellere, sicut Christus, cum esset in forma Dei, non ra- puit aequalitatem Dei, id est, non est usus extra vocationem. Et Petrus inquit: Deus superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam. Syraci- des: Quo maior es, eo magis te humilia, et in- venies gratiam coram Domino.

Cum igitur Paulus inquit: Nemo vos deci- piat volens in humilitate, intelligatur simulans humilitatem, quasi dicat, volens decipere in hu- militate. Talis est hominum natura, ὅμοιον ὁμοίῳ φίλον, pares vel inferiores amantur, et nemini gratum est se contemni. Iustum est enim suum cuique locum proportione geometrica tri- buere. Cum igitur aliquis effert se supra alios, et praesertim cum premit alios, ut quasi eos de loco ipsorum detrudat, venit in odium: denique omnes homines capiuntur assentatione. Grati sunt igitur, qui se subiiciunt aliis et arte adulan- tur, et inflectunt se ad affectus eorum, quibus pla- cere volunt. Ideo facile capiuntur homines illa histrionica, quae arte imitatur gestus humiliores, admirationem etiam parit, videri non appetere voluptates et opes, quia si essent sine avaritia et sine stulta ambitione, haberent excellentem vir- tutem.

Experientia autem ostendit has praestigias, id est, gestus humilitatis seu modestiae, usitatas esse impostoribus, qui prava dogmata spargunt. Tales hypocritae in genere humano semper fue- runt, sunt et erunt. Ideo et in Matthaeo tradi- tur admonitio de cavendis talibus insidiatoribus, qni speciem habent ovium, et intus sunt lupi rapaces. Nominat Paulus et aliud genus praestigia- rum, falso iactare afflatus, Enthusiasmos, illu- minationes, colloquia cum angelis, et videre spe- cies divinitus oblatas. Sicut in urbe Monaste- riensi Anabaptistae falso iactarunt afflatus et sin- gulae aetates habent exempla. Expresse autem accusat eos mendacii Paulus, dicit eos superbe incedere in his quae non viderunt. Graeca phra- sis est, quae superbo incessu elationem animi significat, ut, ἐπιβατεύων τοῦ Σμέρδεως ὀνό- ματι, id est, superbiens nomine Smerdis. Di- citur igitur superbe eos iactare vanissima menda- cia, quod habeant afflatus aut angelorum collo- quia, quae non habent. Sicut multos novi, qui falso gloriabantur, se habere afflatus, quos non habebant. Vocabulum θρησκεία est superstitio, quasi τερασκεία, id est, exercere prodigiosum aliquid, quasi τέρατα ἀσκεῖν. Suidas ait esse quasi θεὸν δέρκειν, Deum videre. Quia vero populus mi- ratur tales, quos putat Deo familiares esse, et superstitiosi similem familiaritatem expetunt, ideo multi eis assentiuntur, sive vera sive falsa docen- tibus. Saepe igitur admonitio de his praestigiis enthusiastarum cavendis repetita est, et Paulus hic inquit, frustra inflatos esse persuasione suae carnis, id est, falsa imaginatione de sua sapien- tia et iusticia tumere, id superbire et sese efferre supra alios, et fingere se Prophetarum similes esse. Ut autem insidiae caveri possint, necesse est normam aliquam esse. Difficilis enim diiudi- catio est, ut etiam in veteri versu dicitur: χαλε- πὸν νόον ἴδμεναι ἀνδρὸς. Item: κιβδήλου δ’ ἀνδρὸς γνῶναι χαλεπώτερον οὐδὲν. Expressa est autem norma universaliter in his dictis: Si quis aliud Evangelium docet, ana- thema sit. Item: Nemo potest fundamentum po- nere, praeter id quod positum est, quod est Chri- stus Iesus. Hanc normam et hic monstrat cum ait: Non tenens caput, scilicet Christum, qui per vocem Evangelii est efficax, et Ecclesiam col- ligit non per alias doctrinas. Ideo hic diserte addit de capite, ut collectio Ecclesiae intelligatur et comprehendatur Evangelium seu doctrinae in- tegritas. Ait ergo: Ex quo capite Christo totum corpus, id est, Ecclesia, per iuncturas et com- pages coagmentatur et crescit, et fit tale corpus, in quo Deus erit omnia in omnibus in aeternitate. Intelligit autem iuncturas et compages consensum in eadem vera doctrina, quo consensu membra Ecclesiae copulantur, et filius Dei efficax est, col- ligens Ecclesiam una et eadem voce Evangelii, sicut inquit: Ego sum vitis, vos palmites. Est- que antithesis opposita enthusiastis, de quibus prius dixit, quasi dicat: Illi gloriantur se esse domicilia Dei et habere enthusiasmos, sed palam mentiuntur, quia nec membra sunt Ecclesiae, nec habitat Deus in impostoribus, qui fingunt genus doctrinae contrarium Evangelio. Sed habitat Deus in his, qui sunt adiuncti capiti Christo, et sunt membra Ecclesiae retinentia eandem vocem Evangelii incorruptam.

Gloriantur Anabaptistae se habere mirandos enthusiasmos, sed certum est, eos esse impostores: quia manifeste discedunt a capite Christo et a doctrina Evangelii, et sunt hostes verae Ecclesiae et doctrinae verae, fingunt se sese iustos suis ementitis afflatibus et sua patientia, et patientiam nominant desertionem politici ordinis etc. Qui tantos errores retinent pugnantes cum Evangelio, nec templa Dei sunt, nec membra Ecclesiae, sed sunt extra compages illas, de quibus hic Paulus loquitur.
