Si mortui estis cum Christo ab elementis mundi, cur tanquam viventes in mundo decreta facitis: Non attingas, non contrectes, non gustes etc.

Initio monendi sunt iuniores, haec verba: Non attingas, non gustes, non contrectes, dici μιμητικῶς, seu recitative, non dispositive, id est, Paulus recitat exempla alienarum legum, qua- les hypocritae condunt: Non gustes carnem die sexto etc. Non inseruit haec verba tanquam leges ferens, ut monachi insulse interpretati sunt, non intelligentes figuram dictionis. Addit autem: Quae sunt omnia interitura ipso usu, ut vestis, pocula atteruntur usu assiduo, cibi usu consu- muntur. Vult enim dicere, novitas in renatis est aeterna lux et vita per filium voce Evangelii et Spiritu sancto accensa, et sunt res aeternae filius Dei et Spiritus sanctus. Non est igitur Evange- lii iusticia res seu observatio rei, quae usu con- sumitur, ut ciborum aut vestium. Ac vocabu- lum ἀπόχρησις non significat abusum, quod est κατάχρησις, sed ἀπόχρησις significat assiduitatem usus seu sufficientiam in usu, ut innumerabilia exempla ostendunt, ut apud Platonem 2. πολι- τειῶν. Ἀποχρῇ, id est, sufficit dicere Deum tantorum bonorum autorem esse.

Secundum mandata et doctrinas hominum, quae habent speciem sapientiae in superstitione etc.

Ut sciri possit in his Pauli concionibus reiici non solum ceremonias Mosaicas, sed etiam alios ritus, qui instituuntur humana autoritate, sive ab Episcopis, sive a Monachis, sive ab aliis hominibus. Ideo expresse hic nominat et reiicit praecepta et doctrinas hominum, et superstitiones, quas nominat ἐθελοθρησκείας, id est, ritus sine mandato Dei excogitatos, seu exercitia vel corporis vexationes non mandatas a Deo, ut aliqui inediam tridui aut plurium dierum sibi indixerunt. Eremitae abdiderunt se in solitudinem etiam familiis relictis. Monachi instituerunt coelibatum et alios ritus. Semper in mundo usitatum fuit fingere cultus, et inde processit audacia hominum, ut etiam nova numina fingerent excogitatis variis cultibus, ut milites finxerunt Martem, mulieres Iunonem, Venerem et alia idola. Alligat autem nos Deus in primo praecepto Decalogi ad unum verum Deum, qui se patefecit hoc ipso verbo, quod tradidit per Prophetas et per filium, et saepissime damnat omnes alias invocationes, ut cum inquit: Non habebis Deos alienos. Item: Dominum Deum tuum adorabis et illi soli servies. Et Esai. 44.: Haec dicit Dominus rex Israël: Praeter me non est Deus. Ac vult nos in invocatione hunc verum Deum alloqui, et segregare nostram invocationem ab aliarum gentium invocationibus. Dicitur et expresse de cultibus Iesai 29.: Frustra colunt me mandatis hominum. Et Ezechiel. 20.: In praeceptis patrum vestrorum nolite incedere, in praeceptis meis ambulate, et sciatis, quod ego sim Dominus Deus vester. Et in Numeris 15.: Non sequantur cogitationes suas et oculos meretricios, id est, respicientes ad varia numina, sed memores praeceptorum Domini faciant ea, sintque sancti Deo suo, ego Dominus Deus vester, qui eduxi vos de terra Aegypti.

Haec illustria et expressa testimonia omnibus notissima sint, ut sciamus, opera non mandata a Deo non esse cultus Dei, et sit nota definitio, videlicet: Cultus Dei est opus a Deo mandatum, factum in fide, cuius finis principalis est, ut Deo hunc honorem tribuamus, id est, ut hac obedientia testemur hunc verum Deum esse, quem sic colimus, et eum sic velle coli.

Sed cur inquit Paulus, traditiones humanas speciem habere sapientiae humanae seu praetextus, qui sapienter cogitati videntur, cum in multis ritibus manifesta sit crudelitas seu turpitudo, ut in mactatione hominum, in Bacchanalibus, in stupris, multa item manifesta mendacia, ut in adoratione statuarum, aut in adoratione panis in circumgestatione, quem fingunt Deum esse? Respondeo: Paulatim ad absurdiora gradus fiunt, initia autem et semina minus conspiciuntur, ut dicitur: Dato uno inconvenienti multa sequuntur. Augent enim diaboli furores in impiis. Loquitur ergo Paulus de multis, quae minus habent absurdidatis, ut initio utilitatis causa constitutum est, ut tres essent praecipui Episcopi, Romanus, Constantinopolitanus et Alexandrinus, quorum singuli haberent autoritatem convocandi synodos vicinorum, et ut ad eos fieret provocatio a vicinis. Hic triumviratus humano iure constitutus est, et tunc utilitas movit synodos. Postea vero Romanus Papa multa tyrannice affinxit, se iure divino summum esse Episcoporum, habere potestatem condendi dogmata et cultus, se habere utrumque gladium, denique ut fit in aulis, multi praestigiatores sine modo amplificaverunt autoritatem pontificiam. Ante paucos annos scripserunt monachi, oblationem in Missa mereri remissionem peccatorum ex opere operato. Id cum sit manifeste absurdum, nunc arte tegunt et verecundius loquuntur, et tamen nervum idolatriae retinent, et multa aliena a re de sacrificiis et de κακοζηλίᾳ Leviticorum sacrificiorum cumulant, quae ornantur verbis, ut de sophistica verum est, quod dicit Euripides in Hippolyto: οἱ καλοὶ λίαν λόγοι evertunt bene ordinatas urbes. Ideo Paulus hic inquit, habere traditiones speciem seu praetextum sapientiae. Sic enim interpretor λόγον, quasi dicas, Verba non rem, ut Graeci usitate de falsis praetextibus dicunt: λόγος ἐστὶ καὶ πρόφασις, id est, verba sunt non res, aliud ostenditur, aliud agitur, ut cum Carolus imperator simulabat se bellum inferre nostris non religionis causa, λόγος ἦν καὶ πρόφασις, verba erant et praetextus. Sic loquitur Plutarchus in Eumene. Ut autem ad praestigias sophisticas apte et perspicue respondeatur, utrunque necessarium est, nosse fontes earum doctrinarum, ex quibus materia disputationis sumitur, et non esse rudem dialectices, ut cum defendunt Papistae traditiones humanas, λόγος καὶ πρόφασις est.

Opportet in Ecclesia esse ordinem, ut Pau- lus inquit: Omnia decore et ordine fiant in Ec- clesia. Ergo pastores possunt condere decreta.

Respondeo ad consequens: Possunt boni or- dinis causa consentiente Ecclesia aliqua lectio- num aut festorum discrimina facere, sed sine opi- nione cultus et sine opinione necessitatis. Papi- stae autem addunt falsas opiniones cultus et ne- cessitatis. Has falsas opiniones taxare et tollere necesse est, quae adduntur dicto Paulino contra regulam, quae vetat plus esse in conclusione quam in praemissis.

Species sapientiae est et Osiandri grandilo- quentia, quae obruit doctrinam Evangelii de iu- sticia fidei. Nos affirmamus in hac misera homi- num natura magna peccata, et magnas sordes manere, etiamsi renatus accepta remissione pec- catorum per fidem factus est templum Dei, et vere in eo accendit filius novam lucem voce Evan- gelii, et dato Spiritu sancto novos motus in corde ciet. Semper igitur in hac vita tenenda est con- solatio, renatos iustos esse, id est, acceptos Deo propter mediatorem per misericordiam sola fide, sicut David inquit: Non iustificabitur in conspe- ctu tuo omnis vivens. Hic Osiander magnificam speciem sapientiae opponit. Solus Deus est iusti- cia, Ergo habens Deum, habet iusticiam. Ita ab- ducit homines a conspectu mediatoris, et delet fidem, id est, fiduciam misericordiae, et docet homines confidere in propria novitate, quam effi- cit Deus.

Est igitur imaginatio Osiandri corruptela, et non est λογομαχία, sed reipsa tollitur ex con- spectu doctrina Evangelii, et movent homines illa θαύματα ῥημάτων, Iusticia essentialis, et haec species sapientiae: Solus Deus est iusticia, quod verum est de sua iusticia aeterna, et immensa iu- dicante, servante et damnante, de fonte et per- fectione iusticiae. Et simul propositio vera est: Obedientia filii est iusticia, quae pro nobis est pretium, et est constituta, ut sit illa iusticia, propter quam nos iusti et accepti simus. Cum ergo additur: Habens Deum, habet iusticiam, intelligas quatenus habet, ut si dicas: Solus Deus est fortitudo, Ergo habens fortitudinem, habet Deum. Concedo quatenus habet, ut Alexander fortiter praelians armatur a Deo, sed non propte- rea iustus est. Ita novitas est opus Dei, et rena- tus habet Deum, sed ita, ut prius accipiat impu- tatam iusticiam propter filium fide. Hoc modo primum persona recipitur, postea novitas, quam efficit Deus, est iusticia, quatenus est opus Dei. Sed simul adhuc in nobis manent multa peccata, ideo persona propter aliud est accepta, videlicet propter obedientiam mediatoris, quae etiam est iusticia, et quidem illa iusticia, propter quam nos sumus fide accepti. In hoc exemplo consideres, quantum caliginis offundat illa species sapientiae, et quam difficilis sit explicatio. Sed annitendum est in bonis causis, ut et confirmationes firmas teneamus, et quantum fieri potest obiectiones perspicue solvamus, ac simus memores dicti Aristotelici: Πολλοὶ πλέξαντες εὖ, κακῶς λύουσι.

## 2:23
By not sparing the body, etc.

Antiquity, which was more severe, loved discipline and exercises of temperance more. Some extended fasting to three days and more, and harmed their bodies. Some even added that such works are worship of God, righteousness, and satisfaction, and that they merit the remission of guilt and punishment, as Thomas expressly wrote. Thus, many sinned in two ways: by the harming of their bodies and by false opinions. Therefore, Paul delivers a most grave admonition to Timothy: Bodily exercise is profitable for a little, but godliness is profitable for all things. Here he wisely distinguishes exercises, such as labors of the body and fasting, which each person takes upon himself by his own judgment, from godliness, that is, necessary acts of worship, and he speaks clearly. He calls necessary works commanded by God 'worship'; he does not call other works not commanded by God 'worship' in this way, but 'exercises,' and he reproves them modestly: They are profitable for a little. He wants it to be understood what their use is, and he wants there to be a limit. And because foolish and superstitious opinions often accompanied those exercises in the Church, many admonitions from others are read concerning this matter. From Athanasius, this saying worthy of memory is recited: καλὸν ἡ ἄσκησις μετὰ ἀληθοῦς γνώσεως καὶ συμμετρίας. A good thing is the exercise of the body with true understanding and a fitting manner, that is, where there is faith without heretical opinions. Likewise, where it is known that these labors taken up by our own judgment are not worship of God, not righteousness, not merit, and where these exercises are moderate, there this custom of restraining oneself is a good thing, because then the custom is nothing other than living in a neat order: for nature loves order.

There were many holy men in prison, among whom was the nobleman Attalus; he reproved another who lived only on bread, salt, and water, and said that by his example he was disturbing others, who might imagine that they themselves were not holy because they did not live so harshly. But just as that age both harmed bodies and added superstitious opinions to exercises, so now, with the bonds of traditions loosened, many sin in the other direction. We do not keep order in food, drink, and labors. Almost no one keeps the proper times for food, drink, prayers, labors, and studies, and if any wish to keep them, they are hindered by barbaric household management. Furthermore, how many there are who gorge themselves for a great part of the night, and they do so more securely because they hear that fasting is not worship of God. These things must be considered, and Paul's admonition must be opposed to the sins of both kinds.

Paul commands us to have honor for the body, that is, he commands us to live in order, and not to harm our bodies by either fasting or gluttony. But why does he name 'honor,' when it would be enough to say, 'live in order'? A physician would speak thus. But Paul names 'honor' so that he may remind us of the reasons for which we must live in order. For honor, first and before all things, is something that is owed to God, that is, to acknowledge and confess that God is the Creator, who revealed Himself by sending His Son, perfectly wise, truthful, beneficent, just, a judge, chaste, caring for men, hearing and saving those who rightly call upon Him.

And these two things pertain to honor, namely, to confess these things and to subject ourselves to God. Afterwards, when honor is attributed to men, it should always be understood to be attributed because of something divine, that is, because God is doing something there through Himself, as honor is owed to Moses and Elijah, because it is certain that they were both sent by God and are dwellings of God, and that God shines and acts in them. Thus, it should be understood that honor is to be attributed to the body because God infuses Himself into our members; in the brain, He kindles light by the thought of the Word, by which we rightly acknowledge Him, and the Holy Spirit wraps Himself in the spirits of the heart, and of the brain, and of the nerves, and as a flame purifies and stirs our flames, so that when David fights, invading and striking down Goliath, the mind looks upon God and thinks that He is present in His Church, repeats the divine promises in thought, and seeks divine help from God. Thus, by this thought of the Word, the Son kindles light, and the Holy Spirit gives strength to the heart and arms the nerves in the arms. Thus, the body of David is the dwelling and instrument of God. Therefore Paul says that honor must be attributed to the body. Let us consider, therefore, how great an evil it is to destroy this instrument and dwelling of God petulantly, either by fasting or by gluttony. And that the intention of thought about God, and pious motions in the heart, are greatly hindered by drunkenness, is shown by the saying of Hosea 4: Whoredom, wine, and drunkenness take away the heart. And experience has brought forth these sayings: And Venus rages in wines, fire in fire. And Odyss. Φ.: Οἷ τ’ αὐτῷ πρώτῳ κακὸν εὕρετο οἰνοβαρείων, that is, He first found evil for himself, weighed down by wine. Wherefore the Lord also says: Beware lest your hearts be weighed down with surfeiting and drunkenness. And 1 Peter 4 it is said: Be sober unto prayers. Let us therefore be temperate in this, that the body in the present may be fit for thoughts about God and for divine motions, and may be more durable and firmer in old age. But as for what Paul says: To the satisfying of the flesh, he commands that honor be attributed to the body in such a way that as much as is sufficient is attributed, of food, drink, sleep, and exercises. He excludes, therefore, both deficiency and excess. For πλησμονὴ does not signify excess or superfluity, but a satisfaction convenient to the body, and I think Paul used a fuller word to tax the hypocrites, who cheated their bodies too much of necessary supports, and brought on diseases and delusions of the brain, and from there feigned that prophecies and specters were shown to them, just as we have seen many.

Latin:

Non parcendo corpori etc.

Vetustas, quae fuit severior, magis amavit disciplinam et exercitia temperantiae. Aliqui extenderunt inediam in triduum et plures dies, et laeserunt corpora. Aliqui etiam affinxerunt talia opera esse cultus Dei, iusticiam et satisfactionem, et mereri remissionem culpae et poenae, ut expresse scripsit Thomas. Ita multi dupliciter peccaverunt, laesione corporum et falsis opinionibus. Ideo ad Timotheum Paulus gravissimam admonitionem tradit: Corporale exercitium ad modicum utile est, pietas ad omnia utilis est. Hic exercitia ut labores corporis et inediam, quae sibi quisque suo iudicio sumit, sapienter discernit a pietate, id est, necessariis cultibus, et loquitur diserte. Cultus nominat opera necessaria mandata a Deo, non sic nominat alia opera non mandata a Deo, sed exercitia, et verecunde reprehendit: Ad modicum utilia sunt. Vult intelligi quis sit eorum usus, et vult modum esse. Ac quia saepe in Ecclesia stultae et superstitiosae opiniones ad illa exercitia accesserunt: multae et aliorum admonitiones de hac re leguntur. Ex Athanasio recitatur hoc dictum memoria dignum: καλὸν ἡ ἄσκησις μετὰ ἀληθοῦς γνώσεως καὶ συμμετρίας. Bona res est exercitium corporis cum vero intellectu et congruente modo, id est, ubi est fides sine haereticis opinionibus. Item, ubi scitur hos labores nostro iudicio sumtos non esse cultus Dei, non iusticiam, non meritum, et ubi haec exercitia sunt mediocria, ibi bona res est haec consuetudo se frenandi, quia tunc consuetudo nihil aliud est, quam concinno ordine vivere: amat autem natura ordinem.

Erant in carcere multi sancti viri, inter quos fuit vir nobilis Attalus, is reprehendit alium, qui tantum pane, sale et aqua victitabat, et dixit eum suo exemplo alios turbare, qui imaginarentur, sese non esse sanctos, quia non tam duriter vive- rent. Ut autem illa aetas et corpora laesit, et superstitiosas opiniones addidit exercitiis, ita nunc laxatis vinculis traditionum, multi in alte- ram partem peccant. Non servamus ordinem in cibo, potu et laboribus. Tempora iusta cibi, po- tus, precationum, laborum, studiorum fere nemo servat, et si qui vellent servare, impediuntur barbaricis oeconomiis. Deinde quam multi sunt, qui helluantur magna parte noctis, idque faciunt securius, quia audiunt inediam non esse cultum Dei. Haec consideranda sunt, et opponenda est Pauli admonitio peccatis utriusque generis.

Praecipit Paulus honorem habere corpori, id est, praecipit ordine vivere, et nec inedia nec helluatione corpora laedere. Sed cur nominat honorem, cum satis esset, ordine vivite? Sic loqueretur medicus. Sed Paulus honorem nomi- nat, ut de causis nos commonefaciat, propter quas ordine vivendum est. Honos enim primum et ante omnia est quiddam quod Deo debetur, id est, agnoscere et fateri, quod fere sit Deus crea- tor, qui se patefecit misso filio, perfecte sapiens, verax, beneficus, iustus, iudex, castus, curans homines, exaudiens et salvans recte invocantes.

Et ad honorem pertinent haec duo, videlicet, haec fateri et subiicere nos Deo. Postea cum ho- minibus honos tribuitur, semper intelligatur tri- bui propter aliquod divinum, id est, quia ibi Deus aliquid per sese agit, ut honos debetur Mosi, Heliae, quia certum est, eos et missos esse a Deo, et domicilia Dei esse, et lucere Deum ac agere in eis. Ita intelligatur honos tribuendus esse cor- pori, quia Deus infundit sese in membra nostra, in cerebro cogitatione verbi accendit lucem, qua eum recte agnoscimus, et involvit sese Spiri- tus sanctus spiritibus cordis, et cerebri et ner- vorum, et ut flamma nostras flammas purificat et agitat, ut cum David praeliatur invadens et prosternens Goliath, mens intuetur Deum, et cogitat eum adesse in Ecclesia sua, repetit cogi- tatione promissiones divinas, et petit a Deo auxi- lium divinum. Ita hac cogitatione verbi lucem accendit filius, et Spiritus sanctus dat robur cordi, armat nervos in brachiis. Ita corpus Davidis est domicilium et organum Dei. Ideo Paulus inquit, honorem tribuendum esse corpori. Cogitemus igitur, quantum mali sit hoc or- ganon et domicilium Dei petulanter destruere, vel inedia vel ingluvie. Et valde impediri ebrie- tate intentionem cogitationis de Deo, et pios mo- tus in corde, ostendit dictum Oseae 4.: Scorta- tio, vinum et ebrietas auferunt cor. Et expe- rientia genuit haec dicta: Et Venus in vinis, ignis in igne furit. Et Odyss. Φ.: Οἷ τ’ αὐτῷ πρώτῳ κακὸν εὕρετο οἰνοβαρείων, id est, Sibi ipsi primo malum invenit vino gravatus. Quare et Dominus inquit: Cavete ne corda vestra graventur crapula et ebrietate. Et 1. Petri 4. dicitur: Sitis sobrii ad precationes. Simus igitur eo temperantes, ut corpus in praesentia sit idoneum ad cogitationes de Deo et ad motus divinos, et sit durabilius et firmius in senecta. Quod autem inquit Paulus: Ad saturitatem carnis, iubet sic tribuere honorem corpori, ut quantum satis est tribuatur, cibi, potus, somni, exercitiorum. Excludit igitur et defectum et ex- cessum. Nam πλησμονὴ non significat exces- sum vel superfluitatem, sed saturitatem conve- nientem corpori, et existimo Paulum verbo ple- niori usum esse ad taxandos hypocritas, qui cor- pora nimium fraudabant necessariis adminiculis, et accersebant morbos et deliria cerebri, inde fingebant sibi ostendi vaticinia et spectra, sicut multos vidimus.

## 3:1 Argument
Chapter three.

In the previous two chapters Paul delivered the sum of the Gospel and an admonition about avoiding corruptions of doctrine; he taxed false opinions about Mosaic ceremonies and about traditions, which are feigned by human audacity in the Church. Now in the third chapter he begins the doctrine of good works, in which there are many sweet descriptions of virtues and certain distinguished precepts, such as this one about assiduity in teaching and thinking on the word handed down from God: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom, and teach and admonish one another. Let us all obey this sweetest admonition, and often read, hear, and think upon the doctrine handed down by God, that we may stir ourselves to the acknowledgment of God, to true invocation, and to the fear of God. For God is effective through the thought of His own word, as the Psalm also teaches: My soul has waited in His word, my soul has hoped in the Lord. And Rom. 1 it is said: The Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believes.

And the ravings of Stencfeld and similar enthusiasts are to be condemned, who feign that God communicates Himself without the thought of the divine word, and lead men away from the ministry of the Gospel and from the reading and thought of doctrine. Paul on the contrary says: Let it dwell among you, and indeed, Richly. In both words there is a notable emphasis. He wants the divine word to be so familiarly known to us as are those who dwell with us in the same family. Nor is there any doubt that God dwells in that breast which, in conversion and faith, thinks upon the word of God, and Paul wants us to think upon it copiously. He adds, however: With all wisdom, that is, he wants it to be read, not so that we may extract mutilated sayings, so that they may be twisted toward depraved desires, toward flatteries, toward cavils and corruptions, as heretics have always played and do play with the tricks of sophisms.

But I return to the beginning of the third chapter. An argument is placed before the discourse on good works, customary to Paul, drawn from cause and effects. The old nature is dead in the converted, Therefore let it not be effective. But Christ lives in you, Therefore let Him be effective, and an objection is inserted. Why do you say that we have not been raised with Christ, when we are nevertheless still subject to death, to huge miseries, to a horrible struggle with sin, to terrors and doubts? To this objection he answers: Your life is hidden with Christ in God, that is, although life has been begun, yet the glory of the Church is not yet seen, to be seen then when the Lord shall appear again. Now we have the beginnings, which are still covered by the death of the body, the remnants of sin, and great miseries, as he says in Rom. 8: If Christ is in you, the body is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness.

Here many distinguished matters are contained, the declaration of the articles of the creed: He ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of God the Father, etc. Likewise, what the properties of the glorified body are. Likewise, how it is said: Christ is in you, Christ is your life. And first concerning the saying: He ascended into heaven. How do these things agree? Elsewhere it is said: The Son who is in the bosom of the Father. Likewise, John 3: The Son of man who is in heaven. I answer: In the creed, let the statement be understood as the letter sounds, both concerning the body and bodily location. He ascended, namely by a bodily and physical location, into heaven, that is, into a heavenly place, wherever it is, because allegories are not to be feigned here. The ascension was visible and bodily, and the whole of antiquity always wrote thus, that Christ is in some place by bodily location wherever He wills, and the bodily ascension took place upwards. Therefore, Paul in this chapter names that place upwards.

But in the proposition: The Son who is in heaven, let the statement be understood by the communication of idioms. The Λόγος is always in heaven, even if by bodily location the body is in the virgin. This narrative is expressed in the exposition of the creed, which is read in the books of Cyprian, even if elsewhere the inscription is: Exposition of Rufinus, He ascended into heaven, not where the Word God had not been before, for He was always in heaven and remained with the Father, but where the Word made flesh had not sat before, that is, where the body had not previously had a bodily location. Thus Augustine speaks, and the words are cited in Lombard, book 3, distinction 22: Christ did not leave the Father when He came into the world, being everywhere whole, everywhere perfect. Then the form of speech is added: He is everywhere whole, but not the whole. Others have spoken more neatly: The proposition is true by the communication of idioms: Christ is everywhere.

Athanasius speaks thus concerning the incarnation of the Word: The Λόγος is not bound to the body, but He Himself contains the body, so that He is both in it and outside all things, and in the bosom of the Father, nor when He is in all things does He become a part of others, but all things receive life and sustenance from Him.

But as it was said concerning the local ascension of human nature: He ascended into heaven, so concerning the exaltation of human nature above all creatures it is said: He sits at the right hand of the Father, as this Paul says here: Where He is sitting at the right hand of God. He says that Christ is upwards, and indeed at the right hand of God, that is, not as blessed angels and men are upwards, but exalted above the angels in that secret light of God, reigning with the Father, and yet the body is locally somewhere according to the manner of a true body, as Augustine says. And let these propositions: Christ is in you, I in them, we will come to him and make our dwelling with him, etc., be understood by the communication of idioms. And concerning this presence of the Son in the preaching of the Gospel and in the saints, it is necessary for the Church to be faithfully instructed, so that we may acknowledge our Lord Jesus Christ to be present to the Church, and to be the head perfecting all things in all.

Now I return to the argument of Paul, who makes an antithesis of our death and resurrection. He says that we are dead, namely, because in true conversion the carnal nature begins to die, and he adds that we have been resurrected, because the vivification has been begun, just as he spoke above. Hence an argument is drawn from the efficient cause, just as he argues in Romans 6. A dead nature is not effective; a living one is effective. But you have been vivified by life, light, and righteousness, which the Son of God, resurrected for this purpose, gives, so that He may resurrect and vivify you. Therefore, let this light and righteousness be effective; let not the vivification begun through the resurrected Son of God be idle in you.

This is the sum of the argument in this place. He interweaves, however, a singular consolation, by which he meets a tacit objection: Why do you say that we have been resurrected, when we still carry around in ourselves death, diseases, the remnants of sin, huge sorrows, and an unspeakable mass of calamities, and nothing seems to be weaker than Christ? He answers: You live and have the beginnings of eternal life, just as the thief hanging on the cross had. But these beginnings are still hidden, as they were hidden in the thief, who nevertheless, feeling the consolation, knew that he already had the beginnings of eternal life, and knew that Christ was effective, although the world thought He was nothing. Thus he says here that Christ is also hidden, namely, because the world does not see His effectiveness and laughs at the Gospel with horrible security as if it were an empty fable.

But the glory of the Son and of the Church will be seen in the final judgment, where all men will see that Christ both was and is effective, and that the Gospel was not an empty fable. He interweaves this consolation with the argument by which he exhorts that we persevere in the begun mortification and vivification, and that we do not lose these effects of Christ, rushing against our conscience into new crimes. This sum is comprehended in this saying: Fight the good fight, keeping faith and a good conscience.

Latin:

Caput tertium.

In prioribus duobus capitibus tradidit Pau- lus summam Evangelii et admonitionem de ca- vendis corruptelis doctrinae, taxavit falsas opinio- nes de ceremoniis Mosaicis et de traditionibus, quae finguntur humana audacia in Ecclesia. Nunc in tertio capite incoat doctrinam de bonis Operibus, in qua sunt multae dulces virtu- tum descriptiones et insignia quaedam praecepta, quale est hoc de assiduitate in docendo et cogi- tando sermone divinitus traditio: Sermo Christi habitet in vobis abunde cum omni sapientia, et docete et commonefacite vos mutuo. Huic dul- cissimae admonitioni omnes obtemperemus, et saepe legamus, audiamus et cogitemus doctrinam a Deo traditam, ut nos excitemus ad agnitionem Dei, ad veram invocationem et ad timorem Dei. Deus enim efficax est cogitatione verbi ipsius, ut et Psalmus docet: Sustinuit anima mea in verbo eius, speravit anima mea in Domino. Et Rom. 1. dicitur: Evangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti.

Suntque damnanda deliramenta Stencfeldii et similium enthusiastarum, qui fingunt Deum sese communicare sine cogitatione verbi divini, et abducunt homines a ministerio Evangelii et a lectione et cogitatione doctrinae. Paulus contra inquit: Habitet inter vos, et quidem, Abunde. In utraque voce insignis emphasis est. Vult sermonem divinum ita familiariter nobis notum esse, ut sunt qui in eadem familia nobiscum habitant. Nec dubium est in illo pectore habitare Deum, quod in conversione et fide cogitat verbum Dei, ac vult Paulus copiose cogitare. Addit autem: Cum omni sapientia, id est, vult legi, non ut excerpamus mutilata dicta, ut ad pravas cupiditates, ad assentationes, ad cavillationes et corruptelas detorqueantur, ut semper haeretici praestigiis sophismatum luserunt et ludunt.

Sed redeo ad initium tertii capitis. Argumentum praeponitur concioni de bonis operibus usitatum Paulo, ductum a causa et effectibus. Vetus natura est mortua in conversis, Ergo non sit efficax. Vivit autem in vobis Christus, Ergo sit efficax, et inserta est occupatio. Cur dicis, non resuscitatos esse cum Christo, cum tamen adhuc simus subiecti morti, ingentibus aerumnis, horribili luctae cum peccato, pavoribus et dubitationibus? Ad hanc obiectionem respondet: Vita vestra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo, id est, etsi incoata est vita, tamen nondum gloria Ecclesiae conspicitur, conspicienda tunc cum Dominus rursus apparebit. Nunc habemus initia, quae adhuc tecta sunt morte corporis, reliquiis peccati et magnis aerumnis, sicut inquit Rom. 8.: Si Christus est in vobis, corpus mortuum est propter peccatum, spiritus autem vita est propter iusticiam.

Hic multae insignes materiae continentur, declaratio articulorum symboli: Ascendit in coelos, sedet ad dexteram Dei patris etc. Item, quae sint proprietates glorificati corporis. Item, quomodo dicatur: Christus est in vobis, Christus est vita vestra. Ac primum de dicto: Ascendit in coelum. Quomodo haec congruunt? Alibi dici- tur: Filius qui est in sinu patris. Item, Io- hann. 3.: Filius hominis qui est in coelo. Re- spondeo: In symbolo intelligatur dictum, ut so- nat litera, et de corpore et de corporali locatione. Ascendit, scilicet corporali et physica locatione, in coelum, id est, in locum coelestem, ubicun- que est, quia hic non sunt fingendae allegoriae. Ascensio fuit visibilis et corporalis, et semper ita scripsit tota antiquitas, Christum corporali locatione in aliquo loco esse ubicunque vult, et ascensio corporalis facta est sursum. Ideo Paulus in hoc capite locum illum nominat sursum.

At in propositione: Filius qui est in coelo, dictum intelligatur communicatione idiomatum. Λόγος semper est in coelo, etiamsi corporali lo- catione corpus est in virgine. Haec narratio ex- pressa est in enarratione symboli, quea legitur in libris Cypriani, etsi alibi inscriptio est: Enarratio Ruffini, Ascendit ad coelos, non ubi verbum Deus antea non fuerat, quippe qui erat semper in coelo, et manebat cum patre, sed ubi verbum caro factum antea non sedebat, id est, ubi corpus antea non habuerat corporalem locationem. Sic Augustinus loquitur, et citantur verba in Longo- bardo lib. 3. distinct. 22.: Non dimisit patrem Christus, cum venit infirmio, ubique totus, ubi- que perfectus. Deinde additur forma sermonis: Ubique totus est, sed non totum. Alii concin- nius locuti sunt: Propositio vera est communi- catione idiomatum: Christus ubique est.

Athanasius sic loquitur de incarnatione verbi: Λόγος non colligatus est corpori, sed ipse corpus continet, ut et in eo sit, et extra omnia, et in sinu patris, neque cum sit in omnibus, fit pars in aliorum, sed omnia vitam, sustentationemque ab ipso accipiunt.

Ut autem de locali ascensione naturae hu- manae dictum est: Ascendit ad coelos, ita de ex- altatione naturae humanae super omnes creaturas dictum est: Sedet ad dexteram patris, ut hic Pau- lus inquit: Ubi est ad dexteram Dei sedens. Ait Christum sursum esse, et quidem ad dexteram Dei, id est, non ut beati angeli et homines sur- sum sunt, sed exaltatus supra angelos in illa ar- cana luce Dei regnans cum patre, et tamen cor- pus localiter alicubi est secundum veri corporis modum, ut Augustinus inquit. Et hae proposi- tiones: Christus in vobis est, Ego in eis, venie- mus ad eum et mansionem apud eum faciemus etc. intelligantur communicatione idiomatum. Et de hac praesentia filii in praedicatione Evangelii et in sanctis, necesse est Ecclesiam fideliter eru- diri, ut agnoscamus Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum adesse Ecclesiae, et esse caput omnia in omnibus perficiens.

Iam ad Argumentum Pauli redeo, qui facit antithesin mortis nostrae et resurrectionis. Dicit nos esse mortuos, scilicet, quia in vera conver- sione natura carnalis incipit mori, et addit nos resuscitaos esse, quia vivificatio incoata est, sicut et supra locutus est. Hinc ducitur argumentum ex efficiente causa, sicut Rom. 6. argumentatur. Mortua natura non sit efficax, viva sit efficax. Estis autem vivificati vita, luce et iusticia, quam dat filius Dei resuscitatus ad hoc, ut vos resusci- tet et vivificet. Ergo haec lux et iusticia sit effi- cax, non sit otiosa in vobis vivificatio incoata per filium Dei resuscitatum.

Haec est argumenti summa hoc loco. In- texit autem singularem consolationem, qua oc- currit tacitae obiectioni: Cur dicis nos resusci- tatos esse, cum adhuc mortem, morbos, reliquias peccati, ingentes dolores et inenarrabilem molem calamitatum in nobis circumferamus, et videatur nihil esse imbecillius Christo? Respondet: Vi- vitis et habetis initia vitae aeternae, sicut habe- bat latro pendens in cruce. Sed haec initia adhuc tecta sunt, ut erant in latrone tecta, qui tamen sentiens consolationem, sciebat se iam habere initia vitae aeternae, et sciebat Christum esse effi- cacem, quanquam mundus putabat eum nihil esse. Ita hic inquit, Christum quoque tectum esse, scilicet, quia mundus non videt eius effi- caciam et ridet Evangelium horribili securitate tanquam inanem fabulam.

Sed gloria filii et Ecclesiae conspicietur in postremo iudicio, ubi omnes homines videbunt Christum, et fuisse et esse efficacem, et Evange- lium non fuisse inanem fabulam. Hanc consola- tionem intexit argumento, quo hortatur, ut in incoata mortificatione et vivificatione persevere- mus, non amittamus hos effectus Christi, ruen- tes contra conscientiam in nova scelera. Haec summa comprehenditur in hoc dicto: Milita bo- nam militiam, retinens fidem et bonam con- scientiam.

## 3:6
Because of which the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience etc.

Let the Hebrew phrase be noted. Sons of disobedience, that is, disobedient men, just as Son of perdition, that is, a lost son, although there is an emphasis in this phrase, as if he were saying, one belonging to perdition (just as a son belongs to a father) or one whom perdition dominates. Son of wrath, a guilty son, belonging to wrath, that is, to guilt. Next, let us also consider the matter. Let this saying of Paul placed in this passage be joined to other testimonies concerning new obedience against the Antinomians. For the rule must be held most firmly: Fight the good fight, keeping faith and a good conscience. And it is most certain that those rushing into crimes against conscience pour out the Holy Spirit, and again become guilty of eternal punishment, unless they are converted again. Because it is expressly said, 1 Cor. 6: Do not err, neither fornicators, nor adulterers shall possess the kingdom of God, that is, then when they are such, they are guilty of eternal death. And Galat. 5: Those doing such things shall not possess the kingdom of God, and 2 Peter 2: If they are again entangled in previous contaminations, the latter things will become worse for them than the former and it will happen to them according to the proverb: The dog returned to its vomit etc. It is most certain that these things are true, and the Antinomians are to be execrated, who imagine that men are righteous by faith, even if they persevere in crimes against conscience.

And we speak clearly concerning new obedience, namely, that new obedience is not the merit or price of eternal life, and yet that new obedience is necessary for this very reason, because this order in God is immovable, that the creature should obey the creator. Likewise: Because the Son of God came to destroy sin, not to confirm the license to rush into crimes. He did not hang on the cross in horrible sufferings for this reason, that you should take for yourself a license to contaminate yourself with lusts and other crimes.

Thirdly, there is also a necessity because of the order of cause and effect, because where the Holy Spirit is in the heart, there sin does not reign, but the Holy Spirit, according to the saying: If you mortify the actions of the flesh by the Spirit, you shall live. Yet we do not use that phrase: Good works are necessary for salvation, because it is understood concerning merit. For at the same time freely on account of the mediator, and through him we receive the remission of sins, the imputation of righteousness and vivification, and we are made heirs of eternal life, just as the Lord himself says: I give them eternal life. Likewise: He who has Christ, has life. Likewise: Justified by faith we have peace with God. Likewise, Rom. 8: If we are sons, we are also heirs. Likewise: This is eternal life, that they may know you the true God, and Jesus whom you sent to be Christ. He names, however, the disobedient in this passage, who depart from the rule: Fight the good fight, keeping faith and a good conscience.

After you have put off the old man etc.

It is a phrase of Paul, in the same reborn man to name the old man, and the oldness and the exterior man, the remnants of the vicious carnal nature. Conversely, the new man and the newness of the spirit, and the interior man, insofar as in the mind, will, and heart a new light and new motions have been kindled by the Son of God, by the voice of the Gospel and the Holy Spirit, as 2 Cor. 4 is said: The interior man is renewed from day to day. And these things must be rightly understood: Newness happens in true conversion, when by the voice of the Gospel a new light is kindled in the mind through the Son, and the Holy Spirit is given, beginning faith, joy, invocation, and other motions such as he himself is. And let there not be here a confusion of the Gospel and philosophy, just as some have falsely written that newness is reason, and the senses are oldness. But it must be known that even reason without the Son of God, without the voice of the Gospel and without the Holy Spirit is oldness and darkness. These things have been explained more copiously elsewhere.

Paul, however, names here the new man the Image of God, where this doctrine may be rightly understood. Augustine interprets the image concerning the powers in this way. In the soul there are the mind itself, thought, and motion. He adapts these three thus. The eternal Father is as it were the Mind, the Son, the Image of the Father begotten by thought, the Holy Spirit, as motion. And to those considering these things piously and prudently, this comparison will not be unwelcome, because certainly the soul is a testimony concerning God, and God wants us to understand that he is an intelligent Essence, thinking of himself, and a mover. But to these sayings of Augustine concerning the powers I add this: that the powers are to be understood not as corrupted, but as either integral or being reborn. Thus it is written to the Ephesians: Put on the new man, who according to God is created, in righteousness and holiness of truth.

Here there is not only a mention of powers, but he wants there to be righteousness and holy truth in the powers, that is, he wants true knowledge of God, firm assent, and righteousness to shine in us, that is, conformity with God, just as man was created in the beginning, having true knowledge and conformity in will and heart with God. And it is most sweetly said here: Let the new man be renewed unto knowledge, so that we may know that a new light is kindled in newness, and indeed by the voice of the Gospel.

Osiander argues certain other things about the image of God: that man is called the image of God because the Son was to assume human nature. This is true, but yet it must be understood that it is the truth and righteousness by which we are made similar to the Son, with God sanctifying us and the Son making us like himself.

Where there is neither Greek nor Jew etc.

Let the doctrine concerning the distinction between the righteousness of the Gospel and political affairs always be in sight. The Gospel does not establish new polities, as Loriothus and many others imagine: but it preaches about the repentance of individuals in the heart, and about the restoration of eternal righteousness and life in individuals, which restoration is made by the Son of God himself quickening hearts by the voice of the Gospel, and giving the Holy Spirit. Outwardly, however, he allows us to use different political laws in bodily life, if they do not fight against natural laws, just as some use different foods, or others different spans of days. Therefore he says here, there is no distinction of Greek and Jew. He often repeated this sentiment, because the Pseudo-apostles wanted to bind the Gentiles to the Jewish polity, just as in our time Carolostadius and others wanted to destroy and remove the Roman law, and judge matters according to the laws of Moses.

Against such errors let us be confirmed by these words of Paul, and let righteousness, for the sake of which the Son of God was sent, and the political order be rightly distinguished. He says, however, that Christ is all in all, all things, namely, that are proper to the new man are Christ, that is, as to merit and as to effect, or as to grace and as to the gift. Christ has been made righteousness for you, so that, namely, for his sake righteousness is imputed, and at the same time he is your quickener, quickening the heart by the voice of the Gospel, and giving the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

Propter quae venit ira Dei super filios inobedientiae etc.

Nota sit phrasis Hebraea. Filii inobedientiae, id est, homines inobedientes, ut Filius perditionis, id est, filius perditus, etsi emphasis est in hac phrasi, quasi dicat, proprius perditionis (ut filius est proprius patris) seu cui dominatur perditio. Filius irae, filius reus, proprius irae, id est, reatus. Deinde et res consideremus. Dictum Pauli hoc loco positum adiungatur aliis testimoniis de nova obedientia contra Antinomos. Firmissime enim tenenda est regula: Milita bonam militiam retinens fidem et bonam conscientiam. Ac certissimum est ruentes in scelera contra conscientiam effundere Spiritum sanctum, et iterum fieri reos aeternae poenae, nisi rursus convertantur. Quia expresse dicitur, 1. Corinth. 6.: Ne erretis, nec scortatores, nec adulteri possidebunt regnum Dei, scilicet, tunc cum sunt tales, sunt rei aeternae mortis. Et Galat. 5.: Talia facientes regnum Dei non possidebunt, et 2. Petri 2. Si rursus implicantur prioribus contaminationibus, fient eis posteriora deteriora prioribus et accidet eis iuxta proverbium: Canis reversus ad vomitum etc. Haec esse vera certissimum est, et execrandi sunt Antinomi, qui fingunt homines esse iustos fide, etiamsi perseverent in sceleribus contra conscientiam.

Ac perspicue loquimur de nova obedientia, videlicet, novam obedientiam non esse meritum seu pretium vitae aeternae, et tamen novam obedientiam eo ipso necessariam esse, quia hic ordo in Deo immotus est, ut creatura creatori obediat. Item: Quia filius Dei venit, ut destruat peccatum, non ut confirmet licentiam ruendi in scelera. Non ideo pependit in cruce in horribilibus doloribus, ut tu sumas tibi licentiam contaminandi te libidinibus et aliis sceleribus.

Tertio necessitas est etiam propter ordinem causae et effectus, quia ubi est in corde Spiritus sanctus, ibi non regnat peccatum, sed Spiritus sanctus, iuxta dictum: Si actiones carnis spiritu mortificabitis, vivetis. Nec tamen illa phrasi utimur: Bona opera sunt necessaria ad salutem, quia intelligitur de merito. Simul enim gratis propter mediatorem, et per eum accipimus remissionem peccatorum, imputationem iusticiae et vivificationem, ac efficimur haeredes vitae aeternae, sicut ipse Dominus inquit: Ego vitam aeternam do eis. Item: Qui habet Christum, habet vitam. Item: Iustificati fide pacem habemus ad Deum. Item, Rom. 8.: Si sumus filii, sumus et haeredes. Item: Haec est vita aeterna, ut agnoscant te verum Deum, et quem misisti Iesum esse Christum. Nominat autem inobedientes hoc loco, qui discedunt a regula: Milita bonam mi- litiam retinens fidem et bonam conscientiam.

Posteaquam exuistis veterem hominem etc.

Phrasis Pauli est, in eodem homine renato nominare veterem hominem, et vetustatem et exteriorem hominem, reliquias naturae carnalis vitiosae. Contra vero novum hominem et novi- tatem spiritus, et interiorem hominem, quatenus in mente, voluntate et corde nova lux et novi motus accensi sunt a filio Dei, voce Evangelii et Spiritu sancto, ut 2. Corinth. 4. dicitur: Interior homo renovatur de die in diem. Et haec recte intelligenda sunt: Novitas fit in vera conver- sione, cum voce Evangelii nova lux in mente per filium accenditur, et datur Spiritus sanctus, fidem, laetitiam, invocationem et alios motus incoans qualis ipse est. Nec fiat hic confusio Evangelii et philosophiae, sicut quidam falso scripserunt novitatem esse rationem, sensus ve- tustatem. Sed sciendum est etiam rationem sine filio Dei, sine voce Evangelii et sine Spiritu sancto esse vetustatem et tenebras. Haec alibi copiosius explicata sunt.

Nominat autem hic Paulus novum hominem Imaginem Dei, ubi recte intelligatur haec doctrina. Augustinus interpretatur imaginem de potentiis hoc modo. In anima sunt mens ipsa, cogitatio et motus. Haec tria sic accommodat. Aeternus Pater est veluti Mens, Filius, Imago Patris cogi- tatione genita, Spiritus sanctus, ut motus. Et pie ac prudenter ista considerantibus non erit in- grata haec collatio, quia certe anima est testimo- nium de Deo, et vult nos Deus intelligere, se esse Essentiam intelligentem, cogitantem sese, et motricem. Sed ad haec Augustini dicta de po- tentiis hoc addo: Potentias intelligendas esse non corruptas, sed vel integras vel renascentes. Sic ad Ephes. scriptum est: Induite novum hominem, qui secundum Deum creatus est, in iustitia et sanctitate veritatis.

Hic non fit tantum potentiarum mentio, sed vult in potentiis esse iusticiam et sanctam verita- tem, id est, vult lucere in nobis veras noticias de Deo, firmam assensionem et iusticiam, id est, conformitatem cum Deo, sicut initio homo con- ditus est, habens veras noticias et conformita- tem in voluntate et corde cum Deo. Et dulcis- sime hic dicitur: Renovetur novus homo ad agni- tionem, ut sciamus in novitate accendi novam lucem, et quidem voce Evangelii.

Osiander alia quaedam disputat de imagine Dei: nominari hominem imaginem Dei, propterea quia filius fuerit assumturus humanam naturam. Hoc verum est, sed tamen comprehendi necesse est, veritatem et iusticiam, qua efficimur similes filio, sanctificante nos Deo et assimilante filio.

Ubi nec Graecus est nec Iudaeus etc.

Semper in conspectu sit doctrina de distin- ctione iusticiae Evangelii et rerum politicarum. Evangelium non condit novas politias, sicut Lo- riothus et alii multi fingunt: sed concionatur de poenitentia singularum in corde, et de restitu- tione aeternae iusticiae et vitae in singulis, quae restitutio fit ipso filio Dei vivificante corda voce Evangelii, et dante Spiritum sanctum. Foris autem sinit nos uti in vita corporali diversis poli- ticis legibus, si non pugnent cum legibus natura- libus, sicut alii aliis cibis utuntur, aut alii aliis spatiis dierum, Ideo hic inquit, non esse discri- men Graeci et Iudaei. Hanc sententiam saepe repetivit, quia Pseudoapostoli volebant Gentes ad politiam Iudaicam alligare, sicut nostro tem- pore Carolostadius et alii volebant delere et tol- lere ius Romanum, et res iudicare ex legibus Mosi.

Contra tales errores confirmati simus his Pauli dictis, et recte discernantur iusticia, propter quam filius Dei missus est, et ordo politicus. Di- cit autem, omnia in omnibus esse Christum, om- nia, videlicet propria novi hominis sunt Chri- stus, scilicet, quo ad meritum et quo ad effe- ctionem, seu quo ad gratiam et quo ad donum. Chrisus factus est tibi iusticia, ut videlicet propter eum imputetur iusticia, et simul est tibi vivifica- tor, vivificans cor voce Evangelii, et dans Spiri- tum sanctum.

## 3:14
Above these things have love, which is the bond of perfection etc.

Love is the bond of perfection. The word perfection here should not be understood as the private perfection of one person or the perfect fulfillment of the law: but it should be understood as the joining together of the body of the Church or the preservation of conjunction and concord. Love is the bond of the joining together of the Church, that is, as long as the teachers retain love, even if it sometimes happens that one thing seems otherwise to another, yet the Church is not immediately torn apart, but the learned tolerate the weaker ones and calmly strive to heal them, and in turn the weaker ones do not grudgingly listen to the more learned ones, just as modest children listen to old parents, as it is said: ᾿Ακέσται δὲ φρένες ἐσθλῶν, that is, the minds of the good are curable.

Latin:

Super haec habete dilectionem, quae est vincu- lum perfectionis etc.

Dilectio est vinculum perfectionis. Voca- bulum Perfectionis hic non intelligatur privata perfectio unius personae seu perfecta impletio legis: sed intelligatur corporis Ecclesiae coagmen- tatio seu coniunctionis et concordiae conservatio. Dilectio est vinculum coagmentationis Ecclesiae, id est, donec retinent doctores dilectionem, etiamsi interdum accidit, ut aliud alteri videatur, tamen non mox dilaceratur Ecclesia, sed docti tolerant infirmiores et placide student sanare, et rursus infirmiores non gravatim audiunt alios doctiores, sicut modesti filii senes parentes, sicut dicitur: ᾿Ακέσται δὲ φρένες ἐσθλῶν, id est, sanabiles sunt animi bonorum.

## 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly with all wisdom etc.

Among the chief sentences of this Epistle one must remember this one, and since it contains many most serious admonitions, especially commending the study of doctrine, it must be diligently and often considered. First, that it is a divine command of the law here that we rightly learn the doctrine of Christ, and there is a significant emphasis in the words: Let it dwell in you, and indeed richly. Those who dwell with us are most familiarly known. You should also know that God himself truly dwells in that breast in which the doctrine concerning conversion to God is thought upon, and in consolation and invocation, just as the Lord expressly says: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my father will love him, and we will come to him, and make our dwelling with him.

Therefore reading and thinking upon doctrine please God, and through it God is effective and dwells in us. He adds, however, With all wisdom. Heretics and all tricksters also read the books of the Prophets and Apostles, but they read without wisdom, that is, they do not rightly learn the sources, which are in those very prophetic and apostolic books, just as Papists do not distinguish the Law and the Promise of grace, worship commanded by God, and superstitions devised by men. Anabaptists confuse the doctrine concerning eternal righteousness in the heart and concerning political life, they imagine the Gospel to be barbarism, which condemns the political order. Antinomians do not distinguish sins against conscience from others etc.

Therefore an admonition is added here, that we wisely consider the order of doctrine and the distinctions of the members, just as elsewhere he commands to ὀρθοτομεῖν the divine word. And Sirach says in chapter 3: What God commands you, think upon these things holily, that is, retain the native meaning of the word of God, and do not attach profane opinions to it, as is customary to all heretics, to all idolaters, and to all sorcerers. Item 2 Tim. 1: Hold fast the form of sound words. But in order that corruptions and deceits may be judged and avoided, it is necessary that men be rightly taught, admonished, and that false opinions be corrected, just as it is said in Proverbs 30: Every word of God is pure; he is a shield unto them that put their trust in him. Pure, he says, just as metals are smelted, so that a separation of the silver and the dross may be made. Thus, by learning, the proper and native meaning must be sought, and filth must be removed. Therefore Paul adds: Teaching and admonishing one another.

Since, therefore, we hear that the study of teaching and learning is commanded, let us obey God, and let us love these labors of teaching and learning because of the command of God, and let us know that they are pleasing to God. But at the same time, let prayer be joined to them, just as the Lord says: Pray that you enter not into temptation. Item: How much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him. Let there also be study without sophistry, without the curiosity of seeking unnecessary things, as Sirach commands: Seek not curiously into the things that are unnecessary for your discourses.

Whatsoever you do in word or deed, etc.

The rule of life is: Commit thy way unto the Lord, and trust in him, and he shall bring it to pass. Psalm 36: Way signifies one's calling and all the duties of that calling, that is, of the honest labor to which we have been rightly called. For a calling is not of impious labor. The Psalm therefore teaches that all our actions ought to be governed by the law of God and the Gospel. The Law shows which actions are pleasing to God; the Gospel shows how they are pleasing, namely, when faith shines forth, acknowledging the Son of God, and receiving the remission of sins and reconciliation, and calling upon Him to help us, just as He says: Without me you can do nothing, Ask and you shall receive, and determining that these labors are pleasing to God, although we are very weak and unworthy, and many impediments are thrown in our way, yet that they will not be in vain, and referring our plans to this end, that God may be rightly acknowledged and celebrated, that the Church may remain, and not be torn apart by scandals and dissensions. Therefore, in this saying of the Psalm, a promise is added: He shall bring it to pass. Commit thy way unto God, that is, in the duties of your calling, which you perform according to the commands of God, rightly call upon God with faith and hope, and do not be deterred by your own unworthiness or weakness, but know that God will help you, so that your labors may be successful, just as Paul says elsewhere: Your labor shall not be in vain in the Lord. John 15: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit. Psalm 1: And his leaf shall not wither, and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper.

Paul embraces this whole rule of the Psalm, saying: Do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, that is, in the true acknowledgment of the Son of God, in faith and invocation, and let all things be referred to the glory of the Son of God.

And let the efficient and final causes of good actions be often considered. The efficient causes are the mind looking upon the precepts of God and thinking upon the Gospel, namely, the promise of grace and other promises. There, the Son in the believer teaches the mind, and kindles light, and at the same time moves the will by the Holy Spirit, so that it obeys and is firm, asks for and hopes for the help of God, and asks for good outcomes, even if great dangers are shown. The final causes are that God may be celebrated, the Church may remain, and punishments may be avoided, etc. Since these causes are very illustrious in Joseph, let us often think of his example. And Paul embraces all these efficient and final causes when he commands us to do all things in the name of Jesus, that is, in the acknowledgment of Him, in faith and invocation.

Latin:

Sermo Christi habitet in vobis opulenter cum omni sapientia etc.

Inter praecipuas sententias huius Epistolae et hanc meminisse oportet, cumque multas gra- vissimas admonitiones contineat, praesertim com- mendantes doctrinae studium, diligenter et saepe consideranda est. Primum hic legis mandatum divinum esse, ut doctrinam Christi recte disca- mus, et emphasis est insignis verbis: Habitet in vobis, et quidem opulenter. Familiarissime noti sunt qui nobiscum habitant. Scias etiam vere in illo pectore Deum ipsum habitare, in quo cogita- tur doctrina de conversione ad Deum, et in con- solatione et invocatione, sicut expresse Dominus inquit: Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum ser- vabit, et pater meus diliget eum, et veniemus ad eum, et mansionem apud eum faciemus.

Placent igitur Deo lectio et cogitatio doctri- nae, et per eam Deus est efficax et habitat in no- bis. Addit autem, Cum omnia sapientia. Le- gunt Prophetarum et Apostolorum libros etiam haeretici et omnes praestigiatores, sed sine sa- pientia legunt, id est, fontes non recte discunt, qui sunt in ipsis libris propheticis et apostolicis, ut Papistae non discernunt Legem et Promissionem gratiae, cultus divinitus mandatos, et supersti- tiones ab hominibus excogitatas. Anabaptistae confundunt doctrinam de iusticia aeterna in cor- de et de vita politica, fingunt Evangelium bar- bariem esse, quae damnet ordinem politicum. Antinomi non discernunt peccata contra conscien- tiam ab aliis etc.

Addita est igitur hic admonitio, ut sapien- ter consideremus ordinem doctrinae et discrimina membrorum, sicuti alibi iubet sermonem divi- num ὀρθοτομεῖν. Et Syracides inquit cap. 3.: Quae praecipit tibi Deus, haec cogita sancte, id est, retine nativam sententiam verbi Dei, nec af- fingito prophanas opiniones, sicut usitatum est omnibus haereticis, omnibus idolorum cultoribus et omnibus praestigiatoribus. Item 2. Timoth. 1.: Formam retine sanorum sermonum. Ut autem iudicari et vitari corruptelae et praestigiae possint, necesse est recte doceri homines, commonefieri et emendari falsas opiniones, sicut et Proverb. 30. dicitur: Omne verbum Dei purgatum clypeus est sperantibus propter ipsum. Purgatum inquit, sicut metalla coquuntur, ut fiat segregatio ar- gendi et scoriae. Sic discendo quaerenda est propria et nativa sententia, et removendae sunt sordes. Ideo Paulus addit: Docentes et emen- dantes vos mutuo.

Cum igitur audimus praecipi studium do- cendi et discendi, obediamus Deo, et hos labo- res docendi et discendi propter mandatum Dei amemus, et placere eos Deo sciamus. Sed simul adiuncta sit invocatio, sicut inquit Dominus: Orate ne intretis in tentationem. Item: Quando magis pater vester coelestis dabit Spiritum san- ctum petentibus. Sit etiam studium sine sophi- stica, sine curiositate quaerendi non necessaria, ut Syracides praecipit: Ne curiose quaeras in ser- monibus tuis non necessaria.

Omne quodcunque facitis in verbo aut opere etc.

Regula vitae est: Commenda Deo viam tuam, et spera in eum, et ipse faciet. Psal. 36.: Via significat vocationem et omnia officia vocatio- nis, id est, laboris honesti, ad quem recte vocati sumus. Vocatio enim non est impii laboris. Do- cet igitur Psalmus omnes nostras actiones regi de- bere lege Dei et Evangelio. Lex ostendit, quae actiones Deo placeant, Evangelium ostendit quo- modo placeant, videlicet, cum praelucet fides, agnoscens filium Dei, et accipiens remissionem peccatorum et reconciliationem, et invocans eum, ut nos adiuvet, sicut inquit: Sine me nihil pote- stis facere, Petite et accipietis, et statuens Deo placere hos labores, quanquam sumus valde in- firmi et indigni, et multa impedimenta obiiciun- tur, nec tamen fore irritos, et referens consilia ad hunc finem, ut Deus recte agnoscatur et cele- bretur, maneat Ecclesia, et non dilaceretur scan- dalis et dissidiis. Ideo in hoc dicto Psalmi ad- ditur promissio: Ipse faciet. Commenda Deo viam tuam, id est, in officiis vocationis, quae iuxta mandata Dei facis, recte invoca Deum fide et spe, nec deterrearis tua indignitate aut infir- mitate, sed scias Deum tibi opitulaturum esse, ut labores sint felices, sicut alibi inquit Paulus: Labor vester non erit inanis in Domino. Iohan. 15.: Qui manet in me et ego in eo, hic feret fru- ctum copiosum. Psalmo 1.: Et folium eius non defluet, et omnia quae faciet, erunt prospera.

Hanc totam regulam Psalmi complectitur Paulus inquiens: Omnia facite in nomine Domini Iesu, id est, in vera agnitione filii Dei, fide et invocatione, et referantur omnia ad gloriam filii Dei.

Ac saepe considerentur actionum bonarum causae efficientes et finales. Efficientes sunt mens intuens praecepta Dei, et cogitans Evangelium, videlicet promissionem gratiae et alias promis- siones. Ibi filius in credente docet mentem, et lucem accendit, et simul movet voluntatem Spi- ritu sancto, ut obtempert et sit firma, petat et speret auxilium Dei, petat bonos eventus, etiamsi magna pericula ostenduntur. Finales causae sunt, ut celebretur Deus, maneat Ecclesia, et vitentur poenae etc. Hae causae cum in Ioseph sint valde illustres, exemplum eius saepe cogitemus. Et has causas omnes efficientes et finales complecti- tur Paulus, cum iubet omnia facere in nomine Iesu, id est, in agnitione eius, fide et invo- catione.

## 4:1 Argument
Chapter four.

Masters, give unto your servants that which is just and equal, etc.

Just signifies that which is owed or ordered by divine and positive laws. For here it is spoken of legal justice, so that it is not just to snatch away the spouses of servants, or to kill them without just cause, or not to provide food. Therefore, Augustus rightly freed a servant whom his master wished to kill because he had accidentally broken a crystal. And because the ancient allowance was generous, it appears that the ancients wisely considered what nature could bear, and were just and beneficent. For to one was given daily bread worth three Meissen coins, also a sextarius of wine, and a certain measure of meat, figs, or other side dishes. These were owed by civil obligation, which Paul calls Just. Even though jurists ask whether there is marriage between a male servant and a female servant, yet the truest rule is: Divine and natural bonds bind both servants and the free.

some civil benefits do not pertain to slaves.

Paul uses two words here; he commands that just things be provided, namely those commanded by divine and positive laws. Seneca speaks thus: It is not permitted to do to a man what the law of nature forbids. Paul adds: Provide equality. He wishes that, beyond those things which are comprehended by civil obligation, benefits be given which are owed by natural obligation, such as that special rewards are to be given to those who have served well, and that the labors of the sick and the elderly are to be lightened. Seneca alleges the example of the mistress hidden by slaves when the city was captured. That also should be considered when equality is spoken of, that it must be considered where equality by geometric proportion has a place, and where there is use for equality by arithmetic proportion. When Paul says: Provide equality, he does not wish slaves to become equal or peers to their master, but he wishes equality to be observed by geometric proportion. Moreover, this whole doctrine must be followed now as well, both in families and in the government of princes. The bonds of divine law remain, which bind both princes and people equally. Princes are not lords in such a way that it is permitted for them to kill subjects without just cause, or to take away their property without just cause, etc.

Latin:

Caput quartum.

Domini, quod iustum est et aequale, servis praestate etc.

Iustum significat debitum seu ordinatum le- gibus divinis et positivis. Hic enim de iusticia legali dicitur, ut non est iustum servis eripere coniuges, aut sine iusta causa eos interficere, aut non dare victum. Ideo Augustus recte liberat servum, quem dominus voluit interficere, quod casu fregerat crystallum. Et quia demensum ve- tus fuit largum, apparet veteres sapienter consi- derasse, quid natura ferre posset, et fuisse iustos et beneficos. Uni enim dabatur quotidie panis valens tribus nummis Misnicis, item sextarius vini, certus modus carnium, ficorum aut aliorum obsoniorum. Haec obligatione civili erant debi- ta, quae Paulus nominat Iusta. Etsi enim Iuris- consulti quaerunt, an coniugium sit servi et an- cillae, tamen regula verissima est: Vincula di- vina et naturalia ligant servos et liberos.

rum aliqua civilia beneficia ad servos non per- tinent.

Usus est autem Paulus hic duobus vocabulis, iubet praestare iusta, scilicet mandata legibus divinis et positivis, Seneca sic loquitur: Non licere in hominem quae ius naturae vetat. Addit autem Paulus : Praestate aequalitatem. Vult praeter illa, quae comprehenduntur obligatione civili dari beneficia, quae obligatione naturali de- bentur, ut benemeritis danda sunt singularia praemia, levandi sunt labores aegrotis et senibus. Seneca exemplum allegat de occultata domina a servis capta urbe. Illud etiam consideretur cum de aequalitate dicitur, considerandum esse, ubi aequalitas geometrica proportione locum habeat, ubi usus sit aequalitatis arithmetica proportione. Cum dicit Paulus: Praestate aequalitatem, non vult servos fieri aequales vel pares domino, sed vult servari aequalitatem geometrica proportione. Tota autem haec doctrina nunc quoque sequenda est, et in familiis et in gubernatione principum. Manent vincula legis divinae, quae pariter ligant et Principes et populum. Principes non sic sunt domini, ut liceat eis subditos sine iusta causa in- terficere, aut auferre facultates eorum sine iusta causa etc.

## 4:6
Let your speech be seasoned with salt in grace, etc.

There is a manifest deformity in the vices of scurrility and insipidity. Scurrility is joined with impudence, vanity, obscenity, or even virulence. A scurra is so called from σκὼρ, that is, dung, so that he is as it were speaking dung, σκὼρ λέγων. In Greek they are named βωμόλοχοι, as if lying at the altar, because many beggars used to run to sacrifices, who begged for money with various trifles, just as also the jugglers who carried around the dust of saints. Insipidity, however, is a stupidity that is excessive and unworthy of a human being. Between these vices, philosophers place a mean, which is wit, which is a moderation of cheerfulness and harshness in speech.

It is an excellent ornament in a man to bring forth sayings and speeches at the right time, whether figuratively or simply, which either soothe the pain of the sorrowful, or by art break the excessive emotions in the angry, or rebuke the proud. Moreover, quickness of wit and the knowledge of many things come together. And when moderation is added to this, this whole thing is said to be a virtue, just as Menenius's fable recalled the citizens from sedition. It was a beautiful saying of Demades, that after Alexander died his army was like a Cyclops with its eye gouged out: and that one: τάμιαι λάμιαι: and this of Erasmus: The Christian mind is a Lutheran stomach. And my own narrative about nations adapting religions to their own natures, and that of the French King Louis: those things which were done previously against the duke do not pertain to the king. And antiquity distinguishes white salt from black, and says that the white belongs to Mercury, such as sayings that increase benevolence, like that of Alexander: It is royal to bear insults while doing good, or that of Plautus: What is done well for the good, that at last is serious and welcome. And concerning this kind, Callimachus asks that the Graces anoint his hands with ambrosia in his poem. They said that black salt belongs to Momus, such as poisonous rebukes, like that of Antiphon to Dionysius, that the best sculptors should be brought to Athens, who would have made statues for the tyrannicides.

But when Paul here names grace in speech, he wishes scurrility, obscenity, insipidity, boasting, virulence, and chicanery to be avoided. Afterwards, when he names salt, he does not speak of salts exactly as the philosophers do, although there is a place for these too: but he understands salt generally as judgment, applying the word of God rightly and skillfully, as it is said in Mark 9: Salt is good; have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves. Where salt signifies the word of God rightly understood, with judgment or discernment applied, lest it be transformed into profane imaginations, like Servetus and Thammer, who say that the λόγος is not ὑφιστάμενον, but is a vanishing voice. Likewise, lest by deleting true and necessary distinctions, things that should not be mixed are mixed into one chaos, as the Anabaptists do not distinguish private vengeance from divinely ordained judgments, and they condemn judgments and the whole political order. Likewise, lest the native meaning of words be changed, just as monks understand faith only as knowledge of history, such as exists even in the impious. Likewise, lest opinions be added that fight with the foundation, as Papists teach that dead men are to be invoked, teach that the works of men merit the remission of sins, pretend that the Mass merits the remission of sins and indeed ex opere operato, and adore the bread in the procession. These absurdities, completely outside the prophetic and apostolic writings, the unlearned have added to the doctrine of the Church by ethnic superstition. In these examples, the insipidity is manifest. Let these sayings, however, be understood: Have salt in yourselves, that is, the word of God rightly applied. Likewise: Let your speech be seasoned with salt, not only regarding doctrine, but universally regarding the reproof of errors and sins, and regarding consolation. Likewise, regarding advice to be given in various matters, as Paul's advice is not insipid concerning the marriage of a believer and a heathen. Likewise, Christ's advice concerning the didrachma, so that sedition might not be stirred up against the ordinary authority, and without doubt Zacharias and those like him were advisors that wars should not be stirred up against the Romans at that time. Finally, many things occur where those who are rightly instructed, fearing and calling upon God, judge differently than those who are not rightly instructed or are profane and superstitious.

Latin:

Sermo vester in gratia sale conditus sit etc.

Manifesta deformitas est vitiorum Scurrili- tatis et Insulsitatis. Scurrilitas cum impudentia, vanitate, obscoenitate, aut etiam virulentia con- iuncta est. Dicitur autem Scurra, a σκὼρ, id est, stercus, ut sit quasi stercora loquens, σκὼρ λέ- γων. Graece nominantur βωμόλοχοι, quasi ad aram cubantes, quia ad sacrificia multi mendici accurrebant, qui variis nugis pecuniam mendica- bant, sicut et praestigiatores, qui pulvisculos sanctorum circumtulerunt. Insulsitas vero stu- por est nimius et indignus homine. Inter haec vitia Philosophi collocant medium, quod est Le- pos, qui est in sermone hilaritatis et asperitatis moderatio.

Est autem excellens in homine ornamentum, dicta et sermones tempestive proferre seu figu- rate seu simpliciter, qui aut moestis dolorem le- niant, aut in iratis nimios motus arte frangant, aus superbos reprehendant. Concurrunt autem ingenii celeritas et cognitio multarum rerum. Ac haec cum accedit moderatio, totum hoc virtus esse dicitur, ut Menenii apologus revocavit cives a seditione. Pulcrum fuit et Demadis dictum, Alexandro mortuo exercitum eius similem esse Cyclopi effosso oculo: et illud: τάμιαι λάμιαι: et hoc Erasmi: Mens Christiana stomachus Lu- theranus est. Et mea narratio de gentibus at- temperantibus religiones ad suas naturas, et re- gis Gallorum Ludovici: non pertinent ad regem, quae antea contra ducem facta sunt. Et vetustas discernit salem candidum a nigro, et candidum dicit esse Mercurii, ut sunt dicta, quae benevo- lentiam augent, ut Alexandri: Regium est bene- facientem ferre maledicta, aut illud Plauti: Bonis bene quod fit, id demum grave ac gratum est. Et de hoc genere petit Callimachus, ut Gratiae alubant manus ambrosia in suo Carmine. Nigrum vero salem dixerunt esse Momo, ut sunt vene- natae reprehensiones, ut Antiphontis ad Diony- sium, optimos statuarios Athenis adducendos esse, qui fecissent statuas tyrannicidis.

Cum autem hic Paulus nominat gratiam in ser- mone, vult vitari scurrilitatem, obscoenitatem, in- sulsitatem, iactantiam, virulentiam et sycophantias. Postea cum salem nominat, non prorsus ut Philo- sophi de salibus loquitur, etsi his quoque locus est: sed generaliter intelligit salem iudicium recte et dextre accommodans verbum Dei, ut Marci 9. dici- tur: Bonus est sal, habete in vobis salem, et pa- cem habete inter vos. Ubi sal significat verbum Dei recte intellectum, adhibito iudicio seu dis- crimine, ne transformetur in prophanas imagina- tiones, ut Servetus, Thammerus, qui dicunt λόγον non esse ὑφιστάμενον, sed esse vocem evane- scentem. Item, ne deletis veris distinctionibus et necessariis, misceantur in unum chaos non mi- scenda, ut Anabaptistae non discernunt vindictam privatam a iudiciis divinitus ordinatis, et dam- nant iudicia et totum politicum ordinem. Item, ne nativa significatio verborum mutetur, sicut monachi fidem tantum intelligunt noticiam histo- riae, qualis est et in impiis. Item, ne addantur opiniones pugnantes cum fundamento, ut Papi- stae docent homines mortuos invocandos esse, docent opera hominum mereri remissionem pec- catorum, fingunt Missam mereri remissionem peccatorum et quidem ex opere operato, adorant panem in circumgestatione. Haec absurda pror- sus extra scripta prophetica et apostolica indocti addiderunt ethnica superstitione ad doctrinam Ecclesiae. In his exemplis manifesta est insul- sitas. Intelligantur autem haec dicta: Habete salem in vobis, id est, verbum Dei recte accommodatum. Item: Sermo sit sale conditus, non solum de doctrina, sed universaliter de reprehensione errorum et peccatorum, et de consolatione. Item, de consiliis dandis in variis negotiis, ut Pauli consilium non est insulsum de coniugio credentis et ethnicae. Item, consilium Christi de didrachmo, ne moveretur seditio contra ordinariam potestatem, et haud dubie Zacharias et similes fuerunt suasores, ne tunc moverentur bella adversus Romanos. Denique multa incidunt ubi recte instituti, timentes et invocantes Deum, aliter iudicant quam non recte instituti aut prophani et superstitiosi.

## 4:10
Aristarchus greets you, etc.

The examples of greetings in the Epistles of Paul show that the Church is not a polity which is governed by the same civil laws and has its own political magistrates, but a congregation agreeing on true doctrine and invocation, and joined by benevolence, even if it is scattered into different political empires, heathen or pious, just as in the time of the Apostles there were Churches, some under heathen Romans, others under Persians or Parthians, etc.

It is necessary to know these things about the Church and to discern it prudently, because very many fanatical and seditious men in all ages have attempted to establish new polities under the pretext of the Gospel, as the Anabaptists have done in our time. Thus also the Roman Bishops unjustly established an empire for themselves, and taught that no one is a member

of the Church of God, unless he embraces human traditions, holiness from the Roman Bishops concerning their own primacy and ceremonies. It is certain that these things are false from the saying: The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them, but you shall not be so. Likewise: Our citizenship is in heaven. Therefore, the rule must be held: Render to God the things that are God's, and to Caesar the things that are Caesar's. This admonition must be especially considered when we read these greetings.

At the same time, however, let this also be considered. Although the Church is not one political empire, yet it is a congregation of many who are joined by the ministry of the Gospel and the Sacraments, and by the same true confession. In these, those who know one another are joined by benevolence, just as the Lord prays to the eternal Father: Make them one in us. These signs of benevolence are seen also in these greetings.

Finally, readers are also to be warned of this, which Eutropius writes, that Laodicea and Colossae were submerged by an earthquake in the year following Paul's death, just as Jerusalem was destroyed after Christ's preaching. In such examples, God shows that He punishes the enemies of the Church and the ungrateful, who, having heard the voice of the Gospel, are not amended. And yet He miraculously delivers His Church, just as before the siege Simeon led his hearers out of Jerusalem across the Jordan. Thus it is consistent that the pious were also led out of those cities beforehand. And now also, in such great confusions and ruins of empires, let us pray to the Son of God that He may preserve the Church and us in it, as He says: No one shall snatch my sheep out of my hands.

Praise be to God.

Latin:

Salutat vos Aristarchus etc.

Salutationum exempla in Epistolis Pauli ostendunt, Ecclesiam non esse politiam, quae iisdem legibus civilibus regatur, et habeat proprios magistratus politicos, sed congregationem consentientem de vera doctrina, et invocatione, et coniunctam benevolentia, etiamsi sparsa est in diversa imperia politica, ethnica vel pia, sicut Apostolorum tempore erant Ecclesiae, aliae sub ethnicis Romanis, aliae sub Persis aut Parthis etc.

Haec de Ecclesia scire, et eam prudenter discernere necesse est, quia plurimi fanatici et seditiosi homines omnibus seculis praetextu Evangelii novas politias constituere conati sunt, ut nostro tempore Anabaptistae fecerunt. Sic et Romani Episcopi iniuste constituerunt sibi imperium, ac docuerunt, neminem esse membrum

Ecclesiae Dei, nisi amplectentem traditiones huma- nas, sanctitas a Romanis Episcopis de ipsorum primatu et ceremoniis. Haec falsa esse certum est ex dicto: Reges gentium dominantur, vos au- tem non sic. Item: Πολίτευμα nostrum in coe- lis.
