Tenenda est igitur regula: Date Deo, quae Dei sunt, Caesari, quae sunt Caesaris. Haec ad- monitio praecipue cogitanda est, cum has saluta- tiones legimus.

Simul autem et haec consideretur. Etsi Ec- clesia non est unum politicum imperium, tamen congregatio est multorum, qui ministerio Evan- gelii et Sacramentorum, et eadem vera confessione coniuncti sunt. In his qui norunt inter se benevo- lentia coniuncti sunt, sicut Dominus orat aeter- num patrem: Fac ut unum sint in nobis. Haec signa benevolentiae conspiciuntur et in his saluta- tionibus.

Postremo et hoc monendi sunt lectores, quod scribit Eutropius, Laodiceam et Colossas terrae motu submersas esse proximo anno post Pauli mortem, sicut Ierosolyma post Christi praedica- tionem deleta est. In talibus exemplis ostendit Deus se punire hostes Ecclesiae et ingratos, qui audita voce Evangelii non emendantur. Et ta- men mirabiliter liberat suam Ecclesiam, sicut ante obsidionem Simeon ex Ierosolyma eduxit suos au- ditores trans Iordanem. Ita consentaneum est et ex illis urbibus pios ante eductos esse. Ac nunc quoque in tantis confusionibus et ruinis imperio- rum precemur filium Dei, ut Ecclesiam et nos in ea servet, sicut inquit: Nemo rapiet oves meas ex manibus meis.

Laus Deo.

# 1 Timothy

## 1:1 Argument
PHILIP MELANCHTHON'S EXPOSITION OF THE FIRST EPISTLE TO TIMOTHY.

Already in the year 1541 there had appeared: 'A Commentary on Paul's first epistle to Timothy, dictated in the school of Wittenberg by Dr. Caspar Cruciger. Strasbourg, 1541. 8vo,' which Mylius in his chronology of Melanchthon's writings claims for him as the author. But later, after Melanchthon's death, the same exposition appeared inscribed thus: Exposition of the 1st Epistle to Timothy and of two chapters of the second, written and dictated in a public lecture in the years 1550 and 1551 by Phil. Mel. Wittenberg, 1561. 17 sheets, 8vo (edited by P. Crellius), which exposition Peucer inserted into the works of Melanchthon, Vol. IV, p. 366 ff., from where we have drawn it.

ARGUMENT OF THE FIRST EPISTLE TO TIMOTHY, WITH A BRIEF COMMEMORATION OF PAUL'S PRINCIPAL JOURNEYS.

Lystra is a town of Lycaonia below Galatia, which is listed also by Ptolemy, not far from Iconium and Derbe. But because it is written in Acts chapter 16 that Timothy lived in Lystra, he is also thought to have been born there. His mother, Eunice, was a Jewess and a believer, as is written there in Acts, and his grandmother was the Jewess Lois. His father, however, was a Gentile. But so that the Jews might be less averse to Timothy's custom, and in those first beginnings of the tender Church, with the abrogation of the law not yet inculcated in everyone, might hear him more easily, Paul wished him to be circumcised. We take the journeys from Acts: when Paul had come to Lystra in the sixteenth year after his conversion, he joined Timothy to himself there. Then he crossed into Macedonia: Timothy was a companion of this first journey into Macedonia and Greece. Afterwards Paul sailed from Corinth to Ephesus, where he stayed for two years; when he was departing from there to visit the churches of Asia, he entrusted the church in Ephesus to Timothy, and on the journey in Phrygia he wrote the first Epistle to him at Laodicea. The argument is appropriate for an Apostle, but he writes briefly about doctrine to a learned disciple, whom he himself had both taught and often heard. But yet he touches upon the principal matters of doctrine, so that both then there might exist testimonies of Paul against Timothy's adversaries, and afterwards these testimonies might be preserved in the Church. Because God in His immense mercy wishes us to be certain about doctrine, He wishes it to be known when, through whom, and by what testimonies it has been propagated. Therefore He adds to the Apostles great companies of companions, and by manifest miracles He testifies that they carry about a divine voice.

Catalogue of the years of Paul.

35. 1. The year of Paul's conversion. The year from the birth of Christ 35.

36. 2. Paul went into Arabia.

39. 5. He went into Tarsus, Acts 9.

42. 8. Barnabas leads Paul from Tarsus to Antioch, Acts 11.

44. 10. He went into Cyprus, Acts 13, with Barnabas accompanying him. And by the command of the Holy Spirit. And there Sergius the proconsul is converted.

45. 11. Having set out into Perga of Pamphylia, Antioch of Pisidia, Iconium and the neighboring cities, Acts 14.

48. 14. The famine predicted by Agabus afflicts the whole world. Josephus.

Year of Christ, Year after conversion.

51. 17. The Synod of Jerusalem at which Paul was present, Acts 15.

52. 18. He returned to Iconium and Lystra, where he joined Timothy to himself and crossed into Macedonia. And he was at Corinth, where he wrote the Epistle to the Romans.

53. 19. 54. 20. 55. 21. He returned to Asia, and when he had been at Ephesus for two years, he commended the Church to Timothy as he was leaving.

56. 22. He returned to Phrygia, where at Laodicea he wrote the first Epistle to Timothy.

57. 23. Paul returned to Macedonia after first traveling through Phrygia and the borders of the Galatians, and when he had come into Macedonia, he wrote both Epistles to the Corinthians at Philippi within a short interval. Afterwards he returned to Asia, and came to Mytilene, likewise to Samos and Miletus, Acts 20.

59. 25. 60. 26. The final journey to Jerusalem, upon arriving at which he is captured, and is held captive for two years at Caesarea.

61. 27. 62. 28. Sent back to Rome. But then he was delivered from the mouth of the lion, as 2 Timothy 4 narrates.

63. 29. 64. 30. 65. 31. 66. 32. 67. 33. He was for two years in a rented house.

68. 34. 69. 35. Paul killed by Nero shortly before his death.

70. 36. The fourteenth year of Nero, in which Nero committed suicide.

Latin:

PHILIPPI MELANTHONIS ENARRATIO EPIST. PRIORIS DA TIMOTHEUM.

Iam anno 1541 prodierat: „In epistolam Pauli ad Timotheum priorem Commentarius, dictatus in schola Witeberg. per D. Casp. Crucigerum. Argentor. 1541. 8." quem Mylius in chronologia scriptorum Melanthonis huic tanquam auctori vindicat. Postea vero, post Melanthonis obitum, eadem enarratio prodiit sic inscripta: Enarratio Epist. 1. ad Timotheum et duorum capitum secundae, scripta et dictata in praelectione publica anno 1550 et 1551 a Phil. Mel. Witeb. 1561. 17. pl. 8. (edidit P. Crellius.), quam enarrationem Peucerus inseruit operibus Melanthonis, Tom. IV, p. 366 seq. unde sic eam hausimus.

ARGUMENTUM EPISTOLAE PRIORIS AD TIMOTHEUM, CUM COMMEMORATIONE BREVI PRAECIPUORUM ITINERUM PAULI.

Lystra oppidum est Lycaonicae infra Galatiam, quod recensetur et a Ptolemaeo, non procul ab Iconio et Therbe. Quia vero in Actis capite 16. scribitur, Timotheum in Lystris vixisse, ibi quo- que natus existimatur. Fuit autem mater Eunice Iudaea, et fidelis, ut ibi in Actis scriptum est, et avia Iudaea Lois. Pater vero fuit Ethnicus. Ut autem a consuetudine Timothei minus abhor- rerent Iudaei, et in illis primis initiis tenerae Ec- clesiae, nondum abrogatione legis inculcata om- nibus, facilius eum audirent, voluit eum Paulus circumcidi. Itinera ex Actis sumimus: cum Paulus sede- cimo anno a conversione venisset Lystram, Ti- motheum ibi sibi adiunxit. Deinde traiecit in Macedoniam: huius primae profectionis in Ma- cedoniam et Graeciam comes fuit Timotheus. Postea ex Corintho navigavit Paulus Ephesum, ubi biennio commoratus est, inde cum discederet visurus Asiae Ecclesias, Timotheo Ecclesiam in Epheso commendavit, et in itinere in Phrygia priorem Epistolam ei Laodiceae scripsit, Argu- mentum est conveniens Apostolo, breviter autem de doctrina scribit ad discipulum eruditum, quem ipse et docuerat et saepe audierat. Sed tamen attingit praecipuas materias doctrinae, ut et tunc extarent testimonia Pauli contra adversarios Ti- mothei, et postea in Ecclesia haec testimonia con- servarentur. Quia Deus immensa misericordia vult nos de doctrina certos esse, vult sciri, quan- do, per quos, quibus testimoniis propagata sit. Ideo addit Apostolis magnos coetus comitum, et manifestis miraculis testatur eos circumferre vo- cem, divinam.

Catalogus annorum Pauli.

35. 1. Annus conversionis Pauli. An- nus a natali Christi 35.

36. 2. Ivit Paulus in Arabiam.

39. 5. Ivit in Tarsum, Acto. 9.

42. 8. Barnabas Paulum ex Tarso An- tiochiam ducit, Acto. 11.

44. 10. Ivit in Cyprum, Acto. 13. comi- tante eum Barnaba. Et iuben- te Spiritu sancto. Ibique Ser- gius proconsul convertitur.

45. 11. Profectus in Pergen Pamphyliae, Antiochiam Pisidiae, Iconium et vicinas urbes, Acto. 14.

48. 14. Fames praedicta ab Agabo to- tum terrarum orbem affligit. Iosephus.

Anno Christi, Anno post converssionem.

51. 17. Synodus Ierosolymae cui Paulus interfuit, Acto. 15.

52. 18. Rediit in Iconium et Lystram, ubi Timotheum sibi adiunxit et traiecit in Macedoniam. Et fuit Corinthi, ubi scripsit Epi- stolam ad Romanos.

53. 19. 54. 20. 55. 21. Rediit in Asiam, et cum fuisset biennio Ephesi, Timotheo Ecclesiam abiens commen- davit.

56. 22. Rediit in Phrygiam, ubi Laodi- ceae scripsit primam Episto- lam ad Timotheum.

57. 23. Rediit Paulus in Macedoniam prius peragrata Phrygia et fini- 58. 24. bus Galatarum, cumque ve- nisset in Macedoniam, scripsit in Philippis utramque Episto- lam ad Corinthios non longo intervallo. Postea rediit in Asiam, ac venit Mytilenen, item in Samum et Miletum, Acto. 20.

59. 25. 60. 26. Postremum iter ad Ierosolymam, quo cum venit capitur, et bien- nio Cesareae captivus tenetur.

61. 27. 62. 28. Remissus Romam. Sed tunc liberatus est ore leonis, ut 2. Timoth. 4. narrat.

63. 29. 64. 30. 65. 31. 66. 32. 67. 33. Fuit biennium in conducto.

68. 34. 69. 35. Interfectus Paulus a Nerone paulo ante eius mortem.

70. 36. Decimus quartus Neronis, quo Nero sibi conscivit mortem.

## 1:1
Paul, Apostle of Jesus Christ.

At the beginning Paul places his name first, because in the Church it is necessary that testimonies exist, and that it be known through whom those testimonies have been delivered: and mention is made of the apostolic office, so that we may know that his doctrine is to be believed, as the voice of God sounding from heaven, just as he himself says to the Galatians, that he did not receive the doctrine from men, and he says many things about his calling, so that he may confirm the authority of his doctrine. And it is profitable for the younger ones to be reminded of the distinction between Prophets, Apostles, and other teachers. Prophets were those who were immediately called by God to teach, and to illustrate the promise concerning the Messiah, and for certain political counsels, and they have divine testimonies that they do not err in doctrine, namely certain peculiar miracles. Apostles were those who were immediately called by Christ to teach the Gospel, not for political governance, and they have divine testimonies that they do not err in doctrine, and they can teach in any place. Bishops and other Doctors are mediately called by God through human election, and they ought to sound forth the doctrine received from the Apostles without any change, but when they change it, they err, as often happens, therefore their doctrine is to be judged from the testimonies of the Apostles. It is necessary to give these warnings at the beginning concerning the title, lest anyone think the name of Apostle was added idly: therefore Paul expressly adds that he is an Apostle sent by divine command. But just as it is necessary for them to teach, so it is necessarily commanded to us to hear this doctrine.

That they teach no other things, and that they do not attend to fables.

The admonition is necessary, and it is the first in the Church, that other doctrines not be proposed while the doctrine delivered by God is omitted. Likewise, that curious questions not be agitated while necessary matters are omitted, because the Church is bound to the foundation, as is said elsewhere: No one can lay another foundation, besides that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ. Likewise: If anyone teaches another Gospel, let him be anathema.

And as a wise Doctor at the beginning he recites the sum, by which he briefly embraces all things which are necessary to be in a man converted to God, The sum of the commandment is love, from a pure heart and a good conscience, and faith unfeigned.

Latin:

Paulus Apostolus Iesu Christi.

Initio Paulus nomen praeponit, quia in Ec- clesia oportet extare testimonia, et sciri per quos ea testimonia tradita sint: et fit mentio muneris apostolici, ut sciamus credendum esse ipsius do- ctrinae, tanquam voci Dei de coelo sonanti, sicut ipse inquit ad Galatas, se doctrinam non acce- pisse ab hominibus, et de sua vocatione multa dicit, ut autoritatem suae doctrinae confirmet. Et prodest commonefieri iuniores de discrimine Prophetarum, Apostolorum, et aliorum docen- tium. Prophetae fuerunt, qui immediate a Deo vocati sunt ad docendum, et ad illustrandam pro- missionem de Messia, et ad aliqua consilia poli- tica, et habent testimonia divina, quod non er- rent in doctrina, videlicet quaedam peculiaria miracula. Apostoli fuerunt, qui immediate a Christo vocati sunt ad docendum Evangelium, non ad gubernationem politicam, et habent testimonia divina, quod non errent in doctrina, et possunt quolibet loco docere. Episcopi et alii Doctores sunt mediate vocati a Deo electione humana, et sonare debent doctri- nam ab Apostolis acceptam sine aliqua mutatione, cum vero mutant, errant, ut saepe fit, ideo earum doctrina iudicanda est ex testimoniis Apostolorum. Haec monere initio de titulo necesse est, ne quis putet nomen Apostoli otiose additum esse: ideo diserte addit Paulus, se esse Apostolum mandato divino missum. Sicut autem ipsi necessarium est docere, ita nobis necessario mandatum est audire hanc doctrinam.

Ne alia doceant, et ne attendant fabulis.

Necessaria est admonitio, est et prima in Ecclesia, ne omissa doctrina divinitus tradita pro- ponantur aliae doctrinae. Item ne curiosae quae- stiones agitentur omissis rebus necessariis, quia Ecclesia alligata est ad fundamentum, ut alibi dicitur: Fundamentum aliud ponere nemo po- test, praeter id quod positum est, quod est Chri- stus Iesus. Item: Si quis aliud Evangelium do- cet, anathema sit.

Ac ut sapiens Doctor initio summam reci- tat, qua breviter complectitur omnia, quae in homine converso ad Deum esse necesse est, Summa mandati est dilectio, ex corde puro et conscientia bona, et fide non ficta.

## 1:5
From a pure heart.

First, what does he call a pure heart, or who at all is there in this weakness of men, whose heart is pure? I answer according to the saying of the Apostles in Acts chapter 15: Purifying their hearts by faith. He calls a pure heart, therefore, one purified by faith, that is, not Epicurean, not Academic, remaining in doubt, not Saulitic, that is, fleeing from God and being angry at God, but now rightly feeling about God, and approaching him in true recognition and trust of the Son of God, and truly acknowledging that we, although unclean, are nevertheless received, and our filth, although many and great, is covered, the cleanliness and righteousness of the Son of God being imputed to us. Thus also David says: You shall sprinkle me, O Lord, with hyssop and I shall be cleansed. And afterwards: Create in me a clean heart, O God, that is, rightly feeling about God, sprinkled with the blood of the Son. And when hearts are thus purified by faith, they receive the Holy Spirit, they submit themselves to God, they now begin to seek the glory of God, and to obey God, and they have the true beginnings of the love of God and neighbor. For Paul includes under the name of love the works of all the commandments of the Decalogue, just as he says elsewhere: Love is the fulfillment of the law. And 1 John 5: This is the love of God, to keep his commandments.

faith and a good conscience. And 1 Peter 3: Keeping a good conscience. Likewise to the Corinthians: This is our boasting, the testimony of our conscience. Nor do these two conflicting things remain at the same time: the action by which a man violates the law of God knowingly and willingly, and that faith which is a trust in mercy receiving remission, because the oath says, As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live. The prayer is copulative, that is, vivification by faith does not happen until no conversion happens, that is, until someone has the purpose of sinning. And such offenses are usually called mortal sins, when the Holy Spirit and trust in mercy are poured out, and thus having fallen, they are then subject to the wrath of God and eternal death, according to those sayings, Because of this the wrath of God comes upon the disobedient. Nor are the fanatical imaginations of those to be received who pretend that those once reborn cannot again pour out the Holy Spirit, since it is manifestly said in 2 Peter 2: If they are again overcome by the defilements which they had escaped, the latter things become worse for them than the former. Likewise: Let him who stands see that he does not fall. Therefore let us be vigilant, so that the righteousness of a good conscience may be retained, that is, a good purpose.

And with faith not feigned.

Let this, therefore, be the definition: Love is a virtue by which, after we have apprehended by faith the mercy of God promised on account of the Son, we now begin to love him and give him thanks, and we submit ourselves to him, and we begin obedience according to all the commandments, with a certain sense of joy in God. But as I said before, that hearts are first purified by faith, so also afterwards it must be known that this begun obedience, even if there are still many impurities in us, nevertheless pleases God on account of the Mediator, nor can love be begun, nor does it please, unless faith precedes. Therefore Paul also soon adds: from faith not feigned.

Latin:

Ex corde puro.

Primum quid nominat cor purum, aut quis est omnino in hac imbecillitate hominum, cuius cor sit purum? Respondeo iuxta dictum Aposto- lorum in Actis capite 15.: Fide purificans corda eorum. Nominat igitur cor purum, fide puri- ficatum, id est, non Epicureum, non Academi- cum, manens in dubitatione, non Sauliticum, id est, fugiens Deum, et irascens Deo, sed iam recte sentiens de Deo, et ad eum accedens in vera agnitione et fiducia filii Dei, et agnoscens vere nos quanquam immundos tamen recipi, et tegi nostras sordes quanquam multas et magnas, im- putata nobis munditie et iusticia filii Dei. Sic et David inquit: Asperges me Domine hyssopo et mundabor. Et postea: Cor mundum crea in me Deus, id est, recte sentiens de Deo, consper- sum sanguine filii. Et cum sic purificantur fide corda, accipiunt Spiritum sanctum, se Deo sub- iiciunt, iam incipiunt quaerere gloriam Dei, et obedire Deo, et habent vera initia dilectionis Dei et proximi. Comprehendit enim Paulus no- mine dilectionis opera omnium praeceptorum De- calogi, sicut alibi inquit: Dilectio est impletio legis. Et 1. Iohannis 5.: Haec est dilectio Dei, mandata eius custodire.

fidem et bonam conscientiam. Et 1. Petri 3.: Con- scientiam bonam retinentes. Item ad Corinth.: Haec est gloriatio nostra, testimonium conscien- tiae nostrae. Nec simul manent haec duo pu- gnantia, Actio qua violat homo legem Dei sciens et volens, et illa fides, quae est fiducia miseri- cordiae accipiens remissionem, quia Iusiurandum dicit, Vivo ego, dicit Dominus, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed ut convertatur et vivat. Oratio copulativa est, id est, non fit vivificatio fide, do- nec nulla fit conversio, id est, donec aliquis ha- bet propositum peccandi. Et talia delicta nomi- nantur usitate peccata mortalia, cum effunduntur Spiritus sanctus et fiducia misericordiae, et sic lapsi, tunc sunt rei irae Dei et aeternae mortis, iuxta illa dicta, Propter hoc venit ira Dei super inobedientes. Nec recipiendae sunt fanaticae imaginationes eorum, qui fingunt semel renatos non posse rursus effundere Spiritum sanctum, cum manifeste dicatur 2. Petri 2.: Si rursus superan- tur ab inquinamentis quae effugerant, fiunt eis posteriora peiora prioribus. Item: Qui stat, vi- deat ne cadat. Ideo simus vigilantes, ut iusticia bonae conscientiae retineatur, id es, bonum propositum.

Et fide non simulata.

Sit igitur haec definitio: Dilectio est virtus, qua postquam misericordiam Dei propter filium promissam fide apprehendimus, iam eum diligere et ei gratias agere incipimus, et nos ei subiicimus, et obedientiam iuxta omnia mandata incoamus, cum quodam sensu laetitiae in Deo. Ut autem antea dixi, prius fide purificari corda, ita et po- stea sciendum est, hanc incoatam obedientiam, etsi adhuc multae sordes in nobis sunt, tamen placere Deo propter mediatorem, nec incoari di- lectio potest, nec placet, nisi praecedat fides. Ideo et Paulus mox addit ex fide non fucata.

## 1:5
From a good conscience, and faith not feigned.

It is necessary that this rule concerning our obedience or good works be known universally. Although our obedience is far from perfection, and sins cling to us, nevertheless it is necessary that such be the obedience in the converted, that there be in us faith and a good conscience, that is, a purpose of not sinning. This degree is necessary in the converted, which is also confirmed by this saying of Paul, and others, as below: Wage the good warfare, having

Nor can the love of God be begun, nor do works please God unless faith precedes. But lest faith be understood only as knowledge, such as is in the devils, he adds the particle, That it be not feigned. Faith not feigned is, therefore, an assent by which we embrace all the sayings of the Gospel, and in these the promise of grace, and it is a trust acquiescing in the Mediator according to that promise. This trust, which indeed, when it consoles and raises up hearts in true sorrows, and draws them as it were from the depths, can be felt, distinguishes idle knowledge from faith not feigned. Of this faith it is said: Being justified by faith we have peace. Nor does Paul understand the word of faith in any other way in this place. And since we know that the corruptions of Paul's doctrine have been devised after the words were falsely understood, let us be diligent in retaining the proper meaning, which being retained, there is neither obscurity nor ambiguity in Paul's speech.

But in order that this brief summary may be understood in this place, the whole doctrine of Justification must be contemplated by the mind, namely, that in true repentance or sorrows the voice of the Gospel must be heard and thought upon, which on account of the Son of God freely, not on account of at the same time this offers all our dignity, the remission of sins, the imputation of righteousness, the Holy Spirit, and the inheritance of eternal life. Moreover, there is an eternal and immovable command of God concerning the Son: Hear him. It is necessary, therefore, to assent to the promise offering reconciliation, namely those goods which I have mentioned. By this faith, man truly receives the remission of sins, the imputation of righteousness, and the Holy Spirit, and becomes an heir of eternal life on account of the Son of God freely, not on account of his own dignity or merit. And to this effect, the prayer is customary in our Churches: We are justified by faith alone. For it signifies that to be justified is to receive the remission of sins and the imputation of righteousness, with which is joined the gift of the Holy Spirit and the inheritance of eternal life.

And it is most manifest that it is said to be by imputation for this reason, because we do not yet have that entire newness, concerning the transfusion of which the monks speak, but we are righteous by the granted remission of sins, and the righteousness of the Son of God imputed to us, and as it were clothed with it by imputation, and yet it is most true that at the same time newness is begun in us, which is brought about by the Holy Spirit poured into our hearts, and kindling faith in us, and other virtues, and joining us to the Son of God, reigning at the right hand of the eternal Father, as it is said in Acts 2: Exalted by the right hand of God, he received the promise of the Holy Spirit, which he poured out upon us.

Furthermore, that imagination must be rejected which feigns that a man is only prepared at the beginning by faith, but afterwards is righteous by his own love, or by his own virtues, as when we say: Motion warms, motion is a preparation, afterwards we are warm with heat. But the person received by faith is thereafter also righteous, that is, accepted by God for eternal life, not on account of his own virtues, because much filth still remains in us, but on account of the Mediator by faith alone, by which we also thereafter have the remission of sins, and are clothed with the imputed righteousness of the Mediator. However, new obedience is pleasing in the reconciled, with this very confession preceding, that many great impurities still cling to us, according to that: No living person is justified in your sight. But yet this begun obedience is also pleasing on account of the Mediator by faith.

These things are often recited more copiously elsewhere, from where a longer explanation may be taken. Now I have only briefly reviewed these things, so that the younger ones, being admonished, may know that Paul speaks of this very faith, concerning which he says elsewhere: Having been justified by faith, we have peace. And let them exercise this in daily invocation and in consolations.

Latin:

Ex conscientia bona, et fide non simulata.

Universaliter hanc regulam de nostra ob- edientia seu de bonis operibus sciri necesse est. Quanquam nostra obedientia procul abest a per- fectione, et haerent in nobis peccata, tamen opor- tet talem esse obedientiam in conversis, ut sint in nobis fides et bona conscientia, id est, propo- situm non peccandi. Hic gradus in conversis ne- cessarius est, quod et hoc dicto Pauli confirmatur, et aliis, ut infra: Milita bonam militiam, habens

Nec incoari dilectio Dei potest, nec placent opera Deo nisi praecedente fide. Ne autem fides intelligatur tantum de noticia, qualis est in dia- bolis, addit particulam, Ne sit simulata. Est igitur fides non simulata assensio, qua amplecti- mur omnia dicta Evangelii, et in his promissio- nem gratiae, et est fiducia acquiescens in media- tore iuxta eam promissionem. Haec fiducia, quae quidem, cum in veris doloribus consoletur et eri- gat corda, et quasi ex inferis retrahat, sentiri potest, discernit otiosam noticiam a non simulata fide. De hac fide dicitur: Iustificati fide pacem habemus. Nec aliter intelligit Paulus vocabulum fidei hoc loco. Cumquae sciamus corruptelas doctrinae Pauli excogitatas esse, postquam voca- bula falso intellecta sunt, simus diligentes in re- tinenda propria significatione, qua retenta, nec obscuritas nec ambiguitas est in Pauli oratione.

Ut autem haec brevis summa hoc loco intel- ligatur, mente intuenda est tota doctrina de Iu- stificatione, videlicet in vera poenitentia seu do- loribus vocem Evangelii audiri et cogitari necesse est, quae propter filium Dei Gratis, non propter ullam nostram dignitatem simul offert haec qua- tuor, remissionem peccatorum, imputationem iusticiae, Spiritum sanctum et haereditatem vitae aeternae. Est autem mandatum Dei aeternum et immotum de Filio: Hunc audite. Necesse est igitur assentiri promissioni offerenti reconciliatio- nem, videlicet illa bona, quae dixi. Hac fide homo vere accipit remissionem peccatorum, im- putationem iusticiae et Spiritum sanctum, et fit haeres vitae aeternae propter filium Dei Gratis, non propter propriam dignitatem aut meritum. Et in hanc sententiam usitata est oratio in nostris Ecclesiis, Sola fide iustificamur. Significat enim iustificari accipere remissionem peccatorum et im- putationem iusticiae, cum qua coniuncta est do- natio Spiritus sancti, et haereditas vitae aeternae.

Et manifestissimum est ideo de imputatione dici, quia nondum habemus illam totam novita- tem, de cuius transfusione monachi dicunt, sed sumus iusti donata remissione peccatorum, et imputata nobis iusticia filii Dei, et quasi ea vestiti per imputationem, et tamen verissimum est, si- mul incoari in nobis novitatem, quae fit Spiritu sancto effuso in corda nostra, et accendente in nobis fidem, et alias virtutes, et copulante nos filio Dei, regnanti ad dexteram aeterni patris, sicut dicitur Actorum 2.: Dextera Dei exaltatus accepit promissionem Spiritus sancti, quem effu- dit in nos.

Prorsus etiam reiicienda est imaginatio, quae fingit hominem tantum initio praeparari fide, po- stea vero iustum esse propria dilectione, seu pro- priis virtutibus, ut cum dicimus: Motus calefacit, Motus praeparatio est, postea calore sumus calidi. Sed persona fide recepta deinceps etiam est iusta, id est, accepta Deo ad vitam aeternam, non pro- pter proprias virtutes, quia multum adhuc manet in nobis sordium, sed propter mediatorem sola fide, qua et deinceps habemus remissionem pec- catorum, et imputata iusticia mediatoris vestiti sumus. Placet autem nova obedientia in recon- ciliato, hac ipsa confessione praecedente, quod adhuc multae magnae sordes in nobis haereant, iuxta illud: Non iustificatur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens. Sed placet tamen et haec incoata obedientia propter mediatorem fide.

Haec saepe alibi copiosius recitantur, unde sumatur explicatio longior. Nunc tantum brevi- ter haec recensui, ut iuniores admoniti sciant Paulum loqui de hac ipsa fide, de qua alibi in- quit: Fide iustificati pacem habemus. Et hanc in quotidiana invocatione et in consolationibus exer- ceant.

## 1:8
The Law is good if one uses it lawfully.

The summary having been recited, he enters into the commemoration concerning the use of the law. For many of the Jews, still dreaming that the Mosaic polity was to remain, contended that the Mosaic rites were necessary, just as this controversy had been recently agitated then in the Synod, which is recited in the Acts, chapter 15. Therefore, as often elsewhere, so here too he reproves those who defend the law of Moses, and adds a few things concerning the use of the law.

Moreover, it is a notable proposition, The Law is good if one uses it lawfully, where he warns that many things must be considered concerning the use of the law, namely both the distinctions of the laws themselves, and the ends of the law. It is known, however, that one part of the law, namely the Moral, which we call the Decalogue, is the eternal wisdom in the divine mind, the knowledge of which has been transfused into men, so that God might be truly acknowledged, and all our powers might correspond with the mind and will of God. And although afterwards the nature of men was turned away from God, yet in the whole human race these knowledges remain in some way, because God wills that his judgment against sin be acknowledged by all, he also wills that men, although not reborn, restrain and coerce their locomotive power.

The other two parts, namely the forensic Laws and the Ceremonies, were the nerves of this polity of Israel, destined to perish with the polity itself. But concerning the use of all parts, this proposition is true: No works of the law, neither moral nor others, merited the remission of sins, nor were they the thing by which David, Jeremiah, Daniel, and the like were righteous before God, but they were discipline, by which the not-reborn were restrained, and exercises in which the reborn declared their obedience and confession. Furthermore, the rites were signs distinguishing this polity from others, because God willed that the people from whom the Redeemer would be born be known, and for that reason he willed that there be a certain seat of his Church at that time. It is necessary to know that by this counsel that polity was so constituted, and distinguished from other nations by peculiar rites.

But now let us speak concerning the Decalogue, that is, concerning the natural and perpetual law, omitting the other laws. For concerning this very part, namely concerning the moral law, Paul says: The Law is laid down for the unjust, that is, it urges and presses upon the unjust. And he adds examples pertaining properly to the moral law: he says it is set for the perjured, for murderers, and for fornicators.

Here, first, let true doctrine be fixed in minds against the Antinomians, that the moral law is not mutable or idle, like the Spartan law concerning iron money, or the Theban law concerning placing debtors who do not pay into a basket: but that it is eternal and immutable wisdom in the divine mind, the knowledge of which has been handed down to the rational creature, so that we may know that God exists, and what kind of being He is, and that He is an avenger, and that He always obligates us. First, that we may obey.

Secondly, if we do not obey, that this stubborn nature may be horribly destroyed. Because God is already angry on account of these things, as it is commonly said: Every law obligates either to obedience or to punishment. And Adam understood this obligation of the law very clearly when, after the fall, he felt the wrath of God and judged that he must be utterly destroyed by the just judgment of God, nor could any creature solve this argument, but the Son of God intervened, who both performed obedience and derived the punishment onto Himself, so that the law would not be void, and yet men would be saved.

These things must be thought upon very often, so that we may learn in some way that these are the greatest matters: the law of God, sin, the wrath of God, the most certain order of God’s justice inflicting punishment. And therefore daily examples are at hand: death, and other huge calamities of men, diseases, pains, slaughters, devastations. These common miseries are the ordered effects of the law, and testimonies of the wrath of God against sins, as it is said in Psalm 38: Because of iniquities You correct man. And it is greatly to be lamented that men rush securely into various crimes, as if the law of God were an empty picture.

Let us know, therefore, that the truth of God exists, and let us rightly understand its use. There are, however, two uses universally against the unregenerate: To Restrain and To Punish. Therefore, even the unregenerate must be taught that they are enclosed in the prison of the law, and that discipline must be maintained for these four reasons.

First: Because God commands it, and all creatures owe obedience to God.

Secondly: That they may avoid present and eternal punishments, because there is no doubt at all that atrocious crimes in this life are accompanied by atrocious punishments, according to those sayings: Gen. 6, Matt. 26: He who takes the sword will perish by the sword. Likewise, Exod. 20: God will not hold him guiltless, etc. Likewise, Heb. 13: God will judge fornicators and adulterers. Likewise, Prov. 12: The Lord will abhor a lying lip. Daily experience shows that these rules are true and that this is the divine order which God executes.

Thirdly: God wishes that individuals spare the lives of others, for we are not born for ourselves alone, but there is a common kinship in the human race, and individuals ought to foster common society, and that voice of Cain is to be execrated, Gen. 4: Am I my brother's keeper? Therefore, impulses in individuals must be curbed, so that others may live, lest society be dissipated, and education and instruction be disturbed. These three causes can be easily understood.

The fourth cause is that of which Paul speaks in the 3rd chapter to the Galatians: The law is a schoolmaster in Christ, that is, men cannot be taught where there is no discipline. Likewise, the benefits of the Son of God are not understood without the acknowledgment of sin. Likewise, they are not received as long as men persevere in crimes against their conscience.

May all these causes exhort to the diligence of governing discipline, which indeed it is possible for a man, even one not regenerate, to govern in some way: because God wills that there remain a freedom of will in man for governing locomotive action.

Discipline, however, is the governance of locomotive action, even if hearts are unclean, so that the fact that Achilles, admonished by reason, withdraws his hand so as not to kill Agamemnon, is the governance of locomotive action, even if the heart burns with a huge fire.

Furthermore, it must be known that, even though God commands and demands discipline, and horribly punishes the violation of discipline, nevertheless discipline by no means merits the remission of sins, nor is it justice before God by which men are just, that is, acceptable to God: but it covers us, just as Adam and Eve covered their uncleanness and horrible contamination with a fig leaf, that is, it is some sort of curb, which is necessary for life and society.

Remember also this saying: The law is laid down for the unjust, that the whole political order, governments, marriage, the distinction of property, contracts, judgments, and punishments may be approved: because the sinews of this order are most properly the precepts of the Decalogue. Since, however, the Decalogue is most truly the wisdom of God, it is manifest that this political order also is in its own kind a good thing. The second use of the law in the unregenerate is to condemn to present and eternal punishments, and present punishments are the beginning of divine judgment and destruction, from which some are delivered, namely those who are converted to God, while others are not delivered, but rush from them into eternal destruction. As the present calamity of Saul is the beginning of the punishments which oppress him for all eternity, so the calamity of David is the beginning of judgment and destruction, but the latter is delivered, because he seeks and receives the remission of sins by trust in the Redeemer. Of this use of the law, namely of condemnation, Paul speaks in 1 Corinthians 15, saying: The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. And Romans 7: Through the law sin becomes sin exceedingly, that is, very guilty, that is, guilt, the wrath of God, and casting away are felt as the law accuses us. Of these pains Hezekiah says, in Isaiah chapter 38: Like a roaring lion he has crushed all my bones.

I have spoken of the uses of the law in the unregenerate, and in the second use, concerning condemnation, those who are converted must be distinguished from others who are not converted. For the converted are delivered from condemnation, and yet they too feel the beginnings of this horrible judgment and many punishments, just as David, Jonathan, and others.

But before we speak of the use in the regenerate, the sentence must first be explained: The law is not laid down for the just. In order for this to be understood rightly and simply, the antithesis between the counsel of the Pseudo-apostles and the counsel of Paul must be considered. The Pseudo-apostles contended that the law must be kept so that by these works men might become just, and become more and more just, just as a mother might say to her daughter, 'For so many hours eat nothing, and afterwards be content with a single dish, and drink twice, and thus you will be temperate, and by this habituation you will be more temperate.' In this way, it is rightly said concerning discipline, but there must by no means be a confusion of discipline and justice before God. The Pseudo-apostles falsely transfer this example to justice before God. Paul therefore opposes this error and confusion with this saying: The law is not laid down for the just, namely with regard to justification. The law is not to be proposed so that a man may become just by the law or by works, or more just, but an entirely different thing is proposed by which a man becomes just before God, namely the Son of God; because of Him you are just by faith, that is, you have the remission of sins and His imputed justice, and because of Him you are gifted with the Holy Spirit and the inheritance of eternal life.

This is the first right and simple explanation: The law is not laid down for the just, namely with regard to justification, so that a man might become just or more just before God by the law, for you already have this benefit from elsewhere: as if we were to say to monks, 'Fools, why do you act thus? Do you wish to institute works and lay down laws so that men may become just?' There is by no means any need for us who believe in the Son of God for any other thing for justice, but because of Him are given the remission of sins, the imputation of justice, the Holy Spirit, and the inheritance of eternal life.

There follow also other interpretations, which are more customary, that the law is not laid down for the just, namely with regard to coercion, and also with regard to condemnation. And the interpretation concerning condemnation contains useful doctrine, and agrees with the sayings in Romans 5: Being justified by faith we have peace. Also, Romans 6: You are not under the law, but under grace. Also, Romans 8: There is now no condemnation for those who walk in Christ Jesus. Thus it is said: The law is not laid down for the just, that is, the law does not condemn the one who is just by faith, even if we still carry around many impurities and sins in this great infirmity of ours, but the saying speaks of the Just, that is, of one who has true faith, who, having been converted to God, has been received by trust in the Son of God. This person acknowledges and deplores the remnants of sin, but nevertheless knows that they are covered by the Son of God, and resists evil opinions and vicious desires. This interpretation is clear and brings consolation to pious minds. And the word κεῖται has a singular emphasis, as if to say: The law does not oppress the believer as if it were immovable and without any mitigation.

To Augustine, the interpretation concerning coercion is more familiar; the regenerate person, by the Holy Spirit, now obeys willingly, just as a mother loves and nourishes her offspring spontaneously, not coerced by law, even if the law also commands it: but because great infirmity remains in this life, many who are even regenerate must be restrained by discipline, as is manifest in the case of children, therefore I leave this interpretation.

What, however, is the use of the law in the regenerate? The answer customary to us is sufficiently neat, if it is taken correctly: Believers are free from the law as far as condemnation is concerned, not as far as obedience is concerned, that is, they are already reconciled and are pleasing to God, although they do not satisfy the law: but it does not follow from that that it is permitted for them to rush against their conscience: because this order always remains, that a rational creature should obey God, but this is of the Gospel benefit, because imperfect obedience is pleasing to God. For the Gospel does not grant contempt of God against conscience; therefore it is said, Matt. 5: Unless your righteousness shall exceed the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven. Likewise: I am not come to destroy the law, but to fulfill. And he himself fulfills, so that he may at the same time restore it in us, as it is said in Rom. 8: He condemned sin for sin, that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh. Likewise, Rom. 8: We establish the law through faith, that is, we are received and renewed for this reason, that the law may now be done and be pleasing.

This sentiment is often repeated in other cruder forms of speaking, 1 Cor. 6: Do not err, fornicators, idolaters, adulterers, etc., shall not possess the kingdom of God. And 1 John 3: Let no man deceive you, he who commits sin is of the devil. And Rom. 8: We are debtors, not to walk according to the flesh. Nor does debt signify violence, but the immovable order by which a rational creature is subject to the creator. And this very thing is the debt, that obedience should be spontaneous. And Zech. 8 it is said: Judge truth and the judgment of peace in your gates, and think no evil against your neighbors, and do not love a false oath: for all these are things that I hate, says the Lord. Likewise, Psalm 5: You are not a God who wills wickedness.

Therefore that will remains in God, eternal and immovable, which distinguishes good and evil, and wills good, and wills the obedience of the creature consistent with his will, and revealed through the son, of whom it is said, Matt. 17: Hear him. Therefore it is also said in the oath, Ezek. 33: As I live, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he may be converted and live. For the oath embraces both: the command concerning conversion, and the promise of reconciliation. From all these things it can be understood that it is rightly said that obedience, which is begun by faith and subjects us to the will of God which the law shows, is necessary.

Secondly, the law remains for the reborn, as far as doctrine is concerned, because it is necessary for them to have an express testimony as to which worship is pleasing to God; therefore it was said to Timothy, 2 Tim. chapter 3: Scripture divinely inspired is useful for teaching.

Thirdly, liberation from the law is more clearly understood when we contemplate the entire liberation, such as it will be in us in eternal life, where we shall live in divine light without sin, without death, without other calamities: but in this life, the remnants of sin, death, and many calamities cling to us. Just as, therefore, death and other punishments remain, so the law remains regarding the remnants of sin: for all these things accuse us at the same time, the law, death, and other punishments. To the afflicted David, his calamity is the voice of the law, but he becomes free from the law and from death in this way, because he struggles out by faith. Thus, therefore, to the just man, insofar as he is just, that is, insofar as he overcomes by faith, the law is not laid down, it does not condemn him. Re-read this doctrine concerning liberation from the law, and concerning the uses of the law, briefly recited here, but explained more copiously elsewhere.

Because I did it in ignorance.

He distinguishes persecutors, as in Rom. 10 and 11, some are converted, some are not converted. Concerning this distinction, it is also said in Matt. 12: Whoever shall speak a word against the son of man, it shall be forgiven him, but whoever shall speak against the Holy Spirit, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this nor in the future life. Here many things are disputed concerning blasphemy or the irremissible sin. Let us first hold this rule: the command concerning conversion is without any doubt universal, and so also without any doubt the promise of grace is universal, just as the Lord says: Come to me all you who labor and are burdened. And it is a horrible insult against the son of God to think the kingdom of the devil is more powerful than Christ, when indeed it has been said in Rom. 5: Grace abounds above sin. And let the promise be holy by the oath, As I live, I do not desire the death of the sinner, etc. Let us therefore flee to the son of God, and sustain ourselves with the promise, and let us resist doubt.

These are the commands divinely given, and such will feel consolation and will be received. Thus let us judge a posteriori, that these did not have the irremissible sin. Thus Paul and many other persecutors were saved: and indeed Paul says that his conversion is an example and testimony of the rule, that God truly wishes to receive sinners who flee to the son, freely for the sake of the son. Thus Aaron and Peter were saved, although they fell knowingly.

On the contrary, however, many persecutors perish in horrible hatred of God, like Judas; concerning these it can be judged a posteriori that they had the irremissible sin: but the same ones knowingly and willingly persevered in that horrible hatred against God, and did not flee to the son of God. Nor let us seek more subtly apriori what the irremissible sin is. Paul indicates some distinction when he says: Because I did it ignorantly.

But here questions arise: Aaron, Peter, Manasseh did not sin out of ignorance, and yet they were received, and the examples show that there is some distinction. Did the devil sin differently, knowing and proudly despising God, and Adam and Aaron differently, knowing but overcome by infirmity? But let us omit these questions, and judge concerning the will of God according to His own word: Hear Him. Everyone who believes in the Son has eternal life. Let us prefer the Son of God and His oath to the whole kingdom of sin. Let us also know that the Son of God is to be preferred to the voice of the law: and although this struggle is difficult and great, yet these rules are true and not to be neglected, according to that of Moses in chapter 18: Whoever will not hear the Son, I will be the avenger.

Let us hold to this true consolation, as I have said, and let us rouse ourselves and exhort all others to repentance and to faith, just as the Apostles also exhort these very people to repentance, to whom they say in Acts 4: But this Jesus you have crucified. And many of them were truly converted to God. And let the examples of Aaron, Paul, and many others be before our eyes, who, although they had been persecutors, were afterwards converted.

But if any do not wish to hear this consolation, what is the point of disputing about them, since they sin horribly by that very fact, that they then deny the voice of the Gospel, Grace abounds above sin. And they burn with such hatred that they would rather be eternal enemies of God than flee to the Son. In this way many perish in all ages, such as Saul, Ahithophel, Judas, Arius, and in our time Latomus of Louvain, Hoffmeister, and many others, at the thought of whose examples let us tremble, and let us ask to be ruled and confirmed by the Holy Spirit. As it is written in Luke 11: How much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him. And let us learn the truth with pious zeal, and let us beware lest we oppose it.

Moreover, there are distinctions between errors of ignorance and sins against conscience, which are also manifold. For even affected ignorance is a sin against conscience: and sometimes affected ignorance becomes blasphemy, as in many Pharisees, when, namely, their hearts being convicted by divine testimonies, they nevertheless burn with hatred and attempt to blot out the voice of God: and to persuade others that it is diabolical. These distinctions of sins can be judged afterwards, when we see some who, indulging in their own rages, have refused to return to repentance.

The saying is certain.

Above he has preached concerning the Law, now he inserts the sum of the Gospel, but very briefly, because he is writing to a hearer who had been his companion for a long time and had well known the whole voice of the doctrine. And at the beginning an assertion is placed, The saying is certain and to be embraced most firmly. By this assertion let us also confirm faith in ourselves, so that we may struggle out of doubts and truly determine that we are received and heard.

But here let everyone repeat to himself the entire doctrine concerning Justification, about which we always speak in the same way, and we take the beginning of the doctrine from the words of the Lord: Go preaching repentance and remission of sins in my name. These things must happen in conversion. First, it is necessary that sin be rebuked, that hearts be terrified, just as the Lord also says, Mark chapter 1: Repent. And 2 Corinthians 7 it is said: Godly sorrow produces repentance unto salvation. And in the last chapter of Isaiah: To whom shall I look? To the contrite and humbled, and him who trembles at my words. And the oath demands conversion in us when He says, Ezekiel 18 and 33: As I live, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live. And the examples agree: Adam, Eve, David are accused and tremble horribly.

These terrors and the sense of the wrath of God they have customarily called contrition, concerning which men must be rightly taught, lest we either flatter ourselves with blind security, or rush into despair, or the glory of the Son of God be injured and the Gospel be blotted out, just as the monks have fashioned foul errors by which the Gospel has been utterly obscured and true consolation has been snatched away from pious minds. For although it is true that there must be some contrition in us, some terrors and sorrows because we have offended God, yet these two errors are most false: that contrition must be sufficient, and that sufficient contrition merits the remission of sins. For first, no contrition can be sufficient, and when sorrow grows without consolation, man is submerged into death and eternal destruction, according to that of Romans 3: The Law works wrath. Likewise, 2 Corinthians 3: The Law kills. Then it is most certain that sins are remitted freely on account of the Son of God, and by no means on account of our contrition or love.

But let terrified minds hear the voice of the Gospel, which Paul recites here. The saying is certain and to be embraced most firmly, that Christ came into this world to save sinners. For Paul wishes to say this, that the voice of the Gospel concerning free reconciliation is by no means known to natural judgment, nor is it the voice of the law, but it is a singular and wonderful decree of the divinity concerning the redemption of the human race through the Son. Therefore he says expressly: Christ Jesus came into the world, as if he were saying: I bid you consider the cause why the Son of God came into the world. He was not sent like Moses or other Prophets, but he was this mediator beforehand, and now he has come to us for this reason, that he might become a victim: and it is necessary to know what benefits he brought, and how they are applied to us. He brings, however, the remission of sins, the imputation of righteousness, the gift of the Holy Spirit and of eternal life, and after this life, the resurrection and eternal life. Moreover, in this life, the remission of sins, the imputation of righteousness, the gift of the Holy Spirit and of eternal life are received on account of him freely, not on account of our merits, by faith alone. This is the proper voice of the Gospel, whose native understanding, so that we may retain it, requires that the terms be rightly understood: for from the depravation of terms other darknesses have arisen.

On the term Righteousness.

It is a Hebrew phrase in the word to be justified, as if I should say, Scipio has been justified by the accusing tribunes of the people, that is, he has been acquitted, and it has been pronounced that he is righteous. Thus here, for men to be justified on account of the mediator is for them to receive the remission of sins, and to be pronounced righteous, that is, to be reckoned righteous or accepted on account of him, with his righteousness imputed to us. And joined with this acceptance is the gift of the Holy Spirit and of eternal life.

And the term Righteousness becomes more clear when the Pauline meaning is distinguished from philosophical modes. For righteous in the philosophical manner signifies one having either universal or particular righteousness. But because we are not righteous before God by the fulfillment of the law, therefore another righteousness is announced in the Gospel, namely, the remission of sins and reconciliation on account of the Son of God. It is necessary, therefore, to distinguish the meaning of the word from philosophical modes. When Paul says, Being justified by faith we have peace, that is, being reconciled or accepted by God on account of Christ, by faith we have peace. And the conscience in great consternation acknowledges that you are unclean, it does not look around at its own qualities, as the Prophet cries out, Psalm 143: No living being shall be justified in your sight, namely, by his own purity or by his own qualities. But we shall speak more about imputation later.

On the term Faith.

It is most certain that by faith in this doctrine is not only signified knowledge, which even the devils possess, but it is signified at the same time knowledge of the history, and assent, by which you apply the promise to yourself, and trust resting in the mediator and in God, according to the promise: and there is no doubt that the Hebrews speak thus, according to that saying, Matthew 15: O woman, great is your faith. And this faith embraces the whole creed, in which he also professes that article, I believe the remission of sins. For here are expressed the benefits of God and of the mediator, of whom the preceding articles speak, and let individuals apply this article to themselves thus, I believe the remission of sins is given not only to others, but to me also. This faith rightly embraces the promise, by which you believe that remission and reconciliation are exhibited to you yourself, just as in Romans 4 Paul affirms that he is speaking of that faith which receives the promise, namely, by which you apply the promise to yourself, when he says: Therefore it is by faith freely, so that the promise may be firm.

But although writers after the Apostles were more negligent, yet sometimes they show what they felt. And the saying of Bernard is to be held, because the testimony is clear, and it is useful for confirming some. It is necessary first of all to believe that you cannot have the remission of sins except through the indulgence of God, but add, that you believe also this, that through him your sins are forgiven you. This is the testimony which the Holy Spirit bears in your heart, saying: Your sins are forgiven you. For thus the Apostle thinks that a man is justified freely by faith. These words exist in the first sermon on the Annunciation.

Let there be, therefore, a definition of faith. Faith is assent, by which we embrace the whole doctrine delivered to us by God, and in this the promise of grace also, and it is a trust resting in the mediator and in God according to the promise, and crying out: Abba Father. In this doctrine it is necessary that the terms Law, Gospel, Sin, and Grace be rightly understood, about which it has been spoken elsewhere; once the terms are explained, the proposition becomes clear: and let us apply it to teaching and comforting ourselves in sorrows, and daily in invocation: not on account of any merits of ours, but on account of the Son of God, we freely receive the remission of sins, and are reputed righteous, the righteousness of the mediator being imputed to us, and we are gifted with the Holy Spirit, and the inheritance of eternal life, by Faith, that is, trust in the mediator. And the command of God is immovable and eternal, that we truly believe we are thus received and pleasing on account of the Son, as it is said in John 3: God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life. And let the other testimonies be in sight, Romans 3 and 4 and elsewhere, not only so that we may be able to refute adversaries, but much more so that we may comfort and confirm ourselves. Let us also remember that these four things are comprehended at the same time: the remission of sins, the imputation of righteousness, the gift of the Holy Spirit, and the inheritance of eternal life.

Let the antithesis also be considered, in which there are two principal members. First, the monks shout that men merit the remission of sins, and are righteous, and merit eternal life on account of their own fulfillment of the law. Then, because no one knows when he has enough merits, they command men to always remain in doubt. These two imaginations are ethnic, arisen from human reasoning, which looks at the law in some way, and does not know the Gospel: just as Socrates, Xenophon, and the like disputed while doubting about the will of God.

But against these shadows, let the preachings of the Gospel concerning free reconciliation on account of the Son, and concerning faith, be opposed, and let us know that it is the command of God that we believe we are thus received on account of the Son by faith, and let us assiduously resist doubt. This antithesis brings some light to the younger ones. These must also be warned about corruptions.

The monks have thus corrupted this proposition, We are justified by faith, namely by formed love, and they understand faith only as knowledge, and they dream that a man is righteous on account of love, that is, the fulfillment of the law. This depravation expressly fights with Paul, because they say: We are not righteous by faith, but on account of love, when Paul clearly says, Romans 3, Galatians 2 and 3: It is impossible for the law to justify. And although others have sought other disguises of words, yet all corruptions tend to the same thing: they pretend that we are righteous by our own newness, and they remove this consolation, that we please God freely on account of the Son of God by faith. Therefore, all corruptions can be refuted by these sayings, Psalm 143: In thy sight shall no man living be justified. And Daniel, chapter 9: Not in our righteousness, but through thy mercy for the Lord's sake, hear us. Likewise, 1 Corinthians. 4: I am conscious of nothing, but in this I am not justified.

The corruption in Origen is similar to the corruption among the monks.

A recent depravation is that we are justified by faith as a preparation, so that afterwards we may be righteous by another thing, as if it were said, Motion warms, but afterwards the body is not warm by motion, but by heat. Thus they want a man to be righteous afterwards by his own newness. I oppose again that saying, In thy sight shall no man living be justified. Likewise, it is necessary that this sentence be retained, that we are righteous by imputation on account of the mediator. And to remove the doctrine concerning imputation, and to substitute for it this error, that a man is already righteous by his own newness, is a manifest impiety fighting with this saying, Genesis 15 and Romans 4: Abraham believed God, and it was imputed to him for righteousness.

Nor does that imagination agree with the Gospel, that a man is righteous on account of a bodily commixture of Christ with our soul or body, because it is properly said of the Holy Spirit that he is poured into our hearts, and is the immediate sanctifying person, as it is said in Acts chapter 2: Being by the right hand of God exalted, and having received of the Father the promise of the Holy Ghost, he hath shed forth this. And Galatians 4: God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts.

It is difficult to judge the labyrinths which are so variously constructed against the truth, but let the younger ones rightly learn the foundations for the glory of God, and for their own salvation. Once the foundations are rightly known, when age and experience approach, they will be able to refute contrary imaginations. And the things which we have said agree with the doctrine concerning Regeneration. For when hearts are sustained in true terrors by the voice of the Gospel, the Holy Spirit is at the same time effective, and it kindles faith and other spiritual motions, as is said in Galatians 3: That we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith. These are the beginnings of regeneration in the converted, concerning which it is said in Romans 8: Those who are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God. Likewise: If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, this one is not his. teach this, that a man is righteous, or is sanctified, or is freed from sin and eternal death by his own powers or actions: but this sanctification and vivification is the work of God, effecting it by His Holy Spirit, and then the reborn are truly the temple of God. For although this sanctification is a property attributed to the Holy Spirit, yet it is true that the whole divinity is present at the same time, as the Lord says in John 14: We will come to him, and make our abode with him. This great good must be acknowledged, and thanks must be given to God, because in His immense mercy He so humbles Himself for the sake of His Son, that He receives this miserable nature, still carrying about great filth, and is truly present in it, rules it, defends it against the devils, and endows it with light and eternal life: and let us take care to retain this great good, and let us not grieve the Holy Spirit with false opinions, or with falls against conscience, on account of which a man is deserted and falls into the kingdom of the devil, as is said in 2 Peter 2.

Although, however, the reborn is the temple of God, and the divinity is truly in him, and it is necessary that new light and sanctification, kindled by the Holy Spirit, grow in him: yet this sentence remains true, that a person is righteous, that is, pleases God not on account of newness, but is reckoned righteous by the righteousness of Christ imputed to him, and pleases Him on account of the Mediator Son by faith alone. Thus let us know both, that renewal happens through the Holy Spirit, and yet that this consolation concerning imputation must be held. And that this faith always shines before other virtues and invocation, according to that, Romans 5: Being justified by faith we have peace. For one cannot approach God without this consolation.

After, however, it has been spoken about the conversion of man: then it is customary to add the doctrine concerning good works, which for the sake of teaching I distribute into these questions. First: What works are to be done. Second: How they can be done. Third: How they please, since the remainder in us is sin. Fourth: For what causes they are to be done. Fifth: What is the distinction of sins. Concerning these questions it has been spoken elsewhere copiously and explicitly.

Latin:

Bona est Lex legitime utenti.

Recitata summa ingreditur in commemora- tionem de usu legis. Nam multi ex Iudaeis ad- huc somniantes mansuram esse politiam Mosai- cam, contendebant ritus Mosaicos necessarios esse, ut recens tunc fuerat agitata haec contro- versia in Synodo, quae recitatur in Actis capite 15. Itaque ut saepe alibi, ita hic quoque repre- hendit illos errores propugnantes legem Moysi, et pauca addit de usu legis.

Est autem insignis propositio, Bona est Lex legitime utenti, ubi monet de usu legis multa consideranda esse, videlicet et ipsarum legum dis- crimina, et fines legis. Notum est autem unam legis partem, scilicet Moralem, quam nomina- mus Decalogum, sapientiam aeternam in mente divina esse, cuius noticia in homines transfusa est, ut vere agnosceretur Deus, et omnes vires nostrae congruerent cum mente et voluntate Dei. Etsi autem postea natura hominum aversa est a Deo, tamen in toto genere humano manent hae noticiae aliquo modo, quia Deus vult ab omni- bus agnosci suum iudicium adversus peccatum, vult etiam homines quanquam non renatos fre- nare et coërcere locomotivam.

Aliae duae partes, videlicet Leges forenses, et Ceremoniae, erant nervi huius politiae Israël, interituri cum ipsa politia. Sed de omnium par- tium usu haec propositio vera est: Nulla opera legis, neque moralia, neque alia, merebantur remissionem peccatorum, nec erant illa res, qua David, Ieremias, Daniel, et similes erant iusti coram Deo, sed erant disciplina, qua non renati frenabantur, et exercitia, in quibus renati decla- rabant suam obedientiam et confessionem. Prae- terea ritus erant signa discernentia hanc politiam ab aliis, quia voluit Deus notum esse populum, ex quo nasceretur redemtor, eamque ob causam voluit tunc certam esse Ecclesiae suae sedem. Hoc consilio politiam illam ita constitutam esse, et peculiaribus ritibus distinctam ab aliis gentibus, sciri necesse est.

Sed iam dicamus de Decalogo, id est, de naturali et perpetua lege, omissis caeteris legi- bus. Nam de hac ipsa parte, videlicet de lege morali, inquit Paulus: Lex est posita iniustis, id est, urget et premit iustos. Et addit exempla per- tinentia proprie ad legem moralem: ait esse po- sitam periuris, homicidis et scortatoribus.

Hic primum sit infixa mentibus vera doctrina contra Antinomos, legem moralem non esse mu- tabilem aut otiosam, sicut lex Spartana de num- mo ferreo, aut lex Thebana de collocandis in cophinum obaeratis non solventibus: sed esse aeternam et immutabilem sapientiam in mente divina, cuius noticia creaturae rationali tradita est, ut sciamus esse Deum, et qualis sit, et quod sit vindex, et quod semper nos obliget. Primum, ut obtemperemus.

Secundo, si non obtemperemus, ut horribi- liter haec natura contumax destruatur. Quia Deus iam propter haec irascitur, sicut usitate dicitur: Omnis lex obligat vel ad obedientiam vel ad poenam. Et hanc obligationem legis valde per- spicue intellexit Adam, cum post lapsum sensit iram Dei, et iudicavit se iusto iudicio Dei peni- tus delendum esse, nec argumentum hoc ulla crea- tura solvere poterat, sed intervenit filius Dei, qui et obedientiam praestitit, et poenam in sese derivavit, ne lex esset irrita, et tamen servaren- tur homines.

Haec saepissime cogitanda sunt, ut aliquo modo discamus res esse maximas, legem Dei, peccatum, iram Dei, ordinem certissimum iusti- ciae Dei irrogantis poenam. Ideoque exempla quotidiana in promptu sunt, mors, et aliae in- gentes calamitates hominum, morbi, dolores, caedes, vastationes. Hae communes miseriae sunt effectus ordinati legis, et testimonia irae Dei adversus peccata, sicut dicitur Psalmo 38.: Pro- pter iniquitates corripis hominem. Et valde do- lendum est, homines securos ruere in varia sce- lera, quasi lex Dei sit inanis pictura.

Sciamus igitur veritatem Dei esse, et usum eius recte intelligamus. Sunt autem usus adver- sus non renatos duo universaliter, Coërcere et Punire. Docendi sunt igitur etiam non renati se inclusos esse carcere legis, et disciplinam prae- standam esse propter haec quatuor.

Primum: Quia Deus eam praecipit, et om- nes creaturae Deo obedientiam debent.

Secundo: Ut vitent poenas praesentes et aeternas, quia nequaquam dubium est atrocia scelera in hac vita atroces poenas comitari, iuxta illa dicta: Gen. 6., Matth. 26.: Qui acceperit gladium, gladio peribit. Item, Exod. 20.: Non habebit Deus insontem eum, etc. Item, Ebr. 13.: Scortatores et adulteros iudicabit Deus. Item, Proverb. 12.: Labium mendax abominabitur Do- minus. Has regulas veras esse et ordinem divi- num, quem Deus exequitur, quotidiana expe- rientia ostendit.

Tertio: Vult Deus singulos et aliorum vitae parcere, non enim nobis tantum nati sumus, sed communis cognatio est in genere humano, et sin- guli communem societatem fovere debent, et exe- cranda est illa vox Cain, Gen. 4.: Nunquid ego custos sum fratris mei? Frenandi sunt igitur im- petus, in singulis, ut alii vivere possint, ne dis- sipetur societas, nec turbentur educatio et insti- tutio. Hae tres causae facile intelligi possunt.

Quarta causa est, de qua Paulus loquitur ad Galatas 3. capite: Lex est paedagogus in Christo, id est, non possunt doceri homines, ubi nulla est disciplina, Item beneficia filii Dei non intelli- guntur sine agnitione peccati, Item non accipiun- tur, donec homines perseverant in sceleribus con- tra conscientiam.

Hae causae omnes ad diligentiam regendae disciplinae hortentur, quam quidem regere ali- quo modo possibile est homini etiam non renato: quia Deus vult reliquam esse libertatem volunta- tis in homine ad regendam locomotivam.

Est autem disciplina gubernatio locomotivae, etiamsi corda sunt immunda, ut quod Achilles admonitus a ratione retrahit manum, ne inter- ficiat Agamemnonem, gubernatio est locomotivae, etiamsi cor ardet ingenti incendio.

Praeterea sciendum est, etiamsi disciplinam praecipit et flagitat Deus, et horribiliter violatio- nem disciplinae punit, tamen disciplina nequa- quam meretur remissionem peccatorum, nec est iusticia coram Deo, qua homines iusti, id est, Deo accepti sint: sed tegit nos, sicut folio fici Adam et Eva suam immunditiem et horrendam contaminationem tegebant, id est, Est qualecun- que frenum, quod vitae et societati necessa- rium est.

Memineris etiam hoc dicto: Lex est iniustis posita, approbari totum ordinem politicum, im- peria, coniugium, distinctionem dominiorum, contractus, iudicia, poenas: quia nervi huius ordinis propriissime sunt praecepta Decalogi. Cum autem Decalogus verissime sit sapientia Dei, manifestum est et hunc ordinem politicum suo genere rem bonam esse. Alter usus legis in non renatis est conde- mnare ad poenas praesentes et aeternas, suntque initium iudicii divini et destructionis poenae praesentes, ex quibus liberantur aliqui, videlicet hi qui ad Deum convertuntur, alii non liberan- tur, sed ruunt ex illis in aeternum exitium. Ut praesens calamitas Saulis initium est poenarum, quae in omni aeternitate ipsum opprimunt, est et Davidis calamitas initium iudicii et destructio- nis, sed hic liberatur, quia petit et accipit re- missionem peccatorum fiducia redemtoris. De hoc usu legis, videlicet de condemnatione loqui- tur Paulus 1. Corinth. 15. inquiens: Aculeus mor- tis peccatum est, potentia vero peccati lex est. Et Roma 7.: Per legem peccatum fit excellenter peccatum, id est, valde reum, id est, reatus, ira Dei, proiectio, sentiuntur lege nos accusante. De his doloribus inquit Ezechias, Esaiae sap. 38.: Sicut leo rugiens contrivit omnia ossa mea.

Dixi de usibus legis in non renatis, ac in secundo usu de condemnatione discernendi sunt hi qui convertuntur, ab aliis qui non conver- tuntur. Nam conversi liberantur a condemna- tione, et tamen hi quoque sentiunt initia huius horrendi iudicii et multas poenas, sicut David, Ionathas et alii.

Priusquam autem dicimus de usu in renatis, prius declaranda est sententia: Iusto non est lex posita. Haec ut recte et simpliciter intelligatur, antithesis consideranda est consilii Pseudoaposto- lorum et consilii Paulini. Contendebant Pseudo- apostoli legem servandam esse, ut his operibus homines fierent iusti, et magis magisque fierent iusti, sicut diceret materfamilias filiae, tot horis nihil gustes, et postea unico ferculo contenta esto, et bis bibas, et sic eris temperans, et hac assuefactione magis temperans eris. Hoc modo de disciplina recte dicitur, sed nequaquam fa- cienda est confusio disciplinae et iusticiae coram Deo. Falso transferunt hoc exemplum Pseudo- apostoli ad iusticiam coram Deo. Opponit igitur Paulus huic errori et confusioni hoc dictum: Iusto non est lex posita, scilicet quo ad iustificationem. Lex non est proponenda, ut homo fiat iustus lege vel operibus, vel magis iustus, sed prorsus alia res proposita est, qua homo fit iustus coram Deo, scilicet filius Dei, propter hunc es iustus fide, id est, habes remissionem peccatorum et imputatam ipsius iusticiam, et propter ipsum: et es donatus Spiritu sancto et haereditate vitae aeternae.

Haec-est prima recta et simplex enarratio: Iusto non est lex posita, scilicet quo ad iustifica- tionem, ut homo lege fiat iustus vel magis iustus coram Deo, iam habes hoc beneficium aliunde: ut si diceremus monachis, Stulti quid agitis, vul- tis instituere opera et condere leges, ut homines fiant iusti: Nequaquam alia re nobis credentibus in filium Dei opus est ad iusticiam, sed propter ipsum donantur remissio peccatorum, imputatio iusticiae, Spiritus sanctus et haereditas vitae aeternae.

Sequunter et aliae interpretationes, quae magis usitatae sunt, Iusto non est lex posita, scilicet quo ad coactionem, item quo ad conde- mnationem. Ac interpretatio de condemnatione continet utilem doctrinam, et congruit cum dictis, Roma. 5.: Iustificati fide pacem habemus. Item, Roma. 6.: Non estis sub lege, sed sub gratia. Item, Roma. 8.: Nulla nunc condemnatio est his, qui in Christo Iesu ambulant. Sic dicitur: Iusto non est lex posita, id est, lex non condemnat fide iustum, etiamsi multum adhuc sordium et peccatorum in hac tanta infirmitate nostra cir- cumferimus, sed loquitur dictum de Iusto, id est, de habente veram fidem, qui conversus ad Deum fiducia filii Dei receptus est. Hic agnoscit et deplorat reliquias peccati, sed tamen scit eas tegi per filium Dei, et repugnat malis opinioni- bus et vitiosis cupiditatibus, Haec interpreta- tio perspicua est, et consolationem piis mentibus affert. Et verbum κεῖται singularem habet em- phasin, quasi dicat: Credentem lex non opprimit tanquam immota et sine ulla mitigatione.

Augustino familiarior est interpretatio de coactione, Renatus Spiritu sancto iam volens ob- temperat, ut mater sponte amat et alit sobolem non coacta lege, etiamsi lex quoque id praecipit: sed quia magna infirmitas in hac vita manet reli- qua, multi etiam renati disciplina frenandi sunt, ut de pueris manifestum est, ideo hanc interpre- tationem relinquo.

Quis est autem usus legis in renatis? Usitata nobis responsio est et satis concinna, si dextre accipiatur, Credentes liberi sunt a lege, quod ad condemnationem attinet, non quod ad obedien- tiam attinet, id est, sunt iam reconciliati, et pla- cent Deo, quanquam legi non satisfaciant: sed inde non sequitur, licere eis ruere contra con- scientiam: quia semper manet hic ordo, ut crea- tura rationalis Deo obediat, sed hoc est Evangelii beneficium, quod obedientia imperfecta Deo pla- cet. Nec enim concedit Evangelium comtemtum Dei contra conscientiam, ideo dicitur, Matth. 5.: Nisi iusticia vestra excellet supra iusticiam Phari- saeorum, non intrabitis in regnum coelorum. Item: Non veni solvere legem, sed implere. Et implet ipse, ut simul in nobis restituat, ut Ro- ma. 8. dicitur: De peccato damnavit peccatum, ut iusticia legis impleatur in nobis, non secundum carnem ambulantibus. Item, Roma. 8.: Legem stabilimus per fidem, id est, ideo recipimur et renovamur, ut iam fiat lex et placeat.

Haec sententia saepe repetita est aliis crassio- ribus formis loquendi, 1. Corinth. 6.: Ne erretis, scortatores, idolatrae, adulteri etc. non possi- debunt regnum Dei. Et 1. Ioannis 3.: Nemo de- cipiat vos, qui facit peccatum, ex diabolo est. Et Roma 8.: Debitores sumus, ut non secundum carnem ambulemus. Nec debitum significat vio- lentiam, sed immotum ordinem, quo creatura rationalis creatori subiecta est. Et hoc ipsum est debitum, ut obedientia sit spontanea. Et Zacha. 8. dicitur: Veritatem et iudicium pacis iudicate in portis vestris, et malum contra proximos non cogitate, et iuramentum mendax ne diligatis: omnia enim haec sunt quae odi, dicit Dominus. Item, Psalm. 5.: Non Deus volens impieta- tem tu es.

Manet igitur illa voluntas in Deo aeterna et immota, quae discernit bona et mala, et vult bo- na, et vult obedientiam creaturae congruentem suae voluntati, et patefactam per filium, de quo dicitur, Matth. 17.: Hunc audite. Ideo et in iuramento dicitur, Ezech. 33.: Vivo ego, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed ut convertatur et vivat. Utrumque enim complectitur Iusiurandum, man- datum de conversione, et promissionem recon- ciliationis. Ex his omnibus intelligi potest recte dici, obedientiam, quae incoatur fide, et subii- cit nos voluntati Dei, quam lex ostendit, neces- sarium esse.

Secundo manet lex renatis, quod ad doctri- nam attinet, quia oportet eos habere testimonium expressum, qui cultus Deo placeant, ideo dictum est ad Timotheum, 2. Timoth 3. capite: Scri- ptura divinitus inspirata utilis est ad docendum.

Tertio liberatio a lege clarius intelligitur, cum intuemur integram liberationem, qualis erit in nobis in vita aeterna, ubi in luce divina vive- mus sine peccato, sine morte, sine aliis calamita- tibus: sed in hac vita haerent in nobis reliquiae peccati, mors, et multae calamitates.
