Sicut igitur manent mors et aliae poenae, ita manet lex quo ad reliquias peccati: nam haec omnia simul nos accusant, lex, mors et aliae poenae. Pulso Davidi sua calamitas est vox legis, sed ita fit liber a lege et a morte, quia fide eluctatur. Sic igitur iusto, quatenus est iustus, id est, quatenus fide vincit, non est lex posita, non condemnat eum. Hanc doctrinam de liberatione a lege, et de usibus legis breviter hic recitatam, alibi copiosius expositam relegite.

Quia ingnorans feci.

Discernit persecutores, ut Roma. 10. et 11. aliqui convertuntur, aliqui non convertuntur. De hoc discrimine et Matthaei 12. dicitur: Qui dixerit sermonem contra filium hominis, remittetur ei, Qui autem dixerit contra Spiritum sanctum, non remittetur ei, neque in hac neque in futura vita. Hic multa disputantur de blasphemia seu de peccato irremissibili. Nos prius teneamus hanc regulam, Mandatum de conversione sine ulla dubitatione universale est, sic et sine ulla dubitatione promissio Gratiae universalis est, sicut Dominus inquit: Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis et onerati estis. Et horrenda contumelia est adversus filium Dei, cogitare regnum diaboli potentius esse Christo, cum quidem dictum sit Roma. 5.: Gratia exuberat supra peccatum. Et sancta sit promissio iureiurando, Vivo ego, nolo mortem peccatoris, etc. Confugiamus igitur ad filium Dei, et sustentemus nos promissione, et repugnemus dubitationi.

Haec sunt mandata divinitus, et tales sentient consolationem et recipientur. Ita iudicemus a posteriore, hos non habuisse peccatum irremissibile. Sic servatus est Paulus et alii multi persecutores: et quidem Paulus inquit, suam conversionem exemplum et testimonium esse regulae, quod Deus vere velit Gratis propter filium recipere peccatores confugientes ad filium. Sic servati sunt Aaron et Petrus, quanquam scientes lapsi sunt.

Contra vero multi persecutores pereunt horribili odio Dei, ut Iudas, de his a posteriori iudicari potest, habuisse eos peccatum irremissibile: sed iidem scientes et volentes perseverarunt in illo horribili odio adversus Deum, nec confugerunt ad filium Dei. Nec subtilius quaeramus a priori, quod sit peccatum irremissibile. Paulu aliquod discrimen indicat, cum ait: Quia igno rans feci.

Sed hic oriuntur quaestiones, Aaron, Petrus, Manasses, non peccaverunt ignorantia, et tamen recepti sunt, et esse aliquod discrimen exempla ostendunt. Aliter deliquit diabolus sciens et superbe despiciens Deum, aliter Adam, Aaron, scientes, sed superati infirmitate? Sed nos omittamus has quaestiones, et iudicemus de voluntate Dei iuxta verbum ipsius: Hunc audite. Omnis qui credit in filium, habet vitam aeternam, Anteferamus filium Dei, et iusiurandum toti regno peccati. Sciamus etiam anteferendum esse filium Dei voci legis: etsi autem haec pugna difficilis et magna est, tamen hae regulae verae sunt, et non negligendae, iuxta illud Moysi capite 18.: Qui non audierit filium, ego ultor ero.

Hanc consolationem veram, ut dixi, teneamus, et nos ipsos exuscitemus, et alios omnes hortemur ad poenitentiam et ad fidem, sicut et Apostoli hos ipsos hortantur ad poenitentiam, quibus Acto. 4. dicunt: Hunc autem Iesum vos crucifixistis. Et multi ex his vere conversi sunt ad Deum. Et sint nobis in conspectu exempla Aaron, Pauli et multorum aliorum, qui cum fuissent persecutores, postea conversi sunt.

Si qui vero nolunt audire hanc consolationem, quid attinet de eis disputare, cum eo ipso horribiliter peccent, quod tunc negant vocem Evangelii, Gratia exuberat supra peccatum. Et ita ardent odio, ut potius malint fieri aeterni hostes Dei, quam confugere ad filium. Hoc modo pereunt multi omnibus aetatibus, ut Saul, Achitophel, Iudas, Arius, et nostro tempore Latomus Lovaniensis, Hoffmeister, et alii multi, quorum exemplorum cogitatione expavescamus, et petamus nos regi et confirmari Spiritu sancto. Sicut scriptum est Luc, 11.: Quanto magis pater vester coelestis dabit Spiritum sanctum petentibus. Et pio studio discamus veritatem, et caveamus ne eam oppugnemus.

Caeterum sunt discrimina inter errata ignorantiae, et delicta contra conscientiam, quae etiam multiplicia sunt. Nam et affectata ignorantia delictum est contra conscientiam: et interdum fit affectata ignorantia blasphemia, ut in multis Pharisaeis, cum videlicet corda convicta testimoniis divinis, tamen ardent odio, et conantur delere vocem Dei: et aliis persuadere, esse eam diabo- licam. Haec discrimina peccatorum iudicari postea possunt, cum videmus aliquos indulgentes suis furoribus ad poenitentiam redire noluisse.

Certus est sermo.

Supra de Lege concionatus est, nunc inserit summam Evangelii, sed valde breviter, quia scribit ad auditorem, qui fuerat ipsius comes longo tempore, et bene cognoverat totam doctrinae vocem. Ac initio asseveratio posita est, Certus est sermo et firmissime amplectendus. Hac asseveratione in nobis quoque fidem confirmemus, ut ex dubitationibus eluctemur, et vere statuamus nos recipi et exaudiri.

Hic autem repetat unusquisque apud sese integram doctrinam de Iustificatione, de qua semper eodem modo dicimus, et exordium doctrinae ex verbis Domini sumimus: Ite praedicantes poenitentiam et remissionem peccatorum in nomine meo. Haec fieri oportet in conversione. Primum oportet argui peccatum, perterrefieri corda, sicut et Dominus inquit, Marc. 1. cap.: Agite poenitentiam. Et 2. Corinth. 7. dicitur: Tristitia secundum Deum poenitentiam efficit ad salutem. Et Esaiae ultimo: Ad quem respiciam? ad contritum et humiliatum, et trementem sermones meos. Et iusiurandum flagitat in nobis conversionem cum inquit, Ezech. 18. et 33.: Vivo ego, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed ut convertatur et vivat. Et Exempla congruunt, Adam, Eva, David, accusantur et horribiliter expavescunt.

Hos pavores et sensum irae Dei vocaverunt usitate contritionem, de qua recte docendi sunt homines, ne vel nobis ipsi blandiamur coeca securitate, vel ruamus in desperationem, vel laedatur gloria filii Dei, et deleatur Evangelium, sicut monachi tetros errores finxerunt, quibus Evangelium prorsus obscuratum est, et vera consolatio piis mentibus erepta est. Quanquam enim verum est, oportere in nobis esse aliquam contritionem, aliquos pavores, et dolores quod Deum offenderimus, tamen hi duo errores falsissimi sunt, quod oporteat sufficientem esse contritionem, et quod sufficiens contritio mereatur remissionem peccatorum. Primum enim nulla potest esse sufficiens contritio, et cum crescit dolor sine consolatione, mergitur homo in mortem et in aeternum exitium, iuxta illud Roma. 3.: Lex iram efficit. Item, 2. Corinth. 3.: Lex occidit. Deinde certissimum est remitti peccata Gratis propter filium Dei, et nequaquam propter nostram contritionem vel dilectionem.

Sed perterrefactae mentes audiant vocem Evangelii, quam hic recitat Paulus. Certus est sermo et firmissime amplectendus, quod Christus venerit in hunc mundum salvos facere peccatores. Vult enim hoc dicere Paulus, vocem Evangelii de gratuita reconciliatione nequaquam notam esse iudicio naturali, nec esse vocem legis, sed singulare et mirandum decretum esse divinitatis de redemtione generis humani per filium. Ideo diserte inquit: Christus Iesus venit in mundum, quasi dicat: Iubeo te causam considerare, cur in mundum venerit filius Dei. Non est missus sicut Moyses aut alii Prophetae, sed fuit hic mediator antea, et nunc ideo ad nos venit, ut fieret victima: et sciri oportet quae beneficia attulerit, et quomodo nobis adplicentur. Adfert autem remissionem peccatorum, imputationem iusticiae, donationem Spiritus sancti et vitae aeternae, et post hanc vitam resurrectionem et vitam aeternam. Accipiuntur autem in hac vita propter ipsum Gratis, non propter nostra merita, Sola Fide, remissio peccatorum, imputatio iusticiae, donatio Spiritus sancti et vitae aeternae. Haec est vox Evangelii propria, cuius intellectum nativum, ut retineamus, vocabula recte intelligenda sunt: nam ex depravatione vocabulorum aliae tenebrae ortae sunt.

De vocabulo Iusticiae.

Hebraica phrasis est in verbo Iustificari, ut si dicam, Scipio iustificatus est accusantibus tribunis plebis, id est, absolutus est, et, pronunciatum est eum esse iustum. Ita hic iustificari homines propter mediatorem, est accipere eos remissionem peccatorum, et pronunciari iustos, id est, reputari iustos seu acceptos propter ipsum, imputata nobis iusticia ipsius. Et cum hac acceptatione coniuncta est donatio Spiritus sancti et vitae aeternae.

Et fit magis perspicuum vocabulum Iusticiae, cum significatio Paulina discernitur a modis philosophicis. Nam Iustus more philosophico significat habentem seu iusticiam universalem seu particularem. Sed quia non sumus iusti coram Deo impletione legis, ideo in Evangelio annunciatur alia iusticia, scilicet remissio peccatorum et reconciliatio propter filium Dei. Necesse est igitur significationem vocabuli discernere a philosophi- cis modis. Cum ait Paulus, Iustificati fide pacem habemus, id est, reconciliati seu accepti Deo propter Christum fide pacem habemus. Et conscientia in magnis consternationibus agnoscit te immundum esse, non circumspectat suas qualitates, sicut clamat Propheta, Psalm. 143.: Non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens, scilicet propria munditie seu propriis qualitatibus. Sed de imputatione postea plura dicemus.

De vocabulo Fidei.

Certissimum est fide in hac doctrina non tantum significari noticiam, quam et diaboli tenent, sed significari simul noticiam historiae, et assensionem, qua promissionem tibi applicas, et fiduciam acquiescentem in mediatore et in Deo, iuxta promissionem: et sic loqui Hebraeos non dubium est, iuxta illud dictum, Matth. 15.: O mulier, magna est fides tua. Et complectitur haec fides totum symbolum, in quo et illum articulum profitetur, Credo remissionem peccatorum. Hic enim exprimuntur beneficia Dei et mediatoris, de quo articuli praecedentes loquuntur, et hunc articulum sic ad sese applicent singuli, Credo remissionem peccatorum non tantum aliis dari, sed mihi quoque. Haec fides recte amplectitur promissionem, qua tibi ipsi credis exhiberi remissionem et reconciliationem, ut Rom. 4. adfirmat Paulus se de ea fide loqui, quae promissionem accipit, videlicet, qua tibi ipsi promissionem applicas, cum inquit: Ideo ex fide gratis, ut firma sit promissio.

Etsi autem scriptores post Apostolos fuerunt negligentiores, tamen interdum quid senserint ostendunt. Estque dictum Bernardi tenendum, quia testimonium perspicuum est, et ad confirmandos aliquos prodest. Necesse est primo omnium credere, quod remissionem peccatorum habere non possis, nisi per indulgentiam Dei, sed adde, ut credas et hoc, quod per ipsum peccata tibi donantur. Hoc est testimonium, quod perhibet Spiritus sanctus in corde tuo, dicens: Dimissa sunt tibi peccata tua. Sic enim arbitratur Apostolus Gratis iustificari hominem per fidem. Haec verba extant in prima concione de annunciatione.

Sit igitur definitio fidei. Fides est assensus, quo amplectimur totam doctrinam a Deo nobis traditam, et in hac promissionem Gratiae quoque, et est fiducia acquiescens in mediatore et in Deo iuxta promissionem, et clamans: Abba Pater. In hac doctrina necesse est et recte intelligi vocabula Legis, Evangelii, Peccati, Gratiae, de quibus alibi dictum est, enarratis vocabulis, propositio fit perspicua: et eam accommodemus ad nos docendos et consolandos in doloribus, et quotidie in invocatione: non propter ulla merita nostra, sed propter filium Dei Gratis, certo accipimus remissionem peccatorum, et reputamur iusti, imputata nobis iusticia mediatoris, et donamur Spiritu sancto, et haereditate vitae aeternae, Fide, id est, fiducia mediatoris. Et mandatum Dei immotum et aeternum est, ut credamus vere nos sic recipi et placere propter filium, ut Iohannis 3. dicitur: Sic dilexit Deus mundum, ut filium suum unigenitum daret, ut omnis qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam. Ac sint in conspectu testimonia caetera, Roma. 3. et 4. et alibi, non solum ut refutare adversarios possimus, sed multo magis ut nos ipsos consolemur et confirmemus. Meminerimus etiam simul haec quatuor comprehendi, Remissionem peccatorum, imputationem iusticiae, donationem Spiritus sancti, et haereditatem vitae aeternae.

Antithesis etiam consideretur, in qua duo sunt praecipua membra. Primum monachi vociferantur, homines mereri remissionem, et esse iustos et mereri vitam aeternam propter propriam legis impletionem. Deinde, quia nemo scit, quando satis habeat meritorum, iubent homines semper manere in dubitatione. Hae duae imaginationes sunt ethnicae, ortae ex humana ratiocinatione, quae utcunque legem intuetur, et non novit Evangelium: sicut Socrates, Xenophon, et similes de voluntate Dei ambigentes disputarunt.

Contra vero opponantur his tenebris conciones Evangelii de gratuita reconciliatione propter filium, et de fide, et sciamus mandatum Dei esse, ut credamus nos sic recipi propter filium fide, et assidue repugnemus dubitationi. Haec antithesis iunioribus aliquid lucis adfert. Hi praemonendi sunt etiam de corruptelis.

Monachi sic corruperunt hanc propositionem, Fide iustificamur, scilicet formata dilectione, ac fidem intelligunt tantum noticiam, et somniant hominem iustum esse propter dilectionem, id est, legis impletionem. Haec depravatio ex- presse pugnat cum Paulo, quia dicunt: Non fide, sed propter dilectionem sumus iusti, cum Paulus clare dicat, Roma. 3., Galat. 2. et 3.: Impossi- bile est legi iustificare. Etsi autem alii alios fu- cos verborum quaesiverunt, tamen eodem ten- dunt omnes corruptelae: fingunt nos iustos esse nostra novitate, et removent hanc consolationem, nos propter filium Dei Gratis Deo placere fide. Refutari igitur omnes corruptelae possunt per haec dicta, Psalmo 143.: Non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens. Et Daniel. 9. cap.: Non in iusticia nostra, sed per misericordiam tuam propter Dominum exaudias nos. Item, 1. Corinth. 4.: Nihil mihi conscius sum, sed in hoc non iusificatus sum.

Corruptela apud Origenem similis est cor- ruptelae apud monachos.

Recens depravatio est, fide scilicet praepa- rante iustificamur, ut deinde alia re simus iusti, ut si dicatur, Motus calefacit, postea vero corpus non calet motu, sed calore. Sic volunt isti po- stea hominem sua novitate iustum esse. Oppono rursus dictum illud, Non iustificabitur in conspe- ctu tuo omnis vivens. Item, Retineri necesse est hanc sententiam, quod imputatione propter me- diatorem simus iusti. Ac tollere doctrinam de imputatione, et pro ea subiicere hunc errorem, quod homo sua novitate iam sit iustus, manifesta impietas est pugnans cum hoc dicto, Genes. 15. et Roma. 4.: Credidit Abraham Deo, et imputa- tum est ei ad iusticiam.

Nec illa imaginatio congruit cum Evangelio, quod homo sit iustus propter commixtionem cor- poralem Christi cum anima vel corpore nostro, quia proprie de Spiritu sancto dictum est, quod effundatur in corda nostra, et sit immediata per- sona sanctificans, ut in Actis capite 2. dicitur: Dextra Dei exaltatus, accipiens promissionem Spiritus sancti a patre, effudit eum in nos. Et Galat. 4.: Misit Deus spiritum filii sui in corda nostra.

Difficile est iudicare labyrinthos, qui tam varie struuntur contra veritatem, sed iuniores recte discant fundamenta propter gloriam Dei, et propter propriam salutem. Recte cognitis fun- damentis, cum accedet aetas et usus, refutare contrarias imaginationes poterunt. Et quae dixi- mus congruunt ad doctrinam de Regeneratione. Cum enim in veris pavoribus corda voce Evange- lii sustentantur, Spiritus sanctus simul est efficax, et accendit fidem et alios motus spirituales, sicut ad Galatas 3. dicitur: Ut promissionem Spiritus accipiamus per fidem. Haec sunt initia regene- rationis in conversis, de qua dicitur Roma. 8.: Qui spiritu Dei ducuntur, hi sunt filii Dei, Item: Si quis spiritum Christi non habet, hic non est eius. Nequaquam enim hoc docemus, hominem iustum esse, aut sanctificari, aut libe- rari a peccato et a morte aeterna propriis viribus, aut actionibus: sed haec sanctificatio et vivifica- tio opus est Dei, efficientis eam suo Spiritu san- cto, et tunc renati vere sunt templum Dei. Etsi enim haec sanctificatio est proprietas attributa Spiritui sancto, tamen verum est, simul totam divinitatem esse, sicut inquit Dominus Ioh. 14.: Veniemus ad eum, et mansionem apud eum fa- ciemus. Hoc ingens bonum agnoscendum est, et Deo gratiae agendae, quod immensa misericordia ita se propter filium demittit, ut hanc miseram naturam et magnas sordes adhuc circumferentem tamen recipiat, et vere in ea adsit, eam regat, defendat contra diabolos, et luce et vita aeterna donet: et curemus hoc tantum bonum retinere, nec contristemus Spiritum sanctum falsis opinio- nibus, aut lapsibus contra conscientiam, propter quos deseritur homo et ruit in regnum diaboli, ut 2. Petri 2. dicitur.

Quanquam autem renatus est templum Dei, et in eo revera est divinitas, et crescere in eo no- vam lucem et sanctificationem accensam a Spiritu sancto oportet: tamen haec sententia manet ve- ra, personam iustam esse, id est, placere Deo non propter novitatem, sed reputari iustam impu- tata ei iusticia Christi, et placere propter filium mediatorem sola fide. Ita utrumque sciamus, fieri renovationem per Spiritum sanctum, et ta- men hanc consolationem de imputatione tenen- dam esse. Et hanc fidem caeteris virtutibus et invocationi semper praelucere, iuxta illud, Ro- ma. 5.: Iustificati fide pacem habemus. Non enim accedi potest ad Deum sine hac conso- latione.

Postquam autem de conversione hominis dictum est: deinde usitatum est addere doctri- nam de bonis operibus, quam docendi causa in has quaestiones distribuo. Prima: Quae opera sint facienda. Secunda: Quomodo fieri possint. Tertia: Quomodo placeant, cum reliquum in nobis sit peccatum. Quarta: Propter quas causas facienda sint. Quinta: Quod sit discrimen pec- catorum. De his quaestionibus alibi copiose et explicate dictum est.

## 1:18
According to the preceding prophecies.

That is: As you previously had testimonies of the Holy Spirit about yourself or over yourself.

Latin:

Secundum praecedentes prophetias.

Id est: Sicut antea habuisti de te vel super te testimonia Spiritus sancti.

## 1:19
Having faith and a good conscience.

At the end of the first chapter there is a return corresponding to the beginning. Just as I exhorted you to charge others to teach salutary things, that command I now also entrust to you. Again, however, he inserts a brief saying, which is as it were the sum of the doctrine necessary in the Church: Fight the good fight, keeping faith and a good conscience. By these two titles he embraces the whole Christian life: wherefore let it be most known to all, and let it be as a rule of life. Since, however, the words have been explained above in a similar saying, The end of the commandment is love etc., I do not add a longer explanation here: I will only add this, that both must be ruled, faith and a good conscience, not by human imaginations, but by the word of God. As is said in Galatians, the first chapter: If anyone teaches another Gospel, let him be anathema. Likewise, Psalm 118: Your word is a lamp to my feet. Likewise, Ezekiel chapter 20: Walk in my precepts. Nor let men fashion for themselves either dogmas, or acts of worship, or conscience by their own imaginations without the word of God or against the word of God.

Latin:

Habens fidem et bonam conscientiam.

In fine primi capitis redditio est congruens ad initium. Sicut hortatus sum, ut praecipias aliis, ut doceant salutaria, id mandatum nunc quoque tibi commendo. Rursus autem inserit breve dictum, quod velut summa est doctrinae in Ecclesia necessariae: Milites bonam militiam, retinens fidem et bonam conscientiam. His duobus titulis complectitur totam vitam Christia- nam: quare notissimum sit omnibus, et sit tan- quam regula vitae. Cum autem vocabula supra enarrata sint in simili dicto, Finis mandati est dilectio etc., non addo hic longiorem enarratio- nem: tantum hoc addam, utrumque oportet regi, fidem et bonam conscientiam, non imaginationi- bus humanis, sed verbo Dei. Sicut dicitur Ga- lat. primo capite: Si quis aliud Evangelium do- cet, anathema sit. Item, Psalm. 118.: Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum. Item, Ezechielis capite 20.: In praeceptis meis ambulate. Nec fin- gant sibi homines vel dogmata, vel cultus, vel conscientiam suis imaginationibus sine verbo Dei vel contra verbum Dei.

## 2:1 Argument
Chapter two.

Above, it has been spoken about the two principal chapters of doctrine, namely about the Law and the Gospel. Now he adds the doctrine concerning good works, and begins from the highest work, which is prayer, about which he also speaks here. First of all make prayers, signifying that this work is the first and highest in the believer, and proper to the Church of God. This passage contains, however, a most ample doctrine concerning many things, concerning prayer, concerning governments, concerning the ends or duties of governments, concerning the calling of all men, likewise against προσωποληψίαν [respect of persons], likewise concerning the Mediator. Then precepts and consolations are handed down to mothers.

But first let the reader here think to himself of the entire doctrine concerning invocation, what kind of invocation ought to be in the Church. First, true invocation must be distinguished from ethnic, just as the Lord says in John 4: You worship what you do not know. It must be known what you are addressing in invocation, and then why and how God hears. Thus, invocation must be governed by the word of God and faith. And Paul below, 1 Timothy 2, admonishes us concerning the manner: Pray without anger and without hesitation: where with wonderful brevity, as in an Epistle, he embraces a most copious doctrine. When he says, without hesitation, he embraces promises and faith. Let the mind contemplate the mediator, and with true faith establish that you are received, and that your groans and your invocation are heard, according to that of John 16: Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give to you. But when he says, without anger, namely against God, he delivers the doctrine concerning patience. He wants us not to be angry at God, not to rage against him, but in some way to bend our hearts to obedience in punishments and calamities, just as Psalm 4 says: Be angry, and do not sin. Likewise, 1 Peter 5: Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God. In this part, the entire doctrine concerning Christian patience must also be considered.

Paul speaks here also of these duties, he names four degrees. Let the government be such that we live in true piety, that men are rightly taught about God, and that they rightly invoke God. Then he names honesty, that is, the morals of the people should be honest, that is, license should not be granted to lusts, thefts, robberies, debaucheries, just as among the Ethnics many horrendous crimes were not punished. Thirdly, he makes mention of peace. Fourthly, of tranquility. For he names a quiet and tranquil life. Quiet is opposed to wars, tumults, seditions, robberies, devastations, in which it is manifest that many are killed and scattered, but all are hindered in education, in instructing offspring, in seeking food and other things necessary for life. Tranquility indeed signifies εὐταξίαν, order and the harmonious connection of citizens, namely mutual reverence, and beneficence, and modesty, so that it is not enough for cities to have peace, just as we do not wage wars against the Tartars, but their life is without order, there are no degrees of men, no reverence, no mutual beneficence, no distinct times for actions, no culture of the arts, much petulance, much brawling, libelous pamphlets, rash and confused rushing about of men, and factions, such as there were in Rome in the petitioning for Magistracies, and later in the election of Bishops, in which often because of the diverse pursuits of the voters many slaughters occurred. And by such examples it can be understood in some way what Paul calls tranquility.

Secondly, he commands that we pray for empires, just as Jeremiah also commands in chapter 29: Seek the peace of the city, in which you will be guests, and pray for it. Here many things are signified at once: that empires are good things, and that their dangers are great: because the tumults of the devils move without end, and horribly tear apart the human race, so that they may increase impious opinions, blasphemies, and other furies, and cause devastation and eternal evils. Let the thought of these greatest dangers and most sad spectacles excite a greater intention in praying. It is also signified that God wishes to protect our hospices and empires, since he commands us to seek this benefit.

He therefore most wisely paints the good state of the city in brief words: He wants true invocation of God to shine in it. Then he adds honest discipline, peace, and εὐταξίαν. Thus he has truly embraced all things necessary in good government. And let this image be in the sight not only of governors, who ought to direct their counsels to this idea, but also of individual men in their own place, so that we may aid such a state, first by ardent prayer, then by our obedience and examples. Let us not violate peace with injuries, let us not disturb order with petulance and barbaric morals.

The ends or duties of empires should be taken from the Decalogue: for it is aptly said, the Magistrate is the guardian of the law, namely of the first and second Table, as far as external discipline pertains. First, let him take care that men are rightly taught about God, just as the second Psalm also commands, And now, O kings, understand, and let him delete manifest idols, punish blasphemers and perjurers. For although he cannot change hearts, yet he ought to prohibit and punish external crimes, according to the saying of Leviticus 24: Whoever blasphemes the name of the Lord, shall die by death. Thus in the second Table, let him prohibit and punish external offenses. When he does these things, he protects discipline and peace.

Here also the entire doctrine which is delivered in the Church concerning political matters must be considered, which should be taken from books where it is recited more copiously, but especially let the rule be known: It is necessary to obey not only because of anger, that is, because of punishment, but also because of conscience. This rule is the principal nerve of political government in the whole human race, and it protects empires more than any other wisdom or power. And to this rule must be referred the saying of Paul in this place. This is honest and acceptable before our savior God, he says these very duties, prayer for authority, piety, to maintain honest discipline, peace and εὐταξίαν, are works pleasing to God, namely in the believer in his own order, just as it is said elsewhere about good works.

Who wants all men to be saved, and to arrive at the knowledge of the truth, etc.

This is the interpretation of Augustine: God wants all men, that is, some of all ranks and nations, to be saved. Then they add labyrinths about predestination, by which it is by no means useful for minds to be troubled: and those turbulent disputes arise from the fact that the distinction between the law and the free promise is not considered, and minds are led away from the free promise.

But let us look not at men disputing with idle minds, but at those oppressed by true sorrows, such as those who are already being led to punishment; to these, questions about predestination are not to be proposed, but the doctrine must be held, of which it is said in John 1: The Son who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him to us. This will concerning the grace and immense mercy of God has been revealed by an express decree, and God wants it to be known from this promise of his, and the promise is universal, according to these sayings, Matthew 11: Come to me all you who labor etc. And Acts 10: To him all the Prophets bear witness, that all who believe in him receive remission of sins through his name. And the universal particle has been repeated often, and whence would there be certainty, if the promise were not universal?

To this universal promise and revealed will I also accommodate these sayings of Paul: God wants all men to be saved, by the will revealed in the promise, by which he is also most truly effective in those who sustain themselves with the word. Likewise it is said: With God there is no respect of persons.

And it is most manifest in true terrors that minds cannot be raised by any other consolation than the knowledge of the Son, and the command is universal, pertaining to the whole human race, sounding in the whole human race concerning the Son: Hear him. When these sayings of Paul are accommodated to this consolation, they will become most sweet, and it is pleasing in God to see equality. For the thought of inequality, that God is more harshly angry at the sins of some, neglects the foul falls of others, and has singled out some to whom he wishes to be more familiar while spurning the rest, attributes to God προσωποληψίαν, which is tyrannical, and tortures minds with horrible doubt.

But the divine voice draws us back to the revelation, which affirms without any doubt that God is truly angry at sins in all, as much in David as in Saul. Again, also without doubt, that God receives all who flee to the Son: the express promise, which is universal, compels us to judge thus. And let there be some limit to disputes, nor let cavils be sought to undermine the promise. Let us be content with this simple explanation: God wants all men to be saved, as far as his will is concerned, according to the revealed promise, by which he is without any doubt effective in those who receive the word and sustain themselves with the word.

He adds the reason why God wants to save all men: because, he says, the Son paid the price for all. At the same time, however, he teaches us here about the knowledge of the true God, about true invocation, and about the mode of salvation. And first he distinguishes the true God from fictitious deities: There is one God, he says, namely that one who sent the mediator Jesus Christ. For it is always necessary to apprehend God in such a way that we establish that this one is truly God, and we look upon him with faith and call upon him, who revealed himself by giving a promise about the mediator, and by adding testimonies. Just as it is said in the first commandment: I am the Lord your God, who led you out of Egypt. Likewise: The God of our fathers Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, that is, who gave promises to our fathers. But all other revelations are to be referred to this principal one, by which God revealed himself by sending his Son. And when he says, There is one God, he embraces three persons. For he opposes this saying to all fictitious deities, as in Deuteronomy, chapter 6: Hear O Israel, the Lord your God, the Lord is one.

Afterwards he speaks of the Son as of the mediator, where he says expressly: The man Christ Jesus, so that he may signify that he is naming the Son now for this reason, not that he excludes him from divinity, but because he is now speaking about the mediator, in whom there are two natures, divine and human. It is, however, among all the highest works of the wisdom of God the supreme and most secret of all this plan, the union of the divine and human nature in the redeemer, and this wisdom we shall learn throughout all eternity: but now both must be considered piously and reverently, both what a mediator is, and why God willed to appoint a mediator, and why he is such, God and man.

Latin:

Caput secundum.

Supra de duobus praecipuis capitibus doctri- nae dictum est, videlicet de Lege et Evangelio. Nunc doctrinam de bonis operibus addit, et or- ditur a summo opere quod est precatio, de quo et hic dicit. Primum omnium facite precationes, significans id opus esse primum et summum in credente, et proprium Ecclesiae Dei. Continet autem hic locus amplissimam doctrinam de multis rebus, de precatione, de imperiis, de finibus seu officiis imperiorum, de vocatione omnium hominum, item contra προσωποληψίαν, item de mediatore. Deinde praecepta et consolationes matribus traduntur.

Primum autem hic lector integram doctri- nam de invocatione apud sese cogitet, qualem esse invocationem in Ecclesia oporteat. Primum discernenda est invocatio vera ab ethnica, sicut Dominus inquit Ioan. 4.: Vos adoratis quod nescitis. Sciendum est quid alloquaris in invo- catione, et deinde cur et quomodo exaudiat Deus. Ita regenda est invocatio verbo Dei et fide. Et Paulus infra, 1. Timoth. 2. nos de modo admo- net, Orate sine ira et sine haesitatione: ubi mira brevitate, ut in Epistola, copiosissimam doctri- nam complectitur. Cum ait, sine haesitatione, complectitur promissiones et fidem, Mens intuea- tur mediatorem, et vera fide statuas te recipi, et exaudiri tuos gemitus et tuam invocationem, iuxta illud Iohannis 16.: Quicquid petieritis patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis. Cum autem inquit, sine ira, scilicet adversus Deum, tradit doctri- nam de patientia. Vult nos non irasci Deo, non fremere adversus eum, sed aliquo modo flecti corda ad obedientiam in poenis et calamitatibus, sicut Psalmus 4. inquit: Irascimini, nolite pec- care. Item, 1. Petr. 5.: Humiliamini sub po- tenti manu Dei. In hac parte etiam cogitanda est integra doctrina de patientia Christiana.

De his officiis et hic Paulus loquitur, nomi- nat quatuor gradus, Sit gubernatio talis, ut viva- mus in vera pietate, ut recte doceantur homines de Deo, et Deum recte invocent. Deinde nomi- nat honestatem, id est, mores populi sint hone- sti, id est, non concedatur licentia libidinibus, furtis, latrociniis, helluationibus, ut apud Eth- nicos multa horrenda scelera non puniebantur. Tertio facit mentionem pacis. Quarto tranquil- litatis. Nominat enim vitam quietam et tranquil- lam, Quies opponitur bellis, tumultibus, sedi- tionibus, latrociniis, vastationibus, in quibus multos interfici et dissipari manifestum est, om- nes vero impediuntur in educatione, in insti- tuenda sobole, in quaerendo victu et aliis rebus vitae necessariis. Tranquillitas vero significat εὐταξίαν, ordinem et concinnam connexionem civium, videlicet mutuam reverentiam, et bene- ficentiam, et modestiam, ut, non satis est civi- tates habere pacem, sicut Tartaris non inferimus bella, sed vita eorum est sine ordine, non sunt gradus hominum, non reverentia, non mutua beneficentia, non distincta tempora actionum, non cultura artium, multum petulantiae, multum rixarum, famosi libelli, temerariae et confusa- neae concursationes hominum, et factiones, qua- les Romae fuerunt in petitione Magistratuum, et postea in electione Episcoporum, in qua saepe propter diversa studia suffragatorum multae cae- des fiebant. Et talibus exemplis utcunque intel- ligi potest, quid nominet Paulus tranquillitatem.

Secundo iubet orari pro imperiis, sicut et Ieremias capite 29. praecipit: Quaerite pacem civitatis, in qua eritis hospites, et pro ea orate. Hic multa simul significantur, imperia res bonas esse, et magna eorum pericula esse: quia diaboli tumultus sine fine movent, et horribiliter dilace- rant genus humanum, ut augeant impias opinio- nes, blasphemias et alios furores, et faciant va- stitatem et aeterna mala. Horum maximorum periculorum et tristissimorum spectaculorum co- gitatio, exuscitet maiorem intentionem in pre- cando. Significatur etiam, Deum velle tueri ho- spitia nostra et imperia, cum nos iubeat hoc be- neficium petere.

Pingit igitur sapientissime bonum statum ci- vitatis brevibus verbis: Vult in ea lucere veram Dei invocationem. Deinde addi honestam disci- plinam, pacem et εὐταξίαν. Ita revera com- plexus est omnia necessaria in bona gubernatione. Et sit haec imago in conspectu non solum guber- natoribus, qui ad hanc ideam sua consilia diri- gere debebant, sed etiam singulis hominibus suo loco, ut talem statum adiuvemus, primum ar- denti precatione, deinde nostris obsequiis et exemplis, Non violemus pacem iniuriis, non tur- bemus ordinem petulantia et barbaricis moribus.

Fines seu officia imperiorum sumantur ex Decalogo: apte enim dicitur, Magistratus est cu- stcs legis, videlicet primae et secundae Tabulae, quod ad externam disciplinam attinet. Primum curet recte doceri homines de Deo, sicut et Psal- mus secundus praecipit, Et nunc reges intelligite, Et deleat manifesta idola, puniat blasphemos et periuros. Etsi enim non potest corda mutare, tamen externa scelera prohibere et punire debet, iuxta dictum Levit 24.: Qui blasphemaverit no- men Domini, morte morietur. Sic in secunda Tabula prohibeat et puniat externa delicta. Haec cum facit, disciplinam et pacem tuetur.

Hic quoque integra doctrina, quae in Eccle- sia traditur de rebus politicis cogitanda est, quae sumatur ex libris, ubi copiosius recitatur, prae- cipue vero nota sit regula: Necesse est obedire non solum propter iram, id est, propter poenam, sed etiam propter conscientiam. Haec regula est praecipuus nervus gubernationis politicae in toto genere humano, et magis munit imperia quam ulla alia sapientia vel potentia. Et ad hanc regu- lam referendum est dictum Pauli hoc loco. Hoc honestum et acceptum est coram salvatore nostro Deo, dicit haec ipsa officia, precationem pro potestate, pietatem, tueri honestam disciplinam, pacem et εὐταξίαν, esse opera Deo placentia, vi- delicet in credente suo ordine, sicut alibi de bonis operibus dicitur.

Qui vult omnes homines salvos fieri, et ad ve- ritatis agnitionem pervenire, etc.

Augustini interpretatio haec est: Deus vult omnes homines, id est, omnium graduum et gen- tium aliquos salvos fieri. Deinde addunt labyrin- thos de praedestinatione, quibus turbari mentes nequaquam utile est: et illae turbulentae disputa- tiones inde oriuntur, quod non consideratur dis- crimen lgis et gratuitae promissionis, et abdu- cuntur mentes a gratuita promissione.

Intueamur autem non homines otiosis men- tibus disputantes, sed oppressos veris doloribus, ut eos qui iam ad supplicia ducuntur, his non sunt proponendae quaestiones de praedestina- tione, sed tenenda est doctrina, de qua dicitur Ioan 1.: Filius qui est in sinu patris, ipse enarra- vit nobis. Haec voluntas de gratia et immensa misericordia Dei expresso decreto patefacta est, et vult eam Deus ex hac sua promissione cognosci, et promissio est universalis, iuxta haec dicta, Matth. 11.: Venite ad me omnes qui laboratis etc. Et Acto. 10.: Huic omnes Prophetae testi- monium perhibent, remissionem peccatorum ac- cipere per nomen eius omnes qui credunt in eum. Et saepe repetita est universalis particula, et unde certitudo esset, si promissio non esset uni- versalis?

Ad hanc universalem promissionem et reve- latam voluntatem accommodo et haec dicta Pauli: Deus vult omnes homines salvos fieri, voluntate revelata in promissione, qua et verissime efficax est in iis, qui verbo se sustentant. Item dicitur: Apud Deum non est acceptio personarum.

Ac manifestissimum est in veris pavoribus, non alia consolatione mentes erigi posse, nisi agnitione filii, et mandatum est universale ad to- tum genus humanum pertinens, sonans in toto genere humano de filio: Hunc audite. Ad hanc consolationem cum haec dicta Pauli accommo dan- tur, fient dulcissima, et gratum est in Deo aequa- litatem videre. Nam cogitatio inaequalitatis, quod Deus aliorum peccatis durius irasca- tur, aliorum tetros lapsus negligat, et aliquos excerpserit, quibus velit esse familiarior spretis caeteris, tribuit Deo προσωποληψίαν, quae est tyrannica, et excruciat mentes horribili dubi- tatione.

Retrahit autem nos vox divina ad patefactio- nem, quae affirmat sine ulla dubitatione Deum vere irasci peccatis in omnibus, tam in Davide quam in Saule. Rursus etiam sine dubitatione Deum recipere omnes confugientes ad filium: sic iudicare nos cogit expressa promissio, quae est universalis. Et sit modus aliquis disputationum, nec quaerantur cavillationes ad labefactandam promissionem. Hac simplici enarratione contenti simus: Deus vult omnes homines salvos fieri, quod ad suam voluntatem attinet, iuxta revela- tam promissionem, qua sine ulla dubitatione effi- cax est in accipientibus verbum, et se sustentan- tibus verbo.

Causam addit, quare Deus velit omnes ho- mines salvos facere: quia, inquit, pro omnibus filius persolvit pretium. Simul autem hic docet nos de agnitione veri Dei, de vera invocatione, et de modo salvationis. Ac primum discernit verum Deum a commentitiis numinibus: Unus est Deus, inquit, ille scilicet, qui misit mediatorem Iesum Christum. Semper enim oportet sic appre- hendi Deum, ut hunc vere esse Deum statuamus, et fide intueamur et compellemus, qui se patefe- cit data promissione de mediatore, et additis te- stimoniis. Sicut in primo praecepto dicitur: Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus, qui eduxi te de Aegy- pto. Item: Deus patrum nostrorum Abraham, Isaac, Iacob, id est, qui dedit promissiones pa- tribus nostris. Omnes autem aliae patefactiones referendae sunt ad hanc praecipuam, qua se Deus patefecit misso filio. Et cum ait, Unus est Deus, complectitur tres personas. Opponit enim hoc dictum omnibus commentitiis numinibus, ut in Deutero. 6. capite: Audi Israël, Dominus Deus tuus, Dominus unus est.

Postea de filio ut de mediatore loquitur, ubi diserte inquit: Homo Christus Iesus, ut significet se ideo nunc nominare Filium, non quod excludat eum a divinitate, sed quod iam de mediatore lo- quatur, in quo duae naturae sunt, divina et hu- mana. Est autem inter omnia summa opera sa- pientiae Dei supremum et arcanissimum omnium hoc consilium, copulatio naturae divinae et hu- manae in redemtore, et hanc sapientiam in omni aeternitate discemus: sed iam utrunque pie et re- verenter considerandum est, et quid sit mediator, et quare voluerit Deus constituere mediatorem, et quare talis sit, Deus et homo.

## 2:5
On the Mediator.

There are, however, four properties of the mediator.

I. That he be a person established between God, who is angry at sin, and the human race, guilty of sin and of the wrath of God, so that he may satisfy the justice of God, sustain the wrath for sin, and intercede for us.

II. That this mediator be revealed, and by the express testimony of God ordained for this purpose, that he be a propitiator, just as it is expressly said of the Son of God, Rom. 3: Whom he appointed as propitiator. And in Psalm 110: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek. And the same places are the promises which testify that this mediator is heard.

III. That the merits of the mediator be applied to those who call upon him, and be valid for them, just as it is said of the Son: Through the obedience of one, many are constituted righteous, Rom. 5.

IV. That he be named in invocation; and that we approach God with confidence in this mediator, and that he himself may carry our prayers to God, and see the hearts of all, discern those who call upon him truly and those who do not, and be effective in those who call upon him, so that they may now become one with God, just as it is said to the Ephesians and Colossians: That the Son may bring all things under one head, and join us to the eternal Father.

But why did he will a mediator?

Because he willed that redemption be accomplished in such a way that the divine justice would nevertheless be satisfied, therefore a mediator was appointed, into whom the true and not feigned wrath of divine justice against our sins would be poured, and that such a mediator would be the price for the human race.

Latin:

De Mediatore.

Sunt autem proprietates mediatoris quatuor.

I. Ut sit persona inter Deum irascentem pec- cato, et genus humanum reum peccati et irae Dei constituta, ut iusticiae Dei satisfaciat, sustineat iram pro peccato et deprecetur pro nobis.

II. Ut sit revelatus hic mediator, et expresso testimonio Dei ad hoc ordinatus, ut sit propicia- tor, sicut de filio Dei expresse dictum est, Roma. 3.: Quem constituit propiciatorem. Et in Psalmo 110.: Tu es sacerdos in aeternum secun- dum ordinem Melchisedech. Et eadem loca sunt promissiones, quae testantur exaudiri hunc me- diatorem.

III. Ut merita mediatoris applicentur invocan- tibus, et valeant pro eis, sicut de filio dicitur: Per unius obedientiam iusti constituuntur multi, Roma. 5.

IV. Ut in invocatione nominetur; et fiducia huius mediatoris ad Deum accedamus, et ipse nostra vota ad Deum perferat, et videat omnium corda, discernat vere et non vere invocantes, et sit efficax in invocantibus, ut iam fiant unum cum Deo, sicut ad Ephesios et Colossenses dicitur: Quod filius redigat sub unum caput, et adiungat nos aeterno patri.

Quare autem voluit mediatorem?

Quia redemtionem ita fieri voluit, ut iusti- ciae divinae tamen satisfieret, ideo mediator con- stitutus est, in quem effunderetur vera et non simulata ira iusticiae divinae adversus nostra pec- cata, et ut talis mediator esset pretium pro ge- nere humano.

## 2:5
But why is he such, God and man?

Because when the human race had sinned, the order of justice was that man should sustain the punishments, therefore Paul says clearly in this place: The man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a price for all men. And yet that same mediator is God, so that he may be an equivalent price, and so that he may be able to sustain the wrath of the eternal Father, overcome death, restore justice and life, enter into the secret counsel of the eternal Father, intercede for us, see and judge the hearts of all, help and sanctify. Therefore Paul says elsewhere: In him dwells all the fullness of the divinity bodily, that is, personally, Colos. 2. Likewise: Through him all things were created, Ephes. 1, where he spoke expressly of the divinity. Here also a comparison must be considered. In the Epistle to the Galatians chapter 3, Paul says of Moses: The law was given by the hand of a mediator. These words are taken from the history which is recounted in Exodus 20 and 34, where the people, dismayed by hearing the voice of God, say: Speak you to us and we will hear, let not the Lord speak to us, lest we die. In this history it is signified that human nature cannot sustain the voice of God judging, or the judgment of God. Just as it is also said in Deut. 4: God is a consuming fire. But Moses is there a typical mediator: for not even he could have heard God, had not the Son been a shelter. Just as it is said in Exodus 33: No man shall see me and live, but he adds: I will protect you with my right hand. Moses does not sustain the wrath of God, nor is he a propitiator, nor can he transfuse the rays of justice and life into others, therefore he is veiled, so that it may be signified that a Type is being proposed, but another is the true mediator, our Lord Jesus Christ, who both sustains the wrath of God, and is a propitiator, and transfuses the rays of his justice and life into those who hear him. Therefore Paul says here: There is one mediator, because he is speaking not of a typical, but of a true mediator, whom he names Propitiator in Romans 3, just as it was said above that it pertains to the office of a mediator that he should sustain the punishment for us and be a propitiator. Let readers observe here that the universal is repeated, who gave himself ἀντίλυτρον for all men, and let them consider the force of the word, which signifies compensation and price. For Paul wishes such a mediator, or such a propitiator, to be understood, who derived the punishment into himself. And contemplating this so great a price, let us acknowledge that God is truly and horribly angry at sins, because by a wonderful and ineffable wisdom justice and mercy are joined in the redemption. Nor was the human race received, except in such a way that at the same time the justice of God was satisfied. God wishes this just anger to be seen. Again, he also wishes faith to be raised up and mercy to be acknowledged, when we consider that this price far exceeds our sins. This is the fountain of all consolations in the greatest sorrows. Nor can this admirable doctrine be explained in words with sufficient fullness, but yet its beginnings must be thought upon here in some way, and it must be repeated in daily invocation, and it must be prayed that the Son of God himself, the mediator, may transfuse the rays of his wisdom and righteousness into us.

Latin:

Quare autem talis est, Deus et homo?

Quia cum genus humanum peccasset, ordo iusticiae erat, ut homo poenas sustineret, ideo Paulus hoc loco diserte inquit: Homo Christus Iesus, qui dedit se pretium pro omnibus homini- bus. Et tamen idem ille mediator est Deus, ut sit aequivalens pretium, et ut possit sustinere iram aeterni patris, vincere mortem, reddere iusticiam et vitam, ingredi in arcanum consilium aeterni patris, intercedere pro nobis, videre et iudicare omnium corda, opitulari et sanctificare. Ideo alibi inquit Paulus: In eo habitat omnis plenitudo divinitatis corporaliter, id est, personaliter, Colos. 2. Item: Per eum condita sunt omnia, Ephes. 1., ubi expresse de divinitate locutus est. Hic et collatio consideranda est. In Epistola ad Galatas capite 3. Paulus de Moyse inquit: Lex est data per manum mediatoris. Haec verba sumta sunt ex historia, quae recitatur Exodi 20. et 34., ubi populus consternatus audita voce Dei inquit: Loquere tu nobis et audiemus, non loquatur nobis Dominus, ne moriamur. In hac historia significatum est, humanam naturam non posse sustinere vocem Dei iudicantis, seu iudicium Dei. Sicut et Deut. 4. dicitur: Deus est ignis consumens. Est autem ibi Moyses mediator typicus: nam nec ipse audire Deum potuisset, nisi filius fuisset umbraculum. Sicut Exodi 33. dicitur: Non videbit me homo et vivet, sed addit: Protegam te dextra mea. Non sustinet Moyses iram Dei, nec est propiciator, nec potest transfundere radios iusticiae et vitae in alios, ideo velatus est, ut significetur Typum proponi, sed alius est verus mediator Dominus noster Iesus Christus, qui et sustinet iram Dei, et est propiciator, et transfundit radios suae iusticiae et vitae in eos, qui ipsum audiunt. Ideo Paulus hic inquit: Unus est mediator, quia non de typico, sed de vero mediatore, loquitur, quem Roman. 3. nominat Propiciatorem, sicut supra dictum est, Ad mediatoris officium pertinere, ut sustineat poenam pro nobis, et sit propiciator. Observent autem lectores hic repetitam esse universalem, qui dedit se ἀντίλυτρον pro omnibus hominibus, et vim vocabuli considerent, quod significat compensationem et pretium. Vult enim intelligi Paulus talem mediatorem, seu talem propiciatorem, qui in sese derivavit poenam. Et hoc tam grande pretium intuentes, agnoscamus Deum vere et horribiliter irasci peccatis, quia mirabili et inenarrabili sapientia copulatae sunt iusticia et misericordia in redemtione. Nec receptum est genus humanum, nisi ita, ut simul iusticiae Dei satisfieret. Hanc iustam iram Deus vult conspici. Rursus etiam vult erigi fidem et agnosci misericordiam, cum consideramus hoc pretium longe antecellere nostris peccatis. Hic fons est omnium consolationum in summis dolo- ribus. Nec potest haec admiranda doctrina satis copiose verbis exponi, sed tamen initia hic ut- cunque cogitanda sunt, et in quotidiana invoca- tione repetenda est, et precandum, ut ipse filius Dei mediator radios suae sapientiae et iusticiae in nos transfundat.

## 2:8
Lifting up pure hands.

Let the entire doctrine concerning prayer always be in sight, and let the consideration of the will of God kindle us to invocation and to faith, which becomes the more illustrious for that very reason, because the precept concerning invocation has been repeated so often, just as Tauler says most sweetly: Never is the breast of man as eager to receive as the will of God is eager to give grace and salvation on account of the Son.

What things, however, ought to concur in prayer has often been said elsewhere. Included among these are these circumstances, of which Paul makes mention in this place. Lift up pure hands, that is, not polluted by evil purpose, according to that, John 9: God does not hear sinners.

Latin:

Levantes puras manus.

Semper in conspectu sit integra doctrina de precatione, et accendat nos ad invocationem et ad fidem consideratio voluntatis Dei, quae eo ipso fit illustrior, quia tam saepe repetitum est praeceptum de invocatione, sicut Taulerus dul- cissime inquit: Nunquam pectus hominis tam avidum est ad accipiendum, quam avida est vo- luntas Dei ad dandam gratiam et salutem propter filium.

Quae res autem concurrere in precatione de- beant, saepe alias dictum est. In his comprehen- duntur et hae circumstantiae, quarum Paulus hoc loco mentionem facit. Levate puras manus, id est, non pollutas malo proposito, iuxta illud, Iohan. 9.: Peccatores Deus non exaudit.

## 2:8
Without anger.

That is, without indignation and raging against God, but let hearts be bent in some way toward patience, according to that 1 Peter 5: Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God. Let not hearts, overcome by indignation, fail, so that they rush either into Epicurean contempt of God or into blasphemies, like Saul, Judas, and the like. For it is necessary that there be in us the beginnings of new obedience.

Without hesitation.

That is, let there be faith that is victorious over doubts. And let us truly establish that we are received by God on account of the Son, that we are a care to God, and that our groans are not in vain on account of the Son. These things are declared more fully elsewhere. But let this very sentence also rouse us to prayer and to faith: because he both commands that invocation be made, and wills that hesitations be overcome.

Latin:

Sine ira.

Id est, sine indignatione et fremitu adver- sus Deum, sed flectantur corda aliquo modo ad patientiam, iuxta illud 1. Petr. 5.: Humiliamini sub potenti manu Dei. Non deficiant corda su- perata indignatione, ut ruant vel in Epicureum comtemtum Dei, vel in blasphemias, ut Saul, Iudas et similes. Oportet enim in nobis esse initia novae obedientiae.

Sine haesitatione.

Id est, adsit fides victrix dubitationum. Ac vere statuamus, nos propter filium recipi a Deo, curae esse Deo, et nostros gemitus non esse irri- tos propter filium. Haec alibi copiosius decla- rantur. Exuscitet autem nos et haec ipsa senten- tia ad precationem et ad fidem: quia et praecipit fieri invocationem, et vult vinci haesitationes.

## 2:15
The woman is saved through the bearing of children.

There is no doubt that the Holy Spirit has opposed this sweetest sermon concerning the duties of the female sex to manifold superstition. And the notable praise of marriage is to be observed for the refuting of all fanatical spirits who have condemned marriage and domestic duties, as there have always been many such, like Marcion, Tatian, Hierax, ἐγκρατήται, Popes, Monks. To all these let this voice of Paul be opposed: The woman is saved through the bearing of children, if they have remained in faith.

But first, the younger students must be admonished concerning the grammar: he said 'if they have remained' in the plural number, because he is speaking of the sex, as we say: The crowd rush. Therefore, the insipid interpretation of many is to be exploded, who explain the word 'have remained' as referring to the children, since it is manifestly false that mothers are not made saved unless the children are made saved. Romans 14: Each one of us will give an account of himself to God.

Secondly, one must respond to the argument: We are saved by faith alone, therefore not by domestic duties. I respond. The antecedent is true; on account of the merit of the Son of God alone are given reconciliation, justification, and the inheritance of eternal life, and these must be received by faith: which faith new obedience necessarily follows. For just as eternal life itself in its consummation will formally be light and a burning of virtues, which will be in us when we are suffused with divine light, as it is written: God will be all in all, 1 Corinthians 15: So now is the beginning of virtues, which the Son of God kindles in us through the Holy Spirit, just as Paul says elsewhere, 2 Corinthians 5: We shall be clothed upon, if indeed we shall not be found naked.

See therefore the prudence of Paul, when he had praised the work, he soon makes mention of faith, to which he adds the other virtues, because he is no longer disputing about merits, but includes the virtues which are necessarily kindled together with faith. Moreover, as often as mention is made of obedience, a beginning must be made with the mention of the calling, just as the woman was especially created so that she might bear and cherish and nourish her weak offspring. This first work Paul includes among the virtues of the woman.

At the same time, however, these propositions are true: The just man is justified by faith freely on account of the Son of God, and through Him is an heir of eternal life. And the other: In this just man, new obedience is necessary, because consolation and vivification through faith happen in such a way that at the same time new light and new obedience are kindled by the Holy Spirit, according to that of Jeremiah chapter thirty-three: I will put my law in their hearts. Therefore Paul says in 1 Corinthians 9: Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel. Item 2 Cor. 5: We shall be clothed upon, if yet we shall be found not naked. Item, Matt. 5: Unless your righteousness shall exceed that of the Scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven. Nor do these conflict; new obedience is necessary in the justified, and yet it is not the merit or price of eternal life, because we never satisfy the law of God in this life, and we are never without sin, according to that 1 John 1: If we say that we have no sin, we are liars. Faith, therefore, looking upon the Son of God, has certain consolation, and knows that you are an heir of eternal life because of the merit of the Son of God, and through him, not because of your merit.

Thus Paul here signifies that new obedience is necessary, he does not mean it to be merit. And among the virtues of new obedience he recounts domestic duties, justice, and patience in the common troubles of a mother, which are many and great. He names, however, these virtues: the labors of childbirth and upbringing, faith, love, sanctification, and modesty. That faith is necessary in all things is manifest, and here let the entire doctrine of faith be considered, which is trust resting in the Son of God, and receiving through him freely the remission of sins, the imputation of righteousness, true consolation, and vivification, by which renewal is begun in us because of the Son of God, and through him. This faith, however, must be exercised assiduously in every invocation, in all dangers, and with it we understand Hope and Tolerance to be included, as was said above concerning prayer. The exercises of these virtues are the chief consolations in this whole life, concerning which it is said Phil. 4: Let the peace of God govern your hearts. Item, Psalm 124: They who trust in the Lord shall not be moved, like Mount Zion, forever.

Love, as elsewhere, signifies love of God and neighbor, and includes fear and obedience toward God. Then, in the love of neighbor, in a mother of a family the first virtue is love of husband and offspring, gentleness of spirit, lest the marriage become sad through her own irascibility and rage, nor the husband's spirit be alienated. Item, Patience, lest she desert her husband in adverse fortune. Item, let her be just in contracts, let her not be a defrauder. Item, let her be beneficent toward the poor. All these virtues are included in love, and can be distinguished by inspecting the Decalogue. They become, however, more conspicuous when examples are contemplated, such as Sarah, Abigail, the widow of Zarephath, Elizabeth the mother of the Baptist, Elizabeth of Thuringia. Item, Elizabeth the sister of Charles, who was married to the Danish king, and was a companion of exiles and great troubles, nor did she wish to receive the kingdom offered without her husband. Sanctification in the Hebrew phrase often signifies chastity, as in 1 Thessalonians 4: This is the will of God, your sanctification, that you abstain from fornication, and that each one possess his vessel in sanctification and honor. Since, however, he said above that women are saved by childbearing, it is certain that the conjugal custom is not prohibited, but that adulteries are prohibited. Now here let good minds consider that chastity is both a necessary and beautiful virtue, which is, whether in marriage or in the celibate life, to avoid all prohibited comminglings and emissions of seed. And concerning its necessity it is expressly said, 1 Cor. 6: Do not err, fornicators and adulterers shall not possess the kingdom of God. Item, Gal. 5: Those who do such things shall not possess the kingdom of God. Item, to Heb. 12: Without sanctification, that is, chastity, no one shall see God. And not only do eternal punishments accompany lusts in those who are not converted, but also present punishments in this life oppress both the converted and the unconverted, although they are mitigated for the converted, as the example of David shows. And it is expressly said Heb. 13: God will judge fornicators and adulterers, namely, both in this life and after this life, if they have not been converted. God judges, however, sometimes immediately, just as he destroys Sodom, in which example it must be considered most diligently that that horrible execution of punishment is done by the Son of God himself, who is a guest of Abraham on that journey, where later the text says: The Lord rained fire and sulfur from the Lord upon Sodom, Gen. 19. Sometimes he punishes mediately through empires and other calamities, as Antony is punished by Augustus. There are, however, also the legitimate punishments of the divine judgment by magistrates, and there is no doubt that promiscuous lusts are the causes of many huge wars and great devastations, as histories show: for even among the causes of the flood mention is made of lusts. Later the destructions of Sodom, the Canaanites, and almost the entire tribe of Benjamin are recounted, the princes are hanged in the desert, David's adultery was followed by sedition, Greek histories are full of examples, Sybaris, Thebes, Sparta: and now Africa, Asia, Egypt, Syria, Greece, are either wildernesses or foul stables of barbarians without churches, without laws, without discipline, without doctrine, because of idols, heresies, and lusts.

By the contemplation of these most sad examples let us rouse ourselves, that we may be more vigilant in defending true doctrine, in true invocation, and in avoiding the pollutions of lusts. Let us also look around at daily punishments: many great and small families are overturned daily because of the confusions of lusts. Wherefore let us strive to piously guard chastity, both in marriage and in the celibate life. There is also a certain tenderness of age, which can still easily retain purity, if it avoids evil companionships and debaucheries, and adds to sobriety and honest labors the thought of the judgment of God, and of punishments, and prayer.

But I have already spoken of bodily punishments. In Paul, Eph. 4, mention is made of much graver punishments, namely blindness and insensibility, as when the Ptolemaeans pollute themselves in various ways, afterwards they rush blind into domestic robberies, and bring destruction upon themselves: and there are in sight examples of pontiffs, priests, and monks, there these two evils dominate, Blindness and Insensibility. Very many are openly Epicurean. A few others, superstitious and fascinated by false persuasions, attempt to destroy the truth, then secure, without any groan of repentance, they live in great crimes, and in the Sybaritic manner seek all kinds of pleasures, until they rush into eternal destruction.

Fearing these greatest punishments, blindness and insensibility, let us guard chastity with greater care, and let us pray to the Son of God, that since He Himself most loves chastity for the sake of His own glory, He may help us, that we may not be contaminated, and that we may not provide the devil with the pleasure of our fall, who celebrates manifold triumphs when he overturns some in this way, and rejoices in the hatred of God; because those works are done which greatly displease God. Also, because it deforms the creature of God, and disturbs the order divinely instituted, because it tears man away from God, and grieves the Holy Spirit, because it provides an occasion for many other evils to follow: for the devil weaves a long web. Finally, what is sadder than to live in such a way that you know for certain that God is angry with you, and you cannot approach Him by invocation, or seek from Him help, or defense in any matter. These such great miseries are to be thought of often and much, and our examples and those of others are to be looked upon, so that we may rouse ourselves to repentance and to prayer, and avoid the occasions of falls, and restrain our members, as Paul says in Eph. 5: Walk accurately, not as fools. It is useful to rightly understand the appellations of the virtues, and to think often of their sources, duties, and dignity. In this weakness of nature we do not see how great things wisdom, truth, and virtue are. Nor on the other hand do we sufficiently perceive how horrible evils lying, the worship of idols, injustice, and being polluted by lusts are. Furthermore, we either think coldly of the Law, or we are indignant that we are as it were unjustly enclosed in this prison, just as Gorgias said, that the Law is a tyrant. Let us know that this darkness and contumacy in our nature are great and sad wounds and horrible sins, of which it is said, Rom. 8: The mind of the flesh is enmity against God. Therefore let us in some way acknowledge and deplore our diseases, and flee to the mediator the Son of God, to our Samaritan, and seek help from Him. And when we think of the virtues, let us look upon God Himself, and know Him to be such, shining with true and immense light, wisdom, goodness, beneficence, truth, rectitude, and purity, and that He wills us to be like Him: thus the nature and beauty of the virtues can be better considered, when we behold them as it were in God Himself. For although the law is a doctrine which narrates what God is like, yet we think more narrowly of the virtues while looking at the law, from which we shrink as if from a prison. You should love justice in not harming others, because God is such, namely beneficent and equal, and He wills us to be like Him, and think that this virtue is for that reason a most beautiful thing, because God is such. Thus you should love truth, because God is such, and He wills us to be like Him. You should transfer this thought also to the other virtues, and let the terms be rightly explained. But let the enumerations and descriptions be taken from the Decalogue, as we often say. The term σωφροσύνη in this place, as often elsewhere, signifies both temperance and modesty. But properly temperance is named as moderation in food and drink. This virtue is necessary by itself, because it is manifest by itself that the contrary vices are destructive to the body, as it is said, More perish by intemperance than by the sword: And it is the nurse of many other virtues, of invocation, of intention, of deliberation, of diligence, of circumspection, of chastity, since intemperance hinders the sense of the fear of God, repentance, meditation, invocation, and confirms security, and increases many fires of desires. Concerning invocation it is said, Mark 9: This kind of demons is not cast out, except by fasting and prayer. And Peter says, 1 Pet. 5: σωφρονήσατε and be sober unto prayer. Concerning chastity, And Venus rages in wines, fire in fire. And Juvenal, For what does a drunken Venus care? And let the saying of Seneca always be in sight, Vices hardened by the habit of insanity conceived in wine, are strong even without wine.

Nor is there any doubt that public and private calamities are increased, because God punishes intemperance, which indeed many other vices usually accompany, according to that epigram: ἥλις καὶ μεθυεῖ καὶ ψεύδεται, οἷος ἕκαστον οἶκος, τοίη ἢ καὶ ξυναπᾶσα πόλις. The Heliacan city is at once lying and drunken, such is the whole city, as any house is wont to be, that is, a bad public state arises from this, because individuals do not wish to amend themselves, but each one wishes to impose laws on others, not to rule himself and his own, since it has been said: The just man is the first accuser of himself.

Modesty indeed is a virtue in opinion, speech, gesture, and the conduct of business, preserving propriety, that is, drawing us back within the limits appropriate to a person.

From this definition it can be understood that Modesty as a whole comprises many parts or species, some of which are distinguished by names, and illustrious differences are made when opposing vices are compared: with Modesty fight pride, Thrasonic vanity, or boasting. Likewise garrulity, futility, scurrility, petulance, obscenity: Likewise luxury, and ineptitudes in dress, and most of all curiosity, or πολυπραγμοσύνη, which thrusts itself into the affairs of others, fights with modesty.

Although, however, all vices which fight with temperance and modesty are pernicious and deformed in all men, men and women, yet in women the deformity is more conspicuous, because this sex ought to remain hidden on account of its infirmity. Therefore a drunken woman in an assembly is a very shameful spectacle, and she falls more easily then into other disgraces: thus deformity is more conspicuous in a garrulous, curious woman, mixing herself in the affairs of government, as Tiberius used to call his mother Livia a Ulysses in a stola, because she astutely moved many affairs in the republic. Therefore many precepts are handed down which command women to care for domestic economy at home, and to omit affairs which are to be governed by men. Therefore the saying of Sophocles from the Ajax is often cited: γυναῖξι κόσμον ἡ σιγὴ φέρει, Silence brings ornament to women.

Although this enumeration of virtues in Paul is brief, yet the attentive reader will see that the form of the whole matronly life is wisely comprehended here. Nor shall I be more prolix, because the Decalogue, which is the fountain of doctrine concerning all virtues, ought to be most known to all.

Again, however, I admonish the reader to consider here the testimony concerning the praise of marriage, and to think of the causes, God in immense wisdom thus founded the human race and joined it in a certain way, He wishes chastity to be understood and performed, either in marriage, or in the celibate life of those who are fit for the celibate life, He wishes the disturbance of this order to be avoided, and He horribly punishes wandering lusts with private and public calamities, and then with eternal punishments, unless conversion takes place. For these causes the conjugal life has been praised.

Since, however, it is necessary that we be ruled by the word of God, and no worships please God without the word of God, it is manifest that the vows of monks are not worships of God, and monks and mass-priests have accumulated many other errors, and worships of idols, to which is joined the prohibition of marriage, which Paul below expressly names the doctrine of demons. This title signifies many great evils, the devil burns with hatred of God, and in order to affect God with insult, he first sows false worships and lies in the human race. Then he attempts to horribly deform and destroy the work of God, namely the human race, he kindles discords and wars, he impels many to be contaminated with most foul lusts, because he knows that God is greatly angered by the confusions of lusts. And he does all these things so that he may drag as many men as possible into eternal destruction, and to eternal blasphemies of God. With the same design he impelled hypocrites to impose the law concerning celibacy upon priests, and to devise the impious bonds of vows, which manifoldly offend God, because they are both the nerves of false worships, and are causes of horrible contaminations, on account of which huge crowds of men rush into eternal punishments.

It is necessary that these evils and their sources be understood, and the impious law concerning celibacy is to be condemned, and For those who depart from the defenders of idols and the law concerning celibacy, there is great consolation, because Paul expressly names that law a doctrine of demons, so that we may know most certainly that it displeases God, and that consciences may know that the society of that defense is to be shunned, according to that saying: If anyone teaches another Gospel, let him be anathema. But let us depart from them in such a way that we do not retain former filth, but are made members of the son of God by true invocation, chastity, and other true acts of worship.

Latin:

Salvatur mulier per filiorum generationem.

Non dubium est Spiritum sanctum hanc dul- cissimam concionem de officiis sexus muliebris opposuisse multiplici superstitioni. Et laudatio insignis coniugii est observanda ad refutandos omnes fanaticos spiritus, qui coniugium et oeconomica officia damnaverunt, ut semper tales multi fuerunt, ut Marcion, Tatianus, Hierax, ἐγκρατήται, Papae, Monachi. His omnibus opponatur haec vox Pauli: Salvatur mulier per filiorum generationem, si manserint in fide.

Primum autem de Grammatica iuniores admonendi sunt, si manserint, dixit plurali numero, quia de sexu loquitur, ut dicimus: Turba ruunt. Explodenda est igitur multorum insulsa interpretatio, qui verbum manserint de filiis enarrant, Cum manifeste falsum sit, matres non fieri salvas, nisi filii fiant salvi. Roman. 14.: Unusquisque nostrum de seipso rationem reddet Deo.

Secundo, Respondendum est ad argumetum: Sola fide salvamur, Ergo non officiis oeconomicis. Respondeo. Antecedens verum est, propter solius filii Dei meritum dantur, reconciliatio, iustificatio, et haereditas vitae aeternae, et haec fide accipi oportet: Quam fidem nova obedientia necessario sequitur. Ut enim ipsa aeterna vita in consummatione formaliter erit lux et virtutum incendium, quae erunt in nobis perfusis luce divina, sicut scriptum est: Deus erit omnia in omnibus, 1. Corinth. 15.: Ita nunc inchoatio virtutum, quas filius Dei per Spiritum sanctum in nobis accendit, sicut alibi inquit Paulus, 2. Corinth. 5.: Superinduemur, si tamen non nudi reperiemur.

Vide igitur Pauli prudentiam, cum laudasset opus, mox et fidei mentionem facit, cui caeteras virtutes addit, quia non iam de meritis disputat, sed comprehendit virtutes, quae cum fide necessario simul accenduntur. Quotiescunque autem de obedientia dicitur, initio facienda est mentio vocationis, ita cum mulier praecipue condita sit, ut pariat et imbecillem foetum foveat ac alat. Hoc primum opus complectitur Paulus inter virtutes mulieris.

Simul autem vera sunt hae propositiones: Iustus fide Gratis propter filium Dei, et per eum est haeres vitae aeternae. Et altera: In hoc iusto necessaria est nova obedientia, quia ita fit consolatio et vivificatio per fidem, ut simul a Spiritu sancto nova lux et nova obedientia accendantur, iuxta illud Ieremiae capite tricesimo tertio: Dabo legem meam in corda eorum. Ideo inquit Paulus 1. Corinth. 9.: Vae mihi, si non evangelizem. Item 2. Corinth. 5.: Superinduemur, si tamen non nudi reperiemur. Item, Matth. 5.: Nisi abundaverit iusticia vestra plus quam Scribarum et Pharisaeorum, non intrabitis regnum coelorum. Nec pugnant haec, Nova obedientia in iustificato necessaria est, et tamen non est meritum vel pretium vitae aeternae, quia nunquam in hac vita legi Dei satisfacimus, et nunquam sumus sine peccato, iuxta illud 1. Iohann. 1.: Si dixerimus, quod peccatum non habemus, mendaces sumus. Fides igitur intuens filium Dei, habet certam consolationem, et scit te haeredem esse vitae aeternae propter meritum filii Dei, et per ipsum, non propter tuum meritum.

Ita Paulus hic novam obedientiam necessariam esse significat, non vult esse meritum. Et inter virtutes novae obedientiae recenset officia oeconomica, iusticiam et patientiam in communibus aerumnis matris, quae multae et magnae sunt. Nominat autem has virtutes, labores partus et educationis, fidem, dilectionem, sanctificationem et modestiam. Fidem necessariam esse in omnibus manifestum est, et hic cogitetur integra doctrina de fide, quae est fiducia acquiescens in filio Dei, et accipiens propter eum gratis remissionem peccatorum, imputationem iusticiae, veram consolationem et vivificationem, qua incoatur in nobis renovatio propter filium Dei, et per eum. Haec autem fides assidue in omni invocatione, in omnibus periculis exercenda est, et cum ea comprehendi intelligimus Spem et Tolerantiam, ut supra de precatione dictum est. Harum virtutum exercitia sunt praecipuae consolationes in tota hac vita, de quibus dicitur Philip. 4.: Pax Dei gubernet corda vestra. Item Psalmo 124.: Qui confidunt in Domino, sicut mons Sion non movebuntur in aeternum.

Dilectio sicut alibi significat dilectionem Dei et proximi, et comprehendit timorem et obedientiam erga Deum. Deinde in dilectione proximi, in matrefamilias prima virtus est dilectio mariti et sobolis, lenitas animi, ne iracundia et rabie ipsius fiat triste coniugium, Nec abalienetur viri animus. Item, Patientia, ne maritum in adversa fortuna deserat. Item sit iusta in contractibus, non sit defraudatrix. Item sit benefica erga pauperes. Hae virtutes omnes dilectione comprehenduntur, et discerni possunt inspecto Decalogo. Fiunt autem magis conspicuae, cum exempla intuentur, ut Sarae, Abigail, viduae Sareptanae, Elizabeth matris Baptistae, Elisabeth Thuringicae. Item, Elizabeth sororis Caroli, quae fuit nupta regi Da- nico, et comes exiliorum et magnarum aerumna- rum socia, nec voluit regnum recipere oblatum sine marito. Sanctificatio phrasi hebraea saepe castitatem significat, ut primae Thessalonicenses 4.: Haec est voluntas Dei sanctificatio vestra, ut abstineatis a scortatione, et possideat quisque vas suum in san- ctificatione et honore. Cum autem supra dixerit, mulieres pariendo salvas fieri, constat non prohi- beri consuetudinem coniugalem, sed adulteria prohiberi. Iam hic cogitent bonae mentes, et necessariam et pulcram virtutem esse castitatem, quae est vel in coniugio vel in vita coelibe vitare omnes prohibitas commixtiones, et seminis pro- fusiones. Ac de necessitate expresse dictum est, 1. Corinth. 6.: Ne erretis, scortatores et adulteri non possidebunt regnum Dei. Item, Galat. 5.: Qui talia faciunt, regnum Dei non possidebunt. Item, ad Hebr. 12.: Sine sanctificatione, id est, castitate nemo Deum videbit. Nec tantum aeternae poenae comitantur libi- dines in his, qui non convertuntur, sed etiam praesentes poenae in hac vita et conversos et non conversos opprimunt, quanquam conversis miti- gantur, ut ostendit exemplum Davidis. Et ex- presse dictum est Hebr. 13.: Scortatores et adul- teros iudicabit Deus, scilicet et in hac vita et post hanc vitam, si non fuerint conversi. Iudicat au- tem Deus aliquando immediate, sicut delet Sodo- ma, in quo exemplo diligentissime consideran- dum est, illam horrendam executionem poenae ab ipso filio Dei fieri, qui in eo itinere hospes est Abrahae, ubi postea textus inquit: Pluit Dominus ignem et sulphur a Domino super Sodoma, Gene. 19. Aliquando punit mediate per imperia et alias calamitates, ut Antonius punitur ab Augusto. Sunt autem et magistratuum legitimae poenae iu- dicii divini, nec dubium est vagas libidines mul- torum ingentium bellorum et magnarum vastatio- num causas esse, ut ostendunt historiae: nam et inter diluvii causas fit mentio libidinum.
