Postea narrantur exitia Sodomae, Cananaeorum, et fere totius tribus Beniamin, Principes suspenduntur in deserto, adulterium Davidis secuta est seditio, Graecae historiae plenae sunt exemplorum, Siba- ris, Thebae, Spartae: et nunc Africa, Asia, Ae- gyptus, Syria, Graecia, sunt aut solitudines, aut tetra Barbarorum stabula sine Ecclesiis, sine le- gibus, sine disciplina, sine doctrina, propter idola, haereses et libidines.

Horum tristissimorum exemplorum cogita- tione nos exuscitemus, ut simus vigilantiores in tuenda vera doctrina, in vera invocatione, et vi- tandis inquinamentis libidinum. Circumspicia- mus etiam quotidianas poenas: multae magnae et parvae familiae quotidie evertuntur propter libi- dinum confusiones. Quare castitatem pie tueri studeamus, tum in coniugio, tum in vita coelibe. Est etiam quaedam aetatis teneritas, quae adhuc facile potest retinere puritatem, si vitet mala so- dalitia et helluationes, et ad sobrietatem ac ad la- bores honestos adiungat cogitationem de iudicio Dei, et de poenis, et precationem.

Dixi autem iam de poenis corporalibus. Apud Paulum Ephes. 4. fit mentio multo gra- viorum poenarum, videlicet coecitatis et indo- lentiae, ut cum Ptolomaei polluunt se variis mo- dis, postea ruunt coeci in domestica latrocinia, et sibi ipsis exitia accersunt: et sunt in conspectu exempla pontificum, sacrificulorum et monacho- rum, ibi dominantur haec duo mala, Coecitas et Indolentia. Plurimi sunt palam Epicurei. Alii pauci superstitiosi et fascinati falsis persuasionibus delere veritatem conantur, deinde securi, sine ullo poenitentiae gemitu in magnis sceleribus vi- vunt, et Sibaritico more omnia voluptatum genera quaerunt, donec ruunt in aeternum exitium.

Has maximas poenas, coecitatem et indolen- tiam, formidantes, majore cura tueamur castita- tem, et filium Dei oremus, ut cum ipse maxime castitatem amet propter suam gloriam, nos adiu- vet, ne contaminemur, ac ne diabolo voluptatem nostri lapsus praebeant, qui multiplices triumphos agit, cum hoc modo aliquos evertit, et laetatur odio Dei; quod fiant opera, quae valde displi- ceant Deo. Item, quod deformet creaturam Dei, et turbet ordinem divinitus institutum, quod avellit hominem a Deo, et contristat Spiritum sanctum, quod praebet occasionem aliis multis malis secuturis: nam diabolus longam telam texit. Postremo, quid est tristius quam ita vivere, ut certo scias Deum tibi irasci, nec possis ad eum accedere invocatione, aut petere ab eo auxilium, aut defensionem ulla in re. Hae tantae miseriae saepe multumque cogitandae sunt, et exempla nostra, et aliena intuenda, ut nos ad poeniten- tiam et ad precationem exuscitemus, et vitemus occasiones lapsuum, et coërceamus nostra mem- bra, sicut Paulus inquit Ephes. 5.: Ambulate ac- curate, non ut fatui. Utile est recte intelligere appellationes virtu- tum, et de earum fontibus, officiis et dignitate saepe cogitare. In hac imbecillitate naturae non videmus, quantae res sint sapientia, veritas, vir- tus. Nec econtra satis cernimus, quam horrenda mala sint mendacium, cultus idolorum, iniusti- cia, pollui libidinibus. Praeterea aut frigide co- gitamus de Lege, aut indignamur nos quasi iniu- ste in hunc carcerem inclusos esse, sicut Gorgias dixit, Legem tyrannum esse. Hanc in nostra natura caliginem et contumaciam sciamus esse magna et tristia vulnera et horrenda peccata, de quibus dicitur, Rom. 8.: Sensus carnis inimici- tia est adversus Deum. Ideo morbos nostros ali- quo modo agnoscamus et deploremus, et confu- giamus ad mediatorem filium Dei, ad Samarita- num nostrum, et ab eo petamus auxilium. Et cum de virtutibus cogitamus, Deum ipsum intueamur, et sciamus talem esse, fulgentem vera et immensa luce, sapientia, bonitate, beneficentia, veritate, rectitudine et puritate, et velle nos sibi similes esse: ita melius considerari natura et pulcritudo virtutum potest, cum quasi in ipso Deo eas aspi- cimus. Etsi enim lex est doctrina, quae narrat qua- lis sit Deus, tamen de virtutibus angustius cogi- tamus intuentes legem, a qua velut a carcere ab- horremus. Ames iusticiam in non laedendis aliis, quia Deus talis est, videlicet beneficus et aequa- lis, et vult nos sibi similes esse, et cogita hanc virtutem ideo rem esse pulcerrimam, quia Deus talis est. Ita ames veritatem, quia Deus talis est, et vult nos sibi similes esse. Hanc cogitationem et ad caeteras virtutes transferas, et vocabula recte enarrentur. Sumantur autem enumerationes et descriptiones ex Decalogo, ut saepe dicimus. Vocabulum σωφροσύνη hoc loco ut saepe alias significat et temperantiam et modestiam. Proprie autem temperantia nominatur convenien- tia in cibo et potu. Haec virtus per sese necessa- ria est, quia vitia contraria corpori exitiosa esse per sese manifestum est, ut dicitur, Plures intem- perantia quam gladio perire: Et nutrix est multa- rum aliarum virtutum, invocationis, intentionis, deliberationis, diligentiae, circumspectionis, ca- stitatis, cum intemperantia impediat sensum ti- moris Dei, poenitentiam, meditationem, invo- cationem, et confirmat securitatem, et multa in- cendia cupiditatum augeat. De invocatione dici- tur, Marci 9.: Hoc genus daemoniorum non eii- citur, nisi ieiunio et oratione. Et Petrus inquit, 1. Petr. 5.: σωφρονήσατε et sobrii estote ad pre- cationem. De castitate, Et Venus in vinis, ignis in igne furit. Et Iuvenalis, Quid enim Venus ebria curat? Et semper sit in conspectu dictum Senecae, Consuetudine insaniae durata vitia vi- no concepta, etiam sine vino valent.

Nec dubium est augeri publicas et privatas calamitates, propterea quia Deus intemperantiam punit, quam quidem plerunqve et alia multa vi- tia comitantur, iuxta illud Epigramma: ἥλις καὶ μεθυεῖ καὶ ψεύδεται, οἷος ἕκαστον οἶκος, τοίη ἢ καὶ ξυναπᾶσα πόλις. Heliaca urbs simul est mendax ac ebria, talis tota urbs est, domus ut quaelibet esse solet, id est, publicus malus status inde oritur, quia singuli nolunt sese emendare, sed quilibet aliis vult leges ferre, non sese et suos regere, cum dictum sit: Iustus primum accusator est sui.

Modestia vero est virtus in opinione, ser- mone gestu, actione negotiorum, servans conve- nientiam, id est, retrahens nos intra metas per- sonae convenientes.

Ex hac definitione intelligi potest, Mode- stiam tanquam totum complecti multas partes seu species, quarum aliquae appellationibus discer- nuntur, et fiunt discrimina illustria, cum confe- runtur opposita vitia: cum Modestia pugnant su- perbia, Thrasonica vanitas, seu iactantia. Item garrulitas, futilitas, scurrilitas, petulantia, ob- scoenitas: Item luxus, et ineptiae in vestitu, et multo maxime pugnat cum modestia curiositas, seu πολυπραγμοσύνη ingerens se in aliena ne- gotia.

Etsi autem vitia omnia, quae pugnant cum temperantia et modestia in omnibus hominibus, viris et foeminis perniciosa et deformia sunt, ta- men in mulieribus magis conspicua est deformi- tas, quia hic sexus propter infirmitatem latere de- bet. Itaque valde turpe spectaculum est in coetu mulier ebria, et facilius tunc ruit in alia dede- cora: sic deformitas magis conspicua est in mu- liere garrula, curiosa, admiscente se negotiis gu- bernationis, ut Liviam matrem Tyberius nomina- bat Ulyssem stolatum, propterea quia in republica multa negotia astute movebat. Itaque multa prae- cepta traduntur, quae iubent mulieres oeconomica domi curare, et omittere negotia quae a viris gubernanda sunt. Ideo saepe citatur dictum Sophoclis ex Aiace: γυναῖξι κόσμον ἡ σιγὴ φέρει, Mulieribus silentium decus est.

Etsi autem brevis est haec apud Paulum enumeratio virtutum, tamen lector attentus videbit formam totius vitae matronalis hic sapienter comprehensam esse. Nec ero prolixior, quia oportet Decalogum omnibus notissimum esse, qui est fons doctrinae de omnibus virtutibus.

Rursus autem admoneo lectorem, ut testimonium de laude coniugii hic consideret, et causas cogitet, Deus immensa sapientia sic condidit genus humanum et certo modo coniunxit, vult intelligi et praestari castitatem, vel in coniugio, vel in vita coelibe eorum, qui sunt idonei ad vitam coelibem, vult vitari huius ordinis conturbationem, et horribiliter punit vagas libidines privatis et publicis calamitatibus, et deinde poenis aeternis, nisi fiat conversio. Propter has causas laudata est vita coniugalis.

Cum autem oporteat regi nos verbo Dei, et nulli cultus Deo placeant sine verbo Dei, manifestum est monachorum vota non esse cultus Dei, et cumulaverunt monachi et sacrificuli multos alios errores, et cultus idolorum, quibus adiuncta est prohibitio coniugii, quam infra Paulus expresse nominat doctrinam daemoniorum. Significat autem hic titulus multa magna mala, ardet diabolus odio Dei, et ut Deum contumelia afficiat, primum falsos cultus et mendacia in genere humano serit. Deinde opus Dei, scilicet genus humanum, horribiliter deformare et perdere conatur, accendit discordias et bella, multos impellit, ut teterrimis libidinibus contaminentur, quia scit Deum valde irasci confusionibus libidinum. Et haec facit omnia, ut quam plurimos homines pertrahat in aeternum exitium, et ad aeternas blasphemias Dei. Eodem consilio impulit hypocritas ad legem de coelibatu imponendam sacerdotibus, et ad excogitanda impia vincula votorum, quae multipliciter offendunt Deum, quia et nervi sunt falsorum cultuum, et sunt causae horribilium contaminationum, propter quae peccata ingentia hominum agmina ruunt in aeternas poenas.

Haec mala et eorum fontes intelligi necesse est, et impia lex de coelibatu damnanda est, ac iis qui discedunt a defensoribus idolorum et legis de coelibatu, magna consolatio est, quod Paulus expresse nominat illam legem doctrinam daemoniorum, ut certissime sciamus eam displicere Deo, et conscientiae sciant fugiendam esse societatem eius defensionis, iuxta illud: Si quis aliud Evangelium docet, anathema sit. Sic autem ab illis discedamus, non ut priores sordes retineamus, sed efficiamur membra filii Dei vera invocatione, castitate, et aliis veris cultibus.

## 3:1 Argument
Chapter III.

Latin:

Caput III.

## 3:1
If anyone desires the office of a Bishop, he desires a good work.

He previously delivered brief admonitions concerning the doctrine of faith and works; now he adds an admonition concerning the ministers of the Gospel, as if establishing the polity of the Church. Here, therefore, we must speak of vocation and ordination. But first it must be known that there is a twofold vocation: The one which happens immediately from God. The other which happens mediately through men in a lawful manner. The former is immediate, because God, out of immense goodness for the sake of the son and through the son, wishes to gather an eternal Church for himself; therefore, he first appointed the son as high priest. This one first brings forth the Gospel from the bosom of the eternal father; this one was ordained and anointed with the fullness of the holy Spirit, as it is said in Isaiah 61: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me. And in the forty-fourth Psalm: God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness because of your companions. This son then, in order to begin and subsequently restore the Church, calls and sends Fathers, Prophets, and Apostles immediately by his own voice, anoints them with the gifts of the holy Spirit, and is effective through their ministry, as it is said in Ephesians 4: He gives gifts to men, some indeed as Prophets, others as Apostles, others as Pastors.

Although, however, this vocation and mission happens by divine authority, yet God himself adds testimonies, so that the Church and the called themselves may know that this mission is divine: nor does he wish such great things to be done in the Church without testimonies. And the called themselves have great need, even for the sake of their own conscience, to have a testimony of their vocation, because consciences are greatly tormented when they are struck by that voice: They ran and I did not send them, in Jeremiah twenty-third.

Therefore, so that both the Church and the conscience of the one called may be without doubt as to whether this ministry is from God, divine testimonies are added, just as manifest testimonies are attributed to Abel, Noah, Joseph, Moses, Elijah, Elisha, and the other Prophets and Apostles.

Sometimes God also reveals the mission to certain men, as Moses knows that Joshua is appointed leader, and he lays hands upon him, as it is written in the last chapter of Deuteronomy. Eli knows that Samuel is being called, and concerning Paul it is said in the Acts, chapter 18: Separate for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have called them. And in such cases the divine mission itself is the ordination, in which the son of God simultaneously anoints them and lays hands upon them, that is, he blesses them, and is effective in their ministry, just as he says to Moses, Exodus 4: I will be in your mouth and in his mouth. And Jeremiah 10: Behold, I put my words in your mouth. And Isaiah 55: The word which goes forth from my mouth shall not return to me empty. These things are to be observed first concerning immediate vocation.

The other is mediate vocation, which happens through men in a lawful manner. Because God adds this also to that other benefit, he wishes the Church itself to call ministers, and affirms that he is effective even through the ministry of these. This great good must be acknowledged, and thanks must be given to God: and the consolation must be held that in this way God gathers the Church to himself in a continuous series, and is present with the ministry of those who teach rightly.

It is expressly written to Titus: Appoint presbyters through the cities, as I commanded. Likewise 2 Timothy 2: The things which you have heard from me before many witnesses, these entrust to faithful men, who may be fit to teach others. Likewise, 1 Timothy 5: Lay hands on no one hastily.

These sayings manifestly show that it is commanded to the Church that it should elect ministers. And therefore Paul gives precepts as to what kind of men are to be elected, because he wishes the election, which happens by the voice of the Church, to be valid.

Now let testimonies concerning the ministry be added here, which affirm that God is effective through the ministry of the Gospel, that is, through the voice of the Gospel, which Paul, Titus, and the hearer of Titus, retaining the uncorrupted doctrine, sound forth the same. Romans 1: The Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes. 2 Corinthians 3: He made us ministers of the new testament, not of the letter, but of the spirit. Ephesians 4: He ascended, he gave gifts to men, Pastors and

Doctors. Namely, those called either immediately or mediately. Luke 10: He who hears you, hears me. John 15: I am the vine, you are the branches; he who abides in me and I in him, he will bear much fruit. John chapter 18: I pray not for these only, but for all who will believe through their word. It is necessary for these things to be known for many reasons. First, so that this mediate calling of ministers is not despised and omitted, just as we remember the wandering Anabaptists despise this whole calling, and say that ministers are to be awaited whom God would send immediately. Let us be fortified against these fanatical delusions. Then, this doctrine is also derived from here: where there is no prophetic and apostolic calling, let us know that the ministry of the Gospel is by no means to be invaded without a mediate calling, because Peter says in 1 Peter 4: Let no one be an ἀλλοτριοεπίσκοπος. And generally, it is commanded to the Thessalonians in 1 Thess. 4: Do your own work. And there is a sad rebuke in Jeremiah 23: They ran, and I did not send them. And God destroys Korah and Dathan, who invade the ministry without a calling. Formerly, however, this calling or election took place by the votes of the Church, with some Bishop or Pastor brought in for the examination of doctrine, as the Nicene Synod expressly says, in the Tripartite History, book 2, page 325: ὁ λάος αἵρειτο συνεπιψηφίζοντος καὶ συνεπισφραγίζοντος ἐπισκόπου, that is, Let the people elect, with the Bishop approving and confirming at the same time. And book 9 of the Tripartite History, page 558, in the Epistle to Damasus, the Bishops of the East write that they, in the presence of the Emperor Theodosius, ordained a Bishop elected by the votes of the whole clergy and the whole city. And in the same place regarding another location: κοινονικῶς ἐχειροτόνησαν πάσης συμψήφου τῆς ἐκκλησίας, they ordained canonically by votes, with the whole Church approving. Now the calling is done through the principal members of the Church, as in cities through the Senate, with some from the college of ministers of the Gospel brought in, because at that time when election was done by the votes of the entire multitude, tumults often arose and slaughters were committed, therefore the restriction to fewer people was made. However, it is necessary that pious Doctors from the college of ministers of the Gospel be brought in for the examination of doctrine, concerning which it is manifestly commanded to Timothy in 2 Timothy 2: Entrust the doctrine to faithful men, who are fit to teach.

Afterwards, it is also necessary for the elected or called person to be judged by the Churches, because if the Church knew that he did not think rightly, it could reject the one called, but when it receives one who thinks rightly, it confirms the calling. Afterwards, it adds prayer: and it was an ancient rite to lay hands on the elected. This sign showed the calling and the confirmation of the calling: meanwhile, without any doubt, the Son of God brings it about that the ministry of this person is effective; thus He Himself lays on hands and anoints him.

In this ancient custom, it must be seen which members are necessary and of divine right, which rites are mutable, and how the depravation was brought about by the Pope and the Bishops addicted to him.

There are, however, many depravations. They do not institute a calling to the ministry, but say that they ordain Priests to sacrifice, and they feign that it is necessary for there to be a certain crowd of Mass-priests who offer for the living and the dead, and that no one has the power of consecrating the bread and the cup except those who have received the power from a Bishop confirmed by the Roman pontiff. In these opinions, there is a great chaos of errors.

Afterwards, they add unjust bonds of Canons, concerning celibacy and other traditions; likewise, they anoint with oil, which has been consecrated with magical blasphemies.

At this time, they add new blasphemies, such as that the one to be ordained must first swear that he does not wish to embrace the doctrine that censures their errors and idols.

Where these great depravations are retained, ordination is by no means to be sought from such Bishops: nor let us be moved by the clamors of the unlearned, who shout that the ordination performed in our Churches is not valid because there are no Bishops among us confirmed by this title by the Roman pontiff. But the firmest rule must be opposed: If anyone teaches another Gospel, let him be anathema. Nothing can be said more expressly, since it is manifest that those who stubbornly defend manifest errors and manifest idols are to be fled, and it is certain that such are the Pope and the Bishops addicted to him. We are most certain that they are not members of the true Church of God.

Let us, however, seek which and where the true Church of God is, and let us join ourselves to it, according to the saying of Psalm 26: One thing I ask of the Lord, that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life.

Item, Psalm 25: I will wash my hands among the innocent, and I will go about your altar, O Lord. That the true ministry of the Gospel exists in the true Church is most certain from the saying: He ascended on high, he gave gifts to men, Prophets, Apostles, Pastors and Teachers etc. Ephesians 4. Wherefore the right of vocation remains with this one, because it was said to the true Church: Appoint elders.

The necessary members of ordination are these: Vocation to the ministry, examination of doctrine, indicating the called to the Church, approving the vocation, and prayer. Therefore it is most certain that ordination pertains to the true Church, not to the enemies of the Church.

Moreover, there were immediately in the ancient Church ceremonies in the external rite of ordination, the laying on of hands and the placing of a book upon the head, etc. I say that such signs are mutable, but yet, since it is fitting that all things be done in order in the Church, it is useful that there be some public rite of ordination without superstition: 1. For this purpose, that the testimonies of the vocation and the approval of the one called may be more illustrious. 2. And that it may be seen whose Church doctrine the one called embraces. 3. And that a public prayer may be made there. 4. This very rite is also useful for the confirmation of many, so that they may know that the right of ordination pertains to the true Church. 5. And that they may consider what the errors of the adversaries are. 6. And of which Church they wish to be citizens. 7. Finally, there are many utilities, when it is judged without calumny and without superstition.

These things have been said for the instruction of the younger ones concerning vocation and ordination.

There is a dispute here also concerning ambition, whether one sins by seeking the office of pastor? I answer: There is a twofold petition. The one is pious, which is done in such a way that you offer your labors, and have the προαίρεσιν (purpose) of rightly performing the office, and you leave the judgment concerning yourself to those who are employed, and you do not contend by illicit means. This petition is praised by Paul in this saying: If anyone aspires to the office of Bishop, he desires a noble work. He praises the will of the one seeking, and admonishes him to consider the magnitude of the work: as it is manifest that the most difficult things are the explanation of doctrine, governance, and the circumspection necessary to avoid scandals.

Nor is it unjust to seek a reward in one's own order. And such a petition does not hinder the vocation, but rather thanks are owed to the one seeking, because he makes himself known, since those who preside do not know as many as are needed for the ministry. But then the vocation is said to have been made, when the judgment and approval of the one calling has been added.

The other petition is ambitious, which is done in such a way that it hinders judgment and contends by illicit means. This ambition fights against the vocation, because it attempts to hinder the judgment which is necessary for the vocation: and many vices concur, labors are not sought, but revenues or splendor. Moreover, they are most pernicious thieves who, having omitted the labor, devour the revenues, and concerning pride it is said, Proverbs 16: Everyone who is proud in heart is an abomination before God.

Let the explanation of the argument be noted here: Let no one seek or receive a burden that exceeds his strength. Administration in the Church and in polities without any doubt exceeds human strength, therefore it is not to be sought or received? I answer to the major premise: Let no one seek or receive it, when a vocation does not approach. Item: Let no one seek or receive it by trust in himself, but when a vocation has approached, then the administration becomes a work of obedience owed to God, and it is to be done by trust in divine aid, and in the acknowledgment and invocation of God.

Then I answer to the minor premise: Administration exceeds human strength, that is true, but it becomes possible and effective with God helping. And God wills to gather the Church in this way by the voice of ministers, as Paul says 1 Corinthians 3: We are God's fellow workers, you are God's field, I planted, Apollos watered, God gave the increase. Nor is it required that we ourselves be sufficient, but our sufficiency is from God, 2 Corinthians 3. But this is required, that we be faithful, 1 Corinthians 4. Faithfulness, however, embraces a good will and one that is not slothful, but with a good conscience seeking the things necessary for administration, namely a moderate knowledge of doctrine, diligence, constancy in confession, and similar virtues, a catalog of which Paul recounts in this place.

That a vocation or election made by men is pleasing to God, and that the ministry through such is effective, is manifest from this, because Paul commands ministers to be chosen, and narrates what kind are to be chosen; now if no election were to be made by men, why would there be a need to hand down a form of what kind are to be chosen.

Furthermore, concerning this form, let us know that it is necessary for individual men to know the sum of doctrine, which is the directress of faith and morals. And there is one common sum of all things which he recited above: Fight the good fight, having faith and a good conscience.

But in order that the conscience may have a norm, let us look at the Decalogue, and let us understand it rightly. Let us know that works conflicting with the Decalogue are works polluting the conscience and offending God, and conscience is a judgment in us approving deeds according to the word of God, or according to the law of nature, and condemning the contrary, which condemnation is followed in a certain order in rational nature by horrible torments, which are witnesses and the work of the judgment of God, according to that saying: God is a consuming fire.

The general sum of doctrine having been considered, let each one afterwards see what things are proper to his own vocation: this part also pertains to the Decalogue. Let the Minister of the Gospel know that he ought to sound forth doctrine. Let him not therefore be ignorant of doctrine, and let him be in some way fit for teaching. Then, let the Decalogue rightly understood be the norm of morals for him also: This sum Paul proposes here as well.

At the beginning, however, he sets down the genus or sum suitable for those choosing: A Bishop must be irreprehensible, in Greek ἀνεπίληπτον. And to Titus, chapter 1, it is called ἀνέγκλητον, that is, not guilty of any crime which can be truly accused before human judgment. For ἐπιλαμβάνομαι signifies I reprehend, I rebuke, as in Plato in the Gorgias, If I seem to say anything not rightly, ἐπιλάμβανε, that is, rebuke it. And ἐγκαλεῖν signifies to accuse or to call into judgment, because Paul is speaking here of election, it is certain that it is said concerning accusation before human judgment, he wishes the Bishop not to be infamous. And let the crimes be known, on account of which either civil courts mark men with infamy, or the Church forbids communion.

God has so ordained life that he wills that on account of manifest crimes men should either be put to death by the political power, or otherwise be cast out from the rest of society. As on account of blasphemies, perjuries, magic, manifest worship of idols, seditions, homicides, wandering and incestuous lusts, adulteries, thefts, calumnies, the crime of forgery.

A most insipid interpretation is that which some have invented, A Bishop must be without sin: this interpretation is false, when it is understood of sin before God, according to that saying of John, 1 John 1: If we say that we have no sin, we are liars. There remain in this miserable nature, even in the saints in this life, many great stains and sins, just as Jeremiah says, chapter 17: The heart of man is perverse and wretched. And in the daily exercises of repentance these interior sins are to be acknowledged and deplored before God. But Paul is not speaking of these here; the interpreter translates to Titus, without crime.

Let the younger ones therefore learn the phrase, it is one thing to say without sin, another without crime, that is, without such a crime as is condemned in the judgments of the Church or of the state.

But here we ourselves object many things to ourselves. First, no one is so firm that he does not also sometimes fall shamefully, as Solomon says, Eccles. chapter 7: There is no just man on earth who does not sin. Likewise, Prov. 24: The just man shall fall seven times. Likewise, that saying of Simonides is known: It is impossible to be a tetragon, that is, perfect. And it is manifest that in every government there are many errors of omission and ignorance.

Secondly, no one can avoid detractions and calumnies. For evil speaking is a sweet and customary evil, as Pindar says: ὄψον πολίταις αἱ κακηγορίαι.

Concerning the former question I answer: Let the rule be held in all duties, that we be faithful, as is said in 1 Corinthians 4, that is, let there be a good purpose, and let us strive to do rightly, and for the most part let us do rightly, but having fallen, let us allow ourselves to be healed. Furthermore, since we all know that all men can most easily fall and err: and the horrible snares of the devil are assiduous, let us be more ardent in the invocation of the Son of God, nor let us forget the saying, John 15: Without me you can do nothing. Likewise: Without your divinity there is nothing in man.

Concerning the second question I answer, both must be provided: First, that the conscience be without stain. Second, that the reputation be intact among the more honest who judge rightly, as is said in Psalm 149: His praise is in the Church of the saints. And the maxim is known: I have need of a good conscience for the sake of God, a good reputation for the sake of my neighbor. And in Ecclesiasticus, chapter 39: The Church declares their praise.

But that in the meantime many are slanderous is not the fault of those who serve faithfully, as is said: There is no remedy against the bite of a sycophant, and there are many dispositions full of arrogance and poison, restless and sophisticated, which often can even plausibly construct calumnies. Concerning these it is said in Proverbs 17: The evil man always seeks quarrels, and a cruel messenger will be sent against him. However, the rule in Matthew 5 must be held: Blessed are you when they shall revile you, lying. Likewise, in Psalm 18: They

And it is a necessary virtue in life to bear such injuries wisely, as David and Fabius do not answer calumniators.

Here also the question concerning the Donatists is agitated. Although infamous men are not to be chosen, and those who later become infamous when they are in the ministry were to be removed, nevertheless the error of the Donatists is to be exploded, who contended that the ministry is not valid when men polluted against their conscience perform it; against these the doctrine must be opposed that the efficacy of the ministry does not depend upon the dignity of the minister, but is truly the work of God, as John says in Luke 3: I baptize you with water, but another will baptize you with fire and the Holy Spirit. In Matthew 13 the Church is compared to a net, in which there are good and bad fish: so also in the whole Church and in the ministry there are good and bad, but yet they are in agreement concerning doctrine. Let us be content with these admonitions in this place.

Latin:

Si quis Episcopi munus desiderat, honestum opus desiderat.

Admonitiones breves antea de doctrina fidei et operum tradidit, nunc addit admonitionem de ministris Evangelii, quasi Ecclesiae politiam constituens. Hic igitur de vocatione et ordinatione dicendum est. Primum autem sciendum est, duplicem esse vocationem: Alteram quae fit immediate a Deo. Alteram quae fit mediate per homines iusto modo. Immediata prior est, quia Deus immensa bonitate propter filium et per filium sibi vult aeternam Ecclesiam colligere, ideo primum constituit summum sacerdotem filium, hic primus ex sinu aeterni patris profert Evangelium, hic ordinatus et unctus est plenitudine Spiritus sancti, ut Esaiae 61. dicitur: Spiritus Domini super me, eo quod unxit me. Et Psalmo quadragesimo quarto: Unxit te Deus, Deus tuus oleo laetitiae propter consortes tuos. Hic filius deinde, ut incoët et subinde instauret Ecclesiam, Patres, Prophetas et Apostolos immediate sua voce vocat et mittit, ungit eos donis Spiritus sancti, et est efficax per ministerium eorum, ut Ephes. 4. dicitur: Dona dat hominibus, alios quidem Prophetas, alios Apostolos, Pastores.

Quanquam autem haec vocatio et missio fit autoritate divina, tamen ipse Deus addit testimonia, ut Ecclesia et ipsi vocati sciant hanc missionem esse divinam: nec vult fieri res tantas in Ecclesia sine testimoniis. Ac ipsis vocatis valde opus est etiam propter suam conscientiam habere testimonium vocationis, quia valde anguntur conscientiae, cum illa voce feriuntur: Currebant et non mittebam eos, Ieremiae vicesimo tertio.

Itaque ut et Ecclesia et conscientia vocati sint sine dubitatione, an hoc ministerium sit a Deo, adduntur divina testimonia, ut Abel, Noae, Ioseph, Moysi, Eliae, Helisaeo et caeteris Prophetis et Apostolis tribuuntur manifesta testimonia.

Interdum et patefacit Deus missionem certis hominibus, ut Moyses scit constitui ducem Iosue, et ei manus imponit, ut scriptum est Deuteronomii ultimo. Eli scit vocari Samuelem, et de Paulo in Actis dicitur, capite 18.: Segregate mihi Paulum et Barnabam ad opus ad quod vocavi eos. Et in talibus ipsa missio divina est ordinatio, in qua filius Dei simul et ungit eos, et manus imponit eis, id est, benedicit eis, et est efficax in ministerio eorum, sicut ad Moysen dicit, Exod. 4.: Ego ero in ore tuo et in ore illius. Et Ieremiae 10.: Ecce do verba mea in ore tuo. Et Esaiae 55.: Verbum quod egreditur de ore meo, non revertetur ad me vacuum. Haec de vocatione immediata primum observanda sunt.

Altera est vocatio mediata, quae fit per homines iusto modo. Quia Deus ad illud alterum beneficium hoc quoque adiungit, vult Ecclesiam ipsam vocare ministros, et affirmat se horum ministerio etiam efficacem esse. Hoc ingens bonum agnoscendum est, et Deo gratiae agendae sunt: ac tenenda consolatio, quod hoc modo Deus continua serie sibi colligit Ecclesiam, et ministerio recte docentium adest.

Expresse scriptum est ad Titum: Constituas presbyteros per civitates, sicut iussi. Item 2. Timoth. 2.: Quae audivisti a me multis testibus, haec commenda fidelibus hominibus, qui sint idonei ad docendos alios. Item, 1. Timoth. 5.: Nemini cito manus imponito.

Haec dicta manifeste ostendunt Ecclesiae praecipi, ut ministros eligat. Ideoque Paulus dat praecepta quales sint eligendi, quia vult electionem, quae fit voce Ecclesiae, ratam esse.

Iam huc addantur testimonia de ministerio, quae affirmant Deum esse efficacem per ministerium Evangelii, id est, per vocem Evangelii, quam sonant eandem Paulus, Titus, et Titi auditor retinens doctrinam incorruptam. Roman. 1.: Evangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti. 2. Corinth. 3.: Fecit nos ministros novi testamenti, non literae, sed spiritus. Ephes. 4.: Ascendit, dedit dona hominibus, Pastores et

Doctores. Scilicet vel immediate vel mediate vocatos. Lucae 10.: Qui vos audit, me audit. Iohann. 15.: Ego sum vitis, vos palmites, qui manet in me et ego in eo, feret fructum copiosum. Iohannis capite 18.: Rogo non pro eis tantum, sed pro omnibus credituris per verbum eorum. Haec sciri necesse est propter multas causas. Primum, ne contemnatur et omittatur haec mediata vocatio ministrorum, sicut meminimus errones Anabaptistas contemnere totam hanc vocationem, et dicere expectandos esse ministros, quos Deus immediate mitteret. Adversus haec fanatica deliria muniti simus. Deinde et haec doctrina hinc sumitur, ubi non est vocatio prophetica et apostolica, sciamus sine vocatione mediata nequaquam invadendum esse ministerium Evangelii, quia Petrus inquit 1. Petri 4.: Nemo sit ἀλλοτριοεπίσκοπος. Et generaliter praeceptum est ad Thessalonicenses 1. Thess. 4.: Propria facite. Et tristis reprehensio est Ierem. 23.: Currebant et non mittebam eos. Et Deus perdit Chore et Dathan, qui sine vocatione invadunt ministerium. Olim autem fiebat haec vocatio seu electio per suffragia Ecclesiae, adhibito Episcopo aliquo, vel Pastore, propter explorationem doctrinae, ut expresse Synodus Nicena inquit, in tripartita historia, libro 2. pag. 325.: ὁ λάος αἵρειτο συνεπιψηφίζοντος καὶ συνεπισφραγίζοντος ἐπισκόπου, id est, Populus eligat simul comprobante et confirmante Episcopo. Et lib. 9. Tripart. hist. pag. 558. in Epistola ad Damasum scribunt Episcopi Orientis, se praesente Theodosio imperatore ordinasse Episcopum, electum suffragiis totius cleri, et totius civitatis. Et ibidem de alio loco: κοινονικῶς ἐχειροτόνησαν πάσης συμψήφου τῆς ἐκκλησίας, Canonice elegerunt per suffragia comprobante tota Ecclesia. Nunc fit vocatio per praecipua membra Ecclesiae, ut in urbibus per Senatum, adhibitis aliquibus ex collegio ministrorum Evangelii, quia tunc cum fiebat electio suffragiis universae multitudinis, saepe tumultus orti sunt et factae caedes, ideo restrictio ad pauciores facta est. Oportet autem adhiberi pios Doctores ex collegio ministrorum Evangelii, propter explorationem doctrinae, de qua ad Timotheum manifeste praecipitur 2. Timoth. 2.: Commenda doctrinam hominibus fidelibus, qui sunt ad docendum idonei.

Postea etiam iudicari Ecclesiis electum seu vocatum oportet, quia si sciret Ecclesia eum non recte sentire, reiicere vocatum posset, sed cum recte sentientem recipit, confirmat vocationem. Postea addit precationem: et fuit antiquus ritus imponere manus electis. Hoc signum ostendebat vocationem et vocationis confirmationem: interea sine ulla dubitatione filius Dei efficit, ut ministerium huius sit efficax, sic ipse manus imponit et ungit eum.

In hac antiqua consuetudine videndum est, quae membra sint necessaria et iuris divini, qui ritus sint mutabiles, et quomodo facta sit depravatio per Papam et Episcopos ipsi addictos.

Sunt autem multae depravationes. Non instituunt vocationem ad ministerium, sed dicunt se ordinare Sacerdotes ad sacrificandum, et fingunt oportere certam turbam esse Sacrificulorum, qui offerant pro vivis et mortuis, et neminem habere potestatem consecrandi panem et calicem nisi tales, qui potestatem acceperint ab Episcopo confirmato a Romano pontifice. In his opinionibus magnum chaos est errorum.

Postea addunt iniusta vincula Canonum, de coelibatu et aliis traditionibus, item ungunt oleo, quod magicis blasphemiis consecratum est.

Hoc tempore addunt novas blasphemias, ut primum ordinandus iurei, se nolle amplecti doctrinam taxantem ipsorum errores et idola.

Ubi hae tantae depravationes retinentur, nequaquam a talibus Episcopis ordinatio petenda est: nec moveamur clamoribus indoctorum, qui vociferantur, non valere ordinationem factam in Ecclesiis nostris, quia non sint apud nos Episcopi, hoc titulo confirmati a Romano pontifice. Sed opponenda est regula firmissima: Si quis aliud Evangelium docet, anathema sit. Nihil potest dici expressius, cum manifestum sit eos, qui pertinaciter defendunt manifestos errores, et manifesta idola, fugiendos esse, et constet tales esse Papam et Episcopos ipsi addictos, Sumus certissimi eos non esse membra verae Ecclesiae Dei.

Quaeramus autem quae et ubi sit vera Ecclesia Dei, et nos ad eam adiungamus, iuxta dictum Psalmi 26.: Unum hoc requiro a Domino, ut habitem in domo Domini omnibus diebus vitae meae.

Item, Psal. 25.: Lavabo inter innocentes manus meas, et altare tuum circundabo Domine. Esse autem verum ministerium Evangelii in vera Ec- clesia certissimum est ex dicto: Ascendit in altum, dedit dona hominibus, Prophetas, Apostolos, Pastores et Doctores etc. Ephesios 4. Quare apud hanc manet ius vocationis, quia verae Ecclesiae dictum est: Constitue presbyteros.

Necessaria autem membra ordinationis haec sunt. Vocatio ad ministerium, exploratio doctri- nae, indicare vocatos Ecclesiae, approbare voca- tionem, et precatio. Ideo certissimum est ordi- nationem pertinere ad veram Ecclesiam, non ad hostes Ecclesiae.

Fuerunt autem in externo ritu ordinationis statim in veteri Ecclesia ceremoniae, impositio manuum et collocatio libri supra caput etc. Talia signa dico mutabilia esse, sed tamen cum in Ec- clesia deceat omnia fieri ordine, esse aliquem pu- blicum ritum ordinationis sine superstitione, utile est; 1. Ad hoc, ut magis illustria sint testimonia vocationis et approbationis vocati. 2. Et ut con- spiciatur cuius Ecclesiae doctrinam vocatus am- plectatur. 3. Et ut ibi publica precatio fiat. 4. Prodest etiam hic ipse ritus ad multorum confirmationem, ut sciant ius ordinationis pertinere ad veram Ecclesiam. 5. Et cogitent qui sint errores adversariorum. 6. Et cuius Ec- clesiae velint esse cives. 7. Denique multae sunt utilitates, cum sine calumnia et sine super- stitione iudicatur.

Haec de vocatione et ordinatione ad iuniores commonefaciendos dicta sunt.

Disputatur hic et de ambitione, an peccet petens officium pastoris? Respondeo: Duplex est petitio. Altera est pia, quae ita fit, ut offeras tuos labores, et habeas προαίρεσιν recte faciendi officium, et iudicium de te permittas iis qui ad- hibentur, nec pugnes illicitis modis. Haec peti- tio laudata est a Paulo in hoc dicto: Si quis Epi- scopi functionem expetit, honestum opus expetit. Laudat voluntatem petentis, et commonefacit, ut operis magnitudinem consideret: sicut manife- stum est, res difficilimas esse explicationem do- ctrinae, gubernationem, circumspectionem neces- sariam ad vitanda scandala.

Nec iniustum est appetere mercedem suo or- dine. Ac talis petitio non impedit vocationem, sed potius gratia debetur petenti, quod se indicat, quia hi qui praesunt non norunt tam multos, quam multis opus est ad ministerium. Tunc au- tem dicitur vocatio facta esse, cum accessit iudi- cium et approbatio vocantis.

Alia petitio ambitiosa est, quae ita fit, ut iudicium impediat, et pugnet illicitis modis. Haec ambitio pugnat cum vocatione, quia conatur im- pedire iudicium, quod ad vocationem necessarium est: et concurrunt multa vitia, non quaeruntur labores, sed reditus aut splendor. Sunt autem perniciosissimi fures, qui omisso labore devo- rant reditus, et de superbia dictum est, Pro- verb. 16.: Abominatio est coram Deo omnis su- perbus corde.

Hic et argumenti explicatio nota sit, Nemo petat vel recipiat onus, quod superat vires. Ad- ministratio in Ecclesia et in politiis sine ulla du- bitatione superat vires humanas, Ergo non est pe- tenda vel recipienda? Respondeo ad maiorem: Nemo petat vel recipiat, cum non accedit vocatio. Item: Nemo petat vel recipiat fiducia sui, sed cum accessit vocatio, iam administratio fit opus obedientiae Deo debitae, et id faciendum est fidu- cia auxilii divini, et in agnitione et invocatio- ne Dei.

Deinde ad minorem respondeo: Admini- stratio superat vires humanas, id verum est, sed fit possibilis et efficax Deo iuvante. Ac vult Deus hoc modo colligere Ecclesiam voce ministrorum, sicut inquit Paulus 1. Corint. 3.: Dei cooperato- res sumus, Dei agricultura estis, Ego plantavi, Apollo rigavit, Deus incrementum dedit. Nec requiritur, ut nos ipsi sufficientes simus, sed suf- ficientia nostra ex Deo est, 2. Corinth. 3. Sed hoc requiritur, fideles ut simus, 1. Corinth. 4. Fidelitas autem complectitur bonam voluntatem et non ignavam, sed bona conscientia quaerentem res necessarias administrationem, scilicet medio- crem cognitionem doctrinae, diligentiam, con- stantiam in confessione et similes virtutes, qua- rum catalogum hoc in loco Paulus recenset.

Quod placeat Deo vocatio seu electio per ho- mines facta, et quod ministerium per tales sit ef- ficax, hinc manifestum est, quia Paulus iubet eligi ministros, et narrat quales sint eligendi, iam si nulla per homines facienda esset electio, quor- sum opus esset tradere formam, quales sint eli- gendi.

Caeterum de forma hac sciamus oportere sin- gulos homines scire summam doctrinae, quae sit rectrix fidei et morum. Et una communis est omnium summa quam supra recitavit: Milita bonam militiam habens fidem et bonam conscientiam.

Ut autem conscientia normam habeat, intueamur Decalogum, et eum recte intelligamus. Sciamus opera pugnantia cum Decalogo esse opera polluentia conscientiam, et offendentia Deum, et conscientia iudicium est in nobis approbans facta secundum verbum Dei, vel iuxta legem naturae, et condemnans contraria, quam condemnationem certo ordine in natura rationali sequuntur horrendi cruciatus, qui sunt testes et opus iudicii Dei, iuxta illud: Deus ignis consumens est.

Considerata generali summa doctrinae, postea videat quisque, quae sint suae vocationis propria: haec pars etiam pertinet ad Decalogum, Minister Evangelii sciat se debere sonare doctrinam. Non sit igitur ignarus doctrinae, et sit aliquo modo ad docendum idoneus. Deinde huic quoque norma morum sit Decalogus recte intellectus: Hanc summam Paulus et hic proponit.

Initio autem ponit genus seu summam convenientem eligentibus, Episcopum oportet irreprehensibilem esse, Graece ἀνεπίληπτον. Et ad Titum cap. 1. dicitur ἀνέγκλητον, id est, non reum alicuius criminis, quod iudicio humano vere accusari potest. Nam ἐπιλαμβάνομαι significat reprehendo, corripio, ut apud Platonem in Gorgia, Si quid non recte dicere videor, ἐπιλάμβανε, id est, reprehendito. Et ἐγκαλεῖν significat accusare seu in iudicium vocare, quia Paulus hic loquitur de electione, certum est dici de accusatione coram iudicio humano, vult Episcopum non esse infamem. Et sint nota scelera, propter quae aut iudicia civilia homines notant infamia, aut Ecclesia interdicit communionem.

Sic ordinavit Deus vitam aeternam, ut velit propter manifesta scelera homines vel interfici a potestate politica, vel alioqui eiici ex reliqua societate. Ut propter blasphemias, periuria, magiam, manifestum cultum idolorum, seditiones, homicidia, vagas et incestas libidines, adulteria, furta, calumnias, crimen falsi.

Interpretatio insulsissima est, quam aliqui finxerunt, Oportet Episcopum esse sine peccato: haec interpretatio falsa est, cum intelligitur de peccato coram Deo, iuxta illud Iohannis, 1. Iohan. 1.: Si dicimus, quod peccatum non habe- mus, mendaces sumus. Manent in hac misera natura etiam in sanctis in hac vita multae magnae sordes et peccata, sicut inquit Ieremias cap. 17.: Cor hominis perversum est et aerumnosum. Ac in quotidianis exercitiis poenitentiae haec inte- riora peccata coram Deo agnoscenda et deploranda sunt. De his autem Paulus hic non loquitur, ad Titum vertit interpres, sine crimine.

Discant igitur iuniores phrasin, aliud est di- cere sine peccato, aliud sine crimine, id est, sine tali scelere, quod in iudiciis Ecclesiae, seu poli- ticis damnatur.

Sed hic nobis ipsi multa obiicimus. Primum nemo est tam firmus, qui non etiam aliquando turpiter labatur, ut inquit Salomo Eccles. 7. cap.: Non est iustus in terra qui non peccet. Item, Proverb. 24.: Iustus cadet in die septies. Item notum est illud Simonidis: Impossibile est esse tetragonum, id est, perfectum. Et manifestum est in omni gubernatione multa esse errata omis- sionis et ignorantiae.

Secundo, nemo potest vitare obtrectationes et calumnias. Est enim dulce et usitatum malum maledicentia, ut Pindarus inquit: ὄψον πολίταις αἱ κακηγορίαι.

De priore quaestione respondeo: Regula teneatur in omnibus officiis, ut fideles simus, ut dicitur 1. Corinth. 4., id est, sit bonum proposi- tum, et studeamus recte facere, et plerunqne recte faciamus, lapsi vero sanari nos patiamur. Praeterea cum omnes sciamus facilime posse labi et errare omnes homines: et assidue sint insidiae diaboli horrendae, Simus in invocatione filii Dei ardentiores, nec obliviscamur dicti, Iohan. 15.: Sine me nihil potestis facere. Item: Sine tuo nu- mine nihil est in homine.

De secunda quaestione respondeo, utrunque praestandum est: Primum, ut sit conscientia sine labe. Secundo, ut fama sit integra apud hone- stiores recte iudicantes, sicut dicitur Psalmo 149.: Laus eius in Ecclesia sanctorum. Et nota est sen- tentia: Bona conscientia mihi opus est propter Deum, bona fama propter proximum. Et in Ec- clesiastico cap. 39.: Laudem eorum nunciat Ec- clesia.

Quod autem interea multi sunt maledici, non est culpa eorum, qui fideliter serviunt, ut dicitur: Non est remedium adversus sycophantae morsum, Et multa sunt ingenia plena arrogantiae et veneni, inquieta et sophistica, quae saepe etiam plausibiliter instruere calumnias possunt. De his dicitur Proverb. 17.: Semper iurgia quae- rit malus, et nuncius crudelis mittetur contra eum. Tenenda est autem regula, Matth. 5.: Beati estis cum maledicent vobis mentientes. Item, Psalmo 18.: Illi maledicent et tu be- nedices.

Et necessaria virtus est in vita sapienter ferre tales iniurias, ut David, Fabius, non respondent calumniatoribus.

Hic et quaestio de Donatistis agitatur. Etsi non sunt eligendi infames, et removendi erant ii, qui postea cum sunt in ministerio fiunt infames, tamen error Donatistarum explodendus est, qui contendebant non valere ministerium, cum eo fungerentur homines polluti contra conscientiam, contra hos opponenda est doctrina, quod efficacia ministerii non pendeat ex ministri dignitate, sed vere sit opus Dei, sicut Iohannes inquit, Lucae 3.: Ego baptizo vos aqua, alius autem baptizabit vos igni et Spiritu sancto. Matth. 13. confertur Ecclesia sagenae, in qua boni et mali pisces sunt: ita et in tota Ecclesia et in ministerio sunt boni et mali, sed tamen de doctrina consentientes. His admonitionibus hoc loco contenti simus.

## 3:2
The husband of one wife.

He wishes the minister of the Gospel to be chaste, whether married or celibate. And because few are suited for a celibate life, he placed the other part, he orders an honest married man to be chosen: and he makes mention of marriage also for this very reason, to show that marriage is granted to all ministers of the Gospel. I omit, however, the disputes concerning bigamy. Antiquity called those bigamists who at the same time had several spouses, as the father of Samuel was a bigamist, but later many foolish opinions were born, which it is not pleasing to recite.

However, the doctrine must be held in the Church that marriage is a legitimate and inseparable union, of only one male and one female, according to the first institution: and the Lord recalls the Church to the first institution. They shall be two into one flesh, that is, one male and one female inseparably joined. But when either the husband or the wife dies, it is permitted to contract another legitimate marriage, as will be said below concerning widows.

The word σώφρων explained above signifies modest in general: sometimes the name σωφροσύνη is also used for temperance and for continence. The name of modesty is more general: for it signifies a virtue which maintains propriety even in opinions, speech, and gesture, as in Romans 12 he opposes the proud, the arrogant, the boastful, the Thrasos, and the busybodies.

Κόσμιον.

It is near to σωφροσύνῃ, but properly it signifies being alien to levity or scurrility. Not given to unworthy games or follies, in dress and gesture, just as the French Cardinals, having returned from the election of Pope Paul, invited harlots at Venice, and danced French dances with them.

Latin:

Unius uxoris virum.

Vult ministrum Evangelii castum esse, sive maritum, sive coelibem. Et quia pauci sunt ad vitam coelibem idonei, posuit alteram partem, iubet eligi maritum honestum: ac mentionem coniugii facit etiam hanc ipsam ob causam, ut ostendat concedi coniugium omnibus Evangelii ministris. Omitto autem disputationes de diga- mia. Vetustas digamos nominabat eos, qui eo- dem tempore plures coniuges habebant, ut pa- ter Samuelis fuit digamus, sed postea multae fatuat opiniones natae sunt, quas non libet re- citare.

Tenenda est autem in Ecclesia doctrina, quod coniugium sit legitima et inseparabilis con- iunctio, tantum unius maris et unius foeminae, iuxta primam institutionem: et Dominus revocat Ecclesiam ad primam institutionem. Erunt duo in carnem unam, id est, unas mas et una foemina inseparabiliter iuncti. Cum autem moritur aut maritus aut uxor, concessum est aliud legitimum coniugium contrahere, ut infra de viduis di- cetur.

Vocabulum σώφρων supra enarratum signi- ficat modestum in genere: interdum et pro tempe- rantia et pro continentia usurpatur nomen σω- φροσύνη. Nomen modestiae generalius est: si- gnificat enim virtutem, quae etiam in opinioni- bus, sermone et gestu convenientiam servat, ut Roman. 12. opponit superbis, arrogantibus, iactabundis, Thrasonibus, Ardelionibus.

Κόσμιον.

Vicinum est σωφροσύνῃ, sed proprie signi- ficat a levitate seu scurrilitate alienum. Non de- ditum indignis ludis aut ineptiis, in vestitu et ge- stu, sicut Cardinales Gallici reversi ex electione Pauli pontificis, Venetiis invitarunt meretrices, et apud eas saltarunt saltationes Gallicas.

## 3:2
Hospitable.

This species of beneficence is often praised in divine sermons, and is especially necessary in the Church, on account of the frequent exiles of the pious. But God wishes us to consider why the Church is in exile in the world, namely, He wishes us to remember the first exile, in which we lost our heavenly fatherland. Then He wishes us to remember the exile of the Son, who for our sake was made an exile, so that He might lead us back into our fatherland. Often a huge multitude has been expelled from cities at once, and troops of horsemen have been sent in, who trampled the old, the children, and the women. Sometimes God has taken some up into heaven in the sight of others, as is read concerning the old man Chaeremon and his aged wife, who, when they were being expelled from the Egyptian city of Nilopolis and could not proceed on account of the weakness of old age, were translated into heaven with the rest of the multitude.

Διδακτικὸν apt for teaching.

He requires not only that ministers hold the doctrine of the Church, but also that they be apt to teach, just as he says below in 2 Timothy 2: Entrust the doctrine to faithful men, who may be apt to teach. And to Titus chapter 1 he says: Let him be powerful to teach, and to refute those who contradict. And he enjoins study in 1 Timothy 4: Be diligent and attentive in reading, doctrine, and consolation.

Let these sayings be most familiarly known to all, so that we may rouse ourselves to learning. Let us know, therefore that this labor of learning is pleasing to God, and that the defense of those who teach and those who learn is a concern to God, just as He says concerning the Priesthood in Deut. 18: The Lord is your inheritance. Likewise Isa. 58: I have put my word in your mouth, and I will protect you with my right hand, that you may plant the heavens.

It is also certain that negligence in learning is most severely punished, as it is said in Hosea 4: Because you have rejected knowledge, I will reject you, that you may not serve me as priest. Let these admonitions excite diligence; let the younger ones know that it is a difficult thing to rightly grasp the whole body of doctrine, but that it is much more difficult to explain it rightly and clearly, and let them prepare themselves for these great works for the sake of the glory of God, their own salvation, and the utility of the Church. And at the same time let them ask that God may rule their minds, just as the Prophet asks in Psalm 118: Deal with your servant according to your mercy, and teach me your statutes. These labors are pleasing to God and are adorned with rewards, according to that saying of Luke 19: To him who has, it shall be given.

There follows an enumeration of many virtues in men and women, so that their order and sum may be comprehended: let the younger ones know that the doctrine of all virtues is to be distributed into the Decalogue, from which their longer explanation can also be taken, and it is handed down in Ethics.

And it is sufficiently apparent that Paul is not only an excellent herald of the Gospel, but also a political monitor. For he names virtues not only private, such as temperance, but also political, necessary in government, such as that a Bishop should not be a striker. Here he distinguishes the ministry of the Gospel from the political magistracy, which has a mandate in its own order to punish with bodily force, as has been said often elsewhere.

He also commands that he not be a brawler, that is, that he not stir up unnecessary conflicts; nay, he should even see where harshness is to be softened by ἐπιεικείᾳ (gentleness), he should tolerate some inconveniences in the weak and curable: he should wisely bear some injuries, lest dissensions inflamed by mutual conflicts grow. Concerning this matter, it has been most wisely prescribed that many great diseases are cured by abstinence and quiet.

The younger age does not yet understand these political precepts, but nevertheless let them learn to recognize the names of these virtues somehow and to bend themselves toward moderation. Let those who are older know that this consideration pertains to them, so that they may see where it is necessary to fight, and where it is not necessary.

Latin:

Hospitalem.

Haec species beneficentiae saepe laudatur in concionibus divinis, et inprimis necessaria est in Ecclesia, propter crebra exilia piorum. Vult au- tem Deus nos cogitare cur in mundo exulet Ec- clesia, videlicet, vult nos recordari primum exi- lium, in quo patriam coelestem amisimus. Deinde vult nos recordari exilium filii, qui propter nos factus est exul, ut nos reducat in patriam. Saepe ingens multitudo simul ex urbibus expulsa est, et turmae equitum immissae, quae senes, pueros, mulieres conculcarunt. Interdum Deus in con- spectu aliorum aliquos in coelum abduxit, ut le- gitur de sene Chaeremone et eius coniuge anu, qui cum ex urbe Aegypti Nilopoli expellerentur, et propter senectae imbecillitatem non possent procedere, cum reliqua multitudine in coelum translati sunt.

Διδακτικὸν idoneum ad docendum.

Postulat non solum ut teneant ministri do- ctrinam Ecclesiae, sed etiam ut sint idonei ad docendum, sicut et infra inquit 2. Timoth. 2.: Commenda doctrinam hominibus fidelibus, qui ad docendum idonei sint. Et ad Titum cap. 1. inquit: Sit potens ad docendum, et ad refutan- dos contradicentes. Et studium praecipit 1. Ti- moth. 4.: Sis assiduus et attentus in lectione, do- ctrina et consolatione.

Haec dicta familiarissime nota sint omnibus, ut nos ad discendum excitemus. Sciamus igitur hunc laborem discendi placere Deo, et Deo curae esse defensionem docentium et discentium, sicut de Sacerdotio inquit Deut. 18.: Dominus est hae- reditas vestra. Item Isa. 58.: Posui in ore tuo verbum meum, et dextera mea protegam te, ut plantes coelos.

Severissime etiam puniri negligentiam in discendo certum est, ut Oseae 4. dicitur: Quia scientiam repulisti, repellam te, ne sacerdotio fun- garis mihi. Hae commonefactiones excitent dili- gentiam, sciant iuniores rem difficilem esse recte complecti totum doctrinae corpus, multo autem difficilius esse recte et perspicue exponere, et se ad haec tanta opera propter gloriam Dei, propriam salutem et utilitatem Ecclesiae praeparent. Ac si- mul petant, ut Deus regat mentes, sicut petit Propheta Psalmo 118.: Fac cum servo tuo secun- dum misericordiam tuam, et iustificationes tuas doce me. Hi labores Deo placent et ornantur praemiis, iuxta illud Lucae 19.: Habenti da- bitur.

Sequitur enumeratio multarum virtutum in viris et mulieribus, quarum ut ordo et summa comprehendi possit: sciant iuniores omnium vir- tutum doctrinam in Decalogum distribuendam esse, inde et explicatio earum longior sumi potest, et in Ethicis traditur.

Ac satis apparet Paulum non solum Evange- lii praeconem excellentem esse, sed etiam politi- cum monitorem. Nominat enim virtutes non tan- tum privatas, ut temperantiam, sed etiam politi- cas in gubernatione necessarias, ut ne Episcopus sit percussor. Hic discernit ministerium Evan- gelii a magistratu politico, qui mandatum habet suo ordine puniendi vi corporali, ut alibi saepe dictum est.

Iubet item, ne sit rixator, id est, ne certa- mina moveat non necessaria, imo videat etiam ubi asperitas lenienda sit ἐπιεικείᾳ, toleret in in- firmis et sanabilibus aliqua incommoda: sapienter ferat aliquas iniurias, ne crescant dissidia inflam- mata mutuis certaminibus. Hac de re sapientis- sime praeceptum est, multos magnos morbos cu- rari abstinentia et quiete.

Haec politica praecepta nondum intelligit ae- tas minor, sed tamen harum virtutum nomina utcunque agnoscere et flectere se ad moderatio- nem discant. Alii grandiores sciant hanc consi- derationem ad se pertinere, ut videant ubi ne- cesse sit pugnare, ubi non necesse sit.

## 3:15
The Church of the living God, the pillar and seat of truth.

Here he inserts a description of the Church and is kindled with great emotion of mind in this very commemoration, and he celebrates the magnitude of the goodness of God, who by a wondrous counsel sent his son, and gathers an eternal Church by the voice of the Gospel, and in the human race, amidst the furies of devils, amidst the tumults of kings and the impious, amidst the ruins of the impious, always preserves the remnants of the Church. This perpetuity of the Church is an illustrious testimony of the presence of God and the truth of the doctrine.

But first, let the definition of the Church be noted, which it is necessary to hold rightly constituted for many reasons. For many name the Church simply the pontifical kingdom, just as Caiaphas named the Church the host joined with him, with errors, sacrifices, offices, and traditions. Others, altogether removing the external appearance, speak of the invisible Church as if of a Platonic idea, which is nowhere seen or heard. And therefore they wander, and wish to be citizens of no congregation: this imagination is also to be reprehended. For although the pontifical kingdoms are for the most part great, and obscure the true Church, and the number of those rightly invoking is very small, just as in the time of Zechariah the kingdom of the Pharisees and Sadducees was great: nevertheless there is always some visible assembly, at times larger, at times smaller, which is the guardian of the foundation; this assembly is to be sought, and to this the pious, wherever they are, ought to join themselves by their confession and similar invocation. Thus, therefore, this definition.

The Church in this life is a visible assembly of those embracing the Gospel and rightly using the sacraments, in which assembly God is effective through the ministry and sanctifies many to eternal life; yet there are many in the same assembly who are not holy, but nevertheless agree with the holy ones concerning true doctrine in external profession. As in the time of Mary there was a visible Church, Zechariah, Simeon, Joseph, Mary, Elizabeth, Anna, and many others, hearing the doctrine of these and feeling with them, and worshiping God with the same invocation, of whom some had more, some less light.

Such an assembly, although it does not hold the kingdom, but rather many are scattered here and there, nevertheless it is seen and heard. For God wishes his Son to be acknowledged in the human race, just as he says to all nations, Psalm 2: Kiss the Son. Therefore he wishes the Church both to be seen and to be heard sounding the Gospel concerning the Son, just as it is written in Psalm 18: Their sound has gone out into all the earth.

visible, and the necessary safeguards for the defense of the king, the laws, the judgments, and the people, and the king has the power of establishing some laws and interpreting ambiguous ones. And the interpretation is valid on account of royal authority.

As in the French kingdom there are laws in some circumstances different from the laws of other polities, and judgments are established for certain persons and places: nor is it permitted to refer French controversies to the judgments of other kingdoms. There is also a visible king, and he is fortified with necessary safeguards, and he has the power of interpreting laws and establishing some new ones. Such is the kingdom of the Roman pontiff. Such also was the kingdom of the impious pontiffs in Israel. Many have dreamed of such kingdoms in the Church at all times.

But it is often horribly oppressed and obscured by idolatrous kingdoms, as it is said in Isaiah 1: Unless the Lord had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom. And Matthew 24: Unless these days had been shortened, all flesh would have perished. And yet remnants survive and the Church is restored from time to time, as it is said in Isaiah 46: Even in old age I will carry you, etc. And Isaiah 59: This is my covenant with them, says the Lord, my spirit which is in you, and my words which I have put in your mouth, shall not depart from your mouth, nor from the mouth of your seed forever. Likewise, Matthew 28: I am with you until the end of the age. And in the creed we profess this daily: I believe there is a holy catholic Church, I believe therefore that the promises delivered to the Church are firm, I believe that I am heard and received according to those promises.

But let us learn that these imaginations are to be fled, and that the Church, even though it is visible, is nevertheless unlike political empires. And those pontifical kingdoms were signified when the Son of God was clothed in purple and lacerated with a crown of thorns; thus the pontiffs and writers who transform the Church into such a kingdom, where both laws and worship are instituted without the command of God, concerning private Masses, celibacy, and other superstitions, treat the Son of God with contumely: and other men who do not observe these rites are expressly condemned, and the Roman Bishop is set over them as a king armed with the power of establishing new laws and new forms of worship, and with the power of interpretation, and fortified by his own armies and those of kings.

And it is a great consolation that there are always some elect in such a gathering of the called, because since there is always some number of the elect, and it is only among the called, as Paul says in Romans 8: Those whom he chose, these he also called. Let us know that the elect are not to be sought elsewhere outside the gathering of the called, and let us willingly gather ourselves to this gathering: therefore it has been said, In this gathering God is effective through the ministry, for there the elect are converted.

Let us know therefore that the external appearance of the Church is unlike political empires. Although it is in some way similar to a pious school, and yet it is true that the Monarchy or kingdom in this visible gathering is invisibly, namely, because the Son of God is most truly present in this gathering, and is truly the king and head of the believers, whom he rules by his word and Holy Spirit, and joins to the eternal Father, just as it is written in Ephesians 1: He subjected all things under his feet, and gave him as head over all things to the Church, which is his body, the complete congregation of him who fills all in all. Thus he himself says in Matthew 18: I am in the midst of them. Likewise, John 17: I am in them. Psalm 2: But I establish my king upon Zion my holy hill.

But in this life this dissimilarity remains, that some who are not elect and hypocrites, who are not sanctified, are mixed with the elect in the external society, as is said in Matthew 13 concerning the good and bad fish. The dreams of the Anabaptists, who wanted to constitute a Church in which there would only be saints, must therefore be removed.

And because we are speaking of the visible gathering, external signs must be considered, namely, the purity of doctrine and the legitimate use of the Sacraments. Sometimes, however, God also adds external miracles.

The external appearance of the ministers of the Gospel and the hearers is in some way similar to an Aristocracy, but bound to the Gospel, and without the power of po- But although we are speaking of the visible Church, nevertheless the imagination and zeal without knowledge must be removed, which transforms the Church into a political or worldly kingdom, whose proper characteristics are these: Laws concerning the form of government in morals, judgments, and certain rites, the order of persons, places, King litical and without bodily defenses, as in Hosea 1: Not by bow and sword, but I will save them by the Lord their God, etc. Likewise in Zechariah chapter 4: Not by an army, not by strength, but by my spirit etc. Nor is it to be imagined that the Church is enclosed in the polity of one kingdom, as it is written in Matthew 24: Behold here it is, behold there it is. But the members of the true Church are scattered in diverse places, and somewhere God provides lodgings for the public congregation and for the studies of true doctrine, in some places more, in others less convenient.

However, this deformed appearance, which seems to be anarchy and dissipation, greatly offends the eyes of the wise, nor does it seem to be divinely associated and guarded, what is so variously torn, without a visible head, without a certain seat, without order. Since therefore the wise abhor this appearance, they run to the defense of the ordinary power, as they name it. And great struggles arise from this difference of judgment.

It is necessary to consider these things regarding the external appearance of the Church, so that we are not deterred from the truth by the deformity of dissipation, but hold to the rule: If anyone teaches another Gospel, let him be anathema. After we have said what and where the true Church is, and what its appearance is like, these questions now follow.

First: Whether truth is always in it without errors. Second: What the power of the ministers is like. Third: What authority there is in judging, and in interpretation.

On the first Question.

Whether there is always truth in the Church without errors.

I answer: These propositions, the Church errs, and likewise the Church is the pillar and seat of truth, are synecdoches, and one is understood of other congregations, and they speak of different kinds of errors.

Often there is a great multitude, which has the title of Church, which nevertheless is not the true Church, but a hostile assembly waging war with the elect. Just as the Pontiffs, Pharisees, and Sadducees were in the time of Zechariah. These did not even retain the foundation, which Paul names thus in 1 Corinthians 3: No other foundation can be laid, besides that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ. For the Pharisees and Sadducees defended many errors against the articles of faith. Such a multitude, even if it arrogates the title to itself, and dominates in the Church, is nevertheless by no means the true Church or a part of the true Church. Therefore it is written in John 8: You are from your father the devil. And that such a multitude existed in Israel is manifest, that such would also exist after the Apostles was predicted, and the matter shows it, Matthew 24: Many false prophets will arise and will seduce many. And 1. Timothy 4: The Spirit says certainly that in the last times many will depart from the faith, and will believe in impostor spirits. And the description of the Antichrist in 2 Thessalonians 2 is horrible: Dominating in the temple of God, establishing with horrible fury idols and lies, which fight against the articles of faith. This most sad description speaks of those dominating widely, and of a great multitude, and of horrible idols and lies. Hence it is sufficiently clear that many who have the title of Church err: and it is necessary to remember these testimonies, so that they may be opposed to those alleging the name of the Church regarding an impious congregation. But let us speak of the other part, which is the true Church. Even if in this one too there are many who are weak, and in some places there is more darkness, in others less, nevertheless the foundation is retained in it, otherwise there would be no Church at all. However, the Lord shows that there are always some elect, when he says in Matthew 24: These days will be shortened for the sake of the elect. Likewise, the article of faith is always true: I believe there is a holy catholic Church. Likewise: I am with you even to the consummation of the age. Likewise, Isaiah 59: This is my covenant with them, says the Lord, my spirit which is in you, and my words, which I have put in your mouth, will not depart from your mouth and from the mouth of your seed, from now on and forever. Matthew 24: At the coming of the son of man there will be two in the field, one will be taken, the other will be left. And although this true Church also issues a confession, is heard, and is seen, nevertheless that dominating Synagogue far surpasses it in multitude and splendor, just as in the time of the passion of Christ there was a great paucity. And Isaiah says in chapter 1: Unless the Lord had left us a seed. And here let the immense goodness of God be considered: for just as in Paradise the devil tried to destroy the whole human race, so he perpetually rages and destroys very many. But nevertheless the son of God restrains him, so that he does not [destroy] the universe the human race perish, he snatches and saves many, and from time to time restores the Church; therefore, concerning this small group of those who call upon him, it is said in Daniel 11: And the learned among the people shall teach many, and they shall fall by the sword and flame. However, there remain in this life, and in this true Church, many infirmities, and indeed the elders more recognize and deplore their own darkness, and that of others, and their own filth. Therefore Paul says in 1 Corinthians 3: Some build gold upon the foundation, others silver, others stubble. They build gold and silver when they refute heresies and illustrate the articles of faith. He calls the contagions of opinions stubble, in which there is some error, as concerning Ceremonies; as Augustine and other saints built much stubble upon the foundation. When, therefore, Paul says that the Church is the pillar and seat of truth, let us know that he is speaking of the true Church retaining the foundation, and not stubbornly defending idols and lies that conflict with the articles of faith: because God always wishes to be acknowledged in some part of the human race, even if it is small. To this pertains also the saying in Ephesians 5: That he might present to himself a Church not having a spot, and that it might be holy and blameless, namely in true doctrine, and calling upon God in true faith, and righteous because of the Son of God, by imputation and beginning.

On the second Question.

On the power of ministers.

There is an express command in the last chapter of Mark: Preach the Gospel to every creature. And 2 Corinthians 3: We are ministers of the new testament, not of the letter, but of the spirit. And John, last chapter: As the Father has sent me, so I send you. This command embraces those things which pertain to the substance of the evangelical ministry, namely the preaching of the Gospel, the administration of the Sacraments, the excommunication of the contumacious, the Absolution of those doing penance, and judgments concerning those called to the evangelical ministry. Rightly also can be added judgments concerning doctrine, because this part is necessary in the preaching of the Gospel. But by no means does any creature have the power of establishing new dogmas concerning the essence or will of God, or of instituting new forms of worship, But the Son who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him to us. Concerning this it is said in Matthew 17: Hear him. Likewise he himself says in John 17: Father, sanctify them in the truth; Thy word is truth. Likewise Matthew 15: In vain do they worship me with the commandments of men. Therefore, the imagination of Bishops and similar people who attribute to Bishops or others the power of establishing new forms of worship is false and impious.

However, there is a due obedience in those things which properly pertain to the ministry, sanctioned in this saying, Luke 10: He who hears you, hears me; he who rejects you, rejects me. In these sayings the Lord leads us to the very voice of the Gospel; he wishes himself to be heard in the preaching of the ministers, nor does this sentence establish any kingdom outside the ministry, just as Bishops demand that obedience be rendered to traditions which are outside the voice of the Gospel. Furthermore, the ministers of the Gospel do not have the power of coercing with the sword or physical force. Concerning which matter it is often said elsewhere.

On the third Question.

It is manifest that controversies arise even in the true Church, as appears in Acts 15; therefore, concerning judgments it is asked: Who are the judges, and what is the norm according to which it is necessary to judge, and what is the authority of the judges, and how is it necessary to obey what has been judged.

Here, first, let political judgments be considered; there the judge is the king himself or the magistrate with the greater part of the council. The norm in any kingdom is its own laws, which both the judge and the litigants must obey. The authority of the judges is such that when there is ambiguity in the law, they can add a certain declaration, and this addition afterwards has the force of law because of the rank of the magistrate, and obedience is owed to it, even if it seems otherwise to some litigant.

Thus it is said that a judgment is valid by royal or magisterial authority, because God has armed the political magistrate with this power, and affairs are subject to reason. A wise magistrate can see a probable reason why it should be pronounced in such a way. However, obedience is owed to him because of his rank, so that there may be peace and an end to lawsuits, and when the condemned do not obey, it is just to compel them. Let us know that such is the order and authority of political judgments.

Afterwards, let it be considered to what extent this image corresponds to the judgments of the Church, which are in some way dissimilar to political judgments.

First, this can rightly be said: that the Ministers of the Gospel ought to preside over judgments and have the mandate to convene the Church for examination, as in Acts chapter 15 the Apostles preside over the examination and employ others from the assembly of elders. The norm, however, is the word of God and the symbols, which are certainly brief articles taken only from the word of God; according to this norm, it is necessary to judge now indeed after the Apostles, according to this saying, Galatians chapter 1: If anyone teaches another Gospel, let him be anathema.

But what if there is ambiguity? Here I first answer: There is no ambiguity in the foundation, that is, in the necessary parts of doctrine, in the prophetic and apostolic books and the symbols, when the sentences are considered rightly without sophistry and the entire body of doctrine is compared. So that, even if Samosatenus contends that there is ambiguity in the saying: In the beginning was the Word, nevertheless the circumstance of the text convinces him, which shows that the Word there must be understood as a person, because the text says: All things were made through him. Likewise: And the Word was made flesh. Likewise John 8: Before Abraham was born, I am. And: Abraham saw my day.

Furthermore, even if someone sophistically contends that there is ambiguity, as the Anabaptists clamor about the Baptism of infants, nevertheless, since there is always a true Church, the true light always remains in some, whether many or few. These, in judging, pronounce, show their confession, relate what they understand, and are certain from the prophetic and apostolic discourse itself, and the testimonies of the Holy Spirit in them, according to that Ephesians 1: You were sealed with the Holy Spirit.
