First, because he approves of the study of letters, when he says, Be diligent in reading: for which purpose there is need of a manifold knowledge of languages and arts. Since therefore you know it is a commandment that you read the sacred books, you understand that these labors of teaching and learning are pleasing to God, and you can ask for and hope for help from him, and in all dangers and adversities you have a primary consolation, according to those sayings, Psalm 36: Commit your way to God, and hope in him, and he will do it. Likewise, 1 Corinthians 15: Your labor will not be in vain in the Lord.

For a rule must be held universally. First, it must be known whether a labor or a way of life is pleasing to God, according to that in Romans 14: Whatever is not of faith is sin. Then, no one can call upon God, ask for or expect help in a business that God disapproves, according to that in Psalm 5: You are not a God who wills impiety. The sentence is therefore, Commit your way to God, that is, your vocation, warfare, labor, and way of life approved by him.

Paul also warns here that the Church is bound to certain books, just as it is often commanded elsewhere concerning prophetic and apostolic doctrine, as Isaiah says, chapter 8: To the law and to the testimonies. It is therefore necessary to reject doctrines and illuminations that conflict with these books. Likewise opinions and worship outside these books.

Thirdly, he commands private and public reading, and shows that it was the custom in the Churches to read the prophetic books in order, just as it was customary in the Synagogues, and Moses commands the Levites, Deut. 31, to read the entire law. Therefore it is said in Malachi 2: The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and I will seek the law from his mouth, because he is the messenger of the Lord of hosts. And in Hosea 4, a penalty is denounced against the negligent: Because you have rejected knowledge, I will reject you, so that you may not serve as priest to me.

Let these sayings and similar ones be fixed in our hearts, so that they may rouse us to diligence in learning, teaching, and reading. Moreover, let prayer be added, so that God may rule our minds, that we may properly receive the divine sayings, just as the Prophet prays, Psalm 118: Deal with your servant according to your mercy, and teach me your justifications. And Isaiah prays that the truth may be retained in some hearers, Isaiah 8: Seal the law among my disciples.

There is also a necessity for comparison with others, just as it is written, Luke 22: And you, when you have turned, strengthen your brothers. And Samson says in Judges 14: Unless you had plowed with my heifer, you would not have found out, that is, unless you had been helped by the labor of the Church. Let us therefore listen to the Apostles and the guardians of apostolic doctrine.

Let us also consider who have departed from apostolic doctrine and how. In some, a diabolical audacity has completely changed the whole doctrine of the Church and spread horrible frenzies, as in Marcion, the Manichaeans, and the like. In others, superstition has bent their minds toward new forms of worship.

This entire consideration pertains to reading, in which the series of the whole Church and the histories of all times must be known.

However, a brief distribution of these kinds—reading, doctrine, and consolation—must be observed. Why does it start from reading? Because there is a great dissimilarity between philosophy and the Gospel. We do not begin arithmetic with reading, but we bring in many pieces of information which are a path to the art; but God has published by His own voice an arcane doctrine about the Son, and about redemption, and about the whole restoration of the human race; He wishes to be known according to this revelation of His, and He willed for this to be written by the Prophets and Apostles. Therefore, the Church is bound to the reading of these books, and these books are the foundation and norm of all doctrine in the Church, according to that passage in 1 Corinthians 3: No other foundation can be laid than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ. It is therefore necessary that these writings be read assiduously both privately and publicly.

Let doctrine follow reading, just as in the medication of the body the end is healing. And the medical art contains two parts: doctrine and the method of curing. Doctrine indeed shows the nature of the human body, qualities, temperaments, causes of diseases, and remedies. Afterward, the method of curing applies the remedies. And the wisdom of a physician is to understand what pertains to his art and to direct his counsels toward healing as the ultimate and principal end. Thus, let the preacher know that he is like a physician, and that the ultimate end of the evangelical ministry is healing, by which men are freed from eternal death through the Son of God by the voice of the Gospel. For he does not merely govern morals, as a political magistrate does.

There are therefore two members here as well: doctrine and consolation. Doctrine speaks of the articles of faith, distinguishes between Law and Gospel, recites the description of sin, the use of the sacraments, and the difference between eternal righteousness and political life. But it is necessary for consolation to be added as a healing, lest man be left in sin and eternal death.

And doctrine is this very thing which we customarily call Catechesis, that is, a summary of dogmas reciting the articles of faith, the description of sin, the difference between Law and Gospel, the use of the sacraments, and the difference between eternal righteousness and political life, taken from the divine voice itself, which is read first; and this very Catechesis is an interpretation of the reading, whether long or short. For since in learning it is necessary to grasp the entire body of doctrine with the mind, brief summaries of the principal topics must be handed down in order to the more unlearned, and afterward, firm testimonies must be shown in the reading itself, so that faith may lean upon the divine voice.

With this intention, symbols were first established and Catechisms written. For although the reading sounds exactly the same, and the prophetic and apostolic books themselves are the fountain of doctrine, yet for this reason books are not only read through in the Church by boys, but the voice of an interpreter is also added, so that they may explain the type of discourse to the more unlearned, show the heads of the matters about which it is spoken, and illustrate them with definitions and distinctions, just as it is necessary to do in teaching. And let these things be done without sophistry, but rightly according to the methods of the arts, and let not foreign materials be mixed in.

Since, therefore, there is need for some form in teaching, Paul commands that a Bishop be chosen who is apt for teaching. He calls this form doctrine here, which is Catechesis, whether short or long, which indeed is itself an interpretation of the sacred books: because the Catechesis must be taken from there, and testimonies must be shown there.

The third member is consolation: because it is not enough to recite the heads of doctrine unless the application is shown. Let the preacher understand the degrees of his office; let him read the prophetic and apostolic books to the people in order, and from time to time propose the body of true doctrine, so that the hearers may rightly grasp the summary, as it is handed down in the Catechesis; and let not the sermon be without affections, but let the commemoration of the wrath of God stir up fear, yet let not minds be left in dread and doubt, as the tragedies of the poets show only punishments, but let consolation from the voice of the Gospel be added; let the hearers be reminded to apply to themselves by faith the eternal promises and those of present goods, and to exercise faith, hope, invocation, thanksgiving, and the other virtues.

Thus this third degree speaks properly of the application of the Gospel, by which liberation from sin and eternal death is effected, and pains in this life are alleviated by the recognition of the goodness of God, by faith, and by the hope of divine aid. Since, therefore, the Pauline distribution most wisely shows the parts of the preacher's office, let the faithful preacher follow this norm, let him be a faithful reader of the sacred books, and let him remember that all opinions conflicting with the sacred books are to be rejected. Then let him propose the entire body of doctrine in order, and add testimonies without sophistry. Finally, let him also show the application, so that the fear of God, repentance, faith, invocation, hope, and other virtues may grow, and the beginning of eternal life may be made.

Latin:

Omnis creatura Dei bona est.

Opponit regulam fanaticis spiritibus, qui damnant coniugium, cibos, ordinem politicum, distinctionem dominiorum, iudicia. Semper enim multi fuerunt, sunt et erunt tales hypocri- tae, ut olim Marcion, Tatianus, Manichaei, Papa, Monachi, et nunc Anabaptistae, qui de distinctione dominiorum sic argumentantur: Ne- mini licet appetere alienum. Omnes res extra spiritum sunt alienae, ergo non licet appetere ul- las tales res, ut facultates.

Ac omnino amplissimam sapientiam signifi- cat Paulus, cum inquit, usum fieri sanctum per verbum Dei, id est, agnitione totius doctrinae Dei de iusticia aeterna, et de vita corporali, in qua vult incoari aeternam Ecclesiam.

Iubet autem Paulus et precationem addi, id est, petitionem auxilii, confessionem et gra- tiarum actionem: quia et hanc corporalem vitam vult Deus esse occasionem exercendae et ostenden- dae obedientiae, quare de coniugio, de castitate, de educatione et institutione sobolis, de communi societate, de toto ordine politico, de vitandis homicidiis et furtis, tradidit nobis verbum, et in hoc pulcherrimo ordine, in quo lucent ipsius sa- pientia et bonitas, vult exerceri timorem, fidem, spem, invocationem, dilectionem, castitatem, beneficentiam, et alias virtutes.

Respondeo: Maior vera est de alieno, quod politica distinctione dominiorum pertinet ad alte- rius dominium, iuxta illud: Non concupiscas alterius uxorem, neque res alterius. Minor est falsa, ut manifestum est: propria uxor est res extra spiritum: non dicitur isto modo res aliena, cibi sunt res extra spiritum, et tamen appetendi sunt.

Sic Tatianus argumentabatur. Scriptum est in Evangelio secundum Aegyptios dixisse Chri- stum ad Salomonem, Veni ut solvam opera mu- lieris, Parere est opus mulieris, Ergo Christus abolet coniugium.

Necessaria sapientia est in Ecclesia. recte intelligere discrimen legis et Evangelii, et iusti- ciae aeternae in cordibus, et usus rerum corpora- lium, quem Deus suo verbo certo modo ordina- vit: quia in hac mortali vita Ecclesiam vult col- ligi, et in harum ipsarum rerum usu lucere fidem, invocationem, et alias virtutes.

Sed manichaea et anabaptistica colluvies fascinata a diabolo ostentat novam sanctitatem, quasi reliquerint terram, et volitent in coelo ex- tra hanc vitae societatem, et iactat interea se ha- bere mirandos afflatus. Et quia haec hypocrisis mendacium est, nec carent rebus in hac vita, fa- ciunt postea confusiones libidinum, et movent seditiones, et volunt novam Ierosolymam consti- tuere, sicut saepe accidit. Nam et olim similis Tragoedia Monasteriensi accidit in Phrygia in oppido Pepuza, quam nominabant novam Iero- solymam, et habebant ibi fanaticos vates.

Haec admonitio contra Anabaptistas et simi- les spiritus fanaticos, diligenter consideranda est. Ac Paulus ideo inquit: Sanctificatur cibus per verbum Dei, ut doceat utentes quomodo bona conscientia rebus uti possint, sicut alibi inquit: Quicquid non est ex fide, peccatum est, Roma. 14. Eius dicti sententia nativa recte tenenda est. Non tantum est legale dictum, sicut multi interpre- tantur hoc modo: Quicquid prohibitum est man- datis divinis ad nos pertinentibus peccatum est.

Quanquam autem hic legalis intellectus ve- rus est, tamen nondum reddit totam sententiam, dicti Paulini: sed quia fit mentio fidei, oportet complecti Evangelium. Nec tantum intelligatur fides de noticia historiae, sicut dicunt: Honesta opera hominis ethnici non placent Deo, quia non est in professione Christiana: sed intelligi oportet veram fidem, quae accedit ad Deum fidu- cia mediatoris, et invocat eum. Ubi talis fides non est, sed cor agit contra conscientiam, aut manet in dubitatione, ut suspendens furem, et tamen existimans se contra Deum facere, non potest invocare Deum, et agit cum contemtu Dei.

Sit igitur nota haec regula Pauli, et recte intelligatur et praeluceat omnibus actionibus, et ne quid faciamus contra conscientiam, et ut con- scientia regatur verbo Dei, ac possit accedere in- vocatio, videlicet omne quod non est ex fide, peccatum est.

Corporalis exercitatio ad modicum est utilis, pietas ad omnia, etc.

Utilis distinctio est inter necessaria et non necessaria opera, electa exercitii nostri causa, ut sunt ieiunia, vel alii labores suscepti ad frenan- dum corpus. Ac semper in Ecclesia externae ob- servationes multum disputationum pepererunt, quia vel propter ordinem, vel propter exercitia, externae aliquae observationes humano consilio instituuntur aut suscipiuntur, quae postea super- stitione depravantur, cum affingitur opinio me- riti, cultus aut necessitatis. Ideo etiam vetustas taxavit superstitionem, iuxta dictum memorabile Athanasii: καλὸν ἡ ἄσκησις μεάτα ἀληθοῦς γνώ- σεως, καὶ συμμετρίας.

Ut autem recte iudicetur de ritibus humanis, totum corpus doctrinae tenendum est, sicut hic quoque Paulus facit antithesin necessariorum et non necessariorum. Pietas utilis est ad omnia. Nominat autem pietatem simul fidem et omnes necessarias virtutes, seu omnia opera nobis man- data divinitus. Et valde insignis sententia est, quod ait promissiones praesentis et futurae vitae pietati propositas esse, et addit expressam asseve- rationem: Certus est sermo et firma assensione amplectendus.

Hanc dulcissimam et maxime necessariam doctrinam, de duobus generibus promissionum oportet familiarissime notam esse. Ac primum quod ad Evangelium attinet, continet promissio- nem remissionis peccatorum, et restitutionem vitae aeternae per filium Dei, et propter eum, quod manifestissimum est. Constat enim hanc esse principalem vocem Evangelii, missum esse filium Dei, ut aboleat peccatum et mortem, et restituat vitam aeternam.

Sed cur dicit, Evangelium habere praesentis vitae promissionem, cum Ecclesia sit subiecta cruci? Item cum dicit Dominus Matth. 24.: In- terficient vos et eritis odio omnibus hominibus propter nomen meum. Et Lucae 9.: Filius ho- minis non habet ubi reclinet caput? Haec sunt praedictiones mortis, non vitae praesentis? Sed respondeo: Utraque propositio verissima est, et subiecta est Ecclesia cruci, et tamen habet pro- missionem bonorum corporalium, sicut coniun- git haec Dominus Marc. 10.: Recipiet centuplum, sed cum tribulatione. Et Esaiae 30.: Audiet clamorem tuum, et dabit vobis panem et aquam in angustia et dolore.

Cum enim Deus velit in hac mortali vita ita incoari et colligi Ecclesiam, servat eam, praebet ei hospitia, fruges, oeconomias, politias, facul- tatem propagandi sobolem, et Ecclesiam, sicut ipse Dominus inquit Matth. 6.: Scit pater vester coelestis his omnibus vobis opus esse, Primum quaerite regnum Dei, et caetera adiicientur vobis. Item, Psalmo 32.: Enutriet et alet eos in fame: imo propter Ecclesiam Deus et caeteras gentes et bona corporalia conservat. Postquam autem uni- versa Ecclesia collecta fuerit, nec fuerint plures electi in genere humano, mox cessabit haec mor- talis vita, et fiet extremum iudicium.

Est autem promissio bonorum corporalium generalis, non alligata certo loco, ut Israëlitis alligata erat ad certum locum, et semper in hac vita rata est universo coetui. Ideo semper in hac vita servat Deus aliquam suam Ecclesiam, etiamsi multa membra interficiuntur, ut si victoria pro- missa esset exercitui, rata et vera est promissio, etiamsi aliqui milites interficiuntur.

Secundo, promissio corporalis semper intel- ligatur cum exceptione castigationis et crucis. Vult Deus utrumque exerceri in petentis bonis corporalibus, fidem et obedientiam. Vult Abra- hae vitam et familiam custodire, sed ita, ut rega- tur Abraham non solum humanis consiliis, sed fide, invocatione Dei, et a Deo petat et expectet auxilium, iuxta dicta Ierem. 17.: Maledictus qui confidit in homine et ponit carnem brachium suum. Item, Zachar. 4.: Non in robore, non in exercitu, sed in spiritu meo, dicit Dominus.

Vult etiam hoc scire homines, se vere irasci peccatis, et horribiliter punire lapsus, ut simus diligentiores in nobis frenandis: sicut tristissimae poenae secutae sunt lapsus Davidis, Salomonis etc. Et tamen inter has poenas aliquod semen Ecclesiae semper servatum est, ut in exilio Ba- bylonico.

Ita videmus promissionem corporalem simi- liter ratam esse propter gloriam Dei, ne extin- guatur agnitio Dei in genere humano, et in peti- tione hunc finem intueamur, Psalm. 114.: Non nobis Domine, non nobis, sed nomini tuo da glo- riam. Item: Non mortui laudabunt te Domine. Exerceamus igitur et fidem et obedientiam in pe- titione, et expectatione corporalium bonorum, sicut Dominus iubet petere panem quotidianum, et illas stultas superstitiones eorum execremur, qui hanc petitionem nolunt interpretari de rebus corporalibus.

Semper autem in conspectu sint hae quatuor causae, propter quas Deus et tradidit promissio- nes corporales, et vult ea bona peti. Prima est, Quia vult intelligi haec bona non spargi casu sine consilio et voluntate Dei, sed Deum suo consilio vel fovere naturae vires, vel deserere, vel dare facultates, vel non dare. Primum igitur sit in nobis haec fides de pro- videntia, quod non casu spargantur haec bona sine consilio Dei. Nam haec fides est fundamen- tum petitionis et gratiarum actionis. Et sint nota aliqua testimonia Deut. 8.: Non in solo pane vivet homo, sed ex omni verbo, quod procedit ex ore divino. Deut. 30.: Ipse est vita tua, et longitudo dierum tuorum. Acto. 17.: In ipso vivimus, movemur et sumus. Matth. 10.: Omnes capilli capitis vestri numerati sunt. Proverb. 10.: Benedictio Domini divites facit. Proverb. 3.: Egestas a Domino in domo impii. Iere. in Thre- nis cap. 3.: Quis est iste, qui dicit fieri haec non iubente Domino, Ex ore Domini nec bona nec mala egredientur? Sequitur ergo deinde altera causa. Cum certissimum sit haec bona divinitus dari, utroque modo vult Deus exerceri fidem, petitione et gra- tiarum actione, vult se agnosci creatorem esse et datorem vitae et victus, vult hoc celebrari in pe- titione et gratiarum actione. Sicut dicit Psalm. 50.: Invoca me in die tribulationis, et eripiam te, et glorificabis me. Tertia causa est, Hae promissiones sunt te- stimonia de conservatione Ecclesiae in hac mortali vita, ideo enim dantur, ne intereat Ecclesia, iuxta illud Psalmi 114.: Non mortui laudabunt te Domine. Item Matth. 6.: Primum quaerite regnum Dei, et caetera adiicientur vobis. Quarta, Omnes promissiones corporales sunt commonefactiones de spirituali, videlicet, de filio Dei, quia nec invocare Deum possumus, nisi prius sciamus nos recipi et exaudiri propter me- diatorem. Haec fides in omni petitione etiam corporalium bonorum praeluceat: ita perspicuum est, cum fides petit corporalia, simul oportere exerceri petitionem spiritualem. Haec tota doctrina de promissionibus spiri- tualibus et corporalibus notissima sit omnibus, et quotidie in invocatione exerceatur, in qua publica et privata bona petenda sunt, salutaria regimina, pax, victus, bona valetudo et alia bona. In his exercitiis fiet doctrina magis perspicua, et crescet fides, quae experietur hanc invocationem non esse irritam. Sciamus etiam Deum haec exer- citia postulare, et hanc invocationem esse cul- tum Deo placentem in credentibus. Sicut inquit

Psalmo 50.: Invoca me in die tribulationis, et eripiam te.

Esto typus fidelium in sermone, etc.

Quanquam exempla in gubernantibus magis conspicua sunt, tamen haec sententia Pauli com- munis regula est, quam singuli intueantur in to- tius vitae gubernatione. Nominat autem ordine haec membra. Esto typus in sermone, id est, in doctrina, recte doceas, recte et non sophistice loquaris de doctrina, et moneto alios, ut vitent curiosas quaestiones, falsa, improprie et per- plexe dicta. Denique sit doctrina perspicua, ne- cessaria ad exercitia fidei, et ad invocationem, et ad bonos mores, ut supra dictum est, Doctrina prosit ad aedificationem.

Secundo inquit, in conversatione. Hic si- gnificat iusticiam universalem, id est, honestas actiones iuxta omnia praecepta Dei, non sis infa- mis ex ulla causa.

In dilectione. Addit aliquid priori membro: non solum vult externam conversationem hone- stam esse, et non famosam, sed vult etiam in corde erga Deum et erga homines dilectionem esse, vult de esse amantem communis consociationis vero corde, placitum et beneficum. Fur est in- famis, sed vult Paulus non solum vitari furta, sed insuper etiam te beneficum esse vero corde.

In spiritu, id est, Zelo, vult ita te placi- dum esse, ut tamen non conniveas ad scelera, et ad perniciosa dogmata. Sed legitimo modo re- prehendas digna reprehensione.

In fide, id est, in consolatione, in omni- bus periculis, videant alii te fide praestare pa- tientiam et constantiam in persecutione et aliis doloribus, non quaerere iniusta auxilia, sed ex- pectare auxilium Dei, et tua consolatione alii eru- diantur et confirmentur, sicut Ieremias regit et consolatur sua fide Ecclesiam sui temporis.

Nominatim et castitatem addit, quae est vi- tare omnes prohibitas commixtiones, et necessa- ria virtus est, iuxta hoc dictum, 1. Corinth. 6.: Nolite errare, scortatores et adulteri non possi- debunt regnum Dei, et fiunt domicilia diabolo- rum, qui se polluunt prohibitis commixtionibus.

Sis assiduus in lectione, consolatione et doctrina.

Propter multas causas hoc dictum familiaris- sime notum sit omnibus. Primum, quia studia literarum approbat, cum ait, Sis assiduus in le- ctione: quam ad rem opus est multiplici cognitio- ne linguarum et artium. Cum igitur scis prae- ceptum esse, ut legas sacros libros, intelligis Deo placere hos labores docendi et discendi, et potes ab eo petere et sperare auxilium, et in omnibus periculis et adversitatibus habes praecipuam con- solationem, iuxta illa dicta, Psalmo 36.: Com- menda Deo viam tuam, et spera in eum, et ipse faciet. Item, 1. Corinth. 15.: Labor vester non erit inanis in Domino.

Universaliter enim regula tenenda est. Pri- mum sciri oportere, an labor aut genus vitae pla- ceat Deo, iuxta illud Roma. 14.: Quidquid non est ex fide, peccatum est. Deinde, nemo potest invocare Deum, petere aut expectare auxilium in negotio quod Deus improbat, iuxta illud Psalmo 5.: Non Deus volens impietatem tu es. Est igi- tur sententia, Commenda Deo viam tuam, id est, vocationem, militiam, laborem, vitae genus ab ipso approbatum.

Monet etiam Paulus hic Ecclesiam alligatam esse ad certos libros, sicut saepe alias praecipitur de doctrina prophetica et apostolica, ut Esaias inquit, cap. 8.: Ad legem et ad testimonia. Ne- esse est igitur reiici doctrinas et illuminationes pugnantes cum his libris. Item opiniones et cul- tus extra hos libros.

Tertio mandat privatam et publicam lectio- nem, et ostendit morem in Ecclesiis fuisse, or- dine propheticos libros legere, sicut et in Syna- gogis fuit usitatum, et Moyses praecipit Levitis, Deut. 31. lectionem integrae legis. Ideo Ma- lach. 2. dicitur: Labia sacerdotis custodiunt scien- tiam, et legem requiram ex ore eius, quia ange- lus Domini exercituum est. Et Oseae 4. denun- ciatur poena negligentibus: Quia repulisti scien- tiam, repellam te, ne sacerdotio fungaris mihi.

Haec dicta et similia sint infixa pectoribus, ut nos ad diligentiam in discendo, docendo, et legendo exuscitent. Accedat autem precatio, ut Deus mentes nostras regat, ut dicta divina pro- prie accipiamus, sicut Propheta orat, Psal. 118.: Fac cum servo tuo secundum misericordiam tuam, et iustificationes tuas doce me. Et Esaias orat, ut retineatur in aliquibus auditoribus veritas, Isaiae 8.: Obsigna legem in discipulis meis.

Est et collatio cum aliis necessaria, sicut scriptum est, Luc. 22.: Et tu conversus confirma fratres tuos. Et Samson inquit Iudic. 14.: Nisi arassetis mea vitula, non invenissetis, id est, nisi essetis adiuti labore Ecclesiae. Audiamus igitur Apostolos et custodes doctrinae apostolicae.

Consideremus etiam, qui a doctrina aposto- lica quomodo discesserint. In aliis prorsus dia- bolica audacia totam Ecclesiae doctrinam mutavit, et horrendos furores sparsit, ut in Marcione, Ma- nichaeis et similibus. In aliis superstitio inflexit animos ad novos cultus.

Haec tota consideratio ad lectionem pertinet, in qua universae Ecclesiae series, et omnium tem- porum historiae cognoscendae sunt.

Observanda est autem brevis distributio ho- rum generum, lectionis, doctrinae et consolatio- nis. Cur a lectione orditur? Quia magna dissi- militudo est philosophiae et Evangelii. Arithme- ticam non incipimus a lectione, sed afferimus multas noticias, quae sunt via ad artem, Deus autem sua voce edidit arcanam doctrinam de filio, et de redemtione, et tota restitutione generis hu- mani, iuxta hanc suam revelationem vult agnosci, et hanc scribi voluit per Prophetas et Apostolos. Ideo ad horum librorum lectionem alligata est Ecclesia, et hi libri sunt fundamentum et norma universae doctrinae in Ecclesia, iuxta illud 1. Co- rinth. 3.: Fundamentum aliud poni non potest, praeter id quod positum est, quod est Iesus Chri- stus. Necesse est igitur assidue legi haec scripta privatim et publice.

Lectionem sequatur doctrina, ut in medica- tione corporis finis est sanatio. Et ars medica continet duas partes, doctrinam et modum cu- randi. Doctrina vero ostendit naturam corporis humani, qualitates, temperamenta, causas mor- borum, remedia. Postea modus curandi applicat remedia. Ac medici sapientia est intelligere, quae ad suam artem pertinent, et consilia dirigere ad sanationem tanquam ad ultimum et principalem finem. Ita sciat concionator se medici similem esse, et finem ministerii evangelici ultimum esse sanationem, qua per filium Dei voce Evangelii liberentur homines ex morte aeterna. Non enim tantum regit mores, ut magistratus politicus.

Sunt igitur et hic duo membra, doctrina et consolatio. Doctrina loquitur de articulis fidei, discernit Legem et Evangelium, recitat descri- ptionem peccati, usum sacramentorum, discri- men iusticiae aeternae et vitae politicae. Sed ne- eesse est accedere consolationem tanquam sana- tionem, ne homo relinquatur in peccato et morte aeterna.

Estque doctrina hoc ipsum, quod usitate nominamus Catechesin, id est, summa dogma- tum recitans articulos fidei, descriptionem pec- cati, discrimen Legis et Evangelii, usum sacra- mentorum, discrimen iusticiae aeternae et vitae politicae, sumta ex ipsa voce divina, quae prius legitur, et haec ipsa Catechesis est interpretatio lectionis seu longa seu brevis. Cum enim in di- scendo necesse sit integrum corpus doctrinae mente complecti, rudioribus tradendae sunt or- dine breves summae principalium locorum, et postea in ipsa lectione monstranda sunt firma te- stimonia, ut fides nitatur voce divina.

Hoc consilio primum condita sunt symbola, et scripti Catechismi. Quanquam enim prorsus eadem sonat lectio, et ipsi libri prophetici et apostolica fons sunt doctrinae, tamen ideo non tantum praeleguntur libri in Ecclesia a pueris, sed etiam accedit vox interpretis, ut rudioribus enarrent genus sermonis, ostendant capita rerum, de quibus dicitur, illustrent ea definitionibus et distinctionibus, sicut in docendo fieri necesse est. Et fiant haec sine sophistica, sed recte iuxta ar- tium vias, Nec misceantur peregrinae materiae.

Cum igitur opus sit forma aliqua in docendo, iubet Paulus eligi Episcopum idoneum ad docen- dum. Hanc formam hic doctrinam nominat, quae est Catechesis seu brevis seu longa, quae quidem et ipsa librorum sacrorum interpretatio est: quia inde sumenda est Catechesis, et testi- monia ibi monstranda sunt.

Tertium membrum consolatio est: quia non satis est recitare capita doctrinae, nisi ostendatur applicatio. Intelligat concionator officii sui gra- dus, legat populo ordine libros propheticos et apostolicos, subinde et corpus verae doctrinae proponat, ut auditores summam recte complecti possint, sicut in Catechesi traditur: nec sit concio sine affectibus, sed commemoratio de ira Dei, exuscitet timorem, nec tamen relinquantur men- tes in pavore et dubitatione, ut poëtarum tra- goediae tantum poenas ostendunt, sed accedat consolatio ex voce Evangelii, commonefiant audi- tores, ut sibi fide applicent promissiones aeternas et praesentium bonorum, et exerceant fidem, spem, invocationem, gratiarum actionem, et caeteras virtutes.

Ita tertius hic gradus proprie de applicatione Evangelii loquitur, qua fit liberatio a peccato et a morte aeterna, et leniuntur dolores in hac vita, agnitione bonitatis Dei, fide, et spe auxilii divini. Cum igitur distributio Paulina sapientissime ostendat partes officii concionatoris, fidelis concionator hanc normam sequatur, sit lector fidelis sacrorum librorum, et meminerit omnes pugnantes opiniones cum sacris libris reiiciendas esse. Deinde integrum corpus doctrinae ordine proponat, et addat testimonia sine sophistica. Postremo et applicationem ostendat, ut crescant timor Dei, poenitentia, fides, invocatio, spes et aliae virtutes, et fiat incoatio vitae aeternae.

## 5:1 Argument
Chapter V.

Thus far many things have been said about doctrine; here he adds some particular admonitions concerning forensic and economic affairs, and it is a notable testimony that duties owed to relatives are pleasing to God. Let them learn, he says, to treat their own house lovingly, and to render a return to their elders, for this is honest and acceptable to God. He exaggerates the same sentiment afterwards, saying: If anyone does not care for his own, and especially those of his household, he has denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel. This amplification must be diligently considered. He signifies, moreover, that στοργὰς (natural affections) are virtues founded by God in nature, which, like other virtues, are necessary in the reborn and are pleasing to God. If anyone, therefore, acts against these virtues, as if someone hates or petulantly harms parents or a spouse, or children, or brothers, or benefactors, he pours out the Holy Spirit, according to those words in 1 John 3: He who does not love his brother remains in death. Likewise in the same place: He who commits sin is of the devil. Likewise 1 Timothy 1: Wage the good warfare, holding faith and a good conscience. These cuckoos, however, namely the ἄστοργοι (those without natural affection), have great wounds of conscience.

We have briefly warned of these things in this place, so that students may consider the whole doctrine concerning natural στοργῇ (affection), which indeed is also a reminder of the love of the eternal Father toward the Son, and toward us, and of the love of the Son toward the human nature which He assumed, and toward us brothers. These secret and wonderful works of God we now look upon from afar, but in eternal life we shall know them more closely.

Latin:

Caput V.

Hactenus plurima de doctrina dicta sunt, hic addit admonitiones particulares aliquot de negotiis forensibus et oeconomicis, et insigne testimonium est, quod Deo placeant officia debita cognatis. Discant, inquit, propriam domum amanter tractare, et reddere vicem maioribus, hoc enim honestum et Deo acceptum est. Eandem sententiam exaggerat postea, dicens: Si quis suos et maxime domesticos non curat, fidem abnegavit, et est infideli deterior. Haec amplificatio diligenter consideranda est. Significat autem στοργὰς esse virtutes a Deo conditas in natura, quae ut caeterae virtutes in renatis necessariae sunt, et Deo placent. Si quis igitur contra has virtutes facit, ut si quis odit aut petulanter laedit parentes aut coniugem, aut natos, aut fratres, aut benefactores, is effundit Spiritum sanctum, iuxta illa dicta 1. Iohann. 3.: Qui non diligit fratrem, manet in morte. Item ibidem: Qui facit peccatum, ex diabolo est. Item 1. Timoth. 1.: Milita bonam militiam, retinens fidem et bonam conscientiam. Habent autem hi cuculi, videlicet ἄστοργοι, magna vulnera conscientiae.

Haec breviter hoc loco monuimus, ut considerent studiosi totam doctrinam de naturali στοργῇ, quae quidem et commonefactrix est de amore aeterni patris erga filium, et erga nos, et de amore filii erga naturam humanam, quam assumsit, et erga nos fratres. Haec arcana et miranda opera Dei nunc procul aspicimus, sed in vita aeterna propius cognoscemus.

## 5:9
Let a widow be chosen, etc.

At the temple of Jerusalem there were women who served by cooking, washing, mending clothes, and providing medication for the Levites and the poor. The Apostles imitated this custom and transferred it to the Church; they ordered that elderly matrons be chosen who would serve the sick or strangers, and these had wages from the alms which the Church then liberally contributed. Paul speaks of this custom, not of monastic vows, and the rest is clear.

But concerning monastic vows, the adversaries clamor loudly in this place, because Paul seems to condemn those contracting marriages after a vow, when he says, Having damnation, because they have made void their first faith. Although there are many firm responses, let us nevertheless hold to this one especially. Even if there had been a custom at that time of making vows, which Paul does not say, those vows would nevertheless have been very different from monastic vows, which without any doubt are idolatrous.

A true and immovable rule must therefore be held: It is most certain that vows which bind one to the worship of idols or to the committing of other sins are void, as if someone had bound himself to sacrifice to Juno to obtain riches, because the voice of the first commandment is manifest, Exodus 20: You shall have no other gods. Likewise 1 Corinthians 11: Flee from idols.

Such, however, have monastic vows been for many centuries. First, there are impious opinions, and rather frenzies, to imagine that monastic rites merit the remission of sins, that they are righteousness, that they are worship of God, that they are evangelical perfection. Second, the offering for the living and the dead in the Mass is a manifest idol, likewise the invocation of dead men, and many other superstitions which are customary in monasteries.

Paul's statement is by no means to be twisted toward the monastic vows of these recent times, in which there are many manifest idols.

Nor does 'first faith' signify a vow of celibacy, but either the faith by which they had promised fidelity in serving, or the Christian faith by which they embraced all the articles of faith. For some curious and lustful women were casting off this also, who, having obtained such offices, wandered about more. And they came into conversations with many, and because they had wages from elsewhere, they lived more lavishly and indulged in pleasures. Paul therefore does not condemn marriage, but he condemns either the desertion of the faith itself, or other sins which followed wantonness and curiosity. Paul used significant words: σπαταλῶσα, that is, abounding in delights and indulging in wantonness; this, he says, is dead while she lives, namely on account of wantonness. Σπατάω in Aristophanes means to live prodigally, hence σπατάλαι are profusions and delights, as Suidas cites the saying: Now the mice dance, enjoying the delights of the flesh of cats.

Moreover, the neighboring virtues are frugality, temperance, and continence, just as these three virtues are especially conspicuous in bees. They are also good things in themselves, and pleasing to God, and they are nurses of other greater virtues: wisdom, justice, and fortitude. There are also neighboring vices: prodigality, intemperance, and incontinence, and this deformity is more conspicuous in women, because it is the duty of a woman in household management to guard faithfully the things acquired, and to dispense them sparingly, chosen with skill for necessary uses. Concerning intemperance it is said: For what does a drunken Venus care?

I believe, however, that Paul alluded to certain descriptions known at that time, because he takes illustrious words from the Comedies. For the following word is also significant: When they have grown wanton against Christ from the alms themselves. The word στρηνιᾶν means to live luxuriously, to be burdened with gluttony, as in Athenaeus: I have lived luxuriously, having consumed the food of four elephants. And in the Apocalypse, chapter 18: The kings who have committed fornication and lived luxuriously with her.

There are also other significant words here, the weight of which if the reader observes, he will understand that Paul is wisely indicating what are the proper virtues of matrons, and what are the contrary vices. It is useful to consider these, and to flee the sophistry which maliciously and foolishly twists Paul to establish the impious and foolish superstitions of monasteries. Paul says expressly: I want the younger women to marry, to be mothers and nurses of families. Here he aptly recounts the principal duties of the female sex, about which it was also said above in the sentence: The woman shall be saved through the bearing of children. Nor do I add a longer exposition: for there are many writings on household management extant, which it behooved many both to know and to follow.

Latin:

Vidua eligatur, etc.

Apud templum Ierosolymae fuerunt mulie- res, quae serviebant coquendo, lavando, sar- ciendis vestibus, medicatione Levitis et pauperi- bus. Hunc morem Apostoli imitati transtulerunt et ad Ecclesiam, iusserunt eligi grandes natu ma- tronas, quae aegrotis aut peregrinis servirent, et hae mercedes habebant ex eleemosynis, quas Ecclesia tunc liberaliter conferebat. De hoc more loquitur Paulus, non de votis monasticis, ac caetera perspicua sunt.

Sed de votis monasticis hoc loco valde voci- ferantur adversarii, quia Paulus videatur damnare contrahentes coniugia post votum, cum ait, Dam- nationem habentes, quia primam fidem irritam fecerunt. Etsi autem multae firmae responsiones sunt, tamen hanc praecipue teneamus. Etiamsi tunc consuetudo fuisset faciendi vota, quod non dicit Paulus, tamen ea vota dissimilima fuissent votis monasticis, quae sine ulla dubitatione sunt idolatrica.

Tenenda est igitur regula vera et immota: Vota quae obligant ad cultus idolorum aut ad alia peccata facienda, certissimum est irrita esse, ut si quis obligasset se sacrificaturum Iunoni ad im- petrandas divitias, quia manifesta est vox primi mandati, Exod. 20.: Non habebis deos alienos. Item 1. Corinth. 11.: Fugite idola.

Talia sunt autem vota monastica iam multis seculis. Primum opiniones impiae sunt, ac fu- rores potius, fingere ritus monasticos mereri re- missionem peccatorum, esse iusticiam, esse cul- tus Dei, esse perfectionem evangelicam. Secundo manifesta idola sunt oblatio pro vivis et mortuis in Missa, item invocatio hominum mortuorum, et aliae multae superstitiones, quae usitatae sunt in monasteriis.

Nequaquam igitur detorquendum est Pauli dictum ad vota monastica horum recentium tem- porum, in quibus multa manifesta idola sunt.

Nec prima fides significat votum coelibatus, sed aut fidem, qua promiserant fidelitatem in ser- viendo, aut fidem Christianam, qua omnes arti- culos fidei amplectebantur. Nam hanc quoque aliquae curiosae et salaces mulieres abiiciebant, quae nactae talia officia magis vagabantur. Et cum multis veniebant in colloquia, et quia habe- bant mercedes aliunde, victitabant largius et in- dulgebant voluptatibus. Non igitur damnat Paulus nuptias, sed dam- nat vel ipsam fidei desertionem, vel alia peccata, quae salacitatem et curiositatem sequebantur. Usus est Paulus verbis significantibus: σπατα- λῶσα, id est, deliciis affluens et lasciviae indul- gens, haec inquit, vivens mortua est, scilicet propter lasciviam. Σπατάω apud Aristophanem significat prodigaliter profundo, inde σπατάλαι profusiones et deliciae, ut Suidas citat dictum: Nunc saltant mures fruentes deliciis carne felium.

Sunt autem virtutes vicinae frugalitas, tem- perantia et continentia, ut in apibus simul hae tres virtutes inprimis conspicuae sunt. Sunt autem et per sese res bonae, et Deo gratae, et sunt nu- trices aliarum maiorum virtutum, sapientiae, iu- stitiae, fortitudinis. Sunt et vitia vicina prodi- galitas intemperantia et incontinentia, et in mu- lieribus haec deformitas conspectior est, quia mu- lieris officium est in oeconomia res partas fideliter custodire, et ad necessarios usus arte electas parce promere. De intemperantia dicitur: Quid enim Venus ebria curat?

Existimo autem Paulum ad descriptiones ali- quas tunc notas allusisse, quia verba illustria Co- moediarum sumit. Nam et sequens verbum in- signe est: Cum saginatae sunt ex ipsis eleemo- synis contra Christum. Verbum στρηνιᾶν est helluari, ingluvie onerari, ut apud Athenaeum: Helluatus sum absumto cibo quatuor elephanto- rum. Et in Apocalypsi capite 18.: Reges qui cum ea scortati et helluati sunt.

Sunt et alia verba hic insignia, quorum pon- dera lector si observabit, intelliget Paulum sa- pienter significare, quae sint propriae matrona- rum virtutes, et quae sint contraria vitia. Haec considerare utile est, et fugienda sophistica, quae malitiose et stulte detorquet Paulum ad stabilien- das impias et fatuas superstitiones monasteriorum. Expresse inquit Paulus: Volo iuniores nubere, esse matres et nutrices familiarum. Hic apte recenset praecipua officia sexus muliebris, de qui- bus et supra dictum est in sententia: Salvabitur mulier per filiorum generatioem. Nec addo lon- giorem enarrationem: extant enim multa oecono- mica scripta, quae et nosse et sequi multos opor- tebat.

## 5:17
Let them be considered worthy of double honor.

That is, with sustenance and reverence. It must be considered why he distinguishes these, and first, that sustenance is owed to teachers is manifest, according to the precept of the Lord, Luke 10: The laborer is worthy of his hire. And here Paul adapts the saying in the law, Deut. 25: You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain, which rite was an image signifying that wages owed should be paid to those who labor, just as the law in Leviticus 19 expressly commands: You shall not keep the wages of a laborer with you until the morning.

And this care pertains to governors, so that aid may be brought from the public to the Pastors of the Churches, and to others who serve the studies of the Church by teaching and learning, just as it is said in Isaiah chapters 49 and 60: Kings shall be your foster fathers, and queens your nurses.

The other part is reverence, of which there are many degrees. The first and most necessary is obedience in those things which pertain to the ministry of the Gospel, according to these sayings, Luke 10: He who hears you, hears me; he who rejects you, rejects me. Likewise to the Hebrews, chapter 13: Obey and be subject to your leaders.

For although these sayings do not constitute kingdoms for Pastors outside the Gospel, nevertheless they affirm that obedience is owed to Pastors in those things which are proper to the evangelical ministry, and these most severe precepts are not to be despised.

Then let other degrees in the mind be added to external obedience: a good opinion of the whole ministry and of the Pastors themselves, and benevolence toward them; because without these interior virtues, external obedience is hypocrisy; let there be no contempt in souls, let there be no hatred, just as Paul says, 1 Corinthians 4, that the Apostles are in hatred as offscourings.

Although there always have been, are, and will be those who think irreverently of the ministry, nevertheless let the sounder ones understand its dignity. Dignity itself is the goodness of the thing, which is seen in the efficient and final cause. The efficient and preserving cause of the evangelical ministry is God himself, gathering the eternal Church by the immense goodness of the voice of the Gospel, and again joining to himself the human race torn away from him. He indeed commands the ministry to be heard and venerated, as was said above.

The final cause is that by this voice God is most truly efficacious, he forgives sins to those who believe, he gives them the Holy Spirit, and makes them heirs of eternal life. He imparts these highest benefits through the voice of the Gospel sounding even through the most miserable men, as the Lord says in John 20: As my Father has sent me, so I send you, that is, it is most certain that I will be effective through you, just as the Father was effective through me, as the resurrection from the dead shows, so also Paul says in Romans 1: The Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth. Likewise, 2 Corinthians 3: The Gospel is the ministry of the spirit.

These statements will be more clear when we learn the true exercises of faith in true consolations, and sustain ourselves by the thought of the promises. Enthusiasts, such as the Anabaptists, Stenckfeld, and the like, reject this use of the ministry, who seek illuminations and raptures outside the Gospel. But in true sorrows and true consolation we learn that God is effective through the thought of the Gospel, as Paul says in Romans 10: Faith comes by hearing. Likewise, Romans 5: Being justified by faith we have peace.

Therefore, let us together give thanks to God for the published promise, for the effectiveness through the Gospel, for the establishment, preservation, and restorations of the evangelical ministry, for the gathering of the Church through the Gospel and the Holy Spirit, for the gift of righteousness and eternal life, for the mitigation of present punishments, for the remission of eternal punishment. Let us acknowledge and celebrate these great goods, and let us also show the due benevolence to those whose labor in this pious ministry serves the Church.

Latin:

Duplici honore digni ducantur.

It est, victu et reverentia. ‘Haec cur dis- cernat considerandum est, ac primum deberi victum docentibus manifestum est, iuxta praeceptum Domini, Lucae 10.: Dignus est operarius mercede. Et hic Paulus accommodat dictum in lege, Deut. 25.: Non ligabis os bovi trituranti, qui ritus imago fuit significans, ut mercedes debitae laborantibus solvantur, sicut expresse praecipit lex Levit. 19.: Non retineas mercedem operarii apud te in crastinum.

Ac pertinet haec cura ad gubernatores, ut Pastoribus Ecclesiarum, et caeteris, qui serviunt studiis Ecclesiae docendo et discendo, de publico auxilium feratur, sicut in Esaia capite 49 et 60. dicitur: Reges erunt nutritores tui, et reginae nutrices.

Altera pars est reverentia, cuius multi sunt gradus. Primus et maxime necessarius est obedientia in his, quae ad ministerium Evangelii pertinent, iuxta haec dicta, Lucae 10: Qui vos audit, me audit, Qui vos spernit, me spernit. Item ad Hebraeos capite 13.: Obedite et subditi estote praepositis vestris.

Etsi enim haec dicta non constituunt regna Pastoribus extra Evangelium, tamen affirmant deberi Pastoribus obedientiam in his, quae sunt propria ministerii evangelici, nec spernenda sunt haec severissima praecepta.

Deinde accedant ad externam obedientiam et alii gradus in mente, Bona opinio de toto ministerio et de ipsis Pastoribus, et benevolentia erga eos: quia sine his interioribus virtutibus externa obedientia est hypocrisis, non sit comtemtus in animis, non sit odium, sicut Paulus inquit, 1. Corinth. 4., Apostolos in odio esse tanquam καθάρματα.

Etsi autem semper multi fuerunt, sunt et erunt de ministerio irreverenter sentientes: tamen saniores intelligant eius dignitatem. Est autem dignitas ipsa rei bonitas, quae in causa efficiente et finali conspicitur. Causa efficiens et conservans ministerii evangelici, est ipse Deus immensa bonitate voce Evangelii colligens aeternam Ecclesiam, et genus humanum avulsum ab ipso rursus sibi copulans. Qui quidem praecipit audiri ac venerari ministerium, ut supra dictum est.

Causa finalis est, quod hac voce Deus verissime est efficax, remittit peccata credentibus, dat eis Spiritum sanctum, et facit haeredes vitae aeternae. Haec summa beneficia impertit per vocem Evangelii sonantem etiam per miserrimos homi- nes, sicut inquit Dominus Ioann. 20.: Sicut pa- ter meus misit me, sic ego mitto vos, id est, cer- tissimum est me efficacem fore per vos, sicut pa- ter per me fuit efficax, ut resuscitatio ex morte ostendit, ita et Paulus inquit Roma. 1.: Evange- lium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti. Item, 2. Corinth. 3.: Evangelium est ministe- rium spiritus.

Haec dicta erunt magis perspicua cum in ve- ris consolationibus discemus vera exercitia fidei, et sustentabimus nos cogitatione promissionum. Hunc usum ministerii abiiciunt enthusiastae, qua- les sunt Anabaptistae, Stenckfeldius, et similes, qui quaerunt illuminationes et raptus extra Evan- gelium. Sed in veris doloribus et vera consola- tione discimus Deum efficacem esse cogitatione Evangelii, ut Paulus inquit Roma. 10.: Fides ex auditu est. Item, Roma. 5.: Iustificati fide pa- cem habemus.

Simul igitur Deo gratias agamus pro edita promissione, pro efficacia per Evangelium, pro constitutione, conservatione, et instaurationibus ministerii evangelici, pro collectione Ecclesiae per Evangelium et Spiritum sanctum, pro dona- tione iusticiae et vitae aeternae, pro mitigatione poenarum praesentium, pro remissione poenae ae- ternae. Haec tanta bona agnoscamus, et cele- brcmus, praestemus etiam benevolentiam debi- tam iis, quorum labor in hoc ministerio pio ser- vit Ecclesiae.

## 5:21
Without prejudice, etc.

He ordains certain forensic matters, which, since they are both known by nature and expressed in the law of God, and are repeated in common law, are not obscure. Let the younger ones learn to understand the terms.

Prejudice signifies to decide a matter not yet duly examined, whether this is done by emotion or by the persuasion of one's own wisdom. Thus in Deuteronomy 16 it is expressly commanded: Hear them, and judge what is just. And the sayings are well known: μήδε δίκην δικάσεις πρὶν ἀμφοῖν μῦθον ἀκούσῃς. Likewise: δεῖ ἀμφοῖν ὁμοίως ἀκροᾶσθαι.

And because judgments are often corrupted by emotions, he therefore adds: Do nothing according to inclination, that is, do not depart from the rule of justice by any private emotion. Thus it can happen either through pride, when someone does not wish to yield to another's opinion, even if the will toward the parties is equal, or when the will is not equal toward the parties, that is called προσωποληψία. Therefore, several species are joined in Deuteronomy 16: You shall not decline to the other side, you shall not accept a person, and from that Paul took the word inclination, by which he here also comprehends προσωποληψίαν, which is to be unequal toward equals, and equal toward unequals.

For God wishes it to be understood that justice is equality toward equals, which indeed has as its norm the divine mind, which loves things similar to its own will and rejects things dissimilar to its own will. Thus a just king preserves all the just and punishes all the unjust. But it is called acceptance of persons when some appearance or shadow outside the case is preferred to the rule of justice, as when a judge spares an adulterer because he is noble, according to that: He grants pardon to the crows, he harasses the doves with censure. Therefore, the acceptance of persons is unjust, because it departs from the rule of justice and creates inequality.

This whole admonition must be diligently considered, so that the term may be weighed, and this sweetest consolation, often repeated in the scriptures, may be familiarly known, which says that there is no προσωποληψίαν with God, as in Romans chapter 2, Acts 10. And in Isaiah 42 it is said of the Messiah: He will not accept a person, that is, he will not be unjust, he will not be unequal, God is truly equal to equals. He condemns sins in all, and receives all who flee to the Son, etc.

Latin:

Sine praeiudicio, etc.

Ordinat forensia quaedam, quae cum et na- tura nota et in lege Dei expressa sunt, et in iure usitato repetuntur, non sunt obscura. Iuniores vocabula discant intelligere.

Praeiudicium significat statuere re nondum ordine cognita, sive id fiat affectu, sive persua- sione propriae sapientiae. Ita Deut. 16. expresse mandatum est: Audite illos, et quod iustum est iudicate. Et nota sunt dicta: μήδε δίκην δικά- σεις πρὶν ἀμφοῖν μῦθον ἀκούσῃς. Item: δεῖ ἀμ- φοῖν ὁμοίως ἀκροᾶσθαι.

Et quia saepe corrumpuntur iudicia affecti- bus, ideo addit: Nihil facias secundum inclina- tionem, id est, non discedas a regula iusticiae ullo privato affectu. Sic potest accidere vel su- perbia, cum non vult quispiam cedere alienae sententiae, etiamsi voluntas erga partes aequalis est, vel cum voluntas non aequalis est erga par- tes, id nominatur προσωποληψία. Species igi- tur plures coniunguntur Deut. 16.: Non declines in alteram partem, non accipias personam, et ex eo sumsit Paulus verbum inclinationem, quo hic et προσωποληψίαν comprehendit, quae est esse inaequalem erga aequales, et aequalem erga in- aequales.

Vult enim Deus intelligi, iusticiam esse ae- qualitatem erga aequales, quae quidem habet nor- mam mentem divinam, quae diligit similia suae voluntati, et reiicit dissimilia suae voluntati. Ita iustus rex servat omnes iustos, et punit omnes in- iustos. Dicitur autem acceptio personae, cum aliqua species seu umbra extra causam antefertur regulae iusticiae, ut cum parcit iudex adultero, quia est nobilis, iuxta illud: Dat veniam corvis, vexat censura columbas. Est igitur acceptio personarum iniusta, quia discedit a regula iusticiae, et efficit inaequali- tatem.

Haec tota commonefactio diligenter conside- randa est, ut vocabulum expendatur, et haec dulcissima consolatio saepe repetita in scripturis familiariter nota sit, quae dicit, apud Deum non esse προσωποληψίαν, ut Roman. 2. cap. Acto. 10. Et Esaiae 42. de Messia dicitur: Non accipiet per- sonam, id est, non erit iniustus, non erit inae- qualis, Deus vere aequalis est aequalibus. Damnat peccata in omnibus, et recipit omnes confugien- tes ad filium, etc.

## 5:22
Lay hands suddenly on no man, etc.

It embraces useful doctrine. First, it confirms the calling and ordination which is done through men in the Church, because he approves the ordination which Timothy was performing by laying hands on those whom the Church or he himself had chosen. But it is a huge benefit of God that He wishes ministers to be called or chosen by the Church, and through us He truly wishes to be effective, as the Lord says in John 20: As my Father has sent me, so I send you. And afterwards Paul commands Titus in chapter 1: Appoint presbyters.

We ought to acknowledge this huge benefit with thanks, and exercise the ministry with this faith, and use the ministry, and conclude that God is truly effective by the voice of these ministers. And above it was said more copiously about the double calling of ministers.

The second admonition contained here is this: that he wishes for an examination of doctrine and morals to take place, and that those not examined should not be admitted to the ministry, just as he also commands below in 2 Timothy 2: Commit the ministry to faithful men, who are fit to teach. He wishes, therefore, for doctrine and morals to be inspected, and for no one to be admitted to the ministry who is not moderately fit.

Here someone will ask: What degree must be observed? I answer: Both propositions must be held. The first, that no one's erudition, wisdom, and diligence is equal to such a ministry, just as it is expressly said in 2 Corinthians 3: We are not sufficient. Our infirmity must therefore be acknowledged, and our audacity curbed, so that we do not disturb the rightly delivered doctrine by reliance on our own wisdom, nor invent new dogmas or new forms of worship. The second proposition must be added, that it is necessary to obey the command which orders those called to serve the Church; it is required there that we be faithful, as is said in 1 Corinthians 4.

Faithfulness, however, is opposed to two vices: affected ignorance and affected negligence in those things which necessarily had to be done. Faithfulness therefore includes moderate erudition and moderate diligence in doing those things which are necessary. Here, however, moderate erudition should be considered that which nevertheless fully embraces the foundation, that is, all the articles of the creed, the Decalogue, the distinction between Law and Gospel, the understanding of the doctrine of justification, of the use of the sacraments, and of true and fictitious forms of worship.

Although no one sufficiently understands this divine wisdom, nevertheless, regarding all these matters, it is necessary for every Pastor to know the form of teaching which exists correctly in the Churches, contained in the Catechisms.

For it is necessary to know the distinction between insufficiency and faithfulness in any vocation, so that we may know why it is necessary to serve, and what things we ought to bring, and from where help must be sought and expected: and so that, having acknowledged our infirmity, we may attempt nothing outside our vocation, just as many great men have fallen through reliance on their own power, or justice, or wisdom, or authority, such as Gideon, Nebuchadnezzar, Pompey, and countless others.

Paul adds here, however, a rule: Do not share in the sins of others. Which agrees with the common saying: The doer and the consenter are to be punished alike.

Then he gathers other precepts, concerning chastity, likewise concerning the preservation of health, and others.

The doctrine concerning chastity is often repeated, which it is most certain is a necessary virtue, according to the saying in 1 Corinthians 6: Fornicators and adulterers will not possess the kingdom of God. Likewise, Hebrews 13: God will judge fornicators and adulterers.

On the preservation of health. This justice pertains to the commandment: You shall not kill. Always, however, very many men have killed themselves, and are killing themselves, through intemperance; some have even harmed their bodies through immoderate abstinence. Paul in the twelfth chapter to the Colossians used a remarkable word; he orders that honor be held for the body. For since it is the lodging and organ of the Holy Spirit, it is such a thing that it must not only be cherished, just as you cherish a tree or cattle, but it must also be so magnified that the opinion arises that the body is the dwelling and organ of divine actions in all eternity. And because of these goods, so that God may not be hindered, it must be held reverently, and the very art of its construction is more to be admired than in other bodies, because many more testimonies about God are impressed upon us, namely, the rays of divine wisdom, the knowledge of numbers and order, and the distinction between honorable and shameful things. It is impossible that these things are always such by chance. But it must be confessed that there is an architectonic mind. Finally, for this reason also, honor is owed to the body, because God commands that it not be harmed. May this consideration invite us to diligence in protecting and governing the body.

Latin:

Nemini cito manus imponito, etc.

Complectitur utilem doctrinam. Primum confirmat vocationem et ordinationem, quae fit per homines in Ecclesia, quia approbat ordina- tionem, quam Timotheus faciebat imponens ma- nus iis, quos Ecclesia vel ipse elegerat. Est au- tem ingens beneficium Dei, quod vult ab Eccle- sia vocari vel eligi ministros, et per nos vere vult esse efficax, sicut inquit Dominus Ioann. 20.: Sicut pater meus misit me, ita ego mitto vos. Et postea praecipit Tito Paulus capite 1.: Consti- tue presbyteros.

Hoc ingens beneficium grati agnoscere debe- mus, et hac fide exercere ministerium, et uti mi- nisterio, ac statuere, quod Deus vere efficax sit voce horum ministrorum. Ac supra copiosius dictum est de duplici vocatione ministrorum.

Altera admonitio hic comprehensa haec est, Quod vult fieri explorationem doctrinae et morum, nec admitti ad ministerium inexploratos, sicut et infra praecipit 2. Timoth. 2.: Commenda mini- sterium hominibus fidelibus, qui sunt idonei ad docendum. Vult ergo inspici doctrinam et mo- res, et nullos admitti ad ministerium, qui non sunt mediocriter idonei.

Hic quaeret aliquis: Quis gradus observan- dus est? Respondeo: Utraque propositio tenenda est. Prima, Nullius eruditionem, sapientiam, et diligentiam parem esse tanto ministerio, sicut 2. Corinth. 3. expresse dicitur: Non sumus suffi- cientes, Agnoscenda est igitur nostra infirmitas, et frenanda audacia, ne fiducia nostrae sapientiae doctrinam recte traditam turbemus, nec nova dogmata, nec novos cultus fingamus. Altera pro- positio addenda est, Necesse est obedire mandato, quod iubet servire Ecclesiae vocatos, ibi requiri- tur ut fideles simus, ut dicitur 1. Corinth. 4.

Fidelitas autem opponitur duobus vitiis, Af- fectatae ignorantiae, et affectatae negligentiae in iis, quae necessario facienda erant. Comprehen- dit igitur fidelitas mediocrem eruditionem, et me- diocrem diligentiam in faciendis iis, quae neces- saria sunt. Hic autem mediocris eruditio ea exi- stimetur esse, quae tamen fundamentum integre complectitur, id est, omnes articulos symboli, Decalogum, discrimen Legis et Evangelii, intellectum doctrinae de iustificatione, de usu sacramentorum, de veris cultibus et ficticiis.

Etsi autem nemo satis intelligit hanc divi- nam sapientiam, tamen de his materiis omnibus utcunque oportet quemlibet Pastorem scire for- mam docendi, quae in Ecclesiis emendate extat, comprehensa in Catechismis.

Nam distinctionem de insufficientia et fideli- tate, in qualibet vocatione nosse necessarium est, ut sciamus cur necesse sit servire, et quas res nos afferre oporteat, et unde petendum et expectan- dum sit auxilium: et ut agnita infirmitate nostra nihil extra vocationem tentemus, sicut multi summi viri lapsi sunt fiducia suae potentiae, vel iusticiae, vel sapientiae, vel autoritatis, ut Ge- deon, Nabogdonosor, Pompeius et alii innume- rabiles.

Addit autem hic Paulus regulam: Non com- munices alienis peccatis. Quae congruit cum usi- tato dicto: Faciens et consentiens similiter pu- niendus est.

Deinde congerit alia praecepta, de castitate, item de tuenda valetudine, et alia.

Saepe autem repetitur doctrina de castitate, quam certissimum est virtutem esse necessariam, iuxta dictum 1. Corinth. 6.: Scortatores et adul- teri non possidebunt regnum Dei. Item, He- brae. 13.: Scortatores et adulteros iudicabit Deus.

De tuenda valetudine. Pertinet haec iusti- cia ad praeceptum: Non occides. Semper autem valde multi homines se interfecerunt, et interfi- ciunt intemperantia, aliqui etiam immoderata abs- tinentia laeserunt corpora. Paulus ad Colossens. capite duodecimo insigni verbo usus est, iubet honorem haberi corpori. Cum enim sit hospitium et organum Spiritus sancti, tale quiddam est, quod non solum fovendum est, sicut foves arbo- rem aut pecus, sed etiam ita magnificiendum est, ut accedat opinio, quod corpus sit domicilium et organum actionum divinarum in omni aeternitate. Et propter haec bona ne Deus impediatur, reve- renter tenendum est, et ars ipsa fabricationis ma- gis admiranda est, quam in aliis corporibus, quia multo plura testimonia de Deo nobis impressa sunt, videlicet radii sapientiae divinae, noticia numerorum et ordinis, discrimen honestorum et turpium. Haec casu semper talia esse impossi- bile est. Sed fatendum est mentem architectatri- cem esse. Postremo ideo quoque debetur honos corpori, quia Deus praecipit, ne laedatur. Haec consideratio nos ad diligentiam invitet in tuendo et regendo corpore.

## 5:24
The sins of some go before judgment, etc.

He is not speaking of the final judgment, but since he had spoken earlier of election and the censure of morals, he now adds an admonition about the same matter, and he speaks of human judgment in governance; he says that morals, whether good or bad, do not remain hidden for long, but are either quickly detected before governance, or if there was any simulation, it cannot be long-lasting during governance, as it is said: ἀρχὴ ἄνδρα δείκνυσι. This rule should be observed, because in life it is necessary to take care not to entangle yourself in the familiarities of evil men, as Sirach says in the eleventh chapter: Do not bring just anyone into your house, because there are many deceitful snares. Therefore, the signs of intentions and morals must be considered, which Many things can be observed, such as lies, ostentation, detraction, associations with evil people, not paying debts, a type of study and labor, gluttony. Paul speaks here of such human judgments, and he wants us to be vigilant and attentive in discerning the feelings and natures of those whom we join to ourselves.

Latin:

Quorundam peccata praecedunt iudicium etc.

Non loquitur de extremo iudicio, sed cum antea dixerit de electione et de censura morum, nunc eadem de re admonitionem addit, et loqui- tur de iudicio humano in gubernatione, non diu latent inquit mores, seu boni seu mali, sed aut cito deprehenduntur ante gubernationem, aut si qua fuit simulatio, tamen in gubernatione non potest esse diuturna, sicut dicitur: ἀρχὴ ἄνδρα δείκνυσι. Haec regula observetur, quia in vita necesse est cavere, ne implices te malorum homi- num familiaritatibus, ut Syrach capite undecimo inquit: Non quemlibet inducas in domum tuam, quia multae sunt insidiae dolosae. Signa igitur voluntatum et morum consideranda sunt, quae multa animadverti possunt, ut mendacia, osten- tatio, obtrectatio, familiaritates malorum, non solvere debita, genus studii et laborum, hellua- tiones. De talibus iudiciis humanis hic loquitur Paulus, et vult nos vigilantes et intentos esse in diiucandis sensibus et naturis eorum, quos nobis adiungimus.

## 6:1 Argument
Chapter VI.

In the sixth chapter, at the beginning, he gives a commandment to servants, where the younger ones should remember that the common rule is confirmed, which is often repeated: the Gospel does not abolish economies and polities, but preaches about other things, namely about eternal goods, about eternal justice and life, which God effects in the hearts of men, whom he nevertheless wills in this mortal life to be subject to this order, which according to the will of God is suitable for bodily life. He wills us to be sustained by food and drink, he wills there to be legitimate marriages and propagation, he wills there to be the ordinary association of the human race, the distinction of dominions, defense through empires, contracts, laws, judgments, punishments. Thus, here we see servitude approved, such as it was described in the laws at that time. It is profitable, moreover, both for consciences and for peace to understand this doctrine of the approval of the political order.

Latin:

Caput VI.

In sexto capite initio servis praeceptum dat, ubi meminerint iuniores communem regulam con- firmari, quae saepe, repetitur, Evangelium non abolet oeconomias et politias, sed concionatur de aliis rebus, videlicet de aeternis bonis, de aeterna iusticia et vita, quam Deus efficit in cordibus ho- minum, quos tamen vult in hac vita mortali sub- iectos esse huic ordini, qui iuxta voluntatem Dei convenit vitae corporali. Vult nos cibo et potu sustentari, vult esse legitima coniugia, et propa- gationem, vult esse consociationem ordinariam generis humani, distinctionem dominiorum, de- fensionem per imperia, contractus, leges, iudi- cia, poenas. Ita hic videmus approbari servitu- tem, qualis tunc in legibus descripta fuit. Pro- dest autem et conscientiis, et ad pacem intelligere hanc doctrinam approbatione ordinis politici.

## 6:3
If anyone teaches otherwise etc.

The commandment concerning guarding the purity of doctrine has been repeated very often in all the writings of the Prophets and Apostles, according to that in Galatians 1: If anyone teaches another Gospel etc. This is also repeated here with a long commemoration, which warns both what kind of people they are who spread corruptions of doctrine, and what kind of matters they are, and how great evils arise from useless questions.

Afterwards he introduces the saying: They think that godliness is a means of gain, that is, they think that doctrine and the name of religion are a lure for gain, and they carry themselves in such a way that for the sake of gain some practice arts that are entirely useless, such as street performing, rope-walking, and the like.

He uses, moreover, the word τετύφωται, which means he is stunned, or struck by lightning, so that judgment and discernment are lost. Demosthenes and others have used this word to mean I am out of my mind. For it is from τυφὼν, which means a whirlwind, and antiquity used it for a type of lightning.

It signifies, therefore, that such people are hallucinating, who invent corruptions of true doctrine so that they err in judgment, and like the blind, they grasp at nearby things, not those which they seek. Then they also add hyperboles, such as we have seen many in our age: as when Paul says, our citizenship is in heaven, signifying that the Gospel does not establish a worldly polity. Anabaptists simply condemn all political offices, the distinction of dominions, magistrates, judgments, and oaths.

When antiquity had said, justice is the communication of God with equality, namely ordered, heretics added a hyperbole, with equality, namely universal, so that individuals might have access to others' wives equally. Such examples show what he calls stunned or stupefied, so that madness follows.

The beginnings, however, of this madness are these: when a man has not rightly learned the foundation, and without the fear of God and without prayer judges, and fascinated by the admiration of his own wisdom, loves his own imaginations, the devil approaches and hinders his judgment even more, as it is written in Luke 22: Satan entered into him. Likewise, They are held captive by the snares of the devil, says Paul in 2 Timothy 2. Since, therefore, our weakness is great, and the devil as a roaring lion seeks whom he may devour, let us studiously learn the foundation, and with assiduous prayer let us ask, as the Prophet sounding the voice of all the saints says in Psalm 118: Deal with thy servant according to thy mercy, and teach me thy statutes.

But someone might say: From where shall I discern useful questions from useless ones? I answer: Let the norm be the foundation, as Paul says in 1 Corinthians 3: Other foundation can no man lay than that which is laid, which is Christ Jesus. The foundation, however, embraces the prophetic and apostolic writings, and the creeds, and there is an illustrious distinction between Law and Gospel. Likewise between the justice of faith and of works. Likewise between true worship instituted by God and false worship instituted by men, etc. Within these boundaries thoughts must be restrained, and curiosity must be curbed, as it is said in Ecclesiastes 5: Be not rash to speak before God. And a little before in chapter 4: Draw near to the temple, that you may hear. Romans 12: Think modestly according to the measure given to each one, etc.

And those plagues are to be entirely avoided: Ostentation of subtleties, Sophistomania, and the love of contention, which are condemned by all sayings that enjoin truth and forbid lying, according to that: Do not speak false testimony. Eph. 4: Putting away lying, speak truth. And let us also follow the rules: The custom of false teachers is to be avoided, according to the saying in 1 Corinthians 15: Evil communications corrupt good manners. Likewise in Luke 12: Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees.

Latin:

Si quis aliter docet etc.

Praeceptum de custodienda puritate doctri- nae saepissime repetitum est in omnibus scriptis Prophetarum et Apostolorum, iuxta illud Gal. 1.: Si quis aliud Evangelium docet etc. Id hic quo- que longa commemoratione repetitum est, quae monet et quales sint qui doctrinae corruptelas spargunt, et quales sint materiae, et quanta mala ex inutilibus quaestionibus oriantur.

Postea infert dictum: Putant pietatem quaestum esse, id est, putant doctrinam et no- men religionis esse aucupium quaestus, et ita cir- cumferunt, ut quaestus causa exerceant aliqui ar- tes prorsus inutiles, circulatoriam, funambulato- riam, et similia.

Utitur autem verbo τετύφωται, quod signi- ficat, attonitus est, seu fulmine stupefactus, ut iudicium et delectus amissus sit. Demosthenes et alii hoc verbo usi sunt, pro amens sum. Est enim a τυφὼν, quod significat turbinem, et vetustas pro specie fulminum usurpavit.

Significat ergo tales esse alucinatores, qui corruptelas verae doctrinae fingunt, ut iudicio errent, et velut coeci vicina apprehendant, non ea quae petunt. Deinde et hyperbolas addunt, quales nostra aetate multos vidimus: ut cum Paulus inquit, πολίτευμα nostrum in coelis est, significans Evangelium non constituere politiam mundanam. Anabaptistae simpliciter damnant omnia politica officia, distinctionem dominiorum, magistratus, iudicia, iuramenta.

Cum vetustas dixisset, iusticia est communicatio Dei cum aequalitate, scilicet ordinata, haeretici addebant hyperbolen, cum aequalitate, scilicet universali, ita ut aequaliter ad alienas uxores singuli accederent. Talia exempla ostendunt, quid nominet attonitos seu stupefactos, ita ut amentia sequatur.

Initia autem huius amentiae haec sunt, quando homo non recte didicit fundamentum, et sine timore Dei et sine precatione iudicat, et admiratione suae sapientiae fascinatus amat suas imaginationes, accedit diabolus et magis impedit iudicium, sicut scriptum est Lucae 22.: Intravit in eum Satanas. Item, Tenentur captivi laqueis diaboli, inquit Paulus 2. Timoth. 2. Cum igitur et magna sit infirmitas nostra, et diabolus tanquam leo rugiens quaerat quem devoret, studiose discamus fundamentum, et assidua precatione petamus, sicut Propheta sonans vocem omnium sanctorum, Psalmo 118.: Fac cum servo tuo secundum misericordiam tuam, et iustificationes tuas doce me.

Dicat autem aliquis: Unde discernam quaestiones utiles ab inutilibus? Respondeo: Norma sit fundamentum, ut Paulus inquit 1. Corinth. 3.: Fundamentum aliud poni non potest, nisi id quod positum est, quod est Christus Iesus. Complectitur autem fundamentum scripta prophetica et apostolica, et symbola, et illustre discrimen est Legis et Evangelii. Item iusticiae fidei et operum. Item veri cultus a Deo instituti, et falsi cultus ab hominibus instituti etc. Intra has metas coërcendae sunt cogitationes, et frenanda est curiositas, ut Ecclesiastae 5. dicitur: Non sis velox ad loquendum coram Deo. Et paulo ante capite 4.: Accede ad templum, ut audias. Roman. 12.: Sapite modeste secundum mensuram unicui que datam etc.

Et prorsus fugiendae sunt illae pestes, Ostentatio argutiarum, Sophistomania, et amor con- tentionis, quae damnantur omnibus dictis, quae praecipiunt veritatem, et prohibent mendacium, iuxta illud: Non dicas falsum testimonium. Ephe. 4.: Deponentes mendacium, loquimini veritatem. Et regulas etiam sequamur: Fugienda consuetudo falsa docentium, iuxta dictum 1. Corinth. 15.: Corrumpunt bonos mores colloquia prava. Item Lucae duodecimo: Cavete fermentum Pharisaeorum.

## 6:6
Godliness with αὐταρκείᾳ (contentment) is great gain.

He has used the word 'gain' twice, first speaking of hunting for profit, and censuring impious men who treat religion as a source of gain, which is always common in the world. Afterwards, he opposes another meaning of the word, saying that religion is in reality great gain, which is said for this reason, not because he wishes it to be venal, but because he wishes it to be understood that for one who possesses it rightly, it is in itself an eternal good, to which God also adds bodily goods, according to that in Matthew 6: Seek first the kingdom of God, and the rest shall be added unto you. Likewise, 1 Timothy 4: Godliness has promises of the present and future life.

He adds, however, that it is gain in such a way that we ought also to be content with little, and indeed if we lived in an orderly fashion, nature could be content with little. But expenses are increased by many most foolish causes, which harm both resources, and morals, and the soul, and the Republics. And Paul censures these vices, profusions, rapacities, and avarice. Furthermore, when he names αὐτάρκειαν (contentment), he wishes us to be obedient under the cross, and to remember the doctrine concerning the understanding of bodily promises, namely that they are to be understood with the exception of chastisement and the cross. Then also let the mind be content, according to that in 1 Peter 5: Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, and let it seek mitigation from God.

Latin:

Magnum lucrum est pietas cum αὐταρκείᾳ.

Bis usus est vocabulo Quaestus, primum de aucupio loquens, et taxans impios homines, qui religionem quaestui habent, quod semper in mundo usitatum est. Postea opponit aliam significationem vocabuli, inquiens, religionem revera esse magnum lucrum, quod eo dicitur, non quod velit esse venalem, sed quia vult intelligi, recte habenti eam per sese bonum aeternum esse, cui Deus etiam addit bona corporalia, iuxta illud Matthaei 6.: Primum quaerite regnum Dei, et caetera adiicientur vobis. Item, 1. Timoth. 4.: Pietas habet promissiones praesentis et futurae vitae.

Addit autem, sic esse lucrum, ut tum etiam oporteat nos parvo contentos esse, et quidem si ordine viveremus, natura parvo contenta esse posset. Sed augentur sumtus multis stultissimis causis, quae et facultatibus, et moribus, et animae, et Rebuspublicis nocent. Ac Paulus taxat haec vitia, profusiones, rapacitates, avaritiam. Praeterea cum nominat αὐτάρκειαν, vult nos obedire in cruce, ac meminisse doctrinam de promissionum corporalium intellectu, quod videlicet intelligendae sint cum exceptione castigationis et crucis. Tunc quoque animus contentus sit, iuxta illud 1. Petri 5.: Humiliamini sub potenti manu Dei, et petat mitigationem a Deo.

## 6:13
I charge thee, etc.

Finally, he repeats the precept concerning the guarding of the purity of doctrine, and mixes in the saying: Before God who quickens all things. This particle pertains to the doctrine which is handed down in the explanation of the creed concerning creation, namely that God has not departed from created things, as a craftsman departs from a ship that has been constructed, but always sustains things as long as they exist: and indeed sustains them most freely. Thus it is said in Acts chapter 17: In him we are, we live, and we move. Likewise, Luke 12: Two sparrows are sold for a farthing, and one of them does not fall upon the ground without your Father. But the very hairs of your head are all numbered. Likewise, Psalm 144: Who gives them their food, and to the young ravens that call upon him.

It is necessary to think of this free presence and will of God in every invocation, because those who retain imaginations that pretend nature is carried along thus without God, or that God is bound to secondary causes, do not invoke God, but treat him with insult, like the Epicureans or Stoics. Let faith resist these impious thoughts with great effort. And this struggle is to be learned in daily invocation. To the same doctrine pertains the saying placed below in 1 Timothy 6: Let them hope in the living God, and who provides us all things to enjoy, where he also testifies that sustenance is given to us by God, but given to be enjoyed, that is, for use convenient to nature, not for Antonian profusions, etc.

The end of the first Epistle.

Latin:
