Praecipio tibi etc.

Tandem repetit praeceptum de tuenda puri- tate doctrina, et miscet dictum: Coram Deo qui vivificat omnia. Haec particula pertinet ad doctrinam, quae traditur in enarratione symboli de creatione, quod videlicet Deus non discesserit a rebus conditis, sicut discedit faber a navi con- structa, sed semper sustentet res, donec sunt: et quidem sustentet liberrime. Ita dicitur in Actis capite. 17.: In ipso sumus, vivimus et movemur. Item, Lucae 12.: Duo passeres asse veneunt, et unus ex illis non cadit super terram sine patre ve- stro. Vestri autem capilli capitis omnes numerati sunt. Item, Psalmo 144.: Qui dat escam ipso- rum, et pullis corvorum invocantibus eum.

Hanc liberam praesentiam et voluntatem Dei cogitare necesse est in omni invocatione, quia qui retinent imaginationes, quae fingunt naturam sic ferri sine Deo, aut Deum ad causas secundas alli- gatum esse, non invocant Deum, sed contumelia eum adficiunt, ut Epicurei aut Stoici. His im- piis cogitationibus fides magno labore repugnet. Et haec pugna in quotidiana invocatione discenda est. Ad eandem doctrinam pertinet dictum infra positum 1. Timoth. 6.: Sperent in Deo vivente, et praebente nobis omnia ad fruendum, ubi etiam testatur victum nobis a Deo dari, sed dari ad fruendum, id est, ad usum convenientem natu- rae, non ad profusiones Antonianas etc.

Finis primae Epistolae.

# 2 Timothy

## 1:1 Argument
A commentary by Lord Philipp Melanchthon on the Second Epistle to Timothy.

Paul wrote the Second Epistle to Timothy while a prisoner in Rome, when he was calling him to himself from Ephesus. He confirms and consoles him, and commands him to guard the purity of doctrine and to choose suitable teachers. He mixes in admonitions concerning the sum of doctrine, the reading of the prophetic books, the cross, and future dissensions. And many illustrious words are scattered in this short Epistle, such as when he commands ἀναζωπυρεῖν, that is, to stir up like a fire the gifts of God in us. He commands ὀρθοτομεῖν, that is, to rightly divide the word of God. The speech of heretics creeps like the disease gangrene. There will be men who are ἄστοργοι, ἄσπονδοι, τετυφώμενοι, and many other things worthy of singular consideration.

At the beginning, however, mention is made of Timothy's grandmother and mother. Let the younger ones know there those things which are written about the fatherland and parents of Timothy in Acts chapter 16. Timothy was born in the town of Lystra, which is situated in Lycaonia, under Galatia, not far from Iconium, which city is not far from Mount Taurus, and is often celebrated in histories, and because of the name εἰκὼν many fables have been handed down about it: but I think it was so called because of a notable idol. Timothy's father was a Gentile; his mother and grandmother were Jewish women, to whom indeed Paul attributes the testimony of true invocation. Thus, long ago, the recognition of the true God was propagated among the nations.

At the beginning, however, he commands him to stir up the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and he used the illustrious word ἀναζωπυρεῖν, which signifies to stir up again a fire that is almost extinguished, and it is often used for that which we say, to rekindle the heat in a body that is almost extinguished. He used a fuller word for this reason, that he might tax sloth and hypocrisy; he wants us to be neither idle nor to loosen the rein to our desires. Furthermore, where there is diligence, let it not be hypocritical, as are the superstitious exercises of monks, but let the works be useful. And let there be in the mind true knowledge of the Son of God, repentance, fear, faith, and true invocation.

But someone might say: How are the gifts stirred up? I answer: A reborn man is not like a statue, but the Holy Spirit is given for this reason, that liberty may be begun in us, and we can now begin obedience; nor is the Holy Spirit idleness, but it is a flame and a divine agitation resisting the devil and the infirmity of the flesh, and approaching such motions as the Holy Spirit himself is. Therefore it was said to the Romans in the eighth chapter: The Spirit helps our infirmity. Likewise, Eph. 5: Walk accurately, not as fools. Likewise, 1 Cor. 6: We exhort you not to receive the grace in vain. Likewise, Luke 16: How much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask. Likewise, 1 Pet. 5: Be sober unto prayer. The gifts are therefore stirred up first of all by the contemplation of doctrine: then by invocation, exercises of repentance, consideration of our infirmity, by resisting the sudden fires of the passions, and by sustaining struggles and dangers in confession. In such actions Paul wants the gifts to grow, as it is said in Luke 19: To him who has, it shall be given. And the whole parable of the merchants pertains to this.

Latin:

IN ALTERAM AD TIMOTHEUM ENARRATIO DOMINI PHILIPPI MELANTHONIS.

Secundam Epistolam ad Timotheum scripsit Paulus Romae captivus, cum eum ad se ex Epheso vocaret. Confirmat et consolatur eum, praecipit, ut doctrinae puritatem custodiat, et eligat idoneos doctores. Miscet admonitiones de summa doctri- nae, de lectione propheticorum librorum, de cruce, de venturis dissidiis. Et multa illustria verba sparsa sunt in hanc brevem Epistolam, ut, iubet ἀναζωπυρεῖν, id est, excitare velut ignem dona Dei in nobis. Iubet ὀρθοτομεῖν, id est, recte secare verbum Dei. Sermo haereticorum serpit ut Gangraena morbus. Erunt homines ἄστοργοι, ἄσπονδοι, τετυφώμενοι, et alia multa digna sin- gulari consideratione.

Initio autem fit mentio aviae et matris Ti- mothei. Sciant iuniores ibi ea quae de patria et parentibus Timothei scripta sunt in Actis cap. 16. Natus est Timotheus in oppido Lystris, quod in Lycaonia situm est, sub Galatia, non procul ab Iconio, quae urbs non procul abest a Tauro monte, et saepe celebratur in historiis, et propter nomen εἰκὼν multae fabulae de ea traditae sunt: sed existimo propter insigne idolum sic appella- tum esse. Pater Timothei Ethnicus fuit, mater et avia fuerunt mulieres Iudaicae, quibus quidem tribuit Paulus testimonium verae invocationis. Sic olim inter gentes propagata est agnitio veri Dei.

Initio autem iubet eum excitare dona Spiri- tus sancti, et illustri verbo usus est ἀναζωπυ- ρεῖν, quod significat ignem pene extinctum rur- sus excitare, et saepe usurpatur pro eo quod dici- mus, rursus accendere calorem in corpore pene extinctum. Ideo autem pleniore verbo usus est, ut taxet ignaviam et hypocrisin, vult nos nec otiosos esse, nec laxare frenum cupiditatibus. Deinde ubi est diligentia, non sit hypocritica, ut sunt superstitiosa exercitia monachorum, sed sint opera utilia. Et sint in mente vera noticia filii Dei, poenitentia, timor, fides, vera invocatio.

Sed dicat aliquis: Quomodo exuscitantur dona? Respondeo: Homo renatus non est ut statua, sed ideo datur Spiritus sanctus, ut incoë- tur in nobis libertas, et possumus iam incoare obedientiam, nec Spiritus sanctus est otium, sed est flamma et agitatio divina repugnans diabolo et infirmitati carnis, et accedens motus tales, qua- lis ipse Spiritus sanctus est. Ideo dictum est ad Romanos octavo capite: Spiritus opitulatur infir- mitati nostrae. Item, Ephes. 5.: Ambulate accur- rate, non ut fatui. Item, 1. Corinth. 6.: Ad- hortamur vos, ne frustra gratiam accipiatis. Item, Lucae 16.: Quanto magis dabit pater vester coe- lestis Spiritum sanctum petentibus. Item, 1. Pe- tri 5.: Sitis sobrii ad precationem. Excitantur igitur dona primum omnium cogitatione doctri- nae: deinde invocatione, exercitiis poenitentiae, consideratione nostrae infirmitatis, repugnando subitis incendiis affectuum, sustinendo certamina et pericula in confessione. In talibus actionibus vult Paulus crescere dona, sicut dicitur Lucae 19.: Habenti dabitur. Et huc pertinet tota parabola de negociantibus.

## 1:7
Not the spirit of fear etc.

Let us retain the customary distinction: One is servile fear, namely dread without faith, with which there are rumblings and indignation against God, and a horrible flight from God and from punishments, as in Saul, Judas, and the like. Another is filial fear, namely true dread with faith, that is, consolation, by which the heart now rests in the mediator, does not flee from God, but having recognized his mercy, struggles with dread, and begins to believe in God, to invoke him, and to submit itself to him with true reverence. Such fear is in Joseph and in all the saints. Let these things be considered in experience, in daily invocation, and not be entangled in obscure doubts.

Let this therefore be a plain answer: God has not given us the spirit of fear, that is, servile fear, indignation against God, and horrible flight, not doubts.

On the contrary, he names the Spirit of power, that is, a powerful or strong Spirit, first of all vivifying hearts by faith and consoling them, so that they may approach God, not flee, not be angry, not be overwhelmed by despair and death. He is likewise powerful or constant in retaining assent to doctrine against devils, and against the enemies of the Gospel. He is also strong in enduring hatreds and tortures, in confession. From these effects it can be understood what he calls a powerful Spirit. Thus also in the first chapter to the Ephesians he says: Believing according to the efficacy of the power of his might, which power he wrought through Christ raising him from the dead, that is, God is efficacious in conversion, and by faith he vivifies and delivers from death, confirms assent in the heart, and constancy in confession.

Latin:

Non Spiritum timoris etc.

Retineamus usitatam distinctionem: Alius est timor servilis, videlicet pavor sine fide, cum quo sunt fremitus et indignatio adversus Deum, et horribilis fuga Dei, et poenarum, ut in Saul, Iuda et similibus. Alius est timor filialis, videli- cet verus pavor cum fide, id est, consolatione, qua cor iam acquiescit in mediatore, non fugit Deum, sed agnita eius misericordia luctatur cum pavore, et incipit credere Deo, invocare eum, et se ei subiicere vera reverentia. Talis timor est in Ioseph et in omnibus sanctis. Haec in expe- rientia, in quotidiana invocatione considerentur, non involvantur obscuris dubitationibus.

Sit igitur haec plana responsio: Non dedit nobis Deus Spiritum timoris, id est, timorem servilem, indignationem adversus Deum, et hor- ribilem fugam, non dubitationes.

Econtra nominat Spiritum potentiae, id est, Spiritum potentem seu fortem, primum fide vivi- ficantem corda et consolantem, ut ad Deum acce- dant, non fugiant, non irascantur, non oppri- mantur desperatione et morte. Est item potens seu constans in retinenda assensione doctrinae contra diabolos, et contra hostes Evangelii. Est et fortis in perferendis odiis et cruciatibus, in con- fessione. Ex his effectibus intelligi potest, quid nominet Spiritum potentem. Sic et in primo capite ad Ephesios inquit: Credentes secundum efficaciam potentiae roboris eius, quam poten- tiam effecit per Christum excitans eum a mor- tuis, id est, Deus efficax est in conversione, et fide vivificat et liberat ex morte, confirmat assen- sionem in corde, et constantiam in confessione.

## 1:7
The Spirit of love etc.

Previously he named the powerful Spirit, so that with an illustrious term he might tax sloth and hypocrisy. For he understands true motions, by which we are vivified in terrors, and are aroused to invocation, and are confirmed in confession and in all the dangers and labors of the ministry against devils and their instruments. Now he names the Spirit of love. For just as he spoke before of our vivification, so now he speaks of virtues toward others.

Although the term Love is otherwise used in other ways, yet here it embraces love toward God and toward men on account of God, as when it is said in Romans 13: Love is the fulfilling of the law. And it signifies that by the Holy Spirit love toward God is kindled, that is, fervor and zeal in the preservation of doctrine, invocation, thanksgiving, and joy in God, patience in the cross and confession. Then toward men it signifies a love of concord, care to avoid hatreds and the seeds of dissensions, the repression of pride and the desire for vengeance, to admonish and hear others calmly. Finally, let the declaration of love be taken from the Decalogue itself. And the Holy Spirit is given, so that he may kindle motions consistent with the divine law. And he himself is such as the motions described in the law.

However, as often as it is spoken of our love toward God, let the hearers know that it is necessary for faith to precede love, and the sense of God's love toward us, because the heart does not approach God unless it rests in the mediator by faith, and determines that God is reconciled, as is said to the Ephesians 4: Through him we have access to God by faith. When this happens, consolation is felt, which is the recognition of the love of God toward us, of which it is said to the Romans 15: The love of God is poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, that is, we feel that we are loved by God.

And to Romans 8: You have received the spirit of adoption of sons, by which we cry Abba Father. Likewise in Zechariah chapter 12: I will pour out upon the house of David the spirit of grace and of supplications. He is named the Spirit of grace, by which we feel that we are in grace, in true consolation, in the struggle of repentance. When this consolation is in us, in turn our love toward God is begun, and invocation, thanksgiving, joy in God, patience in the cross follow: because the Prophet has encompassed these interior acts of worship under the name of invocation. This consideration concerning the term of love and concerning faith shining before is very necessary.

The Spirit of modesty.

Consider the restriction, the powerful or strong Spirit is sharp, he conducts difficult business, and approaches great dangers. But yet the saints look to the goals, they are not carried beyond their calling, like many who, first burning with the spirit, did useful things, afterwards being puffed up by prosperous affairs, attempted some things outside their calling, when indeed they thought they were doing right, which afterwards had sad outcomes, such as Samson, Josiah, and others.

Profane histories have innumerable examples, because leaders who do not know God are not restrained by the Holy Spirit, such as Hercules, Themistocles, Pausanias, Marius, Pompey, Julius. Of all these the voice was true: He puts down the mighty from their seat. Likewise, 1 Peter 5: God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. These examples of warriors strike the eyes more.

Then, however they may be considered, let the examples of those ruling the Churches be considered. Many by a certain zeal of their own did many things rightly, afterwards by self-confidence they either invented dogmas, or moved other things outside their calling, as Gregory instituted many things, and Bishops often under the pretext of religion moved seditions, and many at all times by a certain foolish zeal, under the pretext of religion, wish to establish new polities. Concerning all such he says to the Romans chapter 12: Be wise, but unto modesty, that is, remain within the word and the calling. And 2 Peter 1: In faith into virtue, in faith into knowledge, that is, let faith not be slothful, but let it be ardent, yet let it burn with judgment and discernment.

Thus because in this place he added the restriction, God has given us a strong spirit, but yet one that moderates impulses, and restrains minds, lest being puffed up they invent dogmas, or new forms of worship, lest they be trumpets of seditions, lest they tear the Church apart with logomachies or other unnecessary quarrels. Thus, against foolish zeal, against pride, against the desire for revenge, against polypragmosynen, and against petulance, he names the spirit of modesty, that is, the spirit that restrains and moderates disordered impulses.

Moreover, it is known that in apostolic discourse the term sophrosynes encompasses modesty, temperance, and chastity. Likewise, since mention has been made of the virtues which are kindled in the converted by the Holy Spirit, the admonition concerning the doctrine of justification must be repeated. Although it is most certain that the Holy Spirit is in the converted, whom the Father and the Son breathe into their hearts, and obedience has been begun in them: nevertheless, they must establish that they are not righteous by that newness, that is, having the remission of sins and being accepted for eternal life, but on account of the mediator the Son of God, by whose merit the wrath of God is appeased, and who is the perpetual intercessor, whose merits are given to us, so that righteousness is imputed to us. This mediator must be apprehended by faith, and this perpetual consolation must be retained, that on account of this mediator we are pleasing, not on account of our newness, with which there is still much filth, according to the saying of Psalm 143: No one living shall be justified in your sight, namely by their own dignity or qualities, but being justified by faith we have peace.

But as for what some say, that we are righteous by the indwelling of the divinity, it must be known that the indwelling is the effectuation of newness. This effectuation happens in such a way when the heart first apprehends the remission of sins and consolation, looking upon the mediator the Son of God, and establishing that you have remission on account of that mediator, and are righteous, that is, pleasing to God, not on account of the effectuation of newness or the newness itself. Thus the true proposition remains: the converted Paul has the remission of sins, and is righteous, that is, accepted by God on account of the merit of Christ, or on account of the propitiator by faith alone, according to that: Whom he set forth as a propitiator through faith, by his blood. Let this consolation always be in sight, by which, when hearts are ruled, at the same time vivification occurs, and that which is said in John chapter fourteen: We will come to him, and make our abode with him. Consolation must, however, be distinguished from newness, because in the true struggle we perceive our sins and the wrath of God, nor can righteousness rely on our newness, according to those sayings of Exodus 34: Before you, the innocent is not innocent. Likewise Job 9: I know truly that a man is not righteous before God.

Therefore, let not the testimony of our Lord shame you. He said that the spirit given is not one of timidity, but one effective in consolation and constant in confession. Now he adds an exhortation as a consequence. Therefore, be constant in confession, let not the testimony, that is, the confession, shame you, do not be broken by the appearance of the cross, and conversely by the authority and wisdom of the adversaries, just as he says elsewhere in 1 Corinthians 9: I am not ashamed of the Gospel. As it is manifest that for a moderate nature it is a huge pain to stand among the few and despised, and to seem to oppose foolishly or petulantly the greatest men, who excel in wisdom, virtue, and authority, and judgments, and to disturb the public state, to be called a torch of seditions, a trumpet of wars. Against this temptation Isaiah says in chapter 59: Do not fear the reproaches of men.

Endure evils with the Gospel according to the power of God, who made us safe, etc. Afterwards he inserts the often-repeated saying: By the works of the law shall no flesh be justified before God. He affirms that our works are by no means the cause or merit of the remission of sins or of reconciliation, but says that we are saved and called according to the purpose of God and grace. Understand grace as the gratuitous mercy of God toward us promised on account of the Son, just as he speaks most often in Romans 5: Much more does grace and the gift abound through grace or in grace. Where grace signifies relatively gratuitous acceptance, but the gift signifies the donation of the Holy Spirit, new and eternal righteousness and life. For it embraces the entire benefits, nor does the Son of God take away sins only in such a way that he does not impute them, and yet nature remains in these filthinesses and in death, but he takes them away in reality, when he restores eternal life.

Latin:

Spiritum dilectionis etc.

Antea nominavit Spiritum potentem, ut il- lustri vocabulo ignaviam et hypocrisin taxaret. Intelligit enim veros motus, quibus vivificamur in pavoribus, et exuscitamur ad invocationem, et confirmamur in confessione et in omnibus pericu- lis et laboribus ministerii contra diabolos et eo- rum organa. Nunc nominat Spiritum dilectionis. Ut enim prius de vivificatione nostri dixit, ita iam de virtutibus erga alios loquitur.

Etsi autem vocabulum Dilectionis alias aliter usurpatur, tamen hic complectitur dilectionem erga Deum et erga homines propter Deum, ut cum dicitur Roman. 13.: Dilectio est impletio le- gis. Et significat Spiritu sancto accendi dilectio- nem erga Deum, id est, feruorem et zelum in conservatione doctrinae, invocationem, gratia- rum actionem, et laetitiam in Deo, patientiam in cruce et confessione. Deinde erga homines signi- ficat amorem concordiae, curam vitandi odia et semina dissidiorum, repressionem superbiae et cupiditatis vindictae, placide monere et audire alios. Denique sumatur declaratio dilectionis ex ipso Decalogo. Ac datur Spiritus sanctus, ut ac- cendat motus congruentes legi divinae. Et talis est ipse, quales motus in lege describuntur.

Quoties autem dicitur de dilectione nostra erga Deum, sciant auditores oportere dilectioni fidem antecedere, et sensum dilectionis Dei erga nos, quia cor non accedit ad Deum, nisi fide acquiescat in mediatore, et statuat Deum recon- ciliatum esse, ut dicitur ad Ephesios 4.: Per hunc habemus accessum ad Deum fide. Hoc cum fit, sentitur consolatio, quae est agnitio dilectionis Dei erga nos, de qua dicitur ad Romanos 15.: Dilectio Dei effusa est in corda nostra per Spiri- tum sanctum, id est, sentimus nos diligi a Deo.

Et ad Roman. 8.: Accepistis spiritum adoptionis filiorum, quo clamamus Abba pater. Item apud Zachariam capite 12.: Effundam super domum David spiritum gratiae et precum. Nominatur Spiritus gratiae, quo sentimus nos esse in gratia, in vera consolatione, in lucta poenitentiae. Haec consolatio cum sit in nobis, vicissim incoatur di- lectio nostra erga Deum, et sequuntur invocatio, gratiarum actio, laetitia in Deo, patientia in cruce: quia hos interiores cultus Propheta com- plexus est nomine invocationis. Haec considera- tio de vocabulo dilectionis et de fide praelucente valde necessaria est.

Spiritum modestiae.

Considera restrictionem, Spiritus potens seu fortis est acer, agit negotia difficilia, et adit ma- gna pericula. Sed tamen sancti prospiciunt me- tas, non evehuntur extra vocationem, sicut multi, qui primum spiritu ardentes egerunt res utiles, postea elati rebus secundis tentarunt aliqua extra vocationem, cum quidem existimarent se recte fa- cere, quae postea exitus tristes habuerunt, ut Samson, Iosias et alii.

Historiae prophanae habent innumerabilia exempla, quia duces ignorantes Deum non fre- nantur Spiritu sancto, ut Hercules, Themisto- cles, Pausanias, Marius, Pompeius, Iulius. De his omnibus vera fuit vox: Deponit potentes de sede. Item, 1. Petri 5.: Superbis Deus resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam. Haec bellatorum exempla magis incurrunt in oculos.

Inde utcunque considerentur exempla regen- tium Ecclesias. Multi suo quodam zelo multa recte fecerunt, postea fiducia sui vel dogmata fin- xerunt, vel alias res extra vocationem moverunt, ut Gregorius multa instituit, et Episcopi saepe praetextu religionis moverunt seditiones, et multi omnibus temporibus quodam stulto zelo, prae- textu religionis volunt constituere novas politias. De talibus omnibus dicit ad Romanos capite 12.: Sapite, sed ad modestiam, id est, manete intra verbum et vocationem. Et 2. Petri 1.: In fide in virtutem, in fide in scientiam, id est, fides non sit ignava, sed sit ardens, ardeat autem cum iu- dicio et delectu.

Ita quia hoc loco addidit restrictionem, Deus nobis dedit spiritum fortem, sed tamen impetus moderantem, et compescentem animos, ne elati dogmata fingant, aut novos cultus, ne sint tubae seditionum, ne Ecclesiam dilacerent λογομαχίαις aut aliis non necessariis rixis. Ita contra stultum zelum, contra superbiam, contra cupiditatem vindictae, contra πολυπραγμοσύνην, et contra petulantiam nominat spiritum modestiae, id est, spiritum compescentem et moderantem inordina- tos impetus.

Caeterum notum est in sermone apostolico vocabulo σωφροσύνης comprehendi modestiam, temperantiam et castitatem. Item cum dictum sit de virtutibus, quae in conversis accenduntur a Spiritu sancto, repetenda est et admonitio de do- ctrina iustificationis. Quanquam in conversis certissimum est esse Spiritum sanctum, quem pa- ter et filius in corde eorum spirant, et obedien- tia in eis incoata est: tamen statuere debent, se non illa novitate iustos esse, id est, habentes re- missionem peccatorum, et acceptos esse ad vi- tam aeternam, sed propter mediatorem filium Dei, cuius merito placata est ira Dei, et qui est perpetuus intercessor, cuius merita nobis donan- tur, ut imputetur nobis iusticia. Hunc mediato- rem fide apprehendi oportet, et retineri hanc per- petuam consolationem, quod propter hunc me- diatorem placeamus, non propter nostram novi- tatem, cum qua multum adhuc sordium est, iuxta dictum Psalmi 143.: Non iustificabitur in con- spectu tuo omnis vivens, scilicet propria digni- tate seu qualitatibus, sed iustificati fide pacem habemus.

Quod autem aliqui dicunt, nos esse iustos inhabitatione divinitatis, sciendum est, inhabi- tationem esse effectionem novitatis. Haec effectio ita fit, cum cor prius apprehendit remissionem peccatorum et consolationem, intuens in media- torem Filium Dei, et statuens te propter illum mediatorem habere remissionem, et iustum esse, id est, placentem Deo, non propter effectionem novitatis aut novitatem. Ita manet vera proposi- tio: Paulus conversus habet remissionem pecca- torum, et est iustus, id est, acceptus Deo pro- pter meritum Christi, seu propter propiciatorem sola fide, iuxta illud: Quem posuit propiciato- rem per fidem, per sanguinem eius. Haec con- solatio semper sit in conspectu, qua cum regun- tur corda, simul fit vivificatio, et illud quod di- citur Iohannis decimo quarto: Veniemus ad eum, et mansionem apud eum faciemus. Discernenda tamen est consolatio a novitate, quia in vero agone cernimus nostra peccata, et iram Dei, nec potest niti iusticia, nostra novitate, iuxta illa di- cta Exodi 34.: Coram te innocens non est inno- cens. Item Iob. nono: Vere scio, quod non sit iustus homo coram Deo.

Ne igitur te pudeat testimonii Domini nostri. Dixit datum esse spiritum non timiditatis, sed efficacem in consolatione, et constantem in confessione. Nunc addit adhortationem tanquam consequens. Ergo esto constans in confessione, non pudeat te testimonii, id est, confessionis, non frangaris specie crucis, et econtra autoritate et sapientia adversantium, sicut alibi inquit 1 Co- rinth. 9.: Non pudet me Evangelii. Sicut ma- nifestum est, moderatae naturae ingentem dolo- rem esse, stare inter paucos et spretos, et videri stulte aut petulanter adversari summorum homi- num, qui antecellunt sapientia, virtute et auto- ritate, iudiciis, et turbare publicum statum, dici facem seditionum, tubam bellorum esse. Adver- sus hanc tentationem Esaias inquit capite 59.: Ne timete probra hominum.

Sustineas mala cum Evangelio secundum poten- tiam Dei, qui fecit nos salvos etc. Postea inserit saepe repetitum dictum: Ex operibus legis non iustificabitur omnis caro co- ram Deo. Affirmat nostra opera nequaquam esse causam vel meritum remissionis peccatorum seu reconciliationis, sed dicit nos secundum proposi- tum Dei et gratiam salvari et vocari. Intellige gratiam gratuitam misericordiam Dei erga nos promissam propter filium, sicut saepissime loqui- tur Roma 5.: Multo magis exuberat gratia et do- num per gratiam vel in gratia. Ubi gratia signifi- cat relative gratuitam acceptationem, donum vero significat donationem Spiritus sancti, novam et aeternam iusticiam et vitam. Complectitur enim integra beneficia, nec filius Dei sic tantum aufert peccata, ut non im- putet, et tamen natura maneat in his sordibus et in morte, sed reipsa aufert, cum restituit vitam aeternam.

## 1:12
I know whom I have believed, etc.

Here, disputes are raised concerning doubt, whether the converted ought to remain in doubt as to whether he has the remission of sins, and whether he is in grace? Here it must be answered plainly: Although Although doubt naturally clings to men, yet it is a most certain doctrine, and a clear voice of the Gospel, that those who have been converted ought to overcome doubt, and to establish that they have the remission of sins, and are in grace. For the promises were delivered by God for this reason, that natural doubt might be removed, and to one not believing or remaining in doubt, the promise is a vain sound. Therefore Paul says to the Romans in the fourth chapter: Therefore it is of faith, that it might be by grace, to the end the promise might be sure. This faith is opposed to doubt, according to that in the fifth chapter of Romans: Being justified by faith we have peace and access to God. And although trepidation is felt, yet let hearts know the saying in Mark chapter nine: I believe Lord, but help my unbelief. Thus let us also ask to be confirmed, according to that: How much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask. And let this faith look upon the promise, and grow in invocation. When this is done, the consolation itself in us is a testimony, by which we recognize that we are freed from eternal death, concerning which consolation Paul says in the eighth chapter of Romans: You have received the Spirit crying Abba Father. This Spirit gives testimony to our spirit, that we are the children of God. And to this effect Augustine says: He who believes knows that he believes. It is true, however, that the Prophets and Apostles had singular testimonies, which even if they were given to them because of their ministry and because of the hearers, yet they also confirm them privately, and yet their faith relied not on those gifts and miracles, but on the mercy promised because of the Son of God. Monks seek this certainty not in the promise, but in their own qualities, where when they find impurity, they command one to remain in doubt. On the contrary, however, it must be known that faith looks upon the promise, not our qualities, just as it was rightly said by Augustine: The certainty of all confidence ought to be in the precious blood of Christ.

Latin:

Scio cui credidi etc.

Hic moventur disputationes de dubitatione, An conversus debeat manere in dubitatione, utrum habeat remissionem peccatorum, et an sit in gra- tia? Hic plane respondendum est: Quanquam naturaliter haeret in hominibus dubitatio, tamen certissima doctrina est, et vox Evangelii perspi- cua, conversos oportere vincere dubitationem, et statuere quod habeant remissionem peccatorum, et sint in gratia. Ideo enim promissiones divinitus traditae sunt, ut naturalis dubitatio tollatur, et non cre- denti seu manenti in dubitatione promissio inanis sonitus est. Ideo Paulus inquit ad Romanos ca- pite quarto: Ideo ex fide Gratis, ut sit firma pro- missio. Haec fides opposita est dubitationi, iuxta illud ad Romanos capite quinto: Iustificati fide pacem habemus et accessum ad Deum. Quan- quam autem sentitur trepidatio, tamen sciant corda dictum in Marco capite nono: Credo Do- mine, sed opem fer diffidentiae meae. Sic peta- mus et nos confirmari, iuxta illud: Quanto ma- gis dabit pater coelestis Spiritum sanctum peten- tibus. Et haec fides intueatur promissionem, et crescat in invocatione. Hoc cum fit, consolatio ipsa in nobis est testimonium, quo agnoscimus nos liberari ex morte aeterna, de qua consolatione inquit Paulus ad Romanos capite octavo: Acce- pistis Spiritum clamantem Abba pater. Hic spi- ritus dat testimonium spiritui nostro, quod si- mus filii Dei. Et in hanc sententiam ait Augu- stinus: Credens scit se credere. Verum est autem, Prophetas et Apostolos habuisse singularia testimonia, quae etiamsi pro- pter ministerium et propter auditores ipsis data sunt, tamen etiam ipsos privatim confirmant, et tamen ipsorum fides nitebatur non illis donis et miraculis, sed misericordia propter filium Dei promissa. Quaerunt monachi hanc certitudinem non in promissione, sed in qualitatibus suis ubi cum inveniant immunditiem, iubent manere in dubitatione. Contra vero sciendum est, fidem intueri promissionem, non qualitates nostras, sicut recte dictum est ab Augustino: Totius fidu- ciae certitudo esse debet in pretioso sanguine Christi.

## 1:13
Hold fast the form of sound words.

He repeats the commandment concerning preserving the purity of doctrine, which is very often recited in divine assemblies. And the sum is comprised in this saying: If anyone shall have taught another Gospel, let him be anathema. Paul used a singular word here: Hold fast the form of sound words, that is, which was previously delineated for you. He wishes both the things themselves to be held fast, and the modes of speaking to be clear, and customary to the Prophets and Apostles. For although he does not superstitiously demand that the same words be recited everywhere: yet he wishes ambiguities and logomachias to be avoided.

He exaggerates the commandment, however, when he orders the doctrine to be guarded as a precious deposit. It is established, however, that in guarding a deposit, good faith is most strictly required. Nor does he add in vain: that he may guard through the Holy Spirit. He wishes the hearers not to indulge in reason seeking cavils against things rightly delivered, he wishes hearts to be confirmed by the invocation of God, so that they may be firm in holding fast to things rightly delivered. Many, indulging in their own speculations, and having a zeal for contradicting, cast out the Holy Spirit, such as he names here, certain ones, Phygellus and Hermogenes and the rest. He commands, therefore, to the Corinthians, 2 Cor. 10, that thoughts be brought into captivity to Christ.

Latin:

Formam retineto sanorum verborum.

Repetit praeceptum de conservanda puritate doctrinae, quod saepissime in divinis concioni- bus recitatur. Et summa comprehensa est in hoc dicto: Si quis aliud Evangelium docuerit, ana- thema sit. Usus est autem Paulus hic singulari verbo: Retineas formam sanorum verborum, id est, quae tibi antea delineata est. Vult et res ipsas retineri, et modos loquendi perspicuos, et usitatos Prophetis et Apostolis. Quanquam enim non superstitiose postulat ubique eadem verba recitari: tamen vult vitari ambiguitates et λογομαχίας.

Exaggerat autem praeceptum, cum iubet custodiri doctrinam tanquam praeclarum depositum. Constat autem in custodiendo deposito severissime postulari bonam fidem. Nec frustra addit: ut custodiat per Spiritum sanctum. Vult non indulgere auditores rationi quaerenti cavillationes contra recte tradita, vult invocatione Dei confirmari corda, ut sint firma in retinendis recte traditis. Multi indulgentes suis speculationibus, et habentes studium contradicendi excutiunt Spiritum sanctum, quales hic nominat quosdam, Phigellum et Hermogenem et reliquos. Praecipit igitur ad Corinthios 2. Corinth. 10. redigi mentes in captivitatem Christo.

## 1:16
May he grant mercy to the house.

The examples which Paul recounts here are not to be passed over, the first of which is concerning Apostates or corrupters of doctrine, because it reminds us of the snares of the devil, and of our own infirmity. For since these have failed, who were familiar to the Apostles, and were spectators of miracles, what will happen afterwards? Let us therefore be terrified and let us pray to be confirmed, and let us remember those sayings of Luke 12: The devil has demanded you, that he might sift you as wheat, but I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail.

The other example is of a man beneficent toward the Church, concerning which kind of alms there exist commandments, promises, reminders, and examples, all of which are known. Genesis 12: I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse those who curse you. And Deuteronomy thirty-third: Your doctrine from your holy man. Who says to father and mother, to wife and children, I do not know you, these will be the keepers of my law. I will bless your burnt offering, those who hate him will not rise up. You see more members. The first binds the priests to a certain kind of doctrine delivered by divine testimonies through the Prophets, Christ, and the Apostles. Afterwards he adds a commandment, what kind of teachers he wishes them to be, namely, of such strength of faith, that they prefer the confession of faith to life. Afterwards he adds the promise that he will hear this priesthood divinely ordained. Finally, he threatens the enemies of this priesthood in Sirach chapter seven: Fear the Lord and honor the priests, and give them their portion. Proverbs chapter three: Honor the Lord with the first fruits of your produce, and your barns will be filled with abundance, and your wine presses with wine. And Matthew chapter ten: Whoever gives a drink of cold water to one of the least of mine for the sake of doctrine, Amen I say to you, he shall not lose his reward. First Corinthians chapter nine: No one serves as a soldier at his own expense. And 2 Corinthians 9: He who gives seed to the sower will increase your seed.

Let examples also be considered: God did good to the Egyptian midwives, who refused to kill the Hebrew infants. He returned thanks for the hospitality of Obadiah, who had hidden the Prophets in caves against Jezebel, 1 Kings 9. Likewise Abdemelech, who did good to Jeremiah, as is narrated in Jeremiah 39. And in this place Paul prays well for the family of Onesiphorus, and below he gives thanks to Philemon for his benefits toward the Church, and indeed he used the sweetest words: The hearts of the saints are refreshed through you, that is, in great dangers and sorrows they have defense and hospitality with you, so that dangers are warded off and sorrows are alleviated by your services, in which there is nothing feigned. Therefore, in turn, the saints rest with the sincere joy of the heart without fear and suspicions.

Now these precepts, promises, threats, and examples teach first that we also ought to be obliging in this kind. Second, it consoles the beneficent, so that they in turn may expect help from God. Third, they signify that hospitality is not lacking to the Church in this life, and what kind it is, namely: rare among the highest princes, but more frequent among those of moderate status, such as were Obadiah, Abdemelech, Sergius, Onesiphorus, Philemon, and others like them.

Latin:

Det misericordiam domui.

Non praetereunda sunt hic exempla, quae hic recenset Paulus, quorum prius est de Apostatis vel corruptoribus doctrinae, quod commonefaciat nos de insidiis diaboli, et de nostra infirmitate. Cum enim hi defecerint, qui familiares fuerunt Apostolis, et spectatores fuerunt miraculorum, quid postea fiet? Expavescamus igitur et oremus nos confirmari, ac meminerimus illa dicta Lucae 12.: Diabolus depoposcit vos, ut cribraret vos tanquam triticum, veruntamen ego rogavi pro te, ne deficiat fides tua Petre.

Alterum exemplum est hominis benefici erga Ecclesiam, de quo genere eleemosynae extant praecepta, promissiones, commonefactiones et exempla, quae omnia nota sunt. Genesis 12.: Benedicam benedicentibus tibi, et maledicam maledicentibus tibi. Et Deuteronom. trigesimo tertio: Doctrina tua a viro sancto tuo. Qui dicit patri et matri uxori et liberis, nescio vos, hi erunt custodes legis meae. Benedicam holocausto tuo, Qui oderunt eum, non consurgent. Vides plura membra. Primum alligat sacerdotes ad certum genus doctrinae divinis testimoniis traditum per Prophetas, Christum et Apostolos. Postea addit praeceptum, quales esse velit doctores, videlicet, tali robore fidei, ut anteferant confes- sionem vitae. Postea addit promissionem quod sit exauditurus hoc sacerdotium divinitùs ordina- tum. Postremo minatur hostibus huius sacer- dotii Syrach capite septimo: Time Dominum et honore afficito sacerdotes, et des eis partem eo- rum. Proverbiorum tertio: Honora Dominum de primitiis frugum tuarum, et replebuntur hor- rea tua abundantia, et vino torcularia tua. Et Matthaei capite decimo: Qui dederit potum aquae frigidae uni ex minimis meorum propter doctri- nam, Amen dico vobis, non perdet mercedem suam. Primae Corinth. nono: Nemo militat suis stipendiis. Et 2. Corinth. 9.: Qui dat se- men seminanti, augebit semen vestrum.

Considerentur et exempla: Deus benefecit obstetricibus Aegyptiis, quae noluerunt interfi- cere infantes Hebraeos. Reddidit gratiam hospi- tii Abdiae, qui abdiderat Prophetas in specubus contra Iesabel, 1. Reg. 9. Item Abdemelech, qui benefecit Ieremiae, ut narratur Ieremiae 39. Et hoc loco Paulus bene precatur Onesiphori fa- miliae, et infra agit gratias Philemoni propter be- neficia erga Ecclesiam, et quidem dulcissimis ver- bis usus est: Viscera sanctorum per te reficiun- tur, id est, in magnis periculis et doloribus ha- bent defensionem, et hospitium apud te, ita ut pericula depellantur, et leniantur dolores tuis of- ficiis, in quibus nihil est fucatum. Vicissim igi- tur acquiescunt sancti sincera laetitia cordis sine metu et suspicionibus.

Iam haec praecepta, promissiones, commi- nationes et exempla primum docent, nos quoque debere in hoc genere officiosos esse. Secundo consolatur beneficos, ut vicissim expectent auxi- lium a Deo. Tertio significant Ecclesiae non deesse hospitia in hac vita, et qualia sint, videli- cet: rara apud summos principes, sed frequen- tiora apud mediocres, quales fuerunt Abdias, Abdemelech, Sergius, Onesiphorus, Philemon et alii similes.

## 2:1 Argument
Chapter II.

In the second chapter at the beginning there stands again a testimony of ordination, that God wills the ministers of the Gospel to be chosen through the Church, and approves the election of these. Wherefore without any doubt the ministry of these is effective, according to the saying in Romans 1: The Gospel is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes,

Then he warns what kind he wishes to be chosen, where by name he demands two virtues, the ability to teach, and faithfulness, that is, assiduity and constancy in the truth. But when mention is made of the ability to teach, it is manifest that many things are comprehended. Thus above he commands one to be chosen who is διδακτικόν. Likewise to Titus chapter 1 he commands such a one to be chosen who can refute adversaries. For these difficult works it is necessary for the younger to be prepared by learning. By such sayings all are commanded, and the studies of doctrine are approved. Erected by this consolation, let us learn more willingly and bear the common difficulties of our order, and let us expect help and defense from God. According to that 1 Corinthians 15: Your labor is not in vain in the Lord.

No one serving as a soldier entangles himself in the affairs of a livelihood etc.

The simile is taken from soldiers, who cannot stay at home to manage a household, nor wander about for the sake of business, but the soldier serves entirely in his function: Thus he wants the minister of the Gospel to serve entirely in his own vocation, and not to thrust himself into others, into political governance. Let not the minister of the Gospel have one foot in the temple, the other in the court. And Peter says 1 Peter 4: Do not be ἀλλοτριοεπίσκοποι. Likewise 1 Thessalonians 4: In this be φιλότιμοι, that you may be quiet, and do your own things.

The laboring farmer must be the first to partake of his own labors etc.

God wills the understanding of justice and other virtues to shine in men, so that we may recognize him for what he is, and distinguish him from evil natures. But since he is good and preserves his creatures, he is also equal, good to the good, that is, preserving the good, and punishing the bad. This equality in him is called justice. And he teaches us also that justice is equality, and he demands it from us. Therefore he instituted this order, that man should preserve equality toward men, not harm others, give things for things, reward for labor. Concerning this equality speak the sayings in Leviticus 19: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another. Luke 10: The laborer is worthy of his reward. Such is equality, that he who has cultivated a field with his own labor should enjoy the things growing there.

But since Paul previously commanded that teachers should not be entangled in the affairs of a livelihood, which hinder their duty, soon he adds a response to that question which could be posed: Whence then shall those who teach live? He answers with a proposed simile: Let the farmer enjoy his own labor, so let those who teach have their sustenance from the contribution of the Church. This precept is often repeated, but because Paul adds the admonition: Consider what I say, may the Lord give you understanding in all things, he signifies that he is speaking not only of bodily reward, but also of the increase of gifts, which God increases for those who teach faithfully. As the farmer first enjoys his own labor, so the faithful teacher first perceives the rewards of his labor, God will kindle in him greater light, greater strength of faith, and other gifts, because he teaches faithfully, just as the parable about the merchants teaches, Luke 19: To him who has it will be given, and from him who has not, even that which he has will be taken away.

Present yourself as a minister rightly dividing the word of truth etc.

I think the metaphor is taken from the division of members in victims, which it was not permitted to divide rashly, but the breast and the shoulders had to be cut away from the fat, and given to the priests, who lived from them: The fat, the kidneys, the tail were burned. And the law applied a reason not only of signification, but also of utility, for it attributed to the priests those parts which are more fleshy, the rest were burned. The tail signified that all actions must be referred to God as to the end. The fat or suet signified that all things are watered by God. The kidneys signified that carnal affections must be burned.

From that art of cutting the victim, therefore, he takes the simile, when he commands the word of God to be rightly cut. He embraces, however, the entire diligence of teaching rightly, and because in teaching there is great power in divisions and definitions: it is necessary for the teacher to hold the order of the members of the whole doctrine rightly distributed, as it is manifest that horrible confusions follow when the kinds of doctrines, of Law and Gospel, of spiritual and political doctrine, are not rightly mixed. Let the teacher also accustom the hearers, so that he himself may also be able to comprehend the entire body of doctrine with his mind, and see the series of members, the beginnings, the progressions, and the outcomes. This sentence also testifies that the studies of learners please God, because no one can teach rightly unless he has learned, just as also above 1 Tim. 4.

he admonishes, saying: Attend to reading, to consolation and to doctrine.

Avoid profane empty talk.

Gangrene is a word made from the verb grainein, which means to gnaw away. It is, however, an evil more savage than a cancer, burning and gnawing away flesh and bones, so that they are immediately reduced as if to ash. But unless the member is quickly cut off, it kills the man.

By this image he signifies that impious dogmas both spread quickly and widely, and are very pernicious. In which matter not only the vanity and levity of human nature must be recognized and deplored, which delights in lies, but also the malice and power of the devils must be considered, who freely, without any inconvenience to themselves, scatter and confirm foul frenzies, only so that they may afflict God with insult, and destroy men out of hatred for Christ.

Let us also shudder thinking about the power, of which it was said in Luke 22: Satan entered into him. And the ethnic idols of all times of the world, the Bacchanalia, human victims, and other frenzies, are testimonies of his power, and among those who wish to be named the Church of God, there have always been many foul delusions.

Even times near to the apostolic ones had most shameful sects, defiled by abominable opinions and confusions of lusts. These examples must be considered, so that we may be mindful of the most grave admonitions of Matt. 26: Pray, that you may not enter into temptation. Likewise 1 Peter last: The devil as a roaring lion goes about, seeking whom he may devour. Let the thought of dangers excite in us fear and invocation, lest we be oppressed while idle, secure, drunk, or by pleasures, or by ambition, or by other desires, and let faith oppose to the power of the devils the power of Christ, who says John 10: No one shall snatch my sheep from my hands. Likewise 1 John 3: The son of God appeared, that he might destroy the works of the devil. Likewise Gen. 3: The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent.

This also must be considered, that Paul says those fascinated by the devil fall little by little into greater impiety, just as he says elsewhere, Rom. 1: He gave them up to a reprobate mind.

Latin:

Caput II.

In secundo capite initio rursus testimonium extat ordinationis, velle Deum eligi ministros Evangelii per Ecclesiam, et approbare horum electionem. Quare sine ulla dubitatione horum ministerio est efficax, iuxta dictum Rom. 1.: Evangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti,

Deinde monet, quales eligi velit, ubi nominatim duas virtutes flagitat, facultatem docendi, et fidelitatem, id est, assiduitatem et constantiam in veritate. Cum autem fit mentio facultatis docendi, manifestum est multa comprehendi. Ita supra iubet eligi διδακτικόν. Item ad Titum caput 1. iubet eligi talem, qui possit refutare adversarios. Ad haec difficilia opera necesse est iuniores discendo praeparari. Talibus dictis omnibus praecipiuntur, et approbantur studia doctrinae. Hac erecti consolatione libentius discamus et feramus communes difficultates nostri ordinis, et expectemus auxilium et defensionem a Deo. Iuxta illud 1. Corinth. 15.: Non est inanis labor vester in Domino.

Nemo militans implicat se negotiis victus etc.

Similitudo sumta est a militibus, qui non possunt domi manere, ut regant oeconomiam, neque vagari negociationum causa, sed miles totus servit suae functioni: Ita vult ministrum Evangelii totum servire propriae vocationi, et non ingerere se in alienas, in gubernationem politicam. Non habeat minister Evangelii alterum pedem in templo, alterum in curia. Et Petrus inquit 1. Petri 4.: Non sitis ἀλλοτριοεπίσκοποι. Item 1. Thess. 4.: In hoc sitis φιλότιμοι, ut sitis quieti, et propria agatis.

Laborantem agricolam oportet primum suorum laborum participem esse etc.

Vult Deus intellectum iusticiae et aliarum virtutum in hominibus lucere, ut agnoscamus ipsum qualis sit, et discernamus eum a malis naturis. Cum autem sit bonus et servans creaturas, est etiam aequalis, bonus bonis, id est, servans bonos, et puniens malos. Haec in eo aequalitas nominatur iusticia. Ac docet nos quoque iusticiam esse aequalitatem, et eam a nobis flagitat. Hunc igitur ordinem instituit, ut homo servet aequalitatem erga homines, non noceat aliis, det res pro rebus, pro labore mercedem. De hac aequalitate loquuntur dicta Levit. 19.: Diligas proximum sicut teipsum. Quod tibi non vis fieri, alteri ne feceris. Lucae 10.: Dignus est operarius mercede. Talis est aequalitas, ut is qui suo labore coluit agrum, fruatur rebus ibi nascentibus.

Cum autem Paulus antea praeceperit, ne implicentur doctores negotiis victus, quae im- pediunt officium, mox addit responsionem ad eam quaestionem, quae opponi poterat: Unde igitur vivent docentes? Respondet proposita similitu- dine: Agricola fruatur suo labore, ita docentes victum habeant ex collatione Ecclesiae. Hoc prae- ceptum saepe repetitum est, quia vero addit Pau- lus admonitionem: Considera quod dico, det tibi Dominus intellectum in omnibus, significat non tantum loqui se de mercede corporali, sed etiam de incremento donorum, quae fideliter do- centibus auget Deus. Ut agricola primum frui- tur suo labore, sic doctor fidelis primum perci- piet sui laboris praemia, accendet Deus in ipso maiorem lucem, maius robur fidei, et alia dona, quia fideliter docet, sicut parabola de negocian- tibus docet, Lucae 19.: Habenti dabitur, et a non habente etiam id quod habet auferetur.

Praesta te ministrum recte secantem sermonem veritatis etc.

Existimo sumtam esse metaphoram a divi- sione membrorum in victimis, quas non licuit temere partiri, sed pectus et harmos oportuit abscindi ab adipe, et dari sacerdotibus, qui inde victitabant: Adeps, renes, cauda cremabantur. Et lex non solum significationis, sed etiam uti- litatis rationem adhibuit, attribuit enim eas partes sacerdotibus, quae sunt magis carnosae, reliqua comburebantur. Cauda significabat omnes actio- nes referendas esse ad Deum tanquam ad finem. Adeps seu pinguedo significabat rigari omnia a Deo. Renes significabant carnales affectus esse cremandos.

Ab illa igitur arte secandi victimam sumit similitudinem, cum iubet recte secari verbum Dei. Complectitur autem universam diligentiam recte docendi, et quia in docendo divisionum et definitionum magna vis est: doctorem tenere ne- cesse est ordinem membrorum totius doctrinae recte distributum, ut manifestum est, horrendas confusiones sequi, quando non recte miscentur genera doctrinarum, Legis et Evangelii, doctri- nae spiritualis et politicae. Assuefaciat etiam do- ctor auditores, ut ipse quoque integrum doctri- nae corpus mente comprehendere possint, et vi- deant seriem membrorum, initia, progressiones et exitus. Haec sententia etiam testatur placere Deo studia discentium, quia nemo potest recte docere nisi didicerit, sicut et supra 1. Tim. 4.

monet, inquiens: Attendite lectioni, consola- tioni et doctrinae.

Prophanas verborum inanitates vitato.

Gangraena vocabulum est factum a verbo γραίνειν, quod significat arrodere. Est autem malum saevius cancro, urens et arrodens carnem et ossa, ut statim velut in cinerem redigantur. At nisi membrum cito praecidatur, occidit ho- minem.

Hac imagine significat impia dogmata, et celeriter late vagari, et valde perniciosa esse. Qua in re non solum vanitas et levitas humanae naturae agnoscenda et deploranda est, quae de- lectatur mendaciis, sed etiam diabolorum mali- tia, et potentia consideranda est, qui gratis, sine ullo suo incommodo spargunt et confirmant te- tros furores, tantum ut Deum contumelia affi- ciant, et odio Christi perdunt homines.

Cohorrescamus etiam cogitantes de potentia, de qua dictum est Lucae 22.: Satan intravit in eum. Ac idola ethnica omnium temporum mun- di, Bacchanalia, humanae victimae, et alii fu- rores, sunt testimonia eius potentiae, et inter eos, qui nominari volunt Ecclesia Dei, semper fuerunt multa tetra deliramenta.

Etiam tempora vicina apostolicis habue- runt turpissimas sectas, inquinatas abominandis opinionibus et confusionibus libidinum. Haec exempla consideranda sunt, ut simus memores gravissimarum admonitionum Matth. 26.: Orate, ne intretis in tentationem. Item 1. Petri ult.: Diabolus tanquam leo rugiens circumit, quae- rens quem devoret. Exuscitet in nobis cogitatio periculorum, timorem et invocationem, ne op- primamur otiosi, securi, ebrii, aut voluptati- bus, aut ambitione, aut aliis cupiditatibus, et opponat fides potentiae diabolorum potentiam Christi, qui dicit Iohan. 10.: Nemo rapiet oves meas ex manibus meis. Item 1. Iohan. 3.: Ap- paruit filius Dei, ut destruat opera diaboli. Item Gene. 3.: Semen mulieris conculcabit caput serpentis.

Considerandum et hoc est, quod fascinatos a diabolo Paulus inquit, paulatim in maiorem impietatem ruere, sicut alibi dicit, Roma 1.: Tradidit eos in reprobum sensum.

## 2:19
The foundation stands firm etc.

Paul, having entered into this sad commemoration concerning the dissipations of the Church, opposes two consolations, the one public, the other pertaining to individuals. This is the public one: That it is most certain, however, that the Son of God, sitting at the right hand of the eternal Father, reigning and restraining the devils, and assiduously interceding for us, is an eternal priest, and is gathering to himself a Church among the human race, however much the devils may oppose. This decree is firm and immovable.

Therefore, this consolation must be held, that there will always be some Church of God, at times more, at times less frequent, at times more, at times less oppressed by errors, according to the sayings of Christ in Luke 17: It will be as in the days of Noah etc. Likewise, Matthew 24: For the sake of the elect these days will be shortened. There will always be some elect until the end of the world, and they are not elect except in the assembly of the called, according to that in Romans 8: Whom he chose, these he also called. God will therefore always preserve some who rightly teach and learn, whether many or few.

The second consolation. But someone might say, even if the Church of the elect is to remain, what does this pertain to me, whether I also am among the elect? Or where are they to be sought, when everywhere there is much vice and tearing apart? These questions greatly disturb minds, but these sentences divinely and expressly handed down must be held most firmly. First, that there are always some elect in this life, according to that in Matthew 24: For the sake of the elect these days will be shortened. Likewise, Matthew 28: I am with you until the consummation of the world. But let us know that all the elect must arrive into the assembly of the called, according to that in Romans 8: Whom he chose, these he also called.

But when we hear that the elect are only in the assembly of the called, minds seek such a Church as would be a most tranquil, most honest, and most dutiful polity. But from the divine voice it must be known that it is one thing to be the Church, and another to be hospices, namely polities, in which very many are openly enemies of the Gospel and the Church. Furthermore, the visible Church itself in this life is an assembly of good and bad, as the sayings of Christ in Matthew 13 manifestly teach: The kingdom of heaven is like a dragnet etc. And in this very Epistle to Timothy it is said: In a great house there are golden vessels honored, and earthen ones made for deformed uses. Nor for this reason should the pious doubt that the assembly in which there is a profession of true doctrine is the true Church of God, even if they see many stained with manifest vices. By this forewarning it is necessary that all be confirmed, lest they cause dissipations, as the Donatists did. But let us remain in the common congregation of those who teach rightly, even if with great sorrow we perceive that discipline is neglected, and let the invocation of the pious be the more ardent, just as Zechariah, Simeon, and the like remained in the common congregation.

You have heard, therefore, where the elect are to be sought, namely, in the assembly of the called. Now when your mind disputes whether you also are in the number of the elect, you should always hold this rule: That we ought to judge concerning the will of God from his own word; when you perform repentance, and in true consolation believe that you are received on account of the mediator, it is certain then that you are pleasing to God, according to the sayings in Ezekiel 18: As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live. Likewise, Romans 5: Justified by faith we have peace with God. Thus, when in the struggle you persevere in faith and in invocation, it is certain that you are elect, according to those sayings in Matthew 24: He who perseveres to the end, this one will be saved. And Revelation 14: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord. And Revelation 2: Be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown etc. And 2 Corinthians 5: We shall be clothed upon, if indeed we are not found naked.

These sayings together show that sanctification must be begun in this life, and that those are certainly blessed who in this life have been converted to God by true repentance and faith, and in the struggle retain repentance and faith, according to those sayings in John 6: This is the will of God, that everyone who believes in the Son should have eternal life. Likewise, John 17: This is eternal life, that they may know you the true God, and Jesus whom you sent to be Christ. This simple consideration is true, and useful to pious minds.

Moreover, it has often been said elsewhere that the cause of reprobation is sin in those very persons whom God did not choose for salvation, but on the contrary, the cause of election is by no means our merits, but the mercy by which, on account of the Son as intercessor and mediator, the divinity receives those who become members of the mediator, when drawn by the voice of the Gospel they embrace by faith the Son as mediator. There let us not indulge in distrust, nor like enthusiasts expect violent raptures, but feeling the beginnings of faith, let us cry out to God for the sake of the Son, that He may help us with His Holy Spirit, as it is commanded, Luke 16: How much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask.

Human minds are hindered, thinking about election in God, when they imagine a succession of times. When we somehow lead ourselves away from this imagination, many questions are removed, as even the ancient writers said.

Having recited this warning about election and about the Church, it can be better understood why Paul says: If anyone cleanses himself from ignoble vessels, he will be a vessel for honor. This cleansing is not a desertion of the congregation, but is a conversion to God.

But you will say: How can conversion happen if only election is the cause? I answer: Election is a cause in such a way that God also wills to call you. He wills, therefore, that you hear the Gospel, and not resist, not indulge in distrust, but struggle with infirmity, and ask that you be helped by the Holy Spirit. For these causes concur: the Word of God, the Holy Spirit, and a will not resisting, but truly struggling with doubt, and asking to be helped by the Holy Spirit, as it is said, Rom. 8: The Spirit brings aid to our infirmity.

These things become more clear when this foundation is considered, that both preachings are universal, namely the preaching of repentance and the promise of grace, and that both commandments are universal, namely, that all and each of us should repent, and all and each of us should believe in the Son of God. To this foundation these sayings correspond: God wills all men to be saved. Likewise, Acts 10, Rom. 2: With God there is no respect of persons. It is useful to hold these consolations for refuting many questions, and for repressing the temptation concerning particularity.

Thus, therefore, let Paul be understood in this place concerning cleansing: Cleanse yourself, that is, repent, acknowledge errors and faults, and grieve, and believe the Gospel. When these things are done, having heard the voice of the Gospel, at the same time the Holy Spirit is effective in a will that is not resisting, but struggling with doubt and asking for help.

Latin:

Stat firmum fundamentum etc.

Paulus ingressus in hanc tristem commemo- rationem de dissipationibus Ecclesiae, opponit consolationes duas, alteram publicam, alteram pertinentem ad singulos. Publica haec est: Quod certissimum est tamen filium Dei sedentem ad dexteram aeterni patris, regnantem et reprimen- tem diabolos, et assidue intercedentem pro no- bis, esse sacerdotem aeternum, et colligere sibi Ecclesiam in genere humano, quantumcunque adversantibus diabolis. Hoc decretum firmum et immotum est.

Tenenda est igitur haec consolatio, semper fore aliquam Dei Ecclesiam, alias magis, alias minus frequentem, alias magis, alias minus op- pressam erroribus, iuxta dicta Christi Lucae 17.: Erit sicut in diebus Noae etc. Item, Matth. 24.: Propter electos abbreviabuntur istis dies, Erunt semper aliqui electi usque ad finem mundi, et non sunt electi, nisi in coetu vocatorum, iuxta illud Roma 8.: Quos elegit, hos et vocavit. Serva- bit igitur Deus semper aliquos recte docentes et discentes, seu multos seu paucos.

Altera consolatio. Sed dicat aliquis, etiamsi mansura est electorum Ecclesia, quid hoc ad me pertinet, an et ego sum inter electos? Aut ubi illi quaerendi sunt, cum ubique multum sit vi- tiorum et dilacerationum? Hae quaestiones valde turbant mentes, sed firmissime tenendae sunt hae sententiae divinitus expresse traditae. Pri- mum quod semper sint aliqui electi in hac vita, iuxta illud Matth. 24.: Propter electos abbrevia- buntur isti dies. Item, Matth. 28.: Ego vobis- cum sum usque ad consummationem mundi. Omnes autem electos sciamus oportere in coetum vocatorum pervenire, iuxta illud Roma 8.: Quos elegit, hos et vocavit.

Cum vero audimus electos tantum in coetu vocatorum esse, quaerunt mentes talem Eccle- siam, quae sit politia tranquillissima, honestis- sima, et officiosissima. Sed ex voce divina scien- dum est, aliud esse Ecclesiam, et aliud hospitia, scilicet politias, in quibus plurimi palam sunt ho- stes Evangelii et Ecclesiae. Deinde ipsa Ecclesia visibilis in hac vita est coetus bonorum et malo- rum, ut manifeste docent dicta Christi, Matth. 13.: Simile est regnum coelorum sagenae etc. Et in hac ipsa Epistola ad Timotheum dicitur: In magna domo sunt vasa aurea honorata, . et testa- cea ad deformes usus facta. Nec propterea dubitent pii, coetum, in quo est professio verae doctrinae, esse veram Dei Ec- clesiam, etiamsi vident multos inquinatos mani- festis vitiis. Hac praemonitione necesse est om- nes esse confirmatos, ne faciant dissipationes, sicut Donatistae faciebant. Sed maneamus in communi congregatione recte docentium, etiamsi magno cum dolore cernimus negligi disciplinam, et sit invocatio piorum eo ardentior, sicut mane- bant in communi congregatione Zacharias, Si- meon, et similes.

Audivisti igitur ubi sint quaerendi electi, scilicet, in coetu vocatorum. Iam cum disputat tua mens, an et tu sis in numero electorum, sem- per teneas hanc regulam: Nos de voluntate Dei ex verbo ipsius iudicare oportere, cum agis poe- nitentiam, et in vera consolatione credis te recipi propter mediatorem, certum est tunc te placere Deo, iuxta dicta Ezech. 18.: Vivo ego, dicit Do- minus, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed ut conver- tatur et vivat. Item, Roman. 5.: Iustificati fide pacem habemus apud Deum. Sic cum in agone perseveras in fide et in invocatione, certum est te esse electum, iuxta illa dicta Matth. 24.: Qui perseverarit in finem, hic salvus erit. Et Apocalypsis 14.: Beati mortui qui in Domino moriuntur. Et Apocal. 2.: Esto fidelis usque ad mortem, et dabo tibi coronam etc. Et 2. Co- rinth. 5.: Superinduemur, si tamen non nudi reperiemur.

Haec dicta simul ostendunt oportere in hac vita incoari sanctificationem, et certo beatos esse, qui in hac vita ad Deum conversi sunt vera poe- nitentia et fide, et in agone poenitentiam et fidem retinent, iuxta illa dicta Iohan. 6.: Haec est voluntas Dei, ut omnis qui credit in filium, ha- beat vitam aeternam. Item, Ioh. 17.: Haec est vita aeterna, ut agnoscant te verum Deum, et quem misisti Iesum esse Christum. Haec sim- plex consideratio vera est, et utilis piis men- tibus.

Caeterum alibi saepe dictum est, causam re- probationis esse peccatum in illis ipsis, quos Deus non elegit ad salutem, contra vero electionis cau- sam esse nequaquam nostra merita, sed misericor- diam, qua propter filium deprecatorem et me- diatorem divinitas recipit illos, qui fiunt membra mediatoris, cum tracti voce Evangelii fide am- plectuntur filium mediatorem. Ibi non indul- geamus diffidentiae, nec velut enthusiastae ex- pectemus violentos raptus, sed sentientes initia fidei, clamemus ad Deum propter filium, ut Spi- ritu suo sancto nos adiuvet, sicut praeceptum est, Lucae 16.: Quanto magis pater vester coelestis dabit Spiritum sanctum petentibus.

' Impediuntur humanae mentes, de electione in Deo cogitantes, cum imaginantur successionem temporum. Ab hac imaginatione, cum utcunque nos abducimus, multae quaestiones tolluntur, ut etiam veteres scriptores dixerunt.

Recitata hac praemonitione de electione et de Ecclesia, melius intelligi potest, cur Paulus dicat: Si quis mundaverit se a vasis deformio- ribus, erit vas ad honorem. Haec mundatio non est desertio congregationis, sed est conversio ad Deum.

· Dices autem: Quomodo fieri conversio potest, si tantum electio est causa? Respondeo: Electio sic est causa, ut Deus etiam vocare te velit. Vult igitur te audire Evangelium, et non repugnare, non indulgere diffidentiae, sed luctari cum infir- mitate, et petere, ut Spiritu sancto adiuveris. Concurrunt enim hae causae, Verbum Dei, Spi- ritus sanctus, et voluntas non repugnans, vere luctans cum dubitatione, et petens ut iuvetur Spiritu sancto, sicut dictum est, Rom. 8.: Spi- ritus opem fert infirmitati nostrae.

Haec fiunt magis perspicua considerato hoc fundamento, quod utraque praedicatio universa- lis est, scilicet praedicatio poenitentiae, et pro- missio gratiae, et quod utrunque praeceptum universale est, videlicet, ut omnes et singuli aga- mus poenitentiam, et omnes et singuli credamus in filium Dei. Ad hoc fundamentum congruunt haec dicta: Deus vult omnes homines salvos fieri. Item, Acto. 10., Rom. 2.: Apud Deum non est acceptio personarum. Has consolationes tenere utile est ad refutandas multas quaestiones, et ad reprimendam tentationem de particularitate.'

Sic ergo intelligatur Paulus hoc loco de mun- datione: Mundes te, id est, agas poenitentiam, agnoscas errores et delicta, et doleas, et credas Evangelio. Haec cum fiunt, audita voce Evan- gelii, simul Spiritus sanctus est efficax in volun- tate non repugnante, sed luctante cum dubitatione et petente auxilium.

## 2:22
Follow after righteousness, etc.

I understand universal righteousness, that is, obedience according to all the commandments of God. Although, however, the names of species are added afterwards, which are included in universal righteousness, yet it is not unusual, having posited the whole, to then recite some notable parts by name, especially when it is done with a singular purpose, as Paul here wishes to warn that obedience is pleasing when it is joined with faith: therefore he expressly adds the name of faith. Hypocrites also boast of obedience, as in Luke 18, but it is necessary in the Church always to have in sight this rule of Psalm 143: No living person will be justified in your sight. But that we certainly have the remission of sins, and the imputation of righteousness because of the mediator, by faith alone, not because of our own virtues, as that Pharisee in Luke 18 dreams.

Afterwards he names love and peace, so that he may oppose this to the contentious, who under the pretext of righteousness stir up unnecessary disputes, of whom it is said in Rom. 10: They have zeal, but not according to knowledge, just as there were once quarrels about the Passover, about leavened bread, and many now are more futile, such as about the sleep of souls, and whether Noah brought mice into the ark. And from what follows it appears that the names of love and peace are expressed here so that concord may be retained in the Church with greater care: because he soon adds notable admonitions, which contain many illustrious words. It is manifest, however, that virtue, love, and the effort to retain concord are necessary, but this cannot be retained unless we calmly tolerate some infirmities in others, and omit quarrels about some unnecessary questions.

Latin:

Sectare Iusticiam, etc.

Intelligo Iusticiam universalem, id est, obe- dientiam iuxta omnia praecepta Dei. Quanquam autem deinde adduntur nomina specierum, quae inclusae sunt in universali iusticia, tamen non est inusitatum posito toto aliquas insignes partes deinde nominatim recitare, praesertim cum id fit singulari consilio, ut hic vult monere Paulus, ita placere obedientiam, quando coniuncta est cum fide: ideo expresse addit nomen fidei. Iactant obedientiam et hypocritae, ut Luc. 18., sed ne- cesse est in Ecclesia semper in conspectu esse hanc regulam Psalmi 143.: Non iustificabitur in con- spectu tuo omnis vivens. Sed quod certo habea- mus remissionem peccatorum, et imputationem iusticiae propter mediatorem, sola fide, non propter nostras virtutes, sicut ille Pharisaeus Lucae 18. somniat.

Postea nominat dilectionem et pacem, ut opponat hoc contentiosis, qui praetextu iusticiae movent non necessaria certamina, de quibus di- citur Roma. 10.: Habent zelum, sed non secun- dum scientiam, sicut de Paschate, de fermentato olim rixae fuerunt, et multae nunc sunt futilio- res, ut de dormitione animarum, et an Noë mu- res induxerit in arcam. Et ex sequentibus appa- ret, nomina dilectionis et pacis hic expressa esse, ut maiore cura retineatur in Ecclesia concordia: quia mox addit insignes admonitiones, quae con- tinent multa illustria verba. Manifestum est au- tem necessariam esse virtutem, dilectionem et studium retinendae concordiae, haec autem reti- neri non potest, nisi infirmitates aliquas in aliis placide toleremus, et omittamus rixas de aliqui- bus non necessariis quaestionibus.
